docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: You do not need advanced mathematics to call a model API. A practical understanding of vectors, probability, loss, and gradients helps explain what models learn, how embeddings are compared, and why training changes parameters.

docs.title: Scalars, vectors, and matrices
docs.text:
• A scalar is one value, such as a learning rate.
  • A vector is an ordered list of values, such as an embedding or a row of numeric features.
  • A matrix is a grid of values. A dataset with rows for examples and columns for features can be represented as a matrix.
  • A tensor generalizes arrays to more dimensions, such as a batch of images with height, width, and color channels.

Dimensions are part of the meaning. If a batch has 32 examples and each has 10 features, its shape is commonly written (32, 10). Matrix operations require compatible dimensions; shape errors often reveal a mistaken assumption about the data.

docs.title: Dot product and cosine similarity
docs.text:
For vectors (a) and (b), the dot product multiplies corresponding entries and sums the results:

[ a \cdot b = \sum_i a_i b_i ]

Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the vector lengths:

[ \operatorname{cosine}(a,b) = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a||b|} ]

It emphasizes direction rather than raw magnitude. Embedding models and indexes may use cosine similarity, dot product, or another distance; use the metric expected by the specific embedding and index.

from math import sqrt

def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    norm_a = sqrt(sum(x * x for x in a))
    norm_b = sqrt(sum(y * y for y in b))
    if norm_a == 0 or norm_b == 0:
        raise ValueError("cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector")
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b)

print(round(cosine([1, 0], [0.8, 0.2]), 3))  # 0.97

High similarity means the representation is close under the chosen metric. It does not mean that a passage is correct, authorized, or actually answers a question.

In a TaskFlow backend the same calculation ranks stored embeddings against a query embedding. The dimension check matters: vectors from two different embedding models cannot be compared, and mixing them is a common bug after a model upgrade.

// src/ai/similarity.ts: rank stored embeddings by cosine similarity to a query
export function cosine(a: number[], b: number[]): number {
  if (a.length !== b.length) {
    throw new Error(`dimension mismatch: ${a.length} vs ${b.length}`);
  }
  let dot = 0;
  let normA = 0;
  let normB = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    dot += a[i] * b[i];
    normA += a[i] * a[i];
    normB += b[i] * b[i];
  }
  if (normA === 0 || normB === 0) {
    throw new Error("cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector");
  }
  return dot / Math.sqrt(normA * normB);
}

export function topK<T extends { embedding: number[] }>(query: number[], items: T[], k = 3) {
  return items
    .map((item) => ({ item, score: cosine(query, item.embedding) }))
    .sort((x, y) => y.score - x.score)
    .slice(0, k);
}

// Toy 3-dimensional vectors; real embeddings have hundreds or thousands of dimensions
const docs = [
  { id: "billing-faq", embedding: [0.9, 0.1, 0.0] },
  { id: "shipping-faq", embedding: [0.1, 0.9, 0.1] },
  { id: "refund-policy", embedding: [0.8, 0.3, 0.1] },
];

for (const { item, score } of topK([1, 0.2, 0], docs, 2)) {
  console.log(item.id, score.toFixed(3));
}

Output from running it with Node.js 24:

billing-faq 0.996
refund-policy 0.980

A loop like this is fine for a few thousand vectors; beyond that a vector index does the search. Two details from real systems:

  • OpenAI's embeddings guide states that its embeddings "are normalized to length 1", so a plain dot product gives the same ranking as cosine similarity, only faster (OpenAI embeddings guide).
  • MongoDB Vector Search, which a TaskFlow deployment on MongoDB Atlas would use, lets an index choose euclidean, cosine, or dotProduct similarity, and requires vectors normalized to unit length at index and query time for dotProduct (MongoDB vector index fields).

See embedding models and dimensions and vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: Probability, logits, and softmax
docs.text:
A model classifier may return logits, real-valued scores that are not probabilities. The softmax function converts a vector of logits into positive values that sum to one:

[ \operatorname{softmax}(z_i) = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} ]

In practice, subtract the largest logit before exponentiation to reduce overflow:

from math import exp

def softmax(logits):
    peak = max(logits)
    values = [exp(value - peak) for value in logits]
    total = sum(values)
    return [value / total for value in values]

print([round(p, 3) for p in softmax([2.0, 1.0, 0.1])])
# [0.659, 0.242, 0.099]

The resulting values sum to one for this candidate set, but a value such as 0.659 is not automatically a calibrated 65.9% chance of correctness. Calibration must be measured against outcomes.

Language models apply a temperature (T) by computing (\operatorname{softmax}(z / T)). For the same logits [2.0, 1.0, 0.1]:

Temperature Probabilities 0.5 [0.864, 0.117, 0.019] 1.0 [0.659, 0.242, 0.099] 2.0 [0.502, 0.304, 0.194]

A low temperature sharpens the distribution toward the top token; a high temperature flattens it, so sampling picks unlikely tokens more often. Inference and decoding shows how this combines with top-p sampling.

docs.title: Loss and cross-entropy
docs.text:
A loss function assigns a numeric penalty to model predictions during training. For a classification task with a correct class (y) and predicted probabilities (p), cross-entropy loss is:

[ L = -\log(p_y) ]

Assigning higher probability to the correct class reduces this loss. If the correct class received 0.659, the loss is (-\log(0.659) \approx 0.417); if it received only 0.1, the loss is about 2.303. Confident wrong predictions are penalized much more than hesitant ones, and next-token training of language models uses the same loss over the vocabulary. Training usually averages or otherwise aggregates losses across examples. The training objective is a useful signal, not a complete measure of product quality, truthfulness, or safety.

docs.title: Gradients and gradient descent
docs.text:
A gradient describes how a small change in parameters would change a loss. Gradient descent updates parameters in the direction that reduces loss:

[ \theta_{\text{new}} = \theta_{\text{old}} - \eta \nabla_\theta L ]

Here, (\theta) represents model parameters and (\eta) is the learning rate. If the learning rate is too large, optimization can overshoot; if too small, learning can be slow. Backpropagation applies the chain rule to calculate gradients through a neural network.

For a tiny linear regression example, use the model (y = wx + b). The following pseudocode-like Python sketch shows the repeated update:

for x, target in examples:
    prediction = weight * x + bias
    error = prediction - target
    weight_gradient += 2 * error * x / len(examples)
    bias_gradient += 2 * error / len(examples)

weight -= learning_rate * weight_gradient
bias -= learning_rate * bias_gradient

This sketch omits initialization and the outer training loop; it illustrates the update only. In deep networks, automatic differentiation libraries calculate these gradients over many tensor operations.

docs.title: Batches, epochs, and generalization
docs.text:
• A batch is a subset of training examples used for one parameter update.
  • An epoch is one pass through a training dataset.
  • A learning rate schedule changes the update size during training.
  • Regularization discourages some forms of overly complex fitting.
  • A validation set helps compare choices; a test set should remain held out for a final estimate.

Training well on examples is not enough. A model must generalize to cases that represent its actual use. See Machine Learning and Deep Learning for data splits, metrics, and leakage.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: For application work, these ideas explain why embeddings have dimensions, why similarity is only a ranking signal, why classifiers need thresholds, and why training loss is not a user-facing success metric. You usually use a library or API for the calculations, but you should still understand what its scores and metrics do—and do not—mean.

docs.title: Model Context Protocol and Agent Integrations
Introduction
docs.text: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and context sources through a common client-server model. An MCP server can expose capabilities such as tools, resources, or prompts. MCP standardizes parts of the connection; it does not make a server trustworthy or decide whether a user may perform an action.

docs.title: Main concepts
docs.text:
• Host: the AI application that manages the user's session and model interaction.
  • Client: the protocol component in the host that connects to a particular server.
  • Server: a process or service that advertises capabilities.
  • Tools: operations the model may request through the host.
  • Resources: data the host may retrieve through the protocol.
  • Prompts: reusable prompt templates or workflows provided by a server.

The exact protocol version, transports, and capability details evolve. Consult the current MCP specification when implementing a client or server. As of November 2026 the current revision is 2026-07-28, which replaced 2025-11-25. Its biggest change is that MCP is now stateless: there is no initialize handshake or protocol session, every request carries its protocol version and client capabilities in _meta, and servers advertise their versions and capabilities through a server/discover call. The official TypeScript SDK implements this revision in its v2 packages (@modelcontextprotocol/server and @modelcontextprotocol/client); v1 (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk) speaks 2025-11-25 and earlier.

docs.title: What can an MCP server provide?
docs.text:
The server advertises capabilities; the host decides which ones to expose to the model or user.

Capability Direction and purpose Example Tools The model may request an operation through the host Search an issue tracker or create a draft Resources The host can read data exposed by a server A document, record, or application context Prompts The server can provide a reusable prompt template A guided code-review or research prompt

Depending on protocol version and negotiated capabilities, client-side features can include roots, sampling, elicitation, and tasks. In 2026-07-28, roots, sampling, and logging are deprecated (they still work during a deprecation window of at least twelve months), elicitation remains, and tasks for long-running work moved into an optional official extension. A capability is not automatically available just because the other side implements MCP; client and server must both support it.

docs.title: How an MCP connection is established
docs.text:
1. A user or administrator configures a trusted server for an MCP-capable host.
  2. The host creates an MCP client and selects a compatible transport.
  3. Client and server agree on a protocol version and capabilities. Older revisions used an initialize handshake; since 2026-07-28 the client can call server/discover and then sends its version and capabilities with every request.
  4. The client discovers server capabilities and presents only approved tools, resources, or prompts to the model.
  5. When the model proposes a tool call, the host applies policy and confirmation before invoking the server.
  6. Results return through the client, are treated as untrusted data, and may be added to the model's context.

The protocol connection is between host/client and server. The model typically does not open an MCP socket or directly execute a server tool.

docs.title: Standard transports and deployment choices
docs.text:
The current MCP specification defines two standard transports:

Transport How it connects Typical use Main security considerations stdio The host launches a local server process and exchanges newline-delimited JSON-RPC messages over standard input/output Local tools and developer integrations The configured command runs as a process with the host user's permissions; review its executable, arguments, working directory, and environment Streamable HTTP A client sends JSON-RPC messages to one HTTP endpoint; responses may be JSON or a request-scoped server-sent-event stream Remote or shared servers Authenticate and authorize requests, protect transport, validate origin/host behavior, and isolate tenants

Streamable HTTP replaced the older HTTP+SSE transport in protocol 2025-03-26, and 2026-07-28 formally marks HTTP+SSE as Deprecated. The same revision removed the Mcp-Session-Id header and stream resumability: a server that needs state across calls returns its own handle as an ordinary tool argument, and a client re-issues a request whose stream broke. Older clients may still support HTTP+SSE for compatibility; new integrations should follow the current specification and verify the client/server versions. Transport and capability details can change, so check compatibility rather than assuming every host supports every mode.

docs.title: Illustrative host configuration
docs.text:
Some desktop hosts use a JSON configuration shaped like this for a local stdio server:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "project-search": {
      "command": "python",
      "args": ["server.py"],
      "env": {}
    }
  }
}

Remote-server configuration may instead specify a URL and authentication settings. Configuration schemas and file locations are host-specific; mcpServers is an example convention, not a field required by the MCP protocol. Do not copy tokens or secrets into a checked-in config file.

Conceptually, a remote client connects to a configured MCP endpoint:

MCP client -> HTTPS endpoint -> authenticated MCP server

The host may start the stdio process itself, or a platform may manage that process. For remote services, follow the server's authentication and deployment guidance. MCP authorization supports OAuth-based patterns for HTTP transports; stdio normally relies on local process configuration and OS permissions instead of HTTP OAuth. In 2026-07-28, OAuth Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated in favor of Client ID Metadata Documents.

docs.title: A minimal read-only server in TypeScript
docs.text:
This TaskFlow server exposes one search tool over stdio with the v2 TypeScript SDK. Zod schemas become the tool's JSON Schema, and the SDK rejects invalid arguments before the handler runs.

// taskflow-mcp/server.ts: a read-only MCP server exposing one TaskFlow search tool over stdio
import { McpServer } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server";
import { StdioServerTransport } from "@modelcontextprotocol/server/stdio";
import * as z from "zod";

// In the real server this is a MongoDB query scoped to the user the server was configured for.
const tasks = [
  { id: "T-101", title: "Prepare release notes for 1.9", status: "open" },
  { id: "T-102", title: "Fix login rate limit", status: "done" },
  { id: "T-103", title: "Review release checklist", status: "open" },
];

const server = new McpServer({ name: "taskflow-tasks", version: "1.0.0" });

server.registerTool(
  "search_tasks",
  {
    title: "Search TaskFlow tasks",
    description: "Find tasks whose title contains the query. Read-only.",
    inputSchema: z.object({
      query: z.string().min(2).max(100),
      status: z.enum(["open", "done"]).optional(),
      limit: z.number().int().min(1).max(20).default(5),
    }),
    outputSchema: z.object({
      tasks: z.array(z.object({ id: z.string(), title: z.string(), status: z.string() })),
    }),
    annotations: { readOnlyHint: true },
  },
  async ({ query, status, limit }) => {
    const q = query.toLowerCase();
    const found = tasks
      .filter((t) => t.title.toLowerCase().includes(q) && (!status || t.status === status))
      .slice(0, limit);
    const output = { tasks: found };
    return { content: [{ type: "text", text: JSON.stringify(output) }], structuredContent: output };
  },
);

// stdout carries the protocol; log to stderr only
await server.connect(new StdioServerTransport());
console.error("taskflow-tasks MCP server ready on stdio");

A test client built with @modelcontextprotocol/client that starts this server and calls the tool printed:

tools: search_tasks readOnly=true
call: {"tasks":[{"id":"T-101","title":"Prepare release notes for 1.9","status":"open"},{"id":"T-103","title":"Review release checklist","status":"open"}]}
invalid input -> isError: true [{"type":"text","text":"Input validation error: Invalid arguments for tool search_tasks: query: Too small: expected string to have >=2 characters"}]

readOnlyHint is advice to the host, not enforcement. Write tools should act with a TaskFlow user token from the host's authorization flow, not a shared admin credential.

docs.title: Tool use through a host
docs.text:
1. The host connects to a configured server and discovers supported capabilities.
  2. The application decides which capabilities are appropriate for the current user and task.
  3. The model may propose a tool call with structured arguments.
  4. The host validates the request, checks authorization, and obtains any required user confirmation.
  5. The host invokes the tool and returns a bounded result to the model.
  6. The application validates and presents the final answer or action.

docs.title: MCP and custom tool calling
docs.text:
Choice Advantages Considerations Provider-specific function calling Direct integration with one model API Tied to that provider's tool format Application-defined tools Full control over exposed operations Each integration needs custom schemas and maintenance MCP Common protocol for capability discovery and integrations Requires client/server lifecycle, version, security, and compatibility management

MCP can improve interoperability; it does not replace application authorization, business rules, audit logging, or user confirmation.

docs.title: Where A2A fits
docs.text: MCP connects an agent to tools and data. The Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol connects an agent to other agents that it cannot see inside: each side keeps its memory, tools, and logic private. A2A started at Google in 2025, is governed under the Linux Foundation, and is at specification version 1.0 as of November 2026. An agent publishes an Agent Card (a JSON document, usually at /.well-known/agent-card.json) with its skills, endpoint, and authentication requirements; work happens in tasks with states such as working, input required, and completed, exchanged as messages and artifacts over JSON-RPC 2.0, gRPC, or HTTP+JSON. For TaskFlow, an MCP server exposes task search to the assistant; A2A would matter only if TaskFlow's agent had to hand work to another organization's agent. Patterns and trade-offs are in agent protocols and interoperability.

docs.title: What MCP servers and integrations are available?
docs.text:
The ecosystem includes local or remote servers for categories such as files and project search, source-control and issue trackers, databases, documentation, communications, and other business systems. Implementations may be first-party, community-maintained, or vendor-provided. Availability, maintenance, and trustworthiness are not implied by being listed in a catalog or appearing in a host's UI.

Before connecting one, verify its publisher and source code where appropriate, supported protocol version, requested permissions, data handling, update process, and whether it transmits information to another service. Prefer the narrowest server and access scope that satisfies the task. A database server should expose task-specific operations rather than unrestricted credentials or query execution when a narrower interface is possible.

docs.title: Security checklist
docs.text:
• Trust only reviewed, explicitly configured servers.
  • Authenticate remote connections and protect transport credentials.
  • Use least privilege for each server and tool.
  • Validate all arguments and outputs against schemas and business rules.
  • Treat resource contents and tool results as untrusted input.
  • Require confirmation for destructive, financial, or external actions.
  • Record useful audit events without retaining unnecessary sensitive data.
  • Set network, time, size, and call-count limits.
  • Review dependencies and update protocol implementations.

Trusted servers can still be turned against you. In May 2025 Invariant Labs showed how a prompt injection in an issue on a public GitHub repository could make an agent connected to the GitHub MCP server read the user's private repositories and publish their contents in a pull request on the public one (Invariant Labs). The researchers stressed that this was not a bug in the server's code but a "toxic agent flow": untrusted content, private data, and a public write tool in one session. Their advice was the checklist above: scope each session to the repositories it needs and monitor tool calls. Defenses are covered in prompt injection and defenses.

docs.title: Agent design
docs.text: An agent is a model-directed control loop that can select tools, inspect results, and continue. Keep the loop bounded by allowed tools, step count, time, token budget, and user permissions. Prefer a deterministic workflow when the task has a known sequence. Make state, retries, and side effects explicit and idempotent. See tool calling in practice and agent orchestration patterns.

docs.title: Images, Audio, and Video Formats for AI
Introduction
docs.text: An image, audio recording, or video file is encoded data—not a model input format by itself. An application must decode a file, interpret its dimensions, color or timing, apply any required preprocessing, and send a representation the selected model accepts.

docs.title: Raster and vector images
docs.text:
Raster images store a grid of pixels. Each pixel has color samples, often represented by red, green, and blue channels (RGB), and may include an alpha channel for transparency. Resolution is the number of pixels; a larger image can carry detail but use more memory and model context.

Vector graphics describe shapes and paths mathematically, often with text and style rules. They can scale cleanly for diagrams and icons, but they must be rendered to pixels for many computer-vision models.

Format Kind and typical properties Useful fit and caveat PNG Raster; lossless compression; transparency supported Screenshots, diagrams, and sharp edges; can be large for photographs JPEG / JPG Raster; lossy photographic compression Photos; repeated re-encoding can add artifacts and it does not support alpha WebP Raster; lossy and lossless options, transparency and animation supported Web delivery; confirm target tool and model accept it AVIF Raster image format based on AV1 image coding Efficient web images in supported pipelines; decoding support varies GIF Palette-based raster; animation supported Simple short animations; limited color compared with modern formats SVG XML-based vector description Logos, icons, and diagrams; sanitize untrusted SVG before serving or rendering

PNG was developed by the PNG Development Group and is now specified by standards organizations including W3C. JPEG is specified through the Joint Photographic Experts Group standards process (including ISO/IEC and ITU-T publications). SVG is maintained by the W3C SVG Working Group. Google introduced WebP as a web image format. AVIF builds on the AV1 image coding work from the Alliance for Open Media. These names describe standards or organizations rather than one individual inventor.

docs.title: What an image model receives
docs.text:
A vision pipeline commonly decodes an image into pixel values, applies orientation and color handling, resizes or crops it, and converts it into numeric tensors. Some vision transformer systems split an image into patches. Multimodal systems may encode patches or crops into representations that are combined with text tokens. Exact pipelines vary by model.

The model may resize a large image, sample several crops, or impose a resolution limit. A small chart can become unreadable if the application resizes it too aggressively. Strip unnecessary metadata and enforce upload limits, but preserve task-relevant resolution.

docs.title: A small image-inspection example
docs.text:
Using Pillow in a Python environment, inspect dimensions and color mode before deciding on preprocessing:

# inspect_image.py: print an image's format, size, and color mode, then convert it to RGB
from PIL import Image

with Image.open("diagram.png") as image:
    print(image.format, image.size, image.mode)
    rgb_image = image.convert("RGB")

This reads and converts pixels; it does not call an AI model. The Pillow decoder must support the input format, and uploaded data should be validated and size-limited before decoding. Pillow has a built-in guard: as of Pillow 13, Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS defaults to 89,478,485 pixels, above which opening an image warns, and above twice that it raises DecompressionBombError. Set a lower limit that fits your product.

Provider limits are specific and change, so read them for your provider. As an example, Anthropic's vision documentation (November 2026) lists JPEG, PNG, GIF, and WebP as supported, uses only the first frame of an animation, accepts up to 8000 x 8000 pixels and 10 MB per image (base64-encoded) on its API, downscales images beyond a per-model long edge such as 1,568 pixels, and estimates cost as (\lceil w/28 \rceil \times \lceil h/28 \rceil) visual tokens, so a 1000 x 1000 image costs about 1,296 tokens (Claude vision). Resizing an image to the size the model will use anyway saves upload time and gives predictable cost. Base64 encoding in a JSON request adds a third to the file size.

docs.title: Checking what an upload really is
docs.text:
A TaskFlow attachment endpoint should decide the type from the file's first bytes (its signature), not from the filename or the client's Content-Type header:

// src/uploads/sniff-media.ts: identify an upload by its first bytes, not by its name or MIME header
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

type Kind = "png" | "jpeg" | "gif" | "webp" | "wav" | "mp4" | "pdf" | "unknown";

export function sniff(buf: Buffer): Kind {
  const ascii = (start: number, end: number) => buf.subarray(start, end).toString("latin1");
  if (buf.subarray(0, 8).equals(Buffer.from([0x89, 0x50, 0x4e, 0x47, 0x0d, 0x0a, 0x1a, 0x0a]))) return "png";
  if (buf[0] === 0xff && buf[1] === 0xd8 && buf[2] === 0xff) return "jpeg";
  if (ascii(0, 6) === "GIF87a" || ascii(0, 6) === "GIF89a") return "gif";
  if (ascii(0, 4) === "RIFF" && ascii(8, 12) === "WEBP") return "webp";
  if (ascii(0, 4) === "RIFF" && ascii(8, 12) === "WAVE") return "wav";
  if (ascii(4, 8) === "ftyp") return "mp4"; // ISO base media: MP4, MOV, and similar
  if (ascii(0, 5) === "%PDF-") return "pdf";
  return "unknown";
}

// PNG stores width and height in its first chunk, so the size can be checked before decoding
export function pngSize(buf: Buffer): { width: number; height: number } {
  return { width: buf.readUInt32BE(16), height: buf.readUInt32BE(20) };
}

const MAX_PIXELS = 25_000_000; // reject before decoding: a small file can expand to gigabytes

for (const name of process.argv.slice(2)) {
  const buf = readFileSync(name);
  const kind = sniff(buf);
  let note = "";
  if (kind === "png") {
    const { width, height } = pngSize(buf);
    note = `${width}x${height}${width * height > MAX_PIXELS ? " too large" : ""}`;
  }
  console.log([name, kind, note].filter(Boolean).join(" "));
}

Output from running it with Node.js 24 on four test files, where photo.png is a JPEG file renamed with a .png extension:

diagram.png png 640x360
photo.jpg jpeg
icon.webp webp
photo.png jpeg

Signature checks catch renamed and mislabeled files cheaply. They do not prove that the rest of the file is valid, so still decode with limits, preferably in a background job, and re-encode images you keep.

docs.title: Video: container, codec, frames, and timestamps
docs.text:
A container such as MP4 or WebM packages streams and metadata. A codec such as H.264, VP9, AV1, or H.265 compresses video frames; audio may use codecs such as AAC or Opus. A filename extension alone does not guarantee that the content uses a particular codec.

Video models may consume a video file, sampled frames, audio, or a mixture. For frame sampling, the application chooses times or a rate; sparse sampling can miss short events, while dense sampling costs more. Retain timestamps so an answer can link to the relevant moment. Audio may be transcribed separately or processed by an audio-capable model.

# Inspect a local file's streams and codecs when FFmpeg is installed.
ffprobe -hide_banner -show_streams -show_format ./meeting.mp4

Review the command output before passing media to an external provider. FFmpeg tools are optional; model providers may accept different containers, codecs, durations, and sizes.

docs.title: Audio representation
docs.text:
Digital audio is a sequence of samples. Sample rate describes samples per second; bit depth describes the precision of each sample; channels describe separate streams such as left and right stereo. Compression may be lossless (for example FLAC) or lossy (for example MP3, AAC, or Opus). A container such as WAV can store uncompressed PCM, while other containers can carry compressed streams.

Speech models may require a particular encoding, sample rate, channel layout, and duration. Resampling and channel mixing must be deliberate; they can change speech quality. Uncompressed size is simple arithmetic: 16-bit mono PCM at 16 kHz is 32,000 bytes per second, about 1.9 MB per minute, which is why recordings are usually sent compressed or streamed. Realtime speech APIs often expect raw PCM at a fixed rate; see speech and multimodal AI. Preserve timestamps and speaker segments when the application needs a transcript users can verify.

docs.title: Web delivery versus model input
docs.text: The best browser asset is not necessarily the best model input. WebP or AVIF may reduce download size, while a provider endpoint may accept only a different set of formats. A browser can display SVG while a vision model expects raster pixels. Keep the delivery format and inference preprocessing as separate decisions.

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text: Validate actual file content, not only its extension or client-supplied MIME type. Bound size, pixel dimensions, duration, and decompression work. Treat metadata, embedded text, subtitles, and OCR output as untrusted. Images and recordings can contain faces, locations, voices, or other sensitive data; minimize processing and apply the product's consent, retention, and access policies.

docs.text:

  • MDN: Image file type and format guide
  • MDN: Web video codec guide

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: MLOps applies software delivery and operations practices to machine learning systems. It covers reproducible data and training pipelines, model and prompt versioning, evaluation gates, deployment, monitoring, and retirement. For a full-stack AI feature, the lifecycle also includes retrieval indexes, tool definitions, policy configuration, and application code.

docs.title: Lifecycle components
docs.text:
1. Data pipeline: ingest, validate, transform, and version inputs.
  2. Experiment tracking: record code, configuration, data, model parameters, metrics, and artifacts.
  3. Evaluation gate: compare a candidate with a baseline on a held-out suite; test safety, latency, and cost constraints as well as quality.
  4. Model registry: store approved artifacts and metadata with reproducible identifiers.
  5. Deployment: release through staged environments, shadow testing, canary traffic, or a rollback plan.
  6. Monitoring: track system health and quality signals, investigate drift, and re-evaluate when data or model behavior changes.
  7. Retirement: remove unsupported versions and clean up dependent indexes, endpoints, and credentials.

docs.title: Version more than model weights
docs.text:
A reproducible AI feature may depend on:

  • model provider, model identifier, and version;
  • prompt and tool schemas;
  • retrieval index and embedding-model version;
  • data transformations and chunking configuration;
  • safety policy and output validator;
  • application code and evaluation set.

If one of these changes, compare system behavior before and after the change. A provider alias that silently points to a new model can alter quality, latency, or cost. Providers also retire model versions on published schedules, so a pinned version eventually needs a planned migration (see LLMOps: prompt and model versioning).

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
Track service availability, latency percentiles, timeouts, rate limits, queue depth, resource use, and cost. Where appropriate and privacy-safe, track task completion, user corrections, citation validity, refusal and escalation rates, and evaluation results. Log identifiers and aggregate signals rather than sensitive prompts by default.

Model quality is harder to monitor than CPU or HTTP status. Add sampled human review, user feedback, offline regression suites, and privacy-aware incident investigation. A change in model output may come from input distribution, retrieval, prompt, provider version, or code.

Service health, dashboards, SLOs, and alerting work as for any API; see Monitoring and Logging. LLM evaluation sets and tracing are covered in Evaluation and Monitoring, and drift in classic models in production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: Rollback and incidents
docs.text:
Keep a known-good version and a safe fallback. Define how to disable a feature, revoke a key, rebuild an index, or route a task to human review. Do not use a previous model blindly if its license, safety status, or data dependencies differ. A rollback target can also disappear: providers retire old model versions, so check that the version you would return to is still served.

Model releases use the same mechanics as application releases: versioned artifacts, staged rollouts, feature flags, and rehearsed rollbacks. See Release Engineering and rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
• Experiment tracking and model registry: record runs with MLflow, promote versions with registry aliases, and make training reproducible.
  • LLMOps: prompt and model versioning: prompts as code, release manifests, A/B tests, rollbacks, and migrating off deprecated provider models.
  • Production monitoring and drift: data and concept drift measured with PSI and the KS test, monitoring classic models, feedback loops, and retraining triggers.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: Model serving exposes a trained model through an interface that an application can call. A serving system loads model weights, accepts requests, runs inference on available hardware, and returns results. It may be a hosted provider, a managed cloud endpoint, or infrastructure operated by your team.

docs.title: Serving choices
docs.text:
Option Team operates Trade-offs Hosted provider API Application integration and policy controls Fastest setup; provider terms, quotas, latency, and price apply Managed cloud endpoint Model selection, application integration, and configuration Less infrastructure work than self-hosting; availability and hardware choices vary Self-hosted inference server Model runtime, hardware, scaling, upgrades, security, and observability More control; high operational and capacity-planning burden On-device runtime Packaging, supported hardware, updates, and local UX Can work offline and keep inference local; device capability and model size constrain quality and speed

Choose by measured quality, data policy, availability, latency, throughput, operational capability, and total cost. "Open weights" does not remove license obligations or operational work.

docs.title: What happens inside a serving system?
docs.text:
1. A gateway checks authentication, quotas, request size, and model access.
  2. A scheduler queues requests and may combine compatible work into a batch.
  3. The runtime tokenizes or otherwise prepares the input, loads model weights, and uses CPU, GPU, or another accelerator.
  4. The model produces output; a decoder or task-specific postprocessor formats it.
  5. A response layer streams or returns the result and emits operational metrics.

docs.title: Example: an OpenAI-compatible server with vLLM
docs.text:
vLLM is a widely used open-source engine for serving open-weight models on GPUs. vllm serve starts an OpenAI-compatible API (Chat Completions, Completions, Responses, Embeddings, and more) on port 8000 by default:

# Pick a model whose license and size fit your GPU; keep the ID in configuration
export MODEL_ID="<org>/<model>"

vllm serve "$MODEL_ID" \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key "$VLLM_API_KEY" \
  --served-model-name taskflow-chat \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --gpu-memory-utilization 0.90

# Smoke test, then read the serving metrics
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $VLLM_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "taskflow-chat", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Reply with: ready"}], "max_tokens": 10}'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/metrics | grep -E "vllm:(num_requests_waiting|num_requests_running)"
  • --served-model-name gives the deployment a stable alias, so TaskFlow's CHAT_MODEL setting does not change when you swap the underlying weights.
  • --max-model-len caps prompt plus output tokens; a smaller value leaves more GPU memory for the KV cache and therefore for concurrent requests.
  • --gpu-memory-utilization is the fraction of GPU memory vLLM may claim. Check the default for your version in the vllm serve reference.
  • --api-key protects only the API path prefixes such as /v1; endpoints like /metrics stay open, so bind to loopback or a private network and put the server behind your gateway.

The TaskFlow client from running models locally works unchanged with LOCAL_LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1.

docs.title: Performance techniques and trade-offs
docs.text:
• Quantization: represents weights or activations with lower precision to reduce memory or improve throughput. Quality changes must be evaluated; support varies by model and hardware.
  • Batching: executes multiple requests together to use accelerators efficiently. Waiting to form a batch can add latency.
  • Continuous batching: adds and removes sequences while a batch is running, improving utilization in some generation workloads.
  • KV caching: retains attention state for active generation, reducing repeated computation while consuming memory.
  • Model parallelism: splits a large model across devices, adding communication and operational complexity.
  • Autoscaling: adds capacity when demand rises, but model loading, accelerator availability, and warm-up time make scaling slower than ordinary stateless web workers.

Optimize only after measuring queue time, time to first token, generation speed, tail latency, memory, throughput, and cost per completed task. vLLM, for example, exports these on /metrics as vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:time_to_first_token_seconds, vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds, vllm:e2e_request_latency_seconds, and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc (metrics docs). A rising waiting count with a full KV cache means you need more memory or replicas, not a faster model.

These techniques matter in practice. When the vLLM team introduced PagedAttention, which stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks instead of one contiguous buffer per request, they reported up to 24 times the throughput of Hugging Face Transformers and up to 3.5 times that of Text Generation Inference in their benchmarks. LMSYS, which served Vicuna and Chatbot Arena on vLLM (30,000 requests a day on average, with peaks of 60,000), reported cutting the GPUs used for that traffic by 50% (vLLM blog, June 2023). Treat such "up to" numbers as a starting point and benchmark your own prompts.

docs.title: Reliability and security
docs.text: Limit request and output size, protect model endpoints, isolate tenants, patch the runtime, and monitor GPU or accelerator health. Use deadlines, bounded queues, cancellation, and explicit overload responses. Do not allow an internal inference endpoint to become publicly reachable without authentication and rate controls.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text:
Most full-stack developers should begin with a hosted API or managed endpoint. Self-host when privacy, latency, control, economics at measured scale, or product requirements justify the operational cost.

Keep the application side boring: one client module that reads the base URL, API key, and model alias from configuration, sets a request timeout, streams long answers, and records tokens and latency per request. Then the same code can call a hosted API, a managed endpoint, or your own vLLM fleet. The deep dives are in serving open models, latency optimization, cost optimization for LLM apps, and GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: "AI model" describes many systems with different input and output types. Before selecting a provider or architecture, describe the task: what information goes in, what should come out, how errors are handled, and whether a person must review the result.

docs.title: Common model categories
docs.text:
Model category Typical input Typical output Example use Chat and language generation Text and conversation context Text, structured fields, or tool-call requests Assistant, drafting, Q&A Reasoning-oriented language model Text or structured task Multi-step answer or plan Complex analysis with verification; cost and latency may be higher Code model Source code, tests, instructions Code completion, explanation, or patch suggestion Developer assistance; generated code still needs review and tests Embedding model Text, image, or other supported content Numeric vector Semantic search, clustering, retrieval Classifier Example and candidate labels Category or score Routing support tickets or detecting content categories Image generation model Text prompt, sometimes reference images Generated or edited image Concept art, assets, design exploration Speech model Audio or text Transcription, translation, or generated speech Voice interface, captions, audio summaries Video model Text, images, or video, depending on model Video, summary, or extracted description Creative generation, scene search, summarization Multimodal model Multiple modalities such as text and images Text or other supported outputs Ask questions about a chart or image Recommendation/ranking model User, item, and context features Ranking or recommendation scores Product or media discovery OCR / document understanding Page image or document file Extracted text, fields, or layout Invoice review and searchable scans Anomaly detector Events or measurements Unusualness score or flag Operations review and equipment monitoring Computer-use (agent) model A goal plus screenshots of a screen Mouse and keyboard actions for your code to execute Operating a web app that has no API

Categories overlap. A multimodal model might accept images and audio; a single product can combine several specialized models in one workflow. Capabilities and limits vary by model version and deployment.

docs.title: Agents and computer use
docs.text:
An agent is not a separate kind of model. It is a language model in a loop: it can call tools, read their results, and choose the next step until the task is done. TaskFlow Assistant becomes an agent when it can call createTask and updateTask itself instead of only describing what to do. Computer use applies the same loop to graphical interfaces: the model receives screenshots and returns actions such as clicks and keystrokes, and your code carries them out in a controlled environment.

As of November 2026, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google each document a computer-use tool for their APIs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google). The guides agree on the basics: run actions in an isolated browser, VM, or container with minimal privileges, keep credentials and sensitive data away from the model, and have a person confirm consequential actions. Anthropic also warns that the model may follow instructions it finds in on-screen content "even when they conflict with your instructions", which is prompt injection through the interface.

The task is still hard for models. When the OSWorld benchmark of real desktop tasks was published in 2024, people completed over 72% of its tasks and the best model about 12% (OSWorld); check current results before relying on a model for a workflow. Prefer a real API or an MCP tool when one exists: screen automation is slower, costs more per step because every screenshot is input, and breaks when the interface changes.

GitHub's Copilot coding agent shows the bounded pattern in production. It works in an environment such as a GitHub Actions runner, opens a pull request per task, and GitHub's documentation tells you to "review and test the output before using it in production" (GitHub Docs). See tool calling in practice, computer use and browser agents, and MCP and agent integrations.

docs.title: Generative and predictive models
docs.text:
Generative models produce content such as text, an image, or audio. Discriminative models estimate labels, scores, or distinctions for inputs. These are broad modeling categories; real model designs can blur the line.

Choose deterministic code or a conventional model when it is easier to validate than free-form generation. For example, calculate a tax total with application code rather than asking a chatbot to perform arithmetic that must be exact.

docs.title: Open weights, source, and hosted access
docs.text:
• Hosted model/API: a provider runs the model and exposes an interface. The model's weights may not be available to the customer.
  • Open-weight model: weights are available under a license for permitted use, but training data, code, or full reproducibility may not be available.
  • Open-source AI system: the term can mean different things; inspect the license, weights, data and documentation available, and usage restrictions instead of assuming every component is open.
  • Commercial product: may combine models, tools, safety systems, retrieval, and proprietary infrastructure.

Model access and license terms change. Confirm the current license, allowed use, retention behavior, and deployment terms for the exact model and version.

docs.title: Public examples
docs.text:
Examples of public AI products and model platforms include OpenAI's ChatGPT/API offerings, Google's Gemini products and APIs, Anthropic's Claude products and API, GitHub Copilot for coding assistance, Adobe Firefly for creative workflows, and Meta's Llama model family. These are examples of different product and provider categories, not an endorsement, a complete market list, or a claim that every product uses one model for every feature.

Public product names and capabilities evolve. Prefer current official documentation when selecting a model for a project.

docs.title: How a full-stack application may combine models
docs.text:
A study-notes app could use:

  1. A speech-to-text model to transcribe a lecture.
  2. A language model to draft a summary.
  3. An embedding model to index notes for semantic search.
  4. A language model with retrieved passages to answer a question with citations.
  5. Application code to enforce access permissions and store the user's notes.

A shopping application might instead use a ranking model to sort eligible items, an image model to describe product photos, and ordinary business rules to filter unavailable items. Eligibility and price calculations should remain deterministic backend operations.

Each step has a distinct contract and should be evaluated separately.

docs.title: Model routing: selecting a model for a task
docs.text:
Model routing is the application-level decision about which model or processing path should handle a request. A system may route an image question to a vision-capable model, a semantic-search query to an embedding model, or a simple deterministic calculation to ordinary code.

Routing can be implemented with:

  • Explicit application rules: choose a model from a known feature, input type, account setting, or user selection. This is predictable and easy to inspect.
  • A lightweight classifier: classify the task into a small set of allowed routes. The backend still validates the route and permissions.
  • A model-based router: ask a model to select from a bounded set of tools or model choices. This can handle less structured requests, but adds another model call and can choose incorrectly.

An example policy might send ordinary note questions to a lower-cost text model, image questions only to a model that supports images, and questions requiring current private information through an authorized retrieval workflow. A request to calculate a total should normally use application code rather than a language model.

Keep the router separate from authorization. A route is a technical choice, not permission to read a user's data or perform an action. Define allowed routes on the server, validate the selected model's actual input and output capabilities, and provide a safe fallback when no route fits. Compare the routed result with a fixed baseline for task quality, latency, and cost; otherwise routing can add complexity without improving the experience.

Do not route solely by a model's name, size, or marketing category. Provider capabilities, limits, and model versions change, so keep model configuration replaceable and verify the current provider documentation.

Explicit rules are a few lines of code. Model IDs stay in configuration, so a model change is a deploy-time setting, not a code change:

// src/ai/router.ts: choose a processing path with explicit rules; model IDs come from configuration
type ModelRoute = "fast-text" | "vision" | "reasoning" | "embedding";
type Route = "code" | ModelRoute;
type AssistantRequest = { task: "total" | "answer" | "search" | "plan"; hasImage?: boolean };

const MODELS: Record<ModelRoute, string | undefined> = {
  "fast-text": process.env.FAST_MODEL,
  vision: process.env.VISION_MODEL,
  reasoning: process.env.REASONING_MODEL,
  embedding: process.env.EMBEDDING_MODEL,
};

export function route(req: AssistantRequest): Route {
  if (req.task === "total") return "code"; // exact arithmetic stays in application code
  if (req.task === "search") return "embedding";
  if (req.hasImage) return "vision";
  if (req.task === "plan") return "reasoning";
  return "fast-text";
}

export function modelFor(r: ModelRoute): string {
  const id = MODELS[r];
  if (!id) throw new Error(`no model configured for route "${r}"`);
  return id;
}

const examples: AssistantRequest[] = [
  { task: "total" },
  { task: "answer" },
  { task: "answer", hasImage: true },
  { task: "plan" },
];
for (const req of examples) console.log(JSON.stringify(req), "->", route(req));

try {
  modelFor("vision");
} catch (err) {
  console.log((err as Error).message); // fail at startup or in a health check, not mid-request
}

Output from running it with Node.js 24 and no model variables set:

{"task":"total"} -> code
{"task":"answer"} -> fast-text
{"task":"answer","hasImage":true} -> vision
{"task":"plan"} -> reasoning
no model configured for route "vision"

Fill the variables from each provider's current model list, and check at startup that every route has a model. See choosing models and providers.

docs.title: Developer perspective
docs.text: Choose based on task quality, latency, cost, availability, data policy, language or modality coverage, output constraints, and operational requirements. Use task-specific tests instead of comparing model names or parameter counts alone.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A chatbot, a model, and an AI product are not the same thing.
  • "Open weight" does not automatically mean unrestricted commercial use.
  • A coding model can generate plausible but insecure or incorrect code.
  • Image, audio, video, and text models have different input, output, and evaluation requirements.
  • A model router does not grant access to data or tools; authorization remains an application responsibility.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A neural network is a mathematical model made of connected operations with parameters adjusted during training. A transformer is a neural network architecture that uses attention to process relationships among items in a sequence or other structured input. Transformers underpin many modern language models and are also used for images, audio, video, and multimodal tasks.

docs.title: Neural-network basics
docs.text:
A network receives numeric inputs, applies parameterized operations and nonlinear transformations through layers, then produces outputs. During training, an objective (loss) measures how far predictions are from training targets. An optimization algorithm calculates how to adjust parameters to reduce that loss.

  • Forward pass: compute a model output from an input.
  • Loss: numeric training objective measuring some prediction error.
  • Backpropagation: calculate how the loss changes with model parameters.
  • Optimizer: update parameters using those calculated gradients.
  • Epoch: one pass through the training dataset, in training setups that use epochs.

Inference uses the learned parameters to produce outputs; it usually does not update them.

docs.title: Attention and the transformer idea
docs.text:
Attention lets a model compute which parts of an input are relevant to processing another part. In a language sequence, the representation for a token can incorporate information from other tokens. Self-attention computes these relationships within the same sequence.

The transformer architecture commonly combines attention with feed-forward layers, residual connections, normalization, and positional information. Details differ across model architectures. The key idea is that attention helps model long-range relationships and can be parallelized during training more readily than recurrent sequence processing.

In a simplified self-attention operation, each input representation is projected into a query (Q), key (K), and value (V). Similarity between a query and keys determines weights over the values. Multiple attention heads learn different relationships in parallel and their results are combined. This helps the model contextualize tokens, but the weights are not a human-readable explanation of why an answer is true.

The core operation from the original transformer paper is:

[ \operatorname{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V ]

A few lines of NumPy show it for four tokens. Decoder-style models add a causal mask so that each token can only use itself and earlier tokens:

# attention.py: scaled dot-product self-attention with a causal mask, as in decoder-style models
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
tokens, d_model, d_k = 4, 8, 8  # 4 tokens, 8 numbers per token

x = rng.normal(size=(tokens, d_model))  # token embeddings with position information
W_q, W_k, W_v = (rng.normal(size=(d_model, d_k)) / np.sqrt(d_model) for _ in range(3))  # learned in training
Q, K, V = x @ W_q, x @ W_k, x @ W_v

scores = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d_k)  # (4, 4): query-key similarity for every pair of tokens
mask = np.triu(np.ones((tokens, tokens), dtype=bool), k=1)
scores[mask] = -np.inf  # causal mask: a token cannot look at later tokens

weights = np.exp(scores - scores.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
weights /= weights.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)  # softmax over each row
output = weights @ V  # (4, 8): one contextual vector per token

print(np.round(weights, 2))
print(output.shape)

Output from running it with NumPy 2.5:

[[1.   0.   0.   0.  ]
 [0.39 0.61 0.   0.  ]
 [0.34 0.33 0.33 0.  ]
 [0.08 0.4  0.29 0.22]]
(4, 8)

Each row holds one token's attention weights and sums to 1; the zeros above the diagonal are the mask. The score matrix has one entry for every pair of tokens, which is where the quadratic cost in sequence length comes from. A real model repeats this in every layer, with many heads and vectors of thousands of numbers.

docs.title: Encoder, decoder, and encoder-decoder patterns
docs.text:
Pattern Broad behavior Common use Encoder-style Build contextual representations of the input Classification, search embeddings, extraction Decoder-style Generate an output sequence one token at a time Chat, completion, code generation Encoder-decoder Encode an input and generate a related output Translation, summarization, speech or text transformations

These are useful architectural families, not a complete list of current designs. Some systems combine components or use other architectures.

Encoder-style models are less visible than chat models but widely deployed. When Google added BERT, an encoder-style transformer, to Search in October 2019, it said BERT would help Search "better understand one in 10 searches in the U.S. in English" (Google). Embedding models for semantic search and RAG use the same idea: they output one vector per input instead of generating text. Some are built on encoder models such as BERT, others on decoder models adapted for embeddings.

Vision transformers commonly split an image into patches and process them as a sequence of representations. Audio models may use frames, learned tokens, or other encodings. Their inputs and training objectives are specialized; a text-only decoder cannot automatically process raw media.

docs.title: From text to model input
docs.text:
Text is split into tokens, which are converted to numeric identifiers and then to learned embeddings (vectors). The model processes these representations and produces output scores. A decoder-style language model selects or samples a next token, appends it to the context, and repeats until a stopping condition is met.

The output is generated token by token. This is why a long response takes time, why context limits matter, and why the model can produce a plausible continuation that is not factually grounded.

docs.title: Why use transformers?
docs.text:
Attention gives models a flexible way to relate different positions in an input, and large-scale training can produce representations useful across many tasks. Trade-offs include substantial compute and memory requirements, quadratic attention cost in some common designs with sequence length, latency for autoregressive generation, and difficult-to-predict behavior. Modern systems use optimizations and architectures that change these costs; do not assume one cost profile fits every model.

Refinements found in many current models:

Refinement What it changes Source Mixture of experts (MoE) A router sends each token to a few expert feed-forward blocks, so only part of the parameters run per token. Mixtral 8x7B picks 2 of 8 experts per layer: 47B parameters, 13B active Mixtral paper Grouped-query attention (GQA) Several query heads share one key-value head, which shrinks the KV cache that inference keeps per token GQA paper Rotary position embeddings (RoPE) Encodes token positions by rotating query and key vectors RoFormer paper FlashAttention Computes exact attention in tiles to cut GPU memory traffic FlashAttention paper

MoE explains why a model's total parameter count and its per-token compute can differ widely. Inference and decoding covers the KV cache, and serving open models covers what these choices mean for GPU memory.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: You generally call an inference endpoint rather than implement backpropagation or attention yourself. Knowing the high-level flow helps explain prompt length, context windows, streaming responses, embeddings, and latency. For a production feature, treat the model version and its input format as dependencies that can change.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• Attention is a model operation, not human attention or an explicit source citation.
  • A transformer is an architecture, not a single model or product.
  • An embedding is a learned numeric representation, not a guaranteed definition of meaning.
  • Neural networks do not retrieve exact training examples on command like a database query.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Attention Is All You Need
  • The Illustrated Transformer
  • Hugging Face: How do Transformers work?

docs.title: AI Project Learning Paths
docs.text:
Use these as step-by-step learning paths, not as instructions to build every feature at once. Pick one project, complete one small milestone, and decide whether to continue before adding the next capability. The study-notes path below is a suggested capstone because it connects AI concepts with ordinary full-stack engineering.

The hands-on labs are short exercises within the learning path; there is no separate testing project to complete. Evaluation and safety checks belong alongside the feature they assess.

docs.title: Suggested capstone: study-notes assistant
docs.text:
Treat each item as a learning step. Stop after any step once it meets your learning goal; the later steps are optional extensions, not a requirement to build a complete product.

  1. Define one small task. For example, answer a question using one fictional note. Decide what a useful answer and a no-answer result look like.
  2. Choose an existing model. Start with a hosted API or an available local model; do not train a model. Compare only what matters for this task, such as answer quality, data handling, latency, and cost.
  3. Understand model selection. Decide whether this task needs a text model, embedding model, or both. Keep the choice fixed initially; study model routing as a later extension.
  4. Try the simplest prompt-based version. Give the model the small note directly and ask it to answer only from that material. Check a question the note answers and one it does not.
  5. Add retrieval when needed. Learn how chunking and embeddings select relevant passages as the note collection grows. Keep the note's source and access information with each passage.
  6. Connect retrieval to answers. Provide the selected passages to the model and show links to those actual sources. Do not treat generated citations as verified until the application checks them.
  7. Add access boundaries. Use fictional notes to understand ownership filtering and why the backend, not the model, enforces permissions. Include prompt injection in a note and observe why retrieved content must remain untrusted.
  8. Add a user interface only after the flow is clear. A minimal screen can submit a question, show the answer and sources, and explain when there is not enough information.
  9. Evaluate each milestone as you learn it. Keep a few expected question/source pairs, check whether retrieval found the right passage, verify that citations point to it, and try a missing-answer or cross-user case. This is part of each step, not a separate testing module.
  10. Consider optional extensions. Add a second model, a local runtime, document upload, or a narrow MCP search tool only when you can explain what the extension teaches and what new risks it introduces.

Related lessons: Model Types and Capabilities, RAG, AI Security, and Building AI Features.

docs.title: 1. Hosted-model API playground
docs.text:
Build a backend endpoint that accepts a user prompt, validates its length, calls a hosted model, and returns a bounded response.

  • Keep the API key on the server.
  • Add authentication, rate limiting, timeout handling, and usage tracking.
  • Show loading, cancellation, error, and retry states in the UI.
  • Test that an invalid request never reaches the provider.
  • Do not log the key or unnecessary prompt content.

Prerequisites: Hosted Model APIs, Building AI Features, and Deployment, Cost, and Performance.

What you practice: secure server-side model calls, backend validation, provider adapters, UI states, quotas, and explicit failure handling. Choose this first if API integration is new to you; it builds the smallest reusable foundation for the later projects.

docs.title: 2. Local-model comparison
docs.text:
Run one small model locally and compare it with a permitted hosted model on the same set of fictional tasks. Record quality, latency, context limits, hardware use, and operational work. Keep the sample data non-sensitive.

Prerequisites: Model Types and Running Models Locally.

What you practice: model selection, local serving, resource measurement, and controlled comparisons. Choose this if you want to understand local-versus-hosted trade-offs before choosing an inference platform; it does not require training a model.

docs.title: 3. Structured support-ticket triage
docs.text:
Create a small set of fictional tickets and allowed categories. Ask a model for structured output, validate it on the backend, and route uncertain cases to a human review screen.

  • Test malformed, ambiguous, and out-of-scope messages.
  • Do not let the model execute ticket changes.
  • Compare against a simple keyword or rules baseline.

Prerequisites: Prompting and Structured Output and Evaluation and Monitoring.

What you practice: schemas, a deterministic baseline, thresholds, review queues, and classification metrics. Choose this if you want to build a bounded business workflow where the model suggests a result but ordinary backend code retains authority.

docs.title: 4. Searchable study notes with RAG
docs.text:
Let a signed-in user add notes, index chunks, ask questions, and open cited source passages.

  • Enforce note ownership before indexing and retrieval.
  • Store source IDs and locations with each chunk.
  • Test that one user's query never retrieves another user's notes.
  • Test deletion and re-indexing when a note changes.
  • Say when no useful source was found instead of inventing an answer.

Prerequisites: Embeddings and Vector Search, RAG, and Security and Responsible AI.

What you practice: ingestion, chunking, vector search, source citations, tenant isolation, data deletion, and answer evaluation. Choose this if you want a flagship project that connects AI retrieval to backend, database, security, and UI skills.

docs.title: 5. Fine-tune a narrow behavior (optional)
docs.text:
Only after establishing a baseline, use a small permitted dataset and a supported model to explore fine-tuning. Compare it with prompting on the same held-out examples. Document the model, data, terms, cost, and regressions. Do not upload personal or confidential data without approval.

Prerequisites: Fine-Tuning and Training Models.

What you practice: data curation, held-out tests, adapters, experiment tracking, and regression analysis. Choose this only after a baseline demonstrates a repeatable behavior gap that prompting and application logic do not solve.

docs.title: 6. Media understanding pipeline
docs.text:
Build a small workflow that accepts a user-selected image or short video, validates its format and size, extracts a few timestamped frames or a transcript, and asks a suitable model for a source-linked description. Show the user which frames or transcript segments support the result and let them remove the uploaded media.

Prerequisites: Images, Audio, and Video Formats for AI, Speech and Multimodal AI, and Security, Privacy, and Responsible AI.

What you practice: codecs and decoding, media limits, asynchronous processing, timestamps, consent, and multimodal evaluation. Choose this if media-based AI is relevant to your goals; begin with still images before adding longer videos or audio.

docs.title: 7. MCP project-search server
docs.text:
Create a read-only local MCP server that searches a small, synthetic project-notes folder. Expose one narrow search tool and one resource, run it over stdio from a compatible host, and inspect how the host discovers and invokes capabilities. Do not start with a shell-execution tool or credentials.

Prerequisites: MCP and Agent Integrations, Terminal Tools and Operating-System Access, and Security, Privacy, and Responsible AI.

What you practice: host/client/server roles, stdio transport, capability discovery, tool schemas, process permissions, and approval boundaries. Choose this if you want to learn how reusable AI integrations connect to external systems without giving a model unrestricted OS access.

docs.title: 8. Model evaluation harness
docs.text:
Build a small test runner that loads fictional task cases, calls a selected model adapter, validates structured outputs, and reports task-specific metrics, latency, and estimated usage. Compare a prompt or model change against the same baseline cases.

Prerequisites: Evaluation and Monitoring, MLOps and Model Lifecycle, and Mathematics for Machine Learning.

What you practice: reproducible fixtures, grading rules, regression testing, model versioning, and operational metrics. Choose this before fine-tuning or switching providers if you need evidence that a change actually improves your task.

docs.title: Choosing a project
docs.text: Your goal Start with Why Learn safe API integration Hosted-model API playground Smallest useful end-to-end feature Understand model hosting choices Local-model comparison Measures quality and resource trade-offs Build a bounded business task Support-ticket triage Practices schemas, metrics, and human review Connect private knowledge safely Searchable study notes with RAG Integrates retrieval, authorization, and citations Learn AI connector protocols MCP project-search server Shows discovery and OS process boundaries Improve multimodal understanding Media understanding pipeline Adds media decoding and modality-specific evaluation Compare model or prompt changes Model evaluation harness Provides evidence before adding complexity Explore model adaptation Fine-tuning experiment Requires a clear behavior gap and evaluation baseline

docs.title: Suggested project quality checklist
docs.text:
• Define the user problem and a measurable success criterion.
  • Keep authorization, validation, and side effects in ordinary backend code.
  • Set input, output, rate, time, and cost limits.
  • Add tests for errors, retries, permissions, and sensitive data.
  • Evaluate representative successes and failures before deployment.
  • Explain generated content and uncertainty to users.
  • Provide deletion and correction paths for stored or derived data.
  • Document which model and prompt versions were used.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: A prompt is the input and instruction context sent to a model for inference. It may include system instructions, developer rules, user input, conversation history, examples, retrieved information, and tool definitions. Prompt engineering is the practice of designing and testing that context for a specific task.

docs.title: Why prompt design matters
docs.text: Models respond to the information and instructions in their context. Ambiguous goals, conflicting requirements, missing data, and irrelevant history can lead to inconsistent outputs. A clear prompt makes the task, constraints, and expected format easier to evaluate.

docs.title: A practical prompt structure
docs.text:
1. Role or task: state what work is requested.
  2. Context: provide only the relevant background and source material.
  3. Constraints: define safety boundaries, audience, length, or allowed actions.
  4. Output format: specify fields or a schema when predictable data is needed.
  5. Uncertainty behavior: say what to do when information is missing, such as ask a question or return an explicit unknown.
  6. Examples: provide representative input and output examples only when they clarify the desired behavior.

docs.title: Example: note summary
docs.text:
Task: Summarize the supplied meeting notes for a project team.
Rules:
- Use only the supplied notes.
- Separate decisions, action items, and open questions.
- Include the source heading for each item.
- If an owner or date is missing, write "not specified".
Output: JSON with decisions, action_items, and open_questions arrays.

This prompt improves clarity, but the application must still validate JSON, check source references, and allow correction. The instruction "use only the notes" is not a technical security boundary.

docs.title: Structured output
docs.text:
When an application expects data, use a provider's structured-output or schema-constrained feature when available. Define required fields, types, enums, and bounds. Then validate the response on the server with an ordinary schema validator before using it.

Do not assume JSON-looking text is valid JSON or that valid JSON is factually correct. A schema can ensure priority is one of three strings; it cannot prove that the selected priority is appropriate.

docs.title: Parameters and reproducibility
docs.text:
Prompts and model behavior can change with model version, provider defaults, sampling parameters, and context. Keep prompts in version control without embedding secrets or personal data. Record model identifiers and relevant configuration so a test can be reproduced as closely as possible.

Reasoning models add an effort or thinking setting, and as of November 2026 some providers reject or deprecate sampling parameters such as temperature for their newest models. Record the effort level with the model identifier, and read model identifiers from configuration rather than hard-coding them.

docs.title: Prompt injection
docs.text:
Prompt injection is untrusted input that attempts to override instructions or influence model behavior. It can appear in user text, documents, web pages, or tool results. The model should not be treated as an authorization engine.

Keep sensitive operations behind application code. A model may suggest a tool call, but the backend must validate arguments, check the user's permissions, and constrain the operation before execution. Treat retrieved content as data, not instructions.

docs.title: Testing prompts
docs.text:
Build a small set of realistic inputs, including ambiguous, malformed, adversarial, and out-of-scope examples. Evaluate:

  • whether required information is present;
  • whether the model follows the requested format;
  • factual support and source attribution;
  • refusals and uncertainty handling;
  • latency and token consumption;
  • behavior after changing model or prompt versions.

Change one important prompt component at a time and compare outputs. A single impressive example is not evidence of reliability.

docs.title: Full-stack developer perspective
docs.text: Keep prompts and provider logic on the server when they contain private instructions or access to tools. Prompt text is not a substitute for input validation, output encoding, authorization, or rate limiting.

docs.title: Common misconceptions
docs.text:
• A longer prompt is not automatically a better prompt.
  • Telling a model to "be accurate" does not verify its answer.
  • JSON output can be syntactically valid and semantically wrong.
  • A system prompt is not a secret or a hard security boundary.

docs.title: Go deeper
docs.text:
• Prompt design and templates: system and user messages, the instruction hierarchy, few-shot examples, delimiting untrusted content, and versioned, tested prompt templates in TypeScript.
  • Structured output and validation: JSON mode, schema-constrained output, and tool-based extraction, zod validation and repair retries, refusals, streaming partial JSON, and end-to-end task creation for TaskFlow.
  • Reasoning models and thinking: test-time compute, effort and thinking settings per provider, when to use reasoning models, prompting them, and evaluating them by outcome.
