docs.title: Parse the event stream
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/sse.ts
export interface SseEvent { event: string; data: string; id?: string }

// Parses a text/event-stream body. Network chunks can split an event (or a
// multi-byte character) anywhere, so text is buffered until a blank line.
export async function* parseSse(body: ReadableStream<Uint8Array>): AsyncGenerator<SseEvent> {
  const reader = body.getReader();
  const decoder = new TextDecoder(); // { stream: true } keeps split UTF-8 bytes
  let buffer = "";
  try {
    while (true) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      buffer += decoder.decode(value, { stream: true }).replace(/\r\n?/g, "\n");
      let end: number;
      while ((end = buffer.indexOf("\n\n")) !== -1) {
        const block = buffer.slice(0, end);
        buffer = buffer.slice(end + 2);
        const event = parseBlock(block);
        if (event) yield event;
      }
    }
  } finally {
    reader.releaseLock();
  }
}

function parseBlock(block: string): SseEvent | undefined {
  let event = "message", id: string | undefined;
  const data: string[] = [];
  for (const line of block.split("\n")) {
    if (line === "" || line.startsWith(":")) continue; // comments are keep-alives
    const colon = line.indexOf(":");
    const field = colon === -1 ? line : line.slice(0, colon);
    const value = colon === -1 ? "" : line.slice(colon + 1).replace(/^ /, "");
    if (field === "event") event = value;
    else if (field === "data") data.push(value);
    else if (field === "id") id = value;
  }
  return data.length ? { event, data: data.join("\n"), id } : undefined;
}

docs.title: Model the turn as a reducer
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/chatState.ts
export interface Source { id: string; title: string; url: string; snippet: string }

export interface UiMessage {
  id: string;
  role: "user" | "assistant";
  text: string;
  sources: Source[];
  state: "sending" | "sent" | "failed" | "waiting" | "streaming" | "complete" | "stopped" | "error";
}

export type ChatStatus = "idle" | "submitted" | "streaming" | "error";
export interface ChatState { messages: UiMessage[]; status: ChatStatus; error?: string }

export type ChatAction =
  | { type: "submit"; userId: string; assistantId: string; text: string }
  | { type: "regenerate"; assistantId: string }
  | { type: "accepted"; assistantId: string }
  | { type: "delta"; assistantId: string; text: string }
  | { type: "sources"; assistantId: string; sources: Source[] }
  | { type: "done"; assistantId: string }
  | { type: "stopped"; assistantId: string }
  | { type: "failed"; assistantId: string; error: string; requestReached: boolean };

export const initialChat: ChatState = { messages: [], status: "idle" };

const patch = (messages: UiMessage[], id: string, change: (m: UiMessage) => Partial<UiMessage>) =>
  messages.map((m) => (m.id === id ? { ...m, ...change(m) } : m));

export function chatReducer(state: ChatState, action: ChatAction): ChatState {
  switch (action.type) {
    case "submit": // optimistic: show the user's message and a placeholder at once
      return {
        status: "submitted",
        messages: [
          ...state.messages,
          { id: action.userId, role: "user", text: action.text, sources: [], state: "sending" },
          { id: action.assistantId, role: "assistant", text: "", sources: [], state: "waiting" },
        ],
      };
    case "regenerate": { // drop the last answer and wait for a new one
      const lastUser = state.messages.findLastIndex((m) => m.role === "user");
      return {
        status: "submitted",
        messages: [
          ...state.messages.slice(0, lastUser + 1),
          { id: action.assistantId, role: "assistant", text: "", sources: [], state: "waiting" },
        ],
      };
    }
    case "accepted": // the server stored the user message
      return { ...state, messages: state.messages.map((m) => (m.state === "sending" ? { ...m, state: "sent" } : m)) };
    case "delta":
      return {
        status: "streaming",
        messages: patch(state.messages, action.assistantId, (m) => ({ text: m.text + action.text, state: "streaming" })),
      };
    case "sources":
      return { ...state, messages: patch(state.messages, action.assistantId, () => ({ sources: action.sources })) };
    case "done":
      return { status: "idle", messages: patch(state.messages, action.assistantId, () => ({ state: "complete" })) };
    case "stopped": // keep the partial text, clearly marked
      return { status: "idle", messages: patch(state.messages, action.assistantId, () => ({ state: "stopped" })) };
    case "failed": {
      // If the request never reached the server, the user's text must not be lost.
      const messages = action.requestReached
        ? patch(state.messages, action.assistantId, () => ({ state: "error" }))
        : state.messages
            .filter((m) => m.id !== action.assistantId)
            .map((m) => (m.state === "sending" ? { ...m, state: "failed" as const } : m));
      return { status: "error", error: action.error, messages };
    }
  }
}

docs.title: The streaming hook: send, stop, regenerate
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/useChatStream.ts
import { useCallback, useEffect, useReducer, useRef } from "react";
import { parseSse } from "./sse.js";
import { chatReducer, initialChat, type Source } from "./chatState.js";
import { ChatHttpError, describeChatError } from "./errors.js";

export function useChatStream(conversationId: string) {
  const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(chatReducer, initialChat);
  const controller = useRef<AbortController | null>(null);

  const run = useCallback(async (text: string, regenerate: boolean) => {
    controller.current?.abort(); // one generation at a time
    const abort = new AbortController();
    controller.current = abort;
    const assistantId = crypto.randomUUID();
    dispatch(regenerate
      ? { type: "regenerate", assistantId }
      : { type: "submit", userId: crypto.randomUUID(), assistantId, text });

    let requestReached = false;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`/api/conversations/${conversationId}/messages`, {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json", Accept: "text/event-stream" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ text, regenerate }),
        signal: abort.signal,
      });
      if (!res.ok || !res.body) {
        const retryAfter = Number(res.headers.get("Retry-After")) || undefined;
        throw new ChatHttpError(res.status, retryAfter);
      }
      requestReached = true;
      dispatch({ type: "accepted", assistantId });
      for await (const event of parseSse(res.body)) {
        const data = JSON.parse(event.data);
        if (event.event === "delta") dispatch({ type: "delta", assistantId, text: data.text as string });
        else if (event.event === "sources") dispatch({ type: "sources", assistantId, sources: data.sources as Source[] });
        else if (event.event === "error") throw new Error(String(data.message));
        else if (event.event === "done") { dispatch({ type: "done", assistantId }); return; }
      }
      throw new Error("The stream ended without a done event");
    } catch (err) {
      if (abort.signal.aborted) dispatch({ type: "stopped", assistantId });
      else dispatch({ type: "failed", assistantId, requestReached, error: describeChatError(err).title });
    } finally {
      if (controller.current === abort) controller.current = null;
    }
  }, [conversationId]);

  const stop = useCallback(() => controller.current?.abort(), []);
  useEffect(() => () => controller.current?.abort(), []); // leaving the page stops the stream

  const lastUserText = state.messages.findLast((m) => m.role === "user")?.text ?? "";
  return {
    ...state,
    send: (text: string) => run(text, false),
    regenerate: () => run(lastUserText, true),
    stop,
  };
}

A stream that ends without done is treated as an error, not as a complete answer: a proxy timeout or deploy can cut the connection cleanly, and a truncated answer must not look finished. The error helper maps failures to the messages in the table above:

// src/web/chat/errors.ts
export class ChatHttpError extends Error {
  constructor(readonly status: number, readonly retryAfterSeconds?: number) {
    super(`HTTP ${status}`);
  }
}

// Problem first, then what the user can do. No raw provider errors in the UI.
export function describeChatError(err: unknown): { title: string; detail: string; canRetry: boolean } {
  if (err instanceof ChatHttpError) {
    if (err.status === 401) return { title: "Your session expired.", detail: "Sign in again to continue.", canRetry: false };
    if (err.status === 413) return { title: "That message is too long.", detail: "Shorten it or attach the text as a file.", canRetry: false };
    if (err.status === 429) {
      const wait = err.retryAfterSeconds ? `in ${err.retryAfterSeconds} seconds` : "in a moment";
      return { title: "Too many requests right now.", detail: `Try again ${wait}.`, canRetry: true };
    }
    if (err.status >= 500) return { title: "The assistant is unavailable.", detail: "Try again. Your message was kept.", canRetry: true };
  }
  if (typeof navigator !== "undefined" && navigator.onLine === false) {
    return { title: "You appear to be offline.", detail: "Reconnect, then retry.", canRetry: true };
  }
  return { title: "Something went wrong.", detail: "Try again. Your message was kept.", canRetry: true };
}

docs.title: Render markdown safely
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/SafeMarkdown.tsx
import Markdown, { type Components } from "react-markdown";
import remarkGfm from "remark-gfm";

// Images load from our own file host only: a remote image URL in model output
// can carry data out of the page the moment the browser fetches it.
const IMAGE_HOSTS = new Set(["files.example.com"]);

function allowedImage(src: unknown): string | undefined {
  if (typeof src !== "string") return undefined;
  try {
    const url = new URL(src, window.location.origin);
    return url.protocol === "https:" && IMAGE_HOSTS.has(url.host) ? url.href : undefined;
  } catch {
    return undefined;
  }
}

const components: Components = {
  a({ href, children }) {
    if (href?.startsWith("#source-")) { // citation markers produced by linkCitations
      return <sup><a href={href} className="citation">{children}</a></sup>;
    }
    return <a href={href} target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">{children}</a>;
  },
  img({ src, alt }) {
    const safe = allowedImage(src);
    return safe ? <img src={safe} alt={alt ?? ""} loading="lazy" /> : <span>[image not shown]</span>;
  },
};

// react-markdown never renders raw HTML (skipHtml drops it entirely) and its
// default urlTransform removes javascript: and other unsafe link protocols.
export function SafeMarkdown({ text }: { text: string }) {
  return (
    <Markdown remarkPlugins={[remarkGfm]} skipHtml components={components}>
      {text}
    </Markdown>
  );
}

A test renders hostile input with renderToString and asserts on the HTML. This is the real output for four of the payloads (the <script> and raw <img onerror> lines produced nothing at all):

<p><a href="" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow">click me</a></p>
<p><span>[image not shown]</span></p>
<p><img src="https://files.example.com/logo.png" alt="logo" loading="lazy"/></p>
<p><strong>bold</strong> and <code>code</code></p>

The javascript: link survives as harmless text with an empty href; if that looks odd in your UI, render links with an empty href as plain text in the a override.

docs.title: Link citations and show sources
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/citations.ts
import type { Source } from "./chatState.js";

// The model is asked to cite with markers such as [S2] or [S1, S3]. Markers are
// turned into links to the sources panel; markers for unknown IDs are removed
// and counted, because a citation to a source that was never retrieved is invented.
export function linkCitations(text: string, sources: Source[]) {
  const order = new Map(sources.map((s, i) => [s.id, i + 1]));
  let invalid = 0;
  const linked = text.replace(/\[(S\d+(?:\s*,\s*S\d+)*)\]/g, (_marker, ids: string) =>
    ids.split(",").map((raw) => {
      const id = raw.trim();
      const n = order.get(id);
      if (n === undefined) { invalid++; return ""; }
      return `[${n}](#source-${id})`;
    }).join(""));
  return { markdown: linked, invalid };
}

// src/web/chat/AssistantMessage.tsx
import { linkCitations } from "./citations.js";
import { SafeMarkdown } from "./SafeMarkdown.js";
import { FeedbackButtons } from "./FeedbackButtons.js";
import type { UiMessage } from "./chatState.js";

export function AssistantMessage({ message }: { message: UiMessage }) {
  const { markdown } = linkCitations(message.text, message.sources);
  const finished = message.state === "complete" || message.state === "stopped";
  return (
    <article aria-label="Assistant message" aria-busy={message.state === "streaming"}>
      {message.state === "waiting" ? <p className="thinking">Thinking...</p> : <SafeMarkdown text={markdown} />}
      {message.state === "stopped" && <p className="note">Stopped. This answer is incomplete.</p>}
      {message.state === "error" && <p className="note" role="alert">The answer was interrupted.</p>}
      {message.sources.length > 0 && (
        <section aria-label="Sources">
          <h3>Sources</h3>
          <ol>
            {message.sources.map((source) => (
              <li key={source.id} id={`source-${source.id}`}>
                <a href={source.url}>{source.title}</a>
                <blockquote>{source.snippet}</blockquote>
              </li>
            ))}
          </ol>
        </section>
      )}
      {finished && <FeedbackButtons messageId={message.id} />}
    </article>
  );
}

With sources S1 and S2, the input Budget is fixed [S1, S9]. becomes Budget is fixed [1](#source-S1). and invalid is 1: the test asserts exactly that. Send the invalid count to your telemetry with the message's trace ID.

docs.title: Feedback buttons and the endpoint behind them
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/FeedbackButtons.tsx
import { useState } from "react";

type Rating = "up" | "down";
const REASONS = ["Incorrect", "Not helpful", "Wrong or missing source", "Unsafe or offensive"];

export function FeedbackButtons({ messageId }: { messageId: string }) {
  const [rating, setRating] = useState<Rating | null>(null);
  const [reasons, setReasons] = useState<string[]>([]);
  const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);

  async function submit(next: Rating | null, nextReasons: string[]) {
    const previous = rating;
    setRating(next); // optimistic; roll back if the request fails
    setSaved(false);
    const res = await fetch("/api/feedback", {
      method: "PUT", // idempotent: one rating per user per message, changeable
      headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ messageId, rating: next, reasons: nextReasons }),
    }).catch(() => undefined);
    if (!res?.ok) setRating(previous);
    else setSaved(true);
  }

  const toggleReason = (reason: string) => {
    const next = reasons.includes(reason) ? reasons.filter((r) => r !== reason) : [...reasons, reason];
    setReasons(next);
    void submit("down", next);
  };

  return (
    <div className="feedback">
      {/* With icon-only buttons, keep these texts as aria-label values. */}
      <button type="button" aria-pressed={rating === "up"}
              onClick={() => submit(rating === "up" ? null : "up", [])}>Helpful</button>
      <button type="button" aria-pressed={rating === "down"}
              onClick={() => submit(rating === "down" ? null : "down", reasons)}>Not helpful</button>
      {rating === "down" && (
        <fieldset>
          <legend>What went wrong? (optional)</legend>
          {REASONS.map((reason) => (
            <label key={reason}>
              <input type="checkbox" checked={reasons.includes(reason)} onChange={() => toggleReason(reason)} />
              {reason}
            </label>
          ))}
        </fieldset>
      )}
      <span role="status">{saved ? "Thanks for the feedback." : ""}</span>
    </div>
  );
}

// src/routes/feedback.ts
import { Router } from "express";
import { ObjectId, type Db } from "mongodb";
import { z } from "zod";

const FeedbackBody = z.object({
  messageId: z.string().refine(ObjectId.isValid, "invalid message id"),
  rating: z.enum(["up", "down"]).nullable(),       // null clears an earlier vote
  reasons: z.array(z.string().max(60)).max(5).default([]),
  comment: z.string().max(1_000).optional(),
});

export function feedbackRoutes(db: Db) {
  const router = Router();
  const messages = db.collection("messages");
  const feedback = db.collection("feedback");

  router.put("/feedback", async (req, res) => {
    const owner = res.locals.owner as { userId: string; workspaceId: string };
    const body = FeedbackBody.safeParse(req.body);
    if (!body.success) return res.status(400).json({ error: "Invalid feedback." });

    // Model, prompt version, and trace come from the stored message, not the client.
    const messageId = new ObjectId(body.data.messageId);
    const message = await messages.findOne(
      { _id: messageId, userId: owner.userId, role: "assistant" },
      { projection: { conversationId: 1, model: 1, promptVersion: 1, traceId: 1 } },
    );
    if (!message) return res.status(404).end();

    await feedback.updateOne(
      { messageId, userId: owner.userId },
      {
        $set: {
          ...body.data, messageId, workspaceId: owner.workspaceId,
          conversationId: message.conversationId, model: message.model,
          promptVersion: message.promptVersion, traceId: message.traceId,
          reviewStatus: body.data.rating === "down" ? "unreviewed" : "none",
          updatedAt: new Date(),
        },
        $setOnInsert: { createdAt: new Date() },
      },
      { upsert: true },
    );
    res.status(204).end();
  });

  return router;
}

reviewStatus: "unreviewed" is what the review queue queries. A unique index on { messageId: 1, userId: 1 } makes the upsert safe under double clicks.

docs.title: Put it together with accessible states
docs.text:
// src/web/chat/ChatView.tsx
import { useState, type KeyboardEvent } from "react";
import { useChatStream } from "./useChatStream.js";
import { AssistantMessage } from "./AssistantMessage.js";

export function ChatView({ conversationId }: { conversationId: string }) {
  const chat = useChatStream(conversationId);
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");
  const busy = chat.status === "submitted" || chat.status === "streaming";
  const last = chat.messages.at(-1);

  function send() {
    const text = draft.trim();
    if (!text || busy) return;
    setDraft(""); // the reducer already holds the text, so a failure cannot lose it
    void chat.send(text);
  }

  function onKeyDown(e: KeyboardEvent<HTMLTextAreaElement>) {
    if (e.key === "Enter" && !e.shiftKey) { e.preventDefault(); send(); }
    if (e.key === "Escape" && busy) chat.stop();
  }

  // One short announcement per state change, instead of one per streamed token.
  const announcement =
    chat.status === "submitted" ? "Assistant is responding." :
    last?.state === "complete" ? "Response complete." :
    last?.state === "stopped" ? "Response stopped." :
    chat.status === "error" ? (chat.error ?? "Something went wrong.") : "";

  return (
    <div className="chat">
      <section aria-label="Conversation">
        {chat.messages.map((m) =>
          m.role === "user"
            ? <p key={m.id} className={`user ${m.state}`}>{m.text}{m.state === "failed" && " (not sent)"}</p>
            : <AssistantMessage key={m.id} message={m} />)}
      </section>

      <div role="status" className="visually-hidden">{announcement}</div>

      {!busy && (last?.state === "stopped" || last?.state === "error" || last?.state === "complete") && (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void chat.regenerate()}>Regenerate</button>
      )}

      <form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); send(); }}>
        <label htmlFor="chat-input">Message TaskFlow Assistant</label>
        <textarea id="chat-input" value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)}
                  onKeyDown={onKeyDown} rows={2} />
        {busy
          ? <button type="button" onClick={chat.stop}>Stop generating</button>
          : <button type="submit" disabled={!draft.trim()}>Send</button>}
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}

The real test run for this module set:

ok 1 - SSE parser survives events and UTF-8 characters split across chunks
ok 2 - reducer: optimistic send, stream, stop keeps partial text, regenerate replaces it
ok 3 - reducer: a request that never reached the server keeps the user's text
ok 4 - citations: known markers become links, invented ones are removed and counted
ok 5 - errors: 429 shows the Retry-After wait
ok 6 - SafeMarkdown neutralizes XSS and exfiltration payloads

docs.title: The same chat with the AI SDK
docs.text:
If the backend streams the AI SDK's UI message format (for example with streamText(...).toUIMessageStreamResponse()), useChat replaces the hook and the reducer. Messages arrive as typed parts, so text, sources, tool calls, and reasoning each get their own component:

// src/web/chat/AssistantChatSdk.tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { useChat } from "@ai-sdk/react";
import { DefaultChatTransport } from "ai";
import { SafeMarkdown } from "./SafeMarkdown.js";

export function AssistantChatSdk({ conversationId }: { conversationId: string }) {
  const { messages, sendMessage, status, stop, regenerate, error, clearError } = useChat({
    id: conversationId,
    transport: new DefaultChatTransport({ api: "/api/chat" }),
    throttle: 50, // re-render at most every 50 ms while tokens arrive
  });
  const [draft, setDraft] = useState("");
  const busy = status === "submitted" || status === "streaming";

  return (
    <div className="chat">
      <section aria-label="Conversation">
        {messages.map((message) => (
          <article key={message.id} aria-label={`${message.role} message`}>
            {message.parts.map((part, i) => {
              if (part.type === "text") return <SafeMarkdown key={i} text={part.text} />;
              if (part.type === "source-url") return <a key={i} href={part.url}>{part.title ?? part.url}</a>;
              return null; // tool calls, reasoning, and files get their own components
            })}
          </article>
        ))}
      </section>
      <div role="status" className="visually-hidden">{status === "submitted" ? "Assistant is responding." : ""}</div>
      {error && (
        <div role="alert">
          The assistant is unavailable. <button type="button" onClick={() => { clearError(); void regenerate(); }}>Retry</button>
        </div>
      )}
      <form onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); if (draft.trim() && !busy) { void sendMessage({ text: draft }); setDraft(""); } }}>
        <label htmlFor="sdk-input">Message TaskFlow Assistant</label>
        <input id="sdk-input" value={draft} onChange={(e) => setDraft(e.target.value)} />
        {busy ? <button type="button" onClick={() => stop()}>Stop generating</button> : <button type="submit">Send</button>}
      </form>
    </div>
  );
}

The safe markdown component, the feedback buttons, and the accessibility rules apply unchanged. useChat also supports resuming an interrupted stream (resume: true with a server that stores streams), which pairs with the resumable patterns in conversation state and memory. How the SDK compares with other frameworks is the subject of AI frameworks and SDKs.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Model each turn as an explicit state machine and derive every button from the state.
  • Use fetch with a stream reader for POST-based chat; parse events with a buffer and a streaming TextDecoder.
  • Make Stop abort the request end to end, keep and label partial text, and treat a stream without a done event as an error.
  • Show the user's message optimistically and never lose its text on failure.
  • Batch token updates and memoize finished markdown blocks.
  • Render model output with react-markdown (or a sanitizer), never with dangerouslySetInnerHTML; allowlist image hosts and add a CSP.
  • Build source URLs on the server, validate citation markers in the client, and show snippets.
  • Attach model, prompt version, and trace ID to feedback on the server, and route thumbs-down cases into a review queue that feeds eval sets.
  • Announce state changes through one role="status" region; keep focus in the input; make Stop keyboard reachable.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The browser tab freezes during long answers. Detect: long tasks in the browser's performance profile while streaming; real-user interaction latency spikes on long chats. Cause: re-rendering and re-parsing the full message on every token. Fix: throttle updates, memoize completed blocks, and virtualize long transcripts.
  • An answer looks complete but stops mid-sentence. Detect: answers without a final done event in client telemetry; users report truncated answers after deploys. Cause: a proxy timeout or server restart closed the stream cleanly and the UI treated the end of the body as success. Fix: require the done event, mark anything else interrupted with Retry, and raise the proxy's streaming timeouts (see streaming responses end to end).
  • Users press Stop but token usage does not drop. Detect: provider usage for stopped messages matches full-length answers. Cause: the relay does not cancel the upstream request when the browser disconnects. Fix: propagate the abort to the provider call and record the stop in telemetry.
  • A security review finds a model-produced image leaking data. Detect: requests from users' browsers to unknown image hosts in CSP violation reports or proxy logs. Cause: markdown images rendered from any URL, combined with prompt injection in retrieved content. Fix: allowlist image hosts in the renderer, add img-src to the CSP, and add an injection test case to the eval set.
  • Screen reader users cannot use the assistant. Detect: accessibility audit or user reports of nonstop announcements. Cause: the streaming message is a live region, so every token is announced. Fix: remove the live region from the message, announce state changes through one status element, and test with screen readers.
  • Feedback volume is high but nothing improves. Detect: thousands of votes, no new eval cases, and no change in the Not helpful rate between prompt versions. Cause: votes stored without model, prompt version, or trace, and no review process. Fix: attach context on the server, sample thumbs-down votes into a review queue, and turn reviewed cases into eval set entries that run in CI.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Time to first token (TTFT): Delay between sending a request and the first streamed text appearing.
  • Server-sent events (SSE): A text format for a stream of named events over one HTTP response.
  • AbortController: The browser API that cancels a fetch and closes its connection.
  • Optimistic UI: Showing the result of a user action before the server confirms it, with rollback on failure.
  • Regenerate: Requesting a new answer to the same user message, replacing or paging past the previous one.
  • Improper output handling: Passing model output to a browser or system without validation or encoding (OWASP LLM05).
  • Image exfiltration: Leaking data through the URL of an image that the browser loads automatically.
  • Citation marker: A placeholder such as [S2] that the UI turns into a link to a retrieved source.
  • Explicit and implicit feedback: Ratings users give on purpose, and signals inferred from what they do.
  • Live region: An element whose changes assistive technologies announce without moving focus.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using EventSource for a POST chat endpoint, or parsing each network chunk as if it were one complete event.
  • Treating the end of the response body as success without a done event.
  • A Stop button that hides the stream but leaves the model generating.
  • Clearing the input before the request is safely stored, so a failure loses the user's text.
  • Rendering model markdown through innerHTML, or allowing images from any host.
  • Trusting URLs or citation IDs that the model wrote.
  • Storing a thumbs down without the model, prompt version, or trace that produced the answer.
  • Making the streaming message a live region.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does TaskFlow read the chat stream with fetch instead of EventSource, and why must the parser buffer across chunks?
  2. A model streams 40 tokens per second and the first token arrives after 800 ms. How long until a 1,000-token answer completes, and how long is the user waiting before they can start reading? (Answer: 0.8 + 1,000 / 40 = 25.8 seconds to finish; 0.8 seconds before reading starts.)
  3. What must happen on the server when the user presses Stop, and what should the UI do with the partial text?
  4. Describe the optimistic update for sending a message and what happens when the request never reaches the server.
  5. List three ways rendered model markdown can harm a user, and the defense against each.
  6. Why are source URLs built on the server, and what does the UI do with a citation marker whose ID was never retrieved?
  7. What context must a feedback record carry to be useful for evaluations, and why should the server add it?
  8. How do you make a streaming answer accessible without flooding a screen reader?

docs.title: Building AI Applications Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review conversation state and memory, frontend patterns for AI features, AI frameworks and SDKs, and realtime voice applications. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. Does a model remember earlier API requests?
docs.text: No. Each request is stateless: the model sees only what that request contains. Memory is state your application stores and sends back (history, summaries, saved facts), or state a provider holds for you through features such as previous_response_id or a conversation object.

docs.title: 2. Where can conversation history live, and which should own it?
docs.text: In your database (you resend it), with the provider (chained response IDs or conversation objects), or in a framework checkpointer. For any chat a user can see, export, or delete, your own database should be the source of truth; provider state can be an optimization stored next to it.

docs.title: 3. How do you compute the input budget for a request?
docs.text:
Take the model's context window from its documentation, subtract the output tokens you will request, and keep a safety margin:

input budget = (context window - reserved output) x (1 - margin)
(128,000 - 4,000) x 0.95 = 117,800 tokens

Without reserving output, a long prompt can leave no room for the answer.

docs.title: 4. In what order do you fill the budget?
docs.text: Fixed parts first (instructions, tool definitions, saved memories, the rolling summary, the new message), then pinned turns, then the newest turns until the next one would not fit. Everything older is evicted and folded into the summary rather than silently dropped.

docs.title: 5. Why must a tool call and its result be kept or evicted together?
docs.text: A tool result is only valid immediately after the assistant turn that requested it; sending one without the other is rejected by most APIs or confuses the model. Budgeting code groups each assistant turn with its tool results and treats the group as one unit.

docs.title: 6. Why does resending full history get expensive?
docs.text: Turn n carries roughly n turns of history, so total input grows with the square of the conversation length. At 500 tokens per exchange, 40 turns send 410,000 input tokens in total; capping history at 6,000 tokens sends about 207,000. Chaining with previous_response_id does not avoid this, because earlier input tokens are still billed.

docs.title: 7. What is a rolling summary, and what can go wrong with it?
docs.text: A stored summary of evicted turns, updated by a background job and saved with the last sequence number it covers (throughSeq). Risks are drift (details lost or distorted across re-summaries) and races (an older run overwriting a newer summary). Keep identifiers verbatim, keep raw turns searchable, and only accept a summary whose throughSeq is newer.

docs.title: 8. When is server-side compaction a good fit, and when is it not?
docs.text: It suits agent loops whose history no user reads and that stay on one provider: the provider shrinks the context automatically past a threshold. Its output is opaque, so you cannot show it, test it for drift, or move it to another provider; keep your own summary when the user owns the conversation.

docs.title: 9. What kinds of long-term memory are there, and where does each belong?
docs.text: Profile facts with a known shape (time zone, preferred view) belong in structured fields. Free-form facts ("prefers due dates on Fridays") suit a searchable store with embeddings. Episodic memory is past conversation summaries. Procedural memory, such as team conventions, belongs in instructions that people edit.

docs.title: 10. How do you keep one user's memories away from another user?
docs.text: Every memory document carries owner fields, the vector index declares them as filter fields, and every query adds the owner filter from the authenticated session in server code, never from the request body or model output. Add automated tests that query with one user's session and assert another user's data never appears.

docs.title: 11. Why is a stored memory a prompt-injection risk?
docs.text: Memories are user-influenced text that is replayed into future prompts. A planted "memory" such as an instruction to email data elsewhere persists across sessions. Insert memories as labeled data, filter what gets saved, show users their memories, and let them delete any of them.

docs.title: 12. Why store messages in their own collection rather than an array in the conversation document?
docs.text: A MongoDB document is limited to 16 mebibytes, which long chats with tool output can approach; every append would rewrite a growing document; and a streamed reply is easier to update as its own small document. A unique index on { conversationId, seq } keeps ordering safe.

docs.title: 13. How do you make a long AI job resumable?
docs.text: Return 202 Accepted with a job ID, make submission idempotent, claim jobs with a time-limited lease using one atomic update, save a checkpoint after each step (conditioned on still holding the lease), retry failed steps with backoff up to a limit, and let any worker claim a job whose lease expired. Steps run at least once, so make them safe to repeat.

docs.title: 14. Why does streaming matter if the total time is the same?
docs.text: Perceived speed. A 600-token answer at about 50 tokens per second takes 12 seconds; if the first words arrive after a second, the user reads for 11 of those seconds instead of watching a spinner.

docs.title: 15. Why use fetch with a stream reader instead of EventSource for chat?
docs.text: EventSource only sends GET requests without a body or custom headers, but a chat turn is a POST with a JSON body. fetch exposes the response body as a ReadableStream you can read and parse yourself.

docs.title: 16. What must an SSE parser handle?
docs.text: Network chunks split events, and even multi-byte characters, at arbitrary points. Buffer decoded text until a blank line ends an event, decode bytes with TextDecoder in streaming mode, skip comment lines used as keep-alives, and join multi-line data fields.

docs.title: 17. What does a correct Stop button do?
docs.text: It aborts the request with an AbortController, which closes the connection; the backend must notice and cancel the provider request, or generation and billing continue. The UI keeps the partial text and labels it incomplete, because the user often has what they needed.

docs.title: 18. How should regenerate work?
docs.text: Drop or page past the last answer and request a new one for the same user message, with a flag so the server does not store the user message twice. Record which answer the user kept; a regeneration is an implicit thumbs down on the first.

docs.title: 19. What is optimistic UI in a chat, and what must never be optimistic?
docs.text: Showing the user's message immediately, marked as sending, before the server confirms it. If the request never reaches the server, the message stays visible as "not sent" with its text intact for retry. Assistant content is never faked.

docs.title: 20. Why treat a stream that ends without a done event as an error?
docs.text: A proxy timeout or deploy can close the connection cleanly, and the body simply ends. Without a terminal event the answer may be truncated, so the UI marks it interrupted and offers retry instead of presenting it as complete.

docs.title: 21. How do you keep long streamed answers from freezing the page?
docs.text: Batch updates (apply text every 30 to 50 ms; the AI SDK's useChat has a throttle option), memoize finished markdown blocks so only the growing one re-renders, and use a streaming-aware renderer or plain text while streaming to avoid flicker from half-written syntax.

docs.title: 22. Why is rendering model markdown a security issue?
docs.text: Model output is untrusted; it can carry instructions planted in retrieved content. Raw HTML becomes script execution, javascript: links run code, and an image URL can carry private data to another server as soon as the browser loads it (OWASP LLM05, improper output handling).

docs.title: 23. How does react-markdown keep output safe, and what do you add?
docs.text: It builds React elements instead of setting innerHTML, does not render raw HTML unless you add a raw-HTML plugin (skipHtml drops it entirely), and its default urlTransform removes unsafe protocols. You add component overrides: links with rel="noopener noreferrer nofollow" and images only from hosts you control, plus a Content-Security-Policy as a second layer.

docs.title: 24. How should a citations UI work?
docs.text: The server sends sources as structured data with server-built URLs; the model cites with markers such as [S2]; the UI turns known markers into numbered links to a sources panel with snippets, and removes and counts markers whose IDs were never retrieved, because those citations are invented.

docs.title: 25. What makes thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback useful for evaluation?
docs.text: Context attached by the server: the model ID, prompt version, and trace ID of the exact answer. Votes are idempotent per user and message. Sampled thumbs-down cases go to a review queue, and reviewed cases, with personal data removed, become eval set entries that run in CI.

docs.title: 26. How do you make a streaming chat accessible?
docs.text: Do not make the growing message a live region. Announce state changes ("Assistant is responding", "Response complete") through one role="status" element, set aria-busy on the streaming message, keep focus in the input, make Stop reachable by keyboard, give icon buttons accessible names, and respect reduced motion.

docs.title: 27. What layers sit between your code and a model provider?
docs.text: Provider HTTP APIs; official provider SDKs; unified model APIs such as the Vercel AI SDK; orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph, LangChain, and LlamaIndex; and agent SDKs that run the tool loop. Each layer up saves code and adds abstraction you must understand when debugging.

docs.title: 28. What do official provider SDKs give you, and what do they not?
docs.text: Typed requests and responses, streaming helpers, structured-output helpers, built-in retries (the openai client retries twice by default), and day-one access to new features. They do not give a common shape: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google differ in message formats, tool definitions, and events.

docs.title: 29. What are the parts of the Vercel AI SDK?
docs.text: AI SDK Core (generateText, streamText, tool(), Output.object(), stopWhen) gives one call shape; provider packages adapt it to each API; AI SDK UI (useChat) consumes its streaming protocol. Provider-specific settings pass through providerOptions.

docs.title: 30. What does LangGraph add over a plain agent loop?
docs.text: A graph runtime with checkpointers that save state after each step: durable execution (resume after a crash), human-in-the-loop interrupts, and inspectable history per thread. LangChain v1's createAgent is built on it. Use it when the workflow itself must survive restarts or wait for a person.

docs.title: 31. When is LlamaIndex a good choice?
docs.text: When retrieval over many document types is the core of the product: loaders, chunking, indexes, and query engines come ready-made. As of November 2026 its Python package is the most active; the TypeScript @llamaindex/* packages are marked deprecated on npm, which matters for a Node backend.

docs.title: 32. What do agent SDKs such as the OpenAI Agents SDK provide?
docs.text: The agent loop (call the model, run requested tools, feed results back, repeat), handoffs between agents, guardrails, sessions, and tracing. The OpenAI Agents SDK was still pre-1.0 in November 2026, so expect breaking changes; in Node.js it traces runs by default.

docs.title: 33. Where does framework lock-in actually live?
docs.text: In what the library owns: stored message and checkpoint formats, prompts assembled inside library classes, tool definitions written against its helpers, tracing wired to one vendor, and provider features exposed only partially. Swapping imports is the easy part.

docs.title: 34. How do you limit lock-in?
docs.text: Put AI behind a small interface your team owns (for example parseTask() and answerQuestion()), keep prompts and zod schemas in your repository, keep conversations in your database, and run evals against the interface. Adapters for an SDK or framework then become replaceable.

docs.title: 35. Why cap agent loops, and how?
docs.text: A confused model can call tools repeatedly, burning tokens and time. Set a step or turn limit (stopWhen: isStepCount(5) in the AI SDK, maxTurns in the OpenAI Agents SDK), return clear tool errors, and alert on steps per run.

docs.title: 36. Why can adding a framework package break your types?
docs.text: Frameworks bring their own versions of shared libraries. In November 2026 the LangGraph MongoDB checkpointer depended on the 6.x MongoDB driver, so an app on driver 7 got two copies and a "MongoClient is not assignable" error. Check npm ls <package> and align versions.

docs.title: 37. What maturity signals do you check before adopting a framework?
docs.text: Release activity and recency, 1.0 status and how often majors arrive, the language it is primarily developed in, the size of its dependency tree, whether successors or merges have been announced, and how easy it is to see the exact requests it sends.

docs.title: 38. What does Anthropic recommend about frameworks?
docs.text: To start with the LLM APIs directly, since many patterns take a few lines of code, and, when using a framework, to understand the underlying code, because abstractions can obscure prompts and responses and make debugging harder.

docs.title: 39. Compare a cascaded pipeline with a speech-to-speech model.
docs.text: Cascaded (speech-to-text, a text model, text-to-speech) lets you choose each component and gives text to log and moderate, but adds latency per hop and loses tone of voice, and is usually cheaper per minute. Speech-to-speech is faster and more natural, handles interruptions in the session, but costs more and is harder to inspect.

docs.title: 40. When do you use WebRTC, WebSocket, or SIP?
docs.text: WebRTC for browsers and mobile clients: UDP media with jitter buffering and echo cancellation. WebSocket between your server and the model, or for phone media bridges. SIP when a telephony provider routes calls directly to a model API that accepts them.

docs.title: 41. How do you keep the provider key out of the browser in a voice app?
docs.text: Create the session on the server: the browser posts its WebRTC offer, the server calls the provider with the real key and returns the answer (the unified interface), or the server mints a short-lived client secret the browser uses once.

docs.title: 42. What are the audio format numbers to remember?
docs.text: G.711 phone audio is 8,000 one-byte samples per second, so a 20 ms frame is 160 bytes. 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz is 32,000 bytes per second, about 42,700 as base64. The Google Live API takes 16 kHz PCM in and sends 24 kHz out; the OpenAI Realtime API also accepts audio/pcmu and audio/pcma.

docs.title: 43. What dominates voice latency, and what do you do about it?
docs.text: Often the end-of-turn wait. Tune turn detection first, then stream every stage, start speech on the first sentence, keep tools off the critical path with a spoken acknowledgment, deploy close to users and the provider, and keep the session prefix stable for caching.

docs.title: 44. How does silence-based turn detection trade speed for accuracy?
docs.text: The turn ends after silence_duration_ms of quiet, and that time is added to every reply: with 500 ms, a user who stops at 200 ms is answered no earlier than 700 ms. Too short cuts people off mid-thought; semantic turn detection waits longer when the words sound incomplete.

docs.title: 45. What are the steps of barge-in handling?
docs.text: Detect the user's speech, stop playback and discard queued audio immediately, truncate the stored reply to what was actually heard (conversation.item.truncate with audio_end_ms), and cancel the rest of the generation.

docs.title: 46. Why truncate the history after an interruption?
docs.text: Otherwise the conversation records the full reply, and the model's next answer assumes the user heard parts they never did, such as a confirmation question.

docs.title: 47. What causes false barge-ins, and how do you reduce them?
docs.text: Echo of the assistant's own voice into the microphone, and backchannels such as "uh-huh" or coughs. Keep echo cancellation on, prefer headsets, raise the VAD threshold, and require a minimum speech duration.

docs.title: 48. What are the two generic ways to connect phone calls to a voice model?
docs.text: Media streaming, where the telephony provider sends audio frames over a WebSocket to your server, which bridges them to the model with full control; and SIP, where calls go to a model API that accepts SIP and your server accepts, configures, transfers, and ends them through webhooks and API calls.

docs.title: 49. What obligations does a phone assistant carry?
docs.text: Disclosing that it is an AI, consent for recording or transcription as the caller's jurisdiction requires, transfer to a person, keypad input, and never handling emergency calls with a bot; plus maximum call lengths and idle timeouts.

docs.title: 50. Why do later minutes of a voice call cost more?
docs.text: The whole conversation is processed for every reply, so input grows each turn. In the OpenAI Realtime API, user audio counts as 1 token per 100 ms and assistant audio as 1 per 50 ms; a 30-turn call with 5-second user and 8-second assistant turns sends about 97,650 input tokens against 4,800 output tokens.

docs.title: 51. Long TaskFlow chats start failing with "context length exceeded". What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the token count of failing requests and how the budget is computed for the model in use.

How to confirm: the failures cluster on long conversations or after a large paste, and the configured window does not match the current model.

Likely causes and fixes: no budget, a budget for a different model, or one oversized message. Read the window per model from configuration, reserve output tokens, count exactly near the limit, and truncate oversized messages. See conversation state and memory.

docs.title: 52. The assistant forgets a decision made earlier in a long chat. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the decision is in the stored summary or only in raw messages.

How to confirm: the turn was evicted, and the summary either dropped it or was never updated (summarizer lag).

Likely causes and fixes: summary drift or a stalled summarizer. Keep decisions in a fixed summary section, alert on summarizer lag, and add long-chat recall cases to the eval set. See conversation state and memory.

docs.title: 53. A user reports seeing another user's saved preference. How do you respond?
docs.text:
What to check first: the code path that read memories, and whether the owner filter came from the session.

How to confirm: reproduce with two test users; inspect the vector index for filter fields and the query for the owner filter.

Likely causes and fixes: a missing filter field or owner condition, or an owner ID taken from the request. Treat it as a security incident, fix the index and the repository layer, and add cross-user tests. See conversation state and memory.

docs.title: 54. Meeting summaries are generated twice and users get duplicate notifications. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: job documents with two completion writes and the lease duration compared with the slowest model call.

How to confirm: logs show two workers processing the same job ID after a lease expired mid-step.

Likely causes and fixes: writes not conditioned on the lease owner, or no lease renewal. Condition every write on leaseOwner, renew after each step, and make the final write idempotent. See conversation state and memory.

docs.title: 55. Answers sometimes look complete but end mid-sentence. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: client telemetry for streams without a done event.

How to confirm: truncations line up with deploys or proxy timeouts.

Likely causes and fixes: the UI treats the end of the body as success. Require the terminal event, mark other endings as interrupted with Retry, and raise the proxy's streaming timeouts. See frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: 56. Users press Stop, but token usage does not drop. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: provider usage for messages stored as stopped.

How to confirm: stopped messages show full-length output token counts.

Likely causes and fixes: the relay does not cancel the upstream request when the browser disconnects. Propagate the abort to the provider call and record stops in telemetry. See frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: 57. A security review finds that an assistant answer made the browser load an image from an unknown host. What now?
docs.text:
What to check first: CSP violation reports and proxy logs for image requests, and how markdown images are rendered.

How to confirm: a retrieved document contains injected text telling the model to emit an image URL with data in the query string.

Likely causes and fixes: images rendered from any host. Allowlist image hosts in the renderer, add img-src to the CSP, and add the injection case to the eval set. See frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: 58. Thousands of thumbs-down votes, but quality never improves. What is missing?
docs.text:
What to check first: what a feedback record contains and whether anyone reviews it.

How to confirm: records lack model, prompt version, or trace ID, and no eval cases were added from feedback.

Likely causes and fixes: feedback is collected but not connected. Attach context on the server, sample thumbs-down votes into a review queue, and turn reviewed cases into eval set entries that run in CI. See frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: 59. After a minor framework upgrade, answers change though prompts did not. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: the dependency diff and the outgoing requests before and after.

How to confirm: the framework changed a default prompt, parsing rule, or retry setting.

Likely causes and fixes: unpinned versions and no upgrade gate. Pin versions, log requests at your adapter boundary, and require the eval suite to pass on upgrade branches. See AI frameworks and SDKs.

docs.title: 60. An agent's cost per request spikes overnight. What do you look at?
docs.text:
What to check first: steps per run and token usage per step in traces.

How to confirm: some runs show dozens of repeated tool calls.

Likely causes and fixes: no step limit, or a tool error the model keeps retrying. Set stopWhen or maxTurns, return clear tool errors, and alert on steps per run. See AI frameworks and SDKs.

docs.title: 61. Adding a checkpointer package produces "MongoClient is not assignable to MongoClient". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: npm ls mongodb.

How to confirm: two driver versions are installed, one nested under the framework package.

Likely causes and fixes: the package depends on a different major version of the driver. Align the app's driver with the package, or keep the framework's connection separate until it supports your version. See AI frameworks and SDKs.

docs.title: 62. In the browser voice mode, the assistant keeps interrupting itself. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: speech_started events that arrive while the assistant is speaking, and the microphone constraints.

How to confirm: recordings show the assistant's own voice in the input, with no user speech.

Likely causes and fixes: echo without echo cancellation. Keep echoCancellation on, suggest headsets, raise the VAD threshold, and require a minimum speech duration. See realtime voice applications.

docs.title: 63. Phone callers hear fast, garbled speech, while the browser sounds fine. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the declared audio formats on both sides of the phone bridge.

How to confirm: a known test tone played through the bridge comes out at the wrong pitch or speed.

Likely causes and fixes: a sample-rate or encoding mismatch, such as 24 kHz PCM sent to an 8 kHz mu-law line. Declare formats explicitly, use G.711 end to end where the API supports it, otherwise resample with filtering, and keep a tone test in CI. See realtime voice applications.

docs.title: 64. Voice replies take over two seconds. Where does the time go?
docs.text:
What to check first: per-stage timings from the end of the user's speech to the first audio played.

How to confirm: the end-of-turn wait or a synchronous tool call takes most of the time.

Likely causes and fixes: a conservative silence setting, a tool on the critical path, or a distant region. Tune turn detection (or use semantic detection), speak an acknowledgment while tools run, and move the voice server closer to users and the provider. See realtime voice applications.
