docs.title: Realtime Voice Applications
docs.text:
TaskFlow's voice mode lets a user say "add a task to send the Q3 deck by Friday" in the web app, or call a phone number and ask what is due today. Voice looks like chat with a microphone, but it is a different engineering problem: audio streams both ways at the same time, replies must start within about a second, people interrupt, phones carry low-quality audio, and every extra minute of conversation costs more than the last.

This lesson covers realtime speech APIs over WebRTC and WebSocket, the choice between a cascaded speech-to-text, text model, and text-to-speech pipeline and a single speech-to-speech model, the latency budget, turn-taking and barge-in, a generic overview of connecting phone calls, and the relative costs. Speech recognition and synthesis as model tasks are introduced in speech and multimodal AI.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Silence reads as failure. In a chat window a spinner is tolerable; on a call, two seconds of silence makes people say "hello?" and talk over the reply. Every stage of the pipeline has to stream.
  • Interruptions are normal. People cut in to correct a date or skip a long answer. A system that keeps talking, or that later assumes the caller heard the whole reply, feels broken.
  • Audio fails in new ways. Echo makes the assistant interrupt itself, background noise starts false turns, and a sample-rate mismatch turns speech into noise.
  • Cost grows with time, not just words. Realtime speech APIs bill audio by duration, and the conversation so far is processed again for every reply, so the tenth minute of a call costs more than the first.
  • Phones bring obligations. Disclosing that the caller is talking to an AI, getting consent before recording, transferring to a person, and never handling emergency calls with a bot are product requirements, not extras.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI Realtime API. The Realtime API guide documents WebRTC for browsers and mobile apps and WebSocket for server-to-server use; a separate guide covers SIP for telephony. Its WebRTC guide describes a "unified interface", where your server creates the session from the browser's connection offer, and ephemeral keys as the alternative.
  • Interruptions, documented. OpenAI's realtime conversations guide says that when the user interrupts, the client should stop playback immediately, discard queued audio, and send conversation.item.truncate with the number of milliseconds the user actually heard.
  • Google Live API. The Live API overview specifies 16-bit PCM input at 16 kHz and output at 24 kHz over a stateful WebSocket, and recommends ephemeral tokens for client connections; its session management guide limits audio-only sessions to 15 minutes without context compression and offers session resumption.
  • Cost behavior. OpenAI's voice cost optimization guide states that user audio counts as 1 token per 100 ms and assistant audio as 1 token per 50 ms, and that the entire conversation is sent to the model for each response, so later turns cost more.
  • Open-source pipelines. Pipecat describes itself as an open source ecosystem for building voice and multimodal AI agents, the kind of framework teams use to assemble cascaded pipelines from interchangeable speech and model providers.

Popular tools and providers: the OpenAI Realtime API, the Google Live API, Pipecat, LiveKit Agents, the AI SDK's experimental realtime hook, streaming speech-to-text and text-to-speech services from cloud and speech vendors, browser WebRTC, and telephony providers that offer phone numbers, SIP trunks, and media streaming.

docs.title: Two architectures
docs.text:
Cascaded (STT, text model, TTS) Speech-to-speech (realtime model) Latency Sum of three streaming stages Lowest: one model hears and speaks Component choice Any STT, any text model, any voice One provider's model and voices Understanding tone Lost: the model sees a transcript Kept: hesitation and emphasis reach the model Inspecting and moderating Easy: text between every stage Harder: work from transcripts of audio Interruptions You coordinate STT, model, and TTS Built in to the session Relative cost Usually lower per minute; text tokens are cheap Higher: audio tokens cost more than text

Many products mix them: speech-to-speech for the conversation, plus a separate transcription stream for logs, captions, and moderation.

docs.title: Transports: WebRTC, WebSocket, and SIP
docs.text:
Transport Typical use Audio What you handle WebRTC Browser and mobile clients Media tracks; the browser handles codecs, jitter, and echo cancellation Session creation on your server, a data channel for events WebSocket Your server to the model Base64 audio chunks inside JSON events Buffering, playback position, interruptions, reconnects SIP Phone calls routed to the model provider Telephony codecs such as G.711 Accepting, transferring, and ending calls from your server

WebRTC runs over UDP with built-in jitter buffering and packet-loss handling, which suits unreliable mobile networks. A WebSocket runs over TCP, so one lost packet delays everything behind it; that is fine between data centers and poor on a phone's cellular connection. Whatever the transport, the provider API key stays on your server: either the server creates the session from the browser's offer (the unified interface used in the examples), or it mints a short-lived client secret that the browser uses once.

docs.title: Audio formats and the numbers behind them
docs.text:
Phone networks carry G.711 audio: 8,000 samples per second, one byte per sample (mu-law in North America and Japan, A-law elsewhere), so one second is 8,000 bytes and a 20 ms frame is 160 bytes. Speech models usually want 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz or 24 kHz: one second at 16 kHz is 32,000 bytes, and base64 inside JSON adds a third, about 42,700 bytes per second. Some realtime APIs accept G.711 directly (audio/pcmu and audio/pcma in the OpenAI Realtime API), which avoids transcoding phone audio; others need it decoded and resampled, in both directions.

Mismatched rates are a classic bug: 24 kHz audio played as 16 kHz sounds slow and deep, and 8 kHz audio sent as 16 kHz sounds fast and garbled.

docs.title: The latency budget
docs.text:
Measure from the moment the user stops talking to the moment they hear the first syllable of the reply. The values in the diagram are an illustration, not a benchmark, but the shape is typical: the wait for the end of the turn is often the largest single item, so tuning turn detection pays off before buying a faster model. Other levers:

  • Stream every stage. Feed partial transcripts forward, start speech synthesis on the first sentence of the reply, and play audio as it arrives.
  • Keep tools off the critical path. If a lookup takes a second, have the assistant say a short acknowledgment ("Let me check your tasks") while the tool runs.
  • Make the first sentence short. Instruct the model to lead with the answer; a long preamble delays the useful part.
  • Stay close and warm. Run the voice server near your users and the provider region, and reuse connections.
  • Keep the session prefix stable. Changing instructions or tools in the middle of a session lowers prompt-cache hits, which costs latency and money.

General latency techniques are covered in latency optimization.

docs.title: Turn-taking
docs.text:
Turn detection decides when the user has finished. Three approaches:

  • Voice activity detection (VAD): detect speech in the audio and end the turn after a set amount of silence. Realtime APIs offer it on the server, for example server_vad with silence_duration_ms in the OpenAI Realtime API. A short silence setting replies faster but cuts people off when they pause to think; a long one feels sluggish.
  • Semantic turn detection: a model judges whether the utterance sounds complete, so "my task is to..." waits longer than "add a task for Friday." The OpenAI Realtime API calls this semantic_vad, with an eagerness setting from low to high.
  • Push-to-talk: the user holds a button. It has no false turns and suits noisy places, at the cost of a less natural feel.

The energy-based detector in the examples shows the cost of the silence setting in its real test output: the user stops talking at 200 ms, and with a 500 ms silence threshold the turn ends at 700 ms. Every millisecond of that threshold is added to every reply.

docs.title: Barge-in
docs.text:
Barge-in means the user can interrupt the assistant. Handling it well takes four steps, in this order:

  1. Detect the user's speech while the assistant is talking (the speech_started event in server VAD).
  2. Stop the audio now. Clear the playback queue on the device or phone line; every queued millisecond the user still hears makes the system feel deaf.
  3. Correct the history. Tell the model how much of its reply was actually heard (conversation.item.truncate with audio_end_ms), so the stored reply ends there and the next answer does not refer to things the user never heard.
  4. Cancel generation of the rest of the reply. With server_vad, the interrupt_response setting lets the server cancel automatically.

Over WebRTC the provider knows what was played and handles much of this; over WebSocket and phone bridges, your server must track playback, which is what PlaybackTracker in the examples does. Two side problems need care: echo, where the assistant's own voice leaks into the microphone and triggers barge-in (keep the browser's echo cancellation on and use headsets where you can), and backchannels, where "uh-huh" or a cough interrupts a reply that should continue (raise the VAD threshold or require a minimum speech duration).

docs.title: Tools in a voice session
docs.text: A voice assistant uses the same tools as the chat agent (create task, list tasks due), with voice-specific rules: confirm before any write ("Create 'Send the Q3 deck', due Friday?"), read results as short sentences rather than lists, and speak dates and IDs naturally. Run tools on the server: the session can be created by the server, and a server can attach to the same call by its ID over WebSocket to execute tools and watch events, so the browser never holds business logic or credentials. Tool safety is covered in tool calling in practice.

docs.title: Connecting phone calls
docs.text:
A phone call reaches your application through a telephony provider that owns the phone numbers and the connection to the public network. There are two generic integration patterns:

  • Media streaming. The provider opens a WebSocket to your voice server and sends the call's audio as small frames (typically 20 ms of 8 kHz G.711), and plays audio frames you send back. Your server bridges them to the model and has full control: logging, tools, and custom interruption logic. Each provider has its own message format; the example uses a neutral one.
  • SIP. The provider routes the call over a SIP trunk to a model API that accepts SIP directly. The API notifies your server with a webhook, your server accepts the call and configures the session, and it can later transfer the call (SIP REFER) or hang up. Less audio plumbing, less control of individual frames.

Both patterns need the same call control: transfer to a person on request or when the assistant is stuck, keypad (DTMF) input for numbers and menus, an AI disclosure and, where recording or transcription happens, consent that follows the laws where the caller is. Emergency numbers must never reach a bot. Calls also outlive sessions: provider sessions have duration limits (15 minutes for audio-only Live API sessions without compression), so long calls need session resumption or a planned handover.

docs.title: Relative costs
docs.text:
• Speech-to-speech audio costs more than text. A cascaded pipeline pays for transcription by duration, the text model by (cheaper) text tokens, and synthesis by characters; for long calls it is usually the cheaper option, and the slower one.
  • The assistant's voice is denser. In the OpenAI Realtime API, assistant audio counts as 1 token per 50 ms, twice the rate of user audio (1 token per 100 ms).
  • Every reply re-reads the conversation. Input therefore grows with each turn, and the tenth minute costs more than the first. A 30-turn call where the user speaks 5 seconds (50 tokens) and the assistant 8 seconds (160 tokens) per turn adds 210 tokens of history per turn; summing 210 x (1 + 2 + ... + 30) = 97,650 input tokens across the call, against 30 x 160 = 4,800 output tokens. Input dominates, so cached prefixes, shorter sessions, and truncating or summarizing old turns matter more than shorter answers.
  • Silence is mostly free with server VAD, which filters empty input audio, but streaming silence into a manually managed buffer is not.
  • Phones add their own charges: per-minute telephony costs on top of model costs, so a stuck call that never hangs up is expensive. Set maximum call durations and idle timeouts.

Cost control in general is covered in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Choice Use when Avoid when A voice interface at all Hands-busy or eyes-busy use, phone support, accessibility Dense information users must scan or compare: show it on screen Speech-to-speech Natural conversation where speed matters most You must inspect or moderate text before it is spoken, or use a specific voice vendor Cascaded pipeline Component choice, strict moderation, long calls on a budget Interruption-heavy conversation where every 300 ms matters WebRTC Browser and mobile clients Server-to-server bridges WebSocket Your server to the model, phone media bridges End-user devices on lossy networks SIP to the model provider Simple phone agents with standard call control You need frame-level control or a different model per call stage Semantic turn detection Users who pause mid-sentence (dictating tasks) Very short commands where fixed silence is fine

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The examples type-check against openai 7.57, @google/genai 3.3, and ws; the audio utilities ran under test, with real output shown. Model IDs and voices come from configuration: choose a realtime-capable model from the provider's current model list.

docs.title: Create a browser voice session on the server
docs.text:
// src/voice/voiceRoutes.ts
import express, { Router } from "express";
import OpenAI from "openai";

const client = new OpenAI(); // the real API key never leaves the server

const INSTRUCTIONS = `You are TaskFlow's voice assistant. Keep answers to one or two short
sentences. Read dates as words. Ask before creating or changing a task.`;

export function voiceRoutes() {
  const router = Router();

  // The browser posts its WebRTC SDP offer; we create the session and return the answer.
  router.post("/voice/session", express.text({ type: "application/sdp", limit: "20kb" }), async (req, res) => {
    const answer = await client.realtime.calls.create({
      sdp: req.body as string,
      session: {
        type: "realtime",
        model: process.env.REALTIME_MODEL!, // a realtime model ID from the provider's model list
        instructions: INSTRUCTIONS,
        audio: {
          input: {
            turn_detection: { type: "semantic_vad", eagerness: "auto" },
            transcription: { model: process.env.TRANSCRIPTION_MODEL }, // enables user transcript events
          },
          output: { voice: process.env.REALTIME_VOICE },
        },
      },
    });
    res.type("application/sdp").send(await answer.text());
  });

  return router;
}

Put this route behind the same authentication and per-user rate limits as the chat API: each session is a billable, long-lived connection.

docs.title: Connect from the browser with WebRTC
docs.text:
// src/web/voice/voiceClient.ts
export interface VoiceCallbacks {
  onUserSpeaking(): void;
  onTranscript(role: "user" | "assistant", text: string): void;
  onEnded(reason: string): void;
}

export async function startVoiceSession(cb: VoiceCallbacks) {
  // Echo cancellation keeps the assistant's own voice from triggering barge-in.
  const mic = await navigator.mediaDevices.getUserMedia({
    audio: { echoCancellation: true, noiseSuppression: true, autoGainControl: true },
  });

  const pc = new RTCPeerConnection();
  const speaker = new Audio();
  speaker.autoplay = true;
  pc.ontrack = (e) => { speaker.srcObject = e.streams[0]; };
  pc.addTrack(mic.getTracks()[0], mic);

  const events = pc.createDataChannel("oai-events"); // JSON events in both directions
  events.onmessage = (msg) => {
    const event = JSON.parse(msg.data);
    if (event.type === "input_audio_buffer.speech_started") cb.onUserSpeaking();
    if (event.type === "conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.completed") cb.onTranscript("user", event.transcript);
    if (event.type === "response.output_audio_transcript.done") cb.onTranscript("assistant", event.transcript);
    if (event.type === "error") cb.onEnded(event.error?.message ?? "error");
  };

  const offer = await pc.createOffer();
  await pc.setLocalDescription(offer);
  const res = await fetch("/api/voice/session", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/sdp" },
    body: offer.sdp,
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Voice session failed: ${res.status}`);
  await pc.setRemoteDescription({ type: "answer", sdp: await res.text() });

  pc.onconnectionstatechange = () => {
    if (pc.connectionState === "failed" || pc.connectionState === "disconnected") cb.onEnded(pc.connectionState);
  };

  return {
    // Push-to-talk style manual interruption, for example a Stop button.
    interrupt: () => events.send(JSON.stringify({ type: "response.cancel" })),
    hangUp: () => { mic.getTracks().forEach((t) => t.stop()); pc.close(); },
  };
}

The transcripts feed the visible conversation and accessibility captions, and the UI shows a clear listening, thinking, and speaking state. Browsers only grant microphone access on secure (HTTPS) pages after a user gesture, so start the session from a button.

docs.title: Track turns and playback
docs.text:
These two small classes make turn-taking and barge-in concrete. The VAD is deliberately simple; production systems use the provider's VAD or a model-based detector.

// src/voice/turns.ts

// A minimal energy-based end-of-turn detector, to show what server VAD settings
// mean. Production systems use model-based VAD or semantic turn detection.
export class EnergyVad {
  private speaking = false;
  private silentMs = 0;

  constructor(private readonly threshold = 500,        // RMS level that counts as speech
              private readonly silenceDurationMs = 500) {} // pause that ends a turn

  // Feed one frame; returns an event when the user starts or stops speaking.
  push(frame: Int16Array, frameMs: number): "speech_started" | "speech_stopped" | null {
    let sum = 0;
    for (const s of frame) sum += s * s;
    const rms = Math.sqrt(sum / frame.length);
    if (rms >= this.threshold) {
      this.silentMs = 0;
      if (!this.speaking) { this.speaking = true; return "speech_started"; }
      return null;
    }
    if (!this.speaking) return null;
    this.silentMs += frameMs;
    if (this.silentMs >= this.silenceDurationMs) { this.speaking = false; return "speech_stopped"; }
    return null;
  }
}

// Tracks how much of each assistant reply the caller has actually heard, so an
// interruption can cut the stored reply at that point (barge-in).
export class PlaybackTracker {
  private itemId: string | null = null;
  private sentMs = 0;
  private playedMs = 0;

  audioSent(itemId: string, ms: number) {
    if (itemId !== this.itemId) { this.itemId = itemId; this.sentMs = 0; this.playedMs = 0; }
    this.sentMs += ms;
  }

  // Called when the playback side confirms progress (for example a mark that came back).
  played(ms: number) { this.playedMs = Math.min(this.sentMs, this.playedMs + ms); }

  // On interruption: what to keep, and how much queued audio to discard.
  interrupt() {
    if (!this.itemId) return null;
    const result = { itemId: this.itemId, audioEndMs: this.playedMs, discardedMs: this.sentMs - this.playedMs };
    this.itemId = null;
    return result;
  }
}

Real test output: ten loud 20 ms frames followed by silence, and a reply interrupted after 640 ms of 1,000 ms sent:

[ 'speech_started@20ms', 'speech_stopped@700ms' ]
{ itemId: 'item_1', audioEndMs: 640, discardedMs: 360 }

docs.title: Bridge phone calls over a media WebSocket
docs.text:
The telephony provider connects to this server for each call. Because the OpenAI Realtime API accepts mu-law in both directions, no transcoding is needed:

// src/voice/phoneBridge.ts
import type { WebSocket } from "ws";
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { OpenAIRealtimeWS } from "openai/realtime/ws";
import { PlaybackTracker } from "./turns.js";

// Messages on the telephony media WebSocket. Every provider names these
// differently; this neutral shape stands in for yours.
type PhoneIn =
  | { type: "start"; callId: string }
  | { type: "audio"; payload: string }   // base64 mu-law, 8 kHz, 20 ms
  | { type: "played"; ms: number }       // playback progress reported by the phone side
  | { type: "stop" };
type PhoneOut = { type: "audio"; payload: string } | { type: "clear" };

const client = new OpenAI();
const FRAME_MS = 20;

export function bridgeCall(phone: WebSocket) {
  const model = new OpenAIRealtimeWS({ model: process.env.REALTIME_MODEL! }, client);
  const playback = new PlaybackTracker();
  const toPhone = (m: PhoneOut) => phone.send(JSON.stringify(m));

  model.socket.on("open", () => {
    model.send({
      type: "session.update",
      session: {
        type: "realtime",
        instructions: "You are TaskFlow's phone assistant. Be brief. Offer a transfer to a person.",
        audio: {
          // Phone audio in and out: no transcoding needed with mu-law on both sides.
          input: { format: { type: "audio/pcmu" }, turn_detection: { type: "server_vad", silence_duration_ms: 500 } },
          output: { format: { type: "audio/pcmu" }, voice: process.env.REALTIME_VOICE },
        },
      },
    });
  });

  model.on("response.output_audio.delta", (e) => {
    toPhone({ type: "audio", payload: e.delta });
    playback.audioSent(e.item_id, (Buffer.from(e.delta, "base64").length / 8_000) * 1_000);
  });

  // Barge-in: the caller started talking over the assistant.
  model.on("input_audio_buffer.speech_started", () => {
    const cut = playback.interrupt();
    if (!cut) return;
    toPhone({ type: "clear" }); // drop audio queued on the phone side
    model.send({ type: "conversation.item.truncate", item_id: cut.itemId, content_index: 0, audio_end_ms: cut.audioEndMs });
  });

  model.on("error", (err) => console.error(JSON.stringify({ msg: "realtime error", error: err.message })));

  phone.on("message", (raw) => {
    const msg = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) as PhoneIn;
    if (msg.type === "audio") model.send({ type: "input_audio_buffer.append", audio: msg.payload });
    else if (msg.type === "played") playback.played(msg.ms);
    else if (msg.type === "stop") model.close();
  });
  phone.on("close", () => model.close());
  return { frameMs: FRAME_MS };
}

The duration of each chunk comes straight from the format: mu-law is 8,000 bytes per second, so bytes divided by 8 is milliseconds. A production bridge also records call events with the call ID, enforces a maximum call length, and implements the transfer tool through the provider's call control API.

docs.title: Convert phone audio for PCM-only models
docs.text:
When the model needs 16-bit PCM (the Live API wants 16 kHz in and sends 24 kHz out), the bridge decodes mu-law and resamples:

// src/voice/audio.ts
// Phone audio is G.711 mu-law: 8,000 samples per second, 1 byte per sample.
// Many speech models want 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz or 24 kHz instead.

const BIAS = 0x84;
const CLIP = 32_635;

export function muLawDecode(bytes: Uint8Array): Int16Array {
  const out = new Int16Array(bytes.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < bytes.length; i++) {
    const u = ~bytes[i] & 0xff;
    const exponent = (u >> 4) & 0x07;
    const sample = ((((u & 0x0f) << 3) + BIAS) << exponent) - BIAS;
    out[i] = u & 0x80 ? -sample : sample;
  }
  return out;
}

export function muLawEncode(samples: Int16Array): Uint8Array {
  const out = new Uint8Array(samples.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < samples.length; i++) {
    let s = samples[i];
    const sign = s < 0 ? 0x80 : 0;
    if (s < 0) s = -s;
    s = Math.min(s, CLIP) + BIAS;
    let exponent = 7;
    for (let mask = 0x4000; (s & mask) === 0 && exponent > 0; mask >>= 1) exponent--;
    const mantissa = (s >> (exponent + 3)) & 0x0f;
    out[i] = ~(sign | (exponent << 4) | mantissa) & 0xff;
  }
  return out;
}

// Linear interpolation is enough for speech going UP in rate (8 -> 16 kHz).
// Going DOWN (24 -> 8 kHz) needs a low-pass filter first, or high frequencies alias.
export function resampleLinear(input: Int16Array, fromRate: number, toRate: number): Int16Array {
  const outLength = Math.round((input.length * toRate) / fromRate);
  const out = new Int16Array(outLength);
  for (let i = 0; i < outLength; i++) {
    const pos = (i * fromRate) / toRate;
    const left = Math.floor(pos);
    const right = Math.min(left + 1, input.length - 1);
    const frac = pos - left;
    out[i] = Math.round(input[left] * (1 - frac) + input[right] * frac);
  }
  return out;
}

export const frameSamples = (rateHz: number, frameMs: number) => (rateHz * frameMs) / 1000;

Real test output: a 20 ms phone frame is 160 samples, which becomes 320 samples at 16 kHz and 480 at 24 kHz, and a mu-law round trip of a speech-level tone stays within about 2.4% of the original samples:

{ worstRelativeError: '0.0238', bytesPerSecond: 8000 }
ok 1 - a 20 ms phone frame: 160 bytes of mu-law, 320 samples at 16 kHz
ok 2 - mu-law round trip keeps speech-level samples within a few percent

Mu-law is lossy by design (it spends its bits where speech is), so never decode, process, and re-encode audio more often than the pipeline needs.

docs.title: The same session with the Google Live API
docs.text:
// src/voice/liveGoogle.ts (the equivalent session with the Google Gen AI SDK)
import { GoogleGenAI, Modality } from "@google/genai";

const ai = new GoogleGenAI({}); // GEMINI_API_KEY on the server

export async function openLiveSession(onAudio: (pcm24k: string) => void, onInterrupted: () => void) {
  const session = await ai.live.connect({
    model: process.env.LIVE_MODEL!, // a Live API model ID from Google's model list
    config: {
      responseModalities: [Modality.AUDIO],
      systemInstruction: "You are TaskFlow's voice assistant. Be brief.",
    },
    callbacks: {
      onmessage: (message) => {
        if (message.serverContent?.interrupted) onInterrupted(); // the user talked over the model
        for (const part of message.serverContent?.modelTurn?.parts ?? []) {
          if (part.inlineData?.data) onAudio(part.inlineData.data); // base64 PCM16, 24 kHz
        }
      },
      onerror: (e) => console.error(JSON.stringify({ msg: "live error", error: e.message })),
      onclose: () => undefined,
    },
  });
  return {
    // Input must be 16-bit PCM at 16 kHz: decode and resample phone audio first.
    sendAudio: (pcm16k: string) => session.sendRealtimeInput({ audio: { data: pcm16k, mimeType: "audio/pcm;rate=16000" } }),
    close: () => session.close(),
  };
}

The shape is the same (connect, stream audio in, play audio out, react to interruptions), but the formats and event names differ. In React apps, the AI SDK also ships an experimental_useRealtime hook (experimental as of November 2026) that wraps browser capture and playback for realtime providers.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep provider keys on the server; create sessions server-side or issue short-lived client secrets.
  • Use WebRTC for end-user devices and WebSocket for server bridges.
  • Measure mouth-to-ear latency per stage, and tune turn detection before changing models.
  • Stream every stage, keep tools off the critical path, and lead replies with the answer.
  • Implement barge-in fully: stop playback, truncate history to what was heard, cancel generation.
  • Keep echo cancellation on, and tune VAD thresholds against real recordings, including noisy ones.
  • Confirm every write action aloud, and offer transfer to a person at any time.
  • Disclose the AI, handle recording consent, and keep emergency calls away from bots.
  • Cap call length and idle time, keep the session prefix stable, and summarize or truncate long sessions to control cost.
  • Store transcripts with the same ownership, retention, and deletion rules as chat messages.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The assistant keeps interrupting itself. Detect: speech_started events while the assistant is speaking with no user speech in recordings; replies cut off mid-sentence. Cause: speaker output leaking into the microphone without echo cancellation. Fix: keep echoCancellation on, prefer headsets, raise the VAD threshold, and require a minimum speech duration before barge-in.
  • Users complain they get cut off mid-sentence. Detect: short user turns followed by "no, I wasn't finished"; transcripts that end mid-clause. Cause: a silence threshold too short for how people dictate tasks. Fix: lengthen silence_duration_ms or switch to semantic turn detection with lower eagerness, and evaluate with recorded calls.
  • Replies take two seconds or more. Detect: per-stage timings show a long end-of-turn wait or a tool call before the first audio. Cause: a conservative VAD, a synchronous tool on the critical path, or a distant region. Fix: tune turn detection, speak an acknowledgment while tools run, and move the voice server closer to users and the provider.
  • Callers hear fast, garbled, or deep, slow speech. Detect: audio sounds wrong only on one path (phone but not browser). Cause: a sample-rate or encoding mismatch, such as 24 kHz PCM sent to an 8 kHz mu-law line. Fix: declare formats explicitly on both sides, resample with filtering when going down in rate, and add an automated test that plays a known tone through the bridge.
  • Long calls drop at the same point. Detect: disconnects clustered at a fixed duration. Cause: a provider session limit, such as 15 minutes for audio-only Live API sessions without compression. Fix: enable context compression or session resumption, or hand over to a new session with a summary.
  • Voice costs grow faster than call volume. Detect: cost per call minute rises with call length; a few long or stuck calls dominate spend. Cause: the whole conversation is processed for every reply, plus calls that never hang up. Fix: cap call duration, add idle timeouts, keep instructions stable for caching, and truncate or summarize old turns.
  • The conversation log is missing what the user said. Detect: assistant transcripts are stored but user turns are empty. Cause: input transcription was never enabled in the session. Fix: configure input transcription and store both sides with the call ID.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Realtime speech API: A model API that streams audio in and out over a long-lived connection.
  • Cascaded pipeline: Speech-to-text, a text model, and text-to-speech chained together.
  • Speech-to-speech model: One model that takes audio in and produces audio out.
  • WebRTC: The browser standard for real-time media over UDP, with jitter buffering and echo cancellation.
  • SDP offer and answer: The messages two WebRTC peers exchange to agree on media formats and network paths.
  • Voice activity detection (VAD): Detecting when speech starts and stops in an audio stream.
  • Semantic turn detection: Ending a turn when the words sound complete, not only after a fixed silence.
  • Barge-in: The user interrupting the assistant while it speaks.
  • Mouth-to-ear latency: Time from the user finishing speaking to hearing the first audio of the reply.
  • G.711 (mu-law, A-law): The 8 kHz, 8-bit telephony audio encodings.
  • SIP trunk: A connection that carries phone calls between a telephony provider and another system over SIP.
  • DTMF: The tones produced by phone keypad presses.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Putting the provider API key in the browser instead of creating sessions on the server.
  • Using a WebSocket from mobile clients on lossy networks.
  • Blaming the model for latency that comes from the end-of-turn wait.
  • Stopping playback on interruption but leaving the full reply in the history, so the model assumes the user heard it.
  • Turning off echo cancellation, then fighting self-interruptions with VAD tweaks.
  • Sending audio at the wrong sample rate or encoding.
  • Letting the assistant act on spoken commands without confirming writes.
  • Forgetting AI disclosure, recording consent, transfer to a person, or emergency-call handling on phone lines.
  • Estimating voice cost from output length, when input grows with every turn.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare a cascaded pipeline with a speech-to-speech model on latency, control, moderation, and relative cost.
  2. Why is WebRTC preferred for browsers and mobile clients, and a WebSocket for server-to-server bridges?
  3. How many bytes per second does 16 kHz 16-bit PCM need, and how many as base64 in JSON? How many bytes is a 20 ms G.711 frame? (Answer: 32,000; about 42,700; 160.)
  4. Using the example budget, which single change would cut the most latency, and what is the trade-off?
  5. List the four steps of barge-in handling and explain why truncating the history matters.
  6. A 20-turn call has user turns of 4 seconds and assistant turns of 6 seconds, with all audio kept in the conversation. Estimate total input and output audio tokens using 1 token per 100 ms for the user and 1 per 50 ms for the assistant. (Answer: 40 + 120 = 160 tokens of history per turn; input about 160 x 210 = 33,600 tokens; output 20 x 120 = 2,400 tokens.)
  7. Describe the media-streaming and SIP patterns for phone calls and what your server controls in each.
  8. Which obligations does a phone voice assistant carry that a chat assistant does not?

docs.text:
# k8s/vllm-chat-autoscaling.yaml (excerpt): scale vLLM on queue length with KEDA
spec:
  minReplicaCount: 1 # keep one warm replica for interactive traffic
  maxReplicaCount: 6 # no more than the GPU quota allows
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc:9090
        query: sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{namespace="taskflow", model_name="taskflow-chat"})
        threshold: "4" # average waiting requests per replica

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A new feature with uncertain demand A hosted API No idle GPUs; pay per token Many users on data-center GPUs vLLM or SGLang Continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching A laptop, CPU, or edge device Ollama or llama.cpp with GGUF Minutes to set up, OpenAI-style API To leave an existing TGI deployment vLLM or SGLang TGI is in maintenance mode and archived A faster first token A shorter, cacheable prompt, and streaming Prefill grows with uncached input A faster finish Fewer output tokens, a smaller model Decode dominates long answers Cheaper work nobody waits for A batch API or flex tier Half the price, results within 24 hours Cheaper easy requests Per-feature routing, then a cascade Most savings with no runtime logic More concurrency on one GPU FP8 KV cache, then 4-bit weights after evaluation The cache, not the weights, sets concurrency A model too large for one GPU Quantize first; tensor parallelism if 16-bit is required Splitting buys fit, not efficiency Lowest cost per token Hosted or serverless for spiky load, reserved GPUs for steady high load Utilization decides

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value KV cache per token 2 × layers × KV heads × head_dim × bytes; 8B shape: 128 KiB, so 1 GiB per 8K conversation 8B model on a 24 GB GPU 14.9 GiB weights, about 4.7 conversations at 8K; 9.4 with an FP8 cache; 15.6 with 4-bit weights End-to-end latency TTFT + (output tokens − 1) × TPOT: 1.2 s + 399 × 0.025 s = 11.2 s Speculative decoding (1 − a^(k+1)) / (1 − a) tokens per pass: a = 0.7, k = 4 gives 2.77 Decode bound Steps/s ≤ bandwidth / bytes per step: 16 GB at 2 TB/s ≤ 125 Self-hosted cost per token G / (T × utilization): 10% utilization costs 8 times as much as 80% Cascade cost small + escalation × large: 1 + 0.3 × 10 = 4 units instead of 10 Batch APIs 50% off at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google; up to 24 hours Cached input OpenAI up to 95% off (1,024-token minimum on recent models); Anthropic reads 0.1× (0.05× or 0.025× on some newer models), writes 1.25× (5 min) or 2× (1 h) Defaults vLLM port 8000, prefix caching on; SGLang 30000; Ollama 11434, OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1, queue 512; llama-server 127.0.0.1:9931 vLLM --api-key Covers only /v1, /v2, /inference, /cohere KEDA threshold: "4" 13 waiting requests → ceil(13 / 4) = 4 replicas Spot GPUs AWS gives a 2-minute interruption notice

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Scaling GPU servers on CPU. Scale on vllm:num_requests_waiting or KV cache usage; scale out early and in slowly.
  • Leaving --max-model-len at the model maximum. Cap it at what the feature needs; context is paid for in cache.
  • Relying on the engine's API key. Keep the server internal behind a network policy and authenticate at a gateway.
  • Putting variable text at the top of a cached prompt. Stable content first, and alert on the cache hit ratio.
  • Trimming the prompt when output length dominates. Ask for the length the UI needs and set an output limit.
  • Putting tenant IDs in metric labels. Label by feature, model, and token type; keep tenants in logs and a usage store.
  • Shipping a 4-bit model without evaluation. Compare it with the original on your evaluation set and keep the original for rollback.
  • Scaling interactive model servers to zero. Keep a warm replica; scale to zero only for batch work.

docs.title: Cost Optimization for LLM Apps
docs.text:
An LLM feature has a meter attached to every request. Hosted models bill by tokens (input, cached input, output, and hidden reasoning tokens) and by some tool calls; self-hosted models bill by the GPU-hour whether or not anyone is using them. This lesson shows how to account for that spend precisely, how to find the feature and the token type that dominate it, and how to reduce it with caching, batching, routing to smaller models, distillation, output limits, and context trimming, without breaking quality.

All costs here are relative. Prices change often and differ by provider and model, so the examples use units where one uncached input token costs 1, and you multiply by your provider's current price list when you need money. The running examples are TaskFlow's Assistant (task creation with structured output), project Q&A over documents, the task agent, and meeting-notes summaries.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Usage-based pricing scales with traffic times tokens, and both grow quietly. A prompt template gains a paragraph, retrieval returns eight passages instead of four, an agent takes two extra steps, a model upgrade produces longer answers, and the monthly bill doubles without a single traffic change. Output tokens usually cost several times as much as input tokens (five times at several providers' list prices in November 2026), and reasoning models add hidden output tokens on top. Retries and validation failures bill again for the same user action.

Cost is also a product decision. A feature that costs more per request than the user pays per month cannot ship to everyone. Knowing the cost per completed task, per feature and per tenant, is what lets a team set limits, price plans, and choose where to spend engineering effort. And many cost fixes (shorter outputs, smaller models, cached prefixes) make the feature faster too, as described in latency optimization.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI Batch API. The Batch guide offers a "50% cost discount compared to synchronous APIs", a separate pool of higher rate limits, and completion "within 24 hours (and often more quickly)". The flex processing guide offers batch-level prices on ordinary requests "in exchange for slower response times and occasional resource unavailability".
  • OpenAI and Anthropic prompt caching. OpenAI's prompt caching guide describes cached input tokens "discounted up to 95%". Anthropic's prompt caching documentation prices 5-minute cache writes at 1.25 times the base input price, 1-hour writes at 2 times, and cache reads at 0.1 times (0.05 or 0.025 times on some newer models), and its batch processing guide offers "a 50 percent discount on all usage" that stacks with caching.
  • FrugalGPT. Chen, Zaharia, and Zou, FrugalGPT, route each query through a cascade of models from cheap to expensive and report matching the best single model's performance "with up to 98% cost reduction" on their benchmarks.
  • RouteLLM. Ong and colleagues, RouteLLM: Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data, train routers that choose between a strong and a weak model per query and report reducing costs "by over 2 times in certain cases" without hurting response quality.
  • Gemini Batch API. Google's Batch API guide prices batch requests "at 50% of the standard interactive API cost" with a 24-hour target turnaround.

Popular tools and providers: provider usage dashboards and usage APIs, batch APIs and flex tiers, prompt caching, token counting endpoints (OpenAI responses.inputTokens.count, Anthropic messages.countTokens, Google models.countTokens), local tokenizers such as gpt-tokenizer, Prometheus and OpenTelemetry for per-feature metrics, and AI gateways that add budgets and routing in front of several providers.

docs.title: The cost of one request
docs.text:
Every provider's bill reduces to the same shape:

request cost = uncached input tokens x input price
             + cached input tokens   x cached-input price   (much cheaper)
             + cache-write tokens    x cache-write price    (some providers charge extra)
             + output tokens         x output price         (includes reasoning tokens)
             + tool and other fees   (web search, images, audio, ...)

Relative units used in this lesson: input 1, cached input 0.1, output 5

TaskFlow Assistant (task creation): 2,000 input tokens, 1,800 of them a cached
system prompt and tool schema; 80 output tokens
  uncached: 200 x 1 = 200;  cached: 1,800 x 0.1 = 180;  output: 80 x 5 = 400
  = 780 units  (2,400 units without caching)

Project Q&A: 150 cached instruction tokens, 8 passages x 500 tokens, 300 output tokens
  150 x 0.1 + 4,000 x 1 + 300 x 5 = 15 + 4,000 + 1,500 = 5,515 units
  with the top 4 passages instead of 8:  15 + 2,000 + 1,500 = 3,515 units

Meeting summary: 6,000 input tokens of notes (never repeated, so never cached),
400 output tokens
  6,000 x 1 + 400 x 5 = 8,000 units;  with a five-bullet limit (150 tokens): 6,750

Then account for what the user actually gets. If 4% of Assistant calls fail validation and are retried once, and 2% hit a timeout and are retried, the cost per completed task is about 6% higher than the cost per request. Agents are worse: every step re-sends the growing conversation, so input tokens grow roughly with the square of the number of steps unless the history is cached or trimmed.

docs.title: Where the money goes: per feature, not per request
docs.text: Multiplying cost per request by volume changes the picture. Task creation is cheap per request but frequent; summaries are expensive per request but rare; project Q&A combines high volume with long retrieved context and dominates the bill. The highest-value change is often a boring one (fewer, better passages) rather than a model switch. You only see that if usage is recorded per feature, which the practical examples show how to do.

docs.title: Counting tokens: estimate before, record after
docs.text:
Two different numbers matter:

  • Before the call, estimate input size to enforce budgets: trim history, cap retrieved context, or refuse a request that would exceed a tenant's quota. A local tokenizer such as gpt-tokenizer (OpenAI's o200k_base encoding by default) is fast and free; other providers tokenize differently, so treat it as an estimate with a margin, or call the provider's token counting endpoint when precision matters.
  • After the call, record the usage object the provider returns. That is what you are billed for, including cached and reasoning tokens that no local count can predict.

The usage fields differ by provider, and so does their arithmetic:

Provider Input Cached input Output OpenAI Responses input_tokens (includes cached and cache-write tokens) input_tokens_details.cached_tokens output_tokens (includes output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens) OpenAI-style Chat Completions prompt_tokens (includes cached) prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens completion_tokens (includes reasoning) Anthropic Messages input_tokens (only tokens after the last cache breakpoint) cache_read_input_tokens; writes in cache_creation_input_tokens output_tokens Google Gen AI promptTokenCount (includes cached) cachedContentTokenCount candidatesTokenCount plus thoughtsTokenCount

Normalize them once, in one module, so dashboards do not mix "input including cache" with "input excluding cache".

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Three kinds of caching cut cost, with very different risks:

Cache What is reused Saves Main risk Provider prompt caching Processed prefix of the prompt Most of the input price of the cached part Low; needs an identical prefix Exact response cache (yours) The whole answer for an identical request The entire call Serving one tenant's answer to another; stale answers Semantic cache (yours) An answer to a similar earlier question The entire call Wrong answers for questions that look alike but differ

Prompt caching is nearly free to adopt: put stable content first and measure hit ratios. An exact response cache fits deterministic, non-personal calls, such as classifying a support ticket or summarizing a public changelog; its key must include the model, the prompt version, the tenant and permission scope, the full input, and the data version (see cache fundamentals). Semantic caching needs an evaluation of false hits before it is trusted, and should never cross tenant or permission boundaries.

docs.title: Batching and flex tiers
docs.text: Work nobody waits for should not pay interactive prices. Nightly meeting summaries for inactive projects, re-summarizing a backlog after a prompt change, evaluation runs, and data enrichment can all go through a batch API: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all price batch requests at half the interactive rate as of November 2026, in exchange for asynchronous results within 24 hours. OpenAI's flex tier applies similar pricing to individual requests that can tolerate slow responses and occasional unavailability. For self-hosted models the equivalent is filling the GPU: an offline job that keeps continuous batching saturated lowers the cost of every token the GPU produces.

docs.title: Routing to smaller models
docs.text:
Many requests do not need the largest model. Three routing patterns, from simple to sophisticated:

  1. Per-feature routing. Each feature has a configured model: a small model for task creation and ticket classification, a large one for multi-step agent work. This is configuration, not code, and captures most of the savings.
  2. Cascade. Try the small model first, validate the result (schema checks, a confidence field, or a cheap verifier), and escalate to the large model only on failure. FrugalGPT studies this pattern.
  3. Learned router. A classifier predicts which model a query needs, as in RouteLLM. It needs training data and monitoring, so start with the first two.

The arithmetic of a cascade decides whether it pays:

small model = 1 unit, large model = 10 units per request

always large:                          10 units
cascade, 30% escalate:   1 + 0.3 x 10 = 4 units   (60% cheaper)
cascade, 85% escalate:   1 + 0.85 x 10 = 9.5 units, and escalated requests are slower

A cascade only helps when most requests succeed on the small model, so track the escalation rate per feature, and evaluate quality on the same evaluation set as the large model (see building evaluation sets).

docs.title: Distillation
docs.text: When one narrow, high-volume task (task extraction from a sentence, ticket labeling) runs on a large model, you can distill it: collect the large model's outputs on real inputs, review them, and fine-tune a small model to reproduce them. The small model then serves the task at a fraction of the cost and latency, and can often be self-hosted. It costs an evaluation set, a training pipeline, and ongoing retraining when the task changes; check the provider's terms on training with its outputs before you start. The method is covered in preference tuning and distillation, and the decision in when to fine-tune.

docs.title: Limits: output caps, context trimming, and step caps
docs.text:
• Output caps. Set an output limit per feature (max_output_tokens, max_tokens) and ask for the length the UI needs. For reasoning models, choose the lowest reasoning effort that passes evaluation.
  • Context trimming. Keep the last few conversation turns verbatim and replace older ones with a running summary, or drop them; see conversation state and memory.
  • Retrieval caps. Fewer, reranked passages usually answer as well as many raw ones, at a fraction of the input cost.
  • Agent step caps and tool output limits. Cap the number of steps, truncate large tool results before they go back into the context, and stop runaway loops.
  • Per-tenant quotas. Enforce token budgets per tenant and plan, and degrade gracefully (a smaller model, a shorter answer, a clear message) instead of failing silently.

docs.title: Self-hosting economics
docs.text:
A self-hosted GPU costs the same per hour at 5% load and at 95% load, so its cost per token depends on utilization:

G = cost of one GPU-hour (relative units), T = tokens per hour at full load
cost per token = G / (T x utilization)

T = 7.2 million tokens per hour (2,000 tokens/s across all streams)
  80% utilization: G / 5.76 million tokens
  10% utilization: G / 0.72 million tokens  -> 8 times the cost per token

Self-hosting is cheaper than a hosted API only when sustained utilization is high enough that G / (T x utilization) falls below the API's price per token for a model of similar quality, after adding engineering and on-call time. Spiky or low traffic usually favors hosted APIs; steady, high volume, or strict data-control requirements favor self-hosting. GPU options and their relative costs are in GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: Per-feature cost tracking
docs.text:
Cost tracking works when it is impossible to bypass:

  • One wrapper for every model call, taking a feature name, so no code path calls an SDK directly.
  • Labels with low cardinality in metrics (feature, model, token type). Tenant ids go to logs and a usage store, not to Prometheus labels, where thousands of tenants would explode the series count.
  • No prompt content in cost records. Usage numbers and ids are enough; prompts may hold personal data (see privacy, PII, and data retention).
  • Outcomes next to costs. Record whether the task completed (task created, answer accepted) so you can compute cost per completed task, not just cost per call.
  • Trace attributes. OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions define attributes such as gen_ai.request.model, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens; they are still marked Development, so pin the version you follow (see LLM observability and tracing).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Technique Watch out for Long, repeated instructions or documents Prompt caching Variable text at the top of the prompt Identical, non-personal requests Exact response cache Key must include tenant, model, prompt and data versions Work nobody waits for Batch API or flex tier Results arrive later; design for asynchronous completion Most requests are easy Per-feature routing or a cascade Escalation rate and quality must be measured One narrow task at high volume Distillation to a small model Training pipeline, evaluation, provider terms Long answers or chats Output caps, history trimming Truncated answers, lost context Retrieval-heavy features Fewer, reranked passages Recall drops if you cut too far Steady high volume, data control needs Self-hosting Utilization; idle GPUs are expensive Spiky, low volume Hosted APIs Rate limits and provider dependency

docs.title: Estimating tokens and trimming history before the call
docs.text:
// src/ai/token-budget.ts
import { countTokens } from "gpt-tokenizer"; // o200k_base by default: an estimate for other providers

export interface ChatTurn {
  role: "system" | "user" | "assistant";
  content: string;
}

// Keep the system prompt and as many of the newest turns as fit the budget.
export function fitToBudget(turns: ChatTurn[], budgetTokens: number): ChatTurn[] {
  const [system, ...rest] = turns;
  if (!system || system.role !== "system") throw new Error("first turn must be the system prompt");

  let used = countTokens(system.content);
  const kept: ChatTurn[] = [];
  for (let i = rest.length - 1; i >= 0; i -= 1) {
    const turn = rest[i] as ChatTurn;
    const cost = countTokens(turn.content) + 4; // small allowance for message framing
    if (used + cost > budgetTokens) break;
    used += cost;
    kept.unshift(turn);
  }
  return [system, ...kept];
}

// scripts/token-budget-demo.ts
import { countTokens } from "gpt-tokenizer";
import { fitToBudget, type ChatTurn } from "../src/ai/token-budget.js";

const turns: ChatTurn[] = [
  { role: "system", content: "You are TaskFlow Assistant. Turn requests into tasks." },
  ...Array.from({ length: 30 }, (_, i): ChatTurn => ({
    role: i % 2 === 0 ? "user" : "assistant",
    content: `Turn ${i}: please move the launch checklist task to next week and notify the design team.`,
  })),
];

const all = turns.reduce((sum, t) => sum + countTokens(t.content), 0);
const trimmed = fitToBudget(turns, 300);
const kept = trimmed.reduce((sum, t) => sum + countTokens(t.content), 0);
console.log(`all turns: ${turns.length} turns, ${all} tokens`);
console.log(`trimmed:   ${trimmed.length} turns, ${kept} tokens (budget 300)`);

# Output from a local run
all turns: 31 turns, 581 tokens
trimmed:   13 turns, 239 tokens (budget 300)

In production, replace the dropped turns with a short running summary rather than discarding them, and keep the budget per feature in configuration.

docs.title: Normalizing usage and computing relative cost
docs.text:
// src/ai/usage.ts
import type Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import type { GenerateContentResponseUsageMetadata } from "@google/genai";
import type OpenAI from "openai";

export interface NormalizedUsage {
  uncachedInput: number;
  cachedInput: number;
  cacheWrite: number;
  output: number; // includes reasoning tokens
  reasoning: number; // informational subset of output
}

export function fromOpenAIResponses(u: OpenAI.Responses.ResponseUsage): NormalizedUsage {
  const cached = u.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens;
  const writes = u.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens ?? 0;
  return {
    uncachedInput: Math.max(0, u.input_tokens - cached - writes),
    cachedInput: cached,
    cacheWrite: writes,
    output: u.output_tokens,
    reasoning: u.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens,
  };
}

export function fromChatCompletions(u: OpenAI.CompletionUsage): NormalizedUsage {
  const cached = u.prompt_tokens_details?.cached_tokens ?? 0;
  return {
    uncachedInput: u.prompt_tokens - cached,
    cachedInput: cached,
    cacheWrite: 0,
    output: u.completion_tokens,
    reasoning: u.completion_tokens_details?.reasoning_tokens ?? 0,
  };
}

export function fromAnthropic(u: Anthropic.Messages.Usage): NormalizedUsage {
  return {
    uncachedInput: u.input_tokens, // Anthropic reports cache reads and writes separately
    cachedInput: u.cache_read_input_tokens ?? 0,
    cacheWrite: u.cache_creation_input_tokens ?? 0,
    output: u.output_tokens,
    reasoning: 0,
  };
}

export function fromGemini(u: GenerateContentResponseUsageMetadata): NormalizedUsage {
  const cached = u.cachedContentTokenCount ?? 0;
  const thoughts = u.thoughtsTokenCount ?? 0;
  return {
    uncachedInput: (u.promptTokenCount ?? 0) - cached,
    cachedInput: cached,
    cacheWrite: 0,
    output: (u.candidatesTokenCount ?? 0) + thoughts,
    reasoning: thoughts,
  };
}

// Prices per million tokens, loaded from configuration and kept in sync with
// the provider's price list. Relative units work for comparisons.
export interface ModelPrice {
  input: number;
  cachedInput: number;
  cacheWrite: number;
  output: number;
}

export function loadPrices(json = process.env.MODEL_PRICES_JSON ?? "{}"): Map<string, ModelPrice> {
  return new Map(Object.entries(JSON.parse(json) as Record<string, ModelPrice>));
}

export function costOf(usage: NormalizedUsage, price: ModelPrice): number {
  return (
    (usage.uncachedInput * price.input +
      usage.cachedInput * price.cachedInput +
      usage.cacheWrite * price.cacheWrite +
      usage.output * price.output) /
    1_000_000
  );
}

// scripts/usage-demo.ts
import { costOf, fromAnthropic, fromOpenAIResponses, loadPrices } from "../src/ai/usage.js";

// Relative prices per million tokens: input 1, cached 0.1, cache write 1.25, output 5
const prices = loadPrices(
  JSON.stringify({ "taskflow-large": { input: 1, cachedInput: 0.1, cacheWrite: 1.25, output: 5 } }),
);
const price = prices.get("taskflow-large");
if (!price) throw new Error("no price configured");

// Usage shaped like the provider responses for the same Assistant call
const openai = fromOpenAIResponses({
  input_tokens: 2_000,
  input_tokens_details: { cached_tokens: 1_800, cache_write_tokens: 0 },
  output_tokens: 80,
  output_tokens_details: { reasoning_tokens: 0 },
  total_tokens: 2_080,
});
const anthropic = fromAnthropic({
  input_tokens: 200,
  cache_read_input_tokens: 1_800,
  cache_creation_input_tokens: 0,
  output_tokens: 80,
  cache_creation: null,
  inference_geo: null,
  output_tokens_details: null,
  server_tool_use: null,
  service_tier: "standard",
  speed: null,
});

for (const [name, usage] of Object.entries({ openai, anthropic })) {
  const units = costOf(usage, price) * 1_000_000;
  console.log(`${name.padEnd(9)} ${JSON.stringify(usage)} -> ${units} units`);
}

# Output from a local run
openai    {"uncachedInput":200,"cachedInput":1800,"cacheWrite":0,"output":80,"reasoning":0} -> 780 units
anthropic {"uncachedInput":200,"cachedInput":1800,"cacheWrite":0,"output":80,"reasoning":0} -> 780 units

The two providers report the same call differently (OpenAI's input_tokens includes the cached 1,800; Anthropic's excludes them), and the normalized records agree. The price table lives in configuration, keyed by the configured model alias, so no real prices or model IDs are hard-coded.

docs.title: Recording cost per feature
docs.text:
// src/ai/cost-tracking.ts
import { Counter } from "prom-client";
import { costOf, type ModelPrice, type NormalizedUsage } from "./usage.js";

const tokens = new Counter({
  name: "taskflow_llm_tokens_total",
  help: "Model tokens by feature, model, and token type",
  labelNames: ["feature", "model", "type"] as const,
});
const cost = new Counter({
  name: "taskflow_llm_cost_units_total",
  help: "Model cost in price-table units by feature and model",
  labelNames: ["feature", "model"] as const,
});

export interface LlmCallRecord {
  feature: "assistant" | "project-qa" | "agent" | "meeting-summary";
  model: string;
  promptVersion: string;
  tenantHash: string; // hashed tenant id: logs and usage store only, never a metric label
  usage: NormalizedUsage;
  completed: boolean; // did the user get the outcome (task created, answer shown)?
}

export function recordLlmCall(record: LlmCallRecord, price: ModelPrice | undefined): void {
  const { feature, model, usage } = record;
  tokens.inc({ feature, model, type: "input_uncached" }, usage.uncachedInput);
  tokens.inc({ feature, model, type: "input_cached" }, usage.cachedInput);
  tokens.inc({ feature, model, type: "cache_write" }, usage.cacheWrite);
  tokens.inc({ feature, model, type: "output" }, usage.output);
  const units = price ? costOf(usage, price) : 0;
  cost.inc({ feature, model }, units);

  // One structured line per call: ids and numbers, never prompt or answer text
  console.info(
    JSON.stringify({
      event: "llm_usage",
      feature,
      model,
      promptVersion: record.promptVersion,
      tenantHash: record.tenantHash,
      ...usage,
      costUnits: units,
      completed: record.completed,
    }),
  );
}

# PromQL: daily cost per feature, and cost per completed Assistant task
sum by (feature) (increase(taskflow_llm_cost_units_total[1d]))

sum(increase(taskflow_llm_cost_units_total{feature="assistant"}[1d]))
  / sum(increase(taskflow_assistant_tasks_created_total[1d]))

The second query divides cost by outcomes (a counter the Assistant increments when a task is actually created), so retries and validation failures show up as a higher cost per task. Per-tenant totals come from the structured log lines or a daily usage collection in MongoDB, which also feeds quota checks before each call. Metrics and dashboards are covered in metrics and dashboards.

docs.title: A cascade for task creation
docs.text:
// src/ai/cascade.ts
export interface TaskDraft {
  title: string;
  dueDate: string | null;
  confidence: number; // the model's own 0-1 estimate, requested in the schema
}

export type Complete = (model: string, prompt: string) => Promise<string>;

function parseDraft(text: string): TaskDraft | null {
  try {
    const value = JSON.parse(text) as Partial<TaskDraft>;
    if (typeof value.title !== "string" || value.title.trim() === "") return null;
    if (value.dueDate !== null && typeof value.dueDate !== "string") return null;
    if (typeof value.confidence !== "number") return null;
    return { title: value.title, dueDate: value.dueDate ?? null, confidence: value.confidence };
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
}

// Try the small model; escalate when its output is invalid or unsure.
export async function draftTask(
  sentence: string,
  complete: Complete,
  models = { small: process.env.SMALL_MODEL ?? "", large: process.env.CHAT_MODEL ?? "" },
  minConfidence = 0.7,
): Promise<{ draft: TaskDraft; escalated: boolean }> {
  const prompt = `Extract a task as JSON {title, dueDate (ISO date or null), confidence}: ${sentence}`;

  const small = parseDraft(await complete(models.small, prompt));
  if (small && small.confidence >= minConfidence) return { draft: small, escalated: false };

  const large = parseDraft(await complete(models.large, prompt));
  if (!large) throw new Error("both models returned invalid task drafts");
  return { draft: large, escalated: true };
}

// scripts/cascade-demo.ts
import { draftTask, type Complete } from "../src/ai/cascade.js";

// A fake client: the small model is unsure about relative dates
const fake: Complete = async (model, prompt) =>
  model === "small" && /next/.test(prompt)
    ? JSON.stringify({ title: "Plan launch", dueDate: null, confidence: 0.4 })
    : JSON.stringify({ title: "Plan launch", dueDate: "2026-11-20", confidence: 0.9 });

const models = { small: "small", large: "large" };
for (const sentence of ["Plan the launch by 2026-11-20", "Plan the launch next Friday"]) {
  const { draft, escalated } = await draftTask(sentence, fake, models);
  console.log(`${escalated ? "large" : "small"}: ${JSON.stringify(draft)}`);
}

# Output from a local run
small: {"title":"Plan launch","dueDate":"2026-11-20","confidence":0.9}
large: {"title":"Plan launch","dueDate":"2026-11-20","confidence":0.9}

The injected complete function keeps the router testable; in production it wraps the provider SDK with structured output (see structured output and validation). Self-reported confidence is a weak signal, so calibrate the threshold on an evaluation set and track the escalation rate per feature.

docs.title: Moving nightly summaries to the Batch API
docs.text:
// scripts/submit-summary-batch.ts
import { createReadStream, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { CHAT_MODEL, llm } from "../src/ai/llm-client.js";

interface PendingNote {
  meetingId: string;
  notes: string;
}

export async function submitSummaryBatch(pending: PendingNote[]): Promise<string> {
  const lines = pending.map((note) =>
    JSON.stringify({
      custom_id: `meeting-${note.meetingId}`, // maps each result back to its meeting
      method: "POST",
      url: "/v1/responses",
      body: {
        model: CHAT_MODEL,
        instructions: "Summarize meeting notes in at most five bullets, then list action items.",
        input: note.notes,
        max_output_tokens: 400,
      },
    }),
  );
  const path = "/tmp/summary-batch.jsonl";
  writeFileSync(path, lines.join("\n") + "\n");

  const file = await llm.files.create({ file: createReadStream(path), purpose: "batch" });
  const batch = await llm.batches.create({
    input_file_id: file.id,
    endpoint: "/v1/responses",
    completion_window: "24h",
  });
  return batch.id; // store it; a scheduled job polls llm.batches.retrieve(id) and saves results
}

Each line is an ordinary request body, so the same prompt and limits apply at half the price. The scheduled poller downloads the output file when the batch completes, matches results by custom_id, and retries only the lines that failed. Anthropic's Message Batches and Google's Batch API follow the same shape with their own request formats.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Record normalized usage for every model call, labeled by feature and model, with outcomes next to costs.
  • Report cost per completed task per feature, not only total spend.
  • Start optimization with the feature that dominates spend; it is often retrieval context, not the model.
  • Put stable prompt content first and track cache hit ratios.
  • Send asynchronous work through batch APIs or flex tiers.
  • Route by feature first; add a cascade where evaluation shows a small model handles most cases.
  • Cap outputs, retrieved context, conversation history, and agent steps.
  • Keep price tables in configuration and update them when prices change.
  • Enforce per-tenant budgets before the call and degrade gracefully.
  • Self-host only when sustained utilization beats hosted per-token prices.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The bill doubled while traffic was flat. Detect: input tokens per request rose after a release; cost by feature points at one feature. Cause: a prompt template or retrieval change added context to every call, or a cached prefix stopped matching. Fix: per-feature token dashboards with release annotations, a prompt-size check in CI, and cache hit ratio alerts.
  • One tenant consumed a large share of monthly spend. Detect: per-tenant usage store shows one tenant far above its plan. Cause: an automated integration looping on the agent endpoint. Fix: per-tenant token quotas checked before each call, rate limits, and step caps on agents.
  • Reasoning model costs exceed estimates by a wide margin. Detect: output tokens per call far above visible answer length; reasoning_tokens large. Cause: hidden reasoning billed as output, at a high default effort. Fix: lower reasoning effort for simple features, route them to non-reasoning models, and include reasoning tokens in dashboards.
  • The cascade saved nothing. Detect: escalation rate above 70%; latency up. Cause: the small model is not good enough for this feature, or the confidence threshold is too strict. Fix: evaluate per feature, route that feature directly to the large model, or distill a better small model.
  • A response cache returned another customer's data. Detect: support report of foreign task names in an answer. Cause: the cache key omitted the tenant and permission scope. Fix: include tenant, permission scope, model, prompt version, and data version in the key; purge the cache; add a test that two tenants never share entries.
  • The batch job silently left meetings without summaries. Detect: summaries missing for some meetings; batch status shows partial failures or expiry. Cause: failed lines were never retried, or the batch expired after 24 hours. Fix: reconcile by custom_id, retry failed lines, and alert when a batch expires.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Input, cached input, and output tokens: The token classes providers bill at different rates.
  • Reasoning tokens: Hidden tokens a reasoning model generates before answering; billed as output.
  • Cost per completed task: Spend divided by successful user outcomes, including retries and failures.
  • Prompt caching: Provider-side reuse of a repeated prompt prefix at a discounted input price.
  • Response cache: Your own store of full answers for identical requests.
  • Semantic cache: Reusing answers for similar, not identical, requests.
  • Batch API: Asynchronous, discounted processing of many requests.
  • Cascade: Trying a cheap model first and escalating on failure.
  • Router: Logic or a model that picks which model handles a request.
  • Distillation: Training a small model to imitate a large model on a task.
  • Utilization: The share of a GPU's capacity actually used; drives self-hosted cost per token.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Tracking total spend but not spend per feature and per completed task.
  • Assuming input tokens dominate; output and reasoning tokens often do.
  • Comparing providers' "input tokens" without normalizing cache accounting.
  • Putting tenant ids in metric labels.
  • Caching full responses without tenant and permission scope in the key.
  • Running offline jobs at interactive prices.
  • Building a learned router before trying per-feature routing.
  • Believing self-hosting is cheaper regardless of utilization.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Write the cost of a request in terms of token classes and prices. Which class does each provider's usage object report, and how do they differ?
  2. A feature sends 3,000 input tokens (2,500 cached) and receives 200 output tokens. In units of input 1, cached 0.1, output 5, what does one call cost, and what without caching? (500 + 250 + 1,000 = 1,750; 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000.)
  3. Why should you estimate tokens before a call and record usage after it?
  4. Compare provider prompt caching, an exact response cache, and a semantic cache.
  5. A cascade escalates 40% of requests from a small model (1 unit) to a large one (10 units). What is the expected cost per request, and when does a cascade stop paying off? (1 + 0.4 x 10 = 5 units; when escalation approaches 90%, the cascade costs as much as always using the large model.)
  6. Which TaskFlow work belongs in a batch API, and what does it trade away?
  7. Why must tenant ids stay out of Prometheus labels, and where should per-tenant usage go instead?
  8. A GPU sustains 3.6 million tokens per hour at full load. How does its cost per token change between 60% and 15% utilization? (It becomes 4 times higher.)
