docs.title: GPU Capacity and Scaling
docs.text:
Self-hosting a model turns capacity planning into GPU arithmetic. Will the model fit on one card? How many conversations can it hold at once? How much does 4-bit quantization buy, and what does it cost in quality? How long does a new replica take to start, and what should trigger it? This lesson sizes GPU memory from first principles (weights plus KV cache plus runtime overhead) with a calculator you can run, explains the quantization formats you will meet (FP8, INT8, 4-bit GPTQ and AWQ, and GGUF), and shows how to autoscale model servers on Kubernetes when every new replica needs minutes to become ready. It closes with the hosted GPU options and how their costs compare.

The serving engines themselves are covered in serving open models; this lesson is about the hardware and the fleet underneath them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
GPUs are the most expensive and the least elastic part of an AI stack. A GPU you size too small cannot load the model, or runs it with so little cache that requests queue and preempt each other. A GPU you size too large, or keep running idle at night, costs the same every hour as a busy one. Unlike web servers, model servers cannot be added in seconds: a new replica may need a new GPU node, a multi-gigabyte image, tens of gigabytes of weights, and a warm-up, so an autoscaler that reacts late leaves users waiting for minutes.

The numbers are knowable in advance. Weights take parameters times bytes per parameter; the KV cache takes a fixed number of bytes per token that follows from the model's shape; the rest is overhead you can measure once. Doing this arithmetic before buying or reserving capacity prevents the two classic mistakes: a model that does not fit, and a model that fits but serves only three users at a time.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• vLLM memory settings. The vLLM engine arguments define --gpu-memory-utilization as "the fraction of GPU memory to be used for the model executor", a per-instance limit, and add --kv-cache-memory-bytes for setting the cache size directly. At startup vLLM logs its KV cache size in tokens and the "Maximum concurrency" for the configured context length, which is the number to compare with your estimate.
  • GPTQ. Frantar and colleagues, GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-trained Transformers, quantize models of 175 billion parameters "in approximately four GPU hours, reducing the bitwidth down to 3 or 4 bits per weight, with negligible accuracy degradation", with inference speedups of around 3.25x on high-end GPUs.
  • AWQ. Lin and colleagues, AWQ: Activation-aware Weight Quantization for LLM Compression and Acceleration, protect the small share of weights that matter most to activations and report a 4-bit inference framework with "more than 3x speedup over the Huggingface FP16 implementation".
  • LLM.int8(). Dettmers and colleagues, LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale, show 8-bit inference that "cut the memory needed for inference by half while retaining full precision performance".
  • Tooling status (November 2026). The AutoAWQ README states that "AutoAWQ is officially deprecated and will no longer be maintained" and that it "has been adopted by the vLLM Project" in LLM Compressor; the AutoGPTQ repository is archived, and vLLM's quantization documentation lists GPTQModel instead.
  • KEDA. The KEDA Prometheus scaler scales a workload on the result of any PromQL query, which is how GPU servers scale on queue length instead of CPU.

Popular tools and providers: vLLM and SGLang (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, and compressed-tensors models), LLM Compressor and GPTQModel for producing quantized checkpoints, llama.cpp's llama-quantize for GGUF files, bitsandbytes for 4-bit and 8-bit loading in Transformers, the NVIDIA GPU Operator on Kubernetes, KEDA and Prometheus for autoscaling, and GPU capacity from cloud providers, GPU clouds, and serverless GPU platforms.

docs.title: What fills GPU memory
docs.text:
Serving memory has four parts:

GPU memory used = weights + KV cache + runtime (activations, CUDA graphs, workspace)
                  + whatever the engine leaves free (vLLM's utilization setting)

weights  = parameters x bytes per parameter (+ ~5-10% for scales in 4-bit formats)
KV cache = bytes per token x tokens held by all active sequences
bytes per token = 2 x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per cache value

8B shape:  32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 -> 128 KiB per token at 16 bits
70B shape: 80 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 -> 320 KiB per token at 16 bits

The weights are a fixed cost per replica. The KV cache is what turns into concurrency: whatever memory remains after weights and runtime holds the cache, and the cache divided by the context each conversation uses is how many conversations fit at once. Grouped-query attention (several query heads sharing one key-value head, as in the shapes above) is why modern models need far less cache than older ones with as many KV heads as query heads.

Concurrency is about actual tokens, not configured maximums. Engines with paged caches allocate blocks as tokens arrive, so a server whose conversations average 2,000 tokens holds about four times as many of them as the "full 8K context" numbers suggest, until a burst of long conversations fills the cache and preemptions start.

docs.title: Running the numbers
docs.text:
The calculator in the practical examples produces this table (planning numbers; the engine's startup log is the ground truth):

model weights kv    GPU      weights GiB KiB/token  KV GiB 8K seqs
8b    bf16    bf16  1x24GB          14.9       128     4.7     4.7
8b    int4    bf16  1x24GB           4.0       128    15.6    15.6
8b    bf16    fp8   1x24GB          14.9        64     4.7     9.4
8b    bf16    bf16  1x80GB          14.9       128    55.1    55.1
70b   bf16    bf16  1x80GB         131.5       320   -61.5  no fit
70b   bf16    bf16  2x80GB         131.5       320     8.5     3.4
70b   int4    fp8   1x80GB          35.5       160    34.5    27.6

The table holds the main decisions of GPU sizing:

  • An 8B model in 16-bit runs on a 24 GB card, but holds fewer than five full-length conversations. Fine for a developer server, not for TaskFlow's production traffic.
  • 4-bit weights free 11 GiB on the same card, more than tripling the cache. An FP8 cache halves bytes per token, doubling concurrency without touching the weights.
  • A 70B model in 16-bit does not fit one 80 GB GPU. Two GPUs with tensor parallelism fit it but leave little cache. With 4-bit weights and an FP8 cache, one GPU holds the model and about 28 full-length conversations, traded against the quality loss of quantization, which you must measure.

docs.title: Decode speed and memory bandwidth
docs.text:
Decoding is limited by memory bandwidth: every step reads the weights (and each sequence's cache) from GPU memory. A rough upper bound for one sequence alone:

steps per second <= memory bandwidth / bytes read per step

16 GB of weights on a GPU with 2 TB/s of bandwidth: <= 125 steps/s at batch size 1
the same model in 4-bit (about 4.3 GB):             <= 465 steps/s at batch size 1

Real numbers are lower, but the ratio explains two things. Quantization speeds up decoding even when memory is not short, because fewer bytes move per step. And batching is nearly free at small batch sizes: one weight read serves every sequence in the step, which is why continuous batching multiplies throughput. As batches grow, the work becomes compute-bound and those gains level off, so benchmark at your real concurrency.

docs.title: Quantization formats
docs.text:
Format Bits per weight Where it runs Notes BF16 / FP16 16 Any modern GPU The usual reference format; best quality FP8 (weights and activations) 8 GPUs with FP8 support (vLLM lists Ada and Hopper and newer) Small quality loss on most models; fast on supported hardware; also used for the KV cache INT8 (W8A8 or weight-only) 8 Most GPUs SmoothQuant-style W8A8 or LLM.int8(); halves weight memory GPTQ 3-4 (usually 4) GPUs via vLLM, SGLang, Transformers Post-training, uses calibration data; produce with GPTQModel or LLM Compressor AWQ 4 GPUs via vLLM, SGLang Activation-aware; produce with LLM Compressor (AutoAWQ is deprecated) bitsandbytes NF4 / INT8 4 or 8 Transformers, vLLM Quantizes at load time; common for QLoRA fine-tuning GGUF (for example Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M) about 4.5-8.5 llama.cpp, Ollama, LM Studio; CPUs, Apple silicon, GPUs Single-file format; Hugging Face documents Q4_K at 4.5 bits per weight

Three rules keep quantization safe:

  1. Measure quality on your tasks. Run TaskFlow's evaluation sets (task-creation accuracy, Q&A faithfulness) on the quantized model before switching; general benchmark scores hide task-specific regressions, especially in long-context and structured-output tasks (see building evaluation sets).
  2. Prefer published, reputable quantized checkpoints or produce your own with maintained tools; check that the engine version supports the exact format.
  3. Quantize the cache separately. An FP8 KV cache (--kv-cache-dtype fp8 in vLLM) doubles concurrency at a small quality cost and is independent of weight quantization.

docs.title: More than one GPU
docs.text:
When a model does not fit one GPU, engines split it:

  • Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs in one server (--tensor-parallel-size 2 in vLLM). It needs fast GPU-to-GPU links, and each GPU holds a share of the weights and of the cache.
  • Pipeline parallelism places different layers on different GPUs or nodes. It reaches larger models but adds latency between stages.
  • Data parallelism (more replicas) is how you add throughput once one replica fits.

Splitting a model buys fit, not efficiency: two GPUs running one 70B replica at 16 bits held about 3 full-length conversations in the table above. Often a quantized model on one GPU per replica, scaled out with more replicas, serves more users per GPU.

docs.title: Autoscaling model servers
docs.text:
Model servers need different autoscaling than web servers:

  • Scale on queue and cache signals. CPU usage is meaningless and GPU utilization saturates early. Use the engine's metrics: requests waiting (vllm:num_requests_waiting), KV cache usage (vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc), or measured TTFT p95.
  • Scale out early, scale in slowly. A new replica takes minutes, so trigger on a modest queue and keep headroom; scale in only after a long stabilization window, and drain in-flight generations first.
  • Scale to zero only where cold starts are acceptable. Internal batch jobs can wait minutes; the interactive Assistant cannot. Keep at least one warm replica for interactive features.

A cold start is a chain of slow steps, and each has a fix:

Step Why it is slow Fix GPU node provisioning GPUs are scarce; nodes take minutes to boot and join Keep a warm node, reserve capacity, use node pools with minimum size Image pull Engine images are several gigabytes Pre-pull or bake into the node image; pin tags Weight download Tens of gigabytes per model Model cache on a persistent volume or local NVMe; avoid downloading at startup Load to GPU Read and copy the weights Fast local disk; streaming loaders such as vLLM's --load-format runai_streamer Warm-up Kernel compilation, CUDA graph capture Keep it, but exclude it from readiness only with a startup probe

Spot (preemptible) GPUs cost much less and fit batch work and extra replicas, but they can disappear: AWS gives a two-minute interruption notice, and Google Cloud's default notice for Spot VMs is shorter. Never put all interactive capacity on spot.

docs.title: Hosted GPU options
docs.text:
Option Examples Pays for idle time? Relative cost per unit of work Operations work Per-token API for open models Inference providers that host open-weight models No Low at low or spiky volume; higher than your own busy GPUs at sustained volume Lowest Serverless GPU containers Cloud Run with GPUs, Azure Container Apps serverless GPUs, Modal, RunPod Serverless No (scale to zero) Higher per GPU-second than VMs; nothing while idle; cold starts Low Managed model endpoints Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints, Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, cloud AI platforms' managed compute Yes, while running Above raw VMs; you pay for management Medium GPU VMs and Kubernetes node pools EC2 accelerated instances, Compute Engine GPUs, Azure GPU VMs, EKS, GKE, AKS Yes Lowest per GPU-hour at high utilization, lower still when reserved, lowest on spot Highest GPU clouds Specialized GPU providers with VMs and Kubernetes Yes Often below hyperscaler on-demand prices; fewer surrounding services High

Choose by utilization and control. TaskFlow's sensible path is a hosted API first, a serverless GPU or managed endpoint for an open model when privacy requires it at low volume, and a reserved GPU node pool only once steady traffic keeps the GPUs busy. The arithmetic is in cost optimization for LLM apps, and the general cloud cost levers in cost optimization and cloud bills.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choose Avoid 8B-class model, few users, one card 16-bit weights on a 24 GB GPU Promising production concurrency from it More concurrency on the same GPU FP8 KV cache, then 4-bit weights after evaluation Raising --max-num-seqs without cache to back it Model too large for one GPU Quantize first; tensor parallelism if quality requires 16-bit Pipeline parallelism across slow networks for interactive use Interactive traffic with daily peaks Warm minimum replicas plus queue-based scale-out Scale to zero for interactive features Offline batch inference Spot GPUs or scale-to-zero serverless GPUs Reserved capacity sized for the batch peak Laptop, CPU, or edge GGUF with llama.cpp or Ollama Data-center formats that need GPU kernels Steady, high utilization Reserved GPU nodes Per-second serverless pricing

docs.title: Estimating memory and concurrency
docs.text:
# scripts/vram_estimate.py
"""Estimate GPU memory and concurrency for serving a decoder-only model.

Rough planning numbers only: confirm with the engine's startup log, which
reports the real KV cache size. Shapes come from the model's config.json
(num_hidden_layers, num_attention_heads, num_key_value_heads, hidden_size,
optional head_dim); the parameter count comes from the model card.
"""
import argparse
import json

GIB = 1024**3
BYTES = {"fp16": 2.0, "bf16": 2.0, "fp8": 1.0, "int8": 1.0, "int4": 0.5}


def kv_bytes_per_token(cfg: dict, kv_dtype: str) -> float:
    heads = cfg["num_attention_heads"]
    kv_heads = cfg.get("num_key_value_heads", heads)  # fewer with grouped-query attention
    head_dim = cfg.get("head_dim") or cfg["hidden_size"] // heads
    return 2 * cfg["num_hidden_layers"] * kv_heads * head_dim * BYTES[kv_dtype]


def estimate(cfg: dict, params_b: float, weight_dtype: str, kv_dtype: str,
             gpu_gib: float, gpus: int = 1, context: int = 8192,
             mem_fraction: float = 0.9, runtime_gib_per_gpu: float = 2.0) -> dict:
    # 4-bit formats also store scales and zero points: add about 8%
    overhead = 1.08 if weight_dtype == "int4" else 1.0
    weights = params_b * 1e9 * BYTES[weight_dtype] * overhead
    usable = gpus * gpu_gib * GIB * mem_fraction
    runtime = gpus * runtime_gib_per_gpu * GIB  # activations, CUDA graphs, workspace
    kv_budget = usable - weights - runtime
    per_token = kv_bytes_per_token(cfg, kv_dtype)
    tokens = max(0.0, kv_budget / per_token)
    return {
        "weights_gib": weights / GIB,
        "kv_kib_per_token": per_token / 1024,
        "kv_budget_gib": kv_budget / GIB,
        "kv_tokens": int(tokens),
        "full_context_sequences": tokens / context,
        "fits": kv_budget > per_token * context,
    }


SHAPES = {
    # Generic shapes of popular open models; read real ones from config.json
    "8b": {"num_hidden_layers": 32, "num_attention_heads": 32,
           "num_key_value_heads": 8, "hidden_size": 4096},
    "70b": {"num_hidden_layers": 80, "num_attention_heads": 64,
            "num_key_value_heads": 8, "hidden_size": 8192},
}

SCENARIOS = [
    # (shape, billions of params, weights, kv cache, GPU GiB, GPUs)
    ("8b", 8.0, "bf16", "bf16", 24, 1),
    ("8b", 8.0, "int4", "bf16", 24, 1),
    ("8b", 8.0, "bf16", "fp8", 24, 1),
    ("8b", 8.0, "bf16", "bf16", 80, 1),
    ("70b", 70.6, "bf16", "bf16", 80, 1),
    ("70b", 70.6, "bf16", "bf16", 80, 2),
    ("70b", 70.6, "int4", "fp8", 80, 1),
]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--config", help="path to a model's config.json")
    parser.add_argument("--params-b", type=float, help="parameters in billions")
    parser.add_argument("--weights", default="bf16", choices=BYTES)
    parser.add_argument("--kv", default="bf16", choices=BYTES)
    parser.add_argument("--gpu-gib", type=float, default=80)
    parser.add_argument("--gpus", type=int, default=1)
    parser.add_argument("--context", type=int, default=8192)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    if args.config:
        with open(args.config, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            cfg = json.load(f)
        print(estimate(cfg, args.params_b, args.weights, args.kv,
                       args.gpu_gib, args.gpus, args.context))
    else:
        print(f"{'model':5} {'weights':7} {'kv':5} {'GPU':8} {'weights GiB':>11} "
              f"{'KiB/token':>9} {'KV GiB':>7} {'8K seqs':>7}")
        for shape, params, w, kv, gib, n in SCENARIOS:
            r = estimate(SHAPES[shape], params, w, kv, gib, n)
            gpu = f"{n}x{gib}GB"
            seqs = f"{r['full_context_sequences']:.1f}" if r["fits"] else "no fit"
            print(f"{shape:5} {w:7} {kv:5} {gpu:8} {r['weights_gib']:11.1f} "
                  f"{r['kv_kib_per_token']:9.0f} {r['kv_budget_gib']:7.1f} {seqs:>7}")

# The scenario table shown earlier in this lesson
python scripts/vram_estimate.py

# One real model: its config.json from the model repository, a 24 GB GPU, 4K context
python scripts/vram_estimate.py --config config.json --params-b 8 --gpu-gib 24 --context 4096
# {'weights_gib': 14.90..., 'kv_kib_per_token': 128.0, 'kv_budget_gib': 4.69...,
#  'kv_tokens': 38492, 'full_context_sequences': 9.39..., 'fits': True}

The runtime reserve (2 GiB per GPU) and the 90% memory fraction are assumptions; replace them with what your engine reports. Then compare the estimate with vLLM's startup line ("KV cache size: ... tokens, Maximum concurrency for ... tokens per request") and keep the measured value.

docs.title: Producing a quantized checkpoint
docs.text:
# scripts/quantize_fp8.py
# FP8 weights and dynamic FP8 activations with LLM Compressor; no calibration data needed.
# Follows the LLM Compressor README (November 2026); needs a GPU and the model's license.
import os

from llmcompressor import oneshot
from llmcompressor.modifiers.quantization import QuantizationModifier
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

MODEL_ID = os.environ["MODEL_ID"]  # chosen from the model hub after license review
SAVE_DIR = os.environ.get("SAVE_DIR", "model-fp8-block")

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)

recipe = QuantizationModifier(targets="Linear", scheme="FP8_BLOCK", ignore=["lm_head"])
oneshot(model=model, recipe=recipe)

model.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR)
tokenizer.save_pretrained(SAVE_DIR)

# GGUF for llama.cpp and Ollama: convert to a 16-bit GGUF, then quantize to Q4_K_M
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ./model-dir --outtype bf16 --outfile model-bf16.gguf
./build/bin/llama-quantize model-bf16.gguf model-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M

Either way, run the evaluation set against the quantized model and the original side by side, and keep the original for rollback. The quantized directory is served with the same vllm serve command as any other model.

docs.title: Scaling vLLM on queue length with KEDA
docs.text:
# k8s/vllm-chat-autoscaling.yaml
apiVersion: monitoring.coreos.com/v1
kind: PodMonitor
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: vllm-chat
  podMetricsEndpoints:
    - port: http
      path: /metrics
      interval: 15s
---
apiVersion: keda.sh/v1alpha1
kind: ScaledObject
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    name: vllm-chat # the Deployment from the serving lesson
  minReplicaCount: 1 # keep one warm replica for interactive traffic
  maxReplicaCount: 6 # also bounded by GPU quota and node pool size
  pollingInterval: 15
  advanced:
    horizontalPodAutoscalerConfig:
      behavior:
        scaleUp:
          policies:
            - type: Pods
              value: 2
              periodSeconds: 60
        scaleDown:
          stabilizationWindowSeconds: 900 # replicas are slow to replace
          policies:
            - type: Pods
              value: 1
              periodSeconds: 300
  triggers:
    - type: prometheus
      metadata:
        serverAddress: http://prometheus-operated.monitoring.svc:9090
        query: sum(vllm:num_requests_waiting{namespace="taskflow", model_name="taskflow-chat"})
        threshold: "4" # target average waiting requests per replica
  • The PodMonitor (a Prometheus Operator resource) scrapes each vLLM pod's /metrics. vLLM labels metrics with model_name, which is the --served-model-name.
  • KEDA turns the query into a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler target: with the default average-value metric type, it aims for about 4 waiting requests per replica, so 13 waiting requests ask for 4 replicas.
  • Scale-up adds at most 2 pods per minute; scale-down waits 15 minutes and removes one pod every 5 minutes, because a replica removed too early costs minutes to bring back.
  • maxReplicaCount must match what the GPU node pool and your cloud GPU quota can actually provide; a pending pod waiting for a GPU is not capacity. The node side is in scaling and resource management and the general autoscaling patterns in autoscaling server fleets.

docs.title: Measuring cold start
docs.text:
# Time a fresh replica from creation to Ready, and see where the time went
kubectl -n taskflow scale deployment vllm-chat --replicas=2
kubectl -n taskflow get pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=vllm-chat -w

# Events show scheduling, image pull, and probe timing for the new pod
kubectl -n taskflow describe pod <new-pod-name> | sed -n '/Events:/,$p'
kubectl -n taskflow logs <new-pod-name> | grep -E "Loading|KV cache size|startup complete"

Record each stage (pod scheduled, image pulled, weights loaded, ready) and size the startup probe, the autoscaler's lead time, and the minimum replica count from the measurements.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Size GPUs from weights plus KV cache for your real context lengths, and confirm with the engine's startup log.
  • Cap --max-model-len at what features need; context is paid in cache.
  • Try an FP8 KV cache before buying more GPUs, then quantized weights.
  • Evaluate every quantized model on your own tasks and keep the original for rollback.
  • Prefer quantization plus more replicas over splitting one replica across many GPUs when quality allows.
  • Autoscale on queue length or cache usage, scale out early, and scale in slowly.
  • Keep warm replicas for interactive features; reserve scale to zero for batch work.
  • Cache images and weights near the GPUs to shorten cold starts.
  • Put only interruptible work on spot GPUs.
  • Re-check hosting options as utilization changes; idle GPUs are the most common waste.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The engine fails to start after a model upgrade. Detect: startup errors while allocating the cache, or a log saying the context does not fit. Cause: the new model has more layers or KV heads, or a larger default context, so weights plus minimum cache exceed the GPU. Fix: recompute with the calculator, set --max-model-len, use an FP8 cache or quantized weights, or move to a larger GPU.
  • A burst of long documents stalls every user. Detect: vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc near 100%, preemptions rising, queue growing. Cause: long conversations consume the cache that short ones need. Fix: separate long-document traffic onto its own replicas, cap context per feature, and scale out on queue length.
  • Autoscaling adds pods that never become ready. Detect: pods stay Pending with "Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu", or nodes never arrive. Cause: GPU quota or node pool maximum reached, or the region has no capacity. Fix: align maxReplicaCount with quota, request quota ahead of launches, reserve capacity, or add a second region or GPU type.
  • Users wait minutes during the morning peak. Detect: queue length rises at the same time daily; new replicas become ready ten minutes later. Cause: reactive scaling with long cold starts. Fix: scheduled scale-up before the peak, a higher minimum, pre-pulled images, and cached weights.
  • Answers got worse after a cost-saving change. Detect: evaluation scores or user feedback drop after switching to a 4-bit model. Cause: quantization hurt this model on this task, often in structured output or long context. Fix: compare against the original on the evaluation set, try an 8-bit format or another quantization method, or keep 16-bit for the affected feature.
  • The GPU bill stays high at night. Detect: low request rates but a constant replica count. Cause: a high minReplicaCount or no scale-in. Fix: time-based minimums, scale-in policies, and moving batch work to hours when interactive capacity is idle.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• VRAM: The GPU's own memory, which holds weights, cache, and activations.
  • KV cache: Stored keys and values for every active token; the memory that sets concurrency.
  • Grouped-query attention: Sharing each key-value head among several query heads, shrinking the KV cache.
  • Quantization: Storing weights, activations, or the cache in fewer bits.
  • FP8 / INT8 / 4-bit: Common reduced precisions for serving.
  • GPTQ / AWQ: Post-training 4-bit weight quantization methods.
  • GGUF: llama.cpp's single-file model format with its own quantization types.
  • Tensor parallelism: Splitting each layer of a model across GPUs.
  • Cold start: The time for a new replica to become ready to serve.
  • Scale to zero: Removing all replicas when idle, at the cost of cold starts.
  • Spot (preemptible) capacity: Discounted capacity the provider can reclaim at short notice.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Sizing GPUs from the weights alone and forgetting the KV cache.
  • Assuming a model that loads will serve many users.
  • Treating quantization as free; it must pass your own evaluation.
  • Splitting a model across GPUs when a quantized single-GPU replica would serve more users.
  • Autoscaling GPU servers on CPU or GPU utilization.
  • Scaling interactive model servers to zero.
  • Setting maxReplicaCount above the GPU quota.
  • Comparing hosting options by hourly price instead of cost per unit of work at your utilization.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which four things occupy GPU memory when serving a model, and which of them sets concurrency?
  2. A model has 48 layers, 8 KV heads, and head dimension 128, with a 16-bit cache. How much KV cache does one token need, and how many 8K-token conversations fit in 30 GiB of cache? (2 x 48 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 196,608 bytes = 192 KiB per token; 8,192 tokens = 1.5 GiB per conversation; 20 conversations.)
  3. Why does 4-bit quantization speed up decoding even when memory is not short?
  4. Compare FP8, GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF: where does each run, and how is each produced?
  5. When is tensor parallelism the right answer, and when is a quantized model on more replicas better?
  6. Which metrics should trigger autoscaling of a vLLM deployment, and why not CPU?
  7. List the steps of a cold start and one fix for each.
  8. For steady, high traffic and for spiky, low traffic, which hosting options are cheapest, and why?

docs.title: Deployment Cost and Performance Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: Questions and answers on serving open models, latency, cost, and GPU capacity, grouped by lesson, followed by production scenarios. Answers are short enough to say aloud; follow the links for depth.

docs.title: 1. Why does a dedicated serving engine outperform calling a model's generate function once per request?
docs.text: Decoding produces one token per forward pass, and each pass reads all the weights from GPU memory, so a single sequence leaves the GPU's arithmetic units mostly idle. An engine such as vLLM or SGLang runs many sequences in the same pass (continuous batching), reusing every weight read for all of them, and manages the KV cache efficiently so more sequences fit. The same GPU serves many times more users.

docs.title: 2. What are prefill and decode, and why do they behave differently?
docs.text: Prefill processes the whole prompt in one parallel pass, fills the KV cache, and produces the first token; it is compute-bound. Decode then generates one token per step; it is memory-bandwidth-bound because each step moves the weights and the sequence's cache for little arithmetic. Prefill mostly sets time to first token, decode sets the rest of the latency.

docs.title: 3. What is the KV cache, and how do you size it per token?
docs.text: The stored attention keys and values for every token of every active sequence, so attention does not recompute the history at each step. Bytes per token = 2 x layers x KV heads x head dimension x bytes per value. For 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and 16-bit values, that is 128 KiB per token, or 1 GiB for an 8,192-token conversation.

docs.title: 4. What problem does PagedAttention solve?
docs.text: Older servers reserved one contiguous slab of cache per request, sized for the maximum length, wasting most of it; the vLLM paper measured that only 20-38% of cache memory held real tokens. PagedAttention splits the cache into fixed-size blocks (16 tokens by default in the paper) mapped through per-sequence block tables, allocates blocks as tokens arrive, and lets sequences share prefix blocks. Waste drops to part of one block per sequence.

docs.title: 5. What is continuous batching, and how does it differ from static batching?
docs.text: Static batching runs a batch until its longest sequence finishes, so short sequences leave idle slots and new requests wait. Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling, introduced by Orca) decides at every decode step: finished sequences leave, waiting requests join, and the batch stays full. Throughput rises and queueing falls.

docs.title: 6. What is chunked prefill, and what does vLLM's --max-num-batched-tokens trade?
docs.text: Chunked prefill splits a long prompt's prefill into pieces mixed into decode steps, so one huge prompt does not freeze everyone's streaming. --max-num-batched-tokens caps the tokens processed per step: smaller values keep other streams smooth, larger values give long prompts a faster first token.

docs.title: 7. What is preemption in a serving engine, and what does frequent preemption mean?
docs.text: When the KV cache fills, the engine pauses a running sequence, frees its blocks, and later recomputes or reloads them. Occasional preemption during bursts is normal; a steady rate means the server admits more concurrent work than its memory holds. Fix it with fewer concurrent sequences, shorter context caps, output limits, cache quantization, or more replicas.

docs.title: 8. How does prefix caching work, and how should prompts be laid out for it?
docs.text: The engine keeps KV blocks of finished requests keyed by a hash of their tokens; a new prompt that starts with the same tokens reuses them and skips that prefill. vLLM enables it by default, and SGLang's RadixAttention is built around it. Put stable content first (instructions, tool definitions, shared documents) and variable content last, byte-for-byte identical across requests.

docs.title: 9. When would you choose vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, or Ollama?
docs.text: vLLM or SGLang for multi-user serving on data-center GPUs; SGLang is especially strong with shared prefixes (agents, multi-turn chat). llama.cpp for CPUs, Apple silicon, single GPUs, and edge devices with GGUF models. Ollama for developer laptops and quick prototypes, accepting less control. Benchmark with your own prompts and concurrency before deciding.

docs.title: 10. What is the status of Text Generation Inference, and what should a team using it do?
docs.text: Its README says it is in maintenance mode and recommends vLLM, SGLang, or local engines such as llama.cpp and MLX; as of November 2026 the repository is archived, with the last release in December 2025. Existing users should plan a migration and benchmark the replacement on their workload; new projects should not start on it.

docs.title: 11. What does "OpenAI-compatible" guarantee, and what does it not?
docs.text: It guarantees routes and request and response shapes for common fields (/v1/chat/completions, /v1/models, often /v1/responses and /v1/embeddings), so the official SDKs work by changing the base URL. It does not guarantee identical behavior for tool calling, structured output, reasoning output, or every sampling parameter; those depend on the engine and the model's chat template, so test the features you use.

docs.title: 12. How do you secure a self-hosted model server?
docs.text: Keep it internal: a ClusterIP Service, no public IP, and a network policy that admits only the backend. Do not rely on the engine's API key: vLLM's --api-key covers only routes under /v1, /v2, /inference, and /cohere, leaving others such as /invocations open. Authenticate at a gateway, log access, and audit exposed ports.

docs.title: 13. What does a model server on Kubernetes need that a web API does not?
docs.text: A GPU request (nvidia.com/gpu) with the device plugin or GPU operator, tolerations for tainted GPU nodes, a startup probe sized for minutes of weight loading, a persistent or node-local model cache, a memory-backed /dev/shm volume, the Hugging Face token from a Secret, and autoscaling on queue metrics rather than CPU.

docs.title: 14. Why give a deployment a served-model alias?
docs.text: --served-model-name taskflow-chat decouples the application from the underlying model ID. Configuration says CHAT_MODEL=taskflow-chat; swapping the model behind it is an infrastructure change with no code release, and metrics carry the alias in their model_name label.

docs.title: 15. How do you prove a new deployment serves the right model correctly?
docs.text: A /health check only proves the process is up. A smoke test after each deploy lists /v1/models to confirm the alias is served, sends a short real request through the same client code, and checks the output is plausible (for example, that owners named in meeting notes appear in the summary).

docs.title: 16. Define TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end latency, and how they relate.
docs.text: TTFT is time to first token (network, queue, and prefill). TPOT, or inter-token latency, is the average gap between later tokens. End-to-end latency is approximately TTFT + (output tokens - 1) x TPOT, plus application work.

docs.title: 17. Why does output length usually dominate latency? Give an example.
docs.text: Each output token is a sequential decode step. With a TTFT of 1.2 s and 40 tokens per second, 400 output tokens take 1.2 + 399 x 0.025 = 11.2 s; cutting output to 150 tokens gives about 4.9 s even with no other change. Prompt changes mostly move TTFT; output changes move everything.

docs.title: 18. How does prompt length affect latency?
docs.text: Prefill time grows with the number of input tokens that must be processed, so long prompts delay the first token, especially when most of the input is new. Send fewer, better retrieved passages, trim conversation history, strip unneeded markup, and make the stable part cacheable.

docs.title: 19. How does prompt caching reduce latency, and what breaks it?
docs.text: The provider or engine reuses the processed prefix of a prompt it has seen recently, skipping that prefill. It requires an identical prefix and a minimum length (1,024 tokens on recent OpenAI models; it varies elsewhere). A timestamp, request id, or shuffled list near the top of the prompt makes every request a miss. Monitor cached tokens per request after each deploy.

docs.title: 20. When should you stream, and when is it pointless?
docs.text: Stream any answer a person reads: the first text appears at TTFT instead of at the end. Streaming does not make generation faster. For output parsed as a whole, such as task-creation JSON, streaming adds complexity without helping the user; shrink the output instead.

docs.title: 21. How do you measure TTFT correctly in code?
docs.text: Start a timer before the request, record the time of the first chunk that contains text (earlier chunks may carry only a role), and record the end. Request usage in the stream (stream_options.include_usage on OpenAI-compatible servers) so tokens per second uses real token counts, not chunk counts.

docs.title: 22. Which latency statistics should you report?
docs.text: Percentiles (p50, p95, p99) per feature and model, for TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end latency, measured at the client and at the server. Averages hide the slow tail that users notice, and a fast server can still feel slow behind blocking retrieval or a slow client connection.

docs.title: 23. Why do per-stream speed and aggregate throughput move in opposite directions?
docs.text: More concurrent sequences per decode step raise total tokens per second for the server but give each stream a smaller share of each step, so every user sees slower text. Engine settings such as maximum concurrent sequences set the balance.

docs.title: 24. How do you reduce an agent's latency?
docs.text: Fewer sequential model calls: coarser tools ("create these three tasks"), parallel tool calls, combining planning with acting, a cap on steps, and streaming an early status update. Each removed round trip saves a full model call plus network time.

docs.title: 25. How do you parallelize independent calls safely?
docs.text: Start lookups that do not depend on each other together (document search, open tasks, permission check) with a concurrency limit and a timeout on each, so one slow dependency cannot stall the answer or exhaust connection pools and rate limits. The combined wait becomes the slowest lookup instead of the sum.

docs.title: 26. How does speculative decoding work, and why does it not change output quality?
docs.text: A cheap proposer (a draft model, extra prediction heads, or n-gram lookup) guesses several tokens; the target model checks them all in one forward pass, keeps the longest agreed prefix, and adds one token of its own. With the right acceptance rule the output follows the target model's distribution, so quality is unchanged; the gain comes from verifying several tokens for roughly the cost of one memory-bound step.

docs.title: 27. With acceptance rate a and k drafted tokens, how many tokens does one target pass yield?
docs.text: (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a), from Leviathan and colleagues. For a = 0.7 and k = 4: (1 - 0.168) / 0.3 = 2.77 tokens per pass; for a = 0.3 it is only 1.42, before paying for the drafting.

docs.title: 28. When does speculative decoding hurt?
docs.text: At high load, decode steps are already full of other users' work, so extra verification competes with them; and with unpredictable output, acceptance is low and drafted tokens are wasted. vLLM positions it for low to medium QPS; benchmark at real concurrency and disable or switch methods if inter-token latency worsens.

docs.title: 29. How does regional placement affect latency?
docs.text: Light in fiber covers about 200 km per millisecond, so cross-continent calls add tens of milliseconds per round trip, multiplied by every sequential call an agent makes. Put the backend next to the model endpoint, reuse connections, and use regional or global endpoints deliberately, checking that global routing still meets data residency rules.

docs.title: 30. What are provider service tiers, and when are they worth it?
docs.text: Options that trade price for speed or availability, such as OpenAI's service_tier values priority (or fast) for faster processing at a higher price and flex for cheaper, slower processing with occasional unavailability. Use fast tiers only on the few latency-critical paths and flex or batch for work nobody waits for.

docs.title: 31. What makes up the cost of one model request?
docs.text: Uncached input tokens at the input price, cached input at a much lower price, cache writes where a provider charges for them, output tokens (including hidden reasoning tokens) at a higher price, and tool fees. Output usually costs several times as much per token as input.

docs.title: 32. Why track cost per completed task instead of cost per request?
docs.text: Retries, validation failures, and abandoned requests bill without producing an outcome. Dividing spend by successful outcomes (tasks created, answers shown) shows the real unit cost and exposes failures that per-request averages hide.

docs.title: 33. Why estimate tokens before a call and record usage after it?
docs.text: Before the call, a local tokenizer estimate enforces budgets cheaply: trim history, cap context, check a tenant's quota. After the call, the provider's usage object is what you are billed for, including cached and reasoning tokens no local count can predict. Different providers tokenize differently, so estimates need a margin or the provider's counting endpoint.

docs.title: 34. How do providers' usage objects differ?
docs.text: OpenAI's input_tokens and Chat Completions' prompt_tokens include cached tokens, reported as a subset; Anthropic's input_tokens counts only tokens after the last cache breakpoint, with cache reads and writes reported separately; Gemini's promptTokenCount includes cached content, and thinking tokens come separately. Normalize them once so dashboards compare like with like.

docs.title: 35. Compare provider prompt caching, an exact response cache, and a semantic cache.
docs.text: Prompt caching reuses a processed prefix, saves most of its input cost, and is low risk. An exact response cache reuses the whole answer for identical requests and saves the whole call but can leak data or serve stale answers if keyed badly. A semantic cache reuses answers to similar questions and risks wrong answers for questions that differ in a detail.

docs.title: 36. What must a response cache key include?
docs.text: The model, the prompt version, the full input, the tenant and permission scope, and the version of any data the answer depends on. Missing tenant or permission scope can serve one customer's answer to another.

docs.title: 37. When should work go through a batch API, and what does it trade?
docs.text: When nobody waits for it: nightly summaries, backfills after prompt changes, evaluation runs, data enrichment. OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google price batch work at half the interactive rate as of November 2026, in exchange for asynchronous completion within 24 hours, so the application must poll, reconcile results by id, and retry failed lines.

docs.title: 38. What routing patterns reduce cost?
docs.text: Per-feature routing (each feature configured with a model size), a cascade (small model first, escalate on invalid or unsure output), and a learned router that predicts which model a query needs, as in RouteLLM. Start with per-feature routing; it captures most of the savings with no runtime logic.

docs.title: 39. When does a cascade stop paying off?
docs.text: Expected cost = small + escalation rate x large. With a small model at 1 unit and a large one at 10, 30% escalation costs 4 units versus 10, but 90% escalation costs 10 units and adds latency to most requests. Track the escalation rate per feature and route features that usually escalate straight to the large model.

docs.title: 40. What is distillation, and when is it worth it?
docs.text: Training a small model to reproduce a large model's outputs on one narrow, high-volume task, such as extracting tasks from sentences. It cuts cost and latency per request but needs reviewed training data, an evaluation set, a training pipeline, retraining as the task changes, and a check of the provider's terms on training with its outputs.

docs.title: 41. How do output caps and context trimming save money?
docs.text: Output caps bound the most expensive tokens; ask for the length the UI needs and set max_output_tokens or max_tokens, checking the finish reason for truncation. Context trimming keeps recent turns verbatim and summarizes or drops older ones, and retrieval caps send fewer, reranked passages.

docs.title: 42. Why do an agent's input tokens grow roughly with the square of its steps?
docs.text: Each step re-sends the whole conversation so far, which grows by each step's output and tool results. The total input over n steps is a sum of growing contexts, roughly proportional to n squared, unless the prefix is cached or old tool results are truncated.

docs.title: 43. How do you track cost per feature without overloading metrics?
docs.text: Route every model call through one wrapper that takes a feature name, normalizes usage, and increments counters labeled only by feature, model, and token type. Tenant ids go to structured logs and a per-tenant usage store, never to metric labels, and no prompt text is recorded.

docs.title: 44. When is self-hosting cheaper than a hosted API?
docs.text: Cost per token = GPU-hour cost / (tokens per hour at full load x utilization). At 10% utilization a GPU's tokens cost eight times what they cost at 80%. Self-hosting wins only when sustained utilization pushes that below the API's price for a model of similar quality, after engineering and on-call time.

docs.title: 45. Why can reasoning models cost far more than expected?
docs.text: They generate hidden reasoning tokens billed as output before the visible answer, often far more tokens than the answer itself. Use the lowest reasoning effort that passes evaluation, route simple features to non-reasoning models, and include reasoning tokens in dashboards.

docs.title: 46. What occupies GPU memory when serving a model?
docs.text: The weights (parameters x bytes per parameter), the KV cache for active tokens, runtime memory (activations, CUDA graphs, workspace), and whatever headroom the engine leaves. Weights are fixed per replica; the remaining memory becomes cache, and the cache sets concurrency.

docs.title: 47. Estimate how many 8K-token conversations an 8B model serves on a 24 GB GPU.
docs.text: Weights in 16-bit take about 14.9 GiB. Using 90% of 24 GiB (21.6 GiB) and about 2 GiB of runtime leaves about 4.7 GiB of cache. At 128 KiB per token, an 8K conversation needs 1 GiB, so about 4.7 full conversations. With 4-bit weights, the cache grows to about 15.6 GiB; with an FP8 cache instead, concurrency doubles to about 9.4.

docs.title: 48. How does grouped-query attention change serving capacity?
docs.text: Several query heads share one key-value head, so the cache stores fewer KV heads per layer. A model with 8 KV heads instead of 32 needs a quarter of the cache per token, quadrupling the conversations that fit in the same memory.

docs.title: 49. Why is decoding limited by memory bandwidth, and what bound does that give?
docs.text: Each step reads the weights and caches from memory for little arithmetic. Steps per second at batch size 1 are at most bandwidth / bytes read per step: 16 GB of weights on a GPU with 2 TB/s gives at most about 125 steps per second; the same model in 4-bit (about 4.3 GB) allows about 465.

docs.title: 50. Compare FP8, INT8, GPTQ, AWQ, and GGUF.
docs.text: FP8 (8-bit floating point) runs fast on GPUs with FP8 support, usually with a small quality loss. INT8 (W8A8 or weight-only, as in LLM.int8()) halves weight memory on most GPUs. GPTQ and AWQ are post-training 4-bit weight methods served by vLLM and SGLang, produced with GPTQModel or LLM Compressor. GGUF is llama.cpp's single-file format with its own quant types (Q8_0, Q5_K_M, Q4_K_M) for CPUs, Apple silicon, and GPUs.

docs.title: 51. Why quantize the KV cache separately from the weights?
docs.text: The cache, not the weights, sets concurrency. An FP8 cache (--kv-cache-dtype fp8 in vLLM) halves bytes per token and roughly doubles concurrency at a small quality cost, independent of the weight format, so it is often the first lever to try.

docs.title: 52. What changed in the quantization tooling recently?
docs.text: AutoAWQ is officially deprecated and was adopted into the vLLM project's LLM Compressor; the AutoGPTQ repository is archived, and vLLM's documentation lists GPTQModel instead. Use maintained tools and check that the engine version supports the exact format before deploying.

docs.title: 53. Compare tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism for serving.
docs.text: Tensor parallelism splits each layer across GPUs in one server and needs fast GPU links. Pipeline parallelism puts different layers on different GPUs or nodes, reaching larger models at the cost of inter-stage latency. Data parallelism adds whole replicas for throughput once a replica fits. Splitting buys fit, not efficiency; a quantized one-GPU replica scaled out often serves more users per GPU.

docs.title: 54. Which metrics should drive autoscaling of a vLLM deployment, and why not CPU?
docs.text: Requests waiting (vllm:num_requests_waiting), KV cache usage (vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc), or measured TTFT p95. CPU usage says nothing about GPU work, and GPU utilization saturates long before users suffer; queue length shows waiting users directly.

docs.title: 55. How does a KEDA Prometheus trigger with threshold: "4" scale a deployment?
docs.text: KEDA feeds the query result to a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler with an average-value target of 4 per replica, so 13 waiting requests ask for ceil(13 / 4) = 4 replicas, within the minimum and maximum replica counts and the scaling behavior policies.

docs.title: 56. What steps make up a model replica's cold start, and how do you shorten each?
docs.text: Provisioning a GPU node (keep warm nodes or reserve capacity), pulling a multi-gigabyte image (pre-pull or bake it into the node image), downloading weights (persistent or node-local model cache), loading them onto the GPU (fast local disk or a streaming loader such as vLLM's runai_streamer), and warm-up (unavoidable; cover it with a startup probe). Cold paths can take many minutes against one or two on a warm path.

docs.title: 57. When is scaling a model server to zero appropriate?
docs.text: For batch or internal workloads where waiting minutes for a cold start is acceptable, and on serverless GPU platforms that bill per second. Interactive features such as the TaskFlow Assistant need at least one warm replica.

docs.title: 58. Where do spot GPUs fit?
docs.text: Batch inference, evaluation runs, and extra replicas above a reserved baseline. The provider can reclaim them at short notice (AWS gives a two-minute warning; Google Cloud's default for Spot VMs is shorter), so interactive capacity must not depend on them alone.

docs.title: 59. Compare hosted GPU options by relative cost.
docs.text: Per-token APIs for open models have no idle cost and the least operations work, and cost more per token than your own busy GPUs at sustained volume. Serverless GPU containers bill per second and scale to zero, with cold starts. Managed endpoints add management on top of instance prices. GPU VMs and Kubernetes node pools are cheapest per GPU-hour, especially reserved or spot, but you pay while idle and run everything.

docs.title: 60. How would you choose GPU capacity for a newly adopted open model?
docs.text: Read the model's shape from its config, compute weights and per-token cache for the formats you consider, estimate concurrency from real context lengths, and pick the smallest GPU and format that meets it. Then evaluate quality of any quantized format, load the model, compare the engine's reported KV cache size with the estimate, and load-test TTFT and TPOT at expected concurrency before committing to reservations.

docs.title: 61. After a prompt change, the Assistant's time to first token doubled with no traffic change. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: cached input tokens per request before and after the deploy, and the first lines of the new prompt template.

How to confirm: compare cached_tokens (or cache_read_input_tokens) across releases; diff the rendered prompt for content that changes per request, such as a date, user name, or request id.

Likely causes and fixes: variable text moved into the stable prefix, breaking prompt caching; move it after the stable content, add a test that the prefix is identical across requests, and alert on cache hit ratio. See latency optimization.

docs.title: 62. A self-hosted vLLM server shows rising TTFT while GPU utilization looks normal.
docs.text:
What to check first: vllm:num_requests_waiting, vllm:request_queue_time_seconds, and vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc.

How to confirm: queue time grows with traffic while per-token decode speed stays flat; the cache sits near full.

Likely causes and fixes: more concurrent requests than cache and --max-num-seqs admit, so requests queue. Add replicas and autoscale on queue length, lower --max-model-len, or use an FP8 cache or quantized weights. See serving open models.

docs.title: 63. The model bill doubled while traffic stayed flat.
docs.text:
What to check first: token counts per request by feature and token type, annotated with recent releases.

How to confirm: find the feature whose input or output tokens per request jumped, and the release that changed its prompt, retrieval settings, model, or reasoning effort.

Likely causes and fixes: more retrieved passages, a longer template, a broken cache prefix, longer answers from a new model, or higher reasoning effort. Revert or cap the change, add prompt-size checks to CI, and alert on tokens per request. See cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: 64. Under bursts, self-hosted latency becomes erratic and throughput drops.
docs.text:
What to check first: vllm:num_preemptions and cache usage during the bursts.

How to confirm: preemptions rise exactly when cache usage hits 100%, often during long-document requests.

Likely causes and fixes: admitted sequences outgrow the cache, so the engine evicts and recomputes them. Lower --max-num-seqs, cap output and context per feature, isolate long-document traffic on separate replicas, and add capacity. See GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: 65. Model server pods restart in a loop after a model upgrade.
docs.text:
What to check first: pod events and the last log lines before each restart.

How to confirm: liveness probe failures during weight loading, or a CUDA out-of-memory error while allocating the cache.

Likely causes and fixes: no startup probe or one shorter than the new cold start; or the larger model plus its default context no longer fits. Add a startup probe sized from a measured cold start, set --max-model-len, recompute memory, and use a quantized format or a larger GPU. See serving open models.

docs.title: 66. Tool calls work against the hosted API but fail against the self-hosted model.
docs.text:
What to check first: the raw responses from both backends for the same request, and the engine's tool-calling configuration for that model.

How to confirm: the self-hosted response returns tool calls as plain text or in another shape; the chat template or tool parser differs.

Likely causes and fixes: "OpenAI-compatible" does not mean identical behavior. Enable the engine's tool parser for the model family, test with the model's chat template, and keep an evaluation set that runs against every backend. See serving open models.

docs.title: 67. Meeting summaries take twenty seconds, but TTFT is under a second.
docs.text:
What to check first: output tokens per summary and the finish reason.

How to confirm: summaries average hundreds of tokens more than the UI shows, and the prompt sets no length.

Likely causes and fixes: decode time from long outputs. Ask for a fixed format and length, set an output limit, stream the answer, and consider a faster model for summaries. See latency optimization.

docs.title: 68. Users say the task agent "thinks" for a long time before doing anything.
docs.text:
What to check first: traces of one agent run: the number of sequential model calls and tool calls before the first visible action.

How to confirm: several planning calls run in series before the first tool result; each adds a full round trip.

Likely causes and fixes: fine-grained tools, a planning call on every step, and no parallel tool calls. Use coarser tools, allow parallel calls, cap steps, and stream a status update early. See latency optimization.

docs.title: 69. A small-model-first cascade was added to save money, but costs did not fall.
docs.text:
What to check first: the escalation rate per feature.

How to confirm: most requests escalate; cost per request is close to always using the large model, and latency rose.

Likely causes and fixes: the small model is not good enough for that feature, or the confidence threshold is miscalibrated. Evaluate per feature, route that feature straight to the large model, calibrate the threshold on an evaluation set, or distill a better small model. See cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: 70. Autoscaling created new model server pods that stay Pending.
docs.text:
What to check first: pod events and the GPU node pool's size and quota.

How to confirm: events show "Insufficient nvidia.com/gpu"; the node autoscaler cannot add nodes because of quota or regional capacity.

Likely causes and fixes: maxReplicaCount exceeds what the cluster and quota can supply. Align it with real capacity, request quota ahead of launches, reserve capacity, or allow another GPU type or region. See GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: 71. Every weekday morning, users wait minutes for answers.
docs.text:
What to check first: queue length and replica readiness times around the morning ramp.

How to confirm: the queue grows at the same time each day, and new replicas become ready many minutes after scaling starts.

Likely causes and fixes: reactive scaling with a long cold start. Scale up on a schedule before the peak, raise the minimum replicas during working hours, pre-pull images, and cache weights near the GPUs. See GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: 72. Answer quality dropped after switching to a 4-bit model to save money.
docs.text:
What to check first: evaluation scores of the original and quantized models on the same set, by feature.

How to confirm: the drop concentrates in specific tasks, often structured output or long context, and reproduces offline.

Likely causes and fixes: quantization error affects this model on these tasks. Try an 8-bit or FP8 format, another 4-bit method or checkpoint, or keep 16-bit for the affected feature; never ship a quantized model without running the evaluation set. See GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: 73. A customer saw another customer's task names in an answer.
docs.text:
What to check first: any response cache in the path and how its key is built.

How to confirm: the same cache key is produced for two tenants with the same question; cache hit logs show the entry crossing tenants.

Likely causes and fixes: the key omits the tenant and permission scope. Purge the cache, add tenant, permission scope, model, prompt version, and data version to the key, add a test that two tenants never share entries, and treat it as a security incident. See cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: 74. Speculative decoding was enabled, and peak-hour streaming got slower.
docs.text:
What to check first: inter-token latency and speculation acceptance metrics, at peak and off-peak.

How to confirm: acceptance is low and the slowdown appears only under high load.

Likely causes and fixes: a busy server with unpredictable output, so verification work is wasted. Disable it at high load, switch to a model-based method if the model supports one, and benchmark at real concurrency. See latency optimization.

docs.text:
