docs.title: Latency Optimization
docs.text:
An LLM feature feels slow for one of two reasons: nothing appears for a long time, or text appears and then takes ages to finish. Those are different problems with different fixes. This lesson splits a request's latency into its parts (network, queueing, prefill, and decode), defines the metrics that separate them (time to first token, time per output token, end-to-end latency), and works through the levers in order of how often they matter: generating fewer tokens, sending fewer and more cacheable input tokens, streaming, making fewer and parallel calls, choosing smaller or faster models, placing compute near users, and, for self-hosted models, speculative decoding and engine settings.

The running examples are TaskFlow's features: the Assistant that turns a sentence into a task, project Q&A over documents, the agent that updates tasks through tools, and meeting-notes summaries. Each has a different latency profile, so each gets a different mix of fixes.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Users judge an interactive feature by how quickly something useful appears. A meeting summary that starts streaming after half a second feels fast even if it finishes eight seconds later; a task-creation call that shows a spinner for four seconds feels broken, even though it produced only fifty tokens. Knowing which part of the request dominates tells you whether to stream, trim the prompt, shorten the answer, or pick another model.

Latency also compounds. An agent that makes five sequential model calls, each with a two-second answer, takes ten seconds before any tool result reaches the user. A RAG answer that embeds the query, searches, reranks, and then generates pays every step in series unless some run in parallel. And tail latency matters more than the average: if 5% of Assistant calls take twelve seconds, many users see one of them in a session.

Finally, latency and cost are coupled. Output tokens cost the most money and the most time, so many latency fixes (shorter answers, smaller models, cached prefixes) also cut the bill, which is covered in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI latency guide. The latency optimization guide organizes the work into seven principles: "Process tokens faster. Generate fewer tokens. Use fewer input tokens. Make fewer requests. Parallelize. Make your users wait less." and "Don't default to an LLM." It notes that "a long prompt can delay the first token, especially when much of the input is new".
  • OpenAI prompt caching. The prompt caching guide lists among the benefits to "reduce the time spent processing input before the response starts", states that prompt caching is enabled by default for supported models, and that caches "cannot be reused across regional processing boundaries".
  • Speculative decoding. Leviathan, Kalman, and Matias, Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding, show that a small draft model's guesses can be verified by the large model in parallel, reporting "a 2X-3X acceleration compared to the standard T5X implementation, with identical outputs".
  • vLLM speculative decoding. The vLLM guide positions the feature for reducing "inter-token latency under medium-to-low QPS (queries per second), memory-bound workloads", and ranks model-based methods (EAGLE, MTP, draft models) above simpler n-gram and suffix methods for latency.
  • Disaggregated serving. The DistServe paper, Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-optimized Large Language Model Serving, shows that running prefill and decode on the same GPUs makes them interfere, and that separating them lets a system meet time-to-first-token and time-per-output-token targets at higher load.

Popular tools and providers: streaming in every provider SDK; prompt caching at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google; priority or fast service tiers at hosted providers; regional and global endpoints at cloud AI platforms; vLLM and SGLang for self-hosted speculative decoding and chunked prefill; OpenTelemetry and Prometheus for measuring each stage.

docs.title: Where the time goes
docs.text:
One request to a model passes through these stages:

Stage What happens Grows with Typical lever Network and TLS Connect, send the prompt, receive bytes Distance, new connections Keep-alive, nearby region Queueing Wait for a provider or GPU slot Load, rate limits, capacity Capacity, priority tiers, fewer requests Prefill Process every input token, produce the first token Input tokens not already cached Shorter prompts, prompt caching Decode Generate the remaining tokens one by one Output tokens (and reasoning tokens) Fewer output tokens, faster models, speculative decoding Application work Retrieval, tool calls, validation, rendering Number of sequential steps Parallel calls, fewer round trips

Two derived numbers describe most of it:

TTFT  (time to first token)   = network + queue + prefill
TPOT  (time per output token) = average gap between tokens after the first
end-to-end latency            = TTFT + (output tokens - 1) x TPOT

Meeting summary, before: TTFT 1.2 s, 400 output tokens at 40 tokens/s (TPOT 25 ms)
  1.2 s + 399 x 0.025 s = 11.2 s
After: cached prefix and less context (TTFT 0.6 s), five bullets (150 tokens)
  0.6 s + 149 x 0.025 s = 4.3 s

The arithmetic explains the most common surprise: for answers longer than a few sentences, decode time dominates. Halving the prompt improves TTFT; halving the answer halves the whole request.

docs.title: The metrics to collect
docs.text:
Metric Measures Where TTFT Time until the first token arrives Client side, per request TPOT, also called inter-token latency (ITL) Smoothness of streaming Client or engine metrics Output tokens per second, per stream How fast one user's text appears Client side Aggregate tokens per second Throughput of a server or account Engine metrics, provider dashboards End-to-end latency What the user waited in total Client and backend traces Queue time Waiting before processing starts Engine metrics (vllm:request_queue_time_seconds)

Measure percentiles (p50, p95, p99), split by feature and by model, and measure both at the client and at the server: a fast server with a slow client connection or a blocking retrieval step still feels slow. Per-stream speed and aggregate throughput move in opposite directions under load, because a server that admits more concurrent streams gives each one a smaller share of every decode step. Tracing each stage is covered in LLM observability and tracing.

docs.title: Generate fewer tokens
docs.text:
Output tokens are the most expensive part of a request in time and money, so start here:

  • Ask for the length the UI needs. "Return five bullets" or "reply with one sentence" shortens answers more reliably than hoping.
  • Set an output limit (max_output_tokens in OpenAI's Responses API, max_tokens in Chat Completions-style servers and the Anthropic Messages API). It caps the worst case, though a capped answer is truncated, so check the finish reason.
  • Keep structured output compact. Task creation needs a small JSON object, not prose around it; short field names and no echoed input save tokens on every call (see structured output and validation).
  • Control reasoning. Reasoning models generate hidden reasoning tokens before the answer; they cost time even though the user never sees them. Use a lower reasoning effort for simple tasks, as described in reasoning models and thinking.

docs.title: Send fewer, more cacheable input tokens
docs.text:
Prefill time grows with the input tokens that must be processed. Two levers apply:

  1. Send less. Retrieve fewer, better passages for project Q&A, trim old conversation turns, and strip markup the model does not need.
  2. Make the rest cacheable. Hosted providers and self-hosted engines reuse the work for a prompt prefix they have seen recently. Put stable content first (instructions, tool definitions, shared documents) and the variable part last, and keep the stable part byte-for-byte identical. A timestamp in the first line of the system prompt defeats caching for every request.

Provider details differ and change; check the current documentation:

Provider How caching is triggered (November 2026) How to see hits OpenAI Automatic for supported models; minimum 1,024 input tokens on recent models usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens Anthropic A top-level cache_control field (automatic) or explicit breakpoints (up to 4); 5-minute default lifetime, optional 1 hour usage.cache_read_input_tokens Google Gemini API Implicit caching on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer; explicit caches on some models usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount vLLM, SGLang Automatic prefix caching (vLLM default on) vllm:prefix_cache_hits, vllm:prefix_cache_queries

Caching affects cost as well as latency, which prompt caching and batch processing covers in depth.

docs.title: Stream to cut perceived latency
docs.text: Streaming sends tokens as they are generated (server-sent events for most providers). It does not make the model faster; it moves the moment the user sees something from the end of the request to the first token. For the meeting summary above, that is 0.6 s instead of 4.3 s. Stream any answer a person reads; do not bother for calls whose output is parsed as a whole, such as task-creation JSON, unless you parse partial output deliberately. The backend relay is covered in streaming responses end to end and the UI side in frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: Make fewer requests, and run independent ones in parallel
docs.text:
Every sequential step adds its full latency. Two habits remove most of it:

  • Combine steps when one call has all the information it needs. A separate "rewrite the question" call before every search costs a whole round trip; folding it into the main call, or skipping it for short questions, often works as well.
  • Run independent work concurrently. Retrieval, a user-profile lookup, and a permission check do not depend on each other, so they can start together. Bound the concurrency so a burst does not exhaust connection pools or provider rate limits.

Agents need special care: each tool round trip is another model call. Allowing parallel tool calls, giving tools coarse operations ("create these three tasks") instead of fine ones, and capping the number of steps keep agent latency predictable (see agent orchestration patterns).

docs.title: Smaller, faster models and tiers
docs.text:
A smaller model has fewer weights to read per token, so it decodes faster and usually starts faster. For classification, routing, extraction, and short task creation, a small model is often as accurate as a large one for a fraction of the latency; measure it on an evaluation set before switching. Routing between models is covered in cost optimization for LLM apps.

Hosted providers also sell processing tiers. OpenAI's service_tier parameter, for example, accepts priority (or fast) for faster, more expensive processing and flex for slower, cheaper processing with occasional unavailability. Use a fast tier only for the few latency-critical paths that justify the price.

docs.title: Regional placement
docs.text:
Network distance adds a floor that no model change removes: light in fiber covers about 200 km per millisecond, so a backend in Europe calling a model endpoint in North America pays at least 50-60 ms per round trip before any processing, and realistic routes add more. An agent that makes eight sequential calls pays that eight times. Options:

  • Put the backend next to the model endpoint. Most latency-sensitive traffic is backend-to-model, not browser-to-backend, and an agent multiplies it.
  • Use the provider's regional or global endpoints deliberately. Azure's Microsoft Foundry offers global, data zone, and regional deployment types; Amazon Bedrock offers cross-Region inference profiles for a geography or globally; Google Cloud offers regional endpoints and a global endpoint that "provide higher availability and reliability than single regions"; Anthropic's API lets you set inference_geo per request. Global options usually improve capacity and availability but do not guarantee where data is processed, so check data residency rules first.
  • Keep connections warm. SDK clients reuse HTTP connections; creating a new client per request pays a fresh TCP and TLS handshake each time.
  • Self-hosted: run GPUs in the region where the backend runs, and use global traffic management when users are spread across continents.

docs.title: Speculative decoding
docs.text:
Decode is memory-bound: verifying several proposed tokens in one forward pass costs about the same as generating one. Speculative decoding exploits that. A cheap proposer (a small draft model, extra prediction heads, or an n-gram lookup in the prompt) guesses the next k tokens; the target model scores them all at once and keeps the longest prefix it agrees with, then adds one token of its own. With the right acceptance rule the output follows the target model's distribution, so quality does not change.

Expected tokens per target pass, with acceptance rate a and k drafted tokens
(from Leviathan and colleagues):
  (1 - a^(k+1)) / (1 - a)

a = 0.7, k = 4:  (1 - 0.7^5) / 0.3 = (1 - 0.168) / 0.3 = 2.77 tokens per pass
a = 0.3, k = 4:  (1 - 0.3^5) / 0.7 = 1.42 tokens per pass, minus the drafting cost

It helps most when the server is lightly loaded (decode steps are not already full of other users' work) and when the output is predictable, such as code edits or answers that copy text from the prompt. Under heavy load the extra verification work competes with other requests, which is why vLLM recommends it for low to medium QPS. Hosted providers apply such techniques internally; OpenAI exposes a related feature, Predicted Outputs, for edits where most of the output is known in advance. It is supported only on some model families, and rejected prediction tokens are still billed as output.

docs.title: Engine settings for self-hosted models
docs.text:
On vLLM or SGLang, a few settings trade time to first token against smoothness and throughput:

  • Chunked prefill and --max-num-batched-tokens. Smaller chunks keep other users' streams smooth while a long prompt is read; larger chunks give that prompt a faster first token.
  • --max-num-seqs. More concurrent sequences raise throughput and slow each stream; fewer do the opposite.
  • Prefix caching (on by default in vLLM) shortens TTFT for shared prefixes.
  • Quantized weights and an FP8 cache reduce the bytes read per decode step, which speeds up memory-bound decoding; see GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Symptom Technique Watch out for Blank screen for seconds, then fast text Shorter or cached prompt, streaming, a nearby region Caching needs an identical prefix Text starts fast but finishes slowly Fewer output tokens, smaller or faster model Truncated answers if limits are too tight Agent takes many seconds before acting Fewer steps, parallel tool calls, coarse tools Parallel side effects need idempotency Several independent lookups before the model call Run them concurrently with a limit Rate limits and connection pools Only a few critical paths are too slow A priority or fast tier for those paths It costs more per token Self-hosted, low load, predictable output Speculative decoding Gains shrink or reverse at high load Self-hosted, many users, long prompts Chunked prefill tuning, more replicas Trading one user's TTFT for others' smoothness Output parsed as a whole (task JSON) Do not stream; shrink the output instead Partial JSON is not useful to users

docs.title: Measuring TTFT and tokens per second
docs.text:
// scripts/measure-latency.ts
import { CHAT_MODEL, llm } from "../src/ai/llm-client.js";

interface Sample {
  ttftMs: number;
  totalMs: number;
  outputTokens: number;
  tokensPerSecond: number;
}

async function measureOnce(prompt: string): Promise<Sample> {
  const started = performance.now();
  let firstTokenAt: number | undefined;
  let outputTokens = 0;

  const stream = await llm.chat.completions.create({
    model: CHAT_MODEL,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: prompt }],
    max_tokens: 300,
    stream: true,
    stream_options: { include_usage: true }, // the last chunk carries token usage
  });

  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    if (firstTokenAt === undefined && chunk.choices[0]?.delta?.content) {
      firstTokenAt = performance.now();
    }
    if (chunk.usage) outputTokens = chunk.usage.completion_tokens;
  }

  const ended = performance.now();
  const first = firstTokenAt ?? ended;
  const decodeSeconds = (ended - first) / 1000;
  return {
    ttftMs: first - started,
    totalMs: ended - started,
    outputTokens,
    tokensPerSecond: outputTokens > 1 && decodeSeconds > 0 ? (outputTokens - 1) / decodeSeconds : 0,
  };
}

function percentile(values: number[], p: number): number {
  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const index = Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.max(0, Math.ceil((p / 100) * sorted.length) - 1));
  return sorted[index] ?? Number.NaN;
}

const prompt =
  process.argv[2] ??
  "Summarize these meeting notes in five bullets: Ana will draft the release notes by Friday.";
const runs = Number(process.env.RUNS ?? 20);
const samples: Sample[] = [];
for (let i = 0; i < runs; i += 1) samples.push(await measureOnce(prompt));

for (const key of ["ttftMs", "totalMs", "tokensPerSecond"] as const) {
  const values = samples.map((s) => s[key]);
  console.log(
    `${key.padEnd(16)} p50=${percentile(values, 50).toFixed(0)} p95=${percentile(values, 95).toFixed(0)}`,
  );
}

# Output from a run against a local OpenAI-compatible stub server configured
# for about 30 ms of prefill and 20 ms per token (Windows timers stretch the
# 20 ms sleeps); real numbers depend on the model, hardware, and load
ttftMs           p50=47 p95=49
totalMs          p50=635 p95=668
tokensPerSecond  p50=32 p95=33
  • The first chunk with text marks TTFT; chunks before it can carry only a role or nothing.
  • stream_options.include_usage makes OpenAI-compatible servers send a final chunk with token counts, so tokens per second uses real counts rather than chunk counts (one chunk can hold several tokens).
  • The script runs requests one at a time, so it measures latency without load. Latency under concurrent load is a load test; see load testing with k6.
  • Point the same script at the hosted API and at a self-hosted server by changing LLM_BASE_URL, and compare like with like: same prompt, same output limit.

docs.title: Running independent calls in parallel with a limit
docs.text:
// src/ai/parallel.ts
// Run fn over items with at most `limit` calls in flight; keeps result order.
export async function mapWithLimit<T, R>(
  items: readonly T[],
  limit: number,
  fn: (item: T, index: number) => Promise<R>,
): Promise<R[]> {
  const results = new Array<R>(items.length);
  let next = 0;

  async function worker(): Promise<void> {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const index = next;
      next += 1;
      results[index] = await fn(items[index] as T, index);
    }
  }

  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, () => worker()));
  return results;
}

// scripts/parallel-demo.ts
// Three independent lookups before a project Q&A answer, run two ways.
import { mapWithLimit } from "../src/ai/parallel.js";

const sleep = (ms: number) => new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
const lookups = [
  { name: "search project docs", ms: 120 },
  { name: "list open tasks", ms: 80 },
  { name: "check permissions", ms: 30 },
];

let started = performance.now();
for (const lookup of lookups) await sleep(lookup.ms);
console.log(`sequential: ${Math.round(performance.now() - started)} ms`);

started = performance.now();
await mapWithLimit(lookups, 3, (lookup) => sleep(lookup.ms));
console.log(`parallel:   ${Math.round(performance.now() - started)} ms`);

# Output from a local run
sequential: 257 ms
parallel:   135 ms

The parallel version finishes when the slowest lookup does. In real code each lookup should also carry a timeout (AbortSignal.timeout(ms) passed to fetch or the SDK call), so one slow dependency cannot stall the whole answer.

docs.title: Laying out a prompt for caching and checking hits
docs.text:
// src/ai/project-qa.ts
import { CHAT_MODEL, llm } from "./llm-client.js";

// Stable for every request: identical text first, so the provider can reuse it.
const QA_INSTRUCTIONS = [
  "You answer questions about one TaskFlow project.",
  "Use only the passages provided. Cite passage ids like [p3].",
  "If the passages do not contain the answer, say so in one sentence.",
].join("\n");

export async function answerProjectQuestion(question: string, passages: string[]) {
  const response = await llm.responses.create({
    model: CHAT_MODEL,
    instructions: QA_INSTRUCTIONS, // stable prefix
    input: [
      { role: "user", content: `Passages:\n${passages.join("\n\n")}` },
      { role: "user", content: `Question: ${question}` }, // variable part last
    ],
    max_output_tokens: 300,
  });

  const cached = response.usage?.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens ?? 0;
  const input = response.usage?.input_tokens ?? 0;
  console.info({ feature: "project-qa", input, cached, hitRatio: input ? cached / input : 0 });
  return response.output_text;
}

This uses OpenAI's Responses API; vLLM also serves /v1/responses. Watch the hit ratio per feature: a sudden drop after a deploy usually means someone put changing text (a date, a request id, a shuffled list) into the stable prefix. With Anthropic, mark the end of the stable part with a cache_control breakpoint; with Gemini, implicit caching works the same way for long, identical prefixes.

docs.title: Turning on speculative decoding in vLLM
docs.text:
# n-gram speculation: proposes tokens by matching earlier text in the prompt.
# Cheap to enable; best when answers copy from the input (edits, extraction).
vllm serve "$MODEL_ID" --served-model-name taskflow-chat \
  --speculative-config '{"method": "ngram", "num_speculative_tokens": 4, "prompt_lookup_min": 2, "prompt_lookup_max": 5}'

# Compare inter-token latency and acceptance before and after, at your real load
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/metrics \
  | grep -E "^vllm:(inter_token_latency_seconds_(sum|count)|spec_decode_)"

Benchmark at the load you actually run. If acceptance is low or the server is busy, speculation adds verification work without saving steps; switch to a model-based method (EAGLE or MTP where the model supports it) or turn it off.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Measure TTFT, TPOT, and end-to-end latency per feature at p50 and p95 before changing anything.
  • Shorten outputs first: explicit length instructions, output limits, and compact structured output.
  • Keep prompts lean and put stable content first; watch cache hit ratios after every deploy.
  • Stream answers people read; do not stream output you parse as a whole.
  • Remove sequential round trips, and run independent lookups concurrently with a limit and timeouts.
  • Use a small model where an evaluation shows it is good enough.
  • Place the backend near the model endpoint and reuse SDK clients.
  • Reserve priority tiers for the few paths that need them.
  • On self-hosted engines, tune chunked prefill and concurrency against measured TTFT and TPOT targets; try speculative decoding at low load.
  • Budget latency per feature (for example "first text in 1 s, done in 6 s") and alert on p95, not the average.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The Assistant got slower after a prompt change, with no traffic change. Detect: TTFT p50 doubled after a deploy; cached tokens per request fell to zero. Cause: a timestamp or per-user detail moved into the top of the instructions, so the prefix no longer matches. Fix: move variable content after the stable prefix and alert on cache hit ratio.
  • Meeting summaries take twenty seconds. Detect: output tokens per request are far above the UI's needs; TTFT is normal. Cause: no length instruction or output limit, so the model writes long summaries. Fix: ask for a fixed format and length, set an output limit, and check the finish reason.
  • Agent runs feel stuck before the first visible action. Detect: traces show five or more sequential model calls before the first tool result. Cause: fine-grained tools and a planning call on every step. Fix: coarser tools, parallel tool calls, a step cap, and streaming a status update early.
  • Latency is fine in tests but p95 explodes at peak. Detect: queue time or provider rate-limit errors rise with traffic; per-request processing time is flat. Cause: capacity or quota exhaustion, made worse by retries. Fix: request higher limits or add replicas, cap concurrency per feature, and retry with backoff and jitter.
  • Self-hosted streams stutter whenever someone uploads a long document. Detect: inter-token latency spikes coincide with long prompts. Cause: large prefill work shares decode steps with everyone. Fix: smaller prefill chunks (--max-num-batched-tokens), a separate pool for long-document work, or more replicas.
  • Speculative decoding made things slower. Detect: higher inter-token latency at peak after enabling it; low acceptance metrics. Cause: busy server and unpredictable output, so verification work is wasted. Fix: disable it at high load or switch to a better-matched method; benchmark at real concurrency.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• TTFT (time to first token): Time from sending a request to receiving the first output token.
  • TPOT / ITL (time per output token, inter-token latency): The average gap between output tokens after the first.
  • End-to-end latency: Total time until the last token and any application work finish.
  • Prefill: Processing the input tokens; sets most of TTFT.
  • Decode: Generating output tokens one at a time; sets most of the rest.
  • Prompt caching: Reusing processed work for a repeated prompt prefix.
  • Streaming: Sending tokens to the client as they are generated.
  • Speculative decoding: Drafting several tokens cheaply and verifying them in one pass of the large model.
  • Acceptance rate: The share of drafted tokens the target model keeps.
  • Service tier: A provider option that trades price for speed or availability.
  • Tail latency: High percentiles (p95, p99) of the latency distribution.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Optimizing the prompt when the answer length is the real cost.
  • Believing streaming makes generation faster.
  • Reporting average latency instead of percentiles.
  • Putting dates or request ids at the top of a cached prompt.
  • Chaining calls that do not depend on each other.
  • Assuming a bigger model is needed for every feature.
  • Enabling speculative decoding without benchmarking at real load.
  • Creating a new SDK client per request and paying new handshakes.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define TTFT and TPOT. Which stages of a request does each include?
  2. A request has a TTFT of 0.8 s and generates 600 tokens at 50 tokens per second. What is its end-to-end latency, and what is it if the answer is cut to 200 tokens? (0.8 + 599 x 0.02 = 12.8 s; 0.8 + 199 x 0.02 = 4.8 s.)
  3. Why does prompt caching need an identical prefix, and how should a prompt be laid out to benefit from it?
  4. When does streaming help, and when is it pointless?
  5. Three independent lookups take 400 ms, 250 ms, and 900 ms before a model call. What do you save by running them in parallel? (Sequential 1,550 ms; parallel 900 ms; saving 650 ms.)
  6. Explain speculative decoding and why its output matches the target model. With an acceptance rate of 0.8 and 3 drafted tokens, how many tokens does one target pass yield on average? ((1 - 0.8^4) / 0.2 = 2.95.)
  7. Why can speculative decoding hurt at high load?
  8. How does regional placement affect an agent that makes many sequential model calls?

docs.title: Serving Open Models
docs.text:
A hosted model API hides everything between "send a prompt" and "receive tokens". When you run open-weight models yourself, that hidden part becomes yours: a serving engine that loads the weights onto a GPU, schedules many requests at once, manages the attention state of every conversation, and exposes an HTTP API your backend can call. This lesson explains how modern engines (vLLM, SGLang, the llama.cpp server, Ollama, and the now-archived Text Generation Inference) work inside: the KV cache, paged attention, continuous batching, and prefix caching.

It then covers the OpenAI-compatible endpoints that let TaskFlow's backend switch between a hosted provider and a self-hosted model by changing a base URL, and how to run an engine on Kubernetes with GPU nodes, long startup probes, a model cache, and queue-based autoscaling. Latency tuning, cost accounting, and GPU sizing get their own lessons in this subject.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A naive server that calls a model's generate function once per request leaves most of an expensive GPU idle. Generating text is a loop: one forward pass per output token, and each pass for a single sequence reads all the model weights from GPU memory to produce one token. The GPU's arithmetic units mostly wait for memory. Processing many sequences in the same pass reuses each weight read for all of them, which is why a good engine serves many times more users on the same card than a request-at-a-time loop.

The constraint that decides how many sequences fit is GPU memory, and most of it is not the weights but the KV cache: the attention keys and values of every token in every active conversation. Engines differ mainly in how well they pack that cache, how quickly they admit new requests into a running batch, and how much of a shared prompt they can reuse. Choosing an engine, and setting its memory and concurrency limits, decides throughput, time to first token, and cost per request far more than small model differences do.

Operationally, a model server is a stateful, slow-starting, GPU-bound service. It takes minutes to start, it fails differently from a web server (out of memory, queueing, preemption), and its HTTP API is easy to expose by accident. Knowing those properties is what lets you deploy it safely.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• vLLM and PagedAttention. The paper Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention (Kwon and colleagues, SOSP 2023) measured that in earlier systems "only 20.4% - 38.2% of the KV cache memory is used to store the actual token states", and that managing the cache in pages lets vLLM improve throughput "by 2-4x with the same level of latency".
  • Orca and iteration-level scheduling. The OSDI 2022 paper Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models introduced scheduling at the granularity of one decoding iteration, so finished sequences leave the batch and new ones join without waiting for the whole batch. Engines now call this continuous batching.
  • SGLang and RadixAttention. The paper SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs describes RadixAttention, which keeps a tree of cached prefixes for reuse across requests, and reports "up to 6.4x higher throughput" on workloads such as agents and multi-turn chat.
  • Text Generation Inference (TGI). The TGI repository README states that "text-generation-inference is now in maintenance mode" and recommends vLLM, SGLang, and local engines such as llama.cpp or MLX going forward. As of November 2026 the repository is archived (read-only), and its last release is v3.3.7 from December 2025.
  • vLLM on Kubernetes. The vLLM guide Using Kubernetes shows a GPU Deployment with a Hugging Face token Secret, a model cache volume, a shared-memory volume, and /health probes, and lists higher-level projects that build on it, such as KServe, llm-d, KubeAI, NVIDIA Dynamo, and the vLLM production stack.

Popular tools and providers: vLLM, SGLang, the llama.cpp server (llama-server), Ollama, and LM Studio for engines; KServe, llm-d, KubeAI, and the vLLM production stack for Kubernetes; KEDA for queue-based autoscaling; Hugging Face Hub for model weights; managed endpoints from cloud providers when you want open models without operating GPUs.

docs.title: Prefill, decode, and the scheduler
docs.text:
Every request passes through two phases with very different costs:

  1. Prefill. The engine runs the whole prompt through the model in one large, parallel pass, computing attention keys and values for every prompt token and producing the first output token. Prefill is compute-bound: a 4,000-token prompt is a lot of matrix arithmetic, done efficiently.
  2. Decode. The engine then generates one token per step. Each step processes only the newest token per sequence, but it must read the weights and that sequence's cached keys and values. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound: the GPU spends most of the step moving bytes.

A scheduler loop runs continuously: it picks which waiting requests to admit, which running sequences take a decode step, how much prefill work fits into the same step, and which requests to pause when memory runs out. Its limits (maximum running sequences, maximum tokens per step, memory reserved for the cache) are the main knobs you set when deploying.

docs.title: The KV cache
docs.text:
Attention lets each new token look at every earlier token. Recomputing keys and values for the whole history at each step would be wasteful, so the engine stores them: two vectors (key and value) per layer, per key-value head, per token. That store is the KV cache, and it grows with every token of every active sequence:

KV bytes per token = 2 (K and V) x layers x kv_heads x head_dim x bytes per value

An 8-billion-parameter model shape: 32 layers, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, 16-bit values
  2 x 32 x 8 x 128 x 2 bytes = 131,072 bytes = 128 KiB per token
  one 8,192-token conversation = 1 GiB of KV cache
  weights: about 8 billion x 2 bytes = about 16 GB

Keeping about 10% of GPU memory back for the runtime:
24 GB GPU: 21.6 GB - 16 GB weights - activations -> roughly 4-5 GB of cache
           -> about 4 conversations at full 8K context
80 GB GPU: 72 GB - 16 GB - activations -> roughly 55 GB of cache
           -> about 55 conversations at full 8K context

Two consequences follow. The number of users one GPU can serve at once is set mostly by cache space, not by arithmetic. And context length is expensive: allowing 32K-token conversations instead of 8K cuts the number of concurrent full-length conversations by four. The full sizing method, including quantized weights and an FP8 cache, is in GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: Paged attention
docs.text:
Early servers reserved one contiguous slab of cache per request, sized for the maximum possible output. A request that might produce 2,048 tokens but stops after 200 held 90% of its slab empty, and gaps between slabs could not be used by anyone.

PagedAttention borrows the idea of virtual memory. The cache is split into small fixed-size blocks (the paper uses 16 tokens per block by default). Each sequence has a block table mapping its logical blocks to physical blocks anywhere in GPU memory, and the attention kernel follows the table. Blocks are allocated only as tokens are produced, so waste is limited to the unfilled part of each sequence's last block. Because blocks are referenced through tables, sequences can also share blocks: parallel samples of one prompt, or requests with the same system prompt, point to the same physical prefix blocks and copy a block only when they diverge.

docs.title: Continuous batching
docs.text:
Static batching waits to collect a batch, runs it until the longest sequence finishes, and only then starts the next batch. Short answers sit finished while the long one completes, and new requests wait at the door.

Continuous batching (iteration-level scheduling) makes the decision at every decode step. When a sequence finishes, its slot and cache blocks are freed and a waiting request starts its prefill in the next step. Modern engines combine this with chunked prefill: a long prompt is processed in pieces mixed into decode steps, so one 30,000-token document does not freeze every other user's stream while it is read. vLLM's --max-num-batched-tokens caps the tokens processed per step, which trades prefill speed against the smoothness of everyone's streaming.

When the cache fills up anyway, an engine must preempt: pause a running sequence and free its blocks, then recompute or reload them later. A few preemptions under bursts are normal; a steady stream means the server is admitting more concurrent work than its memory can hold.

docs.title: Prefix caching
docs.text:
Many TaskFlow requests start with the same long text: the Assistant's system prompt and tool definitions, or a project's documents in a Q&A session. Prefix caching keeps the KV blocks of finished requests in a lookup keyed by a hash of the tokens they contain. A new request whose prompt begins with the same tokens reuses those blocks and skips their prefill, which cuts time to first token and frees compute for others.

vLLM's automatic prefix caching is enabled by default (enable_prefix_caching defaults to true in vLLM 0.33), and its Prometheus metrics report queries and hits. SGLang's RadixAttention organizes cached prefixes as a radix tree and is designed around this reuse. The rule for your prompts is the same as with hosted prompt caching: put stable content first (instructions, tools, shared documents) and variable content last (the user's message), and keep the stable part byte-for-byte identical.

docs.title: The engines compared
docs.text:
Engine Best fit Model format Concurrency model Notes (November 2026) vLLM Production GPU serving, many users Hugging Face safetensors, many quantized formats Continuous batching, paged KV cache, prefix caching vllm serve; OpenAI-compatible server; very broad model and hardware support; v0.33 SGLang Production GPU serving, agent and multi-turn workloads with shared prefixes Hugging Face safetensors and quantized formats Continuous batching, RadixAttention prefix tree sglang serve; OpenAI-compatible; its quickstart uses port 30000 llama.cpp server CPU, Apple silicon, single GPUs, edge devices GGUF (often 4- to 8-bit) Slots (-np) with continuous batching on by default llama-server; OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible routes; binds to 127.0.0.1 by default Ollama Developer laptops, internal tools, quick prototypes GGUF-based models from its library One request per model at a time by default (OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=1), queue of 512 OpenAI-compatible at http://localhost:11434/v1; easiest setup TGI Existing deployments only Hugging Face safetensors Continuous batching In maintenance mode; repository archived; plan a migration

The split is roughly: vLLM or SGLang when the model runs on data-center GPUs for many users; llama.cpp or Ollama when it runs on one machine, a laptop, or hardware without a large GPU. Ollama also runs GGUF models and trades control for convenience. Whatever you pick, benchmark it with your own prompts and concurrency, because results depend heavily on the model, the GPU, and the request mix.

docs.title: OpenAI-compatible endpoints
docs.text:
Every engine above exposes routes shaped like OpenAI's API, so the official OpenAI SDK, the Vercel AI SDK, and most frameworks work against them by changing the base URL:

Engine Base URL (example) Chat route Also offers vLLM http://vllm.taskflow.svc.cluster.local/v1 /v1/chat/completions /v1/completions, /v1/responses, /v1/embeddings (embedding models), /v1/models, /health, /metrics SGLang http://localhost:30000/v1 /v1/chat/completions /v1/completions, /v1/models llama.cpp server http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 /v1/chat/completions /v1/responses, /v1/embeddings, /v1/messages (Anthropic-style), /health, /metrics with --metrics Ollama http://localhost:11434/v1 /v1/chat/completions Native /api/* routes

"Compatible" means the request and response shapes match for the common fields, not that every parameter behaves the same. Structured output, tool calling, reasoning output, and some sampling parameters differ by engine and by model chat template, so test the features TaskFlow uses against the engine you deploy.

Authentication is the part teams get wrong. vLLM's documentation warns that --api-key (or VLLM_API_KEY) "only authenticates requests to endpoints under the /v1, /v2, /inference, and /cohere path prefixes", that other routes such as /invocations stay open, and that you should not rely on it alone. llama.cpp's /health is public by design, and Ollama's OpenAI routes require an API key field that they ignore. Treat a model server as an internal service: no public IP, a network policy that admits only your backend, and authentication at a gateway in front of it.

docs.title: Running on Kubernetes
docs.text:
A model server on Kubernetes is an ordinary Deployment with unusual settings, built from the pieces covered in pods, Deployments, and Services:

  • GPU scheduling. The container requests nvidia.com/gpu: 1 (or more for tensor parallelism), which requires the NVIDIA device plugin or GPU operator on the nodes. GPU node pools are usually tainted, so the pod needs a matching toleration.
  • Startup time. Downloading tens of gigabytes of weights and loading them onto the GPU takes minutes. A startup probe with a generous budget keeps the liveness probe from killing a pod that is still loading, as explained in health probes and rolling updates.
  • Model cache. Weights go on a persistent volume or a node-local cache so a restart does not download them again; see stateful workloads and jobs.
  • Shared memory. PyTorch uses /dev/shm between processes, so the pod mounts a memory-backed emptyDir there (the Docker equivalent is --ipc=host or --shm-size).
  • Configuration and secrets. The model ID comes from a ConfigMap and the Hugging Face token from a Secret, as in configuration and secrets.
  • Scaling. CPU usage says nothing useful about a GPU server. Scale on the engine's own queue metric (vllm:num_requests_waiting) through KEDA, and keep headroom, because a new replica needs minutes. Details are in GPU capacity and scaling and scaling and resource management.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Choose Why A new AI feature, uncertain demand A hosted API No GPUs to buy or run; pay per token while you learn the demand Developers need a local model for TaskFlow features Ollama or llama.cpp server Minutes to set up, runs on laptops, same OpenAI-style API Data must not leave your infrastructure, steady traffic vLLM or SGLang on your GPUs Full control of data path and model version; high throughput per GPU Many requests share long prefixes (agents, document Q&A) SGLang or vLLM with prefix caching Reused prefixes skip prefill CPU-only or edge hardware llama.cpp with a quantized GGUF model Runs where no data-center GPU exists An existing TGI deployment Plan a move to vLLM or SGLang TGI is in maintenance mode and archived Spiky, low-volume traffic A hosted API or a managed endpoint An idle self-hosted GPU still costs money every hour

Self-hosting is not automatically cheaper. A GPU costs the same whether it serves one request an hour or fifty a second, so it pays off only at sustained utilization, or when privacy, control, or latency requirements justify it. The trade-off is worked through in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: Running vLLM with Docker
docs.text:
# Start vLLM on one GPU host; the model ID comes from configuration, not code.
# Choose MODEL_ID from the model's Hugging Face page after checking its license.
export MODEL_ID="<org>/<model-name>"
export VLLM_API_KEY="<random-internal-key>"

docker run --rm --runtime nvidia --gpus all \
  -v ~/.cache/huggingface:/root/.cache/huggingface \
  --env "HF_TOKEN=$HF_TOKEN" \
  --env "VLLM_API_KEY=$VLLM_API_KEY" \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  --ipc=host \
  vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0 \
  --model "$MODEL_ID" \
  --served-model-name taskflow-chat \
  --max-model-len 8192 \
  --max-num-seqs 64

# Once the log says the server is ready:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/health -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n"
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer $VLLM_API_KEY"
  • Arguments after the image name are engine arguments; the image's entry point runs the OpenAI-compatible server on port 8000.
  • --served-model-name taskflow-chat gives the deployment a stable alias. TaskFlow's configuration says CHAT_MODEL=taskflow-chat, so swapping the underlying model is an infrastructure change, not a code change.
  • --max-model-len 8192 caps prompt plus output length. A smaller cap leaves more cache for concurrent requests; the default is the model's own maximum, which can be far larger than the feature needs.
  • --max-num-seqs caps concurrently running sequences. Too high and the cache thrashes with preemptions; too low and the GPU idles.
  • Publishing on 127.0.0.1 keeps the port off the network while you test.
  • Pin the image tag (v0.33.0 here) and upgrade deliberately; engine releases change defaults.

docs.title: A local engine for development
docs.text:
# Option 1: Ollama. Pull a model from its library, then serve with 4 parallel slots.
ollama pull "$OLLAMA_MODEL"
OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL=4 OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=8192 ollama serve
# OpenAI-compatible base URL: http://localhost:11434/v1 (the API key is ignored)

# Option 2: llama.cpp server with a GGUF file from Hugging Face (quant after the colon).
llama-server -hf "$GGUF_REPO:Q4_K_M" \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 \
  -c 16384 -np 4 \
  --api-key "$LLAMA_API_KEY" \
  --metrics
# OpenAI-compatible base URL: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1

OLLAMA_NUM_PARALLEL defaults to 1, so without it every TaskFlow developer request queues behind the previous one; Ollama's documentation notes that memory grows with parallel requests times context length. Its default context length depends on VRAM (4K below 24 GiB, 32K for 24-48 GiB, 256K at 48 GiB or more, per the context length page), so set it explicitly to get the same behavior on every machine. -np sets llama.cpp's parallel slots, and -c must leave enough context for all of them. Set --port explicitly: current releases listen on 127.0.0.1:9931 by default, and the default has changed before.

docs.title: One client for hosted and self-hosted models
docs.text:
// src/ai/llm-client.ts
import OpenAI from "openai";

function requireEnv(name: string): string {
  const value = process.env[name];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`${name} is not configured`);
  return value;
}

// LLM_BASE_URL: unset for the provider's own API, or a self-hosted
// OpenAI-compatible server such as http://vllm-chat.taskflow.svc.cluster.local/v1
export const llm = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: process.env.LLM_BASE_URL || undefined,
  apiKey: requireEnv("LLM_API_KEY"),
  timeout: 30_000, // a stuck GPU server must not hold the request forever
  maxRetries: 1, // retries add load to a busy server; keep them few
});

// CHAT_MODEL is a provider model ID chosen from its current model list,
// or the --served-model-name alias of the self-hosted deployment.
export const CHAT_MODEL = requireEnv("CHAT_MODEL");

export async function summarizeMeetingNotes(
  notes: string,
  signal?: AbortSignal,
): Promise<string> {
  const completion = await llm.chat.completions.create(
    {
      model: CHAT_MODEL,
      messages: [
        {
          role: "system",
          content:
            "Summarize meeting notes for a task tracker. Return at most five " +
            "bullet points, then a list of action items with owners.",
        },
        { role: "user", content: notes },
      ],
      max_tokens: 400, // self-hosted servers read max_tokens; it bounds cost and time
      temperature: 0.2,
    },
    { signal },
  );

  const text = completion.choices[0]?.message?.content;
  if (!text) throw new Error("empty completion");
  return text;
}

Chat Completions is used here because every engine supports it. OpenAI's own API also offers the Responses API (llm.responses.create), and for the hosted path OpenAI prefers max_completion_tokens over the older max_tokens. The Anthropic SDK (messages.create) and the Google Gen AI SDK (models.generateContent) are not OpenAI-shaped; to switch freely between them as well, use a layer such as the Vercel AI SDK, covered in AI frameworks and SDKs.

docs.title: The Kubernetes manifests
docs.text:
# k8s/vllm-chat.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat
  namespace: taskflow
data:
  MODEL_ID: "<org>/<model-name>" # chosen after a license and evaluation review
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: vllm-chat
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: vllm-chat
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 120 # let in-flight generations finish
      tolerations:
        - key: nvidia.com/gpu
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
      containers:
        - name: vllm
          image: vllm/vllm-openai:v0.33.0
          args:
            - "--model"
            - "$(MODEL_ID)"
            - "--served-model-name"
            - "taskflow-chat"
            - "--max-model-len"
            - "8192"
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: vllm-chat
          env:
            - name: HF_TOKEN
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: hf-token
                  key: token
            - name: VLLM_API_KEY
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: vllm-api-key
                  key: key
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "4"
              memory: 24Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
            limits:
              memory: 32Gi
              nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: model-cache
              mountPath: /root/.cache/huggingface
            - name: shm
              mountPath: /dev/shm
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 90 # up to 15 minutes to download and load weights
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 6
      volumes:
        - name: model-cache
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: vllm-model-cache
        - name: shm
          emptyDir:
            medium: Memory
            sizeLimit: 2Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: vllm-chat
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: vllm-chat-ingress
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: vllm-chat
  policyTypes: ["Ingress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
      ports:
        - port: 8000
  • $(MODEL_ID) in args is expanded by Kubernetes from the container's environment, which envFrom fills from the ConfigMap.
  • The startup probe allows 90 x 10 s = 15 minutes before liveness checks begin. Measure your real cold start and size the budget from it.
  • A ReadWriteOnce volume works for one replica. With several replicas, use a ReadWriteMany volume, a per-node cache, or weights baked into a pre-pulled image, so replicas do not fight over one disk.
  • The network policy admits only TaskFlow API pods on port 8000, which also covers the routes --api-key does not protect. It only takes effect if the cluster's network plugin enforces policies.
  • Prometheus scraping of /metrics and the KEDA ScaledObject that scales this Deployment are shown in GPU capacity and scaling.

docs.title: A smoke test after every deploy
docs.text:
// scripts/smoke-llm.ts
import { CHAT_MODEL, llm, summarizeMeetingNotes } from "../src/ai/llm-client.js";

const started = Date.now();
const models = await llm.models.list();
const served = models.data.map((m) => m.id);
if (!served.includes(CHAT_MODEL)) {
  throw new Error(`server does not serve ${CHAT_MODEL}; it serves ${served.join(", ")}`);
}

const summary = await summarizeMeetingNotes(
  "Ana will draft the release notes by Friday. Ben owns the database upgrade.",
);
if (!/Ana/.test(summary) || !/Ben/.test(summary)) {
  throw new Error(`summary lost the owners: ${summary}`);
}
console.log(`ok: ${CHAT_MODEL} answered in ${Date.now() - started} ms`);

The check proves three things a /health probe cannot: the alias TaskFlow uses is actually served, the chat template works, and output is plausible. Run it in the deployment pipeline before shifting traffic.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with a hosted API; self-host when privacy, control, latency, or sustained volume justify a GPU fleet.
  • Use vLLM or SGLang for multi-user GPU serving, llama.cpp or Ollama for local and edge use; migrate off TGI.
  • Give each deployment a stable served-model alias and keep the real model ID in configuration.
  • Cap --max-model-len at what the feature needs; context length is paid for in cache space.
  • Put stable prompt content first so prefix caching can reuse it.
  • Keep model servers internal: network policies, no public addresses, and authentication at a gateway rather than the engine's API key alone.
  • Pin engine image versions and re-run benchmarks and smoke tests on every upgrade.
  • Budget startup probes from measured cold starts, and cache weights so restarts do not download them again.
  • Scale on queue depth and cache usage, not CPU.
  • Test the exact features you use (tools, structured output, streaming) against the engine and model you deploy.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Time to first token climbs while GPU utilization looks fine. Detect: vllm:num_requests_waiting grows and vllm:request_queue_time_seconds rises; tokens per second per stream is normal. Cause: more concurrent requests than the cache and --max-num-seqs admit, so requests queue. Fix: add replicas, lower --max-model-len, quantize the cache or weights, and scale on queue depth.
  • Throughput collapses under bursts and logs show preemptions. Detect: vllm:num_preemptions increases; latency becomes erratic; vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc sits near 100%. Cause: admitted sequences outgrow the cache and the engine keeps evicting and recomputing them. Fix: lower --max-num-seqs, cap output with max_tokens, and size the cache from real context lengths.
  • Pods restart in a loop after a deploy. Detect: restart count rises; events show liveness probe failures during weight loading. Cause: no startup probe, or a budget shorter than the cold start after the model grew. Fix: a startup probe sized from a measured cold start, and a cached copy of the weights.
  • The pod is killed with OOM, or the engine fails at startup with a CUDA out-of-memory error. Detect: OOMKilled status, or an engine error while allocating the cache. Cause: the container memory limit is below what the engine uses on the host side, or the model plus requested context does not fit the GPU. Fix: raise the container memory limit, reduce --max-model-len, use a quantized model, or add GPUs with tensor parallelism.
  • The model server answered requests from outside the cluster. Detect: unknown client addresses in access logs; usage that matches no TaskFlow traffic. Cause: a LoadBalancer Service or port-forward left open, relying on --api-key, which does not cover every route. Fix: ClusterIP Service, network policies, authentication at a gateway, and an audit of exposed ports.
  • Tool calls or structured output fail only on the self-hosted path. Detect: parse errors or missing tool calls that never happen with the hosted provider. Cause: the engine's tool parser or the model's chat template differs from the provider's behavior. Fix: enable and test the engine's tool and structured-output options for that model, and keep an evaluation set that runs against every backend.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Serving engine: Software that loads a model, schedules requests, and serves an API, such as vLLM or SGLang.
  • Prefill: The parallel pass over the prompt that fills the KV cache and produces the first token.
  • Decode: The token-by-token generation phase; bound by memory bandwidth.
  • KV cache: Stored attention keys and values for every token of every active sequence.
  • PagedAttention: Managing the KV cache in fixed-size blocks mapped through per-sequence block tables.
  • Continuous batching: Admitting and retiring sequences at every decode step instead of per batch.
  • Chunked prefill: Splitting a long prompt's prefill into pieces mixed with decode steps.
  • Prefix caching: Reusing KV blocks of an identical prompt prefix across requests.
  • Preemption: Pausing a running sequence and freeing its cache when memory runs out.
  • Served model name: The alias a server exposes in its API, independent of the underlying model ID.
  • GGUF: The single-file model format used by llama.cpp, usually holding quantized weights.
  • OpenAI-compatible endpoint: An API that accepts and returns OpenAI-shaped requests at routes such as /v1/chat/completions.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing GPU arithmetic is the limit; for chat serving, KV cache memory usually is.
  • Leaving --max-model-len at the model maximum "just in case".
  • Assuming "OpenAI-compatible" means every parameter and feature works.
  • Exposing a model server on a public address protected only by its API key.
  • Scaling GPU servers on CPU utilization.
  • Using Ollama's single-request default for a shared team server.
  • Starting a new project on TGI.
  • Treating /health as proof the right model is being served.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is decoding memory-bandwidth-bound, and why does batching many sequences raise throughput?
  2. Explain the KV cache. What does its size per token depend on?
  3. A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head dimension 128, and a 16-bit cache. How much cache does one 16,384-token conversation need? (2 x 40 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 163,840 bytes per token, times 16,384 tokens = about 2.5 GiB.)
  4. What problem does PagedAttention solve, and how do block tables enable prefix sharing?
  5. Compare static and continuous batching. What does chunked prefill add?
  6. When would you choose vLLM or SGLang, and when llama.cpp or Ollama? What should an existing TGI user do?
  7. Which vLLM routes does --api-key protect, and how should a model server be secured instead?
  8. Why does a model server on Kubernetes need a startup probe, a model cache volume, and a shared-memory volume?
