docs.title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
docs.text:
Vector search is good at meaning and weak at exact strings. Ask TaskFlow "how do we undo a broken release?" and embeddings find the rollback runbook even though it never says "undo". Ask "TF-1432 rollback" and the same embeddings may rank three generic rollback notes above the one ticket that matters, because a ticket number carries little meaning for them. Keyword search has the opposite profile.

This lesson covers hybrid search, which runs keyword (BM25) and vector retrieval side by side and fuses the two result lists, most often with reciprocal rank fusion (RRF). It then covers rerankers, the cross-encoder models that reorder a short candidate list far more accurately than either retriever, and the retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR, and nDCG) that tell you whether each stage earns its latency. The end-to-end RAG pipeline around these steps is covered in building a RAG pipeline.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Retrieval quality is decided twice: once when candidates are gathered (anything missed here is gone for good) and once when they are ordered (only the top few reach the model or the user). Hybrid search improves the first step, because keyword and vector retrievers fail on different queries. A reranker improves the second, because it reads the query and each candidate together instead of comparing two precomputed vectors.

Both add cost and latency, and both can make results worse if tuned blindly: a noisy keyword leg can push good semantic hits down, and a reranker can truncate long chunks. Retrieval metrics on labeled queries are what turn "it feels better" into a decision, which is why this lesson treats measurement as part of the design rather than an afterthought.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Anthropic. In Introducing Contextual Retrieval (September 2024), Anthropic measured retrieval failures as 1 minus recall@20. Contextual embeddings alone cut the failure rate by 35%, adding contextual BM25 (fused with rank fusion and deduplicated) cut it by 49%, and adding a reranker that scored the top 150 chunks and kept 20 cut it by 67%, from 5.7% to 1.9%.
  • Microsoft. The Azure AI Search post Outperforming vector search with hybrid retrieval and reranking (2023) reports NDCG@3 on customer datasets of 40.6 for keyword, 43.8 for vector, 48.4 for hybrid (top 50 from each, fused with RRF), and 60.1 for hybrid plus its semantic reranker, with the same ordering on BEIR and on the multilingual MIRACL benchmark.
  • BEIR. The BEIR benchmark (NeurIPS 2021) evaluated retrieval models zero-shot on 18 datasets. It found BM25 to be a robust baseline and re-ranking and late-interaction models to give the best zero-shot results on average, at high computational cost.
  • Spotify. Its natural language podcast search (2022) added dense retrieval as an extra source next to the existing Elasticsearch retrieval rather than replacing it, noting that dense retrieval often underperforms on exact term matching, and feeds the query-episode cosine similarity into a final reranking model.

Popular tools and providers: Elasticsearch and OpenSearch (BM25, vector search, and RRF), MongoDB $rankFusion, Weaviate hybrid search, Qdrant's Query API, PostgreSQL full-text search with pgvector, Cohere Rerank, Voyage AI rerankers, Azure AI Search's semantic ranker, and sentence-transformers cross-encoders.

docs.title: The hybrid retrieval pipeline
docs.text: A production retrieval path for TaskFlow's project-knowledge Q&A has four steps: two retrievers in parallel, fusion, and reranking. Each retriever filters by workspace on its own, fusion works on ranks, and the reranker only ever sees a short list. The rest of this section takes the steps one at a time.

docs.title: What keyword search catches that embeddings miss
docs.text:
Embeddings compress a passage into one vector that captures its gist. Details that do not change the gist get blurred: ticket and order numbers, error codes, version strings, product and person names, rare technical terms, and exact quotations. Those are often exactly what users type. Keyword search treats every distinct term as a separate dimension, so a rare token such as tf-1432 dominates the score of the one note that contains it.

Query Keyword search Vector search TF-1432 rollback Finds the ticket note first Prefers generic rollback notes "how do we undo a broken release" Needs the same words; misses "roll back a bad deploy" Finds the runbook by meaning "Ana's notes from the billing sync" Matches the name exactly May match any meeting about billing A question in Spanish about English notes Fails without translation Works with a multilingual model

docs.title: BM25 in one formula
docs.text:
BM25 scores a document for a query by summing, over the query terms it contains:

score(term, doc) = IDF(term) * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * docLength / avgDocLength))
IDF(term)        = ln(1 + (N - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5))

Here f is how often the term appears in the document, N is the number of documents, and n is how many contain the term. Three ideas are packed in: rare terms matter more (IDF), repeating a term helps with diminishing returns (k1), and long documents are discounted (b). Elasticsearch, whose default similarity is BM25, uses k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75, and the TypeScript example below uses the same values.

The formula is only as good as the text analysis in front of it. Tokenizers, stemming, and stop words decide what a "term" is, and that is where hybrid search most often goes wrong:

  • In a real run of the PostgreSQL example below, the english text search configuration split TF-1432 into tf and -1432, so a different ticket, TF-1398, matched on tf and ranked second. Index identifiers in a separate keyword field matched exactly, or normalize them before indexing.
  • Without stop-word removal, the TypeScript BM25 example ranked a note titled "How to write a postmortem" first for "how do we undo a broken release?", because "how" was rare in the small corpus.

PostgreSQL's built-in ranking (ts_rank, ts_rank_cd) is not BM25: it has no corpus-wide IDF. It works as a hybrid leg, and extensions add true BM25 when you need it.

docs.title: Fusing result lists with reciprocal rank fusion
docs.text:
The two retrievers produce scores on unrelated scales: BM25 scores are unbounded and vary by query, while cosine similarity sits between -1 and 1. Adding them directly lets one leg dominate. Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke, and Buettcher, SIGIR 2009) ignores scores and uses only positions:

RRF(d) = sum over result lists L containing d of  weight(L) / (k + rank_L(d))

With k = 60, rank 1 contributes 1/61 and rank 10 contributes 1/70, so being found by both retrievers matters more than being first in one. Elasticsearch's RRF retriever defaults rank_constant to 60 and its documentation notes that RRF needs no tuning; MongoDB's $rankFusion uses 60 and accepts per-pipeline weights. Defaults differ across products, though: as of November 2026, Qdrant's RRF uses k = 2 with zero-based ranks unless you set it, and Weaviate's default hybrid fusion is relativeScoreFusion, which normalizes scores instead of using ranks. Check before comparing results between systems.

Practical settings:

  • Candidate depth. Take 20 to 100 results from each leg; Microsoft's experiments used the top 50 from each. Fusion cannot promote a document neither leg returned.
  • Weights. Start equal. Raise the keyword weight for ID-heavy queries or the vector weight for conversational ones, and measure.
  • Score fusion. Normalizing scores (min-max, or mean and standard deviation as in Qdrant's DBSF) and taking a weighted sum keeps more information than ranks, but is more sensitive to outliers and needs tuning per query type.

docs.title: Rerankers: reading the query and the document together
docs.text:
Embedding models are bi-encoders: the query and the document are encoded independently, so document vectors can be computed once and compared with any query in microseconds. That independence is also their limit: the model never sees the query and the document side by side.

A cross-encoder reranker takes the pair as one input and outputs a relevance score. It can notice that the question asks about undoing a release and that the passage describes a rollback, or that a passage mentions the right ticket but says the fix is still pending. Voyage's documentation describes its rerankers exactly this way: a cross-encoder processing each query-document pair jointly, which is why it predicts relevance more accurately than embeddings.

The cost is that nothing can be precomputed: every candidate is a model call, so rerankers run only on a short list. Typical shapes:

  • Retrieve 50 to 150 candidates with hybrid search, rerank, keep 5 to 20 for the model's context (Anthropic's experiment: 150 in, 20 out).
  • As of November 2026, Cohere's Rerank 5 models accept 32,768 tokens of query plus document and cover 100+ languages; Voyage's rerank-3 and rerank-3-lite accept up to 1,000 documents per request. Long chunks are truncated or split, so keep chunks within the limit.
  • Open cross-encoders run locally through sentence-transformers' CrossEncoder; language models can also rerank by judging relevance, at a higher cost per candidate.
  • Late-interaction models (ColBERT-style) sit in between: they keep a vector per token, so they can be precomputed yet still compare at the word level, at the cost of much more storage.

docs.title: When to rerank
docs.text:
Rerank when the candidate list is broad and the top positions matter: RAG answers that use only the top few chunks, search pages where users read the first results, and agent tools that must pick one document. Skip it, or make it optional, when:

  • the candidate set is already small and precise, such as filtering a single project's ten notes;
  • the latency budget is tight, as in autocomplete, because a reranker adds a network call and model time proportional to the candidates;
  • candidate recall is the real problem: a reranker cannot recover a document that retrieval never returned, so fix recall first;
  • you cannot measure the gain, because then you cannot tell whether it helps.

Reranker scores are also useful beyond ordering. Cohere describes Rerank 5's scores as calibrated between 0 and 1, which makes a threshold such as "answer only if the best chunk scores above X" practical, provided X is chosen on labeled data for that specific model.

docs.title: Retrieval metrics
docs.text:
Each metric answers a different question about a ranked list, given relevance judgments for the query:

Metric Question it answers Formula Use it for Recall@k Did the relevant documents make it into the top k? relevant found in top k / all relevant The candidate stage (k = 50 to 150), and context sent to a model Precision@k How much of the top k is relevant? relevant in top k / k Noise in the context window MRR How soon does the first relevant result appear? mean of 1 / rank of first relevant Single-answer lookups, navigation nDCG@k Are the most relevant results at the top? DCG@k / ideal DCG@k Final ordering with graded relevance

nDCG (Järvelin and Kekäläinen, 2002) adds up each result's gain discounted by its position, DCG@k = sum of (2^grade - 1) / log2(position + 1), and divides by the DCG of the ideal ordering, so 1.0 means perfect order. Graded judgments (3 for "answers it", 1 for "related") let it distinguish a list that puts the answer first from one that puts a merely related note first. Some tools use the grade itself as the gain instead of 2^grade - 1; pick one and keep it fixed.

In the diagram's example, both lists have the same recall@3 of 0.667, but the fused list puts both answers on top: its MRR is 1.0 against 0.5 and its nDCG@3 is 0.958 against 0.664. Recall tells you whether the evidence is there; MRR and nDCG tell you whether it is where the model and the user will look.

docs.title: Building a retrieval evaluation set
docs.text:
Metrics need judgments. A useful first set for TaskFlow has 100 to 300 queries:

  • real questions from logs or support tickets, plus ID-heavy queries ("TF-1432"), name queries, multilingual queries, and questions with no answer in the data;
  • for each query, the chunks that answer it, graded (3 answers it, 1 related), judged by people who know the content, with a language model as an assistant at most;
  • the workspace each query belongs to, so the evaluation also proves that nothing from other tenants appears.

Run every configuration (BM25 only, vector only, hybrid, hybrid plus reranker, different k values) over the same set, report metrics per query type, and keep the set versioned as the data changes. Building and maintaining such sets in general is covered in building evaluation sets, and evaluating whole RAG answers in evaluating and debugging RAG.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choose Why Queries mix natural language with IDs, codes, or names Hybrid search with RRF Each retriever covers the other's blind spots Answers use only the top few chunks Hybrid plus a reranker over 50 to 150 candidates Cross-encoders order the shortlist best Autocomplete or type-ahead Keyword or prefix search, no reranker Every millisecond counts; queries are fragments Exact lookups (ticket number, email address) A database query or keyword field No similarity needed Short conversational questions over prose Vector search, then measure whether hybrid helps Keyword overlap may be low anyway Tight budget per query Hybrid without a reranker, or rerank only when top scores are close Reranking costs a model call per request Many languages Multilingual embeddings plus per-language analyzers, multilingual reranker Keyword search needs language-aware analysis

docs.title: BM25 in TypeScript
docs.text:
// src/search/bm25.ts
// Okapi BM25 over an in-memory corpus, with Lucene's IDF and default k1 and b.
// Small enough to read; production systems use a search engine's index instead.
export interface Doc {
  id: string;
  text: string;
}

export interface Hit {
  id: string;
  score: number;
}

// Lowercase words and numbers; keeps hyphenated IDs such as "tf-1432" whole.
export const tokenize = (text: string): string[] =>
  text.toLowerCase().match(/[\p{L}\p{N}]+(?:-[\p{L}\p{N}]+)*/gu) ?? [];

export function buildBm25(docs: Doc[], { k1 = 1.2, b = 0.75 } = {}) {
  const docTokens = docs.map((d) => tokenize(d.text));
  const avgLength = docTokens.reduce((sum, t) => sum + t.length, 0) / docs.length;
  const docFreq = new Map<string, number>();
  for (const tokens of docTokens) {
    for (const term of new Set(tokens)) docFreq.set(term, (docFreq.get(term) ?? 0) + 1);
  }
  // Rare terms (ticket IDs, names) get a high IDF; common words get a low one.
  const idf = (term: string) => {
    const n = docFreq.get(term) ?? 0;
    return Math.log(1 + (docs.length - n + 0.5) / (n + 0.5));
  };

  return function search(query: string, limit = 10): Hit[] {
    const queryTerms = tokenize(query);
    const hits: Hit[] = [];
    docs.forEach((doc, i) => {
      const termFreq = new Map<string, number>();
      for (const term of docTokens[i]) termFreq.set(term, (termFreq.get(term) ?? 0) + 1);
      const lengthNorm = 1 - b + (b * docTokens[i].length) / avgLength;
      let score = 0;
      for (const term of queryTerms) {
        const f = termFreq.get(term) ?? 0;
        if (f > 0) score += (idf(term) * f * (k1 + 1)) / (f + k1 * lengthNorm);
      }
      if (score > 0) hits.push({ id: doc.id, score });
    });
    return hits.sort((x, y) => y.score - x.score).slice(0, limit);
  };
}

The tokenizer deliberately keeps hyphenated identifiers whole, which is the behavior you want for ticket numbers. A real deployment uses a search engine or database index, but the scoring is the same idea.

docs.title: Reciprocal rank fusion
docs.text:
// src/search/rrf.ts
// Reciprocal rank fusion: score(d) = sum over lists of weight / (k + rank(d)),
// with ranks starting at 1. Only ranks matter, so BM25 and cosine scores
// never have to be put on the same scale.
export interface RankedList {
  name: string;
  ids: string[];   // best first, as returned by one retriever
  weight?: number; // default 1
}

export interface FusedHit {
  id: string;
  score: number;
  ranks: Record<string, number>; // where each retriever placed it
}

export function reciprocalRankFusion(
  lists: RankedList[],
  { k = 60, limit = 10 } = {},
): FusedHit[] {
  const fused = new Map<string, FusedHit>();
  for (const { name, ids, weight = 1 } of lists) {
    ids.forEach((id, index) => {
      const hit = fused.get(id) ?? { id, score: 0, ranks: {} };
      if (hit.ranks[name] !== undefined) return; // ignore duplicates within a list
      hit.ranks[name] = index + 1;
      hit.score += weight / (k + index + 1);
      fused.set(id, hit);
    });
  }
  return [...fused.values()].sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score).slice(0, limit);
}

Keeping ranks on each fused hit makes debugging easy: you can log which retriever found a chunk and where, which is the first thing to check when a result looks wrong.

docs.title: Retrieval metrics
docs.text:
// src/eval/retrieval-metrics.ts
// Offline retrieval metrics. `ranked` is a result list (best first); `labels`
// maps each judged document ID to a relevance grade (0 = not relevant).
export type Labels = Map<string, number>;

const relevantIds = (labels: Labels) => [...labels].filter(([, g]) => g > 0).map(([id]) => id);

// Share of all relevant documents that appear in the top k.
export function recallAtK(ranked: string[], labels: Labels, k: number): number {
  const relevant = relevantIds(labels);
  if (relevant.length === 0) return 0;
  const top = new Set(ranked.slice(0, k));
  return relevant.filter((id) => top.has(id)).length / relevant.length;
}

// 1 / rank of the first relevant result, 0 if none is returned.
export function reciprocalRank(ranked: string[], labels: Labels): number {
  const index = ranked.findIndex((id) => (labels.get(id) ?? 0) > 0);
  return index === -1 ? 0 : 1 / (index + 1);
}

// Normalized discounted cumulative gain with graded relevance (gain 2^grade - 1).
export function ndcgAtK(ranked: string[], labels: Labels, k: number): number {
  const dcg = (grades: number[]) =>
    grades.slice(0, k).reduce((sum, g, i) => sum + (2 ** g - 1) / Math.log2(i + 2), 0);
  const ideal = dcg([...labels.values()].sort((a, b) => b - a));
  return ideal === 0 ? 0 : dcg(ranked.map((id) => labels.get(id) ?? 0)) / ideal;
}

export const mean = (values: number[]) => values.reduce((s, v) => s + v, 0) / values.length;

Math.log2(i + 2) is the position discount for zero-based index i (position 1 divides by log2(2) = 1). Average each metric over all queries; MRR is the mean of reciprocalRank.

docs.title: Comparing BM25, vector, and hybrid on labeled queries
docs.text:
// src/scripts/hybrid-demo.ts
// Run: node --experimental-strip-types src/scripts/hybrid-demo.ts
import { buildBm25, type Doc } from "../search/bm25.ts";
import { reciprocalRankFusion } from "../search/rrf.ts";
import { mean, ndcgAtK, recallAtK, reciprocalRank, type Labels } from "../eval/retrieval-metrics.ts";

const notes: Doc[] = [
  { id: "n1", text: "Runbook: roll back a bad deploy with the previous image tag, then check health." },
  { id: "n2", text: "TF-1432: payment webhook retries fail after the release; rollback planned for Friday." },
  { id: "n3", text: "Release notes for 3.2: new calendar view and faster search." },
  { id: "n4", text: "Incident review: the broken release on March 3 was undone by turning off its feature flag." },
  { id: "n5", text: "TF-1398: calendar sync drops recurring tasks for some users." },
  { id: "n6", text: "Meeting notes: freeze releases during the billing migration." },
  { id: "n7", text: "How to write a postmortem: timeline, impact, causes, and actions." },
  { id: "n8", text: "Rollback checklist for database migrations: expand, migrate, contract." },
];

// Ranks an embedding model might return (assumed for the demo, not computed here):
// it understands "undo" ~ "roll back" but blurs the ticket ID.
const vectorRanks: Record<string, string[]> = {
  "TF-1432 rollback": ["n8", "n1", "n4", "n2", "n5"],
  "how do we undo a broken release": ["n1", "n4", "n8", "n3", "n6"],
};

// Relevance judgments: 3 = answers the question, 1 = related.
const judgments: Record<string, Labels> = {
  "TF-1432 rollback": new Map([["n2", 3], ["n8", 1]]),
  "how do we undo a broken release": new Map([["n1", 3], ["n4", 3], ["n8", 1]]),
};

const bm25 = buildBm25(notes);
const scores: Record<string, number[][]> = { bm25: [], vector: [], rrf: [] };

for (const [query, labels] of Object.entries(judgments)) {
  const lexical = bm25(query, 5).map((h) => h.id);
  const semantic = vectorRanks[query];
  const fused = reciprocalRankFusion(
    [{ name: "bm25", ids: lexical }, { name: "vector", ids: semantic }],
    { k: 60, limit: 5 },
  );
  console.log(`\n${query}`);
  console.log("  bm25:  ", lexical.join(" "));
  console.log("  vector:", semantic.join(" "));
  console.log("  rrf:   ", fused.map((h) => `${h.id}(${h.score.toFixed(4)})`).join(" "));
  const lists = { bm25: lexical, vector: semantic, rrf: fused.map((h) => h.id) };
  for (const [name, ranked] of Object.entries(lists)) {
    scores[name].push([recallAtK(ranked, labels, 3), reciprocalRank(ranked, labels), ndcgAtK(ranked, labels, 3)]);
  }
}

console.log("\nmean over both queries   recall@3   MRR    nDCG@3");
for (const [name, rows] of Object.entries(scores)) {
  const [r, m, n] = [0, 1, 2].map((c) => mean(rows.map((row) => row[c])).toFixed(3));
  console.log(`  ${name.padEnd(22)} ${r}      ${m}  ${n}`);
}

Output of a real run on Node.js 22 (the BM25 rankings, the fusion, and the metrics are computed; the vector rankings are the assumed inputs above):

TF-1432 rollback
  bm25:   n2 n8
  vector: n8 n1 n4 n2 n5
  rrf:    n8(0.0325) n2(0.0320) n1(0.0161) n4(0.0159) n5(0.0154)

how do we undo a broken release
  bm25:   n7 n4 n1 n3 n2
  vector: n1 n4 n8 n3 n6
  rrf:    n1(0.0323) n4(0.0323) n3(0.0313) n7(0.0164) n8(0.0159)

mean over both queries   recall@3   MRR    nDCG@3
  bm25                   0.833      0.750  0.832
  vector                 0.750      1.000  0.566
  rrf                    0.833      1.000  0.834

Fusion matched the best single retriever on every metric without being told which query type it faced. It did not fix everything: for the ticket query it put the generic checklist n8 just above the ticket n2, which is the kind of near-tie a reranker resolves. Two queries prove nothing statistically; the same script over a few hundred judged queries is how the decision should be made.

docs.title: Hybrid search in PostgreSQL
docs.text:
-- db/queries/hybrid_search.sql
-- Hybrid search in one statement: full-text and vector candidates fused with RRF (k = 60).
-- $1 = query text, $2 = query embedding as '[...]', $3 = workspace id
WITH q AS (
  -- OR the terms together: natural-language questions rarely contain every word of a note
  SELECT replace(plainto_tsquery('english', $1)::text, ' & ', ' | ')::tsquery AS query
),
lexical AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS rank
  FROM (
    SELECT id, ts_rank_cd(search_tsv, q.query) AS score
    FROM note_chunks, q
    WHERE workspace_id = $3 AND search_tsv @@ q.query
    ORDER BY score DESC
    LIMIT 50
  ) AS l
),
semantic AS (
  SELECT id, row_number() OVER (ORDER BY distance) AS rank
  FROM (
    SELECT id, embedding <=> $2::vector AS distance
    FROM note_chunks
    WHERE workspace_id = $3
    ORDER BY distance
    LIMIT 50
  ) AS s
)
SELECT id,
       COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + lexical.rank), 0)
         + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + semantic.rank), 0) AS rrf_score,
       lexical.rank AS lexical_rank,
       semantic.rank AS semantic_rank
FROM lexical FULL OUTER JOIN semantic USING (id)
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC
LIMIT 10;

It assumes a stored full-text column and index on note_chunks:

-- db/migrations/005_note_chunks_fulltext.sql
ALTER TABLE note_chunks
  ADD COLUMN search_tsv tsvector
  GENERATED ALWAYS AS (to_tsvector('english', content)) STORED;
CREATE INDEX note_chunks_search_tsv ON note_chunks USING gin (search_tsv);
  • plainto_tsquery ANDs every word, so a natural-language question rarely matches anything; replacing & with | turns it into an OR query, and ts_rank_cd ranks the matches.
  • Each leg limits itself to 50 candidates before numbering, so the vector leg can use the HNSW index, and both legs filter by workspace.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN keeps documents found by only one leg, with COALESCE adding nothing for the missing rank.

This query was run in PGlite on the eight demo notes plus a note from another workspace (which never appeared). Two findings from that run are worth knowing before you ship it. The query text "how do we undo a broken release" became 'undo' | 'broken' | 'releas', so the stemmer handled "release" and "releases" alike. The query "TF-1432 rollback" became 'tf' | '-1432' | 'rollback', so the ticket TF-1398 matched on tf: keep identifiers in their own column and match them exactly.

docs.title: Hybrid search in MongoDB with $rankFusion
docs.text:
// src/search/mongo-text-index.ts
// Full-text index for the lexical half of hybrid search (MongoDB Search, Lucene-based).
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI ?? "mongodb://localhost:27017");
try {
  await client.db("taskflow").collection("note_chunks").createSearchIndex({
    name: "note_chunks_text",
    type: "search",
    definition: {
      mappings: {
        dynamic: false,
        fields: {
          text: { type: "string", analyzer: "lucene.english" }, // stemming and stop words
          workspaceId: { type: "objectId" },                    // for the equals filter
        },
      },
    },
  });
} finally {
  await client.close();
}

// src/search/mongo-hybrid-search.ts
// Hybrid retrieval in one aggregation: $rankFusion merges a full-text $search
// and a $vectorSearch with reciprocal rank fusion (MongoDB 8.0 or later).
import { MongoClient, type ObjectId } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI ?? "mongodb://localhost:27017");
const chunks = client.db("taskflow").collection("note_chunks");

export interface HybridHit {
  _id: ObjectId;
  noteId: ObjectId;
  text: string;
  score: number; // the RRF score
}

export async function hybridSearch(
  workspaceId: ObjectId,
  queryText: string,
  queryVector: number[],
  { limit = 50, vectorWeight = 1, textWeight = 1 } = {},
): Promise<HybridHit[]> {
  return chunks
    .aggregate<HybridHit>([
      {
        $rankFusion: {
          input: {
            pipelines: {
              vector: [
                {
                  $vectorSearch: {
                    index: "note_chunks_vector",
                    path: "embedding",
                    queryVector,
                    numCandidates: Math.min(limit * 20, 10_000),
                    limit,
                    filter: { workspaceId },
                  },
                },
              ],
              text: [
                {
                  $search: {
                    index: "note_chunks_text",
                    compound: {
                      must: [{ text: { query: queryText, path: "text" } }],
                      filter: [{ equals: { path: "workspaceId", value: workspaceId } }],
                    },
                  },
                },
                { $limit: limit },
              ],
            },
          },
          combination: { weights: { vector: vectorWeight, text: textWeight } },
        },
      },
      { $limit: limit },
      { $project: { noteId: 1, text: 1, score: { $meta: "score" } } },
    ])
    .toArray();
}
  • $rankFusion runs each named pipeline, deduplicates, and scores every document with weight * 1 / (60 + rank) summed over the pipelines it appears in. Each input pipeline may contain only selection and ranking stages such as $search, $vectorSearch, $match, $sort, and $limit, all on the same collection.
  • Both legs filter by workspaceId: the vector leg through its filter field, the text leg through a compound filter clause.
  • Add scoreDetails: true and project { $meta: "scoreDetails" } to see each document's rank in each pipeline while tuning.

These modules were type-checked against the MongoDB Node.js driver; they need MongoDB 8.0 or later with MongoDB Search and Vector Search enabled.

docs.title: Reranking the fused candidates
docs.text:
// src/search/rerank.ts
// Reorders retrieval candidates with a hosted cross-encoder (Cohere Rerank shown).
// The model ID comes from configuration; choose it from the provider's model list.
import { CohereClientV2 } from "cohere-ai";

const cohere = new CohereClientV2({ token: process.env.COHERE_API_KEY });

export interface Candidate {
  id: string;
  text: string;
}

export interface Reranked extends Candidate {
  relevance: number; // 0 to 1 for this provider; calibrate any threshold per model
}

export async function rerank(query: string, candidates: Candidate[], topN = 8): Promise<Reranked[]> {
  if (candidates.length === 0) return [];
  const model = process.env.RERANK_MODEL;
  if (!model) throw new Error("RERANK_MODEL is not set");

  const response = await cohere.rerank(
    {
      model,
      query,
      documents: candidates.map((c) => c.text),
      topN: Math.min(topN, candidates.length),
    },
    { timeoutInSeconds: 3, maxRetries: 1 }, // reranking must not stall the answer
  );
  // Results come back best first; `index` points into the documents we sent.
  return response.results.map((r) => ({ ...candidates[r.index], relevance: r.relevanceScore }));
}

// Use the reranker when it answers in time; otherwise keep the fused order.
export async function rerankOrFallback(query: string, candidates: Candidate[], topN = 8) {
  try {
    return { results: await rerank(query, candidates, topN), reranked: true };
  } catch (err) {
    console.warn("rerank failed, using fused order", err);
    return { results: candidates.slice(0, topN).map((c) => ({ ...c, relevance: Number.NaN })), reranked: false };
  }
}
  • Results reference candidates by index, so the original IDs, metadata, and tenant checks stay on your side.
  • The short timeout and the fallback keep a slow reranker from turning into a slow answer; record how often the fallback runs.
  • Equivalents: Voyage AI's rerank endpoint takes the same query and document list, Azure AI Search has a built-in semantic ranker, and a local model works through sentence-transformers.

The module was type-checked against the cohere-ai SDK and exercised against a local stub of the rerank endpoint, with every outgoing request redirected to the stub: the SDK sent the configured model, the query, the documents, and top_n, results were mapped back to candidate IDs, and a 503 from the stub triggered the fallback.

A local cross-encoder in Python looks like this:

# scripts/rerank_local.py
# Reranks candidates with an open cross-encoder on your own hardware.
import os

from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder

model = CrossEncoder(os.environ["RERANK_MODEL"])  # a Hugging Face cross-encoder ID

query = "how do we undo a broken release"
candidates = [
    "Incident review: the broken release on March 3 was undone by turning off its feature flag.",
    "Release notes for 3.2: new calendar view and faster search.",
    "Runbook: roll back a bad deploy with the previous image tag, then check health.",
]
for hit in model.rank(query, candidates, top_k=2, return_documents=True):
    print(f"{hit['score']:.3f}  {hit['text']}")

This script was not run here because it downloads model weights; the rank() signature (query, documents, top_k, return_documents, returning corpus_id, score, and text) was checked against the sentence-transformers 6.3 source.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run keyword and vector retrieval side by side when queries contain IDs, names, or codes, and fuse with RRF before reaching for score blending.
  • Give identifiers their own exactly matched field, and check what your text analyzer does to them.
  • Retrieve deep (50 to 150 candidates), rerank, and send only the top few to the model.
  • Keep tenant filters inside every leg, not only after fusion.
  • Put a timeout and a fallback around the reranker, and monitor latency and fallback rate.
  • Measure recall@k for candidate generation and nDCG or MRR for the final order on a labeled, versioned query set, broken down by query type.
  • Re-run the evaluation whenever the embedding model, analyzer, chunking, fusion weights, or reranker changes.
  • Calibrate any relevance threshold per model on labeled data.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Searches for ticket numbers return the wrong ticket. Detect: queries matching an ID pattern have low MRR; logs show other tickets ranked first. Cause: the text analyzer splits identifiers (TF-1432 into tf and -1432), or only vector search runs. Fix: index IDs in a keyword field, route ID-shaped queries to exact match, and keep a BM25 leg in hybrid search.
  • Hybrid results got worse than vector-only for conversational questions. Detect: nDCG drops for long natural-language queries after enabling hybrid. Cause: a noisy keyword leg (OR queries, no stop words) pushes semantic hits down through fusion. Fix: tune the analyzer, lower the keyword weight for conversational queries, or rerank the fused list.
  • Answer latency doubled after adding a reranker. Detect: p95 latency rises in step with candidate count; traces show the rerank span dominating. Cause: too many or too long candidates per request, or a slow region. Fix: rerank fewer candidates, trim chunks, set a timeout with fallback, and cache results for repeated queries.
  • The reranker ignores the end of long chunks. Detect: answers miss facts that appear late in long chunks. Cause: the reranker truncates documents beyond its token limit (Cohere's maxTokensPerDoc defaults to 4,096). Fix: chunk to fit the limit and check the provider's truncation behavior.
  • "No relevant results" appears for questions that have answers. Detect: abstention rate rises after a model change. Cause: a fixed score threshold carried over from another embedding or rerank model. Fix: recalibrate thresholds per model on labeled data.
  • Offline metrics look great but users still complain. Detect: nDCG on the evaluation set is stable while thumbs-down rates rise. Cause: the evaluation set no longer matches real queries (new features, new languages, more ID searches). Fix: refresh the set from recent logs and report metrics per query type.
  • Results from another workspace appear after fusion. Detect: cross-tenant tests fail only on hybrid queries. Cause: one leg (often the keyword index) lacks the tenant filter. Fix: filter inside every leg and keep cross-tenant tests for each retrieval path.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Lexical (keyword) search: Retrieval by matching terms, usually ranked with BM25.
  • BM25: A ranking function based on term frequency with saturation, inverse document frequency, and document length normalization.
  • Analyzer: The tokenizer and filters (lowercasing, stemming, stop words) that turn text into index terms.
  • Hybrid search: Running lexical and vector retrieval together and fusing their results.
  • Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF): Fusing ranked lists by summing 1 / (k + rank) for each list a document appears in.
  • Bi-encoder: A model that embeds queries and documents separately.
  • Cross-encoder (reranker): A model that scores a query and a document together.
  • Late interaction: Comparing per-token vectors of query and document, as in ColBERT-style models.
  • Recall@k: The share of relevant documents found in the top k.
  • MRR: The mean over queries of 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result.
  • nDCG@k: Position-discounted gain of a ranking divided by that of the ideal ranking.
  • Relevance judgments: Labels saying which documents answer a query, often graded.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming vector search makes keyword search obsolete.
  • Adding raw BM25 and cosine scores together.
  • Fusing or reranking too few candidates, so the right chunk never enters the pool.
  • Expecting a reranker to fix poor candidate recall.
  • Filtering by tenant after fusion instead of inside each leg.
  • Comparing RRF results across products without checking their k and fusion defaults.
  • Tuning on a handful of queries and calling it an evaluation.
  • Reporting only recall, which ignores order, for a feature that only shows the top three results.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Give two kinds of queries where keyword search beats vector search and two where vector search wins. Why does each fail where it does?
  2. Explain the three ideas inside the BM25 formula and what k1 and b control.
  3. A document is ranked 3rd by BM25 and 7th by vector search. Another is ranked 1st by vector search only. With k = 60, which wins under RRF?
  4. Why does RRF use ranks instead of scores, and when might score fusion be the better choice?
  5. Explain why a cross-encoder is more accurate than a bi-encoder but cannot be used to search a whole collection.
  6. Your reranker adds 300 ms at the 95th percentile. What would you measure and change before removing it?
  7. For a list whose relevance grades are 0, 3, 0, 1, 3 at positions 1 to 5, compute recall@3 and MRR, given three relevant documents in total.
  8. Which metric would you use for the candidate stage of a RAG pipeline, and which for the final top five? Explain why.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Reciprocal Rank Fusion paper (Cormack et al., 2009)
  • Elasticsearch: Reciprocal rank fusion
  • MongoDB: $rankFusion
  • Qdrant: Hybrid and multi-stage queries
  • Weaviate: Hybrid search
  • Cohere: Rerank
  • Voyage AI: Rerankers
  • BEIR benchmark (arXiv)
  • Next: embeddings and vector search interview questions and answers. Back to the embeddings and vector search overview.

docs.title: Embeddings and Vector Search Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review embedding models and dimensions, vector databases and indexes, filtering and tenant isolation, hybrid search and reranking, and retrieval metrics. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is an embedding, and why is it useful for search?
docs.text: An embedding is a fixed-length vector produced by a model so that inputs with related meaning end up close together. Search becomes "find the stored vectors nearest to the query vector", which matches paraphrases and even other languages that share no keywords with the query. It complements keyword search rather than replacing it.

docs.title: 2. How does an embedding model turn text into one vector?
docs.text: Usually a transformer encoder tokenizes the input, produces a vector per token, and pools them (often by averaging) into one vector with a fixed number of dimensions, whatever the input length. Training pulls related pairs together and pushes unrelated ones apart, so distance approximates relatedness for the tasks it was trained on.

docs.title: 3. Why can't you compare vectors from two different embedding models?
docs.text: Each model defines its own coordinate system. A cosine between vectors from two models is a number without meaning, so mixing them in one index silently degrades results. Store the model, version, and dimension setting with every vector. The only exceptions are spaces a provider explicitly documents as shared, such as Cohere's Embed 5 Pro and Fast or Voyage's 4 series (as of November 2026).

docs.title: 4. What is asymmetric retrieval, and how do providers handle it?
docs.text: Queries are short needs; documents are long answers. Many models embed them differently: Cohere requires inputType (search_query or search_document), Voyage takes input_type, Gemini uses task types or task prefixes, Qwen3 Embedding expects an instruction before queries, and sentence-transformers offers encode_query and encode_document. OpenAI's text-embedding-3 models use the same call for both. Using the wrong mode lowers recall without any error.

docs.title: 5. How would you choose between a hosted embedding API and an open-weight model?
docs.text: Hosted APIs are fastest to adopt, often strong and multilingual, and bill per token, but text leaves your network and the provider retires models on its schedule. Open models need serving hardware and operations, are cheaper at steady high volume, keep data local, and can be fine-tuned. Shortlist two or three candidates and compare them on your own labeled questions with recall@10.

docs.title: 6. Where should the embedding model ID live in an application?
docs.text: In configuration (for example EMBEDDING_MODEL and EMBEDDING_DIMENSIONS), never hard-coded. The evaluation, the dual-write migration, and rollback all need to switch it without a code change, and every stored vector should record the version that made it.

docs.title: 7. What do embedding dimensions cost?
docs.text: Storage, memory, and compute all scale with dimensions. A float32 value is 4 bytes, so one million 1,536-dimension vectors need about 6.1 GB raw and 3,072-dimension vectors about 12.3 GB, before index overhead. Distance calculations scale too: 3,072 dimensions mean roughly three times the arithmetic of 1,024.

docs.title: 8. What is Matryoshka Representation Learning?
docs.text: A training method (Kusupati et al., 2022) that makes every prefix of an embedding a useful embedding by itself, like nested dolls. You can keep only the first 256 or 768 values of a 3,072-dimension vector and lose quality gradually rather than suddenly. The paper reports up to 14 times smaller embeddings at the same accuracy for ImageNet-1K classification.

docs.title: 9. How do you shorten an embedding safely?
docs.text:
Either ask the API for fewer dimensions (OpenAI's dimensions, Gemini's outputDimensionality, Voyage's output_dimension) or slice the vector yourself and re-normalize, because a prefix of a unit vector is shorter than 1. It only works for Matryoshka-trained models; slicing an ordinary model's vector discards information and can wreck results.

// Slice, then restore unit length
const short = normalize(vector.slice(0, 256));

docs.title: 10. When do dot product, cosine similarity, and Euclidean distance give the same ranking?
docs.text: When all vectors are unit length. Then cosine equals the dot product, and squared Euclidean distance equals 2 - 2 * cosine, so all three sort results identically. OpenAI documents that its embeddings are normalized to length 1, which is why it notes that cosine can be computed with a dot product.

docs.title: 11. What goes wrong if you use a dot-product index with vectors that are not normalized?
docs.text: Longer vectors get higher scores regardless of direction, so long chunks crowd the top of every result list. In the lesson's demo, a long, partly related note scored 2.32 on raw dot product against 0.955 for the note that actually matched, while cosine ranked them 0.842 and 0.997. Normalize at write and query time or use cosine.

docs.title: 12. Can you set a fixed similarity threshold such as 0.8?
docs.text: Only per model, after calibration on labeled data. Score distributions differ widely between models, so a threshold that works for one model returns far too much or too little with another. Prefer top-k plus a reranker, and recalibrate any threshold after every model change.

docs.title: 13. What is a multilingual embedding model, and what should you check before relying on it?
docs.text: A model trained so that texts with the same meaning in different languages map close together, enabling cross-lingual retrieval. Check that the family is not English-only, evaluate each language your users write in (benchmarks such as MMTEB publish per-language results), and remember that keyword search needs per-language analyzers.

docs.title: 14. Why do embedding models have input limits, and what do you do about them?
docs.text: Models accept a maximum number of tokens per input (8,192 for OpenAI's embedding models; 32,000 for Voyage's 4 series; 128,000 for Cohere's Embed 5, as of November 2026). Longer text is cut or rejected, so documents are chunked before embedding, and very long chunks also dilute relevance.

docs.title: 15. What are int8 and binary embeddings?
docs.text: Quantized representations that store each dimension in 1 byte or 1 bit instead of 4 bytes, cutting storage to a quarter or a thirty-second. Recall drops somewhat; the usual remedy is two-stage retrieval: search the compact copy with a larger candidate count, then rescore the best candidates with full-precision vectors.

docs.title: 16. Are embeddings safe to store with weaker controls than the source text?
docs.text: No. Research (Morris et al., 2023) recovered 92% of 32-token inputs exactly from their embeddings and recovered full names from clinical notes. Treat vectors as sensitive as the text: same access controls, encryption, retention, and deletion.

docs.title: 17. Why must you re-embed when you change the model, and how do you do it without downtime?
docs.text: Old and new vectors live in different spaces, so every stored vector must be recomputed and the two must never share an index. Use a parallel migration: add a second field and index, dual-write new and edited chunks, backfill the rest in resumable batches, compare recall on an evaluation set, cut over through configuration (canary first), keep the old field for a rollback window, then drop it.

docs.title: 18. How long does a re-embedding backfill take?
docs.text: Estimate tokens and divide by your rate limit. For example, 600,000 chunks of 300 tokens are 180 million tokens; at 2,000,000 tokens per minute that is at least 90 minutes of embedding time, plus retries and writes. Make the job resumable and log progress.

docs.title: 19. Why do vector databases use approximate nearest-neighbor search?
docs.text: Exact search compares the query with every vector, about N x d work per query, which grows linearly with the collection. ANN indexes examine only a promising neighborhood and answer far faster, at the price of occasionally missing a true neighbor. The miss rate is a setting you choose.

docs.title: 20. What is recall@k for an ANN index, and how do you measure it?
docs.text: The share of the true top-k neighbors (from an exact scan) that the index returns. Take a few hundred representative queries, compute exact results (in PostgreSQL, SET LOCAL enable_indexscan = off inside a transaction), run them through the index at several settings, and compare. Recall 0.95 at k = 10 means 9.5 of the 10 true neighbors on average.

docs.title: 21. How does an HNSW index search?
docs.text: It builds layered proximity graphs: each vector gets a random maximum layer with exponentially decaying probability, so upper layers are sparse with long links. A search starts at the top, moves greedily toward the query, drops a layer, repeats, and finally explores the bottom layer with a candidate list of size ef_search before returning the best k.

docs.title: 22. What do m, ef_construction, and ef_search control in pgvector?
docs.text: m (default 16) is links per node: higher means better recall, more memory, slower builds. ef_construction (default 64) is the candidate list while building: a better graph at the cost of build time. hnsw.ef_search (default 40) is the candidate list while searching: higher recall at higher latency.

docs.title: 23. How does an IVF index work, and how can it miss a neighbor?
docs.text: It runs k-means to find lists centroids, files every vector under its nearest centroid, and at query time scans only the nearest probes lists. A true neighbor just across a cluster boundary is missed unless its cluster is probed. More probes raise recall and latency together.

docs.title: 24. What does pgvector recommend for IVFFlat settings?
docs.text: Create the index after loading data, start with rows / 1000 lists up to one million rows and sqrt(rows) above that, and start with sqrt(lists) probes (the default is 1). Rebuild when the data distribution drifts, because the clusters reflect the data at build time.

docs.title: 25. Compare HNSW and IVF.
docs.text: HNSW usually reaches higher recall at the same latency, needs no training, accepts inserts immediately, and can be created on an empty table, but it uses more memory and builds slowly. IVF builds fast, uses less memory, and combines with product quantization for huge collections, but needs representative data and periodic rebuilds. In the lesson's measured run, HNSW took 38.4 s to build and IVFFlat 2.1 s.

docs.title: 26. Describe the recall-latency trade-off you measured.
docs.text: On 50,000 clustered 128-dimension vectors in pgvector (PGlite), an exact scan took 29.6 ms at recall 1.0. HNSW went from recall 0.647 at 1.5 ms (ef_search 10) to 0.851 at 1.7 ms (40) and 0.963 at 5.1 ms (320). IVFFlat with 50 lists went from 0.464 at 1.6 ms (1 probe) to 0.747 at 4.0 ms (8 probes). Recall climbs fast, then flattens while latency keeps rising, so tune to a target.

docs.title: 27. How would you choose ef_search for production?
docs.text: Pick a recall target (for example 0.95 recall@10), measure recall and latency percentiles on representative queries at several values, choose the cheapest setting that meets the target, and re-check as the collection grows. Supabase's benchmark needed ef_search 100 for 0.98 accuracy@10 and 250 for 0.99 on its data.

docs.title: 28. What is product quantization?
docs.text: A compression method that splits each vector into sub-vectors and replaces each with the ID of its nearest centroid from a small codebook, so a vector becomes a short code (Meta's FAISS post describes 20-byte codes). Distances are approximated from the codes. It is how billion-scale indexes fit in memory, usually combined with IVF (IVF-PQ).

docs.title: 29. How much memory does an HNSW index need?
docs.text: Raw vectors plus graph links. For 10 million 768-dimension float32 vectors: 3,072 bytes each, about 30.7 GB, plus roughly 256 bytes of links per vector at M = 32 (FAISS's estimate is M x 2 x 4 bytes), about 2.6 GB more. The graph should stay in RAM, so plan for both.

docs.title: 30. When is exact search the right choice?
docs.text: For small collections (tens of thousands of chunks), for small tenants selected by a filter, and for measuring recall. It is simple and has recall 1.0. pgvector does it without an index, MongoDB with exact: true, FAISS with IndexFlatIP or IndexFlatL2.

docs.title: 31. When would you use pgvector rather than a dedicated vector database?
docs.text: When PostgreSQL already holds the data: vectors sit next to relational rows, filters are SQL, row-level security and backups already exist, and there is no second system to sync. Choose a dedicated database when you need billions of vectors, very heavy filtering, or thousands of strictly isolated tenants beyond what the database handles well.

docs.title: 32. What does MongoDB Vector Search offer a MongoDB application such as TaskFlow?
docs.text: Chunks stay next to notes, a vectorSearch index defines vector fields (numDimensions up to 8,192; cosine, dotProduct, or euclidean; optional scalar or binary quantization; hnsw or flat) and filter fields, and the $vectorSearch aggregation stage queries them with pre-filters. $rankFusion (MongoDB 8.0 and later) adds hybrid search.

docs.title: 33. Write a $vectorSearch stage for one workspace.
docs.text:
{ $vectorSearch: {
    index: "note_chunks_vector",
    path: "embedding",
    queryVector,
    numCandidates: 200,      // at least 20x limit; at most 10,000
    limit: 10,
    filter: { workspaceId }, // field indexed with type "filter"
} }

It must be the first stage of the pipeline; project the score with { $meta: "vectorSearchScore" }, which is normalized to 0 to 1.

docs.title: 34. What is FAISS, and why is it not a vector database?
docs.text: FAISS is Meta's C++ and Python library of exact and approximate indexes (flat, HNSW, IVF, PQ, on CPU and GPU). It returns positions of nearest vectors, but storage, IDs, metadata filtering, replication, and access control are yours to build, so it suits batch jobs and custom services better than a multi-tenant API.

docs.title: 35. Which pgvector operator matches cosine similarity, and what does it return?
docs.text: <=> returns cosine distance, which is 1 - cosine similarity, and needs an index built with vector_cosine_ops. <#> returns the negative inner product (because PostgreSQL index scans order ascending), and <-> is Euclidean distance.

docs.title: 36. Why are vector indexes sometimes eventually consistent, and what do you do about it?
docs.text: Some systems update the vector index asynchronously; MongoDB Vector Search follows the collection's change stream in a separate search process, so a just-written chunk may not be searchable for a moment. Monitor ingestion lag, show indexing status where it matters, and avoid read-your-write assumptions in tests.

docs.title: 37. What is the difference between pre-filtering and post-filtering?
docs.text: Post-filtering finds the nearest candidates first and then drops those that fail the filter, which can leave few or none when the filter is selective. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set first and searches only within it. Iterative or filter-aware scans sit between them: they keep searching until enough matching results appear.

docs.title: 38. Why did a selective filter return zero rows from an HNSW index?
docs.text: With ef_search at 40 and iterative scans off, pgvector took the 40 nearest candidates from the whole table; none belonged to a workspace holding 0.2% of the rows, so the query returned nothing. Setting hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order returned 10 rows, and a B-tree index on the filter column let PostgreSQL run an exact scan for that workspace.

docs.title: 39. What are pgvector's iterative index scans?
docs.text: A pgvector 0.8 feature: with hnsw.iterative_scan set to strict_order or relaxed_order, the index keeps scanning until enough rows pass the filter, up to hnsw.max_scan_tuples (default 20,000). Relaxed order can return slightly unordered rows, so wrap the query in a materialized CTE and sort again outside it.

docs.title: 40. What are the options for isolating tenants in vector search?
docs.text: From most shared to most isolated: one index with a mandatory tenant filter (plus row-level security in PostgreSQL), a partition or shard per tenant (PostgreSQL partitions, Weaviate tenants, Milvus partition key), a namespace or collection per tenant (Pinecone namespaces), and a database or cluster per tenant. Isolation, cost, and operational effort rise together.

docs.title: 41. Where must the tenant ID come from?
docs.text: From the authenticated session in server code, never from the request body and never from a language model's tool arguments, which an attacker can influence through prompt injection. Retrieval tools get the tenant injected by the application.

docs.title: 42. How does PostgreSQL row-level security help with vector search?
docs.text: A policy such as USING (workspace_id = current_setting('app.workspace_id')::bigint) filters every query for the application role. Set the value per transaction with set_config('app.workspace_id', $1, true). Because current_setting raises an error when the setting is missing, a forgotten setting fails closed. Superusers and table owners bypass it, so connect as a dedicated role.

docs.title: 43. Why does Pinecone recommend one namespace per tenant?
docs.text: On serverless indexes each namespace is stored separately, so tenants are physically isolated, a query only pays for the namespace it reads, and deleting a tenant is nearly instant. A shared namespace with a metadata filter scans every tenant's data on each query.

docs.title: 44. How do you test tenant isolation in retrieval?
docs.text: Keep automated tests that search as tenant A for content that exists only in tenant B and expect nothing, for every retrieval path (vector, keyword, hybrid, reranked), plus tests that a missing tenant context fails rather than returning everything.

docs.title: 45. What does keyword search catch that vector search misses?
docs.text: Exact strings that carry little meaning: ticket and order numbers, error codes, versions, names, rare terms, and quotations. Embeddings blur these details into the gist, while BM25 gives a rare token such as tf-1432 a high weight in the one document that contains it.

docs.title: 46. Explain BM25.
docs.text:
BM25 sums, over query terms in a document, the term's inverse document frequency times a saturating function of its frequency, discounted by document length:

IDF * f * (k1 + 1) / (f + k1 * (1 - b + b * docLength / avgDocLength))

k1 controls term-frequency saturation and b length normalization; Elasticsearch defaults them to 1.2 and 0.75.

docs.title: 47. Why is the text analyzer so important for hybrid search?
docs.text: It decides what a term is. In the lesson's PostgreSQL run, the english configuration split TF-1432 into tf and -1432, so another ticket matched on tf; without stop-word removal, "how" made a postmortem guide the top BM25 hit. Index identifiers in an exactly matched field and check stemming and stop words per language.

docs.title: 48. Why not just add the BM25 score and the cosine similarity?
docs.text: They are on unrelated scales: BM25 is unbounded and varies by query, cosine lies between -1 and 1. One retriever dominates the sum. Either fuse by rank (RRF) or normalize scores first (min-max, or mean and standard deviation as in Qdrant's DBSF) and weight them.

docs.title: 49. How does reciprocal rank fusion work?
docs.text: Each document scores sum of weight / (k + rank) over the lists it appears in, with ranks starting at 1 and k commonly 60 (Cormack et al., 2009). Rank 1 adds 1/61 and rank 10 adds 1/70, so appearing in both lists matters more than topping one. It needs no score calibration.

docs.title: 50. Compute RRF: document A is 3rd in BM25 and 7th in vector search; document B is 1st in vector search only. Which wins with k = 60?
docs.text: A: 1/63 + 1/67 = 0.01587 + 0.01493 = 0.0308. B: 1/61 = 0.0164. A wins, because being found by both retrievers outweighs a single first place.

docs.title: 51. Do all products use the same RRF defaults?
docs.text: No. Elasticsearch's rank_constant defaults to 60 and MongoDB's $rankFusion uses 60. As of November 2026, Qdrant's RRF uses k = 2 with zero-based ranks unless configured, and Weaviate's default hybrid fusion is relativeScoreFusion, a score-based method. Check before comparing systems.

docs.title: 52. How many candidates should each retriever return before fusion?
docs.text: Typically 20 to 100 each; Microsoft's Azure AI Search experiments used the top 50 from keyword and vector search. Fusion and reranking can only reorder what the legs returned, so too few candidates caps recall.

docs.title: 53. What is the difference between a bi-encoder and a cross-encoder?
docs.text: A bi-encoder embeds the query and documents separately, so document vectors are computed once and searched quickly, but the model never sees both texts together. A cross-encoder reads the query and one document as a single input and outputs a relevance score: more accurate, but one model call per pair, so it is used only to rerank a short list.

docs.title: 54. When should you add a reranker, and when not?
docs.text: Add one when only the top few results matter (RAG context, a results page, an agent picking a document) and candidates are broad. Skip it when the candidate set is already small and precise, the latency budget is tight, or candidate recall is the real problem, because a reranker cannot recover a document retrieval never returned.

docs.title: 55. What are typical reranking shapes and limits?
docs.text: Retrieve 50 to 150 candidates, rerank, keep 5 to 20 (Anthropic's experiment: 150 in, 20 out). As of November 2026, Cohere's Rerank 5 models accept 32,768 tokens of query plus document and Voyage's rerankers up to 1,000 documents per request; long chunks are truncated or split, so chunk to fit.

docs.title: 56. How do you keep a reranker from hurting availability and latency?
docs.text: Give it a short timeout and few retries, fall back to the fused order on failure, cap candidate count and chunk length, and monitor latency and fallback rate. Results reference candidates by index, so IDs and tenant checks stay in your code.

docs.title: 57. What evidence shows that hybrid search and reranking help?
docs.text: Anthropic reported that contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 cut retrieval failures (1 minus recall@20) by 49%, and adding reranking by 67%. Microsoft reported NDCG@3 of 40.6 for keyword, 43.8 for vector, 48.4 for hybrid with RRF, and 60.1 with its semantic reranker. BEIR found BM25 a robust baseline and rerankers best zero-shot, at high computational cost.

docs.title: 58. Define recall@k, MRR, and nDCG@k.
docs.text: Recall@k is relevant results in the top k divided by all relevant results. MRR is the mean over queries of 1 divided by the rank of the first relevant result. nDCG@k sums each result's gain (often 2^grade - 1) divided by log2(position + 1) and divides by the same sum for the ideal ordering, so 1.0 means perfect order.

docs.title: 59. Which metric fits which stage?
docs.text: Recall@k with a large k (50 to 150) for candidate generation, because anything missed there is lost. nDCG@k or MRR with a small k for the final order the model or user sees. Precision@k shows how much noise reaches the context window.

docs.title: 60. Two lists have the same recall@3. How can one be much better?
docs.text: Recall ignores order. In the lesson's example both lists had recall@3 of 0.667, but the fused list put both answers first: MRR 1.0 against 0.5 and nDCG@3 0.958 against 0.664.

docs.title: 61. Compute recall@3 and reciprocal rank for grades 0, 3, 0, 1, 3 at positions 1 to 5, with three relevant documents in total.
docs.text: The top 3 contain one relevant document (position 2), so recall@3 is 1/3 = 0.333. The first relevant result is at position 2, so the reciprocal rank is 0.5.

docs.title: 62. How would you build a retrieval evaluation set for TaskFlow?
docs.text: Collect 100 to 300 queries from logs and support tickets, including ID-heavy, name, multilingual, and no-answer queries. Have people who know the content grade the chunks that answer each (3 answers it, 1 related), record the workspace for tenant checks, version the set, and run every configuration over it, reporting metrics per query type.

docs.title: 63. Why is a strong offline metric not enough?
docs.text: The evaluation set can drift from real traffic (new features, languages, more ID searches), and retrieval quality is not answer quality. Refresh the set from recent logs, segment by query type, and pair offline metrics with online signals and end-to-end RAG evaluation.

docs.title: 64. After switching to a new embedding model, answer quality dropped sharply but nothing errors. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the embeddingVersion values stored in the index and the model used for query embeddings.

How to confirm: count chunks per version and run the evaluation set against the index, comparing recall@10 with the previous release.

Likely causes and fixes: queries embedded with the new model are being compared with documents embedded by the old one, or one index holds both spaces. Roll the query path back, finish the backfill into a separate field and index, evaluate, then cut over. See embedding models and dimensions.

docs.title: 65. You shortened vectors from 1,536 to 512 dimensions to save memory and recall collapsed. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the model supports Matryoshka shortening and whether the shortened vectors were re-normalized.

How to confirm: check the norms of stored vectors and measure recall at several sizes on the evaluation set.

Likely causes and fixes: the model was not trained for truncation, or sliced vectors were left shorter than unit length in a dot-product index. Use the API's dimensions parameter or re-normalize, and choose a Matryoshka model if you need small vectors. See embedding models and dimensions.

docs.title: 66. The same few long documents appear at the top of almost every search. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the index metric and whether vectors are unit length.

How to confirm: compute the norms of the top-ranked vectors and re-rank a sample with cosine similarity.

Likely causes and fixes: a dot-product index over vectors that are not normalized, so length wins over direction. Normalize at write and query time, or switch the index to cosine. See embedding models and dimensions.

docs.title: 67. Users in small workspaces get zero or two results while large workspaces work fine. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the tenant filter is applied (post-filter, pre-filter, or iterative scan) and the candidate settings.

How to confirm: run the same query with a larger ef_search or numCandidates, or with exact search, and see whether results appear.

Likely causes and fixes: post-filtering of a small ANN candidate list. Enable pgvector iterative scans, index the filter field for pre-filtering, raise numCandidates, or use a flat index, partition, or namespace for small tenants. See vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: 68. A customer reports seeing another company's note in an AI answer. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the retrieval logs for that request: which query ran, with which tenant filter, against which index.

How to confirm: reproduce with the same inputs and run cross-tenant tests on every retrieval path, including hybrid and reranked ones.

Likely causes and fixes: a path without the tenant filter (often the keyword leg), a tenant taken from the request body or tool arguments, or a stale copy in a second store. Fix the path, take the tenant from the session, add row-level security or namespaces, and treat it as a security incident. See vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: 69. Recall@10 on your monitoring queries has slipped every month for half a year with no code changes. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: collection size growth and the ANN settings (ef_search, probes, numCandidates).

How to confirm: compare index results with exact search on the same queries now and against the original measurements.

Likely causes and fixes: settings tuned for a smaller collection, or IVF clusters built on old data. Retune to the recall target, rebuild IVF indexes, and schedule recall checks. See vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: 70. Vector search p99 latency jumped and the database server is swapping. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: index size against available memory.

How to confirm: compare the HNSW index size (vectors plus graph) with RAM, and watch disk reads during queries.

Likely causes and fixes: the graph no longer fits in memory. Add memory, store halfvec or quantized vectors with rescoring, shorten dimensions with a Matryoshka model, or move to a disk-based index. See vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: 71. A note saved a few seconds ago does not show up in search. Is it a bug?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the vector index is updated asynchronously and how long ingestion takes.

How to confirm: measure the delay between the write and the first successful search, and check the ingestion queue or change-stream lag.

Likely causes and fixes: eventual consistency (MongoDB Vector Search follows the change stream) or a delayed embedding job. Monitor lag, show indexing status, and do not assume read-your-write in tests. See vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: 72. Searching for "TF-1432" returns a different ticket first. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: what the text analyzer does to the identifier and whether a keyword leg runs at all.

How to confirm: inspect the parsed query (in PostgreSQL, plainto_tsquery('english', 'TF-1432')) and the tokens stored for the document.

Likely causes and fixes: the analyzer split the ID into tf and -1432, so other tickets matched on tf, or only vector search runs. Index identifiers in an exactly matched field, route ID-shaped queries to exact lookup, and keep BM25 in a hybrid pipeline. See hybrid search and reranking.

docs.title: 73. After enabling hybrid search, long conversational questions got worse results than vector-only. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: per-query-type metrics and the keyword leg's results for those queries.

How to confirm: compare nDCG for vector-only, keyword-only, and hybrid on conversational queries, and look at the fused ranks.

Likely causes and fixes: a noisy keyword leg (OR queries, missing stop words) pushes good semantic hits down through fusion. Tune the analyzer, lower the keyword weight for conversational queries, or rerank the fused candidates. See hybrid search and reranking.

docs.title: 74. Answer latency doubled after you added a reranker. What do you look at?
docs.text:
What to check first: the rerank span in traces, candidate count, and average candidate length.

How to confirm: plot rerank latency against candidates per request and check timeouts and fallback rate.

Likely causes and fixes: too many or too long candidates per request. Rerank fewer candidates, trim chunks to the model's limit, set a timeout with a fallback to fused order, and cache repeated queries. See hybrid search and reranking.

docs.title: 75. Answers miss facts that appear near the end of long chunks, even though the right chunks are retrieved. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: chunk lengths against the reranker's and the embedding model's token limits.

How to confirm: find the token position of the missed facts and the truncation settings (Cohere's maxTokensPerDoc defaults to 4,096).

Likely causes and fixes: truncation inside the reranker or embedding model. Chunk to fit the limits, keep headings with each chunk, and check the provider's truncation behavior. See hybrid search and reranking.

docs.title: 76. The assistant now says "I found nothing relevant" far more often after a model change. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: any fixed similarity or relevance threshold in the retrieval path.

How to confirm: plot score distributions for relevant and irrelevant results under the old and new models on labeled data.

Likely causes and fixes: a threshold calibrated for the old model. Recalibrate per model on labeled data or rely on top-k plus a reranker with a calibrated score. See embedding models and dimensions.

docs.title: 77. Offline nDCG is stable but user thumbs-down on answers keeps rising. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: how recent the evaluation set is and how today's query mix compares with it.

How to confirm: sample recent queries, label them, and compare metrics with the existing set, broken down by query type.

Likely causes and fixes: the evaluation set no longer reflects traffic (new features, languages, ID searches), or the failures are in generation rather than retrieval. Refresh the set, report per segment, and evaluate end-to-end answers as in evaluating and debugging RAG. See hybrid search and reranking.

docs.text:
