docs.title: Evaluation and Monitoring Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the evaluation and monitoring lessons: use it before an interview or before wiring evals and tracing into a TaskFlow feature.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does npx promptfoo eval -c evals/promptfoo/promptfooconfig.yaml Run every test against every provider, apply assertions --grader "openai:responses:$JUDGE_MODEL" Model that grades llm-rubric assertions -o results.json -o report.html Write results; repeatable (JSON, HTML, JUnit XML, ...) --repeat 3 Run each test several times (nightly, flakiness) --filter-metadata critical=true Run only tests whose metadata matches (smoke suite) --filter-sample N Random sample of N tests on very large suites -j 4 / --max-concurrency 4 Stay under provider rate limits --no-cache, --no-share Fresh outputs; no shareable URL npx tsx scripts/dataset-manifest.ts check Fail CI if the eval set changed without a new version npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts base.json results.json Paired gate: critical cases, drop, McNemar p otelcol-contrib validate --config=otel-collector.yaml Check a Collector file before deploying it

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/llm-evals.yml (excerpt): let the paired gate decide, not the raw pass rate
env:
  CHAT_MODEL: ${{ vars.CHAT_MODEL }}      # model IDs in repository variables
  JUDGE_MODEL: ${{ vars.JUDGE_MODEL }}
  PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD: "0"      # default 100: any failure exits with code 100

# otel-collector.yaml (excerpt): mask content attributes and personal data in every service's spans
processors:
  redaction:
    allow_all_keys: true
    blocked_key_patterns: ['^gen_ai\.(input|output)\.messages$', '^gen_ai\.system_instructions$']
    blocked_values: ['[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+', '\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b']
    summary: info
GenAI attribute Holds gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.provider.name Required on a model-call span (chat <model>, CLIENT) gen_ai.request.model / gen_ai.response.model Configured alias / dated snapshot that actually ran gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, .output_tokens, .cache_read.input_tokens Token usage gen_ai.prompt.name, gen_ai.prompt.version Which prompt produced the answer gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages Content: opt-in, off by default

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Grade structured output Code checks (schema, equality, properties) Instant, free, deterministic Grade faithfulness or completeness Pointwise pass/fail judge per criterion, calibrated Absolute numbers for gates and dashboards Pick between two prompts Pairwise judge in both orders Cancels position bias; flip rate measures it Gate a pull request Critical cases + floors + paired McNemar test Catches real regressions without blocking on noise Catch model drift with no code change Nightly full run, no cache, repeats An alias can move without a pull request Report reliability of a user-facing feature pass^k or the mean pass rate pass@k flatters Trace LLM calls across vendors Manual spans + OpenTelemetry Collector fan-out One place for redaction, sampling, and backends Debug with full prompts Content capture in staging, redacted, short retention Production keeps content out of telemetry

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Margin of error of a pass rate 1.96 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n): +/- 8.3 points at n = 50, 5.9 at 100, 3.8 at 240, 2.9 at 400 (p = 0.9) Rule of three All n cases pass: true failure rate may still be about 3 / n Cohen's kappa (p_obs - p_exp) / (1 - p_exp); 0.61 to 0.80 is "substantial" Rogan-Gladen correction p_true = (p_obs + TNR - 1) / (TPR + TNR - 1) McNemar (exact) 16 regressions vs 3 fixes: p = 0.004; 7 vs 5: p = 0.77 Starting set sizes 20 to 50 cases (prototype), 100 to 300 (launch), 100 to 200 calibration labels promptfoo exit code 100 when the pass rate is below PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD (default 100%) GenAI conventions Development status; moved to semantic-conventions-genai in semconv v1.42.0 (June 2026) Attribute rename gen_ai.system became gen_ai.provider.name in semconv v1.37 Prometheus names gen_ai.client.token.usage becomes gen_ai_client_token_usage; counters add _total Sampling parameters OpenAI Responses: temperature, no seed; Anthropic API 2026-10-21: no temperature, top_p, top_k

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• One overall score. Report per-slice pass rates with Wilson intervals.
  • Editing released cases. Retire them, add a new id, and check the manifest in CI.
  • Judging what code can check. Move schema, dates, and length into code checks first.
  • An uncalibrated judge gating releases. Measure TPR and TNR on held-out expert labels.
  • One-order pairwise comparisons. Judge both orders and report the flip rate.
  • Gating on a raw pass-rate drop. Use a paired test against the committed baseline.
  • Full prompts in production traces. Keep capture off; redact at the source and in the Collector.
  • User IDs as metric labels. Keep high-cardinality values on spans only.

docs.title: Where to go deeper
docs.text:

Back to the Evaluation and monitoring overview.

docs.title: Evals in CI and Regression Testing
docs.text:
An evaluation set and a set of graders are only useful if they run every time something that affects the model's behavior changes: the prompt template, the model ID, the retrieval settings, a tool definition, or the code that parses the output. Running them by hand means they run before the big release and are skipped for the "small" change that breaks production. Running them in CI makes them a gate, like unit tests, with one important difference: the system under test is not deterministic, so a failing number is evidence, not proof.

This lesson wires the TaskFlow Assistant's evaluation set into GitHub Actions. It compares eval tools (promptfoo in depth, plus DeepEval, Braintrust, the OpenAI Evals API, and Inspect), shows how to turn the versioned dataset and the code-based checks from the previous lessons into a promptfoo suite, designs gates and thresholds that catch real regressions without blocking on noise, handles nondeterminism with repeats and paired comparisons, and keeps the bill under control with caching and tiered runs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
LLM regressions are quiet. A prompt edit that fixes one complaint changes behavior on hundreds of other inputs, and nothing crashes: the API still returns 200, the JSON still parses, and the drafts are just a little more often wrong. Model updates are worse, because they change behavior without any change in your repository. The only reliable way to notice is to rerun the same cases and compare.

At the same time, a naive gate does harm. If the gate is "pass rate must not drop", it fails on random fluctuation, people learn to rerun it until it is green, and the gate becomes noise. If the gate calls a paid model for 2,000 cases on every push, the eval bill outgrows the feature's. The techniques in this lesson are what make an LLM gate both trustworthy and affordable.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• promptfoo. The open-source (MIT) eval runner used in this lesson documents its CI use in CI/CD integration, including caching the promptfoo cache directory keyed on the prompt files and configuration, and publishes a GitHub Action that evaluates a pull request and posts a summary comment. On March 9, 2026, OpenAI announced that it would acquire Promptfoo and said it would keep developing the open-source project; check the project's repository for its current status before you depend on it.
  • Error bars for evals. Evan Miller's Adding Error Bars to Evals (2024) argues that evaluations are experiments and recommends standard errors, clustered standard errors for related questions, variance reduction by resampling, analysis of question-level paired differences when comparing two models, and power analysis to size an eval.
  • pass^k. The tau-bench paper, tau-bench (2024), proposed the pass^k metric for the reliability of agent behavior over multiple trials: a task counts only if it succeeds in all k attempts, which is closer to what users experience than a single lucky run.
  • OpenAI. Evaluation best practices recommends eval-driven development ("evaluate early and often"), scoped tests at every stage, and structuring evaluations for automated scoring.
  • DeepEval. The DeepEval quickstart shows the Python side of the same idea: DeepEval plugs into Pytest, so deepeval test run collects eval files and runs them like tests, which is what makes it easy to drop into an existing CI job.

Popular tools and providers: promptfoo, DeepEval, Braintrust, the OpenAI Evals API, Inspect, LangSmith and Langfuse experiments, and GitHub Actions or any CI system that can run Node.js or Python.

docs.title: Where evals run
docs.text:
Evals run at several points, each with a different budget:

Where What runs Budget Purpose Every commit Unit tests: prompt rendering, parsers, code checks, judge plumbing with stubs Seconds, free Catch broken code, not model behavior Pull request touching AI code The test split with code checks and a few judge criteria, cached Minutes, low Block clear regressions before merge Nightly on main The full suite, no cache, several repeats per case, all judge criteria Tens of minutes, moderate Detect drift from model updates; measure flakiness Before a model or provider switch Full suite on old and new, paired comparison, human review of differences Hours, planned Decide the switch with evidence Production Code checks on all traffic, a judge on a sample, user feedback Continuous Catch what offline sets miss (see LLM observability and tracing)

Keep unit tests and evals separate. Unit tests must be deterministic and never call a model; they belong in npm test. Evals call models, cost money, and are noisy; they get their own job, their own gate, and their own schedule.

docs.title: Eval tools
docs.text:
All of these run cases, apply graders, and report scores; they differ in language, where results live, and how much they assume about your app:

Tool Language and style Where results live Good fit promptfoo YAML config with JavaScript, TypeScript, or Python extensions; CLI Local files and a local web viewer; optional sharing Any stack; prompt and model comparisons; red teaming DeepEval Python, Pytest-style test files Local, optional hosted platform Python services and RAG pipelines Braintrust TypeScript or Python SDK (Eval() with data, task, scores), autoevals library Hosted platform Teams that want hosted experiment tracking OpenAI Evals API Hosted evals: data source config plus testing criteria (graders) OpenAI platform Apps already on the OpenAI platform Inspect Python framework from the UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs; inspect eval Local logs and viewer Capability and agentic evaluations evalite TypeScript, built on Vitest, local UI; deprecated and archived on November 9, 2026, with Langfuse as the maintainer's suggested replacement Local Existing suites only; plan a migration LangSmith, Langfuse SDKs that run experiments over hosted datasets Their platforms Teams already tracing with them

A good rule is to keep the dataset and the checks in your repository, in your own formats, and treat the tool as a runner. The case schema and checkDraft from the earlier lessons stay the same whichever runner you choose; only the glue changes.

docs.title: promptfoo in a TaskFlow repository
docs.text:
promptfoo reads a configuration with prompts, providers, and tests, runs every test against every provider, applies each test's assertions, and writes results. For an application feature, the most faithful setup does not let promptfoo call the model directly. It uses a custom provider that calls the same code path production uses, here draftTaskAsText from prompt design and templates, so the eval exercises the real template, the real parameters, and the real parsing.

The pieces:

File Role promptfooconfig.yaml Wires the provider, the test generator, and options together taskflow-provider.ts Calls the app's code for each case, with a response cache load-cases.ts Turns the versioned JSONL dataset into promptfoo tests, with metadata for filtering assert-draft.ts Reuses the code-based checks as a promptfoo javascript assertion llm-rubric assertions Judge criteria where code cannot decide, graded by the model given with --grader

Exit codes make it CI-friendly. promptfoo eval exits with code 100 when the pass rate is below PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD (default 100%, so any failure fails the job); setting the threshold to 0 leaves the decision to a separate gate script, while errors such as a failed provider call still fail the run. Useful flags for CI are -o (JSON, HTML, JUnit XML, and other formats; repeatable), --repeat, -j/--max-concurrency, --filter-metadata, --filter-sample, --no-cache, and --no-share.

docs.title: Gates and thresholds
docs.text:
A gate turns a run into a merge decision. Four kinds of rules work well together:

Rule Example for the Assistant Why Critical cases always pass late-evening-tz, injection-in-request Known incidents and security cases must never regress, whatever the average does Absolute floors Schema validity 100%; overall pass rate at least 88% Catches a collapse, even without a baseline Paired regression against the baseline Fail if the pass rate drops more than 2 points and the paired test says the drop is unlikely to be chance Compares like with like, case by case Operational budgets Median output tokens and p95 latency within 20% of the baseline Quality changes often come with cost or latency changes

The baseline is a committed results file for the current main (evals/baseline/task-assistant.json). Comparing against a baseline on the same dataset version, case by case, is much more sensitive than comparing two pass rates: a change that fixes 5 cases and breaks 7 has almost the same average, but the list of 7 regressions is exactly what a reviewer needs. When a change in scores is intended (a new model, a corrected label), update the baseline in the same reviewed pull request that causes it, never automatically.

docs.title: Handling nondeterminism
docs.text:
The same prompt, model, and input can give different outputs. Sources of variation include sampling, provider-side batching and hardware effects, silent model updates behind an alias, and timing in tool-using agents. You cannot remove all of it, so design the evals to measure through it:

  • Pin what you can. Read a specific model snapshot from configuration rather than a moving alias, and record it with each run. Most behavior changes "with no code change" turn out to be a model alias that moved.
  • Do not rely on sampling parameters. Setting a low temperature reduces variation where it is supported, but it is not a guarantee of identical outputs, and support differs by provider and API version: OpenAI's Responses API accepts temperature but has no seed parameter, and Anthropic's API version 2026-10-21 removed temperature, top_p, and top_k entirely (requests that send them get a 400 error). Check the current API reference instead of copying old settings.
  • Repeat cases and choose an aggregation deliberately. With k runs per case, pass@k (at least one success) measures what is possible, pass^k (all succeed) measures reliability, and the mean pass rate estimates a typical single run. For a user-facing feature, pass^k or the mean is the honest number; pass@k flatters.
  • Know the noise band. The 95% margin of a pass rate on n cases is about 1.96 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n). With 240 cases at 90%, that is plus or minus 3.8 points, so a run that scores 88.3% instead of 90.8% has not regressed by itself.
  • Compare pairs, not averages. When two versions run on the same cases, only the cases where they disagree carry information. McNemar's test asks whether the regressions and fixes are too unbalanced to be chance; it is far more sensitive than comparing two independent pass rates, which is the point Miller's paper makes about paired analysis.
  • Track flaky cases. A case that passes on some repeats and fails on others is either ambiguous (fix the label or the guide) or sitting on a real weakness. List flaky cases in every nightly report; do not silently drop them.

docs.title: Controlling cost
docs.text:
Eval cost is the number of cases, times repeats, times calls per case (the feature plus each judge criterion), times tokens per call. Every lever reduces one of those factors:

Lever How Trade-off Path filters Run evals only when src/ai/**, evals/**, or dependencies change Model alias changes are invisible to it, so keep the nightly run Response cache on pull requests Cache outputs keyed on prompt hash, model, and input; reruns are nearly free Cached outputs hide nondeterminism, so the nightly run disables the cache Code checks first Skip judge calls for cases whose code checks already failed None; it is pure saving Tiered suites Critical and smoke cases on pull requests, the full suite nightly (--filter-metadata) Some regressions are found the next morning instead of before merge Sampling --filter-sample with a fixed seed on very large suites Wider confidence intervals Cheaper judges A smaller judge model once it is calibrated for a criterion Needs re-calibration; see the judge lesson Batch APIs Nightly runs through a provider's batch endpoint Slower turnaround; see prompt caching and batch processing Concurrency limits --max-concurrency keeps runs under rate limits Longer runs

The broader cost picture for LLM features is in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: Secrets and safety in CI
docs.text: Eval jobs need provider API keys, which makes them a target. Store keys as encrypted secrets, scope them to the eval job, and use a separate key with its own spending limit for evals so a runaway job cannot exhaust production quota. Pull requests from forks do not receive secrets in GitHub Actions, so the workflow skips the eval job for them instead of failing. Keep model IDs in repository variables, not secrets, so they are visible in logs and reviews. The general practices are in secrets management and GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Prompt, model, retrieval, or tool definition changes Pull-request evals with a paired gate against the baseline Provider or model upgrade Full suite with repeats on both, paired comparison, and a human read of the differences Nothing changed in the repository Nightly runs to detect upstream model drift Purely deterministic code around the model Unit tests only; evals add cost without information Tiny prototype with a handful of cases Run evals locally before merging; add CI once the set has dozens of cases Very large suites (thousands of cases) Sampled or tiered pull-request runs, full runs nightly or before releases

Do not gate merges on a single unrepeated run of a judge-graded criterion with a tight threshold; it will block on noise. Do not let evals call production systems with side effects (sending email, creating real tasks); stub the side effects in the provider or point it at a test project.

docs.title: The promptfoo configuration
docs.text:
# evals/promptfoo/promptfooconfig.yaml: TaskFlow Assistant regression suite
description: TaskFlow Assistant on the task-assistant dataset
prompts:
  - "{{request}}"            # the provider renders the real, versioned template itself
providers:
  - file://taskflow-provider.ts
tests:
  - path: file://load-cases.ts
    config:
      split: test
evaluateOptions:
  maxConcurrency: 4

The prompt entry exists because promptfoo requires one; the provider ignores it and renders the real template. File paths in the configuration are resolved relative to the configuration file.

docs.title: The provider: running the real code path
docs.text:
// evals/promptfoo/taskflow-provider.ts: run the real Assistant code path for each test case
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { existsSync, mkdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { join } from "node:path";
import type { ApiProvider, CallApiContextParams, ProviderResponse } from "promptfoo";
import type { EvalCase } from "../case-schema.js";
import { draftTaskAsText } from "../../src/ai/assistant-client.js";
import { PROMPT_HASH, PROMPT_ID, PROMPT_VERSION } from "../../src/ai/prompts/task-assistant.js";

const CACHE_DIR = process.env.EVAL_CACHE_DIR ?? ".eval-cache";

export default class TaskAssistantProvider implements ApiProvider {
  id() {
    return `taskflow:${PROMPT_ID}@${PROMPT_VERSION}#${PROMPT_HASH}`;
  }

  async callApi(_prompt: string, context?: CallApiContextParams): Promise<ProviderResponse> {
    const c = context?.vars.evalCase as unknown as EvalCase;
    // Same prompt, model, and input give the same cache key; a prompt or model change misses.
    const key = createHash("sha256")
      .update(JSON.stringify([PROMPT_HASH, process.env.CHAT_MODEL, c.request, c.members, c.now, c.tz]))
      .digest("hex");
    const file = join(CACHE_DIR, `${key}.json`);
    if (process.env.EVAL_NO_CACHE !== "1" && existsSync(file)) {
      return { output: JSON.parse(readFileSync(file, "utf8")).output, cached: true };
    }
    const started = Date.now();
    try {
      const output = await draftTaskAsText(
        { projectName: "Eval project", currentUser: c.members[0] ?? "Eval user", members: c.members, now: new Date(c.now), timeZone: c.tz },
        c.request,
      );
      mkdirSync(CACHE_DIR, { recursive: true });
      writeFileSync(file, JSON.stringify({ output }));
      return { output, latencyMs: Date.now() - started };
    } catch (err) {
      return { error: `assistant call failed: ${(err as Error).message}` };
    }
  }
}

The provider id includes the prompt's id, version, and hash, so every result records exactly which template produced it. The cache key includes the prompt hash and CHAT_MODEL, so editing the template or switching the model invalidates the cache automatically; EVAL_NO_CACHE=1 turns it off for nightly runs. promptfoo's own disk cache covers its built-in providers; a custom provider is responsible for its own, which is why this one implements a small file cache.

docs.title: Loading the versioned dataset as tests
docs.text:
// evals/promptfoo/load-cases.ts: turn the versioned JSONL dataset into promptfoo test cases
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { parseCases } from "../case-schema.js";

const DATASET = new URL("../datasets/task-assistant/cases.jsonl", import.meta.url);

export default async function loadCases(config?: { split?: "dev" | "test" }) {
  const split = config?.split ?? "test";
  const cases = parseCases(readFileSync(DATASET, "utf8"), "cases.jsonl")
    .filter((c) => c.status === "active" && c.split === split);

  return cases.map((c) => ({
    description: c.id,
    vars: { request: c.request, evalCase: c },   // array vars would expand into extra tests, so pass the case whole
    metadata: { critical: String(c.critical), ...c.slices },     // for --filter-metadata and reports
    assert: [
      { type: "javascript", value: "file://assert-draft.ts", metric: "contract" },
      ...(c.expect.clarifyingQuestion === "present"
        ? [{
            type: "llm-rubric",
            metric: "clarifying-question",
            value: "The clarifyingQuestion asks who should own the task, and the draft does not assign it to anyone.",
          }]
        : []),
    ],
  }));
}

Two details matter. The case is passed as one object, because promptfoo expands array-valued variables into one test per element: passing members as an array would have multiplied the tests. And the slices and the critical flag go into metadata, which makes --filter-metadata critical=true a ready-made smoke suite and lets reports group results by slice. The llm-rubric assertion is added only to cases where code cannot judge the quality of the clarifying question.

docs.title: Reusing the code-based checks as an assertion
docs.text:
// evals/promptfoo/assert-draft.ts: a promptfoo assertion that applies the code-based checks
import type { AssertionValueFunctionContext, GradingResult } from "promptfoo";
import type { EvalCase } from "../case-schema.js";
import { checkDraft } from "../draft-checks.js";

export default function assertDraft(output: string, context: AssertionValueFunctionContext): GradingResult {
  const evalCase = context.vars.evalCase as unknown as EvalCase;
  const { pass, checks } = checkDraft(output, evalCase);
  const failed = checks.filter((x) => !x.pass);
  return {
    pass,
    score: (checks.length - failed.length) / checks.length,
    reason: pass ? `${checks.length} checks passed` : failed.map((x) => `${x.name}: ${x.detail}`).join("; "),
  };
}

checkDraft is the function from the LLM-as-judge lesson; the assertion only adapts its result to promptfoo's GradingResult shape.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
A dry run in a scratch copy of the repository, with the Assistant client replaced by a stub that returns canned drafts (including a deliberate time-zone bug) and llm-rubric graded by a stub grader, so no API key is needed:

$ npx promptfoo eval -c evals/promptfoo/promptfooconfig.yaml --grader file://stub-grader.ts \
    -o results.json --no-progress-bar --no-share --no-table
Running 5 test cases (up to 4 at a time)...
✓ Eval complete (ID: eval-K1N-2026-11-14T15:16:32)

Results:
  ✓ 4 passed (80.00%)
  ✗ 1 failed (20.00%)
  0 errors (0%)
$ echo $?
100

The failure in results.json is late-evening-tz with the reason dueDate: got 2026-11-15, expected 2026-11-14, the time-zone bug the critical case exists to catch. In the same dry run, rerunning used the response cache for every case; --filter-metadata critical=true ran only the two critical cases; PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD=75 turned the 80% run into exit code 0; and on the dev split the llm-rubric assertion produced a separate clarifying-question metric next to contract. In CI, --grader "openai:responses:$JUDGE_MODEL" replaces the stub with a real judge model chosen from the provider's current model list.

docs.title: The regression gate
docs.text:
The gate compares the candidate run with the committed baseline, case by case. With --repeat, a case passes only if all its repeats pass (pass^k), and cases whose repeats disagree are listed as flaky:

// evals/compare-runs.ts: paired comparison of a candidate eval run against the baseline
// Usage: npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json results.json
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

interface Row { testCase: { description: string; metadata?: Record<string, string> }; success: boolean }
interface CaseResult { passes: number; runs: number; critical: boolean }

const MAX_DROP = 0.02;          // tolerated drop in pass rate, in absolute terms
const ALPHA = 0.05;             // significance level for the paired test

function load(file: string): Map<string, CaseResult> {
  const rows: Row[] = JSON.parse(readFileSync(file, "utf8")).results.results;
  const byCase = new Map<string, CaseResult>();
  for (const r of rows) {        // with --repeat N, each case appears N times
    const id = r.testCase.description;
    const c = byCase.get(id) ?? { passes: 0, runs: 0, critical: r.testCase.metadata?.critical === "true" };
    c.runs++;
    if (r.success) c.passes++;
    byCase.set(id, c);
  }
  return byCase;
}

/** Two-sided exact McNemar test: are regressions and fixes too unbalanced to be chance? */
function mcnemarP(regressions: number, fixes: number): number {
  const n = regressions + fixes;
  if (n === 0) return 1;
  const k = Math.min(regressions, fixes);
  let logC = 0, tail = 0;                       // sum of C(n, i) / 2^n for i = 0..k
  for (let i = 0; i <= k; i++) {
    if (i > 0) logC += Math.log(n - i + 1) - Math.log(i);
    tail += Math.exp(logC - n * Math.LN2);
  }
  return Math.min(1, 2 * tail);
}

const [baseFile, candFile] = process.argv.slice(2);
const base = load(baseFile), cand = load(candFile);
const shared = [...cand.keys()].filter((id) => base.has(id));
const passed = (c: CaseResult) => c.passes === c.runs;   // strict: every repeat must pass (pass^k)

const regressions = shared.filter((id) => passed(base.get(id)!) && !passed(cand.get(id)!));
const fixes = shared.filter((id) => !passed(base.get(id)!) && passed(cand.get(id)!));
const flaky = shared.filter((id) => { const c = cand.get(id)!; return c.passes > 0 && c.passes < c.runs; });
const rate = (m: Map<string, CaseResult>) => shared.filter((id) => passed(m.get(id)!)).length / shared.length;
const drop = rate(base) - rate(cand);
const p = mcnemarP(regressions.length, fixes.length);
const criticalRegressions = regressions.filter((id) => cand.get(id)!.critical);

console.log(`paired cases: ${shared.length}; pass rate ${(100 * rate(base)).toFixed(1)}% -> ${(100 * rate(cand)).toFixed(1)}%`);
console.log(`regressions: ${regressions.length} ${regressions.join(" ")}`);
console.log(`fixes: ${fixes.length} ${fixes.join(" ")}`);
console.log(`flaky (repeats disagree): ${flaky.length} ${flaky.join(" ")}`);
console.log(`McNemar exact p = ${p.toFixed(3)}`);

const reasons = [
  ...(criticalRegressions.length ? [`critical cases regressed: ${criticalRegressions.join(", ")}`] : []),
  ...(drop > MAX_DROP && p < ALPHA ? [`pass rate dropped ${(100 * drop).toFixed(1)} points (p = ${p.toFixed(3)})`] : []),
];
if (reasons.length) {
  console.log(`GATE: FAIL - ${reasons.join("; ")}`);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log(drop > MAX_DROP ? "GATE: PASS with warning - drop is not significant; review the regressions" : "GATE: PASS");

Three candidate runs of a 240-case suite with three repeats each, compared with the same baseline (generated result files, run through the real script):

$ npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json runs/candidate-ok.json
paired cases: 240; pass rate 90.8% -> 90.0%
regressions: 7 case-013 case-014 case-015 case-016 case-023 case-024 case-025
fixes: 5 case-031 case-034 case-038 case-040 case-059
flaky (repeats disagree): 3 case-023 case-024 case-025
McNemar exact p = 0.774
GATE: PASS

$ npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json runs/candidate-bad.json
paired cases: 240; pass rate 90.8% -> 85.4%
regressions: 16 case-013 case-014 case-015 case-016 case-017 case-018 case-019 case-020 case-021 case-022 case-023 case-024 case-025 case-026 case-035 case-036
fixes: 3 case-031 case-034 case-038
flaky (repeats disagree): 2 case-035 case-036
McNemar exact p = 0.004
GATE: FAIL - pass rate dropped 5.4 points (p = 0.004)

$ npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json runs/candidate-critical.json
paired cases: 240; pass rate 90.8% -> 91.3%
regressions: 1 case-004
fixes: 2 case-031 case-034
flaky (repeats disagree): 0 
McNemar exact p = 1.000
GATE: FAIL - critical cases regressed: case-004

The first run is noise: seven regressions against five fixes, three of them flaky, and a p-value of 0.774. The second is a real regression: 16 against 3 is very unlikely to be chance (p = 0.004). The third improves the average but breaks a critical case, which no average-based gate would catch. Note the effect of the strict rule in the first run: the three flaky cases count as regressions, which is why flaky cases need their own list and follow-up.

docs.title: The GitHub Actions workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/llm-evals.yml: LLM regression evals for the TaskFlow Assistant
name: LLM evals

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "src/ai/**"
      - "evals/**"
      - "package-lock.json"
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * *"                 # nightly: full suite, fresh samples, repeats
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: llm-evals-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  CHAT_MODEL: ${{ vars.CHAT_MODEL }}      # model IDs live in repository variables, not in code
  JUDGE_MODEL: ${{ vars.JUDGE_MODEL }}
  PROMPTFOO_DISABLE_TELEMETRY: "1"
  PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD: "0"      # compare-runs.ts decides pass or fail, not the raw rate

jobs:
  pr-evals:
    # Pull requests from forks get no secrets, so they cannot call the model.
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    env:
      OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
      EVAL_CACHE_DIR: .eval-cache
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test                                     # unit tests, including the judge plumbing
      - run: npx tsx scripts/dataset-manifest.ts check    # no silent edits to the eval set
      - uses: actions/cache@v6
        with:
          path: .eval-cache
          key: llm-evals-${{ vars.CHAT_MODEL }}-${{ hashFiles('src/ai/prompts/**', 'evals/datasets/**') }}
          restore-keys: llm-evals-${{ vars.CHAT_MODEL }}-
      - name: Run the eval suite
        run: >-
          npx promptfoo eval -c evals/promptfoo/promptfooconfig.yaml
          --grader "openai:responses:$JUDGE_MODEL"
          -o results.json -o report.html --no-progress-bar --no-share
      - name: Gate on the paired comparison with the baseline
        run: npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json results.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: llm-evals-pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          path: |
            results.json
            report.html
          retention-days: 14

  nightly-evals:
    if: github.event_name != 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 60
    env:
      OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
      EVAL_NO_CACHE: "1"                                  # fresh outputs every night
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsx scripts/dataset-manifest.ts check
      - name: Run the eval suite three times per case
        run: >-
          npx promptfoo eval -c evals/promptfoo/promptfooconfig.yaml
          --repeat 3 --max-concurrency 4
          --grader "openai:responses:$JUDGE_MODEL"
          -o nightly.json -o nightly.html --no-progress-bar --no-share
      - name: Compare with the baseline
        run: npx tsx evals/compare-runs.ts evals/baseline/task-assistant.json nightly.json
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        if: always()
        with:
          name: llm-evals-nightly-${{ github.run_id }}
          path: |
            nightly.json
            nightly.html
          retention-days: 30

What each part does:

  • Triggers. Pull requests run evals only when AI code, eval files, or dependencies change. The nightly schedule catches upstream model changes that no pull request would trigger.
  • Model IDs from variables. vars.CHAT_MODEL and vars.JUDGE_MODEL are repository variables; changing a model is a reviewed settings change, recorded in every run's environment, and the cache key includes the model so old outputs are not reused.
  • Fork safety. The if condition skips the eval job for forks, which have no access to secrets, instead of failing it.
  • Cache. The response cache is restored before the run and saved after it, keyed on the model and the hash of the prompts and the dataset, so an unchanged pull request reruns at almost no cost.
  • Gate. PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD: "0" stops promptfoo from failing the job on its own, while provider errors still fail it; the paired comparison in compare-runs.ts makes the decision.
  • Artifacts. The JSON and HTML reports are uploaded even when the gate fails, so reviewers can read the regressed cases.

actionlint 1.7.12 reports no problems for this workflow. The action versions follow the rest of these notes; for the general workflow syntax see GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run evals in their own job, separate from deterministic unit tests.
  • Exercise the production code path through a custom provider instead of re-implementing the prompt in the eval tool.
  • Keep the dataset, checks, and baseline in the repository; treat the eval tool as a replaceable runner.
  • Gate on critical cases, absolute floors, and a paired comparison with the baseline, not on a raw pass rate.
  • Pin model snapshots in configuration and record them with every run.
  • Use repeats and report pass^k or the mean, plus a list of flaky cases.
  • Cache responses on pull requests and disable the cache nightly.
  • Update the baseline only in reviewed pull requests that explain the change.
  • Give evals their own API key with a spending limit, and skip them for forks.
  • Upload reports as artifacts so failures are readable without rerunning.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The eval job fails on random pull requests. Detect: the same commit passes on rerun; failures cluster on judge criteria. Cause: a raw pass-rate threshold tighter than the noise band, often with a single run per case. Fix: gate on the paired comparison with a significance test, add repeats to the nightly run, and quarantine flaky cases for relabeling.
  • Scores dropped overnight with no merged changes. Detect: the nightly comparison fails while main has not changed. Cause: the model alias moved to a new snapshot, or the provider changed behavior. Fix: pin a snapshot in CHAT_MODEL, compare the old and new snapshots explicitly, and update the baseline only after review.
  • The eval bill exceeds the feature's bill. Detect: the eval API key's usage grows with every push. Cause: no path filter, no cache, judge calls for every criterion on every case. Fix: add path filters and the response cache, short-circuit judges on code failures, tier the suites, and move broad runs to the nightly job.
  • Pull requests from contributors fail the eval job. Detect: fork pull requests fail with authentication errors from the provider. Cause: forks get no secrets. Fix: skip the job for forks with an if condition and run evals after a maintainer merges or re-runs the change from a branch.
  • A regression shipped although CI was green. Detect: an incident on a kind of request the suite covers poorly. Cause: a coverage gap, or a baseline that was updated to accept the regression. Fix: add the incident as a critical case, require a written reason for baseline updates, and review slice reports, not only the overall gate.
  • Eval results are not reproducible. Detect: nobody can tell which prompt or dataset produced a score from last month. Cause: results were not tied to versions. Fix: include the prompt hash in the provider id, check the dataset manifest before every run, and keep artifacts long enough to compare.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Eval suite: The dataset, graders, and configuration that produce scores for one feature.
  • Custom provider: A promptfoo provider that calls your own code instead of a model API directly.
  • Baseline: The committed results of the current version, used for comparison.
  • Regression gate: The rules that turn eval results into a merge decision.
  • Critical case: A case that must pass on every run.
  • Paired comparison: Comparing two versions case by case on the same inputs.
  • McNemar's test: A test of whether paired binary changes (regressions and fixes) are balanced.
  • pass@k: At least one success in k attempts.
  • pass^k: Success in all k attempts.
  • Flaky case: A case whose repeats disagree.
  • Noise band: The range of scores expected from random variation alone.
  • Tiered suite: Smaller suites on pull requests and the full suite on a schedule.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Putting model-calling evals in npm test, so unit tests become slow, flaky, and expensive.
  • Re-implementing the prompt in the eval tool, so the eval tests a copy of the feature.
  • Gating on "pass rate must not drop" with a single run.
  • Believing a low temperature makes outputs reproducible.
  • Comparing two independent pass rates when the same cases were run on both versions.
  • Updating the baseline automatically after every merge.
  • Running the full judge suite on every push.
  • Letting evals create real tasks or send real emails.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why should model-calling evals run in a separate CI job from unit tests, and what belongs in each?
  2. What does a custom promptfoo provider give you that a built-in provider does not? Why does it need its own cache?
  3. Describe four kinds of gate rules and what each one catches.
  4. A suite has 400 cases at a 90% pass rate. What is the approximate 95% noise band, and would a run at 88.5% concern you on its own? (1.96 * sqrt(0.09 / 400), about 2.9 points; 88.5% is inside it.)
  5. A candidate has 9 regressions and 2 fixes against the baseline. Why is this stronger evidence than the change in pass rate alone, and which test would you use? (Paired: McNemar's exact test, p is about 0.065, so borderline; look at the cases.)
  6. Explain pass@k and pass^k. Which would you report for the TaskFlow Assistant, and why?
  7. List five ways to reduce eval cost and the trade-off of each.
  8. Scores dropped in last night's run and nothing was merged. What do you check first?

docs.title: Evaluation and Monitoring Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review how to build evaluation sets, grade outputs with code and LLM judges, run evals as regression tests in CI, and observe LLM features in production with traces, metrics, and user feedback. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is an evaluation set, and how is it different from a benchmark?
docs.text: A fixed, versioned list of cases for one feature, each with an input exactly as the feature receives it and an expectation a correct output must satisfy. A public benchmark measures general model ability on someone else's task; an evaluation set measures your feature, with your prompts, tools, and data, on the inputs your users send.

docs.title: 2. What are the parts of a good evaluation case?
docs.text: The input (for the TaskFlow Assistant: request, project members, server time, time zone), the expectation (only the keys that matter, such as dueDate and intent), and metadata: a stable id, slice tags, the split, a critical flag, the source and a trace or incident reference, who labeled it, the dataset version that added it, and its status.

docs.title: 3. Why should expectations often be partial?
docs.text: Many outputs are correct for the same input: "Call the bank" and "Phone the bank" are both fine titles. Pinning one exact value makes good outputs fail and trains people to ignore the eval. Check what the case is about, and leave other qualities to other cases or to a rubric.

docs.title: 4. What kinds of expectations can a case hold?
docs.text: Reference values (exact dueDate), properties every output must satisfy (assignee is a member or null), a reference answer plus criteria (cite note X and state the launch date), criteria only (a rubric for a summary), and pairwise preferences between two outputs. Prefer the first two; they are graded by code.

docs.title: 5. Where do good cases come from?
docs.text: Hand-written cases from the spec before launch; sampled production traces; failure signals such as thumbs-down, edited drafts, and retries; incidents and bug reports; and synthetic variations to fill thin slices. Each source covers a gap the others leave. Reading real traces (error analysis) finds most of the useful ones.

docs.title: 6. How do you sample cases from production responsibly?
docs.text: Use only traffic you may reuse (consent and policy), scrub personal data before anything is stored, keep the trace ID rather than the raw request, deduplicate on normalized and scrubbed text, and stratify: take failure signals first, fill every slice to a minimum, then add random traffic. Repeat the sampling regularly as traffic changes.

docs.title: 7. Why is random sampling of production traffic not enough?
docs.text: It mirrors traffic, so a slice that is 0.5% of requests gets one case in 200, which measures nothing. Rare but important inputs (injection attempts, other languages, late-evening time zones) need deliberate minimum counts, often filled with hand-written or synthetic cases because production contains too few of them.

docs.title: 8. What is leakage in an evaluation set?
docs.text: Anything that lets the system see the answer or lets tuning inflate the test score: a production request that is also a few-shot example in the prompt, the same or a near-duplicate request in both the dev and test splits, or test cases copied into prompt instructions.

docs.title: 9. How do you make labels trustworthy?
docs.text: Write a labeling guide that answers ambiguous questions with product sign-off, prefer pass/fail with a written reason, use domain experts for domain judgments, double-label a share of every round, measure agreement, and adjudicate every disagreement, updating the guide when a rule was unclear.

docs.title: 10. How do you compute Cohen's kappa, and why not raw agreement?
docs.text: kappa = (p_observed - p_expected) / (1 - p_expected), where p_expected is the agreement two labelers would reach by chance given how often each uses each label. Raw agreement overstates consistency when one label dominates: with 75% passing outputs, random guessing already agrees most of the time. Example: 85% raw agreement with p_expected = 0.60 is a kappa of 0.63.

docs.title: 11. Why report scores per slice, and how many cases does a slice need?
docs.text: One overall score hides concentrated failures. The 95% margin of a pass rate is about 1.96 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n): plus or minus 8 points for 50 cases at 90%, 6 for 100, 3 for 400. If all n cases pass, the true failure rate can still be about 3 / n (the rule of three), so 12 out of 12 proves little. Report intervals and add cases where slices matter.

docs.title: 12. How do you version an evaluation set?
docs.text: Keep it in the repository as JSONL, release immutable versions with semantic numbers, never edit a released case (retire it with a reason and add a new id), record a manifest with the content hash and counts, check it in CI before every run, and store dataset@version with every result.

docs.title: 13. Why should code-based checks come before an LLM judge?
docs.text: They are instant, free, deterministic, and exact for anything a program can decide: JSON validity, schema, field equality, membership, date rules, length, citations that exist, tool-call arguments. Every check moved from a judge to code removes cost and noise. A judge is for what remains: faithfulness, completeness, usefulness.

docs.title: 14. What is the grader ladder?
docs.text: Code checks, then reference comparison, then an LLM judge, then human review. Each rung up handles more nuance but costs more, is slower, and varies more. Push every check as low as it can go, and use humans mainly for calibration labels and hard cases.

docs.title: 15. What makes a good rubric?
docs.text: One criterion per judgment, binary verdicts, PASS and FAIL definitions with real examples, reasoning before the verdict in a structured output, graded text treated as data inside escaped tags, and code-checkable criteria such as length kept out of the judge.

docs.title: 16. Why prefer pass/fail over a 1-to-10 scale?
docs.text: People and models apply binary criteria much more consistently, the result is easier to act on, and agreement with human labels is easier to measure. A scale mixes several qualities into one number and drifts. If a scale is truly needed, define every point.

docs.title: 17. Compare pointwise, pairwise, and reference-guided judging.
docs.text: Pointwise grades one output against criteria and gives absolute numbers for thresholds and monitoring. Pairwise picks the better of two outputs, which is easier and more consistent but needs two versions and is exposed to position bias. Reference-guided compares an output with a labeled answer, which anchors the judge but needs references.

docs.title: 18. What is position bias, and how do you counter it?
docs.text: A judge's verdict depends on which answer it sees first. Judge both orders, score a flip as a tie, and report the flip rate. In a simulation where the judge picked the first slot 30% of the time, one fixed order reported a 32% win rate for a prompt that was truly better 54% of the time; both orders brought it back near 51%.

docs.title: 19. What are verbosity bias and self-preference?
docs.text: Verbosity bias: judges favor longer answers even when length adds nothing; counter it with criteria that say length is not a merit, a length check in code, and comparisons at similar lengths. Self-preference: judges favor text from their own model family; use a judge from a different family or calibrate for it.

docs.title: 20. How do you calibrate a judge?
docs.text: Collect 100 to 200 real outputs with enough failures, have experts label them with critiques, develop the judge prompt on one part and measure it on a held-out part, and look at the confusion matrix: true positive rate, true negative rate, and kappa. Re-calibrate when the judge model, prompt, or rubric changes.

docs.title: 21. Why is accuracy a misleading summary of a judge?
docs.text: If 85% of outputs are good, a judge that passes everything is 85% accurate and catches nothing. The true negative rate (the share of expert-failed outputs the judge fails) shows whether the judge catches problems; a judge with 87% accuracy and a TNR of 64% misses about a third of real failures.

docs.title: 22. How can you correct a judge's observed pass rate?
docs.text: With known error rates, the Rogan-Gladen estimator gives p_true = (p_obs + TNR - 1) / (TPR + TNR - 1). With TPR 0.964, TNR 0.639, and an observed 88.0%, the estimate is 86.0%. It is unstable when TPR + TNR is close to 1, and only as good as the calibration sample.

docs.title: 23. What is criteria drift?
docs.text: The finding by Shankar and colleagues that people need criteria to grade outputs, but grading outputs is what helps them define the criteria. Rubrics and labels change during labeling and calibration; when a judge and experts keep disagreeing on the same cases, fix the criterion rather than tuning the judge to an unclear label.

docs.title: 24. How do you get structured verdicts from a judge model?
docs.text: Use the provider's structured output support so the verdict is always parseable: in the OpenAI SDK, client.responses.parse() with zodTextFormat(schema, "verdict") and read output_parsed; in the Anthropic SDK, client.messages.parse() with output_config: { format: zodOutputFormat(schema) }; in the Google Gen AI SDK, responseMimeType: "application/json" with responseJsonSchema. Read the judge model ID from configuration.

docs.title: 25. How do you test judge code without paying for API calls?
docs.text: Make the grader an injected function and test the plumbing with a stub: every criterion is graded, one failing criterion fails the output, and graded text cannot close its data tags. The tests check wiring; calibration measures judgment.

docs.title: Evals in CI and regression testing
26. Why keep model-calling evals out of npm test?
docs.text: Unit tests must be fast, free, and deterministic; evals call models, cost money, and are noisy. Mixing them makes unit tests flaky and expensive. Give evals their own job, gate, and schedule, and keep unit tests for rendering, parsing, checks, and judge plumbing with stubs.

docs.title: 27. Where in the delivery process should evals run?
docs.text: Unit tests on every commit; a cached eval suite on pull requests that touch AI code; the full suite nightly without a cache and with repeats to catch model drift and flakiness; a full paired comparison before a model or provider switch; and code checks, sampled judges, and feedback in production.

docs.title: 28. Name some eval tools and when you would use each.
docs.text: promptfoo (YAML config with JavaScript, TypeScript, or Python extensions, any stack), DeepEval (Pytest-style, Python), Braintrust (hosted, Eval() plus autoevals), the OpenAI Evals API (hosted graders), Inspect (Python framework from the UK AI Security Institute and Meridian Labs, for capability and agentic evals). evalite (TypeScript on Vitest) was deprecated in November 2026. Keep the dataset and checks in your repository and treat the tool as a runner.

docs.title: 29. Why use a custom provider in promptfoo for an application feature?
docs.text: It runs the same code path production uses (template, parameters, parsing) instead of a copy of the prompt in YAML, so the eval tests what ships. Its id can include the prompt version and hash, so every result records which template produced it. A custom provider handles its own response caching.

docs.title: 30. How does promptfoo signal failure to CI?
docs.text: promptfoo eval exits with code 100 when the pass rate is below PROMPTFOO_PASS_RATE_THRESHOLD (default 100%) and with an error code when providers fail. Setting the threshold to 0 leaves the decision to a separate gate script that compares with a baseline.

docs.title: 31. Why can't you pass an array as a promptfoo test variable for one case?
docs.text: promptfoo expands array-valued variables into one test per element, so a members array would multiply the tests. Pass the case as a single object and read it in the provider and assertions.

docs.title: 32. What rules should a regression gate include?
docs.text: Critical cases must always pass; absolute floors (schema validity 100%, a minimum overall pass rate); a paired comparison with the committed baseline that fails only if the drop exceeds a tolerance and is statistically significant; and budgets for tokens and latency.

docs.title: 33. Why compare runs case by case instead of comparing pass rates?
docs.text: Only the cases where the versions disagree carry information. A change that fixes 5 cases and breaks 7 barely moves the average but produces a list of 7 regressions to read. McNemar's test on regressions and fixes is far more sensitive than comparing two independent rates.

docs.title: 34. Compute a McNemar test example.
docs.text: 16 regressions and 3 fixes: under "no real change", each discordant case is a coin flip, so the two-sided exact p-value is 2 * P(X <= 3) for X ~ Binomial(19, 0.5), about 0.004. That is very unlikely to be chance, so the gate fails. With 7 regressions and 5 fixes, p is about 0.77: noise.

docs.title: 35. Where does nondeterminism come from, and how do you handle it?
docs.text: Sampling, provider-side batching and hardware effects, model aliases that move, and timing in agents. Pin model snapshots in configuration, do not rely on sampling parameters, repeat cases, aggregate deliberately, know the noise band, compare pairs, and track flaky cases.

docs.title: 36. Does temperature 0 make LLM evals reproducible?
docs.text: No. It reduces variation where supported but does not guarantee identical outputs, and support differs by API: OpenAI's Responses API accepts temperature but has no seed, and Anthropic's API version 2026-10-21 removed temperature, top_p, and top_k (requests that send them get a 400 error). Design the evals to measure through the noise instead.

docs.title: 37. Explain pass@k and pass^k.
docs.text: With k runs per case, pass@k counts a case if at least one run succeeds (what is possible); pass^k counts it only if all runs succeed (reliability), a metric proposed in the tau-bench paper. For user-facing features, report pass^k or the mean pass rate; pass@k flatters.

docs.title: 38. How do you control the cost of evals?
docs.text: Path filters, a response cache on pull requests (disabled nightly), code checks before judges, tiered suites (critical cases on pull requests, everything nightly), sampling with a fixed seed, cheaper calibrated judges, batch APIs for nightly runs, and concurrency limits. Give evals a separate API key with a spending limit.

docs.title: 39. How do you handle secrets and forks in an eval workflow?
docs.text: Store provider keys as secrets scoped to the eval job, keep model IDs in repository variables, and skip the eval job for pull requests from forks, which receive no secrets, instead of letting it fail. Never let evals trigger real side effects such as sending email.

docs.title: 40. What does LLM observability add to ordinary observability?
docs.text: Model-aware signals: tokens (input, cached, output, reasoning) per feature and model, model calls per request, prompt versions and model snapshots on every span, provider errors and incomplete responses, schema-validation failures, and quality signals such as user feedback and judge scores on sampled traces.

docs.title: 41. What do the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions define, and what is their status?
docs.text: Span names, attributes, and metrics for model calls, embeddings, retrieval, tool execution, and agents. As of November 2026 they are in Development status. In core semantic conventions v1.42.0 (June 2026) they moved to the dedicated semantic-conventions-genai repository, which had not yet published a release.

docs.title: 42. How is a model-call span named, and which attributes are required?
docs.text: {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}, for example chat <model>, as a CLIENT span. gen_ai.operation.name and gen_ai.provider.name are required; request and response model, response id, token usage, and finish reasons are recommended. Tool execution is execute_tool {tool name} and retrieval is retrieval, both INTERNAL.

docs.title: 43. Why record both the requested and the returned model?
docs.text: The request often uses an alias; the response names the dated snapshot that actually ran. When behavior changes without a deploy, comparing gen_ai.response.model before and after shows whether the provider moved the alias.

docs.title: 44. Should prompts and answers be recorded in traces?
docs.text: Not by default. The conventions say instrumentations should not capture instructions, inputs, and outputs by default because they are sensitive, and describe three patterns: record nothing, record content on spans (for example in pre-production), or store content externally and record only a reference, which they recommend for production.

docs.title: 45. How do you keep personal data out of traces?
docs.text: Content off by default; redact at the source when it is captured; redact again in the Collector with the redaction processor; store full content separately with its own access control and short retention when truly needed; pseudonymize user IDs; and set retention and deletion for the tracing backend like any database of user data.

docs.title: 46. Why route telemetry through an OpenTelemetry Collector?
docs.text: It enforces policy for every service in one place (redaction, sampling), fans out to several backends, and lets you change vendors by editing one file instead of every service. Tail sampling there keeps every error and slow trace while sampling the rest.

docs.title: 47. What is the catch with tail sampling?
docs.text: It decides after a trace completes, so all spans of a trace must reach the same Collector instance; a scaled deployment needs routing by trace ID first. It also holds traces in memory while waiting, which needs capacity planning.

docs.title: 48. Compare Langfuse, LangSmith, and Arize Phoenix.
docs.text: Langfuse: open source (MIT core), owned by ClickHouse since January 2026, cloud or self-hosted, OTLP endpoint, traces plus prompts, datasets, and scores. LangSmith: LangChain's commercial platform, SDK tracing with wrapOpenAI and traceable, also accepts OTLP. Phoenix: Elastic License 2.0, self-hosted, built on OpenTelemetry and OpenInference, with evaluations and experiments next to traces.

docs.title: 49. What is OpenInference, and why does it matter when mixing tools?
docs.text: Arize's conventions and instrumentations used by Phoenix. They use their own attribute names, such as openinference.span.kind and llm.token_count.prompt, rather than gen_ai.*, so dashboards and queries built for one convention do not automatically work with spans from the other.

docs.title: 50. How do you build token and cost dashboards safely?
docs.text: Record token usage and duration as metrics with low-cardinality labels (feature, operation, provider, model, prompt version), compute cost from token counts and a price table in configuration, and never use user IDs, trace IDs, or prompt text as labels. Through a Prometheus exporter, gen_ai.client.token.usage becomes gen_ai_client_token_usage.

docs.title: 51. Why can a reasoning model cost more than its per-token price suggests?
docs.text: Reasoning tokens are billed as output tokens, so a long thinking phase adds output tokens the user never sees. Cached input tokens usually cost less than uncached ones. Track reasoning and cached tokens separately to see where the money goes.

docs.title: 52. How do you connect user feedback to what produced an answer?
docs.text: Return the trace ID with every AI response, send it back with the feedback, check that the trace belongs to the user, store the feedback in your own database, and attach it to the trace as a score. The trace then shows the prompt version, model, retrieval, and tool calls behind the complaint.

docs.title: 53. Why is user feedback not an accuracy measurement?
docs.text: It is biased: unhappy users click more, and some errors (a subtly wrong date) are never noticed. Use feedback rates as trends and triage signals, turn triaged failures into evaluation cases, and keep the offline set as the source of truth.

docs.title: 54. The eval suite's pass rate rose for five releases, but thumbs-down rates are flat. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether prompts mention test cases, how old the test split is, and how its slices compare with current traffic.

How to confirm: score a fresh sample of recent production traces with the same checks; compare with the test split's score.

Likely causes and fixes: overfitting to the test cases, or a set that no longer reflects traffic. Refresh the test split from production, remove test material from prompts, and keep a dev split for iteration. See building evaluation sets.

docs.title: 55. The overall score clears the target, but a customer in Los Angeles keeps getting tasks due a day late. Why didn't the eval catch it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the per-slice report for late-evening and time zone slices.

How to confirm: count active cases with relative dates late in the evening in western time zones; check their pass rate and interval.

Likely causes and fixes: a coverage gap: too few cases to move the score, and the date computed from UTC. Add the incident as a critical case, fill the slice, and add a code check that compares against the user's local date. See building evaluation sets.

docs.title: 56. Two engineers report 91% and 87% for the same prompt on the same day. Who is right?
docs.text:
What to check first: the dataset version, hash, and case counts in each result.

How to confirm: run the manifest check on both checkouts; diff the cases files.

Likely causes and fixes: different datasets: someone edited labels without a version bump. Release a proper version, run the manifest check in CI before every eval, and compare only runs with the same dataset@version. See building evaluation sets.

docs.title: 57. The judge reports a 95% pass rate on summaries, but support tickets about wrong summaries keep coming. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the judge's calibration results, especially its true negative rate.

How to confirm: have experts label a fresh production sample and compare with the judge's verdicts.

Likely causes and fixes: a lenient judge that misses real failures. Sharpen FAIL definitions with examples from the missed cases, measure on held-out labels, and report corrected rates meanwhile. See LLM-as-judge and automated evals.

docs.title: 58. A pairwise eval says the new summary prompt wins 70% of comparisons, but users like it less. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the comparison ran in both orders and how output lengths differ.

How to confirm: rerun with both orders, report the flip rate, and compare win rates on length-matched pairs.

Likely causes and fixes: position or verbosity bias. Judge both orders, add a length check, and tell the judge that length is not a merit. See LLM-as-judge and automated evals.

docs.title: 59. Judge scores dropped five points overnight, but nothing in the app changed. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the judge model ID and the judge prompt version recorded with each run.

How to confirm: rerun yesterday's outputs through today's judge; if the verdicts change, the judge changed.

Likely causes and fixes: a judge model alias moved, or the judge prompt was edited. Pin the judge model in configuration, version the judge prompt with the rubric, and re-calibrate before accepting a new baseline. See LLM-as-judge and automated evals.

docs.title: 60. The eval job fails on about one pull request in five, and reruns pass. How do you fix the gate?
docs.text:
What to check first: the gate rule and the number of runs per case.

How to confirm: run the same commit several times and look at the spread of pass rates and which cases flip.

Likely causes and fixes: a raw pass-rate threshold tighter than the noise band. Gate on a paired comparison with a significance test, add repeats nightly, and list flaky cases for relabeling. See evals in CI and regression testing.

docs.title: 61. The nightly eval failed although nothing was merged. Where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: gen_ai.response.model in the nightly results compared with the previous night.

How to confirm: run the old and new snapshots side by side on the suite and compare case by case.

Likely causes and fixes: upstream model drift behind an alias. Pin a snapshot, compare explicitly, and update the baseline only in a reviewed pull request. See evals in CI and regression testing.

docs.title: 62. The monthly bill for the eval API key is higher than for the feature itself. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: how often evals run, cache hit rates, and judge calls per case.

How to confirm: break down tokens by job type and by grader in the eval reports.

Likely causes and fixes: no path filters, no cache, and judges on every criterion for every case. Add path filters and the response cache, short-circuit judges on code failures, tier suites, and move broad runs to the nightly job. See evals in CI and regression testing.

docs.title: 63. Token usage for the agent doubled overnight with flat traffic. How do you find the cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: model calls per request and output tokens per call, by prompt version.

How to confirm: open traces with the most model calls and look at the tool spans between them.

Likely causes and fixes: an agent loop retrying a failing tool, or a prompt change that lengthened answers. Cap calls per request, fix the tool, alert on calls per request and tokens per hour, and compare output tokens across prompt versions. See LLM observability and tracing.

docs.title: 64. A privacy review finds customer email addresses in the tracing backend. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which spans and attributes contain them, and whether content capture or an instrumentation library put them there.

How to confirm: search the backend for email patterns by service and attribute; check the instrumentation's content-capture settings.

Likely causes and fixes: content captured in production without redaction. Turn capture off, add the Collector redaction processor, purge the data through your incident process, and set retention on the backend. See LLM observability and tracing.

docs.title: 65. After upgrading an instrumentation library, the token dashboard went blank. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the metric and attribute names the new version emits.

How to confirm: list metric names in the backend before and after the upgrade.

Likely causes and fixes: the GenAI conventions changed names (for example gen_ai.system to gen_ai.provider.name, or the token histogram to counters) and the library followed. Pin instrumentation versions, keep names in one module, and update queries with the upgrade. See LLM observability and tracing.

docs.title: 66. Thumbs-down reports pile up, but nobody can reproduce them. What is missing?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether responses return trace IDs and whether those traces were kept by sampling.

How to confirm: take a recent thumbs-down record and try to find its trace, prompt version, and input.

Likely causes and fixes: no trace ID in responses, or traces sampled away. Return the trace ID with every answer, store it with the feedback, and keep traces with errors or negative feedback. Then triage weekly and turn failures into evaluation cases. See LLM observability and tracing.
