docs.title: LLM Observability and Tracing
docs.text:
Offline evaluation tells you how a feature behaves on the cases you thought of. Production tells you how it behaves on everything else. LLM observability is the practice of recording enough about each model call, tool call, and retrieval step to answer questions like "why did the assistant create this task for the wrong date?", "which feature doubled the token bill last week?", and "do users trust the new prompt more than the old one?", without turning your tracing backend into a copy of every user's private messages.

This lesson builds on the general observability practice in section 07, especially distributed tracing and metrics and dashboards, and covers only what is specific to LLM features: the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions and their current status, tracing model calls, tool calls, and retrieval in TaskFlow, the LLM-focused backends Langfuse, LangSmith, and Arize Phoenix, keeping personal data out of traces, token and cost dashboards, and the loop that turns user feedback into evaluation cases.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
An LLM feature fails in ways that ordinary monitoring does not see. The HTTP request succeeds, latency is normal, and the error rate is zero, while the agent calls create_task twice, the Q&A answer cites a note the user cannot open, or a prompt change quietly doubles the output tokens. Seeing these needs telemetry that knows what a model call, a tool call, and a retrieval step are, and that records tokens, models, and prompt versions in a consistent way.

Cost is the second reason. Token usage is the main variable cost of an LLM feature, and it moves with prompt edits, model switches, retries, and agent loops. Without per-feature token metrics, the first sign of a runaway agent is the monthly bill.

The third reason is the feedback loop. The cases that most improve an evaluation set come from production: the request that confused the assistant, the answer a user marked as wrong. Traces with stable IDs connect a thumbs-down to the exact prompt version, model, retrieved documents, and tool calls behind it, which turns a complaint into a reproducible test case.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. The conventions define span names, attributes, and metrics for model calls, embeddings, retrieval, tool execution, and agents. Their status is still Development. In core semantic conventions v1.42.0 (released June 12, 2026) they moved to a dedicated repository, semantic-conventions-genai, which had not published a release as of November 2026. The conventions say instrumentations "SHOULD NOT capture" instructions, inputs, and outputs by default, because they are considered sensitive.
  • Langfuse. An open-source (MIT, except enterprise directories) LLM engineering platform for tracing, prompt management, and evaluation; ClickHouse announced it had acquired Langfuse on January 16, 2026 (announcement), and it remains available as a cloud service and for self-hosting. It accepts OpenTelemetry traces on its OTLP endpoint and maps gen_ai.* attributes to its own model.
  • LangSmith. LangChain's platform traces any app through its SDK (wrapOpenAI and traceable in TypeScript, per its tracing quickstart) and also accepts OpenTelemetry traces at its API URL plus /otel.
  • Arize Phoenix. Phoenix is "built on top of OpenTelemetry and is powered by OpenInference instrumentation", and adds evaluation, datasets, experiments, and prompt management. It is source-available under the Elastic License 2.0 and can be self-hosted. Its OpenInference conventions use their own attribute names (openinference.span.kind, llm.token_count.prompt) rather than gen_ai.*.
  • OpenTelemetry Collector. The contrib distribution's redaction processor (beta for traces) masks attribute values that match patterns, and the tail sampling processor (beta) keeps whole traces based on errors, latency, or a percentage. Both appear in the Collector configuration later in this lesson.

Popular tools and providers: Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize Phoenix, Braintrust, OpenLLMetry instrumentations from Traceloop, the OpenTelemetry Collector, and general-purpose backends such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, and Prometheus for traces and metrics.

docs.title: What LLM observability adds
docs.text:
Everything in ordinary observability still applies: request rates, errors, latency percentiles, SLOs, and alerts. LLM features add a layer on top:

Question Classic signal LLM-specific signal Is it up? HTTP errors, latency Provider errors and rate limits, incomplete responses, schema-validation failures Is it fast? Request latency Time to first token, output tokens per call, number of model calls per request What does it cost? Instance hours Input, cached, output, and reasoning tokens per feature and model Is it correct? Rarely observable User feedback, edits to drafts, judge scores on sampled traces What changed? Deploy markers Prompt version, model snapshot, retrieval index version on every span Why did this request fail? A trace through services A trace through model calls, tool calls, and retrieval, with token counts and versions

docs.title: Anatomy of a trace for an AI request
docs.text:
A TaskFlow agent request ("move the launch review to Friday and tell Ana") becomes one trace. The HTTP server span is the root; inside it, each model call, each tool execution, and each database call is a child span, so the waterfall shows where time and tokens went:

The value is in the structure. "4.1 seconds" alone says the request was slow; the waterfall says that the second model call took half of it, that the first call reused 1,024 cached input tokens, and which prompt version and model snapshot produced the answer. The same structure works for project Q&A, where a retrieval span sits before the model call and records which index was searched and how many documents came back.

docs.title: The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions
docs.text:
The conventions give every tool the same vocabulary, so a trace produced by your code can be read by Langfuse, Phoenix, LangSmith, or a general tracing backend. The parts used most:

Span Name Kind Key attributes Model call (inference) {gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}, for example chat <model> CLIENT Required: gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.provider.name; recommended: request and response model, gen_ai.response.id, token usage, finish reasons Embeddings embeddings {gen_ai.request.model} CLIENT gen_ai.embeddings.dimension.count, input tokens Retrieval retrieval INTERNAL gen_ai.retrieval.top_k, gen_ai.data_source.id; documents and query text are opt-in Tool execution execute_tool {gen_ai.tool.name} INTERNAL gen_ai.tool.name, gen_ai.tool.call.id, gen_ai.tool.type; arguments and results are opt-in Agent invocation invoke_agent {gen_ai.agent.name} CLIENT, or INTERNAL in-process gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.agent.id, gen_ai.agent.version

Other details worth knowing:

  • Operation names include chat, generate_content, text_completion, embeddings, retrieval, execute_tool, create_agent, invoke_agent, and invoke_workflow, among others.
  • Provider names are well-known values such as openai, anthropic, gcp.gemini, gcp.vertex_ai, aws.bedrock, and azure.ai.openai. The attribute was called gen_ai.system before semantic conventions v1.37; older instrumentations still emit that name.
  • Usage is recorded as gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, with gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens when the provider reports them.
  • Prompt identity has its own attributes, gen_ai.prompt.name and gen_ai.prompt.version, which are exactly what you need to compare two prompt versions in production.
  • Content (gen_ai.system_instructions, gen_ai.input.messages, gen_ai.output.messages, gen_ai.tool.definitions) is opt-in. The conventions describe three patterns: record nothing (the default), record content on span attributes (for example in pre-production), or store content externally and record only a reference (*_ref attributes), which they recommend for production when volume or sensitivity is a concern.

Because the conventions are still in Development, names change between versions, and instrumentations lag behind. Two practical consequences. Older guidance (up to semantic conventions v1.41) asks instrumentations to offer OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=gen_ai_latest_experimental to emit the latest experimental attributes, so check what your library emits by default. And metrics are in flux: the released conventions define a gen_ai.client.token.usage histogram with a gen_ai.token.type attribute (input or output) and a gen_ai.client.operation.duration histogram, while the development version in the new repository replaces the token histogram with per-category counters such as gen_ai.client.inference.usage.input_tokens. This lesson's code uses the released names; keep all attribute and metric names in one module so a rename is a one-line change.

docs.title: Instrumenting the code
docs.text:
Approach Example Strengths Weaknesses Manual spans around your own wrapper tracedResponse() in this lesson Exact control over attributes, prompt versions, and redaction You maintain it OpenTelemetry instrumentation libraries OpenLLMetry (@traceloop/instrumentation-openai), OpenInference (@arizeai/openinference-instrumentation-openai) Automatic for every call through the SDK Each library follows its own conventions and version; content capture defaults vary Vendor SDKs Langfuse (@langfuse/tracing, built on OpenTelemetry), LangSmith (wrapOpenAI, traceable) Rich features in that vendor's UI Tighter coupling to one backend

TaskFlow already calls every model through one function (the client in calling model APIs from a backend), so a manual span in that function covers every feature with one change and keeps redaction under the team's control. HTTP, Express, and MongoDB spans still come from the standard Node.js auto-instrumentation set up in the distributed tracing lesson.

docs.title: Backends and the Collector
docs.text:
Backend License and hosting Ingestion Strengths Langfuse MIT core; cloud or self-hosted OTLP at /api/public/otel, SDKs Traces, prompts, datasets, scores, and evaluations in one open-source tool LangSmith Commercial; cloud or self-hosted SDKs, OTLP at the API URL plus /otel Deep integration with LangChain and LangGraph; datasets and experiments Arize Phoenix Elastic License 2.0; self-hosted OTLP; OpenInference instrumentation Evaluations and experiments next to traces General tracing (Jaeger, Grafana Tempo) Open source OTLP One place for all services; less LLM-specific UI

Send telemetry from the app to an OpenTelemetry Collector rather than directly to a vendor. The Collector is where you enforce policy for every service at once: redact values that must not leave your network, sample whole traces, and fan out to more than one backend (for example Langfuse for the AI team and the general tracing system for everyone else). Switching vendors then means editing one Collector file, not every service. It also avoids version coupling: in November 2026, Langfuse's own span processor (@langfuse/otel 6.1) still declared the OpenTelemetry JS SDK 2 packages as peer dependencies, while @opentelemetry/sdk-node 0.301 is built on SDK 3, so a TaskFlow service on SDK 3 sends plain OTLP and lets the Collector deliver it to Langfuse's endpoint.

docs.title: Keeping personal data out of traces
docs.text:
Prompts and answers are user data. A request to the Assistant can contain a name, an email address, or a health detail, and the answer repeats it. Telemetry backends usually have broader access, longer retention, and weaker deletion workflows than the primary database, so copying content into them by default creates exactly the risk that privacy rules forbid. Use several layers:

  1. Do not capture content by default. Record token counts, models, versions, latencies, and IDs. They answer most operational questions.
  2. Redact at the source when content is captured, before it reaches a span: emails, phone numbers, card numbers, and anything that looks like a key.
  3. Redact again in the Collector as a safety net for every service, including ones that forgot step 2 or use an instrumentation library that captures more than you expected.
  4. Store full content separately when you truly need it, in a store with its own access control and short retention, and put only a reference on the span, as the conventions recommend for production.
  5. Pseudonymize users with an internal ID or an HMAC of the user ID, never an email address, and never put user IDs in metric labels.
  6. Set retention and access for the tracing backend as you would for any database of user data, and include it in deletion requests.

The full privacy picture, including data retention and provider data handling, is in privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: Token and cost dashboards
docs.text:
Traces answer questions about one request; metrics answer questions about all of them. Record token usage and duration as metrics with a few low-cardinality attributes (feature, operation, provider, model), and compute cost from tokens and a price table kept in configuration. Never use user IDs, trace IDs, or prompt text as metric attributes: every distinct value creates a new time series.

With the Collector's Prometheus exporter, OpenTelemetry names are translated: dots become underscores, a unit in braces such as {token} is dropped, seconds add _seconds, and counters add _total, so gen_ai.client.token.usage becomes gen_ai_client_token_usage and the duration histogram becomes gen_ai_client_operation_duration_seconds. A useful first dashboard:

Panel Question it answers Tokens per hour by feature and type Which feature drives usage, and is it input or output? Average output tokens per call Did a prompt change make answers longer? p95 latency by feature Is the assistant getting slower? Error share by feature Are provider errors or rate limits rising? Estimated cost per day by feature Where does the money go? Cost per successful task Is the feature getting more or less efficient per user outcome? Thumbs-down share by prompt version Did the new prompt change how users judge answers?

Cost estimates multiply token counts by per-token prices from the provider's current pricing page, kept in configuration rather than code because prices change. Cached input tokens are usually billed at a lower rate than uncached ones, and reasoning tokens are billed as output, so a model with a long thinking phase can cost more per answer than its per-token price suggests. Broader cost strategy is covered in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: The user-feedback loop
docs.text:
Explicit and implicit feedback are the cheapest quality signals in production, but only if each one can be traced back to what produced it:

  • Explicit feedback: thumbs up or down, a reason ("wrong", "incomplete", "unsafe"), an optional comment.
  • Implicit feedback: the user edits the Assistant's draft before saving it, regenerates an answer, abandons the flow, or opens a support ticket.

The mechanism is simple: every AI response returns its trace ID, the UI sends that ID back with the feedback, and the backend stores the feedback in its own database and attaches it to the trace as a score. From there, a weekly triage reads the thumbs-down and edited traces, groups the failures, and turns the important ones into evaluation cases (the sampling and labeling process from building evaluation sets), which the CI gate from evals in CI then protects. Running a calibrated judge on a small sample of production traces adds a third signal that does not depend on users speaking up.

Feedback is biased: unhappy users click more than satisfied ones, and some failures (a subtly wrong date) are never noticed. Treat feedback rates as trends and triage signals, not as accuracy measurements, and keep the offline evaluation set as the source of truth. Slow shifts in inputs and outputs over months, and the model-lifecycle response to them, are the subject of production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Any production LLM feature Spans with GenAI attributes and token metrics, content off Debugging a prompt in development or staging Content capture on, redacted, short retention Agents with tool calls A span per model call and per tool execution; alert on calls per request RAG features A retrieval span with the index and counts; content opt-in Teams that want an LLM-specific UI Collector fan-out to Langfuse, LangSmith, or Phoenix, plus the general backend Regulated or sensitive data Content never in telemetry; references to a restricted store if needed

Do not record full prompts and answers in production telemetry just because a tool makes it easy, do not put high-cardinality values in metric labels, and do not let the tracing vendor's SDK become the only place your feedback data lives: keep your own copy.

docs.title: Starting the SDK
docs.text:
The app sends traces and metrics over OTLP to the Collector. Load this file before the app with node --import, so instrumentation is active before Express and the MongoDB driver are imported:

// src/telemetry.ts: start OpenTelemetry before the app (node --import ./dist/telemetry.js dist/server.js)
import { OTLPMetricExporter } from "@opentelemetry/exporter-metrics-otlp-proto";
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from "@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto";
import { resourceFromAttributes } from "@opentelemetry/resources";
import { PeriodicExportingMetricReader } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-metrics";
import { NodeSDK } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-node";
import { ATTR_SERVICE_NAME, ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION } from "@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions";

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({
    [ATTR_SERVICE_NAME]: "taskflow-api",
    [ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION]: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev",
  }),
  // Both exporters read OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: point it at your Collector, not at a vendor.
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter(),
  metricReaders: [
    new PeriodicExportingMetricReader({ exporter: new OTLPMetricExporter(), exportIntervalMillis: 30_000 }),
  ],
});
sdk.start();

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  sdk.shutdown().finally(() => process.exit(0));
});

This targets the OpenTelemetry JS SDK 3 line (@opentelemetry/sdk-node 0.301 and @opentelemetry/api 1.10 in November 2026). Add the HTTP, Express, and MongoDB instrumentations through the instrumentations option, as shown in the distributed tracing lesson.

docs.title: Attribute names in one module
docs.text:
// src/ai/genai-attributes.ts: GenAI attribute names in one place, because the conventions are still in Development
export const GEN_AI = {
  OPERATION_NAME: "gen_ai.operation.name",            // chat, embeddings, retrieval, execute_tool, invoke_agent
  PROVIDER_NAME: "gen_ai.provider.name",              // openai, anthropic, gcp.gemini, ...
  REQUEST_MODEL: "gen_ai.request.model",
  REQUEST_MAX_TOKENS: "gen_ai.request.max_tokens",
  RESPONSE_ID: "gen_ai.response.id",
  RESPONSE_MODEL: "gen_ai.response.model",
  RESPONSE_STATUS: "gen_ai.response.status",
  CONVERSATION_ID: "gen_ai.conversation.id",
  PROMPT_NAME: "gen_ai.prompt.name",
  PROMPT_VERSION: "gen_ai.prompt.version",
  USAGE_INPUT_TOKENS: "gen_ai.usage.input_tokens",
  USAGE_OUTPUT_TOKENS: "gen_ai.usage.output_tokens",
  USAGE_CACHE_READ_INPUT_TOKENS: "gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens",
  USAGE_REASONING_OUTPUT_TOKENS: "gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens",
  TOKEN_TYPE: "gen_ai.token.type",                    // metric attribute: input | output
  TOOL_NAME: "gen_ai.tool.name",
  TOOL_CALL_ID: "gen_ai.tool.call.id",
  TOOL_TYPE: "gen_ai.tool.type",
  RETRIEVAL_TOP_K: "gen_ai.retrieval.top_k",
  DATA_SOURCE_ID: "gen_ai.data_source.id",
  INPUT_MESSAGES: "gen_ai.input.messages",            // opt-in content
  OUTPUT_MESSAGES: "gen_ai.output.messages",          // opt-in content
  OPENAI_API_TYPE: "openai.api.type",                 // chat_completions | responses
  ERROR_TYPE: "error.type",
} as const;

The @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions package has an incubating entry point with constants for unstable attributes, but its README recommends copying unstable definitions into your own code base rather than importing that entry point at runtime, because it may break in minor versions. This module does exactly that.

docs.title: Tracing model, tool, and retrieval calls
docs.text:
// src/ai/traced-llm.ts: one span and two metrics per model call, following the GenAI conventions
import { metrics, SpanKind, SpanStatusCode, trace } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import type OpenAI from "openai";
import type { ResponseCreateParamsNonStreaming } from "openai/resources/responses/responses";
import { GEN_AI as A } from "./genai-attributes.js";
import { redactForTelemetry } from "./redact.js";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("taskflow-ai");
const meter = metrics.getMeter("taskflow-ai");
const tokenUsage = meter.createHistogram("gen_ai.client.token.usage", {
  unit: "{token}",
  description: "Number of input and output tokens used",
});
const duration = meter.createHistogram("gen_ai.client.operation.duration", {
  unit: "s",
  description: "GenAI operation duration",
});

// Off by default. Turn on only where telemetry storage is approved for user content (see the PII section).
const CAPTURE_CONTENT = process.env.GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT === "true";

export interface CallInfo {
  feature: string;          // task-assistant, project-qa, meeting-summary, agent
  promptName: string;
  promptVersion: string;
  conversationId?: string;
}

export async function tracedResponse(
  client: OpenAI,
  params: ResponseCreateParamsNonStreaming & { model: string },
  info: CallInfo,
) {
  // Low-cardinality attributes, shared by the span and the metrics.
  const common = {
    [A.OPERATION_NAME]: "chat",
    [A.PROVIDER_NAME]: "openai",
    [A.REQUEST_MODEL]: params.model,
    "taskflow.feature": info.feature,
  };
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(
    `chat ${params.model}`,
    {
      kind: SpanKind.CLIENT,
      attributes: {
        ...common,
        [A.OPENAI_API_TYPE]: "responses",
        [A.PROMPT_NAME]: info.promptName,
        [A.PROMPT_VERSION]: info.promptVersion,
        ...(info.conversationId ? { [A.CONVERSATION_ID]: info.conversationId } : {}),
        ...(params.max_output_tokens ? { [A.REQUEST_MAX_TOKENS]: params.max_output_tokens } : {}),
      },
    },
    async (span) => {
      const started = performance.now();
      let errorType: string | undefined;
      try {
        const response = await client.responses.create(params);
        const u = response.usage;
        span.setAttributes({
          [A.RESPONSE_ID]: response.id,
          [A.RESPONSE_MODEL]: response.model,
          [A.RESPONSE_STATUS]: response.status ?? "unknown",
          ...(u && {
            [A.USAGE_INPUT_TOKENS]: u.input_tokens,
            [A.USAGE_OUTPUT_TOKENS]: u.output_tokens,
            [A.USAGE_CACHE_READ_INPUT_TOKENS]: u.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens,
            [A.USAGE_REASONING_OUTPUT_TOKENS]: u.output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens,
          }),
        });
        if (u) {
          tokenUsage.record(u.input_tokens, { ...common, [A.TOKEN_TYPE]: "input" });
          tokenUsage.record(u.output_tokens, { ...common, [A.TOKEN_TYPE]: "output" });
        }
        if (CAPTURE_CONTENT) {
          span.setAttribute(A.OUTPUT_MESSAGES, [
            { role: "assistant", parts: [{ type: "text", content: redactForTelemetry(response.output_text) }] },
          ]);
        }
        return response;
      } catch (err) {
        errorType = (err as { status?: number }).status ? String((err as { status: number }).status) : (err as Error).name;
        span.setAttribute(A.ERROR_TYPE, errorType);
        span.recordException(err as Error);
        span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
        throw err;
      } finally {
        duration.record((performance.now() - started) / 1000, { ...common, ...(errorType && { [A.ERROR_TYPE]: errorType }) });
        span.end();
      }
    },
  );
}

/** A tool execution inside the agent loop, as its own INTERNAL span. */
export function tracedTool<T>(name: string, callId: string, run: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(
    `execute_tool ${name}`,
    { kind: SpanKind.INTERNAL, attributes: { [A.OPERATION_NAME]: "execute_tool", [A.TOOL_NAME]: name, [A.TOOL_CALL_ID]: callId, [A.TOOL_TYPE]: "function" } },
    async (span) => {
      try {
        return await run();
      } catch (err) {
        span.setAttribute(A.ERROR_TYPE, (err as Error).name);
        span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR });
        throw err;
      } finally {
        span.end();
      }
    },
  );
}

/** A retrieval step for project Q&A: record what was searched and how much came back, not the text. */
export function tracedRetrieval<T extends { id: string; score: number }[]>(source: string, topK: number, run: () => Promise<T>): Promise<T> {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(
    "retrieval",
    { kind: SpanKind.INTERNAL, attributes: { [A.OPERATION_NAME]: "retrieval", [A.DATA_SOURCE_ID]: source, [A.RETRIEVAL_TOP_K]: topK } },
    async (span) => {
      try {
        const docs = await run();
        span.setAttributes({ "taskflow.retrieval.returned": docs.length, "taskflow.retrieval.top_score": docs[0]?.score ?? 0 });
        return docs;
      } finally {
        span.end();
      }
    },
  );
}

How the parts fit:

  • Span name and kind follow the conventions: chat <model> as a CLIENT span for the model call, execute_tool <name> and retrieval as INTERNAL spans. startActiveSpan makes each one the parent of anything that runs inside it, such as the MongoDB call inside a tool.
  • The request model and the response model differ on purpose: the request carries the configured ID (often an alias), the response the dated snapshot that actually ran, which is what you need when behavior changes "without a deploy".
  • Usage details map the Responses API's input_tokens_details.cached_tokens and output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens to the conventions' cache-read and reasoning attributes.
  • Errors set error.type (the HTTP status from the SDK's error, or the error name), record the exception, and mark the span as an error, so tail sampling keeps the trace and the duration metric can be split by error.
  • Content is recorded only when GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT=true, as a structured value after redaction. Structured attribute values are supported from @opentelemetry/api 1.10, whose AnyValue type allows maps and arrays.

Running the helpers against a fake client and an in-memory exporter, for an agent request with one tool call, prints the spans they produce (trimmed to one model call):

POST /api/agent  [SERVER]
chat example-model  [CLIENT]  parent: POST /api/agent
    gen_ai.operation.name = "chat"
    gen_ai.provider.name = "openai"
    gen_ai.request.model = "example-model"
    taskflow.feature = "agent"
    openai.api.type = "responses"
    gen_ai.prompt.name = "task-agent"
    gen_ai.prompt.version = "7"
    gen_ai.conversation.id = "conv_42"
    gen_ai.response.id = "resp_demo_1"
    gen_ai.response.model = "example-model-2026-10-01"
    gen_ai.response.status = "completed"
    gen_ai.usage.input_tokens = 1250
    gen_ai.usage.output_tokens = 64
    gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens = 1024
    gen_ai.usage.reasoning.output_tokens = 0
execute_tool create_task  [INTERNAL]  parent: POST /api/agent
    gen_ai.operation.name = "execute_tool"
    gen_ai.tool.name = "create_task"
    gen_ai.tool.call.id = "call_1"
    gen_ai.tool.type = "function"
chat example-model  [CLIENT]  parent: POST /api/agent

With content capture turned on, the second model call's answer, which mentioned an email address, was recorded with the address already replaced:

gen_ai.output.messages = [{"role":"assistant","parts":[{"type":"text","content":"Created 'Call the bank' for Nov 14. Questions: <email>"}]}]

Outside the Node SDK, spans nest only if a context manager is registered; NodeSDK registers one automatically.

docs.title: Redacting content at the source
docs.text:
// src/ai/redact.ts: scrub obvious personal data before any text reaches telemetry
const PATTERNS: [RegExp, string][] = [
  [/[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+/g, "<email>"],
  [/\+?\d[\d\s().-]{7,}\d/g, "<phone>"],
  [/\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b/g, "<card>"],
  [/\b(sk|pk|rk)[-_][A-Za-z0-9_-]{16,}\b/g, "<secret>"],
];

export function redactForTelemetry(text: string, maxLength = 2_000): string {
  let out = text;
  for (const [pattern, replacement] of PATTERNS) out = out.replace(pattern, replacement);
  return out.length > maxLength ? `${out.slice(0, maxLength)}...[truncated]` : out;
}

Pattern-based redaction catches structured identifiers, not names or free-text personal details ("my diagnosis is ..."), which is why content capture stays off by default and the Collector adds a second layer. The truncation also protects backends from oversized attribute values.

docs.title: The Collector: redaction, sampling, and export
docs.text:
# otel-collector.yaml: one Collector between TaskFlow and its tracing and metrics backends
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 20
  redaction:
    allow_all_keys: true                  # keep attribute keys, mask the values below
    blocked_key_patterns:                 # content is opt-in in the app; mask it here as well
      - '^gen_ai\.(input|output)\.messages$'
      - '^gen_ai\.system_instructions$'
      - '^gen_ai\.tool\.call\.(arguments|result)$'
      - '^gen_ai\.retrieval\.(documents|query\.text)$'
    blocked_values:
      - '[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.-]+'        # email addresses
      - '\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b'          # card-like numbers
    summary: info
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: keep-errors
        type: status_code
        status_code: { status_codes: [ERROR] }
      - name: keep-slow
        type: latency
        latency: { threshold_ms: 8000 }
      - name: sample-the-rest
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic: { sampling_percentage: 10 }

exporters:
  otlphttp/langfuse:
    endpoint: https://cloud.langfuse.com/api/public/otel
    headers:
      Authorization: "Basic ${env:LANGFUSE_AUTH}"   # base64 of public key and secret key
      x-langfuse-ingestion-version: "4"
  prometheus:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:8889

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, redaction, tail_sampling]
      exporters: [otlphttp/langfuse]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter]
      exporters: [prometheus]

What each part does:

  • redaction keeps every attribute key (allow_all_keys: true) but masks the values of content attributes and any value that matches the email or card patterns. The processor fails closed when allow_all_keys is false, so an allow-list of keys is the stricter alternative for high-risk services.
  • tail_sampling waits until a trace is complete, then keeps all errors, all traces slower than 8 seconds, and 10% of the rest. It needs every span of a trace to reach the same Collector instance, so a horizontally scaled deployment routes by trace ID first.
  • otlphttp/langfuse sends traces to Langfuse's OTLP endpoint (the EU cloud region in this example; self-hosted instances use their own URL). The credentials come from an environment variable, never from the file.
  • prometheus exposes the metrics for Prometheus to scrape.

otelcol-contrib validate (version 0.165.0) accepts this file. Sending a test span through a local copy of the pipeline with a debug exporter showed the redaction at work:

Attributes:
     -> gen_ai.operation.name: Str(chat)
     -> gen_ai.output.messages: Str(****)
     -> taskflow.note: Str(contact ****, card ****)
     -> gen_ai.usage.input_tokens: Int(1250)
     -> redaction.masked.count: Int(2)

docs.title: Cost per call
docs.text:
// src/ai/cost.ts: estimated cost per call from token usage and a price table kept in configuration
import { metrics } from "@opentelemetry/api";
import type { ResponseUsage } from "openai/resources/responses/responses";
import { z } from "zod";

// LLM_PRICES holds the provider's current per-million-token prices, copied from its pricing page:
// {"<model id>": {"input": <price>, "cachedInput": <price>, "output": <price>}}
const Prices = z.record(z.string(), z.object({ input: z.number(), cachedInput: z.number(), output: z.number() }));
const PRICES = Prices.parse(JSON.parse(process.env.LLM_PRICES ?? "{}"));

const cost = metrics.getMeter("taskflow-ai").createCounter("taskflow.llm.cost", {
  unit: "{cost_unit}",
  description: "Estimated model cost in the billing currency of the price table",
});

export function recordCost(model: string, usage: ResponseUsage, feature: string): number | undefined {
  const p = PRICES[model];
  if (!p) return undefined;                            // unknown model: alert on this, do not guess
  const cached = usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens;
  const estimate =
    ((usage.input_tokens - cached) * p.input + cached * p.cachedInput + usage.output_tokens * p.output) / 1_000_000;
  cost.add(estimate, { "gen_ai.request.model": model, "taskflow.feature": feature });
  return estimate;
}

Call recordCost(response.model, response.usage, feature) after each call. The price table is keyed by the model ID the provider returns, so a model switch without a matching price shows up as a missing estimate instead of a wrong one. Treat the result as an estimate and reconcile it with the provider's usage reports.

Queries for the dashboard, using the metric names as the Collector's Prometheus exporter produced them in a local test:

# tokens per hour, by feature and type (input or output)
sum by (taskflow_feature, gen_ai_token_type) (increase(gen_ai_client_token_usage_sum[1h]))

# average output tokens per call, by feature
sum by (taskflow_feature) (increase(gen_ai_client_token_usage_sum{gen_ai_token_type="output"}[1h]))
  / sum by (taskflow_feature) (increase(gen_ai_client_token_usage_count{gen_ai_token_type="output"}[1h]))

# p95 model-call latency, by feature
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, taskflow_feature) (rate(gen_ai_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

# share of model calls that failed, by feature
sum by (taskflow_feature) (rate(gen_ai_client_operation_duration_seconds_count{error_type!=""}[5m]))
  / sum by (taskflow_feature) (rate(gen_ai_client_operation_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

# estimated cost per day, by feature
sum by (taskflow_feature) (increase(taskflow_llm_cost_total[1d]))

Alerts follow the patterns in alerting and on-call: page on error share and latency against the feature's SLO, and send a ticket, not a page, when tokens per hour or cost per day jump well above their usual level.

docs.title: The feedback endpoint
docs.text:
Every AI response includes the ID of the trace that produced it. Inside the request handler, after the model call:

// src/routes/assistant.ts (excerpt): return the trace ID with the answer
import { trace } from "@opentelemetry/api";

const traceId = trace.getActiveSpan()?.spanContext().traceId;   // 32 lowercase hex characters
if (traceId) await feedbackStore.rememberTrace(req.user.id, traceId);   // so feedback can be checked later
res.json({ draft, traceId });

The UI sends the ID back with the user's rating, and this route stores the feedback and attaches it to the trace as a score:

// src/routes/ai-feedback.ts: thumbs up or down on an AI answer, tied to the trace that produced it
import { LangfuseClient } from "@langfuse/client";
import { Router } from "express";
import { z } from "zod";

const Feedback = z.object({
  traceId: z.string().regex(/^[0-9a-f]{32}$/),          // returned with every AI answer
  feature: z.enum(["task-assistant", "project-qa", "meeting-summary", "agent"]),
  rating: z.enum(["up", "down"]),
  reason: z.enum(["wrong", "incomplete", "unsafe", "slow", "other"]).optional(),
  comment: z.string().max(1_000).optional(),
});
export type Feedback = z.infer<typeof Feedback>;

export interface FeedbackStore {
  rememberTrace(userId: string, traceId: string): Promise<void>;  // called when an answer is served
  ownsTrace(userId: string, traceId: string): Promise<boolean>;
  save(doc: Feedback & { userId: string; at: Date }): Promise<void>;
}

const langfuse = new LangfuseClient();   // reads LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY, LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY, LANGFUSE_BASE_URL

export function aiFeedbackRouter(store: FeedbackStore) {
  const router = Router();
  router.post("/api/ai/feedback", async (req, res) => {
    const parsed = Feedback.safeParse(req.body);
    const userId = (req as { user?: { id: string } }).user?.id;   // set by the auth middleware
    if (!userId) { res.status(401).end(); return; }
    if (!parsed.success) { res.status(400).json({ error: "invalid feedback" }); return; }
    const f = parsed.data;
    if (!(await store.ownsTrace(userId, f.traceId))) { res.status(404).end(); return; }

    await store.save({ ...f, userId, at: new Date() });            // your own copy, joinable with eval sets
    langfuse.score.create({
      id: `${f.traceId}-user-feedback`,     // idempotency key: a second click updates the score
      traceId: f.traceId,
      name: "user-feedback",
      value: f.rating === "up" ? 1 : 0,
      dataType: "BOOLEAN",
      ...(f.reason && { comment: f.reason }),   // free text stays in your database, not the trace tool
    });
    res.status(204).end();
  });
  return router;
}

Design choices worth copying:

  • Ownership check. Users can only rate traces that were served to them, so nobody can flood another user's answers with feedback.
  • Your own copy first. The feedback lives in TaskFlow's database, joinable with users and features and usable for building evaluation sets, whatever tracing tool you use next year.
  • A score on the trace. Langfuse uses OpenTelemetry trace IDs (32 lowercase hex characters) as its trace IDs, so the ID from the answer attaches the score to the right trace. score.create queues the score and sends it in batches; it never throws, so feedback never fails the request. The id makes a repeated click update the score rather than add a second one.
  • Free text stays home. Comments can contain personal data; only the structured reason goes to the tracing tool.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Wrap every model call in one traced function, and record the prompt name, prompt version, requested model, and returned model on every span.
  • Follow the GenAI semantic conventions, keep the names in one module, and note which convention version your instrumentation emits.
  • Keep content capture off in production; when you need it, redact at the source, redact again in the Collector, and prefer references to a restricted store.
  • Send telemetry to a Collector and fan out from there, so vendors can change without code changes.
  • Use tail sampling to keep every error and slow trace, and sample the rest.
  • Record tokens and durations as metrics with low-cardinality labels only; compute cost from a price table in configuration.
  • Return the trace ID with every AI response and attach feedback to it.
  • Triage thumbs-down and edited outputs weekly and turn them into evaluation cases.
  • Alert on error share and latency against SLOs, and ticket on token or cost anomalies.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The token bill doubled overnight. Detect: tokens per hour for the agent feature jumped while request volume stayed flat; traces show many model calls per request. Cause: an agent loop that retries a failing tool, or a prompt change that made answers longer. Fix: cap model calls per request, alert on calls per request and tokens per hour, and compare output tokens by prompt version.
  • A user's email address appears in the tracing backend. Detect: a privacy review or a search of span attributes finds raw emails. Cause: content capture turned on in production, or an instrumentation library that captures prompts by default. Fix: turn capture off, add the Collector redaction processor, purge the affected data per your incident process, and set retention on the backend.
  • Behavior changed with no deploy. Detect: thumbs-down share rises; spans show a new gen_ai.response.model snapshot behind the same requested model. Cause: the provider moved the alias to a new snapshot. Fix: pin a snapshot in configuration, run the evaluation suite on old and new, and upgrade deliberately.
  • Dashboards stopped updating after a library upgrade. Detect: token panels are empty while traffic continues; the metrics backend shows new metric or attribute names. Cause: the GenAI conventions changed names (for example gen_ai.system to gen_ai.provider.name, or the token histogram to counters) and the instrumentation followed. Fix: pin instrumentation versions, keep names in one module, and update queries in the same change as the upgrade.
  • Feedback cannot be matched to anything. Detect: thumbs-down records exist, but nobody can find the trace, prompt version, or input behind them. Cause: responses did not return trace IDs, or traces were sampled away. Fix: return the trace ID with every answer and add a tail-sampling policy that keeps traces with negative feedback or errors.
  • The metrics backend runs out of memory. Detect: active series grow without bound after an instrumentation change. Cause: a high-cardinality label such as a user ID, trace ID, or prompt text on a metric. Fix: remove the label, keep such values on spans only, and add a cardinality limit in the Collector or backend.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• LLM observability: Telemetry that records model calls, tool calls, and retrieval with tokens, versions, and quality signals.
  • GenAI semantic conventions: OpenTelemetry's names for spans, attributes, and metrics of generative AI operations.
  • Inference span: The span for one model call, named {operation} {model}.
  • Content capture: Recording prompts, instructions, and outputs in telemetry; opt-in by convention.
  • OTLP: The OpenTelemetry protocol used to send traces, metrics, and logs.
  • OpenTelemetry Collector: A service that receives, processes, and exports telemetry.
  • Redaction processor: A Collector component that masks attribute values by key or pattern.
  • Tail sampling: Deciding which traces to keep after they complete.
  • Cardinality: The number of distinct label combinations of a metric.
  • Trace ID: The identifier shared by all spans of one request.
  • Score: A quality value attached to a trace, from a user, a judge, or a reviewer.
  • OpenInference: Arize's conventions and instrumentations for AI tracing, used by Phoenix.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating HTTP 200 and normal latency as proof that an AI feature works.
  • Logging full prompts and answers in production because it is convenient for debugging.
  • Recording the requested model but not the returned model snapshot.
  • Putting user IDs or prompt text in metric labels.
  • Assuming every tool uses the same attribute names (OpenInference and the GenAI conventions differ).
  • Assuming the GenAI conventions are stable and will not rename anything.
  • Collecting thumbs-down clicks without the trace ID that explains them.
  • Treating feedback rates as accuracy rather than as triage signals.
  • Sending telemetry straight to a vendor from every service, so a redaction rule has to be added in ten places.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which questions about an LLM feature can classic request metrics not answer, and which signals answer them?
  2. Describe the spans of a TaskFlow agent request that calls two tools. What are their names and kinds under the GenAI conventions?
  3. What is the status of the GenAI semantic conventions in November 2026, and what changed in semantic conventions v1.42.0? How do you protect dashboards from renames?
  4. Name the three content-capture patterns the conventions describe and when each fits.
  5. Why should telemetry go through a Collector, and what do the redaction and tail sampling processors add?
  6. A feature makes 40,000 model calls a day with 1,200 input tokens (900 of them cached) and 150 output tokens each. How many uncached input, cached input, and output tokens is that per day, and which one would you reduce first if output tokens cost several times more than input? (12 million uncached, 36 million cached, 6 million output; output and uncached input usually dominate, so trim answer length and the uncached part of the prompt.)
  7. Why must the feedback endpoint check that the trace belongs to the user, and why store feedback in your own database?
  8. Dashboards went blank after an instrumentation upgrade while traffic continued. What happened, and how do you prevent it?

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does pip install "transformers>=5.23" "peft>=0.21" "trl>=1.18" datasets accelerate Installs the training stack used in the lessons (plus PyTorch and a CUDA GPU) python scripts/build_dataset.py examples.jsonl data Deduplicates, validates gold answers, and group-splits into train, validation, and test python scripts/eval_task_parser.py data/test.jsonl preds/base.jsonl preds/tuned.jsonl Scores JSON validity, schema, per-field accuracy, and exact match per model python scripts/lora_params.py Counts LoRA parameters and training memory before you rent GPUs trainer.model.print_trainable_parameters() Confirms the adapter's share (about 0.5% of an 8B model at rank 16) PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, path).merge_and_unload() Folds the adapter into a 16-bit base for a standalone model vllm serve "$BASE_MODEL" --enable-lora --lora-modules name=path --max-lora-rank 16 Serves adapters by name over one shared base model client.fine_tuning.jobs.create(..., method={"type": "supervised", ...}) Starts a managed SFT job on Microsoft Foundry's OpenAI-compatible API

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# scripts/train_lora.py (excerpt): the starting point used in the lessons
peft_config = LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, lora_dropout=0.05,
                         target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM")
args = SFTConfig(output_dir="runs/lora", learning_rate=2e-4, num_train_epochs=2,
                 warmup_steps=0.03, lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
                 per_device_train_batch_size=4, gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
                 max_length=1024, eval_strategy="steps", eval_steps=50,
                 load_best_model_at_end=True, metric_for_best_model="eval_loss")
# QLoRA: also pass quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True,
#   bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
#   bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16) to SFTTrainer

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Answers from changing or private documents RAG with citations Fine-tuning learns facts slowly and can raise hallucination Valid JSON every time Structured output with a schema Fixes the shape without training The same quality from a smaller model at high volume SFT a small model with LoRA Shorter prompts and faster tokens repay the one-off cost A model you cannot download The provider's managed fine-tuning No weights, so no adapter of your own A base that does not fit your GPU QLoRA 4-bit base, 16-bit adapter Many features on one base model Separate adapters, multi-LoRA serving One base in memory, swap by name Several valid answers, some better DPO on pairs from your SFT model Comparisons are cheaper than perfect answers Only thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback KTO Learns from unpaired binary labels Quality that code can check GRPO or managed reinforcement fine-tuning Optimizes the real requirement A large model that works but costs too much Distillation into a smaller student Keeps most quality on a narrow task

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Full fine-tuning with Adam About 16 bytes per parameter: 8B model = 128 GB before activations LoRA and QLoRA, 8B, rank 16 About 16.7 GB and 4.7 GB; adapter file about 84 MB LoRA parameters per layer r x (d_in + d_out): 131,072 for 4,096 x 4,096 at rank 16 (under 1%) PEFT LoraConfig defaults r=8, lora_alpha=8, lora_dropout=0.0; scale alpha / r LoRA starting point Rank 16, alpha 32, learning rate 2e-4, effective batch under 32 TRL guide ranks 256 for SFT at post-training scale; 1-32 for RL TRL SFTConfig learning_rate=2e-5, max_length=1024 (cuts the end), gradient checkpointing on TRL DPO and GRPO DPO beta=0.1, learning_rate=1e-6; GRPO 8 generations, beta=0.0 DPO loss at step 0 -log sigmoid(0) = log 2 = 0.693 Test set of 50 examples Each error moves the score 2 points Data to start About 100 examples (Google's guidance); LIMA: 1,000 curated Break-even One-off cost / saving per request, then divide by daily volume Hosted availability OpenAI: no new orgs since May 7, 2026, no new jobs from January 6, 2027; Gemini API: no tuning since May 2025

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Fine-tuning to add facts. Use retrieval; fine-tune behavior.
  • Beating only a naive prompt. Compare with the best prompted baseline on the same held-out set.
  • Leaky splits. Split by project or customer and deduplicate normalized text.
  • A full fine-tuning learning rate for LoRA. Use about 2e-4, and check that outputs differ from the base model.
  • Attention-only adapters. Use target_modules="all-linear".
  • max_length shorter than the examples. Truncation cuts the answer; measure token lengths first.
  • Merging a QLoRA adapter into 4-bit weights. Merge into the 16-bit base.
  • Distilling without checks. Validate teacher outputs and confirm the teacher's terms allow it.

docs.title: Fine-Tuning Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review deciding when to fine-tune, LoRA and PEFT in practice, preference tuning and reinforcement methods, and distillation. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is fine-tuning, and what does it change?
docs.text: Fine-tuning continues training a pretrained model on a smaller, task-specific dataset, which updates some or all of its weights. It changes behavior: format, style, classification boundaries, tool-use patterns, and how much prompting a task needs. It is not a reliable way to add facts, citations, or permissions.

docs.title: 2. Why do prompting, structured output, and retrieval come before fine-tuning?
docs.text: They are cheaper, faster to change, and easy to undo: a prompt change ships in minutes, while fine-tuning needs a dataset, an evaluation set, training runs, deployment, and retraining when the base model retires. Many problems blamed on the model (invalid JSON, missing knowledge) are solved by a schema or retrieval.

docs.title: 3. Why is fine-tuning a poor way to add knowledge?
docs.text: Models learn new facts slowly through fine-tuning, and Gekhman et al. (2024) found that once new facts are learned they increase the tendency to hallucinate. Ovadia et al. (2023) found RAG consistently outperformed unsupervised fine-tuning for knowledge injection. Weights also cannot cite sources, follow document updates, or enforce per-user access.

docs.title: 4. What problems does fine-tuning solve well?
docs.text: Consistent output formats and styles, stable classification with a house taxonomy, tool-selection patterns on a fixed tool set, and compressing a long few-shot prompt into the weights. The most common business case is getting the same quality from a smaller, cheaper, faster model.

docs.title: 5. How do RAG and fine-tuning combine?
docs.text: Retrieval supplies current, permission-filtered facts per request, and fine-tuning teaches the model how to use them: answer only from the passages, cite them in a fixed format, and say when the passages do not contain the answer.

docs.title: 6. What does "evaluate first" mean in practice?
docs.text: Build the held-out evaluation set and metrics before collecting training data, score the best prompted baseline on it, and treat that baseline as the contender to beat. Without a baseline, you cannot tell whether training helped.

docs.title: 7. Why must the comparison be against the best prompted baseline, not a naive prompt?
docs.text: A fine-tuned model that only beats a weak prompt may lose to a better prompt that costs nothing to maintain. The decision is "is the tuned model better than our best non-tuned option on the same test set", including cost and latency.

docs.title: 8. What metrics would you use for a structured-output task such as a task parser?
docs.text: JSON validity, schema validity, per-field accuracy, exact match of all fields, and operational metrics such as input tokens and latency at the 50th and 95th percentile. Per-field accuracy shows which behavior is wrong; exact match is the user-visible success rate.

docs.title: 9. How big should a test set be?
docs.text: Big enough that one error barely moves the score. With 50 examples each error is 2 percentage points, so small differences are noise; with a few hundred, each error is worth well under 1 point.

docs.title: 10. How many training examples do you need?
docs.text: Providers publish minimums that are floors, not targets; Google's guidance for Gemini tuning on its Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) is to start with 100 examples and scale to thousands if needed. LIMA showed strong instruction following from 1,000 curated examples. Consistency, coverage of edge cases, and correct labels matter more than volume.

docs.title: 11. What is a group split, and why use it?
docs.text: Assigning examples to train, validation, and test by a shared key such as project, customer, or time period, for example by hashing the project ID. It prevents near-duplicate phrasing from the same source appearing on both sides of the split, which inflates scores.

docs.title: 12. What makes a good fine-tuning dataset?
docs.text: Representative real inputs (with permission), edge cases and refusals, consistent labels written to rules, no duplicates or leakage, minimal personal data, and a documented source and right to use each example.

docs.title: 13. What are the risks of synthetic training data?
docs.text: It inherits the generator's mistakes and biases, can be less varied than real traffic, and may carry restrictions from the generator's terms. Review a sample, label synthetic rows in metadata, and keep real examples in the test set.

docs.title: 14. How do you reason about the cost of fine-tuning without exact prices?
docs.text: In relative units: one-off cost (data work and training runs), any hosting fee for the custom model, and per-request savings from fewer input tokens and a smaller model. Break-even requests = one-off cost / saving per request, then compare with real volume.

docs.title: 15. Which managed fine-tuning services exist as of November 2026?
docs.text: Microsoft Foundry offers SFT, DPO, and reinforcement fine-tuning for selected OpenAI and open models; Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) offers SFT, preference tuning, and RL fine-tuning for selected Gemini models; Amazon Bedrock offers SFT, reinforcement fine-tuning, and distillation; Together AI offers LoRA and full fine-tuning of open models. OpenAI is winding down self-serve fine-tuning, and the Gemini developer API has no tuning.

docs.title: 16. Hosted fine-tuning or an open-weight model you train yourself?
docs.text: Hosted services need little infrastructure but limit methods to what the provider supports, keep the model on their platform, and can change. Open-weight training gives any method, portability, and ownership of the adapter (within the license), at the cost of running GPUs, serving, and security yourself.

docs.title: 17. What should you check about a base model before building the dataset?
docs.text: Which tuning methods the platform supports for it, its size against your latency and cost targets, how close its prompted baseline already is, its license or terms, and its retirement date. Read its ID from configuration and record the exact version.

docs.title: 18. How do you roll out a fine-tuned model safely?
docs.text: Behind a canary: a deterministic per-user bucket sends a small share of traffic to the candidate, outputs are validated, invalid answers fall back to the baseline, and the fallback rate is monitored before raising the percentage.

docs.title: 19. Why does full fine-tuning need so much memory?
docs.text: With Adam in mixed precision each parameter needs about 16 bytes: a 16-bit weight and gradient (4 bytes) plus a 32-bit master weight and two moment estimates (12 bytes). An 8B model needs about 128 GB before activations.

docs.title: 20. What is PEFT?
docs.text: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning: methods that freeze the base model and train a small number of new or selected parameters, so gradients and optimizer state exist only for those. LoRA is the most widely used; others include prompt tuning and IA3.

docs.title: 21. How does LoRA work?
docs.text: For a frozen linear layer W, LoRA adds a trainable low-rank path: h = W x + (alpha / r) B A x, with A of shape r x d_in and B of shape d_out x r. Only A and B train, so a layer adds r x (d_in + d_out) parameters instead of d_in x d_out.

docs.title: 22. Why is B initialized to zero?
docs.text: So the adapter is a no-op at the start: the model initially behaves exactly like the base model, and training moves away from it smoothly. That is PEFT's default initialization.

docs.title: 23. How many parameters does rank 16 add to a 4,096 x 4,096 projection?
docs.text: 16 x (4,096 + 4,096) = 131,072, versus 16,777,216 weights in the layer, under 1%.

docs.title: 24. What do rank and alpha control?
docs.text: Rank sets the adapter's capacity. Alpha scales the update by alpha / r, so changing rank with a fixed alpha changes the effective step size. rsLoRA scales by alpha / sqrt(r) instead so higher ranks do not learn more slowly.

docs.title: 25. Which layers should LoRA target?
docs.text: All linear layers (target_modules="all-linear" in PEFT). The Thinking Machines "LoRA Without Regret" study found attention-only LoRA underperforms even when its rank is raised to match the parameter count.

docs.title: 26. What learning rate does LoRA need?
docs.text: Higher than full fine-tuning: the same study found the optimal LoRA rate about 10 times the full fine-tuning rate, and TRL's guide uses 2e-4 for LoRA SFT. Using TRL's full fine-tuning default of 2e-5 often makes the adapter barely change the model.

docs.title: 27. When does LoRA underperform full fine-tuning?
docs.text: When the dataset exceeds the adapter's capacity, such as continued pretraining on billions of tokens or very large instruction sets. Biderman et al. (2024) found LoRA "learns less and forgets less": weaker on the target domain at low ranks, but better at preserving other abilities.

docs.title: 28. What is QLoRA?
docs.text: LoRA on a frozen base stored in 4-bit, with 16-bit adapters. It adds the NF4 data type, double quantization of the scaling constants, and paged optimizers, and the paper fine-tuned a 65B model on a single 48 GB GPU while matching 16-bit fine-tuning quality.

docs.title: 29. What does QLoRA cost compared with LoRA?
docs.text: Speed: every forward pass dequantizes 4-bit blocks to the compute type, so steps are slower than LoRA on a 16-bit base. Use it when memory is the constraint.

docs.title: 30. How do you configure QLoRA in Transformers and TRL?
docs.text:
A BitsAndBytesConfig with load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, and bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16, passed to SFTTrainer as quantization_config together with a peft_config.

trainer = SFTTrainer(model=BASE_MODEL, args=args, train_dataset=train,
                     peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear"),
                     quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"))

docs.title: 31. Why use a prompt-completion dataset for SFT?
docs.text: TRL then computes the loss only on the completion by default, so the model is trained on the answer it must produce rather than on reproducing the system prompt and user message.

docs.title: 32. What do TRL's SFTConfig defaults mean for a LoRA run?
docs.text: learning_rate=2e-5 is a full fine-tuning value (raise it for LoRA), max_length=1024 truncates longer examples from the end, and gradient checkpointing is on to save memory.

docs.title: 33. Why does max_length matter so much for structured outputs?
docs.text: Truncation cuts the end of an example, which in a prompt-completion pair is the answer. The model then learns incomplete JSON. Measure token lengths and set max_length above the longest example.

docs.title: 34. How do you choose the number of epochs?
docs.text: Watch validation loss: when training loss keeps falling and validation loss rises, the adapter is memorizing. Keep the best checkpoint (load_best_model_at_end=True with metric_for_best_model="eval_loss") and judge it by task metrics on the test set.

docs.title: 35. What effective batch size suits LoRA?
docs.text: Moderate: the TRL guide recommends an effective batch under 32, because LoRA is less tolerant of large batches than full fine-tuning. Effective batch = per-device batch x gradient accumulation steps x GPUs.

docs.title: 36. Name some LoRA variants and when to try them.
docs.text: DoRA (use_dora=True) when plain LoRA lags full fine-tuning; rsLoRA for high ranks; PiSSA, OLoRA, or LoftQ initializations for faster convergence or quantized bases; modules_to_save when new token embeddings must be learned. Start with plain LoRA.

docs.title: 37. What checks should an adapter pass before release?
docs.text: Task metrics on the held-out test set, a general regression set for forgetting, safety and refusal cases, and a smoke test that its outputs differ from the base model's.

docs.title: 38. Merge an adapter or keep it separate?
docs.text: Merge (merge_and_unload()) for a standalone model with no adapter overhead. Keep it separate to serve many adapters on one base model in memory, to swap or roll back by name, and to limit the adapter to the feature it was trained for.

docs.title: 39. How does multi-LoRA serving work in vLLM?
docs.text: Start the server with --enable-lora, register adapters with --lora-modules name=path, and set --max-lora-rank to the highest adapter rank. Clients select an adapter by putting its name in the request's model field.

docs.title: 40. Why must an adapter be stored with its exact base model?
docs.text: An adapter is a set of deltas for specific weight matrices. It only works on the base model and revision it was trained on; on a similarly named model it fails to load or silently produces poor output.

docs.title: 41. Why merge into a 16-bit base rather than the 4-bit one after QLoRA?
docs.text: Merging into quantized weights adds rounding error to the result. Load the base in 16-bit, merge there, and quantize the merged model afterward if needed.

docs.title: 42. What does preference tuning add beyond SFT?
docs.text: SFT teaches what a good answer looks like; preference tuning teaches which of two plausible answers is better, from comparisons or ratings that are cheaper to collect than perfect answers.

docs.title: 43. Describe the RLHF pipeline.
docs.text: SFT on demonstrations; a reward model trained on human rankings (with the Bradley-Terry model, P(A beats B) = sigmoid(r(A) - r(B))); then reinforcement learning, usually PPO, to maximize the reward minus a KL penalty that keeps the policy near the SFT model.

docs.title: 44. Why is the KL penalty needed?
docs.text: The reward model is an imperfect proxy. Without a penalty for drifting from the reference model, the policy finds answers that score well without being good, which is reward hacking.

docs.title: 45. What does DPO change compared with RLHF?
docs.text: It shows the RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy, so training becomes a classification-style loss on preference pairs. No reward model, no sampling during training, and only two models (policy and reference).

docs.title: 46. What does beta do in DPO?
docs.text: It controls how far the policy may move from the reference model; TRL's default is 0.1. Higher values keep the policy closer to the reference.

docs.title: 47. Compute a DPO loss.
docs.text: With beta = 0.1, a chosen log-ratio of +2.0 and a rejected log-ratio of -1.0, the margin is 0.1 x 3.0 = 0.3 and the loss is -log sigmoid(0.3) = 0.554. At the start, both log-ratios are 0 and the loss is log 2 = 0.693.

docs.title: 48. What are DPO's common failure modes?
docs.text: Length bias when raters preferred longer answers; pairs collected from a different model (off-policy) that do not fit your model; and falling likelihoods of both chosen and rejected answers, which an added SFT term (loss_type=["sigmoid", "sft"] in TRL) counters.

docs.title: 49. What are KTO, ORPO, and SimPO?
docs.text: KTO learns from single answers labelled desirable or undesirable, such as thumbs up or down. ORPO adds an odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss so SFT and alignment happen in one stage without a reference model. SimPO uses the average log-probability as the reward, adds a target margin, and needs no reference model.

docs.title: 50. What is RLVR, and what is GRPO?
docs.text: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards uses a reward computed by code, such as tests or schema and field checks, instead of a learned reward model. GRPO samples a group of answers per prompt and uses each answer's reward relative to the group mean (divided by the group's standard deviation) as its advantage, so no value model is needed.

docs.title: 51. What happens when every answer in a GRPO group gets the same reward?
docs.text: The advantages are all zero and the prompt teaches nothing. TRL logs the share of such groups as frac_reward_zero_std; fix it with partial credit, prompts of the right difficulty, or more sampling diversity.

docs.title: 52. How do you design a verifiable reward?
docs.text: Make it as strict as the real requirement, give partial credit where it helps learning (valid shape, then each correct field), and test it on correct, partly correct, and adversarial answers before training.

docs.title: 53. What is distillation, and why use it?
docs.text: Training a smaller student to imitate a larger teacher, usually to cut cost and latency for a narrow task. DistilBERT, for example, kept 97% of BERT's language understanding while being 40% smaller and 60% faster.

docs.title: 54. Compare logit, off-policy, and on-policy distillation.
docs.text: Logit distillation matches the teacher's full probability distribution and needs those probabilities and a shared vocabulary. Off-policy distillation fine-tunes the student on teacher-written answers and works with an API teacher. On-policy distillation (GKD, TRL's DistillationTrainer) lets the student generate and the teacher grade each token, which fixes the train-inference mismatch but needs an open teacher with the same vocabulary.

docs.title: 55. What is the main weakness of off-policy distillation?
docs.text: The student only learns from the teacher's clean answers and never practices recovering from its own mistakes, so it can be brittle on real inputs. Validated, real prompts and on-policy distillation reduce this.

docs.title: 56. Why validate teacher outputs before training a student?
docs.text: The student inherits the teacher's mistakes. Keep only answers that pass schema and evaluation checks, match gold labels where they exist, and review a sample by hand.

docs.title: 57. What legal check comes before distilling a hosted model?
docs.text: Its terms of service. Anthropic's commercial terms, for example, prohibit accessing the services "to build a competing product or service, including to train competing AI models." Open models you are licensed to use, or your own models, avoid the question.

docs.title: 58. When is distillation worth it?
docs.text: When the task is narrow and stable, volume is high or latency matters, and the student reaches the quality bar on the same held-out evaluation. It is rarely worth it for low-volume features or broad open-ended tasks.

docs.title: 59. A team wants to fine-tune a model on the product documentation so the assistant answers support questions. What do you recommend?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the failure is missing or outdated knowledge, and whether answers need citations or per-customer access.

How to confirm: give the model the relevant documentation page in the prompt and see whether it answers correctly; if it does, the gap is knowledge, not behavior.

Likely causes and fixes: a knowledge problem being treated as a behavior problem. Use retrieval with citations and access filters; if the answer style still needs work, fine-tune on answer format and citation behavior, not on the documents. See when to fine-tune.

docs.title: 60. The fine-tuned parser scored 12 points above the baseline offline, but production fallbacks went up. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the training and test data were collected compared with live requests.

How to confirm: score the tuned model on a fresh sample of real requests labelled after the release; compare phrasing and length distributions with the training set.

Likely causes and fixes: tidy, synthetic, or old training data, or leakage that inflated the test score. Add real requests to training and evaluation, split by group, and re-evaluate before raising the canary. See when to fine-tune.

docs.title: 61. A new evaluation set shows much lower scores than the original test set. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: overlap between training and the original test set.

How to confirm: search for near-duplicates and shared projects or customers across the splits; check whether the test set was used to pick hyperparameters.

Likely causes and fixes: leakage through near-duplicates or shared groups, or tuning against the test set. Split by group, deduplicate on normalized text, keep a separate validation set, and refresh the test set periodically. See when to fine-tune.

docs.title: 62. After switching to a tuned small model, the monthly bill went up. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: hosting charges for the custom model deployment, not just per-token costs.

How to confirm: break the bill down by deployment, hosting hours, and training jobs; compare with request volume.

Likely causes and fixes: an hourly hosting fee or provisioned capacity at low traffic, idle deployments, or repeated training runs. Include hosting in the break-even calculation, use per-token deployments for low volume, and delete unused deployments. See when to fine-tune.

docs.title: 63. Your LoRA adapter's outputs look identical to the base model's. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: that the adapter is actually loaded and selected for the request.

How to confirm: log the adapter name per request, compare outputs with and without PeftModel.from_pretrained, and check the training logs for the learning rate and validation loss.

Likely causes and fixes: a wrong adapter path, the base model's name in the request instead of the adapter's, or a full fine-tuning learning rate such as 2e-5. Fix the loading, log adapter selection, and retrain with a LoRA learning rate. See LoRA and PEFT in practice.

docs.title: 64. Some JSON answers from the tuned model stop in the middle. What is the cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether truncated outputs correlate with long requests.

How to confirm: measure token lengths of training examples against max_length, and check max_new_tokens at inference.

Likely causes and fixes: training examples longer than max_length were truncated from the end, so the model learned incomplete answers, or generation stopped at a low max_new_tokens. Raise or respect the limits and drop over-long examples. See LoRA and PEFT in practice.

docs.title: 65. Training crashes with out-of-memory errors on the first steps. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: the model's 16-bit size against GPU memory, then batch size and max_length.

How to confirm: estimate weights plus adapter state before activations, and test with batch size 1.

Likely causes and fixes: a base that barely fits, or batches and sequences too large. Lower the per-device batch and raise gradient accumulation, keep gradient checkpointing on, shorten max_length, or switch to QLoRA. See LoRA and PEFT in practice.

docs.title: 66. vLLM refuses to load a new adapter. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the adapter's rank and base model.

How to confirm: read adapter_config.json for r and the base model name and compare with the server's --max-lora-rank and model.

Likely causes and fixes: a rank above --max-lora-rank, or an adapter trained on a different base or revision. Raise the limit to the highest rank in use and pin the base revision in training and serving. See LoRA and PEFT in practice.

docs.title: 67. After merging the parser adapter into the base model, other features got worse. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the merged model replaced the base for every feature.

How to confirm: run the general regression set on the base and the merged model.

Likely causes and fixes: the narrow task's weight changes now apply everywhere. Serve the adapter only for the parser and keep the base for other features, or add general examples to the training data. See LoRA and PEFT in practice.

docs.title: 68. Summaries became noticeably longer after DPO. Why, and what do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the share of preference pairs where the chosen answer is longer.

How to confirm: compare average length before and after, and inspect pairs where length was the main difference.

Likely causes and fixes: raters preferred longer answers and DPO learned length as the signal. Rebalance the pairs, add brevity to the rubric, or try a length-normalized method such as SimPO. See preference tuning and distillation.

docs.title: 69. GRPO's training reward keeps rising, but held-out exact match is falling. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the highest-reward samples.

How to confirm: read them and score them with the evaluation script; look for outputs that satisfy the reward function without being correct.

Likely causes and fixes: reward hacking through a loophole in the verifier. Tighten the reward, test it on adversarial answers, add a KL penalty or train for fewer steps, and select checkpoints by the evaluation. See preference tuning and distillation.

docs.title: 70. A GRPO run shows a flat reward and a high frac_reward_zero_std. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: how often groups contain only perfect or only failing answers.

How to confirm: sample prompts and generate several answers each at the training temperature.

Likely causes and fixes: prompts too easy or too hard for the model, or an all-or-nothing reward. Keep prompts the model sometimes solves, add partial credit, and raise sampling diversity. See preference tuning and distillation.

docs.title: 71. A distilled student fails many of the same cases as the teacher, plus others. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether teacher outputs were validated before training.

How to confirm: score the teacher's training answers against gold labels or the schema and evaluation checks.

Likely causes and fixes: the student learned the teacher's errors, and off-policy training left it brittle on its own mistakes. Filter teacher answers, keep only those matching gold labels where available, add real prompts, and consider on-policy distillation. See preference tuning and distillation.

docs.title: 72. The fine-tuned model must be retrained before a fixed date. How do you make that routine?
docs.text:
What to check first: the base model's retirement date and whether the dataset, evaluation, and training configuration are versioned.

How to confirm: try retraining on a newer base from the stored artifacts in a staging run.

Likely causes and fixes: hosted fine-tuned models usually follow their base model's retirement schedule, and providers change their offerings. Keep datasets in a provider-neutral chat JSONL format, keep the evaluation runnable against any compatible endpoint, schedule retraining before the deadline, and keep an open-weight fallback. See when to fine-tune.
