docs.title: LoRA and PEFT in Practice
docs.text:
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is the default way to fine-tune open-weight language models today. Instead of updating billions of weights, it freezes the base model and trains a pair of small matrices next to selected layers, producing an "adapter" of tens of megabytes. This lesson explains why full fine-tuning is so memory-hungry, how LoRA and QLoRA work, how rank, alpha, and target modules interact, and how to train, evaluate, merge, and serve an adapter for the TaskFlow Assistant's task parser with the Hugging Face PEFT and TRL libraries. Code was checked against the installed packages as of November 2026: peft 0.21, trl 1.18, and transformers 5.23.

The previous lesson, when to fine-tune, built the dataset and the evaluation script used here.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Full fine-tuning updates every weight, so the optimizer must keep gradients and its own statistics for every weight too. For an 8-billion parameter model that is well over 100 GB of accelerator memory before a single activation is stored, which means several data-center GPUs for a job that only teaches the model to emit tidy JSON. Each fine-tuned copy is also a full-size model to store and serve.

LoRA changes both sides of that equation. Training needs memory for the frozen weights plus a fraction of a percent of trainable parameters, so a single GPU is often enough, and with QLoRA even a large model can fit. The result is a small adapter file: many adapters can share one base model in memory, one per feature or customer, and a bad adapter can be rolled back by switching a name. Knowing the knobs (rank, alpha, which layers, learning rate) is the difference between an adapter that matches full fine-tuning and one that quietly learns nothing.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• LoRA paper (Microsoft), 2021. LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models reports that, compared with fully fine-tuning GPT-3 175B with Adam, LoRA "can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times," performs on par in quality, and adds "no additional inference latency" because the update can be merged into the weights.
  • QLoRA, 2023. QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs backpropagates through a frozen 4-bit base model into LoRA adapters, which "reduces memory usage enough to finetune a 65B parameter model on a single 48GB GPU while preserving full 16-bit finetuning task performance," using the NF4 data type, double quantization, and paged optimizers.
  • Apple Intelligence, 2024. Apple's foundation models overview describes LoRA adapters for features such as summarization that "can be dynamically loaded, temporarily cached in memory, and swapped," and notes that a rank-16 adapter for its roughly 3-billion-parameter on-device model "typically require[s] 10s of megabytes."
  • Thinking Machines, "LoRA Without Regret", 2025. The study finds that LoRA matches full fine-tuning on small and medium post-training datasets when applied to all layers (especially the MLP layers), with a learning rate about 10 times higher than full fine-tuning's, and that LoRA is "less tolerant of large batch sizes." Hugging Face reproduced the settings in TRL's LoRA Without Regret guide.
  • Biderman et al., 2024. LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less finds that on large code and math datasets standard low-rank LoRA "substantially underperforms full finetuning," but "better maintains the base model's performance on tasks outside the target domain": the capacity trade-off behind choosing a rank.

Popular tools and providers: Hugging Face PEFT, TRL, Transformers, and bitsandbytes; Unsloth, Axolotl, and LLaMA-Factory as training front ends; vLLM and LoRAX for serving many adapters on one base model. (PyTorch's torchtune is no longer actively maintained, according to its repository.)

docs.title: Why full fine-tuning is heavy
docs.text:
Training with the Adam optimizer in mixed precision keeps, for every weight, a 16-bit copy of the weight (2 bytes), a 16-bit gradient (2 bytes), and in 32-bit a master copy plus Adam's two moment estimates (12 bytes): about 16 bytes per parameter, the figure analyzed in the ZeRO paper. Activations come on top and grow with batch size and sequence length.

8B parameters x 16 bytes = 128 GB   (full fine-tuning, before activations)
8B parameters x  2 bytes =  16 GB   (the same model, frozen, in 16-bit)
8B parameters x 0.5 byte =   4 GB   (frozen in 4-bit, as QLoRA stores it)

If only a small set of new parameters is trainable, the 14 bytes per parameter of gradient and optimizer state apply only to them. That is the whole idea of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT).

docs.title: The LoRA update
docs.text:
A linear layer computes h = W x, where W has shape d_out x d_in. LoRA freezes W and adds a low-rank path:

h = W x + (alpha / r) * B (A x)

A: r x d_in    (trainable, random init)
B: d_out x r   (trainable, initialized to zero)
r: the rank, much smaller than d_in and d_out (for example 16)

Because B starts at zero, the adapter is a no-op before training: the model behaves exactly like the base model at step 0, which keeps early training stable (PEFT's default initialization). The trainable weights per layer are r x (d_in + d_out) instead of d_in x d_out. For a 4096 x 4096 projection at rank 16, that is 131,072 weights instead of 16,777,216, under 1%.

The bet behind LoRA is that the change a fine-tuning task needs has low "intrinsic rank": a narrow behavior can be expressed as a small number of directions in weight space. That bet holds well for format, style, and task behavior, and less well for absorbing large amounts of new knowledge, which is where a higher rank or full fine-tuning helps.

docs.title: Rank, alpha, and scaling
docs.text:
• Rank r sets capacity. Small ranks (8-32) suit narrow tasks such as the TaskFlow parser; TRL's guide recommends rank 256 for SFT at "post-training scale" and 1-32 for reinforcement learning, which needs very little capacity.
  • Alpha scales the update by alpha / r. Changing r while keeping alpha fixed changes the effective step size, which is why ranks and learning rates interact. A common habit is alpha = 2r or a fixed alpha such as 16 or 32; PEFT's defaults are r=8 and lora_alpha=8.
  • rsLoRA (use_rslora=True in PEFT) scales by alpha / sqrt(r) instead, from Kalajdzievski (2023), which keeps higher ranks from learning more slowly.
  • Dropout on the LoRA path (lora_dropout, default 0.0) is a mild regularizer for small datasets.

docs.title: Which layers to adapt
docs.text:
Early LoRA work often adapted only the attention query and value projections. Current evidence favors adapting every linear layer: the Thinking Machines study found attention-only LoRA underperforms even when its rank is raised to match the parameter count. In PEFT, target_modules="all-linear" selects every linear layer except the output head. The parameter cost for an 8B-class decoder (32 layers, hidden size 4,096, MLP size 14,336, 8 key-value heads) is small either way:

Rank Attention only All linear Share of 8B 8 6,815,744 20,971,520 0.26% 16 13,631,488 41,943,040 0.52% 64 54,525,952 167,772,160 2.10% 256 218,103,808 671,088,640 8.39%

The numbers come from the parameter calculator in the practical examples.

docs.title: QLoRA: a 4-bit base under a 16-bit adapter
docs.text:
QLoRA keeps LoRA's trainable matrices in 16-bit but stores the frozen base in 4-bit, with three tricks from the paper:

  1. NF4 (4-bit NormalFloat), a data type whose 16 levels are spaced for normally distributed weights, losing less information than plain 4-bit integers.
  2. Double quantization, which quantizes the per-block scaling constants themselves to save a little more memory.
  3. Paged optimizers, which move optimizer state to CPU memory during spikes instead of crashing with out-of-memory errors.

During the forward pass each 4-bit block is dequantized to the compute type (usually bfloat16) on the fly, so QLoRA trades some speed for memory. In Transformers this is a BitsAndBytesConfig with load_in_4bit=True, bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4", bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True, and bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16; the bitsandbytes library has the most complete support on NVIDIA GPUs.

docs.title: Variants worth knowing
docs.text:
PEFT implements dozens of methods; a few matter in practice:

Option What it changes When to try it use_dora=True DoRA splits each weight into magnitude and direction and applies LoRA to the direction (Liu et al., 2024) When plain LoRA lags full fine-tuning; slower to train use_rslora=True Rank-stabilized scaling alpha / sqrt(r) High ranks init_lora_weights="pissa" and others Initializes A and B from the base weights (PiSSA, OLoRA, LoftQ, and more) instead of zeros Faster convergence; LoftQ pairs with quantized bases modules_to_save=[...] Trains and saves full copies of chosen modules New tokens whose embeddings must be learned

Start with plain LoRA on all linear layers; reach for variants only when evaluation shows a gap.

docs.title: Training with TRL
docs.text:
TRL's SFTTrainer handles tokenization, chat templates, loss masking, and the PEFT wrapping. Three behaviors matter for a task like TaskFlow's:

  • Dataset format. A prompt-completion dataset, where prompt holds the system and user messages and completion holds the assistant answer, computes the loss on the completion only by default (completion_only_loss=None means "decide from the dataset"). The model is graded on the JSON it writes, not on reproducing your system prompt.
  • PEFT integration. Passing peft_config=LoraConfig(...) wraps the model; passing quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(...) as well loads the base in 4-bit, which together is QLoRA.
  • Defaults. TRL's SFTConfig defaults to learning_rate=2e-5, a full-fine-tuning value, max_length=1024 with truncation from the end, and gradient checkpointing on. For LoRA, raise the learning rate.

docs.title: Hyperparameters
docs.text:
Setting Starting point Why r 16 for a narrow task; up to 256 for large SFT datasets Capacity must match the dataset lora_alpha 32 (with r=16) Sets the update scale alpha / r target_modules "all-linear" Attention-only adapters underperform learning_rate 2e-4 About 10x a full fine-tuning rate; TRL's guide uses it for SFT Effective batch size 16 (per_device_train_batch_size x gradient_accumulation_steps x GPUs) LoRA prefers effective batches under 32 num_train_epochs 1-3 Watch validation loss; small datasets overfit fast warmup_steps 0.03 (a float below 1 is a fraction of all steps) Transformers 5 replaced warmup_ratio with this lr_scheduler_type "cosine" Smooth decay after warmup max_length Longer than your longest example Truncation cuts the end, which is the answer

Change one setting at a time and compare on the validation set. The learning rate matters most: too low and the adapter barely moves (its output looks like the base model's); too high and validation loss climbs after a few hundred steps.

docs.title: Evaluating an adapter
docs.text:
Training loss falling is necessary, not sufficient. Use four checks:

  1. Task metrics on the held-out test set, with the same eval_task_parser.py used for the baseline: JSON validity, field accuracy, exact match.
  2. Validation loss per checkpoint. When training loss keeps falling but validation loss rises, the adapter is memorizing; keep the best checkpoint (load_best_model_at_end=True).
  3. A regression set of general tasks the product still relies on (summaries, other prompts), to catch forgetting. LoRA forgets less than full fine-tuning, but not nothing.
  4. Safety and refusal cases, because a narrow dataset with no refusals can erode refusal behavior.

The evals in CI lesson shows how to run these checks automatically on every new adapter.

docs.title: Serving: separate adapters or a merged model
docs.text: An adapter can be merged into the base (merge_and_unload() adds (alpha/r) B A into W), producing an ordinary model with no extra latency, or kept separate, so one base model in GPU memory serves many adapters. vLLM supports the second pattern: start it with --enable-lora and --lora-modules name=path, and clients select an adapter by passing its name as the model in an OpenAI-compatible request. Serving at scale is covered in serving open models.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choice Why Narrow task behavior on an open model LoRA, r 8-32, all linear layers Small, fast, matches full fine-tuning at this scale Large instruction dataset (hundreds of thousands of examples) LoRA with a high rank, or full fine-tuning Low ranks run out of capacity Continued pretraining on billions of domain tokens Full fine-tuning LoRA "learns less" at this scale A large model that does not fit on available GPUs QLoRA 4-bit base, 16-bit adapter Many features or tenants sharing one base model Separate adapters with multi-LoRA serving One base in memory; swap by name Lowest possible latency for one task Merge the adapter No adapter overhead at inference A hosted model you cannot download The provider's fine-tuning service No weights, so no LoRA of your own

docs.title: Count parameters and memory before you train
docs.text:
This calculator reproduces the table above and the memory estimate, so you can plug in your own model's dimensions from its config.json.

# scripts/lora_params.py
"""Count LoRA parameters and estimate training memory for an 8B-class decoder."""
LAYERS, HIDDEN, MLP, KV_OUT = 32, 4096, 14336, 1024  # 8 KV heads x 128 dims
TOTAL_PARAMS = 8.0e9
LINEAR = {  # module name: (in_features, out_features), per decoder layer
    "q_proj": (HIDDEN, HIDDEN),
    "k_proj": (HIDDEN, KV_OUT),
    "v_proj": (HIDDEN, KV_OUT),
    "o_proj": (HIDDEN, HIDDEN),
    "gate_proj": (HIDDEN, MLP),
    "up_proj": (HIDDEN, MLP),
    "down_proj": (MLP, HIDDEN),
}
ATTENTION = {"q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj"}


def lora_params(rank: int, modules: set[str]) -> int:
    """A LoRA pair adds A (rank x in) and B (out x rank): rank * (in + out) weights."""
    return LAYERS * sum(rank * (i + o) for name, (i, o) in LINEAR.items() if name in modules)


def gb(n_bytes: float) -> str:
    return f"{n_bytes / 1e9:,.1f} GB"


print(f"{'rank':>4} {'attention only':>16} {'all linear':>14} {'% of model':>11}")
for rank in (8, 16, 64, 256):
    attn, every = lora_params(rank, ATTENTION), lora_params(rank, set(LINEAR))
    print(f"{rank:>4} {attn:>16,} {every:>14,} {every / TOTAL_PARAMS:>10.2%}")

adapter = lora_params(16, set(LINEAR))
print("\nMemory before activations (r=16, all linear, Adam):")
print("full fine-tuning, mixed precision:", gb(TOTAL_PARAMS * 16))  # 2 + 2 + 12 bytes per weight
print("LoRA on a 16-bit base:           ", gb(TOTAL_PARAMS * 2 + adapter * 16))
print("QLoRA on a 4-bit base:           ", gb(TOTAL_PARAMS * 0.5 + adapter * 16))
print("adapter file in 16-bit:          ", f"{adapter * 2 / 1e6:,.0f} MB")

Output:

rank   attention only     all linear  % of model
   8        6,815,744     20,971,520      0.26%
  16       13,631,488     41,943,040      0.52%
  64       54,525,952    167,772,160      2.10%
 256      218,103,808    671,088,640      8.39%

Memory before activations (r=16, all linear, Adam):
full fine-tuning, mixed precision: 128.0 GB
LoRA on a 16-bit base:            16.7 GB
QLoRA on a 4-bit base:            4.7 GB
adapter file in 16-bit:           84 MB

docs.title: Train a LoRA adapter with TRL
docs.text:
The script turns the chat-format splits from the previous lesson into prompt-completion rows and trains an adapter. The base model comes from the BASE_MODEL environment variable: choose an instruct model whose license fits your use, whose prompted baseline is already close, and that fits your hardware.

# requirements: a CUDA GPU; versions as checked for this lesson
pip install "torch>=2.6" "transformers>=5.23" "peft>=0.21" "trl>=1.18" datasets accelerate

# scripts/train_lora.py
"""Train a LoRA adapter for the TaskFlow task parser with TRL's SFTTrainer."""
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import SFTConfig, SFTTrainer

BASE_MODEL = os.environ["BASE_MODEL"]  # a Hub model ID or local path, from configuration


def to_prompt_completion(row: dict) -> dict:
    *prompt, answer = row["messages"]  # system + user messages, then the gold answer
    return {"prompt": prompt, "completion": [answer]}


data = load_dataset(
    "json", data_files={"train": "data/train.jsonl", "validation": "data/validation.jsonl"}
)
data = data.map(to_prompt_completion, remove_columns=["messages"])

peft_config = LoraConfig(
    r=16,
    lora_alpha=32,
    lora_dropout=0.05,
    target_modules="all-linear",
    task_type="CAUSAL_LM",
)

args = SFTConfig(
    output_dir="runs/taskflow-parser-lora",
    num_train_epochs=2,
    learning_rate=2e-4,
    lr_scheduler_type="cosine",
    warmup_steps=0.03,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,  # effective batch size 16 on one GPU
    max_length=1024,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=50,
    save_steps=50,
    load_best_model_at_end=True,
    metric_for_best_model="eval_loss",
    bf16=True,
    report_to="none",
    seed=42,
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=BASE_MODEL,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=data["train"],
    eval_dataset=data["validation"],
    peft_config=peft_config,
)
trainer.model.print_trainable_parameters()
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("adapters/taskflow-parser")  # writes the adapter weights and config only

Parts: to_prompt_completion makes the loss cover only the assistant's JSON; LoraConfig adapts every linear layer at rank 16 with scale 32 / 16 = 2; SFTConfig raises the learning rate to a LoRA value, evaluates and checkpoints every 50 steps, and restores the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss at the end; print_trainable_parameters() should report roughly half a percent for an 8B-class model; and save_model writes adapter_model.safetensors plus adapter_config.json, which records the base model it belongs to.

docs.title: Switch to QLoRA when the model does not fit
docs.text:
Only the model loading changes. TRL applies the quantization when it loads the model from the ID, and the LoRA layers stay in 16-bit.

# scripts/train_qlora.py: the same as train_lora.py except for these lines
import torch
from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig

quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(
    load_in_4bit=True,
    bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
    bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True,
    bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)

trainer = SFTTrainer(
    model=BASE_MODEL,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=data["train"],
    eval_dataset=data["validation"],
    peft_config=peft_config,
    quantization_config=quantization_config,  # requires the bitsandbytes package
)

Expect slower steps than LoRA on a 16-bit base, because every forward pass dequantizes the weights. Use QLoRA when memory is the constraint, not by default.

docs.title: Generate predictions and compare with the base model
docs.text:
To evaluate, load the base model, attach the adapter, and write the predictions file that eval_task_parser.py expects. Running the same script with none instead of an adapter path produces the base model's predictions.

# scripts/predict.py
"""Write test-set predictions for the base model, optionally with a LoRA adapter."""
import json
import os
import sys

import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

BASE_MODEL = os.environ["BASE_MODEL"]
adapter_dir, test_path, out_path = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3]

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map="auto")
if adapter_dir != "none":
    model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, adapter_dir)
model.eval()

with open(test_path, encoding="utf-8") as src, open(out_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
    for index, line in enumerate(src):
        messages = json.loads(line)["messages"][:-1]  # drop the gold answer
        inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
            messages, add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt"
        ).to(model.device)
        with torch.no_grad():
            output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=128, do_sample=False)
        new_tokens = output[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:]
        text = tokenizer.decode(new_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
        out.write(json.dumps({"index": index, "output": text}) + "\n")

python scripts/predict.py none data/test.jsonl preds/base.jsonl
python scripts/predict.py adapters/taskflow-parser data/test.jsonl preds/lora.jsonl
python scripts/eval_task_parser.py data/test.jsonl preds/base.jsonl preds/lora.jsonl

apply_chat_template uses the same chat template the trainer used, which matters: a model trained with one template and served with another often ignores what it learned. In Transformers 5 it returns a dictionary of tensors by default, hence **inputs. Greedy decoding (do_sample=False) makes runs repeatable.

docs.title: Merge the adapter, or serve it next to the base model
docs.text:
Merging gives a standalone model for runtimes that do not support adapters. Merge into the 16-bit base, never into a 4-bit one.

# scripts/merge_adapter.py
"""Fold the LoRA update into the base weights and save a standalone model."""
import os

import torch
from peft import PeftModel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer

BASE_MODEL = os.environ["BASE_MODEL"]

base = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL, dtype=torch.bfloat16)
merged = PeftModel.from_pretrained(base, "adapters/taskflow-parser").merge_and_unload()
merged.save_pretrained("models/taskflow-parser-merged")
AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(BASE_MODEL).save_pretrained("models/taskflow-parser-merged")

To keep adapters separate, start vLLM with the base model and register each adapter under a name:

# one base model in GPU memory, adapters selected per request by name
vllm serve "$BASE_MODEL" \
  --enable-lora \
  --lora-modules taskflow-parser=./adapters/taskflow-parser \
  --max-lora-rank 16

curl -s http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"model": "taskflow-parser", "temperature": 0,
       "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Today is 2026-11-16.\nFix the login page by Friday"}]}'

The TaskFlow API code from the previous lesson works unchanged: set AI_BASE_URL to the vLLM server's /v1 URL and TASK_PARSER_MODEL to taskflow-parser. --max-lora-rank must be at least the highest rank among the adapters; setting it much higher wastes memory. vLLM can also load adapters at runtime through an API, but its documentation warns that this is for trusted, isolated environments only.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Count trainable parameters and memory before renting hardware.
  • Start with plain LoRA on all linear layers, rank 16, alpha 32, and a learning rate around 2e-4; change one setting at a time.
  • Use a prompt-completion dataset so the loss covers only the answer.
  • Set max_length above your longest example and check how many examples would be truncated.
  • Keep the best checkpoint by validation loss, and judge it by task metrics on the held-out test set.
  • Run a general regression set and a safety set on every adapter.
  • Store the adapter with the exact base model ID and revision it was trained on; an adapter only works on that base.
  • Merge into a 16-bit base when you need a standalone model, and keep adapters separate when several features share one base.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The tuned model answers exactly like the base model. Detect: predictions are identical with and without the adapter; validation loss barely moved. Cause: the adapter was never loaded (a wrong path or a missing PeftModel.from_pretrained), the request used the base model's name instead of the adapter's, or the learning rate was a full fine-tuning value such as 2e-5. Fix: log which adapter served each request, assert that outputs differ on a smoke test, and use a LoRA learning rate.
  • JSON answers are cut off in the middle. Detect: truncated outputs cluster on long requests; the training data has examples longer than max_length. Cause: truncation dropped the end of long examples, so the model learned incomplete answers. Fix: measure token lengths, raise max_length or drop over-long examples, and set max_new_tokens high enough at inference.
  • Validation loss rises while training loss keeps falling. Detect: the curves diverge after the first epoch; test exact match drops for later checkpoints. Cause: overfitting a small dataset with too many epochs or too high a rank. Fix: keep the best checkpoint, reduce epochs, add data, or lower the rank and learning rate.
  • The server refuses to load the adapter. Detect: vLLM startup or load errors mentioning rank or shapes. Cause: the adapter rank exceeds --max-lora-rank, or the adapter was trained on a different base model or revision. Fix: set --max-lora-rank to the highest adapter rank, and pin the base model revision in both training and serving.
  • Quality drops after merging a QLoRA adapter. Detect: the merged model scores lower than the base plus adapter. Cause: the adapter was merged into the quantized 4-bit weights, adding rounding error. Fix: load the base in 16-bit, merge there, and re-quantize the merged model for serving if needed.
  • Other features get worse after the adapter ships. Detect: the general regression set or user feedback shows weaker summaries or chat after a merged model replaced the base. Cause: the merged weights now carry the narrow task everywhere. Fix: serve the adapter only for its feature (keep the base for everything else) or mix general examples into the training data.
  • Training crashes with out-of-memory errors. Detect: CUDA out-of-memory at the first steps or on long batches. Cause: batch size and max_length too large for the GPU, or a base model that does not fit in 16-bit. Fix: lower the per-device batch and raise gradient accumulation, keep gradient checkpointing on (TRL's default), shorten max_length, or switch to QLoRA.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning): Methods that train a small number of parameters while the base model stays frozen.
  • LoRA: Adds a trainable low-rank update (alpha/r) B A beside frozen linear layers.
  • Adapter: The saved LoRA weights and configuration, usable only with their base model.
  • Rank (r): The inner dimension of the LoRA matrices; sets capacity.
  • Alpha: The scale numerator; the update is multiplied by alpha / r (or alpha / sqrt(r) with rsLoRA).
  • Target modules: The layers that receive adapters; all-linear in PEFT covers every linear layer except the output head.
  • QLoRA: LoRA on a frozen base stored in 4-bit NF4, with double quantization and paged optimizers.
  • Merging: Adding the LoRA update into the base weights to produce a standalone model.
  • Multi-LoRA serving: One base model in memory serving many adapters chosen per request.
  • Completion-only loss: Computing the training loss only on the answer tokens, not the prompt.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using a full fine-tuning learning rate for LoRA and concluding that LoRA does not work.
  • Adapting only attention projections and compensating with a higher rank.
  • Believing a higher rank is always better; capacity should match the dataset, and higher ranks overfit small ones.
  • Training on the whole conversation, so the model spends capacity learning to repeat the system prompt.
  • Loading an adapter onto a different base model, or a different revision of the same one.
  • Merging a QLoRA adapter into 4-bit weights.
  • Judging an adapter by training loss instead of held-out task metrics.
  • Assuming QLoRA is free; it is slower per step than LoRA on a 16-bit base.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does full fine-tuning with Adam need about 16 bytes per parameter, and which of those bytes does LoRA avoid?
  2. Write the LoRA forward pass and explain why B is initialized to zero.
  3. A layer maps 4,096 inputs to 14,336 outputs. How many LoRA parameters does rank 32 add, and what fraction of the layer is that? (32 x (4,096 + 14,336) = 589,824, about 1% of 58,720,256.)
  4. What does alpha / r control, and what happens if you double r without changing alpha?
  5. Explain the three QLoRA techniques and the speed cost.
  6. Why does a prompt-completion dataset produce a better task parser than training on full conversations?
  7. When would you merge an adapter, and when keep it separate?
  8. Your adapter's outputs are identical to the base model's. List three possible causes.

• Hugging Face PEFT: LoRA developer guide

docs.title: Preference Tuning and Distillation
docs.text:
Supervised fine-tuning teaches a model what a good answer looks like. Preference tuning teaches it which of two plausible answers is better, and reinforcement methods let it improve against a score you can compute. Distillation goes the other way: it moves the behavior of a large, slow "teacher" model into a small, fast "student". This lesson covers the classic RLHF pipeline, Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) and the newer methods built on it, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards such as GRPO, and teacher-to-student distillation, with TRL code for the TaskFlow Assistant's meeting-notes summaries and task parser. Code was checked against trl 1.18 and peft 0.21 as of November 2026.

It builds on LoRA and PEFT in practice: every method here can train a LoRA adapter instead of the full model.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Many qualities users care about have no single correct answer. Two summaries of the same meeting can both be accurate while one is clearly more useful: it names owners, skips small talk, and stays short. Writing the perfect summary for every training example is slow and subjective; picking the better of two is fast and consistent. Preference methods turn those cheap comparisons into training signal, which is how chat models learned to be helpful in the first place.

Reinforcement methods go further when quality can be checked by code: a parsed task either matches the expected fields or it does not, a SQL query either returns the right rows or it does not. Training against such a check can push a model past the examples you could write by hand.

Distillation addresses the bill. A large model may do the TaskFlow tasks well but too slowly and expensively for every keystroke; a student a fraction of its size, trained on the teacher's outputs, can often keep most of the quality for that narrow task. Knowing which of these tools fits, and their failure modes (length bias, reward hacking, inherited mistakes), keeps a team from spending weeks on the wrong one.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• InstructGPT (OpenAI), 2022. Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback describes the three-stage pipeline (demonstrations for SFT, rankings for a reward model, reinforcement learning) and reports that outputs from the 1.3B InstructGPT model "are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters."
  • DPO (Stanford), 2023. Direct Preference Optimization shows that the RLHF objective can be solved "with only a simple classification loss," which is "stable, performant, and computationally lightweight, eliminating the need for sampling from the LM during fine-tuning."
  • Tulu 3 (Allen Institute for AI), 2024. Tulu 3 publishes a fully open post-training recipe that combines SFT, DPO, and a method it calls Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with data, code, and evaluations.
  • DeepSeekMath and DeepSeek-R1, 2024-2025. DeepSeekMath introduced Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), and DeepSeek-R1 shows that reasoning abilities "can be incentivized through pure reinforcement learning" on verifiable tasks and that the resulting reasoning patterns "can be systematically harnessed to guide and enhance the reasoning capabilities of smaller models", that is, distilled.
  • DistilBERT (Hugging Face), 2019. DistilBERT showed that distillation can "reduce the size of a BERT model by 40%, while retaining 97% of its language understanding capabilities and being 60% faster."
  • Amazon Bedrock Model Distillation. Bedrock's distillation feature generates responses from a chosen teacher for your prompts and fine-tunes a smaller student on them, the off-policy distillation pattern described below, as a managed service.

Popular tools and providers: Hugging Face TRL (DPOTrainer, KTOTrainer, RewardTrainer, GRPOTrainer, RLOOTrainer, and DistillationTrainer), verl, and OpenRLHF for open models; Microsoft Foundry (DPO and reinforcement fine-tuning), Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI (preference tuning and RL fine-tuning), and Amazon Bedrock (reinforcement fine-tuning and distillation) as managed services.

docs.title: Where preference tuning fits
docs.text:
A typical post-training stack runs in this order:

  1. SFT on demonstrations teaches the format and the task.
  2. Preference tuning on comparisons teaches which of the model's own plausible answers people prefer.
  3. Reinforcement learning against a reward model or a verifier improves further where quality can be scored.

Skipping step 1 rarely works: preference methods adjust the relative likelihood of answers the model can already produce. If the model never writes a three-bullet summary with owners, no amount of comparing two bad summaries will teach it.

docs.title: RLHF: the classic pipeline
docs.text:
Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), as InstructGPT used it, has three stages:

  1. Supervised fine-tuning on human-written demonstrations.
  2. Reward modeling. Labelers rank several model answers per prompt; a reward model learns a score so that preferred answers score higher. With the Bradley-Terry model, the probability that answer A beats answer B is sigmoid(r(A) - r(B)), and training maximizes that probability for the observed preferences.
  3. Policy optimization. The SFT model (now the "policy") generates answers, the reward model scores them, and an RL algorithm, usually PPO, updates the policy to raise the reward, minus a penalty beta x KL(policy || reference) that keeps it close to the SFT model.

The KL penalty is essential. A reward model is an imperfect proxy, and a policy optimized hard against it finds answers that score well without being good: reward hacking, such as very long or flattering answers. Staying near the reference model limits how far it can drift. The cost is complexity: PPO-based RLHF keeps four models busy (policy, frozen reference, reward model, and a value model that estimates expected reward), and it is sensitive to hyperparameters.

docs.title: DPO: preferences without the RL loop
docs.text:
DPO starts from the same objective (maximize reward, stay close to the reference) and shows that the optimal policy can be written in closed form, so the reward model and the RL loop disappear. What remains is a loss over preference pairs (prompt x, chosen y_w, rejected y_l):

loss = -log sigmoid( beta * [ (log p(y_w|x) - log p_ref(y_w|x))
                            - (log p(y_l|x) - log p_ref(y_l|x)) ] )

In words: raise the policy's probability of the chosen answer relative to the reference model, lower it for the rejected answer, and stop pushing once the margin is comfortable. beta controls how strongly the policy may move away from the reference; TRL's default is 0.1.

A worked example with beta = 0.1. At the start of training the policy equals the reference, both log-ratios are 0, and the loss is -log sigmoid(0) = log 2 = 0.693. Later, the chosen answer's log-ratio is +2.0 and the rejected one's is -1.0:

margin = 0.1 x (2.0 - (-1.0)) = 0.3
loss   = -log sigmoid(0.3) = -log 0.574 = 0.554

DPO needs only two models (policy and reference), no sampling during training, and ordinary supervised-style batches. In TRL, if you pass no reference model, the trainer uses the initial policy (the model as it was before DPO started), which with a LoRA adapter costs no extra copy. TRL logs rewards/chosen, rewards/rejected, rewards/margins, and rewards/accuracies (how often the chosen answer wins); accuracy near 100% after a few steps usually means the pairs are too easy or the model is memorizing.

Three known weaknesses shape how DPO is used:

  • Length bias. If people preferred longer answers in the data, DPO learns "longer is better". Check how often the chosen answer is longer before training.
  • Off-policy data. Pairs collected from a different model may describe answers your model would never produce. Pairs sampled from your own SFT model work better.
  • Falling likelihoods. The probabilities of both chosen and rejected answers can decrease while their gap grows. Adding an SFT term on the chosen answers (TRL accepts loss_type=["sigmoid", "sft"] with loss_weights) keeps the chosen answers likely.

docs.title: Newer preference methods
docs.text:
DPO started a family of variants. TRL includes several, with different maturity levels as of version 1.18:

Method Key idea Data In TRL IPO Replaces DPO's log-sigmoid with a squared loss to resist overfitting deterministic preferences Pairs DPOConfig(loss_type="ipo") KTO Learns from a binary "desirable or not" signal; "matches or exceeds" pairwise methods "at scales from 1B to 30B" Single answers with a label, such as thumbs up or down KTOTrainer (stable) ORPO Adds an odds-ratio penalty to the SFT loss, so SFT and preference alignment happen in one stage with no reference model Pairs ORPOTrainer (experimental) SimPO Uses the average log-probability as the implicit reward and adds a target margin; no reference model Pairs Experimental CPO trainer with loss_type="simpo"

KTO deserves attention for products like TaskFlow: a thumbs-up or thumbs-down on a single summary is far easier to collect than a careful side-by-side comparison. "Experimental" in TRL means the API may change between releases, so pin the version if you use those trainers.

docs.title: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards
docs.text:
When quality can be checked by code, the reward model can be replaced by the check itself. Tulu 3 calls this RLVR; DeepSeek used it with GRPO to train reasoning on math and code. For the TaskFlow parser the check is the evaluation logic: valid JSON, the right keys, correct fields.

GRPO is the most common algorithm for this. For each prompt it samples a group of answers (TRL's default is 8), scores each one, and uses the score relative to the group as the advantage:

advantage_i = (reward_i - mean(group rewards)) / std(group rewards)

rewards    1.00   0.75   0.25   0.00     mean 0.50, std 0.40
advantage  +1.26  +0.63  -0.63  -1.26    (population standard deviation)

Answers better than their siblings are reinforced and worse ones are discouraged, without a value model, which saves memory compared with PPO. Two consequences follow. If every answer in a group gets the same reward (all perfect or all failing), the advantages are zero and the prompt teaches nothing; TRL logs this as frac_reward_zero_std. And the policy will exploit any gap in the reward function, so the verifier must be as strict as the real requirement. TRL's GRPO defaults to beta=0.0 (no KL penalty against a reference model, so no reference copy in memory), and TRL's LoRA Without Regret guide reports that RL needs very little adapter capacity (ranks of 1-32).

Managed services offer the same idea under the name reinforcement fine-tuning: Microsoft Foundry scores samples with graders you define, Amazon Bedrock calls reward functions you write in AWS Lambda, and Google's Agent Platform trains a LoRA adapter "to maximize the reward."

docs.title: Distillation: teacher to student
docs.text:
Distillation trains a small student to imitate a large teacher. There are three practical forms:

  1. Logit (classic) distillation. Hinton et al. (2015) train the student to match the teacher's full probability distribution over outputs ("soft targets"), which carries more information than the single correct label. It needs the teacher's probabilities and, for language models, a shared vocabulary.
  2. Off-policy (sequence-level) distillation. The teacher writes answers for a set of prompts, a validator filters them, and the student is fine-tuned on the result with ordinary SFT. This works with any teacher behind an API, which is why managed services offer it: Bedrock's distillation generates teacher responses and fine-tunes the student, and Foundry supports distillation "through teacher-generated SFT data". Zephyr applied the same idea to preferences, using a teacher's rankings for "distilled DPO" with no human annotation (Tunstall et al., 2023).
  3. On-policy distillation. The student generates its own answers and the teacher's token distribution grades every token, as in Generalized Knowledge Distillation. This fixes the mismatch of off-policy distillation, where the student only ever learns from the teacher's perfect paths and never from recovering after its own mistakes. TRL's DistillationTrainer implements it; the teacher must be an open model that "must share the student's vocabulary."

Two cautions apply to every form. The student inherits the teacher's mistakes, so validate teacher outputs as strictly as you would human labels. And check the teacher provider's terms: Anthropic's commercial terms, for example, prohibit accessing the services "to build a competing product or service, including to train competing AI models." Distilling an open model you are licensed to use, or your own fine-tuned model, avoids that question.

docs.title: When distillation is worth it
docs.text:
The arithmetic is the same break-even reasoning as in when to fine-tune, with the teacher's labeling cost added to the one-off side. In relative units, if the teacher costs 1.0 per request and the student 0.1, each request saves 0.9; generating and validating 20,000 teacher answers costs 20,000, and training and evaluation another 30,000, so the project breaks even after about 55,000 requests (50,000 / 0.9). Distillation is worth it when:

  • the task is narrow and stable, so the student's smaller capacity is enough and you will not redo the work monthly;
  • volume is high or latency matters (a student also runs on cheaper hardware or on-device);
  • the student reaches your quality bar on the same held-out evaluation used for the teacher.

It is not worth it for low-volume features, for broad open-ended tasks where the student's capacity limits quality, or when the teacher's terms forbid it.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Method Why A clear correct answer per input SFT Simplest; preference methods add nothing Several valid answers, some better (summaries, tone) DPO on pairs from your SFT model Cheap comparisons become signal Only thumbs up or down feedback KTO Works with unpaired binary labels Quality can be checked by code (JSON fields, SQL results, tests) GRPO or managed reinforcement fine-tuning Optimizes the real requirement A large model works, but cost or latency is too high Distillation into a smaller student Keeps most of the quality for a narrow task No SFT baseline yet SFT first Preference methods refine existing behavior Subjective quality with no reliable labels or checks None yet Build the evaluation and labeling guide first

docs.title: Build DPO pairs from summary comparisons
docs.text:
TaskFlow's meeting-notes feature can show two candidate summaries and let users pick one. The script turns those logged choices into the conversational preference format TRL and the managed DPO services expect, drops ties and duplicates, and reports how often the chosen answer is longer, an early warning for length bias.

# scripts/build_pairs.py
"""Turn logged summary comparisons into DPO preference pairs and report label bias.

Each input line: {"prompt": [messages], "a": str, "b": str, "winner": "a" | "b" | "tie"}
Each output line: {"prompt": [messages], "chosen": [message], "rejected": [message]}
"""
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path


def main(source: str, target: str) -> None:
    pairs, skipped, chosen_longer = [], {"tie": 0, "identical": 0, "duplicate": 0}, 0
    seen = set()
    for line in Path(source).read_text(encoding="utf-8").splitlines():
        row = json.loads(line)
        if row["winner"] == "tie":
            skipped["tie"] += 1
            continue
        chosen, rejected = (row["a"], row["b"]) if row["winner"] == "a" else (row["b"], row["a"])
        if chosen.strip() == rejected.strip():
            skipped["identical"] += 1
            continue
        key = (json.dumps(row["prompt"]), chosen, rejected)
        if key in seen:
            skipped["duplicate"] += 1
            continue
        seen.add(key)
        chosen_longer += len(chosen) > len(rejected)
        pairs.append({
            "prompt": row["prompt"],
            "chosen": [{"role": "assistant", "content": chosen}],
            "rejected": [{"role": "assistant", "content": rejected}],
        })

    with open(target, "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        for pair in pairs:
            f.write(json.dumps(pair, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
    print(f"pairs written: {len(pairs)}  skipped: {skipped}")
    # Preference data often rewards length; DPO will learn that bias if it is there.
    print(f"chosen answer is longer in {chosen_longer / max(len(pairs), 1):.0%} of pairs")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

On a 12-line sample file:

pairs written: 8  skipped: {'tie': 2, 'identical': 1, 'duplicate': 1}
chosen answer is longer in 62% of pairs

A share well above half means raters lean toward longer summaries. Decide whether that is a real preference or a rater habit before DPO amplifies it; options include rebalancing pairs or adding a length rule to the labeling guide.

docs.title: Train with DPO on top of the SFT model
docs.text:
DPO starts from the SFT model, here a merged SFT checkpoint whose path comes from configuration, and trains a new LoRA adapter on the pairs.

# scripts/train_dpo.py
"""Preference-tune the meeting-summary model with DPO and a fresh LoRA adapter."""
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import DPOConfig, DPOTrainer

SFT_MODEL = os.environ["SFT_MODEL"]  # path or ID of the SFT model, from configuration

pairs = load_dataset("json", data_files="data/pairs.jsonl", split="train")
splits = pairs.train_test_split(test_size=0.1, seed=42)

args = DPOConfig(
    output_dir="runs/summary-dpo",
    beta=0.1,  # how far the policy may move from the reference
    loss_type=["sigmoid", "sft"],  # DPO plus an SFT term on the chosen answers
    loss_weights=[1.0, 0.2],
    learning_rate=1e-5,  # a LoRA value; TRL's default of 1e-6 suits full fine-tuning
    num_train_epochs=1,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    max_length=1024,
    eval_strategy="steps",
    eval_steps=50,
    bf16=True,
    report_to="none",
)

trainer = DPOTrainer(
    model=SFT_MODEL,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=splits["train"],
    eval_dataset=splits["test"],
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("adapters/summary-dpo")

Watch rewards/margins grow and rewards/accuracies rise on the evaluation split, but judge the result with a summary evaluation (for example a rubric scored by people or by an LLM judge), not by the training metrics. The same pairs format, with input, preferred_output, and non_preferred_output field names instead, is what Microsoft Foundry's managed DPO expects.

docs.title: Write a verifiable reward
docs.text:
The reward function scores a parser answer between 0 and 1. TRL passes it the completions plus every extra dataset column, so a ground_truth column carries the gold task.

# scripts/rewards.py
"""A verifiable reward for the TaskFlow task parser, usable by TRL's GRPOTrainer.

TRL calls reward functions with the generated completions plus every extra
dataset column as a keyword argument; here the dataset has a "ground_truth"
column holding the gold task as a JSON string.
"""
import json

FIELDS = ("title", "due_date", "priority")


def _text(completion) -> str:
    # Conversational datasets produce [{"role": "assistant", "content": ...}].
    return completion[0]["content"] if isinstance(completion, list) else completion


def task_reward(completions, ground_truth, **kwargs) -> list[float]:
    rewards = []
    for completion, gold_json in zip(completions, ground_truth):
        try:
            task = json.loads(_text(completion))
        except json.JSONDecodeError:
            rewards.append(0.0)  # not JSON at all
            continue
        if not isinstance(task, dict) or set(task) != set(FIELDS):
            rewards.append(0.1)  # JSON, wrong shape
            continue
        gold = json.loads(gold_json)
        title_ok = " ".join(str(task["title"]).lower().split()) == " ".join(gold["title"].lower().split())
        hits = [title_ok, task["due_date"] == gold["due_date"], task["priority"] == gold["priority"]]
        rewards.append(0.25 + 0.25 * sum(hits))  # 0.25 for valid shape, up to 1.0
    return rewards


if __name__ == "__main__":
    gold = json.dumps({"title": "Fix the login page", "due_date": "2026-11-20", "priority": "high"})
    samples = [
        '{"title": "Fix the login page", "due_date": "2026-11-20", "priority": "high"}',
        '{"title": "Fix login page", "due_date": "2026-11-20", "priority": "high"}',
        '{"title": "Fix the login page", "due_date": null}',
        "Sure! I created the task for you.",
        [{"role": "assistant", "content": '{"title": "fix the LOGIN page", "due_date": "2026-11-21", "priority": "high"}'}],
    ]
    for sample, reward in zip(samples, task_reward(samples, [gold] * len(samples))):
        print(f"{reward:.2f}  {str(sample)[:70]}")

Running the self-test:

1.00  {"title": "Fix the login page", "due_date": "2026-11-20", "priority":
0.75  {"title": "Fix login page", "due_date": "2026-11-20", "priority": "hig
0.10  {"title": "Fix the login page", "due_date": null}
0.00  Sure! I created the task for you.
0.75  [{'role': 'assistant', 'content': '{"title": "fix the LOGIN page", "du

The partial credit is deliberate: if every early sample scored 0 or 1, most groups would have identical rewards and teach nothing. Test a reward function like this one on correct, partly correct, and adversarial answers before training, exactly as the managed services advise for graders.

docs.title: Train the parser with GRPO
docs.text:
The training script reuses the SFT splits: the prompt is the system and user messages, and the gold answer becomes the ground_truth column.

# scripts/train_grpo.py
"""Reinforcement fine-tuning of the task parser with GRPO and the verifiable reward."""
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from rewards import task_reward
from trl import GRPOConfig, GRPOTrainer

SFT_MODEL = os.environ["SFT_MODEL"]  # start from SFT so most samples are already valid JSON


def to_rl_row(row: dict) -> dict:
    *prompt, answer = row["messages"]
    return {"prompt": prompt, "ground_truth": answer["content"]}


train = load_dataset("json", data_files="data/train.jsonl", split="train")
train = train.map(to_rl_row, remove_columns=["messages"])

args = GRPOConfig(
    output_dir="runs/parser-grpo",
    num_generations=8,  # answers sampled per prompt; advantages are relative within the group
    max_completion_length=128,  # the JSON answer is short
    learning_rate=5e-5,  # the LoRA value used in TRL's LoRA Without Regret guide
    per_device_train_batch_size=8,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,  # 32 answers per step, a multiple of num_generations
    num_train_epochs=1,
    logging_steps=5,
    bf16=True,
    report_to="none",
)

trainer = GRPOTrainer(
    model=SFT_MODEL,
    reward_funcs=task_reward,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=train,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=8, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("adapters/parser-grpo")

Watch the logged reward rise and frac_reward_zero_std stay low. If the reward climbs while the held-out evaluation does not improve, the model has found a way to score without doing the task; tighten the reward function. Generation dominates GRPO's run time, and TRL can hand sampling to vLLM (use_vllm=True) to speed it up.

docs.title: Distill off-policy: let a teacher label prompts
docs.text:
This script asks a teacher model behind an OpenAI-compatible endpoint to answer TaskFlow prompts and keeps only answers that pass validation. The endpoint and model ID come from configuration; the output is ready for the SFT scripts from the earlier lessons.

# scripts/generate_teacher_data.py
"""Off-policy distillation, step 1: have a teacher model label prompts, keep only valid answers.

Environment: TEACHER_BASE_URL, TEACHER_API_KEY, TEACHER_MODEL (all from configuration).
Input: prompts.jsonl with {"messages": [system, user]} per line.
Output: SFT-ready chat JSONL with the teacher's answer appended as the assistant turn.
"""
import json
import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url=os.environ["TEACHER_BASE_URL"], api_key=os.environ["TEACHER_API_KEY"])
TEACHER = os.environ["TEACHER_MODEL"]
FIELDS = {"title", "due_date", "priority"}


def valid(answer: str) -> bool:
    try:
        task = json.loads(answer)
    except json.JSONDecodeError:
        return False
    return isinstance(task, dict) and set(task) == FIELDS and task["priority"] in ("low", "medium", "high")


def main(prompts_path: str, out_path: str) -> None:
    kept = dropped = 0
    with open(prompts_path, encoding="utf-8") as src, open(out_path, "w", encoding="utf-8") as out:
        for line in src:
            messages = json.loads(line)["messages"]
            reply = client.chat.completions.create(model=TEACHER, messages=messages, temperature=0)
            answer = (reply.choices[0].message.content or "").strip()
            if not valid(answer):
                dropped += 1  # never train the student on answers that fail validation
                continue
            out.write(json.dumps({"messages": messages + [{"role": "assistant", "content": answer}]}) + "\n")
            kept += 1
    print(f"kept {kept}, dropped {dropped} invalid teacher answers")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main(sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2])

Against a local stub server that returns one non-JSON answer out of four, the script printed kept 3, dropped 1 invalid teacher answers. For a real run, also compare a sample of kept answers with human labels, because a valid-looking answer can still have the wrong date; where gold labels exist, keep only teacher answers that match them. For large prompt sets, the provider's batch API (see prompt caching and batch processing) is usually cheaper than one request at a time.

docs.title: Distill on-policy with TRL
docs.text:
When the teacher is an open model you can load, TRL's DistillationTrainer lets the student generate and the teacher grade every token.

# scripts/train_distill.py
"""On-policy distillation: the student writes answers, the teacher's token probabilities grade them."""
import os

from datasets import load_dataset
from peft import LoraConfig
from trl import DistillationConfig, DistillationTrainer

STUDENT_MODEL = os.environ["STUDENT_MODEL"]  # the small model you will serve
TEACHER_MODEL = os.environ["TEACHER_MODEL"]  # a larger open model with the same vocabulary

prompts = load_dataset("json", data_files="data/train.jsonl", split="train")
prompts = prompts.map(lambda row: {"prompt": row["messages"][:-1]}, remove_columns=["messages"])

args = DistillationConfig(
    output_dir="runs/parser-distill",
    beta=0.5,  # 0.0 forward KL, 0.5 Jensen-Shannon, 1.0 reverse KL (the default)
    max_completion_length=128,
    learning_rate=1e-5,
    per_device_train_batch_size=4,
    gradient_accumulation_steps=4,
    bf16=True,
    report_to="none",
)

trainer = DistillationTrainer(
    model=STUDENT_MODEL,
    teacher_model=TEACHER_MODEL,
    args=args,
    train_dataset=prompts,
    peft_config=LoraConfig(r=16, lora_alpha=32, target_modules="all-linear", task_type="CAUSAL_LM"),
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model("adapters/parser-distilled")

Teacher and student are both in memory during training, so this needs more GPU memory than SFT; the payoff is a student that has practiced on its own outputs. Evaluate the student with the same eval_task_parser.py used for the teacher and the baseline.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run SFT first; use preference and reinforcement methods to refine behavior the model can already produce.
  • Collect preference pairs from your own model's outputs, with a written rubric for raters, and check the data for length bias before training.
  • Use KTO when you only have thumbs-up and thumbs-down feedback.
  • Make reward functions strict, give partial credit where it helps learning, and test them on adversarial answers before training.
  • Judge every method by the held-out task evaluation, not by training rewards or margins.
  • Validate teacher outputs as strictly as human labels before distilling, and confirm the teacher's license or terms allow it.
  • Keep a reference to the starting model's scores so regressions on other behavior are visible.
  • Pin the TRL version when you use trainers marked experimental.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Summaries get longer after DPO. Detect: average summary length jumps after the release; reviewers call them verbose. Cause: raters preferred longer answers, and DPO learned length as the signal. Fix: measure the chosen-longer share, rebalance pairs, add brevity to the rubric, or try a length-normalized method such as SimPO.
  • Training rewards climb but the evaluation gets worse. Detect: GRPO's reward or DPO's rewards/accuracies rise while held-out exact match falls. Cause: reward hacking (the policy exploits a loophole in the verifier) or memorized preference pairs. Fix: inspect high-reward samples, close the loophole, add a KL penalty (beta) or fewer steps, and select checkpoints by the evaluation.
  • GRPO training does not move. Detect: frac_reward_zero_std stays high and the reward is flat. Cause: prompts are so easy or so hard that every sampled answer gets the same reward. Fix: filter prompts to ones the model sometimes gets right, add partial credit, or raise sampling temperature.
  • Chosen answers become less likely during DPO. Detect: rewards/chosen goes negative even though margins grow; output quality drops. Cause: DPO only pushes the gap, so both likelihoods can fall. Fix: add an SFT term (loss_type=["sigmoid", "sft"]), lower the learning rate, or use pairs sampled from the current model.
  • The distilled student repeats the teacher's errors. Detect: the student fails the same evaluation cases as the teacher, plus more. Cause: unvalidated teacher outputs were used as labels. Fix: validate outputs, keep only answers that match gold labels where available, and review a sample by hand.
  • The student is good on test prompts but brittle on real traffic. Detect: the canary shows more fallbacks than the offline evaluation predicted. Cause: off-policy distillation never showed the student how to recover from its own mistakes, and the prompts did not cover real phrasing. Fix: add real prompts and use on-policy distillation or a GRPO stage with the verifier.
  • Legal review blocks the distilled model. Detect: a terms-of-service review flags the training data source. Cause: teacher outputs came from a provider whose terms prohibit training competing models. Fix: check terms before generating data, and prefer open teachers or models you own.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Preference tuning: Training from comparisons or ratings of model outputs rather than from target answers.
  • RLHF: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: SFT, a reward model from rankings, then policy optimization.
  • Reward model: A model that scores answers, trained so preferred answers score higher.
  • KL penalty: A term that keeps the trained policy close to a reference model.
  • Reward hacking: Finding outputs that score highly without meeting the real goal.
  • DPO: Direct Preference Optimization, a classification-style loss on preference pairs with no separate reward model or RL loop.
  • KTO: A preference method that learns from single answers labelled desirable or undesirable.
  • GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization; scores a group of samples per prompt and uses within-group relative advantages.
  • RLVR: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards computed by code.
  • Distillation: Training a smaller student to imitate a larger teacher.
  • On-policy distillation: The student generates and the teacher grades the student's own outputs token by token.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Running DPO on a base model that cannot yet produce the desired answers.
  • Treating rewards/accuracies or the GRPO reward curve as proof of better quality.
  • Collecting preference pairs from a different model and expecting them to fit your model.
  • Writing a lenient reward function and assuming the model will not find the loophole.
  • Believing preference tuning adds knowledge; like SFT, it shapes behavior.
  • Distilling from a teacher whose terms prohibit it.
  • Assuming a distilled student matches the teacher on everything; it matches on the distribution it was trained on, at best.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the three stages of RLHF and why the KL penalty is needed.
  2. What does DPO remove from the RLHF pipeline, and what does it keep?
  3. With beta = 0.2, the chosen log-ratio is +1.0 and the rejected one is -1.5. What is the DPO margin and loss? (0.2 x 2.5 = 0.5; loss = -log sigmoid(0.5), about 0.474.)
  4. When would you choose KTO over DPO?
  5. A GRPO group gets rewards 1, 1, 1, 1. What are the advantages, and what does that mean for training?
  6. Why does a verifiable reward need partial credit and adversarial testing?
  7. Compare off-policy and on-policy distillation, including what each needs from the teacher.
  8. Distillation costs 40,000 units one-off and saves 0.8 units per request. At 2,000 requests a day, when does it break even? (50,000 requests, 25 days.)
