docs.title: Choosing Models and Providers
docs.text:
TaskFlow has four AI features with very different needs: parsing a sentence into a task must be fast and cheap, project Q&A must cite the right documents, meeting summaries read long notes, and the task agent plans several tool calls where a mistake creates real tasks. No single model is the best choice for all four. This lesson shows how to choose: a decision matrix covering capability, latency, cost, context size, and data policy; model tiers and routing between them; evaluating candidates on your own cases; lock-in and the choice between closed and open-weight models; and the data-retention and BAA terms that rule some providers out before quality is even measured.

Model names below are a snapshot from the providers' official pages in November 2026 and will age quickly. The method does not: read the current lineup from each provider's model list, keep model IDs in configuration, and let your evaluation set decide.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The model is usually the biggest lever on an AI feature's quality, speed, and cost at the same time, and the levers pull in different directions. Within one provider's lineup, the strongest model can cost many times more per token than the smallest and respond noticeably more slowly. Using the strongest model everywhere makes high-volume features expensive and slow; using the cheapest everywhere quietly lowers quality where it matters.

The choice also has a long tail. Prompts get tuned to one model's habits, code starts depending on provider-only features, and contracts (data retention, a business associate agreement for health data, data residency) decide which providers are allowed at all. Providers retire models and features on their own schedule, so a choice made without an evaluation set and a migration path becomes an emergency later.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI's model guidance. The models page (November 2026) recommends GPT-6 Astra as the flagship for complex reasoning and coding, GPT-6.1 Sol to balance intelligence and cost, and GPT-6 Luna for cost-sensitive, high-volume workloads, all with a context window of about 1 million tokens.
  • Anthropic's comparison table. The models overview lists Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 with "moderate" comparative latency for demanding reasoning and agentic work, Claude Sonnet 5.5 as "fast" with the best balance of speed and intelligence, and Claude Haiku 5.5 as "fastest" for high-volume classification, extraction, and routing.
  • Features retire, not only models. OpenAI's deprecations page shows the Assistants API shut down on August 26, 2026, and reusable prompt objects (/v1/prompts) shutting down on November 30, 2026, with the advice to "move prompt content into your application code".
  • API behavior changes. Anthropic's API versions page records that version 2026-10-21 removed the temperature, top_p, and top_k request parameters; requests that send them return 400 on every model.
  • Data use depends on the tier, not just the provider. The Gemini API terms say content sent to unpaid services (Google AI Studio, the free quota) is used to improve Google's products and may be read by human reviewers, while paid services do not use prompts or responses to improve products.

Popular tools and providers: direct APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google; the same or similar models through cloud platforms (Microsoft Foundry, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, formerly Vertex AI); gateways such as LiteLLM and OpenRouter; open-weight models served by inference providers or yourself.

docs.title: Start from the task, not the model
docs.text:
Before comparing models, write a short task card for each feature. The card turns "which model is best?" into questions that have answers:

Question Parse task Project Q&A Meeting summary Task agent Input size One sentence Docs excerpt plus question Up to 2 hours of notes Growing transcript Output Strict JSON Text with citations 300-600 words Tool calls Latency budget Under 2 s First token under 2 s Streamed Seconds per step Volume High Medium Medium Low Cost of a mistake Low (user edits the draft) Medium (wrong answer) Medium High (real changes) Data User text Private project docs Private notes Private tasks

The categories of models and capabilities are described in model types and capabilities; this page is about choosing among the language models that fit.

docs.title: The decision matrix
docs.text:
Dimension What to measure Where to find it Watch out for Capability Pass rate on your own cases; required modalities, tools, structured output, reasoning effort settings Your evaluation set; provider model pages Public benchmarks measure other tasks Latency Time to first token, output speed, p95 for your prompt sizes Your own measurements; providers' comparative latency labels Long inputs and reasoning raise time to first token Cost Cost per successful task, not per token Pricing pages, as ratios between candidates Output and reasoning tokens often dominate; caching and batch change the math Context size Input you really send; maximum output Model pages (context window, max output) A large window is not a reason to send everything Data policy Training use, retention, zero-retention options, BAA, region Providers' data and terms pages Free tiers and some features have different terms

Capability is the one dimension you cannot read from a page. Two models with similar benchmark scores can differ sharply on TaskFlow's JSON schema, citation style, or tool-calling behavior, which is why every decision below runs through the evaluation set.

Cost needs one more step than reading a price list. A cheaper model that fails one case in five and triggers a retry or an escalation may cost more per successful task than a mid-tier model that passes almost every case. Compare cost per passing case, in relative units against the model you use today.

docs.title: The current lineups (November 2026)
docs.text:
Each provider describes its own tiers. Summarized from the official model pages:

Provider Strongest tier Balanced tier Fast, high-volume tier Context window Source OpenAI GPT-6 Astra GPT-6.1 Sol; GPT-6.1 Terra (fast, efficient) GPT-6 Luna About 1.05M tokens, 128K output Models Anthropic Claude Fable 5.2; Claude Opus 5.5 Claude Sonnet 5.5 Claude Haiku 5.5 1M tokens, 128K output Models overview Google Gemini 4 Carbon Gemini 4 Argon (efficient frontier reasoning) Gemini 4 Hydrogen; Flash and Flash-Lite models 1M tokens Gemini models

Treat this table as a dated example. Production code reads model IDs from configuration (see calling model APIs from a backend), and a daily job checks each configured ID against the providers' models endpoints, which report lifecycle data: OpenAI's shutdown_date, and Anthropic's lifecycle (active, deprecated, or retired), deprecated_at, and retires_at.

docs.title: Model tiers and routing
docs.text:
Most applications settle on two or three tiers rather than one model:

  • Fast tier for short, well-specified, high-volume work: parsing, classification, extraction, routing.
  • Standard tier for most generation: answers, summaries, drafts.
  • Deep tier for multi-step reasoning and agentic work where errors are expensive. Many models also expose a reasoning-effort setting (OpenAI lists levels from none or low up to max on its current models), which acts as a tier dial within one model; how to prompt reasoning models and set thinking budgets is covered in reasoning models and thinking.

Routing then decides which tier serves a request. The simplest and most predictable router is a table from feature to tier, as described in the routing section of model types and capabilities. A cascade adds one rule: try the cheaper tier, validate the output (schema, citations present, tool arguments valid), and escalate to the next tier only when validation fails.

The cascade's economics are easy to estimate. If the fast tier costs a tenth of the standard tier per request and passes validation 85% of the time, the average cost is 0.1 + 0.15 x 1.0 = 0.25 of always using the standard tier, a 75% saving, paid for with extra latency on the 15% of requests that run twice. The cascade only works when validation can actually detect a bad answer; for open-ended text where "bad" is subtle, route by feature instead.

docs.title: Evaluating candidates
docs.text:
Selection is a funnel. Apply the hard constraints first, because no quality score can justify sending health data to a provider without a BAA. Then run the same evaluation set against every remaining candidate, then check latency and cost among the ones that pass the quality bar.

The evaluation set is the most valuable artifact in this process: a few hundred real, anonymized TaskFlow cases per feature with graders (exact field checks for parsed tasks, citation checks for Q&A, rubric-based LLM judges for summaries). Building it is covered in building evaluation sets, judges in LLM-as-judge and automated evals, and running it on every prompt or model change in evals in CI and regression testing. With that set, comparing a new model takes minutes instead of a week of anecdotes, and the result is the same table every time: pass rate, p50 and p95 latency, and cost per passing case.

Two practical rules keep evaluations honest. Run candidates on identical prompts first, then give each candidate a short prompt-tuning pass, because a prompt written for one model can understate another. And re-run the evaluation when a provider updates a model behind an alias: the name stays, the behavior may not.

docs.title: Lock-in, and open versus closed models
docs.text:
Lock-in is rarely about the model ID; that is one line of configuration. It comes from the layers underneath:

  • API shape. Request formats, streaming events, error types, and usage fields differ by provider. An internal adapter (as in calling model APIs from a backend) confines them to one module. Some providers offer OpenAI-compatible endpoints (Google documents one for the Gemini API), which helps with basic calls but not with provider-specific features.
  • Prompts. Prompts drift toward one model's habits. Keeping them in the repository (as OpenAI now recommends for production prompts) and pairing them with an evaluation set is what makes a switch a measured change.
  • Provider-only features. Stored conversations, background responses, hosted prompts, specific caching modes, and batch formats are useful but provider-shaped, and they retire: the Assistants API, reusable prompt objects, and OpenAI's Evals dashboard (read-only from November 30, 2026, with a recommendation to migrate to Promptfoo) all changed during 2026. Wrap them, and know what you would do without them.
  • API versions. Parameters can disappear, as temperature, top_p, and top_k did in Anthropic's 2026-10-21 API version. Code that depends on sampling settings for correctness is more fragile than code that validates outputs.
  • Contracts. Data-processing terms, a BAA, and residency commitments take weeks to put in place, so a second provider for health data needs its paperwork before it can be a fallback.

Open-weight models change the trade-off rather than remove it. You can call them through hosted inference providers (an API like any other, with that provider's terms) or serve them yourself, which gives control over the data path, the model version, and capacity at the price of running GPUs, scaling, and monitoring. They are attractive when data must stay on infrastructure you control, when a fixed model version matters for years, or when steady high volume makes owned capacity cheaper than per-token pricing. Closed hosted models usually lead on the hardest tasks and need no operations. Serving open models is covered in depth in serving open models, local experimentation in running models locally, and the cost crossover in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: Data retention, training use, and BAAs
docs.text:
The table summarizes each offering's official data pages as checked in November 2026. It is a starting point for a review with whoever owns privacy and contracts, not legal advice; terms change, and features inside one API can have their own retention. Privacy engineering in depth is covered in privacy, PII and data retention.

Offering Used for training? Retention by default Zero-retention option HIPAA and BAA Source OpenAI API No, unless you opt in (since March 1, 2023) Abuse-monitoring logs up to 30 days; Responses API application state 30 days unless store: false Zero Data Retention or Modified Abuse Monitoring, after approval BAA-eligible endpoints under a Business Associate and Healthcare Addendum Data controls Anthropic Claude API Not without your express permission Per Anthropic's commercial retention policy; features that store data document their own retention, and some models require 30-day retention ZDR by arrangement with Anthropic HIPAA readiness with a signed BAA, enabled in the Claude Console, for supported features API and data retention Gemini API, unpaid (AI Studio, free quota) Used to improve Google products; human review possible Per the terms No Not mentioned in the terms; do not send sensitive data Gemini API terms Gemini API, paid Not used to improve products Logged for a limited period for abuse detection No Not mentioned in the terms Gemini API terms Google Cloud Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) Not without permission (training restriction) Some prompt logging for abuse monitoring Zero retention possible with specific customer actions Google Cloud BAA for covered products Zero data retention, HIPAA Microsoft Foundry (models sold by Azure, including OpenAI models) Not used to train foundation models without permission; not available to OpenAI or other model providers Abuse monitoring; data at rest in the customer's geography Approved customers can modify abuse monitoring Covered under Microsoft's terms; check the product terms Data, privacy, and security Amazon Bedrock Model providers cannot access prompts or completions See the Bedrock documentation See the Bedrock documentation Check AWS HIPAA-eligible services Data protection

Three consequences for TaskFlow:

  • Turn off what you do not need. store: false on OpenAI's Responses API avoids 30 days of application state when TaskFlow keeps its own conversation history.
  • Never use a free tier for user data. A developer's AI Studio key in production silently changes the data terms for every request.
  • Fallbacks inherit the strictest requirement. If a feature processes health information, every route in its fallback list needs a BAA and the matching configuration, or the fallback is not allowed for that feature.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Decision Choose When One provider or several One provider with tiers Most teams; simpler contracts and keys; fallback within the provider A second provider Availability matters more than identical behavior, and the second is evaluated and contracted One model or tiers One model Low volume, one feature, or no evaluation set yet Tiers with routing Several features with different cost and latency needs Direct API or cloud platform Cloud platform (Foundry, Bedrock, Agent Platform) Existing cloud contracts, regional processing, private networking, consolidated billing Direct API Newest features first, simpler setup Closed or open-weight Closed hosted Hardest tasks, no GPU operations Open-weight (hosted or self-served) Data must stay on your infrastructure, a frozen model version, steady high volume

Do not choose by leaderboard position or by the newest release alone, and do not switch models in production without running the evaluation set. Do not add a cascade where the validator cannot tell a good answer from a bad one.

docs.title: Tiers from configuration and a cascade
docs.text:
// src/ai/tiers.ts
// Model tiers from configuration, a feature-to-tier table, and a cascade that
// escalates to a stronger tier only when the cheaper answer fails validation.
export type Tier = "fast" | "standard" | "deep";
export type Feature = "parse-task" | "project-qa" | "meeting-summary" | "agent-plan";

export interface TierModel {
  provider: "openai" | "anthropic" | "google";
  model: string;
}

// MODEL_FAST="openai:<model id>", MODEL_STANDARD=..., MODEL_DEEP=...
export function loadTiers(env: NodeJS.ProcessEnv = process.env): Record<Tier, TierModel> {
  const parse = (name: string): TierModel => {
    const value = env[name];
    const [provider, ...rest] = (value ?? "").split(":");
    const model = rest.join(":");
    if (!model || !["openai", "anthropic", "google"].includes(provider ?? "")) {
      throw new Error(`${name} must look like "openai:<model id>"`);
    }
    return { provider: provider as TierModel["provider"], model };
  };
  return { fast: parse("MODEL_FAST"), standard: parse("MODEL_STANDARD"), deep: parse("MODEL_DEEP") };
}

// Start each feature on the cheapest tier that passed its evaluation set.
export const FEATURE_TIER: Record<Feature, Tier> = {
  "parse-task": "fast", // short input, strict schema, high volume
  "project-qa": "standard", // retrieval answers with citations
  "meeting-summary": "standard", // long input, moderate reasoning
  "agent-plan": "deep", // multi-step tool use, mistakes are costly
};

const NEXT: Record<Tier, Tier | null> = { fast: "standard", standard: "deep", deep: null };

// Cascade: try the feature's tier; if the output fails validation, escalate once per tier.
export async function runWithCascade<T>(
  feature: Feature,
  call: (tier: Tier) => Promise<string>,
  validate: (output: string) => T | null,
  onEscalate?: (from: Tier, to: Tier) => void,
): Promise<{ value: T; tier: Tier }> {
  for (let tier: Tier | null = FEATURE_TIER[feature]; tier; tier = NEXT[tier]) {
    const value = validate(await call(tier));
    if (value !== null) return { value, tier };
    const next = NEXT[tier];
    if (next) onEscalate?.(tier, next);
  }
  throw new Error(`No tier produced a valid ${feature} result`);
}
  • The environment names the provider and model per tier, so moving the standard tier to another provider is a configuration change plus an evaluation run.
  • onEscalate feeds a metric: a rising escalation rate for a feature means the fast tier no longer fits it (or a prompt change broke it).
  • The call function is the adapter from calling model APIs from a backend, so retries and fallback still apply inside each tier.

docs.title: Comparing candidates on TaskFlow cases
docs.text:
// scripts/compare-candidates.ts
// Summarize an evaluation run of several candidate models on the same TaskFlow
// cases: pass rate, latency percentiles, and cost per passing case (relative units).
export interface CaseResult {
  candidate: string; // e.g. "openai:<model id>"
  caseId: string;
  passed: boolean; // from the grader (exact fields, schema, or an LLM judge)
  latencyMs: number;
  inputTokens: number;
  outputTokens: number;
}

// Relative price per token, normalized so the current model's input price is 1.
export interface RelativePrice {
  input: number;
  output: number;
}

export function percentile(values: number[], p: number): number {
  if (values.length === 0) return NaN;
  const sorted = [...values].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const rank = Math.ceil((p / 100) * sorted.length) - 1; // nearest-rank method
  return sorted[Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.max(0, rank))]!;
}

export interface CandidateSummary {
  candidate: string;
  cases: number;
  passRate: number;
  p50Ms: number;
  p95Ms: number;
  costPerPass: number; // relative units: lower is cheaper
}

export function summarize(results: CaseResult[], prices: Record<string, RelativePrice>): CandidateSummary[] {
  const byCandidate = Map.groupBy(results, (r) => r.candidate);
  return [...byCandidate].map(([candidate, rows]) => {
    const price = prices[candidate];
    if (!price) throw new Error(`No relative price for ${candidate}`);
    const passes = rows.filter((r) => r.passed).length;
    const cost = rows.reduce((sum, r) => sum + r.inputTokens * price.input + r.outputTokens * price.output, 0);
    return {
      candidate,
      cases: rows.length,
      passRate: passes / rows.length,
      p50Ms: percentile(rows.map((r) => r.latencyMs), 50),
      p95Ms: percentile(rows.map((r) => r.latencyMs), 95),
      costPerPass: passes === 0 ? Infinity : cost / passes,
    };
  });
}

// The cheapest candidate that meets every bar wins; ties go to lower p95 latency.
export function pick(
  summaries: CandidateSummary[],
  bar: { minPassRate: number; maxP95Ms: number },
): CandidateSummary | undefined {
  return summaries
    .filter((s) => s.passRate >= bar.minPassRate && s.p95Ms <= bar.maxP95Ms)
    .sort((a, b) => a.costPerPass - b.costPerPass || a.p95Ms - b.p95Ms)[0];
}

Relative prices keep the comparison stable when list prices change: set the current model's input price to 1 and express the others as multiples read from the pricing pages on the day of the comparison. Map.groupBy needs Node 21 or later (the section's examples use Node 24).

Running the summary on a synthetic set of results (made-up numbers, 100 cases per candidate, used only to show the shape of the output) with a bar of 90% pass rate and 2.5 seconds p95:

candidate   cases  passRate  p50Ms  p95Ms  costPerPass
A-large     100    0.96      2388   2928   10938
B-medium    100    0.94      1194   1464   2181
C-small     100    0.81      547    682    247
picked: B-medium

The large model is best on quality but misses the latency bar, and the small one is far cheaper but fails too many cases, so the medium model wins for this feature. A different feature, with a different bar, can pick differently from the same run.

docs.title: Watching model lifecycles
docs.text:
// scripts/check-model-lifecycle.ts
// Daily job: warn when a configured model is deprecated or has a shutdown date.
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { loadTiers } from "../src/ai/tiers.js";

const WARN_DAYS = 60;

function daysUntil(date: string | number | null | undefined): number | null {
  if (date === null || date === undefined) return null;
  const ms = typeof date === "number" ? date * 1000 : Date.parse(date);
  return Math.round((ms - Date.now()) / 86_400_000);
}

export async function checkLifecycle(): Promise<string[]> {
  const warnings: string[] = [];
  const openai = new OpenAI();
  const anthropic = new Anthropic();

  for (const [tier, { provider, model }] of Object.entries(loadTiers())) {
    if (provider === "openai") {
      const info = await openai.models.retrieve(model);
      const days = daysUntil(info.shutdown_date);
      if (days !== null && days <= WARN_DAYS) warnings.push(`${tier}: ${model} shuts down in ${days} days`);
    } else if (provider === "anthropic") {
      const info = await anthropic.models.retrieve(model);
      const days = daysUntil(info.retires_at);
      if (info.lifecycle !== "active" || (days !== null && days <= WARN_DAYS)) {
        warnings.push(`${tier}: ${model} is ${info.lifecycle}${days !== null ? `, retires in ${days} days` : ""}`);
      }
    }
    // Google: compare against the Gemini models page and its deprecation notices.
  }
  return warnings;
}

Sixty days is enough time to run the evaluation set against candidate replacements, tune prompts, and roll out through the usual release process, instead of discovering a retirement from 404 errors.

docs.title: A model decision record
docs.text:
# docs/decisions/0007-meeting-summary-model.md
Feature:        meeting summaries (streamed, private notes)
Constraints:    paid API terms, store: false, EU processing not required, no PHI
Candidates:     3 standard-tier models from 2 providers (IDs in config/models.env)
Evaluation:     220 anonymized meetings, rubric judge + action-item recall
Result:         candidate B: rubric 4.4/5, recall 0.93, p95 first token 1.1 s,
                cost per passing summary 0.45 of the previous model
Fallback:       candidate C (other provider), rubric 4.1/5, contract signed
Review:         on model shutdown notices, provider data-page changes, or every 6 months

A one-page record like this (the values above are examples), next to the code, explains the choice to the next engineer and lists exactly what to re-run when something changes.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write a task card per feature (input, output, latency, volume, cost of mistakes, data sensitivity) before comparing models.
  • Apply hard constraints first: data terms, BAA, region, modalities, context, required features.
  • Decide with your own evaluation set and compare cost per passing case, in relative units.
  • Use two or three tiers and route by feature; add a cascade only where a validator can detect bad output.
  • Keep model IDs and tiers in configuration, and check lifecycle fields daily.
  • Keep prompts in the repository and wrap provider-only features behind your own interfaces.
  • Give every fallback route the same evaluation and the same contractual coverage as the primary.
  • Re-run evaluations when a provider updates a model, when prompts change, and before every switch.
  • Record each decision with its evidence and its review triggers.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Quality drops with no code change. Detect: evaluation scores in the nightly run fall; user edits of drafts rise. Cause: configuration uses an alias whose underlying model changed, or the provider updated the model. Fix: pin dated model IDs where the provider offers them, run the evaluation set nightly, and treat model changes like deploys.
  • Requests fail with 400 after an SDK upgrade. Detect: every Anthropic call returns 400 mentioning temperature. Cause: the new SDK sends a newer API version (2026-10-21) that removed temperature, top_p, and top_k. Fix: remove the parameters and rely on prompts and validation instead of sampling settings.
  • Costs tripled after moving the agent to a stronger tier. Detect: output tokens per request jump; usage shows many reasoning tokens. Cause: reasoning effort set high for every step, with reasoning tokens counted as output. Fix: compare effort levels on the evaluation set and use high effort only for planning steps.
  • Private user data reached a free tier. Detect: an audit finds an AI Studio key, or a key from an unpaid project, in production configuration. Cause: a development key was promoted. Fix: separate keys per environment, block unpaid keys in production, and follow the incident process for the exposed data.
  • A fallback sent health data to an uncovered provider. Detect: routing logs show PHI-bearing requests served by the second provider. Cause: the fallback list was shared across features regardless of data class. Fix: fallback lists per data class, and a test that fails if a route without a BAA serves a PHI feature.
  • A retired model takes a feature down. Detect: 404 or "model not found" errors for one route. Cause: the shutdown date passed unnoticed. Fix: a daily lifecycle check with warnings 60 days ahead, and a pre-evaluated replacement in configuration.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Model tier: A class of model in your configuration (fast, standard, deep) chosen for a cost, latency, and quality profile.
  • Routing: Choosing which tier or model serves a request.
  • Cascade: Trying a cheaper tier first and escalating when its output fails validation.
  • Evaluation set: A versioned collection of real cases with graders, used to compare models and prompts.
  • Cost per passing case: Total cost of an evaluation run divided by the cases that passed; a fairer comparison than price per token.
  • Open-weight model: A model whose weights are published under a license, so it can be served by you or by any inference provider.
  • Lock-in: The cost of moving away from a provider, mostly in prompts, provider-only features, and contracts.
  • Zero data retention (ZDR): An arrangement where the provider does not store prompts or outputs after responding, with documented exceptions.
  • BAA: A business associate agreement, required under HIPAA before a provider may process protected health information for you.
  • Model lifecycle: The stages a model goes through (active, deprecated, retired), with announced shutdown or retirement dates.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Picking the top model on a public leaderboard for every feature.
  • Comparing price per token instead of cost per successful task.
  • Assuming a bigger context window means you should send more context.
  • Treating a second provider as a drop-in fallback without evaluation or contracts.
  • Believing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint removes all lock-in.
  • Relying on sampling parameters for correctness.
  • Using free-tier keys anywhere near user data.
  • Hard-coding model IDs, and learning about a retirement from errors.
  • Assuming open-weight models are free; serving them costs hardware and operations.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What goes on a task card, and why write it before comparing models?
  2. Name the five dimensions of the decision matrix and one pitfall for each.
  3. A fast tier costs 0.08 of the standard tier and passes validation 80% of the time. What is the cascade's average cost relative to always using the standard tier? (0.08 + 0.2 x 1.0 = 0.28, a 72% saving.)
  4. Why is cost per passing case a better comparison than price per token?
  5. Which hard constraints would rule a provider out of a TaskFlow feature that summarizes clinical notes?
  6. Describe the layers of lock-in and one mitigation for each.
  7. When would you choose an open-weight model served by yourself over a closed hosted model?
  8. What should happen, technically and procedurally, when the models endpoint reports a shutdown date for a configured model?

docs.title: Hosted Model APIs Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review calling model APIs from a backend, streaming responses end to end, prompt caching and batch processing, and choosing models and providers. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: Calling model APIs from a backend
1. Why should the browser never call a model provider directly with your API key?
docs.text: The key authorizes spending on your account, and anything shipped to the browser is public: a key in a Vite variable is compiled into the bundle whatever its name. The browser should call your backend with its normal session; the backend authorizes the user, chooses the model and prompt, enforces quotas, and calls the provider with a server-side key.

docs.title: 2. What timeout and retry defaults do the official SDKs ship with?
docs.text: As of November 2026, the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs wait up to 10 minutes per attempt and retry twice, with backoff from 0.5 seconds up to 8 seconds and some jitter. The Google Gen AI SDK does not retry unless httpOptions.retryOptions is set, and its timeout applies per attempt. Set these explicitly instead of inheriting them.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between an attempt timeout and a time budget?
docs.text: The attempt timeout caps a single HTTP request to the provider. The time budget caps everything the caller waits for: every attempt, every backoff sleep, and any fallback. Only the budget matches the product promise, so attempt timeouts should shrink as the budget runs down.

docs.title: 4. Which errors should be retried, and which should not?
docs.text: Retry temporary failures: timeouts, connection errors, 408, rate-limit 429s, 500, 503, and Anthropic's 529 overloaded. Do not retry bad requests (400, 413, 422), authentication errors, or billing and quota 429s; they fail the same way again. Some non-retryable errors (a 404 for a retired model, a quota error at one provider) can still go to another route.

docs.title: 5. How can code tell a temporary 429 from one that will not clear?
docs.text: By the error code and headers. OpenAI uses codes such as credit_balance_exhausted and organization_spend_limit_exceeded (often with the error type insufficient_quota) for billing problems and slow_down for ramping too fast. Anthropic's spend-cap 429 carries error.details.error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached and no retry-after header. Ordinary rate limits usually come with Retry-After.

docs.title: 6. What is full jitter, and why use it?
docs.text:
Exponential backoff sets a ceiling that doubles with each attempt, capped at a maximum; full jitter waits a random time between zero and that ceiling. Clients that failed together then retry at different moments instead of in a synchronized wave that hits the provider again.

const ceiling = Math.min(maxDelayMs, baseDelayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1));
const delay = Math.random() * ceiling;

docs.title: 7. Why should retries happen in only one layer?
docs.text: Because layers multiply. SDK retries inside application retries inside a proxy or client retry turn one user action into many provider requests, exactly when the provider is struggling. Amazon's Builders' Library example: three retries at each of five layers multiplies load on the failing component by 243. Pick one layer, usually the application, and set maxRetries: 0 in the SDK.

docs.title: 8. Is calling a model idempotent? How do you make an endpoint safe to retry?
docs.text: No: each call produces a different answer and a new bill, and the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs send no idempotency header for generation requests. The client sends an Idempotency-Key per user action; the backend claims it with a unique index before calling the model, stores the result, and replays it for repeats. Side effects triggered by the result need their own idempotency.

docs.title: 9. What is an error taxonomy, and why define one?
docs.text: A small, provider-neutral set of failure kinds (aborted, timeout, rate_limited, overloaded, quota_exhausted, auth, not_found, bad_request, incomplete), each with two decisions attached: retry the same route, and try another route. The rest of the application acts on the kind, logs it, and shows a fitting message, without knowing provider-specific error classes.

docs.title: 10. How do fallback routes work, and what makes them safe?
docs.text: An ordered list of routes (primary model, a cheaper model at the same provider, optionally another provider) behind one adapter interface. The router moves to the next route after non-retryable route failures or after retries are exhausted. It is safe only if every route passes the same evaluation set and is covered by the same data terms as the primary.

docs.title: 11. What does a circuit breaker add to fallback?
docs.text: It stops paying the attempt timeout on every request while a route is down. After several consecutive failures, the route is skipped for a cooldown period, then probed again. Without it, every request waits for the broken route to time out before falling back.

docs.title: 12. Why do you need per-user quotas when providers already rate-limit?
docs.text: Provider limits apply to your whole account, so one user's script can use the shared tokens-per-minute budget and break the feature for everyone, or run up a large bill. Per-user daily token budgets, per-minute request limits, and concurrency caps protect fairness and cost; a hashed safety_identifier lets the provider's abuse detection target one user.

docs.title: 13. How can a token quota be enforced atomically in MongoDB?
docs.text: Reserve an estimate with one conditional update: filter on { userId, day, tokens: { $lte: limit - estimate } }, $inc the tokens, and upsert. If the user is over the limit, the filter does not match, the upsert tries to insert a duplicate { userId, day }, and the unique index rejects it. After the call, settle the difference between the estimate and the real usage.

docs.title: 14. Why abort the provider call when the client disconnects?
docs.text: Nobody will read the answer, but the provider keeps generating and billing until the connection closes. Listening for the response close event (when the response did not finish) and aborting an AbortController whose signal was passed to the SDK closes the provider request.

docs.title: 15. What does streaming improve, and what does it not?
docs.text: It improves time to first token and perceived speed, lets users stop a bad answer, and avoids long non-streaming timeouts. It does not make total generation faster: the model produces tokens at the same rate either way.

docs.title: 16. Describe the three streams in a streamed answer.
docs.text: Provider to backend: server-sent events parsed by the SDK into typed events. Backend to proxy: the relay writes its own SSE events as each provider event arrives. Proxy to browser: nginx, the load balancer, or the CDN passes bytes through, and the browser reads them with fetch and a stream reader. Any hop that buffers delays everything.

docs.title: 17. Why re-encode provider events instead of piping them to the browser?
docs.text: Provider events contain internal ids, tool-call fragments, reasoning summaries, and usage fields, and differ by provider. A small vocabulary of your own (delta, done, error) keeps the browser independent of the provider and model, and keeps internals private.

docs.title: 18. What does the SSE wire format look like?
docs.text:
Plain text with Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each message is event: and data: lines ended by a blank line; lines starting with : are comments, which make good heartbeats.

event: delta
data: {"text":"Decision: ship v2 "}

: ping

docs.title: 19. Why does TaskFlow Web use fetch instead of EventSource?
docs.text: EventSource only makes GET requests, cannot send custom headers such as Authorization, and reconnects automatically, which would restart a paid generation. fetch with POST and a ReadableStream reader gives full control, at the cost of parsing events yourself.

docs.title: 20. Which response headers does the relay send, and why?
docs.text: Content-Type: text/event-stream; Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform so caches do not store it and intermediaries do not transform (and buffer) it; X-Accel-Buffering: no so nginx does not buffer this response; then res.flushHeaders() so the status and headers leave before the first token.

docs.title: 21. How does nginx break streaming, and how do you fix it?
docs.text: proxy_buffering is on by default, so nginx collects the upstream response in page-sized buffers (4 or 8 KB) and sends text in bursts or at the end. Turn it off for the stream location or send X-Accel-Buffering: no. Also set proxy_read_timeout longer than the longest silent gap (it defaults to 60 seconds between reads) and keep gzip off the route.

docs.title: 22. Why send heartbeat comments?
docs.text: Proxies and load balancers close connections that stay idle too long (nginx's read timeout and an AWS ALB's idle timeout both default to 60 seconds). A reasoning model can be silent longer than that before its first token. A : ping comment every 15 seconds resets idle timers and is ignored by SSE parsers.

docs.title: 23. How does a cancel travel from the browser to the provider?
docs.text: The browser aborts its fetch; nginx (with the default proxy_ignore_client_abort off) closes its upstream connection; Express emits close on the response before it finished; the route calls controller.abort(); the SDK, created with that signal, closes its request to the provider, and generation stops.

docs.title: 24. What is the trap in checking for an aborted OpenAI stream?
docs.text: When the OpenAI SDK's stream is aborted, the for await loop ends quietly instead of throwing. Code after the loop must check signal.aborted; otherwise it treats a cancelled answer as if the stream had ended normally.

docs.title: 25. What is backpressure in a streaming relay, and how is it handled?
docs.text: When a client reads slowly, res.write() returns false because the socket buffer is full. Ignoring it queues data in Node's memory. The relay waits for drain (or close) before writing more, which also slows how fast it reads from the provider.

docs.title: 26. How should partial failures be reported once the 200 is sent?
docs.text: As events. An output limit becomes done with status: "incomplete"; a provider error event or a dropped upstream connection becomes error with partial: true; a client disconnect is recorded as cancelled. The stored status must match what happened, and a stream with no done event is incomplete by definition.

docs.title: 27. Can you retry a stream that failed halfway?
docs.text: Not silently: the user has seen part of the answer. Either start over visibly (clear and regenerate), or resume where it stopped if the provider supports it, such as OpenAI's background mode with responses.retrieve(id, { stream: true, starting_after }). Falling back to another model is only safe before the first token was sent.

docs.title: 28. What does a prompt cache store, and why only prefixes?
docs.text: The provider keeps the processed state of a prompt prefix for a while, so a later request starting with exactly the same tokens skips that work and pays a reduced rate for it. Processing runs from the beginning of the prompt, so only an identical beginning can be reused; one changed token invalidates everything after it.

docs.title: 29. How does OpenAI's caching work on current models?
docs.text: Caching is automatic. On GPT-5.6 and later, implicit mode (the default) places a breakpoint at the end of the latest eligible message, while explicit mode caches only blocks marked with prompt_cache_breakpoint, up to four writes per request. prompt_cache_options.ttl is "30m" or "12h", the minimum prefix is 1,024 tokens, and usage reports cached_tokens and cache_write_tokens.

docs.title: 30. How does Anthropic's caching differ?
docs.text: It is opt-in: a top-level cache_control field turns on automatic caching (the breakpoint moves forward with the conversation), and cache_control on individual blocks sets explicit breakpoints, up to four per request. Entries live 5 minutes, refreshed on each read, or 1 hour at a higher write price; the prefix order is tools, then system, then messages.

docs.title: 31. What are Gemini's two caching mechanisms?
docs.text: Implicit caching is on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer models, with savings when requests hit but no guarantee. Explicit caching creates a cache object with a TTL (1 hour by default) that requests reference via cachedContent; savings are guaranteed and storage is billed for the lifetime. Explicit caching is not available for Gemini 4 models or the Interactions API.

docs.title: 32. How should a prompt be ordered for caching?
docs.text: From most stable to least stable: tool definitions, instructions, shared reference material (versioned), the append-only conversation, and finally the new input and anything per-request (dates, user names, retrieved chunks).

docs.title: 33. Name three things that silently break prompt caching.
docs.text: A timestamp or request id in the instructions; non-deterministic serialization, such as tools or JSON keys in a different order; and rewriting earlier conversation turns. Per-user content early in the prompt also splits the cache per user.

docs.title: 34. How do you know whether caching works?
docs.text: Read the usage fields on every response (cached and cache-write tokens) and track the hit ratio, cached / input. Log a hash of the stable prefix too: if it differs between two requests that should match, something volatile is in the prefix. On Anthropic, both cache fields at zero mean the prompt was not cached, often because it is below the model's minimum.

docs.title: 35. Work through the value of caching for a reused prefix.
docs.text: With a write multiplier of 1.25 and a read multiplier of 0.1, a 20,000-token prefix used by 50 questions of 300 tokens costs 25,000 + 49 x 2,000 + 15,000 = 138,000 input-token equivalents, against 50 x 20,300 = 1,015,000 without caching: about 14% of the uncached cost.

docs.title: 36. Why can a burst of parallel requests all miss the cache?
docs.text: On Anthropic, a new cache entry only becomes available after the first response starts. Parallel requests with the same new prefix all write instead of read. Send one request first and release the rest after it starts streaming; OpenAI also offers a prewarm option.

docs.title: 37. When are long cache lifetimes (1 hour, 12 hours) worth it?
docs.text: Only when the same prefix is reused across gaps longer than the default lifetime, such as project documents queried all day, or batch jobs with shared context. Long-lifetime writes cost more, so a prefix read once or twice loses money.

docs.title: 38. What do batch APIs trade, and what do they cost relatively?
docs.text: They accept many requests at once and return results within a window (up to 24 hours; Anthropic says most batches finish within an hour) at about half the interactive price, with separate, higher rate limits. The trade is latency: the window, not the typical case, is the promise.

docs.title: 39. How do you process batch results correctly?
docs.text: Match each result to its request by custom_id, because output order is not guaranteed. Read both the output file and the error file (OpenAI); each line can succeed or fail on its own, and expired or cancelled batches still return what finished. Resubmit only the failed lines, and make submission idempotent per job and day.

docs.title: 40. What is a flex service tier, and when would you use it?
docs.text: A cheaper tier for ordinary synchronous requests with slower and less guaranteed processing: OpenAI's Flex processing is priced at Batch API rates and can return uncharged 429 resource-unavailable errors, and Gemini's Flex inference offers a 50% reduction with best-effort availability. It suits work that should finish within minutes, such as evaluation runs in CI.

docs.title: 41. What goes on a task card, and why write one?
docs.text: Input size, output format, latency budget, volume, cost of a mistake, and data sensitivity for one feature. It turns "which model is best?" into measurable requirements and usually shows that different features need different tiers.

docs.title: 42. What are the dimensions of a model decision matrix?
docs.text: Capability (measured on your own cases), latency (time to first token and p95), cost (per successful task, in relative terms), context size (input and maximum output), and data policy (training use, retention, zero retention, BAA, region).

docs.title: 43. Why compare cost per passing case instead of price per token?
docs.text: A cheap model that fails often costs extra through retries, escalations, and human fixes. Dividing the total cost of an evaluation run by the passing cases captures quality and price together.

docs.title: 44. Why not choose models from public leaderboards?
docs.text: Leaderboards measure other tasks, prompts, and formats. Two models with similar scores can differ sharply on your JSON schema, citations, or tool calls. Leaderboards can shortlist; your evaluation set decides.

docs.title: 45. What are model tiers, and how are features routed to them?
docs.text: Two or three classes of model (fast, standard, deep) chosen for different cost, latency, and quality profiles. A table from feature to tier is the simplest router: parsing on the fast tier, Q&A and summaries on the standard tier, agent planning on the deep tier.

docs.title: 46. What is a cascade, and when does it work?
docs.text: Try the cheaper tier, validate the output, and escalate only if validation fails. If the fast tier costs 0.1 of the standard tier and passes 85% of the time, the average cost is 0.1 + 0.15 = 0.25 of always using the standard tier. It works only when a validator can detect bad output, such as schema or citation checks.

docs.title: 47. How do you evaluate candidate models fairly?
docs.text: Apply hard constraints first, then run the same versioned evaluation set with the same graders against every candidate, report pass rate, p50 and p95 latency, and cost per passing case, and give each candidate a short prompt-tuning pass so a prompt written for one model does not understate another.

docs.title: 48. Where does provider lock-in really come from?
docs.text: Rarely from the model ID, which is configuration. It comes from the API shape, prompts tuned to one model, provider-only features (stored state, hosted prompts, batch formats, caching modes), API version changes, and contracts such as BAAs and data-processing agreements.

docs.title: 49. Give recent examples of provider features changing under applications.
docs.text: OpenAI's Assistants API shut down on August 26, 2026; reusable prompt objects (/v1/prompts) shut down on November 30, 2026, with the advice to keep prompts in application code; OpenAI's Evals dashboard became read-only on the same date. Anthropic's API version 2026-10-21 removed temperature, top_p, and top_k.

docs.title: 50. How do you keep a model choice from becoming an outage?
docs.text: Keep model IDs in configuration, check the providers' lifecycle fields daily (OpenAI's shutdown_date; Anthropic's lifecycle, deprecated_at, retires_at), warn weeks ahead, and keep a pre-evaluated replacement ready. Pin dated model versions where offered, because an alias can change behavior underneath you.

docs.title: 51. When would you pick an open-weight model over a closed hosted one?
docs.text: When data must stay on infrastructure you control, a model version must stay frozen for a long time, or steady high volume makes owned capacity cheaper than per-token prices. The cost is GPU operations, scaling, and monitoring; closed hosted models usually lead on the hardest tasks and need no operations.

docs.title: 52. Does the provider's data policy depend on how you use it?
docs.text: Yes. Gemini's unpaid services (AI Studio, the free quota) use content to improve Google's products, paid services do not; OpenAI's Responses API keeps application state for 30 days unless store: false; zero-retention arrangements need approval or a contract. Read the terms for the exact tier and feature.

docs.title: 53. What must be true of a fallback for a feature that handles health data?
docs.text: The fallback provider needs a signed BAA and the HIPAA-ready configuration it requires (for example Anthropic's HIPAA readiness in the Console, OpenAI's BAA-eligible endpoints, or Google Cloud's BAA for covered products), and it must pass the feature's evaluation set. Otherwise it is not an allowed route for that feature.

docs.title: 54. During a provider incident, assistant requests hang for minutes and API servers run out of connections. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the SDK client options (timeout and retries) and whether calls have a total time budget.

How to confirm: attempt logs show few completions and very long durations; the client still uses the 10-minute default timeout with two retries.

Likely causes and fixes: SDK defaults and no budget. Set attempt timeouts from the expected output size, wrap calls in a budget, fall back or fail with a clear "busy" message, and add a circuit breaker. See calling model APIs from a backend.

docs.title: 55. Every assistant request fails with 429, but traffic is normal. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: the error code and headers on the 429 responses.

How to confirm: codes such as insufficient_quota, credit_balance_exhausted, or enforced_spend_limit_reached, and no retry-after header.

Likely causes and fixes: a billing limit or spend cap, not a rate limit. Stop retrying those codes, alert the account owner, fall back to another route if one is configured and allowed, and raise the limit. See calling model APIs from a backend.

docs.title: 56. After an outage the provider's dashboard shows many times more requests than user actions. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how many layers retry: the SDK, application code, the API gateway, and the client.

How to confirm: attempt logs show several provider calls per user action, each layer retrying independently.

Likely causes and fixes: stacked retries multiply load. Retry in one layer with full jitter and a budget, set maxRetries: 0 elsewhere, and add a breaker. See calling model APIs from a backend.

docs.title: 57. Users report duplicate tasks after clicking "Create with assistant" once. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether requests carry an Idempotency-Key and whether the server de-duplicates it.

How to confirm: two model calls with the same user and nearly the same timestamp; two task inserts.

Likely causes and fixes: double submits or client retries without idempotency. Generate a key per user action, claim it with a unique index, replay stored results, and make task creation itself idempotent. See calling model APIs from a backend.

docs.title: 58. Summaries appear all at once after several seconds in production, but stream locally. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: response headers and the proxy configuration on the production path.

How to confirm: curl -N against the API server directly streams; through the public URL it does not.

Likely causes and fixes: nginx proxy buffering, response compression, or a buffering CDN. Send X-Accel-Buffering: no or set proxy_buffering off, exclude the route from compression, and check CDN streaming settings. See streaming responses end to end.

docs.title: 59. Long answers always stop at about 60 seconds. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: idle and read timeouts on nginx and the load balancer, and whether the relay sends heartbeats.

How to confirm: streams end at the same duration without a done event; proxy logs show upstream timeouts.

Likely causes and fixes: a silent gap (often a reasoning model before its first token) exceeds a 60-second idle timeout. Send : ping comments every 15 seconds and raise timeouts above the longest gap. See streaming responses end to end.

docs.title: 60. Output token spend is far higher than the text users actually receive. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether client disconnects abort the provider request.

How to confirm: many summaries end as abandoned in logs, yet the provider reports full-length outputs; a slow-stream test shows the provider connection staying open after the browser leaves.

Likely causes and fixes: no abort propagation. Abort an AbortController on early response close, pass its signal to the SDK, and check signal.aborted after the stream loop. See streaming responses end to end.

docs.title: 61. Stored meeting summaries sometimes end mid-sentence but are marked complete. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the relay decides the final status.

How to confirm: the code saves whatever text exists when the loop ends; failed or cancelled streams were saved as completed.

Likely causes and fixes: status not derived from completion events. Set completed or incomplete only from the provider's completion events and store everything else as failed or cancelled; the client treats a stream without done as cut off. See streaming responses end to end.

docs.title: 62. Prompt caching was enabled weeks ago, but costs did not change. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the cached-token fields in usage and the prefix fingerprint in logs.

How to confirm: cached tokens are always zero and the fingerprint differs on every request.

Likely causes and fixes: volatile content in the prefix (current time, user name, request id) or non-deterministic serialization, or a prompt below the model's minimum. Move volatile content to the end, stabilize serialization, and check the minimum. See prompt caching and batch processing.

docs.title: 63. Some projects did not get their nightly digest. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the batch's final status and request counts, and how results are matched.

How to confirm: the batch completed or expired with failures; the collector read only the output file or matched by position.

Likely causes and fixes: line-level failures and partial results ignored. Read the output and error files, match by custom_id, and resubmit the failed lines. See prompt caching and batch processing.

docs.title: 64. Answer quality dropped this week with no code changes. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the configured model IDs and the nightly evaluation results.

How to confirm: the configuration uses an alias, the provider updated the model behind it, and evaluation scores fell on the same day.

Likely causes and fixes: an unpinned model changed. Pin dated model versions where offered, run the evaluation set nightly, and treat model changes like deploys with a decision record. See choosing models and providers.

docs.title: 65. After an SDK upgrade, every Anthropic request returns 400. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the error message and the request parameters.

How to confirm: the error names temperature (or top_p, top_k), and the upgraded SDK sends the 2026-10-21 API version.

Likely causes and fixes: that API version removed the sampling parameters. Remove them, rely on prompts and output validation, and pin SDK upgrades behind the evaluation set. See choosing models and providers.

docs.title: 66. An audit finds health data processed by a fallback provider. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: routing logs for the affected feature and the fallback list it uses.

How to confirm: PHI-bearing requests were served by a route whose provider has no BAA or HIPAA-ready configuration.

Likely causes and fixes: one fallback list shared by all features. Keep fallback lists per data class, add a test that fails if a non-BAA route can serve a PHI feature, and follow the incident process. See choosing models and providers.
