docs.title: Prompt Caching and Batch Processing
docs.text:
Two provider features cut the cost of model calls without changing the model or the answer. Prompt caching lets the provider reuse the work it already did on a prompt prefix it has seen recently, so TaskFlow's project-knowledge Q&A does not pay full price for the same 20,000 tokens of project documents on every question. Batch processing accepts a file of requests, runs them asynchronously within a day, and charges much less, which suits TaskFlow's nightly project digests and evaluation runs. This lesson explains how each provider implements caching (automatic prefix caching versus explicit cache breakpoints), how to structure prompts so the cache actually hits, how batch APIs work, and when to use each one.

Costs on this page are relative ("cheaper", "a fraction of the input price"); provider price lists change and are linked at the end. Wider cost strategy is covered in cost optimization for LLM apps.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
For many applications, input tokens dominate the bill. A retrieval question sends instructions, tool definitions, retrieved documents, and the conversation so far, often thousands of tokens, to get a few hundred tokens back. Agents are worse: every step resends the whole growing transcript. Most of that input is identical from one request to the next. Prompt caching turns that repetition into savings and also shortens time to first token, because the provider skips recomputing the cached prefix.

Caching only works if the prefix is byte-for-byte identical. One timestamp in the instructions, one reordered tool definition, or one rewritten earlier turn makes every request a miss, and nothing in the response tells you so unless you read the usage fields. Teams regularly "enable caching" and see no change because of a single volatile line.

Batch APIs address a different waste: paying interactive prices and competing for interactive rate limits with work nobody is waiting for. Nightly summaries, backfills, re-classification of old tasks, and evaluation runs can all wait hours. Moving them to a batch API makes them substantially cheaper and keeps them from eating the rate limit the TaskFlow Assistant needs during the day.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Anthropic prompt caching. The prompt caching guide offers automatic caching (one top-level cache_control field) and explicit breakpoints on content blocks, a 5-minute lifetime refreshed on every use or a 1-hour lifetime at a higher write price, cache reads at a small fraction of the input price, and a prefix that always runs tools, then system, then messages.
  • OpenAI prompt caching. The prompt caching guide describes caching that works with no code changes, plus implicit and explicit breakpoint modes, 30-minute and 12-hour lifetimes, and a 1,024-token minimum on GPT-5.6 and later models. It includes a break-even formula for deciding whether to pad a short prefix up to the minimum.
  • Gemini context caching. The caching page explains that implicit caching is on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer models with no guaranteed savings, while explicit caches (on Gemini 3 and 2.5 models through generateContent) guarantee the discount but add a storage charge for their lifetime.
  • Batch APIs at about half price. OpenAI's Batch API guide (a 50% discount, separate higher rate limits, completion within 24 hours), Anthropic's batch processing guide (50% off, most batches done within an hour, discounts that stack with caching), and Gemini's Batch API page (50% of the standard cost, a 24-hour target) describe the same trade: wait longer, pay less.

Popular tools and providers: prompt caching and batch APIs at OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google; cheaper slower service tiers such as OpenAI's Flex processing and Gemini's Flex inference; job schedulers (cron, BullMQ, a cloud scheduler) that submit and collect batches.

docs.title: What a prompt cache saves
docs.text:
Before a model generates anything, it processes the whole input. For a long prompt that processing is a large share of the time and cost. A prompt cache keeps the processed state of a prompt prefix for a while, so a later request that starts with exactly the same tokens skips that work for the shared part and pays a reduced rate for it. The rest of the request (everything after the longest cached prefix) is processed normally.

Three properties follow from "prefix" and "exactly":

  • Only the beginning of a prompt can be reused. A shared paragraph in the middle of two different prompts saves nothing.
  • Any change in the prefix, even one character, makes everything after it a miss.
  • Caches are scoped: OpenAI caches are not shared across organizations or across regional processing boundaries, Anthropic caches are isolated per organization and, on the Claude API, per workspace, and Gemini explicit caches are objects in your project.

docs.title: Automatic prefix caching versus explicit breakpoints
docs.text:
The providers agree on the idea and differ on who decides what is cached. The details below were checked against each provider's documentation in November 2026; minimums and multipliers vary by model, so check the table for the model you configure.

OpenAI caches automatically. On GPT-5.6 and later models, prompt_cache_options.mode selects how breakpoints are placed:

  • Implicit (the default): OpenAI places a breakpoint at the end of the latest eligible message (a user message, the last of a run of tool results, or the initial developer messages) and can reuse prefixes that end at up to 20 earlier message boundaries.
  • Explicit: only content blocks you mark with prompt_cache_breakpoint are written to the cache, up to four writes per request. Content after the last breakpoint is billed as ordinary input with no write charge. With no breakpoints, the request is not cached.

You can mix the two: in implicit mode, up to three explicit breakpoints are written alongside the implicit one. prompt_cache_options.ttl sets the minimum lifetime, "30m" (the default) or "12h"; a 12-hour write costs more than a 30-minute write, and reads cost the same for both. Breakpoints cannot go in the top-level instructions field, so reusable instructions belong in a developer message. prompt_cache_key groups related requests; on models before GPT-5.6 it helps route them to the same cache, and on newer models it mainly keeps cache accounting separate per customer. Usage reports input_tokens_details.cached_tokens and input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens.

Anthropic caches only when asked:

  • Automatic caching: one top-level cache_control field. The API puts the breakpoint on the last cacheable block and moves it forward as the conversation grows, which suits multi-turn chat.
  • Explicit breakpoints: cache_control on individual blocks (a tool definition, a system block, a message block), up to four per request, with automatic caching using one of the four slots.

The default lifetime is 5 minutes, refreshed for free each time the entry is read, and measured from the start of the request; ttl: "1h" keeps it longer at a higher write price. Writes cost somewhat more than ordinary input, reads cost a small fraction of it. When looking for a cached prefix, the API checks at most 20 blocks back from each breakpoint. A prompt shorter than the model's minimum (512 to 4,096 tokens depending on the model) is processed without caching and without an error; usage then shows both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens as zero. A new entry only becomes available once the first response has started, so a burst of parallel requests with the same new prefix all miss: send one first and the rest after its response begins. Cached reads also do not count against Anthropic's input-tokens-per-minute limit, which raises effective throughput.

Gemini offers two mechanisms:

  • Implicit caching is enabled by default on Gemini 2.5 and newer models. Savings are passed on automatically when a request hits, but there is no guarantee. Google's advice is to put large, common content at the beginning and send requests with similar prefixes close together.
  • Explicit caching creates a cache object (caches.create) holding system instructions and content with a TTL (1 hour by default), which requests then reference with cachedContent. Savings are guaranteed, and storage is billed for the lifetime. It is available for Gemini 3 and 2.5 models through generateContent, but not for Gemini 4 models or the Interactions API, which support implicit caching only.

docs.title: Structuring prompts so the cache hits
docs.text:
The rule is to order the prompt from most stable to least stable, and to keep anything volatile out of the stable part:

  1. Tools and instructions first, identical for every request. Build tool definitions in a fixed order from code, and serialize JSON deterministically: the same object with keys in a different order is a different prefix.
  2. Shared reference material next: for TaskFlow, the project's glossary and documents. Include a version identifier and change it only when the documents change, so a whole project's questions share one cache entry until then.
  3. The conversation, append-only. Each turn adds to the end, so the previous request is a prefix of the next one. Rewriting or summarizing earlier turns saves context but invalidates the cache from that point; do it rarely and deliberately.
  4. The new question, and anything per-request, last: the current time, the user's name, retrieved chunks that differ per question.

Two caveats. Retrieval-augmented prompts put different chunks in every request, so only what comes before the chunks is cacheable; keep stable material ahead of them. And per-user content in the prefix (a user's profile, permissions text) splits the cache per user, which is fine when each user sends many requests in a short time and wasteful otherwise.

docs.title: Measuring whether the cache works
docs.text:
Usage fields are the only reliable signal. TaskFlow logs, for every request, the input tokens, the cached tokens, the cache-write tokens, and a short hash of the stable part of the prompt. The hit ratio is cached_tokens / input_tokens. A healthy project Q&A route might show 80% or more after the first question in a session; a ratio stuck at zero means the prefix changes, the prompt is below the minimum, or requests are too far apart for the cache lifetime. A prefix hash that differs between two requests that should match points straight at the volatile content.

A worked example of what caching is worth, using the multipliers in OpenAI's guide for GPT-5.6 and later (30-minute writes at 1.25 times the uncached input rate, reads at 0.1 times): a 20,000-token prefix is used by 50 questions of 300 tokens within half an hour.

  • Without caching: 50 x 20,300 = 1,015,000 input-token equivalents.
  • With caching: one write (20,000 x 1.25 = 25,000), 49 reads (49 x 20,000 x 0.1 = 98,000), and the questions (50 x 300 = 15,000): 138,000 equivalents, about 14% of the uncached cost.

The same guide gives a break-even rule for padding a short prefix up to the minimum cacheable length: with minimum M, read multiplier r, write multiplier w, and N requests, expanding pays off when the original prefix is longer than M x (r + (w - r) / N). With M = 1,024, r = 0.1, w = 1.25, and N = 10, that is 220.2 tokens, so a prefix of 221 tokens or more is worth expanding.

docs.title: Batch APIs: asynchronous, cheaper, slower
docs.text:
A batch API takes many independent requests at once and promises results within a window instead of seconds. In exchange it charges roughly half the interactive price and draws on separate, higher rate limits, so a large job does not compete with interactive traffic.

OpenAI Batch API Anthropic Message Batches Gemini Batch API Relative price 50% discount 50% discount, stacks with caching 50% of the standard cost Turnaround Within 24 hours, often sooner Most within 1 hour; expires after 24 hours 24-hour target, usually faster Input Uploaded JSONL file (purpose batch), up to 50,000 requests or 200 MB Requests in the create call, up to 100,000 or 256 MB Inline requests (under 20 MB) or an uploaded JSONL file (up to 2 GB) Matching results custom_id per line custom_id per request A key per request Results Output file plus an error file Streamed JSONL results, available for 29 days Inline responses or an output file

Four rules make batch jobs dependable:

  • Match by custom_id. Output order is not guaranteed, so every request carries an identifier that maps back to the record it belongs to (TaskFlow uses the project id).
  • Handle partial results. A batch that expires or is cancelled still returns the requests that finished. Each line can succeed or fail on its own; the failed ones go into the next batch or are retried as normal requests.
  • Collect in a separate job. Submission records the batch id; a scheduled job polls status and processes results. Neither should block a web request.
  • Make submission idempotent. Record "digest batch for 2026-11-14 submitted as batch X" before or atomically with submitting, so a restarted scheduler does not pay for the same night twice.

Caching and batching combine. Anthropic's guide recommends the 1-hour cache lifetime for batches with shared context, because batch requests run over longer periods than 5 minutes. Gemini's batch mode supports context caching too.

A middle ground exists for work that should finish within minutes rather than hours: cheaper, slower service tiers for ordinary synchronous requests. OpenAI's Flex processing (service_tier: "flex", in beta for some models) is priced at Batch API rates with slower responses and occasional 429 "resource unavailable" errors that are not charged. Gemini's Flex inference (serviceTier: FLEX, in preview) offers a 50% reduction with variable latency and best-effort availability.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Workload Caching Batch or flex Why Project Q&A with large shared docs Yes, explicit breakpoint after the docs No Users wait; the prefix repeats Multi-turn assistant or agent loop Yes, automatic or implicit No Each turn's prompt extends the last Nightly digests for every project Little to share Batch Nobody waits; half the price Re-classifying 200,000 old tasks Shared instructions only Batch Large, independent, not urgent Evaluation runs in CI or nightly Shared instructions Batch (nightly) or flex (CI) Cost matters more than latency One-off short prompts No No Below the cache minimum; nothing repeats A prefix reused once every few hours Probably not Depends Writes cost more than plain input; the entry expires before reuse

Avoid the 1-hour or 12-hour lifetimes unless reuse really spans that long: the write premium is wasted if the entry is read only once or twice. Avoid batch APIs for anything a user is waiting for, even if most batches finish within an hour; the promise is the window, not the typical case.

docs.title: A cache-friendly request for project Q&A
docs.text:
// src/ai/project-qa.ts
// Project-knowledge Q&A with a cache-friendly prompt: stable content first,
// the user's question last, and nothing volatile in the prefix.
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import OpenAI from "openai";

export interface ProjectContext {
  projectId: string;
  docsVersion: string; // changes only when the project's docs change
  docs: string; // glossary, conventions, current docs (thousands of tokens)
}
export interface Turn {
  role: "user" | "assistant";
  text: string;
}

const INSTRUCTIONS = [
  "You answer questions about one TaskFlow project using only the project documents.",
  "Cite the document title for every claim. If the documents do not say, answer 'Not documented.'",
].join("\n");

export function buildRequest(model: string, ctx: ProjectContext, history: Turn[], question: string) {
  const request = {
    model,
    max_output_tokens: 600,
    store: false,
    prompt_cache_key: `project:${ctx.projectId}`, // groups related requests (helps older models route)
    prompt_cache_options: { mode: "implicit", ttl: "30m" }, // GPT-5.6 and later
    input: [
      // 1. Stable for every request in the deployment.
      { role: "developer", content: [{ type: "input_text", text: INSTRUCTIONS }] },
      // 2. Stable per project and docs version; reused all day, so cache it longer.
      {
        role: "developer",
        content: [
          {
            type: "input_text",
            text: `Project documents (version ${ctx.docsVersion}):\n${ctx.docs}`,
            prompt_cache_breakpoint: { mode: "explicit", ttl: "12h" },
          },
        ],
      },
      // 3. Grows by appending; the implicit breakpoint follows the latest user message.
      ...history.map((t) => ({ role: t.role, content: t.text })),
      // 4. Changes every request: always last.
      { role: "user", content: question },
    ],
  } satisfies OpenAI.Responses.ResponseCreateParamsNonStreaming;
  return request;
}

// Hash of everything before the conversation: log it with each request.
// If it changes between two requests that should share a cache, something
// volatile (a timestamp, a random id, reordered JSON) leaked into the prefix.
export function prefixFingerprint(req: ReturnType<typeof buildRequest>): string {
  const stable = JSON.stringify([req.model, req.input[0], req.input[1]]);
  return createHash("sha256").update(stable).digest("hex").slice(0, 12);
}

// Share of input tokens served from cache, from the usage the provider returns.
export function cacheHitRatio(usage: OpenAI.Responses.ResponseUsage | undefined): number {
  if (!usage || usage.input_tokens === 0) return 0;
  return usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens / usage.input_tokens;
}
  • The documents get an explicit 12-hour breakpoint because the same project's questions arrive all day; the conversation relies on the implicit 30-minute breakpoint because sessions are short.
  • satisfies checks the object against the SDK's request type without widening it, so a misspelled cache option fails the type check.
  • prompt_cache_options applies to GPT-5.6 and later models. For an older model in CHAT_MODEL, drop it and the breakpoint, and rely on automatic caching plus prompt_cache_key.
  • The function never puts the date, the user's name, or retrieved chunks before the conversation. If the assistant needs today's date, it goes into the final user message.

docs.title: The Anthropic and Gemini equivalents
docs.text:
// src/ai/cache-equivalents.ts
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai";

const anthropic = new Anthropic();
const genai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY });

// Anthropic: an explicit 1-hour breakpoint after the project documents, plus
// top-level automatic caching that moves its breakpoint along the conversation.
export async function anthropicAnswer(docs: string, history: Anthropic.MessageParam[], question: string) {
  const message = await anthropic.messages.create({
    model: process.env.ANTHROPIC_MODEL!,
    max_tokens: 600,
    cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" }, // automatic: last cacheable block, 5-minute TTL
    system: [
      { type: "text", text: "Answer questions about one TaskFlow project using only its documents." },
      { type: "text", text: docs, cache_control: { type: "ephemeral", ttl: "1h" } },
    ],
    messages: [...history, { role: "user", content: question }],
  });
  const u = message.usage;
  console.log({ cacheWrite: u.cache_creation_input_tokens, cacheRead: u.cache_read_input_tokens, uncached: u.input_tokens });
  return message;
}

// Gemini: implicit caching needs no code. Explicit caching creates a cache
// object (Gemini 3 and 2.5 models through generateContent) and references it.
export async function geminiWithExplicitCache(docs: string, question: string) {
  const model = process.env.GEMINI_CHAT_MODEL!;
  const cache = await genai.caches.create({
    model,
    config: {
      displayName: "taskflow-project-docs",
      systemInstruction: "Answer questions about one TaskFlow project using only its documents.",
      contents: [{ role: "user", parts: [{ text: docs }] }],
      ttl: "3600s", // the default is 1 hour; storage is billed for the TTL
    },
  });
  const response = await genai.models.generateContent({
    model,
    contents: question,
    config: { cachedContent: cache.name },
  });
  console.log({ cachedTokens: response.usageMetadata?.cachedContentTokenCount });
  return response.text;
}
  • In the Anthropic request, the order is fixed by the API: tools, then system, then messages. Putting the documents in system with their own breakpoint keeps them cached even while the automatic breakpoint moves along the messages.
  • In Anthropic usage, input_tokens counts only the tokens after the last breakpoint; add the three fields to get the full prompt size.
  • A real application creates one Gemini cache per project and docs version, stores its name, and deletes or lets it expire when the documents change, rather than creating a cache per question as this short example does.

docs.title: Nightly digests with the Batch API
docs.text:
// src/jobs/nightly-digests.ts
// Nightly "what happened in your project today" digests through the Batch API:
// one JSONL line per project, submitted at night, collected by a later job.
import OpenAI, { toFile } from "openai";

export interface DigestInput {
  projectId: string;
  activity: string; // the day's task changes and comments, as text
}

interface BatchLine {
  custom_id: string; // how results are matched back: output order is not guaranteed
  method: "POST";
  url: "/v1/responses";
  body: OpenAI.Responses.ResponseCreateParamsNonStreaming;
}

const DIGEST_INSTRUCTIONS =
  "Write a short digest of today's activity in this TaskFlow project: completed work, new blockers, overdue tasks.";

export function buildBatchFile(model: string, inputs: DigestInput[]): string {
  return inputs
    .map((input): BatchLine => ({
      custom_id: input.projectId, // unique within the batch; the day is in the batch metadata
      method: "POST",
      url: "/v1/responses",
      body: { model, instructions: DIGEST_INSTRUCTIONS, input: input.activity, max_output_tokens: 400, store: false },
    }))
    .map((line) => JSON.stringify(line))
    .join("\n");
}

export async function submitDigestBatch(client: OpenAI, jsonl: string, day: string): Promise<string> {
  const file = await client.files.create({
    file: await toFile(Buffer.from(jsonl, "utf8"), `digests-${day}.jsonl`),
    purpose: "batch",
  });
  const batch = await client.batches.create({
    input_file_id: file.id,
    endpoint: "/v1/responses",
    completion_window: "24h",
    metadata: { job: "nightly-digests", day },
  });
  return batch.id; // store it; a later job collects the results
}

export interface DigestResult {
  projectId: string;
  text?: string;
  error?: string;
}

// Called by a scheduled job every few minutes until the batch is final.
export async function collectDigestBatch(client: OpenAI, batchId: string): Promise<DigestResult[] | null> {
  const batch = await client.batches.retrieve(batchId);
  if (["validating", "in_progress", "finalizing", "cancelling"].includes(batch.status)) return null; // not yet
  if (batch.status === "failed") throw new Error(`Batch ${batchId} failed validation`);

  const results: DigestResult[] = [];
  // "completed", "expired" and "cancelled" batches can all have partial output.
  for (const fileId of [batch.output_file_id, batch.error_file_id]) {
    if (!fileId) continue;
    const body = await (await client.files.content(fileId)).text();
    for (const line of body.split("\n").filter(Boolean)) results.push(parseResultLine(line));
  }
  return results;
}

export function parseResultLine(line: string): DigestResult {
  const row = JSON.parse(line) as {
    custom_id: string;
    response: { status_code: number; body: OpenAI.Responses.Response } | null;
    error: { code: string; message: string } | null;
  };
  const projectId = row.custom_id;
  if (row.error || !row.response || row.response.status_code !== 200) {
    return { projectId, error: row.error?.message ?? `HTTP ${row.response?.status_code}` };
  }
  // output_text is an SDK convenience getter; raw JSON needs the output items.
  const text = row.response.body.output
    .flatMap((item) => (item.type === "message" ? item.content : []))
    .flatMap((part) => (part.type === "output_text" ? [part.text] : []))
    .join("");
  return { projectId, text };
}
  • Each line of the input file is a complete request with its own custom_id, HTTP method, endpoint path, and body. The whole file must target the endpoint given to batches.create.
  • toFile turns an in-memory buffer into an upload; for very large jobs, write the JSONL to disk and stream it instead.
  • Results arrive in two files: the output file holds lines with an HTTP status and body (a 429 or 500 on one line is possible), and the error file holds lines that could not be processed at all. Both are parsed into the same result shape.
  • The collector returns null while the batch is running, so a scheduler can call it every few minutes without special cases.

The Anthropic version sends the requests directly in the create call and streams results back:

// src/jobs/nightly-digests-anthropic.ts
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import type { DigestInput, DigestResult } from "./nightly-digests.js";

const anthropic = new Anthropic();

export async function submit(inputs: DigestInput[]): Promise<string> {
  const batch = await anthropic.messages.batches.create({
    requests: inputs.map((input) => ({
      custom_id: input.projectId, // results come back in any order
      params: {
        model: process.env.ANTHROPIC_MODEL!,
        max_tokens: 400,
        system: "Write a short digest of today's activity in this TaskFlow project.",
        messages: [{ role: "user", content: input.activity }],
      },
    })),
  });
  return batch.id;
}

export async function collect(batchId: string): Promise<DigestResult[] | null> {
  const batch = await anthropic.messages.batches.retrieve(batchId);
  if (batch.processing_status !== "ended") return null;
  const results: DigestResult[] = [];
  for await (const row of await anthropic.messages.batches.results(batchId)) {
    if (row.result.type === "succeeded") {
      const text = row.result.message.content.flatMap((b) => (b.type === "text" ? [b.text] : [])).join("");
      results.push({ projectId: row.custom_id, text });
    } else {
      results.push({ projectId: row.custom_id, error: row.result.type }); // errored, canceled, or expired
    }
  }
  return results;
}

docs.title: Testing both features without a provider
docs.text:
The pure parts run locally: the prefix fingerprint stays the same across conversation turns and changes when the documents' version changes, and the hit ratio of a usage object with 9,600 cached tokens out of 12,000 is 0.8. The batch flow runs against a stub server that implements the files and batches endpoints, with the real OpenAI SDK. Output of that test run (no provider called):

fingerprint  426c41d51fa2 for turn 1 and turn 3; different for docs v13
batch        uploaded 3 lines with purpose "batch"; batch_1 created
poll 1       in_progress -> collector returned null
poll 2       completed -> 3 results matched by custom_id:
             p1  text: "Done: 3 tasks."
             p2  error: "HTTP 429"            (line-level failure in the output file)
             p3  error: "max_output_tokens too large"  (from the error file)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Order prompts from most stable to least stable: tools, instructions, shared documents, conversation, then the new input.
  • Keep timestamps, user names, request ids, and retrieved chunks out of the cached prefix.
  • Serialize tool definitions and JSON deterministically, and version shared documents.
  • Keep conversations append-only; summarize old turns rarely and on purpose.
  • Log cached and cache-write tokens and a prefix fingerprint for every request; alert when the hit ratio drops.
  • Choose cache lifetimes from measured reuse intervals; long lifetimes cost more to write.
  • Send the first request with a new prefix before a parallel burst on providers where entries appear only after the first response starts.
  • Move work nobody waits for to batch APIs, match results by custom_id, retry only failed lines, and make submission idempotent.
  • Consider flex service tiers for work that should finish in minutes and can tolerate slower responses and occasional capacity errors.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Caching was enabled but the bill did not change. Detect: cached_tokens (or cache_read_input_tokens) stays at zero; the prefix fingerprint differs on every request. Cause: a volatile value (current time, request id, user name) or non-deterministic JSON in the prefix. Fix: move volatile content to the end, sort and stabilize serialization, and add the fingerprint to logs.
  • The hit ratio collapsed after a deploy. Detect: cached tokens drop to zero at the deploy time for every route. Cause: a changed tool schema or instruction text invalidated every cached prefix (expected once), or a new field was added to the start of the prompt (a lasting regression). Fix: expect one cold period after prompt changes; if it persists, compare fingerprints before and after.
  • Costs rose after switching to the 1-hour (or 12-hour) cache. Detect: cache-write tokens are high and reads per write are low. Cause: entries are written at the higher long-lifetime rate but rarely reused. Fix: measure reuse intervals per route and use the default lifetime unless reuse spans it.
  • A burst of identical requests all miss the cache. Detect: parallel requests at the same moment each show cache writes. Cause: the entry becomes available only after the first response starts. Fix: send one request first (or pre-warm where the provider supports it) and release the rest after it starts.
  • Some projects never get their nightly digest. Detect: the batch ended with fewer successes than lines; failed lines are not retried. Cause: line-level errors or an expired batch, with results matched by position or only the output file read. Fix: read both files, match by custom_id, and resubmit failed lines.
  • The nightly batch ran twice. Detect: two batches with the same metadata day; doubled batch spend. Cause: the scheduler retried submission after a timeout without checking for an existing batch. Fix: record the submission per day with a unique key before submitting, and look it up on retry.
  • The explicit Gemini cache bill keeps growing. Detect: storage charges for caches nobody uses. Cause: caches created per request or per user with long TTLs. Fix: one cache per shared context and version, short TTLs, and deletion when the content changes.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Prompt caching: Reusing the provider's processed state for an identical prompt prefix across requests.
  • Prefix: The beginning of a prompt, up to a cache breakpoint.
  • Cache breakpoint: The position up to which a prefix is written to the cache.
  • Automatic (implicit) caching: Caching where the provider chooses what to cache with little or no configuration.
  • Explicit caching: Caching where the developer marks breakpoints or creates cache objects.
  • Cache write: Storing a new prefix, usually billed above the normal input rate.
  • Cache read (hit): Reusing a stored prefix, billed at a fraction of the input rate.
  • TTL: How long a cache entry or batch result remains available.
  • Batch API: An asynchronous interface that processes many requests within a window at a lower price.
  • custom_id: The identifier that matches each batch result to its request.
  • Flex tier: A cheaper service tier for synchronous requests with slower and less guaranteed processing.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming caching works because it was "turned on", without reading the usage fields.
  • Putting the date or user details in the system prompt.
  • Expecting a shared paragraph in the middle of prompts to be cached.
  • Rewriting earlier conversation turns on every request.
  • Using long cache lifetimes for prefixes that are rarely reused.
  • Firing a burst of parallel requests with a brand-new prefix.
  • Matching batch results by position instead of custom_id.
  • Ignoring the error file and line-level failures of a batch.
  • Using a batch API for anything a user is waiting for.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can a prompt cache only reuse a prefix, and what does that imply for the order of a prompt?
  2. Compare OpenAI's implicit and explicit modes with Anthropic's automatic and explicit caching. Who decides where the breakpoint goes in each?
  3. A request shows cache_creation_input_tokens: 0 and cache_read_input_tokens: 0 although cache_control is set. Give two possible reasons.
  4. Using a write multiplier of 1.25 and a read multiplier of 0.1, what is the relative input cost of reusing a 10,000-token prefix for 20 requests with 500-token questions, compared with no caching? (Cached: 12,500 + 19 x 1,000 + 10,000 = 41,500; uncached: 20 x 10,500 = 210,000; about 20%.)
  5. Where should TaskFlow put today's date if the assistant needs it, and why?
  6. Which TaskFlow workloads belong in a batch API, and which do not?
  7. How do you make nightly batch submission safe against a scheduler that retries?
  8. When would you choose a flex service tier over a batch API?

docs.title: Streaming Responses End to End
docs.text:
When a TaskFlow user opens a meeting and asks for a summary, the first words should appear in well under a second, even though the whole summary takes several seconds to generate. That is streaming: the model provider sends text as it is produced, and every hop between the provider and the browser passes it on immediately. This lesson follows one streamed answer end to end: the provider's server-sent events, the SDK's stream, an Express relay that re-encodes them for TaskFlow Web, the reverse proxy that must not buffer them, and the browser code that reads them. It then covers cancelling generation when the user leaves, backpressure, and what to do when a stream fails halfway through.

Rendering streamed text in React (stop and regenerate buttons, scroll behavior, partial markdown) is covered in frontend patterns for AI features; this lesson owns the backend relay and the wire format.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Two numbers describe a model response: time to first token (how long until anything appears) and total generation time (how long until the last token). Generation speed is bounded by the model, so a 600-token summary takes the same total time whether it is streamed or not. What streaming changes is perception and control: the user reads from the first second instead of staring at a spinner, can stop a summary that is going in the wrong direction, and a long answer never runs into a non-streaming request timeout.

Streaming also moves failures to awkward places. The HTTP status 200 is sent before the model has produced anything, so an error that happens halfway cannot change the status code. A proxy that buffers responses silently turns the stream back into one late response. A user who closes the tab leaves the provider generating (and billing) tokens nobody will read, unless the cancel travels back through every hop. Each of these is invisible in a quick local test and obvious in production.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI streaming events. The streaming responses guide describes the Responses API's typed server-sent events, such as response.created, response.output_text.delta, response.completed, and error, which clients handle by type instead of parsing raw chunks.
  • Anthropic streaming events. The streaming messages page documents the event flow (message_start, content_block_delta, message_delta, message_stop), ping events that can appear at any time, and error events such as overloaded_error that arrive inside a stream that started with 200.
  • nginx buffering by default. The proxy module documentation shows proxy_buffering on as the default, explains that buffering can be switched off per response with an X-Accel-Buffering: no header, and that proxy_read_timeout (60 seconds by default) applies between two successive reads.
  • Compression and SSE. The README of the Express compression middleware warns that it "does not work out of the box with server-sent events" because compression buffers output, and that res.flush() must be called to push data to the client.
  • The SSE format. The HTML standard's server-sent events section defines the event: and data: fields, blank-line-terminated messages, and comment lines starting with a colon.

Popular tools and providers: the streaming helpers in the OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google Gen AI SDKs; the Vercel AI SDK (streamText and UI message streams); nginx, cloud load balancers, and CDNs on the path; fetch with ReadableStream in the browser.

docs.title: Three streams in a row
docs.text:
A streamed answer passes through three different streams, and each one is your responsibility to keep flowing:

  1. Provider to backend. The provider sends server-sent events (SSE) over one long HTTP response. The SDK parses them into typed event objects and exposes them as an async iterator.
  2. Backend to proxy. The Express route writes its own SSE events to its response as soon as each provider event arrives.
  3. Proxy to browser. nginx, a load balancer, or a CDN forwards the bytes. TaskFlow Web reads them with fetch and a stream reader.

The relay re-encodes instead of piping the provider's bytes through. The provider's events contain internal ids, reasoning summaries, tool-call fragments, and usage fields the browser should not depend on, and their format differs per provider. TaskFlow defines three events of its own:

Event Data Meaning delta {"text": "..."} Append this text done {"status": "completed" or "incomplete", ...} The answer ended normally, or hit the output limit error {"message": "...", "partial": true} Generation failed; any text shown so far is incomplete

A small vocabulary like this survives a change of provider or model without touching TaskFlow Web.

docs.title: What the providers send
docs.text:
Provider and API Text arrives in End of answer Errors inside the stream OpenAI Responses (stream: true) response.output_text.delta (delta) response.completed, or response.incomplete with a reason such as max_output_tokens response.failed, error Anthropic Messages (stream: true) content_block_delta with a text_delta message_delta (with stop_reason), then message_stop error events such as overloaded_error; ping events in between Gemini (generateContentStream) Each chunk's text The iterator ends; check finishReason on the final chunk's candidate Thrown by the iterator

Usage (token counts) arrives at the end: in response.completed for OpenAI and in the cumulative usage of message_delta for Anthropic. Quotas and cost tracking from calling model APIs from a backend must read it there, not from a non-streaming response object.

docs.title: The SSE wire format
docs.text:
SSE is plain text over a normal HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream. Each message is a set of field: value lines ended by a blank line:

event: delta
data: {"text":"Decision: ship v2 "}

: ping

event: done
data: {"status":"completed"}
  • event: names the message type; without it the type is message.
  • data: carries the payload. Several data: lines join with newlines, so encoding each payload as one line of JSON avoids framing bugs when the text itself contains newlines.
  • A line starting with : is a comment. Comments are ideal heartbeats: they keep idle timers on proxies from firing and are ignored by parsers.

The browser's built-in EventSource only makes GET requests and cannot send custom headers such as Authorization, and it reconnects automatically, which would restart a paid generation. TaskFlow Web therefore uses fetch with POST and reads the body as a stream.

docs.title: Headers, flushing, and compression
docs.text:
Four details decide whether the first byte leaves the server promptly:

  • Content-Type: text/event-stream tells every hop what this is.
  • Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform stops caches from storing it and intermediaries from transforming (and buffering) it.
  • X-Accel-Buffering: no asks nginx not to buffer this one response, even if buffering stays on for the rest of the site.
  • res.flushHeaders() sends the status and headers immediately, before the first model token, so the browser knows the request was accepted.

Response compression is the classic hidden buffer. The compression middleware collects output to compress it efficiently, so either exclude stream routes from it or call res.flush() after every write. Validation, authentication, and authorization must all happen before flushHeaders(): once the 200 is out, failures can only be reported as events.

docs.title: Proxies, load balancers, and timeouts
docs.text:
With proxy_buffering on, nginx reads the upstream response into buffers of one memory page (4 or 8 KB, depending on the platform) and forwards them as they fill or when the response ends. Small SSE events then arrive in bursts. Turning buffering off for the stream location, or sending X-Accel-Buffering: no from Express, restores token-by-token delivery.

Idle timeouts are the second trap. nginx closes an upstream connection when nothing arrives for proxy_read_timeout (60 seconds by default, measured between two reads, not for the whole response), and cloud load balancers have their own idle timeouts (60 seconds by default on an AWS Application Load Balancer, as covered in load balancers in depth). A reasoning model can think silently for longer than that before its first text token. A heartbeat comment every 15 seconds keeps every hop's idle timer from firing without the browser seeing anything. Since nginx 1.29.7 proxy_http_version defaults to 1.1; on older versions set it explicitly, because HTTP/1.0 upstream connections handle long responses poorly.

docs.title: Aborting when the client disconnects
docs.text:
A provider keeps generating as long as the connection to it is open, and output tokens are billed whether or not anyone reads them. The cancel must therefore travel back through every hop:

  1. The browser aborts its fetch (Stop button) or the tab closes.
  2. nginx, with the default proxy_ignore_client_abort off, closes its connection to Express.
  3. Express emits close on the response before it finished. The route checks res.writableFinished to tell a disconnect from a normal end, and calls controller.abort().
  4. The SDK request was created with that signal, so the SDK closes its connection to the provider, and generation stops.

One SDK detail matters here. When the OpenAI SDK's stream is aborted, its iterator ends quietly instead of throwing (the source comments say it should "exit without throwing"), so code after the for await loop must check signal.aborted to know whether the answer finished. The relay below does exactly that and records the summary as cancelled.

The worked example shows why this matters for cost: if 1,000 users a day close the tab 2 seconds into a 600-token summary that streams at 100 tokens per second, the remaining 400 tokens each add up to 400,000 output tokens a day that are generated, billed, and thrown away when the abort is not wired up.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text: res.write() returns false when the socket's buffer is full, which happens when a client on a slow mobile connection reads more slowly than the model writes. Ignoring the return value keeps queueing data in the Node process's memory. The relay awaits the drain event (or close, if the client leaves) before writing more, which also slows how fast it consumes the provider stream.

docs.title: Partial failures
docs.text:
Once streaming has started, failures fall into a few shapes, and each one needs a deliberate response:

What happened How the relay sees it What it sends What it stores Output limit reached response.incomplete (max_output_tokens) or stop_reason: "max_tokens" done with status: "incomplete" Text, status incomplete Provider error mid-stream response.failed, error, or an Anthropic error event error with partial: true Text so far, status failed Upstream connection dropped The iterator throws error with partial: true Text so far, status failed User left Response close before finishing Nothing (nobody is listening) Text so far, status cancelled A proxy cut the stream Nothing on the server, or a write error Nothing arrives Depends where it was cut

The browser applies one rule: an answer is complete only if a done event arrived. A stream that ends without done was cut off somewhere, however it ended, and the UI should say so and offer to try again.

Retrying a failed stream is not the same as retrying a normal request. The user has already seen part of the answer, so a silent retry would show different text, or the same text twice. The usual choices are:

  • Start over visibly. Clear the partial text and generate again (a "Retry" button). Simple and honest.
  • Resume where it stopped. OpenAI's background mode (background: true) keeps a response on the provider side for roughly 10 minutes, and responses.retrieve(id, { stream: true, starting_after: <sequence number> }) resumes the event stream after a dropped connection, as described in the background mode guide. This requires storing the response id and the last sequence number, and it is a provider-specific feature.

Never store a partial answer as if it were complete: a summary saved with status completed after a dropped connection is a silent data-quality bug that resurfaces later as "the summary is missing the action items".

docs.title: Timeouts for streams
docs.text: A total-time timeout makes little sense for a stream that legitimately runs for a minute. Two other limits work better: time to first byte (if the provider has not started within N seconds, fail or fall back before anything was shown) and maximum idle gap (if no event arrives for N seconds, the stream is stuck). Falling back to another model is only safe before the first delta has been sent to the browser.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Stream? Why Summaries, answers, drafts shown to a waiting user Yes First words in under a second; Stop saves cost Long outputs (thousands of tokens) Yes Avoids long non-streaming timeouts Structured output the server must validate before use Usually no The result is only usable once complete; stream progress events instead of tokens Background jobs (nightly summaries, batch work) No Nobody is watching; use a queue or a batch API Very short answers (a label, a yes or no) No The overhead buys nothing A path through proxies you cannot configure Test first A buffering hop removes the benefit

docs.title: The Express relay
docs.text:
// src/routes/summary-stream.ts
// POST /api/meetings/:id/summary/stream: relay a model stream to the browser as SSE.
import express, { type Request, type Response } from "express";
import OpenAI from "openai";

export interface SummaryStore {
  loadNotes(userId: string, meetingId: string): Promise<string | null>;
  saveSummary(meetingId: string, text: string, status: "completed" | "incomplete" | "failed" | "cancelled"): Promise<void>;
}

const INSTRUCTIONS =
  "Summarize the meeting notes for the TaskFlow project team: decisions, owners, open questions.";
const HEARTBEAT_MS = 15_000;

// One SSE event. JSON keeps newlines inside the data out of the framing.
function sseEvent(event: string, data: unknown): string {
  return `event: ${event}\ndata: ${JSON.stringify(data)}\n\n`;
}

// Respect backpressure: wait for "drain" when the socket buffer is full.
async function write(res: Response, chunk: string): Promise<void> {
  if (!res.write(chunk)) {
    await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
      const done = () => {
        res.off("drain", done);
        res.off("close", done);
        resolve();
      };
      res.on("drain", done);
      res.on("close", done);
    });
  }
}

export function summaryStreamRouter(deps: { client: OpenAI; store: SummaryStore; model: string }): express.Router {
  const router = express.Router();

  router.post("/api/meetings/:id/summary/stream", async (req: Request, res: Response) => {
    const userId = res.locals.userId as string | undefined;
    const meetingId = String(req.params.id);
    if (!userId) return res.status(401).json({ error: "Sign in first." });
    const notes = await deps.store.loadNotes(userId, meetingId); // authorization happens here
    if (!notes) return res.status(404).json({ error: "Meeting not found." });

    // Errors before this point are normal JSON responses. After it, only SSE events.
    res.status(200).set({
      "Content-Type": "text/event-stream; charset=utf-8",
      "Cache-Control": "no-cache, no-transform",
      "X-Accel-Buffering": "no", // tell nginx not to buffer this response
    });
    res.flushHeaders();

    const controller = new AbortController();
    res.on("close", () => {
      if (!res.writableFinished) controller.abort(); // the browser went away
    });
    const heartbeat = setInterval(() => res.write(": ping\n\n"), HEARTBEAT_MS);

    let text = "";
    let status: "completed" | "incomplete" | "failed" | "cancelled" = "failed";
    try {
      const stream = await deps.client.responses.create(
        { model: deps.model, instructions: INSTRUCTIONS, input: notes, max_output_tokens: 800, stream: true, store: false },
        { signal: controller.signal, timeout: 60_000 },
      );
      for await (const event of stream) {
        if (event.type === "response.output_text.delta") {
          text += event.delta;
          await write(res, sseEvent("delta", { text: event.delta }));
        } else if (event.type === "response.completed") {
          status = "completed";
          await write(res, sseEvent("done", { status, usage: event.response.usage }));
        } else if (event.type === "response.incomplete") {
          status = "incomplete";
          const reason = event.response.incomplete_details?.reason ?? "unknown";
          await write(res, sseEvent("done", { status, reason }));
        } else if (event.type === "response.failed" || event.type === "error") {
          await write(res, sseEvent("error", { message: "The summary stopped early.", partial: text.length > 0 }));
        }
      }
      // An aborted SDK stream ends the loop quietly instead of throwing.
      if (controller.signal.aborted && status !== "completed") status = "cancelled";
    } catch (err) {
      if (controller.signal.aborted) {
        status = "cancelled"; // client left; provider connection already closed by the SDK
      } else {
        console.error(JSON.stringify({ msg: "summary_stream_failed", meetingId, error: String(err) }));
        await write(res, sseEvent("error", { message: "The summary stopped early.", partial: text.length > 0 }));
      }
    } finally {
      clearInterval(heartbeat);
      await deps.store.saveSummary(meetingId, text, status); // never store a partial as completed
      res.end();
    }
  });

  return router;
}
  • loadNotes takes the user id, so authorization happens before the 200 is committed; a user cannot stream another team's meeting.
  • The timeout passed to the SDK covers waiting for the response to start; once events flow, the heartbeat and the proxies' idle timeouts take over.
  • store: false and the meeting text: summaries of private notes are exactly the content whose retention matters; see choosing models and providers.
  • The finally block runs for every outcome, so the status written to MongoDB always matches what the user actually received.

docs.title: The nginx location for the stream
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow.conf (excerpt)
location /api/ {
    proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;          # default since nginx 1.29.7; explicit for older versions
    proxy_set_header Connection "";  # keep upstream connections reusable
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
}

location ~ ^/api/meetings/[^/]+/summary/stream$ {
    proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Connection "";
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_buffering off;             # pass each event through as it arrives
    proxy_read_timeout 120s;         # longer than the longest silent gap; heartbeats every 15 s
    gzip off;                        # compression buffers output
}

The X-Accel-Buffering: no header from Express already disables buffering for this response, so the dedicated location is belt and braces; it also documents the stream route for whoever maintains the proxy. Other nginx basics for TaskFlow are in running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.title: Reading the stream in TaskFlow Web
docs.text:
// src/lib/read-sse.ts (TaskFlow Web)
// Parse a fetch() response body as server-sent events. EventSource cannot
// POST or send an Authorization header, so the web app reads the stream itself.
export interface SseMessage {
  event: string;
  data: string;
}

export async function* readSse(response: Response): AsyncGenerator<SseMessage> {
  if (!response.ok || !response.body) throw new Error(`Stream failed with HTTP ${response.status}`);
  const reader = response.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
  let buffer = "";
  for (;;) {
    const { value, done } = await reader.read();
    if (done) return;
    buffer += value.replace(/\r\n/g, "\n");
    let boundary: number;
    while ((boundary = buffer.indexOf("\n\n")) !== -1) {
      const block = buffer.slice(0, boundary);
      buffer = buffer.slice(boundary + 2);
      let event = "message";
      const data: string[] = [];
      for (const line of block.split("\n")) {
        if (line.startsWith(":")) continue; // comment, e.g. a heartbeat
        if (line.startsWith("event:")) event = line.slice(6).trim();
        else if (line.startsWith("data:")) data.push(line.slice(5).replace(/^ /, ""));
      }
      if (data.length > 0) yield { event, data: data.join("\n") };
    }
  }
}

// Usage: stream a summary; resolve with its final status, or throw if it broke.
export async function streamSummary(
  url: string,
  onText: (t: string) => void,
  signal: AbortSignal,
): Promise<"completed" | "incomplete"> {
  const response = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", signal });
  let status: "completed" | "incomplete" | undefined;
  for await (const msg of readSse(response)) {
    const payload = JSON.parse(msg.data);
    if (msg.event === "delta") onText(payload.text);
    else if (msg.event === "done") status = payload.status;
    else if (msg.event === "error") throw new Error(payload.message);
  }
  // No "done" event means a proxy or the network cut the stream.
  if (!status) throw new Error("The connection closed before the summary finished.");
  return status;
}
  • TextDecoderStream decodes UTF-8 correctly even when a multi-byte character is split across two network chunks; decoding each chunk separately with new TextDecoder().decode(chunk) does not.
  • The parser keeps incomplete blocks in buffer, because an event can be split anywhere between two reads.
  • The signal comes from the Stop button's AbortController; aborting it starts the chain shown in the disconnect diagram.

docs.title: The same relay with other SDKs
docs.text:
// src/ai/stream-equivalents.ts
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai";
import { pipeTextStreamToResponse, streamText, toTextStream } from "ai";
import { openai } from "@ai-sdk/openai";
import type { Response } from "express";

const anthropic = new Anthropic({ maxRetries: 0 });
const genai = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY });

// Anthropic: raw events; text arrives in content_block_delta events of type text_delta.
export async function* anthropicText(notes: string, signal: AbortSignal): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  const stream = await anthropic.messages.create(
    { model: process.env.ANTHROPIC_MODEL!, max_tokens: 800, messages: [{ role: "user", content: notes }], stream: true },
    { signal },
  );
  for await (const event of stream) {
    if (event.type === "content_block_delta" && event.delta.type === "text_delta") yield event.delta.text;
    if (event.type === "message_delta" && event.delta.stop_reason === "max_tokens") yield "\n[truncated]";
  }
}

// Gemini: each chunk is a partial GenerateContentResponse.
export async function* geminiText(notes: string, signal: AbortSignal): AsyncGenerator<string> {
  const stream = await genai.models.generateContentStream({
    model: process.env.GEMINI_CHAT_MODEL!,
    contents: notes,
    config: { maxOutputTokens: 800, abortSignal: signal },
  });
  for await (const chunk of stream) {
    if (chunk.text) yield chunk.text;
  }
}

// Vercel AI SDK: plain text stream piped straight into an Express response.
export async function aiSdkRelay(notes: string, res: Response, signal: AbortSignal): Promise<void> {
  const result = streamText({
    model: openai(process.env.CHAT_MODEL!),
    instructions: "Summarize the meeting notes: decisions, owners, open questions.",
    prompt: notes,
    abortSignal: signal,
  });
  await pipeTextStreamToResponse({ response: res, stream: toTextStream({ stream: result.stream }) });
}

The generator versions plug into the same relay loop: replace the OpenAI event handling with for await (const text of anthropicText(...)). AI SDK 7's standalone pipeTextStreamToResponse helper writes plain text without event framing (the older result.pipeTextStreamToResponse() method is deprecated); the UI message stream (toUIMessageStream with pipeUIMessageStreamToResponse) carries typed parts for the React hooks covered in frontend patterns for AI features.

docs.title: Testing the relay without a provider
docs.text:
A stub server that speaks the provider's SSE format lets the real SDK, the real relay, and the real parser run together locally. The stub reads the scenario from the request and either streams normally, streams slowly, drops the connection after two deltas, or ends with response.incomplete. Results from a run of that test suite against the code on this page (dummy keys, no provider called):

normal      deltas arrived at 99, 143, 189, 234, 279, 325, 375 ms; saved "completed"
slow        browser aborted after 2 deltas; stub saw its connection close after
            4 events of 20; saved "cancelled" with the partial text
drop        stub destroyed the socket after 2 deltas; browser got an "error"
            event; saved "failed" with "Decision: ship v2 "
incomplete  stream ended with response.incomplete; browser resolved "incomplete"
parser      heartbeat comments, CRLF line endings, and an event split across
            two chunks all parsed correctly

The "slow" scenario is the important one: it proves that a closed browser tab really closes the provider connection, which is otherwise hard to see until the bill arrives.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Re-encode provider events into a small event vocabulary of your own (delta, done, error).
  • Authenticate, authorize, and validate before flushHeaders(); after the 200, report problems only as events.
  • Send Cache-Control: no-cache, no-transform and X-Accel-Buffering: no, and keep compression off stream routes.
  • Send a heartbeat comment more often than the shortest idle timeout on the path.
  • Pass an AbortSignal to the SDK and abort it when the response closes early; check the signal after the stream loop.
  • Respect backpressure with drain.
  • Treat an answer as complete only after a done event, and store partial results with an explicit status.
  • Use time-to-first-byte and idle-gap limits instead of a total timeout, and fall back to another model only before the first token was sent.
  • Test streaming through the real proxy chain, not only against localhost.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The whole summary appears at once after several seconds. Detect: curl -N against the API directly streams, but through the public URL it does not; browser dev tools show one large chunk. Cause: proxy buffering, response compression, or a CDN that buffers. Fix: X-Accel-Buffering: no or proxy_buffering off, disable compression on the route, and check CDN settings for streaming.
  • Long answers stop at exactly 60 seconds. Detect: streams end at the same duration; proxy logs show upstream timeouts; the browser receives no done. Cause: an idle or read timeout on nginx or the load balancer while the model was thinking. Fix: heartbeat comments every 15 seconds and timeouts longer than the longest silent gap.
  • Output token spend is much higher than tokens shown to users. Detect: provider usage exceeds the sum of completed summaries; many summaries end as abandoned. Cause: client disconnects are not propagated, so generation continues. Fix: abort on response close, pass the signal to the SDK, and verify with a slow-stream test.
  • Saved summaries are missing their last section. Detect: summaries stored as completed end mid-sentence. Cause: the code saved whatever text it had when the loop ended, without checking for a completion event. Fix: set the status only from completed or incomplete events and store everything else as failed or cancelled.
  • Node memory grows during busy hours. Detect: heap usage rises with concurrent streams; slow mobile clients correlate with spikes. Cause: res.write() return values ignored, so output queues in memory. Fix: await drain, and cap concurrent streams per user.
  • Users see raw JSON or "undefined" when a stream fails. Detect: error reports with fragments of event payloads in the UI. Cause: a mid-stream provider error was forwarded as a delta, or the client did not handle error events. Fix: map provider errors to an error event and handle it explicitly in the client.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Server-sent events (SSE): A text format for a stream of events over one long HTTP response.
  • Time to first token: The delay between sending a request and receiving the first generated text.
  • Delta: A small piece of newly generated text in a stream event.
  • Relay: A backend route that consumes the provider's stream and writes its own stream to the client.
  • Heartbeat: A periodic comment line that keeps idle connections from timing out.
  • Proxy buffering: A proxy collecting response data before passing it on, which delays streamed events.
  • Backpressure: Slowing the producer when the consumer cannot keep up, signalled in Node by write() returning false.
  • Partial failure: A stream that ends with an error after some output was already delivered.
  • Background mode: An OpenAI Responses option that runs a response asynchronously and allows resuming its event stream.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing streaming makes the model faster; it changes when output is seen, not how long generation takes.
  • Using EventSource for a POST endpoint with an Authorization header.
  • Piping the provider's raw events to the browser.
  • Forgetting that the 200 is sent before generation, then trying to return an error status mid-stream.
  • Leaving compression or proxy buffering on for stream routes.
  • Not aborting the provider request when the client disconnects.
  • Saving a partial answer as complete.
  • Retrying silently after some text was already shown.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which two latency numbers describe a model response, and which one does streaming improve?
  2. Why does TaskFlow re-encode provider events instead of forwarding them?
  3. List the headers the relay sends and what each one prevents.
  4. Walk through what happens, hop by hop, when a user closes the tab mid-summary.
  5. Why must code after an OpenAI SDK stream loop check signal.aborted?
  6. A proxy has a 60-second idle timeout and a reasoning model can be silent for 90 seconds before its first token. What breaks, and what are two fixes?
  7. An abandoned summary would have produced 600 tokens; users leave after about 150 tokens on average, 2,000 times a day. How many output tokens a day does aborting save? (2,000 x 450 = 900,000.)
  8. How should TaskFlow Web decide whether a summary is complete, and what should it do if it is not?

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Building features with future data. Compute them point in time (merge_asof, strictly earlier outcomes) and test that flipping future labels changes nothing.
  • Splitting at random when the model predicts the future. Split by time and report the test set once.
  • Reporting accuracy or ROC-AUC alone on rare positives. Add PR-AUC, the base rate, and precision and recall at the chosen threshold.
  • Keeping the 0.5 threshold. Pick it from costs or capacity on validation, version it, and revisit it when the base rate changes.
  • Trusting predict_proba after class weights. Recalibrate on held-out data with FrozenEstimator and CalibratedClassifierCV.
  • Shuffled KFold with several rows per entity. Use GroupKFold; on the same sessions, KFold said 0.958 and GroupKFold 0.725.
  • A rolling z-score on a seasonal metric. Compare each point with the same slot on normal days, using the median and MAD.
  • Judging recommenders on recall alone. Report NDCG, coverage, and new-item recall, and correct in-batch popularity bias with logQ.
