docs.title: Recommender Systems
docs.text:
A recommender system chooses, for one user at one moment, a short list from a catalog too large to browse: the videos on a home page, the products under "customers also bought", or, in TaskFlow, the project templates offered when someone starts a new project. This lesson builds that TaskFlow template recommender from simple to modern.

It covers implicit feedback, the two-stage retrieval and ranking architecture, collaborative filtering (item-item similarity and matrix factorization), content-based filtering, embedding-based retrieval with a two-tower model trained from scratch in NumPy, offline evaluation with recall@k and NDCG, and the cold-start problem for new items and new users. Embedding models and vector indexes are covered in depth in vector databases and indexes.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Recommendations decide what users discover. For TaskFlow, a good template suggestion gets a team productive in minutes and spreads the templates that work; a bad one teaches users to ignore the panel. The same techniques power "related tasks", "suggested assignees", and "docs you may need" in the project-knowledge assistant.

Recommenders also fail in characteristic ways that are easy to miss offline: they recommend only what is already popular, never surface new items, trap users in more of the same, and train on their own output. Knowing the mechanics (what each method can and cannot see) is how you avoid shipping a system that looks accurate on a dashboard and feels stale to users.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• YouTube: two stages. Covington, Adams, and Sargin, Deep Neural Networks for YouTube Recommendations (RecSys 2016), describe one of the largest recommenders in industry, split according to the classic two-stage information retrieval dichotomy: a deep candidate generation model, then a separate deep ranking model.
  • YouTube: two-tower retrieval and sampling bias. Yi and others, Sampling-Bias-Corrected Neural Modeling for Large Corpus Item Recommendations (RecSys 2019), train two-tower networks with in-batch negatives, show that the batch loss is biased against popular items under a power-law item distribution, correct it with streaming item-frequency estimates, and deploy the result to retrieve from tens of millions of videos.
  • Amazon. Smith and Linden, Two Decades of Recommender Systems at Amazon.com (IEEE Internet Computing, 2017), revisit their original article on Amazon's recommendations and how the approach changed as the store grew.
  • Implicit feedback. Hu, Koren, and Volinsky, Collaborative Filtering for Implicit Feedback Datasets (ICDM 2008), point out that clicks and views carry no negative feedback (a user who never watched a show may simply not know it) and treat observations as preferences with varying confidence, in a system that recommended television shows.
  • Cold start by design. Volkovs, Yu, and Poutanen, DropoutNet: Addressing Cold Start in Recommender Systems (NIPS 2017), show that neural recommenders can be trained explicitly for cold start by applying dropout to the preference inputs, so content features learn to stand in for missing history.

Popular tools and providers: scikit-learn and SciPy sparse matrices for baselines, the implicit library (ALS and BPR), LightFM, TensorFlow Recommenders and TorchRec for two-tower and ranking models, LightGBM's LGBMRanker for learning to rank, FAISS, ScaNN, and vector databases for approximate nearest-neighbour retrieval; managed options include Amazon Personalize and Google Cloud's AI Commerce Search (formerly Vertex AI Search for commerce), which covers product recommendations as well as search.

docs.title: Feedback: explicit and implicit
docs.text: Explicit feedback (stars, thumbs) says what users think but is rare. Implicit feedback (used, opened, starred, completed, dwell time) is plentiful but one-sided: an unused template may be unwanted or simply unseen. TaskFlow records "team created a project from this template", a strong positive signal. Everything else is unknown, not negative, which is why recommenders sample negatives and evaluate by ranking rather than by classification accuracy.

docs.title: Two stages: retrieval, then ranking
docs.text:
A large catalog cannot be scored with an expensive model for every request. Production recommenders work in stages:

Stage Job Typical method Measured by Candidate generation (retrieval) Find a few hundred plausible items fast Two-tower plus ANN, item-item CF, popularity, content Recall@k Ranking Order the candidates precisely Gradient-boosted trees or neural rankers with many features NDCG, AUC, online metrics Re-ranking Apply product rules Filters, diversity, freshness, business constraints Guardrail metrics

Retrieval only needs to keep the right items in the candidate set; ranking spends its feature budget on a few hundred items instead of the whole catalog. For a catalog of 600 templates TaskFlow could score everything, but the structure is the same at a million items.

docs.title: Collaborative filtering
docs.text:
Collaborative filtering (CF) recommends from behaviour alone: users who used the same things in the past will want similar things next.

  • Item-item CF: compute the similarity between items from the users who used both (cosine similarity between columns of the user-item matrix), then score each item by its summed similarity to the user's history. It is simple, explainable ("because you used Sprint board"), and easy to precompute.
  • Matrix factorization: approximate the sparse user-item matrix as the product of a user-factor matrix and an item-factor matrix with a few dozen dimensions. Each factor captures a hidden pattern, such as "teams that run formal sprints", that no text describes. Methods include truncated SVD, alternating least squares weighted for implicit feedback, and BPR.

CF's blind spots are the reverse of its strengths: it knows nothing about an item until people use it (item cold start), nothing about a user without history (user cold start), and it amplifies whatever is already popular.

docs.title: Content-based filtering
docs.text:
Content-based filtering describes items by their own features (title, tags, topic, category, author, embeddings of the description) and builds each user's profile from the items they used. Scoring is a similarity between the profile and each item. It handles new items from day one and can explain itself ("matches your engineering templates"), but it only finds more of what the user already did, and it cannot see what the text does not say: two "Sprint board" templates may differ completely in quality.

Hybrids combine both: blend scores, use content features inside a factorization model, or let a neural model learn from IDs and content together. The two-tower model below is one such hybrid.

docs.title: Embedding-based retrieval and the two-tower model
docs.text:
A two-tower model has a user (query) tower and an item (candidate) tower. Each maps its inputs to an embedding of the same size, and the score is their dot product. Because the towers do not interact until that dot product, item embeddings can be computed offline, stored in an approximate nearest-neighbour index, and searched in milliseconds with the user embedding computed at request time.

Training details that matter:

  • In-batch negatives. Each training example is a (user, item) pair that happened. The other items in the same batch serve as negatives, and a softmax over the batch is the loss. It is cheap and works well.
  • Sampling-bias correction. Popular items appear in many batches, so they are used as negatives far more often than rare ones and get pushed down. Subtracting log(frequency) of each item from its logit during training (the "logQ correction") removes that bias.
  • ID embeddings and cold start. A learned ID embedding per item captures what content cannot, but new items have none. Training some examples with the ID hidden (ID dropout) teaches the content path to carry the prediction alone, which is what new items need.
  • No leakage from the target. The user features for a training pair must not include the target item itself.

Serving is a vector search: see vector databases and indexes for HNSW and IVF indexes, recall trade-offs, and filtering. Text embeddings from a modern embedding model can replace TF-IDF as item features without changing the architecture.

docs.title: Ranking
docs.text: The ranking stage scores a few hundred candidates with a richer model, often gradient-boosted trees trained with a learning-to-rank objective (LightGBM's LGBMRanker with objective="lambdarank") or a neural model. It can use features retrieval cannot afford: how recently the team used a similar template, the project's size, the time of year, the candidate's retrieval scores from each source, and its historical click rate in this position. Labels come from logged impressions: shown and used, shown and ignored.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Offline, hold out each user's most recent interactions, recommend from the rest, and check whether the held-out items appear near the top.

Metric Measures Note Recall@k Share of held-out items found in the top k The main retrieval metric Precision@k Share of the top k that were held-out items Bounded by how many items are held out NDCG@k Recall weighted by position (higher is better) Rewards putting hits at the top MRR Average of 1 / rank of the first hit When one good item is enough Coverage Share of the catalog ever recommended Low values mean popularity bias Novelty and diversity How unpopular or varied the lists are Guardrails against "more of the same"

Split by time, not at random: a random split lets the model see a user's future to predict their past. Exclude items the user already has from the candidates, compare everything against a popularity baseline, and report cold-start segments separately.

Online, the real measure is behaviour: click-through and adoption rate of recommended templates, projects that stay active, and longer-term retention, compared in an A/B test. Offline gains often shrink online because offline data only contains items the old system showed (exposure bias), and a model trained on its own recommendations keeps reinforcing them (feedback loops). Keep a small share of traffic for exploration (random or diverse candidates) so the logs contain evidence about items the current model would never show.

docs.title: Cold start
docs.text: Case What is missing Strategies New item Interaction history Content features or embeddings, ID dropout in training, a guaranteed exploration slot, editorial picks New user History Popular items in the user's context (team size, industry), an onboarding question ("what do you manage?"), session-based signals from the first clicks New system Everything Popularity and rules first; log impressions from day one so a model has data later

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Approach A small catalog and little data Popularity per segment, rules, and editorial lists Plenty of interactions, mostly known items Item-item CF or matrix factorization Many new or long-tail items, rich item text Content-based or a hybrid with content features Large catalog, many signals, strict latency Two-tower retrieval with ANN, then a ranking model Recommendations with legal or safety impact Transparent rules and human review; a model only as an input Very few users or items Do not build a recommender; a curated list is better

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: Tested with Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5, pandas 3.1.1, and scikit-learn 1.9.1 in November 2026. The data is synthetic: each simulated user has a preference over 8 topics, visible in template titles, and over 6 hidden "ways of working" that no text reveals, and template popularity follows a long-tailed distribution.

docs.title: A synthetic template catalog and usage log
docs.text:
# ml/make_interactions.py: synthetic TaskFlow template catalog and who used which template
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
TOPICS = {
    "engineering": ["sprint", "bug", "release", "code review", "incident", "API"],
    "marketing": ["campaign", "content", "SEO", "launch", "newsletter", "social"],
    "sales": ["pipeline", "lead", "deal", "account", "quota", "demo"],
    "design": ["wireframe", "user research", "design review", "prototype", "brand", "UX"],
    "hr": ["onboarding", "hiring", "interview", "offboarding", "review cycle", "policy"],
    "finance": ["budget", "invoice", "expense", "forecast", "audit", "payroll"],
    "support": ["ticket", "escalation", "knowledge base", "SLA", "customer", "FAQ"],
    "operations": ["vendor", "inventory", "facilities", "procurement", "travel", "office"],
}
KINDS = ["template", "checklist", "board", "tracker", "playbook", "plan"]
names = list(TOPICS)

n_items, n_new, n_users = 600, 60, 2_000
item_topic = rng.integers(0, len(names), n_items)
item_style = rng.integers(0, 6, n_items)                          # hidden: way of working, not in the text
items = pd.DataFrame({
    "item": np.arange(n_items),
    "topic": [names[t] for t in item_topic],
    "title": [f"{rng.choice(TOPICS[names[t]])} {rng.choice(KINDS)}".capitalize() for t in item_topic],
    "is_new": np.arange(n_items) >= n_items - n_new,              # added after the training cutoff
})
popularity = rng.pareto(1.2, n_items) + 1                          # a long tail of rarely used items

rows = []
for user in range(n_users):
    taste = rng.dirichlet(np.full(len(names), 0.15))              # most users care about 1-2 topics
    style = rng.dirichlet(np.full(6, 0.2))                        # and work in one or two styles
    weights = taste[item_topic] * style[item_style] * popularity ** 0.7
    n_events = int(rng.integers(8, 40))
    chosen = rng.choice(n_items, size=n_events, replace=False, p=weights / weights.sum())
    old = chosen[~items["is_new"].to_numpy()[chosen]]
    new = chosen[items["is_new"].to_numpy()[chosen]]
    order = list(rng.permutation(old)) + list(new)                # new items can only come last
    for step, item in enumerate(order):
        rows.append((user, int(item), step))

events = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["user", "item", "step"])
Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
items.to_csv("data/items.csv", index=False)
events.to_csv("data/events.csv", index=False)
print(f"{len(items)} items ({n_new} new), {n_users} users, {len(events)} events")
print(items.sample(4, random_state=1)[["item", "topic", "title"]].to_string(index=False))

$ python make_interactions.py
600 items (60 new), 2000 users, 47138 events
 item     topic             title
  446     sales   Quota checklist
  404    design     Brand tracker
  509 marketing Content checklist
  455        hr   Hiring playbook

docs.title: The split, item features, and the metrics
docs.text:
# ml/rec_common.py: leave-last-two-out split, item text features, and top-k evaluation
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer

items = pd.read_csv("data/items.csv")
events = pd.read_csv("data/events.csv")
n_users, n_items = events["user"].max() + 1, len(items)
is_new = items["is_new"].to_numpy()

last = events.groupby("user")["step"].transform("max")
test = events[events["step"] > last - 2]                        # each user's two most recent
train = events[(events["step"] <= last - 2) & ~is_new[events["item"]]]   # new items: unseen

X = np.zeros((n_users, n_items), dtype=np.float32)              # user x item, 1 = used
X[train["user"], train["item"]] = 1.0
truth = test.groupby("user")["item"].apply(set)

text = items["title"] + " " + items["topic"]                    # what a new template comes with
content = TfidfVectorizer().fit_transform(text).toarray().astype(np.float32)
content /= np.linalg.norm(content, axis=1, keepdims=True)


def evaluate(scores, k=10):
    """Recall@k and NDCG@k over each user's two held-out items, plus catalog coverage."""
    scores = np.where(X > 0, -np.inf, scores)                   # never re-recommend used items
    top = np.argsort(-scores, axis=1)[:, :k]
    recall, ndcg, cold_hits, cold_total = [], [], 0, 0
    for u, held in truth.items():
        ranked = list(top[u])
        hits = [1 if i in held else 0 for i in ranked]
        recall.append(sum(hits) / len(held))
        ideal = sum(1 / np.log2(r + 2) for r in range(len(held)))
        ndcg.append(sum(h / np.log2(r + 2) for r, h in enumerate(hits)) / ideal)
        for i in held:
            if is_new[i]:
                cold_total += 1
                cold_hits += i in ranked
    return {f"recall@{k}": np.mean(recall), f"NDCG@{k}": np.mean(ndcg),
            "coverage": len(np.unique(top)) / n_items, "new-item recall": cold_hits / cold_total}

Every user's two most recent templates are the test set. The 60 new templates never appear in training: they model templates published after the cutoff, the item cold-start case. Item features are TF-IDF vectors of title and topic, normalized so dot products are cosine similarities.

docs.title: Popularity, collaborative filtering, and content-based filtering
docs.text:
# ml/recommend.py: popularity, item-item collaborative filtering, matrix factorization, content-based
import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD

from rec_common import X, content, evaluate, n_users, test, train

print(f"train events {len(train)}, test events {len(test)}, users {n_users}")
results = {}

popularity = X.sum(axis=0)                                       # how many users used each item
results["most popular"] = np.tile(popularity, (n_users, 1))

norms = np.linalg.norm(X, axis=0) + 1e-9
item_sim = (X.T @ X) / np.outer(norms, norms)                    # cosine between item columns
np.fill_diagonal(item_sim, 0)
results["item-item CF"] = X @ item_sim                           # sum of similarities to my items

svd = TruncatedSVD(n_components=32, random_state=0).fit(X)      # low-rank user and item factors
V = svd.components_.T                                            # item factors (n_items x 32)
results["matrix factorization"] = (X @ V) @ V.T

profile = X @ content                                            # the user's taste in text space
results["content-based"] = profile @ content.T

print(f"{'model':22} {'recall@10':>9} {'NDCG@10':>8} {'coverage':>8} {'new-item recall':>15}")
for name, scores in results.items():
    m = evaluate(scores)
    print(f"{name:22} {m['recall@10']:9.3f} {m['NDCG@10']:8.3f} {m['coverage']:8.2f} "
          f"{m['new-item recall']:15.3f}")

$ python recommend.py
train events 41548, test events 4000, users 2000
model                  recall@10  NDCG@10 coverage new-item recall
most popular               0.019    0.013     0.03           0.000
item-item CF               0.113    0.081     0.90           0.000
matrix factorization       0.106    0.079     0.88           0.000
content-based              0.077    0.041     1.00           0.079

Reading the results:

  • Popularity is a weak baseline here (recall@10 0.019) because users care about different topics, and it recommends the same 3% of the catalog to everyone.
  • Item-item CF and matrix factorization are about six times better. They see the hidden "way of working" that no title reveals, because users who share it use the same templates.
  • Content-based is weaker on known items (0.077) but is the only one of the four that ever recommends a new template (new-item recall 0.079).
  • Coverage shows how much of the catalog each method uses; all but popularity spread recommendations widely.

The matrix factorization here is truncated SVD of the 0/1 matrix, a strong and simple baseline; weighted ALS (the implicit library) usually does better on real implicit data.

docs.title: A two-tower model in NumPy
docs.text:
The model is small enough to train with plain NumPy and hand-written gradients, which makes every moving part visible. In production use TensorFlow Recommenders, TorchRec, or PyTorch.

# ml/two_tower.py: a small two-tower retrieval model in NumPy, trained with in-batch negatives
import argparse

import numpy as np

from rec_common import X, content, evaluate, n_items, train

parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("--id-dropout", type=float, default=0.3)   # share of examples trained on text only
parser.add_argument("--no-logq", action="store_true")          # turn off the popularity correction
args = parser.parse_args()
ID_DROPOUT, LOGQ = args.id_dropout, not args.no_logq
D, BATCH, EPOCHS, LR = 32, 256, 15, 0.01
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n_words = content.shape[1]
pairs = train[["user", "item"]].to_numpy()
freq = np.bincount(pairs[:, 1], minlength=n_items) + 1
log_q = np.log(freq / freq.sum())                             # how often each item is a negative


def user_input(history):
    """User tower input: the items used (multi-hot) and their average text, both length-normalized."""
    n = np.maximum(history.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True), 1)
    return np.hstack([history / n, (history @ content) / n])


params = {"Wu": rng.normal(0, 0.05, (n_items + n_words, D)),   # user tower: one linear layer
          "Wi": rng.normal(0, 0.05, (n_words, D)),             # item tower: text ...
          "E": np.zeros((n_items, D))}                         # ... plus a learned ID embedding
moments = {k: (np.zeros_like(v), np.zeros_like(v)) for k, v in params.items()}
step = 0
for epoch in range(EPOCHS):
    order, total = rng.permutation(len(pairs)), 0.0
    for start in range(0, len(pairs), BATCH):
        u, i = pairs[order[start:start + BATCH]].T
        history = X[u].copy()
        history[np.arange(len(u)), i] = 0                     # leave the target out of the history
        keep_id = (rng.random(len(u)) >= ID_DROPOUT)[:, None]  # sometimes hide the ID: cold-start practice
        xu, xi = user_input(history), content[i]
        eu = xu @ params["Wu"]
        ei = xi @ params["Wi"] + keep_id * params["E"][i]
        logits = eu @ ei.T                                     # other items in the batch act as negatives
        if LOGQ:
            logits -= log_q[i][None, :]                        # correct for popular items' extra negatives
        logits -= logits.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        prob = np.exp(logits) / np.exp(logits).sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        total -= np.log(np.diag(prob) + 1e-12).sum()
        g = (prob - np.eye(len(u))) / len(u)                   # gradient of the softmax loss
        g_eu, g_ei = g @ ei, g.T @ eu
        grads = {"Wu": xu.T @ g_eu, "Wi": xi.T @ g_ei, "E": np.zeros_like(params["E"])}
        np.add.at(grads["E"], i, keep_id * g_ei)
        step += 1
        for k, (m, v) in moments.items():                      # Adam
            m[:] = 0.9 * m + 0.1 * grads[k]
            v[:] = 0.999 * v + 0.001 * grads[k] ** 2
            params[k] -= LR * (m / (1 - 0.9 ** step)) / (np.sqrt(v / (1 - 0.999 ** step)) + 1e-8)
    if epoch in (0, EPOCHS - 1):
        print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2}: mean in-batch loss {total / len(pairs):.3f}")

user_emb = user_input(X) @ params["Wu"]                       # computed per request in production
item_emb = content @ params["Wi"] + params["E"]                # precomputed, indexed for ANN search
m = evaluate(user_emb @ item_emb.T)
print(f"two-tower: recall@10 {m['recall@10']:.3f}  NDCG@10 {m['NDCG@10']:.3f}  "
      f"coverage {m['coverage']:.2f}  new-item recall {m['new-item recall']:.3f}")

What each part does:

  • The user tower sees the multi-hot list of templates used (the collaborative signal) and their average text (the content signal), through one linear layer. During training the target template is removed from the history so the model cannot simply look it up.
  • The item tower maps the template's text through a linear layer and adds a learned ID embedding. New templates have an all-zero ID embedding, so their vectors come from text alone.
  • The loss is a softmax over the batch, with gradients written out (prob - I), and Adam updates the three parameter matrices.
  • Serving computes item_emb once for the whole catalog, ready for an ANN index, and only user_emb per request.

Three runs show what the two training details are worth:

$ python two_tower.py --id-dropout 0 --no-logq
epoch  1: mean in-batch loss 4.778
epoch 15: mean in-batch loss 3.355
two-tower: recall@10 0.080  NDCG@10 0.050  coverage 0.92  new-item recall 0.001

$ python two_tower.py --id-dropout 0
epoch  1: mean in-batch loss 4.805
epoch 15: mean in-batch loss 3.377
two-tower: recall@10 0.088  NDCG@10 0.060  coverage 0.93  new-item recall 0.002

$ python two_tower.py
epoch  1: mean in-batch loss 4.893
epoch 15: mean in-batch loss 3.819
two-tower: recall@10 0.164  NDCG@10 0.099  coverage 1.00  new-item recall 0.106
  • Without ID dropout, the model leans on per-item IDs, memorizes the training pairs, and generalizes worse than plain item-item CF; new templates, which have no trained ID, are almost never recommended.
  • The logQ correction adds a little on its own (recall@10 0.080 to 0.088).
  • With 30% ID dropout, the text path has to work on its own for some examples. The result is the best model on both known items (0.164, against 0.113 for item-item CF) and new items (0.106, against 0.079 for content-based). Its training loss is higher; the metric that matters is better. That is a regularization lesson as much as a recommender one.

These numbers come from synthetic data with a known structure; on real data, compare the same way against the same baselines before adopting a more complex model.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with popularity per segment and item-item CF; adopt anything more complex only when it beats them on the same split.
  • Treat implicit feedback as positive-only; sample negatives and evaluate by ranking.
  • Split by time, hold out each user's latest interactions, and exclude already-used items from the candidates.
  • Report recall@k and NDCG@k with coverage, and report new-item and new-user segments separately.
  • Use a two-stage design for large catalogs: high-recall retrieval from several sources, then a feature-rich ranker.
  • In two-tower training, remove the target from the user features, correct for in-batch sampling bias, and train part of the time without IDs.
  • Keep an exploration slot so new and long-tail items earn data.
  • Log impressions with position and source, not just clicks; they are the ranker's training data.
  • Apply permission filters before showing anything: never recommend a template or document the user cannot open.
  • Confirm offline gains with an A/B test on adoption, not only click-through.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The same few templates are recommended to everyone. Detect: catalog coverage and novelty fall; most clicks go to the top 1% of items. Cause: popularity bias from CF and in-batch training without correction, reinforced by a feedback loop. Fix: logQ correction, diversity re-ranking, an exploration share, and coverage as a guardrail metric.
  • New templates never get recommended. Detect: new items have near-zero impressions for weeks; new-item recall offline is zero. Cause: ID-only models with no content path. Fix: content features in the item tower, ID dropout during training, and a guaranteed exploration slot for fresh items.
  • Offline recall rose but the A/B test is flat. Detect: a new model wins offline and loses or ties online. Cause: exposure bias (logs only contain what the old model showed), a random instead of temporal split, or an offline metric unlinked to adoption. Fix: temporal splits, exploration traffic for unbiased data, and an agreed online success metric.
  • A user sees a recommendation for something they cannot access. Detect: support tickets, or 403 responses after clicks on recommended items. Cause: candidates from a global index without permission filtering. Fix: filter by permissions in retrieval and again before rendering, and test that path (see privacy, PII, and data retention).
  • Recommendations go stale after a product change. Detect: click-through drops after a catalog reorganization or a new feature. Cause: item embeddings and similarity tables computed before the change; retrieval index not rebuilt. Fix: scheduled retraining, index rebuilds tied to catalog changes, and freshness monitoring of embeddings.
  • Latency spikes on the home page. Detect: p99 of the recommendation call grows with catalog size. Cause: scoring every item with the ranking model, or exact nearest-neighbour search. Fix: two stages, an ANN index, a candidate cap, and caching per user for a few minutes.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Implicit feedback: Behaviour such as use or clicks, positive-only.
  • Explicit feedback: Ratings or votes stated by the user.
  • Candidate generation (retrieval): Selecting a few hundred plausible items from the whole catalog.
  • Ranking: Ordering the candidates with a richer model.
  • Collaborative filtering: Recommending from patterns in many users' behaviour.
  • Item-item CF: Scoring items by similarity to items the user used.
  • Matrix factorization: Approximating the user-item matrix with low-dimensional user and item factors.
  • Content-based filtering: Recommending items whose features match the user's profile.
  • Two-tower model: Separate user and item networks whose embeddings meet in a dot product.
  • In-batch negatives: Using the other items in a training batch as negative examples.
  • LogQ correction: Subtracting each item's log sampling frequency from its logit to remove popularity bias.
  • Recall@k and NDCG@k: The share of held-out items in the top k, and that share weighted by position.
  • Cold start: Missing history for a new user or item.
  • Exposure bias: Logs that only contain items the previous system chose to show.
  • Feedback loop: A model trained on data shaped by its own earlier recommendations.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating unused items as disliked.
  • Evaluating with a random split, so the model sees each user's future.
  • Recommending items the user already used and counting them as hits.
  • Comparing a new model only against other complex models, not against popularity and item-item CF.
  • Reporting average recall only, hiding that new items are never shown.
  • Training two-tower models with the target item inside the user features.
  • Ignoring permissions and privacy in candidate generation.
  • Assuming offline gains will carry over to the A/B test.
  • Judging a model by its training loss rather than the ranking metric.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is implicit feedback "positive-only", and how does that change training and evaluation?
  2. Why do large recommenders use separate retrieval and ranking stages?
  3. A user has two held-out templates and one of them appears at rank 3 of the top 10. What are recall@10 and NDCG@10 for that user? (Recall 0.5; NDCG = (1 / log2(4)) / (1 + 1 / log2(3)) = 0.5 / 1.631 = 0.307.)
  4. Why can item-item CF not recommend a template published yesterday, and what can?
  5. What does the logQ correction fix in in-batch training?
  6. Why did ID dropout improve the two-tower model on old items as well as new ones?
  7. How would you recommend templates to a user who signed up five minutes ago?
  8. Name two reasons an offline improvement might not appear in an A/B test.

docs.title: Tabular ML and Gradient Boosting
docs.text:
Most machine learning in a business application works on tables: one row per task, user, invoice, or event, and one column per fact about it. This lesson builds a real tabular model for TaskFlow: predicting, at the moment a task is created, how likely it is to miss its due date, so the web app can flag at-risk work and TaskFlow Assistant can suggest a realistic deadline.

It covers framing a tabular problem, feature engineering, honest train, validation, and test splits, how gradient-boosted decision trees work, LightGBM and XGBoost through their scikit-learn APIs, a linear baseline to compare against, feature importance, and data leakage: the mistake that makes a model look excellent offline and fail in production. Metrics are used here and explained in depth in model evaluation and validation.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Tabular prediction is where classic machine learning still pays its way: churn risk, fraud review queues, delivery estimates, lead scoring, and "which tasks will slip". A language model is the wrong tool for most of these. A gradient-boosted tree model trains in seconds on a laptop, answers in well under a millisecond, costs almost nothing to serve, and is usually the most accurate option on rows-and-columns data.

The hard part is not the algorithm. It is deciding what one row means, which facts are really known at prediction time, and how to split the data so the offline score predicts the production score. Get those wrong and the model is confidently useless: the leaky example on this page scores ROC-AUC 0.888 offline and 0.535, barely better than a coin, on the inputs it would really receive.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Tree models win on typical tabular data. Grinsztajn, Oyallon, and Varoquaux, Why do tree-based models still outperform deep learning on typical tabular data? (2022), benchmark 45 datasets and find that tree-based models such as XGBoost and random forests remain state of the art on medium-sized data (about 10,000 samples), partly because neural networks struggle with uninformative features and irregular functions.
  • XGBoost. Chen and Guestrin, XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System (KDD 2016), report that 17 of the 29 winning solutions published on Kaggle's blog during 2015 used XGBoost, and that every team in the top 10 of KDD Cup 2015 used it.
  • LightGBM. Ke and others, LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (NeurIPS 2017), introduce gradient-based one-side sampling and exclusive feature bundling, and report training up to over 20 times faster than conventional gradient boosting at almost the same accuracy.
  • Leakage is common, even in published research. Kapoor and Narayanan, Leakage and the Reproducibility Crisis in ML-based Science (2022), found leakage-related errors in 17 scientific fields, affecting 329 papers, and describe 8 types of leakage, from textbook errors to open research problems.
  • scikit-learn. The common pitfalls guide defines data leakage as using information that would not be available at prediction time, and recommends pipelines so that preprocessing is fitted on training data only.

Popular tools and providers: LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost, scikit-learn (HistGradientBoostingClassifier, pipelines, metrics), pandas and Polars, Optuna for tuning, SHAP for explanations; managed options include BigQuery ML boosted tree models (built on XGBoost), the built-in XGBoost algorithm in Amazon SageMaker AI, and automated ML in Azure Machine Learning.

docs.title: Framing a tabular problem
docs.text:
Before any code, write down four things:

Question TaskFlow overdue-risk answer What is one row? One task, at the moment it is created When is the prediction made? When POST /tasks succeeds (the prediction time) What is the label? late = 1 if the task was completed after due_at When is the label known? After the due date passes or the task is completed

The prediction time decides everything else. A feature is usable only if the API knows its value at that moment. The label time decides how fresh the training data can be: a task due in 30 days cannot be labelled until 30 days after it was created.

The positive rate matters too. In the synthetic history used on this page, 31% of tasks finish late. That is balanced enough for plain log loss; rare-event problems (2% fraud, 0.5% churn) need the techniques in model evaluation and validation.

docs.title: Feature engineering
docs.text:
A feature is a column the model learns from. Tree models are forgiving (no scaling, missing values allowed), but the features still decide most of the accuracy.

Feature type TaskFlow examples How to prepare it Numeric estimate_hours, days_to_due, n_subtasks Trees use raw values; linear models need scaling, and logs for skewed values Ratios and domain logic pressure = estimate / (6 working hours x days to due) Encode what experts already know; often the strongest features Categorical priority, source, team One-hot for linear models; native categorical support in LightGBM, XGBoost, and scikit-learn Dates created weekday, December, days to due Calendar parts, durations, and holidays, never the raw timestamp History aggregates assignee's late rate before this task Computed point in time: only from outcomes known before the prediction High-cardinality IDs assignee (320 people) Rarely raw; use history aggregates or carefully cross-fitted target encoding Text title, description Length and flags, or embeddings (see embedding models and dimensions)

History aggregates deserve special care. "This person finishes 40% of their tasks late" is a powerful feature, and it leaks the label unless it is computed only from tasks that finished before the current task was created. The practical example builds it with pandas.merge_asof and tests it.

Two more rules for categorical features:

  • Fix the vocabulary at training time. Categories seen in production but not in training (a new team) must map to "unknown", not crash or silently become another category.
  • Shrink small groups. A person with two finished tasks has a late rate of 0%, 50%, or 100%. Blending towards the global rate (here with a weight of 10 tasks) keeps those noisy values from dominating.

docs.title: Train, validation, and test splits
docs.text:
Each split has one job:

Split Job Touched Training Fit the trees (or the coefficients) Every run Validation Early stopping, tuning, threshold choice, model choice Many times Test One final, unbiased estimate of production performance Once, at the end

The split must mirror how the model is used. TaskFlow predicts the future from the past, so the split is by time, and the training set contains only tasks whose labels were known at the cutoff (due before 1 January 2026). Tasks created before the cutoff but due after it are left out; in a real retraining run on 1 January, their outcomes would not exist yet.

Split strategy Use when Risk if misused Random (train_test_split) Rows are independent and the world does not change Optimistic on time-ordered data Time-based Predicting the future from the past Fewer training rows; seasons can be missing Group (GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit) Many rows per user, team, or document Without it, the model memorizes entities Stratified Rare classes in small datasets Does not fix time or group leakage

Cross-validation with these splitters (TimeSeriesSplit, GroupKFold) is covered in model evaluation and validation.

docs.title: How gradient boosting works
docs.text:
A decision tree splits rows with questions such as "is pressure above 0.5?" and predicts a value per leaf. One deep tree overfits; one shallow tree underfits. Gradient boosting builds an additive model from many shallow trees, each one trained to fix the errors of the trees before it:

  1. Start with a constant prediction: the mean (regression) or the log-odds of the positive rate (classification).
  2. Compute, for every row, the gradient of the loss at the current prediction. For squared error that is simply the residual.
  3. Fit a small tree to those gradients (gradient-boosting libraries also use the second derivative to set each leaf's value).
  4. Add the tree, multiplied by the learning rate, to the model.
  5. Repeat until the validation loss stops improving (early stopping).

Several implementation details make modern libraries fast and accurate:

  • Histograms. Feature values are bucketed into bins (255 by default in LightGBM, max_bin), so finding the best split scans bins, not rows.
  • Tree growth. LightGBM grows trees leaf-wise (best-first, controlled by num_leaves); XGBoost grows depth-wise by default (max_depth), with a leaf-wise grow_policy="lossguide" option.
  • Missing values. Both learn a default direction for missing values at every split, so NaN needs no imputation.
  • Regularization. Minimum rows per leaf, L1 and L2 penalties on leaf values, row and column subsampling, and a small learning rate all trade a little training fit for better generalization.

A smaller learning rate needs more trees but usually generalizes better, so the standard recipe is a small rate (0.01 to 0.1), a large n_estimators, and early stopping on the validation set.

docs.title: LightGBM and XGBoost through the scikit-learn API
docs.text:
Both libraries ship scikit-learn estimators (LGBMClassifier, XGBClassifier), so they work with fit, predict_proba, pipelines, and permutation_importance. The parameter names differ:

Concept LightGBM 4.7 (default) XGBoost 3.4 (default) Number of trees n_estimators (100) n_estimators (100) Learning rate learning_rate (0.1) learning_rate (0.3) Tree size num_leaves (31), max_depth (-1, no limit) max_depth (6), max_leaves Minimum leaf size min_child_samples (20) min_child_weight (1, a hessian sum) Row subsampling subsample (1.0) with subsample_freq (0, off) subsample (1) Column subsampling colsample_bytree (1.0) colsample_bytree (1) L2 penalty reg_lambda (0.0) reg_lambda (1) Categorical columns pandas category dtype, used automatically pandas category with enable_categorical=True Validation data fit(..., eval_X=..., eval_y=...) fit(..., eval_set=[(X, y)]) Early stopping callbacks=[lightgbm.early_stopping(100)] early_stopping_rounds=100 in the constructor

Two version notes, current in November 2026. LightGBM 4.7.0 added eval_X and eval_y and deprecated eval_set, which still works with a warning. XGBoost has taken early_stopping_rounds in the constructor since 1.6, and after early stopping its predict methods use the best iteration automatically, as LightGBM's do.

LightGBM's tuning guide gives the key rule for leaf-wise trees: num_leaves is the main complexity control, keep it below 2^max_depth, and raise min_child_samples (alias min_data_in_leaf) to fight overfitting on large data.

docs.title: Data leakage
docs.text:
Data leakage is any path by which information that would not exist at prediction time reaches training or evaluation. It inflates offline scores and is invisible until production.

Kind TaskFlow example Prevention Target leakage comment_count from the export: late tasks stay open longer and collect comments Only features known at prediction time; snapshot features when predicting Aggregate leakage Assignee's late rate over all tasks, including this one and later ones Point-in-time aggregates (merge_asof, strictly earlier outcomes) Temporal leakage Random split of time-ordered data Time-based splits; train only on labels known at the cutoff Group leakage The same recurring task template in training and test Group splits by template, user, or team Preprocessing leakage Scaler, encoder, or feature selection fitted on all rows Fit inside a pipeline, on training data only Duplicate leakage Imported or copied tasks present in both splits De-duplicate before splitting

The warning signs are recognizable: a score far above what the domain suggests is possible, one feature dominating importance, a feature whose name describes something that happens after the event, and a large gap between validation and the first weeks of production.

docs.title: Feature importance and explanations
docs.text:
Feature importance answers "what does the model rely on?", which is the fastest way to spot leakage and to explain the model to product owners.

  • Split and gain importance (feature_importances_, with importance_type="split" by default in LightGBM or "gain") are cheap but computed on training data and biased towards features with many distinct values.
  • Permutation importance (sklearn.inspection.permutation_importance) shuffles one column of the validation set and measures how much the metric drops. It reflects what the model needs on unseen data, but correlated features share credit.
  • SHAP values explain individual predictions as additive contributions, which suits "why was this task flagged?" in the UI.

Importance shows reliance, not causation. A model that leans on team may be learning workload, not anything about the team.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Use Notes Rows and columns, thousands to millions of rows Gradient-boosted trees The default first serious model Few hundred rows Regularized linear model or small trees Boosting overfits; cross-validate carefully Decisions that must be explained line by line (credit, hiring) Linear models, GAMs, or monotone constraints Check the regulations that apply first Images, audio, free text Deep learning or embeddings Embeddings can become features of a tree model A rule already captures the business logic The rule Learn only what rules cannot express Labels arrive months later and the world keeps changing Boosting plus frequent retraining and monitoring See production monitoring and drift

Do not reach for boosting (yet) when there is no agreed label, when the label is not known until long after the decision, or when a baseline has not been measured.

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text:
The code runs in a Python virtual environment and was tested with Python 3.12, scikit-learn 1.9.1, pandas 3.1.1, LightGBM 4.7.0, and XGBoost 3.4.1 in November 2026. All data is synthetic.

cd ml
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
pip install scikit-learn pandas lightgbm xgboost pytest
python make_tasks.py && python train.py && python leakage.py && pytest -q

On PyPI, the CPU-only xgboost-cpu package is a much smaller download than xgboost and provides the same xgboost module.

docs.title: A synthetic TaskFlow task history
docs.text:
# ml/make_tasks.py: a synthetic TaskFlow task history (no real data), saved as CSV
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 24_000
created = pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(
    np.sort(rng.uniform(0, 546, n)), unit="D").floor("min")

team = rng.integers(0, 40, n)
assignee = team * 8 + rng.integers(0, 8, n)              # 8 people per team
skill = rng.normal(0, 0.8, 320)                          # hidden: how often each person runs late
priority = rng.choice(["low", "medium", "high", "urgent"], n, p=[0.25, 0.45, 0.22, 0.08])
days_to_due = np.where(priority == "urgent", rng.integers(1, 4, n), rng.integers(1, 31, n))
estimate_hours = np.round(rng.lognormal(1.3, 0.7, n), 1)
n_subtasks = rng.poisson(1.5, n)
has_description = rng.random(n) < 0.7
source = rng.choice(["web", "api", "assistant"], n, p=[0.6, 0.25, 0.15])
december = created.month == 12
open_tasks = rng.poisson(4 + 3 * december)               # assignee's open tasks at creation
month = (created.year - 2025) * 12 + created.month - 1
crunch = rng.normal(0, 0.7, (40, 18))[team, month]       # hidden: busy months per team

pressure = estimate_hours / (6 * days_to_due)            # share of the working time it needs
logit = (-2.2 + 2.2 * (pressure > 0.5) + 1.2 * np.clip(pressure, 0, 0.5)   # a threshold effect
         + 0.9 * (days_to_due > 21)                                        # long deadlines drift
         + 0.8 * ((priority == "low") & (days_to_due > 14))                # interactions
         + 1.0 * ((priority == "urgent") & (estimate_hours > 4))
         + 0.08 * open_tasks + skill[assignee] + crunch + 0.12 * n_subtasks - 0.35 * has_description
         + 0.25 * (created.day_of_week == 4)                               # created on a Friday
         + 0.6 * december + 0.3 * (created >= "2026-02-01"))               # season and drift
late = rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))

due_at = created + pd.to_timedelta(days_to_due, unit="D")
delay_days = np.where(late, rng.exponential(4, n) + 0.1, -rng.uniform(0, 1, n) * days_to_due)
completed_at = (due_at + pd.to_timedelta(delay_days, unit="D")).floor("min")
days_open = (completed_at - created).days.to_numpy()
comment_count = rng.poisson(0.5 + 0.35 * days_open)      # counted at export time, not at creation

tasks = pd.DataFrame({
    "task_id": np.arange(1, n + 1), "created_at": created, "due_at": due_at,
    "completed_at": completed_at, "team": "team-" + pd.Series(team).astype(str),
    "assignee": "user-" + pd.Series(assignee).astype(str), "priority": priority,
    "estimate_hours": estimate_hours, "days_to_due": days_to_due, "n_subtasks": n_subtasks,
    "has_description": has_description, "source": source, "assignee_open_tasks": open_tasks,
    "comment_count": comment_count, "late": late.astype(int),
})
Path("data").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
tasks.to_csv("data/tasks.csv", index=False)
print(tasks.shape, f"late rate {tasks['late'].mean():.3f}")
by_quarter = tasks.groupby(tasks["created_at"].dt.to_period("Q"))["late"].mean()
print("late rate by quarter:", ", ".join(f"{q} {r:.3f}" for q, r in by_quarter.items()))

$ python make_tasks.py
(24000, 15) late rate 0.310
late rate by quarter: 2025Q1 0.299, 2025Q2 0.286, 2025Q3 0.295, 2025Q4 0.335, 2026Q1 0.332, 2026Q2 0.314

The generator hides structure a real history would have: people who are usually late, busy months per team, a deadline-pressure threshold, interactions (low priority with a long deadline), a December effect, and a small drift from February 2026. Because the true rules are known, you can check what each model finds. comment_count is deliberately recorded at export time, which makes it a trap.

docs.title: Point-in-time features
docs.text:
# ml/features.py: features known when a task is created, computed point in time
import pandas as pd

NUMERIC = ["estimate_hours", "days_to_due", "pressure", "n_subtasks", "assignee_open_tasks",
           "done_before", "assignee_late_rate", "created_weekday"]
CATEGORICAL = ["priority", "source", "team"]


def load_tasks(path="data/tasks.csv"):
    return pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["created_at", "due_at", "completed_at"])


def add_history(tasks, m=10):
    """Each assignee's late rate over tasks that finished BEFORE this task was created."""
    done = tasks[["assignee", "completed_at", "late"]].sort_values("completed_at")
    done["done_before"] = done.groupby("assignee").cumcount() + 1
    done["late_before"] = done.groupby("assignee")["late"].cumsum()
    done["global_rate"] = done["late"].expanding().mean()
    left = tasks[["task_id", "created_at", "assignee"]].sort_values("created_at")
    asof = dict(left_on="created_at", right_on="completed_at", direction="backward",
                allow_exact_matches=False)                     # strictly earlier outcomes only
    person = pd.merge_asof(left, done[["assignee", "completed_at", "done_before", "late_before"]],
                           by="assignee", **asof)
    overall = pd.merge_asof(left, done[["completed_at", "global_rate"]], **asof)
    hist = person[["task_id", "done_before", "late_before"]].assign(
        global_rate=overall["global_rate"].to_numpy())
    hist = hist.fillna({"done_before": 0, "late_before": 0, "global_rate": 0.3})  # 0.3: a neutral start
    # Shrink towards the global rate so a person with two finished tasks is not 0% or 100% late.
    hist["assignee_late_rate"] = (hist["late_before"] + m * hist["global_rate"]) / (hist["done_before"] + m)
    return tasks.merge(hist[["task_id", "done_before", "assignee_late_rate"]], on="task_id")


def build_features(tasks):
    t = add_history(tasks)
    t["pressure"] = t["estimate_hours"] / (6 * t["days_to_due"])   # share of working hours needed
    t["created_weekday"] = t["created_at"].dt.day_of_week
    return t


def time_split(tasks, cutoff="2026-01-01", test_start="2026-04-01"):
    cutoff, test_start = pd.Timestamp(cutoff), pd.Timestamp(test_start)
    train = tasks[tasks["due_at"] < cutoff]                    # labels already known at the cutoff
    val = tasks[(tasks["created_at"] >= cutoff) & (tasks["created_at"] < test_start)]
    test = tasks[tasks["created_at"] >= test_start]
    return train, val, test


def to_xy(df, train, features):
    X = df[features].copy()
    for col in CATEGORICAL:
        if col in features:   # the training categories only: unseen values become missing
            X[col] = pd.Categorical(X[col], categories=sorted(train[col].unique()))
    return X, df["late"]

What each part does:

  • add_history sorts finished tasks by completion time and keeps running counts per assignee. merge_asof then attaches, to each new task, the counts from the last completion strictly before its creation (allow_exact_matches=False). The global rate is computed the same way, so even the shrinkage prior uses no future data.
  • time_split trains only on tasks due before the cutoff, so every training label already existed on the cutoff day.
  • to_xy converts categorical columns to the pandas category dtype with the training vocabulary. A team created after the cutoff becomes missing, which LightGBM and XGBoost handle, instead of a new code the model never saw.
  • Pandas 3 deprecates DatetimeIndex.dayofweek; day_of_week is the current name.

docs.title: A leakage test for features
docs.text:
# ml/test_features.py: a point-in-time feature must not change when the future changes
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from features import build_features, load_tasks


def test_history_features_ignore_the_future():
    tasks = load_tasks()
    cut = pd.Timestamp("2025-09-01")
    future = tasks["completed_at"] >= cut
    flipped = tasks.assign(late=np.where(future, 1 - tasks["late"], tasks["late"]))

    before = build_features(tasks).set_index("task_id")
    after = build_features(flipped).set_index("task_id")
    created_before_cut = before["created_at"] < cut
    for col in ["done_before", "assignee_late_rate"]:
        pd.testing.assert_series_equal(before.loc[created_before_cut, col],
                                       after.loc[created_before_cut, col])

$ pytest -q test_features.py
.                                                                        [100%]
1 passed in 0.83s

The test flips every label that became known after 1 September 2025 and checks that no feature of a task created before that date moves. A leaky "late rate over all tasks" fails it immediately: in a check against this dataset it changed for 10,628 of the 10,715 earlier tasks. Run tests like this in CI next to the training code.

docs.title: Baselines, LightGBM, and XGBoost on the same split
docs.text:
# ml/train.py: time-based splits, two baselines, LightGBM, and XGBoost on the same features
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.compose import make_column_transformer
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import average_precision_score, log_loss, roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

from features import CATEGORICAL, NUMERIC, build_features, load_tasks, time_split, to_xy

tasks = build_features(load_tasks())
train, val, test = time_split(tasks)
print(f"train {len(train)}, validation {len(val)}, test {len(test)}, "
      f"left out {len(tasks) - len(train) - len(val) - len(test)}")

FEATURES = NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL
(X_tr, y_tr), (X_va, y_va), (X_te, y_te) = (to_xy(d, train, FEATURES) for d in (train, val, test))

prior = DummyClassifier(strategy="prior").fit(X_tr, y_tr)
linear = make_pipeline(
    make_column_transformer((StandardScaler(), NUMERIC),
                            (OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), CATEGORICAL)),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

gbm = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.03, num_leaves=31,
                         min_child_samples=40, subsample=0.8, subsample_freq=1,
                         colsample_bytree=0.8, reg_lambda=1.0, random_state=42, verbose=-1)
gbm.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_X=X_va, eval_y=y_va, eval_metric="binary_logloss",
        callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100, verbose=False)])   # pandas category columns = categorical

xgb = XGBClassifier(n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.03, max_depth=5, min_child_weight=5,
                    subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, reg_lambda=1.0, tree_method="hist",
                    enable_categorical=True, early_stopping_rounds=100, eval_metric="logloss",
                    random_state=42)
xgb.fit(X_tr, y_tr, eval_set=[(X_va, y_va)], verbose=False)
print(f"best iterations: LightGBM {gbm.best_iteration_}, XGBoost {xgb.best_iteration}")


def report(name, model, X, y):
    p = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    print(f"{name:31} ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y, p):.3f}   PR-AUC {average_precision_score(y, p):.3f}"
          f"   log loss {log_loss(y, p):.3f}")


for name, model in [("prior", prior), ("logistic regression", linear),
                    ("LightGBM", gbm), ("XGBoost", xgb)]:
    report(f"validation {name}", model, X_va, y_va)
report("test LightGBM (once)", gbm, X_te, y_te)

imp = permutation_importance(gbm, X_va, y_va, scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=5, random_state=0)
ranked = sorted(zip(FEATURES, imp.importances_mean), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])
print("permutation importance (drop in validation ROC-AUC):")
print("  " + ", ".join(f"{name} {value:.3f}" for name, value in ranked[:6]))

$ python train.py
train 15252, validation 4018, test 4081, left out 649
best iterations: LightGBM 154, XGBoost 147
validation prior                ROC-AUC 0.500   PR-AUC 0.332   log loss 0.638
validation logistic regression  ROC-AUC 0.715   PR-AUC 0.558   log loss 0.580
validation LightGBM             ROC-AUC 0.724   PR-AUC 0.590   log loss 0.561
validation XGBoost              ROC-AUC 0.725   PR-AUC 0.589   log loss 0.562
test LightGBM (once)            ROC-AUC 0.712   PR-AUC 0.531   log loss 0.559
permutation importance (drop in validation ROC-AUC):
  assignee_late_rate 0.089, pressure 0.041, days_to_due 0.041, priority 0.011, team 0.007, assignee_open_tasks 0.006

Reading the results:

  • The prior baseline predicts the training late rate for everyone. Its ROC-AUC is 0.5 by definition and its PR-AUC equals the positive rate (0.332); every real model must beat those numbers.
  • Logistic regression is a strong baseline. It reaches 0.715. Boosting adds a modest but consistent gain (PR-AUC 0.590 against 0.558) because it finds the pressure threshold and the priority-deadline interactions without hand-made features. On some datasets the linear model wins; you only know because you measured it.
  • LightGBM and XGBoost tie. With equivalent settings, the choice is about ecosystem, speed, and team familiarity, not accuracy.
  • Early stopping chose about 150 trees out of 2,000, at a learning rate of 0.03.
  • The test score is lower than validation (0.712 against 0.724). Validation was used for early stopping, so it is slightly optimistic, and the test quarter differs from the validation quarter. The test number is the one to report.
  • Permutation importance ranks the point-in-time assignee history first, then deadline pressure, matching how the data was generated. No single feature dominates suspiciously.

docs.title: Measuring what leakage does
docs.text:
# ml/leakage.py: the same LightGBM model with an honest setup and three leaky ones
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

from features import CATEGORICAL, NUMERIC, build_features, load_tasks, time_split, to_xy

HONEST = NUMERIC + CATEGORICAL


def auc(train, val, features, scored=None):
    """Fit on train, return validation ROC-AUC; `scored` replaces the inputs at prediction time."""
    X_tr, y_tr = to_xy(train, train, features)
    X_va, y_va = to_xy(val if scored is None else scored, train, features)
    model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=150, learning_rate=0.05, random_state=42, verbose=-1)
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)
    return roc_auc_score(val["late"], model.predict_proba(X_va)[:, 1])


tasks = build_features(load_tasks())
train, val, _ = time_split(tasks)
print(f"honest features, time split          {auc(train, val, HONEST):.3f}")

# 1. Target leakage: comment_count is the value at export time, after the task finished.
with_comments = HONEST + ["comment_count"]
print(f"+ comment_count from the export      {auc(train, val, with_comments):.3f}")
print(f"  same model, creation-time inputs   "
      f"{auc(train, val, with_comments, scored=val.assign(comment_count=0)):.3f}")

# 2. Leaky aggregate: each person's late rate over ALL their tasks, this one and future ones included.
tasks["late_rate_all"] = tasks.groupby("assignee")["late"].transform("mean")
train, val, _ = time_split(tasks)
print(f"+ late rate over all tasks           {auc(train, val, HONEST + ['late_rate_all']):.3f}")

# 3. A random split mixes months: the model is tested on the past it was trained around.
rand_train, rand_val = train_test_split(tasks, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
print(f"honest features, random split        {auc(rand_train, rand_val, HONEST):.3f}")

$ python leakage.py
honest features, time split          0.713
+ comment_count from the export      0.888
  same model, creation-time inputs   0.535
+ late rate over all tasks           0.751
honest features, random split        0.723

Each line is a mistake that happens in real projects:

  • Target leakage looks spectacular (0.888) and collapses to 0.535 when the model receives what the API knows at creation: zero comments. The model learned "many comments means late", which is a consequence of lateness, not a predictor.
  • The all-tasks late rate includes the row's own label and future outcomes, adding 0.038 of fake ROC-AUC.
  • The random split estimates 0.723 where the honest time split gets 0.713. The gap is small here because the synthetic rows are almost independent; with real drift, seasonality, and correlated rows it is often much larger.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write down the prediction time and the label time before choosing features; reject every feature not known at prediction time.
  • Build history features point in time, and test them by changing the future and checking nothing earlier moves.
  • Split the way the model will be used: by time for forecasts of the future, by group when entities repeat.
  • Keep the test set for one final estimate; tune and early-stop on validation only.
  • Always train a prior baseline and a regularized linear model next to the boosted trees, and report all three.
  • Use a small learning rate, many trees, and early stopping; tune num_leaves or max_depth and the minimum leaf size first.
  • Fix categorical vocabularies at training time and handle unseen values explicitly.
  • Fit every preprocessing step inside a pipeline, on training data only.
  • Check permutation importance on validation data; investigate any feature that dominates.
  • Store the feature code with the model version, and compute features in production with the same code as in training.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The model was excellent offline and mediocre from day one. Detect: production ROC-AUC or precision on the first labelled weeks is far below validation; one feature dominates importance. Cause: target leakage, such as a field measured after the prediction time or an aggregate that includes the label. Fix: audit every feature against the prediction time, rebuild aggregates point in time, add a leakage test, and retrain.
  • Predictions differ between the training notebook and the API. Detect: the same task scored offline and online gets different probabilities; logged online features differ from recomputed ones. Cause: training-serving skew: features computed twice with different code, time zones, or defaults. Fix: one feature module used by both paths, logged features at prediction time, and a daily comparison job.
  • A new team breaks the model. Detect: errors or odd scores for tasks from a team created after training. Cause: an unseen category mapped to an arbitrary code, or an encoder that raises on unknown values. Fix: fix the vocabulary at training time, map unknowns to missing or "other", and test the path.
  • Accuracy decays month by month. Detect: rolling precision and calibration on newly labelled tasks drift down; input distributions shift. Cause: data or concept drift, such as a new workflow or seasonal load. Fix: monitor inputs and outcomes, retrain on a schedule with a time-based validation gate (see production monitoring and drift).
  • Retraining quietly uses unfinished labels. Detect: the newest training rows show a lower late rate than older ones. Cause: tasks not yet due are labelled "on time" by default. Fix: train only on rows whose label window has closed, as time_split does with the due date.
  • The model is slow or large in the API. Detect: p99 latency or memory grows after deployment. Cause: thousands of deep trees, or rebuilding a pandas frame per request. Fix: early stopping, fewer leaves, batch scoring where possible, and predicting from a NumPy array or the native booster in the hot path.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Tabular data: Rows of entities with columns of typed facts.
  • Feature: An input column the model learns from.
  • Label (target): The value the model learns to predict.
  • Prediction time: The moment the model is asked; features must be known then.
  • Point-in-time feature: A feature computed only from data that existed at the prediction time.
  • Gradient boosting: An additive model of trees, each fitted to the gradient of the loss at the current predictions.
  • Learning rate (shrinkage): The factor applied to each new tree.
  • Early stopping: Stopping training when the validation metric stops improving.
  • Leaf-wise growth: Splitting the leaf with the best gain next (LightGBM); depth-wise growth splits level by level (XGBoost default).
  • Data leakage: Information unavailable at prediction time reaching training or evaluation.
  • Target encoding: Replacing a category with a statistic of the label; must be cross-fitted or point in time.
  • Permutation importance: The drop in a metric when one feature's values are shuffled.
  • Training-serving skew: Features computed differently in training and in production.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Deep learning is always better." On typical tabular data, boosted trees are usually stronger and far cheaper.
  • Splitting time-ordered data randomly and trusting the score.
  • Computing history aggregates over the whole dataset.
  • Using columns from an export without asking when each value was written.
  • Tuning on the test set, or looking at it after every change.
  • Skipping the baseline, so nobody knows whether the model adds anything.
  • Scaling or encoding all rows before splitting.
  • Treating feature importance as causation.
  • Training on rows whose labels are not final yet.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are the prediction time and the label time for TaskFlow's overdue-risk model, and why does each matter?
  2. Why does time_split train only on tasks due before the cutoff instead of tasks created before it?
  3. Explain gradient boosting in four steps. What does the learning rate trade off?
  4. In the three-task example, round 1 predicts 4, 7, and 7 for actual hours 2, 6, and 10. Tree 2 outputs -1.5, -1.5, and +3 and the learning rate is 0.5. What are the new predictions and the squared error? (3.25, 6.25, 8.5; 1.5625 + 0.0625 + 2.25 = 3.875.)
  5. Name four kinds of data leakage and one prevention for each.
  6. A feature gives ROC-AUC 0.89 offline, but the model scores 0.54 in production. What do you check first?
  7. Map these LightGBM parameters to XGBoost: num_leaves, min_child_samples, eval_X, and early stopping.
  8. Why can permutation importance spread credit between two correlated features?
