docs.title: MLOps and Model Lifecycle Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review experiment tracking and model registries, prompt and model versioning for LLM features, and production monitoring and drift. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What problem does experiment tracking solve?
docs.text: It records every training run with its code version, data, parameters, environment, metrics, and artifacts, so runs can be compared, explained, and rebuilt. Without it, model history lives in notebooks and file names, and nobody can say which data or code produced a model that is misbehaving in production.

docs.title: 2. What must a run record to be reproducible?
docs.text: The Git commit (and whether the tree was dirty), an immutable data snapshot with a content digest, every hyperparameter and feature list, the library and runtime versions, and the random seeds. Metrics make a run comparable; these inputs make it reproducible.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between a parameter, a metric, and a tag in MLflow?
docs.text: A parameter is an input fixed for the run, such as learning_rate. A metric is a measured result, optionally logged at many steps, such as test_roc_auc. A tag is mutable descriptive metadata, such as git_dirty=True or owner=ml-team. Keeping them separate makes runs queryable.

docs.title: 4. What is a model registry, and how is it different from the tracking UI?
docs.text: A registry holds named models with immutable, numbered versions and records which version is approved for which purpose. The tracking UI shows experiments; a good run there is not a release. The registry is where promotion decisions, approvals, and rollbacks happen and are audited.

docs.title: 5. What are MLflow model aliases, and why did they replace stages?
docs.text: An alias is a movable, named pointer to one model version, such as @champion or @challenger, loaded with models:/taskflow-priority@champion. Stages (Staging, Production, Archived) were a fixed list with one meaning per version; they were deprecated in MLflow 2.9 and still warn in MLflow 3. Aliases and tags express any workflow, including several production models.

docs.title: 6. Why should a deployment use a concrete version rather than the alias?
docs.text: A server resolves an alias when it loads the model, so replicas that start at different times can serve different versions, and logs cannot say which version answered. The deploy step should resolve the alias once, deploy models:/name/<version>, and record that version with every prediction.

docs.title: 7. How does a rollback work with aliases?
docs.text: Before promotion, record the old champion (for example in a @previous alias). Rolling back moves @champion back to that version and redeploys or reloads, with no retraining or rebuild. The version that failed is tagged rolled_back so the history stays intact.

docs.title: 8. What belongs in a promotion gate?
docs.text: Score the challenger and the champion on the same, newer holdout data that neither trained on; compare overall and per slice; check the signature, latency, and size; record the decision as tags; and move aliases only if all checks pass. Online validation (shadow or canary) follows before full traffic.

docs.title: 9. Why compare models on a later holdout instead of a random split?
docs.text: A random split of the training period shares that period's patterns, so it flatters models that memorize them. A later period resembles what the model will see in production and exposes models that do not generalize over time.

docs.title: 10. Why check slices and not only the overall metric?
docs.text: An overall gain can hide a regression for one segment, such as one project type, language, or customer size. In the lesson's example a challenger lost 0.0211 AUC on marketing tasks; a gate with a 0.02 slice budget rejected it.

docs.title: 11. What is a model signature, and why log one?
docs.text: It is the declared input and output schema of a model. MLflow infers it from a sample and the scoring server enforces it, returning HTTP 400 (INVALID_PARAMETER_VALUE) for requests that do not match. It turns interface mismatches into clear errors instead of wrong predictions.

docs.title: 12. Why should preprocessing live inside the model artifact?
docs.text: If encoding or feature transformations happen outside the artifact, the serving code must reimplement them, which invites training-serving skew. A pipeline (encoder plus model) logged as one artifact accepts the raw values the API sends.

docs.title: 13. Name common causes of runs that cannot be reproduced.
docs.text: Training from mutable tables, unseeded randomness (scikit-learn's HistGradientBoostingClassifier enables early stopping with a random validation split above 10,000 samples), unpinned library versions, nondeterministic GPU kernels, and features computed differently in training and serving.

docs.title: 14. Why does MLflow 3 save scikit-learn models with skops instead of pickle?
docs.text: Loading a pickle can execute arbitrary code, so a tampered model file is a code-execution risk. Skops refuses types it does not trust; when it reports one, review that specific type and pass it in skops_trusted_types rather than falling back to pickle.

docs.title: 15. How do Weights & Biases and MLflow compare?
docs.text: Both track runs and version models. W&B is hosted (or self-managed), with strong dashboards, sweeps, and artifact lineage; models are artifacts linked into W&B Registry collections. MLflow is open source, self-hosted or managed by several platforms, with registered models, versions, and aliases. The concepts map one to one.

docs.title: 16. What should you check before adopting a hosted tracking service?
docs.text: That metadata and models can be exported in bulk, that production does not depend on the tracking UI to load models, and what happens if the vendor changes. Neptune.ai's hosted service shut down in March 2026 and deleted remaining data after a transition period.

docs.title: 17. What does "the model" mean for a feature built on a hosted LLM?
docs.text: A combination of the prompt version, the provider's model ID, request parameters, the output schema, tools, and any retrieval index. Changing any one changes behavior, so all of them together are versioned as one release.

docs.title: 18. Why keep production prompts in the repository?
docs.text: They are reviewed in pull requests, typed, tested and evaluated in CI, and released with the code that parses their output. OpenAI's own guidance (2026) is to store production prompts in application code, and its reusable prompt objects are being retired.

docs.title: 19. What rules make prompt versions safe?
docs.text: A version is immutable: any text change is a new version. Old versions stay in the build while a release refers to them, so rollback is a configuration change. Inputs are typed parameters, and user text stays separate from instructions.

docs.title: 20. How can CI detect a prompt edited in place?
docs.text: Keep a lock file of hashes of each prompt version rendered with a fixed sample input. CI recomputes the hashes: a new version adds a line the developer commits; a changed hash for an existing version fails the build.

docs.title: 21. What is a release fingerprint?
docs.text: A hash of a release's effective parts: the prompt text, the resolved model ID, and parameters. Logged with every request, it reveals changes that bypassed the release process, such as a model variable changed in one environment.

docs.title: 22. How should code choose a model ID?
docs.text: It should not: each feature reads its model ID from configuration. To choose a value, read the provider's models page and models.list(), shortlist by capability, relative cost, and latency, run your evaluation set, and configure a pinned version.

docs.title: 23. What is the difference between a pinned version and a moving alias?
docs.text: A pinned version keeps fixed behavior until its retirement date. A moving alias is repointed by the provider to newer models (Google repoints its "latest" aliases with two weeks' notice). Aliases suit prototypes; production should pin.

docs.title: 24. What should every LLM request log?
docs.text: The release ID, prompt version, model requested and model reported by the provider, fingerprint, latency, token counts, and the outcome of output validation. These fields let you break down quality and cost by release and answer "what changed?" during an incident.

docs.title: 25. Describe a release process for a prompt or model change.
docs.text: A pull request adds a new release; CI runs type checks, the prompt lock, and offline evaluations for the current and new release; reviewers read the prompt and evaluation diffs; staging; optional shadow traffic; a sticky canary or A/B test behind a flag; full rollout; then retirement of the old release when nothing refers to it.

docs.title: 26. Why assign A/B variants per user rather than per request?
docs.text: Per-request assignment shows one user two behaviors, which makes the product inconsistent and contaminates both groups' outcomes. Hashing "<experiment>:<user id>" gives a sticky bucket without storing assignments, and changing the experiment key reshuffles users.

docs.title: 27. What metrics would you use for an A/B test of the task parser?
docs.text: A primary metric tied to user value, such as the share of drafts saved without edits, plus guardrails: p95 latency, error and schema-failure rates, refusal rate, and cost per request. A win on the primary metric does not ship if a guardrail regresses.

docs.title: 28. How many users per variant are needed to detect a lift from 62% to 64%?
docs.text: With 5% two-sided significance and 80% power, n = (1.96 + 0.84)² × (0.62 × 0.38 + 0.64 × 0.36) / 0.02², about 9,144 users per variant. Smaller tests can only detect larger effects.

docs.title: 29. Why should you not stop an A/B test as soon as p < 0.05?
docs.text: Checking repeatedly and stopping at the first significant result inflates false positives. Fix the sample size and duration in advance (full weeks), or use a sequential method designed for repeated looks. LLM output varies between calls, which adds noise.

docs.title: 30. What is shadow testing, and what are its costs?
docs.text: A sample of requests also runs the candidate in the background; its output is logged and compared but never shown. It doubles model calls for the sample, uses rate limit, and may send user data to a second model or provider, so keep it small, time-boxed, read-only, and allowed by your data policy.

docs.title: 31. List the ways to roll back an LLM feature.
docs.text: Flip the rollout flag back to the previous release (seconds), use the kill switch to fall back to a non-AI path (seconds), revert the model configuration (minutes), or redeploy the previous build. Flags only work if the old release and prompt are still in the build.

docs.title: 32. Why can a rollback fail for an LLM feature specifically?
docs.text: The previous release's model may have been retired by the provider, or the old prompt was deleted from the code. Also, outputs produced by the bad release persist in the database and may need cleanup.

docs.title: 33. How much notice do providers give before retiring models?
docs.text: As of November 2026: OpenAI states at least 6 months for generally available models, 3 months for specialized variants and image models, and about 2 weeks for previews; Anthropic at least 60 days for publicly released models; Google at least 2 weeks for Gemini previews; Microsoft Foundry a standard 18-month GA lifecycle with notices at least 60 days ahead. Plan for the shortest notice you depend on.

docs.title: 34. Outline a migration off a deprecated model.
docs.text: Inventory every use; shortlist candidates (including but not limited to the recommended replacement); evaluate offline on your data with cost and latency; adapt prompts and parameters as new releases; shadow, then canary; switch; keep the old release as a rollback until shortly before shutdown; remove its configuration.

docs.title: 35. Why is a recommended replacement model not a drop-in swap?
docs.text: It may follow prompts differently, reject parameters the old model accepted (Anthropic removed temperature, top_p, and top_k in API version 2026-10-21), count tokens differently, or format structured output differently. Each difference needs evaluation and often a new prompt version.

docs.title: 36. How can you detect upcoming retirements automatically?
docs.text: A daily job asks the provider about every configured model: OpenAI's models endpoint returns shutdown_date, Anthropic's returns lifecycle and retires_at, and Microsoft Foundry's Models API returns lifecycleStatus and deprecation dates. The job fails CI or alerts when a model is within your migration window.

docs.title: 37. Prompt registry service or prompts in code: how do you choose?
docs.text: Code fits most teams: reviewed, tested, and released with the parsing code. A registry (Langfuse, MLflow Prompt Registry, LangSmith) fits many non-developer prompt authors, but needs the same review and evaluation gates, or production behavior changes without them. A common hybrid exports approved registry versions into the build.

docs.title: 38. How do platform auto-upgrades affect versioning?
docs.text: Some platforms upgrade deployments to a new model version on a schedule unless you opt out (Microsoft Foundry's versionUpgradeOption). That is a model change you did not deploy: evaluate the new version before the scheduled date and log the model the provider reports.

docs.title: 39. Why do ML models need monitoring beyond service metrics?
docs.text: A drifted model keeps returning confident predictions with HTTP 200, so error and latency dashboards stay green while quality decays. Google's Rules of ML calls this out as "Watch for silent failures". You must monitor data, predictions, and performance as well.

docs.title: 40. Explain data drift, label shift, and concept drift.
docs.text: Data drift: the input distribution P(X) changes. Label shift: the outcome distribution P(Y) changes. Concept drift: the relationship P(Y | X) changes, so the same input now has a different correct answer. Input monitoring can detect the first two; only labels reveal concept drift.

docs.title: 41. What is training-serving skew, and how is it different from drift?
docs.text: Skew is a difference between features in training and serving caused by different code or data paths, such as characters versus words. It is a bug present from day one, often visible as many features "drifting" at once after a deploy. Fix it by logging served features and reusing feature code.

docs.title: 42. What does a prediction log contain, and why?
docs.text: Request ID, timestamp, model version, the features as the model saw them, and the score. It is the source for drift statistics, skew checks, per-version analysis, and joining labels that arrive later.

docs.title: 43. How is PSI computed?
docs.text: Cut bins at the reference quantiles, compute each bin's share in the reference and current samples, and sum (current − reference) × ln(current / reference), with a small floor for empty bins. Every bin adds a positive amount, whether it gained or lost data.

docs.title: 44. What are the usual PSI thresholds, and how far should you trust them?
docs.text: Below 0.10 little shift, 0.10 to 0.25 investigate, above 0.25 significant. They come from credit-scoring practice and are used without reference to error rates, and PSI is biased upward on small samples, so tune thresholds per feature after a baseline period.

docs.title: 45. Compute PSI for reference shares 0.5/0.5 and current 0.7/0.3.
46. What does the two-sample KS test measure?
docs.text: Its statistic D is the largest vertical gap between the two empirical cumulative distribution functions; its p-value is the probability of a gap that large if both samples came from the same distribution. It works for continuous numeric features.

docs.title: 47. Why are p-values poor alert signals on large samples?
docs.text: The p-value answers "is there any difference?", and with enough data the answer is always yes. In the lesson, a 0.03 standard-deviation shift had p = 0.087 at 1,000 rows and p = 7e-14 at 200,000 rows, while PSI stayed near 0.001. Alert on effect sizes instead.

docs.title: 48. How many false alarms do you expect from daily tests on 7 features at 5%?
docs.text: About 7 × 365 × 0.05 ≈ 128 a year from a stable system. Reduce them with effect-size thresholds, persistence rules (for example two days above 0.25), and weekly reports instead of pages.

docs.title: 49. Why check missing values separately from drift?
docs.text: PSI and KS run on present values, so a field that goes missing can look stable. In the lesson, days_until_due had PSI 0.007 while its null share rose by 0.28. Monitor null shares, schemas, and vocabularies as data-quality checks.

docs.title: 50. How do you monitor performance when labels arrive days later?
docs.text: Join labels to the prediction log by request ID, report by prediction week, show label coverage with each metric, add confidence intervals (such as Wilson intervals), and slice by key segments. Do not judge a week until enough of its labels have arrived.

docs.title: 51. What can you monitor before labels arrive?
docs.text: Proxies: input drift, the score distribution, the share of predictions above the threshold, and estimated performance such as NannyML's CBPE from calibrated scores. CBPE does not work under concept drift, so proxies only buy time until labels confirm.

docs.title: 52. What is a feedback loop in ML, and how do you break it?
docs.text: The model's outputs influence its future training data: users keep suggested priorities, so labels copy the model and errors confirm themselves. Keep a small holdout without suggestions, prefer outcome-based labels, log exposure, and evaluate on holdout data.

docs.title: 53. What retraining triggers exist, and which would you use?
docs.text: On demand, on a schedule, on new training data, on performance degradation, and on significant distribution change, as Google Cloud's MLOps guide lists. Combine a schedule with performance and data-volume triggers, and treat drift alone as a reason to investigate.

docs.title: 54. Why should a retraining trigger never promote a model?
docs.text: Retraining can produce a worse model, especially on biased or old labels. The trigger only starts the pipeline; the new version passes the same holdout and slice gate and canary as any release.

docs.title: 55. Right after a deploy of the TaskFlow API, every feature of the priority model shows PSI above 0.5. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the API or a feature pipeline changed in that deploy.

How to confirm: compare the served feature values in the prediction log with values the training pipeline computes for the same tasks.

Likely causes and fixes: training-serving skew from a code change (units, encoding, a renamed field), not real drift. Roll back or fix the code path, add a skew check to CI, and reuse feature code between training and serving. See production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: 56. Suggestion acceptance fell 6 points over two weeks, with no deploys and no input drift. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: weekly precision and AUC by slice from labeled predictions, and any process or product change in that period.

How to confirm: performance dropped for one segment while input PSI stayed near zero; the business owner confirms a change in how that segment is handled.

Likely causes and fixes: concept drift. Gather labels from after the change, retrain on recent data, evaluate on recent weeks, and consider disabling suggestions for the affected segment meanwhile. See production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: 57. Drift alerts fire every day and the team has started ignoring them. How do you fix the alerting?
docs.text:
What to check first: what the alerts are based on, the sample sizes, and how many features are tested.

How to confirm: most alerts are p-values below 0.05 on large daily samples, with tiny PSI values and no performance impact.

Likely causes and fixes: p-value alerts on large samples and multiple testing. Alert on effect sizes with persistence rules, page only for sustained large shifts, and move the rest to a weekly report. See production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: 58. During an incident, nobody can tell which model version produced a bad suggestion. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the prediction log records a model version and how serving loads the model.

How to confirm: servers load models:/taskflow-priority@champion at startup and log only the model name.

Likely causes and fixes: unresolved aliases. Resolve the alias in the deploy step, deploy a concrete version, and log it with every prediction. See experiment tracking and model registry.

docs.title: 59. The same task gets different priority scores depending on which pod answers. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the model version loaded by each pod and when each pod started.

How to confirm: pods started after the latest promotion report the new version; older pods report the previous one.

Likely causes and fixes: an alias resolved at pod startup. Treat a promotion as a deployment: resolve once and roll out like any release. See experiment tracking and model registry.

docs.title: 60. A new model version beats the champion offline but suggestion acceptance drops after release. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: what data and metric the offline comparison used.

How to confirm: the gate used a random split of the training month and overall AUC only, with no slices or online validation.

Likely causes and fixes: an unrepresentative comparison. Gate on a later holdout with slice checks, add the business metric, and run a canary before full traffic. See experiment tracking and model registry.

docs.title: 61. An auditor asks you to rebuild the model that was in production in August, and the retrained model scores differently. What is missing?
docs.text:
What to check first: the run's recorded commit, data source, seeds, and environment.

How to confirm: the run read a live table rather than a snapshot, or did not log random_state, or the environment was not pinned.

Likely causes and fixes: incomplete run records. Train only from dated snapshots with digests, log seeds and environments, and run a scheduled reproducibility check. See experiment tracking and model registry.

docs.title: 62. Task-parser quality dropped overnight with no code release. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the model reported in response logs and the release fingerprints before and after.

How to confirm: the configured model is a moving alias that the provider repointed, or a platform auto-upgrade ran, or a model variable changed in one environment.

Likely causes and fixes: an unversioned model change. Pin versions, manage model variables through reviewed configuration, alert on fingerprint changes within a release, and evaluate auto-upgrades before their date. See LLMOps: prompt and model versioning.

docs.title: 63. Requests to the meeting-summary feature started failing with "model not found" at midnight. What happened, and how do you prevent it next time?
docs.text:
What to check first: the provider's deprecation page and the configured model's shutdown date.

How to confirm: the configured model's retirement date was yesterday; errors began at that time.

Likely causes and fixes: a missed retirement. Switch the flag to a release on a supported model or use the kill switch, then add a daily lifecycle check that fails CI weeks before any shutdown. See LLMOps: prompt and model versioning.

docs.title: 64. After migrating to the provider's recommended replacement model, 3% of requests return HTTP 400. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the error messages and which parameters those requests send.

How to confirm: the errors name a parameter, such as a sampling parameter that the new model or API version rejects.

Likely causes and fixes: a parameter incompatibility. Remove or replace the parameter in a new release, and run every migration through a canary so such errors reach a small share of users first. See LLMOps: prompt and model versioning.

docs.title: 65. A prompt A/B test showed a significant win, but after full rollout the metric is back where it was. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how users were assigned, how long the test ran, and when it was stopped.

How to confirm: assignment was per request, or the test ran only a few days and stopped at the first significant result.

Likely causes and fixes: a flawed experiment. Assign per user, fix the sample size and duration in advance (full weeks), and keep a small holdback after rollout to confirm. See LLMOps: prompt and model versioning.

docs.title: 66. You tried to roll the task parser back to last month's release and it failed. Why might that be?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the old prompt version is still in the build and whether the old release's model is still served.

How to confirm: the old prompt was deleted when the new one shipped, or the provider retired the old model.

Likely causes and fixes: a rollback target that no longer exists. Keep old prompt versions while any release refers to them, check that rollback targets use supported models, and rehearse rollbacks. See LLMOps: prompt and model versioning.

docs.title: 67. Each retrained priority model wins offline, yet users override suggestions more and more. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: where training and evaluation labels come from.

How to confirm: most labels are "kept the suggested priority", and there is no group of tasks without suggestions to compare with.

Likely causes and fixes: a feedback loop. Create a small holdout without suggestions, train and evaluate on holdout and outcome-based labels, and log whether a suggestion was shown. See production monitoring and drift.

docs.title: 68. A required feature has been empty for a third of requests for weeks, and no alert fired. How did that happen?
docs.text:
What to check first: the null share of each feature in the prediction log over time.

How to confirm: the null share rose when a client release stopped sending the field, while that feature's PSI stayed low.

Likely causes and fixes: drift statistics ignore missing values and no data-quality check existed. Alert on null shares of required features and validate the schema at the API boundary. See production monitoring and drift.

docs.text:
• MLflow: model registry
  • Google: Rules of Machine Learning
  • Google Cloud: MLOps continuous delivery and automation pipelines
  • OpenAI: deprecations

docs.title: LLMOps: Prompt and Model Versioning
docs.text:
When a feature calls a hosted model, there are no weights to train or register, yet there is still a model to version. What you ship is a combination: the prompt text, the provider's model ID, the request parameters, the output schema, and sometimes tools and a retrieval index. Change any one of them and the feature behaves differently for every user, without a compiler error or a failing unit test. LLMOps is the discipline of versioning, testing, releasing, and retiring that combination.

This lesson applies it to the TaskFlow Assistant task parser, which turns "urgent: fix the login bug by Friday" into a structured task. It covers prompts as code, release manifests and fingerprints, the release process, A/B tests and shadow traffic, rollbacks, and migrating when a provider deprecates a model. Building evaluation sets, LLM-as-judge scoring, CI evals, and tracing are covered in Evaluation and Monitoring; this page uses their results to make release decisions. Code is TypeScript, type-checked with TypeScript 7.0, the OpenAI SDK 7.57, the Anthropic SDK 1.8, and the Google Gen AI SDK 3.3 (November 2026).

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
LLM features fail quietly. A prompt edit that "just clarifies the wording" can change date handling for one language; a provider model update can change the output format a parser depends on. The request still returns HTTP 200, so error dashboards stay green while users retype half their tasks. Without versions, the first question of every incident, "what changed?", has no answer.

The ground also moves under you. Providers retire models on their own schedule, rename parameters, and repoint aliases such as "latest" to new models. A team that has not pinned its versions, recorded which release served each request, and practiced switching releases will meet these changes as outages instead of planned work. The good news is that the release engineering you already use for code (versioned artifacts, staged rollouts, feature flags, rollbacks) applies almost unchanged.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI moved prompts back into code. OpenAI's text generation guide now says: "Store production prompts in your application code instead of creating reusable prompt objects." Its deprecations page lists /v1/prompts and reusable prompt objects as deprecated (notice June 3, 2026, shutdown November 30, 2026), with the replacement "Move prompt content into your application code." The same page states minimum notice periods for model retirements and recommends comparing outputs, latency, and cost on representative requests before moving traffic.
  • GitHub Copilot. In How we evaluate AI models and LLMs for GitHub Copilot (January 2025), GitHub describes running "more than 4,000 offline tests, most of them as part of our automated CI pipeline", followed by live internal evaluations "similar to canary testing", for all major changes and not only new models, and warns that "just because a model is newer doesn't mean it will perform better for your use case."
  • Microsoft Foundry. The Foundry Models lifecycle and support policy describes a standard 18-month lifecycle for generally available models, automatic upgrades for some deployment types with an opt-out setting, and the advice "Don't wait for Microsoft to name an official replacement before you begin evaluating newer models."
  • Anthropic. The model deprecations page defines Active, Legacy, Deprecated, and Retired states and promises at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model. It also lists a parameter deprecation: temperature, top_p, and top_k were removed in API version 2026-10-21, so a migration can break on request parameters, not only on model IDs.
  • Langfuse. The open-source LLM platform's prompt A/B testing guide labels two prompt versions (prod-a, prod-b), picks one per request, and compares latency, tokens, cost, and evaluation scores per version: the same loop this page builds by hand.

Popular tools and providers: Git and CI (prompts as code), Langfuse, MLflow Prompt Registry, LangSmith, Braintrust, PromptLayer, LaunchDarkly AgentControl (formerly AI Configs) and other flag platforms such as GrowthBook and Statsig, and LLM gateways such as LiteLLM and Portkey for central routing and fallbacks.

docs.title: What a release of an LLM feature is
docs.text:
Part Example for the task parser Changes behavior because Prompt version task-parser@4 Instructions decide date handling, priorities, refusals Model ID Value of TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT Different models follow the same prompt differently Parameters max_output_tokens: 400 Truncation, length, and cost Output schema task_draft, strict JSON Downstream code parses it Tools and their schemas (none for this feature) The agent's options and arguments Retrieval index version (none for this feature; RAG features have one) What context the model sees Application code Git commit Pre- and post-processing, validation

A release is a named, immutable bundle of these parts, such as task-parser-2026-11-10. Everything downstream refers to the release ID: the rollout configuration, every request's log line, CI evaluation reports, and dashboards. A fingerprint (a hash of the prompt text, model ID, and parameters) detects the case where someone changed a part without creating a new release.

docs.title: Prompts as code
docs.text:
There are three places to keep prompts:

Where Strengths Weaknesses Fits In the repository, as code Reviewed in pull requests, typed inputs, tested in CI, released with the code that parses the output Product staff need a developer to change wording Most production features A prompt registry service (Langfuse, MLflow Prompt Registry, LangSmith) Non-developers can edit, versions and labels, per-version metrics A runtime dependency; changes can bypass code review; prompts and parsing code can drift apart Teams with many prompt authors and an approval workflow Provider-hosted prompt objects No storage of your own Tied to one provider; OpenAI's are being retired Avoid for new work

Prompts in code follow a few rules:

  • A version is immutable. Any change to the text, even a typo fix, is a new version (task-parser@5). A lock file of hashes, checked in CI, enforces this (example below).
  • Old versions stay in the build while any release refers to them, so rolling back is a configuration change, not an emergency deploy.
  • Typed inputs. A prompt is a function of named, typed values (today, projects, text), not string concatenation scattered through the code.
  • Instructions and user data are separate. The user's text goes in the input field, never inside the instructions, which also limits prompt injection (see security, privacy, and responsible AI).
  • No real names or data in examples inside prompts; models copy them. Use neutral placeholders.

A registry service can still be the editing surface: some teams export approved registry versions into the repository in CI, so production loads prompts from the build while authors keep a friendly editor.

docs.title: Choosing and pinning model IDs
docs.text:
Code never contains a model ID. Each feature reads its own from configuration (TASK_PARSER_MODEL, SUMMARY_MODEL), which lets you change models per feature and per environment without a code change. To choose a value:

  1. Read the provider's current models page (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini API) and list what your account can use with the SDK's models.list().
  2. Shortlist by capability (structured output, context length, tool use), relative cost, and latency; see choosing models and providers.
  3. Run your offline evaluation set on the shortlist, then pick the cheapest model that meets the quality bar.
  4. Configure a pinned version for production, not a moving alias.
Kind of identifier Behavior Production use Pinned or stable version Fixed behavior until its retirement date Yes: the default Moving alias ("latest" style) Repointed by the provider to new releases; Google gives two weeks' email notice for its "latest" aliases Prototypes, or features that tolerate silent change Preview Can be retired at short notice (two weeks for Gemini previews and for OpenAI previews) Experiments behind a flag Experimental Google says these "will typically not be suitable for production use" No

Some platforms upgrade deployments for you. In Microsoft Foundry, a standard deployment's versionUpgradeOption can be OnceNewDefaultVersionAvailable, OnceCurrentVersionExpired, or NoAutoUpgrade (which stops working at retirement). An automatic upgrade is still a model change: treat it as a release and run your evaluations before the scheduled date. Whatever you configure, log the model the provider reports in each response, so you can see when what answered differs from what you asked for.

docs.title: The release process
docs.text:
An LLM release goes through the same gates as any change, with evaluations in place of most unit tests:

  1. Pull request: a new prompt version or a model change creates a new release entry. CI type-checks, runs the prompt lock check, and runs the offline evaluation suite for both the current and the new release (see evals in CI and regression testing).
  2. Review: reviewers read the prompt diff and the evaluation diff, including per-slice scores, cost, and latency, not just an average.
  3. Staging: the release runs against staging traffic or a replay of recent anonymized requests.
  4. Shadow (optional): a sample of production requests also runs the candidate; its output is logged and compared, never shown.
  5. Canary or A/B test: a flag sends a small, sticky share of users to the new release, then ramps up while guardrails hold.
  6. Full rollout, with the previous release kept deployable.
  7. Retirement: once nothing refers to it, the old release and its prompt version are removed.

This is the release engineering of section 07 applied to prompts and model configuration: version naming as in versioning patterns, promotion across environments as in environments and promotion, and staged exposure as in feature flags and progressive delivery.

docs.title: A/B testing prompts and models
docs.text:
Offline evaluations tell you whether a release is acceptable; an online test tells you whether users are better off. For the task parser:

  • Primary metric: the share of drafts the user saves without editing any field (the acceptance rate).
  • Guardrails: p95 latency, error and schema-failure rate, refusal rate, and cost per request. A candidate that wins on acceptance but doubles cost or latency does not ship automatically.
  • Unit of assignment: the user, not the request. Per-request random choice (as in many tool examples) is fine for offline-style comparisons, but a user who sees two behaviors on two tasks gets an inconsistent product and contaminates both groups.

Sticky assignment needs no database: hash the experiment key and the user ID, as in section 07's flag bucketing. SHA-256 of "<experiment>:<user id>", first 4 bytes, modulo 10,000 gives a bucket from 0 to 9999; buckets below 9000 get the control release.

How many users you need depends on the effect you want to detect. To detect a lift from 62% to 64% acceptance at 5% significance with 80% power, each variant needs about 9,144 users:

n per variant = (1.96 + 0.84)^2 × (0.62 × 0.38 + 0.64 × 0.36) / 0.02^2
              = 7.85 × 0.466 / 0.0004 ≈ 9,144

A 10% candidate slice of 10,000 users (1,000 users) can only detect large effects, such as the 4.8-point lift in the diagram. Decide the sample size and the test duration before starting, run full weeks to cover weekday patterns, and do not stop the test the first time the p-value dips below 0.05. Also remember that model output varies between calls, so small tests are noisier than they look.

docs.title: Shadow testing
docs.text:
Shadow traffic answers "how would the candidate have behaved on real inputs?" without exposing users to it. For a sample of requests (5% in the example below), the API calls the candidate in the background after answering with the current release, and logs agreement metrics: same due date, same project, same priority. Disagreements are the cases to review by hand or with an LLM judge.

Shadowing doubles model calls for the sampled requests, so it costs more and uses rate limit; keep the sample small and time-boxed. Check that your data policy allows sending the same user data to a second model or provider, and never let the shadow call write anything: shadow output is for logs only.

docs.title: Rollbacks
docs.text:
Rollback path How Time Requires Flag change Set the rollout split back to 100% of the previous release Seconds The previous release and prompt still in the build Kill switch enabled: false: the UI falls back to the plain task form Seconds A non-AI fallback path Configuration revert Restore the previous model ID value Minutes (config reload) The previous model still served by the provider Code rollback Redeploy the previous build A normal deploy Section 07's rollback tooling

Two traps are specific to LLM features. First, the rollback target may no longer exist: providers retire models, so a release whose model is retired cannot be rolled back to. Second, outputs persist: drafts or summaries produced by the bad release stay in the database, so rollbacks may need a cleanup or re-generation job, as data migrations do. See rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: When a provider deprecates a model
docs.text:
Provider policies as of November 2026:

Provider Lifecycle terms Minimum notice before retirement OpenAI Active, Deprecated, shutdown date Generally available models at least 6 months; specialized variants and image models at least 3 months; previews about 2 weeks. The models endpoint returns shutdown_date. Anthropic Active, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired At least 60 days for publicly released models. The models endpoint returns lifecycle and retires_at. Google Gemini API Stable, Preview, Latest alias, Experimental Previews at least 2 weeks; "latest" aliases repointed with 2 weeks' notice Microsoft Foundry Preview, GA, Legacy, Deprecated, Retired Standard GA lifecycle of 18 months; notices at least 60 days (GA) and 30 days (preview)

These terms change; read the pages linked above before planning. Plan for the shortest notice among the providers you use, because that is the one that will catch you:

A migration checklist:

  1. Inventory. Search configuration for the model ID across all environments and features, and check usage by key and model in the provider's console (Anthropic's Usage page can export a CSV broken down by API key and model).
  2. Shortlist candidates, starting from the provider's recommended replacement but not limited to it.
  3. Evaluate offline on your own data, overall and per slice, with cost and latency. Public benchmarks do not tell you how your prompt behaves.
  4. Adapt. Newer models may need prompt changes, reject parameters the old one accepted, count tokens differently (changing cost and context limits), or format structured output differently. Each fix is a new prompt version and release.
  5. Shadow, then canary the new release with the usual guardrails.
  6. Switch, keep the old release as a rollback until shortly before the shutdown date, then delete its configuration so nothing calls a retired model.

Automate the early warning: a daily job that asks the provider about every configured model and fails when one is close to retirement (see the example below).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use release versioning for any LLM feature that users rely on, that other code parses, or that costs enough to monitor. Use A/B tests when you have enough traffic and a measurable user outcome; use shadow tests when the risk of showing a worse answer is high.

Keep it lighter when:

  • The feature is an internal prototype with a handful of users: version prompts in Git and skip online experiments.
  • Traffic is too low for an A/B test to reach a useful sample size: rely on offline evaluations, a careful canary, and human review.
  • Outputs are not user-visible (offline batch jobs): compare releases on the batch itself, no traffic splitting needed.
Change Minimum process Typo or wording fix in a prompt New prompt version, CI evals, canary New instructions or output fields New version, evals including slices, A/B test if traffic allows Same model family, new pinned version Evals, shadow or canary, then switch Different provider or model family Full migration checklist, A/B test, longer canary Provider retirement notice Migration plan sized to the notice period Parameter change (max_output_tokens) New release, evals focused on truncation and cost

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The code below type-checks with TypeScript 7.0 in strict mode and runs on Node.js 24 (tested on Node.js 22). The logged outputs were produced against local stub servers that imitate the OpenAI API, so no real API was called.

docs.title: Prompt versions in code
docs.text:
// src/ai/prompts/taskParser.ts: every live version of the task-parser prompt
export interface TaskParserInput {
  text: string;        // what the user typed (untrusted)
  today: string;       // YYYY-MM-DD in the user's time zone
  projects: string[];  // projects this user can file tasks under
}

export interface BuiltPrompt {
  instructions: string;
  input: string;
}

const v3 = (i: TaskParserInput): BuiltPrompt => ({
  instructions: [
    "Turn the user's request into one TaskFlow task.",
    `Today is ${i.today}. Resolve relative dates against it.`,
    `Projects: ${i.projects.join(", ")}.`,
  ].join("\n"),
  input: i.text,
});

const v4 = (i: TaskParserInput): BuiltPrompt => ({
  instructions: [
    "Turn the user's request into one TaskFlow task.",
    `Today is ${i.today}. Resolve relative dates such as "next Friday" against it.`,
    "Set dueDate to null when the request names no date; never guess one.",
    `Choose project only from: ${i.projects.join(", ")}. Use null if none fits.`,
    'Use priority "high" only for explicit urgency words such as "urgent" or "blocker".',
  ].join("\n"),
  input: i.text,
});

// Old versions stay here until no release refers to them, so rollback is a config change
export const TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS = {
  "task-parser@3": v3,
  "task-parser@4": v4,
} as const satisfies Record<string, (i: TaskParserInput) => BuiltPrompt>;

export type TaskParserPromptVersion = keyof typeof TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS;

Version 4 fixes two problems found in evaluation: version 3 guessed due dates for requests without one, and marked too many tasks as high priority. Both versions stay in the module while releases use them.

docs.title: Releases, rollout configuration, and sticky bucketing
docs.text:
// src/ai/releases.ts: named releases of the task parser and who gets which one
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { z } from "zod";
import { TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS, type TaskParserPromptVersion } from "./prompts/taskParser.js";

export interface AiRelease {
  id: string;                            // unique and never reused
  promptVersion: TaskParserPromptVersion;
  modelEnv: string;                      // env var that holds the provider's model ID
  maxOutputTokens: number;
}

export const RELEASES = {
  "task-parser-2026-10-02": {
    id: "task-parser-2026-10-02",
    promptVersion: "task-parser@3",
    modelEnv: "TASK_PARSER_MODEL",
    maxOutputTokens: 400,
  },
  "task-parser-2026-11-10": {
    id: "task-parser-2026-11-10",
    promptVersion: "task-parser@4",
    modelEnv: "TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT",
    maxOutputTokens: 400,
  },
} as const satisfies Record<string, AiRelease>;

export type ReleaseId = keyof typeof RELEASES;

// Rollout settings come from the flag service or config, so they change without a deploy
export const RolloutConfig = z.object({
  enabled: z.boolean(),                  // kill switch: false turns the feature off
  experiment: z.string(),                // bucketing key; a new key reshuffles users
  splits: z.array(z.object({
    release: z.enum(Object.keys(RELEASES) as [ReleaseId, ...ReleaseId[]]),
    percent: z.number().int().min(0).max(100),
  })).refine((s) => s.reduce((sum, x) => sum + x.percent, 0) === 100, "splits must sum to 100"),
});
export type RolloutConfig = z.infer<typeof RolloutConfig>;

// SHA-256 of "<experiment>:<user id>", first 4 bytes, modulo 10,000: stable per user
export function bucketOf(experiment: string, userId: string): number {
  return createHash("sha256").update(`${experiment}:${userId}`).digest().readUInt32BE(0) % 10_000;
}

export function resolveRelease(config: RolloutConfig, userId: string): AiRelease | null {
  if (!config.enabled) return null;
  const bucket = bucketOf(config.experiment, userId);
  let upper = 0;
  for (const split of config.splits) {
    upper += split.percent * 100;
    if (bucket < upper) return RELEASES[split.release];
  }
  return null;
}

// Changes whenever the prompt text, model ID, or parameters change
export function releaseFingerprint(release: AiRelease, env = process.env): string {
  const sample = TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS[release.promptVersion]({
    text: "<text>", today: "<today>", projects: ["<project>"],
  });
  const material = JSON.stringify({
    prompt: sample.instructions,
    model: env[release.modelEnv] ?? null,
    maxOutputTokens: release.maxOutputTokens,
  });
  return createHash("sha256").update(material).digest("hex").slice(0, 12);
}

The rollout configuration lives in the flag service (or a config file reloaded at runtime) and is validated before use:

{
  "enabled": true,
  "experiment": "task-parser-2026-11",
  "splits": [
    { "release": "task-parser-2026-10-02", "percent": 90 },
    { "release": "task-parser-2026-11-10", "percent": 10 }
  ]
}

Checking the behavior with 100,000 simulated users, a kill switch, an invalid configuration, and fingerprints (model IDs are placeholders):

assignment of 100,000 users: { 'task-parser-2026-10-02': 89960, 'task-parser-2026-11-10': 10040 }
sticky: true bucket of user-42: 2658
kill switch: null
bad config rejected: true
task-parser-2026-10-02 fingerprint 48543e08b07b
task-parser-2026-11-10 fingerprint f64a7f2544d8
model change -> d45ac29116a3

The split lands within 0.05 points of 90/10, a user always gets the same release, a configuration that does not sum to 100 is rejected before it can route traffic, and changing only the model ID changes the fingerprint. Because the release type refers to TaskParserPromptVersion, a release that names a deleted prompt version does not compile.

docs.title: Calling the model with the assigned release
docs.text:
The OpenAI Responses API in full; equivalents for other SDKs follow.

// src/ai/runTaskParser.ts: parse a request with the release this user is assigned to
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { z } from "zod";
import { TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS, type TaskParserInput } from "./prompts/taskParser.js";
import {
  bucketOf, releaseFingerprint, resolveRelease, type AiRelease, type RolloutConfig,
} from "./releases.js";

const client = new OpenAI(); // reads OPENAI_API_KEY

export const TaskDraft = z.object({
  title: z.string(),
  dueDate: z.string().nullable(),   // YYYY-MM-DD
  project: z.string().nullable(),
  priority: z.enum(["low", "normal", "high"]),
});
export type TaskDraft = z.infer<typeof TaskDraft>;
const { $schema: _draftSchemaUri, ...TASK_DRAFT_SCHEMA } = z.toJSONSchema(TaskDraft);

async function callModel(release: AiRelease, input: TaskParserInput): Promise<TaskDraft> {
  const model = process.env[release.modelEnv];
  if (!model) throw new Error(`${release.modelEnv} is not set`);
  const prompt = TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS[release.promptVersion](input);
  const started = performance.now();
  const response = await client.responses.create({
    model,
    instructions: prompt.instructions,
    input: prompt.input,
    max_output_tokens: release.maxOutputTokens,
    text: { format: { type: "json_schema", name: "task_draft", strict: true, schema: TASK_DRAFT_SCHEMA } },
  });
  console.log(JSON.stringify({
    event: "llm_call",
    release: release.id,
    promptVersion: release.promptVersion,
    model,
    fingerprint: releaseFingerprint(release),
    latencyMs: Math.round(performance.now() - started),
    inputTokens: response.usage?.input_tokens,
    outputTokens: response.usage?.output_tokens,
  }));
  return TaskDraft.parse(JSON.parse(response.output_text));
}

export async function runTaskParser(
  userId: string, input: TaskParserInput, rollout: RolloutConfig, shadow?: AiRelease,
): Promise<{ draft: TaskDraft; release: string } | null> {
  const release = resolveRelease(rollout, userId);
  if (!release) return null; // switched off: the UI shows the plain task form
  const draft = await callModel(release, input);

  // Shadow: a sample of requests also runs the candidate; its answer is logged, never shown
  if (shadow && shadow.id !== release.id && bucketOf("task-parser-shadow", userId) < 500) {
    void callModel(shadow, input)
      .then((candidate) => console.log(JSON.stringify({
        event: "shadow_compare",
        primary: release.id,
        candidate: shadow.id,
        sameDueDate: candidate.dueDate === draft.dueDate,
        sameProject: candidate.project === draft.project,
        samePriority: candidate.priority === draft.priority,
      })))
      .catch((err: unknown) => console.log(JSON.stringify({
        event: "shadow_error", candidate: shadow.id, error: String(err),
      })));
  }
  return { draft, release: release.id };
}
  • The Zod schema is the single source for the JSON schema sent to the model (Zod 4's z.toJSONSchema(), minus its $schema key) and for validating the answer.
  • Every call logs the release, prompt version, model, fingerprint, latency, and token counts as one structured line (see structured logging); in production these become span attributes in your tracing (see LLM observability and tracing).
  • Shadow calls use their own bucketing key, so the 5% shadow sample is independent of the A/B split.

Run against a local stub server with placeholder model IDs, one shadowed request logs (example output from the stub, not a real model):

{"event":"llm_call","release":"task-parser-2026-10-02","promptVersion":"task-parser@3","model":"model-a","fingerprint":"57138fe92cdc","latencyMs":39,"inputTokens":120,"outputTokens":30}
{"draft":{"title":"Fix login bug","dueDate":null,"project":"engineering","priority":"high"},"release":"task-parser-2026-10-02"}
{"event":"llm_call","release":"task-parser-2026-11-10","promptVersion":"task-parser@4","model":"model-b","fingerprint":"07f690c924f8","latencyMs":7,"inputTokens":120,"outputTokens":30}
{"event":"shadow_compare","primary":"task-parser-2026-10-02","candidate":"task-parser-2026-11-10","sameDueDate":false,"sameProject":true,"samePriority":true}

The same release maps directly onto the other SDKs: the instructions become Anthropic's system field or Google's systemInstruction, and the schema moves to each provider's structured-output setting.

// src/ai/equivalents.ts: the same release on Anthropic and Google Gen AI SDKs
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";
import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai";
import type { BuiltPrompt } from "./prompts/taskParser.js";

export async function viaAnthropic(model: string, prompt: BuiltPrompt, schema: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const anthropic = new Anthropic(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
  return anthropic.messages.create({
    model,
    system: prompt.instructions,
    messages: [{ role: "user", content: prompt.input }],
    max_tokens: 400,
    output_config: { format: { type: "json_schema", schema } },
  });
}

export async function viaGoogle(model: string, prompt: BuiltPrompt, schema: Record<string, unknown>) {
  const ai = new GoogleGenAI({}); // reads GEMINI_API_KEY or GOOGLE_API_KEY
  return ai.models.generateContent({
    model,
    contents: prompt.input,
    config: {
      systemInstruction: prompt.instructions,
      maxOutputTokens: 400,
      responseMimeType: "application/json",
      responseJsonSchema: schema,
    },
  });
}

Moving a release between providers is therefore a new release with new evaluations, never a drop-in swap: limits such as max_tokens and schema support differ, and the prompt usually needs tuning.

docs.title: Blocking silent prompt edits in CI
docs.text:
// scripts/check-prompt-lock.ts: fail CI when a released prompt version was edited in place
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS } from "../src/ai/prompts/taskParser.js";

const LOCK = "prompts.lock.json";
const sample = { text: "<text>", today: "<today>", projects: ["<project>"] };
const lock: Record<string, string> = JSON.parse(readFileSync(LOCK, "utf8"));

let failed = false;
for (const [version, build] of Object.entries(TASK_PARSER_PROMPTS)) {
  const hash = createHash("sha256").update(JSON.stringify(build(sample))).digest("hex").slice(0, 16);
  if (!(version in lock)) {
    lock[version] = hash; // a new version: record it
    console.log(`added   ${version} ${hash}`);
  } else if (lock[version] !== hash) {
    failed = true;
    console.log(`CHANGED ${version}: locked ${lock[version]}, now ${hash}; add a new version instead`);
  } else {
    console.log(`ok      ${version} ${hash}`);
  }
}
writeFileSync(LOCK, JSON.stringify(lock, null, 2) + "\n");
process.exitCode = failed ? 1 : 0;

Output after someone edited version 3 in place:

CHANGED task-parser@3: locked 0000000000000000, now 26831ec372851f7f; add a new version instead
ok      task-parser@4 d977707d20fc2bf8

The lock file is committed. A new version adds a line that the developer commits with the change; an edit to an existing version fails the build. It is the prompt equivalent of never re-tagging a released container image.

docs.title: Reading an A/B result
docs.text:
// scripts/ab-analysis.ts: compare acceptance rates of two releases, and size the test
// Normal CDF via the Abramowitz-Stegun erf approximation (error below 1.5e-7)
function normalCdf(z: number): number {
  const t = 1 / (1 + 0.3275911 * (Math.abs(z) / Math.SQRT2));
  const poly = t * (0.254829592 + t * (-0.284496736 + t * (1.421413741
    + t * (-1.453152027 + t * 1.061405429))));
  const erf = 1 - poly * Math.exp(-(z * z) / 2);
  return z >= 0 ? (1 + erf) / 2 : (1 - erf) / 2;
}

// Two-sided two-proportion z-test with a pooled standard error
export function compareRates(acceptedA: number, totalA: number, acceptedB: number, totalB: number) {
  const pA = acceptedA / totalA;
  const pB = acceptedB / totalB;
  const pooled = (acceptedA + acceptedB) / (totalA + totalB);
  const se = Math.sqrt(pooled * (1 - pooled) * (1 / totalA + 1 / totalB));
  const z = (pB - pA) / se;
  return { pA, pB, lift: pB - pA, z, pValue: 2 * (1 - normalCdf(Math.abs(z))) };
}

// Users per variant to detect `delta` at 5% significance (two-sided) with 80% power
export function sampleSizePerVariant(baseline: number, delta: number): number {
  const zAlpha = 1.959964;
  const zBeta = 0.841621;
  const p2 = baseline + delta;
  const variance = baseline * (1 - baseline) + p2 * (1 - p2);
  return Math.ceil(((zAlpha + zBeta) ** 2 * variance) / delta ** 2);
}

const r = compareRates(5_580, 9_000, 668, 1_000);
console.log(`control ${(r.pA * 100).toFixed(1)}%, candidate ${(r.pB * 100).toFixed(1)}%, ` +
  `lift ${(r.lift * 100).toFixed(1)} points, z=${r.z.toFixed(2)}, p=${r.pValue.toFixed(4)}`);
console.log(`users per variant to detect +2 points at 62%: ${sampleSizePerVariant(0.62, 0.02)}`);

control 62.0%, candidate 66.8%, lift 4.8 points, z=2.97, p=0.0029
users per variant to detect +2 points at 62%: 9144

Experimentation platforms do this math for you (and handle repeated looks at the data more carefully); the point of the script is to know what the numbers mean before you trust a dashboard.

docs.title: Failing the build before a model retires
docs.text:
// scripts/check-model-lifecycle.ts: fail CI or alert when a configured model is retiring
import OpenAI from "openai";

const MODEL_ENVS = ["TASK_PARSER_MODEL", "TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT", "SUMMARY_MODEL"];
const MIN_DAYS_LEFT = Number(process.env.MODEL_MIN_DAYS_LEFT ?? 45);
const client = new OpenAI();

let failed = false;
for (const env of MODEL_ENVS) {
  const id = process.env[env];
  if (!id) continue;
  try {
    const model = await client.models.retrieve(id);
    if (!model.shutdown_date) {
      console.log(`ok    ${env}=${id}: no shutdown date announced`);
      continue;
    }
    const daysLeft = Math.floor((Date.parse(model.shutdown_date) - Date.now()) / 86_400_000);
    const tooSoon = daysLeft < MIN_DAYS_LEFT;
    failed ||= tooSoon;
    console.log(`${tooSoon ? "FAIL" : "warn"}  ${env}=${id}: shuts down ${model.shutdown_date} (${daysLeft} days)`);
  } catch (err) {
    if (!(err instanceof OpenAI.NotFoundError)) throw err;
    failed = true;
    console.log(`FAIL  ${env}=${id}: not available to this project`);
  }
}
process.exitCode = failed ? 1 : 0;

Against a stub that announces a shutdown in 20 days for one model (example output, placeholder IDs):

FAIL  TASK_PARSER_MODEL=model-current: shuts down 2026-12-04 (19 days)
ok    TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT=model-next: no shutdown date announced
warn  SUMMARY_MODEL=model-summary: shuts down 2027-06-02 (199 days)

For Claude models the same check reads lifecycle and retires_at:

// scripts/check-anthropic-lifecycle.ts: the same check for a Claude model
import Anthropic from "@anthropic-ai/sdk";

const anthropic = new Anthropic(); // reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
const id = process.env.SUMMARY_MODEL;
if (id) {
  const info = await anthropic.models.retrieve(id);
  if (info.lifecycle !== "active") {
    console.log(`${info.id} is ${info.lifecycle}; retires ${info.retires_at ?? "date not set"}`);
    process.exitCode = 1;
  }
}

Microsoft Foundry exposes lifecycleStatus and deprecation dates through its Models API. Where a provider exposes nothing, subscribe to its deprecation notices and add the dates to configuration by hand.

docs.title: Wiring the checks into the pipeline
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ai-release-checks.yml
name: ai-release-checks
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["src/ai/**", "prompts.lock.json", "evals/**"]
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * *" # daily: catch newly announced shutdown dates
jobs:
  checks:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx tsc -p tsconfig.json
      - name: Prompt versions are immutable
        run: node dist/scripts/check-prompt-lock.js && git diff --exit-code prompts.lock.json
      - name: Offline evaluations for current and candidate releases
        if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
        run: npm run evals
        env:
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
          TASK_PARSER_MODEL: ${{ vars.TASK_PARSER_MODEL }}
          TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT: ${{ vars.TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT }}
      - name: Configured models are not retiring soon
        run: node dist/scripts/check-model-lifecycle.js
        env:
          OPENAI_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.OPENAI_API_KEY }}
          TASK_PARSER_MODEL: ${{ vars.TASK_PARSER_MODEL }}
          TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT: ${{ vars.TASK_PARSER_MODEL_NEXT }}
          SUMMARY_MODEL: ${{ vars.SUMMARY_MODEL }}

Model IDs live in repository or environment variables (vars), not in the workflow, so the same pipeline checks whatever each environment uses. The npm run evals script is the evaluation suite from the evaluation lessons; the daily schedule skips it to avoid paying for evaluations nobody asked for.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep production prompts in the repository as typed functions, with every version immutable and a lock file enforced in CI.
  • Read every model ID from configuration, per feature, and pin versions rather than moving aliases in production.
  • Give every combination of prompt, model, parameters, and schema a release ID, and log it (with the model the provider reports) on every request.
  • Change behavior through flags: sticky per-user splits, a kill switch with a non-AI fallback, and old releases kept deployable.
  • Gate releases on offline evaluations of both the current and the candidate release, including slices, cost, and latency.
  • Size A/B tests before starting them, use user-level assignment, and guard latency, error rate, and cost.
  • Run a daily lifecycle check against provider APIs, and plan migrations for the shortest notice period you depend on.
  • Treat provider auto-upgrades as releases: evaluate before the scheduled date.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Acceptance drops with no deploy. Detect: the share of drafts saved without edits falls on a day with no code release; logs show the same release ID throughout. Cause: the configured model is a moving alias that the provider repointed, or a platform auto-upgrade ran. Fix: compare the model reported in responses before and after, pin a version, and rerun evaluations on the new one before adopting it.
  • Behavior changed but every release looks the same. Detect: the fingerprint in log lines differs between two days for one release ID. Cause: someone edited a prompt in place or changed a model variable in one environment. Fix: enforce the prompt lock in CI, manage model variables through reviewed configuration, and alert on fingerprint changes within a release.
  • Requests start failing with 404 or "model not found". Detect: an error spike on one feature at midnight UTC of a known date. Cause: the model reached its shutdown date. Fix: switch the feature's flag to a release on a supported model (or the kill switch), then add the daily lifecycle check so the next retirement fails CI weeks earlier.
  • A migration to a newer model returns 400 errors. Detect: errors only for the new release, mentioning a parameter. Cause: the new model or API version rejects a parameter the old one accepted, such as sampling parameters on newer Claude models. Fix: remove the parameter in a new release; run a canary before any migration so these errors hit 1% of users, not all.
  • An A/B test "wins" and the gain disappears after rollout. Detect: acceptance after full rollout is close to the old control. Cause: the test was stopped at the first significant result, ran for only part of a week, or randomized per request. Fix: fix the sample size and duration in advance, assign per user, and keep a small holdback after rollout.
  • Shadow traffic causes rate-limit errors for real users. Detect: 429 responses rise when shadowing starts. Cause: the shadow calls share the production key and quota. Fix: use a separate project or key with its own limits, sample fewer requests, and drop shadow calls first when limits are near.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• LLMOps: Operating LLM features: versioning, evaluating, releasing, monitoring, and retiring prompts, models, and their configuration.
  • Prompt version: An immutable, named version of a prompt's text and structure.
  • Release (of an LLM feature): A named bundle of prompt version, model ID, parameters, schema, tools, and index versions.
  • Fingerprint: A hash of a release's effective parts, used to detect unrecorded changes.
  • Pinned version / moving alias: A model identifier with fixed behavior / one the provider repoints to newer models.
  • Deprecation / retirement (shutdown): The announcement that a model will go away / the date after which requests to it fail.
  • Shadow traffic: Running a candidate on real inputs without showing its output.
  • Sticky assignment: Giving the same user the same variant on every request, usually by hashing the user ID.
  • Guardrail metric: A metric that must not get worse (latency, errors, cost) while the primary metric is optimized.
  • Kill switch: A flag that turns an AI feature off and falls back to a non-AI path.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Editing a prompt "just slightly" in place instead of creating a new version.
  • Hard-coding model IDs, or using "latest" aliases in production and calling it pinned.
  • Believing a newer model is automatically better for your task.
  • Deleting old prompt versions as soon as a new one ships, which turns a rollback into an emergency deploy.
  • Running A/B tests per request, stopping them early, or judging only the primary metric without cost and latency guardrails.
  • Treating a provider's recommended replacement as a drop-in swap without evaluations, prompt changes, or parameter checks.
  • Waiting for the shutdown email to start a migration.
  • Letting a prompt registry change production behavior without the same review and evaluation gates as code.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. List the parts of an LLM feature release and explain how each one can change behavior.
  2. Why does a prompt lock file help, and what should a developer do when it fails?
  3. Compare keeping prompts in code, in a prompt registry, and in provider-hosted prompt objects.
  4. Your acceptance rate is 62%. How many users per variant do you need to detect a 2-point lift at 5% significance and 80% power? What if you only have 3,000 users per week in the candidate group?
  5. Why should an A/B test of a prompt assign users rather than requests to variants?
  6. A provider announces that the model behind your summary feature retires in 60 days. Outline your plan, week by week.
  7. Rollback to the previous release fails during an incident. Name two LLM-specific reasons this can happen and how to prevent them.
  8. What is the difference between a moving alias and a pinned version, and when is each acceptable?

docs.text:
• OpenAI: deprecations
  • Anthropic: model deprecations
  • Gemini API: models and version types
