docs.title: Production Monitoring and Drift
docs.text:
A model is trained on yesterday's data and serves today's users. The moment it ships, the world starts moving away from what it learned: users change habits, products add features, upstream systems change formats. Unlike a crashed service, a model that has drifted keeps answering with full confidence and HTTP 200. Production monitoring for machine learning watches for that: whether inputs still look like the training data, whether predictions still behave as expected, and, once labels arrive, whether the model is still right.

This lesson monitors the TaskFlow priority suggestion model from experiment tracking and model registry. It covers the kinds of drift, measuring them with the population stability index (PSI) and the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test, performance monitoring when labels arrive late, feedback loops, and when to retrain. All code was run with Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5, pandas 3.1, SciPy 1.18, and scikit-learn 1.9; the outputs are from those runs. Service-level monitoring (latency, errors, SLOs, alerting) works as for any API and is covered in section 07's Monitoring and Logging; quality monitoring of LLM features is covered in Evaluation and Monitoring.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Google's Rules of Machine Learning has a rule just for this, #10, "Watch for silent failures", noting that a decaying system keeps behaving "reasonably good, decaying gradually". Nobody files a bug for "suggestions are a bit worse than in March". Without monitoring, the first sign of drift is a business metric that slipped for months, and by then nobody can say whether the cause was the data, the model, or a product change.

Monitoring also protects you from the opposite mistake: retraining on every alarm. Drift statistics are noisy, and many shifts do not hurt the model at all. Good monitoring tells you which changes matter, gives you labels to prove it, and feeds a retraining process that still goes through the same gates as any release.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google's Rules of ML. Besides rule #10, the guide recommends logging the features used at serving time (rule #29) and measuring training/serving skew (rule #37, "Measure Training/Serving Skew"), because a discrepancy "probably indicates an engineering error". Many production "drift" alerts are such skew bugs.
  • Google Cloud's MLOps guide. MLOps: continuous delivery and automation pipelines lists retraining triggers: on demand, on a schedule, on availability of new training data, on model performance degradation, and on significant changes in the data distributions. It also requires tracking summary statistics of the data and the online performance of the model.
  • Banking and PSI. A study of the statistical properties of the population stability index (Western Michigan University, 2018) describes PSI as the measure banks use to monitor whether a model still fits the current population, where a high value can trigger an internal investigation or a regulator's audit. It notes that the usual thresholds (below 0.10 "little shift", above 0.25 "significant shift, action required") are used "without reference to Type I or Type II error rates".
  • Failing Loudly (NeurIPS 2019). An empirical study of methods for detecting dataset shift compared detectors across many shifts and found that "a two-sample-testing-based approach, using pre-trained classifiers for dimensionality reduction, performs best": two-sample tests such as KS are the workhorse, applied to the right representation.
  • Evidently's defaults. The open-source library's drift method documentation uses the KS test (numeric) and chi-squared test (categorical) with a 0.95 confidence level for reference data up to 1,000 rows, and switches to Wasserstein distance and Jensen-Shannon divergence with a 0.1 threshold above that, which avoids leaning on p-values for large samples. It also warns that drift tests do not react to more missing values, so null shares must be checked separately.

Popular tools and providers: Evidently and NannyML (open source), Arize, Fiddler, Azure Machine Learning model monitoring, Google Cloud model monitoring (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), and Prometheus with Grafana for the resulting metrics. Amazon SageMaker Model Monitor, an earlier managed option, is no longer open to new customers (November 2026).

docs.title: What can go wrong after deployment
docs.text:
Failure TaskFlow example First signal Service failure The model server runs out of memory Errors and latency (section 07 monitoring) Broken input data A client stops sending days_until_due Null share and schema checks Training-serving skew The API computes title_length in characters, training used words Feature distributions differ from day one Data drift A new "quick add" creates many short tasks without due dates Input PSI and KS Label shift A deadline-heavy quarter makes more tasks urgent Label rate, predicted score share Concept drift A new triage team takes urgent support work, so support tasks stop being urgent Only performance on labels Feedback loop Users accept suggested priorities, so labels copy the model Holdout comparison

The first three are bugs with a fix in code or data pipelines. The next three are the world changing. The last one is the model changing the world it learns from.

docs.title: Monitoring layers
docs.text:
Layer What to measure How often Needs labels Service Request rate, errors, latency, saturation Continuously No Data quality Schema, null shares, value ranges, category vocabulary Every batch or day No Input drift PSI and KS per feature against the training reference Daily No Prediction drift Distribution of scores, share above the threshold Daily No Performance Precision, recall, AUC, calibration, per slice Weekly, as labels arrive Yes Outcome Suggestion acceptance, time to triage Weekly Product data

The service layer reuses metrics and dashboards and alerting and on-call. The other layers need one thing the service layer does not: a prediction log that stores, for each request, the request ID, the model version, the features as the model saw them, and the score. It is the only reliable source for drift statistics, skew checks, and joining labels later (Rules of ML #29).

docs.title: Kinds of drift
docs.text:
• Data drift (covariate shift): the distribution of inputs changes, P(X). The model may still be right for each input, but it now sees inputs it rarely trained on.
  • Label shift (prior shift): the share of each class changes, P(Y). Thresholds and calibration go off even if the inputs look similar.
  • Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and outcome changes, P(Y | X). The same task now means something else. This is the dangerous one, because input monitoring cannot see it.

Drift can be sudden (a product launch), gradual (habits changing), or recurring (weekends, quarter ends). Recurring patterns argue for comparing against a reference from the same period, or for alerting on persistent changes only.

docs.title: Measuring drift: PSI
docs.text:
The population stability index compares the share of data in each bin between a reference (training) sample and a current sample:

PSI = Σ over bins (current share − reference share) × ln(current share / reference share)

Bins are cut at the reference quantiles (deciles are common), so every reference bin holds the same share. Empty bins get a small floor so the logarithm stays finite. Each bin adds a positive amount whether it gained or lost data, and the total grows with the size of the shift.

Working the first bin by hand: (0.35 − 0.20) × ln(0.35 / 0.20) = 0.15 × 0.560 = 0.084. The common rule of thumb reads PSI below 0.10 as little shift, 0.10 to 0.25 as worth investigating, and above 0.25 as a significant shift. Treat these as starting points to tune per feature: they come from credit scoring practice, not from a statistical test, and PSI is biased upward on small samples (500 rows of unchanged data gave PSI values of 0.01 to 0.03 in the daily example below).

docs.title: Measuring drift: the KS test and other tests
docs.text:
The two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test compares the empirical cumulative distributions of two samples. Its statistic D is the largest vertical gap between the two curves (0 = identical, 1 = no overlap), and its p-value is the probability of a gap at least that large if both samples came from the same distribution.

Method Data type Output Watch out for PSI Numeric (binned) or categorical Effect size, rule-of-thumb thresholds Binning choices; small-sample bias KS test Numeric, continuous D statistic and p-value p-values shrink with sample size Chi-squared test Categorical Statistic and p-value Same; needs enough counts per category Wasserstein distance Numeric Distance in the feature's units Scale-dependent; normalize to compare features Jensen-Shannon distance Categorical or binned Bounded distance (0 to 1) Needs a threshold choice like PSI Domain classifier Many features or text at once AUC of telling old from new data Shows that, not where, data differs

A p-value answers "is there any difference?", not "is the difference big enough to matter?". With enough data the answer to the first question is always yes. The same shift of 0.03 standard deviations, measured three times:

n=  1,000: KS statistic 0.0560, p-value 8.69e-02, PSI 0.0369
n= 20,000: KS statistic 0.0139, p-value 4.16e-02, PSI 0.0013
n=200,000: KS statistic 0.0124, p-value 7.17e-14, PSI 0.0010

At 200,000 rows the test is overwhelmingly "significant" about a shift no model would notice, while PSI correctly stays near zero. Use effect sizes (PSI, D itself, distances) for alerts and keep p-values for small samples. There is also a multiple-testing cost: testing 7 features daily at a 5% significance level produces about 7 × 365 × 0.05 ≈ 128 false alarms a year from a perfectly stable system. Alert on effect sizes, require persistence, and review a weekly report instead of paging on every test.

docs.title: Missing values hide from drift statistics
docs.text: PSI and KS run on the values that are present. When a client stops sending a field, the remaining values can look perfectly stable while a quarter of the rows are empty. In the comparison below, days_until_due has PSI 0.007, yet its null share rose by 0.28. Track null shares, schema, and category vocabularies as separate data-quality checks; they catch broken pipelines faster than drift statistics do.

docs.title: Monitoring performance when labels arrive late
docs.text:
Drift tells you something changed; only labels tell you whether the model is still right. For TaskFlow, a suggestion's label arrives when the task's real urgency is known: the user changed or kept the priority over the next days, or the task was escalated. That label delay shapes the monitor:

  • Join the prediction log with labels by request ID, and report by the week of the prediction, not the week the label arrived.
  • Show label coverage next to every metric: a week that is 55% labeled is not comparable with a complete one.
  • Show confidence intervals. Precision on 100 flagged tasks has an interval about 20 points wide; a dip inside it is noise. The Wilson interval behaves well for small counts.
  • Slice by the segments that matter (project type, team size, language).

In the simulation below, support tasks stop being urgent from week 5 (a new triage team handles them), while the inputs do not change at all:

      label_coverage  precision precision_ci  recall   auc  project_type_psi
week
1              1.000      0.623    0.54-0.70   0.200 0.717             0.000
2              1.000      0.578    0.48-0.67   0.165 0.711             0.001
3              1.000      0.613    0.53-0.69   0.200 0.705             0.004
4              1.000      0.638    0.56-0.71   0.212 0.732             0.000
5              1.000      0.472    0.39-0.56   0.203 0.660             0.000
6              1.000      0.378    0.30-0.47   0.159 0.660             0.003
7              1.000      0.408    0.33-0.49   0.196 0.665             0.001
8              0.550      0.539    0.43-0.65   0.247 0.641             0.000

Precision falls from about 0.61 to about 0.42 and AUC from 0.72 to 0.66, while the project-type PSI stays at zero: concept drift is invisible to input monitoring. Week 8 also shows why coverage matters: with 55% of labels in, its precision bounces up and its interval is wide.

Before labels arrive you can watch proxies: the score distribution, the share of high-confidence predictions, and estimated performance. NannyML's confidence-based performance estimation (CBPE) estimates classification metrics from calibrated scores without labels, but its documentation is explicit that it "will not work under concept drift i.e. when P(Y|X) changes". Proxies buy time; they do not replace labels.

docs.title: Feedback loops
docs.text:
A model that influences its own future training data creates a feedback loop, a risk Google's Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems describes as direct and hidden feedback loops. TaskFlow's suggestion sets the default priority in the form. Users often keep defaults, so "kept the suggested priority" becomes the label, and the next model learns to agree with the last one. Errors become self-confirming.

Mitigations:

  • A holdout group. A small share of tasks (5%, chosen by hashing the task ID) gets no suggestion. Their labels show how users prioritize unaided, and give an unbiased evaluation set.
  • Label from outcomes, not defaults. Prefer signals the suggestion does not set directly, such as escalations or completion times.
  • Record exposure. Log whether a suggestion was shown, so training can weight or exclude influenced labels.
  • Watch position and presentation effects. Rules of ML #36, "Avoid feedback loops with positional features", makes the same point for ranked lists.

docs.title: Retraining triggers
docs.text:
Trigger Example rule Strength Weakness Schedule Every 28 days Simple, predictable Retrains when nothing changed; late when things change fast New data 5,000 new labels since the last run Uses fresh information Labels may be biased (feedback loops) Performance Latest precision's upper bound below baseline minus 0.05 Acts on real harm Waits for labels Drift A key feature's PSI above 0.25 for 3 days Early Many drifts do not hurt; risk of churn Event A product launch or upstream schema change Planned Needs people to remember it

Two rules keep retraining safe. First, a trigger starts the training pipeline; it never promotes. The new version goes through the same gate as any other: a newer holdout, slice checks, a canary (see the promotion gate). Second, retraining fixes drift only when fresh, correct labels exist. After a concept change, a model retrained on mostly old labels learns the old world again; sometimes the right response is a rule change, a feature change, or turning the suggestion off until enough new labels arrive.

docs.title: Alerting on model health
docs.text:
Model alerts follow the same principles as service alerts: page a human only for urgent, actionable problems, and send the rest to a ticket or weekly report (see SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets). For the priority model:

Signal Page Ticket Weekly report Scoring errors or latency SLO burn rate Null share of a required feature above 5% Yes Feature PSI above 0.25 on two consecutive days Yes Feature PSI above 0.10 for three days Yes Precision below baseline with confidence Yes Single-day drift blips, p-values Yes

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Every model in production needs the service, data-quality, and prediction-log layers from day one: they are cheap and catch most incidents. Drift and performance monitoring scale with the stakes.

Situation Monitoring to add A low-stakes suggestion with an easy override Service, data quality, weekly drift report, quarterly performance check A model that drives decisions (fraud, pricing, credit) Daily drift with alerts, weekly performance by slice, holdout groups, documented retraining policy Labels arrive in minutes (clicks) Near-real-time performance; drift matters less Labels arrive in months (loan defaults) Strong drift and proxy monitoring, cohort-based performance later Very low traffic Weekly or monthly windows; PSI and tests are noise on tiny samples LLM features without trained models Use the evaluation and tracing practices in the evaluation lessons

docs.title: Drift functions
docs.text:
# drift.py: PSI and two-sample tests for one feature at a time
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

EPS = 1e-4  # floor for empty bins, so log() stays finite


def psi_numeric(reference: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray, bins: int = 10) -> float:
    """Population stability index with bins cut at the reference deciles."""
    reference, current = reference[~np.isnan(reference)], current[~np.isnan(current)]
    edges = np.unique(np.quantile(reference, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1)))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf
    ref = np.histogram(reference, edges)[0] / len(reference)
    cur = np.histogram(current, edges)[0] / len(current)
    ref, cur = np.clip(ref, EPS, None), np.clip(cur, EPS, None)
    return float(np.sum((cur - ref) * np.log(cur / ref)))


def psi_categorical(reference: pd.Series, current: pd.Series) -> float:
    cats = sorted(set(reference.dropna()) | set(current.dropna()))
    ref = reference.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(cats, fill_value=0).to_numpy()
    cur = current.value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(cats, fill_value=0).to_numpy()
    ref, cur = np.clip(ref, EPS, None), np.clip(cur, EPS, None)
    return float(np.sum((cur - ref) * np.log(cur / ref)))


def compare_feature(reference: pd.Series, current: pd.Series) -> dict:
    """Effect size (PSI) plus a test statistic and p-value, and the change in missing values."""
    result = {"null_share_change": current.isna().mean() - reference.isna().mean()}
    if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(reference) and not pd.api.types.is_bool_dtype(reference):
        ref, cur = reference.to_numpy(float), current.to_numpy(float)
        ks = stats.ks_2samp(ref[~np.isnan(ref)], cur[~np.isnan(cur)])
        result.update(psi=psi_numeric(ref, cur), test="ks", statistic=ks.statistic, p_value=ks.pvalue)
    else:
        table = pd.crosstab(pd.concat([reference, current]).astype(str),
                            np.r_[np.zeros(len(reference)), np.ones(len(current))])
        chi2 = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
        result.update(psi=psi_categorical(reference.astype(str), current.astype(str)),
                      test="chi2", statistic=chi2.statistic, p_value=chi2.pvalue)
    return result
  • Bins come from the reference only, so today's data cannot move the bin edges. np.unique merges duplicate edges for integer features with many ties.
  • compare_feature returns an effect size, a test, and the null-share change together, so a report never shows a p-value without its context.
  • Booleans and strings go to the categorical branch with a chi-squared test on a contingency table.

docs.title: Comparing last week with the training data
docs.text:
# compare_week.py: compare one week of production inputs and scores with the training data
import mlflow
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from drift import compare_feature, psi_numeric
from make_dataset import make_tasks

FEATURES = ["title_length", "has_due_date", "days_until_due", "assignee_open_tasks",
            "project_type", "mentions_blocker", "created_hour"]

reference = pd.read_parquet("data/tasks-2026-10.parquet")[FEATURES]

# Stand-in for last week's prediction log: 40% of tasks now come from the new "quick add"
current = make_tasks(3_000, seed=20261109)[FEATURES]
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
quick = rng.random(len(current)) < 0.4
current.loc[quick, "has_due_date"] = False
current.loc[quick, "days_until_due"] = np.nan
current.loc[quick, "title_length"] = rng.integers(2, 6, quick.sum())

rows = {name: compare_feature(reference[name], current[name]) for name in FEATURES}
report = pd.DataFrame(rows).T[["test", "statistic", "p_value", "psi", "null_share_change"]]
print(report.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.4f}"))

model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/taskflow-priority@champion")
ref_scores = model.predict_proba(reference.sample(3_000, random_state=1))[:, 1]
cur_scores = model.predict_proba(current)[:, 1]
print(f"\nprediction PSI {psi_numeric(ref_scores, cur_scores):.4f}, "
      f"mean score {ref_scores.mean():.3f} -> {cur_scores.mean():.3f}")

In production current is read from the prediction log; here it is generated with make_tasks from the previous lesson, then 40% of tasks are changed the way the quick-add feature changes them.

                     test statistic p_value    psi null_share_change
title_length           ks    0.3285  0.0000 0.5269            0.0000
has_due_date         chi2  931.0224  0.0000 0.3334            0.0000
days_until_due         ks    0.0270  0.3650 0.0070            0.2824
assignee_open_tasks    ks    0.0093  0.9749 0.0005            0.0000
project_type         chi2   13.5029  0.0037 0.0053            0.0000
mentions_blocker     chi2    0.4039  0.5251 0.0002            0.0000
created_hour           ks    0.0146  0.6318 0.0058            0.0000

prediction PSI 0.2097, mean score 0.195 -> 0.200

Reading the report:

  • title_length (PSI 0.53) and has_due_date (PSI 0.33) moved a lot: the quick-add effect, clearly above the 0.25 rule of thumb.
  • days_until_due looks stable by PSI and KS, but 28% more rows are empty: the real change hides in the null share.
  • project_type did not change at all, yet its chi-squared p-value is 0.004. With seven tests a day, such false alarms are routine; its PSI of 0.005 says the difference is negligible.
  • The scores shifted (prediction PSI 0.21) while the mean score barely moved (0.195 to 0.200). Averages hide distribution changes; compare distributions.

docs.title: Why p-values alone mislead
docs.text:
# sample_size_effect.py: the same tiny shift, measured with more and more data
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

from drift import psi_numeric

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for n in (1_000, 20_000, 200_000):
    reference = rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, n)
    current = rng.normal(0.03, 1.0, n)  # a shift of 0.03 standard deviations
    ks = stats.ks_2samp(reference, current)
    print(f"n={n:>7,}: KS statistic {ks.statistic:.4f}, p-value {ks.pvalue:.2e}, "
          f"PSI {psi_numeric(reference, current):.4f}")

The output is shown in the KS section above: the p-value falls from 0.087 to 7e-14 as the sample grows, while the KS statistic and PSI settle near their true, tiny values.

docs.title: Alerts that need persistence
docs.text:
# daily_monitor.py: turn daily PSI values into alerts that need persistence
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from drift import psi_numeric
from make_dataset import make_tasks


def alert_level(psi_history: list[float]) -> str:
    """psi_history holds one value per day, newest last."""
    if len(psi_history) >= 2 and min(psi_history[-2:]) > 0.25:
        return "page"    # large shift on two days in a row
    if len(psi_history) >= 3 and min(psi_history[-3:]) > 0.10:
        return "ticket"  # moderate shift for three days: investigate in working hours
    return "ok"


reference = pd.read_parquet("data/tasks-2026-10.parquet")["title_length"].to_numpy(float)
quick_add_share = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, 0.4, 0.4]  # the feature launches on day 5
history: list[float] = []
for day, share in enumerate(quick_add_share, start=1):
    today = make_tasks(500, seed=day)["title_length"].to_numpy(float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(100 + day)
    quick = rng.random(len(today)) < share
    today[quick] = rng.integers(2, 6, quick.sum())
    history.append(psi_numeric(reference, today))
    print(f"day {day:>2}: quick add {share:.0%}, PSI {history[-1]:.3f} -> {alert_level(history)}")

day  1: quick add 0%, PSI 0.034 -> ok
day  2: quick add 0%, PSI 0.023 -> ok
day  3: quick add 0%, PSI 0.009 -> ok
day  4: quick add 0%, PSI 0.012 -> ok
day  5: quick add 10%, PSI 0.072 -> ok
day  6: quick add 20%, PSI 0.184 -> ok
day  7: quick add 30%, PSI 0.411 -> ok
day  8: quick add 40%, PSI 0.575 -> page
day  9: quick add 40%, PSI 0.528 -> page
day 10: quick add 40%, PSI 0.662 -> page

The first four days show the noise floor of PSI on 500 rows (0.01 to 0.03). Day 7 is the first day above 0.25, but the rule waits for a second day, so a one-day blip would never wake anyone; the cost is one day of delay. Export the daily values as gauge metrics so dashboards and alert rules live with the rest of your monitoring.

docs.title: Performance with delayed labels
docs.text:
# weekly_performance.py: join predictions with labels that arrive later, week by week
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score


def wilson_interval(successes: int, n: int, z: float = 1.96) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """95% confidence interval for a proportion; honest for small n."""
    if n == 0:
        return float("nan"), float("nan")
    p = successes / n
    denom = 1 + z**2 / n
    center = (p + z**2 / (2 * n)) / denom
    half = z * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n + z**2 / (4 * n**2)) / denom
    return center - half, center + half


def weekly_performance(predictions: pd.DataFrame, labels: pd.DataFrame,
                       threshold: float = 0.5) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """predictions: request_id, week, score. labels: request_id, is_urgent (arrives later)."""
    joined = predictions.merge(labels, on="request_id", how="left")
    rows = []
    for week, part in joined.groupby("week"):
        labeled = part.dropna(subset=["is_urgent"])
        y = labeled["is_urgent"].astype(bool)
        flagged = y[labeled["score"] >= threshold]
        low, high = wilson_interval(int(flagged.sum()), len(flagged))
        rows.append({
            "week": week,
            "label_coverage": len(labeled) / len(part),
            "precision": flagged.mean(),
            "precision_ci": f"{low:.2f}-{high:.2f}",
            "recall": flagged.sum() / y.sum(),
            "auc": roc_auc_score(y, labeled["score"]),
        })
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("week")

The simulation that produced the table in "Monitoring performance when labels arrive late" scores eight weeks of tasks with the champion model, flips 70% of support tasks to "not urgent" from week 5, and keeps only 55% of week 8's labels:

# simulate_weeks.py: eight weeks of predictions; from week 5 support tasks stop being urgent
import mlflow
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from drift import psi_categorical
from make_dataset import make_tasks
from weekly_performance import weekly_performance

model = mlflow.sklearn.load_model("models:/taskflow-priority@champion")
reference = pd.read_parquet("data/tasks-2026-10.parquet")
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
predictions, labels, drift = [], [], {}

for week in range(1, 9):
    tasks = make_tasks(2_000, seed=1_000 + week)
    tasks["request_id"] = [f"w{week}-{i}" for i in range(len(tasks))]
    tasks["week"] = week
    tasks["score"] = model.predict_proba(tasks.drop(columns=["is_urgent", "request_id", "week"]))[:, 1]
    if week >= 5:  # concept drift: a new triage team now handles urgent support work
        support = tasks["project_type"] == "support"
        tasks.loc[support & (rng.random(len(tasks)) < 0.7), "is_urgent"] = False
    labeled = tasks if week < 8 else tasks.sample(frac=0.55, random_state=week)  # labels lag
    predictions.append(tasks[["request_id", "week", "score"]])
    labels.append(labeled[["request_id", "is_urgent"]])
    drift[week] = psi_categorical(reference["project_type"], tasks["project_type"])

report = weekly_performance(pd.concat(predictions), pd.concat(labels))
report["project_type_psi"] = pd.Series(drift)
print(report.to_string(float_format=lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"))

In production the two inputs are queries: predictions from the prediction log, labels from the task history, both with the request ID the API wrote when it made the suggestion.

docs.title: Retraining triggers as code
docs.text:
# retrain_trigger.py: decide whether to start the training pipeline (never to promote)
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import date


@dataclass
class MonitorState:
    last_trained: date
    labels_since_training: int
    baseline_precision: float        # from the weeks after the last promotion
    latest_precision_ci_high: float  # upper bound of the latest week's 95% interval
    days_with_feature_psi_above_025: int


def retraining_reasons(s: MonitorState, today: date) -> list[str]:
    reasons = []
    if (today - s.last_trained).days >= 28:
        reasons.append("schedule: 28 days since the last training run")
    if s.labels_since_training >= 5_000:
        reasons.append(f"data: {s.labels_since_training:,} new labels")
    if s.latest_precision_ci_high < s.baseline_precision - 0.05:
        reasons.append(f"performance: precision upper bound {s.latest_precision_ci_high:.2f} "
                       f"is below baseline {s.baseline_precision:.2f} minus 0.05")
    if s.days_with_feature_psi_above_025 >= 3:
        reasons.append("drift: a feature has PSI above 0.25 for 3 days")
    return reasons


state = MonitorState(last_trained=date(2026, 10, 20), labels_since_training=4_200,
                     baseline_precision=0.61, latest_precision_ci_high=0.49,
                     days_with_feature_psi_above_025=0)
for reason in retraining_reasons(state, today=date(2026, 11, 14)):
    print(reason)

performance: precision upper bound 0.49 is below baseline 0.61 minus 0.05

Using the upper bound of the interval means the trigger fires only when even the optimistic reading of week 7 is clearly worse than the baseline. The reasons are recorded with the training run as tags, so the registry shows why each version was trained. Because this is concept drift, the pipeline should train on the weeks after the change, and the gate should evaluate on those weeks too, or the "new" model will learn the old behavior.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Log every prediction with request ID, model version, the features as served, and the score; it is the foundation of all other monitoring.
  • Check data quality (schema, nulls, ranges, vocabularies) separately from drift; it catches most incidents first.
  • Alert on effect sizes such as PSI, with persistence rules; use p-values only on small samples and in reports.
  • Monitor prediction distributions, not only averages.
  • Report performance by prediction week, with label coverage, confidence intervals, and slices.
  • Keep a small holdout without the model's influence to get unbiased labels.
  • Let triggers start training, never promotion; every retrained model passes the same gate and canary.
  • Tune thresholds per feature after a few weeks of baseline data; document them with the model.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every feature drifted overnight. Detect: PSI above 0.25 on most features at once, starting at a deploy time. Cause: training-serving skew or a pipeline bug (units, encoding, a renamed field), not the world changing. Fix: compare served feature values with the training pipeline's values for the same records, fix the code path, and add a skew check to CI.
  • Drift alerts fire daily and everyone ignores them. Detect: dozens of drift tickets closed as "no impact". Cause: p-value alerts on large samples and many features. Fix: switch to effect-size thresholds, require persistence, and move single-day signals into a weekly report.
  • A field went missing and nobody noticed. Detect: weeks later, days_until_due is null for a third of rows. Cause: drift statistics ignore nulls; no data-quality check existed. Fix: alert on null shares of required features and validate schema at the API boundary.
  • Precision dropped but drift dashboards are green. Detect: weekly precision below its confidence band for two weeks, input PSI near zero. Cause: concept drift, such as a process change that alters what "urgent" means. Fix: confirm with the business owner, gather labels from after the change, retrain on recent data only, and consider disabling the suggestion meanwhile.
  • Retrained models keep getting worse. Detect: each new version wins offline but acceptance declines. Cause: a feedback loop: labels are mostly accepted suggestions, so the model learns to copy itself. Fix: build evaluation and training sets from a holdout without suggestions, and from outcome-based labels.
  • Performance numbers jump around every Monday. Detect: the latest week's metrics swing far more than earlier weeks. Cause: incomplete labels for recent predictions. Fix: show label coverage, report a week only when coverage passes a threshold, and plot confidence intervals.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Data drift (covariate shift): A change in the distribution of inputs, P(X).
  • Label shift (prior shift): A change in the distribution of outcomes, P(Y).
  • Concept drift: A change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, P(Y | X).
  • Training-serving skew: A difference between features in training and in serving caused by different code or data paths.
  • PSI (population stability index): A binned measure of how far a current distribution has moved from a reference.
  • KS test: A two-sample test whose statistic is the largest gap between two empirical cumulative distributions.
  • Reference window: The data that drift is measured against, usually the training data or a stable recent period.
  • Label delay: The time between a prediction and knowing its correct outcome.
  • Label coverage: The share of predictions in a window that have labels yet.
  • Feedback loop: A model's predictions influencing the data it is later trained or evaluated on.
  • Holdout group: Users or items deliberately not exposed to the model, used for unbiased measurement.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Equating drift with degradation: many shifts do not hurt the model, and concept drift can hurt it with no input drift at all.
  • Paging on p-values from large samples.
  • Comparing averages instead of distributions.
  • Forgetting missing values, which drift statistics silently ignore.
  • Judging last week's performance before its labels have arrived.
  • Retraining automatically on every alert, and promoting the result without a gate.
  • Using accepted suggestions as ground truth without a holdout.
  • Monitoring only the model and not the pipeline that feeds it.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain data drift, label shift, and concept drift with a TaskFlow example of each. Which one can input monitoring not detect?
  2. Compute the PSI for two bins with reference shares 0.5 and 0.5 and current shares 0.7 and 0.3. Which rule-of-thumb band is it in?
  3. Why does a KS test on 200,000 rows flag shifts that do not matter, and what should alerts use instead?
  4. You test 7 features daily at 5% significance. How many false alarms do you expect in a year from a stable system, and how do you reduce them?
  5. Precision fell from 0.61 to 0.42, but no feature drifted. What happened, and what would you do?
  6. Describe a feedback loop in a suggestion feature and two ways to break it.
  7. Compare schedule-based and performance-based retraining triggers. Why should a trigger never promote a model by itself?
  8. What fields must a prediction log contain, and why does each matter?

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Data for code to use Schema-constrained output plus domain checks The shape is enforced while decoding; values are not The model to pick between actions Strict tools, permission checks before running Arguments match the schema; the action is still checked A model without schema support Constrained decoding in the serving stack, or JSON mode plus validation JSON mode guarantees syntax only User text or documents in the prompt Delimit, label, and escape them Concatenated text can rewrite your rules Per-request lists (members, prices) Prompt data plus code checks, not enums Changing schemas defeat the grammar cache Drafts, extraction, classification A fast model, reasoning off or minimal Short, frequent, checked by code Planning under hard constraints A reasoning model, effort from a sweep, a code checker Pays off only on multi-step problems A fix for a rule violation One repair with the exact problems Never repair refusals or truncation

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Concatenating user text into instructions. Delimit, label, and escape every untrusted value, and enforce permissions in code.
  • Trusting valid JSON. Run domain checks (real dates, real members) and map names to IDs in code.
  • Parsing before checking the stop reason. Handle truncation and refusals first, and never repair them.
  • Putting every rule in the schema. Keep the model schema portable; lengths, ranges, and lookups belong in domain checks.
  • Acting on partial JSON from a stream. Use partial objects for display only; validate the final object.
  • Editing prompts without a version. Log id@version#hash with the served model and add a lock-file test.
  • Prompting reasoning models like old ones. Drop "think step by step" and sampling parameters; set effort from a sweep.
  • Hard-coding model IDs or inheriting defaults. Read the model and effort from configuration and pin dated snapshots.

docs.title: Prompting and Structured Output Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review prompt design and templates, structured output and validation, and reasoning models and thinking. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What are the parts of a production prompt, and who writes each part?
docs.text: The developer writes the instructions (role, rules, output contract) and the few-shot examples. Application code adds context it looked up, such as the project's members and today's date in the user's time zone. The user supplies the request, and tools or retrieval may add documents. Each part has a different level of trust, which is why a template assembles them in a fixed order with clear boundaries.

docs.title: 2. What is the instruction hierarchy?
docs.text: The trained ranking of who may instruct the model. OpenAI's Model Spec calls it a chain of command: root and system rules, then developer instructions, then user instructions, then guidelines. Quoted text, files, and tool outputs carry no authority by default, so instructions inside them are information, not commands. When two instructions conflict, the higher layer wins.

docs.title: 3. Where do developer instructions go in the main APIs?
docs.text: OpenAI Responses API: the instructions parameter, or a developer message in input. Anthropic Messages API: the top-level system parameter. Google Interactions API: system_instruction. Vercel AI SDK: the instructions option (system is deprecated in version 7).

docs.title: 4. Does the instruction hierarchy make prompt injection impossible?
docs.text: No. It is trained behaviour that makes injection much less likely to succeed; OpenAI's instruction hierarchy paper reports large robustness gains, not immunity. Anything that must never happen, such as assigning a task in another team's project, is enforced by backend code that checks permissions regardless of what the model outputs.

docs.title: 5. What does a well-written rule look like?
docs.text: It states the rule, the reason, and what to do instead: "The assignee must be one of the listed members, because TaskFlow can only notify members. If the request names anyone else, set assigneeName to null and ask who should own the task." The reason lets the model generalize, and the alternative stops it from replacing one wrong action with another.

docs.title: 6. Why avoid "CRITICAL: you MUST" phrasing?
docs.text: Recent models follow system prompts closely, and Anthropic notes that aggressive language written for older models now causes over-triggering. Plain, specific instructions with reasons work better and are easier to maintain.

docs.title: 7. In what order should a prompt be assembled?
docs.text: Stable content first (identity, rules, output contract, examples), then per-request context, then the user's input last. Stable content first lets provider prompt caching reuse the prefix, and OpenAI recommends putting reusable content at the start. For long documents, Anthropic recommends placing them above the question, which improved quality by up to 30 percent in its tests.

docs.title: 8. How many few-shot examples should you use, and which ones?
docs.text: A few, typically three to five (Anthropic's guidance), chosen to sit on the decision boundaries: for TaskFlow, an urgent request for a member, a request naming a non-member, and a request that is not a task. Easy middle-of-the-road examples teach little. For reasoning models, try zero examples first.

docs.title: 9. How can examples make answers worse?
docs.text: Models copy what examples have in common: if every example uses the same name or a Friday due date, those details leak into real answers. An example that contradicts a rule often wins over the rule because it is more concrete. Vary surface details, keep examples consistent with the rules, and test with and without them.

docs.title: 10. Should examples be sent as conversation turns or inside the instructions?
docs.text: Either works if they are clearly marked. As earlier user and assistant turns they look exactly like real exchanges; inside <example> tags in the instructions they stay part of the stable prefix. Both keep examples separate from the real request, which is what matters.

docs.title: 11. How do you delimit untrusted content safely?
docs.text:
Wrap each untrusted value in a tag that names its source (<user_request>, <email>), state in the developer instructions that tagged content is data, and escape < and > in the value so it cannot close the tag. Escape everything user-controlled, including project and member names.

const escapeForTag = (s: string) =>
  s.replace(/&/g, "&").replace(/</g, "<").replace(/>/g, ">");

docs.title: 12. What is spotlighting?
docs.text: A family of techniques from Microsoft researchers that mark untrusted text so the model can tell where it came from: delimiting, datamarking (interleaving a marker character through the text), and encoding (for example base64). In their experiments it reduced indirect prompt injection success from above 50 percent to below 2 percent; it costs tokens and can hurt quality on some models.

docs.title: 13. Why keep prompt templates in application code?
docs.text: Code gives review, diffs, type checking, tests, and deployment with the code that depends on the prompt. OpenAI's prompt engineering guide (as of November 2026) recommends storing production prompts in application code and announces that its reusable prompt objects are deprecated, with v1/prompts shutting down on November 30, 2026.

docs.title: 14. Why must the server, not the model, provide today's date?
docs.text: The model does not know the current date or the user's time zone, so it guesses. The template renders today's date from the server clock in the user's IANA time zone. Getting this wrong produces off-by-one due dates for users west or east of UTC near midnight.

docs.title: 15. How do you version a prompt?
docs.text: Give it an ID, a human version, and a hash of its stable text (for example task-assistant@3#0ed2b14868b0). Log all three with the served model ID on every call. Keep a lock file mapping each prompt ID to its version and hash, with a unit test that fails when the text changes without a version bump.

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between unit tests and evaluations for prompts?
docs.text: Unit tests check the rendering without a model: escaping, order, dates, size, and the lock file; they run on every commit in milliseconds. Evaluations call the model on golden, edge, adversarial, and regression cases and score the answers; they run when the prompt or model changes and compare versions on the same cases.

docs.title: 17. How do you roll out a prompt change safely?
docs.text: Bump the version, run unit tests and the evaluation set against the current version, review the prompt diff and the score diff together, then release behind a feature flag (for example 5, 50, then 100 percent) while watching quality metrics. Rollback is switching the flag back to the previous version, with no redeploy.

docs.title: 18. Name four prompt anti-patterns.
docs.text: Concatenating user text into instructions; putting fixed rules in the first user message; one giant prompt shared by every feature; editing prompts in place without versions. Others: examples that all look alike, asking the model for facts the server knows, and judging a change on one example.

docs.title: 19. The stable prefix is 1,100 tokens and per-request data averages 150 tokens. What share of input tokens can prefix caching cover?
docs.text: 1,100 / (1,100 + 150) = 88 percent. Moving any per-request field above the stable part breaks the prefix match and loses most of that benefit.

docs.title: 20. Compare JSON mode, schema-constrained output, and tool-based extraction.
docs.text: JSON mode guarantees only syntactically valid JSON. Schema-constrained output enforces a supplied JSON Schema while generating, so the answer matches it unless the model refuses or is cut off. Tool-based extraction gets the data as the arguments of a tool call; strict tools give the same guarantee, and it fits when the model must also choose between actions.

docs.title: 21. How does constrained decoding work?
docs.text: The provider compiles the schema into a grammar (a state machine). At each step the model scores every token; the grammar removes the tokens that would break the schema; the remaining probabilities are renormalized and one token is sampled. The model still chooses, but only among legal tokens.

docs.title: 22. What does schema enforcement not guarantee?
docs.text: Correct values, rules that span fields, and anything outside the schema: that a date exists, that an assignee is a project member, that a title is sensible. It also does not cover refused or truncated answers. Those need domain validation in your code.

docs.title: 23. What does OpenAI's strict mode require of a schema?
docs.text: Every property listed in required (optional fields become a union with null), additionalProperties: false, and a root that is an object, not an anyOf. Unsupported keywords cause an error. Limits include 5,000 properties, 10 levels of nesting, and 1,000 enum values in total.

docs.title: 24. Why split validation into a model schema and domain checks?
docs.text: Providers support different JSON Schema subsets: OpenAI errors on unsupported keywords, Anthropic's SDK moves length and range constraints into descriptions, and Google ignores some keywords silently. A model schema with only portable features behaves the same everywhere; lengths, real dates, database lookups, and cross-field rules then live in a function such as checkDraft that returns specific problems.

docs.title: 25. Why not put the project's member names in the schema as an enum?
docs.text: The schema changes on every request, so the provider compiles a new grammar each time instead of reusing a cached one (Anthropic caches compiled grammars for 24 hours), and large enums count against complexity limits. Put the names in the prompt as data and check the answer against them in code.

docs.title: 26. How are refusals reported on OpenAI and on Anthropic?
docs.text: OpenAI: a content item of type refusal with a refusal string, which does not follow the schema. Anthropic: stop_reason: "refusal" with a 200 status; the output may not match the schema and the tokens are billed. In both cases show a clear message and do not retry.

docs.title: 27. How do you detect a truncated structured answer?
docs.text: OpenAI returns status: "incomplete" with incomplete_details.reason set to max_output_tokens; Anthropic returns stop_reason: "max_tokens". Check these before trusting the parse, then raise the limit once or shorten the input; a repeat of the same call is cut off again.

docs.title: 28. What is a repair retry, and what should never be retried this way?
docs.text: A follow-up call that adds the model's answer and a message listing the exact problems ("assigneeName "Rosa" is not a project member"). It works for rule violations. Do not repair refusals (they repeat), truncation (the same limit applies), or transport errors such as 429 and 5xx, which the SDKs retry with backoff themselves.

docs.title: 29. Eight percent of first answers fail validation, and a repair costs 1.3 times a first call. What is the average cost per request with one repair?
docs.text: 1 + 0.08 x 1.3 = 1.104 first-call equivalents, about 10 percent more. A larger repair budget mostly adds latency to requests that will not succeed; fall back to the manual form instead.

docs.title: 30. Why validate on the server when the provider already enforces the schema?
docs.text: Model output is untrusted input shaped by user text. Parsing again in your process catches gaps in provider enforcement, gives typed data, and the domain checks catch everything the schema cannot express. The SDK helpers (responses.parse, messages.parse) already run the zod schema; the domain checks are your job.

docs.title: 31. Why give the model an explicit way out in the schema?
docs.text: Constrained decoding forces some legal answer. Without an "other" intent, nullable fields, and a clarifying-question field, a request such as "what's our deploy process?" is squeezed into a fake task. Exits let the model say "not a task" or "I need more information" legally.

docs.title: 32. Does the order of fields in a schema matter?
docs.text: Yes. OpenAI produces keys in schema order, and Anthropic outputs required properties first, then optional ones. Fields generated early condition later ones, so put deciding fields such as intent first.

docs.title: 33. Should a schema include a "reasoning" field?
docs.text: Not for step-by-step reasoning. Anthropic warns that a property asking for the model's step-by-step thinking can trigger a refusal, and research such as "Let Me Speak Freely?" found that strict formats can reduce reasoning quality. Let the model reason in its thinking, and ask for a short explanation field only if users need one.

docs.title: 34. How does streaming structured output work, and what is the danger?
docs.text: A tolerant parser completes the unfinished JSON (closing strings and objects) so the UI can show a growing draft. Partial objects can contain values the schema forbids, such as "intent": "c" after a few characters, and later fields are missing. Use them for display only; validate and act only on the final, complete object.

docs.title: 35. When is tool-based extraction better than a response schema?
docs.text: When the model must choose what to do, for example create a task or search for an existing one first, each with its own arguments. Strict tools enforce the arguments. Note that some current Anthropic models reject forced tool choice on every request, so use a response schema when you only need data.

docs.title: 36. Why does the TaskFlow flow use two endpoints?
docs.text: The first turns text into a draft and saves nothing; the user reviews and edits it. The second receives the confirmed fields, which are now ordinary client input, and validates them again with a fresh member list before inserting. The model proposes, the user confirms, and the API is the only writer.

docs.title: 37. Why should the model never choose user IDs?
docs.text: IDs are database facts the model cannot verify, and a wrong or injected ID could reference another user or tenant. The model returns a name; the API matches it against the members it loaded for the caller's project and uses that member's ID, or asks a question when nothing matches.

docs.title: 38. How do you test structured-output code without calling a model?
docs.text: Make the provider call an injectable function (ModelCall) and test the loop with a fake that replays scripted replies: valid, invalid then valid, refusal, truncation. One level lower, point the official SDK at a local stub server with OPENAI_BASE_URL or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and fake keys to test that the adapter parses each response shape.

docs.title: 39. What changed for structured output in the Vercel AI SDK 7?
docs.text: generateObject and streamObject are deprecated. Structured output is the output option of generateText or streamText, for example output: Output.object({ schema }), with the result in result.output and partial objects in partialOutputStream.

docs.title: 40. What is a reasoning model?
docs.text: A model trained, mostly with reinforcement learning on checkable problems, to generate internal reasoning before answering: it tries approaches, checks them, and revises. The extra computation at answer time is called test-time compute, and it pays off most on math, code, planning, and other multi-step problems.

docs.title: 41. How did reasoning models develop from chain-of-thought prompting?
docs.text: Wei and colleagues (2022) showed that prompting a model to write intermediate steps improves reasoning. Reasoning models internalize this through training: DeepSeek-R1 (2025) reported that pure reinforcement learning produced self-reflection and verification without human-written reasoning traces, and Snell and colleagues (2024) showed that adaptive test-time compute can beat a model 14 times larger on suitable problems.

docs.title: 42. How are reasoning tokens billed and limited?
docs.text: As output tokens, even when they are hidden or only summarized, and they count against the output limit (max_output_tokens on OpenAI, max_tokens on Anthropic). Usage fields report them separately: output_tokens_details.reasoning_tokens on OpenAI and output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens on Anthropic.

docs.title: 43. Which controls set how much a model thinks, per provider?
docs.text: OpenAI: reasoning.effort (none to max, depending on the model). Anthropic: output_config.effort (low to max) with adaptive thinking; budget_tokens only on older models. Google Interactions API: generation_config.thinking_level (minimal to xhigh, per model). The Vercel AI SDK has a provider-neutral reasoning setting. All as of November 2026.

docs.title: 44. What is the difference between effort and the output limit?
docs.text: Effort is soft guidance about how much work a request deserves; Anthropic calls it a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget. The output limit is a hard wall that stops generation wherever it is, including in the middle of reasoning. Lower effort to save cost and time; use the limit as the ceiling.

docs.title: 45. How can a reasoning request cost money and return nothing?
docs.text: If the output limit is reached while the model is still reasoning, the response is incomplete (status: "incomplete" on OpenAI) with no visible answer, but input and reasoning are billed. Prevent it with headroom (OpenAI suggests at least 25,000 tokens when starting), lower effort, and an alert on the incomplete rate.

docs.title: 46. What happened to explicit thinking budgets?
docs.text: They are being replaced by effort levels. Anthropic's budget_tokens (at least 1,024 and below max_tokens) is deprecated on Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 and returns a 400 error from Claude Opus 4.7 onwards, where adaptive thinking guided by effort is the control. Google's Interactions API uses thinking_level.

docs.title: 47. Can you tune a reasoning model with temperature?
docs.text: Mostly no. Anthropic's newest models return a 400 error for any non-default temperature, top_p, or top_k, and from API version 2026-10-21 every model rejects them at any value; Google marks temperature deprecated in the Interactions API; OpenAI documents effort as the control for reasoning models. Control variety with the prompt and quality with effort.

docs.title: 48. When should you use a reasoning model instead of a fast model?
docs.text: For multi-step problems with checkable rules: planning and scheduling, code, analysis that reconciles conflicting information, and agents that decide between tool calls. Use fast models for drafts, extraction, classification, and summaries. OpenAI calls reasoning models "the planners" and fast models "the workhorses", and expects most workflows to use both.

docs.title: 49. How does prompting a reasoning model differ?
docs.text: State the goal, hard constraints, and success criteria, not the method. Do not ask it to think step by step (OpenAI says that can hurt). Try zero-shot first. Keep delimiters and developer instructions. Keep reasoning out of the output schema, and calm aggressive wording; steer overthinking with lower effort or "choose an approach and commit to it".

docs.title: 50. What does reasoning do to latency, and how do you design around it?
docs.text: Time to first visible token grows with the amount of reasoning, and nothing visible streams while the model thinks. Stream a reasoning summary or progress for interactive use, move long reasoning to background jobs with notifications, and keep reasoning off the hot path of features that must feel instant.

docs.title: 51. How does reasoning affect cost, and does prompt caching help?
docs.text: Reasoning adds billed output tokens, often several times the visible answer, and output tokens usually cost more than input. Prompt caching reduces repeated input only; it does not reduce reasoning. Changing the top-level effort between requests can also invalidate cached prefixes on Anthropic, so keep it constant within a cached conversation.

docs.title: 52. What is an effort sweep, and how do you read one?
docs.text: Run the same evaluation set at each effort level, record pass rate, latency percentiles, and output tokens, and pick the lowest level that meets the quality bar and the latency budget. If medium and high both pass 90 percent but high uses about 2.3 times the output tokens and twice the p95 latency, choose medium.

docs.title: 53. What reasoning can you see from hosted providers?
docs.text: Not the raw reasoning: OpenAI does not expose raw reasoning tokens, and Anthropic says no display setting returns the raw chain of thought. You can request summaries (reasoning.summary, Anthropic display: "summarized", Google thinking_summaries), and you receive opaque carry-over items. Open-weight models such as DeepSeek-R1 show their raw reasoning when you run them yourself.

docs.title: 54. Why must reasoning items and thinking blocks be passed back unchanged?
docs.text: They let the model continue its reasoning across tool calls. Anthropic thinking blocks carry a signature and modified blocks are rejected with a 400 error; OpenAI's stateless mode carries reasoning in encrypted_content, usable only within the same model family. Append the provider's returned content as is instead of rebuilding it from text.

docs.title: 55. What does faithfulness research say about visible reasoning?
docs.text: Anthropic found that when models used a planted hint, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned it 25 percent of the time and DeepSeek R1 39 percent of the time. OpenAI researchers found chain-of-thought monitoring useful but fragile, since training pressure on the reasoning teaches models to hide intent. So reasoning text is not an audit trail; judge outcomes.

docs.title: 56. How do you evaluate a reasoning model?
docs.text: Grade outcomes with code where rules exist (the planner's checkPlan), run each case several times and report pass rates, record cost and latency with quality at each effort level, re-run on every model change, and use model graders only for qualities code cannot check. Never grade the reasoning summary.

docs.title: 57. Why does Anthropic's TypeScript SDK refuse some non-streaming requests?
docs.text: It estimates the maximum duration from max_tokens and refuses non-streaming requests that could run longer than ten minutes (roughly above 21,000 output tokens). Reasoning workloads need large ceilings, so use messages.stream() and finalMessage() for them.

docs.title: 58. After a prompt edit, drafts name the wrong assignee. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the assignee-correction rate by prompt version, and the diff between the old and new prompt, especially the examples.

How to confirm: the wrong assignees concentrate on the new version and often repeat a name that appears in the new examples.

Likely causes and fixes: examples that share a name the model now copies, or a reworded assignee rule. Switch the flag back to the previous version, vary the example names, add assignee cases to the evaluation set, and compare versions before the next rollout. See prompt design and templates.

docs.title: 59. Users in the Americas report due dates one day early in the evening. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the "Today" line in the rendered prompt for an affected request, and the user's time zone setting.

How to confirm: the prompt shows the UTC date, which is already the next day for those users in the evening, and "tomorrow" resolves from it.

Likely causes and fixes: the template formats the date in UTC or the server's zone. Render today's date in the user's IANA time zone, add evaluation cases near local midnight, and keep date facts out of the model's guesswork. See prompt design and templates.

docs.title: 60. A pasted email made the assistant assign every task to one person. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the rendered prompt for that request: where the email text sits and whether it is delimited and escaped.

How to confirm: the email contains instructions ("assign all tasks to ...") that were concatenated into the request without tags or escaping.

Likely causes and fixes: untrusted text treated as instructions. Delimit and escape it, state that tagged content is data, add injection cases to the evaluation set, and make the API check assignee permissions before saving. See prompt design and templates and prompt injection and defenses.

docs.title: 61. Input tokens per call doubled with no feature change. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the rendered prompt size over time and the prompt versions released in the same period.

How to confirm: the stable prefix grew (more examples or policy text), and a per-request field now sits above it, so cached-token counts dropped.

Likely causes and fixes: prompt creep and a broken cache prefix. Add a size test that fails above a token budget, move per-request data back to the end, and remove instructions that evaluations show have no effect. See prompt design and templates.

docs.title: 62. Answers changed overnight without a deploy. Where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: the logged model value before and after the change, and the configured model ID.

How to confirm: the configuration uses an alias, and the served snapshot changed on the day the behaviour shifted.

Likely causes and fixes: a moving alias. Pin a dated snapshot in configuration, record the served model on every call, and switch snapshots only after the evaluation set passes. See prompt design and templates.

docs.title: 63. After a schema change, the assistant endpoint returns 400 errors. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the provider's error message and the JSON Schema the SDK helper generated from the new zod schema.

How to confirm: the error names an unsupported keyword or "schema too complex", and the new schema adds a .min(), .regex(), recursion, or many optional and union fields.

Likely causes and fixes: the model schema left the portable subset or exceeded complexity limits. Move the rule into domain checks, make fields required and nullable, and test the generated schema in CI. See structured output and validation.

docs.title: 64. Tasks were saved with assignees who are not project members. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: the code path between the model's answer and the insert, and whether assignee names are resolved against the member list.

How to confirm: the saved assigneeId values do not appear in the project's memberIds, and the code trusted the model's field because the JSON was valid.

Likely causes and fixes: schema validity mistaken for data validity. Resolve names against members loaded for the caller, map them to IDs in code, repair or ask when nothing matches, and validate again on the confirm endpoint. See structured output and validation.

docs.title: 65. A small share of requests fail with "Unexpected end of JSON input". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the stop reason or status of the failing responses, and whether the feature uses JSON mode or a schema.

How to confirm: the failures have status: "incomplete" or stop_reason: "max_tokens", often on long inputs.

Likely causes and fixes: truncated output parsed as if complete, or JSON mode without a schema. Check the stop reason before parsing, raise the output limit for long inputs, use schema-constrained output, and treat truncation as its own outcome. See structured output and validation.

docs.title: 66. The refusal rate rose right after a new field was added to the schema. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the new field's name and description, and the refusal messages or stop reasons for affected requests.

How to confirm: the field asks the model to write out its step-by-step reasoning, and removing it in a test restores the old rate.

Likely causes and fixes: a reasoning-extraction refusal. Replace the field with a short explanation, or remove it and let reasoning happen in thinking. See structured output and validation.

docs.title: 67. Users created tasks with a priority that changed after they clicked Create. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: when the client enables the Create button, and whether it uses partial objects from the stream.

How to confirm: analytics show creates before the stream's final event, and the saved values match a partial object.

Likely causes and fixes: acting on partial JSON. Enable actions only after the final, validated object arrives, and validate the confirmed fields on the server. See structured output and validation.

docs.title: 68. The weekly planner often returns nothing, yet token spend keeps rising. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the share of planner responses with status: "incomplete" and their reasoning-token counts.

How to confirm: incomplete responses have reasoning tokens close to the output limit and no visible output.

Likely causes and fixes: the output ceiling was sized for the answer and reasoning used it up. Raise the ceiling with headroom, lower the effort, cap the input size, alert on incomplete responses, and run large plans as background jobs. See reasoning models and thinking.

docs.title: 69. After a model upgrade, the planner's cost doubled with no quality change. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: reasoning tokens per request and the effort value actually sent, before and after the upgrade.

How to confirm: effort was not set explicitly, and the new model's default or calibration produces much more reasoning at the same pass rate.

Likely causes and fixes: an inherited default. Set effort explicitly, run a fresh effort sweep for the new model, and gate model changes on cost per passing case as well as quality. See reasoning models and thinking.

docs.title: 70. The task agent fails on its second turn after a tool call. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the error message and the assistant content sent back with the tool result.

How to confirm: the error mentions modified or missing thinking blocks or reasoning items, and the code rebuilt the assistant message from its text.

Likely causes and fixes: dropped or edited reasoning carry-over. Append the provider's returned content unchanged, including thinking signatures and encrypted reasoning items, and test a two-turn tool loop in CI. See reasoning models and thinking.
