docs.title: CI/CD
docs.text: CI/CD automates the path from a code change to running software. Continuous integration (CI) merges every developer's work into a shared main line frequently and verifies each change automatically with builds and tests. Continuous delivery (CD) keeps every verified change releasable, so deploying is a routine, low-risk, push-button decision; continuous deployment goes one step further and releases every change that passes the pipeline without a manual step. Together they turn releases from rare, stressful events into small, frequent, reversible ones.

docs.title: What CI/CD provides
docs.text:
• Fast feedback: a broken build or failing test is reported minutes after the push, while the change is still fresh in the author's mind.
  • A main line that always works: automated checks gate every merge, so main stays deployable.
  • Repeatable releases: the same scripted steps build, test, and deploy every time, instead of a checklist someone follows by hand.
  • Traceability: every artifact and deployment links back to a commit, a pipeline run, and the checks it passed.
  • Smaller, safer changes: frequent deploys of small batches are easier to review, test, diagnose, and roll back.
  • Measurable delivery: pipelines make DORA metrics such as deployment frequency and change lead time visible.

A pipeline is also software: it needs maintenance, security review, and speed budgets, and a green check only means the configured checks passed.

docs.title: How a typical CI/CD pipeline works
docs.text:
A change to the TaskFlow API travels through these steps:

  1. A developer pushes a commit or opens a pull request.
  2. CI runs automatically: install dependencies, lint, type-check, run unit and integration tests, and build.
  3. On main, the pipeline produces one artifact, such as a container image identified by its digest.
  4. The pipeline deploys that artifact to staging and runs smoke and end-to-end tests against it.
  5. An approval gate (for example, a required reviewer on the production environment) decides when to release. In continuous deployment this gate is automated.
  6. The same artifact is deployed to production, often gradually.
  7. Monitoring checks error rates and latency; problems lead to a rollback or a fix-forward commit, which starts the loop again.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml: the smallest useful CI for TaskFlow API
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc   # same Node version as production
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci                   # exact versions from package-lock.json
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm test

Every pull request and every push to main now gets a pass or fail status. Marking the test check as required in the branch rules turns it into a merge gate. The full pipeline, with a MongoDB service container, build artifacts, and deployments, is built up in GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Make the pipeline run the same commands you run locally (npm ci, npm test), keep it fast enough that people wait for it (around ten minutes for pull requests), and treat a red main as the team's top priority. Build once and promote the same artifact; keep secrets out of untrusted code paths; give workflows the least permissions they need.

  • CI is not "having a build server". It is the practice of integrating small changes into the main line at least daily; a server testing month-old branches is not CI.
  • Continuous delivery does not mean deploying every commit to production; that is continuous deployment. Delivery means every commit could be deployed.
  • A green pipeline does not prove the software is correct, only that the checks you wrote passed. Flaky or missing tests make it lie.
  • Rebuilding the code separately for staging and production means production runs something that was never tested.
  • Pipelines are an attack surface: they hold credentials and run code from pull requests and third-party actions.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies
docs.text: A deployment strategy is the plan for replacing the running version of an application with a new one: in what order instances change, how user traffic moves from the old version to the new one, how you notice that something is wrong, and how you get back to safety when it is. The same build can be shipped with minutes of downtime or with none, to every user at once or to 1% first; the strategy decides which.

docs.title: What deployment strategies provide
docs.text:
• Less or no downtime: rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments keep healthy instances serving while others change.
  • A smaller blast radius: canary releases, rings, and feature flags expose a bad change to a small share of users before everyone.
  • Fast recovery: keeping the previous version runnable (an old environment, an old image, a flag you can switch off) turns an outage into a short incident.
  • Separation of deploy and release: code can reach production turned off and be released later, to chosen users, without another deploy.
  • Evidence: each step is checked against health and business metrics before more traffic moves.

Every strategy also has costs: extra capacity, two versions running side by side (so the database and APIs must work with both), more automation, and more things to monitor.

docs.title: How a typical safe deployment works
docs.text:
A common path for a web API such as TaskFlow API:

  1. CI builds one immutable artifact (a container image tagged with the commit) and runs the tests.
  2. The artifact is deployed to staging, where smoke tests and checks run against production-like configuration.
  3. A database migration that is backward compatible runs first, so both the old and the new code work against the schema.
  4. The new version starts beside the old one and must pass its readiness check before receiving any traffic.
  5. Traffic shifts gradually (for example 1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) while error rate and latency are compared with the old version.
  6. If a check fails, traffic returns to the old version automatically; if all checks pass, the old version is retired after a bake period.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A canary rollout described declaratively with Argo Rollouts, a Kubernetes controller that shifts traffic in steps and pauses between them:

# k8s/taskflow-api-rollout.yaml (Argo Rollouts canary steps)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  replicas: 10
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: taskflow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: taskflow-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
        - setWeight: 10          # 10% of pods run the new version
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        # after the last step the rollout goes to 100%

Without a traffic router, Argo Rollouts approximates the weight by the ratio of new to old pods; with a service mesh or gateway it can shift an exact percentage of requests. The deep pages explain both.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Choose the simplest strategy that meets your downtime and risk needs. A small internal tool can accept a 20-second restart; a payment API cannot. Whatever you choose, make every deploy repeatable from one script or pipeline, keep the previous artifact ready, and decide in advance which metrics mean "roll back".

  • Zero-downtime deployment is not a property of the tool; it also needs graceful shutdown, readiness checks, and backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Blue-green does not make database changes reversible. Both colors usually share one database.
  • A canary only helps if someone, or something, compares its metrics with the baseline and acts on the difference.
  • Rolling back code does not roll back data that the new code already wrote.
  • Deploying is not releasing: with feature flags, new code can sit in production, switched off, for days.

docs.title: DevOps Fundamentals
docs.text: DevOps is a way of building and running software in which the people who write a change also deliver it, operate it, and learn from how it behaves in production, supported by automation and shared measurements. It grew out of the friction between development teams, rewarded for shipping features, and operations teams, rewarded for keeping systems stable. Instead of a hand-off between two groups with opposite goals, DevOps sets up one short feedback loop that small changes travel around many times a day.

docs.title: What DevOps provides
docs.text:
• Faster delivery of small changes: a fix moves from commit to production in hours instead of waiting for the next monthly release.
  • Fewer and smaller failures: small batches are easier to review, test, and roll back. DORA's research keeps finding that delivery speed and stability rise together rather than trading off.
  • Fast feedback from production: the team that built a change sees its errors, latency, and user impact directly, not through a ticket days later.
  • Shared ownership: one team owns a service end to end, so problems are fixed where they start instead of bouncing between departments.
  • Measurable improvement: delivery metrics show whether a change to the process actually helped.
  • Sustainable operations: repetitive manual work is automated away, and on-call load is kept small enough for people to stay healthy.

DevOps also asks for things in return: investment in tests and automation, a blameless culture, product teams willing to carry a pager, and leaders who judge outcomes rather than activity.

docs.title: How a typical DevOps loop works
docs.text:
Follow one change to the TaskFlow API, the Express and MongoDB task service used throughout this site:

  1. Plan small. The team slices the feature so each piece can ship on its own within a day or two, hidden behind a feature flag if it is not ready for users.
  2. Integrate continuously. A developer opens a small pull request, CI tests it, and it merges into main the same day.
  3. Deliver automatically. The pipeline builds one artifact and deploys it through staging to production with no manual hand-off.
  4. Release progressively. A canary or a flag exposes the change to a few users first, and an automatic rollback fires if error rates rise.
  5. Operate what you build. The same team watches the dashboards, receives the pages, and fixes what breaks.
  6. Learn and adjust. Incidents become blameless postmortems, metrics show where work waits, and the next change starts with those lessons.

Each step has its own subject in this section: Git and GitHub, CI/CD, deployment strategies, and monitoring and logging. This subject explains the ideas and team practices that connect them.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deliver.yml: every merge to main is tested, deployed, and recorded
name: Deliver
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: deliver-production
  cancel-in-progress: false      # never stop a deploy halfway

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production      # GitHub records a deployment for every run
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "$GITHUB_SHA"
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh https://api.example.com/healthz

Small as it is, this file encodes the core habits. Every merge to main becomes its own small deployment instead of waiting for a release train. Tests gate the deploy, and a smoke test checks the running service afterwards. The concurrency group lets only one deployment run at a time. The team that owns deploy.sh is the team that gets paged. The environment: production key makes GitHub keep a deployment history, which is raw material for the delivery metrics in measuring delivery performance.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
For a developer, DevOps means your work is not finished at merge. You will deploy it, watch it, and support it, so build in what makes that easy from the first commit: health checks, structured logs, metrics, a feature flag for risky behavior, and a way to roll back. Before writing code, ask "how will I know this works in production?".

  • DevOps is not a job title or a team that sits between development and operations. Adding a "DevOps team" in the middle creates one more hand-off.
  • DevOps is not a tool. Pipelines, containers, and dashboards support the practices; buying them does not create the practices.
  • "You build it, you run it" does not mean developers do everything alone. Platforms, SREs, and enabling teams make ownership affordable.
  • Going faster does not mean taking more risk. Small, frequent changes fail less often and are fixed sooner than large, rare ones.
  • DevOps does not remove control. Peer review, automated checks, and an audit trail can replace slow approval boards and still satisfy auditors.
  • Delivery metrics are for learning, not for ranking teams. Once a number becomes a target, people optimize the number.

docs.title: DevSecOps and Cloud Security
docs.text: DevSecOps builds security into every stage of software delivery instead of checking it once, at the end, by a separate team. Code is scanned on every pull request, builds produce images that are scanned and signed, deploys use short-lived credentials, and production runs behind edge protection, least-privilege identities, and segmented networks that are watched by audit logs. Cloud security is the part of this work that protects the environment the software runs in: identities, networks, the edge, and the data, under a shared responsibility model with the cloud provider.

docs.title: What DevSecOps and cloud security provide
docs.text:
• Earlier, cheaper fixes: a vulnerable dependency caught in a pull request costs a version bump; the same flaw found in production costs an incident.
  • A smaller blast radius: least-privilege roles, short-lived credentials, and private networks limit what one stolen token or one compromised container can reach.
  • Protection at the edge: managed DDoS mitigation, a web application firewall (WAF), rate limits, and bot controls absorb attacks before they reach the application.
  • A fast response to new vulnerabilities: an inventory of what runs where, plus severity and exploitation data, turns a new CVE into a prioritized, time-boxed fix instead of a panic.
  • Evidence for customers and auditors: audit logs, access reviews, and policy as code show that controls exist and keep working, which is what SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, HIPAA, GDPR, and PCI DSS assessments ask for.

docs.title: How a typical DevSecOps pipeline works
docs.text:
Follow one change to TaskFlow API through the pipeline:

  1. Code: a pre-commit hook and GitHub push protection stop a pasted token before it leaves the laptop. The pull request runs static analysis, dependency review, and an infrastructure-as-code scan; only new, high-confidence findings block the merge.
  2. Build: CI builds the image, scans it, and fails on fixable high or critical vulnerabilities. It records an SBOM and signed provenance for the image digest.
  3. Deploy: the deploy job assumes a cloud role through OIDC, verifies the image's provenance, and ships to staging, where a DAST scan probes the running API. Production needs an approval in a protected environment.
  4. Run: requests pass through DDoS protection, a WAF, and rate limits at the edge. The API runs in private subnets with a role that can read only its own secrets and bucket prefix, and every API call to the cloud lands in an audit log.
  5. Feedback: continuous scanning turns newly published CVEs into tickets with deadlines set by severity and exploitation, and incidents end with postmortems that add the missing control.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The cheapest useful gate: fail the build when a production dependency has a known high or critical vulnerability.

# .github/workflows/security.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  dependency-audit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read                 # the job can read code and nothing else
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev

--audit-level=high sets the threshold for a non-zero exit code, and --omit=dev ignores tooling that never ships. Real pipelines add SAST, image scanning, and a way to accept known findings, as the first lesson shows.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat security controls like tests: automated, fast, owned by the team that writes the code, and tuned so that a failure means something. Start with the controls that remove whole classes of risk (no long-lived cloud keys, no public databases, patched base images) before buying tools.

  • A green scanner run does not mean the code is secure; scanners find known patterns and known CVEs, not design flaws or broken access control.
  • Passing an audit is not the same as being secure. Compliance proves that agreed controls exist; attackers do not read the audit scope.
  • The cloud provider secures the cloud, not your configuration. A public bucket or an over-privileged role is the customer's side of the shared responsibility model.
  • A private network is not a trust boundary on its own. Zero trust checks identity and context on every request, inside the network too.
  • Blocking every finding does not make teams safer; it teaches them to ignore or bypass the scanner. Gate on new, fixable, high-impact issues.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text: Docker packages an application together with everything it needs to run (a runtime such as Node.js, system libraries, configuration defaults, and the code itself) into an image, and runs that image as an isolated process called a container. Containers share the host's Linux kernel, so they start in milliseconds to seconds and use far less memory than virtual machines, while still giving each application its own filesystem, network, and process view. The same image runs unchanged on a laptop, in CI, and in production, which is why containers became the standard unit of deployment.

docs.title: What Docker provides
docs.text:
• A reproducible package: an image built from a Dockerfile contains the exact runtime, libraries, and dependency versions, so "works on my machine" becomes "works in this image".
  • Isolation without a full VM: Linux namespaces give each container its own process tree, network stack, and filesystem; cgroups cap its CPU and memory.
  • Fast, cached builds: images are stacks of layers, and unchanged layers are reused between builds and shared between images.
  • Distribution: registries such as Docker Hub and GitHub Container Registry store images by name, tag, and content digest.
  • Local environments: Docker Compose starts an application with its database, cache, and tools from one file.
  • A common format: Docker images follow the Open Container Initiative (OCI) specifications, so Kubernetes, cloud container services, and other runtimes can run them.

Containers also add responsibilities: keeping images small and patched, running as a non-root user, handling shutdown signals correctly, and never baking secrets into image layers.

docs.title: How a typical Docker workflow works
docs.text:
1. A developer writes a Dockerfile describing how to build the image: the base image, the files to copy, the commands to run, and the start command.
  2. docker build sends the build context to BuildKit, which executes each instruction, caches every resulting layer, and produces an image.
  3. The image is tagged, for example ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0, and identified by an immutable content digest (sha256:...).
  4. docker push uploads only the layers the registry does not already have.
  5. A server (or Kubernetes node) pulls the image and docker run creates a container: the read-only image layers plus a thin writable layer, started as an isolated process.
  6. The same image is promoted from CI to staging to production, so what was tested is exactly what runs.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A minimal image for the TaskFlow API (an Express + MongoDB service):

# Dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev
COPY src ./src
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

# Build, run, and check the container
docker build -t taskflow-api:dev .
# host.docker.internal reaches MongoDB on your machine with Docker Desktop;
# on Linux, also pass --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway
docker run -d --name taskflow-api -p 3000:3000 \
  -e MONGODB_URI="mongodb://host.docker.internal:27017/taskflow" \
  taskflow-api:dev
docker logs -f taskflow-api
curl http://localhost:3000/healthz

Copying the lockfile and installing dependencies before copying the source means a code change reuses the cached npm ci layer, so rebuilds take seconds. USER node runs the process as the unprivileged user that the official Node.js images provide. The production Dockerfiles lesson turns this into a multi-stage build with health checks and graceful shutdown.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat the image as the release artifact: build it once in CI, tag it with the commit SHA, scan it, and promote that exact image through every environment. Keep configuration and secrets outside the image (environment variables, mounted files, a secret manager), keep the image small, and make the process handle SIGTERM so deploys do not drop requests.

  • A container is not a lightweight VM. It is a normal Linux process with restricted views of the system; it shares the host kernel.
  • Containers are not secure by default just because they are isolated. A root process with extra capabilities or the Docker socket mounted can take over the host.
  • Data written inside a container's filesystem disappears when the container is removed. Persistent data belongs in volumes or a managed database.
  • latest is just a tag name, not "the newest version", and it can point to different images over time.
  • Docker is not required to run containers in production: Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O directly, and they run the same OCI images.

docs.title: Domains, DNS and Email
docs.text: A domain name such as example.com is the address people and other systems use to reach everything you run: the website, the API, the mail servers, and the email your application sends. You rent the name from a registrar, the registry for its top-level domain points the internet at your nameservers, and those nameservers publish the zone: records that send app.example.com to a CDN, api.example.com to a load balancer, inbound mail to a mail provider, and the policies that let mailbox providers trust TaskFlow's email. When this is right nobody notices; when it is wrong the site disappears, password-reset emails land in spam, or certificate renewals start failing.

docs.title: What domains, DNS and email setup provide
docs.text:
• A stable name that outlives servers: moving TaskFlow API to a new load balancer or host means changing one record, not every client.
  • Routing per hostname: each name (app, api, www, the apex) can point at a different service, provider, or region.
  • Proof of control: verification records (TXT or CNAME) prove to hosting platforms and certificate authorities that you own the domain, and CAA records limit which authorities may issue certificates for it.
  • Email trust: SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records tell receiving servers which senders may use your domain, so your mail can reach the inbox and spoofed mail can be rejected.
  • Edge delivery: pointing a hostname at a CDN puts caching, compression, and protection in front of your origin.

These pieces also bring duties: renewing the domain, keeping an inventory of records and their owners, planning TTLs before changes, and monitoring both DNS answers and email reputation.

docs.title: How a typical domain setup works
docs.text:
1. You register example.com at a registrar and choose a DNS host (it can be the same company). The registrar sends the DNS host's nameservers to the .com registry.
  2. The registry publishes the delegation: NS records for example.com in the .com zone, plus a DS record if DNSSEC is on.
  3. In the DNS host you create the zone's records: app as a CNAME to the CDN, api as an address or alias for the load balancer, MX records for inbound mail, TXT records for SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and verification, and a CAA record for certificates.
  4. A browser asks a recursive resolver for app.example.com. The resolver follows the root, the .com servers, and your nameservers, returns the answer, and caches it for the record's TTL.
  5. The browser connects to the CDN edge, which serves TaskFlow Web from its cache or fetches from the origin. Mail servers sending to @example.com look up the MX records, and mailbox providers that receive TaskFlow's email check its SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A zone excerpt for TaskFlow in standard zone-file format (the addresses and provider names are documentation placeholders):

; example.com zone (excerpt): one domain, several services
$TTL 3600
example.com.        IN  NS     ns1.dns-host.example.net.
example.com.        IN  NS     ns2.dns-host.example.net.
www.example.com.    300  IN  CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.
app.example.com.    300  IN  CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.
api.example.com.    60   IN  A      198.51.100.20
example.com.        IN  MX     10 mx1.mail.example.net.
example.com.        IN  MX     20 mx2.mail.example.net.
example.com.        IN  TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"
_dmarc.example.com. IN  TXT    "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"
example.com.        IN  CAA    0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

Each line answers one question: where the web app lives, where the API lives, who receives mail, who may send mail as example.com, and which certificate authority may issue certificates. The deep pages explain each record type, how to choose TTLs, and why the apex (example.com itself) cannot simply be a CNAME.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat DNS as production configuration. Keep the zone in code (Terraform or DNSControl), review changes like any other deploy, lower TTLs before planned changes, give every record an owner, and protect the registrar account with MFA, a transfer lock, and auto-renewal. The protocol itself (resolvers, root and TLD servers, record basics) is covered in DNS in the Networking section, and routing users to regions with DNS is covered in global traffic management.

  • "Propagation" is not a push. Your change is live on the authoritative servers within seconds; resolvers keep serving their cached copy until its TTL runs out.
  • The registrar and the DNS host are different roles. Changing nameservers moves the whole zone, so every record (including MX and TXT) must exist at the new host first.
  • A CNAME cannot sit at the zone apex. Use an A or AAAA record, or a provider feature such as an alias record or CNAME flattening.
  • DNS only says where to connect. TLS certificates, redirects, and which site a server shows for a hostname are configured on the host or CDN.
  • SPF, DKIM, and DMARC do not guarantee the inbox; they make mail eligible for it. Complaint rates, list quality, and sending patterns decide the rest.

docs.title: Environment Variables and Secrets
docs.text: Environment variables are named string values that the operating system passes to a process when it starts. They are the most common way to give an application its configuration (which port to listen on, which database to use, how much to log) without changing its code, so that one build can run in development, staging, and production. Secrets, such as database passwords and API keys, often travel the same way, but they need much more care: who can read them, how they are rotated, and what happens when one leaks.

docs.title: What environment variables and secrets management provide
docs.text:
• One artifact, many environments: the same container image or release runs everywhere; only its configuration differs.
  • Configuration outside the code: values change without a rebuild, and are not committed to the repository.
  • A standard interface: every language, runtime, process manager, container platform, and CI system can set and read them.
  • Controlled secrets: a secret store adds encryption, access control, audit logs, rotation, and short-lived credentials on top.

They also bring well-known problems: values are untyped strings, tools load .env files with different and surprising precedence rules, frontend build tools bake variables into public JavaScript, and secrets in environment variables can leak through logs, crash reports, and child processes.

docs.title: How a typical configuration flow works
docs.text:
For TaskFlow API running in production:

  1. The deploy system (Kubernetes, systemd, PM2, or a PaaS) starts the process with environment variables from its own configuration.
  2. Secrets are injected from a secret store at deploy or start time, never committed to Git.
  3. In local development, a .env file supplies the same variable names with development values.
  4. At startup, one config module reads process.env, converts strings to numbers, booleans, and lists, validates every value, and exits with a clear error if anything is missing or invalid.
  5. The rest of the application imports the typed, frozen config object and never touches process.env directly.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
// src/config.js: validate environment variables once, at startup
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  APP_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "staging", "production"]),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
  MONGODB_URI: z.string().startsWith("mongodb"),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32),
});

const result = schema.safeParse(process.env);
if (!result.success) {
  // Name the problem, never print the values
  for (const issue of result.error.issues) {
    console.error(`config error: ${issue.path.join(".")}: ${issue.message}`);
  }
  process.exit(1);
}

export const config = Object.freeze(result.data);

# .env (local development only; listed in .gitignore)
APP_ENV=development
PORT=3000
MONGODB_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow
JWT_SECRET=<at-least-32-random-characters>

node --env-file=.env src/server.js

A missing or malformed variable stops the process immediately with a message naming the variable, instead of failing on the first request an hour later.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Keep configuration boring: one documented list of variables (an .env.example file), one module that validates them, the same names in every environment, and secrets that come from a secret store rather than from files people pass around. When something behaves differently between environments, compare the effective configuration each process actually received.

  • .env files are a development convenience, not a secrets management system.
  • Different tools load .env files differently; Node, dotenv, Vite, Next.js, Bun, and Docker Compose each have their own rules for which file wins.
  • Anything in a VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable ends up in public JavaScript. It is never a secret.
  • Environment variables are strings. "false" is truthy in JavaScript.
  • Removing a leaked secret from Git history does not un-leak it; rotate it first.

docs.title: Git and GitHub
docs.text: Git is a distributed version control system: every clone holds the full history of a project as a graph of snapshots, so you can record changes, work on branches in parallel, compare any two versions, and undo almost any mistake without a network connection. GitHub hosts Git repositories and adds the collaboration layer around them: pull requests, code review, branch protection, issues, releases, and GitHub Actions for automation. Git is the tool; GitHub is one of several platforms (with GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps) built on top of it.

docs.title: What Git and GitHub provide
docs.text:
• A complete, verifiable history: every commit records who changed what, when, and why, and is identified by a hash of its content, so history cannot be altered silently.
  • Safe parallel work: branches are cheap pointers, so each feature, fix, or experiment can live on its own line of work and be merged when ready.
  • Review before change: pull requests show a diff, run automated checks, and collect approvals before code reaches the main branch.
  • Recovery: reverts, the reflog, and git bisect let you undo a bad change, recover "lost" commits, and find the commit that introduced a bug.
  • The trigger for automation: pushes, pull requests, and tags start the CI/CD pipelines that test, build, and deploy your code.
  • Releases: tags mark exact versions, and GitHub Releases attach notes and build artifacts to them.

Git also asks for discipline: clear commit messages, small focused changes, an agreed branching strategy, and care with commands that rewrite history.

docs.title: How a typical change flows through Git
docs.text:
A change to the TaskFlow API moves through four areas:

  1. You edit files in the working tree, the checked-out copy of the project on your disk.
  2. git add copies the chosen changes into the staging area (the index), which holds the snapshot your next commit will record.
  3. git commit stores that snapshot as a new commit in the local repository (the .git directory) and moves your branch to it.
  4. git push uploads the new commits to the remote repository on GitHub, usually on a feature branch.
  5. You open a pull request; CI runs, teammates review, and the branch is merged into main.
  6. Others run git fetch to download the new commits (which moves their remote-tracking branch origin/main), then merge or rebase to update their own branches. git pull does both steps at once.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
# Make a change to TaskFlow API and propose it for review
git clone git@github.com:example/taskflow-api.git
cd taskflow-api
git switch -c feat/task-due-dates        # new branch from main

# ...edit src/routes/tasks.js...
git status                               # what changed?
git add -p src/routes/tasks.js           # stage chosen hunks only
git commit -m "feat(tasks): add due dates to tasks"
git push -u origin feat/task-due-dates   # publish the branch, set upstream

gh pr create --fill --base main          # open a pull request (GitHub CLI)

git add -p lets you review each hunk before staging it, which keeps commits focused. The -u flag records origin/feat/task-due-dates as the branch's upstream, so later git push and git pull need no arguments.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Learn the model before memorizing commands. Once you see commits as snapshots in a graph and branches as movable labels, merge, rebase, reset, and recovery all become predictable. Commit small, coherent changes with messages that explain why; keep branches short-lived; and never rewrite history that others have already pulled.

  • Git does not store diffs between versions; it stores snapshots and computes diffs when you ask for them.
  • A branch is not a copy of the code; it is a name that points to one commit hash, which is why creating one is instant.
  • git pull is not a simple download; it fetches and then merges or rebases, which can create merge commits or conflicts.
  • Deleting a file in a new commit does not remove it from history. A leaked secret must be rotated, not just deleted.
  • GitHub is not Git. Pull requests, reviews, and Actions are platform features; plain Git knows only commits, branches, tags, and remotes.

docs.title: Hosting and Cloud Platforms
docs.text: Hosting is the decision about where your software runs and where its data lives: on a virtual machine you manage, in containers on a managed service, as functions that run per request, as static files on a CDN, or on a developer platform that hides all of that behind git push. Every option trades control for convenience and a predictable bill for one that follows your traffic. This subject explains what each option is, what you manage and what the provider manages, how each one bills, which well-known companies use it and why, and how to pick one for a given situation.

docs.title: What hosting and cloud platforms provide
docs.text:
• Compute: virtual machines, containers, functions, and edge runtimes that run your code, from one small server to thousands of instances.
  • Managed data services: relational and document databases, caches, queues, and object storage that someone else patches, backs up, and fails over.
  • Delivery: load balancers, CDNs, TLS certificates, and DNS that put your application in front of users worldwide.
  • Elasticity: capacity you can add in minutes and remove when traffic drops, so you pay for what you use instead of buying for the peak.
  • Compliance building blocks: audited data centers, encryption, and contracts (such as a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement) that you could not easily build yourself.

Each of these also creates a bill with several meters (instance-hours, requests, GB-seconds, GB stored, GB transferred), responsibilities you keep (your code, your data, your access settings), and some degree of lock-in to the provider's APIs.

docs.title: How a typical hosting decision works
docs.text:
1. List the workloads. For TaskFlow these are a React frontend (TaskFlow Web), a Node.js API (TaskFlow API), a MongoDB database, uploaded files, and a few background jobs.
  2. Pick a level of control for each. Static files rarely need a server; an API can run on a platform, in containers, or as functions; a database is almost always better managed.
  3. Check the hard constraints: long-lived WebSocket connections, request duration limits, data residency, compliance contracts, and the regions your users are in.
  4. Price it with real units for your expected traffic, including the meters people forget: data transfer out, NAT gateways, load balancer hours, public IPv4 addresses, and log ingestion.
  5. Estimate the exit cost: how much code and data would have to change to move, and what moving the data out would cost in egress fees.
  6. Start with the simplest option that meets the constraints, write down the traffic or cost level at which you would revisit it, and measure.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The same TaskFlow API container image can run on several of these options. On Google Cloud Run, one command deploys it as a serverless container that scales to zero when idle:

# Deploy the TaskFlow API image to Cloud Run (request-based billing)
gcloud run deploy taskflow-api \
  --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/example-project/apps/taskflow-api:1.4.0 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --port=3000 \
  --cpu=1 --memory=512Mi \
  --min-instances=0 --max-instances=10 \
  --set-secrets=MONGODB_URI=taskflow-mongodb-uri:latest \
  --allow-unauthenticated

What that costs at TaskFlow's launch traffic:

Prices checked November 2026

The estimate below uses Google Cloud us-central1 list prices in USD from the Cloud Run pricing page in November 2026. Prices change often and differ by region; re-check them with the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator before deciding.

TaskFlow API, 2 million requests a month, 120 ms each, 1 vCPU, 512 MiB
(us-central1 list prices, checked November 2026). Billable time is
rounded up to 100 ms, so an isolated 120 ms request is billed as 200 ms:

  billable time   2,000,000 x 0.2 s                = 400,000 instance-seconds
  CPU             400,000 vCPU-s - 180,000 free    = 220,000 x $0.000024 = $5.28
  memory          200,000 GiB-s, under the 360,000 GiB-s free tier      = $0.00
  requests        2,000,000, inside the 2 million free tier             = $0.00
  total                                                                 ~ $5.28 / month

Requests that overlap on one instance share billable time, so the real figure is usually lower. The same image could run on AWS Fargate behind a load balancer for a steady monthly price, or on a $12 virtual machine. Which one is cheapest depends on traffic shape, and the backend servers lesson works out where the lines cross.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Choose per workload, not per company: static files on a CDN, the API on whatever your team can operate well, and the database on a managed service. Keep the application portable where it is cheap to do so (a container image, standard SQL or the MongoDB wire protocol, environment configuration), and accept lock-in deliberately where it buys real value. Put a budget alert on every account on day one.

  • "Serverless is always cheaper." It is cheapest at low or spiky traffic; at steady high traffic, per-request pricing usually costs more than instances that run all month.
  • "The cloud is always more expensive than your own servers." For small teams, the operations work you avoid usually outweighs the price difference; the comparison changes only at large, steady scale.
  • "The price on the pricing page is the bill." Data transfer, NAT gateways, load balancers, logs, and idle resources often add more than the compute itself.
  • "A managed service means no operations." You still own schema design, capacity choices, access control, cost, and restore testing.
  • "Free tiers are a hosting plan." Many free tiers sleep, expire, or forbid commercial use; read the limits before launching on one.

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code
docs.text: Infrastructure as code (IaC) means describing servers, networks, databases, buckets, permissions, and DNS records in files that are versioned, reviewed, and applied by tools, instead of creating them by clicking through a cloud console. The files say what should exist; a tool such as Terraform, OpenTofu, CloudFormation, or Pulumi works out what to create, change, or delete to make reality match, and records what it manages.

docs.title: What infrastructure as code provides
docs.text:
• Repeatability: the same code builds staging and production, or rebuilds an environment after a disaster.
  • Review and history: every change is a pull request with a diff and a plan, and Git shows who changed what and why.
  • Safety: tools show exactly what they will change before they do it, and automation applies only the reviewed change.
  • Drift detection: comparing code with reality reveals manual changes made outside the process.
  • Documentation that stays true: the code is the inventory of what exists and how it is connected.

It also brings new things to learn and protect: state files that contain sensitive data, provider and module versions, refactoring without destroying resources, and the discipline of never "just fixing it in the console".

docs.title: How a typical IaC change works
docs.text:
For TaskFlow, adding an S3 bucket for user uploads:

  1. An engineer adds a module call to the production Terraform code in a branch and opens a pull request.
  2. CI runs terraform init, fmt -check, validate, and plan. The plan reads the remote state (what Terraform already manages) and shows the difference: for example 6 resources to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
  3. A reviewer reads the plan, not just the code, and approves.
  4. On merge, CI runs apply with the saved plan. Terraform takes the state lock, calls the cloud APIs, and writes the new state.
  5. A scheduled plan later compares code, state, and reality, and reports drift if someone changed the bucket by hand.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
# envs/prod/main.tf: production uploads bucket for TaskFlow, built from a module
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

module "uploads" {
  source                            = "../../modules/uploads-bucket"
  bucket_name                       = "taskflow-prod-uploads-example"
  noncurrent_version_retention_days = 90
}

output "uploads_bucket" {
  value = module.uploads.bucket_name
}

terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan     # review: what will be created, changed, destroyed
terraform apply tfplan         # apply exactly the reviewed plan

The module (shown in full in Terraform in practice) creates a private, versioned, encrypted bucket and an IAM policy that the API can use. Running plan again right after apply shows no changes: the code and reality match.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Start small: put one new resource under code, then import existing ones gradually. Keep state remote, locked, encrypted, and access-controlled from day one; review plans, not only code; and make the pipeline the only thing with permission to change production.

  • IaC is not just "scripts that call the cloud API"; declarative tools compare desired state with actual state and change only the difference.
  • A clean terraform plan does not mean the infrastructure is correct; it means it matches the code.
  • The state file is not a cache you can delete; it is how the tool knows which real resources it owns, and it often contains secrets.
  • IaC does not replace configuration management or application deployment; it provisions the platform they run on.
  • Renaming a resource in code can destroy and recreate it unless you tell the tool it moved.

docs.title: Kubernetes
docs.text: Kubernetes is an open-source system that runs containers across a cluster of machines and keeps them running the way you declared. You describe the desired state in YAML (which image, how many replicas, how much CPU and memory, how traffic reaches them, how to check their health) and Kubernetes continuously compares that with reality and fixes the difference: it schedules containers onto machines, restarts them when they crash, replaces them when a machine dies, rolls out new versions gradually, and gives them stable names and load-balanced addresses.

docs.title: What Kubernetes provides
docs.text:
• Scheduling: places each container on a machine with enough free CPU and memory, following your placement rules.
  • Self-healing: restarts crashed containers, replaces Pods on failed nodes, and stops sending traffic to Pods that fail health checks.
  • Rollouts and rollbacks: replaces old versions gradually and can undo a release with one command.
  • Service discovery and load balancing: a stable DNS name and virtual IP for a changing set of Pods.
  • Scaling: more or fewer replicas by hand or automatically from CPU, memory, or custom metrics, and more nodes when the cluster is full.
  • Configuration and secrets: injected into containers at runtime, kept out of images.
  • A common API: the same manifests work on Amazon EKS, Google GKE, Azure AKS, and on-premises clusters, and an ecosystem of tools builds on it.

Kubernetes also brings real operating cost: a control plane to run or pay for, networking and storage plugins, upgrades every few months, and a large set of concepts every team member needs to understand.

docs.title: How a typical deployment works
docs.text:
When you deploy the TaskFlow API:

  1. kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml sends the manifest to the API server, which authenticates you, checks your permissions, runs admission checks, and validates the object.
  2. The API server stores the desired state in etcd, the cluster's key-value store.
  3. The Deployment controller notices the new Deployment and creates a ReplicaSet; the ReplicaSet controller creates the requested number of Pods.
  4. The scheduler sees Pods with no node and binds each to a node that has room.
  5. The kubelet on each chosen node sees its new Pods and asks the container runtime (containerd) to pull the image and start the containers.
  6. The kubelet reports status back. When the readiness probe passes, the Pod's address is added to its Service, and traffic starts to arrive.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api.yaml: three replicas of the API behind a Service
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: taskflow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: taskflow-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: taskflow-api
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000

kubectl apply -f k8s/taskflow-api.yaml
kubectl get deployments,pods,services -l app=taskflow-api
kubectl delete pod -l app=taskflow-api --wait=false   # watch them come back
kubectl get pods -l app=taskflow-api --watch

Deleting the Pods does not shut the API down: the ReplicaSet notices that fewer than three exist and creates replacements within seconds. That is reconciliation, the core idea of Kubernetes. A production version of this manifest adds resource requests, liveness and startup probes, security settings, and configuration, built up in the lessons below.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
As an application developer on a Kubernetes platform, your job is to make the app a good citizen: stateless processes, configuration from the environment, health endpoints that mean something, graceful handling of SIGTERM, honest resource requests, and logs on stdout. Kubernetes can only keep promises the application helps it keep.

  • Kubernetes is not required to run containers. One service and a small team are usually better served by a managed container platform (Cloud Run, ECS with Fargate, Azure Container Apps) or Compose on a VM.
  • Kubernetes does not make an application highly available by itself. A single replica, a missing readiness probe, or a database on one disk is still a single point of failure.
  • Kubernetes does not need Docker on its nodes; it runs the same OCI images through containerd or CRI-O.
  • kubectl apply does not run anything directly. It records desired state; controllers and kubelets make it happen asynchronously.
  • Secrets are not encrypted just because they are Kubernetes Secrets: their values are only base64-encoded unless the cluster encrypts them at rest.

docs.title: Linux Server Operations
docs.text: Linux server operations is the work of running software on Linux machines you manage yourself: reaching them securely over SSH, turning a fresh virtual machine into a hardened server, running applications as supervised services behind a reverse proxy, scheduling jobs, keeping logs and disks under control, and finding out quickly what is wrong when something breaks. Even teams that deploy only containers rely on these skills, because every container host, Kubernetes node, and CI runner is a Linux server underneath. This section uses Ubuntu Server 26.04 LTS ("Resolute Raccoon", released in April 2026 and supported until 2031) and the TaskFlow API as its running example.

docs.title: What Linux server operations provide
docs.text:
• Full control at a predictable price: one virtual machine can run nginx, two Node.js instances, and scheduled jobs; you choose versions, limits, and tuning, and you pay for the VM, not per request.
  • An understanding of what platforms do for you: a PaaS or Kubernetes restarts crashed processes, collects logs, and terminates TLS. On a server you configure each of those yourself, which teaches you what to expect, and what to check, on any platform.
  • Debugging skills that transfer: uptime, free, df, ss, and journalctl work the same on a VPS, a container host, and a Kubernetes node.
  • A secure baseline: key-only SSH, a default-deny firewall, automatic security updates, and services that run as unprivileged users.

The price of that control is ownership: patching, monitoring, backups, capacity, and being on call for the machine are your job. Choosing between a VM and a managed platform is covered in running backend servers and APIs.

docs.title: How a typical Linux server works
docs.text:
1. An engineer connects from a laptop with ssh and an Ed25519 key. Password logins and direct root logins are disabled.
  2. The cloud firewall and ufw on the host allow only SSH (ideally from known addresses), HTTP, and HTTPS. Everything else is dropped.
  3. A user's HTTPS request reaches nginx on port 443, which terminates TLS, enforces body-size limits and timeouts, and proxies the request to the app on 127.0.0.1.
  4. systemd runs two TaskFlow API instances (taskflow-api@3001 and taskflow-api@3002) as the unprivileged taskflow user, restarts an instance if it crashes, and stops instances gracefully during deploys.
  5. Everything the app writes to stdout and stderr lands in the systemd journal, read with journalctl; nginx writes its own access and error logs, which logrotate rotates daily.
  6. systemd timers start scheduled work: database backups, log rotation, certificate renewal, and apt's automatic security updates.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
The first minute on an unfamiliar server: what is it, is anything broken, and what is listening?

# first-look.sh: read-only checks to run when you log in to a server
hostnamectl                               # OS release, kernel, virtualization
uptime                                    # load averages over 1, 5, and 15 minutes
systemctl --failed                        # units that crashed or failed to start
systemctl status 'taskflow-api@*'         # the app instances: state, PID, memory, last log lines
journalctl -u 'taskflow-api@*' --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager | tail -n 50
sudo ss -tlnp                             # listening TCP ports and the process behind each
df -h / && free -h                        # disk and memory headroom

Every command only reads state, so the checklist is safe on a production machine. journalctl stores a Node.js app's output at the info priority unless the app adds a priority prefix, so filtering with -p err hides its errors; search the structured log fields instead, as the troubleshooting lesson shows.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat a server as something you can rebuild from a script in minutes, not a pet you repair by hand. Keep its setup in a script or in infrastructure as code, keep secrets out of Git, ship logs off the machine, and back up data to somewhere the server cannot delete. The concepts underneath (processes, memory, file systems) are introduced in the Operating Systems and Linux section; this section applies them to a production server.

  • "The cloud provider secures the server." The provider secures the hypervisor and network; the operating system, SSH, firewall rules, and patches are yours.
  • free showing almost no free memory is normal: Linux uses spare RAM as page cache. The available column is the number that matters.
  • A process running in tmux or with nohup is not a service. It does not restart after a crash or a reboot; systemd does both.
  • Changing the SSH port is not a security control on its own; key-only authentication is.
  • A high load average does not always mean busy CPUs. On Linux it also counts tasks waiting on disk I/O.
  • Containers do not remove the need for these skills; the host still needs patching, disk space, and log rotation.

docs.title: Load Balancing and Multi-Server Architecture
docs.text: A multi-server architecture runs the same application on several machines at once, and a load balancer spreads incoming requests across them, stops sending traffic to machines that fail, and lets you add or remove machines without users noticing. The same idea repeats at every scale: two Node.js processes behind Nginx, a fleet of instances behind a cloud load balancer in three data centers, or whole regions behind DNS and anycast. It is how a service grows past one machine and survives the failure of any single one.

docs.title: What load balancing and multi-server architecture provide
docs.text:
• Capacity: ten instances handle roughly ten times the requests of one, as long as nothing they share (usually the database) becomes the bottleneck.
  • Availability: when an instance, a zone, or a region fails, health checks remove it and the remaining capacity keeps serving.
  • Zero-downtime changes: instances can be drained, replaced, and re-added one at a time, which is what rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments are built on.
  • Lower latency for distant users: DNS, anycast, and edge locations send each user to a nearby entry point.
  • Fault isolation: zones, regions, and cells limit how many users a single failure can reach.

These benefits have a price: the application must be stateless (no sessions, files, or schedules that live on one machine), the load balancer itself must be redundant, and every extra zone or region adds data replication, cost, and failure modes to understand.

docs.title: How a typical multi-server request path works
docs.text:
A request for the TaskFlow API travels through several layers, each of which can route around a failure:

  1. The client looks up api.taskflow.example.com. DNS answers with the address of a nearby edge location (GeoDNS or latency-based routing, or one anycast address announced from many places).
  2. The client opens an HTTPS connection to the edge (a CDN point of presence or a global load balancer), which terminates TLS, answers cached static content, and filters attacks.
  3. API calls and cache misses continue to a region, where a regional load balancer receives them on nodes in several Availability Zones.
  4. The load balancer picks a healthy instance with its balancing algorithm. Instances that fail health checks get no new requests; instances being replaced are drained first.
  5. The instance reads and writes the data tier: a database replicated across zones, Redis for sessions, rate limits, and locks, and object storage for uploads. Because no state lives on the instance, any instance can serve any user.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Nginx as a load balancer in front of three TaskFlow API instances:

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-api.conf
upstream taskflow_api {
    least_conn;                                 # fewest active connections wins
    server 10.0.1.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.2.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.3.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 32;                               # idle connections kept open to the app
}

server {
    listen 80;                                  # TLS ends at the edge or cloud LB in front
    server_name api.taskflow.example.com;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;                 # default since nginx 1.29.7; set for older versions
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
        proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;
    }
}

If an instance refuses connections or times out three times within 10 seconds, Nginx stops using it for 10 seconds, and the failed request is retried once on another instance. Nginx never retries a POST or PATCH that already reached an instance unless you add non_idempotent, which protects against creating a task twice.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Scale out only after the application is stateless and the database can take the extra connections; then add instances, then zones, and only add regions when a measured need (latency for distant users, a regional outage you cannot accept, data residency) justifies the cost.

  • A load balancer does not make an application scalable. An app that keeps sessions or uploads in local memory breaks the moment a second instance appears.
  • More instances do not fix a slow database; they usually add connections and make it worse.
  • "The process is running" is not a health check. The load balancer needs a readiness endpoint that says whether the instance can serve now.
  • The load balancer is also a single point of failure unless it is a managed, multi-zone service or a redundant pair.
  • DNS failover is not instant: resolvers and clients cache answers, and open connections stay where they are.
  • Multi-region is not a free upgrade from multi-AZ; it turns data replication and write conflicts into everyday problems.

docs.title: Monitoring and Logging
docs.text: Monitoring and logging are how a team finds out what its software is doing in production. The running application emits evidence (log lines, numeric metrics, and traces of individual requests), a pipeline collects and stores that evidence, and people and alert rules read it to answer two questions: "Are users being hurt right now?" and "Why?". The broader property of a system that lets you answer new questions without shipping new code is called observability.

docs.title: What monitoring and logging provides
docs.text:
• Detection: alerts fire when users are affected, ideally before the first support ticket arrives.
  • Diagnosis: logs, metrics, and traces narrow a symptom ("checkout is slow") down to a cause ("one MongoDB query lost its index").
  • Reliability targets you can measure: service level objectives (SLOs) turn "the API should be fast and available" into numbers you track.
  • Safer releases: comparing error rate and latency before and after a deploy tells you whether to continue or roll back.
  • Capacity planning: saturation trends show when you will run out of CPU, memory, connections, or disk.
  • Audit and security evidence: who did what, and when.

None of this comes for free. Every signal costs storage and attention, and an alert that wakes someone up for nothing is worse than no alert.

docs.title: How a typical observability pipeline works
docs.text:
Follow TaskFlow API, the Express and MongoDB task service used throughout this site, from a line of code to a person being paged:

  1. Instrument. The API writes structured JSON logs to stdout with pino, exposes request counters and latency histograms at /metrics with prom-client, and records spans for each request with the OpenTelemetry SDK.
  2. Collect. A log agent (Fluent Bit or Vector) tails container output, Prometheus scrapes /metrics every 15 seconds, and an OpenTelemetry Collector receives spans over OTLP, batches and samples them.
  3. Store. Each signal lands in a store built for it: a log store (Loki, Elasticsearch), a time-series database (Prometheus, Mimir), and a trace store (Tempo, Jaeger), each with its own retention.
  4. Look. Grafana dashboards show request rate, errors, and duration per service; a trace ID in a log line opens the matching trace.
  5. Alert. Rules evaluate SLO burn rates; Alertmanager groups, deduplicates, and routes firing alerts, paging the on-call engineer with a runbook link only when users are affected.
  6. Learn. After an incident, a blameless postmortem produces action items, often new or better signals.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
A request handled by TaskFlow API produces evidence in all three signals. The logger and the latency metric come from a few lines of setup; pino-http and the OpenTelemetry pino instrumentation (covered in the deep pages) add the request and trace fields to each log line:

// src/observability.js
import pino from "pino";
import client from "prom-client";

export const logger = pino({
  base: { service: "taskflow-api", env: process.env.NODE_ENV },
  redact: ["req.headers.authorization", "req.headers.cookie"],
});

client.collectDefaultMetrics(); // process CPU, memory, event loop lag, GC
export const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: "http_request_duration_seconds",
  help: "HTTP request duration in seconds",
  labelNames: ["method", "route", "status_code"],
  buckets: [0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5],
});

{"level":30,"time":1763030401123,"service":"taskflow-api","env":"production","reqId":"5b0c...","trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736","msg":"request completed","res":{"statusCode":201},"responseTime":38}

# PromQL: 95th percentile latency per route over the last 5 minutes
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

The metric tells you that p95 latency on POST /tasks doubled; the trace_id in the log line leads to a trace that shows which downstream call got slower. Each deep page below builds one piece of this.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat observability as a feature of the code you ship, not something an operations team bolts on later. Every new endpoint should come with a request id in its logs, a latency histogram, and a span, and every alert should be tied to something a user would notice. The application-level basics (log levels, what to log in a handler) are covered in logging and monitoring in the Backend section; this subject covers the production pipeline around them.

  • More dashboards do not mean better monitoring. A few dashboards that follow the request path beat hundreds nobody opens.
  • Logging everything is not observability. Unstructured, high-volume logs are expensive and hard to query; structure and correlation IDs matter more than volume.
  • Averages hide pain. Track percentiles (p95, p99) from histograms.
  • Alerting on CPU or memory usually pages people for things users never feel. Alert on symptoms such as error rate and latency.
  • 100% availability is the wrong target; it is unachievable and blocks every change. Choose an SLO and spend the error budget deliberately.
  • Monitoring does not end at the server. Users experience DNS, certificates, CDNs, and the browser too, so check from the outside as well.

docs.title: Performance and Reliability Testing
docs.text: Performance testing puts a system under a controlled, realistic load and measures how fast it responds, how much work it completes, and what breaks first. Reliability testing goes further: it holds the load for hours, injects failures on purpose (chaos engineering), and rehearses the human response (game days). Together they replace "it should cope with the launch" with evidence such as "TaskFlow API serves 120 requests per second with p95 under 300 ms, loses one instance without user-visible errors, and recovers on its own".

docs.title: What performance and reliability testing provides
docs.text:
• Capacity numbers: the throughput one instance sustains within the SLO, which feeds capacity planning and autoscaling limits.
  • Regression protection: a short load test with thresholds in CI fails the build when a change makes p95 latency or the error rate worse.
  • Bottleneck discovery: load reveals the first resource to saturate (the event loop, a connection pool, the database, a downstream API) before users find it.
  • Proof that failure handling works: timeouts, retries, failover, and autoscaling are only proven when you watch them work under load and under injected failure.
  • Practised people: game days rehearse the incident response, so the first real outage is not the first time anyone opens the runbook.

None of this is free. Tests need a production-like environment, realistic data, and someone who can read the results. A load test against the wrong environment, or with an unrealistic workload model, produces confident and wrong numbers.

docs.title: How a typical load test works
docs.text:
1. Ask one question and set pass criteria from the SLO: "Can TaskFlow API serve the expected weekday peak of 120 requests per second with p95 under 300 ms and fewer than 0.1% errors?"
  2. Model the workload: the endpoint mix and arrival rate from production metrics, think time between user actions, test users, and data volume.
  3. Prepare the environment: production-sized instances and data, the same configuration, and a load generator with spare capacity of its own.
  4. Run a smoke test first (one virtual user for a minute) to prove the script and the environment, then run the chosen load shape.
  5. Watch both sides: client-side throughput, latency percentiles, and errors from the load tool; server-side saturation (CPU, event-loop delay, connection pools, database) from monitoring.
  6. Compare with thresholds and the last baseline. When a limit is hit, find the bottleneck, change one thing, and run the same test again.
  7. Keep the script, the results, and the environment description so the next run is comparable.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
An average-load test for TaskFlow API with Grafana k6 (version 2.x). The arrival-rate executor starts a fixed number of requests per second, so slow responses cannot quietly reduce the load:

// perf/tasks-average-load.js: TaskFlow API at its expected weekday peak
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    list_tasks: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate", // open model: k6 starts N requests per second
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { target: 120, duration: "5m" },  // ramp to the expected peak: 120 requests/s
        { target: 120, duration: "20m" }, // hold it
        { target: 0, duration: "2m" },    // ramp down
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],                // fewer than 0.1% errors
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"],  // latency SLO, in ms
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/tasks?limit=20`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}` },
  });
  check(res, { "status is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

k6 run -e BASE_URL=https://staging.taskflow.example.com \
  -e API_TOKEN="$PERF_TEST_TOKEN" perf/tasks-average-load.js
# exit code 0: every threshold passed; 99: at least one threshold failed

The thresholds turn the SLO into a pass or fail result, which is what lets a pipeline gate on it. Each deep page below builds one piece of this: choosing the shape, writing realistic scripts, explaining a failure, and testing what happens when parts of the system break.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat performance like any other requirement: write it down as a threshold derived from the SLO, check it automatically, and run the same test again after every change that could affect it. The theory this subject builds on lives elsewhere on the site: latency, percentiles, and queueing basics in performance and latency, targets in SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets, and the patterns that chaos experiments verify in resilience patterns across servers.

  • A test on a laptop, or against a database with a hundred rows, does not predict production. Size, data volume, and configuration all matter.
  • More virtual users is not more realism. A closed workload model slows down together with a slow server and hides the very problem you are looking for.
  • An average that passes says nothing about the tail. Gate on p95 and p99 latency and on the error rate.
  • A test that ends without errors has not found the limit. Only stress and breakpoint tests tell you where the system breaks and how.
  • Chaos engineering is not breaking things at random in production. It is a controlled experiment with a hypothesis, a small blast radius, and a way to stop.
  • A passing result is valid for the version, data, configuration, and environment you tested, and for nothing else.
