docs.title: DevOps and Deployment Projects
docs.text: Build these to practice the DevOps lessons on a running system. Most of them take the TaskFlow API from the Backend section (Express and MongoDB) from a project on your laptop to a service you could run for real users. Do them in order: each one builds on the pipeline, image, server, or domain from the projects before it.

docs.title: Ship It Pipeline
docs.text:
Put TaskFlow under a real workflow: protect main, require pull requests with a passing check, and add a GitHub Actions pipeline that lints, type checks, and runs unit and integration tests against MongoDB in a service container. Cache dependencies on the lockfile hash and keep the pipeline under five minutes. Finish by tagging a release with a generated changelog. Practices Git and GitHub and CI/CD.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Production Image
docs.text:
Write a multi-stage Dockerfile that produces a small image running as a non-root user, handles SIGTERM gracefully, and has a health check. Build it in CI, tag it with the commit SHA, scan it for vulnerabilities, and push it to a registry. Add a Docker Compose stack (API, MongoDB, and a database UI) that starts in the right order using health conditions. Practices Docker.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: TaskFlow on Kubernetes
docs.text:
Run a local cluster (kind or minikube) and deploy TaskFlow with a Deployment, Service, ConfigMap, and Secret. Add readiness and liveness probes, resource requests and limits, and a HorizontalPodAutoscaler. Put load on it with a load-testing tool, watch it scale, roll out a new image, then roll back with kubectl rollout undo while requests keep succeeding. Package it all as a Helm chart. Practices Kubernetes.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Config and Secrets Hardening
docs.text:
Replace every hard-coded setting with environment variables validated at startup, so a missing value stops the process with a clear error. Move the database password into a secret store, have the app fetch it at startup, then rotate it with zero downtime using two valid passwords during the switch. Commit a fake secret to a test repository and practice the full response: revoke, rotate, and purge it from history. Practices Environment Variables and Secrets.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Canary Release Lab
docs.text:
Deploy two versions of TaskFlow behind a load balancer or ingress and shift traffic in steps (5%, 25%, 50%, 100%). Ship a deliberately broken version and have the rollout stop automatically when its error rate rises. Add a feature flag that turns a new endpoint on for 10% of users with stable bucketing, and rename a database field with expand and contract across three deploys without downtime. Practices Deployment Strategies.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Version Everything
docs.text:
Give every TaskFlow artifact a version a person can trace: semantic versions and tags for the API, a build ID baked into TaskFlow Web, and the image digest in each deployment record. Deprecate one API field the way the release engineering lessons describe, announce the deprecation and sunset dates to clients, and keep the old field working until the date passes. Make open browser tabs notice a new frontend release and reload safely, and give a desktop or mobile build a minimum supported version that the API enforces with a clear upgrade message. Practices Release Engineering.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Production Server from Scratch
docs.text:
Rent a small virtual server and set it up by hand from a fresh Ubuntu LTS image: a non-root user with sudo, key-only SSH, a firewall, automatic security updates, and Node.js installed by a supported method. Run TaskFlow under a hardened systemd unit behind Nginx, deploy with release folders and a symlink switch so a rollback is one command, rotate the logs, and schedule a nightly job that cannot overlap itself. Then fill the disk and exhaust memory on purpose, and diagnose each problem with the tools from the troubleshooting lesson. Practices Linux Server Operations.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Your Own Domain, Properly
docs.text:
Point a domain you own at TaskFlow: the apex and www with one redirecting to the other, an api subdomain for the backend, and a CAA record naming your certificate authority. Put a CDN in front of TaskFlow Web with cache rules per path and a purge step in the deploy pipeline. Rehearse moving DNS to another provider by lowering TTLs first and copying every record, then send transactional email with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, moving DMARC from p=none to p=reject once the reports are clean. Practices Domains, DNS and Email.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: TLS Everywhere
docs.text:
Serve TaskFlow over HTTPS behind Nginx or Caddy with a certificate from Let's Encrypt (use its staging environment while testing), redirect HTTP to HTTPS, and add HSTS. Confirm automatic renewal works with a dry run, add an expiry alert, and use openssl s_client to diagnose a deliberately broken certificate chain. Practices SSL Certificates.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Three Servers, One Address
docs.text:
Run three TaskFlow instances behind a load balancer such as Nginx or HAProxy. Move sessions to a shared store and uploads to object storage so any instance can serve any request, then prove it by stopping instances one at a time under load. Add health checks and connection draining so a rolling deploy drops no requests, make a scheduled job run once per scheduled time across the fleet, and protect a slow dependency with timeouts, retries with jittered backoff, and a circuit breaker. Practices Load Balancing and Multi-Server Architecture.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Pick a Host and Price It
docs.text:
Write down what TaskFlow needs (traffic, data size, regions, compliance), then price three ways to host the web app, API, and database: for example a static host with a container platform and a managed database, an all-in-one platform, and a single virtual server. Estimate each at 10,000, 1 million, and 50 million monthly page views with the providers' official pricing calculators, deploy the two cheapest, and compare deploy time, cold starts, and the real bill after a month. Set a budget alert on every account before you start. Practices Hosting and Cloud Platforms.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Infrastructure from Code
docs.text:
Use Terraform to create the cloud resources for TaskFlow: a network with public and private subnets, storage for uploads with versioning, and the permissions the app needs, with remote state and locking. Run plan on every pull request and apply only after merge. Destroy everything and recreate it from code to prove nothing was configured by hand. Practices Infrastructure as Code.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Secure the Pipeline
docs.text:
Add security checks to the TaskFlow pipeline: static analysis, dependency and secret scanning, a scan of the Terraform code, and an image scan that fails the build only on fixable critical findings. Replace any long-lived cloud keys with OIDC and a least-privilege role, run a DAST scan against staging, and put a WAF rate-limit rule in front of the login endpoint. Triage what the scanners report with CVSS, EPSS, and the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. Practices DevSecOps and Cloud Security.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Observability Lab
docs.text:
Instrument TaskFlow with JSON logs that carry a request ID, Prometheus metrics for request rate, errors, and duration, and OpenTelemetry traces that follow a request into MongoDB. Define an availability and a latency SLO, build a dashboard, and add a burn-rate alert with a runbook link. Break something on purpose, follow the alert to the trace and the log line that explain it, and write a blameless postmortem. Practices Monitoring and Logging.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Load Test and Break It
docs.text:
Write k6 tests for TaskFlow's main user journeys with thresholds on p95 latency and error rate, and run a short version in CI that fails the build when a threshold is crossed. Raise the load until latency bends upward, find the bottleneck with the USE method and a CPU profile, fix it, and measure again. Finish with a small game day: add latency between the API and MongoDB with a fault-injection proxy such as Toxiproxy, write down what you expect to happen, and compare it with what does. Practices Performance and Reliability Testing.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Backup and Restore Drill
docs.text:
Schedule encrypted MongoDB backups to object storage with a retention policy and an immutable copy. Then run a drill: drop a collection, restore to the minute before the mistake, verify the data with counts and a smoke test, and record how long it really took. Compare the result with the RPO and RTO you would promise users. Practices Backups and Disaster Recovery.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Measure Your Delivery
docs.text:
Compute the DORA metrics for your own TaskFlow work with a small script over git history, deployment records, and the incidents from the earlier projects. Choose one metric to improve and say why, write a one-page team charter covering ownership, on-call, and how changes are approved, and record one architecture decision as an ADR. Practices DevOps Fundamentals.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Publish These Notes
docs.text:
Deploy a MkDocs site like this one to GitHub Pages with a workflow that builds on every push to main, fails on broken links with mkdocs build --strict, and publishes only from the default branch. Add a pull-request check that builds without deploying. Practices CI/CD and deploying static sites.

Guide: one-page plan

docs.title: Release Engineering
docs.text: Release engineering is the discipline of turning source code into versions that people and machines can install, run, and trust, and of managing how those versions coexist once they are out. Google's SRE book describes it concisely as building and delivering software. In practice it answers questions that a single deploy pipeline does not: which version is running where, which versions must still work together, how installed software updates itself, when a release ships, and how dozens of services or apps in one repository are released without stepping on each other.

docs.title: What release engineering provides
docs.text:
• Identifiable versions: every artifact (image, bundle, installer, schema, event) says exactly what it is and where it came from, so an incident starts with facts instead of guesses.
  • Compatibility across versions in flight: old clients keep working against new servers, new servers keep reading old data, and breaking changes happen in a deliberate order.
  • Safe update paths: desktop, mobile, and web clients update through signed, staged, observable mechanisms that can be paused.
  • A predictable cadence: release trains, cut-offs, hotfix branches, and long-term support lines that customers and teams can plan around.
  • Independent delivery at scale: many services, or many apps in one monorepo, each released on its own schedule without lock-step deploys.

docs.title: How a typical release works
docs.text:
A TaskFlow release that renames a field touches every layer of the product, one layer at a time:

  1. A change merges to main. CI builds each artifact once and stamps it with a version such as 2.4.1+build.873.g3f2a1c and its commit.
  2. The database migration expands the schema so both the old and the new column exist; the running API version keeps working.
  3. The TaskFlow API deploys with a rolling update. For a few minutes both versions serve traffic, so the new version accepts the old and the new request shapes.
  4. TaskFlow Web deploys. New tabs load the new bundle; tabs opened earlier keep running the old one, so old assets stay available and those tabs are prompted to reload.
  5. Desktop and mobile clients update over days or weeks through their updaters and stores. The API keeps serving every supported client version, and clients below the minimum version are asked to update.
  6. When usage of the old field drops to zero (or its announced sunset date passes), a final release removes it: the contract step.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Many teams record each product release as a small manifest that names every component version that shipped together. CI writes it; humans and tools read it during incidents and audits.

{
  "release": "2026.11.2",
  "createdAt": "2026-11-13T10:42:00Z",
  "api": {
    "version": "2.4.1+build.873.g3f2a1c",
    "image": "ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest>",
    "apiVersions": { "current": "v2", "deprecated": { "v1": "2027-06-30" } }
  },
  "web": { "build": "873", "commit": "3f2a1c9" },
  "schema": { "lastMigration": "0042_add_due_object" },
  "clients": {
    "minSupported": { "desktop": "1.6.0", "ios": "3.0.0", "android": "3.0.0" },
    "latest": { "desktop": "1.9.1", "ios": "3.2.0", "android": "3.2.0" }
  }
}

The manifest answers "what exactly is TaskFlow 2026.11.2?" without anyone reconstructing it from deploy logs, and it gives the API, the updater, and support tooling one source for the minimum supported client versions.

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Think of every interface in your product as something that will exist in at least two versions at the same moment: the one before your deploy and the one after. Design each change so that both can run side by side, stamp every artifact with its exact version, and make the update path for installed software as safe as your server pipeline.

  • "We deploy frontend and backend together, so skew cannot happen." Any rolling deploy mixes versions for minutes, and browser tabs keep old code for hours or days.
  • A version number is not a release process. It only helps when it is stamped into the artifact and visible at runtime.
  • An installed client cannot be rolled back. A bad version is replaced by shipping a newer one.
  • Microservices do not make deploys independent by themselves; shared databases and breaking contracts turn them into a distributed monolith.
  • A monorepo does not mean one deploy. Each app should still build and ship on its own when it is affected.

docs.title: SSL Certificates
docs.text: An SSL (more accurately, TLS) certificate is a signed document that binds a domain name such as api.example.com to a public key. During the TLS handshake the server presents its certificate, proves it holds the matching private key, and the client checks that a certificate authority it already trusts vouched for that binding. The result is an encrypted connection to the server the user actually meant to reach. Every HTTPS site, API, and internal service call relies on this, and an expired or misconfigured certificate takes a service down as completely as a crashed server.

docs.title: What SSL certificates provide
docs.text:
• Authentication: the client knows it is talking to the real api.example.com, not an impostor on the network.
  • Confidentiality: traffic is encrypted, so passwords, tokens, and task data cannot be read in transit.
  • Integrity: any modification of data in transit is detected.
  • A prerequisite for the modern web: browsers mark HTTP pages as not secure, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 are used over TLS in browsers, and many web APIs (service workers, geolocation) require a secure context.

Certificates also bring operational duties: they expire, must be renewed automatically, must be served with the right intermediate chain, and their private keys must be protected.

docs.title: How a typical HTTPS connection is verified
docs.text:
When a TaskFlow Web user's browser connects to https://api.example.com:

  1. The browser opens a TCP connection and sends a ClientHello with the server name it wants (SNI) and a key share for the key exchange.
  2. The server replies with its own key share, its certificate chain (leaf certificate plus intermediate certificates), and a signature made with its private key.
  3. The browser verifies the chain: each certificate is signed by the next one up, ending at a root certificate already in its trust store.
  4. It checks that api.example.com matches a name in the certificate's subject alternative name list and that the current date is within the validity period.
  5. Both sides confirm the handshake with Finished messages, derive the same session keys, and send HTTP requests and responses encrypted.

docs.title: Practical example
docs.text:
Check the certificate a server is actually presenting, its issuer, its validity dates, and the names it covers:

# Ask for api.example.com explicitly (SNI), then decode the leaf certificate
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

subject=CN=api.example.com
issuer=C=US, O=Example Trust Services, CN=Example TLS CA R1
notBefore=Oct 31 09:12:44 2026 GMT
notAfter=Jan 29 09:12:43 2027 GMT
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:api.example.com

notAfter is the date that matters for outages; the subject alternative name list is what browsers match against the hostname. The troubleshooting lesson builds on this command.

Review

docs.title: Developer perspective and common misconceptions
docs.text:
Treat certificates as automated infrastructure, not a yearly chore. Public certificate lifetimes are shrinking under CA/Browser Forum rules (a 200-day maximum since March 2026, falling to 47 days by 2029), so manual renewal no longer scales: use ACME (Let's Encrypt, Caddy, cert-manager) or managed certificates at your load balancer, and monitor the certificate that is actually served. The protocol itself is covered in TLS and SSL in the Networking section.

  • "SSL" is a historical name. SSL 2.0 and 3.0 are broken and disabled; everything today is TLS 1.2 or 1.3.
  • HTTPS proves who you are talking to and protects data in transit. It does not prove the site is honest or that the server is secure.
  • A free, automated DV certificate gives the same encryption strength as an expensive one. Paid options add validation of the organization, support, or warranties, not stronger cryptography.
  • Never "fix" certificate errors by disabling verification (curl -k, rejectUnauthorized: false, NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0). That removes authentication and invites man-in-the-middle attacks.
  • Renewing a certificate is not enough; the server must load the new one, and with the full intermediate chain.
  • Internal services need TLS too: networks inside a data center or cloud VPC are not automatically trustworthy.

docs.title: Backup Fundamentals and Strategies
docs.text: A backup strategy answers four questions: what to copy, how often, where to keep the copies, and for how long, so that you can restore within the time and data loss the business accepts. This lesson separates backups from replication and snapshots, compares full, incremental, and differential backups with a storage and restore-time example, explains the 3-2-1 rule and its 3-2-1-1-0 extension, immutable backups against ransomware, encryption and key management, grandfather-father-son retention, and what besides the database needs backing up.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most data loss is not caused by disks dying, which redundancy handles well. It is caused by people and software: a migration that drops the wrong field, a script run against production instead of staging, a bug that overwrites records for a week before anyone notices, an attacker who encrypts or deletes everything they can reach. Redundant systems copy these mistakes faithfully and immediately. Only an independent copy from before the mistake lets you recover.

Strategy matters because backups are easy to get superficially right and deeply wrong: copies in the same account an attacker controls, an incremental chain too long to restore in time, encrypted backups whose key was deleted, or a job that has quietly produced empty files for months. GitLab's 2017 outage is the classic example of several backup mechanisms all failing at once.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitLab (2017). The postmortem of the January 31 database outage describes how an engineer accidentally removed the primary database's data directory, and how the regular pg_dump backups had been failing silently (a version mismatch, with failure emails rejected), disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers, and replication could not help. GitLab restored from a snapshot taken about six hours earlier for staging, losing database records created in that window.
  • Google SRE book. The chapter Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote argues that what users need is restores, not backups, and describes defence in depth: soft deletion, backups with tested recovery, and replication, each covering different failure modes.
  • CISA ransomware guidance. The #StopRansomware Guide recommends offline, encrypted backups of critical data, regular testing of backup integrity and restore procedures, golden images, and keeping infrastructure-as-code templates backed up offline, because attackers look for and destroy reachable backups.
  • The 3-2-1 rule. US-CERT's paper Data Backup Options states the rule: keep 3 copies of important data (1 primary and 2 backups), on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Backup, Azure Backup, Google Cloud Backup and DR, MongoDB Atlas backups, Percona Backup for MongoDB, pgBackRest, Barman, restic, BorgBackup, Velero (Kubernetes), rclone, and Veeam.

docs.title: Backups, replication, and snapshots
docs.text:
Backup Replication Snapshot What it is An independent copy from a point in time, kept for a retention period A continuously updated copy (replica set member, read replica, cross-region bucket replication) A point-in-time image of a volume or database, often copy-on-write Protects against Deletion, corruption, bad deploys, ransomware (if isolated), disasters (if offsite) Hardware and zone failures; enables fast failover Quick rollback after a risky change; base for backups Does not protect against Data written after the last backup Mistakes and attacks, which it copies within seconds Loss of the storage system or account that holds it, unless copied elsewhere Typical RPO Hours (or minutes with log capture) Seconds or zero At snapshot time Restore speed Minutes to hours Seconds (failover) Fast within the same system

Replication is about availability; backups are about recoverability. TaskFlow needs both: a MongoDB replica set to survive a node failure, and backups to survive db.tasks.deleteMany({}). A snapshot becomes a backup once it is copied somewhere independent, with its own retention.

docs.title: Full, incremental, and differential backups
docs.text:
• A full backup copies everything.
  • An incremental backup copies what changed since the previous backup of any kind.
  • A differential backup copies what changed since the last full backup.

Worked example: 500 GB of data, 25 GB (5%) of new changes each day, assuming each day changes different data, one week of backups:

Daily fulls:     7 x 500 GB                         = 3,500 GB
Incremental:     500 + 6 x 25 GB                    =   650 GB
Differential:    500 + (25 + 50 + 75 + 100 + 125 + 150) GB = 1,025 GB

Restore Saturday's state, at 200 MB/s from backup storage:
Daily fulls:     read 500 GB                        = 2,500 s, about 42 min (1 piece)
Incremental:     read 500 + 150 GB = 650 GB         = 3,250 s, about 54 min (7 pieces, in order)
Differential:    read 500 + 150 GB = 650 GB         = 3,250 s, about 54 min (2 pieces)

The incremental and differential restores read the same amount of data here, but the incremental restore depends on seven pieces applied in order, so any missing or corrupt piece breaks everything after it, and real chains are often weeks long. Differentials grow every day until the next full.

Modern tools blur these categories:

  • Block-level and deduplicating backups (restic, BorgBackup, cloud snapshots, Percona Backup and pgBackRest incrementals) store only new or changed chunks, but each snapshot can be restored as if it were a full.
  • Synthetic fulls build a new full backup from the previous full and its incrementals on the backup server, so the chain stays short without re-reading production.
  • Continuous log capture (MongoDB oplog, PostgreSQL WAL) records every change between base backups, enabling point-in-time recovery, covered in database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: The 3-2-1 rule and 3-2-1-1-0
docs.text:
3-2-1: keep 3 copies of the data (production plus 2 backups), on 2 different types of storage, with 1 copy offsite. Each part defends against a different failure: multiple copies against loss of one, different media against a flaw shared by one storage type, offsite against losing a site.

In the cloud, "different media" and "offsite" translate to different services, regions, and, most importantly, different accounts and credentials: a copy that the same administrator credentials can delete is not independent.

3-2-1-1-0 extends the rule for the ransomware era:

  • +1 immutable or offline copy that cannot be modified or deleted during its retention period, even by an administrator.
  • 0 errors: backups are verified by automated restore tests, not assumed (see restore testing and runbooks).

docs.title: Immutable backups against ransomware
docs.text:
Attackers who gain administrator access look for backups first, because destroying them makes a ransom far more likely to be paid. Defences:

  • Write once, read many (WORM) storage. Amazon S3 Object Lock stores object versions that cannot be deleted or overwritten until a retention date passes. In compliance mode nobody, including the root account, can shorten the retention or delete the version; in governance mode users with a special permission can. A legal hold blocks deletion with no end date until it is removed. Object Lock requires versioning.
  • Backup vault locks. AWS Backup Vault Lock, Azure immutable vaults, and similar features enforce minimum retention on backup vaults.
  • Separate accounts and credentials. Backups are copied into an account where production roles cannot delete anything; the backup writer role can write but not delete.
  • Retention longer than detection time. Attackers can sit in a network for weeks before encrypting; if backups expire after 7 days, every copy may already contain their changes or tooling. Keep at least some copies for months.
  • Offline copies for the most critical data: storage not reachable from the network at all.

Immutability has costs: you cannot delete data early (including data you are legally required to erase), and mistakes in retention settings are expensive. Use compliance mode deliberately, with short default retention and longer retention only where needed.

docs.title: Encryption and key management
docs.text:
Backups contain everything sensitive in production, often for longer, so:

  • Encrypt at rest with server-side encryption (for example SSE-KMS) or client-side encryption before upload (restic, BorgBackup, and age encrypt by default or on request), and in transit with TLS.
  • Keep keys separate from the backups. A KMS key in the backup account, or a client-side key stored in a different system, so stealing the backups alone is useless.
  • Protect the keys as carefully as the data. If the key is deleted or lost, the backups are permanently unreadable. Cloud KMS keys have a deletion waiting period (7 to 30 days in AWS KMS) precisely so mistakes can be cancelled; alert on scheduled key deletions.
  • Restrict who can restore. A restore role can read all historical data; grant it narrowly and audit its use.
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypting each tenant's data with its own key lets you make that tenant's data in old backups unreadable by destroying the key, which helps with deletion obligations.

docs.title: Retention schedules: grandfather-father-son
docs.text:
Keeping every daily backup forever is expensive and rarely useful. Grandfather-father-son (GFS) keeps:

  • Sons: daily backups for 7 to 14 days (recover yesterday's mistake).
  • Fathers: one weekly backup for 4 to 5 weeks.
  • Grandfathers: one monthly backup for 12 months or more, sometimes yearly backups for several years.

23 restore points cover a year instead of 365. Retention is driven by three inputs: how far back mistakes are typically discovered (silent corruption can take weeks to notice), legal and contractual requirements, and cost. Personal data adds a constraint the other way: privacy laws such as the GDPR limit how long you keep it, so document how deletion requests interact with backups (usually: deleted data expires with the backups and is never restored into production).

docs.title: What to back up beyond the database
docs.text:
Data Why How for TaskFlow MongoDB data The system of record Snapshots plus continuous oplog, or Atlas Cloud Backup with point-in-time restore Object storage (uploaded attachments) Users' files; replication alone copies deletions Versioning, Object Lock or backup copies to another account, lifecycle rules Secrets and keys Without them, restored systems cannot start or decrypt data Secrets manager replication or export to a separate, encrypted store; KMS key protection Configuration Feature flags, tenant settings, DNS zones Keep in Git or IaC; export what lives in SaaS consoles Infrastructure-as-code state Terraform state maps code to real resources; losing it makes changes dangerous Remote state in a versioned, access-controlled bucket Source code and CI configuration Rebuilding requires code and pipelines Hosted Git plus a mirror elsewhere; Git hosting is not itself a backup Container images and build artifacts Redeploying an exact old version Registry replication or rebuild from tagged source Logs and audit trails Investigations and compliance Retention in the log store and archive tier Runbooks and contact lists Needed when your systems are down Offline or independently hosted copies

Not everything needs a backup: caches (Redis used as a cache), search indexes, and derived tables can be rebuilt from the source, as long as the rebuild procedure is documented and its duration fits the RTO. Write down, for every data store, whether it is restored or rebuilt.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Strategy Small database (under tens of GB) Nightly logical dumps plus continuous log capture, copied offsite Large database (hundreds of GB and more) Storage or database-native snapshots with incremental change capture; logical dumps only for subsets Managed database (Atlas, RDS) Enable its backups and point-in-time recovery, plus cross-region or cross-account copies you control Files in object storage Versioning plus a copy in another account, ideally with Object Lock Critical data, ransomware risk 3-2-1-1-0: separate account, immutable copy, tested restores Data you can regenerate Document the rebuild instead of backing it up Personal data with deletion obligations Short retention, encryption, documented deletion handling; avoid indefinite immutability

Do not treat a replica, RAID array, or same-account snapshot as your only protection, and do not add backup layers you never test.

docs.title: A backup inventory for TaskFlow
docs.text:
What Method Frequency Retention Where Restore test MongoDB taskflow Atlas Cloud Backup snapshots + continuous backup Snapshots every 6 h, continuous oplog 7 d PITR, 4 w weekly, 12 m monthly Primary region + copy to second region Weekly automated restore to scratch cluster Uploads bucket Versioning + replication to backup account with Object Lock Continuous 35 d locked, about 430 d total (400 d + 30 d for old versions) Backup account, second region Monthly sample restore of 100 files Terraform state Versioned S3 backend Every apply 90 d of versions Infrastructure account Quarterly terraform plan from a restored version Secrets Secrets manager replica Continuous Managed Second region Quarterly DR drill Runbooks Markdown in Git + exported copy On change All versions Git mirror, offline copy Reviewed in DR drill

The inventory itself is a deliverable: it is what you check during a disaster, so keep a copy outside the systems it describes.

docs.title: File backups with restic and GFS retention
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/backup-uploads.sh: encrypted, deduplicated backup of local uploads to S3
set -euo pipefail

export RESTIC_REPOSITORY="s3:s3.amazonaws.com/taskflow-backups-example/uploads"
export RESTIC_PASSWORD_FILE="/etc/taskflow/credentials/restic-password"   # root-only 0600, not in the repository
# AWS credentials come from the instance role or standard AWS environment variables.

# One-time setup: restic init

restic backup /srv/taskflow/shared/uploads --tag uploads --host taskflow-files-1

# Grandfather-father-son retention, then remove unreferenced data
restic forget --tag uploads --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 --prune

# Verify repository structure and read back a sample of the stored data
restic check --read-data-subset=5%

restic encrypts and deduplicates on the client, so the bucket owner cannot read the data without the password, and each snapshot restores as a full even though only changed chunks are uploaded. Losing /etc/taskflow/credentials/restic-password makes every backup unreadable, so store it in a secrets manager as well. The paths follow the server layout in setting up a production server.

docs.title: An immutable, encrypted backup bucket (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/backup-bucket.tf (applied in the separate backup account)
resource "aws_kms_key" "backups" {
  description             = "TaskFlow backup encryption"
  deletion_window_in_days = 30
  enable_key_rotation     = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "backups" {
  bucket              = "taskflow-backups-example"
  object_lock_enabled = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "backups" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.backups.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_object_lock_configuration" "backups" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.backups.id
  rule {
    default_retention {
      mode = "COMPLIANCE" # nobody can delete a version before 35 days, not even root
      days = 35
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "backups" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.backups.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm     = "aws:kms"
      kms_master_key_id = aws_kms_key.backups.arn
    }
    bucket_key_enabled = true
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "backups" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.backups.id
  rule {
    id     = "expire-old-backups"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter {}
    expiration {
      days = 400
    }
    noncurrent_version_expiration {
      noncurrent_days = 30
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "backups" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.backups.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

Object Lock retention protects each version for 35 days; lifecycle rules expire objects after that, so storage does not grow forever. Pair the bucket with a policy that lets production's backup role write but not delete, and test the setup with a short retention period first, because compliance-mode retention cannot be undone.

docs.title: A backup plan with cross-region copies and a vault lock (AWS Backup)
docs.text:
# infra/backup-plan.tf
resource "aws_backup_vault" "primary" {
  name        = "taskflow-primary"
  kms_key_arn = aws_kms_key.backups.arn
}

resource "aws_backup_vault_lock_configuration" "primary" {
  backup_vault_name   = aws_backup_vault.primary.name
  min_retention_days  = 7
  max_retention_days  = 400
  changeable_for_days = 3 # after 3 days the lock can no longer be changed or removed
}

resource "aws_backup_plan" "taskflow" {
  name = "taskflow"

  rule {
    rule_name         = "daily"
    target_vault_name = aws_backup_vault.primary.name
    schedule          = "cron(0 3 * * ? *)" # 03:00 UTC every day
    lifecycle {
      delete_after = 14
    }
    copy_action {
      destination_vault_arn = var.dr_vault_arn # vault in another region and account
      lifecycle {
        delete_after = 14
      }
    }
  }

  rule {
    rule_name         = "monthly"
    target_vault_name = aws_backup_vault.primary.name
    schedule          = "cron(0 4 1 * ? *)" # 04:00 UTC on the 1st of each month
    lifecycle {
      delete_after = 365
    }
    copy_action {
      destination_vault_arn = var.dr_vault_arn
      lifecycle {
        delete_after = 365
      }
    }
  }
}

A backup selection (aws_backup_selection) then assigns resources, for example by tag, to the plan. Setting changeable_for_days puts the vault lock in compliance mode after the grace period.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start from RPO and RTO for each data store, then choose methods that meet them.
  • Never rely on replication, RAID, or same-account snapshots alone.
  • Follow 3-2-1-1-0: an offsite copy in a separate account, at least one immutable copy, and zero untested backups.
  • Encrypt backups, keep keys separate, and protect keys from deletion.
  • Use GFS retention driven by detection time, legal needs, and cost.
  • Back up object storage, secrets, configuration, IaC state, and runbooks, not just databases; document what is rebuilt instead.
  • Alert on backup job failures, on the age of the last successful backup, and on unexpected size changes.
  • Keep restore chains short (periodic or synthetic fulls).
  • Keep an inventory of every backup, with owner and restore test status.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Backups have been empty for weeks and nobody noticed. Detect: backup sizes dropped sharply, or a restore test fails; the job "succeeded" every night. Cause: the script ignores the dump tool's exit code, or a version mismatch or permission error produces an empty file (as at GitLab). Fix: set -euo pipefail, check exit codes, alert on size anomalies and on the age of the last verified backup, and run automated restore tests.
  • Ransomware encrypted production and deleted the backups. Detect: backup vaults or buckets are empty, or deletion events from a production role appear in the audit log. Cause: backups lived in the same account with credentials the attacker obtained. Fix: copies in a separate account, Object Lock or vault lock in compliance mode, and backup writer roles without delete permissions.
  • A restore takes two days instead of two hours. Detect: a DR drill or real restore stalls while applying a long chain of incrementals or downloading from cold storage. Cause: months since the last full, or backups moved to an archive tier with slow retrieval. Fix: periodic or synthetic fulls, keep recent restore points in a fast tier, and measure restore time in drills.
  • Backups cannot be decrypted. Detect: restore fails with access denied or key errors. Cause: the KMS key was disabled or scheduled for deletion, or a client-side password was lost with the server. Fix: key policies that restrict deletion, alerts on key deletion scheduling, and key material or passwords stored independently of the backups.
  • The database restores, but files referenced by tasks are missing. Detect: restored tasks link to attachments that return 404. Cause: the uploads bucket was not backed up, or only replicated, so deletions propagated. Fix: versioning and separate-account copies for object storage, and restore tests that check references between data stores.
  • The backup bill keeps growing. Detect: storage cost rises month over month regardless of data size. Cause: no retention expiry, noncurrent object versions kept forever, or every backup a full. Fix: lifecycle rules, GFS retention, and incremental or deduplicating tools.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Backup: An independent, point-in-time copy kept for restoring data.
  • Restore: Recreating data from a backup.
  • Replication: Continuously copying data to another location for availability.
  • Snapshot: A point-in-time image of a volume or database.
  • Full / incremental / differential backup: Everything; changes since the last backup; changes since the last full.
  • Synthetic full: A full backup assembled from earlier backups without reading the source again.
  • 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 storage types, 1 offsite.
  • 3-2-1-1-0: Adds 1 immutable or offline copy and 0 restore errors.
  • Immutable backup (WORM): A copy that cannot be changed or deleted until its retention expires.
  • Object Lock (governance / compliance mode): S3's WORM feature, with and without an override permission.
  • GFS retention: Daily, weekly, and monthly tiers of restore points.
  • Crypto-shredding: Making data unreadable by destroying its encryption key.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating replication, RAID, or high availability as a backup.
  • Keeping all copies in the same account, region, or credentials.
  • Backing up only the database and forgetting files, secrets, and IaC state.
  • Never testing restores, or testing only that a file exists.
  • Encrypting backups with a key stored next to them, or losing the key.
  • Retention shorter than the time it takes to notice corruption or an intrusion.
  • Unbounded retention that turns backups into an expensive privacy liability.
  • Long incremental chains that make restores slow and fragile.
  • Assuming a managed database provider's default backups meet your RPO, RTO, and isolation needs.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is replication not a backup? Give a failure that replication makes worse.
  2. For 800 GB of data changing 40 GB per day, how much storage does a week of daily fulls, of incrementals, and of differentials use, starting with a full on Sunday? (5,600 GB; 800 + 6 x 40 = 1,040 GB; 800 + (40 + 80 + 120 + 160 + 200 + 240) = 1,640 GB.)
  3. In that example, how many pieces does each scheme need to restore Saturday, and what is the risk with the incremental chain?
  4. Explain the 3-2-1 rule and the extra "1" and "0" in 3-2-1-1-0.
  5. What is the difference between S3 Object Lock governance and compliance modes, and when would you use each?
  6. Why must backup retention be longer than the time it takes to detect an intrusion?
  7. What should a backup strategy cover besides the primary database? Name five things for TaskFlow.
  8. How do you keep encrypted backups recoverable if the production account is lost?

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does mongodump --uri="$MONGODB_URI" --readPreference=secondary --oplog --archive --gzip Consistent dump to stdout, for aws s3 cp - mongorestore --uri="$RESTORE_URI" --archive --gzip --oplogReplay --drop Restore into a scratch cluster, replaying the dump's oplog mongorestore ... --nsFrom="taskflow.tasks" --nsTo="recovery.tasks_20261112" Restore one collection side by side, under a new name pbm config --set pitr.enabled=true, then pbm restore --time="2026-11-10T14:30:59" Percona Backup for MongoDB: continuous oplog capture, then PITR pg_dump --format=directory --jobs=4 --file=<dir> "$DATABASE_URL" Parallel, compressed PostgreSQL dump pg_dumpall --globals-only Dump roles, which pg_dump leaves out pg_restore --jobs=4 ... --dbname="$SCRATCH_DATABASE_URL" <dir> Restore a dump in parallel pg_basebackup --pgdata=<dir> --wal-method=stream --checkpoint=fast Physical base backup for PITR aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time ... --restore-time 2026-11-10T14:30:59Z RDS PITR into a new instance restic forget --tag uploads --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 4 --keep-monthly 12 --prune GFS retention for file backups restic check --read-data-subset=5% Read back and verify 5% of the data

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# postgresql.conf on the primary: archive every completed WAL segment
wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'test ! -f /mnt/wal-archive/%f && cp %p /mnt/wal-archive/%f'
archive_timeout = 300   # switch segments at least every 5 min (bounds the RPO)

# postgresql.conf on the restore server (plus an empty recovery.signal file)
restore_command = 'cp /mnt/wal-archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-10 14:30:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A small database (up to tens of GB) Nightly logical dumps plus continuous log capture, copied offsite Portable; restores one collection or table A large database Physical or snapshot backups with PITR (pgBackRest, WAL-G, Percona Backup for MongoDB) Logical restores reinsert every record and rebuild every index A managed database (Atlas, RDS) Its backups and PITR, plus cross-region or cross-account copies you control Defaults may not meet your RPO, RTO, and isolation needs Files in object storage Versioning plus a copy in another account with Object Lock Replication alone copies deletions Ransomware resilience 3-2-1-1-0 Attackers look for backups first A major-version or platform migration Logical dump and restore Physical backups are tied to the same engine and major version Recovery of one deleted collection or table Restore to a scratch instance, then copy the records back Never restore over production DR with hours of tolerable downtime Backup and restore, rebuilt with IaC Lowest cost An RTO under an hour Pilot light or warm standby Data is already replicated to the DR region Near-zero downtime Multi-site active/active, plus point-in-time backups Highest cost; replication still copies corruption

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value 3-2-1-1-0 3 copies, 2 types of storage, 1 offsite, 1 immutable or offline, 0 errors in restore tests GFS retention Daily for 7 to 14 days, weekly for 4 to 5 weeks, monthly for 12 months or more Achieved RPO Time since the last recoverable copy (backup interval, or replication lag) Achieved RTO Detect + decide + provision + restore + verify + switch traffic Nightly backups only Worst-case RPO about 24 h DR strategies Backup and restore: hours; pilot light: tens of minutes; warm standby: minutes; active/active: near zero archive_timeout = 300 At most about 5 min of PostgreSQL commits at risk RDS automated backups Daily snapshot plus logs about every 5 min; PITR within a retention of 1 to 35 days AWS KMS key deletion 7 to 30 day waiting period; alert on scheduled deletions S3 Object Lock Compliance mode: nobody, not even root, can shorten retention or delete; governance mode: specially permitted users can; needs versioning Failover DNS TTL About 60 s, set before the disaster Restore tests Automated weekly for tier 0 and 1 (daily for the most critical); regional failover drill at least yearly

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating replication, RAID, or high availability as a backup. They copy deletions and corruption; keep point-in-time backups as well.
  • Keeping every copy in one account, region, or set of credentials. Copy into a separate backup account with Object Lock.
  • Backing up only the database. Include files, secrets and keys, configuration, IaC state, images, and runbooks.
  • Running mongodump without --oplog on a busy replica set. Dump with --oplog and restore with --oplogReplay.
  • Never testing restores, or only checking that files exist. Restore to scratch on a schedule, validate counts and invariants, and time it.
  • Restoring over production. Restore side by side into a new instance, then copy back or switch.
  • Retention shorter than the time to notice damage. Keep some copies for months; intruders can wait weeks before encrypting.
  • Encrypting backups with a key stored next to them. Keep keys separate, back them up, and alert on scheduled key deletions.

docs.title: Database Backups and Point-in-Time Recovery
docs.text: Databases are the hardest thing to back up well: they change constantly, they must be captured in a consistent state, they are often large, and the backup itself puts load on the system users depend on. This lesson compares logical and physical backups, shows mongodump/mongorestore (with the oplog and its caveats) and pg_dump/pg_restore, explains what makes a backup consistent, how point-in-time recovery works by replaying the MongoDB oplog or the PostgreSQL write-ahead log on top of a base backup, what managed services such as MongoDB Atlas and Amazon RDS do for you, and why backups are usually taken from a replica rather than the primary.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A nightly backup gives you yesterday's database. If a bad migration runs at 14:31, restoring last night's backup throws away fourteen hours of every user's work. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) lets you restore to 14:30:59 instead, losing almost nothing that happened before the mistake. Without it, the choice during an incident is between living with corrupted data and losing a day.

How you back up also decides how long a restore takes. A logical dump of a 500 GB database can take many hours to restore because every document is reinserted and every index rebuilt, which may exceed the recovery time the business can accept. Choosing the method is therefore a decision about RPO and RTO, not just about tools.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• MongoDB. The manual's backup methods page compares MongoDB Atlas backups, Ops Manager, filesystem snapshots, and mongodump, and notes that mongodump and mongorestore suit small deployments, while larger systems use snapshot-based methods.
  • PostgreSQL. The documentation chapter Continuous Archiving and Point-in-Time Recovery explains combining a file-system-level base backup with archived WAL files to restore to any moment since the base backup.
  • Amazon RDS. The guide to restoring to a specified time describes how RDS uses automated backups and archived transaction logs to restore to any second within the retention period, creating a new DB instance.
  • GitLab (2017). The postmortem of its database outage lists investigating point-in-time recovery with continuous WAL archiving among its action items, after restoring from a six-hour-old snapshot.

Popular tools and providers: mongodump/mongorestore, MongoDB Atlas Cloud Backup, Percona Backup for MongoDB, MongoDB Ops Manager, pg_dump/pg_restore, pg_basebackup, pgBackRest, Barman, WAL-G, Amazon RDS and Aurora backups, Google Cloud SQL backups, and EBS or persistent disk snapshots.

docs.title: Logical and physical backups
docs.text:
• A logical backup asks the database for its data and writes it in a portable format: BSON for mongodump, SQL or a custom archive for pg_dump. It can be restored into a different version or platform, and you can restore a single collection or table. It is slow for large data, and the restore must reinsert every record and rebuild every index.
  • A physical backup copies the database's files or disk blocks: a volume snapshot, pg_basebackup, or a physical backup tool. It is fast to take (snapshots are often incremental at the block level) and fast to restore (copy files, start the server), but it is tied to the same database engine and major version, and usually restores everything.

Rule of thumb: logical for small databases (up to roughly tens of GB), migrations between versions, and extracting subsets; physical for large production databases where restore time matters. Many teams run both.

docs.title: Consistency
docs.text:
A backup is useful only if it represents a state the database actually had:

  • Point-in-time consistent: every record as of one moment. pg_dump achieves this automatically by running in a single transaction snapshot, so concurrent writes do not appear half-applied.
  • Inconsistent: a dump that reads collections one after another while writes continue. A plain mongodump without --oplog on a busy replica set can capture a task in one collection but not the related record in another collection written a second later.
  • Crash-consistent: a snapshot equivalent to pulling the power plug. Databases with a write-ahead journal recover from this on startup, if the journal is in the same snapshot. For MongoDB with WiredTiger, a snapshot of a single volume holding both data and journal is consistent; if they are on different volumes, or for multi-volume setups, lock writes (db.fsyncLock()) or use a tool that coordinates.
  • Sharded clusters need coordination across shards and the config servers, which is what Atlas, Ops Manager, and Percona Backup for MongoDB provide. mongodump through mongos requires pausing the balancer, cross-shard transactions, and schema changes, and cannot use --oplog.

docs.title: MongoDB logical backups: mongodump and mongorestore
docs.text:
mongodump reads data through the database and writes BSON plus metadata (collection options and index definitions). Important options and caveats from the official documentation:

  • --oplog also captures oplog entries written during the dump, so the result is consistent to the moment the dump finished; restore it with mongorestore --oplogReplay. It requires a full dump of a replica set member: it cannot be combined with --db, --collection, or --query, and cannot be used on a sharded cluster through mongos.
  • A dump with --oplog fails if certain operations run during it, including collection renames, aggregations with $out, mapReduce, and changes to users or roles. Schedule dumps away from such jobs.
  • --readPreference=secondary reads from a secondary instead of the primary.
  • --archive writes one archive (or a stream to stdout, for piping to object storage) and --gzip compresses it.
  • --numParallelCollections (default 4) controls parallelism.
  • Restore into a deployment with the same major version or feature compatibility version as the source.
  • mongorestore rebuilds indexes after inserting data, which is often the slowest part of a large restore. --nsInclude, --nsFrom, and --nsTo restore selected collections, optionally under new names.

docs.title: PostgreSQL logical backups: pg_dump and pg_restore
docs.text:
• pg_dump dumps one database consistently, without blocking normal reads and writes. Formats: plain SQL (-Fp), custom (-Fc, compressed, selective restore), directory (-Fd, supports parallel dump with --jobs), and tar.
  • pg_restore restores custom, directory, and tar dumps, in parallel with --jobs, and can restore single tables (-t).
  • pg_dump does not include cluster-wide objects such as roles; dump them with pg_dumpall --globals-only.

docs.title: Physical backups
docs.text:
• Volume snapshots (EBS, persistent disks) are block-level, incremental after the first, and nearly instant to start. Copy them to another region and account to make them real backups.
  • pg_basebackup copies a running PostgreSQL cluster's data directory over the replication protocol, including the WAL needed to make it consistent (--wal-method=stream). PostgreSQL 17 added incremental base backups (pg_basebackup --incremental with WAL summarization enabled) and pg_combinebackup to merge them.
  • pgBackRest, Barman, and WAL-G manage full, differential, and incremental physical backups, parallelism, compression, encryption, retention, and WAL archiving.
  • Percona Backup for MongoDB offers logical and physical backups and point-in-time recovery for replica sets and sharded clusters.

docs.title: Point-in-time recovery
docs.text:
Every change to a database is first recorded in a log: the write-ahead log (WAL) in PostgreSQL, the oplog in a MongoDB replica set. PITR combines two things:

  1. A base backup (snapshot, pg_basebackup, or dump) taken at a known point.
  2. An unbroken archive of the log from that point onward.

To recover, restore the base backup, then replay the log until a recovery target: a timestamp, a log position, or a named restore point. The database ends up exactly as it was at that moment.

Practical details:

  • The RPO is the unarchived tail of the log. With WAL segments shipped at least every 5 minutes (archive_timeout = 300), at most about 5 minutes of committed data is at risk if the server is destroyed. Managed services quote similar figures (RDS can typically restore to within the last five minutes).
  • The chain must be complete. One missing WAL segment or an oplog gap (for example because the oplog window was shorter than the time between captures) stops replay at that point. Monitor archive failures and the oplog window.
  • Pick the target carefully. Find the exact time of the bad operation from application logs, audit logs, or the oplog itself, and stop just before it.
  • RTO includes replay. Restoring a base backup and replaying two days of log can take much longer than restoring a fresh snapshot; take base backups often enough to keep replay short.
  • Restore next to production, not over it. Recover into a new instance, verify, then either switch traffic or copy the affected records back. This keeps good writes made after the mistake.

docs.title: Managed database backups
docs.text:
MongoDB Atlas provides Cloud Backup (scheduled snapshots with configurable retention, copies to other regions) and Continuous Cloud Backup, which captures the oplog so you can restore to any point within a configured window. Restores go to the same or a different cluster.

Amazon RDS provides:

  • Automated backups: a daily snapshot during the backup window plus transaction logs uploaded about every five minutes, giving PITR to any second within a retention period of 1 to 35 days (0 disables them).
  • Manual snapshots, kept until you delete them.
  • Restores always create a new DB instance with a new endpoint, so the application's connection settings must change (or DNS must point to the new instance).
  • Cross-region automated backup replication and integration with AWS Backup for copies to other accounts.

Managed backups remove most of the mechanics, but not the decisions: retention long enough for slow-to-detect corruption, copies outside the account and region, protection against someone deleting the instance and its backups, and restore tests that measure the real RTO.

docs.title: Backing up a replica, not the primary
docs.text:
Backups read a lot of data. On the primary, that competes with application traffic for disk I/O, CPU, and memory, and a full scan from mongodump evicts the application's hot data from the WiredTiger cache. Common practice:

  • Take backups from a secondary, or better, a hidden member (hidden: true, priority: 0) that applications never read from and that can never become primary.
  • Remember that a replica can lag. A backup from a member that is 10 minutes behind is 10 minutes older than you think; check replication lag before and during backups.
  • A delayed member (secondaryDelaySecs) that stays, say, an hour behind gives a fast way to recover data from a mistake noticed within the hour. It is a convenience, not a backup: it is in the same cluster, the same account, and eventually applies every mistake.
  • PostgreSQL can take pg_basebackup from a standby; WAL archiving can also be done from a standby.

docs.title: Backup windows and impact
docs.text:
• Schedule heavy backups at low traffic, and measure their duration as data grows: a nightly dump that took 40 minutes a year ago may now run into business hours.
  • Throttle where tools allow (parallelism, bandwidth limits) and watch latency during backups.
  • Prefer snapshots for large data: copy-on-write snapshots start instantly and run in the storage layer, although the first snapshot of a volume copies every block.
  • Separate concerns: a short RPO comes from continuous log capture, not from running full backups more often.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Database situation Recommended approach TaskFlow on Atlas or another managed service Managed snapshots plus continuous backup (PITR), copies to another region, restore tests Self-managed MongoDB replica set, under tens of GB mongodump --oplog from a hidden member plus oplog capture, or Percona Backup for MongoDB Self-managed MongoDB, large or sharded Coordinated snapshot-based backups with PITR (Percona Backup for MongoDB, Ops Manager) PostgreSQL, small pg_dump nightly plus WAL archiving for PITR PostgreSQL, large pgBackRest, Barman, or WAL-G with physical base backups and WAL archiving Migrating to a new major version or platform Logical dump and restore (or logical replication) Recovering one deleted collection or table Restore a backup to a scratch instance, then copy the records back

Do not use logical dumps as the only backup for a large database whose restore time would exceed the RTO, and do not rely on replicas or delayed members instead of backups.

docs.title: MongoDB: a hidden backup member
docs.text:
// mongosh, connected to the primary: add a member used only for backups
rs.add({
  host: "mongo-backup-1.internal.example.com:27017",
  priority: 0, // can never become primary
  hidden: true, // invisible to application drivers
});

// Optional: a delayed member that stays one hour behind the primary
rs.add({
  host: "mongo-delayed-1.internal.example.com:27017",
  priority: 0,
  hidden: true,
  secondaryDelaySecs: 3600,
});

rs.printSecondaryReplicationInfo(); // check how far behind each member is

docs.title: MongoDB: dump with the oplog and restore selectively
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/mongo-backup.sh: consistent nightly dump from the hidden member
set -euo pipefail
STAMP="$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H%M%SZ)"

mongodump \
  --uri="mongodb://backup-user@mongo-backup-1.internal.example.com:27017/?authSource=admin&directConnection=true" \
  --oplog --archive="/var/backups/taskflow-${STAMP}.archive.gz" --gzip

aws s3 cp "/var/backups/taskflow-${STAMP}.archive.gz" \
  "s3://taskflow-backups-example/mongodb/taskflow-${STAMP}.archive.gz"

# Reached only if both commands succeeded: do not let local dumps fill the disk
rm -f "/var/backups/taskflow-${STAMP}.archive.gz"

# Full restore into a scratch deployment, replaying the oplog captured during the dump
mongorestore --uri="$SCRATCH_URI" --archive=taskflow-2026-11-12T020000Z.archive.gz \
  --gzip --oplogReplay --drop

# Selective restore: only the tasks collection, under a new name, for comparison and repair
mongorestore --uri="$SCRATCH_URI" --archive=taskflow-2026-11-12T020000Z.archive.gz --gzip \
  --nsInclude="taskflow.tasks" --nsFrom="taskflow.tasks" --nsTo="recovery.tasks_20261112"

Run the script from a systemd timer with failure alerts rather than a bare crontab line; the timer, overlap protection, and OnFailure= notification are shown in scheduled jobs and log rotation. The backup user only needs the built-in backup role, and the restore user the restore role. The connection string's password comes from the environment or a secrets manager (here the URI omits it). Restoring selectively into a new namespace lets you copy back only the deleted documents with an aggregation or a script, instead of overwriting the whole collection.

docs.title: MongoDB: point-in-time recovery with Percona Backup for MongoDB
docs.text:
# Enable continuous oplog capture (PITR) alongside scheduled backups
pbm config --set pitr.enabled=true
pbm backup --type=physical     # or logical (the default)
pbm list                       # shows backups and the PITR time ranges available

# Restore the cluster to just before the bad migration
pbm restore --time="2026-11-10T14:30:59"

On Atlas the same operation is a point-in-time restore from the Backup page, CLI, or Admin API, targeting a timestamp within the continuous backup window.

docs.title: PostgreSQL: logical backups
docs.text:
# Parallel, compressed directory-format dump of one database
pg_dump --format=directory --jobs=4 --file=/var/backups/taskflow-2026-11-12 "$DATABASE_URL"

# Roles and other cluster-wide objects are not in pg_dump; dump them separately
pg_dumpall --globals-only --file=/var/backups/globals-2026-11-12.sql

# Parallel restore into a scratch database
pg_restore --jobs=4 --clean --if-exists --no-owner \
  --dbname="$SCRATCH_DATABASE_URL" /var/backups/taskflow-2026-11-12

docs.title: PostgreSQL: continuous archiving and PITR
docs.text:
# postgresql.conf on the primary: archive every completed WAL segment
wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'test ! -f /mnt/wal-archive/%f && cp %p /mnt/wal-archive/%f'
archive_timeout = 300   # force a segment switch at least every 5 minutes (bounds the RPO)

# Base backup, streaming the WAL needed to make it consistent
pg_basebackup --pgdata=/var/backups/base-2026-11-09 --format=plain \
  --wal-method=stream --checkpoint=fast --progress

# postgresql.conf on the restore server (data directory copied from the base backup)
restore_command = 'cp /mnt/wal-archive/%f %p'
recovery_target_time = '2026-11-10 14:30:59+00'
recovery_target_action = 'promote'

# Ask PostgreSQL to enter targeted recovery on startup, then start it
touch "$PGDATA/recovery.signal"
pg_ctl -D "$PGDATA" start
# The log shows WAL being replayed and "recovery stopping before commit of transaction ..."

The archive_command shown is the documentation's simple example; in production use a tool such as pgBackRest or WAL-G that copies WAL to object storage, verifies it, and handles retention.

docs.title: Amazon RDS: restore to a point in time
docs.text:
# How far forward can we restore?
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier taskflow-prod \
  --query 'DBInstances[0].LatestRestorableTime'

# Restore into a NEW instance, one second before the bad migration
aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time \
  --source-db-instance-identifier taskflow-prod \
  --target-db-instance-identifier taskflow-restore-20261110 \
  --restore-time 2026-11-10T14:30:59Z \
  --db-subnet-group-name taskflow-private \
  --no-publicly-accessible

aws rds wait db-instance-available --db-instance-identifier taskflow-restore-20261110

Verify the restored instance, then either repoint the application to it or copy the affected rows back to production.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Combine base backups with continuous log capture (oplog or WAL) for point-in-time recovery.
  • Choose logical or physical backups by data size and RTO; test how long a full restore really takes.
  • Make backups consistent: --oplog for mongodump, single-volume or coordinated snapshots, tools that coordinate sharded clusters.
  • Take backups from a hidden secondary or standby, and watch replication lag.
  • Monitor log archiving failures and the oplog window, since a gap breaks PITR.
  • Restore into a new instance and copy data back, rather than restoring over production.
  • Back up roles, users, and configuration alongside data.
  • Keep managed-service backups, but add cross-region or cross-account copies and retention that matches your detection time.
  • Record the backup window duration and its impact on latency, and revisit as data grows.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• PITR stops hours short of the target time. Detect: PostgreSQL stops with "recovery ended before configured recovery target was reached", or the oplog capture shows a missing range. Cause: WAL archiving failed for a while (full disk, expired credentials) or the oplog rolled over before it was captured. Fix: alert on archive failures (pg_stat_archiver.failed_count), size the oplog for a long enough window, and take a fresh base backup after any gap.
  • The nightly dump makes the API slow every night. Detect: p99 latency and cache eviction rise during the backup window. Cause: mongodump reads from the primary and evicts the working set from the cache. Fix: dump from a hidden member, throttle parallelism, or switch to snapshots.
  • A restored dump has orphaned or inconsistent references. Detect: tasks reference projects that do not exist in the restored data. Cause: mongodump without --oplog ran while writes continued, so collections were captured at different times. Fix: use --oplog with --oplogReplay, or snapshot-based backups.
  • mongodump --oplog fails intermittently. Detect: the backup job exits with an error about an operation not allowed during the dump. Cause: a $out aggregation, collection rename, or user change ran during the dump. Fix: schedule those jobs outside the backup window, or move to a backup tool that handles them.
  • A restore exceeds the RTO by hours. Detect: a drill shows mongorestore or pg_restore still rebuilding indexes long after data loaded. Cause: a logical backup of a database that has outgrown it. Fix: physical backups for full restores, keep logical dumps for selective recovery, and measure restore time regularly.
  • Restored RDS instance works, but the app still writes to the old one. Detect: writes keep arriving at the damaged instance after the "restore". Cause: PITR creates a new instance with a new endpoint. Fix: include connection switching (DNS name or configuration change) in the runbook, and practise it.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Logical backup: A dump of records through the database (BSON, SQL).
  • Physical backup: A copy of data files or blocks.
  • Base backup: The starting point for point-in-time recovery.
  • Write-ahead log (WAL): PostgreSQL's log of every change, written before data files.
  • Oplog: MongoDB's capped collection recording every write on a replica set.
  • Oplog window: How far back the oplog reaches before old entries are overwritten.
  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR): Restoring a base backup and replaying the log to a chosen moment.
  • Recovery target: The time, log position, or restore point where replay stops.
  • Crash-consistent: Equivalent to a power loss; recoverable with a journal.
  • Hidden member / delayed member: Replica set members not visible to applications, optionally lagging on purpose.
  • Archive timeout: The maximum time before PostgreSQL ships a partly filled WAL segment.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Running mongodump without --oplog on a busy replica set and calling the result consistent.
  • Assuming nightly backups give a small RPO.
  • Never checking that WAL or oplog capture is continuous.
  • Taking backups from the primary during peak hours.
  • Treating a delayed member as a backup.
  • Restoring over production instead of into a new instance.
  • Forgetting roles, users, and configuration when restoring.
  • Assuming a managed service's default retention (often a week) covers corruption discovered a month later.
  • Never measuring how long a full restore takes.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare logical and physical backups on portability, speed, selective restore, and impact.
  2. What does mongodump --oplog do, what are its restrictions, and how is the dump restored?
  3. Why is pg_dump consistent even while the database is being written to?
  4. Explain point-in-time recovery step by step. What breaks it?
  5. With archive_timeout = 300 and WAL shipped to another region, what is the worst-case RPO if the primary's region is lost? (About 5 minutes of committed transactions, plus any archiving backlog.)
  6. A base backup of 400 GB restores at 250 MB/s, and 60 GB of WAL replays at 100 MB/s. Roughly how long is the restore, and how could you shorten it? (1,600 s plus 600 s, about 37 minutes; take base backups more often or use faster storage.)
  7. Why back up from a hidden member, and what should you check about it first?
  8. What changes in your runbook when RDS PITR creates a new instance?
