docs.title: Disaster Recovery, RPO, and RTO
docs.text: Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan and the machinery for bringing a service back after an event that its normal redundancy cannot absorb: a whole region down, a database corrupted, an account compromised, a critical provider gone. It is measured with two numbers: the recovery point objective (RPO), how much data you may lose, and the recovery time objective (RTO), how long you may be down. This lesson defines both with worked examples, shows how a business impact analysis sets them, compares the standard DR strategies (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active/active) by cost and recovery time, and covers regions and availability zones, DNS failover, third-party dependencies, and what a DR plan contains.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Every architecture has a failure that takes everything down at once. For TaskFlow running in one cloud region, that could be a regional outage, an engineer's script that deletes the production database, or ransomware that encrypts every volume the attacker can reach. Without a plan, the response is improvised under maximum pressure: nobody knows which backup to use, whether the infrastructure code still works, who can approve spending on a second region, or how to tell customers.

DR is also a business decision with real money attached. Running a full second copy of production can double infrastructure cost; a plan that needs two days to restore may be unacceptable for a product whose customers run their work on it. RPO and RTO turn that trade-off into explicit, agreed numbers that engineering can design and test against.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• AWS disaster recovery whitepaper. AWS's Disaster recovery options in the cloud describes four strategies (backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and multi-site active/active) in order of increasing cost and complexity and decreasing recovery time, and recommends relying on data plane rather than control plane operations during failover.
  • AWS Well-Architected Framework. The reliability pillar's Plan for disaster recovery (DR) section asks teams to define recovery objectives per workload, use defined recovery strategies, test DR implementations, and manage configuration drift in the DR site.
  • NIST contingency planning. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, the Contingency Planning Guide for Federal Information Systems, defines the business impact analysis and the relationship between maximum tolerable downtime, RTO, and RPO used in many organizations' DR plans.
  • Amazon S3 (2017). Amazon's summary of the S3 service disruption in us-east-1 shows the reach of a single-region dependency: many services in the region depended on S3, and AWS's own status dashboard could not be updated at first because it depended on the failing service.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery, Route 53 health checks and Application Recovery Controller, AWS Global Accelerator, Azure Site Recovery, Google Cloud Backup and DR, MongoDB Atlas multi-region clusters, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, Cloudflare load balancing, and Terraform for rebuilding infrastructure.

docs.title: RPO and RTO
docs.text:
• Recovery point objective (RPO): the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured in time before the disaster. If the RPO is 1 hour, you must always have a recoverable copy no older than 1 hour.
  • Recovery time objective (RTO): the maximum acceptable time from the disaster until the service works again for users.
  • Maximum tolerable downtime (MTD): from the business impact analysis, the point after which the damage becomes unacceptable. The RTO must sit comfortably inside it.

What determines the numbers you actually achieve:

Achieved RPO  ~ time since the last recoverable copy
              = backup interval, or replication/log-shipping lag if data is copied continuously

Achieved RTO  = time to detect + time to decide + time to provision infrastructure
              + time to restore data + time to verify + time to switch traffic

Worked example 1: nightly backups only.

TaskFlow takes a full backup at 02:00 and copies it to another region.
A region outage starts at 17:00.

Data loss: everything written between 02:00 and 17:00 = 15 hours.
Worst case (outage just before 02:00):            nearly 24 hours  -> RPO is 24 h

Restore in the other region:
  detect and decide                          20 min
  terraform apply for network, cluster, app  45 min
  restore 200 GB at 100 MB/s                 ~33 min (2,000 s)
  rebuild indexes, verify, smoke test        30 min
  switch DNS (TTL 60 s) and watch            10 min
  total                                      ~2 h 20 min                -> RTO about 2.5 h

Worked example 2: continuous log shipping to the DR region.

Oplog captured continuously to the DR region with a typical lag of under 1 minute.
Data loss: about 1 minute of writes                                   -> RPO about 1 min
If a database replica is already running in the DR region (pilot light):
  detect and decide 15 min, promote replica 5 min, start app servers from IaC 15 min,
  verify and switch 10 min                                             -> RTO about 45 min

The second design costs more (a running replica, cross-region data transfer), but cuts the RPO from a day to a minute and the RTO by more than half.

docs.title: Business impact analysis
docs.text:
A business impact analysis (BIA) decides the targets instead of letting engineers guess:

  1. List the business functions TaskFlow supports (sign in, create and view tasks, reminders, reports, billing) and the systems each depends on.
  2. Estimate the impact of losing each function over time: lost revenue, contract penalties, regulatory exposure, customer churn, and manual workarounds.
  3. Determine the maximum tolerable downtime and acceptable data loss per function.
  4. Group systems into tiers with RTO and RPO targets, and check that dependencies have targets at least as strict as what depends on them.
Tier TaskFlow functions RTO RPO Implied strategy 0 Authentication, task create/read/update 1 hour 5 minutes Pilot light or warm standby with continuous replication 1 Reminders and notifications 4 hours 1 hour Backup and restore with frequent snapshots, or pilot light 2 Reports and analytics 24 hours 24 hours Backup and restore, or rebuild from source data 3 Internal admin tools 72 hours 24 hours Backup and restore

docs.title: Disaster scenarios differ
docs.text:
"Disaster" is not one event, and each needs a different mechanism:

Scenario What helps What does not Single server or disk failure Redundancy, replicas, auto-healing DR plan (overkill) Data center (availability zone) failure Multi-AZ deployment and database replicas Single-AZ backups only Whole region unavailable Data and capacity in another region (any DR strategy) Multi-AZ alone Data corruption or accidental deletion Point-in-time backups Replication (copies the damage) Ransomware or account compromise Immutable backups in a separate account, rebuildable infrastructure Anything the attacker's credentials can reach Provider or critical SaaS outage Fallbacks, alternative providers, graceful degradation More replicas with the same provider

A design that is excellent against a region outage (active/active replication) can be useless against corruption, which replicates to every region within seconds. Every DR strategy still needs point-in-time backups.

docs.title: DR strategies
docs.text:
Strategy What runs in the DR region Typical RPO / RTO (AWS whitepaper characterization) Relative cost TaskFlow example Backup and restore Only backups (and IaC to rebuild) Hours Lowest Snapshots copied cross-region; terraform apply builds everything on demand Pilot light Live data replication; core infrastructure defined, compute switched off Tens of minutes Low MongoDB replica in the DR region; API autoscaling group at 0 instances Warm standby A complete, scaled-down, working copy Minutes Medium Two small API instances running against the DR replica, scaled up on failover Multi-site active/active Full production in two or more regions, all serving users Near zero (real time) Highest Users routed to the nearest region; multi-region database with conflict handling

Notes that matter in practice:

  • Backup and restore depends entirely on infrastructure as code. If the network, cluster, and services cannot be recreated by a tested pipeline, restoring data alone does not bring the service back (see infrastructure as code).
  • Pilot light versus warm standby: pilot light cannot serve requests until servers are started; warm standby can serve immediately at reduced capacity and only needs to scale up.
  • Active/active removes failover as an event but adds the hardest problem: writes in several regions. Options include routing all writes to one region (with fast promotion of another), partitioning writes by user, or databases with multi-region writes and conflict resolution.
  • Capacity and quotas: a DR region needs enough service quota and instance capacity to take full production load, verified in advance.
  • Prefer data plane operations for failover. Control planes (APIs that create or reconfigure resources) are more likely to be impaired during a regional event than data planes (serving traffic, health checks), which is why AWS recommends failover mechanisms such as health-check-driven DNS over "create resources during the disaster" where RTO is tight.

docs.title: Regions and availability zones
docs.text:
• An availability zone (AZ) is one or more isolated data centers in a region, with independent power and networking, connected to other AZs in the region by low-latency links. Spreading TaskFlow's instances and database members across three AZs protects against the most common large failures with synchronous-ish replication and no DR process at all.
  • A region is a separate geographic area with its own set of AZs and largely independent control planes. Multi-region designs protect against regional outages and some provider-wide issues, at the cost of cross-region latency (tens of milliseconds or more), asynchronous replication (so a non-zero RPO), data transfer charges, and data residency rules about where personal data may be stored.

Multi-AZ is the default for production; multi-region is a DR decision driven by the BIA.

docs.title: DNS failover
docs.text:
The usual way to move users to the recovery region is DNS:

  • Health-checked failover records (for example Amazon Route 53 failover routing): a primary record is returned while its health check passes, and a secondary record otherwise.
  • TTL matters: resolvers and clients cache answers for the record's TTL, so a 1-hour TTL means up to an hour of users still going to the dead region. DR-critical records use TTLs of 60 seconds or so, set before the disaster. Some clients cache longer than the TTL.
  • Anycast and global load balancers (AWS Global Accelerator, Cloudflare load balancing, Google Cloud's global load balancer) shift traffic without waiting for DNS caches.
  • Automatic or manual? Automatic failover reacts fastest but can fail over on a false alarm, which itself causes data loss (RPO) and downtime. Many teams automate every step but keep the decision to a human, so failover is "one button".
  • Failback is a second migration: the original region's data is now stale, so it must be resynchronized before traffic returns.

docs.title: Dependencies on third parties and shared services
docs.text:
A DR region is useless if the service cannot start there. Check every dependency:

  • Identity and access: can engineers log in to the cloud account and the DR region if single sign-on is down?
  • Secrets and keys: are secrets and KMS keys available in the DR region (multi-region keys, replicated secrets)?
  • Container images and artifacts: is the registry replicated, or does the deploy pull images from the failed region?
  • CI/CD: can you deploy if the CI system or its runners are affected?
  • DNS provider, CDN, email and SMS providers, payment gateways, auth providers: what are their SLAs and their own DR, and does TaskFlow degrade gracefully without them?
  • Monitoring and the status page: are they outside the failed region, so you can see and communicate during the disaster?

docs.title: DR plans
docs.text:
A DR plan is the document people follow when it happens. It contains:

  1. Scope and objectives: systems covered, tiers, RTO and RPO targets.
  2. Scenarios and which strategy applies to each.
  3. Roles and contacts: who can declare a disaster, incident roles, vendor support contacts, escalation paths.
  4. Decision criteria: when to fail over versus wait for the provider, based on expected duration and RPO cost.
  5. Runbooks: step-by-step failover, data restore, verification, and failback procedures (see restore testing and runbooks).
  6. Communication: internal updates, status page, customer messages.
  7. Dependencies and prerequisites: quotas, accounts, keys, images.
  8. Testing schedule and results: when the plan was last exercised and what the measured RTO and RPO were.

Keep the plan versioned, reviewed after every test and architecture change, and available outside the systems it describes (an offline copy, a separate wiki, printed for the most critical steps).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Early-stage product, internal tool, or tolerant users Multi-AZ plus backup and restore to another region; tested yearly Business-critical API with hours of tolerable downtime Backup and restore with fast IaC rebuild, or pilot light for the database Revenue-critical service with an RTO under an hour Pilot light or warm standby with continuous replication and rehearsed failover Global product needing near-zero downtime Multi-site active/active, with point-in-time backups for corruption Regulated workloads Strategy per regulation and BIA, with documented tests and evidence

Do not build active/active for a service whose BIA allows hours of downtime, and do not claim an RTO you have never measured in a drill.

docs.title: An RPO and RTO worksheet
docs.text:
Service: TaskFlow API (tier 0)                Target RTO: 1 h     Target RPO: 5 min

Current design: backup and restore; nightly snapshot copied to the DR region
  Achieved RPO (worst case): 24 h                         FAILS target
  Achieved RTO (last drill):  2 h 40 min                  FAILS target

Proposed design: pilot light
  MongoDB member in the DR region (priority 0) + continuous backup with PITR
  API servers defined in Terraform, scaled to 0; images replicated to the DR registry
  Route 53 failover record, TTL 60 s
  Expected RPO: replication lag, p99 < 30 s                 MEETS target
  Expected RTO: detect 10 + decide 10 + promote 5 + scale API 15 + verify 10 = 50 min   MEETS target
  Added monthly cost: DR database member, cross-region transfer, replicated storage

Decision: approved by <product owner>, <engineering manager>; first drill scheduled <date>

docs.title: Health-checked DNS failover (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/dns-failover.tf
resource "aws_route53_health_check" "api_primary" {
  fqdn              = "api-primary.example.com"
  port              = 443
  type              = "HTTPS"
  resource_path     = "/readyz"
  failure_threshold = 3
  request_interval  = 30
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "api_primary" {
  zone_id         = var.zone_id
  name            = "api.example.com"
  type            = "CNAME"
  ttl             = 60
  set_identifier  = "primary"
  health_check_id = aws_route53_health_check.api_primary.id
  records         = ["api-primary.example.com"]

  failover_routing_policy {
    type = "PRIMARY"
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "api_secondary" {
  zone_id        = var.zone_id
  name           = "api.example.com"
  type           = "CNAME"
  ttl            = 60
  set_identifier = "secondary"
  records        = ["api-dr.example.com"]

  failover_routing_policy {
    type = "SECONDARY"
  }
}

Route 53 returns the primary while its health check (which probes the readiness endpoint from several locations) passes, and the DR endpoint otherwise. The 60-second TTL bounds how long clients keep using a dead answer. In a pilot light setup, the DR endpoint must already be able to serve, or the failover will route users to nothing; many teams therefore make the secondary switch manual until the DR stack is scaled up.

docs.title: A pilot light switch in infrastructure as code
docs.text:
# infra/dr-region/api.tf (applied in the DR region)
variable "dr_active" {
  description = "Set to true during a disaster to bring the API up in this region"
  type        = bool
  default     = false
}

resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "api" {
  name                = "taskflow-api-dr"
  min_size            = var.dr_active ? 3 : 0
  max_size            = var.dr_active ? 12 : 0
  desired_capacity    = var.dr_active ? 3 : 0
  vpc_zone_identifier = var.private_subnet_ids
  target_group_arns   = [aws_lb_target_group.api.arn]

  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.api.id
    version = "$Latest"
  }
}

# Failover step from the runbook: switch the pilot light on
terraform -chdir=infra/dr-region apply -var 'dr_active=true'

The network, load balancer, launch template, and database replica exist all the time; only compute is off. Because this step calls the cloud control plane, practise it and know its duration; a warm standby with instances already running removes this dependency.

docs.title: Promoting a MongoDB member in the DR region
docs.text:
// mongosh, connected to the surviving DR member, ONLY when the primary region is lost
// and a majority of voting members is unreachable (the documented forced reconfiguration).
cfg = rs.conf();
cfg.members = cfg.members.filter((m) => m.host.startsWith("mongo-dr-"));
cfg.members.forEach((m) => { m.priority = 1; m.votes = 1; });
rs.reconfig(cfg, { force: true });

A forced reconfiguration can roll back writes that the lost members had but the DR member had not replicated: that loss is your real RPO. Follow MongoDB's procedure for reconfiguring a replica set with unavailable members, and plan how to rejoin the old region's members afterwards. Managed services such as Atlas multi-region clusters handle elections across regions for you.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run a business impact analysis and agree RTO and RPO per tier with the business, in writing.
  • Use multiple availability zones by default; add multi-region only where the BIA requires it.
  • Keep point-in-time backups in every strategy; replication does not protect against corruption.
  • Make infrastructure fully reproducible from code, including the DR region, and keep it free of drift.
  • Pre-create everything a failover needs: quotas, keys, secrets, images, DNS records with short TTLs.
  • Automate failover steps, keep a human decision for the trigger, and plan failback.
  • Inventory third-party dependencies and their DR posture.
  • Keep the DR plan outside the systems it protects, and test it on a schedule, recording measured RTO and RPO.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Failover worked, but users kept hitting the dead region for an hour. Detect: traffic to the DR endpoint ramps slowly; some resolvers still return the old address. Cause: a long TTL on the API record (for example 3,600 seconds) set before the incident. Fix: lower TTLs on DR-critical records in advance, or use an anycast or global load balancer.
  • The DR region could not start the application. Detect: deployments in the DR region fail pulling images or reading secrets. Cause: the container registry and secrets existed only in the primary region. Fix: replicate images, secrets, and keys, and include "deploy from scratch in the DR region" in drills.
  • Scaling up in the DR region failed with capacity or quota errors. Detect: autoscaling activities fail during a drill. Cause: the DR account or region had default service quotas, or the instance type was scarce. Fix: raise quotas ahead of time, allow several instance types, and keep warm capacity for tier 0 services.
  • More data was lost than the RPO allowed. Detect: after failover, recent orders or tasks are missing beyond the expected window. Cause: replication lag had grown unnoticed (minutes or hours) before the disaster. Fix: alert on replication and log-shipping lag against the RPO, not just on replication being "up".
  • Failback corrupted data. Detect: duplicate or conflicting records after returning to the primary region. Cause: the old primary came back and accepted writes (split brain), or was promoted without resynchronizing. Fix: fence the old primary during failover, resynchronize before failback, and script failback as carefully as failover.
  • The DR plan was out of date when needed. Detect: runbook steps reference services or commands that no longer exist. Cause: the architecture changed and the plan did not. Fix: review the plan in every architecture change and run regular drills.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Disaster recovery (DR): Restoring service after events beyond normal redundancy.
  • RPO (recovery point objective): The maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time.
  • RTO (recovery time objective): The maximum acceptable time to restore service.
  • MTD (maximum tolerable downtime): The outage length beyond which harm is unacceptable.
  • Business impact analysis (BIA): The assessment that sets recovery priorities and objectives.
  • Backup and restore / pilot light / warm standby / active-active: DR strategies of increasing cost and decreasing recovery time.
  • Availability zone: An isolated data center group within a region.
  • Failover / failback: Moving service to the recovery site, and back.
  • Split brain: Two sites both accepting writes as primary.
  • Data plane / control plane: The parts that serve traffic versus the APIs that configure resources.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Setting RTO and RPO without the business, or never writing them down.
  • Believing multi-AZ or replication is a complete DR strategy.
  • Forgetting that active/active still needs backups for corruption.
  • Planning a backup and restore strategy without tested infrastructure as code.
  • Long DNS TTLs on records that must fail over.
  • Ignoring third-party dependencies, secrets, images, and quotas in the DR region.
  • Automatic failover on noisy health checks, causing unnecessary data loss.
  • Never testing failback.
  • Keeping the only copy of the DR plan in the system that just failed.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define RPO, RTO, and MTD, and explain how they relate.
  2. TaskFlow takes backups every 6 hours and copies them to another region. What is the worst-case RPO? If a region fails 4 hours after the last backup, how much data is lost? (6 hours; 4 hours.)
  3. A restore needs 15 minutes to decide, 40 minutes to rebuild infrastructure, 300 GB of data at 150 MB/s, 20 minutes to verify, and 5 minutes to switch DNS. What RTO can you claim? (300 GB at 150 MB/s is 2,000 s, about 33 minutes; total about 1 h 53 min.)
  4. Compare backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, and active/active by cost, RPO, and RTO.
  5. Why does active/active not remove the need for point-in-time backups?
  6. What is the difference between an availability zone failure and a region failure, and which strategies cover each?
  7. Why should DR-critical DNS records have short TTLs, and what are the alternatives?
  8. List five dependencies that could stop TaskFlow from starting in its DR region.

docs.text:
• AWS whitepaper: Disaster Recovery of Workloads on AWS
  • AWS whitepaper: Business continuity plan and objectives
  • Amazon Route 53: DNS failover
  • MongoDB: Reconfigure a replica set with unavailable members
  • NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: Contingency Planning Guide

docs.title: Backups Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review backup fundamentals and strategies, database backups and point-in-time recovery, disaster recovery with RPO and RTO, and restore testing and runbooks. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between a backup, replication, and a snapshot?
docs.text: A backup is an independent, point-in-time copy kept for a retention period so you can restore after loss or corruption. Replication keeps a continuously updated copy for availability and fast failover. A snapshot is a point-in-time image of a volume or database, which becomes a backup only when copied somewhere independent with its own retention.

docs.title: 2. Why is replication not a backup?
docs.text: Replication copies every change, including mistakes and attacks, within seconds. A dropped collection, a bad migration, or ransomware encryption reaches every replica. Only a copy from before the event, kept independently, lets you recover.

docs.title: 3. Compare full, incremental, and differential backups.
docs.text: A full copies everything. An incremental copies changes since the previous backup of any kind, so it is small but a restore needs the full plus every incremental in order. A differential copies changes since the last full, so it grows each day but a restore needs only the full and the latest differential.

docs.title: 4. With 500 GB of data and 25 GB of daily changes, how much does a week of each scheme store?
docs.text: Daily fulls: 7 x 500 = 3,500 GB. Incremental: 500 + 6 x 25 = 650 GB. Differential: 500 + (25 + 50 + 75 + 100 + 125 + 150) = 1,025 GB, assuming each day changes different data. Restoring Saturday needs 1, 7, and 2 pieces respectively.

docs.title: 5. What is a synthetic full backup?
docs.text: A full backup assembled on the backup system from the previous full and later incrementals, without reading the production source again. It keeps restore chains short while preserving the low production impact of incrementals.

docs.title: 6. What is the 3-2-1 rule, and what does 3-2-1-1-0 add?
docs.text: Keep 3 copies of the data (production plus 2 backups), on 2 different storage types, with 1 copy offsite. 3-2-1-1-0 adds 1 immutable or offline copy that cannot be changed or deleted, and 0 errors, proven by verified restore tests.

docs.title: 7. How do immutable backups protect against ransomware?
docs.text: Write-once storage such as S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, or a locked backup vault, prevents anyone, including administrators and the root account, from deleting or overwriting backups before their retention expires. Combined with a separate account and credentials, an attacker who takes over production cannot destroy the recovery path.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between S3 Object Lock governance and compliance modes?
docs.text: In governance mode, users with a special permission can shorten retention or delete locked versions; in compliance mode nobody can, until the retention date passes. Governance suits testing and internal controls; compliance suits backups that must survive account compromise. Object Lock requires bucket versioning.

docs.title: 9. How should backups be encrypted, and what is the key risk?
docs.text: Encrypt at rest (server-side with a KMS key or client-side before upload) and in transit, with keys kept separately from the backups and protected by restrictive policies. The risk is losing the key: if it is deleted or inaccessible, every backup encrypted with it is permanently unreadable.

docs.title: 10. What is grandfather-father-son retention?
docs.text: A schedule with daily backups (sons) kept for about a week, weekly backups (fathers) kept for about a month, and monthly backups (grandfathers) kept for a year or more. About 23 restore points cover a year, fine-grained for recent data and coarse for old data.

docs.title: 11. How do you choose a retention period?
docs.text: From how long it takes to discover corruption or an intrusion (often weeks), legal and contractual requirements, privacy rules that limit how long personal data may be kept, and cost. Retention shorter than detection time means every backup already contains the damage.

docs.title: 12. What besides the database should be backed up?
docs.text: Object storage (uploaded files), secrets and encryption keys, configuration, infrastructure-as-code state, source code mirrors, container images or the ability to rebuild them, logs needed for audits, and runbooks. Caches and search indexes can be rebuilt instead, if the rebuild is documented and fits the RTO.

docs.title: 13. Why is object storage replication not enough to protect uploaded files?
docs.text: Replication propagates deletions and overwrites. Use versioning so old versions survive, and copy objects to another account with Object Lock or backup retention, so a mistake or attacker in the source account cannot remove every copy.

docs.title: 14. How do backups interact with privacy rules such as the right to erasure?
docs.text: Rewriting every backup to delete one person's data is usually impractical and, with immutable storage, impossible. Common practice is short, documented retention so deleted data expires with the backups, never restoring deleted records into production (re-applying deletions after a restore), and per-tenant or per-user encryption keys whose destruction makes old copies unreadable (crypto-shredding).

docs.title: 15. Compare logical and physical database backups.
docs.text: Logical backups (mongodump, pg_dump) read records through the database into portable files; they allow selective restores and version migrations but are slow for large data and slow to restore because indexes are rebuilt. Physical backups (snapshots, pg_basebackup) copy files or blocks; they are fast to take and restore but tied to the same engine and version, usually restoring everything.

docs.title: 16. What makes a database backup consistent?
docs.text: It represents a state the database actually had at one moment. pg_dump runs in a single transaction snapshot. mongodump --oplog captures oplog entries during the dump and replays them on restore. Snapshots are crash-consistent if the journal is on the same volume; multi-volume and sharded setups need locks or coordinated tools.

docs.title: 17. What does mongodump --oplog do, and what are its limits?
docs.text: It records oplog entries written during the dump so mongorestore --oplogReplay brings the restore to a single consistent point. It needs a full dump of a replica set member, cannot be combined with --db, --collection, or --query, is not supported through mongos on sharded clusters, and fails if operations such as collection renames, $out aggregations, or user changes run during the dump.

docs.title: 18. How do pg_dump formats differ?
docs.text: Plain (-Fp) is a SQL script; custom (-Fc) is compressed and allows selective restore with pg_restore; directory (-Fd) also allows parallel dumps with --jobs; tar is another archive format. Roles and other cluster-wide objects need pg_dumpall --globals-only.

docs.title: 19. Explain point-in-time recovery.
docs.text: Restore a base backup, then replay the database's change log (PostgreSQL WAL or the MongoDB oplog) up to a chosen recovery target: a timestamp, log position, or named restore point. It requires an unbroken log archive from the base backup to the target.

docs.title: 20. What determines the RPO of a PITR setup?
docs.text: How much committed log has not yet been archived when the disaster hits: for PostgreSQL, bounded by archive_timeout and archiving speed; for MongoDB, by how continuously the oplog is captured. Gaps in the archive or an oplog window shorter than the capture interval break recovery entirely after the gap.

docs.title: 21. Why restore into a new instance rather than over production?
docs.text: It keeps the damaged system available for investigation, lets you verify the restore before committing, and allows copying back only the affected records, preserving good writes made after the recovery target. Restoring in place can destroy data you still need.

docs.title: 22. What do managed services such as Atlas and RDS provide, and what remains your job?
docs.text: They take scheduled snapshots and capture logs for point-in-time restore within a retention window (RDS: 1 to 35 days, with restores creating a new instance). You still choose retention, copy backups to other regions and accounts, protect against deletion of the instance and its backups, and test restores and connection switching.

docs.title: 23. Why back up from a replica, and which kind?
docs.text: Backups read a lot of data and evict the working set from cache; on the primary they slow user traffic. A hidden MongoDB member (priority 0, hidden) or a PostgreSQL standby serves backups without application load. Check replication lag, because the backup is only as fresh as the replica.

docs.title: 24. Is a delayed replica a backup?
docs.text: No. A delayed member that stays an hour behind is a convenient way to recover from a mistake noticed within that hour, but it lives in the same cluster and account and eventually applies every change, including the mistake. It complements backups.

docs.title: 25. Why might a logical backup be the wrong choice for a large database?
docs.text: Restoring requires reinserting every document and rebuilding every index, which can take many hours for hundreds of gigabytes and exceed the RTO. Physical or snapshot-based backups restore by copying files and starting the server.

docs.title: 26. How do you back up a sharded MongoDB cluster?
docs.text: Use a tool that coordinates a consistent point across every shard and the config servers: Atlas Cloud Backup, Ops Manager, or Percona Backup for MongoDB. mongodump through mongos needs the balancer, cross-shard transactions, and schema changes paused, cannot use --oplog, and is not a sound production backup strategy for sharded clusters.

docs.title: 27. Define RPO and RTO.
docs.text: RPO (recovery point objective) is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time before the disaster. RTO (recovery time objective) is the maximum acceptable time from the disaster until the service works again. Both must fit within the maximum tolerable downtime from the business impact analysis.

docs.title: 28. Backups run every 6 hours. What is the worst-case RPO?
docs.text: Six hours (plus any copy delay): a disaster just before the next backup loses almost everything since the previous one. Continuous log capture is the way to get an RPO of minutes.

docs.title: 29. What makes up the RTO?
docs.text: Time to detect, decide, provision infrastructure, restore data, verify, and switch traffic. Restoring data is often less than half; decision making, access problems, and DNS caching are commonly underestimated.

docs.title: 30. What is a business impact analysis?
docs.text: An assessment of each business function's dependence on systems and the impact of losing it over time (revenue, contracts, regulation, reputation). It sets maximum tolerable downtime and acceptable data loss, which become RTO and RPO targets per tier.

docs.title: 31. Describe the four DR strategies.
docs.text: Backup and restore keeps only backups and rebuilds everything (hours). Pilot light replicates data live and keeps core infrastructure ready but compute switched off (tens of minutes). Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy (minutes). Multi-site active/active serves users from several regions (near zero), at the highest cost and complexity.

docs.title: 32. What is the difference between pilot light and warm standby?
docs.text: Pilot light cannot serve requests until servers are started and scaled; warm standby can serve immediately at reduced capacity and only needs to scale up. Warm standby costs more and recovers faster.

docs.title: 33. Does active/active remove the need for backups?
docs.text: No. It protects against losing a region, but corruption, accidental deletion, and ransomware replicate to every region. Point-in-time backups are still required, and data recovery from them still has a non-zero RPO.

docs.title: 34. How do availability zones and regions differ for DR?
docs.text: Availability zones are isolated data centers within a region with low-latency links, protecting against data center failures; multi-AZ is the production default. Regions are separate geographic areas protecting against regional outages, with asynchronous replication, higher latency, and data residency considerations.

docs.title: 35. How does DNS failover work, and what are its pitfalls?
docs.text: Health-checked DNS returns the primary endpoint while it is healthy and a secondary otherwise. Clients and resolvers cache answers for the TTL, so DR records need short TTLs set in advance; anycast or global load balancers avoid DNS caching. Automatic failover on noisy checks can cause unnecessary data loss, so many teams keep a human decision.

docs.title: 36. Why prefer data plane over control plane operations during failover?
docs.text: Control planes (APIs that create or change resources) are more likely to be impaired during a regional event than data planes (serving traffic, health checks). Failover that only flips health-checked routing is more reliable than one that must create resources at the worst moment.

docs.title: 37. What should a DR plan contain?
docs.text: Scope and objectives, scenarios and strategies, roles and contacts, criteria for declaring a disaster, runbooks for failover, restore, and failback, communication plans, dependencies and prerequisites, and the testing schedule with measured results, stored outside the systems it protects.

docs.title: 38. What third-party dependencies can block recovery in a DR region?
docs.text: Identity and single sign-on, secrets and keys, container registries, CI/CD systems, DNS and CDN providers, email and payment providers, and monitoring and status pages hosted in the failed region.

docs.title: 39. What is the difference between RTO and maximum tolerable downtime?
docs.text: Maximum tolerable downtime, from the business impact analysis, is the outage length beyond which harm becomes unacceptable. The RTO is the engineering target for restoring service and must be shorter, leaving a margin for verification and for things going wrong during recovery.

docs.title: 40. Why is an untested backup not a backup?
docs.text: Backups fail silently: empty or truncated files, version mismatches, missing collections, missing keys or permissions, or restores far slower than the RTO. Only a verified restore proves the backup works.

docs.title: 41. What should an automated restore test verify?
docs.text: That the restore completes without errors, document counts match a manifest recorded at backup time within a tolerance, invariants hold (no orphaned references, required indexes present), the data is fresh (newest record within the RPO), and the application runs against the restored data in a smoke test. It also records the restore duration.

docs.title: 42. What is a backup manifest?
docs.text: Facts recorded when the backup is taken, such as the document count per collection and the newest update timestamp, stored with the backup. The restore test compares the restored data with it to detect missing or stale data.

docs.title: 43. What metrics should you alert on for backups?
docs.text: Backup job failures, the age of the last successful backup, unexpected changes in backup size, the age of the last successful restore test, restore duration against the RTO, and replication or log-shipping lag against the RPO.

docs.title: 44. What is the difference between a tabletop exercise and a DR drill?
docs.text: A tabletop exercise is a discussion that walks through a scenario on paper to find gaps in plans and knowledge, touching no systems. A drill actually performs the restore or failover, following the runbook, and measures the real RTO and RPO.

docs.title: 45. What makes a good runbook?
docs.text: A clear purpose and scope, owner and last-tested date, prerequisites, explicit decision points, numbered steps with copy-pasteable commands and expected output, verification, abort or rollback steps, communication points, and post-steps. It is stored where it is available during an outage and updated after every use.

docs.title: 46. How do you measure the actual RTO and RPO in a drill?
docs.text: Record UTC timestamps at every phase (scenario start, decision, restore complete, verification, traffic switched), sum them for the RTO, and compare the newest restored write with the time of the simulated damage for the RPO. Trend the results across drills.

docs.title: 47. Why should someone other than the runbook author run drills?
docs.text: The author fills gaps from memory without noticing. A different engineer exposes ambiguous steps, missing access, and unwritten knowledge, which is exactly what an on-call engineer will face during a real incident.

docs.title: 48. The nightly backup job has reported success for months, but a restore test finds the archives are empty. What happened, and what do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: the backup script's handling of exit codes and the dump tool's logs and version.

How to confirm: the dump command fails (for example a version mismatch or authentication error) while the script continues and uploads an empty file, as in GitLab's 2017 incident.

Likely causes and fixes: missing set -euo pipefail and exit-code checks, and no size or restore verification. Fail the job on errors, alert on size anomalies and on the age of the last verified restore, and run weekly automated restore tests. See restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: 49. A migration deleted a field from every task at 14:31. Nightly backups ran at 02:00. How do you recover with minimal data loss?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether point-in-time recovery is available (continuous backup in Atlas, PBM PITR, or archived oplog) and the exact time of the migration in UTC.

How to confirm: the PITR window covers 14:30:59, and logs show the migration's start time.

Likely causes and fixes: restore to 14:30:59 into a new cluster, verify, then copy the field values back to production for the affected tasks, keeping good writes made after 14:31. Without PITR, the best option is the 02:00 backup plus manual reconstruction. See database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: 50. Ransomware encrypted production servers, and the attacker also deleted the backup snapshots. How could this have been prevented?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the backups lived and which credentials could delete them.

How to confirm: audit logs show deletions by a production administrator role in the same account.

Likely causes and fixes: backups in the same account with deletable retention. Copy backups to a separate account, enable Object Lock or vault lock in compliance mode, give backup writers no delete permission, keep retention longer than typical intrusion dwell time, and keep an offline copy of critical data. See backup fundamentals and strategies.

docs.title: 51. A restore of the 400 GB MongoDB database took nine hours against a two-hour RTO. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the time went: download, data insertion, or index builds.

How to confirm: the drill timeline shows mongorestore spending most of the time rebuilding indexes after loading data.

Likely causes and fixes: a logical backup used for a database too large for it. Move to snapshot or physical backups for full restores, keep logical dumps for selective recovery, consider warm standby for tier 0, and track restore duration in weekly tests. See database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: 52. Point-in-time recovery stopped three hours short of the target time. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the WAL or oplog archive for gaps around where recovery stopped.

How to confirm: archiving failures (pg_stat_archiver.failed_count rising) or a missing oplog range during that period.

Likely causes and fixes: an archive destination that was full or unreachable, expired credentials, or an oplog window shorter than the capture interval. Alert on archiving failures and lag, size the oplog generously, and take a new base backup after any gap. See database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: 53. After failing over to the DR region, users still reach the dead region for an hour. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the TTL on the API's DNS record and what resolvers return.

How to confirm: the record has a TTL of 3,600 seconds and resolvers still serve the old answer.

Likely causes and fixes: a long TTL set before the incident. Lower TTLs on DR-critical records to about 60 seconds in advance, or use anycast or a global load balancer. See disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: 54. The DR region's infrastructure exists, but the application will not start there during a drill. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: image pulls, secret reads, and key access in the DR region.

How to confirm: pods fail with image pull errors from the primary region's registry, or access denied reading secrets and KMS keys.

Likely causes and fixes: registries, secrets, or keys that exist only in the primary region. Replicate images, secrets, and keys, raise quotas in advance, and include deploying from scratch in the DR region in every drill. See disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: 55. After a regional failover, more data was lost than the 5-minute RPO allowed. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: replication or log-shipping lag to the DR region before the outage.

How to confirm: metrics show lag had grown to 40 minutes days earlier, with no alert.

Likely causes and fixes: monitoring checked that replication was running, not how far behind it was. Alert on lag against the RPO, investigate bandwidth or write-volume growth, and consider stronger write concerns for critical data. See disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: 56. A restored database looks complete, but tasks link to attachments that return 404. What is missing?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the uploads bucket is backed up and at what point in time.

How to confirm: the attachments were deleted from the bucket (or never copied), and only replication protected it.

Likely causes and fixes: object storage outside the backup scope. Enable versioning, copy objects to a separate account with retention, and make restore tests check references between the database and storage. See backup fundamentals and strategies.

docs.title: 57. During an incident, the on-call engineer cannot decrypt the backups. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the state of the KMS key and the restore role's permissions on it.

How to confirm: the key is disabled or pending deletion, or its policy does not allow the restore role.

Likely causes and fixes: key management outside the backup design. Restrict key deletion, alert on scheduled deletions and policy changes, document key ownership, and exercise the restore role and key in every restore test. See backup fundamentals and strategies.

docs.title: 58. The weekly restore test passes, but a real restore last month surprised everyone. Why might the test be misleading?
docs.text:
What to check first: what the test actually verifies and how it differs from the real procedure.

How to confirm: it only checks that the archive exists and decompresses, restores a much smaller staging backup, or skips the application switch and DNS steps.

Likely causes and fixes: verification stopped at a shallow level. Restore the real production backup, validate counts, freshness, and invariants, run a smoke test, time the restore, and run periodic drills that include switching traffic. See restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: 59. The team restored the database to "14:30" but lost an extra hour of data. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the time zone of the recovery target and of the logs used to choose it.

How to confirm: the incident was at 14:31 local time (UTC-1), but the target was interpreted as 14:30 UTC, an hour earlier than intended.

Likely causes and fixes: mixed time zones. Use UTC everywhere, set the target as an explicit variable in the runbook, and verify the newest restored write against the intended target before switching. See restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: 60. Backup storage costs double every few months although the database grows slowly. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: retention settings, lifecycle rules, and whether backups are full or incremental.

How to confirm: old backups and noncurrent object versions are never expired, and every nightly backup is a full copy.

Likely causes and fixes: missing lifecycle expiry and retention policy. Apply GFS retention, expire noncurrent versions, move older backups to cheaper tiers where restore time allows, and use incremental or deduplicating tools. See backup fundamentals and strategies.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Backups overview

docs.title: Restore Testing and Runbooks
docs.text: A backup that has never been restored is an assumption. The only proof that you can recover is a restore that worked recently, produced the right data, and finished within the RTO. This lesson explains why untested backups fail, how to schedule restore tests and verify them automatically (counts, checksums, freshness, and an application smoke test), how to run game days and DR drills, how to write a runbook people can follow under pressure, with a complete restore runbook for TaskFlow's MongoDB database, how to measure the real RTO and RPO in drills, and the restore failures that catch teams most often.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Backup jobs fail in ways that look like success: the job exits 0 but writes an empty file, a version mismatch produces an unusable dump, a new collection is never included, the encryption key is gone, the restore tool needs a version nobody has installed. These are discovered at the worst possible moment, during an incident, when the original data is already lost. GitLab's 2017 postmortem is the well-known example: several backup mechanisms existed, and none worked as expected when needed.

Even when backups are fine, recovery depends on people executing a long, unfamiliar procedure under stress. Restore time in a drill is usually far longer than anyone estimated: downloads are slower, index builds take hours, access is missing, a step is ambiguous. Testing turns these surprises into calm Tuesday-afternoon fixes instead of extended outages.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitLab (2017). The database outage postmortem lists automated testing of database backup recovery and backup monitoring among its improvements, after discovering during the incident that regular backups had not been working.
  • AWS disaster recovery guidance. The whitepaper section Testing disaster recovery and the Well-Architected best practice Test disaster recovery implementation to validate the implementation call for regularly testing failover and restores so you know the strategy works and meets its RTO and RPO.
  • AWS Backup restore testing. AWS Backup offers a restore testing feature that restores recovery points on a schedule, records restore duration, and lets you run validation before the test resources are deleted, a managed form of the pipeline in this lesson.
  • Google SRE. The SRE book's Data Integrity chapter stresses continuously testing the recovery process, and the chapter Accelerating SREs to On-Call and Beyond describes "Wheel of Misfortune" role-play exercises that rehearse incident response before it is needed.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Backup restore testing, MongoDB Atlas restore APIs, Percona Backup for MongoDB, pgBackRest (verify, restore), restic (check), Velero, CI schedulers (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI), AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin, LitmusChaos, and Chaos Mesh for game days.

docs.title: Why untested backups are not backups
docs.text:
Common ways a "successful" backup turns out to be useless:

  • Silent job failures: the script ignores a non-zero exit code, or alert emails go nowhere.
  • Incomplete scope: a new database, collection, bucket, or service was never added to the backup configuration.
  • Corrupted or truncated files: network interruptions, full disks, or storage bugs.
  • Missing keys or credentials: the encryption key or restore role no longer exists.
  • Tool and version drift: the restore needs a specific tool or database version.
  • Too slow: the restore works but takes three times longer than the RTO.
  • Unusable result: data restores, but the application cannot run on it (missing indexes, users, configuration, or migrations).
  • Lost knowledge: the one person who knew the procedure is unavailable.

Only an actual restore, verified against expectations, catches all of these.

docs.title: Levels of verification
docs.text:
Level Check Catches Typical frequency 0 Job exit code and logs Crashes, permission errors Every run 1 Backup exists, size within the expected range Empty or truncated files, missing runs Every run 2 Integrity check (checksums, restic check, pgbackrest verify) Corruption in storage Daily to weekly 3 Restore completes in a scratch environment Tool drift, missing keys or permissions Weekly for tier 0 4 Data validation: counts, checksums, invariants, freshness Incomplete scope, inconsistent dumps, stale data With every restore test 5 Application smoke test on restored data Missing indexes, users, config; schema mismatch With every restore test 6 Full DR drill: failover, traffic, measured RTO and RPO Process, people, and dependency gaps Quarterly to yearly

Levels 0 to 2 are cheap and run every time; levels 3 to 5 are the automated restore test; level 6 is a scheduled drill with people.

docs.title: Automated restore verification
docs.text:
The pipeline's checks, and why each matters:

  • Restore completed: the tool exited cleanly, logged no errors, and rebuilt every index. Restores that "mostly worked" are failures.
  • Counts against a manifest: at backup time, record the document count of every collection (and other facts, such as the newest updatedAt). After restoring, compare. A tolerance allows for writes during the dump; a missing collection or a large drop is a failure.
  • Checksums and invariants: for data that should not change between backup and verification, MongoDB's dbHash command returns a hash per collection; for live data, check invariants instead: every task's projectId exists, no task has a null owner, totals reconcile.
  • Freshness: the newest record should be no older than the RPO before the backup time. A backup of a stale replica passes every other check and still fails this one.
  • Smoke test: start TaskFlow API against the restored data and run a few real requests. This catches missing indexes (timeouts), missing users, and schema mismatches.
  • Timing: record the restore duration every time. It is your evidence for the RTO, and it grows with the data.

Handle the scratch environment as production data: same access controls, encryption, region, and deletion after the test.

docs.title: Game days and DR drills
docs.text:
Automated tests prove the data; drills prove the people and the process. Types, from cheapest to most realistic:

  • Tabletop exercise: the team walks through a scenario on paper ("the primary region is gone; what do we do first?") and finds gaps in knowledge and documentation. No systems are touched.
  • Component restore drill: restore the production database to a point in time in a separate environment, following the runbook, as the on-call engineer would during an incident.
  • Failover drill (game day): fail over a real service to the DR site, in staging or in production during a planned window, and measure the RTO end to end, including DNS, verification, and communication.
  • Chaos experiments: deliberately inject failures (instance loss, network faults) with tools such as AWS Fault Injection Service to verify resilience continuously.

A good drill has a written plan: scenario, hypothesis ("we can restore tier 0 data within 1 hour with less than 5 minutes of data loss"), success criteria, blast radius limits, an abort condition, assigned roles, and observers whose only job is to write down what happens and when. Rotate who executes the runbook; a drill where the author runs it proves little.

docs.title: Runbook structure
docs.text:
A runbook is a step-by-step procedure for a specific operational task, written for someone competent but unfamiliar with this system, at 3 a.m. A useful structure:

  1. Header: purpose, scope, owner, last tested date and result, expected duration.
  2. When to use it: symptoms or decisions that lead here, and when not to.
  3. Prerequisites: access and roles, tools and versions, where credentials live, people to involve.
  4. Decision points: explicit choices (restore to a new cluster or in place? which recovery time?) with guidance.
  5. Steps: numbered, one action each, with copy-pasteable commands and the expected output.
  6. Verification: how to know it worked.
  7. Rollback or abort: how to stop safely at each stage.
  8. Communication: who to update and when.
  9. After the procedure: cleanup, follow-up tickets, postmortem.

Principles: commands use variables declared once at the top; steps are safe to re-run where possible; dangerous steps are marked and require a second person; the runbook lives somewhere available during an outage; and it is updated after every use or drill.

docs.title: Measuring actual RTO and RPO
docs.text:
During a drill or real restore, the scribe records a timestamp at every phase boundary:

Drill: restore TaskFlow MongoDB to a point in time (tier 0, target RTO 60 min, RPO 5 min)

10:00  scenario announced (simulated: bad migration at 09:41)
10:06  decision made: PITR to 09:40:59 into a new cluster              decide:   6 min
10:31  restore finished on the new cluster                              restore: 25 min
10:44  verification passed (counts, invariants, smoke test)             verify:  13 min
10:52  application switched to the new cluster, error rate normal      switch:   8 min
                                                         measured RTO: 52 min  (target 60)
Newest restored write: 09:40:57; bad migration at 09:41:00   measured RPO:  3 s  (target 5 min)
Gaps found: restore role missing on one account (fixed during drill, +4 min); runbook step 7 unclear.

Trend these numbers across drills. A measured RTO that creeps toward the target as data grows is an early warning that the strategy needs to change before a real disaster proves it.

docs.title: Common restore failures
docs.text: Symptom during restore Typical cause Prevention Access denied reading backups Restore role or cross-account permission missing Test the restore role in every drill; least privilege, but exercised Decryption fails KMS key disabled, deleted, or in another account Key policies, deletion alerts, documented key ownership mongorestore errors on version or FCV Restoring into a different major version Pin restore environments to the source version Restore takes hours longer than planned Slow downloads, index rebuilds, cold storage retrieval Measure in drills, keep recent backups in fast storage, prefer physical backups for large data Data restored but app fails Missing users, roles, indexes, config, or secrets Back up and restore those too; smoke test PITR stops early Gap in oplog or WAL archive Monitor archiving and the oplog window Wrong data restored Wrong backup chosen, time zone mistakes in the target time Use UTC everywhere; verification step compares with expectations Restore overwrote good data Restored in place instead of side by side Restore to a new cluster first, then copy back or switch

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Test type Use for Frequency Automated restore verification Every tier 0 and tier 1 data store Weekly (daily for the most critical) Integrity checks All backup repositories Daily or weekly Tabletop exercise New DR plans, new team members, after architecture changes Quarterly Component restore drill Database and storage recovery procedures Monthly to quarterly Regional failover drill Pilot light, warm standby, active/active At least yearly, ideally quarterly Chaos experiments in production Mature teams with good observability and guardrails Continuous, in limited blast radius

Do not run production failover drills without an abort plan, monitoring, and stakeholder notice, and do not let restore tests touch production data stores: they write to scratch environments only.

docs.title: Recording a manifest at backup time
docs.text:
# scripts/mongo-manifest.sh: run right after the dump; stored next to the archive
# STAMP is the same UTC timestamp the backup script used in the archive name
set -euo pipefail
STAMP="${STAMP:?set STAMP to the archive timestamp, e.g. 2026-11-12T020000Z}"
mongosh "$BACKUP_SOURCE_URI" --quiet --eval '
  const tf = db.getSiblingDB("taskflow");
  const counts = {};
  for (const name of tf.getCollectionNames()) {
    counts[name] = tf.getCollection(name).countDocuments({});
  }
  const newest = tf.tasks.find({}, { updatedAt: 1 }).sort({ updatedAt: -1 }).limit(1).toArray()[0];
  print(JSON.stringify({ takenAt: new Date(), counts, newestTaskUpdate: newest?.updatedAt ?? null }));
' > "manifest-${STAMP}.json"
aws s3 cp "manifest-${STAMP}.json" \
  "s3://taskflow-backups-example/mongodb/manifest-${STAMP}.json"

docs.title: An automated restore test
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/restore-test.sh: restore the latest backup into a scratch MongoDB and verify it
set -euo pipefail
START=$(date +%s)
BUCKET="s3://taskflow-backups-example/mongodb"
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'docker rm -f restore-test >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT

# 1. Fetch the newest archive and its manifest (read-only role in the backup account)
LATEST=$(aws s3 ls "$BUCKET/" | awk '{print $4}' | grep '\.archive\.gz$' | sort | tail -n 1)
STAMP="${LATEST#taskflow-}"; STAMP="${STAMP%.archive.gz}"
aws s3 cp "$BUCKET/$LATEST" "$WORK/backup.archive.gz"
aws s3 cp "$BUCKET/manifest-${STAMP}.json" "$WORK/manifest.json"

# 2. Restore into a throwaway MongoDB pinned to the production major version
docker run -d --name restore-test -p 27018:27017 mongo:8.0 >/dev/null
until mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27018" --quiet --eval 'db.runCommand({ ping: 1 }).ok' >/dev/null 2>&1; do sleep 2; done
mongorestore --uri="mongodb://localhost:27018" --archive="$WORK/backup.archive.gz" --gzip --oplogReplay
RESTORE_SECONDS=$(( $(date +%s) - START ))

# 3. Verify counts, freshness, and invariants against the manifest
MANIFEST="$(cat "$WORK/manifest.json")" MAX_AGE_SECONDS=$(( 26 * 3600 )) \
  mongosh "mongodb://localhost:27018" --quiet --file scripts/verify-restore.js

# 4. Smoke test: run the API image against the restored data
docker run --rm --network host \
  -e MONGODB_URI="mongodb://localhost:27018/taskflow" -e NODE_ENV=restore-test \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:current npm run smoke-test

# 5. Report success and timing (picked up by Prometheus via the Pushgateway)
cat <<EOF | curl --fail --silent --data-binary @- \
  "http://pushgateway.monitoring.internal.example.com:9091/metrics/job/taskflow_restore_test"
# TYPE taskflow_last_successful_restore_timestamp_seconds gauge
taskflow_last_successful_restore_timestamp_seconds $(date +%s)
# TYPE taskflow_restore_duration_seconds gauge
taskflow_restore_duration_seconds ${RESTORE_SECONDS}
EOF
echo "restore test passed in ${RESTORE_SECONDS}s"

// scripts/verify-restore.js: run by mongosh against the restored database
const manifest = JSON.parse(process.env.MANIFEST);
const maxAge = Number(process.env.MAX_AGE_SECONDS);
const tf = db.getSiblingDB("taskflow");
const failures = [];

// Counts: every collection present, within 0.5% of the manifest
for (const [name, expected] of Object.entries(manifest.counts)) {
  const actual = tf.getCollection(name).countDocuments({});
  const drift = expected === 0 ? actual : Math.abs(actual - expected) / expected;
  if (drift > 0.005) failures.push(`${name}: expected ~${expected}, got ${actual}`);
}

// Freshness: newest task update close to the backup time
const newest = tf.tasks.find({}, { updatedAt: 1 }).sort({ updatedAt: -1 }).limit(1).toArray()[0];
const ageSeconds = (new Date(manifest.takenAt) - newest.updatedAt) / 1000;
if (ageSeconds > maxAge) failures.push(`data is ${ageSeconds}s older than the backup time`);

// Invariants: no orphaned tasks, required indexes present
const orphans = tf.tasks.aggregate([
  { $lookup: { from: "projects", localField: "projectId", foreignField: "_id", as: "p" } },
  { $match: { p: { $size: 0 } } },
  { $count: "n" },
]).toArray()[0]?.n ?? 0;
if (orphans > 0) failures.push(`${orphans} tasks reference missing projects`);
const indexNames = tf.tasks.getIndexes().map((i) => i.name);
if (!indexNames.includes("userId_1_dueAt_1")) failures.push("index userId_1_dueAt_1 missing");

if (failures.length) {
  print("RESTORE VERIFICATION FAILED:\n- " + failures.join("\n- "));
  quit(1);
}
print("restore verification passed");

# .github/workflows/restore-test.yml
name: weekly-restore-test
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 6 * * 1" # Mondays 06:00 UTC
  workflow_dispatch: {}
permissions:
  id-token: write # OIDC to assume the read-only restore-test role
  contents: read
jobs:
  restore-test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 120
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::<backup-account-id>:role/taskflow-restore-test
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - name: Restore and verify the latest backup
        run: ./scripts/restore-test.sh

The script assumes mongosh, mongorestore, and Docker are available on the runner (install them in an earlier step or use a prepared image), and the API image provides a smoke-test script. An alert fires when time() - taskflow_last_successful_restore_timestamp_seconds exceeds 8 days, so a broken pipeline is noticed even if nobody reads its logs, and a dashboard shows taskflow_restore_duration_seconds against the RTO.

docs.title: A restore runbook for TaskFlow's MongoDB
docs.text:
RUNBOOK: Restore TaskFlow MongoDB after data loss or corruption
Owner: tasks-team        Last tested: <date> (drill, measured RTO 52 min)     Expected duration: 45-75 min
Severity: SEV1/SEV2      Requires: incident commander + one operator + second person for step 8

WHEN TO USE
- Data was deleted or corrupted (bad migration, script, bug), or the cluster is unrecoverable.
- NOT for a single failed node or a primary election: the replica set handles those.

PREREQUISITES
- Roles: backup-restore role in the backup account; Atlas project owner (or PBM operator access).
- Tools: mongosh and MongoDB Database Tools matching the cluster's major version.
- Decide the recovery target time in UTC from logs/audit trail. Write it in the incident channel.

VARIABLES (set once)
  export TARGET_TIME="2026-11-10T14:30:59Z"     # one second before the damaging operation
  export RESTORE_CLUSTER="taskflow-restore-20261110"

DECISION 1: Scope
  a) Small, identifiable damage (one collection, some documents)  -> restore side by side, copy back  (steps 1-6, 9)
  b) Widespread corruption or cluster lost                         -> restore side by side, switch over (steps 1-5, 7-9)

STEPS
1. Freeze the damage: stop or disable the job/migration/feature that caused it. Confirm writes of bad data have stopped.
2. Announce: IC posts the plan, target time, and expected duration; comms lead updates the status page.
3. Create the restore target: a NEW cluster "$RESTORE_CLUSTER" in the same region and version as production.
   (Atlas: Backup > Restore > Point in Time > target $TARGET_TIME > restore to $RESTORE_CLUSTER.)
   (Self-managed with PBM: provision new replica set, then: pbm restore --time="${TARGET_TIME%Z}")
   Expected: restore job status "completed". Record the timestamp.
4. Verify the restored data:
   mongosh "$RESTORE_URI" --quiet --eval 'db.getSiblingDB("taskflow").tasks.find({}, {updatedAt: 1}).sort({updatedAt: -1}).limit(1)'
   Expected: the newest updatedAt is just before $TARGET_TIME. Run the invariant checks from scripts/verify-restore.js
   (orphans, required indexes) and spot-check that the damaged records are intact.
5. Smoke test: run the API smoke tests against "$RESTORE_URI". Expected: all pass.
6. (Scope a) Copy back: export only the affected documents from the restored cluster and import them into production,
   e.g. mongoexport --uri="$RESTORE_URI" --db=taskflow --collection=tasks --query='{"projectId": {"$oid": "<id>"}}' --out=fix.json
        mongoimport --uri="$PROD_URI" --db=taskflow --collection=tasks --mode=upsert --file=fix.json
   Then go to step 9.
7. (Scope b) Put the API in maintenance mode (feature flag "maintenance=on"); confirm writes stop.
8. (Scope b) SECOND PERSON REQUIRED. Update the MONGODB_URI secret to "$RESTORE_URI" and restart the API (rolling).
   Expected: /readyz healthy on all pods; error rate normal for 10 minutes. Disable maintenance mode.
   ABORT: revert the secret to the previous value and restart; production cluster is untouched until step 10.
9. Verify with users: check SLO dashboards, error tracker, and a sample of support tickets.
10. Afterwards: keep the damaged cluster read-only for 7 days for investigation, then delete it. Record measured RTO
    (start to step 8/9) and RPO (target time vs. damaging operation). Open the postmortem. Update this runbook.

The runbook uses one decision point to choose between copying back a few documents (keeping good writes made after the target time) and switching to the restored cluster (losing writes after it). Measured RTO and RPO go into the drill log and the DR plan.

docs.title: A game day plan
docs.text:
Game day: TaskFlow regional failover (staging), <date> 14:00-16:00 UTC
Hypothesis: with the pilot light design, staging recovers in the DR region within 60 minutes
            with no more than 1 minute of data loss.
Scenario:   block all traffic to the primary region's staging subnets (network ACL change).
Roles:      IC <name>; operators <name>, <name> (not the runbook authors); observers <name> (timeline);
            comms <name> (internal channel updates every 15 minutes).
Success:    API healthy in the DR region; synthetic checks green; RPO and RTO measured.
Abort if:   impact spreads beyond staging, or 120 minutes elapse; revert the ACL change.
Afterwards: blameless review within 3 days; action items in the backlog; runbook and DR plan updated.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Treat a backup as valid only after a verified restore; track "last verified restore" per data store.
  • Automate restore tests on a schedule, with counts, invariants, freshness, and an application smoke test.
  • Record the restore duration every time and compare it with the RTO.
  • Alert on the age of the last successful restore test, not only on backup jobs.
  • Restore side by side, never over production, unless the runbook says otherwise for a reason.
  • Write runbooks with copy-pasteable commands, expected outputs, decision points, and abort steps; keep them available during outages.
  • Run drills with people who did not write the runbook, and rotate them.
  • Use UTC for every timestamp in runbooks, logs, and recovery targets.
  • Feed every drill's findings back into the runbook, DR plan, and backlog.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The restore test has been "green" for months, but it tests nothing. Detect: reading the pipeline shows it only checks that a file exists in the bucket. Cause: verification stopped at level 1. Fix: restore the backup, run data validation and a smoke test, and fail on any mismatch.
  • A real restore takes six hours against a one-hour RTO. Detect: the incident timeline shows hours of index builds after data loaded. Cause: restore duration was never measured as the data grew. Fix: track restore_duration_seconds from weekly tests, alert when it approaches the RTO, and move to physical backups or warm standby.
  • The on-call engineer cannot access the backups during an incident. Detect: access denied in the backup account; the person with access is on holiday. Cause: the restore role was never exercised by on-call engineers. Fix: use the same role in automated tests, include access checks in drills, and document break-glass access.
  • The restored database is missing a collection. Detect: verification reports a collection absent from the restore but present in production. Cause: the backup job lists collections or databases explicitly, and a new one was added later. Fix: back up everything by default, and compare the manifest with production's collection list.
  • A drill succeeded, but only because the author ran it. Detect: a different engineer gets stuck at an ambiguous step. Cause: the runbook relies on unwritten knowledge. Fix: rotate operators, make observers note every question asked, and rewrite unclear steps.
  • Restoring to the wrong time destroys more data. Detect: the restored data lacks records from the hour before the incident. Cause: the target time was given in local time and interpreted as UTC. Fix: UTC everywhere, an explicit variable in the runbook, and verification that compares the newest restored write with the intended target.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Restore test: Restoring a backup into a separate environment to prove it works.
  • Manifest: Facts recorded at backup time (counts, newest timestamps) used to verify a restore.
  • Smoke test: A small set of real requests that prove the application works on the restored data.
  • Runbook: A step-by-step procedure for a specific operational task.
  • Game day: A planned exercise that injects a failure to test systems and people.
  • Tabletop exercise: A discussion-based walk-through of a scenario.
  • DR drill: A rehearsal of the disaster recovery plan, measuring RTO and RPO.
  • Measured RTO / RPO: Recovery time and data loss observed in a test, as opposed to targets.
  • Restore side by side: Restoring into a new environment instead of over the original.
  • Break-glass access: An emergency access path used only when normal access is unavailable.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Equating "the backup job succeeded" with "we can restore".
  • Testing only that backup files exist or decompress.
  • Running restore tests against production clusters.
  • Never timing restores, so the RTO is a guess.
  • Runbooks without commands, expected outputs, or abort steps.
  • Keeping runbooks only in systems that may be down during the incident.
  • Letting only the runbook author run drills.
  • Treating drills as pass or fail rather than as a source of improvements.
  • Mixing time zones in recovery targets.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name five ways a backup can be unusable even though the backup job reported success.
  2. Describe the levels of backup verification, and which ones a weekly automated restore test should cover.
  3. Why record a manifest at backup time, and what should it contain for TaskFlow?
  4. Why is a freshness check needed when counts already match?
  5. In a drill, the decision took 9 minutes, the restore 31, verification 14, and switching 6. The newest restored write was 2 minutes before the damaging operation. What are the measured RTO and RPO, and do they meet targets of 60 minutes and 5 minutes? (RTO 60 minutes, exactly at the target with no margin; RPO 2 minutes, within target.)
  6. What are the main sections of a good runbook?
  7. Why should restores normally happen side by side rather than in place?
  8. Compare a tabletop exercise, a component restore drill, and a regional failover drill.
