docs.title: Artifacts and Environment Promotion
docs.text:
An artifact is the thing you actually deploy: a container image, a package tarball, a binary, or a bundle of static files. Environment promotion is the practice of moving that one artifact, unchanged, from development to staging to production, with checks and approvals between the steps and only configuration differing per environment.

This lesson covers what counts as an artifact, how to identify and version it (container images by digest), artifact registries, promotion without rebuilding, injecting environment-specific configuration at deploy time, approvals and protected environments, and deployment records that make every release traceable.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: "It worked in staging" only means something if production runs the same bits. Teams that rebuild for each environment, or deploy mutable tags such as latest, cannot be sure of that: a dependency release, a new base image, or a retagged image can change what runs between one environment and the next. Promotion by immutable identifier turns the pipeline into evidence: this exact artifact passed these tests, was approved by this person, and has run in production since this time. It also makes rollback trivial, because the previous artifact still exists and can be redeployed in seconds.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Twelve-Factor apps. Build, release, run separates the build (an executable bundle) from the release (that build plus an environment's config), and says every release must have a unique ID and never be modified; Config says configuration that varies between deploys belongs in the environment, not in the code or build.
  • Google release engineering. The SRE book's Release Engineering chapter describes hermetic builds, packages versioned with a unique hash and signed, labels that reference a package by build ID, binaries that report their build date, revision, and build identifier, and an audit trail of every release step.
  • OCI content addressing. The OCI image specification identifies image manifests and layers by digest (for example sha256: plus a hash of the content), which is what makes "deploy exactly this image" possible.
  • GitHub deployments. Jobs that reference an environment create deployment records, and the deployments REST API exposes them, linking environment, commit, and status.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub Container Registry, Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry, Docker Hub, JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus, the npm registry, docker buildx imagetools, crane, skopeo, and GitOps tools such as Argo CD and Flux for promotion.

docs.title: What an artifact is
docs.text:
Artifact Identity Stored in TaskFlow example Container image Manifest digest sha256:... Container registry ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:9f2c... npm package Name + version (immutable once published) + integrity hash npm registry @example/taskflow-sdk@2.4.0 Static web bundle Content-hashed file names, archive checksum Object storage or CDN TaskFlow Web dist/ Binary or installer File checksum, signature Release assets, object storage Desktop client installer Helm chart or config bundle Chart version, digest (OCI charts) OCI registry or chart repo taskflow-api chart 1.8.0

Good artifacts share four properties: they are immutable (never changed after creation), uniquely identified (by digest or an immutable version), traceable (they record the commit and build that produced them), and environment-neutral (no environment's settings baked in).

docs.title: Digests versus tags
docs.text:
A container tag (:2.4.0, :main, :latest) is a movable name; the registry lets anyone with push rights point it at a different image. A digest is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest, so it identifies exactly one image and can never point anywhere else. Multi-platform images have an index digest that covers each platform's image.

docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:2.4.0
# Name:      ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:2.4.0
# MediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
# Digest:    sha256:9f2c...   (index digest covering amd64 and arm64)

Use tags as human-friendly labels (2.4.0, sha-a1b2c3d...) and deploy by digest (image@sha256:...). Some registries can make tags immutable (Amazon ECR's tag immutability setting, for example), which prevents overwriting a release tag. Image tagging conventions are covered in images, registries, and tagging.

docs.title: Versioning artifacts
docs.text:
Every artifact should carry at least:

  • the commit SHA it was built from (tag sha-<commit> and label org.opencontainers.image.revision),
  • a release version if it is a release (2.4.0), and
  • the build run that produced it (a link or ID, recorded in labels or attestations).

Never deploy latest or branch-name tags to shared environments: two nodes pulling :main an hour apart can run different code, and a restart can silently upgrade a running service.

docs.title: Artifact registries
docs.text:
Registries store artifacts and control who can push and pull them. Things to configure deliberately:

  • Access: CI pushes with short-lived credentials (GITHUB_TOKEN for GHCR, OIDC-issued cloud credentials for ECR or Artifact Registry); runtime environments pull with read-only identities.
  • Immutability: protect release tags from being overwritten.
  • Retention: delete untagged and old development images automatically, but keep everything that is or recently was deployed, because rollback needs it.
  • Scanning: most registries scan images for known vulnerabilities on push.
  • Proximity: use a registry in the same cloud region as the runtime, or a pull-through cache, to speed up deploys and survive outages of public registries.

Workflow artifacts in GitHub Actions (actions/upload-artifact) are for passing files between jobs and keeping reports; they expire (90 days by default) and are not a release store.

docs.title: Promotion without rebuilding
docs.text:
Promotion means "this artifact is now approved for the next environment". There are several mechanisms, all of which keep the artifact unchanged:

Mechanism How Notes Deploy by digest per environment The pipeline passes the digest from the build job to each deploy job Simplest; the deployment record is the promotion record Add a tag docker buildx imagetools create --tag ...:2.4.0 ...@sha256:... No rebuild; copies the manifest reference Copy between registries crane copy or skopeo copy from a dev registry to a prod registry Preserves the digest; separates prod pull permissions GitOps Commit the new digest into the environment's config repository Argo CD or Flux applies it; Git history is the audit log (see immutable infrastructure and GitOps)

docs.title: Environment-specific configuration at deploy time
docs.text:
If one artifact runs everywhere, everything that differs must come from outside it:

  • Environment variables and secrets injected by the platform (Kubernetes Secrets and ConfigMaps, ECS task definitions, a secrets manager), never baked into the image.
  • Configuration files mounted at runtime.
  • Feature flags read at runtime.

Backend services read configuration at startup, so this is natural. Frontends are harder: Vite and similar bundlers inline import.meta.env.VITE_* values at build time, which forces a build per environment. To promote one TaskFlow Web bundle, load runtime configuration (a config.json written at deploy time) instead; the trade-offs are covered in build-time versus runtime configuration.

docs.title: Approvals and protected environments
docs.text:
Promotion to sensitive environments passes through gates:

  • Automated gates decide whether promotion is safe: tests pass, error rates in staging are normal, a canary is healthy.
  • Manual approval decides whether promotion is wanted now: a required reviewer on the production environment, often the release owner. Give approvers context (the diff since the last production deploy, test results, the change ticket) or approvals become rubber stamps.
  • Environment protection keeps the rules enforceable: only main (or release tags) can deploy to production, the person who triggered the run cannot approve it, and production secrets are only released to jobs that passed the gates.

Continuous deployment replaces the manual approval with automated analysis; the environment protections stay.

docs.title: Deployment records and traceability
docs.text:
Every deployment should record what (artifact digest and version), from where (commit SHA, pipeline run), to where (environment), who (triggering user and approver), when, and result. With these records you can answer, in seconds:

  • What is running in production right now, and since when?
  • Which commits shipped in the deploy that started the incident?
  • What do we roll back to?
  • What are our deployment frequency and change lead time? (See continuous integration fundamentals.)

GitHub records a deployment for every job that references an environment; artifact attestations add signed provenance linking the digest to the workflow that built it (see pipeline and supply chain security).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Practice Use when Adapt when Promote by digest Always for container deployments Platforms that only accept tags: use immutable tags derived from the digest or commit Separate dev and prod registries with copy-on-promote Strict separation of who can pull production images Small teams: one registry with read-only prod pulls is fine Manual approval before production Regulated changes, low test confidence, business-timed releases Mature continuous deployment with automated canary analysis Runtime config for frontends Promoting one web bundle across environments Static sites with no environment differences GitOps promotion Kubernetes platforms with Argo CD or Flux Simple single-service deployments (direct deploy jobs suffice) Retention policies Every registry Never delete images that production might roll back to

docs.title: Build once, promote by digest through staging and production
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  build-image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write                       # push to ghcr.io
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v6
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api
          tags: |
            type=sha,format=long
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}   # includes org.opencontainers.image.revision
          build-args: |
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-image
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    with:
      environment: staging
      image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ needs.build-image.outputs.digest }}

  e2e-staging:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - env:
          BASE_URL: ${{ needs.deploy-staging.outputs.url }}
        run: npx playwright test

  deploy-production:
    needs: [build-image, e2e-staging]
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml        # the production environment requires approval
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    with:
      environment: production
      image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ needs.build-image.outputs.digest }}

The image is built once; both deploy jobs receive the same digest from needs.build-image.outputs.digest. deploy.yml is the reusable workflow from GitHub Actions in depth: its job references the environment named in its input, so the production job pauses for the environment's required reviewers, then receives production variables and secrets.

docs.title: Add release tags and copy between registries without rebuilding
docs.text:
DIGEST=sha256:<digest-from-the-build-job>

# Add a human-friendly release tag to the exact image that passed staging
docker buildx imagetools create \
  --tag ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:2.4.0 \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@"$DIGEST"

# Copy it into the production account's registry; the digest stays the same
crane copy \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@"$DIGEST" \
  123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/taskflow-api:2.4.0

crane digest 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/taskflow-api:2.4.0
# sha256:<same digest>

Neither command rebuilds anything: they add references to, or copy, the existing manifest and layers.

docs.title: Runtime configuration so one TaskFlow Web bundle serves every environment
docs.text:
// src/config.js (TaskFlow Web): configuration loaded at runtime, not build time
let config;

export async function loadConfig() {
  const res = await fetch("/config.json", { cache: "no-store" });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Cannot load config.json: ${res.status}`);
  config = await res.json(); // for example { "apiBaseUrl": "https://api.example.com" }
  return config;
}

export function getConfig() {
  if (!config) throw new Error("Config not loaded yet");
  return config;
}

// src/main.jsx
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { loadConfig } from "./config.js";
import App from "./App.jsx";

loadConfig().then(() => {
  createRoot(document.getElementById("root")).render(<App />);
});

#!/bin/sh
# docker-entrypoint.d/40-runtime-config.sh: runs when the nginx container starts
envsubst < /usr/share/nginx/html/config.template.json > /usr/share/nginx/html/config.json

The same image serves staging and production; each environment sets API_BASE_URL (referenced in config.template.json) at deploy time. The official nginx image runs executable scripts in /docker-entrypoint.d/ before starting. Only non-secret values belong in config.json, because browsers can read it.

docs.title: What is running, and since when?
docs.text:
# Last five production deployments with commit, time, and who triggered them
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/deployments?environment=production&per_page=5" \
  --jq '.[] | {id, sha: .sha[0:7], created_at, creator: .creator.login}'

# Status history of one deployment
gh api "repos/{owner}/{repo}/deployments/<deployment-id>/statuses" \
  --jq '.[] | {state, created_at, log_url}'

Pair this with a /version endpoint on the service (see versioning, tags, and releases) to confirm that the running process matches the record.

docs.title: A registry retention policy that protects rollbacks
docs.text:
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Delete untagged images after 14 days",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "untagged",
        "countType": "sinceImagePushed",
        "countUnit": "days",
        "countNumber": 14
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    },
    {
      "rulePriority": 2,
      "description": "Keep only the newest 300 commit-tagged images",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPrefixList": ["sha-"],
        "countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
        "countNumber": 300
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    }
  ]
}

This is an Amazon ECR lifecycle policy. Images tagged only with a version (2.4.0) match no rule, so they are kept, and development images are pruned. A rule selects an image if any of its tags matches, so a release image that still has its sha- tag can be expired by rule 2; keep releases in their own repository, as the crane copy example does. Before enabling any cleanup, check that every digest deployed in the last few months is protected.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Build each artifact once per commit; never rebuild for an environment.
  • Deploy by digest; treat tags as labels and make release tags immutable.
  • Stamp commit SHA, version, and build ID into every artifact.
  • Keep artifacts environment-neutral; inject configuration and secrets at deploy time.
  • Give CI short-lived push credentials and runtimes read-only pull access.
  • Gate production with automated checks plus, where needed, a required reviewer with context; restrict which branches can deploy.
  • Record every deployment (what, from where, to where, who, when, result).
  • Set retention policies that delete clutter but keep rollback targets.
  • Use Actions artifacts for files between jobs and reports, registries for releases.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Production behaves differently from staging with "the same version". Detect: the image digests in the two environments differ for the same version tag. Cause: per-environment builds or a moved tag. Fix: build once, deploy by digest, and make release tags immutable.
  • A node restart silently upgraded a service. Detect: pods on different nodes report different /version values under one Deployment. Cause: the manifest referenced a mutable tag (:latest, :main) and nodes pulled at different times. Fix: reference images by digest in manifests and set pull policies accordingly.
  • Rollback failed because the previous image was deleted. Detect: manifest unknown when redeploying the last good version. Cause: an aggressive registry cleanup rule. Fix: restore from another registry or rebuild from the tag as a last resort; change the policy to exclude release tags and recently deployed digests.
  • Staging's web app calls the production API. Detect: production logs show staging traffic. Cause: the frontend bundle had the API URL baked in at build time and the production build was copied to staging. Fix: load the API URL from runtime configuration and promote one bundle.
  • Production deploys wait hours for approval. Detect: long gaps between staging success and production start in deployment records. Cause: a single approver, no notifications, no context. Fix: several eligible reviewers, notifications, a summary of changes and test results on the run, and automated gates so approval is a quick decision.
  • Nobody can say which commits are in production. Detect: incident responders compare timestamps by hand. Cause: no deployment records or version endpoint. Fix: deploy through environments that create records, expose /version, and tag telemetry with the release.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Artifact: The deployable output of a build.
  • Image digest: The SHA-256 hash identifying an exact image manifest.
  • Tag: A mutable, human-friendly name pointing at an image.
  • Immutable tag: A tag the registry will not allow to be repointed.
  • Artifact registry: A service that stores and serves artifacts.
  • Promotion: Approving an existing artifact for the next environment.
  • Build once, deploy many: One build per commit, deployed everywhere.
  • Runtime configuration: Settings supplied when the artifact starts, not when it is built.
  • Protected environment: An environment with deployment rules such as required reviewers and branch restrictions.
  • Deployment record: A log entry linking artifact, commit, environment, approver, time, and result.
  • Retention policy: Rules for deleting old artifacts.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rebuilding "the same version" for each environment.
  • Deploying latest or branch tags to shared environments.
  • Baking API URLs, feature flags, or secrets into images or bundles.
  • Treating GitHub Actions workflow artifacts as long-term release storage.
  • Registry cleanup rules that delete rollback targets.
  • Approvals without context, which become rubber stamps.
  • Assuming a version tag identifies an image uniquely; only the digest does.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What four properties should a deployable artifact have?
  2. Why is a digest a safer deployment reference than a tag? When are tags still useful?
  3. Describe three ways to promote an image without rebuilding it.
  4. A frontend embeds VITE_API_URL at build time. What problem does that cause for promotion, and how do you fix it?
  5. What should a deployment record contain, and which DORA metrics can you compute from such records?
  6. Your registry holds 4,000 images using 1.2 TB. Production deploys about 10 times a day and you need 90 days of rollback history. Roughly how many deployed images must a cleanup policy protect? (About 900.)
  7. Which gates are automated and which are human in a typical production promotion, and why keep environment protections even with continuous deployment?
  8. Why are GitHub Actions workflow artifacts not a good release store?

docs.title: CI/CD Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the CI/CD lessons, for the day before an interview or before you write a pipeline.

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (the shape of a TaskFlow API pipeline)
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:                          # required with a merge queue
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read                        # grant more only per job
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15                 # the default is 360
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm                    # caches ~/.npm, keyed on the lockfile
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run ci
  ci-ok:                                # the one required check
    if: always()
    needs: [test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - if: contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1
Key What it does needs: [a, b] Builds the job graph; a job is skipped when a job it needs fails if: always() Runs even after failures (aggregator jobs, test reports) $GITHUB_OUTPUT, outputs: steps.<id>.outputs.x, then needs.<job>.outputs.x env:, vars, secrets File values; visible settings; masked secrets, none for fork PRs environment: production Protection rules, environment secrets, a deployment record permissions: GITHUB_TOKEN scopes; unlisted scopes become none id-token: write Lets the job request an OIDC token for cloud login

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does npm ci Installs exactly the lockfile; fails if it is out of sync actionlint .github/workflows/*.yml Lints workflows, contexts, and expressions gh run view <id> --json jobs Job start and end times, to find the critical path docker buildx imagetools create --tag <repo>:2.4.0 <repo>@sha256:<digest> Adds a tag without rebuilding crane copy <src>@sha256:<digest> <dst>:2.4.0 Copies to another registry; same digest gh attestation verify oci://<image>@sha256:<digest> --owner example Verifies provenance before deploying

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Checks on every PR pull_request (+ merge_group) Fork PRs get a read-only token, no secrets Deploys after merge push to main with environments Approvals, environment secrets, records Cloud credentials OIDC, role bound to repo and environment No long-lived keys to leak Reuse Composite action (steps) or reusable workflow (jobs) Jobs get their own runners and secrets Several Node.js versions A matrix For libraries; an app tests its one runtime A slow suite Sharding (--shard=2/4) About the slowest shard plus setup Required checks in a monorepo Change detection and conditional jobs Path filters leave checks pending A production release The digest staging tested What was tested is what runs One web bundle everywhere Runtime config.json Vite inlines VITE_* at build time

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text:
• PR pipeline about 10 minutes; at 30 to 45, people batch changes. Flaky failures well under 1% of runs.
  • Critical path, the longest chain of jobs: 4 + 3 + 2 + 6 + 3 = 18 minutes in the example, against 22 run serially.
  • Matrix jobs = combinations - excludes + new includes (3 x 2 = 6).
  • Caches: immutable per key, 10 GB per repository by default, evicted after 7 days unused; a branch reads its own and the default branch's. Artifacts are kept 90 days by default.
  • Concurrency (default): one running and one pending run per group; a newer pending run replaces the older one. queue: max keeps up to 100 pending (not with cancel-in-progress: true).
  • schedule: UTC, every 5 minutes at most, disabled in public repositories after 60 days without activity.
  • Required reviewers: up to 6, one approval. In private repositories, required reviewers and wait timers need GitHub Enterprise.
  • GITHUB_TOKEN expires with the job (24 hours at most); events it creates start no runs, except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch. Reusable workflows nest up to ten levels.
  • Dependabot waits 3 days before proposing a new version by default; security updates are not delayed.
  • DORA change fail rate: 6 failed of 60 deployments = 10%.

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Requiring a job that needs the tests. Require an if: always() aggregator; a skipped job counts as passing.
  • Path filters on required workflows. Run them always and decide inside with a change-detection job.
  • Rebuilding for each environment. Build once and deploy the digest.
  • Caching node_modules, or keys without the lockfile hash. Cache ~/.npm keyed on the OS and the lockfile hash.
  • ${{ github.event.* }} inside run:. Pass values through env: and quote them.
  • pull_request_target with a checkout of the PR head. Run PR code under pull_request; privileged follow-ups use workflow_run.
  • Third-party actions pinned by tag. Pin full commit SHAs.
  • Long-lived cloud keys in secrets. Use OIDC with a tight sub.

docs.title: Continuous Integration Fundamentals
docs.text:
Continuous integration (CI) is a development practice, not a tool: everyone merges small changes into a shared main line at least daily, and every merge is verified by an automated build and test run. Continuous delivery extends CI so that every verified change is ready to release; continuous deployment releases each one automatically.

This lesson explains the differences between CI, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment, why fast feedback and small batches matter, how teams keep the build green, what a minimum CI pipeline should check, and how to measure delivery performance with DORA's metrics.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Integration problems grow with the time between integrations. Two developers who merge every few hours meet small conflicts while the context is fresh; two who merge after three weeks meet a tangle that takes days to unpick, and the bugs they find could have been introduced by any of hundreds of changes. CI turns integration from a risky phase into a continuous background activity. It is also the foundation of everything later in the pipeline: you cannot deploy safely and often if the main line is not reliably green, and you cannot improve delivery performance you do not measure.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The definition. Martin Fowler's Continuous Integration defines CI as each team member merging changes into the codebase at least daily, with each integration verified by an automated build and tests. Its practices include "Fix Broken Builds Immediately" (quoting Kent Beck: "nobody has a higher priority task than fixing the build") and "Keep the Build Fast", with the Extreme Programming guideline of a ten-minute build.
  • Google. The CI chapter of Software Engineering at Google describes TAP, Google's continuous build, which handles more than 50,000 unique changes and runs more than four billion test cases a day. Teams run a fast, reliable subset of tests before submit; a change that passes it has a 95%+ chance of passing everything else, and the rest run after submit, with fast rollback when something breaks.
  • DORA. DORA's software delivery performance metrics (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, and deployment rework rate) are the standard way to measure whether CI/CD is working, and its continuous integration capability page ties CI to trunk-based development and fast automated tests.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD, Jenkins, CircleCI, Buildkite, Azure Pipelines, AWS CodeBuild and CodePipeline, Google Cloud Build, and TeamCity.

docs.title: Integration, delivery, and deployment
docs.text:
Practice Promise What is automated Who decides to release Continuous integration main always builds and passes tests Build and test on every change Release is a separate process Continuous delivery Every change on main is releasable Build, test, package, deploy to test environments, release mechanics A person, with one approval Continuous deployment Every change that passes goes to production Everything, including the release decision The pipeline's automated gates

Continuous delivery does not require deploying every commit; it requires that you could. The release decision becomes a business choice (wait for marketing, a regulatory sign-off, an app store window) instead of an engineering project.

docs.title: Fast feedback
docs.text:
The value of a check depends on how soon it reports. Feedback arrives in layers, from fastest and cheapest to slowest and most expensive:

Layer Typical delay Examples Editor Seconds Type errors, lint warnings Pre-commit hook Seconds Formatting, secrets in staged files Pull request CI Minutes Unit and integration tests, build Post-merge pipeline Minutes to an hour Full test suite, staging deploy, e2e tests Production Minutes to days Error rates, latency, user reports

The aim is to catch each class of problem at the earliest layer that can catch it reliably. A pull request pipeline of about ten minutes keeps developers waiting for the result instead of switching tasks; at 45 minutes they stop waiting, start batching changes, and the feedback loop breaks.

docs.title: Trunk and small batches
docs.text:
CI requires a shared main line that everyone integrates into frequently, which is why DORA calls trunk-based development a required practice for CI (see branching strategies). Small batches make every later step cheaper:

  • Review: a 150-line change is read; a 3,000-line change is skimmed.
  • Diagnosis: if a build that contains 1 change fails, you know the culprit; if it contains 40, you start bisecting.
  • Rollback: reverting a small change removes little else.
  • Conflicts: less divergence means fewer and smaller conflicts.

A useful rule of thumb from DORA: three or fewer active branches, merged to trunk at least daily, and no code freezes.

docs.title: Keeping the build green
docs.text:
The main line is shared infrastructure; when it is red, nobody can trust their own results, and changes pile up on top of a failure. Teams that do CI well treat a red main as a stop-the-line event:

  • Revert first, investigate second. Restoring green takes minutes; debugging may take hours.
  • Make the culprit obvious: small commits, required checks on PRs, and clear failure output.
  • Own it: the author of the breaking change fixes it, or a rotating "build cop" makes sure someone does (Google's practice).
  • Fight flakiness: a test that fails randomly teaches people to ignore red, which destroys the signal. Quarantine and fix flaky tests (see testing and quality gates).
  • Prevent combination failures: require PR branches to be up to date or use a merge queue, so main is tested as it will be.

docs.title: What a minimum CI pipeline checks
docs.text:
Step Purpose Typical time for TaskFlow API Check out the exact commit Test what was pushed Seconds Set up the runtime from .nvmrc Same Node.js version as production Seconds npm ci Install exactly the lockfile's versions, fail if it is out of sync 20-60 s (faster with caching) Lint and format check Catch errors and style issues mechanically Seconds Type check (TypeScript projects) Catch type errors Seconds to a minute Unit tests Logic in isolation Under a minute Integration tests API plus a real MongoDB 1-3 minutes Build The build that would ship actually works Under a minute Dependency and secret scanning Known vulnerabilities, leaked credentials Seconds to a minute

Later stages add packaging (a container image), deployment to staging, end-to-end tests, and security scanning of the artifact; those are covered in pipeline design and the pages after it.

Two principles keep CI honest:

  • CI runs the same commands developers run. Put the logic in package.json scripts (or a Makefile), and keep the CI file thin. If CI does something special that nobody can run locally, failures are hard to reproduce.
  • CI uses the same versions as production: runtime version, lockfile, and ideally the same base image.

docs.title: Presubmit and post-submit
docs.text:
Not every test belongs before merge. Google's rule of thumb is to run only fast, reliable tests before submit and the slower, larger tests after, accepting some rollbacks in exchange for developer speed. A typical split:

Before merge (PR) After merge (main) Lint, type check, unit tests, integration tests with service containers, build Full end-to-end suite against staging, performance tests, long-running security scans, multi-platform builds

Whatever runs after merge must have a clear owner and a fast revert path, because failures there affect everyone.

docs.title: Measuring delivery: the DORA metrics
docs.text:
DORA's research program measures software delivery performance with these metrics, defined on dora.dev:

Group Metric Definition (DORA) Throughput Change lead time Time for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed in production Throughput Deployment frequency Number of deployments over a period, or the time between deployments Throughput Failed deployment recovery time Time to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention Instability Change fail rate Ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment Instability Deployment rework rate Ratio of deployments that are unplanned and happen as a result of an incident in production

The first four are the long-standing "four keys" (failed deployment recovery time replaced the older "time to restore service" or MTTR naming in 2023); deployment rework rate was added in 2024. Measurement rules, the history of these changes, and DORA's published benchmarks are covered in measuring delivery performance.

DORA's guidance on using them well:

  • Measure one application or service at a time; blending very different systems hides the signal.
  • Use them to track improvement over time, not as targets or to rank teams; mandated targets invite gaming.
  • Use several metrics together: throughput and instability can pull against each other, so improving one while the other collapses is visible. DORA's research finds they usually improve together.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Context Recommendation Any team writing code together CI: always, from the first commit Web service or API with good tests and fast rollback Continuous delivery, moving to continuous deployment as confidence grows Regulated releases needing documented approval Continuous delivery with a recorded approval gate (protected environment) Mobile apps in app stores Continuous delivery to internal and beta tracks; store release is gated by review Desktop or on-premises software Continuous delivery of signed builds; customers choose when to install Database migrations and irreversible changes Automate them, but gate with expand-and-contract patterns (see zero-downtime database migrations)

Continuous deployment is not a fit when you cannot detect a bad release quickly (no monitoring or automated rollback), when releases are irreversible, or when external commitments fix release dates. Those teams still benefit from continuous delivery.

docs.title: Scripts as the contract between laptops and CI
docs.text:
{
  "name": "taskflow-api",
  "type": "module",
  "engines": { "node": ">=24" },
  "scripts": {
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check .",
    "test": "node --test \"test/unit/**/*.test.js\"",
    "test:integration": "node --test \"test/integration/**/*.test.js\"",
    "build": "node scripts/build.js",
    "ci": "npm run lint && npm run format:check && npm test && npm run test:integration && npm run build"
  }
}

# .nvmrc
24

A developer runs npm run ci before pushing and gets the same verdict CI will give. The workflow file only sets up the environment and calls these scripts.

docs.title: A minimum CI workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      mongo:
        image: mongo:8.0
        ports: ["27017:27017"]
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.adminCommand({ ping: 1 })'"
          --health-interval 5s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 10
    env:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow_test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run ci

concurrency cancels superseded runs on pull requests (a new push makes the old run pointless) but never cancels a main run that has started. timeout-minutes stops a hung job long before the six-hour default. Each part is explained in GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: Computing DORA metrics from deployment records
docs.text:
// scripts/dora.js: compute DORA metrics for one service from deployment records
// Usage: node scripts/dora.js deployments.json
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const records = JSON.parse(await readFile(process.argv[2], "utf8"));
// Each record: { deployedAt, commits: [{ committedAt }], failed, recoveredAt, unplanned }

const minutes = (a, b) => (new Date(b) - new Date(a)) / 60_000;
const median = (xs) => {
  const s = [...xs].sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const mid = Math.floor(s.length / 2);
  return s.length % 2 ? s[mid] : (s[mid - 1] + s[mid]) / 2;
};

const times = records.map((r) => new Date(r.deployedAt));
const days = (Math.max(...times) - Math.min(...times)) / 86_400_000 || 1;

const leadTimes = records.flatMap((r) =>
  r.commits.map((c) => minutes(c.committedAt, r.deployedAt)),
);
const failed = records.filter((r) => r.failed);
const recovery = failed.map((r) => minutes(r.deployedAt, r.recoveredAt));

console.log({
  deploymentsPerDay: +(records.length / days).toFixed(2),
  medianLeadTimeMinutes: median(leadTimes),
  changeFailRate: +(failed.length / records.length).toFixed(3),
  meanRecoveryMinutes: recovery.length
    ? recovery.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / recovery.length
    : 0,
  reworkRate: +(records.filter((r) => r.unplanned).length / records.length).toFixed(3),
});

The records can come from GitHub deployments (gh api repos/example/taskflow-api/deployments), your deploy tool's history, or incident tickets. Lead time uses each commit's timestamp, so a deploy that ships five commits contributes five lead times; the median resists outliers such as a commit that waited on a long-lived branch.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Integrate into main at least daily, in small batches.
  • Build and test every push and every pull request automatically.
  • Keep the PR pipeline around ten minutes; measure it and treat regressions as bugs.
  • Fix or revert a broken main immediately; make "revert first" the default.
  • Make CI run the same scripts and versions as developers and production.
  • Run fast, reliable tests before merge and slower suites after merge, each with a clear owner.
  • Quarantine flaky tests and fix them; never normalize re-running until green.
  • Track DORA metrics per service as trends, not targets, and use throughput and instability together.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Developers stop waiting for CI and batch their changes. Detect: median PR pipeline time above 30 minutes; PR size and lead time grow. Cause: a slow, serial pipeline with no caching. Fix: parallelize jobs, cache dependencies, move slow suites after merge, and set a time budget (see pipeline design).
  • main stays red for hours while people keep merging. Detect: the main branch status is red across several merges. Cause: no stop-the-line norm; nobody owns the breakage. Fix: revert the first failing merge immediately, block merges while main is red (required checks or a merge queue), and rotate a build-cop role.
  • "Works on my machine" failures in CI. Detect: tests pass locally but fail in CI, or the reverse. Cause: different Node.js versions, npm install instead of npm ci, or hidden local state. Fix: pin the runtime in .nvmrc, use npm ci everywhere, and run the same npm run ci script locally.
  • The team re-runs failed jobs until they pass. Detect: many runs with attempt numbers above 1; failures that vanish on retry. Cause: flaky tests. Fix: track flaky tests, quarantine them out of the required checks with an owner and deadline, and fix the root causes (timing, shared state, order dependence).
  • Change fail rate rises after the pipeline got faster. Detect: more rollbacks per deploy over the last month. Cause: tests were dropped or moved after merge without compensating checks. Fix: restore coverage at the right stage, add canary analysis, and review throughput and instability metrics together.
  • Leadership compares teams by deployment frequency and numbers inflate. Detect: deployments that change nothing, or metrics that diverge from incident data. Cause: metrics used as targets. Fix: follow DORA's guidance: use metrics per service for improvement conversations, not rankings.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Continuous integration: Merging small changes into a shared main line at least daily, each verified automatically.
  • Continuous delivery: Keeping every change releasable, with release as a push-button decision.
  • Continuous deployment: Releasing every change that passes the pipeline automatically.
  • Main line (trunk): The shared branch everyone integrates into.
  • Build: The automated compile, test, and package run for a change.
  • Green / red build: A passing or failing pipeline run.
  • Stop the line: Treating a broken main line as everyone's top priority.
  • Presubmit / post-submit: Checks before merging and after merging.
  • Change lead time: Time from commit to running in production.
  • Deployment frequency: How often deployments happen.
  • Change fail rate: Share of deployments needing immediate intervention.
  • Failed deployment recovery time: Time to recover from a failed deployment.
  • Deployment rework rate: Share of deployments that are unplanned fixes for production incidents.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Equating CI with owning a CI server while branches live for weeks.
  • Confusing continuous delivery with continuous deployment.
  • Letting the pipeline grow to an hour, then wondering why batches grow.
  • Re-running flaky tests instead of fixing them.
  • Running special commands in CI that developers cannot run locally.
  • Using npm install in CI, which may change the lockfile, instead of npm ci.
  • Treating DORA metrics as targets or comparing unrelated teams with them.
  • Assuming a green build means the change is correct; it means the checks you wrote passed.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define continuous integration, continuous delivery, and continuous deployment, and give one context where each is the right stopping point.
  2. Why does a ten-minute PR pipeline matter more than it seems?
  3. What does "stop the line" mean for a red main, and why is reverting usually the first step?
  4. List the checks in a minimum CI pipeline for a Node.js API and why each is there.
  5. Which tests belong before merge and which after, and what must be true of the post-merge ones?
  6. In one month a service had 60 deployments; 6 needed a rollback or hotfix, recovering in 20, 30, 30, 45, 60, and 90 minutes; 4 deployments were unplanned fixes. Compute the change fail rate, mean failed deployment recovery time, and deployment rework rate. (10%, 45.8 minutes, about 6.7%.)
  7. Why does DORA warn against using its metrics as targets or to compare teams?
  8. Why should CI call package.json scripts rather than contain the logic itself?

docs.text:
• Martin Fowler: Continuous Integration
  • Software Engineering at Google: Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery
  • DORA: Software delivery performance metrics
  • DORA: Continuous integration and Continuous delivery

docs.title: GitHub Actions in Depth
docs.text:
GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in automation platform. A YAML workflow in .github/workflows/ declares which events start it and which jobs to run; each job runs on a runner and executes steps, which are shell commands or reusable actions. Because it is part of the repository, the pipeline is versioned, reviewed, and protected like the code it builds.

This lesson walks through the moving parts in the order you meet them: events, jobs, steps, and runners; contexts and expressions; needs, if, and outputs; environment variables, configuration variables, and secrets; environments with protection rules; concurrency; caching; reusable workflows and composite actions; and the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions block. It ends with a complete CI workflow for TaskFlow API with a MongoDB service container.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most teams on GitHub run their whole delivery pipeline in Actions, so Actions knowledge decides how fast, cheap, and safe that pipeline is. The details matter: a missing merge_group trigger blocks a merge queue, an unscoped GITHUB_TOKEN turns a compromised dependency into write access to your repository, a cache key without the lockfile hash breaks builds, and a missing concurrency group lets two deploys race. The syntax is small, but the semantics (which context is available where, what a skipped job reports, which events see secrets) are where real pipelines succeed or fail.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's own documentation. Understanding GitHub Actions and the workflow syntax reference define every key used on this page; the events reference lists each trigger, its activity types, and which ref and commit the run uses.
  • Security hardening guidance. GitHub's secure use reference recommends least-privilege GITHUB_TOKEN permissions, pinning third-party actions to full commit SHAs, and avoiding untrusted input in scripts, practices applied in every example below and expanded in pipeline and supply chain security.
  • Reusable workflows at scale. GitHub's reusing workflow configurations page compares reusable workflows and composite actions: reusable workflows contain jobs, can use secrets, log each step, and can be nested up to ten levels; composite actions bundle steps that run inside the caller's job. Platform teams use them to give hundreds of repositories one maintained deployment pipeline.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub-hosted and larger runners, self-hosted runners with Actions Runner Controller on Kubernetes, the GitHub CLI (gh workflow, gh run), actionlint for workflow linting, and the Marketplace of actions (actions/*, docker/*, cloud providers' official actions).

docs.title: Events, workflows, jobs, steps
docs.text: Concept What it is Key facts Workflow A YAML file in .github/workflows/ Several workflows can run for one event Event What starts a run (on:) Push, pull request, manual, schedule, release, and many more Job A set of steps on one runner Jobs run in parallel unless linked with needs; each gets a fresh machine on hosted runners Step One command (run:) or action (uses:) Steps share the job's file system and environment, in order Action Reusable step logic JavaScript, Docker container, or composite; referenced as owner/repo@ref or ./path Runner The machine executing a job GitHub-hosted or self-hosted

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
The events used most in CI/CD:

on:
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]
    tags: ["v*"]
    paths-ignore: ["docs/**", "**/*.md"]
  pull_request:                       # default types: opened, synchronize, reopened
    branches: [main]
  merge_group:                        # required when using a merge queue
  workflow_dispatch:                  # manual "Run workflow" button and API
    inputs:
      environment:
        description: Where to deploy
        type: environment
        required: true
      dry-run:
        type: boolean
        default: true
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * 1-5"            # 03:17 UTC, Monday to Friday
  release:
    types: [published]
Event Runs on Typical use Notes push The pushed commit Build and deploy main, tag releases Filters: branches, tags, paths and their -ignore forms pull_request A merge commit of the PR into its base PR checks From forks: read-only GITHUB_TOKEN, no secrets merge_group The merge queue's temporary branch Required checks with a merge queue Without it, queued PRs never get their checks workflow_dispatch The chosen branch Manual deploys, maintenance jobs Typed inputs; gh workflow run deploy.yml -f environment=staging schedule Latest commit on the default branch Nightly scans, dependency checks, cleanup Cron in UTC; shortest interval 5 minutes; can be delayed under load; disabled in public repos after 60 days without activity release The release's tag Publish packages and assets Choose types, usually published workflow_call Inherits the caller's event Reusable workflows See below

pull_request_target and workflow_run also exist; they run with elevated privileges in the context of the base repository and are covered as security risks in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Runners
docs.text:
GitHub-hosted Self-hosted Machine Fresh VM per job (Linux, Windows, macOS; larger and ARM sizes available) Your VM, container, or server State between jobs None: clean every time Persists unless configured as ephemeral Maintenance GitHub patches images You patch, scale, and secure them Network Public internet Can reach private networks (databases, clusters) Cost Free for public repositories on standard runners; per-minute beyond plan quotas for private ones Your infrastructure cost Security caveat Isolated per job Never let untrusted code (public fork PRs) run on persistent self-hosted runners

runs-on: ubuntu-latest picks the current Ubuntu image; pin a version label such as ubuntu-24.04 when you need stability across image upgrades. Self-hosted runners are selected by labels (runs-on: [self-hosted, linux, x64]), and Actions Runner Controller autoscales ephemeral runners on Kubernetes.

docs.title: Contexts and expressions
docs.text:
Expressions, written ${{ <expression> }}, read contexts:

Context Contains Example github The event and run: event_name, ref, sha, actor, repository, event.* github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' env Environment variables set with env: env.NODE_ENV vars Configuration variables (org, repo, environment) vars.AWS_REGION secrets Encrypted secrets, masked in logs secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK_URL inputs workflow_dispatch or workflow_call inputs inputs.environment matrix, strategy Current matrix values matrix.node steps Outputs and outcomes of earlier steps in the job steps.meta.outputs.version needs Results and outputs of jobs this job needs needs.build.outputs.digest job, runner The current job's container/services; the runner's OS, temp dir runner.os

Operators (==, !=, &&, ||, !) and functions such as contains(), startsWith(), format(), join(), toJSON(), fromJSON(), and hashFiles() are available. Status functions control whether a step or job runs: success() (the default), failure(), cancelled(), and always().

Two rules prevent confusion:

  • Expressions are evaluated before the step runs, by the runner, and the result is pasted into the script. Untrusted values (PR titles, branch names) must therefore never be interpolated into run: directly; pass them through env: instead.
  • Not every context is available everywhere: for example, secrets cannot be referenced directly in if: conditions, and env cannot be used in runs-on. The contexts reference has an availability table.

docs.title: needs, if, and outputs
docs.text:
needs builds the job graph and gives access to upstream outputs. if decides whether a job or step runs. Outputs are written to files the runner provides:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}   # job output from a step output
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - id: meta
        run: echo "version=$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  report:
    needs: build
    if: github.event_name == 'push' && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          VERSION: ${{ needs.build.outputs.version }}
        run: echo "Built $VERSION" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
File variable Effect $GITHUB_OUTPUT name=value lines become step outputs (steps.<id>.outputs.name) $GITHUB_ENV NAME=value lines become environment variables for later steps $GITHUB_PATH Directories added to PATH for later steps $GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY Markdown shown on the run's summary page

When a job fails, the jobs that need it are skipped, and a skipped job counts as successful for required checks. Use an aggregator job with if: always() as the required check (see pipeline design).

docs.title: env, vars, and secrets
docs.text:
env: Configuration variables (vars) Secrets (secrets) Defined in The workflow file (workflow, job, or step level) Repository, organization, or environment settings Repository, organization, or environment settings Visible in logs Yes Yes Masked (***) Use for Non-sensitive values tied to the workflow Non-sensitive settings that differ per repo or environment (region, URLs) Tokens, passwords, keys Fork pull requests Available Available Not available (except a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN)

Environment-level secrets and variables override repository-level ones with the same name, and are only available to jobs that reference that environment, after its protection rules pass. Prefer OIDC federation over long-lived cloud keys stored as secrets wherever the provider supports it.

docs.title: Environments and protection rules
docs.text:
An environment (staging, production) is a named deployment target with its own secrets, variables, and deployment protection rules:

  • Required reviewers: up to six people or teams; one approval lets the job proceed, and you can prevent the person who triggered the run from approving it.
  • Wait timer: delay the job by a number of minutes.
  • Deployment branches and tags: only main (or v* tags) may deploy to production.
  • Custom protection rules: GitHub Apps that check external conditions (change tickets, monitoring).
jobs:
  deploy-production:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://api.taskflow.example.com

A job that names the environment pauses until the rules pass, and every run creates a deployment record visible on the repository's deployments page, linking commit, run, environment, and status. Availability in private repositories depends on the plan: environments need GitHub Pro, Team, or Enterprise, and required reviewers and wait timers need GitHub Enterprise.

docs.title: concurrency
docs.text:
concurrency limits how many runs or jobs in the same group run at once:

# Cancel superseded PR runs, never a main run that has started
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

# Serialize deploys to one environment
jobs:
  deploy-production:
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-production
      cancel-in-progress: false

With cancel-in-progress: false, a new run waits while one is in progress, and if a newer run arrives while one is already pending, the older pending run is cancelled; so a deploy queue holds at most one running and one waiting run, and the waiting one is always the newest. That is usually what you want for deployments (the latest commit wins), but it means intermediate commits are not deployed individually.

docs.title: Caching
docs.text:
Two ways to cache dependencies:

  • Built into setup actions: actions/setup-node with cache: npm caches npm's download cache keyed on the lockfile. Recent versions also enable npm caching automatically when package.json declares npm as its package manager, which you can turn off with package-manager-cache: false (worth doing in privileged release workflows).
  • actions/cache for anything else, with an explicit key and restore-keys (examples in pipeline design).

Caches are immutable per key, scoped to branches (a branch can read its own and the default branch's caches), limited per repository (10 GB by default), and evicted after 7 days without use.

docs.title: Reusable workflows and composite actions
docs.text:
Two ways to avoid copy-pasting YAML across jobs and repositories:

Composite action Reusable workflow Defined in action.yml with runs.using: composite A workflow with on: workflow_call Called from A step: uses: ./.github/actions/setup A job: uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml or org/repo/.github/workflows/deploy.yml@v3 Contains Steps Jobs (with their own runners, services, environments) Secrets Receive values only as inputs Declared secrets, or secrets: inherit Logs One step in the caller's log Each job and step logged separately Best for Setup sequences (install, configure, login) Whole standardized pipelines (build, deploy)

Details that trip people up: a reusable workflow cannot inherit the caller's workflow-level env:; the called workflow can only reduce, never raise, the GITHUB_TOKEN permissions the caller grants; and called workflows from other repositories should be pinned to a tag or, better, a commit SHA.

docs.title: GITHUB_TOKEN and the permissions block
docs.text:
Each run receives an automatically generated GITHUB_TOKEN, scoped to the repository and expiring when the job ends (or after 24 hours at most). Its permissions come from the repository or organization default (read-only for repositories created since early 2023), overridden by the workflow's permissions: block:

permissions:            # workflow level: applies to every job
  contents: read

jobs:
  release:
    permissions:        # job level: replaces the workflow-level set for this job
      contents: write   # create tags and releases
      packages: write   # push to ghcr.io
      id-token: write   # request an OIDC token for cloud login or attestations
      attestations: write
Scope Grants contents Read code; write to push commits, tags, releases pull-requests Comment on, label, or update pull requests issues Create and edit issues packages Read or publish GitHub Packages (GHCR) id-token write lets the job request an OIDC token actions, checks, statuses, deployments Manage runs, check runs, commit statuses, deployments security-events Upload code scanning results attestations Create artifact attestations

Any scope not listed is none once a permissions block exists, so permissions: {} disables everything. Two more rules: events created with GITHUB_TOKEN do not start new workflow runs (except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch), and actions/checkout persists the token in the job for later Git commands unless you set persist-credentials: false.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Need Use Avoid Checks on every PR pull_request (+ merge_group with a queue) pull_request_target for running PR code Deploy after merge push to main with environments Deploying from PR workflows Manual operations workflow_dispatch with typed inputs Editing the workflow to trigger it Nightly jobs schedule (UTC cron, off the hour) Relying on exact timing Repeated setup steps Composite action Copy-pasted steps Standard pipeline across many repos Reusable workflow, pinned Forked copies of YAML that drift Private network access Ephemeral self-hosted runners Persistent self-hosted runners on public repositories Cloud credentials OIDC with id-token: write Long-lived access keys in secrets

docs.title: Complete CI workflow for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npm run format:check

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      mongo:
        image: mongo:8.0
        ports:
          - 27017:27017
        options: >-
          --health-cmd "mongosh --quiet --eval 'db.adminCommand({ ping: 1 })'"
          --health-interval 5s
          --health-timeout 5s
          --health-retries 12
    env:
      NODE_ENV: test
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow_test
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Unit tests
        run: npm test
      - name: Integration tests against MongoDB
        run: |
          mkdir -p reports
          npm run test:integration
      - name: Upload test report
        if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: integration-report
          path: reports/
          retention-days: 14

  build:
    needs: [lint, test]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build
      - id: meta
        run: echo "version=$(node -p "require('./package.json').version")-${GITHUB_SHA::7}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: dist-${{ steps.meta.outputs.version }}
          path: dist/

  ci-ok:
    if: always()
    needs: [lint, test, build]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Fail if any required job failed or was cancelled
        if: contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1

{
  "scripts": {
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check .",
    "test": "node --test \"test/unit/**/*.test.js\"",
    "test:integration": "node --test --test-concurrency=1 --test-reporter=spec --test-reporter-destination=stdout --test-reporter=junit --test-reporter-destination=reports/integration.xml \"test/integration/**/*.test.js\"",
    "build": "node scripts/build.js"
  }
}

How the pieces fit:

  • Triggers: PRs, the merge queue, pushes to main, and a manual button. concurrency cancels outdated PR runs but never cancels a main run that has started.
  • Least privilege: the whole workflow only reads the repository, and persist-credentials: false stops checkout from leaving the token configured for later Git commands, so test code and dependencies cannot reuse it.
  • Service container: mongo:8.0 starts before the steps; the health check (using mongosh, which the official image includes) makes the job wait until MongoDB answers. Because the job runs directly on the runner, the mapped port is reachable at localhost:27017. (If the job itself ran in a container, it would use the service name mongo as the host.) Service containers require Linux runners.
  • Isolation: integration test files run one at a time (--test-concurrency=1) because they share one database; each test cleans up its own data.
  • Reports: the JUnit report is uploaded even when tests fail (!cancelled()), so failures can be inspected.
  • One required check: ci-ok fails if any job failed or was cancelled, so branch protection requires just ci-ok.

docs.title: A manual deployment with typed inputs
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy-manual.yml
name: deploy (manual)
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: environment
        required: true
      image-digest:
        description: "sha256:... digest to deploy"
        type: string
        required: true

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: ${{ inputs.environment }}
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-${{ inputs.environment }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Validate the digest format
        env:
          DIGEST: ${{ inputs.image-digest }}
        run: |
          [[ "$DIGEST" =~ ^sha256:[0-9a-f]{64}$ ]] || { echo "invalid digest"; exit 1; }
      - name: Deploy
        env:
          ENVIRONMENT: ${{ inputs.environment }}
          IMAGE: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ inputs.image-digest }}
        run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "$ENVIRONMENT" "$IMAGE"

gh workflow run deploy-manual.yml -f environment=staging -f image-digest=sha256:<digest>
gh run watch                          # follow the run in the terminal

User input reaches the shell only through env: and is validated before use, which closes the script-injection hole.

docs.title: A composite action for shared setup
docs.text:
# .github/actions/setup-taskflow/action.yml
name: Set up TaskFlow
description: Install Node.js from .nvmrc and dependencies with npm ci
inputs:
  npm-ci-args:
    description: Extra arguments for npm ci
    required: false
    default: ""
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
      with:
        node-version-file: .nvmrc
        cache: npm
    - shell: bash
      env:
        NPM_CI_ARGS: ${{ inputs.npm-ci-args }}
      run: npm ci $NPM_CI_ARGS

# usage in any job of the same repository (after checkout)
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-taskflow
  - run: npm test

Composite run steps must declare shell. A local action needs the repository checked out first, because the runner reads action.yml from the workspace.

docs.title: A reusable deployment workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: deploy
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      environment:
        type: string
        required: true
      image:
        type: string
        required: true
    outputs:
      url:
        description: URL of the deployed environment
        value: ${{ jobs.deploy.outputs.url }}

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: ${{ inputs.environment }}
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-${{ inputs.environment }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    outputs:
      url: ${{ steps.deploy.outputs.url }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: ${{ vars.AWS_REGION }}
      - id: deploy
        env:
          ENVIRONMENT: ${{ inputs.environment }}
          IMAGE: ${{ inputs.image }}
        run: |
          ./scripts/deploy.sh "$ENVIRONMENT" "$IMAGE"
          echo "url=https://$ENVIRONMENT.taskflow.example.com" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

# Caller (excerpt of .github/workflows/release.yml)
jobs:
  deploy-staging:
    needs: build-image
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write          # the called job needs OIDC; the caller must grant it
    with:
      environment: staging
      image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ needs.build-image.outputs.digest }}

  smoke-test:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          URL: ${{ needs.deploy-staging.outputs.url }}
        run: curl --fail --retry 5 --retry-all-errors "$URL/healthz"

The environment's protection rules and environment-scoped variables (vars.AWS_DEPLOY_ROLE_ARN can differ between staging and production) apply inside the called job, so every repository using this workflow gets the same guarded deployment.

docs.title: Lint your workflows
docs.text:
# actionlint catches syntax errors, unknown contexts, and shell issues in run: blocks
actionlint .github/workflows/*.yml

Running actionlint in CI on changes under .github/workflows/ catches mistakes (a typo in needs, an undefined output, an invalid cron expression) before they reach main.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set permissions: contents: read at the top of every workflow and grant more per job only where needed.
  • Pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs; at least pin official actions to a major version and keep them updated with Dependabot.
  • Pass untrusted values to scripts through env:, never inline ${{ }} in run:.
  • Use concurrency to cancel superseded PR runs and to serialize deploys.
  • Give every job timeout-minutes; the six-hour default hides hangs.
  • Cache with setup actions or lockfile-keyed actions/cache; never cache secrets.
  • Use environments with required reviewers and branch restrictions for production, and OIDC instead of stored cloud keys.
  • Extract repeated steps into composite actions and whole pipelines into reusable workflows.
  • Require one aggregator check, include merge_group when using a merge queue, and lint workflows with actionlint.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The merge queue never merges anything. Detect: queued PRs time out waiting for required checks; no runs appear for gh-readonly-queue/* refs. Cause: the workflow lacks the merge_group trigger. Fix: add merge_group: to every workflow that provides required checks.
  • Integration tests fail with "connection refused" to MongoDB. Detect: errors at the first database call, only in CI. Cause: tests start before MongoDB is ready, or they connect to mongo while running directly on the runner (or to localhost while running in a container). Fix: add a service health check, and use localhost with port mapping for runner jobs or the service name for container jobs.
  • Fork contributors' PRs fail with empty credentials. Detect: steps using secrets.* fail only on PRs from forks. Cause: secrets are not passed to pull_request runs from forks, by design. Fix: keep PR checks secret-free (service containers, mocks), and run secret-dependent jobs after merge; do not switch to pull_request_target to get secrets.
  • Two deployments to production ran at the same time. Detect: overlapping runs in the deployments history; mixed versions. Cause: no concurrency group for the deploy job. Fix: concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }.
  • A workflow suddenly fails with "Resource not accessible by integration". Detect: a step calling the GitHub API or pushing gets 403. Cause: the GITHUB_TOKEN lacks the needed scope (a permissions block was added, or the org default became read-only). Fix: grant exactly the missing scope at the job level.
  • Nightly scheduled job stopped running. Detect: no runs for weeks; a banner says the workflow was disabled. Cause: scheduled workflows in public repositories are disabled after 60 days without repository activity. Fix: re-enable it (gh workflow enable) and add a keep-alive only if it is genuinely needed.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Workflow: A YAML automation file in .github/workflows/.
  • Event (trigger): The activity that starts a workflow run.
  • Job: Steps executed on one runner; jobs form a graph via needs.
  • Step: A single run command or uses action within a job.
  • Action: A reusable unit of steps (JavaScript, Docker, or composite).
  • Runner: The machine that executes a job, GitHub-hosted or self-hosted.
  • Context: An object available to expressions, such as github, needs, or secrets.
  • Expression: ${{ }} syntax evaluated before a step runs.
  • Service container: A container (for example MongoDB) started for a job's duration.
  • Environment: A deployment target with protection rules, secrets, and variables.
  • Concurrency group: A key that limits simultaneous runs or jobs.
  • Reusable workflow: A workflow triggered by workflow_call and used as a job.
  • Composite action: An action that bundles several steps.
  • GITHUB_TOKEN: The per-run token whose scopes are set by permissions.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming jobs share files; each job runs on a fresh runner.
  • Interpolating ${{ github.event.* }} into run: scripts.
  • Granting write-all or relying on a permissive org default.
  • Expecting secrets in fork PRs, then reaching for pull_request_target.
  • Requiring a check that can be skipped into a pass.
  • Using env or secrets in places where those contexts are not available.
  • Forgetting that schedule uses UTC and runs on the default branch.
  • Running untrusted PR code on persistent self-hosted runners.
  • Treating cancel-in-progress: false as a full queue; only the newest pending run waits.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the relationship between an event, a workflow, a job, a step, and a runner.
  2. Which events would you use for PR checks, deploying main, a manual rollback, and a nightly scan, and what are the caveats of each?
  3. Why should ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} never appear inside a run: script, and what is the safe alternative?
  4. How do step outputs become job outputs, and how does a later job read them?
  5. Compare env, vars, and secrets, including what fork PRs can see.
  6. A deploy workflow uses concurrency: { group: deploy-prod, cancel-in-progress: false }. Commits A, B, C, and D merge one minute apart while each deploy takes ten minutes. Which commits get deployed? (A, then D; B and C are cancelled while pending.)
  7. When do you choose a composite action and when a reusable workflow?
  8. What does permissions: {} do, and which scopes does a job that pushes an image to GHCR and logs in to AWS with OIDC need?
