docs.title: Testing and Quality Gates
docs.text:
A quality gate is an automated check a change must pass before it moves to the next stage: merging, deploying to staging, or reaching production. The pipeline is a sequence of such gates, each catching a different class of problem at a different cost. Designing them well means putting each kind of test where it gives the most confidence per minute, and keeping every gate trustworthy enough that red always means "stop".

This lesson covers the test pyramid and testing trophy in CI, where lint, formatting, type checks, unit, integration, and end-to-end tests belong, service containers, test sharding, flaky test detection and quarantine, coverage thresholds and their limits, required checks, preview environments for end-to-end tests, and performance budgets.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Tests are only useful in CI if they are fast enough to run on every change and reliable enough to believe. A suite that takes 40 minutes gets skipped or batched; a suite that fails randomly trains people to click "re-run" until green, at which point real failures slip through. Google reported that about 1.5% of its test runs produced a flaky result and that 84% of observed pass-to-fail transitions involved a flaky test, so the cost of unreliable tests is not theoretical. Well-placed gates catch most defects in minutes at low cost, and reserve slow, expensive, realistic tests for changes that already passed everything cheaper.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google on flaky tests. Flaky Tests at Google and How We Mitigate Them reports a continual rate of about 1.5% of test runs with a flaky result, that almost 16% of tests had some flakiness, and that about 84% of pass-to-fail transitions in CI involved a flaky test, which is why flakiness needs active management.
  • The practical test pyramid. Ham Vocke's The Practical Test Pyramid on martinfowler.com explains writing many fast, isolated tests and few slow, broad ones, and how each layer fits a deployment pipeline.
  • The testing trophy. Kent C. Dodds' testing trophy argues for static analysis as the base and integration tests as the largest layer for web applications, because they give the most confidence per test.
  • Hermetic presubmit tests at Google. The CI chapter of Software Engineering at Google describes the Google Takeout team moving sandboxed environment tests to presubmit, which prevented 95% of broken servers caused by bad configuration and cut nightly deployment failures by 50%.

Popular tools and providers: Jest, Vitest, and the Node.js test runner (node:test) for unit and integration tests, Supertest for HTTP APIs, Testcontainers and GitHub Actions service containers for real dependencies, Playwright and Cypress for end-to-end tests, k6 and Lighthouse CI for performance budgets, and Stryker for mutation testing.

docs.title: The pyramid and the trophy in CI
docs.text:
Both models make the same economic argument: lower layers are cheaper, faster, and more precise; higher layers are more realistic but slower and flakier.

Layer Pyramid emphasis Trophy emphasis Typical TaskFlow example Static analysis (assumed) Base of the trophy ESLint, Prettier, TypeScript, secret scanning Unit tests Largest layer Some Due-date validation logic Integration tests Middle Largest layer POST /tasks through Express into a real MongoDB End-to-end tests Small tip Small top Sign in, create a task, see it in TaskFlow Web

For a typical API, integration tests that exercise HTTP routes against a real database catch the bugs that matter (queries, validation, error handling) with few mocks, so many teams weight toward the trophy. For pure logic libraries the pyramid's unit-heavy shape fits better.

docs.title: Where each check runs
docs.text: Check Stage Blocks merge? Target time Format check, lint PR Yes Seconds Type check PR Yes Under a minute Unit tests PR Yes Under a minute Integration tests with service containers PR Yes 1-3 minutes Dependency review and secret scanning PR Yes for high severity Seconds Build and container image scan PR (build) and main (push) Yes A few minutes End-to-end tests PR preview or staging after merge Yes before production 5-15 minutes, sharded Performance budgets PR (web) or staging (API load test) Yes for clear regressions Minutes Canary analysis Production rollout Blocks full rollout Minutes to an hour

docs.title: Real dependencies: service containers and alternatives
docs.text:
Integration tests need a database. Options, from most to least realistic:

Option How Pros Cons Service container services: mongo: image: mongo:8.0 in the job Real MongoDB, same version as production, no code changes Linux runners only; one instance shared by the job Testcontainers Library starts containers from test code Per-suite isolation, works locally the same way Needs Docker on the runner; slower startup In-memory server mongodb-memory-server downloads and runs mongod No Docker needed Binary download; may differ from production setup Mocks Replace the driver in tests Fast Misses query, index, and validation bugs

Whatever you choose, keep tests isolated: each test creates the data it needs and cleans up, test files that share one database run serially (or use a database per worker), and nothing depends on test order.

docs.title: Test sharding
docs.text:
When one suite is too slow, split it across parallel jobs. Each shard runs a deterministic subset:

Tool Command Node.js test runner node --test --test-shard=2/4 Jest jest --shard=2/4 Vitest vitest run --shard=2/4 Playwright npx playwright test --shard=2/4

With a matrix of four shards, a 12-minute end-to-end suite takes roughly 3 minutes plus per-job setup. Shards finish unevenly when test files vary in length, so split long files. Merge the shards' reports afterwards (Playwright's blob reporter and merge-reports exist for this).

docs.title: Flaky tests
docs.text:
A flaky test passes and fails on the same code. Typical causes:

  • Fixed sleeps and races (waiting 500 ms for something that usually takes 400).
  • Shared state: a database, files, or globals left behind by another test.
  • Order dependence: a test passes only after another one ran.
  • Real external services, networks, and DNS.
  • Dates, time zones, and randomness without fixed seeds.
  • Resource limits: slow shared runners, timeouts set too tight.

A sound policy:

  1. Detect. Retries that turn a failure into a pass mark a test as flaky (Playwright reports these as "flaky"). Track flaky counts per test over time.
  2. Quarantine tests that block many PRs: move them out of the required checks into a non-blocking job, with an issue, an owner, and a deadline. The quarantine list must stay short.
  3. Fix the root cause: replace sleeps with waiting for a condition, isolate data, fake time, stub external services.
  4. Verify by running the test many times in a loop before restoring it.

Automatic retries (for example retries: 2 in CI) keep the pipeline moving but hide flakiness unless you report it; Playwright's --fail-on-flaky-tests turns "passed on retry" into a failure when you want to enforce zero tolerance.

docs.title: Coverage thresholds and their limits
docs.text:
Coverage tools report which lines, branches, and functions ran during tests. A threshold fails the build when coverage drops below a number:

node --test --experimental-test-coverage \
  --test-coverage-lines=80 --test-coverage-branches=70 \
  "test/unit/**/*.test.js"

Coverage is useful as a floor (to stop untested code piling up) and as a map (to find untested areas), but it measures execution, not verification: a test that calls a function and asserts nothing earns full coverage. Practical guidance:

  • Set thresholds a little below the current level and ratchet up; never chase 100%.
  • Prefer "no decrease on changed files" over a global number.
  • Review what tests assert, not only what they execute; mutation testing (Stryker) measures whether tests catch deliberately injected bugs.
  • Exclude generated code and configuration from coverage.

docs.title: Required checks
docs.text: A gate only protects main if branch rules require it. Combine the quality gates into one aggregator job and require that job (see pipeline design and pull requests and code review). Optional checks are informative, but people learn that they can be ignored.

docs.title: Preview environments for end-to-end tests
docs.text:
A preview environment is a short-lived deployment of one pull request: TaskFlow Web and API built from the PR, with seeded test data, at a unique URL. End-to-end tests run against it before merge, and reviewers can click through the change. Frontend platforms such as Vercel and Netlify create deploy previews automatically; for APIs, teams deploy to a per-PR Kubernetes namespace or run the stack with Docker Compose inside the CI job.

Rules that keep previews safe and cheap:

  • Use test data and test credentials only; never production data.
  • Tear down on PR close (pull_request with types: [closed]) and with a scheduled sweeper for leftovers.
  • Do not deploy fork PRs with secrets; run previews only for branches in the same repository.

docs.title: Performance budgets
docs.text:
A performance budget is a limit the build must not exceed: p95 latency, error rate, page weight, Largest Contentful Paint. In CI, budgets catch regressions the moment they are introduced:

Target Tool Example budget API latency and errors k6 thresholds p95 under 300 ms, error rate under 1% at 20 virtual users Web page performance Lighthouse CI assertions Performance score at least 0.9, LCP under 2.5 s JavaScript bundle size Bundler output checks Main bundle under a set number of kilobytes

Short smoke load tests fit in PR or staging pipelines; full load tests run on a schedule against a production-like environment (see performance testing).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Test type Use when Avoid when Unit tests Pure logic, edge cases, error handling Testing framework glue or simple data passing Integration tests with a real database Routes, queries, validation, transactions Behavior that a unit test covers more precisely Contract tests Several services or clients depend on an API's shape A single app with one client in the same repo End-to-end tests A few critical user journeys (sign in, create task, pay) Every edge case (too slow and flaky) Coverage thresholds Preventing untested code from accumulating As the measure of test quality Preview environments UI changes, end-to-end tests before merge When the cost per PR is high and staging tests suffice Performance budgets in PRs Web pages and hot API endpoints Full-scale load tests (run on a schedule instead)

docs.title: An integration test against the service container
docs.text:
// test/integration/tasks.test.js
import { test, before, after, beforeEach } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import request from "supertest";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import { createApp } from "../../src/app.js";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
let app;
let db;

before(async () => {
  await client.connect();
  db = client.db();                  // database name from the URI: taskflow_test
  app = createApp({ db });
});

beforeEach(async () => {
  await db.collection("tasks").deleteMany({});   // each test starts clean
});

after(async () => {
  await client.close();
});

test("POST /tasks creates a task that GET /tasks/:id returns", async () => {
  const created = await request(app)
    .post("/tasks")
    .send({ title: "Write CI docs" })
    .expect(201);

  const res = await request(app).get(`/tasks/${created.body.id}`).expect(200);
  assert.equal(res.body.title, "Write CI docs");
});

test("POST /tasks rejects an empty title with 400", async () => {
  await request(app).post("/tasks").send({ title: "" }).expect(400);
});

In CI, MONGODB_URI points at the mongo service container (mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow_test); locally it points at a Docker Compose MongoDB. The same test file runs in both places. Testing Express APIs in depth is covered in testing Express APIs.

docs.title: Sharded Playwright end-to-end tests for TaskFlow Web
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/e2e.yml
name: e2e
on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  e2e:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        shardIndex: [1, 2, 3, 4]
        shardTotal: [4]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --shard=${{ matrix.shardIndex }}/${{ matrix.shardTotal }} --grep-invert @quarantine
      - if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: blob-report-${{ matrix.shardIndex }}
          path: blob-report
          retention-days: 3

  merge-reports:
    if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
    needs: e2e
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          path: all-blob-reports
          pattern: blob-report-*
          merge-multiple: true
      - run: npx playwright merge-reports --reporter html ./all-blob-reports
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: playwright-report
          path: playwright-report
          retention-days: 14

  quarantined:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    continue-on-error: true            # informative only, not a required check
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
      - run: npx playwright test --grep @quarantine --repeat-each 5

// playwright.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from "@playwright/test";

export default defineConfig({
  testDir: "./e2e",
  retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0,          // passing on retry is reported as flaky
  reporter: process.env.CI ? "blob" : "html",
  use: {
    baseURL: process.env.BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:4173",
    trace: "on-first-retry",                 // keep a trace when a retry happens
  },
});

// e2e/create-task.spec.ts (a quarantined test is tagged, not deleted)
import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("create a task from the board", { tag: "@quarantine" }, async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "New task" }).click();
  await page.getByLabel("Title").fill("Write CI docs");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save" }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText("Write CI docs")).toBeVisible();
});

Four shards run in parallel; fail-fast: false lets every shard finish so the merged report shows all failures. Quarantined tests run separately, five times each, so their flakiness stays visible without blocking PRs.

docs.title: Coverage floor in package.json
docs.text:
{
  "scripts": {
    "test": "node --test \"test/unit/**/*.test.js\"",
    "test:coverage": "node --test --experimental-test-coverage --test-coverage-lines=80 --test-coverage-branches=70 --test-coverage-functions=80 \"test/unit/**/*.test.js\""
  }
}

The process exits with code 1 when a threshold is missed, which fails the CI step. The coverage flags are still marked experimental in Node.js; Jest (coverageThreshold) and Vitest (coverage.thresholds) offer the same gate if you use those runners.

docs.title: A preview environment per pull request
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/preview.yml
name: preview
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, closed]

permissions:
  contents: read
  pull-requests: write          # comment the preview URL
  id-token: write               # OIDC login to the cluster's cloud account

jobs:
  deploy-preview:
    # same-repository branches only: fork PRs get no secrets or cloud access
    if: github.event.action != 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: preview
    concurrency:
      group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
      cancel-in-progress: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Build, push, and deploy to a per-PR namespace
        env:
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: ./scripts/preview-deploy.sh "pr-$PR"
      - name: Comment the URL
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: |
          gh pr comment "$PR" --body "Preview: https://pr-$PR.preview.taskflow.example.com"

  teardown-preview:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed' && github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: preview
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - env:
          PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
        run: ./scripts/preview-teardown.sh "pr-$PR"

docs.title: Performance budgets for the API and the web app
docs.text:
// perf/tasks-smoke.js: k6 smoke test with pass/fail thresholds
import http from "k6/http";
import { check } from "k6";

export const options = {
  vus: 20,
  duration: "1m",
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],      // under 1% errors
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],    // 95% of requests under 300 ms
  },
};

export default function () {
  const res = http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/tasks?limit=20`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}` },
  });
  check(res, { "status is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

k6 run -e BASE_URL=https://staging.taskflow.example.com -e API_TOKEN="$STAGING_TEST_TOKEN" perf/tasks-smoke.js
# k6 exits non-zero when a threshold fails, which fails the CI step

{
  "ci": {
    "collect": {
      "startServerCommand": "npm run preview",
      "url": ["http://localhost:4173/"],
      "numberOfRuns": 3
    },
    "assert": {
      "assertions": {
        "categories:performance": ["error", { "minScore": 0.9 }],
        "largest-contentful-paint": ["error", { "maxNumericValue": 2500 }],
        "total-byte-weight": ["warn", { "maxNumericValue": 350000 }]
      }
    },
    "upload": { "target": "temporary-public-storage" }
  }
}

The JSON is TaskFlow Web's lighthouserc.json; npx @lhci/cli autorun builds a report from three runs and fails on the error assertions. Three runs reduce noise, because single Lighthouse runs vary.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Put each test where it catches its class of bug most cheaply; keep the PR pipeline around ten minutes.
  • Prefer integration tests against real dependencies (service containers) over heavy mocking for APIs.
  • Keep tests isolated: own data, cleanup, no order dependence, fixed time and seeds.
  • Shard slow suites and merge reports; split long test files so shards balance.
  • Track flaky tests, quarantine quickly with an owner, and fix root causes; report retries instead of hiding them.
  • Use coverage as a floor and a map, not a target; ratchet, do not chase 100%.
  • Require one aggregate check; keep optional checks few.
  • Run end-to-end tests on preview or staging environments with test data, limited to critical journeys.
  • Gate performance with budgets in CI and run full load tests on a schedule.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Everyone re-runs failed jobs and the "re-run" button is the fix. Detect: a high share of runs with more than one attempt; failures that disappear on retry. Cause: flaky tests in required checks. Fix: measure flakiness per test, quarantine the worst offenders with owners, and fix timing and shared-state problems.
  • Integration tests pass alone but fail in the full suite. Detect: failures depend on which tests ran before; running a file alone passes. Cause: shared database state or parallel test files writing to the same collections. Fix: clean data per test, run files serially (--test-concurrency=1) or give each worker its own database.
  • Coverage is 92% but a basic bug reached production. Detect: the buggy branch shows as covered. Cause: tests executed the code without asserting the outcome. Fix: review assertions, add behavior-focused tests, and try mutation testing on critical modules.
  • The end-to-end suite takes 40 minutes and blocks deploys. Detect: the e2e job dominates the critical path. Cause: too many end-to-end tests covering edge cases, run serially. Fix: move edge cases down to integration tests, keep critical journeys, and shard the rest.
  • A performance regression shipped unnoticed. Detect: p95 latency jumped after a deploy; no CI check failed. Cause: no performance budget in the pipeline. Fix: add a k6 smoke test with thresholds against staging and Lighthouse budgets for the web app.
  • Preview environments pile up and the cloud bill grows. Detect: namespaces or deployments for long-closed PRs. Cause: teardown only on closed events, which can be missed. Fix: add a scheduled sweeper that deletes previews whose PRs are closed, and set resource quotas.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Quality gate: An automated check that must pass before a change moves forward.
  • Test pyramid: Many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, few end-to-end tests.
  • Testing trophy: Static analysis base, with integration tests as the largest layer.
  • Service container: A dependency container started alongside a CI job.
  • Hermetic test: A test whose environment is fully self-contained.
  • Test sharding: Splitting a suite across parallel jobs.
  • Flaky test: A test that both passes and fails on the same code.
  • Quarantine: Removing a flaky test from blocking checks while it is fixed.
  • Code coverage: The share of code executed by tests.
  • Mutation testing: Injecting small bugs to see whether tests catch them.
  • Preview environment: A temporary deployment of one pull request.
  • Performance budget: A limit on a performance metric enforced in CI.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating coverage percentage as proof of quality.
  • Mocking the database in every test and missing query bugs.
  • Writing end-to-end tests for every edge case.
  • Using fixed sleeps instead of waiting for conditions.
  • Retrying flaky tests silently forever.
  • Leaving checks optional and expecting people to honor them.
  • Running previews with production data or secrets available to fork PRs.
  • Running one-off full load tests on every PR instead of short budgets.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare the test pyramid and the testing trophy. Which would you favor for TaskFlow API, and why?
  2. Place lint, type check, unit, integration, end-to-end, and performance checks in a pipeline, with target times.
  3. What are three ways to provide MongoDB to integration tests in CI, and their trade-offs?
  4. An end-to-end suite takes 24 minutes. With 6 shards and 1 minute of setup per shard, roughly how long does it take, assuming even shards? What makes shards uneven? (About 5 minutes; long test files.)
  5. Describe a flaky-test policy from detection to restoration.
  6. Why can 90% coverage coexist with poor tests? What complements coverage?
  7. How would you build preview environments safely for a repository that accepts fork PRs?
  8. Write k6 thresholds for "fewer than 0.5% errors and p99 under 800 ms".

docs.title: Advanced Deployment Patterns
docs.text:
The core strategies (recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary) answer "how do I replace version 1 with version 2?". Large systems add patterns that answer harder questions: how do I test a new version on real traffic without users seeing it, how do I keep WebSocket users connected through ten deploys a day, how do I make sure one bad deploy can only ever reach a small slice of customers, and how do I change an API without breaking clients I do not control?

This lesson covers red/black, ramped (incremental) rollouts, immutable deployments, rainbow deployments, shadow (mirrored) traffic, dark launches, ring and wave deployments, the one-box to one-AZ to one-region to everywhere progression, cell-based deployments, and pinned-version clients with gradual API migration. For each: what it is, how it works, when to use it, and what it costs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
As a system grows, the cost of a bad release grows faster than the system. A bug that reaches every region at once is a global outage; the same bug reaching one host for an hour is a log line. The patterns here all apply one idea, limit and measure exposure, along different axes: time (ramps, bake times), audience (rings, dark launches), infrastructure (one-box, AZ, region, cell), traffic (shadowing), and client versions (pinned APIs).

They are also how real outages are prevented. Google's report on its June 2025 Cloud outage noted that a code path was deployed region by region but was never exercised during the rollout, and that a global data replication then triggered it everywhere at once; its remediations include feature flags for critical binaries and incremental propagation of globally replicated data. CrowdStrike's July 2024 analysis committed to deploying content updates through canary rings instead of to every customer at once. Knowing these patterns is knowing how such incidents are kept small.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon: one box, then waves. The Amazon Builders' Library article Automating safe, hands-off deployments describes production pipelines that deploy first to one box (typically serving at most 10% of requests for a Region or Availability Zone), then in waves: a low-traffic Region one AZ at a time, then a high-traffic Region, then more Regions in parallel. A typical pipeline waits at least one hour after each one-box stage and at least 12 hours after the first regional wave, rolls back automatically on alarms, and avoids nights, weekends, and holidays.
  • Netflix and Spinnaker: red/black. Spinnaker, the delivery platform Netflix open-sourced, calls its blue-green variant red/black: deploy a new server group beside the old one, send traffic to it, then disable the old one while keeping it for rollback. The Spinnaker rollout strategies guide notes that Blue/Green replaces the Red/Black name in Spinnaker 1.30 and later, and also lists "highlander" (destroy the old versions) and "dark" (deploy without routing traffic) rollouts.
  • Slack: cells. Slack's migration to a cellular architecture describes making each AWS Availability Zone a cell: services only send traffic within their own AZ, and operators can drain an AZ at the edge load balancers in 1% steps, with a goal of removing its traffic within 5 minutes, without first knowing the root cause.
  • AWS: cell-based architecture. The whitepaper Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture explains how AWS service teams have used cells for more than a decade to apply the fault isolation of AZs and Regions inside a workload.
  • Microsoft: rings and tiers. Microsoft's Safe deployment practices guide shows a five-tier model used by a Microsoft team, from tier 0 (internal users, highest risk tolerance) to tier 4 (everyone), with a bake time of about a day per tier including a period of peak usage.
  • Stripe: pinned API versions. In APIs as infrastructure: future-proofing Stripe with versioning, Stripe explains that an account is pinned to the newest API version on its first request, can override it per request with the Stripe-Version header, and that older versions are served by "version change modules" that transform responses backward.
  • GitHub: Scientist. Scientist: Measure Twice, Cut Once describes running old and new code paths side by side on real requests, comparing results, and always returning the old result, which GitHub used to rewrite its permissions code safely: shadowing inside one process.
  • Rainbow deploys. Brandon Dimcheff's Rainbow Deploys with Kubernetes describes naming a Deployment per git commit instead of per color, so chat backends holding WebSocket connections that drain over 24 to 48 hours could still deploy many times a day.

Popular tools and providers: Spinnaker, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, AWS CodeDeploy and CodePipeline, Istio and Envoy (mirroring and weighted routing), nginx mirror, Diffy-style response comparison, GitHub Scientist and its ports, LaunchDarkly and other flag services for dark launches, and GitHub environments or Azure Pipelines stages for rings.

docs.title: Red/black
docs.text:
What it is. Netflix's name, carried into Spinnaker, for a blue-green variant built on immutable server groups (auto scaling groups or Kubernetes ReplicaSets).

How it works. The pipeline creates a new server group with the new image beside the old one and waits until it is healthy. It then enables the new group in the load balancer and disables the old group: the old instances stay running but receive no traffic. Rollback re-enables the old group, which is warm and immediate. After a bake period the old group is destroyed. A "highlander" rollout ("there can be only one") destroys the old group as soon as the new one is healthy.

When to use it. Instance-based services in an auto-scaled fleet where fast rollback matters more than briefly paying for double capacity.

Downsides. Double capacity during the bake period, the same shared database constraints as blue-green, and, like blue-green, everyone moves at once unless combined with a canary first.

docs.title: Ramped (incremental) rollout
docs.text:
What it is. Traffic or instances move to the new version in fixed increments on a timer: for example 10% more every minute (CodeDeployDefault.LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute), or rolling batches that grow (1 instance, then 10%, then 25%, then the rest).

How it differs from a canary. A canary waits for analysis to pass before each step; a ramp moves on a schedule and relies on alarms to stop it. A ramp is simpler and needs less traffic for statistics, but it can push a subtle regression to everyone before anyone notices.

When to use it. Services with good alarms but too little traffic for meaningful canary statistics, or as the "finish" phase after a canary has passed its first steps.

Downsides. Exposure grows whether or not the version is healthy; choose step sizes and intervals long enough for alarms to fire (an alarm that needs 5 minutes of data is useless on a 1-minute ramp).

docs.title: Immutable deployments
docs.text:
What it is. Servers or containers are never changed after they start. To deploy, you build a new image (container image, VM image), start new instances from it, move traffic, and terminate the old instances. Nobody runs apt upgrade, git pull, or edits configuration on a live server.

How it works. The deploy unit is the image, identified by a digest or image ID. Every strategy above can be implemented immutably: a rolling update of a Kubernetes Deployment replaces pods, and red/black replaces whole server groups.

When to use it. Almost always for stateless services. It removes configuration drift ("works on server 3 only"), makes every instance identical to what was tested, and makes rollback "start the previous image".

Downsides. Every change, even a one-line config fix, needs a build and a rollout, so pipelines must be fast. Local state on instances is lost on every deploy, so state must live in databases, object storage, or volumes. Boot time matters. See immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: Rainbow deployments
docs.text:
What it is. Blue-green with as many colors as you need: every release gets its own Deployment (named by commit SHA or version), and several versions stay alive at once.

How it works. The router (a Kubernetes Service selector, a load balancer target group) sends new connections to the newest version. Older versions keep only their existing long-lived connections and are deleted once those connections have drained to near zero. Rollback is pointing the router back at the previous version, which is still running.

When to use it. Long-lived connections that you do not want to cut: WebSockets for chat or live collaboration, streaming, long-running consumer sessions, game servers. TaskFlow Web's live task board uses a WebSocket per open browser tab; a rolling deploy would disconnect thousands of tabs and cause a reconnect storm.

Downsides. Many versions run at once, so compatibility rules (schema, events, caches) must hold across several versions, not two. Capacity and cost grow with each live version. Cleanup needs automation that watches connection counts; without it, old versions run for weeks. A security fix must reach old versions too, which may mean forcing reconnects after all.

docs.title: Shadow (mirrored) traffic
docs.text:
What it is. A copy of real production requests is sent to the new version, and its responses are thrown away (or only compared). Users always get the old version's answer.

How it works. A proxy duplicates requests: nginx's mirror module, Istio's mirror with mirrorPercentage, Envoy's request mirroring, or recording and replaying traffic. Tools in the Diffy family compare the two responses; GitHub's Scientist does the same inside one process by running old and new code and returning the old result.

When to use it. Rewrites and migrations where correctness is hard to test with fixtures: a new search backend, a rewritten pricing engine, a database migration (read from both, compare), or performance testing a new version with real traffic shapes.

Downsides and dangers.

  • Side effects. A shadow that writes to the production database, sends email, charges cards, or publishes events causes real damage twice. Shadow only read paths, or point the shadow at sandboxed dependencies and disable side effects with a request marker.
  • Load. Mirroring 100% doubles the load on everything the shadow touches. Start with a small mirror percentage.
  • Noise. Responses legitimately differ (timestamps, generated IDs, ordering). Comparison needs normalization rules.
  • Proxy cost. Keep mirror timeouts short; a slow mirror target ties up proxy resources.

docs.title: Dark launches
docs.text:
What it is. Deploying a feature to production and exercising it without users seeing it: either by running its code path for real requests and discarding the result, or by enabling it only for staff.

How it works. A feature flag guards the new code. In the dark phase the flag is off for users; the code still runs for internal accounts, or runs in the background ("compute the new recommendations, log them, show the old ones"). When metrics look good, the flag is turned on for 1% of users, then more.

When to use it. Features that depend on production scale or data: load on a new storage path, a new ranking algorithm, a new integration. Also to separate the technical risk (does it work under load?) from the product launch date.

Downsides. Hidden load: a dark-launched code path consumes real capacity. Flags left behind after launch become debt. Dark results must be kept away from users, including through caches and logs.

docs.title: Rings and waves
docs.text:
What it is. Users or infrastructure are grouped into rings ordered by risk tolerance, and every release goes through them in order with a bake time in each:

Ring Typical members What it catches 0 The owning team, test tenants Obvious breakage, before any customer 1 All employees ("dogfood") Everyday workflows, real usage patterns 2 Opted-in beta customers or a small region Diversity of real customer data and devices 3 A larger slice (one large region, 25%) Scale problems 4 Everyone Remaining long-tail issues

How it works. The pipeline is a sequence of stages, one per ring, each gated by health checks and a bake time. For server software, rings are usually infrastructure (hosts, AZs, regions); for client software they are audiences (internal, beta channel, staged percentages).

When to use it. Any software with a large user base where a bad release has a high cost, including server fleets, desktop apps, mobile apps, and configuration or content pushes.

Downsides. Total rollout time grows to days, so an urgent fix needs a documented expedited path (Microsoft's guide lets the most severe hotfixes skip tiers with approval). Inner rings must be representative, or problems slip through: employees may all use the same browser, region, and account type.

docs.title: One box, then one AZ, then one Region, then everywhere
docs.text:
This is the infrastructure version of rings, as described in the Amazon Builders' Library:

  1. One box: a single host (or a single container task) receives a small share of one AZ's traffic. Its own metrics are compared with the rest of the fleet, and it bakes for at least an hour.
  2. First wave: a low-traffic Region, one Availability Zone at a time, so a failure affects one AZ, which the system is already built to survive.
  3. Later waves: a high-traffic Region, then several Regions in parallel, each still one AZ at a time, with shorter bake times as confidence grows.
  4. Automatic rollback at every stage when alarms fire, and a block on promotion while any high-severity alarm is active.

Worked example: TaskFlow API runs in 3 Regions with 3 AZs each and 10 hosts per AZ. The one box is 1 of 30 hosts in a Region, about 3.3% of that Region's traffic and about 1.1% of global traffic. The first AZ in the first Region is about 11% of global traffic, but if it fails, the other two AZs in that Region can absorb its load. A bug that slips past the one box therefore reaches at most a fraction of users for minutes, not everyone.

The cost is time: one hour, twelve hours, a few hours per later wave, and no deploys at night or on weekends add up to days for a global rollout. Amazon's article reports that its default pipelines take roughly four to five business days to deploy globally.

docs.title: Cells and blast radius
docs.text:
What it is. The whole stack (load balancer, API instances, queues, database) is copied into several independent cells, and each customer lives in exactly one cell. A thin cell router maps a request's tenant or customer ID to its cell.

How it works for deployments. Deploy to one cell, bake, then the next. A bad deploy, a poison message, a runaway query, or a corrupted index can only affect the customers of the cells it has reached. With N cells, the first deploy step exposes 1/N of customers, and so does any failure that stays inside a cell. Cells also cap the maximum size of each database and fleet, so a cell can be load-tested at its full size.

When to use it. Multi-tenant services with strict availability targets, or where one customer's behavior (a noisy tenant) must not affect others. Slack's AZ-based cells show a lighter variant: cells by AZ, which makes draining a failing AZ a routine action.

Downsides. Cells multiply infrastructure and operations; you now run N databases. Anything that crosses cells (global search, admin reports, a customer who must move between cells) needs extra design. The cell router and any global control plane become the most critical components: a bad change there reaches every cell, so they need the same cautious, staged rollout themselves.

docs.title: Pinned-version clients and gradual API migration
docs.text:
Server deploys finish in hours; clients you do not control (mobile apps, partner integrations, customers' scripts) upgrade over months or never. A deployment strategy for an API therefore includes a strategy for changing the API contract.

What it is. Each client is pinned to an API version: an explicit version header, a version in the URL (/v2/tasks), or a version stored on the account when it first called the API (Stripe's approach). The server keeps serving every supported version.

How it works. The core code produces only the newest response shape. Each breaking change ships with a small transform that converts a newer response into the previous version's shape (and, for requests, the old request shape into the new one). A request pinned to an old version passes through the transforms in reverse order. Additive changes (a new optional field) need no new version at all.

Gradual migration then looks like this:

  1. Ship the new version; new clients use it, old clients keep their pin.
  2. Measure usage per version and per client.
  3. Announce deprecation with a date; return a Deprecation or Sunset header and notify the owners of clients still on old versions.
  4. Retire the old version only when its traffic is near zero or the notice period has ended.

When to use it. Public and partner APIs, and APIs behind mobile apps. For an internal API whose only client is your own SPA, backward compatibility for one or two releases (expand and contract) is usually enough.

Downsides. Every supported version is code you must test. Transform chains grow, and without usage data old versions are never retired. API versioning strategies are compared in keeping frontend and backend in sync, and deprecation and sunset policies are covered in release trains and release management.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Problem Pattern Avoid it when Need instant rollback for an instance-based fleet Red/black Capacity cannot double, even briefly Too little traffic for canary statistics Ramped rollout with alarms Alarms are slow or missing Configuration drift, snowflake servers Immutable deployments Never; but state must be externalized first Long-lived WebSocket or streaming connections Rainbow deployments Versions cannot stay compatible across several releases Rewrite whose correctness is hard to test Shadow traffic or in-process comparison The path has side effects you cannot stub Feature needs production scale before launch Dark launch behind a flag You cannot afford the hidden load Large user base, high cost of a bad release Rings or waves with bake times A single small service with few users (the delay costs more than it saves) Global, multi-region service One box, one AZ, one Region, then everywhere Single-region systems (use one box plus AZ by AZ) Multi-tenant service with strict availability goals Cells, deployed cell by cell Small systems where N copies cost more than the risk Clients you do not control Pinned versions and gradual migration Only your own client calls the API

docs.title: Mirroring a share of traffic with nginx
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-shadow.conf
upstream taskflow_v1        { server 10.0.1.10:3000; server 10.0.2.10:3000; }
upstream taskflow_v2_shadow { server 10.0.3.10:3000; }

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    server_name api.taskflow.example.com;
    # ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key as in the main config

    # Mirror only the read-heavy search endpoint
    location /tasks/search {
        mirror /mirror;
        mirror_request_body off;          # GET requests have no body to copy
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_v1;
    }

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_v1;    # everything else is not mirrored
    }

    location = /mirror {
        internal;
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_v2_shadow$request_uri;
        proxy_set_header X-Shadow-Request "1";
        proxy_connect_timeout 1s;
        proxy_read_timeout 2s;
    }
}

Mirroring is configured per location, so mirror only endpoints that are read-only by design. The X-Shadow-Request header tells the shadow it must not cause side effects, and the guard below refuses writes even if one slips through.

docs.title: Mirroring with Istio
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-virtualservice.yaml
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  hosts:
    - taskflow-api
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: taskflow-api
            subset: v1
          weight: 100
      mirror:
        host: taskflow-api
        subset: v2
      mirrorPercentage:
        value: 10.0        # copy 10% of requests to v2; responses are ignored

docs.title: Guarding side effects in a shadow instance
docs.text:
// src/middleware/shadow-guard.js: make shadow requests side-effect free
export function shadowGuard({ email, payments, events }) {
  const noop = async () => ({ skipped: "shadow" });

  return (req, res, next) => {
    const isShadow =
      process.env.APP_ROLE === "shadow" || req.get("X-Shadow-Request") === "1";

    // Request-scoped adapters: real ones for users, no-ops for shadows
    req.deps = isShadow
      ? { email: { send: noop }, payments: { charge: noop }, events: { publish: noop } }
      : { email, payments, events };

    if (isShadow && req.method !== "GET") {
      return res.status(202).json({ shadow: true }); // never apply writes
    }
    next();
  };
}

Route handlers call req.deps.email.send(...) instead of importing the email client directly, so a shadow can never reach the real provider. Running the shadow with its own database user that only has read permissions adds a second, independent guard.

docs.title: A rainbow deploy script for Kubernetes
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/rainbow-deploy.sh: one Deployment per commit; old ones drain
# usage: rainbow-deploy.sh <commit-sha>
set -euo pipefail
sha="$1"
name="taskflow-realtime-${sha:0:7}"

# 1. Create this version's Deployment from a template (labels include the sha)
sed -e "s/__NAME__/$name/g" -e "s/__SHA__/$sha/g" k8s/realtime-deployment.tpl.yaml |
  kubectl apply -f -
kubectl rollout status "deployment/$name" --timeout=5m

# 2. Point new connections at it; existing sockets stay where they are
kubectl patch service taskflow-realtime \
  -p "{\"spec\":{\"selector\":{\"app\":\"taskflow-realtime\",\"version\":\"$sha\"}}}"

# 3. Delete older versions whose open connections have drained below 20
for old in $(kubectl get deployments -l app=taskflow-realtime \
              -o jsonpath='{.items[*].metadata.name}'); do
  [ "$old" = "$name" ] && continue
  open=$(./scripts/open-connections.sh "$old")   # reads the app's metric
  if [ "$open" -lt 20 ]; then
    echo "deleting $old ($open connections left)"
    kubectl delete deployment "$old"
  fi
done

Run step 3 on a schedule as well as after each deploy, so drained versions are cleaned up even when no new release happens. Rollback is step 2 with the previous SHA.

docs.title: Waves with bake times in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/release-waves.yml
name: Release in waves

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      image:
        description: Image digest to release
        required: true

env:
  IMAGE: ${{ inputs.image }}   # scripts read "$IMAGE"; never inline inputs in run:

jobs:
  one-box:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod-one-box
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh one-box "$IMAGE"
      - run: ./scripts/bake.sh one-box 60          # watch alarms for 60 minutes

  wave-1:
    needs: one-box
    runs-on: self-hosted                           # a 12-hour bake: GitHub-hosted jobs stop at 6 hours
    environment: prod-wave-1                       # e.g. required reviewers
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh eu-west-1 "$IMAGE" --az-by-az
      - run: ./scripts/bake.sh eu-west-1 720

  wave-2:
    needs: wave-1
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: prod-wave-2
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh us-east-1 "$IMAGE" --az-by-az
      - run: ./scripts/bake.sh us-east-1 180

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/bake.sh: fail (and trigger rollback) if alarms fire during the bake
# usage: bake.sh <target> <minutes>
set -euo pipefail
target="$1"; minutes="$2"
end=$(( $(date +%s) + minutes * 60 ))
while [ "$(date +%s)" -lt "$end" ]; do
  if ./scripts/alarms-firing.sh "$target"; then
    echo "alarm during bake of $target; rolling back" >&2
    ./scripts/rollback.sh "$target"
    exit 1
  fi
  sleep 60
done
echo "$target baked for $minutes minutes without alarms"

GitHub-hosted runner jobs have a maximum run time (6 hours at the time of writing), so very long bakes are better implemented as a scheduled promotion job or in a dedicated delivery tool. The structure, deploy one target, watch, promote or roll back, stays the same.

docs.title: A cell router lookup
docs.text:
// src/cells/cell-for-tenant.js: map a tenant to its cell
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const CELLS = ["cell-1", "cell-2", "cell-3", "cell-4", "cell-5", "cell-6"];

// Explicit placements win: used to move a tenant or isolate a noisy one
const placements = new Map([
  ["tenant-enterprise-0042", "cell-6"],
]);

export function cellForTenant(tenantId) {
  const placed = placements.get(tenantId);
  if (placed) return placed;
  // Stable hash: the same tenant always lands in the same cell
  const n = createHash("sha256").update(tenantId).digest().readUInt32BE(0);
  return CELLS[n % CELLS.length];
}

In production the placement table lives in a small, highly available store, and the router caches it. Adding a cell changes n % length for most tenants, so real systems record each tenant's cell explicitly once assigned instead of recomputing it.

docs.title: Serving pinned API versions
docs.text:
// src/api/versioning.js: serve old API versions from the newest code
const VERSIONS = ["2024-06-01", "2025-03-15", "2026-11-01"]; // oldest to newest
const LATEST = VERSIONS.at(-1);

// Each entry turns a response of that version into the previous version's shape
const downgrades = {
  "2026-11-01": (task) => ({
    ...task,
    status: task.status === "blocked" ? "open" : task.status,
  }),
  "2025-03-15": ({ due, ...task }) => ({
    ...task,
    dueDate: due ? due.date : null,
  }),
};

export function apiVersion(req, res, next) {
  const requested = req.get("TaskFlow-Version") ?? req.account?.pinnedVersion ?? LATEST;
  if (!VERSIONS.includes(requested)) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: `Unknown API version ${requested}` });
  }
  req.apiVersion = requested;
  res.set("TaskFlow-Version", requested);
  next();
}

export function toVersion(task, version) {
  let out = task;
  for (let i = VERSIONS.length - 1; VERSIONS[i] !== version; i -= 1) {
    out = downgrades[VERSIONS[i]](out); // undo newer changes one by one
  }
  return out;
}

// Usage in a route:
// res.json(toVersion(latestShapeTask, req.apiVersion));

A task built in the latest shape ({ due: { date, timezone }, status: "blocked" }) is returned unchanged to a client on 2026-11-01, with status: "open" to a client on 2025-03-15, and additionally with a plain dueDate string to a client on 2024-06-01. Logging req.apiVersion per client gives the usage data needed to retire old versions.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Combine patterns: one box, then a canary within each wave, behind feature flags, deployed immutably.
  • Put the cheapest, fastest-failing stage first (one box, ring 0) and the slowest, broadest last.
  • Give every stage automatic rollback on alarms and a bake time long enough to include real peak traffic.
  • Stage configuration and data pushes (feature files, policies, replicated metadata) with the same caution as code.
  • Shadow only side-effect-free paths, or stub every side effect; start with a small mirror percentage.
  • Automate cleanup: rainbow versions, old server groups, and stale flags.
  • Treat the cell router and global control planes as the most critical deploys you have.
  • Track API usage per version and per client before you deprecate anything.
  • Keep a documented, audited expedited path for urgent fixes.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A shadow deployment sent real emails. Detect: customers receive duplicate messages; the provider's logs show sends from the shadow's hosts. Cause: the shadow used live credentials and the mirrored path had a side effect. Fix: sandbox credentials for shadows, request-scoped no-op adapters, and mirroring only GET routes.
  • Production latency rose when mirroring was enabled. Detect: database CPU and p99 latency climb at the moment the mirror percentage changed. Cause: the shadow shares the production database or cache, doubling load. Fix: point the shadow at a replica or copy, and mirror a smaller share.
  • The cluster fills up with old versions. Detect: dozens of taskflow-realtime-* Deployments, rising node count and cost. Cause: rainbow cleanup only runs after deploys, or connection counts never reach the threshold because of idle clients. Fix: scheduled cleanup, a maximum age after which clients are asked to reconnect, and alerts on the number of live versions.
  • A bad router configuration took down every cell. Detect: all cells report errors simultaneously; cell-level deploys were clean. Cause: the shared routing or control-plane layer was changed globally. Fix: deploy router and control-plane changes with the same staged rollout as cells, and keep them as small as possible.
  • An urgent security fix took four days to reach all regions. Detect: the release sat in bake stages while the vulnerability was public. Cause: the pipeline had no expedited path. Fix: a documented hotfix path with shorter bakes and explicit approval, used rarely and reviewed afterwards.
  • An old API version can never be retired. Detect: the oldest version still serves 8% of requests a year after deprecation. Cause: no per-client usage data, no outreach, no sunset date. Fix: log version per client, send Deprecation and Sunset headers, contact remaining clients, and enforce a date.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Red/black: Netflix and Spinnaker's name for blue-green with immutable server groups, where the old group is disabled but kept.
  • Highlander rollout: a rollout that destroys old versions once the new one is healthy.
  • Ramped (linear) rollout: shifting traffic in fixed increments on a schedule.
  • Immutable deployment: replacing instances with new ones built from a new image instead of changing running ones.
  • Rainbow deployment: many live versions at once, each draining its own long-lived connections.
  • Shadow (mirrored, dark) traffic: copies of real requests sent to a new version whose responses are discarded.
  • Dark launch: a feature running in production without being visible to users.
  • Ring: a group of users or infrastructure that receives a release at the same stage.
  • Wave: one stage of a multi-region rollout.
  • One box: a single host that receives a release first.
  • Cell: an independent, complete copy of a service serving a fixed subset of customers.
  • Blast radius: the share of users or systems a failure can affect.
  • Pinned version: the API version a client is locked to until it upgrades.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking more stages always means more safety; stages that are not representative only add delay.
  • Mirroring write traffic and assuming the shadow is harmless.
  • Deploying code carefully in waves while pushing configuration or data globally in seconds.
  • Treating cells as free; they multiply operations and need a strong router.
  • Keeping rainbow versions forever because nothing deletes them.
  • Versioning every API change, including additive ones that need no new version.
  • Forgetting that a dark-launched feature still consumes production capacity.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. How does red/black differ from a highlander rollout, and what does each cost?
  2. When would you choose a ramped rollout over a canary with analysis?
  3. Why do rainbow deployments need compatibility across more than two versions?
  4. List three ways shadow traffic can harm production and how to prevent each.
  5. A service runs in 4 Regions with 3 AZs each and 8 hosts per AZ. What share of global traffic does the one-box stage receive, and what share does the first AZ receive?
  6. With 10 equal cells, what share of customers does a bug in the first deployed cell affect? What component can still cause a global outage?
  7. How does a server serve a client pinned to an API version that is two breaking changes old?
  8. Why should configuration and data pushes go through staged rollouts too? Give a public example.

docs.text: Command What it does kubectl set image deployment/taskflow-api api=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.1 Start a rolling update kubectl rollout status deployment/taskflow-api --timeout=5m Wait for the rollout, with a timeout kubectl rollout undo deployment/taskflow-api Roll back to the previous ReplicaSet kubectl patch service taskflow-api -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"taskflow-api","color":"green"}}}' Blue-green: point the live Service at green pm2 reload ecosystem.config.cjs --env production --update-env Replace cluster workers one at a time npx migrate-mongo up Apply migrations once, as their own pipeline step aws s3 sync dist/assets "$BUCKET/assets" --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" Upload hashed assets first aws s3 cp dist/index.html "$BUCKET/index.html" --cache-control "no-cache" Upload the entry point last aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id "$DISTRIBUTION_ID" --paths "/index.html" "/" Invalidate only the entry points

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300   # mark the rollout failed after 5 min
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: api
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /readyz, port: 3000 } }
          livenessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /livez, port: 3000 } }

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A dev or test environment, an internal tool Recreate Simplest; short downtime is acceptable Zero downtime for a stateless API Rolling, with honest readiness probes Kubernetes default; only surge capacity Instant rollback, budget for double capacity Blue-green Switch back while blue still runs High traffic, costly bad releases Canary with automated analysis 1% first; grows only while metrics stay healthy Safety on a low-traffic service Blue-green or rolling plus strong tests A 1% canary sees too few requests to judge Many users or many regions Rings or waves with bake times Each stage limits the blast radius Code in production before launch, a kill switch A feature flag Release and undo without a deploy A product answer ("does it convert better?") A/B test behind flags Sticky per user, business metrics, days to weeks A column rename or type change Expand and contract over several releases Old and new code work at every step Recovery from a bad app release Halt the rollout, flag off, ship a fix Installed copies cannot be rolled back

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Kubernetes grace period 30 s by default: SIGTERM, wait, then SIGKILL progressDeadlineSeconds 600 by default; marks the rollout failed, does not undo it Shutdown budget Drain (5 s) + longest request (~10 s) + cleanup (~2 s) < app deadline (25 s) < grace period (30 s) Node server.keepAliveTimeout 5 s by default; set above the proxy idle timeout (ALB: 60 s), for example 65 s PM2 kill_timeout About 1.6 s by default; raise it above the drain time Canary sample size To see 0.2% errors double to 0.4% at 3 standard deviations: at least 4,500 requests Bake times (Amazon) At least 1 h after the one box, 12 h after the first Region Error budget 99.9% a month allows 43.2 min of full outage Flag bucketing SHA-256("<flag key>:<user id>"), first 4 bytes mod 10,000 DORA metrics Change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate, deployment rework rate PostgreSQL migration SET lock_timeout = '2s', SET statement_timeout = '30s' Cache-Control Hashed assets public, max-age=31536000, immutable; index.html no-cache Apple phased release 7 days: 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, then 100%

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating a rolling update as safe by default. Gate it on honest readiness probes and metrics, or it rolls a bad version to everyone.
  • Checking the database in the liveness probe. Ping it in readiness only; restarting every instance during an outage fixes nothing.
  • Shipping a rename or drop with the code that needs it. Expand and contract over several releases; drop in the contract step.
  • Running a canary nobody compares. Compare it with the live baseline automatically, with a minimum request count.
  • Using DNS for canaries or fast rollbacks. Use load balancer, gateway, or mesh weights; resolvers cache beyond the TTL.
  • Waiting for a root cause before rolling back. Roll back first and investigate with the old version running.
  • Caching index.html for a long time. Serve it no-cache, cache hashed assets for a year, and upload assets before index.html.
  • Leaving release flags in the code. Remove them within days of 100%, fail CI on expired flags, and never reuse a key.
