docs.title: Deploying Backend Services
docs.text:
Deploying a backend service means getting a new version of a long-running server process (for TaskFlow API, a Node.js Express app talking to MongoDB) onto machines, putting it behind a proxy or load balancer, and switching traffic to it without dropping requests. This lesson covers the main ways to run a Node API, the request path through a reverse proxy, health checks, graceful shutdown, zero-downtime restarts with PM2 and systemd, migrations at deploy time, compiled single-binary deploys, and how to write deploy scripts that are safe to run twice.

The strategies in the next lessons (rolling, blue-green, canary) all rely on the mechanics here. A canary is worthless if every instance drops its in-flight requests when it stops.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A server process is not a static file. When it stops, it may be in the middle of 200 requests, holding database connections, and owning queued work. When it starts, it may need seconds to connect to its database and warm caches. If the deploy process ignores this, every release produces a burst of 502 Bad Gateway and connection-reset errors, users retry, clients double-submit, and teams learn to deploy only at night.

Getting the mechanics right is cheap: a readiness endpoint, a signal handler, a few timeouts that agree with each other, and a deploy script that checks its own work. With them, a small team can deploy during the day, many times a day, without anyone noticing.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Twelve-Factor App (disposability). Factor IX, Disposability, says processes should start fast and shut down gracefully when they receive SIGTERM: a web process stops listening, lets current requests finish, and exits. Every platform from Heroku to Kubernetes assumes this behavior.
  • Express documentation. The Express guide Health checks and graceful shutdown shows the same pattern for Node: on SIGTERM, stop accepting new connections, finish existing ones, close resources, then exit.
  • Kubernetes. The pod termination documentation explains that the kubelet sends SIGTERM, waits for the grace period (30 seconds by default), and then sends SIGKILL, while the pod is removed from Service endpoints in parallel. That race is why a short delay before server.close() is common.
  • AWS Elastic Load Balancing. Target groups have a deregistration delay (300 seconds by default) during which a target being removed receives no new requests but keeps its in-flight ones: connection draining implemented in the load balancer.

Popular tools and providers: PM2, systemd, Docker, Kubernetes, Amazon ECS and Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, Fly.io, Render, Heroku, AWS Lambda, nginx, HAProxy, Caddy, Traefik, and cloud load balancers.

docs.title: Ways to run a Node API
docs.text:
Option You manage Deploy unit Scaling Good for VM + process manager (systemd, PM2) OS, runtime, patches, proxy, deploy scripts Release directory or tarball Add VMs behind a load balancer; PM2 cluster per VM Small teams, steady load, full control Containers on VMs (Docker, Compose) OS and Docker host, orchestration by hand Container image Manual or scripted One or a few hosts, reproducible runtime Orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS, Nomad) Cluster or service definitions Container image + manifest Autoscaling on metrics Many services, many instances PaaS / serverless containers (Cloud Run, App Runner, Fly.io, Render, Heroku) App code and settings Image or source push Platform scales instances, sometimes to zero Teams that want minimal operations Functions (AWS Lambda, Cloud Functions) Handler code Function package Per request, automatic Spiky or event-driven work

The further down the table, the less you operate and the less you control. The deploy mechanics below exist on every row; on a PaaS the platform performs them for you, so you must still give it a health endpoint and handle SIGTERM.

docs.title: The request path
docs.text:
A reverse proxy (nginx, or a cloud load balancer) sits in front of the app instances because it does several jobs the app should not:

  • terminates TLS and holds the certificates,
  • spreads requests across instances and stops sending to unhealthy ones,
  • retries a failed connection on another instance,
  • buffers slow clients so the Node process is not held open by them,
  • adds request IDs and forwarded headers (X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto), and enforces body size and timeouts.

The app must then trust exactly one proxy hop (app.set("trust proxy", 1) in Express) so req.ip and req.protocol are correct. See nginx and load balancing for the proxy itself.

docs.title: Health checks: liveness, readiness, startup
docs.text:
Check Question it answers On failure Should it check the database? Liveness (/livez) Is this process stuck beyond repair? Restart the process No. A database outage would restart every instance, which fixes nothing Readiness (/readyz) Should this instance get new requests now? Stop routing to it, do not restart Yes, cheaply (a ping), plus the draining flag Startup Has it finished starting? Keep waiting, up to a limit Usually the same as readiness

Rules that prevent most health-check incidents:

  • Keep checks fast and cheap (a ping, not a query over a large collection), with a timeout shorter than the probe interval.
  • Never put dependency checks in liveness. A slow database plus a liveness check that queries it makes the orchestrator kill healthy processes in a loop.
  • Return 503 from readiness while draining, so the load balancer stops routing to the instance before it closes.
  • Do not require authentication on probe endpoints, but do not expose details either; serve them on an internal port or path if possible.

In Kubernetes these map directly to livenessProbe, readinessProbe, and startupProbe (see health probes and rolling updates).

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text:
The sequence, in order:

  1. Receive the signal. Kubernetes, Docker, and systemd send SIGTERM. PM2 sends SIGINT by default. Handle both.
  2. Fail readiness. Set a draining flag so /readyz returns 503.
  3. Wait briefly. Load balancers and Kubernetes endpoint lists update asynchronously; new requests may still arrive for a few seconds. A delay of 5 to 10 seconds avoids refusing them.
  4. Stop accepting connections. server.close() stops listening. Since Node 19 it also closes connections that are idle at that moment.
  5. Let in-flight requests finish. close() calls back only when every connection is gone. A keep-alive connection that becomes idle after close() stays open until keepAliveTimeout, so keep calling server.closeIdleConnections() (Node 18.2+) while draining.
  6. Close resources. MongoDB client, Redis, message consumers (stop consuming first, finish the current message), log and trace exporters.
  7. Exit with code 0.
  8. Enforce your own deadline. If anything hangs, exit with code 1 a few seconds before the platform's SIGKILL, so the logs say why.

Timeouts must agree with each other:

drain delay (5 s) + longest request (~10 s) + cleanup (~2 s)
    < your own deadline (25 s)
    < platform grace period (Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30;
      PM2 kill_timeout; systemd TimeoutStopSec; ECS stopTimeout)

Two container-specific traps: the process must be PID 1 or have an init that forwards signals (npm start as PID 1 may not pass SIGTERM to Node; use CMD ["node", "src/server.js"] or docker run --init), and the Dockerfile CMD must use the exec form so no shell sits in between. See writing production Dockerfiles.

docs.title: Keep-alive timeouts between the proxy and Node
docs.text: Node closes idle keep-alive connections after server.keepAliveTimeout (5 seconds by default). Load balancers keep idle connections to targets much longer (the AWS Application Load Balancer idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds). If Node closes a connection at the same instant the load balancer sends a new request on it, the request fails with a 502. Set the server's keep-alive timeout longer than the proxy's idle timeout, for example 65 seconds, so the proxy always closes first.

docs.title: Zero-downtime restarts
docs.text:
With a single process, a restart always has a gap: the old process has stopped listening and the new one is not ready yet. Zero downtime needs a second process to carry traffic during the switch.

  • PM2 cluster mode. PM2 runs several Node workers through the Node cluster module, all sharing one port. pm2 reload replaces them one at a time: it starts a new worker, waits until it is online (with wait_ready, until the worker calls process.send("ready"), up to listen_timeout), then stops the old one with SIGINT, sending SIGKILL after kill_timeout (about 1.6 seconds by default, so raise it). pm2 restart stops and starts everything at once. In fork mode, reload behaves like restart.
  • systemd. systemctl restart is stop then start, with a gap. With socket activation, a .socket unit owns the listening socket and passes it to the service; while the service restarts, the kernel queues new connections instead of refusing them, and Node can listen on the inherited descriptor (server.listen({ fd: 3 })). Requests wait during startup rather than fail, but in-flight requests on the old process still need a graceful shutdown. Most teams run two or more instances behind a proxy instead.
  • Multiple instances behind a load balancer. Take one instance out (drain), deploy to it, wait for readiness, put it back, repeat. This is a rolling deployment, covered in rolling, blue-green, and canary.
  • Orchestrators. Kubernetes Deployments do the same with maxSurge and maxUnavailable; ECS uses minimum and maximum healthy percent.

Capacity check for a rolling restart: four instances each handle 250 requests per second and peak traffic is 800. Removing one instance leaves 750, which is below peak, so a one-at-a-time roll during peak overloads the rest. Either surge first (start a fifth instance before stopping one) or deploy outside peak.

docs.title: Running database migrations at deploy time
docs.text:
Approach How Risk Separate pipeline step or job before rollout npx migrate-mongo up or npx prisma migrate deploy once, then roll out Clean; the migration must be compatible with the old code still running On application startup Every instance runs migrations as it boots Several instances race; slow migrations delay readiness; needs a lock Kubernetes init container Runs before each pod's app container Same race as startup, multiplied by replica count Separate Kubernetes Job or Helm hook One job per release, rollout waits for it Good; failures must stop the rollout

The safe default is a single migration step before the rollout, with the migration itself written to work with both the old and the new code, because during any rolling or canary deploy both versions run at once. Destructive steps (dropping a column) run in a later release. See zero-downtime database migrations.

docs.title: Compiled single-binary deploys
docs.text:
Some backends ship as one executable: Go binaries, bun build --compile, deno compile, and Node's single executable applications. The source code and dependencies are embedded in the binary at build time. Three consequences:

  • Pulling code is not deploying. git pull on the server changes the source files but not the running binary. Until you rebuild and restart, the old code serves, including old routes, so new endpoints return 404 even though the code "is on the server".
  • Configuration loading may differ. A compiled binary reads environment variables at runtime, but whether it auto-loads a .env file depends on the tool and version (recent Bun versions do by default and offer --no-compile-autoload-dotenv; Go never does). Pass configuration through the process manager or orchestrator so behavior does not depend on the working directory.
  • Verify what runs. Bake the version and commit into the binary and expose them at /version; the deploy is not done until that endpoint reports the new commit.

docs.title: Deploy scripts and idempotency
docs.text:
A deploy script should be safe to run twice, safe to interrupt, and able to undo itself:

  • Idempotent: running it again with the same version changes nothing harmful (it reuses the existing release directory, and reload of the same code is harmless).
  • Atomic switch: prepare the new release completely in its own directory, then switch with one atomic operation (renaming a symlink).
  • Locked: two deploys at once must be impossible (flock, or the CI concurrency setting).
  • Verified: after switching, wait for readiness and check /version.
  • Reversible: keep the last few releases on disk and switch back automatically if verification fails.
  • Fail-fast: set -euo pipefail in bash so a failed step stops the script instead of continuing with half a deploy.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Reasonable choice One small API, low traffic, small team One or two VMs with PM2 cluster mode or systemd, nginx in front Need for reproducible runtime across machines Containers, even on plain VMs with Docker Compose Several services, autoscaling, many deploys a day Kubernetes, ECS, or a serverless container platform Very spiky or event-driven work Functions or scale-to-zero containers Long-lived connections (WebSockets) Instances with long drain times, connection-aware load balancing; avoid platforms with short request limits

Do not:

  • run a single instance in production if downtime during deploys is not acceptable;
  • choose Kubernetes for one small service only because large companies use it; the operational cost is real;
  • rely on a platform to make shutdown graceful if the app ignores SIGTERM.

docs.title: An Express server with health checks and graceful shutdown
docs.text:
// src/server.js: TaskFlow API with health checks and graceful shutdown
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import express from "express";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const DRAIN_DELAY_MS = Number(process.env.DRAIN_DELAY_MS ?? 5_000);
const SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS = Number(process.env.SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS ?? 25_000);

// Written by CI at build time: {"version":"1.8.0","commit":"9f3e1c2"}
const buildInfo = JSON.parse(
  readFileSync(new URL("../build-info.json", import.meta.url), "utf8"),
);

const mongo = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, {
  serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 2_000, // fail health checks fast if the DB is gone
});

const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1); // exactly one proxy (nginx or the load balancer)

let draining = false;

// While draining, ask clients to drop keep-alive connections after this response
app.use((req, res, next) => {
  if (draining) res.set("Connection", "close");
  next();
});

// Liveness: can the process serve at all? No dependency checks here.
app.get("/livez", (req, res) => res.send("ok"));

// Readiness: should this instance receive new requests right now?
app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
  if (draining) return res.status(503).send("draining");
  try {
    await mongo.db("admin").command({ ping: 1 });
    res.send("ready");
  } catch {
    res.status(503).send("database unavailable");
  }
});

// Which build is running? The deploy script checks this.
app.get("/version", (req, res) => res.json(buildInfo));

app.get("/tasks", async (req, res) => {
  const tasks = await mongo.db().collection("tasks").find().limit(50).toArray();
  res.json(tasks);
});

await mongo.connect();

const server = app.listen(PORT, () => {
  console.log(`taskflow-api ${buildInfo.version} listening on ${PORT}`);
  process.send?.("ready"); // PM2 wait_ready: this worker may take traffic now
});

// Keep idle connections open longer than the load balancer does (ALB: 60 s)
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;
server.headersTimeout = 66_000;

async function shutdown(signal) {
  if (draining) return;
  draining = true;
  console.log(`${signal} received: draining`);

  // Safety net: exit on our own before the platform's SIGKILL
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.error("graceful shutdown timed out; forcing exit");
    process.exit(1);
  }, SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS).unref();

  // 1. Readiness now fails; give load balancers time to stop routing here
  await new Promise((resolve) => setTimeout(resolve, DRAIN_DELAY_MS));

  // 2. Stop accepting connections. close() calls back once every connection
  //    is gone, so keep closing keep-alive sockets as they become idle.
  const closed = new Promise((resolve) => server.close(resolve));
  server.closeIdleConnections();
  const sweeper = setInterval(() => server.closeIdleConnections(), 1_000);
  await closed;
  clearInterval(sweeper);

  // 3. Release dependencies, then exit cleanly
  await mongo.close();
  console.log("shutdown complete");
  process.exit(0);
}

process.on("SIGTERM", () => shutdown("SIGTERM")); // Kubernetes, Docker, systemd
process.on("SIGINT", () => shutdown("SIGINT"));   // PM2 default, Ctrl+C
  • /livez never touches MongoDB, so a database outage marks instances not ready instead of restarting all of them.
  • The idle-connection sweep matters: without it, a client whose keep-alive socket became idle after close() keeps the server open for the full 65-second keep-alive timeout.
  • The deadline timer is unref()ed so it never keeps a finished process alive.

docs.title: PM2 in cluster mode
docs.text:
// ecosystem.config.cjs
module.exports = {
  apps: [
    {
      name: "taskflow-api",
      script: "src/server.js",
      cwd: "/srv/taskflow/current",
      exec_mode: "cluster",
      instances: "max",        // one worker per CPU core
      wait_ready: true,        // wait for process.send("ready")
      listen_timeout: 10_000,  // ...but no longer than 10 s
      kill_timeout: 30_000,    // time between SIGINT and SIGKILL
      max_memory_restart: "512M",
      env_production: {
        NODE_ENV: "production",
        APP_ENV: "production",
        PORT: 3000,
      },
    },
  ],
};

# First start, then zero-downtime reloads on every deploy
pm2 start ecosystem.config.cjs --env production
pm2 reload ecosystem.config.cjs --env production --update-env
pm2 save   # remember the process list across reboots (with pm2 startup)

kill_timeout must be longer than the app's own shutdown deadline (25 seconds above), otherwise PM2 kills workers mid-drain. --update-env makes a reload pick up changed environment values.

docs.title: A systemd unit
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-api.service
[Unit]
Description=TaskFlow API
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=taskflow
WorkingDirectory=/srv/taskflow/current
EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/api.env
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node src/server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=30
NoNewPrivileges=true
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/srv/taskflow/shared

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

TimeoutStopSec is systemd's grace period before SIGKILL. EnvironmentFile keeps configuration outside the release directory, and the hardening options (NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem) limit what a compromised process can do.

docs.title: nginx in front of two app servers
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-api.conf
upstream taskflow_api {
    server 10.0.1.10:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 10.0.2.10:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 32;                      # reuse upstream connections
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name api.taskflow.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.taskflow.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.taskflow.example.com/privkey.pem;

    client_max_body_size 5m;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Connection "";          # required for upstream keepalive
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $request_id;
        proxy_connect_timeout 5s;
        proxy_read_timeout 60s;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
    }
}

proxy_next_upstream retries a request on the other server when a connection fails or a server answers 502/503. By default nginx does not retry non-idempotent requests such as POST once they were sent to an upstream, which avoids creating a task twice. Open-source nginx has no active health checks; it marks a server failed after max_fails errors, so graceful shutdown on the app side still matters.

docs.title: A release-directory deploy script for a VM
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy-vm.sh: idempotent, verified deploy of one version to one VM
# usage: deploy-vm.sh 1.8.0
set -euo pipefail

VERSION="$1"
APP_DIR=/srv/taskflow
RELEASE="$APP_DIR/releases/$VERSION"
ARTIFACT="https://artifacts.example.com/taskflow-api/taskflow-api-$VERSION.tar.gz"

# Only one deploy at a time on this machine
exec 9>"$APP_DIR/deploy.lock"
flock -n 9 || { echo "another deploy is running" >&2; exit 1; }

previous=$(readlink -f "$APP_DIR/current" || true)

# 1. Prepare the release in its own directory (skipped if already prepared)
if [ ! -d "$RELEASE" ]; then
  rm -rf "$RELEASE.tmp" && mkdir -p "$RELEASE.tmp"
  curl -fsSL "$ARTIFACT" | tar -xz -C "$RELEASE.tmp"
  (cd "$RELEASE.tmp" && npm ci --omit=dev)
  mv "$RELEASE.tmp" "$RELEASE"            # appears only when complete
fi

# 2. Backward-compatible migrations (safe while the old version still runs)
(cd "$RELEASE" && npx migrate-mongo up)

# 3. Atomic switch: rename a new symlink over the old one
ln -sfn "$RELEASE" "$APP_DIR/current.tmp"
mv -T "$APP_DIR/current.tmp" "$APP_DIR/current"

# 4. Zero-downtime reload (starts the app if it is not running yet)
pm2 startOrReload "$APP_DIR/current/ecosystem.config.cjs" --env production --update-env

# 5. Verify: ready, and actually running the new version
for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
  if curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/version | grep -q "\"version\":\"$VERSION\""; then
    echo "deployed $VERSION"
    ls -1dt "$APP_DIR"/releases/*/ | tail -n +6 | xargs -r rm -rf   # keep 5
    exit 0
  fi
  sleep 2
done

# 6. Verification failed: switch back and reload the previous release
echo "verification failed; rolling back to $previous" >&2
if [ -n "$previous" ]; then
  ln -sfn "$previous" "$APP_DIR/current.tmp"
  mv -T "$APP_DIR/current.tmp" "$APP_DIR/current"
  pm2 reload "$APP_DIR/current/ecosystem.config.cjs" --env production --update-env
fi
exit 1

Run it twice with the same version and step 1 is skipped, the migration tool finds nothing new to apply, and the reload replaces workers with the same code. That is what idempotent means in practice.

docs.title: Building a compiled binary that reports its own version
docs.text:
# Go: set a package variable at link time
go build -ldflags "-X main.commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" -o server ./cmd/server

# Bun: bundle the app and runtime into one executable with a build constant
bun build ./src/index.ts --compile \
  --define BUILD_COMMIT="\"$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)\"" \
  --outfile server

# After installing the new binary and restarting the service
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:3000/version
# {"commit":"9f3e1c2"}  <- must match the commit you meant to deploy

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run at least two instances (or a PM2 cluster) wherever deploys must not drop requests.
  • Separate liveness from readiness; keep dependencies out of liveness.
  • Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT: fail readiness, wait, close the server, sweep idle connections, close resources, exit.
  • Line up timeouts: drain delay plus longest request plus cleanup, below your deadline, below the platform's grace period.
  • Set the app's keep-alive timeout above the load balancer's idle timeout.
  • Run migrations once per release, before rollout, and only backward-compatible ones.
  • Expose /version and make verification part of the deploy.
  • Make deploy scripts idempotent, locked, atomic, and self-reverting.
  • Keep the previous release (directory, image, or binary) ready for a fast switch back.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A burst of 502s during every deploy. Detect: load balancer 5xx and target connection errors spike at deploy times, then recover. Cause: instances stop without draining, or receive traffic before they are ready. Fix: add readiness checks, a drain delay before server.close(), and roll instances one at a time.
  • Occasional 502s at low traffic, not tied to deploys. Detect: load balancer logs show target resets on reused connections, often after idle periods. Cause: Node's 5-second keep-alive timeout is shorter than the load balancer's idle timeout. Fix: set server.keepAliveTimeout above the proxy's idle timeout.
  • The deploy "succeeded" but new endpoints return 404. Detect: /version reports the old commit. Cause: a compiled binary was not rebuilt after git pull, or the process manager was never reloaded. Fix: rebuild, reload, and make the deploy script verify /version before reporting success.
  • Every instance restarts in a loop when the database is slow. Detect: restart counts climb on all instances at once; liveness probe failures in events. Cause: the liveness probe checks the database. Fix: make liveness process-only, move the dependency check to readiness.
  • Shutdown always takes the full grace period, then SIGKILL. Detect: logs show "draining" and nothing after; exit code 137. Cause: idle keep-alive sockets, open intervals, or an unclosed client keep the process alive, or SIGTERM never reaches Node (npm start as PID 1). Fix: sweep idle connections, close every resource, run node directly or with an init, and keep a forced-exit deadline.
  • Two instances ran the same migration at the same time. Detect: duplicate-key or lock errors in migration logs at startup. Cause: migrations run on application start in every instance. Fix: run migrations as one pipeline step or job before the rollout.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Reverse proxy: a server in front of the application that receives client requests and forwards them, often terminating TLS.
  • Liveness probe: a check that decides whether to restart a process.
  • Readiness probe: a check that decides whether to send a process traffic.
  • Graceful shutdown: stopping a process without dropping in-flight work.
  • Connection draining: letting existing connections finish while sending no new ones; deregistration delay in AWS terms.
  • Grace period: time the platform waits between SIGTERM and SIGKILL.
  • Cluster mode: running several worker processes that share one port.
  • Socket activation: systemd holding a listening socket and passing it to a service, so connections queue during restarts.
  • Idempotent deploy: a deploy that can run repeatedly with the same result.
  • Single executable: an application compiled with its runtime and code into one binary.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing pm2 restart is zero-downtime; pm2 reload in cluster mode is.
  • Checking the database in the liveness probe.
  • Calling server.close() and assuming it finishes quickly with keep-alive clients.
  • Leaving PM2's kill_timeout at its short default while the app needs 20 seconds to drain.
  • Running the app as npm start in a container and wondering why SIGTERM is ignored.
  • Deploying by git pull on servers, so what runs depends on what each server happened to pull and build.
  • Running destructive migrations in the same release that stops using the column.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between liveness and readiness, and why must liveness not check the database?
  2. List the steps of a graceful shutdown in order and explain why a short delay comes before server.close().
  3. Why can server.close() take as long as the keep-alive timeout, and how do you prevent it?
  4. A load balancer has a 60-second idle timeout and Node uses its default keep-alive timeout. What error appears, and how do you fix it?
  5. Six instances each handle 200 requests per second; peak traffic is 1,100 requests per second. Can you roll them one at a time during peak without surge capacity? Show the numbers.
  6. Why is pm2 reload zero-downtime in cluster mode but not in fork mode with one process?
  7. Why must migrations that run during a rolling deploy be compatible with the old code?
  8. A Go service was deployed with git pull and a restart, but a new route returns 404. What happened?

docs.text:

docs.title: Deploying Frontends and Static Sites
docs.text:
A built frontend (TaskFlow Web, a React app built with Vite) or a static documentation site (this site, built with MkDocs) is a folder of files: one or a few HTML entry points plus scripts, styles, fonts, and images. Deploying it means putting those files on a host or CDN so that every visitor gets a consistent version, quickly, and keeps getting it while the next version is uploaded.

This lesson covers static hosting options, what a build produces, content-hashed filenames and the cache headers that go with them, atomic deploys and why upload order matters, CDN invalidation, fallback routing for single-page apps, environment values baked in at build time, preview deploys, and a complete GitHub Pages deploy for an MkDocs site.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Static files look simple, but they are cached in more places than anything else you ship: the CDN edge, corporate proxies, and every visitor's browser. Get caching wrong one way and users keep running yesterday's JavaScript against today's API. Get it wrong the other way and every page view downloads megabytes again. Upload files in the wrong order and visitors get a blank page for minutes. Delete old files too early and users who opened the app an hour ago crash when they click a lazy-loaded route.

The good news is that the right setup is well known, cheap, and almost the same on every host: hash the asset filenames, cache them forever, always revalidate the HTML, and switch versions atomically.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• web.dev on HTTP caching. The article Prevent unnecessary network requests with the HTTP Cache by Ilya Grigorik and Jeff Posnick recommends Cache-Control: max-age=31536000 for URLs that contain a fingerprint or version (the content at that URL never changes) and no-cache for unversioned URLs such as HTML, so the browser revalidates every time and gets a small 304 when nothing changed.
  • Vite. The Vite guide on building for production notes that a host may delete assets from previous deployments, so a user with an older page can fail to load dynamic imports; Vite emits a vite:preloadError event for that case, and the guide tells you to set Cache-Control: no-cache on the HTML file so it does not keep referencing old assets.
  • Netlify. The deploy overview says Netlify "enforces a strict concept of atomic deploys": no change goes live until all files of the new deploy are uploaded, and then the whole version goes live at once. Every deploy also gets a permanent URL whose content never changes, and pull requests get Deploy Previews.
  • GitHub Pages. The GitHub documentation on using custom workflows with GitHub Pages shows the artifact-based deployment used below: a build job uploads the site with actions/upload-pages-artifact, and a deploy job with pages: write and id-token: write permissions publishes it with actions/deploy-pages.

Popular tools and providers: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages and Workers static assets, GitHub Pages, Amazon S3 with CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps, Firebase Hosting, and nginx or Caddy on your own servers.

docs.title: What a frontend build produces
docs.text:
$ npm run build        # vite build
dist/index.html                    0.46 kB
dist/assets/index-B7x9q2Lc.css    18.20 kB
dist/assets/index-D4kPz8wa.js    142.71 kB
dist/assets/TaskBoard-Cm3fQ1sE.js 31.05 kB   <- lazy-loaded route chunk
  • index.html is the entry point. Its URL never changes (/), and it references the current scripts and styles by their exact filenames.
  • Everything under assets/ has a content hash in its name, computed from the file's content. Change one line of code and the affected file's name changes; leave a file alone and its name stays the same across builds.
  • Route-level chunks (TaskBoard-...js) are loaded later, when the user navigates, which is why old chunks must stay available for a while.

MkDocs Material does the same for its theme bundles; other frameworks (Next.js static export, Angular, SvelteKit) produce the same shape with different folder names.

docs.title: Cache headers that match the file type
docs.text:
Files Cache-Control Why Hashed assets (/assets/*-<hash>.js, .css, fonts, images) public, max-age=31536000, immutable The name changes when the content changes, so a cached copy is never wrong; immutable tells browsers not to revalidate even on reload index.html and other HTML entry points no-cache Always revalidate (cheap 304 with an ETag), so new deploys are seen on the next visit Service worker script (sw.js) no-cache Browsers also check it for updates, but a long cache delays them Unhashed files (favicon.ico, robots.txt, manifest.webmanifest) short, for example public, max-age=300 They can change without a new name Personalized responses (if a server renders them) private, no-store Must never be stored in shared caches

no-cache does not mean "do not cache"; it means "check with the server before using". no-store is the one that forbids storing. See HTTP and CDN caching for the full set of directives.

docs.title: Atomic deploys and why order matters
docs.text:
A deploy is atomic when visitors see either the complete old version or the complete new version, never a mix. Platforms such as Netlify, Vercel, and Cloudflare Pages do this by uploading every file of a deploy first and then switching one pointer. On plain object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob) files are written one at a time, so you create atomicity yourself through ordering:

  1. Upload new assets first. They have new names, so they overwrite nothing and are invisible until something references them.
  2. Upload the entry point last. The moment the new index.html is live, every file it references already exists.
  3. Delete old assets later, not now. A visitor who loaded the app before the deploy still runs the old index.html and will request old route chunks for as long as the tab stays open. Keep previous releases' assets for days, then clean up.

docs.title: Requests through a CDN
docs.text: With this setup, each new version's assets are fetched from the origin about once per edge location, and after that from caches. The HTML costs one small revalidation per page load.

docs.title: CDN invalidation
docs.text:
An invalidation (purge) tells the CDN to drop its copy of a path so the next request goes to the origin. With hashed assets you only ever need to invalidate the entry points (/index.html, and / if the CDN caches it separately). Things to know:

  • Invalidation clears CDN edges, not browsers. Anything already cached in a browser with a long max-age stays there, which is why HTML must never get a long max-age.
  • Invalidations take time to propagate (seconds to minutes) and many CDNs charge for them beyond a free allowance (CloudFront includes a monthly quota of free invalidation paths). Invalidating /* on every deploy throws away the whole cache.
  • Some CDNs support cache tags or surrogate keys to purge groups of objects at once.

docs.title: Fallback routing for single-page apps
docs.text:
A single-page app handles routes such as /tasks/42 in the browser. There is no file at that path, so the host must answer with index.html (status 200) and let the client router render the view. But a missing script must still be a real 404, otherwise the browser receives HTML when it expected JavaScript and fails with a confusing MIME-type error.

Host How to configure the fallback Netlify _redirects: /assets/* /404.html 404, then /* /index.html 200 (existing files always win) Vercel vercel.json rewrites to /index.html, with a source pattern that excludes /assets/ Cloudflare Pages Serves index.html for unknown paths automatically when the project has no top-level 404.html nginx try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; S3 + CloudFront A CloudFront Function that rewrites extensionless paths to /index.html (custom error responses mapping 403/404 to index.html also work but hide missing assets) GitHub Pages No rewrites: use hash-based routing or a 404.html that redirects

docs.title: Environment values are baked in at build time
docs.text:
import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL in TaskFlow Web is replaced with the literal string during vite build. The built files therefore contain the API URL of whatever environment they were built for, and changing it requires a rebuild. Two consequences:

  • Either build once per environment (and accept that staging and production artifacts differ), or load runtime configuration (a config.json fetched at startup) so one build can be promoted.
  • Anything in a VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable is public. Never put secrets there.

Both patterns are covered in build-time vs runtime configuration.

docs.title: Preview deploys
docs.text: Static hosts make per-pull-request previews almost free: every pull request builds and gets its own URL (Netlify Deploy Previews, Vercel Preview Deployments, Cloudflare Pages preview URLs). Point previews at a staging API, keep them out of search engines, and protect them if they show unreleased features. See environments and promotion for the full preview lifecycle.

docs.title: Security headers belong in the hosting configuration
docs.text: A static host is also where security headers are set: Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, Referrer-Policy, and frame restrictions. Configure them in the same file as cache headers (_headers, vercel.json, nginx) so they ship with every deploy.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Option Atomic deploys Custom headers and rewrites Previews Fits Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Pages Yes Yes Built in Most SPAs and static sites; teams that want zero hosting work S3 (or GCS, Azure Blob) + CDN No, use ordering Yes, through object metadata and CDN rules Build it yourself Teams already on that cloud, strict control, large scale GitHub Pages Yes, each publish replaces the site No custom headers; no rewrites No Documentation and project sites, open-source projects nginx or Caddy on your servers With release directories and a symlink switch Full control Build it yourself Apps already running on your own servers, internal networks

Static hosting does not fit pages that must be rendered per request (personalized server-side rendering); those need a server or edge functions, though their static assets still follow the rules on this page.

docs.title: Deploy TaskFlow Web to S3 and CloudFront in a safe order
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy-web.sh: ordered, cache-aware deploy of a Vite build
set -euo pipefail
BUCKET="s3://taskflow-web-production"
DISTRIBUTION_ID="${CLOUDFRONT_DISTRIBUTION_ID:?set by CI}"

npm ci
npm run build                     # dist/index.html + dist/assets/*

# 1. Hashed assets: cache for a year; do NOT delete old files here
aws s3 sync dist/assets "$BUCKET/assets" \
  --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"

# 2. Other unhashed files (favicon, robots.txt): short cache
aws s3 sync dist "$BUCKET" \
  --exclude "assets/*" --exclude "index.html" \
  --cache-control "public, max-age=300"

# 3. The entry point last: always revalidated
aws s3 cp dist/index.html "$BUCKET/index.html" \
  --cache-control "no-cache" \
  --content-type "text/html; charset=utf-8"

# 4. Only the entry point needs to leave the CDN cache
aws cloudfront create-invalidation \
  --distribution-id "$DISTRIBUTION_ID" \
  --paths "/index.html" "/"

Clean up old assets in a separate scheduled job that keeps every file referenced by the last few releases. Enable build.manifest: true in vite.config.js so each build writes a manifest of its files (dist/.vite/manifest.json), store the manifests per release, and delete only assets that no recent manifest mentions. Do not use an age-based bucket rule on assets/: aws s3 sync skips unchanged files, so an unchanged asset still in use keeps its old upload date and would be deleted.

docs.title: Rewrite page routes in CloudFront
docs.text:
// cloudfront/spa-rewrite.js: CloudFront Function, viewer-request event
function handler(event) {
  var request = event.request;
  var uri = request.uri;
  var lastSegment = uri.substring(uri.lastIndexOf("/") + 1);

  // Page routes have no file extension; assets keep their real 404s
  if (!uri.startsWith("/assets/") && lastSegment.indexOf(".") === -1) {
    request.uri = "/index.html";
  }
  return request;
}

docs.title: nginx serving a single-page app
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-web.conf
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name app.taskflow.example.com;
    root /srv/taskflow-web/current;     # a symlink switched atomically per release

    location /assets/ {
        add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
        try_files $uri =404;            # missing assets are real 404s
    }

    location = /index.html {
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
    }

    location / {
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;   # page routes fall back to the app
    }
}

Deploy by uploading the new build into /srv/taskflow-web/releases/<id>, copying the previous releases' assets/ files into it (so old tabs keep working), and switching the current symlink with ln -sfn and mv -T, the same atomic switch used for backend releases.

docs.title: Netlify headers and redirects
docs.text:
# public/_headers (copied into dist/ by the build)
/assets/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
/index.html
  Cache-Control: no-cache
/*
  X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
  Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin

# public/_redirects: the first matching rule wins
/assets/*  /404.html    404
/*         /index.html  200

The 200 makes the catch-all a rewrite rather than a redirect, and files that exist are still served directly, because a rule does not apply where a file exists. A missing file under /assets/ would otherwise fall through to index.html, so the first rule answers it with a real 404 (with a public/404.html as the body).

docs.title: Vercel configuration
docs.text:
{
  "rewrites": [{ "source": "/:path((?!assets/).*)", "destination": "/index.html" }],
  "headers": [
    {
      "source": "/assets/(.*)",
      "headers": [{ "key": "Cache-Control", "value": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" }]
    }
  ]
}

Saved as vercel.json at the project root. The negative lookahead keeps /assets/ out of the rewrite, so a missing asset stays a 404. Check both a deep link and a missing asset path on a preview deploy before relying on it.

docs.title: Recover when an old tab cannot load a new chunk
docs.text:
// src/main.jsx: reload once if a lazy chunk from an old build is gone
window.addEventListener("vite:preloadError", (event) => {
  event.preventDefault(); // we handle it
  const key = "reloaded-for-new-build";
  if (!sessionStorage.getItem(key)) {
    sessionStorage.setItem(key, "1");
    window.location.reload(); // fetches the new index.html and new chunks
  }
});

The sessionStorage guard stops a reload loop if the asset is missing for some other reason. Keeping old assets available is still the main defense; this handles the rare tab that outlives them. "New version available" prompts for long-open tabs and the other version skew defenses are covered in keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: Worked example: publish an MkDocs site to GitHub Pages
docs.text:
This site is built with MkDocs and Material for MkDocs. There are two common ways to publish such a site.

Option A, the Pages artifact workflow (GitHub's recommended custom workflow; set the repository's Pages source to GitHub Actions):

# .github/workflows/docs.yml
name: Publish documentation

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write       # deploy to Pages
  id-token: write    # verify the deployment comes from this workflow

concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: false   # let a running publish finish

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v7
        with:
          python-version: "3.x"
          cache: pip
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: mkdocs build --strict          # fail on broken links and warnings
      - uses: actions/configure-pages@v6
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5
        with:
          path: site

  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v5
  • mkdocs build --strict turns warnings (such as links to missing pages) into failures, so a broken page never ships.
  • The build job has no write access to the repository; only the deploy job can publish, and only to Pages.
  • Each run publishes a complete, new version of the site; there is no partially updated state.

Option B, mkdocs gh-deploy. The Material for MkDocs publishing guide uses a workflow that runs mkdocs gh-deploy --force, which builds the site and force-pushes it to a gh-pages branch that Pages serves. It needs contents: write permission. It is simpler to set up and keeps the built site in Git history; Option A keeps the repository clean and grants the workflow fewer permissions.

Either way, set site_url in mkdocs.yml to the published address (including the repository path for project sites), so canonical links and the sitemap are correct.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Hash asset filenames and cache them for a year with immutable.
  • Serve HTML entry points with no-cache and validators (ETag).
  • Upload new assets first and the entry point last; delete old assets days later, by reference, not by age.
  • Invalidate only unhashed entry points at the CDN.
  • Fall back to index.html for page routes only; keep real 404s for missing assets.
  • Treat every build-time variable as public; use runtime configuration for values that differ per environment if you want to promote one build.
  • Use preview deploys for every pull request.
  • Set security headers in the hosting configuration, version-controlled.
  • Build with strict settings (mkdocs build --strict, failing type checks and lint) so broken output never deploys.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users see a blank page right after a deploy. Detect: console errors such as "Failed to load module script" or 404s for index-<hash>.js. Cause: index.html was uploaded before its assets, or the CDN still serves an old HTML that references deleted files. Fix: upload assets first and HTML last, keep old assets, and serve HTML with no-cache.
  • Some users still run last week's version. Detect: error reports from old asset hashes; the HTML response has a long max-age. Cause: the entry point was cached by browsers. Fix: no-cache on HTML; until old caches expire, a version check in the app can prompt a reload.
  • Navigating to a route crashes with a chunk load error. Detect: ChunkLoadError or vite:preloadError events spike after deploys, from long-open tabs. Cause: old route chunks were deleted. Fix: keep previous releases' assets, and reload once on preload errors.
  • Refreshing /tasks/42 returns 404. Detect: direct links and reloads fail; navigation inside the app works. Cause: no SPA fallback on the host. Fix: configure a rewrite for page routes.
  • A missing script returns HTML and the app fails with a MIME error. Detect: "Refused to execute script ... MIME type text/html". Cause: a catch-all fallback (or a CDN error rule) serves index.html for missing assets. Fix: exclude /assets/ and paths with extensions from the fallback.
  • The production build calls the staging API. Detect: network requests go to the wrong host. Cause: the build ran with staging VITE_* values, or one artifact was promoted although values are baked in. Fix: build per environment with explicit values checked in CI, or move to runtime configuration.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Static site: a site served as prebuilt files, with no per-request rendering.
  • Entry point: the HTML file that references the current assets.
  • Content hash (fingerprint): a hash of a file's content included in its name.
  • Immutable caching: caching a URL for a very long time because its content never changes.
  • Revalidation: asking the server whether a cached copy is still current, answered by 304 Not Modified if it is.
  • Atomic deploy: switching all files of a site to a new version at once.
  • Invalidation (purge): removing an object from CDN caches.
  • SPA fallback: serving index.html for client-side routes.
  • Build-time variable: a value inlined into the output during the build.
  • Preview deploy: a temporary deployment of a pull request.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Caching index.html for a long time.
  • Not hashing asset filenames, then fighting stale caches with invalidations.
  • Invalidating /* on every deploy instead of only entry points.
  • Deleting old assets in the same step as the upload (sync --delete).
  • Believing a CDN purge clears browser caches.
  • A catch-all fallback that turns missing assets into HTML.
  • Putting API keys in VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables.
  • Expecting one frontend build to work in every environment when values are inlined at build time.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can content-hashed assets be cached for a year while index.html cannot?
  2. In what order should files be uploaded to object storage, and why?
  3. Why should old assets stay available after a deploy, and for how long?
  4. What does no-cache mean, and how does it differ from no-store?
  5. A site's HTML had max-age=86400 and a bad release was replaced after one hour. How long could some users keep the bad HTML, and would a CDN purge help them?
  6. How do you configure a SPA fallback that still returns real 404s for missing assets?
  7. Why does an age-based deletion rule on assets/ break a site deployed with aws s3 sync?
  8. Compare publishing MkDocs with the Pages artifact workflow and with mkdocs gh-deploy.

docs.text:

  • MDN: Cache-Control
  • Vite: Deploying a static site
  • Amazon CloudFront: Invalidating files
  • GitHub Docs: Using custom workflows with GitHub Pages

docs.title: Environments and Promotion
docs.text:
An environment is a complete, running copy of a system (code, configuration, data, and the infrastructure around them) used for one purpose: developing, testing, rehearsing a release, or serving real users. Promotion is the act of moving a tested build from one environment to the next until it reaches production.

This lesson covers the usual environment ladder, why environments drift apart and how to keep them close, per-pull-request preview environments, the difference between deploying and releasing, approvals and gates, rules for test and production data, and how configuration differs per environment while the artifact stays the same.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most production incidents caused by a change share one story: the change behaved differently in production than it did where it was tested. The database was larger, a setting was different, the cache was shared, the third-party API returned a real error instead of a sandbox success. A well-designed set of environments exists to find those differences before users do. A badly designed one gives false confidence: a staging environment that nobody trusts, an artifact rebuilt for production that was never tested, or a test database that is really a copy of customer data and therefore a privacy breach waiting to happen.

Promotion rules also decide how fast a team can ship. Every gate costs time. Automated gates are cheap and consistent; manual approvals are slow and tend to batch many changes into one risky release. Choosing which checks run where is part of designing the delivery pipeline.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Twelve-Factor App (dev/prod parity). Factor X of The Twelve-Factor App names three gaps between development and production: the time gap (code waits days or weeks before deploy), the personnel gap (developers write, operators deploy), and the tools gap (for example SQLite locally and PostgreSQL in production). It recommends keeping all three small, including using the same type and version of backing services everywhere.
  • Slack. The post Deploys at Slack describes a ladder in practice: each release goes to staging (no public traffic, automated smoke tests plus manual checks), then to "dogfood" hosts serving internal workspaces, then to a canary receiving about 2% of production traffic, and then to 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of production while charts and alerts are watched.
  • Heroku Pipelines. The Heroku Pipelines documentation describes promotion as copying the exact build (the slug) that ran in staging to production, instead of rebuilding it: the "build once, promote the same artifact" rule built into a platform.
  • GitHub environments. The GitHub Actions documentation on managing environments for deployment shows the gates most teams use: required reviewers, wait timers, restrictions on which branches may deploy, and secrets that only jobs targeting that environment can read.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI/CD environments, Argo CD and Flux (promotion by pull request), Vercel, Netlify, and Cloudflare Pages (preview deployments), Heroku Pipelines, Octopus Deploy, Spinnaker, and Kubernetes namespaces with Helm for ephemeral environments.

docs.title: The usual environments
docs.text:
Environment Purpose Who uses it Data How code arrives Local Write and debug code One developer Small seeded fixtures Running from source CI (ephemeral) Unit and integration tests The pipeline Created per run, then discarded Every push Preview (per PR) Review a change running for real Reviewers, designers, QA Synthetic, seeded per preview Every push to a pull request Development (shared) Integrate merged work early The team Seeded, can be reset any time Automatically on merge to main Test / QA Automated end-to-end and exploratory tests QA and the pipeline Fixtures known to the tests Promoted after integration tests pass Staging (pre-production) Rehearse the production release Release owners Production-like volume, never raw customer data Promoted after end-to-end tests pass Production Serve real users Customers Real data Promoted after approval and checks

Not every team needs all of these. A small product can work well with local, CI, preview, and production. What matters is that each environment answers a question the others cannot: preview answers "does this change work and look right?", staging answers "will this exact release work with production-like configuration, scale, and migrations?".

docs.title: Build once, promote the same artifact
docs.text:
The single most important promotion rule: build the artifact once and deploy that exact artifact to every environment. For a container this means the image is identified by its digest (sha256:...), not rebuilt per environment and not referred to by a mutable tag like latest.

Rebuilding per environment breaks the chain of evidence. A second npm install can resolve a different dependency version, a base image tag can point to a newer image, and build-time variables can differ. What reaches production would then be an artifact nobody tested. Twelve-Factor calls this separation build, release, run: the build produces an artifact, the release combines it with one environment's configuration, and the run stage executes it.

What changes between environments is configuration: URLs, credentials, log levels, replica counts, feature flag defaults. That is why configuration must live outside the artifact (see configuration fundamentals).

docs.title: Environment parity and where it breaks
docs.text:
Parity means environments differ only where they must. In practice they drift in predictable places:

Aspect Typical gap What goes wrong How to close it Backing service versions MongoDB 6 locally, 8 in production Query or index behaves differently Pin the same versions in Docker Compose and infrastructure code Topology Standalone database locally, replica set in production Multi-document transactions need a replica set, so code paths differ Run a single-node replica set locally Data volume 50 tasks locally, 40 million in production A query without an index is fast in test, times out in production Load-test staging with production-sized synthetic data Scale One instance in staging, many in production In-memory sessions or caches "work" until there are two instances Run at least two instances everywhere above local Third parties Sandbox payment and email APIs Real errors, rate limits, and latency never seen Contract tests, fault injection, sandbox error simulation Edge No CDN or TLS in test Caching headers, redirects, and cookies behave differently Put the same proxy or CDN configuration in front of staging Configuration Hand-edited values per environment A setting exists only in production Keep configuration in version control and validate it at startup Flags Feature flags on in staging, off in production Staging tests a combination users never see Test the production flag state too

Perfect parity is impossible and expensive (a full copy of production data and scale for every environment). Aim for parity in the kinds of things (same software, same topology, same configuration shape) and accept differences in size.

docs.title: Preview environments per pull request
docs.text:
A preview (ephemeral, review) environment is a short-lived copy of the application created for one pull request and destroyed when it closes. Reviewers click a link and test the change running for real, instead of reading a diff and imagining it.

Design points:

  • Isolation: each preview gets its own namespace (or app), hostname, and database. Previews must never share a writable database with each other or with staging.
  • Data: seed synthetic data at creation so every preview starts in a known state.
  • Secrets: previews get sandbox credentials only. Pull requests from forks must not receive secrets at all; GitHub does not pass secrets to pull_request workflows triggered from forks for this reason.
  • Access: previews are not public by default. Put them behind single sign-on or a shared password, and add noindex headers so search engines do not index half-finished work.
  • Callbacks: OAuth redirect URIs and webhook endpoints often require exact URLs. Use a fixed callback host that routes to the right preview, or test those flows in staging.
  • Cost: a preview costs money while it exists, so teardown is part of the design, not an afterthought.

Worked example: previews cost about $0.06 per hour each (API plus a small database). The team opens 40 pull requests a week and each stays open for 3 days on average. By Little's law the average number running is arrival rate times lifetime: 40 / 7 per day × 3 days ≈ 17 previews, or 17 × 0.06 × 730 h ≈ $745 a month. If 10% of close events are missed and nothing reaps them, 4 orphaned previews accumulate every week; after six months there are about 100 of them costing 100 × 0.06 × 730 ≈ $4,380 a month, more than everything else combined. The TTL reaper exists for that reason.

docs.title: Deploy versus release
docs.text:
Deploy Release What it is Installing a new version of the code in an environment Exposing new behavior to users Who triggers it The pipeline A product decision (flag change, schedule) Risk it carries Technical: crashes, latency, resource use Product: wrong behavior, confused users, business impact How it is undone Roll back the artifact Turn the flag off

When the two are coupled, every deploy is a release and every release needs a deploy. Decoupling them with feature flags means code can reach production switched off ("dark"), be tested there by staff, and be released later to 1% of users, then everyone, without another deploy. This is the basis of trunk-based development: unfinished work is merged and deployed behind a flag instead of living on a long branch.

docs.title: Promotion, gates, and approvals
docs.text:
A gate is a condition that must hold before a build moves up a rung.

  • Automated gates: tests passing, a vulnerability scan with no critical findings, smoke tests against the newly deployed environment, error rate and latency within limits during a soak period, a migration dry run succeeding.
  • Manual gates: an approval from a named group, a QA sign-off, a change-management ticket, or a deployment window.
  • Time gates: a minimum bake time in staging, or a wait timer before production.

Manual approvals feel safe but often are not. When approving is slow, changes queue up and are released in large batches, and a large batch is riskier and harder to debug than many small ones. The DORA research on change approval found heavyweight external approval processes are associated with worse delivery performance, while peer review plus automation works better. Keep manual gates for genuinely high-risk steps and make everything else automatic.

Common promotion triggers:

  • Merge to main deploys to development or staging automatically.
  • Creating a release tag (for example v1.8.0) or approving a GitHub environment promotes to production.
  • In GitOps, a pull request that changes the image digest in the production folder of an environment repository is the promotion (see immutable infrastructure and GitOps).

docs.title: Test data and production data rules
docs.text:
• Do not copy raw production data into lower environments. Staging is usually accessible to more people, has weaker controls, and is logged less carefully. Privacy laws such as the GDPR apply to personal data wherever it is stored.
  • Prefer synthetic data, generated to realistic volume and shape. If production-derived data is truly needed (for a migration rehearsal), mask or anonymize it in a controlled job and document who approved it.
  • Never let lower environments act on the real world. Use sandbox payment keys, an email catcher or an allowlist of internal addresses, and fake SMS providers. A staging job that emails real customers is a classic incident.
  • Never connect a lower environment to production resources. No shared databases, queues, or buckets. Separate cloud accounts or projects per environment make this enforceable.
  • Guard destructive scripts. Seed and reset scripts check the environment name and refuse to run against production.

docs.title: Configuration per environment
docs.text:
The artifact is identical; configuration differs. For TaskFlow API:

Setting Development Staging Production APP_ENV development staging production NODE_ENV development production production LOG_LEVEL debug info info MONGODB_URI local container staging cluster production cluster (secret) EMAIL_TRANSPORT local catcher (for example Mailpit) provider sandbox, internal allowlist provider, live PAYMENTS_MODE test test live Replicas 1 2 6, autoscaled

Notice that NODE_ENV is production in staging. Express and many libraries change behavior based on NODE_ENV (Express caches view templates and returns less detailed errors in production), so staging should run the production code paths. Use a separate variable such as APP_ENV to name the environment.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Environments that pay off Solo project or early prototype Local, CI, production; maybe previews from your hosting platform Small team, web app, low regulatory risk Local, CI, previews, production with canary or quick rollback Several services, shared database migrations Add staging to rehearse migrations and cross-service releases Regulated domain (health, finance) Staging with formal sign-off, audit trail of promotions, strict data rules Mobile or desktop clients Beta channels and staged rollouts act as extra "environments" (see releasing desktop and mobile apps)

Avoid:

  • Long-lived environments per developer or per feature branch; they drift, cost money, and nobody owns them. Use previews instead.
  • A shared staging that is permanently broken or occupied. If teams queue for staging, it has become a bottleneck; previews and canaries can take over much of its job.
  • Treating staging success as proof. Staging reduces risk; production progressive delivery and monitoring are still needed.

docs.title: Build once, deploy to staging, promote to production with approval
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: Build and deploy TaskFlow API

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

concurrency:
  group: deploy-main
  cancel-in-progress: false   # never cancel a deploy halfway

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      image: ${{ steps.ref.outputs.image }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${{ github.sha }}
      - id: ref
        # Refer to the image by digest from here on, never by tag
        run: echo "image=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  deploy-staging:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: staging
      url: https://staging.taskflow.example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh staging "${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}"
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh https://staging.taskflow.example.com

  deploy-production:
    needs: [build, deploy-staging]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production          # required reviewers are set on this environment
      url: https://taskflow.example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production "${{ needs.build.outputs.image }}"
      - run: ./scripts/smoke-test.sh https://taskflow.example.com
  • The build job is the only place an image is created. Both deploy jobs receive the same digest through the job output.
  • environment: production pauses the job until a required reviewer approves it (configured under the repository's environment settings), and only then exposes production-scoped secrets to the job.
  • concurrency makes deploys run one at a time and never cancels one in progress, which could leave an environment half-updated.

docs.title: A preview environment per pull request
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/preview.yml
name: Preview environment

on:
  pull_request:
    types: [opened, synchronize, reopened, closed]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: preview-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    if: github.event.action != 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: preview
      url: https://pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}.preview.example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}
      - run: >
          ./scripts/preview.sh up
          "pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}"
          "${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}"
      - if: github.event.action == 'opened'
        uses: actions/github-script@v9
        with:
          script: |
            await github.rest.issues.createComment({
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              body: `Preview: https://pr-${context.issue.number}.preview.example.com`,
            });

  destroy:
    if: github.event.action == 'closed'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/preview.sh down "pr-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/preview.sh: create or delete one preview environment
set -euo pipefail
action="$1"
ns="$2"

case "$action" in
  up)
    sha="$3"
    kubectl create namespace "$ns" --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
    kubectl label namespace "$ns" preview=true --overwrite
    kubectl annotate namespace "$ns" preview-last-deploy="$(date -u +%s)" --overwrite
    helm upgrade --install taskflow ./charts/taskflow \
      --namespace "$ns" \
      --set image.tag="$sha" \
      --set ingress.host="$ns.preview.example.com" \
      --set mongodb.enabled=true \
      --wait --timeout 5m
    kubectl -n "$ns" exec deploy/taskflow-api -- node scripts/seed.js
    ;;
  down)
    helm uninstall taskflow --namespace "$ns" || true
    kubectl delete namespace "$ns" --ignore-not-found
    ;;
  *)
    echo "usage: preview.sh up <namespace> <sha> | down <namespace>" >&2
    exit 2
    ;;
esac

The script is idempotent: running up twice upgrades the same release, and running down on a missing preview succeeds. A scheduled job reaps previews whose last deploy is older than 72 hours:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/reap-previews.sh: delete previews idle for more than 72 hours
set -euo pipefail
now=$(date -u +%s)
max_age=$((72 * 3600))

kubectl get namespaces -l preview=true \
  -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}{" "}{.metadata.annotations.preview-last-deploy}{"\n"}{end}' |
while read -r ns last; do
  if [ -n "${last:-}" ] && [ $((now - last)) -gt "$max_age" ]; then
    echo "deleting idle preview $ns"
    kubectl delete namespace "$ns" --wait=false
  fi
done

docs.title: A seed script that refuses to touch production
docs.text:
// scripts/seed.js: synthetic data for preview and test environments
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const allowed = new Set(["development", "test", "preview"]);
if (!allowed.has(process.env.APP_ENV)) {
  console.error(`Refusing to seed APP_ENV=${process.env.APP_ENV}`);
  process.exit(1);
}

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
await client.connect();
const db = client.db();

await db.collection("users").deleteMany({ seeded: true });
await db.collection("tasks").deleteMany({ seeded: true });

const users = Array.from({ length: 20 }, (_, i) => ({
  email: `user${i + 1}@example.test`, // reserved test domain, never deliverable
  name: `Test User ${i + 1}`,
  seeded: true,
}));
const { insertedIds } = await db.collection("users").insertMany(users);

const tasks = Object.values(insertedIds).flatMap((userId, u) =>
  Array.from({ length: 25 }, (_, t) => ({
    userId,
    title: `Task ${t + 1} for user ${u + 1}`,
    done: t % 3 === 0,
    createdAt: new Date(Date.UTC(2026, 0, 1 + t)),
    seeded: true,
  })),
);
await db.collection("tasks").insertMany(tasks);

console.log(`seeded ${users.length} users and ${tasks.length} tasks`);
await client.close();

The allowlist check uses the environment name, not the database URL, because URLs are easy to mistype. The seeded: true marker lets the script reset only its own data.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Build one immutable artifact per commit and promote it by digest.
  • Keep configuration outside the artifact, versioned, and validated at startup in every environment.
  • Keep backing service types and versions identical across environments; let only size differ.
  • Run at least two instances in every shared environment so state bugs appear before production.
  • Give each environment its own credentials, ideally its own cloud account or project, and never share writable resources between them.
  • Use synthetic data; mask any production-derived data in a controlled, audited job.
  • Make previews isolated, access-controlled, and automatically destroyed.
  • Automate gates wherever possible and keep manual approvals for real risk; record who approved what and when.
  • Decouple deploy from release with feature flags.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The release works in staging but fails in production. Detect: errors start at the production deploy and do not appear in staging logs for the same digest. Cause: configuration drift (a missing variable, a different flag state) or a scale difference (data volume, instance count). Fix: diff the effective configuration of both environments, validate configuration at startup, and add the missing case to staging.
  • Customers receive emails from staging. Detect: support tickets about test messages; the email provider's logs show sends from the staging API key. Cause: staging used live credentials, or production data with real addresses was copied in. Fix: sandbox or allowlist outbound email in lower environments, rotate the leaked key, and stop copying production data.
  • Production runs something that was never tested. Detect: the image digest in production differs from the one that passed staging. Cause: the pipeline rebuilds per environment or deploys a mutable tag such as latest. Fix: pass the digest from the build job to every deploy job and reject tag-only deploys.
  • The cloud bill grows every month without new features. Detect: cost reports show many pr-* namespaces or apps, some months old. Cause: preview teardown depends on a close event that was sometimes missed. Fix: add a TTL reaper and a label on every preview resource, and alert when the preview count exceeds a threshold.
  • Releases get bigger and riskier over time. Detect: the number of commits per production deploy rises; deploys per week fall. Cause: a slow manual approval gate makes teams batch changes. Fix: automate the checks the approver performs, approve smaller batches, and reserve manual approval for high-risk changes.
  • Staging is always broken. Detect: staging smoke tests fail for days and people stop looking. Cause: shared, long-lived data and manual changes. Fix: rebuild staging from code regularly, reset its data from seeds, and treat a red staging as a blocker.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Environment: a complete running copy of the system used for one purpose.
  • Promotion: moving an already-tested artifact to the next environment.
  • Artifact: the immutable output of a build, such as a container image identified by digest.
  • Environment parity: how closely environments match in software, topology, and configuration.
  • Preview (ephemeral) environment: a short-lived environment created for one pull request.
  • Gate: a condition, automated or manual, that must pass before promotion.
  • Deploy: installing a version of the code in an environment.
  • Release: making new behavior available to users.
  • Configuration drift: unplanned differences in settings between environments or between servers that should be identical.
  • Synthetic data: generated data with realistic shape and volume but no real personal information.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Rebuilding the artifact for each environment and assuming it is the same thing that was tested.
  • Using NODE_ENV to name environments, so staging runs development code paths.
  • Copying the production database into staging "to make it realistic".
  • Believing staging success proves production will work; it proves less the more the two differ.
  • Adding more manual approvals after each incident, which grows batch size and makes the next incident more likely.
  • Letting previews or feature environments live forever.
  • Sharing one database between staging and previews, so tests corrupt each other's data.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why should the same artifact, identified by digest, be promoted through every environment instead of rebuilt?
  2. Name the three gaps from the Twelve-Factor dev/prod parity factor and one practical way to shrink each.
  3. Give two examples of parity gaps that hide bugs until production.
  4. What is the difference between deploying and releasing, and what technique decouples them?
  5. Previews cost $0.08 per hour. The team opens 30 pull requests a week and each stays open 4 days on average. How many previews run on average, and what is the monthly cost (use 730 hours)?
  6. Why can a slow manual approval gate increase the risk of each release?
  7. What rules should apply to data and outbound side effects (email, payments) in staging?
  8. Why is NODE_ENV=production usually correct for staging?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App: Dev/prod parity
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Build, release, run
  • GitHub Docs: Managing environments for deployment
  • DORA: Streamlining change approval
  • Next: deploying backend services. Back to the deployment strategies overview.

docs.title: Feature Flags and Progressive Delivery
docs.text:
A feature flag (feature toggle) is a switch in the code whose position is decided at runtime, per request, from configuration you can change without deploying. Progressive delivery is the practice of releasing a change to gradually larger audiences (staff, 1% of users, 10%, everyone) while measuring it, using flags together with the deployment strategies from the previous lessons.

This lesson covers the four kinds of flags, how flags are evaluated on servers and in clients, targeting rules, percentage rollouts with stable hashing (with a worked example), dark launches, the flag lifecycle and how flag debt builds up, the OpenFeature standard, the main tools, testing code that has flags, and a small flag service you can read end to end.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Flags separate two decisions that deployment alone ties together: when code reaches production and when users get the behavior. That gives teams three abilities:

  • Merge and deploy unfinished work safely (trunk-based development), so there are no long-lived branches and painful merges.
  • Release to a small audience first, watch metrics, and widen or stop, without a deploy and at the speed of a configuration change.
  • Turn something off in seconds when it misbehaves: an expensive query, a failing integration, a new UI that confuses users.

Flags also carry real risk. Every flag doubles the number of code paths, flags left in the code become confusing and dangerous, and a flag evaluated wrongly can expose an unreleased feature or hide a working one. Treating flags as first-class, owned, short-lived configuration is what makes them safe.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Pete Hodgson on martinfowler.com.
