The article Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags) defines the four categories used on this page (release, experiment, ops, and permission toggles), compares them by how long they live and how dynamic their decisions are, and warns that toggles are inventory with a carrying cost that teams must actively remove.
  • Google Cloud, June 2025. The incident report for the June 12, 2025 outage states that the change which failed "did not have appropriate error handling nor was it feature flag protected", and that "if this had been flag protected, the issue would have been caught in staging". Its remediations include requiring feature flags, disabled by default, for changes to critical binaries.
  • Knight Capital, 2012. The U.S. SEC's order against Knight Capital describes how new code was not deployed to one of eight servers and how a flag that previously activated retired "Power Peg" code was repurposed for the new feature. On that one server the flag reactivated the old code, and the firm lost about $460 million in roughly 45 minutes: a lesson in flag debt and in never reusing flag names.
  • Facebook. The SOSP 2015 paper Holistic Configuration Management at Facebook describes Gatekeeper, the system that controls feature rollouts by user attributes and percentages, alongside the configuration system whose changes are code-reviewed, tested, and canaried like code.

Popular tools and providers: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, GrowthBook, ConfigCat, PostHog, AWS AppConfig, Firebase Remote Config, flagd, and the vendor-neutral OpenFeature SDKs.

docs.title: What a flag looks like in code
docs.text:
// In a route handler: the flag decides which code path runs
const showNewBoard = flags.get("new-task-board", { userId: req.user.id, plan: req.user.plan }, false);
res.json(showNewBoard ? await boardV2(req.user) : await boardV1(req.user));

Three parts matter in every call: the flag key, the evaluation context (who is asking: user ID, organization, plan, country, app version), and the default value used if the flag service is unreachable or the flag does not exist. The default must always be the safe, old behavior.

docs.title: Kinds of flags
docs.text:
Kind Purpose Typical lifetime Who changes it Decision changes Release Hide unfinished or not-yet-launched code; roll out gradually Days to weeks Developers, release owner Per user during rollout Experiment A/B and multivariate tests of product ideas Weeks, until the result is significant Product, data team Per user, sticky Ops (kill switch) Turn off expensive or failing functionality; degrade gracefully Long-lived by design On-call engineers Rarely, in incidents Permission Enable features for plans, beta programs, internal users Long-lived, often permanent Product, sales, support Per account

The kinds differ in how long they live and how they must be governed. A release flag that is still in the code six months later is debt; a kill switch that is removed is a missing safety mechanism. Some teams move long-lived permission flags out of the flag system into a proper entitlements model once they stabilize.

docs.title: Evaluation: server-side and client-side
docs.text:
Server-side SDK Client-side SDK (browser, mobile) Where rules live Downloaded into the server process, refreshed by polling or streaming Usually not on the client; the client receives evaluated values for one user Cost per evaluation A local function call, microseconds Read from a local cache; network only on refresh Security Rules and targeting data stay on the server Anything sent to the client is visible to the user Typical use API behavior, backend paths, kill switches UI changes, mobile features that must change without a store release Failure mode Service unreachable: keep last known rules, else code defaults Offline: last cached values, else code defaults

Two client-side cautions. First, never ship the full rule set (all flag keys, targeting lists, internal email domains) to browsers; send only the values for the current user, ideally evaluated by your server or the vendor's edge. Second, avoid "flicker", where the old UI renders and then switches: bootstrap the page with flag values computed on the server, or wait briefly for flags before first render.

docs.title: Targeting rules
docs.text:
A flag definition is an ordered list of decisions:

  1. Enabled? A disabled flag serves its off value to everyone. This is also the kill switch.
  2. Individual targets: specific user or account IDs (QA accounts, a customer who asked for early access).
  3. Rules and segments: attribute matches such as plan in [beta], email ends with @taskflow.example.com, country in [NZ], appVersion >= 3.2. Reusable groups of rules are segments.
  4. Percentage rollout: a share of everyone else.
  5. Fallthrough (default rule): what everyone else gets.

The first matching step decides. Order matters: a staff rule placed after a 0% rollout never runs.

docs.title: Percentage rollouts with stable hashing
docs.text:
A percentage rollout must be sticky: the same user must get the same answer on every request, every server, every day, or they will see the feature appear and disappear. Random numbers per request do not work. Instead, hash a stable identifier:

bucket = first 4 bytes of SHA-256("<flag key>:<user id>") as an integer, mod 10,000
on     = bucket < percentage x 100

Worked example with real SHA-256 values for the flag new-task-board:

User First 4 bytes of the hash As integer Bucket (mod 10,000) On at 10%? 25%? 50%? user-16 3aa3e84c 983,820,364 364 yes yes yes user-1 4356a514 1,129,751,828 1828 no yes yes user-512 6cfbac84 1,828,433,028 3028 no no yes user-17 63a8c7c1 1,672,005,569 5569 no no no

Properties worth knowing:

  • Monotonic: raising 10% to 25% only adds users (buckets 1000 to 2499); nobody who had the feature loses it. Lowering the percentage removes the most recently added users first.
  • Uniform: a good hash spreads users evenly. Simulating 100,000 user IDs gives 10.1% in the 10% bucket range. (The modulo adds a bias too small to matter: 2^32 is not a multiple of 10,000, which skews bucket probabilities by about 0.0002%.)
  • Independent across flags: because the flag key is part of the hashed string, each flag picks a different 10%. In the same simulation, only 9.9% of the users inside flag A's 10% were also inside flag B's 10%, which is what independence predicts. Without the flag key in the hash, the same unlucky 10% of users would get every new feature first.
  • Choose the unit deliberately: bucket by userId for consumer features, by organizationId in a B2B product so a whole team sees the same UI, and by a device or session ID only for anonymous users. Changing the unit or the salt reshuffles everyone.

Unleash documents the same approach: it hashes the chosen stickiness field with the strategy's group ID (the flag name by default) using MurmurHash and compares the result with the rollout percentage.

docs.title: Dark launches
docs.text: A dark launch deploys and runs a feature in production without showing it to users: the flag is off for users but on for staff, or the new code runs in the background and its result is logged and discarded. It answers "does this work at production scale?" before "do users like it?". See advanced deployment patterns for dark launches alongside shadow traffic.

docs.title: Progressive delivery
docs.text:
Progressive delivery combines the pieces:

  1. Deploy the code with the flag off (dark), using a rolling or canary deployment for the technical risk.
  2. Turn the flag on for staff and test accounts.
  3. Roll out to 1%, 5%, 25%, 50%, 100% of users, watching guardrail metrics for the flagged population (errors, latency, and the business metric the feature should move or must not harm).
  4. If a guardrail regresses, turn the flag off; some flag platforms can do this automatically when metrics cross a threshold.
  5. At 100%, wait a short bake period, then remove the flag from the code.

Deployment strategies control which servers run new code; flags control which users see new behavior. Mature teams use both: a canary catches a crash in the new binary, a flag rollout catches a confusing UI or a slow query that only some users trigger.

docs.title: Flag lifecycle and flag debt
docs.text:
Flag debt is what accumulates when flags reach 100% and stay in the code:

  • Dead code paths that nobody tests but that can still be switched on.
  • Confusing combinations (with 20 flags there are about a million theoretical states).
  • The Knight Capital failure mode: a flag or an old code path that means something different on some servers than on others.

Controls that work:

  • Every flag has an owner and an expiry or review date when it is created.
  • CI fails when a release flag passes its expiry date (example below).
  • The flag service reports flags that served a single value for 30 days.
  • Removing the flag is part of the feature's definition of done.
  • Flag keys are never reused; a new purpose gets a new key.
  • Keep flag checks at the edges (route handlers, top-level components), not deep inside libraries, so removal is a small change.

docs.title: The OpenFeature standard
docs.text:
OpenFeature is a CNCF project that defines a vendor-neutral API for flag evaluation. Application code calls the OpenFeature API; a provider connects it to a flag system (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith, flagd, your own service, or an in-memory provider for tests). Switching vendors then means changing the provider, not every call site.

Core concepts:

  • Evaluation API: getBooleanValue, getStringValue, getNumberValue, getObjectValue, each with a flag key, a default value, and an optional context; get...Details variants also return the reason and variant.
  • Evaluation context: attributes about the subject, with targetingKey as the stable identifier used for bucketing.
  • Providers: adapters to flag back ends.
  • Hooks: code that runs before and after evaluations, for logging, metrics, or validation.
  • Domains: named clients bound to different providers.

docs.title: Testing with flags
docs.text:
• Test both states of every flag the change introduces, with other flags at their production values. Testing every combination is impossible; testing each new flag on and off is cheap.
  • Inject flags through an interface (or OpenFeature's in-memory provider) so tests set values directly instead of calling a network service.
  • Make the default value the old behavior, and test that the code behaves correctly when the flag service is down.
  • Run end-to-end tests with the flag states that production currently serves, not just "all on".

docs.title: Choosing a tool
docs.text:
Tool Model Notes LaunchDarkly SaaS Mature targeting, experimentation, streaming updates, wide SDK coverage Unleash Open source (self-host) and SaaS Strategies such as gradual rollout with stickiness; strong self-hosting story Flagsmith Open source (self-host) and SaaS Flags plus remote configuration values GrowthBook Open-source core, self-host or cloud Strong on experimentation and warehouse-native analysis ConfigCat SaaS Simple pricing, config files evaluated locally by SDKs AWS AppConfig Managed AWS service Feature flags and config with validators and deployment strategies that can roll back on alarms flagd Open source, OpenFeature project A small flag daemon that reads flag definitions from files or other sources

A home-grown flag service is reasonable for a handful of release flags and kill switches (the example below). Once you need audit logs, approval workflows, experimentation statistics, and a UI for non-engineers, a dedicated tool usually costs less than building those.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a flag for Do not use a flag for Merging unfinished work into main Secrets or credentials Gradual rollout of a risky behavior change Per-environment infrastructure settings (use configuration) A kill switch around an expensive or fragile dependency Database schema changes (use expand and contract) Beta programs and early access Permanent authorization rules that belong in your permission model A/B experiments on product ideas Trivial changes where the flag costs more than the risk

Also avoid flags in code that runs before the flag system is available (startup configuration), and avoid nesting flags inside flags.

docs.title: A small flag service with stable bucketing
docs.text:
// src/flags/flag-service.js: a small flag service with stable percentage bucketing
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const BUCKETS = 10_000; // 0.01% resolution

// Same flag + same unit (user, org) -> same bucket, on every server, forever.
export function bucketFor(flagKey, unitId, salt = flagKey) {
  const digest = createHash("sha256").update(`${salt}:${unitId}`).digest();
  return digest.readUInt32BE(0) % BUCKETS;
}

function matches(rule, ctx) {
  const actual = ctx[rule.attribute];
  switch (rule.operator) {
    case "in":
      return rule.values.includes(actual);
    case "notIn":
      return !rule.values.includes(actual);
    case "endsWith":
      return typeof actual === "string" && rule.values.some((v) => actual.endsWith(v));
    default:
      return false; // unknown operators never match
  }
}

export function evaluate(flag, ctx, defaultValue) {
  if (!flag) return { value: defaultValue, reason: "FLAG_NOT_FOUND" };
  if (!flag.enabled) return { value: flag.offValue, reason: "DISABLED" };

  const unitId = ctx[flag.bucketBy ?? "userId"];

  if (unitId && flag.targets?.[unitId] !== undefined) {
    return { value: flag.targets[unitId], reason: "TARGET_MATCH" };
  }
  for (const rule of flag.rules ?? []) {
    if (matches(rule, ctx)) return { value: rule.value, reason: "RULE_MATCH" };
  }
  if (flag.rollout && unitId) {
    const bucket = bucketFor(flag.key, unitId, flag.salt);
    const inRollout = bucket < flag.rollout.percentage * (BUCKETS / 100);
    return {
      value: inRollout ? flag.rollout.value : flag.fallthroughValue,
      reason: "PERCENTAGE_ROLLOUT",
      bucket,
    };
  }
  return { value: flag.fallthroughValue, reason: "FALLTHROUGH" };
}

export class FlagService {
  #flags = new Map();
  #timer;

  constructor({ source, refreshMs = 30_000, logger = console }) {
    this.source = source; // async () => array of flag definitions
    this.refreshMs = refreshMs;
    this.logger = logger;
  }

  async start() {
    await this.refresh();
    this.#timer = setInterval(() => this.refresh(), this.refreshMs);
    this.#timer.unref();
  }

  stop() {
    clearInterval(this.#timer);
  }

  async refresh() {
    try {
      const defs = await this.source();
      this.#flags = new Map(defs.map((f) => [f.key, f]));
    } catch (err) {
      // Keep serving the last good rules; never crash because flags are unavailable
      this.logger.error({ err }, "flag refresh failed; using last known rules");
    }
  }

  get(key, ctx, defaultValue) {
    return evaluate(this.#flags.get(key), ctx, defaultValue).value;
  }

  explain(key, ctx, defaultValue) {
    return evaluate(this.#flags.get(key), ctx, defaultValue);
  }
}

// Example source: a JSON file shipped by the flag pipeline (or an HTTP endpoint)
export const fileSource = (path) => async () => JSON.parse(await readFile(path, "utf8"));

The flag definitions, flags/flags.json (JSON has no comments, so the owner and expiry are ordinary fields):

[
  {
    "key": "new-task-board",
    "enabled": true,
    "offValue": false,
    "fallthroughValue": false,
    "bucketBy": "userId",
    "targets": { "user-qa-1": true },
    "rules": [
      { "attribute": "email", "operator": "endsWith", "values": ["@taskflow.example.com"], "value": true },
      { "attribute": "plan", "operator": "in", "values": ["beta"], "value": true }
    ],
    "rollout": { "percentage": 10, "value": true },
    "owner": "team-boards",
    "expires": "2027-01-31"
  },
  {
    "key": "search-backend-v2",
    "enabled": false,
    "offValue": false,
    "fallthroughValue": false,
    "owner": "team-search",
    "expires": "2026-12-15"
  }
]

Evaluating new-task-board with this file gives:

{ userId: "user-16", plan: "free" }               -> true   PERCENTAGE_ROLLOUT (bucket 364)
{ userId: "user-1",  plan: "free" }               -> false  PERCENTAGE_ROLLOUT (bucket 1828)
{ userId: "user-17", plan: "beta" }               -> true   RULE_MATCH
{ userId: "user-99", email: "ana@taskflow.example.com" } -> true RULE_MATCH
{ userId: "user-qa-1" }                           -> true   TARGET_MATCH
search-backend-v2 for anyone                      -> false  DISABLED
an unknown flag                                   -> the caller's default, FLAG_NOT_FOUND

Design choices worth copying: evaluation is a pure function (easy to test), the service keeps the last good rules when a refresh fails, the default value is chosen by the caller, and explain returns the reason so logs can show why a user saw a feature.

docs.title: Using it in an Express route
docs.text:
// src/routes/board.js
import { Router } from "express";
import { flags } from "../flags/index.js"; // a started FlagService instance

export const board = Router();

board.get("/board", async (req, res) => {
  const ctx = { userId: req.user.id, plan: req.user.plan, email: req.user.email };
  const { value: useNewBoard, reason } = flags.explain("new-task-board", ctx, false);

  req.log.info({ flag: "new-task-board", value: useNewBoard, reason }, "flag evaluated");
  res.json(useNewBoard ? await buildBoardV2(req.user) : await buildBoardV1(req.user));
});

docs.title: The same call through OpenFeature
docs.text:
// src/flags/openfeature.js: vendor-neutral evaluation (in-memory provider shown)
import { OpenFeature, InMemoryProvider } from "@openfeature/server-sdk";

await OpenFeature.setProviderAndWait(
  new InMemoryProvider({
    "new-task-board": {
      disabled: false,
      variants: { on: true, off: false },
      defaultVariant: "off",
      contextEvaluator: (ctx) => (ctx.plan === "beta" ? "on" : "off"),
    },
  }),
);

const client = OpenFeature.getClient("taskflow-api");

export async function useNewBoard(user) {
  return client.getBooleanValue("new-task-board", false, {
    targetingKey: user.id, // the stable ID providers use for bucketing
    plan: user.plan,
  });
}

// On shutdown: await OpenFeature.close();

In production you replace InMemoryProvider with the provider package for your flag system; the call sites do not change.

docs.title: Testing both states
docs.text:
// test/board.test.js
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { evaluate } from "../src/flags/flag-service.js";

const flag = {
  key: "new-task-board",
  enabled: true,
  offValue: false,
  fallthroughValue: false,
  rollout: { percentage: 10, value: true },
};

test("a user inside the 10% rollout gets the new board", () => {
  assert.equal(evaluate(flag, { userId: "user-16" }, false).value, true); // bucket 364
});

test("a user outside the rollout keeps the old board", () => {
  assert.equal(evaluate(flag, { userId: "user-1" }, false).value, false); // bucket 1828
});

test("a disabled flag acts as a kill switch", () => {
  assert.equal(evaluate({ ...flag, enabled: false }, { userId: "user-16" }, false).value, false);
});

test("an unknown flag falls back to the caller's default", () => {
  assert.equal(evaluate(undefined, { userId: "user-16" }, false).value, false);
});

docs.title: Failing CI on expired flags
docs.text:
// scripts/check-flag-expiry.js: fail the build when a release flag is past its date
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const flags = JSON.parse(await readFile("flags/flags.json", "utf8"));
const today = new Date().toISOString().slice(0, 10); // YYYY-MM-DD compares as text

const expired = flags.filter((f) => f.expires && f.expires < today);
for (const f of expired) {
  console.error(`flag "${f.key}" (owner ${f.owner}) expired on ${f.expires}: remove it or extend it`);
}
if (expired.length > 0) process.exit(1);

Add node scripts/check-flag-expiry.js to the CI pipeline. Extending a date is allowed, but it becomes a visible, reviewed decision instead of silent drift.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Default every flag call to the safe, old behavior.
  • Give every flag an owner, a kind, and an expiry or review date.
  • Hash a stable ID salted with the flag key for percentage rollouts; bucket by organization in B2B products.
  • Keep rules on the server; send clients only their evaluated values.
  • Log the flag value and reason with requests, so incidents can be traced to flag states.
  • Watch guardrail metrics per flag cohort during rollouts.
  • Remove release flags within days of reaching 100%; never reuse keys.
  • Keep kill switches for expensive or fragile dependencies and test them regularly.
  • Put flag checks at the edges of the code, not deep in shared libraries.
  • Use OpenFeature (or your own thin interface) so call sites do not depend on one vendor's SDK.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A user sees the new feature appear and disappear. Detect: support reports of a flickering UI; logs show the same user with different flag values. Cause: bucketing on a value that changes (session ID, random number), or rules that depend on an attribute not always present. Fix: bucket on a stable user or organization ID and always send the same context.
  • The flag service had an outage and the API slowed to a crawl. Detect: latency matches the flag client's timeout. Cause: flags were evaluated by a network call per request. Fix: use an SDK that evaluates locally from cached rules, with code defaults if rules never loaded.
  • An unreleased feature name leaked. Detect: someone posts flag keys found in the browser's network tab. Cause: the client SDK received the full rule set. Fix: evaluate on the server or vendor edge and send only values; use neutral flag keys.
  • Turning a flag off did not stop the problem. Detect: errors continue after the flag change. Cause: the slow code was not behind the flag, values were cached in the app for a long time, or a second flag also controlled the path. Fix: keep refresh intervals short, test kill switches, and map which code each flag guards.
  • An old flag reactivated retired code. Detect: unexpected behavior after a config change to a flag "nobody uses". Cause: flag debt; the dead path was never deleted, or a key was reused. Fix: expiry dates enforced in CI, cleanup as part of done, and new keys for new purposes.
  • A 10% rollout hit the same customers as the last three rollouts. Detect: the same accounts report every new bug. Cause: bucketing hashed only the user ID, without the flag key. Fix: include the flag key (or a per-flag salt) in the hashed string.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Feature flag (toggle): a runtime switch that selects a code path.
  • Evaluation context: the attributes describing who or what a flag is evaluated for.
  • Targeting rule: a condition on context attributes that selects a variant.
  • Segment: a reusable group of targeting rules.
  • Variant: one of the values a flag can serve.
  • Percentage rollout: serving a variant to a share of units chosen by hashing.
  • Bucketing (stickiness): mapping a stable ID to a fixed bucket so the decision is consistent.
  • Kill switch: an ops flag that turns off functionality quickly.
  • Dark launch: running a feature in production without exposing it to users.
  • Progressive delivery: releasing to growing audiences with measurement and automatic or manual stop points.
  • Flag debt: flags and dead code paths left after their purpose ended.
  • OpenFeature: a CNCF project defining a vendor-neutral flag evaluation API.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using flags as a substitute for testing; a flag limits blast radius, it does not make the code correct.
  • Evaluating flags with a network call on every request.
  • Choosing an unsafe default value, so an outage of the flag service turns features on.
  • Shipping all flag rules to browsers.
  • Hashing only the user ID, so the same users are always first.
  • Leaving release flags in the code indefinitely, and reusing old keys.
  • Treating permission and kill-switch flags like release flags and deleting them.
  • Assuming a flag can protect a database schema change; both code paths still need a compatible schema.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are the four kinds of feature flags, and how do their lifetimes differ?
  2. Why must percentage rollouts hash a stable identifier instead of using a random number per request?
  3. With buckets 0 to 9,999, a user's bucket is 2,731. At which rollout percentages is the user included: 10%, 25%, 30%, 50%?
  4. Why should the flag key be part of the hashed string?
  5. When would you bucket by organization ID instead of user ID?
  6. What should happen when the flag service is unreachable, and how should the SDK be built to make that safe?
  7. Explain how flag debt contributed to the Knight Capital incident.
  8. What does OpenFeature standardize, and what stays vendor-specific?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Pete Hodgson: Feature Toggles (aka Feature Flags)
  • OpenFeature specification
  • OpenFeature: JavaScript server SDK
  • Unleash: Stickiness
  • Google Cloud incident report, June 12, 2025
  • Next: zero-downtime database migrations. Back to the deployment strategies overview.

docs.title: Deployment Strategies Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review environments and promotion, deploying backend services, rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments, advanced patterns, feature flags, zero-downtime migrations, rollbacks, frontend deploys, and client app releases. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. Why should you build an artifact once and promote it, instead of building per environment?
docs.text: Rebuilding can produce a different artifact: dependency resolution, base image tags, and build-time variables can change between builds, so what reaches production would not be what was tested. Building once and promoting the same image by digest keeps a chain of evidence from test to production; only configuration changes per environment.

docs.title: 2. What is environment parity, and where does it usually break?
docs.text: Parity means environments differ only where they must. It breaks in backing service versions, topology (standalone database locally, replica set in production), data volume, instance count, third-party sandboxes, edge configuration (CDN, TLS), configuration values, and flag states. Aim for the same kinds of things everywhere and accept differences in size.

docs.title: 3. What is a preview environment, and what must it get right?
docs.text: A short-lived copy of the application per pull request, with its own URL, namespace, and seeded database, destroyed when the pull request closes. It needs isolation, synthetic data, sandbox-only credentials (none for fork pull requests), access control, and reliable teardown, including a TTL reaper for missed close events.

docs.title: 4. What is the difference between deploying and releasing?
docs.text: Deploying installs a version in an environment; releasing exposes new behavior to users. Feature flags decouple them, so code can reach production switched off and be released later, gradually, without another deploy.

docs.title: 5. Why can heavy manual approval gates increase risk?
docs.text: Slow approvals make teams batch changes into bigger releases, which are harder to test, debug, and roll back. DORA's research associates heavyweight external change approval with worse delivery performance; peer review plus automated checks works better, with manual gates kept for genuinely high-risk steps.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between liveness and readiness probes?
docs.text: Liveness answers "is this process stuck beyond repair?" and failing it restarts the process. Readiness answers "should this instance receive traffic now?" and failing it removes the instance from load balancing. Liveness must not check dependencies; otherwise a database outage restarts every instance.

docs.title: 7. Describe a graceful shutdown for a Node API.
docs.text: On SIGTERM (or PM2's SIGINT): set a draining flag so readiness returns 503, wait a few seconds for load balancers to stop routing, call server.close(), keep closing idle keep-alive connections, wait for in-flight requests, close the database client and consumers, and exit 0. A forced exit before the platform's SIGKILL covers hangs.

docs.title: 8. Why can server.close() take as long as the keep-alive timeout?
docs.text: close() calls back only when all connections are closed. Since Node 19 it closes connections that are idle at that moment, but a connection that becomes idle afterwards stays open until keepAliveTimeout. Calling server.closeIdleConnections() repeatedly while draining fixes it.

docs.title: 9. Why set Node's keep-alive timeout above the load balancer's idle timeout?
docs.text: If Node closes an idle connection (5 seconds by default) at the moment the load balancer reuses it (AWS ALB keeps idle connections 60 seconds by default), the request fails with a 502. With Node's timeout longer, the load balancer always closes first.

docs.title: 10. What is the difference between pm2 restart and pm2 reload?
docs.text: restart stops and starts all processes, leaving a gap. reload in cluster mode replaces workers one at a time, starting a new worker and waiting until it is ready (optionally until it calls process.send("ready")) before stopping the old one. In fork mode with one process, reload behaves like restart.

docs.title: 11. Why is git pull not a deploy for a compiled binary?
docs.text: The code is embedded in the binary at build time. Pulling changes the source but not the running program, so the old code serves (including old routes) until you rebuild and restart. Expose the commit at /version and verify it after every deploy.

docs.title: 12. Where should database migrations run in a deploy?
docs.text: Once, as a separate pipeline step or job before the rollout, not on every instance's startup. The migration must be compatible with the old code still running, and destructive steps belong to a later release.

docs.title: 13. Compare recreate and rolling deployments.
docs.text: Recreate stops everything and starts the new version: simple, no version mixing, but downtime. Rolling replaces instances in batches with no downtime, but both versions serve traffic during the rollout and there is no metric gate or automatic rollback by default.

docs.title: 14. What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control?
docs.text: How far above (surge) or below (unavailable) the desired replica count a Kubernetes rolling update may go. maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 adds one new pod at a time and removes an old one only after the new one is ready, keeping full capacity.

docs.title: 15. How does blue-green deployment work, and what is its main limitation?
docs.text: Two full environments run; one is live. The new version goes to the idle one, is warmed and tested privately, and the router switches to it; switching back is the rollback. The limitation is the shared database: the schema must work for both versions, and blue-green does nothing to undo data changes. It also exposes everyone at the switch.

docs.title: 16. What makes a canary release effective?
docs.text: A small, representative share of traffic, a baseline running at the same time for comparison, user-facing metrics (errors, latency, saturation, business events), enough traffic for statistics, step-by-step increases with soak times, and automated abort when analysis fails.

docs.title: 17. Why compare a canary with a baseline running at the same time?
docs.text: Traffic and behavior vary by time of day and day of week, so comparing with yesterday mixes the change with unrelated variation. A simultaneous baseline (ideally a fresh one of the same size, as Kayenta does) isolates the effect of the change.

docs.title: 18. A service handles 200 requests per second with a 0.2% error rate. Can a 1% canary for 10 minutes detect the error rate doubling?
docs.text: The canary sees 1,200 requests; 2.4 errors are expected if healthy and 4.8 if doubled, a difference smaller than the noise (about sqrt(2.4) ≈ 1.5). Detecting the doubling at three standard deviations needs about 4,500 requests: 37 minutes at 1%, under 4 minutes at 10%. A 5% failure, by contrast, shows up as about 60 errors immediately.

docs.title: 19. How do the main traffic-shifting mechanisms compare?
docs.text: Load balancer weights, Gateway API routes, and service meshes split precisely per request and roll back in seconds. Replica ratios are coarse. DNS weights are imprecise and slow because resolvers and clients cache beyond the TTL. Platform features (Cloud Run revisions, Lambda aliases) are precise but platform-specific.

docs.title: 20. How does a canary differ from an A/B test?
docs.text: A canary checks whether a new version is safe, using technical metrics, over minutes to hours, ending in promotion or rollback. An A/B test compares product variants on user behavior with sticky assignment and a pre-planned sample size, over days or weeks, ending with the winner shipped. Canaries use traffic routing; A/B tests usually use flags inside one version.

docs.title: 21. What state-related problems appear when two versions run side by side?
docs.text: In-memory sessions lost on switches, users bouncing between versions without stickiness, long-lived connections staying on the old version, cache entries in new formats crashing old code, queue messages one version cannot parse, scheduled jobs running twice, and schema changes that only one version understands.

docs.title: 22. What is red/black deployment?
docs.text: Netflix's and Spinnaker's name for blue-green with immutable server groups: a new group is created, enabled in the load balancer, and the old group is disabled but kept running for fast rollback, then destroyed after a bake. Spinnaker 1.30 and later call it blue/green.

docs.title: 23. When would you use a rainbow deployment?
docs.text: When long-lived connections (WebSockets, streams) take hours to drain. Each release gets its own Deployment; new connections go to the newest, old versions keep their existing connections and are deleted when nearly empty. Several versions run at once, so compatibility must hold across all of them.

docs.title: 24. What are the risks of shadow (mirrored) traffic?
docs.text: Side effects (writes, emails, payments, events) happening twice, doubled load on shared dependencies, noisy response comparisons, and proxy resources tied up by slow mirrors. Mirror only read paths, sandbox the shadow's dependencies, and start with a small percentage.

docs.title: 25. What is the "one box, then one AZ, then one region" progression?
docs.text: A staged production rollout described in the Amazon Builders' Library: a single host first, then a low-traffic region one Availability Zone at a time, then a high-traffic region, then more regions in parallel, each with bake time and automatic rollback on alarms. A failure therefore reaches a small, fault-isolated slice first.

docs.title: 26. How do cells reduce blast radius, and what is their weak point?
docs.text: Each cell is an independent copy of the stack serving a fixed subset of customers, so a bad deploy or failure in one cell affects only 1/N of customers. The weak point is anything shared: the cell router and global control plane must be changed with the same staged caution.

docs.title: 27. How can an API serve clients pinned to old versions without branching all its code?
docs.text: The core builds only the newest response shape; each breaking change adds a small transform that converts a response to the previous version's shape. Requests pinned to an old version pass through the transforms in reverse. Stripe describes this with "version change modules". Usage per version tells you when an old version can be retired.

docs.title: 28. What are the four kinds of feature flags?
docs.text: Release flags (hide unfinished work, short-lived), experiment flags (A/B tests), ops flags or kill switches (turn off fragile or expensive functionality, long-lived), and permission flags (features per plan or group, long-lived).

docs.title: 29. How do you implement a sticky percentage rollout?
docs.text: Hash a stable identifier together with the flag key (for example SHA-256 of "new-task-board:user-16"), take the result modulo 10,000 as a bucket, and enable the flag when the bucket is below the percentage times 100. The same user always gets the same answer, raising the percentage only adds users, and different flags select different users.

docs.title: 30. Why include the flag key in the hash?
docs.text: Without it, every flag selects the same users for its first 10%, so the same customers always receive every new feature (and every new bug) first. Including the key makes rollouts independent.

docs.title: 31. Should flags be evaluated server-side or client-side?
docs.text: Server-side SDKs keep rules in memory and evaluate locally, keeping targeting rules private. Client apps should receive only the evaluated values for the current user, not the full rule set, and should bootstrap values to avoid UI flicker.

docs.title: 32. What is flag debt, and how do you control it?
docs.text: Flags and dead code paths left after their purpose ended: untested paths, confusing combinations, and the risk of reactivating old behavior, as in the Knight Capital incident. Control it with an owner and expiry date per flag, CI that fails on expired flags, stale-flag reports, removal as part of done, and never reusing keys.

docs.title: 33. What does OpenFeature standardize?
docs.text: A vendor-neutral evaluation API (typed get...Value calls with a key, default, and context), the evaluation context with a targetingKey, providers that connect to flag systems, hooks, and domains. Call sites stay the same when you change vendors.

docs.title: 34. What should happen when the flag service is unreachable?
docs.text: The SDK keeps serving the last known rules; if it never loaded rules, it returns the default value passed in the code, which must be the safe, old behavior. Flag evaluation must never block requests on a network call.

docs.title: 35. Why must a migration be compatible with the code already running?
docs.text: The migration runs before the new code rolls out, and during the rollout old and new versions share the schema. A rollback runs the old code again. Any change that only the new code understands breaks the old instances still serving traffic.

docs.title: 36. Explain expand and contract with a column rename.
docs.text: Add the new column (expand); deploy code that writes both and reads the old; backfill old rows in batches; deploy code that reads the new and still writes both; deploy code that uses only the new column; later drop the old column (contract). Each step changes either schema or code, so each deploy can be undone by one step.

docs.title: 37. How should a large backfill be run?
docs.text: In small batches by primary-key range (keyset pagination), each committed separately, with pauses and throttling on replication lag, idempotent (only rows that still need it) and resumable, never overwriting values the dual-writing application already set, and verified afterwards.

docs.title: 38. Why can a fast ALTER TABLE still cause an outage?
docs.text: It needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock. If a long query holds a conflicting lock, the ALTER waits, and every later query on the table queues behind it. Setting a short lock_timeout makes the migration fail and retry instead of blocking the application.

docs.title: 39. How do you add NOT NULL to a large PostgreSQL table safely?
docs.text: Add CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID (brief lock), run VALIDATE CONSTRAINT (scans without blocking reads or writes), then SET NOT NULL, which on PostgreSQL 12+ uses the validated constraint and skips the scan, and drop the check.

docs.title: 40. What are the caveats of CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY?
docs.text: It is slower, cannot run in a transaction block, and on failure leaves an invalid index that IF NOT EXISTS will silently skip. Drop the invalid index concurrently and build again.

docs.title: 41. How do MongoDB index builds affect a live collection?
docs.text: Since 4.2, builds hold an exclusive lock only briefly at the start and end, allowing reads and writes in between, and since 4.4 replica set members build simultaneously and commit by quorum. Builds still consume resources, so run large ones off-peak and watch replication lag.

docs.title: 42. Why do teams roll forward rather than run down migrations?
docs.text: Down migrations cannot restore dropped data, may destroy data written in the new shape, and are rarely tested. Expand steps rarely need undoing, contract steps happen after stability is proven, and true data recovery uses backups.

docs.title: 43. When do you roll back and when do you roll forward?
docs.text: Roll back when a release correlates with the problem and rollback is safe: restore service first, diagnose later. Roll forward when the new version wrote data the old one cannot read, when there are irreversible side effects, or when a tiny, certain fix ships faster than a rollback. Turning off a flag is the fastest option when it applies.

docs.title: 44. What makes a rollback possible?
docs.text: A retained immutable artifact, a still-valid configuration for the old version, a schema and data the old version can read, compatible messages and caches, a plan for irreversible side effects, compatible clients, and practice.

docs.title: 45. What is the prepare-then-activate technique?
docs.text: For a data format change, first deploy a version that reads both formats but writes the old one (prepare); once it is everywhere, deploy the version that writes the new format (activate). Any rollback then leaves servers able to read everything written.

docs.title: 46. How long should a release bake?
docs.text: Long enough to include a traffic peak and scheduled jobs and to reveal slow failures such as memory leaks. Amazon's pipelines bake at least an hour after the first host and at least 12 hours after the first region; Microsoft's guidance suggests about a day per tier.

docs.title: 47. What are the DORA instability metrics?
docs.text: Change fail rate (the share of deployments requiring immediate intervention) and deployment rework rate (the share of unplanned deployments caused by production incidents); since 2024 DORA groups failed deployment recovery time with throughput. With 120 deploys and 9 needing a rollback or hotfix, the change fail rate is 7.5%.

docs.title: 48. What are the trade-offs of change freezes?
docs.text: They reduce change during high-risk periods but cause a backlog that ships as a large, risky batch afterwards. Keep them short, allow small low-risk changes, keep an emergency path, and release the backlog gradually.

docs.title: 49. What cache headers should a built SPA use?
docs.text: Content-hashed assets: public, max-age=31536000, immutable, because the name changes when content changes. HTML entry points: no-cache, so browsers revalidate on every load and pick up new asset names. Unhashed files: a short max-age.

docs.title: 50. In what order should a static deploy upload files?
docs.text: New hashed assets first, then the entry point (index.html) last, then invalidate only the entry point at the CDN. Delete old assets days later, so open tabs from the previous version can still load their chunks.

docs.title: 51. Does a CDN purge fix stale content in users' browsers?
docs.text: No. A purge clears CDN edge caches only. Browsers keep anything cached with a long max-age until it expires, which is why HTML must not get a long max-age.

docs.title: 52. How do you configure SPA fallback routing correctly?
docs.text: Serve index.html with status 200 for page routes that have no file, but keep real 404s for missing assets (paths under /assets/ or with a file extension). Otherwise a missing script returns HTML and fails with a MIME type error.

docs.title: 53. Why can one frontend build not always be promoted across environments?
docs.text: Values such as import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL are inlined at build time, so the build contains one environment's values. Either build per environment or fetch runtime configuration at startup.

docs.title: 54. Why can a mobile or desktop release not be rolled back?
docs.text: Installed copies are on users' devices. Halting a staged rollout stops new installs, but existing ones stay until users install a newer version. The fix is to halt, disable the feature remotely, and ship a fix forward.

docs.title: 55. What do code signing, timestamping, and notarization do?
docs.text: Signing identifies the publisher and proves the binary is unchanged. Timestamping keeps the signature valid after the certificate expires. Notarization (macOS) is Apple's automated check of Developer ID software, whose ticket Gatekeeper verifies before first launch.

docs.title: 56. How does a secure auto-update system work?
docs.text: The app asks an update endpoint (with version, platform, channel, and install ID), receives a manifest with the version, URL, and signature, downloads the file, verifies the signature with a public key embedded in the app, installs, and reports its new version. The server controls channels, rollout percentage, and halts.

docs.title: 57. How do Apple and Google stage mobile releases?
docs.text: Apple's phased release offers an update to 1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, and 100% of automatic-update users over 7 days, with pauses up to 30 days. Google Play's staged rollout uses a percentage you raise manually and can halt; users who already received it keep it.

docs.title: 58. How do you keep old clients working as the API evolves?
docs.text: Send client version on every call, only add fields, make clients ignore unknown fields, version breaking changes, ship server support before clients that use it, keep remote switches for client features, and enforce a minimum version only for emergencies after checking who it affects.

docs.title: 59. Every deploy of the API causes a burst of 502 errors for about 20 seconds. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether instances drain before stopping and receive traffic only when ready.

How to confirm: load balancer logs show 502s from targets being deregistered or just started; app logs show no SIGTERM handling, or readiness that returns 200 before the database connects.

Likely causes and fixes: no graceful shutdown, readiness that lies, or npm start as PID 1 swallowing SIGTERM. Add readiness checks, a drain delay before server.close(), idle-connection sweeping, and exec-form CMD. See deploying backend services.

docs.title: 60. Occasional 502s appear at low traffic, unrelated to deploys. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: the app's keep-alive timeout compared with the load balancer's idle timeout.

How to confirm: 502s cluster after idle periods; load balancer logs show target connection resets on reused connections.

Likely causes and fixes: Node closes idle connections after 5 seconds while the load balancer reuses them for up to 60. Set server.keepAliveTimeout above the proxy's idle timeout. See deploying backend services.

docs.title: 61. A rolling deploy completed, all pods were Ready, and the error rate went to 30%. Why did nothing stop it?
docs.text:
What to check first: what the readiness probe checks and whether any metric gate exists.

How to confirm: the probe returns 200 without exercising real dependencies; the rollout had no analysis step.

Likely causes and fixes: rolling updates only gate on readiness and do not roll back automatically. Add canary analysis or a post-deploy metric watch with automatic rollout undo. See rolling, blue-green, and canary.

docs.title: 62. The rollback of a bad release took 25 minutes. How do you make it faster next time?
docs.text:
What to check first: how traffic was shifted back and whether the old version was still running.

How to confirm: the switch used DNS and clients cached it, or the blue environment had been scaled to zero and had to start cold.

Likely causes and fixes: use load balancer or mesh weights instead of DNS, keep the previous version warm during the bake period, and automate the rollback decision on alarms. See rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: 63. The deploy pipeline ran a migration and the whole API froze for 40 seconds. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: pg_stat_activity during the migration and the locks involved.

How to confirm: many sessions waited on a lock behind an ALTER TABLE, which itself waited for a long-running report query.

Likely causes and fixes: the lock queue. Set lock_timeout for migrations and retry, cancel long queries first, and run risky DDL off-peak. See zero-downtime database migrations.

docs.title: 64. Right after deploying v2, the still-running v1 pods started throwing "column does not exist". What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the migration that ran with this release.

How to confirm: it renamed or dropped a column v1 still uses.

Likely causes and fixes: a contract step shipped with the code change. Restore the column (or roll forward with a compatibility view), then redo the change with expand and contract. See zero-downtime database migrations.

docs.title: 65. The same handful of customers report every new feature's bugs first. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how percentage rollouts choose users.

How to confirm: the bucketing hashes only the user ID, so each flag's first 10% is the same set of users.

Likely causes and fixes: include the flag key (or a per-flag salt) in the hashed value. See feature flags and progressive delivery.

docs.title: 66. A flag nobody had touched for a year was switched on and reactivated retired behavior. How do you prevent this?
docs.text:
What to check first: the flag's history, owner, and the code it guards.

How to confirm: the flag reached 100% (or was abandoned) long ago and its old code path was never removed, or the key was reused.

Likely causes and fixes: flag debt. Enforce owners and expiry dates in CI, delete flags and dead code after rollout, and never reuse keys. See feature flags and progressive delivery.

docs.title: 67. After a frontend deploy, some users see a blank page. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the browser console and the HTML response's Cache-Control and referenced asset names.

How to confirm: 404s for index-<hash>.js; the new HTML was uploaded before its assets, or old assets were deleted while old HTML was cached.

Likely causes and fixes: upload assets first and HTML last, keep old assets for days, serve HTML with no-cache, and reload once on preload errors. See deploying frontends and static sites.

docs.title: 68. The desktop app's 1.9.0 release crashes on startup for some users. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: crash-free sessions by release and the share of installs on 1.9.0.

How to confirm: crash reports cluster on 1.9.0 with one stack trace.

Likely causes and fixes: halt the rollout in the update server, disable the failing feature by remote flag for 1.9.0 if possible, and ship 1.9.1 through the stages quickly. Installed copies cannot be recalled. See releasing desktop and mobile apps.

docs.title: 69. A server change broke older mobile app versions. How do you prevent a repeat?
docs.text:
What to check first: API errors by client version since the deploy.

How to confirm: a field was removed or a parameter made required that old versions do not send.

Likely causes and fixes: revert the change, keep APIs compatible with every supported client version, run contract tests per version, and only raise the minimum version after usage drops. See releasing desktop and mobile apps.

docs.title: 70. Staging passed, production failed on the same image digest. Where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: the effective configuration of both environments and differences in scale or data.

How to confirm: a variable, flag state, or dependency version differs, or a query is slow only on production-sized data.

Likely causes and fixes: configuration drift or parity gaps. Validate configuration at startup, keep it versioned, and load-test staging with production-sized synthetic data. See environments and promotion.

docs.title: Releasing Desktop and Mobile Apps
docs.text:
Server software runs on machines you control: you deploy, and minutes later every user runs the new version. Desktop and mobile apps run on machines your users control: they install when they choose, sometimes never, and every version you ever shipped may still be running somewhere. Releasing client software therefore needs its own techniques: code signing so operating systems trust the app, auto-update systems that verify what they install, channels and staged rollouts, minimum supported versions, APIs that keep old clients working, app store review, and crash reporting by release.

This lesson covers those techniques at a practical level, using a TaskFlow desktop app (built with Tauri) and TaskFlow mobile apps as examples.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Three properties make client releases riskier than server releases:

  • No rollback. Once a version is installed, you cannot remove it from users' devices. A halted rollout stops new installs; it does not undo existing ones. The only fix is a newer version, or a remote switch built into the app beforehand.
  • Old versions live forever. Some users disable updates, some devices cannot run the latest OS, and enterprise customers pin versions. Your API serves many client versions at once, for months or years.
  • Slow fixes. A server hotfix ships in minutes. A mobile fix waits for store review and for users to update; even after the fix is approved, it reaches users over days.

The CrowdStrike incident of July 2024 shows the scale of the problem: a content update pushed to Windows endpoints crashed machines worldwide, and because the affected machines could not boot normally, they could not receive a fix automatically either. Its root cause analysis committed to staged deployment through rings with canary testing. Client software that updates itself is a deployment system and needs the same safety as a server pipeline.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Apple App Store phased release. Apple's documentation on releasing a version update in phases describes a 7-day schedule (1%, 2%, 5%, 10%, 20%, 50%, then 100% of users with automatic updates), pausing for up to 30 days in total, and notes that anyone can still download the update manually from the App Store during the phase.
  • Google Play staged rollouts. Google's staged rollout documentation says you choose the percentage of users who receive an update, that it never increases automatically, that halting stops further users from getting it while users who already have it keep it, and that staged rollouts apply to updates, not first releases.
  • Tauri updater. The Tauri updater plugin requires every update to be signed ("This cannot be disabled"), embeds the public key in the app, and warns that losing the private key means you can no longer publish updates to existing installs.
  • Apple notarization. Apple's guide to notarizing macOS software before distribution explains that software distributed outside the Mac App Store with a Developer ID is submitted to Apple's notary service, and that Gatekeeper checks for the notarization ticket before first launch.
  • Sentry release health. Sentry's release health documentation describes tracking crash-free sessions and users per release, the signal most teams use to decide whether to continue or halt a client rollout.

Popular tools and providers: Tauri updater, electron-updater (electron-builder), Squirrel.Windows, Sparkle (macOS), MSIX and the Microsoft Store, App Store Connect and TestFlight, Google Play Console and its testing tracks, Firebase App Distribution, fastlane, and crash reporting with Sentry or Firebase Crashlytics.

docs.title: Why client releases differ
docs.text: Server Desktop or mobile client Who installs You The user, or the OS on their behalf Time to reach 100% Minutes Days to never Rollback Redeploy the previous version Impossible for installed copies; ship a newer one Versions running at once One or two Dozens Gatekeepers Your pipeline OS trust (signing), app store review Configuration changes Instant Only through remote config built into the app Observability Logs and metrics you own Crash reports and analytics the app sends

docs.title: Code signing
docs.text:
Code signing proves who published a binary and that it has not been changed since. Operating systems warn about or block unsigned software.

  • Windows (Authenticode). Executables and installers are signed with a code signing certificate using signtool. Always add a timestamp from a timestamping service, so the signature stays valid after the certificate expires. Since mid-2023, the CA/Browser Forum's code signing requirements mean the private keys of publicly trusted code signing certificates must be kept in hardware (a token or a hardware security module, including cloud HSM signing services), so CI pipelines sign through such a service rather than a key file. Microsoft Defender SmartScreen also uses reputation, so a new certificate or a new file may still show warnings until reputation builds.
  • macOS. Apps distributed outside the Mac App Store are signed with a Developer ID certificate, built with the hardened runtime, notarized by Apple's notary service (xcrun notarytool), and the ticket is stapled to the app or disk image (xcrun stapler) so Gatekeeper can verify it offline.
  • iOS and Android. Store apps are always signed. iOS uses Apple-issued certificates and provisioning profiles; Android apps are signed with an app signing key, which with Play App Signing is managed by Google while you sign uploads with a separate upload key.
  • Linux. Packages in apt or rpm repositories are verified through the repository's signing key; formats such as Flatpak and Snap have their own signing models.

Signing keys are among the most sensitive secrets a company has: anyone holding them can ship software your users' machines will trust. See secrets management.

docs.title: Auto-update architecture
docs.text:
The parts:

  • Update manifest: a small document (JSON or YAML) per channel and platform listing the latest version, download URL, signature or hash, release notes, and optionally a rollout percentage. It can be a static file on a CDN or computed per request by an update server.
  • Signature verification: the app embeds an update-signing public key and refuses any download whose signature does not verify. This is separate from OS code signing and protects against a compromised CDN or update server.
  • Download and install: in the background where possible, applied on restart, with a prompt for large or disruptive updates.
  • Channels: stable, beta, and sometimes nightly or canary. Users or administrators choose; staff run beta. Chrome's Stable, Beta, Dev, and Canary channels are the best-known example of this model.
  • Reporting: the app reports its version (anonymously) so you know the version distribution and can measure crash rates per release.

Tauri, electron-updater, Sparkle, and Squirrel all implement this shape with different file formats. Updater design in depth (static manifests versus update servers, signing-key rotation, delta updates, cohort rollouts and roll-forward, over-the-air JavaScript updates, and service workers for web apps) is covered in update mechanisms and updaters.

docs.title: Staged rollouts and halting
docs.text:
A staged rollout offers a new version to a growing share of installs. App stores provide it (Apple's phased release, Google Play's staged rollouts); for desktop apps the update server or manifest provides it (electron-updater reads a stagingPercentage field; a custom update server can bucket install IDs exactly like a feature flag).

Typical gates between stages: crash-free sessions and users for the new release compared with the previous one, error rates of API calls made by that version, and support tickets. When a gate fails:

  1. Halt the rollout so no new users receive the version.
  2. Mitigate with remote configuration: turn off the broken feature by flag for that app version.
  3. Ship a fix forward and roll it out, often faster, to replace the bad version where it landed.

docs.title: Minimum supported version and forced updates
docs.text:
Every API call from a client should carry its platform and version (for example X-Client-Platform: desktop and X-Client-Version: 1.8.0). That gives you the version distribution and a way to enforce a floor:

  • Soft update: the app shows a banner suggesting the update.
  • Hard (forced) update: below the minimum version, the API returns a specific error and the app shows a blocking "please update" screen. On Android, Google Play's in-app updates API offers an "immediate" flow for this; on iOS the app links to its App Store page.
  • Raise the floor carefully: only after the old version's usage is small, with notice, and never as a substitute for keeping APIs compatible. Forcing an update that the store has not yet approved, or that some OS versions cannot install, locks users out.

Minimum and recommended versions, contract tests for every supported client release, and support windows are covered in more depth in keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: Backward-compatible APIs for old clients
docs.text:
Because many client versions call the API at once:

  • Add fields; do not remove or rename them while supported clients use them. Make clients ignore unknown fields and unknown enum values.
  • Version breaking changes and serve old versions from the same code (see pinned-version clients in advanced deployment patterns).
  • Ship server support first, then the client that uses it; never the other way round.
  • Keep server-side switches for client features, so a broken feature in an installed version can be disabled remotely.

docs.title: App store review and phased release
docs.text:
• Review. Both Apple and Google review submissions, so a release cannot be shipped at a moment of your choosing; build review time into plans. Apple offers expedited review requests for critical fixes.
  • Testing tracks. TestFlight (iOS) and Google Play's internal, closed, and open testing tracks give staff and beta users builds before production, the client equivalent of rings.
  • Phased release. Use Apple's 7-day phased release and Play's staged rollouts for every production update, and watch crash rates at each step.
  • Release timing. Submitting early in the week leaves time to react before a weekend.

docs.title: Crash reporting by release
docs.text:
Crash and error reporting must be tagged with the release (version and build number) so you can compare releases:

  • Crash-free sessions and crash-free users per release are the main health signals.
  • Symbols must be uploaded for each build (dSYM files for Apple platforms, R8/ProGuard mapping files for Android, source maps for JavaScript, PDB files for Windows), or stack traces are unreadable.
  • New issues that appear only in the new release point at the change.
  • Gates: promote the rollout only if crash-free sessions for the new release are at least as good as the previous release's.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Consumer mobile app Store phased release or staged rollout on every update, remote flags for risky features, a minimum version for emergencies Desktop app distributed directly Signed builds, a signed auto-update manifest, beta and stable channels, server-side percentage rollout Enterprise desktop deployments Let administrators control versions (MSI or MSIX with management tools), support pinned versions longer, communicate deprecations Internal tool used by a few staff A simple signed auto-update to everyone may be enough Critical security fix Expedited review or accelerated rollout, but still in fast stages if possible; consider raising the minimum version

Avoid forced updates as a routine tool, and avoid shipping a client that depends on a server change that is not yet live.

docs.title: Tauri: updater configuration
docs.text:
{
  "bundle": {
    "createUpdaterArtifacts": true
  },
  "plugins": {
    "updater": {
      "pubkey": "<contents of the public key file, not a path>",
      "endpoints": [
        "https://updates.taskflow.example.com/desktop/{{target}}/{{arch}}/{{current_version}}"
      ]
    }
  }
}

These are the relevant parts of src-tauri/tauri.conf.json. createUpdaterArtifacts makes the bundler produce update packages and their .sig files. The private key is generated once with the Tauri CLI's signer generate command and provided to the build through the TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY environment variable (and TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY_PASSWORD) from the CI secret store; the Tauri docs note that .env files do not work for this.

docs.title: Tauri: checking for updates in the app
docs.text:
// src/updater.js: check, download, verify, install, relaunch
import { check } from "@tauri-apps/plugin-updater";
import { relaunch } from "@tauri-apps/plugin-process";

export async function updateIfAvailable(installId) {
  const update = await check({ headers: { "X-Install-Id": installId } });
  if (!update) return false; // server answered 204: nothing to do

  let downloaded = 0;
  await update.downloadAndInstall((event) => {
    if (event.event === "Progress") downloaded += event.data.chunkLength;
  }); // the plugin verifies the signature before installing

  await relaunch();
  return true;
}

docs.title: An update server with staged rollout and halt
docs.text:
// src/update-server.js: returns an update manifest or 204
import express from "express";
import semver from "semver";
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

// In practice this comes from a database or a release config file
const release = {
  version: "1.9.1",
  notes: "Fixes a crash when opening large boards.",
  pubDate: "2026-11-12T09:00:00Z",
  rolloutPercent: 25,     // raise in steps: 1, 5, 25, 50, 100
  halted: false,          // set true to stop offering this version
  minVersion: "1.6.0",    // older installs always get the update
  assets: {
    "windows-x86_64": { url: "https://downloads.taskflow.example.com/1.9.1/TaskFlow_1.9.1_x64-setup.exe", signature: "<contents of the .sig file>" },
    "darwin-aarch64": { url: "https://downloads.taskflow.example.com/1.9.1/TaskFlow.app.tar.gz", signature: "<contents of the .sig file>" },
  },
};

function inRollout(installId, percent) {
  const n = createHash("sha256").update(`desktop-${release.version}:${installId}`).digest().readUInt32BE(0);
  return n % 10_000 < percent * 100;
}

const app = express();

app.get("/desktop/:target/:arch/:currentVersion", (req, res) => {
  const { target, arch, currentVersion } = req.params;
  const asset = release.assets[`${target}-${arch}`];
  const installId = req.get("X-Install-Id");

  if (!asset || !semver.valid(currentVersion)) return res.status(204).end();
  if (!semver.gt(release.version, currentVersion)) return res.status(204).end();

  const belowFloor = semver.lt(currentVersion, release.minVersion);
  const offered = !release.halted && installId && inRollout(installId, release.rolloutPercent);
  if (!belowFloor && !offered) return res.status(204).end();

  res.json({
    version: release.version,
    notes: release.notes,
    pub_date: release.pubDate,
    url: asset.url,
    signature: asset.signature,
  });
});

app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3001));

The target and arch values come from the Tauri endpoint template. Because buckets depend on the install ID and the version, each release picks a different subset of users, and raising the percentage only adds installs. Halting is one field change, with no new build.

docs.title: Enforcing a minimum client version in the API
docs.text:
// src/middleware/min-client-version.js
import semver from "semver";

const MIN_VERSION = { desktop: "1.6.0", ios: "3.0.0", android: "3.0.0" };

export function minClientVersion(req, res, next) {
  const platform = req.get("X-Client-Platform");
  const version = req.get("X-Client-Version");
  const min = MIN_VERSION[platform];

  if (min && semver.valid(version) && semver.lt(version, min)) {
    return res.status(426).json({
      error: "client_update_required",
      message: "This version of TaskFlow is no longer supported. Please update.",
      minVersion: min,
    });
  }
  next();
}

HTTP 426 Upgrade Required was defined for protocol upgrades; many APIs reuse it for this purpose, others use a 400-class status with an error code. What matters is a stable, documented error that every client version knows how to show.

docs.title: Signing and notarizing a macOS build in CI
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/sign-macos.sh: sign with Developer ID, notarize, staple, verify
set -euo pipefail
APP="TaskFlow.app"
IDENTITY="Developer ID Application: Example Ltd (TEAMID1234)"

# Nested frameworks and helpers must be signed first (inside out); Tauri and
# Electron packaging tools do that before this step.
codesign --force --options runtime --timestamp --sign "$IDENTITY" "$APP"
ditto -c -k --keepParent "$APP" TaskFlow.zip

# Credentials were stored earlier with: xcrun notarytool store-credentials taskflow-notary ...
xcrun notarytool submit TaskFlow.zip --keychain-profile "taskflow-notary" --wait
xcrun stapler staple "$APP"
spctl --assess --type execute --verbose "$APP"

--options runtime enables the hardened runtime required for notarization, and --wait makes the script fail if Apple rejects the submission. Signing tools for Tauri and Electron can run these steps for you when given the same credentials.

docs.title: Signing a Windows installer
docs.text:
signtool sign /fd SHA256 /td SHA256 /tr "<timestamp-server-url>" /n "Example Ltd" TaskFlowSetup.exe
signtool verify /pa /v TaskFlowSetup.exe

/tr adds an RFC 3161 timestamp from your certificate authority's timestamping service and /td its digest algorithm; /n selects the certificate by subject name from the store, which is where hardware tokens and cloud signing services surface the key.

docs.title: Staged store releases with fastlane
docs.text:
# fastlane/Fastfile
lane :android_release do
  upload_to_play_store(track: "production", rollout: "0.05")  # 5% of users
end

lane :ios_release do
  upload_to_app_store(submit_for_review: true, phased_release: true)
end

The Play rollout is raised later from the Play Console or another upload_to_play_store call with a higher rollout; the App Store phased release then follows Apple's 7-day schedule automatically once approved.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Sign everything, with timestamps, using keys held in hardware or a managed signing service; protect update-signing keys as top secrets and back them up securely.
  • Verify update signatures in the app with an embedded public key.
  • Offer channels (beta, stable) and use staged rollouts for every production release.
  • Gate rollout steps on crash-free sessions per release; upload symbols for every build.
  • Send client platform and version on every API call; watch the version distribution.
  • Keep APIs backward compatible for every supported client version; ship server changes before the clients that need them.
  • Build remote kill switches into the app for risky features.
  • Set and enforce a minimum supported version for emergencies, with notice.
  • Plan for store review time; submit early in the week.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A bad version is out and cannot be recalled. Detect: crash-free sessions for the new release drop; crash reports share one stack trace. Cause: a defect that testing missed, now on installed devices. Fix: halt the rollout, disable the feature with a remote flag, and ship a fix forward through an expedited review.
  • Users see "unknown publisher" or Gatekeeper blocks the app. Detect: support tickets and install funnel drop after a release. Cause: signing or notarization failed or was skipped, or the certificate expired without a timestamp. Fix: fail the build when signing or notarization fails, always timestamp, and track certificate expiry.
  • Auto-update stopped working for everyone. Detect: the version distribution freezes; update checks return errors or signature failures. Cause: the update-signing key was rotated or lost, or the manifest URL changed. Fix: treat the public key and endpoint as long-term contracts; ship key rotation as a normal update signed with the old key, well before it is needed.
  • An API change broke older apps. Detect: errors from specific client versions in API logs right after a server deploy. Cause: a removed field or new required parameter. Fix: revert the server change, keep the API compatible with supported versions, and add contract tests per supported client version.
  • Forced update locked out part of the user base. Detect: sessions from some OS versions fall to zero. Cause: the new minimum version requires an OS those devices cannot run. Fix: check OS support before raising the floor and offer a degraded mode instead of a hard block.
  • Crash reports are unreadable. Detect: stack traces with memory addresses or minified names. Cause: symbols, mapping files, or source maps were not uploaded for that build. Fix: upload them in the release pipeline and fail the release if they are missing.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Code signing: a cryptographic signature that identifies the publisher and proves the binary is unchanged.
  • Timestamping: recording when a signature was made so it stays valid after the certificate expires.
  • Notarization: Apple's automated check of Developer ID software, producing a ticket Gatekeeper trusts.
  • Update manifest: the document that tells clients which version is available and where to get it.
  • Update channel: a release stream such as stable or beta.
  • Staged (phased) rollout: offering an update to a growing share of users.
  • Halt: stopping a rollout so no further users receive it.
  • Minimum supported version: the oldest client version the service still accepts.
  • Forced update: blocking use until the user updates.
  • Crash-free sessions: the share of app sessions that did not crash, per release.
  • Symbols: files that map compiled code back to source for readable crash reports.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming a halted rollout removes the bad version from devices.
  • Shipping a client that needs a server change before that change is live.
  • Removing API fields because "the new app does not use them".
  • Keeping the update-signing private key on a laptop, or in a .env file in the repository.
  • Skipping timestamps when signing.
  • Raising the minimum version without checking who it locks out.
  • Releasing without uploading symbols, then being unable to debug the crash spike.
  • Treating client configuration and content pushes as harmless; they are releases too.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can a client release not be rolled back the way a server release can, and what are the alternatives?
  2. What do code signing, timestamping, and notarization each protect against?
  3. Why should an app verify update signatures even when downloads use HTTPS?
  4. With Apple's phased release, what share of automatic-update users has the update after day 3, and can other users still get it?
  5. A desktop rollout uses buckets 0 to 9,999. At 25%, which buckets get the update? What happens to installs in buckets 2,500 to 9,999 if the rollout is halted?
  6. When should you raise the minimum supported version, and what must you check first?
  7. Which signals should gate each step of a client rollout?
  8. Why must API changes be deployed before the client versions that use them?
