docs.title: Rollbacks and Safe Releases
docs.text: A rollback returns production to the last version that worked. A safe release is one designed so that a bad change is caught early, affects few users, and can be undone quickly. This lesson covers rollback versus roll forward, what has to be true for a rollback to work at all, automated rollback driven by health checks and metrics, post-deploy verification with smoke tests and synthetic checks, bake time, release checklists, change freezes and deployment windows, blast radius reduction with rings, regions, and cells, and how all of this shows up in the DORA metrics.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most outages are caused by change. The Google SRE book's introduction states that SRE has found roughly 70% of outages are due to changes in a live system, and recommends progressive rollouts, quick and accurate detection of problems, and safe rollback when problems arise. You cannot stop changing software, so the practical goal is that a bad change is cheap: few users see it, for a short time, and recovery needs no heroics.

The time a bad release hurts users is detection time plus decision time plus recovery time. Each can be designed: detection with good metrics and canaries, decision with a pre-agreed rule ("if the error rate doubles, roll back"), and recovery with a previous version that is ready to run. Teams that leave any of the three to improvisation at 3 a.m. have long incidents.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon: rollback-safe changes. The Amazon Builders' Library article Ensuring rollback safety during deployments describes a two-phase technique for changes in data or protocol formats: first deploy a version that can read the new format but still writes the old one (prepare), and only after it is everywhere deploy the version that writes the new format (activate), so a rollback at any point leaves servers able to read what was written.
  • Amazon: automated rollback. Automating safe, hands-off deployments describes pipelines that roll back automatically when alarms fire, bake for at least an hour after the first production host, block deploys while high-severity alarms are active, and avoid nights, weekends, and holidays.
  • DORA. The DORA metrics guide measures delivery with throughput (change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time) and instability (change fail rate, deployment rework rate). Change fail rate is "the ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment"; failed deployment recovery time is how long recovery from such a deployment takes.
  • CrowdStrike, July 2024. The root cause analysis executive summary for the Channel File 291 incident describes a content update delivered to Windows hosts that crashed them, and commits to staged deployment of such content through rings with canary testing. A configuration or content push is a release and needs the same safety as code.
  • Cloudflare, November 2025. The post-incident report for 18 November 2025 explains how a generated feature file that doubled in size propagated quickly across the network and crashed the proxy software, and lists remediations including hardening ingestion of internally generated configuration "in the same way we would for user-generated input" and more global kill switches.

Popular tools and providers: Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker, AWS CodeDeploy (automatic rollback on CloudWatch alarms), Kubernetes rollout undo, Helm rollback, feature flag platforms, Prometheus and Alertmanager, Datadog, Grafana, synthetic monitoring tools (Checkly, Datadog Synthetics, Grafana Synthetic Monitoring), and error trackers with release health such as Sentry.

docs.title: Rollback or roll forward
docs.text:
Roll back Roll forward What it is Return to the previous known-good version Ship a new version that fixes the problem Speed Fast if the previous version is ready (seconds to minutes) As fast as your pipeline: build, test, deploy Risk Low if compatibility was preserved; dangerous if data changed shape A rushed fix can add a second bug Needs Previous artifact, compatible schema and data, no irreversible effects A clear diagnosis and a fast, trustworthy pipeline Typical choice Default when the cause is unclear or impact is high When rollback is unsafe, or the fix is tiny and certain

The rule most teams adopt: restore service first, diagnose later. If a release correlates with the problem and rollback is safe, roll back without waiting for a root cause. A feature flag switched off counts as the fastest rollback of all.

docs.title: What makes rollback possible
docs.text:
Rollback is a property you build in advance, not a button:

  • Immutable, retained artifacts. The previous image or package must still exist and be identical to what ran before. Registry cleanup policies that delete "old" images can delete your rollback target.
  • The previous version is runnable. Its configuration, secrets, and dependencies still exist. If you rotated a credential and the old version reads it from a different place, rollback fails.
  • Compatible schema and data. The database still has everything the old code needs, and data written by the new code is readable by the old code (expand and contract, prepare and activate). See zero-downtime database migrations.
  • Compatible messages and caches. Events, queue messages, and cache entries written by the new version must not crash the old one.
  • No irreversible side effects, or a plan for them. Emails sent, payments taken, and webhooks delivered cannot be rolled back; a bug in those paths needs compensation, not just a rollback.
  • Clients. Browsers that loaded new frontend assets may call APIs the old backend lacks; mobile apps cannot be rolled back at all (see releasing desktop and mobile apps).
  • Practice. A rollback path that has never been exercised is a guess. Roll back in staging regularly and occasionally in production on purpose.

docs.title: Automated rollback on health and metrics
docs.text:
The slowest part of most incidents is a human noticing, deciding, and acting. Automation removes it: the deployment tool watches health checks and metrics during and after the rollout, and reverts on its own when they cross agreed thresholds.

  • Kubernetes Deployments stop a rollout whose pods never become ready, but do not roll back by themselves.
  • AWS CodeDeploy can roll back automatically when a deployment fails or when a CloudWatch alarm attached to the deployment group fires.
  • Argo Rollouts and Flagger run analysis during canary steps and abort to the stable version when it fails.
  • Feature flag platforms can switch a flag off when guardrail metrics regress.

Worked example: suppose the bad version failed every request. A 99.9% monthly availability target allows 30 x 24 x 60 x 0.001 = 43.2 minutes of full outage per month. The automatic path above (about 7 minutes) spends 16% of the month's budget; the manual path (about 17 minutes) spends 39%. With a 10% canary in front, the same failures reach one tenth of the traffic, about 1.6% and 3.9% of the budget.

Thresholds need care. Too sensitive and normal noise triggers rollbacks (at low traffic, two errors can be "a 5% error rate"); too loose and real regressions pass. Require several consecutive data points, a minimum request count, and compare with a baseline where possible.

docs.title: Deployment verification
docs.text:
Check When What it proves Readiness probes As each instance starts The process can serve Version check Right after the deploy The intended version is actually running everywhere Smoke tests Right after the deploy, against production Key flows work end to end (sign in, list tasks, create a task in a test account) Canary analysis During progressive rollout The new version behaves no worse than the old one under real traffic Synthetic checks Continuously, every minute Key flows keep working, from outside, even with no real users active Error tracker release health Hours after the deploy New errors and crash rates by release Business metrics Hours to days Sign-ups, tasks created, payments are not quietly down

Smoke tests must exercise real paths, not just /readyz. Use dedicated test accounts or tenants so writes in production are harmless and easy to clean up.

docs.title: Bake time
docs.text:
Bake time is how long a version runs at one stage before it is promoted further. Some failures need time to appear:

  • memory leaks and slow resource exhaustion,
  • daily or hourly jobs (a nightly report, a cache refresh, log rotation),
  • traffic peaks (the Monday-morning login rush),
  • rare paths (month-end billing, a specific locale, a certificate renewal).

Amazon's pipelines bake at least an hour after the first production host and at least 12 hours after the first region; Microsoft's guidance suggests about a day per tier, including a period of peak usage. Shorter bakes are fine for low-risk changes; the point is to choose them deliberately rather than promote the moment the dashboard looks green.

docs.title: Release checklists
docs.text:
A short checklist, kept in the repository and used for risky releases, catches the predictable mistakes:

  • Is the previous version's artifact retained and its configuration unchanged?
  • Are database changes expand-only in this release?
  • Is the change behind a flag, and is the flag's default the old behavior?
  • What metrics and thresholds mean "roll back", and who decides?
  • Are on-call engineers aware, and is this inside a deployment window?
  • Are dependent teams (mobile, partners, support) informed of visible changes?

Go/no-go criteria, release captains, and coordinating one release across web, API, and mobile are covered in release trains and release management.

docs.title: Change freezes and deployment windows
docs.text:
• Deployment windows restrict deploys to times when people are available to respond: working hours, not Friday evening, not during a holiday. Amazon's and Microsoft's guidance both favor deploying during working hours, early in the week.
  • Change freezes stop non-urgent changes during high-risk periods (a major sales event, year-end, a big launch).

Both reduce risk during the window and increase it afterwards: changes queue up and ship as one large batch when the freeze lifts, which is harder to test and debug. Keep freezes short, allow small low-risk changes where possible, keep an approved path for emergency fixes, and release the backlog gradually after the freeze.

docs.title: Reducing blast radius
docs.text:
Blast radius is the share of users or systems a failure can reach. Ways to shrink it, from finest to coarsest:

  • Feature flags: 1% of users, or only staff.
  • Canary traffic: a small share of requests.
  • Rings: team, employees, beta customers, everyone.
  • One box, one AZ, one region: infrastructure stages.
  • Cells: independent copies of the stack, each serving a fixed set of customers.

These combine. Advanced deployment patterns covers waves, cells, and rings in depth. The same staging applies to configuration and data pushes, which are releases too, as the Google, Cloudflare, and CrowdStrike reports show.

docs.title: Measuring it: DORA metrics
docs.text:
Two DORA metrics measure release safety directly:

  • Change fail rate: of 120 production deployments in a quarter, 9 needed immediate intervention (rollback, hotfix, or flag off), a change fail rate of 9 / 120 = 7.5%.
  • Failed deployment recovery time: how long those 9 took to recover, typically reported as a median.

DORA's research consistently finds that speed and stability go together: teams that deploy small changes often also tend to have lower change fail rates and faster recovery. Small batches, automated verification, and fast rollback are what make that possible. How to compute these metrics from deployment and incident records is shown in measuring delivery performance.

docs.title: Rolling back things that are not code
docs.text: What changed How to undo it Application version Redeploy the previous image or release Feature flag Switch it back; keep an audit log of who changed what Runtime configuration Revert the commit in the config repository and redeploy, or restore the previous version in the config service Infrastructure (Terraform) Revert the commit and apply; some changes (deleted data stores) cannot be undone by code Database schema Usually roll forward with a new migration Data Restore from backup or point-in-time recovery, or run a corrective job DNS Revert the record, then wait for TTLs and caches

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Choose A release correlates with errors, rollback is compatible Roll back immediately The problem is behind a flag Switch the flag off The new version already wrote data the old version cannot read Roll forward, or mitigate and then roll forward The fix is one line, certain, and the pipeline takes 5 minutes Roll forward is acceptable, with an expedited review Cause unclear, high impact Roll back first, investigate with the old version running Mobile or desktop client release You cannot roll back installed apps: halt the rollout, disable the feature by flag, and ship a fix

Avoid automatic rollback where its trigger cannot be trusted, for example a service with so little traffic that one error trips the threshold. Use minimum request counts or longer windows, or alert a human instead.

docs.title: Verify after deploying, and roll back automatically
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/deploy-and-verify.sh: deploy, verify, watch metrics, roll back on failure
# usage: deploy-and-verify.sh <image>
set -euo pipefail
IMAGE="$1"
PROM="http://prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090"
QUERY='sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="taskflow-api",code=~"5.."}[2m])) / sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="taskflow-api"}[2m]))'
THRESHOLD=0.01      # 1% errors
WATCH_MINUTES=10
BAD_LIMIT=3         # consecutive bad samples before rolling back

rollback() {
  echo "rolling back: $1" >&2
  kubectl rollout undo deployment/taskflow-api
  kubectl rollout status deployment/taskflow-api --timeout=5m
  exit 1
}

kubectl set image deployment/taskflow-api api="$IMAGE"
kubectl rollout status deployment/taskflow-api --timeout=5m || rollback "rollout did not become ready"

./scripts/smoke-test.sh https://api.taskflow.example.com || rollback "smoke tests failed"

bad=0
for _ in $(seq 1 "$WATCH_MINUTES"); do
  sleep 60
  rate=$(curl -fsS --get "$PROM/api/v1/query" --data-urlencode "query=$QUERY" |
         jq -r '.data.result[0].value[1] // "0"')
  echo "5xx rate: $rate"
  if awk -v r="$rate" -v t="$THRESHOLD" 'BEGIN { exit !(r > t) }'; then
    bad=$((bad + 1))
    [ "$bad" -ge "$BAD_LIMIT" ] && rollback "5xx rate above $THRESHOLD for $bad minutes"
  else
    bad=0
  fi
done
echo "release verified"
  • rollout status fails when the new pods do not become ready in time.
  • Smoke tests run against production before the watch begins.
  • The metric must be bad for three consecutive minutes, so one noisy sample does not trigger a rollback.

docs.title: A smoke test that exercises real paths
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/smoke-test.sh: real requests against a dedicated test tenant
# usage: smoke-test.sh <base-url>
set -euo pipefail
BASE="$1"
AUTH="Authorization: Bearer $SMOKE_TEST_TOKEN"   # injected by CI, test tenant only

curl -fsS "$BASE/readyz" > /dev/null
curl -fsS "$BASE/version" | jq -e '.version' > /dev/null

# Read path
curl -fsS -H "$AUTH" "$BASE/tasks?limit=1" | jq -e 'type == "array"' > /dev/null

# Write path, then clean up
id=$(curl -fsS -H "$AUTH" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
       -d '{"title":"smoke test"}' "$BASE/tasks" | jq -r '.id')
curl -fsS -H "$AUTH" -X DELETE "$BASE/tasks/$id" > /dev/null
echo "smoke tests passed"

docs.title: Automatic rollback in AWS CodeDeploy
docs.text:
aws deploy update-deployment-group \
  --application-name taskflow-api \
  --current-deployment-group-name production \
  --auto-rollback-configuration enabled=true,events=DEPLOYMENT_FAILURE,DEPLOYMENT_STOP_ON_ALARM \
  --alarm-configuration 'enabled=true,alarms=[{name=taskflow-api-5xx-high},{name=taskflow-api-p99-high}]'

When either CloudWatch alarm fires during a deployment, CodeDeploy stops it and redeploys the last known-good revision.

docs.title: Rolling back a Helm release
docs.text:
helm history taskflow -n production        # list revisions with status and chart version
helm rollback taskflow 41 -n production --wait --timeout 5m

Helm rollback restores the Kubernetes manifests of revision 41. It does not touch the database, so it is only safe when the schema is compatible with that revision.

docs.title: Keep rollback targets in the registry
docs.text:
An Amazon ECR lifecycle policy, saved as ecr-lifecycle.json:

{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Release images expire only after a year",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPrefixList": ["release-"],
        "countType": "sinceImagePushed",
        "countUnit": "days",
        "countNumber": 365
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    },
    {
      "rulePriority": 2,
      "description": "Keep the 50 most recent other images",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "any",
        "countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
        "countNumber": 50
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    }
  ]
}

Applied with aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy, it keeps tagged release images for a year and only trims other images beyond the newest 50. In ECR, an image matched by a higher-priority rule's tag selection is not expired by a lower-priority rule, so the catch-all rule cannot remove release images.

docs.title: A release checklist for risky changes
docs.text:
# docs/release-checklist.md
[ ] Previous release image is retained (tag and digest noted below)
[ ] Migrations in this release are expand-only; contract is scheduled later
[ ] New behavior is behind flag ______, default off
[ ] Rollback triggers agreed: 5xx > 1% for 3 min, p99 > 800 ms for 5 min
[ ] Smoke tests and synthetic checks cover the changed flow
[ ] Deploying inside the window (Mon-Thu, 09:00-15:00 local), on-call aware
[ ] Support and mobile teams told about visible changes
Previous release: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:________

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Make rollback the default response to a release-correlated incident when it is safe; diagnose afterwards.
  • Keep every release artifact immutable and retained; never deploy mutable tags.
  • Keep schema, data, messages, and caches compatible with the previous version (expand and contract, prepare and activate).
  • Automate verification: version check, smoke tests, canary analysis, synthetic checks.
  • Automate rollback on clear, noise-resistant signals.
  • Bake long enough to cover peaks and scheduled jobs.
  • Release in small batches, during working hours, through rings.
  • Treat configuration, flags, and data pushes as releases with the same safety.
  • Practice rollbacks; track change fail rate and recovery time.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The rollback failed because the old image was gone. Detect: ImagePullBackOff or "manifest unknown" during rollback. Cause: a registry lifecycle policy deleted older images. Fix: retention rules that protect release tags, and record the previous digest in every deploy.
  • The rollback made things worse. Detect: new errors from the old version, such as parse failures or missing columns. Cause: the new version wrote data in a format the old version cannot read, or a migration removed something. Fix: prepare-then-activate format changes, expand-only migrations, and testing rollback in staging.
  • Automatic rollbacks keep firing on healthy releases. Detect: rollbacks with no user complaints; the metric spiked on a handful of requests. Cause: thresholds without minimum volume or consecutive-sample rules. Fix: require a minimum request count, several bad samples in a row, and baseline comparison.
  • Smoke tests passed but users could not sign in. Detect: support tickets after a "green" deploy. Cause: smoke tests checked only health endpoints. Fix: smoke tests and synthetic checks that exercise sign-in and the main flows with test accounts.
  • Rolling back the code did not fix it. Detect: errors persist with the previous version running. Cause: the real change was a configuration value, flag, or infrastructure change made alongside the deploy. Fix: record every change (code, config, flags, infra) on one timeline and version configuration like code.
  • The first release after a freeze caused a long outage. Detect: an unusually large release (many PRs) right after the freeze. Cause: batched changes, hard to verify and debug. Fix: shorter freezes, small low-risk changes allowed, gradual release of the backlog.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Rollback: returning to the previous known-good version.
  • Roll forward: fixing a problem with a new release.
  • Known-good version: the last release that met its health criteria.
  • Automated rollback: a rollback triggered by the deployment system from health checks or metrics.
  • Smoke test: a quick end-to-end check of key flows right after a deploy.
  • Synthetic check: a scripted request run continuously against production from outside.
  • Bake time: how long a release runs at a stage before promotion.
  • Deployment window: the times when deploys are allowed.
  • Change freeze: a period when non-urgent changes are blocked.
  • Blast radius: the share of users or systems a failure can affect.
  • Change fail rate: the share of deployments needing immediate intervention.
  • Failed deployment recovery time: how long recovery from such a deployment takes.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming rollback is always possible because "we can redeploy the old version".
  • Waiting for a root cause before rolling back.
  • Treating down migrations as a rollback plan for data.
  • Smoke tests that only call a health endpoint.
  • Automatic rollback on a single noisy sample.
  • Freezes that create one enormous release afterwards.
  • Forgetting that configuration, flag, and data changes need rollbacks too.
  • Counting only code deploys when measuring change fail rate.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. List five conditions that must hold for a rollback to be safe.
  2. When is rolling forward the better choice?
  3. Explain the prepare-then-activate technique for changing a data format.
  4. A 99.95% monthly target allows how many minutes of full outage in a 30-day month? How much of it does a 9-minute full outage consume?
  5. Why must an automated rollback trigger require more than one bad data point?
  6. Why can change freezes increase risk after they end?
  7. In a quarter, 200 deploys led to 14 rollbacks or hotfixes. What is the change fail rate?
  8. Why did the CrowdStrike and Cloudflare incidents lead to staged rollouts for content and configuration, not only code?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Amazon Builders' Library: Ensuring rollback safety during deployments
  • Amazon Builders' Library: Automating safe, hands-off deployments
  • DORA: Software delivery performance metrics
  • Google SRE book: Release engineering
  • AWS CodeDeploy: Redeploy and roll back a deployment
  • Helm: helm rollback
  • Next: deploying frontends and static sites. Back to the deployment strategies overview.

docs.title: Rolling, Blue-Green, and Canary Deployments
docs.text:
These are the four core ways to replace a running version of a service: recreate (stop the old, start the new), rolling (replace instances in batches), blue-green (run a full second environment and switch), and canary (send a small, growing share of traffic to the new version while measuring it). This lesson explains each in depth, how traffic is actually shifted, how canary analysis decides to promote or abort, how a canary differs from an A/B test, and what sessions, caches, queues, and the database need so that two versions can run side by side.

The next lesson, advanced deployment patterns, builds on these with red/black, rainbow, shadow traffic, rings, waves, and cells.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The strategy decides three numbers for every release: how long users are affected if the release is bad, how many users are affected, and how fast you can undo it. With recreate, a bad version hits 100% of users until a full redeploy finishes. With a canary at 1%, the same bug reaches 1% of requests for a few minutes before automation pulls it back. The Google SRE Workbook puts it simply: the impact on the error budget is directly proportional to the share of traffic exposed to the defect.

Every strategy except recreate also means two versions run at the same time, which is where most surprises come from: an old instance reading data written by a new one, a cached object in a new format, a queue message the old consumer cannot parse. Choosing a strategy is therefore also choosing which compatibility rules your code and data must follow.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Martin Fowler, blue-green. The bliki entry BlueGreenDeployment describes two identical production environments with a router in front: you release by switching the router to the idle one and roll back by switching back. It also notes that the database is the hard part, because both environments usually share it.
  • Google SRE Workbook, canarying. The chapter Canarying Releases defines a canary as "a partial and time-limited deployment of a change in a service and its evaluation", recommends comparing the canary with a control population at the same time rather than before and after, and advises evaluating user-facing metrics such as error rate and latency instead of noisy ones such as CPU.
  • Google and Netflix, Kayenta. The Google Cloud post Introducing Kayenta describes automated canary analysis used with Spinnaker: a small share of traffic goes to the canary, a new baseline cluster runs the old version (to avoid comparing fresh instances with long-running ones), a judge scores each chosen metric statistically, and the 0 to 100 score promotes, escalates to a human, or rolls back.
  • Slack. Deploys at Slack describes a canary at about 2% of production traffic, followed by 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% while dashboards and alerts are watched.
  • AWS CodeDeploy. The predefined deployment configurations encode these strategies as products: CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime and HalfAtATime (rolling) for servers, and ECSCanary10Percent5Minutes or LambdaLinear10PercentEvery1Minute (canary and linear traffic shifting) for containers and functions.

Popular tools and providers: Kubernetes Deployments, Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker with Kayenta, AWS CodeDeploy, Amazon ECS, Istio, Linkerd, Gateway API implementations, AWS Application Load Balancer weighted target groups, Amazon Route 53 weighted records, and the traffic splitting built into Cloud Run and AWS Lambda aliases.

docs.title: Recreate
docs.text:
Recreate stops every old instance, then starts the new ones. In Kubernetes it is strategy.type: Recreate; on a single VM it is systemctl restart.

  • Downtime: from the moment the last old instance stops until the first new one is ready. For a Node API that connects to MongoDB and warms up, 10 to 60 seconds is typical.
  • Advantage: only one version ever runs, so no compatibility rules apply. Recreate is the only strategy that allows a breaking schema change in a single step (inside a maintenance window).
  • Rollback: another full recreate with the old version, with another outage.
  • Fits: development and test environments, internal tools, batch workers that can pause, single-instance software that cannot run two copies (some licensed or stateful software), and planned maintenance.

docs.title: Rolling
docs.text:
A rolling deployment replaces instances in batches. Two parameters control the pace (Kubernetes names, with equivalents elsewhere):

  • maxSurge: how many extra instances may exist above the desired count. Higher surge means a faster rollout and more temporary cost.
  • maxUnavailable: how many instances may be missing below the desired count. Zero means full capacity throughout; higher means faster but thinner.

With replicas: 4, maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0, Kubernetes starts one new pod, waits until it passes its readiness probe (plus minReadySeconds), removes one old pod, and repeats. The rollout depends entirely on readiness: a probe that returns 200 before the app can serve turns a rolling deploy into a rolling outage.

What rolling does not give you:

  • No traffic control. The share of requests reaching the new version equals its share of instances, and the rollout keeps going unless readiness fails. A version that is "ready" but returns wrong answers rolls all the way out.
  • No automatic rollback. If new pods never become ready, Kubernetes stops and marks the rollout as failed after progressDeadlineSeconds (600 by default), but leaves it there. Someone or something must run kubectl rollout undo.
  • Mixed versions for the whole rollout. Every request might hit either version, so APIs, events, and schemas must be compatible both ways.

docs.title: Blue-green
docs.text:
Blue-green keeps two complete production environments. One (blue) is live; the other (green) receives the new version, is warmed up, and is tested through a private route. The release is a single routing change; the rollback is the same change reversed.

How the switch is made:

Switch point How Speed and caveats Load balancer Change the listener's target group, or the nginx upstream Seconds; existing keep-alive connections finish on blue Kubernetes Service Change the Service selector from color: blue to color: green Seconds; endpoints update cluster-wide DNS Point the record at the green load balancer Minutes to hours; resolvers and clients cache beyond the TTL Platform Swap deployment slots (Azure App Service), or move traffic between revisions Seconds; platform-specific

Design points:

  • Warm-up first. Green must have the same instance count as blue and warm caches and connection pools before the switch, or the first minute after the switch is slow.
  • Keep blue for a bake period. Leave blue running (at full or reduced size) for an hour or a day. Rollback is only instant while blue exists.
  • The database is shared. Blue and green almost always use the same database, so the schema must work for both versions. Blue-green makes code rollback instant; it does nothing for data.
  • Everyone moves at once. Unlike a canary, the switch exposes 100% of users simultaneously. A gradual weighted shift between blue and green turns it into a canary, which the SRE Workbook recommends when possible.
  • Background work runs twice. If schedulers or queue consumers run in both colors, cron jobs fire twice and messages are consumed by both versions. Disable schedulers in the idle color or run them separately.
  • Cost: double capacity during the deploy, permanently if both colors stay at full size.

docs.title: Canary
docs.text:
A canary sends a small share of real traffic to the new version, compares it with the old version, and increases the share step by step while the comparison stays good. Three decisions define a canary:

  1. Who goes to the canary. A random share of requests (simplest), a random share of users (sticky, so one user sees one version), staff and internal accounts first, or one region or cell first.
  2. The steps. For example 1% for 10 minutes, 10% for 10 minutes, 50% for 20 minutes, then 100%. The first step catches crashes and obvious errors; later steps catch problems that appear only under load.
  3. The analysis. Which metrics, compared with what, and what result means abort.

docs.title: Canary analysis
docs.text:
Good canary metrics are user-facing and attributable to the change:

  • 5xx error rate (exclude 4xx caused by clients),
  • latency percentiles (p50, p99) for the main endpoints,
  • saturation signals that predict trouble (event-loop lag, memory growth, database connection pool waits),
  • a few business events (tasks created per minute, sign-ins succeeded).

Compare the canary with a baseline running at the same time, not with yesterday: traffic changes by hour and day. Ideally the baseline is a separate set of old-version instances of the same size and age as the canary, which is what Kayenta does, because freshly started instances behave differently from instances that have run for days.

docs.title: How much traffic a canary needs: a worked example
docs.text:
TaskFlow API serves 200 requests per second with a normal 5xx rate of 0.2%.

Canary at 1% = 2 requests/s; a 10-minute step sees 1,200 requests.
Expected errors if the canary is as good as the baseline: 1,200 x 0.002 = 2.4

Case A: v2 fails 5% of requests -> about 60 errors.
        60 versus an expected 2.4 is unmistakable: abort within minutes.

Case B: v2 raises the error rate to 0.4% (doubles it).
        Error counts are roughly Poisson, so noise is about sqrt(expected).
        To see the extra errors (0.002 n) above 3 standard deviations of
        noise (3 x sqrt(0.002 n)):
            0.002 n >= 3 x sqrt(0.002 n)  ->  0.002 n >= 9  ->  n >= 4,500
        At 1%  (2 req/s):  4,500 / 2  = 2,250 s, about 37 minutes
        At 10% (20 req/s): 4,500 / 20 =   225 s, under 4 minutes

The lesson: a small canary catches large regressions quickly and safely; subtle regressions need more traffic or more time. That is why canaries go up in steps, and why analysis tools use statistical tests instead of eyeballing one dashboard.

docs.title: Traffic shifting mechanisms
docs.text:
Mechanism How the split happens Precision Rollback Caveats Replica ratio 1 new pod among 10 gets about 10% Coarse, in steps of one instance As fast as scaling Depends on even load balancing; 1% needs 100 pods Load balancer weights AWS ALB weighted target groups (weights 0 to 999), nginx weight Exact, per request Seconds Enable stickiness if users must stay on one version Gateway API HTTPRoute backendRefs with weight Exact, per request (implementation-dependent) Seconds Portable across implementations; supports header matches Service mesh Istio VirtualService weights, Linkerd Exact, plus header and cookie targeting Seconds Adds a mesh to operate Ingress annotations Controller-specific canary annotations Exact Seconds Not portable; the widely used ingress-nginx project was retired in March 2026 DNS weighted records Route 53 weighted records (weights 0 to 255) Coarse, per resolver Slow Resolvers and clients cache beyond the TTL; open connections stay on the old target Platform built-in Cloud Run revision traffic, Lambda alias weights Exact Seconds Tied to one platform

DNS deserves a warning: lowering a TTL to 60 seconds does not mean all clients move within 60 seconds. Some resolvers enforce minimum TTLs, operating systems and browsers cache, mobile apps hold connections for long periods, and a client that has an open connection keeps using the old address. DNS is fine for moving whole regions over hours; it is a poor tool for a 1% canary or a fast rollback.

docs.title: Automatic promotion and abort
docs.text: Tools such as Argo Rollouts, Flagger, Spinnaker with Kayenta, and AWS CodeDeploy run the loop for you: set weight, wait, query metrics, compare with thresholds or the baseline, then continue, pause, or abort. When analysis fails, the controller sets the canary weight back to 0% and marks the rollout aborted. Manual promotion still has a place for the first canary of a risky change, but a human watching dashboards at 2 a.m. is the weakest part of a canary.

docs.title: A/B testing compared with canary
docs.text:
Canary A/B test Question Is the new version safe to roll out? Which variant achieves the product goal better? Variants Old and new version of the software Two (or more) intended behaviors, both expected to work Assignment Random requests or users; often not sticky Sticky per user (hash of user ID), so each user has one consistent experience Metrics Errors, latency, saturation Conversion, retention, engagement, revenue Duration Minutes to hours Days to weeks, until the planned sample size is reached Ends with 100% of the new version, or rollback The winning variant for everyone; the losing code removed Usually implemented with Traffic routing (load balancer, mesh, rollout controller) Feature flags or an experimentation platform inside one version

The two are often confused because both split traffic. They answer different questions, need different statistics (an A/B test needs a sample size calculated in advance and protection against stopping early when results look good), and live in different tools. An A/B test runs inside one deployed version, usually through feature flags; a canary compares two deployed versions.

docs.title: Sessions, state, and database concerns
docs.text:
Running two versions side by side, or switching between them, raises the same questions in every strategy except recreate:

  • Sessions. If session data lives in instance memory, any switch logs users out. Store sessions in Redis or a database, or use stateless tokens, and keep the session format readable by both versions.
  • Sticky routing. Per-request weights can send one user's requests to both versions in the same minute. If the UI or API changed, enable stickiness (a cookie or user-ID hash) for the canary period.
  • Long-lived connections. WebSockets and server-sent event streams do not move when the router changes; they stay on the old version until they close. Plan drain times, or ask clients to reconnect (see rainbow deployments in advanced deployment patterns).
  • Caches. If v2 writes cache entries in a new format, v1 may read and fail on them. Version cache keys (task:42:v2) so each version reads its own format.
  • Queues and events. Both versions may consume the same queue, and each may produce messages the other consumes. Add fields, never remove or rename them in one step, and make consumers ignore unknown fields.
  • Scheduled jobs. Make sure only one version runs each scheduled job (blue-green idle colors especially).
  • Database schema. Every change must be readable and writable by both versions during the rollout and the rollback window. This is the expand-and-contract discipline in zero-downtime database migrations.
  • Clients. A browser that loaded the old SPA calls the API after the switch. Keep API changes backward compatible for at least one release.

docs.title: Pattern chooser
docs.text: Recreate Rolling Blue-green Canary Downtime Yes, seconds to minutes None if readiness is correct None None Extra capacity cost None Small (surge instances) Up to 2x during the deploy and bake Small (a few canary instances) Rollback speed Slow: full redeploy with another outage Medium: roll the old version back in Instant: switch back while blue exists Fast: weight to 0%, often automatic Risk exposure 100% of users at once Grows batch by batch, with no metric gate by default 100% of users at the switch 1% first, grows only while metrics stay healthy Complexity Lowest Low (default in Kubernetes) Medium: two environments, switch, warm-up High: traffic routing plus metric analysis Database and sessions Breaking changes allowed in one step Two versions share data throughout: compatible schema, versioned caches, external sessions Shared database: schema compatible both ways; sessions external; idle color must not run jobs Like rolling, plus sticky assignment if behavior differs visibly

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Good fit Avoid Dev or test environment, internal tool Recreate Anything heavier Stateless API on Kubernetes, moderate risk Rolling with good readiness probes Recreate (needless downtime) Instant rollback required, budget for double capacity Blue-green Rolling (slow rollback) High traffic, high cost of a bad release Canary with automated analysis Blue-green alone (all users at once) Very low traffic (a few requests a minute) Blue-green or rolling plus strong tests; canary statistics will be weak Pure canary analysis Breaking schema change that cannot be split Recreate in a maintenance window Any strategy that runs two versions Product question ("does the new flow convert better?") A/B test behind feature flags A canary

docs.title: A rolling update in Kubernetes
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  replicas: 4
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5        # old ReplicaSets kept for rollout undo
  minReadySeconds: 10            # must stay ready 10 s before counting
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300   # mark the rollout failed after 5 min
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: taskflow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: taskflow-api
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: 3000
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /livez
              port: 3000
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3

kubectl set image deployment/taskflow-api api=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/taskflow-api --timeout=5m
# If it fails or misbehaves:
kubectl rollout undo deployment/taskflow-api
kubectl rollout history deployment/taskflow-api

kubectl rollout status exits non-zero when the progress deadline is exceeded, so a pipeline can run rollout undo automatically on failure.

docs.title: Blue-green with two Deployments and a Service selector
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-service.yaml: the live Service selects one color
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  selector:
    app: taskflow-api
    color: blue          # switch to green to release
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
---
# A preview Service always points at green for smoke tests
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-preview
spec:
  selector:
    app: taskflow-api
    color: green
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/blue-green-switch.sh: release green, keep blue for rollback
set -euo pipefail
kubectl set image deployment/taskflow-api-green api="$1"
kubectl rollout status deployment/taskflow-api-green --timeout=5m
./scripts/smoke-test.sh http://taskflow-api-preview.default.svc.cluster.local
kubectl patch service taskflow-api \
  -p '{"spec":{"selector":{"app":"taskflow-api","color":"green"}}}'
echo "green is live; blue stays up for rollback"
# Rollback: patch the selector back to color: blue

docs.title: A weighted canary with Gateway API
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-httproute.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public-gateway
  hostnames:
    - api.taskflow.example.com
  rules:
    # Staff can force the canary with a header for manual checks
    - matches:
        - headers:
            - name: x-taskflow-canary
              value: "always"
      backendRefs:
        - name: taskflow-api-canary
          port: 80
    # Everyone else: 90/10 split
    - backendRefs:
        - name: taskflow-api-stable
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: taskflow-api-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10

Changing the weights (and committing the change, in a GitOps setup) is the whole promotion step. Setting the canary weight to 0 is the rollback.

docs.title: Automated canary analysis with Argo Rollouts
docs.text:
# k8s/taskflow-api-rollout.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
spec:
  replicas: 10
  revisionHistoryLimit: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: taskflow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: taskflow-api
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
  strategy:
    canary:
      canaryService: taskflow-api-canary
      stableService: taskflow-api-stable
      trafficRouting:
        istio:
          virtualService:
            name: taskflow-api
            routes:
              - primary
      analysis:                      # runs in the background from step 1
        templates:
          - templateName: taskflow-canary-health
        startingStep: 1
        args:
          - name: service
            value: taskflow-api-canary
      steps:
        - setWeight: 1
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 10
        - pause: { duration: 10m }
        - setWeight: 50
        - pause: { duration: 20m }
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: taskflow-canary-health
spec:
  args:
    - name: service
  metrics:
    - name: error-rate
      interval: 2m
      failureLimit: 1
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.01
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090
          query: |
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service}}",code=~"5.."}[2m]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_requests_total{service="{{args.service}}"}[2m]))
    - name: p99-latency-seconds
      interval: 2m
      failureLimit: 1
      successCondition: result[0] < 0.5
      provider:
        prometheus:
          address: http://prometheus.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:9090
          query: |
            histogram_quantile(0.99,
              sum by (le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{service="{{args.service}}"}[2m])))

If either metric fails more than once, Argo Rollouts aborts: traffic goes back to the stable Service and the canary pods scale down. Fixed thresholds are a simple start; comparing against the stable version (baseline) is more robust when error rates vary by time of day.

docs.title: Weighted target groups on an AWS Application Load Balancer
docs.text:
# Send 10% of the listener's traffic to the green target group
aws elbv2 modify-listener \
  --listener-arn "<listener-arn>" \
  --default-actions '[{
    "Type": "forward",
    "ForwardConfig": {
      "TargetGroups": [
        { "TargetGroupArn": "<blue-target-group-arn>",  "Weight": 90 },
        { "TargetGroupArn": "<green-target-group-arn>", "Weight": 10 }
      ],
      "TargetGroupStickinessConfig": { "Enabled": true, "DurationSeconds": 3600 }
    }
  }]'

The same call with weights 0 and 100 completes a blue-green switch; with 100 and 0 it rolls back. Stickiness keeps each client on one target group for an hour so a user does not bounce between versions.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Get readiness and graceful shutdown right first; every strategy depends on them.
  • Default to rolling for low-risk services, and add canary analysis where a bad release is expensive.
  • Compare canaries with a baseline running at the same time, on user-facing metrics, and automate the abort.
  • Start canaries small (1% or internal users), then increase in steps that leave enough requests for a meaningful comparison.
  • Keep the previous version runnable (old ReplicaSet, blue environment, previous image) for the whole bake period.
  • Make every schema, cache, event, and API change compatible with both versions during the rollout and rollback window.
  • Avoid DNS for fast traffic shifts; use load balancer, gateway, or mesh weights.
  • Turn off schedulers in idle environments and version your cache keys.
  • Run one canary at a time per service, so a failure is attributable.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A rolling deploy took the service down even though pods were "ready". Detect: errors climb with each batch; pods show Ready while the app fails requests. Cause: the readiness probe returns 200 before the app can serve (database not connected, cache not warm). Fix: make readiness check what requests need, add minReadySeconds, and gate the rollout on error rate, not just readiness.
  • The canary looked healthy and the full rollout still failed. Detect: errors appear only above 50% traffic. Cause: a capacity or shared-resource problem (connection pool, cache stampede, lock contention) that 1% of traffic could not reveal. Fix: add a larger step with a longer soak, and include saturation metrics in the analysis.
  • After a blue-green switch, users were logged out. Detect: a spike in sign-ins and session-not-found errors at the switch time. Cause: sessions stored in instance memory, or a session format change. Fix: external session store, format compatible across versions.
  • The rollback took 20 minutes. Detect: traffic graphs show the old version receiving requests only slowly after the rollback command. Cause: the switch used DNS and clients cached the record, or blue had been scaled to zero. Fix: shift with load balancer weights and keep blue warm during the bake period.
  • Nightly emails went out twice. Detect: duplicate job logs from two deployments. Cause: the idle blue environment still ran its scheduler. Fix: enable schedulers only in the live color or run jobs as a separate single-instance workload.
  • Old instances crash during a rolling deploy. Detect: errors only on v1 pods, parsing cache entries or messages. Cause: v2 writes data in a format v1 cannot read. Fix: version cache keys, make consumers tolerant of unknown fields, and split format changes across releases.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Recreate: stop all old instances, then start new ones.
  • Rolling update: replace instances in batches.
  • maxSurge / maxUnavailable: how far above or below the desired instance count a rolling update may go.
  • Blue-green deployment: two full environments with a router switch.
  • Canary: a small, measured share of traffic sent to a new version.
  • Baseline: the old version, running at the same time, used for comparison.
  • Canary analysis: the automated comparison that decides promote or abort.
  • Bake time: how long a version runs at a step before moving on.
  • Weighted routing: splitting traffic between targets by configured weights.
  • Stickiness: keeping a client on the same target across requests.
  • A/B test: a controlled experiment between product variants, measured on user behavior.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating a rolling update as safe by default; without metric gates it rolls a bad version to everyone.
  • Running a canary and not looking at it, or comparing it with last week's numbers.
  • Expecting statistical certainty from a 1% canary on a low-traffic service.
  • Thinking blue-green makes database changes reversible.
  • Using DNS for canaries or fast rollbacks.
  • Calling an experiment a canary (or a canary an experiment) and using the wrong metrics and duration.
  • Forgetting long-lived connections, schedulers, caches, and queue consumers when two versions run at once.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control, and what happens with maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 and four replicas?
  2. Why does a Kubernetes rolling update not roll back automatically, and what does progressDeadlineSeconds do?
  3. Name three things that must stay compatible when blue and green share one database.
  4. Why should a canary be compared with a baseline running at the same time rather than with the previous day?
  5. A service handles 50 requests per second with a 0.5% error rate. A canary at 5% runs for 10 minutes. How many requests does it see, and roughly how many errors are expected if it is healthy? Could it detect an increase to 1%?
  6. Why is DNS a poor mechanism for a 1% canary or a fast rollback?
  7. Give three differences between a canary and an A/B test.
  8. Which strategy would you choose for a breaking schema change that cannot be split, and why?
