docs.title: DevOps, SRE, and Platform Engineering
docs.text:
Job advertisements use "DevOps engineer", "site reliability engineer", and "platform engineer" almost interchangeably, yet the three names come from different places and describe different mechanisms. DevOps is a philosophy about how development and operations work together. Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) is Google's concrete implementation of the reliability side of it, with error budgets and limits on manual work. Platform engineering builds internal products that make good practice self-service for every team.

This lesson defines each one from its primary sources, shows how they fit together, explains toil and the SRE time budget with a worked example, describes the common ways SRE teams are organized, and introduces Team Topologies' four team types and three interaction modes, applied to the teams that build TaskFlow.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Organizations regularly get these models wrong in ways that cost years. An operations team is renamed "SRE" but still spends all its time on tickets. A "DevOps team" is created to own every deployment and becomes the new bottleneck. A platform team builds a portal nobody asked for and then mandates it. Each failure comes from copying a name without the mechanism behind it: SRE works because it caps operational work and ties releases to an error budget; platforms work because they are run as products for developers; DevOps works because the people who build a service also run it.

Knowing the mechanisms also helps you choose. A five-person startup needs DevOps habits but not an SRE organization. A company with forty product teams that each built their own pipeline probably needs a platform team. A service with strict reliability needs may justify dedicated SREs.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google's definition of SRE. In the introduction to the SRE book, Benjamin Treynor Sloss writes: "SRE is what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team." He describes joining Google in 2003 to run a production team of seven engineers, and the rule that "Google places a 50% cap on the aggregate 'ops' work for all SREs."
  • SRE and DevOps. The SRE Workbook chapter How SRE Relates to DevOps sums up the relationship as "class SRE implements interface DevOps", and clarifies that "product development teams in Google own their service by default"; SRE "is neither available nor warranted for the bulk of services."
  • How SRE teams are organized. Google Cloud's 2019 post How SRE teams are organized, and how to get started describes six implementations, from a "kitchen sink" team that does everything to consulting teams that advise without changing code, with the pros and cons of each.
  • Platform engineering. DORA's platform engineering capability defines an internal developer platform as shared tools, services, and "golden paths", and reports that by 2025, 90% of organizations used an internal developer platform and 76% had dedicated platform teams.
  • Team Topologies. The Team Topologies key concepts describe four fundamental team types (stream-aligned, enabling, complicated subsystem, and platform) and three interaction modes (collaboration, X-as-a-Service, and facilitating), and call stream-aligned teams "You Built It, You Run It" teams.

Popular tools and providers: SLO tooling such as Prometheus with Sloth or Pyrra, Grafana SLO, and Datadog SLOs; incident and on-call tools such as PagerDuty and incident.io; platform building blocks such as Kubernetes, Argo CD, Crossplane, and Terraform; and developer portals such as Backstage.

docs.title: Three names for answers to one problem
docs.text:
All three respond to the same problem from the previous lesson: work and knowledge split between people who change systems and people who run them. They answer it at different levels.

DevOps SRE Platform engineering What it is A culture and set of practices A job role and a set of practices, defined at Google A discipline that builds internal products for developers Origin Practitioner movement, 2008 to 2009 Google, from 2003 Grew from DevOps and SRE as organizations scaled Core mechanism Shared ownership, CALMS, the Three Ways SLOs and error budgets, a cap on operational work, toil reduction Self-service golden paths, run as a product Primary customer Users of the product Users of the service, through its reliability Internal developers Typical measures DORA delivery metrics SLO compliance, error budget, share of time on toil, pages per shift Adoption, developer satisfaction, product teams' DORA metrics Typical failure A "DevOps team" that becomes a new silo An operations team renamed SRE, still doing tickets all day A ticket queue or a mandated portal nobody wants

docs.title: SRE as Google defines it
docs.text:
The SRE book describes the traditional "sysadmin" model, in which an operations team grows linearly with the service, because every new server, customer, and feature adds manual work. SRE's answer is to staff operations with software engineers who will "quickly become bored by performing tasks by hand" and have the skills to automate them. The book lists the core tenets every Google SRE team follows:

  • Ensuring a durable focus on engineering: at most 50% of SRE time on operational work, at most two events per 8 to 12-hour on-call shift so each gets proper follow-up, and blame-free postmortems for all significant incidents.
  • Pursuing maximum change velocity without violating the SLO: the error budget, described below.
  • Monitoring: software interprets signals, and humans are notified only when they need to act: alerts for action now, tickets for action later; logs are kept for diagnosis and notify no one.
  • Emergency response: reliability depends on time to repair, and the book reports that playbooks written in advance produce "roughly a 3x improvement in MTTR" compared with "winging it".
  • Change management: "roughly 70% of outages are due to changes in a live system", so SRE automates progressive rollouts, fast detection, and safe rollback.
  • Demand forecasting, capacity planning, provisioning, efficiency and performance: SRE owns capacity because capacity is availability (see load testing fundamentals and autoscaling server fleets).

The 50% cap is enforced, not aspirational. Google measures how SRE time is spent, and when operational work exceeds the cap the excess is redirected to the product development team: bugs and tickets go to development managers, and developers rejoin the pager rotation. The SRE Workbook suggests thinking of the limit less as a cap than as "a guarantee": an explicit promise that engineering time exists to remove the work, rather than toiling at it forever.

docs.title: Error budgets: the contract between development and SRE
docs.text:
SRE replaces the argument between "ship faster" and "change nothing" with a number. The product owners choose an availability target, and "the error budget is one minus the availability target." A 99.9% SLO over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of full outage, or 0.1% of requests failing. While budget remains, teams spend it on launches and experiments; when it is gone, an agreed policy slows or stops risky releases until reliability recovers. In the SRE book's words, "SRE's goal is no longer 'zero outages'; rather, SREs and product developers aim to spend the error budget getting maximum feature velocity."

SLIs, SLO targets, burn rates, and error budget policies are covered in depth in SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets.

docs.title: Toil
docs.text:
The SRE book's chapter Eliminating Toil defines toil as "the kind of work tied to running a production service that tends to be manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and that scales linearly as a service grows."

Attribute Test TaskFlow example Manual A human does it, even if only by running a script Running npm run migrate on the production host by hand Repetitive Done over and over, not a one-off Resetting staging test data every few days Automatable A machine could do it, or the need could be designed away Granting read access to production logs via tickets Tactical Interrupt-driven and reactive; the book counts handling pager alerts Restarting a stuck reminder worker at 3 a.m. No enduring value The service is in the same state afterwards Answering "is the API down?" in chat O(n) with growth Grows with traffic, users, or services Rotating API keys for every new partner by hand

Not all unpleasant work is toil. Team meetings, goal setting, and HR paperwork are overhead, and cleaning up a messy alert configuration may be grungy but has lasting value. Google reports that its SREs spend on average about 33% of their time on toil, with wide variation between individuals, against a target of under 50%.

A worked example. The four engineers on the TaskFlow tasks team (160 hours a week) keep a toil log for a month:

toil: 15.5 h/week of 160 h team time (9.7%)

task                                   h/week   hours to automate   payback
Reset staging test data                   2.0                   6   3.0 weeks
Answer is-the-API-down questions          3.0                  10   3.3 weeks
Rotate partner API keys by hand           4.0                  24   6.0 weeks
Grant read access to production logs      2.0                  12   6.0 weeks
Run database migrations by hand           3.0                  20   6.7 weeks
Restart stuck reminder worker             1.5                  16  10.7 weeks

Ranking by payback (hours to automate divided by hours saved per week) tells the team what to automate first: a staging reset script pays for itself in three weeks, a public status page in just over three. The script that produces this report is in the practical examples below.

docs.title: How SRE teams are organized
docs.text:
Google Cloud's 2019 post describes six implementations, roughly in the order organizations adopt them:

Implementation Scope Main strength Main risk Kitchen sink ("everything SRE") Every service and workflow, usually the first SRE team Easy to start without reorganizing Unbounded scope; day-to-day demands crowd out SRE practices Infrastructure Shared infrastructure such as clusters, CI/CD, monitoring, networking Defines production standards as code that simplify every team's work Can drift away from customer experience Tools Software that helps others measure and improve reliability Reusable reliability tooling Solving the wrong problems if far from front-line teams Product or application One critical application or business area Clear link between business priorities and SRE effort Duplicated infrastructure and divergent practices across many such teams Embedded SREs work inside development teams for a period, changing code and configuration Hands-on teaching of SRE practices Divergent practices; embedded SREs lose contact with peers Consulting Advises teams without changing their code Scales the impact of an experienced SRE group Advice without enough context; seen as hands-off

The post recommends starting even earlier, with a few engineers spending part of their time as SRE advocates, before staffing any dedicated team. It also notes that an SRE team can act as the company's "reliability standards and practices" group, defining how production may be changed, how incidents run, and how error budgets work.

docs.title: Platform engineering
docs.text:
DORA defines platform engineering as "a sociotechnical discipline" focused on "automation, self-service, and repeatability", which designs and builds toolchains and workflows, "often called an 'Internal Developer Platform'", that provide shared tools, services, and "golden paths". It stresses that the platform is "an internal product designed specifically for developers", not a collection of infrastructure tickets.

The idea is not new. In his 2012 post against "DevOps teams", Jez Humble described the one central team he did support, listing its first job as "Builds a platform that allows developers to self-service environments for testing and production", and added: "This platform is a product." Google SRE reached a similar place from the other direction. The SRE book chapter The Evolving SRE Engagement Model describes how reviewing services one at a time did not scale, so SRE built shared frameworks and a common production platform; services built on it become "production ready" by design, SRE supports the platform, and development teams provide on-call support for bugs in their own application code.

Platforms are covered in depth in platform engineering and developer portals.

docs.title: How the three relate
docs.text:
Read the diagram as an interface and two implementations:

  • DevOps says what good looks like: shared ownership, small batches, fast feedback, continuous learning. The SRE Workbook notes it is "relatively silent on how to run operations at a detailed level."
  • SRE says how to run reliable services: an "opinionated intellectual framework (including concepts like error budgets)" with measurable limits on toil and paging.
  • Platform engineering says how to make the right way the easy way for many teams: a product that turns repeated decisions (how to build, deploy, observe, and secure a service) into self-service defaults.
  • Product teams remain the owners. Neither SRE nor a platform team should take ownership of other teams' services away from them. Their job is to make that ownership affordable.

A small organization may have all three in one person's head: a team that owns its service (DevOps), sets an SLO with an error budget (SRE), and reuses one shared deploy workflow (a very thin platform).

docs.title: Team Topologies
docs.text:
Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that "organizations which design systems (in the broad sense used here) are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations" (How Do Committees Invent?). Team Topologies, by Matthew Skelton and Manuel Pais (second edition 2025), turns that observation into a design tool: decide how teams should interact so that the architecture you want, and fast flow of change, become the natural result.

Team type Purpose (from the key concepts page) TaskFlow example Stream-aligned "aligned to a flow of work from (usually) a segment of the business domain"; owns it end to end Tasks team (API), Web team, Reminders team Platform "provide a compelling internal product to accelerate delivery by Stream-aligned teams" Delivery platform team: CI/CD templates, Kubernetes, observability Enabling "helps a Stream-aligned team to overcome obstacles"; temporarily boosts skills, then moves on Reliability enabling team teaching SLOs and on-call practice Complicated subsystem "where significant mathematics/calculation/technical expertise is needed" Scheduling engine that suggests due dates Interaction mode Meaning When to use it Collaboration Working closely together for a defined period to discover new things A new capability whose interface is not yet known; high bandwidth, high cost, so time-box it X-as-a-Service One team provides and the other consumes, with minimal interaction Mature, well-understood capabilities such as the deploy pipeline Facilitating One team helps and mentors another Teaching a practice until the receiving team can do it alone

The approach is built around team cognitive load: a team can only own so much before quality and speed fall. Platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams exist to reduce the load on stream-aligned teams, and the key concepts page warns that "most internal platforms become bloated monstrosities" unless they follow the Thinnest Viable Platform idea: provide just enough capability to make stream-aligned teams faster.

docs.title: Job titles in practice
docs.text:
Titles vary between companies, so read the job description, not the label. Typical scopes are:

Title Usually means Watch out for DevOps engineer Builds pipelines, infrastructure as code, and deployment tooling, often inside or alongside product teams A role that owns everyone's deployments, recreating the wall Site reliability engineer Owns reliability of services with SLOs, incident response, capacity, and automation; spends a bounded share of time on operations An operations job renamed, with no engineering time or error budget Platform engineer Builds and runs the internal platform as a product: golden paths, self-service APIs, developer portal A ticket-driven infrastructure team with a new name

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Context Good fit Not yet One team, one product, early stage DevOps habits: the team owns build, deploy, and on-call; one SLO per critical journey A separate SRE team or a platform team 3 to 10 product teams, each solving deployment differently A thin platform: shared pipeline templates, one deploy path, a service catalog A large portal project before the common needs are known A critical service whose outages are expensive Dedicated SRE support (product or embedded), with a production readiness review SRE for every service; most should stay with their developers Many teams, high cognitive load, repeated reliability problems Platform team plus an SRE "standards and practices" or enabling team Mandating tools without user research An operations team that wants to "become SRE" Measure toil, set SLOs, cap operational work, automate the top toil Renaming the team and keeping the ticket queue

The SRE Workbook calls renaming without changing practices "rename-and-shame" and warns it is "a hollow one, unlikely to yield benefit." The same is true of renaming an infrastructure team "platform".

docs.title: A toil log and payback report
docs.text:
Keep a simple log of recurring operational work for a few weeks:

# toil.csv
task,kind,per_week,minutes_each,automation_hours
Restart stuck reminder worker,manual fix,3,30,16
Rotate partner API keys by hand,ticket,2,120,24
Answer is-the-API-down questions,interrupt,12,15,10
Reset staging test data,ticket,4,30,6
Run database migrations by hand,release chore,3,60,20
Grant read access to production logs,ticket,6,20,12

// scripts/toil-report.js: weekly toil, share of team time, and automation payback
// Usage: node scripts/toil-report.js toil.csv <engineers> <hours per engineer per week>
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const [file, engineers = "4", hoursEach = "40"] = process.argv.slice(2);
const teamHours = Number(engineers) * Number(hoursEach);

const [header, ...rows] = (await readFile(file, "utf8")).trim().split(/\r?\n/);
const cols = header.split(",");
const items = rows.map((line) => {
  const v = Object.fromEntries(line.split(",").map((x, i) => [cols[i], x]));
  const weekly = (Number(v.per_week) * Number(v.minutes_each)) / 60;
  return { task: v.task, weekly, automate: Number(v.automation_hours) };
});

const total = items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.weekly, 0);
console.log(`toil: ${total.toFixed(1)} h/week of ${teamHours} h team time (${((100 * total) / teamHours).toFixed(1)}%)`);
console.log("payback  h/week  build h  task");
for (const i of items.sort((a, b) => a.automate / a.weekly - b.automate / b.weekly)) {
  const payback = `${(i.automate / i.weekly).toFixed(1)} wk`;
  console.log(`${payback.padStart(7)}  ${i.weekly.toFixed(1).padStart(6)}  ${String(i.automate).padStart(7)}  ${i.task}`);
}

$ node scripts/toil-report.js toil.csv 4 40
toil: 15.5 h/week of 160 h team time (9.7%)
payback  h/week  build h  task
 3.0 wk     2.0        6  Reset staging test data
 3.3 wk     3.0       10  Answer is-the-API-down questions
 6.0 wk     4.0       24  Rotate partner API keys by hand
 6.0 wk     2.0       12  Grant read access to production logs
 6.7 wk     3.0       20  Run database migrations by hand
10.7 wk     1.5       16  Restart stuck reminder worker

The parser is deliberately simple (no quoted commas in fields). The numbers are estimates; their job is to rank the work, not to be precise. Notice that the cheapest fix is not always to automate the task: the stuck reminder worker should be fixed so it stops getting stuck.

docs.title: A production readiness checklist
docs.text:
Google SRE runs a Production Readiness Review (PRR) before taking on a service, to "verify that a service meets accepted standards of production setup and operational readiness". A lightweight version is useful for any team launching a service it will run itself:

# docs/production-readiness.yaml: TaskFlow reminders service
service: taskflow-reminders
owner: reminders-team
review_date: 2026-11-10
checks:
  slos:
    - "Freshness SLO: 99% of reminders sent within 5 minutes of the due time"
    - "Dashboard shows every SLI in the SLO document"
  alerting:
    - "Burn-rate alerts page the owning team's rotation"
    - "Every paging alert links to a runbook"
  operations:
    - "On-call rotation has at least two people per shift (primary and secondary)"
    - "Rollback tested in staging within the last 30 days"
    - "Graceful shutdown drains in-flight jobs on SIGTERM"
  capacity:
    - "Load test at 3x the expected peak reminders per minute"
    - "Queue depth alert before the backlog breaks the freshness SLO"
  data:
    - "Backups restored successfully in the last quarter"
  dependencies:
    - "Behavior documented and tested when the email provider is down"
open_items:
  - "Add a runbook for 'reminder backlog growing' (owner: reminders-team, due 2026-11-24)"

The format is illustrative; the value is in reviewing the answers with someone who has operated similar services, before users depend on them.

docs.title: A team charter with Team Topologies vocabulary
docs.text:
Writing down each team's type, ownership, and interactions makes dependencies explicit and shows when an interaction mode should change:

# teams/reminders-team.yaml
team: reminders-team
type: stream-aligned
owns:
  services: [taskflow-reminders]
  on_call: true                       # you build it, you run it
interactions:
  - team: delivery-platform
    mode: x-as-a-service              # uses pipelines, clusters, dashboards
  - team: reliability-enabling
    mode: facilitating
    purpose: "Define SLOs and set up burn-rate alerting"
    until: 2026-12-18                 # enabling help ends; the skill stays
  - team: tasks-team
    mode: x-as-a-service              # consumes the tasks API, versioned contract
cognitive_load_review: quarterly

Interactions that never end are a warning sign: a facilitating engagement that runs for a year has become a dependency, and a collaboration that never settles into X-as-a-Service usually means the interface between the teams is still unclear.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with DevOps habits in every team: own the service, automate the path to production, and learn from incidents.
  • Adopt SRE mechanisms, not just the title: SLOs with error budget policies, a cap on operational work, and measured toil.
  • Keep ownership with product teams by default; reserve dedicated SRE support for services that justify it.
  • Measure toil for a few weeks before automating, and rank work by payback.
  • Build platforms as products with user research, a roadmap, and measured adoption; start with the thinnest platform that helps.
  • Name team types and interaction modes explicitly, time-box collaboration and facilitation, and revisit them as needs change.
  • Watch cognitive load: when a team owns too much, split ownership or move undifferentiated work to a platform.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The new SRE team spends every day on tickets. Detect: a time-tracking sample shows 80% or more of SRE time on tickets and pages; no automation projects ship for a quarter. Cause: an operations team was renamed without a cap on operational work or a mechanism to push excess back. Fix: measure the ops share, agree a 50% cap with leadership, redirect excess work to the owning development teams, and fund the top toil fixes.
  • Releases are blocked by the SRE team on every launch. Detect: launch reviews queue for weeks and developers route around them with "small" changes. Cause: reliability is enforced by gatekeeping instead of an agreed error budget. Fix: define SLOs and an error budget policy with product leadership, and let the budget, not a reviewer, decide when releases slow down.
  • Developers carry the pager and burn out. Detect: rising after-hours pages per person and people leaving the rotation. Cause: ownership was handed to product teams without runbooks, sane alerts, or platform support. Fix: cap pages per shift, give the team time to fix noisy alerts, and provide platform defaults for deploys, rollbacks, and dashboards.
  • The platform team's backlog is all tickets. Detect: most platform work items are "create a database for team X" requests; developers wait days. Cause: "ticket-ops", which DORA lists as a platform pitfall. Fix: turn the most frequent requests into self-service APIs or templates, and measure time from request to use.
  • Each product team built its own pipeline and observability stack. Detect: a dozen different deploy scripts and logging formats; security fixes take months to roll out everywhere. Cause: DevOps ownership without any shared platform. Fix: extract the common path into a thin, optional platform and migrate teams by making it clearly easier than their own tooling.
  • An enabling team has been "helping" the same team for a year. Detect: the receiving team still cannot operate the practice without the enabling team. Cause: facilitation turned into dependency; the enabling team does the work instead of teaching it. Fix: agree an end date and a skill to transfer, and pair rather than do the work for them.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• DevOps: The culture and practices of shared ownership between building and running software.
  • Site Reliability Engineering (SRE): Google's approach of running operations as a software problem, with SLOs, error budgets, and a cap on operational work.
  • Error budget: One minus the availability target; the amount of unreliability a service may spend.
  • Toil: Manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical operational work with no enduring value that grows with the service.
  • Overhead: Administrative work that is not tied to running a production service, such as meetings.
  • Production Readiness Review (PRR): A review of a service's operational readiness before SRE support or launch.
  • Platform engineering: Building internal developer platforms as products that make delivery self-service.
  • Internal developer platform (IDP): The tools, services, and golden paths a platform team provides to developers.
  • Stream-aligned team: A team aligned to a flow of work that owns it end to end.
  • Enabling team: A team that helps others gain a capability, then moves on.
  • Complicated-subsystem team: A team owning a part that needs deep specialist knowledge.
  • Interaction modes: Collaboration, X-as-a-Service, and facilitating.
  • Cognitive load: The mental effort a team needs to own its work.
  • Conway's law: Systems mirror the communication structures of the organizations that design them.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating DevOps, SRE, and platform engineering as competing alternatives rather than layers that fit together.
  • Renaming an operations team "SRE" without SLOs, error budgets, or a limit on toil.
  • Believing SRE means a separate team must run every service.
  • Counting all disliked work as toil; meetings are overhead, and cleanup with lasting value is not toil.
  • Automating toil that should have been designed away.
  • Building a platform before several teams share the same need.
  • Mandating a platform instead of making it the easiest path.
  • Ignoring Conway's law: drawing an architecture that the team structure cannot produce.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain "class SRE implements interface DevOps". What does SRE add that DevOps leaves open?
  2. What happens at Google when operational work exceeds 50% of SRE time, and why is that a feedback mechanism rather than a punishment?
  3. Name the six attributes of toil and give a TaskFlow example of each. Why are team meetings not toil?
  4. A team of five engineers works 40 hours a week each. A toil log shows 70 hours a week of toil, including a 10-hour weekly task that would take 40 hours to automate. What share of time is toil before and after automating that task, and what is the payback period? (35% of 200 hours; 60 / 200 = 30% afterwards; 4 weeks.)
  5. Compare the kitchen sink, embedded, and consulting SRE implementations. Which would you start with in a company of 60 engineers, and why?
  6. Why did Jez Humble accept a central team that builds a self-service platform while rejecting a "DevOps team"?
  7. Describe the four Team Topologies team types and when each interaction mode is appropriate.
  8. Your organization wants to "become SRE" next quarter. What would you measure first and what would you change before the name?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Google SRE book: Introduction
  • Google SRE book: Eliminating Toil
  • Google SRE Workbook: How SRE Relates to DevOps
  • Google Cloud: How SRE teams are organized, and how to get started
  • DORA: Platform engineering
  • Team Topologies: Key concepts
  • Next: measuring delivery performance. Back to the DevOps fundamentals overview.

docs.title: DevOps Fundamentals Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review what DevOps is, how it relates to SRE and platform engineering, how delivery performance is measured, the team practices behind ownership, and internal platforms and developer portals. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is DevOps, in one or two sentences?
docs.text: DevOps is the set of cultural habits, practices, and automation that lets one team change a system quickly and safely and learn from how it behaves in production. AWS describes it as "the combination of cultural philosophies, practices, and tools" that increases an organization's ability to deliver at high velocity; the emphasis on culture and shared ownership is what separates it from a toolchain.

docs.title: 2. What problem was DevOps created to solve?
docs.text: The split between development, rewarded for shipping features, and operations, rewarded for stability. The split produced large, infrequent releases, hand-offs "over the wall", slow feedback to the people who wrote the code, and blame when things broke. Google's SRE book describes the result as structural conflict between pace of change and stability.

docs.title: 3. Where did the DevOps movement come from?
docs.text: Patrick Debois presented agile infrastructure ideas at Agile 2008 in Toronto. In June 2009 John Allspaw and Paul Hammond gave the Velocity talk "10+ Deploys Per Day: Dev and Ops Cooperation at Flickr", and Debois organized the first devopsdays in Ghent, Belgium, on 30 and 31 October 2009. Books followed: Continuous Delivery (2010), The Phoenix Project (2013), The DevOps Handbook (2016), and Accelerate (2018).

docs.title: 4. What does CALMS stand for, and where does it come from?
docs.text: Culture, Automation, Lean, Measurement, Sharing. John Willis summarized DevOps as CAMS in a July 2010 post; Lean was added later, and Google's SRE Workbook credits CA(L)MS to John Willis, Damon Edwards, and Jez Humble. Culture comes first: in Willis's words, "If you don't have culture, all automation attempts will be fruitless."

docs.title: 5. Explain the Three Ways.
docs.text: From Gene Kim's 2012 article: the First Way is flow and systems thinking (optimize the whole value stream, never pass known defects downstream); the Second Way amplifies right-to-left feedback loops; the Third Way builds a culture of continual experimentation and learning, with time to improve daily work and practice through repetition. Faster flow without feedback only ships problems faster.

docs.title: 6. Why is a "DevOps team" between development and operations an anti-pattern?
docs.text: It adds another functional silo and another hand-off, which is the problem DevOps tries to remove. Jez Humble's 2012 post put it bluntly: "THERE IS NO SUCH THING AS A DEVOPS TEAM." He did accept a central team that builds a self-service platform and coaches others, as long as it is not on the hook for running other teams' systems.

docs.title: 7. Can you buy DevOps?
docs.text: No. Tools support the practices but do not create them. Willis warned that a vendor claiming a "Devops product" does not "have a clue of what Devops is." Organizations that buy tools without changing ownership, batch size, and feedback usually see no improvement in lead time or stability.

docs.title: 8. What is value stream mapping, and what is flow efficiency?
docs.text:
Value stream mapping draws the steps from request (or commit) to production with the work time and the wait time of each step.

lead time       = work time + wait time
flow efficiency = work time / lead time

A change with 5 hours of work and 158 hours of waiting has a lead time of about 163 hours and a flow efficiency near 3%: removing a queue helps far more than working faster.

docs.title: 9. Why do small batches reduce risk? Show it with numbers.
docs.text: If each change has a 2% chance of causing a problem, a release of 40 changes contains at least one bad change with probability 1 - 0.98^40, about 55%, and finding it takes about six rounds of bisection. Deploying each change alone keeps every deploy at 2%, points to one suspect, and makes rollback remove only that change. Feedback also arrives while the code is fresh.

docs.title: 10. What is a WIP limit, and how does Little's law explain it?
docs.text: A WIP limit caps how many items may be in a stage at once, so the team finishes before starting. Little's law says average lead time equals average work in progress divided by average throughput: a team finishing 10 items a week with 30 in progress has a 3-week lead time; with 10 in progress, 1 week, without working any faster.

docs.title: 11. Does delivering faster make systems less stable?
docs.text: DORA's research consistently says no: throughput and stability tend to move together, and its 2025 report calls the "speed vs. stability" trade-off a myth. The mechanism is batch size: small, frequent changes are easier to test, diagnose, and roll back than large, rare ones.

docs.title: 12. How does Google define Site Reliability Engineering?
docs.text: Benjamin Treynor Sloss: "SRE is what happens when you ask a software engineer to design an operations team." SREs are engineers who automate operational work, manage services to SLOs with error budgets, and keep operational work capped so engineering time remains. SRE started at Google in 2003.

docs.title: 13. What does "class SRE implements interface DevOps" mean?
docs.text: From the SRE Workbook: DevOps is a broad philosophy that is "relatively silent on how to run operations at a detailed level"; SRE is one concrete implementation with an opinionated framework (SLOs, error budgets, toil limits, blameless postmortems). Both share the goals of fewer silos, gradual change, measurement, and treating accidents as normal.

docs.title: 14. What is Google's 50% rule for SRE, and how is it enforced?
docs.text: At most 50% of SRE time goes to operational work (tickets, on-call, manual tasks); the rest goes to engineering. Google measures it, and when operational work exceeds the cap, the excess is redirected to the product development team: tickets go to development managers and developers rejoin the pager. That feedback pushes developers to build systems that need less manual work.

docs.title: 15. What is toil, and what is not toil?
docs.text: Toil is work tied to running a production service that is manual, repetitive, automatable, tactical, devoid of enduring value, and scales linearly with the service. Meetings and HR paperwork are overhead, not toil, and cleanup with lasting value is not toil even if it is unpleasant. Google reports its SREs average about 33% toil against a target under 50%.

docs.title: 16. How do error budgets resolve the conflict between developers and operations?
docs.text: The product owners set an availability target, and the error budget is one minus that target. While budget remains, teams spend it on launches and experiments; when it is exhausted, an agreed policy slows risky releases. The decision comes from a number agreed in advance instead of an argument during each launch.

docs.title: 17. How would you decide which toil to automate first?
docs.text: Log recurring tasks with frequency and duration, estimate the effort to automate or eliminate each, and rank by payback: hours to automate divided by hours saved per week. A 6-hour script that saves 2 hours a week pays back in 3 weeks. Prefer eliminating the cause (fix the stuck worker) over automating the symptom (restart it faster).

docs.title: 18. What SRE team implementations does Google Cloud describe?
docs.text: Six, roughly in order of adoption: kitchen sink (everything), infrastructure, tools, product or application, embedded (SREs working inside development teams, changing code), and consulting (advising without changing code). Before any of them, it recommends part-time SRE advocates. Embedded teams teach hands-on; consulting scales an experienced group but risks advice without context.

docs.title: 19. What is platform engineering, and how is it different from a traditional infrastructure team?
docs.text: Platform engineering builds an internal developer platform as a product: self-service tools, services, and golden paths designed around developers' needs, with a product owner, roadmap, and adoption measures. A traditional infrastructure team fulfills requests; a platform team removes the need for requests by making capabilities self-service.

docs.title: 20. What are the four Team Topologies team types?
docs.text: Stream-aligned teams own a flow of work end to end ("You Built It, You Run It" teams). Platform teams provide a compelling internal product that speeds them up. Enabling teams help others gain capabilities, then move on. Complicated-subsystem teams own parts that need deep specialist knowledge.

docs.title: 21. What are the three interaction modes, and when do you use each?
docs.text: Collaboration: working closely for a defined period to discover something new, such as a new interface; high bandwidth and high cost, so time-box it. X-as-a-Service: consume a well-defined capability with minimal interaction, such as the deploy pipeline. Facilitating: one team mentors another until it can work alone.

docs.title: 22. What is Conway's law, and why does it matter for DevOps?
docs.text: Melvin Conway wrote in 1968 that organizations "are constrained to produce designs which are copies of the communication structures of these organizations." If teams are split by function, systems end up with hand-offs at the same seams. Team Topologies uses this deliberately: design team boundaries and interactions for the architecture and flow you want.

docs.title: 23. What is team cognitive load, and what is the Thinnest Viable Platform?
docs.text: Cognitive load is the mental effort a team needs to own its work; past a point, quality and speed drop. Platform, enabling, and complicated-subsystem teams exist to reduce the load on stream-aligned teams. The Thinnest Viable Platform provides just enough capability to make those teams faster, instead of a bloated platform that adds dependencies.

docs.title: 24. What are DORA's five software delivery metrics?
docs.text: Throughput: change lead time, deployment frequency, and failed deployment recovery time. Instability: change fail rate and deployment rework rate. DORA's guide says they are meant to be applied at the application or service level and used together, not as single targets.

docs.title: 25. How have DORA's metrics changed over time?
docs.text: Research began in 2014 with four variables, including mean time to recover (MTTR). In 2023 MTTR was renamed and redefined as failed deployment recovery time, to separate failures caused by software changes from external failures. In 2024 deployment rework rate was added, recovery time moved into the throughput group, and change fail and rework rates formed the stability (now "instability") group. The 2025 report published per-metric distributions and seven team profiles instead of a four-level table.

docs.title: 26. How do you measure change lead time precisely?
docs.text: From commit time to the first successful production deployment that contains the commit. Re-deploys after a rollback must not reset the clock, and staging deploys do not count. Squash and rebase merges create commits whose committer date is the merge time, hiding review wait; if review time matters, start at the pull request's first commit and say so.

docs.title: 27. What counts as a deployment for deployment frequency?
docs.text: A successful deployment to production of one service, planned or unplanned (rollbacks and hotfixes count). Failed pipeline runs that never reached production do not. Report deployments per week, the share of working days with a deployment, or the time between deployments.

docs.title: 28. How do you decide which deployments count toward change fail rate?
docs.text: Those that required immediate intervention after reaching production: a rollback, hotfix, fix forward, or patch, which is how DORA's 2025 survey describes it. Decide explicitly whether disabling a feature flag counts, write the rule down, and link each incident to the deployment that caused it, or the rate will silently read zero.

docs.title: 29. Why was MTTR replaced by failed deployment recovery time?
docs.text: MTTR mixed recovery from failed changes with recovery from anything else, such as a data center outage. The new metric measures only how quickly a team recovers from a deployment that failed and needed immediate intervention, which is what delivery practices control. Other outages belong in SLO and incident metrics.

docs.title: 30. Why report median and p90 lead time instead of the mean?
docs.text: Lead times are skewed. In a two-week TaskFlow sample, the median was 2.3 hours, the mean 12.2 hours, and the p90 20.9 hours, because a few commits waited over a weekend or on a branch. The median describes the typical change; a high percentile describes the tail you want to shrink; the mean moves when one forgotten commit ships.

docs.title: 31. What benchmarks does DORA publish, and how should you use them?
docs.text: The 2024 report's four clusters, for example elite: lead time under one day, deploys on demand, 5% change fail rate, recovery under one hour (19% of respondents). The 2025 report instead shows answer distributions per metric. DORA's advice: "the best teams are those that achieve elite improvement, not necessarily elite performance". Compare a service with its own past, not with other teams.

docs.title: 32. In 2024, why did the medium cluster have a lower change fail rate than the high cluster?
docs.text: The clusters emerged from the data: one group was faster but less stable (high, 20% change fail rate), another slower but more stable (medium, 10%). DORA chose to call the faster group "high" and noted there may be no universal answer to which is better; it depends on the service and its users.

docs.title: 33. What are flow metrics, and how do they differ from DORA's metrics?
docs.text: The Flow Framework measures from work start to work complete across four flow item types (features, defects, risks, and debt): flow velocity (items completed), flow time, flow efficiency (active share of flow time), flow load (work in progress), and flow distribution (the mix of item types). DORA starts at commit; flow metrics include the waiting before it and show whether debt and risk work is being starved.

docs.title: 34. What is the SPACE framework?
docs.text: SPACE (Forsgren and colleagues, ACM Queue, 2021) says developer productivity cannot be captured by one metric. Its five dimensions are satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, and efficiency and flow. Measure at least three, mixing survey data with system data, and never judge productivity by activity counts alone.

docs.title: 35. Explain Goodhart's law with an example of gaming delivery metrics.
docs.text: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" (the popular phrasing, credited to Marilyn Strathern). If leadership demands "multiple deployments per day", teams can deploy unchanged code or split one change into many deploys; if change fail rate is a target, incidents stop being linked to deployments. DORA lists "Setting metrics as a goal" as its first pitfall.

docs.title: 36. How would you compute lead time from git and deployment data?
docs.text:
Record each production deployment with its SHA and time, use git rev-list <previous sha>..<sha> to list the commits it shipped, and load commit times from git log --format='%H,%cI'. Lead time per commit is its first successful deployment time minus its commit time:

SELECT dc.sha, MIN(julianday(d.finished_at)) AS deployed_jd
FROM deployment_commits dc
JOIN deployments d ON d.id = dc.deployment_id
WHERE d.environment = 'production' AND d.status = 'success'
GROUP BY dc.sha

Then subtract julianday(committed_at) and take the median per week.

docs.title: 37. Why store raw delivery events instead of computed numbers?
docs.text: Raw events let you recompute every metric when a definition changes or a bug in the calculation is found. Vendor histories also expire: GitHub, for example, retains previous deployment statuses for 90 days. Export events into your own store, in UTC, with the service name on each one.

docs.title: 38. What does "you build it, you run it" mean, and where does it come from?
docs.text: The team that builds a service also operates and supports it, including on-call. The phrase comes from Werner Vogels's 2006 ACM Queue interview: "Giving developers operational responsibilities has greatly enhanced the quality of the services ... You build it, you run it." It closes the feedback loop: teams paged for their own bugs fix the causes.

docs.title: 39. What does a team need before it can run its own services sustainably?
docs.text: Netflix's "full cycle developer" post lists the prerequisites: tooling that makes deploying, monitoring, and rolling back easy, training, partnerships with central teams that build shared tools, and staffing "with enough headroom" for operational work. Without these, it warns, "teams risk overload and burnout."

docs.title: 40. How large should an on-call rotation be?
docs.text: The SRE book caps on-call at 25% of an engineer's time. With a primary and a secondary on every weekly shift, that needs at least eight engineers for a single-site 24/7 rotation, or six per site for two sites. A team of five on the same rotation would be on call 40% of the time.

docs.title: 41. How do you know whether on-call is fair?
docs.text: Look beyond shift counts: pages per person, pages outside working hours, the share handled by the busiest person compared with an even share, the actionable rate, and how often shifts are swapped or uncovered. One person handling far more than their share usually points to a noisy alert, which should be fixed rather than rescheduled around.

docs.title: 42. What is blameless culture, and does it mean nobody is accountable?
docs.text: It treats failures as information about the system: what made an action seem reasonable, and what safeguard was missing. Punishing individuals creates incentives to hide the truth. Accountability remains: owners complete the action items, and deliberate malicious acts follow other processes.

docs.title: 43. What is the Westrum typology?
docs.text: Ron Westrum's three cultures, distinguished by how information flows: pathological (power-oriented; messengers punished; failure leads to scapegoating), bureaucratic (rule-oriented; messengers neglected; failure leads to justice), and generative (performance-oriented; messengers trained; failure leads to inquiry). DORA found generative, high-trust culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance.

docs.title: 44. What is an architecture decision record, and what does it contain?
docs.text: A short, numbered document recording one architecturally significant decision, introduced by Michael Nygard in 2011: title, context, decision ("We will ..."), status (proposed, accepted, deprecated, or superseded), and consequences, positive and negative. ADRs live in the repository, numbers are never reused, and reversed decisions are kept and marked superseded.

docs.title: 45. What did DORA find about change advisory boards?
docs.text: That heavyweight approval by people outside the team has a negative impact on software delivery performance, and that "no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates." It slows delivery, which creates larger batches and more risk per release.

docs.title: 46. How can you meet segregation of duties without a CAB?
docs.text: Use peer review: a change is approved by someone other than its author in the pull request, with the review recorded in the development platform. Add automated tests and checks, flag high-risk changes (migrations, authentication, infrastructure) for extra review, and keep the pipeline as the audit trail. Use the same fast path for emergency changes.

docs.title: 47. Why does documentation quality matter to delivery performance?
docs.text: DORA found "a clear link between documentation quality and organizational performance", and that documentation quality drives the implementation of every technical practice it studied; for example, trunk-based development lifted organizational performance far more for teams with above-average documentation. Keep docs next to code and update them in the same pull requests.

docs.title: 48. What conditions define trunk-based development in DORA's research?
docs.text: Three or fewer active branches, merging to trunk at least once a day, and no code freezes or integration phases. The habits behind it are social: small pull requests, reviews within hours, a red main branch fixed first, and unfinished work merged behind feature flags.

docs.title: 49. What is an internal developer platform?
docs.text: A set of shared tools, services, and golden paths, offered through self-service interfaces and run as a product for internal developers. The CNCF defines a platform as "an integrated collection of capabilities defined and presented according to the needs of the platform's users"; Evan Bottcher calls it "a compelling internal product."

docs.title: 50. What are golden paths, paved roads, and golden cages?
docs.text: A golden path, in Spotify's words, is "the 'opinionated and supported' path to 'build something'". Netflix's paved road is its supported set of tools, encouraged by being "a far better experience" rather than mandated. A golden cage, a DORA pitfall, is a rigid path with no exits that ignores the needs of different kinds of teams.

docs.title: 51. What is ticket-ops, and why is it a trap?
docs.text: A platform team that fulfills infrastructure requests manually, like a "vending machine" for tickets. It stays trapped in toil, becomes the bottleneck, and never builds self-service. Forty requests a month at 45 minutes each is 30 hours of platform time plus days of waiting for every team; a self-service path removes both.

docs.title: 52. What is Backstage?
docs.text: "An open source framework for building developer portals", created at Spotify and open-sourced in March 2020. Its core features are the software catalog, software templates, TechDocs, and plugins. It was accepted to the CNCF in September 2020 and moved to Incubating in March 2022. Spotify reported a 55% decrease in onboarding time, measured as time to a new engineer's 10th pull request.

docs.title: 53. What goes in a catalog-info.yaml, and why does spec.owner matter?
docs.text: The entity's apiVersion, kind (Component, API, Resource, System, and so on), metadata (name, description, annotations, links), and spec (type, lifecycle, owner, system, dependencies, provided APIs). spec.owner names the team that "bears ultimate responsibility" for the entity, which turns the catalog into an ownership map that answers "who do I call?".

docs.title: 54. How do software templates encode a golden path?
docs.text: A template defines form parameters and steps: fetch a skeleton project with best practices built in, publish it as a new repository, and register it in the catalog with its owner. Every new service starts with the standard pipeline, SLO document, dashboards, and runbook links, instead of drifting toward them later. Calling a shared, versioned reusable workflow instead of copying the pipeline keeps existing services current too: a security fix ships once, to every caller.

docs.title: 55. How do you measure whether a platform succeeds?
docs.text: Combine delivery outcomes of product teams (DORA's metrics) with developer experience (surveys such as CSAT or NPS), adoption and retention, task success for key journeys, and efficiency measures such as time to provision a database or to deploy a brand-new service. Backstage's guide adds onboarding time, measured as time to a new engineer's 10th merged pull request.

docs.title: 56. What did DORA's 2024 report find about internal developer platforms?
docs.text: Users had 8% higher individual productivity and 10% higher team performance, and organizational performance rose 6%, but throughput fell 8% and change stability 14%. Mandatory, exclusive use was linked to a 6% throughput decrease. Performance followed a J-curve: early gains, a dip, then recovery as the platform matured.

docs.title: 57. When should a small team not build a platform, and what are the cheaper options?
docs.text: When only one to three teams share the need, or nobody can run the platform as a product. Cheapest: a shared template repository, a wiki page, and managed services. Next: a managed or commercial product with your defaults on top, trading a subscription for engineering time. Most expensive: self-building a platform and portal, because it needs a dedicated team to build, upgrade, support, and be on call for it.

docs.title: 58. Leadership created a "DevOps team" a year ago, but lead time and stability have not changed. What do you look at?
docs.text:
What to check first: who deploys, who is paged, and where tickets go between product teams and the new team.

How to confirm: a value stream map shows changes waiting in the DevOps team's queue; product teams still hand off deploys and never see alerts.

Likely causes and fixes: a new silo between development and operations. Give product teams ownership of deploys and on-call, and turn the central team into a platform or enabling team that builds self-service tools and coaches. See what is DevOps.

docs.title: 59. The CI pipeline takes 10 minutes, but change lead time is 12 days. Where is the time going?
docs.text:
What to check first: the gap between merge and production: release trains, approval meetings, manual QA, deploy windows.

How to confirm: map the value stream with work and wait times per step; most of the 12 days will be waiting.

Likely causes and fixes: queues, not slow work. Remove the biggest wait first: deploy on merge instead of a weekly release cut, replace external approval with peer review and automated checks, and automate regression tests. See what is DevOps.

docs.title: 60. Deployment frequency doubled the month after leadership set a target. Should you celebrate?
docs.text:
What to check first: commits per deployment and lead time over the same period.

How to confirm: many deployments ship no new commits, or one change is split into several deploys; lead time is unchanged.

Likely causes and fixes: Goodhart's law: the metric became the goal. Withdraw the target, track throughput and instability together per service, and discuss trends with teams instead of ranking them. See measuring delivery performance.

docs.title: 61. The delivery dashboard shows a 0% change fail rate, yet production incidents happen every week. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether incidents record the deployment that caused them.

How to confirm: incident records have no link to deployments, and rollbacks are not marked as unplanned deployments.

Likely causes and fixes: the numerator is never populated. Add a required "triggering deployment" field to incident records and a reason input to rollback and hotfix workflows, then recompute from raw events. See measuring delivery performance.

docs.title: 62. Median lead time is two hours, but product managers say features take months. Who is right?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the clock starts and the merge strategy.

How to confirm: squash merges stamp commits at merge time; pull requests stay open for days; flow time from work start is far longer.

Likely causes and fixes: both are right about different spans. Add lead time from the pull request's first commit and flow time from work start, and look for waiting in backlogs and reviews. See measuring delivery performance.

docs.title: 63. Your newly formed SRE team spends 85% of its time on tickets and manual tasks. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: a time sample of where SRE hours go, and whether any cap on operational work exists.

How to confirm: no automation projects shipped for a quarter; the top toil items repeat weekly.

Likely causes and fixes: an operations team renamed SRE without the mechanisms. Agree a 50% cap with leadership, redirect excess work to the owning development teams, and fund the top toil fixes ranked by payback. See DevOps, SRE, and platform engineering.

docs.title: 64. After moving to "you build it, you run it", developers are burning out. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: pages per person, after-hours pages, rotation size, and how much planned capacity goes to operational work.

How to confirm: a rotation of three or four people, noisy alerts, and no time budgeted for fixing them.

Likely causes and fixes: ownership without support. Merge rotations until each person is on call about a quarter of the time or less, fix the noisiest alerts, provide platform defaults for deploys and rollbacks, and reserve capacity for operability work. See team practices and ownership.

docs.title: 65. One engineer in a six-person rotation handled 39% of last month's pages. The schedule is equal. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which alerts paged that engineer and when.

How to confirm: an on-call report shows one alert firing repeatedly during their week, mostly at night, and rarely needing action.

Likely causes and fixes: a noisy alert, not an unfair schedule. Tune or delete the alert, give the engineer recovery time, and review per-person load monthly. See team practices and ownership.

docs.title: 66. Every change waits for a weekly change advisory board, yet incidents are not decreasing. What do you propose?
docs.text:
What to check first: how long changes wait for approval and how many changes each release bundles.

How to confirm: approval wait dominates lead time, and change fail rate has not improved since the board was added.

Likely causes and fixes: external approval as the main control, which DORA found slows delivery without lowering change fail rates. Move approval into peer review, automate checks, flag high-risk paths for extra review, keep an audit trail, and give the board a coordination role. See team practices and ownership.

docs.title: 67. Postmortems have become vague since a manager named an engineer in one. How do you recover?
docs.text:
What to check first: recent postmortem timelines and near-miss reports.

How to confirm: timelines with gaps, phrases like "a configuration issue occurred", and no near misses reported.

Likely causes and fixes: blame broke psychological safety. Leadership restates the blameless policy publicly, reviews focus on system changes, and people are thanked for candid accounts. See team practices and ownership.

docs.title: 68. A developer portal launched three months ago and few teams use it. What next?
docs.text:
What to check first: which journeys teams actually struggle with, from interviews and usage data.

How to confirm: low weekly active users; templates rarely run; features chosen without user research.

Likely causes and fixes: "build it and they will come". Pick the most painful journey, ship a minimal golden path for it, measure task success and satisfaction, and remove any mandates. See platform engineering and developer portals.

docs.title: 69. The platform team's backlog is almost entirely "create X for team Y" tickets. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the most frequent request types and how long each waits.

How to confirm: the same few requests (databases, environments, access) make up most tickets and wait days.

Likely causes and fixes: ticket-ops. Automate the top requests behind an API, CLI, or portal form with secure defaults, and measure time from request to use. See platform engineering and developer portals.

docs.title: 70. After a mandated move to the internal platform, lead time and deployment frequency got worse. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: where changes wait in the new pipeline and which teams' needs it does not fit.

How to confirm: extra handoffs and approval steps appear in the value stream; teams with unusual needs work around the platform.

Likely causes and fixes: a mandatory, one-size-fits-all path, the pattern DORA linked to lower throughput. Remove the mandate, make the platform composable, and fix the slowest steps. See platform engineering and developer portals.
