docs.title: Measuring Delivery Performance
docs.text:
Teams argue about whether delivery is "fast" or "stable" until someone measures it. This lesson goes deeper than the introduction to DORA's metrics in continuous integration fundamentals: it covers the current five metrics and how DORA has changed them, the exact timestamps and edge cases needed to compute each one from git, pipeline, and incident data, the benchmarks DORA publishes and how to read them, flow metrics, the SPACE framework, and the ways measurement goes wrong.

The practical examples build a small, working implementation: four tables, a script that exports git history, and SQL that computes lead time, deployment frequency, and the instability metrics for two weeks of TaskFlow API deployments, with the real output of the run.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without measurement, improvement is a matter of opinion: the team that argues most confidently wins. With careless measurement it is worse, because a wrong number looks authoritative. Delivery metrics, done well, answer concrete questions: Did moving to trunk-based development shorten lead time? Did the new canary step reduce failed changes? Is the on-call rotation recovering faster?

DORA describes its software delivery metrics as both leading and lagging indicators: leading indicators for organizational performance and employee well-being, and lagging indicators for software development and delivery practices. That makes them useful for checking whether a practice change worked, and for seeing problems before they show up as missed business goals. The same numbers become harmful the moment they are used to rank teams or set targets, which is why the pitfalls section of this lesson matters as much as the formulas.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• DORA's metrics guide. The software delivery performance metrics guide (updated January 2026) defines five metrics in two groups, throughput and instability, says they "are meant to be applied at the application or service level", and lists pitfalls such as "Setting metrics as a goal" and "Having one metric to rule them all".
  • DORA's history of the metrics. Nathen Harvey's A history of DORA's software delivery metrics (January 2026) explains how the original four keys became the current five: mean time to recover was renamed and redefined as failed deployment recovery time in 2023, and deployment rework rate was added in 2024.
  • Published performance levels. The 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report found four clusters of software delivery performance, with elite performers reporting 127 times faster lead time and 182 times more deployments per year than low performers. The 2025 report, State of AI-assisted Software Development, instead publishes the distribution of answers for each metric and seven team profiles.
  • SPACE. Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Houck, and Butler's The SPACE of Developer Productivity (ACM Queue, 2021) argues that productivity "cannot be measured by a single metric or dimension". Microsoft's Developer Velocity Lab announcement lists its five dimensions and recommends measuring at least three.
  • Flow metrics. Planview's Flow Metrics documentation describes the Flow Framework from Mik Kersten's Project to Product: flow velocity, time, efficiency, load, and distribution across features, defects, risks, and debt.

Popular tools and providers: the DORA Quick Check, source-available tools listed on DORA's resources page (Apache DevLake, Middleware, OpenDORA, and a Backstage DORA plugin), commercial engineering-metrics platforms, and plain SQL over your own pipeline and incident events, as in this lesson.

docs.title: The five metrics today
docs.text:
DORA's guide lists five software delivery performance metrics:

Factor Metric DORA's definition Typical unit Throughput Change lead time "The amount of time it takes for a change to go from committed to version control to deployed in production." Hours or days; report the median and a high percentile Throughput Deployment frequency "The number of deployments over a given period or the time between deployments." Deployments per day or week Throughput Failed deployment recovery time "The time it takes to recover from a deployment that fails and requires immediate intervention." Minutes or hours Instability Change fail rate "The ratio of deployments that require immediate intervention following a deployment." Percent of deployments Instability Deployment rework rate "The ratio of deployments that are unplanned but happen as a result of an incident in production." Percent of deployments

Recovery time sits with throughput because it measures how fast changes of any kind, including fixes, move through the system. The 2024 report explains that change fail rate and rework rate together form a reliable "software delivery stability" factor; DORA's guide now calls the same group instability, so lower is better. You will also see "lead time for changes", "change failure rate", and "rework rate" in DORA's reports; they refer to the same metrics.

docs.title: What changed, and why
docs.text:
Period Change Notes 2014 Research starts with four variables: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, mean time to recover (MTTR), change fail rate Change fail rate did not correlate with the others, so the first definition of IT performance used three 2015 Metrics grouped as throughput (deployment frequency, lead time) and stability (MTTR, change fail rate) The "duality of throughput and stability" 2018 Availability added; "IT performance" becomes "software delivery and operational (SDO) performance"; the elite cluster appears The first measure of operational performance joins the delivery metrics 2021 Availability broadened to reliability The history article notes that calling reliability the "fifth metric" was inaccurate, because it measures operations, not delivery 2023 MTTR renamed and redefined as failed deployment recovery time To separate failures caused by software changes from external failures such as data center outages 2024 Deployment rework rate added; recovery time grouped with throughput, change fail and rework rates with stability Change fail rate was long suspected to be a proxy for rework, and the data confirmed the two are related 2025 Report reorganized around AI-assisted development; distributions per metric and seven team profiles instead of a four-level table Delivery metrics "tell you what is happening, but they don't explain why"

The number of clusters has never been fixed in advance. DORA's FAQ notes three clusters before 2018, four from 2018 to 2021, three in 2022, and four again in 2023 and 2024. Treat any "elite" threshold as a snapshot of that year's respondents, not a standard.

docs.title: Where each timestamp comes from
docs.text:
Each metric needs a precise rule for its start and end. Write the rules down, because every edge case changes the numbers:

  • Change lead time starts when the change is committed and ends at the first successful production deployment that contains it. A re-deploy after a rollback does not reset the clock, and staging deploys do not count. Merge strategy matters: squash and rebase merges create new commits whose committer date is the merge time, so the wait for review disappears from the measurement. If review time is part of what you want to improve, start the clock at the first commit of the pull request instead, and say so.
  • Deployment frequency counts successful deployments to production for one service, planned or not. A pipeline run that failed before reaching production is not a deployment. Report deployments per week, the share of working days with at least one deployment, or the time between deployments.
  • Change fail rate needs a definition of "requires immediate intervention". DORA's 2025 survey describes changes that lead to service impairment or outage and require "a hotfix, rollback, fix forward or patch". Decide whether turning off a feature flag counts, write it down, and link each incident to the deployment that caused it.
  • Failed deployment recovery time runs from the failed deployment (or from detection, if you prefer, but be consistent) to the moment service is restored, usually by a rollback, flag change, or fix. Outages that were not caused by a deployment, such as a cloud region failure, belong in your SLOs and incident metrics, not here. That separation is why DORA renamed MTTR.
  • Deployment rework rate counts deployments that were not planned but happened because of a production incident: rollbacks, hotfixes, emergency patches. Your deploy tooling needs a way to mark them, such as a required "reason" input on the rollback workflow.

All of this is measured per application or service. Mixing a mobile app that ships monthly through store review with a web API that deploys hourly produces a number that describes neither.

docs.title: A data model you can trust
docs.text:
Store raw events rather than finished numbers. If you keep only "lead time this week: 2.3 hours", you cannot recompute it when you change the definition, fix a bug in the calculation, or want a different percentile. With raw events, every number is a query.

A few rules keep the events trustworthy:

  • Record deployments at the source, from the pipeline step that performs them, including failures and rollbacks. Reconstructing them later from chat messages or tickets loses events.
  • Use UTC and ISO 8601 everywhere (2026-10-05T10:20:00Z). SQLite, PostgreSQL, and JavaScript all parse it, including offsets such as +02:00.
  • Map deployments to commits with git, not by guessing: git rev-list <previous deployed sha>..<deployed sha> lists exactly the commits a deployment shipped.
  • Keep your own copy. Vendor histories have retention limits; for example, GitHub retains previous deployment statuses for 90 days.

docs.title: Distributions, not averages
docs.text:
Lead times are heavily skewed: most changes are quick, and a few wait days on a branch or over a weekend. In the sample data used below, the median commit reached production in 2.3 hours while the mean was 12.2 hours, more than five times higher, pulled up by two commits that waited 65 and 96 hours. The 90th percentile, 20.9 hours, tells a different story again: about one change in four or five waits overnight for the next morning's deploy. (The histogram's bins are deliberately unequal, so it shows the minutes-to-days range in one picture.)

Report the median for the typical change and a high percentile (p85 or p90) for the tail you want to shrink. Averages move when one commit sits on a forgotten branch, which says little about the team's normal flow.

docs.title: Benchmarks as published by DORA
docs.text:
The 2024 report's performance levels, from a cluster analysis of the original four metrics (rework rate was not part of the clustering):

Performance level Change lead time Deployment frequency Change fail rate Failed deployment recovery time Share of respondents Elite Less than one day On demand (multiple deploys per day) 5% Less than one hour 19% High Between one day and one week Between once per day and once per week 20% Less than one day 22% Medium Between one week and one month Between once per week and once per month 10% Less than one day 35% Low Between one month and six months Between once per month and once every six months 40% Between one week and one month 25%

Two details are easy to miss. The medium cluster has a lower change fail rate than the high cluster: DORA chose to call faster teams "high" and slower but more stable teams "medium", and notes there may be no universal answer to which is better. And the report's own advice is that "the best teams are those that achieve elite improvement, not necessarily elite performance."

The 2025 report replaced the four-level table with the distribution of survey answers for each metric ("How do you compare?"). Reading off where the middle respondent falls:

Metric Typical (median) respondent Best answer offered, and share choosing it Change lead time Between one day and one week Less than one hour: 9.4% (less than one day: 24.4% in total) Deployment frequency Between once per week and once per month On demand, multiple deploys per day: 16.2% Failed deployment recovery time Less than one day Less than one hour: 21.3% (less than one day: 56.5% in total) Change fail rate 8% to 16% 0% to 2%: 8.5% Deployment rework rate 8% to 16% 0% to 2%: 6.9%

These are self-reported survey answers about each respondent's primary application. Use them for orientation, then compare your service with its own past, which is the comparison DORA recommends.

docs.title: Flow metrics
docs.text:
DORA's metrics start at commit. Much of the waiting happens earlier: in backlogs, design, and review. The Flow Framework measures the whole value stream, from when work starts to when it is complete, using flow items of four types: features, defects, risks, and debt. Planview's documentation defines the metrics:

Flow metric Definition (Planview) Question it answers Flow velocity Number of flow items of each type completed over a period (throughput) Is value delivery accelerating? Flow time Time from "work start" to "work complete", active and waiting Is time to value getting shorter? Flow efficiency Active time as a share of total flow time How much of the time is work actually progressing? Flow load Number of flow items in progress, active or waiting (WIP) Is demand outweighing capacity? Flow distribution Ratio of the four flow item types completed in a period Are features crowding out defects, risk, and debt?

Flow load and flow time are linked by Little's law, as shown in What is DevOps: more work in progress at the same throughput means longer flow time. Flow distribution catches a pattern DORA metrics miss: a team can deploy often and fast while spending nothing on debt and risk, until it cannot.

docs.title: SPACE: productivity has more than one dimension
docs.text:
The SPACE framework names five dimensions of developer productivity: satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, and efficiency and flow. Microsoft's announcement recommends including measures from at least three of them. Combine what people report in surveys with what systems record, since each sees things the other misses. The examples below are illustrative choices for the TaskFlow team, not a list from the paper:

Dimension Example measures What it guards against Satisfaction and well-being Quarterly survey: satisfaction with tools and process, burnout risk Shipping faster by exhausting people Performance SLO compliance, change fail rate, customer-reported defects Activity that produces no good outcomes Activity Deployments, pull requests merged, incidents handled Invisible work; meaningless alone Communication and collaboration Review turnaround time, onboarding time, findability of documentation Fast individuals, slow team Efficiency and flow Change lead time, flow efficiency, interruptions per day Hidden waiting and constant context switching

DORA's article Choosing measurement frameworks compares SPACE, DevEx, HEART, and DORA's metrics, and distinguishes self-reported data (surveys, interviews) from logs-based data (counts, durations, frequencies), warning that it is "a common misconception that logs-based metrics are objective."

docs.title: Pitfalls: Goodhart's law and gaming
docs.text:
Economist Charles Goodhart observed in 1975 that a statistical regularity tends to collapse once it is used for control; the popular phrasing, usually credited to Marilyn Strathern, is "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." DORA's guide cites Goodhart's law in the first of its listed pitfalls:

  • "Setting metrics as a goal", for example "Every application must deploy multiple times per day by year's end".
  • "Having one metric to rule them all", instead of several metrics "with a healthy amount of tension between them".
  • "Using industry as a shield against improving."
  • "Making disparate comparisons" between very different applications.
  • "Having siloed ownership", with each team owning one metric.
  • "Competing" against other teams instead of improving over time.
  • "Focusing on measurement at the expense of improvement."

Typical ways each metric gets gamed, and what exposes it:

Metric How it gets gamed Counter-signal Deployment frequency Deploying unchanged code, splitting one change into many deploys Lead time and commits per deploy Change lead time Squash-merging to hide review time, measuring from merge Pull request age, flow time Change fail rate Not linking incidents to deployments, renaming rollbacks "maintenance" Incident records, rework rate, SLO burn Recovery time Closing incidents before users are really unaffected SLO error budget, customer reports Any of them Ranking teams, so people hide problems Blameless reviews, trends per service

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Approach A team wants to know if a process change helped DORA metrics for its service, as a trend before and after No data or tooling yet Start with a conversation and the DORA Quick Check, not a data platform Delivery looks fast but users wait months for features Add flow metrics from work start, and a value stream map Leadership asks "how productive are developers?" SPACE-style mix of at least three dimensions, including surveys Comparing teams for performance reviews or bonuses Do not; it invites gaming and hides problems A service deploys a few times a year by design (firmware, regulated device) Use lead time and change fail rate per release; frequency is not a goal Many services in a monorepo Compute per deployable service, mapping commits by path (see monorepo builds and deployments)

docs.title: Record every deployment at the source
docs.text:
The deploy job sends one event per attempt, success or failure, to the team's metrics store (any database or HTTP endpoint you control):

# .github/workflows/deliver.yml (excerpt): record every production deployment
jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "$GITHUB_SHA"
      - name: Record the deployment
        if: always()                     # record failed attempts too
        env:
          METRICS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.METRICS_TOKEN }}
          JOB_STATUS: ${{ job.status }}
        run: |
          status=failed
          if [ "$JOB_STATUS" = "success" ]; then status=success; fi
          curl -fsS -X POST https://metrics.example.com/api/deployments \
            -H "Authorization: Bearer $METRICS_TOKEN" \
            -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
            -d "{\"service\":\"taskflow-api\",\"environment\":\"production\",\"sha\":\"$GITHUB_SHA\",\"status\":\"$status\",\"finished_at\":\"$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)\"}"

job.status is success, failure, or cancelled at that point in the job, and if: always() makes the step run even after a failed deploy. The rollback and hotfix workflows send the same event with an extra "unplanned": 1, which is what the rework rate counts. Export the events as deployments.csv with the columns of the deployments table.

docs.title: Export commits and deployment ranges from git
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/export-dora.sh: turn git history and a deployment log into CSV files
# Input: deployments.csv (id,service,environment,sha,finished_at,status,unplanned), oldest first
set -euo pipefail

echo "sha,committed_at" > commits.csv
git log --format='%H,%cI' main >> commits.csv

echo "deployment_id,sha" > deployment_commits.csv
prev=""
while IFS=, read -r id service environment sha finished_at status unplanned; do
  [ "$environment" = "production" ] && [ "$status" = "success" ] || continue
  if [ -n "$prev" ]; then
    # commits reachable from this deploy but not from the previous one
    git rev-list "$prev..$sha" | sed "s/^/$id,/" >> deployment_commits.csv
  fi
  prev="$sha"
done < <(tail -n +2 deployments.csv)

%cI prints the committer date in strict ISO 8601 with its offset. The first deployment in the file has no previous one, so start the export from a known baseline. After a rollback, the next range includes commits that were already deployed once; the lead time query handles that by taking each commit's first successful deployment.

docs.title: Create the tables and load the data
docs.text:
-- schema.sql: delivery events for one service (SQLite)
CREATE TABLE commits (
  sha          TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
  committed_at TEXT NOT NULL              -- ISO 8601, for example 2026-10-05T09:15:00Z
);

CREATE TABLE deployments (
  id          INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  service     TEXT NOT NULL,
  environment TEXT NOT NULL,              -- 'staging' or 'production'
  sha         TEXT NOT NULL,              -- the commit that was deployed
  finished_at TEXT NOT NULL,              -- when the deployment completed
  status      TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (status IN ('success', 'failed')),
  unplanned   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- 1 = rollback or hotfix for an incident
);

-- Every commit a deployment shipped: git log <previous deployed sha>..<sha>
CREATE TABLE deployment_commits (
  deployment_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES deployments(id),
  sha           TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES commits(sha),
  PRIMARY KEY (deployment_id, sha)
);

-- Production incidents caused by a deployment
CREATE TABLE incidents (
  id            INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  deployment_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES deployments(id),
  detected_at   TEXT NOT NULL,
  restored_at   TEXT NOT NULL
);

sqlite3 dora.db < schema.sql
sqlite3 dora.db ".import --csv --skip 1 commits.csv commits"
sqlite3 dora.db ".import --csv --skip 1 deployments.csv deployments"
sqlite3 dora.db ".import --csv --skip 1 deployment_commits.csv deployment_commits"

docs.title: Change lead time per week
docs.text:
-- lead-time.sql: change lead time per week, median and 90th percentile
WITH first_deploy AS (
  -- A commit counts as deployed the first time a successful production
  -- deployment ships it; later re-deploys (after a rollback) do not reset it.
  SELECT dc.sha, MIN(julianday(d.finished_at)) AS deployed_jd
  FROM deployment_commits dc
  JOIN deployments d ON d.id = dc.deployment_id
  WHERE d.environment = 'production' AND d.status = 'success'
  GROUP BY dc.sha
),
lead AS (
  SELECT date(f.deployed_jd, 'weekday 0', '-6 days') AS week_of,  -- Monday
         ROUND((f.deployed_jd - julianday(c.committed_at)) * 1440) AS minutes
  FROM first_deploy f
  JOIN commits c ON c.sha = f.sha
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT week_of, minutes,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY week_of ORDER BY minutes) AS rn,
         COUNT(*)     OVER (PARTITION BY week_of)                  AS n
  FROM lead
)
SELECT week_of,
       n AS changes,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN rn IN ((n + 1) / 2, (n + 2) / 2) THEN minutes END) / 60.0, 1) AS median_h,
       ROUND(MAX(CASE WHEN rn <= (9 * n + 9) / 10 THEN minutes END) / 60.0, 1)            AS p90_h,
       ROUND(AVG(minutes) / 60.0, 1)                                                     AS mean_h
FROM ranked
GROUP BY week_of, n
ORDER BY week_of;

$ sqlite3 -header -column dora.db < lead-time.sql
 week_of    changes  median_h  p90_h  mean_h
----------  -------  --------  -----  ------
2026-10-05       14       2.5   20.9    10.4
2026-10-12       13       2.3   20.7    14.1

How it works: first_deploy takes each commit's earliest successful production deployment, so c06 and c07 count from deployment 4, not from the re-deploy after the rollback. The modifier pair 'weekday 0', '-6 days' moves any date to the Monday of its week. The median averages the middle one or two rows; (9 * n + 9) / 10 is integer arithmetic for the nearest-rank 90th percentile, ceil(0.9 × n), without needing SQLite's optional math functions. In PostgreSQL, percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) gives the same median and percentile_disc(0.9) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY minutes) the same nearest-rank 90th percentile.

Reading it: the median is stable at about two and a half hours, but the mean jumped from 10.4 to 14.1 hours in the second week because of one commit that waited four days on a branch. The p90 of about 21 hours says the slowest changes regularly wait overnight; a team that wants to improve should look at why afternoon merges are not deployed the same day.

docs.title: Deployment frequency per week
docs.text:
-- deploy-frequency.sql: successful production deployments per week
WITH prod AS (
  SELECT finished_at, unplanned,
         date(finished_at, 'weekday 0', '-6 days') AS week_of,
         (julianday(finished_at)
           - julianday(LAG(finished_at) OVER (ORDER BY finished_at))) * 24 AS gap_h
  FROM deployments
  WHERE environment = 'production' AND status = 'success'
)
SELECT week_of,
       COUNT(*)                         AS deploys,
       COUNT(DISTINCT date(finished_at)) AS deploy_days,
       ROUND(COUNT(*) / 5.0, 1)         AS per_workday,
       SUM(unplanned)                   AS unplanned,
       ROUND(MAX(gap_h), 1)             AS longest_gap_h
FROM prod
GROUP BY week_of
ORDER BY week_of;

$ sqlite3 -header -column dora.db < deploy-frequency.sql
 week_of    deploys  deploy_days  per_workday  unplanned  longest_gap_h
----------  -------  -----------  -----------  ---------  -------------
2026-10-05        9            5          1.8          1           23.6
2026-10-12        8            5          1.6          1           66.8

The failed pipeline run (deployment 9) is excluded, while the rollback and the hotfix count: they are real production deployments. Deploy days (5 of 5 working days) is a useful second view, because it shows whether deployment is routine or bunched. The 66.8-hour longest gap is the weekend; the 23.6-hour gap in the first week runs from Tuesday's 11:10 deploy to Wednesday's 10:45 deploy.

docs.title: Change fail rate, rework rate, and recovery time
docs.text:
-- instability.sql: change fail rate, rework rate, failed deployment recovery time
WITH prod AS (
  SELECT id, finished_at, unplanned
  FROM deployments
  WHERE environment = 'production' AND status = 'success'
),
failed AS (
  SELECT p.id,
         MAX(julianday(i.restored_at) - julianday(p.finished_at)) * 1440 AS recovery_min
  FROM prod p
  JOIN incidents i ON i.deployment_id = p.id
  GROUP BY p.id
)
SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod)                                         AS deploys,
       (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM failed)                                       AS failed_changes,
       ROUND(100.0 * (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM failed)
                   / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod), 1)                       AS change_fail_pct,
       ROUND(100.0 * (SELECT SUM(unplanned) FROM prod)
                   / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM prod), 1)                       AS rework_pct,
       (SELECT ROUND(AVG(recovery_min)) FROM failed)                       AS mean_recovery_min;

$ sqlite3 -header -column dora.db < instability.sql
deploys  failed_changes  change_fail_pct  rework_pct  mean_recovery_min
-------  --------------  ---------------  ----------  -----------------
     17               2             11.8        11.8               80.0

Two of 17 deployments needed immediate intervention (11.8%), and two deployments were unplanned fixes (also 11.8%, a coincidence in this sample). Recovery took 35 minutes for the rollback and 125 minutes for the hotfix, a mean of 80 minutes; with so few failures, list them individually rather than trusting any average. These SQL files run unchanged with the sqlite3 command-line shell and with Python's built-in sqlite3 module.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Measure one service at a time, as trends, and look at throughput and instability together.
  • Write down the definition of every start and end timestamp, including how rollbacks, flags, and squash merges are handled.
  • Record events automatically at the source: commits from git, deployments from the pipeline, incidents from the incident tool.
  • Keep raw events in your own store, in UTC, so numbers can be recomputed.
  • Report medians and a high percentile, never only averages.
  • Add flow metrics and surveys when the question goes beyond "commit to production".
  • Use metrics to choose and check experiments; never set them as targets or compare unlike teams.
  • Start small: a conversation and the DORA Quick Check can be enough to pick the first improvement.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Lead time looks excellent, but features still take months. Detect: change lead time is a few hours while product managers report long waits; pull requests stay open for days. Cause: the clock starts at the squash-merge commit, and most waiting happens before commit. Fix: measure from the pull request's first commit as well, add flow time from work start, and map the value stream.
  • Deployment frequency doubled right after leadership set a target. Detect: many deployments ship no new commits, and commits per deploy fell to zero. Cause: Goodhart's law: the number became the goal. Fix: withdraw the target, track deploys together with lead time and commits per deploy, and discuss trends with the team instead of ranking it.
  • The DORA dashboard lost last year's data. Detect: history before a certain date is empty or shows no failures. Cause: metrics were computed from a vendor API with limited retention; GitHub, for instance, keeps previous deployment statuses for 90 days. Fix: export events nightly into your own database and compute everything from there.
  • Change fail rate is 0% while incidents keep happening. Detect: the incident tracker shows deploy-related incidents, yet no deployment is marked failed. Cause: incidents are not linked to the deployment that caused them. Fix: add a required "triggering deployment" field to incident records and a reason input on rollback workflows.
  • Every service in the monorepo shows the same deployment frequency. Detect: identical numbers for unrelated services. Cause: each deploy of the repository is counted for every service. Fix: record the service on each deployment event and map commits to services by path.
  • Recovery times jumped after a cloud outage. Detect: one incident of several hours dominates the month's recovery time. Cause: an outage that was not caused by a deployment was counted as a failed deployment. Fix: keep only deployment-caused failures in this metric, which is the point of DORA's 2023 rename, and track the outage against the SLO instead.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Change lead time: Time from commit to that change running in production.
  • Deployment frequency: Number of production deployments in a period, or the time between them.
  • Failed deployment recovery time: Time to recover from a deployment that needed immediate intervention.
  • Change fail rate: Share of deployments that needed immediate intervention.
  • Deployment rework rate: Share of deployments that were unplanned fixes for production incidents.
  • Throughput / instability: DORA's two groupings of the five metrics.
  • Performance cluster: A group of survey respondents with similar metric values, found by cluster analysis.
  • Median / p90: The middle value, and the value 90% of observations fall below.
  • Flow item: A unit of work in the Flow Framework: feature, defect, risk, or debt.
  • Flow time / flow load / flow efficiency: Start-to-finish time, work in progress, and the active share of flow time.
  • SPACE: Satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, efficiency and flow.
  • Goodhart's law: A measure used as a target stops being a good measure.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using DORA metrics to rank teams or individuals.
  • Averaging lead times instead of reporting the median and a percentile.
  • Counting staging deployments or failed pipeline runs as deployments.
  • Starting lead time at merge without saying so, after squash merges.
  • Counting outages unrelated to deployments as failed deployments.
  • Treating the 2024 "elite" thresholds as a permanent standard.
  • Believing system data is objective while surveys are not; both need care.
  • Measuring only activity (commits, pull requests) and calling it productivity.
  • Building a large metrics platform before having the first improvement conversation.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name DORA's five software delivery metrics, their two groupings, and what changed in 2023 and 2024.
  2. Why does failed deployment recovery time exclude a data center outage that no deployment caused?
  3. How do squash merges affect a lead time measured from commit timestamps, and how would you correct for it?
  4. A service had 40 production deployments in a month; 3 needed a rollback or hotfix, recovering in 20, 40, and 90 minutes; 5 deployments were unplanned fixes. Compute the change fail rate, mean recovery time, and rework rate. (7.5%; 50 minutes; 12.5%.)
  5. Seven lead times in hours are 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 20, and 70. Compute the mean, the median, and the nearest-rank 90th percentile. Which would you report? (Mean 14.1; median 2; p90 is rank ceil(6.3) = 7, so 70. Report the median and the p90.)
  6. In the 2024 performance levels, why is the medium cluster's change fail rate lower than the high cluster's, and what does DORA advise about chasing "elite"?
  7. Name the five flow metrics and the four flow item types. What does flow distribution reveal that DORA metrics do not?
  8. Your director wants every team to reach "multiple deployments per day" by year end. What do you recommend instead, and why?

docs.title: Platform Engineering and Developer Portals
docs.text:
"You build it, you run it" asks a lot of every team: pipelines, infrastructure, monitoring, security scanning, secrets, documentation. When ten teams each solve all of that alone, the organization pays ten times for the same work and gets ten slightly different answers. Platform engineering builds the shared answers once, as an internal product that teams use by choice because it is the easiest way to do the right thing.

This lesson explains what an internal developer platform is and how it is layered, golden paths and paved roads, self-service instead of tickets, the Backstage developer portal and its software catalog and templates, running a platform as a product, measuring whether it works, and when a small team should not build a platform at all. The examples register TaskFlow in a catalog, scaffold a new service from a template, share one pipeline as a reusable workflow, and check every repository against the golden path.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The more a team owns, the more it has to know. A product team that must also become expert in Kubernetes, cloud networking, CI runners, and security policy spends its attention on infrastructure instead of users. Team Topologies calls this cognitive load; DORA's platform engineering capability says a platform's primary goal is to reduce it by "abstracting away underlying complexity".

Platforms also cut the hidden cost of fragmentation. When every service deploys, logs, and stores secrets differently, a security fix takes months to reach all of them, and moving between teams means relearning everything. A shared, well-run path changes that. But platforms fail in predictable ways too, and DORA's 2024 research found that the same platforms that raise productivity can lower delivery throughput and change stability when they add handoffs or force a poor fit. Building one well is product work, not just infrastructure work.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix's paved road. In Full Cycle Developers at Netflix (2018), Netflix describes centralized teams that "act as force multipliers by turning their specialized knowledge into reusable building blocks", and a "paved road" of tools and practices that is not mandated: adoption is encouraged "by ensuring that development and operations using those technologies is a far better experience than not using them." Netflix's infrastructure itself is one of the case studies in how top companies run at scale.
  • Spotify's golden paths. Spotify's 2020 post How We Use Golden Paths to Solve Fragmentation in Our Software Ecosystem defines the Golden Path as "the 'opinionated and supported' path to 'build something'", created to replace what it called "rumour-driven development".
  • Backstage. Spotify open-sourced its developer portal in March 2020 (announcement), reporting a 55% decrease in onboarding time, measured as time until a new engineer's 10th pull request. According to the CNCF project page, Backstage was accepted to the CNCF on September 8, 2020 and moved to the Incubating maturity level on March 15, 2022.
  • CNCF Platforms White Paper. The white paper from CNCF's TAG App Delivery defines a platform as "an integrated collection of capabilities defined and presented according to the needs of the platform's users", lists the attributes of a good platform, and proposes ways to measure one.
  • DORA's research. The 2024 Accelerate State of DevOps Report found internal developer platform users had 8% higher individual productivity and 10% higher team performance, alongside 8% lower throughput and 14% lower change stability, and DORA's capability page reports that by 2025, 90% of organizations used an internal developer platform.

Popular tools and providers: developer portals such as Backstage (open source) and commercial portals such as Port, Cortex, and OpsLevel; platform building blocks such as Kubernetes, Argo CD, Crossplane, Terraform, and OpenTofu; and GitHub Actions reusable workflows or GitLab CI templates for shared pipelines.

docs.title: What an internal developer platform is
docs.text:
Three definitions, from different angles:

  • DORA: platform engineering designs and builds "toolchains and workflows, often called an 'Internal Developer Platform', that provide shared, high-quality tools, services, and 'golden paths'", treated as "an internal product designed specifically for developers."
  • CNCF: "an integrated collection of capabilities defined and presented according to the needs of the platform's users", offered through consistent experiences such as "Web portals, project templates, and self-service APIs."
  • Evan Bottcher (2018), What I Talk About When I Talk About Platforms: "A digital platform is a foundation of self-service APIs, tools, services, knowledge and support which are arranged as a compelling internal product."

The common thread is product: users, a roadmap, support, and a reason to choose it. A pile of Terraform modules that only the platform team can run is infrastructure, not a platform.

docs.title: The layers of a platform
docs.text:
The CNCF white paper is explicit that a platform team "doesn't necessarily run compute, network, storage or other services", and that it "should rely on externally-provided services and capabilities as much as possible". The platform's value is in the top two layers: consistent interfaces and well-integrated capabilities. A very small platform can be nothing more than, in the paper's words, "a wiki page with links to standard operating procedures to provision capabilities from providers."

The paper's attributes of a good platform make a useful checklist:

Attribute What it means TaskFlow example Platform as a product Built from users' needs, prioritizing the most common use cases The deploy path every service uses comes first; exotic needs later User experience Consistent interfaces where users already work: portal, CLI, IDE, API platform db create and a portal form call the same API Documentation and onboarding Docs, examples, and templates that bundle a "golden path" A new service is scaffolded with CI, dashboards, and an SLO document Self-service Capabilities requested and delivered "autonomously and automatically" A database arrives in minutes, not after a ticket Reduced cognitive load Hides implementation details; users do not operate platform services Teams never manage the database servers, only their schemas Optional and composable Teams can use parts of it, and go outside it when needed A team that needs a graph database can run one itself Secure by default Compliance and validation built in Encryption, backups, least-privilege access, and pipeline security checks are defaults

docs.title: Golden paths and paved roads
docs.text:
Spotify's golden path is "the 'opinionated and supported' path to 'build something' (for example, build a backend service, put up a website, create a data pipeline)." Its original internal write-up added: "If you are an adventurer you can of course leave the Golden Path and do your own thing, but then you will not have the same support." Netflix's paved road works the same way: supported tools that are "a far better experience than not using them", with no mandate.

Three lessons from those posts are worth copying:

  • The path is the product; the tutorial only describes it. When engineers complained that the golden path tutorials were too long, Spotify's response was that the tutorials "just reflect the actual Golden Path. That's what we need to shorten."
  • Check conformance, do not police it. Spotify's "Golden State" is "a list of checks that engineers can use to know if their systems are following the Golden Path", so teams can see where they stand.
  • Avoid the golden cage. DORA lists a "one-size-fits-all" platform as a pitfall: a rigid "golden cage" that ignores the different needs of, say, data science and mobile teams.

docs.title: Self-service instead of tickets
docs.text:
DORA names the "ticket-ops" trap: a platform team that works like "a reactive 'vending machine' for infrastructure tickets" stays trapped in toil and becomes the bottleneck it was meant to remove. The worked numbers in the diagram are typical of the trade: 40 database requests a month at 45 minutes each is 30 hours of platform engineers' time, plus about three days of waiting for each requesting team. Building the self-service path costs engineering time once; after that, each request costs minutes and no platform engineer at all, and the defaults (backups, encryption, tagging) are applied every time instead of when someone remembers.

DORA's 2024 data supports the direction: when developers could complete their tasks without involving an enabling team, the report measured a 5% productivity improvement at both the individual and team level.

docs.title: Backstage: catalog, templates, and docs
docs.text:
Backstage is "an open source framework for building developer portals", powered by a centralized software catalog. Out of the box it includes:

  • Software Catalog: every component, API, resource, and owner in one searchable place, described by catalog-info.yaml files that live in each repository.
  • Software Templates: wizards that create new projects "with your organization's best practices", the usual way to encode golden paths.
  • TechDocs: documentation written as Markdown next to the code ("docs like code") and rendered in the portal.
  • Plugins: an ecosystem that brings CI status, deployments, costs, alerts, and other tools into the same interface.

The catalog's system model has three core entities, components (individual pieces of software), APIs (the boundaries between components), and resources (the infrastructure a component needs, such as databases), plus systems and domains to group them and users and groups to own them. Every component's spec.owner names "the singular entity (commonly a team) that bears ultimate responsibility for the component". That one required field is what turns the catalog into an ownership map.

Backstage itself is a framework you assemble, deploy, and upgrade. Its adoption guide is direct about the organizational cost: "you will need a central team that owns your Backstage deployment and treats it like a product", with operations, support, and eventually on-call. For a small organization, that team usually costs more than the portal saves.

docs.title: Platform as a product
docs.text:
DORA's capability page turns "platform as a product" into concrete advice:

  • Assign a product manager and map critical user journeys, such as "spinning up a new service" or "debugging a production issue", to find the worst friction.
  • Start with a minimum viable platform: identify "the golden path for the most common workflow" and make that one journey demonstrably better before building anything else. Team Topologies calls the same idea the Thinnest Viable Platform.
  • Design for extensibility, so other teams can contribute tools and the platform team does not become a bottleneck.
  • Prioritize clear feedback: in DORA's 2025 data, the platform capability most correlated with a positive user experience is giving "clear feedback on the outcome of my tasks".

And it lists the anti-patterns: "Build it and they will come" (no user research), the "Ivory tower" (rigid standards dictated from above), the "Ticket-ops" trap, the "Big bang" release, and the "one-size-fits-all" golden cage. The CNCF white paper adds that platform teams "that rely on top-down mandates to achieve adoption are almost certain to find resistance and resentment from their users". DORA's 2024 report saw this in the data: respondents required to use the platform exclusively for every lifecycle task reported a 6% decrease in throughput.

docs.title: Measuring platform success
docs.text:
What to measure Example measures Source of the idea User satisfaction and productivity Active users and retention, NPS or CSAT, SPACE-style measures CNCF white paper; DORA Organizational efficiency Time from request to a usable database or environment; time to build and deploy a brand-new service; time for a new engineer's first change CNCF white paper Delivery outcomes of product teams Change lead time, deployment frequency, recovery time, change fail rate, rework rate DORA Adoption and retention Teams onboarding to the platform and continuing to use it DORA, using the HEART framework Onboarding and complexity Time until a new engineer's 10th merged pull request; number of tools touched to ship one change Backstage adoption guide

Expect a dip. DORA describes a "J-curve" for platforms: early gains, a drop as complexity grows, then recovery to a higher level as the platform matures. Its 2024 report saw gains in productivity and organizational performance but losses in throughput and stability, and suggests one cause: more handoffs between systems as each change passes through more automated checks. Measure both sides, delivery speed and developer experience, and watch the trend rather than one quarter.

docs.title: When a small team should not build a platform
docs.text:
Netflix's post includes its own warning: "many companies won't have the staffing to invest in centralized teams like at Netflix, nor will they need the complexity that Netflix's scale requires", and advises bringing "in the least complexity necessary."

Costs rise in this order, so start at the top and move down only when the need is proven:

  • Cheapest: templates, a wiki page, and managed services. A shared template repository and the provider's managed databases, queues, and CI cost almost nothing to maintain. This is enough for one to three teams.
  • Middle: a managed or commercial product with your defaults on top. You pay a subscription or usage fee instead of engineering time, and your effort goes into conventions and one golden path.
  • Most expensive: a self-built platform and portal. Open-source tools such as Backstage carry no license fee, but the platform needs a dedicated team to build, upgrade, support, and be on call for it. That ongoing staffing is the largest cost, so it pays off only when many teams share the need.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Recommendation One or two product teams No platform team: shared templates, managed services, good READMEs Several teams repeat the same pipeline, infrastructure, and monitoring work A thin platform: one golden path for the most common service type, owned by a small team Dozens of teams, many services, nobody knows who owns what A software catalog first; ownership data pays off before any templates Strong compliance or security requirements across many services Secure defaults in the platform (policy checks, encryption, audit) instead of manual reviews A platform already exists but nobody uses it User research and task-success measures before any new features; remove mandates Highly diverse teams (data science, mobile, backend) Composable capabilities and several golden paths, not one rigid path

docs.title: Register TaskFlow in the software catalog
docs.text:
Each repository describes its own entities. One file may hold several entities separated by ---, as Backstage's file format allows:

# catalog-info.yaml (in the taskflow-api repository)
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  description: Task API for TaskFlow (Express and MongoDB)
  annotations:
    github.com/project-slug: example/taskflow-api
    backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.
  tags:
    - nodejs
    - express
  links:
    - url: https://grafana.example.com/d/taskflow-slo
      title: SLO dashboard
      icon: dashboard
    - url: https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api
      title: Runbooks
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: production
  owner: tasks-team
  system: taskflow
  dependsOn:
    - resource:default/taskflow-db
  providesApis:
    - tasks-api
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: API
metadata:
  name: tasks-api
  description: REST API for creating and listing tasks
spec:
  type: openapi
  lifecycle: production
  owner: tasks-team
  system: taskflow
  definition:
    $text: ./openapi.yaml
---
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Resource
metadata:
  name: taskflow-db
  description: MongoDB replica set that stores tasks
spec:
  type: database
  owner: tasks-team
  system: taskflow

The parts: spec.type, spec.lifecycle (experimental, production, or deprecated are the well-known values), and spec.owner are required for a component. owner: tasks-team is a short entity reference that defaults to a Group. The github.com/project-slug annotation lets plugins find the repository, and backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:. tells TechDocs to build documentation from this repository. The API's definition uses the $text substitution to load the OpenAPI file from the same folder, so the spec is not duplicated.

docs.title: Scaffold a new service from a golden-path template
docs.text:
# templates/node-service/template.yaml: golden path for a new Node.js service
apiVersion: scaffolder.backstage.io/v1beta3
kind: Template
metadata:
  name: node-service
  title: Node.js service (golden path)
  description: Express service with CI/CD, an SLO document, dashboards, and on-call wiring
spec:
  owner: platform-team
  type: service
  parameters:
    - title: Service details
      required: [name, owner]
      properties:
        name:
          title: Name
          type: string
          description: Lowercase and dash-separated, for example taskflow-reminders
        owner:
          title: Owner
          type: string
          ui:field: OwnerPicker
          ui:options:
            catalogFilter:
              kind: Group
    - title: Repository
      required: [repoUrl]
      properties:
        repoUrl:
          title: Repository location
          type: string
          ui:field: RepoUrlPicker
          ui:options:
            allowedHosts:
              - github.com
  steps:
    - id: fetch
      name: Fetch the golden path skeleton
      action: fetch:template
      input:
        url: ./skeleton
        values:
          name: ${{ parameters.name }}
          owner: ${{ parameters.owner }}
    - id: publish
      name: Publish to GitHub
      action: publish:github
      input:
        description: ${{ parameters.name }}, created from the node-service golden path
        repoUrl: ${{ parameters.repoUrl }}
        defaultBranch: main
    - id: register
      name: Register in the catalog
      action: catalog:register
      input:
        repoContentsUrl: ${{ steps.publish.output.repoContentsUrl }}
        catalogInfoPath: /catalog-info.yaml
  output:
    links:
      - title: Repository
        url: ${{ steps.publish.output.remoteUrl }}
      - title: Open in catalog
        icon: catalog
        entityRef: ${{ steps.register.output.entityRef }}

# templates/node-service/skeleton/catalog-info.yaml: filled in by fetch:template
apiVersion: backstage.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
metadata:
  name: ${{ values.name }}
  annotations:
    backstage.io/techdocs-ref: dir:.
spec:
  type: service
  lifecycle: experimental
  owner: ${{ values.owner }}

The parameters render as form steps in the portal; fetch:template copies the skeleton/ folder and replaces ${{ values.* }} in every file; publish:github creates the repository (it comes from the @backstage/plugin-scaffolder-backend-module-github module); and catalog:register adds the new service to the catalog with its owner. The skeleton would also contain the pipeline caller shown next, an SLO document, a README with runbook links, and .nvmrc, so a new service starts on the golden path instead of drifting toward it later.

docs.title: Share one pipeline as a reusable workflow
docs.text:
The platform team owns the pipeline once; each service calls it:

# platform-workflows/.github/workflows/node-service.yml: the shared golden-path pipeline
name: Node service
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      service:
        description: Service name used for deploys and metrics
        required: true
        type: string
      node-version:
        required: false
        type: string
        default: "24"

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: ${{ inputs.node-version }}
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint --if-present
      - run: npm test

  deploy:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    concurrency:
      group: deploy-${{ inputs.service }}
      cancel-in-progress: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh "$GITHUB_SHA"
        env:
          SERVICE: ${{ inputs.service }}

# .github/workflows/deliver.yml (in the taskflow-reminders repository)
name: Deliver
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  pipeline:
    uses: example/platform-workflows/.github/workflows/node-service.yml@v1
    with:
      service: taskflow-reminders
    secrets: inherit

A reusable workflow is declared with on: workflow_call and referenced as {owner}/{repo}/.github/workflows/{filename}@{ref}. Pinning to a tag such as v1 lets the platform team ship compatible improvements to every service at once; GitHub's documentation notes that a commit SHA is the safest reference if you need exact reproducibility. secrets: inherit passes the caller's secrets through, including environment secrets for the production environment. The deploy job runs only on main, so pull requests get tests but never deploy.

docs.title: Check every repository against the golden path
docs.text:
A small "golden state" check, in the spirit of Spotify's, shows each team where it stands:

// scripts/golden-state.js: check service repositories against the golden path
// Usage: node scripts/golden-state.js <repo dir> [<repo dir> ...]
import { existsSync, readFileSync, readdirSync } from "node:fs";
import { basename, join } from "node:path";

const read = (dir, file) => (existsSync(join(dir, file)) ? readFileSync(join(dir, file), "utf8") : "");
const workflows = (dir) => {
  const wf = join(dir, ".github", "workflows");
  return existsSync(wf) ? readdirSync(wf).map((f) => readFileSync(join(wf, f), "utf8")).join("\n") : "";
};

const checks = [
  ["catalog entry with an owner", (d) => /^\s+owner:\s*\S+/m.test(read(d, "catalog-info.yaml"))],
  ["CODEOWNERS", (d) => existsSync(join(d, ".github", "CODEOWNERS"))],
  ["Node.js 24", (d) => read(d, ".nvmrc").trim() === "24"],
  ["platform pipeline", (d) => /uses: example\/platform-workflows\/\.github\/workflows\/node-service\.yml@/.test(workflows(d))],
  ["SLO document", (d) => existsSync(join(d, "docs", "slo"))],
  ["runbook link", (d) => /runbook/i.test(read(d, "README.md"))],
];

let missing = 0;
for (const dir of process.argv.slice(2)) {
  const failed = checks.filter(([, test]) => !test(dir)).map(([name]) => name);
  missing += failed.length;
  const score = `${checks.length - failed.length}/${checks.length}`;
  console.log(`${basename(dir).padEnd(20)} ${score}${failed.length ? `  missing: ${failed.join(", ")}` : ""}`);
}
process.exitCode = missing ? 1 : 0;

Run against three checked-out repositories:

$ node scripts/golden-state.js repos/*
taskflow-api         6/6
taskflow-reminders   2/6  missing: catalog entry with an owner, CODEOWNERS, platform pipeline, runbook link
taskflow-web         4/6  missing: Node.js 24, SLO document

The reminders service, built before the golden path existed, has its own pipeline and no registered owner; the web app only needs a runtime upgrade and an SLO document. Publishing these results (on the portal or in a weekly summary) works better than mandates: teams see the gap, and the platform team learns which checks are hardest to meet and makes those steps easier. The script exits with a non-zero code when anything is missing, so it can also run in CI as a warning.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start from user research: map the journeys developers struggle with most, and fix the most common one first.
  • Treat the platform as a product with an owner, a roadmap, support, and published measures.
  • Make the golden path the easiest path, and keep it optional; earn adoption instead of mandating it.
  • Prefer managed services and existing tools; build only the thin layer of interfaces and defaults that is specific to your organization.
  • Offer self-service through APIs first, with portals and CLIs on top.
  • Put ownership in the catalog from day one: every component has an owning team.
  • Encode best practices in templates and shared workflows, and version them so improvements reach every service.
  • Measure delivery outcomes and developer experience together, and expect a J-curve.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The new portal launched and almost nobody uses it. Detect: low weekly active users and few templates run after the launch announcement. Cause: "build it and they will come": features chosen without user research, solving problems teams do not have. Fix: interview teams, pick the most painful journey, ship a minimal golden path for it, and measure task success.
  • The platform team's backlog is all provisioning tickets. Detect: most work items are "create X for team Y" and requests wait days. Cause: ticket-ops instead of self-service. Fix: automate the three most frequent requests behind an API or template, then measure time from request to use.
  • Throughput dropped after everyone moved to the platform. Detect: lead time and deployment frequency fell after a mandated migration, while developer surveys report more waiting. Cause: extra handoffs and a path that does not fit some teams, the pattern DORA's 2024 data showed for exclusive, mandatory use. Fix: remove the mandate, make the path composable, and find where changes now wait in the new pipeline.
  • The catalog says one thing and reality another. Detect: owners listed in the catalog no longer exist; services in production are missing. Cause: catalog entries maintained by hand in a central file. Fix: keep catalog-info.yaml in each repository, register through templates, and add a golden-state check for a valid owner.
  • A security fix takes months to reach every service. Detect: weeks after a vulnerable base image is fixed, many services still run it. Cause: each team copied the pipeline instead of calling a shared one. Fix: move common steps into a versioned reusable workflow and track which services use which version.
  • The self-hosted portal became a maintenance burden. Detect: the portal is several versions behind and plugin upgrades keep breaking; nobody is on call for it. Cause: a framework adopted without the central owning team its own guide calls for. Fix: staff it as a product, cut it back to the catalog and one template, or move to a managed option.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Platform engineering: Building internal platforms as products that make software delivery self-service.
  • Internal developer platform (IDP): The shared tools, services, and golden paths a platform team provides.
  • Developer portal: The user interface to the platform, often built on Backstage: catalog, templates, docs.
  • Golden path: The opinionated and supported way to build a common kind of software.
  • Paved road: Netflix's term for its supported, recommended set of tools and practices.
  • Thinnest viable platform: The smallest platform that makes teams faster.
  • Self-service: Users get capabilities on demand, without tickets or waiting for another team.
  • Software catalog: A registry of components, APIs, resources, systems, and their owners.
  • Software template: A scaffolding definition that creates new projects with built-in best practices.
  • Reusable workflow: A GitHub Actions workflow with on: workflow_call that other workflows can call.
  • Golden state: A list of checks showing whether a system follows the golden path.
  • Ticket-ops: A platform team that fulfills requests manually instead of offering self-service.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Equating "platform" with Kubernetes, or with a developer portal.
  • Building a platform before several teams share the same need.
  • Mandating adoption instead of making the platform clearly better.
  • Building capabilities that managed services already provide.
  • Treating Backstage as a product you install rather than a framework that needs a team.
  • Measuring the platform by features shipped rather than by users' outcomes.
  • Allowing the golden path to become a golden cage with no exits.
  • Keeping the catalog in a central spreadsheet instead of in each repository.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare the DORA, CNCF, and Bottcher definitions of a platform. What do they all agree on?
  2. Explain golden paths and paved roads. Why are both described as supported but not mandatory?
  3. A platform team receives 60 environment requests a month at 30 minutes each. How many hours a month does that cost, and what changes with self-service? (30 hours a month of platform time; with self-service that time goes to improving the path instead, and teams stop waiting in a queue.)
  4. Name Backstage's main features and its core catalog entities. What does spec.owner add?
  5. What does DORA mean by a "minimum viable platform", and which anti-patterns does it warn about?
  6. DORA's 2024 report found platform users more productive but with lower throughput and stability. Give two plausible causes and how you would check them.
  7. Which measures would you use to show that a platform succeeded, and why include developer surveys as well as delivery metrics?
  8. A startup with two product teams wants to adopt Backstage. Using the cost drivers in this lesson, what would you advise instead, and when would you revisit the decision?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• DORA: Platform engineering
  • CNCF TAG App Delivery: Platforms White Paper and Platform Engineering Maturity Model
  • Backstage: What is Backstage? and Writing templates
  • Spotify: How We Use Golden Paths
  • GitHub Docs: Reuse workflows
  • Next: DevOps fundamentals interview questions and answers. Back to the DevOps fundamentals overview.

docs.title: Team Practices and Ownership
docs.text:
The culture behind DevOps lives in a handful of team habits: who owns a service, how on-call is shared, how failures are discussed, how repetitive work gets removed, how knowledge and decisions are written down, how changes are approved, and how work is integrated. None of these needs a new tool. Each needs an explicit agreement and someone who keeps it alive.

This lesson covers "you build it, you run it" and what owning a service really includes, on-call rotations that people can sustain, blameless culture, toil reduction as a routine, documentation and runbooks, architecture decision records, change approval without a heavyweight change advisory board, and trunk-based habits. The examples show how TaskFlow's tasks team encodes these habits in its repository.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Tools copy easily; habits do not. Two teams can run the same pipeline and dashboards with opposite results: one deploys daily and learns from every incident, the other deploys monthly and hides its mistakes. The difference is how the people work together. DORA's research ties these habits to outcomes: generative, high-trust culture predicts software delivery and organizational performance; documentation quality amplifies the benefit of every technical practice studied; and external change approval slows delivery without making it safer.

Ownership also has a cost. Developers who run their services lose sleep when alerts are noisy, rotations are too small, or nobody budgets time for operational work. The practices in this lesson are what make ownership sustainable instead of a fast route to burnout.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon, 2006. In A Conversation with Werner Vogels (ACM Queue, Volume 4, issue 4), Amazon's CTO described teams that are "completely responsible for the service": "Giving developers operational responsibilities has greatly enhanced the quality of the services ... You build it, you run it." AWS's Prescriptive Guidance still cites the interview as the source of the phrase.
  • Netflix, 2018. The post Full Cycle Developers at Netflix explains "operate what you build": the team that develops a system is also responsible for operating and supporting it, supported by centralized teams that build shared tools, and staffed "with enough headroom" for operations. Without that, the authors warn, "teams risk overload and burnout."
  • Google SRE on-call. The SRE book chapter Being On-Call caps on-call at 25% of an SRE's time, derives a minimum of eight engineers for a single-site 24/7 rotation (six per site for two sites), and offers time off in lieu or cash compensation, capped to limit any one person's load.
  • DORA on change approval. DORA's streamlining change approval capability, based on the 2019 State of DevOps Report, found that approval by external bodies such as a change advisory board (CAB) has a negative impact on software delivery performance, and that "no evidence was found to support the hypothesis that a more formal, external review process was associated with lower change fail rates."
  • Architecture decision records. Michael Nygard's 2011 post Documenting Architecture Decisions introduced short, numbered records with a title, context, decision, status, and consequences, kept in the repository.

Popular tools and providers: PagerDuty and incident.io for rotations and paging; GitHub CODEOWNERS, rulesets, and deployment environments for ownership and approvals; Markdown in the repository with MkDocs or Backstage TechDocs for documentation; and adr-tools or a plain docs/adr/ folder for decision records.

docs.title: You build it, you run it
docs.text:
Vogels described the old model precisely: "you take your software to the wall that separates development and operations, and throw it over and then forget about it. Not at Amazon. You build it, you run it. This brings developers into contact with the day-to-day operation of their software." The point is the feedback loop. A team that is paged for its own bugs fixes the causes; a team that is never paged keeps producing them.

The model has prerequisites, and Netflix's post lists them candidly: tooling that makes deploying, monitoring, and rolling back easy, training for developers who have never operated software, partnerships with central teams, and enough people that someone can take operational work without the team's roadmap collapsing. Team Topologies describes the same arrangement as stream-aligned teams supported by platform and enabling teams (see DevOps, SRE, and platform engineering).

docs.title: What owning a service includes
docs.text:
Ownership is a list of things someone must answer for, not a name in a wiki. A useful test: if this service failed at 3 a.m., is it obvious who is paged, what they look at first, how they roll back, and who decided the design they are debugging?

Area The owning team provides Kept where Code and reviews Reviewers for every change; CODEOWNERS for paths that need specialist review .github/CODEOWNERS Delivery One automated path to production, including rollback .github/workflows/ Reliability SLOs, dashboards, and burn-rate alerts docs/slo/, alert rules in the repository On-call A rotation, escalation policy, and handoff notes Paging tool, linked from the README Knowledge README, runbooks, ADRs docs/ in the repository Dependencies Known consumers and providers, contracts, behavior when a dependency fails Service catalog, API specs Cost and capacity Budget alerts, load tests before big launches Dashboards, docs/capacity.md

docs.title: On-call that people can sustain
docs.text:
The SRE book's numbers are a good default even outside Google. At most 25% of time on call; with a primary and a secondary on every weekly shift, that needs at least eight people in a single-site rotation. It also targets at most two incidents per 8 to 12-hour shift, so each one can be handled properly and followed by a postmortem, and treats "operational underload" as a risk too: engineers who are on call too rarely lose touch with production.

Fairness is more than equal shift counts. Track, per person and per quarter:

Signal Why it matters Healthy direction Pages per shift Load on the responder At most two incidents per shift Pages outside working hours Sleep and recovery Falling over time Share of pages handled by the busiest person Hidden unfairness, often caused by one noisy alert Close to an even share Actionable rate Alert quality Most pages lead to action Swaps and uncovered shifts Whether the rotation still works for people Rare, and easy to arrange

Fair rotations also need compensation or time off after bad nights, a written swap and holiday policy, and handoffs between shifts. The mechanics of routing, escalation, and handoff notes are covered in alerting and on-call.

docs.title: Blameless culture
docs.text:
When an engineer runs a command that deletes data, two responses are possible: find out who did it and punish them, or find out why the system made that action easy and its effects so large. The SRE Workbook states the second view as "Accidents Are Normal": accidents result "from missing safeguards for when things inevitably go wrong", and punishing the person "creates incentives to confuse issues, hide the truth, and blame others."

DORA's generative organizational culture capability builds on Ron Westrum's typology of how organizations handle information:

Pathological Bureaucratic Generative Orientation Power Rules Performance Messengers (people who bring bad news) Punished Neglected Trained Failure leads to Scapegoating Justice Inquiry Novelty Crushed Leads to problems Implemented

DORA also cites a large two-year study at Google that found high performing teams need psychological safety, meaningful work, and clarity. In practice, blameless culture shows up as small, consistent habits:

  • Postmortem timelines describe actions and the information available at the time, never "X failed to".
  • Reviews ask "what made this action make sense?" and "what would have stopped it?", not "who?".
  • Leaders thank people for reporting near misses and their own mistakes.
  • Action items change systems: guardrails, defaults, tests, alerts.
  • Accountability remains: owners complete the action items.

How to run the incident itself and write the postmortem is covered in incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: Toil reduction as a routine
docs.text:
Toil, as defined in DevOps, SRE, and platform engineering, grows quietly unless a team budgets against it. Habits that work:

  • Log it. Keep a running list of manual operational tasks with how often they occur and how long they take.
  • Budget for it. Reserve a fixed share of each iteration (the TaskFlow team's working agreement uses 20%) for automation and reliability work, and protect it.
  • Rank by payback. Hours to automate divided by hours saved per week.
  • Prefer elimination to automation. A worker that gets stuck needs a fix, not a faster restart script.
  • Close the loop. Review the toil log in retrospectives and celebrate removed work, not heroic effort.

docs.title: Documentation and runbooks
docs.text:
DORA's documentation quality capability reports "a clear link between documentation quality and organizational performance", and found documentation quality driving the implementation of every technical practice it studied. In its 2022 data, for example, trunk-based development lifted organizational performance by 36% for teams with below-average documentation and by 1525% for teams with above-average documentation.

Docs that stay correct share a few properties:

  • Kept next to the code (docs/ in the service repository) and changed in the same pull request as the behavior they describe.
  • Small and specific: a README that answers "what is this, who owns it, how do I run it locally, how is it deployed, where are the dashboards and runbooks"; separate runbooks per alert.
  • Owned and reviewed: stale documentation is a bug, filed and fixed like any other.
  • Written for the reader under pressure: runbooks start with what the alert means and the safest mitigation, then the diagnosis.

The structure of an alert runbook is described in alerting and on-call.

docs.title: Architecture decision records
docs.text:
Nygard's argument is that a new team member who does not know why a decision was made can only "blindly accept" or "blindly change" it, and both are dangerous. An architecture decision record (ADR) captures one "architecturally significant" decision in a page or two:

Section Content Title A short noun phrase, numbered: "ADR 7: Send reminders from a queue worker" Context The forces at play, stated as facts, including the ones in tension Decision "We will ..." in full sentences Status Proposed, accepted, deprecated, or superseded (with a link to the replacement) Consequences All the results, positive, negative, and neutral

ADRs are numbered sequentially and never reused; a reversed decision is kept and marked superseded, because knowing what was decided before is still useful. They live in the repository, so they are reviewed like code and travel with it. For architecture decision-making in general, see architecture fundamentals.

docs.title: Change approval without a heavyweight CAB
docs.text:
Change control exists for good reasons: reduce the risk of changes and satisfy requirements such as segregation of duties ("changes must be approved by someone other than the author"). DORA's research found that the traditional way of meeting those goals, approval by a CAB or senior manager outside the team, has a negative impact on software delivery performance and no measurable benefit for change fail rate. It slows delivery, which leads to "the release of larger batches less frequently", which raises the risk of each release.

DORA's recommended alternative:

  • Peer review for segregation of duties, with reviews and approvals recorded in the development platform.
  • Automation to catch bad changes early: continuous testing, continuous integration, monitoring, and observability.
  • Risk-based scrutiny instead of "treating all changes equally": detect and flag high-risk changes so they get additional review.
  • One fast path for everything, so that "you can use it to make emergency changes too."
  • A new role for the CAB: coordinating between teams, improving the process, and making business trade-offs, rather than reviewing code.

Jez Humble called the spreadsheet-and-meeting version of change control "risk management theatre". John Willis's 2010 post gives the opposite example, from a bank using ITIL: services that need no change approval are provisioned automatically in under five minutes, and only the rest wait for approval. The audit trail an auditor needs (who reviewed, which checks passed, who approved the production deployment) is a by-product of the pipeline. The automated security checks are covered in security in the delivery pipeline, and what auditors expect as evidence in compliance and audit readiness.

docs.title: Trunk-based culture
docs.text: Daily integration is a team habit before it is a branching model. DORA's trunk-based development capability lists the conditions: three or fewer active branches, merging to trunk at least once a day, and no code freezes or integration phases. The habits that make it work are social: small pull requests, reviews that start within hours, a red main branch treated as everyone's top priority, and unfinished work merged behind flags. The strategies themselves are compared in branching strategies.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Practice Use when Adapt or avoid when You build it, you run it The team changes the service and can be given tools and time to operate it The team cannot deploy or roll back itself yet; fix that first, with platform help Team-owned on-call The rotation has enough people (about eight for one site) or shares a rotation with a neighbor team Two or three people would be on call every other week; merge rotations or cover business hours only Blameless postmortems Always, for incidents and near misses Never "blameless" for deliberate malicious acts; those follow security and HR processes ADRs Decisions that affect structure, dependencies, interfaces, or quality attributes Small, easily reversed choices; a code comment is enough Peer review instead of CAB Changes flow through an automated pipeline with an audit trail Regulated contexts may still need a named approver: put that approval in the pipeline, not a meeting Risk-based extra review Paths with real blast radius: migrations, authentication, infrastructure Everything; adding reviewers everywhere recreates the CAB

docs.title: Ownership and specialist review with CODEOWNERS
docs.text:
# .github/CODEOWNERS: the last matching pattern takes precedence
*                    @example/tasks-team
/migrations/         @example/data-reliability
/infra/              @example/platform-team
/src/auth/           @example/security-champions
/docs/adr/           @example/tasks-team @example/architecture-guild

With the branch rule "require review from code owners" enabled on main, an ordinary pull request needs an approval from the tasks team, while a change under migrations/ needs one from the data reliability team instead. The file can live in .github/, the repository root, or docs/, and code owners are only requested when the file is on the pull request's base branch.

docs.title: Extra approval only for risky changes
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deliver.yml (excerpt): extra approval only for risky paths
jobs:
  classify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
