docs.title: Compliance and Audit Readiness
docs.text:
Compliance means showing, to customers, auditors, and regulators, that agreed security and privacy controls exist and keep working. For an engineering team it is mostly operational: who can access production, whether data is encrypted, what is logged and for how long, how changes are reviewed, how data is deleted, and whether you can prove all of it for a whole audit period. This lesson covers what SOC 2, ISO/IEC 27001, HIPAA, GDPR, and PCI DSS ask of operations, the shared responsibility model, encryption at rest and in transit, audit logs, access reviews, evidence collection, data retention and deletion, business associate agreements for health data, and policy as code.

It builds on the previous lessons: least privilege and access reviews in identity and access management, and patch deadlines in vulnerability and patch management.

Not legal advice

This page summarizes frameworks at a high level for engineers. Which laws and standards apply to you, and what they require in your case, depends on your contracts, data, and jurisdictions, and the texts change: proposals to amend the GDPR and the HIPAA Security Rule, and draft 2027 SOC 2 criteria, were all pending at the time of writing. Confirm with your legal, privacy, or compliance owner and the official texts linked below.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Customers increasingly ask for a SOC 2 report or an ISO/IEC 27001 certificate before they sign, hospitals need a business associate agreement before they share health data, and card brands require PCI DSS compliance before you touch card numbers. Regulators can fine heavily: GDPR Article 83 allows fines of up to EUR 20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover for the most serious infringements.

For engineers, the expensive part is not the controls themselves (most are good practice anyway) but proving them after the fact. Teams that build evidence into their pipelines, such as reviewed pull requests, policy checks, locked audit logs, and recorded access reviews, pass audits with an export. Teams that do not spend weeks assembling screenshots and discover that a control silently stopped working months ago.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• AICPA SOC 2. The AICPA describes SOC 2 as a report on controls at a service organization relevant to security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, or privacy, the five Trust Services Criteria categories. A Type 1 report covers the design of controls at a point in time; a Type 2 report also covers how they operated over a period. Reports use the 2017 Trust Services Criteria (with revised points of focus, 2022); in October 2026 the AICPA published exposure drafts of proposed 2027 criteria, which are not yet in effect.
  • ISO/IEC 27001:2022. The current edition of ISO/IEC 27001 specifies requirements for an information security management system (ISMS); Amendment 1:2024 added climate action changes to the context clauses. Its Annex A lists 93 controls grouped into organizational, people, physical, and technological themes.
  • HHS and HIPAA. The US Department of Health and Human Services publishes the HIPAA Security Rule (administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic protected health information) and guidance on cloud computing, which explains that a cloud provider storing electronic PHI is a business associate even if it only stores encrypted data it cannot read.
  • GDPR. Regulation (EU) 2016/679, the General Data Protection Regulation on EUR-Lex, requires security appropriate to the risk (Article 32, which names encryption and pseudonymisation), breach notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours where feasible (Article 33), and erasure on request when its conditions are met (Article 17).
  • PCI Security Standards Council. The Council's announcement Just Published: PCI DSS v4.0.1 describes the June 2024 limited revision of PCI DSS v4.0, which clarified requirements without adding or removing any. PCI DSS v4.0 was retired at the end of 2024, so v4.0.1 is the version assessments use.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Artifact, AWS Config conformance packs, AWS Security Hub CSPM, AWS Audit Manager, CloudTrail, Azure Policy and Microsoft Defender for Cloud regulatory compliance, Google Cloud Audit Logs and Security Command Center, Open Policy Agent, Checkov, Kyverno, and compliance automation platforms such as Vanta, Drata, and Secureframe.

docs.title: What each framework asks of operations
docs.text:
Framework What it is Who it applies to What it asks of operations (high level) SOC 2 An attestation report by a CPA firm against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria Service organizations whose customers ask for it (common for B2B SaaS) Controls for access, change management, monitoring, incident response, vendor management, and backups, with evidence that they operated through the audit period (Type 2) ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A certifiable standard for an information security management system Any organization that wants certification A risk assessment, a Statement of Applicability choosing Annex A controls, internal audits, management review, and continual improvement, checked by surveillance audits HIPAA US law and regulations for protected health information Covered entities (health plans, clearinghouses, most providers) and their business associates Risk analysis, access control, audit controls, integrity, authentication, transmission security, contingency plans, BAAs, breach notification, documentation kept 6 years GDPR EU regulation on personal data Organizations processing personal data of people in the EU, under its territorial rules Security of processing, data protection by design, records of processing, processor contracts, data subject rights such as access and erasure, breach notification within 72 hours PCI DSS v4.0.1 An industry standard from the PCI Security Standards Council Anyone who stores, processes, or transmits payment card account data Network controls, secure configuration, protected stored card data, strong cryptography in transit, patching, need-to-know access, MFA, logging, regular testing

A few concrete operational numbers that come up constantly:

  • PCI DSS 10.5.1: keep audit log history for at least 12 months, with at least the most recent three months immediately available for analysis.
  • PCI DSS 7.2.4: review all user accounts and their access privileges at least once every six months.
  • PCI DSS 6.3.3: install critical-severity security patches within one month of release.
  • HIPAA: retain required Security Rule documentation for six years. Notify affected individuals of a breach of unsecured PHI without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 days after discovery.
  • GDPR Article 12(3): answer data subject requests (such as erasure) without undue delay and within one month, extendable by two further months where necessary.

In January 2025 HHS published a proposed rule to update the HIPAA Security Rule (for example, making encryption and multi-factor authentication required rather than "addressable"). At the time of writing it was still a proposal, and the current rule remains in force; check HHS for its status.

docs.title: Shared responsibility
docs.text:
A cloud provider's certifications cover its side of the line: the AWS shared responsibility model calls it security of the cloud, while the customer is responsible for security in the cloud. Practically:

  • Download the provider's reports (AWS Artifact, the Microsoft Service Trust Portal, Google's compliance reports manager) and give them to your auditor for the inherited controls, such as physical security.
  • Everything you configure is yours to prove: bucket policies, security groups, IAM, encryption settings, logging, backups, and your application's access control.
  • Each vendor that handles regulated data for you adds its own line and its own contract (a data processing agreement under GDPR, a BAA under HIPAA).

docs.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
docs.text:
At rest In transit What Disks, databases, object storage, backups, snapshots, logs Browser to edge, edge to load balancer, service to service, service to database How Provider-managed encryption on by default, or customer-managed keys in a KMS with envelope encryption TLS 1.2 or later (1.3 preferred), HSTS for websites, TLS to databases and caches, mTLS in a service mesh What auditors check Encryption enabled everywhere, who can use the keys, key rotation, encrypted backups No plaintext protocols, current TLS versions and ciphers, certificates managed and renewed Framework hooks GDPR Art. 32, HIPAA addressable encryption, PCI DSS requirement 3, ISO A.8.24 GDPR Art. 32, HIPAA transmission security, PCI DSS requirement 4, ISO A.8.24

Encryption at rest in the cloud mostly protects against lost media and some insider paths; it does not protect against a stolen credential that can read the data through the API. That is why key policies matter: customer-managed keys let you separate who can administer data from who can decrypt it, and every decryption is logged. Under HIPAA, data encrypted consistently with HHS guidance counts as "secured", which affects whether a lost device or leaked file is a reportable breach. For secrets and signing keys see secrets management; for TLS see TLS and certificate fundamentals and network security in the cloud.

docs.title: Audit logs
docs.text:
Every framework asks for a record of who did what, when, and from where, protected from tampering and kept long enough to investigate. Collecting is not enough: the HIPAA Security Rule, for example, requires regularly reviewing records of information system activity such as audit logs and access reports, so pair logs with alerts and a review routine.

  • AWS CloudTrail records API calls. Event history keeps 90 days of management events per Region for free; for anything longer, create a multi-Region trail (an organization trail for all accounts) that delivers to an S3 bucket, ideally in a separate log-archive account. Turn on log file integrity validation, which writes signed hourly digest files that prove whether log files were modified or deleted, and protect the bucket with S3 Object Lock so not even an administrator can delete logs early. Data events (such as S3 object reads) are not recorded by default and cost extra; enable them for buckets holding regulated data.
  • Google Cloud Audit Logs: Admin Activity logs are always written; Data Access logs, except for BigQuery, are disabled by default and must be enabled for services holding sensitive data.
  • Azure: the Activity log records control-plane operations and keeps them for 90 days; export it with diagnostic settings for longer retention, alongside Microsoft Entra ID sign-in and audit logs.
  • Application audit logs are your responsibility: who viewed which patient record, who exported which report, who changed whose role. Log identifiers, not the sensitive data itself, and treat these logs as regulated data (see structured logging).

docs.title: Access reviews
docs.text: Access reviews confirm, on a fixed cadence, that every person and workload still needs the access it has. The mechanics (identity center exports, unused-access findings, one ticket per removal) are covered in identity and access management. For compliance, what matters is that the review happens on schedule (PCI DSS sets a maximum of six months; quarterly is common for production), that a named owner signs off, and that every removal is recorded. A review nobody can show did not happen.

docs.title: Evidence collection
docs.text:
Auditors usually work with a population and samples: "list every production change in the period", then "for these 25, show the approval, the tests, and the deploy". Design so that the answer is a query:

  • One control, many frameworks. Map each internal control (such as "production changes are reviewed") to every framework it satisfies, and collect its evidence once.
  • Evidence from systems, not people: pull request approvals and branch protection settings, CI logs, Terraform plans and policy results, cloud configuration rule results, access review tickets, backup and restore test reports, incident postmortems, training records.
  • Timestamped and append-only: store exports in a bucket with versioning or Object Lock so evidence cannot be edited afterwards.
  • Continuous, not annual: a control that silently broke in month two fails a Type 2 audit in month twelve. Alert when a check fails.

docs.title: Data retention and deletion
docs.text:
GDPR's storage limitation principle (Article 5) and most customer contracts require that personal data is kept no longer than needed, and deleted when a valid erasure request arrives. Make it operational:

  • A retention schedule: for each data type, how long, why (contract, law, legitimate need), and the mechanism that enforces it.
  • Mechanisms, not intentions: MongoDB TTL indexes, S3 lifecycle rules, log group retention settings, and scheduled jobs.
  • Erasure across copies: primary databases, search indexes, caches, analytics, data warehouses, file storage, and processors (email and support tools). Keep a record that the erasure happened without keeping the data.
  • Backups: editing backups is impractical; common practice is short backup retention, encrypted backups, and re-applying completed erasures after any restore. Write that down in your policy.
  • Exceptions: legal holds and legal obligations (such as accounting records) override deletion for specific data; restrict access to it.
  • Crypto-shredding: encrypting each tenant's data with its own key lets you make it unreadable everywhere, including backups, by destroying the key.

docs.title: BAAs for health data
docs.text:
Under HIPAA, a covered entity (or a business associate) must have a business associate agreement with any vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on its behalf. HHS publishes sample BAA provisions. For cloud providers, rely only on what their official pages state:

  • AWS offers a Business Associate Addendum that customers review and accept in AWS Artifact, and its HIPAA page says to process, store, and transmit PHI only in HIPAA-eligible services.
  • Microsoft states on its Azure HIPAA page that the HIPAA BAA is available by default to covered entities and business associates through the Microsoft Product Terms and Data Protection Addendum, for in-scope services.
  • Google Cloud states on its HIPAA page that it enters into BAAs as necessary, covering its infrastructure and the listed products, and that unsupported services should not be used for PHI.

For every other vendor in the data path (error tracking, email, SMS, analytics, support desks), check its official documentation; if it does not offer a BAA, PHI must not reach it. A BAA is necessary but not sufficient: Microsoft's page notes that using a BAA-covered service does not by itself make your solution compliant.

docs.title: Policy as code
docs.text:
Policy as code turns rules such as "no public buckets" or "databases are encrypted" into automated checks:

  • Before deploy: check Terraform plans with Open Policy Agent, Checkov, or Trivy in pull requests (see IaC fundamentals and Terraform in practice).
  • In the cloud: AWS Config rules and conformance packs, Azure Policy, and Google Cloud organization policies evaluate or block the live configuration, including changes made outside Terraform.
  • In Kubernetes: admission controllers such as Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper reject non-compliant workloads.
  • As evidence: every evaluation is timestamped, which is exactly what a Type 2 auditor wants to sample.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Typical starting point B2B SaaS selling to mid-size and enterprise customers in the US SOC 2 Type 1, then Type 2 Customers in Europe or regulated industries asking for certification ISO/IEC 27001 Handling PHI for US covered entities HIPAA safeguards, BAAs with every vendor in the PHI path Personal data of people in the EU GDPR: records of processing, DPAs, rights handling, breach process Taking card payments PCI DSS; minimize scope with a hosted payment page or tokenization so card numbers never touch your servers Early-stage product with no regulated data and no customer demand Good security practice and a short security page; start formal programs when customers or data require them

Avoid buying a compliance tool before you have controls to measure, and avoid expanding scope: keeping card numbers or PHI out of systems that do not need them is the cheapest control there is.

docs.title: An audit trail that cannot be deleted
docs.text:
# audit-trail.tf: every API call in every Region, written to a write-once bucket
data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}
data "aws_region" "current" {}

locals {
  trail_name = "taskflow-audit"
  trail_arn  = "arn:aws:cloudtrail:${data.aws_region.current.region}:${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}:trail/${local.trail_name}"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "audit" {
  bucket              = "example-taskflow-audit-logs"
  object_lock_enabled = true # must be set when the bucket is created
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "audit" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.audit.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_object_lock_configuration" "audit" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.audit.id
  rule {
    default_retention {
      mode = "COMPLIANCE" # nobody, not even the root user, can delete or shorten it
      days = 400
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "audit" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.audit.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "cloudtrail_write" {
  statement {
    sid       = "CloudTrailAclCheck"
    actions   = ["s3:GetBucketAcl"]
    resources = [aws_s3_bucket.audit.arn]
    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "aws:SourceArn"
      values   = [local.trail_arn]
    }
  }

  statement {
    sid       = "CloudTrailWrite"
    actions   = ["s3:PutObject"]
    resources = ["${aws_s3_bucket.audit.arn}/AWSLogs/${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}/*"]
    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "s3:x-amz-acl"
      values   = ["bucket-owner-full-control"]
    }
    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "aws:SourceArn"
      values   = [local.trail_arn]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "audit" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.audit.id
  policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.cloudtrail_write.json
}

resource "aws_cloudtrail" "audit" {
  name                          = local.trail_name
  s3_bucket_name                = aws_s3_bucket.audit.id
  is_multi_region_trail         = true # one trail records every Region
  include_global_service_events = true # IAM, STS, and other global services
  enable_log_file_validation    = true # hourly signed digests prove nothing was altered

  depends_on = [aws_s3_bucket_policy.audit]
}

Four hundred days of compliance-mode retention covers PCI DSS's 12-month minimum with margin. In an AWS Organization, put this bucket in a dedicated log-archive account and make the trail an organization trail, so that workload accounts cannot touch it.

docs.title: Continuous configuration checks as evidence
docs.text:
# config-rules.tf: continuous checks that double as audit evidence
# (assumes an AWS Config recorder and delivery channel already exist in the account)
locals {
  managed_rules = {
    "cloudtrail-enabled"               = "CLOUD_TRAIL_ENABLED"
    "s3-bucket-versioning"             = "S3_BUCKET_VERSIONING_ENABLED"
    "s3-bucket-public-read-prohibited" = "S3_BUCKET_PUBLIC_READ_PROHIBITED"
    "ebs-volumes-encrypted"            = "ENCRYPTED_VOLUMES"
    "rds-storage-encrypted"            = "RDS_STORAGE_ENCRYPTED"
    "iam-user-mfa-enabled"             = "IAM_USER_MFA_ENABLED"
  }
}

resource "aws_config_config_rule" "managed" {
  for_each = local.managed_rules

  name = each.key
  source {
    owner             = "AWS"
    source_identifier = each.value
  }
}

Each rule evaluates resources continuously and keeps a compliance history, so "were all volumes encrypted during the audit period?" becomes a report instead of a guess. Note that some rule names differ from their identifiers (cloudtrail-enabled is CLOUD_TRAIL_ENABLED). There is no rule for default S3 encryption here: since January 2023 Amazon S3 encrypts all new objects with SSE-S3 by default. Both files validate with Terraform 1.17.2 and AWS provider 6.73.0.

docs.title: Guardrails on every Terraform plan with Open Policy Agent
docs.text:
# policy/terraform.rego: guardrails checked against `terraform show -json` output
package terraform.guardrails

# Changes that create or update something (ignore deletes and no-ops)
changes contains rc if {
    some rc in input.resource_changes
    some action in rc.change.actions
    action in {"create", "update"}
}

deny contains msg if {
    some rc in changes
    rc.type == "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block"
    some setting in ["block_public_acls", "block_public_policy", "ignore_public_acls", "restrict_public_buckets"]
    rc.change.after[setting] != true
    msg := sprintf("%s: %s must be true", [rc.address, setting])
}

deny contains msg if {
    some rc in changes
    rc.type == "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule"
    rc.change.after.cidr_ipv4 == "0.0.0.0/0"
    rc.change.after.from_port != 443
    msg := sprintf("%s: only port 443 may be open to the internet", [rc.address])
}

deny contains msg if {
    some rc in changes
    rc.type == "aws_db_instance"
    not rc.change.after.storage_encrypted
    msg := sprintf("%s: database storage must be encrypted", [rc.address])
}

# policy/terraform_test.rego: unit tests for the guardrails (run with `opa test policy/`)
package terraform.guardrails_test

import data.terraform.guardrails

test_open_ssh_is_denied if {
    count(guardrails.deny) == 1 with input as {"resource_changes": [{
        "address": "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.ssh",
        "type": "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule",
        "change": {"actions": ["create"], "after": {"cidr_ipv4": "0.0.0.0/0", "from_port": 22}},
    }]}
}

test_unencrypted_database_is_denied if {
    count(guardrails.deny) == 1 with input as {"resource_changes": [{
        "address": "aws_db_instance.main",
        "type": "aws_db_instance",
        "change": {"actions": ["create"], "after": {"storage_encrypted": false}},
    }]}
}

terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
opa test policy/
opa eval --fail-defined --format pretty \
  --data policy/terraform.rego --input plan.json "data.terraform.guardrails.deny[msg]"

Run against a plan that adds a public access block with block_public_acls = false and an SSH rule open to 0.0.0.0/0, the evaluation prints:

[
  "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.exports: block_public_acls must be true",
  "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule.ssh_anywhere: only port 443 may be open to the internet"
]

--fail-defined makes the command exit with code 1 when any deny message exists, so it can gate a pull request. The policy uses the Rego v1 syntax of OPA 1.x (contains and if), passes opa fmt, and was tested with OPA 1.22.4 against a real terraform show -json plan. Conftest, a CLI built on OPA for testing configuration files, accepts the same syntax if you prefer it in CI.

docs.title: Keeping the policy run as evidence in CI
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/terraform-policy.yml (excerpt)
jobs:
  policy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write
    defaults:
      run:
        working-directory: infra/envs/prod
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@dfe3c3f87815947d99a8997f908cb6525fc44e9e # v4.0.1
        with:
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-terraform-plan
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -lock=false -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform show -json tfplan > plan.json
      - name: Install OPA
        run: |
          curl -fsSL -o /usr/local/bin/opa \
            https://github.com/open-policy-agent/opa/releases/download/v1.22.4/opa_linux_amd64_static
          chmod +x /usr/local/bin/opa
      - name: Evaluate guardrails
        run: |
          opa eval --format pretty --data ../../../policy/terraform.rego --input plan.json \
            "data.terraform.guardrails.deny" | tee policy-result.txt
          opa eval --fail-defined --format pretty --data ../../../policy/terraform.rego \
            --input plan.json "data.terraform.guardrails.deny[msg]" > /dev/null
      - if: always()
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: policy-evidence-${{ github.sha }}
          path: infra/envs/prod/policy-result.txt

The uploaded result ties a commit to the policies it passed. Artifact storage has its own retention limits, so for audit periods copy the results to the evidence bucket as well.

docs.title: Retention by TTL and an erasure job
docs.text:
// scripts/retention-indexes.js: let MongoDB delete expiring data on its own
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI);
await client.connect();
const db = client.db();

// Sessions disappear 30 days after the user was last seen
await db.collection("sessions").createIndex(
  { lastSeenAt: 1 },
  { expireAfterSeconds: 60 * 60 * 24 * 30, name: "ttl_sessions_30d" },
);

// Password reset tokens live for one hour
await db.collection("passwordResets").createIndex(
  { createdAt: 1 },
  { expireAfterSeconds: 60 * 60, name: "ttl_password_resets_1h" },
);

await client.close();

// src/privacy/erase-user.js: one job deletes a user's personal data everywhere we hold it
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

export async function eraseUser(db, userId, { searchIndex, emailProvider }) {
  const user = await db.collection("users").findOne({ _id: userId });
  if (!user) return { status: "not_found" };

  await db.collection("tasks").deleteMany({ ownerId: userId });
  await db.collection("comments").deleteMany({ authorId: userId });
  await db.collection("sessions").deleteMany({ userId });
  await searchIndex.deleteByOwner(userId);           // copies outside MongoDB
  await emailProvider.deleteContact(user.email);      // processors too

  // Invoices stay (legal obligation); detach them from the person's profile
  await db.collection("invoices").updateMany(
    { userId },
    { $set: { customerName: "erased", customerEmail: null } },
  );

  await db.collection("users").deleteOne({ _id: userId });

  // Record that the erasure happened, without keeping who it was
  await db.collection("erasures").insertOne({
    subject: createHash("sha256").update(String(userId)).digest("hex"),
    completedAt: new Date(),
  });
  return { status: "erased" };
}

A TTL index removes a document once its date field is older than expireAfterSeconds; MongoDB's background task runs about every minute, so expiry is not instant. The erasures collection lists the users to re-delete after any backup restore, and it is evidence that requests were handled on time. Whether invoices may keep a name depends on local accounting law; this is where your privacy owner decides, not the code.

docs.title: A retention schedule
docs.text: Data Retention Basis Mechanism Active account data While the account exists Contract Erasure job on account deletion Sessions 30 days after last use Security, legitimate need TTL index Application logs 90 days Operations, security Log retention setting; identifiers only Cloud audit logs 400 days PCI DSS 10.5.1, security investigations Object Lock on the audit bucket Backups 35 days Disaster recovery Backup retention policy; erasures re-applied on restore Invoices As required by accounting law Legal obligation Restricted access, scheduled deletion after the period Audit evidence Audit period plus one year Certification and attestation Versioned evidence bucket

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Map each internal control to every framework it satisfies, and collect its evidence once, automatically.
  • Know your side of the shared responsibility line, and keep the provider's reports for the rest.
  • Encrypt everything at rest and in transit by default; control and log who can use the keys.
  • Send audit logs from every account and Region to a separate, locked account with integrity validation, kept at least as long as your strictest framework requires.
  • Run access reviews on schedule with named owners, and record every removal.
  • Check policies on every Terraform plan and continuously in the cloud; alert when a check fails.
  • Write a retention schedule and enforce it with TTLs, lifecycle rules, and jobs; plan erasure across every copy, including processors and backups.
  • Sign BAAs or DPAs before regulated data reaches a vendor, and keep regulated data out of systems that do not need it.
  • Rehearse the breach process, including the 72-hour GDPR clock and HIPAA's 60-day limit.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The auditor asks for a year of change approvals and nobody can produce them. Detect: evidence requests take weeks; some changes have no linked review. Cause: direct pushes, console changes, and approvals in chat. Fix: branch protection with required reviews, deploys only from CI, and exports of pull request and pipeline records to the evidence store.
  • CloudTrail had gaps for weeks. Detect: the cloudtrail-enabled rule reports non-compliance; digest validation shows missing files. Cause: a trail stopped or a bucket policy changed. Fix: an organization trail managed in code, Object Lock, Config rules and alerts on logging changes.
  • A departed engineer still had production access during the audit period. Detect: the access review sample shows an active account weeks after their last day. Cause: offboarding not tied to the identity provider, or IAM users outside single sign-on. Fix: single sign-on with automatic deprovisioning, no IAM users for people, and recorded reviews.
  • A restore brought back users who had asked to be erased. Detect: a complaint from a person who requested erasure. Cause: backups restored without re-applying erasures. Fix: keep the erasure list and run it as part of every restore procedure.
  • PHI showed up in a third-party error tracker without a BAA. Detect: a search of error events finds patient names in payloads. Cause: full request bodies attached to error reports. Fix: scrub or allowlist fields before sending, sign a BAA if the vendor offers one or stop sending such data, and assess whether a breach notification is required.
  • Encryption was enabled, but the same role could administer and read everything. Detect: key policies grant broad decrypt access. Cause: default keys with permissive access. Fix: customer-managed keys with separated administration and usage permissions, and alerts on unusual decrypt activity.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• SOC 2 Type 1 / Type 2: attestation reports on the design of controls at a point in time / on design and operating effectiveness over a period.
  • Trust Services Criteria: the AICPA criteria for security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy.
  • ISMS: an information security management system, the subject of ISO/IEC 27001.
  • Statement of Applicability: the ISO/IEC 27001 document stating which Annex A controls apply and why.
  • PHI / ePHI: protected health information / in electronic form.
  • Covered entity / business associate: organizations HIPAA applies to directly / vendors handling PHI on their behalf.
  • BAA: a business associate agreement required between those parties.
  • Controller / processor: under GDPR, who decides why and how data is processed / who processes it on the controller's behalf.
  • DPA: a data processing agreement between controller and processor.
  • Cardholder data environment (CDE): the systems that store, process, or transmit card data, which PCI DSS scopes.
  • Shared responsibility model: the split of security duties between cloud provider and customer.
  • Evidence: records that show a control operated, collected for auditors.
  • Retention schedule: how long each type of data is kept, why, and how deletion is enforced.
  • Crypto-shredding: making data unreadable by destroying its encryption key.
  • Policy as code: compliance and security rules written as automated, version-controlled checks.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a cloud provider's certification makes your system compliant.
  • Treating compliance as a yearly project instead of continuous evidence.
  • Assuming a BAA or DPA with the cloud provider covers every other vendor.
  • Logging sensitive data (PHI, card numbers, passwords) in application logs to make debugging easier.
  • Keeping data "just in case", which increases risk and conflicts with storage limitation.
  • Promising deletion without accounting for backups, analytics, and processors.
  • Thinking encryption at rest stops attackers who hold valid credentials.
  • Equating passing an audit with being secure.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a SOC 2 Type 1 and a Type 2 report, and why does Type 2 need continuous evidence?
  2. Which parts of a deployment on managed containers are your responsibility under the shared responsibility model?
  3. A breach affecting EU users is discovered on Friday at 16:00. By when must the supervisory authority normally be notified under GDPR Article 33, and what if not all facts are known yet?
  4. How do you make CloudTrail logs trustworthy as audit evidence?
  5. PCI DSS requires 12 months of audit log history with three months immediately available. Design a storage setup that meets this.
  6. Why can a cloud provider be a HIPAA business associate even if it only stores encrypted data? How do you check whether a vendor offers a BAA?
  7. How would you handle an erasure request for data that also exists in backups and in invoices?
  8. Give two examples of policy as code, one before deploy and one in the running cloud, and explain how each produces audit evidence.

docs.title: Edge Protection: WAF, DDoS, and Bots
docs.text:
The edge is the first place a request meets your infrastructure: a CDN, a global load balancer, or the provider network in front of a regional load balancer. It is also the cheapest place to stop bad traffic, because the provider's capacity is far larger than yours and nothing has reached your servers yet. This lesson explains what attacks look like at each layer and how edge services stop them.

It covers the three kinds of DDoS attack (volumetric, protocol, and application layer), managed protection from AWS Shield, Cloudflare, Google Cloud Armor, and Azure DDoS Protection, web application firewall (WAF) rules from managed rule groups and the OWASP Core Rule Set, rate limiting, bot management, origin cloaking, and example rules for TaskFlow API. Setting up a CDN itself is covered in CDN setup and edge caching, routing users to the right region in global traffic management, and per-user rate limits inside the application in rate limiting and throttling.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Attacks at the edge are fast and large. Cloudflare reported a 31.4 Tbps attack in late 2025 that lasted 35 seconds: over before anyone could open a dashboard, let alone change a rule. Protection against floods therefore has to be automatic and always on.

Application-layer attacks are cheaper for the attacker and harder to spot, because each request looks legitimate. A few thousand bots requesting TaskFlow's search endpoint can exhaust the database without saturating any link. The same edge that absorbs floods can also run WAF rules that block exploit payloads (for example, the Log4Shell ${jndi: strings that filled logs in December 2021) while the team patches, and bot controls that stop credential stuffing on the login page.

Cost matters too. Autoscaling can absorb a flood, but every extra request that reaches the origin is compute, database load, and data transfer you pay for. Requests stopped or cached at the edge cost you the least.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub, 2018. GitHub's February 28th DDoS incident report describes a memcached amplification attack that peaked at 1.35 Tbps and 126.9 million packets per second, with an amplification factor of up to 51,000x. GitHub moved its traffic to its DDoS mitigation provider's edge and was fully available again about ten minutes after the attack began.
  • Google Cloud, 2023. Google's post Google mitigated the largest DDoS attack to date, peaking above 398 million rps explains the HTTP/2 "Rapid Reset" technique (CVE-2023-44487), which was 7.5 times larger than the previous record of 46 million requests per second, and how global load balancing and edge capacity kept customers' services up.
  • Cloudflare, 2025. The 2025 Q4 DDoS threat report describes a record 31.4 Tbps attack lasting 35 seconds from the Aisuru-Kimwolf botnet, 47.1 million DDoS attacks over 2025, and autonomous detection and mitigation without human involvement.
  • OWASP Core Rule Set. The OWASP CRS is the open-source rule set behind many WAFs: Google Cloud Armor's preconfigured rules are based on it, Azure WAF offers CRS 3.2 next to its own Default Rule Set, and Cloudflare offers an implementation as a managed ruleset. Its anomaly-scoring model is the standard way to tune false positives.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Shield Standard and Advanced, AWS WAF with AWS Managed Rules, Bot Control, and fraud control rule groups, Amazon CloudFront; Cloudflare DDoS protection, WAF, rate limiting rules, and bot products; Google Cloud Armor Standard and Enterprise with Adaptive Protection; Azure DDoS Protection and Azure WAF on Application Gateway and Front Door; Akamai and Fastly; ModSecurity (now an OWASP project) and Coraza running the OWASP CRS.

docs.title: DDoS attacks by layer
docs.text:
Type Examples What it exhausts Where it is stopped Volumetric (layer 3) UDP floods, amplification through open DNS, NTP, or memcached servers Bandwidth of links and routers Provider backbone and anycast edge, with scrubbing Protocol (layers 3 and 4) SYN floods, fragmented packets Connection tables in servers, load balancers, and firewalls Edge network and load balancers (SYN cookies and proxies) Application (layer 7) HTTP floods, HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, expensive endpoints such as search, slow-request attacks Application servers, databases, worker pools WAF, rate limits, bot management, caching, and a resilient application

Volumetric and protocol attacks are measured in bits and packets per second, and only a large network can absorb them, which is why they are handled by the provider. Application attacks are measured in requests per second and look like real traffic, so they need rules that understand HTTP and your application.

docs.title: Managed DDoS protection
docs.text:
Every major provider protects its own edge, and offers a paid tier with more help:

Provider Included at no extra charge Paid tier adds AWS Shield Standard: automatic protection against common layer 3 and 4 attacks for all AWS customers Shield Advanced: protection for EC2 Elastic IPs, load balancers, CloudFront, Global Accelerator, and Route 53, automatic application-layer mitigation through AWS WAF, the Shield Response Team (with a Business or Enterprise support plan), and DDoS cost protection; a large fixed monthly subscription with a one-year commitment, plus data transfer fees Cloudflare Unmetered DDoS protection for layers 3 to 7 on all plans Higher plans add WAF features, more rate limiting rules, bot management, and support Google Cloud Always-on layer 3 and 4 protection for applications behind its load balancers; Cloud Armor Standard is pay-as-you-go Cloud Armor Enterprise (pay-as-you-go or annual): Adaptive Protection, threat intelligence, named IP lists; DDoS response support and bill protection on the annual option Azure DDoS infrastructure protection for every service with a public IP DDoS IP Protection per protected IP, or DDoS Network Protection with rapid response support, cost protection, and a WAF discount

The relative cost decides the choice. The included tiers cost nothing extra and cover most attacks most applications will see. The premium tiers are a large fixed subscription, worth it when an outage costs more than the subscription or when expert help during an attack is needed; a small team behind a CDN usually starts with the included protection plus a WAF.

docs.title: The edge as a pipeline
docs.text: Order matters for both cost and accuracy. Cheap checks (IP reputation, rate limits) run before expensive ones, and the WAF should see a request before the cache serves anything personalized. Each layer also labels or logs what it saw, so later layers and humans can act on it.

docs.title: WAF rules: managed groups, custom rules, and the OWASP CRS
docs.text:
A web application firewall inspects layer-7 requests (method, path, query string, headers, cookies, and the body up to a size limit) and applies rules in priority order. Each rule has an action: allow, block, count (log only), or challenge with a CAPTCHA or a silent browser check.

  • Managed rule groups are maintained by the provider or a vendor. In AWS WAF, the core rule set (AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet) covers common OWASP-style attacks, known bad inputs (AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet) includes rules for Log4j JNDI lookups in headers, query strings, bodies, and paths, the Amazon IP reputation list blocks addresses AWS threat intelligence has seen attacking, and paid groups add Bot Control, account takeover prevention (ATP), account creation fraud prevention (ACFP), and an anti-DDoS group. Cloudflare offers its Managed Ruleset, an OWASP Core Ruleset implementation, and a Free Managed Ruleset on every plan; Azure WAF offers its Default Rule Set (DRS 2.2 is the latest) and CRS 3.2.
  • Custom rules encode what only you know: TaskFlow's login path, its bulk import endpoint that accepts large bodies, the countries it never serves, the header its mobile app sends.

The OWASP Core Rule Set works by anomaly scoring rather than by blocking on the first match:

  • Each matching rule adds points by severity: CRITICAL 5, ERROR 4, WARNING 3, NOTICE 2.
  • After all request rules run, the total is compared with the inbound anomaly score threshold (5 by default, so a single critical match blocks); responses have their own outbound threshold (4 by default).
  • The paranoia level (1 to 4) selects how many rules run. Level 1, the default, is designed to rarely cause false positives; each higher level adds stricter rules and more tuning work. CRS 4 separates the blocking paranoia level from an optional higher detection level, so stricter rules can be observed in the logs before they are allowed to block.

CRS 4 is the current major version (the project publishes both a latest and a long-term-support release), and CRS 3.3 has reached end of life. Engines include ModSecurity, which moved to OWASP in 2024 as its original sponsor ended commercial support, and Coraza.

docs.title: Tuning a WAF without breaking the application
docs.text:
A WAF that blocks real users is worse than none, because it gets switched off. The safe rollout is the same everywhere:

  1. Deploy in count or detection mode (AWS WAF count, ModSecurity SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly) and send logs to a central store.
  2. Read what would have been blocked for a representative period, including releases and batch jobs.
  3. Fix false positives narrowly: override one rule to count instead of disabling a group, scope a rule away from one path, or exclude one field. AWS WAF labels make this precise: a managed rule can be set to count, and a later custom rule can block requests carrying its label except on the one endpoint that needs it.
  4. Switch to blocking, keep watching the block rate, and alert on sudden changes after deploys.

Know the inspection limits. WAFs inspect only the first part of large request bodies and offer an "oversize handling" choice for the rest, and AWS's core rule set blocks request bodies over 8 KB by default. Redact sensitive fields such as the Authorization header from WAF logs.

docs.title: Rate limiting at the edge
docs.text:
Rate limits at the edge stop floods and brute force before they reach the application; rate limits in the application enforce business rules per user or API key. Use both.

  • Choose the key. Per IP is the default, but many users can share one address (offices, mobile carriers using carrier-grade NAT), and attackers spread across thousands. Better keys include IP plus path, an API key or session header, or a TLS fingerprint where the provider supports it.
  • Know the counting model. AWS WAF rate-based rules look back over a window of 60, 120, 300 (the default), or 600 seconds, accept a minimum limit of 10, and enforce limits approximately. Cloudflare counts per data center, so a client spread across locations can exceed the configured rate. Google Cloud Armor offers throttle (limit the rate) and rate-based ban (block a client for a period after it exceeds the threshold).
  • Limit the expensive paths most tightly: login, password reset, signup, search, and exports.

A worked example shows why per-IP limits alone do not stop credential stuffing:

limit on POST /api/auth/login:   10 requests per minute per IP
one attacker IP:                 at most 10 guesses per minute    (blocked beyond)
2,000 IPs from a botnet:         2,000 x 10 = 20,000 guesses per minute
                                 = 1,200,000 guesses per hour, none of them rate limited

and the other side of the same limit:
an office of 300 people behind one NAT address shares the same 10 requests per minute

Distributed attacks need signals beyond the address: bot detection, login failure rates per account, breached-password checks, and MFA.

docs.title: Bot management
docs.text:
Not all automation is bad. Search engine crawlers, uptime monitors, and partners' integrations are wanted; credential stuffers, scrapers, fake account creators, and inventory hoarders are not; AI crawlers are a policy decision. Bot management classifies traffic using IP reputation, TLS and HTTP fingerprints (JA3 and JA4), behavior over time, JavaScript detections in browsers, and machine-learning models, then allows, challenges, or blocks it.

  • AWS WAF: Bot Control (common and targeted protection levels), ATP for login pages, and ACFP for signup pages, with CAPTCHA and challenge actions.
  • Cloudflare: Bot Fight Mode on the Free plan, Super Bot Fight Mode on Pro and Business, and Bot Management for Enterprise, which exposes a bot score from 1 (almost certainly automated) to 99 (almost certainly human) and a verified-bot flag that custom rules can use.
  • Google Cloud Armor: bot management with reCAPTCHA assessments and rate limiting based on reCAPTCHA exemption tokens.
  • Azure WAF: Bot Manager rule sets that classify good, bad, and unknown bots.

Challenges work only for browsers. Mobile apps and API clients cannot solve a JavaScript challenge, so API endpoints need other signals: API keys, signed requests, attestation where available, and per-key rate limits.

docs.title: Origin cloaking: making the edge the only way in
docs.text:
Every protection at the edge is optional for an attacker who can reach the origin directly. Origin addresses leak through old DNS records, subdomains that are not proxied, mail servers on the same host, and certificate transparency logs, so assume the address is known and make it useless:

  • Network allowlist: on AWS, allow the origin load balancer's security group to accept traffic only from the managed prefix list com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing. With Cloudflare, allow only Cloudflare's published address ranges.
  • Shared secret: CloudFront adds a custom header with a random value, and the load balancer's listener forwards only requests that carry it, answering everything else with a fixed 403. Rotate the value like any secret. Cloudflare's Authenticated Origin Pulls use mutual TLS instead.
  • No public origin at all: CloudFront VPC origins can serve from an internal load balancer in private subnets, and Cloudflare Tunnel connects outbound from the origin, which then needs no inbound ports.

For S3 origins, origin access control lets only the CloudFront distribution read the bucket.

docs.title: Responding to an attack
docs.text:
1. Confirm and classify: is it volumetric (provider dashboards and network metrics), protocol, or application layer (request rate by path, status codes, origin latency)?
  2. Let automation work, then tighten: lower rate limits on the targeted path, raise challenge levels (as a last resort, Cloudflare's Under Attack mode shows every visitor an interstitial check page and blocks suspicious traffic), block abusive autonomous systems or countries you do not serve, and cache what can be cached.
  3. Protect the expensive dependencies: shed load on non-essential endpoints, cap autoscaling so a flood does not become a bill, and use the resilience patterns in resilience patterns across servers.
  4. Escalate: contact the provider's response team if you have one, and run the incident as described in incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Reasonable protection Usually not needed yet Static site or SPA on a CDN Included DDoS protection, CDN caching, origin access control A WAF with custom tuning Public API with logins (TaskFlow) Included DDoS protection, WAF with managed rules in front of the API, rate limits on auth paths, origin cloaking Premium DDoS tier, unless outages are very costly High-value target (payments, elections, gaming, large retail) Premium DDoS tier with response team, bot management, Adaptive Protection or equivalent Nothing: these are the services attackers pick Internal tools Identity-aware proxy, no public exposure at all A public WAF configuration API used only by mobile apps Per-key and per-account rate limits, signed or attested requests JavaScript challenges, which mobile clients cannot pass

Do not put a WAF in blocking mode without a count-mode period, do not rely on per-IP limits as the only login protection, and do not leave the origin reachable around the edge.

docs.title: A web ACL for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# infra/waf.tf: regional web ACL in front of the TaskFlow API load balancer
resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl" "api" {
  name        = "taskflow-api"
  description = "Edge rules for TaskFlow API"
  scope       = "REGIONAL"

  default_action {
    allow {}
  }

  # 1. Addresses that AWS threat intelligence has seen attacking
  rule {
    name     = "aws-ip-reputation"
    priority = 10
    override_action {
      none {}
    }
    statement {
      managed_rule_group_statement {
        name        = "AWSManagedRulesAmazonIpReputationList"
        vendor_name = "AWS"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "aws-ip-reputation"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  # 2. Core rule set; its 8 KB body rule only counts here, rule 4 decides instead
  rule {
    name     = "aws-common"
    priority = 20
    override_action {
      none {}
    }
    statement {
      managed_rule_group_statement {
        name        = "AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet"
        vendor_name = "AWS"
        rule_action_override {
          name = "SizeRestrictions_BODY"
          action_to_use {
            count {}
          }
        }
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "aws-common"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  # 3. Known bad inputs, including Log4j JNDI lookups
  rule {
    name     = "aws-known-bad-inputs"
    priority = 30
    override_action {
      none {}
    }
    statement {
      managed_rule_group_statement {
        name        = "AWSManagedRulesKnownBadInputsRuleSet"
        vendor_name = "AWS"
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "aws-known-bad-inputs"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  # 4. Large bodies are blocked everywhere except the bulk import endpoint
  rule {
    name     = "large-body-except-import"
    priority = 40
    action {
      block {}
    }
    statement {
      and_statement {
        statement {
          label_match_statement {
            scope = "LABEL"
            key   = "awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body"
          }
        }
        statement {
          not_statement {
            statement {
              byte_match_statement {
                search_string         = "/api/tasks/import"
                positional_constraint = "STARTS_WITH"
                field_to_match {
                  uri_path {}
                }
                text_transformation {
                  priority = 0
                  type     = "NONE"
                }
              }
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "large-body-except-import"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  # 5. Password guessing: at most 100 login requests per IP in 5 minutes
  rule {
    name     = "login-rate-limit"
    priority = 50
    action {
      block {}
    }
    statement {
      rate_based_statement {
        limit                 = 100
        evaluation_window_sec = 300
        aggregate_key_type    = "IP"
        scope_down_statement {
          byte_match_statement {
            search_string         = "/api/auth/login"
            positional_constraint = "EXACTLY"
            field_to_match {
              uri_path {}
            }
            text_transformation {
              priority = 0
              type     = "NONE"
            }
          }
        }
      }
    }
    visibility_config {
      cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
      metric_name                = "login-rate-limit"
      sampled_requests_enabled   = true
    }
  }

  visibility_config {
    cloudwatch_metrics_enabled = true
    metric_name                = "taskflow-api"
    sampled_requests_enabled   = true
  }
}

resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl_association" "api" {
  resource_arn = aws_lb.api.arn
  web_acl_arn  = aws_wafv2_web_acl.api.arn
}
  • Rules run in priority order, lowest first. override_action { none {} } keeps each managed group's own actions; managed groups cannot be nested inside other statements, which is why they sit at the top level.
  • Rule 2 changes one managed rule to count. The rule still adds its label (awswaf:managed:aws:core-rule-set:SizeRestrictions_Body), and rule 4 blocks labeled requests except on the import endpoint: one exception, everything else still protected.
  • Rule 5 counts login requests per client IP over a 5-minute window and blocks an IP above 100 until its rate falls again.
  • For a CloudFront distribution the same web ACL would use scope = "CLOUDFRONT", be created in us-east-1, and be attached to the distribution instead of the load balancer.

docs.title: Logging WAF decisions without leaking credentials
docs.text:
# infra/waf-logging.tf
resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "waf" {
  name              = "aws-waf-logs-taskflow-api"   # the aws-waf-logs- prefix is required
  retention_in_days = 90
}

resource "aws_wafv2_web_acl_logging_configuration" "api" {
  resource_arn            = aws_wafv2_web_acl.api.arn
  log_destination_configs = [aws_cloudwatch_log_group.waf.arn]

  redacted_fields {
    single_header {
      name = "authorization"
    }
  }
}

The logs show which rule matched each request and what action it took, which is exactly what the count-mode period needs. Redacting the Authorization header keeps bearer tokens out of the log store.

docs.title: A login rate limit on Cloudflare
docs.text:
{
  "description": "Login attempts per client IP",
  "expression": "(http.request.uri.path eq \"/api/auth/login\")",
  "action": "block",
  "ratelimit": {
    "characteristics": ["cf.colo.id", "ip.src"],
    "period": 60,
    "requests_per_period": 10,
    "mitigation_timeout": 600
  }
}

This is the body of a rule in the zone's http_ratelimit phase, created through Cloudflare's Rulesets API. cf.colo.id is always part of the key, so the count is per data center. A 60-second period with a 10-minute mitigation timeout needs the Pro plan or higher; the Free plan allows only 10-second periods.

docs.title: A bot rule for the login page on Cloudflare
docs.text:
# Cloudflare WAF custom rule: expression (action: Managed Challenge)
(http.request.uri.path eq "/api/auth/login" and cf.bot_management.score lt 30 and not cf.bot_management.verified_bot)

Requests to the login page that Bot Management scores as likely automated (below 30), and that do not come from a verified bot, get a Managed Challenge instead of reaching the API. Bot scores in custom rules require Enterprise Bot Management; Pro and Business plans use Super Bot Fight Mode settings instead.

docs.title: Running the OWASP CRS yourself
docs.text:
# crs-setup.conf (excerpt): block at paranoia level 1 with the default thresholds
SecAction \
    "id:900000,\
    phase:1,\
    pass,\
    t:none,\
    nolog,\
    setvar:tx.blocking_paranoia_level=1"

SecAction \
    "id:900110,\
    phase:1,\
    pass,\
    t:none,\
    nolog,\
    setvar:tx.inbound_anomaly_score_threshold=5,\
    setvar:tx.outbound_anomaly_score_threshold=4"

These are the CRS defaults made explicit, which documents the decision. Start the engine with SecRuleEngine DetectionOnly, tune exclusions from the audit log, then switch to SecRuleEngine On. To observe paranoia level 2 rules without blocking on them, set tx.detection_paranoia_level=2 while keeping the blocking level at 1.

docs.title: Locking the origin to CloudFront
docs.text:
# infra/origin-lockdown.tf
data "aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list" "cloudfront" {
  name = "com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "alb_from_cloudfront" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.alb.id
  prefix_list_id    = data.aws_ec2_managed_prefix_list.cloudfront.id
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  description       = "HTTPS from CloudFront origin-facing servers only"
}

Combine this with the secret origin header and a listener rule that answers requests without it with a fixed 403. The CloudFront prefix list counts heavily against the security group rules quota, which AWS documents as the prefix list's weight. When the load balancer can be internal, a CloudFront VPC origin removes the public endpoint altogether.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep the provider's included DDoS protection on everything, put a CDN or global load balancer in front of public services, and cache aggressively.
  • Run a WAF with managed rule groups in front of every public API; add custom rules for your own sensitive paths.
  • Roll out WAF rules in count mode first, fix false positives narrowly, then block; review logs after every major release.
  • Rate-limit authentication, signup, password reset, search, and export endpoints at the edge, and per user or key in the application.
  • Combine rate limits with bot management and account-level protections for logins; per-IP limits alone do not stop distributed attacks.
  • Make the edge the only way in: allowlist the edge's addresses, require a secret header or mTLS, or remove the public origin entirely.
  • Cap autoscaling and alert on unusual traffic, so an attack does not turn into an unbounded bill.
  • Keep a runbook for attacks, including who can change edge rules and how to reach the provider's response team.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The site is down, but servers show normal CPU. Detect: edge dashboards show a spike in packets or bits per second, and the load balancer reports connection errors. Cause: a volumetric or protocol attack saturating a component in front of the servers, often an origin exposed outside the CDN. Fix: make sure traffic flows through the protected edge, cloak the origin, and engage the provider's response team if you have a premium tier.
  • The database is overloaded by search requests from thousands of IPs. Detect: request rate on /api/tasks/search jumps while other paths are flat; each IP sends only a few requests. Cause: a distributed layer-7 attack on an expensive endpoint. Fix: add a rate limit keyed on a better identity than IP, challenge suspected bots, cache common queries, and shed load on search while protecting core paths.
  • Mobile app users get 403 after a WAF change. Detect: 403 responses from the edge rise right after a deploy; WAF logs show a challenge or a rule such as a missing User-Agent check matching the app's requests. Cause: a rule or challenge that assumes a browser. Fix: return the rule to count, scope it away from API paths, and identify app traffic with keys or signed requests.
  • Large task imports fail with 403. Detect: WAF logs show SizeRestrictions_BODY blocking POST /api/tasks/import. Cause: the core rule set blocks bodies over 8 KB. Fix: override that rule to count and re-block by label except on the import path, as in the example above.
  • Attackers bypass the WAF entirely. Detect: origin access logs show requests whose source addresses are not the CDN's, and they never appear in WAF logs. Cause: the origin is reachable directly. Fix: restrict the origin to the edge's prefix list and a secret header, or move it behind a VPC origin or tunnel.
  • Credential stuffing continues despite a login rate limit. Detect: login failures are high across many accounts while each IP stays under the limit. Cause: a botnet spreading attempts across thousands of addresses. Fix: add bot detection or account takeover protection on the login path, per-account failure throttling, breached password checks, and MFA.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• DDoS: Distributed denial of service; overwhelming a target with traffic from many sources.
  • Volumetric, protocol, and application-layer attacks: Attacks that exhaust bandwidth, connection state, or application resources.
  • Amplification: Spoofed requests to open servers that send much larger responses to the victim.
  • Anycast: Announcing the same address from many locations so traffic goes to the nearest one and attacks are spread out.
  • WAF: A web application firewall that inspects and filters HTTP requests.
  • Managed rule group: A rule set maintained by a provider or vendor.
  • OWASP CRS: The open-source Core Rule Set for WAF engines.
  • Anomaly scoring: Adding points per matched rule and blocking above a threshold.
  • Paranoia level: The CRS setting that selects how strict the active rules are.
  • Rate-based rule: A rule that acts on clients exceeding a request rate.
  • Bot score: A per-request estimate of how likely the client is automated.
  • Origin cloaking: Making the origin unreachable except through the edge.
  • Credential stuffing: Trying leaked username and password pairs at scale.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming autoscaling is DDoS protection; it absorbs load by spending money and still fails behind exhausted dependencies.
  • Turning on a WAF in blocking mode on day one and switching it off after the first false positive.
  • Disabling a whole managed rule group to fix one false positive.
  • Relying on per-IP rate limits against distributed bots, or blocking whole offices that share one address.
  • Leaving the origin reachable directly, so the edge is optional.
  • Serving JavaScript challenges to API clients that cannot solve them.
  • Treating the WAF as a replacement for fixing vulnerabilities; it buys time while you patch.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain volumetric, protocol, and application-layer DDoS attacks, and which part of the stack stops each.
  2. What does AWS Shield Standard include, and when would you pay for Shield Advanced or an equivalent premium tier?
  3. Using the CRS defaults, will a request matching one CRITICAL rule and one NOTICE rule be blocked? What about a request matching only two NOTICE rules? (5 + 2 = 7, at or above 5, so blocked; 2 + 2 = 4, below 5, so allowed and logged.)
  4. A login rate limit allows 10 requests per minute per IP. How many guesses per hour can a botnet of 2,000 addresses make without hitting it, and what else would you add? (2,000 x 10 x 60 = 1,200,000; bot detection, per-account throttling, breached-password checks, and MFA.)
  5. How would you roll out a new managed rule group without breaking real users?
  6. Why can a mobile API not rely on JavaScript challenges, and what can it use instead?
  7. List three ways to make sure attackers cannot bypass the CDN and reach the origin directly.
  8. Why does Cloudflare's per-data-center counting matter when you choose a rate limit?

docs.text:
