docs.title: Identity and Access Management
docs.text:
In the cloud, every action is an API call, and every API call is checked by identity and access management (IAM): who is calling, what are they trying to do, to which resource, and under what conditions. There is no network cable to unplug; a stolen credential with the right permissions is as good as being inside the data center. That makes IAM the most important control plane in a cloud deployment.

This lesson covers principals, users and roles, least privilege, AWS IAM policies with conditions and how AWS evaluates them, MFA, single sign-on and identity providers, short-lived credentials for people and workloads, break-glass accounts, access reviews, separating production into its own account with AWS Organizations and a landing zone, and what a leaked key really costs. Examples use AWS, with the Google Cloud and Azure equivalents named where they differ. The basic IAM principles are introduced in cloud building blocks, and workload identity for secrets in secrets management.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most cloud breaches do not break encryption or exploit the hypervisor. They use a credential: an access key in a public repository, a token printed in a CI log, a session stolen from a laptop, or a workload role that can do far more than the workload needs. Once inside, the attacker's reach is exactly the reach of that identity. Good IAM design makes each credential short-lived, narrowly scoped, and attributable to one person or workload, so a single leak becomes a small, visible, recoverable event instead of a company-wide incident.

IAM also decides how fast a team can safely move. Engineers who can get the access they need through a well-designed single sign-on flow do not keep personal admin keys "just in case". Production that lives in its own account turns "I ran it against the wrong environment" into a permission error.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Uber, 2016. The US Federal Trade Commission's settlement announcement explains that intruders reached data in a third-party cloud provider "by using an access key an Uber engineer had posted on a code-sharing website", downloading files with more than 25 million names and email addresses, and that the breach was not disclosed until November 2017. One long-lived key unlocked the data store.
  • Microsoft Exchange Online, 2023. The Cyber Safety Review Board's review describes attackers forging authentication tokens with a consumer signing key created in 2016 that should have been retired in 2021; manual rotation had stopped, and the key's scope was not enforced. The board calls signing keys a cloud provider's "crown jewels". The lessons apply to any team's keys: rotate automatically, scope narrowly, and alert on old credentials.
  • AWS IAM best practices. AWS's IAM best practices recommend federation with temporary credentials for people, IAM roles for workloads, MFA, least privilege, and regularly removing unused users, roles, and permissions.
  • AWS quarantines exposed keys. When AWS detects that an IAM user's keys were exposed publicly, it can attach the managed policy AWSCompromisedKeyQuarantine, which denies certain actions "to limit the potential damage that may be caused by fraud-related activity leading to unauthorized charges", and opens a support case. The existence of an automated quarantine shows how routinely exposed keys are abused.
  • Emergency access done deliberately. The Well-Architected practice SEC03-BP03 Establish emergency access process recommends a dedicated emergency access account with pre-created roles or users, SCPs protecting those roles, alerts whenever the account is used, and regular testing.

Popular tools and providers: AWS IAM, IAM Identity Center, AWS Organizations, AWS Control Tower, and IAM Access Analyzer; Google Cloud IAM, organization policies, and Workload Identity Federation; Microsoft Entra ID, Azure RBAC, managed identities, and Privileged Identity Management; identity providers such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, and Google Workspace; HashiCorp Vault for dynamic credentials.

docs.title: Principals and credentials
docs.text:
A principal is anything that can make a request: a person, a workload (an EC2 instance, an ECS task, a Lambda function, a Kubernetes pod), a CI job, another AWS account, or an AWS service acting for you. A principal proves who it is with credentials, and the kind of credential decides most of the risk.

Credential Lifetime Typical holder Main risk IAM user password plus MFA Until changed Break-glass users only Phishing, shared accounts IAM user access key Until deleted Legacy tools, third-party integrations Leaks into code, logs, and laptops; valid from anywhere Role session (STS) 15 minutes to the role's maximum (1 to 12 hours) People through SSO, workloads, CI Theft during the session; limited by expiry Instance or task role credentials Rotated automatically EC2, ECS, Lambda, EKS pods Theft through SSRF or a compromised container OIDC token exchanged for a role Minutes, then a role session CI jobs, workloads in other clouds Over-broad trust policy conditions

An IAM user has long-lived credentials. An IAM role has none: a principal assumes it through AWS STS and receives temporary credentials (an access key ID, a secret key, and a session token) that expire. AWS's guidance is that people sign in through federation and workloads use roles, so long-lived access keys become rare exceptions with an owner and a rotation date.

docs.title: Policies and how AWS evaluates them
docs.text:
A policy is a JSON document of statements. Each statement has an Effect (Allow or Deny), an Action (such as s3:GetObject), a Resource (an ARN), and optionally a Condition that must be true, such as aws:SourceIp, aws:PrincipalOrgID, or s3:prefix. Policies come in several types:

  • Identity-based policies attach to users, groups, and roles: what this principal may do.
  • Resource-based policies attach to resources such as S3 buckets, KMS keys, and SQS queues: who may use this resource. A role's trust policy is the resource-based policy that says who may assume it.
  • Permissions boundaries cap what an identity-based policy can grant, which lets a team create roles without being able to create administrators.
  • Session policies narrow a single role session.
  • Service control policies (SCPs) and resource control policies (RCPs) in AWS Organizations cap the permissions of every principal or resource in an account or organizational unit. They never grant anything.

Two rules explain almost every "access denied" message. Everything is denied by default, and an explicit deny always wins over any allow. Within one account, an allow in either the identity-based or the resource-based policy is enough, but SCPs, RCPs, boundaries, and session policies must all allow as well. Across accounts, both sides must allow: the caller's identity policy and the resource's policy.

docs.title: Least privilege in practice
docs.text:
Least privilege means each principal can do what its job needs and nothing more. In practice it is a process, not a single policy:

  1. Start from the actions the workload performs. TaskFlow API reads its own secrets, reads and writes objects under one bucket prefix, and nothing else. Write exactly that.
  2. Scope resources by ARN and prefix, not *. A role that may read taskflow/prod/* secrets cannot read the billing service's secrets.
  3. Add conditions where they express intent: only through a given service (kms:ViaService), only from your organization (aws:PrincipalOrgID), only over TLS (aws:SecureTransport).
  4. Generate and trim. IAM Access Analyzer can generate a policy from the actions a role actually used in CloudTrail, and its unused access analyzer reports roles, keys, and permissions that have not been used for a chosen number of days.
  5. Watch the dangerous permissions. iam:PassRole on * lets a principal hand any role, including an administrator role, to a service it controls. iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachRolePolicy, and sts:AssumeRole on broad resources are similar escalation paths.

Attribute-based access control (ABAC) adds tags to the picture: a condition such as "aws:ResourceTag/project": "${aws:PrincipalTag/project}" lets one policy serve many teams, each limited to resources carrying its own tag.

docs.title: People: single sign-on, MFA, and short sessions
docs.text:
Engineers should not have IAM users at all. They sign in to the company's identity provider (IdP) such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, or Google Workspace, which enforces MFA and knows who has joined, moved, or left. IAM Identity Center connects the IdP to every AWS account: groups map to permission sets, and each permission set becomes a role in the assigned accounts.

  • Session length: a new permission set defaults to a 1-hour session, configurable up to 12 hours. Shorter sessions for production limit what a stolen laptop session can do.
  • MFA: enforce it in the IdP, preferably with phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys or security keys. The IAM condition key aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent is only present when temporary credentials were used, and AWS documents that it is not present for federated identities or for requests signed with access keys, so it cannot enforce MFA for SSO users by itself.
  • Joiners, movers, leavers: provision users and groups from the IdP (SCIM), so removing someone in one place removes their access to every account.
  • Elevated access: keep everyday permission sets read-only in production and grant write access through a separate, time-limited permission set or a just-in-time approval tool.

The Google Cloud equivalent is Cloud Identity or Workspace with IAM roles on projects and folders; on Azure, Microsoft Entra ID with Azure RBAC and Privileged Identity Management for just-in-time roles.

docs.title: Workloads: identities without keys
docs.text:
Workloads should receive credentials from the platform they run on, never from a file or an environment variable:

  • EC2: an instance profile; the role's credentials come from the instance metadata service. Require IMDSv2 (session-token based), which blocks the simple server-side request forgery (SSRF) tricks that read credentials through a vulnerable proxy; see network security in the cloud.
  • ECS and Fargate: a task role per service; Lambda: an execution role; EKS: Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts.
  • CI: an OIDC token from GitHub Actions exchanged for a role whose trust policy names one repository and environment; see pipeline and supply chain security.
  • Other clouds: Google Cloud's Workload Identity Federation and Azure managed identities follow the same idea.

When an AWS service assumes a role on your behalf, add the aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn condition to the trust policy, as the ECS documentation recommends, so that another customer cannot trick the service into using your role (the confused deputy problem).

docs.title: Accounts as blast-radius boundaries
docs.text:
An AWS account is a hard isolation boundary: resources, IAM, quotas, and billing are separate. Putting production in its own account is the simplest way to guarantee that a staging credential, a sandbox experiment, or a mistyped profile cannot touch production.

  • AWS Organizations groups accounts into organizational units (OUs). SCPs attached to an OU set the maximum permissions for every principal in its accounts; RCPs do the same for resources. Neither affects the management account, which is one reason to run no workloads there. Declarative policies set service configurations (for example, requiring IMDSv2 for new EC2 instances) across the organization.
  • A landing zone is the standard multi-account setup most teams copy: a log archive account that receives every account's audit logs, an audit or security tooling account, workload accounts per environment, and sandboxes. AWS Control Tower builds one, provisions new accounts through Account Factory, and applies preventive, detective, and proactive controls.
  • Root users: with centralized root access management, the management account can delete the root user credentials of member accounts and run the few tasks that need root through short-term privileged sessions.
  • Elsewhere: Google Cloud uses an organization, folders, projects, and organization policies; Azure uses management groups, subscriptions, and Azure Policy.

docs.title: Break-glass access
docs.text: Single sign-on is a dependency: if the IdP is down, or its federation certificate expires, nobody can sign in. A break-glass process provides a second path for a small set of administrators, and AWS's Well-Architected guidance describes it as a dedicated emergency access account with pre-created IAM users (each tied to one person) or a vaulted root user with multiple hardware MFA devices, cross-account roles protected by SCPs, logs in the central log archive, and alerts whenever the account is used outside a declared emergency. Credentials are rotated after every use, and the path is tested in game days, because a break-glass procedure that has never been tried will fail when it is needed.

docs.title: Access reviews
docs.text: Permissions accumulate: people change teams, projects end, and temporary access is never removed. An access review asks each owner, on a fixed cadence (often quarterly for production), to confirm who has which access and to remove what is no longer needed. Make reviews cheap by generating the evidence: permission set assignments per account from Identity Center, unused access findings from IAM Access Analyzer, IAM credential reports for the few remaining IAM users, and a ticket per removal. Auditors for SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 ask for exactly this record; see compliance and audit readiness.

docs.title: The cost of a leaked key
docs.text: A long-lived key in a public repository should be considered stolen as soon as it is pushed. Attackers use leaked cloud keys to start compute in every Region they can reach (often for cryptocurrency mining), copy data, and create new users or keys so they keep access after the original key is revoked. The compute bill grows with three multipliers: instances per Region, Regions reached, and hours until someone notices. Thirty large instances in each of 4 Regions over a 72-hour weekend is 30 x 4 x 72 = 8,640 instance-hours that the account pays for, before any data-loss cost. Each multiplier maps to a control on this page: an SCP that denies unused Regions cuts the Regions, budget alerts and threat detection (Amazon GuardDuty, Google Security Command Center, Microsoft Defender for Cloud) cut the hours, least-privilege policies cut what the key can start, and having no long-lived keys removes the event entirely.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Need Use Avoid Engineers accessing AWS IAM Identity Center federated to the company IdP, MFA, short sessions IAM users with personal access keys A service running on AWS A role per service (task role, instance profile, execution role) Access keys in environment variables or files CI deploying to AWS OIDC federation to a role bound to repository and environment Repository secrets holding access keys A third-party tool that only accepts keys An IAM user with a minimal policy, key rotation, and monitoring Sharing an engineer's key Separating environments Separate accounts per environment under Organizations Tags or naming conventions as the only boundary Emergency access A tested break-glass process with alerts Shared admin passwords kept "for emergencies" Org-wide rules SCPs and RCPs as guardrails Expecting SCPs to grant access; they only restrict

docs.title: A least-privilege task role for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
The API running on ECS reads its own secrets and stores attachments under one prefix of the uploads bucket.

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "ReadOwnSecrets",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "secretsmanager:GetSecretValue",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:secretsmanager:eu-west-1:123456789012:secret:taskflow/prod/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DecryptSecretsThroughSecretsManagerOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "kms:Decrypt",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:eu-west-1:123456789012:key/<key-id>",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "kms:ViaService": "secretsmanager.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ReadWriteAttachments",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-uploads/attachments/*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ListAttachmentsPrefixOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "s3:ListBucket",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-uploads",
      "Condition": {
        "StringLike": {
          "s3:prefix": "attachments/*"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
  • Secrets are limited to the taskflow/prod/ path; Secrets Manager adds a random six-character suffix to secret ARNs, which the trailing * also covers.
  • kms:Decrypt is needed only when the secrets use a customer managed KMS key, and kms:ViaService limits it to decryption performed by Secrets Manager, so the role cannot decrypt arbitrary data with that key.
  • Object actions apply to attachments/* only. s3:ListBucket is a bucket-level action, so its prefix restriction is a condition on s3:prefix rather than a resource path.
  • There is no s3:*, no Resource: "*", and no IAM permission at all.

docs.title: The trust policy: who may assume the role
docs.text:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Service": "ecs-tasks.amazonaws.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRole",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnLike": {
          "aws:SourceArn": "arn:aws:ecs:eu-west-1:123456789012:*"
        },
        "StringEquals": {
          "aws:SourceAccount": "123456789012"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Only ECS tasks may assume the role, and only when the request comes from ECS acting for this account in this Region, which closes the confused deputy path.

docs.title: Organization guardrails with SCPs
docs.text:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyLeavingTheOrganization",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": "organizations:LeaveOrganization",
      "Resource": "*"
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ProtectAuditTrails",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Action": [
        "cloudtrail:DeleteTrail",
        "cloudtrail:StopLogging",
        "cloudtrail:UpdateTrail",
        "cloudtrail:PutEventSelectors"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:role/security-admin"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyRootUserExceptBucketPolicyRecovery",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "NotAction": [
        "s3:GetBucketPolicy",
        "s3:PutBucketPolicy",
        "s3:DeleteBucketPolicy"
      ],
      "Resource": "*",
      "Condition": {
        "ArnLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::*:root"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Attached to the Workloads OU, this SCP stops any principal in staging or production from removing the account from the organization, stops anyone except the security team's role from turning off audit trails, and denies the root user everything except fixing a bucket policy that locked everyone out. These statements follow AWS's published SCP examples, which also include a Region restriction: a Deny with NotAction listing global services and a StringNotEquals condition on aws:RequestedRegion. Use the full list of exempt global services from that example (IAM, for instance, is always called in us-east-1), and test every SCP on a test OU before attaching it widely.

docs.title: Permission sets as code
docs.text:
# infra/identity/production-access.tf
data "aws_ssoadmin_instances" "this" {}

locals {
  sso_instance_arn  = tolist(data.aws_ssoadmin_instances.this.arns)[0]
  identity_store_id = tolist(data.aws_ssoadmin_instances.this.identity_store_ids)[0]
}

resource "aws_ssoadmin_permission_set" "prod_view_only" {
  name             = "ProdViewOnly"
  description      = "Resources and metadata in production, no data access"
  instance_arn     = local.sso_instance_arn
  session_duration = "PT1H"
}

resource "aws_ssoadmin_managed_policy_attachment" "prod_view_only" {
  instance_arn       = local.sso_instance_arn
  permission_set_arn = aws_ssoadmin_permission_set.prod_view_only.arn
  managed_policy_arn = "arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/job-function/ViewOnlyAccess"
}

data "aws_identitystore_group" "oncall" {
  identity_store_id = local.identity_store_id

  alternate_identifier {
    unique_attribute {
      attribute_path  = "DisplayName"
      attribute_value = "taskflow-oncall"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_ssoadmin_account_assignment" "oncall_production" {
  instance_arn       = local.sso_instance_arn
  permission_set_arn = aws_ssoadmin_permission_set.prod_view_only.arn
  principal_id       = data.aws_identitystore_group.oncall.group_id
  principal_type     = "GROUP"
  target_id          = var.production_account_id
  target_type        = "AWS_ACCOUNT"
}

The on-call group gets a one-hour, view-only session in production. ViewOnlyAccess shows resources and metadata without reading data such as object contents, unlike ReadOnlyAccess. Because the assignment is code, every change to production access is a reviewed pull request, which is also access review evidence.

docs.title: Finding unused access
docs.text:
# One analyzer for the whole organization, run from the management account
# or the delegated administrator account
aws accessanalyzer create-analyzer \
  --analyzer-name org-unused-access \
  --type ORGANIZATION_UNUSED_ACCESS \
  --configuration '{"unusedAccess": {"unusedAccessAge": 90}}'

# Findings: unused roles, access keys, passwords, and permissions (90+ days)
aws accessanalyzer list-findings-v2 --analyzer-arn <analyzer-arn>

Review the findings in each access review and remove what nobody used.

docs.title: Responding to a leaked access key
docs.text:
# 1. Disable the key at once (re-enable later if it was a false alarm)
aws iam update-access-key --user-name ci-legacy \
  --access-key-id <access-key-id> --status Inactive

# 2. What did it do? Event history keeps 90 days of management events per Region
aws cloudtrail lookup-events --region eu-west-1 \
  --lookup-attributes AttributeKey=AccessKeyId,AttributeValue=<access-key-id> \
  --max-results 50

# 3. Look for persistence the attacker may have created
aws iam list-users --query 'Users[].[UserName,CreateDate]' --output table
aws iam list-access-keys --user-name ci-legacy

# 4. Delete the key and move the workload to a role
aws iam delete-access-key --user-name ci-legacy --access-key-id <access-key-id>

Check every Region the account can use, not only the one you normally deploy to, and check the organization trail in the log archive account, which keeps events longer than the 90-day event history. Then treat it as a security incident: see incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Federate people through one identity provider with phishing-resistant MFA; give engineers no IAM users and no access keys.
  • Give every workload its own role, and every CI pipeline an OIDC-assumed role bound to repository and environment.
  • Write policies per workload with explicit actions and resource ARNs; add conditions that express intent; review iam:PassRole carefully.
  • Put production in its own account; use SCPs for guardrails, a log archive account for audit logs, and no workloads in the management account.
  • Keep production sessions short and default to read-only; grant write access through a separate, time-limited path.
  • Remove root user credentials from member accounts, and protect the management account's root user with multiple hardware MFA devices.
  • Maintain and test a break-glass process, with alerts on every use.
  • Run access reviews on a schedule with generated evidence, and remove unused access found by IAM Access Analyzer.
  • Treat any exposed key as compromised: disable, investigate, rotate, and replace it with a role.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Deploys fail with "AccessDenied" after a new SCP was attached. Detect: CloudTrail shows errorCode: AccessDenied for the deploy role starting at the time of the SCP change, and the error message names an explicit deny in a service control policy. Cause: a guardrail (often a Region restriction) blocks an action the deploy needs, such as a global service called through us-east-1. Fix: detach or narrow the SCP, exempt the global service, and test SCPs on a test OU first.
  • An access key appears in a public commit. Detect: GitHub secret scanning, a provider notification, or AWS attaching a quarantine policy and opening a case. Cause: a long-lived key in a file or test. Fix: deactivate the key, review CloudTrail for its activity in every Region, remove anything the attacker created, then replace the key with a role or OIDC.
  • A service can read another service's secrets. Detect: IAM Access Analyzer or a policy review shows secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on *; CloudTrail shows reads of unrelated secrets. Cause: a shared, over-broad task role. Fix: one role per service with secret ARNs scoped by path, and an alert on cross-service secret reads.
  • Nobody can sign in during an identity provider outage. Detect: SSO sign-in fails for everyone while the IdP status page reports an incident. Cause: no tested emergency path. Fix: invoke the break-glass process; afterwards, rotate the break-glass credentials and schedule regular tests.
  • A departed engineer's access key is still active months later. Detect: the IAM credential report or an unused-access finding shows a key with a recent "last used" date after the person left. Cause: an IAM user created outside the IdP, so offboarding never reached it. Fix: deactivate and investigate, remove IAM users for people, and include IAM users in access reviews.
  • A role can escalate itself to administrator. Detect: a privilege-escalation check (Access Analyzer policy checks, a third-party IAM scanner) flags iam:PassRole or iam:CreatePolicyVersion on *. Cause: a convenience policy written for a deploy tool. Fix: restrict iam:PassRole to the specific role ARNs and the service (iam:PassedToService), and add a permissions boundary for roles the tool creates.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Principal: An entity that makes requests: a user, role session, service, or account.
  • IAM role: An identity without long-term credentials that principals assume to receive temporary credentials.
  • Trust policy: The resource-based policy on a role that says who may assume it.
  • Least privilege: Granting only the permissions a task needs.
  • Explicit deny: A Deny statement, which overrides any allow.
  • Permissions boundary: A policy that caps the permissions an identity-based policy can grant.
  • SCP and RCP: Organization policies that cap the permissions of principals (SCP) or resources (RCP) in member accounts.
  • Permission set: An IAM Identity Center template that becomes a role in each assigned account.
  • Federation: Signing in with an external identity provider instead of local credentials.
  • Workload identity: Credentials issued to software by the platform it runs on.
  • Confused deputy: A trusted service tricked into acting for the wrong party.
  • Break-glass access: A tested emergency path used only when normal access fails.
  • Landing zone: A standard multi-account environment with shared logging, security, and guardrails.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Creating IAM users with access keys for people because "SSO is extra work".
  • Believing SCPs grant permissions; they only limit them.
  • Using "Resource": "*" because finding the ARN format took too long.
  • Expecting aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent to enforce MFA for SSO users; MFA for federated users is enforced in the identity provider.
  • Sharing one role across services, which makes every service as powerful as the most powerful one.
  • Running workloads in the management account, where SCPs do not apply.
  • Deleting a leaked key from Git history but leaving it active.
  • Having a break-glass account that nobody has tested.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why are IAM roles safer than IAM users for both people and workloads?
  2. Walk through how AWS evaluates a request when an SCP, an identity policy, and a permissions boundary all apply. What happens when only one of them lacks an allow?
  3. Write the statements a service needs to list and read objects only under reports/ in one bucket, and explain why s3:ListBucket needs a condition rather than a resource path.
  4. What problem do aws:SourceArn and aws:SourceAccount solve in a trust policy?
  5. An access key leaked at 09:00 on Friday starts 30 instances in each of 4 Regions, and nobody notices until 09:00 on Monday. How many instance-hours does the account pay for, and which control shrinks each multiplier? (30 x 4 x 72 = 8,640 instance-hours; an SCP denying unused Regions cuts the Regions, budget alerts and threat detection cut the hours, and having no long-lived keys prevents the event.)
  6. Why should production live in its own account, and what belongs in the management account?
  7. Describe a break-glass process and how you would know it was used.
  8. What evidence makes an access review fast and credible?

docs.title: DevSecOps and Cloud Security Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review security in the delivery pipeline, identity and access management, network security, edge protection, vulnerability and patch management, and compliance. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What does "shift left" mean, and why is it not enough on its own?
docs.text: Shift left means running a check as early in the delivery path as it can run (on the laptop, in the pull request), because the author still has the context and nothing is deployed yet. It is not enough on its own: new CVEs are published against code that has not changed, some problems exist only in a built image or a running service, and console changes never pass through a pull request. Mature pipelines also rescan main, registries, and production continuously.

docs.title: 2. What do SAST, SCA, secret scanning, IaC scanning, image scanning, and DAST each find, and what do they miss?
docs.text: SAST reads source code and follows untrusted data to dangerous operations; it misses missing logic such as broken access control. SCA matches dependencies against advisory databases; it finds nothing new. Secret scanning finds credentials in known formats. IaC scanning finds public buckets and open ports before they exist, but not console drift. Image scanning finds known CVEs in OS and language packages. DAST probes the running app over HTTP and misses code paths it never reaches.

docs.title: 3. How does taint tracking find an injection bug? Use a NoSQL example.
docs.text: The analyzer follows data from a source an attacker controls (req.body.owner) to a sink where it is dangerous (Task.find()); if no sanitizer sits in between, it raises an alert. With the body {"owner": {"$ne": null}}, the filter matches every task whose owner is not null. Validating the input as a string first (z.string().parse()) breaks the taint, and non-string input fails with a 400.

docs.title: 4. Which findings should block a merge, and what happens to the rest?
docs.text: Block only on findings that are new in the change, high or critical from a high-confidence rule, and fixable. Everything else is reported and becomes a ticket with a deadline. A gate that blocks on old, unfixable, or noisy findings trains people to bypass it, and then the one important finding is ignored too. New scanners start in report-only mode and are tuned before they enforce.

docs.title: 5. What is the difference between a baseline and an exception?
docs.text:
A baseline is a recorded snapshot of existing findings that a gate ignores so only new ones fail (Checkov's --create-baseline, for example); the debt itself goes into tickets. An exception accepts one specific finding, with an owner, a reason, and an expiry date:

# .trivyignore: accepted by the API team lead; reviewed at expiry
CVE-YYYY-NNNNN exp:2026-12-31

After the expiry date the finding returns and the gate fails again.

docs.title: 6. Why is ignoring unfixed vulnerabilities a sensible default for an image gate, and what risk remains?
docs.text: A gate the author cannot satisfy gets bypassed, and a CVE without a fixed version cannot be fixed by a version bump. Gating on fixable findings (Trivy's --ignore-unfixed) keeps the gate meaningful. The risk is that an exploitable vulnerability without a fix stays open, so it needs a separate track: a mitigation, a time-boxed exception, and a subscription to the advisory.

docs.title: 7. What should happen when a secret is found in a commit?
docs.text: Treat it as an incident, not a lint error: revoke and rotate the credential first, then check what it was used for, then clean up the history. Rewriting Git history does not make a pushed secret safe. Prevent recurrence with layers: a pre-commit hook, platform push protection, a CI scan of every push, and a scan of built images and bundles. TruffleHog can verify a candidate against the provider to separate live keys from test strings.

docs.title: 8. What is SARIF, and why send every scanner's results to one place?
docs.text: SARIF is a JSON standard for static analysis results (rule, location, severity). Uploading every tool's SARIF to code scanning gives one list with pull request annotations, deduplication across runs, and auditable dismissal reasons, so a finding is triaged once. The upload job needs security-events: write, and each tool should use its own category.

docs.title: 9. What did the 2026 compromise of the Trivy GitHub Action teach about running scanners in CI?
docs.text: In March 2026 attackers force-pushed 76 of 77 version tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action (CVE-2026-33634) to code that stole credentials from the runner before the real scan ran. Scanners are dependencies too: pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs, pin the scanner binary, give scanner jobs read-only permissions and no secrets, and rotate everything the affected workflows could read. A pin protects only the code it names, so prefer actions that pin their own dependencies.

docs.title: 10. Where should DAST run, and how do ZAP's baseline, API, and full scans differ?
docs.text: Against staging or a disposable environment you own, never against production without explicit approval. The baseline scan spiders for a minute and runs passive checks only. The API scan imports an OpenAPI, SOAP, or GraphQL definition and actively attacks each operation. The full scan spiders and actively attacks a web app, filling it with junk data. A rules file marks each alert IGNORE, INFO, WARN, or FAIL.

docs.title: 11. Why are IAM roles safer than IAM users?
docs.text: An IAM user's access key works from anywhere until someone deletes it. A role has no long-term credentials: a principal assumes it through STS and receives temporary credentials that expire (role sessions last from 15 minutes up to the role's maximum of 1 to 12 hours). People should sign in through federation and workloads should use roles, so long-lived keys become rare exceptions with an owner and a rotation date.

docs.title: 12. How does AWS evaluate a request when several policy types apply?
docs.text: Everything is denied by default, and an explicit deny anywhere wins. Then, in an organization, SCPs and RCPs must allow the request; an identity-based or resource-based policy must allow it (either one within an account, both across accounts); and a permissions boundary and a session policy must allow it if they exist. If any required layer lacks an allow, the request is denied.

docs.title: 13. What is a role's trust policy, and what is the confused deputy problem?
docs.text: The trust policy is the resource-based policy on a role that says who may assume it. The confused deputy problem arises when a trusted service, such as ECS, can be tricked by another customer into using your role. Adding aws:SourceAccount or aws:SourceArn conditions to the trust policy limits assumption to the service acting for your account and resources.

docs.title: 14. Why can't aws:MultiFactorAuthPresent enforce MFA for single sign-on users?
docs.text: AWS documents that the key is present only when temporary credentials were used, and is absent for federated identities and for requests signed with access keys. MFA for people who sign in through IAM Identity Center is enforced in the identity provider, preferably with phishing-resistant methods such as passkeys or security keys.

docs.title: 15. What do SCPs and RCPs do, and what can they not do?
docs.text: They set the maximum permissions for every principal (SCPs) or resource (RCPs) in member accounts and organizational units: guardrails such as "no unused Regions" or "nobody may stop CloudTrail". They never grant anything, and they do not affect the management account, which is one reason to run no workloads there. Test them on a test OU first, because a guardrail can block a deploy that needs a global service.

docs.title: 16. How should a GitHub Actions workflow authenticate to AWS?
docs.text:
With OIDC instead of stored keys. The job requests an ID token (id-token: write), and STS exchanges it for short-lived role credentials if the trust policy's conditions match:

{"StringEquals": {
  "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
  "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:example/taskflow-api:environment:production"}}

Binding sub to one repository and environment means another repository, branch, or pull request cannot assume the production role. Never use a wildcard such as repo:example/* for a deploy role.

docs.title: 17. Which IAM permissions are classic privilege-escalation paths?
docs.text: iam:PassRole on * lets a principal hand any role, including an administrator role, to a service it controls. iam:CreatePolicyVersion, iam:AttachRolePolicy, and broad sts:AssumeRole are similar. Restrict iam:PassRole to specific role ARNs and services (iam:PassedToService), add permissions boundaries to roles that tools create, and run policy checks that flag these patterns.

docs.title: 18. What is a break-glass process, and how do you keep it both safe and usable?
docs.text: It is a second way in for a few administrators when single sign-on fails (an identity provider outage or an expired federation certificate): a dedicated emergency account with pre-created users tied to individuals, or a vaulted root user with hardware MFA, protected by SCPs. Every use raises an alert, credentials are rotated after use, logs go to the log archive, and the path is tested in game days so it works when needed.

docs.title: 19. What makes an access review fast and credible?
docs.text: Generated evidence instead of spreadsheets: permission set assignments per account from Identity Center, unused-access findings from IAM Access Analyzer, credential reports for the remaining IAM users, and one ticket per removal, signed off by a named owner on a fixed cadence (often quarterly for production; PCI DSS 7.2.4 requires at least every six months). Managing permission set assignments as code makes every change a reviewed pull request.

docs.title: 20. A leaked key starts 30 instances in each of 4 Regions over a 72-hour weekend. What does it cost, and which controls shrink each factor?
docs.text: 30 x 4 x 72 = 8,640 instance-hours before any data-loss cost. An SCP that denies unused Regions cuts the Regions; budget alerts and threat detection (GuardDuty, Security Command Center, Defender for Cloud) cut the hours; least privilege limits what the key can start; and having no long-lived keys removes the event.

docs.title: 21. What belongs in public, private, and isolated subnets?
docs.text: Public subnets hold only what must accept internet traffic: load balancers and NAT gateways. Private app subnets hold the API tasks, which accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group. Isolated data subnets have no route to an internet gateway or NAT at all, and the database accepts connections only from the API's security group or through a private endpoint.

docs.title: 22. Why write security group rules by reference to other groups instead of IP addresses?
docs.text: "The API accepts port 3000 from the load balancer's group" stays correct as tasks are replaced and IPs change, and it reads like a policy. Know the defaults: the default security group allows all traffic between members and all outbound traffic, and new groups start with allow-all egress (Terraform's aws_security_group removes it, so egress must be declared). Keep rules in code and scan them in pull requests.

docs.title: 23. When do you use network ACLs instead of security groups?
docs.text: Security groups are stateful allow-lists on network interfaces and do most of the work. Network ACLs are stateless, ordered allow and deny lists on subnets; use them for coarse, subnet-wide decisions such as denying an address range during an incident or making data subnets refuse anything from public subnets. Their explicit deny is something security groups cannot express.

docs.title: 24. Why is a NAT gateway not a security control, and how do you control egress?
docs.text: NAT gives private subnets outbound access but filters nothing. Egress controls, from coarse to fine: security group egress rules (IP ranges, prefix lists, groups), VPC endpoints for AWS APIs, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall for domain names (which a client can bypass with a raw IP), and AWS Network Firewall or an egress proxy that filters by TLS SNI or HTTP Host. Endpoints often lower NAT charges as well.

docs.title: 25. How does IMDSv2 protect instance credentials from SSRF?
docs.text: The metadata service starts each session with an HTTP PUT that returns a token, and every read must carry that token. Open WAFs, reverse proxies, and most SSRF bugs can only make GET requests, so they cannot fetch the role's credentials. Require IMDSv2 as an account default (or through a declarative policy), keep the hop limit low on hosts without containers, and prefer task or pod roles, which do not come from instance metadata.

docs.title: 26. Compare a bastion host, Session Manager, and Identity-Aware Proxy for administrative access.
docs.text: A bastion is an internet-facing server with SSH open to known ranges: a host to patch, keys to issue and revoke, and logs on the box an attacker would target. Session Manager's agent connects outbound, users start sessions through the AWS API with IAM (so SSO and MFA), and sessions are logged centrally with no inbound port. Google's IAP lets SSH in only from 35.235.240.0/20 and requires the roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor role, so the VM needs no external IP.

docs.title: 27. What does zero trust change compared with a client VPN?
docs.text: A VPN checks the user once at the edge and then the network trusts them, so a stolen VPN login reaches everything on it. Zero trust authenticates and authorizes each request using identity, device state, and context, per application: identity-aware proxies for people, workload identity and mutual TLS for services. Segmentation still matters; zero trust means the network is not the only check, not that the network is flat.

docs.title: 28. Is traffic inside a VPC encrypted, and why add TLS anyway?
docs.text: AWS documents that traffic between Availability Zones is encrypted and that many Nitro-based instance types encrypt traffic between instances automatically when both sides qualify; VPC Encryption Controls can report and enforce this. Application TLS is still the norm: it protects against a compromised host inside the network, it authenticates the server (and the client with mTLS), and it does not depend on instance types that can change.

docs.title: 29. What is a data perimeter, and why does aws:SourceIp stop working with VPC endpoints?
docs.text: A data perimeter keeps data reachable only by trusted identities from expected networks, built from endpoint policies and resource policies such as a bucket policy that requires aws:SourceVpce. Requests that arrive through a VPC endpoint do not include the aws:SourceIp key, so a bucket policy that allows only certain IP addresses denies the API's own requests once an endpoint is added. Use aws:SourceVpce instead, with a tested exception role.

docs.title: Edge protection: WAF, DDoS, and bots
30. What are the three kinds of DDoS attack, and where is each stopped?
docs.text: Volumetric attacks (UDP floods, amplification through open DNS, NTP, or memcached servers) exhaust bandwidth and are absorbed by the provider's backbone and anycast edge. Protocol attacks (SYN floods, fragments) exhaust connection tables and are stopped by the edge network and load balancers. Application-layer attacks (HTTP floods, HTTP/2 Rapid Reset, expensive search requests) look like real traffic and need WAF rules, rate limits, bot management, caching, and a resilient application.

docs.title: 31. What does AWS Shield Standard include, and when is a premium DDoS tier worth it?
docs.text: Shield Standard protects every AWS customer against common layer 3 and 4 attacks at no extra charge. Shield Advanced adds protection for more resource types, automatic application-layer mitigation through AWS WAF, a response team, and DDoS cost protection, for a large fixed subscription with a one-year commitment. It pays off when an outage costs more than the subscription or expert help during an attack is needed; a small team behind a CDN usually starts with the included tier plus a WAF.

docs.title: 32. How does the OWASP Core Rule Set decide whether to block a request?
docs.text: By anomaly scoring. Each matching rule adds points by severity (CRITICAL 5, ERROR 4, WARNING 3, NOTICE 2), and after all request rules run the total is compared with the inbound threshold, 5 by default, so one critical match blocks. Responses have their own threshold (4). The paranoia level (1 to 4) chooses how many rules run; level 1 rarely causes false positives, and CRS 4 can log a higher detection level without blocking on it.

docs.title: 33. How do you roll out a WAF without breaking real users?
docs.text: Deploy in count or detection mode and send logs to a central store; read what would have been blocked over a representative period, including releases and batch jobs; fix false positives narrowly (override one rule to count, scope it away from one path, or exclude one field, using labels in AWS WAF); then switch to blocking and alert on sudden changes in the block rate after deploys.

docs.title: 34. Why don't per-IP rate limits stop credential stuffing?
docs.text: The attack is distributed. With a limit of 10 login requests per minute per IP, a botnet of 2,000 addresses still makes 2,000 x 10 x 60 = 1,200,000 guesses an hour without hitting it, while an office of 300 people behind one NAT address shares the same 10 requests. Add bot detection, per-account failure throttling, breached-password checks, and MFA, and choose better keys than IP where you can.

docs.title: 35. Why can't an API used by mobile apps rely on JavaScript challenges?
docs.text: Challenges and CAPTCHAs run in browsers. A mobile app or API client cannot solve them, so a challenge simply breaks it. API endpoints need other signals: API keys or session tokens, signed requests, app attestation where available, and per-key or per-account rate limits.

docs.title: 36. What is origin cloaking, and how do you implement it?
docs.text: Making the origin unreachable except through the edge, because every edge protection is optional for an attacker who can reach the origin directly, and origin addresses leak through old DNS records, unproxied subdomains, mail headers, and certificate logs. Allow only the edge's addresses (on AWS, the com.amazonaws.global.cloudfront.origin-facing prefix list), require a secret header or mutual TLS, or remove the public origin with a CloudFront VPC origin or Cloudflare Tunnel.

docs.title: 37. Does a WAF rule replace patching?
docs.text: No. A WAF rule is a virtual patch: it blocks known exploit patterns (such as the Log4j JNDI rules in AWS's known bad inputs group) and buys time while you patch. Attackers obfuscate payloads to get around it, and CISA's KEV entry for Log4Shell accepted temporary mitigations only until updates were available. Patch, rebuild, and redeploy as fast as the deadline requires.

docs.title: 38. What is the difference between a CVE, a CWE, and an advisory such as a GHSA?
docs.text: A CVE is a unique ID and record for one publicly known vulnerability, assigned by a CVE Numbering Authority, often the vendor itself. A CWE is a class of weakness (Log4Shell is CWE-917, expression language injection). A GHSA advisory in the GitHub Advisory Database maps a vulnerability to exact vulnerable and fixed package versions in an ecosystem such as npm, which is what dependency scanners match against.

docs.title: 39. What does a CVSS score tell you, and what does it not?
docs.text: CVSS (version 4.0, maintained by FIRST) describes severity: how bad exploitation would be for a generic installation. Its base metrics are intrinsic; threat metrics add exploit maturity and environmental metrics add your own controls. Most published scores are base-only (CVSS-B), so they say nothing about whether anyone is exploiting the vulnerability or whether your deployment is exposed. Use CVSS to order work, not to set deadlines.

docs.title: 40. What is EPSS, and how should it be combined with CVSS and KEV?
docs.text: FIRST's Exploit Prediction Scoring System gives a daily probability that a CVE will see exploitation activity in the next 30 days; version 5 has published scores since June 2026. Confirmed exploitation (a KEV entry) overrides any score, and EPSS must not be multiplied by CVSS, which is an ordinal scale. Probabilities add up: 100 findings at 0.05 mean about 5 exploited in a month, and 1 - 0.95^100 ≈ 99.4% odds of at least one.

docs.title: 41. What is the CISA KEV catalog, and why check it first?
docs.text: A list of vulnerabilities with an assigned CVE, reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild, and a clear remediation action; the November 2026 catalog holds 1,779 entries, 361 marked as used in ransomware campaigns. It is the strongest single signal and small enough to drive to zero. It is published as a JSON feed that scripts can read, and CISA recommends that every organization address KEV entries immediately.

docs.title: 42. How does CISA's BOD 26-04 set remediation deadlines?
docs.text: It replaced BOD 22-01's fixed deadlines (two weeks for recent CVEs, six months for older ones) in June 2026 for US federal civilian agencies. Four decision points (publicly exposed, in KEV, automatable, technical impact) map to 3, 14, or 60 days, or "fix on system upgrade". KEV entries with total impact in the 3-day class also need forensic triage. The clock starts at the KEV addition or at discovery, whichever comes first, and moves when the facts change.

docs.title: 43. What is VEX, and when is a not_affected statement justified?
docs.text: VEX records whether a product is affected by a vulnerability, with the statuses not_affected, affected, fixed, and under_investigation. A not_affected statement needs a justification such as component_not_present or vulnerable_code_not_present (kernel headers flagged in a container image, for example). Trivy reads OpenVEX, CycloneDX, and CSAF with --vex. Treat it as a reviewed claim with an owner and a review date, never as a mute button.

docs.title: 44. What changed at the NVD in 2026, and how should a team adapt?
docs.text: Since April 15, 2026, NIST enriches priority CVEs (KEV entries, software used by the federal government, and critical software) and leaves the rest "not scheduled for immediate enrichment"; it also no longer routinely adds its own severity score when one exists. A process that waits for an NVD score stalls. Use the CNA's score, GHSA and OSV data, distribution severities, KEV, EPSS, and CISA's SSVC data instead.

docs.title: 45. How should a team keep container base images patched?
docs.text: Images are snapshots, so rebuild on a schedule, not only on code changes: docker build --pull --no-cache picks up a moved base tag and fresh OS packages. If the base is pinned by digest, a bot (Renovate pinDigests or Dependabot) opens pull requests when the digest changes. Either way, deploy the rebuilt image, alert on the age of what is running, and prefer slim or distroless bases with fewer packages to patch.

docs.title: 46. Compare patching servers in place with replacing them.
docs.text: In place, unattended-upgrades (on by default on Ubuntu Server) or a managed service such as AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager installs updates on running hosts; reboots and service restarts must be scheduled. By replacement, a new golden image is baked weekly and rolled through the fleet with an instance refresh, so patching becomes a tested, reversible deploy with no drift. Containers are always replaced, never patched in place. Either way, a patch is not active until the process restarts.

docs.title: 47. How do Dependabot and Renovate keep dependencies current without adding risk?
docs.text: They open pull requests for advisories and new versions. Security updates skip the release-age delay (Dependabot's cooldown, Renovate's minimumReleaseAge), while ordinary updates wait a few days so a malicious or broken release can be caught first. Automerge only patch versions and digest bumps after tests pass, and let humans start major upgrades. npm's overrides field in the root package.json can force a patched transitive version until the parent package catches up.

docs.title: 48. How do SBOMs help during a zero-day, and what did Log4Shell show?
docs.text: An SBOM per release and per deployed image digest turns "are we affected?" into a query, and rescanning stored SBOMs daily (trivy sbom, Grype) checks old releases against new advisories without rebuilding them. The Cyber Safety Review Board found that groups representing organizations already using SBOMs reported none had used them to find vulnerable Log4j deployments. Store them, cover hosts and vendor tools, and rehearse the query before you need it.

docs.title: 49. Walk through the first hours of a Log4Shell-class zero-day.
docs.text: Declare an incident; query every SBOM, image, and host inventory for the component and contact vendors; rank exposure (internet-facing first); apply mitigations immediately (WAF rules, configuration changes, egress filtering, isolation); patch, rebuild, and redeploy, and expect follow-up fixes (Log4j needed 2.15.0, 2.16.0, 2.17.0, and 2.17.1 in under three weeks); verify by rescanning what is running; check exposed systems for compromise; then communicate and write the postmortem.

docs.title: 50. What is the difference between a SOC 2 Type 1 and a Type 2 report?
docs.text: Both are attestation reports by a CPA firm against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, not certifications. Type 1 covers the design of controls at a point in time; Type 2 also covers how they operated over a period. A Type 2 therefore needs continuous evidence: a control that silently broke in month two fails the audit in month twelve.

docs.title: 51. What does the shared responsibility model mean for compliance?
docs.text: The provider's certifications cover security of the cloud (data centers, hardware, hypervisors), which you inherit by giving its reports (AWS Artifact and equivalents) to your auditor. Everything you configure is yours to prove: IAM, bucket policies, security groups, encryption settings, logging, backups, and application access control. Each vendor that handles regulated data adds its own contract, such as a DPA or a BAA.

docs.title: 52. How do you make CloudTrail trustworthy as audit evidence?
docs.text: Use an organization trail for every account and Region, delivered to a bucket in a separate log archive account; enable log file integrity validation, which writes signed digest files that reveal modified or deleted logs; protect the bucket with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode; add data events for buckets holding regulated data (they are not recorded by default); and alert on any change to logging. Event history alone keeps only 90 days.

docs.title: 53. What does "evidence from systems, not people" mean in an audit?
docs.text: Auditors take a population ("every production change this year") and samples ("for these 25, show approval, tests, and deploy"). If pull request approvals, CI logs, policy results, configuration rule results, and access review tickets are exported automatically to an append-only, timestamped store mapped to controls, the answer is a query instead of weeks of screenshots, and one control's evidence serves several frameworks.

docs.title: 54. How do you handle a GDPR erasure request when the data also exists in backups and invoices?
docs.text: Run one erasure job across every live copy (database, search index, caches, processors) and record that it happened without keeping the data. Backups are not edited: keep their retention short and re-apply the list of completed erasures after any restore. Data kept under a legal obligation, such as invoices, stays with restricted access until its retention period ends. The request must be answered within one month, extendable by two further months where necessary.

docs.title: 55. When do you need a BAA, and does the cloud provider's BAA cover your other vendors?
docs.text: Under HIPAA, every vendor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI for you needs a business associate agreement; HHS treats a cloud provider that stores encrypted ePHI it cannot read as a business associate too. The cloud provider's BAA covers only its eligible services. Error trackers, email, SMS, analytics, and support tools need their own BAA, or PHI must not reach them, and a BAA alone does not make your solution compliant.

docs.title: 56. What is policy as code, and how does it produce audit evidence?
docs.text: Rules such as "no public buckets" written as automated checks: Open Policy Agent, Checkov, or Trivy on every Terraform plan before deploy; AWS Config rules, Azure Policy, or Google organization policies on the live cloud, which also catch console changes; and admission controllers such as Kyverno in Kubernetes. Every evaluation is timestamped and tied to a commit or resource, which is exactly what a Type 2 auditor samples.

docs.title: 57. A breach is discovered. What are the GDPR and HIPAA notification deadlines?
docs.text: GDPR Article 33 requires notifying the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours of becoming aware of the breach, unless it is unlikely to result in a risk; information can be provided in phases if not all facts are known yet. HIPAA requires notifying affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. Rehearse both clocks before an incident.

docs.title: 58. A new security scanner went live on Monday, and by Tuesday nearly every pull request fails the same check. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the gate fails on all findings or only on findings the change introduces.

How to confirm: the failing pull requests touch unrelated code, and the findings are in files the authors never changed.

Likely causes and fixes: the scanner blocks on existing debt. Switch it to report-only, record a baseline, block only new high-confidence findings, and turn the backlog into tickets with owners and deadlines. See security in the delivery pipeline.

docs.title: 59. An access key appears in a public commit and was pushed 20 minutes ago. What are your first steps?
docs.text:
What to check first: which principal owns the key and whether it is still active.

How to confirm: CloudTrail lookup-events filtered by the access key ID in every Region shows any calls from unknown addresses or new Regions, plus any users, keys, or roles created as persistence.

Likely causes and fixes: a long-lived key committed in a file or test. Deactivate it at once, investigate its activity everywhere (including the organization trail), remove anything the attacker created, then replace it with a role or OIDC and enable push protection. See identity and access management.

docs.title: 60. Deploys start failing with AccessDenied an hour after the security team attached a new SCP. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the exact error message and the deploy role's failing API calls in CloudTrail.

How to confirm: the error names an explicit deny in a service control policy, and the failures start at the time of the SCP change.

Likely causes and fixes: a guardrail, often a Region restriction, blocks an action the deploy needs, such as a global service called through us-east-1. Exempt the global services as AWS's example does, narrow or detach the SCP, and test SCPs on a test OU before attaching them widely. See identity and access management.

docs.title: 61. GuardDuty reports that an instance role's credentials were used from an address outside AWS. Where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: the instance's metadata settings (is IMDSv1 still allowed?) and its application logs.

How to confirm: the logs show requests to 169.254.169.254 triggered through a user-supplied URL, and CloudTrail shows the role's calls from the foreign address.

Likely causes and fixes: an SSRF bug reached the metadata service because IMDSv1 accepted a simple GET. Revoke the role's active sessions, require IMDSv2 by account default, fix the SSRF, narrow the role, and check what the attacker did with the credentials. See network security in the cloud.

docs.title: 62. After moving build agents into private subnets, NAT gateway charges jump and builds slow down. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which destinations account for the NAT gateway's processed bytes.

How to confirm: flow logs show most traffic going to ECR and S3 address ranges.

Likely causes and fixes: image pulls and artifacts flow through NAT. Add an S3 gateway endpoint and interface endpoints for ECR, which cuts NAT data processing and removes an internet path at the same time. See network security in the cloud.

docs.title: 63. Login failures are high across thousands of accounts, but no client IP exceeds the login rate limit. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: failed logins per account and per IP, and the number of distinct source addresses.

How to confirm: each IP makes only a few attempts, the attempted passwords match known breach lists, and attempts are spread over many accounts.

Likely causes and fixes: credential stuffing from a botnet. Add bot detection or account takeover protection on the login path, per-account failure throttling, breached-password checks, and MFA, and key rate limits on more than the IP. See edge protection: WAF, DDoS, and bots.

docs.title: 64. Large task imports started failing with 403 right after the WAF's managed core rule set was enabled. How do you fix it without weakening the WAF?
docs.text:
What to check first: the WAF logs for the failing requests: which rule matched and with which action.

How to confirm: the logs show the core rule set's body size rule blocking POST /api/tasks/import, because its bodies exceed 8 KB.

Likely causes and fixes: a managed rule that does not fit one endpoint. Override only that rule to count, then add a custom rule that blocks requests carrying its label except on the import path, so every other path stays protected. See edge protection: WAF, DDoS, and bots.

docs.title: 65. Origin access logs show attack traffic that never appears in the WAF logs. How did it get in?
docs.text:
What to check first: the source addresses of the requests at the origin load balancer.

How to confirm: they are not the CDN's addresses, and the origin's security group accepts traffic from anywhere.

Likely causes and fixes: the origin is reachable directly, so the edge is optional. Allow only the edge's prefix list, require a secret header or mutual TLS, answer everything else with a fixed 403, or move the origin behind a VPC origin or tunnel. See edge protection: WAF, DDoS, and bots.

docs.title: 66. On a Friday afternoon, CISA adds a CVE to KEV that affects a library in your internet-facing API. How do you decide how fast to act?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the vulnerable component is in the image that is actually running, and whether attacker input can reach it.

How to confirm: query the SBOM for the deployed digest, rescan that digest, and read the CVE record's SSVC data (automatable, technical impact) and the fixed version from the advisory.

Likely causes and fixes: publicly exposed plus KEV means a 3-day deadline in a BOD 26-04-style policy, with forensic triage if the impact is total. Mitigate now (a WAF rule, a disabled feature), then upgrade, rebuild, redeploy through the normal pipeline, verify with a rescan, and check for signs of earlier compromise. See vulnerability and patch management.

docs.title: 67. Every container image scan shows dozens of Linux kernel CVEs, some of them in KEV. Is the API exploitable?
docs.text:
What to check first: which package the findings are reported against.

How to confirm: they sit on linux-libc-dev (kernel headers) or similar packages in the image, not on anything the application executes.

Likely causes and fixes: build tools and headers shipped in the runtime image, while containers run on the host's kernel. Move to a multi-stage build on a slim or distroless base, record a VEX vulnerable_code_not_present statement for anything that remains, and patch the hosts' kernels as a separate asset with their own deadline. See vulnerability and patch management.

docs.title: 68. Patch Manager reports the fleet as patched, but a scanner still finds the old OpenSSL in use. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: pending reboots and long-running processes on the hosts.

How to confirm: describe-instance-patch-states shows InstalledPendingRebootCount above zero, /var/run/reboot-required exists, or running processes still map the old library.

Likely causes and fixes: packages were installed without a reboot or service restart (for example with RebootOption=NoReboot). Schedule rolling reboots behind the load balancer, use needrestart for services, and consider replacing instances with a freshly baked image instead. See vulnerability and patch management.

docs.title: 69. The image pipeline rebuilds TaskFlow API every night, yet production runs a three-month-old image. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: the digest that is actually running compared with the newest digest in the registry.

How to confirm: the rebuild workflow pushes images but never calls the deploy workflow, or the deploy manifest still pins the old digest.

Likely causes and fixes: a rebuild without a deploy protects nothing. Deploy rebuilt images through the normal pipeline (with its canary and rollback), and alert when the running image is older than the rebuild cadence allows. See vulnerability and patch management.

docs.title: 70. The auditor asks for every production change in the audit period, with approvals for a sample of 25. Several changes have no review. What went wrong, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the unreviewed changes reached production: direct pushes, console edits, or approvals given in chat.

How to confirm: the commits bypassed branch protection or the resources were changed outside Terraform, as CloudTrail and configuration history show.

Likely causes and fixes: controls that existed on paper only. Require reviews through branch protection, deploy only from CI, detect console changes with configuration rules, and export pull request and pipeline records continuously to an append-only evidence store. See compliance and audit readiness.
