docs.title: Network Security in the Cloud
docs.text:
IAM decides who may call an API; the network decides what can connect to what. Together they give defense in depth: an attacker who steals a credential still needs a network path, and an attacker who finds an open port still needs a credential. This lesson treats the cloud network as a security control rather than plumbing.

It covers private subnets for data tiers, security groups and network ACLs used deliberately, ingress and egress control, private endpoints and PrivateLink, administrative access with bastions compared with Session Manager and identity-aware proxies, VPNs, zero trust, encryption in transit inside the VPC, segmentation, and the flow and DNS logs that show what actually happened. VPC basics (subnets, route tables, gateways, and the security group table) are in cloud building blocks; hands-on server firewalls are in setting up a production server.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Anything reachable from the internet is found within hours by automated scanners that sweep the whole IPv4 address space. A database with a public IP and a weak password, an SSH port open to the world, or an admin panel on a forgotten instance is not "hidden"; it is in someone's list. Most cloud network incidents come from a short list of mistakes: something public that should not be, a flat network where one compromised host reaches every other, and unrestricted outbound traffic that lets an attacker pull tools in and push data out.

The network also limits the damage of application bugs. A server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw lets an attacker make TaskFlow API send requests on their behalf; whether that reaches the instance metadata service, an internal admin API, or an attacker's server depends on network and metadata settings, not on the bug.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google BeyondCorp. In BeyondCorp: A New Approach to Enterprise Security (;login:, 2014), Google explains that once a perimeter is breached "an attacker has relatively easy access to a company's privileged intranet", and describes removing the requirement for a privileged intranet by moving corporate applications to the internet behind checks on users and devices. This is the origin of most zero-trust access products.
  • NIST zero trust architecture. NIST SP 800-207 (August 2020) defines zero trust as moving defenses "from static, network-based perimeters to focus on users, assets, and resources", with "no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location."
  • AWS IMDSv2. The AWS Security Blog post Add defense in depth against open firewalls, reverse proxies, and SSRF vulnerabilities (2019) explains why the metadata service now starts sessions with an HTTP PUT that returns a token: open WAFs, reverse proxies, and most SSRF paths cannot send that request, so they cannot fetch the instance role's credentials.
  • AWS Session Manager. The Session Manager documentation states that it provides node access "without the need to open inbound ports, maintain bastion hosts, or manage SSH keys", with access decided by IAM and session activity logged.
  • AWS VPC Encryption Controls. AWS announced in November 2025 a VPC setting that can monitor whether traffic is encrypted in transit and, in enforce mode, prevent resources that do not encrypt traffic, a sign that "encrypted inside the VPC" is becoming an auditable property.

Popular tools and providers: AWS security groups, network ACLs, VPC Block Public Access, AWS Network Firewall, Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall, VPC endpoints and PrivateLink, Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, AWS Verified Access, and AWS Client VPN; Google Cloud firewall rules, Private Service Connect, and Identity-Aware Proxy; Azure network security groups, Azure Firewall, Private Link, and Azure Bastion; Cloudflare Access and Tunnel; WireGuard and Tailscale; Istio and Linkerd for mutual TLS between services.

docs.title: Two layers: who may call, and what may connect
docs.text: Layer Control Stops Identity IAM policies, SSO, MFA Calls by principals without permission Network edge Only load balancers and CDNs are public; WAF, DDoS protection Direct access to servers and databases from the internet Inside the VPC Security groups by reference, isolated data subnets Lateral movement from one compromised host to everything Outbound Egress rules, VPC endpoints, DNS and domain filtering Data exfiltration, malware downloads, callbacks Transport TLS and mutual TLS, provider encryption Reading or tampering with traffic on the wire Visibility Flow logs, DNS query logs, threat detection Attacks that would otherwise go unnoticed

docs.title: Zones: public, private, and isolated
docs.text:
• Public subnets hold only what must accept internet traffic: load balancers and NAT gateways. Nothing else gets a public IP.
  • Private app subnets hold the API tasks, which accept traffic only from the load balancer's security group.
  • Isolated data subnets have no route to an internet gateway or NAT at all. The database accepts connections only from the API's security group or through a private endpoint.
  • Account-level guardrails catch mistakes: VPC Block Public Access can block internet gateway traffic for a whole account with explicit exclusions, and S3 creates new buckets with public access blocked by default.

docs.title: Security groups and network ACLs as security controls
docs.text:
Security groups are stateful allow-lists attached to network interfaces; network ACLs are stateless, ordered allow and deny rules on subnets. The comparison table is in cloud building blocks. From a security point of view:

  • Reference groups, not addresses. "The API accepts 3000 from the load balancer's group" stays correct as tasks come and go, and it reads like a policy: identity-like rules at the network layer.
  • Know the defaults. The default security group allows all traffic between its members and all outbound traffic, and every new security group starts with an outbound rule that allows everything. Terraform's aws_security_group removes that default egress rule, so egress must be declared explicitly, which is what you want.
  • Use NACLs for coarse, subnet-wide decisions, such as denying an address range during an incident or making the data subnets refuse anything from the public subnets. Their explicit deny is something security groups cannot express.
  • Treat rules as code. Keep them in Terraform, review them in pull requests, and let an IaC scanner fail changes that open administrative ports to 0.0.0.0/0 (Checkov's CKV_AWS_24 does this for port 22).

docs.title: Egress control
docs.text:
Inbound rules get attention; outbound rules usually stay "allow all". Yet outbound access is how a compromised container downloads tools, reaches a command-and-control server, or uploads stolen data, and how an SSRF bug reaches places it should not. Options, from coarse to fine:

Mechanism Filters by Good for Limits Security group egress rules IP ranges, prefix lists, other groups Limiting tiers to the ports and peers they need Cannot express domain names VPC endpoints Destination service (S3, Secrets Manager, ECR) Keeping AWS API traffic off the internet and NAT Only for services with endpoints Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall Domain names in DNS queries Blocking known-bad domains or allowing only listed ones A client can still connect to a raw IP address AWS Network Firewall or an egress proxy Domain via TLS SNI or HTTP Host, IPs, protocols Allowlisting the third-party APIs a service calls Cost and operational effort NAT gateway alone Nothing Giving private subnets outbound access Not a security control

For TaskFlow, the API needs AWS APIs (through endpoints), MongoDB (through a private endpoint), and a payment provider (through the filtered egress path). Everything else can be denied. Cost points the same way: NAT gateways charge per hour and per gigabyte processed, an S3 gateway endpoint has no additional charge, and interface endpoints charge per hour and per gigabyte, so moving heavy AWS API traffic to endpoints often lowers the bill while it removes an internet path.

Two controls protect the instance role's credentials from SSRF: require IMDSv2, which needs a token obtained with a PUT request (an account default, or a declarative policy across an organization), and keep the metadata hop limit low on hosts that do not run containers. On ECS and EKS, task and pod credentials come from the platform, not from the instance's metadata, which is another reason to give each workload its own role.

docs.title: Private connectivity: endpoints and PrivateLink
docs.text:
• Gateway endpoints (S3 and DynamoDB) add routes to a route table. Traffic to the service never leaves the AWS network or touches the NAT gateway.
  • Interface endpoints (AWS PrivateLink) place network interfaces with private IPs in your subnets for services such as Secrets Manager, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, and STS. With private DNS enabled, the normal service hostname resolves to those private IPs, so SDKs need no changes.
  • PrivateLink to partners: many SaaS providers, MongoDB Atlas among them, offer private endpoints, so the database never needs a public address.
  • Endpoint and resource policies form a data perimeter. An endpoint policy can limit which buckets or principals the endpoint may be used for, and a bucket policy can require aws:SourceVpce so the bucket is reachable only through your endpoint. Remember that aws:SourceIp is not present in requests that arrive through a VPC endpoint, so IP-based bucket policies and endpoints do not mix.

docs.title: Administrative access without open ports
docs.text:
A bastion host (jump box) is a hardened server with SSH open to known addresses, used to reach private servers. It works, but it is an internet- facing server to patch, SSH keys to issue and revoke, and logs that live on the box an attacker would target. Managed alternatives remove all three:

  • AWS Systems Manager Session Manager: the SSM agent on the instance makes an outbound connection; users start shell or port-forwarding sessions through the AWS API, authorized by IAM (so by SSO and MFA), with shell sessions logged to S3 or CloudWatch Logs and every session start in CloudTrail. AWS notes that session logging does not cover port-forwarding or SSH sessions, whose contents are encrypted end to end.
  • EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint: SSH or RDP to instances without public IPs and without a bastion, controlled by IAM, with every connection attempt logged to CloudTrail.
  • Google Cloud Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding: the VM has no external IP; its firewall accepts SSH only from IAP's range 35.235.240.0/20, and users need the roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor role.
  • Azure Bastion provides the same managed pattern on Azure.

Server-side SSH hardening and ProxyJump are covered in SSH and remote access.

docs.title: VPNs and zero trust
docs.text:
A VPN extends a private network to a laptop (client VPN) or connects two networks (site-to-site VPN). Site-to-site VPNs remain the normal way to link an office or data center to a VPC. As a way to give people access to applications, a client VPN has a structural weakness: one check at the edge admits the user to a network, and the network then trusts them. Protocol details are in VPNs and tunneling.

Zero trust removes that implicit trust. Each request is authenticated and authorized on its own merits, using the user's identity, the device's state, and context such as time and location, and access is granted per application rather than per network. In practice:

  • For people: identity-aware proxies (Google IAP, AWS Verified Access, Cloudflare Access) put internal tools behind SSO and device checks instead of behind a VPN.
  • For services: every call carries a workload identity, usually through mutual TLS issued by a service mesh or the platform, and the receiving service authorizes the caller, not just the source IP.
  • For networks: segmentation still matters as a second layer; zero trust does not mean "flat network", it means the network is not the only check.

docs.title: Encryption in transit inside the VPC
docs.text:
Is traffic inside a VPC already encrypted? Partly, and the details matter for audits. AWS documents that all traffic between Availability Zones is encrypted, and that many current instance types (Nitro-based) automatically encrypt traffic between instances with 256-bit AEAD encryption when both sides meet the requirements. VPC Encryption Controls can report which flows are encrypted and, in enforce mode, block resources that are not.

Application-level TLS is still the norm for three reasons: it protects against anyone inside the network (including a compromised host) and not just against the physical link; it authenticates the server, and with mutual TLS the client; and it does not depend on instance types and configuration that can change. For TaskFlow that means TLS from the load balancer to the tasks when the data is sensitive, TLS to MongoDB (managed MongoDB services typically require it), and mTLS between services if a mesh is introduced. Termination choices are in TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Visibility: flow logs and DNS logs
docs.text:
• VPC Flow Logs record metadata for IP traffic on a VPC, subnet, or interface: addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, and whether the traffic was ACCEPTed or REJECTed. They contain no payloads. Send them to the log archive account.
  • Route 53 Resolver query logs record DNS lookups, which often reveal malware and exfiltration before any connection succeeds.
  • Amazon GuardDuty uses CloudTrail management events, VPC Flow Logs, and DNS query logs as its foundational data sources to flag, for example, instances talking to known malicious addresses.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use Avoid Public web traffic A load balancer or CDN in public subnets; WAF in front Public IPs on application servers Database access from the app Security group reference or a private endpoint in isolated subnets A public database endpoint "protected" by an IP allowlist Calling AWS APIs from private subnets VPC endpoints Sending S3 or ECR traffic through NAT Shell access for engineers Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, or IAP SSH open to 0.0.0.0/0; long-lived personal keys Internal tools for staff An identity-aware proxy with SSO A client VPN that exposes the whole network Office or data center to cloud Site-to-site VPN or a dedicated link Exposing internal services publicly instead Outbound third-party calls Domain allowlisting for sensitive tiers Assuming NAT filters anything

A small team with one service can start with the zones, security groups by reference, endpoints for AWS APIs, and Session Manager; domain-level egress filtering and a mesh are worth their cost when the data is sensitive or the number of services grows.

docs.title: Private AWS access and tight egress for the API tier
docs.text:
The security groups aws_security_group.api and the VPC module come from the reference architecture in cloud building blocks.

# infra/network-security.tf
data "aws_region" "current" {}

# S3 through a gateway endpoint: a route, no internet path, no NAT charges
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = module.vpc.vpc_id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.${data.aws_region.current.region}.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = module.vpc.private_route_table_ids
}

# Secrets Manager through an interface endpoint (PrivateLink)
resource "aws_security_group" "endpoints" {
  name        = "taskflow-endpoints"
  description = "Interface endpoints, reachable only from the API tasks"
  vpc_id      = module.vpc.vpc_id
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule" "endpoints_from_api" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.endpoints.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.api.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 443
  to_port                      = 443
  description                  = "HTTPS from the API tasks only"
}

resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "secretsmanager" {
  vpc_id              = module.vpc.vpc_id
  service_name        = "com.amazonaws.${data.aws_region.current.region}.secretsmanager"
  vpc_endpoint_type   = "Interface"
  subnet_ids          = module.vpc.private_subnets
  security_group_ids  = [aws_security_group.endpoints.id]
  private_dns_enabled = true
}

# Egress for the API: only what it needs (Terraform removed the default allow-all)
resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "api_to_endpoints" {
  security_group_id            = aws_security_group.api.id
  referenced_security_group_id = aws_security_group.endpoints.id
  ip_protocol                  = "tcp"
  from_port                    = 443
  to_port                      = 443
  description                  = "AWS APIs through interface endpoints"
}

resource "aws_vpc_security_group_egress_rule" "api_to_s3" {
  security_group_id = aws_security_group.api.id
  prefix_list_id    = aws_vpc_endpoint.s3.prefix_list_id
  ip_protocol       = "tcp"
  from_port         = 443
  to_port           = 443
  description       = "S3 through the gateway endpoint"
}

# Flow logs for the whole VPC, delivered to the log archive account's bucket
resource "aws_flow_log" "vpc" {
  vpc_id                   = module.vpc.vpc_id
  traffic_type             = "ALL"
  log_destination_type     = "s3"
  log_destination          = var.flow_logs_bucket_arn
  max_aggregation_interval = 60
}
  • The gateway endpoint exports a prefix list of S3's addresses in the Region, so the egress rule can say "S3 on 443" without hard-coding IPs.
  • The interface endpoint has its own security group that accepts HTTPS only from the API, and private DNS makes the SDK's normal Secrets Manager hostname resolve to it.
  • The API's remaining egress rules (to the database's private endpoint and to the egress filter for the payment provider) follow the same pattern; anything not listed is dropped.
  • Flow logs capture every flow with a one-minute aggregation interval (the default is ten minutes), which helps during investigations.

docs.title: A bucket reachable only through your VPC endpoint
docs.text:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "DenyInsecureTransport",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-exports",
        "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-exports/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "Bool": {
          "aws:SecureTransport": "false"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "DenyAccessOutsideTheVpcEndpoint",
      "Effect": "Deny",
      "Principal": "*",
      "Action": "s3:*",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-exports",
        "arn:aws:s3:::taskflow-prod-exports/*"
      ],
      "Condition": {
        "StringNotEquals": {
          "aws:SourceVpce": "vpce-<endpoint-id>"
        },
        "ArnNotLike": {
          "aws:PrincipalArn": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/storage-admin"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

The first statement refuses plain HTTP. The second denies every request that does not arrive through the named endpoint, unless it comes from the storage-admin role (both conditions must be true for the deny to apply), so a stolen credential used from a laptop is useless against this bucket. Two cautions: test with the exception role first, because a mistake can lock everyone out, including the console; and do not apply it to the uploads bucket, because browsers upload there directly with presigned URLs and their requests never pass through your endpoint. AWS services that read the bucket on your behalf may need their own exception.

docs.title: Session Manager instead of SSH
docs.text:
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Sid": "StartSessionsOnTaskflowNodes",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "ssm:StartSession",
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ec2:eu-west-1:123456789012:instance/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "ssm:resourceTag/app": "taskflow"
        }
      }
    },
    {
      "Sid": "AllowedSessionDocuments",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": "ssm:StartSession",
      "Resource": [
        "arn:aws:ssm:eu-west-1:123456789012:document/SSM-SessionManagerRunShell",
        "arn:aws:ssm:eu-west-1:*:document/AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost"
      ]
    },
    {
      "Sid": "ManageOwnSessionsOnly",
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "ssm:TerminateSession",
        "ssm:ResumeSession",
        "ssmmessages:OpenDataChannel"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:ssm:*:*:session/*",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "ssm:resourceTag/aws:ssmmessages:session-id": "${aws:userid}"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

Attached to the on-call permission set, this allows sessions only to instances tagged app=taskflow, only with the standard shell and remote-port-forwarding documents (the * in the account field covers documents owned by AWS), and lets users end or resume only their own sessions, following AWS's sample policies.

# A shell on a private instance: no inbound port, no SSH key
aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id>

# Forward a private service to the laptop (here the API's internal port)
aws ssm start-session --target <instance-id> \
  --document-name AWS-StartPortForwardingSessionToRemoteHost \
  --parameters '{"host":["api.internal.example.com"],"portNumber":["3000"],"localPortNumber":["3000"]}'
curl http://localhost:3000/healthz

The instance needs the SSM agent, an instance role that allows it to register with Systems Manager, and a path to the Systems Manager endpoints (through NAT or, better, interface endpoints for ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages). Security groups need no inbound rule at all.

docs.title: IAP TCP forwarding on Google Cloud
docs.text:
# Allow SSH only from IAP's forwarding range
gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-ssh-ingress-from-iap \
  --direction=INGRESS --action=allow --rules=tcp:22 \
  --source-ranges=35.235.240.0/20

# Grant one engineer the right to open tunnels
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding <project-id> \
  --member=user:oncall@example.com --role=roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor

# SSH through IAP; the VM has no external IP
gcloud compute ssh taskflow-worker-1 --zone=europe-west1-b --tunnel-through-iap

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give public IPs only to load balancers, CDNs, and NAT gateways; keep data stores in subnets with no internet route.
  • Write security group rules by reference to other groups, keep them in code, and scan them in pull requests.
  • Declare egress explicitly: VPC endpoints for AWS APIs, private endpoints for databases, and a filtered path for the few external APIs a service needs.
  • Require IMDSv2 everywhere and give every workload its own role.
  • Replace bastions and open SSH with Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint, or IAP, behind SSO and MFA.
  • Put internal tools behind an identity-aware proxy rather than a VPN that opens the whole network.
  • Use TLS for every hop that carries sensitive data, even inside the VPC.
  • Turn on flow logs and DNS query logs, store them in the log archive, and run threat detection over them.
  • Use account-level guardrails such as VPC Block Public Access and S3 Block Public Access as a safety net under every change.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The database is suddenly reachable from the internet. Detect: a posture tool (Security Hub CSPM, a third-party scanner) reports a public endpoint or 0.0.0.0/0 on the database port, or flow logs show accepted connections from unknown addresses. Cause: a "temporary" rule added in the console for debugging. Fix: remove the rule, check the database logs for access, move debugging to Session Manager port forwarding, and enforce through IaC scanning and drift detection.
  • An SSRF bug was used to read instance credentials. Detect: GuardDuty reports credentials of an instance role used from an address outside AWS, or application logs show requests to 169.254.169.254. Cause: IMDSv1 still allowed, so a single forged GET returned the role's credentials. Fix: rotate by stopping the instance or revoking role sessions, require IMDSv2 by account default, fix the SSRF, and narrow the role.
  • A compromised container downloaded tools and sent data to an unknown host. Detect: flow logs and DNS query logs show connections to a never-seen domain; GuardDuty flags the destination. Cause: allow-all egress through NAT. Fix: isolate the task, rotate its credentials, then add endpoints and domain allowlisting so only required destinations are reachable.
  • Builds became slow and expensive after moving to private subnets. Detect: NAT gateway processed bytes and charges jump; most traffic goes to ECR and S3. Cause: image pulls and artifacts flow through NAT. Fix: add an S3 gateway endpoint and interface endpoints for ECR, which cuts NAT data processing and removes an internet path.
  • Session Manager cannot reach a new instance. Detect: the instance is missing from Fleet Manager and sessions fail to start. Cause: no instance role permission to register, no route to the Systems Manager endpoints, or the agent is not running. Fix: attach the managed instance policy to the role, add the ssm, ssmmessages, and ec2messages endpoints, and check the agent.
  • After adding a VPC-endpoint-only bucket policy, nobody can open the bucket in the console. Detect: AccessDenied for every human request. Cause: console and laptop requests do not come through the endpoint, and the exception was missing or misspelled. Fix: recover through the exception role (or the root user of that account if needed), correct the condition, and test policies on a non-critical bucket first.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Public, private, and isolated subnets: Subnets with a route to an internet gateway, with outbound access through NAT only, and with no internet route at all.
  • Security group: A stateful allow-list on network interfaces.
  • Network ACL: A stateless, ordered allow and deny list on subnets.
  • Egress filtering: Restricting which destinations workloads may connect to.
  • VPC endpoint: A private path from a VPC to a service; gateway endpoints add routes, interface endpoints add private network interfaces (PrivateLink).
  • Data perimeter: Policies that keep data reachable only by trusted identities from expected networks.
  • Bastion host: A hardened server used as a jump point into private networks.
  • Identity-aware proxy: A gateway that authorizes each request by identity and context before passing it to an internal application.
  • Zero trust: A security model that grants no implicit trust based on network location.
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): TLS in which both client and server present certificates.
  • SSRF: Server-side request forgery; tricking a server into making requests for the attacker.
  • IMDSv2: The token-based version of the EC2 instance metadata service.
  • Flow logs: Records of IP traffic metadata with accept or reject decisions.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating "in a private subnet" as "secure"; private resources still need narrow security groups, IAM, and TLS.
  • Leaving egress open because "outbound is harmless".
  • Believing a NAT gateway is a firewall.
  • Restricting S3 by aws:SourceIp and then adding a VPC endpoint, where that key is not present.
  • Keeping a bastion with SSH open to the world "for emergencies".
  • Assuming zero trust means removing all network segmentation.
  • Assuming traffic inside a VPC needs no TLS, without checking what the provider encrypts and what auditors require.
  • Enabling flow logs but never reading or alerting on them.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a NAT gateway not a security control, and what would you add to restrict TaskFlow API's outbound traffic?
  2. Describe the three subnet zones for TaskFlow and which resources belong in each.
  3. How does IMDSv2 defend against SSRF, and why do ECS task roles reduce the risk further?
  4. Compare a bastion host, Session Manager, and IAP on inbound exposure, key management, and audit logging.
  5. A bucket policy allows access only from the office IP range. After a VPC endpoint is added, the API can no longer read the bucket. Why, and how do you fix it?
  6. What does zero trust change for an engineer who uses a VPN today to reach internal tools?
  7. A team moved its build agents to private subnets and the NAT data processing charges jumped. Which traffic is the likely cause, and which change makes it cheaper and safer?
  8. Is traffic between two instances in the same VPC encrypted? What would you check, and why might you add TLS anyway?

docs.title: Security in the Delivery Pipeline
docs.text:
Every change to TaskFlow API passes through the same pipeline: a commit on a laptop, a pull request, a build, a deploy to staging, and a release. Each of those steps is a place where a machine can look for a class of security problem faster and more consistently than a human reviewer. This lesson explains what each kind of scanner looks at, where it belongs in the pipeline, and how to turn its output into decisions that a team will actually act on.

It covers shifting security left, static analysis (SAST) with CodeQL and Semgrep, dependency scanning (SCA) with npm audit, Dependabot, Snyk, and OSV-Scanner, secret scanning, infrastructure-as-code (IaC) scanning with Checkov and Trivy, container image scanning, and dynamic testing (DAST) of the running API with ZAP. Hardening the pipeline itself (least-privilege tokens, pinned actions, OIDC, SBOMs, and provenance) is covered in pipeline and supply chain security; this page summarizes it and links there.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most successful attacks do not need a novel technique. They use a known vulnerability in a dependency, an injection flaw a scanner would have flagged, a key committed to a repository, or a cloud resource left open to the internet. The OWASP Top 10:2025 lists Software Supply Chain Failures third and Security Misconfiguration second, both of which automated checks catch well.

The cheapest moment to fix such a problem is while its author is still in the pull request: the context is fresh, the change is small, and nothing is deployed. The same flaw found in production needs an incident, a hotfix, and perhaps a breach notification. That is the whole argument for scanning in the pipeline.

The opposite failure is just as real. A scanner that floods every pull request with hundreds of old, low-impact, or false findings teaches the team to click past it. Then the one finding that matters is ignored too. Good pipeline security is therefore as much about which findings stop a change as about which tools run.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google: static analysis people actually use. In Lessons from Building Static Analysis Tools at Google (Communications of the ACM, 2018), Google engineers describe surfacing analysis results in code review and requiring checks shown there to produce less than 10% "effective false positives", meaning issues on which developers took no positive action. Precision and timing, not the number of rules, made developers fix issues by their own choice.
  • DORA: security as part of daily work. The DORA capability Pervasive security recommends addressing security early, preapproved libraries and tools, and automated testing at scale, and reports that high-performing teams spend 50 percent less time remediating security issues than low-performing teams.
  • Trivy, March 2026: the scanner is a dependency too. The advisory GHSA-69fq-xp46-6x23 (CVE-2026-33634) describes attackers force-pushing 76 of 77 version tags of aquasecurity/trivy-action and all tags of setup-trivy to an infostealer that ran before the real scan, dumped runner memory, and exfiltrated credentials. It recommends pinning actions to full commit SHAs and treating every secret the affected pipelines could reach as exposed.
  • OWASP Top 10:2025. The 2025 edition adds A03 Software Supply Chain Failures and keeps Broken Access Control first. The categories map well onto pipeline checks (supply chain to SCA and pinning, misconfiguration to IaC scanning, injection to SAST), and equally show what scanners miss: access control and design flaws need tests and review.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub code scanning with CodeQL and Copilot Autofix, Semgrep, SonarQube, Snyk, Dependabot and Renovate, OSV-Scanner, npm audit, GitHub secret scanning and push protection, gitleaks, TruffleHog, Checkov, Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout, KICS, and ZAP.

docs.title: Shift left, and keep scanning on the right
docs.text:
"Shift left" means moving a check as early in the delivery path as it can run, because early feedback is cheap feedback. It does not mean "only left": some problems exist only in a built image, only in a running service, or only after a new CVE is published against code that has not changed in months. A mature pipeline does both.

Scanner Looks at Finds Misses Typical placement SAST Source code Injection paths, unsafe APIs, dangerous data flows Runtime config, broken business rules, most access-control bugs PR (new alerts only) and a full scan on main SCA Lockfiles, manifests, built artifacts Known CVEs in dependencies, licenses Zero-days, flaws in your own code PR, build, and daily rescans Secret scanning Commits, history, images, bundles Tokens and keys in known formats Secrets in unknown formats, secrets only at runtime Pre-commit, push, CI, artifacts IaC scanning Terraform, Kubernetes, Dockerfiles Public buckets, open ports, missing encryption, root containers Console changes (drift), runtime posture PR and plan scan Image scanning Image layers: OS and language packages Known CVEs in the base image and dependencies Application logic After build, then continuous rescans DAST The running app over HTTP Missing headers, injection that shows in responses, exposed endpoints Code paths the scan never reaches Staging after each deploy

docs.title: SAST: following untrusted data through the code
docs.text:
Static application security testing reads source code without running it. Simple linters match patterns line by line. The tools that find real injection bugs go further: they build a model of the program and follow tainted data from a source (anything an attacker controls, such as req.body, headers, or uploaded files) to a sink (an operation that is dangerous with attacker input: a database query, child_process.exec, a redirect, HTML output). If the data reaches the sink without passing a sanitizer (validation, casting, escaping), the tool raises an alert.

This is exactly the NoSQL injection TaskFlow is exposed to. With a JSON body of {"owner": {"$ne": null}}, a handler that passes req.body.owner straight into Task.find() asks MongoDB for every task whose owner is not null. CodeQL's js/sql-injection query covers both SQL and NoSQL queries built from user input. (Express 5's default "simple" query parser no longer turns ?owner[$ne]=x into a nested object, but JSON bodies still carry objects, so validation remains necessary. Mongoose's sanitizeFilter option, off by default, is a useful second layer.)

  • CodeQL turns the code into a database and runs queries over it. GitHub's default setup enables it with no workflow file; advanced setup uses a workflow where you choose languages, query suites (security-extended adds lower-precision queries to the default set), and triggers. For JavaScript and TypeScript, build-mode: none analyzes the source without a build. The actions language analyzes the repository's own workflow files for problems such as script injection.
  • Semgrep matches patterns written to look like the code they find, which makes custom rules cheap: a team can encode its own conventions ("every query on Task must filter by the current user") in a few lines of YAML. The open-source engine is now called Semgrep Community Edition; the commercial platform adds cross-file analysis and triage features.

SAST is weakest where the problem is missing logic rather than bad data flow: an endpoint that never checks whether the caller owns the task looks perfectly normal to a scanner. Those bugs need tests and review, see authentication and authorization.

docs.title: SCA: known vulnerabilities in dependencies
docs.text:
Software composition analysis reads what you depend on (the lockfile, or the packages inside a built image) and matches each package and version against advisory databases such as the GitHub Advisory Database and OSV.dev. It finds nothing new; it tells you which already-published vulnerabilities you ship.

  • npm audit checks the installed tree against the registry's advisory data. --audit-level=high makes it exit non-zero only for high or critical findings, and --omit=dev leaves out development tooling that never runs in production. npm audit fix --force may install semver-major upgrades, so never run it unattended.
  • Dependabot raises alerts, opens security update pull requests, and can group them into one pull request per ecosystem. Security updates are not delayed by the cooldown setting that applies to version updates, and they have their own limit of 10 open pull requests.
  • OSV-Scanner is Google's open-source scanner for the OSV database across many ecosystems. Its pull request workflow compares the base and head branches and fails only on vulnerabilities the change introduces.
  • Snyk is a commercial platform with a free tier; snyk test --severity-threshold=high reports only high and critical issues, and --fail-on=upgradable fails only when a fix exists.

A CVE in a dependency is not automatically exploitable in your service: the vulnerable function may never be called. That judgment (and how to record it with VEX) belongs to vulnerability and patch management. Dependency review on pull requests, lockfiles, npm ci, and Dependabot's configuration are covered in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Secret scanning
docs.text:
Secret scanners look for strings in the shape of known credentials (AWS access key IDs, GitHub tokens, Stripe keys, private key headers) and for high-entropy strings. Layer them, because each layer catches what the previous one let through: a pre-commit hook on the laptop, platform push protection on push, a CI job that scans the commits in each push or pull request, and a scan of built images and frontend bundles. TruffleHog can also verify a candidate by calling the provider's API, which separates live keys from test strings; --results=verified,unknown reports both verified and unverifiable ones.

A found secret is an incident, not a lint error: revoke and rotate first, then clean up. The full runbook is in secrets management.

docs.title: IaC scanning: misconfiguration before it exists
docs.text:
TaskFlow's infrastructure is Terraform, so a public bucket or a security group open to 0.0.0.0/0 exists in a pull request before it exists in the cloud. IaC scanners parse the code (or the JSON output of terraform show -json for a plan, where computed values are known) and evaluate policies against each resource.

  • Checkov ships with a large policy library (IDs such as CKV_AWS_24, "no security group allows ingress from 0.0.0.0/0 to port 22"), supports Terraform, CloudFormation, Kubernetes, Helm, and Dockerfiles, can write a baseline of today's findings so only new ones fail, and accepts inline skip comments with a written reason.
  • Trivy scans IaC with trivy config (and in trivy fs with the misconfig scanner). The older tfsec project has been folded into Trivy, and its README asks users to migrate.

IaC scanning cannot see changes made by hand in the console. Cloud posture tools (AWS Security Hub CSPM, AWS Config rules, Google Security Command Center, Microsoft Defender for Cloud) check the live environment; see compliance and audit readiness.

docs.title: Container image scanning
docs.text: An image contains an operating system's packages as well as TaskFlow's node_modules, and either can carry known CVEs. The scan belongs right after the build, before the image is pushed for deployment, with a gate on fixable high and critical findings (--ignore-unfixed in Trivy): blocking on a CVE that has no fix only teaches people to disable the check. Registries and runtime tools rescan stored and running images, because a clean image becomes vulnerable the day a new CVE is published. Base image choice, digests, and signing are covered in container security.

docs.title: DAST: testing the running API on staging
docs.text:
Dynamic application security testing sends real HTTP requests to a running service. It finds what only appears at runtime: missing security headers, verbose error pages, injection that changes a response, endpoints that should not be reachable. It needs an environment that behaves like production, so it runs against staging after each deploy, never against production without explicit approval, and only ever against systems you own or are authorized to test.

ZAP (formerly OWASP ZAP; since 2024 the open-source project is maintained by its core team as "ZAP by Checkmarx") provides packaged scans:

  • The baseline scan spiders the target for one minute by default and runs only passive checks; it does not attack.
  • The API scan imports an OpenAPI, SOAP, or GraphQL definition and runs an active scan tuned for APIs, which sends attack payloads.
  • The full scan spiders and actively attacks a web application; use it on a disposable environment because it submits forms and calls endpoints with junk data.

A rules file sets each alert to IGNORE, INFO, WARN, or FAIL, and the scripts exit with 1 when any FAIL rule matches and 2 when there are only warnings.

docs.title: Gating without drowning the team
docs.text:
A gate is a rule that turns findings into a pass or a fail. The useful question for each finding is not "is it bad?" but "should it stop this change?"

The techniques that keep gates trustworthy:

  • Severity thresholds per tool. Block on high and critical; report medium and low. Calibrate per tool, because severities are not comparable across scanners.
  • New findings only. Code scanning shows alerts inside the pull request's diff; Semgrep scans pull requests diff-aware; OSV-Scanner compares base and head; Checkov and gitleaks accept baseline files. Existing debt becomes tickets with deadlines instead of a wall of red on every unrelated change.
  • Fixable only, for dependencies and images. A gate the author cannot satisfy is a gate that gets bypassed.
  • Exceptions with expiry. Accepting a risk is legitimate when it is written down: who accepted it, why, and until when. .trivyignore lines accept an exp: date; Checkov skip comments carry a reason; ZAP rules files say IGNORE per alert. Review them like code.
  • Monitor before enforcing. Run a new scanner in report-only mode for a few weeks, tune or disable noisy rules, then turn on blocking.
  • Measure the noise. Track how many findings are dismissed as false positives, how long fixes take, and how many critical findings are open.

A worked example shows why precision matters. Suppose a scanner raises 400 findings a week, 70% of them false positives, and each takes 6 minutes to triage:

before:  400 findings x 6 min = 2,400 min = 40 hours/week
         wasted on false positives: 280 x 6 min = 28 hours/week

after (new findings only, tuned to 10% false positives):
          25 findings x 6 min =   150 min = 2.5 hours/week
         wasted on false positives:   2.5 x 6 min = 15 min/week

The tuned gate catches the same new problems for a sixteenth of the attention, and people trust it.

docs.title: One place for results: SARIF
docs.text: Most scanners can write SARIF (Static Analysis Results Interchange Format), a JSON standard for findings with locations, rules, and severity. Uploading SARIF to GitHub code scanning with github/codeql-action/upload-sarif puts CodeQL, Semgrep, Checkov, and Trivy results in one list with annotations on pull requests, deduplication across runs, and dismissal reasons that are auditable later. The upload needs security-events: write, and each tool should use its own category so results do not overwrite each other.

docs.title: The pipeline is attack surface too
docs.text: Every scanner runs with the job's token and whatever secrets the job can read, so the security pipeline needs the same hardening as the release pipeline: read-only permissions by default, third-party actions pinned to full commit SHAs, no secrets in jobs that run fork pull request code, OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, and SBOMs and provenance for what ships. The Trivy advisory also shows the limit of pinning: workflows pinned to recent trivy-action commits were safe, but older pinned commits still pulled the setup-trivy action through a mutable reference, and that was retagged too. A pin protects only the code it names, so pin scanner versions as well and prefer actions that pin their own dependencies. Those controls are explained in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Minimum sensible set Add later Small team, one repository CodeQL default setup, Dependabot alerts and security updates, push protection, npm audit gate Secret scan in CI, image scan Containers and Terraform in production The above plus Trivy image scan, Checkov or Trivy config on PRs, TruffleHog or gitleaks Semgrep custom rules, DAST on staging Regulated data or many teams All of the above, SARIF in one place, exceptions with expiry, DAST after each staging deploy Metrics on noise and fix time, a security champions program

Avoid these common traps:

  • Do not run active DAST or full scans against production; use staging or a disposable environment with seeded data.
  • Do not block pull requests on existing findings in legacy code; baseline them and schedule the fixes.
  • Do not stack three SCA tools on the same lockfile; they report the same CVEs three times. Pick one source of truth and one gate.
  • Do not give scanners secrets in workflows that run code from forks.

docs.title: Practical examples
docs.text: The examples use major-version tags for GitHub's own actions, matching the rest of this site, and full commit SHAs with a version comment for third-party actions, as recommended after the Trivy compromise.

docs.title: A security workflow for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/security.yml
name: security

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  schedule:
    - cron: "17 3 * * 1"             # weekly: new CVEs appear in unchanged code

permissions:
  contents: read                     # every job starts read-only

jobs:
  codeql:
    name: CodeQL (${{ matrix.language }})
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write         # upload results to code scanning
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        language: [javascript-typescript, actions]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: github/codeql-action/init@v4
        with:
          languages: ${{ matrix.language }}
          build-mode: none
          queries: security-extended
      - uses: github/codeql-action/analyze@v4
        with:
          category: /language:${{ matrix.language }}

  dependencies:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci --ignore-scripts   # the audit needs the tree, not install scripts
      - run: npm audit --audit-level=high --omit=dev

  secrets:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0             # scan every commit in the push or pull request
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: trufflesecurity/trufflehog@3bd2b5887eb0efb8fa18bfd1d296032924e4ffdc # v3.99.9
        with:
          version: 3.99.9            # pin the scanner image as well as the action
          extra_args: --results=verified,unknown

  iac:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: bridgecrewio/checkov-action@3f0caf0c3aa9f56ade6b49f6e60b63aaeafb75a3 # v12.3141.0
        with:
          directory: infra
          framework: terraform
          baseline: infra/.checkov.baseline
          output_format: cli,sarif
          output_file_path: console,checkov.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        if: success() || failure()   # upload even when the gate fails
        with:
          sarif_file: checkov.sarif
          category: checkov

  image:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: docker build --tag taskflow-api:ci .
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: taskflow-api:ci
          version: v0.76.2           # pin the Trivy binary, not only the action
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true       # gate only on findings that have a fix
          exit-code: "1"
          trivyignores: .trivyignore
          format: sarif
          output: trivy.sarif
          limit-severities-for-sarif: true
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        if: success() || failure()
        with:
          sarif_file: trivy.sarif
          category: trivy-image

What each part does:

  • permissions: contents: read at the top makes every job read-only; only the jobs that upload SARIF get security-events: write.
  • The CodeQL matrix analyzes the JavaScript code and the workflow files themselves. On pull requests, its alerts appear inside the diff.
  • The dependencies job fails on high or critical advisories in production dependencies. --ignore-scripts avoids running package install scripts in a job that only needs the dependency tree.
  • The secrets job lets TruffleHog work out the commit range from the event (the pull request's base and head, or the pushed commits; the weekly run scans the branch) and fail on verified or unverifiable secrets.
  • The iac job fails only on findings that are not in the committed baseline and uploads all results for triage.
  • The image job builds the image locally and fails on fixable high and critical CVEs. In a real pipeline, scan the exact image the build job produced (by digest) instead of building it twice.
  • The schedule trigger rescans main weekly, because new advisories arrive even when the code does not change.

docs.title: A custom Semgrep rule for TaskFlow's data access
docs.text:
The rule encodes a TaskFlow convention: MongoDB filters are never built from raw request input.

# .semgrep/taskflow.yml
rules:
  - id: taskflow-mongo-filter-from-request
    languages: [javascript, typescript]
    severity: ERROR
    message: >-
      MongoDB filter built from raw request input. A value such as
      {"$ne": null} changes what the query matches. Validate and cast the
      input (for example with zod) before using it in a filter.
    metadata:
      cwe: "CWE-943: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements in Data Query Logic"
    patterns:
      - pattern-either:
          - pattern: |
              $MODEL.$METHOD({..., $KEY: req.query.$FIELD, ...}, ...)
          - pattern: |
              $MODEL.$METHOD({..., $KEY: req.body.$FIELD, ...}, ...)
      - metavariable-regex:
          metavariable: $METHOD
          regex: ^(find|findOne|countDocuments|updateOne|updateMany|deleteOne|deleteMany|findOneAndUpdate)$

// src/routes/tasks.js (excerpt)
const unsafe = await Task.find({ owner: req.body.owner });          // flagged
const owner = z.string().parse(req.body.owner);                     // throws on objects
const safe = await Task.find({ owner });                            // not flagged

The {..., $KEY: req.body.$FIELD, ...} pattern matches an object literal with that property anywhere in it, and the metavariable-regex limits the rule to query methods. Run it next to the community rules in CI:

# .github/workflows/semgrep.yml
name: semgrep
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  semgrep:
    if: github.actor != 'dependabot[bot]'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      security-events: write
    container:
      image: semgrep/semgrep:1.185.0  # pin the engine version
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - run: semgrep scan --config p/default --config .semgrep/ --error --sarif-output=semgrep.sarif
      - uses: github/codeql-action/upload-sarif@v4
        if: success() || failure()
        with:
          sarif_file: semgrep.sarif
          category: semgrep

--error makes Semgrep exit with 1 when it has findings, which fails the job, and --sarif-output writes a SARIF copy for code scanning while the log keeps the readable output. Semgrep's own documentation runs the CLI in the semgrep/semgrep image like this, and skips Dependabot's pull requests, which cannot read the repository's secrets.

docs.title: IaC scanning with a baseline and justified skips
docs.text:
# Run once, review the output, and commit infra/.checkov.baseline
checkov --directory infra --framework terraform --create-baseline

# Locally or in CI: only findings that are not in the baseline fail
checkov --directory infra --framework terraform --baseline infra/.checkov.baseline

# infra/uploads.tf (excerpt)
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "uploads" {
  #checkov:skip=CKV_AWS_144:Uploads are copied to the backup account by AWS Backup, not by replication
  #checkov:skip=CKV2_AWS_62:No service consumes object events from this bucket
  bucket = "taskflow-prod-uploads"
}

The baseline freezes today's debt so the gate only fails on new problems; the debt itself gets tickets. A skip comment sits inside the resource and states the reason, so reviewers and auditors can judge it later.

docs.title: Accepting a finding with an expiry date
docs.text:
# .trivyignore
# CVE in a library function TaskFlow never calls; vendor fix expected this quarter.
# Accepted by the API team lead. Review at expiry.
CVE-2026-12345 exp:2026-12-31

After the expiry date, Trivy reports the CVE again and the gate fails, so an accepted risk cannot quietly become permanent. (The CVE ID above is a placeholder.)

docs.title: DAST against staging after each deploy
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/dast-staging.yml
name: dast-staging
on:
  workflow_run:
    workflows: [deploy-staging]
    types: [completed]
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 2 * * *"              # nightly, against the current staging build

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  zap-api-scan:
    if: github.event_name == 'schedule' || github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7      # only to read .zap/rules.tsv from the default branch
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: zaproxy/action-api-scan@5158fe4d9d8fcc75ea204db81317cce7f9e5453d # v0.10.0
        env:
          ZAP_AUTH_HEADER_VALUE: Bearer ${{ secrets.STAGING_SCAN_TOKEN }}
        with:
          target: https://staging-api.example.com/openapi.json
          format: openapi
          rules_file_name: .zap/rules.tsv
          fail_action: true
          allow_issue_writing: false

# .zap/rules.tsv (tab-separated: alert ID, action, name)
10038   IGNORE  (Content Security Policy (CSP) Header Not Set)
10021   FAIL    (X-Content-Type-Options Header Missing)
10035   FAIL    (Strict-Transport-Security Header)
90020   FAIL    (Remote OS Command Injection)
90022   WARN    (Application Error Disclosure)
  • The scan imports TaskFlow's OpenAPI definition and actively tests each operation on staging, authenticated as a dedicated low-privilege test user whose token is stored as STAGING_SCAN_TOKEN.
  • fail_action: true turns a failing scan into a failed job; allow_issue_writing: false keeps findings out of public issues.
  • The rules file ignores the CSP alert for JSON responses (TaskFlow API serves no HTML), fails on missing transport headers and command injection, and only warns on error disclosure while that is being fixed.

docs.title: Dependabot security updates in one pull request
docs.text:
# .github/dependabot.yml (excerpt)
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: npm
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    groups:
      npm-security:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns: ["*"]

With Dependabot security updates enabled for the repository, this groups every npm security fix into one pull request, which is easier to test and merge than ten separate ones. Version updates, cooldowns, and action pinning are configured as shown in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run each scanner where its feedback is cheapest, and keep rescanning main, registries, and production for newly published CVEs.
  • Block only on new, high-severity, high-confidence, fixable findings; report everything else into tickets with deadlines.
  • Introduce every new scanner in report-only mode, tune it, then enforce.
  • Record accepted risks with an owner, a reason, and an expiry date, and review them like code.
  • Send all results to one place (SARIF in code scanning or one platform) so findings are deduplicated and triaged once.
  • Write custom rules for your own conventions; they are often the highest-signal checks a team has.
  • Pin third-party scanner actions to commit SHAs and pin scanner versions; give scanner jobs the least permissions and no secrets.
  • Run DAST only against environments you own, starting with passive scans and keeping active scans on staging or disposable environments.
  • Measure false-positive rates and time to fix, and remove rules nobody acts on.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A new scanner went live and the pull request queue stopped. Detect: dozens of PRs fail the same new check, and developers ask for admin merges. Cause: the gate blocks on all existing findings, not only on those the change introduces. Fix: switch to report-only, create a baseline, block only new findings, and file the backlog as tickets with owners.
  • A critical CVE blocks every build, but no fixed version exists. Detect: the image or dependency gate fails on the same CVE in every pipeline, and the advisory lists no patched release. Cause: the gate does not distinguish fixable from unfixable findings. Fix: gate on fixable findings (--ignore-unfixed), add a time-boxed exception for this CVE with a mitigation note, and subscribe to the advisory.
  • Credentials leaked from CI after a scanner action was compromised. Detect: an advisory such as the Trivy one names your action, and workflow logs show runs during the exposure window. Cause: the action was referenced by a mutable tag and ran with secrets in reach. Fix: rotate every secret those workflows could read, pin actions to full SHAs, pin scanner versions, and remove secrets from scanner jobs.
  • The nightly DAST scan filled staging with junk and broke demos. Detect: thousands of strange tasks and users appear after the scan window. Cause: an active scan submits real requests to every operation. Fix: run active scans against a disposable environment or a dedicated tenant, reset data afterwards, and exclude destructive operations that need separate tests.
  • SARIF upload fails with "Resource not accessible by integration". Detect: the scan succeeds but the upload step fails, and no alerts appear in code scanning. Cause: the job lacks security-events: write (private repositories may also need actions: read), or the event is a fork pull request with a read-only token. Fix: grant the permission on that job only, and accept that fork pull requests report results through logs.
  • Developers dismiss every alert from one SAST rule as a false positive. Detect: the dismissal rate for one rule is close to 100%. Cause: a low-precision rule or a sanitizer the tool does not recognize. Fix: tune or disable the rule, model the project's sanitizer, and track dismissal rates per rule.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Shift left: Moving a check earlier in the delivery path, where feedback is faster and fixes are cheaper.
  • SAST: Static application security testing; analysis of source code without running it.
  • SCA: Software composition analysis; finding known vulnerabilities and licenses in dependencies.
  • DAST: Dynamic application security testing; probing a running application over its interfaces.
  • IaC scanning: Policy checks on infrastructure code before it is applied.
  • Source, sink, sanitizer: Where untrusted data enters, where it is dangerous, and what makes it safe in between.
  • Taint tracking: Following untrusted data through a program from sources to sinks.
  • Baseline: A recorded set of existing findings that a gate ignores so that only new findings fail.
  • Effective false positive: A finding on which developers take no positive action, whatever its technical correctness.
  • SARIF: A JSON standard format for static analysis results.
  • Security gate: A pipeline rule that fails a change based on findings.
  • Exception (risk acceptance): A recorded, time-limited decision to accept a known finding.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a clean scan means secure code; scanners miss design and access-control flaws.
  • Blocking on every severity and every existing finding, which trains people to bypass the gate.
  • Treating a dismissed finding as a closed one, with no reason or expiry.
  • Running active DAST against production, or against systems you are not authorized to test.
  • Scanning only on pull requests and never rescanning, so new CVEs in unchanged code go unnoticed.
  • Referencing scanner actions by tag and giving them secrets they do not need.
  • Installing several overlapping tools and triaging the same CVE three times.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does "shift left" not remove the need for scans after deployment? Give two kinds of problem that only appear later.
  2. Explain sources, sinks, and sanitizers using TaskFlow's Task.find({ owner: req.body.owner }) as the example.
  3. A scanner reports 300 findings a week, 60% false positives, 5 minutes of triage each. How much time is wasted per week on false positives, and what would a new-findings-only gate with 10% false positives at 20 findings a week cost? (900 minutes, or 15 hours; 20 x 5 = 100 minutes in total, of which 10 minutes are false positives.)
  4. Which findings should block a merge, and what should happen to the others?
  5. Why is --ignore-unfixed a sensible default for an image gate, and what risk does it leave open?
  6. What is the difference between ZAP's baseline, API, and full scans, and where should each run?
  7. What did the 2026 Trivy compromise teach about running security tools in CI?
  8. Why should every accepted risk have an owner and an expiry date?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• GitHub Docs: About code scanning with CodeQL and workflow configuration options
  • Semgrep: CLI reference and sample CI configurations
  • OSV-Scanner GitHub Action
  • Checkov: suppressing and skipping policies
  • Trivy: filtering findings
  • ZAP: baseline scan and API scan
  • OWASP DevSecOps Guideline
  • Next: identity and access management. Back to the DevSecOps and cloud security overview.

docs.title: Vulnerability and Patch Management
docs.text:
Scanners in the pipeline answer one question: which known vulnerabilities are in what we ship? This lesson is about everything that happens after that answer. Which findings actually matter, how fast each one must be fixed, and how every layer (npm packages, the Node.js runtime, the base image, the hosts, and the managed services underneath) stays patched month after month. New CVEs are published every day against code that has not changed, so this is continuous work, not a gate you pass once.

It covers CVEs and the databases around them, CVSS v4.0 severity, EPSS exploit probability, CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog and SSVC decisions, reachability and VEX, remediation deadlines by risk, operating system patching with unattended-upgrades and managed patch services, base image rebuild cadence, dependency update automation with Dependabot and Renovate, SBOMs as the inventory that answers "are we affected?", and how to handle a critical zero-day, with Log4Shell as the public case. Scanner placement and gates are covered in security in the delivery pipeline, and generating SBOMs in pipeline and supply chain security; this page uses their output.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Many breaches do not need an unknown flaw; they use a known one that already had a fix. In 2017, Equifax was alerted to a critical Apache Struts vulnerability on March 8 and emailed more than 400 employees an order to patch within 48 hours, as its policy required. The email never reached the person responsible for the consumer dispute portal, and the follow-up scan was not configured to look at every public-facing system. Attackers exploited the unpatched portal from May 13 to July 30, and the breach affected about 147 million people. The policy existed; the inventory, the verification, and the ownership did not.

The opposite failure is just as common: treating every finding as urgent. FIRST counts about 61,000 published CVEs in a 12-month period, just over 10% of them rated Critical by CVSS, while only about 1.5% to 3% of published vulnerabilities see exploitation activity in any 30-day window. A team that patches strictly by CVSS spends most of its effort on vulnerabilities nobody attacks and still misses exploited ones that are not rated Critical: HTTP/2 Rapid Reset (CVE-2023-44487) and the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2024-1086 are both in KEV with High scores of 7.5 and 7.8. CISA, citing Verizon's 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report, notes that only 26% of KEV-listed vulnerabilities were fully remediated in 2025, with a median of 43 days to full resolution.

Good vulnerability management therefore has three parts: know exactly what runs where (inventory), decide which vulnerabilities are exploited or likely to be (prioritization), and make routine patching so automatic that the long tail disappears without meetings.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Equifax and the FTC (2019). The FTC's complaint and its business guidance post describe a 48-hour patch policy that failed because the alert missed the system's owner, the scanner was not configured for all assets, and there was no accurate inventory of public-facing systems running Apache Struts (CVE-2017-5638). The unpatched system went unnoticed for more than four months; suspicious traffic was found only after expired security certificates were replaced.
  • Log4Shell and the Cyber Safety Review Board (2022). The CSRB review of the December 2021 Log4j event calls Log4j an "endemic vulnerability" whose unpatched versions will remain "perhaps a decade or longer". Many organizations could not find where they ran it, and of the groups representing organizations that already used SBOMs, none reported having used them to find vulnerable Log4j deployments. Its recommendations include an accurate asset inventory, a documented vulnerability response program, and better SBOM tooling.
  • CISA BOD 26-04 (June 2026). Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk replaced the fixed deadlines of BOD 22-01 and BOD 19-02 for US federal civilian agencies with a risk table: public exposure, KEV status, automatable exploitation, and technical impact decide whether a fix is due in 3, 14, or 60 days or at the next system upgrade. CISA's Patch Smarter, Not Harder reports that in one large agency's first analysis about 1% of vulnerability instances fell into the three-day class and over 60% could wait for the next upgrade.
  • FIRST EPSS. The Using EPSS guide explains why a probability of exploitation complements CVSS severity: confirmed exploitation (such as a KEV entry) takes precedence over any score, and an EPSS score should never be multiplied by a CVSS score to invent a "risk score".
  • NIST NVD (2026). Since April 15, 2026 the NVD prioritizes three groups for enrichment: KEV entries (with a goal of one business day), software used by the federal government, and critical software as defined by Executive Order 14028. Other CVEs are "not scheduled for immediate enrichment", and NIST no longer routinely adds its own severity score when the CVE already has one. A process that waits for an NVD score can wait forever.

Popular tools and providers: Dependabot and Renovate, Trivy, Grype, OSV-Scanner, Snyk, Amazon Inspector, Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Google Security Command Center, OWASP Dependency-Track, AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager, Azure Update Manager, Google Cloud VM Manager, unattended-upgrades, and the public data feeds: CVE records, the GitHub Advisory Database, OSV.dev, CISA KEV, and FIRST EPSS.

docs.title: From disclosure to a fix in production
docs.text:
A vulnerability passes through several hands before it reaches a backlog:

  1. A researcher finds it and reports it privately to the maintainer (coordinated disclosure).
  2. A CVE Numbering Authority (CNA), often the vendor or project itself (the Apache Software Foundation is one), assigns an ID such as CVE-2021-44228 and publishes a CVE record with a description, affected versions, and usually a CVSS score and a CWE.
  3. Advisories follow: the vendor's own, the GitHub Advisory Database (GHSA-... IDs mapped to exact npm package versions), OSV.dev, distribution trackers such as Debian's and Ubuntu's, and, for priority CVEs, NVD enrichment.
  4. A fixed version ships, scanner databases update, and your next scan matches the vulnerable version in a lockfile, an image, or a host.
  5. You triage, fix, deploy, and verify.

The exposure window runs from public disclosure (or first exploitation) until the fix is running in production. Steps 1 to 4 belong to others; measure the rest, because that is the part you control: time to detect, time to decide, time to deploy.

Source What it tells you Notes CVE record (cve.org) ID, description, affected versions, the CNA's CVSS and CWE The canonical identifier NVD (NIST) Enrichment: CVSS, CWE, affected product data Since April 2026, routinely only for priority CVEs GitHub Advisory Database, OSV.dev Exact vulnerable and fixed package versions per ecosystem What npm audit, Dependabot, and OSV-Scanner match against Distribution trackers Whether the distro's build is affected, and the fixed package The source for OS package findings in images and hosts CISA KEV Exploited in the wild, plus a required action 1,779 entries in the November 2026 catalog FIRST EPSS Probability of exploitation activity in the next 30 days Daily, for every published CVE CISA Vulnrichment (SSVC) Exploitation, automatable, technical impact Added to CVE records by CISA

A CWE names a class of weakness (Log4Shell is CWE-917, expression language injection); a CVE is one concrete vulnerability in one product.

docs.title: CVSS: severity, not risk
docs.text:
The Common Vulnerability Scoring System, maintained by FIRST, is at version 4.0 (released November 2023). Version 3.1 scores are still what most records and tools show.

CVSS v4.0 metric group Describes Who can fill it in Base Intrinsic properties: attack vector, complexity, privileges, user interaction, impact The CNA or vendor Threat Exploit maturity: Attacked, Proof-of-Concept, or Unreported Anyone with threat intelligence Environmental Your controls and how much the affected system matters to you Only you Supplemental Extra context (safety, automatable, recovery, and more) that does not change the score The CNA or vendor; you decide how to use it

FIRST asks that every published number names the groups behind it: CVSS-B (base only), CVSS-BT, CVSS-BE, or CVSS-BTE. The optional severity scale is None 0.0, Low 0.1-3.9, Medium 4.0-6.9, High 7.0-8.9, and Critical 9.0-10.0.

Log4Shell's NVD vector shows how much a base score encodes:

CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H   = 10.0 Critical

AV:N  attack vector: network           PR:N  no privileges needed
AC:L  attack complexity: low           UI:N  no user interaction
S:C   scope changed (impact spreads)   C:H/I:H/A:H  total loss of
                                                    confidentiality,
                                                    integrity, availability

A base score describes a generic worst case, not your deployment. Most published scores are CVSS-B, and the same CVE can carry different scores from the CNA, NVD, and a Linux distribution. The specification itself says consumers "should enrich the Base metrics with Threat and Environmental metric values". Use CVSS to order work inside a deadline class, not to set the deadline.

docs.title: EPSS: how likely exploitation is
docs.text:
The Exploit Prediction Scoring System "estimates the probability that a published CVE will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days". FIRST publishes a score between 0 and 1 and a percentile for every CVE every day; version 5 (model v2026.06.15) has published scores since 15 June 2026. The percentile says what share of all CVEs score at or below this one. Because exploitation is rare, the distribution is long-tailed: FIRST gives the mean as about 2.8% and the median as about 0.7%.

curl -s "https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss?cve=CVE-2021-44228,CVE-2024-29041"
# {"status":"OK","status-code":200, ... "data":[
#   {"cve":"CVE-2024-29041","epss":"0.007860000","percentile":"0.566660000","date":"2026-11-13"},
#   {"cve":"CVE-2021-44228","epss":"0.999990000","percentile":"1.000000000","date":"2026-11-13"}]}

Express's open redirect, CVE-2024-29041, scores below 0.8% yet sits at the 57th percentile: most CVEs score lower still. Scores move as evidence appears: FIRST's Log4Shell write-up shows the score at 0.355 the day after publication, 0.633 when exploit code reached ExploitDB, and 0.944 when a Metasploit module appeared on 17 December 2021. Small probabilities also add up: 100 open vulnerabilities at 0.05 each mean an expected 5 exploited in a month, and 1 - 0.95^100 ≈ 99.4% odds that at least one is.

FIRST's guidance for combining signals: effort equivalent to patching all CVSS Critical findings corresponds to an EPSS threshold of roughly 0.04 (about the 90th percentile); confirmed exploitation overrides the score; and EPSS must not be multiplied by CVSS, which is an ordinal scale.

docs.title: KEV: known exploitation
docs.text:
CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog lists vulnerabilities that meet three criteria: an assigned CVE ID, reliable evidence of active exploitation in the wild, and a clear remediation action. It started on 3 November 2021 with 287 entries; the 10 November 2026 version holds 1,779, of which 361 are marked as known to be used in ransomware campaigns. Each entry has a dateAdded, a requiredAction, a dueDate for federal agencies, knownRansomwareCampaignUse, notes, CWE IDs, and a forensicTriage flag. The whole catalog is one JSON file that a script can read: https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json.

KEV is the strongest single signal you have. It is small enough to drive to zero, and CISA "strongly recommends" that every organization include a requirement to address KEV vulnerabilities immediately in its vulnerability management plan. Entries go back years (the oldest CVE in it is from 2002), so a KEV check also finds old, forgotten software.

docs.title: SSVC and BOD 26-04: decisions instead of scores
docs.text:
SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization), developed by Carnegie Mellon's SEI with CISA, replaces a number with a decision. CISA's tree uses exploitation status, technical impact, automatable, mission prevalence, and public well-being impact, and ends in one of four outcomes: Track, Track*, Attend (remediate sooner than standard timelines), or Act (as soon as possible, with leadership attention).

CISA's Vulnrichment program adds SSVC data to CVE records as an extra container, so the decision points are machine-readable. The record for Log4Shell, from the public CVE API, contains:

{"type": "ssvc", "content": {"id": "CVE-2021-44228", "role": "CISA Coordinator",
  "options": [{"Exploitation": "active"}, {"Automatable": "yes"}, {"Technical Impact": "total"}],
  "version": "2.0.3"}}

BOD 26-04, issued on 10 June 2026 and binding only on US federal civilian agencies, turns these signals into deadlines. It is the most concrete public example of a risk-based SLA, and a good model to adapt:

Publicly exposed In KEV Automatable Technical impact Deadline (calendar days) Yes Yes Yes Total 3 days and forensic triage Yes Yes Yes Partial 3 days Yes Yes No Total 3 days and forensic triage Yes Yes No Partial 14 days Yes No Yes Total 3 days Yes No Yes Partial 14 days Yes No No Total 14 days Yes No No Partial 60 days No Yes Yes Total 3 days and forensic triage No Yes Yes Partial 14 days No Yes No Total 14 days No Yes No Partial 14 days No No Yes Total 60 days No No Yes Partial 60 days No No No Total Fix on system upgrade No No No Partial Fix on system upgrade

Details that make it work:

  • Exposure is a property of your asset, not of the CVE: "publicly exposed" means reachable by unauthenticated or untrusted parties over public networks. Only your inventory can answer it.
  • The clock starts when the CVE is added to KEV or when you identify it, whichever comes first, and the deadline changes when the facts do: taking a system off the internet lengthens it, a new KEV entry shortens it.
  • Missing metadata defaults to caution: without SSVC data, treat the vulnerability as not automatable but with total technical impact.
  • Forensic triage means checking whether the system was already compromised, not only patching it. CISA's implementation guidance suggests scoping within the first two hours after a KEV addition, preserving evidence and patching critical systems within 2 to 24 hours, and an escalation decision within 48 to 72 hours.

docs.title: Reachability and VEX: is it exploitable here?
docs.text:
A scanner finding means "this package at this version matches an advisory". It does not mean the vulnerability can be exploited in your service. Common reasons it cannot:

  • The component is not in the running artifact: a development dependency, a build-stage tool, or a package removed by a multi-stage build.
  • The vulnerable code is not present: a scanner flags linux-libc-dev (kernel headers) in an image for a Linux kernel CVE, but containers run on the host's kernel.
  • The vulnerable function is never called, or attacker-controlled input never reaches it.
  • A mitigation already blocks it (a disabled feature, a configuration flag).

VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange) records such a decision in a machine-readable form, so scanners stop reporting it and auditors can see why.
