The OpenVEX specification (v0.2.0) defines four statuses: not_affected, affected, fixed, and under_investigation. A not_affected statement needs a justification or an impact statement; the justification labels are component_not_present, vulnerable_code_not_present, vulnerable_code_not_in_execute_path, vulnerable_code_cannot_be_controlled_by_adversary, and inline_mitigations_already_exist. CycloneDX and CSAF can carry the same information. Trivy reads all three formats with --vex (still marked experimental) and filters findings whose package URL (PURL) matches a not_affected statement; Grype also supports OpenVEX.

Treat VEX as a reviewed claim, not a mute button. Reachability analysis is easy to get wrong, a refactor can make dead code live, and a KEV entry deserves a second reviewer before anyone declares it unexploitable. Put an owner and a review date on every statement, exactly like the exceptions in security in the delivery pipeline.

docs.title: Remediation deadlines that teams can meet
docs.text:
TaskFlow adopts the BOD 26-04 table as its policy, with three additions:

  1. Ordering inside a class follows EPSS, then CVSS: two findings due in 14 days are fixed most-likely-exploited first.
  2. Payment scope: PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirement 6.3.3 requires patches for critical vulnerabilities (as ranked by the entity's own process under 6.3.1) within one month of release. Nothing rated critical in the cardholder data environment may wait for "next upgrade" if that is later.
  3. "Fix on system upgrade" needs upgrades to happen. A weekly image rebuild and a monthly host image make that class mean "within 7 days" for containers and "within 30 days" for hosts. Without a cadence it means "never".

The cadence is what makes the table affordable. Suppose a weekly scan of TaskFlow's images and hosts shows 180 open findings: 2 in the 3-day class, 9 in the 14-day class, 25 in the 60-day class, and 144 that can wait for the next upgrade. With weekly image rebuilds and monthly host images, the 144 disappear on schedule with no tickets at all. Engineers spend attention on 36 findings, and urgent attention on 2.

Every finding that cannot meet its deadline gets a written exception: an owner, the reason, the compensating control (a WAF rule, a disabled feature, a network restriction), and an expiry date. The numbers worth watching are the count of open KEV findings (target: zero), the share of findings fixed within their deadline per class, the age of the oldest overdue finding, and scan coverage: the share of assets that were scanned at all. A system the scanner never sees always reports zero findings, as Equifax learned.

docs.title: Patching every layer
docs.text:
Layer TaskFlow example Who fixes it How Application dependencies Express, Mongoose, and their transitive packages The team Bot pull requests, CI, normal deploy Language runtime Node.js 24 inside the image The team Move the base image to a Node release with the fix Container OS packages Debian packages in node:24-slim Image publisher fixes, the team rebuilds Scheduled rebuilds and digest-bump pull requests Host OS Ubuntu on VMs and Kubernetes worker nodes The team unattended-upgrades or a patch service, or a new image and instance replacement Cluster Kubernetes version and node images The team, with the provider Planned upgrades following provider releases Managed services MongoDB Atlas, load balancers, caches The provider Maintenance windows you choose Hypervisor and hardware The cloud's hosts The provider Invisible to you

The shared responsibility model decides where your work stops: on managed services you pick the maintenance window and keep major versions supported, and the provider does the patching.

docs.title: Operating system patching: in place or by replacement
docs.text:
In place (mutable hosts). On Ubuntu Server, unattended-upgrades is installed and enabled by default: it applies security updates once a day, configured in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades and 50unattended-upgrades. It does not reboot unless Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot is set to "true", and it signals pending reboots through /var/run/reboot-required. Since Ubuntu 24.04, needrestart restarts services that use updated libraries automatically. The step-by-step setup is in setting up a production server.

For fleets, a managed service schedules and reports the same work:

  • AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager runs Scan (report) or Install operations with the AWS-RunPatchBaseline document. Patch baselines auto-approve patches a chosen number of days after release; AWS recommends patch policies in Quick Setup to cover every account and Region. Two warnings from its documentation: AWS does not test patches before making them available, and the default RebootOption, RebootIfNeeded, reboots after any installed patch, whether or not the patch requires it. It uses the publisher's severity, not CVSS or NVD scores, and "compliant" with a baseline does not mean secure.
  • Azure Update Manager assesses Windows and Linux machines (every 24 hours with periodic assessment) and installs updates in maintenance windows you define, including Azure Arc servers outside Azure.
  • Google Cloud VM Manager runs patch jobs and scheduled patch deployments across Compute Engine VMs and reports patch compliance.

Do not run two patchers on one host. Patch Manager's documentation warns that a patch already installed by unattended-upgrades can stop its operation from rebooting the node as expected.

By replacement (immutable hosts). Bake a new golden image every week with the latest updates (see immutable infrastructure and GitOps), then roll it through the fleet with an instance refresh or rolling update (see autoscaling server fleets). Patching becomes a deploy: tested in staging, rolled out gradually, and reversible. Containers are always immutable: never run apt-get upgrade inside a running container; rebuild the image and redeploy.

Either way, a patch is not active until the process restarts. An updated OpenSSL library on disk does nothing for a Node.js process that loaded the old one, and a kernel fix needs a reboot. Restart or replace instances in batches behind the load balancer, one Availability Zone at a time.

docs.title: Base images: rebuild on a schedule, not only on code changes
docs.text:
Docker's build best practices put it plainly: "Docker images are immutable. Building an image is taking a snapshot of that image at that moment." A TaskFlow image built in March still carries March's OpenSSL in November, however many fixes Debian has shipped since. Upstream images move on their own schedule: the Docker Official Images maintainers "strive to publish updated images at least monthly for Debian" and rebuild earlier for a critical security need. Your image picks those fixes up only when you rebuild it.

Two ways to pull fixes in, and many teams use both:

  • Tag plus scheduled rebuild. FROM node:24-slim and a weekly build with --pull (fetch the newest image behind the tag) and --no-cache (rerun the apt-get steps instead of reusing cached layers) picks up base and OS package fixes automatically, at the cost of exact reproducibility. npm ci still installs exactly what the lockfile says, so npm fixes arrive through dependency pull requests, not rebuilds.
  • Digest pin plus bot pull requests. FROM node:24-slim@sha256:... always builds the same base; Renovate (pinDigests) or Dependabot opens a pull request when the tag's digest changes, and the update goes through CI and review like any change. Reproducible, but a fix waits for the bot's schedule and the merge. Pinning is covered in container security.

Three rules keep this honest:

  • A rebuild is not a deploy. A fresh image sitting in the registry protects nothing. Deploy rebuilt images through the normal pipeline, and alert on the age of the image actually running.
  • Runtimes have end-of-life dates. Node.js 20 has reached end of life and gets no more security fixes; the Node.js project says production applications should only use Active LTS or Maintenance LTS releases. Major runtime upgrades need planning, not a bot.
  • Smaller images mean fewer findings. Every package you do not ship is one you never patch; multi-stage builds onto slim or distroless images remove compilers, shells, and header packages from production.

docs.title: Dependency updates on autopilot
docs.text:
Bots turn new advisories into pull requests. Dependabot's configuration, grouping, and cooldown are covered in pipeline and supply chain security; its security updates are not delayed by the cooldown, and up to 10 can be open at once. Renovate offers the same ideas with more control:

  • vulnerabilityAlerts configures pull requests for known vulnerabilities. By default they ignore the schedule and any minimumReleaseAge, are created immediately, and add a [SECURITY] suffix to the commit message.
  • osvVulnerabilityAlerts: true adds advisories from OSV.dev.
  • minimumReleaseAge (for example "3 days") holds back ordinary version updates until a release has aged, which gives the community time to spot and pull a malicious or broken release before you adopt it. Security fixes skip the wait.
  • automerge merges low-risk updates (patch versions, digest bumps) only after the branch's tests pass; Renovate's ignoreTests defaults to false.
  • lockFileMaintenance regularly refreshes the lockfile, which updates transitive dependencies that no direct upgrade touches.

When a vulnerable package is buried several levels deep and its parent has not released a fix, npm's overrides field in the root package.json forces a patched version for the whole tree. Treat it as temporary: a comment, an owner, and removal once the parent catches up.

docs.title: SBOMs: the inventory that answers "are we affected?"
docs.text:
When the next Log4Shell is announced, the first question is "where do we run it?" An SBOM per artifact turns that into a query instead of a week-long search. SBOMs are generated in CI (see pipeline and supply chain security); using them well means:

  • Keep one per release and per deployed image digest, so you can answer for what is running, not only for what is on main.
  • Rescan stored SBOMs every day. trivy sbom and Grype read CycloneDX and SPDX, so yesterday's releases are checked against today's advisories without rebuilding them. Platforms such as OWASP Dependency-Track ingest CycloneDX SBOMs and "continuously match every component against multiple vulnerability sources".
  • Cover more than the app. Host images, CI runners, self-hosted tools, and vendor software need inventories too; Syft can catalog a directory or a whole host filesystem, and suppliers can be asked for their SBOMs.
  • Practice the query. The CSRB found SBOM users who still did not use their SBOMs during Log4Shell. A query nobody has run before an incident is not a capability.

The two standard formats are CycloneDX (version 1.7, released October 2025, and also standardized by Ecma International as ECMA-424) and SPDX (version 3.0; SPDX is also the international standard ISO/IEC 5962:2021). npm sbom currently writes CycloneDX 1.5 or SPDX 2.3, which every major scanner reads.

docs.title: Handling a critical zero-day: Log4Shell
docs.text:
What happened. Log4j 2, a popular open-source Java logging library built into thousands of other software packages, evaluated ${jndi:ldap://...} lookups inside logged strings. Any attacker who could get a string into a log line (a header, a username, a chat message) could make the server load and run remote code: CVSS 10.0, network-reachable, no authentication. Details became public on 9 December 2021; Apache published version 2.15.0 and the CVE on 10 December, and CISA added it to KEV the same day. The first fix was incomplete: CVE-2021-45046 led to 2.16.0, which removed message lookups, CVE-2021-45105 (a denial of service) to 2.17.0, and CVE-2021-44832 to 2.17.1. Teams upgraded up to four times in under three weeks.

Why it was hard. Log4j was rarely a direct dependency. It sat inside other Java libraries, vendor appliances, build servers, and search and logging clusters. TaskFlow API is Node.js and never loaded Log4j, but its platform could still run Java tools, so the honest answer to "are we affected?" needed an inventory of everything, not one lockfile.

A runbook that works for the next one:

  1. Declare an incident and run it like one: a lead, a channel, a cadence of updates (see incident response and postmortems).
  2. Scope: query every stored SBOM, image, and host inventory for the component; list vendor products and ask their vendors.
  3. Rank exposure: internet-facing systems first, then systems that process untrusted input indirectly (logs, queues), then the rest.
  4. Mitigate now, while patching: the CSRB lists the measures defenders used: egress filtering, deleting the JndiLookup class, hot patches, WAF rules that block exploit strings (see edge protection), and taking systems offline. WAF rules are a virtual patch; attackers obfuscate payloads, so they buy time and nothing more. The KEV entry put it precisely: temporary mitigations were acceptable only until updates were available.
  5. Patch, rebuild, redeploy, and expect follow-up releases: watch the advisory and re-run the scope query after each one.
  6. Verify by rescanning running artifacts, not only repositories.
  7. Hunt: assume exposed systems may already be compromised and check (forensic triage); patching does not remove an attacker who got in first.
  8. Communicate and learn: customer notices if needed, then a postmortem that adds the missing inventory or automation.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Small team, containers on a managed platform Dependabot or Renovate, weekly image rebuild and deploy, KEV check in CI, managed databases Fleet of VMs you patch in place A patch service (Patch Manager, Azure Update Manager, VM Manager) with baselines, maintenance windows, and compliance reports Immutable VM or Kubernetes fleet Weekly golden images or node images rolled with instance refresh or node upgrades; no in-place patching Payment card data in scope Documented risk ranking (PCI DSS 6.3.1), critical patches within one month (6.3.3), evidence of both Hundreds of findings and no prioritization KEV first, then the BOD 26-04-style table with EPSS ordering; cadence for the rest Many products, many teams Central SBOM store with continuous rescans (Dependency-Track or a scanner platform), findings routed to owning teams

What not to do:

  • Do not patch running containers or hand-edit servers in an immutable fleet; the next deploy silently reverts it.
  • Do not automerge major versions or let bots deploy straight to production without tests and a staged rollout.
  • Do not chase "zero CVEs by CVSS"; it buries the few findings attackers use.
  • Do not mark findings not_affected without evidence and a reviewer.
  • Do not let NVD scores gate your process; many new CVEs will not get one.

docs.title: Turn a scan into a patch plan with KEV, EPSS, and SSVC
docs.text:
The script reads a Trivy JSON report, produced with trivy image --format json --output trivy-report.json <image>, looks up each CVE in the KEV feed, FIRST's EPSS API, and CISA's SSVC data in the CVE record, and applies the BOD 26-04 table. Exposure comes from you, because only you know whether the service is internet-facing. It uses only Node.js 24 built-ins.

// scripts/triage.mjs: turn a Trivy JSON report into a patch plan with deadlines
// usage: node scripts/triage.mjs trivy-report.json [--exposed]
import { readFile } from "node:fs/promises";

const KEV_FEED =
  "https://www.cisa.gov/sites/default/files/feeds/known_exploited_vulnerabilities.json";
const EPSS_API = "https://api.first.org/data/v1/epss";
const CVE_API = "https://cveawg.mitre.org/api/cve/";

// Deadlines from BOD 26-04 Table 1, keyed by exposed, in KEV, automatable
// (Y/N each) and technical impact (T = total, P = partial).
// days: null means "fix at the next scheduled rebuild or upgrade".
const D = (days, triage = false) => ({ days, triage });
const DEADLINES = {
  YYYT: D(3, true), YYYP: D(3), YYNT: D(3, true), YYNP: D(14),
  YNYT: D(3), YNYP: D(14), YNNT: D(14), YNNP: D(60),
  NYYT: D(3, true), NYYP: D(14), NYNT: D(14), NYNP: D(14),
  NNYT: D(60), NNYP: D(60), NNNT: D(null), NNNP: D(null),
};

async function getJson(url) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(20_000) });
  if (res.status === 404) return null;
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`${res.status} ${res.statusText}: ${url}`);
  return res.json();
}

async function loadKev() {
  const feed = await getJson(KEV_FEED);
  return new Set(feed.vulnerabilities.map((v) => v.cveID));
}

async function loadEpss(cves) {
  const scores = new Map();
  for (let i = 0; i < cves.length; i += 100) {   // the cve parameter takes up to 2,000 characters
    const body = await getJson(`${EPSS_API}?cve=${cves.slice(i, i + 100).join(",")}`);
    for (const row of body?.data ?? []) scores.set(row.cve, Number(row.epss));
  }
  return scores;
}

// CISA's Vulnrichment adds SSVC decision points to CVE records as an ADP container.
async function loadSsvc(cve) {
  const record = await getJson(CVE_API + cve);
  const adp = record?.containers?.adp?.find((a) => a.providerMetadata?.shortName === "CISA-ADP");
  const ssvc = adp?.metrics?.find((m) => m.other?.type === "ssvc")?.other.content;
  const options = Object.assign({}, ...(ssvc?.options ?? []));
  return {
    // No metadata yet: treat as not automatable but total impact, as CISA's guidance does
    automatable: options.Automatable === "yes",
    totalImpact: options["Technical Impact"] !== "partial",
  };
}

async function mapLimit(items, limit, fn) {
  const results = new Array(items.length);
  let next = 0;
  const worker = async () => {
    while (next < items.length) {
      const i = next++;
      results[i] = await fn(items[i]);
    }
  };
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: Math.min(limit, items.length) }, worker));
  return results;
}

const [file, ...flags] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!file) {
  console.error("usage: node scripts/triage.mjs <trivy-report.json> [--exposed]");
  process.exit(64);
}
const exposed = flags.includes("--exposed");
const report = JSON.parse(await readFile(file, "utf8"));

const findings = (report.Results ?? []).flatMap((result) =>
  (result.Vulnerabilities ?? []).map((v) => ({
    id: v.VulnerabilityID,
    pkg: v.PkgName,
    hasFix: Boolean(v.FixedVersion),
  })),
);
const cves = [...new Set(findings.map((f) => f.id).filter((id) => id.startsWith("CVE-")))];

const [kev, epss, ssvcList] = await Promise.all([
  loadKev(),
  loadEpss(cves),
  mapLimit(cves, 4, loadSsvc),
]);
const ssvc = new Map(cves.map((cve, i) => [cve, ssvcList[i]]));

const yn = (b) => (b ? "Y" : "N");
const plan = findings.map((f) => {
  const s = ssvc.get(f.id) ?? { automatable: false, totalImpact: true };
  const inKev = kev.has(f.id);
  const key = yn(exposed) + yn(inKev) + yn(s.automatable) + (s.totalImpact ? "T" : "P");
  const { days, triage } = DEADLINES[key];
  const due = days === null
    ? "next rebuild"
    : new Date(Date.now() + days * 86_400_000).toISOString().slice(0, 10);
  return { ...f, ...s, inKev, days, triage, due, epss: epss.get(f.id) ?? 0 };
});

// Deadline first; within the same deadline, the likelier exploit first
plan.sort((a, b) => (a.days ?? Infinity) - (b.days ?? Infinity) || b.epss - a.epss);

const cols = [["due", 13], ["id", 16], ["pkg", 16], ["kev", 5], ["epss", 7], ["auto", 5], ["impact", 8], ["fix", 4]];
console.log(cols.map(([name, width]) => name.padEnd(width)).join(""));
for (const p of plan) {
  const row = {
    due: p.due, id: p.id, pkg: p.pkg, kev: p.inKev ? "yes" : "-",
    epss: (Math.floor(p.epss * 1000) / 1000).toFixed(3), auto: p.automatable ? "yes" : "no",
    impact: p.totalImpact ? "total" : "partial", fix: p.hasFix ? "yes" : "NO",
  };
  console.log(cols.map(([name, width]) => String(row[name]).padEnd(width)).join("") +
    (p.triage ? "+ forensic triage" : ""));
}

// A non-zero exit lets a scheduled CI job page someone for 3-day items
process.exitCode = plan.some((p) => p.days === 3) ? 2 : 0;

A run against an older TaskFlow image on 13 November 2026 (EPSS and CISA data change daily, so your numbers will differ):

$ node scripts/triage.mjs trivy-report.json --exposed
due          id              pkg             kev  epss   auto impact  fix
2026-11-16   CVE-2023-44487  libnghttp2-14   yes  0.999  yes  partial yes
2026-11-16   CVE-2024-1086   linux-libc-dev  yes  0.280  no   total   yes + forensic triage
2026-11-16   CVE-2021-44906  minimist        -    0.045  yes  total   yes
2026-11-27   CVE-2022-24999  qs              -    0.156  yes  partial yes
2027-01-12   CVE-2024-29041  express         -    0.007  no   partial yes

Reading the result:

  • CVE-2023-44487 (HTTP/2 Rapid Reset) is in KEV and automatable: 3 days.
  • CVE-2024-1086 is a Linux kernel privilege escalation in KEV, flagged here in linux-libc-dev, the kernel headers package. The container never runs this kernel code, so the image needs a VEX statement (next example) and, better, a multi-stage build that drops the package; the hosts' kernels are a separate asset with their own deadline (not publicly exposed: 14 days).
  • CVE-2021-44906 in minimist (CVSS 9.8, EPSS about 0.045) lands in 3 days because SSVC rates it automatable with total impact, and the service is exposed. If it is only a development dependency, the honest fix is npm ci --omit=dev in the image, which removes it entirely.
  • The same report run without --exposed, as for an internal worker, moves most items to 14 or 60 days and express to the next rebuild.

docs.title: Record a not_affected decision with OpenVEX
docs.text:
Save the statement in the repository (here as .vex/taskflow-api.openvex.json), next to the code it describes. The product @id must be the exact package URL Trivy reports, which is the PkgIdentifier.PURL field in its JSON output.

{
  "@context": "https://openvex.dev/ns/v0.2.0",
  "@id": "https://vex.example.com/taskflow-api/2026-11-13-001",
  "author": "TaskFlow platform team <security@example.com>",
  "timestamp": "2026-11-13T21:00:00Z",
  "version": 1,
  "statements": [
    {
      "vulnerability": { "name": "CVE-2024-1086" },
      "products": [
        { "@id": "pkg:deb/debian/linux-libc-dev@<version-from-the-scan>" }
      ],
      "status": "not_affected",
      "justification": "vulnerable_code_not_present",
      "impact_statement": "linux-libc-dev contains kernel headers only. Containers use the host kernel, which the node image pipeline patches. Review by 2027-02-13 or when the base image changes."
    }
  ]
}

trivy image --vex .vex/taskflow-api.openvex.json \
  --severity HIGH,CRITICAL ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0
# The CVE-2024-1086 finding for linux-libc-dev is filtered out;
# every other finding is reported as before.

The statement matches one package version, so it lapses when the package changes, which forces a fresh look. Review VEX files in pull requests like code, and keep the hosts' kernel patching tracked separately: VEX for the image does not make the host safe.

docs.title: A weekly rebuild that picks up base image fixes
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/rebuild.yml
name: rebuild

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "41 4 * * 1"             # Mondays 04:41 UTC: pick up base image and OS fixes
  workflow_dispatch:                 # and on demand during a zero-day

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: rebuild
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write                # push to GitHub Container Registry
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@f87e5991a6d7451dcb8d9637bfbc97413f497069 # v4.4.1
      - uses: docker/login-action@8aa5831fb8d48d8f76594c7ddde61ae58019f550 # v4.8.0
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          pull: true                 # resolve FROM again: a moved tag brings a patched base
          no-cache: true             # rerun apt-get steps instead of reusing cached layers
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${{ github.sha }}-r${{ github.run_number }}
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@ed142fd0673e97e23eac54620cfb913e5ce36c25 # v0.36.0
        with:
          image-ref: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}
          version: v0.76.2           # pin the Trivy binary, not only the action
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH
          ignore-unfixed: true
          exit-code: "1"
          trivyignores: .trivyignore

  deploy:
    needs: build
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write                # the deploy workflow assumes a cloud role with OIDC
    uses: ./.github/workflows/deploy.yml
    with:
      image-digest: ${{ needs.build.outputs.digest }}

What each part does:

  • The schedule rebuilds even when no code changed, and workflow_dispatch gives the same pipeline an emergency button.
  • pull: true and no-cache: true are the action's equivalents of docker build --pull --no-cache. With a digest-pinned FROM, the base stays the same and only package steps refresh; the base itself then moves through the bot's digest pull requests.
  • The scan gates on fixable high and critical findings for the exact digest that was pushed. A failed scan stops the deploy job; the image stays in the registry but never runs.
  • The deploy job calls the same reusable deploy workflow that releases use (it declares on: workflow_call with an image-digest input), so a patch rollout gets the same canary, checks, and rollback as a feature.
  • The Trivy action is pinned to a full commit SHA. Its tags were force-pushed to a credential stealer in March 2026 (CVE-2026-33634), as security in the delivery pipeline describes.

docs.title: Renovate for security fixes, digests, and safe automerge
docs.text:
// renovate.json5 (JSON5 allows comments)
{
  $schema: "https://docs.renovatebot.com/renovate-schema.json",
  extends: ["config:recommended"],
  osvVulnerabilityAlerts: true,        // add OSV.dev advisories to the platform's alerts
  vulnerabilityAlerts: {
    labels: ["security"],              // security PRs: no schedule, no release-age wait
  },
  minimumReleaseAge: "3 days",         // ordinary updates wait until a release has aged
  pinDigests: true,                    // FROM image:tag@sha256:..., bumped by PRs
  lockFileMaintenance: { enabled: true },  // refresh transitive dependencies weekly
  packageRules: [
    {
      matchUpdateTypes: ["patch", "digest"],
      automerge: true,                 // only after the branch's tests pass
    },
    {
      matchUpdateTypes: ["major"],
      dependencyDashboardApproval: true,   // a human starts every major upgrade
    },
  ],
}

Patch versions and image digests merge themselves once CI is green, major versions wait for someone to approve them on the Dependency Dashboard, and security fixes skip both the schedule and the three-day wait. Pair automerge with a staged rollout so that a bad patch release stops at the canary.

docs.title: Patching a VM fleet with Patch Manager
docs.text:
# Report missing patches on every TaskFlow API instance (no changes, no reboots)
aws ssm send-command \
  --document-name "AWS-RunPatchBaseline" \
  --targets "Key=tag:app,Values=taskflow-api" \
  --parameters "Operation=Scan" \
  --timeout-seconds 600

# Install, a quarter of the fleet at a time; stop at the first failure
aws ssm send-command \
  --document-name "AWS-RunPatchBaseline" \
  --targets "Key=tag:app,Values=taskflow-api" \
  --parameters "Operation=Install,RebootOption=RebootIfNeeded" \
  --max-concurrency "25%" \
  --max-errors "0" \
  --comment "Weekly security patching" \
  --timeout-seconds 600

# Which instances still wait for a reboot, and how many critical gaps remain?
aws ssm describe-instance-patch-states \
  --instance-ids $(aws ec2 describe-instances \
      --filters "Name=tag:app,Values=taskflow-api" "Name=instance-state-name,Values=running" \
      --query 'Reservations[].Instances[].InstanceId' --output text) \
  --query 'InstancePatchStates[*].[InstanceId,InstalledPendingRebootCount,CriticalNonCompliantCount]' \
  --output table

--max-concurrency and --max-errors are the safety rails: with 25% concurrency, three quarters of the instances keep serving while one batch installs and reboots, provided each instance leaves the load balancer before it reboots (for example through a pre-install hook in the AWS-RunPatchBaselineWithHooks document). For a recurring schedule across accounts and Regions, use a patch policy in Quick Setup instead of ad hoc commands.

docs.title: "Are we affected?" across every release
docs.text:
# scripts/affected.sh: which stored SBOMs contain a component, and which versions?
# usage: scripts/affected.sh log4j-core
set -euo pipefail
component="$1"
for sbom in sboms/*.cdx.json; do
  # CycloneDX nests components, so search the whole document
  jq -r --arg name "$component" --arg file "$sbom" \
    '.. | objects | select(.name? == $name and has("purl")) | "\($file)\t\(.version)\t\(.purl)"' \
    "$sbom"
done

# Re-check yesterday's releases against today's advisories, without rebuilding
for sbom in sboms/*.cdx.json; do
  trivy sbom --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed "$sbom"
done

# Host images need inventories too: catalog the filesystem while baking the image
syft / -o cyclonedx-json=host-sbom.cdx.json
grype sbom:./host-sbom.cdx.json

Keep the SBOM store indexed by image digest, so the first output answers "which running services contain it?" rather than "which repositories mention it?".

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep an inventory of every service, image digest, host image, and vendor product, with an owner; you cannot patch what you do not know you run.
  • Check KEV first and drive open KEV findings to zero; then apply a risk table based on exposure, exploitation, automation, and impact.
  • Use EPSS and CVSS to order work inside a deadline, never to replace confirmed exploitation data.
  • Rebuild images and host images on a fixed cadence, deploy them, and alert on the age of what is running.
  • Automate dependency updates, merge low-risk ones on green tests, and delay ordinary version updates by a few days; let security fixes through immediately.
  • Record not_affected decisions as reviewed VEX statements with an owner and a review date.
  • Store an SBOM per release and per deployed digest, rescan them daily, and rehearse the "are we affected?" query.
  • Treat a critical, exploited zero-day as an incident: scope, mitigate, patch, verify, hunt, and communicate.
  • Restart or replace processes after patching; a patch on disk is not a patch in memory.
  • Measure deadline compliance per class, open KEV count, and scan coverage, and report them where leadership sees them.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A KEV vulnerability stayed open for weeks. Detect: the open-KEV count on the dashboard is above zero for longer than the deadline, and the finding has no assignee. Cause: findings go to a shared security queue instead of the team that owns the service. Fix: route findings by asset ownership (service tags, CODEOWNERS), page the owner for 3-day items, and report overdue items weekly.
  • Every image scan shows dozens of Linux kernel CVEs. Detect: findings cluster on linux-libc-dev or kernel packages in container images. Cause: build tools and kernel headers ship in the runtime image; containers use the host kernel. Fix: multi-stage builds onto slim or distroless images, VEX vulnerable_code_not_present for what remains, and kernel patching tracked on the hosts.
  • Images were rebuilt nightly, yet production ran a three-month-old image. Detect: the running digest's build date is far older than the newest image in the registry. Cause: the rebuild pipeline pushed images but nothing deployed them. Fix: deploy rebuilds through the normal pipeline and alert when a running image is older than the cadence allows.
  • Patched hosts were still vulnerable. Detect: package versions are current, but /var/run/reboot-required exists, Patch Manager reports InstalledPendingReboot, or processes still map the old library. Cause: no restart or reboot after installing. Fix: rolling reboots in a maintenance window, needrestart for services, and replacement instead of in-place patching where possible.
  • An automerged patch release broke production on a weekend. Detect: errors start minutes after a bot pull request merged and deployed. Cause: automerge with thin test coverage and no staged rollout. Fix: automerge only patch and digest updates with good tests, add a release-age delay for ordinary updates, and send every deploy through a canary.
  • New findings sat as "unknown severity" for months. Detect: the triage queue fills with CVEs that have no NVD score, rising since April 2026. Cause: the process waits for NVD enrichment, which now covers mainly priority CVEs. Fix: use the CNA's score, GHSA and OSV data, distribution severities, KEV, EPSS, and SSVC instead.
  • "Are we affected?" took four days during a zero-day. Detect: the incident timeline shows days spent grepping repositories and asking teams. Cause: no SBOMs for running images, hosts, or vendor tools. Fix: SBOMs per digest and per host image, a rehearsed query, and an inventory of third-party products with contacts.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• CVE: A unique identifier and record for one publicly known vulnerability.
  • CNA: CVE Numbering Authority; an organization allowed to assign CVE IDs, often the vendor itself.
  • CWE: A category of software weakness, such as injection or use-after-free.
  • CVSS: FIRST's severity score (v4.0) built from base, threat, environmental, and supplemental metrics.
  • EPSS: FIRST's daily probability that a CVE will see exploitation activity in the next 30 days.
  • KEV: CISA's catalog of vulnerabilities with reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild.
  • SSVC: A decision-tree method that maps exploitation, automation, impact, and mission context to Track, Track*, Attend, or Act.
  • Vulnrichment: CISA's program that adds SSVC data to CVE records.
  • VEX: A machine-readable statement of whether a product is affected by a vulnerability, and why.
  • Reachability: Whether vulnerable code can actually be executed with attacker-controlled input in your service.
  • SBOM: A machine-readable list of an artifact's components, in CycloneDX or SPDX.
  • Exposure window: The time between disclosure or first exploitation and the fix running in production.
  • Patch baseline: The rules that decide which patches a managed node must have to be compliant.
  • Virtual patch: A temporary control, such as a WAF rule, that blocks exploitation without fixing the code.
  • Forensic triage: Checking whether a vulnerable system was already compromised, in addition to fixing it.
  • End of life (EOL): The date after which a product receives no more security fixes.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Prioritizing by CVSS alone, and treating "critical" as "exploited".
  • Believing a clean scan means no exposure, when the scanner never covered half the assets.
  • Waiting for an NVD score before triaging a CVE.
  • Thinking a rebuilt image or an installed package protects production before it is deployed or the process is restarted.
  • Pinning base images by digest without a bot to move the pin, so patches never arrive.
  • Declaring findings not_affected without evidence, review, or expiry.
  • Patching once during a zero-day and missing the follow-up fixes.
  • Assuming the cloud provider patches everything; on VMs, containers, and dependencies, you do.
  • Running end-of-life runtimes or operating systems because "it still works".

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a CVSS 10.0 base score not tell you how urgently to fix a vulnerability in your own system? Which CVSS v4.0 groups would add that context?
  2. What does an EPSS score of 0.03 mean, and why should it not be multiplied by a CVSS score?
  3. You have 40 open vulnerabilities, each with an EPSS score of 0.02. What is the expected number exploited in the next 30 days, and the chance that at least one is? (0.8 expected; 1 - 0.98^40 ≈ 55%.)
  4. Using the BOD 26-04 table: an internal service (not publicly exposed) has a KEV-listed vulnerability that is not automatable and has partial technical impact. What is the deadline? (14 days.) What changes if the service is moved behind a public endpoint?
  5. A scanner reports a kernel CVE in linux-libc-dev inside your container image. Is the container exploitable? What do you record, and what do you still have to patch?
  6. Your base image is pinned by digest and you rebuild weekly. Why might a Debian security fix still not reach production? Name two ways to fix that.
  7. A patched base image is published on a Tuesday morning. Your images rebuild every Sunday night and deploys finish within a day. When does the fix reach production, and what is the worst case for any weekly rebuild? (About six and a half days later, by Monday night. The worst case is a fix published just after a rebuild: seven days plus the deploy.)
  8. Outline the first five steps of your response when a Log4Shell-class vulnerability is announced on a Friday evening.

docs.text: Quick revision after the Docker lessons, before an interview or a task.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does docker build -t taskflow-api:dev . Builds an image from the Dockerfile here docker build --target build . Stops at one stage of a multi-stage build docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc . Passes a secret that never lands in a layer docker build --check . Lints the Dockerfile with BuildKit's checks docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push -t <image> . Builds and pushes one multi-platform image docker run -d --name api -p 3000:3000 taskflow-api:dev Starts a container and publishes a port docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image> Opens a shell in an image whose app crashes docker exec -it api sh Runs a shell in a running container docker logs --tail 100 api Shows the last lines of stdout and stderr docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' api Reads the exit code and whether memory ran out docker events Shows who stopped, killed, or restarted what docker history --no-trunc <image> Lists layers and the commands behind them docker system df -v Shows disk used by images, volumes, and cache docker compose watch Syncs or rebuilds services as files change docker compose config Prints the merged, interpolated Compose file

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile (shape): dependencies, build, and a small non-root runtime
FROM node:24-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app

FROM base AS deps
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

FROM base AS build
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM base AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

# compose.yaml (excerpt): start the API after a healthy database
services:
  api:
    build: { context: ., target: build }
    command: npm run dev
    depends_on:
      mongo:
        condition: service_healthy
    develop:
      watch:
        - { action: sync, path: ./src, target: /app/src }
        - { action: rebuild, path: package-lock.json }
  mongo:
    image: mongo:8.0
    volumes: ["mongo-data:/data/db"]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"]
volumes:
  mongo-data:

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• A shell as PID 1. Use exec-form CMD so SIGTERM reaches Node.
  • Secrets in ARG, ENV, or a copied .npmrc. Use build secrets.
  • COPY . . before npm ci. Copy the lockfile first; add .dockerignore.
  • Running as root. Set USER node and drop capabilities.
  • Deploying :latest. Deploy a digest or an immutable version tag.
  • Publishing a database on all interfaces. Bind it to 127.0.0.1.
  • down -v or volume prune --all by habit. Both delete named volumes and the data in them.
  • depends_on without a condition. Add a health check and service_healthy.

docs.title: Container Fundamentals
docs.text:
A container is an ordinary Linux process that the kernel has been told to isolate: it gets its own view of the process list, network, filesystem, and hostname, and it is limited in how much CPU and memory it may use. Nothing about it is virtual hardware. This lesson explains the kernel features that make containers possible (namespaces and cgroups), how images are built from stacked read-only layers, the standards that let any runtime run any image, the chain of programs between docker run and your process, and the states a container moves through.

Understanding the mechanism pays off quickly: it explains why a container starts in a second, why data written inside it disappears, why it can be killed with exit code 137, why an image built on an Apple-silicon laptop can fail on a server, and why Kubernetes can run Docker images without Docker.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Before containers, a deployment meant installing the right runtime, system libraries, and dependency versions on every server and hoping they matched the developer's machine. Virtual machines solved the mismatch by shipping a whole operating system, at the cost of gigabytes per copy and slow boots. Containers ship only the application and its user-space files, share the host kernel, and start almost as fast as a normal process, so a single server can run dozens of isolated services and the same artifact can move unchanged from a laptop to production.

The same design creates the problems you will debug in production: containers share one kernel (weaker isolation than VMs), their writable layer is temporary, their limits are enforced by the kernel without warning, and the image still depends on the CPU architecture it was built for.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google (Borg). The ACM Queue article Borg, Omega, and Kubernetes (2016) describes more than a decade of running workloads in containers at Google, explains why the container became the unit of deployment there, and shows how those lessons shaped Kubernetes.
  • The Linux kernel. The namespaces(7) and cgroups(7) manual pages document the two kernel features every container runtime is built on. Docker, Podman, containerd, and CRI-O all call the same system calls.
  • Open Container Initiative. The OCI was formed in 2015 by Docker and other industry members to standardize the image format and runtime. Docker contributed runc, which is still the reference runtime most engines use.
  • Kubernetes without Docker. The Kubernetes blog post Don't Panic: Kubernetes and Docker explains that images built with Docker keep working on clusters that use containerd or CRI-O directly, because they are standard OCI images.

Popular tools and providers: Docker Engine and Docker Desktop, Podman, containerd with nerdctl, CRI-O, runc and crun, gVisor and Kata Containers for stronger isolation, Rancher Desktop, and Colima.

docs.title: Containers compared with virtual machines
docs.text:
A virtual machine emulates hardware. A hypervisor gives each VM virtual CPUs, memory, and disks, and each VM boots its own kernel and full operating system. A container emulates nothing: it is a process on the host kernel, started with restricted views (namespaces) and resource limits (cgroups).

Virtual machine Container What is isolated Whole machine, including the kernel A process tree, using kernel features Kernel One per VM Shared with the host Typical size Gigabytes (full OS) Megabytes to a few hundred MB Start time Tens of seconds (OS boot) Usually under a second plus app startup Density Tens of VMs per host Hundreds of containers per host Isolation strength Strong: a kernel bug in one VM rarely affects others Weaker: a kernel exploit can escape to the host Can run a different OS Yes (Windows on Linux, any kernel) No: Linux containers need a Linux kernel

The two are often combined. Cloud servers are VMs, and containers run inside them. Projects such as Kata Containers and Firecracker-based services wrap each container in a tiny VM when tenants do not trust each other.

docs.title: Namespaces: what a container can see
docs.text:
A namespace wraps a global system resource so that processes inside it see their own isolated instance. When a runtime starts a container, it creates a new namespace of each type and places the process in it.

Namespace Isolates Effect inside the container PID Process IDs The app sees itself as PID 1 and cannot see host processes Network (net) Interfaces, IP addresses, routes, ports, firewall rules Own eth0 and localhost; port 3000 does not clash with the host's Mount (mnt) Mount points Own root filesystem, assembled from the image UTS Hostname and domain name Own hostname (the short container ID by default) IPC System V IPC and POSIX message queues Cannot attach to other processes' shared memory User User and group IDs Root inside can map to an unprivileged UID outside Cgroup View of the cgroup tree Sees its own cgroup as the root Time Some clock offsets Rarely used by container engines

Two details matter in practice. First, Docker does not enable user namespaces by default: root inside a default container is UID 0 on the host, limited only by dropped capabilities, seccomp, and AppArmor or SELinux. Rootless Docker, Podman's rootless mode, and Docker's userns-remap setting change that (see container security). Second, namespaces can be shared on purpose: docker run --network host skips the network namespace, and --pid container:<name> joins another container's process namespace, which is how debugging sidecars see the app's processes.

docs.title: cgroups: what a container can use
docs.text:
Control groups (cgroups) account for and limit the resources a group of processes uses. Modern distributions use cgroup v2, a single unified hierarchy under /sys/fs/cgroup. Docker creates one cgroup per container and writes the limits you pass:

Docker flag cgroup v2 file What happens at the limit --memory 512m memory.max = 536870912 The kernel reclaims memory, then the OOM killer kills a process (exit code 137) --cpus 1.5 cpu.max = 150000 100000 The group may use 150 ms of CPU time per 100 ms period, then is throttled until the next period --pids-limit 200 pids.max = 200 fork() fails, so a fork bomb cannot exhaust the host --cpu-shares 512 cpu.weight (converted) Only a relative weight when CPUs are contended

Memory and CPU behave differently at the limit, and this difference is the root of many production incidents: CPU is compressible (a container over its CPU quota just runs slower), while memory is not (a container over its memory limit is killed). The limits apply to the whole container, but tools inside it often do not know about them. For example, Node's os.cpus() still reports every host CPU, so size worker pools from configuration rather than from the CPU count.

docs.title: Images: stacked read-only layers
docs.text:
An image is an ordered list of filesystem layers plus a JSON configuration (environment variables, working directory, user, entry point, command, exposed ports). Each Dockerfile instruction that changes files (RUN, COPY, ADD) produces a layer containing only the files it added, changed, or deleted. Layers are tar archives identified by the SHA-256 digest of their content, so identical layers are stored once and shared between every image and container that uses them.

When a container starts, the runtime stacks the image layers read-only and adds one thin writable layer on top. On Linux this is done with overlayfs: the image layers are the lowerdir, the writable layer is the upperdir, and the container sees the merged view as its root filesystem. Docker's classic storage driver for this is overlay2; newer installations increasingly use the containerd image store, whose overlayfs snapshotter achieves the same result.

This design has consequences you can predict:

  • Copy-on-write is per file. Changing one byte of a 500 MB file that came from the image first copies the whole file into the writable layer. Databases and other write-heavy workloads must use volumes.
  • Deleting in a later layer does not shrink the image. If one RUN downloads a 300 MB archive and the next RUN deletes it, the first layer still contains it. Download, use, and delete in the same RUN, or use a multi-stage build.
  • The writable layer dies with the container. docker rm deletes it. Anything worth keeping belongs in a volume, a database, or object storage.
  • Shared layers save disk and pull time. Ten services built on the same node:24-slim base store that base once, and a server that already has it pulls only the small application layers.

docs.title: The OCI specifications
docs.text:
The Open Container Initiative maintains three specifications that make images and runtimes interchangeable:

Specification Defines Why it matters Image spec The manifest, the image configuration, the layer format, and the image index for multiple platforms An image built by Docker, Buildah, or Kaniko runs anywhere Runtime spec A "bundle" (config.json plus a root filesystem) and the operations create, start, kill, and delete Engines can swap runc for crun, gVisor's runsc, or Kata Distribution spec The HTTP API registries expose under /v2/ for pushing and pulling Any client can push to and pull from any compliant registry

"Docker image" and "OCI image" are, for practical purposes, the same thing today. Docker's own manifest format predates OCI and both are accepted everywhere.

docs.title: From docker run to a process
docs.text:
docker is only a command-line client. Every command becomes a call to the Docker Engine API, and the actual work is split across several programs.

  1. docker CLI parses docker run and calls the API, by default over the Unix socket /var/run/docker.sock. With contexts or DOCKER_HOST it can drive a remote engine.
  2. dockerd (the Docker Engine) resolves the image, creates networks and volumes, and asks containerd to create the container.
  3. containerd stores images and snapshots and supervises container lifecycles. Kubernetes nodes run containerd (or CRI-O) without dockerd; the kubelet talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI).
  4. containerd-shim-runc-v2 is started once per container. It stays as the container's parent, holds its standard streams and exit status, and lets containerd and dockerd restart without killing containers.
  5. runc reads the OCI bundle, creates the namespaces and cgroup, sets up the root filesystem and security settings, starts the container's process, and exits.

Because every step speaks a standard (Engine API, CRI, OCI), the pieces are replaceable. Podman, for example, has no daemon at all: the podman command starts conmon and an OCI runtime directly.

docs.title: The container lifecycle
docs.text:
State Meaning Reached by created Filesystem and configuration prepared; no process yet docker create running The main process is alive docker start, docker run (create + start) paused All processes frozen by the cgroup freezer docker pause restarting The daemon is restarting it under its restart policy A restart policy after an exit exited The main process ended; exit code and writable layer kept Process exit, docker stop, docker kill removing Removal in progress docker rm dead Removal partly failed (for example a busy mount) Rare error cases

docker stop sends the image's stop signal (SIGTERM unless STOPSIGNAL says otherwise), waits up to 10 seconds by default (--timeout changes it), then sends SIGKILL. docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately unless you pass --signal. A container lives exactly as long as its main process (PID 1): when that process exits, the container exits, even if other processes were still running inside it.

docs.title: Why containers fix "works on my machine"
docs.text:
An image freezes everything above the kernel: the OS packages, the runtime version, every dependency at its locked version, the file layout, the user, and the start command. The same digest therefore behaves the same on a laptop, a CI runner, and a server.

Some differences remain, and they explain most "but it works in Docker on my laptop" bugs:

  • CPU architecture. Images contain compiled binaries. An arm64 image built on an Apple-silicon Mac does not run on an amd64 server without emulation. Build multi-platform images (see images, registries, and tagging).
  • Kernel. The host kernel's version, enabled features, and cgroup version come from the server, not the image.
  • Runtime inputs. Environment variables, mounted files, secrets, networks, and resource limits are supplied when the container starts.
  • External services. The database, queues, and third-party APIs are not inside the image.

docs.title: Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS
docs.text:
Linux containers need a Linux kernel, so Docker Desktop on Windows and macOS runs a small Linux virtual machine and runs dockerd inside it. On Windows the recommended backend is WSL 2; on macOS it uses Apple's virtualization framework. The docker CLI on your desktop talks to the engine inside that VM. This explains several behaviours:

  • Bind-mounted project folders cross the VM boundary, so file access is slower than on native Linux. On Windows, keep projects inside the WSL 2 filesystem rather than under C:\.
  • Published ports are forwarded from the VM to your desktop, and the special name host.docker.internal reaches services on your host.
  • CPU and memory for all containers come from the VM's allocation, set in Docker Desktop's settings.
  • Windows containers (Windows Server images) are a separate mode that needs a Windows kernel; they are unrelated to the Linux containers this section uses.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use containers when:

  • You deploy services that must behave identically across developer machines, CI, and production.
  • You want to run several services with conflicting dependencies on the same machines.
  • You deploy to Kubernetes, a cloud container service (Cloud Run, ECS, Azure Container Apps), or any platform that accepts OCI images.
  • You need fast, disposable environments for tests and local development.

Think twice when:

  • Tenants do not trust each other and need kernel-level isolation: use VMs, or sandboxed runtimes such as gVisor or Kata Containers.
  • The workload needs a different OS or kernel (Windows services, custom kernel modules).
  • The application is a single static site or a serverless function where the platform already handles packaging.
  • The team cannot yet patch base images and scan them; an unmaintained image is an unpatched server.
Need Better fit Package a Node.js API with exact dependencies Container Run untrusted customer code MicroVM (Firecracker, Kata) or gVisor Run a Windows-only application Windows VM or Windows containers Isolate several services on one Linux host Containers with resource limits A database that needs tuned disks and backups Managed database service, or a VM

docs.title: See the namespaces from inside and outside
docs.text:
# Inside: the container's process list starts at PID 1
docker run --rm alpine:3.22 ps
# PID   USER     TIME  COMMAND
#     1 root      0:00 ps

# Inside: own hostname and network interfaces
docker run --rm alpine:3.22 sh -c 'hostname; ip addr show eth0'

# Outside: the same container is a normal host process
docker run -d --name demo nginx:1.30-alpine
pid=$(docker inspect --format '{{.State.Pid}}' demo)
ps -o pid,user,cmd -p "$pid"           # nginx master, visible on the host
sudo ls -l /proc/"$pid"/ns             # its namespace handles
sudo lsns -p "$pid"                    # which namespaces it is in
docker rm -f demo

The host sees nginx with a normal host PID; inside the container the same process is PID 1. On Docker Desktop the host-side commands must run inside the Linux VM, so try them on a Linux machine.

docs.title: Build a "container" by hand with unshare
docs.text:
# On a Linux host: new PID, mount, UTS, and network namespaces
sudo unshare --pid --fork --mount-proc --uts --net bash

# Now inside the new namespaces:
hostname sandbox && hostname   # does not change the host's hostname
ps aux                         # bash is PID 1; host processes are invisible
ip link                        # only a loopback interface, and it is down
exit

This is the core of what a runtime does. runc adds a separate root filesystem, a cgroup with limits, dropped capabilities, and a seccomp filter on top.

docs.title: Read the cgroup limits a container got
docs.text:
docker run --rm --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 --pids-limit 200 alpine:3.22 \
  sh -c 'cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max /sys/fs/cgroup/pids.max'
# 536870912
# 150000 100000
# 200

The memory limit is 512 × 1024 × 1024 bytes. The CPU quota of 150,000 microseconds per 100,000-microsecond period equals 1.5 CPUs.

docs.title: Inspect an image's layers
docs.text:
docker pull node:24-slim
docker history node:24-slim                       # one row per instruction
docker image inspect node:24-slim \
  --format '{{json .RootFS.Layers}}'              # layer digests
docker image inspect node:24-slim \
  --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'            # e.g. linux/amd64

docker history shows the instruction that created each layer and its size. Rows with 0B come from instructions that only change metadata (ENV, CMD, EXPOSE).

docs.title: Watch copy-on-write with docker diff
docs.text:
docker run -d --name cow nginx:1.30-alpine
docker exec cow sh -c 'echo hello > /usr/share/nginx/html/hello.html'
docker exec cow rm /usr/share/nginx/html/50x.html
docker diff cow
# C /usr/share/nginx/html
# A /usr/share/nginx/html/hello.html
# D /usr/share/nginx/html/50x.html
# (other entries, such as nginx's runtime files, omitted)
docker rm -f cow   # the writable layer, and these changes, are gone

A means added, C changed, and D deleted. The deleted file still exists in the image; the writable layer only records a whiteout.

docs.title: Walk through the lifecycle
docs.text:
docker create --name life nginx:1.30-alpine
docker ps -a --filter name=life --format '{{.Names}}: {{.Status}}'   # Created
docker start life                                                    # Up ...
docker pause life                                                    # Up ... (Paused)
docker unpause life
docker stop life                                                     # Exited (0) ...
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}' life # exited 0
docker rm life

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Treat containers as disposable: anything that must survive goes into a volume, a database, or object storage, never the writable layer.
  • Run one main process per container and let it be PID 1 (or use a tiny init such as tini), so signals and exit codes behave predictably.
  • Set memory limits on every production container, and size the application (for example Node's heap) below them.
  • Keep images small and few: share a common base image across services so layers are reused.
  • Build images for the architecture of the servers that run them, or publish multi-platform images.
  • Remember that containers share the kernel: keep hosts patched, drop privileges, and use VMs or sandboxed runtimes for untrusted code.
  • Learn the engine-independent tools (ctr, crictl, nerdctl) if you operate Kubernetes nodes, where dockerd is usually absent.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The container exits immediately with exec format error. Detect: docker logs shows exec /usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh: exec format error, and the container restarts in a loop. Cause: the image was built for another CPU architecture, typically arm64 on an Apple-silicon laptop deployed to an amd64 server. Fix: check docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}', build in CI for the target platform, or publish a multi-platform image with docker buildx.
  • A container is killed under load with exit code 137. Detect: docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}' returns true, and the host kernel log shows a memory cgroup out-of-memory kill. Cause: the process exceeded the container's memory limit; memory cannot be throttled, so the kernel killed it. Fix: raise the limit, cap the Node heap with --max-old-space-size at roughly 75% of the limit, and look for leaks.
  • Uploaded files vanish after a redeploy. Detect: files saved before the deploy return 404 afterwards, and docker diff on the old container showed them as added files. Cause: the application wrote to the container's writable layer, which was deleted when the container was recreated. Fix: mount a named volume, or store uploads in object storage.
  • The host's disk fills up. Detect: df -h /var/lib/docker is near 100% and docker system df reports gigabytes of images, stopped containers, and build cache. Cause: old images and containers are never removed, logs are not rotated, or an application writes heavily to its writable layer. Fix: prune regularly, configure log rotation, and move write-heavy paths to volumes (see debugging and operating containers).
  • Upgrading Docker restarts every service on the host. Detect: all containers stop when dockerd restarts during a package upgrade. Cause: by default, containers do not survive a daemon restart. Fix: set "live-restore": true in /etc/docker/daemon.json so running containers keep running while the daemon is down (not available in Swarm mode), or drain the host first.
  • A service with --cpus 2 starts 64 worker threads and is slow. Detect: CPU throttling counters (nr_throttled in cpu.stat) climb while latency rises. Cause: the application sized its thread or worker pool from the host's CPU count, which a CPU quota does not change. Fix: set worker counts explicitly from configuration to match the quota.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Container: An isolated, resource-limited process (or process tree) started from an image.
  • Image: An immutable, layered filesystem plus configuration from which containers are created.
  • Namespace: A kernel feature that gives a process its own isolated view of a global resource such as PIDs or the network.
  • cgroup (control group): A kernel feature that limits and accounts for the CPU, memory, I/O, and process count of a group of processes.
  • Layer: One read-only filesystem diff in an image, identified by its SHA-256 digest.
  • Writable layer: The per-container layer that receives every change the container makes; deleted with the container.
  • Copy-on-write: Copying a file from a lower layer into the writable layer only when it is first modified.
  • overlayfs: The Linux union filesystem that merges image layers and the writable layer into one view.
  • OCI: The Open Container Initiative and its image, runtime, and distribution specifications.
  • Container runtime: Low level (runc, crun) creates the isolated process; high level (containerd, CRI-O) manages images and lifecycles.
  • CRI: The Container Runtime Interface Kubernetes uses to talk to a high-level runtime.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Calling a container a lightweight VM. It has no kernel of its own and no virtual hardware.
  • Assuming root in a container is harmless. Without user namespaces it is host root with some capabilities removed.
  • Writing data to the container filesystem and expecting it to survive a redeploy.
  • Deleting files in a later RUN to shrink the image; the earlier layer still contains them.
  • Assuming the image pins the kernel. Kernel version and features come from the host.
  • Forgetting CPU architecture when building on one machine and running on another.
  • Believing Kubernetes "dropped Docker support" means Docker images stop working. Only the Docker Engine integration was removed; OCI images run as before.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which kernel features provide a container's isolation and its resource limits, and what does each control?
  2. Why can a container start in well under a second when a VM takes tens of seconds?
  3. A host runs 20 containers from the same 250 MB image, and each writes 30 MB to its writable layer. How much disk do the image and writable layers use, and why is it not 20 × 280 MB?
  4. A container runs with --cpus 0.5. What value appears in cpu.max, and what happens when the process tries to use more CPU?
  5. Why does deleting a file in a later Dockerfile instruction not make the image smaller?
  6. Trace docker run from the CLI to the running process. Which component would a Kubernetes node use instead of dockerd?
  7. Name three differences between environments that a container image does not remove.
  8. What happens to a container's other processes when its PID 1 exits?
