docs.title: Container Networking and Storage
docs.text: Every container gets its own network stack and its own filesystem, and both are thrown away when the container is removed. This lesson explains how containers talk to each other, to the host, and to the outside world (network drivers, the default and user-defined bridges, embedded DNS, port publishing), and how they keep data that must outlive them (named volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts), including backups, file ownership problems, and the performance quirks of Docker Desktop.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most "it works on my machine but not in Docker" problems are networking or storage problems: an API that connects to localhost and finds nothing, a database port accidentally published to the whole internet, a container that cannot reach a service on the host, data that vanished with a container, or a bind mount that the container user cannot write to.

These are also security and reliability decisions. A port published on 0.0.0.0 is reachable by every machine that can reach the host, and on Linux it can bypass the host firewall. A database stored in a container's writable layer is lost on the next deploy. Knowing exactly where packets go and where bytes are stored prevents both.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Docker: firewalls. The packet filtering and firewalls documentation explains that Docker writes its own NAT and filter rules for published ports, and warns that this makes published ports incompatible with simple host firewalls such as ufw and firewalld rules that only filter the host's input chain.
  • Docker: user-defined bridges. The bridge network driver page lists why user-defined bridges are better than the default bridge: automatic DNS resolution between containers, better isolation, and attaching or detaching containers without restarting them.
  • Docker: volumes. The volumes guide describes volumes as the preferred mechanism for persisting data generated and used by containers, because Docker manages them and they work the same on Linux and Docker Desktop.
  • Docker Desktop on Windows. The WSL best practices page recommends storing project files in the Linux file system rather than the Windows one for bind-mount performance and file-change events.

Popular tools and providers: Docker networks and volumes, the netshoot debugging image, nsenter, ss and tcpdump, CNI plugins in Kubernetes (Calico, Cilium), and volume plugins and CSI drivers for network storage.

docs.title: Network drivers
docs.text:
Driver What the container gets Typical use bridge Its own network namespace on a virtual switch on the host, with a private IP and NAT to the outside The default for single-host containers host No network isolation: it uses the host's interfaces and ports directly Network-heavy tools on Linux; avoids NAT none Only a loopback interface Batch jobs that must not use the network overlay A virtual network spanning several Docker hosts (Swarm) Multi-host Swarm services macvlan, ipvlan An address directly on the physical network Legacy apps that need to look like physical hosts

On Docker Desktop the "host" is the Linux VM, so host networking behaves differently from native Linux; treat it as a Linux-only feature. Kubernetes does not use these drivers at all: it uses CNI plugins that give every pod a routable IP (see pods, deployments, and services).

docs.title: The default bridge compared with user-defined bridges
docs.text:
Docker creates a bridge called docker0 (network name bridge) at install time, and containers started without --network join it. It is kept for backwards compatibility and lacks the features you want:

Default bridge (docker0) User-defined bridge Resolve other containers by name No (only the legacy --link flag) Yes, through embedded DNS Isolation Every unconfigured container shares it Only containers you attach Attach or detach a running container Requires a restart docker network connect / disconnect Created by Docker at install docker network create, or Compose per project

Always create a network for an application (Compose does this automatically). Inside each container, /etc/resolv.conf points to Docker's embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11, which answers for container names, service names, and --network-alias names on that network and forwards everything else to the host's resolvers. Several containers can share an alias, in which case DNS returns all their addresses.

docs.title: How port publishing works
docs.text:
A container's ports are reachable from other containers on the same network, but not from outside the host, until you publish them. docker run -p 8080:3000 tells Docker to forward the host's port 8080 to the container's port 3000.

What happens underneath on Linux:

  1. Docker adds a destination NAT (DNAT) rule: packets arriving at the host on port 8080 are rewritten to 172.18.0.2:3000.
  2. Filter rules allow the forwarded traffic to reach the bridge.
  3. For connections from the host itself to localhost:8080, Docker by default also runs a small docker-proxy process that listens on the port.
  4. Outbound traffic from containers is masqueraded (source NAT) to the host's address, so containers can reach the internet without being reachable from it.

The forms of -p you need:

Flag Listens on Reachable from -p 8080:3000 All host addresses (0.0.0.0 and ::) Every machine that can reach the host -p 127.0.0.1:8080:3000 Host loopback only Only the host itself -p 3000 A random high host port Every machine; see it with docker port -P Random ports for every EXPOSEd port Every machine (no -p) Nothing on the host Only containers on the same network

EXPOSE in a Dockerfile documents a port; it publishes nothing.

Because published ports are handled by NAT before the host's normal input rules, a firewall such as ufw that blocks port 27017 does not stop a container published with -p 27017:27017. Publish databases on 127.0.0.1 or not at all, and put your own filtering rules in Docker's DOCKER-USER chain if you must filter published ports.

docs.title: Reaching the host from a container
docs.text:
localhost inside a container is the container itself. To reach a service running on your machine (a database you started outside Docker, a mock server):

  • On Docker Desktop, use the special name host.docker.internal.
  • On Linux, add it yourself with --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway (or extra_hosts in Compose). host-gateway resolves to the host's address on the bridge.
  • The host service must listen on an address the container can reach. A database bound only to 127.0.0.1 on a Linux host is not reachable from the bridge; bind it to the bridge address or 0.0.0.0 behind a firewall.

docs.title: Storage options
docs.text:
A container's own filesystem is the image plus a writable layer that is deleted with the container. Anything that must survive, or must be fast, or must be shared with the host, needs a mount.

Named volume Bind mount tmpfs Syntax -v mongo-data:/data/db -v "$(pwd)/src:/app/src" --tmpfs /tmp Long syntax --mount type=volume,src=mongo-data,dst=/data/db --mount type=bind,src=$(pwd)/src,dst=/app/src --mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=64m Where the data is Docker's storage area on the host (inside the VM on Docker Desktop) The host path you name Host memory Survives docker rm Yes Yes (host files) No Pre-filled from the image Yes, if empty on first mount No: it hides the image's files at that path No Portable across hosts and OSes Yes No: depends on host paths Yes Typical use Databases, uploads, caches Source code in development, config files Secrets, scratch space, --read-only containers

-v with a host path that does not exist silently creates an empty directory owned by root; --mount fails with an error instead, which is why scripts and production configurations should prefer --mount. Append :ro (or readonly in --mount) to mount read-only.

docs.title: Volume lifecycle
docs.text:
• Named volumes are created by docker volume create, by the first docker run -v name:/path, or by Compose. They persist until removed explicitly with docker volume rm or a prune.
  • Anonymous volumes are created by -v /path without a name or by a VOLUME instruction in the image. They get a random name and are removed together with the container only if it was started with --rm or removed with docker rm -v.
  • Pruning: docker volume prune removes unused anonymous volumes; add --all to include unused named volumes (Docker Engine 23 changed the default to anonymous-only).
  • docker volume inspect shows the Mountpoint on the host; do not edit files there while a database is running.

docs.title: Backing up a volume
docs.text: A volume is just a directory, so a helper container can archive it. For a database, a file-level copy is only consistent if the database is stopped (or the storage supports snapshots); otherwise use the database's own backup tool, such as mongodump, which produces a consistent logical backup while it runs. Backups in depth are covered in database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: File ownership and UIDs
docs.text:
The kernel compares numeric user IDs, not names. Inside the official Node image the node user is UID 1000; on your Linux host, UID 1000 is whoever was created first. With a bind mount:

  • Files the container creates appear on the host owned by the container's UID (root-owned files in your project folder if the container runs as root).
  • A container running as UID 1000 cannot write to a host directory owned by UID 1001 with mode 755.

Fixes: run the container with your own IDs (--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"), create and chown directories in the image for named volumes, or use named volumes instead of bind mounts for data. On SELinux systems (Fedora, RHEL), bind mounts also need the :z or :Z option to relabel the files. Docker Desktop's file-sharing layer usually hides UID mismatches, which is why these errors often appear only on Linux servers and CI.

docs.title: Docker Desktop file-sharing performance
docs.text:
On macOS and Windows, a bind mount crosses from your OS into the Linux VM, and every file operation pays for that crossing. Directories with tens of thousands of small files (node_modules, .git) make it worst.

  • Windows: keep the project inside the WSL 2 Linux filesystem (for example ~/code/taskflow in your distribution), not under C:\. Bind mounts from the Windows filesystem are slower and do not deliver file-change events reliably, so watchers miss edits.
  • macOS: the VirtioFS file-sharing implementation is much faster than the older ones; select it in Docker Desktop's settings if it is not already the default.
  • Both: never bind-mount the host's node_modules into the container. Use docker compose watch to sync only source files, or mount the project and put node_modules in a volume.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Choose Containers of one app talking to each other A user-defined bridge (Compose's default network) Access to the API from your browser -p 3000:3000 (or 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 on shared machines) Access to a local database from your tools -p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017 A database that must never be reachable from outside No -p at all Maximum network performance on Linux --network host, accepting port conflicts and no isolation Persist database files Named volume (or a managed database in production) Live-edit source code Compose watch, or a bind mount on Linux A secret or scratch files that must not touch disk tmpfs Share files between hosts Object storage or a network volume driver, not a bind mount

Do not use host networking to work around a misunderstanding of localhost, and do not run production databases on bind mounts to arbitrary host folders without backups and permission management.

docs.title: A user-defined network and name resolution
docs.text:
docker network create taskflow-net

docker run -d --name mongo --network taskflow-net \
  -v mongo-data:/data/db mongo:8.0

docker run -d --name api --network taskflow-net -p 3000:3000 \
  -e MONGODB_URI=mongodb://mongo:27017/taskflow \
  taskflow-api:dev

# How names resolve inside the network
docker run --rm --network taskflow-net busybox:1.37 nslookup mongo
# Server:    127.0.0.11
# Name:      mongo
# Address:   172.18.0.2

docker network inspect taskflow-net --format '{{json .Containers}}'

The same nslookup from a container on the default bridge fails, because the default bridge has no embedded DNS for container names.

docs.title: Publishing ports safely and checking them
docs.text:
# API for the browser; MongoDB only for tools on this machine
docker run -d --name api -p 3000:3000 taskflow-api:dev
docker run -d --name mongo -p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017 mongo:8.0

docker port mongo
# 27017/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:27017

sudo ss -ltnp | grep -E ':3000|:27017'   # what is listening, on which address

docs.title: Reaching a service on the host
docs.text:
# Docker Desktop: works out of the box
docker run --rm curlimages/curl:8.15.0 http://host.docker.internal:4000/health

# Linux: map the name to the host's bridge gateway first
docker run --rm --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  curlimages/curl:8.15.0 http://host.docker.internal:4000/health

# compose.yaml (excerpt): the same mapping in Compose
services:
  api:
    extra_hosts:
      - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway"

docs.title: Backing up and restoring a volume
docs.text:
# File-level archive of a volume (stop the database first for consistency)
docker compose stop mongo
docker run --rm \
  -v taskflow_mongo-data:/data:ro \
  -v "$(pwd)":/backup \
  alpine:3.22 tar czf /backup/mongo-data-$(date +%F).tgz -C /data .
docker compose start mongo

# Restore into a new, empty volume
docker volume create taskflow_mongo-data-restored
docker run --rm \
  -v taskflow_mongo-data-restored:/data \
  -v "$(pwd)":/backup \
  alpine:3.22 tar xzf /backup/mongo-data-2026-11-13.tgz -C /data

# Logical backup while MongoDB keeps running (-T: no TTY, binary-safe)
docker compose exec -T mongo mongodump --archive --gzip > taskflow-$(date +%F).archive.gz
docker compose exec -T mongo mongorestore --archive --gzip --drop < taskflow-2026-11-13.archive.gz

docs.title: Fixing ownership on a bind mount
docs.text:
# Files created in ./output belong to your user, not root
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$(pwd)/output:/out" \
  taskflow-api:dev node dist/scripts/export.js /out/tasks.json

# Dockerfile (excerpt): a writable directory for a named volume
RUN mkdir -p /app/uploads && chown node:node /app/uploads
USER node
VOLUME ["/app/uploads"]

An empty named volume mounted at /app/uploads copies the directory's ownership from the image on first use, so the node user can write to it. (This is one of the few good reasons to declare VOLUME; many teams still prefer to declare the mount only in Compose or Kubernetes.)

docs.title: A read-only container with tmpfs scratch space
docs.text:
docker run -d --name api --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=64m \
  -p 3000:3000 taskflow-api:dev

The root filesystem cannot be modified, which blocks a whole class of attacks, while /tmp still works for libraries that need scratch files. This pattern returns in container security.

docs.title: Compose: keep node_modules out of a bind mount
docs.text:
# compose.yaml (excerpt): bind-mount the code, keep dependencies in the image
services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: build
    volumes:
      - ./:/app                # project from the host
      - /app/node_modules      # anonymous volume masks the host's node_modules

The anonymous volume at /app/node_modules is pre-filled from the image on first creation, so the container uses the Linux dependencies installed during the build. When dependencies change, recreate it with docker compose up -d --build --renew-anon-volumes. Compose Watch avoids this trick entirely.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Create a network per application; never rely on the default bridge.
  • Connect services by name; never hard-code container IP addresses.
  • Publish only what a human or external client needs, and bind development and database ports to 127.0.0.1.
  • Remember that published ports bypass simple host firewalls on Linux.
  • Store data in named volumes (or managed services), never in the writable layer.
  • Prefer --mount in scripts so a missing host path is an error.
  • Back up databases with their own tools, and test restores.
  • Run containers as a non-root user and plan ownership of writable paths.
  • On Docker Desktop, keep projects in the VM-friendly location and avoid bind-mounting node_modules.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A database is reachable from the internet although ufw blocks it. Detect: an external port scan shows 27017 open; docker ps shows 0.0.0.0:27017->27017/tcp. Cause: -p 27017:27017 publishes on all interfaces, and Docker's NAT rules are evaluated before ufw's input rules. Fix: do not publish database ports, or bind them to 127.0.0.1; filter in the DOCKER-USER chain or a cloud firewall; enable authentication regardless.
  • The API logs ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:27017. Detect: the error appears only in the container, and the same configuration works outside Docker. Cause: the connection string uses localhost, which inside the container is the container itself. Fix: use the service name (mongodb://mongo:27017), or host.docker.internal for a database on the host.
  • Containers cannot resolve each other's names. Detect: getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND mongo; docker inspect shows the containers on the bridge network. Cause: containers started without --network join the default bridge, which has no name DNS. Fix: create a user-defined network (or use Compose) and attach both.
  • Some corporate addresses become unreachable when Docker starts. Detect: VPN or office subnets in the 172.17.0.0/16 to 172.31.0.0/16 range stop responding while Docker networks exist. Cause: Docker's default address pools overlap the corporate ranges. Fix: set bip and default-address-pools in /etc/docker/daemon.json (or Docker Desktop's settings) to unused ranges, then recreate the networks.
  • EACCES: permission denied writing to a mounted directory. Detect: the error appears on Linux servers but not on Docker Desktop; ls -ln shows a different numeric owner. Cause: the container's UID does not own the host directory. Fix: match UIDs with --user, chown the directory, or use a named volume prepared in the image.
  • The host disk fills up with volumes nobody recognizes. Detect: docker system df -v lists many anonymous volumes with 64-character names. Cause: images with VOLUME instructions and containers removed without -v. Fix: docker volume prune, run short-lived containers with --rm, and avoid VOLUME in your images.
  • File watching is slow or misses changes on Windows. Detect: saves take seconds to appear, or the dev server never reloads. Cause: the project is bind-mounted from the Windows filesystem through the VM. Fix: move the project into the WSL 2 filesystem or use Compose Watch.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Network namespace: The kernel feature that gives a container its own interfaces, routes, and ports.
  • Bridge network: A virtual switch on the host connecting containers with private IPs and NAT to the outside.
  • User-defined bridge: A bridge created with docker network create (or by Compose) that provides name resolution.
  • Embedded DNS: Docker's DNS server at 127.0.0.11 inside containers on user-defined networks.
  • Port publishing: Mapping a host port to a container port with -p, implemented with NAT rules.
  • DNAT / masquerading: Rewriting a packet's destination (inbound) or source (outbound) address.
  • Named volume: Docker-managed persistent storage referenced by name.
  • Anonymous volume: A volume with a random name, created by VOLUME or -v /path.
  • Bind mount: A host file or directory mounted into a container.
  • tmpfs mount: A memory-backed filesystem that disappears when the container stops.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing EXPOSE makes a port reachable.
  • Using localhost to reach another container or the host.
  • Publishing every port on 0.0.0.0 and trusting the host firewall.
  • Hard-coding container IP addresses, which change on every recreation.
  • Copying a running database's files and calling it a backup.
  • Assuming docker volume prune only deletes anonymous volumes in every version, or that it never deletes named ones (--all does).
  • Expecting bind mounts to behave the same on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can the API reach mongo:27017 on a Compose network but not on the default bridge?
  2. What is the difference between -p 27017:27017 and -p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017, and why does ufw not protect the first?
  3. A container connects to localhost:5432 for a PostgreSQL server running on the host. Why does it fail, and what are two fixes?
  4. Compare named volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs for persistence, performance, and portability.
  5. A volume holds 12 GB of MongoDB data. A tar backup runs at 60 MB/s. How long must MongoDB stay stopped for a consistent file-level copy, and what would you use instead to avoid the downtime?
  6. Why do permission errors on bind mounts often appear on Linux servers but not on a developer's Mac?
  7. What happens to the image's files at /app/uploads when you mount an empty named volume there, and when you bind-mount an empty host directory there?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Docker documentation: Networking overview
  • Docker documentation: Port publishing and mapping
  • Docker documentation: Bind mounts
  • Docker documentation: tmpfs mounts
  • Linux manual: network_namespaces(7)
  • Next: container security. Back to the Docker overview.

docs.title: Container Security
docs.text: Containers isolate processes, but the isolation is only as strong as the way you build and run them. A default container runs as root, keeps a set of Linux capabilities, has a writable filesystem, and shares the host's kernel with every other container. This lesson works through the attack surface layer by layer, from the image contents and the build process to the running process, the kernel, and the host: non-root users, read-only filesystems, dropped capabilities, no-new-privileges, rootless Docker, keeping secrets out of layers, minimal base images, vulnerability scanning, pinning by digest, signing images, and why the Docker socket is effectively root on the host.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Container security failures tend to be quiet and severe. A token copied into a layer is readable by anyone who can pull the image, for as long as the image exists. A compromised process running as root with extra capabilities, the Docker socket, or --privileged can take over the host and every container on it. An image built a year ago carries a year of unpatched vulnerabilities into production on every deploy.

Most of the defenses cost a few lines in a Dockerfile or a run configuration. They also map directly onto Kubernetes securityContext settings, so learning them once pays off on every platform.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• NIST. Special Publication 800-190, Application Container Security Guide groups container risks into image, registry, orchestrator, container, and host-OS risks, and recommends countermeasures such as minimal images, vulnerability management, and treating the shared kernel as a risk boundary.
  • OWASP. The Docker Security Cheat Sheet lists rules that this page applies: do not expose the Docker socket, set a user, limit capabilities, prevent privilege escalation with no-new-privileges, use read-only filesystems, and scan images.
  • Docker. The Docker Engine security documentation explains that only trusted users should control the daemon, because access to it is equivalent to root on the host, and describes the default capability set, seccomp, and AppArmor profiles.
  • CIS. The CIS Docker Benchmark is a widely used checklist for host configuration, daemon settings, images, and runtime flags that auditors and scanners measure against.

Popular tools and providers: Trivy, Grype with Syft, Docker Scout, Snyk Container, Sigstore cosign, Notation, distroless images, Chainguard Images, Docker Hardened Images, gVisor, Kata Containers, and Falco for runtime threat detection.

docs.title: The threat model
docs.text:
Four things can go wrong, and each needs different controls:

  1. A vulnerable or malicious image. Known CVEs in base packages or dependencies, or a compromised upstream image.
  2. Leaked secrets. Credentials in image layers, environment variables, logs, or build metadata.
  3. A compromised process escalating. An attacker who gets code execution in the app tries to become root in the container, then to reach the host.
  4. Escape through the host interface. Mounted sockets, host paths, privileged mode, or a kernel vulnerability let the attacker leave the container entirely.

docs.title: Run as a non-root user
docs.text:
Root inside a default container is UID 0 on the host kernel. It is restricted by capabilities, seccomp, and AppArmor or SELinux, but every kernel or runtime vulnerability is more dangerous when the attacker is already root. Set a non-root user in the image (USER node in the official Node images, UID 1000) and keep application files owned by root so the process cannot modify them.

Use a numeric UID when an orchestrator must verify it: Kubernetes' runAsNonRoot: true cannot check a user name like node and refuses to start the pod, while USER 1000 passes the check.

docs.title: Drop Linux capabilities
docs.text: Linux splits root's power into about 40 capabilities. Docker grants a default set of 14 to every container: AUDIT_WRITE, CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE, FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, MKNOD, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SETFCAP, SETGID, SETPCAP, SETUID, and SYS_CHROOT. A Node.js API needs none of them when it runs as a non-root user on port 3000. --cap-drop ALL removes them all; --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE adds back only the one you need (binding ports below 1024). NET_RAW, for example, allows crafting raw packets for spoofing attacks inside the container network.

docs.title: Prevent privilege escalation
docs.text: A setuid binary (such as su or passwd) runs with its owner's privileges, which can turn a non-root foothold into root. --security-opt no-new-privileges:true sets the kernel's no_new_privs flag so no process in the container can gain privileges through setuid or file capabilities. Kubernetes exposes the same flag as allowPrivilegeEscalation: false.

docs.title: Read-only root filesystem
docs.text: --read-only mounts the container's root filesystem read-only. An attacker cannot drop tools, modify the app, or plant persistence, and accidental writes to the container layer (which would be lost anyway) fail loudly. Paths that genuinely need writes get a tmpfs (--tmpfs /tmp) or a volume.

docs.title: seccomp, AppArmor, and SELinux
docs.text: Docker applies a default seccomp profile that blocks dozens of system calls rarely needed by applications (for example those that load kernel modules or change the system clock), plus an AppArmor (docker-default) or SELinux policy on hosts that support them. Keep the defaults. --privileged disables seccomp and AppArmor, grants every capability, and exposes host devices: it is effectively running on the host and should be reserved for system tools you fully trust.

docs.title: Rootless Docker and user namespaces
docs.text:
Two options remove "root in the container is root on the host":

  • Rootless mode runs the Docker daemon and containers as an ordinary user. A container escape lands in that user's account, not root. Some features are limited (privileged ports, some network and storage drivers, cgroup limits on older setups).
  • User-namespace remapping (userns-remap in daemon.json) keeps a root daemon but maps container UID 0 to an unprivileged range of host UIDs.

Podman runs rootless by default. Kubernetes supports user namespaces for pods through the hostUsers: false field on recent versions.

docs.title: The Docker socket is root on the host
docs.text:
The Docker API lets its caller start a container with the host's root filesystem mounted and --privileged set. Therefore:

  • Membership in the docker group is root-equivalent on that host.
  • Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives that container full control of the host. CI runners, dashboards, and "Docker in Docker" setups that do this must be treated as root on the host.
  • Exposing the daemon on TCP without TLS client authentication gives the host to anyone who can reach the port.

Alternatives: rootless daemons, a per-job VM for CI builds, a socket proxy that allows only specific read-only API calls, or daemonless builders (BuildKit in rootless mode, Buildah).

docs.title: Secrets never belong in layers
docs.text:
Every layer is a tar archive anyone with pull access can extract with docker save. A file copied in one layer and deleted in the next is only hidden by a whiteout; the earlier layer still contains it. Build arguments are recorded too: docker history shows the command line of every RUN, including ARG values used in it.

Build-time secrets go through BuildKit secret mounts. Runtime secrets are injected when the container starts, preferably as files (Compose and Swarm mount them under /run/secrets/, Kubernetes as volumes) rather than environment variables, which appear in docker inspect, crash reports, and child processes. Where secrets come from is covered in secrets management.

docs.title: Minimal base images
docs.text:
Every package in the image is something to patch and something an attacker can use. Smaller bases have fewer packages and therefore fewer CVEs to triage:

Base Shell and package manager Typical CVE count Debugging node:24 (full Debian) Yes, plus compilers and tools Highest Easiest node:24-slim Yes Lower Easy node:24-alpine sh and apk Low Easy Distroless (gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13) None Lowest of the Debian-based options Needs ephemeral debug containers Hardened images (Chainguard, Docker Hardened Images) Usually none in runtime variants Very low, frequently rebuilt As distroless

Distroless images contain the runtime and its libraries but no shell, so an attacker who gets code execution cannot simply run sh, curl, or apt-get. Their :nonroot variants run as UID 65532 by default.

docs.title: Image scanning
docs.text:
Scanners build an inventory of the image (OS packages from the package database, language packages from lockfiles and node_modules) and match it against vulnerability databases. Run them:

  • in CI, failing the build for fixable high and critical findings;
  • in the registry or continuously, because new CVEs are published against images that were clean when built;
  • with judgment: a CVE in a library the app never loads is lower priority than one in Node itself. VEX documents and ignore files with expiry dates record those decisions.

The usual fix is not a code change but a rebuild on a patched base: which is why images should be rebuilt on a schedule, not only when the code changes.

docs.title: Pinning base images by digest
docs.text: FROM node:24-slim resolves to whatever the tag points to at build time, so two builds of the same commit can produce different images. FROM node:24-slim@sha256:<digest> always resolves to the same bytes. Pinning gives reproducibility and protects against a compromised or broken upstream tag, but it also freezes security patches, so pair it with a bot (Renovate or Dependabot) that opens pull requests when the tag's digest changes.

docs.title: Signing images
docs.text: A digest proves which bytes you have, not who built them. Signing adds that proof. Sigstore's cosign supports keyless signing: in CI, the workflow's OIDC identity is exchanged for a short-lived certificate, the signature is stored in the registry next to the image, and the event is recorded in a public transparency log. At deploy time, an admission policy (Kyverno, Sigstore policy-controller, or a cloud provider's binary authorization) rejects images not signed by your CI identity. Provenance attestations and SLSA levels extend the same idea to "how was it built"; see pipeline and supply-chain security.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Control Local development Production Untrusted code (multi-tenant) Non-root user Yes Required Required --cap-drop ALL Optional Yes Required no-new-privileges Optional Yes Required Read-only root filesystem Optional Yes, with tmpfs where needed Required Default seccomp and AppArmor Yes Yes Plus stricter custom profiles Distroless or hardened base Slim is fine Recommended Required Scanning Occasionally Every build plus continuous Every build plus continuous Signing and admission policy No Recommended Required Rootless or user namespaces Optional Recommended where supported Plus gVisor, Kata, or VMs

Do not skip the basics because "it is only internal": most container compromises start with an ordinary application vulnerability, and the controls above decide what happens next. Conversely, do not use a container boundary alone for code you do not trust; use a sandboxed runtime or a VM.

docs.title: A hardened docker run
docs.text:
docker run -d --name taskflow-api \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m \
  --cap-drop ALL \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --memory 512m --cpus 1 --pids-limit 200 \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 \
  --env-file ./api.env \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest>

Each line closes one layer of the attack surface: an unprivileged user, an immutable root filesystem, a small non-executable scratch area, no capabilities, no setuid escalation, resource limits that stop fork bombs and memory exhaustion, a port reachable only through a local reverse proxy, and an image pinned by digest.

docs.title: The same settings in Compose
docs.text:
# compose.prod.yaml (excerpt): hardened TaskFlow API service
services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest>
    user: "1000:1000"
    read_only: true
    tmpfs:
      - /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=64m
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt:
      - no-new-privileges:true
    pids_limit: 200
    mem_limit: 512m
    cpus: 1.0
    secrets:
      - mongodb_uri
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI_FILE: /run/secrets/mongodb_uri
    restart: unless-stopped

secrets:
  mongodb_uri:
    file: ./secrets/mongodb_uri.txt      # not committed; created on the server

The connection string arrives as a file at /run/secrets/mongodb_uri instead of an environment variable; the app reads MONGODB_URI_FILE when it is set.

docs.title: A distroless runtime stage
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile: TaskFlow API on a distroless, non-root runtime
# (keep the Node major version and the Debian release the same in every
# stage: node:24-trixie-slim and distroless nodejs24 are both Debian 13)

FROM node:24-trixie-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:24-trixie-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13:nonroot AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
EXPOSE 3000
# The image's ENTRYPOINT is the node binary, so CMD is only the script
CMD ["dist/server.js"]

There is no shell in the final image, so health checks and debugging must use node itself or an ephemeral debug container that shares the container's namespaces.

docs.title: Scanning in CI and locally
docs.text:
# Trivy: fail on fixable HIGH or CRITICAL findings
trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-3f9c2e1

# Docker Scout: summary, then the CVE list
docker scout quickview ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-3f9c2e1
docker scout cves --only-severity critical,high ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-3f9c2e1

# Grype: generate the inventory with Syft, then scan it
syft ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-3f9c2e1 -o spdx-json > sbom.spdx.json
grype sbom:./sbom.spdx.json --fail-on high

docs.title: Proving a leaked secret is in the image
docs.text:
# The image history shows build commands, including ARG values used in RUN
docker history --no-trunc taskflow-api:bad

# Every layer can be extracted and searched
mkdir leak && docker save taskflow-api:bad -o leak/image.tar
tar -xf leak/image.tar -C leak
grep -rl "_authToken" leak/ || echo "no token found"

If a secret is found in a published image, deleting the tag is not enough: copies may already exist in caches, mirrors, and other people's machines. Revoke and rotate the credential first, then rebuild with a secret mount.

docs.title: Keyless signing in GitHub Actions and verification
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/image.yml (excerpt, after the build step with id "build")
permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write
  id-token: write            # lets the job request an OIDC token for Sigstore

steps:
  - uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@756fe2d284c7292c4e9b62c8a28f1e5629c59532 # v4.1.3
  - name: Sign the pushed image by digest
    run: cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}

# Anyone can verify who signed it
cosign verify ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest> \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/example/taskflow-api/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com

Sign the digest, never a tag, so the signature cannot be moved to other content. The installer action is pinned to a full commit SHA, like every third-party action in a job that can sign or push: in March 2026 the tags of Trivy's setup-trivy installer action were repointed to code that stole CI secrets (CVE-2026-33634). The cosign version changes only when you upgrade the pinned installer.

docs.title: Pinning a base image by digest
docs.text:
# The "Digest:" line near the top is the digest of the multi-platform index
docker buildx imagetools inspect node:24-slim

# Dockerfile (excerpt): readable tag plus the digest that is actually used
FROM node:24-slim@sha256:<digest> AS base

Renovate and Dependabot both understand this tag@digest form and update the digest when the tag moves.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run as a non-root numeric UID, with application files owned by root.
  • Drop all capabilities and add back only those you can justify.
  • Set no-new-privileges and keep the default seccomp and AppArmor or SELinux profiles; never use --privileged for applications.
  • Run with a read-only root filesystem and explicit tmpfs or volume mounts for writable paths.
  • Never mount the Docker socket into application containers, and treat the docker group as root.
  • Keep secrets out of COPY, ARG, and ENV; use secret mounts at build time and files at runtime.
  • Use slim, distroless, or hardened base images, pinned by digest and updated automatically.
  • Scan in CI and continuously; rebuild images on a schedule.
  • Sign images in CI and verify signatures before deploy.
  • Set memory, CPU, and PID limits on every container.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A CI runner can control the whole host. Detect: docker inspect on the runner container shows /var/run/docker.sock mounted or "Privileged": true. Cause: the runner builds images by talking to the host's daemon. Fix: use ephemeral VMs per job, rootless BuildKit, or a remote builder, and treat existing hosts as fully trusted infrastructure.
  • A registry token is found inside a public image. Detect: a secret scanner or a researcher reports the token; docker history --no-trunc or an extracted layer shows .npmrc. Cause: the file was copied into a layer and deleted later, or passed as an ARG. Fix: revoke and rotate the token immediately, rebuild with secret mounts, delete the affected images, and add secret scanning to CI.
  • Every scan reports hundreds of vulnerabilities. Detect: scanner output is dominated by OS packages from the base image. Cause: a full node base image with compilers, rarely rebuilt. Fix: multi-stage build onto slim or distroless, --ignore-unfixed for gating, and scheduled rebuilds with --pull.
  • The app crashes with EROFS: read-only file system after hardening. Detect: the error names a path such as /tmp or a cache directory. Cause: the application or a library writes to the root filesystem. Fix: mount a tmpfs or volume at exactly those paths, or configure the library to write elsewhere.
  • A service fails to start after --cap-drop ALL. Detect: EACCES when binding port 80 or Operation not permitted on chown. Cause: the process needed NET_BIND_SERVICE or ran ownership changes at startup as root. Fix: listen on a high port (for nginx, the unprivileged image on 8080) or add back the single capability required.
  • Secrets appear in logs and support bundles. Detect: docker inspect output, crash dumps, or debug endpoints show MONGODB_URI with credentials. Cause: secrets passed as environment variables are visible to anyone who can inspect the container and are often dumped wholesale. Fix: mount secrets as files, redact configuration in logs, and restrict who can run docker inspect.
  • The same commit builds an image with different contents. Detect: digests differ between two builds of one commit, and a new CVE or behaviour change appears without a code change. Cause: the base tag moved upstream. Fix: pin the base by digest and let a bot propose updates through reviewed pull requests.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Attack surface: Everything an attacker can interact with or use.
  • Capability: One of the privileges Linux splits root's power into, such as NET_BIND_SERVICE or SYS_ADMIN.
  • no-new-privileges: A kernel flag that stops processes from gaining privileges through setuid binaries or file capabilities.
  • seccomp: A kernel filter that restricts which system calls a process may make.
  • AppArmor / SELinux: Mandatory access control systems that confine what a container's processes may access.
  • Rootless mode: Running the container engine and containers without root privileges on the host.
  • User namespace: A mapping of container UIDs to different, unprivileged host UIDs.
  • Distroless image: A base image with only the application runtime and its libraries.
  • CVE: A publicly catalogued vulnerability identifier.
  • SBOM: A software bill of materials: the inventory of packages in an image.
  • Image signing: Attaching a verifiable signature to an image digest to prove who built it.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing containers are a security boundary as strong as VMs.
  • Running as root because "it is inside a container".
  • Mounting the Docker socket to let a dashboard or CI job "just work".
  • Using --privileged to fix a permission error.
  • Deleting a secret in a later RUN and assuming it is gone.
  • Passing secrets with --build-arg.
  • Scanning only once at build time and never again.
  • Pinning digests without automation, so patches never arrive.
  • Signing a tag instead of a digest.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is a process running as root in a default Docker container more dangerous than the same process running as UID 1000?
  2. Which Docker flags implement a non-root user, no capabilities, no privilege escalation, and an immutable filesystem?
  3. Explain how a token copied into a layer and then deleted can still be recovered. How does a BuildKit secret mount avoid this?
  4. Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock equivalent to giving a container root on the host?
  5. A scan finds 180 vulnerabilities in a node:24 based image, 150 of them in OS packages. Which two changes would remove most of them, and why?
  6. What do pinning by digest and signing each prove, and why do you need both?
  7. When would you choose gVisor, Kata Containers, or a VM over a hardened container?

docs.text:
• Docker documentation: Rootless mode

  • Trivy documentation

docs.title: Debugging and Operating Containers
docs.text: Running containers in production means answering questions quickly: why did this container stop, why does it keep restarting, why is it slow, what is it doing right now, and why is the disk full. This lesson is the operator's toolkit: docker logs, exec, inspect, stats, top, events, and cp; a systematic way to debug a crash loop; what each exit code means; restart policies; memory and CPU limits and exactly what happens when a container reaches them; logging drivers and log rotation; health-check status; and keeping disk usage under control.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Containers fail differently from processes on a server you can log in to. The filesystem may have no shell, the process may already be gone, restart policies can hide a crash behind a fresh container every few seconds, and the kernel can kill a container silently when it reaches its memory limit. Without a method, debugging turns into guessing.

The same knowledge prevents incidents: unrotated logs and unpruned images are among the most common reasons a Docker host runs out of disk, and missing memory limits let one leaking container take down every other service on the machine.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Docker: resource constraints. The resource constraints documentation explains that without limits a container can use as much memory as the host kernel allows, that the kernel OOM killer may then kill any process including the Docker daemon, and how --memory, --memory-swap, and --cpus change that.
  • Docker: logging. The logging drivers guide notes that the default json-file driver does not rotate logs unless configured and recommends the local driver, which rotates and compresses by default, to prevent disk exhaustion.
  • Docker: restart policies. The start containers automatically page defines no, on-failure, always, and unless-stopped, and the increasing delay Docker adds between restarts.
  • The Twelve-Factor App. The logs factor says an app should write its event stream unbuffered to standard output and let the execution environment collect and route it: exactly what docker logs and logging drivers expect.

Popular tools and providers: the Docker CLI, nicolaka/netshoot for network debugging, ctop and lazydocker for terminal dashboards, Dozzle for viewing logs, cAdvisor and Prometheus for container metrics, and log shippers such as Fluent Bit and Vector.

docs.title: The debugging toolbox
docs.text: Question Command What is running, and what stopped? docker ps -a What did it print? docker logs --tail 100 -f <name> Why did it stop? docker inspect --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}' <name> What is its full configuration? docker inspect <name> What is happening inside right now? docker exec -it <name> sh Which processes run in it? docker top <name> How much CPU, memory, I/O does it use? docker stats What happened to it over time? docker events --filter container=<name> How do I get a file out (or in)? docker cp <name>:/path ./local What changed in its filesystem? docker diff <name> Where did the disk space go? docker system df -v

docs.title: Logs
docs.text:
docker logs shows what the container's main process wrote to standard output and standard error. Useful flags: -f to follow, --tail 100 to start near the end, --since 10m or a timestamp, and --timestamps. Logs survive while the container exists, so you can read the output of a container that has already exited; they are deleted with docker rm.

Two consequences for applications: log to stdout and stderr, not to files inside the container (those are invisible to docker logs and fill the writable layer), and write structured, one-line JSON entries so log pipelines can parse them (see structured logging).

docs.title: Getting inside a container
docs.text:
• docker exec -it api sh starts a new process in the running container's namespaces. Add -u 0 to run it as root when the container runs as a non-root user and you need to install a tool temporarily.
  • Distroless and other shell-less images cannot run sh. Start a debugging container that joins the target's namespaces instead: docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api nicolaka/netshoot. It sees the app's processes and shares its localhost, and /proc/<pid>/root exposes the app's filesystem. Docker Desktop also offers docker debug for the same purpose.
  • A container that exits immediately cannot be execed into. Start the same image with a different entry point: docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image>.

docs.title: inspect, stats, top, and events
docs.text:
docker inspect returns the full JSON state and configuration. The fields you will read most often are State (status, exit code, OOMKilled, start and finish times, health), RestartCount, Config.Env and Config.Cmd, HostConfig (limits, restart policy, mounts), Mounts, and NetworkSettings. Go templates with --format extract single fields.

docker stats streams per-container CPU percentage (where 100% is one full core), memory usage against the limit, network and block I/O, and the number of processes. docker top lists processes as the host sees them. docker events streams lifecycle events (create, start, die, oom, kill, stop, restart, health_status) with timestamps, which answers "who stopped this container, and when?".

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text:
When a container stops, its exit code is the main process's exit code. Codes above 128 mean a signal killed the process.

The most misread code is 137. It means "killed by SIGKILL", which happens when the kernel kills the process for exceeding its memory limit (then OOMKilled is true), but also on docker kill and when a process ignores SIGTERM until docker stop's timeout runs out. Check OOMKilled before raising memory limits.

docs.title: Debugging a crash loop
docs.text:
A container with a restart policy that keeps failing shows a status such as Restarting (1) 3 seconds ago and a climbing RestartCount. Work through it in order:

  1. Read the state: exit code, OOMKilled, restart count, and the last health-check output.
  2. Read the logs of the failed run with docker logs --tail 100. Most crash loops are configuration errors that print a clear message: a missing environment variable, a wrong connection string, a port already in use.
  3. Check what killed it with docker events when the code is a signal.
  4. Reproduce interactively: run the image with --entrypoint sh, or override the command with sleep infinity and exec in, then start the app by hand and watch it fail.

docs.title: Restart policies
docs.text:
Policy Restarts when After a daemon restart no (default) Never Not started on-failure[:N] The process exits with a non-zero code, optionally at most N times Not restarted always The process exits for any reason Started again, even if you had stopped it manually unless-stopped The process exits for any reason Started again unless you had stopped it

Docker waits before each restart, doubling the delay from 100 ms, and resets the delay once a container has run for at least 10 seconds. A manual docker stop is respected until the daemon or the container is restarted. Restart policies are the single-host equivalent of an orchestrator's self-healing; they do not move containers to another machine and do not react to an unhealthy health status.

docs.title: Limits and what happens at the limit
docs.text:
Resource Flag At the limit Memory --memory 512m The kernel reclaims page cache, then the OOM killer kills a process in the container (exit 137, OOMKilled: true) Memory + swap --memory-swap 512m Equal to --memory disables swap; unset, the container may also use swap up to the same amount if the host has swap Soft memory --memory-reservation 256m Only enforced when the host is short of memory CPU quota --cpus 1.5 The process is throttled for the rest of each 100 ms period: slower, never killed CPU weight --cpu-shares 512 Only matters when CPUs are contended CPU pinning --cpuset-cpus 0,1 Runs only on those cores Processes --pids-limit 200 New processes and threads fail to start

For Node.js, memory needs extra care: V8's heap is only part of the process's memory (buffers, native modules, and thread stacks add more), and the default maximum heap size may not match the container limit. Set --max-old-space-size (in MB) explicitly to roughly 75% of the container limit so the garbage collector works harder before the kernel steps in. A process that hits the heap limit dies with a JavaScript "heap out of memory" error you can read in the logs; a process that hits the container limit is killed without a message.

docs.title: Logging drivers and rotation
docs.text:
Docker captures stdout and stderr through a logging driver:

Driver Where logs go Rotation by default docker logs works json-file (default) JSON files under /var/lib/docker/containers/ No: grows without limit Yes local Compressed files in an optimized format Yes: 5 files of 20 MB per container Yes journald The systemd journal By journald's settings Yes syslog, fluentd, gelf, awslogs, gcplogs, ... External systems Handled by the receiver Yes, through Docker's local cache (dual logging)

Set the driver and options for the whole host in /etc/docker/daemon.json; they apply to containers created afterwards. In production, the usual pattern is the local or json-file driver with rotation on each host plus a log shipper (Fluent Bit, Vector, the cloud provider's agent) that sends logs to central storage.

docs.title: Health status
docs.text: When an image or Compose file defines a health check, docker ps shows (health: starting), (healthy), or (unhealthy) after the status, and docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' shows the last five check results with their output. A health_status event is emitted on every change. Docker Engine does not restart unhealthy containers; Compose dependencies, Swarm, monitoring, or a small watchdog must act on the status.

docs.title: Disk usage and cleanup
docs.text:
docker system df summarizes space used by images, containers, local volumes, and the build cache, including how much is reclaimable; -v lists every item.

Command Removes docker container prune Stopped containers docker image prune Dangling images (untagged leftovers of rebuilds) docker image prune -a Every image not used by a container docker builder prune Build cache (-a for all of it) docker volume prune Unused anonymous volumes (--all adds unused named volumes) docker network prune Networks no container uses docker system prune Stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images, and unused build cache; -a and --volumes widen it

All prune commands accept --filter until=<duration> so a scheduled job can remove only old objects. Never run --volumes or volume prune --all on a host whose databases might be temporarily stopped.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Tool Avoid A container exited docker ps -a, inspect, logs Recreating it before reading its state It restarts in a loop Crash-loop method above Raising limits blindly It is slow docker stats, throttling in cpu.stat, app metrics Restarting it and hoping Network problem exec with curl, or netshoot in its namespace Installing tools in the production image Need a file from it docker cp Bind-mounting host paths after the fact Disk is full docker system df -v, targeted prunes system prune -a --volumes on a database host Many hosts Central logs and metrics SSH-ing to each host to run docker logs

Interactive debugging is for diagnosis. The fix belongs in the image or the configuration, followed by a new deploy: changes made with exec are lost when the container is recreated.

docs.title: The first five commands for any broken container
docs.text:
docker ps -a --filter name=taskflow-api
docker inspect --format \
  'status={{.State.Status}} exit={{.State.ExitCode}} oom={{.State.OOMKilled}} restarts={{.RestartCount}} finished={{.State.FinishedAt}}' \
  taskflow-api
docker logs --tail 100 --timestamps taskflow-api
docker events --since 30m --filter container=taskflow-api \
  --format '{{.Time}} {{.Action}} exit={{.Actor.Attributes.exitCode}}'
docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' taskflow-api

docs.title: A crash loop caused by configuration
docs.text:
docker run -d --name taskflow-api --restart on-failure:5 \
  -p 3000:3000 taskflow-api:1.4.0

docker ps -a --filter name=taskflow-api --format '{{.Status}}'
# Restarting (1) 2 seconds ago

docker logs --tail 5 taskflow-api
# Error: MONGODB_URI is not set
#     at loadConfig (file:///app/dist/config.js:12:11)

docker rm -f taskflow-api
docker run -d --name taskflow-api --restart on-failure:5 -p 3000:3000 \
  --env-file ./api.env taskflow-api:1.4.0

Exit code 1 plus a clear log line: the configuration was missing, so the fix is the run configuration, not the image. on-failure:5 stops after five attempts instead of retrying forever.

docs.title: Keeping a crashing image alive to inspect it
docs.text:
# Override the entry point and get a shell in the same image
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh taskflow-api:1.4.0
# inside: ls -la /app; node -e "console.log(process.versions.node)"; node dist/server.js

# Or keep a container running and exec into it
docker run -d --name api-debug --entrypoint sleep taskflow-api:1.4.0 infinity
docker exec -it api-debug sh
docker rm -f api-debug

docs.title: Debugging a distroless container from a sidecar
docs.text:
docker run --rm -it \
  --network container:taskflow-api \
  --pid container:taskflow-api \
  nicolaka/netshoot

# inside netshoot:
ps aux                                  # the app's node process is visible
curl -s localhost:3000/healthz          # same localhost as the app
dig mongo                               # name resolution from the app's network
ss -tnp                                 # the app's open connections
ls /proc/1/root/app/dist                # the app's filesystem

docs.title: Watching resources and adjusting limits
docs.text:
docker stats --no-stream --format \
  'table {{.Name}}\t{{.CPUPerc}}\t{{.MemUsage}}\t{{.MemPerc}}\t{{.PIDs}}'

# Raise the memory limit of a running container (no restart needed)
docker update --memory 768m --memory-swap 768m taskflow-api

# Was it throttled? Read the cgroup counters
docker exec taskflow-api cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
# nr_periods 51231
# nr_throttled 8452        <- 16% of periods hit the quota
# throttled_usec 912834120

# Size the Node heap to the container limit (512 MB -> about 384 MB of heap)
docker run -d --name taskflow-api --memory 512m \
  -e NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=384 \
  taskflow-api:1.4.0

docs.title: Log rotation for the whole host and for one service
docs.text:
{
  "log-driver": "local",
  "log-opts": {
    "max-size": "20m",
    "max-file": "5"
  },
  "live-restore": true
}

sudo cp daemon.json /etc/docker/daemon.json
sudo systemctl restart docker      # live-restore keeps running containers up
docker info --format '{{.LoggingDriver}}'

# compose.yaml (excerpt): per-service rotation with the default driver
services:
  api:
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "10m"
        max-file: "3"

docs.title: A cleanup routine
docs.text:
docker system df
docker container prune -f --filter until=72h
docker image prune -af --filter until=168h      # unused images older than 7 days
docker builder prune -f --filter until=168h
docker system df

Run it from a systemd timer or cron on build hosts and single-server deployments. Leave volumes to an explicit, reviewed process.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Read the exit code, OOMKilled, and logs before changing anything.
  • Log to stdout and stderr in a structured format; never to files inside the container.
  • Set memory limits on every container and size runtimes (such as the Node heap) below them.
  • Prefer on-failure with a retry limit for jobs and unless-stopped for long-running services on single hosts; alert on restart counts.
  • Configure log rotation on every host and ship logs centrally.
  • Enable live-restore so daemon upgrades do not stop containers.
  • Keep production images free of debugging tools and debug from a sidecar container instead.
  • Schedule pruning of old images, containers, and build cache; never prune volumes automatically.
  • Watch CPU throttling, not just CPU percentage, for latency-sensitive services.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A container restarts every few hours with exit code 137. Detect: docker inspect shows OOMKilled: true, docker events shows oom events, and memory in docker stats climbs steadily before each restart. Cause: a memory leak or a limit below the real working set; the kernel killed the process at the cgroup limit. Fix: take heap snapshots to find the leak, set --max-old-space-size below the limit, and size the limit from measured peak usage.
  • The host's disk is full and every container fails. Detect: df -h shows /var/lib/docker at 100%, and du -sh /var/lib/docker/containers/* shows multi-gigabyte *-json.log files. Cause: the default json-file driver without rotation. Fix: set rotation in daemon.json (new containers) and logging options in Compose, recreate the containers, and ship logs off the host.
  • A crash loop goes unnoticed for days. Detect: RestartCount is in the hundreds, and the logs show the same error repeating. Cause: restart: always hides failures because the service keeps coming back briefly. Fix: alert on restart counts or die events, and use on-failure with a limit for things that should not restart forever.
  • An unhealthy container keeps receiving traffic. Detect: docker ps shows (unhealthy) while the reverse proxy still routes to it. Cause: Docker Engine only reports health; nothing acts on it. Fix: use an orchestrator (Swarm, Kubernetes) or a watchdog that restarts unhealthy containers, and make the proxy check health too.
  • p99 latency doubles under load though CPU usage looks moderate. Detect: nr_throttled in cpu.stat rises with traffic; docker stats shows CPU pinned at the --cpus value. Cause: the CPU quota throttles bursts within each 100 ms period. Fix: raise --cpus, run more replicas, or reduce CPU work per request.
  • A container exits immediately with code 0. Detect: docker ps -a shows Exited (0) seconds after start, and the logs end normally. Cause: the main process finished: a command that starts the server in the background (npm start &), or a daemon that forks away (nginx without daemon off). Fix: run the server in the foreground as the container's main process.
  • The build host runs out of space although few images exist. Detect: docker system df shows tens of gigabytes of build cache. Cause: BuildKit cache from many builds and branches is never collected. Fix: docker builder prune on a schedule, or configure BuildKit garbage collection limits for the builder.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Exit code: The main process's exit status; 128 + N means killed by signal N.
  • OOMKilled: A flag set when the kernel killed the container's process for exceeding its memory limit.
  • Crash loop: A container that repeatedly starts and fails, restarted by a restart policy or an orchestrator.
  • Restart policy: The rule Docker uses to restart a container after it exits.
  • CPU throttling: Pausing a cgroup's processes for the rest of a period after they used their CPU quota.
  • Logging driver: The plugin that receives a container's stdout and stderr and stores or forwards it.
  • Log rotation: Capping log size by rolling to a new file and deleting the oldest.
  • Health status: starting, healthy, or unhealthy, from the container's health check.
  • Dangling image: An untagged image layer set left behind by a rebuild.
  • Live restore: A daemon setting that keeps containers running while dockerd restarts.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating every 137 as out-of-memory without checking OOMKilled.
  • Deleting and recreating a failed container before reading its logs and state.
  • Writing logs to files inside the container.
  • Running production hosts with the default unrotated json-file logs.
  • Expecting Docker to restart an unhealthy container.
  • Using restart: always and assuming a service is healthy because it is "Up".
  • Installing debugging tools in production images instead of using a debugging sidecar.
  • Running docker system prune -a --volumes on a server that holds data.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. A container exited with code 137. List three possible causes and the command that distinguishes the out-of-memory case.
  2. What do exit codes 126, 127, and 139 each suggest, and where would you look next?
  3. Describe the steps you would follow to debug a container in a crash loop.
  4. A host runs 20 containers, each logging 2 MB per minute with the default json-file driver. How much disk do the logs use per day, and what configuration fixes it?
  5. What is the difference between always and unless-stopped after a daemon restart?
  6. What happens when a container reaches its memory limit compared with its CPU limit?
  7. How do you debug a distroless container that has no shell?
  8. Why should automatic cleanup jobs avoid pruning volumes?

docs.title: Further learning
