docs.title: Docker Compose for Development
docs.text:
Docker Compose describes a multi-container application in one YAML file and runs it with one command. Instead of starting MongoDB, Redis, and the API by hand with long docker run lines, you declare the services, their images or build instructions, ports, environment, volumes, health checks, and dependencies, and docker compose up creates the network, volumes, and containers in the right order.

This lesson covers the structure of a Compose file, every key the TaskFlow stack uses, how service names become hostnames, how to start services only when their dependencies are healthy, profiles for optional tools, override files for personal and environment-specific settings, docker compose watch for live code sync, and the commands you will use every day.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A new developer should be able to clone the repository and run the whole system in minutes, with the same database and cache versions that production uses. Without Compose, onboarding means a page of installation steps, everyone's local MongoDB is a different version, and "start Redis first" lives only in someone's memory.

Compose turns that knowledge into a reviewed file in the repository. It also gives integration tests and CI a reproducible environment, and it is a reasonable way to run small production deployments on a single server.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App. The dev/prod parity factor argues that developers should use the same type and version of backing services (database, queue, cache) locally as in production, and names lightweight tools such as Docker as the way to make that practical.
  • Docker. The documentation on controlling startup order explains that Compose starts containers in dependency order but only waits for readiness when you use health checks with condition: service_healthy, the pattern this page uses for MongoDB.
  • The Compose Specification. The open Compose Specification defines the file format that Docker Compose v2 implements. It made the old top-level version field obsolete, which is why modern files start directly with services:.
  • Docker. The Compose Watch guide shows develop.watch rules that sync source files into a running container and rebuild it when dependency manifests change, replacing slow bind mounts on macOS and Windows for many projects.

Popular tools and providers: Docker Compose v2 (docker compose), Podman Compose, Docker Desktop, Rancher Desktop, Testcontainers (for containers started from test code), Tilt, and Dev Containers.

docs.title: The Compose file
docs.text:
Compose looks for compose.yaml (preferred), compose.yml, or the older docker-compose.yaml in the current directory. The main top-level keys:

Key Purpose name Project name; defaults to the directory name services The containers to run, one entry per service volumes Named volumes the services mount networks Extra networks; one default network is created automatically configs, secrets Files mounted into services include Pulls in other Compose files as sub-projects

There is no version: key in current files. Compose v2 ignores it and prints a warning that it is obsolete.

Compose names everything after the project: containers become taskflow-api-1, the default network taskflow_default, and a volume called mongo-data becomes taskflow_mongo-data. Two checkouts of the same repository in folders with the same name share these resources, so set name: or use -p when that matters.

docs.title: Services: build or image
docs.text:
Each service either uses an existing image (image: mongo:8.0) or builds one (build:). A service can have both: Compose builds the image and tags it with the image name.

Key Example Notes image mongo:8.0 Pin at least a major version; never rely on latest build.context . The build context, as with docker build build.target build Stop at a Dockerfile stage (a stage with dev dependencies) command npm run dev Overrides the image's CMD ports "3000:3000" HOST:CONTAINER; quote them so YAML does not misread them environment MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/taskflow Variables set in the container env_file .env.local File of NAME=value lines loaded into the container volumes mongo-data:/data/db Named volume or bind mount depends_on mongo: {condition: service_healthy} Start order and readiness healthcheck test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"] Overrides or adds the image's health check restart unless-stopped Restart policy profiles ["tools"] Start only when the profile is enabled

docs.title: Environment variables: two different mechanisms
docs.text:
Compose uses environment variables in two separate ways, and mixing them up is a classic source of confusion:

  1. Interpolation in the Compose file. ${MONGO_TAG:-8.0} in compose.yaml is replaced when Compose reads the file, using your shell environment and the project's .env file. ${NAME:?message} stops with an error if NAME is unset.
  2. Variables inside the container. environment: and env_file: decide what the process sees in process.env. The project .env file is not passed into containers unless you list it in env_file.

When both set the same variable, environment: wins over env_file:. docker compose config prints the fully resolved file, which is the quickest way to see what Compose actually did. Precedence rules in more depth are in env files and precedence.

docs.title: Networks and service-name DNS
docs.text:
Compose creates one user-defined bridge network per project and attaches every service to it. Docker's embedded DNS server resolves each service name to the container's IP address on that network, so the API connects to mongodb://mongo:27017, not to localhost. Inside a container, localhost means the container itself.

Two consequences:

  • Services talk to each other on the container port (27017), whatever host port you publish. Publishing a port is only needed for access from your machine.
  • A service that is not published at all (Redis above) is reachable only from inside the network, which is a sensible default for databases.

docs.title: Startup order and health conditions
docs.text:
depends_on controls the order in which containers start. In its short form (depends_on: [mongo]) it only waits for the mongo container to be created and started, not for MongoDB to accept connections. MongoDB needs a few seconds to initialize, so an API that connects at startup can fail with ECONNREFUSED or a server-selection timeout.

The long form adds a condition:

Condition Waits until service_started The dependency's container has started (the default) service_healthy The dependency's health check reports healthy service_completed_successfully The dependency ran to completion and exited with code 0

service_healthy requires a healthcheck on the dependency. Adding restart: true under a dependency also restarts the dependent service when that dependency is restarted by a Compose command. Health conditions make startup reliable, but the application should still retry its connections: in production nothing waits for the database for you.

docs.title: Health checks in Compose
docs.text:
A healthcheck block has the same fields as the Dockerfile instruction, written in YAML:

healthcheck:
  test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"]
  interval: 5s
  timeout: 5s
  retries: 10
  start_period: 10s

test in ["CMD", ...] form runs the program directly; ["CMD-SHELL", "..."] runs it through /bin/sh. The command must exist in the image: the official mongo images ship mongosh, the redis images ship redis-cli, and Node images can use node -e with fetch.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text: Services with profiles: start only when one of their profiles is enabled, with --profile <name> or the COMPOSE_PROFILES variable. Services without profiles always start. This keeps optional tools (an admin UI, a mail catcher, a load generator) in the same file without running them for everyone.

docs.title: Override files
docs.text:
Compose automatically merges compose.override.yaml on top of compose.yaml when it exists. With -f, you choose the files and their order explicitly: docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml up. Merge rules:

  • Single-value keys (image, command, restart) are replaced by the later file.
  • Multi-value keys (ports, expose, dns) are combined.
  • environment, labels, and volumes are merged by key or by container path, with the later file winning.

Common uses: a git-ignored compose.override.yaml for personal settings, a compose.ci.yaml that runs tests, and a production file that removes bind mounts and sets restart policies.

docs.title: docker compose watch
docs.text:
The develop.watch section tells Compose what to do when files on the host change:

Action What happens Use it for sync Copies changed files into the running container Source code with a watcher inside (tsx, nodemon, Vite) rebuild Rebuilds the image and recreates the container package.json, package-lock.json, the Dockerfile sync+restart Syncs files, then restarts the container Config files read only at startup

docker compose watch (or docker compose up --watch) starts the stack and the watcher. Compared with bind-mounting the whole project, syncing avoids the slow cross-VM file access of Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows, and it never mounts the host's node_modules (built for the host OS) over the container's.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use Compose for Prefer something else for Local development stacks with databases and caches Multi-host production clusters (Kubernetes, ECS) Integration tests in CI Unit tests that need no services Demo environments and reproducible bug reports Autoscaling and zero-downtime rolling deploys Small production deployments on one VM Highly available databases (use managed services) Trying out a new tool next to your app Containers created per test case (Testcontainers)

Compose on a single server is a legitimate production choice for small internal tools: add restart: unless-stopped, log rotation, backups, and no bind mounts of source code. It cannot spread containers across machines, fail over when the host dies, or roll out new versions without a brief gap, which is where Kubernetes or a managed container platform takes over.

docs.title: The full TaskFlow stack
docs.text:
# compose.yaml: TaskFlow local development stack
name: taskflow

services:
  api:
    build:
      context: .
      target: build                 # Dockerfile stage with dev dependencies
    command: npm run dev            # package.json: "dev": "tsx watch src/server.ts"
    ports:
      - "3000:3000"
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      PORT: "3000"
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/taskflow
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    env_file:
      - path: .env.local            # personal overrides, git-ignored
        required: false
    depends_on:
      mongo:
        condition: service_healthy
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 20s
    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync
          path: ./src
          target: /app/src
        - action: rebuild
          path: package-lock.json

  migrate:
    build:
      context: .
      target: build
    command: npm run migrate        # idempotent: safe to run on every "up"
    environment:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/taskflow
    depends_on:
      mongo:
        condition: service_healthy

  mongo:
    image: mongo:8.0
    volumes:
      - mongo-data:/data/db
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 10s

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

  mongo-express:
    image: mongo-express:1.0
    profiles: ["tools"]
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8081:8081"
    environment:
      ME_CONFIG_MONGODB_URL: mongodb://mongo:27017/
      ME_CONFIG_BASICAUTH_USERNAME: admin
      ME_CONFIG_BASICAUTH_PASSWORD: ${MONGO_EXPRESS_PASSWORD:?set MONGO_EXPRESS_PASSWORD in .env}
    depends_on:
      mongo:
        condition: service_healthy

volumes:
  mongo-data:

What each part does:

  • api builds the build stage of the Dockerfile from writing production Dockerfiles, which has dev dependencies, and runs a watcher. It reaches MongoDB and Redis by service name and starts only after both are healthy and the migrations have finished.
  • migrate is a one-off task. service_completed_successfully means a failing migration stops the API from starting, which is exactly what you want.
  • mongo keeps its data in the named volume mongo-data, so docker compose down and up keep your local data. It publishes no port; tools on your machine use the override file below.
  • redis is reachable only inside the project network.
  • mongo-express starts only with --profile tools, binds to 127.0.0.1 so other machines on your network cannot reach it, and refuses to start without a password.

The local MongoDB here has no authentication, which is acceptable only because nothing outside this machine can reach it. Never copy this service definition to a server.

docs.title: Project .env for interpolation
docs.text:
# .env (read by Compose for ${...} in compose.yaml; not passed to containers)
MONGO_EXPRESS_PASSWORD=<choose-a-local-password>
COMPOSE_PROFILES=

docs.title: A personal override file
docs.text:
# compose.override.yaml: local-only tweaks (listed in .gitignore)
services:
  api:
    environment:
      LOG_LEVEL: debug
  mongo:
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:27017:27017"     # for MongoDB Compass or mongosh on this machine

environment is merged by key and ports are added, so this file only contributes the debug log level and the published database port.

docs.title: Everyday commands
docs.text:
docker compose up -d                  # create and start everything in the background
docker compose up -d --build          # rebuild images first
docker compose watch                  # start and sync ./src on every save
docker compose --profile tools up -d  # also start mongo-express
docker compose ps                     # services, state, health, ports
docker compose logs -f api            # follow one service's logs
docker compose exec api sh            # shell in the running api container
docker compose run --rm api npm test  # one-off container with the api's settings
docker compose exec mongo mongosh taskflow   # database shell
docker compose restart api            # restart one service
docker compose config                 # print the fully resolved configuration
docker compose down                   # stop and remove containers and the network
docker compose down -v                # ...and delete named volumes (local data!)

docs.title: Running integration tests in CI
docs.text:
# compose.ci.yaml: used as docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml ...
services:
  api:
    command: npm run test:integration
    develop: !reset {}

docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml up -d --wait mongo redis
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml run --rm api
docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.ci.yaml down -v

--wait returns only when the listed services are running and healthy. The !reset tag removes the develop section inherited from the base file. Tests then run against real MongoDB and Redis of the same versions as development.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Name the file compose.yaml, leave out version:, and set name:.
  • Pin image versions for every service, matching production's versions.
  • Add health checks to databases and caches and use service_healthy; still make the application retry connections.
  • Connect services by service name; publish only the ports you use from the host, bound to 127.0.0.1.
  • Keep data in named volumes and remember that down -v deletes them.
  • Keep secrets in a git-ignored .env or env_file, never in compose.yaml.
  • Put optional tools behind profiles and personal tweaks in an ignored override file.
  • Prefer develop.watch over bind-mounting the whole project, especially on macOS and Windows.
  • Check what Compose will do with docker compose config.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The API crashes on docker compose up with ECONNREFUSED. Detect: docker compose logs api shows a MongoDB connection error in the first seconds, then a restart. Cause: depends_on without a condition waits only for the container to start, not for MongoDB to be ready. Fix: add a health check to mongo, use condition: service_healthy, and add connection retries in the app.
  • dependency failed to start: container taskflow-mongo-1 is unhealthy. Detect: docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' taskflow-mongo-1 shows the check output, such as executable file not found. Cause: the health check calls a tool missing from the image (the legacy mongo shell is not in current MongoDB images), or the timeout is too short for the first start. Fix: use mongosh, and raise start_period and retries.
  • All local data disappeared. Detect: collections are empty after a restart, and docker volume ls no longer lists taskflow_mongo-data. Cause: someone ran docker compose down -v, or the project name changed so a new, empty volume was created. Fix: set name: explicitly, avoid -v unless you mean it, and keep a seed script for local data.
  • Bind for 0.0.0.0:3000 failed: port is already allocated. Detect: docker compose up fails for one service. Cause: another container or a local process already uses the host port. Fix: stop the other process (docker ps shows containers), or change the host side of the mapping ("3001:3000"); the container port stays the same.
  • Code changes do not show up in the running API. Detect: the response is unchanged after saving a file. Cause: the stack was started with up instead of watch, the watch path does not match the folder, or the process inside does not reload. Fix: use docker compose watch, check path and target, and run a watcher (tsx watch, node --watch) as the command.
  • A variable is set in .env but process.env does not have it. Detect: docker compose exec api env lacks the variable. Cause: the project .env file is only used for interpolation in the Compose file. Fix: reference it in environment: (FOO: ${FOO}) or list the file under env_file:.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Project: All resources Compose manages for one Compose file, named by name: or the directory.
  • Service: A named container definition that Compose runs as one or more containers.
  • Default network: The bridge network Compose creates per project; service names resolve on it.
  • Named volume: Docker-managed storage that survives container recreation.
  • Health check: A command whose exit status marks a container healthy or unhealthy.
  • Dependency condition: service_started, service_healthy, or service_completed_successfully in depends_on.
  • Profile: A label that makes a service start only on request.
  • Override file: A Compose file merged on top of another, such as compose.override.yaml.
  • Interpolation: Substituting ${VAR} in the Compose file from the shell and .env.
  • Compose Watch: Rules in develop.watch that sync files or rebuild services when the host files change.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using localhost to reach another service; inside a container it is the container itself.
  • Assuming depends_on waits until a database is ready.
  • Expecting the project .env file to appear in containers.
  • Writing version: "3.8" and believing it changes behaviour; it is ignored.
  • Publishing database ports on 0.0.0.0, exposing them to the whole network.
  • Bind-mounting the host's node_modules into a Linux container.
  • Treating docker compose down -v as a harmless cleanup.
  • Using the legacy docker-compose (v1) binary; the current command is docker compose.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does the API use mongodb://mongo:27017 instead of mongodb://localhost:27017?
  2. What is the difference between depends_on: [mongo] and depends_on: {mongo: {condition: service_healthy}}?
  3. In the timeline above, MongoDB becomes healthy at 8 seconds and the migration takes 3 seconds. If MongoDB's health check interval were 10 seconds instead of 5, roughly when could the API start, and why?
  4. Where do ${MONGO_EXPRESS_PASSWORD} and env_file values each come from, and which one does the container see?
  5. How would you run mongo-express only when you need it?
  6. What happens to the ports list and the command when an override file sets both?
  7. Why can docker compose watch be faster than a bind mount on macOS?
  8. When is Compose a reasonable production tool, and what does it lack compared with Kubernetes?

docs.title: Images, Registries, and Tagging
docs.text: Once an image is built, it has to be named, stored, moved to the machines that run it, and eventually deleted. This lesson covers how image references are structured, what a registry actually stores (manifests, configs, and layers addressed by digest), why tags can move but digests cannot, a tagging strategy that keeps deploys reproducible, the major registries, multi-architecture images with docker buildx, sharing the build cache through a registry, retention policies, and pull rate limits.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The image reference in a deployment file is the single link between "the code we tested" and "the code that runs". If it says taskflow-api:latest, nobody can tell which commit is in production, two servers can run different code under the same name, and a rollback has nothing exact to return to. If it says taskflow-api@sha256:..., every node runs identical bytes and the deploy history is the history of that reference.

Registries are also production dependencies. A registry outage, an anonymous pull limit, or a cleanup policy that deleted an image still in use can block every deploy and every autoscaling event at the worst possible moment.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• OCI Distribution Specification. The distribution spec defines the HTTP API that Docker Hub, GHCR, ECR, Artifact Registry, ACR, and Harbor all implement for pushing and pulling manifests and blobs by digest. That shared API is why one docker push command works against any of them.
  • Kubernetes. The Images documentation recommends avoiding the :latest tag in production, explains that latest (or no tag) changes the default pull policy to Always, and shows pinning an image by digest so every node runs the same version.
  • Docker Hub. Docker's usage and limits documentation describes the pull rate limits that apply to anonymous and authenticated users, which is why CI systems and clusters authenticate or use a mirror.
  • Amazon ECR. The lifecycle policies guide shows rules that expire untagged images and cap the number of images per tag prefix, the standard way to keep registry storage from growing without bound.

Popular tools and providers: Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry (GHCR), Amazon ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry, Harbor, Quay, and JFrog Artifactory; docker buildx, crane, skopeo, and regctl for inspecting and copying images.

docs.title: Anatomy of an image reference
docs.text:
A reference has up to five parts: [registry/][namespace/]repository[:tag][@digest].

Part Example Rules and defaults Registry ghcr.io, 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Recognized by a dot, a port, or localhost; defaults to Docker Hub (docker.io) Namespace example An account, organization, or project; Docker Hub's Official Images use library Repository taskflow-api Lowercase letters, digits, and separators Tag 1.4.0, sha-3f9c2e1 Up to 128 characters of letters, digits, _, ., -; defaults to latest Digest sha256:9f86d0... The SHA-256 of the manifest; if present, the tag is ignored for pulling

latest is not special to the registry. It is just the tag Docker uses when you do not give one, and nothing forces it to point to the newest image.

docs.title: What a registry stores
docs.text:
A registry stores three kinds of objects, each addressed by the SHA-256 digest of its content:

  • Layers (blobs): compressed tar archives of filesystem changes.
  • The image config (a blob): JSON with the environment, entry point, command, user, and the ordered list of uncompressed layer digests.
  • The manifest: a small JSON document that references the config and the layers by digest and size.
{
  "schemaVersion": 2,
  "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
  "config": {
    "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.config.v1+json",
    "digest": "sha256:<config-digest>",
    "size": 7023
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip",
      "digest": "sha256:<base-layer-digest>",
      "size": 28230000
    },
    {
      "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.layer.v1.tar+gzip",
      "digest": "sha256:<node-modules-layer-digest>",
      "size": 12900000
    }
  ]
}

The image digest you deploy is the digest of this manifest. Because the manifest contains the digests of everything below it, the digest pins the entire image: change one byte in any layer and every digest above it changes. A tag is just a named pointer from a repository to a manifest digest.

Pushing and pulling move these objects separately. docker push first asks the registry whether each layer digest already exists (and prints Layer already exists when it does), uploads only the missing ones, and then uploads the manifest and moves the tag. docker pull reads the manifest and downloads only the layers the local machine lacks. That is why a code-only change to the TaskFlow API pushes a 1 MB layer, not the whole 250 MB image.

docs.title: Tags are mutable, digests are immutable
docs.text:
Anyone with push access can move a tag at any time, and CI does it routinely when it rebuilds 1.4 with a patched base image. A deployment that references a tag therefore depends on when each node pulled it. Kubernetes makes this worse with latest: the default pull policy becomes Always and every restart may fetch something new.

A digest can never point to different content. Deploying by digest, or by a tag the registry refuses to overwrite, makes every node run the same bytes and makes rollbacks exact. Several registries can enforce this: Amazon ECR repositories can be set to immutable tags, and Google Artifact Registry Docker repositories have an immutable-tags option.

docs.title: A tagging strategy
docs.text:
Tag Example Moves? Use it for Commit SHA sha-3f9c2e1 or the full SHA Never (one build per commit) The canonical, traceable build identity Full version 1.4.0 Should never move Releases; what changelogs and humans refer to Minor / major 1.4, 1 Yes, to the newest patch Consumers who accept updates automatically Branch main Yes, on every merge Development environments that track a branch latest latest Yes Local convenience only; never in deploy manifests Environment production Yes Avoid: hides which build is where; use digests in GitOps instead

A practical recipe that many teams use:

  1. CI tags every build with the commit SHA and pushes it once.
  2. A release adds 1.4.0 (and moves 1.4 and 1) to the same digest; it does not rebuild.
  3. Deployment manifests reference the digest, or the immutable SHA tag plus digest (taskflow-api:sha-3f9c2e1@sha256:...) so people can read it and machines can verify it.
  4. Every image carries OCI labels such as org.opencontainers.image.source and org.opencontainers.image.revision so anyone can trace it back to the repository and commit. GHCR uses the source label to link a package to its repository.

Promoting the same digest through environments is covered in artifacts and environment promotion, and version numbering in versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: Registries
docs.text:
Registry Reference format Authentication Good fit Docker Hub docker.io/<namespace>/<repo> docker login with an access token Public images, Official Images GitHub Container Registry ghcr.io/<owner>/<image> GITHUB_TOKEN in Actions, or a token with package scopes Code on GitHub, open source Amazon ECR <account>.dkr.ecr.<region>.amazonaws.com/<repo> aws ecr get-login-password piped to docker login; IAM roles on AWS EKS, ECS, Lambda containers Google Artifact Registry <region>-docker.pkg.dev/<project>/<repo>/<image> gcloud auth configure-docker <region>-docker.pkg.dev GKE, Cloud Run Azure Container Registry <name>.azurecr.io/<repo> az acr login --name <name>; managed identities AKS, Azure Container Apps Harbor (self-hosted) <your-host>/<project>/<repo> Users, robot accounts, OIDC On-premises, air-gapped, proxy caches

Choose the registry that sits in the same cloud and region as the workloads that pull from it: pulls are faster, often free of egress charges, and authenticate through the platform's identity system instead of stored passwords. Google's older Container Registry (gcr.io) has been replaced by Artifact Registry.

docs.title: Multi-architecture images
docs.text:
Images contain compiled binaries (the node executable, native modules, system libraries), so an image built for linux/amd64 does not run natively on linux/arm64 machines such as Apple-silicon laptops and AWS Graviton or other Arm servers. A multi-platform image solves this with an image index (Docker calls it a manifest list): one tag points to an index, and the index points to one manifest per platform.

docker buildx builds every platform in one command. It has three ways to produce non-native binaries:

Method How Trade-off QEMU emulation Runs the other architecture's instructions in an emulator Works for any Dockerfile; npm ci with native modules can be several times slower Native nodes A builder with one machine per architecture (docker buildx create --append) Fast; needs an Arm machine or runner Cross-compilation Build stage runs on $BUILDPLATFORM and outputs for $TARGETPLATFORM Fastest; only for steps whose output does not depend on the CPU

For a TypeScript service, compiling to JavaScript produces the same files on any CPU, so the build stage can run natively on the build machine. Production node_modules may contain native modules and must be installed on (or emulated for) each target platform.

BuildKit also attaches attestations when pushing (a minimal build provenance record by default, and an SBOM if you ask for one). They are stored in the index as extra entries with the platform unknown/unknown, which is why even a single-platform push can produce an index. A few older registries and tools do not understand them; --provenance=false disables them, at the cost of losing supply-chain metadata.

docs.title: Sharing the build cache through a registry
docs.text:
CI runners are usually fresh machines with an empty BuildKit cache. Export the cache after each build and import it before the next:

Cache backend Flags Notes Registry --cache-to type=registry,ref=<image>:buildcache,mode=max --cache-from type=registry,ref=<image>:buildcache Works with any CI; stored as a separate image reference GitHub Actions --cache-to type=gha,mode=max --cache-from type=gha Uses the Actions cache service; subject to its size limits Inline --cache-to type=inline Embeds cache metadata in the image itself; only min mode

mode=min exports only the layers of the final image. mode=max also exports the layers of intermediate stages, which is what makes multi-stage builds fast in CI: without it, the build and deps stages are rebuilt every time.

docs.title: Retention and cleanup
docs.text:
Every CI build pushes an image, so a busy repository accumulates thousands of them. Registries offer rules to delete old ones:

  • Amazon ECR: lifecycle policies that expire untagged images after N days or keep only the newest N images matching a tag prefix.
  • Google Artifact Registry: cleanup policies with delete and keep conditions (tag state, tag prefixes, age, and a "keep most recent N").
  • Azure Container Registry: retention for untagged manifests and the acr purge command run as a scheduled task.
  • GHCR: delete package versions through the API or a scheduled workflow.

Design rules so that cleanup cannot break a rollback: keep every release tag (1.4.0) indefinitely or for your support window, keep the last 30 to 100 commit builds, expire untagged manifests after a week, and never delete a digest that a running deployment, or the previous release, still references.

docs.title: Pull rate limits and availability
docs.text:
Docker Hub limits how many pulls an IP address or account can make per hour, with much lower limits for anonymous pulls than for authenticated ones; check Docker's documentation for the current numbers. A CI fleet or a cluster behind one NAT address can hit the anonymous limit quickly and fail with toomanyrequests. The fixes, in order of robustness:

  1. Authenticate every pull (CI secrets, Kubernetes imagePullSecrets).
  2. Use a pull-through cache: ECR pull-through cache rules, Artifact Registry remote repositories, ACR artifact cache, or a Harbor proxy project.
  3. Copy the base images you depend on into your own registry and build from there, which also protects you if an upstream tag changes or disappears.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Decision Recommendation Reference in production manifests Digest (optionally with the SHA tag for readability) Reference in a Dockerfile FROM Version tag for readability, plus digest when you need full reproducibility and have automated updates latest Local experiments only Registry for a cloud workload The registry of that cloud, same region Registry for open-source images Docker Hub or GHCR Multi-platform builds When any developer, CI runner, or server uses a different architecture Registry cache Every CI pipeline that builds images

Multi-platform builds cost build time; skip them if every machine that runs the image is amd64 and nobody develops on Arm. Do not pin every image by digest by hand without a bot (such as Dependabot or Renovate) to update the digests, or patches will never arrive.

docs.title: Tag and push the TaskFlow API to GHCR
docs.text:
# Log in with a token read from stdin (never on the command line)
echo "$GHCR_TOKEN" | docker login ghcr.io -u <github-user> --password-stdin

SHA=$(git rev-parse --short=12 HEAD)
docker build \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/example/taskflow-api \
  --label org.opencontainers.image.revision="$(git rev-parse HEAD)" \
  -t ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-"$SHA" .
docker push ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-"$SHA"

# Release: add a version tag to the SAME image, without rebuilding
docker tag ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-"$SHA" ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
docker push ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0

# The digest to put in deployment manifests
docker image inspect --format '{{index .RepoDigests 0}}' \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
# ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api@sha256:<digest>

docs.title: Build multi-platform images locally
docs.text:
# One-time: a builder that can produce multi-platform images
docker buildx create --name multi --driver docker-container --use
docker run --privileged --rm tonistiigi/binfmt --install arm64,amd64   # QEMU handlers

docker buildx build \
  --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 \
  -t ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-"$SHA" \
  --push .

docker buildx imagetools inspect ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-"$SHA"
# Output, abbreviated:
#   MediaType: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json
#   Manifests:
#     Platform: linux/amd64
#     Platform: linux/arm64
#     Platform: unknown/unknown   (an attestation manifest)

Multi-platform results must be pushed (or exported) because the classic local image store holds one platform per tag; Docker Desktop's containerd image store can keep all of them locally.

docs.title: Cross-compile the platform-independent stage
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile (excerpt): compile once natively, install deps per platform

# Runs on the build machine's own CPU: TypeScript output is the same everywhere
FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# Runs once per target platform: native modules must match the CPU
FROM node:24-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev

FROM node:24-slim AS runtime
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

BuildKit sets BUILDPLATFORM and TARGETPLATFORM automatically. Only the deps stage runs under emulation for the non-native platform, so the slow part of a multi-platform build shrinks to one npm ci.

docs.title: A CI workflow: build, tag, cache, push
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/image.yml
name: image
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    tags: ["v*.*.*"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-qemu-action@v4
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: meta
        uses: docker/metadata-action@v6
        with:
          images: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api
          flavor: latest=false
          tags: |
            type=sha,format=long
            type=semver,pattern={{version}}
            type=semver,pattern={{major}}.{{minor}}
      - id: build
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.tags }}
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          cache-from: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:buildcache
          cache-to: type=registry,ref=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:buildcache,mode=max
      - run: echo "Pushed digest ${{ steps.build.outputs.digest }}" >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

metadata-action produces a sha-<full commit> tag on every push and 1.4.0 plus 1.4 when a v1.4.0 Git tag is pushed, and fills in the OCI labels; latest=false stops it from also moving a latest tag. The registry cache in mode=max keeps the deps and build stages warm between runs. The digest output is what a deployment step or GitOps commit should record. The workflow structure itself is covered in GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: An ECR lifecycle policy
docs.text:
{
  "rules": [
    {
      "rulePriority": 1,
      "description": "Expire untagged images after 7 days",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "untagged",
        "countType": "sinceImagePushed",
        "countUnit": "days",
        "countNumber": 7
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    },
    {
      "rulePriority": 2,
      "description": "Keep only the 50 newest commit builds",
      "selection": {
        "tagStatus": "tagged",
        "tagPrefixList": ["sha-"],
        "countType": "imageCountMoreThan",
        "countNumber": 50
      },
      "action": { "type": "expire" }
    }
  ]
}

aws ecr put-lifecycle-policy \
  --repository-name taskflow-api \
  --lifecycle-policy-text file://lifecycle.json

Release tags such as 1.4.0 match neither rule, so they are kept. Test a new policy with the lifecycle policy preview before applying it.

docs.title: Inspect without pulling
docs.text:
docker buildx imagetools inspect node:24-slim            # index and platforms
docker buildx imagetools inspect --raw ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
skopeo inspect docker://ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0   # labels, digest, layers
crane digest ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0              # just the digest

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give every build an immutable, traceable tag (the commit SHA) and push it exactly once.
  • Add release tags to an existing digest instead of rebuilding.
  • Deploy by digest; keep human-readable tags alongside for people.
  • Turn on tag immutability where the registry supports it.
  • Label images with their source repository and revision.
  • Use the registry in the same cloud and region as the workloads.
  • Authenticate all pulls and mirror the public base images you rely on.
  • Publish multi-platform images when any consumer runs a different architecture.
  • Export the build cache from CI with mode=max.
  • Write retention rules that keep releases and anything still deployed.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Pulls fail with toomanyrequests. Detect: CI jobs or new pods fail at image pull, and the error mentions the pull rate limit. Cause: anonymous Docker Hub pulls from many runners or nodes sharing one IP address. Fix: authenticate pulls, configure a pull-through cache or mirror, and copy base images into your own registry.
  • Some servers run old code after a deploy. Detect: responses differ between instances; docker inspect shows different image IDs for the same tag. Cause: the deployment references a mutable tag, and each node pulled it at a different time (or reused a cached copy). Fix: deploy by digest or an immutable SHA tag.
  • no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8 in the manifest list entries. Detect: the pull fails only on Arm machines (Apple silicon, Graviton). Cause: the image was built for amd64 only. Fix: build with --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64, or pin the platform explicitly where emulation is acceptable.
  • A rollback fails with manifest unknown. Detect: the previous release's image cannot be pulled. Cause: a cleanup rule deleted it because it fell outside "keep the last N". Fix: exempt release tags from expiry, keep enough history for your rollback window, and check deployed digests before deleting.
  • CI image builds stay slow despite caching. Detect: build logs show the dependency install running on every pipeline although the lockfile did not change. Cause: no cache import on fresh runners, or cache exported with mode=min so intermediate stages are missing. Fix: --cache-from and --cache-to with mode=max to a registry or the CI cache.
  • Pushing to GHCR from CI fails with denied. Detect: login succeeds but docker push is rejected. Cause: the workflow token lacks packages: write, or the package is not linked to the repository. Fix: add the permission to the workflow and link the package (the org.opencontainers.image.source label does this automatically).
  • The registry storage bill grows every month. Detect: thousands of untagged manifests and commit images in the repository. Cause: no retention policy. Fix: lifecycle or cleanup rules that expire untagged and old commit images while keeping releases.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Image reference: The registry, namespace, repository, tag, and/or digest naming an image.
  • Registry: A server implementing the OCI distribution API that stores manifests and blobs.
  • Repository: A named collection of images (all versions of taskflow-api).
  • Tag: A mutable, human-readable pointer to a manifest.
  • Digest: The SHA-256 hash of content; for an image, the hash of its manifest. Immutable by construction.
  • Manifest: JSON that lists an image's config and layers by digest.
  • Image index (manifest list): JSON that lists one manifest per platform under one tag.
  • Platform: An OS and CPU architecture pair such as linux/arm64.
  • Attestation: Signed or unsigned metadata about how an image was built (provenance) or what it contains (SBOM).
  • Pull-through cache: A registry that fetches and stores images from an upstream registry on first pull.
  • Lifecycle (retention) policy: Rules that delete old images automatically.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking latest means newest. It means "no tag was given".
  • Deploying mutable tags and expecting every node to run the same code.
  • Rebuilding for each environment instead of promoting one digest.
  • Assuming pure JavaScript images are architecture-independent; the Node binary and native modules are not.
  • Deleting old images without checking which digests are deployed or needed for rollback.
  • Pulling anonymously from Docker Hub in CI and clusters.
  • Pinning base images by digest without automation to update them, so security patches never arrive.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Break ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0@sha256:... into its parts and say which part decides what is pulled.
  2. What does nginx expand to, and why is latest not guaranteed to be the newest release?
  3. Why does a code-only change push a 1 MB layer rather than the whole image?
  4. A tag 1.4 is rebuilt on day 5. A deployment that references :1.4 scales from 2 to 6 replicas on day 6. How many replicas run the day-1 image, and how would you prevent the mix?
  5. How does a laptop on linux/arm64 end up with different layers than a server on linux/amd64 when both pull the same tag?
  6. Why does a multi-stage build need mode=max cache export to stay fast in CI?
  7. Design a retention policy that saves storage but can never break a rollback to the previous two releases.
  8. Name two ways to avoid Docker Hub rate limits in a Kubernetes cluster.

docs.text:
• Docker documentation: Multi-platform builds
  • Docker documentation: Cache storage backends
  • OCI image specification: image index
  • GitHub documentation: Working with the Container registry
  • Google Cloud: Artifact Registry cleanup policies

docs.title: Docker Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review container fundamentals, production Dockerfiles, images and registries, Docker Compose, networking and storage, security, and day-to-day operations. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is a container, and how is it different from a virtual machine?
docs.text: A container is an ordinary Linux process (or process tree) isolated with kernel namespaces and limited with cgroups. It shares the host kernel. A VM runs its own kernel on virtual hardware provided by a hypervisor. So containers are smaller (megabytes instead of gigabytes) and start in about a second, while VMs give stronger isolation and can run a different OS kernel.

docs.title: 2. Which kernel features make containers possible?
docs.text: Namespaces decide what a process can see: PID, network, mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, user, cgroup, and time namespaces. cgroups decide what it can use: memory, CPU, I/O, and number of processes. Security features (capabilities, seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux) further restrict what it may do.

docs.title: 3. What happens at the cgroup memory limit compared with the CPU limit?
docs.text: Memory is not compressible: when a container exceeds --memory, the kernel reclaims what it can and then the OOM killer kills a process (exit 137, OOMKilled: true). CPU is compressible: a container over its --cpus quota is throttled until the next scheduling period, so it gets slower but keeps running.

docs.title: 4. What is an image made of?
docs.text: An ordered list of read-only filesystem layers plus a JSON configuration (environment, user, working directory, entry point, command). Each layer is a tar archive of the files an instruction added, changed, or deleted, identified by its SHA-256 digest. A manifest lists the config and layers; its digest identifies the image.

docs.title: 5. How does copy-on-write work in a container?
docs.text: The runtime stacks the image layers read-only and adds a writable layer using overlayfs. Reads come from the highest layer that has the file. The first write to an image file copies the whole file up into the writable layer; deletions create whiteouts. The writable layer is deleted with the container, which is why data and write-heavy workloads belong in volumes.

docs.title: 6. What sits between docker run and the running process?
docs.text: The docker CLI calls the Docker Engine API on /var/run/docker.sock; dockerd asks containerd over gRPC to create the container; containerd starts a containerd-shim-runc-v2 per container; the shim calls runc with an OCI bundle; runc creates the namespaces and cgroups, starts the process, and exits. Kubernetes nodes skip dockerd and talk to containerd through the CRI.

docs.title: 7. What is the OCI, and why does it matter?
docs.text: The Open Container Initiative maintains the image, runtime, and distribution specifications. Because Docker images are OCI images, the same image runs on containerd, CRI-O, Podman, and every cloud container service, and registries expose a common push and pull API.

docs.title: 8. What states can a container be in?
docs.text: created, running, paused, restarting, exited, plus the transient removing and the rare dead. A container lives exactly as long as its main process: when PID 1 exits, the container exits, whatever else was running inside.

docs.title: 9. Why does Docker Desktop need a virtual machine on macOS and Windows?
docs.text: Linux containers need a Linux kernel. Docker Desktop runs a lightweight Linux VM (WSL 2 on Windows, Apple's virtualization framework on macOS) with dockerd inside. That is why bind mounts are slower there, why host.docker.internal exists, and why resources come from the VM's allocation.

docs.title: 10. Why copy package.json and the lockfile before the source code?
docs.text: The build cache reuses a step only if its instruction and inputs are unchanged and every previous step was reused. Copying the manifests and running npm ci first means a source-only change reuses the cached dependency layer; only the final COPY and later steps rebuild, so the build takes seconds instead of a full reinstall.

docs.title: 11. What is a multi-stage build, and what does it achieve?
docs.text: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where later stages copy only selected outputs with COPY --from=<stage>. Build tools, dev dependencies, source files, and caches stay in earlier stages, so the final image is smaller, has fewer vulnerabilities, and contains only what runs.

docs.title: 12. What is the difference between exec form and shell form?
docs.text: Exec form (CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]) runs the program directly as PID 1. Shell form (CMD node dist/server.js) runs it under /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and usually does not forward signals; it does expand variables. Use exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT.

docs.title: 13. How do ENTRYPOINT and CMD interact?
docs.text: ENTRYPOINT is the executable; CMD supplies default arguments (or the whole command if there is no entry point). docker run <image> <args> replaces CMD only; --entrypoint replaces the entry point. An entry point script must end with exec "$@" so the app replaces the shell.

docs.title: 14. Why is PID 1 special, and how do you handle signals in Node?
docs.text: The kernel applies no default signal actions to PID 1, so a signal it has no handler for is ignored, and PID 1 should reap orphaned zombies. Node has no default SIGTERM handler, so as PID 1 it ignores docker stop and is killed after 10 seconds. Use exec form, handle SIGTERM in the app (stop accepting, finish requests, close pools, exit), and use --init or tini when the app spawns children.

docs.title: 15. What does a graceful shutdown handler in Express do?
docs.text:
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  server.close(async () => {          // stop accepting; wait for in-flight requests
    await mongoose.disconnect();      // release pools
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 8000).unref(); // before the platform's SIGKILL
});

docs.title: 16. What is the difference between ARG and ENV?
docs.text: ARG exists only during the build (from --build-arg) and is not in the running container's environment; ENV is set during the build and at runtime and can be overridden with docker run -e. Neither is safe for secrets: ARG values used in RUN appear in the image history.

docs.title: 17. What does .dockerignore protect against?
docs.text: It excludes files from the build context: the host's node_modules (possibly built for another OS), .git (which breaks the cache on every commit), .env files and credentials, and build outputs. A smaller context also uploads faster.

docs.title: 18. Which BuildKit features matter most for production builds?
docs.text: Cache mounts (RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm) keep package caches between builds without storing them in layers; secret mounts (--mount=type=secret) expose credentials to one step only; parallel and skipped stages; --target to stop at a stage; and cache export to a registry for CI.

docs.title: 19. Does a HEALTHCHECK make Docker restart an unhealthy container?
docs.text: No. Docker Engine only records healthy or unhealthy. Compose uses it for depends_on: condition: service_healthy, Swarm replaces unhealthy tasks, and monitoring can alert on it. Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK and uses probes.

docs.title: 20. What are the parts of an image reference?
docs.text: registry/namespace/repository:tag@digest, for example ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0@sha256:.... The registry defaults to docker.io, Docker Hub Official Images use the library namespace, and the tag defaults to latest only when neither a tag nor a digest is given.

docs.title: 21. Why should production deployments reference digests instead of tags?
docs.text: Tags are mutable pointers that anyone with push access (including CI) can move; nodes that pull at different times can run different code under the same tag. A digest is the hash of the manifest, so it always names the same bytes. Deploying by digest makes every node identical and rollbacks exact.

docs.title: 22. Describe a good tagging strategy.
docs.text: Tag every CI build with its commit SHA and push it once; add semantic version tags (1.4.0, 1.4) to that same digest at release time without rebuilding; reference the digest in deployment manifests; never deploy latest; enable tag immutability where the registry supports it; add OCI labels for the source repository and revision.

docs.title: 23. How does a multi-architecture image work?
docs.text: The tag points to an image index (manifest list) containing one manifest per platform, such as linux/amd64 and linux/arm64. The client picks the entry matching its own platform and pulls only those layers. docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --push builds and publishes all of them.

docs.title: 24. What are the ways to build for another CPU architecture?
docs.text: QEMU emulation (works for anything, slow for heavy steps), native builder nodes per architecture (fast, needs the hardware), and cross-compilation with FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM for steps whose output does not depend on the CPU, such as compiling TypeScript.

docs.title: 25. How do you keep Docker builds fast in CI?
docs.text: Order the Dockerfile for the cache, use BuildKit cache mounts, and export and import the cache across runs with --cache-to and --cache-from (a registry reference or the CI cache) in mode=max, so intermediate stages are cached too.

docs.title: 26. Why do pulls fail with toomanyrequests, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Docker Hub limits pulls per hour, with much lower limits for anonymous pulls, and many runners or nodes behind one NAT address share the anonymous quota. Authenticate pulls, use a pull-through cache or mirror, or copy base images into your own registry.

docs.title: 27. How do you clean up a registry safely?
docs.text: Use lifecycle or cleanup policies: expire untagged manifests after some days, keep the newest N commit builds, and keep release tags for the support window. Never delete a digest that is deployed or needed for a rollback.

docs.title: 28. What problem does Docker Compose solve?
docs.text: It declares a multi-container application (services, images or builds, ports, environment, volumes, networks, health checks, dependencies) in one file, so docker compose up reproduces the whole stack for development, tests, demos, or small single-host deployments.

docs.title: 29. How do services find each other in Compose?
docs.text: Compose creates a user-defined bridge network per project, and Docker's embedded DNS resolves each service name to its container. The API connects to mongodb://mongo:27017; localhost inside a container means the container itself. Services use container ports, not published ports.

docs.title: 30. Does depends_on wait until a database is ready?
docs.text: Only with a condition. The short form waits for the container to start. condition: service_healthy waits for the dependency's health check to pass, and service_completed_successfully waits for a one-off task such as a migration to exit with 0. Apps should still retry connections.

docs.title: 31. What is the difference between .env, env_file, and environment?
docs.text: The project .env file feeds ${VAR} interpolation in the Compose file and is not passed into containers by itself. env_file and environment set variables inside the container, with environment winning on conflicts. docker compose config shows the resolved result.

docs.title: 32. What are profiles and override files for?
docs.text: Profiles mark optional services (an admin UI, a mail catcher) that start only with --profile. compose.override.yaml is merged automatically on top of compose.yaml for local tweaks; -f combines files explicitly, for example a CI or production overlay.

docs.title: 33. What does docker compose watch do?
docs.text: It applies develop.watch rules: sync copies changed source files into the running container, rebuild rebuilds and recreates the service when files such as package-lock.json change, and sync+restart syncs then restarts. It avoids slow bind mounts on Docker Desktop and never mounts the host's node_modules.

docs.title: 34. Is Docker Compose suitable for production?
docs.text: For small, single-host deployments, yes, with restart policies, log rotation, backups, and no source bind mounts. It cannot schedule across hosts, fail over when the host dies, autoscale, or roll out without a brief gap; that is where Kubernetes or a managed container platform fits.

docs.title: 35. Why should applications use a user-defined bridge instead of the default bridge?
docs.text: User-defined bridges provide DNS resolution by container name, isolate the application from unrelated containers, and allow connecting or disconnecting containers without restarts. The default bridge has none of these.

docs.title: 36. How does -p 8080:3000 work, and what is the security catch?
docs.text: Docker adds NAT rules that forward the host's port 8080 to the container's port 3000, listening on all interfaces by default. Those rules are evaluated before simple host-firewall input rules such as ufw, so a published port can be reachable even when the firewall "blocks" it. Bind sensitive ports to 127.0.0.1 or do not publish them.

docs.title: 37. Does EXPOSE publish a port?
docs.text: No. It documents the port the app listens on and is used by -P. Publishing requires -p or ports:.

docs.title: 38. How does a container reach a service running on the host?
docs.text: Use host.docker.internal, which Docker Desktop provides; on Linux add --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway (or extra_hosts). The host service must listen on an address reachable from the bridge, not only on 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: 39. Compare named volumes, bind mounts, and tmpfs mounts.
docs.text: Named volumes are Docker-managed, persist past docker rm, are pre-filled from the image when empty, and suit databases and uploads. Bind mounts map a specific host path, hide the image's files at the target, and suit source code and config. tmpfs mounts live in memory, vanish when the container stops, and suit secrets and scratch space.

docs.title: 40. How do you back up a Docker volume?
docs.text: For general files, archive the volume from a helper container: docker run --rm -v vol:/data:ro -v "$(pwd)":/backup alpine tar czf /backup/vol.tgz -C /data .. For a database, stop it first or, better, use the database's own tool (mongodump) for a consistent backup while it runs, and test restores.

docs.title: 41. Why do bind mounts cause permission errors on Linux but rarely on Docker Desktop?
docs.text: The kernel checks numeric UIDs: a container running as UID 1000 cannot write to a host directory owned by another UID, and files a root container creates become root-owned on the host. Docker Desktop's file-sharing layer translates ownership, hiding the mismatch. Fix with --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)", ownership changes, or named volumes.

docs.title: 42. Why run containers as a non-root user?
docs.text: Without user namespaces, root in a container is UID 0 on the host kernel, limited only by capabilities, seccomp, and AppArmor or SELinux. Any escape or kernel bug is far more dangerous from root. Use USER with a numeric UID so orchestrators can verify it, and keep app files read-only to that user.

docs.title: 43. Which runtime flags harden a container?
docs.text: --user 1000:1000, --read-only with --tmpfs /tmp, --cap-drop ALL (adding back only what is needed), --security-opt no-new-privileges:true, memory, CPU, and PID limits, publishing on 127.0.0.1, and never --privileged.

docs.title: 44. Why is mounting /var/run/docker.sock dangerous?
docs.text: Whoever can call the Docker API can start a privileged container with the host's root filesystem mounted, so socket access equals root on the host. The same applies to membership in the docker group and to an unauthenticated TCP daemon.

docs.title: 45. How can a secret end up in an image, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: COPY of a credentials file (even if a later RUN rm deletes it, the earlier layer keeps it), ARG or ENV values (visible in history and config), or an unignored .env in the context. Use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time secrets, a .dockerignore, and runtime injection as files for runtime secrets.

docs.title: 46. What do distroless images give you?
docs.text: Only the language runtime and its libraries: no shell, no package manager, far fewer packages. That reduces CVEs and leaves an attacker without the usual tools. Debugging needs an ephemeral sidecar container that shares the target's namespaces.

docs.title: 47. How does image scanning fit into a pipeline?
docs.text: Scanners (Trivy, Grype, Docker Scout) inventory OS and language packages and match them against vulnerability databases. Scan in CI and fail on fixable high or critical issues, scan continuously in the registry because new CVEs appear after the build, and fix mostly by rebuilding on patched bases.

docs.title: 48. What do pinning by digest and signing each prove?
docs.text: Pinning a base image by digest makes builds reproducible and immune to a moved or compromised tag (pair it with an update bot). Signing an image digest with cosign proves who built it; admission policies can then reject unsigned images. Together they answer "which bytes" and "from whom".

docs.title: 49. What does exit code 137 mean, and how do you confirm the cause?
docs.text: 128 + 9: the process received SIGKILL. Check docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}': true means the memory limit was hit. Otherwise it was docker kill, or a process that ignored SIGTERM until docker stop's timeout.

docs.title: 50. What do exit codes 125, 126, 127, 139, and 143 indicate?
docs.text: 125: the docker run command itself failed. 126: the command could not be executed (permissions, not a program). 127: the command was not found. 139: segmentation fault (128 + 11), usually native code. 143: terminated by SIGTERM (128 + 15) without a handler that exited cleanly.

docs.title: 51. How do you debug a container in a crash loop?
docs.text: Read the state (docker inspect: exit code, OOMKilled, restart count, health), read the failed run's logs (docker logs --tail 100), check docker events for kills and stops, then reproduce interactively with docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh <image> or by overriding the command with sleep infinity and execing in.

docs.title: 52. Compare the restart policies.
docs.text: no never restarts. on-failure[:N] restarts on non-zero exits, up to N times. always restarts on any exit and again after a daemon restart, even if you stopped it. unless-stopped is like always but stays stopped after a daemon restart if you stopped it. Docker doubles the delay between restarts, starting at 100 ms.

docs.title: 53. Why do Docker hosts run out of disk, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: Unrotated json-file logs, old images and stopped containers, build cache, anonymous volumes, and apps writing into container layers. Set log rotation (or the local driver) in daemon.json, prune images, containers, and build cache on a schedule, run short-lived containers with --rm, and monitor /var/lib/docker.

docs.title: 54. How do you debug a container that has no shell?
docs.text: Start a debugging container in its namespaces: docker run --rm -it --network container:api --pid container:api nicolaka/netshoot. It shares the app's localhost, sees its processes, and can read its filesystem through /proc/<pid>/root. Docker Desktop's docker debug does the same.

docs.title: 55. A one-line code change makes the CI image build take four minutes. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Dockerfile's instruction order and whether npm ci shows CACHED in the build log.

How to confirm: the dependency install runs on commits that only change source files; the .dockerignore is missing .git, or CI imports no cache.

Likely causes and fixes: COPY . . before npm ci, a context that changes on every commit, or fresh runners with no cache. Copy the manifests first, add .dockerignore, and export the cache with --cache-to ... mode=max. See writing production Dockerfiles.

docs.title: 56. Every deploy takes ten extra seconds per container, and some requests fail with 502. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the exit code of the old containers and the CMD form.

How to confirm: docker stop always takes the full timeout and the old container exits with 137.

Likely causes and fixes: PID 1 is a shell or npm, or the app has no SIGTERM handler. Use exec-form CMD ["node", ...], add a graceful shutdown handler, and use --init or tini. See writing production Dockerfiles.

docs.title: 57. An image built on a developer's MacBook fails on the server with exec format error. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the image's architecture with docker image inspect --format '{{.Architecture}}'.

How to confirm: it reports arm64 while the server is amd64.

Likely causes and fixes: the image was built on Apple silicon for the local platform. Build in CI for the target platform or publish a multi-platform image with docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64. See images, registries, and tagging.

docs.title: 58. After a "deploy", half of the servers still run the old version. How do you fix the process?
docs.text:
What to check first: the image reference in the deployment configuration.

How to confirm: it uses a mutable tag (latest or 1.4), and docker inspect shows different image IDs on different servers.

Likely causes and fixes: nodes pulled the tag at different times or reused cached images. Deploy by digest or an immutable commit-SHA tag and promote the same digest through environments. See images, registries, and tagging.

docs.title: 59. docker compose up fails because the API cannot connect to MongoDB, but a second up works. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the depends_on definition and MongoDB's health check.

How to confirm: the API logs ECONNREFUSED in the first seconds while MongoDB is still initializing.

Likely causes and fixes: depends_on without a condition only waits for the container to start. Add a mongosh ping health check, use condition: service_healthy, and add connection retries. See Docker Compose for development.

docs.title: 60. The API container logs ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:27017, but MongoDB is running. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the connection string.

How to confirm: it uses localhost, and MongoDB runs in another container or on the host.

Likely causes and fixes: localhost inside a container is the container itself. Use the service name (mongo) on a shared network, or host.docker.internal for a database on the host. See container networking and storage.

docs.title: 61. A security scan of the internet finds your MongoDB port open although ufw denies it. How?
docs.text:
What to check first: docker ps port mappings on that host.

How to confirm: the container shows 0.0.0.0:27017->27017/tcp.

Likely causes and fixes: published ports are handled by Docker's NAT rules before ufw's input rules. Remove the mapping or bind it to 127.0.0.1, filter in DOCKER-USER or a cloud firewall, and enable database authentication. See container networking and storage.

docs.title: 62. Users' uploaded files disappear after every deploy. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the API writes uploads and the container's mounts.

How to confirm: docker inspect shows no volume at the upload path, and docker diff on a running container lists the files as added.

Likely causes and fixes: files go to the writable layer, which is deleted with the container. Mount a named volume there, or better, store uploads in object storage so any instance can serve them. See container networking and storage.

docs.title: 63. A registry token is discovered in a public image. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which credential leaked and in which layers and tags.

How to confirm: docker history --no-trunc or an extracted layer shows .npmrc or the token in an ARG.

Likely causes and fixes: a COPY of the file or a build argument. Revoke and rotate the token immediately, rebuild with a secret mount, delete the affected images, and add secret scanning to CI. See container security.

docs.title: 64. A monitoring dashboard container has /var/run/docker.sock mounted. Is that a problem?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the dashboard is reachable by other users and whether the mount is read-write.

How to confirm: docker inspect shows the socket mount; anyone who compromises the dashboard can call the Docker API.

Likely causes and fixes: socket access is root on the host (a read-only mount does not change that, because API calls are still possible). Remove it, use a socket proxy that allows only read-only endpoints, or run the tool on an isolated host. See container security.

docs.title: 65. A service restarts every few hours with exit code 137. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: OOMKilled and the memory trend in docker stats or metrics.

How to confirm: OOMKilled: true, oom events, and memory climbing steadily before each restart.

Likely causes and fixes: a leak or a limit below the working set. Take heap snapshots, set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the limit, and size the limit from measured peaks. See debugging and operating containers.

docs.title: 66. A Docker host runs out of disk space overnight. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: docker system df -v and the size of /var/lib/docker/containers/*/*-json.log.

How to confirm: one container's log file is many gigabytes, or images and build cache dominate.

Likely causes and fixes: unrotated json-file logs, accumulated images, or build cache. Configure log rotation in daemon.json, recreate containers, prune on a schedule, and ship logs centrally. See debugging and operating containers.

docs.title: 67. A container shows (unhealthy) for an hour but still serves traffic. Why didn't Docker fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: what consumes the health status on this host.

How to confirm: the container uses only a restart policy; nothing listens to health_status events.

Likely causes and fixes: Docker Engine reports health but never restarts unhealthy containers. Use an orchestrator or a watchdog that restarts them, and make the load balancer check health. See debugging and operating containers.

docs.title: 68. A container with --cpus 1 has high p99 latency at peak, but average CPU looks fine. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: throttling counters in the container's cpu.stat.

How to confirm: nr_throttled rises with traffic, and docker stats shows bursts at 100%.

Likely causes and fixes: the CPU quota throttles bursts within each 100 ms period even when the average is low. Raise the quota, add replicas, or reduce CPU work per request. See container fundamentals.
