docs.title: Writing Production Dockerfiles
docs.text:
A Dockerfile is a recipe: each instruction runs in order and records its result as an image layer or as image metadata. Writing one that merely works takes five lines. Writing one that builds in seconds, produces a small image, runs as an unprivileged user, shuts down cleanly, reports its health, and never leaks a secret takes understanding how the build cache, stages, and the container's PID 1 behave.

This lesson walks through every common instruction, the build context and .dockerignore, the cache rules that decide build speed, multi-stage builds for the TaskFlow API (Node.js) and TaskFlow Web (a Vite build served by nginx), exec and shell forms, ENTRYPOINT and CMD, signal handling and graceful shutdown, health checks, build arguments, and the BuildKit features that keep secrets out of images.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The Dockerfile decides properties you cannot fix later at runtime:

  • Build speed. A badly ordered Dockerfile reinstalls every dependency on each one-line code change. Ten developers and a CI pipeline turn that into hours of waiting per day.
  • Image size. Every megabyte is pulled by every node on every deploy and every scale-out. A 1.3 GB image can add tens of seconds to an autoscaling event that a 250 MB image would not.
  • Security. Compilers, package managers, shells, and a root user in the final image are tools an attacker can use. Secrets copied into any layer can be extracted by anyone who can pull the image.
  • Reliability. A process that ignores SIGTERM is killed mid-request on every deploy. A missing health check lets a hung process keep receiving traffic.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Docker. The official Building best practices guide recommends multi-stage builds, a .dockerignore file, pinned base images, ordering instructions for the cache, and one concern per container: the same rules this page applies to the TaskFlow images.
  • The Node.js Docker team. The docker-node best practices document, maintained with the official Node.js images, recommends setting NODE_ENV=production, running as the built-in node user, using --init or handling signals because Node is not designed to run as PID 1, and calling node directly instead of npm start.
  • Google Cloud. The architecture guide Best practices for building containers explains PID 1 signal handling and zombie reaping, building the smallest image possible, and making the most of the build cache.
  • Snyk. The article 10 best practices to containerize Node.js web applications with Docker walks through deterministic installs with npm ci, least-privilege users, graceful shutdown, multi-stage builds, and keeping secrets out of images, applied to a Node.js service.

Popular tools and providers: Docker BuildKit and docker buildx, Hadolint (a Dockerfile linter), dive (an image layer explorer), Docker Scout, docker init (generates starter files), Buildah, and Cloud Native Buildpacks (Paketo) as an alternative to writing Dockerfiles.

docs.title: The instructions
docs.text:
Start every Dockerfile with the parser directive # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1. It tells BuildKit to use the latest stable 1.x Dockerfile frontend, which enables features such as cache and secret mounts regardless of the Docker version installed.

Instruction What it does Layer or metadata FROM image AS name Starts a stage from a base image Base layers ARG NAME=default Declares a build-time variable Metadata (build only) ENV NAME=value Sets an environment variable for later steps and at runtime Metadata WORKDIR /app Sets (and creates) the working directory Metadata (may create a small layer) COPY src dst Copies files from the build context or another stage (--from) Layer ADD src dst Like COPY, but also fetches URLs and Git repositories and unpacks local tar archives Layer RUN command Runs a command at build time Layer USER node Sets the user for later RUN steps and for the container Metadata EXPOSE 3000 Documents the port the app listens on; publishes nothing Metadata ENTRYPOINT [...] The executable the container always runs Metadata CMD [...] Default arguments (or the default command) Metadata HEALTHCHECK CMD ... A command Docker runs periodically to test health Metadata LABEL key=value Adds metadata, such as the source repository Metadata VOLUME /data Declares a mount point that gets an anonymous volume by default Metadata STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT Changes the signal docker stop sends Metadata SHELL ["bash", "-c"] Changes the shell used by shell-form instructions Metadata ONBUILD ... Defers an instruction to images built from this one Metadata (rarely used)

Prefer COPY over ADD: its behaviour is explicit, and ADD's automatic extraction and remote downloads can surprise you. Avoid VOLUME in application images: it creates anonymous volumes nobody manages.

docs.title: The build context and .dockerignore
docs.text:
docker build . sends the build context, the directory given as the last argument, to BuildKit. COPY . . can only copy files from it, and every file in it can affect the cache. Without a .dockerignore, the context includes:

  • the host's node_modules, possibly compiled for another OS or CPU, which then overwrites the clean install inside the image;
  • .git, which can be hundreds of megabytes and changes on every commit, breaking the cache for COPY . .;
  • .env files and local credentials, which end up inside an image layer.

A .dockerignore uses the same pattern syntax as .gitignore (*, **, ! to re-include). Keep it next to the Dockerfile and treat it as part of the build definition.

docs.title: The layer cache
docs.text:
BuildKit stores the result of every step and reuses it on the next build when nothing that step depends on has changed:

  1. A step is reused only if its parent layer was reused and the instruction text is identical.
  2. For COPY and ADD, the content checksums of the copied files must also match (modification times are ignored).
  3. For RUN, only the command string is compared. RUN apt-get update stays cached for months even though the package mirrors moved on; rebuild with --pull --no-cache on a schedule to pick up patches.
  4. Once one step misses the cache, every later step is rebuilt, even if its own inputs did not change.

The practical rule: order steps from least to most frequently changing. Copy the dependency manifests, install, and only then copy the source.

Worked example: the TaskFlow API team builds 40 times a day, and 5 of those builds change package-lock.json. With the slow order every build reinstalls dependencies: 40 × 65 s ≈ 43 minutes. With the fast order only the 5 lockfile changes reinstall: 5 × 65 s + 35 × 2 s ≈ 6.6 minutes. The registry also stores and transfers a 1 MB layer instead of a 40 MB layer for most builds.

CI runners start with an empty cache. Export the cache to a registry or the CI provider's cache so CI gets the same benefit (see images, registries, and tagging).

docs.title: Multi-stage builds
docs.text:
A multi-stage build has several FROM instructions. Each starts a new stage, and later stages copy only what they need from earlier ones with COPY --from=<stage>. Everything else (dev dependencies, compilers, source files, caches) stays behind and never reaches the final image.

Useful properties of stages:

  • BuildKit builds only the stages the target needs and runs independent stages in parallel (here, deps and build).
  • docker build --target build . stops at a named stage, which CI can use to run tests in the build environment.
  • The last stage is the default target, so put the runtime stage last.
  • A stage can start FROM another stage (FROM base AS deps) to share common settings.

docs.title: Running as a non-root user
docs.text:
Containers run as root unless the image says otherwise. The official Node images include a node user (UID 1000), and USER node switches to it for later RUN instructions and for the running container. Two details matter:

  • Files copied with COPY are owned by root by default. That is good for application code: the node user can read it but not modify it, so a compromised process cannot rewrite the app. Use COPY --chown=node:node or a RUN mkdir ... && chown only for directories the app must write.
  • Unprivileged users cannot bind ports below 1024 without extra capabilities. Listen on 3000 or 8080 inside the container and map the port when publishing it.

docs.title: Exec form compared with shell form
docs.text:
CMD, ENTRYPOINT, and RUN accept two syntaxes:

Exec form: CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"] Shell form: CMD node dist/server.js What actually runs node directly /bin/sh -c "node dist/server.js" PID 1 node The shell (Docker's docs warn the app will not receive signals) Signals from docker stop Delivered to node Delivered to the shell, which usually does not forward them Variable expansion ($PORT) None: passed literally Yes, by the shell Needs a shell in the image No (works in distroless images) Yes

Use the exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT. If you need variable expansion, use a small entrypoint script that ends with exec "$@" so the app replaces the shell as PID 1. Shell form is fine for RUN.

docs.title: ENTRYPOINT compared with CMD
docs.text:
ENTRYPOINT is the executable; CMD provides default arguments that docker run <image> <args> replaces.

ENTRYPOINT CMD Process started (none) ["node", "dist/server.js"] node dist/server.js; docker run img node -v runs node -v instead ["node"] ["dist/server.js"] node dist/server.js; docker run img dist/migrate.js runs node dist/migrate.js ["/usr/bin/tini", "--"] ["node", "dist/server.js"] tini -- node dist/server.js ["docker-entrypoint.sh"] ["node", "dist/server.js"] The script runs, then exec "$@" starts node as PID 1 Shell form anything The shell-form entry point ignores CMD and run arguments

The official Node images set ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"], a script that ends in exec "$@", so a CMD ["node", ...] still ends up with node as PID 1. If you replace ENTRYPOINT, keep that property.

docs.title: PID 1, signals, and graceful shutdown
docs.text:
The first process in a PID namespace is special. The kernel does not apply default signal actions to it: a signal that PID 1 has no handler for is simply ignored. PID 1 is also expected to reap orphaned child processes (zombies). Node.js installs no SIGTERM handler by default, so node as PID 1 ignores docker stop, and Docker sends SIGKILL 10 seconds later.

Three fixes, usually combined:

  1. Exec form, so the signal reaches node and not a shell. Run node directly rather than npm start: npm adds a process in between, and its signal forwarding has varied between versions.
  2. A SIGTERM handler in the app that stops accepting connections, lets in-flight requests finish, closes database pools, and exits.
  3. A tiny init process as PID 1 that forwards signals and reaps zombies: docker run --init (Docker's bundled tini), init: true in Compose, or tini installed in the image when the platform has no --init option (Kubernetes does not).

docker stop waits 10 seconds by default (--timeout or stop_grace_period in Compose); Kubernetes waits terminationGracePeriodSeconds, 30 seconds by default. The app's own shutdown timeout must be shorter than the platform's.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
HEALTHCHECK tells Docker how to test whether the container is working. Docker runs the command inside the container on a schedule and records the status as starting, healthy, or unhealthy.

Option Default Meaning --interval 30s Time between checks --timeout 30s A check taking longer counts as a failure --start-period 0s Grace period while the app boots; failures do not count --start-interval 5s Check interval during the start period (Docker Engine 25+) --retries 3 Consecutive failures before unhealthy

Docker Engine itself does not restart an unhealthy container. The status is used by Docker Swarm, by Compose's depends_on: condition: service_healthy, and by monitoring. Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK entirely and uses its own probes (see health probes and rolling updates). Slim and distroless images usually have no curl, so use the runtime you already ship: Node 18 and later have a global fetch.

docs.title: ARG compared with ENV
docs.text:
ARG ENV Available during the build Yes, in the stage that declares it Yes Present in the running container No Yes Set from the command line docker build --build-arg NAME=value Only by changing the Dockerfile Override at runtime Not applicable docker run -e NAME=value Scope Ends at the stage; an ARG before the first FROM is usable only in FROM lines unless redeclared Inherited by later stages built FROM this one Safe for secrets No: values can appear in docker history and provenance metadata No: visible to anyone with the image

Use ARG for build-time choices (a Node version, a public API URL baked into a frontend bundle) and ENV for runtime defaults. Use neither for secrets; use secret mounts.

docs.title: BuildKit features worth using
docs.text:
BuildKit has been the default builder since Docker Engine 23. With the # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 line you can use:

  • Cache mounts: RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci keeps npm's download cache between builds without putting it in a layer, so a lockfile change re-downloads only the changed packages.
  • Secret mounts: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc makes a file available to one RUN step only. It is never written to a layer or the image history.
  • SSH mounts: RUN --mount=type=ssh forwards the host's SSH agent for cloning private repositories.
  • Heredocs: RUN <<EOF followed by several lines and EOF writes multi-line scripts without && \ chains.
  • COPY --link: creates a layer that does not depend on the layers below it, so changing the base image does not invalidate it.
  • Build checks: docker build --check . runs Dockerfile lint rules without building.

docs.title: Base images and image size
docs.text:
Sizes below are approximate, uncompressed, for linux/amd64, and change with every release. Measure your own with docker image ls.

Base image Approximate size What is inside Typical use node:24 ~1.1 GB Debian with compilers, Python, Git, and Node Build stage for native modules node:24-slim ~200-250 MB Minimal Debian and Node Default runtime for Node services node:24-alpine ~150-170 MB Alpine (musl libc) and Node Smaller images when musl is fine gcr.io/distroless/nodejs24-debian13 ~150-200 MB Node and glibc; no shell or package manager Smallest attack surface nginx:1.30 ~190 MB Debian and nginx Rarely needed for static files nginx:1.30-alpine ~50 MB Alpine and nginx Serving a built frontend

The Node.js binary alone is on the order of 100 MB, so a Node image will not get much smaller than that whatever the base. Alpine's musl libc behaves differently from glibc for some native modules and DNS resolution, and the Node.js project treats musl builds as an experimental platform. Choose -slim by default and Alpine or distroless when you have tested them.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommendation Any service you deploy Multi-stage build, slim base, non-root user, exec-form CMD Plain JavaScript with no native modules Two stages: production deps and runtime TypeScript or a bundler Three stages: deps, build, runtime Native modules (bcrypt, sharp) Build on the same libc as the runtime (glibc to glibc) A static frontend Build with Node, serve the output with nginx or a CDN Many similar services A shared internal base image, or Cloud Native Buildpacks Highest security requirements Distroless or hardened base images, pinned by digest

Do not use a single-stage image built FROM node:24 with dev dependencies for production, and do not hand-tune Dockerfiles for dozens of near-identical services when a buildpack or shared base would give the same result with less maintenance.

docs.title: .dockerignore for the TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# .dockerignore
node_modules
dist
coverage
npm-debug.log*
.git
.github
.vscode
.env
.env.*
!.env.example
Dockerfile*
compose*.yaml
*.md

node_modules and dist are rebuilt inside the image, .git would break the cache on every commit, and .env files must never reach a layer. Ignoring the Dockerfile and Compose files keeps edits to them from invalidating COPY . ..

docs.title: Production Dockerfile for the TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile: TaskFlow API (Express + MongoDB, TypeScript)

ARG NODE_VERSION=24

# ---- base: settings shared by every stage ----
FROM node:${NODE_VERSION}-slim AS base
WORKDIR /app

# ---- deps: production dependencies only ----
FROM base AS deps
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --omit=dev

# ---- build: all dependencies, then compile ----
FROM base AS build
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci
COPY tsconfig.json ./
COPY src ./src
RUN npm run build

# ---- runtime: the image that ships ----
FROM base AS runtime
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
COPY package.json ./
USER node
EXPOSE 3000
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --start-period=20s --retries=3 \
  CMD ["node", "-e", "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:3000/healthz').then(r => process.exit(r.ok ? 0 : 1)).catch(() => process.exit(1))"]
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

How the parts fit together:

  • ARG NODE_VERSION before the first FROM lets CI test a new Node major with --build-arg NODE_VERSION=26 without editing the file.
  • NODE_ENV=production is set only in the runtime stage. Setting it in base would make the build stage's npm ci skip dev dependencies, because npm omits them when NODE_ENV is production, and the TypeScript compiler would be missing.
  • The cache mounts keep npm's download cache between builds without adding it to any layer.
  • The application files stay owned by root; the process runs as node and can read but not change them.
  • The health check uses Node's built-in fetch, so the image needs no curl.
  • For plain JavaScript, delete the build stage and replace the dist copy with COPY src ./src and CMD ["node", "src/server.js"].
docker build -t taskflow-api:dev .
docker build --target build -t taskflow-api:build .   # stop at the build stage
docker image ls taskflow-api                          # compare sizes
docker history taskflow-api:dev                       # inspect the layers
# On Linux, also pass --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway
docker run -d --name api -p 3000:3000 \
  -e MONGODB_URI="mongodb://host.docker.internal:27017/taskflow" \
  taskflow-api:dev
docker inspect --format '{{.State.Health.Status}}' api   # starting, then healthy

docs.title: Graceful shutdown in the API
docs.text:
// src/server.ts
import express from "express";
import mongoose from "mongoose";

const app = express();
let shuttingDown = false;

// Liveness: the process is up and its event loop responds
app.get("/healthz", (_req, res) => {
  res.status(200).send("ok");
});

// Readiness: only take traffic while connected and not shutting down
app.get("/readyz", (_req, res) => {
  const ready = !shuttingDown && mongoose.connection.readyState === 1;
  res.status(ready ? 200 : 503).send(ready ? "ready" : "not ready");
});

// app.use("/tasks", tasksRouter);

async function main(): Promise<void> {
  await mongoose.connect(process.env.MONGODB_URI ?? "mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow");
  const port = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
  const server = app.listen(port, () => console.log(`TaskFlow API listening on ${port}`));

  const shutdown = (signal: NodeJS.Signals): void => {
    if (shuttingDown) return;
    shuttingDown = true;
    console.log(`${signal} received, shutting down`);

    // Give up before the platform's SIGKILL (Docker waits 10 s by default)
    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
      console.error("Graceful shutdown timed out");
      process.exit(1);
    }, 8_000);
    timer.unref();

    // Stop accepting connections; requests in flight still complete.
    // Since Node 19, close() also closes idle keep-alive connections.
    server.close(async (err) => {
      await mongoose.disconnect();
      process.exit(err ? 1 : 0);
    });
  };

  process.on("SIGTERM", shutdown);
  process.on("SIGINT", shutdown);
}

main().catch((err) => {
  console.error(err);
  process.exit(1);
});

server.close() stops new connections at once, and its callback runs when the last open connection has finished. The timer guarantees an exit with a clear log line if something hangs. The /readyz endpoint is used later by Kubernetes readiness probes.

docs.title: TaskFlow Web: a Vite build served by nginx
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile: TaskFlow Web (React + Vite, served by nginx)

FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci
COPY . .
# Vite inlines VITE_* variables into the bundle at build time.
# ARG values are visible to RUN steps as environment variables.
ARG VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.30-alpine AS runtime
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s \
  CMD wget -q -O /dev/null http://127.0.0.1/ || exit 1

# nginx.conf: single-page app hosting for TaskFlow Web
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name _;
    root /usr/share/nginx/html;
    index index.html;

    # Hashed build assets never change: cache them for a year
    location /assets/ {
        add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable";
        try_files $uri =404;
    }

    # Everything else is the app shell: revalidate on every visit,
    # and send unknown paths to index.html for client-side routing
    location / {
        add_header Cache-Control "no-cache";
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }
}

The final image contains nginx and the static files only: no Node, no node_modules, no source. Because VITE_API_URL is compiled into the JavaScript, one image works for one API URL; building per environment or loading configuration at runtime is discussed in build-time vs runtime configuration. The base nginx image runs its worker processes as the nginx user but the master as root; the nginxinc/nginx-unprivileged images run entirely as a non-root user and listen on port 8080.

docs.title: Installing from a private registry with a secret mount
docs.text:
# .npmrc (on the build machine or CI runner; never committed or copied)
@example:registry=https://npm.example.com/
//npm.example.com/:_authToken=<token>

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile (deps stage): private packages without leaking the token
FROM node:24-slim AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm \
    npm ci --omit=dev

docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=$HOME/.npmrc -t taskflow-api:dev .
docker history --no-trunc taskflow-api:dev | grep -c _authToken   # 0

The .npmrc exists only while that one RUN executes. Compare this with COPY .npmrc . followed by RUN rm .npmrc, which leaves the token in the earlier layer forever (see container security).

docs.title: Adding tini when the platform has no --init
docs.text:
# Dockerfile (runtime stage excerpt): tini as PID 1
FROM base AS runtime
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ENV NODE_ENV=production
COPY --from=deps /app/node_modules ./node_modules
COPY --from=build /app/dist ./dist
USER node
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--"]
CMD ["node", "dist/server.js"]

tini forwards SIGTERM to node and reaps zombie processes. You still need the SIGTERM handler in the app to shut down gracefully; tini only makes sure the signal arrives.

docs.title: Linting and inspecting
docs.text:
docker build --check .                                   # BuildKit lint rules
docker run --rm -i hadolint/hadolint < Dockerfile        # Hadolint rules
dive taskflow-api:dev                                    # browse layers and wasted space
docker run --rm taskflow-api:dev id                      # uid=1000(node) gid=1000(node)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1 and a .dockerignore.
  • Copy dependency manifests, install, then copy the source.
  • Use multi-stage builds; ship only runtime files.
  • Use npm ci --omit=dev for production dependencies; never npm install in an image build.
  • Pin the base image to at least a major version and a variant (node:24-slim), and to a digest for full reproducibility.
  • Run as a non-root user and keep application files read-only to it.
  • Use the exec form for CMD and ENTRYPOINT, run node directly, and handle SIGTERM in the app.
  • Add a HEALTHCHECK that uses tools already in the image.
  • Keep secrets out of ARG, ENV, and COPY; use secret mounts.
  • Combine download, use, and cleanup in one RUN (apt-get update, install, rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*).
  • Rebuild regularly with --pull so base image patches reach production.
  • Lint Dockerfiles in CI.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every build reinstalls all dependencies. Detect: CI build logs show npm ci running for a minute on commits that only change source files, and docker build output lacks CACHED for that step. Cause: COPY . . before npm ci, a missing .dockerignore (so .git changes every build), or no cache import in CI. Fix: reorder the steps, add .dockerignore, and export the build cache to the registry or CI cache.
  • Deploys take 10 extra seconds per container and drop requests. Detect: docker stop always takes the full timeout, and the stopped container shows exit code 137. Cause: PID 1 is a shell (shell-form CMD) or npm, or the app has no SIGTERM handler. Fix: exec-form CMD ["node", ...], a shutdown handler, and --init or tini.
  • The image is over a gigabyte and scale-outs are slow. Detect: docker image ls shows 1 GB or more, and new nodes spend tens of seconds pulling. Cause: a single-stage build on the full node image with dev dependencies and build tools. Fix: a multi-stage build on a slim base with production dependencies only.
  • The container crashes with invalid ELF header or a native module error. Detect: the error names a .node file such as bcrypt or sharp. Cause: the host's node_modules (built for macOS or Windows) was copied over the image's, or a module built against glibc runs on Alpine (musl). Fix: ignore node_modules in .dockerignore and build native modules on the same libc as the runtime.
  • EACCES: permission denied after adding USER node. Detect: the app fails when writing to /app/uploads or a cache directory. Cause: the directory is owned by root. Fix: create only that directory with the right owner, or better, write uploads to a mounted volume or object storage.
  • The container is permanently unhealthy though the app works. Detect: docker inspect --format '{{json .State.Health}}' shows curl: not found in the check output. Cause: the health check calls a tool missing from the slim image. Fix: use node -e "fetch(...)", wget on Alpine, or a small health-check binary.
  • Known-fixed vulnerabilities keep appearing in scans. Detect: the scanner reports base-image CVEs that upstream fixed weeks ago. Cause: builds reuse a cached base image and cached apt-get layers. Fix: rebuild on a schedule with --pull (and --no-cache for OS package steps), and automate base-image updates.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Build context: The files sent to the builder; the only files COPY can read.
  • .dockerignore: Patterns excluded from the build context.
  • Layer cache: Stored step results reused when instructions and inputs are unchanged.
  • Multi-stage build: A Dockerfile with several FROM stages where the final stage copies artifacts from earlier ones.
  • Exec form: The JSON-array syntax that runs a program directly, without a shell.
  • PID 1: The first process in the container; it receives docker stop's signal and has no default signal handling.
  • Init process: A minimal PID 1 such as tini that forwards signals and reaps zombie processes.
  • Graceful shutdown: Stopping new work, finishing in-flight work, releasing resources, then exiting.
  • Cache mount: A BuildKit mount that persists a directory (such as npm's cache) between builds without storing it in a layer.
  • Secret mount: A BuildKit mount that exposes a secret to one RUN step without writing it to the image.
  • Distroless image: A base image with only the runtime and its libraries, no shell or package manager.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using npm install instead of npm ci, so the lockfile is not enforced.
  • Thinking EXPOSE publishes a port; only -p or ports: does.
  • Deleting files in a later RUN and expecting the image to shrink.
  • Setting NODE_ENV=production in a stage that needs dev dependencies.
  • Using CMD npm start and wondering why shutdown takes 10 seconds.
  • Passing secrets through --build-arg; they can appear in the image metadata and history.
  • Believing a HEALTHCHECK makes Docker restart a broken container; it only reports status.
  • Using latest or an unpinned base and getting a different base image on every build.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why should package.json and package-lock.json be copied before the source code?
  2. A team builds 40 times a day and changes the lockfile in 5 of those builds. Installing dependencies takes 60 seconds and the other steps take 5 seconds when uncached and 2 seconds in total when cached. How much build time per day does correct ordering save?
  3. What ends up in the final image of a multi-stage build, and what does not?
  4. Explain why CMD node dist/server.js can make docker stop take 10 seconds. Give two fixes.
  5. How do ENTRYPOINT and CMD combine, and what does docker run <image> <args> replace?
  6. Why must NODE_ENV=production not be set in the build stage of the TaskFlow API Dockerfile?
  7. Compare ARG, ENV, and a secret mount for passing an npm token.
  8. Does a failing HEALTHCHECK restart the container? Which tools use its status?

docs.title: CDN Setup and Edge Caching
docs.text:
A content delivery network puts servers between TaskFlow's users and its origins: the S3 bucket holding TaskFlow Web and the load balancer in front of TaskFlow API. This lesson is the operator's view: configuring origins and protecting them, designing cache keys, writing cache rules per path, purging, origin shields and tiered caches, compression, image optimization at the edge, putting an API behind a CDN, edge functions at a high level, and how CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, and Bunny differ.

The HTTP caching theory (Cache-Control directives, freshness, revalidation with ETag, shared versus private caches) is covered in HTTP and CDN caching, and deploying hashed assets with the right headers and invalidations in deploying frontends and static sites. This lesson assumes both.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: A well-configured CDN serves most requests from a location a few milliseconds from the user, absorbs traffic spikes, terminates TLS close to users, and leaves the origin handling a small fraction of the load. A badly configured one has a 20% hit ratio, serves one user's account page to another, floods the origin after every purge, or keeps showing yesterday's site. Because the CDN sits in front of everything, its configuration is production code: a wrong rule is wrong for every user in every region at once, and the CDN itself becomes a dependency whose outage is your outage.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Fastly (June 2021). Fastly's summary of the June 8 outage explains how a valid customer configuration change triggered a latent software bug that made 85% of its network return errors. Monitoring detected it within a minute and 95% of the network recovered within 49 minutes, but every site behind those servers was down meanwhile.
  • CloudFront Origin Shield. The Origin Shield documentation describes an extra caching layer through which all requests from CloudFront's caches pass, consolidating misses for the same object into as few as one origin request, at an extra charge.
  • Cloudflare Tiered Cache. Cloudflare's Tiered Cache documentation explains that lower-tier data centers ask an upper tier before going to the origin, and that Smart Tiered Cache, available on all plans, picks the closest upper tier for each origin from latency data.
  • Fastly Instant Purge. Fastly's post Fastly Instant Purge: under 150ms for over a decade explains why purges that reach every location in about 150 milliseconds on average let publishers cache content until it changes and purge on publish.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon CloudFront, Cloudflare, Fastly, Akamai, Bunny CDN, Google Cloud CDN, and Azure Front Door; curl -I, CDN logs and analytics, and WebPageTest for checking behaviour.

docs.title: The path of a request
docs.text:
An edge location receives the request, computes the cache key, and looks it up. On a hit it answers immediately. On a miss it asks the next tier (a regional cache or origin shield), and only if that misses too does it ask the origin, storing the response on the way back according to the response headers and the CDN's rules. Even uncacheable requests benefit: TLS ends close to the user and the CDN reuses warm connections to the origin.

The arithmetic is worth doing for your own traffic. With an edge hit ratio of 90% and a shield hit ratio of 80% on the remaining misses, the origin sees 0.10 × 0.20 = 2% of requests: 20,000 out of a million. Without the shield, every edge location fetches each object separately, so a new release's assets hit the origin once per location instead of once in total.

docs.title: Origins and how to protect them
docs.text:
An origin is wherever the CDN fetches from on a miss: an S3 bucket, a load balancer, a single server, or another platform. Configure:

  • HTTPS to the origin, with a certificate that matches the name the CDN connects to. A mismatch shows up as 502 errors at the edge.
  • The Host header. Either forward the viewer's Host (the origin must accept every public name) or let the CDN send the origin's own name. CloudFront's managed policy AllViewerExceptHostHeader exists for origins such as API Gateway and Lambda function URLs that expect their own name.
  • Timeouts and failover. Know the CDN's origin read timeout (Cloudflare's proxy read timeout is 125 seconds by default and returns 524 when exceeded) and use origin failover groups where offered.
  • Origin lock-down. If the origin is reachable directly, attackers and scrapers bypass the CDN's cache and protections. Use CloudFront's origin access control for S3, allow only the CDN's published address ranges at the load balancer or firewall, require a secret header that only the CDN adds, or connect through a tunnel. Edge security as a whole is covered in edge protection, WAF, DDoS and bots.
  • The client's IP. The origin sees the CDN's addresses; read the client IP from the CDN's header (CF-Connecting-IP, X-Forwarded-For, or CloudFront's viewer address header), and trust it only from the CDN.

docs.title: Cache keys: what makes two requests the same
docs.text:
The key decides correctness and hit ratio at the same time:

  • Include every input that changes the response: path, the query parameters that matter, and headers such as Accept-Language only if the response really varies by them.
  • Exclude everything else: tracking parameters (utm_*, gclid), parameter order, and high-variety headers such as User-Agent. Each unnecessary input splits one popular object into many rarely hit ones.
  • Never use session cookies or Authorization in a shared cache key for content that differs per user; route those requests around the cache instead.

CloudFront separates two policies, and confusing them causes bugs: the cache policy lists what goes into the key, while the origin request policy lists extra values forwarded to the origin without being in the key. If the origin varies its response on a value that is forwarded but not keyed, the CDN serves the first variant to everyone.

docs.title: Cache rules per path
docs.text:
One distribution usually needs several behaviors. For TaskFlow:

Path At the edge Headers or policy Key /assets/* Cache for a year public, max-age=31536000, immutable Path only / and /index.html Store, revalidate every time no-cache Path only /images/* Cache, resize at the edge public, max-age=2592000 Path plus allowed width and format /api/public/* Cache briefly, shared public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300 Path and query /api/* Never cache private, no-store; caching disabled at the CDN Not cached

The CDN's own settings can override the origin's headers, which is the source of nasty surprises. CloudFront's managed CachingOptimized policy has a minimum TTL of one second, and AWS warns that a minimum TTL above zero makes CloudFront cache responses for at least that long even if the origin sends no-cache, no-store, or private. Never attach such a policy to personalized API paths; use CachingDisabled there.

docs.title: Headers the CDN reads and writes
docs.text:
Header Role Cache-Control Freshness for all caches; s-maxage targets shared caches like CDNs CDN-Cache-Control / Surrogate-Control Instructions for the CDN only (RFC 9213 and Fastly's equivalent), so browser and edge TTLs can differ Vary Request headers the response depends on; every value becomes a separate variant Cache-Tag (Cloudflare), Surrogate-Key (Fastly), a configured header (CloudFront) Tags for purging groups of objects Age Seconds the response has spent in a shared cache CF-Cache-Status, X-Cache The CDN's hit or miss verdict, useful in debugging

Cloudflare's CF-Cache-Status values are worth memorizing: HIT, MISS, EXPIRED, STALE (served because the origin was unreachable), UPDATING, REVALIDATED, BYPASS (the origin response was not cacheable), and DYNAMIC (the request was never eligible for caching).

docs.title: Purging and invalidation
docs.text:
• Version URLs instead of purging wherever possible; then only entry points (/index.html) need invalidating after a deploy.
  • Purge by tag for content that appears on many URLs: tag responses (Cache-Tag: template-42) and purge the tag when the template changes. Cloudflare offers purge by URL, tag, prefix, hostname, and everything on all plans, with rate limits per plan; Fastly purges surrogate keys in about 150 ms on average and supports soft purges that mark content stale instead of deleting it; CloudFront invalidates by path and, when the distribution has a cache tag configuration, by tag, with the first 1,000 paths each month free and a wildcard counting as one path; Akamai's Fast Purge completes in seconds.
  • Avoid purging everything. Every edge then misses at once and the origin takes the full load; tiered caching softens this but does not remove it.
  • Purges do not reach browsers. Anything a browser cached with a long max-age stays there.

docs.title: Origin shield and tiered caching
docs.text:
Provider Mid-tier feature Notes CloudFront Regional edge caches, plus Origin Shield Choose the Origin Shield Region with the lowest latency to the origin; extra charge per request Cloudflare Tiered Cache Smart topology on all plans; regional and custom topologies on Enterprise Fastly Shielding Pick a shield POP near the backend; shield hits and edge misses are both counted in statistics Akamai Tiered Distribution Interim parent servers near the origin, for cacheable content Bunny Origin Shield (and Perma-Cache) Origin Shield at no extra cost

A shield matters most for origins that are expensive per request (image processing, video packaging, small servers) and for global audiences, where many edge locations would otherwise miss separately. It adds a hop on misses, so it helps little for content that is rarely requested or never cacheable.

docs.title: Compression
docs.text: Let the CDN compress text at the edge. On CloudFront, enable "compress objects automatically" and both Gzip and Brotli in the cache policy; CloudFront then compresses responses between 1,000 and 10,000,000 bytes with a compressible Content-Type and a Content-Length header, prefers Brotli when the browser accepts both, and never recompresses a response that already has Content-Encoding. Do not compress images, video, or archives again; they are already compressed.

docs.title: Images at the edge
docs.text:
Image services resize and convert images on request and cache each variant: Cloudflare Images transformations, Fastly Image Optimizer, Akamai Image and Video Manager, Bunny Optimizer, and on AWS the Dynamic Image Transformation for Amazon CloudFront solution (formerly Serverless Image Handler), which you deploy into your account. Two rules keep them cheap and safe:

  • Allow only a few sizes and formats. Free-form width parameters let anyone create unlimited variants, and Cloudflare, for example, bills each unique transformation per month.
  • Key on the parameters you allow, and let the service choose AVIF or WebP from the browser's Accept header rather than adding Vary: Accept yourself.

Large media files and video belong in object storage and a video service, as covered in video storage and streaming.

docs.title: A CDN in front of an API
docs.text:
Even with caching disabled, putting TaskFlow API behind a CDN gives TLS termination near users, connection reuse to the origin, a WAF, and DDoS absorption. Rules for doing it safely:

  • Disable caching for everything except explicitly public GET endpoints, and forward Authorization, cookies, and the query string to the origin.
  • Cache public endpoints with s-maxage and short TTLs, never responses that set cookies or depend on the caller's identity.
  • Check the CDN's limits: request body size, the origin timeout, and WebSocket support for real-time features.
  • Make sure rate limiting and logging use the real client IP from the CDN's header.

docs.title: Edge functions
docs.text:
Most CDNs run small programs at the edge:

Product Runtime Typical use CloudFront Functions JavaScript, viewer request and response only, sub-millisecond, no network access Redirects, header changes, cache key normalization, token checks Lambda@Edge Node.js or Python, also origin request and response, network access Heavier logic, calling other services, reading request bodies Cloudflare Workers JavaScript and WebAssembly in V8 isolates Full request handling, APIs, rewriting, A/B routing Fastly Compute WebAssembly Programmable routing and caching Akamai EdgeWorkers JavaScript Custom logic inside Akamai's delivery Bunny Edge Scripting JavaScript Middleware and small apps on Bunny's network

Use them for logic that depends only on the request: redirects, header rules, key normalization, bucketing users for experiments, and verifying signed tokens. Keep business logic that needs the database at the origin; a function far from its data is slower, not faster.

docs.title: Choosing a provider
docs.text:
Provider Strengths Fits CloudFront Deep AWS integration (S3 origin access control, ACM, WAF, Route 53 alias), Origin Shield, cache tags, flat-rate plans Origins already in AWS Cloudflare DNS, proxy, WAF, and CDN in one place; Tiered Cache and all purge types on every plan; static asset requests on Workers free Small teams to large sites, especially when DNS moves to Cloudflare Fastly Instant purge with surrogate keys, VCL and Compute programmability, shielding Content that changes often and must be purged precisely Akamai Very large network, Tiered Distribution, Fast Purge, media delivery products Large enterprises and media Bunny Low prices, Origin Shield at no extra cost, Perma-Cache, Optimizer Cost-sensitive delivery, video, small teams

Pricing changes often and is compared in hosting websites and frontends.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a CDN when:

  • Users are spread across regions or the site has heavy static assets.
  • Traffic is spiky (launches, campaigns) and the origin should not see the spikes.
  • You want TLS, WAF, and DDoS protection at the edge, even for an API.

Think twice, or keep it simple, when:

  • Every response is personalized and uncacheable, and users are close to a single region: a CDN still helps with TLS and protection, but not with load.
  • The team cannot yet explain its cache keys and headers; start with hashed assets and no-cache HTML, and cache API responses later.
  • Data must not leave a jurisdiction and the CDN cannot restrict where it caches.
Content Strategy Hashed static assets Cache for a year at edge and browser; never purge HTML entry points no-cache; invalidate after deploys if the CDN stores it Public, slowly changing API data s-maxage plus stale-while-revalidate, tag purges on change Images Edge resizing with an allowlist of sizes Per-user data Bypass the cache; private, no-store

docs.title: CloudFront in front of TaskFlow Web and API (Terraform)
docs.text:
This extends the distribution from hosting websites and frontends with an API origin and per-path behaviors. Only the parts that change are shown.

# infra/web/cdn-api.tf: API origin, origin shield, and per-path behaviors
data "aws_cloudfront_cache_policy" "disabled" {
  name = "Managed-CachingDisabled"
}

data "aws_cloudfront_origin_request_policy" "all_viewer_except_host" {
  name = "Managed-AllViewerExceptHostHeader"
}

# Public API responses: honor the origin's s-maxage, never key on cookies
resource "aws_cloudfront_cache_policy" "public_api" {
  name        = "taskflow-public-api"
  min_ttl     = 0
  default_ttl = 0
  max_ttl     = 300

  parameters_in_cache_key_and_forwarded_to_origin {
    enable_accept_encoding_brotli = true
    enable_accept_encoding_gzip   = true

    cookies_config {
      cookie_behavior = "none"
    }
    headers_config {
      header_behavior = "none"
    }
    query_strings_config {
      query_string_behavior = "all"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_cloudfront_distribution" "web" {
  # ... default origin (S3), default_cache_behavior, viewer_certificate as before ...

  origin {
    origin_id   = "api-alb"
    domain_name = "origin-api.example.com" # a name on the load balancer's certificate

    custom_origin_config {
      http_port              = 80
      https_port             = 443
      origin_protocol_policy = "https-only"
      origin_ssl_protocols   = ["TLSv1.2"]
    }

    origin_shield {
      enabled              = true
      origin_shield_region = "us-east-1" # the Region closest to the origin
    }

    custom_header {
      name  = "X-Origin-Verify"
      value = var.origin_verify_secret # the load balancer rejects requests without it
    }
  }

  # Most specific pattern first: CloudFront evaluates ordered behaviors in order
  ordered_cache_behavior {
    path_pattern             = "/api/public/*"
    target_origin_id         = "api-alb"
    viewer_protocol_policy   = "https-only"
    allowed_methods          = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"]
    cached_methods           = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    compress                 = true
    cache_policy_id          = aws_cloudfront_cache_policy.public_api.id
    origin_request_policy_id = data.aws_cloudfront_origin_request_policy.all_viewer_except_host.id
  }

  ordered_cache_behavior {
    path_pattern             = "/api/*"
    target_origin_id         = "api-alb"
    viewer_protocol_policy   = "https-only"
    allowed_methods          = ["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS", "PUT", "POST", "PATCH", "DELETE"]
    cached_methods           = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    compress                 = true
    cache_policy_id          = data.aws_cloudfront_cache_policy.disabled.id
    origin_request_policy_id = data.aws_cloudfront_origin_request_policy.all_viewer_except_host.id
  }
}
  • max_ttl = 300 caps how long the origin can ask the CDN to keep a public API response; min_ttl = 0 means no-store from the origin is respected.
  • AllViewerExceptHostHeader forwards headers, cookies, and query strings, but sends Host: origin-api.example.com, which matches the load balancer's certificate.
  • The secret header plus a load balancer rule that rejects requests without it (and a security group allowing only CloudFront's managed prefix list) keeps clients from bypassing the CDN. Store the secret in a secrets manager and rotate it.

docs.title: Tagging API responses for purges (Express)
docs.text:
// src/routes/public-templates.js: cacheable at the CDN, purgeable by tag
import express from "express";
import { Templates } from "../models/templates.js";

export const router = express.Router();

router.get("/api/public/templates/:id", async (req, res) => {
  const template = await Templates.findById(req.params.id);
  if (!template) return res.status(404).json({ error: "not found" });

  // Browsers revalidate; the CDN may serve it for 60 s, and stale for 300 s while refreshing
  res.set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=0, s-maxage=60, stale-while-revalidate=300");
  // Cloudflare reads Cache-Tag (comma-separated); Fastly uses Surrogate-Key (space-separated);
  // CloudFront reads whichever header name its cache tag configuration specifies
  res.set("Cache-Tag", `template-${template.id},templates`);
  res.json(template);
});

# Purge one template everywhere after it changes (Cloudflare API)
curl -s -X POST "https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/zones/${CF_ZONE_ID}/purge_cache" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer ${CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN}" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{"tags":["template-42"]}'

# CloudFront equivalents: a path, and a tag (needs a cache tag configuration)
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id "$DIST_ID" --paths "/index.html"
aws cloudfront create-invalidation --distribution-id "$DIST_ID" --paths "#template-42"

Purge from the code path that changes the data (after the database commit), not by hand, and keep the TTL as a safety net if a purge is lost.

docs.title: Normalizing the cache key with a CloudFront Function
docs.text:
// cloudfront/strip-tracking-params.js: viewer-request function
// For behaviors whose cache key includes all query strings
function handler(event) {
  var request = event.request;
  var query = request.querystring;
  for (var name in query) {
    if (name.indexOf("utm_") === 0 || name === "gclid" || name === "fbclid") {
      delete query[name];
    }
  }
  return request;
}

Newsletter links with ?utm_source=... now share one cache entry with everyone else. Associate the function with the viewer request event of the /api/public/* behavior.

docs.title: Checking what the CDN did
docs.text:
curl -sI https://www.example.com/assets/index-B7x9q2Lc.js \
  | grep -iE '^(cache-control|age|x-cache|cf-cache-status)'
curl -sI https://www.example.com/api/tasks -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" \
  | grep -iE '^(cache-control|age|x-cache|cf-cache-status)'

; Example output (CloudFront)
cache-control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
age: 5321
x-cache: Hit from cloudfront

cache-control: private, no-store
x-cache: Miss from cloudfront

The asset was served from cache and has been there for about 90 minutes; the personal API response was fetched from the origin, as it must be. An Age header on a personalized response is an incident.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Hash asset filenames and cache them for a year; serve HTML with no-cache.
  • Send an explicit Cache-Control header on every response, including errors.
  • Keep cache keys minimal but complete; strip tracking parameters and never key shared content on cookies or Authorization.
  • Disable caching for personalized paths at the CDN, not only in headers, and never attach a minimum TTL above zero to them.
  • Purge by tag from code after data changes; avoid purge-everything.
  • Enable a shield or tiered cache for global audiences and expensive origins.
  • Lock the origin so only the CDN can reach it, and log the real client IP from the CDN's header.
  • Allowlist image sizes and formats for edge transformations.
  • Treat the CDN as a dependency: monitor hit ratio, error rates, and origin load, and know your fallback if it fails.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The hit ratio is stuck at 20%. Detect: CDN analytics show many distinct keys for the same path, differing by utm_* parameters, cookies, or User-Agent. Cause: unnecessary inputs in the cache key, or Vary: User-Agent from the origin. Fix: remove them from the key, normalize query strings, and stop sending high-variety Vary headers.
  • One user sees another user's data. Detect: responses for a personal endpoint carry an Age header or a HIT status. Cause: the path uses a cache policy with a minimum TTL above zero, or the origin forgot private, no-store. Fix: treat it as a security incident: purge, switch the behavior to CachingDisabled, add private, no-store, and test that two users get different responses.
  • The origin falls over right after a deploy. Detect: origin requests per second spike just after an invalidation of /*. Cause: purge-everything turned every edge cold at once. Fix: hash assets, invalidate only entry points, and enable a shield or tiered cache.
  • The edge returns 502 for the API. Detect: CDN logs show origin TLS or connection errors; the origin sees no requests. Cause: the origin certificate does not match the origin domain name the CDN uses, or the origin firewall blocks the CDN's ranges. Fix: align the origin name and certificate (or the Host policy) and allow the CDN's published ranges.
  • The image bill grows every month. Detect: unique transformations far exceed the number of images times the sizes you use. Cause: free-form width and quality parameters, sometimes abused by bots. Fix: allowlist sizes and formats and reject others at the edge.
  • The whole site is down while the origin is healthy. Detect: errors come from the CDN's own error pages in many regions; the provider's status page reports an incident. Cause: a CDN outage, as in Fastly's 2021 incident. Fix: for critical sites, keep a tested fallback (a second CDN or a direct origin path behind a short-TTL DNS record) and practice switching.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Edge location (PoP): A CDN site that serves users nearby.
  • Origin: The server or bucket the CDN fetches from on a miss.
  • Cache key: The request properties that identify a cached object.
  • Cache behavior / cache rule: The settings applied to a path pattern.
  • Cache policy and origin request policy: CloudFront's split between values in the key and values only forwarded to the origin.
  • Origin shield / tiered cache: A mid-tier cache that collapses edge misses before they reach the origin.
  • Request collapsing: Merging simultaneous misses for the same object into one origin request.
  • Purge (invalidation): Removing objects from CDN caches before they expire.
  • Surrogate key / cache tag: A label on cached objects used to purge them as a group.
  • Soft purge: Marking objects stale instead of deleting them, so they can still be served while refreshing.
  • Edge function: Code that runs at CDN locations on requests or responses.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming a CDN speeds up everything; uncacheable responses gain only TLS and connection benefits.
  • Including cookies, User-Agent, or tracking parameters in the cache key.
  • Forwarding a header to the origin that changes the response without putting it in the key.
  • Attaching a policy with a nonzero minimum TTL to personalized paths.
  • Purging everything after each deploy instead of versioning assets.
  • Leaving the origin open to direct traffic.
  • Believing a purge clears browsers' caches.
  • Letting arbitrary image sizes be generated on demand.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Walk through what happens to a request on an edge miss with an origin shield enabled.
  2. With an edge hit ratio of 95% and a shield hit ratio of 60%, what fraction of 20 million daily requests reaches the origin? (0.05 × 0.40 = 2%, so 400,000 requests.)
  3. What is the difference between CloudFront's cache policy and origin request policy, and what goes wrong if you confuse them?
  4. Why can a cache policy with a one-second minimum TTL leak personal data even when the origin sends no-store?
  5. Design cache rules for /assets/*, /index.html, /api/public/*, and /api/* for TaskFlow, including the order of the behaviors.
  6. When would you purge by tag instead of by URL, and what do Cloudflare, Fastly, and CloudFront call the tag header?
  7. What does an edge function do well, and what should stay at the origin?
  8. How would you keep TaskFlow Web available if its CDN had a global outage?

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does dig @ns1.dns-host.example.net api.example.com +norecurse Asks the authoritative server what the zone really says dig +trace api.example.com Walks the delegation from the root down to your nameservers dig @1.1.1.1 api.example.com Shows a public resolver's cached answer and its remaining TTL dig +cd example.com Skips DNSSEC validation; an answer only with +cd means a broken chain dig +short example.com MX (or TXT, CAA) Checks mail, SPF, and certificate authority records curl --resolve api.example.com:443:198.51.100.40 https://api.example.com/healthz Tests a new target with the real hostname before DNS points at it curl -sI https://www.example.com/ Shows redirects and cache headers (age, x-cache, cf-cache-status)

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
; example.com zone (excerpt): web, API, mail, and certificates
www      300  IN  CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.
api      60   IN  A      198.51.100.20
@             IN  MX     10 mx1.mail.example.net.
@             IN  TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"
_dmarc        IN  TXT    "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"
@             IN  CAA    0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

; example.org zone (excerpt): a parked domain that sends and receives no mail
@        IN  MX   0 .
@        IN  TXT  "v=spf1 -all"
_dmarc   IN  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=reject; sp=reject; adkim=s; aspf=s"

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A subdomain on a platform or CDN A CNAME to the hostname the dashboard shows The platform can change IPs and steer traffic The apex on a platform or CDN An alias, a flattened CNAME, the documented A record, or a redirect to www A CNAME cannot sit at the apex A load balancer A Route 53 alias, or a CNAME to its DNS name Its IPs change, so its DNS TTL is 60 s A Workers custom domain or a Pages apex Cloudflare nameservers Both need the zone on Cloudflare CDN and WAF on Cloudflare Proxied web records, Full (strict), DNS-only mail Flexible loops; MX and TXT are never proxied Per-PR preview hostnames A one-label wildcard and a DNS-01 wildcard certificate TLS wildcards cover one label A move to another DNS host Inventory, diff, DS removed a day ahead, both zones identical The .com delegation is cached for up to two days Purging content shown on many URLs Tags: Cache-Tag, Surrogate-Key, CloudFront cache tags One precise purge, not purge-everything Password resets and newsletters Marketing on its own subdomain and stream; custom DKIM and Return-Path Campaign complaints cannot sink resets

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value TTLs 60 to 300 s for names you may move; 3600 s for stable ones; 86400 s for NS and MX Planned change Lower the TTL one old TTL ahead; after a change, the worst case is one TTL Negative caching The smaller of the SOA record's TTL and its minimum field (RFC 2308) .com delegation NS cached for 172,800 s (2 days); DS for 86,400 s (1 day) Cloudflare proxy Automatic 300 s TTL (ttl = 1); 524 after the 125 s read timeout Registration 30-day redemption grace; 60-day transfer lock after registration, a transfer, or a registrant change TXT and SPF 255 bytes per string; one SPF record per name; max 10 lookups (nested count) and 2 void lookups DKIM RSA of at least 1024 bits, 2048 recommended; never rsa-sha1 DMARC (RFC 9989) adkim, aspf default r; sp defaults to p; t=y applies one level weaker; no pct, rf, ri Gmail and Yahoo Spam rate under 0.3% (Google: aim under 0.1%); Gmail bulk: close to 5,000 a day, permanent; unsubscribe in 2 days Outlook.com Over 5,000 a day: SPF and DKIM pass plus aligned DMARC, or 550 5.7.515 Amazon SES Sandbox: 200 a day, 1 per second; review at 5% bounces or 0.1% complaints; 45-day IP warm-up CloudFront ACM certificate in us-east-1; CachingOptimized has a 1 s minimum TTL Shield arithmetic Origin share = edge miss x shield miss (0.10 x 0.20 = 2%)

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Moving nameservers to attach one subdomain. Add a CNAME; a nameserver change moves every record, including MX and TXT.
  • Lowering the TTL when you make the change. Lower it at least one old TTL before.
  • A CNAME at the apex or next to MX and TXT. Use an alias, CNAME flattening, or the platform's documented A record.
  • Two SPF records, or more than 10 lookups. Merge into one record, drop unused a and mx, and give senders their own subdomains.
  • Jumping to p=reject without reports. Start at p=none with rua and align every sender first; RFC 9989 advises against p=reject where users post to mailing lists.
  • Flexible mode with an origin that redirects to HTTPS. Use Full (strict) with a valid origin certificate.
  • A nonzero minimum TTL on personal API paths. Use CachingDisabled and send private, no-store.
  • Deleting a cloud resource before its DNS record. Remove the record first, or the subdomain can be taken over.
