docs.title: Connecting Domains to Hosting
docs.text:
Attaching www.example.com to TaskFlow Web or api.example.com to TaskFlow API is where DNS, hosting, TLS, and redirects meet. This lesson covers choosing a canonical host (apex or www), the exact records for Vercel, Netlify, CloudFront, a load balancer, and a single server, the verification records platforms ask for, wildcard and per-pull-request preview subdomains, redirects between the apex and www, certificates for custom domains, Route 53 alias records, what Cloudflare's proxy (the "orange cloud") changes, and how a forgotten record lets someone else take over a subdomain.

Choosing a host and understanding its bill is covered in hosting websites and frontends; deploying files onto it safely is covered in deploying frontends and static sites.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The platform's dashboard says "invalid configuration", the apex works but www shows a certificate warning, enabling a CDN creates an infinite redirect loop, or moving nameservers to a hosting platform silently deletes the company's mail records: these are the everyday failures of domain hookups, and each one is visible to every user at once. The mechanics are small (a CNAME here, an alias there), but each platform has its own rules for the apex, verification, certificates, and wildcards, and the defaults are not always safe.

There is also a security side. A DNS record that points at a deleted cloud resource can be claimed by a stranger, who then serves content, and can obtain a valid certificate, on your subdomain.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Vercel recommends www. Vercel's deploying and redirecting domains guide recommends www as the primary domain with a CNAME, plus a redirect from the apex, because a CNAME avoids hard-coding IP addresses and lets Vercel steer traffic for reliability and DDoS mitigation; it notes the apex can still use an A record served over anycast.
  • Netlify and the apex. Netlify's external DNS guide points apex domains at apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com with an ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME (or an A record as a fallback), explains that the apex then cannot use direct DNS routing on its CDN, and recommends a subdomain as the primary domain.
  • Microsoft on dangling DNS. Microsoft's guide Prevent dangling DNS entries and avoid subdomain takeover walks through the takeover sequence (a CNAME left pointing at a deleted resource, then claimed by an attacker) and lists the risks: lost control of content, harvested cookies, phishing, and valid certificates for the attacker.
  • Cloudflare proxy status. Cloudflare's proxy status documentation explains that proxied records answer with Cloudflare's anycast addresses instead of the origin's, that only A, AAAA, and CNAME records can be proxied, and that proxied records use an automatic TTL of 300 seconds.

Popular tools and providers: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare (DNS, proxy, Pages, Workers), Amazon Route 53 with CloudFront, Elastic Load Balancing, and AWS Certificate Manager, Azure DNS with Front Door, Google Cloud DNS with Cloud Load Balancing, and Caddy or nginx with certbot on a single server.

docs.title: Choose one canonical host
docs.text:
Pick the address users and search engines should see, then send every other variant there with a permanent redirect.

www.example.com canonical example.com (apex) canonical DNS record A plain CNAME to the platform Alias, flattened CNAME, or the platform's documented IPs Traffic steering The platform's DNS sees the user's resolver Depends on anycast or on your DNS host's features Recommended by Vercel, and Netlify when you use external DNS Fine on Cloudflare, Route 53 alias, or anycast platforms The other name Apex redirects to www www redirects to the apex

Whichever you choose, use it everywhere: in links, OAuth redirect URIs, CORS allow lists, cookie settings, sitemaps, and the site_url of static site generators. Keep APIs on their own name (api.example.com) and never put a redirect in front of an API, because many HTTP clients do not follow redirects for POST requests the way browsers do.

docs.title: Pointing names at common hosts
docs.text:
Host Subdomain (www, app) Apex Watch out for Vercel CNAME to the project-specific vercel-dns hostname shown in the project's Domains settings A record with the value the dashboard shows, or Vercel's nameservers Wildcards need Vercel's nameservers or an NS delegation of _acme-challenge to Vercel; a _vercel TXT record proves access when the domain is used by another account Netlify CNAME to the site's netlify.app hostname ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com, or an A record fallback Adding either the apex or www adds both; prefer a subdomain as primary with external DNS CloudFront CNAME to the distribution's name, such as d111111abcdef8.cloudfront.net Route 53 alias A and AAAA (and optionally HTTPS) records; without Route 53, CloudFront's Anycast static IPs The name must be an alternate domain name on exactly one distribution, covered by an ACM certificate in us-east-1 AWS load balancer CNAME to the load balancer's DNS name Route 53 alias Never A records to its IPs: they change, which is why its DNS TTL is 60 seconds Single server (VPS) A and AAAA to a reserved static IP The same The web server must also be configured for the name, and needs its own certificate Cloudflare Pages / Workers Pages: CNAME from any DNS host Requires Cloudflare nameservers Workers custom domains require Cloudflare nameservers

Always copy the exact values from the platform's dashboard: several providers now issue per-project targets, and old blog posts contain retired IP addresses. Details for Cloudflare's products are in the hosting lesson.

docs.title: Verification records
docs.text:
Before a platform serves your domain or a CA signs a certificate, it asks for proof that you control DNS. Common forms:

Purpose Typical record Hosting platform ownership TXT at the apex or at a label such as _vercel.example.com Azure App Service custom domain TXT at asuid.<subdomain> holding the verification ID AWS Certificate Manager DNS validation CNAME from an underscore name to an acm-validations.aws target ACME DNS-01 challenge TXT at _acme-challenge.<name> (or a CNAME delegating it) Email sending services DKIM CNAMEs or TXT keys, plus SPF and return-path records

Two rules: keep a verification record for as long as the service uses it (ACM renewals stop working when the validation CNAME is deleted, as obtaining and renewing certificates explains), and record which service each one belongs to, so a later cleanup does not guess.

docs.title: Certificates for custom domains
docs.text:
Most platforms issue and renew certificates themselves once DNS points at them. What can still go wrong is on your side:

  • CAA must allow the platform's CA. Check it before moving a domain (see domains and DNS records).
  • Wildcards need the DNS-01 challenge, so the platform needs your nameservers or a delegated _acme-challenge name.
  • CloudFront needs an ACM certificate in us-east-1 that covers every alternate domain name, and checks that it does before accepting the name.
  • Cloudflare's Universal SSL covers the apex and first-level subdomains only; pr-42.preview.example.com needs Advanced Certificate Manager (Total TLS or an advanced certificate) or an uploaded certificate.

Termination choices and debugging are covered in TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Wildcard subdomains and per-pull-request previews
docs.text:
A wildcard record such as *.preview.example.com CNAME preview-ingress.example.net. sends every preview hostname to one ingress or platform, so each pull request can get pr-42.preview.example.com without a DNS change. Three subtleties:

  • DNS wildcards match only names that do not exist. Per RFC 4592, *.preview.example.com answers for pr-42.preview.example.com, and even for deeper names whose parents do not exist, but not for a name that has records of its own. A name also "exists" when something below it has records: create _acme-challenge.pr-42.preview.example.com and the wildcard stops answering for pr-42.preview.example.com itself.
  • TLS wildcards cover exactly one label. *.preview.example.com covers pr-42.preview.example.com but not api.pr-42.preview.example.com. Name previews with one label, such as pr-42-api.preview.example.com.
  • Previews are public by default. Protect them with the platform's deployment protection or an identity proxy, keep them out of search engines, and point them at a staging API.

Platforms also offer this ready-made: Vercel's Preview Deployment Suffix (Pro and Enterprise plans) replaces vercel.app with your domain in preview URLs. The preview lifecycle itself is covered in environments and promotion.

docs.title: Redirects between the apex and www
docs.text:
• Use a permanent redirect: 301, or 308 when the method and body must be preserved. Redirect in one hop and keep the path and query.
  • Do it where it is cheapest: the platform's domain redirect setting, a Cloudflare redirect rule, an nginx return 301, or a CloudFront Function. A redirect service still needs a valid certificate for the name it redirects from.
  • With HSTS preload, the order is fixed by the preload rules: redirect http://example.com to https://example.com first (same host), serve the HSTS header there with max-age of at least 31536000, includeSubDomains, and preload, then redirect to https://www.example.com. Preloading forces HTTPS on every subdomain and is slow to undo, so audit all subdomains first.

docs.title: Route 53 alias records
docs.text:
An alias record is Route 53's way to point a name at an AWS resource:

  • It works at the zone apex, which a CNAME cannot.
  • Route 53 answers with the resource's current addresses, so a load balancer can change IPs without any DNS change on your side.
  • Queries to alias records that target AWS resources are not charged.
  • You cannot set the TTL for an AWS target; Route 53 uses the resource's default (60 seconds for Elastic Load Balancing).
  • To dig, an alias looks like an ordinary A or AAAA record. Create both when the target serves IPv6 (CloudFront with IPv6 enabled, a dual-stack load balancer).
  • evaluate_target_health lets Route 53 skip unhealthy targets in routing policies such as failover, covered in global traffic management.

docs.title: Cloudflare's proxy: what the orange cloud changes
docs.text:
DNS only (grey cloud) Proxied (orange cloud) DNS answer Your origin's IP Cloudflare anycast IPs TTL The value you set Automatic (300 seconds) TLS for visitors Your origin's certificate Cloudflare's edge certificate Origin connection Direct from the visitor From Cloudflare, per the SSL/TLS mode Caching, WAF, DDoS protection None from Cloudflare Applied Visitor IP at the origin The TCP source address CF-Connecting-IP header (and X-Forwarded-For) Protocols Anything HTTP and HTTPS on supported ports; other TCP or UDP needs Spectrum Record types All Only A, AAAA, and CNAME; MX and TXT are always DNS-only

Consequences to plan for:

  • Use Full (strict) mode. Flexible mode connects to the origin over plain HTTP; if the origin redirects HTTP to HTTPS, every request loops. Full (strict) validates the origin's certificate (a free Cloudflare origin certificate works). Cloudflare's Automatic SSL/TLS setting picks the most secure mode the origin supports.
  • Log the right client IP. Behind the proxy every TCP connection comes from Cloudflare; read CF-Connecting-IP (and only trust it from Cloudflare's address ranges).
  • Know the limits. Request bodies are capped per plan (larger uploads get 413), and an origin that does not answer within the proxy read timeout (125 seconds by default) produces 524. Upload large files directly to object storage and move long work to background jobs.
  • Hide the origin. A DNS-only record on the same server, an old record, or historical DNS data can reveal the origin's IP. Allow only Cloudflare's ranges (or use a tunnel), and rotate the IP if it leaked. Edge protection in depth is covered in edge protection, WAF, DDoS and bots.
  • Keep mail DNS-only. An MX target such as mail.example.com must resolve to the mail server, not to Cloudflare.

Moving nameservers to Cloudflare (a full setup) is a DNS migration; the partial (CNAME) setup that keeps your current DNS host is available only on Business and Enterprise plans.

docs.title: Subdomain takeover
docs.text:
The sequence Microsoft describes is short:

  1. You create a cloud resource (a web app, a bucket website, a CDN endpoint) and a CNAME such as promo.example.com pointing at its provider-assigned name.
  2. The campaign ends; someone deletes the resource but not the CNAME.
  3. An attacker notices the dangling name, creates a resource with the same provider-assigned name in their own account, and now serves content on promo.example.com, with a valid certificate.

Cookies scoped to example.com are sent to the attacker's page, and a dangling MX record can even receive your mail. Prevention is procedural: remove or repoint DNS before deleting a resource, keep platform verification records (they stop other accounts from attaching your name), and regularly check that every CNAME target still exists and belongs to you.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended setup TaskFlow Web on Vercel or Netlify, DNS elsewhere www CNAME as canonical; apex alias or flattened CNAME, or the documented A record; apex redirects to www TaskFlow Web on S3 and CloudFront, DNS in Route 53 Alias A and AAAA for the apex and www; redirect the non-canonical name with a CloudFront Function TaskFlow API behind a load balancer api alias or CNAME to the load balancer; no redirects One VPS A and AAAA to a reserved IP; Caddy or nginx with certbot A CDN, WAF, and DDoS protection in front of everything Cloudflare full setup with proxied web records and DNS-only mail records Preview environment per pull request Wildcard record plus a wildcard certificate via DNS-01, or the platform's preview domain feature

When not to:

  • Do not move a domain's nameservers to a hosting platform just to attach one subdomain; a CNAME is enough, and a nameserver change moves every record, including mail.
  • Do not proxy non-HTTP services (SSH, SMTP, databases) through an HTTP proxy; keep those records DNS-only or use a dedicated product.
  • Do not use A records to a platform's IPs unless the platform documents them as stable for that purpose.

docs.title: TaskFlow Web and API in Route 53 (Terraform)
docs.text:
This attaches the apex and www to the CloudFront distribution from hosting websites and frontends and api to an Application Load Balancer.

# infra/web/dns.tf: alias records for TaskFlow Web and TaskFlow API
data "aws_route53_zone" "main" {
  name = "example.com"
}

locals {
  web_names = toset(["example.com", "www.example.com"])
}

# IPv4 and IPv6 aliases to CloudFront for both web names
resource "aws_route53_record" "web" {
  for_each = { for pair in setproduct(local.web_names, ["A", "AAAA"]) : "${pair[0]}-${pair[1]}" => pair }

  zone_id = data.aws_route53_zone.main.zone_id
  name    = each.value[0]
  type    = each.value[1]

  alias {
    name                   = aws_cloudfront_distribution.web.domain_name
    zone_id                = aws_cloudfront_distribution.web.hosted_zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = false
  }
}

# API: alias to the load balancer; Route 53 follows its changing IPs
resource "aws_route53_record" "api" {
  for_each = toset(["A", "AAAA"]) # AAAA requires a dual-stack load balancer

  zone_id = data.aws_route53_zone.main.zone_id
  name    = "api.example.com"
  type    = each.value

  alias {
    name                   = aws_lb.api.dns_name
    zone_id                = aws_lb.api.zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = true
  }
}
  • setproduct creates four records (two names times two types) from one resource block, keyed like www.example.com-AAAA.
  • The distribution must list both names as aliases (its aliases argument) and carry an ACM certificate from us-east-1 that covers them, or CloudFront rejects the names.
  • The zone_id inside alias is the target's hosted zone (CloudFront's or the load balancer's), not your own zone.

docs.title: The same site on Cloudflare (Terraform, provider v5)
docs.text:
# infra/cloudflare/dns.tf: proxied web records, DNS-only mail
terraform {
  required_providers {
    cloudflare = {
      source  = "cloudflare/cloudflare"
      version = "~> 5.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "cloudflare" {} # reads CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN from the environment

variable "zone_id" {
  type = string
}

resource "cloudflare_dns_record" "www" {
  zone_id = var.zone_id
  name    = "www.example.com"
  type    = "CNAME"
  content = "taskflow-web.cdn.example.net"
  ttl     = 1 # 1 means automatic; proxied records always use it
  proxied = true
}

resource "cloudflare_dns_record" "apex" {
  zone_id = var.zone_id
  name    = "example.com"
  type    = "CNAME" # flattened automatically at the apex
  content = "taskflow-web.cdn.example.net"
  ttl     = 1
  proxied = true
}

resource "cloudflare_dns_record" "mx" {
  zone_id  = var.zone_id
  name     = "example.com"
  type     = "MX"
  content  = "mx1.mail.example.net"
  priority = 10
  ttl      = 3600
  proxied  = false # MX records are never proxied
}

Create the API token with permission to edit DNS for this one zone only. In version 5 of the provider the resource is cloudflare_dns_record and ttl is required; older configurations use cloudflare_record.

docs.title: Redirects and HSTS on a single server (nginx)
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/example.com.conf
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name example.com www.example.com;
    return 301 https://$host$request_uri;   # HTTPS on the same host first
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
    return 308 https://www.example.com$request_uri;   # one hop to the canonical host
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name www.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
    root /srv/taskflow-web/current;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;
    }
}

The certificate must cover both names (certbot certonly ... -d example.com -d www.example.com). Add preload to the HSTS header only after every subdomain serves HTTPS. Running TaskFlow behind nginx on one server end to end is covered in running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.title: Verifying a hookup from the command line
docs.text:
dig +short www.example.com CNAME            # the platform hostname you expect
dig +short example.com A                    # alias, flattened, or redirect IPs
dig +short example.com AAAA                 # a stale AAAA sends IPv6 users elsewhere

curl -sI http://example.com    | grep -iE '^(HTTP|location)'
curl -sI https://example.com   | grep -iE '^(HTTP|location|strict-transport-security)'
curl -sI https://www.example.com | grep -iE '^(HTTP|server|age)'

openssl s_client -connect www.example.com:443 -servername www.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -ext subjectAltName

; Example output for a healthy setup
HTTP/1.1 301 Moved Permanently
Location: https://example.com/
HTTP/2 308
location: https://www.example.com/
strict-transport-security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains
HTTP/2 200
X509v3 Subject Alternative Name:
    DNS:example.com, DNS:www.example.com

Check from IPv4 and IPv6 (curl -4, curl -6) as well: a forgotten AAAA record is a common reason why "it works for me" while some users reach an old server.

docs.title: Decommissioning without leaving a dangling record
docs.text:
1. Find every record that points at the resource: dig +short promo.example.com CNAME, and search the zone (in code) for the provider-assigned name.
  2. Delete or repoint those records, and wait for their TTL.
  3. Only then delete the resource.
  4. Remove its verification records and any CAA entry no other service needs.
  5. Watch Certificate Transparency logs for certificates issued for your names that you did not request.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pick one canonical host, redirect everything else to it in one hop, and use it consistently in configuration.
  • Point names at platform hostnames (CNAME or alias), not copied IPs.
  • Copy record values from the platform's dashboard, every time.
  • Attach subdomains with CNAMEs; move nameservers only when you mean to move all DNS.
  • Check CAA, IPv6 (AAAA), and verification records as part of every hosting change.
  • Use Full (strict) with Cloudflare, read CF-Connecting-IP, and lock the origin to the proxy.
  • Name previews with a single label under one wildcard, and protect them.
  • Remove DNS records before deleting the resources they point to.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The platform dashboard says "invalid configuration". Detect: dig shows extra A or AAAA records next to the CNAME, or a different target from the one in the dashboard. Cause: leftover records from the previous host, or values copied from old documentation. Fix: remove conflicting records and use the exact values the platform shows.
  • Browsers report too many redirects after enabling Cloudflare. Detect: curl -sI shows a 301 to the same HTTPS URL again and again; the SSL/TLS mode is Flexible. Cause: Cloudflare fetches the origin over HTTP, and the origin redirects HTTP to HTTPS. Fix: switch to Full (strict) with a valid origin certificate.
  • The apex shows a certificate error while www works. Detect: openssl s_client for the apex shows a certificate without example.com in its SAN list, or the platform shows the apex pending. Cause: the apex was never added to the platform or certificate, CAA blocks the CA, or an old AAAA points elsewhere. Fix: add the apex, fix CAA, remove stale records, and re-check over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • The origin is attacked directly although Cloudflare is in front. Detect: origin logs show traffic from addresses outside Cloudflare's ranges. Cause: the origin IP leaked through a DNS-only record or old DNS data. Fix: firewall the origin to Cloudflare's ranges or use a tunnel, then rotate the IP.
  • A forgotten subdomain serves a scam page. Detect: a Certificate Transparency alert for promo.example.com, or dig shows a CNAME to a resource you no longer own. Cause: a dangling CNAME was claimed by someone else. Fix: delete the record, treat it as a security incident (cookies scoped to the parent domain may have leaked), and add DNS removal to the decommissioning checklist.
  • Large uploads fail with 413, long reports with 524, after proxying. Detect: Cloudflare-branded error responses in the browser and logs. Cause: the plan's request body limit and the proxy read timeout. Fix: upload directly to object storage with presigned URLs, and run long work asynchronously.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Canonical host: The one hostname users should see; the others redirect to it.
  • Alternate domain name: CloudFront's term for a custom domain attached to a distribution.
  • Alias record: Route 53's apex-capable pointer to an AWS resource.
  • Verification record: A TXT or CNAME record that proves domain control to a platform or CA.
  • Wildcard record: A record such as *.preview.example.com that answers for names that do not otherwise exist.
  • Proxied record: A Cloudflare record answered with Cloudflare's addresses so traffic passes through its network.
  • SSL/TLS mode: Cloudflare's setting for how it connects to the origin (Off, Flexible, Full, Full (strict), Strict).
  • HSTS preload: A browser-shipped list of domains that are only ever contacted over HTTPS.
  • Dangling DNS record: A record pointing at a resource that no longer exists or that you no longer own.
  • Subdomain takeover: Claiming a dangling target to serve content on someone else's subdomain.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Changing nameservers to a platform to attach one subdomain, and losing mail and verification records.
  • Using A records to load balancer or platform IPs that can change.
  • Forgetting the apex, or www, when adding a domain to a platform or a certificate.
  • Leaving an old AAAA record that sends IPv6 users to a retired server.
  • Running Cloudflare in Flexible mode with an origin that redirects to HTTPS.
  • Assuming the proxy hides the origin while a DNS-only record on the same IP exists.
  • Expecting *.preview.example.com to cover two-level names, in DNS or in TLS.
  • Deleting cloud resources before their DNS records.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why do Vercel and Netlify recommend www as the canonical host when DNS is hosted elsewhere?
  2. Which records would you create to put the apex and www of example.com on CloudFront with Route 53, and why both A and AAAA?
  3. Why should an API hostname never sit behind an apex-to-www-style redirect?
  4. A preview environment uses *.preview.example.com. Which of these get an answer and a valid wildcard certificate: pr-7.preview.example.com, api.pr-7.preview.example.com, preview.example.com? (DNS answers the first and, if nothing else exists, the second; the certificate covers only the first; the third is not matched by either wildcard.)
  5. List four things that change when a Cloudflare record goes from DNS-only to proxied.
  6. Explain the redirect loop caused by Flexible mode, and the fix.
  7. Describe the subdomain takeover sequence and three controls that prevent it.
  8. HSTS preload requires a specific redirect order for example.com. What is it, and why?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Vercel: Adding and configuring a custom domain
  • Netlify: Configure external DNS for a custom domain
  • Amazon CloudFront: Use custom URLs by adding alternate domain names
  • Cloudflare: Encryption modes
  • Cloudflare: Proxied records limitations
  • HSTS preload list submission requirements
  • RFC 4592: The Role of Wildcards in the Domain Name System
  • Next: DNS migrations and troubleshooting. Back to the domains, DNS and email overview.

docs.title: DNS Migrations and Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Sooner or later TaskFlow moves: the API to a new load balancer, the web app to another platform, or the whole zone from the registrar's free DNS to Route 53 or Cloudflare. This lesson turns DNS caching into a runbook for changing records with zero downtime, moving a zone to a new provider without losing mail or certificates, and handling DNSSEC during a move. It then covers the tools for finding out what DNS is really answering (dig +trace, asking authoritative servers directly, comparing public resolvers) and a troubleshooting flow for the failures you will meet.

Record types and TTL basics are covered in domains and DNS records; moving traffic between regions with health-checked DNS is covered in global traffic management.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: DNS changes are rare, so teams are out of practice, and they are unforgiving: a wrong answer is cached by thousands of resolvers you do not control, for as long as the TTL you set. A nameserver change that forgets the MX records breaks inbound mail for days; a DNSSEC key that does not match its DS record makes the whole domain unresolvable for validating resolvers; and because the .com delegation is cached for two days, there is no quick undo. The outages below show that when DNS fails, everything behind it fails at once, including the tools you would use to fix it.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Meta (October 2021). In More details about the October 4 outage, Meta explains that when its backbone failed, its DNS servers withdrew their BGP route announcements because they could not reach the data centers. "The end result was that our DNS servers became unreachable even though they were still operational," which took every Meta service off the internet and slowed the recovery itself.
  • AWS (October 2025). The summary of the DynamoDB disruption in us-east-1 describes a race condition in DynamoDB's DNS automation that left the regional endpoint with an empty DNS record, so clients could not connect. DNS was restored in under three hours, but cached answers had to expire before everyone recovered, and AWS disabled the automation worldwide until it was fixed.
  • Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 (July 2025). The incident report explains how a configuration error withdrew the resolver's prefixes for 62 minutes. Users whose devices relied only on 1.1.1.1 lost all name resolution: a reminder that resolvers are dependencies too, and that checking from several resolvers is part of every diagnosis.
  • Route 53 zone import. The Route 53 guide on importing a zone file lists the rules that trip up migrations: at most 1,000 records per import, the SOA and apex NS records are ignored, names without a trailing dot get the zone appended (creating mail.example.com.example.com), and Route 53 cannot export zone files.

Popular tools and providers: dig, delv, kdig, drill, nslookup and Resolve-DnsName, DNSViz, DNSControl and OctoDNS for DNS as code, Terraform, and the cache flush pages of Google Public DNS and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1.

docs.title: "Propagation" is cache expiry
docs.text:
Nothing is pushed anywhere when you change a record. The authoritative servers serve the new data within seconds; every recursive resolver keeps its cached copy until that copy's TTL runs out, then asks again. Because each resolver cached the record at a different moment, users see a mix of old and new answers until the last cached copy expires. Several caches are involved:

Cache Controlled by Typical lifetime Record answers in recursive resolvers The record's TTL Your TTL, sometimes clamped by the resolver "Does not exist" answers SOA TTL and minimum (RFC 2308) Often minutes to an hour The delegation (NS records at the parent) The TLD registry 172,800 s (2 days) for .com DS records at the parent The TLD registry 86,400 s (1 day) for .com Operating system and browser caches OS and browser Short, but they exist Application caches The runtime and your code Varies; long-lived processes may keep connections to old IPs

Two consequences shape every runbook. A low TTL only helps if it was lowered at least one old TTL before the change. And a nameserver change cannot be rolled back quickly: whatever you publish at the registry, many resolvers keep using the previous delegation for up to two days.

docs.title: Changing a record with zero downtime
docs.text:
1. Lower the TTL early. If the record's TTL is 86400, lower it to 300 at least a day before the change (better two). Until the old TTL has passed, some resolvers still hold the long-lived copy.
  2. Prepare the new target fully. It must serve the same hostname: certificate, virtual host or alternate domain name, firewall rules, and capacity.
  3. Test it before DNS points at it. curl --resolve sends a real request with the real hostname (and SNI) to the new address.
  4. Change the record, ideally through code review.
  5. Run old and new in parallel. For at least one new TTL, and in practice until the old target's traffic reaches zero, both serve users. The old target must keep working (and keep its certificate).
  6. Verify on the authoritative servers, on several public resolvers, over IPv4 and IPv6, and in your monitoring.
  7. Raise the TTL again, then decommission the old target (and remove any DNS records that still point at it).

docs.title: Moving a zone to a new DNS provider
docs.text:
Changing nameservers moves every record at once, so the work is in making the new provider an exact copy before anyone notices.

  1. Inventory everything. Export a zone file where the old provider offers one, or list records through its API (aws route53 list-resource-record-sets for Route 53, which cannot export zone files). Include the records nobody remembers: DKIM selectors, the DMARC record, platform verification tokens, ACM validation CNAMEs, CAA, SRV, wildcards, and NS records that delegate subdomains to other providers.
  2. Translate provider-specific records. Route 53 alias records, Cloudflare proxied records, and flattened CNAMEs have no standard zone file form. Recreate them with the new provider's equivalent.
  3. Import and compare. Query the new provider's nameservers directly (dig @<new-ns> ... +norecurse) for every name and type and diff against the old ones (a script follows below).
  4. Handle DNSSEC first. Either remove the DS record at the registrar and wait out the DS record's TTL, a day or more, before the move (the simple path; Route 53's domain-transfer guide asks for 24 hours), or use a multi-signer setup (RFC 8901) in which both providers' keys are published. Never change nameservers while a DS record points at keys the new provider does not have.
  5. Change the nameservers at the registrar.
  6. Keep the old zone serving identical data for at least two days (the .com delegation TTL) plus a margin; a week is common. Freeze changes, or apply each change to both providers, which DNS as code makes easy.
  7. Verify and finish. dig +trace shows the new nameservers, query counts at the old provider fall to zero, the new provider signs the zone and you publish its DS, then delete the old zone.

Moving the registration to another registrar is a separate operation that does not need to touch DNS; see domains and DNS records for its rules.

docs.title: Asking the right server
docs.text:
Most DNS confusion comes from asking the wrong question. Separate three:

Question Command Tells you What does my zone say? dig @ns1.dns-host.example.net api.example.com +norecurse The authoritative truth, no caches involved Where does the world look for my zone? dig +trace api.example.com The delegation at every level, from the root down What are users getting right now? dig @1.1.1.1 api.example.com (and 8.8.8.8, 9.9.9.9, your office resolver) Cached answers and the TTL they have left

Supporting tools:

  • dig +dnssec shows signatures; dig +cd (checking disabled) asks a validating resolver to skip validation. An answer that fails normally but works with +cd is a DNSSEC problem. delv validates locally and explains why a chain fails, and DNSViz draws the chain.
  • dig -x 198.51.100.20 checks reverse DNS (PTR).
  • On Windows, Resolve-DnsName -Server 8.8.8.8 -Name api.example.com and nslookup api.example.com 8.8.8.8 do the same jobs; ipconfig /flushdns clears the local cache. On Linux with systemd-resolved, resolvectl flush-caches; on macOS, sudo dscacheutil -flushcache; sudo killall -HUP mDNSResponder.
  • Google Public DNS and Cloudflare's 1.1.1.1 each have a page to flush a name from their own cache. That fixes those resolvers only; every other resolver still waits for its TTL.

docs.title: A troubleshooting flow
docs.text: Work from the source outward: first prove the zone is right, then the delegation, then DNSSEC, then caches. Only when all four are clean is the problem somewhere else; the troubleshooting lesson for Linux servers covers the network checks that come next.

docs.title: Failure patterns
docs.text: Symptom Usual cause How to confirm Mail stops after a nameserver change MX, SPF, or DKIM records were not copied dig @<new-ns> example.com MX +norecurse is empty The site works but certificate renewal fails CAA does not list the CA, or an ACM validation CNAME was deleted dig example.com CAA; the CA or ACM error message The console refuses a record, or mail breaks after adding one A CNAME at the apex or next to other records The record list at that name A record exists but nobody can find it The zone name was appended: _dmarc.example.com.example.com dig the doubled name SERVFAIL for some users only DNSSEC: DS and keys disagree dig +cd works; DNSViz shows the break A new subdomain is NXDOMAIN for some users Negative caching of a lookup made before the record existed The SOA minimum and TTL; it clears by itself Half the answers old, half new, for days Two delegated nameserver sets with different data dig @ each NS listed in dig +trace Some clients use the old IP for hours Long-lived processes or connection pools that resolved once Client logs; restart or add connection max age

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Change Approach Point one name at a new target Lower the TTL early, test with curl --resolve, change, run old and new in parallel Move a zone to another DNS provider Full migration: inventory, translate, compare, DNSSEC first, keep both zones identical for the delegation TTL Move only the registration Registrar transfer; DNS does not change (move DNS first if the old registrar hosts it) Survive a DNS provider outage Two providers serving the same zone at all times, kept in sync by DNS as code, prepared in advance Fail over between regions automatically Health-checked DNS routing, covered in global traffic management

When not to:

  • Do not keep very low TTLs permanently "just in case". They add query volume and cost, and make your DNS provider's outages hit users sooner.
  • Do not plan to "switch nameservers" during an outage: the delegation is cached for days. Redundant DNS must already be in place.
  • Do not change nameservers, DNSSEC, and records in the same step; each one has its own cache and its own rollback.

docs.title: Testing the new target before the switch
docs.text:
# Send a real request for api.example.com to the NEW load balancer's address
curl -sv --resolve api.example.com:443:198.51.100.40 \
  https://api.example.com/healthz -o /dev/null 2>&1 \
  | grep -E 'subject:|subjectAltName|HTTP/'

--resolve host:port:address overrides DNS for that one request, so TLS uses the real server name and the request carries the real Host header. A certificate or virtual host problem shows up here, not in front of users.

docs.title: Walking the delegation with dig +trace
docs.text:
; Example output of: dig +trace www.example.com (trimmed, documentation names)
.                    518400  IN  NS     a.root-servers.net.
com.                 172800  IN  NS     a.gtld-servers.net.
example.com.         172800  IN  NS     ns1.dns-host.example.net.
example.com.         172800  IN  NS     ns2.dns-host.example.net.
www.example.com.     300     IN  CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.

Read it top to bottom: the root refers the resolver to the .com servers, the .com servers refer it to your nameservers (this is the delegation, cached for two days), and your nameservers answer. During a nameserver migration the third block is what changes; if it still lists the old provider, the registrar change has not happened or has not reached the registry.

docs.title: What are different resolvers seeing?
docs.text:
for r in 1.1.1.1 8.8.8.8 9.9.9.9; do
  printf '%-8s ' "$r"
  dig +noall +answer @"$r" api.example.com A | awk '{print "ttl=" $2, $5}'
done

; Example output a few minutes after a change
1.1.1.1  ttl=212 198.51.100.40
8.8.8.8  ttl=41 198.51.100.20
9.9.9.9  ttl=287 198.51.100.40

One resolver still serves the old address with 41 seconds left; it will switch on its own. A remaining TTL far above the TTL you set means a record or a resolver you did not expect is involved.

docs.title: Comparing two providers before a cutover
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/compare-zones.sh: diff answers from the old and new nameservers
# Usage: scripts/compare-zones.sh names.txt   (one fully qualified name per line)
set -euo pipefail
OLD_NS="ns1.old-dns.example.net"
NEW_NS="ns1.new-dns.example.net"
TYPES=(A AAAA CNAME MX TXT CAA SRV)   # apex NS and SOA differ by design

status=0
while read -r name; do
  [[ -z "$name" || "$name" == \#* ]] && continue
  for type in "${TYPES[@]}"; do
    old=$(dig +short +norecurse @"$OLD_NS" "$name" "$type" | sort)
    new=$(dig +short +norecurse @"$NEW_NS" "$name" "$type" | sort)
    if [[ "$old" != "$new" ]]; then
      printf 'DIFF %s %s\n  old: %s\n  new: %s\n' "$name" "$type" "${old:-<none>}" "${new:-<none>}"
      status=1
    fi
  done
done < "${1:?names file required}"
exit "$status"

Build names.txt from the old provider's export, including underscore names such as _dmarc.example.com and s1._domainkey.example.com. Expect real differences only where a provider-specific feature answers differently by design (a proxied record returns the proxy's addresses); every other DIFF is a missing or wrong record.

docs.title: One source of truth for both providers (DNSControl)
docs.text:
During the overlap, DNSControl can push the same records to the old and the new provider. A SERVICE() with 0 as its second argument manages records without listing that provider's nameservers in the delegation.

// dns/dnsconfig.js: the same zone pushed to the old and the new provider
D("example.com", REGISTRAR("none"),
  SERVICE("old_dns"),     // currently delegated: serves real traffic
  SERVICE("new_dns", 0),  // kept identical, not delegated yet
  DefaultTTL(300),
  A("api", "198.51.100.20"),
  AAAA("api", "2001:db8::20"),
  CNAME("www", "taskflow-web.cdn.example.net."),
  MX("@", 10, "mx1.mail.example.net."),
  MX("@", 20, "mx2.mail.example.net."),
  TXT("@", "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"),
  TXT("_dmarc", "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"),
  CAA("@", "issue", "letsencrypt.org"),
);

{
  "none": { "TYPE": "NONE" },
  "old_dns": {
    "TYPE": "ROUTE53",
    "KeyId": "$AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID",
    "SecretKey": "$AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY",
    "Token": "$AWS_SESSION_TOKEN"
  },
  "new_dns": {
    "TYPE": "CLOUDFLAREAPI",
    "accountid": "$CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID",
    "apitoken": "$CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN"
  }
}

The second file is dns/creds.json; values starting with $ are read from environment variables, so no secret is committed. dnscontrol preview prints the changes for each provider and dnscontrol push applies them. On the cutover day you change the nameservers at the registrar, swap the 0 to the old provider's SERVICE(), and after the overlap remove it.

docs.title: Running DNS changes through CI
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/dns.yml
name: DNS

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["dns/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["dns/**"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write   # OIDC for AWS

concurrency:
  group: dns
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  dns:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-dns
          aws-region: us-east-1

      - name: Preview DNS changes
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD/dns:/dns" \
            -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY -e AWS_SESSION_TOKEN \
            -e CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID -e CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN \
            ghcr.io/dnscontrol/dnscontrol preview
        env:
          CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ vars.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
          CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_DNS_TOKEN }}

      - name: Push DNS changes
        if: github.event_name == 'push'
        run: |
          docker run --rm -v "$PWD/dns:/dns" \
            -e AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID -e AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY -e AWS_SESSION_TOKEN \
            -e CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID -e CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN \
            ghcr.io/dnscontrol/dnscontrol push
        env:
          CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID: ${{ vars.CLOUDFLARE_ACCOUNT_ID }}
          CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.CLOUDFLARE_DNS_TOKEN }}
  • Pull requests get a preview, so reviewers see exactly which records change at each provider; only merges to main push.
  • AWS credentials come from OIDC (configure-aws-credentials exports short-lived keys as environment variables); the Cloudflare token is scoped to DNS edits on this zone. Short-lived credentials and OIDC are covered in pipeline and supply chain security.
  • concurrency stops two pushes from racing each other.
  • The image is shown untagged, as in DNSControl's documentation; in a real pipeline pin it to a release tag or digest so a new DNSControl version cannot change behaviour unreviewed.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Manage zones as code and review every change; keep an export of each zone outside the provider.
  • Lower TTLs at least one old TTL before planned changes, and raise them afterwards.
  • Test new targets with curl --resolve before changing DNS.
  • Keep old targets serving until their traffic is gone.
  • For nameserver moves: inventory, translate, diff, handle DNSSEC first, and keep both zones identical for at least the delegation TTL.
  • Diagnose from the source outward: authoritative answer, delegation, DNSSEC, caches, then other layers.
  • Check from several resolvers and over IPv4 and IPv6.
  • Prepare secondary DNS before you need it; it cannot be added in the middle of an outage.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Inbound mail disappears after moving DNS to a new provider. Detect: senders' bounces or a drop in received mail; dig @<new-ns> example.com MX +norecurse returns nothing. Cause: only web records were copied before the nameserver change. Fix: add the MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records at the new provider immediately; diff every name and type before future cutovers.
  • The domain returns SERVFAIL for many users right after a move. Detect: validating resolvers fail, dig +cd succeeds, DNSViz shows a DS without a matching DNSKEY. Cause: the DS record at the registrar still points at the old provider's key. Fix: remove the DS (or add the new provider's key) and wait for the cached DS to expire; next time, remove DS a day before the move.
  • Half the users get old answers days after an edit. Detect: dig +trace lists nameservers from two providers, and they answer differently. Cause: the old provider's zone is still delegated (or cached as delegated) and was not updated. Fix: apply the change to both providers until the old delegation has expired everywhere.
  • The cutover went fine, but the API still gets traffic on the old load balancer. Detect: the old target's request count stays above zero long after the TTL. Cause: clients with connection pools or DNS caches that resolved once (long-running workers, mobile apps). Fix: keep the old target up longer, set a maximum connection age on clients, and restart long-lived workers.
  • A freshly created subdomain is NXDOMAIN for some people. Detect: authoritative servers answer, some resolvers say the name does not exist. Cause: those resolvers looked it up before it existed and cached the negative answer. Fix: wait out the negative TTL (the SOA minimum), flush the public resolvers you can, and create records before announcing them.
  • Certificate renewals fail after the DNS move. Detect: ACM shows renewal pending, or the ACME client reports a CAA or validation error. Cause: the ACM validation CNAME or a CAA entry was left behind. Fix: restore the record, and include underscore names in every inventory.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Propagation: The informal name for resolvers' caches expiring at different times after a change.
  • Delegation TTL: How long resolvers cache the parent's NS records for your zone (two days at .com).
  • Negative caching: Caching the answer that a name does not exist.
  • Authoritative answer: An answer from a server that holds the zone, marked with the aa flag in dig output.
  • Lame delegation: A nameserver listed in the delegation that does not actually serve the zone.
  • dig +trace: Resolving a name step by step from the root, showing each delegation.
  • --resolve (curl): Overriding DNS for one request to test a target with the real hostname.
  • Multi-signer DNSSEC: Two providers serving one signed zone with both sets of keys published (RFC 8901).
  • DNS as code: Managing zones in version-controlled files applied by tools such as DNSControl, OctoDNS, or Terraform.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing "DNS propagation takes 48 hours" for every change; ordinary record changes take one TTL, while nameserver changes are bounded by the delegation TTL.
  • Lowering the TTL at the same moment as the change.
  • Copying only web records when changing nameservers, forgetting MX, TXT, DKIM, CAA, and validation records.
  • Changing nameservers while a DS record points at the old provider's keys.
  • Testing only from one's own laptop, whose resolver may have been flushed or may have just cached the new answer.
  • Shutting down the old target as soon as DNS is changed.
  • Expecting to switch DNS providers quickly during an outage.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is "propagation" a misleading word? What actually happens after you change a record?
  2. A record has a TTL of 86400. You plan to change it on Thursday at 10:00. When must you lower the TTL, and to what? (By Wednesday 10:00 at the latest, so every cached copy of the long TTL has expired; 300 seconds is typical.)
  3. Why must the old zone stay identical for about two days after a .com nameserver change, and what sets that number?
  4. Describe the safe order of steps for moving a DNSSEC-signed zone to a new provider.
  5. Which three questions separate "zone wrong", "delegation wrong", and "caches stale", and which commands answer each?
  6. A domain fails with SERVFAIL on 8.8.8.8 but resolves with dig +cd. What do you suspect, and what tool shows the broken link?
  7. Why test a new target with curl --resolve rather than by editing DNS and waiting?
  8. Your DNS provider is down. Why can you not simply switch the nameservers to another provider, and what should have been prepared?

docs.text:
• RFC 2308: Negative Caching of DNS Queries
  • RFC 8901: Multi-Signer DNSSEC Models

docs.title: Domains and DNS Records
docs.text:
Every hostname TaskFlow uses, from app.example.com to the address its password-reset emails come from, hangs off one registered domain and one DNS zone. This lesson explains who does what in the domain system (registrants, registrars, registries, and DNS hosts), how registration data is published and protected, the domain lifecycle from registration to expiry and transfer, every record type you will meet in practice, how TTLs decide how long an answer lives, and what DNSSEC adds.

The resolution path itself (recursive resolvers, root and TLD servers, caching) is covered in DNS in the Networking section; this lesson builds on it from the operator's side.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A domain is a single point of failure that most teams never test. If it expires, the website, the API, inbound mail, and outbound mail all stop at once. If someone takes over the registrar account, they control where every name points and can pass the DNS checks certificate authorities use, so they can obtain valid certificates for your domain. And DNS mistakes have long tails: a wrong answer is cached by thousands of resolvers for as long as its TTL allows, so a five-minute typo can mean an hour of partial outage.

Records also carry security policy, not only addresses. CAA decides which certificate authorities may issue for you, SPF and DMARC decide whether mail claiming to be from you is accepted, and DNSSEC decides whether validating resolvers trust your answers at all. Knowing each record's exact rules is what separates a routine change from an incident.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• ICANN and RDAP. ICANN's RDAP page explains that the Registration Data Access Protocol was created as the replacement for WHOIS and gives registration data in standardized formats. Since 28 January 2025, gTLD registries and registrars must provide RDAP and are, with few exceptions, no longer required to run WHOIS services.
  • Slack's DNSSEC rollout (2021). In The Case of the Recursive Resolvers, Slack describes how enabling DNSSEC on slack.com caused about 24 hours of failures for less than 1% of users. A signing bug in how wildcard records were denied made some resolvers cache "nothing exists here", and when the team rolled back, the DS record was already cached: the .com zone asks resolvers to keep it for 24 hours, and the domain owner cannot shorten that.
  • Let's Encrypt and CAA. The Let's Encrypt CAA documentation says it checks CAA records before every certificate it issues, follows CNAMEs while doing so, and supports the accounturi and validationmethods parameters that pin issuance to one ACME account or challenge type.
  • Route 53 alias records. The Route 53 guide Choosing between alias and non-alias records documents the provider-specific answer to the "no CNAME at the apex" rule: an alias record can sit at the zone apex, answers with the target resource's current IP addresses, and is not charged for queries to AWS resources.

Popular tools and providers: registrars such as Cloudflare Registrar, Amazon Route 53 Domains, Namecheap, GoDaddy, and Gandi; DNS hosts such as Amazon Route 53, Cloudflare DNS, Google Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, and DNSimple; and tools such as dig, delv, nslookup, PowerShell's Resolve-DnsName, ICANN's RDAP lookup, and DNSViz.

docs.title: Registrant, registrar, registry, and DNS host
docs.text:
Role Who What it does Registrant You (TaskFlow's company) Holds the right to use example.com; its contact details receive renewal and transfer messages Registrar The company you pay Registers the name with the registry, renews it, and sends your nameservers (and DS records) to the registry Registry operator The operator of .com, .org, a country code TLD, and so on Keeps the database of names in its TLD and runs the TLD's nameservers, which publish the delegation DNS host Route 53, Cloudflare, your registrar's DNS, your own servers Runs the authoritative nameservers that serve your zone's records Recursive resolver Your ISP, 1.1.1.1, 8.8.8.8, a corporate resolver Looks up names for clients and caches the answers

ICANN accredits registrars for generic TLDs (.com, .org, .dev, .app, and over a thousand more), while country code TLDs (.uk, .in, .de) are run by national registries with their own rules on who may register and how transfers work. One company can be both your registrar and your DNS host, but the two jobs stay separate: you can keep the registration at one company and point the nameservers at another.

When you choose a domain, check the renewal price (not only the first year), whether the TLD has residency or eligibility rules, and register the variants you care about before launch. Never invent private top-level domains for internal services; use a subdomain of a domain you own, such as internal.example.com, so nobody else can ever register it.

docs.title: Registration data: WHOIS, RDAP, and privacy
docs.text:
Registries and registrars publish registration data: creation and expiry dates, status codes, nameservers, and the registrar. RDAP returns it as JSON over HTTPS, with a standard bootstrap file at IANA that tells clients which server to ask for each TLD. Personal contact details are usually redacted (data protection laws such as the GDPR pushed the industry this way), and many registrars offer a privacy or proxy service on top.

Two practical consequences:

  • The registrant email must be real and monitored. Renewal notices, transfer approvals, and registrant verification emails go there. Some registries require the registrant to confirm the address, and an unverified contact can get the domain suspended. Use a role mailbox such as domains@example.com, never one person's inbox.
  • Monitor the expiry date like a certificate. RDAP gives you the expiration event in machine-readable form, so a scheduled check can alert months ahead.

docs.title: Domain lifecycle, locks, and transfers
docs.text:
ICANN's Expired Registration Recovery Policy sets the minimum rules for generic TLDs: the registrar must send notices about a month and about a week before expiry, interrupt the domain's DNS after it expires (while still letting the registrant renew), and registries must offer a 30-day redemption grace period after deletion. Registrars set their own prices and exact windows inside those rules, so read yours before you need it.

Locks protect a domain from hijacking and mistakes. Their state shows up as EPP status codes in RDAP:

Status Set by Effect clientTransferProhibited Registrar (the "transfer lock" toggle) Blocks transfers to another registrar clientUpdateProhibited / clientDeleteProhibited Registrar Blocks changes to nameservers or contacts, and deletion serverTransferProhibited and other server* codes Registry The same, enforced at the registry; with a registry lock, changes need an out-of-band verification redemptionPeriod, pendingDelete Registry The domain is expired and being deleted

Moving the registration to another registrar is a transfer: unlock the domain, get the authorization (EPP) code from the old registrar, request the transfer at the new one, and approve it. Typical rules, as listed in the Route 53 transfer guide: no transfer within 60 days of registration or a previous transfer, a 60-day lock after a change of registrant (some registrars let you opt out before the change), and for most generic TLDs the transfer adds a year to the registration. Two traps:

  • If your old registrar also hosts your DNS for free, it may switch that DNS off when the transfer starts. Move DNS hosting first, then the registration.
  • If the domain uses DNSSEC and the DNS host will change, remove the DS record first and wait at least a day for cached copies to expire.

docs.title: Record types
docs.text: Type Holds TaskFlow example A An IPv4 address api.example.com A 198.51.100.20 AAAA An IPv6 address api.example.com AAAA 2001:db8::20 CNAME Another name; the resolver restarts the lookup there app.example.com CNAME taskflow-web.cdn.example.net. ALIAS / ANAME / alias record Provider feature: the DNS host resolves a target and answers with its addresses example.com alias to a CDN distribution MX Priority and mail server hostname example.com MX 10 mx1.mail.example.net. TXT Text strings: SPF, DMARC, DKIM keys, verification tokens _dmarc.example.com TXT "v=DMARC1; p=none; ..." CAA Which certificate authorities may issue example.com CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org" NS Nameservers for a zone (at the apex and at the parent) example.com NS ns1.dns-host.example.net. SOA Zone metadata: primary server, contact, serial, timers One per zone, managed by most providers SRV Priority, weight, port, and target for a service _mongodb._tcp.db.example.com SRV 0 0 27017 db-1.example.com. PTR Reverse DNS: the name for an IP address 20.100.51.198.in-addr.arpa PTR api.example.com. HTTPS / SVCB Connection hints such as supported protocols Covered in DNS DS, DNSKEY, RRSIG DNSSEC keys and signatures See DNSSEC below

docs.title: A and AAAA
docs.text: Address records are the end of every lookup. Publish AAAA alongside A when the target supports IPv6, and point them only at addresses you control for as long as the record exists: a static or reserved IP for a VPS, never an address a provider can hand to someone else.

docs.title: CNAME and its rules
docs.text:
A CNAME says "this name is an alias; ask for that one instead". The rules come from the core DNS specifications (RFC 1034 and RFC 2181):

  • No other data at the same name. A name with a CNAME cannot also have MX, TXT, or A records. This is why the zone apex, which must hold SOA and NS records, can never be a CNAME.
  • MX and NS targets must not be aliases. Point them at names with real A/AAAA records.
  • A CNAME applies to every query type. A TXT lookup for a CNAMEd name follows the alias, which surprises people adding verification records.
  • Chains cost time. Each hop can be another lookup; keep chains short.

docs.title: The apex problem: alias records and CNAME flattening
docs.text:
Hosting platforms and CDNs want you to point at a hostname they control, so they can change IP addresses and steer traffic. Subdomains can do that with a CNAME; the apex cannot. DNS hosts solve it with non-standard features that resolve the target on the authoritative side:

  • Route 53 alias records answer with the current addresses of an AWS resource (CloudFront, a load balancer, an S3 website, and others), can sit at the apex, and appear to clients as plain A or AAAA records.
  • Cloudflare CNAME flattening happens automatically for a CNAME at the apex on all plans and for proxied records; paid plans can flatten every CNAME.
  • ALIAS and ANAME records at other DNS hosts work the same way.

Because the DNS host resolves the target from its own servers, a platform that steers users by DNS no longer sees the user's resolver. That is why Netlify recommends a subdomain such as www as the primary domain when you use external DNS, and Vercel recommends www with a CNAME so its CDN keeps more control over traffic. The apex then becomes a redirect, as shown in connecting domains to hosting.

docs.title: MX: where mail for the domain goes
docs.text:
Each MX record has a preference (lower is tried first) and a hostname that must have address records. Several MX records with different preferences give fallbacks. A domain that should never receive mail publishes a null MX (MX 0 ., RFC 7505) so senders fail fast instead of retrying for days. example.com itself is a good model of a domain that neither sends nor receives mail:

$ dig +short example.com MX
0 .
$ dig +short example.com TXT
"v=spf1 -all"
$ dig +short _dmarc.example.com TXT
"v=DMARC1;p=reject;sp=reject;adkim=s;aspf=s"

These are the real answers for example.com in November 2026 (TXT output trimmed to the SPF record): no mail exchanger, no authorized sender, and a DMARC policy telling receivers to reject anything claiming to come from it. Every parked or redirect-only domain you own should publish the same three records so spammers cannot borrow it.

docs.title: TXT: the general-purpose record
docs.text:
TXT records carry SPF (at the domain itself), DMARC (at _dmarc), DKIM public keys (at <selector>._domainkey), and verification tokens from platforms and certificate authorities. Details that matter:

  • One TXT record can hold several strings of up to 255 bytes each; receivers join them without spaces. Long DKIM keys are split this way.
  • A name can have many TXT records, but only one SPF record (v=spf1 ...). Two SPF records make every SPF check a permanent error.
  • Some DNS consoles want quotes around the value, some add them, and some append the zone name to whatever you type in the name field. Always check the published result with dig.

SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are explained in depth in email deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

docs.title: CAA: which CAs may issue
docs.text:
A CAA record (RFC 8659) lists the certificate authorities allowed to issue for a name. Public CAs must check it before issuing.

example.com.  CAA  0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
example.com.  CAA  0 issue "amazon.com"
example.com.  CAA  0 issuewild "letsencrypt.org"
example.com.  CAA  0 iodef "mailto:security@example.com"
  • issue allows a CA for normal certificates; issuewild controls wildcard certificates, and when any issuewild record exists, issue records are ignored for wildcard requests.
  • The CA looks for CAA at the exact name, then climbs toward the root and uses the first name that has any CAA records. A CAA set at example.com therefore governs api.example.com too, unless api.example.com has its own.
  • No CAA records anywhere means any CA may issue. issue ";" means none may.
  • Each CA documents its identifier: Let's Encrypt uses letsencrypt.org, and AWS Certificate Manager needs one of amazon.com, amazontrust.com, awstrust.com, or amazonaws.com. Cloudflare adds CAA records for its own CAs automatically once you create any CAA record, so its Universal SSL keeps renewing.
  • 0 issue "letsencrypt.org; accounturi=<account-url>" (RFC 8657) restricts issuance to one ACME account.

CAA is cheap protection, but it is also the classic cause of "renewal suddenly fails after we moved hosting": the new platform's CA is not on the list. Certificate issuance itself is covered in obtaining and renewing certificates.

docs.title: NS and SOA
docs.text: NS records appear twice: at the parent (the .com servers' delegation, plus glue addresses when the nameservers are inside the zone) and at the apex of your zone. They should match. The SOA record holds the primary nameserver, a contact mailbox, a serial number, timers for secondary servers, and the value used for negative caching: per RFC 2308, a "no such name" answer is cached for the smaller of the SOA record's TTL and its minimum field. Managed DNS hosts maintain SOA for you.

docs.title: SRV and PTR
docs.text:
SRV records publish a service's priority, weight, port, and host under _service._protocol.name. TaskFlow meets them through MongoDB: a mongodb+srv://db.example.com/ connection string makes the driver look up _mongodb._tcp.db.example.com SRV records for the replica set members and a TXT record on db.example.com for options such as replicaSet and authSource, and it turns TLS on by default. Keep such internal names in a private zone.

PTR records live in the reverse zones in-addr.arpa and ip6.arpa, which belong to whoever owns the IP address. For a cloud server you set them through the provider. Reverse DNS matters mostly for mail: Gmail requires sending IPs to have a PTR record whose hostname resolves back to the same IP.

docs.title: TTL: how long an answer lives
docs.text:
Every record has a TTL in seconds. A resolver that fetched the record may answer from its cache until the TTL runs out, then must ask again.

TTL Good for Trade-off 60 to 300 s Records you may change soon: api, app, anything before a migration More queries, and an outage of your DNS host hurts sooner 3600 s Most stable records A mistake lingers for up to an hour 86400 s NS, MX, and other rarely changed records Changes take up to a day to reach everyone

Worked example: api.example.com has a TTL of 3600. A resolver caches it at 09:59:30, and you change the record at 10:00. That resolver keeps returning the old address until 10:59:30, so the worst case is one full TTL after the change, plus whatever applications cache on top. Lowering the TTL helps only if you do it at least one old TTL before the change; DNS migrations and troubleshooting turns this into a runbook. Alias records inherit their TTL from the target (AWS load balancers use 60 seconds), and Cloudflare proxied records use an automatic TTL of 300 seconds.

docs.title: DNSSEC at a high level
docs.text:
DNSSEC adds signatures so a validating resolver can prove an answer came from the zone owner and was not altered. It does not encrypt anything; DNS over HTTPS or TLS does that, between client and resolver.

  • DNSKEY records hold the zone's public keys, RRSIG records hold signatures over each record set, and NSEC or NSEC3 records prove that a name does not exist.
  • The parent zone holds a DS record, a hash of your key, which you submit through the registrar. That link is what connects your zone to the chain of trust.
  • If the DS at the parent and the key in your zone disagree, every validating resolver (and that includes the large public resolvers) returns SERVFAIL. Because the DS is cached for a day at .com, the failure outlives the fix, as Slack's incident showed.

Managed providers (Route 53, Cloudflare, Google Cloud DNS, Azure DNS) sign the zone for you, but how much key work remains varies: Route 53, for example, manages the zone-signing key while the key-signing key is a customer managed key in AWS KMS that you own and rotate. Your other jobs are publishing the DS at the registrar and planning provider migrations around it. Enable DNSSEC for high-value domains when signing is automated and your team has a written migration procedure.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use Avoid Point a subdomain at a platform or CDN CNAME to the hostname the platform gives you Copying the platform's current IPs into A records Point the apex at a platform, CDN, or load balancer Alias record, flattened CNAME, the platform's documented static IPs, or a redirect to www A CNAME at the apex A VPS with a fixed address A and AAAA to a reserved static IP Ephemeral IPs that change on restart A load balancer Alias or CNAME to its DNS name A records to its current IPs (they change) A domain that sends and receives no mail Null MX, v=spf1 -all, DMARC p=reject Leaving it without email records Restrict certificate issuance CAA listing every CA you actually use Forgetting the CA of a new hosting platform Discovering a service's hosts and ports SRV (for example MongoDB's +srv strings) Hard-coding host lists in many clients High-value domain integrity DNSSEC with provider-managed signing DNSSEC without a migration plan

Do not use DNS round robin as load balancing or failover: resolvers cache answers and DNS does not know whether a server is healthy. Use a load balancer or health-checked DNS routing instead (see load balancing and global traffic management). Avoid wildcard records unless you need them: they make typos resolve and hide missing records.

docs.title: A complete zone for TaskFlow
docs.text:
; example.com zone file (BIND format); documentation addresses only
$ORIGIN example.com.
$TTL 3600
@       IN SOA  ns1.dns-host.example.net. hostmaster.example.com. (
                2026111301 ; serial (YYYYMMDDnn)
                7200       ; refresh
                3600       ; retry
                1209600    ; expire
                300 )      ; minimum: negative-caching TTL
@       IN NS     ns1.dns-host.example.net.
@       IN NS     ns2.dns-host.example.net.

; Web: www is the primary site; the apex redirects to it
@       300  IN A      203.0.113.10        ; redirect service
@       300  IN AAAA   2001:db8::10
www     300  IN CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.
app     300  IN CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.

; API behind a load balancer with fixed addresses
api     60   IN A      198.51.100.20
api     60   IN AAAA   2001:db8::20

; Inbound mail and sender policy
@       IN MX     10 mx1.mail.example.net.
@       IN MX     20 mx2.mail.example.net.
@       IN TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"
_dmarc  IN TXT    "v=DMARC1; p=none; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"

; Certificates
@       IN CAA    0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
@       IN CAA    0 iodef "mailto:security@example.com"
  • $ORIGIN makes unqualified names relative: www means www.example.com.. A name with a trailing dot is absolute; a name without one gets the origin appended, which is the source of records such as mx1.example.com.example.com.
  • Record-level TTLs override $TTL: names you may change soon get 60 to 300 seconds.
  • The SOA minimum (300) bounds how long resolvers remember that a name does not exist, which matters when you create a record someone already looked up.

docs.title: Querying records with dig and Resolve-DnsName
docs.text:
dig +short api.example.com A                 # just the answer
dig +noall +answer app.example.com           # answer section with TTLs; shows the CNAME chain
dig +short example.com MX
dig +short _dmarc.example.com TXT
dig +short example.com CAA
dig example.com SOA +multiline               # serial and timers, readable
dig @ns1.dns-host.example.net api.example.com A +norecurse   # ask the authoritative server directly

; Example output of: dig +noall +answer app.example.com
app.example.com.                300  IN  CNAME  taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.
taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.    60  IN  A      203.0.113.50
taskflow-web.cdn.example.net.    60  IN  A      203.0.113.51

The TTL column counts down in a resolver's cache: run the command twice a few seconds apart and a cached answer shows a smaller number. On Windows:

Resolve-DnsName -Name app.example.com -Type A -Server 1.1.1.1
Resolve-DnsName -Name example.com -Type MX
nslookup -type=TXT _dmarc.example.com

docs.title: Checking registration data with RDAP
docs.text:
# The IANA bootstrap file says which RDAP server serves each TLD
curl -s https://data.iana.org/rdap/dns.json | jq -r '.services[] | select(.[0][] == "com") | .[1][]'

# Ask that server about the domain, keep the fields worth monitoring
curl -s https://rdap.verisign.com/com/v1/domain/example.com \
  | jq '{name: .ldhName, status, events: [.events[] | {(.eventAction): .eventDate}], dnssec: .secureDNS.delegationSigned}'

{
  "name": "EXAMPLE.COM",
  "status": ["client delete prohibited", "client transfer prohibited", "client update prohibited"],
  "events": [
    { "registration": "1995-08-14T04:00:00Z" },
    { "expiration": "2027-08-13T04:00:00Z" },
    ...
  ],
  "dnssec": true
}

This is the real (trimmed) answer for example.com in November 2026: all three client locks are on, the delegation is signed, and the expiry date is machine-readable. A scheduled job that alerts when expiration is less than 60 days away, for every domain you own, prevents the most embarrassing outage in this lesson.

docs.title: Managing core records in Terraform (Route 53)
docs.text:
# infra/dns/records.tf: core records for example.com in Route 53
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

resource "aws_route53_zone" "main" {
  name = "example.com"
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "mx" {
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.main.zone_id
  name    = "example.com"
  type    = "MX"
  ttl     = 3600
  records = ["10 mx1.mail.example.net.", "20 mx2.mail.example.net."]
}

# All TXT strings for one name live in ONE record set
resource "aws_route53_record" "apex_txt" {
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.main.zone_id
  name    = "example.com"
  type    = "TXT"
  ttl     = 3600
  records = [
    "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all",
    "example-site-verification=<token>",
  ]
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "caa" {
  zone_id = aws_route53_zone.main.zone_id
  name    = "example.com"
  type    = "CAA"
  ttl     = 3600
  records = [
    "0 issue \"letsencrypt.org\"",
    "0 issue \"amazon.com\"",
    "0 issuewild \"letsencrypt.org\"",
    "0 iodef \"mailto:security@example.com\"",
  ]
}

output "nameservers" {
  value = aws_route53_zone.main.name_servers # give these to the registrar
}
  • Route 53 stores one record set per name and type, so the SPF record and a verification token must share the apex_txt resource; a second resource for the same name and type fails.
  • The nameservers output is what you enter at the registrar to delegate the domain to this zone.
  • Keeping records in code gives you review, history, and a quick way to rebuild the zone at another provider.

docs.title: Locking down a domain
docs.text:
• Turn on auto-renew, keep a valid payment method, and register important domains for several years.
  • Enable the registrar's transfer lock, and a registry lock for the main production domain if your registrar offers it.
  • Protect the registrar and DNS accounts with MFA (security keys if possible), few administrators, and API tokens scoped to one zone.
  • Use a role mailbox for registrant and technical contacts.
  • Alert on expiry dates (RDAP), on unexpected NS or DS changes, and on certificates issued for your names (Certificate Transparency monitoring).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Separate the questions "who registers the domain" and "who hosts DNS", and document both, with account owners.
  • Manage zones as code and review every change.
  • Point names at hostnames the platform controls (CNAME or alias), not at IP addresses you copied.
  • Choose TTLs per record: short for names you may move, long for stable ones, and lower them a full TTL before planned changes.
  • Publish null MX, v=spf1 -all, and DMARC p=reject on domains that send no mail.
  • Keep CAA in sync with every CA your platforms use.
  • Keep internal names in private zones and out of public DNS.
  • Enable DNSSEC only with provider-managed signing and a migration plan.
  • Verify every change with dig against the authoritative servers and at least one public resolver.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The whole product is down, and DNS returns a parking page. Detect: RDAP shows an expiration date in the past and a status such as redemptionPeriod; the A record now points at the registrar's parking IPs. Cause: auto-renew was off, the card expired, or the renewal notices went to a former employee. Fix: renew immediately (or restore during redemption, usually with a fee), move contacts to a role mailbox, and add expiry alerts.
  • Certificate renewal fails with "CAA record prevents issuance". Detect: the ACME client or the platform reports a CAA error; dig example.com CAA lists only another CA. Cause: a new hosting platform or CDN uses a CA missing from the CAA set. Fix: add that CA's identifier, and make CAA review part of every hosting change.
  • Some users get SERVFAIL, others resolve fine. Detect: dig example.com returns SERVFAIL through a validating resolver but works with dig +cd; DNSViz shows a broken chain. Cause: the DS record at the registry does not match the zone's keys, often after a DNS provider change. Fix: publish the matching DNSKEY or remove the DS, then wait out the DS TTL; plan DNSSEC into migrations.
  • Mail stops arriving after a new record is added at the apex. Detect: MX lookups now return a CNAME, or the DNS console silently replaced records. Cause: a CNAME was created at a name that also had MX and TXT records. Fix: use the provider's alias or flattening feature at the apex and restore the mail records.
  • A verification record "exists" but the platform cannot see it. Detect: dig _dmarc.example.com TXT is empty, while dig _dmarc.example.com.example.com TXT returns the value. Cause: the console appended the zone name to a fully qualified name. Fix: enter the relative name (_dmarc) or add a trailing dot, and verify with dig.
  • Changed records keep returning old values for hours. Detect: dig @<authoritative> shows the new value; public resolvers show the old one with a large remaining TTL. Cause: the old TTL was long and was not lowered beforehand. Fix: wait it out (flush the public resolvers' caches where they offer it) and lower TTLs a full TTL ahead next time.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Registrant: The holder of a domain registration.
  • Registrar: The company that registers and renews domains with the registry for you.
  • Registry: The operator of a TLD's database and nameservers.
  • Delegation: NS records in the parent zone that point a domain at its authoritative nameservers.
  • Authoritative nameserver: A server that holds a zone's records and answers for them.
  • Zone apex: The domain's own name (example.com), which holds the SOA and NS records.
  • TTL: How many seconds a resolver may cache an answer.
  • Negative caching: Caching the fact that a name or record does not exist.
  • RDAP: The JSON-over-HTTPS protocol for registration data that replaced WHOIS.
  • EPP status code: A registry status such as clientTransferProhibited that shows locks and lifecycle state.
  • Redemption grace period: A 30-day window after deletion when only the previous registrant can restore a gTLD domain.
  • CNAME flattening / alias record: A DNS host feature that resolves a target hostname and answers with its addresses, allowed at the apex.
  • CAA: A record listing the certificate authorities allowed to issue for a name.
