  • DS record: The parent zone's hash of a child zone's DNSSEC key.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating the registrar and the DNS host as the same thing, and losing records when changing nameservers.
  • Putting a CNAME at the apex, or next to MX and TXT records.
  • Publishing two SPF records at one name.
  • Copying a platform's current IP addresses into A records instead of using its hostname.
  • Believing a low TTL helps a change that is already live; it must be lowered beforehand.
  • Thinking DNSSEC encrypts DNS. It signs answers; encryption is DoH or DoT.
  • Assuming a domain renews itself with a lapsed card or a dead contact email.
  • Leaving CAA records unchanged when moving to a platform that uses a different CA.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the roles of the registrant, registrar, registry, and DNS host for example.com, and what each controls.
  2. Why can the zone apex not be a CNAME, and what are three ways to point the apex at a CDN?
  3. What three records should a domain that sends and receives no email publish, and why?
  4. api.example.com has a TTL of 14400 seconds. You change it at 09:00, and a resolver cached it at 08:59. Until what time can that resolver serve the old address? (Until about 12:59, four hours after it cached the record.)
  5. A CAA set at example.com lists only letsencrypt.org. Can AWS Certificate Manager issue a certificate for api.example.com? What would you change?
  6. What happens to a validating resolver's answers if the DS record at the registry no longer matches the zone's key, and why does the fix take time?
  7. Which EPP status codes would you expect on a well-protected production domain, and what does each block?
  8. Why should a mongodb+srv:// hostname's SRV and TXT records live in a private zone?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 1035: Domain Names, Implementation and Specification
  • RFC 8659: DNS Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) Resource Record
  • RFC 7505: A "Null MX" No Service Resource Record
  • ICANN: Expired Registration Recovery Policy
  • IANA: Root Zone Database
  • Amazon Route 53: Transferring registration for a domain to Route 53
  • Cloudflare: CNAME flattening
  • Next: connecting domains to hosting. Back to the domains, DNS and email overview.

docs.title: Email Deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
docs.text:
TaskFlow sends invitations, password resets, and "tasks due today" reminders. Whether those messages reach the inbox depends less on the code that sends them than on DNS records, sending reputation, and how bounces and complaints are handled. This lesson covers why application email lands in spam, transactional versus marketing email, choosing a sending provider (Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, Resend), SPF and its 10-lookup limit, DKIM signing, DMARC alignment, policies, reports, and a safe rollout, the 2026 update to the DMARC standard, the sender requirements of Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.com, bounce and complaint handling, and dedicated IPs and warm-up.

How mail moves between servers (SMTP, MX lookups, IMAP) is covered in email protocols, and designing a notification service with queues, retries, and provider failover in the notification system case study.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A password reset that lands in spam is an outage for that user, and support usually hears about it before monitoring does. Mailbox providers decide where a message goes from two kinds of evidence: authentication (is this message really from example.com?) and reputation (does mail from this domain and these IPs get marked as spam, bounce, or hit spam traps?). Since 2024 Gmail and Yahoo, and since 2025 Outlook.com, require authentication from bulk senders and reject or junk mail that lacks it.

There is a security side too. Without SPF, DKIM, and an enforced DMARC policy, anyone can send phishing email that claims to come from example.com, and your users have no way to tell.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Gmail's sender guidelines. Google's Email sender guidelines require every sender to personal Gmail accounts to use SPF or DKIM, valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, and a spam rate below 0.3%; bulk senders (close to 5,000 or more messages a day to Gmail accounts) also need SPF and DKIM, a DMARC policy (at least p=none), alignment, and one-click unsubscribe. The FAQ adds that bulk status is permanent and that from November 2025 Gmail is ramping up enforcement, with temporary and permanent rejections.
  • Yahoo's Sender Hub. Yahoo's sender best practices set the same baseline: SPF or DKIM for everyone; SPF, DKIM, and a passing DMARC policy of at least p=none for bulk senders; one-click unsubscribe honored within two days; and a spam rate below 0.3%.
  • Outlook.com high-volume senders. Microsoft's announcement requires domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to Outlook.com consumer addresses (outlook.com, hotmail.com, live.com) to pass SPF and DKIM and publish DMARC of at least p=none, aligned with SPF or DKIM, from May 5, 2025. An April 2025 update dropped the planned Junk-folder stage: non-compliant mail is rejected with 550 5.7.515.
  • DMARC as a proposed standard. The original DMARC specification, RFC 7489, was published as an informational document in 2015. In May 2026 the IETF published RFC 9989 ("DMARCbis") on the Standards Track, obsoleting RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, with aggregate and failure reporting split into RFC 9990 and RFC 9991.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon SES, SendGrid, Postmark, Mailgun, and Resend for sending; Google Postmaster Tools, Yahoo's Sender Hub, and Microsoft's SNDS for reputation data; DMARC report processors such as the open-source parsedmarc or a hosted service; and DNSControl's SPF_BUILDER for managing SPF records in code.

docs.title: Why application email lands in spam
docs.text:
Signal What receivers look at What you control Authentication SPF, DKIM, DMARC results and alignment with the visible From DNS records and provider configuration Domain and IP reputation Spam complaints, bounces, spam traps, history of the domain and IPs List quality, consent, volume patterns, shared or dedicated IPs Engagement Opens, replies, deletions without reading, "not spam" clicks Sending only mail people asked for and want Infrastructure Reverse DNS, TLS, standards-compliant messages Mostly the provider's job Content Links, formatting, misleading subjects Honest, plain templates

Authentication is the entry ticket; reputation decides the folder. Google asks senders to keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.1% and never to reach 0.3%.

docs.title: Transactional and marketing email
docs.text:
Transactional Marketing (broadcast) Examples Password reset, invitation, receipt, security alert Newsletter, product announcement, promotion Trigger One user's action A campaign to many people Expectation Must arrive within seconds Can wait; must respect consent Unsubscribe Not for security mail; offer it for optional notifications Required, including one-click for bulk senders Risk Low complaint rate when done right Higher complaint rate

Keep the two apart so a campaign's complaints cannot sink password resets: send marketing from its own subdomain (for example news.example.com) and its own provider stream or IP pool. Postmark, for example, runs transactional and broadcast message streams on separate infrastructure. Note that Gmail counts mail from subdomains toward the primary domain when deciding whether you are a bulk sender.

docs.title: Choosing a sending provider
docs.text:
Provider DNS you add Notable details Amazon SES Three Easy DKIM CNAMEs (2048-bit keys by default); a custom MAIL FROM subdomain with an MX to feedback-smtp.<region>.amazonses.com and SPF include:amazonses.com New accounts start in a sandbox (verified recipients only, 200 messages a day, 1 per second); account-level suppression list on by default; review at 5% bounces or 0.1% complaints, possible pause at 10% or 0.5% SendGrid Domain authentication with automated security: CNAMEs em<number>, s1._domainkey, s2._domainkey, plus link-branding CNAMEs SendGrid updates the SPF and DKIM targets behind the CNAMEs for you Postmark A DKIM TXT record; a custom Return-Path CNAME such as pm-bounces pointing to pm.mtasv.net Separate transactional and broadcast streams on separate IP pools Mailgun A sending subdomain such as mg.example.com with SPF include:mailgun.org, a DKIM TXT key, and an optional tracking CNAME Mailgun recommends a subdomain rather than the root domain Resend DKIM and SPF records (TXT and MX or CNAME) generated per domain; Return-Path defaults to send.<your domain> Recommends sending from subdomains; do not proxy its CNAMEs through Cloudflare

Whichever you choose, the pattern is the same: prove the domain with DKIM, give the provider a bounce (Return-Path) subdomain so SPF aligns, and publish DMARC yourself.

docs.title: The three identities in every message
docs.text:
• Header From (reminders@example.com): what the user sees. DMARC protects this domain.
  • Envelope MAIL FROM (the Return-Path, bounce@bounce.example.com): where bounces go. SPF checks this domain, not the header From.
  • DKIM signing domain (d=example.com in the DKIM-Signature header): the domain whose key signed the message.

docs.title: SPF: which servers may send
docs.text:
An SPF record is a TXT record on the envelope sender's domain:

bounce.example.com.  TXT  "v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all"
example.com.         TXT  "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"
  • Mechanisms are checked left to right: ip4: and ip6: ranges, include: another domain's SPF, a and mx (the domain's own hosts), and all at the end. The qualifier on all decides the default: -all fails anything not listed, ~all soft-fails it.
  • One SPF record per name. Two records make every check a permanent error.
  • SPF breaks when mail is forwarded, because the forwarder's IP is not in your record. DKIM survives forwarding, which is why DMARC accepts either.

The 10-lookup limit. RFC 7208 caps the DNS lookups an SPF check may trigger at 10. The include, a, mx, ptr, and exists mechanisms and the redirect modifier each count, including those inside included records; ip4, ip6, and all do not. Going over the limit is a permerror, so SPF fails for every message, not just the last sender. RFC 7208 also asks receivers to allow at most two "void" lookups (names that return nothing).

Ways to stay under the limit: remove mechanisms for hosts that do not send mail (a, mx), never use ptr, give each third-party sender its own subdomain (each name has its own budget of 10), and use the custom MAIL FROM or Return-Path subdomain your provider offers. Flattening includes into IP ranges works but breaks silently when the provider changes its IPs; DNSControl's documentation recommends flattening only when it is the only way under 10.

docs.title: DKIM: a signature from your domain
docs.text:
The provider signs selected headers and a hash of the body with a private key and adds a header such as:

DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256; d=example.com; s=s1; c=relaxed/relaxed;
        h=from:to:subject:date:message-id:list-unsubscribe:list-unsubscribe-post;
        bh=<body-hash>; b=<signature>

The receiver fetches the public key from s1._domainkey.example.com:

s1._domainkey.example.com.  TXT  "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkq...truncated...IDAQAB"
  • Key size: RFC 8301 requires at least 1024-bit RSA keys and recommends 2048; rsa-sha1 must no longer be used. SES Easy DKIM uses 2048-bit keys by default.
  • Selectors (s=) let several keys coexist, which is how keys are rotated: publish a new selector, switch signing to it, and remove the old key after mail in transit has been delivered. When the provider gives you CNAMEs for the selectors (SES, SendGrid), it can rotate keys without you touching DNS.
  • What breaks DKIM: anything that changes signed headers or the body, such as mailing lists that add footers. ARC (RFC 8617) lets such intermediaries vouch for the original results.

docs.title: DMARC: alignment, policy, and reports
docs.text:
DMARC is a TXT record at _dmarc.<domain>:

_dmarc.example.com.  TXT  "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; sp=quarantine; adkim=r; aspf=r; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"

A message passes DMARC when SPF or DKIM passes and the passing domain aligns with the header From domain.

Tag Meaning p Policy for the domain: none (monitor), quarantine (treat as suspicious, usually the spam folder), reject sp Policy for existing subdomains (defaults to p) np Policy for subdomains that do not exist (from RFC 9091, now part of RFC 9989) adkim, aspf Alignment mode: r relaxed (same organizational domain, the default) or s strict (exact match) rua Where to send daily aggregate reports ruf Where to send per-message failure reports (few receivers send them) t Test mode in RFC 9989: t=y asks receivers to apply the next weaker policy

Reports are what make DMARC safe to enforce. Aggregate reports are XML files, usually daily, listing every IP that sent mail as your domain with counts and SPF and DKIM results. They reveal the CRM, the support desk, and the forgotten script that send as example.com. If rua points at another domain (a reporting service), that domain must publish a record authorizing it, which hosted services set up for you.

What changed in RFC 9989. The pct tag (apply the policy to a percentage of mail) was removed because receivers rarely applied it accurately except at 0 and 100; t=y replaces its main use. The rf and ri tags were removed, np and psd were added, and receivers now find the organizational domain with a DNS tree walk instead of the Public Suffix List. It also makes explicit (Section 7.4) that domains whose users might post to mailing lists should not publish p=reject; any such domain that still wants it should first run p=none, then p=quarantine, for at least a month each. Receivers ignore tags they do not know, so existing records keep parsing, but receivers that still implement RFC 7489 ignore t, so treat every step to a stricter p as real.

docs.title: Rolling DMARC out safely
docs.text:
1. Publish p=none with rua and collect reports for a few weeks.
  2. For each legitimate source, make it align: DKIM with d=example.com (or the subdomain it sends from) and a custom Return-Path where possible. Move hard-to-fix senders to their own subdomain.
  3. Move to p=quarantine (optionally first with t=y), and watch.
  4. Move to p=reject (optionally first with t=y), and set sp and np deliberately.
  5. Keep reading reports; a new SaaS tool sending as your domain shows up there first.

Domains that never send mail should go straight to p=reject together with a null MX and v=spf1 -all, as shown in domains and DNS records.

docs.title: What Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.com require
docs.text:
Requirement Gmail (personal accounts) Yahoo Outlook.com (consumer) Who is covered All senders; extra rules for bulk senders (close to 5,000+ messages a day, status permanent) All senders; extra rules for bulk senders Domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day SPF and DKIM All: SPF or DKIM. Bulk: both All: SPF or DKIM. Bulk: both SPF must pass and DKIM must pass DMARC Bulk: published (p=none allowed), with alignment Bulk: at least p=none, must pass; relaxed alignment is fine At least p=none, aligned with SPF or DKIM Unsubscribe Bulk marketing and subscribed mail: one-click (RFC 8058) plus a visible link; honor within 48 hours Bulk: one-click (POST highly recommended, mailto accepted) plus a visible link; honor within 2 days A clear, working unsubscribe is recommended Spam rate Below 0.3%, aim below 0.1% Below 0.3% Not stated as a number Other Valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS, RFC 5322 format Valid forward and reverse DNS, RFC 5321 and 5322 Valid, reply-capable From or Reply-To Enforcement Since February 2024; ramping up from November 2025 with rejections Since February 2024 Since May 5, 2025: rejected with 550 5.7.515

These rules do not apply to mail sent to Google Workspace business accounts, but meeting them everywhere is simpler than tracking exceptions.

docs.title: Bounces, complaints, and suppression lists
docs.text:
Event Meaning Action Hard bounce Permanent failure, such as an address that does not exist Stop sending to the address immediately Soft bounce Temporary failure, such as a full mailbox Retry; suppress after repeated failures Complaint The recipient marked the message as spam (reported through a feedback loop) Stop sending that kind of mail to them immediately Unsubscribe The recipient opted out of a category Stop that category; keep security mail

Providers keep their own suppression lists (SES's account-level list holds addresses that hard-bounced or complained until you remove them), but keep yours too, per message category, so it survives a provider change. Two details matter. SES places an account under review at a 5% bounce rate or a 0.1% complaint rate, and recommends staying below 2% bounces. And Gmail does not send complaint data to SES, so for Gmail users your signals are the spam rate in Postmaster Tools and the unsubscribes you receive, which is one more reason to offer one-click unsubscribe on optional mail.

docs.title: Shared and dedicated IPs, and warm-up
docs.text: Providers send most customers' mail from shared IP pools whose reputation they manage. A dedicated IP gives you your own reputation, good or bad, and needs steady volume: SES advises sending around 1,000 emails a day to each mailbox provider you want to keep a good reputation with. New IPs have no history, so they must be warmed up: volume rises gradually over weeks (SES's automatic warm-up for standard dedicated IPs takes 45 days, and mailbox providers need roughly two to six weeks), starting with the most engaged recipients. Choose dedicated IPs only for high, steady volume; for most applications a reputable shared pool plus good domain reputation is the better choice.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended setup Password resets and invitations for TaskFlow A transactional provider (Postmark, SES, Resend, SendGrid, or Mailgun) on a shared pool, DKIM with d=example.com, a custom Return-Path, DMARC Optional reminders and digests The transactional setup plus List-Unsubscribe and List-Unsubscribe-Post headers and per-category preferences Newsletters and announcements A separate subdomain and broadcast stream, explicit consent, one-click unsubscribe High, steady volume Dedicated IPs with warm-up and monitoring per mailbox provider Third-party tools sending as you (CRM, help desk) Their custom DKIM for your domain, or their own subdomain Domains that send no mail Null MX, v=spf1 -all, DMARC p=reject

Do not:

  • Send marketing through the transactional stream or IPs.
  • Buy, rent, or scrape lists; spam traps and complaints follow.
  • Send from a no-reply address that bounces replies; Microsoft asks for a valid, reply-capable From or Reply-To.
  • Jump to p=reject before reports show every legitimate sender aligned.

docs.title: TaskFlow's email DNS records
docs.text:
; Inbound mail (a hosted mailbox provider)
example.com.                    MX     10 mx1.mail.example.net.
example.com.                    MX     20 mx2.mail.example.net.
; Only the mailbox provider sends directly as @example.com
example.com.                    TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.mail.example.net -all"

; Transactional mail through Amazon SES, From: reminders@example.com
; Easy DKIM: three CNAMEs; copy the exact names and targets from the SES console
<token1>._domainkey.example.com. CNAME  <token1>.dkim.amazonses.com.
<token2>._domainkey.example.com. CNAME  <token2>.dkim.amazonses.com.
<token3>._domainkey.example.com. CNAME  <token3>.dkim.amazonses.com.
; Custom MAIL FROM, so SPF aligns with example.com
bounce.example.com.             MX     10 feedback-smtp.us-east-1.amazonses.com.
bounce.example.com.             TXT    "v=spf1 include:amazonses.com ~all"

; Newsletters from a separate subdomain and provider
news.example.com.               TXT    "v=spf1 include:_spf.news-provider.example.net -all"
nl1._domainkey.news.example.com. TXT   "v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=MIIBIjANBgkq...truncated...IDAQAB"

; One DMARC policy for the domain and its subdomains
_dmarc.example.com.             TXT    "v=DMARC1; p=quarantine; sp=quarantine; np=reject; rua=mailto:dmarc-reports@example.com"
  • SES's MAIL FROM subdomain must be used only for that purpose (not for sending from or receiving mail) and must have exactly one MX record.
  • news.example.com has its own SPF budget and its own reputation, and the _dmarc record at example.com covers it through sp.
  • np=reject tells receivers to reject mail from subdomains that do not exist, which phishers like to invent; receivers that only implement RFC 7489 ignore it.

docs.title: Sending through SES with unsubscribe headers (Node.js)
docs.text:
// src/email/send-reminder.js: send a "tasks due today" email via Amazon SES (API v2)
import { SESv2Client, SendEmailCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-sesv2";
import { isSuppressed } from "./suppressions.js";
import { renderReminder } from "./templates.js";

const ses = new SESv2Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });

export async function sendReminder({ to, tasks, unsubscribeUrl }) {
  if (await isSuppressed(to, "reminders")) return null; // bounced, complained, or opted out

  const { subject, text, html } = renderReminder(tasks, unsubscribeUrl);
  const result = await ses.send(new SendEmailCommand({
    FromEmailAddress: "TaskFlow <reminders@example.com>",
    ReplyToAddresses: ["support@example.com"],
    Destination: { ToAddresses: [to] },
    ConfigurationSetName: "taskflow-transactional", // publishes bounce and complaint events
    Content: {
      Simple: {
        Subject: { Data: subject },
        Body: { Text: { Data: text }, Html: { Data: html } },
        Headers: [
          { Name: "List-Unsubscribe", Value: `<${unsubscribeUrl}>` },
          { Name: "List-Unsubscribe-Post", Value: "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click" },
        ],
      },
    },
  }));
  return result.MessageId; // store it to match later bounce and complaint events
}
  • The unsubscribe headers go on optional mail such as reminders, never on password resets or security alerts.
  • RFC 8058 requires both headers to be covered by the DKIM signature, and receivers should not offer one-click unsubscribe otherwise. Check the h= list in the DKIM-Signature of a delivered message to confirm your provider signs them.
  • Run sends from a background job with retries rather than inside the HTTP request, as described in background jobs and scheduling.

docs.title: The one-click unsubscribe endpoint (Express)
docs.text:
// src/routes/unsubscribe.js: RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe plus a page for humans
import express from "express";
import { verifyUnsubscribeToken } from "../email/tokens.js";
import { Preferences } from "../models/preferences.js";

export const router = express.Router();
const CATEGORIES = new Map([["reminders", "task reminders"], ["digests", "weekly digests"]]);

async function optOut(req) {
  const { category } = req.params;
  if (!CATEGORIES.has(category)) return false; // never use raw input as a field name
  const userId = verifyUnsubscribeToken(req.query.t, category); // signed, expiring token
  if (!userId) return false;
  await Preferences.updateOne(
    { userId },
    { $set: { [`email.${category}`]: false } },
    { upsert: true },
  );
  return true;
}

// Mail clients POST the body "List-Unsubscribe=One-Click" with no cookies or login
router.post("/unsubscribe/:category", async (req, res) => {
  res.status((await optOut(req)) ? 200 : 400).end(); // no redirect: RFC 8058 forbids one
});

// The visible link in the email body opens a confirmation page instead
router.get("/unsubscribe/:category", (req, res) => {
  const label = CATEGORIES.get(req.params.category);
  if (!label) return res.status(404).end();
  res.send(`<form method="post"><button>Unsubscribe from ${label}</button></form>`);
});

The token in the URL identifies the user and category, because the request carries no cookies or authentication. Categories come from an allowlist, so URL input is never echoed into HTML or used as a database field name. The GET route does not unsubscribe by itself: link scanners and prefetchers follow links in emails, and must not opt users out. The form has no action, so it posts back to the same URL, token included.

docs.title: Handling SES bounce and complaint events (Lambda)
docs.text:
// src/email/ses-events.js: SES events delivered through SNS to a Lambda function
import { Suppressions } from "../models/suppressions.js";

export async function handler(event) {
  for (const record of event.Records) {
    const msg = JSON.parse(record.Sns.Message);
    const type = msg.eventType ?? msg.notificationType; // configuration set events vs identity notifications

    if (type === "Bounce" && msg.bounce.bounceType === "Permanent") {
      for (const r of msg.bounce.bouncedRecipients) {
        await suppress(r.emailAddress, "hard-bounce", msg.mail.messageId);
      }
    } else if (type === "Complaint") {
      for (const r of msg.complaint.complainedRecipients) {
        await suppress(r.emailAddress, "complaint", msg.mail.messageId);
      }
    }
    // Transient bounces are retried by SES; count them and suppress after repeats
  }
}

async function suppress(email, reason, messageId) {
  await Suppressions.updateOne(
    { email: email.toLowerCase() },
    { $setOnInsert: { reason, messageId, createdAt: new Date() } },
    { upsert: true },
  );
}

SES reports bounceType as Permanent, Transient, or Undetermined. Many mailbox providers redact who complained, so complainedRecipients lists every recipient of that message on the complaining domain; for one-recipient transactional mail that is exactly the person.

docs.title: Reading the verdict on a received message
docs.text:
; Example header added by a receiving server
Authentication-Results: mx.receiver.example.org;
       dkim=pass header.i=@example.com header.s=s1;
       spf=pass smtp.mailfrom=bounce.example.com;
       dmarc=pass (p=QUARANTINE sp=QUARANTINE) header.from=example.com

Send a test message to a mailbox you control and open the raw headers: all three should pass, and the domains after header.i, smtp.mailfrom, and header.from should share example.com.

docs.title: Reading an aggregate report
docs.text:
; Excerpt of a DMARC aggregate report (XML), one record
<record>
  <row>
    <source_ip>203.0.113.77</source_ip>
    <count>1250</count>
    <policy_evaluated><disposition>none</disposition><dkim>fail</dkim><spf>fail</spf></policy_evaluated>
  </row>
  <identifiers><header_from>example.com</header_from></identifiers>
  <auth_results>
    <dkim><domain>crm.example.net</domain><result>pass</result></dkim>
    <spf><domain>crm.example.net</domain><result>pass</result></spf>
  </auth_results>
</record>

1,250 messages claiming to be from example.com came from a CRM: SPF and DKIM passed for the CRM's own domain, but neither aligned, so DMARC failed (disposition is none only because the policy was still p=none). Enabling the CRM's custom DKIM for example.com, or moving it to crm.example.com, fixes it before enforcement.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Authenticate everything: DKIM with your domain, a custom Return-Path for SPF alignment, and DMARC with rua reporting.
  • Roll DMARC out from none to reject on evidence from reports, and give non-sending domains p=reject from day one.
  • Separate transactional and marketing mail by subdomain and stream.
  • Keep each name's SPF under 10 lookups; prefer subdomains to flattening.
  • Use 2048-bit DKIM keys and rotate them through selectors.
  • Add one-click unsubscribe to optional mail and honor it within two days.
  • Suppress hard bounces and complaints immediately, in your own store as well as the provider's.
  • Watch Postmaster Tools, your provider's reputation metrics, and DMARC reports; alert on bounce and complaint rates.
  • Use dedicated IPs only with steady volume and a warm-up plan.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Password resets go to spam at Gmail only. Detect: raw headers show dmarc=fail or spf=pass with smtp.mailfrom on the provider's domain; Postmaster Tools shows a rising spam rate. Cause: no alignment (default provider Return-Path and DKIM signed with the provider's domain), or a marketing stream sharing the domain and IPs. Fix: custom DKIM and Return-Path for example.com, separate marketing onto its own subdomain and stream.
  • Every message fails SPF after a new tool was added. Detect: reports and headers show spf=permerror. Cause: the new include pushed the record past 10 lookups, or a second SPF record was created. Fix: merge into one record, remove unused mechanisms, and move the tool to its own subdomain.
  • Mail to Outlook.com addresses bounces with 550 5.7.515. Detect: bounce events carry that code for hotmail.com and outlook.com recipients. Cause: the domain sends more than 5,000 messages a day and fails SPF, DKIM, or aligned DMARC. Fix: make both SPF and DKIM pass and publish an aligned DMARC record.
  • The provider pauses sending. Detect: an account review or pause notice; SES's Reputation.BounceRate above 5%. Cause: sending to stale or imported addresses, or ignoring bounce events. Fix: suppress bounces automatically, confirm addresses with double opt-in, and stop sending to inactive recipients.
  • Legitimate mail is rejected right after moving to p=reject. Detect: complaints from a team whose tool's mail vanished; reports show a source with failing alignment. Cause: a sender that was never fixed during the p=none phase. Fix: step back to quarantine, fix the sender, and only advance when reports are clean.
  • Email stops entirely after a DNS migration. Detect: DKIM fail (no key) or missing SPF in headers. Cause: DKIM selectors, SPF, or the MAIL FROM MX were not copied to the new DNS provider. Fix: restore them; include underscore names in every zone inventory (see DNS migrations and troubleshooting).

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Header From: The address the recipient sees; DMARC protects its domain.
  • Envelope MAIL FROM (Return-Path): The bounce address used in SMTP; SPF checks its domain.
  • SPF: A TXT record listing which servers may send for a domain.
  • DKIM: A signature over headers and body, verified with a public key published under a selector.
  • Selector: The label (s=) that tells receivers which DKIM key to fetch.
  • DMARC: A policy that requires SPF or DKIM to pass and align with the header From domain, plus reporting.
  • Alignment: The authenticated domain matching the From domain, exactly (strict) or by organizational domain (relaxed).
  • Aggregate report (rua): Daily XML summaries of authentication results per sending IP.
  • One-click unsubscribe: RFC 8058's List-Unsubscribe-Post mechanism that lets mail clients unsubscribe with one POST.
  • Hard and soft bounce: Permanent and temporary delivery failures.
  • Feedback loop: A mailbox provider's channel for reporting spam complaints to the sender.
  • IP warm-up: Gradually increasing volume on a new IP to build reputation.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing SPF protects the visible From address; it checks the envelope sender, and only DMARC ties authentication to the From.
  • Publishing two SPF records, or one with more than 10 lookups.
  • Letting providers sign with their own domain, so DKIM passes but DMARC fails.
  • Jumping to p=reject without reading aggregate reports.
  • Sending newsletters and password resets from the same stream.
  • Treating "accepted by the provider" as "delivered to the inbox".
  • Unsubscribing users on GET requests that link scanners trigger.
  • Assuming a dedicated IP improves deliverability by itself.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name the three domains involved in authenticating one message and which check uses each.
  2. Why can a message pass both SPF and DKIM and still fail DMARC?
  3. Count the lookups in v=spf1 a mx include:x.example.net -all if x.example.net includes two more records, one of which includes one more. Is it under the limit? (a 1, mx 1, x 1, its two includes 2, the nested one 1: 6 lookups, under 10.)
  4. Describe a safe DMARC rollout from p=none to p=reject, and what evidence allows each step.
  5. What did RFC 9989 change compared with RFC 7489, and what replaces pct?
  6. Which headers does RFC 8058 require, and why must the GET handler for an unsubscribe link not unsubscribe by itself?
  7. TaskFlow sends 8,000 reminders a day to Gmail users. Which Gmail requirements apply, and how long does that status last?
  8. When is a dedicated IP worth it, and how would you warm one up?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 7208: Sender Policy Framework (SPF)
  • RFC 6376: DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) Signatures
  • RFC 9989: Domain-Based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC)
  • RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers
  • Google: Postmaster Tools dashboards
  • Amazon SES: Authenticating email with DKIM
  • Amazon SES: Using a custom MAIL FROM domain
  • Postmark: Message streams
  • Next: domains, DNS and email interview questions and answers. Back to the domains, DNS and email overview.

docs.title: Domains, DNS and Email Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review domains and DNS records, connecting domains to hosting, DNS migrations and troubleshooting, CDN setup and edge caching, and email deliverability with SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between a registrar, a registry, and a DNS host?
docs.text: The registry operates a top-level domain: its database of names and the TLD's nameservers. The registrar is the company you pay; it registers and renews the name with the registry and sends it your nameservers and DS records. The DNS host runs the authoritative nameservers that serve your zone's records. One company can be registrar and DNS host, but the roles stay separate.

docs.title: 2. What is a delegation, and where does it live?
docs.text: The NS records for your domain in the parent zone (for example.com, in the .com zone), plus glue addresses when the nameservers are inside the zone. It tells resolvers which servers are authoritative. The .com servers publish it with a 172,800-second (two-day) TTL, which is why nameserver changes settle slowly.

docs.title: 3. What replaced WHOIS, and why does registration data matter to operators?
docs.text: RDAP, which returns registration data as JSON over HTTPS; since 28 January 2025, gTLD registries and registrars must provide RDAP and are mostly no longer required to run WHOIS. Operators use it to monitor expiry dates and lock statuses, and must keep the registrant email real, because renewal notices, transfer approvals, and verification requests go there.

docs.title: 4. What happens when a generic TLD domain expires?
docs.text: The registrar must send notices about a month and a week before expiry. After expiry it interrupts DNS (often showing a parking page) while you can still renew. Once deleted, the name enters a 30-day redemption grace period with DNS off, where only the previous registrant can restore it, usually for a fee. After a short pending-delete stage anyone can register it.

docs.title: 5. How do you protect a production domain from hijacking or accidental changes?
docs.text: Auto-renew with a valid payment method, a registrar transfer lock (clientTransferProhibited, plus update and delete locks), a registry lock for the most important domain, MFA on registrar and DNS accounts, zone-scoped API tokens, and alerts on expiry dates, NS and DS changes, and Certificate Transparency entries for your names.

docs.title: 6. What are the rules of a CNAME record?
docs.text: A name with a CNAME can hold no other records, so the zone apex (which needs SOA and NS) can never be a CNAME. MX and NS targets must not be aliases. A CNAME applies to every query type, including TXT lookups. Each hop in a chain can cost another lookup.

docs.title: 7. How do you point the apex at a CDN or hosting platform?
docs.text: With a provider feature that resolves the target on the authoritative side: a Route 53 alias record, Cloudflare's CNAME flattening (automatic at the apex), or an ALIAS/ANAME record at other hosts. Alternatives are the platform's documented static or anycast IPs, or making www the canonical host and redirecting the apex to it.

docs.title: 8. What is the trade-off of CNAME flattening and alias records?
docs.text: The DNS host resolves the target from its own servers, so a platform that steers users by DNS sees the DNS host's location rather than the user's resolver. That is why Netlify recommends a subdomain as the primary domain with external DNS, and Vercel recommends www with a CNAME.

docs.title: 9. What should a domain that never sends or receives email publish?
docs.text: A null MX (MX 0 ., RFC 7505) so senders fail fast, v=spf1 -all so no server is authorized to send, and _dmarc with p=reject so receivers reject mail claiming to be from it. example.com itself publishes exactly these records.

docs.title: 10. What does a CAA record do, and how does a CA find the relevant one?
docs.text:
It lists the certificate authorities allowed to issue for a name (issue, issuewild, iodef). The CA looks at the exact name, then climbs toward the root and uses the first name that has CAA records. No CAA anywhere means any CA may issue; issue ";" means none may. Each CA has an identifier, such as letsencrypt.org or amazon.com for ACM.

example.com.  CAA  0 issue "letsencrypt.org"
example.com.  CAA  0 issuewild "letsencrypt.org"

docs.title: 11. What is negative caching?
docs.text: Resolvers cache the answer that a name or record does not exist. Per RFC 2308 the duration is the smaller of the SOA record's TTL and the SOA minimum field. A record created after someone looked it up can stay invisible to that resolver until the negative entry expires.

docs.title: 12. How does TTL affect a change? Give an example.
docs.text: A resolver may answer from cache until the TTL expires. With a TTL of 3600, a resolver that cached the record at 09:59:30 serves the old value until 10:59:30 even if you change it at 10:00. Lowering the TTL helps only if done at least one old TTL before the change.

docs.title: 13. What does DNSSEC protect, and what is its main operational risk?
docs.text: It lets validating resolvers verify, through a chain of DS and DNSKEY records from the root, that answers came from the zone owner unaltered. It does not encrypt queries. The risk is a broken chain: if the DS at the parent does not match the zone's key, validating resolvers return SERVFAIL, and the cached DS (a day at .com) makes the outage outlive the fix.

docs.title: 14. What is an SRV record, and where might a Node.js developer meet one?
docs.text: It publishes priority, weight, port, and target host for a service under _service._proto.name. MongoDB's mongodb+srv:// connection strings make the driver look up _mongodb._tcp.<host> SRV records for the members and a TXT record for options such as replicaSet, and turn TLS on by default.

docs.title: 15. Why do platforms recommend www as the canonical host?
docs.text: www can be a plain CNAME, so the platform controls where it points and can steer traffic by DNS for performance and DDoS mitigation; the apex needs an A record or flattening. The apex then redirects to www with a permanent redirect that browsers cache.

docs.title: 16. How do you attach a subdomain and the apex to Vercel or Netlify?
docs.text: Subdomain: a CNAME to the target the dashboard shows (a project-specific Vercel DNS name, or the site's netlify.app name). Apex: the A record value Vercel shows or its nameservers; for Netlify an ALIAS, ANAME, or flattened CNAME to apex-loadbalancer.netlify.com, or an A record as a fallback. Always copy values from the dashboard.

docs.title: 17. What does CloudFront need before it serves a custom domain?
docs.text: The name must be an alternate domain name on exactly one distribution, covered by a trusted certificate (an ACM certificate in us-east-1), and DNS must point at the distribution: a CNAME for subdomains, or Route 53 alias A and AAAA records, including at the apex.

docs.title: 18. Why should you never create A records with a load balancer's IP addresses?
docs.text: Managed load balancers scale and replace nodes, so their IPs change; AWS load balancers publish their DNS name with a 60-second TTL for exactly this reason. Use an alias record or a CNAME to the load balancer's DNS name.

docs.title: 19. What are verification records, and why must you keep them?
docs.text: TXT or CNAME records that prove domain control to a platform or CA, such as Vercel's _vercel TXT, Azure's asuid TXT, or ACM's validation CNAMEs. Deleting them can block later renewals (ACM stops renewing when its CNAME disappears) or let another account claim the domain. Record which service owns each one.

docs.title: 20. How does a Route 53 alias record differ from a CNAME?
docs.text: It can sit at the apex, answers with the current addresses of an AWS resource (so it looks like an A or AAAA record to clients), only matches the record type you created, is free for queries to AWS resources, and takes its TTL from the target instead of your setting.

docs.title: 21. What changes when a Cloudflare record is switched from DNS-only to proxied?
docs.text: DNS answers with Cloudflare anycast IPs and an automatic 300-second TTL, TLS for visitors ends at Cloudflare with an edge certificate, caching, WAF, and DDoS rules apply, the origin sees Cloudflare's addresses (the visitor's is in CF-Connecting-IP), and only HTTP and HTTPS are carried. Only A, AAAA, and CNAME records can be proxied; MX and TXT stay DNS-only.

docs.title: 22. What causes a redirect loop after enabling Cloudflare, and how do you fix it?
docs.text: Flexible mode connects to the origin over plain HTTP; if the origin redirects HTTP to HTTPS, every request loops. Switch to Full (strict) with a valid origin certificate, so Cloudflare connects over HTTPS and validates the origin.

docs.title: 23. How do DNS wildcards and TLS wildcards differ?
docs.text: A DNS wildcard (*.preview.example.com) answers for any name below it that does not exist, even several labels deep, but not for names that exist, including names that exist only because something below them has records. A TLS wildcard certificate covers exactly one label: pr-7.preview.example.com, not api.pr-7.preview.example.com.

docs.title: 24. What is subdomain takeover, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text: A DNS record (usually a CNAME) points at a cloud resource that was deleted; an attacker creates a resource with the same provider name and serves content, with a valid certificate, on your subdomain. Prevent it by removing DNS records before deleting resources, keeping verification records, and regularly checking that every CNAME target still exists and belongs to you.

docs.title: 25. In what order should example.com redirect when you use HSTS preload?
docs.text: http://example.com first redirects to https://example.com on the same host, which serves the HSTS header (max-age of at least a year, includeSubDomains, preload), and only then redirects to https://www.example.com. Preloading forces HTTPS on every subdomain, so audit them first.

docs.title: 26. What does "DNS propagation" actually mean?
docs.text: Nothing is pushed. The authoritative servers serve a change within seconds; each resolver keeps its cached copy until that copy's TTL expires, at different moments, so users see a mix of old and new answers for up to one TTL (or up to the delegation TTL for nameserver changes).

docs.title: 27. How do you change a record with zero downtime?
docs.text: Lower the TTL at least one old TTL ahead, prepare the new target fully, test it with curl --resolve using the real hostname, change the record, keep the old target serving until its traffic is gone, verify from several resolvers over IPv4 and IPv6, then raise the TTL and decommission the old target.

docs.title: 28. How do you move a zone to a new DNS provider safely?
docs.text: Inventory every record (including MX, DKIM, DMARC, verification, CAA, SRV, and subdomain delegations), translate provider-specific records such as aliases, import, diff both providers' answers name by name, handle DNSSEC first, change the nameservers at the registrar, and keep both zones identical for at least the delegation TTL before deleting the old one.

docs.title: 29. Why can't you quickly roll back a .com nameserver change?
docs.text: Resolvers cache the delegation from the .com servers for up to two days (172,800 seconds), and you cannot shorten that TTL. Whatever you publish at the registry, some resolvers keep using the previous nameservers until their cached delegation expires.

docs.title: 30. How do you handle DNSSEC when changing DNS providers?
docs.text: Either remove the DS record at the registrar and wait at least a day for cached copies to expire before moving (then sign at the new provider and publish its DS), or use a multi-signer setup (RFC 8901) in which both providers' keys are published. Never move while the DS points at keys the new provider does not have.

docs.title: 31. How do you tell whether a problem is in the zone, the delegation, or caches?
docs.text: Ask the authoritative server directly (dig @ns1... name +norecurse) to check the zone, walk the delegation with dig +trace, and query several public resolvers (dig @1.1.1.1, @8.8.8.8) to see cached answers and their remaining TTL. Work outward from the zone.

docs.title: 32. What does it mean when dig returns SERVFAIL but dig +cd works?
docs.text: +cd asks the resolver to skip DNSSEC validation. If the answer only works without validation, the DNSSEC chain is broken, typically a DS that does not match the zone's keys. delv and DNSViz show where the chain breaks.

docs.title: 33. How do you test a new server before DNS points at it?
docs.text: curl --resolve api.example.com:443:198.51.100.40 https://api.example.com/healthz sends a real request to the new address with the real hostname in SNI and Host, so certificate and virtual host problems appear before users are switched.

docs.title: 34. How does DNS as code help a migration?
docs.text: The zone lives in version control and changes go through review. Tools like DNSControl can push the same records to the old and new providers during the overlap (SERVICE("new_dns", 0) manages records without delegating), and dnscontrol preview in CI shows each provider's changes before push.

docs.title: 35. What is a cache key, and what belongs in it?
docs.text: The request properties that decide whether two requests share a cached object. Include every input that changes the response (path, meaningful query parameters, headers the response really varies by) and nothing else: drop tracking parameters and high-variety headers, and never key shared content on session cookies or Authorization.

docs.title: 36. What is the difference between CloudFront's cache policy and origin request policy?
docs.text: The cache policy defines what goes into the cache key; the origin request policy defines extra values forwarded to the origin without being keyed. If the origin varies its response on a value that is forwarded but not keyed, CloudFront serves the first variant to everyone.

docs.title: 37. Why can a policy with a minimum TTL above zero leak private data?
docs.text: CloudFront caches for at least the minimum TTL even when the origin sends no-cache, no-store, or private; the managed CachingOptimized policy has a one-second minimum. Attached to personalized API paths, it can serve one user's response to another. Use CachingDisabled there.

docs.title: 38. What does an origin shield or tiered cache do? Give the arithmetic.
docs.text: It adds a mid-tier cache near the origin that collapses misses from many edge locations. With a 90% edge hit ratio and an 80% shield hit ratio on the misses, the origin sees 0.10 × 0.20 = 2% of requests. CloudFront Origin Shield, Cloudflare Tiered Cache, Fastly shielding, Akamai Tiered Distribution, and Bunny Origin Shield all do this.

docs.title: 39. How should you invalidate cached content?
docs.text: Prefer versioned (hashed) URLs so only entry points need invalidating. Purge groups by tag (Cloudflare Cache-Tag, Fastly Surrogate-Key, CloudFront cache tags) when content changes, avoid purge-everything, which turns every edge cold at once, and remember purges never reach browsers.

docs.title: 40. How do you protect an origin that sits behind a CDN?
docs.text: Use CloudFront origin access control for S3, allow only the CDN's published ranges at the firewall or load balancer, require a secret header that only the CDN adds, or connect through a tunnel. Otherwise attackers bypass the cache and the WAF by hitting the origin directly.

docs.title: 41. How do you put an API behind a CDN safely?
docs.text: Disable caching for everything except explicitly public GET endpoints, forward Authorization, cookies, and query strings, cache public responses with short s-maxage, never cache responses that depend on the caller, check body size and timeout limits, and read the client IP from the CDN's header.

docs.title: 42. When would you use CloudFront Functions instead of Lambda@Edge?
docs.text: CloudFront Functions run sub-millisecond JavaScript on viewer requests and responses only, without network access, at very high scale: redirects, header changes, cache key normalization, token checks. Lambda@Edge (Node.js or Python) adds origin-side events, network and body access, and longer execution for heavier logic.

docs.title: 43. How do you keep edge image transformations under control?
docs.text: Allow only a small set of widths and formats, reject others at the edge, and include the allowed parameters in the cache key. Free-form parameters let anyone create unlimited variants, and services such as Cloudflare bill each unique transformation per month.

docs.title: 44. What do Cloudflare's DYNAMIC and BYPASS cache statuses mean?
docs.text: DYNAMIC means the request was never eligible for caching under the current rules, so it went straight to the origin. BYPASS means it was eligible, but the origin's response was not cacheable (for example because of its Cache-Control header).

docs.title: Email deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC
45. Why does application email land in spam?
docs.text: Mailbox providers decide on authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC with alignment) and reputation: complaints, bounces, spam traps, engagement, and the history of the domain and IPs. Authentication is required to be eligible for the inbox; reputation decides the folder. Google asks for a spam rate below 0.1% and never reaching 0.3%.

docs.title: 46. Why separate transactional and marketing email?
docs.text: Marketing draws more complaints. Sending it from its own subdomain and provider stream or IP pool keeps a campaign's complaints from pushing password resets into spam. Note that Gmail still counts subdomains toward the primary domain for its bulk-sender threshold.

docs.title: 47. What does SPF check, and what is the 10-lookup limit?
docs.text: SPF checks the envelope MAIL FROM (Return-Path) domain against the servers listed in its TXT record, not the visible From. RFC 7208 limits an evaluation to 10 lookups from include, a, mx, ptr, exists, and redirect, including nested includes; ip4, ip6, and all are free. Exceeding it is a permerror, so SPF fails for every message.

docs.title: 48. How does DKIM work, and how are its keys rotated?
docs.text: The sender signs selected headers and a body hash with a private key and adds a DKIM-Signature with d= (domain) and s= (selector); the receiver fetches the public key from <selector>._domainkey.<domain>. Keys should be 2048-bit RSA (RFC 8301 requires at least 1024 and forbids rsa-sha1). Rotate by publishing a new selector, switching signing, and removing the old key later.

docs.title: 49. What does a message need to pass DMARC?
docs.text: SPF or DKIM must pass, and the passing domain must align with the header From domain: in relaxed mode (the default) it must share the organizational domain, in strict mode it must match exactly. The policy (p=none, quarantine, reject) says what to do when neither aligned check passes.

docs.title: 50. Why can SPF and DKIM both pass while DMARC fails?
docs.text: Because they passed for someone else's domain: the provider's default Return-Path (for example amazonses.com) and DKIM signed with the provider's domain. Neither aligns with example.com. Fix it with custom DKIM for your domain and a custom MAIL FROM or Return-Path subdomain.

docs.title: 51. How do you roll out DMARC safely?
docs.text: Publish p=none with rua, read aggregate reports for a few weeks, inventory and fix every legitimate sender (aligned DKIM, custom Return-Path, or its own subdomain), then move to quarantine and later reject, optionally with t=y first. Advance only when reports are clean, and keep reading them afterwards.

docs.title: 52. What changed when DMARC was updated in 2026?
docs.text: RFC 9989 (May 2026) put DMARC on the Standards Track, obsoleting RFC 7489 and RFC 9091, and moved reporting to RFC 9990 and RFC 9991. It removed pct, rf, and ri, added t (test mode, which applies the next weaker policy), np, and psd, and replaced the Public Suffix List with a DNS tree walk for finding the organizational domain. Receivers still on RFC 7489 ignore the new tags.

docs.title: 53. What do Gmail, Yahoo, and Outlook.com require from bulk senders?
docs.text: Gmail (close to 5,000+ messages a day to personal accounts, a permanent status) and Yahoo require SPF and DKIM, DMARC of at least p=none with alignment, one-click unsubscribe honored within about two days, and a spam rate below 0.3%. Outlook.com requires SPF and DKIM to pass and an aligned DMARC record for domains above 5,000 messages a day, enforced since May 5, 2025 with 550 5.7.515 rejections.

docs.title: 54. What is one-click unsubscribe, and how do you implement it?
docs.text: RFC 8058: the message carries List-Unsubscribe with an HTTPS URL and List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click, both covered by DKIM. The mail client sends a POST without cookies; the endpoint must unsubscribe from a token in the URL and must not redirect. The GET link should show a confirmation page, because link scanners follow links.

docs.title: 55. How should bounces and complaints be handled?
docs.text: Suppress hard bounces and complaints immediately, retry soft bounces and suppress after repeats, and keep your own suppression store per category as well as the provider's. Watch rates: SES reviews accounts at 5% bounces or 0.1% complaints. Gmail does not send complaint data to SES, so watch Postmaster Tools too.

docs.title: 56. When is a dedicated IP worth it, and what is warm-up?
docs.text: Only for high, steady volume: a dedicated IP carries your reputation alone and needs regular sending (SES suggests around 1,000 emails a day per mailbox provider). A new IP has no history, so volume must rise gradually over weeks, starting with engaged recipients; SES's automatic warm-up takes 45 days.

docs.title: 57. After moving DNS from the registrar to a new provider, the website works but nobody receives email. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the MX records at the new provider, queried directly: dig @<new-ns> example.com MX +norecurse.

How to confirm: the old provider's export lists MX, SPF, DKIM, and DMARC records that the new zone lacks; senders report bounces.

Likely causes and fixes: only web records were copied before the nameserver change. Add the mail records immediately, then diff every name and type between the providers. See DNS migrations and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 58. The whole product is unreachable and the domain now shows a parking page. The servers are healthy. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the domain's registration status and expiry date with an RDAP lookup.

How to confirm: RDAP shows an expiration date in the past and a status such as redemptionPeriod; the A record points at the registrar's parking IPs.

Likely causes and fixes: the domain expired because auto-renew was off, the card failed, or notices went to a former employee. Renew or restore it, move contacts to a role mailbox, and alert on expiry dates. See domains and DNS records.

docs.title: 59. After moving TaskFlow Web to a new platform, its certificate cannot be issued: the platform reports a CAA error. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: dig example.com CAA and dig app.example.com CAA.

How to confirm: the relevant CAA set lists only the old platform's CA, not the one the new platform uses.

Likely causes and fixes: CAA was never updated. Add the new CA's identifier (keeping any still in use), and add a CAA review to the hosting change checklist. See connecting domains to hosting.

docs.title: 60. Right after a DNS provider change, some users get SERVFAIL while others resolve fine. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: compare dig example.com and dig +cd example.com through a validating resolver such as 8.8.8.8.

How to confirm: the answer works only with +cd; DNSViz shows the parent's DS record matching no DNSKEY at the new provider.

Likely causes and fixes: the DS record still points at the old provider's key. Remove it (or publish matching keys) and wait for the cached DS to expire; next time remove DS a day before the move. See DNS migrations and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 61. An hour after switching api.example.com to a new load balancer, a third of requests still reach the old one. Is DNS broken?
docs.text:
What to check first: the record's TTL before the change and the remaining TTL at public resolvers.

How to confirm: resolvers still hold the old address with a large remaining TTL, or the old load balancer's traffic comes from a few long-lived clients.

Likely causes and fixes: the TTL was not lowered beforehand, or clients reuse old connections or cached lookups. Keep the old target serving, restart long-lived workers or limit connection age, and lower TTLs a full TTL ahead next time. See DNS migrations and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 62. After turning on Cloudflare's proxy, browsers show "too many redirects". What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the zone's SSL/TLS encryption mode and the origin's HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect.

How to confirm: curl -sI shows 301 responses to the same HTTPS URL repeatedly, and the mode is Flexible.

Likely causes and fixes: Cloudflare fetches the origin over HTTP and the origin redirects to HTTPS. Install a valid origin certificate and use Full (strict). See connecting domains to hosting.

docs.title: 63. A security researcher reports that promo.example.com serves a phishing page. Nobody on the team deployed it. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: dig promo.example.com and what its CNAME target points to.

How to confirm: the CNAME targets a provider-assigned name for a resource your account no longer owns; Certificate Transparency shows a certificate you did not request.

Likely causes and fixes: subdomain takeover through a dangling CNAME. Delete the record, treat it as a security incident (cookies scoped to the parent domain may have leaked), audit all CNAMEs, and remove DNS before deleting resources. See connecting domains to hosting.

docs.title: 64. The platform shows "invalid configuration" for www.example.com, and some users reach an old server. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: all records at www: dig www.example.com CNAME, A, and AAAA.

How to confirm: an old AAAA record or a stray A record still points at the previous host; IPv6 users (curl -6) reach it.

Likely causes and fixes: leftover records from the previous host. Remove them, use exactly the target the dashboard shows, and test over IPv4 and IPv6. See connecting domains to hosting.

docs.title: 65. The CDN hit ratio for TaskFlow's public pages is 15%. How do you raise it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the cache key configuration and the variety of query strings, cookies, and headers in requests.

How to confirm: CDN logs show many distinct keys per path that differ only by utm_* parameters, a cookie, or User-Agent.

Likely causes and fixes: unnecessary inputs in the key or a Vary: User-Agent from the origin. Remove them from the key, strip tracking parameters at the edge, and add a shield or tiered cache. See CDN setup and edge caching.

docs.title: 66. A user reports seeing another user's task list. Responses pass through CloudFront. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the cache behavior and cache policy that match /api/*, and the response headers (Age, X-Cache).

How to confirm: the API path uses a policy with a minimum TTL above zero, or the response lacks private, no-store, and X-Cache shows a hit.

Likely causes and fixes: a personalized path is cached. Invalidate it, attach CachingDisabled to API behaviors, send private, no-store, test with two users, and handle it as a security incident. See CDN setup and edge caching.

docs.title: 67. Every deploy is followed by a spike that overloads the origin for several minutes. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the deploy's invalidation paths and whether a shield or tiered cache is enabled.

How to confirm: origin requests per second jump right after an invalidation of /*.

Likely causes and fixes: purge-everything makes every edge miss at once. Hash asset filenames, invalidate only entry points, and enable Origin Shield or tiered caching. See CDN setup and edge caching.

docs.title: 68. Password reset emails land in spam at Gmail but arrive fine elsewhere. Where do you look?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Authentication-Results header of a message delivered to a Gmail test account, and Postmaster Tools.

How to confirm: dmarc=fail, or SPF and DKIM passing only for the provider's domains; or a rising spam rate caused by marketing mail on the same domain and IPs.

Likely causes and fixes: missing alignment or shared reputation. Set up custom DKIM and a custom Return-Path for example.com, and move marketing to its own subdomain and stream. See email deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

docs.title: 69. After the marketing team added a new tool, every message from example.com fails SPF. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: dig +short example.com TXT for SPF records.

How to confirm: headers show spf=permerror; there are two SPF records, or counting nested includes gives more than 10 lookups.

Likely causes and fixes: a second SPF record or the lookup limit. Merge into one record, remove unused mechanisms such as a and mx, and give the tool its own subdomain with its own SPF. See email deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC.

docs.title: 70. Mail to hotmail.com and outlook.com addresses now bounces with 550 5.7.515. What does it mean?
docs.text:
What to check first: your daily volume to Outlook.com addresses and the SPF, DKIM, and DMARC results on those messages.

How to confirm: the domain sends more than 5,000 messages a day there, and messages fail SPF or DKIM, or have no aligned DMARC record.

Likely causes and fixes: Outlook.com's high-volume sender requirements. Make SPF and DKIM both pass for the sending domain and publish an aligned DMARC record of at least p=none. See email deliverability: SPF, DKIM and DMARC.
