docs.title: Build-Time vs Runtime Configuration
docs.text:
Some configuration is read when a program runs: a Node server reads process.env.MONGODB_URI at startup, in whatever environment it was started. Other configuration is consumed when a program is built: a Vite or Next.js frontend replaces import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL or process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_API_URL with a literal string while bundling, so the value is frozen into the files you ship. Mixing the two up causes wrong API URLs in production, secrets published in JavaScript bundles, and builds that cannot be promoted from staging to production.

This lesson covers build-time inlining in frontends, why inlined values are public, why changing them needs a rebuild, runtime configuration patterns for single-page apps, ARG versus ENV and build secrets in container images, the one-image-for-all-environments rule, and what "configuration" means for desktop and mobile apps that ship to every device.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The rule "build once, promote the same artifact" from environments and promotion only works if environment-specific values are read at runtime. A frontend built with the staging API URL inlined will call the staging API wherever it is deployed. Teams then either rebuild per environment (and ship to production an artifact that never ran in staging) or invent fragile search-and-replace scripts.

The security side is sharper. Anything inlined into a browser bundle, mobile app, or desktop binary is delivered to every user and can be read by anyone. A secret API key in a VITE_* variable is a published secret.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Next.js. The environment variables guide explains that NEXT_PUBLIC_* values are inlined into the browser bundle at next build, that "after being built, your app will no longer respond to changes to these environment variables", including when one Docker image is deployed to several environments, and that server code can read environment variables at runtime during dynamic rendering so a single image can be promoted.
  • Vite. The env variables and modes guide says VITE_* variables are exposed in client-side source code after bundling and should not contain sensitive information such as API keys.
  • Docker. The build variables documentation warns that build arguments and environment variables "are inappropriate for passing secrets to your build, because they're exposed in the final image", notes that build arguments may persist in image metadata and history, and recommends secret mounts instead.
  • The Twelve-Factor App. Factor V, Build, release, run, separates the build (code into an executable bundle), the release (bundle plus one environment's config), and the run stage, which is exactly the boundary build-time inlining blurs.

Popular tools and providers: Vite, Next.js, webpack DefinePlugin, esbuild and Bun --define, Docker ARG, ENV, and BuildKit secret mounts, the official nginx image's entrypoint scripts, Kubernetes ConfigMaps, and remote configuration services such as Firebase Remote Config for mobile apps.

docs.title: Two moments: build and run
docs.text: Build-time value Runtime value Read by The bundler or compiler The running program Where it ends up Inside the artifact (bundle, image layer, binary) In process memory, from the environment or a fetched file To change it Rebuild and redeploy Restart, reload, or refetch Same artifact in every environment? No Yes Visibility Anyone who can download the artifact Whoever can read the process environment or config endpoint

docs.title: Build-time inlining in frontends
docs.text:
Bundlers replace specific expressions with literal values while building:

// src/api.js (source)
export const API_URL = import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL;
if (import.meta.env.DEV) console.debug("API", API_URL);

// dist/assets/index-D4kPz8wa.js (production build, simplified)
const API_URL = "https://api.staging.taskflow.example.com";
  • import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL became a string literal.
  • import.meta.env.DEV became false, and the bundler removed the whole if block as dead code. That is the legitimate use of build-time values: removing development-only code.
  • Next.js does the same for process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_*, but only for direct references; process.env[name] or destructuring is not inlined, which is a common source of undefined in the browser.

docs.title: Why inlined values are public, always
docs.text:
The browser downloads the bundle. Anyone can open DevTools, the Network panel, or the source map, and read every inlined string. So:

Fine as a public build-time value Never as a build-time value Public API base URL API keys that grant write access or cost money Analytics site ID Database URLs or credentials Error tracker DSN (designed to be public, restrict by origin) JWT signing keys, session secrets Payment provider publishable key Payment provider secret key Feature defaults, build version Admin tokens, internal hostnames you consider confidential

When a frontend needs a secret-backed capability (calling a paid API, reading private data), the frontend calls your backend, which holds the secret and enforces authorization. A prefix such as VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ is a deliberate "this is public" marker; treat adding one like publishing the value.

docs.title: Changing a build-time value needs a rebuild
docs.text:
Because the value lives inside the files, changing the environment of a running deployment does nothing. Teams handle this in one of three ways:

  1. Build per environment. Simple and common for static sites. The price: the production artifact is not the one that was tested, and every environment needs its own build.
  2. Runtime configuration. Keep environment-specific values out of the bundle and load them when the app starts (next section). One build is promoted everywhere.
  3. Avoid configuration. Call the API at a relative path (/api) on the same origin, and let each environment's reverse proxy route it. No URL to configure at all, and no CORS.

docs.title: Runtime configuration patterns for single-page apps
docs.text:
Pattern How Pros Cons config.json fetched at startup The app fetches /config.json (served per environment, no-cache) before rendering Simple, one build, works on any static host One extra request before first render Server-injected config The server or edge inserts window.__APP_CONFIG__ = {...} into index.html No extra request Needs a server or edge function; must escape values to avoid script injection Container entrypoint writes config A script in the web container writes config.json from environment variables when the container starts Fits "one image, many environments" Only works when you serve the SPA from your own container Same-origin relative API Frontend calls /api; proxy routes per environment No config for the API URL at all Requires a proxy in front of both

Whatever the pattern, the runtime values are still public: they are sent to the browser. Runtime configuration fixes promotion, not secrecy.

docs.title: Container images: ARG, ENV, and build secrets
docs.text: ARG ENV Secret mount (RUN --mount=type=secret) Available during build Yes, from its declaration Yes, after its declaration Only in the RUN step that mounts it Present in running containers No, unless copied into ENV or a file Yes No Visible in image metadata or history It can be (history, provenance) Yes, in the image config No Use for Build options (versions, flags) Safe runtime defaults (NODE_ENV=production, PORT) Tokens needed only to build (private registry credentials) Never use for Secrets Secrets or per-environment values Runtime configuration

docs.title: One image for all environments
docs.text: The image should contain the runtime, dependencies, code, and safe defaults, and nothing that differs per environment. The platform supplies the rest when the container starts. That gives you a single digest to test, scan, sign, and promote.

docs.title: Desktop and mobile apps: every value ships to every device
docs.text:
A desktop or mobile app is a build artifact installed on devices you do not control. Any value compiled into it, including "hidden" ones in native code or obfuscated JavaScript, can be extracted.

  • Never embed secrets. Not API secret keys, not database passwords, not signing keys. Use your backend as the intermediary, with per-user authentication.
  • Expect old builds to live for months. A URL compiled into version 1.2 is called by 1.2 for as long as it is installed. Prefer stable public endpoints that you can route on the server side.
  • Use remote configuration for values that must change after release (feature switches, endpoints, minimum versions), fetched at startup, cached, with safe defaults when offline.
  • Restrict keys that must be public. Some providers issue client keys that are meant to be embedded but can be restricted to your app's bundle ID, package name, or website origin.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Value Build time Runtime Removing development-only code (import.meta.env.DEV) Yes App version and build commit Yes (it describes the build) API base URL that differs per environment Only if you build per environment Preferred (or use a relative /api path) Analytics or error tracker public IDs per environment Acceptable Preferred if you promote builds Server database URLs, secret keys Never Yes, on the server only Values that must change without a release (mobile) Never Remote config Credentials needed only to install dependencies during a Docker build Secret mount, never ARG

docs.title: Fail the frontend build if a required public value is missing
docs.text:
// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig, loadEnv } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

const REQUIRED = ["VITE_SENTRY_DSN"];

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => {
  const env = loadEnv(mode, process.cwd()); // only VITE_* keys by default
  const missing = REQUIRED.filter((key) => !env[key]);
  if (mode === "production" && missing.length > 0) {
    throw new Error(`Missing build-time variables: ${missing.join(", ")}`);
  }
  return { plugins: [react()] };
});

// src/vite-env.d.ts: type the variables you read
/// <reference types="vite/client" />
interface ImportMetaEnv {
  readonly VITE_SENTRY_DSN: string;
}
interface ImportMeta {
  readonly env: ImportMetaEnv;
}

A missing value now fails CI instead of shipping undefined to users.

docs.title: Runtime configuration for TaskFlow Web with config.json
docs.text:
// src/runtime-config.js: load and validate per-environment values at startup
import { z } from "zod";

const schema = z.object({
  apiBaseUrl: z.url(),
  environment: z.enum(["development", "staging", "production"]),
  sentryDsn: z.string().optional(),
});

let current;

export async function loadRuntimeConfig() {
  const res = await fetch("/config.json", { cache: "no-store" });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`config.json: HTTP ${res.status}`);
  current = Object.freeze(schema.parse(await res.json()));
  return current;
}

export function runtimeConfig() {
  if (!current) throw new Error("runtime config not loaded yet");
  return current;
}

// src/main.jsx: render only after configuration is loaded
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client";
import { loadRuntimeConfig } from "./runtime-config.js";
import { App } from "./App.jsx";

const root = createRoot(document.getElementById("root"));

loadRuntimeConfig()
  .then(() => root.render(<App />))
  .catch((err) => {
    console.error(err);
    root.render(<p>TaskFlow could not start. Please try again later.</p>);
  });

Each environment serves its own /config.json with Cache-Control: no-cache; the JavaScript bundle is identical everywhere.

docs.title: One web image, configured when the container starts
docs.text:
#!/bin/sh
# deploy/40-runtime-config.sh: runs from /docker-entrypoint.d/ before nginx starts
set -eu
: "${API_BASE_URL:?API_BASE_URL is required}"
: "${APP_ENV:?APP_ENV is required}"

# Values are public and validated again by the app; keep them to simple URLs and names
cat > /usr/share/nginx/html/config.json <<EOF
{
  "apiBaseUrl": "${API_BASE_URL}",
  "environment": "${APP_ENV}",
  "sentryDsn": "${SENTRY_DSN:-}"
}
EOF
echo "runtime config written for ${APP_ENV}"

# Dockerfile (TaskFlow Web): build once, configure at container start
FROM node:24-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM nginx:1.30-alpine
COPY --from=build /app/dist /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY deploy/nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --chmod=0755 deploy/40-runtime-config.sh /docker-entrypoint.d/40-runtime-config.sh

The official nginx image runs executable *.sh files from /docker-entrypoint.d/ before starting nginx, so the same image writes a different config.json in each environment. :? makes the container exit at startup if a required value is missing, just like a backend config check. Serve config.json with no-cache in nginx.conf.

docs.title: ARG, ENV, and a build secret in one Dockerfile
docs.text:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# Dockerfile (TaskFlow API)
FROM node:24-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Build option: which version label to bake in (not a secret)
ARG APP_VERSION=dev
# Deliberately persisted: the app reports it at /version
ENV APP_VERSION=$APP_VERSION \
    NODE_ENV=production \
    PORT=3000

COPY package*.json ./
# The private registry token exists only during this RUN step, in no layer
RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci --omit=dev

COPY src ./src
USER node
CMD ["node", "src/server.js"]

docker build \
  --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.8.0 \
  --secret id=npmrc,src="$HOME/.npmrc" \
  -t ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0 .

# Same image, different environments
docker run --rm -e APP_ENV=staging --env-file ./staging.env ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.8.0

Never write ARG NPM_TOKEN and RUN echo "//registry...:_authToken=$NPM_TOKEN" > .npmrc: the token ends up in the image history or a layer, and anyone who can pull the image can read it.

docs.title: Reading runtime values on the server in Next.js
docs.text:
// app/status/page.tsx: rendered per request, reads the environment at runtime
import { connection } from "next/server";

export default async function StatusPage() {
  await connection(); // opt into dynamic rendering, so this runs per request
  const region = process.env.DEPLOY_REGION ?? "unknown"; // server-only, not inlined
  return <p>Served from {region}</p>;
}

Server-only variables (no NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix) read during dynamic rendering come from the running environment, so one Next.js image can be promoted; NEXT_PUBLIC_* values in client components remain frozen at build time.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Decide for every value whether it is build-time or runtime, and document it.
  • Treat every VITE_*, NEXT_PUBLIC_*, and mobile or desktop compiled value as public.
  • Use build-time values for build facts (version, commit, dev-only code removal), runtime values for environment facts.
  • Prefer a same-origin /api path or runtime config.json so one frontend build can be promoted.
  • Validate runtime configuration in the browser too; fail visibly if it is missing.
  • Keep container images free of secrets and environment-specific values; use ENV only for safe defaults.
  • Use BuildKit secret mounts for build-time credentials.
  • Use remote configuration with safe offline defaults for installed apps.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The production frontend calls the staging API. Detect: browser network requests go to the staging host; errors or data from staging appear. Cause: the build was made with staging VITE_* values and then promoted. Fix: runtime configuration or a relative API path, or build per environment with checks in CI that the inlined URL matches the target.
  • An API secret key was found in the JavaScript bundle. Detect: secret scanning alert, or a researcher's report. Cause: a secret placed in a public build-time variable. Fix: revoke and rotate the key immediately, move the call behind your backend, and add a CI check that greps built assets for known secret patterns.
  • A private registry token was exposed in an image. Detect: docker history or an image scanner shows the token in a layer or build argument. Cause: ARG or ENV used for a build credential. Fix: rotate the token, rebuild with a secret mount, and delete the exposed images from the registry.
  • A config change did nothing in the browser. Detect: the environment variable changed but users see the old behavior. Cause: the value is inlined at build time, or config.json is cached by the CDN or browser. Fix: rebuild (for build-time values) or serve config.json with no-cache.
  • process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_X is undefined in the browser. Detect: client code logs undefined although the variable is set. Cause: dynamic access (process.env[key]) that the bundler cannot inline, or the variable was not set during next build. Fix: use direct property access and set the value at build time, or move to runtime configuration.
  • Old mobile app versions call a retired endpoint. Detect: 404s on an old path from specific app versions. Cause: the URL was compiled into the app. Fix: keep or redirect the old path server-side, and use remote configuration for endpoints in future versions.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Build time: when source is compiled or bundled into an artifact.
  • Runtime: when the artifact runs in an environment.
  • Inlining (static replacement): substituting an expression with a literal value during the build.
  • Dead-code elimination: removing code that a build-time constant makes unreachable.
  • Public prefix: a variable name prefix (VITE_, NEXT_PUBLIC_) marking values that will be shipped to browsers.
  • Runtime configuration: values an app loads after it starts, from the environment, a file, or an endpoint.
  • ARG: a Dockerfile build-time variable.
  • ENV: a Dockerfile variable that persists into the image and its containers.
  • Build secret mount: a BuildKit feature exposing a secret to a single RUN step without storing it in the image.
  • Remote configuration: values an installed app fetches from a server after release.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a VITE_ or NEXT_PUBLIC_ value is hidden because it came from an environment variable.
  • Expecting environment changes on the server to change an already-built frontend.
  • Promoting a frontend build whose environment-specific values were inlined.
  • Using ARG or ENV for tokens during Docker builds.
  • Baking environment-specific settings into container images.
  • Embedding secrets in desktop or mobile apps and relying on obfuscation.
  • Thinking runtime configuration makes values secret; it only makes them changeable.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What happens to import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL during vite build?
  2. Why is every NEXT_PUBLIC_* value public, and what should you do when a frontend needs a secret-backed capability?
  3. Give three ways to let one frontend build run in staging and production.
  4. Compare ARG, ENV, and secret mounts in a Dockerfile: which ones appear in running containers, and which can leak in image metadata?
  5. Why should a container image contain no environment-specific values?
  6. Why is process.env[name] not inlined by Next.js, and what symptom does that cause?
  7. What must never be compiled into a mobile app, and what replaces it?
  8. A runtime config.json change does not reach users for an hour. What is the likely cause?

docs.title: Environment Variables and Secrets Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the environment variables and secrets lessons, for the day before an interview or a configuration task.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text:
Command What it does node --env-file=.env app.js Loads the file before your code runs; a missing file is an error node --env-file-if-exists=.env app.js Same, but a missing file is fine process.loadEnvFile(".env") Loads a file from inside your code; keeps variables already set node -r dotenv/config app.js Loads .env with the dotenv package bun --env-file=extra.env app.js Loads only the named files instead of Bun's automatic list docker compose config --no-interpolate The Compose file before interpolation (without the flag, secrets can show) docker compose exec api printenv LOG_LEVEL What the container actually received (non-secret keys only) docker history --no-trunc IMAGE Build arguments and commands that may contain leaked tokens 
# "It is in the file, but the app does not see it" (never print values)
env | cut -d= -f1 | sort     # names already exported in your shell
cat -A .env                  # tab = ^I, CRLF = ^M$, trailing spaces
head -c 4 .env | od -c       # a byte order mark shows as 357 273 277
file .env                    # reports UTF-16

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
Precedence, highest first:

Tool Order Node --env-file Existing environment, later --env-file, earlier --env-file dotenv Existing environment (unless override: true), first file in path, later files Vite Real environment (VITE_* keys), .env.[mode].local, .env.[mode], .env.local, .env Next.js process.env, .env.$(NODE_ENV).local, .env.local (not in test), .env.$(NODE_ENV), .env Bun Shell, .env.[NODE_ENV].local, .env.local (not in test), .env.[NODE_ENV], .env Compose container run -e, interpolated environment/env_file values, plain environment, env_file, image ENV

Read process.env in one config module: coerce types, validate every key, print problems by name only, exit 1 on failure, and export a frozen object.

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why .env loading in a Node service node --env-file-if-exists=.env or dotenv Built in since v20.6.0; dotenv adds options such as override Shared defaults plus personal overrides Committed .env with safe values, Git-ignored .env.local Vite ranks .env.[mode] above .env.local; Next.js and Bun do the opposite A value inside a Compose container env_file: or environment: KEY: ${KEY} The project .env only fills ${VAR} in compose.yaml Per-user, gradual, or live changes A feature flag or dynamic config service No restart, and changes can target users One frontend build for every environment Runtime config.json or a same-origin /api path Build-time values are frozen into the bundle A credential during docker build RUN --mount=type=secret Never stored in a layer; ARG can persist in history Secrets on one systemd server LoadCredential= or a 0600 EnvironmentFile= Root-only files, read before the service starts Secrets for pods, VMs, and CI A secret store, workload identity, OIDC (id-token: write) Audited reads, short-lived credentials, no stored keys Encrypted secrets in Git SOPS or Sealed Secrets Readable diffs; no dynamic secrets or per-read audit

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text:
• Every value is a string: Boolean("false") is true, and "30" > "100" is true.
  • Node --env-file: added in v20.6.0, no longer experimental since v24.10.0 and v22.21.0; --env-file-if-exists since v22.9.0.
  • dotenv 18 prints injected env (N) from .env by default; quiet: true silences it.
  • Vite mode: development for vite, production for vite build. Next.js inlines NEXT_PUBLIC_* at next build, but not process.env[name].
  • Bun expands ${VAR}; Node's loader and dotenv keep it literally. Compiled Bun executables autoload .env unless built with --no-compile-autoload-dotenv.
  • Kubernetes never updates a running container's environment variables; mounted ConfigMap files update eventually. Secrets are base64, not encrypted, unless etcd encryption at rest is configured.
  • Invalid configuration means exit code 1 at startup: the rolling deploy halts and the old version keeps serving.
  • JWT_SECRET: at least 32 characters (openssl rand -base64 48). After a key change, accept the old key for at least the token lifetime.

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Editing .env while the variable is exported in the shell. Unset it; the existing environment wins in Node, dotenv, Vite, Next.js, and Bun.
  • A secret in a VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable. Rotate it, and move the call behind your backend.
  • Parsing booleans with Boolean(). Use z.stringbool() or an explicit list of allowed spellings.
  • Defaults for database URLs and secrets. Make them required and fail fast at startup.
  • Expecting the Compose project .env inside the container. Pass the key with environment: or env_file:.
  • Env files with a BOM, UTF-16, or whitespace-only lines. Use plain UTF-8 with LF endings, enforced by .editorconfig.
  • A build token passed with ARG. Use a BuildKit secret mount.
  • Only purging a leaked secret from Git history. Rotate it first; clones and forks keep the old value.

docs.title: Configuration Fundamentals
docs.text: Configuration is everything that can differ between deployments of the same code: the port to listen on, the database to use, the log level, the URL of a partner API, a connection pool size, a credential. This lesson explains how configuration differs from code and from secrets, what the Twelve-Factor App recommends and where that advice stops, how to give each environment its own values, how to load configuration into a typed, validated module that fails fast, why defaults can be dangerous, how feature configuration differs from operational configuration, and how configuration drift happens and is detected.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Configuration bugs are production bugs that tests rarely catch. The code was reviewed and tested; the value it was given in production was not. A missing variable that falls back to localhost, a log level string with a typo, a timeout of "30" compared as a string, a boolean "false" that JavaScript treats as true: each passes every unit test and fails in production, often long after startup.

Large public incidents show the same pattern at scale. Google's report on its June 2025 outage describes policy data with unintended blank fields replicated globally within seconds and hitting a code path that had no error handling; Cloudflare's November 2025 report describes a generated configuration file that doubled in size and exceeded a limit in its proxy. Treating configuration as code, with structure, validation, review, and staged rollout, is how teams stop these.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App. Factor III, Config, requires strict separation of config from code, gives the litmus test "whether the codebase could be made open source at any moment, without compromising any credentials", and recommends storing config in environment variables, because they are easy to change between deploys, unlikely to be committed, and language-agnostic. It also warns against grouping config into named environments inside the code, because that does not scale.
  • Kubernetes ConfigMaps. The ConfigMap documentation describes ConfigMaps as a way to decouple environment-specific configuration from container images, exposed to pods as environment variables, command-line arguments, or files in a volume, and notes that ConfigMaps are not for confidential data.
  • Facebook. The SOSP 2015 paper Holistic Configuration Management at Facebook describes managing configuration like code: stored in version control, changed through code review, checked by automated validators, and rolled out with canaries, because configuration changes are frequent and can break production as easily as code.
  • Google Cloud, June 2025. The incident report traces a global outage to policy data with blank fields that a binary did not validate or handle, and lists propagating globally replicated data incrementally, with validation, as a remediation.

Popular tools and providers: zod, envalid, convict, Joi, dotenv, Kubernetes ConfigMaps, AWS AppConfig and Systems Manager Parameter Store, Azure App Configuration, HashiCorp Consul KV, and etcd.

docs.title: Code, configuration, and secrets
docs.text:
• Code is the same in every environment. If a value would be the same in development and production forever (a business rule, a retry algorithm), it belongs in code, under review and tests.
  • Configuration is what legitimately differs per deploy. Keep the set of keys the same in every environment and let only the values differ.
  • Secrets are configuration that grants access. They need everything configuration needs plus restricted access, audit, rotation, and protection from leaks (see secrets management).

docs.title: Twelve-factor config and where it stops
docs.text:
Environment variables are a good default carrier, and the Twelve-Factor rule (config in the environment, not in code) holds up well. In practice teams add three refinements:

  • Structured or large configuration (routing tables, lists of tenants, certificate bundles) is awkward as flat strings. Mount it as a file (a Kubernetes ConfigMap volume, a JSON or YAML file) and still validate it at startup.
  • Secrets are better fetched from or injected by a secret store than passed around as plain environment variables, for reasons covered in the secrets lesson.
  • Values that change at runtime (feature flags, rate limits) belong in a flag or dynamic configuration service, not in variables that need a restart.

What Twelve-Factor warns against is still common: code such as if (env === "production") { dbHost = "db.internal" }. Each new environment then needs a code change, and staging tests different code paths from production. Put the value in configuration instead.

docs.title: Per-environment values
docs.text:
The same keys, different values:

Key Development Staging Production APP_ENV development staging production PORT 3000 3000 3000 LOG_LEVEL debug info info MONGODB_URI mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow staging cluster (secret) production cluster (secret) CORS_ORIGINS http://localhost:5173 https://staging.taskflow.example.com https://app.taskflow.example.com EMAIL_ENABLED false true (allowlist only) true MONGO_POOL_SIZE 5 10 50

Document every key once, in an .env.example file (names, meaning, example values, no real secrets), and keep it in the repository. Code review then sees every new variable.

docs.title: A typed config module that fails fast
docs.text:
The rules:

  1. Read process.env in exactly one module. Everything else imports the result. This makes the full list of configuration discoverable and testable.
  2. Coerce types explicitly. Every environment variable is a string: "3000", "true", "a,b,c". Convert to numbers, booleans, and lists on purpose. In JavaScript Boolean("false") is true and "30" > "100" is true (string comparison), which are classic bugs.
  3. Validate everything at startup: required keys, allowed values, ranges, formats (URLs, connection strings), and cross-field rules (trace logging is not allowed in production).
  4. Fail fast. On any problem, print every issue by name and exit with a non-zero code. A process that never becomes ready cannot take traffic; in a rolling deploy the rollout stops and the old version keeps serving. That is much better than a process that starts and fails on the first request that needs the bad value.
  5. Never print secret values, not even in validation errors.
  6. Freeze the result so no code changes configuration at runtime by accident.

docs.title: Defaults and their dangers
docs.text:
Defaults make local development pleasant and production dangerous:

Default Why it hurts in production Better MONGODB_URI defaults to mongodb://localhost:27017 A missing variable starts the app against nothing, or against a local database on the host, instead of failing Required, no default JWT_SECRET defaults to "secret" Anyone can forge tokens Required, minimum length, no default EMAIL_ENABLED defaults to true Development and test environments send real email Default false; production sets true explicitly CORS_ORIGINS defaults to * Any site can call the API from a browser Required in production LOG_LEVEL defaults to info Harmless; this is a fine default Keep PORT defaults to 3000 Usually harmless Keep, or let the platform set it

A useful rule: defaults are allowed for values where any wrong guess is safe and obvious, and forbidden for addresses of dependencies, anything security-related, and anything with side effects. Some teams also allow defaults only when APP_ENV is development.

docs.title: Feature configuration and operational configuration
docs.text:
Operational configuration Feature configuration (flags) Dynamic operational settings Examples Database URL, pool size, timeouts, log level new-task-board on for 10% of users Rate limits, kill switches Varies by Environment User, account, percentage Time, incident Changes With a deploy or restart Often, by product or release owners During incidents, by operators Delivered by Environment variables, ConfigMaps, files A flag service and SDK A config service with live reload Reload Restart (rolling) Live, per request Live, with validation

Mixing them causes trouble: a feature toggle in an environment variable needs a restart to change and cannot target users; a database URL in a flag service can be changed by the wrong person without review. See feature flags and progressive delivery.

docs.title: Configuration drift
docs.text:
Configuration drift is the difference between what configuration should be and what it actually is, or between environments that should match. Common causes:

  • Someone edits a value directly on a server, in a cloud console, or with kubectl edit, and the change is not recorded anywhere.
  • A new release needs a new variable; it was added to production but not to staging (or the other way round).
  • Each environment has a hand-maintained file that slowly diverges.
  • A value was set temporarily during an incident and never reverted.

Prevention and detection:

  • Keep configuration as code (in the application repository, a config repository, or infrastructure code) and change it only through review and automation.
  • Validate configuration at startup, so a missing variable fails loudly.
  • Log a fingerprint (a hash) of the non-secret configuration at startup and expose it, so you can see which instances run with which config.
  • Compare the names of variables across environments in CI.
  • Use infrastructure drift detection (terraform plan, GitOps reconciliation) for platform-level settings; see IaC fundamentals.

docs.title: Reloading configuration
docs.text: Most services read configuration once at startup and restart (through a rolling deploy) to change it, which keeps behavior predictable: every instance runs with the configuration it validated. Live reload (for example on SIGHUP or by watching a mounted file) is worth its complexity only for values that must change without a restart, and it needs the same validation, plus a rule for what happens to in-flight work. Kubernetes updates files from a mounted ConfigMap eventually, but never updates environment variables of a running container; those need a restart.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Value Where it belongs Same in every environment, part of behavior Code Differs per environment, small, not sensitive Environment variable (or ConfigMap exposed as one) Large or structured (lists, maps, files) Mounted config file, validated at startup Grants access (passwords, keys, tokens) Secret store, injected at deploy or start Changes per user or gradually Feature flag service Must change live during incidents Dynamic config service or kill switch Public frontend settings Build-time variable or runtime config.json (never secrets)

docs.title: A complete config module for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
// src/config/schema.js: one place that knows every configuration key
import { z } from "zod";

export const schema = z.object({
  NODE_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "production"]).default("development"),
  APP_ENV: z.enum(["development", "test", "preview", "staging", "production"]),
  PORT: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(65535).default(3000),
  LOG_LEVEL: z.enum(["fatal", "error", "warn", "info", "debug", "trace"]).default("info"),
  MONGODB_URI: z.string().startsWith("mongodb", "must be a MongoDB connection string"),
  MONGO_POOL_SIZE: z.coerce.number().int().min(1).max(500).default(10),
  JWT_SECRET: z.string().min(32, "must be at least 32 characters"),
  CORS_ORIGINS: z
    .string()
    .transform((s) => s.split(",").map((o) => o.trim()).filter(Boolean))
    .pipe(z.array(z.url())),
  EMAIL_ENABLED: z.stringbool().default(false), // "true"/"false", "1"/"0", "yes"/"no"...
  REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS: z.coerce.number().int().positive().default(10_000),
});

export class ConfigError extends Error {
  constructor(problems) {
    super(`Invalid configuration:\n${problems.map((p) => `  - ${p}`).join("\n")}`);
    this.problems = problems;
  }
}

// Pure function: easy to test with any env object
export function parseConfig(env) {
  const result = schema.safeParse(env);
  if (!result.success) {
    // zod messages describe the problem without echoing the value
    throw new ConfigError(result.error.issues.map((i) => `${i.path.join(".")}: ${i.message}`));
  }
  const c = result.data;

  const crossField = [];
  if (c.APP_ENV === "production" && c.LOG_LEVEL === "trace") {
    crossField.push("LOG_LEVEL: trace is not allowed in production");
  }
  if (c.APP_ENV === "production" && c.NODE_ENV !== "production") {
    crossField.push("NODE_ENV: must be production when APP_ENV is production");
  }
  if (crossField.length > 0) throw new ConfigError(crossField);

  return Object.freeze({
    env: c.APP_ENV,
    isProduction: c.APP_ENV === "production",
    port: c.PORT,
    logLevel: c.LOG_LEVEL,
    mongo: Object.freeze({ uri: c.MONGODB_URI, poolSize: c.MONGO_POOL_SIZE }),
    jwtSecret: c.JWT_SECRET,
    corsOrigins: Object.freeze(c.CORS_ORIGINS),
    emailEnabled: c.EMAIL_ENABLED,
    requestTimeoutMs: c.REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS,
  });
}

// src/config/index.js: load once; exit with a clear message if invalid
import { parseConfig, ConfigError } from "./schema.js";

function load() {
  try {
    return parseConfig(process.env);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof ConfigError) {
      console.error(err.message);
      process.exit(1);
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

export const config = load();

Started with bad values, the process prints and exits with code 1:

Invalid configuration:
  - APP_ENV: Invalid option: expected one of "development"|"test"|"preview"|"staging"|"production"
  - PORT: Invalid input: expected number, received NaN
  - MONGODB_URI: must be a MongoDB connection string
  - JWT_SECRET: must be at least 32 characters
  - CORS_ORIGINS.0: Invalid URL

z.stringbool() (zod 4) accepts the usual spellings of booleans in environment variables and rejects anything else, instead of treating every non-empty string as true. z.coerce.number() turns "abc" into NaN, which the schema then rejects.

docs.title: Documenting every key in .env.example
docs.text:
# .env.example: every configuration key, with safe example values.
# Copy to .env for local development. Never put real secrets here.

# Which deployment this is: development | test | preview | staging | production
APP_ENV=development
# development | test | production (library behavior; staging uses production)
NODE_ENV=development
PORT=3000
# fatal | error | warn | info | debug | trace
LOG_LEVEL=debug

MONGODB_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow
MONGO_POOL_SIZE=5

# At least 32 random characters. Generate: openssl rand -base64 48
JWT_SECRET=<generate-a-local-value>

# Comma-separated list of allowed browser origins
CORS_ORIGINS=http://localhost:5173
EMAIL_ENABLED=false
REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS=10000

docs.title: Logging a safe configuration summary
docs.text:
// src/config/summary.js: what the process is running with, minus secrets
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

const SECRET_KEYS = new Set(["jwtSecret"]);

export function configSummary(config) {
  const visible = {
    ...config,
    mongo: { ...config.mongo, uri: redactUri(config.mongo.uri) },
  };
  for (const key of SECRET_KEYS) visible[key] = "[set]";

  // A fingerprint lets you compare instances without exposing values
  const fingerprint = createHash("sha256")
    .update(JSON.stringify(config))
    .digest("hex")
    .slice(0, 12);
  return { ...visible, fingerprint };
}

function redactUri(uri) {
  try {
    const u = new URL(uri);
    if (u.password) u.password = "***";
    return u.toString();
  } catch {
    return "[unparseable]";
  }
}

// At startup: logger.info({ config: configSummary(config) }, "configuration loaded");

The fingerprint changes whenever any value changes (including secrets) without revealing them. Two instances with different fingerprints are running with different configuration, which is the first thing to check when "only some requests fail".

docs.title: Testing the config module
docs.text:
// test/config.test.js
import { test } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import { parseConfig, ConfigError } from "../src/config/schema.js";

const valid = {
  APP_ENV: "staging",
  NODE_ENV: "production",
  MONGODB_URI: "mongodb://db.internal:27017/taskflow",
  JWT_SECRET: "x".repeat(32),
  CORS_ORIGINS: "https://staging.taskflow.example.com",
};

test("parses and converts types", () => {
  const c = parseConfig({ ...valid, PORT: "8080", EMAIL_ENABLED: "false" });
  assert.equal(c.port, 8080);
  assert.equal(c.emailEnabled, false); // not the truthy string "false"
});

test("reports every missing required key", () => {
  assert.throws(() => parseConfig({}), (err) => {
    assert.ok(err instanceof ConfigError);
    assert.ok(err.problems.some((p) => p.startsWith("MONGODB_URI")));
    assert.ok(err.problems.some((p) => p.startsWith("JWT_SECRET")));
    return true;
  });
});

test("rejects trace logging in production", () => {
  assert.throws(
    () => parseConfig({ ...valid, APP_ENV: "production", LOG_LEVEL: "trace" }),
    ConfigError,
  );
});

docs.title: Catching drift: compare variable names across environments
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/compare-env-keys.sh: list env var NAMES (not values) per deployment
# usage: compare-env-keys.sh <namespace-a> <namespace-b>
set -euo pipefail
keys() {
  kubectl -n "$1" get deployment taskflow-api \
    -o jsonpath='{range .spec.template.spec.containers[0].env[*]}{.name}{"\n"}{end}' | sort
}
diff <(keys "$1") <(keys "$2") && echo "same variable names in $1 and $2"

Run it in CI after every infrastructure change. It catches the most common drift, a variable that exists in one environment and not the other, without ever reading a value.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Separate code, configuration, and secrets; keep the same keys in every environment.
  • Read process.env in one module; export a typed, frozen object.
  • Coerce and validate every value at startup; fail fast with clear, value-free messages.
  • Allow defaults only where a wrong guess is safe; require explicit values for dependencies, security settings, and side effects.
  • Document every key in .env.example and review new keys in pull requests.
  • Use files for structured configuration, a secret store for secrets, and a flag service for per-user or live changes.
  • Change configuration through version control and automation; log a configuration fingerprint at startup.
  • Restart (with a rolling deploy) to apply configuration unless live reload is truly needed.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The app started fine but every request to one feature fails. Detect: errors only in code paths that use one setting; logs show undefined or NaN in URLs or timeouts. Cause: a missing or malformed variable that nothing validated at startup. Fix: validate all configuration at startup and fail fast.
  • Staging sent real emails. Detect: complaints from customers; provider logs show sends from staging. Cause: EMAIL_ENABLED defaulted to true, or staging used production credentials. Fix: safe defaults (off), allowlists in non-production environments, separate credentials.
  • A feature that was "turned off" is still on. Detect: behavior does not match the variable you changed. Cause: Boolean("false") is true, or the process was not restarted after the change. Fix: explicit boolean parsing (z.stringbool()), and roll the deployment after configuration changes.
  • Only some instances misbehave. Detect: errors correlate with specific pods or hosts; config fingerprints differ. Cause: drift from manual edits or a partial rollout of a config change. Fix: manage configuration as code and redeploy every instance from it.
  • A deploy failed because of a variable that exists only in production. Detect: the new version fails validation in staging (good) or worse, only in production. Cause: environments maintained by hand. Fix: compare variable names across environments in CI and add new keys to all environments in the same change.
  • Secrets appeared in the logs. Detect: log search finds connection strings with passwords. Cause: the whole config or process.env was logged, or a validation error printed values. Fix: log a redacted summary only, rotate the exposed secrets.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Configuration: values that differ between deployments of the same code.
  • Environment variable: a named string passed by the operating system to a process at start.
  • Config module: the single place that reads, converts, and validates configuration.
  • Coercion: converting a string value into the intended type.
  • Fail fast: stopping at startup on invalid configuration instead of failing later.
  • Default value: a value used when a key is not set.
  • Operational configuration: settings that control how the service runs in an environment.
  • Feature configuration: settings that control what users see, usually through flags.
  • Configuration drift: unplanned differences between intended and actual configuration, or between environments.
  • Configuration fingerprint: a hash of the effective configuration used to compare instances.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Reading process.env all over the code base.
  • Treating "false" and "0" as false without parsing them.
  • Giving dependencies and secrets defaults "for convenience".
  • Branching on APP_ENV === "production" for values that should be configuration.
  • Logging all of process.env to debug a problem.
  • Editing configuration on live servers and forgetting it.
  • Expecting a running container to see changed environment variables without a restart.
  • Using environment variables for per-user feature toggles.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between code, configuration, and secrets? Give two examples of each for TaskFlow API.
  2. What is the Twelve-Factor litmus test for configuration?
  3. Why should process.env be read in only one module?
  4. What does Boolean("false") return, and how should boolean variables be parsed?
  5. Which settings should never have a default value, and why?
  6. During a rolling deploy, a new version fails configuration validation. What do users experience, and why is that better than starting with the bad value?
  7. How do feature flags differ from operational configuration in who changes them and how they reload?
  8. How can you detect configuration drift between staging and production without reading any secret values?

docs.title: .env Files and Precedence
docs.text:
A .env file is a plain text file of KEY=value lines that a tool reads and turns into environment variables, so developers do not have to export a dozen variables by hand. The format looks universal, but it is not a standard: Node.js, the dotenv package, Vite, Next.js, Bun, and Docker Compose each parse it slightly differently, load different files, and decide differently which value wins when the same key is set in several places.

This lesson covers the .env format, how each of those tools loads files and resolves precedence (only rules stated in their official documentation, plus behavior tested for this page), the parser differences that cause silent bugs, and a debugging recipe for "the variable is in the file but the app does not see it".

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
When a value comes from the wrong place, nothing crashes. The app simply runs with a different database, a different API URL, or a missing key that a default quietly replaces. Typical surprises:

  • A variable exported in your shell overrides the .env file, so editing the file "does nothing".
  • .env.local wins in one framework and loses in another.
  • A Docker Compose .env file is used to fill ${VAR} in compose.yaml but is not passed into the container at all.
  • A line with only spaces, a byte order mark, or an unclosed quote makes one parser drop or merge keys while another reads the same file fine.

Knowing each tool's rules turns an afternoon of confusion into a two-minute check.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Node.js. The command-line documentation for --env-file states: "If the same variable is defined in the environment and in the file, the value from the environment takes precedence", and that with several --env-file flags, "subsequent files override pre-existing variables defined in previous files". The flag was added in v20.6.0 and is no longer experimental as of v24.10.0 and v22.21.0.
  • dotenv. The dotenv README says "By default, we will never modify any environment variables that have already been set", offers override: true to change that, and, for several files, "the first value set for a variable will win, unless the options.override flag is set".
  • Vite. The env variables and modes guide lists .env, .env.local, .env.[mode], and .env.[mode].local, says mode-specific files take priority over generic ones and that variables already in the environment when Vite runs "have the highest priority and will not be overwritten by .env files", and warns that VITE_* variables "should not contain sensitive information".
  • Next.js. The environment variables guide gives the lookup order process.env, .env.$(NODE_ENV).local, .env.local (not checked when NODE_ENV is test), .env.$(NODE_ENV), then .env.
  • Docker Compose. The page on environment variable precedence ranks docker compose run -e highest, then environment or env_file values interpolated from the shell or an environment file, then plain environment entries, then env_file, then ENV in the image.

Popular tools and providers: Node.js --env-file and process.loadEnvFile, dotenv and dotenv-expand, Vite, Next.js and @next/env, Bun, Docker Compose, direnv, and secret-manager CLIs that inject variables into a command (doppler run, op run, infisical run).

docs.title: The .env format
docs.text:
# .env: one KEY=value per line; this line is a comment
APP_ENV=development
PORT=3000
LOG_LEVEL=debug            # inline comment (unquoted values only)
GREETING="Hello, world"    # quotes are removed from the value
PASSWORD_HINT="has a # sign"
export MONGODB_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow   # 'export ' is ignored
TLS_CERT="-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----
...multi-line values inside double quotes...
-----END CERTIFICATE-----"

Rules that hold across the tools on this page:

  • Keys are usually uppercase letters, digits, and underscores.
  • Everything after an unquoted # is a comment, so a value containing # must be quoted.
  • Quotes around the whole value are removed. Single, double, and backtick quotes are accepted by Node and dotenv.
  • Multi-line values work inside double quotes in Node (since v20.12.0 / v21.7.0), dotenv (since v15), Next.js, and Bun.
  • A leading export is ignored (tested with Node, dotenv, and Bun).
  • Variable expansion differs: Node's loader and the dotenv package keep ${HOST} literally (tested); Bun, Vite (through dotenv-expand), and Next.js expand references to earlier variables. Escape $ with \ in the tools that expand.
  • There is no type information: every value is a string.

docs.title: Node.js: --env-file, process.loadEnvFile, util.parseEnv
docs.text:
API What it does Precedence node --env-file=.env app.js Loads the file before your code runs (v20.6.0+). Errors if the file is missing Existing environment variables win; with several flags, later files override earlier ones node --env-file-if-exists=.env app.js Same, but a missing file is not an error (v22.9.0+) Same process.loadEnvFile(path = "./.env") Loads a file from inside your code (v20.12.0 / v21.7.0+) In testing on v22.12, an already-set variable was not overwritten util.parseEnv(content) Parses a string and returns an object; does not touch process.env Not applicable

With --env-file, variables that configure Node itself (such as NODE_OPTIONS) are applied; the documentation notes that NODE_OPTIONS inside a file loaded with process.loadEnvFile() has no effect, because Node is already running.

docs.title: The dotenv package
docs.text:
import "dotenv/config";                         // load ./.env as a side effect
// or, with options:
import dotenv from "dotenv";
dotenv.config({ path: [".env.local", ".env"] }); // first value set wins
dotenv.config({ path: ".env.test", override: true }); // file beats existing variables
  • Existing variables are never overwritten unless override: true.
  • With several files, the first file that sets a key wins (unless override), which is the opposite of Node's "later --env-file wins".
  • Recent major versions print a short "injected env" line when they load a file (version 18 does by default, as tested); pass quiet: true to silence it.
  • dotenv does not expand ${VAR} references; the separate dotenv-expand package does.

docs.title: Vite
docs.text:
Vite loads, for the current mode (development for vite, production for vite build, or --mode staging):

Priority Source 1 (highest) Variables already set in the environment when Vite runs, for keys with the VITE_ prefix 2 .env.[mode].local 3 .env.[mode] 4 .env.local 5 (lowest) .env

Vite's source merges the files in the order .env, .env.local, .env.[mode], .env.[mode].local, with later files overwriting earlier ones, and then copies prefixed keys from the real environment on top. Only keys with the VITE_ prefix (configurable with envPrefix) are exposed to client code as import.meta.env.VITE_*, and they are inlined into the JavaScript bundle at build time. .local files are meant to be ignored by Git. Inside vite.config.js, .env values are not yet in process.env; use Vite's loadEnv(mode, process.cwd(), "") to read them there.

docs.title: Next.js
docs.text:
Priority Source 1 (highest) process.env 2 .env.$(NODE_ENV).local 3 .env.local (not checked when NODE_ENV is test) 4 .env.$(NODE_ENV) 5 (lowest) .env

Compare with Vite: Next.js puts .env.local above .env.production, Vite puts .env.production above .env.local. A value in .env.local therefore wins in a local Next.js production build but loses in a local Vite production build. Next.js inlines only NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables into browser code, at build time. Outside the Next.js runtime (an ORM config, a test runner), loadEnvConfig from @next/env loads files the same way.

docs.title: Bun
docs.text:
Bun's runtime reads .env files automatically, in increasing order of precedence: .env, then .env.production, .env.development, or .env.test depending on NODE_ENV, then .env.local (skipped when NODE_ENV=test), then .env.[NODE_ENV].local. Variables already set in the shell are not overwritten (tested with --env-file). Other details from the Bun documentation and CLI:

  • --env-file replaces the automatic choice of files; it can be given several times.
  • --no-env-file, or env = false in bunfig.toml, turns automatic loading off.
  • Bun.env and import.meta.env are aliases of process.env.
  • Values are expanded: URL=mongodb://${HOST}:27017 becomes mongodb://db:27017 when HOST=db (tested).
  • Standalone executables built with bun build --compile also autoload .env by default in recent versions (--no-compile-autoload-dotenv disables it, per bun build --help in Bun 1.4), so a compiled binary's configuration can depend on the directory it is started from.

docs.title: Docker Compose
docs.text:
Compose uses .env files for two different things:

  1. Interpolation of compose.yaml. A .env file in the project directory (or the file given with docker compose --env-file) fills in ${VAR} references in the Compose file itself. Shell variables take precedence over it for interpolation. These values do not reach the container unless the Compose file passes them on.
  2. The container's environment. Set by environment: and env_file: in the service definition.
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${API_TAG:-latest}   # interpolated from shell or .env
    env_file:
      - ./config/api.env                                      # file contents become container env
    environment:
      LOG_LEVEL: debug                                         # beats the same key in env_file
      MONGODB_URI: ${MONGODB_URI}                              # interpolated, then passed in

Container environment precedence, highest first: docker compose run -e; environment or env_file values interpolated from the shell or an environment file; plain environment values; env_file values; ENV from the image.

docs.title: Kubernetes and process managers do not read .env files
docs.text: In production, variables come from the platform: Kubernetes env and envFrom entries referencing ConfigMaps and Secrets, systemd Environment= and EnvironmentFile=, PM2 ecosystem files, or a PaaS dashboard. systemd's EnvironmentFile uses its own parsing rules (# starts a comment only at the beginning of a line, export is not accepted, and ${VAR} is not expanded), so a file that works with dotenv is not guaranteed to work there. Keep .env files for local development and treat production configuration as a separate, managed source.

docs.title: Parser differences and gotchas
docs.text:
These results come from feeding identical files to Node v22.12.0 (--env-file and util.parseEnv), dotenv 18.0.10, and Bun 1.4.4 while writing this page. Other versions may behave differently: Node v24.22.3 skips whitespace-only and tab-only lines, but its byte order mark and unclosed-quote results match v22.12. The point is that parsers disagree, so test with the loader you actually use.

File content Node 22.12 dotenv 18 Bun 1.4 A line containing only spaces between two keys The next key is merged into a broken name ("\nB"), so B is missing Line skipped, B set Line skipped, B set A line containing only a tab Same as above: next key lost Skipped Skipped UTF-8 byte order mark at the start First key's name starts with \uFEFF, so it is missing Handled Handled A="hello with no closing quote, and a later line such as C="x" Lines up to the next " are swallowed into A; B and C lost Only A affected Same as Node File saved as UTF-16 Nothing is loaded, silently Nothing is loaded Nothing is loaded CRLF line endings Handled Handled Handled The same key twice Last one wins Last one wins Last one wins KEY = value with spaces around = Handled Handled Handled

Practical rules:

  • Keep .env files boring: no indentation, no whitespace-only lines, no trailing spaces, plain ASCII or UTF-8 without a byte order mark, LF line endings, and quotes only where needed.
  • Add an .editorconfig rule (trim_trailing_whitespace = true, charset = utf-8, end_of_line = lf) for .env* files.
  • Validate configuration at startup, so a key that a parser dropped becomes an immediate, named error instead of a silent default.

docs.title: Debugging recipe: "it is in the file, but the app does not see it"
docs.text:
1. Ask the process, not the file. Print, for each expected key, whether it is set and what kind of value it has, never the value.
  2. Check what is already exported in your shell (env | cut -d= -f1 | sort, names only). In most tools the shell wins.
  3. Check which files the tool loads in this mode (Vite mode, Next.js NODE_ENV, Bun NODE_ENV, Compose project directory).
  4. Inspect the file's bytes: cat -A .env shows tabs (^I), line endings (^M$ for CRLF), and trailing spaces; head -c 4 .env | od -c shows a byte order mark; file .env reports UTF-16.
  5. Compare loaders: run the same check under the loader you use in production and the one you use locally.
  6. In containers, check the container, not the Compose file: docker compose exec api printenv LOG_LEVEL for non-secret keys.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Use Local development of a Node service node --env-file-if-exists=.env (no dependency) or dotenv Several local layers (shared defaults plus personal overrides) .env committed with safe defaults, .env.local ignored by Git, loaded in a documented order Frontend builds The framework's own loader (Vite, Next.js); only public values Docker Compose development stacks env_file: for container variables, a project .env only for interpolation Production The platform's configuration (Kubernetes, systemd, PaaS) and a secret store, not .env files CI CI variables and secrets, not committed .env files

Do not commit .env files containing secrets, do not copy .env files between people over chat, and do not rely on implicit autoloading in production binaries.

docs.title: Loading .env in Node without a dependency
docs.text:
{
  "scripts": {
    "dev": "node --watch --env-file-if-exists=.env --env-file-if-exists=.env.local src/server.js",
    "start": "node src/server.js"
  }
}

In package.json, the dev script loads .env and then .env.local (later file wins for keys set in both), but anything already exported in the shell still wins. start loads nothing: production variables come from the platform.

docs.title: A key checker that never prints values
docs.text:
// scripts/check-env.js: show which expected keys are set, and their shape
const EXPECTED = ["APP_ENV", "PORT", "LOG_LEVEL", "MONGODB_URI", "JWT_SECRET", "CORS_ORIGINS"];

function shape(value) {
  if (value === undefined) return "MISSING";
  if (value === "") return "empty string";
  if (/^\s|\s$/.test(value)) return "has leading/trailing whitespace";
  if (/^\d+$/.test(value)) return "integer";
  if (/^(true|false|1|0|yes|no)$/i.test(value)) return "boolean-like";
  if (/^[a-z][a-z0-9+.-]*:\/\//i.test(value)) return `URL (${value.split(":")[0]})`;
  return `string, ${value.length} chars`;
}

for (const key of EXPECTED) {
  console.log(`${key.padEnd(14)} ${shape(process.env[key])}`);
}

// Keys that look broken: names containing whitespace or a byte order mark
const odd = Object.keys(process.env).filter((k) => /[\s\uFEFF]/.test(k));
if (odd.length > 0) console.log("suspicious key names:", odd.map((k) => JSON.stringify(k)));

node --env-file=.env scripts/check-env.js        # what Node's loader produced
node -r dotenv/config scripts/check-env.js        # what dotenv produced
bun scripts/check-env.js                          # what Bun's autoloading produced

Run against the file from the whitespace example, Node 22.12 prints MONGODB_URI MISSING and a suspicious key name starting with a newline, while the other two print URL (mongodb). The URL scheme is shown, but never credentials.

docs.title: Vite: reading env values inside vite.config.js
docs.text:
// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig, loadEnv } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

export default defineConfig(({ mode }) => {
  // Third argument "" loads all keys, not only VITE_*; use them for the dev server only
  const env = loadEnv(mode, process.cwd(), "");
  return {
    plugins: [react()],
    server: {
      proxy: { "/api": env.DEV_API_PROXY_TARGET ?? "http://localhost:3000" },
    },
  };
});

Values read here configure the build and the dev server; only VITE_* keys reach browser code.

docs.title: Docker Compose: see what the container actually received
docs.text:
docker compose config --no-interpolate | less     # the file before interpolation
docker compose exec api printenv APP_ENV LOG_LEVEL   # non-secret values inside the container
docker compose exec api node scripts/check-env.js    # shapes of everything, values hidden

docker compose config without --no-interpolate prints the fully resolved file, which includes any secrets passed through interpolation; avoid pasting its output anywhere.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use one loader per project and know its precedence rules.
  • Commit .env.example (names and safe examples), never .env with real secrets; add .env* (except the example) to .gitignore.
  • Remember that shell variables usually win; unset stale exports.
  • Keep .env files plain: no whitespace-only lines, no indentation, UTF-8 without BOM, LF endings.
  • Use .local files for personal overrides, and learn which way your framework ranks them.
  • Never put secrets in VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variables.
  • Do not use .env files in production; configure the platform and a secret store.
  • Validate configuration at startup and debug with name-and-shape checks, never by printing values.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "I changed the .env file and nothing happened." Detect: the process still shows the old value. Cause: the variable is also exported in the shell or CI environment, which wins in Node, dotenv, Vite, Next.js, and Bun; or the process was not restarted. Fix: unset the exported variable, restart, and check with a key checker.
  • A value works in development and differs in a local production build. Detect: vite build and next build pick different values from the same files. Cause: different ranking of .env.local against .env.production. Fix: avoid setting the same key in both, or document the order for your framework.
  • The container does not see a variable from .env. Detect: docker compose exec api printenv KEY prints nothing. Cause: the project .env file is only used for interpolation of compose.yaml. Fix: pass it with environment: KEY: ${KEY} or put it in an env_file:.
  • One key silently disappeared after someone edited the file. Detect: the key checker shows it missing and a suspicious key name with whitespace. Cause: a whitespace-only or indented line, a BOM, or an unclosed quote, read by a strict parser. Fix: clean the file, enforce .editorconfig, and validate at startup.
  • A compiled binary uses different settings depending on where it is started. Detect: the same binary behaves differently in two directories. Cause: the runtime autoloads .env from the working directory. Fix: disable autoloading for production builds and pass configuration through the process manager.
  • A secret showed up in a CI log. Detect: log search; secret scanning alert. Cause: a debug step printed env or docker compose config. Fix: rotate the secret, remove the step, and use name-only checks.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• .env file: a text file of KEY=value lines loaded into environment variables by a tool.
  • Precedence: the rule deciding which source wins when a key is set more than once.
  • Override: letting a file replace a variable that is already set.
  • Mode (Vite): the named configuration (development, production, or custom) that selects which env files load.
  • Interpolation (Compose): replacing ${VAR} in compose.yaml with values from the shell or an env file.
  • Expansion: replacing ${VAR} references inside env file values.
  • Byte order mark (BOM): invisible bytes at the start of some text files that can corrupt the first key.
  • Autoloading: a runtime loading .env files without being asked.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing the .env file always wins over shell variables.
  • Assuming every tool loads the same files in the same order.
  • Expecting Compose's project .env to appear inside containers.
  • Expecting ${VAR} references to expand in Node's loader or in dotenv.
  • Committing .env "just for the team" with real credentials.
  • Debugging by printing process.env to logs.
  • Saving env files from editors that add a BOM or UTF-16 encoding.
  • Using .env files on production servers instead of platform configuration.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. In Node with --env-file=.env, PORT=4000 is in the file and PORT=5000 is exported in the shell. Which value does the app see?
  2. With node --env-file=a.env --env-file=b.env, which file wins for a key set in both? With dotenv.config({ path: ["a.env", "b.env"] })?
  3. List Vite's env files from highest to lowest priority and say where real environment variables fit.
  4. Why can the same .env.local value win in a Next.js build and lose in a Vite build?
  5. What are the two different uses of .env files in Docker Compose?
  6. A colleague's MONGODB_URI disappears with Node's loader but works with dotenv. Name three file problems that could cause this.
  7. How would you debug a missing variable without ever printing a secret?
  8. Why should production not rely on .env files?

docs.text:
• Node.js: --env-file
  • Node.js: process.loadEnvFile
  • dotenv README
  • Vite: Env variables and modes
  • Next.js: Environment variables
  • Bun: Environment variables
