docs.title: Environment Variables and Secrets Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review configuration fundamentals, .env files and precedence rules, build-time versus runtime configuration, and secrets management. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between code, configuration, and secrets?
docs.text: Code is behavior that is the same in every environment. Configuration is what differs between deployments of the same code (ports, URLs, log levels, pool sizes). Secrets are configuration that grants access (passwords, API keys, signing keys) and additionally need restricted access, audit, rotation, and leak protection.

docs.title: 2. What does the Twelve-Factor App say about configuration?
docs.text: Store config in the environment, strictly separated from code. Its litmus test is whether the codebase could be made open source at any moment without compromising credentials. It warns against named environment groups inside code, because each new environment then needs a code change.

docs.title: 3. Why should process.env be read in only one module?
docs.text: It makes the full set of configuration discoverable, lets one place convert and validate every value, makes testing easy (pass any object to a parse function), and prevents scattered string handling bugs. The rest of the code imports a typed, frozen config object.

docs.title: 4. Why must configuration be validated at startup?
docs.text: Because invalid values otherwise surface later, in the first request that needs them, often far from the cause. Failing at startup with a message naming each bad variable stops a rolling deploy before the new version takes traffic, while the old version keeps serving.

docs.title: 5. What is wrong with Boolean(process.env.EMAIL_ENABLED)?
docs.text: Every non-empty string is truthy, so "false" and "0" become true. Parse booleans explicitly from an allowed set of spellings (zod 4's z.stringbool() does this) and reject anything else.

docs.title: 6. Which configuration values should never have defaults?
docs.text: Addresses of dependencies (database URLs), anything security-related (signing secrets, CORS origins), and anything with side effects (sending email, charging cards). A missing value should stop the process, not silently point at localhost or use "secret".

docs.title: 7. How do feature flags differ from operational configuration?
docs.text: Operational configuration (database URL, pool size, timeouts) differs by environment and changes with deploys or restarts. Feature flags differ by user or percentage, change often, are owned by product or release owners, and reload live through a flag service.

docs.title: 8. What is configuration drift, and how do you detect it?
docs.text: Unplanned differences between intended and actual configuration, or between environments that should match, usually from manual edits or partial changes. Detect it by managing config as code, validating at startup, logging a config fingerprint, comparing variable names across environments in CI, and using infrastructure drift detection.

docs.title: 9. When should configuration be a file instead of environment variables?
docs.text: When it is large or structured (routing tables, lists, certificate bundles). Mount it as a file (for example a ConfigMap volume) and validate it at startup like any other configuration.

docs.title: 10. Does changing a Kubernetes ConfigMap update a running container's environment variables?
docs.text: No. Environment variables are set when the container starts. Files from a mounted ConfigMap are updated eventually, but the app must re-read them. To apply new variables, restart the pods (a rolling restart).

docs.title: 11. How do you log configuration safely?
docs.text: Log a redacted summary: non-secret values in clear, secret keys as [set], credentials inside URLs masked, plus a short hash fingerprint of the effective configuration so instances can be compared without revealing values.

docs.title: 12. Why is NODE_ENV a poor way to name environments?
docs.text: Libraries use NODE_ENV to switch behavior (production optimizations, error detail), so staging should use NODE_ENV=production. A separate variable such as APP_ENV names the deployment environment.

docs.title: 13. If a variable is exported in the shell and also set in .env, which wins with node --env-file=.env?
docs.text: The shell. Node's documentation says that if a variable is defined in the environment and in the file, the environment value takes precedence. The same is true by default for dotenv, Vite (for prefixed keys), Next.js, and Bun.

docs.title: 14. With two env files, which value wins in Node and in dotenv?
docs.text: With node --env-file=a.env --env-file=b.env, later files override earlier ones, so b.env wins. With dotenv.config({ path: ["a.env", "b.env"] }), the first value set wins, so a.env wins, unless override: true is set.

docs.title: 15. What is the precedence of Vite's env files?
docs.text: Highest first: variables already in the environment (for VITE_-prefixed keys), then .env.[mode].local, .env.[mode], .env.local, and .env. Only VITE_* keys reach client code, inlined at build time.

docs.title: 16. How does Next.js order its env files, and how does that differ from Vite?
docs.text: process.env, then .env.$(NODE_ENV).local, .env.local (skipped when NODE_ENV=test), .env.$(NODE_ENV), and .env. Next.js ranks .env.local above .env.production; Vite ranks .env.production above .env.local.

docs.title: 17. Which .env files does Bun load automatically?
docs.text: In increasing precedence: .env, .env.[NODE_ENV], .env.local (skipped in test), and .env.[NODE_ENV].local. --env-file replaces the automatic choice, and --no-env-file or env = false in bunfig.toml disables it. Bun also expands ${VAR} references.

docs.title: 18. What are the two uses of .env files in Docker Compose?
docs.text: A project .env (or --env-file) supplies values for ${VAR} interpolation in compose.yaml. The container's environment comes from environment: and env_file: entries. A key in the project .env does not reach the container unless the Compose file passes it on.

docs.title: 19. What is Docker Compose's precedence for a container's variables?
docs.text: Highest first: docker compose run -e; environment or env_file values interpolated from the shell or an environment file; plain environment values; env_file values; and ENV from the image.

docs.title: 20. Which parser edge cases can silently drop variables?
docs.text: Whitespace-only or tab-only lines (Node 22.12's loader merged the following key into a broken name in testing), a byte order mark corrupting the first key, an unclosed quote swallowing lines until the next quote (Node and Bun), and UTF-16 encoding (nothing loads). Keep files plain UTF-8, LF, without stray whitespace, and validate at startup.

docs.title: 21. Do Node's loader and dotenv expand ${VAR} references?
docs.text: No; both keep the text literally (tested). Bun, Vite (through dotenv-expand), and Next.js expand references to earlier variables; escape $ there when you need a literal dollar sign.

docs.title: 22. How do you debug "the variable is in the file but the app doesn't see it"?
docs.text: Ask the process: print each expected key with whether it is set and its shape, never its value. Check shell exports, which files load in the current mode, and the file's bytes (cat -A for whitespace and CRLF, a hex dump for a BOM, file for UTF-16), and compare loaders. In containers, check inside the container.

docs.title: 23. Should production use .env files?
docs.text: Generally no. Production configuration should come from the platform (Kubernetes, systemd, a PaaS) and secrets from a secret store, managed as code with access control and audit. .env files are a development convenience; implicit autoloading in production binaries makes behavior depend on the working directory.

docs.title: 24. What happens to import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL during a build?
docs.text: Vite replaces the expression with the literal string value from the build environment. The value is now part of the JavaScript files and cannot change without a rebuild.

docs.title: 25. Why are VITE_* and NEXT_PUBLIC_* values public?
docs.text: They are inlined into JavaScript that every visitor downloads, so anyone can read them in DevTools or source maps. Use them only for values meant to be public; route secret-backed operations through your backend.

docs.title: 26. How can one frontend build be promoted from staging to production?
docs.text: Keep environment-specific values out of the bundle: fetch a runtime config.json at startup, inject configuration into index.html from a server or edge function, write config from the container entrypoint, or call the API at a same-origin relative path so no URL is needed.

docs.title: 27. Does runtime configuration make frontend values secret?
docs.text: No. Runtime values are still sent to the browser. Runtime configuration solves promotion, not secrecy.

docs.title: 28. What is the difference between ARG and ENV in a Dockerfile?
docs.text: ARG exists during the build (and can persist in image metadata and history); ENV persists into the image and every container started from it. Neither is suitable for secrets; use ENV only for safe runtime defaults such as NODE_ENV=production.

docs.title: 29. How do you use a credential during a Docker build without leaking it?
docs.text: Use a BuildKit secret mount: RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc,target=/root/.npmrc npm ci with docker build --secret id=npmrc,src=.... The secret is available only in that step and is not stored in any layer.

docs.title: 30. Why should a container image contain no environment-specific values?
docs.text: So one image, identified by digest, can be tested, scanned, signed, and promoted to every environment, with the platform supplying configuration at start. Baked values force per-environment builds and can leak.

docs.title: 31. Why does process.env[name] return undefined in a Next.js client component?
docs.text: Only direct references such as process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_X are inlined at build time. Dynamic lookups and destructuring are not, so the browser has no value.

docs.title: 32. What configuration can safely be compiled into a mobile app?
docs.text: Only public values: public endpoints, publishable keys restricted to the app, feature defaults. Anything compiled in can be extracted from every device. Secrets stay on the backend, and values that must change after release come from remote configuration.

docs.title: 33. Which values are legitimately build-time?
docs.text: Facts about the build: version, commit, and constants that remove development-only code (import.meta.env.DEV). Environment facts (API URLs, database addresses) belong at runtime.

docs.title: 34. Why are environment variables an imperfect carrier for secrets?
docs.text: They are inherited by child processes, readable through process inspection by the same user or root, visible in container and pod metadata, easy to print in logs or CI output, readable by compromised dependencies, and static until restart.

docs.title: 35. What does a secret store add over environment variables?
docs.text: Encryption at rest, fine-grained access policies, versioning, audit logs of every read, rotation support, and in some stores dynamic, short-lived credentials.

docs.title: 36. Compare injecting secrets at deploy time with fetching them at startup.
docs.text: Deploy-time injection (CI or a sync controller writes a Kubernetes Secret or PaaS config) keeps app code simple but copies secrets to another place and needs a restart to rotate. Fetching at startup with the workload's identity avoids copies and audits each read, but the app depends on the store and needs caching and retries.

docs.title: 37. What is workload identity?
docs.text: An identity the platform gives a workload (a service account token, an instance role) that it can exchange for short-lived cloud credentials, so no long-lived key needs to be stored anywhere.

docs.title: 38. How does GitHub Actions OIDC federation with AWS work?
docs.text: The job requests an OIDC token (permissions: id-token: write), and aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials exchanges it with STS for a role whose trust policy checks the token's audience and subject (repository, branch, or environment). The job gets temporary credentials; no AWS key is stored in GitHub.

docs.title: 39. What are dynamic secrets?
docs.text: Credentials generated on demand with a lease, such as a database user created by Vault for one application instance and dropped when the lease ends. Leaked values expire automatically and are traceable to their holder.

docs.title: 40. Describe safe secret rotation.
docs.text: Create the new secret; make every verifier or server accept both old and new; switch every user of the secret to the new one; wait for anything issued with the old one to expire or drain; revoke the old one. Two valid secrets overlap, so nothing breaks.

docs.title: 41. How do you rotate a JWT signing key without logging users out?
docs.text: Put a key ID (kid) in each token, sign with the current key, and verify against a set of current and previous keys. Add the new key as accepted, then make it current, wait at least the token lifetime, then remove the old key.

docs.title: 42. What is the "alternating users" rotation strategy?
docs.text: Two database users exist; rotation changes the password of the user not currently in use and then switches the application to it. A valid credential exists at every moment. AWS Secrets Manager offers it as a managed rotation strategy.

docs.title: 43. Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted?
docs.text: Not by default: values are base64-encoded and stored in etcd, which should be configured with encryption at rest. Access is controlled by RBAC, and anyone who can create pods in a namespace can usually read its Secrets through a pod. Many teams sync them from an external store.

docs.title: 44. What do SOPS and Sealed Secrets do?
docs.text: SOPS encrypts values in YAML, JSON, .env, or INI files with keys protected by KMS, age, or PGP, so encrypted secrets can live in Git with readable diffs. Sealed Secrets encrypts a Kubernetes Secret with a cluster controller's public key so only that controller can decrypt it. Neither provides dynamic secrets or per-read audit.

docs.title: 45. Where should secret scanning run?
docs.text: Before commit (pre-commit hook), on push (push protection), in CI over history and new commits, on artifacts (container images, frontend bundles), and continuously through provider partner programs.

docs.title: 46. What is the first thing to do when a secret leaks?
docs.text: Revoke or rotate it, assuming it is already in an attacker's hands. Then check audit logs for misuse, contain any incident, remove the secret from where it leaked (including Git history), and prevent recurrence.

docs.title: 47. Why is purging a secret from Git history not enough?
docs.text: Forks, clones, CI caches, pull request references, and anyone who already fetched the repository still have it. History cleanup reduces future exposure; only rotation makes the leaked value useless.

docs.title: 48. A new release crashes in production with "Cannot read properties of undefined" an hour after deploy. Staging was fine. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the configuration the production process received, especially variables added in this release.

How to confirm: the key is missing in production, or present with a different shape; there was no startup validation.

Likely causes and fixes: a variable added to staging but not production. Add it, validate all configuration at startup, and compare variable names across environments in CI. See configuration fundamentals.

docs.title: 49. Staging started sending real emails to customers. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: EMAIL_ENABLED and the email credentials used by staging, and whether staging holds real customer data.

How to confirm: the flag defaulted to true or was parsed from "false" as truthy, and staging used a live provider key.

Likely causes and fixes: unsafe defaults, boolean parsing bugs, and shared credentials. Default side effects off, parse booleans strictly, use sandbox keys and allowlists outside production. See configuration fundamentals.

docs.title: 50. A developer edits .env, restarts, and the app still uses the old database. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the same variable is exported in the developer's shell or set by the IDE or a tool.

How to confirm: env | grep -c MONGODB_URI (count only) shows it is set before the app starts.

Likely causes and fixes: the existing environment wins over .env in Node, dotenv, Vite, Next.js, and Bun. Unset the stale export or use a fresh shell. See .env files and precedence.

docs.title: 51. MONGODB_URI works with dotenv but is missing with node --env-file. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the bytes of the file around that line.

How to confirm: cat -A .env shows a whitespace-only line just before it (this breaks Node 22.12's parser; Node 24 skips such lines), or the key checker shows a strange key name containing a newline; or the file starts with a BOM.

Likely causes and fixes: parser differences. Remove whitespace-only lines and the BOM, enforce .editorconfig, and validate at startup. See .env files and precedence.

docs.title: 52. A Docker Compose service does not see API_KEY, which is in the project .env. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether compose.yaml passes the variable to the service.

How to confirm: docker compose exec api printenv API_KEY is empty; the Compose file never references it.

Likely causes and fixes: the project .env is only for interpolating the Compose file. Add environment: API_KEY: ${API_KEY} or put it in an env_file:. See .env files and precedence.

docs.title: 53. The production frontend calls the staging API. How did this happen and how do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the API URL inside the deployed JavaScript bundle.

How to confirm: searching the built assets finds the staging host; the build was made once with staging values and promoted.

Likely causes and fixes: build-time inlining. Switch to runtime configuration or a relative /api path, or build per environment with a CI check of the inlined URL. See build-time vs runtime configuration.

docs.title: 54. A security researcher reports a payment API secret key in your JavaScript bundle. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which key it is and its permissions.

How to confirm: the key is in a VITE_* or NEXT_PUBLIC_* variable and appears in the built assets.

Likely causes and fixes: a secret placed in a public build-time variable. Revoke and rotate the key immediately, review its usage, move the operation to the backend, and add a bundle secret scan to CI. See build-time vs runtime configuration.

docs.title: 55. An image scanner flags a token in a Docker image layer. How did it get there?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Dockerfile's ARG, ENV, COPY, and RUN steps that touch credentials.

How to confirm: docker history --no-trunc shows the token in a build argument, or a layer contains a .npmrc or .env file.

Likely causes and fixes: ARG or ENV used for a build credential, or credential files copied in. Rotate the token, use a secret mount, add .dockerignore entries, and delete exposed images. See build-time vs runtime configuration.

docs.title: 56. After rotating the database password, every instance failed to connect for five minutes. How do you avoid that next time?
docs.text:
What to check first: the order of the rotation steps and how instances obtain credentials.

How to confirm: the old password was invalidated before instances picked up the new one.

Likely causes and fixes: rotation without overlap. Use alternating users or a dual-password window, and make instances refetch credentials on authentication errors. See secrets management.

docs.title: 57. A JWT signing key was replaced and all users were logged out. What should have happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether tokens carry a key ID and verifiers accept more than one key.

How to confirm: verification failures spiked at the deploy; old tokens were rejected.

Likely causes and fixes: single-key verification. Use kid, accept current and previous keys, switch signing, wait the token lifetime, then remove the old key. See secrets management.

docs.title: 58. GitHub reports a cloud access key committed to a public repository three days ago. What is your runbook?
docs.text:
What to check first: the key's permissions and the cloud audit logs since the commit time.

How to confirm: audit logs show whether anyone else used the key.

Likely causes and fixes: revoke the key immediately and issue a new one through a secret store; investigate any misuse as an incident; then purge the file from history; finally replace static keys with workload identity or OIDC and add pre-commit scanning. See secrets management.

docs.title: 59. A third-party CI provider announces a breach of customer environment variables. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which secrets your pipelines stored with that provider.

How to confirm: list the project and organization secrets and the period of exposure the provider reports.

Likely causes and fixes: treat every stored secret as compromised: rotate all of them, review their usage, and reduce what CI stores in future by using OIDC federation and short-lived credentials. See secrets management.

docs.title: 60. Only some API instances behave differently after a configuration change. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: the configuration fingerprint each instance logged at startup.

How to confirm: fingerprints differ between pods or hosts; some were not restarted or were edited by hand.

Likely causes and fixes: drift or a partial rollout of configuration. Redeploy all instances from configuration as code and stop manual edits. See configuration fundamentals.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Environment variables and secrets overview
  • Configuration fundamentals · .env files and precedence · Build-time vs runtime configuration · Secrets management
  • The Twelve-Factor App: Config
  • OWASP: Secrets Management Cheat Sheet

docs.title: Secrets Management
docs.text:
A secret is any value that grants access: a database password, an API key, a private key, a token. Secrets management is how an organization creates, stores, distributes, uses, rotates, audits, and revokes those values, so that the right workloads and people get exactly the access they need, for as short a time as practical, and a leak is noticed and contained quickly.

This lesson covers what counts as a secret, why environment variables are a common but imperfect way to deliver secrets, the main secret stores, injection patterns, workload identity and short-lived credentials, rotation with an overlap window, least privilege and audit, encrypting secrets in Git with SOPS and Sealed Secrets, secret scanning, and a runbook for when a secret leaks.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Leaked credentials are one of the most common starting points of breaches, and leaks rarely look dramatic: a key pasted into a config file and committed, a token printed in a CI log, an .env file copied into a Docker image, a secret in a frontend bundle. Automated scanners watch public repositories and package registries continuously, so a secret pushed to a public place should be treated as stolen within minutes.

Two well-documented incidents show how environment variables in particular become a target. In 2021, a modified Codecov uploader script sent the full env output of customers' CI jobs to an attacker's server for about two months. In January 2023, CircleCI reported that an attacker had exfiltrated customer environment variables, tokens, and keys, and asked every customer to rotate their secrets. In both cases, teams with short-lived credentials, narrow permissions, and practiced rotation had far less to clean up.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• CircleCI, January 2023. The incident report describes malware on an engineer's laptop stealing a 2FA-backed single sign-on session, access to customer environment variables, tokens, and keys (encrypted at rest, but the attacker extracted encryption keys from a running process), and the recommendation that customers rotate all secrets and treat those stored during the period as compromised.
  • Codecov, 2021. The security update explains that unauthorized changes to the Bash Uploader sent the output of env and git remote -v from customers' CI runners to an outside server from January 31 to April 1, 2021, and advises re-rolling all credentials that were in CI environment variables.
  • GitHub secret scanning. GitHub's documentation on secret scanning describes scanning repositories for known credential formats and push protection that blocks commits containing secrets before they reach the remote.
  • OWASP. The Secrets Management Cheat Sheet covers centralization, least privilege, automated rotation, dynamic secrets, auditing, and handling secrets in CI/CD and containers.
  • AWS Secrets Manager rotation. The rotation documentation describes managed rotation with versions labeled AWSCURRENT, AWSPENDING, and AWSPREVIOUS, and strategies such as alternating between two database users so a valid credential always exists.

Popular tools and providers: HashiCorp Vault and its open-source fork OpenBao, AWS Secrets Manager and Systems Manager Parameter Store, Google Cloud Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, Kubernetes Secrets with the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI Driver, SOPS, Sealed Secrets, Doppler, Infisical, 1Password, GitHub Actions secrets and OIDC, and secret scanners such as gitleaks, TruffleHog, and GitHub secret scanning.

docs.title: What counts as a secret
docs.text:
• Passwords and connection strings with credentials (MONGODB_URI with a user and password).
  • API keys and tokens for third parties (payments, email, SMS, AI APIs).
  • Signing and encryption keys: JWT signing keys, session secrets, webhook signing secrets, TLS private keys, code signing and update signing keys.
  • Cloud credentials: access keys, service account keys.
  • OAuth client secrets and refresh tokens.
  • SSH private keys and deploy keys.

Not secrets, though often treated as such: public API base URLs, publishable keys designed to be public, usernames without passwords. They still belong in configuration, not code.

docs.title: Environment variables: common, convenient, imperfect
docs.text:
Environment variables are the default way to hand a secret to a process, and for many teams that is acceptable. Know their weaknesses:

Weakness How it leaks Inherited by child processes Every subprocess, script, or tool the app starts receives all variables Readable by the same user and by root On Linux, /proc/<pid>/environ; process inspection tools Visible in platform metadata docker inspect, container definitions, Kubernetes pod specs to anyone allowed to read them Printed by debugging console.log(process.env), env in CI steps, error reports that capture the environment Captured by supply chain attacks A compromised dependency or CI step can read and send process.env, as in the Codecov incident Static Rotation needs a restart; nothing expires on its own

Mitigations: keep secrets out of logs (redact by key), avoid passing the full environment to child processes, prefer reading secrets from mounted files or fetching them at startup with the workload's own identity, and prefer short-lived credentials so a leaked value expires.

docs.title: Secret stores
docs.text: Store Notable features HashiCorp Vault / OpenBao Many secret engines, including dynamic secrets (per-request database users with leases), PKI, encryption as a service, fine-grained policies, audit devices; self-hosted or managed AWS Secrets Manager Versioned secrets, managed rotation through Lambda functions, IAM policies, CloudTrail audit, cross-account access AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Hierarchical parameters, SecureString encrypted with KMS, cheaper for simple values, no built-in rotation Google Cloud Secret Manager Versioned secrets, IAM per secret, rotation notifications, audit logs Azure Key Vault Secrets, keys, and certificates, with hardware-backed key options, RBAC, and logging Kubernetes Secrets Delivered to pods as files or variables; base64-encoded, not encrypted by default in etcd unless encryption at rest is configured; usually fed from an external store

docs.title: Injection patterns
docs.text:
Pattern How Pros Cons At deploy time CI or a sync controller (External Secrets Operator) copies secrets into the platform (Kubernetes Secret, PaaS config), exposed as variables or files App code stays simple Secrets are copied to another place; rotation needs a sync and a restart At startup The app uses its identity to fetch secrets with the store's SDK No copies; access is audited per workload Startup depends on the store; needs caching and retries Agent or sidecar Vault Agent or a CSI driver fetches secrets and writes files, refreshing them Apps read files; rotation without code changes Another component to run; apps must re-read files Per use with cache The app fetches on demand and caches with a TTL Picks up rotations quickly More calls; must handle store outages

Files in a memory-backed volume (tmpfs) are generally safer than variables: they are not inherited by child processes and do not appear in docker inspect.

docs.title: Workload identity and short-lived credentials
docs.text:
The most dangerous secret is the one that unlocks all the others: a long-lived cloud access key in a CI variable or a config file. Workload identity removes it.

  • In Kubernetes: a projected service account token is exchanged for cloud credentials (EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts, GKE Workload Identity, AKS Workload Identity).
  • On VMs: an instance role, delivered through the metadata service.
  • In CI: GitHub Actions and other CI systems issue OIDC tokens per job, which cloud IAM can trust for a specific repository, branch, or environment (example below).
  • Dynamic secrets: Vault's database engine creates a database user per application instance with a lease (for example one hour) and drops it when the lease ends. A leaked credential stops working on its own, and the audit log shows exactly which instance it belonged to.

docs.title: Rotation with an overlap window
docs.text:
Rotation replaces a secret with a new one. Done naively (change the value, restart everything) it causes an outage: some instances still use the old value while others already use the new one, or old tokens are rejected the moment the key changes. The safe pattern always has two valid secrets for a while:

  1. Create the new secret (v2). Nothing uses it yet.
  2. Accept both everywhere a secret is checked (token verifiers, webhook receivers, database accepting two users).
  3. Switch everything that uses the secret (signers, clients, connection pools) to v2.
  4. Wait for anything issued with v1 to expire or drain (the longest token lifetime, open connections).
  5. Revoke v1.

Concrete forms:

  • JWT signing keys: include a key ID (kid) in each token, sign with the current key, verify with any key in the current set (example below).
  • Database passwords: alternate between two database users (AWS calls this the "alternating users" strategy), or let the database accept the old and new password during the window where supported.
  • Third-party API keys: most providers allow two active keys; create the second, deploy it, then delete the first.
  • Webhook secrets: verify signatures against both secrets during the window.

docs.title: Least privilege and audit
docs.text:
• One secret per service and environment. TaskFlow API in staging and production use different database users, API keys, and signing keys.
  • Narrow policies. The production API role may read taskflow/prod/* and nothing else; CI deploy roles may not read application secrets at all.
  • Read-only where possible. Reporting jobs get a read-only database user.
  • Humans by exception. Engineers do not need production secrets for daily work; access is requested, time-limited, and logged ("break-glass").
  • Audit every read. Store audit logs where the secret's users cannot change them, and alert on unusual access (a new principal, a burst of reads, a read from an unexpected network).

docs.title: Encrypting secrets in Git: SOPS and Sealed Secrets
docs.text:
Sometimes teams want secrets versioned next to the configuration that uses them (GitOps). Two common approaches keep them encrypted in Git:

  • SOPS encrypts the values in YAML, JSON, .env, or INI files, leaving keys readable so diffs stay reviewable. The data key is protected by one or more master keys: a cloud KMS key, age, or PGP. Only identities allowed to use the master key can decrypt, at deploy time.
  • Sealed Secrets (for Kubernetes) encrypts a Secret with the public key of a controller running in the cluster (kubeseal). The resulting SealedSecret is safe to commit; only that controller can decrypt it into a normal Secret inside the cluster.

Both still require key management (who can decrypt, how keys rotate) and do not provide dynamic secrets or per-read audit. Many teams use them for low-volume, static secrets and an external store for the rest.

docs.title: Secret scanning
docs.text:
Scan at every stage, because each catches different mistakes:

  • Before commit: a pre-commit hook (gitleaks) blocks secrets on the developer's machine.
  • On push: platform push protection (GitHub) blocks known credential formats.
  • In CI: scan the full history and new commits; fail the build on findings.
  • In artifacts: scan container images and built frontend bundles for secrets that came in through files or build arguments.
  • Continuously: provider partner programs notify cloud and SaaS providers about leaked keys, which may revoke them automatically.

docs.title: When a secret leaks: the runbook
docs.text:
Order matters. Rotation comes first; history cleanup comes later.

  1. Revoke or rotate immediately. Assume the secret is already in an attacker's hands. Create a new secret, deploy it, revoke the old one, using the overlap pattern if there is time, or accept a short outage if there is not.
  2. Assess use. Check the provider's and store's audit logs for activity with the leaked credential since the earliest possible exposure time.
  3. Contain. If there was misuse, treat it as a security incident: block sources, review data access, notify as required.
  4. Remove from where it leaked. Delete it from the file, log, or image. Rewriting Git history (git filter-repo) helps reduce future exposure, but forks, clones, caches, and pull request refs may still contain it, which is why step 1 is not optional.
  5. Prevent recurrence. Add scanning where it was missed, move the secret to a store, shorten its lifetime, and write down what happened.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Reasonable approach Solo project, one server Environment variables from the process manager (EnvironmentFile with tight file permissions), never in Git; a password manager for humans Small team on a PaaS The platform's encrypted config variables; secret scanning on the repository Kubernetes on a cloud A cloud secret store plus External Secrets Operator or the CSI driver; workload identity; encryption at rest for etcd Multi-cloud, many services, strict compliance Vault or OpenBao with dynamic secrets, audit devices, and policies per service GitOps with a few static secrets SOPS or Sealed Secrets, with key access tightly controlled CI deploying to a cloud OIDC federation instead of stored cloud keys

Avoid building your own encryption scheme, sharing secrets over chat or email, and storing secrets in the same repository as code in plain text, even if the repository is private.

docs.title: Fetch a secret at startup with the workload's own identity
docs.text:
// src/secrets/aws.js: read secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, cached, no stored keys
import { SecretsManagerClient, GetSecretValueCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-secrets-manager";

// Region and credentials come from the environment: workload identity or instance role
const client = new SecretsManagerClient({});
const TTL_MS = 5 * 60_000;
const cache = new Map(); // secretId -> { value, expiresAt, pending }

export async function getSecretJson(secretId) {
  const entry = cache.get(secretId);
  if (entry?.value && entry.expiresAt > Date.now()) return entry.value;
  if (entry?.pending) return entry.pending; // one fetch at a time per secret

  const pending = client
    .send(new GetSecretValueCommand({ SecretId: secretId }))
    .then((out) => {
      const value = JSON.parse(out.SecretString);
      cache.set(secretId, { value, expiresAt: Date.now() + TTL_MS });
      return value;
    })
    .catch((err) => {
      if (entry?.value) {
        // Store unreachable: keep serving the last good value and retry later
        cache.set(secretId, { value: entry.value, expiresAt: entry.expiresAt });
        return entry.value;
      }
      cache.delete(secretId);
      throw err;
    });

  cache.set(secretId, { ...entry, pending });
  return pending;
}

// src/db.js: build the connection string from secret parts at startup
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import { getSecretJson } from "./secrets/aws.js";

export async function connectMongo() {
  // MONGODB_SECRET_ID is configuration ("taskflow/prod/mongodb"), not a secret
  const s = await getSecretJson(process.env.MONGODB_SECRET_ID);
  const uri = `mongodb+srv://${encodeURIComponent(s.username)}:${encodeURIComponent(s.password)}@${s.host}/taskflow`;
  const client = new MongoClient(uri, { serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5_000 });
  await client.connect();
  return client;
}

The process environment holds only the secret's name. If the database password is rotated with alternating users, an authentication failure is the signal to refetch the secret and reconnect.

docs.title: Rotating a JWT signing key without logging anyone out
docs.text:
// src/auth/jwt-keys.js: sign with the current key, accept current and previous
import { SignJWT, jwtVerify, errors } from "jose";

const enc = new TextEncoder();
const keys = new Map([[process.env.JWT_KEY_ID, enc.encode(process.env.JWT_SECRET)]]);
if (process.env.JWT_PREVIOUS_KEY_ID && process.env.JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET) {
  keys.set(process.env.JWT_PREVIOUS_KEY_ID, enc.encode(process.env.JWT_PREVIOUS_SECRET));
}
const currentKid = process.env.JWT_KEY_ID;

export function signAccessToken(userId) {
  return new SignJWT({ sub: userId })
    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "HS256", kid: currentKid })
    .setIssuedAt()
    .setExpirationTime("15m")
    .sign(keys.get(currentKid));
}

export async function verifyAccessToken(token) {
  const { payload } = await jwtVerify(
    token,
    async (header) => {
      const key = keys.get(header.kid);
      if (!key) throw new errors.JWSSignatureVerificationFailed("unknown key id");
      return key;
    },
    { algorithms: ["HS256"] },
  );
  return payload;
}

Rotation steps for TaskFlow API: deploy with the new key as JWT_PREVIOUS_* (verifiers accept it), then swap so the new key is current and the old one is previous (new tokens use the new key), wait at least 15 minutes (the token lifetime), then remove the previous key.

docs.title: GitHub Actions deploying to AWS without stored keys
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (excerpt)
permissions:
  id-token: write   # allow the job to request an OIDC token
  contents: read

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-deploy-production
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: ./scripts/deploy.sh production

The role's trust policy, trust-policy.json, accepts only this repository's production environment:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:oidc-provider/token.actions.githubusercontent.com"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com",
          "token.actions.githubusercontent.com:sub": "repo:example/taskflow:environment:production"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

There is no AWS key in GitHub at all. A job from another repository, or from a branch not deploying to the production environment, cannot assume the role.

docs.title: Dynamic database credentials with Vault
docs.text:
# Each instance gets its own short-lived database user
vault read database/creds/taskflow-api
# Key                Value
# lease_id           database/creds/taskflow-api/<lease-id>
# lease_duration     1h
# username           v-taskflow-api-<random>
# password           <generated>

vault lease revoke database/creds/taskflow-api/<lease-id>   # remove it early, for example on leak

docs.title: Encrypting a secrets file with SOPS
docs.text:
# .sops.yaml: which key encrypts which files
creation_rules:
  - path_regex: secrets/.*\.prod\.yaml$
    age: <production-age-recipient>
  - path_regex: secrets/.*\.staging\.yaml$
    age: <staging-age-recipient>

sops --encrypt --in-place secrets/api.prod.yaml   # values become ENC[AES256_GCM,...]
sops secrets/api.prod.yaml                         # edit in $EDITOR, re-encrypted on save
sops --decrypt secrets/api.prod.yaml | kubectl apply -f -   # at deploy time only

docs.title: Scanning for secrets before they leave the laptop and in CI
docs.text:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.1
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

gitleaks git --redact -v          # scan the repository history, hide secret values in output
gitleaks dir --redact -v dist/    # scan a built frontend bundle before publishing

docs.title: Purging a leaked file from history (after rotating it)
docs.text:
# 1. Rotate the secret first. Then, in a fresh clone:
git filter-repo --invert-paths --path config/production.json
git push --force --all && git push --force --tags
# 2. Ask collaborators to re-clone; contact the host to purge cached views if needed

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep secrets out of code, images, bundles, logs, and chat; store them in a secret store.
  • Give every service and environment its own secrets with narrow access.
  • Prefer workload identity and short-lived credentials over static keys, especially for CI.
  • Rotate with an overlap window; automate rotation where the store supports it; practice it.
  • Deliver secrets as files or fetch them at startup where possible; never print the environment.
  • Audit every read and alert on unusual access.
  • Scan for secrets at commit, push, CI, and artifact stages.
  • On a leak: rotate first, investigate second, clean history third.
  • Encrypt Kubernetes Secrets at rest and restrict who can read them.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A cloud key from CI appears in an attacker's activity. Detect: cloud audit logs show API calls from unknown networks with a CI key; billing spikes. Cause: a long-lived key in CI variables, exfiltrated by a compromised step or dependency. Fix: revoke the key, review activity, and switch CI to OIDC federation.
  • Rotating the database password caused an outage. Detect: authentication failures across instances right after rotation. Cause: the old password was invalidated while instances still used it. Fix: alternating users or a dual-password window, and instances that refetch credentials on authentication errors.
  • All users were logged out after a key change. Detect: a spike in token verification failures and sign-ins. Cause: the JWT signing key was replaced without accepting the old one. Fix: key IDs and a verification key set with current and previous keys.
  • A secret was found in a public repository's history. Detect: secret scanning or a provider notification. Cause: a committed config file or .env. Fix: rotate immediately, check usage, then purge history and add pre-commit scanning and push protection.
  • A token shows up in CI logs. Detect: log review or scanner alert. Cause: a debug env step or a tool echoing its configuration. Fix: rotate, remove the step, rely on the CI system's masking only as a safety net, and add log scanning.
  • The app cannot start because the secret store is down. Detect: startup failures with store timeouts. Cause: a hard dependency on fetching secrets at every start, without caching or retries. Fix: retries with backoff, longer-lived cached values for restarts, and multi-region store replicas where available.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Secret: a value that grants access to something.
  • Secret store: a system that stores secrets encrypted, controls access, versions them, and audits reads.
  • Injection: delivering a secret to a workload, as a variable, file, or fetched value.
  • Workload identity: an identity the platform gives a workload, which can be exchanged for credentials without a stored key.
  • OIDC federation: trusting tokens from an external identity provider (such as a CI system) to obtain cloud credentials.
  • Dynamic secret: a credential generated on demand with a lease and automatic expiry.
  • Rotation: replacing a secret with a new one.
  • Overlap window: the period when both old and new secrets are valid during rotation.
  • Least privilege: granting only the access a workload needs.
  • Secret scanning: automatically detecting secrets in code, history, logs, or artifacts.
  • Envelope encryption: encrypting data with a data key that is itself encrypted with a master key (used by SOPS and cloud KMS services).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating a private repository as a safe place for plaintext secrets.
  • Believing base64 in a Kubernetes Secret is encryption.
  • Rotating by replacing the value everywhere at once.
  • Purging Git history and skipping rotation.
  • Giving CI broad, long-lived cloud credentials.
  • Sharing one set of production credentials across services.
  • Logging process.env or full configuration objects.
  • Assuming CI log masking catches every format of a secret.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name four ways a secret in an environment variable can leak.
  2. Compare injecting secrets at deploy time with fetching them at startup.
  3. How does workload identity remove the need for a stored cloud key?
  4. Describe the five steps of rotating a secret with an overlap window, and apply them to a JWT signing key with a 15-minute token lifetime.
  5. Why must you rotate a leaked secret before cleaning Git history?
  6. What do SOPS and Sealed Secrets each protect, and what do they not provide compared with a secret store?
  7. What should the trust policy of a CI deploy role restrict?
  8. A team has 12 services in 3 environments, each needing a database credential and two API keys. How many distinct secrets should exist under least privilege, and why not fewer?

docs.title: Branching, Merging, and Rebasing
docs.text:
Branches let several lines of work proceed at once; merging and rebasing bring them back together. Every team uses these three operations dozens of times a day, and most painful Git incidents (lost work, duplicated commits, broken shared branches, bad conflict resolutions) come from misunderstanding them.

This lesson explains branches as movable pointers, fast-forward and three-way merges, merge commits, conflicts and the tools for resolving them, how rebase replays commits, interactive rebase for cleaning up a branch, the golden rule of rebasing, the trade-offs between merge, rebase, and squash merging, and cherry-picking.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: How you integrate branches shapes your history, and history is a working tool: git log, git blame, git bisect, and git revert all depend on it. A messy history full of "fix typo" and "WIP" commits makes bisecting and reviewing slow. Rewriting history that teammates already pulled causes duplicated commits and lost work. A conflict resolved carelessly can silently drop a bug fix. Knowing exactly what each operation does to the commit graph lets you choose the right one, keep main clean and deployable, and recover calmly when something goes wrong.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Linux kernel. The kernel's maintainer guide Rebasing and merging states that history exposed beyond your private system should usually not be changed, that you should not rebase a branch containing other people's history, and that the kernel community "is not scared by seeing merge commits", because at its scale avoiding merges would be nearly impossible.
  • The Git project itself. The gitworkflows manual describes how Git is developed: one topic branch per feature, topic branches merged into integration branches, and the rule that published history is not rewritten.
  • GitHub pull requests. GitHub's About merge methods page documents the three ways a pull request can land (merge commit, squash, rebase) and notes that GitHub's rebase-and-merge always creates new commit SHAs, even when a fast-forward would be possible.

Popular tools and providers: the Git CLI, GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket merge buttons, merge tools such as VS Code's merge editor, JetBrains IDEs, Meld, KDiff3, and Beyond Compare, and stacked-branch helpers such as Git's own rebase --update-refs.

docs.title: Branches are movable pointers
docs.text:
A branch is a ref that points to one commit. Creating a branch writes a new pointer; committing on a branch moves its pointer forward to the new commit. Nothing is copied.

git switch -c feat/task-due-dates    # create and switch (same as checkout -b)
git branch                           # list local branches, * marks HEAD
git branch -vv                       # with tip commit and upstream status
git switch main                      # move HEAD to another branch
git branch --merged main             # branches whose tips are reachable from main
git branch -d feat/task-due-dates    # delete only if merged
git branch -D experiment             # force delete (commits remain in the reflog)

Because branches are cheap, Git workflows use them for everything: one branch per feature, bug fix, or experiment, merged and deleted within days.

docs.title: Fast-forward and three-way merges
docs.text:
git merge <branch> integrates another branch into the current one. What happens depends on the shape of the graph.

Fast-forward. If the current branch has not moved since the other branch started (its tip is an ancestor of the other branch's tip), Git simply moves the pointer forward. No new commit is created and history stays linear.

Three-way merge. If both branches have new commits, Git finds the merge base (the best common ancestor, git merge-base main feature) and compares three snapshots: the base, "ours" (the current branch), and "theirs" (the branch being merged). For each region of each file:

Base vs ours Base vs theirs Result unchanged unchanged keep the base changed unchanged take ours unchanged changed take theirs changed changed identically take the change once changed changed differently conflict

The result is recorded as a merge commit with two parents.

You can control which kind you get:

git merge --ff-only feature   # fast-forward or fail: never creates a merge commit
git merge --no-ff feature     # always create a merge commit, even if ff is possible
git merge --squash feature    # stage the combined changes; you commit them yourself

Since Git 2.34 the default merge strategy is ort ("Ostensibly Recursive's Twin"), a faster rewrite of the older recursive strategy that also handles renames better. Two options are often confused:

  • -X ours / -X theirs are options to the strategy: merge normally, but resolve conflicting hunks in favor of one side.
  • -s ours is a different strategy: record a merge but keep our tree entirely, discarding all of their changes. It is rarely what you want.

docs.title: Merge commits and first-parent history
docs.text: A merge commit's first parent is the branch you were on; the second is the branch you merged. That ordering is useful: on a main where every change lands through a merged pull request, git log --first-parent main shows one entry per merged PR, hiding the individual branch commits. git revert -m 1 <merge> (see undoing mistakes) also relies on it.

docs.title: Conflicts and how to resolve them
docs.text:
A conflict means Git cannot decide; it is not an error. Git stops, writes conflict markers into the file, and records the three versions in the index (stages 1, 2, and 3). Here is a real conflict from TaskFlow API, where main changed the page size to 25 and a feature branch changed it to 50:

<<<<<<< HEAD
const PAGE_SIZE = 25;
=======
const PAGE_SIZE = 50;
>>>>>>> feat/bigger-pages
module.exports = { PAGE_SIZE };

With merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3 (or diff3), Git also shows the common ancestor, which often reveals the right answer:

<<<<<<< HEAD
const PAGE_SIZE = 25;
||||||| 555a272
const PAGE_SIZE = 20;
=======
const PAGE_SIZE = 50;
>>>>>>> feat/bigger-pages
module.exports = { PAGE_SIZE };

Now you can see both sides changed the original value 20, so the team must decide. The resolution workflow:

  1. git status lists the conflicted paths ("both modified").
  2. Edit each file to the correct final content and delete all markers. An editor or merge tool helps (git mergetool).
  3. Run the tests. A merge that compiles can still be wrong.
  4. git add <file> marks it resolved (stage 0 again).
  5. git commit (for a merge) or git rebase --continue (for a rebase). git merge --abort or git rebase --abort returns to where you started.

To take one side wholesale for a file, git restore --ours <file> or git restore --theirs <file> (or git checkout --ours/--theirs). During a rebase the sides are swapped: "ours" is the branch you are rebasing onto and "theirs" is your commit being replayed. Check before you choose.

git mergetool opens each conflicted file in a configured three-way tool. For VS Code:

git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait --merge $REMOTE $LOCAL $BASE $MERGED'
git mergetool

git rerere ("reuse recorded resolution") remembers how you resolved a conflict and replays that resolution automatically the next time the same conflict appears, which helps when you rebase a long branch repeatedly or test-merge the same branches often.

git config --global rerere.enabled true
# resolve a conflict once; Git records it in .git/rr-cache
# next time: "Resolved 'config.js' using previous resolution."
git rerere forget config.js   # if a recorded resolution was wrong

docs.title: Rebase: replaying commits
docs.text:
git rebase main (run on feature) moves the branch so it starts from the tip of main:

  1. Find the commits on feature that are not on main (main..feature).
  2. Save the current tip as ORIG_HEAD, then check out the tip of main.
  3. Re-apply each commit's changes in order, creating a new commit for each one. A commit's hash covers its parent, so every replayed commit gets a new hash even if its changes are identical.
  4. Move feature to the last new commit.

Commits whose changes already exist upstream (same patch, for example a cherry-picked fix) are skipped automatically.

If a replayed commit conflicts, the rebase pauses on that commit. Resolve, git add, then git rebase --continue; or git rebase --skip to drop that commit, or git rebase --abort to restore the original branch. Because commits are replayed one at a time, a conflict in a file touched by five of your commits can mean resolving it up to five times (rerere helps).

--onto gives full control over the new base. To move only the commits of feature-b that are not in feature-a onto main:

git rebase --onto main feature-a feature-b

docs.title: Interactive rebase
docs.text:
git rebase -i <base> opens a todo list of the commits after <base>, oldest first, and lets you rewrite them before anyone else sees them:

Command Effect pick Keep the commit as is reword Keep the changes, edit the message edit Stop after applying, so you can amend or split the commit squash Meld into the previous commit and combine both messages fixup Meld into the previous commit and discard this message drop Remove the commit exec Run a shell command, stopping if it fails update-ref Move another branch to this point (used by --update-refs)

Reordering lines reorders commits. Autosquash automates the common "fix an earlier commit" case:

git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d          # creates "fixup! Add dueDate field"
git rebase -i --autosquash main     # the fixup is moved under a1b2c3d and marked fixup
git config --global rebase.autoSquash true   # make it the default

git rebase -i --exec "npm test" main runs the tests after every commit, proving each commit builds on its own (which keeps git bisect useful). For stacked branches (feat-api built on feat-model), git rebase --update-refs rebases the top branch and moves the lower branch pointers along with it.

docs.title: The golden rule
docs.text:
Do not rebase commits that exist outside your repository and that others may have built on. Rebasing creates new commits and abandons the old ones. Anyone who based work on the old commits now has a diverged history; when they pull, Git sees two sets of commits with the same changes and different hashes, producing duplicates and repeated conflicts.

In practice:

  • Rebase your own local commits and your own pushed feature branch freely (then push with git push --force-with-lease).
  • Never rebase or force-push main, release branches, or a branch someone else is committing to. Protect them with branch protection rules that block force pushes.
  • To update a shared branch, merge (or use the platform's "Update branch" button) instead.

docs.title: Merge commit, squash, or rebase?
docs.text:
Pull requests can land on main in three ways, and each produces a different history:

Merge commit Squash and merge Rebase and merge Commits added to main All branch commits + one merge commit One new commit Copies of all branch commits History shape Non-linear, shows branches Linear Linear Original hashes preserved Yes No No Revert a whole PR git revert -m 1 <merge> git revert <sha> Revert each commit (or a range) git bisect granularity Fine (each commit) One commit per PR Fine (each commit) Needs clean branch commits Yes, every commit lands on main (WIP commits hurt bisect) No Yes, every commit lands on main Common in Large projects, kernel-style trees Most product teams on GitHub Teams that curate commits

A practical default for application teams: squash and merge with the PR title as a Conventional Commit message (see versioning, tags, and releases), so main gets one meaningful, revertable commit per PR. Use merge commits when branch history matters (long-lived release branches, integrating large subsystems), and rebase-merge when your team writes carefully curated commits.

One side effect of squash merging: the branch's original commits never become reachable from main, so git branch -d refuses to delete the local branch (use -D once you have confirmed the PR merged), and a branch stacked on top of it must be rebased with --onto.

docs.title: Cherry-pick
docs.text:
git cherry-pick <sha> applies the changes of one commit as a new commit on the current branch. It is the tool for backporting: a fix merged to main also needs to reach the release/2.3 branch.

git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 4f9e2c1        # -x appends "(cherry picked from commit 4f9e2c1...)"
git cherry-pick main~3..main      # a range: the last three commits of main (start excluded)
git cherry-pick -m 1 <merge-sha>  # pick a merge, diffing against its first parent

The new commit has a different hash; -x records the link so reviewers and tools can trace it. Cherry-picking is for moving individual fixes, not for keeping two branches in sync; doing that routinely creates duplicate commits and confusing conflicts.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Use Avoid Bring your private feature branch up to date with main git rebase main (or git pull --rebase) Merging main in repeatedly, which adds noise merge commits Update a branch others also commit to git merge main Rebase plus force push Clean up "WIP" and "fix typo" commits before review git rebase -i with fixup/squash Pushing them to main Land a PR on a product team's main Squash and merge Merging branches full of WIP commits Keep a record of when a large branch was integrated git merge --no-ff Squash (loses the branch's commits) Ship a fix from main to a release branch git cherry-pick -x Merging all of main into the release branch Move a branch that was built on another branch git rebase --onto Manual re-creation of commits Undo a commit already on main git revert Rebasing it out of shared history

docs.title: Resolve a conflict end to end
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull
git merge feat/bigger-pages
# CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in config.js
git status --short
# UU config.js                         <- both modified

git diff                               # shows the conflict hunks
# edit config.js: agree on PAGE_SIZE = 50, delete the markers
npm test                               # prove the merged result works
git add config.js
git commit                             # message pre-filled: "Merge branch 'feat/bigger-pages'"
git show --remerge-diff HEAD           # Git 2.36+: how the resolution differs from an automatic merge

--remerge-diff re-runs the merge and shows only what the human changed while resolving, which is exactly what a reviewer of a merge commit needs to check.

docs.title: Keep a feature branch current
docs.text:
# Option A: rebase (your branch only)
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main                 # replay your commits on the latest main
npm test
git push --force-with-lease            # refuses if someone else pushed meanwhile

# Option B: merge (shared branch, or you prefer not to rewrite)
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
git push

--force-with-lease overwrites the remote branch only if it still points where your remote-tracking ref says it does. Plain --force would silently delete a teammate's pushed commits.

docs.title: Tidy a branch before review with fixups
docs.text:
git log --oneline main..
# 9c1d2e3 Add tests
# 7b6a5f4 fix typo
# 3e2d1c0 Add dueDate field

# Found a bug in the first commit? Commit the fix as a fixup of it:
git add src/models/task.js
git commit --fixup=3e2d1c0
git rebase -i --autosquash main        # the todo list is pre-arranged; save and close
git log --oneline main..
# 5a4b3c2 Add tests
# 1f0e9d8 Add dueDate field             <- now includes the fix
git push --force-with-lease

docs.title: Backport a hotfix to a release branch
docs.text:
git switch release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x 4f9e2c1             # the fix already merged on main
npm test
git push origin release/2.3
git tag -a v2.3.1 -m "TaskFlow API 2.3.1" && git push origin v2.3.1

docs.title: Move a stacked branch after its base was squash-merged
docs.text:
feat-api was built on feat-model. feat-model was squash-merged into main, so its original commits will never appear in main. Move only the feat-api commits:

git fetch origin
git rebase --onto origin/main feat-model feat-api
# commits in feat-api that are not in feat-model now sit on origin/main
git push --force-with-lease origin feat-api

docs.title: Check that a rebase changed nothing unexpected
docs.text:
git rebase origin/main
git range-diff origin/main ORIG_HEAD HEAD
# 1:  3e2d1c0 = 1:  9a8b7c6 Add dueDate field      <- "=" identical change
# 2:  9c1d2e3 ! 2:  5d4e3f2 Add tests              <- "!" changed while resolving

git range-diff compares the two versions of the series commit by commit, so you can review exactly what conflict resolution altered.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep branches short-lived (hours to a few days) and small; the longer a branch lives, the bigger the conflicts.
  • Integrate from main often, by rebase for private branches and merge for shared ones.
  • Enable merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3 and rerere.enabled = true.
  • Run tests after every conflict resolution, before committing.
  • Choose one PR merge method per repository and enforce it in the repository settings.
  • Never rebase or force-push shared branches; protect main and release branches against force pushes.
  • Use --force-with-lease, never bare --force, on your own branches.
  • Use cherry-pick -x for backports so the source commit is traceable.
  • Write commits that build and pass tests on their own, so bisect and revert stay useful.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Teammates get duplicate commits and repeated conflicts after pulling. Detect: git log --oneline --cherry-mark main...origin/main shows pairs of equivalent commits (=) with different hashes. Cause: someone rebased and force-pushed a branch others had pulled. Fix: agree on the correct remote state, have each person rebase their own new commits onto it with git rebase --onto, and enable branch protection to block force pushes on shared branches.
  • A bug fix "disappeared" after a merge. Detect: git log -S "<removed line>" shows the fix landed, and git show --remerge-diff <merge-sha> shows the resolution dropped it. Cause: a conflict resolved by taking one side wholesale. Fix: restore the fix in a new commit, require tests to pass on the merge result (merge queue or "require branches to be up to date"), and review merge resolutions.
  • Every dependency PR conflicts in package-lock.json. Detect: conflicts appear only in the lockfile. Cause: parallel branches each regenerate the lockfile. Fix: resolve package.json by hand, then run npm install --package-lock-only to regenerate a merged lockfile instead of editing it; group dependency updates so fewer PRs touch it at once.
  • git branch -d refuses to delete branches that were merged on GitHub. Detect: "error: the branch 'feat/x' is not fully merged". Cause: the PR was squash- or rebase-merged, so the original commits are not reachable from main. Fix: confirm the PR is merged, then git branch -D; enable "Automatically delete head branches" on the repository.
  • A long-lived branch takes hours to rebase. Detect: the same conflicts recur commit after commit. Cause: weeks of divergence and many commits touching the same files. Fix: squash the branch first, or merge main in once instead of rebasing, enable rerere, and split future work into shorter branches behind feature flags.
  • main contains "WIP" and "fix tests" commits that break git bisect. Detect: bisect lands on commits that do not build. Cause: rebase-merging or merge commits of uncurated branches. Fix: switch the repository to squash merging, or require authors to clean up with rebase -i --exec "npm test" before merging.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Branch: A movable ref pointing to the tip commit of a line of work.
  • Merge base: The best common ancestor of two commits, used for three-way merges.
  • Fast-forward: Moving a branch pointer forward along existing history without creating a commit.
  • Three-way merge: Combining two branches by comparing each with their merge base.
  • Merge commit: A commit with two or more parents.
  • First parent: The parent that was the current branch when the merge was made.
  • Conflict: A region both sides changed differently, needing a human decision.
  • Rebase: Replaying commits on a new base, producing new commits.
  • Interactive rebase: A rebase driven by an editable todo list to reorder, squash, edit, or drop commits.
  • Autosquash: Automatically placing fixup! and squash! commits next to their targets.
  • Squash merge: Combining a branch's changes into a single new commit with one parent.
  • Cherry-pick: Applying the changes of an existing commit as a new commit elsewhere.
  • rerere: Git's record of conflict resolutions, reused automatically.
  • ORIG_HEAD: A ref Git sets before risky operations (rebase, reset, merge) to the previous tip.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking rebase "moves" commits. It creates new ones and abandons the originals.
  • Rebasing a shared branch and force-pushing it.
  • Using git push --force instead of --force-with-lease.
  • Confusing -X ours (prefer ours on conflicts) with -s ours (discard their changes entirely).
  • Forgetting that "ours" and "theirs" swap during a rebase.
  • Committing conflict markers because git add was run without checking the file (a pre-commit check for <<<<<<< helps).
  • Believing a clean merge means a correct merge; two changes can merge without conflict and still break each other at runtime.
  • Cherry-picking routinely between long-lived branches instead of merging or fixing the branching strategy.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. When does git merge fast-forward, and how do you force or forbid a merge commit?
  2. Explain how a three-way merge decides each region of a file, using the merge base.
  3. Your feature branch has 12 commits; 4 of them edit the same function that main also changed. Roughly how many times might you resolve that conflict with git rebase main, and with git merge main? What reduces the work?
  4. Why does every rebased commit get a new hash, even when its changes are identical?
  5. State the golden rule of rebasing and describe what happens to a teammate when it is broken.
  6. Compare merge commit, squash merge, and rebase merge in terms of history shape, reverting a whole PR, and bisect granularity.
  7. What do fixup, squash, and reword do in an interactive rebase, and how does --autosquash help?
  8. When is git cherry-pick -x the right tool, and when is it a symptom of a bad branching strategy?
