docs.title: Branching Strategies
docs.text:
A branching strategy is a team agreement about where work happens, how long branches live, how changes reach the main line, and how releases and fixes are cut. Git does not enforce any of it; the strategy lives in team habits, branch protection rules, and CI configuration.

This lesson covers trunk-based development with short-lived branches and feature flags, GitHub flow, GitFlow and why many teams moved away from it, release branches for versioned, desktop, and mobile products, the environment-branch anti-pattern, how to choose by team size and release cadence, and how the choice shows up in your CI/CD pipeline and DORA metrics.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The branching strategy sets the batch size of integration. When branches live for weeks, every merge is large, conflicts pile up, testing happens late, and releases need stabilization phases and code freezes. When everyone integrates small changes into one main line every day, problems surface while they are small and cheap, and any commit can become a release. DORA's research links these practices directly to delivery performance: the strategy you pick influences how fast changes reach users and how often releases fail. It also determines how simple your CI triggers, deployment pipelines, and hotfix process can be.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• DORA research. DORA's trunk-based development capability reports that teams achieve higher delivery and operational performance when they have three or fewer active branches, merge branches to trunk at least once a day, and have no code freezes or integration phases. It calls trunk-based development a required practice for continuous integration.
  • GitFlow's author. Vincent Driessen's 2010 post A successful Git branching model defined GitFlow. In a 2020 "note of reflection" at the top of the same post he recommends that teams doing continuous delivery of web apps adopt a much simpler workflow such as GitHub flow, and keep GitFlow for explicitly versioned software or when several versions must be supported in the wild.
  • GitHub flow. GitHub documents GitHub flow as a lightweight, branch-based workflow: create a branch, make changes, open a pull request, address review comments, merge, and delete the branch.
  • Martin Fowler's patterns catalogue. Patterns for Managing Source Code Branches describes mainline, healthy branch, release branch, environment branch, and integration frequency as named patterns, with the trade-offs that explain why high-frequency integration usually wins.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub and GitLab branch protection and rulesets, merge queues, feature flag services (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Flagsmith) and the vendor-neutral OpenFeature API, and release automation such as release-please and semantic-release.

docs.title: What a strategy decides
docs.text: Question Trunk-based GitHub flow GitFlow Release branches Where does daily work land? main main via PRs develop main How long do work branches live? Hours to 1-2 days Days Days to weeks Hours to days Long-lived branches main only main only main and develop main plus one per supported release How is a release made? Tag or deploy any green main commit Deploy main after merge release/* branch, merged to main and tagged Cut release/x.y, stabilize, tag How does a hotfix ship? Fix on main, deploy Fix on main via PR, deploy hotfix/* from main, merged to main and develop Fix on main, cherry-pick to release branch Unfinished features Hidden behind feature flags Kept on the branch, or flags Kept on the feature branch Hidden behind flags

docs.title: Trunk-based development
docs.text:
In trunk-based development (TBD), every developer integrates into one shared branch, the trunk (main), at least daily. Small teams may commit to main directly after local tests; most teams use very short-lived branches and pull requests that merge within a day. CI runs on every change, and keeping main green is everyone's first priority: if a merge breaks the build, it is fixed or reverted within minutes.

Large features still ship in small slices, using two techniques:

  • Feature flags (toggles): the code for an unfinished feature is merged but switched off, so it is deployed "dark" and turned on later, possibly for a percentage of users. Deploying code and releasing a feature become separate decisions. Flags carry a cost: every flag is a branch in the code that must be tested and later removed. See feature flags and progressive delivery.
  • Branch by abstraction: to replace a component (say, the TaskFlow notification sender), first introduce an interface in front of the old implementation, build the new implementation behind it in small merged steps, switch callers over, then delete the old code. The main line stays releasable throughout.

TBD needs a solid safety net: fast automated tests, quick code review, and the discipline to keep changes small. Without that net, merging to main daily just spreads breakage faster.

docs.title: GitHub flow
docs.text:
GitHub flow is a simple branch-per-change workflow built around pull requests. Its one rule is that main is always deployable.

  1. Create a descriptively named branch from main.
  2. Commit and push.
  3. Open a pull request, early as a draft if you want feedback.
  4. CI runs and teammates review; push fixes to the same branch.
  5. Merge into main once checks pass and reviewers approve.
  6. Deploy main (usually automatically) and delete the branch.

GitHub flow and trunk-based development converge when branches are short: a team that merges small PRs several times a day is doing trunk-based development with pull requests. The difference shows when branches start living for a week; GitHub flow tolerates that, TBD does not.

docs.title: GitFlow
docs.text:
GitFlow uses two long-lived branches and three kinds of supporting branches:

Branch Branches from Merges into Purpose main (permanent) (permanent) Released code only; every commit is a tagged release develop main (permanent) Integration branch for the next release feature/* develop develop One feature, often long-lived release/* develop main and develop Stabilize, bump version, release hotfix/* main main and develop Urgent fix to the released version

GitFlow brought order to teams that shipped boxed or scheduled releases, and it still fits software that is explicitly versioned with long QA cycles. Many web teams moved away from it because:

  • Integration is delayed. Work sits on feature branches and on develop; main sees it only at release time, so problems surface late and in large batches.
  • Merges multiply. Release and hotfix branches must be merged twice; a forgotten merge back to develop makes a fix silently disappear from the next release.
  • It fights continuous delivery. If every merge to main can be deployed, a separate develop and release branches add ceremony without adding safety.
  • History is complex, which makes bisecting and reasoning about "what is in production" harder.

docs.title: Release branches for versioned products
docs.text:
Desktop applications, mobile apps, on-premises products, SDKs, and libraries often have several versions in use at once, and mobile builds pass through app store review before reaching users. These teams usually combine trunk-based development with release branches:

  • Development always happens on main.
  • At release time, cut release/2.3 from a green main commit. Only stabilization fixes go there; new features keep landing on main.
  • Fixes follow upstream first: land on main, then cherry-pick to each supported release branch (git cherry-pick -x). Fixing only the release branch guarantees the bug returns in the next release.
  • Every shipped build is a tag on the release branch (v2.3.0, v2.3.1).
  • Release branches are never merged back into main; they are deleted or archived when the version leaves support.

The release-branch process for desktop and mobile apps continues in releasing desktop and mobile apps.

docs.title: Environment branches: an anti-pattern
docs.text:
Some teams map branches to environments: dev, staging, and prod, and "deploy" by merging from one to the next. This looks tidy but causes problems:

  • Drift. The branches diverge through hotfixes, reverts, and partial merges, so what was tested in staging is not what reaches production.
  • Rebuilds per environment. Each branch builds its own artifact, so production runs a binary that was never tested.
  • Merge noise and conflicts between branches that should contain the same code.
  • Configuration in code. Environment differences end up as code differences on branches instead of configuration.

The fix is to build once from main, then promote the same artifact through environments with environment-specific configuration injected at deploy time. See artifacts and environment promotion and environments and promotion.

docs.title: Choosing by team size and release cadence
docs.text: Context Good fit Why 1-5 developers, web service, deploy on merge Trunk-based (direct commits or tiny PRs) Minimal ceremony; review by pairing or quick PRs 5-50 developers, SaaS, continuous deployment GitHub flow trending to trunk-based, with a merge queue PRs give review and checks; short branches keep integration daily Hundreds of developers, monorepo Trunk-based with merge queues, flags, and strong CI Only constant integration scales; long branches would never merge Mobile or desktop app, weekly or monthly releases Trunk + release branches Store review and installed versions need stable release lines Library or SDK with LTS versions Trunk + release branches per major version Security fixes must reach older versions Regulated release trains with long manual QA GitFlow or release branches The process requires a stabilization branch; accept the cost Open source with outside contributors GitHub flow from forks PRs from forks are the contribution model

docs.title: How strategy affects CI/CD and DORA metrics
docs.text:
Four of DORA's five delivery metrics (deployment frequency, change lead time, change fail rate, and failed deployment recovery time; see continuous integration fundamentals and measuring delivery performance) respond directly to branching:

  • Change lead time includes the time a commit waits on a branch. A commit that waits on develop for a two-week release cycle has a lead time of weeks, however fast the pipeline is.
  • Deployment frequency is capped by how often releasable code reaches the release branch. Trunk-based teams can deploy every merge.
  • Change fail rate usually improves with small batches: a 50-line change is easier to review, test, and diagnose than a 5,000-line release merge.
  • Recovery time improves when a fix travels the normal path (PR to main to deploy) in minutes, instead of a special hotfix process.

The strategy also shapes the pipeline itself: which branches trigger CI, which trigger deployments, whether a merge queue is needed to keep main green, and whether artifacts are promoted from main or rebuilt from several long-lived branches.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Strategy Use when Avoid when Trunk-based development One production version, fast CI, team comfortable with flags and small changes Tests are slow or flaky and reviews take days (fix those first) GitHub flow Most web teams and open source; PR review is valued Branches routinely live for weeks; you need parallel supported versions GitFlow Explicitly versioned software with scheduled releases and long QA Continuous delivery of a web app Release branches Several versions supported at once, app store releases, LTS A single always-current web service (adds unneeded branches) Environment branches Never as a deployment mechanism Always: promote artifacts instead

docs.title: A minimal feature flag in TaskFlow API
docs.text:
Merge the due-dates feature to main while it is unfinished, turned on for a percentage of users through configuration:

// src/flags.js: minimal percentage-based feature flags
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

// Percent of users (0-100) who get each feature, from configuration
const FLAGS = {
  taskDueDates: Number(process.env.FLAG_TASK_DUE_DATES_PERCENT ?? 0),
};

// Stable bucket 0-99 for a user and flag, so a user always gets the same answer
function bucket(flag, userId) {
  const digest = createHash("sha256").update(`${flag}:${userId}`).digest();
  return digest.readUInt32BE(0) % 100;
}

export function isEnabled(flag, userId) {
  const percent = FLAGS[flag] ?? 0;
  if (percent >= 100) return true;
  if (percent <= 0 || !userId) return false;
  return bucket(flag, userId) < percent;
}

// src/routes/tasks.js (excerpt)
import { isEnabled } from "../flags.js";

router.post("/", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const task = { title: req.body.title, ownerId: req.user.id };
    if (isEnabled("taskDueDates", req.user.id) && req.body.dueDate) {
      task.dueDate = new Date(req.body.dueDate); // new behavior, dark by default
    }
    const created = await req.app.locals.db.collection("tasks").insertOne(task);
    res.status(201).json({ id: created.insertedId, ...task });
  } catch (err) {
    next(err);
  }
});

With FLAG_TASK_DUE_DATES_PERCENT=0 the code is deployed but inactive; raise it to 10, then 100, then delete the flag and the old path. Teams with many flags use a flag service or the OpenFeature SDK instead of environment variables, so flags change without a redeploy.

docs.title: CI triggers for trunk-based development with release branches
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (trigger section)
on:
  pull_request:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]   # PRs into main or any release branch
  push:
    branches: [main, "release/**"]   # every merge is built and tested
    tags: ["v*"]                     # version tags trigger the release job

There is no develop, staging, or prod branch to trigger on: the pipeline builds main once and promotes the artifact, while release branches build only the versions they ship. Pipelines are covered in pipeline design.

docs.title: Cutting and patching a release branch
docs.text:
# Cut release/2.3 from a known-green commit on main
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git switch -c release/2.3
git push -u origin release/2.3
git tag -a v2.3.0 -m "TaskFlow 2.3.0" && git push origin v2.3.0

# Later: a fix merged on main (upstream first) is backported
git switch release/2.3 && git pull --ff-only
git cherry-pick -x 4f9e2c1
git push
git tag -a v2.3.1 -m "TaskFlow 2.3.1" && git push origin v2.3.1

docs.title: GitFlow with plain Git commands
docs.text:
If your process requires GitFlow, you do not need special tooling:

# start a feature
git switch develop && git switch -c feature/task-labels

# finish it (usually through a PR into develop)
git switch develop && git merge --no-ff feature/task-labels

# cut and finish a release
git switch -c release/1.1 develop
# ...bump version, fix bugs...
git switch main && git merge --no-ff release/1.1 && git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "1.1.0"
git switch develop && git merge --no-ff release/1.1   # the merge teams forget
git branch -d release/1.1

# hotfix from main
git switch -c hotfix/1.1.1 main
# ...fix...
git switch main && git merge --no-ff hotfix/1.1.1 && git tag -a v1.1.1 -m "1.1.1"
git switch develop && git merge --no-ff hotfix/1.1.1

docs.title: Migrating from GitFlow to trunk-based development
docs.text:
1. Make main the default branch and the merge target for new PRs; stop creating new feature branches from develop.
  2. Merge develop into main one last time, then archive develop.
  3. Introduce feature flags for work that cannot ship yet.
  4. Speed up CI until a PR gets a result in about 10 minutes, and fix or quarantine flaky tests.
  5. Set a branch age limit (for example, two days) and track it.
  6. Deploy from main automatically to staging, then to production with an approval, and keep release branches only if you support multiple versions.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep work branches short-lived: merge at least daily where possible.
  • Keep main releasable at all times; treat a red main as a stop-the-line event.
  • Use feature flags or branch by abstraction instead of long-lived feature branches, and remove flags once rolled out.
  • Land fixes upstream first, then backport to release branches with cherry-pick -x.
  • Never use branches to represent environments; promote one artifact.
  • Protect long-lived branches (no force pushes, required reviews and checks), as covered in pull requests and code review.
  • Write the strategy down in CONTRIBUTING.md, and encode it in branch protection and CI triggers so the tools enforce it.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The week before each release is "merge hell". Detect: conflict counts and failed builds spike before release dates; release branches need days of stabilization. Cause: long-lived feature branches integrating late. Fix: move to short-lived branches with daily integration and hide unfinished work behind flags.
  • A bug fixed in a hotfix reappears in the next release. Detect: the same issue is reopened after the next scheduled release; git branch --contains <fix-sha> shows the fix is not on develop or main. Cause: a hotfix or release branch was not merged back, or a fix was made only on a release branch. Fix: upstream first (fix on main, then cherry-pick), and automate the merge-back check in CI.
  • Staging passed, production failed with the "same" code. Detect: git diff staging prod between environment branches is not empty, or the image digests differ. Cause: environment branches drifted, or each environment rebuilt its own artifact. Fix: delete environment branches; build once and promote the same artifact by digest.
  • main is red for hours and nobody can merge. Detect: the main branch status check stays failed; PRs queue up. Cause: PRs passed against an older main and broke when combined. Fix: revert the breaking merge immediately, then require branches to be up to date or adopt a merge queue.
  • Lead time is measured in weeks despite a 10-minute pipeline. Detect: DORA change lead time far exceeds pipeline duration; commits wait on develop or release branches. Cause: batching in the branching model. Fix: deploy from main continuously; keep release branches only for genuinely versioned products.
  • Feature flags pile up and nobody knows which are safe to remove. Detect: dozens of flags permanently at 100% or 0%. Cause: no removal step in the process. Fix: give each flag an owner and an expiry date, and add flag removal to the definition of done.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Trunk / mainline: The single shared branch everyone integrates into, usually main.
  • Trunk-based development: Integrating small changes into trunk at least daily, with short-lived branches or direct commits.
  • Short-lived branch: A branch merged within about a day.
  • Feature flag (toggle): Runtime configuration that turns a code path on or off without a deploy.
  • Dark launch: Deploying code that is present but not active for users.
  • Branch by abstraction: Replacing a component behind an interface in small, always-releasable steps.
  • GitHub flow: Branch, pull request, review, merge, deploy; main is always deployable.
  • GitFlow: A model with main, develop, and feature, release, and hotfix branches.
  • Release branch: A branch cut for one version, receiving only fixes.
  • Upstream first: Fixing on main before backporting to release branches.
  • Environment branch: A branch per deployment environment; an anti-pattern for deployment.
  • Code freeze: A period when no new changes may merge; a symptom of late integration.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing GitFlow is "the standard". Its own author recommends simpler flows for continuously delivered software.
  • Calling a workflow trunk-based while branches live for weeks.
  • Merging unfinished features without a flag, or leaving flags in the code forever.
  • Fixing a bug only on a release branch.
  • Using branches to model environments and rebuilding per environment.
  • Assuming direct commits to main mean no review; trunk-based teams review through pairing or very fast PRs.
  • Adopting trunk-based development without fast, reliable tests, then blaming the strategy for a broken main.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What three practices does DORA associate with trunk-based development and higher delivery performance?
  2. How do feature flags and branch by abstraction let a large feature ship without a long-lived branch?
  3. List the five branch types in GitFlow and where release and hotfix branches merge. Why is a forgotten merge dangerous?
  4. Why does Vincent Driessen recommend GitHub flow for continuously delivered web apps?
  5. A commit merges into develop on a Tuesday. Release branches are cut every second Thursday (the next cut is 9 days later), QA takes 5 days, and the production deploy happens 5 days after QA ends. Estimate the change lead time, and compare it with trunk-based development deploying about 1 hour after merge. (Roughly 19 days versus 1 hour.)
  6. When are release branches the right choice, and what does "upstream first" mean for fixes?
  7. Explain three problems with environment branches and the alternative.
  8. How does the branching strategy influence each of the four DORA delivery metrics discussed above?

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why To update your private branch git rebase origin/main Linear history; only your commits change To update a branch others use git merge origin/main Nothing is rewritten To undo a commit already on main git revert Adds an inverse commit; clones stay valid One revertable commit per PR Squash and merge Clean main; revert without -m A record of a big branch's merge Merge commit (--no-ff) Keeps branch commits and the merge point A fix on a release branch Fix main first, then cherry-pick -x No lost fixes; traceable source One production version, fast CI Trunk-based development Daily integration; flags hide unfinished work Several supported versions Trunk plus release branches Stable lines for apps, SDKs, and LTS Different environments Promote one artifact Environment branches drift and rebuild A green main at high merge rates A merge queue Tests the exact combination that lands Large binaries Git LFS Clones fetch only checked-out versions Fast CI checkouts Shallow default; filter: blob:none with history Download only what the job uses

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Rebasing or force-pushing a shared branch. Merge instead, and block force pushes on shared branches.
  • Using bare --force. Use --force-with-lease --force-if-includes, and only on your own branches.
  • Deleting a leaked secret in a new commit. Rotate it first, then rewrite history with git filter-repo and contact GitHub Support.
  • Re-merging a reverted branch. Revert the revert first, then merge the fixes.
  • Running reset --hard over uncommitted work. Commit or stash first; never-committed edits cannot be recovered.
  • Adding a tracked file to .gitignore. Untrack it with git rm --cached; ignore rules affect only untracked files.
  • Required checks that never report. Do not path-filter required workflows, and add merge_group for merge queues.
  • Treating hooks as enforcement. Anyone can skip them; run the same checks in CI and rulesets.

docs.title: Git Fundamentals and Internals
docs.text:
Git looks like a collection of commands, but underneath it is a small, elegant data model: a content-addressed object database plus a set of named pointers into it. Once you understand that model, commands that seem magical (branching, merging, rebasing, resetting, recovering "lost" work) become predictable consequences of moving pointers around a graph.

This lesson explains how Git stores snapshots, how objects are named by their hashes, what refs, HEAD, and the index really are, how commits form a graph, how packfiles keep repositories small, and how remotes and remote-tracking branches work. You will explore a real repository with git cat-file and git ls-tree along the way.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most Git confusion comes from a wrong mental model: thinking a branch is a folder copy, that commits store diffs, or that git pull is a simple download. These models break down exactly when it matters, during a conflicted merge, a botched rebase, or an urgent recovery. Engineers who understand the object model can answer questions like "is my work really gone?", "why did this push get rejected?", or "why is our clone 4 GB?" quickly and safely. The internals are also the foundation for everything that builds on Git: CI systems check out commits by hash, deployments are traced to a commit SHA, and release tooling reads tags and history.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Linux kernel. Git was written by Linus Torvalds in 2005 for Linux kernel development after the project lost access to its previous tool; the Pro Git history chapter lists its design goals: speed, simple design, strong support for thousands of parallel branches, and a fully distributed model. The snapshot-and-hash design described here is what delivers those goals.
  • GitHub engineering. The GitHub blog post Commits are snapshots, not diffs walks through the same object model (blobs, trees, commits) and shows how Git computes diffs on demand, which explains behaviors such as rename detection and why history rewriting creates new commit IDs.
  • SHA-1 to SHA-256. In 2017 the SHAttered research produced the first practical SHA-1 collision. Git responded by hashing with collision detection and by designing a move to SHA-256, documented in Git's hash function transition plan. SHA-256 repositories are supported today, and Git's published plans for Git 3.0 make SHA-256 the default for new repositories.

Popular tools and providers: the Git command line, GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Azure Repos, libgit2 and JGit (Git libraries embedded in IDEs and servers), and graphical clients such as GitHub Desktop and the source control panels in VS Code and JetBrains IDEs.

docs.title: Snapshots, not diffs
docs.text:
Many older version control systems store a file's first version and then a chain of changes. Git instead records a snapshot of the whole project with every commit. That sounds expensive, but two tricks make it cheap:

  1. Every piece of content is stored once, named by the hash of its bytes. An unchanged file in the next commit has the same hash, so the new snapshot simply points to the existing copy.
  2. Objects are later compressed together into packfiles, where similar versions of a file are stored as deltas of each other.

Diffs are computed when you ask for them (git diff, git show), by comparing two snapshots. This is why Git can show a rename it never recorded: it notices that a removed file and an added file have very similar content.

docs.title: The four object types
docs.text:
Everything Git stores lives in the object database under .git/objects. There are only four kinds of object:

Object Stores Created by Blob The raw bytes of one file. No name, no permissions. git add Tree One directory: a list of entries, each with a mode, type, hash, and name git commit (from the index) Commit A pointer to one root tree, zero or more parent commits, author, committer, timestamps, and the message git commit, git merge Annotated tag A pointer to another object (usually a commit), a tag name, the tagger, a message, and optionally a signature git tag -a

A tree entry's mode tells Git what the entry is: 100644 for a normal file, 100755 for an executable, 120000 for a symbolic link, 040000 for a subdirectory (another tree), and 160000 for a submodule commit. A filename lives in the tree, not in the blob, which is why two files with identical content share one blob.

docs.title: Content addressing: names are hashes
docs.text:
An object's name is the hash of its type, its size, and its content. For a blob containing hello followed by a newline, Git hashes the bytes blob 6\0hello\n:

printf 'hello\n' | git hash-object --stdin
# ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a

printf 'blob 6\0hello\n' | sha1sum
# ce013625030ba8dba906f756967f9e9ca394464a  -

Every Git installation in the world computes the same name for the same content. This content addressing gives Git three properties:

  • Deduplication: identical content is stored once, no matter how many files, directories, or commits contain it.
  • Integrity: if a single bit of an object changes on disk, its hash no longer matches its name, and git fsck reports the corruption.
  • Tamper evidence: a commit hash covers its tree hash, which covers every blob and subtree hash, and its parent hashes, which cover all earlier history. Changing anything in the past changes every descendant commit's hash. This chain is a Merkle tree (more precisely, a Merkle DAG).

The default hash is SHA-1 (40 hexadecimal characters). Since the SHAttered collision in 2017, Git uses a hardened SHA-1 implementation that detects the known collision attack patterns. Git also supports SHA-256 repositories (64 hexadecimal characters):

git init --object-format=sha256 taskflow-sha256
git -C taskflow-sha256 rev-parse --show-object-format   # sha256

SHA-256 support was added in Git 2.29 and is no longer labelled experimental, but SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories cannot yet exchange objects with each other, and hosting services and tools must support the format. Check your hosting platform before creating one. Git's documented plans for Git 3.0 switch the default for new repositories to SHA-256; existing SHA-1 repositories keep working.

You rarely type full hashes: any unique prefix works, and Git prints at least 7 characters by default (more in large repositories).

docs.title: Exploring a repository with plumbing commands
docs.text:
Git's commands are split into porcelain (friendly commands such as commit and switch) and plumbing (low-level commands that scripts and curious engineers use). Here is a tiny TaskFlow API repository with two commits, explored with plumbing. The hashes below are real output from this repository.

git cat-file -t HEAD          # object type
# commit

git cat-file -p HEAD          # pretty-print the commit object
# tree 0cb06922109a8f04db81bf4624cca1d9960b8d90
# parent 7bfe7eda1967d4cc66439f90d934b13566eee8b7
# author Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1794564300 +0000
# committer Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1794564300 +0000
#
# Create the Express app

git ls-tree HEAD              # the root tree of that commit
# 100644 blob 713d5006dabfe2792c6ee1dbb4fdbdff2c44e304    .gitignore
# 100644 blob 1e7637db6064c79a959274780f73a883f1e69b3d    package.json
# 040000 tree 523ce736b6d0b50927c955a9017254faa15342f0    src

git ls-tree HEAD~1            # the root tree of the parent commit
# 100644 blob 713d5006dabfe2792c6ee1dbb4fdbdff2c44e304    .gitignore
# 100644 blob 1e7637db6064c79a959274780f73a883f1e69b3d    package.json
# 040000 tree 3fb9f4de81bd6da1f5558790cf2dd07c01508d68    src

git cat-file -p v1.0.0        # an annotated tag is its own object
# object c115592ebd421fdeef7d772e101d28907d339443
# type commit
# tag v1.0.0
# tagger Ada Lovelace <ada@example.com> 1794564300 +0000
#
# TaskFlow API 1.0.0

Notice what the second commit changed. Only src/app.js was edited, so the commit created exactly four new objects: a blob for the new app.js, a new src tree that lists it, a new root tree that lists the new src tree, and the commit itself. The .gitignore and package.json blobs are reused, with identical hashes in both trees. The author line stores a Unix timestamp and a time zone offset, so the commit hash also depends on when and by whom it was made.

docs.title: Refs and HEAD
docs.text:
Hashes are not friendly, so Git keeps refs: names that point to objects.

Ref Example Points to Moves when Local branch refs/heads/main a commit you commit, merge, reset, or rebase on it Remote-tracking branch refs/remotes/origin/main a commit you fetch from origin Tag refs/tags/v1.0.0 a tag object or a commit normally never HEAD .git/HEAD usually another ref you switch branches

A branch is just a ref under refs/heads/. Creating one writes a single hash; that is why branching in Git is instant. With the default "files" storage, a ref is a small file (or a line in .git/packed-refs); newer Git versions also offer a binary "reftable" format that Git 3.0 plans to make the default. Either way, the idea is the same: a name and a hash.

HEAD answers "what am I on?". Normally it is a symbolic ref that names a branch:

cat .git/HEAD
# ref: refs/heads/main
git symbolic-ref HEAD
# refs/heads/main

When you commit, Git creates the commit with the current HEAD commit as its parent and then moves the branch that HEAD names. HEAD itself does not change, because it still names the same branch.

Detached HEAD means HEAD holds a commit hash directly instead of a branch name. It happens when you check out a tag, a commit, or a remote-tracking branch:

git switch --detach v1.0.0
cat .git/HEAD
# c115592ebd421fdeef7d772e101d28907d339443
git status
# HEAD detached at v1.0.0

Detached HEAD is safe for looking around and for building old versions (CI systems often check out a detached commit). The danger is committing there: the new commits belong to no branch, and once you switch away, nothing points to them. They stay recoverable through the reflog until garbage collection, but the simple fix is to create a branch before you leave: git switch -c hotfix/login-timeout.

docs.title: The index (staging area)
docs.text:
The index (.git/index) is a binary file listing every tracked path with its mode, its blob hash, and cached file system metadata such as size and modification time. It is the proposed next commit: git commit turns the index into trees and a commit, not your working files.

git ls-files --stage
# 100644 713d5006dabfe2792c6ee1dbb4fdbdff2c44e304 0       .gitignore
# 100644 1e7637db6064c79a959274780f73a883f1e69b3d 0       package.json
# 100644 dfcefac908bf213230f5b45bd141706e6af843f3 0       src/app.js

The 0 is the stage number. During a merge conflict the index holds up to three versions of a conflicted path: stage 1 (the common ancestor), stage 2 (ours), and stage 3 (theirs). Resolving the conflict and running git add collapses them back to stage 0.

The cached metadata is why git status is fast: Git compares file sizes and timestamps first and only rehashes files that look changed.

Staging exists so that a commit can contain exactly what you intend. git add -p stages individual hunks, letting you split unrelated edits in one file into separate, focused commits.

docs.title: The commit graph
docs.text:
Each commit names its parents, so commits form a directed acyclic graph (DAG): arrows point backwards in time from child to parent and never form a loop. A normal commit has one parent, the first commit has none, and a merge commit has two (or more).

Because history is a graph, Git answers questions with graph operations. Revision syntax names commits relative to others:

Syntax Meaning HEAD~1, HEAD~3 The first parent, the third first-parent ancestor HEAD^2 The second parent of a merge commit main..feature Commits reachable from feature but not from main main...feature Commits on either side but not both (symmetric difference) @{u} The upstream of the current branch, for example origin/main HEAD@{2} Where HEAD was two moves ago (from the reflog) v1.0.0^{commit} The commit an annotated tag points to 
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate   # draw the graph
git merge-base main feature/due-dates        # best common ancestor
git log main..feature/due-dates              # what the PR would add

"Reachable" is the key word: a commit belongs to a branch if you can walk parent links from the branch tip to it. Commits that no ref can reach are unreachable and will eventually be deleted.

docs.title: Loose objects, packfiles, and garbage collection
docs.text:
New objects are first written as loose objects: one zlib-compressed file each, at .git/objects/<first 2 hex chars>/<remaining 38>. Thousands of small files are wasteful, so Git periodically packs them:

  • git gc (also run automatically as git gc --auto after some commands) combines objects into a packfile (.pack) plus an index (.idx) for fast lookup. Inside a pack, similar objects are stored as deltas against each other, so 300 versions of app.js cost little more than one plus the changes.
  • git gc --auto runs when there are more than about 6,700 loose objects (gc.auto) or too many packs (gc.autoPackLimit, default 50).
  • Unreachable objects are pruned only after a grace period (gc.pruneExpire, two weeks by default), and reflog entries expire after 90 days, or 30 days for entries no longer reachable from the ref (gc.reflogExpire, gc.reflogExpireUnreachable). This is what makes recovery possible.
  • git maintenance start schedules background tasks (prefetching, repacking, and updating the commit-graph file that speeds up history walks), which is useful for large repositories.
git count-objects -vH
# count: 11            <- loose objects before gc
git gc
git count-objects -vH
# count: 0
# in-pack: 11
# packs: 1
# size-pack: 2.20 KiB

Network transfers use the same format: git fetch and git push negotiate which commits each side already has, then send a single pack containing only the missing objects.

docs.title: Remotes and remote-tracking branches
docs.text:
A remote is a named URL for another copy of the repository, usually origin. Git does not talk to the remote unless you run fetch, pull, push, or clone; everything else is local.

When you fetch, Git downloads missing objects and updates remote-tracking branches such as origin/main, read-only refs that record where the remote's branches were at the last fetch. The mapping comes from the remote's refspec:

git config --get remote.origin.fetch
# +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*

This reads: "for every branch on the remote (refs/heads/*), update my refs/remotes/origin/* to match, even if that is not a fast-forward (+)". Your local main and origin/main are different refs that can point to different commits.

A local branch can have an upstream (its tracking branch), which lets git status report how far apart they are and lets push and pull run without arguments:

git branch -vv
# * main  c115592 [origin/main: ahead 1, behind 2] Create the Express app
git rev-list --left-right --count main...origin/main
# 1       2

Fetch versus pull:

  • git fetch only downloads commits and moves remote-tracking branches. Your branches, index, and files are untouched, so fetching is always safe.
  • git pull runs git fetch and then integrates the upstream into your current branch, by merging (default) or rebasing (git pull --rebase, or pull.rebase=true). If your branch and the upstream have diverged and you have not configured a preference, recent Git versions stop and ask you to choose (pull.rebase or pull.ff).

Many teams prefer git fetch followed by an explicit git merge or git rebase, because you can inspect what arrived (git log main..origin/main) before changing your branch.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use the porcelain commands for everyday work and reach for plumbing when you need to understand, script, or repair something:

Task Everyday command Lower-level tool See what a commit contains git show <sha> git cat-file -p <sha>, git ls-tree Script "which commit is deployed?" git log -1 git rev-parse HEAD List branches for a script git branch git for-each-ref --format='%(refname:short)' refs/heads Find what is making the repo large (none) git rev-list --objects --all with git cat-file --batch-check Check repository health (none) git fsck

Git itself is the right tool for source code, configuration, and text documents. It is a poor fit for:

Content Why Better choice Large binaries (videos, datasets, design files) Every version stays in history forever and cannot be delta-compressed well Git LFS or object storage Secrets and credentials History is copied to every clone and is hard to purge A secrets manager Build output and dependencies (dist/, node_modules/) Regenerable, noisy, and conflict-prone .gitignore plus CI artifacts Databases and frequently rewritten binary files Merges are impossible and history balloons Backups and migrations

docs.title: Build a commit by hand with plumbing
docs.text:
This shows that git commit is only a convenience over four plumbing steps:

# Run in an empty scratch directory
git init -b main plumbing-demo && cd plumbing-demo

# 1. Store a blob and get its hash
BLOB=$(printf '# TaskFlow API\n' | git hash-object -w --stdin)

# 2. Put it in the index under a path and mode
git update-index --add --cacheinfo 100644,"$BLOB",README.md

# 3. Turn the index into a tree object
TREE=$(git write-tree)

# 4. Create a commit object for that tree, then point main at it
COMMIT=$(echo "Add README" | git commit-tree "$TREE")
git update-ref refs/heads/main "$COMMIT"

git log --oneline        # fd36d15 Add README (hash varies with author and time)
git status --short       #  D README.md: the file exists only in Git, not on disk
git restore README.md    # materialize it from the index

The commit exists, but the file was never written to the working tree. That is the separation between the object database, the index, and the working tree made visible.

docs.title: Find the largest objects in history
docs.text:
When a clone is slow, find out what is taking the space:

# Every object in history with its type and size, largest first
git rev-list --objects --all |
  git cat-file --batch-check='%(objecttype) %(objectname) %(objectsize) %(rest)' |
  awk '$1 == "blob"' |
  sort -k3 -n -r |
  head -10

The last column is the path where the blob was found. Large blobs that no longer exist in the current tree still cost every clone; the fix (Git LFS or rewriting history) is covered in hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories and undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: Inspect where you are relative to the remote
docs.text:
git fetch --prune                     # update origin/* and drop deleted branches
git status -sb
# ## feat/task-due-dates...origin/feat/task-due-dates [ahead 2]

git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD   # my commits not yet on main
git log --oneline HEAD..origin/main   # new commits on main I do not have
git diff origin/main...HEAD           # changes since my branch left main

The three-dot diff compares against the merge base, which is exactly what a pull request shows.

docs.title: Sensible global defaults
docs.text:
# ~/.gitconfig
[init]
    defaultBranch = main          # name for new repositories
[pull]
    rebase = true                 # pull = fetch + rebase, no surprise merge commits
[fetch]
    prune = true                  # remove origin/* refs for deleted branches
[push]
    autoSetupRemote = true        # first push of a new branch sets its upstream
[merge]
    conflictStyle = zdiff3        # show the common ancestor in conflict markers
[rerere]
    enabled = true                # remember and reuse conflict resolutions
[diff]
    algorithm = histogram         # often clearer diffs than the default

Each line is a real Git setting: init.defaultBranch (Git 2.28 and later), push.autoSetupRemote (Git 2.37), and merge.conflictStyle = zdiff3 (Git 2.35). Teams that prefer merge-based pulls set pull.rebase = false or pull.ff = only instead; the important thing is choosing deliberately.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Learn the model: snapshots, four object types, refs, and the graph. Most "Git problems" are pointer questions.
  • Commit small, coherent snapshots; use git add -p to keep unrelated changes apart.
  • Fetch often and look before you integrate (git log main..origin/main).
  • Configure pull.rebase or pull.ff explicitly so git pull never surprises you.
  • Create a branch before committing on a detached HEAD.
  • Keep large binaries, generated files, and secrets out of history from the start; removing them later means rewriting history.
  • In scripts and CI, use plumbing commands (rev-parse, for-each-ref, cat-file) whose output is stable, not porcelain output meant for humans.
  • Record the commit SHA in every build artifact so you can always trace production back to an exact snapshot.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Clones and CI checkouts take minutes and .git is several gigabytes. Detect: git count-objects -vH shows a large size-pack; the largest-objects script above lists big blobs. Cause: binaries, datasets, or build output committed in the past; deleting them in a new commit does not shrink history. Fix: move such files to Git LFS, rewrite history with git filter-repo if the size is unacceptable, and use shallow or partial clones in CI.
  • A developer's commits "disappeared" after switching branches. Detect: git reflog shows commits made while HEAD detached at <sha>. Cause: work committed on a detached HEAD that no branch points to. Fix: git switch -c recovered <sha> from the reflog entry, and teach git switch -c before committing on a checked-out tag.
  • The release job fails with fatal: No names found, cannot describe anything. Detect: git describe or a version script fails only in CI. Cause: CI checkouts are shallow (actions/checkout fetches one commit by default) and contain no tags. Fix: set fetch-depth: 0 (full history and tags) on the checkout step, only in the jobs that need history; fetch-tags alone helps only when the built commit is tagged.
  • git push is rejected with "non-fast-forward". Detect: the push error and git status showing ahead 1, behind 3. Cause: someone pushed to the same branch; your branch and the remote have diverged. Fix: git fetch, then rebase or merge onto origin/<branch> and push again. Never "fix" this with --force on a shared branch.
  • Developers see branches that were deleted on GitHub weeks ago. Detect: git branch -r lists many stale origin/* refs. Cause: fetch does not delete remote-tracking refs by default. Fix: git fetch --prune, or set fetch.prune = true globally.
  • git fsck reports missing or corrupt objects. Detect: errors such as error: object file ... is empty or missing blob. Cause: a crash or full disk during a write, or a damaged file system. Fix: keep the broken copy for analysis, then re-clone or fetch the missing objects from a healthy remote; because objects are named by hash, any good copy is a valid replacement.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Blob: An object holding one file's content, without its name.
  • Tree: An object listing a directory's entries (mode, type, hash, name).
  • Commit: An object pointing to a root tree and its parent commits, with author, committer, and message.
  • Annotated tag: An object that names and describes another object, usually a release commit.
  • Content addressing: Naming data by the hash of its content, so identical content has an identical name.
  • Ref: A name that points to an object, such as refs/heads/main.
  • HEAD: The ref that says what is checked out, usually pointing to a branch.
  • Detached HEAD: HEAD pointing directly at a commit instead of a branch.
  • Index (staging area): The file that holds the proposed next commit.
  • DAG: Directed acyclic graph; the shape of commit history.
  • Reachable: A commit that can be found by walking parents from some ref.
  • Packfile: A compressed file containing many objects, often stored as deltas.
  • Remote-tracking branch: A read-only ref such as origin/main recording a remote branch's position at the last fetch.
  • Upstream: The remote-tracking branch a local branch is configured to follow.
  • Plumbing / porcelain: Low-level, script-friendly commands versus user-facing ones.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing commits store diffs. They store snapshots; diffs are computed on demand.
  • Believing a branch contains commits. A branch is a pointer; commits are reachable from it.
  • Thinking git fetch changes your files. It only updates remote-tracking branches; commands such as merge, rebase, pull, switch, checkout, restore, reset, stash, cherry-pick, and revert are the ones that change the working tree.
  • Thinking a deleted file is gone from the repository. It remains in every earlier snapshot.
  • Using git pull without knowing whether it merges or rebases.
  • Committing on a detached HEAD and switching away without creating a branch.
  • Assuming short hashes are permanent identifiers; a prefix that is unique today may become ambiguous as the repository grows. Store full hashes in deployment records.
  • Parsing porcelain output (git status, git branch) in scripts instead of using plumbing or --porcelain formats.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can Git store a full snapshot on every commit without the repository growing by the full project size each time?
  2. You edit only src/routes/tasks.js (where src/routes/ sits inside src/) and commit. How many new objects does the commit create, and which ones? (Answer: five: the new blob, the src/routes tree, the src tree, the root tree, and the commit.)
  3. What exactly is stored in .git/HEAD when you are on main, and what changes when you check out v1.0.0?
  4. Why does changing a commit message deep in history change the hash of every later commit?
  5. What is the difference between main, origin/main, and the main branch on GitHub?
  6. What does git pull do when your branch and its upstream have diverged, and how do you control it?
  7. When are unreachable commits actually deleted, and why does that delay matter for recovery?
  8. What are stages 1, 2, and 3 in the index, and when do they appear?

docs.text:

docs.title: Hooks, .gitignore, and Large Repositories
docs.text:
A repository is more than its code. Hooks run checks automatically at key moments, .gitignore keeps generated files and secrets out of history, .gitattributes controls line endings, diffs, and binary handling, Git LFS stores large files outside the normal object database, and partial clones and sparse checkouts keep huge repositories usable.

This lesson covers client-side hooks and the tools that manage them (husky, lint-staged, commitlint, and the pre-commit framework), server-side enforcement, .gitignore patterns and precedence, .gitattributes, Git LFS, shallow and partial clones, sparse-checkout, and the trade-offs between monorepos and polyrepos.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most repository problems are preventable at the edges. A pre-commit secret scan stops a leaked key before it exists in any history; a correct .gitignore keeps node_modules/ and .env out from day one; a .gitattributes file ends the "every line changed" diffs between Windows and macOS teammates; and Git LFS keeps a 300 MB design file from making every clone slow forever. As repositories grow, the cost of a full clone lands on every developer laptop and every CI job, many times a day, so clone strategy becomes a real lever on CI time and cost.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google's monorepo. The paper Why Google Stores Billions of Lines of Code in a Single Repository describes a single repository serving tens of thousands of developers, the custom tooling that makes it workable, and the trade-offs of the monorepo model compared with many separate repositories.
  • GitHub's clone guidance. The GitHub blog post Get up to speed with partial clone and shallow clone recommends blobless clones (--filter=blob:none) for developers and build machines reused across builds, treeless clones for one-off builds that still need history, and shallow clones only for throwaway builds, strongly discouraging shallow clones for developers.
  • GitHub file size limits. GitHub's About large files on GitHub page states that Git warns above 50 MiB and GitHub blocks files larger than 100 MiB, which must be stored with Git LFS instead.
  • Git hooks. The githooks reference documents every hook, when it runs, and which ones can abort an operation.

Popular tools and providers: husky, lint-staged, commitlint, the pre-commit framework, gitleaks, Git LFS, Scalar (bundled with Git), monorepo tools such as Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, and npm or pnpm workspaces.

docs.title: Client-side hooks
docs.text:
Hooks are executable scripts in .git/hooks/ (or in the directory set by core.hooksPath) that Git runs at specific points. The .git directory is not versioned, so teams use a tool that installs hooks from a committed directory.

Hook Runs Can abort? Typical use pre-commit Before the commit message is requested Yes Lint and format staged files, scan for secrets prepare-commit-msg Before the editor opens Yes Insert a template or a ticket ID from the branch name commit-msg After the message is written Yes Validate the message format (commitlint) post-commit After the commit is created No Notifications post-checkout, post-merge After switching branches or merging No Remind to run npm install when the lockfile changed pre-push Before objects are sent Yes Fast tests, block pushes to main

Hooks are conveniences, not controls. Anyone can skip them (git commit --no-verify, git push --no-verify, or simply not installing them), so every rule a hook enforces must also run in CI or on the server. Keep them fast: a pre-commit hook that takes a minute will be bypassed.

husky installs hooks for JavaScript projects: npx husky init creates a .husky/ directory with a pre-commit script and adds a prepare script ("prepare": "husky") so hooks are set up on npm install. lint-staged runs commands only on the files staged for the commit, which keeps the hook fast in large codebases. commitlint validates commit messages against a convention such as Conventional Commits.

The pre-commit framework (pre-commit.com) does the same for any language: a .pre-commit-config.yaml lists hook repositories pinned to versions, and pre-commit install wires them into Git. It is common in polyglot and Python-heavy repositories.

docs.title: Server-side checks
docs.text:
Server hooks run on the Git server and cannot be skipped by clients: pre-receive (once per push, can reject everything), update (once per ref), and post-receive (after the update, cannot reject). Self-hosted Git servers and GitHub Enterprise Server support custom pre-receive hooks. GitHub.com does not run custom server hooks; the equivalents are:

Goal GitHub.com mechanism Block secrets in pushes Secret scanning push protection Block large files, certain paths, or extensions Push rulesets (private and internal repositories) Enforce commit message or author email patterns Ruleset metadata restrictions Require tests, lint, signatures, reviews before merge Rulesets and required status checks React to pushes Webhooks and GitHub Actions on: push

docs.title: .gitignore patterns and precedence
docs.text:
.gitignore lists paths Git should treat as untracked and not offer to add. Pattern rules:

Pattern Matches node_modules/ A directory named node_modules anywhere (trailing / means directories only) /dist dist only at the level of this .gitignore (leading / anchors) *.log Any file ending in .log, in any directory logs/*.log .log files directly inside logs/ (a middle / also anchors) **/coverage coverage at any depth build/** Everything inside build/ !.env.example Re-include a file excluded by an earlier pattern # comment A comment; use \# for a literal leading #

Two rules surprise people:

  • A file cannot be re-included if a parent directory is excluded. logs/ followed by !logs/keep.txt does not work, because Git never looks inside an ignored directory. Use logs/* then !logs/keep.txt.
  • Ignore rules only affect untracked files. Adding .env to .gitignore after committing it does nothing; untrack it with git rm --cached .env (and rotate anything it contained).

Git reads ignore rules from several sources. From highest to lowest precedence:

  1. Patterns given on the command line (for commands that accept them).
  2. .gitignore files in the path's directory and its parents; a deeper file overrides a shallower one.
  3. .git/info/exclude: personal, per-repository, not committed.
  4. The file named by core.excludesFile (default ~/.config/git/ignore): personal, for every repository.

Within one file, the last matching pattern wins. Put project artifacts (node_modules/, dist/, .env) in the committed .gitignore, and personal clutter (.DS_Store, editor folders) in your global ignore file. git check-ignore -v <path> tells you exactly which rule matched.

docs.title: .gitattributes: line endings, binaries, and diffs
docs.text:
.gitattributes assigns attributes to paths, and unlike personal configuration it is committed, so it applies to everyone.

Line endings. Windows uses CRLF and Linux and macOS use LF. Without rules, editors and core.autocrlf settings fight, producing diffs where every line changed and shell scripts that fail with /bin/sh^M: bad interpreter. The robust fix is to declare it in the repository:

Attribute Effect * text=auto Git detects text files and stores them with LF in the repository *.sh text eol=lf Always check out with LF (scripts run in Linux containers) *.ps1 text eol=crlf Always check out with CRLF *.png binary Never convert or diff as text (binary = -text -diff -merge) package-lock.json linguist-generated=true Collapse in GitHub diffs, exclude from language statistics vendor/** linguist-vendored Treat as third-party code in GitHub statistics docs/internal/** export-ignore Leave out of git archive tarballs *.psd filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text Store with Git LFS (written by git lfs track)

After adding or changing .gitattributes, run git add --renormalize . and commit, so existing files are stored with the new rules.

docs.title: Git LFS
docs.text:
Git keeps every version of every file forever, and binary files do not delta-compress well, so ten versions of a 200 MB video cost roughly 2 GB in every clone. Git LFS (Large File Storage) replaces such files in Git with small text pointer files, and stores the real content on an LFS server (GitHub provides one):

version https://git-lfs.github.com/spec/v1
oid sha256:4d7a214614ab2935c943f9e0ff69d22eadbb8f32b1258daaa5e2ca24d17e2393
size 12345

Git LFS hooks into Git with a clean/smudge filter: on git add the file is copied into the local LFS cache and the pointer is staged, and git push uploads the content to the LFS server; on checkout the pointer is replaced with the real file, downloaded on demand for the commit you check out. Clones therefore only download the large files of the checked-out version. LFS storage and bandwidth are billed or limited by the hosting plan, and LFS supports file locking (git lfs lock) for unmergeable files such as design documents.

docs.title: Large repositories: shallow, partial, and sparse
docs.text:
When a repository has years of history or a huge tree, three independent techniques reduce what you download and what you check out.

Technique Command What you lose Best for Shallow clone git clone --depth 1 History beyond the depth; some commands (merge-base, blame, describe) misbehave Throwaway CI builds Blobless partial clone git clone --filter=blob:none Nothing; old file contents download on demand Developers, long-lived CI machines Treeless partial clone git clone --filter=tree:0 Nothing; but git log -- path and blame trigger many fetches One-off builds that need commit history Sparse-checkout git sparse-checkout set <dirs> Files outside the chosen directories are not in the working tree Monorepos where you work on a few directories

Partial clone needs server support; GitHub, GitLab, and modern Git servers provide it. Sparse-checkout in cone mode (the default) takes a list of directories, which keeps it fast; combined with a blobless clone, Git downloads only the blobs for the directories you check out. Scalar, shipped with Git, configures all of this (partial clone, sparse-checkout, file system monitor, background maintenance) in one command for very large repositories.

Other settings that help large repositories:

git config core.fsmonitor true        # built-in file system monitor (Windows, macOS)
git config core.untrackedCache true   # cache untracked-file scans
git maintenance start                 # background prefetch, commit-graph, repack

docs.title: Monorepos versus polyrepos
docs.text:
Monorepo (one repository, many projects) Polyrepo (one repository per project) Cross-project changes One atomic commit and PR Coordinated PRs and releases across repositories Dependency versions Usually one version of each shared dependency Each repository chooses; drift is common Code sharing and refactoring Easy; refactor callers in the same change Requires publishing packages and upgrading consumers CI Needs path filters, affected-project detection, and caching to stay fast Simple per-repository pipelines Ownership and access CODEOWNERS per directory; access control is coarser Natural boundaries and per-repository permissions Tooling needs Workspaces, build tools such as Nx, Turborepo, or Bazel; partial and sparse clones at scale Standard tooling per repository Scale limits Git performance must be managed as it grows Each repository stays small

Neither is universally better. Monorepos fit teams that share a lot of code and change it together (for example, TaskFlow API, TaskFlow Web, and a shared validation package); polyrepos fit independent services owned by separate teams with separate release cycles.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Tool Use when Avoid when Pre-commit hooks (husky, pre-commit) Fast checks that save a CI round trip: format, lint changed files, secret scan Slow suites (full tests belong in CI), or as the only enforcement commit-msg linting Automation reads commit messages (release tooling) You squash-merge and lint PR titles instead Global ignore file Personal OS and editor clutter Project build output (belongs in the committed .gitignore) .gitattributes line endings Mixed Windows and Unix teams, shell scripts in containers Never skip it on cross-platform teams Git LFS Large binaries that change: media, design files, datasets Build artifacts (use CI artifacts and registries), huge datasets (object storage) Shallow clone Single-use CI jobs that need only the latest snapshot Developer machines; jobs needing tags or history Blobless clone Large-history repositories for developers and reused CI Offline work needing all history locally Sparse-checkout Large monorepos Small repositories (adds confusion)

docs.title: husky, lint-staged, and commitlint for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
npm install --save-dev husky lint-staged @commitlint/cli @commitlint/config-conventional
npx husky init                         # creates .husky/pre-commit and the prepare script

{
  "name": "taskflow-api",
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "prepare": "husky",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "test": "node --test"
  },
  "lint-staged": {
    "*.{js,mjs,cjs}": ["eslint --fix", "prettier --write"],
    "*.{json,md,yml,yaml}": "prettier --write"
  }
}

# .husky/pre-commit
npx lint-staged

# .husky/commit-msg
npx --no -- commitlint --edit "$1"

// commitlint.config.js
export default { extends: ["@commitlint/config-conventional"] };

Now git commit -m "update stuff" fails with type may not be empty, while git commit -m "fix(tasks): reject an empty title" passes, and only the staged JavaScript files are linted and formatted. In CI and Docker builds, set HUSKY=0 so the prepare script does not try to install hooks; when installing production dependencies only, husky is not present, so use "prepare": "husky || true" or skip prepare there.

docs.title: The pre-commit framework with a secret scanner
docs.text:
# .pre-commit-config.yaml
repos:
  - repo: https://github.com/pre-commit/pre-commit-hooks
    rev: v6.0.0
    hooks:
      - id: trailing-whitespace
      - id: end-of-file-fixer
      - id: check-merge-conflict      # blocks committed conflict markers
      - id: check-added-large-files   # default limit 500 KB
        args: ["--maxkb=1024"]
  - repo: https://github.com/gitleaks/gitleaks
    rev: v8.30.1
    hooks:
      - id: gitleaks

pipx install pre-commit        # or pip install pre-commit
pre-commit install             # writes .git/hooks/pre-commit
pre-commit run --all-files     # run once over the whole repository (also in CI)
pre-commit autoupdate          # bump the pinned revs

docs.title: A .gitignore for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# .gitignore
# Dependencies and build output
node_modules/
dist/
coverage/

# Environment files: keep secrets out, keep the template in
.env
.env.*
!.env.example

# Logs and runtime files
*.log
logs/*
!logs/.gitkeep
*.pid

# Local tooling
.cache/
.eslintcache

git check-ignore -v .env.local
# .gitignore:9:.env.*    .env.local
git rm --cached .env           # if it was committed before the rule existed

Personal clutter goes in ~/.config/git/ignore (.DS_Store, Thumbs.db, .idea/), not in the project file.

docs.title: A .gitattributes for a cross-platform team
docs.text:
# .gitattributes
* text=auto

# Scripts that run in Linux containers must keep LF
*.sh   text eol=lf
Dockerfile text eol=lf

# Windows-only scripts
*.ps1  text eol=crlf
*.cmd  text eol=crlf

# Binary assets: no line-ending conversion, no text diff
*.png  binary
*.jpg  binary
*.pdf  binary

# Generated files: collapsed in GitHub diffs
package-lock.json linguist-generated=true

git add --renormalize .
git commit -m "chore: normalize line endings"

docs.title: Git LFS for TaskFlow Web design assets
docs.text:
git lfs install                          # once per machine
git lfs track "design/**/*.fig" "*.mp4"  # adds lines to .gitattributes
git add .gitattributes design/onboarding.fig
git commit -m "chore: store design files in LFS"
git lfs ls-files                         # what is stored in LFS

# Move existing large files out of history (rewrites history: coordinate first)
git lfs migrate import --include="*.mp4" --everything

docs.title: Faster CI checkouts
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml (checkout step variants)
- uses: actions/checkout@v7          # default: shallow, fetch-depth 1
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
  with:
    fetch-depth: 0                   # full history and tags (versioning, changelogs)
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
  with:
    filter: blob:none                # partial clone
    fetch-depth: 0                   # full history without all blobs
- uses: actions/checkout@v7
  with:
    sparse-checkout: |               # monorepo: only what this job builds
      apps/api
      packages/shared

docs.title: Working in a large monorepo
docs.text:
git clone --filter=blob:none --sparse git@github.com:example/taskflow.git
cd taskflow
git sparse-checkout set apps/api packages/shared   # cone mode: directories
git sparse-checkout list
git sparse-checkout add apps/web                   # widen later

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Commit a .gitignore and .gitattributes in the very first commit.
  • Never commit .env; commit a .env.example with placeholders.
  • Keep hooks fast (seconds) and run the same checks in CI, because hooks can be skipped.
  • Install hooks automatically (husky's prepare script, pre-commit install in onboarding docs) and pin hook versions.
  • Scan for secrets both before commit (gitleaks) and on the server (push protection).
  • Put large binaries in Git LFS before they enter history; migrating later rewrites history.
  • Use blobless clones for developers and shallow or filtered checkouts in CI; avoid shallow clones for daily work.
  • In monorepos, combine CODEOWNERS, path-filtered CI, and sparse-checkout.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every line of a file shows as changed in a PR. Detect: git diff --stat shows whole-file changes; git ls-files --eol reports mixed crlf/lf. Cause: line endings converted by one developer's editor or core.autocrlf setting. Fix: add .gitattributes with * text=auto and explicit eol rules, run git add --renormalize ., and commit once.
  • A container fails with /bin/sh^M: bad interpreter. Detect: the entrypoint script fails only in images built on Windows machines. Cause: the script was checked out with CRLF and copied into the image. Fix: *.sh text eol=lf in .gitattributes, renormalize, and rebuild.
  • git push is rejected because a file exceeds 100 MiB. Detect: remote: error: File ... exceeds GitHub's file size limit of 100.00 MB. Cause: a large binary in one of the commits being pushed, even if a later commit deletes it. Fix: remove it from the unpushed commits (git reset or git lfs migrate import on unpushed history), track the type with LFS, and push again.
  • CI checkout takes minutes and dominates pipeline time. Detect: the checkout step is the slowest step; size-pack is several GB. Cause: full clones of a large history on every job. Fix: default shallow checkout where history is not needed, filter: blob:none where it is, sparse-checkout for monorepo jobs, and remove big blobs from history if appropriate.
  • Hooks silently stop running for some developers. Detect: commits with unformatted code or bad messages reach PRs. Cause: hooks were not installed (npm install skipped, core.hooksPath changed) or bypassed with --no-verify. Fix: enforce the same checks in CI as required status checks; treat hooks as fast feedback only.
  • .env is ignored, but secrets still reached GitHub. Detect: secret scanning alerts on .env. Cause: the file was tracked before it was added to .gitignore. Fix: rotate the secrets, git rm --cached .env, and follow the history clean-up in undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Git hook: A script Git runs at a specific point, such as before a commit.
  • Client-side hook: A hook in a developer's clone; it can be skipped.
  • Server-side hook: A hook on the Git server (pre-receive, update, post-receive); clients cannot skip it.
  • husky / lint-staged / commitlint: Tools to install hooks, run tasks on staged files, and validate commit messages.
  • pre-commit framework: A language-agnostic hook manager configured by .pre-commit-config.yaml.
  • .gitignore: Patterns for untracked files Git should ignore.
  • core.excludesFile: A personal, global ignore file.
  • .gitattributes: Per-path attributes for line endings, diffs, merges, LFS, and GitHub Linguist.
  • Git LFS: An extension storing large files outside Git, referenced by pointer files.
  • Shallow clone: A clone with truncated history.
  • Partial clone: A clone that omits some objects (blobs or trees) and fetches them on demand.
  • Sparse-checkout: Checking out only part of the tree.
  • Monorepo / polyrepo: One repository for many projects versus one per project.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing hooks enforce policy. They are skippable; enforcement lives in CI and server rules.
  • Adding a file to .gitignore and expecting Git to stop tracking it.
  • Trying to re-include a file inside an ignored directory.
  • Relying on each developer's core.autocrlf instead of .gitattributes.
  • Committing large binaries "temporarily"; history keeps them forever.
  • Using --depth 1 clones for development and then fighting missing history.
  • Choosing a monorepo without investing in path-filtered CI and build caching.
  • Long-running pre-commit hooks that run the whole test suite.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which hooks can abort a commit, and why must their checks also run in CI?
  2. Why does logs/ followed by !logs/keep.txt fail to re-include the file, and what pattern works?
  3. List the sources of ignore rules from highest to lowest precedence.
  4. What problem does * text=auto solve, and when do you also need eol=lf?
  5. A repository stores 40 versions of a 150 MB video. Roughly how much does every full clone download with plain Git, and with Git LFS when checking out the latest version? (About 6 GB, compressed only slightly by Git; about 150 MB of LFS content plus small pointer files.)
  6. Compare shallow, blobless, and treeless clones, and say where each fits.
  7. How do GitHub.com repositories get server-side enforcement without custom pre-receive hooks?
  8. Give two advantages and two costs of a monorepo.

docs.text:
• Git reference: githooks
  • Git reference: gitignore and gitattributes
  • GitHub Docs: Configuring Git to handle line endings
  • husky, lint-staged, and commitlint
  • pre-commit framework
