docs.title: Git and GitHub Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review Git internals, branching, merging and rebasing, branching strategies, pull requests and code review, versioning and releases, recovery, and repository hygiene at scale. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. Does Git store diffs or snapshots?
docs.text: Snapshots. Each commit points to a tree describing the whole project at that moment. Unchanged files are not duplicated, because identical content has the same hash and is stored once; packfiles later delta-compress similar objects. Diffs are computed on demand by comparing two snapshots.

docs.title: 2. What are Git's four object types?
docs.text: Blobs (file content), trees (directory listings of mode, type, hash, and name), commits (a root tree, parent commits, author, committer, and message), and annotated tags (a named, signed or described pointer to another object). Everything in .git/objects is one of these.

docs.title: 3. What does content addressing mean in Git, and what does it give you?
docs.text: An object's name is the hash of its type, size, and content (blob 6\0hello\n for a 6-byte file). This gives deduplication, integrity checking (a corrupted object no longer matches its name), and tamper evidence: a commit hash covers its tree and parents, so changing history changes every later hash.

docs.title: 4. What is the status of SHA-256 in Git?
docs.text: Git supports SHA-256 repositories (git init --object-format=sha256) since 2.29, and the format is no longer labelled experimental. SHA-1 and SHA-256 repositories cannot yet interoperate, and hosting support varies. Git's published plans make SHA-256 the default for new repositories in Git 3.0. SHA-1 in Git already uses collision detection against the known attacks.

docs.title: 5. What is a branch, technically?
docs.text: A ref under refs/heads/ that stores one commit hash. Committing moves the branch to the new commit. Creating a branch writes one small ref, which is why branching is instant and cheap.

docs.title: 6. What is HEAD, and what is a detached HEAD?
docs.text: HEAD records what is checked out, normally as a symbolic ref such as ref: refs/heads/main. Detached HEAD means it holds a commit hash directly, which happens when you check out a tag or commit. Commits made there belong to no branch; create one with git switch -c <name> before switching away, or recover them from the reflog later.

docs.title: 7. What is the index (staging area) for?
docs.text: It is the proposed next commit: a file listing each tracked path with its mode and blob hash plus cached file metadata. git commit builds trees from the index, not from the working tree. It lets you commit exactly the changes you choose (git add -p) and speeds up git status. During a conflict it holds stages 1, 2, and 3 for the base, ours, and theirs.

docs.title: 8. What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?
docs.text: fetch downloads new objects and updates remote-tracking branches such as origin/main; your branches and files do not change. pull is fetch followed by integrating the upstream into the current branch, by merge (default) or rebase (--rebase or pull.rebase=true). Since recent Git versions, a pull with diverged branches and no configured preference stops and asks you to choose.

docs.title: 9. What are remote-tracking branches and upstreams?
docs.text: Remote-tracking branches (refs/remotes/origin/*) record where the remote's branches were at the last fetch, as set by the refspec +refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*. An upstream is the remote-tracking branch a local branch follows, which enables ahead/behind counts and argument-less push and pull.

docs.title: 10. What are packfiles, and when are unreachable commits deleted?
docs.text: Packfiles store many objects compressed together, often as deltas, with an index for lookup; git gc creates them from loose objects. Unreachable objects are pruned only after a grace period (two weeks by default), and reflog entries keep commits reachable for 90 days (30 for entries no longer reachable from the ref), which is what makes recovery possible.

docs.title: 11. What is the difference between a fast-forward and a three-way merge?
docs.text: A fast-forward happens when the current branch has not moved since the other branch started: Git just moves the pointer, and no commit is created. Otherwise Git finds the merge base, compares base, ours, and theirs, and records a merge commit with two parents. --ff-only forbids merge commits; --no-ff always creates one.

docs.title: 12. How does Git decide what conflicts in a three-way merge?
docs.text: For each region, if only one side changed it relative to the merge base, that side wins; if both changed it identically, the change is taken once; if both changed it differently, it is a conflict. The default strategy since Git 2.34 is ort.

docs.title: 13. How do you resolve a merge conflict?
docs.text: Inspect with git status and the conflict markers (use merge.conflictStyle=zdiff3 to see the base), edit to the correct final content, run the tests, git add the files, then git commit or git rebase --continue. --abort returns to the start. git mergetool opens a three-way tool, and rerere remembers resolutions.

docs.title: 14. What happens during a rebase?
docs.text: Git finds your commits not in the new base, saves the old tip as ORIG_HEAD, checks out the new base, and replays each commit as a new commit with a new parent and therefore a new hash, then moves the branch. Conflicts are resolved commit by commit. Commits whose patches already exist upstream are skipped.

docs.title: 15. What is the golden rule of rebasing, and why?
docs.text: Do not rebase commits that others may have based work on. Rebasing abandons the original commits; collaborators who have them get diverged history, duplicate commits with different hashes, and repeated conflicts. Rebase your own branches freely and push with --force-with-lease.

docs.title: 16. What can you do with interactive rebase?
docs.text: Reorder, reword, edit, squash, fixup, drop, or run commands (exec) between commits before sharing them. git commit --fixup=<sha> with git rebase -i --autosquash places fix commits under their targets automatically. --exec "npm test" verifies each commit builds.

docs.title: 17. Compare merge commit, squash and merge, and rebase and merge for pull requests.
docs.text: Merge commit keeps all branch commits plus a two-parent merge commit (non-linear, original hashes). Squash creates one new commit per PR (linear, easy single-commit revert, coarse bisect). Rebase-merge copies each commit onto the base (linear, fine-grained, new hashes, needs clean commits). Pick one per repository and enforce it.

docs.title: 18. What is the difference between -X ours and -s ours?
docs.text: -X ours is a strategy option: merge normally but resolve conflicting hunks in favor of the current branch. -s ours is a strategy that records a merge while keeping the current tree entirely, discarding all of the other branch's changes.

docs.title: 19. When do you use git cherry-pick, and why -x?
docs.text: To apply specific commits elsewhere, typically backporting a fix from main to a release branch. -x appends "(cherry picked from commit ...)" so the origin is traceable. Routine cherry-picking between long-lived branches signals a branching problem.

docs.title: 20. What does git rebase --onto do?
docs.text: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> moves the commits in <branch> that are not in <upstream> onto <newbase>. It is used to move a stacked branch onto main after its base branch was squash-merged.

docs.title: 21. What is trunk-based development?
docs.text: Everyone integrates small changes into one shared trunk (main) at least daily, through direct commits or very short-lived branches, with CI on every change and a stop-the-line rule for a red build. Unfinished work hides behind feature flags or branch by abstraction. DORA associates it with three or fewer active branches, daily merges, and no code freezes.

docs.title: 22. What is GitHub flow?
docs.text: A branch per change, a pull request, CI and review, merge into main, deploy, and delete the branch. The rule is that main is always deployable. With short branches it converges with trunk-based development.

docs.title: 23. Describe GitFlow and why many teams moved away from it.
docs.text: GitFlow has long-lived main and develop, plus feature/*, release/*, and hotfix/* branches; release and hotfix branches merge into both main and develop. It delays integration, multiplies merges (forgotten merge-backs lose fixes), and fights continuous delivery. Its author's 2020 note recommends simpler flows for continuously delivered web apps and keeps GitFlow for explicitly versioned software.

docs.title: 24. When do you need release branches?
docs.text: When several versions are supported at once or releases need a stable line: mobile and desktop apps, on-premises products, SDKs with LTS versions. Cut release/x.y from a green main, ship tags from it, and backport fixes from main with cherry-pick -x (upstream first).

docs.title: 25. Why are environment branches (dev, staging, prod) an anti-pattern?
docs.text: They drift through partial merges and hotfixes, so what was tested is not what ships; each branch rebuilds its own artifact; and environment differences become code differences. Build once from main and promote the same artifact with per-environment configuration.

docs.title: 26. What are feature flags, and what do they cost?
docs.text: Runtime switches that turn code paths on or off without a deploy, letting unfinished features merge dark and roll out gradually. They add code paths to test, configuration to manage, and cleanup work; each flag needs an owner and a removal date.

docs.title: 27. How does the branching strategy affect DORA metrics?
docs.text: Waiting on long-lived branches adds directly to change lead time, batching caps deployment frequency, large merges raise change fail rate, and a special hotfix path slows recovery. Small batches into trunk improve all four, and DORA's fifth metric, deployment rework rate, as well.

docs.title: 28. What makes a good pull request?
docs.text: Small and focused (Google's guidance: about 100 lines is reasonable, 1,000 is usually too large), a description of what and why, how to test, and the risks, linked to an issue, with mechanical checks automated so reviewers can focus on correctness and design.

docs.title: 29. What is CODEOWNERS, and how is it evaluated?
docs.text: A file in .github/, the root, or docs/ mapping path patterns to owners. The last matching pattern wins. Owners are requested automatically, and with "require review from Code Owners" one of them must approve. Owners need write access; CODEOWNERS and workflows should themselves be owned.

docs.title: 30. How do rulesets differ from branch protection rules?
docs.text: Many rulesets can apply to a branch and their rules are aggregated (most restrictive wins), they can target tags and pushes, have enforcement status and explicit bypass lists, are visible to anyone with read access, and can be defined at the organization level on eligible plans. Only one branch protection rule applies per branch. Both can coexist.

docs.title: 31. What does "require branches to be up to date" do, and what is its cost?
docs.text: It requires the PR to contain the latest base before merging, so CI tested the combination. Without it, two green PRs can break main together. The cost is constant rebasing and re-running CI as other PRs merge; a merge queue solves that at scale.

docs.title: 32. How does a merge queue work?
docs.text: Approved PRs join a queue; for each, GitHub builds a temporary branch with the latest base, the PRs ahead of it, and the PR, runs required checks (workflows must handle merge_group), and merges passing PRs in order. A failing PR is removed and the groups behind it are rebuilt.

docs.title: 33. Why might a required check never report?
docs.text: The workflow was skipped by a paths or branch filter (a skipped workflow leaves the check pending, unlike a job skipped by if:, which reports success), the job was renamed, or the workflow lacks the merge_group trigger when a merge queue is used.

docs.title: 34. What review settings prevent sneaking in unreviewed code?
docs.text: Required approvals, dismiss stale approvals on push, require approval of the most recent reviewable push, require code owner review (including for CODEOWNERS and .github/workflows/), require conversation resolution, and no bypass for administrators.

docs.title: 35. What are stacked pull requests?
docs.text: Dependent PRs where each targets the previous PR's branch so each diff stays small. GitHub retargets a PR to main when its base branch is deleted after merging; after a squash merge, the upper branch needs git rebase --onto. git rebase --update-refs keeps a local stack in sync.

docs.title: 36. Explain Semantic Versioning.
docs.text: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH: increment MAJOR for incompatible API changes, MINOR for backward-compatible features, PATCH for backward-compatible fixes, resetting lower parts. 0.y.z means the API is not yet stable. Released versions are immutable. Pre-releases (-rc.1) sort before the release; build metadata (+sha.1a2b3c4) is ignored for precedence.

docs.title: 37. How do ^ and ~ ranges in npm relate to SemVer?
docs.text: ^2.4.1 allows >=2.4.1 <3.0.0 (compatible minors and patches); ~2.4.1 allows >=2.4.1 <2.5.0 (patches). For 0.x versions the caret treats the minor as breaking (^0.4.1 is <0.5.0). A breaking change shipped as a minor therefore reaches every consumer automatically.

docs.title: 38. What is the difference between lightweight, annotated, and signed tags?
docs.text: A lightweight tag is just a ref to a commit. An annotated tag is an object with tagger, date, and message. A signed tag is an annotated tag with a GPG, SSH, or X.509 signature. Releases should use annotated or signed tags; git describe and push --follow-tags consider annotated tags by default.

docs.title: 39. What are Conventional Commits?
docs.text: A message format type(scope)!: description with optional body and footers. fix maps to a patch, feat to a minor, and ! or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer to a major. Tools use it to compute versions, generate changelogs, and write release notes.

docs.title: 40. How do release-please and semantic-release differ?
docs.text: release-please maintains a Release PR with the version bump and changelog; merging it creates the tag and GitHub Release, so a human decides when. semantic-release runs in CI on each push to a release branch and, if commits warrant it, tags, creates the release, and publishes in one run. semantic-release needs full history (fetch-depth: 0).

docs.title: 41. Why might a workflow triggered by tags not run after a bot created the tag?
docs.text: Events created with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger new workflow runs, to prevent recursion. Run the publish job in the same workflow, or use a GitHub App or fine-grained token for the bot.

docs.title: 42. How do you make a deployed artifact traceable to its source?
docs.text: Stamp the version and commit SHA at build time: image tags plus OCI labels (org.opencontainers.image.version, .revision), a /version endpoint, and the release field in logs and error tracking. Never rebuild the same version; promote one artifact by digest.

docs.title: 43. Compare git reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard.
docs.text: All move the branch and HEAD. --soft keeps the index and working tree, so the undone changes are staged. --mixed (default) resets the index, leaving changes as unstaged edits. --hard resets the index and working tree, discarding changes; uncommitted edits are lost permanently.

docs.title: 44. When do you use git revert instead of git reset?
docs.text: When the commit is on a shared branch. Revert adds a new commit with the inverse change, preserving history for everyone; reset rewrites history and breaks collaborators' clones.

docs.title: 45. How do you revert a merge commit, and what is the catch?
docs.text: git revert -m 1 <merge> undoes the changes relative to the first parent (the mainline). The branch's commits still count as merged, so re-merging the fixed branch brings only new commits; you must revert the revert first.

docs.title: 46. How do you recover commits after a bad reset or rebase?
docs.text: git reflog shows every previous position of HEAD and branches; find the hash and run git reset --hard <sha> or git branch rescue <sha>. Immediately after a reset or rebase, ORIG_HEAD points at the old tip. Never-committed changes cannot be recovered this way.

docs.title: 47. How does git bisect work, and how many steps does it take?
docs.text: Binary search between a known good and a known bad commit: test the midpoint, mark it, and halve the range. It needs about log2(N) tests: 4 for 16 commits, about 10 for 1,000. git bisect run <script> automates it, with exit code 0 good, 1-127 bad (except 125), and 125 skip.

docs.title: 48. What is the difference between --force and --force-with-lease?
docs.text: --force overwrites the remote branch unconditionally, deleting anyone else's pushed commits. --force-with-lease fails if the remote moved since your last fetch; adding --force-if-includes also protects against background fetches that updated your remote-tracking ref.

docs.title: 49. A secret was pushed. What do you do, in order?
docs.text: Revoke or rotate it immediately, check provider logs for misuse, then, if needed, rewrite history with git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal, force push, ask GitHub Support to clean PR refs and caches, have collaborators re-clone, and enable secret scanning push protection and a pre-commit scanner. Deleting the file in a new commit is not enough.

docs.title: 50. How do you recover a deleted branch?
docs.text: Use the hash printed by git branch -D or find it in git reflog, then git branch <name> <sha>. On GitHub, the pull request page offers "Restore branch". Another clone that still has the branch can push it back.

docs.title: 51. Why are client-side hooks not a security control?
docs.text: They live in each clone, must be installed, and can be skipped with --no-verify. Use them for fast feedback and enforce the same rules in CI, rulesets, and push protection.

docs.title: 52. What do husky, lint-staged, and commitlint do?
docs.text: husky installs Git hooks from a committed .husky/ directory via the prepare script; lint-staged runs linters and formatters only on staged files; commitlint validates commit messages, typically in the commit-msg hook.

docs.title: 53. Why does adding .env to .gitignore not stop Git from tracking it?
docs.text: Ignore rules apply only to untracked files. Untrack it with git rm --cached .env, commit, and rotate any secrets it held, because they remain in history.

docs.title: 54. What does .gitattributes solve that core.autocrlf does not?
docs.text: It is committed, so line-ending rules apply to everyone regardless of personal settings (* text=auto, *.sh text eol=lf). It also marks binaries, controls diffs and merges, configures LFS, and sets GitHub Linguist attributes.

docs.title: 55. When should you use Git LFS?
docs.text: For large binaries that change over time (media, design files, models of modest size): Git stores small pointers and LFS stores the content, so clones download only the versions they check out. GitHub blocks files over 100 MiB without LFS. Build artifacts belong in CI artifacts or registries instead.

docs.title: 56. Compare shallow, blobless, and treeless clones, and sparse-checkout.
docs.text: Shallow (--depth 1) truncates history: for throwaway CI only. Blobless (--filter=blob:none) has all commits and trees and fetches file contents on demand: best for developers. Treeless (--filter=tree:0) also fetches trees on demand: for one-off builds needing history. Sparse-checkout limits the working tree to chosen directories, typically combined with a blobless clone in monorepos.

docs.title: 57. A developer ran git reset --hard HEAD~3 on their feature branch and wants the commits back. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: git reflog for the entry just before the reset.

How to confirm: git show <sha> on that entry shows the latest of the lost commits; git log <sha> shows all three.

Likely causes and fixes: a reset that went too far. Run git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD (if nothing moved since) or git reset --hard <sha>; uncommitted edits at the time are not recoverable. See undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: 58. After a teammate pushed, your git push is rejected as non-fast-forward. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: git fetch then git status (ahead/behind counts).

How to confirm: git log --oneline HEAD..origin/<branch> shows their commits.

Likely causes and fixes: the branches diverged. Rebase or merge onto origin/<branch>, run tests, and push. Do not force push a shared branch. See Git fundamentals and internals.

docs.title: 59. Everyone on the team gets duplicate commits and repeated conflicts after pulling a shared feature branch. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the remote branch's history for a forced update (git reflog show origin/<branch> in someone's clone).

How to confirm: git log --cherry-mark --oneline HEAD...origin/<branch> shows equivalent commits with different hashes.

Likely causes and fixes: someone rebased and force-pushed shared history. Agree on the correct tip, rebase each person's new work onto it with --onto, and block force pushes on shared branches. See branching, merging, and rebasing.

docs.title: 60. main is broken although every merged PR passed CI. How do you prevent this?
docs.text:
What to check first: the failing commit and which PRs merged just before it.

How to confirm: each PR passed against an older main; combining them fails.

Likely causes and fixes: semantic conflicts between PRs tested in isolation. Revert to restore green, then require up-to-date branches or adopt a merge queue with merge_group CI. See pull requests and code review.

docs.title: 61. A PR has been stuck on "Expected: waiting for status to be reported" for hours. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the required check's workflow ran at all for the PR's latest commit.

How to confirm: the Actions tab shows no run, or a run whose job name differs from the required check name.

Likely causes and fixes: a paths filter skipped the workflow, a job was renamed, or merge_group is missing for the merge queue. Make the workflow always run and skip inside jobs, update the check names, and add the trigger. See pull requests and code review.

docs.title: 62. A feature was reverted on main, fixed on its branch, and merged again, but most of it is missing. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the original merge was undone with git revert -m 1.

How to confirm: git log shows the revert commit; the re-merge diff contains only the new fix commits.

Likely causes and fixes: the old commits still count as merged. Revert the revert, then merge the fixes. See undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: 63. A database password was found in the repository's history. What is your plan?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the credential is still valid and where else it is used.

How to confirm: secret scanning alerts or git log -p -S '<part of the value>' show the commits containing it.

Likely causes and fixes: a .env committed before it was ignored. Rotate the password now and review database logs, then rewrite history with git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal, contact GitHub Support for PR refs and caches, have collaborators re-clone, and enable push protection. See undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: 64. A pagination bug exists now but did not in v2.3.0, 900 commits ago. How do you find the cause quickly?
docs.text:
What to check first: that a test reliably reproduces the bug.

How to confirm: the test passes on v2.3.0 and fails on HEAD.

Likely causes and fixes: use git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0 and git bisect run with the test (about 10 steps); use exit code 125 to skip unbuildable commits and --first-parent to identify the PR. See undoing mistakes and recovery.

docs.title: 65. The week before every release is spent resolving merge conflicts. What would you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: branch lifetimes and how many long-lived branches exist.

How to confirm: feature branches live for weeks and integrate only at release time; conflicts cluster before release dates.

Likely causes and fixes: late integration. Move to trunk-based development or GitHub flow with short-lived branches, feature flags, and fast CI; keep release branches only for versioned products. See branching strategies.

docs.title: 66. A hotfix shipped last month and the same bug reappeared in this release. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: git branch -a --contains <fix-sha>.

How to confirm: the fix exists only on a release or hotfix branch, not on main or develop.

Likely causes and fixes: the fix was not merged back (GitFlow) or was made only on the release branch. Land fixes upstream first and cherry-pick to release branches, and add a CI check for merge-backs. See branching strategies.

docs.title: 67. Consumers of your npm package broke after a minor release. What went wrong and how do you prevent it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the diff between the two versions for removed or changed public API.

How to confirm: a field or function was removed or its behavior changed, and the commit lacked ! or BREAKING CHANGE.

Likely causes and fixes: a breaking change released as minor. Publish a patch restoring compatibility, release the change as a major later, add API contract tests, and lint PR titles. See versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: 68. The release job runs git describe and fails in CI with "No names found". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the checkout step's fetch-depth and fetch-tags settings.

How to confirm: git tag in the job prints nothing.

Likely causes and fixes: a shallow checkout without tags. Use fetch-depth: 0 (history and tags) in the jobs that need history; fetching tags alone is not enough, because git describe walks back from HEAD through history to find one. See versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: 69. CI spends four minutes cloning a repository with a large history. How do you speed it up?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the job needs history, and the repository's pack size.

How to confirm: the checkout step dominates job time; git count-objects -vH shows gigabytes.

Likely causes and fixes: full clones of history with large blobs. Use the default shallow checkout where history is not needed, a blobless partial clone where it is, sparse-checkout for monorepo jobs, Git LFS for binaries, and consider removing large blobs from history. See hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories.

docs.title: 70. A Windows developer's PR shows every line changed, and a shell script now fails in the container. What is the fix?
docs.text:
What to check first: git ls-files --eol for the affected files.

How to confirm: the files have CRLF in the working tree or index, and the container error mentions ^M.

Likely causes and fixes: inconsistent line-ending conversion. Add .gitattributes with * text=auto and *.sh text eol=lf, run git add --renormalize ., and commit. See hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories.

docs.title: Pull Requests and Code Review
docs.text:
A pull request (PR) proposes merging one branch into another and wraps that proposal in a conversation: a diff, automated checks, review comments, approvals, and a record of the decision. On GitHub the pull request is the main quality gate between a developer's branch and the code that gets deployed.

This lesson covers the PR lifecycle, draft PRs, keeping PRs small, review checklists and etiquette, CODEOWNERS, branch protection rules and repository rulesets, required status checks and reviews, linear history, merge queues, stacked PRs, PR templates, linking issues, and auto-merge.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Code review catches defects, spreads knowledge of the codebase, and keeps design consistent; required checks stop broken code from reaching main. But the same process can become the bottleneck of the whole delivery pipeline: large PRs wait days for review, reviewers skim instead of reading, and main still breaks because two individually green PRs conflict when combined. Good teams design the PR process deliberately: small changes, fast reviews, the right owners, and automated gates that the platform enforces rather than relying on memory.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google. The paper Modern Code Review: A Case Study at Google analyzes review logs for 9 million reviewed changes, plus interviews and a survey. Google's public code review guidelines say that 100 lines is usually a reasonable size for a change and 1,000 lines is usually too large, that one business day is the maximum time to respond to a review request, and that reviewers should seek continuous improvement rather than perfection, marking optional polish with "Nit:".
  • GitHub. In How GitHub uses merge queue to ship hundreds of changes every day, GitHub reports that over 500 engineers merge about 2,500 pull requests a month into its large monorepo through the merge queue, and that the average wait time to ship a change fell by 33% after replacing its older "deploy train" system.
  • GitHub Docs. The protected branches and rulesets documentation describe the enforcement options used below, including that multiple rulesets can apply to the same branch and the most restrictive rule wins.

Popular tools and providers: GitHub pull requests, GitLab merge requests, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps pull requests, Gerrit, the GitHub CLI (gh), merge queues (GitHub's built-in queue, Mergify, Aviator), and stacked-PR tools.

docs.title: The pull request lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Push a branch and open a PR against the target branch (usually main).
  2. Optionally open it as a draft: drafts cannot be merged and do not request code owner reviews, but CI runs and teammates can comment.
  3. Mark it ready for review; GitHub requests reviews from the code owners of the changed files.
  4. CI runs on the pull_request event and reports status checks.
  5. Reviewers leave comments and submit a review: Comment, Approve, or Request changes.
  6. The author pushes fixes to the same branch; CI re-runs, and depending on settings, earlier approvals are dismissed.
  7. When the merge requirements pass, the PR is merged (directly, by auto-merge, or through a merge queue), and the branch is deleted.

The GitHub CLI covers the whole loop from the terminal:

gh pr create --draft --fill --base main     # open a draft PR from the current branch
gh pr ready                                 # mark it ready for review
gh pr checks --watch                        # follow CI status
gh pr checkout 128                          # check out someone else's PR locally
gh pr review 128 --approve --body "Looks good; one nit inline."
gh pr merge 128 --squash --delete-branch    # merge now (if requirements pass)
gh pr merge 128 --squash --auto             # or merge automatically once they pass

docs.title: Small pull requests
docs.text:
Review quality drops as size grows: a reviewer can reason about a 150-line change, but a 2,000-line change gets skimmed. Small PRs are reviewed faster, are easier to revert, conflict less, and keep branches short-lived. Ways to keep them small:

  • Split by layer or step: a migration PR, then the API, then the UI.
  • Separate refactoring from behavior changes ("move this file" and "change this logic" in different PRs).
  • Merge incomplete work behind a feature flag.
  • Stack dependent PRs (below) instead of one giant PR.

docs.title: What reviewers look for
docs.text:
A practical review checklist, roughly in order of importance:

Area Questions Correctness Does it do what the PR says? Edge cases, error paths, concurrency, time zones? Design Is this the right place and the right abstraction? Will it be easy to change? Tests Do tests cover the behavior and the failure modes, and would they fail if the code were wrong? Security Input validation, authorization checks, injection, secrets, sensitive data in logs? Data and compatibility Are migrations backward compatible? Do API changes break existing clients? Operability Logs, metrics, timeouts, retries, and a safe rollout or flag? Readability Names, comments that explain why, consistency with the codebase Style Left to formatters and linters, not humans

Automate everything mechanical (formatting, linting, type checks, dependency and secret scanning) so human attention goes to design and correctness.

docs.title: Review etiquette
docs.text:
• Authors: write a description that explains what and why, link the issue, point reviewers at the risky parts, review your own diff first, and respond to every comment (fix it, or explain why not).
  • Reviewers: respond quickly (within a business day at most), comment on the code rather than the person, explain the reasoning behind a request, distinguish blocking issues from "Nit:" suggestions, and approve when the change improves the codebase even if it is not how you would have written it.
  • Both: move long debates to a short call, then record the outcome in the PR.

docs.title: CODEOWNERS
docs.text:
A CODEOWNERS file maps paths to the people or teams responsible for them. GitHub looks for it in .github/, then the repository root, then docs/, on the branch the PR targets. When a PR touches owned files, the owners are requested automatically, and with "require review from Code Owners" enabled, one of them must approve.

# .github/CODEOWNERS
# Later lines take precedence: the LAST matching pattern wins.
# Owners must have write access to the repository.

*                          @example/taskflow-maintainers
/src/auth/                 @example/security
/src/db/migrations/        @example/data-platform
/.github/workflows/        @example/platform
/.github/CODEOWNERS        @example/platform

Patterns follow most .gitignore rules, with exceptions: ! negation and [ ] character ranges do not work. Owning the CODEOWNERS file itself and the workflow directory prevents someone from quietly removing a required reviewer or weakening CI in the same PR.

docs.title: Branch protection rules and rulesets
docs.text:
GitHub offers two ways to enforce rules on branches:

Branch protection rules Repository rulesets How many apply to a branch One (the matching rule) Many; rules are aggregated, most restrictive wins Targets Branches Branches, tags, and (for private/internal repos) pushes by path, size, or extension Visibility Repository admins Anyone with read access can see active rulesets Turning off temporarily Delete or edit the rule Set enforcement to disabled, keep the definition Bypass Admins (unless "do not allow bypassing") Explicit bypass list of roles, teams, or apps Organization-wide No Yes, on eligible plans

Both can apply at once; GitHub enforces the union, taking the most restrictive value of any rule that conflicts. New setups usually prefer rulesets because they layer cleanly (an org-wide baseline plus repository-specific additions) and are visible to everyone.

The rules that matter most for main:

  • Require a pull request before merging, with a number of approvals.
  • Dismiss stale approvals when new commits are pushed.
  • Require review from Code Owners.
  • Require approval of the most recent reviewable push, so the person who pushed last cannot be the only approver of their own change.
  • Require status checks to pass, optionally requiring the branch to be up to date with the base before merging.
  • Require conversation resolution before merging.
  • Require linear history: blocks merge commits, allowing only squash or rebase merges.
  • Require signed commits, require a merge queue, and require deployments to succeed before merging (for example, to a preview environment).
  • Block force pushes and deletions.

docs.title: Required status checks
docs.text:
A status check is a result reported on a commit, usually one per CI job, named after the job (for example test or CI / test). Marking a check as required means the PR cannot merge until that check succeeds on the PR's latest commit. Three details catch teams out:

  • Up-to-date branches. Without "require branches to be up to date", CI may have tested the PR against an old main. Two PRs can each pass and still break main when combined. Requiring up-to-date branches fixes this but forces authors to update and re-run CI after every merge, which does not scale; a merge queue does.
  • Skipped workflows. If a workflow does not run at all because of a paths or branches filter, its required check stays "Expected: waiting for status" and the PR is blocked. A job skipped by an if: condition, in contrast, reports success. Design path-filtered CI with that in mind (see pipeline design).
  • Renamed jobs. Renaming a job changes the check name, so the old required check never reports. Update the rule in the same change.

docs.title: Merge queues
docs.text:
A merge queue keeps main green at high merge rates. Instead of requiring each PR to be up to date and re-tested by hand, approved PRs join a queue. For each entry the queue creates a temporary branch (prefixed gh-readonly-queue/main/) containing the latest main, every PR ahead of it, and this PR, and runs the required checks on that exact combination. PRs that pass merge in order; a PR that fails is removed and the groups behind it are rebuilt without it.

Workflows that provide required checks must listen for the merge_group event; otherwise the checks never report, and the queue fails the merge when its status check timeout runs out:

# .github/workflows/ci.yml (trigger section)
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:        # required for merge queue checks

Queue settings include the merge method, how many groups build concurrently, minimum and maximum group sizes, a wait time for filling groups, a status check timeout, and whether only non-failing PRs may merge. Availability depends on the plan and repository ownership; check GitHub's merge queue documentation for your account type.

docs.title: Stacked pull requests
docs.text: When work has dependent steps (model, then API, then UI), you can stack PRs: PR 2's base branch is PR 1's branch instead of main, so each PR shows only its own diff. When PR 1 merges and its branch is deleted, GitHub automatically retargets PR 2 to main. If PR 1 was squash-merged, PR 2's branch still contains PR 1's original commits; rebase it with git rebase --onto (see branching, merging, and rebasing). Locally, git rebase --update-refs keeps all branches of a stack in sync when you edit a lower commit, and dedicated stacked-PR tools automate the rest.

docs.title: PR templates, linked issues, and auto-merge
docs.text:
A pull request template pre-fills the description:

<!-- .github/pull_request_template.md -->
## What and why

## How to test

## Risk and rollout
<!-- Migrations? Feature flag? Anything to watch after deploy? -->

## Checklist
- [ ] Tests added or updated
- [ ] No secrets or personal data in code, logs, or fixtures
- [ ] Database changes are backward compatible
- [ ] Docs and changelog updated if behavior changed

Closes #

Multiple templates can live in .github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE/, chosen with a template= query parameter on the PR creation URL.

Linking issues: writing a closing keyword such as Closes #142, Fixes #142, or Resolves #142 in the PR description links the issue and closes it when the PR is merged into the default branch.

Auto-merge: once enabled in the repository settings, an author can mark a PR to merge automatically when all requirements pass (gh pr merge --auto --squash), so nobody has to wait around for CI to finish. With a merge queue, the same action adds the PR to the queue.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Practice Use when Skip or adapt when Required PR reviews Any shared, deployed codebase A solo prototype; pair-programmed trunk-based commits (pairing is the review) CODEOWNERS with required owner review Clear ownership areas (security, data, CI config) Tiny teams where everyone owns everything Require up-to-date branches Low merge rate (a few PRs a day) High merge rate: use a merge queue instead Merge queue Many PRs per day, slow CI, frequent "main broke" incidents Low traffic repositories Draft PRs Early design feedback, CI on unfinished work Trivial changes Stacked PRs Large features that split into dependent steps Independent changes (open separate PRs from main) Linear history Squash-merge teams that want a simple log Teams that rely on merge commits for history

docs.title: A ruleset for main as code
docs.text:
Rulesets can be created in the UI or through the REST API, which makes them reviewable and repeatable across repositories:

{
  "name": "protect-main",
  "target": "branch",
  "enforcement": "active",
  "conditions": {
    "ref_name": { "include": ["~DEFAULT_BRANCH"], "exclude": [] }
  },
  "bypass_actors": [],
  "rules": [
    { "type": "deletion" },
    { "type": "non_fast_forward" },
    { "type": "required_linear_history" },
    {
      "type": "pull_request",
      "parameters": {
        "required_approving_review_count": 1,
        "dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push": true,
        "require_code_owner_review": true,
        "require_last_push_approval": true,
        "required_review_thread_resolution": true
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "required_status_checks",
      "parameters": {
        "strict_required_status_checks_policy": false,
        "required_status_checks": [
          { "context": "lint" },
          { "context": "test" },
          { "context": "build" }
        ]
      }
    }
  ]
}

# Apply it to a repository with the GitHub CLI
gh api --method POST repos/example/taskflow-api/rulesets --input ruleset-main.json

non_fast_forward blocks force pushes, deletion blocks deleting main, and an empty bypass_actors list means nobody, including admins, skips the rules. strict_required_status_checks_policy is false here because a merge queue (added as another rule or in settings) handles up-to-date testing.

docs.title: A CI workflow that works with required checks and a merge queue
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    needs: [lint, test]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with: { node-version-file: .nvmrc, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run build

The job IDs lint, test, and build become the check names listed in the ruleset. The full TaskFlow API workflow, with a MongoDB service container, is in GitHub Actions in depth.

docs.title: Reviewing a PR locally
docs.text:
gh pr checkout 131                     # fetch the PR branch
git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD    # its commits
git diff origin/main...HEAD --stat     # files changed since it left main
npm ci && npm test                     # run it yourself when the change is risky
gh pr review 131 --request-changes --body "Blocking: the new endpoint skips the ownership check (see inline)."

docs.title: Stacking two PRs
docs.text:
git switch -c feat/due-date-model main
# ...commit the schema change...
git push -u origin feat/due-date-model
gh pr create --base main --title "feat(tasks): add dueDate to the task model"

git switch -c feat/due-date-api        # built on top of the model branch
# ...commit the API change...
git push -u origin feat/due-date-api
gh pr create --base feat/due-date-model --title "feat(tasks): accept dueDate in the API"
# After the first PR merges (and its branch is deleted), GitHub retargets the second to main.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep PRs small (roughly a few hundred changed lines at most) and focused on one purpose.
  • Write a clear description: what, why, how to test, and the risks.
  • Automate formatting, linting, type checks, and scanning; review humans' time for design and correctness.
  • Use CODEOWNERS for sensitive paths, including CODEOWNERS itself and .github/workflows/.
  • Protect main with rulesets: required PR, approvals, code owners, last-push approval, required checks, no force pushes or deletions, and no bypass.
  • Use a merge queue once merge volume makes "update branch and re-run CI" painful.
  • Respond to reviews within a business day; agree on review expectations as a team.
  • Prefer auto-merge over watching CI.
  • Link every PR to an issue or ticket for traceability.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A PR is stuck on "Expected: waiting for status to be reported". Detect: the required check never appears in the PR's checks list. Cause: the workflow was skipped by a paths filter, the job was renamed, or (with a merge queue) the workflow lacks the merge_group trigger. Fix: make the workflow always run and skip work inside jobs with if: (skipped jobs report success), update the required check names, and add merge_group.
  • main is red although every PR passed CI. Detect: the failing commit on main is a merge of two PRs that each passed. Cause: CI tested each PR against an outdated main; the changes conflict semantically. Fix: revert, then require up-to-date branches or enable a merge queue.
  • PRs wait days for review and pile up. Detect: time-to-first-review and PR age metrics climb; PRs over 1,000 lines are common. Cause: large PRs, unclear ownership, review seen as optional work. Fix: size guidelines, CODEOWNERS for routing, a review response target, and splitting work into stacked PRs.
  • A change was merged with an unreviewed last-minute commit. Detect: the audit log shows a push after the final approval. Cause: approvals were not dismissed on new pushes. Fix: enable "dismiss stale approvals" and "require approval of the most recent reviewable push".
  • An admin merged a failing PR during an incident and broke production. Detect: the PR shows "merged without passing required checks" by a bypass actor. Cause: rules allow admin bypass. Fix: remove bypass for main, and create a documented, audited emergency path (for example a separate hotfix ruleset with a required post-incident review).
  • A contributor removed themselves as a required reviewer by editing CODEOWNERS. Detect: the diff touches .github/CODEOWNERS and owner reviews disappear from the PR. Cause: CODEOWNERS and workflows were not themselves owned. Fix: assign owners for CODEOWNERS and .github/workflows/, and require code owner review.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Pull request (merge request): A proposal to merge a branch, with a diff, checks, and review.
  • Draft PR: A PR marked not ready; it cannot be merged.
  • Status check: A pass/fail result reported on a commit by CI or an app.
  • Required check: A status check that must succeed before merging.
  • Code owner: A person or team responsible for paths listed in CODEOWNERS.
  • Branch protection rule: A per-branch set of merge and push restrictions.
  • Ruleset: A named, layered set of rules for branches, tags, or pushes, with enforcement status and a bypass list.
  • Stale approval: An approval given before newer commits were pushed.
  • Linear history: A history without merge commits.
  • Merge queue: A system that tests PRs combined with the latest base and the PRs ahead of them before merging them in order.
  • Stacked PRs: Dependent PRs where each one targets the previous PR's branch.
  • Auto-merge: Merging automatically once all requirements pass.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating approval count as quality; one careful review beats three rubber stamps.
  • Huge PRs "because the feature is big"; split the work.
  • Reviewing style by hand instead of automating it.
  • Making checks required without making sure the workflow always reports them.
  • Assuming a green PR means a green main when branches need not be up to date.
  • Leaving admin bypass on for main.
  • Forgetting merge_group when enabling the merge queue.
  • Letting .github/workflows/ and CODEOWNERS change without owner review.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Walk through a PR from draft to merge, naming each gate.
  2. What does "require approval of the most recent reviewable push" prevent?
  3. How do rulesets differ from branch protection rules, and what happens when both apply to main?
  4. Why can main break even though every PR passed CI, and what two settings prevent it?
  5. CI takes 20 minutes. With "require branches to be up to date" and one PR merging at a time, at most how many PRs can land in an 8-hour day? With a merge queue building 5 groups concurrently? (At most 24; up to about 120, ignoring failures and rebuilds.)
  6. Why should CODEOWNERS and .github/workflows/ have owners?
  7. Why might a required check stay "expected" forever, and how do you fix each cause?
  8. What are stacked PRs, and what extra step is needed after the lower PR is squash-merged?

docs.title: Undoing Mistakes and Recovery
docs.text:
Everyone commits to the wrong branch, resets too far, merges something broken, or pushes a file that should never have left their machine. Git is unusually forgiving: almost everything that was ever committed can be recovered, and most mistakes can be undone in one command, if you pick the right one.

This lesson covers git restore, the three modes of git reset, git revert (including reverting a merge), recovering with the reflog, finding a bad commit with git bisect, git stash, safe force pushing with --force-with-lease, removing a leaked secret from history, and recovering a deleted branch.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: The difference between a five-minute fix and a lost afternoon (or a security incident) is usually knowing which undo command fits the situation. Rewriting history that others have pulled creates more damage than the original mistake; using reset --hard on uncommitted work destroys it permanently; deleting a leaked API key in a new commit leaves it readable in history forever. Knowing the safe options, and knowing that the reflog keeps a safety net under most of them, lets you fix mistakes calmly and quickly, including during incidents when main needs a revert right now.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub's sensitive data guidance. GitHub's Removing sensitive data from a repository says to revoke or rotate a leaked secret first, then rewrite history with git-filter-repo 2.47 or later using --sensitive-data-removal, force push, and contact GitHub Support to clean pull request refs and cached views, because pull request refs are read-only and forks keep their own copies.
  • Reverting faulty merges. Git's own how-to Revert a faulty merge explains that reverting a merge undoes its changes but not its history, so a later re-merge of the same branch brings nothing back unless you first "revert the revert".
  • Bisecting in the Linux kernel. The kernel documentation Bisecting a regression shows git bisect as the standard way to find the change that caused a regression across thousands of commits, which is how many kernel regressions are reported to the right developer.

Popular tools and providers: the Git CLI (restore, reset, revert, reflog, bisect, stash), git-filter-repo and the BFG Repo-Cleaner for history rewriting, GitHub's "Restore branch" and "Revert" buttons on pull requests, and secret scanning with push protection to stop leaks before they happen.

docs.title: Pick the right undo
docs.text:
Situation Command Rewrites history? Discard unstaged edits to a file git restore <file> No Unstage a file but keep the edits git restore --staged <file> No Fix the last commit's message or add a forgotten file (not pushed) git commit --amend Yes (last commit) Undo the last commit, keep its changes staged git reset --soft HEAD~1 Yes Undo the last commit, keep changes as edits git reset HEAD~1 Yes Throw away commits and edits entirely git reset --hard <commit> Yes Undo a commit that is already on a shared branch git revert <sha> No (adds a commit) Undo a merged pull request (merge commit) git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> No Get back commits after a bad reset or rebase git reflog, then git reset --hard <sha> or git branch <name> <sha> Moves a ref Find which commit introduced a bug git bisect No Set work aside temporarily git stash No Remove a secret from all history Rotate the secret, then git filter-repo Yes (whole repository)

The dividing line: if the commits are only in your repository, rewrite freely; if others have them, add new commits that undo the change.

docs.title: git restore: working tree and index
docs.text:
git restore (Git 2.23 and later) copies file content from one place to another without touching commits:

git restore src/app.js                    # discard unstaged edits (copy index -> working tree)
git restore --staged src/app.js           # unstage (copy HEAD -> index), edits stay
git restore --staged --worktree src/app.js  # both: back to the committed version
git restore --source=HEAD~3 src/app.js    # bring back the file as it was 3 commits ago
git restore --source=v2.3.0 -- package.json

git restore <file> without --staged is destructive for that file's uncommitted edits; they were never saved in Git, so they cannot be recovered. Older guides use git checkout -- <file> and git reset HEAD <file> for the same operations.

docs.title: git reset: move the branch, optionally reset the index and files
docs.text:
git reset <commit> moves the current branch (and HEAD) to <commit>. The mode decides what happens to the index and working tree:

Mode Branch/HEAD Index Working tree Typical use --soft moves unchanged unchanged Squash the last few commits into one, or recommit with a new message --mixed (default) moves reset unchanged Undo commits but keep the changes to re-stage selectively --hard moves reset reset Throw away commits and all local changes --keep moves reset reset, but aborts if a locally modified file would change A safer --hard

Before a reset, Git saves the old tip in ORIG_HEAD, so an immediate git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD undoes the reset.

git reset --soft HEAD~3     # turn the last 3 commits into one staged change
git commit -m "feat(tasks): add due dates"

docs.title: git commit --amend
docs.text:
--amend replaces the last commit with a new one (new hash) containing the current index and, optionally, a new message:

git add src/forgotten-file.js
git commit --amend --no-edit          # same message, file added
git commit --amend -m "fix(auth): reject expired refresh tokens"

Amending is a rewrite. If the commit was pushed to a branch only you use, follow with git push --force-with-lease; if others may have it, make a new commit instead.

docs.title: git revert: undo by adding a commit
docs.text:
git revert <sha> creates a new commit that applies the inverse of <sha>'s changes. History is preserved, nobody's clone breaks, and the revert itself is reviewable, which makes it the right tool for shared branches and for production incidents:

git revert 4f9e2c1                    # opens an editor with "Revert ..." message
git revert --no-edit 4f9e2c1 7a1b2c3  # several commits, newest first is usual
git revert --no-commit HEAD~3..HEAD   # stage the inverse of a range, commit once

Reverting a merge. A merge commit has two parents, so Git needs to know which side is the "mainline" to keep. On main, the first parent is the previous main:

git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>   # undo everything the merged branch brought in

The catch: the revert removes the changes, but the branch's commits remain in history as merged. If the team fixes the branch and merges it again, Git sees those commits as already merged and only brings in the new fix commits. The correct sequence is to revert the revert first, then merge the fix:

git revert <revert-sha>       # re-apply the original feature
git merge feat/due-dates      # now brings in only the new fixes

With squash merging, a whole PR is a single ordinary commit, so git revert <sha> works without -m, and GitHub's "Revert" button on a merged PR opens a revert PR for you.

docs.title: The reflog: Git's safety net
docs.text:
Every time HEAD or a branch tip moves (commit, reset, rebase, checkout, merge, pull), Git appends an entry to that ref's reflog. The reflog is local to your clone and is not pushed.

git reflog
# a1b2c3d (HEAD -> feat/due-dates) HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD~2
# 9f8e7d6 HEAD@{1}: commit: add due-date validation
# 5c4b3a2 HEAD@{2}: commit: add dueDate field
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{3}: checkout: moving from main to feat/due-dates

git reflog show feat/due-dates   # the branch's own history of positions
git log -g --oneline             # reflog as a log
git show main@{yesterday}        # where main was yesterday (time-based)

Recovery is always the same two steps: find the hash in the reflog, then point a ref at it (git branch rescue <sha>, or git reset --hard <sha> on the current branch). Commits that no ref or reflog entry reaches are "dangling"; git fsck --lost-found lists them, which can even recover a dropped stash.

docs.title: git bisect: binary search for the bad commit
docs.text:
When something worked in v2.3.0 and is broken now, git bisect finds the first bad commit by binary search. You mark one good and one bad commit; Git checks out the midpoint; you test and mark it; the range halves each time.

The number of tests is about log2 of the number of commits in the range: 16 commits need 4 tests, 1,000 need about 10, and 100,000 only about 17. With an automated test, git bisect run does the whole search:

git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0          # bad first, then good
git bisect run npm test -- tests/pagination.test.js
# ...
# 7440a9ddffa19bdcd28e9cd9286abbec4b314b26 is the first bad commit
git bisect reset                      # return to where you started

The script's exit code drives the search: 0 means good, 1 to 127 (except 125) means bad, and 125 means "cannot test this commit, skip it" (for example, it does not build). Manual steps are git bisect good, git bisect bad, and git bisect skip. Useful options:

  • git bisect start --first-parent follows only the first parent, so on a main built from merged PRs it identifies the PR that broke things.
  • Alternate terms (git bisect old and new, or your own with --term-old and --term-new) work for non-bugs, such as "when did this endpoint get slow?".
  • git bisect log > bisect.log and git bisect replay bisect.log save and repeat a session.

Bisect works best when every commit builds and passes tests on its own, which is one more reason for clean, small commits.

docs.title: git stash: set work aside
docs.text:
git stash saves uncommitted changes as special commits on a stack and cleans the working tree, so you can switch context:

git stash push -m "wip: due-date validation"   # tracked changes only
git stash push -u -m "wip incl. new files"     # include untracked files
git stash push --staged -m "only what is staged"   # Git 2.35+
git stash list
# stash@{0}: On feat/due-dates: wip incl. new files
git stash show -p stash@{0}                    # see the diff
git stash pop                                  # apply and drop the newest
git stash apply stash@{1}                      # apply, keep it in the list
git stash branch feat/validation stash@{1}     # new branch from the stash's base
git stash drop stash@{1}

Stashes are local, easy to forget, and conflict-prone when popped onto a branch that moved on. For anything you will not return to within the hour, a "WIP" commit on a branch is safer.

docs.title: Force pushing safely
docs.text:
After rewriting your own pushed branch (rebase, amend, reset), the remote rejects a normal push because it is not a fast-forward. Your options:

Command Behavior Risk git push --force Overwrite the remote branch unconditionally Silently deletes commits others pushed git push --force-with-lease Overwrite only if the remote still points where your origin/<branch> says Safe unless something fetched in the background and updated origin/<branch> git push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes Also requires that the remote tip you are overwriting was integrated into your local branch (Git 2.30+) The safest form 
git config --global alias.pushf "push --force-with-lease --force-if-includes"
git pushf

Protected branches (main, release branches) should block force pushes entirely, so these commands only ever apply to your own feature branches.

docs.title: Removing a leaked secret from history
docs.text:
Suppose .env with a database password was committed and pushed. A new commit deleting the file does not help: the password is in history, in every clone, possibly in forks and CI logs. The order of operations matters:

  1. Rotate the secret first. Revoke the key or change the password immediately. Once the old value is useless, the leak is contained, and for many secrets this is the only step that truly matters, because you cannot know who already copied it.
  2. Check for misuse in the provider's audit logs for the window the secret was exposed.
  3. Decide whether to rewrite history. If the data itself is sensitive (personal data, a key that cannot be rotated), rewrite:
# In a fresh clone with all refs (git-filter-repo 2.47+)
git clone --mirror git@github.com:example/taskflow-api.git
cd taskflow-api.git
git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --invert-paths --path .env
# or replace strings in every file of every commit:
# git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal --replace-text ../expressions.txt
git push --force --mirror origin
  1. Clean what you cannot push to. Pull request refs on GitHub are read-only, and forks have their own copies; GitHub Support can dereference PRs, remove cached views, and run garbage collection, given the "First Changed Commit(s)" printed by git filter-repo.
  2. Have collaborators re-clone (or carefully rebase their branches); merging old branches would reintroduce the secret.
  3. Prevent recurrence: add the file to .gitignore, enable secret scanning with push protection, and add a pre-commit secret scanner (see hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories).

Every commit hash from the leak onward changes, signatures on rewritten commits are dropped, and open PRs may become unusable, so merge or close open PRs first and announce the rewrite.

docs.title: Recovering a deleted branch
docs.text:
git branch -D feat/due-dates           # oops
# Deleted branch feat/due-dates (was 9f8e7d6).
git branch feat/due-dates 9f8e7d6      # the hash is in the delete message...
git reflog | grep due-dates            # ...or in the reflog

If the branch only existed on GitHub and was deleted after its PR merged or closed, the pull request page offers a Restore branch button. If it is gone from GitHub but a teammate or CI runner still has it, push it back from their clone.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Tool Use when Do not use when restore Discarding or unstaging local file changes You might want those edits later (stash or commit instead) reset --soft / --mixed Reshaping local, unpushed commits The commits are on a shared branch reset --hard Abandoning local work you are sure about You have uncommitted edits you might need commit --amend Fixing the latest unpushed commit Others have pulled it revert Undoing anything already shared, especially on main Cleaning up your private branch (rewrite instead) reflog Recovering after reset, rebase, amend, or branch deletion Recovering never-committed edits (they were never stored) bisect A regression with a known good point No reliable way to test a commit stash Short context switches Long-term storage of work History rewrite for secrets Data that cannot be rotated or must not remain anywhere Instead of rotating the secret

docs.title: Committed to main instead of a feature branch (not pushed)
docs.text:
git branch feat/due-dates          # new branch pointing at the commits
git reset --hard origin/main       # move main back to the remote state
git switch feat/due-dates          # continue on the branch

docs.title: Roll back a bad deploy caused by a merged PR
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
git log --oneline --first-parent -5
# 3c2b1a0 Merge pull request #212 from example/feat/due-dates
git revert -m 1 3c2b1a0 --no-edit
git push                            # or open a PR if main is protected

Rolling back the deployment (redeploying the previous artifact) is usually faster than waiting for a revert to build; do both, so the next deploy does not reintroduce the bug. See rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: Find a pagination regression automatically
docs.text:
#!/bin/sh
# tests/bisect-pagination.sh: exit 0 = good, 1 = bad, 125 = skip
npm ci --silent || exit 125         # cannot build this commit: skip it
node --test tests/pagination.test.js

git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0
git bisect run sh tests/bisect-pagination.sh
# Bisecting: 7 revisions left to test after this (roughly 3 steps)
# ...
# 7440a9d... is the first bad commit
git bisect reset

Keep the bisect script outside the tree (or untracked) when older commits would not contain it; Git checks out old commits while bisecting.

docs.title: Recover from a rebase that went wrong
docs.text:
git rebase origin/main              # conflicts resolved badly, tests now fail
git reset --hard ORIG_HEAD          # back to the pre-rebase tip, immediately after
# Later, if ORIG_HEAD has moved on:
git reflog
# 5d4e3f2 HEAD@{6}: rebase (start): checkout origin/main
# 9c1d2e3 HEAD@{7}: commit: Add tests        <- the tip before the rebase
git reset --hard 9c1d2e3

docs.title: Split one commit into two
docs.text:
git reset HEAD~1                   # undo the commit, keep changes as edits
git add -p src/models/task.js      # stage only the model change
git commit -m "feat(tasks): add dueDate to the model"
git add src/routes/tasks.js
git commit -m "feat(tasks): accept dueDate in the API"

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Prefer revert on shared branches and reserve rewriting for your own unpushed or unshared work.
  • Commit early; committed work is recoverable, uncommitted edits are not.
  • Check git status and git stash list before reset --hard.
  • Use --force-with-lease --force-if-includes, never bare --force.
  • Protect main and release branches against force pushes and deletion.
  • Rotate leaked secrets before anything else; history rewriting is cleanup, not containment.
  • Keep commits small and buildable so revert and bisect stay precise.
  • Use squash merging if you want "undo this PR" to be a single, simple revert.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A deploy broke checkout and the culprit is a merged PR. Detect: error rates rose at deploy time; git log --first-parent shows the merges in that deploy. Cause: a regression in one PR. Fix: roll back the deployment to the previous artifact, then git revert -m 1 the merge (or revert the squash commit) so main is safe to deploy again.
  • A re-merged feature branch "lost" most of its changes. Detect: after merging the fixed branch, only the latest fix commits appear in the diff. Cause: the original merge was reverted, and Git treats the branch's old commits as already merged. Fix: revert the revert commit, then merge the branch with its fixes.
  • A teammate's commits vanished from a shared branch. Detect: git reflog show origin/feat/x on someone's clone shows the branch moved backwards in a forced update. Cause: git push --force over newer remote commits. Fix: restore the lost tip from any clone or the PR's commit list and push it back; enforce --force-with-lease and block force pushes on shared branches.
  • A cloud key was found in a public repository's history. Detect: a secret scanning alert, a provider notification, or an unexpected bill. Cause: .env or a config file committed before .gitignore covered it. Fix: revoke and rotate the key immediately, review provider logs for misuse, then rewrite history with git filter-repo --sensitive-data-removal and contact GitHub Support for PR refs and caches; enable push protection.
  • A developer ran reset --hard and lost a day of work. Detect: the work never appears in git reflog. Cause: the changes were never committed or stashed. Fix: check the editor's local history (many IDEs keep one); for the future, commit WIP to a branch frequently.
  • Bisect points at a commit that obviously cannot be the cause. Detect: the reported first bad commit only changed docs. Cause: a flaky test or an environment difference marked a good commit bad. Fix: make the test deterministic, use git bisect skip for commits that cannot be tested, replay with git bisect log, and consider --first-parent.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• git restore: Copy file content from the index or a commit into the working tree or index.
  • git reset: Move the current branch to another commit, with soft, mixed, or hard effects on the index and files.
  • ORIG_HEAD: The previous tip saved before a reset, rebase, or merge.
  • Amend: Replace the latest commit with a modified one.
  • Revert: A new commit that applies the inverse of an earlier commit.
  • Mainline (-m): The parent number to keep when reverting or cherry-picking a merge.
  • Reflog: The local log of every position a ref has had.
  • Dangling commit: A commit no ref or reflog entry reaches.
  • Bisect: Binary search through history for the first bad commit.
  • Stash: Uncommitted changes saved on a local stack.
  • --force-with-lease: A force push that fails if the remote moved since you last fetched.
  • git filter-repo: A tool that rewrites an entire repository's history by rules.
  • Secret rotation: Replacing a credential and invalidating the old one.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Deleting a leaked secret in a new commit and considering it handled.
  • Rewriting history before rotating the secret.
  • Using reset --hard to "clean up" with uncommitted work present.
  • Reverting a merge without -m, or forgetting to revert the revert before re-merging.
  • Believing the reflog is shared; it exists only in your clone.
  • Believing git stash is a backup; stashes are local and easy to drop.
  • Using --force on a branch someone else uses.
  • Bisecting with a flaky test.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which command undoes a commit that is already on main, and why not reset?
  2. Compare git reset --soft, --mixed, and --hard in terms of the branch, the index, and the working tree.
  3. You reverted a merged feature branch, fixed it, and merged it again, but most of the feature is missing. Why, and what should you have done?
  4. How do you recover commits after git reset --hard HEAD~5? What can never be recovered?
  5. A regression appeared somewhere in 2,000 commits since the last good release. About how many test runs will git bisect need? (About 11, since 2^11 = 2,048.)
  6. What do exit codes 0, 1, and 125 mean to git bisect run?
  7. What is the difference between --force, --force-with-lease, and --force-if-includes?
  8. List, in order, the steps to handle a database password committed and pushed to GitHub.

docs.text:
• Pro Git: Undoing Things
  • Pro Git: Reset Demystified
  • Git how-to: Revert a faulty merge
  • Git reference: git bisect and git reflog
  • GitHub Docs: Removing sensitive data from a repository
  • GitHub Docs: Deleting and restoring branches in a pull request
  • git-filter-repo
