docs.title: Versioning, Tags, and Releases
docs.text:
A release is a named, immutable snapshot of your software that someone can install, deploy, or roll back to. Versioning gives each release a name that communicates what changed; Git tags pin that name to an exact commit; and release tooling turns commits into changelogs, version bumps, and published artifacts.

This lesson covers Semantic Versioning (including pre-release and build metadata), lightweight, annotated, and signed tags, Conventional Commits, changelog generation, release automation with release-please and semantic-release, GitHub Releases and release assets, calendar versioning, and how to stamp the version into the artifacts you deploy.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Versions are a contract with the people and systems that depend on you. A library that ships a breaking change as a patch release breaks every consumer whose lockfile allowed it; an API team that cannot say which commit is running in production cannot reproduce a bug or roll back confidently. Automated, consistent versioning removes the "what is in this release?" meeting, produces accurate changelogs for free, and links every running artifact back to a tag, a commit, and the pull requests that went into it.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Semantic Versioning. The SemVer 2.0.0 specification defines MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, pre-release and build metadata, and precedence rules. npm's dependency ranges (^1.4.0, ~1.4.0) assume packages follow it, which is why a mislabelled breaking change spreads so quickly through the JavaScript ecosystem.
  • Conventional Commits. The Conventional Commits 1.0.0 specification maps commit types to SemVer: fix to a patch, feat to a minor release, and ! or a BREAKING CHANGE footer to a major release, so tools can compute the next version from history.
  • release-please at Google. Google's release-please is used across its open-source client libraries. It maintains a standing "Release PR" with the version bump and changelog, and creates the tag and GitHub Release when that PR is merged.
  • Calendar versioning. CalVer documents date-based schemes used by well-known projects; Ubuntu's YY.0M releases (for example 24.04, April 2024) are the classic example.

Popular tools and providers: release-please, semantic-release, Changesets (popular in JavaScript monorepos), commitlint, npm version, GitHub Releases and the gh release CLI, and docker/metadata-action for deriving image tags from Git tags.

docs.title: Semantic Versioning
docs.text:
A semantic version is MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH, for example 2.4.1:

Part Increment when Example MAJOR You make an incompatible change to the public API 2.4.1 to 3.0.0 MINOR You add functionality in a backward-compatible way 2.4.1 to 2.5.0 PATCH You make backward-compatible bug fixes 2.4.1 to 2.4.2

Incrementing a part resets the parts to its right to zero. Rules worth knowing precisely:

  • A released version's contents must never change. Fixing a release means publishing a new version.
  • 0.y.z is for initial development: anything may change at any time, and the public API is not considered stable. 1.0.0 defines the public API.
  • The public API must be declared: for TaskFlow API it is the HTTP endpoints, request and response shapes, and status codes clients rely on; for a library it is the exported functions and types.
  • v2.4.1 is a common tag name, but the v is not part of the semantic version itself.

Pre-release versions append a hyphen and dot-separated identifiers: 3.0.0-alpha.1, 3.0.0-beta.2, 3.0.0-rc.1. A pre-release has lower precedence than the normal version, and identifiers compare part by part, numerically when numeric:

1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0-alpha.1 < 1.0.0-alpha.beta < 1.0.0-beta
            < 1.0.0-beta.2 < 1.0.0-beta.11 < 1.0.0-rc.1 < 1.0.0

Note beta.2 < beta.11 (numeric comparison), a classic bug in hand-rolled version sorting.

Build metadata appends a plus sign: 2.4.1+build.517 or 2.4.1+sha.1a2b3c4. It is ignored when comparing precedence, so two versions differing only in build metadata are the same version.

How consumers use SemVer in npm (see npm and package management):

Range Matches Meaning ^2.4.1 >=2.4.1 <3.0.0 Any compatible minor or patch ~2.4.1 >=2.4.1 <2.5.0 Patches only ^0.4.1 >=0.4.1 <0.5.0 For 0.x, the caret treats the minor as breaking 2.4.1 exactly 2.4.1 Pinned

docs.title: Git tags
docs.text:
A tag is a ref under refs/tags/ that names a commit permanently. There are three kinds:

Kind Command Stores Use for Lightweight git tag v2.4.0 Just a ref to the commit Private bookmarks Annotated git tag -a v2.4.0 -m "TaskFlow API 2.4.0" A tag object: tagger, date, message Releases Signed git tag -s v2.4.0 -m "..." An annotated tag plus a GPG, SSH, or X.509 signature Releases where provenance matters

Annotated tags are objects with their own metadata (see Git fundamentals), and several tools treat them specially: git describe uses only annotated tags unless you pass --tags, and git push --follow-tags pushes only annotated tags reachable from the pushed commits.

Tags are not pushed by default:

git push origin v2.4.0          # push one tag
git push --follow-tags          # push commits plus their annotated tags
git ls-remote --tags origin     # list tags on the remote

Treat release tags as immutable. Moving a published tag (git tag -f plus a force push) means two people can build "v2.4.0" from different code, and caches, package registries, and lockfiles that recorded the old commit will disagree. If a release is bad, publish v2.4.1.

git describe names any commit relative to the nearest tag, which is useful for development builds:

git describe --tags --dirty
# v2.4.0-5-g1a2b3c4          5 commits after v2.4.0, at commit 1a2b3c4
# v2.4.0-5-g1a2b3c4-dirty    ...with uncommitted changes

docs.title: Conventional Commits
docs.text:
Conventional Commits is a lightweight convention for commit messages:

<type>[optional scope][!]: <description>

[optional body]

[optional footer(s)]

feat(tasks): add dueDate to tasks
fix(auth): reject expired refresh tokens
perf(db): add index on tasks.ownerId
docs: document the pagination parameters
feat(api)!: return 404 instead of 200 with null for missing tasks

BREAKING CHANGE: clients that checked for a null body must handle 404.
Type Meaning Default effect on version feat A new feature MINOR fix A bug fix PATCH ! after type/scope, or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer Incompatible change MAJOR perf, refactor, docs, test, build, ci, chore, style Other changes (types beyond feat and fix are allowed by the spec) None by default; tools can be configured

With squash merging, the PR title becomes the commit message on main, so teams lint PR titles rather than every commit on the branch. Commit message linting with commitlint is covered in hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories.

docs.title: Changelogs and release notes
docs.text:
A changelog is a human-readable list of notable changes per version. Generated from Conventional Commits, it groups entries by type:

## [2.4.0] (2026-11-13)      <- tools link this heading to the v2.3.1...v2.4.0 compare view

### Features
* **tasks:** add dueDate to tasks (#212)

### Bug Fixes
* **auth:** reject expired refresh tokens (#215)

GitHub can also generate release notes from merged pull requests, grouped by label, configured in .github/release.yml:

# .github/release.yml
changelog:
  exclude:
    labels: [skip-changelog]
  categories:
    - title: Breaking changes
      labels: [breaking-change]
    - title: New features
      labels: [enhancement]
    - title: Bug fixes
      labels: [bug]
    - title: Other changes
      labels: ["*"]

docs.title: Release automation
docs.text:
Two widely used tools compute the next version from Conventional Commits.

release-please semantic-release Release trigger Merging the Release PR Any push to a release branch with releasable commits Human checkpoint Yes: the Release PR is reviewed and merged No, unless you add one Writes to the repo Version files and CHANGELOG.md via the PR Nothing by default (version lives in tags and the registry) Typical fit Applications and services, multi-package repos with a manifest Libraries published on every merge Monorepos Built-in manifest mode, one version per package Via community plugins

release-please watches the default branch. On each push it creates or updates a Release PR containing the version bump (for example in package.json with release-type: node) and the new changelog section. When you merge that PR, it tags the merge commit, creates a GitHub Release, and exposes outputs such as release_created, tag_name, and version for later jobs.

semantic-release runs in CI after tests pass. It reads commits since the last release tag, decides the bump, generates notes, creates the tag and GitHub Release, and publishes (for example to npm) in one run. It needs the full Git history and tags, so the checkout must use fetch-depth: 0.

Changesets takes a different approach popular in JavaScript monorepos: contributors add small "changeset" files describing the bump for each package, and a release PR aggregates them.

A practical detail for both: GitHub does not start new workflow runs for events created with the default GITHUB_TOKEN (to prevent loops). A Release PR opened with GITHUB_TOKEN will not trigger your CI checks, and a tag pushed with it will not trigger an on: push: tags workflow. Use a GitHub App token or a fine-grained token for the release bot, or run the publish steps in the same workflow, as in the example below.

docs.title: GitHub Releases and release assets
docs.text:
A GitHub Release is attached to a tag and adds a title, notes, and downloadable assets (binaries, archives, checksums, SBOMs). Each release can hold up to 1,000 assets, each under 2 GiB. Releases can be drafts (not public yet) or marked as pre-releases, and one release is marked "latest".

With immutable releases enabled for a repository (generally available since October 2025), a published release's tag and assets cannot be changed or deleted, and GitHub generates an attestation for the release. Create the release as a draft, attach every asset, then publish.

Container images and packages usually go to a registry (GHCR, npm, Docker Hub) rather than release assets; the release notes link to them by version and digest.

docs.title: Calendar versioning
docs.text:
CalVer uses dates instead of compatibility signals: 24.04 (YY.0M), 2026.11.1 (YYYY.MM.MICRO). It suits products whose users care about "how recent" rather than "is it compatible": operating systems, applications on a release train, internal services. It does not tell consumers whether an upgrade is safe, so libraries should prefer SemVer.

Scheme Says Good for SemVer Compatibility Libraries, SDKs, public APIs CalVer Age, release cadence OS releases, apps on time-based trains Build number or commit SHA Exact build Internal services deployed continuously

Many continuously deployed services do not version releases for humans at all: every deployment is identified by its commit SHA and image digest. That is fine, as long as each artifact is traceable.

docs.title: The version inside the artifact
docs.text:
Whatever scheme you use, stamp it into the artifact so a running system can tell you what it is:

  • Container image tags and labels: tag 2.4.0, 2.4, and the commit SHA, and add the OCI labels org.opencontainers.image.version and org.opencontainers.image.revision.
  • An endpoint or log line: GET /version returning the version and commit, and the same values in the startup log and in error tracking "release" fields.
  • Binaries and bundles: embed at build time (environment variables or generated files), never computed at runtime from a Git checkout that production does not have.

Never rebuild a release under the same version: build once, then promote that exact artifact (see artifacts and environment promotion).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended approach Public library or SDK SemVer, Conventional Commits, semantic-release or release-please, signed tags Service with external API consumers SemVer for the API contract (or API versions in the URL), release-please for human-gated releases Internal service deployed many times a day Commit SHA and image digest per deploy; optional CalVer or SemVer tags for milestones Mobile or desktop app SemVer or CalVer marketing version plus an always-increasing build number required by the stores Monorepo with several packages release-please manifest mode or Changesets, one version per package Prototype or pre-1.0 product 0.y.z; do not promise stability you cannot keep

Avoid Conventional Commits automation when your team will not keep the discipline: wrong commit types produce wrong versions. In that case, lint the PR title and squash-merge, so only one message per change matters.

docs.title: Tag and verify a release by hand
docs.text:
git switch main && git pull --ff-only
npm version minor -m "chore(release): %s"   # bumps package.json, commits, tags v2.4.0
git push --follow-tags                      # push the commit and the annotated tag

# Signed tag with an SSH key (Git 2.34+)
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git tag -s v2.4.1 -m "TaskFlow API 2.4.1"
git tag -v v2.4.1                           # verification needs gpg.ssh.allowedSignersFile
git push origin v2.4.1

npm version creates an annotated tag by default when run in a Git repository, using the v prefix.

docs.title: release-please for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/release.yml
name: release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  release-please:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write        # create tags and releases
      pull-requests: write   # open and update the Release PR
      issues: write          # manage release labels
    outputs:
      release_created: ${{ steps.rp.outputs.release_created }}
      tag_name: ${{ steps.rp.outputs.tag_name }}
      version: ${{ steps.rp.outputs.version }}
    steps:
      - id: rp
        uses: googleapis/release-please-action@v5
        with:
          release-type: node
          # A GitHub App or fine-grained token, so CI runs on the Release PR
          token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_TOKEN }}

  publish-image:
    needs: release-please
    if: needs.release-please.outputs.release_created == 'true'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write        # push to ghcr.io
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          ref: ${{ needs.release-please.outputs.tag_name }}
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          build-args: |
            VERSION=${{ needs.release-please.outputs.version }}
            GIT_SHA=${{ github.sha }}
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${{ needs.release-please.outputs.version }}
            ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-${{ github.sha }}

The publish job runs in the same workflow as release-please, so it does not depend on a tag push event triggering another workflow. In practice teams often promote an image already built for that commit instead of building again; see artifacts and environment promotion.

docs.title: semantic-release for a shared npm package
docs.text:
{
  "branches": ["main", { "name": "next", "prerelease": true }],
  "plugins": [
    "@semantic-release/commit-analyzer",
    "@semantic-release/release-notes-generator",
    "@semantic-release/npm",
    "@semantic-release/github"
  ]
}

# .github/workflows/release.yml (taskflow-sdk package)
name: release
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, next]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  release:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write        # tags and GitHub Releases
      issues: write          # comment on released issues
      pull-requests: write   # comment on released PRs
      id-token: write        # npm trusted publishing and provenance
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0     # full history and tags are required
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
      - run: npm audit signatures
      - run: npx semantic-release
        env:
          GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

The first file is .releaserc.json. The next branch publishes pre-releases such as 3.0.0-next.1. With npm trusted publishing configured for the package, no npm token secret is needed: the job's OIDC identity (id-token: write) authorizes the publish, and npm records provenance. OIDC is explained in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Create a GitHub Release with assets from the CLI
docs.text:
npm run build:openapi            # writes dist/openapi.json
sha256sum dist/openapi.json > dist/SHA256SUMS
gh release create v2.4.0 dist/openapi.json dist/SHA256SUMS \
  --title "TaskFlow API 2.4.0" \
  --generate-notes \
  --verify-tag                   # fail if the tag does not exist on GitHub

docs.title: Expose the version from the running service
docs.text:
# Dockerfile (excerpt)
FROM node:24-slim
ARG VERSION=dev
ARG GIT_SHA=unknown
LABEL org.opencontainers.image.version=$VERSION \
      org.opencontainers.image.revision=$GIT_SHA
ENV APP_VERSION=$VERSION \
    GIT_SHA=$GIT_SHA

// src/routes/version.js
import { Router } from "express";

export const versionRouter = Router();

versionRouter.get("/version", (req, res) => {
  res.json({
    version: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev",
    commit: process.env.GIT_SHA ?? "unknown",
  });
});

curl https://api.example.com/version now answers "what is running?" during an incident, and the image labels answer the same question for whoever inspects the registry.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Follow SemVer for anything other teams consume, and define what your public API is.
  • Use annotated (ideally signed) tags for releases, and never move or reuse a published tag.
  • Adopt Conventional Commits for PR titles and squash merge, and lint them in CI.
  • Automate version bumps, changelogs, tags, and release notes; humans decide when, tools decide what number.
  • Build each release once and publish it under one version; record the commit SHA and image digest with it.
  • Stamp version and commit into every artifact and expose them at runtime.
  • Enable immutable releases where your platform supports them, and attach checksums (and SBOMs) to release assets.
  • Use pre-release channels (-rc.1, next branch) to test major versions with early adopters.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Consumers break after a "minor" upgrade. Detect: bug reports appear right after a minor or patch release; the diff removed or renamed a public field. Cause: a breaking change shipped without ! or a BREAKING CHANGE footer. Fix: publish a patch that restores compatibility (or deprecate first), then add contract tests for the public API and lint PR titles.
  • Two builds of "v2.4.0" behave differently. Detect: image digests or checksums for the same version differ. Cause: a tag was moved, or the release was rebuilt from a branch. Fix: treat tags as immutable (protect them with a tag ruleset), publish a new patch version, and promote artifacts by digest.
  • The release workflow never runs after release-please creates a tag. Detect: the tag and GitHub Release exist, but no on: push: tags or on: release run appears. Cause: the tag was created with GITHUB_TOKEN, which does not trigger new workflow runs. Fix: run the publish job in the same workflow gated on release_created, or use a GitHub App token for the release bot.
  • semantic-release decides "no release" or the wrong version in CI. Detect: logs say no previous tag was found, and it tries to release 1.0.0. Cause: a shallow checkout without tags. Fix: fetch-depth: 0 on actions/checkout.
  • Nobody can say which version is running in production. Detect: incident responders compare deploy timestamps with merge times by hand. Cause: no version or commit in the artifact or telemetry. Fix: stamp version and SHA at build, expose /version, and tag logs, metrics, and error reports with the release.
  • Pre-release versions sort wrongly in a dashboard. Detect: 1.0.0-beta.11 appears before 1.0.0-beta.2. Cause: string sorting instead of SemVer precedence. Fix: use a SemVer library (for example the semver npm package) for comparisons.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Semantic Versioning (SemVer): MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH versions that signal compatibility.
  • Public API: The documented surface whose compatibility the version number promises.
  • Pre-release: A version with a hyphenated suffix (-rc.1) that sorts before its normal version.
  • Build metadata: A + suffix ignored for precedence.
  • Lightweight tag: A ref pointing directly at a commit.
  • Annotated tag: A tag object with tagger, date, and message.
  • Signed tag: An annotated tag carrying a cryptographic signature.
  • Conventional Commits: A commit message convention that encodes change type and breaking changes.
  • Changelog: A curated, per-version list of notable changes.
  • Release PR: A pull request maintained by release-please that, when merged, triggers a release.
  • Release asset: A file attached to a GitHub Release.
  • Immutable release: A release whose tag and assets cannot change after publication.
  • CalVer: Versioning based on release dates.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking the version number is marketing. For dependencies it is a compatibility promise that tools act on automatically.
  • Releasing breaking changes as minor versions because "it is a small break".
  • Moving tags to "fix" a release.
  • Using lightweight tags for releases, so git describe and --follow-tags ignore them.
  • Rebuilding the same version for each environment.
  • Assuming GITHUB_TOKEN-created tags and PRs trigger other workflows.
  • Sorting versions as strings.
  • Staying on 0.x forever to avoid committing to compatibility.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does each part of MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH promise, and what resets when you bump one?
  2. Order these versions: 1.0.0, 1.0.0-rc.1, 1.0.0-beta.11, 1.0.0-beta.2, 1.0.0-alpha.
  3. The last release is 3.7.2. Since then: two fix commits, one feat(tasks) commit, and one docs commit. What is the next version? What if one of the fixes was fix(api)!:? (3.8.0; 4.0.0.)
  4. What is the difference between lightweight, annotated, and signed tags, and which should a release use?
  5. How do release-please and semantic-release differ in when a release happens?
  6. Why might a release workflow triggered by tag pushes never run, and how do you fix it?
  7. When is CalVer a better choice than SemVer?
  8. Give three ways to make a running service report its exact version and commit.

docs.title: Backup and Archive Storage
docs.text:
Backups and archives are the data you hope never to read. That makes them perfect for the cheapest storage tiers, which charge very little to keep data and a lot (in money, time, or both) to get it back. This lesson covers where backup copies and archives should live: the hot, warm, cold, and archive tiers; Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Glacier Flexible Retrieval, and Glacier Deep Archive; Azure Cool, Cold, and Archive; Google Cloud Nearline, Coldline, and Archive; Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2 Infrequent Access, and DigitalOcean Spaces Cold Storage; managed backup services such as AWS Backup; retrieval times and fees, minimum storage durations, early-deletion charges, and object lock for immutability. A worked example prices keeping 5 TB for a year with one full restore on every option.

What to back up, how often, and how to prove restores work is covered in the backups subject: backup fundamentals and strategies (3-2-1, immutability, retention schedules), disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO, and restore testing and runbooks. This page is about the storage underneath.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Backup data grows quietly. A nightly 20 GB database dump kept for seven years is about 51 TB. In S3 Standard that would cost more than $1,100 a month; with a lifecycle rule moving it to Glacier Deep Archive, about $69. Storage choices for backups are therefore real money.

The catch is that a backup is only worth its restore. The cheapest tiers add hours of delay before the first byte, per-GB retrieval fees, per-request restore fees, and minimum durations that punish short-lived data. Teams that only look at the storage price discover the rest during an incident, when the database is down and the archive tier says "within 12 hours". Picking a tier means matching three numbers: what it costs to keep, what it costs to read, and how long reading takes compared with the recovery time objective.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE book. The chapter Data Integrity: What You Read Is What You Wrote separates the two jobs this page serves. Backups "can be loaded back into an application" and must be recovered quickly, "well within the uptime needs of a service". Archives "safekeep data for long periods of time to meet auditing, discovery, and compliance needs", and their recovery "generally doesn't need to complete within uptime requirements". Backups belong in fast tiers; archives belong in the cheapest ones. The chapter's summary line: "No one really wants to make backups; what people really want are restores."
  • Amazon S3 Object Lock. The Object Lock feature page states that in compliance mode a protected object version "can't be overwritten or deleted by any user, including the root user", and that Object Lock has been assessed by Cohasset Associates for SEC Rule 17a-4(f), FINRA Rule 4511, and CFTC Regulation 1.31. Regulated firms use this write-once-read-many (WORM) storage for records that must not be altered.
  • Amazon Glacier (the original vault service). The Amazon Glacier developer guide states that the standalone vault-based service no longer accepts new customers and points new users to the S3 Glacier storage classes; the Glacier pricing page gives the date, December 15, 2025. Existing data stays accessible. Archives outlive products, so keep them in formats and APIs you can move.
  • CISA ransomware guidance. The #StopRansomware Guide recommends maintaining offline, encrypted backups of critical data and regularly testing their availability and integrity, because attackers look for and delete reachable backups. Object lock and separate backup accounts are the cloud versions of "offline".

Popular tools and providers: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes, AWS Backup, Azure Blob Storage (Cool, Cold, Archive) and Azure Backup, Google Cloud Storage (Nearline, Coldline, Archive) and Google Cloud Backup and DR, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, DigitalOcean Spaces Cold Storage, and backup tools that write to object storage: restic, rclone, Velero, and pgBackRest.

docs.title: Hot, warm, cold, and archive
docs.text:
Temperature Typical access First byte Minimum stay Typical use Hot Daily Milliseconds None Live data, last night's backup used by restore tests Warm (infrequent access) About monthly Milliseconds About 30 days Recent backups you may need quickly Cold About quarterly Milliseconds on most providers About 90 days Older backups, monthly snapshots Archive Yearly or never Minutes to hours (AWS, Azure); milliseconds (Google) 90 to 365 days Compliance retention, legal holds, year-end copies

Each step colder lowers the storage price and raises the cost of reading: a per-GB retrieval fee, higher request prices, a minimum billed duration, and on some providers an explicit restore step that takes hours.

docs.title: Amazon S3 Glacier storage classes
docs.text:
What they are. Three S3 storage classes for rarely used data. They are ordinary S3 objects in ordinary buckets, set per object or by lifecycle rules. You choose the class, lifecycle rules, and restore requests; AWS stores the data across at least three Availability Zones with the same eleven-nines durability design as S3 Standard.

Class Storage per GB-month Minimum Getting data back Glacier Instant Retrieval $0.004 90 days, 128 KB minimum size Normal GET in milliseconds; $0.03 per GB retrieved; requests $0.02 per 1,000 writes, $0.01 per 1,000 reads Glacier Flexible Retrieval $0.0036 90 days, 40 KB overhead per object Restore first: expedited 1-5 minutes ($0.03 per GB, $10 per 1,000 requests), standard 3-5 hours ($0.01 per GB, $0.05 per 1,000), bulk 5-12 hours (free) Glacier Deep Archive $0.00099 180 days, 40 KB overhead per object Restore first: standard within 12 hours ($0.02 per GB, $0.10 per 1,000 requests), bulk within 48 hours ($0.0025 per GB, $0.025 per 1,000)

Prices are us-east-1 list prices from the S3 pricing page and the AWS Price List; retrieval times are from Understanding archive retrieval options.

How a restore works for Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive:

  1. You call RestoreObject with a tier (Expedited, Standard, Bulk) and a number of days.
  2. S3 creates a temporary copy of the object. While it exists, you pay for both the archived object and the temporary copy at the S3 Standard rate.
  3. When the copy is ready (an event notification or HeadObject shows the Restore header with ongoing-request="false"), you GET it like any object, usually copying it somewhere permanent.
  4. After the days you asked for, S3 deletes the temporary copy; the object stays archived.

Three practical limits: restores run at up to 1,000 restore requests per second per account and up to 1-2 PB per day, so very large datasets take longer than the headline times; expedited capacity can be unavailable at busy times unless you buy provisioned capacity ($100 per unit per month); and each archived object carries 40 KB of metadata (8 KB of it at the Standard rate), so archiving millions of tiny files costs more than bundling them into larger archives first.

Amazon Glacier (vaults) is a separate, older service with its own API for "vaults" and "archives". It no longer accepts new customers (since December 15, 2025); use the S3 storage classes above. Existing customers keep access and AWS publishes guidance for moving vault data into S3.

docs.title: Azure Blob Storage: Cool, Cold, and Archive
docs.text:
What they are. Access tiers on Azure block blobs. Hot, Cool, and Cold are online (millisecond reads); Archive is offline: a blob must be rehydrated to an online tier before it can be read. You set tiers per blob or with lifecycle management policies; Microsoft manages the storage.

East US, locally redundant storage, from the Azure Retail Prices API (see Blob pricing):

Tier Storage per GB-month Minimum Reading Cool $0.0152 30 days $0.01 per GB, milliseconds Cold $0.0036 90 days $0.03 per GB, milliseconds Archive $0.00099 180 days Rehydrate first: standard $0.02 per GB, high priority $0.10 per GB; read operations $5 (standard) or $50 (high priority) per 10,000

From Blob rehydration from the archive tier: standard priority "might take up to 15 hours" for objects under 10 GB; high priority "might complete in less than one hour" for objects under 10 GB; and "a maximum of 10 GiB per storage account can be rehydrated per hour with priority retrieval". Microsoft warns that these timelines "do not scale linearly" for bulk rehydration. A 5 TB emergency restore from Archive is a multi-day job: plan for it, or keep the most recent backups in Cool or Cold. Archive is available on LRS, GRS, and RA-GRS accounts, not on zone-redundant ones, and lifecycle policies cannot rehydrate.

docs.title: Google Cloud Storage: Nearline, Coldline, and Archive
docs.text:
What they are. Storage classes on Cloud Storage objects. Unlike AWS Glacier and Azure Archive, every class is online: an Archive object returns its first byte in milliseconds with a normal read. The trade-off is expressed only in price and minimum duration.

Class Storage per GiB-month (us-central1) Minimum Retrieval per GiB Nearline $0.010 30 days $0.01 Coldline $0.004 90 days $0.02 Archive $0.0012 365 days $0.05

Read and write operations also cost more in colder classes ($0.05 per 1,000 for both on Archive). Source: Cloud Storage pricing. Instant access makes Google's Archive attractive for backups you hope never to read but might need urgently; the one-year minimum makes it wrong for anything deleted sooner.

docs.title: Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, and DigitalOcean Spaces
docs.text:
These providers have no glacier-style archive tier. They compete by making hot or warm storage cheap and restores free or nearly free:

  • Backblaze B2 ($6.95 per TB-month, no minimum duration, egress free up to 3x stored data): popular as the offsite copy for backup tools. Supports S3-compatible Object Lock.
  • Wasabi ($7.99 per TB-month pay as you go, 1 TB minimum charge, 90-day minimum storage duration, no egress or API fees while egress stays at or below stored data): data deleted early is billed as "timed deleted storage" until 90 days pass, which matters for backup rotations shorter than 90 days. Supports Object Lock.
  • Cloudflare R2 Infrequent Access ($0.01 per GB-month, $0.01 per GB retrieval, 30-day minimum, no egress fees): a warm tier with free egress. R2 offers bucket locks that block deletion and overwrites for a period or indefinitely, but anyone with permission to edit the bucket's configuration can remove a lock rule, so it is weaker than S3's compliance mode.
  • DigitalOcean Spaces Cold Storage ($0.007 per GiB-month, $0.01 per GiB retrieved with the fee waived up to your average daily cold storage usage, 30-day minimum): see Spaces pricing.

docs.title: Managed backup services
docs.text:
What they are. Services that schedule, copy, retain, and restore backups of cloud resources for you, so you write policies instead of scripts. AWS Backup covers EBS, RDS and Aurora, DynamoDB, EFS, S3, and more; Azure Backup and Google Cloud Backup and DR do the same for their platforms. You define backup plans (frequency, retention, copy to another region or account) and vault policies; the provider runs the jobs and stores the recovery points.

How AWS Backup bills (AWS Backup pricing, us-east-1): per GB-month of backup storage by resource type and per GB restored. Examples: S3 backups $0.05 per GB-month warm; EFS backups $0.05 warm and $0.01 cold; restores of S3 and EFS warm backups $0.02 per GB. EBS snapshots cost $0.05 per GB-month, or $0.0125 in the snapshot archive tier with a $0.03 per GB restore fee and a 90-day minimum. Logically air-gapped vaults keep backup copies in a separate, locked vault (with their own prices, for example $0.0575 per GB-month for warm S3 backups) so a compromised production account cannot delete them.

Managed backup storage costs more per GB than a raw archive class, and you pay for convenience: consistent snapshots, policies, cross-account copies, and one-click restores. For a database, also compare with the provider's built-in point-in-time recovery (see database backups and point-in-time recovery).

docs.title: Minimum durations, early deletion, and retrieval fees
docs.text:
Provider and tier Minimum billed duration Early deletion Retrieval S3 Standard-IA / One Zone-IA 30 days Prorated remainder $0.01 per GB S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval 90 days Prorated remainder $0.03 per GB S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval 90 days Prorated remainder Free (bulk) to $0.03 per GB S3 Glacier Deep Archive 180 days Prorated remainder $0.0025 to $0.02 per GB Azure Cool / Cold / Archive 30 / 90 / 180 days Prorated remainder $0.01 / $0.03 / $0.02 (standard) per GB Google Nearline / Coldline / Archive 30 / 90 / 365 days Charged as if stored for the minimum $0.01 / $0.02 / $0.05 per GiB Wasabi pay as you go 90 days "Timed deleted storage" until 90 days None (within egress policy) R2 Infrequent Access 30 days Charged for the minimum $0.01 per GB Backblaze B2 None None None (egress free up to 3x stored)

Minimums apply to overwrites and tier changes too, not only deletes. A backup job that rewrites the same key every night in Glacier Instant Retrieval pays 90 days for every version it replaces.

docs.title: Object lock and immutability
docs.text:
Ransomware and careless scripts both delete backups. Write-once-read- many (WORM) settings make deletion impossible for a retention period:

  • S3 Object Lock (requires versioning): governance mode blocks deletes and overwrites except for users granted a special permission; compliance mode blocks everyone, including the root user, and the retention cannot be shortened. Legal holds block deletion with no expiry until removed. A default retention can apply to every new object in the bucket. See Locking objects with Object Lock.
  • Azure immutable storage: time-based retention policies and legal holds at container or version level; a locked time-based policy cannot be removed. See immutable storage for blobs.
  • Google Cloud Storage: bucket retention policies that can be permanently locked with Bucket Lock, and per-object retention configurations.
  • B2 and Wasabi implement S3-style Object Lock; R2 has bucket locks (removable by anyone who can edit the bucket configuration).

Use compliance mode (or a locked policy) only after testing: a mistake, such as a 10-year retention on terabytes of test data, cannot be undone and you will pay for it. Combine immutability with a separate account for backups, so the credentials that run production cannot reach them.

docs.title: Lifecycle policies
docs.text:
A lifecycle rule moves objects to colder tiers by age and deletes them at the end of retention, so tiering needs no scripts.

Since September 2024, S3 lifecycle rules by default do not transition objects smaller than 128 KB, because each transition is a billed request and small objects can cost more to move than they save (see transitioning objects). A single rule also cannot move an object out of a class before that class's minimum duration: if Glacier Instant Retrieval starts at day 30, Deep Archive can start no earlier than day 120.

docs.title: Worked example: 5 TB for a year with one full restore
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices are US-region list prices in USD (AWS us-east-1, Azure East US with locally redundant storage, Google Cloud us-central1), checked in November 2026 on the official pricing pages and price lists linked above. They change often; re-check them in the AWS Pricing Calculator, the Azure Pricing Calculator, or the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator before deciding. Other regions (for example Mumbai or Pune) have different prices; select the region on the pricing page or calculator.

Scenario. TaskFlow keeps 5 TB of backup archives (5,120 GB, stored as 5,120 objects of 1 GB) for 12 months. Once during the year a disaster forces a full restore of all 5 TB to servers in the same region (no internet egress). Request charges are tiny with 1 GB objects but are included.

S3 Standard-IA                 5,120 x $0.0125 x 12       5,120 x $0.01 = $51.20          $819.20   immediate
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval   5,120 x $0.004 x 12        5,120 x $0.03 = $153.60         $399.36   immediate
S3 Glacier Flexible, bulk      5,120 x $0.0036 x 12       free + 3-day temp copy $11.78   $232.96   5-12 hours
S3 Deep Archive, bulk          5,120 x $0.00099 x 12      $12.80 + $0.13 + copy $11.78     $85.54   within 48 hours
S3 Deep Archive, standard      $60.83                     $102.40 + $0.51 + copy $11.78   $175.52   within 12 hours
Azure Archive, standard        5,120 x $0.00099 x 12      $102.40 + reads $2.56           $165.79   hours per blob, days in bulk
Azure Cold                     5,120 x $0.0036 x 12       $153.60 + reads $0.05           $374.83   immediate
Google Archive                 5,120 x $0.0012 x 12       $256.00 + reads $0.26           $329.99   immediate
Google Coldline                5,120 x $0.004 x 12        $102.40 + reads $0.05           $348.21   immediate
Backblaze B2                   5 TB x $6.95 x 12          free (under 3x stored)          $417.00   immediate
Wasabi                         5 TB x $7.99 x 12          free (egress under stored)      $479.40   immediate
Cloudflare R2 IA               5,120 x $0.01 x 12         $51.20 + reads $0.90            $666.50   immediate

The 3-day temporary copy is the restored data held at the S3 Standard rate while it is copied back into service (5,120 x $0.023 x 3/30). If the restore has to leave AWS (for example to on-premises servers), add internet egress: 5,120 GB x $0.09 = $460.80 on S3. Backblaze B2, Wasabi (within its egress policy), and R2 include that egress.

What the example teaches:

  • Archive tiers win when restores are rare. Deep Archive keeps 5 TB for a year and restores it once for about $86, one sixteenth of S3 Standard, if you can wait up to 48 hours.
  • Retrieval fees can flip the ranking. Google Archive costs almost as little to store as Deep Archive, but its $0.05 per GiB retrieval makes one full restore cost more than three times its yearly storage. With two full restores a year, Google Archive (about $586) would cost more than Glacier Instant Retrieval (about $553) or Coldline (about $451).
  • Time is the hidden column. If the recovery time objective is four hours, every option marked "hours" or "days" is disqualified for the copy you restore first, whatever it costs.
  • Egress-inclusive providers win restores that leave the cloud. For an off-site copy you might restore elsewhere, B2 and Wasabi include the transfer that would add $460.80 on S3.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use archive tiers (Deep Archive, Azure Archive, Glacier Flexible, Google Archive) for compliance retention, legal holds, year-end copies, and second or third backup copies whose restore time can be hours. Use warm or cold millisecond tiers (Standard-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Nearline, Coldline, Cool, Cold, B2, R2 IA) for the most recent backups you would restore first. Do not put short-lived data, frequently rewritten keys, or millions of tiny files in tiers with minimum durations or per-object overheads, and do not rely on an archive tier as the only copy when the recovery time objective is minutes.

Backup need Good fit Avoid Last 7-30 days, restore in minutes S3 Standard or Standard-IA, Glacier IR, Azure Cool, Nearline, B2 Any offline archive tier Monthly copies kept a year Glacier IR, Coldline, Azure Cold Deep Archive if you restore often Compliance retention for 7+ years Deep Archive or Azure Archive with object lock Standard (cost), Wasabi without lock Offsite copy outside your main cloud B2 or Wasabi with Object Lock A bucket in the same account as production Many small files (logs, thumbnails) Bundle into archives first, then tier Per-object tiering of tiny objects

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Scenario Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Backblaze B2 Cloudflare R2 10 GB free on both, no minimum duration on B2, restores free Early startup Managed database backups plus S3 lifecycle to Glacier IR and Deep Archive B2 as the off-site copy Built-in PITR covers fast restores; lifecycle makes long retention cheap without scripts Steady high traffic (large, growing backup sets) S3 with lifecycle: Standard-IA or Glacier IR for 30 days, then Deep Archive Azure Cool then Archive Most data ages into the cheapest tier automatically; recent backups stay fast Spiky traffic (backup volume jumps after launches or imports) S3 Intelligent-Tiering with archive tiers for unpredictable data Glacier IR No retrieval fees and automatic tiering when access patterns are unknown Global audience (data in several regions) Per-region backups plus cross-region copies to a cold tier One central archive region if data residency allows Restores should not depend on the region that failed; check residency rules first Compliance-heavy (for example healthcare records) S3 Glacier classes with Object Lock in compliance mode, in a separate account under the AWS BAA Azure Archive with locked immutability under Microsoft's BAA AWS and Microsoft state on their official HIPAA and HIPAA/HITECH pages that they sign BAAs for eligible services; immutability plus retention meets record-keeping rules Large files and heavy egress (restores leave the cloud) Backblaze B2 Wasabi Restore egress is included, so a full restore does not add a surprise transfer bill Team with no ops people AWS Backup (or Azure Backup) with a vault lock B2 with a backup tool such as restic Policies, schedules, and restores without scripts to maintain

docs.title: A lifecycle rule for nightly database dumps (S3)
docs.text:
TaskFlow writes a compressed MongoDB dump every night to backups/mongo/<date>/. Recent dumps stay in Standard for restore tests, then age into Glacier Instant Retrieval and Deep Archive, and expire after seven years:

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "mongo-dumps-tiering",
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Filter": {
        "And": {
          "Prefix": "backups/mongo/",
          "ObjectSizeGreaterThan": 131072
        }
      },
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 30, "StorageClass": "GLACIER_IR" },
        { "Days": 120, "StorageClass": "DEEP_ARCHIVE" }
      ],
      "Expiration": { "Days": 2555 },
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket taskflow-backups \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json
  • ObjectSizeGreaterThan (128 KB) skips small marker files that would cost more to transition than to keep.
  • Day 30 to 120 is exactly Glacier Instant Retrieval's 90-day minimum, so the second transition is allowed and incurs no early-deletion charge.
  • Expiration deletes the current version after 2,555 days (seven years); with versioning, the delete marker is followed 30 days later by removal of the noncurrent version.

docs.title: Locking the bucket with Object Lock
docs.text:
# Create the bucket with Object Lock (versioning is enabled automatically)
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket taskflow-backups --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket

# Every new object version is locked for 35 days in compliance mode
aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration \
  --bucket taskflow-backups \
  --object-lock-configuration '{"ObjectLockEnabled":"Enabled","Rule":{"DefaultRetention":{"Mode":"COMPLIANCE","Days":35}}}'

Thirty-five days covers the 30-day window of daily restore points plus a margin. Start with GOVERNANCE mode in a test bucket until the retention settings are proven. The infrastructure-as-code version of this bucket (separate account, encryption, replication) is in backup fundamentals and strategies.

docs.title: Uploading straight into a cold class and restoring from Deep Archive
docs.text:
# Upload an already-compressed archive straight into Glacier Instant Retrieval
aws s3 cp taskflow-2026-11-13.archive.gz \
  s3://taskflow-backups/backups/mongo/2026-11-13/ --storage-class GLACIER_IR

# Restore a Deep Archive object for 3 days using the cheaper Bulk tier
aws s3api restore-object \
  --bucket taskflow-backups \
  --key backups/mongo/2025-01-31/taskflow.archive.gz \
  --restore-request '{"Days":3,"GlacierJobParameters":{"Tier":"Bulk"}}'

# Check progress: Restore shows ongoing-request="true" until the copy is ready
aws s3api head-object \
  --bucket taskflow-backups \
  --key backups/mongo/2025-01-31/taskflow.archive.gz \
  --query Restore

For thousands of objects, use S3 Batch Operations to submit the restores and an event notification (s3:ObjectRestore:Completed) to start the copy back.

docs.title: The same policy on Azure and Google Cloud
docs.text:
Azure lifecycle management (cool after 30 days, archive after 120, delete after seven years; daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan stops a rehydrated blob from being archived again immediately). Azure prefixes start with the container name, so here the container is backups and the blob names start with mongo/:

{
  "rules": [
    {
      "enabled": true,
      "name": "mongo-dumps-tiering",
      "type": "Lifecycle",
      "definition": {
        "filters": {
          "blobTypes": ["blockBlob"],
          "prefixMatch": ["backups/mongo/"]
        },
        "actions": {
          "baseBlob": {
            "tierToCool": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 30 },
            "tierToArchive": {
              "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 120,
              "daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan": 7
            },
            "delete": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 2555 }
          }
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}

az storage account management-policy create \
  --account-name <storage-account> \
  --resource-group <resource-group> \
  --policy @policy.json

Google Cloud Storage lifecycle (Coldline after 30 days, Archive after 120, delete after seven years):

{
  "rule": [
    {
      "action": { "type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "COLDLINE" },
      "condition": { "age": 30, "matchesStorageClass": ["STANDARD"], "matchesPrefix": ["backups/mongo/"] }
    },
    {
      "action": { "type": "SetStorageClass", "storageClass": "ARCHIVE" },
      "condition": { "age": 120, "matchesStorageClass": ["COLDLINE"], "matchesPrefix": ["backups/mongo/"] }
    },
    {
      "action": { "type": "Delete" },
      "condition": { "age": 2555, "matchesPrefix": ["backups/mongo/"] }
    }
  ]
}

gcloud storage buckets update gs://taskflow-backups --lifecycle-file=lifecycle.json

On Google Cloud, the move to Coldline at day 30 and to Archive at day 120 leaves each object in Coldline for exactly its 90-day minimum.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Decide per copy: the copy you restore first lives in a millisecond tier; long-retention copies live in archive tiers.
  • Write the restore time of each tier into the runbook next to the RTO, including bulk limits (Azure's 10 GiB per hour for priority rehydration, S3's restore request rate).
  • Bundle small files into compressed archives before tiering, to avoid per-object overheads, minimum sizes, and transition request costs.
  • Use lifecycle rules, not scripts, for tiering and expiry; include noncurrent-version and incomplete-multipart rules.
  • Lock backups (Object Lock, immutable policies) and keep them in a separate account or subscription with separate credentials.
  • Price a full restore, not just storage, before choosing a tier; include egress if the restore may leave the provider.
  • Keep one copy with a different provider or region for the 3-2-1 rule.
  • Test restores from every tier on a schedule, including an archive restore, so the hours-long steps are rehearsed before an incident.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A restore from Deep Archive takes two days during an outage. Detect: HeadObject shows ongoing-request="true" long after the incident started; the runbook assumed hours. Cause: the only copy needed was archived, and Bulk was chosen (within 48 hours). Fix: keep the latest backups in a millisecond tier; use Standard (within 12 hours) for urgent archive restores; document times per tier.
  • The bill shows large early-deletion charges. Detect: usage types such as EarlyDelete-GIR, EarlyDelete-GDA, or Azure "Early Delete" meters. Cause: a rotation that deletes or overwrites daily backups before the tier's minimum (often a backup tool writing the same key each night). Fix: write each backup under a new key, align retention with minimum durations, or keep short-lived copies in a tier without minimums.
  • Archiving millions of small files cost more than expected. Detect: storage bytes in Standard grow after archiving, and transition request charges spike. Cause: 40 KB of metadata per archived object (8 KB billed at the Standard rate) and one billed request per transition. Fix: tar or zip small files into large bundles before archiving; use the 128 KB lifecycle size filter.
  • Ransomware deleted the backups along with production. Detect: CloudTrail shows DeleteObject or PutBucketLifecycle calls from a production role on the backup bucket. Cause: backups in the same account, writable by production credentials, without object lock. Fix: separate backup account, Object Lock in compliance mode or a logically air-gapped vault, write-only replication from production.
  • Rehydrated Azure blobs went straight back to Archive. Detect: blobs return to the archive tier the day after rehydration. Cause: the lifecycle rule archives by last-modified age, and rehydration does not change last-modified time. Fix: add daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan to tierToArchive, or rehydrate by copying to a new blob.
  • A compliance-mode lock keeps test data for ten years. Detect: objects cannot be deleted, and the storage bill for a test bucket keeps growing. Cause: compliance mode set with a long default retention before the design was proven. Fix: nothing can shorten it; prevent recurrence by testing in governance mode and reviewing lock settings in code review.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Backup: A copy that can be loaded back into the application for recovery.
  • Archive: Data kept long term for audit, legal, or compliance needs, where recovery speed matters less.
  • Storage tier / class: A price and performance level for stored data (hot, warm, cold, archive).
  • Retrieval fee: A per-GB charge for reading data from colder tiers.
  • Restore (S3 Glacier) / rehydration (Azure): The step that makes archived data readable again, taking minutes to hours.
  • Minimum storage duration: The minimum time billed for each object in a tier, even if deleted, overwritten, or moved sooner.
  • Early deletion charge: The prorated charge for the unused part of a minimum duration.
  • WORM: Write once, read many; data that cannot be changed or deleted during retention.
  • Object Lock (governance / compliance): S3's WORM feature; compliance mode cannot be bypassed by anyone.
  • Legal hold: A lock with no expiry, kept until explicitly removed.
  • Lifecycle rule: A policy that changes tier or deletes objects by age, prefix, size, or version state.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Choosing a tier by storage price alone and ignoring retrieval fees, restore time, and minimums.
  • Keeping the only recent backup in an offline archive tier.
  • Assuming "archive" means slow everywhere; Google's Archive class reads in milliseconds, at a high retrieval fee.
  • Rewriting the same backup key nightly in a tier with a minimum duration.
  • Archiving millions of small files one by one.
  • Believing versioning alone protects against ransomware; versions can be deleted by anyone with the right permissions unless locked.
  • Using compliance-mode locks before testing retention settings.
  • Forgetting that restores which leave the provider pay egress.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a backup and an archive, and how does that difference decide the storage tier?
  2. Explain how restoring an object from S3 Glacier Deep Archive works, step by step, and what it costs besides the retrieval fee.
  3. Why does Azure's Archive tier make a 5 TB emergency restore a multi-day job?
  4. Calculate the yearly cost of keeping 2 TB (2,048 GB) in S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval with one full restore, in us-east-1. (Answer: 2,048 x $0.004 x 12 = $98.30; 2,048 x $0.03 = $61.44; total $159.74.)
  5. A backup tool overwrites latest.tar.gz every night in Glacier Instant Retrieval. What does it pay for each overwrite, and how do you fix it?
  6. When is Google Cloud's Archive class a better choice than S3 Glacier Deep Archive, and when is it worse?
  7. What is the difference between governance and compliance mode in S3 Object Lock, and why test in governance mode first?
  8. Your RTO is 4 hours and your retention requirement is 7 years. Design a tiering plan and say which tiers each copy uses.

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Serving files through the API. Use presigned uploads and downloads and a CDN in front of the bucket.
  • Paying hyperscaler egress for heavy downloads. Use a zero-egress store, a partner CDN, or a flat-rate CDN plan.
  • Tiering tiny or short-lived objects. Respect minimum durations, skip objects under 128 KB, and bundle small files first.
  • Backups that production credentials can delete. Use a separate account, Object Lock, and a copy at another provider (3-2-1).
  • Never timing a restore. Test every tier; a Deep Archive bulk restore can take up to 48 hours.
  • Committing before usage is steady. Wait for a steady quarter, then cover 70-90% of the baseline.
  • Sending S3 traffic through a NAT gateway. Add a free gateway endpoint.
  • Connection pools that ignore autoscaling. Size pools from max_connections and put a pooler in front of functions.
