docs.title: Choosing Where to Run Software
docs.text:
Every program runs on somebody's computer. The real questions are how much of that computer you rent, how much of it you operate yourself, how you are billed for it, and how hard it would be to leave. This lesson explains the hosting models from virtual machines to static hosting, what you and the provider each manage in every model, how each one bills, the costs that never appear in the headline price, lock-in and portability, and the three families of providers: hyperscalers, developer platforms, and budget providers. It ends with a verdict for common situations and a decision tree.

The next lessons apply this to frontends, backend APIs, and databases. How to ship a release onto any of these hosts (pipelines, rollouts, health checks) is covered in deployment strategies; the networking pieces (VPCs, subnets, security groups) are in cloud building blocks.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The hosting model decides four things that are expensive to change later:

  • How much operations work the team owns. A two-person team that picks Kubernetes spends days on cluster upgrades and node patching that a platform would have done for it.
  • The shape of the bill. Per-request pricing is close to free at low traffic and becomes the most expensive option at steady high traffic; instance pricing is the reverse.
  • The failure modes. Functions have cold starts and duration limits; a single VM is a single point of failure; a platform can raise prices, change plans, or stop selling a product.
  • The exit cost. Data, identity, and networking accumulate in one provider, and moving terabytes out is billed per GB.

None of these choices is permanent, but each one gets harder to reverse every month. Writing down why you chose a host, and at what traffic or cost you would reconsider, turns an accident into a decision.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix (moved into the cloud). In Completing the Netflix Cloud Migration (February 2016), Netflix explains that a major database corruption in 2008 stopped DVD shipping for three days and showed it had to move away from "vertically scaled single points of failure". It chose AWS and finished the migration in January 2016. The stated reasons were elasticity ("thousands of virtual servers and petabytes of storage within minutes") and availability; it says cost reduction "was not the main reason", although its per-stream cloud cost ended up lower than in its data centers.
  • 37signals (moved out of the cloud). In Our cloud-exit savings will now top ten million over five years (October 2024), the makers of Basecamp and HEY report cutting their cloud bill from a $3.2 million per year run rate to $1.3 million after moving their applications onto about $700,000 of their own hardware, with the remaining spend being Amazon S3, which they planned to replace with their own storage. Their reasoning, a large and steady workload that no longer benefits from elasticity, is collected at basecamp.com/cloud-exit.
  • Dropbox (moved storage in-house). The post Scaling to exabytes and beyond (March 2016) describes how Dropbox moved over 90% of user data off Amazon S3 onto its own storage system by October 2015, because owning the whole stack let it "customize the entire stack end-to-end", improve performance, and get "better unit economics" at its scale.
  • Platform risk is real. AWS closed App Runner to new customers (availability change) and recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode instead, and in February 2026 Heroku announced a sustaining engineering model focused on stability rather than new features, with Enterprise contracts no longer offered to new customers. Existing users of both keep running, but the roadmap you bought into changed.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Akamai Cloud (Linode), and colocation or owned hardware.

docs.title: Virtual machines (IaaS)
docs.text:
What it is: a rented virtual server with a fixed amount of vCPU, memory, disk, and network. Examples: Amazon EC2 and Lightsail, Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine, DigitalOcean Droplets, Hetzner Cloud, and Akamai Cloud (Linode).

How it works underneath: a hypervisor on a physical host divides the machine into isolated virtual machines. Your VM boots an operating system image, gets a block-storage disk and a network interface, and keeps running (and billing) until you stop it.

You manage: the OS and its patches, the runtime (Node.js version), the process manager, the reverse proxy, TLS, scaling (adding VMs and a load balancer), backups of anything on the disk, and monitoring. The provider manages: the data center, hardware, hypervisor, and the physical network.

Typical use: steady workloads, software that needs a full OS, and teams that want maximum control or the lowest price per CPU.

docs.title: Containers on an orchestrator (CaaS)
docs.text:
What it is: you package the app as a container image and a scheduler decides which machine runs each copy. Examples: Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine, Azure Kubernetes Service, and Amazon ECS on EC2.

How it works underneath: a control plane (managed by the provider on EKS, GKE, and AKS) stores the desired state; worker nodes (VMs you pay for) run the containers; the scheduler restarts failed containers and spreads replicas across nodes and zones.

You manage: images, manifests, node pools and their upgrades (unless you use a node-less mode such as GKE Autopilot), cluster add-ons, autoscaling rules, and networking policy. The provider manages: the control plane and the hardware.

Typical use: many services, teams that already know Kubernetes, and workloads that need fine control over networking or scheduling. See the Kubernetes subject for how it works.

docs.title: Serverless containers
docs.text:
What it is: you hand the provider a container image plus CPU and memory settings, and it runs as many copies as traffic needs, with no nodes to manage. Examples: AWS Fargate (under ECS or EKS), Google Cloud Run, and Azure Container Apps.

How it works underneath: each task or instance runs in an isolated sandbox on the provider's fleet. Cloud Run and Container Apps can scale to zero instances and start one when a request arrives; Fargate tasks run until you stop them or a scaling policy removes them.

You manage: the image (including the runtime and its patches), CPU and memory sizes, minimum and maximum instance counts, and networking choices. The provider manages: servers, OS, scheduling, and (on Cloud Run and Container Apps) the HTTPS endpoint.

Typical use: stateless HTTP APIs and workers, from small teams that want containers without a cluster to large fleets.

docs.title: Platform as a service (PaaS)
docs.text:
What it is: you push code (or an image), and the platform builds it, runs it, routes traffic to it, and gives you logs, TLS, and scaling. Examples: Heroku, Render, Railway, Fly.io, Azure App Service, Google App Engine, AWS Elastic Beanstalk, and DigitalOcean App Platform.

How it works underneath: a build step turns your repository into an image (with buildpacks or your Dockerfile); the platform runs it on its own fleet behind its router. Fly.io runs each app instance as a lightweight VM it calls a Machine; Elastic Beanstalk is different in that it creates EC2 instances and a load balancer inside your own AWS account.

You manage: code, configuration, instance size and count. The provider manages: almost everything else.

Typical use: early startups, internal tools, and teams with no dedicated operations people.

docs.title: Functions (FaaS)
docs.text:
What it is: you write a handler function; the provider runs it per event (an HTTP request, a queue message, a file upload) and bills per invocation and duration. Examples: AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions), Cloudflare Workers, and Vercel Functions.

How it works underneath: on AWS Lambda each execution environment is a lightweight microVM built on Firecracker. A classic Lambda environment handles one request at a time, so concurrency comes from starting more environments. When no warm environment is free, Lambda creates one, downloads your code, and runs your initialization code first: that delay is a cold start. Warm environments are reused for later requests until Lambda reclaims them.

You manage: handler code, memory size, timeouts, and concurrency limits. The provider manages: servers, runtime patching, and scaling.

Typical use: event processing, spiky APIs, scheduled jobs, and glue between services.

docs.title: Edge compute
docs.text:
What it is: small functions that run in a CDN's points of presence, close to users. Examples: Cloudflare Workers, CloudFront Functions, and Lambda@Edge.

How it works underneath: Cloudflare Workers run in V8 isolates (the sandbox technology of the Chrome JavaScript engine) inside every Cloudflare location, which start in milliseconds instead of booting a VM or container; CloudFront Functions run lightweight JavaScript on every request at CloudFront edge locations.

You manage: small handlers with tight CPU and memory limits. The provider manages: global placement and scaling.

Typical use: redirects, authentication checks, A/B routing, header rewrites, and APIs that read from globally replicated data.

docs.title: Static hosting with a CDN
docs.text:
What it is: the host serves pre-built files (HTML, JavaScript, CSS, images) from a CDN. Examples: Amazon S3 with CloudFront, Cloudflare, Vercel, Netlify, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting, and Azure Static Web Apps.

How it works underneath: your build output is uploaded once, copied or cached at edge locations worldwide, and served without running any of your code per request.

You manage: the build output, cache headers, and redirects. The provider manages: everything else.

Typical use: marketing sites, documentation, and single-page apps such as TaskFlow Web. The frontends lesson compares these hosts in detail.

docs.title: Who manages what
docs.text:
The AWS shared responsibility model summarizes the split as the provider being responsible for security "of" the cloud and the customer for security "in" the cloud. Where the line falls depends on the model:

Layer Own servers VMs Kubernetes Serverless containers PaaS Functions Static Hardware, data center You Provider Provider Provider Provider Provider Provider Host OS, hypervisor You Provider Provider Provider Provider Provider Provider Guest OS and patches You You Nodes: you (or Autopilot) Provider Provider Provider Provider Language runtime You You You (in the image) You (in the image) Provider (buildpack) Provider n/a Scaling and capacity You You You configure You set limits You pick size and count Provider Provider Application code You You You You You You Your files Data, identities, access You You You You You You You

The last row never moves. A public S3 bucket, a leaked API key, or a database open to the internet is the customer's problem on every model.

docs.title: How each model bills
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices on this page are US-region list prices (AWS us-east-1, Google Cloud us-central1, Azure East US) in USD as published on the linked official pages in November 2026. They change often; re-check them with the provider's calculator before deciding.

Each model has a different unit of billing, and that unit decides the shape of the bill:

Model Billed for Example list price Source VM Instance-hours (EC2: per second, 60-second minimum) EC2 t4g.small (2 vCPU, 2 GiB, Arm): $0.0168/hour EC2 pricing VM bundle Flat monthly price with transfer included Lightsail 2 GB: $12/month with 3 TB transfer; DigitalOcean 2 GiB Droplet: $12/month with 2,000 GiB Lightsail, DigitalOcean Budget VM Hourly with a monthly cap Hetzner Cloud from €5.49/month excluding VAT Hetzner Kubernetes Nodes (VMs) plus a cluster fee EKS: $0.10 per cluster-hour; GKE: $0.10 per cluster-hour with a $74.40 monthly credit EKS, GKE Serverless containers vCPU-seconds and GB-seconds allocated Fargate: $0.04048 per vCPU-hour + $0.004445 per GB-hour (per second, 1-minute minimum) Fargate Scale-to-zero containers vCPU- and GiB-seconds while serving, plus requests Cloud Run: $0.000024 per vCPU-second, $0.0000025 per GiB-second, $0.40 per million requests Cloud Run PaaS instance Fixed price per instance size Render: $7/month for 512 MB; Heroku Basic dyno: $7/month Render, Heroku PaaS usage Per-second CPU and memory Railway: $0.00000772 per vCPU-second, $0.00000386 per GB-second Railway Functions Requests plus GB-seconds (1 ms granularity) Lambda: $0.20 per million requests + $0.0000166667 per GB-second Lambda Edge functions Requests plus CPU time Workers Paid: $5/month minimum including 10 million requests and 30 million CPU-ms Workers Developer platform Seats or plan fee plus metered usage Vercel Pro: $20 per developer seat per month with a $20 usage credit Vercel

To compare them you convert every unit into a monthly number. Cloud calculators use 730 hours per month:

VM:                    price per hour x 730
Serverless container:  (vCPU x price per vCPU-hour + GB x price per GB-hour) x hours running
Function:              requests x price per request
                       + requests x duration (s) x memory (GB) x price per GB-second

Example: one Fargate task with 0.5 vCPU and 1 GB, running all month
  (0.5 x $0.04048 + 1 x $0.004445) x 730 = $0.024685 x 730 = $18.02

Prices also differ by region. Fly.io, for example, charges $0.02 per GB of outbound data in North America and Europe but $0.12 per GB in Africa and India (Fly.io pricing), while Google lists Mumbai (asia-south1) in the same Tier 1 price group as us-central1 for Cloud Run. To check a region such as India, pick it in the region selector of the pricing page or the calculator.

Free tiers change as well. New AWS accounts now receive up to $200 in credits and choose between a free plan, which closes after six months or when the credits run out, and a paid plan; more than 30 services keep always-free monthly allowances on both (AWS Free Tier). Developer platforms revise their free plans often, so read the current terms before relying on one.

docs.title: The costs that are not in the headline price
docs.text:
A pricing page shows the main meter. A real bill has several more. On AWS (us-east-1) the usual surprises are:

Item List price Why it surprises people Data transfer out to the internet $0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB, after 100 GB per month free across AWS Every API response, download, and image leaves through this meter NAT gateway $0.045 per hour (about $32.85 per month) plus $0.045 per GB processed Private subnets need one per Availability Zone to reach the internet, ECR, or third-party APIs Data between Availability Zones $0.01 per GB in each direction Multi-AZ designs send app-to-database and replication traffic across zones Application Load Balancer $0.0225 per hour (about $16.43 per month) plus $0.008 per LCU-hour Billed even when traffic is zero; one per environment adds up Public IPv4 address $0.005 per hour (about $3.65 per month) per address, in use or idle Every public load balancer node, NAT gateway, and instance address counts CloudWatch Logs $0.50 per GB ingested, $0.03 per GB-month stored Verbose request logging can cost more than the servers EKS cluster $0.10 per hour; $0.50 per hour on extended support An old Kubernetes version quietly multiplies the control-plane fee by five Idle and forgotten resources gp3 volumes $0.08 per GB-month; databases billed per hour Stopped instances still pay for disks; dev databases run all weekend

Sources: EC2 data transfer, VPC pricing, EBS pricing, Elastic Load Balancing pricing, CloudWatch pricing, and the AWS Price List Bulk API.

Here is what that does to a modest TaskFlow API on ECS with Fargate: two tasks (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB each) in private subnets across two zones, behind an Application Load Balancer, with one NAT gateway per zone.

Fargate        2 tasks x $18.02                                   = $ 36.04
ALB            730 h x $0.0225 = $16.43; ~1 LCU x 730 h x $0.008 = $5.84 = $ 22.27
NAT gateways   2 x 730 h x $0.045 = $65.70; 100 GB x $0.045 = $4.50  = $ 70.20
Public IPv4    4 addresses (2 ALB nodes, 2 NAT) x $3.65             = $ 14.60
Logs           30 GB x $0.50 = $15.00; 30 GB stored x $0.03 = $0.90  = $ 15.90
Cross-AZ       200 GB app-to-database x $0.01 x 2 directions        = $  4.00
Internet out   150 GB - 100 GB free = 50 GB x $0.09                 = $  4.50
                                                                  -------
Total                                                             $167.51

Compute is about a fifth of the bill. The fixes are design choices, not discounts: S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints carry that traffic without a NAT gateway and without a charge, other AWS services can be reached through interface endpoints (which have their own hourly fee), a single NAT gateway halves that line at the cost of a zone dependency, and logging only errors and sampled requests cuts the log line. The cost optimization lesson covers these in depth.

docs.title: Lock-in and portability
docs.text:
Lock-in is the cost of leaving: the code you would rewrite, the data you would move, and the people you would retrain. Some of it is worth paying for, but it should be chosen, not accidental.

Layer Portable choice Provider-specific choice Cost of leaving the specific choice Packaging OCI container image Lambda handler signature, Workers APIs Rewrite entry points and local tooling Relational data PostgreSQL or MySQL (RDS, Cloud SQL, Neon, self-hosted) Aurora-only features Usually small: a dump and restore Document data MongoDB protocol (Atlas, self-hosted) DynamoDB, Firestore, Cosmos DB native APIs Rewrite the data-access layer and its access patterns Infrastructure definition Terraform or OpenTofu CloudFormation, Bicep Re-express resources; the concepts carry over Identity and permissions OIDC between systems IAM roles and policies Always provider-specific; rebuild per provider Data volume Small datasets Hundreds of TB in one provider Egress fees and transfer time

Moving 50 TB out of AWS over the internet at list price costs roughly $4,400 (10 TB at $0.09 and 40 TB at $0.085 per GB). AWS says customers who move all their data off AWS can ask AWS Support for free data transfer out for that move (AWS News Blog), but you still pay in time and engineering effort.

docs.title: Three families of providers
docs.text:
Family Examples Strengths Weaknesses Pick it when Hyperscalers AWS, Azure, Google Cloud Every service you could need, many regions, compliance programs and BAAs, commitment discounts, enterprise support Complexity, many metered extras, egress fees, IAM and networking learning curve You need breadth, compliance, specific regions, or long-term scale Developer platforms Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Render, Railway, Fly.io, Heroku Git-push deploys, preview environments, good defaults, almost no operations Price cliffs at plan limits, fewer regions and controls, platform and roadmap risk You want to ship fast with a small team Budget and infrastructure providers Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Akamai Cloud (Linode) Low prices per vCPU, generous included bandwidth, simple pricing Fewer managed services, fewer regions, compliance and support vary Steady workloads, cost-sensitive teams that can run servers

These families mix well: a common and sensible setup is a static frontend on a developer platform, an API on a hyperscaler or budget VM, and a managed database from a specialist such as MongoDB Atlas.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a more managed option (platform, serverless containers, functions) when the team is small, traffic is uncertain or spiky, or speed of delivery matters most. Move toward more control (containers on your own cluster, VMs, owned hardware) when traffic is large and steady, when you need something the platform cannot do (long-running connections, special hardware, unusual networking), or when the platform's markup has become a large share of the budget.

Do not choose Kubernetes because large companies use it, functions because they are fashionable, or owned hardware because of one blog post. Choose the cheapest option, counting people's time, that meets the hard constraints.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Situation Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Static frontend on Cloudflare or GitHub Pages; API on Cloud Run (free tier, scales to zero) A small VPS (DigitalOcean from $4 a month, Hetzner from €5.49) Costs nothing while idle; a VPS teaches Linux but bills every hour Early startup A developer platform (Render, Railway, Fly.io) or Cloud Run, plus a managed database; frontend on Vercel or Netlify ECS Express Mode on AWS (Fargate and a load balancer created for you) Fastest path to production with no operations hire; move when the bill or a constraint says so Steady high traffic Containers or VMs on committed capacity (ECS or EKS on EC2 with Savings Plans, GKE with committed use discounts) Owned or colocated hardware at very large, very steady scale Per-request pricing costs most at constant load; AWS Compute Savings Plans cut compute prices by up to 66% (AWS) Spiky or unpredictable traffic Functions (Lambda) or scale-to-zero containers (Cloud Run, Container Apps) Autoscaled containers with a small warm minimum You pay for the spike, not for idle hours; plan for cold starts and database connection limits Global audience CDN and edge for static and cacheable content; API in one or two regions near most users Multi-region instances on Fly.io or Cloud Run Most latency is distance; data still has a home region, so move reads to the edge first Compliance-heavy (for example healthcare) A hyperscaler under its BAA, using only HIPAA-eligible services: AWS, Google Cloud, Azure Platforms that sign BAAs: Fly.io, Vercel (a paid add-on on Pro, on request for Enterprise), Render (HIPAA workspaces on its Scale plan) You need the contract, audit logs, encryption, and access controls; a BAA alone does not make your app compliant Large files or heavy egress Object storage with low or no egress fees plus a CDN; compute on providers with large included transfer (Hetzner, Lightsail, DigitalOcean) CloudFront flat-rate plans, which include 50 TB of transfer from $15 per month per distribution At $0.09 per GB, egress dominates; see object and file storage Team with no ops people A fully managed platform (Render, Railway, Heroku-style) or Cloud Run with a managed database ECS Express Mode Nobody has to patch servers or run clusters; avoid Kubernetes until someone owns it

docs.title: A cost model you can rerun
docs.text:
Prices change and traffic grows, so keep the comparison as a small script next to the code and rerun it when either changes:

// scripts/hosting-cost.mjs: compare monthly cost of four hosting models
// Prices: US list prices checked November 2026 (see the linked pages)
const PRICE = {
  lambdaPerRequest: 0.20 / 1e6,        // aws.amazon.com/lambda/pricing
  lambdaPerGbSecond: 0.0000166667,
  fargateVcpuHour: 0.04048,            // aws.amazon.com/fargate/pricing
  fargateGbHour: 0.004445,
  albHour: 0.0225,                     // aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/pricing
  albLcuHour: 0.008,
  ec2T4gSmallHour: 0.0168,             // aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/on-demand
  gp3GbMonth: 0.08,
  ipv4Hour: 0.005,                     // aws.amazon.com/vpc/pricing
  cloudRunVcpuSecond: 0.000024,        // cloud.google.com/run/pricing
  cloudRunGibSecond: 0.0000025,
  cloudRunPerRequest: 0.40 / 1e6,
};
const HOURS = 730;

export function monthlyCost({ requests, durationMs, memoryGb }) {
  const seconds = durationMs / 1000;

  // Functions: pay per request and per GB-second (ignoring the free tier)
  const lambda =
    requests * PRICE.lambdaPerRequest +
    requests * seconds * memoryGb * PRICE.lambdaPerGbSecond;

  // Scale-to-zero container, 1 vCPU, concurrency 1 (worst case): billable
  // time is rounded up to 100 ms, so an isolated 120 ms request bills 200 ms
  const billedSeconds = Math.ceil(durationMs / 100) / 10;
  const cloudRun =
    requests * billedSeconds * PRICE.cloudRunVcpuSecond +
    requests * billedSeconds * memoryGb * PRICE.cloudRunGibSecond +
    requests * PRICE.cloudRunPerRequest;

  // Two always-on Fargate tasks (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB) behind an ALB at ~1 LCU
  const fargate =
    2 * (0.5 * PRICE.fargateVcpuHour + 1 * PRICE.fargateGbHour) * HOURS +
    PRICE.albHour * HOURS + PRICE.albLcuHour * HOURS;

  // One small VM with a 20 GB disk and a public IPv4 address (no redundancy)
  const vm =
    PRICE.ec2T4gSmallHour * HOURS + 20 * PRICE.gp3GbMonth + PRICE.ipv4Hour * HOURS;

  return { lambda, cloudRun, fargate, vm };
}

const round = (n) => Math.round(n * 100) / 100;
for (const millions of [1, 2, 10, 50, 100]) {
  const cost = monthlyCost({ requests: millions * 1e6, durationMs: 120, memoryGb: 0.5 });
  console.log(`${millions}M requests/month`, Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(cost).map(([k, v]) => [k, `$${round(v)}`]),
  ));
}

$ node scripts/hosting-cost.mjs
1M requests/month { lambda: '$1.2', cloudRun: '$5.45', fargate: '$58.31', vm: '$17.51' }
2M requests/month { lambda: '$2.4', cloudRun: '$10.9', fargate: '$58.31', vm: '$17.51' }
10M requests/month { lambda: '$12', cloudRun: '$54.5', fargate: '$58.31', vm: '$17.51' }
50M requests/month { lambda: '$60', cloudRun: '$272.5', fargate: '$58.31', vm: '$17.51' }
100M requests/month { lambda: '$120', cloudRun: '$545', fargate: '$58.31', vm: '$17.51' }

The model is deliberately simple: it ignores free tiers, assumes the fixed-price options have enough capacity, and treats Cloud Run as if no two requests ever overlapped on an instance, which overstates its cost for I/O-bound Node.js code that serves many requests per instance. The backend lesson refines it and plots the crossover points.

docs.title: One image, three hosts
docs.text:
A container image is the most portable unit you can build. The same TaskFlow API image can run on three very different hosting models:

# 1. AWS: ECS Express Mode creates a Fargate service, an ALB, scaling, and networking
aws ecs create-express-gateway-service \
  --service-name taskflow-api \
  --execution-role-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/ecsTaskExecutionRole \
  --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/ecsInfrastructureRoleForExpressServices \
  --primary-container '{
      "image": "<account-id>.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/taskflow-api:1.4.0",
      "containerPort": 3000
    }' \
  --health-check-path "/healthz" \
  --scaling-target '{"minTaskCount":2,"maxTaskCount":6}'

# 2. Google Cloud: a scale-to-zero serverless container
gcloud run deploy taskflow-api \
  --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/example-project/apps/taskflow-api:1.4.0 \
  --region=us-central1 --port=3000 --min-instances=0 --max-instances=10

# 3. A plain VM: Docker restarts the container if it or the VM restarts
docker run -d --name taskflow-api --restart=unless-stopped \
  -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 --env-file /etc/taskflow/api.env \
  ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0

The image did not change; only the surrounding responsibilities did. On the VM you also own nginx, TLS, patching, and a second VM for redundancy, which the backend deployment lesson walks through.

docs.title: Find the hidden costs on an AWS account
docs.text:
These read-only AWS CLI queries list the usual hidden-cost items so you can review them each month:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/hidden-costs.sh: read-only checks for common hidden AWS costs
set -euo pipefail
export AWS_PAGER=""

echo "== Unattached EBS volumes (billed per GB-month while unused)"
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query 'Volumes[].{id:VolumeId,gb:Size,created:CreateTime}' --output table

echo "== Elastic IPs not associated with anything (billed per hour)"
aws ec2 describe-addresses \
  --query 'Addresses[?AssociationId==null].PublicIp' --output text

echo "== Network interfaces holding a public IPv4 address"
aws ec2 describe-network-interfaces \
  --query 'NetworkInterfaces[?Association.PublicIp].{ip:Association.PublicIp,type:InterfaceType,desc:Description}' \
  --output table

echo "== NAT gateways (hourly charge each, plus per-GB processing)"
aws ec2 describe-nat-gateways --filter Name=state,Values=available \
  --query 'NatGateways[].{id:NatGatewayId,vpc:VpcId,subnet:SubnetId}' --output table

echo "== Log groups with no retention (stored forever)"
aws logs describe-log-groups \
  --query 'logGroups[?!retentionInDays].[logGroupName,storedBytes]' --output table

echo "== Last month's cost by usage type"
aws ce get-cost-and-usage \
  --time-period Start=2026-10-01,End=2026-11-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics UnblendedCost \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=USAGE_TYPE \
  --query 'ResultsByTime[0].Groups[].[Keys[0],Metrics.UnblendedCost.Amount]' --output text \
  | sort -k2 -n -r | head -20

Usage types containing NatGateway-Hours, DataTransfer-Out-Bytes, PublicIPv4:InUseAddress, and DataProcessing-Bytes (log ingestion), often with a region prefix such as USE1-, point straight at the lines in the table above. Run the script per region (AWS_REGION=eu-west-1 ./scripts/hidden-costs.sh), because most of these resources are regional.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Choose per workload: static files, APIs, background jobs, and databases often belong on different hosting models.
  • Start with the most managed option that meets the hard constraints, and write down the traffic or cost at which you would revisit it.
  • Price every option with the full set of meters (egress, NAT, load balancer, IPv4, logs, cross-zone traffic), not just compute.
  • Keep the application portable where it is cheap: a container image, configuration in environment variables, standard database protocols, and infrastructure as code.
  • Put budgets and anomaly alerts on every account and project from the first day.
  • Tag or label every resource with its service, environment, and owner so the bill can be split and orphaned resources found.
  • Read the free tier and plan limits: whether it sleeps, expires, pauses, or forbids commercial use.
  • Track each provider's status pages and announcements for products you depend on; closures and pricing changes come with notice.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The bill doubled after moving tasks into private subnets. Detect: Cost Explorer shows NatGateway-Hours and NatGateway-Bytes as new top usage types. Cause: each private subnet's zone got a NAT gateway, and image pulls and API calls now go through it. Fix: add S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints, use interface endpoints for ECR and CloudWatch where they cost less than the NAT traffic, and decide deliberately between one NAT gateway per zone and one shared gateway.
  • Small new charges for "public IPv4" on every service. Detect: PublicIPv4:InUseAddress usage in the bill, roughly $3.65 per address per month. Cause: AWS bills every public IPv4 address, including load balancer nodes and instances that get one automatically. Fix: disable auto-assigned public IPs, put instances behind a load balancer, and use IPv6 where clients support it.
  • The Kubernetes control-plane fee jumped five times. Detect: EKS usage type extendedSupport at $0.50 per hour instead of $0.10. Cause: the cluster runs a Kubernetes version past standard support. Fix: schedule regular version upgrades; treat the extended support fee as an alert, not a plan.
  • The first request after a quiet period takes many seconds. Detect: latency spikes only on the first request after idle time; platform logs show the service starting. Cause: a free or scale-to-zero tier: Render spins down a Free web service after 15 minutes without traffic, Heroku Eco dynos sleep after 30 minutes, and Cloud Run with zero minimum instances starts one on demand. Fix: set a minimum of one instance, move to a paid always-on plan, or accept the delay for internal tools.
  • A site went offline at the end of the month. Detect: the platform dashboard shows the project paused for usage. Cause: a hard plan limit, such as Netlify's Free plan credit limit or Vercel Hobby limits, which pause the feature until the next period. Fix: upgrade before launch, set usage alerts, and use spend limits on paid plans instead of hard stops for production.
  • The provider stopped selling the service you depend on. Detect: an availability notice in the documentation, such as App Runner being closed to new customers. Cause: a product lifecycle change. Fix: follow the named replacement (ECS Express Mode for App Runner), keep deployments in infrastructure as code so a migration is a project, not a rewrite, and keep the app containerized.
  • Egress costs spike overnight. Detect: DataTransfer-Out-Bytes jumps; CDN or load balancer logs show one referrer or crawler downloading large files repeatedly. Cause: hotlinking, a scraper, or an uncached large download. Fix: serve files through a CDN with caching, add rate limits and bot rules, and use signed URLs for large private files.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• IaaS (infrastructure as a service): renting virtual machines, disks, and networks that you configure and operate.
  • CaaS (containers as a service): a managed service that runs container images, with or without visible nodes.
  • PaaS (platform as a service): a platform that builds and runs your code and handles routing, TLS, and scaling.
  • FaaS (functions as a service): running handler functions per event, billed per invocation and duration.
  • Edge compute: code that runs in a CDN's locations near users.
  • Shared responsibility model: the split of security and operations duties between provider and customer, which changes by hosting model.
  • Cold start: the delay when a platform must create a new execution environment or instance before handling a request.
  • Egress: data sent out of a provider's network, usually billed per GB.
  • NAT gateway: a managed service that lets resources in private subnets reach the internet; billed per hour and per GB.
  • Lock-in: the cost, in rewriting, retraining, and data transfer, of moving to another provider.
  • Hyperscaler: one of the largest general-purpose clouds (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud).
  • Committed use discount: a lower price in exchange for committing to a level of spend or usage for one or three years.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Comparing only compute prices and ignoring egress, NAT gateways, load balancers, IPv4 addresses, and logs.
  • Choosing Kubernetes before there is anyone to own the cluster.
  • Assuming serverless is always cheaper; at steady high traffic it usually is not.
  • Assuming the cloud is always more expensive than owned hardware without counting people, data center contracts, and spare capacity.
  • Launching a commercial product on a free tier that sleeps, expires, pauses, or forbids commercial use (GitHub Pages and Vercel Hobby both restrict commercial use).
  • Treating "managed" as "no responsibility": data, access control, and configuration mistakes are always yours.
  • Leaving development environments, snapshots, and test databases running indefinitely.
  • Building deep lock-in by accident instead of choosing where it pays off.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe what you manage and what the provider manages for a VM, a serverless container, and a function.
  2. Why does a classic AWS Lambda function have cold starts, and what happens during one?
  3. Name five costs that rarely appear in the headline price on AWS, with the unit each is billed in.
  4. Calculate the monthly cost of one always-on Fargate task with 1 vCPU and 2 GB at the prices on this page. (Answer: (1 x 0.04048 + 2 x 0.004445) x 730 = $36.04.)
  5. A two-zone setup uses two NAT gateways that process 300 GB per month. What do they cost, and what would you change first? (Answer: 2 x 730 x $0.045 + 300 x $0.045 = $65.70 + $13.50 = $79.20; start with gateway endpoints for S3 traffic.)
  6. When is a developer platform a better choice than a hyperscaler, and when is it worse?
  7. Which parts of an application are cheap to keep portable, and which kinds of lock-in can be worth accepting?
  8. A healthcare startup must store patient data. What must be true of its hosting provider before it stores any, and what remains its own job?

docs.title: Cost Optimization and Cloud Bills
docs.text:
A cloud bill is a running total of every design decision: each instance left on, each log line, each byte that crosses a zone or leaves the network. This lesson shows how to read a bill, attribute it to services and teams with tags and accounts, guard it with budgets and anomaly alerts, and reduce it with rightsizing, scaling to zero, commitments (Savings Plans, reservations, committed use discounts), spot capacity, storage lifecycle rules, egress reduction, NAT gateway alternatives, and log volume control. It ends with FinOps as a practice, unit economics (cost per request and per customer), and the cloud-exit debate with both sides.

The individual "hidden" line items (NAT gateways, egress, cross-zone traffic, load balancer hours, public IPv4 addresses, log ingestion) are introduced in choosing where to run software; this page is about finding and fixing them systematically.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
On-premises, cost was decided once, when hardware was bought. In the cloud, cost is decided continuously by engineers: a new feature that logs every request, a cron job that copies data between regions, a test environment nobody turns off. Bills therefore drift upward unless someone watches them, and the people best placed to fix them (the engineers who built the system) often never see them.

Cost also shapes the business. Cloud spend is often the largest part of a software company's cost of goods sold, so it sets gross margin. A team that knows its cost per request or per customer can price its product, spot a regression in a pull request, and decide when a commitment or a re-architecture pays off. A team that does not finds out from the finance department, after the money is spent.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• 37signals (cloud exit, 2022-2025). In We stand to save $7m over five years from our cloud exit (February 2023) the company reported a 2022 cloud bill of $3.2 million, bought about $600,000 of Dell servers, projected about $1.5 million a year in savings, and said the move happened "without changing the size of our ops team". The original reasoning is in Why we're leaving the cloud (2022): steady, predictable workloads at their scale were cheaper on owned hardware.
  • Andreessen Horowitz (2021). The Cost of Cloud, a Trillion Dollar Paradox sums it up as "You're crazy if you don't start in the cloud; you're crazy if you stay on it." The authors report a practitioner rule of thumb that repatriation costs "one-third to one-half the cost of running equivalent workloads in the cloud", cite Dropbox saving nearly $75 million over two years before its IPO, and also stress that repatriation is complex, needs a strong infrastructure team, and is often partial.
  • Netflix (2016). In Completing the Netflix Cloud Migration Netflix wrote that "cost reduction was not the main reason" it moved to AWS: a 2008 database corruption had stopped DVD shipments for three days, and the cloud gave elastic capacity, better availability, and global reach. Its cloud cost per streaming start still ended up a fraction of the data-center cost. The opposite conclusion from 37signals, for a different workload and scale.
  • FinOps Foundation. The FinOps definition describes FinOps as "an operational framework and cultural practice which maximizes the business value of technology", built on collaboration between engineering, finance, and business teams, and the FinOps phases are Inform, Optimize, and Operate. Its FOCUS specification defines a common format for billing data that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud can export.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost Anomaly Detection, AWS Compute Optimizer, AWS Data Exports (Cost and Usage Report 2.0 and FOCUS), Azure Cost Management and Azure Advisor, Google Cloud Billing reports, budgets, and Recommender, OpenCost and Kubecost for Kubernetes, and Infracost for cost estimates in pull requests.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices on this page are AWS us-east-1 list prices in USD, checked in November 2026 from the AWS Price List and the pricing pages linked next to them. They change often; re-check them in the AWS Pricing Calculator, Azure Pricing Calculator, or Google Cloud Pricing Calculator before deciding. Other regions, for example Mumbai (ap-south-1), have different prices; select the region in the calculator.

docs.title: Where the money goes: a TaskFlow bill
docs.text:
Here is a realistic month for TaskFlow API in production on AWS: three m7g.large API instances behind an Application Load Balancer in two Availability Zones, a self-managed three-node MongoDB replica set on m7g.large instances with gp3 volumes, two NAT gateways, attachments in S3, CloudWatch Logs, and a staging environment that runs all the time.

Compute      3 x m7g.large x 730 h x $0.0816                        = $178.70
Database     3 x m7g.large ($178.70) + 600 GB gp3 x $0.08 ($48.00)
             + 600 GB snapshots x $0.05 ($30.00)                    = $256.70
Load balancer 730 h x $0.0225 + 2 LCU x 730 h x $0.008              =  $28.11
NAT gateways 2 x 730 h x $0.045 + 1,000 GB x $0.045                 = $110.70
Public IPv4  4 addresses x 730 h x $0.005                           =  $14.60
Egress       (3,072 GB - 100 GB free) x $0.09                       = $267.48
Cross-AZ     2,048 GB x $0.01 x 2 directions                        =  $40.96
Logs         300 GB ingested x $0.50 + 300 GB stored x $0.03        = $159.00
S3           2,048 GB x $0.023                                      =  $47.10
Idle         staging 3 x t4g.medium x 730 h x $0.0336 ($73.58)
             + 500 GB unattached gp3 x $0.08 ($40.00)               = $113.58
                                                                    ---------
Total                                                               $1,216.94

Sources: EC2 on-demand pricing, EBS pricing, VPC pricing, Elastic Load Balancing pricing, CloudWatch pricing, S3 pricing.

The servers (the API and database instances, $357.40) are under a third of the bill. The rest is data transfer, network plumbing, logs, storage, and waste, which no discount program touches.

docs.title: Reading a bill
docs.text:
A cloud bill is a table of line items. On AWS each line has a service (AmazonEC2), a usage type (what was metered, such as BoxUsage:m7g.large, NatGateway-Bytes, DataTransfer-Out-Bytes, TimedStorage-ByteHrs), an operation, a region, a quantity, and a rate. Usage types often carry a region prefix (for example EUC1- for Frankfurt). Reading a bill well means three habits:

  • Group by usage type, not only by service. "EC2-Other" in Cost Explorer hides NAT gateways, EBS, data transfer, and public IPv4 addresses. Grouping by usage type shows which meter moved.
  • Know the cost views. Unblended cost is what was charged at the rates in effect each hour; amortized cost spreads upfront commitment payments across the period they cover, which is what you want for unit costs; net views subtract discounts and credits.
  • Export the raw data. AWS Data Exports delivers the Cost and Usage Report 2.0 or a FOCUS-format export to S3 for SQL analysis; Azure and Google Cloud export billing data to storage or BigQuery. Dashboards are for spotting trends; the raw export is for answering "why".

Cost Explorer's API is itself metered: $0.01 per request (AWS Price List, AWSCostExplorer), so cache its results in scripts.

docs.title: Tags, accounts, and cost allocation
docs.text:
Nobody can fix spend they cannot attribute. Two tools do the attribution:

  • Accounts (or subscriptions, projects) per environment and team. The strongest boundary: everything in the taskflow-prod account belongs to TaskFlow production, tagged or not. AWS Organizations, Azure management groups, and Google Cloud folders group them for billing.
  • Tags (labels on Google Cloud). Key-value pairs on resources, such as service=taskflow-api, env=production, team=platform. On AWS, user-defined tags must be activated as cost allocation tags before they appear in billing data. Enforce them in infrastructure as code (default_tags in the Terraform AWS provider) and with tag policies in AWS Organizations, because resources created by hand are rarely tagged.

Shared costs (a shared Kubernetes cluster, a shared NAT gateway, support fees) need an allocation rule, for example by share of requests or CPU. Showback reports each team's costs to it; chargeback bills the team's budget. Start with showback.

docs.title: Budgets and anomaly alerts
docs.text:
• Budgets compare actual and forecast spend with a threshold and notify by email or SNS. In the AWS Price List, AWS Budgets themselves cost nothing; action-enabled budgets (which can apply an IAM or service control policy, or stop specific EC2 and RDS instances) are free for the first 62 budget-days a month, then $0.10 per budget per day, and scheduled budget reports cost $0.01 per report delivered. Azure Cost Management and Google Cloud billing budgets work the same way. A budget alerts; it does not cap spending unless you wire an action to it.
  • Anomaly detection learns each service's normal spend and alerts on unusual jumps, which catches what a monthly threshold misses: a $40 a day increase that would only cross the budget in three weeks. AWS enables a default Cost Anomaly Detection monitor for new Cost Explorer users and describes it as available at no additional cost.

docs.title: Rightsizing
docs.text:
Rightsizing means matching instance size and type to measured use:

  1. Collect at least two weeks of CPU, memory, network, and disk metrics (memory needs the CloudWatch agent on EC2). Look at p95 or p99, not the average.
  2. Use the provider's recommendations (AWS Compute Optimizer, Azure Advisor, Google Cloud Recommender) as a starting list, not a verdict.
  3. Downsize, or change family: Arm-based Graviton instances cost less for the same size. In us-east-1, m7i.large (Intel) is $0.1008 an hour and m7g.large (Graviton) is $0.0816, 19% less, for the same 2 vCPU and 8 GiB. A Node.js service usually runs on Arm unchanged, but native modules and container images must be built for arm64.
  4. Move old volume types: gp2 costs $0.10 per GB-month and gp3 $0.08, a 20% saving that modify-volume applies without downtime.
  5. Measure latency and saturation after the change and keep headroom for peaks; rightsizing that causes an outage costs more than it saves.

On Kubernetes, the waste is in requests: pods request more CPU and memory than they use, so nodes fill up with reservations. See scaling and resource management.

docs.title: Scaling to zero and scheduling
docs.text:
The cheapest resource is one that is not running. Two techniques:

  • Schedules. Development and staging rarely need to run nights and weekends. TaskFlow's staging (three t4g.medium) costs $73.58 a month running all the time; running it 50 hours a week (10 hours on 5 weekdays) instead of 168 saves 70%, about $51.68. Tools: EventBridge Scheduler, AWS Instance Scheduler, Azure automation, or a CI job that scales staging up and down.
  • Scale-to-zero platforms. Lambda, Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, and some serverless databases bill nothing (or almost nothing) when idle. For low or spiky traffic they beat always-on capacity; for steady traffic they usually cost more. The crossover is worked out in running backend servers and APIs.

Autoscaling with sensible minimums does the same for production; see autoscaling server fleets.

docs.title: Commitments: Savings Plans, reservations, and committed use discounts
docs.text:
Providers discount steady usage in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment:

  • AWS Savings Plans commit to a dollar amount of compute per hour. Compute Savings Plans apply to EC2 "regardless of instance family, instance size, OS, tenancy, or AWS Region" and also to Fargate and Lambda; EC2 Instance Savings Plans are cheaper but tied to one instance family in one region. AWS states savings of up to 72% (What are Savings Plans?). Reserved Instances still exist for services such as RDS and ElastiCache.
  • Azure offers reservations and a savings plan for compute; Google Cloud offers resource-based and spend-based committed use discounts and automatic sustained use discounts on some machine families.

For m7g.large in us-east-1 (Linux, no upfront payment), from the AWS Savings Plans price list:

Option Hourly rate Discount Monthly cost for one instance (730 h) On-Demand $0.0816 none $59.57 Compute Savings Plan, 1 year $0.0599 27% $43.73 Compute Savings Plan, 3 years $0.0414 49% $30.22 EC2 Instance Savings Plan (m7g), 1 year $0.054 34% $39.42 EC2 Instance Savings Plan (m7g), 3 years $0.037 55% $27.01

The commitment is paid whether or not you use it, so it only pays off above a break-even utilization:

1-year Compute SP:  $43.73 / $0.0816 per hour = 536 hours = 73% of the month
3-year Compute SP:  $30.22 / $0.0816 per hour = 370 hours = 51% of the month

How to commit safely:

  • Commit to the floor, not the peak. Look at the lowest hourly compute spend over the last 30 to 90 days and cover most of it; leave peaks on on-demand, autoscaling, or Spot.
  • Clean up first. Commit after deleting idle resources and rightsizing, or you lock in waste for years.
  • Prefer flexible plans when the architecture may change. A team moving from EC2 to Fargate keeps a Compute Savings Plan's discount but strands an EC2 Instance Savings Plan.
  • Watch utilization and coverage in the provider's reports every month, and ladder new purchases (smaller plans bought quarterly) instead of one large purchase.

docs.title: Spot and preemptible capacity
docs.text:
Spot capacity is the provider's spare capacity at a deep discount, with the condition that it can be taken back:

Provider Discount (provider's statement) Notice before interruption AWS EC2 Spot Up to 90% off On-Demand (EC2 Spot) Two minutes, via instance metadata and EventBridge (interruption notices) Google Cloud Spot VMs Up to 91% (Spot VMs) Configurable 120 seconds or none (default), then up to 30 seconds of shutdown Azure Spot Virtual Machines Variable price by region and size (Spot VMs) 30 seconds, through Scheduled Events

Good fits: stateless workers that read from a queue, CI runners, batch and data processing, rendering, and extra Kubernetes nodes for stateless pods. Bad fits: databases, single instances serving traffic, and long jobs without checkpoints. Make Spot reliable by diversifying across several instance types and zones, using capacity-optimized allocation, draining work when the notice arrives, and keeping an on-demand baseline.

docs.title: Storage lifecycle rules
docs.text: Storage grows forever unless something deletes it. Lifecycle rules tier and expire objects by age (see object and file storage and backup and archive storage); snapshot policies prune old EBS snapshots; log retention settings expire logs; container registries need image lifecycle policies. The rule of thumb: every bucket, log group, snapshot schedule, and registry gets a retention setting when it is created.

docs.title: Egress reduction
docs.text:
Egress is often the largest single line (22% of the TaskFlow bill above). In order of impact:

  1. Cache at a CDN. CloudFront includes 1 TB of transfer out and 10 million requests a month free, fetches from AWS origins free, and charges $0.085 per GB after that in the US; flat-rate plans bundle up to 50 TB. Moving TaskFlow's 2 TB of attachment downloads behind CloudFront changes $184.32 of direct egress into $87.04, saving $97.28.
  2. Compress. Enable gzip or Brotli for JSON, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript at the CDN or proxy; text responses typically shrink several times over. Serve images in modern formats at the right size.
  3. Send less. Paginate, select fields, avoid polling (use ETags and conditional requests), and stop sending debug payloads.
  4. Keep traffic inside the provider and region. Traffic between AWS services in the same region is cheaper than internet egress, and cross-region replication doubles storage and adds transfer. Do not copy data across regions without a reason (residency, DR).
  5. Choose zero-egress storage for downloads when the files are big and popular (R2, B2 with partner CDNs).

Cross-zone traffic ($0.01 per GB each way) is the price of multi-AZ resilience: reduce it with caching and compression, not by giving up zone redundancy.

docs.title: NAT gateway alternatives
docs.text:
A NAT gateway lets instances in private subnets reach the internet. It costs $0.045 per hour plus $0.045 per GB processed, and it processes all outbound traffic, including traffic to AWS services such as S3 and ECR.

Path What it is Cost (us-east-1) Use for NAT gateway Managed NAT per zone $0.045/h + $0.045/GB Third-party APIs and general IPv4 internet access Gateway endpoint A route-table target for S3 or DynamoDB No charge (gateway endpoints) All S3 and DynamoDB traffic from private subnets Interface endpoint A private IP for an AWS service (PrivateLink) $0.01/h per zone + $0.01/GB ECR, CloudWatch Logs, Secrets Manager, STS at volume Egress-only internet gateway Outbound-only IPv6 No gateway charge (docs); data transfer applies IPv6-capable destinations NAT instance NAT on a small EC2 instance you run Instance hours only Low traffic, when you accept patching and availability work Public subnets Tasks with public IPs, no NAT $0.005/h per IPv4 address Small setups where public IPs are acceptable with tight security groups

Sending 1 TB a month to S3 through a NAT gateway costs 1,024 x $0.045 = $46.08; through a gateway endpoint it costs nothing. Interface endpoints cost $0.01 an hour per zone (about $14.60 a month for two zones) plus $0.01 per GB, so they beat NAT processing above roughly 420 GB a month per service. One NAT gateway shared by two zones halves the hourly cost but adds cross-zone charges and makes one zone's failure take out both.

docs.title: Log volume control
docs.text:
Log ingestion is billed per GB ($0.50 per GB in the CloudWatch Logs Standard class, $0.25 in the Infrequent Access class), and log groups default to keeping data forever. Levers:

  • Log less: info in production, debug only when switched on, errors always, and successful requests sampled (for example 1%).
  • Never log health checks and static assets at full volume.
  • Set retention on every log group (for example 30 days for application logs) and archive what compliance requires to S3.
  • Use the cheaper log class for logs you rarely query, after checking that it supports the features you rely on (it offers a subset of Standard's features).
  • Prefer metrics for counts and latencies; a metric is far cheaper than millions of log lines that say the same thing.

TaskFlow ingests 300 GB a month ($150). Sampling successful requests and dropping debug output brings it to 100 GB ($50). See structured logging for how to keep the logs you do write useful.

docs.title: FinOps basics
docs.text:
FinOps is the practice of making cloud cost a shared, continuous concern of engineering, finance, and the business:

  • Inform: allocate costs (accounts, tags), show each team its spend, forecast, and compute unit costs.
  • Optimize: rightsize, clean up, commit, use Spot, change architecture.
  • Operate: budgets, anomaly response, policies (tagging, retention, approved instance types), cost reviews in design and pull requests.

Engineers own usage (what runs and how much); finance or a central team usually owns rates (commitments, negotiated discounts). The cycle repeats: inform, optimize, operate, and back again.

docs.title: Unit economics
docs.text:
Total spend says little on its own: a bill that doubles while traffic triples is good news. Unit costs divide cost by a business driver:

Cost per 1,000 requests = monthly cost / (monthly requests / 1,000)
                        = $1,216.94 / (30,000,000 / 1,000) = $0.0406

Cost per customer team  = $1,216.94 / 400 paying teams = $3.04 per month

Track unit costs over time and per feature. If a plan sells for $20 a team per month, $3.04 of infrastructure is a healthy 15%; if a new feature pushes it to $9, pricing or architecture must change. Use amortized cost so commitment purchases do not distort single months.

docs.title: Applying the levers to the TaskFlow bill
docs.text:
Lever                                                       Monthly saving
Delete 500 GB of unattached gp3 volumes                     $40.00
Run staging 50 h a week instead of 168                      $51.68
S3 gateway endpoint for 700 GB of S3 traffic via NAT        $31.50
Logs 300 GB -> 100 GB ingested (sampling, no debug)         $106.00 ($100 ingest + $6 storage)
CloudFront for 2 TB of attachment downloads                 $97.28
1-year Compute Savings Plan on the 6 always-on m7g.large    $95.05 (6 x ($0.0816 - $0.0599) x 730)
                                                            -------
Total                                                       $421.51 (35%): $1,216.94 -> $795.43

None of these needed a re-architecture, and only one was a discount. Order matters: clean up, then rightsize, then commit to what is left.

docs.title: The cloud-exit debate
docs.text:
The case for leaving (or never fully moving). Steady workloads at scale pay a premium for elasticity they do not use. 37signals reported a $3.2 million 2022 bill and projected about $7 million of savings over five years from owned servers without growing its operations team, then moved its S3 data to its own storage in 2025. Dropbox moved most storage to its own systems. The a16z analysis estimates that repatriation can cost one-third to one-half as much as equivalent cloud workloads for mature, predictable products. Egress-heavy and storage-heavy businesses feel this first.

The case for staying. The same a16z article calls repatriation "an incredibly complex decision", notes it needs a strong infrastructure team, and says even aggressive repatriators kept a share of workloads in the cloud. Netflix moved to the cloud for availability, elasticity, and global reach rather than cost. Owned hardware means capacity planning, hardware refresh cycles, data center contracts, spare parts, security patching, and on-call for physical failures; spiky or fast-growing workloads and small teams rarely win that trade. Managed services (databases, queues, identity) also replace engineering time that a self-hosted setup has to spend.

The usual answer is "it depends, and it is not binary": start in the cloud; measure unit costs; move steady, heavy, well-understood workloads (storage, bandwidth-heavy delivery, stable compute) to cheaper providers or owned hardware when the numbers and the team support it; keep elastic, experimental, and managed-service-heavy parts where they are. Budget providers such as Hetzner or DigitalOcean are a middle ground; see choosing where to run software.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use budgets, anomaly alerts, and tagging from the first day of any cloud account. Use commitments only for usage that has been steady for months and will stay; use Spot only for interruptible work; re-architect (CDN, endpoints, log pipeline) when a line item is large and structural.

Do not chase cost before you have attribution (you will optimize the wrong thing), commit before cleaning up, cut logs that compliance requires you to keep (move them to cheaper storage instead), or trade away reliability (single AZ, no backups) for small savings.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Scenario Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Free tiers plus a budget alert at a few dollars A flat-price VPS A runaway function or public bucket is the main risk; a fixed-price server cannot surprise you Early startup Tags and accounts per environment, budgets, anomaly alerts; on-demand capacity; a 1-year Compute Savings Plan once usage is steady for a quarter Startup credits while they last Flexibility matters more than discounts while the architecture changes; avoid 3-year commitments Steady high traffic Savings Plans or CUDs covering 70-90% of the baseline, reservations for databases, negotiated pricing for egress Owned or rented dedicated hardware for the steady core Predictable load is exactly what commitments and owned hardware reward Spiky traffic Autoscaling or scale-to-zero platforms, Spot for burst workers, commitments only for the floor Flat-rate CDN plans for traffic spikes Paying for peak capacity all month is the biggest waste Global audience CDN first, regional placement close to users, Compute Savings Plans (region-flexible) Edge platforms with bundled transfer Egress and latency dominate; region-flexible commitments follow traffic Compliance-heavy (for example healthcare) Separate accounts per environment, enforced tagging, retention set by policy with cheaper log and archive tiers Committed spend on the compliant provider You often cannot delete logs or move data freely; save on tiers and commitments instead Large files and heavy egress CDN with flat-rate or committed pricing, zero-egress storage Negotiated private pricing Egress is the bill; storage and compute are rounding errors Team with no ops people Managed services, budgets and anomaly alerts, provider recommendations, Compute Savings Plans A developer platform with simple pricing Avoid savings that need operations work (NAT instances, Spot fleets, self-hosted databases)

docs.title: Cost guardrails in Terraform
docs.text:
Default tags on every resource, a monthly budget with actual and forecast alerts, and an anomaly subscription:

# infra/cost-guardrails.tf
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
  default_tags {
    tags = {
      service = "taskflow-api"
      env     = "production"
      team    = "platform"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_budgets_budget" "monthly" {
  name         = "taskflow-production-monthly"
  budget_type  = "COST"
  limit_amount = "1300"
  limit_unit   = "USD"
  time_unit    = "MONTHLY"

  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 80
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "ACTUAL"
    subscriber_email_addresses = ["cloud-costs@example.com"]
  }

  notification {
    comparison_operator        = "GREATER_THAN"
    threshold                  = 100
    threshold_type             = "PERCENTAGE"
    notification_type          = "FORECASTED"
    subscriber_email_addresses = ["cloud-costs@example.com"]
  }
}

# Accounts that enabled Cost Explorer recently already have a default
# AWS-services monitor; import it instead of creating a second one.
resource "aws_ce_anomaly_monitor" "services" {
  name              = "taskflow-services"
  monitor_type      = "DIMENSIONAL"
  monitor_dimension = "SERVICE"
}

resource "aws_ce_anomaly_subscription" "daily" {
  name             = "taskflow-cost-anomalies"
  frequency        = "DAILY"
  monitor_arn_list = [aws_ce_anomaly_monitor.services.arn]

  subscriber {
    type    = "EMAIL"
    address = "cloud-costs@example.com"
  }

  threshold_expression {
    dimension {
      key           = "ANOMALY_TOTAL_IMPACT_ABSOLUTE"
      match_options = ["GREATER_THAN_OR_EQUAL"]
      values        = ["50"]
    }
  }
}
  • default_tags stamps the three tags on every resource this provider creates, so tagging does not depend on memory.
  • The forecast notification fires early in the month when the trend points past the limit, while there is still time to act.
  • The anomaly subscription emails a daily summary of anomalies with a total impact of $50 or more.

Activate the tag keys for billing once per organization:

aws ce update-cost-allocation-tags-status \
  --cost-allocation-tags-status TagKey=service,Status=Active TagKey=env,Status=Active TagKey=team,Status=Active

docs.title: Endpoints, log retention, and the cheaper log class
docs.text:
# infra/network-and-logs.tf: cost-aware defaults for TaskFlow's VPC and logs
resource "aws_vpc_endpoint" "s3" {
  vpc_id            = aws_vpc.main.id
  service_name      = "com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3"
  vpc_endpoint_type = "Gateway"
  route_table_ids   = aws_route_table.private[*].id # S3 traffic skips the NAT gateway
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "api" {
  name              = "/taskflow/api"
  retention_in_days = 30
}

resource "aws_cloudwatch_log_group" "access" {
  name              = "/taskflow/api-access"
  retention_in_days = 14
  log_group_class   = "INFREQUENT_ACCESS" # $0.25 instead of $0.50 per GB ingested
}

docs.title: Sampling successful requests in TaskFlow API
docs.text:
// src/middleware/access-log.js: log every error, sample successful requests
export function accessLog(logger, { sampleRate = 0.01 } = {}) {
  return (req, res, next) => {
    const started = process.hrtime.bigint();
    res.on("finish", () => {
      const failed = res.statusCode >= 400;
      if (!failed && Math.random() >= sampleRate) return; // drop 99% of successes
      logger.info(
        {
          method: req.method,
          route: req.route?.path ?? req.path,
          status: res.statusCode,
          durationMs: Number(process.hrtime.bigint() - started) / 1e6,
          sampled: !failed,
        },
        "request",
      );
    });
    next();
  };
}

Request counts and latency percentiles come from metrics, so the sampled logs only need to show examples. Mark sampled lines so nobody counts them as totals.

docs.title: Finding idle and outdated resources
docs.text:
# Unattached EBS volumes (billed although no instance uses them)
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=status,Values=available \
  --query "Volumes[].{id:VolumeId,sizeGb:Size,type:VolumeType}" --output table

# Elastic IPs not associated with anything (public IPv4 is billed either way)
aws ec2 describe-addresses --query "Addresses[?AssociationId==null].PublicIp"

# gp2 volumes that can move to gp3 (20% cheaper) without downtime
aws ec2 describe-volumes --filters Name=volume-type,Values=gp2 --query "Volumes[].VolumeId"
aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-<id> --volume-type gp3

# Log groups with no retention (kept forever)
aws logs describe-log-groups --query "logGroups[?retentionInDays==null].logGroupName"

docs.title: A monthly unit-cost report
docs.text:
A script that divides last month's amortized cost for everything tagged service=taskflow-api by the requests the load balancer served:

// scripts/unit-cost.js: TaskFlow API cost per 1,000 requests (Node 24, AWS SDK v3)
import { CostExplorerClient, GetCostAndUsageCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-cost-explorer";
import { CloudWatchClient, GetMetricDataCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-cloudwatch";

const ce = new CostExplorerClient({ region: "us-east-1" }); // Cost Explorer's API lives in us-east-1
const cw = new CloudWatchClient({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION ?? "us-east-1" });

const now = new Date();
const start = new Date(Date.UTC(now.getUTCFullYear(), now.getUTCMonth() - 1, 1));
const end = new Date(Date.UTC(now.getUTCFullYear(), now.getUTCMonth(), 1));
const day = (d) => d.toISOString().slice(0, 10);

const cost = await ce.send(
  new GetCostAndUsageCommand({
    TimePeriod: { Start: day(start), End: day(end) }, // End is exclusive
    Granularity: "MONTHLY",
    Metrics: ["AmortizedCost"], // spreads commitment payments over the period
    Filter: { Tags: { Key: "service", Values: ["taskflow-api"] } },
  }),
);
const dollars = Number(cost.ResultsByTime[0].Total.AmortizedCost.Amount);

const metrics = await cw.send(
  new GetMetricDataCommand({
    StartTime: start,
    EndTime: end,
    MetricDataQueries: [
      {
        Id: "requests",
        MetricStat: {
          Metric: {
            Namespace: "AWS/ApplicationELB",
            MetricName: "RequestCount",
            Dimensions: [{ Name: "LoadBalancer", Value: process.env.ALB_DIMENSION }],
          },
          Period: 86400,
          Stat: "Sum",
        },
      },
    ],
  }),
);
const requests = metrics.MetricDataResults[0].Values.reduce((sum, v) => sum + v, 0);

console.log("| Month | Amortized cost | Requests | Cost per 1,000 requests |");
console.log("|---|---|---|---|");
console.log(
  `| ${day(start).slice(0, 7)} | $${dollars.toFixed(2)} | ${requests.toLocaleString("en-US")} | $${((dollars / requests) * 1000).toFixed(4)} |`,
);

Run it monthly from CI with short-lived credentials (OIDC), writing the table to the job summary:

# .github/workflows/unit-cost.yml
name: unit-cost

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "0 8 3 * *" # 08:00 UTC on the 3rd, once last month's data has settled
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write # lets the job request an OIDC token for AWS

jobs:
  report:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version-file: .nvmrc # Node 24, same as production
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: ${{ vars.AWS_COST_READER_ROLE_ARN }}
          aws-region: us-east-1
      - name: Write the unit cost to the job summary
        env:
          ALB_DIMENSION: ${{ vars.TASKFLOW_ALB_DIMENSION }}
        run: node scripts/unit-cost.js >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"

The role needs only read access:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["ce:GetCostAndUsage", "cloudwatch:GetMetricData"],
      "Resource": "*"
    }
  ]
}

OIDC trust policies and pinning actions are covered in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Create accounts per environment and enforce tags from day one; activate cost allocation tags.
  • Set a budget with actual and forecast alerts and an anomaly monitor on every account, routed to people who can act.
  • Review the bill monthly by usage type, not only by service.
  • Track unit costs (per request, per customer) next to product metrics.
  • Clean up and rightsize before buying commitments; commit to the floor and ladder purchases.
  • Use Spot for interruptible work only, diversified across types and zones.
  • Give every bucket, log group, snapshot schedule, and registry a retention rule when you create it.
  • Put a CDN in front of public content, compress text, and keep S3 and DynamoDB traffic on gateway endpoints.
  • Make cost visible in design reviews and pull requests (for example with a cost estimate of infrastructure changes).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The bill jumped 40% this month and nobody knows why. Detect: Cost Explorer grouped by usage type and day shows a step change on one meter, or an anomaly alert fired. Cause: often a new feature's logging, a job copying data across regions, or an autoscaling group stuck at maximum. Fix: find the meter and the tagged owner, fix the cause, and add a budget or anomaly monitor for that service if it was missing.
  • NAT gateway data processing is a top-five line item. Detect: NatGateway-Bytes is high; VPC flow logs show most NAT traffic going to S3 or ECR address ranges. Cause: AWS-service traffic from private subnets going through the NAT gateway. Fix: add S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints and interface endpoints for high-volume services such as ECR.
  • Savings Plan utilization dropped to 60%. Detect: the Savings Plans utilization report shows unused commitment every hour. Cause: a migration (to Fargate, a new instance family, or another region) left an EC2 Instance Savings Plan without matching usage, or traffic fell. Fix: nothing refunds a commitment; buy flexible Compute Savings Plans next time, commit to the floor, and move matching usage back where possible.
  • Batch jobs restart from the beginning several times a day. Detect: job logs show repeated restarts at Spot interruption times; EventBridge shows "EC2 Spot Instance Interruption Warning" events. Cause: Spot capacity reclaimed, jobs without checkpoints, a single instance type. Fix: checkpoint progress, handle the two-minute notice, diversify instance types and zones, and keep an on-demand floor.
  • Forty percent of spend is untagged. Detect: Cost Explorer grouped by the service tag shows a large "No tag key" bucket. Cause: resources created in the console or by tools without default tags; tags not activated for billing. Fix: activate the tags, add default_tags and tag policies, and allocate shared costs with an agreed rule.
  • CloudWatch Logs storage cost grows every month. Detect: TimedStorage-ByteHrs for CloudWatch rises steadily; log groups show no retention. Cause: the default retention keeps logs forever. Fix: set retention on every group, export what compliance needs to S3, and alarm on log groups without retention.
  • Cross-AZ data transfer costs more than the database. Detect: DataTransfer-Regional-Bytes is large and grows with traffic. Cause: chatty service-to-database or service-to-service calls across zones, uncompressed payloads, or replication of large data. Fix: cache, compress, batch calls, and use zone-aware routing where the platform supports it, without removing zone redundancy.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Usage type: The meter on a bill line (for example NatGateway-Bytes).
  • Unblended / amortized cost: Cost at the rates charged each hour / with upfront commitment payments spread over their term.
  • Cost allocation tag: A resource tag activated for use in billing data.
  • Showback / chargeback: Reporting costs to a team / billing them to the team's budget.
  • Budget / budget action: A spending threshold that alerts / that can also apply a policy or stop resources.
  • Rightsizing: Matching resource size and type to measured use.
  • Savings Plan / reservation / committed use discount: A one- or three-year commitment in exchange for lower rates.
  • Coverage / utilization: The share of usage covered by commitments / the share of commitments actually used.
  • Spot (preemptible) capacity: Discounted spare capacity that the provider can reclaim with short notice.
  • Unit cost: Cost divided by a business driver such as requests or customers.
  • FinOps: The practice of shared, continuous ownership of cloud cost across engineering, finance, and the business.
  • FOCUS: The FinOps Open Cost and Usage Specification, a common format for billing data.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Looking only at compute when data transfer, plumbing, and logs are half the bill.
  • Buying three-year commitments before cleaning up and rightsizing.
  • Believing a budget stops spending; without an action it only alerts.
  • Using Spot for stateful or single-instance production services.
  • Cutting logs that compliance requires instead of moving them to cheaper storage.
  • Giving up multi-AZ to save cross-zone transfer.
  • Treating cost as finance's problem; engineers decide most of it.
  • Comparing total spend month to month without normalizing by traffic or customers.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is grouping a bill by usage type more useful than grouping by service? Give two meters hidden inside "EC2-Other".
  2. Explain unblended and amortized cost, and which you would use for a unit-cost report.
  3. A NAT gateway processes 3 TB (3,072 GB) a month of traffic to S3. How much does an S3 gateway endpoint save? (Answer: 3,072 x $0.045 = $138.24 a month.)
  4. Calculate the break-even utilization of a 1-year Compute Savings Plan at $0.0599 per hour for an instance that costs $0.0816 on demand. (Answer: $0.0599 / $0.0816 = 73%, about 536 of 730 hours.)
  5. Which workloads suit Spot capacity, and how do you make them survive interruptions?
  6. Your staging environment costs $300 a month and is used 45 hours a week. What would a schedule save? (Answer: about $300 x (1 - 45/168) = $220 a month.)
  7. Give three ways to reduce internet egress for an API and a file download feature.
  8. Argue both sides of leaving the cloud for a company with steady load, and name the facts you would need before deciding.
