docs.title: Hosting Websites and Frontends
docs.text:
A frontend is either a folder of built files (a static site or a single-page app such as TaskFlow Web) or a server-rendered application (for example Next.js) that needs code running per request. This lesson covers where each kind can be hosted: Amazon S3 with CloudFront, AWS Amplify Hosting, Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, GitHub Pages, Firebase, Azure Static Web Apps, Render, and DigitalOcean App Platform. For each it explains what the product is, what you manage, how it bills, and what it costs at 10 thousand, 1 million, and 50 million page views a month.

How to deploy onto these hosts safely (hashed assets, cache headers, upload order, invalidation, SPA fallback routing, preview deploys) is covered in deploying frontends and static sites. This lesson is about choosing the host and understanding the bill.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Frontend hosting looks like a solved, nearly free problem, and at low traffic it is. The differences appear as traffic grows: one provider charges nothing for static bandwidth, another charges $0.15 per GB, and a third converts bandwidth, requests, and even deploys into credits. At 50 million page views a month the same build output costs anywhere from zero to about five thousand dollars depending on the host.

Rendering mode matters too. A static site or SPA can live anywhere. A server-rendered Next.js app needs compute at request time, which limits the choice and adds per-request cost. Free tiers also carry conditions (non-commercial use only, monthly bandwidth caps, paused projects) that are easy to discover only after launch.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Algolia on Vercel. In Algolia cuts build times in half with ISR, Vercel describes Algolia moving its website off a "complex Gatsby infrastructure" with growing build times to Next.js on Vercel, where build times fell by 50% and the team could publish changes without waiting for daily deployments. Incremental Static Regeneration (ISR) is one of the features named.
  • The Kubernetes website on Netlify. The kubernetes.io site is a Hugo project whose netlify.toml defines separate build commands for production, branch deploys, and deploy-preview contexts, so every pull request to the documentation gets its own preview site before review: the git-push platform workflow at the scale of a large open-source project.
  • Cloudflare's own guidance: start with Workers. In Your frontend, backend, and database, now in one Cloudflare Worker (April 2025), Cloudflare says Pages "will continue to be supported" but that "all of our investment, optimizations, and feature work will be dedicated to improving Workers", and advises that new projects "should start with Workers" now that Workers serves static assets and server-side rendering.

Popular tools and providers: Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare Workers and Pages, Amazon S3 with CloudFront, AWS Amplify Hosting, GitHub Pages, Firebase Hosting and App Hosting, Azure Static Web Apps, Render, DigitalOcean App Platform, and nginx or Caddy on your own server.

docs.title: Three kinds of frontend and what each needs
docs.text:
Kind Example What the host must do Hosting options Static site Documentation built with MkDocs or Hugo Serve files from a CDN with good cache headers Any static host Single-page app (SPA) TaskFlow Web (React + Vite) Serve files and rewrite unknown paths to index.html Any static host with rewrites Server-rendered (SSR, ISR, streaming) A Next.js storefront Run code per request or per revalidation, plus serve static assets Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare, Amplify, Firebase App Hosting, containers, VMs

The single biggest hosting decision for a frontend is whether it needs a server at all. If the HTML can be built ahead of time or rendered in the browser, every option on this page is open and the cheapest ones cost nothing.

docs.title: Amazon S3 with CloudFront
docs.text:
What it is: Amazon S3 stores your build output as objects in a private bucket; Amazon CloudFront is AWS's CDN, which caches and serves those files from edge locations worldwide. An origin access control (OAC) lets only your CloudFront distribution read the bucket, and a free public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager covers your domain.

You manage: the bucket, the distribution, cache policies, the deploy script (upload order and invalidations), redirects or rewrites (with CloudFront Functions), and DNS. AWS manages: storage durability and the global edge network.

Billing: S3 storage at $0.023 per GB-month and requests (S3 pricing), plus CloudFront either pay-as-you-go or on a flat-rate plan. Pay-as-you-go in the US is $0.085 per GB for the first 10 TB and $0.0100 per 10,000 HTTPS requests, with 1 TB of transfer, 10 million requests, and 2 million CloudFront Functions invocations free every month, and origin fetches from S3 are free (pay-as-you-go pricing). The flat-rate plans are priced per distribution per month with no overage charges: Free $0 (1 million requests, 100 GB), Pro $15 (10 million requests, 50 TB), Business $200 (125 million requests, 50 TB), and Premium $1,000 (500 million requests, 50 TB), each bundling WAF rules and some S3 storage (CloudFront pricing). The allowances are not hard caps: the developer guide says sustained use well above them can lead AWS to adjust delivery (for example fewer or more distant edge locations) until you upgrade.

Strengths and weaknesses: the cheapest and most controllable option inside AWS, with your files in your own account; but you assemble the pieces yourself and get no preview deployments unless you build them.

docs.title: AWS Amplify Hosting
docs.text:
What it is: a git-connected build and hosting service. You connect a repository; Amplify builds each push, hosts the result on CloudFront, and gives branch deployments. It also runs server-rendered Next.js by provisioning compute for SSR routes.

You manage: the build settings and environment variables. AWS manages: builds, CDN, TLS, and SSR compute.

Billing (Amplify pricing): build minutes at $0.01 per minute (standard instance), storage at $0.023 per GB-month, data transfer out at $0.15 per GB served, and SSR at $0.30 per million requests plus $0.20 per GB-hour of request duration. The Amplify pricing page lists a 12-month free tier of 1,000 build minutes, 5 GB stored, 15 GB served, and 500,000 SSR requests a month. AWS accounts created since July 15, 2025 are on the newer credit-based Free Tier (up to $200 in credits), and AWS does not say whether this allowance still applies to them, so check your account's Free Tier page.

Strengths and weaknesses: a Vercel-like workflow inside your AWS account; but at $0.15 per GB it costs much more per GB served than CloudFront directly.

docs.title: Vercel
docs.text:
What it is: a frontend platform built by the company behind Next.js. Every git push produces an immutable deployment with its own URL; pull requests get preview deployments; production is an alias that points at one deployment. Static files are served from Vercel's CDN, and server-side code runs as Vercel Functions, billed by active CPU time, provisioned memory, and invocations.

You manage: the code and project settings. Vercel manages: builds, CDN, TLS, functions, and scaling.

Billing (pricing): Hobby is free but, under the terms of service, only for "personal or non-commercial use"; Hobby includes 100 GB of Fast Data Transfer and 1 million function invocations a month, and when a limit is exceeded the feature pauses until 30 days have passed (Hobby plan). Pro costs $20 per deploying seat per month and includes a $20 usage credit. Its CDN usage is billed one of two ways. With Flat Rate CDN, the default for new Pro teams since September 2026, Pro includes 1 million CDN requests and 1 TB of data transfer a month, and higher tiers cost $20, $100, or $300 a month (10, 50, or 150 million requests, each with 50 TB). With usage-based billing there is no CDN allowance beyond the credit: Fast Data Transfer from $0.15 per GB and CDN requests from $2 per million. Functions bill $0.60 per million invocations, active CPU from $0.128 per hour, and provisioned memory from $0.0106 per GB-hour.

Strengths and weaknesses: the best support for Next.js features and an excellent preview workflow; but per-GB transfer costs more than a CDN bought directly, seats add up for larger teams, and some features are Vercel-specific.

docs.title: Netlify
docs.text:
What it is: a git-push platform for static sites and frameworks with atomic deploys, Deploy Previews for every pull request, serverless and edge functions, forms, and redirects.

You manage: the code, netlify.toml, and _redirects and _headers files. Netlify manages: builds, CDN, TLS, and functions.

Billing: since September 4, 2025, new accounts use credit-based plans; teams created earlier can stay on legacy plans. Free includes 300 credits a month with a hard limit (projects pause when they run out), Personal costs $9 for 1,000 credits, and Pro costs $20 for 3,000 credits with unlimited members. Usage converts to credits: 20 credits per GB of bandwidth, 2 credits per 10,000 web requests, 15 credits per production deploy, and 10 credits per GB-hour of compute. Extra credits on Pro cost $10 per 1,500 (pricing).

Strengths and weaknesses: a mature, framework-neutral workflow; but credits make costs harder to predict, and frequent production deploys consume credits on small plans.

docs.title: Cloudflare Workers static assets and Cloudflare Pages
docs.text:
What it is: Cloudflare's network serves your static files from its locations worldwide. Pages is the older git-integrated product for static sites with optional Functions; Workers can now serve static assets and run server-side code from one project, and Cloudflare recommends it for new projects (see Real-world usage). Workers run in V8 isolates, which start in milliseconds.

You manage: the build output and a wrangler configuration file. Cloudflare manages: the network, TLS, and scaling.

Billing: "Requests to static assets are free and unlimited" and there are no charges for data transfer (Workers pricing). Server-side code is billed per request on Workers Paid ($5 a month minimum, including 10 million requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds, then $0.30 per million requests). Pages Free allows 500 builds a month, 20,000 files per site, and files up to 25 MiB (Pages limits).

Strengths and weaknesses: the lowest cost at any static traffic level and a very large network; but Workers custom domains require the domain's DNS to be on Cloudflare (Pages allows a subdomain on external DNS with a CNAME, though an apex domain on Pages also needs Cloudflare nameservers), and server-side code runs in the Workers runtime rather than full Node.js, so some packages need adaptation.

docs.title: GitHub Pages
docs.text:
What it is: free static hosting published from a repository, either from a branch or from a GitHub Actions workflow.

Limits (GitHub Pages limits): published sites up to 1 GB, a soft bandwidth limit of 100 GB per month, a soft limit of 10 builds per hour (not applied to custom Actions workflows), and no use as "a free web-hosting service to run your online business, e-commerce site", or commercial SaaS.

Strengths and weaknesses: zero cost and zero setup for documentation and open-source project sites; but no server-side code, no custom headers, and not for commercial products.

docs.title: Firebase Hosting and Firebase App Hosting
docs.text:
What it is: Firebase Hosting serves static files from Google's CDN and can rewrite paths to Cloud Run services or functions. Firebase App Hosting is a separate product for server-rendered frameworks such as Next.js and Angular; it builds your app and runs it on Google Cloud infrastructure.

Billing (Firebase pricing): Hosting on the no-cost Spark plan includes 10 GB stored and 360 MB of transfer per day; on the pay-as-you-go Blaze plan, usage beyond that costs $0.026 per GB stored and $0.15 per GB transferred. App Hosting requires Blaze; its outgoing bandwidth beyond 10 GiB a month costs $0.15 per GiB when cached and $0.20 per GiB when not.

docs.title: Azure Static Web Apps
docs.text:
What it is: static hosting on Azure with built-in API routes backed by Azure Functions, authentication integration, and preview environments from pull requests.

Billing (pricing and the Azure retail price list): Free and Standard plans; Standard is $9 per app per month with an SLA. Both include 100 GB of bandwidth per subscription; on Standard, extra bandwidth is $0.20 per GB. Free allows 2 custom domains per app and Standard 5.

docs.title: Render static sites
docs.text:
What it is: Render, a general application platform, hosts static sites for free on its CDN with automatic deploys from git.

Billing: static sites themselves are free; their traffic counts toward the workspace's included bandwidth (Hobby 5 GB, Pro 25 GB, Scale 1 TB), and extra outbound bandwidth costs $0.15 per GB (outbound bandwidth).

docs.title: DigitalOcean App Platform (static sites)
docs.text:
What it is: DigitalOcean's PaaS, which also hosts static sites from git with a CDN and automatic HTTPS.

Billing (App Platform pricing): three static-site apps are free, each with a 1 GiB transfer allowance; additional static apps cost $3 a month, and transfer beyond the allowance costs $0.02 per GiB.

docs.title: A git-push platform, step by step
docs.text: The key idea is that a deployment is immutable and production is only a pointer. That gives atomic switches, instant rollbacks, and a preview URL per pull request with no extra infrastructure, which is most of what these platforms charge for.

docs.title: Hosting server-rendered Next.js
docs.text:
The Next.js deployment guide lists four ways to deploy: a Node.js server and a Docker container support all features, a static export supports only features that do not need a server, and platform adapters vary. Through the OpenNext project and Next.js's Deployment Adapter API (stable in Next.js 16.2), other platforms can run Next.js without reverse-engineering its build output.

Where How it runs Next.js Good for Watch out for Vercel Native: functions for SSR, CDN for static and ISR Full feature support with no configuration Per-GB and per-seat costs at scale Netlify Netlify's own Next.js integration Teams already on Netlify Not yet a verified adapter, so support may vary Cloudflare Workers OpenNext Cloudflare adapter Global edge rendering, free static traffic Workers runtime differences from Node.js AWS Amplify Hosting Amplify-managed SSR compute Staying inside AWS with a managed workflow $0.15 per GB served; not a verified adapter OpenNext on AWS (SST) Lambda functions, S3, and CloudFront in your account Full control and AWS pricing You operate the pieces Firebase App Hosting Google-managed build and runtime Firebase and Google Cloud users Requires the Blaze plan Cloud Run, Fargate, any container next start or output: "standalone" in Docker All features, portable You handle CDN caching for static assets A VM next start behind nginx Steady traffic, full control Patching, scaling, and CDN are yours

docs.text: Host What it is You manage Scaling Pricing model Free tier Strengths Weaknesses Lock-in S3 + CloudFront Object storage + AWS CDN Bucket, distribution, deploy script Automatic Per GB and request, or flat-rate plan 1 TB and 10M requests per month (CDN) Cheap, controllable, in your account Assemble it yourself; no previews Low (files are portable) Amplify Hosting Git-connected AWS hosting Build settings Automatic Build minutes, GB served, SSR requests First period for new accounts Managed workflow in AWS $0.15 per GB Low to medium Vercel Frontend platform Code, settings Automatic Seats + included usage + overages Hobby (non-commercial) Best Next.js support, previews Cost at scale, seats Medium (framework features) Netlify Frontend platform Code, netlify.toml Automatic Credits 300 credits per month Framework-neutral, mature Credits hard to predict Low to medium Cloudflare Workers / Pages Edge network with static assets Build output, config Automatic, global Free static; per request for code Generous free plan Free static traffic, fast Workers runtime, DNS on Cloudflare for Workers Medium for Workers code GitHub Pages Static hosting from a repo Repo and workflow Automatic Free Free Simplest for docs No server code; non-commercial Low Firebase Hosting Google CDN static hosting firebase.json Automatic GB stored and served 10 GB stored, 360 MB per day Easy with Firebase backends $0.15 per GB Low Azure Static Web Apps Azure static + Functions API Config file Automatic Per app + GB Free plan, 100 GB Azure integration, SLA on Standard $0.20 per GB beyond 100 GB Low to medium Render static Free static sites on a PaaS Repo settings Automatic Workspace bandwidth Free sites, 5 GB on Hobby Same place as your API $0.15 per GB beyond plan Low DigitalOcean App Platform PaaS static sites Repo settings Automatic Per app + GiB 3 apps free Low per-GB price 1 GiB included per app Low

docs.title: What each host costs at three traffic levels
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices on this page are US-region list prices in USD from the linked official pricing pages in November 2026. They change often; re-check them with each provider's pricing page or the AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud pricing calculator before deciding. Other regions (for example India) are priced differently: choose the region on the pricing page or in the calculator to see its rates.

Assumptions for TaskFlow Web: each page view transfers 500 KB from the CDN on average (first visits download the bundle, repeat visits are mostly cached) and makes 10 CDN requests; the team deploys to production 30 times a month. So:

10,000 page views      ->      5 GB  and       100,000 requests
1,000,000 page views   ->    500 GB  and    10,000,000 requests
50,000,000 page views  -> 25,000 GB  and   500,000,000 requests

The arithmetic for the less obvious rows, at 50 million page views:

S3 + CloudFront pay-as-you-go (US):
  transfer  (10,240 - 1,024 free) GB x $0.085 = $  783.36
            (25,000 - 10,240) GB x $0.080      = $1,180.80
  requests  (500M - 10M free) / 10,000 x $0.0100 = $  490.00
  total                                         ~ $2,454 (plus a few dollars of S3 origin GETs)

Netlify Pro (credits):
  bandwidth 25,000 GB x 20 = 500,000 credits
  requests  500M / 10,000 x 2 = 100,000 credits
  deploys   30 x 15 = 450 credits
  total 600,450 credits - 3,000 included = 597,450 -> 399 packs x $10 = $3,990 + $20 plan = $4,010

Vercel Pro (usage-based CDN billing: no allowance beyond the $20 credit;
the largest Flat Rate CDN tier covers only 150M requests):
  transfer  25,000 GB x $0.15                    = $3,750
  requests  500M / 1M x $2                       = $1,000
  seat $20, minus the $20 usage credit           ~ $4,750
Host (monthly, USD) 10k page views 1M page views 50M page views Cloudflare Workers static assets or Pages $0 $0 $0 CloudFront flat-rate plan + S3 $0 (Free plan) $15 (Pro) $1,000 (Premium) S3 + CloudFront pay-as-you-go $0 $0 (inside the free tier) about $2,454 DigitalOcean App Platform static about $0.07 about $9.29 about $466 Render static (Hobby workspace) $0 about $74 about $3,749 Firebase Hosting (Blaze) $0 about $73 about $3,748 AWS Amplify Hosting about $1.35 about $75.60 about $3,751 Netlify (credit plans) $9 (Personal) about $90 (Pro + 7 credit packs) about $4,010 (list); Enterprise in practice Vercel $0 Hobby if non-commercial, else $20 Pro $40 (Pro seat + $20 Flat Rate CDN tier for 10M requests) about $4,750 (usage-based list); Enterprise in practice Azure Static Web Apps $0 (Free) $89 (Standard) about $4,989 GitHub Pages $0 Not suitable (100 GB soft limit) Not suitable

Three lessons come out of the table. First, below a million page views the difference is a few tens of dollars, so the workflow matters more than the price. Second, at high volume the per-GB price dominates, and it ranges from zero (Cloudflare) through $0.02 (DigitalOcean) and the CDN rates (CloudFront) to $0.15 or $0.20 (platform markups). Third, list prices are where negotiation starts: at tens of terabytes, every platform has an enterprise or flat-rate offer, so get a quote before you migrate.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Use a pure static host whenever the frontend can be built ahead of time or rendered in the browser; it is cheaper, faster, and has fewer moving parts. Use a platform with server rendering only when SEO, first-load performance, or personalization genuinely need HTML generated per request. Do not pick a host for one feature you might use later; moving a static site is easy, so optimize for today's workflow.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Situation Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Cloudflare Workers static assets or Pages GitHub Pages (non-commercial), Vercel Hobby (non-commercial) Free at any realistic traffic, custom domain, TLS included Early startup Vercel or Netlify for previews and speed Cloudflare for a static SPA Preview deployments and zero setup save more than they cost at this stage Steady high traffic S3 + CloudFront (flat-rate plan or committed pricing) or Cloudflare Negotiated Vercel or Netlify Enterprise if the workflow is worth it Per-GB price dominates at tens of terabytes Spiky traffic (launches, campaigns) Any CDN-backed static host; Cloudflare or a CloudFront flat-rate plan to avoid overage risk Vercel or Netlify with spend limits and alerts CDNs absorb spikes; the risk is the bill, not capacity Global audience Cloudflare or CloudFront (large edge networks) Vercel or Netlify Static files are served from the edge; keep API calls few and cacheable Compliance-heavy (healthcare) S3 + CloudFront under the AWS BAA (both are on AWS's HIPAA eligible services list) Vercel with its HIPAA BAA (a paid add-on on Pro, on request for Enterprise) Keep PHI out of static files and URLs entirely; the build output should hold no patient data, so the contract matters for any server-side code Large files or heavy egress Cloudflare (no egress charges) or CloudFront flat-rate DigitalOcean App Platform ($0.02 per GiB) Avoid $0.15 to $0.20 per GB platform transfer pricing Team with no ops people Vercel or Netlify Amplify Hosting inside AWS Git push, previews, TLS, and rollbacks with no infrastructure to manage

docs.title: TaskFlow Web on a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront (Terraform)
docs.text:
This creates a private bucket, an origin access control, a distribution with the managed caching policy, and a bucket policy that only that distribution can use.

# infra/web/main.tf: TaskFlow Web on a private S3 bucket behind CloudFront
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

variable "domain_name" {
  type    = string
  default = "app.example.com"
}

variable "certificate_arn" {
  type        = string
  description = "ACM certificate for domain_name; CloudFront requires us-east-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "web" {
  bucket = "taskflow-web-example"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "web" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.web.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

resource "aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control" "web" {
  name                              = "taskflow-web-oac"
  origin_access_control_origin_type = "s3"
  signing_behavior                  = "always"
  signing_protocol                  = "sigv4"
}

data "aws_cloudfront_cache_policy" "optimized" {
  name = "Managed-CachingOptimized"
}

resource "aws_cloudfront_distribution" "web" {
  enabled             = true
  is_ipv6_enabled     = true
  default_root_object = "index.html"
  aliases             = [var.domain_name]
  price_class         = "PriceClass_100" # North America and Europe edges only

  origin {
    origin_id                = "s3-web"
    domain_name              = aws_s3_bucket.web.bucket_regional_domain_name
    origin_access_control_id = aws_cloudfront_origin_access_control.web.id
  }

  default_cache_behavior {
    target_origin_id       = "s3-web"
    viewer_protocol_policy = "redirect-to-https"
    allowed_methods        = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    cached_methods         = ["GET", "HEAD"]
    compress               = true
    cache_policy_id        = data.aws_cloudfront_cache_policy.optimized.id
  }

  # SPA fallback: S3 returns 403 for missing keys when the policy has no
  # s3:ListBucket, so map it to index.html with a 200
  custom_error_response {
    error_code            = 403
    response_code         = 200
    response_page_path    = "/index.html"
    error_caching_min_ttl = 10
  }

  restrictions {
    geo_restriction {
      restriction_type = "none"
    }
  }

  viewer_certificate {
    acm_certificate_arn      = var.certificate_arn
    ssl_support_method       = "sni-only"
    minimum_protocol_version = "TLSv1.2_2021"
  }
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "web" {
  statement {
    actions   = ["s3:GetObject"]
    resources = ["${aws_s3_bucket.web.arn}/*"]

    principals {
      type        = "Service"
      identifiers = ["cloudfront.amazonaws.com"]
    }

    condition {
      test     = "StringEquals"
      variable = "AWS:SourceArn"
      values   = [aws_cloudfront_distribution.web.arn]
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_policy" "web" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.web.id
  policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.web.json
}

output "cloudfront_domain" {
  value = aws_cloudfront_distribution.web.domain_name
}
  • The bucket stays private: public access is blocked, and the policy lets only the CloudFront service read objects, and only for requests from this distribution (AWS:SourceArn).
  • price_class = "PriceClass_100" serves from fewer, cheaper edge regions; remove it if many users are in Asia or South America.
  • The error mapping turns every missing file, including a mistyped asset URL, into index.html. A CloudFront Function that rewrites only page routes is more precise; the frontend deployment lesson shows one, along with the ordered upload and invalidation script.
  • Point app.example.com at the distribution with a Route 53 alias or a CNAME at your DNS provider.

docs.title: TaskFlow Web on Cloudflare Workers static assets
docs.text:
// wrangler.jsonc
{
  "$schema": "./node_modules/wrangler/config-schema.json",
  "name": "taskflow-web",
  "compatibility_date": "2026-11-01",
  "assets": {
    "directory": "./dist",
    "not_found_handling": "single-page-application"
  }
}

# public/_headers (Vite copies it into dist/)
/assets/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

npm run build          # Vite writes dist/
npx wrangler deploy    # uploads only changed files and switches versions

With only an assets block and no Worker script, every request is a static asset request, which Cloudflare does not bill. not_found_handling: "single-page-application" returns index.html for unknown paths, which is the SPA fallback.

docs.title: TaskFlow Web on Firebase Hosting
docs.text:
The project's firebase.json (plain JSON, so no comments) sets the output folder, the SPA rewrite, and long caching for hashed assets:

{
  "hosting": {
    "public": "dist",
    "ignore": ["firebase.json", "**/.*", "**/node_modules/**"],
    "rewrites": [{ "source": "**", "destination": "/index.html" }],
    "headers": [
      {
        "source": "/assets/**",
        "headers": [
          { "key": "Cache-Control", "value": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

npm run build
npx firebase-tools deploy --only hosting

Rewrites apply only when no file matches the path, so real files are still served directly.

docs.title: TaskFlow Web on Azure Static Web Apps
docs.text:
staticwebapp.config.json in the build output configures the fallback and headers:

{
  "navigationFallback": {
    "rewrite": "/index.html",
    "exclude": ["/assets/*", "/favicon.ico"]
  },
  "routes": [
    {
      "route": "/assets/*",
      "headers": { "cache-control": "public, max-age=31536000, immutable" }
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Server-rendered Next.js on Cloud Run
docs.text:
For full Next.js features outside Vercel, build a standalone server and run it as a container:

// next.config.mjs
/** @type {import('next').NextConfig} */
const nextConfig = {
  output: "standalone", // copies only the files the server needs into .next/standalone
};
export default nextConfig;

# Dockerfile
FROM node:24-slim AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM node:24-slim
WORKDIR /app
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080 HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0
COPY --from=build /app/.next/standalone ./
COPY --from=build /app/.next/static ./.next/static
COPY --from=build /app/public ./public
USER node
EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "server.js"]

gcloud run deploy taskflow-site --source . --region=us-central1 \
  --min-instances=0 --max-instances=20 --allow-unauthenticated

Put a CDN in front (Cloud CDN through a load balancer, or Cloudflare) so /_next/static/* files, which are content-hashed, are served from cache instead of from the container.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Decide the rendering mode first; static and SPA frontends can use the cheapest hosts.
  • Estimate bandwidth from real numbers: average transferred bytes per page view times page views, not bundle size times visits.
  • Read the commercial-use terms of free tiers before launching a business on them.
  • Set spend limits or usage alerts on platforms that bill overages, and know what happens at a hard limit (pause or bill).
  • Keep the frontend portable: plain build output, rewrites and headers in a small config file you could translate to another host.
  • Keep secrets and personal data out of the frontend bundle entirely; anything in it is public.
  • Get a quote before migrating for cost reasons at tens of terabytes; list prices are the upper bound.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The site went down on the last days of the month. Detect: the platform dashboard shows the project paused or a usage limit reached. Cause: a hard limit on a free plan, such as Netlify's Free credit limit or Vercel Hobby's monthly limits, which pause the feature. Fix: move production to a paid plan with spend alerts, and keep free plans for previews and personal projects.
  • The bandwidth bill is ten times the estimate. Detect: the provider's usage page shows transfer far above page views times expected size; top paths are large images or video. Cause: unoptimized images, source maps, or video served as static files, or hotlinking from other sites. Fix: resize and compress images, serve video from a video service, block hotlinking, and move heavy files to a host without egress fees.
  • Users get the old version for hours after a deploy. Detect: curl -I https://app.example.com/ shows a long max-age or an Age header from before the deploy. Cause: index.html cached at the CDN or in browsers. Fix: serve HTML with Cache-Control: no-cache, invalidate only index.html after each deploy, and keep long caching for hashed assets only.
  • Deep links return 404 or 403 on the new host. Detect: / works but /tasks/42 fails on refresh. Cause: no SPA fallback rewrite on the new host. Fix: add the host's fallback (not_found_handling, rewrites, navigationFallback, or a CloudFront Function) as part of the migration checklist.
  • Server-rendered pages are slow and the function bill climbs. Detect: function invocations equal page views, and cold starts show in latency percentiles. Cause: pages that could be static are rendered on every request. Fix: render at build time or with incremental regeneration where content allows, and cache rendered HTML at the CDN with s-maxage.
  • The custom domain does not attach on Workers. Detect: the dashboard refuses the domain or shows it as pending. Cause: Workers custom domains require nameservers managed by Cloudflare. Fix: move DNS to Cloudflare, or use Pages (which supports a subdomain on external DNS with a CNAME; an apex domain still needs Cloudflare nameservers) for that site.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Static site: a site whose HTML is fully generated at build time.
  • Single-page application (SPA): one HTML page plus JavaScript that renders routes in the browser and calls APIs for data.
  • SSR (server-side rendering): generating HTML on a server for each request.
  • ISR (incremental static regeneration): serving pre-rendered pages and regenerating them in the background after a set time or on demand.
  • Origin: the server or bucket the CDN fetches from on a cache miss.
  • Origin access control (OAC): CloudFront's signed access that lets a private S3 bucket accept requests only from a distribution.
  • Immutable deployment: a deployment whose files never change after it is created; production is an alias pointing at one.
  • Preview deployment: a deployment of a branch or pull request at its own URL, used for review.
  • Fast Data Transfer: Vercel's name for data transferred from its CDN to users, billed per GB.
  • Credits: Netlify's unit for usage on credit-based plans.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Choosing a server-rendering platform for a site that could be fully static.
  • Estimating bandwidth from bundle size alone, ignoring images and repeat-visit caching.
  • Launching a commercial product on GitHub Pages or Vercel Hobby.
  • Assuming "unlimited bandwidth" on every free tier; most have soft limits, hard limits, or fair-use clauses.
  • Making the S3 bucket public instead of using an origin access control.
  • Forgetting that Netlify credit plans count production deploys, so a busy CI pipeline consumes credits.
  • Comparing platforms at list price at large scale instead of asking for an enterprise or flat-rate quote.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does a host need to provide for a static site, an SPA, and a server-rendered Next.js app?
  2. Why is an origin access control better than a public S3 bucket for static hosting?
  3. Calculate the CloudFront pay-as-you-go cost in the US for 3 TB of transfer and 20 million HTTPS requests in a month. (Answer: transfer (3,072 - 1,024) GB x $0.085 = $174.08; requests (20M - 10M) / 10,000 x $0.0100 = $10.00; total $184.08.)
  4. On Netlify's credit plans, which three kinds of usage consume credits for a static site, and why does deploy frequency matter?
  5. Why can a Cloudflare-hosted static site cost nothing at 50 million page views while the same site costs thousands of dollars elsewhere?
  6. What are the trade-offs of running Next.js on Vercel versus in a container on Cloud Run?
  7. A startup's marketing site gets 2 million page views a month and its team wants preview deployments. Which host would you pick and what would you check before launch?
  8. What should a healthcare company keep out of its frontend build, and why does that matter for choosing a host?

docs.title: Hosting and Cloud Platforms Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review where to run and store software: hosting models, frontend and backend hosting, managed databases, object and file storage, video delivery, backup and archive tiers, and cloud cost. Prices quoted are the November 2026 US list prices used in the lessons; always re-check them before deciding. Try answering each question before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. Explain IaaS, CaaS, serverless containers, PaaS, FaaS, edge compute, and static hosting in one line each.
docs.text: IaaS rents virtual machines you operate (EC2, Compute Engine, Droplets). CaaS runs your container images on an orchestrator whose nodes you pay for (EKS, GKE, ECS on EC2). Serverless containers run images without nodes (Fargate, Cloud Run, Container Apps). PaaS builds and runs your code from a git push (Render, Heroku, App Service). FaaS runs a handler per event (Lambda, Cloud Run functions). Edge compute runs small functions in CDN locations (Cloudflare Workers, CloudFront Functions). Static hosting serves pre-built files from a CDN.

docs.title: 2. What does the shared responsibility model say, and which responsibility never moves to the provider?
docs.text: The provider secures the cloud itself (data centers, hardware, hypervisor); the customer secures what they put in it. As you move from VMs to platforms and functions, the provider takes over the OS, runtime, and scaling. Data, identities, and access control stay yours on every model: a public bucket or a leaked key is always the customer's problem.

docs.title: 3. What unit does each hosting model bill by?
docs.text: VMs bill instance-hours (EC2 per second with a 60-second minimum); bundled VMs a flat monthly price with transfer included; serverless containers vCPU-seconds and GB-seconds (plus requests on Cloud Run); functions requests plus GB-seconds; PaaS per instance or per second of use; static hosts per GB and request, or a plan. The unit decides the shape of the bill: per-request pricing tracks traffic, per-hour pricing is flat until capacity runs out.

docs.title: 4. Which AWS costs are not in the headline price?
docs.text: Internet egress ($0.09 per GB for the first 10 TB after 100 GB free), NAT gateways ($0.045 per hour plus $0.045 per GB processed), cross-zone traffic ($0.01 per GB each way), load balancer hours ($0.0225 plus LCUs), public IPv4 addresses ($0.005 per hour each), CloudWatch Logs ingestion ($0.50 per GB), and idle resources such as unattached volumes. In a small two-task Fargate setup they add up to more than three times the compute cost.

docs.title: 5. What is lock-in, and how do you keep it under control?
docs.text: Lock-in is the cost of leaving: code to rewrite, data to move, people to retrain. Keep the portable layers portable: OCI container images, standard engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, the MongoDB protocol), Terraform or OpenTofu, OIDC between systems. Accept provider-specific services only where they clearly pay off, and remember data gravity: moving 50 TB out at list price is about $4,400 of egress plus transfer time.

docs.title: 6. Compare hyperscalers, developer platforms, and budget providers.
docs.text: Hyperscalers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) offer every service, many regions, compliance programs, and commitment discounts, at the price of complexity and metered extras. Developer platforms (Vercel, Netlify, Render, Railway, Fly.io) offer git-push deploys and previews with little operations work, but price cliffs and fewer controls. Budget providers (Hetzner, DigitalOcean, Akamai) offer cheap VMs with generous included bandwidth and fewer managed services. Mixing them is normal.

docs.title: 7. Which product changes from 2022-2026 should a team know about?
docs.text: Heroku ended free dynos in November 2022; Google renamed Cloud Functions to Cloud Run functions; Azure Media Services was retired on June 30, 2024; AWS closed App Runner to new customers and recommends ECS Express Mode; the original Amazon Glacier vault service stopped accepting new customers on December 15, 2025 (use the S3 Glacier storage classes); CloudFront added flat-rate plans in November 2025. Products change, so keep deployments in code and data in portable formats.

docs.title: 8. What does the host have to do for a static site, an SPA, and a server-rendered site?
docs.text: A static site only needs files served from a CDN with good cache headers. An SPA also needs unknown paths rewritten to index.html, so client-side routes work on refresh. A server-rendered site (SSR, ISR, streaming) needs code running per request or per revalidation, as functions, containers, or a Node server. If the site needs no server, every host is an option and the cheapest cost nothing.

docs.title: 9. How does S3 with CloudFront serve a private bucket, and how should a deploy upload files?
docs.text: The bucket stays private; an origin access control lets only the CloudFront distribution read it, and ACM provides the certificate. A deploy uploads content-hashed assets first and index.html last, then invalidates only index.html, so users never load HTML that points at assets not yet uploaded. Origin fetches from S3 to CloudFront are not billed as transfer.

docs.title: 10. Why do platforms such as Vercel and Netlify make rollbacks instant?
docs.text: Every build becomes an immutable deployment with its own URL, and production is only an alias pointing at one deployment. Promoting a release switches the alias atomically at every edge, and rolling back points it at the previous deployment. Preview URLs per pull request come from the same model.

docs.title: 11. Where can you run server-rendered Next.js, and what are the trade-offs?
docs.text: Vercel runs it natively with full feature support but per-GB and per-seat costs at scale. OpenNext on AWS uses Lambda, S3, and CloudFront in your own account, with pieces you operate. Cloudflare Workers run it through the OpenNext adapter with runtime differences from Node.js. Amplify Hosting and Firebase App Hosting manage it for you. A container on Cloud Run or Fargate (output: "standalone") supports everything and is portable, but you add CDN caching for static assets yourself.

docs.title: 12. Why do frontend hosting bills diverge so much at high traffic?
docs.text: Because the price of transfer differs by an order of magnitude: requests to Cloudflare Workers static assets are free and unlimited, CloudFront charges $0.085 per GB in the US after its free terabyte, and several frontend platforms charge well above CDN rates per GB. At 50 million page views (about 25 TB) that is the difference between nothing and several thousand dollars a month at list price (the frontend lesson prices each host). Below about a million page views the difference is tens of dollars, so workflow matters more than price.

docs.title: 13. What are CloudFront flat-rate plans, and what is the catch?
docs.text: Monthly plans per distribution with no overage charges: Free $0 (1 million requests, 100 GB), Pro $15 (10 million requests, 50 TB), Business $200 (125 million requests, 50 TB), and Premium $1,000 (500 million requests, 50 TB), bundling WAF, DDoS protection, and other features. The catch: one plan covers one distribution, and sustained use above the allowance can lead AWS to reduce performance (fewer or more distant edge locations) until you upgrade.

docs.title: 14. Compare VMs, platforms, container services, and functions by unit of scale, start time, and idle cost.
docs.text: VMs scale by adding VMs, start in tens of seconds to minutes, and bill while idle. Platforms scale by instances, start in seconds, and usually bill while idle (some sleep). Container services scale tasks or pods, start in seconds, and bill unless they scale to zero. Functions scale by execution environments, start in milliseconds to seconds (cold starts), and do not bill while idle.

docs.title: 15. What is a cold start on AWS Lambda, and how do you reduce it?
docs.text: When no warm execution environment is free, Lambda creates a Firecracker microVM, loads the code, starts the runtime, and runs module-scope initialization before the handler: that is the cold start. Reduce it with a small package, lazy initialization, Provisioned Concurrency for predictable traffic, or (on other platforms) minimum instances such as Cloud Run's --min-instances.

docs.title: 16. Why do functions exhaust database connections, and how do you fix it?
docs.text: Each execution environment opens its own pool, so a traffic spike that creates hundreds of environments multiplies connections past max_connections. Fixes: one or two connections per environment, a cap on reserved concurrency, and a pooler or proxy (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) or a data API built for serverless clients.

docs.title: 17. Which platforms suit WebSockets and long-running work?
docs.text: VMs, ECS, and Kubernetes have no platform request limit (only load balancer idle timeouts). Cloud Run supports WebSockets but each connection is a request bound by the timeout (up to 60 minutes), so clients must reconnect. Heroku must start responding within 30 seconds. Lambda invocations last at most 15 minutes and WebSockets go through API Gateway. Long jobs belong on workers and queues on any platform.

docs.title: 18. At what traffic does an always-on VM become cheaper than Lambda for TaskFlow API?
docs.text: At 120 ms and 512 MB, Lambda costs about $1.20 per million requests ($0.20 per million requests plus 0.12 s x 0.5 GB x $0.0000166667). One t4g.small with disk and an IPv4 address costs $17.51 a month, so the crossover is 17.51 / 1.20 = about 14.6 million requests a month; two Fargate tasks with an ALB ($58.31) cross at about 48.6 million. The flat lines step up when instances fill, and functions save people time below the crossover.

docs.title: 19. What is AWS Fargate, and how is it billed?
docs.text: Fargate runs ECS or EKS tasks without servers you manage: each task gets an isolated environment with the vCPU and memory you request. It bills $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour (x86, us-east-1) per second with a one-minute minimum, so a 0.5 vCPU, 1 GB task costs about $18 a month running all the time.

docs.title: 20. When is Kubernetes the right hosting choice, and when is it not?
docs.text: It fits many services, a team that knows and owns it, and needs for fine control of scheduling and networking. It is wrong for a small team with a few services: the control plane fee (about $73 a month on EKS or GKE), node upgrades, add-ons, and on-call work cost more than the flexibility is worth. Serverless containers or a platform give most of the benefit with none of the cluster work.

docs.title: 21. What does a managed database take off your plate, and what stays with you?
docs.text: The provider handles installation, patching, automated backups and point-in-time recovery, failover, read replicas, and storage growth. You still own the schema, indexes, query performance, connection limits and pooling, capacity choice and cost, and network exposure and access control.

docs.title: 22. Explain a synchronous standby, a read replica, and point-in-time recovery.
docs.text: A synchronous standby (Multi-AZ, HA) receives every commit in another zone before it is acknowledged and is promoted on failure; you pay for two instances. A read replica is an asynchronous copy for read scaling that can lag. Point-in-time recovery combines snapshots with archived transaction logs to restore a new instance to any second within the retention window.

docs.title: 23. Compare provisioned, serverless-capacity, and per-request database billing.
docs.text: Provisioned instances (RDS, Cloud SQL, Atlas dedicated) cost the same every hour, sized for the peak: best for steady load. Serverless capacity (Aurora Serverless v2, Neon) follows load above a floor or scales to zero: good for variable load and preview databases, with a resume delay. Per-request databases (DynamoDB on-demand, Firestore, Cosmos DB serverless) bill each operation: cheap for spiky key lookups, expensive for scans and fan-out reads.

docs.title: 24. Why can a per-request database bill jump without more users?
docs.text: Because cost follows operations, not users: a scan, a query without a selective key, a realtime listener on a large collection, a retry loop, or a new secondary index (which multiplies write cost) all raise reads or writes. Find the operation in the metrics, redesign around keys or indexes, and cache hot reads.

docs.title: 25. How do you size a connection pool against a managed database limit?
docs.text: Divide max_connections minus a reserve for administration and replicas by the maximum number of processes autoscaling allows. With a limit of 100, a reserve of 10, and up to six API processes: (100 - 10) / 6 = 15 connections per pool. Add a pooler when functions or many small instances connect.

docs.title: 26. When does self-hosting a database make sense?
docs.text: When the team has real database skills, a tested restore procedure, and a cost or control reason large enough to pay for backups, replication, failover, upgrades, and security work. Otherwise a managed service is the default: the premium is small next to the risk of losing data.

docs.title: 27. What are object, block, and file storage, and when do you use each?
docs.text: Object storage holds whole objects under keys in buckets over an HTTP API and scales without limit: uploads, media, backups. Block storage is a virtual disk attached to one server in one zone: root disks and self-hosted databases. File storage is a shared NFS or SMB filesystem mounted by many servers: legacy apps and shared datasets. On AWS, gp3 is $0.08 per GB-month and EFS Standard $0.30, against $0.023 for S3 Standard.

docs.title: 28. Walk through the S3 storage classes.
docs.text: Express One Zone ($0.11 per GB-month, single zone, single-digit milliseconds). Standard ($0.023). Intelligent-Tiering (moves objects between $0.023, $0.0125, and $0.004 tiers by access, plus monitoring). Standard-IA ($0.0125, 30-day and 128 KB minimums, $0.01 per GB read). One Zone-IA ($0.01, one zone). Glacier Instant Retrieval ($0.004, 90 days, $0.03 per GB read). Glacier Flexible Retrieval ($0.0036, restore in minutes to hours). Deep Archive ($0.00099, 180 days, restore within 12 or 48 hours).

docs.title: 29. How does S3 Intelligent-Tiering work, and when is it a bad choice?
docs.text: S3 monitors each object: after 30 days without access it moves to the Infrequent Access tier, after 90 days to Archive Instant Access, and optional archive tiers can be enabled for 90 and 180 days. A read moves it back with no retrieval fee. It costs $0.0025 per 1,000 objects monitored, and objects under 128 KB are not monitored and always pay the frequent rate, so it is poor for millions of tiny objects.

docs.title: 30. Why is the storage price a misleading way to compare object stores?
docs.text: Because egress and requests dominate download-heavy workloads. Storing 10 TB and serving 50 TB a month costs about $4,643 straight from S3 and $4,297 through CloudFront pay-as-you-go, but about $154 on Cloudflare R2, $274 on Backblaze B2 direct, and $436 on a CloudFront Business flat-rate plan if the terms fit. Storage is under $240 in every case.

docs.title: 31. What conditions apply to "free egress" on R2, B2, Wasabi, and Spaces?
docs.text: R2 has no egress charge at all. B2 is free up to three times your average stored data, then $0.01 per GB, and unlimited through partner CDNs. Wasabi has no egress fee but its policy says a use case whose monthly egress exceeds active storage is not a good fit, and service can be limited. DigitalOcean Spaces includes 1,024 GiB a month, then $0.01 per GiB.

docs.title: 32. How do presigned uploads work, and what does a POST policy add over a PUT URL?
docs.text: The API checks permissions, chooses the key, and signs a short-lived URL or form; the browser uploads straight to the bucket, so large files never touch the API servers. A presigned POST policy can enforce conditions such as content-length-range and an exact Content-Type; a presigned PUT cannot enforce a size range, so check the size afterwards. R2 supports presigned GET, HEAD, PUT, and DELETE but not HTML form POST.

docs.title: 33. Uploaded files disappear after every deploy. Why?
docs.text: They were written to the local disk of an instance or container, which is replaced on deploy or scale-in. Write uploads to object storage, store the key in the database, and treat servers as disposable; this is also what makes horizontal scaling possible.

docs.title: 34. Describe the stages of a video delivery pipeline.
docs.text: Upload the source (resumable), transcode it into an ABR ladder of renditions, package each rendition into short segments with HLS or DASH playlists, store segments in object storage, deliver them through a CDN, and play them in a player that switches renditions. Upload, transcode, and packaging run once per video; delivery and playback run on every view, which is why delivery dominates the bill.

docs.title: 35. What is adaptive bitrate streaming, and why must keyframes be aligned?
docs.text: The player picks a rendition per segment based on measured bandwidth, moving between, for example, 360p at 0.8 Mbps and 1080p at 5 Mbps. It can switch only at segment boundaries, so every rendition must start each segment with a keyframe at the same timestamp; otherwise switches glitch or stall.

docs.title: 36. What are HLS, DASH, and CMAF?
docs.text: HLS (RFC 8216) uses .m3u8 master and media playlists and plays natively on Apple devices. MPEG-DASH uses an XML .mpd manifest. CMAF is a common fragmented-MP4 segment format both can reference, so one set of segments can serve HLS and DASH players.

docs.title: 37. How do you estimate video delivery egress?
docs.text: GB = minutes watched x 60 x average Mbps / 8 / 1,000. At 3 Mbps, one minute is 22.5 MB, so 500,000 minutes watched is 11,250 GB: about $864 on CloudFront pay-as-you-go, $500 on Cloudflare Stream ($1 per 1,000 minutes), about $400 on Mux at the 1080p tier after 100,000 free minutes, and about $112 on bunny.net at $0.01 per GB.

docs.title: 38. When is per-minute delivery cheaper than per-GB delivery?
docs.text: Convert through the bitrate. CloudFront's first-tier $0.085 per GB costs bitrate x 7.5 MB x $0.085 per minute, which equals $0.001 per minute at about 1.6 Mbps. Above that average bitrate, per-minute platforms (Stream, Mux 1080p) beat CloudFront's list rate; low per-GB CDNs such as bunny.net stay cheaper across the range.

docs.title: 39. What is the difference between signed URLs, HLS AES-128 encryption, and DRM?
docs.text: Signed URLs or tokens stop link sharing but not a logged-in user saving the stream. AES-128 encrypts segments but hands the key to the client. DRM (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady) decrypts inside a protected module using a licence from a licence server; studios require it. Internal training video rarely needs more than signed URLs.

docs.title: 40. What is the difference between a backup and an archive?
docs.text: The Google SRE book puts it this way: backups can be loaded back into the application and must be recovered quickly, within the service's uptime needs; archives keep data for long periods for audit, discovery, and compliance, and their recovery time matters less. Backups belong in fast tiers, archives in the cheapest.

docs.title: 41. Compare S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval, Flexible Retrieval, and Deep Archive.
docs.text: Instant Retrieval: $0.004 per GB-month, 90-day minimum, millisecond reads at $0.03 per GB. Flexible Retrieval: $0.0036, 90 days, restore first: expedited 1-5 minutes, standard 3-5 hours, bulk 5-12 hours (free). Deep Archive: $0.00099, 180 days, standard within 12 hours ($0.02 per GB) or bulk within 48 hours ($0.0025 per GB).

docs.title: 42. What happens, and what do you pay, when you restore from Deep Archive?
docs.text: You call RestoreObject with a tier and a number of days; S3 creates a temporary copy, billed at the S3 Standard rate on top of the archived object, and you copy it somewhere permanent before it expires. You pay the per-GB retrieval fee and per-request restore fee. Large restores are limited to about 1,000 restore requests per second and 1-2 PB a day per account.

docs.title: 43. How does Azure's Archive tier differ from Cool and Cold?
docs.text: Cool and Cold are online, with millisecond reads and 30- and 90-day minimums. Archive ($0.00099 per GB-month, 180 days) is offline: a blob must be rehydrated, which can take up to 15 hours at standard priority. Microsoft documents a limit of 10 GiB per storage account per hour for high-priority rehydration and warns that bulk timelines do not scale linearly, so a multi-terabyte emergency restore takes days.

docs.title: 44. Why is Google Cloud's Archive class unusual?
docs.text: Every Cloud Storage class is online, so Archive returns data in milliseconds with a normal read. The trade-offs are a 365-day minimum and a $0.05 per GiB retrieval fee: keeping 5 TB a year costs about $74, but one full restore adds about $256.

docs.title: 45. A backup job overwrites latest.tar.gz every night in Glacier Instant Retrieval. What does it cost?
docs.text: Each overwrite ends the previous version before its 90-day minimum, so every replaced version is billed for the remainder of 90 days: the job pays about 90 days of storage for every nightly copy. Write each backup under a new key and expire by age, or keep short-lived copies in a tier without minimums.

docs.title: 46. Explain S3 Object Lock governance and compliance modes, and how R2's bucket locks compare.
docs.text: Both block deletes and overwrites of locked versions for a retention period. Governance mode can be bypassed by users granted a special permission; compliance mode cannot be bypassed by anyone, including the root user, and the retention cannot be shortened. Legal holds have no expiry. R2 bucket locks block deletion too, but anyone allowed to edit the bucket configuration can remove the rule, so they are weaker.

docs.title: 47. How do you read a cloud bill to find what changed?
docs.text: Group by usage type, not only by service ("EC2-Other" hides NAT, EBS, transfer, and IPv4), and by day to find the step change. Know the views: unblended cost is what each hour was charged; amortized spreads commitment payments over their term and is the right basis for unit costs. Export the raw data (Cost and Usage Report 2.0 or FOCUS) for SQL analysis.

docs.title: 48. How do you attribute cloud costs to teams and services?
docs.text: Accounts or projects per environment and team are the strongest boundary. Tags add detail, but on AWS they must be activated as cost allocation tags and enforced (provider default_tags, tag policies), because hand-made resources are rarely tagged. Shared costs need an agreed allocation rule. Start with showback (reporting); chargeback bills the team's budget.

docs.title: 49. Does a budget stop spending? What does anomaly detection add?
docs.text: A budget alerts on actual or forecast spend; it only stops anything if you attach an action (on AWS, applying an IAM or SCP policy or stopping specific EC2 and RDS instances). Anomaly detection learns each service's normal spend and alerts on unusual jumps, catching a $40-a-day leak weeks before a monthly threshold would.

docs.title: 50. How do you decide how much to commit to Savings Plans?
docs.text: Commit to the floor of steady usage after cleanup and rightsizing, not to the peak. For m7g.large ($0.0816 on demand), a 1-year Compute Savings Plan at $0.0599 breaks even at 73% utilization (about 536 of 730 hours) and a 3-year plan at $0.0414 at 51%. Prefer Compute Savings Plans when the architecture may change (they also cover Fargate and Lambda), and ladder purchases over time.

docs.title: 51. Which workloads suit Spot capacity, and how much notice do you get?
docs.text: Stateless queue workers, CI runners, batch and data jobs, and extra nodes for stateless pods. Not databases or a single instance serving traffic. AWS gives a two-minute interruption notice, Azure 30 seconds through Scheduled Events, and Google Cloud a configurable 120 seconds (none by default) plus up to 30 seconds of shutdown. Diversify instance types and zones and checkpoint long work.

docs.title: 52. What are the alternatives to sending everything through a NAT gateway?
docs.text: S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints carry that traffic at no charge (1 TB a month through NAT costs $46.08 in processing). Interface endpoints for services such as ECR and CloudWatch Logs cost $0.01 an hour per zone plus $0.01 per GB, cheaper than NAT above roughly 420 GB a month per service in two zones. IPv6 egress-only internet gateways have no gateway charge. NAT instances and public subnets save more but add operations or exposure.

docs.title: 53. How do you cut log costs without losing what you need?
docs.text: Log errors always, sample successful requests, never log health checks at full volume, set retention on every log group (CloudWatch keeps logs forever by default), use a cheaper log class for rarely queried logs ($0.25 instead of $0.50 per GB ingested on CloudWatch), archive what compliance requires to object storage, and use metrics for counts and latencies.

docs.title: 54. What is unit economics in cloud cost, and what is FinOps?
docs.text: Unit cost divides cost by a business driver: TaskFlow's $1,216.94 a month over 30 million requests is $0.0406 per 1,000 requests, or $3.04 per paying team. FinOps is the practice of shared ownership of cloud cost across engineering, finance, and the business, cycling through Inform (allocate and report), Optimize (rightsize, commit, re-architect), and Operate (budgets, policies, reviews).

docs.title: 55. A two-person startup is launching TaskFlow (React SPA, Express API, MongoDB) and has a plan for EKS with a self-hosted database. The estimate is already over budget. What would you choose instead, and why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the hard constraints (WebSockets, long jobs, compliance contracts), expected traffic, and who will be on call.

How to confirm: price each tier with real units: a static host for the SPA, Cloud Run or a PaaS for the API at expected requests, and Atlas Flex or M10 for MongoDB; compare with EKS's control-plane fee, nodes, and database operations time.

Likely causes and fixes: over-engineering for the stage. Put the SPA on Cloudflare or a CloudFront flat-rate plan, the API on Cloud Run, Render, or Railway (or ECS Express Mode inside AWS), and the data on MongoDB Atlas; revisit when the bill or a constraint demands it. See choosing where to run software.

docs.title: 56. TaskFlow API runs on Lambda. After quiet periods p99 latency spikes, and during a marketing spike the database starts refusing connections. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: Init Duration in Lambda REPORT lines on slow requests, function concurrency, and the database's connection count.

How to confirm: slow requests coincide with new environments, and the connection count hits max_connections as concurrency climbs.

Likely causes and fixes: cold starts plus one pool per execution environment. Trim dependencies and initialize lazily, add Provisioned Concurrency for the baseline, cap reserved concurrency, shrink pools to one or two connections, and put RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, or the provider's pooler in front. See running backend servers and APIs.

docs.title: 57. After moving ECS tasks into private subnets, the AWS bill doubled while traffic stayed flat. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: Cost Explorer grouped by usage type for NatGateway-Hours, NatGateway-Bytes, and PublicIPv4:InUseAddress.

How to confirm: VPC flow logs show most NAT traffic going to S3, ECR, and CloudWatch address ranges.

Likely causes and fixes: a NAT gateway per zone processing AWS-service traffic at $0.045 per GB. Add S3 and DynamoDB gateway endpoints (no charge), interface endpoints for ECR and logs where volume justifies them, and decide deliberately between one NAT gateway per zone and one shared gateway. See cost optimization and cloud bills.

docs.title: 58. Product wants training videos in TaskFlow: about 11,000 minutes stored and 500,000 minutes watched a month. The team has no video experience. Which option would you choose, and why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the videos are private, whether live is needed, the expected average bitrate, and whether files must stay in your own account.

How to confirm: price the scenario: DIY S3 + MediaConvert + CloudFront about $931 a month at list prices (or about $82 with a CloudFront Pro flat-rate plan, if its terms fit), Cloudflare Stream about $555, Mux about $413 after its credit, Bunny Stream about $121.

Likely causes and fixes: without video expertise, building the pipeline is the expensive part. Choose a managed platform: Mux for the best API and analytics, Cloudflare Stream for the simplest bill, or Bunny Stream for the lowest delivery price; keep the original uploads in your own storage so you can leave. See video storage and streaming.

docs.title: 59. A healthcare customer will upload patient documents to TaskFlow. Which hosting and storage would you choose?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the customer requires a HIPAA BAA, data residency, retention rules, and audit requirements.

How to confirm: check each service you plan to use on the provider's official HIPAA eligible services list and confirm the BAA covers it.

Likely causes and fixes: a provider without a BAA for the product cannot hold PHI. Use a hyperscaler under its BAA (for example S3 with encryption, Object Lock for records, and a separate account), keep PHI out of static files and URLs, and use smaller providers only where their official page offers a BAA for that product. See object and file storage and choosing where to run software.

docs.title: 60. Users download 50 TB a month of exported files from S3, and egress is now about $4,400 of the bill. What would you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether downloads go straight to S3 or through a CDN, the cache hit ratio, and file sizes.

How to confirm: Cost Explorer shows DataTransfer-Out-Bytes as the top usage type; access logs show repeated downloads of the same files.

Likely causes and fixes: per-GB egress at list price. A CDN alone on pay-as-you-go rates only gets to about $4,297. Real fixes are a different delivery model: Cloudflare R2 (about $154 including storage), B2 with a partner CDN, or a CloudFront flat-rate plan if its terms fit. Compress files and use signed, short-lived download URLs. See object and file storage.

docs.title: 61. The business needs a 4-hour RTO and 7-year retention for TaskFlow's database backups. Design the storage tiers.
docs.text:
What to check first: backup size and growth, how often restores happen, and whether restores may need to leave the provider.

How to confirm: time a real restore from each candidate tier, including bulk limits, and price one full restore per year.

Likely causes and fixes: one tier cannot meet both goals. Keep the last 30 days in a millisecond tier (S3 Standard or Glacier Instant Retrieval, Azure Cool, Nearline, or B2) for the 4-hour RTO; transition older copies to Deep Archive or Azure Archive with object lock for the 7-year retention; keep a copy in a separate account. See backup and archive storage.

docs.title: 62. During an outage, a restore from S3 Glacier Deep Archive has been "in progress" for a day. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Restore header on the objects and the retrieval tier used in the restore requests.

How to confirm: ongoing-request="true" long after the start, with the Bulk tier (within 48 hours) and thousands of objects.

Likely causes and fixes: the only usable copy was archived, and Bulk was chosen. Standard restores finish within 12 hours; there is no expedited tier for Deep Archive. Keep recent backups in a millisecond tier, document per-tier restore times in the runbook, and rehearse an archive restore. See backup and archive storage.

docs.title: 63. To save money, the team moved an uploads bucket to S3 Standard-IA, and the bill went up. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: usage types TimedStorage-SIA-SmObjects, EarlyDelete-SIA, and Retrieval-SIA after the change.

How to confirm: object size and age distribution (S3 Storage Lens or Storage Class Analysis) shows many objects under 128 KB, deleted within 30 days, or read often.

Likely causes and fixes: minimum billable size, minimum duration, and retrieval fees. Use Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access patterns, filter transitions by size and age, and keep small or hot objects in Standard. See object and file storage.

docs.title: 64. TaskFlow API on Lambda now handles a steady 60 million requests a month. Should it move to containers?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether traffic is steady, average duration and memory, whether API Gateway is in the path, and the team's capacity to run containers.

How to confirm: at about $1.20 per million requests Lambda costs about $72 a month (about $132 with an API Gateway HTTP API at $1.00 per million); two Fargate tasks with an ALB cost $58.31 if a load test shows they can carry the peak.

Likely causes and fixes: past the crossover (about 48.6 million requests against Fargate), always-on capacity is cheaper, and a Compute Savings Plan cuts it further. The saving is modest at this volume, so move when it also simplifies WebSockets, connections, or latency, not for the money alone. See running backend servers and APIs.

docs.title: 65. A static marketing site on a developer platform went offline at the end of a launch month, or showed an overage bill of several thousand dollars. Which hosting would you choose instead?
docs.text:
What to check first: the platform's plan limits and the month's transfer and requests.

How to confirm: the dashboard shows the project paused for usage limits, or the invoice shows per-GB transfer overages multiplied by tens of terabytes.

Likely causes and fixes: hard limits on free plans and per-GB markups at scale. For a static site, use Cloudflare Workers static assets (requests to static assets are free and unlimited) or a CloudFront flat-rate plan; on paid platforms set spend alerts and limits before launches. See hosting websites and frontends.

docs.title: 66. Six months after buying an EC2 Instance Savings Plan, its utilization dropped to 60%. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Savings Plans utilization report and recent architecture changes.

How to confirm: usage of the committed instance family fell when services moved to Fargate, another family, or another region.

Likely causes and fixes: a commitment tied to an instance family and region. Nothing refunds it: move matching usage back where it makes sense, buy Compute Savings Plans next time, commit only to the floor, and ladder purchases. See cost optimization and cloud bills.

docs.title: 67. A bucket on Wasabi that serves public downloads received a notice about its usage. What is going on?
docs.text:
What to check first: monthly egress compared with active storage.

How to confirm: egress is several times the stored data (for example 5 TB stored, 20 TB downloaded).

Likely causes and fixes: Wasabi's free egress policy assumes egress at or below active storage. Put a CDN in front so most reads are served from cache, or move public downloads to a store priced for egress (R2, B2 with partner CDNs) and keep Wasabi for backups. See object and file storage.

docs.title: 68. The CEO read about companies leaving the cloud and asks whether TaskFlow should buy servers. How do you answer?
docs.text:
What to check first: the size, steadiness, and composition of the bill, unit costs, and the team's ability to run hardware.

How to confirm: model owned or rented hardware including refresh cycles, data center contracts, staff time, and on-call against the current bill after cleanup and commitments.

Likely causes and fixes: cloud exits pay off for large, steady, storage- or bandwidth-heavy workloads with strong infrastructure teams (37signals projected about $7 million over five years from a $3.2 million yearly bill). At TaskFlow's roughly $1,200 a month, cleanup and commitments save more with less risk; Netflix stayed in the cloud for reliability and elasticity. Revisit with budget providers for steady parts as the bill grows. See cost optimization and cloud bills.

docs.text:
