docs.title: Managed Databases
docs.text:
A managed database is a database server that a provider installs, patches, backs up, replicates, and fails over for you, while you keep the schema, the queries, and the bill. This lesson explains the main options and how each works underneath: Amazon RDS, Amazon Aurora (including Aurora Serverless v2), Amazon DynamoDB, MongoDB Atlas, Supabase, Neon, Google Firestore, Azure Cosmos DB, Google Cloud SQL, managed Redis and Valkey (ElastiCache, Upstash, Redis Cloud), and self-hosting on a virtual machine. It shows how each one bills, which workloads fit which, and what a small and a medium TaskFlow deployment costs on each.

Data modeling, indexes, and query tuning are covered in the Databases section and in database scaling; backups and restores in depth are in the backups subject.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The database is the part of the system that is hardest to move and most expensive to lose. Running it yourself means owning replication, failover, backups, point-in-time recovery, minor-version patching, disk growth, and the 3 a.m. page when a disk fills. A managed service turns most of that into configuration, and the price premium over a raw VM is usually smaller than one engineer's time.

The choice of service also fixes the billing model: per instance-hour, per unit of serverless capacity, or per read and write. The same TaskFlow workload can cost under a dollar a month on one service and more than fifty on another, and the ranking flips as traffic grows. Picking the data model (relational, document, key-value) usually decides the shortlist before price does.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Figma (Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL). In How Figma's databases team lived to tell the scale, Figma explains that its database stack, running on Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL, "has grown almost 100x since 2020". It first split related tables into separate databases (vertical partitioning), then built horizontal sharding on top of RDS Postgres. It evaluated CockroachDB, TiDB, Spanner, and Vitess, but stayed because switching would have required "a complex data migration" and its team's RDS Postgres expertise was the lower-risk path.
  • Notion (sharded PostgreSQL). In Herding elephants: lessons learned from sharding Postgres at Notion (October 2021), Notion describes outgrowing a single PostgreSQL primary when "the Postgres VACUUM process began to stall consistently", and moving to 480 logical shards spread across 32 physical databases.
  • Discord (a self-operated database). In How Discord stores trillions of messages (March 2023), Discord describes moving its messages database from a 177-node Cassandra cluster to 72 ScyllaDB nodes, because of unpredictable latency, garbage-collection pauses, and on-call toil. The post describes Discord's own engineers provisioning the clusters and carrying the on-call load: the control, and the work, that running a database yourself brings at that scale.
  • Amazon Prime Day (DynamoDB). AWS reports in AWS services scale to new heights for Prime Day 2025 that DynamoDB peaked at 151 million requests per second with single-digit millisecond responses, which shows what a per-request, partitioned key-value design can absorb without capacity planning by the application team.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon RDS, Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon ElastiCache, MongoDB Atlas, Supabase, Neon, Google Cloud SQL, Firestore, Azure Cosmos DB, Azure Database for PostgreSQL, Upstash, Redis Cloud, and PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Valkey run on your own VMs.

docs.title: What "managed" covers, and what it does not
docs.text:
Task Self-hosted on a VM Managed service Install, OS and engine patching You Provider (minor versions in a maintenance window) Automated backups and point-in-time recovery You script and test them Provider; you choose retention and test restores High availability and failover You build replication and failover A setting (Multi-AZ, HA, replica set) Read replicas You set up and monitor A button or API call Storage growth You resize disks Automatic or a setting Monitoring You install it Built-in metrics; you set alerts Schema, indexes, queries You You Connection limits and pooling You You Capacity choice and cost You You Access control and network exposure You You

A slow query, a missing index, or a connection storm is still your problem on every managed service.

docs.title: High availability and recovery on a managed service
docs.text:
• Synchronous standby (Multi-AZ, HA): every commit is written in two zones before it is acknowledged; on failure the provider promotes the standby and moves the endpoint. You pay for two instances.
  • Read replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling; they can lag, so read-your-own-writes needs care.
  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR): snapshots plus continuously archived transaction logs let the provider restore a new instance to any second in the retention window, for example just before a bad migration.

docs.title: Amazon RDS
docs.text:
What it is: AWS's managed relational database for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server, and Db2. Each database is an instance with EBS storage; RDS automates backups, patching, Multi-AZ failover, and read replicas.

You manage: instance class, storage, parameter groups, schema, queries, and connections. Billing: instance-hours (Multi-AZ doubles the instance and storage price), storage per GB-month, backup storage beyond the free allocation at $0.095 per GB-month, and data transfer. In us-east-1, PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro costs $0.016 per hour, db.t4g.small $0.032 ($0.065 Multi-AZ), db.m7g.large $0.168 ($0.337 Multi-AZ), and gp3 storage $0.115 per GB-month ($0.23 Multi-AZ) (RDS for PostgreSQL pricing).

docs.title: Amazon Aurora and Aurora Serverless v2
docs.text:
What it is: AWS's MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible engine that replaces the storage layer with a distributed, self-healing volume replicated across three Availability Zones, so replicas share storage and failover does not copy data. Aurora Serverless v2 sizes compute continuously in Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs, about 2 GiB of memory each with matching CPU) between a minimum and a maximum you set; since November 2024 the minimum can be 0 ACUs, which pauses the database after inactivity and resumes it on the next connection (with a delay).

Billing (Aurora pricing): Serverless v2 at $0.12 per ACU-hour for Aurora PostgreSQL; Aurora Standard storage at $0.10 per GB-month plus $0.20 per million I/O requests. The I/O-Optimized configuration removes I/O charges in exchange for higher compute (about a third more on Serverless v2: $0.16 instead of $0.12 per ACU-hour) and $0.225 per GB-month storage, which pays off for I/O-heavy workloads.

docs.title: Amazon DynamoDB
docs.text:
What it is: a serverless key-value and document database. Items are spread across partitions by their partition key; you query by key (and by secondary indexes), not with joins. It is multi-AZ by design and scales without instance sizing.

You manage: the table design, which must match your access patterns up front, and capacity mode. Billing (DynamoDB pricing): on-demand at $0.625 per million write request units and $0.125 per million read request units (one read unit is a strongly consistent read of up to 4 KB; one write unit is a write of up to 1 KB), or provisioned capacity per hour; storage at $0.25 per GB-month after the first 25 GB; continuous backups (PITR) at $0.20 per GB-month.

docs.title: MongoDB Atlas
docs.text:
What it is: MongoDB's own managed service, running replica sets on AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud in the region you choose. It is the natural home for TaskFlow, which already uses MongoDB.

Tiers (pricing): Free (512 MB, shared), Flex ($0.011 per hour, capped at $30 a month, 5 GB, for development and testing), and Dedicated clusters from M10 ($0.08 per hour, "starts at $56.94/month", 2 GB RAM, 2 vCPUs) through M20 ($0.20 per hour) and M30 ($0.54 per hour, 8 GB RAM). The older shared M2 and M5 tiers and serverless instances have been retired in favor of Flex (Flex migration). For self-service accounts, a HIPAA Business Associate Agreement is included in MongoDB's cloud terms.

docs.title: Supabase
docs.text:
What it is: a platform built around a dedicated PostgreSQL database per project, adding authentication, file storage, realtime subscriptions, edge functions, and auto-generated REST and GraphQL APIs.

Billing (pricing): Free (500 MB database, shared CPU, 5 GB egress; projects are paused after a week of inactivity), Pro at $25 a month including $10 of compute credit (enough for one Micro instance with 1 GB RAM), 8 GB disk then $0.125 per GB, 250 GB egress then $0.09 per GB. Compute sizes run from Small ($15) to Large ($110, 2 dedicated vCPUs, 8 GB) and beyond. Team ($599 a month) adds SOC 2 reports and HIPAA as a paid add-on.

docs.title: Neon
docs.text:
What it is: serverless PostgreSQL that separates storage from compute. Compute autoscales and scales to zero after 5 minutes idle, and copy-on-write branches give each pull request its own database copy in seconds. Its pricing page now calls the database Lakebase Postgres.

Billing (pricing): Free (100 CU-hours per project per month, 1 GB storage), Launch at $0.106 per CU-hour and $0.35 per GB-month of storage, and Scale at $0.222 per CU-hour with SLAs and HIPAA. One CU is about 4 GB of RAM with matching CPU, and computes can be as small as 0.25 CU.

docs.title: Google Firestore
docs.text:
What it is: a serverless document database from Google (the database behind many Firebase apps) with realtime listeners and offline sync for mobile and web clients.

Billing (Firestore pricing, Standard edition, single region): $0.03 per 100,000 document reads, $0.09 per 100,000 writes, $0.01 per 100,000 deletes, and about $0.15 per GiB-month stored (listed as $0.000205479 per GiB-hour). The free quota is 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes, and 20,000 deletes per day and 1 GiB stored.

docs.title: Azure Cosmos DB
docs.text:
What it is: Microsoft's globally distributed, multi-API database (including a NoSQL API and a MongoDB-compatible API), with tunable consistency and multi-region writes. Every operation costs Request Units (RUs): a point read of a 1 KB item is about 1 RU, and writes and queries cost more.

Billing (Cosmos DB pricing and the Azure retail price list, East US): provisioned throughput at $0.008 per hour per 100 RU/s, serverless at $0.25 per million RUs, and storage at $0.25 per GB-month. The free tier gives the first 1,000 RU/s and 25 GB of an account free for its lifetime.

docs.title: Google Cloud SQL
docs.text: What it is: Google's managed MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQL Server, much like RDS. Billing (Cloud SQL pricing, Enterprise edition, us-central1): $0.0413 per vCPU-hour and $0.007 per GiB-hour of memory, doubled for HA ($0.0826 and $0.014); SSD storage $0.000232877 per GiB-hour (about $0.17 per GiB-month). The shared-core db-f1-micro costs $0.0105 per hour but is not covered by the Cloud SQL SLA.

docs.title: Managed Redis and Valkey
docs.text:
What it is: in-memory key-value stores for caches, sessions, rate limits, and queues (see Redis). Valkey is the open-source fork of Redis that AWS and others now offer.

  • Amazon ElastiCache: nodes (Valkey cache.t4g.micro at $0.0128 per hour versus $0.016 for Redis OSS) or ElastiCache Serverless (Valkey $0.084 per GB-hour of data plus $0.0023 per million ElastiCache Processing Units, with a 100 MB minimum versus 1 GB for Redis OSS); Valkey is 20% cheaper on nodes and 33% cheaper on serverless (ElastiCache pricing).
  • Upstash: serverless, Redis-compatible, billed per command: free up to 500,000 commands a month and 250 MB of data, then $0.20 per 100,000 commands, or fixed plans from $10 a month (pricing). It works over HTTP as well as TCP, which suits functions and edge runtimes.
  • Redis Cloud: Redis's own service: Free (30 MB), Essentials from $0.007 per hour ($5 a month), and Pro from $0.014 per hour with a $200 monthly minimum (pricing).

docs.title: Self-hosting on a VM
docs.text: What it is: installing PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Valkey on your own VMs. It is the cheapest in dollars (a $12 VM runs a small PostgreSQL comfortably) and gives full control of versions and extensions, but you own backups, restore tests, replication, failover, upgrades, disk monitoring, and security. It makes sense with real database skills on the team, or at a scale where the managed premium is large, as in Discord's case.

docs.title: How each one bills
docs.text:
Billing model Examples You pay for Best for Watch out for Provisioned instance RDS, Cloud SQL, Atlas Dedicated, Supabase compute Instance-hours, doubled for HA Steady load, predictable bills Paying for the peak all night Serverless capacity Aurora Serverless v2, Neon Capacity units per second or hour, with a floor or scale to zero Variable load, dev and preview databases Resume delay from zero; cost at sustained high load Per request DynamoDB on-demand, Firestore, Cosmos DB serverless Each read and write, plus storage Spiky or low traffic, key-based access Scans and fan-out reads multiply cost Per command Upstash Each command, plus storage Caches used by functions Busy caches cost more than a node

Every model adds the same side meters: storage per GB-month, backups beyond the free allowance, data transfer out of the region or across zones, and a second copy for high availability.

docs.title: What TaskFlow costs on each
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices are US-region list prices in USD (AWS us-east-1, Google Cloud us-central1, Azure East US) from the linked official pages and price lists in November 2026. They change often; re-check them with the AWS, Google Cloud, or Azure pricing calculator, or the vendor's pricing page, before deciding. Other regions such as India are priced differently: choose the region in the calculator to compare.

Small app (launch stage): 2 GB of data, 2 million reads and 500,000 writes a month, items around 1 KB, busy about 8 hours a day.

RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.micro, Single-AZ:  730 h x $0.016 = $11.68 + 20 GB x $0.115 = $2.30  -> $13.98
RDS PostgreSQL db.t4g.small, Multi-AZ:   730 h x $0.065 = $47.45 + 20 GB x $0.23  = $4.60  -> $52.05
Aurora Serverless v2, 0.5 ACU minimum:   730 h x 0.5 x $0.12 = $43.80 + storage $0.20 + 5M I/O $1.00 -> $45.00
  with scale to zero (busy 1/3 of time): 243 h x 0.5 x $0.12 = $14.60 + $1.20       -> about $15.80
DynamoDB on-demand:  2M x $0.125/M = $0.25 + 0.5M x $0.625/M = $0.31, 2 GB free    -> $0.56
Firestore:  reads (2M - 1.5M free) x $0.03/100k = $0.15; writes inside free quota;
            storage (2 - 1 free) GiB x $0.15 = $0.15                                -> $0.30
Cosmos DB serverless (assume 1 RU per read, 6 RU per write):
            (2M + 3M) RU x $0.25/M = $1.25 + 2 GB x $0.25 = $0.50                  -> $1.75
Neon Launch, 0.25 CU busy 8 h/day:  0.25 x 243 h = 60.8 CU-h x $0.106 = $6.45 + 2 GB x $0.35 = $0.70 -> $7.15
Cloud SQL db-f1-micro:  730 h x $0.0105 = $7.67 + 10 GiB SSD x $0.17 = $1.70 (no SLA) -> $9.37
Option (small app) Monthly Notes DynamoDB on-demand $0.56 Only if access patterns are key-based; add $0.40 for PITR Firestore $0.30 Mostly inside the free quota Cosmos DB serverless $1.75 $0 on the free tier with provisioned throughput Neon Launch $7.15 Scales to zero; Free plan if under 1 GB Cloud SQL db-f1-micro $9.37 Shared core, no SLA Self-hosted on a $12 VM about $12 Plus backups, patching, and your time RDS db.t4g.micro $13.98 Single-AZ: no automatic failover Aurora Serverless v2 $15.80 to $45.00 Depends on scale to zero Supabase Pro $25 Includes auth, storage, and a Micro instance MongoDB Atlas Flex up to $30 No code change for TaskFlow; Free tier is 512 MB RDS db.t4g.small Multi-AZ $52.05 Automatic failover MongoDB Atlas M10 $56.94 Dedicated, replica set, backups

Medium app (growing): 50 GB of data, 200 million reads and 40 million writes a month (about 77 reads and 15 writes per second on average), high availability required.

RDS PostgreSQL db.m7g.large Multi-AZ: 730 h x $0.337 = $246.01 + 100 GB x $0.23 = $23.00 -> $269.01
Aurora Serverless v2, average 4 ACU:  4 x 730 h x $0.12 = $350.40 + 50 GB x $0.10 = $5.00
                                      + 300M I/O x $0.20/M = $60.00                       -> $415.40
DynamoDB on-demand:  200M x $0.125/M = $25.00 + 40M x $0.625/M = $25.00
                     + (50 - 25) GB x $0.25 = $6.25 + PITR 50 GB x $0.20 = $10.00        -> $66.25
Firestore:  200M / 100k x $0.03 = $60.00 + 40M / 100k x $0.09 = $36.00 + 50 GiB x $0.15 = $7.50 -> $103.50
Cosmos DB serverless:  (200M + 40M x 6) RU = 440M x $0.25/M = $110.00 + 50 GB x $0.25 = $12.50 -> $122.50
MongoDB Atlas M30 (8 GB RAM):  730 h x $0.54                                             -> $394.20
Supabase Pro + Large compute:  $25 + $110 - $10 credit + (50 - 8) GB x $0.125 = $5.25    -> $130.25
Neon Launch, 2 CU always on:  2 x 730 x $0.106 = $154.76 + 50 GB x $0.35 = $17.50        -> $172.26
Cloud SQL HA, 2 vCPU + 8 GiB: (2 x $0.0826 + 8 x $0.014) x 730 = $202.36 + 100 GiB HA SSD $34.00 -> $236.36
Self-hosted: 2 x EC2 m7g.large ($0.0816/h) = $119.14 + 2 x 100 GB gp3 = $16.00           -> $135.14 + people

The medium numbers show the trade-off clearly. Per-request databases are cheapest when every operation is a key lookup on a small item, but a query that reads 100 items costs 100 reads, and a global secondary index doubles write cost; a relational instance costs the same whether a query touches one row or a thousand. Neon and Supabase undercut RDS on list price at this size, but the RDS and Atlas figures include a standby or replica set for automatic failover, so check what high availability adds on the cheaper options before comparing. Aurora's I/O line suggests the I/O-Optimized configuration at this scale. Price the queries you actually run, not an average operation.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a managed database by default: the cost premium is small compared with the risk of losing data or the time spent on failover and backups. Choose the data model first (relational for joins, constraints, and reporting; document for flexible nested records; key-value for predictable key lookups at large or spiky scale), then the billing model that matches your traffic. Self-host only with database expertise on the team, a tested restore, and a cost or control reason that outweighs the operations work.

Do not use a cache as the only copy of data, a per-request database for analytics scans, or a serverless database that scales to zero for a user-facing API that cannot tolerate the resume delay.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Situation Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio MongoDB Atlas Free (TaskFlow), Neon Free, or Supabase Free Firestore within its free quota Free, managed, and enough for small data; watch Supabase's pause after inactivity Early startup Managed PostgreSQL (Neon, Supabase, RDS) or Atlas Flex then M10 for MongoDB apps Aurora Serverless v2 with a low minimum Standard engines keep options open; pay little until traffic arrives Steady high traffic RDS or Cloud SQL with HA on committed pricing, or Atlas dedicated clusters Aurora provisioned; self-hosted with a strong DBA team Instance pricing is cheapest at constant load; commitments cut it further Spiky traffic DynamoDB on-demand, Aurora Serverless v2, or Neon Firestore or Cosmos DB serverless Capacity follows load without paying for the peak all month Global audience DynamoDB global tables, Cosmos DB multi-region, or Atlas global clusters Regional primary with read replicas near users Writes need a home or a conflict strategy; replicate reads first Compliance-heavy (healthcare) RDS, Aurora, or DynamoDB under the AWS BAA; Cloud SQL or Firestore under Google's; Cosmos DB under Microsoft's (check its in-scope list) MongoDB Atlas (BAA in its terms), Neon Scale, or Supabase Team with the HIPAA add-on Encryption, audit logs, PITR, and a contract; check each product is in the provider's eligible list Large data or heavy egress A database in the same region as the app, with read replicas Self-hosted on VMs with large included transfer Cross-region and internet egress from a database add up quickly Team with no ops people Atlas, Supabase, Neon, or RDS with Multi-AZ Firestore or DynamoDB for simple models Backups, failover, and patching are handled; avoid self-hosting

docs.title: PostgreSQL on RDS with Multi-AZ (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/db/rds.tf: PostgreSQL for TaskFlow with failover, backups, and encryption
variable "private_subnet_ids" {
  type = list(string)
}

variable "db_security_group_id" {
  type = string
}

resource "aws_db_subnet_group" "taskflow" {
  name       = "taskflow-db"
  subnet_ids = var.private_subnet_ids # private subnets in at least two AZs
}

resource "aws_db_instance" "taskflow" {
  identifier     = "taskflow-prod"
  engine         = "postgres"
  engine_version = "17"
  instance_class = "db.t4g.small"

  allocated_storage     = 20
  max_allocated_storage = 200 # storage autoscaling ceiling
  storage_type          = "gp3"
  storage_encrypted     = true

  db_name                     = "taskflow"
  username                    = "taskflow_admin"
  manage_master_user_password = true # password generated and kept in Secrets Manager

  multi_az               = true # synchronous standby in a second AZ
  db_subnet_group_name   = aws_db_subnet_group.taskflow.name
  vpc_security_group_ids = [var.db_security_group_id]
  publicly_accessible    = false

  backup_retention_period    = 14 # days of point-in-time recovery
  backup_window              = "03:00-04:00"
  maintenance_window         = "sun:04:30-sun:05:30"
  auto_minor_version_upgrade = true

  deletion_protection       = true
  skip_final_snapshot       = false
  final_snapshot_identifier = "taskflow-prod-final"
}
  • multi_az = true doubles the instance and storage price and buys automatic failover; backup_retention_period sets how far back PITR can restore.
  • manage_master_user_password keeps the admin password out of Terraform state and code.
  • deletion_protection and a final snapshot stop one mistaken terraform destroy from deleting production data.

docs.title: Aurora Serverless v2 that pauses when idle (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/db/aurora.tf: Aurora PostgreSQL Serverless v2 for a preview environment
resource "aws_rds_cluster" "preview" {
  cluster_identifier          = "taskflow-preview"
  engine                      = "aurora-postgresql"
  engine_mode                 = "provisioned" # Serverless v2 uses provisioned mode
  database_name               = "taskflow"
  master_username             = "taskflow_admin"
  manage_master_user_password = true
  storage_encrypted           = true
  skip_final_snapshot         = true # preview data only
  db_subnet_group_name        = aws_db_subnet_group.taskflow.name # from rds.tf
  vpc_security_group_ids      = [var.db_security_group_id]

  serverlessv2_scaling_configuration {
    min_capacity             = 0   # pause when idle
    max_capacity             = 4   # about 8 GiB of memory at most
    seconds_until_auto_pause = 600 # pause after 10 idle minutes
  }
}

resource "aws_rds_cluster_instance" "preview" {
  identifier         = "taskflow-preview-1"
  cluster_identifier = aws_rds_cluster.preview.id
  engine             = aws_rds_cluster.preview.engine
  instance_class     = "db.serverless"
}

A preview or staging database used a few hours a day costs a fraction of an always-on instance. Scaling to 0 ACUs needs a recent Aurora engine version, so check the Aurora documentation for the supported versions. The first connection after a pause waits for the database to resume, so keep min_capacity above zero for anything users hit directly.

docs.title: DynamoDB on-demand with PITR and TTL (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/db/dynamodb.tf: per-request table for TaskFlow activity events
resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "activity" {
  name         = "taskflow-activity"
  billing_mode = "PAY_PER_REQUEST" # on-demand: pay per read and write
  hash_key     = "taskId"
  range_key    = "createdAt"

  attribute {
    name = "taskId"
    type = "S"
  }

  attribute {
    name = "createdAt"
    type = "S"
  }

  point_in_time_recovery {
    enabled = true # $0.20 per GB-month in us-east-1
  }

  ttl {
    attribute_name = "expiresAt" # items expire automatically; TTL deletes are free
    enabled        = true
  }
}

The key design (taskId plus createdAt) serves exactly one query well: "the activity for this task, newest first". A different question, such as "all activity by this user", needs a secondary index, which adds write cost. That is the DynamoDB trade-off in one table.

docs.title: Sizing connection pools against the database limit
docs.text:
Connection limits are where managed databases most often surprise teams. Every API instance holds a pool, and every function environment holds its own:

// src/db.js: one pool per process, sized for the database's limit
import pg from "pg";

// Budget: database max_connections minus a reserve for admin and replicas,
// divided by the maximum number of API processes that can run at once.
// Example: (100 - 10) / 6 processes = 15 connections each.
export const pool = new pg.Pool({
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  max: Number(process.env.PG_POOL_MAX ?? 15),
  idleTimeoutMillis: 30_000,
  connectionTimeoutMillis: 5_000, // fail fast instead of queueing forever
  ssl: { rejectUnauthorized: true, ca: process.env.PG_CA_CERT },
});

export async function getTask(id) {
  const { rows } = await pool.query("SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = $1", [id]);
  return rows[0] ?? null;
}

Check the real limit with SHOW max_connections; on PostgreSQL (or the tier's documented limit on Atlas), count the maximum number of processes your autoscaling allows, and put a pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, or the provider's built-in pooler such as Supabase's or Neon's) in front when functions or many small instances connect.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pick the data model and the access patterns before the vendor.
  • Turn on HA (Multi-AZ, regional HA, replica sets) for production and understand what it costs: usually twice the instance price.
  • Set backup retention and PITR deliberately, and test a restore into a new instance on a schedule; a backup you have not restored is a hope.
  • Keep databases in private networks, require TLS, and use the provider's secret storage for credentials.
  • Size connection pools against the database limit and add a pooler before connecting from functions.
  • Watch storage, I/O, and backup meters as well as the instance or request price.
  • Put development and preview databases on scale-to-zero options, and production on capacity that does not pause.
  • Prefer standard engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL, the MongoDB protocol) unless a proprietary database clearly earns its lock-in.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "Too many connections" errors during a traffic spike. Detect: database errors and a connection-count metric at its maximum while API instances or function concurrency rise. Cause: pools multiplied by instances or environments exceed max_connections. Fix: shrink pools, cap autoscaling or function concurrency, and add RDS Proxy, PgBouncer, or the provider's pooler.
  • The DynamoDB or Firestore bill jumps without more users. Detect: consumed read units or document reads grow much faster than requests. Cause: a scan, a query without a selective key, a realtime listener on a large collection, or a retry loop. Fix: find the operation in metrics, redesign it around the key or an index, and add a cache for hot reads.
  • The first request of the morning times out. Detect: connection timeouts only after idle periods; the database shows a resume event. Cause: Aurora Serverless v2 at 0 ACUs, Neon's scale to zero, or a paused Supabase Free project. Fix: keep a minimum capacity for production, raise client connection timeouts, or retry the first connection.
  • Writes stall for a minute or two and then recover. Detect: an event in the database's event log about a failover, and connection errors from the app. Cause: the primary failed or was patched, and the endpoint moved to the standby. Fix: use the cluster endpoint (never an instance IP), retry transient connection errors, keep DNS caching short in the driver, and test failover before an incident does it for you.
  • The Aurora bill is dominated by I/O. Detect: StorageIOUsage (I/O requests) is the largest Aurora line in Cost Explorer. Cause: an I/O-heavy workload on Aurora Standard. Fix: compare against the I/O-Optimized configuration, which removes per-request I/O charges for higher compute and storage prices, and fix missing indexes that cause excess reads.
  • A restore takes far longer than expected. Detect: a restore drill or real incident runs for hours. Cause: PITR creates a new instance and replays logs, and large databases take time; connection strings must also change. Fix: measure restore time regularly, document the runbook, and see restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Managed database: a database service where the provider handles installation, patching, backups, and failover.
  • Multi-AZ / HA: a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone that takes over automatically.
  • Read replica: an asynchronous copy used to scale reads; it can lag.
  • Point-in-time recovery (PITR): restoring to any moment in a retention window using snapshots plus archived transaction logs.
  • ACU (Aurora Capacity Unit): Aurora Serverless v2's unit of capacity, about 2 GiB of memory with matching CPU.
  • CU (Neon Compute Unit): Neon's unit of compute, about 4 GB of memory with matching CPU.
  • RRU / WRU: DynamoDB on-demand read and write request units.
  • RU (Request Unit): Cosmos DB's unit of throughput for every operation.
  • Connection pooler: a proxy that shares a small number of database connections among many clients.
  • Scale to zero / auto-pause: stopping compute when idle so no compute is billed, at the cost of a resume delay.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Choosing a database by price before choosing the data model.
  • Assuming per-request pricing is always cheap; scans and fan-out reads multiply it.
  • Running production on a single instance without HA, or on a free tier that pauses or expires.
  • Believing backups exist because the setting is on, without testing a restore.
  • Exposing the database to the internet "temporarily".
  • Opening a large pool in every function environment.
  • Treating a Redis or Valkey cache as durable storage.
  • Forgetting storage, I/O, backup, and transfer meters when comparing prices.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does a managed database take off your hands, and what does it leave with you?
  2. Explain the difference between a Multi-AZ standby and a read replica.
  3. Calculate the monthly DynamoDB on-demand cost for 50 million reads and 10 million writes with 40 GB stored. (Answer: 50 x $0.125 = $6.25; 10 x $0.625 = $6.25; storage (40 - 25) x $0.25 = $3.75; total $16.25.)
  4. Why might Aurora Serverless v2 at 0 ACUs be right for a preview environment and wrong for production?
  5. A query reads 100 documents to show one page. How does that change the cost comparison between Firestore and a provisioned PostgreSQL instance?
  6. Why is MongoDB Atlas the lowest-risk first choice for TaskFlow, and when would you reconsider?
  7. How would you size connection pools for six API instances against a database with max_connections of 100?
  8. A healthcare startup needs a database. What must be true of the service and contract, and what remains its own responsibility?

docs.title: Object and File Storage
docs.text:
Almost every application stores files: user uploads, exported reports, build artifacts, images, backups, logs. Where those bytes live decides how much you pay every month, how fast users can download them, and how hard it is to leave a provider later. This lesson explains the three kinds of cloud storage (object, block, and file), every major object store and its storage classes (Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, DigitalOcean Spaces), the block and file services that sit next to virtual machines, the egress economics that decide most storage choices, and presigned uploads that keep large files off your API servers.

It follows managed databases: databases hold structured records; this page covers everything that is a file. Archive tiers for backups get their own lesson in backup and archive storage.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Storage looks cheap on a pricing page, a few cents per gigabyte per month, so teams rarely think about it until the bill arrives. The bill is usually not driven by storage at all. It is driven by egress (data leaving the provider's network), by requests (millions of small reads and writes), and by retrieval and minimum-duration fees on the colder classes. A team that stores 10 TB of user files and lets users download 50 TB a month can pay more than $4,000 a month on one provider and under $200 on another, for the same bytes.

The kind of storage also shapes the architecture. Object storage scales without limits and lets any number of servers share files, which is what makes stateless API servers possible. Block storage is a disk for one server. File storage is a shared network drive. Choosing the wrong one leads to classic failures: uploads saved on an instance's local disk that vanish when the instance is replaced, a shared filesystem used as a database, or a bucket of private documents left publicly readable.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Dropbox (Magic Pocket, 2016). In Scaling to exabytes and beyond Dropbox explains that it moved over 90% of its users' data from Amazon S3 to its own storage system, Magic Pocket. The reasons given are performance, the ability to customize the whole stack end to end for its workload, and better unit economics at its scale. It kept using AWS where that made sense, for example to store data in Germany for European business customers.
  • 37signals (2023-2025). In We stand to save $7m over five years from our cloud exit the company behind Basecamp reported a 2022 cloud bill of $3.2 million, just under $1 million of it for 8 PB in S3. In It's five grand a day to miss our S3 exit (March 2025) it reported spending just under $1.5 million a year on S3 and replacing it with about $1.5 million of storage hardware, and noted that AWS offered a free 60-day egress window for leaving. Storage at petabyte scale with steady growth is the case where owning hardware can win.
  • Cloudflare R2 (2021). Announcing Cloudflare R2 Storage states that R2 was built to cut the egress fees of typical cloud storage "to zero", describing those fees as charges "that don't correspond to any customer value". R2's pricing has no egress line at all, which is why it appears in the worked example below.
  • AWS (2024). Free data transfer out to internet when moving out of AWS announced that customers leaving AWS can request free data transfer out for that move. Egress fees are a real switching cost, and providers now treat them as part of the competitive and regulatory picture.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, DigitalOcean Spaces, Ceph RADOS Gateway (self-hosted, S3-compatible), and the rclone and AWS CLI tools for moving data between them.

docs.title: Object, block, and file storage
docs.text:
Object storage Block storage File storage What you get Buckets of objects addressed by key over HTTPS A raw virtual disk attached to one server A shared network filesystem (NFS or SMB) How you use it PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST through an API or SDK Format it (ext4, XFS) and mount it like a local disk Mount it on many servers at once Who can read it Any client with permission, from anywhere The one server it is attached to (with rare exceptions) Every server that mounts it Edits Replace the whole object; no in-place edits Byte-level random reads and writes File-level reads and writes with locking Scale Practically unlimited; you never resize You choose a size and grow it Grows automatically on most managed services Typical latency Tens of milliseconds per request Sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds Low milliseconds Typical use Uploads, media, static assets, backups, data lakes Root disks, self-hosted databases Shared content for legacy apps, home directories, ML datasets Examples S3, R2, B2, Wasabi, GCS, Azure Blob, Spaces EBS, Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk, Azure Managed Disks EFS, FSx, Azure Files, Filestore

The rule of thumb for a web application such as TaskFlow API: user files go to object storage, the database's disk is block storage (or a managed database that hides it), and file storage appears only when software insists on a shared POSIX filesystem.

docs.title: How object storage works underneath
docs.text:
An object store is a giant key-value store for files. You create a bucket (a namespace with its own settings), then write objects under keys such as tasks/42/attachments/report.pdf. The slashes are part of the key; there are no real folders, only key prefixes that tools display as folders.

  • Immutable objects. You cannot change byte 500 of an object. You upload a new version of the whole object. Large files are uploaded in parts (multipart upload), so a failed part can be retried alone and parts can upload in parallel.
  • Durability by redundancy. Amazon S3 Standard is designed for 99.999999999% (eleven nines) durability and stores data across at least three Availability Zones. Providers use replication and erasure coding (splitting data into fragments plus parity, so lost fragments can be rebuilt) across many disks and buildings.
  • Consistency. Amazon S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020: after a successful write, every read returns the new object. Older articles that warn about eventual consistency in S3 are out of date.
  • Access control. Buckets are private by default. Access comes from identity policies, bucket policies, and short-lived presigned URLs that let a browser upload or download one object without credentials.
  • Metadata and features. Each object carries metadata (content type, custom headers). Buckets add versioning, lifecycle rules, replication, event notifications, and object lock (write-once retention).
  • S3 compatibility. The S3 API became the industry's common language. R2, B2, Wasabi, Spaces, GCS (through its XML API), and self-hosted Ceph accept S3-style requests, so the same SDK often works against all of them with a different endpoint. Compatibility is never total: check the provider's list of supported operations.

docs.title: What you are billed for
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

All prices on this page are US-region list prices (AWS us-east-1, Google Cloud us-central1, Azure East US) in USD, checked in November 2026 from the official pricing pages and price lists linked next to each number. Prices change often; re-check them in the AWS Pricing Calculator, the Google Cloud Pricing Calculator, or the Azure Pricing Calculator before deciding. Other regions, for example Mumbai (ap-south-1) or India Central, are priced differently: select the region in the calculator or on the pricing page.

Every object store bills some combination of these meters:

Meter Unit Notes Storage GB-month (average stored over the month) Lower in colder classes Write requests (PUT, COPY, POST, LIST) Per 1,000 or per million Often called Class A operations Read requests (GET, HEAD) Per 1,000 or per million Often called Class B operations Retrieval Per GB read Only on infrequent-access and archive classes Minimum storage duration Days Deleting early is billed as if the object stayed Minimum billable object size KB Small objects billed as if larger (128 KB on S3 IA classes) Egress Per GB leaving the provider The largest cost for download-heavy apps Management features Per object or per GB Inventory, Intelligent-Tiering monitoring, replication

docs.title: Amazon S3 and its storage classes
docs.text:
What it is. Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object store and the reference design for the whole category. You manage buckets, keys, permissions, lifecycle rules, and the choice of storage class per object; AWS manages the hardware, redundancy, scaling, and durability. A storage class is a per-object setting that trades storage price against access price and speed.

Class What it is for Storage per GB-month Retrieval per GB Minimum duration First byte S3 Express One Zone Latency-critical hot data in one zone you choose (directory buckets) $0.11 $0.0006, plus $0.0032 per GB uploaded None Single-digit milliseconds S3 Standard Default for active data $0.023 (first 50 TB), $0.022 (next 450 TB), $0.021 (over 500 TB) None None Milliseconds S3 Intelligent-Tiering Unknown or changing access; S3 moves each object between tiers $0.023 / $0.0125 / $0.004 by tier, plus $0.0025 per 1,000 objects monitored None None Milliseconds (optional archive tiers: hours) S3 Standard-IA Accessed about once a month, needs millisecond access $0.0125 $0.01 30 days, 128 KB minimum size Milliseconds S3 One Zone-IA Re-creatable data in one zone $0.01 $0.01 30 days, 128 KB minimum size Milliseconds S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval Archive read about once a quarter, instantly $0.004 $0.03 90 days, 128 KB minimum size Milliseconds S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval Archive restored in minutes to hours $0.0036 $0.03 / $0.01 / free (expedited / standard / bulk) 90 days, 40 KB overhead per object 1-5 minutes to 12 hours S3 Glacier Deep Archive Long-term retention, restored in hours $0.00099 $0.02 / $0.0025 (standard / bulk) 180 days, 40 KB overhead per object Within 12 or 48 hours

Sources: Amazon S3 pricing and the public AWS Price List for us-east-1. Requests on S3 Standard cost $0.005 per 1,000 writes and $0.0004 per 1,000 reads; the infrequent-access classes charge more per request ($0.01 per 1,000 writes on Standard-IA, $0.02 per 1,000 on Glacier Instant Retrieval). Durability, availability, and minimums are from the S3 user guide's storage class comparison.

How the classes behave in practice:

  • Intelligent-Tiering watches each object. After 30 days without access it moves to the Infrequent Access tier, after 90 days to Archive Instant Access; optional Archive Access (90+ days) and Deep Archive Access (180+ days) tiers can be switched on for data that tolerates restores. Any read moves the object back to the frequent tier, with no retrieval fee. Objects under 128 KB are not monitored and always pay frequent-tier rates, so it suits large objects with unpredictable access. (How S3 Intelligent-Tiering works)
  • Minimums bite small objects. A 10 KB thumbnail in Standard-IA is billed as 128 KB, so it costs more than in Standard. Glacier Flexible Retrieval and Deep Archive add 40 KB of metadata per object (8 KB at the Standard rate), which dominates for millions of small files: bundle them into archives first.
  • One Zone classes keep a single copy set in one Availability Zone. The data is still durable against disk failures but is lost if that zone is destroyed. Use them only for data you can re-create, such as thumbnails or replicas.
  • Express One Zone is the high-performance class: single-digit millisecond access, lower request prices than Standard, but almost five times the storage price. It suits analytics and ML jobs that read the same data many times from compute in the same zone, not user uploads.

docs.title: Cloudflare R2
docs.text:
What it is. R2 is Cloudflare's S3-compatible object store. It runs on Cloudflare's own network, which is also a large CDN, and its headline feature is no egress fees in any storage class. You manage buckets, keys, tokens, and lifecycle rules; Cloudflare manages everything else. Buckets can be exposed on a custom domain behind Cloudflare's cache, and Workers (edge functions) can read and write R2 directly.

Pricing (R2 pricing): Standard storage $0.015 per GB-month, Class A operations (writes, lists) $4.50 per million, Class B operations (reads) $0.36 per million, egress free. Infrequent Access storage is $0.01 per GB-month with $9.00 and $0.90 per million operations, a $0.01 per GB retrieval fee, and a 30-day minimum. The monthly free tier covers 10 GB-month of Standard storage, 1 million Class A and 10 million Class B operations. Usage is rounded up to the next billing unit (1.1 GB-month is billed as 2).

Trade-offs. No egress fees changes the economics for download-heavy apps. The downsides: fewer storage classes and no deep-archive tier, an S3 API that does not implement every operation (for example S3 Object Lock is listed as unimplemented; R2 has its own bucket locks), presigned URLs for GET, HEAD, PUT, and DELETE but not HTML form POST uploads, and a smaller compliance catalogue than the hyperscalers.

docs.title: Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage
docs.text:
What it is. Backblaze B2 is an S3-compatible object store from a company that started in consumer backup. It has a single storage class and a deliberately simple price.

Pricing (B2 pricing): $6.95 per TB per month, billed by byte-hour, with the first 10 GB free and no minimum file size or storage duration. Egress is free up to three times your average monthly stored data, then $0.01 per GB, and unlimited free egress applies when downloading through partner CDNs and compute providers (the page lists Fastly, Cloudflare, bunny.net, CacheFly, CoreWeave, Equinix Metal, Vultr, and phoenixNAP). Class A, B, and C API calls are free on pay-as-you-go; Class D calls cost $0.004 per 10,000 after 2,500 free per day.

Trade-offs. Very cheap for storage-heavy data with moderate reads. Fewer regions than a hyperscaler, no storage classes or archive tier, and fewer surrounding services (no built-in event-driven compute next to the data).

docs.title: Wasabi Hot Cloud Storage
docs.text:
What it is. Wasabi sells S3-compatible "hot" storage at a flat price per TB with no egress or API request fees.

Pricing (Wasabi pricing): pay as you go from $7.99 per TB per month, with a minimum charge of 1 TB of active storage and a 90-day minimum storage duration (deleted data is billed as "timed deleted storage" until 90 days). Reserved capacity in 1-, 3-, or 5-year terms is cheaper and has a 30-day minimum.

The egress catch. Egress is free under a policy: the pricing FAQ says that if your monthly egress is greater than your active storage, your use case "is not a good fit" for the free egress policy, and Wasabi reserves the right to limit or suspend service for regular overuse. Wasabi suits backups and archives that are written often and read rarely. It does not suit a public download site serving each file many times a month, unless a CDN in front absorbs most of the reads.

docs.title: DigitalOcean Spaces
docs.text:
What it is. Spaces is DigitalOcean's S3-compatible object store with a built-in CDN, aimed at teams already running Droplets or App Platform.

Pricing (Spaces pricing): a $5 monthly subscription includes 250 GiB of storage and 1,024 GiB of outbound transfer; extra storage is $0.02 per GiB-month and extra transfer $0.01 per GiB. The CDN is included, and its traffic counts against the same transfer allowance. Spaces Cold Storage costs $0.007 per GiB-month with a $0.01 per GiB retrieval fee (waived up to your average daily cold storage usage) and a 30-day minimum.

Trade-offs. Predictable and simple, with a CDN in the box. Fewer regions and features than S3, and the $0.01 per GiB transfer price, while low, still adds up for heavy downloads.

docs.title: Google Cloud Storage
docs.text:
What it is. Cloud Storage is Google Cloud's object store. Buckets are regional, dual-region, or multi-region, and each object has one of four classes. It integrates with BigQuery, Cloud Run, and Google's CDN products.

Pricing (Cloud Storage pricing, us-central1 and us-east1): Standard $0.020 per GiB-month, Nearline $0.010 (30-day minimum, $0.01 per GiB retrieval), Coldline $0.004 (90 days, $0.02 per GiB), Archive $0.0012 (365 days, $0.05 per GiB). Operations on Standard cost $0.005 per 1,000 Class A and $0.0004 per 1,000 Class B. Unlike AWS's archive classes, every GCS class returns the first byte in milliseconds; the colder classes are cheaper to keep and dearer to read. Autoclass can move objects between classes automatically, and retrieval fees do not apply in Autoclass buckets.

docs.title: Azure Blob Storage
docs.text:
What it is. Blob Storage is Azure's object store, organised as storage accounts that contain containers that contain blobs. Each block blob has an access tier.

Pricing (Blob pricing, East US, locally redundant storage, from the Azure Retail Prices API): Hot $0.0208 per GB-month (first 50 TB), Cool $0.0152 (30-day minimum, $0.01 per GB read), Cold $0.0036 (90 days, $0.03 per GB), Archive $0.00099 (180 days, $0.02 per GB standard rehydration, $0.10 per GB high priority). Archive is offline: a blob must be rehydrated, which can take up to 15 hours (see Access tiers for blob data).

docs.title: Options compared
docs.text:
Option What it is Storage price Egress Free tier Strengths Weaknesses Lock-in Amazon S3 AWS's object store with eight storage classes $0.023/GB Standard down to $0.00099 Deep Archive $0.09/GB first 10 TB (less via CloudFront) 100 GB/month egress across AWS Most features, classes, integrations, compliance programs Egress and request costs; many knobs Medium: S3 API is portable, the surrounding services are not Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible store on Cloudflare's network $0.015 Standard, $0.01 IA Free 10 GB-month, 1M writes, 10M reads Zero egress, edge integration with Workers Two classes, partial S3 API, no archive tier Low: S3 API, no exit fee Backblaze B2 S3-compatible single-class store $6.95/TB Free up to 3x stored, $0.01/GB after; free via partner CDNs 10 GB Cheapest simple storage, no minimums One class, fewer regions and services Low Wasabi S3-compatible flat-price hot storage $7.99/TB (1 TB minimum) No fee if egress stays at or below stored data None Flat price, no API fees 90-day minimum; not for download-heavy use Low to medium (minimums) DigitalOcean Spaces S3-compatible store with a built-in CDN $5 includes 250 GiB, then $0.02/GiB 1,024 GiB included, then $0.01/GiB Included allowance Built-in CDN, simple bill Fewer regions and features Low Google Cloud Storage Google Cloud's object store with four classes $0.020 Standard down to $0.0012 Archive Per GB, by destination 5 GB-months in us-east1, us-west1, us-central1 Millisecond access on all classes, Autoclass Retrieval fees on cold classes Medium Azure Blob Storage Azure's object store with access tiers $0.0208 Hot down to $0.00099 Archive Per GB, by destination Limited trial credits Fits Microsoft-centric estates, smart tier Archive is offline (hours) Medium

The Google Cloud free tier line comes from the Google Cloud Free Program, which also includes 5,000 Class A and 50,000 Class B operations and 100 GB of outbound transfer from North America per month.

docs.title: Block storage: EBS, Persistent Disk, Managed Disks
docs.text:
What it is. Block storage is a network-attached virtual disk. Amazon EBS, Google Cloud Persistent Disk and Hyperdisk, and Azure Managed Disks all work the same way: you create a volume of a chosen size and performance in one zone, attach it to a VM, and put a filesystem on it. The provider replicates the volume inside the zone; you manage the filesystem, resizing, and snapshots. A volume is tied to its zone, so a VM in another zone cannot attach it without restoring a snapshot.

On AWS, the default gp3 volume costs $0.08 per GB-month and includes a baseline of 3,000 IOPS and 125 MB/s; extra IOPS cost $0.005 per provisioned IOPS-month and extra throughput $0.04 per provisioned MiB/s per month in us-east-1 (price list effective November 2026; see EBS pricing). Snapshots, which are incremental copies stored in S3, cost $0.05 per GB-month, or $0.0125 in the snapshot archive tier with a $0.03 per GB restore fee. Compare $0.08 for a block volume with $0.023 for S3 Standard: block storage is for data a running server needs as a disk, not for piles of files.

docs.title: File storage: EFS, FSx, Azure Files, Filestore
docs.text:
What it is. Managed file storage is a network filesystem that many servers mount at once. Amazon EFS speaks NFS, grows and shrinks automatically, and spans zones; Amazon FSx offers managed Windows File Server, Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, and OpenZFS; Azure Files offers SMB and NFS shares; Google Cloud Filestore offers managed NFS. You manage mounts and permissions; the provider manages servers, replication, and capacity.

EFS Standard storage costs $0.30 per GB-month in us-east-1, more than ten times S3 Standard, with infrequent-access and archive tiers and per-GB charges for elastic throughput (EFS pricing). Use shared file storage when software needs POSIX semantics: a CMS that writes uploads to a directory, a legacy app you cannot change, or a machine-learning job that reads a dataset as files. For new code, object storage is cheaper and scales further.

docs.title: Egress: the cost that decides most storage choices
docs.text:
Storage is billed once per month per byte; egress is billed every time a byte is downloaded. For anything users download repeatedly (images, videos, exports, installers), egress quickly outgrows storage.

Worked example. TaskFlow lets teams attach files to tasks. After two years it stores 10 TB (10,240 GB) of attachments, and users download 50 TB (51,200 GB) a month. Average file size is 5 MiB, so that is about 10.5 million downloads (10,485,760 GET requests). Monthly cost, US list prices:

S3 Standard, downloads straight from S3
  storage   10,240 GB x $0.023                        =   $235.52
  egress    10,240 GB x $0.09 + 40,960 GB x $0.085    = $4,403.20
  requests  10,485,760 / 1,000 x $0.0004              =     $4.19
  total (ignoring the 100 GB/month AWS free allowance)  ~ $4,643

S3 Standard + CloudFront, pay-as-you-go
  storage                                             =   $235.52
  S3 to CloudFront transfer                           =     $0.00  (free from AWS origins)
  CloudFront egress: 1,024 GB free, 9,216 GB x $0.085,
                     40,960 GB x $0.080               = $4,060.16
  HTTPS requests: (10,485,760 - 10,000,000 free)
                  / 10,000 x $0.01                    =     $0.49
  S3 GETs on cache misses (10%): 1,048,576 / 1,000
                  x $0.0004                           =     $0.42
  total                                               ~ $4,297

S3 Standard + CloudFront Business flat-rate plan
  plan ($200/month: 125M requests, 50 TB transfer)    =   $200.00
  storage                                             =   $235.52
  total (if the workload fits the plan's terms)       ~   $436

Cloudflare R2
  storage   (10,240 - 10 free) GB x $0.015            =   $153.45
  reads     485,760 beyond the free 10M, billed as 1M
            x $0.36                                   =     $0.36
  egress                                              =     $0.00
  total                                               ~   $154

Backblaze B2, downloads straight from B2
  storage   10 TB x $6.95                             =    $69.50
  egress    30 TB free (3 x stored), 20,480 GB x $0.01 =   $204.80
  total                                               ~   $274

Backblaze B2 + bunny.net CDN (partner: B2 egress free)
  storage                                             =    $69.50
  CDN       51,200 GB x $0.01 (Europe and North America) = $512.00
  total                                               ~   $582

Wasabi + bunny.net CDN
  storage   10 TB x $7.99                             =    $79.90
  CDN       51,200 GB x $0.01                         =   $512.00
  origin egress ~5 TB at a 90% cache hit ratio: under the 10 TB stored,
            so inside Wasabi's free egress policy     =     $0.00
  total                                               ~   $592

DigitalOcean Spaces (CDN included)
  base      $5 (250 GiB + 1,024 GiB transfer)         =     $5.00
  storage   9,990 GiB x $0.02                         =   $199.80
  transfer  50,176 GiB x $0.01                        =   $501.76
  total                                               ~   $707

Sources: S3 pricing, CloudFront pay-as-you-go pricing, CloudFront flat-rate plans, R2 pricing, B2 pricing, bunny.net CDN pricing, Wasabi pricing, Spaces pricing.

What the numbers teach:

  • Storage is the small part. Every option stores 10 TB for $70 to $236. The spread from $154 to $4,643 is almost entirely egress.
  • A CDN alone does not fix hyperscaler egress. CloudFront's pay-as-you-go rates are only a little below S3's direct rates. What changes the bill is a provider or plan whose model is not per-GB egress: R2, B2's partner egress, or CloudFront's flat-rate plans (launched November 2025; Free $0, Pro $15, Business $200, Premium $1,000 a month). Flat-rate plans cover one distribution, have no overage charges, and may reduce performance if you exceed the allowance, so read the terms and watch the usage alerts.
  • "Free egress" has conditions. B2's is free up to 3x storage or via partners; Wasabi's assumes egress stays at or below stored data; Spaces includes 1 TB. R2 has no egress line at all.
  • Requests matter for small files. At 5 MiB per file, requests cost a few dollars. Serve 100 KB thumbnails instead and the same 50 TB becomes about 537 million requests: R2 would bill about $190 in Class B operations and CloudFront about $527 in HTTPS requests.

docs.title: Presigned uploads: keep files off your servers
docs.text:
If browsers upload files through the API, every byte crosses the API servers twice (in and out), ties up connections, and needs large request size limits. The standard pattern is a presigned upload:

  1. The browser asks TaskFlow API for permission to upload one file, sending its name, type, and size.
  2. The API checks the user's rights and the file type and size, chooses the object key itself (never trust a client-supplied path), and signs a short-lived upload URL or form with its own credentials.
  3. The browser uploads the bytes directly to the bucket.
  4. The browser (or a bucket event) tells the API the upload finished; the API records the key against the task, and optionally triggers a virus scan or thumbnail job.

The bucket stays private: downloads use presigned GET URLs or a CDN with signed URLs. The application-side details (validation, scanning, private downloads) are in file storage and uploads and file uploads in Express; the code below shows the storage side.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Need Use Avoid User uploads, media, exports, static assets Object storage Instance disks (lost on replacement), shared file systems A disk for one server or a self-hosted database Block storage Object storage mounted as a filesystem Many servers need the same POSIX directory Managed file storage A database or object store forced into the role Millisecond reads by the same compute, many times S3 Express One Zone or block storage Cold classes with retrieval fees Data read rarely but instantly Standard-IA, Glacier Instant Retrieval, Nearline, Cool, R2 IA Archive tiers that need restores Heavy public downloads R2, B2 with a partner CDN, a flat-rate CDN plan Per-GB egress straight from a hyperscaler

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Scenario Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Cloudflare R2 Backblaze B2 R2's free tier (10 GB, 10M reads) and zero egress cover most hobby sites at $0; B2 is just as cheap with 10 GB free Early startup on AWS S3 Standard plus lifecycle rules R2 for public downloads S3 integrates with IAM, Lambda, and the rest of the stack; move only download-heavy buckets if egress shows up on the bill Steady high traffic S3 or GCS behind a CDN with a committed or flat-rate CDN plan R2 At steady volume, negotiated or flat-rate delivery beats list egress; keep storage near compute Spiky traffic R2 or a flat-rate CDN plan S3 + CloudFront pay-as-you-go A viral file on per-GB egress becomes a surprise bill; zero or flat egress caps the risk Global audience Any object store behind a global CDN; R2 (Cloudflare network) S3 + CloudFront Users download from the nearest edge; the origin's region matters less than cache hit ratio Compliance-heavy (for example healthcare) S3, GCS, or Azure Blob under the provider's BAA The same in a dedicated, locked-down account AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure state on their official pages that they sign a HIPAA BAA covering eligible services; for any smaller provider, use it for health data only if its official page offers a BAA for that product Large files and heavy egress R2 B2 with a partner CDN Egress is the bill (see the worked example) Team with no ops people The object store of the platform you already use (S3, Spaces, R2) Backblaze B2 One account, one bill, one set of credentials; nothing to operate either way

docs.title: Presigned POST upload for TaskFlow attachments (S3)
docs.text:
A presigned POST lets the bucket itself enforce limits: the signed policy fixes the key, the content type, and a size range, so a client cannot upload a 5 GB file with a URL meant for 25 MB.

// src/storage/attachments.js: presigned uploads and downloads (Node 24, AWS SDK v3)
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { S3Client, GetObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { createPresignedPost } from "@aws-sdk/s3-presigned-post";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";

const s3 = new S3Client({ region: process.env.AWS_REGION });
const BUCKET = process.env.ATTACHMENTS_BUCKET;
const MAX_BYTES = 25 * 1024 * 1024; // 25 MiB
const ALLOWED_TYPES = new Set(["image/png", "image/jpeg", "application/pdf"]);

export async function createUploadForm({ taskId, contentType }) {
  if (!ALLOWED_TYPES.has(contentType)) {
    throw Object.assign(new Error("Unsupported file type"), { status: 400 });
  }
  // The server chooses the key; the client never controls the path.
  const key = `tasks/${taskId}/${randomUUID()}`;

  const { url, fields } = await createPresignedPost(s3, {
    Bucket: BUCKET,
    Key: key,
    Conditions: [
      ["content-length-range", 1, MAX_BYTES],
      ["eq", "$Content-Type", contentType],
    ],
    Fields: { "Content-Type": contentType },
    Expires: 300, // seconds
  });
  return { url, fields, key };
}

export function createDownloadUrl(key, filename) {
  const command = new GetObjectCommand({
    Bucket: BUCKET,
    Key: key,
    ResponseContentDisposition: `attachment; filename="${filename.replace(/"/g, "")}"`,
  });
  return getSignedUrl(s3, command, { expiresIn: 300 });
}
  • content-length-range makes S3 reject bodies outside 1 byte to 25 MiB.
  • eq $Content-Type stops a client from uploading HTML or SVG under an image key, which would otherwise be a stored cross-site scripting risk if the file were ever served inline.
  • Expires: 300 keeps a leaked form useless after five minutes.
  • ResponseContentDisposition forces downloads instead of rendering the file in the browser.

The browser sends every returned field, then the file last (S3 ignores form fields after the file):

// web/src/upload.js: TaskFlow Web uploads directly to the bucket
export async function uploadAttachment(taskId, file) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api/tasks/${taskId}/attachments/upload-form`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ contentType: file.type }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error("Could not start upload");
  const { url, fields, key } = await res.json();

  const form = new FormData();
  for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(fields)) form.append(name, value);
  form.append("file", file); // must be the last field

  const upload = await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: form });
  if (!upload.ok) throw new Error(`Upload rejected: ${upload.status}`);
  return key; // then tell the API the upload finished
}

docs.title: Bucket CORS for browser uploads
docs.text:
Browsers block cross-origin requests unless the bucket allows the app's origin:

{
  "CORSRules": [
    {
      "AllowedOrigins": ["https://app.example.com"],
      "AllowedMethods": ["GET", "PUT", "POST"],
      "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
      "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"],
      "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
    }
  ]
}

# Apply the CORS rules to the attachments bucket
aws s3api put-bucket-cors \
  --bucket taskflow-attachments \
  --cors-configuration file://cors.json

List exact origins. * would let any website use your upload endpoint with a leaked form.

docs.title: The same code against Cloudflare R2
docs.text:
R2 speaks the S3 API, so only the client changes. R2 presigned URLs support GET, HEAD, PUT, and DELETE, with an expiry from 1 second to 7 days; HTML form POST uploads are not supported, so use a presigned PUT:

// src/storage/r2.js: presigned PUT against Cloudflare R2
import { S3Client, PutObjectCommand } from "@aws-sdk/client-s3";
import { getSignedUrl } from "@aws-sdk/s3-request-presigner";

const r2 = new S3Client({
  region: "auto", // required by the SDK, ignored by R2
  endpoint: `https://${process.env.R2_ACCOUNT_ID}.r2.cloudflarestorage.com`,
  credentials: {
    accessKeyId: process.env.R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID,
    secretAccessKey: process.env.R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
  },
});

export function createR2UploadUrl(key, contentType) {
  // The client must send the same Content-Type header, or R2 rejects the upload.
  const command = new PutObjectCommand({
    Bucket: process.env.R2_BUCKET,
    Key: key,
    ContentType: contentType,
  });
  return getSignedUrl(r2, command, { expiresIn: 300 });
}

A presigned PUT cannot enforce a size range the way a POST policy can. Check the object's size after upload (a HEAD request or an event notification) and delete anything over the limit.

# .env for local development against R2 (placeholders only)
R2_ACCOUNT_ID=<account-id>
R2_ACCESS_KEY_ID=<access-key-id>
R2_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=<secret-access-key>
R2_BUCKET=taskflow-attachments

docs.title: Lifecycle rules for an uploads bucket
docs.text:
Attachments are read often for a few weeks, then rarely. This rule moves them to Intelligent-Tiering after a week (most are over 128 KB), deletes old versions, and cleans up abandoned multipart uploads, which are billed as storage but invisible in normal listings:

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "attachments-tiering",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "tasks/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "Transitions": [
        { "Days": 7, "StorageClass": "INTELLIGENT_TIERING" }
      ],
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 },
      "AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload": { "DaysAfterInitiation": 7 }
    }
  ]
}

aws s3api put-bucket-lifecycle-configuration \
  --bucket taskflow-attachments \
  --lifecycle-configuration file://lifecycle.json

Archive-tier rules (Glacier, Deep Archive) and retention locks are covered in backup and archive storage.

docs.title: Mounting shared file storage (EFS)
docs.text:
When an off-the-shelf app needs a shared directory, mount EFS on every instance with the Amazon EFS mount helper and TLS:

# On each instance (Amazon Linux): install the helper, mount, and persist
sudo dnf install -y amazon-efs-utils
sudo mkdir -p /mnt/shared
sudo mount -t efs -o tls fs-<id>:/ /mnt/shared
echo "fs-<id>:/ /mnt/shared efs _netdev,noresvport,tls 0 0" | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep buckets private, turn on S3 Block Public Access (or the provider's equivalent) at the account level, and serve public files through a CDN.
  • Let the server choose object keys; include tenant and task IDs in the key so permissions and lifecycle rules can target prefixes.
  • Use presigned uploads with short expiry and enforced size and type; never proxy large uploads through the API.
  • Estimate egress before choosing a provider: multiply expected downloads by file size, then price it on two or three providers.
  • Put a CDN in front of anything public and measure the cache hit ratio; every miss is origin egress and a request.
  • Add lifecycle rules on day one: abort incomplete multipart uploads, expire old versions, and tier data by age.
  • Respect minimums: do not put small or short-lived objects in IA or archive classes.
  • Tag buckets by owner and environment so storage shows up per team on the bill (see cost optimization).
  • Use the S3 API through an SDK with a configurable endpoint, so moving between S3-compatible providers is a configuration change.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The storage bill is ten times what storage should cost. Detect: Cost Explorer grouped by usage type shows DataTransfer-Out-Bytes or CloudFront data transfer as the top line, not TimedStorage-ByteHrs. Cause: download-heavy files served on per-GB egress, often through a public bucket that bypasses the CDN. Fix: serve through a CDN with a high hit ratio, move public downloads to a zero-egress store or flat-rate plan, and block direct bucket access.
  • Storage keeps growing although users delete files. Detect: S3 Storage Lens or bucket metrics show noncurrent version bytes or incomplete multipart upload bytes rising. Cause: versioning keeps every overwritten and deleted object; failed uploads leave parts behind. Fix: add NoncurrentVersionExpiration and AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload lifecycle rules.
  • Moving to Standard-IA made the bill go up. Detect: new EarlyDelete-SIA, TimedStorage-SIA-SmObjects, and Retrieval-SIA usage types appear after the change. Cause: many objects were under 128 KB, were deleted within 30 days, or were read often. Fix: use Intelligent-Tiering for unknown access, or filter transitions by object size and age; analyse access with S3 Storage Class Analysis first.
  • Browser uploads fail with a CORS error after a domain change. Detect: the browser console shows a blocked preflight to the bucket endpoint; the bucket's CORS rules list the old origin. Cause: bucket CORS is separate from the API's CORS. Fix: add the new origin to the bucket's CORS configuration and redeploy.
  • Uploaded files disappear after a deploy. Detect: files referenced in the database return 404; the instances or containers were replaced. Cause: uploads were written to the local disk of an instance or container. Fix: write uploads to object storage; treat servers as disposable.
  • A bucket of private documents is found publicly readable. Detect: an external report, AWS Trusted Advisor or IAM Access Analyzer findings, or aws s3api get-bucket-policy-status returning IsPublic: true. Cause: a bucket policy or ACL granting * read, often added to "make images work". Fix: enable Block Public Access, remove the grant, serve through a CDN with origin access control, rotate any exposed data, and treat it as a security incident.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Object storage: Storage of whole files (objects) under keys in buckets, accessed over an HTTP API.
  • Block storage: A network-attached virtual disk for one server.
  • File storage: A shared network filesystem mounted by many servers.
  • Bucket: A named container for objects with its own settings.
  • Key: The full name of an object, including any / prefixes.
  • Storage class / access tier: A per-object setting trading storage price against access price and speed.
  • Egress: Data transferred out of a provider's network, usually billed per GB.
  • Minimum storage duration: The period an object is billed for even if deleted sooner.
  • Minimum billable object size: The size small objects are billed at in some classes (128 KB on S3 IA classes).
  • Presigned URL: A time-limited URL signed with server credentials that allows one specific request without credentials.
  • Multipart upload: Uploading a large object in independently retryable parts.
  • S3-compatible: A non-AWS service that accepts S3 API requests.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Comparing providers on storage price alone, when egress and requests dominate download-heavy workloads.
  • Believing a CDN automatically removes egress costs; on per-GB CDN pricing it mostly moves them.
  • Assuming "free egress" is unconditional; read the multiplier, the partner list, or the fair-use policy.
  • Putting small or short-lived objects into IA or archive classes and paying minimums.
  • Storing uploads on instance disks or in container filesystems.
  • Using EFS as a cheap object store; it costs more than ten times as much per GB as S3 Standard.
  • Making a bucket public to serve images instead of using a CDN with origin access control.
  • Assuming every "S3-compatible" service supports every S3 feature (POST policies, Object Lock, event notifications).

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain object, block, and file storage, and give one workload that fits each.
  2. Why can't you edit part of an object in place, and how do multipart uploads help with large files?
  3. What do the minimum storage duration and the minimum billable object size mean, and when do they make Standard-IA more expensive than Standard?
  4. Calculate the monthly cost of storing 2 TB (2,048 GB) in S3 Standard and serving 5 TB (5,120 GB) of downloads directly from S3 in us-east-1, ignoring requests and free allowances. (Answer: 2,048 x $0.023 = $47.10 storage; 5,120 x $0.09 = $460.80 egress; about $508.)
  5. Why does a CDN in front of S3 not, by itself, make heavy downloads cheap? What does?
  6. What conditions apply to the "free egress" of Backblaze B2 and Wasabi?
  7. Why should the server, not the browser, choose an upload's object key, and what does a presigned POST policy enforce that a presigned PUT does not?
  8. A team serves 100 KB thumbnails. Which costs grow, and which storage classes should they avoid?
