docs.title: Running Backend Servers and APIs
docs.text:
A backend API such as TaskFlow API (Node.js, Express, MongoDB) is a process that must be reachable over HTTPS, scale with traffic, survive restarts, and talk to a database. It can run on a virtual machine, on a platform that hides the machine, in containers, or as functions. This lesson explains what each concrete product is (EC2, Lightsail, Azure VMs, Compute Engine, Droplets, Hetzner, Linode, Elastic Beanstalk, Heroku, Render, Railway, Fly.io, App Service, App Engine, App Platform, ECS, Fargate, EKS, Cloud Run, Container Apps, AKS, GKE, Lambda, Azure Functions, Cloud Run functions, Cloudflare Workers, and Vercel Functions), the constraints that rule some out (WebSockets, long jobs, cold starts), and what TaskFlow API costs on each, including where functions stop being the cheapest option.

The mechanics of deploying a Node service without dropping requests (health checks, graceful shutdown, zero-downtime restarts) are in deploying backend services; this lesson is about where the process runs and what that costs.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The compute model decides how the API behaves under load and how the bill grows. Functions scale from zero to thousands of copies in seconds but add cold starts, duration limits, and a database connection per copy. Containers keep connections warm and handle WebSockets, but someone must size them. A VM is the cheapest per CPU but a single one is a single point of failure, and its patching is yours. Platforms remove most of that work and charge for it.

Getting this wrong is common in both directions: steady APIs paying per-request prices ten times higher than a small cluster would cost, and small teams running Kubernetes for a service that two platform instances would serve. The aim of this lesson is to make the trade-offs concrete, with numbers.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Capital One (functions first, containers as the fallback). The AWS case study Capital One saves developer time and reduces costs by going serverless says the bank's "default strategy is to migrate its applications to serverless compute" on AWS Lambda to reduce the operational burden on engineering teams, and that "for use cases when AWS Lambda cannot be used" it runs containers on Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate. One migrated application "achieved 90 percent cost savings".
  • LAAM (serverless containers instead of a cluster). In LAAM's Google Cloud case study, the commerce platform hosts roughly 135 stateless microservices on Cloud Run, which "eliminated the need to operate a complex Kubernetes control plane" and "scales down to zero". Its CTO explains the choice: "we had a tiny team and zero time to operate infrastructure".
  • 37signals (owned servers for steady load). The cloud exit savings post reports moving seven applications, including HEY, from the cloud onto about $700,000 of their own hardware, cutting the cloud bill from a $3.2 million per year run rate to $1.3 million: the economics of a large, predictable workload with an experienced operations team.
  • AWS Lambda at scale. The Firecracker project page describes the open-source microVM technology that isolates Lambda workloads and powers "15 trillion+ monthly Lambda function invocations", which is why a Lambda environment boots fast enough to create on demand.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon EC2, ECS, Fargate, EKS, and Lambda; Google Compute Engine, Cloud Run, and GKE; Azure Virtual Machines, App Service, Container Apps, AKS, and Functions; Cloudflare Workers; Vercel; Heroku; Render; Railway; Fly.io; DigitalOcean; Hetzner; and Akamai Cloud (Linode).

docs.title: Four ways to run a server process
docs.text: Model Unit that scales Typical start time Holds connections between requests Billed while idle Virtual machine A VM Tens of seconds to minutes Yes Yes Platform (PaaS) An instance (dyno, service instance, Machine) Seconds Yes Usually yes (some sleep or scale to zero) Container service A task or pod Seconds Yes Yes, unless it scales to zero Function An execution environment Milliseconds to seconds (cold start) Only while the environment stays warm No

docs.title: Virtual machines
docs.text:
You rent a VM and run TaskFlow API on it with systemd or PM2 behind nginx (see deploying backend services). The products differ mainly in price, included bandwidth, and what else the provider offers around the VM.

  • Amazon EC2: AWS's general VM service with hundreds of instance types, billed per second (60-second minimum). Disks (EBS), public IPv4 addresses, and data transfer are billed separately. Graviton (Arm) instances such as t4g cost less than comparable x86 ones.
  • Amazon Lightsail: simple VM bundles with a fixed monthly price that includes an SSD, a public IPv4 address, and a data transfer allowance; overage is billed per GB. Good for small, predictable servers that do not need the rest of AWS.
  • Azure Virtual Machines and Google Compute Engine: the equivalents on Azure and Google Cloud. Google's free tier includes one e2-micro VM a month in us-west1, us-central1, or us-east1 (free tier).
  • DigitalOcean Droplets: VMs with simple monthly prices and generous included transfer.
  • Hetzner Cloud: a German provider with data centers in Germany, Finland, the US (Ashburn and Hillsboro), and Singapore, known for low prices and large traffic allowances. Prices are in euros, and some plans show as unavailable in some locations when capacity is short.
  • Akamai Cloud (formerly Linode): VMs with included transfer and a low overage rate.

Prices checked November 2026

Prices in this lesson are US-region list prices in USD (AWS us-east-1, Google Cloud us-central1, Azure East US) from the linked official pricing pages in November 2026, except Hetzner, which is priced in euros. They change often; re-check with the provider's pricing page or calculator before deciding. Other regions such as India are priced differently: pick the region in the calculator or on the pricing page.

Provider and size Monthly price Included outbound transfer Source EC2 t4g.small (2 vCPU, 2 GiB, Arm) $0.0168/hour = $12.26, plus disk ($0.08 per GB-month gp3) and IPv4 ($3.65) 100 GB/month free across the account, then $0.09/GB EC2 Lightsail 2 GB (2 vCPU, 60 GB SSD) $12, IPv4 included 3 TB Lightsail Azure B1ms (1 vCPU, 2 GiB), Linux $0.0207/hour = about $15.11 Billed separately Azure VMs DigitalOcean Droplet 2 GiB (1 vCPU, 50 GiB) $12 2,000 GiB DigitalOcean Akamai Linode 2 GB (1 CPU, 50 GB) $12 2 TB, then $0.005/GB Akamai Hetzner Cloud CPX02 (1 vCPU, 1 GB), Regular Performance from €5.49 excluding VAT in EU locations; prices vary by location at least 20 TB in EU locations, 1 TB in US locations Hetzner Google Compute Engine e2-micro free tier: one VM per month in three US regions 1 GB from North America Google Cloud free tier

docs.title: Platforms (PaaS)
docs.text:
• AWS Elastic Beanstalk: creates EC2 instances, an Auto Scaling group, and a load balancer in your account from your code, and manages deployments and platform updates. "There is no additional charge for AWS Elastic Beanstalk": you pay for the resources it creates (pricing).
  • Heroku: the original git-push platform. Apps run in containers called dynos: Eco $5 a month (sleeps after 30 minutes of inactivity), Basic $7, Standard-1X $25, and Standard-2X $50 (pricing). Free dynos ended on November 28, 2022, and in February 2026 Heroku moved to a sustaining engineering model: existing customers continue unchanged, but new feature work is not the focus and Enterprise contracts are not offered to new customers. The router ends any request that takes longer than 30 seconds (request timeout).
  • Render: web services, workers, cron jobs, and managed databases from git or an image. Workspace plans are Hobby ($0), Pro ($25 a month), and Scale ($499 a month) plus compute; a 512 MB, 0.5 CPU instance is $7 a month and 2 GB with 1 CPU is $25. Free web services spin down after 15 minutes without traffic and take about a minute to start again (free tier).
  • Railway: bills actual CPU and memory use per second: $0.00000772 per vCPU-second (about $20 per vCPU-month) and $0.00000386 per GB-second (about $10 per GB-month), with egress at $0.05 per GB. Hobby has a $5 monthly minimum that includes $5 of usage; Pro has a $20 minimum (pricing).
  • Fly.io: runs your container image as Fly Machines, lightweight VMs that start quickly, in the regions you choose, with private networking between them. A shared-cpu-1x Machine costs $2.19 a month with 256 MB and $3.69 with 512 MB; outbound data is $0.02 per GB in North America and Europe (pricing). Fly.io states that it signs BAAs for healthcare apps.
  • Azure App Service: Microsoft's PaaS for web apps and APIs. The Linux Basic B1 plan is $0.017 per hour (about $12.41 a month) in East US, and a Free F1 tier exists for testing (pricing).
  • Google App Engine: Google's original PaaS. In the standard environment, the first 28 F1 instance-hours per day are free and then $0.05 per hour (pricing).
  • DigitalOcean App Platform: containers from git or a registry, from $5 a month (512 MiB, limited to one instance) and $12 a month for a 1 GiB instance size you can run several copies of, with outbound transfer beyond the allowance at $0.02 per GiB (pricing).
  • AWS App Runner (closed to new customers): AWS closed App Runner to new customers; existing customers can keep using it. AWS recommends Amazon ECS Express Mode, which, from one API call with an image and two IAM roles, creates an ECS service on Fargate, an Application Load Balancer, autoscaling, and networking in your account, at no charge beyond those resources.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
• Amazon ECS: AWS's own container orchestrator. You define a task (image, CPU, memory, ports) and a service (how many copies, which load balancer). Tasks run either on EC2 instances you manage in an Auto Scaling group (cheaper at steady load, more work) or on AWS Fargate, which runs each task in its own isolated environment and bills $0.04048 per vCPU-hour and $0.004445 per GB-hour (Arm: $0.03238 and $0.00356), per second with a one-minute minimum (Fargate pricing).
  • Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine, Azure Kubernetes Service: managed Kubernetes control planes. EKS and GKE charge $0.10 per cluster-hour (about $73 a month); GKE's free tier gives $74.40 of monthly credit, enough for one zonal or Autopilot cluster (GKE pricing). AKS has a free tier with no management fee and a Standard tier at $0.10 per cluster-hour with an uptime SLA (AKS pricing). Worker nodes, or Autopilot and Fargate pods, are billed on top. See the Kubernetes subject.
  • Google Cloud Run: runs a container image as an autoscaled HTTPS service that can scale to zero. Each instance can serve many requests at once (the concurrency setting). With request-based billing you pay $0.000024 per vCPU-second and $0.0000025 per GiB-second only while an instance is starting, serving requests, or shutting down, plus $0.40 per million requests; the first 180,000 vCPU-seconds, 360,000 GiB-seconds, and 2 million requests each month are free. Billable time is rounded up to 100 ms (pricing).
  • Azure Container Apps: a serverless container service built on Kubernetes, with scale to zero, revisions, and Dapr integration. The consumption plan bills $0.000024 per active vCPU-second, $0.000003 per GiB-second, and $0.40 per million requests, with the same monthly free amounts as Cloud Run per subscription (pricing).

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
• AWS Lambda: the classic function service. Each execution environment is a Firecracker microVM that handles one request at a time; Lambda creates more environments as concurrent requests grow. Pricing is $0.20 per million requests and $0.0000166667 per GB-second on x86 ($0.0000133334 on Arm), with 1 million requests and 400,000 GB-seconds free each month; one invocation can run for up to 15 minutes (pricing, quotas). An HTTP endpoint comes from a function URL, which has no extra charge, or from API Gateway, whose HTTP APIs cost $1.00 per million requests (API Gateway pricing). Two newer options change the model: Lambda Managed Instances (announced November 2025) run functions on EC2 instances in your VPC for a management fee on top of the EC2 price, and Lambda Web Functions (announced October 2026) let an Express or Hono app listen on a port, serve multiple concurrent requests per environment, and pay for active CPU time rather than time spent waiting on the database.
  • Azure Functions: Microsoft's functions service. The Flex Consumption plan is the recommended serverless plan; the Linux Consumption plan stops being available on September 30, 2028 (Microsoft Learn). Flex Consumption on-demand bills $0.000026 per GB-second after 100,000 free GB-seconds and $0.40 per million executions after 250,000 free (Functions pricing).
  • Cloud Run functions: Google renamed Cloud Functions (2nd gen) to Cloud Run functions; they are deployed and billed as Cloud Run services, so the Cloud Run prices above apply.
  • Cloudflare Workers: functions in V8 isolates at every Cloudflare location. The free plan allows 100,000 requests a day with 10 ms of CPU per request; the paid plan has a $5 monthly minimum with 10 million requests and 30 million CPU milliseconds included, then $0.30 per million requests and $0.02 per million CPU milliseconds, with no charge for egress. HTTP requests have no wall-clock limit, and CPU time per request can be raised to 5 minutes (limits). Workers are not a full Node.js server, so database drivers that need raw TCP need adapting.
  • Vercel Functions: server code deployed with a Vercel project, billed by active CPU time (from $0.128 per hour), provisioned memory (from $0.0106 per GB-hour), and invocations ($0.60 per million). Hobby functions run up to 300 seconds; Pro can configure up to 800 seconds (Hobby plan).

docs.title: WebSockets, long requests, and background work
docs.text:
Real APIs are not only short request-response calls. TaskFlow pushes task updates over WebSockets and generates CSV exports that take minutes. These needs rule options in or out:

Platform Longest request or invocation WebSockets Long background work VM, ECS, Kubernetes No platform limit (load balancer idle timeouts apply; ALB defaults to 60 seconds idle) Yes Any worker process Cloud Run Request timeout up to 60 minutes, default 5 Yes, but each connection is a request bound by the timeout, so clients must reconnect (docs) Cloud Run jobs Heroku 30 seconds to start responding Yes Worker dynos AWS Lambda 15 minutes Through API Gateway WebSocket APIs, which hold the connection and invoke the function per message Asynchronous invokes, SQS, Step Functions Cloudflare Workers No wall-clock limit for HTTP; CPU limit up to 5 minutes Yes, with Durable Objects to coordinate Queues, Cron Triggers Vercel Functions 300 seconds on Hobby, configurable to 800 on Pro Not as a long-lived server Separate background services

docs.title: Cold starts
docs.text:
A cold start is the time to create a new instance before it can serve a request: on Lambda, creating the microVM, starting the runtime, loading your code, and running everything at module scope (such as connecting to MongoDB). Later requests reuse the warm environment and skip all of it.

Ways to reduce cold starts, by platform:

  • Lambda: keep the package small, initialize lazily, and use Provisioned Concurrency to keep a set number of environments initialized (billed while configured).
  • Cloud Run: set --min-instances to keep instances warm (billed at the idle rate) and enable startup CPU boost.
  • Azure Functions Flex Consumption: configure always-ready instances.
  • Cloudflare Workers: isolates start in milliseconds, so cold starts are rarely noticeable.
  • Any platform: a slow-starting framework or a large dependency tree is often the biggest part of the delay.

docs.title: What TaskFlow API costs on each
docs.text:
The scenario: 2 million requests a month, 120 ms average duration, 512 MB of memory, in a US region. The arithmetic (free tiers ignored unless stated):

Lambda (x86, 512 MB, function URL)
  requests  2,000,000 x $0.20 / 1M                       = $0.40
  compute   2,000,000 x 0.12 s x 0.5 GB = 120,000 GB-s
            120,000 x $0.0000166667                      = $2.00
  total                                                  = $2.40
  with the free tier (1M requests, 400,000 GB-s free)    = $0.20
  with API Gateway HTTP API: + 2,000,000 x $1.00 / 1M    = $4.40

Cloud Run (1 vCPU, 512 MiB, request-based, worst case: no request overlap)
  billable time rounds up to 100 ms, so each 120 ms request bills 0.2 s
  CPU       2,000,000 x 0.2 s = 400,000 vCPU-s x $0.000024      = $9.60
  memory    400,000 s x 0.5 GiB = 200,000 GiB-s x $0.0000025    = $0.50
  requests  2 x $0.40                                           = $0.80
  total                                                         = $10.90
  after the free tier: (400,000 - 180,000) vCPU-s x $0.000024   = $5.28

Two Fargate tasks (0.5 vCPU, 1 GB) + Application Load Balancer
  tasks     2 x (0.5 x $0.04048 + 1 x $0.004445) x 730           = $36.04
  ALB       730 x $0.0225 + 730 x 1 LCU x $0.008                 = $22.27
  total                                                         = $58.31 (+ public IPv4 addresses)

One small VM: EC2 t4g.small + 20 GB gp3 + public IPv4
  730 x $0.0168 + 20 x $0.08 + 730 x $0.005                     = $17.51 (no redundancy)
Option TaskFlow API, 2M requests a month Notes Lambda + function URL $0.20 (with free tier), $2.40 (without) Scales to zero; cold starts; a connection pool per environment Cloud Run $5.28 (with free tier), $10.90 (without) Worst case; less when requests overlap on one instance Railway $5 Hobby minimum (about $4 of usage at 0.05 vCPU and 0.3 GB average) Bills actual use, not allocation Fly.io, two shared-cpu-1x 512 MB Machines $7.38 Plus $0.02 per GB egress in North America Render, one 512 MB instance $7 (Hobby workspace) Two instances for redundancy: $14 Lightsail or DigitalOcean 2 GB VM $12 Transfer included; patching is yours Azure App Service B1 (Linux) about $12.41 One instance One EC2 t4g.small $17.51 No redundancy Two Fargate tasks + ALB $58.31 Redundant across zones; the cost floor of an always-on HA setup

Azure Container Apps is missing from the table on purpose: it bills a running replica per second at an active rate ($0.000024 per vCPU-second) while it processes requests and at a lower idle rate ($0.000003 per vCPU-second and per GiB-second) otherwise, and with steady traffic a replica rarely scales to zero. Its cost depends on how much of the month the replica counts as active or idle, so estimate it with the Azure calculator rather than assuming the free grant covers it.

At this traffic every option is cheap, so choose for operations and constraints. The picture changes as traffic grows, because functions and request-billed containers cost a fixed amount per request while always-on instances cost the same until they run out of capacity:

Lambda cost per request (no free tier):
  $0.20 / 1M + 0.12 s x 0.5 GB x $0.0000166667 = $0.0000002 + $0.000001 = $0.0000012
  = $1.20 per million requests

Crossover with one t4g.small VM ($17.51):        17.51 / 1.20 = 14.6 million requests a month
Crossover with two Fargate tasks + ALB ($58.31): 58.31 / 1.20 = 48.6 million requests a month

Two cautions. The flat lines are flat only until the instances are full; then you add instances and the line steps up. And the function line ignores the people cost: below the crossover, functions are often cheaper in total because nobody sizes or patches anything.

docs.title: Reserved capacity, Savings Plans, and spot
docs.text:
Always-on compute can be bought for less if you commit:

  • AWS Savings Plans: Compute Savings Plans reduce EC2, Fargate, and Lambda prices by up to 66% for a one- or three-year commitment to a dollar amount per hour; EC2 Instance Savings Plans reach up to 72% for a specific instance family and region (Savings Plans pricing); the Fargate pricing page states up to 50% for Fargate usage.
  • Spot instances: spare EC2 capacity "at a discount of up to 90% off compared to On-Demand pricing" (Spot pricing), which AWS can reclaim with short notice. Good for stateless workers, CI runners, and batch jobs; risky for the only copy of an API.
  • Google Cloud and Azure: committed use discounts (Cloud Run's pricing page lists 1- and 3-year rates) and Azure reservations and savings plans work the same way.

Commit only to the baseline you are confident you will use for the whole term; keep the spiky part on demand. The cost optimization lesson shows how to size a commitment from past usage.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use functions when work is event-driven, spiky, or mostly idle, and when each request is short and independent. Use serverless containers or a platform when you want a normal Express server without managing machines. Use containers on a cluster or VMs when traffic is steady and large, when you need long-lived connections or long jobs, or when you have people who can operate them.

Avoid functions for chatty WebSocket services, multi-minute jobs, or APIs at steady high traffic. Avoid Kubernetes without a team that owns it. Avoid a single VM for anything that must stay up during a hardware failure or a reboot.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Situation Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio Cloud Run or Azure Container Apps (scale to zero, free grants) Render free (sleeps) or a small VPS (DigitalOcean from $4, Hetzner from €5.49) No cost while idle; a VM teaches operations but bills every hour Early startup Render, Railway, or Fly.io; or Cloud Run ECS Express Mode on AWS A normal Express server, git-push deploys, no infrastructure hire Steady high traffic ECS or EKS on EC2 (or GKE) with Savings Plans or committed use discounts Budget VMs (Hetzner, DigitalOcean) behind a load balancer, or owned hardware at very large scale Past the crossover, per-request pricing costs more; commitments cut 50 to 72% Spiky traffic Lambda or Cloud Run with a small warm minimum Containers with aggressive autoscaling Pay for bursts only; watch database connection counts Global audience Cloud Run or Fly.io in two or three regions, edge caching for public reads Cloudflare Workers for light logic near users Latency follows distance, but data has a home; replicate reads, not writes Compliance-heavy (healthcare) ECS, Lambda, or EC2 on AWS under its BAA; Cloud Run or Azure equivalents under their BAAs Fly.io (signs BAAs) or Render's HIPAA workspaces on the Scale plan Contract, audit logging, encryption, and private networking are all available Large files or heavy egress Budget VMs with large included transfer (Hetzner, Linode, DigitalOcean) or Lightsail; serve files from object storage and a CDN Fly.io at $0.02 per GB Stream files from storage, not through the API; see object and file storage Team with no ops people Render, Railway, Heroku, or Cloud Run ECS Express Mode Patching, scaling, TLS, and logs are handled for you

docs.title: TaskFlow API on Lambda with connection reuse
docs.text:
Code at module scope runs once per execution environment, during INIT. Creating the MongoDB client there lets warm invocations reuse it:

// src/lambda.mjs: GET /tasks/:id as a Lambda handler behind a function URL
import { MongoClient, ObjectId } from "mongodb";

// Runs once per execution environment (the cold start); reused while warm.
const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, {
  maxPoolSize: 2, // one request at a time per environment, so keep the pool tiny
  serverSelectionTimeoutMS: 5000,
});
const connected = client.connect();

export const handler = async (event) => {
  // Function URLs send the HTTP API payload format 2.0
  const method = event.requestContext?.http?.method;
  const match = /^\/tasks\/([a-f0-9]{24})$/.exec(event.rawPath ?? "");
  if (method !== "GET" || !match) {
    return { statusCode: 404, body: JSON.stringify({ error: "not found" }) };
  }

  await connected;
  const task = await client
    .db("taskflow")
    .collection("tasks")
    .findOne({ _id: new ObjectId(match[1]) });

  if (!task) {
    return { statusCode: 404, body: JSON.stringify({ error: "task not found" }) };
  }
  return {
    statusCode: 200,
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify(task),
  };
};

The catch is multiplication: 500 concurrent environments each hold up to two connections, so the database sees up to 1,000 connections during a burst. Cap the function's reserved concurrency, size the pool per environment, and check the connection limit of the database tier (see managed databases).

docs.title: TaskFlow API on Cloud Run with a warm instance
docs.text:
# One warm instance, 80 concurrent requests per instance, faster cold starts
gcloud run deploy taskflow-api \
  --image=us-docker.pkg.dev/example-project/apps/taskflow-api:1.4.0 \
  --region=us-central1 \
  --port=3000 \
  --cpu=1 --memory=512Mi \
  --concurrency=80 \
  --min-instances=1 --max-instances=20 \
  --cpu-boost \
  --timeout=300 \
  --set-secrets=MONGODB_URI=taskflow-mongodb-uri:latest \
  --allow-unauthenticated
  • --concurrency=80 lets one instance serve many requests while they wait on MongoDB, which is what Node.js is good at; the bill is per instance-second, so overlapping requests share it.
  • --min-instances=1 removes cold starts for normal traffic. With request-based billing an idle minimum instance is billed at the idle rate: 730 hours x 3,600 s x ($0.0000025 for 1 vCPU + 0.5 GiB x $0.0000025) = about $9.86 a month.
  • --cpu-boost gives extra CPU during startup to shorten cold starts.
  • --timeout=300 caps request duration at 5 minutes; long exports belong in a Cloud Run job or a queue worker.

docs.title: TaskFlow API on Azure Container Apps
docs.text:
# Create a scale-to-zero container app with external HTTPS ingress
az containerapp create \
  --name taskflow-api \
  --resource-group rg-taskflow \
  --environment taskflow-env \
  --image ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0 \
  --target-port 3000 \
  --ingress external \
  --cpu 0.5 --memory 1.0Gi \
  --min-replicas 0 --max-replicas 5 \
  --secrets mongodb-uri=<connection-string> \
  --env-vars MONGODB_URI=secretref:mongodb-uri

The secret is stored on the app and injected through secretref:, so the connection string never appears in the environment variable definition. Set --min-replicas 1 when cold starts matter more than the idle cost.

docs.title: A capacity check before trusting a flat line
docs.text:
Fixed-price options are cheaper past the crossover only if they can carry the load. A rough check for TaskFlow API on two Fargate tasks:

Measured in a load test: 20 ms of CPU per request (the rest is waiting on MongoDB)
One task has 0.5 vCPU = 500 ms of CPU per second
Max per task at 100% CPU:      500 / 20      = 25 requests per second
Target 60% CPU for headroom:   25 x 0.6      = 15 requests per second per task
Two tasks:                                     30 requests per second
Per month:  30 x 3,600 x 730                 = about 78.8 million requests
Peak-to-average ratio of 3:  78.8M / 3       = about 26 million requests a month

So two tasks handle TaskFlow up to roughly 26 million requests a month with a 3x daily peak. The Lambda crossover at 48.6 million is past that point, which means a third or fourth task (and its cost) belongs in the comparison. Always compare at the capacity you would actually run.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start from constraints (connections, durations, compliance), then team skills, then cost.
  • Keep the app a normal HTTP server in a container image; it then runs on VMs, platforms, Cloud Run, Fargate, and, with Lambda Web Functions, even on Lambda without rewriting.
  • Price at the capacity you would really run, including redundancy and peak headroom, not at one instance.
  • Put database connection pooling in front of function-based APIs, or cap concurrency, before the first traffic spike.
  • Keep a warm minimum for user-facing APIs on scale-to-zero platforms.
  • Commit (Savings Plans, committed use discounts) only to the steady baseline you are sure of.
  • Watch provider announcements for the products you run on, and keep deployment definitions in code so a forced move is routine.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• p99 latency spikes after quiet periods. Detect: traces show an INIT or startup span on slow requests; Lambda reports Init Duration in its REPORT log line. Cause: cold starts on a scale-to-zero or function platform. Fix: set a minimum of warm instances or Provisioned Concurrency, trim dependencies, and defer heavy initialization.
  • The database runs out of connections during a traffic spike. Detect: database errors such as "too many connections" while function concurrency climbs. Cause: every new execution environment opens its own pool. Fix: cap reserved concurrency, shrink the pool to one or two per environment, and use a pooler (RDS Proxy, PgBouncer) or a data API designed for serverless clients.
  • WebSocket clients disconnect every few minutes. Detect: reconnect storms at regular intervals in client logs. Cause: a platform request timeout (Cloud Run's configured timeout) or a load balancer idle timeout. Fix: raise the timeout to the platform's maximum, send heartbeats, make clients reconnect with backoff, or move the WebSocket service to containers or VMs without a request limit.
  • Requests fail with H12 errors on Heroku. Detect: H12 in the router logs. Cause: the request did not start responding within 30 seconds. Fix: move slow work to a worker dyno and a queue, and return 202 Accepted with a status URL.
  • The serverless bill grows faster than traffic. Detect: cost per million requests rising month over month. Cause: longer durations (slower queries, more memory), retries, or polling clients. Fix: profile the handler, fix slow queries, cache reads, and re-run the crossover math; past it, move the steady part to containers.
  • A single VM's reboot takes the API down. Detect: the uptime monitor shows downtime matching a host maintenance event. Cause: no redundancy. Fix: run two instances in different zones behind a load balancer, or move to a managed platform that replaces instances for you.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Execution environment: the isolated sandbox (on Lambda, a Firecracker microVM) in which a function runs.
  • Cold start: the extra latency when a new instance or environment must be created and initialized.
  • Concurrency (Cloud Run): how many requests one instance may serve at the same time.
  • Provisioned Concurrency: Lambda environments kept initialized ahead of demand, billed while configured.
  • Dyno: Heroku's name for a container running your app.
  • Task (ECS) and pod (Kubernetes): the unit of one or more containers that the orchestrator schedules.
  • Fargate: AWS's serverless container compute for ECS and EKS.
  • Function URL: a built-in HTTPS endpoint for a Lambda function.
  • Crossover point: the traffic level at which two pricing models cost the same.
  • Savings Plan / committed use discount: a lower price in exchange for a one- or three-year commitment.
  • Spot capacity: spare capacity sold at a discount that the provider can reclaim.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming functions are always cheapest; past the crossover they are not.
  • Comparing one VM to a multi-zone function service as if both were equally available.
  • Ignoring the 30-second, 5-minute, or 15-minute limits until a slow export fails in production.
  • Opening a large connection pool in every function environment.
  • Running Kubernetes for one or two services without anyone to upgrade it.
  • Building on a free plan that sleeps and treating the wake-up delay as an application bug.
  • Starting new projects on a product that is closed to new customers (App Runner) instead of its named replacement.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain what happens during a Lambda cold start and which code runs only once per environment.
  2. Why can Cloud Run serve the same traffic more cheaply with a higher concurrency setting?
  3. Calculate the monthly Lambda cost for 10 million requests at 200 ms and 1 GB without the free tier. (Answer: requests 10 x $0.20 = $2.00; compute 10,000,000 x 0.2 x 1 = 2,000,000 GB-s x $0.0000166667 = $33.33; total $35.33.)
  4. At what monthly request volume does that same function cost as much as two Fargate tasks with an ALB at $58.31? (Answer: cost per million = $3.53, so about 16.5 million requests.)
  5. Which platforms on this page cannot hold a WebSocket open for an hour, and what are the workarounds?
  6. What did AWS recommend to new customers instead of App Runner, and what does it create in your account?
  7. When does a $12 VM beat every serverless option, and what risks come with it?
  8. A team of two is building a healthcare scheduling API with steady daytime traffic. Which hosting would you pick and why?

docs.title: Video Storage and Streaming
docs.text: Video is the one kind of file you should almost never serve as-is. A single uploaded MP4 is too big for phones on weak networks, too small for large screens, and often in a format some browsers cannot play. Serving video well means turning one upload into several versions, cutting them into small segments, describing them in a playlist, and delivering the segments from a CDN to a player that switches quality as the network changes. This lesson explains that pipeline, live versus on-demand video, DRM, the do-it-yourself route on AWS (S3, AWS Elemental MediaConvert, CloudFront), the managed video platforms (Mux, Cloudflare Stream, Bunny Stream, api.video, Vimeo, Amazon IVS for live, and YouTube for public content), and what each costs with a worked example.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Video dominates bandwidth. One minute of 1080p video at 5 Mbps is about 37.5 MB, so a product that adds training videos or recorded meetings can multiply its egress overnight. Video also has hard user-facing failure modes: a player that buffers, a stream that will not start on iPhones, or a "private" course video that anyone can download because its URL leaked.

The build-versus-buy decision is unusually sharp. Building the pipeline yourself on S3, a transcoder, and a CDN gives control and can be cheap at steady scale, but it is a set of moving parts (encoding settings, ladder design, packaging, signed URLs, DRM key servers, player compatibility) that a small team has to own. Managed platforms turn all of that into an upload API and a player, billed per minute. Knowing the cost drivers lets you see where each choice wins.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix Open Connect. Open Connect is Netflix's own content delivery network. Netflix provides embedded Open Connect Appliances to qualifying internet service providers at no charge and also interconnects at internet exchanges, so video is served from inside or next to the viewer's ISP. Netflix states the aim is the best viewing experience while reducing traffic that would otherwise cross transit providers. At that scale, owning the delivery layer beats any CDN bill.
  • Netflix per-title encoding. In Per-Title Encode Optimization (2015) Netflix described replacing one fixed bitrate ladder for every title with a ladder computed per title, because simple content such as animation reaches the same visual quality at far lower bitrates than complex, grainy action scenes. The lesson for everyone: the encoding ladder is a cost lever, not a constant.
  • Twitch and Amazon IVS. The Amazon IVS page says the service uses "the same live streaming technology and global infrastructure that powers Twitch", with low-latency streams of about 3 to 5 seconds and real-time streams under 300 milliseconds. Live video at scale is specialised enough that AWS sells Twitch's stack as a service.
  • Azure Media Services retirement. Microsoft's retirement guide states that Azure Media Services was retired on June 30, 2024, and points customers to partner solutions. Teams built on it had to migrate encoding, packaging, and playback in a fixed window, a reminder to keep video in portable formats (HLS, DASH, MP4 in your own storage) whichever platform you choose.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Elemental MediaConvert, MediaLive, and MediaPackage, Amazon CloudFront, Amazon IVS, Google Cloud Transcoder API, Live Stream API, and Media CDN, Mux, Cloudflare Stream, Bunny Stream, api.video, Vimeo, YouTube, FFmpeg, Shaka Packager, and the players hls.js, Shaka Player, and Video.js.

docs.title: The video delivery pipeline
docs.text:
1. Upload. The source file (often called the mezzanine) goes straight to storage with a presigned or resumable upload (the tus protocol, S3 multipart). Large video should never pass through your API servers.
  2. Transcode. An encoder decodes the source and re-encodes it into several renditions: the same video at different resolutions and bitrates. Codecs: H.264/AVC plays everywhere; HEVC/H.265 and VP9 give similar quality at lower bitrates on supported devices; AV1 is royalty-free and compresses best but needs newer hardware to decode efficiently. Audio is usually AAC.
  3. Package. Each rendition is cut into short segments (2 to 6 seconds) and described by a playlist. HLS (HTTP Live Streaming, RFC 8216) uses .m3u8 playlists; MPEG-DASH uses an XML .mpd manifest. CMAF is a common fragmented-MP4 segment format both can reference, so one set of segments can serve HLS and DASH players.
  4. Store. Segments and playlists sit in object storage as ordinary files. A 10-minute video with a 4-rung ladder in 4-second segments is about 600 segment files plus playlists.
  5. Deliver. A CDN caches the segments near viewers. Every segment is a normal HTTP GET, which is why video scales with the same tools as static files.
  6. Play. The player downloads the master playlist, picks a rendition, fetches segments ahead of the playhead, measures throughput, and switches renditions between segments. Safari plays HLS natively; other browsers use Media Source Extensions through hls.js, Shaka Player, or Video.js.

docs.title: Adaptive bitrate (ABR) and the encoding ladder
docs.text:
The ladder is the list of renditions you produce. The example above (1080p at 5 Mbps down to 360p at 0.8 Mbps) is a reasonable starting point for talking-head and screen-recording content; fast sports needs more bits, slides need fewer. Rules that make ABR work:

  • Aligned keyframes. Every rendition must start each segment with a keyframe at the same timestamps, or switching causes glitches. Encoders are told to place keyframes at fixed intervals and not at scene cuts.
  • Segment length trade-off. Short segments switch faster and start faster but mean more requests and slightly worse compression. Four to six seconds is common for on-demand video.
  • Bitrate equals cost. Storage grows with the sum of all rungs; egress grows with the rung viewers actually watch. Dropping a 1080p rung that most viewers cannot use saves both.

A minimal HLS master playlist for that ladder:

#EXTM3U
#EXT-X-VERSION:6
#EXT-X-INDEPENDENT-SEGMENTS
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=5500000,AVERAGE-BANDWIDTH=5000000,RESOLUTION=1920x1080,CODECS="avc1.640028,mp4a.40.2"
1080p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=3300000,AVERAGE-BANDWIDTH=3000000,RESOLUTION=1280x720,CODECS="avc1.4d401f,mp4a.40.2"
720p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=1350000,AVERAGE-BANDWIDTH=1200000,RESOLUTION=854x480,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
480p/index.m3u8
#EXT-X-STREAM-INF:BANDWIDTH=900000,AVERAGE-BANDWIDTH=800000,RESOLUTION=640x360,CODECS="avc1.4d401e,mp4a.40.2"
360p/index.m3u8

BANDWIDTH is the peak bits per second, which the player uses to decide whether a rendition fits; CODECS lets a device skip renditions it cannot decode before downloading anything.

docs.title: Live versus on-demand
docs.text:
On-demand (VOD) Live Input A finished file A continuous stream from an encoder (OBS, a hardware encoder, a browser) Ingest protocol HTTP upload RTMPS is the most common; SRT and WebRTC (WHIP) are increasingly supported Encoding Once, can be slow and multi-pass In real time, every second, for as long as the stream runs Playlist Complete (#EXT-X-ENDLIST) A sliding window the player re-fetches Latency Not applicable Segment length x segments buffered, plus encoding and CDN time; low-latency HLS and WebRTC cut it to seconds or less Failure mode A bad encode, fixed by re-encoding A dropped stream in front of a live audience

Live is harder because nothing can be redone. Use a managed live service (Amazon IVS, Cloudflare Stream Live, Mux live streams, AWS Elemental MediaLive) unless video is your product.

docs.title: Protecting video: signed URLs, encryption, and DRM
docs.text:
Three levels, in increasing strength and cost:

  1. Signed URLs or cookies. The CDN only serves segments to requests carrying a valid, expiring signature (CloudFront signed URLs or cookies, Cloudflare Stream signed tokens, Mux signed playback). This stops link sharing but not a logged-in user saving the stream.
  2. HLS AES-128 encryption. Segments are encrypted and the player fetches the key over HTTPS from your server. Better, but the key is available to the client, so a determined user can still decrypt.
  3. DRM. The browser's or device's content decryption module fetches a licence from a DRM licence server and decrypts inside protected code. Three systems cover the market: Widevine (Google: Chrome, Android, many TVs), FairPlay (Apple: Safari, iOS, tvOS), and PlayReady (Microsoft: Edge, Windows, many TVs). Common Encryption (CENC) lets one set of encrypted segments serve several DRM systems. Studios and paid streaming services require DRM; internal training videos rarely need more than signed URLs.

docs.title: Option 1: build it on AWS (S3 + MediaConvert + CloudFront)
docs.text:
What it is. The do-it-yourself route assembles managed building blocks. An S3 bucket receives uploads. AWS Elemental MediaConvert is a file-based transcoding service: you submit a job (input file, output groups such as HLS or DASH, a ladder of outputs) and it writes segments and playlists back to S3. CloudFront serves them with signed URLs or cookies. For DRM and just-in-time packaging, AWS Elemental MediaPackage sits between storage and CDN; for live, AWS Elemental MediaLive encodes the incoming stream.

You manage: the ladder and encoding settings, job orchestration (an S3 event or queue starts a job; an EventBridge rule reacts when it completes), storage layout and lifecycle, signed URL keys, the player, and DRM integration if needed. AWS manages: the encoding fleet, scaling, storage durability, and the CDN.

How it bills (MediaConvert pricing): per minute of output, with each rendition counted separately and normalised by tier, codec, resolution, and frame rate; outputs shorter than 10 seconds are billed as 10 seconds. SD is under 720 lines, HD is 720 to 1080, 4K is above 1080 up to 2160. The Basic tier (for user-generated and short-form content, AVC, HLS and DASH supported) costs $0.0075 per minute for SD and $0.015 per minute for HD at up to 30 fps, single pass, in us-east-1. The Professional tier adds HEVC, AV1, multi-pass quality-optimised encoding, and DRM encryption at higher rates (for example $0.042 per minute for HD AVC multi-pass high quality at up to 30 fps). Storage and CloudFront delivery are billed as on the object storage page.

Google Cloud and Azure. Google Cloud offers the Transcoder API for files, the Live Stream API for live, and Media CDN for delivery. Azure no longer has a first-party media service after the Media Services retirement; Azure customers use partners or run their own encoders.

docs.title: Option 2: managed video platforms
docs.text:
Each of these replaces the whole pipeline with an upload API, automatic encoding and packaging, a CDN, and a player or playback URL.

Mux (pricing, detailed rates). An API-first video platform. You upload (direct uploads from the browser are supported), Mux stores a standardised version and creates renditions with "just-in-time encoding" when viewers request them, then delivers over HLS through multiple CDNs. Billing is per minute: input (encoding) is free on the default basic quality level, which uses a reduced ladder and is on-demand only; plus and premium levels cost from $0.025 per input minute. Storage on basic and plus is $0.0024 per minute per month at up to 720p and $0.003 at 1080p; delivery is $0.0008 per minute at up to 720p and $0.001 at 1080p after the first 100,000 free delivered minutes each month, with volume tiers below that. Assets nobody watches drop to 40% and then 60% cheaper storage after 30 and 90 days. Pay-as-you-go includes a $20 monthly usage credit. Mux Data (playback analytics) is included.

Cloudflare Stream (pricing). Bills on two dimensions only: minutes stored, prepaid at $5 per month per 1,000 minutes, and minutes delivered, $1 per 1,000 minutes. Ingress and encoding are free, and bandwidth is included in delivered minutes. Storage depends on duration, not file size. On-demand and live are billed the same way. Delivery is counted per segment (4-second segments for uploads), and playback from the viewer's browser cache is not billed.

Bunny Stream (pricing). Built on bunny.net's storage and CDN: encoding is free, storage is billed per GB (Standard HDD storage from $0.01 per GB per region), and delivery per GB at CDN rates ($0.01 per GB in Europe and North America on the standard network, $0.005 per GB for the first 500 TB on the volume network, per the CDN pricing), with a $1 monthly minimum. Because delivery is per GB rather than per minute, higher bitrates cost more, and the price is low.

api.video (pricing). An API-first platform with free encoding and pay-as-you-go storage and delivery billed per minute ("as low as" $0.00285 per minute stored and $0.0017 per minute delivered on the pricing page, with volume discounts).

Vimeo (pricing). A video hosting product with a polished player, privacy settings, and team features, sold as subscription plans rather than raw usage. It suits marketing and company videos where a team wants a hosting product, not an API.

Amazon IVS (pricing). Managed live streaming. Billing is per hour of input and per hour of output per viewer, by resolution. In North America, a Standard channel (which transcodes renditions for ABR) costs $2.00 per input hour and a Basic channel $0.20; output costs $0.036 per viewer-hour for SD, $0.072 for HD, and $0.144 for Full HD for the first 10,000 hours a month. Real-time stages (WebRTC, under 300 ms) bill per participant-hour.

YouTube (public content). Free hosting and delivery for public or unlisted videos, with YouTube's player, branding, recommendations, and advertising rules. Ideal for marketing and public tutorials; unsuitable for private customer content, paid courses, or anything you must control.

docs.title: Options compared
docs.text: Option What it is You manage Pricing model Free tier Strengths Weaknesses Lock-in S3 + MediaConvert + CloudFront Building blocks Ladder, jobs, player, signing, DRM Output minutes + GB stored + GB delivered CloudFront 1 TB/month Full control; cheap encoding; flat-rate CDN plans Most moving parts; you own failures Low: standard HLS/DASH files in your bucket Mux API video platform Uploads, player choice Per minute stored and delivered, by quality and resolution 100,000 delivered minutes/month Excellent API, analytics, JIT encoding Per-minute delivery adds up for long viewing Medium: re-encode to leave Cloudflare Stream API video platform on Cloudflare Uploads, player $5 per 1,000 min stored, $1 per 1,000 min delivered None Simplest bill, free encoding and ingress Fewer encoding controls; per-minute delivery Medium Bunny Stream Storage + CDN + encoder Uploads, player Per GB stored and delivered $1 minimum Lowest delivery price per GB Fewer enterprise features; DRM is an add-on Medium api.video API video platform Uploads, player Per minute stored and delivered Free encoding Simple API Smaller provider Medium Vimeo Hosted video product Settings and pages Subscription plans Plan-based Player, privacy, team tools Not built for app-scale APIs Medium Amazon IVS Managed live streaming Encoder setup, player Input hours + viewer-hours by resolution None stated Twitch-grade live, 3 to 5 s latency Live only; viewer-hours grow with audience Medium YouTube Public video platform Uploads, metadata Free Free Free reach and delivery No control, ads, not private High for audience, low for files

docs.title: Cost drivers and a worked example
docs.text:
Prices checked November 2026

Prices here are US-region list prices in USD (AWS us-east-1 and North America), checked in November 2026 from the official pages linked above. Video pricing changes often and volume discounts are common; re-check with the AWS Pricing Calculator and each provider's page before deciding. Other regions, for example India, are priced differently; on AWS select the region in the calculator, and on per-region CDNs check the region table.

Every video bill is a mix of four drivers:

Driver Unit What moves it Encoding Minutes of input or output Number of renditions, codec, resolution, quality tier Storage GB-month or minutes stored Library length x sum of rendition bitrates (plus originals) Delivery GB delivered or minutes watched Viewers x hours watched x average bitrate actually watched Extras Per month, per play, per hour DRM, live input hours, captions, analytics

Egress in GB is minutes watched x 60 x bitrate (Mbps) / 8 / 1,000. At an average of 3 Mbps, one minute watched is 22.5 MB.

Scenario: TaskFlow Academy. TaskFlow adds a library of training videos for customers. The library holds 10,000 minutes at 1080p and grows by 1,000 minutes a month (11,000 minutes stored). Customers watch 500,000 minutes a month (about 8,300 hours) at an average delivered bitrate of 3 Mbps, which is 11,250 GB of egress. Ladder: 1080p 5 Mbps, 720p 3 Mbps, 480p 1.2 Mbps, 360p 0.8 Mbps (10 Mbps in total, 75 MB per minute of video).

DIY: S3 + MediaConvert (Basic tier, AVC, <=30 fps) + CloudFront pay-as-you-go
  encoding  1,000 new min x (2 HD x $0.015 + 2 SD x $0.0075)   =  $45.00
  storage   11,000 min x 75 MB = 825 GB x $0.023 (S3 Standard)  =  $18.98
  originals 825 GB x $0.004 (Glacier Instant Retrieval)        =   $3.30
  delivery  1,024 GB free + 9,216 GB x $0.085 + 1,010 GB x $0.080 = $864.16
  requests  ~8 million segment requests, under the 10M free    =   $0.00
  total                                                          ~ $931
  (one-time backlog encode: 10,000 min x $0.045 = $450)

DIY with a CloudFront Pro flat-rate plan instead
  ($15: 10M requests, 50 TB transfer; one distribution)
  45.00 + 18.98 + 3.30 + 15.00                                   ~  $82
  (only if the workload fits the plan terms; see the object storage page)

Mux (basic quality, 1080p tier)
  input     free on basic quality                              =   $0.00
  storage   11,000 min x $0.003                                =  $33.00
  delivery  (500,000 - 100,000 free) x $0.001                  = $400.00
  total     $433 before the $20 pay-as-you-go credit         ~ $413
  (an upper bound: views at the 720p tier cost $0.0008 per minute)

Cloudflare Stream
  storage   11 blocks of 1,000 minutes x $5                    =  $55.00
  delivery  500,000 / 1,000 x $1                               = $500.00
  encoding and ingress                                          =   $0.00
  total                                                          ~ $555

Bunny Stream (standard network, one storage region)
  storage   ~825 GB of renditions x $0.01                      =   $8.25
  delivery  11,250 GB x $0.01                                  = $112.50
  encoding                                                      =   $0.00
  total                                                          ~ $121
  (volume network at $0.005 per GB: ~$65)

Live example: a two-hour customer webinar every week (8 hours a month), 1,000 viewers each watching the whole stream at HD.

Amazon IVS, Standard channel, North America
  input     8 h x $2.00                                        =  $16.00
  output    1,000 viewers x 8 h = 8,000 viewer-hours x $0.072   = $576.00
  total                                                          ~ $592

Cloudflare Stream Live
  delivery  8,000 h x 60 = 480,000 min / 1,000 x $1            = $480.00
  recording 480 min stored (fits in one $5 block of 1,000)     =   $5.00
  total                                                          ~ $485

What the example shows:

  • Delivery dominates. Encoding and storage are under $100 a month in every option; delivery is $15 to $864.
  • Per-minute versus per-GB pricing crosses at a bitrate. CloudFront's first-tier rate costs bitrate x 7.5 MB x $0.085 per GB per minute, which equals Cloudflare Stream's $0.001 per minute at about 1.6 Mbps. Above that average bitrate, per-minute platforms beat CloudFront's list egress; per-GB CDNs priced like bunny.net stay cheaper still, and flat-rate CDN plans change the picture entirely.
  • You pay for engineering either way. The DIY numbers exclude the work of building and running the pipeline, the player, and signed-URL or DRM integration. For a small team, the difference between $121 and $555 a month is cheaper than one week of engineering time.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use a managed platform when video supports your product rather than being it, the team has no video expertise, or you need live streaming. Build on S3 + a transcoder + a CDN when you need full control of encoding and storage, already run the surrounding AWS pieces, have steady volume where flat-rate or committed CDN pricing applies, or must keep files in your own account for compliance. Use YouTube or Vimeo for public marketing video.

Do not serve a single progressive MP4 for anything longer than a short clip, build your own live pipeline unless video is the product, or pay for DRM when signed URLs meet the requirement.

docs.title: Which to choose
docs.text: Scenario Pick Runner-up Why Side project or portfolio YouTube (unlisted) or Cloudflare Stream Bunny Stream Free or a few dollars; no pipeline to build Early startup adding video to a product Mux Cloudflare Stream Best developer experience, 100,000 free delivered minutes, analytics included; Stream if you want the simplest bill Steady high traffic S3 + MediaConvert + CDN with committed or flat-rate delivery Bunny Stream At steady volume, per-GB delivery at negotiated rates beats per-minute list prices; you control the ladder Spiky traffic (a launch video goes viral) Cloudflare Stream or Mux CloudFront flat-rate plan Per-minute or flat pricing scales without capacity work; no surprise per-GB spikes at list rates Global audience Mux (multiple CDNs) or Cloudflare Stream CloudFront Global edges and multi-CDN delivery matter more than storage location Compliance-heavy (for example healthcare training or patient content) S3 + MediaConvert + CloudFront in an account under the AWS BAA A platform whose official page offers a BAA AWS lists HIPAA-eligible services on its HIPAA reference; check that page for each service you use, and use a video platform for health data only if its official page offers a BAA Large files and heavy egress (long lectures, high bitrate) Bunny Stream DIY with a flat-rate CDN plan Per-GB delivery at $0.005 to $0.01 is far below per-minute or per-GB hyperscaler list prices Team with no ops people Cloudflare Stream Mux One upload API, one bill, free encoding; nothing to operate Live events Amazon IVS Cloudflare Stream Live or Mux Purpose-built low-latency live; choose by latency need and audience size

docs.title: Direct uploads to Cloudflare Stream
docs.text:
TaskFlow API creates a one-time upload URL; the browser uploads straight to Cloudflare, so the video never touches TaskFlow's servers.

// src/video/stream-upload.js: create a direct creator upload (Node 24, built-in fetch)
const ACCOUNT_ID = process.env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID;
const API_TOKEN = process.env.CF_STREAM_TOKEN;

export async function createVideoUpload({ maxMinutes = 60 }) {
  const res = await fetch(
    `https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${ACCOUNT_ID}/stream/direct_upload`,
    {
      method: "POST",
      headers: {
        Authorization: `Bearer ${API_TOKEN}`,
        "Content-Type": "application/json",
      },
      body: JSON.stringify({
        maxDurationSeconds: maxMinutes * 60,
        requireSignedURLs: true, // playback needs a signed token
      }),
    },
  );
  const body = await res.json();
  if (!body.success) throw new Error(`Stream API error: ${JSON.stringify(body.errors)}`);
  // Store uid against the course lesson; give uploadURL to the browser.
  return { uploadURL: body.result.uploadURL, uid: body.result.uid };
}

maxDurationSeconds also reserves that much storage until the real duration is known. Basic POST uploads are limited to 200 MB; larger files must use the resumable tus protocol.

docs.title: DIY: a MediaConvert job from a template
docs.text:
Keep the ladder in a job template (created once in the console or with infrastructure as code), and give each job only the input:

{
  "Inputs": [
    {
      "FileInput": "s3://taskflow-video-uploads/uploads/v_8f2c/source.mp4",
      "AudioSelectors": {
        "Audio Selector 1": { "DefaultSelection": "DEFAULT" }
      }
    }
  ]
}

# Start a transcode with the 4-rung HLS template; tag it with the video ID
aws mediaconvert create-job \
  --role arn:aws:iam::<account-id>:role/taskflow-mediaconvert \
  --job-template taskflow-hls-4-rung \
  --settings file://job-input.json \
  --user-metadata videoId=v_8f2c

An EventBridge rule catches the result and triggers whatever marks the video ready (or alerts on failure):

{
  "source": ["aws.mediaconvert"],
  "detail-type": ["MediaConvert Job State Change"],
  "detail": { "status": ["COMPLETE", "ERROR"] }
}

docs.title: DIY on one machine: FFmpeg to HLS
docs.text:
For small libraries or to understand what a transcoder does, FFmpeg produces a three-rung HLS ladder with aligned keyframes:

# Encode a 3-rung HLS ladder with 2-second keyframes and 4-second segments
mkdir -p out
ffmpeg -i source.mp4 \
  -filter_complex "[0:v]split=3[a][b][c];[a]scale=-2:1080[v1080];[b]scale=-2:720[v720];[c]scale=-2:480[v480]" \
  -map "[v1080]" -c:v:0 libx264 -b:v:0 5000k -maxrate:v:0 5500k -bufsize:v:0 10000k \
  -map "[v720]"  -c:v:1 libx264 -b:v:1 3000k -maxrate:v:1 3300k -bufsize:v:1 6000k \
  -map "[v480]"  -c:v:2 libx264 -b:v:2 1200k -maxrate:v:2 1350k -bufsize:v:2 2400k \
  -map a:0 -map a:0 -map a:0 -c:a aac -b:a 128k -ac 2 \
  -preset veryfast -force_key_frames "expr:gte(t,n_forced*2)" -sc_threshold 0 \
  -f hls -hls_time 4 -hls_playlist_type vod \
  -hls_segment_filename "out/stream_%v_%05d.ts" \
  -master_pl_name master.m3u8 \
  -var_stream_map "v:0,a:0 v:1,a:1 v:2,a:2" \
  "out/stream_%v.m3u8"
  • split and scale=-2:<height> make three resolutions while keeping the aspect ratio (width rounded to an even number).
  • -force_key_frames with -sc_threshold 0 puts a keyframe exactly every 2 seconds in every rendition, so 4-second segments align across rungs.
  • -maxrate and -bufsize cap bitrate peaks so a rendition stays within the BANDWIDTH the player expects.
  • -var_stream_map pairs each video rendition with an audio copy; %v becomes the rendition index, so FFmpeg writes stream_0.m3u8 to stream_2.m3u8, their segments, and master.m3u8 in out/.

Upload the out/ directory to object storage and serve it through a CDN. Running this yourself means owning a worker fleet, retries, and queueing, which is exactly what MediaConvert and the platforms sell.

docs.title: Playing HLS in TaskFlow Web
docs.text:
// web/src/player.js: HLS playback with hls.js, falling back to native HLS
import Hls from "hls.js";

export function attachPlayer(video, src) {
  if (Hls.isSupported()) {
    const hls = new Hls();
    hls.loadSource(src);
    hls.attachMedia(video);
    return () => hls.destroy();
  }
  if (video.canPlayType("application/vnd.apple.mpegurl")) {
    video.src = src; // Safari and iOS play HLS natively
    return () => video.removeAttribute("src");
  }
  throw new Error("HLS is not supported in this browser");
}

src is the master playlist URL, for example https://media.example.com/videos/v_8f2c/master.m3u8, signed if the CDN requires it. The HTML side of <video> is covered in audio and video.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Upload directly from the browser to storage or the platform; never stream video bodies through API servers.
  • Design the ladder for your content and audience; drop rungs few viewers use and measure the bitrate actually delivered.
  • Align keyframes across renditions and keep segment length consistent.
  • Keep the original upload (in an archive class) so you can re-encode with better codecs later; keep a copy of the renditions or originals outside a managed platform if leaving would be costly.
  • Protect private video with signed URLs or tokens at minimum; add DRM only when contracts require it.
  • Estimate delivery as viewers x minutes x bitrate before choosing per-GB or per-minute pricing.
  • Watch playback quality metrics (startup time, rebuffering ratio, average bitrate) with the platform's analytics or a player SDK.
  • Set lifecycle rules: unwatched renditions can be deleted and regenerated from originals; managed platforms often discount unwatched storage.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Videos buffer constantly on mobile networks. Detect: player analytics show a high rebuffering ratio and most sessions stuck on the lowest rendition. Cause: the ladder's lowest rung is too high (for example 720p at 3 Mbps), or segments are too long for fast adaptation. Fix: add a 360p or lower rung, shorten segments, and cap the starting bitrate.
  • Quality switches cause visible glitches or stalls. Detect: errors or decoder resets in player logs at switch points. Cause: keyframes are not aligned across renditions, so segments start at different times. Fix: force fixed keyframe intervals and disable scene-cut keyframes in every rendition.
  • The CDN bill tripled after adding video. Detect: CDN usage grouped by path shows /videos/ dominating bytes; the average delivered bitrate is near the top rung. Cause: a high top rung with the player defaulting to it on desktops, or per-GB delivery at list rates. Fix: review the ladder, cap resolution to the player size, and compare per-minute platforms, per-GB CDNs, and flat-rate plans.
  • Private course videos appear on other sites. Detect: CDN logs show segment requests from unknown referrers or a single URL fetched by many IPs. Cause: unsigned, permanent playlist URLs. Fix: require signed URLs or tokens with short expiry, rotate the signing keys, and add DRM if the content is valuable enough.
  • Uploads of long recordings fail at 90%. Detect: client errors on large uploads, often after minutes; platform logs show partial uploads. Cause: a single-request upload over an unreliable connection or past a size limit (200 MB for basic Cloudflare Stream uploads). Fix: use resumable uploads (tus or S3 multipart) with retry per chunk.
  • Transcode jobs pile up after a bulk import. Detect: MediaConvert queue metrics or job counts in SUBMITTED status grow; videos stay "processing" for hours. Cause: thousands of jobs submitted at once into an on-demand queue. Fix: rate-limit job submission through a work queue, prioritise new user uploads over backfill, and process the backlog off-peak.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Rendition: One encoded version of a video at a given resolution and bitrate.
  • Encoding ladder: The set of renditions produced for adaptive playback.
  • ABR (adaptive bitrate streaming): Playback that switches renditions segment by segment to match the viewer's bandwidth.
  • Segment: A short chunk of a rendition (typically 2 to 6 seconds) fetched with an HTTP GET.
  • HLS / DASH: The two main HTTP streaming formats; HLS uses .m3u8 playlists, DASH uses .mpd manifests.
  • CMAF: A common fragmented-MP4 segment format usable by both HLS and DASH.
  • Mezzanine: The high-quality source file kept for re-encoding.
  • Keyframe (I-frame): A frame decodable on its own; segments and switches must start on one.
  • DRM: Digital rights management; licence-based decryption inside a protected module (Widevine, FairPlay, PlayReady).
  • Viewer-hour / minute delivered: Units used by live and video platforms to bill delivery regardless of bytes.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Serving the original upload as a single MP4 to every device.
  • Thinking encoding is the expensive part; delivery usually dominates.
  • Comparing per-minute and per-GB prices without converting through the average bitrate.
  • Believing signed URLs or AES-128 encryption are DRM.
  • Building a live pipeline for a monthly webinar.
  • Throwing away the originals, which blocks re-encoding with better codecs later.
  • Assuming a managed platform is forever; Azure Media Services customers had to migrate when it was retired.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the steps from upload to playback, and say which run once per video and which run on every view.
  2. Why must keyframes be aligned across renditions, and what happens to playback if they are not?
  3. What do HLS, DASH, and CMAF each define, and how do they relate?
  4. Calculate the egress in GB for 200,000 minutes watched at an average of 2 Mbps, and its cost at $0.085 per GB. (Answer: 200,000 x 60 x 2 / 8 / 1,000 = 3,000 GB; 3,000 x $0.085 = $255.)
  5. At what average bitrate does CloudFront's $0.085 per GB equal a per-minute price of $0.001? Show the formula.
  6. When are signed URLs enough, and when do you need DRM?
  7. A team of two engineers wants to add course videos to its SaaS. Which option would you recommend and why? What would change your answer?
  8. Why is live video harder to run yourself than on-demand video?

docs.title: Infrastructure as Code Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the infrastructure as code lessons, for use before an interview or an infrastructure change.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does terraform init Sets up the backend, providers, modules, and .terraform.lock.hcl terraform init -upgrade Upgrades providers within the constraints; review the lock file diff terraform init -migrate-state Moves existing state into a newly configured backend terraform fmt -check -recursive Fails CI if files are not in the standard format terraform validate Checks syntax, types, and references terraform plan -out=tfplan Saves the computed changes; changes nothing terraform apply tfplan Applies exactly the reviewed plan; a stale plan is refused terraform plan -detailed-exitcode Drift check: exit 0 no changes, 1 error, 2 changes terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf Drafts resource blocks for import blocks terraform plan -replace=<addr> Forces one resource to be recreated terraform state list / state show <addr> Inspects what is in state terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID> Removes a stale lock once no run is active terraform output -raw <name> Reads an output for scripts packer init / validate / build -var image_version=... Installs plugins, checks, and builds a golden image

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# envs/prod/versions.tf: pinned versions, S3 state with native locking
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0" # any 6.x, never 7.0
    }
  }
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "example-taskflow-terraform-state"
    key          = "prod/uploads/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true # lock object: <key>.tflock
  }
}

# refactor.tf: adopt, rename, and forget without recreating anything
import {
  to = module.uploads.aws_s3_bucket.this
  id = "taskflow-prod-uploads-123456789012"
}

moved {
  from = aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.api_s3
  to   = aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.api_uploads
}

removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy_exports
  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

# clusters/prod/taskflow-api.yaml (excerpt): Argo CD automated sync
spec:
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true      # delete resources removed from Git
      selfHeal: true   # revert changes made directly in the cluster

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Many providers (clouds, DNS, CDN, GitHub) Terraform or OpenTofu Largest provider ecosystem One cloud and its native tooling CloudFormation or CDK (AWS), Bicep (Azure) The cloud keeps the state Loops, classes, and unit tests Pulumi or CDK General-purpose languages To configure long-lived machines Ansible Agentless configuration management over SSH Environments with different credentials A root module and account per environment Own state, credentials, and blast radius Stateless servers on VMs Packer golden images, replace instances No drift; roll back by launching the previous image Many clusters, some behind firewalls Pull-based GitOps (Argo CD or Flux) Credentials stay in each cluster A web UI and many clusters from one place Argo CD Application-centric, visual diffs Lightweight controllers in each cluster Flux Configured entirely through Kubernetes resources

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Plan symbols + create, ~ update in place, - destroy, -/+ replace Parallelism 10 operations at a time by default (-parallelism) S3-native locking Terraform 1.10, generally available in 1.11; DynamoDB locking is deprecated Lock permissions s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, s3:DeleteObject on <key>.tflock Refactoring blocks moved 1.1+, import 1.5+, removed 1.7+ Licenses Terraform: Business Source License (August 2023); OpenTofu: MPL 2.0, CNCF sandbox AWS subnet addresses 5 reserved per subnet: a /24 gives 251, a /20 4,091; a /16 VPC holds 65,536 Availability Zones At least 2 for production; 3 is common for databases that elect a leader by majority NAT gateways One per AZ; charged per hour and per GB; an S3 gateway endpoint adds no charge GitOps principles Declarative, versioned and immutable, pulled automatically, continuously reconciled

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Keeping state on a laptop or in Git. Use a remote backend with locking, versioning, encryption, and tight access control.
  • Not committing .terraform.lock.hcl. Commit it; upgrade providers deliberately with terraform init -upgrade.
  • Renaming a resource without a moved block. Add one; the plan should say "has moved to", not destroy and create.
  • Approving without reading the plan. Check every -/+ and destroy; add prevent_destroy to stateful resources.
  • Separating production with workspaces. Give each environment its own root module and state, ideally in its own account.
  • Trusting sensitive = true with secrets. It only hides output; state still holds the value, so restrict access to state.
  • Fixing in the console and leaving it there. Run nightly drift detection; revert or adopt the change within a day.
  • Mutable tags such as latest in GitOps manifests. Pin images by digest; promote by pull request.
