docs.title: Infrastructure as Code Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review IaC fundamentals, Terraform in practice, cloud building blocks, and immutable infrastructure with GitOps. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is infrastructure as code, and what problems does it solve?
docs.text: Managing infrastructure through versioned, reviewed definitions applied by tools. It replaces manual console work ("ClickOps") with reproducible environments, reviewable diffs with previews, history of who changed what and why, and drift detection.

docs.title: 2. What is the difference between declarative and imperative IaC?
docs.text: Declarative code describes the desired end state ("this bucket exists with versioning on"), and the tool computes the changes. Imperative code lists steps ("create a bucket, then enable versioning"), which may fail or duplicate resources on a second run and does not handle deletions or drift by itself.

docs.title: 3. What does idempotent mean in IaC?
docs.text: Applying the same definition once or many times has the same effect. After the first successful apply, applying again changes nothing unless reality drifted from the code.

docs.title: 4. Why does Terraform need a state file?
docs.text: To map resource addresses in code to real objects, remember attributes and dependencies, detect resources removed from code (so it can plan their deletion), and avoid reading every attribute from the cloud on each run.

docs.title: 5. Why is the state file sensitive, and how should it be stored?
docs.text: It contains every attribute of managed resources, including generated passwords and keys in plain text, even when marked sensitive. Store it in a remote backend that is encrypted, versioned, locked, and readable only by the pipeline and a few administrators. Never commit it to Git.

docs.title: 6. What is drift, and how do you detect it?
docs.text: A difference between code and reality caused by changes outside the IaC process, such as console edits. Detect it with scheduled terraform plan -detailed-exitcode runs (exit code 2 means changes), platform drift tools such as CloudFormation drift detection, or continuous reconciliation in GitOps.

docs.title: 7. When you find drift, how do you decide what to do?
docs.text: Revert it (apply the code) if the manual change was a mistake, or adopt it (change the code in a reviewed pull request) if the change was right but made the wrong way. Then reduce the causes, for example by limiting console write access.

docs.title: 8. How does provisioning differ from configuration management?
docs.text: Provisioning creates and manages resources (networks, VMs, databases, buckets) with tools like Terraform or CloudFormation. Configuration management manages what is inside servers (packages, files, services) with tools like Ansible, Chef, or Puppet. Immutable images have reduced the need for the second.

docs.title: 9. Compare Terraform, CloudFormation, and Pulumi.
docs.text: Terraform uses HCL, a state file, and providers for almost any API. CloudFormation uses YAML or JSON templates with state managed by AWS, AWS only. Pulumi uses general-purpose languages with a state backend and many providers. All preview changes before applying them.

docs.title: 10. Why does OpenTofu exist?
docs.text: HashiCorp moved Terraform from the open-source MPL 2.0 license to the Business Source License in August 2023. The community forked the last open-source version as OpenTofu, now hosted by the Linux Foundation and a CNCF sandbox project, kept under MPL 2.0 and largely compatible with Terraform configuration.

docs.title: 11. What does a safe pull request workflow for infrastructure look like?
docs.text: Format, validate, and policy-check on every push; plan with a read-only role and post the plan for review; read the plan, especially replacements and destroys; apply on merge from a saved plan with a write role that only the main-branch pipeline can use.

docs.title: 12. What do required_providers and .terraform.lock.hcl do?
docs.text: required_providers declares which providers a module needs, with source addresses and version constraints. The lock file records the exact versions and checksums chosen by terraform init. Commit the lock file so every machine and CI run uses the same provider builds.

docs.title: 13. What is the difference between a resource and a data source?
docs.text: A resource is something Terraform creates, updates, and deletes. A data source only reads existing information, such as the current account ID or an IAM role managed by another stack.

docs.title: 14. How does Terraform decide the order of operations?
docs.text: It builds a dependency graph from references between blocks; a resource that references another is created after it, and independent resources are created in parallel (10 at a time by default). depends_on adds dependencies that references cannot express.

docs.title: 15. Why apply a saved plan?
docs.text: terraform apply tfplan applies exactly the changes that were reviewed. If state changed after the plan was made, Terraform rejects the stale plan instead of applying something nobody reviewed.

docs.title: 16. How does state locking work with the S3 backend today?
docs.text: With use_lockfile = true, Terraform creates a .tflock object next to the state with a conditional write that fails if it already exists, so only one run holds the lock. It was introduced in Terraform 1.10 and is generally available from 1.11; DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated.

docs.title: 17. Why separate environments by directories instead of workspaces?
docs.text: Separate root modules (ideally in separate cloud accounts) give each environment its own state, credentials, and blast radius, and allow deliberate differences. Workspaces share code and backend credentials, making it easy to apply to the wrong environment; Terraform's own documentation says they are not suitable where separate credentials and access controls are needed.

docs.title: 18. What makes a good Terraform module?
docs.text: A meaningful unit (a private bucket with its policy, a service with its scaling), a small typed and validated interface with useful outputs, no provider configuration inside, and versioning so environments upgrade deliberately.

docs.title: 19. How do you rename a resource without destroying it?
docs.text: Add a moved block from the old address to the new one. The plan shows "has moved to" instead of destroy and create. Remove the block once it has been applied everywhere.

docs.title: 20. How do you bring an existing, hand-made resource under Terraform?
docs.text: Write an import block with the target address and the resource ID (Terraform 1.5+). terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf can draft the resource configuration, which you then clean up and review.

docs.title: 21. How do you stop managing a resource without deleting it?
docs.text: Use a removed block with lifecycle { destroy = false } (Terraform 1.7+). The resource leaves state but stays in the cloud.

docs.title: 22. How do you protect critical resources from accidental deletion?
docs.text: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail. Combine it with reviewing plans for -/+ replacements and with cloud-side protections such as deletion protection on databases.

docs.title: 23. What is the risk of -target?
docs.text: It applies only part of the configuration, leaving the rest unapplied and the state partially updated relative to code. It is for emergencies, not routine use.

docs.title: 24. How do you bootstrap the bucket that stores Terraform state?
docs.text: Create it with a tiny separate configuration using local state (or a documented manual step), with versioning, encryption, public access blocked, and prevent_destroy. Optionally migrate that configuration's own state into the bucket with terraform init -migrate-state.

docs.title: 25. Which credentials should plan and apply use in CI?
docs.text: Plans on pull requests use a read-only role; applies use a separate role with write access that only the main-branch pipeline (often behind an environment approval) can assume, through OIDC federation rather than stored keys.

docs.title: 26. What are regions and Availability Zones, and how should production use them?
docs.text: A region is a geographic area; an Availability Zone is an independent failure domain within it. Production should span at least two AZs in every tier; multiple regions add resilience to regional failures at a large cost in complexity.

docs.title: 27. What makes a subnet public on AWS?
docs.text: Its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to an internet gateway. Only load balancers and NAT gateways usually belong there; compute and databases go in private subnets.

docs.title: 28. What does a NAT gateway do, and why one per AZ?
docs.text: It lets resources in private subnets make outbound connections without accepting inbound ones. Each NAT gateway lives in one AZ, so one per AZ keeps each zone's outbound traffic working if another zone fails.

docs.title: 29. How can you reduce NAT gateway costs?
docs.text: Route traffic to cloud services through VPC endpoints: a gateway endpoint for S3 has no additional charge, and interface endpoints serve other services privately. NAT gateways charge per hour and per gigabyte processed.

docs.title: 30. Compare security groups and network ACLs.
docs.text: Security groups attach to network interfaces, are stateful, allow-only, and can reference other security groups. Network ACLs attach to subnets, are stateless (return traffic must be allowed), support allow and deny rules, and are evaluated in rule-number order.

docs.title: 31. How do you restrict database access to the application only?
docs.text: Put the database in subnets without internet routes and give its security group an ingress rule that references the application's security group on the database port, with no CIDR-based rules.

docs.title: 32. How many usable addresses does a /24 subnet have on AWS?
docs.text: 256 addresses minus 5 that AWS reserves in every subnet: 251.

docs.title: 33. When would you choose VMs, Kubernetes, serverless containers, or functions?
docs.text: VMs for full OS control or special software; Kubernetes for many services with a team able to operate it; serverless containers for container workloads without managing servers or clusters; functions for event-driven or spiky work without long-lived connections.

docs.title: 34. Compare object, block, and file storage.
docs.text: Object storage (S3) holds whole objects behind an HTTP API, ideal for uploads, static assets, and backups. Block storage (EBS) is a disk for one instance, used by databases. File storage (EFS) is a shared file system for several instances.

docs.title: 35. What are the key IAM principles?
docs.text: Least privilege, roles with temporary credentials for workloads, federation and MFA for people, a locked-away root account, separate accounts per environment, organization-wide guardrails, and regular auditing and cleanup of permissions.

docs.title: 36. What is static stability?
docs.text: Designing a service so it keeps working during a failure without needing to create or change resources, for example by running enough spare capacity in each AZ that losing one zone needs no scaling action.

docs.title: 37. What is immutable infrastructure?
docs.text: Instances are never changed after deployment; a change means building a new image and replacing the instances. It eliminates configuration drift, ensures what runs equals what was tested, and makes rollback "launch the previous image".

docs.title: 38. What is the difference between pets and cattle?
docs.text: Pets are individually named, hand-maintained servers that are repaired when sick. Cattle are interchangeable instances that are replaced when unhealthy. Cloud platforms and orchestrators are designed for cattle.

docs.title: 39. What is a golden image, and how is it built?
docs.text: A machine image with the OS, hardening, agents, and runtime (sometimes the application) pre-installed. Packer builds it by launching a temporary instance from a base image, running provisioners, and saving the result. Rebuild it regularly to include security patches.

docs.title: 40. Where does Ansible still fit if infrastructure is immutable?
docs.text: Building images (as a Packer provisioner), managing long-lived machines that cannot be replaced, network devices and on-premises hardware, and one-off fleet operations.

docs.title: 41. What are the four GitOps principles?
docs.text: Desired state is declarative; it is versioned and immutable in a store such as Git; agents pull it automatically; and agents continuously reconcile actual state with it.

docs.title: 42. Compare push-based and pull-based deployment.
docs.text: In push, CI applies changes to environments and must hold their credentials; drift after the run goes unnoticed. In pull, an agent inside each environment fetches desired state and reconciles continuously, so credentials stay inside, Git history is the deployment history, and manual changes are detected or reverted.

docs.title: 43. What do Argo CD's prune and selfHeal options do?
docs.text: prune deletes live resources that were removed from Git. selfHeal reverts changes made directly in the cluster so it matches Git again.

docs.title: 44. How does promotion work in a GitOps environment repository?
docs.text: CI commits a new image digest to the staging overlay; after staging is verified, a pull request copies the same digest into the production overlay. Merging deploys; reverting the commit rolls back.

docs.title: 45. Why pin images by digest rather than tags in GitOps?
docs.text: A digest identifies exact image content and never changes, so Git states precisely what runs. A mutable tag such as latest can point to different images over time, breaking reproducibility and rollback.

docs.title: 46. How are secrets handled in GitOps repositories?
docs.text: Never in plain text. Use SOPS-encrypted files decrypted by the agent, Sealed Secrets decrypted by an in-cluster controller, or references to an external secret store synced by a controller.

docs.title: 47. What is the difference between Argo CD and Flux?
docs.text: Both reconcile Kubernetes from Git. Argo CD centers on Application resources with a strong web UI and can manage many clusters from one place. Flux is a set of composable controllers configured through Kubernetes resources, typically installed in each cluster, CLI-first.

docs.title: 48. A pull request's Terraform plan shows the production database will be replaced. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which attribute forces replacement and whether the resource address changed.

How to confirm: the plan marks the attribute with "forces replacement", or shows destroy at the old address and create at a new one.

Likely causes and fixes: a renamed resource (add a moved block) or a change to an immutable attribute (find an in-place alternative or plan a migration). Add prevent_destroy and deletion protection. See Terraform in practice.

docs.title: 49. Terraform reports "Error acquiring the state lock". What now?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether another plan or apply is running for the same state.

How to confirm: the error shows the lock holder, operation, and time; CI shows an active or crashed run.

Likely causes and fixes: a concurrent run (wait, and serialize CI with concurrency groups) or a stale lock from a crashed run (confirm nothing is running, then terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>). See Terraform in practice.

docs.title: 50. CI and an engineer get different plans for the same commit. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: Terraform and provider versions, and variable inputs.

How to confirm: terraform version and the lock file differ, or different .tfvars files were used.

Likely causes and fixes: an uncommitted lock file or unpinned versions. Commit .terraform.lock.hcl, pin required_version, and run shared-environment plans only in CI. See Terraform in practice.

docs.title: 51. A security group rule added during an incident vanished after an unrelated deploy. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the rule exists in code.

How to confirm: the apply log shows the rule being removed as drift.

Likely causes and fixes: the console change was never adopted into code, so apply reverted it. Adopt emergency changes into code within a day and run nightly drift detection. See IaC fundamentals.

docs.title: 52. The nightly drift job reports that port 22 is open to the internet on the API security group. How do you respond?
docs.text:
What to check first: who made the change and when, from cloud audit logs.

How to confirm: the plan shows the extra ingress rule, and audit logs show a console or CLI call.

Likely causes and fixes: a manual change. Treat it as a security issue: revert by applying the code, review access during the exposure window, and restrict console write permissions in production. See IaC fundamentals.

docs.title: 53. A state file with database passwords was found in a public bucket. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which secrets the state contains and how long it was exposed.

How to confirm: bucket access logs and audit logs for reads of the object.

Likely causes and fixes: state stored without access controls. Rotate every secret in the state, lock down and encrypt the bucket, restrict state access to pipeline roles, and keep secrets out of Terraform where possible. See IaC fundamentals.

docs.title: 54. Someone applied staging configuration to production. How do you prevent a repeat?
docs.text:
What to check first: how environments are separated.

How to confirm: workspaces or a shared set of credentials were used for both.

Likely causes and fixes: move to a root module and state per environment, separate cloud accounts, and roles that can only change their own environment. See Terraform in practice.

docs.title: 55. During an Availability Zone outage, the whole application went down. What was wrong with the design?
docs.text:
What to check first: where instances, NAT gateways, and the database primary ran.

How to confirm: all tasks, or the only NAT gateway, were in the failed zone.

Likely causes and fixes: single-AZ placement. Spread every tier across at least two AZs, run one NAT gateway per AZ, use a multi-AZ database, and keep enough capacity to lose one zone. See cloud building blocks.

docs.title: 56. The monthly bill shows NAT gateway charges larger than compute. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which traffic flows through the NAT gateways.

How to confirm: VPC flow logs show large transfers from private subnets to S3 or other AWS services.

Likely causes and fixes: service traffic routed through NAT. Add an S3 gateway endpoint and interface endpoints for heavily used services. See cloud building blocks.

docs.title: 57. New tasks cannot start during a deploy: "insufficient IP addresses". What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: free IPs in the private subnets.

How to confirm: subnet available-address metrics are near zero during rolling surges.

Likely causes and fixes: subnets sized without headroom for peaks and surge. Add larger or additional subnets and plan capacity including surges and pod IPs. See cloud building blocks.

docs.title: 58. A fix made with kubectl edit in production keeps reverting. Why, and what is the right way?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the application is managed by Argo CD or Flux with self-healing.

How to confirm: the agent's events show a sync restoring the Git state.

Likely causes and fixes: GitOps is working as designed. Make the fix in Git through an emergency pull request, or pause sync through a documented procedure and reconcile afterwards. See immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: 59. Servers in one auto scaling group behave differently. How do you fix it for good?
docs.text:
What to check first: package and configuration differences between hosts.

How to confirm: hosts were patched or edited individually over SSH.

Likely causes and fixes: mutable servers drifting. Build a golden image, replace all instances from it, rebuild images on a schedule, and block in-place changes. See immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: 60. Production is running an image digest that never ran in staging. How did that happen, and how do you prevent it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the history of the production overlay in the environment repository.

How to confirm: a commit set a digest not present in staging's history, made by hand.

Likely causes and fixes: manual edits to production overlays. Automate promotion from staging's recorded digest, protect the branch, and require checks that verify the digest ran in staging. See immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: Terraform in Practice
docs.text:
Terraform (and its open-source fork OpenTofu, which accepts the same configuration for everything on this page) turns HCL files into real infrastructure through providers that talk to cloud and service APIs. This lesson builds a small but real piece of TaskFlow infrastructure, an S3 bucket for user uploads with versioning, encryption, lifecycle rules, and an IAM policy for the API, and uses it to explain providers and required_providers, resources, data sources, variables, locals, outputs, the CLI workflow, the dependency graph, remote state with locking, modules and versioning, separate environments, refactoring with import, moved, and removed blocks, and running plan and apply from CI.

Every Terraform snippet on this page was checked with terraform validate and terraform fmt -check using Terraform 1.17.2 and the AWS provider 6.73.0.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Terraform is the most widely used IaC tool, and most of what goes wrong with it is not syntax but practice: state stored on a laptop, two applies at once, a renamed resource that destroys a production bucket, an apply from a developer's machine with administrator rights, a plan nobody read, or one copy of the code per environment slowly drifting apart. Knowing the language is an afternoon; knowing how to run it safely in a team is what makes infrastructure changes boring.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• S3 backend with native locking. The S3 backend documentation describes use_lockfile, which stores a lock file next to the state object (for state key path/to/key, the lock is path/to/key.tflock) and needs s3:GetObject, s3:PutObject, and s3:DeleteObject on it. It states that DynamoDB-based locking is deprecated and will be removed in a future minor version, and strongly recommends enabling bucket versioning so state can be recovered.
  • Import and refactoring. The Terraform documentation on import blocks and on refactoring modules with moved blocks shows how to adopt existing resources and rename or move resources in code through reviewed plans instead of manual state surgery.
  • Running Terraform in automation. HashiCorp's tutorial Automate Terraform with GitHub Actions describes planning on pull requests, posting the plan for review, and applying on merge to the main branch, the workflow used below.
  • Atlantis. Atlantis is an open-source service that runs terraform plan when a pull request is opened, comments the output, and runs apply on an approved comment, showing how widely the "plan in the PR, apply on approval" model is used.

Popular tools and providers: Terraform CLI, HCP Terraform, OpenTofu, Terragrunt, Atlantis, the hashicorp/setup-terraform GitHub Action, tflint, terraform-docs, Checkov, Trivy, and Infracost.

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
infra/
  modules/
    uploads-bucket/        # reusable building block: inputs, resources, outputs
      versions.tf
      variables.tf
      main.tf
      outputs.tf
  envs/
    staging/               # root module: backend, provider, values for staging
      versions.tf
      main.tf
      variables.tf
      outputs.tf
    prod/                  # root module for production, its own state
      ...

A root module is a directory where you run terraform init, plan, and apply; it has one state. A child module is reusable code called from a root module. Each environment is its own root module with its own backend key, so production and staging never share state.

docs.title: Providers and required_providers
docs.text:
Providers are plugins that know how to talk to one API (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Cloudflare, GitHub, Kubernetes). Declare them with a source address and a version constraint:

terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0" # any 6.x, never 7.0
    }
  }
}

terraform init downloads matching versions and records the exact choice and checksums in .terraform.lock.hcl. Commit the lock file: it makes every machine and CI run use the same provider build. Upgrade deliberately with terraform init -upgrade and review the change.

docs.title: Resources, data sources, variables, locals, outputs
docs.text:
Block Purpose Example resource Something Terraform creates and manages resource "aws_s3_bucket" "this" { ... } data Something Terraform only reads data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {} variable An input, with type, description, default, validation, sensitive variable "bucket_name" { type = string } locals Named expressions computed inside the module bucket_name = "taskflow-${var.environment}-uploads" output A value exported to callers, other tools, or the CLI output "bucket_arn" { value = aws_s3_bucket.this.arn } module A call to a child module module "uploads" { source = "../../modules/uploads-bucket" }

References between blocks (aws_s3_bucket.this.id) are how Terraform learns dependencies.

docs.title: The dependency graph
docs.text: Terraform builds a graph from references: the versioning configuration references the bucket, so the bucket is created first; the IAM policy references the bucket ARN, so it waits too; independent resources are created in parallel (10 at a time by default, -parallelism). Use depends_on only for dependencies Terraform cannot see from references (for example a permission that must exist before a service starts using it). terraform graph prints the graph in DOT format for visualization.

docs.title: The CLI workflow
docs.text:
Command What it does terraform init Configures the backend, downloads providers and modules terraform fmt -recursive Formats files in the standard style (-check in CI) terraform validate Checks syntax, types, and references against provider schemas terraform plan -out=tfplan Computes and saves the changes; changes nothing terraform show tfplan Prints a saved plan for review terraform apply tfplan Applies exactly the saved plan terraform output -raw uploads_bucket Reads an output for scripts terraform state list / state show <addr> Inspects what is in state terraform destroy Plans and applies deletion of everything in this root module

Flags worth knowing: -var-file=prod.tfvars supplies variable values; -replace=<addr> forces one resource to be recreated; -target limits a run to some resources and should be kept for emergencies, because it leaves the rest of the configuration unapplied.

docs.title: Remote state with locking
docs.text:
For a team, state must live in a shared backend with locking. With the S3 backend:

  • use_lockfile = true makes Terraform create a .tflock object next to the state using a conditional write that fails if the object already exists. This S3-native locking was introduced in Terraform 1.10 and is generally available from 1.11, which is why the example requires >= 1.11.
  • The older dynamodb_table option is deprecated. Both can be set at once while migrating from DynamoDB locking.
  • Enable bucket versioning (to recover earlier state), default encryption (or encrypt = true with a KMS key), block all public access, and restrict access to the pipeline roles and a few administrators.
  • The state bucket is created once by a tiny separate configuration (or by hand, documented), because a configuration cannot store its state in a bucket it has not created yet.

Other backends (Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage, HCP Terraform) provide the same two guarantees: shared state and a lock.

docs.title: State is sensitive
docs.text: State contains every attribute of every managed resource, including generated passwords, private keys, and connection strings, in plain text, even when marked sensitive. Treat read access to state like read access to production secrets, keep secrets out of Terraform where you can (reference them from a secret store at runtime instead), and never commit state to Git.

docs.title: Modules and versioning
docs.text:
Good modules:

  • have a small, documented interface: a few required inputs, sensible defaults, typed and validated variables, and the outputs callers need;
  • encapsulate a meaningful unit (a private bucket with its policy, a service with its scaling and alarms), not a single resource;
  • avoid configuring providers inside child modules; the root module passes providers in;
  • are versioned: registry modules with version = "~> 5.1", Git modules with a tag (source = "git::https://github.com/example/tf-modules.git//uploads-bucket?ref=v1.4.0"), so an environment upgrades a module deliberately.

Promote module versions like application releases: staging moves to v1.5.0 first, production follows after it has been applied there.

docs.title: Environments: separate state per environment
docs.text:
Approach How Strengths Weaknesses Directory per environment (recommended) envs/staging, envs/prod, each a root module with its own backend key, often its own cloud account Clear blast radius, different credentials per environment, environments can differ deliberately Some repetition (kept small by modules) Workspaces One root module, terraform workspace select prod switches state Very little duplication Same code and backend credentials for every environment; easy to apply to the wrong workspace; hard to vary structure Wrapper tools (Terragrunt) Generates backend and inputs per environment from one layout Removes repetition at scale Another tool to learn

Terraform's own documentation notes that CLI workspaces are not a suitable isolation mechanism where environments need separate credentials and access controls; separate root modules and accounts are.

docs.title: Refactoring safely: import, moved, and removed
docs.text:
Need Block Effect Adopt a resource created by hand import (Terraform 1.5+) The next plan imports it into state; terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf can draft the resource block Rename or move a resource in code moved (Terraform 1.1+) State is updated to the new address; nothing is destroyed Stop managing a resource without deleting it removed with lifecycle { destroy = false } (Terraform 1.7+) It leaves state but stays in the cloud

All three appear in plans, go through review, and can be removed from the code once applied everywhere. They replace error-prone manual commands such as terraform state mv and terraform import.

docs.title: Plan in CI, apply on merge
docs.text:
• On every pull request: fmt -check, validate, policy scans, and plan with a read-only role; post the plan on the pull request.
  • On merge to main: plan again and apply that saved plan with a write role that only the main-branch pipeline (and an approval in a protected environment) can use.
  • Serialize runs per root module (CI concurrency) in addition to state locking, so applies queue rather than fail.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choice Multi-cloud or many SaaS providers (DNS, CDN, monitoring, GitHub) Terraform or OpenTofu Strictly one cloud with strong native tooling preferences Consider CloudFormation or CDK (AWS) or Bicep (Azure) Team wants loops, classes, and unit tests in a general-purpose language Consider Pulumi or CDK Separate environments with different credentials Directory per environment, not workspaces Short-lived copies of the same stack (per developer, per test) Workspaces can fit Application deploys (new image versions many times a day) Usually not Terraform; use the deployment platform or GitOps, and let Terraform create the platform

docs.title: A reusable module: private, versioned uploads bucket with an IAM policy
docs.text:
# modules/uploads-bucket/versions.tf
terraform {
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = ">= 6.0"
    }
  }
}

# modules/uploads-bucket/variables.tf
variable "bucket_name" {
  description = "Globally unique bucket name."
  type        = string

  validation {
    condition     = can(regex("^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9.-]{1,61}[a-z0-9]$", var.bucket_name))
    error_message = "Bucket names use 3-63 lowercase letters, digits, dots, and hyphens."
  }
}

variable "noncurrent_version_retention_days" {
  description = "How long to keep overwritten or deleted object versions."
  type        = number
  default     = 30
}

# modules/uploads-bucket/main.tf: a private, versioned, encrypted bucket for user uploads
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "this" {
  bucket = var.bucket_name
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "this" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.this.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "this" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.this.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_server_side_encryption_configuration" "this" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.this.id
  rule {
    apply_server_side_encryption_by_default {
      sse_algorithm = "AES256"
    }
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_lifecycle_configuration" "this" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.this.id

  rule {
    id     = "expire-old-versions"
    status = "Enabled"
    filter {}

    noncurrent_version_expiration {
      noncurrent_days = var.noncurrent_version_retention_days
    }
    abort_incomplete_multipart_upload {
      days_after_initiation = 7
    }
  }
}

data "aws_iam_policy_document" "read_write" {
  statement {
    sid       = "ListBucket"
    actions   = ["s3:ListBucket"]
    resources = [aws_s3_bucket.this.arn]
  }
  statement {
    sid       = "ReadWriteObjects"
    actions   = ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject", "s3:DeleteObject"]
    resources = ["${aws_s3_bucket.this.arn}/*"]
  }
}

resource "aws_iam_policy" "read_write" {
  name   = "${var.bucket_name}-read-write"
  policy = data.aws_iam_policy_document.read_write.json
}

# modules/uploads-bucket/outputs.tf
output "bucket_name" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.this.bucket
}

output "bucket_arn" {
  value = aws_s3_bucket.this.arn
}

output "read_write_policy_arn" {
  value = aws_iam_policy.read_write.arn
}
  • Since AWS provider 4, bucket settings are separate resources (aws_s3_bucket_versioning, ..._server_side_encryption_configuration, ..._lifecycle_configuration), each referencing the bucket.
  • The policy grants only what the API needs on this bucket: list the bucket, and get, put, and delete objects in it.
  • Versioning plus a noncurrent-version expiry protects against accidental overwrites without keeping old versions forever.

docs.title: The production root module
docs.text:
# envs/prod/versions.tf: Terraform, provider, and state settings for production
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"

  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }

  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "example-taskflow-terraform-state"
    key          = "prod/uploads/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true # S3-native state locking (no DynamoDB table needed)
  }
}

# envs/prod/main.tf: production wiring for TaskFlow uploads
provider "aws" {
  region = var.region

  default_tags {
    tags = {
      Project     = "taskflow"
      Environment = var.environment
      ManagedBy   = "terraform"
    }
  }
}

data "aws_caller_identity" "current" {}

locals {
  # Account ID keeps the globally unique bucket name predictable per account
  bucket_name = "taskflow-${var.environment}-uploads-${data.aws_caller_identity.current.account_id}"
}

module "uploads" {
  source = "../../modules/uploads-bucket"

  bucket_name                       = local.bucket_name
  noncurrent_version_retention_days = 90
}

# The API's role is created by the platform team's stack; we only attach a policy to it
data "aws_iam_role" "api" {
  name = var.api_role_name
}

resource "aws_iam_role_policy_attachment" "api_uploads" {
  role       = data.aws_iam_role.api.name
  policy_arn = module.uploads.read_write_policy_arn
}

# envs/prod/variables.tf
variable "environment" {
  description = "Deployment environment name."
  type        = string
  default     = "prod"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be dev, staging, or prod."
  }
}

variable "region" {
  type    = string
  default = "eu-west-1"
}

variable "api_role_name" {
  description = "Existing IAM role used by the TaskFlow API workload."
  type        = string
  default     = "taskflow-api-prod"
}

# envs/prod/outputs.tf
output "uploads_bucket" {
  description = "Set as UPLOADS_BUCKET in the API's configuration."
  value       = module.uploads.bucket_name
}

cd envs/prod
terraform init
terraform fmt -check -recursive ../..
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
# Plan: 7 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
terraform apply tfplan
terraform output -raw uploads_bucket   # feed into the API's configuration

default_tags labels every resource with project, environment, and owner without repeating tags in each block. The data sources read the account ID and an IAM role that another team manages, a clean way to connect stacks without sharing state.

docs.title: Bootstrapping the state bucket
docs.text:
# bootstrap/main.tf: run once with local state, then keep this tiny stack separate
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "eu-west-1"
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket" "state" {
  bucket = "example-taskflow-terraform-state"

  lifecycle {
    prevent_destroy = true # a plan that would delete it fails
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "state" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.state.id
  versioning_configuration {
    status = "Enabled"
  }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "state" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.state.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}

After the first apply you can add a backend "s3" block to this bootstrap stack and run terraform init -migrate-state to move its own state into the bucket it created.

docs.title: Refactoring: adopt, rename, and stop managing
docs.text:
# refactor.tf: adopt an existing bucket and record a rename, without recreating anything
import {
  to = module.uploads.aws_s3_bucket.this
  id = "taskflow-prod-uploads-123456789012"
}

moved {
  from = aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.api_s3
  to   = aws_iam_role_policy_attachment.api_uploads
}

# legacy.tf: forget the old exports bucket, keep it in the cloud
removed {
  from = aws_s3_bucket.legacy_exports

  lifecycle {
    destroy = false
  }
}

The plan shows "1 to import" and "has moved to" lines instead of destroy and create. After the change is applied in every environment, the blocks can be deleted.

docs.title: Plan on pull requests, apply on merge
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/terraform-prod.yml
name: Terraform (prod)

on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["infra/envs/prod/**", "infra/modules/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["infra/envs/prod/**", "infra/modules/**"]

permissions:
  contents: read
  id-token: write
  pull-requests: write

concurrency:
  group: terraform-prod
  cancel-in-progress: false

defaults:
  run:
    working-directory: infra/envs/prod

jobs:
  plan:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.17.2"
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-terraform-plan
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: terraform fmt -check -recursive ../..
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform validate
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -lock=false -no-color -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform show -no-color tfplan > plan.txt
      - uses: actions/github-script@v9
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require("fs");
            const fence = "`".repeat(3);
            const plan = fs.readFileSync("infra/envs/prod/plan.txt", "utf8").slice(-60000);
            await github.rest.issues.createComment({
              ...context.repo,
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              body: `### Terraform plan (prod)\n${fence}\n${plan}\n${fence}`,
            });

  apply:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production        # required reviewers before this job runs
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4
        with:
          terraform_version: "1.17.2"
          terraform_wrapper: false
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-terraform-apply
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - run: terraform init -input=false
      - run: terraform plan -input=false -out=tfplan
      - run: terraform apply -input=false tfplan
  • The plan role can read state and resources but change nothing; the apply role can write and trusts only main in the production environment (see the OIDC trust policy in secrets management).
  • Pinning terraform_version keeps CI and laptops on the same release.
  • Posting plans is fine for private repositories; Terraform hides values marked sensitive, but review what your plans print before posting them anywhere public.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pin Terraform and provider versions; commit .terraform.lock.hcl.
  • Keep one root module and one state per environment; prefer separate cloud accounts for production.
  • Store state remotely with locking, versioning, encryption, and tight access; bootstrap the state bucket separately.
  • Build small, versioned modules with typed, validated inputs and useful outputs; promote module versions through environments.
  • Use default_tags for ownership and cost tracking.
  • Refactor with moved, import, and removed blocks, never by editing state.
  • Protect stateful resources with prevent_destroy and read every -/+ in a plan.
  • Plan on pull requests with a read-only role; apply on merge with a separate write role and an approval for production.
  • Run fmt, validate, a linter, and policy checks in CI.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "Error acquiring the state lock." Detect: plan or apply fails with the lock holder's ID and time. Cause: another run is in progress, or a crashed run left the lock behind. Fix: wait, or confirm no run is active and remove the stale lock with terraform force-unlock <LOCK_ID>; serialize CI runs with concurrency.
  • A rename planned to destroy and recreate a bucket. Detect: the plan shows - for the old address and + for the new one. Cause: the resource or module was renamed in code. Fix: add a moved block and plan again; it should show "has moved to".
  • "Saved plan is stale." Detect: apply refuses the plan file. Cause: state changed after the plan was made (another apply ran). Fix: plan again and review the new plan; this is Terraform protecting you.
  • CI and a developer get different plans. Detect: plans differ for the same commit. Cause: different provider versions (lock file not committed) or different variable files. Fix: commit the lock file, pin required_version, and run plans only in CI for shared environments.
  • Someone applied staging code to production. Detect: production resources renamed or resized unexpectedly. Cause: workspaces, or one set of credentials for every environment. Fix: a root module and cloud account per environment, and roles that can only touch their own environment.
  • The state file disappeared or was overwritten. Detect: plan wants to create everything again. Cause: state deleted, overwritten by an old local copy, or a wrong backend key. Fix: restore the previous version from the versioned bucket, and lock down write access to state.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Provider: a plugin that manages resources in one API.
  • Resource: an infrastructure object Terraform manages.
  • Data source: an object Terraform reads but does not manage.
  • Variable, local, output: a module's inputs, internal values, and exported values.
  • Root module: the directory where Terraform runs, with one state.
  • Child module: reusable configuration called from another module.
  • Backend: where state is stored and how it is locked.
  • State lock: a mechanism that prevents concurrent writes to state.
  • Lock file (.terraform.lock.hcl): the record of exact provider versions and checksums.
  • Saved plan: a plan file applied later exactly as reviewed.
  • moved, import, removed blocks: declarative refactoring of what Terraform manages.
  • Workspace: a named state for the same configuration.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Keeping state locally or committing it to Git.
  • Not committing the provider lock file.
  • Using workspaces to separate production from development.
  • Renaming resources without moved blocks.
  • Applying from laptops with administrator credentials.
  • Using -target routinely, leaving configuration partially applied.
  • Putting secrets into variables and assuming sensitive keeps them out of state.
  • Creating one giant root module for everything, so every plan is slow and every change risky.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do required_providers and .terraform.lock.hcl each control?
  2. How does Terraform decide the order in which to create resources?
  3. How does S3-native state locking work, and which Terraform version made it generally available?
  4. Why are separate root modules preferable to workspaces for staging and production?
  5. You renamed aws_s3_bucket.uploads to module.uploads.aws_s3_bucket.this. What block prevents data loss, and what will the plan show?
  6. When would you use an import block, and when a removed block?
  7. A plan reports "Plan: 7 to add". Using the module on this page, list the seven resources.
  8. Describe a CI design in which pull requests can plan but only merges to main can apply to production.

docs.title: Kubernetes Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the Kubernetes lessons, for use before an interview, a deployment, or a debugging task. Commands assume taskflow is the current namespace.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does kubectl diff -f k8s/, then kubectl apply -f k8s/ --server-side Preview against the live cluster, then apply kubectl describe pod <pod> Events: scheduling, image pulls, probe failures kubectl logs <pod> --previous Logs from the crashed container's last run kubectl debug -it <pod> --image=busybox:1.37 --target=api Ephemeral debug container in a running Pod kubectl port-forward svc/taskflow-api 8080:80 Reach a ClusterIP Service from your machine kubectl rollout status deploy/taskflow-api --timeout=5m Wait for a rollout; fails if it does not complete kubectl rollout undo deploy/taskflow-api Back to the previous revision (or --to-revision=3) kubectl rollout restart deploy/taskflow-api Replace all Pods, for example after a config change kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data Evict Pods, respecting PDBs, before node maintenance kubectl top pods, kubectl describe hpa taskflow-api Usage (needs metrics-server); HPA conditions and events helm upgrade --install taskflow-api charts/taskflow-api -f <values file> --wait --timeout 5m Idempotent install or upgrade; fails if not ready helm rollback taskflow-api 2 Roll back to revision 2 (helm history lists them)

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml (excerpt): rollout, probes, resources, shutdown
spec:
  replicas: 4
  strategy:
    rollingUpdate: {maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0}
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
          ports: [{name: http, containerPort: 3000}]
          readinessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /readyz, port: http}, periodSeconds: 5}
          livenessProbe: {httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: http}, periodSeconds: 10}
          resources:
            requests: {cpu: 250m, memory: 384Mi}
            limits: {memory: 384Mi}      # no CPU limit: no throttling
          lifecycle:
            preStop: {sleep: {seconds: 5}}

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A stateless API or web app Deployment + ClusterIP Service Pods are replaced automatically; Services route by label HTTP(S) from the internet Gateway API, or Ingress on a maintained controller One entry point; Ingress is frozen and ingress-nginx is retired Stable identity and storage per replica StatefulSet + headless Service Only for software that replicates itself; prefer a managed database Finite or scheduled work Job, CronJob Run migrations as a Job before the rollout, not in init containers Settings, not secrets ConfigMap Env vars, or a mounted file that can change live Secrets A secret manager synced by External Secrets Operator, or Sealed Secrets Secrets are base64, not encrypted; never commit them Variable load HPA on CPU with at least 2 to 3 replicas; KEDA for queues Utilization is computed against requests Unknown requests VPA in Off mode, or p95 usage plus headroom Do not combine HPA and VPA on the same metric One team, a few services PaaS, serverless containers, or Compose on a VM Kubernetes pays off with many services and teams

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Probes periodSeconds 10, timeoutSeconds 1, failureThreshold 3, initialDelaySeconds 0 Rolling update maxSurge 25% (rounded up), maxUnavailable 25% (rounded down) Deployment progressDeadlineSeconds 600, revisionHistoryLimit 10 Shutdown 30 s grace period from deletion, including preStop, then SIGKILL HPA Every 15 s; desired = ceil(current replicas x current / target); tolerance 0.1; scale-down window 300 s Job backoffLimit 6; retries after 10 s, 20 s, 40 s, capped at 6 min CronJob Keeps 3 successful and 1 failed Job; concurrencyPolicy: Allow ConfigMap or Secret 1 MiB at most CrashLoopBackOff Restart delay doubles, up to 5 min OOMKilled Exit code 137 Node lost Pods evicted after 300 s etcd quorum floor(n/2) + 1: 3 members survive 1 failure, 5 survive 2 Helm 4 --atomic is now --rollback-on-failure

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Checking dependencies in liveness probes. Keep liveness cheap; put dependency checks in readiness.
  • Expecting Kubernetes to roll back a failed rollout. Gate CI on rollout status --timeout and run rollout undo when it fails.
  • Exiting at once on SIGTERM. Add a short preStop sleep, drain in-flight requests, and finish within the grace period.
  • Leaving requests unset. Set CPU and memory requests; BestEffort Pods are evicted first and the HPA cannot compute utilization.
  • Treating base64 Secrets as encrypted, or committing them. Sync from a secret manager or use Sealed Secrets, with encryption at rest.
  • Deploying latest tags. Use immutable version tags so rollouts and rollbacks are predictable.
  • A PDB with minAvailable equal to the replica count. Use maxUnavailable: 1 so node drains can proceed.

docs.title: Configuration and Secrets
docs.text: One image should run in every environment, so everything that differs between development, staging, and production (log levels, feature flags, connection strings, API keys) must be supplied when the container starts. Kubernetes provides two objects for this: ConfigMaps for ordinary configuration and Secrets for sensitive values. This lesson covers how both are created and consumed, why base64 is not encryption, how to protect Secrets with encryption at rest and RBAC, the difference between environment variables and mounted files (one updates, one does not), how to roll Pods automatically when configuration changes, immutable ConfigMaps, and the external tools teams use to keep real secrets out of Git: the External Secrets Operator, the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and Sealed Secrets.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Configuration mistakes are among the most common causes of failed deploys and security incidents. A changed ConfigMap that never reaches running Pods leaves the cluster in a state nobody intended. A Secret manifest committed to Git with base64 values is a plaintext password in the repository history. A developer role that can create Pods can read every Secret in its namespace by mounting it. Understanding exactly how values flow from these objects into a process, and who can read them on the way, prevents all three.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App. The config factor defines configuration as everything that varies between deploys and requires strict separation of config from code, which ConfigMaps and Secrets implement for Kubernetes workloads.
  • Kubernetes project. The good practices for Kubernetes Secrets page recommends enabling encryption at rest, applying least-privilege RBAC to Secrets, restricting which containers can access them, and considering external secret store providers.
  • Kubernetes project. The encrypting confidential data at rest task shows that Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd unless an encryption configuration (ideally a KMS provider) is set on the API server.
  • External Secrets Operator. The External Secrets Operator project documents the controller pattern used by many teams to sync values from AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Google Secret Manager, and Azure Key Vault into Kubernetes Secrets.

Popular tools and providers: External Secrets Operator, Secrets Store CSI Driver, Sealed Secrets, SOPS, HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager, Azure Key Vault, and Stakater Reloader for restarting Pods on configuration changes.

docs.title: ConfigMaps
docs.text: A ConfigMap stores non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs. Values can be short strings (LOG_LEVEL: info) or whole files (features.json: | followed by the file content). A ConfigMap is limited to 1 MiB, lives in one namespace, and can be consumed only by Pods in that namespace.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
A Secret has the same shape but is meant for sensitive data. Kubernetes treats Secrets slightly differently from ConfigMaps: they are sent only to nodes that run Pods using them, mounted into containers on in-memory tmpfs rather than disk, and can be protected separately by RBAC and encryption at rest. Common types:

Type Use Opaque Arbitrary key-value data (the default) kubernetes.io/tls A TLS certificate and key (tls.crt, tls.key) kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Registry credentials for imagePullSecrets kubernetes.io/basic-auth, kubernetes.io/ssh-auth Typed credentials

docs.title: Base64 is encoding, not encryption
docs.text:
Values in a Secret's data field are base64-encoded so that binary data fits in JSON and YAML. Anyone who can read the object can decode them in one command:

kubectl -n taskflow get secret taskflow-api-secrets \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.mongodb-uri}' | base64 -d

You can write plain values under stringData instead; the API server encodes them. Either way, a Secret manifest with real values is a plaintext secret: it must not be committed to Git.

docs.title: Protecting Secrets
docs.text:
Three layers protect Secret values:

  1. Encryption at rest. By default the API server stores Secrets in etcd unencrypted, so an etcd backup or disk is a copy of every credential. An EncryptionConfiguration makes the API server encrypt them before writing; the kms provider (version 2) uses envelope encryption with a key held in a cloud KMS or HSM, so the key never sits on the control plane disk. Managed services encrypt their etcd storage and offer KMS envelope encryption, enabled by default on some platforms; check yours.
  2. RBAC. get, list, and watch on secrets reveal every value. Grant them only to the controllers and people that need them. Note that anyone who can create Pods in a namespace can mount any Secret in that namespace and read it, so Pod creation rights are effectively Secret read rights.
  3. Limiting exposure in the Pod. Mount only the keys a container needs, prefer files over environment variables (environment variables end up in crash dumps, /proc/<pid>/environ, and child processes), and set restrictive file modes (defaultMode: 0400).

docs.title: Environment variables compared with mounted files
docs.text:
Environment variables Mounted files How env with valueFrom, or envFrom for all keys A configMap or secret volume When the ConfigMap or Secret changes Never updated; the process keeps the values it started with Updated in place by the kubelet, typically within a minute or so With subPath Not applicable Never updated App support Every app reads process.env The app must read the file, and re-read it to pick up changes Exposure Visible to child processes and in process dumps Readable only through the filesystem, with file permissions Best for Simple settings that change with a deploy Secrets, larger files, settings that should change without a restart

The kubelet updates mounted files atomically (it swaps a symbolic link to a new directory), so an app that watches the file sees a complete new version. Updating does not restart anything: if the app reads the file only at startup, it still needs a restart.

docs.title: Rolling Pods when configuration changes
docs.text:
Because environment variables never update and many apps read files only at startup, changing a ConfigMap usually requires new Pods. Kubernetes does not do this by itself: a Deployment rolls out only when its Pod template changes. Common patterns:

Pattern How it works kubectl rollout restart deployment/taskflow-api Adds a timestamp annotation to the template, triggering a normal rolling update; manual Checksum annotation (Helm) The chart puts checksum/config: <sha256 of the ConfigMap> in the Pod template, so any config change changes the template Generated names (Kustomize) configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name (taskflow-api-config-7g8k2m) and rewrites references, so a change produces a new name and a rollout A reloader controller A controller such as Stakater Reloader watches referenced ConfigMaps and Secrets and restarts the workload when they change

Generated, hash-suffixed names also make rollbacks correct: rolling back the Deployment points it at the old ConfigMap, which still exists, instead of keeping the new configuration with the old code.

docs.title: Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets
docs.text: Setting immutable: true prevents any change to the object's data. The kubelet stops watching immutable objects, which reduces load on the API server in large clusters, and accidental edits that would affect running Pods become impossible. To change the value you create a new object with a new name and update the reference, which pairs naturally with hash-suffixed names.

docs.title: External secret management
docs.text:
Keeping secret values in an external manager (a cloud secret manager or Vault) gives you a single source of truth, auditing, rotation, and access policies independent of the cluster. Three tools bring those values into Kubernetes:

Tool How it works Strengths Trade-offs External Secrets Operator ExternalSecret objects (safe to commit) tell a controller which keys to copy from a SecretStore into native Secrets, refreshed on an interval Apps unchanged; many providers; rotation flows through Values still exist as Secrets in etcd Secrets Store CSI Driver A CSI volume mounts values from the store directly into the Pod at start; optional sync to a Secret Values need never be stored in etcd Pods depend on the store being reachable when they start Sealed Secrets kubeseal encrypts a Secret with the cluster's public key; the encrypted SealedSecret is committed; a controller decrypts it in the cluster Pure GitOps; no external service Rotation means re-sealing and committing; the controller's key must be backed up

The controller authenticates to the cloud store with workload identity (EKS Pod Identity or IAM roles for service accounts, GKE Workload Identity Federation, Azure Workload Identity), which maps a Kubernetes service account to a cloud identity so no long-lived cloud key is stored in the cluster. Where secrets come from and how they are rotated is covered in secrets management.

docs.title: Other ways to feed configuration in
docs.text:
• Command arguments can reference environment variables with $(VAR_NAME) syntax in command and args.
  • The Downward API exposes Pod metadata (name, namespace, labels, node name) and the container's own resource requests and limits as environment variables or files, useful for logging and for sizing a runtime from its limits.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Value Store it in Deliver it as Log level, page sizes, public URLs, feature defaults ConfigMap Env vars, or a file if it should change live A JSON or YAML config file ConfigMap Mounted file Database password, API keys, signing keys External secret manager, synced to a Secret Mounted file (or env var if the app requires it) TLS certificate and key Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls, usually managed by cert-manager Used by the Ingress or Gateway, or mounted Registry credentials kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson Secret imagePullSecrets Values that differ per build of a frontend Build arguments, not Kubernetes Baked into static files at build time

Do not put large data or binary blobs in ConfigMaps (the 1 MiB limit and etcd load), do not store secrets in ConfigMaps, and do not rely on Secrets alone as your secret management strategy without encryption at rest and tight RBAC.

docs.title: A ConfigMap and how the Secret is created
docs.text:
# k8s/api-config.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-config
  namespace: taskflow
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  TASKS_PAGE_SIZE: "50"
  features.json: |
    {
      "taskComments": true,
      "taskReminders": false
    }

# Create the Secret from a CI secret or a local file, never from a committed manifest
kubectl -n taskflow create secret generic taskflow-api-secrets \
  --from-literal=mongodb-uri='mongodb://<user>:<password>@mongo.example.com:27017/taskflow' \
  --from-file=jwt-secret=./jwt-secret.txt

# Generate a manifest to inspect (do not commit it)
kubectl -n taskflow create secret generic demo --from-literal=key=value \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml

# Build the same ConfigMap from literals and a file
# (--from-env-file cannot be combined with --from-file or --from-literal)
kubectl -n taskflow create configmap taskflow-api-config \
  --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info --from-literal=TASKS_PAGE_SIZE=50 \
  --from-file=config/features.json \
  --dry-run=client -o yaml > k8s/api-config.yaml

docs.title: Consuming configuration in the Deployment
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml (excerpt): pod template spec
spec:
  containers:
    - name: api
      image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
      env:
        - name: LOG_LEVEL
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: taskflow-api-config
              key: LOG_LEVEL
        - name: TASKS_PAGE_SIZE
          valueFrom:
            configMapKeyRef:
              name: taskflow-api-config
              key: TASKS_PAGE_SIZE
        - name: MONGODB_URI
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: taskflow-api-secrets
              key: mongodb-uri
        - name: JWT_SECRET_FILE
          value: /var/run/secrets/taskflow/jwt-secret
        - name: POD_NAME                     # Downward API
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: metadata.name
      volumeMounts:
        - name: features
          mountPath: /etc/taskflow
          readOnly: true
        - name: secrets
          mountPath: /var/run/secrets/taskflow
          readOnly: true
  volumes:
    - name: features
      configMap:
        name: taskflow-api-config
        items:
          - key: features.json
            path: features.json
    - name: secrets
      secret:
        secretName: taskflow-api-secrets
        defaultMode: 0400
        items:
          - key: jwt-secret
            path: jwt-secret

The variables are listed explicitly because this ConfigMap also holds a file. envFrom with a configMapRef would turn every key into a variable, which is convenient for a ConfigMap of plain settings and messy for one that contains files. The JWT secret is read from a file whose path is passed in an environment variable, a convention many libraries and images support (*_FILE).

docs.title: Reading a mounted file that can change
docs.text:
// src/features.js: reload features.json when the kubelet updates it
import { readFileSync, watch } from "node:fs";

const DIR = "/etc/taskflow";
let features = load();

function load() {
  return JSON.parse(readFileSync(`${DIR}/features.json`, "utf8"));
}

// The kubelet swaps a symlink inside the directory, so watch the directory
watch(DIR, () => {
  try {
    features = load();
  } catch (err) {
    console.error("keeping previous features.json:", err);
  }
});

export const isEnabled = (name) => Boolean(features[name]);

docs.title: Rolling out on change with Kustomize and Helm
docs.text:
# k8s/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: taskflow
resources:
  - ../../base
configMapGenerator:
  - name: taskflow-api-config
    envs:
      - production.env
    files:
      - features.json

# charts/taskflow-api/templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  template:
    metadata:
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}

Kustomize generates taskflow-api-config-<hash> and updates the Deployment's references; Helm changes the annotation whenever the rendered ConfigMap changes. Both turn a config edit into a normal rolling update.

docs.title: Encryption at rest on a self-managed control plane
docs.text:
# /etc/kubernetes/enc/encryption-config.yaml (passed with --encryption-provider-config)
apiVersion: apiserver.config.k8s.io/v1
kind: EncryptionConfiguration
resources:
  - resources:
      - secrets
    providers:
      - aescbc:
          keys:
            - name: key1
              secret: <base64-encoded-32-byte-key>
      - identity: {}     # still able to read data written before encryption

# After restarting the API server, rewrite existing Secrets so they are encrypted
kubectl get secrets --all-namespaces -o json | kubectl replace -f -

The first provider encrypts new writes; later providers are used only to read old data. In production prefer the kms provider so the key lives in a KMS rather than in a file on the control plane.

docs.title: Syncing from AWS Secrets Manager with the External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
# k8s/secret-store.yaml: how to reach the store (uses the Pod's service account identity)
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: SecretStore
metadata:
  name: aws-secrets
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef:
            name: taskflow-api
---
# k8s/external-secret.yaml: what to fetch and which Secret to write
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-secrets
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: aws-secrets
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: taskflow-api-secrets
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
    - secretKey: mongodb-uri
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/taskflow/api
        property: mongodb_uri
    - secretKey: jwt-secret
      remoteRef:
        key: prod/taskflow/api
        property: jwt_secret

Both files are safe to commit: they contain references, not values. The taskflow-api service account is mapped to an IAM role that may read only prod/taskflow/*. Older External Secrets Operator releases serve these kinds as external-secrets.io/v1beta1.

docs.title: An immutable, versioned ConfigMap
docs.text:
# k8s/api-config-v7.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-config-v7
  namespace: taskflow
immutable: true
data:
  LOG_LEVEL: info
  TASKS_PAGE_SIZE: "50"

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Build one image and inject all environment-specific values at runtime.
  • Keep secret values out of Git: commit references (ExternalSecret) or encrypted forms (SealedSecret), never plain or base64 Secret manifests.
  • Enable encryption at rest, preferably with a KMS provider.
  • Restrict get, list, and watch on Secrets, and remember that Pod creation rights imply Secret read rights within a namespace.
  • Prefer mounted files for secrets; mount only the keys a container needs, read-only, with mode 0400.
  • Make configuration changes roll Pods automatically (hash-suffixed names or checksum annotations).
  • Use immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets with versioned names in large clusters.
  • Use workload identity for access to cloud secret stores.
  • Validate configuration at application startup and fail fast with a clear message.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A ConfigMap change has no effect. Detect: kubectl get configmap -o yaml shows the new value, but kubectl exec ... -- printenv LOG_LEVEL shows the old one. Cause: environment variables are set only when the container starts, and nothing restarted the Pods. Fix: kubectl rollout restart now; use hash-suffixed ConfigMaps or a checksum annotation so future changes roll out automatically.
  • Pods fail with CreateContainerConfigError. Detect: kubectl describe pod shows secret "taskflow-api-secrets" not found or couldn't find key mongodb-uri. Cause: the Secret or key does not exist in that namespace yet, often because the sync controller failed or the name changed. Fix: create or sync the Secret first, check the ExternalSecret status conditions, and mark optional references with optional: true only when the app truly works without them.
  • A database password is found in the Git history. Detect: a secret scanner flags a Secret manifest with base64 values. Cause: someone committed a Secret, assuming base64 hides it. Fix: rotate the credential immediately, remove the file, move to the External Secrets Operator or Sealed Secrets, and add secret scanning to CI.
  • A mounted file never changes after an update. Detect: the ConfigMap is updated, but cat inside the container shows the old content even after several minutes. Cause: the volume is mounted with subPath, which is never updated. Fix: mount the whole volume at a directory (with items to pick keys) or restart Pods on change.
  • Developers can read production credentials. Detect: an RBAC review (kubectl auth can-i get secrets --as=<user> -n taskflow) or audit logs show reads by people who should not have them. Cause: broad roles in the namespace, including the right to create Pods that mount Secrets. Fix: separate namespaces or clusters for production, least-privilege roles, deployment only through CI or GitOps, and audit logging on Secret access.
  • A secret rotation causes an outage. Detect: authentication errors spike right after a credential is rotated in the store. Cause: the old credential was revoked before all Pods picked up the new one (env vars need a restart; refresh intervals add delay). Fix: rotate with an overlap: create the new credential, let it propagate and roll Pods, then revoke the old one.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• ConfigMap: An object holding non-sensitive configuration as key-value pairs or files.
  • Secret: An object for sensitive values, base64-encoded in the API and handled more carefully by the kubelet.
  • stringData: A write-only Secret field that accepts plain values and is encoded by the API server.
  • Encryption at rest: Encrypting Secret data before it is written to etcd, configured with an EncryptionConfiguration.
  • KMS provider: Envelope encryption where data keys are protected by a key in an external key management service.
  • envFrom / valueFrom: Ways to turn ConfigMap and Secret keys into environment variables.
  • subPath: Mounting a single file from a volume; such mounts never receive updates.
  • Immutable ConfigMap: A ConfigMap or Secret with immutable: true whose data cannot change.
  • External Secrets Operator: A controller that syncs values from external stores into Kubernetes Secrets.
  • Sealed Secrets: Encrypted Secrets safe to commit, decrypted by an in-cluster controller.
  • Workload identity: Mapping a Kubernetes service account to a cloud identity, avoiding stored cloud keys.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing base64-encoded Secrets are encrypted.
  • Committing Secret manifests to Git.
  • Expecting environment variables to update when a ConfigMap changes.
  • Using subPath for files that should update.
  • Granting broad Pod-creation rights while trying to restrict Secret access.
  • Storing large files or binary data in ConfigMaps.
  • Changing a ConfigMap in place and breaking the ability to roll back configuration together with code.
  • Logging the whole configuration object at startup, secrets included.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret, both in intended use and in how Kubernetes handles them?
  2. Decode this Secret value: dGFza2Zsb3c=. What does that tell you about base64 as protection?
  3. A ConfigMap value is consumed both as an environment variable and as a mounted file. You change it. What does the running process see in each case, and when?
  4. Describe two ways to make a ConfigMap change roll out new Pods automatically.
  5. Why does the right to create Pods in a namespace imply the right to read its Secrets?
  6. What does encryption at rest protect against, and what does it not protect against?
  7. Compare the External Secrets Operator, the Secrets Store CSI Driver, and Sealed Secrets.
  8. Why would you mark a ConfigMap immutable?
