docs.title: Health Probes and Rolling Updates
docs.text:
Kubernetes can only keep an application available if it knows two things about each Pod: whether it can take traffic right now, and whether it is broken beyond repair. Health probes answer those questions. Rolling updates then use the answers to replace Pods a few at a time, and graceful termination makes sure the Pods being replaced finish their work before they disappear.

This lesson covers liveness, readiness, and startup probes and exactly what each failure does, how to design probes that do not cause outages, the rolling update parameters maxSurge and maxUnavailable with a worked example, the full Pod termination sequence (endpoint removal, preStop, SIGTERM, the grace period, SIGKILL), PodDisruptionBudgets, and the kubectl rollout commands for watching and undoing a release.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most deploy-time errors in Kubernetes come from these settings, not from the code being deployed. Without a readiness probe, new Pods receive traffic before they can serve it. Without graceful termination, every deploy cuts off in-flight requests and clients see 502 errors. A liveness probe that checks the database turns a short database outage into every API Pod restarting at once. A PodDisruptionBudget that allows no disruption blocks node upgrades indefinitely.

Done well, the same settings give you zero-downtime deploys, automatic removal of unhealthy instances from load balancing, and rollouts that stop themselves when the new version is broken.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google Cloud. The article Kubernetes best practices: Setting up health checks with readiness and liveness probes explains the difference between the two probes, why liveness probes need a generous initial delay or a startup phase, and how misconfigured probes cause restart loops.
  • Google Cloud. The companion article Kubernetes best practices: terminating with grace walks through the termination sequence: the Terminating state, the preStop hook, SIGTERM, the grace period, and SIGKILL.
  • Learnk8s. The guide Graceful shutdown and zero downtime deployments in Kubernetes shows that endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen in parallel, so an app can receive new requests after it was told to stop, and recommends waiting briefly before shutting down.
  • Google SRE. The workbook chapter Canarying releases describes releasing to a small part of the fleet first and judging it by health signals, the same idea that maxSurge, readiness gates, and progress deadlines automate in a rolling update.

Popular tools and providers: kubectl rollout, Argo Rollouts and Flagger for canary and blue-green releases, Helm's --wait, the PodDisruptionBudget API, and cluster upgrade tooling that drains nodes respecting those budgets.

docs.title: Three probes, three different questions
docs.text:
Probe Question On repeated failure Runs startupProbe Has the app finished starting? Container killed and restarted From container start until its first success readinessProbe Can this Pod take traffic now? Endpoint marked not ready: no new traffic; no restart For the container's whole life livenessProbe Is the process stuck beyond self-recovery? Container killed and restarted For the container's whole life, after startup succeeds

A Pod with no probes is considered ready as soon as its containers start, and it is restarted only if its process exits.

Each probe uses one mechanism: httpGet (status 200 to 399 is success), tcpSocket (the port accepts a connection), exec (a command exits with 0), or grpc (the standard gRPC health checking protocol). And each has the same timing fields:

Field Default Meaning initialDelaySeconds 0 Wait before the first probe periodSeconds 10 Time between probes timeoutSeconds 1 A probe slower than this counts as a failure failureThreshold 3 Consecutive failures before acting successThreshold 1 Consecutive successes to count as healthy again (must be 1 for liveness and startup)

The arithmetic matters. A liveness probe with the defaults restarts a container after about 30 seconds of failures (3 × 10 s). A startup probe with periodSeconds: 10 and failureThreshold: 30 allows up to 300 seconds to start, while the liveness probe stays disabled; the moment startup succeeds, liveness takes over with its own short threshold. That is far better than a large initialDelaySeconds on the liveness probe, which delays failure detection forever after.

docs.title: Designing probes that do not cause outages
docs.text:
• Liveness must not depend on other services. If /healthz checks MongoDB and MongoDB has a two-minute outage, every API Pod fails liveness and restarts, losing caches and connections, and all of them reconnect at once when MongoDB returns. Liveness should answer only "is this process able to respond at all?" For Node.js, a cheap HTTP handler on the same event loop already detects a blocked or deadlocked loop.
  • Readiness reflects this instance's ability to serve. Good checks: startup work finished, the app's own connection pool is established, the process is not shutting down. Be careful with shared dependencies: if every replica fails readiness because of one external service, all endpoints disappear together. Often it is better to stay ready and return fast errors (with a circuit breaker) than to vanish from the load balancer.
  • Keep probes cheap and give them time. The default one-second timeout is easy to exceed under CPU throttling or a garbage-collection pause, which turns load into restarts and more load. Use a few seconds of timeout and a failure threshold that tolerates a blip.
  • Use a startup probe for slow starters (migrations, cache warming, JIT-heavy runtimes) instead of stretching liveness timing.
  • Fail readiness during shutdown. Flipping /readyz to 503 on SIGTERM is a cheap extra safety net beside the preStop delay.

docs.title: Rolling updates
docs.text:
A Deployment's default strategy, RollingUpdate, replaces Pods gradually by scaling a new ReplicaSet up and the old one down, within two limits:

  • maxSurge: how many Pods may exist above replicas during the update. Percentages round up.
  • maxUnavailable: how many Pods may be unavailable below replicas. Percentages round down.

Both default to 25%. The alternative strategy, Recreate, deletes all old Pods before creating new ones: downtime, but never two versions at once.

Worked example with 4 replicas: maxSurge = 25% of 4 = 1, and maxUnavailable = 25% of 4 = 1. So at most 5 Pods exist and at least 3 are available at every moment.

The key word is available: a new Pod counts only after its readiness probe passes and it has stayed ready for minReadySeconds (default 0). That is what makes rolling updates safe. If version 2 never becomes ready, the controller cannot remove more old Pods, and the rollout stalls with three old Pods still serving. After progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) without progress, the Deployment's Progressing condition becomes False with reason ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Kubernetes does not roll back automatically; your pipeline or kubectl rollout undo must.

Settings Behaviour Needs maxSurge: 25%, maxUnavailable: 25% (default) Balanced speed and capacity Some spare room maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 Never below full capacity; one extra Pod at a time Room for one extra Pod maxSurge: 0, maxUnavailable: 1 No extra Pods; capacity dips by one No spare room maxSurge: 100%, maxUnavailable: 0 Full new set first, then old removed Double capacity briefly

docs.title: Graceful termination
docs.text:
Every rolling update deletes old Pods, so how a Pod stops matters as much as how a new one starts. When a Pod is deleted:

  1. The API server sets the Pod's deletionTimestamp; it shows as Terminating.
  2. In parallel: the EndpointSlice controller marks the endpoint as terminating (not ready), and every node's kube-proxy and every ingress controller update their rules, which takes from milliseconds to a few seconds; and the kubelet starts shutting the Pod down.
  3. The kubelet runs the container's preStop hook, if any, and waits for it.
  4. The kubelet sends SIGTERM (or the image's STOPSIGNAL) to the container's main process.
  5. The app stops accepting connections, finishes in-flight requests, closes pools, and exits.
  6. If containers are still running when terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30) has elapsed, counted from step 1 and including the preStop time, the kubelet sends SIGKILL.

Because steps 2 and 3 race, an app that exits immediately on SIGTERM can still receive requests from proxies that have not yet updated, and those clients see connection errors. A short preStop sleep (5 to 10 seconds) keeps the app serving until the endpoint removal has spread. Kubernetes has a built-in sleep action for this (enabled by default since 1.30), so the image needs no sleep binary. The app's own shutdown logic is the handler from writing production Dockerfiles, and its total time must fit inside the grace period.

docs.title: PodDisruptionBudgets
docs.text:
Kubernetes distinguishes voluntary disruptions (draining a node for an upgrade, the cluster autoscaler removing a node, an operator evicting Pods) from involuntary ones (a node crashing, a kernel panic). A PodDisruptionBudget (PDB) limits voluntary disruptions: the eviction API refuses to evict a Pod if that would leave fewer than minAvailable (or more than maxUnavailable) Pods of the selected set.

PDBs do not apply to a Deployment's own rolling update (that is governed by maxUnavailable) and cannot prevent involuntary failures. A PDB that allows zero disruptions (minAvailable equal to the replica count) blocks node drains and cluster upgrades until someone intervenes. Setting unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow lets broken Pods be evicted even when the budget is exhausted, so they cannot block a drain.

docs.title: Rollout commands
docs.text:
Command Use kubectl rollout status deploy/taskflow-api --timeout=5m Wait for a rollout; non-zero exit on failure or timeout (use in CI) kubectl rollout history deploy/taskflow-api List revisions and their change causes kubectl rollout undo deploy/taskflow-api Return to the previous revision kubectl rollout undo deploy/taskflow-api --to-revision=3 Return to a specific revision kubectl rollout pause / resume Batch several changes into one rollout kubectl rollout restart deploy/taskflow-api Replace all Pods with the same template (picks up config changes)

The CHANGE-CAUSE column in the history comes from the kubernetes.io/change-cause annotation; set it in your pipeline when you deploy (the old --record flag is deprecated).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Workload Probes Strategy HTTP API (TaskFlow API) Readiness on /readyz, liveness on cheap /healthz, startup if boot is slow RollingUpdate with maxUnavailable: 0 Background worker (no port) Liveness via exec or a small health port; readiness rarely needed RollingUpdate App that must never run two versions at once (incompatible migrations) As above Recreate, or better, make versions compatible Very slow start (JVM, large caches) Startup probe with a generous threshold RollingUpdate with minReadySeconds Batch Job Usually none Not a Deployment

Do not add a liveness probe just because you can: if the process exits when it breaks, the kubelet already restarts it. Add one when the app can hang without exiting.

docs.title: Probe endpoints in the API
docs.text:
// src/health.js: liveness and readiness handlers for Express
import mongoose from "mongoose";

let shuttingDown = false;
export const markShuttingDown = () => { shuttingDown = true; };

// Liveness: the event loop responds. No dependency checks here.
export function healthz(_req, res) {
  res.status(200).send("ok");
}

// Readiness: this instance can serve right now.
export function readyz(_req, res) {
  const dbConnected = mongoose.connection.readyState === 1;
  if (shuttingDown || !dbConnected) {
    return res.status(503).send("not ready");
  }
  res.status(200).send("ready");
}

// src/server.js (excerpt)
import { healthz, readyz, markShuttingDown } from "./health.js";

app.get("/healthz", healthz);
app.get("/readyz", readyz);

process.on("SIGTERM", () => {
  markShuttingDown();               // readiness fails from now on
  server.close(async () => {        // in-flight requests finish
    await mongoose.disconnect();
    process.exit(0);
  });
  setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 20_000).unref();   // below the 30 s grace period
});

docs.title: Probes, rollout strategy, and termination in the Deployment
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml (excerpt)
spec:
  replicas: 4
  minReadySeconds: 5
  progressDeadlineSeconds: 300
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxSurge: 1
      maxUnavailable: 0
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 24          # up to 120 s to start
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 3
            failureThreshold: 3
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              sleep:
                seconds: 5                # let endpoint removal propagate

The time budget adds up: 5 s of preStop, then up to 20 s of draining before the app's own timer exits, which is safely below the 30-second grace period. With maxSurge: 1 and maxUnavailable: 0, capacity never drops below four ready Pods during a release. On clusters older than 1.30, replace the sleep action with exec: {command: ["sleep", "5"]}, which requires a sleep binary in the image.

docs.title: Releasing and rolling back
docs.text:
# Deploy a new version (normally done by CI or GitOps)
kubectl -n taskflow set image deploy/taskflow-api api=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.5.0
kubectl -n taskflow annotate deploy/taskflow-api \
  kubernetes.io/change-cause="release 1.5.0" --overwrite

# Wait for it; roll back automatically if it does not complete
kubectl -n taskflow rollout status deploy/taskflow-api --timeout=5m \
  || kubectl -n taskflow rollout undo deploy/taskflow-api

kubectl -n taskflow rollout history deploy/taskflow-api
kubectl -n taskflow get deploy taskflow-api \
  -o jsonpath='{.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Progressing")].reason}'

docs.title: A PodDisruptionBudget
docs.text:
# k8s/api-pdb.yaml
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  maxUnavailable: 1
  unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api

kubectl -n taskflow get pdb taskflow-api
# NAME           MIN AVAILABLE   MAX UNAVAILABLE   ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS   AGE
# taskflow-api   N/A             1                 1                     2d

maxUnavailable: 1 lets node drains proceed one API Pod at a time, however many replicas the autoscaler has added.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give every serving container a readiness probe; add a liveness probe only for failure modes where the process hangs without exiting.
  • Keep liveness checks local and cheap; never check databases or other services from liveness.
  • Use startup probes for slow starts instead of long liveness delays.
  • Use timeouts of a few seconds and failure thresholds that tolerate a blip.
  • Handle SIGTERM: fail readiness, stop accepting, drain, close pools, exit well within the grace period.
  • Add a short preStop sleep so endpoint removal finishes before shutdown begins.
  • Use maxUnavailable: 0 for user-facing services when capacity allows, and set minReadySeconds and a realistic progressDeadlineSeconds.
  • Fail the pipeline on kubectl rollout status timeouts and roll back.
  • Give multi-replica services a PDB that allows at least one disruption.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every API Pod restarts during a database outage. Detect: RESTARTS climbs on all Pods at the same time, and kubectl describe pod shows Liveness probe failed: HTTP probe failed with statuscode: 503 while MongoDB is down. Cause: the liveness endpoint checks the database. Fix: make liveness local only; reflect dependency trouble in readiness or in request errors.
  • Clients see 502 errors during every deploy. Detect: ingress or load balancer logs show upstream connection refused or reset errors only while a rollout runs. Cause: Pods exit as soon as they get SIGTERM, before every proxy has removed them, or in-flight requests are cut. Fix: a preStop sleep, a SIGTERM handler that drains, and a grace period longer than both.
  • A rollout hangs at "1 of 4 updated replicas are available". Detect: kubectl rollout status waits, the new Pods are Running but 0/1 ready, and the Deployment eventually reports ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Cause: the new version fails its readiness probe (bad config, missing Secret key, a probe path that changed). Fix: read kubectl describe pod and the logs, then kubectl rollout undo; automate the undo in CI.
  • Slow-starting Pods are killed in a loop. Detect: CrashLoopBackOff with Liveness probe failed events in the first minute, especially after adding startup work. Cause: liveness starts before the app can answer. Fix: add a startup probe whose failureThreshold × periodSeconds covers the worst-case start time.
  • Liveness failures under peak load make things worse. Detect: restarts correlate with traffic peaks and CPU throttling; probe events show context deadline exceeded. Cause: a one-second probe timeout on a busy process. Fix: raise timeoutSeconds and failureThreshold, keep the handler trivial, and give the container enough CPU.
  • A node drain never finishes. Detect: kubectl drain repeats Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget. Cause: minAvailable equals the replica count, or some Pods are unhealthy and the budget is already used up. Fix: use maxUnavailable: 1, add replicas, and set unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow.
  • New Pods stay Pending during a rollout. Detect: the surge Pod reports 0/3 nodes are available: Insufficient cpu. Cause: maxSurge needs spare capacity that does not exist. Fix: a cluster autoscaler, smaller requests, or maxSurge: 0 with maxUnavailable: 1.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Liveness probe: Decides whether to restart a container.
  • Readiness probe: Decides whether a Pod receives Service traffic.
  • Startup probe: Protects slow-starting containers; disables the other probes until it succeeds.
  • Rolling update: Replacing Pods gradually by scaling a new ReplicaSet up and the old one down.
  • maxSurge / maxUnavailable: The limits on extra Pods and missing available Pods during a rolling update.
  • minReadySeconds: How long a Pod must stay ready before it counts as available.
  • Progress deadline: The time after which a stalled rollout is marked as failed.
  • preStop hook: An action the kubelet runs before sending SIGTERM.
  • Termination grace period: The total time between deletion and SIGKILL.
  • PodDisruptionBudget: A limit on voluntary evictions for a set of Pods.
  • CrashLoopBackOff: The state of a container that keeps failing and is restarted with increasing delays.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Checking dependencies in liveness probes.
  • Using the same aggressive settings for liveness as for readiness.
  • Expecting a failing readiness probe to restart the container.
  • Using a long initialDelaySeconds instead of a startup probe.
  • Exiting immediately on SIGTERM without a preStop delay.
  • Setting a preStop sleep longer than the grace period allows.
  • Assuming Kubernetes rolls back a failed rollout automatically.
  • Believing PDBs protect against node crashes or apply to rolling updates.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What happens to a Pod when each of the three probes fails repeatedly?
  2. A startup probe has periodSeconds: 5 and failureThreshold: 24. How long may the app take to start, and what are liveness and readiness doing meanwhile?
  3. A Deployment has 10 replicas with the default maxSurge and maxUnavailable of 25%. What is the maximum number of Pods during a rollout, and the minimum number available?
  4. Why should a liveness probe not check MongoDB? What should readiness check instead?
  5. Describe the termination sequence, and explain why a preStop sleep reduces errors during deploys.
  6. A Pod has a 10-second preStop sleep, its app needs 25 seconds to drain, and the grace period is 30 seconds. What happens?
  7. Why does a stalled rollout not take the service down, and what does Kubernetes do after progressDeadlineSeconds?
  8. What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against, and what does it not?

docs.title: Ingress, Networking, and Helm
docs.text: Services give Pods stable addresses inside the cluster. Getting HTTP traffic in from the internet, securing it with TLS, controlling which Pods may talk to which, and packaging all the YAML so it can be installed per environment are the next problems. This lesson covers Ingress and ingress controllers, TLS certificates with cert-manager, the Gateway API that succeeds Ingress, NetworkPolicies, and the two packaging tools almost every team uses: Helm (charts, values, templates, releases, upgrades, and rollbacks) and Kustomize (bases and overlays), with guidance on when to use which.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The entry point is where every user request first meets your cluster, so mistakes there are visible immediately: an Ingress no controller picks up returns 404, a certificate that failed to renew takes the site down, and controller-specific annotations lock you into one implementation. Inside the cluster, the default network is fully open, so one compromised Pod can reach every database unless NetworkPolicies say otherwise. And without a packaging tool, every environment ends up with hand-edited copies of the same manifests that drift apart.

The ecosystem has also shifted. The Gateway API is now the recommended model for new traffic routing work, and the widely used community ingress-nginx controller has been retired, so teams need to understand both the old and the new model.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Kubernetes SIG Network. The announcement Ingress NGINX Retirement: What You Need to Know explains that the community ingress-nginx controller received only best-effort maintenance until March 2026, with no further releases or security fixes afterwards, and recommends migrating to the Gateway API or another maintained controller.
  • Kubernetes project. The post Gateway API v1.0: GA Release describes the role-oriented resources (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) that standardize features such as traffic splitting and header matching, which previously needed controller-specific annotations on Ingress.
  • cert-manager. The cert-manager documentation shows how issuers obtain certificates from ACME providers such as Let's Encrypt, store them in Secrets used by Ingresses and Gateways, and renew them automatically before they expire.
  • Helm. The Helm documentation describes charts, values, releases, and the upgrade and rollback model used by most publicly distributed Kubernetes software, which is published as Helm charts.

Popular tools and providers: Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, NGINX Gateway Fabric and the F5 NGINX Ingress Controller, Traefik, HAProxy, Kong, the AWS Load Balancer Controller, GKE Gateway, cert-manager, Calico and Cilium for NetworkPolicies, Helm, Kustomize, and GitOps tools (Argo CD, Flux) that apply both.

docs.title: Getting traffic into the cluster
docs.text: Option How Suits NodePort Service A port on every node Labs, bare metal behind an external load balancer LoadBalancer Service One cloud load balancer per Service (L4) A few TCP or UDP services Ingress One HTTP(S) entry point; rules route by host and path to ClusterIP Services HTTP applications (stable API, frozen for new features) Gateway API Gateway (listeners, TLS) plus Routes (HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute, and others) HTTP and other protocols; the recommended model for new work

docs.title: Ingress and ingress controllers
docs.text:
An Ingress is only a set of routing rules: hostnames, paths, the backend Service for each, and TLS settings. It does nothing until an ingress controller (a proxy such as Envoy, NGINX, HAProxy, or a cloud load balancer controller) watches Ingress objects and configures itself to implement them. A cluster can run several controllers; spec.ingressClassName says which one should handle an Ingress.

Things to know about Ingress:

  • pathType is Prefix (matches path segments: /api matches /api/v1 but not /apiv1), Exact, or ImplementationSpecific.
  • Anything beyond hosts, paths, and TLS (timeouts, body-size limits, rewrites, rate limits, canary weights) is configured with controller-specific annotations, so an Ingress written for one controller usually does not behave the same on another.
  • The Ingress API is stable but frozen: it receives no new features, which go into the Gateway API instead.
  • The community ingress-nginx controller was retired after March 2026. Existing installations keep working but receive no fixes, so clusters running it should migrate to the Gateway API or another maintained controller (the ingress2gateway tool converts Ingress objects to Gateway API resources).

docs.title: TLS with cert-manager
docs.text:
cert-manager adds certificate resources to the cluster and automates the ACME protocol used by Let's Encrypt and other certificate authorities:

  1. An Issuer (namespaced) or ClusterIssuer describes a certificate authority and how to prove domain control: an HTTP-01 challenge (a file served over port 80 through the ingress) or a DNS-01 challenge (a TXT record, required for wildcard certificates).
  2. A Certificate lists the DNS names and the Secret to write. An annotation such as cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer on an Ingress creates the Certificate for you from its tls section.
  3. cert-manager completes the challenge, stores the certificate and key in a kubernetes.io/tls Secret, and renews it automatically, by default when two thirds of its lifetime has passed.

How certificates and ACME challenges work in general is covered in obtaining and renewing certificates, and where to terminate TLS in TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: The Gateway API
docs.text:
The Gateway API splits the entry point into resources owned by different roles:

Resource Owned by Defines GatewayClass Infrastructure provider Which implementation runs the gateways (like IngressClass) Gateway Cluster operators Listeners: ports, protocols, hostnames, TLS certificates, which namespaces may attach routes HTTPRoute, GRPCRoute (and other routes) Application teams Hostnames, matches on path, headers, query, and method, filters (redirects, header changes), and weighted backends ReferenceGrant Owner of the referenced object Permission for a route in one namespace to reference a Service or Secret in another

Compared with Ingress, features that used to need annotations are part of the portable API: weighted traffic splitting for canaries, header-based routing, redirects, and request mirroring. Application teams can manage their own routes without access to the shared gateway, and the same manifests work across implementations that support the features used. The API is installed as CRDs and implemented by many projects and cloud providers.

docs.title: NetworkPolicies
docs.text:
By default every Pod can connect to every other Pod in the cluster. A NetworkPolicy selects Pods (by label, in its namespace) and lists the traffic allowed to them (ingress) or from them (egress), by Pod selector, namespace selector, IP block, and port.

  • A Pod selected by any policy for a direction becomes default deny for that direction; only listed traffic is allowed. Pods not selected by any policy stay fully open.
  • Policies are additive: the allowed traffic is the union of all policies that select the Pod. There is no "deny" rule.
  • Policies are enforced by the network plugin (Calico, Cilium, most cloud CNIs). On a plugin that does not implement them, they are accepted and silently ignored.
  • When you add egress rules, remember DNS: Pods must still reach CoreDNS on port 53 (UDP and TCP) to resolve Service names.

A common baseline is a default-deny policy per namespace plus explicit allows: from the ingress controller to the web and API Pods, from the API to MongoDB, and DNS for everyone.

docs.title: Helm
docs.text:
Helm packages Kubernetes manifests as charts:

  • Chart.yaml: the chart's name, version (of the chart), and appVersion (of the application it deploys); apiVersion: v2 for current charts.
  • values.yaml: default configuration values.
  • templates/: manifests written as Go templates with Helm's helper functions, plus shared snippets in _helpers.tpl.
  • Optional dependencies on other charts, and hooks (for example a migration Job that runs before an upgrade).

Installing a chart with a set of values creates a release; every install, upgrade, or rollback creates a new revision, recorded as a Secret in the release's namespace.

Command Purpose helm upgrade --install <release> <chart> -f values.yaml Install or upgrade idempotently (the usual CI command) helm template <release> <chart> -f values.yaml Render manifests locally without installing helm lint <chart> Check a chart for problems helm list -n <ns>, helm history <release> See releases and their revisions helm rollback <release> <revision> Re-apply an earlier revision as a new revision helm get values <release> Show the values a release was installed with helm package, helm push <chart>.tgz oci://<registry>/<path> Publish charts to an OCI registry

Helm 4, released in November 2025, keeps these core commands, and existing apiVersion: v2 charts work unchanged. Some flags changed when moving from Helm 3: automatic rollback on a failed upgrade, --atomic in Helm 3, is --rollback-on-failure in Helm 4, and --wait now selects a wait strategy (plain --wait waits for resources to become ready).

docs.title: Kustomize
docs.text: Kustomize, built into kubectl (kubectl apply -k), customizes plain YAML without templates. A base holds the common manifests; each overlay references the base and applies changes: patches, a namespace, labels, name prefixes or suffixes, image tag overrides, and generated ConfigMaps and Secrets with content-hash names. The output is always valid Kubernetes YAML you can read, and there is no release state stored in the cluster.

docs.title: Choosing between Helm, Kustomize, and plain manifests
docs.text:
Plain manifests Kustomize Helm Learning curve None Low Moderate (templating) Environment differences Copies of files Overlays and patches Values files Distributing software to others Poor Possible Excellent: the ecosystem standard Release history and rollback None (Git history) None (Git history) Built in Readability of what is applied Direct Direct Requires rendering Typical use Tiny projects Your own services, GitOps Third-party software, shared internal charts

Many teams install third-party software (cert-manager, monitoring, the gateway implementation) with Helm and manage their own services with Kustomize overlays or a small internal chart, all applied by a GitOps tool (see immutable infrastructure and GitOps).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use HTTP(S) routing for a new cluster Gateway API with a maintained implementation Existing Ingress resources Keep them on a maintained controller; plan a Gateway API migration Automatic TLS certificates cert-manager with ACME (HTTP-01, or DNS-01 for wildcards) Canary traffic split at the edge HTTPRoute backendRefs weights (or Argo Rollouts, Flagger) Limit which Pods can reach the database NetworkPolicies with a CNI that enforces them Install third-party software Its Helm chart Per-environment differences for your services Kustomize overlays or Helm values

Avoid one LoadBalancer Service per HTTP application, avoid relying on controller annotations for behaviour you need to stay portable, and avoid deeply nested Helm templating for a single internal service where a Kustomize overlay would be clearer.

docs.title: An Ingress for the TaskFlow API and web app
docs.text:
# k8s/ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: taskflow
  namespace: taskflow
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx          # the IngressClass of your installed controller
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.example.com
        - app.example.com
      secretName: taskflow-tls
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: taskflow-api
                port:
                  name: http
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: taskflow-web
                port:
                  number: 80

docs.title: A ClusterIssuer for Let's Encrypt
docs.text:
# k8s/cluster-issuer.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: ops@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx

kubectl -n taskflow get certificate                     # READY should become True
kubectl -n taskflow describe certificate taskflow-tls   # events, renewal time
kubectl get challenges -A                               # ACME challenges in progress

Test against Let's Encrypt's staging endpoint first; the production endpoint enforces rate limits.

docs.title: The same routing with the Gateway API, including a canary
docs.text:
# k8s/gateway.yaml: owned by the platform team
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: public
  namespace: infra
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example-gateway-class   # provided by your Gateway API implementation
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: "*.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: wildcard-example-com-tls
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: All
---
# k8s/api-route.yaml: owned by the TaskFlow team
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: public
      namespace: infra
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - api.example.com
  rules:
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        - name: taskflow-api
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: taskflow-api-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10

Ten percent of requests go to the canary Service, with no controller-specific annotation. Shifting the weights step by step is the canary process described in rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.

docs.title: NetworkPolicies: default deny with explicit allows
docs.text:
# k8s/network-policies.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  podSelector: {}                  # every Pod in the namespace
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-dns
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes: ["Egress"]
  egress:
    - to:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: kube-system
          podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              k8s-app: kube-dns
      ports:
        - protocol: UDP
          port: 53
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 53
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: api-traffic
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  policyTypes: ["Ingress", "Egress"]
  ingress:
    - from:
        - namespaceSelector:
            matchLabels:
              kubernetes.io/metadata.name: ingress-controller
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 3000
  egress:
    - to:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels:
              app.kubernetes.io/name: mongo
      ports:
        - protocol: TCP
          port: 27017

The API now accepts connections only from the ingress controller's namespace on port 3000 and may connect only to MongoDB and DNS. Policies refer to the container port (3000), not the Service port (80). The kubernetes.io/metadata.name label is set automatically on every namespace, and CoreDNS Pods carry the k8s-app: kube-dns label in most distributions.

docs.title: A small Helm chart for the API
docs.text:
# charts/taskflow-api/Chart.yaml
apiVersion: v2
name: taskflow-api
description: TaskFlow API
type: application
version: 0.3.0
appVersion: "1.5.0"

# charts/taskflow-api/values.yaml
replicaCount: 3
image:
  repository: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api
  tag: ""                     # defaults to appVersion
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m
    memory: 384Mi
  limits:
    memory: 384Mi
config:
  LOG_LEVEL: info

# charts/taskflow-api/templates/deployment.yaml (excerpt)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: {{ include "taskflow-api.fullname" . }}
  labels:
    {{- include "taskflow-api.labels" . | nindent 4 }}
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      {{- include "taskflow-api.selectorLabels" . | nindent 6 }}
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        {{- include "taskflow-api.selectorLabels" . | nindent 8 }}
      annotations:
        checksum/config: {{ include (print $.Template.BasePath "/configmap.yaml") . | sha256sum }}
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag | default .Chart.AppVersion }}"
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: {{ include "taskflow-api.fullname" . }}
          {{- with .Values.resources }}
          resources:
            {{- toYaml . | nindent 12 }}
          {{- end }}

# charts/taskflow-api/values-production.yaml
replicaCount: 4
config:
  LOG_LEVEL: warn

helm lint charts/taskflow-api
helm template taskflow-api charts/taskflow-api -f charts/taskflow-api/values-production.yaml \
  | kubectl diff -n taskflow -f -                      # preview against the cluster

helm upgrade --install taskflow-api charts/taskflow-api \
  -n taskflow --create-namespace \
  -f charts/taskflow-api/values-production.yaml \
  --set image.tag=1.5.0 \
  --wait --timeout 5m

helm history taskflow-api -n taskflow
helm rollback taskflow-api 2 -n taskflow

helm package charts/taskflow-api
helm push taskflow-api-0.3.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/example/charts

The helper templates (taskflow-api.fullname, labels, selectorLabels) live in _helpers.tpl, which helm create generates. --wait makes the command wait until the resources are ready, so CI fails when the new version does not become healthy.

docs.title: Kustomize base and overlay
docs.text:
# k8s/base/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - api-deployment.yaml
  - api-service.yaml
labels:
  - pairs:
      app.kubernetes.io/part-of: taskflow

# k8s/overlays/production/kustomization.yaml
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
namespace: taskflow
resources:
  - ../../base
  - ingress.yaml
images:
  - name: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api
    newTag: "1.5.0"
patches:
  - target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: taskflow-api
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/replicas
        value: 4

kubectl kustomize k8s/overlays/production     # render
kubectl apply -k k8s/overlays/production      # apply

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Use one entry point (a Gateway or an ingress controller) for HTTP services, with ClusterIP Services behind it.
  • Prefer the Gateway API for new routing; keep controller-specific annotations to a minimum.
  • Run a maintained controller; migrate off retired ones such as the community ingress-nginx.
  • Automate certificates with cert-manager and monitor certificate expiry.
  • Start every namespace with default-deny NetworkPolicies, then allow DNS and the required flows; confirm your CNI enforces them.
  • Keep Helm charts simple, lint them, render them in CI, and install with upgrade --install --wait.
  • Pin chart versions for third-party software and review their values.
  • Use Kustomize overlays (or Helm values) for environment differences, never copies of whole manifests.
  • Apply everything from Git, ideally through a GitOps controller.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• An Ingress returns 404 for every path. Detect: the response comes from the controller's default backend, and kubectl describe ingress shows no address or events. Cause: no controller claims the Ingress: ingressClassName is missing or names a class nobody runs, or the host header does not match. Fix: set the right ingressClassName (kubectl get ingressclass) and check the host.
  • The site returns 503 Service Unavailable. Detect: controller logs show no healthy upstreams for the Service. Cause: the backend Service has no ready endpoints (selector mismatch or failing readiness) or the port name or number is wrong. Fix: check kubectl get endpointslices for the Service and the Ingress backend port.
  • A certificate is never issued. Detect: kubectl get certificate stays READY False, and kubectl describe challenge shows the HTTP-01 self-check failing. Cause: DNS does not point at the load balancer yet, port 80 is blocked, or the solver uses the wrong ingress class. Fix: fix DNS and firewall rules, match the solver's class, and test with the staging issuer.
  • Everything breaks after applying a default-deny policy. Detect: Pods log getaddrinfo EAI_AGAIN or time out on every hostname. Cause: egress to CoreDNS is now denied. Fix: add an egress policy allowing UDP and TCP port 53 to kube-dns before or with the default deny.
  • NetworkPolicies seem to have no effect. Detect: a test Pod can still reach the database despite a policy. Cause: the cluster's CNI does not enforce NetworkPolicies, or the policy's selectors do not match the Pods. Fix: use an enforcing CNI (or enable enforcement on the managed service) and verify the labels.
  • helm upgrade fails with "another operation is in progress". Detect: helm history shows the latest revision as pending-upgrade or pending-install. Cause: an earlier upgrade was interrupted (a cancelled CI job or a timeout). Fix: roll back to the last deployed revision with helm rollback, then rerun the upgrade.
  • The cluster still runs the retired community ingress-nginx. Detect: kubectl get pods -A shows ingress-nginx-controller Pods. Cause: the migration was deferred. Fix: plan a move to a Gateway API implementation or another maintained controller, translating annotations and testing each host before switching DNS.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Ingress: An object with HTTP routing rules (hosts, paths, TLS) for a controller to implement.
  • Ingress controller: The proxy that implements Ingress rules.
  • IngressClass: Names a controller so an Ingress can select it.
  • Gateway API: The successor to Ingress: GatewayClass, Gateway, and Route resources split by role.
  • HTTPRoute: A Gateway API resource that routes HTTP requests by host, path, and headers to weighted backends.
  • cert-manager: A controller that obtains and renews TLS certificates and stores them in Secrets.
  • ACME / HTTP-01 / DNS-01: The protocol and challenge types used to prove domain control to certificate authorities.
  • NetworkPolicy: A rule set selecting Pods and allowing specific ingress and egress traffic.
  • Helm chart / release / revision: A package of templates; one installed instance of it; one version of that installation.
  • Values: The configuration a Helm chart is rendered with.
  • Kustomize base / overlay: Shared manifests and the environment-specific changes applied on top.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Creating an Ingress without an ingress controller running.
  • Assuming annotations work the same on every controller.
  • Exposing every HTTP service with its own LoadBalancer.
  • Forgetting DNS egress when adding default-deny policies.
  • Assuming NetworkPolicies are enforced on any cluster.
  • Writing policies against Service ports instead of container ports.
  • Hand-editing resources that a Helm release manages, which the next upgrade overwrites.
  • Building complex logic into Helm templates for one internal service.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What is the difference between an Ingress and an ingress controller, and what does ingressClassName do?
  2. Why is the Gateway API split into GatewayClass, Gateway, and Route resources?
  3. Walk through how cert-manager obtains a certificate for api.example.com with an HTTP-01 challenge.
  4. A namespace has a default-deny policy and a policy allowing ingress to the API on port 3000 from the ingress namespace. Can the API reach MongoDB? Can it resolve mongo.taskflow? Why?
  5. What does a Helm release revision record, and what does helm rollback actually do?
  6. In what order are values applied when you pass values.yaml, two -f files, and --set?
  7. When would you choose Kustomize over Helm, and the reverse?
  8. A canary should receive 5% of traffic. How would you express that with an HTTPRoute?

docs.title: Kubernetes Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review orchestration fundamentals, Pods, Deployments and Services, configuration and Secrets, probes and rolling updates, scaling and resources, ingress, networking and Helm, and stateful workloads and Jobs. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What problems does a container orchestrator solve?
docs.text: Scheduling containers onto machines with enough resources, restarting and replacing them when they or their machines fail, rolling out new versions gradually with rollback, giving changing sets of containers stable names and load balancing, scaling replicas and nodes, and injecting configuration and secrets, all through one declarative API.

docs.title: 2. What are the control plane components, and what does each do?
docs.text: kube-apiserver is the REST front end and the only component that talks to etcd; etcd stores all cluster state; kube-scheduler assigns Pods to nodes; kube-controller-manager runs the built-in controllers (Deployment, ReplicaSet, node lifecycle, and others); and cloud-controller-manager integrates with the cloud (load balancers, routes, node lifecycle).

docs.title: 3. What runs on every worker node?
docs.text: The kubelet, which starts the Pods bound to the node through the container runtime and reports their status; kube-proxy (or an eBPF replacement), which programs Service routing rules; and a CRI container runtime such as containerd or CRI-O.

docs.title: 4. What does "desired state and reconciliation" mean?
docs.text: You declare the desired state in an object's spec; controllers continuously observe the actual state (status), compute the difference, and act to close it. The loop is level-triggered, so missed events do no harm and manual changes to managed objects are undone. This is why a deleted Pod owned by a ReplicaSet comes back.

docs.title: 5. What happens to running workloads if the API server goes down?
docs.text: Running Pods keep running and Services keep routing, because kubelets and kube-proxy already have their configuration. But nothing can change: no scheduling, no scaling, no self-healing that needs new objects, and no kubectl access until it returns.

docs.title: 6. Why do etcd clusters have an odd number of members?
docs.text: Writes need a quorum of floor(n/2) + 1 members. Three members tolerate one failure and five tolerate two. Four members still tolerate only one failure (quorum is three), so an even count adds cost without adding fault tolerance.

docs.title: 7. What is the difference between imperative and declarative management?
docs.text: Imperative commands (kubectl create, scale, set image) change the cluster directly and leave no record. Declarative management keeps manifests in Git and applies them with kubectl apply or a GitOps tool, so changes are reviewed, repeatable, and recoverable.

docs.title: 8. What are namespaces for, and are they a security boundary?
docs.text: They scope names and are the unit for RBAC, resource quotas, limit ranges, and network policies. By themselves they are not a security boundary: Pods in different namespaces can communicate and share nodes unless network policies and other controls are added.

docs.title: 9. When would you not use Kubernetes?
docs.text: For one or two services run by a small team, where a serverless container platform (Cloud Run, ECS on Fargate, Azure Container Apps), a PaaS, or Compose on a VM delivers deploys, scaling, and HTTPS with far less operational cost. Kubernetes pays off with many services, several teams, or a need for its ecosystem.

docs.title: 10. What is a Pod, and what do its containers share?
docs.text: The smallest deployable unit: one or more containers scheduled together on one node. They share a network namespace (one IP, one port space, localhost), volumes declared in the Pod, and a lifecycle. Pods are disposable and are replaced, never repaired or moved.

docs.title: 11. What are init containers and native sidecar containers?
docs.text: Init containers run sequentially to completion before app containers start, for preparation work. Native sidecars are init containers with restartPolicy: Always: they start before the app, run alongside it, restart if they crash, and stop after the app exits, so they no longer block Jobs from completing (stable since Kubernetes 1.33).

docs.title: 12. How do a Deployment, ReplicaSets, and Pods relate?
docs.text: The Deployment manages ReplicaSets, one per distinct Pod template, and each ReplicaSet keeps a number of identical Pods running. A template change creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods to it; old ReplicaSets are kept at zero replicas up to revisionHistoryLimit so rollbacks are instant.

docs.title: 13. How does a Service find its Pods?
docs.text: Through its label selector, never by name. The EndpointSlice controller lists the IPs and ports of matching Pods with ready, serving, and terminating conditions, and only ready endpoints receive new traffic.

docs.title: 14. Compare the Service types.
docs.text: ClusterIP (default) gives an internal virtual IP and DNS name. NodePort also opens a port (30000-32767) on every node. LoadBalancer also provisions a cloud load balancer. ExternalName is a DNS alias to an outside name. A headless Service (clusterIP: None) has no virtual IP, and DNS returns Pod IPs.

docs.title: 15. What is the DNS name of a Service?
docs.text: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, for example taskflow-api.taskflow.svc.cluster.local. The short name works within the same namespace. StatefulSet Pods behind a headless Service also get <pod>.<service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.

docs.title: 16. How does a packet sent to a ClusterIP reach a Pod?
docs.text: kube-proxy has programmed iptables or nftables rules on every node from the EndpointSlices. The client's own node rewrites the destination to a ready Pod's IP and port, and the CNI network routes it. kube-proxy itself is not in the data path.

docs.title: 17. Why can gRPC traffic be unevenly balanced across Pods?
docs.text: Service load balancing happens per connection. HTTP/2 clients keep one long-lived connection and send all requests over it, so new Pods added by scaling receive no traffic from existing clients. Use client-side load balancing with a headless Service, a service mesh, or an L7 proxy.

docs.title: 18. Why should you not run bare Pods for applications?
docs.text: Nothing recreates a bare Pod when it is deleted, evicted, or its node fails. A controller (Deployment, StatefulSet, Job, DaemonSet) owns Pods and replaces them.

docs.title: 19. What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
docs.text: Both hold key-value data or files for Pods. Secrets are for sensitive values: they are sent only to nodes that run Pods using them, mounted on tmpfs, can be encrypted at rest, and can be restricted separately with RBAC. Their values are base64-encoded, which is not encryption.

docs.title: 20. Is a Kubernetes Secret secure by default?
docs.text: No. Its values are only base64-encoded, and etcd stores them unencrypted unless encryption at rest is configured (ideally with a KMS provider). Anyone with get or list on Secrets, or with the right to create Pods in the namespace, can read them.

docs.title: 21. What happens to a running Pod when its ConfigMap changes?
docs.text: Environment variables never change; the process keeps its startup values. Mounted files are updated in place by the kubelet after a short delay, except files mounted with subPath, which never update. Apps that read config only at startup still need a restart.

docs.title: 22. How do you roll Pods automatically when configuration changes?
docs.text: Make the change alter the Pod template: Kustomize's configMapGenerator appends a content hash to the ConfigMap name, Helm charts add a checksum/config annotation computed from the rendered ConfigMap, or a reloader controller restarts workloads on change. kubectl rollout restart does it manually.

docs.title: 23. What are immutable ConfigMaps for?
docs.text: immutable: true prevents changes to the data, protects running Pods from accidental edits, and lets the kubelet stop watching the object, which reduces API server load in large clusters. Changes are made by creating a new, versioned object.

docs.title: 24. How do teams keep secret values out of Git?
docs.text: The External Secrets Operator syncs values from a cloud secret manager or Vault into Secrets, defined by committed ExternalSecret references; the Secrets Store CSI Driver mounts values directly into Pods; Sealed Secrets commits values encrypted with the cluster's public key. Workload identity avoids storing cloud credentials in the cluster.

docs.title: 25. What is the difference between liveness, readiness, and startup probes?
docs.text: Readiness decides whether a Pod receives traffic; failing removes it from endpoints without a restart. Liveness decides whether the container is restarted. Startup protects slow starters: until it succeeds, liveness and readiness are disabled, and if it fails for long enough the container is restarted.

docs.title: 26. Why should a liveness probe not check the database?
docs.text: A database outage would fail liveness on every replica at once, restarting all of them, losing warm state, and stampeding the database when it returns. Liveness should only detect a process that cannot recover on its own; dependency problems belong in readiness or in request handling.

docs.title: 27. How long does a default liveness probe take to restart a hung container?
docs.text: About 30 seconds: periodSeconds 10 times failureThreshold 3, plus up to the probe timeoutSeconds (1 second by default) per attempt.

docs.title: 28. How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable work?
docs.text: maxSurge is how many Pods may exist above replicas during a rolling update (percentages round up); maxUnavailable is how many may be unavailable below it (percentages round down). Both default to 25%. With 4 replicas: at most 5 Pods and at least 3 available.

docs.title: 29. What happens if a new version never becomes ready?
docs.text: The rollout cannot proceed beyond the maxUnavailable budget, so old Pods keep serving. After progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) the Deployment's Progressing condition becomes False with ProgressDeadlineExceeded. Kubernetes does not roll back automatically; run kubectl rollout undo or let the pipeline do it.

docs.title: 30. Describe the Pod termination sequence.
docs.text: The Pod is marked Terminating; in parallel its endpoint is removed from EndpointSlices (proxies update over the next moments) and the kubelet runs the preStop hook. Then SIGTERM is sent; the app drains and exits. If it is still running when terminationGracePeriodSeconds (default 30, including preStop) elapses, it gets SIGKILL.

docs.title: 31. Why add a preStop sleep?
docs.text: Endpoint removal and SIGTERM happen concurrently, so a Pod can receive new requests after it starts shutting down. A short sleep (5 to 10 seconds) keeps it serving until load balancers and kube-proxy rules have removed it, eliminating errors during deploys.

docs.title: 32. What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against?
docs.text: Voluntary evictions through the eviction API: node drains, cluster upgrades, and autoscaler scale-downs. It does not apply to a Deployment's rolling update or to involuntary failures such as node crashes. A budget that allows zero disruptions blocks drains.

docs.title: 33. What is the difference between requests and limits?
docs.text: Requests reserve capacity: the scheduler places Pods by them, and CPU requests set relative weight under contention. Limits cap usage: a CPU limit throttles the container, a memory limit gets it OOM-killed when reached.

docs.title: 34. What happens when a container exceeds its CPU limit versus its memory limit?
docs.text: CPU: it is throttled for the rest of each 100 ms period, so it runs slower but survives. Memory: the kernel OOM-kills it (OOMKilled, exit code 137) and the kubelet restarts it.

docs.title: 35. What are the QoS classes?
docs.text: Guaranteed: every container has CPU and memory limits equal to requests. Burstable: some requests or limits but not Guaranteed. BestEffort: none. Under node memory pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort Pods and Pods using more than their requests first, and the OOM killer prefers them too.

docs.title: 36. How does the HPA calculate the desired replica count?
docs.text: desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue), skipped when the ratio is within the 10% tolerance. For example, 4 replicas at 90% CPU with a 60% target give ceil(4 × 90 / 60) = 6, bounded by minReplicas and maxReplicas.

docs.title: 37. Why does the HPA need resource requests?
docs.text: CPU and memory utilization targets are percentages of the request. Without requests the HPA cannot compute utilization and reports <unknown>. Changing requests also changes when it scales.

docs.title: 38. Why does HPA scale-down wait longer than scale-up?
docs.text: Scale-down uses a 300-second stabilization window by default, taking the highest recommendation in that window, so brief dips do not remove Pods that will soon be needed. Scale-up reacts immediately (bounded by rate policies) because under-provisioning hurts users.

docs.title: 39. What is the difference between the HPA, the VPA, and the Cluster Autoscaler?
docs.text: The HPA changes the number of Pods. The VPA recommends or applies better requests per Pod. The Cluster Autoscaler (or Karpenter) adds nodes when Pods are Pending for lack of room and removes underused nodes. All of them depend on accurate requests.

docs.title: 40. How do taints, tolerations, and affinity differ?
docs.text: A taint on a node repels Pods that do not tolerate it; a toleration allows a Pod onto tainted nodes but does not attract it there. Node affinity and node selectors attract Pods to nodes with labels. To dedicate a node pool, taint the nodes and give the intended Pods both a toleration and a selector.

docs.title: 41. What is the difference between an Ingress and an ingress controller?
docs.text: An Ingress is a set of HTTP routing rules (hosts, paths, TLS). An ingress controller is the proxy that watches Ingress objects and implements them. Without a controller that claims it through ingressClassName, an Ingress does nothing.

docs.title: 42. Why is the Gateway API replacing Ingress for new work?
docs.text: Ingress is frozen, and everything beyond hosts, paths, and TLS needs controller-specific annotations. The Gateway API splits responsibilities into GatewayClass, Gateway, and Route resources owned by different roles, and standardizes features such as weighted traffic splitting, header matching, and redirects. The community ingress-nginx controller was also retired after March 2026.

docs.title: 43. How does cert-manager obtain and renew a certificate?
docs.text: An Issuer or ClusterIssuer describes an ACME CA such as Let's Encrypt. For a Certificate (often created from an Ingress annotation), cert-manager proves domain control with an HTTP-01 or DNS-01 challenge, stores the certificate in a TLS Secret, and renews it automatically, by default after two thirds of its lifetime.

docs.title: 44. How do NetworkPolicies work?
docs.text: They select Pods and list allowed ingress and egress traffic by Pod selector, namespace selector, IP block, and port. A Pod selected by a policy is default-deny for that direction; policies are additive; and they are enforced only if the CNI supports them. Remember to allow DNS egress.

docs.title: 45. What are a Helm chart, values, a release, and a revision?
docs.text: A chart is a package of templated manifests with default values. Values configure an installation (precedence: chart defaults, then -f files in order, then --set). A release is one installed instance of a chart, and each install, upgrade, or rollback creates a revision stored as a Secret in the release namespace.

docs.title: 46. What does helm rollback do?
docs.text: It re-applies the manifests and values of an earlier revision and records the result as a new revision. It does not undo database changes or anything outside the release's manifests.

docs.title: 47. When would you use Kustomize instead of Helm?
docs.text: For your own services where environments differ by a few patches, image tags, and generated ConfigMaps: Kustomize keeps plain YAML, needs no templating, and is built into kubectl. Helm suits distributing software to others, complex parameterization, and installing third-party software.

docs.title: 48. What does a StatefulSet guarantee that a Deployment does not?
docs.text: Stable ordinal Pod names (mongo-0), stable DNS names through a headless Service, a dedicated PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod from volumeClaimTemplates, and ordered creation, scaling, and updates. It does not make the software replicate itself.

docs.title: 49. Explain PV, PVC, and StorageClass.
docs.text: A PersistentVolume is real storage; a PersistentVolumeClaim is an app's request for storage of a size, access mode, and class; a StorageClass tells a CSI provisioner how to create volumes dynamically, with a reclaim policy and binding mode.

docs.title: 50. Why use volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer?
docs.text: Cloud block disks are zonal. Waiting until a Pod is scheduled creates the disk in that Pod's zone. Immediate binding can create the disk in a zone where the Pod cannot run, leaving it Pending.

docs.title: 51. Why do many teams run databases as managed services instead of in Kubernetes?
docs.text: A StatefulSet provides identity and storage only. Replication, failover, backups, point-in-time recovery, upgrades, tuning, and monitoring remain the team's job, or an operator's. Managed services provide those, so teams often keep primary data there and run stateless services in the cluster.

docs.title: 52. How do Jobs handle failures?
docs.text: Failed Pods are recreated with exponential back-off (10 s, 20 s, 40 s, up to six minutes) until backoffLimit (default 6) is reached, and activeDeadlineSeconds caps total runtime. podFailurePolicy can fail fast on specific exit codes or ignore disruptions.

docs.title: 53. What do CronJob concurrencyPolicy and timeZone do?
docs.text: concurrencyPolicy decides what happens when a run is due while the previous Job is still running: Allow runs both, Forbid skips the new one, Replace stops the old one. timeZone sets the IANA zone for the schedule instead of the controller's default, usually UTC.

docs.title: 54. A Service returns 503 although its Pods are Running. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Service's EndpointSlices with kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>.

How to confirm: there are no endpoints, or all are not ready; compare the Service selector with kubectl get pods --show-labels.

Likely causes and fixes: a selector that does not match the Pod labels, a wrong targetPort, or Pods failing readiness. Fix the labels or port, or the readiness failure shown in kubectl describe pod. See Pods, Deployments, and Services.

docs.title: 55. New Pods are stuck in ImagePullBackOff. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: the events in kubectl describe pod.

How to confirm: the message says not found (bad tag or digest) or unauthorized / denied (credentials).

Likely causes and fixes: a typo or an image never pushed, a deleted image, a private registry without imagePullSecrets or node permissions, or Docker Hub rate limits. Correct the reference, add credentials, or mirror the image. See Pods, Deployments, and Services.

docs.title: 56. A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What is your process?
docs.text:
What to check first: kubectl logs <pod> --previous and the last state in kubectl describe pod (exit code, reason).

How to confirm: the exit code and log identify the failure: a missing environment variable, OOMKilled, or liveness probe failures.

Likely causes and fixes: configuration or Secret missing (fix the reference), memory limit too low (raise it, size the heap), or a liveness probe killing a slow start (add a startup probe). See health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: 57. Every deploy causes a burst of 502 errors at the ingress. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the app handles SIGTERM and whether there is a preStop hook.

How to confirm: ingress logs show upstream connection refused or reset errors only during rollouts, from Pods that were terminating.

Likely causes and fixes: the app exits immediately on SIGTERM while proxies still route to it, or in-flight requests are cut. Add a short preStop sleep, drain on SIGTERM, keep the total under the grace period, and use readiness probes for new Pods. See health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: 58. During a 3-minute MongoDB outage, every API Pod restarted. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the liveness probe definition and the /healthz handler.

How to confirm: Pod events show Liveness probe failed with 503s during the outage on all replicas at once.

Likely causes and fixes: the liveness endpoint checks the database. Make liveness local only, reflect dependency health in readiness or error handling, and add circuit breaking. See health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: 59. A rollout has been stuck for 15 minutes at "1 of 4 updated replicas are available". What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the new Pods' readiness and events.

How to confirm: new Pods are Running but not ready, and the Deployment condition shows ProgressDeadlineExceeded.

Likely causes and fixes: the new version fails readiness (bad config, missing Secret key, changed probe path). Run kubectl rollout undo, fix the cause, and make the pipeline undo automatically when kubectl rollout status --timeout fails. See health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: 60. A ConfigMap was updated an hour ago, but the app still uses old values. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the value reaches the container (env var or mounted file) and whether the Pods restarted.

How to confirm: kubectl exec ... -- printenv shows the old value, and the Pods' start times predate the change.

Likely causes and fixes: environment variables never update, and the Pod template did not change, so nothing rolled. Run kubectl rollout restart and adopt hash-suffixed ConfigMaps or checksum annotations. See configuration and Secrets.

docs.title: 61. Latency rises at peak while CPU usage looks moderate. What do you look at?
docs.text:
What to check first: CPU throttling: the ratio of container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total to container_cpu_cfs_periods_total, or nr_throttled in cpu.stat.

How to confirm: throttling rises with traffic and correlates with p99 latency.

Likely causes and fixes: a CPU limit throttles bursts within each 100 ms period. Raise or remove the CPU limit, raise requests, or add replicas. See scaling and resource management.

docs.title: 62. The HPA shows <unknown>/60% and never scales. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: kubectl describe hpa conditions and whether metrics-server is running.

How to confirm: the HPA reports failed to get cpu utilization or missing request for cpu, and kubectl top pods fails.

Likely causes and fixes: metrics-server missing or unhealthy, or containers without CPU requests. Install or fix metrics-server and set requests on every container. See scaling and resource management.

docs.title: 63. New Pods stay Pending with "Insufficient cpu", but node CPU usage is 20%. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: the sum of requests on nodes with kubectl describe node ("Allocated resources").

How to confirm: requests are near 100% of allocatable while real usage is low.

Likely causes and fixes: inflated requests. The scheduler uses requests, not usage. Right-size requests with measured usage or VPA recommendations, and run a node autoscaler for genuine growth. See scaling and resource management.

docs.title: 64. Users get a certificate error on the new hostname. How do you debug it?
docs.text:
What to check first: kubectl get certificate and the related Challenge resources.

How to confirm: the Certificate is not ready and the HTTP-01 challenge self-check fails, or DNS for the hostname does not point at the load balancer yet.

Likely causes and fixes: DNS not updated, port 80 blocked, the solver's ingress class wrong, or rate limits from repeated failures. Fix DNS and firewall, match the class, and test with the staging issuer. See Ingress, networking, and Helm.

docs.title: 65. After adding a default-deny NetworkPolicy, every service fails to connect. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether DNS egress is allowed.

How to confirm: Pods log name-resolution errors (EAI_AGAIN), and a test Pod cannot resolve kubernetes.default.

Likely causes and fixes: egress to CoreDNS on port 53 is denied, and the required application flows were not yet allowed. Add an allow-DNS policy and explicit allows for each flow, then apply default deny. See Ingress, networking, and Helm.

docs.title: 66. A database StatefulSet Pod is Pending after a node failure. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Pod's events.

How to confirm: volume node affinity conflict: its PersistentVolume is in a zone with no available node.

Likely causes and fixes: zonal disks pin the Pod to a zone. Restore capacity in that zone (node autoscaling per zone), spread replicas across zones, and rely on database replication meanwhile. See stateful workloads and Jobs.

docs.title: 67. Customers received the nightly email twice. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the CronJob's concurrencyPolicy and the Jobs it created around that time.

How to confirm: two Jobs overlapped, or one Job retried a Pod after it had already sent emails.

Likely causes and fixes: Allow with a long run, or a non-idempotent job. Set concurrencyPolicy: Forbid, a startingDeadlineSeconds, and make sending idempotent by recording what was sent. See stateful workloads and Jobs.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Kubernetes overview
  • Orchestration fundamentals · Pods, Deployments, and Services · Configuration and Secrets · Health probes and rolling updates · Scaling and resource management · Ingress, networking, and Helm · Stateful workloads and Jobs
  • Kubernetes documentation
