docs.title: Orchestration Fundamentals
docs.text:
Running one container on one server is easy. Running forty containers of ten services across six servers, replacing them when they crash or a server dies, rolling out new versions without downtime, and routing traffic to whichever copies are healthy is not. That job is called container orchestration, and Kubernetes is the system most teams use for it.

This lesson explains what an orchestrator does, the architecture of a Kubernetes cluster (the control plane components and what runs on every node), the idea that drives everything in Kubernetes (desired state and reconciliation loops), how declarative YAML and kubectl apply fit in, namespaces and API groups, managed compared with self-managed clusters, and when Kubernetes is the wrong tool.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Every concept in later lessons (Deployments, Services, probes, autoscaling) is a controller reconciling some desired state. Once you understand the loop, Kubernetes stops looking like a collection of magic YAML keys and becomes predictable: you can reason about why a Pod came back after you deleted it, why a change you made with kubectl edit disappeared, why a node failure takes minutes to heal, and what each component's outage would break.

Knowing the architecture also tells you what you are paying for. A managed service runs the control plane, but you still own node capacity, upgrades of your manifests across API versions, add-ons, and the applications. Choosing Kubernetes for a single small service often costs more than it saves.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google (Borg). The paper Large-scale cluster management at Google with Borg (EuroSys 2015) describes the cluster manager that ran Google's workloads before Kubernetes: declarative job specifications, bin-packing of tasks onto machines, and automatic rescheduling on failure. Several Kubernetes concepts (Pods, labels, Services) come from lessons the paper and its follow-up articles describe.
  • OpenAI. The post Scaling Kubernetes to 7,500 nodes explains how OpenAI ran very large clusters for machine-learning workloads and which control plane parts (the API servers, etcd, networking, and monitoring) needed attention at that size.
  • Spotify. The CNCF Spotify case study describes moving from Spotify's homegrown orchestrator, Helios, to Kubernetes because a small in-house team could not keep up with a project supported by a much larger community, running the two side by side during the migration.
  • Kubernetes project. The cluster components documentation defines the control plane and node components this page walks through.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon EKS, Google Kubernetes Engine (including Autopilot), Azure Kubernetes Service, Red Hat OpenShift, Rancher and RKE2, k3s, kubeadm for self-managed clusters, and kind, minikube, k3d, or Docker Desktop for local clusters.

docs.title: What an orchestrator does
docs.text: Problem without an orchestrator What Kubernetes does Deciding which server has room for a container Scheduling by CPU and memory requests and placement rules A container crashes at 3 a.m. Self-healing: the kubelet restarts it; controllers replace lost Pods A server dies Pods on it are recreated on healthy nodes Deploying without downtime Rolling updates with health checks and one-command rollback Clients must find changing container IPs Services: stable names, virtual IPs, and load balancing Traffic grows Horizontal autoscaling of Pods, and of nodes with a cluster autoscaler Configuration and credentials per environment ConfigMaps and Secrets injected at runtime Every team scripts deploys differently One declarative API and a tool ecosystem around it

docs.title: Cluster architecture
docs.text:
A cluster has a control plane, which stores the desired state and makes decisions, and worker nodes, which run the application Pods.

Component Where Responsibility kube-apiserver Control plane The REST front door: authentication, authorization (RBAC), admission control, validation, and the only reader and writer of etcd etcd Control plane Consistent, replicated key-value store holding every object; uses the Raft consensus algorithm kube-scheduler Control plane Assigns each unscheduled Pod to a node: filters nodes that fit, scores them, binds the best kube-controller-manager Control plane Runs the built-in controllers: Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, Job, node lifecycle, EndpointSlice, namespace, and more cloud-controller-manager Control plane Cloud-specific controllers: creates load balancers for Services, attaches routes, removes deleted VMs from the cluster kubelet Every node Watches for Pods bound to its node, starts them through the runtime, runs probes, reports status kube-proxy Every node Programs iptables or nftables rules so Service virtual IPs reach Pods (IPVS mode is deprecated since 1.35; some network plugins replace kube-proxy) Container runtime Every node containerd or CRI-O, called by the kubelet through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI) Add-ons Cluster CoreDNS for service names, a CNI network plugin for Pod networking, a CSI driver for volumes, metrics-server

Three plug-in interfaces keep Kubernetes portable: CRI for container runtimes, CNI for networking (Calico, Cilium, the cloud's VPC plugins), and CSI for storage (cloud disks, network file systems).

Two consequences of the design matter in practice. First, every component talks only to the API server; they never call each other. If the API server is unavailable, running Pods keep running and Services keep routing, but nothing new can be scheduled or changed. Second, etcd needs a quorum: with n members it needs floor(n/2) + 1 to agree, so three members tolerate one failure and five tolerate two. Production control planes therefore run three or five etcd members, which managed services do for you.

docs.title: Desired state and reconciliation
docs.text:
Every Kubernetes object has a spec (what you want) and a status (what is true now, written by the system). A controller is a loop that watches objects of some kind and works to make status match spec:

  1. Read the desired state from the spec.
  2. Observe the actual state through watches on the API server.
  3. Compute the difference.
  4. Act: create, update, or delete objects to reduce the difference.
  5. Repeat on every change and periodically.

The loop is level-triggered: controllers act on the current state, not on a history of events. A missed event does no harm, because the next pass sees the same gap. This is why Kubernetes heals itself and why manual changes to managed objects get undone: if you delete a Pod owned by a ReplicaSet, the ReplicaSet creates a new one; if you kubectl edit a Deployment that a GitOps tool manages, the tool reapplies the version in Git.

Controllers chain together. A Deployment controller manages ReplicaSets, a ReplicaSet controller manages Pods, the scheduler fills in each Pod's node, and the kubelet makes containers exist. Each piece reconciles only its own level, which keeps every controller simple.

Note the timing in the node-failure example: Kubernetes waits before evicting Pods from a node that stops responding (by default Pods tolerate an unreachable node for 300 seconds) so that a brief network blip does not cause a stampede of rescheduling. Running several replicas spread across nodes is what keeps the service up during those minutes.

docs.title: Declarative YAML and kubectl apply
docs.text:
Every object has the same four top-level fields:

apiVersion: apps/v1        # API group and version
kind: Deployment           # object type
metadata:                  # name, namespace, labels, annotations
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:                      # desired state; its shape depends on the kind
  replicas: 3

There are two ways to change a cluster:

Imperative Declarative kubectl create deployment, kubectl scale --replicas=5, kubectl set image Files in Git, applied with kubectl apply -f Fast for experiments Reviewable, repeatable, and recoverable The cluster becomes the only record of what you did Git is the record; the cluster can be rebuilt from it

kubectl apply computes what changed between your file and the live object and patches only that. With client-side apply (the default) it records the last applied file in an annotation; with kubectl apply --server-side, the API server tracks which field manager owns each field and reports conflicts when two tools try to own the same one. kubectl diff -f shows what an apply would change. GitOps tools such as Argo CD and Flux run this loop continuously from a Git repository (see immutable infrastructure and GitOps).

docs.title: Namespaces
docs.text:
A namespace is a scope for names: two Deployments called api can exist in taskflow-staging and taskflow-prod. Namespaces are also the unit for RBAC permissions, resource quotas, default limits, and network policies. A fresh cluster has default, kube-system (cluster components), kube-public, and kube-node-lease (node heartbeats).

Namespaces are not a hard security boundary by themselves: Pods in different namespaces can talk to each other unless network policies say otherwise, and all of them share nodes and the kernel. Nodes, PersistentVolumes, StorageClasses, and namespaces themselves are cluster-scoped: they belong to no namespace.

docs.title: API groups and the objects you will use most
docs.text:
API group/version Kinds v1 (core) Pod, Service, ConfigMap, Secret, Namespace, PersistentVolumeClaim, ServiceAccount apps/v1 Deployment, ReplicaSet, StatefulSet, DaemonSet batch/v1 Job, CronJob networking.k8s.io/v1 Ingress, IngressClass, NetworkPolicy autoscaling/v2 HorizontalPodAutoscaler policy/v1 PodDisruptionBudget rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1 Role, ClusterRole, RoleBinding, ClusterRoleBinding gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1 Gateway, HTTPRoute (installed as CRDs)

APIs move from v1alpha1 to v1beta1 to v1, and old versions are removed on a published schedule, so manifests must be updated before cluster upgrades. Custom resource definitions (CRDs) let add-ons define new kinds (a Certificate, an ExternalSecret), each with its own controller, which is how most of the ecosystem extends Kubernetes.

docs.title: Managed compared with self-managed Kubernetes
docs.text:
Managed (EKS, GKE, AKS) Self-managed (kubeadm, k3s, RKE2) Control plane and etcd Run, scaled, and backed up by the provider You install, back up, and secure them Upgrades Provider upgrades the control plane; you upgrade nodes and manifests You upgrade everything Nodes You manage node groups, or the provider does (GKE Autopilot, EKS Auto Mode) You manage machines and their OS Cloud integration Load balancers, disks, IAM built in You install controllers and drivers Cost Control plane fee plus nodes Engineering time plus machines Typical use Most companies in the cloud On-premises, edge, air-gapped, special hardware

Kubernetes ships about three minor versions per year and each receives roughly a year of patches, so every cluster needs an upgrade routine. Managed providers enforce it by ending support for old versions.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Option Good fit Operational cost Docker Compose on one VM One small app or internal tool Lowest; no high availability Platform as a service (Render, Fly.io, Heroku) Web apps and APIs without a platform team Low; less control over networking and runtime Serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS on Fargate, Azure Container Apps) Stateless HTTP services, workers, and jobs Low to medium; scales to zero on some platforms Managed Kubernetes Many services, several teams, need for its ecosystem or portability Medium to high Self-managed Kubernetes On-premises, edge, regulatory or hardware constraints Highest

Choose Kubernetes when you have enough services and teams that a common platform pays for itself, when you need its extensibility (operators, service meshes, custom controllers), or when portability across clouds and data centers matters. Do not choose it for a single API and a frontend run by two developers: a serverless container platform gives the same rolling deploys, autoscaling, and HTTPS with a fraction of the concepts and cost.

docs.title: A local multi-node cluster with kind
docs.text:
# kind-config.yaml: one control-plane node and two workers
kind: Cluster
apiVersion: kind.x-k8s.io/v1alpha4
nodes:
  - role: control-plane
  - role: worker
  - role: worker

kind create cluster --name taskflow --config kind-config.yaml
kubectl cluster-info --context kind-taskflow
kubectl get nodes -o wide

# Use a locally built image without pushing it to a registry
docker build -t taskflow-api:dev .
kind load docker-image taskflow-api:dev --name taskflow

docs.title: Looking at the control plane
docs.text:
kubectl get pods -n kube-system            # etcd, apiserver, scheduler, CoreDNS, kube-proxy ...
kubectl get --raw='/readyz?verbose'        # API server health checks
kubectl api-resources | head -20           # every kind, its group, and whether it is namespaced
kubectl explain deployment.spec.strategy   # built-in field documentation
kubectl version                            # client and server versions

On managed clusters the control plane Pods are hidden from you; only the node-level components and add-ons appear in kube-system.

docs.title: Watching reconciliation happen
docs.text:
kubectl create namespace taskflow
kubectl -n taskflow create deployment taskflow-api \
  --image=ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0 --replicas=3

# Delete a Pod: the ReplicaSet replaces it
kubectl -n taskflow delete pod -l app=taskflow-api --wait=false
kubectl -n taskflow get pods -w

# Take a node out of service: Pods are evicted and rescheduled elsewhere
kubectl cordon taskflow-worker
kubectl drain taskflow-worker --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data
kubectl -n taskflow get pods -o wide
kubectl uncordon taskflow-worker

# What did the controllers do?
kubectl -n taskflow events --for deployment/taskflow-api
kubectl -n taskflow get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

docs.title: A declarative workflow
docs.text:
# k8s/namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: taskflow
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: taskflow

kubectl diff -f k8s/                      # preview changes against the live cluster
kubectl apply -f k8s/ --server-side       # apply the whole directory
kubectl get all -n taskflow

docs.title: Contexts and default namespaces
docs.text:
kubectl config get-contexts
kubectl config use-context kind-taskflow
kubectl config set-context --current --namespace=taskflow   # stop typing -n
kubectl config current-context

Production contexts deserve care: a command meant for staging that runs against production is a classic incident. Use separate kubeconfig files or a prompt that shows the current context.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep every manifest in Git and change clusters declaratively; reserve imperative commands for experiments and emergencies.
  • Use namespaces per application and environment, with RBAC, quotas, and network policies on top.
  • Run at least two replicas of anything that serves traffic, spread across nodes and zones.
  • Prefer a managed control plane unless you have a specific reason and the people to run one.
  • Track API deprecations and upgrade clusters on a regular schedule.
  • Remember that the API server is the single point of entry: protect it with RBAC, private endpoints, and audit logging.
  • Use kubectl diff before kubectl apply in CI and in manual changes.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A cluster upgrade fails because manifests use removed APIs. Detect: kubectl apply returns no matches for kind "PodDisruptionBudget" in version "policy/v1beta1", or the apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis metric lists clients still calling old versions. Cause: the API version was removed in the target release. Fix: scan manifests and Helm charts with a deprecation checker (such as pluto or kubent), migrate to the stable versions, then upgrade.
  • Changes made with kubectl edit keep reverting. Detect: the object's managedFields or the GitOps tool's history shows another manager rewriting the field. Cause: a GitOps controller or a pipeline reconciles the object from Git. Fix: make the change in Git; use server-side apply field ownership to see who owns what.
  • Pods on a failed node take five minutes to come back. Detect: the node shows NotReady, and its Pods stay Running or Terminating for minutes before replacements appear. Cause: the default 300-second toleration for unreachable nodes delays eviction. Fix: run several replicas spread across nodes so the service never depends on one node; shorten tolerations only for workloads that need faster failover.
  • The API server is slow and kubectl commands time out. Detect: API request latency and etcd disk sync durations (etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds) climb. Cause: on self-managed clusters, etcd on slow disks or overloaded control plane nodes; on any cluster, controllers or scripts listing huge numbers of objects. Fix: fast dedicated disks for etcd, scaled control plane nodes, paginated and watch-based clients.
  • A team accidentally deletes another team's workloads. Detect: audit logs show the deletion from a user with cluster-wide rights. Cause: everything lives in default and everyone has cluster-admin. Fix: a namespace per team or application, RBAC roles scoped to namespaces, and separate production credentials.
  • A cluster runs an unsupported Kubernetes version. Detect: the provider's console warns of end of support, or security advisories no longer list fixes for your minor version. Cause: upgrades were postponed. Fix: a scheduled upgrade process: test in staging, check deprecations, upgrade the control plane, then node pools.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Orchestrator: A system that schedules, runs, heals, and connects containers across many machines.
  • Control plane: The components that store state and make decisions (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller managers).
  • Node: A machine (VM or physical) that runs Pods, with a kubelet and a container runtime.
  • Desired state / spec: What you declared; status: what the system observed.
  • Controller: A loop that reconciles actual state toward desired state for one kind of object.
  • Reconciliation: Repeatedly comparing actual and desired state and acting on the difference.
  • etcd quorum: The majority of etcd members that must agree for writes to succeed.
  • Namespace: A named scope for objects, RBAC, and quotas.
  • CRD: A custom resource definition that adds a new kind to the API.
  • CRI, CNI, CSI: The plug-in interfaces for runtimes, networking, and storage.
  • Managed Kubernetes: A cloud service that runs the control plane for you.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking kubectl apply executes the deployment. It stores desired state; controllers act asynchronously.
  • Editing live objects by hand in a GitOps-managed cluster.
  • Treating namespaces as a security boundary without RBAC and network policies.
  • Running one replica and expecting Kubernetes to avoid downtime.
  • Choosing Kubernetes for one or two services because "everyone uses it".
  • Ignoring API deprecations until an upgrade breaks deploys.
  • Assuming the cluster stops working when the API server is down; running workloads continue, but nothing can change.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. List the control plane components and say what each does.
  2. What runs on every worker node, and how does the kubelet know which Pods to run?
  3. Explain the reconciliation loop using a ReplicaSet with three replicas when one Pod is deleted.
  4. An etcd cluster has 5 members. How many can fail before writes stop? How many for 3 members, and why is 4 not better than 3?
  5. What is the difference between imperative and declarative management, and why do teams keep manifests in Git?
  6. What happens to running Pods if the API server becomes unavailable?
  7. Which responsibilities does a managed Kubernetes service take over, and which remain with you?
  8. Name three situations where a simpler platform than Kubernetes is the better choice.

docs.title: Pods, Deployments, and Services
docs.text:
Three objects carry almost every stateless application on Kubernetes. A Pod is the smallest thing Kubernetes runs: one or more containers that share a network identity and storage. A Deployment keeps a set of identical Pods running and replaces them gradually when you change the template. A Service gives that changing set of Pods one stable name and virtual IP address and spreads connections across the ready ones.

This lesson covers how Pods share networking and storage, init and sidecar containers (including native sidecars), labels and selectors, ReplicaSets and Deployments, the Service types (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, headless), EndpointSlices, cluster DNS names, what actually happens to a packet sent to a Service, full manifests for the TaskFlow API, and the kubectl commands you will use every day.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Most Kubernetes debugging comes down to these objects. A Service with no endpoints because one label is misspelled, a Deployment stuck because the image cannot be pulled, gRPC traffic that lands on a single Pod, a sidecar that keeps a Job from finishing: all are explained by how Pods, ReplicaSets, Services, and EndpointSlices fit together. Writing the manifests well (labels, named ports, resource requests, probes, security settings) also decides how safely every later rollout and scaling event behaves.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitHub. The engineering post Kubernetes at GitHub (2017) describes moving the main Ruby on Rails application that serves github.com and its API onto Kubernetes Pods behind Services, and the review-lab environments that made each pull request deployable.
  • Kubernetes project: native sidecars. The blog post Kubernetes v1.28: Introducing native sidecar containers explains why sidecars needed first-class support: ordinary sidecar containers could start after the app and kept Jobs from completing, which the restartPolicy: Always init-container form fixes.
  • Kubernetes project: gRPC load balancing. The post gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears shows that a ClusterIP Service balances connections, not requests, so long-lived HTTP/2 connections pin to one Pod unless the client or a proxy balances per request.
  • Kubernetes documentation. The Service concept page defines the Service types and selectors used throughout this lesson.

Popular tools and providers: kubectl, k9s and Lens for browsing clusters, stern for multi-Pod logs, kubectx and kubens for switching contexts, CoreDNS, and CNI plugins such as Cilium, Calico, and the cloud providers' VPC plugins.

docs.title: Pods
docs.text:
A Pod is a group of containers that are always scheduled together on the same node and share:

  • One network namespace: one IP address, one port space, and localhost. Two containers in a Pod cannot both listen on port 3000.
  • Volumes declared in the Pod spec, which several containers can mount (an emptyDir is the usual way to share files).
  • A lifecycle: the Pod is created, runs, and is deleted as a unit.

Every Pod gets its own cluster-wide IP address, and by default every Pod can reach every other Pod directly without NAT; the CNI plugin implements this flat network. Pod IPs change whenever Pods are replaced, which is why clients use Services instead.

A Pod's status.phase is Pending (accepted, not yet running: waiting for scheduling or image pulls), Running, Succeeded, Failed, or Unknown. Each container also has a state (Waiting with a reason such as ImagePullBackOff or CrashLoopBackOff, Running, or Terminated with an exit code). Pods are disposable: they are never moved or repaired, only replaced. Do not create bare Pods for applications; let a controller such as a Deployment own them.

docs.title: Init containers and sidecars
docs.text:
• Init containers run one after another, each to completion, before the app containers start. They suit one-time preparation: waiting for a dependency, fetching configuration, setting file permissions.
  • Sidecar containers run alongside the app for its whole life: a log shipper, a proxy, a metrics agent. Since Kubernetes 1.29 (stable in 1.33), a sidecar is declared as an init container with restartPolicy: Always. Such native sidecars start before the app containers, keep running, are restarted if they crash, and are stopped only after the app containers have exited, so they no longer block Jobs from completing or lose the app's last log lines.

docs.title: Labels and selectors
docs.text:
Labels are key-value pairs on any object (app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api, env: prod). Selectors pick objects by label, either by equality (matchLabels) or by set expressions (matchExpressions with In, NotIn, Exists). Controllers and Services find their Pods only through selectors, never by name. The recommended labels app.kubernetes.io/name, app.kubernetes.io/instance, app.kubernetes.io/version, app.kubernetes.io/component, and app.kubernetes.io/part-of make tools and dashboards work consistently.

A Deployment's spec.selector is immutable after creation, and it must match the labels in its Pod template, or the API server rejects the object.

docs.title: ReplicaSets and Deployments
docs.text:
A ReplicaSet keeps a given number of Pods matching its selector running: it creates Pods when there are too few and deletes them when there are too many. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets so you can change the Pod template safely. Each distinct template gets its own ReplicaSet, named with a hash of the template (pod-template-hash).

When you change the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and shifts Pods from the old one to the new one according to its strategy (rolling update by default; covered in health probes and rolling updates). Old ReplicaSets are kept, scaled to zero, up to revisionHistoryLimit (default 10), which is what makes kubectl rollout undo instant. Changing only replicas scales the current ReplicaSet without creating a new one.

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A Service selects Pods by label and gives them a stable virtual IP (the ClusterIP) and DNS name. Its port is what clients connect to; its targetPort is the container port (a number or a named port).

Type Reachable from How Typical use ClusterIP (default) Inside the cluster A virtual IP and DNS name Service-to-service traffic; the backend of an Ingress NodePort Outside, via any node's IP Opens the same port (30000-32767 by default) on every node, plus a ClusterIP Bare-metal setups, or as a building block for external load balancers LoadBalancer Outside, via a cloud load balancer The cloud controller provisions a load balancer that targets the nodes or Pods Exposing a TCP or UDP service directly ExternalName Inside the cluster A DNS CNAME to an outside name Giving an external database an in-cluster name Headless (clusterIP: None) Inside the cluster No virtual IP; DNS returns the Pod IPs StatefulSets, client-side load balancing

For HTTP traffic from the internet, one Ingress or Gateway in front of many ClusterIP Services is usually better than one LoadBalancer per Service (see Ingress, networking, and Helm).

docs.title: EndpointSlices
docs.text: The EndpointSlice controller watches each Service's selector and writes EndpointSlice objects listing the matching Pods' IPs and ports, each with ready, serving, and terminating conditions. Readiness is the key: a Pod whose readiness probe fails stays in the slice but is marked not ready, and receives no new traffic. EndpointSlices replaced the older single Endpoints object (now deprecated) because one huge object per Service did not scale for Services with thousands of Pods.

docs.title: Cluster DNS
docs.text:
CoreDNS gives every Service a DNS name: <service>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. Inside the same namespace the short name works (taskflow-api); from another namespace use taskflow-api.taskflow. A ClusterIP Service resolves to its virtual IP; a headless Service resolves to the IPs of its ready Pods, and StatefulSet Pods also get individual names such as mongo-0.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local.

Pods' /etc/resolv.conf contains search domains and ndots:5, so a name with fewer than five dots is first tried with each search suffix. Lookups of external names such as api.example.com therefore generate several failed queries first; a trailing dot (api.example.com.) or a lower ndots in the Pod's dnsConfig avoids that when it matters.

docs.title: What happens when a Pod calls a Service
docs.text:
Three details explain many surprises:

  • kube-proxy is not a proxy in the data path. It watches Services and EndpointSlices and programs kernel rules (iptables or nftables; the older IPVS mode is deprecated) on every node; the kernel rewrites packets. Some CNI plugins (Cilium, for example) replace kube-proxy with eBPF programs that do the same job.
  • Balancing is per connection. With HTTP keep-alive or HTTP/2 (gRPC), one long-lived connection carries many requests to the same Pod. New Pods added by autoscaling get no traffic from existing connections. Clients that need per-request balancing use a headless Service with client-side balancing, or a service mesh or L7 proxy.
  • The ClusterIP works only inside the cluster. You cannot ping it, and it does not exist outside; use kubectl port-forward for local access.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use Run a stateless API or web app Deployment + ClusterIP Service Expose HTTP(S) to the internet ClusterIP Service behind an Ingress or Gateway Expose a non-HTTP TCP or UDP service externally LoadBalancer Service Stable identity and storage per replica StatefulSet + headless Service One Pod per node (agents) DaemonSet Run to completion Job or CronJob A helper that must start before the app Init container A helper that runs beside the app Native sidecar (init container with restartPolicy: Always) A one-off debugging shell kubectl debug or kubectl run --rm -it

Avoid bare Pods for anything that should survive a node failure, avoid NodePort as a public entry point in the cloud, and avoid one LoadBalancer per HTTP service, which multiplies cost and TLS configuration.

docs.title: The TaskFlow API Deployment
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
    app.kubernetes.io/part-of: taskflow
spec:
  replicas: 3
  revisionHistoryLimit: 5
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
        app.kubernetes.io/part-of: taskflow
    spec:
      securityContext:
        runAsNonRoot: true
        runAsUser: 1000
        runAsGroup: 1000
        seccompProfile:
          type: RuntimeDefault
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.4.0
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: PORT
              value: "3000"
            - name: MONGODB_URI
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: taskflow-api-secrets
                  key: mongodb-uri
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 256Mi
            limits:
              memory: 512Mi
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
          securityContext:
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            capabilities:
              drop: ["ALL"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tmp
              mountPath: /tmp
      volumes:
        - name: tmp
          emptyDir: {}

Points worth noticing:

  • The selector and the template labels match, and use the recommended app.kubernetes.io/name key.
  • The port is named http, so probes and the Service refer to the name rather than repeating 3000.
  • The connection string comes from a Secret (see configuration and Secrets).
  • Requests let the scheduler place the Pod; the memory limit bounds a leak (see scaling and resource management).
  • The security settings mirror the hardened docker run from container security: non-root, no privilege escalation, no capabilities, read-only root, and an emptyDir for /tmp.

docs.title: The Service
docs.text:
# k8s/api-service.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
  labels:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: http

kubectl apply -f k8s/
kubectl -n taskflow get deploy,rs,pods,svc -l app.kubernetes.io/name=taskflow-api
kubectl -n taskflow get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=taskflow-api

Other Pods in the namespace now reach the API at http://taskflow-api, and Pods elsewhere at http://taskflow-api.taskflow.

docs.title: An init container and a native sidecar
docs.text:
# k8s/legacy-worker.yaml (excerpt): wait for a dependency, ship a log file
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: legacy-worker
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: legacy-worker
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: legacy-worker
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: wait-for-mongo
          image: busybox:1.37
          command: ["sh", "-c", "until nslookup mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local; do sleep 2; done"]
        - name: log-shipper
          image: alpine:3.22
          restartPolicy: Always          # native sidecar: starts first, stops last
          command: ["sh", "-c", "tail -F /var/log/app/worker.log"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: ghcr.io/example/legacy-worker:2.1.0
          volumeMounts:
            - name: logs
              mountPath: /var/log/app
      volumes:
        - name: logs
          emptyDir: {}

The first init container blocks until the MongoDB Service name resolves. The second has restartPolicy: Always, which turns it into a sidecar: it keeps running beside the worker and prints the log file the legacy worker writes, so the lines appear in kubectl logs -c log-shipper. Apps you control should simply log to stdout instead.

docs.title: Everyday kubectl commands
docs.text:
# Look
kubectl get pods -n taskflow -o wide                  # node and IP per Pod
kubectl get pods -n taskflow --show-labels
kubectl describe pod <pod> -n taskflow                # events: scheduling, pulls, probes
kubectl get events -n taskflow --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp

# Logs and shells
kubectl logs -n taskflow deploy/taskflow-api -f       # one Pod of the Deployment
kubectl logs -n taskflow -l app.kubernetes.io/name=taskflow-api --tail=50 --prefix
kubectl logs -n taskflow <pod> --previous             # the crashed container's last run
kubectl exec -it -n taskflow <pod> -- sh
kubectl debug -it -n taskflow <pod> --image=busybox:1.37 --target=api   # ephemeral container

# Reach things from your laptop
kubectl port-forward -n taskflow svc/taskflow-api 8080:80
curl http://localhost:8080/healthz

# Change things
kubectl apply -f k8s/
kubectl diff -f k8s/
kubectl scale -n taskflow deploy/taskflow-api --replicas=5
kubectl rollout status -n taskflow deploy/taskflow-api
kubectl delete -f k8s/legacy-worker.yaml

# Learn the schema
kubectl explain deployment.spec.template.spec.containers.readinessProbe

docs.title: Testing Service DNS from inside the cluster
docs.text:
kubectl run -n taskflow dns-test --rm -it --restart=Never --image=busybox:1.37 -- \
  sh -c 'nslookup taskflow-api; wget -qO- http://taskflow-api/healthz'

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Never run bare Pods for applications; use Deployments (or StatefulSets, Jobs, DaemonSets).
  • Use the recommended app.kubernetes.io/* labels consistently and keep selectors minimal and stable.
  • Name container ports and reference the names from probes and Services.
  • Run at least two replicas of anything that serves traffic.
  • Give every container resource requests and a memory limit.
  • Set Pod and container securityContext (non-root, no privilege escalation, dropped capabilities, read-only root filesystem).
  • Use ClusterIP Services by default and one Ingress or Gateway for HTTP entry.
  • Use native sidecars for helpers that must outlive the app container.
  • Use fully qualified Service names across namespaces.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The Service returns connection refused or 503 for every request. Detect: kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=taskflow-api shows no endpoints, or all of them not ready. Cause: the Service selector does not match the Pod labels (a typo or a changed label), the targetPort is wrong, or every Pod fails readiness. Fix: compare kubectl get svc -o yaml with kubectl get pods --show-labels, fix the selector or port, and check readiness probe failures in kubectl describe pod.
  • New Pods stay in ImagePullBackOff. Detect: kubectl describe pod shows Failed to pull image ... not found or unauthorized. Cause: a wrong tag or digest, or a private registry without credentials. Fix: correct the reference, and add an imagePullSecrets entry or node-level registry permissions.
  • A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Detect: restarts climb, and the back-off delay between them grows to five minutes. Cause: the container exits on start: missing configuration, an unreachable dependency, or a failing liveness probe. Fix: kubectl logs --previous for the last run's output and kubectl describe pod for the exit code and probe events.
  • gRPC traffic all lands on one or two Pods after scaling out. Detect: per-Pod request metrics are badly uneven; new Pods are idle. Cause: ClusterIP Services balance connections, and HTTP/2 clients keep one connection open. Fix: client-side load balancing over a headless Service, a service mesh, or periodic connection recycling.
  • Changing a Deployment's labels fails with field is immutable. Detect: kubectl apply rejects spec.selector. Cause: selectors cannot change after creation. Fix: create a new Deployment with the new selector, shift traffic, then delete the old one; or keep selectors minimal so they never need to change.
  • Outbound calls to external APIs are slow to start. Detect: DNS latency is high and CoreDNS logs show many NXDOMAIN queries for names like api.example.com.taskflow.svc.cluster.local. Cause: ndots:5 makes each external lookup try every search domain first. Fix: use fully qualified names with a trailing dot or lower ndots in dnsConfig, and consider NodeLocal DNSCache for heavy lookup rates.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Pod: One or more containers scheduled together, sharing a network namespace and volumes.
  • Init container: A container that runs to completion before the app containers start.
  • Native sidecar: An init container with restartPolicy: Always that runs alongside the app for the Pod's life.
  • Label / selector: Key-value metadata, and a query that matches objects by it.
  • ReplicaSet: Keeps a fixed number of identical Pods running.
  • Deployment: Manages ReplicaSets to roll out template changes and roll them back.
  • Service: A stable virtual IP and DNS name for a set of Pods chosen by selector.
  • ClusterIP / NodePort / LoadBalancer / headless: The ways a Service is exposed.
  • EndpointSlice: The generated list of a Service's backend addresses and their readiness.
  • kube-proxy: The node agent that programs kernel rules implementing Service virtual IPs.
  • CoreDNS: The cluster DNS server that resolves Service and Pod names.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Creating Pods directly and expecting them to come back after a node failure.
  • Assuming a Service routes to Pods by name or by Deployment rather than by label.
  • Thinking a ClusterIP can be reached from outside the cluster.
  • Believing kube-proxy forwards traffic itself and is a bottleneck.
  • Expecting even request distribution for long-lived connections.
  • Using latest image tags in Deployments, so kubectl rollout restart silently changes the version.
  • Putting two containers that listen on the same port into one Pod.
  • Using kubectl edit in production instead of changing the manifest in Git.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do containers in the same Pod share, and what consequences does that have for ports?
  2. Why should applications run under a Deployment instead of as bare Pods?
  3. Explain how a Deployment, its ReplicaSets, and Pods relate during an image change and during kubectl rollout undo.
  4. A Service selects app=taskflow-api, and four Pods carry that label, but one fails its readiness probe. How many receive new connections, and where can you see that?
  5. Compare ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, and headless Services.
  6. What DNS name would a Pod in namespace web use to reach the taskflow-api Service in namespace taskflow?
  7. Why can scaling a gRPC backend from 3 to 6 Pods leave the new Pods idle?
  8. What changed with native sidecar containers, and which problem with Jobs did they solve?
