docs.title: Scaling and Resource Management
docs.text: Kubernetes packs Pods onto nodes and grows or shrinks capacity, but it can only do that well if every container says how much CPU and memory it needs. This lesson covers resource requests and limits and what the kernel does at each boundary (CPU throttling compared with memory OOM kills), the three quality-of-service classes and eviction, namespace guardrails with LimitRange and ResourceQuota, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler and its formula with worked numbers, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, node autoscaling with the Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter, and the scheduling controls that decide where Pods land: node selectors, affinity, taints and tolerations, and topology spread constraints.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Resource settings decide cost, reliability, and latency at the same time. Requests that are too high waste nodes you pay for; requests that are too low pack too many Pods on a node, which then starves or evicts them. A memory limit below the real working set restarts Pods under load. A CPU limit can quietly add tens of milliseconds to every request through throttling, while average CPU graphs look healthy. Autoscaling built on wrong requests scales at the wrong times, and replicas that all land on one node or zone fail together.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google Cloud. The article Kubernetes best practices: Resource requests and limits explains how the scheduler uses requests, what happens when containers exceed CPU or memory limits, and how namespace quotas and limit ranges keep teams from starving each other.
  • The Linux kernel. The CFS bandwidth control documentation describes the quota-per-period mechanism behind CPU limits and the throttling statistics (nr_throttled, throttled_time) used to diagnose it.
  • Kubernetes project. The horizontal Pod autoscaling documentation gives the replica formula, the tolerance, the handling of not-yet-ready Pods, and the default scale-up and scale-down behaviour used in the worked example below.
  • Karpenter. The Karpenter project, started at AWS and now a Kubernetes SIG Autoscaling subproject, provisions right-sized nodes directly from the requirements of pending Pods and consolidates underused nodes, an alternative to scaling fixed node groups.

Popular tools and providers: metrics-server, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler, the Vertical Pod Autoscaler, the Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter, KEDA (event-driven autoscaling), Prometheus Adapter for custom metrics, and Goldilocks for request recommendations.

docs.title: Requests and limits
docs.text:
Each container can declare, per resource:

Request Limit Meaning What the container is guaranteed The most it may use Used by the scheduler Yes: a Pod fits on a node only if the sum of requests fits the node's allocatable capacity No CPU enforcement Relative weight under contention (cpu.weight) Hard quota per 100 ms period (cpu.max): throttling Memory enforcement Used for eviction ranking under node memory pressure Hard cap (memory.max): OOM kill at the limit

Units: CPU is measured in cores, with m meaning thousandths (250m is a quarter of a core). Memory uses bytes with binary suffixes (256Mi, 1Gi) or decimal ones (256M). Case matters: 400m of memory means 0.4 bytes, a classic typo.

docs.title: CPU throttling compared with OOM kills
docs.text:
CPU is compressible. With a 500m limit, the container may use 50 ms of CPU time in each 100 ms period, across all its threads. A request that needs 80 ms of CPU therefore cannot finish in one period: it runs for 50 ms, waits about 50 ms for the next period, and finishes 30 ms into it, taking around 130 ms of wall time instead of 80 ms. Multi-threaded runtimes burn through the quota faster, because every thread consumes it in parallel. The container never dies from this; it just gets slower, and the only clue is the throttling counters.

Memory is not compressible. When a container's memory reaches its limit, the kernel reclaims what it can and then the OOM killer kills a process in the container. Kubernetes reports OOMKilled with exit code 137, and the kubelet restarts the container.

That difference leads to common guidance:

  • Always set a memory limit, usually equal to or slightly above the memory request, and size runtimes inside it (for Node.js, set --max-old-space-size to about 75% of the limit).
  • Always set a CPU request. Whether to set a CPU limit is a trade-off: limits make performance predictable and stop noisy neighbours, but cause throttling at bursts. Many teams omit CPU limits for latency-sensitive services and rely on requests for fair sharing; others require them for strict multi-tenant isolation.

docs.title: Quality-of-service classes and eviction
docs.text:
Kubernetes assigns every Pod a QoS class from its resource settings:

QoS class Rule Under node memory pressure Guaranteed Every container has CPU and memory limits equal to its requests Evicted last; lowest OOM-kill priority Burstable At least one container has a request or limit, but not Guaranteed Evicted if using more than requested BestEffort No requests or limits at all Evicted first; killed first

When a node runs low on memory or disk, the kubelet evicts Pods, ranking first those whose usage exceeds their requests, then by Pod priority. Evicted Pods are recreated elsewhere by their controllers, but a BestEffort Pod can be evicted again and again. Every production Pod should at least be Burstable with honest requests.

docs.title: Namespace guardrails: LimitRange and ResourceQuota
docs.text:
• A LimitRange sets per-container defaults (requests and limits applied when a manifest omits them) and minimums and maximums within a namespace.
  • A ResourceQuota caps a namespace's totals: summed CPU and memory requests and limits, number of Pods, PersistentVolumeClaims, Services, and other objects. Once a quota tracks requests.cpu, every new Pod in the namespace must declare a CPU request (or receive one from a LimitRange), or the API server rejects it.

Together they stop one team's runaway deployment from consuming a shared cluster.

docs.title: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler
docs.text:
The HPA (autoscaling/v2) changes a workload's replica count to keep a metric near a target. Every 15 seconds by default it reads the metric and computes:

desiredReplicas = ceil( currentReplicas × currentMetricValue / targetMetricValue )

Worked example for the TaskFlow API (CPU request 250m, target 60%):

4 replicas, average usage 225m           -> utilization 225/250 = 90%
desired = ceil(4 × 90 / 60) = ceil(6.0)  -> 6 replicas
after scale-out: 900m total / 6 Pods     -> 150m each = 60%, ratio 1.0: stay at 6
traffic falls, utilization 20%           -> ceil(6 × 20 / 60) = 2, min 3: scale to 3
                                            (after the 300 s stabilization window)

Details that shape its behaviour:

  • Utilization is relative to requests. Without a CPU request the HPA cannot compute a percentage and shows <unknown>. Changing the request changes when it scales.
  • Tolerance. If the ratio is within 10% of 1.0, nothing happens, which prevents constant small adjustments.
  • Stabilization. Scale-down uses the highest recommendation from the last 300 seconds by default, so a short dip does not remove Pods that will be needed again a minute later. Scale-up has no window by default and may at most double the replicas or add 4 Pods (whichever is more) per 15 seconds.
  • Not-ready Pods and missing metrics are treated conservatively, so new Pods that are still starting do not trigger another scale-up.
  • Metric types: Resource (CPU, memory), Pods (a per-Pod custom metric such as requests per second), Object (a metric of another object, such as an Ingress), and External (a queue length from a cloud service). Custom and external metrics need an adapter such as Prometheus Adapter or KEDA.
  • When an HPA manages a Deployment, remove replicas from the Deployment manifest, or every kubectl apply resets the count.

Memory is usually a poor HPA metric for Node.js and other garbage-collected runtimes, because memory rarely drops when load falls. CPU, request rate, or queue length track load better.

docs.title: The Vertical Pod Autoscaler
docs.text: The VPA (an add-on, autoscaling.k8s.io/v1) watches actual usage and recommends, or applies, better requests. Its update modes are Off (recommendations only), Initial (set requests when Pods are created), Recreate (evict Pods to apply new values; the older Auto mode is a deprecated alias for it), and InPlaceOrRecreate (resize running Pods in place, evicting only when that fails). In-place resizing of a running Pod's resources is on by default since Kubernetes 1.33 and stable since 1.35. Running the VPA in Off mode is a safe way to right-size requests. Do not let the HPA and the VPA act on the same CPU or memory metric for the same workload; they would fight each other.

docs.title: Node autoscaling: Cluster Autoscaler and Karpenter
docs.text:
The HPA adds Pods; something must add nodes when they do not fit.

Cluster Autoscaler Karpenter Trigger Pods Pending because no node has room Same Scales Predefined node groups (cloud auto scaling groups) Provisions individual nodes chosen from Pod requirements (NodePool rules) Instance choice Fixed per node group Picks sizes and types to fit the pending Pods Scale-down Removes underused nodes, respecting PodDisruptionBudgets Consolidation: replaces or removes nodes to pack Pods more cheaply Providers Most clouds AWS, Azure, and others through providers

Both act on requests, not on real usage: a cluster whose Pods request far more than they use autoscales into waste. KEDA complements them by scaling workloads on event sources (queue depth, stream lag, cron windows), including scaling to zero.

docs.title: Scheduling basics
docs.text:
The scheduler filters nodes that can run a Pod (enough allocatable resources, matching selectors and affinities, tolerated taints), scores the rest, and binds the Pod to the best one.

Control What it does Example nodeSelector Only nodes with these labels kubernetes.io/arch: arm64 Node affinity Required or preferred rules with operators (In, NotIn, Exists) Prefer node.kubernetes.io/instance-type in a list Pod affinity / anti-affinity Place near, or away from, Pods with given labels, per topology domain Keep API replicas on different hosts Taints and tolerations A tainted node repels Pods that do not tolerate the taint (NoSchedule, PreferNoSchedule, NoExecute) GPU or batch-only node pools Topology spread constraints Limit the imbalance (maxSkew) of matching Pods across zones or nodes Spread replicas evenly across three zones PriorityClass Higher-priority Pods can preempt lower ones when the cluster is full Critical services over batch jobs

Taints keep the wrong Pods off a node; tolerations only allow a Pod onto tainted nodes and do not attract it there. To dedicate a node pool, combine a taint (to keep others off) with a node selector or affinity (to steer the intended Pods on).

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Stateless API with load that varies over the day HPA on CPU (or requests per second), minimum 2 to 3 replicas Queue workers KEDA or an HPA on an external queue-length metric You do not know the right requests VPA in Off mode, or measured p95 usage plus headroom Bursty, latency-sensitive service CPU request without a CPU limit (if policy allows); memory request equal to limit Shared multi-team cluster LimitRange defaults, ResourceQuotas, PriorityClasses Highly available service Topology spread across zones and nodes, PDB, at least 3 replicas Special hardware or isolated workloads Taints and tolerations plus node affinity

Do not autoscale on memory for garbage-collected runtimes, do not combine HPA and VPA on the same resource metric, and do not let autoscalers compensate for missing or wildly wrong requests.

docs.title: Requests and limits for the TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml (excerpt): container resources
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m          # about the p95 CPU per Pod at normal load
    memory: 384Mi      # steady-state memory plus headroom
  limits:
    memory: 384Mi      # equal to the request: predictable, lowest eviction risk
    # no CPU limit: bursts use idle CPU instead of being throttled
env:
  - name: NODE_OPTIONS
    value: --max-old-space-size=288   # about 75% of the memory limit

kubectl -n taskflow top pods -l app.kubernetes.io/name=taskflow-api   # needs metrics-server
kubectl -n taskflow get pod <pod> -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'
kubectl describe node <node> | grep -A 8 "Allocated resources"

docs.title: A HorizontalPodAutoscaler
docs.text:
# k8s/api-hpa.yaml
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: taskflow-api
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 60
  behavior:
    scaleUp:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
      policies:
        - type: Pods
          value: 4
          periodSeconds: 60
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
      policies:
        - type: Percent
          value: 50
          periodSeconds: 60

kubectl -n taskflow get hpa taskflow-api --watch
# NAME           REFERENCE                 TARGETS       MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
# taskflow-api   Deployment/taskflow-api   cpu: 90%/60%  3         10        4
kubectl -n taskflow describe hpa taskflow-api      # conditions and scaling events

The behavior section adds at most 4 Pods per minute and removes at most half of them per minute after five quiet minutes, which smooths spiky traffic. The 60% target leaves headroom so existing Pods absorb a surge while new ones start.

docs.title: Namespace guardrails
docs.text:
# k8s/namespace-guardrails.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: defaults
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  limits:
    - type: Container
      defaultRequest:
        cpu: 100m
        memory: 128Mi
      default:
        memory: 256Mi
      max:
        memory: 2Gi
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: taskflow-quota
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "8"
    requests.memory: 16Gi
    limits.memory: 24Gi
    pods: "60"
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"

kubectl -n taskflow describe resourcequota taskflow-quota   # used compared with hard

docs.title: Spreading replicas and steering Pods
docs.text:
# k8s/api-deployment.yaml (excerpt): pod template spec scheduling rules
spec:
  topologySpreadConstraints:
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
      whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
    - maxSkew: 1
      topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
      whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
      labelSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: kubernetes.io/arch
                operator: In
                values: ["amd64", "arm64"]

# k8s/report-job.yaml (excerpt): run only on a dedicated, tainted batch pool
spec:
  nodeSelector:
    workload: batch
  tolerations:
    - key: dedicated
      operator: Equal
      value: batch
      effect: NoSchedule

kubectl taint nodes <batch-node> dedicated=batch:NoSchedule
kubectl label nodes <batch-node> workload=batch

The first spread constraint keeps zones within one replica of each other and refuses to break that rule; the second spreads across hosts when possible. The batch Job both tolerates the taint and selects the label, so it lands only on the batch pool while other Pods stay off it.

docs.title: Finding CPU throttling
docs.text:
# Inside a container (cgroup v2): how often the quota was hit
kubectl -n taskflow exec <pod> -- cat /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.stat
# nr_periods 120000
# nr_throttled 18000      <- 15% of periods throttled
# throttled_usec 540000000

In Prometheus, the cAdvisor metrics container_cpu_cfs_throttled_periods_total divided by container_cpu_cfs_periods_total give the same ratio per container.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Set CPU and memory requests on every container from measured usage, and revisit them as the code changes.
  • Set memory limits, usually equal to requests, and size the runtime's heap below them.
  • Decide CPU limits deliberately; watch throttling wherever they exist.
  • Keep production Pods out of BestEffort.
  • Use LimitRanges and ResourceQuotas in shared clusters.
  • Autoscale stateless services with the HPA on CPU or request rate; leave headroom in the target.
  • Run a node autoscaler so HPA scale-outs never wait on manual capacity.
  • Spread replicas across zones and nodes with topology spread constraints.
  • Remove replicas from manifests of HPA-managed workloads.
  • Use taints plus selectors to dedicate node pools.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Latency rises while average CPU looks fine. Detect: p99 latency climbs with traffic, and the ratio of throttled to total CFS periods is above a few percent. Cause: a CPU limit throttles short bursts, especially for multi-threaded processes. Fix: raise or remove the CPU limit, raise the request, or add replicas.
  • Pods are OOMKilled after a traffic spike. Detect: kubectl describe pod shows Last State: Terminated, Reason: OOMKilled, Exit Code: 137, and memory metrics hit the limit first. Cause: the limit is below the peak working set, or the runtime's heap is not sized to the limit. Fix: raise the limit from measured peaks, set the heap size explicitly, and look for leaks.
  • New Pods stay Pending although nodes look idle. Detect: events show 0/6 nodes are available: 6 Insufficient cpu, while node CPU usage is low. Cause: requests are far higher than real usage, so the scheduler sees the nodes as full. Fix: right-size requests using VPA recommendations or usage data.
  • The HPA shows <unknown>/60% and never scales. Detect: kubectl describe hpa reports failed to get cpu utilization or missing request for cpu. Cause: metrics-server is not installed or not healthy, or the containers have no CPU requests. Fix: install or fix metrics-server and set requests on every container in the Pod.
  • Replica count jumps back after every deploy. Detect: the HPA had scaled to 8, a kubectl apply sets 3, then the HPA scales up again. Cause: the Deployment manifest still contains replicas. Fix: remove the field and let the HPA own it.
  • One zone outage takes the service down. Detect: all replicas were on nodes in the failed zone (kubectl get pods -o wide and node zone labels). Cause: no spread constraints, so the scheduler packed them together. Fix: topology spread constraints across zones, at least one replica per zone, and a PDB.
  • New Pods in a namespace are rejected outright. Detect: kubectl apply fails with must specify requests.cpu. Cause: a ResourceQuota tracks CPU requests and the manifest has none. Fix: add requests, or a LimitRange with default requests.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Request: The amount of a resource reserved for a container and used for scheduling.
  • Limit: The maximum a container may use; enforced by cgroups.
  • Allocatable: A node's capacity minus what is reserved for the system and kubelet.
  • CPU throttling: Pausing a container that used its CPU quota until the next period.
  • OOMKilled: A container killed by the kernel for exceeding its memory limit.
  • QoS class: Guaranteed, Burstable, or BestEffort, derived from requests and limits.
  • Eviction: The kubelet removing Pods to relieve node resource pressure.
  • LimitRange / ResourceQuota: Per-container defaults and bounds, and per-namespace totals.
  • HPA: The controller that scales replicas to keep a metric near a target.
  • VPA: The add-on that recommends or applies better requests.
  • Cluster Autoscaler / Karpenter: Controllers that add and remove nodes based on pending Pods.
  • Taint / toleration: A node marking that repels Pods, and a Pod's permission to ignore it.
  • Topology spread constraint: A rule limiting how unevenly Pods are spread across zones or nodes.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Leaving requests unset and getting BestEffort Pods.
  • Treating limits as reservations; only requests reserve capacity.
  • Setting memory limits far above requests and then being surprised by evictions under node pressure.
  • Believing CPU limits never hurt because the container is not killed.
  • Autoscaling on memory for garbage-collected runtimes.
  • Forgetting that the HPA computes utilization against requests.
  • Expecting tolerations to attract Pods to tainted nodes.
  • Relying on the scheduler to spread replicas across zones without telling it to.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What do requests and limits each control, for CPU and for memory?
  2. A container with a 200m CPU limit needs 60 ms of CPU for a request. Roughly how long does the request take, and why?
  3. Classify the QoS class of a Pod whose only container sets requests.memory: 256Mi and limits.memory: 256Mi but no CPU settings.
  4. An HPA targets 70% CPU. Five replicas average 84% utilization. How many replicas does it want? What if they average 72%?
  5. Why does scale-down wait for a stabilization window, and why does scale-up not?
  6. What is the difference between the HPA, the VPA, and a node autoscaler?
  7. How do you keep a GPU node pool for GPU jobs only?
  8. A node has 3.5 CPU allocatable. How many Pods requesting 500m fit, regardless of their actual usage?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Kubernetes documentation: Resource management for Pods and containers
  • Kubernetes documentation: Pod quality of service classes
  • Kubernetes documentation: Node-pressure eviction
  • Kubernetes documentation: Taints and tolerations
  • Kubernetes documentation: Pod topology spread constraints
  • Kubernetes autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler and VPA)
  • KEDA
  • Next: ingress, networking, and Helm. Back to the Kubernetes overview.

docs.title: Stateful Workloads and Jobs
docs.text:
Deployments assume every replica is interchangeable and disposable. Some workloads are not like that: a database replica needs the same name and the same disk every time it restarts, a migration should run once and stop, a nightly report should run on a schedule, and a log agent should run exactly once on every node. Kubernetes has a workload kind for each: StatefulSets, Jobs, CronJobs, and DaemonSets.

This lesson covers StatefulSets (stable names, ordered rollout, one volume per Pod), persistent storage (PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses, dynamic provisioning, and access modes), why many teams still run databases as managed services, Jobs (completions, parallelism, retries, deadlines), CronJobs (schedules, time zones, concurrency policies), and DaemonSets.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Getting these wrong loses data or runs work the wrong number of times. A database in a Deployment with a shared volume corrupts itself, or loses everything when its Pod moves. Deleting a namespace with a Delete reclaim policy destroys the disks behind it. A migration run from an init container executes once per replica at the same moment. A CronJob that overlaps itself sends every customer two emails. Choosing the right kind and the right storage settings prevents all of these.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google Cloud. The article To run or not to run a database on Kubernetes: What to consider compares fully managed databases, self-managed databases on VMs, and databases on Kubernetes, and explains that running them in a cluster means taking on operations such as backups, failover, and upgrades, often with an operator.
  • Kubernetes project. The tutorial Running ZooKeeper, a distributed system coordinator builds a replicated ensemble with a StatefulSet, a headless Service, per-Pod volumes, a PodDisruptionBudget, and anti-affinity, the same ingredients this page uses.
  • Kubernetes project. The CronJob documentation warns that a CronJob creates a Job approximately once per schedule time, so in rare cases two Jobs or none may be created, and that Jobs must therefore be idempotent.
  • CloudNativePG. The CloudNativePG project is an example of a Kubernetes operator that manages PostgreSQL clusters (replication, failover, backups) on top of these primitives, the usual approach when teams do run databases inside Kubernetes.

Popular tools and providers: CSI drivers (AWS EBS, Google Persistent Disk, Azure Disk, Ceph via Rook), VolumeSnapshots, Velero for cluster backups, operators such as CloudNativePG, MongoDB's Kubernetes operators, and Strimzi for Kafka, Argo Workflows for complex batch pipelines, and managed databases such as MongoDB Atlas, Amazon RDS, and Cloud SQL.

docs.title: StatefulSets
docs.text:
A StatefulSet manages Pods that need identity. Compared with a Deployment, it guarantees:

  • Stable, ordinal names. Pods are mongo-0, mongo-1, mongo-2, not random suffixes, and a replacement for mongo-1 is again called mongo-1.
  • Stable network identity. With a headless Service named in serviceName, each Pod gets a DNS record such as mongo-0.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local, so peers and clients can address a specific replica.
  • Stable storage. volumeClaimTemplates create one PersistentVolumeClaim per Pod (data-mongo-0, data-mongo-1, ...), and a rescheduled Pod reattaches the same claim.
  • Ordering. With the default podManagementPolicy: OrderedReady, Pods are created one at a time in order (each waits for the previous to be Running and Ready) and removed in reverse order. Parallel drops the ordering when the application does not need it.

Updates use updateStrategy. RollingUpdate (the default) replaces Pods one at a time in reverse ordinal order (mongo-2 first), waiting for each to be Ready; a partition value updates only Pods with an ordinal at or above it, which allows staged rollouts. OnDelete updates a Pod only when you delete it yourself.

By default, deleting or scaling down a StatefulSet keeps the PVCs, so the data survives and comes back if you scale up again. The persistentVolumeClaimRetentionPolicy field (whenDeleted and whenScaled, each Retain or Delete) changes that.

A StatefulSet provides identity and storage, not clustering. Making mongo-1 a replica of mongo-0, electing a primary, and adding members is the application's (or an operator's) job.

docs.title: Persistent storage: PV, PVC, and StorageClass
docs.text:
Object Who creates it What it is PersistentVolume (PV) A provisioner (or an administrator) A piece of real storage: a cloud disk, an NFS share; cluster-scoped PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) The application A request for storage: size, access mode, StorageClass; namespaced StorageClass The cluster administrator A recipe: which CSI provisioner, disk type, reclaim policy, binding mode

With dynamic provisioning, a new PVC that names a StorageClass makes the CSI driver create a disk and a matching PV, and binds them. Key StorageClass settings:

  • reclaimPolicy: Delete (the disk is destroyed when the PVC is deleted; the default for dynamically provisioned volumes) or Retain (the disk is kept for manual recovery).
  • volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer: create the disk only when a Pod using the claim is scheduled, so the disk is created in that Pod's zone. With Immediate, a disk can land in a zone where the Pod cannot run.
  • allowVolumeExpansion: true: lets you grow a claim by editing its size.

Access modes describe how a volume may be mounted:

Mode Meaning Typical backing ReadWriteOnce (RWO) Read-write by Pods on a single node Cloud block disks (EBS, Persistent Disk, Azure Disk) ReadWriteOncePod (RWOP) Read-write by a single Pod only CSI block disks that support it ReadOnlyMany (ROX) Read-only by many nodes Shared file systems, prepared images ReadWriteMany (RWX) Read-write by many nodes NFS, EFS, Azure Files, CephFS

Block disks are zonal: a Pod whose volume lives in zone a can only run on nodes in zone a. Losing a zone therefore makes that replica unavailable until the zone returns, which is why replicated databases spread replicas (and their disks) across zones. VolumeSnapshots (snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1) take point-in-time copies through the CSI driver, a building block for backups.

docs.title: Why many teams run databases as managed services
docs.text:
Kubernetes can run databases well, but the platform gives you only the building blocks. Everything that makes a database production-grade is still yours to build or install:

Responsibility Managed service (Atlas, RDS, Cloud SQL) Operator on Kubernetes Plain StatefulSet Replication and failover Provider Operator You Backups and point-in-time recovery Provider, configurable Operator, configured by you You Version upgrades Provider-assisted Operator-assisted You Storage performance tuning Provider You (StorageClass, nodes) You Monitoring and alerting Built in You install it You Cost Highest per unit Cluster resources plus your time Cluster resources plus most of your time

Many teams therefore run stateless services in Kubernetes and keep the primary database in a managed service, using StatefulSets for caches, queues, development environments, or databases backed by a mature operator and a team prepared to operate it. Backup and recovery planning is covered in backups and disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
A Job runs Pods until a given number of them complete successfully, then stops.

Field Default Meaning completions 1 Successful Pods required parallelism 1 Pods running at the same time completionMode NonIndexed Indexed gives each Pod an index (in JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX) so it can process its own shard backoffLimit 6 Failed retries before the Job is marked failed activeDeadlineSeconds none Fail the whole Job after this long, whatever the retries ttlSecondsAfterFinished none Delete the finished Job (and its Pods) after this long podFailurePolicy none Rules on exit codes or conditions: fail fast on a fatal code, ignore Pod disruptions

The Pod template's restartPolicy must be Never (each failure creates a new Pod, keeping the failed one for inspection) or OnFailure (the container restarts in the same Pod). The Job controller recreates failed Pods with an exponential back-off: 10 seconds, 20 seconds, 40 seconds, and so on, capped at six minutes.

Good Job workloads: database migrations before a rollout, one-off data fixes, batch processing, and sending a backlog of emails. Every Job should be idempotent, because a node failure can make a Pod run its work twice.

docs.title: CronJobs
docs.text:
A CronJob creates Jobs on a schedule written in standard five-field cron syntax (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week).

Field Default Meaning schedule required Cron expression, such as 0 2 * * * for 02:00 daily timeZone the controller's time zone (usually UTC) IANA time zone name such as Europe/Berlin concurrencyPolicy Allow Allow overlapping runs, Forbid (skip the new run), or Replace (stop the old run) startingDeadlineSeconds none Skip a run that could not start within this many seconds of its time successfulJobsHistoryLimit / failedJobsHistoryLimit 3 / 1 Finished Jobs kept for inspection suspend false Pause future runs without deleting the CronJob

Set timeZone explicitly; otherwise schedules follow the control plane's clock, which is usually UTC. Missed schedule times (while the controller was down or the CronJob was suspended) never produce a backlog: the controller starts at most one Job, for the most recent missed time, and records a TooManyMissedTimes warning if more than 100 were missed. Without startingDeadlineSeconds that late run starts immediately, however late it is, so a sensible deadline is good practice.

docs.title: DaemonSets
docs.text: A DaemonSet runs one Pod on every node (or every node matching a selector) and adds a Pod automatically when a node joins. Typical uses are node-level agents: log collectors, metrics exporters, CNI and CSI node plugins, and security agents. DaemonSet Pods often need tolerations to run on tainted nodes (including control plane nodes on self-managed clusters), host paths to read node files, and modest resource requests because they run on every node. Updates roll node by node, controlled by updateStrategy.rollingUpdate.maxUnavailable.

docs.title: Choosing the workload kind
docs.text: Workload Kind Stateless API or web app Deployment Replicated database, queue broker, or cache with per-replica data StatefulSet (ideally through an operator) Run once to completion Job Run on a schedule CronJob One Pod per node DaemonSet

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Use StatefulSets when each replica needs its own identity and storage and the software knows how to replicate itself. Do not use them to give a stateless app a fixed name; use a Service. Do not run a production primary database on a plain StatefulSet without backups, monitoring, and a tested failover plan; prefer a managed service or an operator.

Use Jobs for finite work, and run database migrations as a Job before the rollout rather than in init containers (which run once per replica, in parallel). Use CronJobs for periodic work that tolerates the "approximately once" guarantee; for work that must run exactly once, add idempotency keys or a lock. Use DaemonSets only for genuinely per-node work; a cluster-wide service belongs in a Deployment.

docs.title: A StorageClass for SSD disks
docs.text:
# k8s/storageclass-fast-ssd.yaml (AWS EBS CSI driver)
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata:
  name: fast-ssd
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com
parameters:
  type: gp3
reclaimPolicy: Retain
volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer
allowVolumeExpansion: true

On other clouds only the provisioner and parameters change (for example pd.csi.storage.gke.io on GKE or disk.csi.azure.com on AKS).

docs.title: A MongoDB replica set for development and testing
docs.text:
# k8s/mongo.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: mongo
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  clusterIP: None                 # headless: DNS returns Pod addresses
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: mongo
  ports:
    - name: mongo
      port: 27017
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: mongo
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  serviceName: mongo
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: mongo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: mongo
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
      containers:
        - name: mongo
          image: mongo:8.0
          args: ["--replSet", "rs0", "--bind_ip_all"]
          ports:
            - name: mongo
              containerPort: 27017
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["mongosh", "--quiet", "--eval", "db.adminCommand('ping').ok"]
            periodSeconds: 10
            timeoutSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 250m
              memory: 1Gi
            limits:
              memory: 1Gi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: data
              mountPath: /data/db
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data
      spec:
        accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
        storageClassName: fast-ssd
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 10Gi

kubectl apply -f k8s/mongo.yaml
kubectl -n taskflow rollout status statefulset/mongo
kubectl -n taskflow get pods,pvc -l app.kubernetes.io/name=mongo

# One-time replica set initialization
kubectl -n taskflow exec mongo-0 -- mongosh --quiet --eval '
rs.initiate({
  _id: "rs0",
  members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "mongo-0.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017" },
    { _id: 1, host: "mongo-1.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017" },
    { _id: 2, host: "mongo-2.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017" }
  ]
})'

The TaskFlow API then connects with mongodb://mongo-0.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017,mongo-1.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017,mongo-2.mongo.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:27017/taskflow?replicaSet=rs0, and the driver discovers which member is primary. This setup has no authentication, backups, or anti-affinity: it is fine for a development cluster, and exactly the work an operator or a managed service does for you in production.

docs.title: A migration Job run before the rollout
docs.text:
# k8s/migrate-job.yaml (the CI pipeline sets a unique name per release)
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: taskflow-migrate-1-5-0
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  backoffLimit: 2
  activeDeadlineSeconds: 600
  ttlSecondsAfterFinished: 86400
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.5.0
          command: ["node", "dist/migrate.js"]
          env:
            - name: MONGODB_URI
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: taskflow-api-secrets
                  key: mongodb-uri

kubectl apply -f k8s/migrate-job.yaml
kubectl -n taskflow wait --for=condition=complete job/taskflow-migrate-1-5-0 --timeout=10m
kubectl -n taskflow logs job/taskflow-migrate-1-5-0
# only then: update the Deployment image

The pipeline waits for the Job to complete before rolling out the new API version. Migrations must stay compatible with the version still running during the rollout; see zero-downtime database migrations.

docs.title: A CronJob for the daily digest
docs.text:
# k8s/digest-cronjob.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata:
  name: task-digest
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  schedule: "0 7 * * *"
  timeZone: Europe/Berlin
  concurrencyPolicy: Forbid
  startingDeadlineSeconds: 600
  successfulJobsHistoryLimit: 3
  failedJobsHistoryLimit: 1
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      backoffLimit: 3
      activeDeadlineSeconds: 1800
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: Never
          containers:
            - name: digest
              image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.5.0
              command: ["node", "dist/jobs/send-digest.js"]
              env:
                - name: MONGODB_URI
                  valueFrom:
                    secretKeyRef:
                      name: taskflow-api-secrets
                      key: mongodb-uri

kubectl -n taskflow get cronjob task-digest
kubectl -n taskflow create job --from=cronjob/task-digest digest-manual-test   # run it now
kubectl -n taskflow get jobs --watch

The digest script should record which users already received today's email, so a retried or duplicated run sends nothing twice.

docs.title: An Indexed Job that processes shards in parallel
docs.text:
# k8s/reindex-job.yaml
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata:
  name: reindex-tasks
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  completions: 8
  parallelism: 4
  completionMode: Indexed
  backoffLimit: 4
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: reindex
          image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.5.0
          command: ["node", "dist/jobs/reindex.js"]
          env:
            - name: SHARD_COUNT
              value: "8"
            # JOB_COMPLETION_INDEX (0-7) is set automatically for Indexed Jobs

Four Pods run at a time; the Job completes when each index from 0 to 7 has succeeded once.

docs.title: A DaemonSet for a node metrics agent
docs.text:
# k8s/node-exporter.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: DaemonSet
metadata:
  name: node-exporter
  namespace: monitoring
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: node-exporter
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: node-exporter
    spec:
      hostNetwork: true
      hostPID: true
      tolerations:
        - operator: Exists          # run on every node, including tainted ones
      containers:
        - name: node-exporter
          image: quay.io/prometheus/node-exporter:v1.9.1
          args:
            - --path.procfs=/host/proc
            - --path.sysfs=/host/sys
          ports:
            - name: metrics
              containerPort: 9100
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
          volumeMounts:
            - name: proc
              mountPath: /host/proc
              readOnly: true
            - name: sys
              mountPath: /host/sys
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: proc
          hostPath:
            path: /proc
        - name: sys
          hostPath:
            path: /sys

In practice you would install this with the Prometheus community Helm chart, which adds security settings and a Service for scraping; the structure is the same.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Prefer managed databases for primary data; use operators when you run databases in Kubernetes.
  • Use WaitForFirstConsumer StorageClasses for zonal disks and allowVolumeExpansion so volumes can grow.
  • Use reclaimPolicy: Retain for valuable data, and back it up with snapshots or the database's own tools; test restores.
  • Spread StatefulSet replicas across zones with topology spread constraints or anti-affinity, and protect them with a PDB.
  • Run migrations as a Job that the pipeline waits for, not in init containers.
  • Make every Job and CronJob idempotent; set backoffLimit, activeDeadlineSeconds, and ttlSecondsAfterFinished.
  • Set timeZone, concurrencyPolicy, and startingDeadlineSeconds on every CronJob.
  • Give DaemonSets small requests, read-only host mounts, and only the tolerations they need.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A StatefulSet Pod stays Pending after a node failure. Detect: events show volume node affinity conflict or didn't match PersistentVolume's node affinity. Cause: its disk lives in a zone with no available node. Fix: make sure every zone has capacity (node autoscaling per zone), spread replicas across zones, and rely on the database's replication while the zone is down.
  • A database volume fills up. Detect: kubectl exec ... -- df -h /data/db near 100%, and database write errors. Cause: the claim was sized for an earlier data volume. Fix: raise spec.resources.requests.storage on the PVC (with allowVolumeExpansion: true), and alert on volume usage well before it is full.
  • Data disappears after a namespace was deleted. Detect: PVs from the namespace are gone, and the cloud console shows the disks deleted. Cause: the StorageClass used reclaimPolicy: Delete. Fix: use Retain for important data, protect production namespaces from deletion, and keep backups outside the cluster.
  • Customers receive the daily email twice. Detect: two Jobs for the same schedule time overlap in kubectl get jobs. Cause: concurrencyPolicy: Allow with a slow run, or a retried Pod that had already sent emails. Fix: Forbid, and idempotent sending that records what was sent.
  • A CronJob silently stops creating Jobs. Detect: kubectl get jobs shows one Job from the CronJob still active hours or days later, and no newer runs. Cause: concurrencyPolicy: Forbid skips every new run while that Job is active, and a hung Pod with no activeDeadlineSeconds never ends. Fix: set activeDeadlineSeconds in the job template, delete the stuck Job, and alert when a CronJob's last successful run is too old.
  • A Job never completes although its work finished. Detect: the main container is Completed but the Pod stays Running because a sidecar is still up. Cause: a regular sidecar container keeps the Pod alive. Fix: declare the sidecar as a native sidecar (an init container with restartPolicy: Always), which stops after the main container exits.
  • A StatefulSet rollout is stuck. Detect: kubectl rollout status statefulset/mongo waits on mongo-2, which is not Ready. Cause: with ordered updates, the controller waits for each Pod before continuing, and the new version fails its readiness check. Fix: inspect and fix that Pod (or roll the template back), then delete it so it is recreated from the corrected template.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• StatefulSet: A workload with stable Pod names, network identities, and per-Pod storage.
  • Headless Service: A Service with clusterIP: None whose DNS returns the individual Pod addresses.
  • volumeClaimTemplates: The PVC template a StatefulSet stamps out once per Pod.
  • PersistentVolume / PersistentVolumeClaim: A piece of storage, and a request that binds to one.
  • StorageClass: The provisioner and parameters used to create volumes dynamically.
  • Dynamic provisioning: Creating a disk automatically when a claim needs one.
  • Access mode: How a volume may be mounted (RWO, RWOP, ROX, RWX).
  • Reclaim policy: What happens to a volume when its claim is deleted (Delete or Retain).
  • Job: Runs Pods until a number of them complete successfully.
  • CronJob: Creates Jobs on a cron schedule.
  • DaemonSet: Runs one Pod per node.
  • Operator: A controller that encodes the operational knowledge for a piece of software, such as a database.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Running a database in a Deployment, or sharing one RWO volume between replicas.
  • Believing a StatefulSet makes software clustered or highly available by itself.
  • Using Immediate binding with zonal disks and getting volumes in the wrong zone.
  • Relying on the default Delete reclaim policy for important data.
  • Running migrations in init containers.
  • Assuming CronJobs run exactly once and never overlap.
  • Leaving finished Jobs to accumulate forever.
  • Using a DaemonSet for a service that does not need to run on every node.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which three guarantees does a StatefulSet give that a Deployment does not?
  2. What is the DNS name of the second replica of the StatefulSet mongo in namespace taskflow, and what makes it resolvable?
  3. Why does volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer matter for zonal disks?
  4. Compare the RWO, RWOP, ROX, and RWX access modes with a typical backing store for each.
  5. A Job has completions: 12 and parallelism: 3, and each Pod takes 5 minutes with no failures. Roughly how long does the Job take?
  6. Why should migrations run as a Job rather than an init container?
  7. A CronJob runs every 10 minutes, but one run takes 25 minutes. What happens under Allow, Forbid, and Replace?
  8. List three responsibilities you take on when you run a database on a StatefulSet instead of a managed service.

docs.title: Linux Server Operations Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the Linux server operations lessons, for the day before an interview or a task on a server.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text:
Command What it does ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow Creates an Ed25519 key pair; -a 100 slows passphrase guessing ssh -J ops@203.0.113.20 ops@10.0.2.10 Reaches a private server through a bastion (ProxyJump) ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:3300:10.0.2.30:3000 taskflow-bastion Forwards a local port to a private service sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh Validates the sshd configuration, then reloads it sudo sshd -T Prints the effective sshd settings after all drop-ins sudo systemctl daemon-reload Loads changed unit files journalctl -u 'taskflow-api@*' -f Follows the logs of every instance sudo systemctl reset-failed taskflow-api@3001 Clears start-limit-hit so the unit can start again sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx Tests the configuration, then reloads gracefully systemd-analyze calendar --iterations=3 'Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC' Shows the next runs of a timer schedule sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/taskflow-worker Dry run of one logrotate rule sudo lsof +L1 Deleted files that a process still holds open 
# The first minute on a slow server
uptime                    # load averages over 1, 5, 15 minutes
sudo dmesg -T | tail      # OOM kills, I/O errors
vmstat 1 5                # r, b, si/so, wa, st
mpstat -P ALL 1           # one CPU at 100% while others idle?
pidstat 1                 # which process is busy
iostat -xz 1              # r_await, w_await, aqu-sz per device
free -h                   # read "available", not "free"
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1         # retransmits
df -h; df -i              # space and inodes
sudo du -xh -d1 / | sort -h | tail -n 10   # where the space went

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-api@.service (excerpt)
[Unit]
StartLimitIntervalSec=120
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
User=taskflow
EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/api.env
Environment=PORT=%i HOST=127.0.0.1
LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node --max-old-space-size=448 src/server.js
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2s
TimeoutStopSec=30s
MemoryHigh=600M
MemoryMax=700M

Release switch: ln -sfn to current.tmp, then mv -T onto current, so the symlink changes atomically.

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why Admin access for a small team Key-only SSH (Ed25519 with a passphrase), port 22 limited to known ranges Removes password guessing Access to private servers A bastion with ProxyJump Agent forwarding lets root on the bastion use your agent Protection for Docker-published ports A cloud firewall Docker's rules apply before ufw's A deploy without downtime on one host Two instances, a rolling restart, an atomic symlink One instance always serves A job that needs app configuration A systemd timer with EnvironmentFile= and LoadCredential= No overlap, catch-up, OnFailure= alerts A job on several servers that must run once A lock in MongoDB (updateOne with upsert) or a managed scheduler Every server's cron fires otherwise Rotation for a program that can reopen logs logrotate create plus a reopen signal copytruncate can lose lines

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text:
• systemd: RestartSec= 100 ms; start limit 5 starts in 10 s; TimeoutStopSec= 90 s; LimitNOFILE= 1024:524288 (Node raises its soft limit to the hard limit).
  • journald: 10,000 messages per 30 s per service, multiplied by 1 to 6 for free disk space; SystemMaxUse= 10% of the file system, at most 4 GiB.
  • nginx: proxy_read_timeout 60 s; client keepalive_timeout 75 s; default gzip_types is text/html only. Upstream keepalive (60 s) must stay below Node's keepAliveTimeout (65 s in TaskFlow).
  • cron: PATH=/usr/bin:/bin, sh (dash on Ubuntu), % ends the command (date +\%F), and day-of-month OR day-of-week when both are set. /etc/cron.d file names must not contain dots.
  • chrony with NTS needs outbound TCP 4460 as well as UDP 123.
  • Load average counts runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep (D); compare it with the CPU count.
  • Node.js: Node 24 is maintenance LTS, Node 26 is active LTS; Ubuntu 26.04's own package is Node 22 (end of life April 2027), so use NodeSource.

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Hardening sshd_config while 50-cloud-init.conf sets the value first. Use 00-hardening.conf and check with sshd -T.
  • Changing the SSH port the classic way on Ubuntu. ssh.socket owns the port: daemon-reload, then restart ssh.socket.
  • Trusting ufw for container ports. Use the cloud firewall, or publish on 127.0.0.1.
  • Putting PORT in the shared EnvironmentFile=. It overrides Environment=; keep per-instance values in the unit.
  • Editing a unit without daemon-reload. systemd keeps running the old definition.
  • Deleting a log file that is still open. The space stays used; find it with lsof +L1 and rotate with logrotate.
  • A job that works in your shell but not in cron. Set PATH, escape %, and send output to the journal with systemd-cat.
  • Overlapping runs of a slow job. Use flock -n or a systemd timer.
