docs.title: Linux Server Operations Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review SSH and remote access, setting up a production server, running apps with systemd and nginx, troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network, and scheduled jobs and log rotation. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What happens, in order, when you connect with ssh?
docs.text: A TCP connection to port 22, an exchange of versions and algorithm lists, and a key exchange (by default mlkem768x25519-sha256 since OpenSSH 10.0) that gives both sides session keys. The server signs the exchange with its host key, which the client checks against known_hosts. Only then does the user authenticate, for example by proving possession of a private key. Finally the connection carries channels: a shell, commands, port forwards, or SFTP.

docs.title: 2. Why is key-based login safer than passwords, even if you accept an impostor's host key?
docs.text: A password is sent to whoever answers, so an impostor learns it. With public key authentication the client only sends a signature over data that includes the session identifier, which is useless for any other session, and the private key never leaves the client.

docs.title: 3. Which key type should you generate today, and how do you protect it?
docs.text: Ed25519 (ssh-keygen -t ed25519, the default in current OpenSSH), or ed25519-sk on a FIDO2 security key for administrators. Protect the file with a passphrase (-a raises the key-derivation rounds), keep ~/.ssh at 700 and private keys at 600, and use one key per person and device so access can be revoked individually.

docs.title: 4. What does ssh-agent do, and why is agent forwarding risky?
docs.text: The agent holds decrypted keys in memory and signs on request. Forwarding it (-A) exposes a socket on the remote host; anyone with root there cannot copy the keys but can use them to log in elsewhere while you are connected. Use ProxyJump instead.

docs.title: 5. How does ProxyJump work?
docs.text:
The client opens an SSH session to the jump host, asks it to open a TCP connection to the target's port 22, and runs a second, end-to-end encrypted SSH session through it. Authentication uses keys on your laptop, and the bastion only relays bytes it cannot read. The bastion needs AllowTcpForwarding local (or yes).

# ~/.ssh/config
Host taskflow-app-*
    ProxyJump taskflow-bastion

docs.title: 6. What does "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" mean, and what do you do?
docs.text: The server presented a different host key than the one in known_hosts: either it was rebuilt, or someone is intercepting the connection. Verify the new fingerprint out of band (the provider's console log, or ssh-keygen -lf on the host key through the console), then ssh-keygen -R host and reconnect. Host certificates remove the problem for rebuilt servers.

docs.title: 7. Why might sshd still accept passwords after you set PasswordAuthentication no?
docs.text: For most keywords sshd uses the first value it reads, and Ubuntu includes /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf at the top of the main file. A drop-in such as 50-cloud-init.conf can set yes first. Put your settings in a file that sorts earlier (00-hardening.conf) and confirm with sudo sshd -T.

docs.title: 8. Explain local, remote, and dynamic port forwarding.
docs.text: -L makes your machine listen and the SSH server connect onward (reach a private admin UI or database). -R makes the server listen and send connections back to your side (bound to the server's loopback by default). -D turns your machine into a SOCKS proxy whose connections the server makes. -N skips the remote command.

docs.title: 9. What problem do SSH certificates solve?
docs.text: They replace per-server authorized_keys lists. A CA signs a user's key with a key ID, principals, and a validity window; servers trust the CA through TrustedUserCAKeys and map principals with AuthorizedPrincipalsFile. With 40 engineers and 30 servers that is one trusted key instead of 1,200 entries, and access ends when a short-lived certificate expires. Host certificates (@cert-authority in known_hosts) remove trust on first use.

docs.title: 10. How can you reach servers without any open SSH port?
docs.text: AWS Systems Manager Session Manager (an agent connects outward; IAM decides who may start sessions), EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint (an identity-aware TCP proxy into the VPC), Google Cloud IAP TCP forwarding (port 22 open only to Google's 35.235.240.0/20), and Azure Bastion. Session Manager cannot log sessions used for SSH or port forwarding, because they are encrypted end to end.

docs.title: 11. How do you let CI deploy over SSH without giving it a shell?
docs.text: A dedicated key in the deploy account's authorized_keys with restrict,command="/usr/local/sbin/taskflow-deploy-gate". The gate validates $SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND (for example a version string) and runs one root-owned deploy script through a narrow sudoers rule. CI pins the server's host key in known_hosts and uses StrictHostKeyChecking=yes.

docs.title: 12. Why does the order of setup steps matter on a fresh server?
docs.text: Updates, a named admin user with a key, a tested key login, SSH hardening, and the firewall each change how you reach the machine. Done in the wrong order (passwords disabled before a key works, the firewall enabled before SSH is allowed) they lock you out. Test each from a second terminal, and know where the provider's console is.

docs.title: 13. Why use both a cloud firewall and ufw?
docs.text: The cloud firewall (security group) drops traffic before it reaches the VM, lives in the provider's API and Terraform, and keeps working if someone disables the host firewall. ufw protects the host itself and travels with the machine. Defense in depth: each layer catches the other's mistakes.

docs.title: 14. How can a Docker container be reachable on a port ufw denies?
docs.text: Ports published with -p are handled by Docker's own NAT rules before ufw's rules see the packets; Docker's documentation calls the two "incompatible". Publish to loopback (-p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017) and rely on the cloud firewall.

docs.title: 15. What do unattended upgrades do by default on Ubuntu, and what do they not do?
docs.text: They install updates from the release and -security pockets (and Ubuntu Pro's ESM origins when attached) daily, through apt-daily.timer and apt-daily-upgrade.timer. They do not install from third-party repositories such as NodeSource, and they do not reboot unless Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot is set, so new kernels wait. Since Ubuntu 24.04, needrestart restarts affected services automatically.

docs.title: 16. Why does accurate time matter, and what keeps it on Ubuntu 26.04?
docs.text: TLS validity checks, JWT expiry, TOTP codes, schedules, and log correlation all depend on it. New Ubuntu 26.04 installations use chrony with Network Time Security against Ubuntu's servers, which needs outbound TCP 4460 for the key exchange plus UDP 123. Keep servers on UTC.

docs.title: 17. When does a swap file help, and when does it hurt?
docs.text: On a small VM it absorbs short memory spikes that would otherwise end in an OOM kill. It hurts when the working set no longer fits: continuous swapping (vmstat si/so above 0) makes everything slow and only delays the OOM killer. Keep it modest and alert on sustained swapping.

docs.title: 18. What does fail2ban add when SSH already accepts keys only?
docs.text: Guessing cannot succeed, but it fills logs and costs CPU. OpenSSH's PerSourcePenalties (on by default since 9.8) refuses repeat offenders inside sshd; fail2ban adds firewall bans and can watch other logs such as nginx. On Ubuntu 26.04 its sshd jail is enabled by default, reading the journal. Put office and VPN ranges in ignoreip.

docs.title: 19. How should Node.js be installed on an Ubuntu server?
docs.text: From a supported repository with one major per channel, such as NodeSource's node_24.x apt repository (pinned above Ubuntu's own package), or from nodejs.org's official binaries. Ubuntu 26.04's archive ships Node.js 22, whose line ends in April 2027; per-user version managers like nvm suit developer machines, not system services.

docs.title: 20. How should the application's users and files be laid out?
docs.text: The app runs as a system user with no shell and no home. Releases live in root-owned, read-only directories with a current symlink, the app may write only to a shared/ directory, and configuration and secrets sit in root-only files under /etc/taskflow. The app can run its code but never change it.

docs.title: 21. Where do configuration and secrets go, and with which permissions?
docs.text: Non-secret settings in an EnvironmentFile= such as /etc/taskflow/api.env, root-owned, because systemd reads it before starting the process. Secrets as systemd credentials: LoadCredential= reads a root-only file and gives the service a private read-only copy under $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY. The systemd manual warns that environment variables "are not suitable for passing secrets". Create secret files with install -m 0600 before writing them.

docs.title: Running apps with systemd and nginx
22. Why run a Node.js app under systemd instead of nohup or tmux?
docs.text: systemd restarts it after crashes and at boot, runs it as a dedicated user, captures its output in the journal, enforces memory and CPU limits through cgroups, sandboxes it, and stops it gracefully with a timeout. A process in tmux gets none of that.

docs.title: 23. What is a template unit, and why use one for an API?
docs.text: A unit named with @, such as taskflow-api@.service, from which instances like taskflow-api@3001 are started; %i expands to the instance name. One file runs several instances, each with its own port, process, restart counter, and logs, so one can restart while another serves.

docs.title: 24. What is the difference between Type=simple, Type=exec, and Type=notify?
docs.text: simple treats the service as started once fork() returns, so even a missing binary looks like a success. exec waits until the program has been executed and is the recommended choice for long-running services. notify waits for the process to report READY=1, which Node.js cannot do without a library. None of them mean "ready to serve"; health checks do.

docs.title: 25. What do Restart=on-failure and the start limit do?
docs.text: on-failure restarts after unclean exit codes, signals, timeouts, watchdog expiry, and OOM kills, after RestartSec= (100 ms by default; RestartSteps= and RestartMaxDelaySec= add backoff). If a unit starts more than StartLimitBurst= times within StartLimitIntervalSec= (defaults: 5 in 10 seconds) it stops with start-limit-hit until systemctl reset-failed.

docs.title: 26. How does systemd stop a service, and how must the timeouts line up?
docs.text: It sends KillSignal= (SIGTERM) to the processes of the unit's cgroup and waits TimeoutStopSec= (default 90 seconds) before SIGKILL. The app's drain delay plus its longest request plus cleanup must fit inside its own deadline, which must be shorter than TimeoutStopSec.

docs.title: 27. How do EnvironmentFile=, Environment=, and LoadCredential= interact?
docs.text: Values from EnvironmentFile= override Environment=, so per-instance values such as PORT=%i must not appear in the shared file. Environment changes take effect on restart; unit file changes need systemctl daemon-reload first. Secrets belong in LoadCredential=, not in either environment setting.

docs.title: 28. What is the difference between MemoryHigh= and MemoryMax=?
docs.text: Above MemoryHigh= the kernel throttles the unit and reclaims its memory aggressively; at MemoryMax= the OOM killer is invoked inside the unit, and systemd records the result oom-kill. Keep V8's --max-old-space-size well below MemoryHigh= so garbage collection works harder before the cgroup throttles.

docs.title: 29. Which systemd sandboxing settings suit a Node.js API, and which break it?
docs.text: Safe: NoNewPrivileges, ProtectSystem=strict with ReadWritePaths=, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, the Protect* kernel settings, RestrictAddressFamilies (including AF_NETLINK), an empty CapabilityBoundingSet, and SystemCallFilter=@system-service. Breaks it: MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes, because V8 is a JIT, and ProcSubset=pid, which hides the /proc/stat that os.cpus() reads.

docs.title: 30. Why does journalctl -p err show none of a Node.js app's errors?
docs.text: journald stores every line from stdout and stderr at priority info unless the line starts with a prefix such as <3>. Filter on the structured log level instead (journalctl -u 'taskflow-api@*' -g '"level":50') or emit prefixes.

docs.title: 31. Why put nginx in front of Node.js on the same server?
docs.text: It terminates TLS, buffers slow clients so the event loop is not tied up by them, rejects oversized bodies (client_max_body_size), compresses responses, balances between instances, and retries a failed connection on the other instance. Node.js then listens only on 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: 32. What is the proxy_set_header inheritance trap?
docs.text: proxy_set_header directives are inherited from the enclosing level only if the current level defines none. A location that sets Upgrade and Connection silently loses X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Put the common headers in a snippet and include it in every proxied location.

docs.title: 33. How do you proxy WebSockets through nginx?
docs.text:
Use HTTP/1.1 to the upstream and pass the hop-by-hop headers explicitly, with a map so non-upgrade requests get Connection: close, and raise the read timeout for long-lived sockets:

# /etc/nginx/sites-available/ws-example.conf (WebSocket proxying essentials)
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 8080;
    server_name ws.example.com;

    location /ws/ {
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3001;
    }
}

docs.title: 34. Why might nginx not compress JSON responses?
docs.text: Ubuntu's nginx.conf turns gzip on but leaves gzip_types commented out, and the default gzip_types is text/html only. Add application/json. gzip_proxied is a different setting: it concerns requests that arrived through another proxy (with a Via header), such as a CDN.

docs.title: 35. What changed in nginx 1.29.7 for reverse proxies?
docs.text: Upstream keep-alive is enabled by default, proxy_http_version defaults to 1.1, and the Connection header is no longer sent by default. Ubuntu 26.04 ships nginx 1.28.3, so configurations still need proxy_http_version 1.1, an empty Connection header, and keepalive in the upstream; they are harmless on newer versions.

docs.title: 36. How do you deploy with zero downtime on a single server?
docs.text: Unpack each release into its own read-only directory, run backward-compatible migrations once, switch the current symlink atomically (ln -sfn to a temporary name, then mv -T), and restart the two instances one at a time, waiting for /readyz and the new /version before the next. nginx sends traffic to whichever instance accepts connections; on failure, switch back and restart again.

docs.title: 37. When would you choose PM2 over plain systemd?
docs.text: PM2's cluster mode is the simplest way to share one port across all cores, and pm2 reload gives zero-downtime restarts with no script. But it is another daemon (itself started by systemd), keeps logs in files that need rotation, and offers no kernel-enforced limits or sandboxing. systemd alone does the same supervision with fewer moving parts.

docs.title: Troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network
38. What do you run in the first minute on a slow server?
docs.text: The Netflix list: uptime, dmesg -T | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1, and top, ideally from a script that saves the output before anything is restarted.

docs.title: 39. What does the load average measure on Linux?
docs.text: Exponentially damped averages, over 1, 5, and 15 minutes, of tasks that are running, runnable, or in uninterruptible sleep (usually waiting for I/O). A load of 8 on 4 CPUs can mean busy CPUs or a stalled disk; the CPU split in vmstat (us, sy, wa) tells which.

docs.title: 40. The API is slow but the 8-core server is only 12% busy. Why?
docs.text: One Node.js instance runs JavaScript on a single thread, so it can be saturated at 100% of one core while the machine is mostly idle. mpstat -P ALL 1 or top shows the pinned core. Profile it, move CPU work to worker threads, and run one instance per core.

docs.title: 41. What is the difference between "free" and "available" memory?
docs.text: Free is RAM nobody uses at all; Linux keeps it small by caching files. Available is the kernel's estimate of memory usable for new work without swapping: free memory plus page cache it can drop. Judge memory pressure by available, swap activity, and OOM messages.

docs.title: 42. How does the OOM killer choose a victim, and how do you tell a global OOM from a cgroup OOM?
docs.text: It kills the process with the highest badness score, roughly its share of memory adjusted by oom_score_adj (-1000 to +1000; -1000 exempts it). The kernel log says "Out of memory: Killed process" for the whole machine and "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process" when one unit reached its MemoryMax=.

docs.title: 43. Why can df and du disagree, and why can a write fail while df -h shows free space?
docs.text: du adds up files it can reach through directory entries; df asks the file system how many blocks are allocated. A deleted file that a process still holds open has no name, so only df counts it; lsof +L1 finds it, and restarting the process or truncating it through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> frees the space. A write can also fail with free blocks when the file system runs out of inodes (df -i, usually millions of small files), and on ext4 ordinary users lose write access when only the 5% root reserve is left.

docs.title: 44. How do you see what is listening and who is connected?
docs.text: ss -tulpn lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with their processes; ss -s summarizes sockets by state; filters such as ss -tn state established '( dport = :27017 )' show specific connections. A service on 127.0.0.1 is reachable only locally.

docs.title: 45. How do you find where an HTTPS request spends its time?
docs.text: curl -w with time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer, and time_total, then subtract consecutive values: DNS, TCP (about one round trip), TLS (one more with TLS 1.3), waiting for the first byte (server time plus a round trip), and transfer. --resolve pins a name to one server to rule DNS out.

docs.title: 46. How do you diagnose "EMFILE: too many open files"?
docs.text: Read the process's real limits in /proc/<pid>/limits (not ulimit -n in your shell) and count /proc/<pid>/fd over time. A steadily rising count is a leak, often sockets stuck in CLOSE-WAIT (the peer closed but the application never closed its side, typically an HTTP client without timeouts); fix it before raising LimitNOFILE=. Node.js raises its soft limit to the hard limit at startup, while nginx needs worker_rlimit_nofile.

docs.title: 47. mtr shows 40% loss at hop 2 but 0% at every later hop. Is there packet loss?
docs.text: No. Loss that does not continue to later hops is a router rate-limiting its own ICMP replies. Real loss starts at a hop and persists all the way to the destination.

docs.title: 48. Why do scripts that work in your shell fail under cron?
docs.text: Cron runs them with sh, a PATH of /usr/bin:/bin unless the crontab sets one, HOME and LOGNAME from /etc/passwd, and nothing from your profile. Use absolute paths or set PATH and SHELL in the crontab, or move the job to a systemd timer whose service declares its environment.

docs.title: 49. What are cron's % and day-field traps?
docs.text: An unescaped % ends the command and turns the rest into standard input, so date +%F must be date +\%F. When both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, either matching is enough: 0 0 13 * 5 runs on the 13th and on every Friday.

docs.title: 50. How does cron behave around daylight saving time?
docs.text: Debian's cron runs jobs from a skipped hour soon after the change and does not re-run jobs in a repeated hour (for changes under three hours), while wildcard jobs follow the new time. It runs everything in the system time zone. Keeping servers on UTC avoids the issue entirely.

docs.title: 51. How do you stop a scheduled job from overlapping with itself?
docs.text: Wrap it in flock -n lockfile command: a run that finds the lock held exits immediately, and the kernel releases the lock when the process exits. A systemd timer does this by design: if the service is still active when the timer elapses, it is left running and no second instance starts.

docs.title: 52. Why are systemd timers usually better than cron?
docs.text: The service unit declares its user, environment file, credentials, limits, sandbox, and timeout; output goes to the journal; failures are recorded and can trigger OnFailure=; Persistent=true catches up after downtime; RandomizedDelaySec= spreads load; schedules can be tested with systemd-analyze calendar and run on demand with systemctl start.

docs.title: 53. How do you run a scheduled job once when three servers run the same image?
docs.text: Choose one runner: a designated job server, a lock in a shared store (for example a MongoDB updateOne with upsert on a lock document that expires, where losers get duplicate key error 11000), a managed or cluster scheduler, or a queue with repeatable jobs. Make the job idempotent anyway, because managed schedulers deliver at least once.

docs.title: 54. What is the difference between logrotate's create and copytruncate?
docs.text: create renames the log and creates a new file; the program keeps writing to the renamed file until it is told to reopen (a postrotate signal). copytruncate copies the log and truncates it in place, which works for programs that cannot reopen but loses lines written between the copy and the truncate.

docs.title: 55. What are journald's default size limits?
docs.text: SystemMaxUse= is 10% of the file system and SystemKeepFree= 15%, each capped at 4 GiB, with individual files up to one eighth of the maximum (at most 128 MiB). Change them with a drop-in in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/; journalctl --rotate --vacuum-size= trims immediately.

docs.title: 56. How do you prevent disk-full incidents?
docs.text: Cap everything that grows: logrotate rules (run hourly for busy logs), journald limits, Docker log options, a fixed number of releases, backups shipped off the server and pruned locally. Alert on disk and inode usage at around 80% and 90%, and keep large data on its own volume.

docs.title: 57. Right after disabling password authentication, nobody can log in over SSH. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the provider's console access, then journalctl -u ssh for the rejection reason.

How to confirm: messages about bad ownership or modes on ~/.ssh or authorized_keys, a user missing from the AllowGroups group, or no key installed for that account.

Likely causes and fixes: keys never installed for the account, StrictModes rejecting group- or world-writable files, or AllowGroups excluding the user. Fix permissions (700 and 600), add the group, and next time test a key login from a second session before reloading. See SSH and remote access.

docs.title: 58. A CI deploy fails with "Host key verification failed" after the server was rebuilt. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the server was really rebuilt and what its new host key fingerprint is.

How to confirm: compare the fingerprint in the provider's console log with what ssh-keyscan returns from the CI network.

Likely causes and fixes: a legitimate rebuild generated new host keys. Update the pinned known_hosts value after verifying it out of band; never switch CI to StrictHostKeyChecking=no. Host certificates avoid the problem on future rebuilds. See SSH and remote access.

docs.title: 59. Users see a burst of 502 errors for a few seconds during every deploy. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: nginx's error log at deploy time and how the deploy restarts the instances.

How to confirm: connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream at the moment of systemctl restart, with both instances restarting together or only one instance configured.

Likely causes and fixes: all instances restarted at once, no graceful shutdown, or no proxy_next_upstream error. Restart one instance at a time, wait for readiness and the new version, keep nginx's retry on connection errors, and make the app drain before closing. See running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.title: 60. File uploads larger than about 1 MB fail with "413 Request Entity Too Large". Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the 413 comes from nginx or the app.

How to confirm: nginx's own error page and no matching request in the app's logs.

Likely causes and fixes: client_max_body_size is at its 1 MB default. Raise it for the server or the upload location only, and keep the app's body limit consistent. See running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.title: 61. WebSocket connections drop after exactly 60 seconds of silence. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the WebSocket location and its timeouts.

How to confirm: close events at regular 60-second intervals while no messages flow.

Likely causes and fixes: proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 seconds. Raise it in the WebSocket location, send application-level pings more often than the timeout, and make sure the location passes Upgrade and Connection. See running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.title: 62. An API instance restarts every few hours. What do you look for?
docs.text:
What to check first: systemctl show taskflow-api@3001 -p Result -p NRestarts and the kernel log.

How to confirm: Result=oom-kill and "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process" in journalctl -k, with memory climbing steadily before each restart.

Likely causes and fixes: a memory leak reaching MemoryMax=. Keep the limit (it protects the server), take heap snapshots to find the leak, and check that the V8 heap limit sits below MemoryHigh=. See troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network.

docs.title: 63. A 4-vCPU server shows a load average of 12, yet the CPUs are mostly idle. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: vmstat 1 5 for wa and b, then iostat -xz 1.

How to confirm: high wa, several blocked tasks, high r_await or w_await, and a process doing heavy I/O in pidstat -d 1.

Likely causes and fixes: tasks in uninterruptible sleep waiting for a slow or throttled disk, often a backup or a burst of logging. Move the heavy job off peak, reduce the I/O, or provision a faster volume. See troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network.

docs.title: 64. The disk is 97% full, but du accounts for only a third of it. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: sudo lsof +L1.

How to confirm: a large file marked (deleted) with NLINK 0, held open by a running process.

Likely causes and fixes: someone deleted a log that a process still writes to. Truncate it through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> or restart the process, then replace manual deletion with logrotate or journald limits. See troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network.

docs.title: 65. A nightly backup job has not produced a backup for three weeks, and nobody noticed. How do you prevent a repeat?
docs.text:
What to check first: systemctl status of the backup service and its journal, or cron's log lines if it runs from cron.

How to confirm: a failed result on every recent run, or cron discarding output because no mail transfer agent exists.

Likely causes and fixes: a failure with no alert, such as expired credentials or a full target. Run it as a timer with OnFailure= notifications, add a dead man's switch that alerts when no success arrives, and schedule restore tests. See scheduled jobs and log rotation.

docs.title: 66. After scaling from one server to three, every user receives the weekly digest three times. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the job is scheduled.

How to confirm: three runs logged at the same time, one per server.

Likely causes and fixes: the same timer is on every instance. Choose one runner (a lock in MongoDB, a managed scheduler, or a queue) and make the job idempotent by recording who already received the digest. See scheduled jobs and log rotation.

docs.title: 67. On one server, TLS handshakes fail with "certificate is not yet valid" and JWTs are rejected as expired. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: timedatectl status and chronyc -N tracking.

How to confirm: System clock synchronized: no, and sudo chronyc -N authdata shows no NTS keys.

Likely causes and fixes: chrony cannot reach its NTS sources because outbound TCP 4460 (or UDP 123) is blocked. Allow both, or point chrony at internal time servers, then confirm synchronization. See setting up a production server.

docs.title: 68. The API restarted in the middle of the day without a deploy. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the journal around the restart and /var/log/apt/history.log.

How to confirm: an apt or unattended-upgrades run that replaced libraries just before the instance stopped and started.

Likely causes and fixes: needrestart restarted services that used replaced libraries, which Ubuntu does automatically since 24.04. This is expected; make shutdown graceful, run two instances so restarts are invisible, and plan manual upgrades. See setting up a production server.

docs.title: 69. Calls to an external API sometimes take 5 seconds longer than usual. How do you narrow it down?
docs.text:
What to check first: curl -w timings for the external host, run several times.

How to confirm: time_namelookup near 5 seconds on slow runs, and resolvectl status listing a DNS server that does not answer.

Likely causes and fixes: one configured resolver times out before the next is tried. Remove or fix it, and give the app's HTTP clients sensible timeouts. See troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network.

docs.title: 70. After a bad release, the service sits in "failed (Result: start-limit-hit)" even though the release was rolled back. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: systemctl status taskflow-api@3001 and the first failure in its journal.

How to confirm: repeated start attempts that exceeded StartLimitBurst= within StartLimitIntervalSec=.

Likely causes and fixes: systemd stopped retrying after the crash loop and keeps the unit failed until told otherwise. Fix the cause, run systemctl reset-failed taskflow-api@3001, start it, and make the deploy script verify readiness so a broken release is rolled back before the limit is reached. See running apps with systemd and nginx.

docs.text:

docs.title: Running Apps with systemd and nginx
docs.text:
This lesson deploys the TaskFlow API on one Ubuntu 26.04 server from end to end: a systemd template unit that runs two instances of the app, the journal that collects their output, an nginx site that terminates TLS and proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic with sensible limits, a certificate from certbot, and a deploy script that unpacks each release into its own directory, switches a symlink, and restarts the instances one at a time so users never see an error.

The application side of this story (health endpoints, graceful shutdown, PM2 cluster mode) is covered in deploying backend services. This lesson goes deeper on the operating-system side: what systemd does with each setting, how to sandbox a Node.js process, how nginx inheritance and timeouts really behave, and how to roll a release across two instances on a single machine.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A Node.js process started by hand in tmux or with nohup is not a service. It stops when it crashes and nobody notices, does not come back after a reboot, runs as whatever user started it, writes logs to a terminal nobody reads, and can use all the memory on the machine. systemd fixes every one of these with a few lines of configuration that the operating system enforces, not your code.

nginx in front of Node.js matters for different reasons. It terminates TLS, absorbs slow clients so the event loop is not tied up waiting for uploads, rejects oversized bodies before they reach the app, and can send each request to whichever instance is up. Together they make the difference between a deploy that drops requests and one that nobody notices.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Express documentation. The production best practices guide says that to make an app restart when the server restarts you should "use the init system built into your OS. The main init system in use today is systemd", that the best place for compression on a high-traffic site is "at a reverse proxy level", and that Express should run "behind a reverse proxy like Nginx or HAProxy in production".
  • systemd documentation. The systemd.service manual states "It is recommended to use Type=exec for long-running services", and the systemd.exec manual warns that environment variables "are not suitable for passing secrets" and offers credentials and dozens of sandboxing options instead.
  • nginx documentation. The WebSocket proxying guide explains that Upgrade and Connection are hop-by-hop headers that must be passed explicitly and that idle WebSocket connections are closed after 60 seconds by default. The nginx changelog shows that version 1.29.7 (March 2026) made upstream keep-alive and HTTP/1.1 the proxy defaults; Ubuntu 26.04 ships nginx 1.28.3, so its configurations must still set them explicitly.
  • PM2 documentation. PM2's startup guide generates an init-system script so the process list survives reboots; on Linux that means PM2 itself runs as a systemd service.

Popular tools and providers: systemd, nginx (Ubuntu's package or nginx.org's own repository), Caddy, HAProxy, Traefik, PM2, certbot, and supervisord on systems without systemd.

docs.title: The request path on one server
docs.text:
Only nginx listens on public interfaces (ports 80 and 443). Each TaskFlow API instance listens on 127.0.0.1, so a firewall mistake cannot expose it, and two instances exist so one can restart while the other serves. The app reads its bind address from the environment:

// src/server.js (excerpt): listen on loopback only; nginx is the public entry point
const PORT = Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3000);
const HOST = process.env.HOST ?? "127.0.0.1";
const server = app.listen(PORT, HOST, () => {
  console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: 30, msg: `listening on ${HOST}:${PORT}` }));
});

docs.title: Unit files, templates, and instances
docs.text:
A unit file describes one thing systemd manages. Administrator units live in /etc/systemd/system/, package units in /usr/lib/systemd/system/, and a unit is changed without editing its file through drop-ins: systemctl edit nginx writes /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service.d/override.conf and reloads systemd. After editing unit files by hand, run systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl cat unit shows exactly what systemd loaded. Lines that start with # or ; are comments, and systemd has no trailing comments: text after a setting on the same line becomes part of its value.

A template has an @ before the suffix: taskflow-api@.service. Starting taskflow-api@3001.service creates an instance in which the specifier %i expands to 3001. One template therefore runs any number of instances, each with its own port, process, cgroup, logs, and restart counter:

Section Purpose Settings used here [Unit] What it is and how it relates to other units Description=, After=/Wants=network-online.target, start limits [Service] How to run, restart, stop, limit, and sandbox the process Type=, User=, ExecStart=, Restart=, MemoryMax=, Protect*= [Install] What systemctl enable hooks it into WantedBy=multi-user.target (start at boot)

After= only orders startup; Wants= pulls the other unit in without failing if it fails. Ordering after network-online.target matters for an app that connects to a remote database at startup.

docs.title: Service types and readiness
docs.text:
Type= systemd considers the service started when... Fit for Node.js simple fork() returned, even if the binary then fails to execute Works, but a typo in ExecStart= still looks like a successful start exec The program has been executed The recommended default for long-running services notify The process sends READY=1 over sd_notify Node.js has no built-in sd_notify; needs a library forking The parent process exits after forking a daemon Old-style daemons only oneshot The process exits Scripts and jobs (used by timers)

Type=exec still does not mean "ready to serve": the app may need a few seconds to connect to MongoDB. That is why the deploy script below waits for /readyz and /version instead of trusting systemctl restart.

docs.title: Restart policy and the start limit
docs.text:
Restart= Restarts after no (default) Never on-failure An unclean exit code, a signal, a timeout, a watchdog timeout, or an OOM kill on-abnormal Signals, timeouts, watchdog, and OOM kills, but not error exit codes always Any exit, including a clean one, except when you stop it yourself
  • RestartSec= (default 100 ms) is the pause before a restart. Since systemd 254, RestartSteps= and RestartMaxDelaySec= grow that pause exponentially, which keeps a crash loop from hammering a database that is struggling.
  • StartLimitIntervalSec= and StartLimitBurst= belong in [Unit] (defaults: 5 starts in 10 seconds). When a unit exceeds them, systemd stops restarting it and the result is start-limit-hit. systemctl reset-failed clears the counter.
  • Choose on-failure when a clean exit means "done"; choose always when the process should never stop on its own, even with exit code 0.

docs.title: Stopping cleanly
docs.text: On systemctl stop (and on every restart), systemd sends KillSignal= (default SIGTERM) to the main process. With the default KillMode=control-group, every other process left in the unit's cgroup gets it too. If anything is still running after TimeoutStopSec= (default 90 seconds, from DefaultTimeoutStopSec=), systemd sends SIGKILL. The app's own shutdown deadline must be shorter than TimeoutStopSec, which must be longer than the drain delay plus the longest request; the Node.js side of that sequence is in deploying backend services.

docs.title: Environment, configuration, and credentials
docs.text:
EnvironmentFile= reads KEY=value lines "shortly before the process is executed". Empty lines and lines starting with # or ; are ignored, single and double quotes work like a POSIX shell's, and a leading - on the path makes a missing file acceptable. Two rules cause most surprises:

  • Values from EnvironmentFile= override Environment=. If api.env contained PORT=3000, both instances would try to use port 3000 and the second would fail. Per-instance values (PORT=%i) must not appear in the shared file.
  • Edits need the right reload. A changed environment file takes effect on the next restart of the service. A changed unit file needs systemctl daemon-reload first, or systemd keeps using the old one and warns that the unit "changed on disk".

Secrets travel better as credentials: LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri makes systemd read the root-only file and expose a read-only copy at $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY/mongodb-uri that only the service's user can read; the app-side helper is in setting up a production server.

docs.title: Resource limits
docs.text:
Every service runs in its own cgroup, so limits apply to the instance and all of its children:

  • MemoryHigh= is "the main mechanism to control memory usage": above it, the kernel throttles the unit and reclaims its memory aggressively. MemoryMax= is the hard ceiling: "If memory usage cannot be contained under the limit, out-of-memory killer is invoked inside the unit." The service then fails with result oom-kill, and Restart=on-failure brings it back. One leaking instance can no longer take down nginx or the other instance.
  • Set V8's old-space limit (--max-old-space-size) well below MemoryHigh, so the garbage collector works harder before the cgroup starts throttling. Buffers, native modules, and thread stacks live outside the V8 heap and need room too.
  • TasksMax= caps processes and threads; CPUQuota=200% would cap a unit at two CPUs' worth of time.
  • LimitNOFILE= sets the open-file limit. systemd's default is 1024:524288 (soft:hard), and Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup, so a Node service rarely hits the soft limit; nginx and most other programs do not do this.

docs.title: Sandboxing the service
docs.text:
systemd can remove most of what a compromised web app could abuse. The settings below suit a typical Node.js API; test them in staging, because an over-tight sandbox shows up as odd runtime errors.

Setting Effect Node.js notes NoNewPrivileges=yes No privilege gain through setuid binaries Safe ProtectSystem=strict The whole file system is read-only except /dev, /proc, /sys Add ReadWritePaths=/srv/taskflow/shared for uploads ProtectHome=yes /home, /root, /run/user look empty Safe; the app needs no home directory PrivateTmp=yes A private /tmp and /var/tmp Safe; temp files vanish with the service PrivateDevices=yes Only pseudo devices such as /dev/null and /dev/urandom Safe ProtectKernelTunables=, ProtectKernelModules=, ProtectKernelLogs=, ProtectControlGroups=, ProtectClock=, ProtectHostname= Kernel settings, modules, logs, cgroups, clock, and hostname become untouchable Safe RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_NETLINK Only these socket types can be created AF_NETLINK is used by glibc's getaddrinfo() to see which address families are configured and by os.networkInterfaces() RestrictNamespaces=yes, RestrictRealtime=yes, RestrictSUIDSGID=yes, LockPersonality=yes No namespaces, real-time scheduling, setuid files, or personality changes Safe CapabilityBoundingSet= (empty) No Linux capabilities, ever Ports above 1024 need none SystemCallFilter=@system-service with SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM Only common system calls; others fail with EPERM instead of killing the process with SIGSYS Covers Node.js; the EPERM setting turns a surprise into a logged error ProtectProc=invisible Other users' processes are hidden in /proc Safe MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes Forbids writable and executable memory Do not use: the manual notes it is incompatible with JIT engines, and V8 is one ProcSubset=pid Hides everything in /proc that is not about processes Avoid: os.cpus() reads /proc/stat and returns an empty array without it

systemd-analyze security taskflow-api@3001.service estimates the result from 0.0 (tightly sandboxed) to 10.0 (fully exposed) and lists every setting it checked with its contribution. It only measures what systemd enforces, not your code, so use it to find settings you missed, not as a security grade. DynamicUser=yes is a further option that allocates a throwaway user per run, but a fixed taskflow user is simpler when the app owns files in shared/.

docs.title: Logs in the journal
docs.text:
By default, a service's stdout and stderr go to systemd-journald, which stores each line with fields such as _SYSTEMD_UNIT, _PID, and SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER (the program name unless SyslogIdentifier= sets one; without it every instance shows up as node). Things to know:

  • Priorities. Every line from stdout or stderr is stored at priority info unless it starts with a kernel-style prefix such as <3> (error) or <4> (warning). journalctl -p err therefore shows none of a Node.js app's errors; search your JSON log level instead (-g '"level":50' for pino's error level), or emit prefixes.
  • Rate limits. journald drops a service's messages beyond 10,000 per 30 seconds, a burst it multiplies by a factor of 1 to 6 based on free disk space (5 for up to 64 GB free), and logs how many it suppressed. LogRateLimitIntervalSec= and LogRateLimitBurst= change it per unit.
  • Storage. Recent systemd versions keep the journal on disk (Storage=persistent), capped by default at 10% of the file system (at most 4 GiB). Size limits and vacuuming are covered in scheduled jobs and log rotation.
  • Shipping. The journal is the server's local buffer, not your log platform. An agent such as Vector, Fluent Bit, or the OpenTelemetry Collector reads it and ships JSON lines to a central store, as described in structured logging.

docs.title: nginx in front of Node.js
docs.text:
nginx accepts client connections and, by default, buffers both request bodies and responses, so a slow mobile client uploading a 5 MB file ties up an nginx connection rather than the Node.js event loop. The rest is configuration, and four behaviors cause most production surprises:

  • proxy_set_header is all-or-nothing per level. The directives are inherited from the enclosing block "if and only if there are no proxy_set_header directives defined on the current level". A location that sets Upgrade and Connection silently loses the server-level X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto. Keep the common headers in a snippet and include it in every proxied location.
  • WebSockets need explicit headers and a longer timeout. Upgrade and Connection are hop-by-hop, so nginx does not forward them unless told to, and proxy_read_timeout (default 60 seconds) closes a quiet WebSocket unless you raise it or send pings.
  • Compression is off for JSON. Ubuntu's nginx.conf turns gzip on but leaves gzip_types commented out, and the default gzip_types is text/html only. API responses stay uncompressed until you add application/json. gzip_proxied is often misread: it concerns requests that arrived through another proxy (detected by a Via header, as CDNs add), not the responses nginx gets from Node.js.
  • Proxy defaults changed in nginx 1.29.7. From that version, nginx speaks HTTP/1.1 to upstreams and keeps upstream connections alive by default. Ubuntu 26.04's nginx 1.28.3 still defaults to HTTP/1.0 with Connection: close, so set proxy_http_version 1.1, an empty Connection header, and keepalive in the upstream yourself; the settings are harmless on newer versions.

Limits and timeouts worth setting deliberately:

Directive Default Set here Why client_max_body_size 1m 10m Larger uploads get 413 Request Entity Too Large from nginx before reaching Node client_body_timeout, client_header_timeout 60s 15s Clients that stall get 408 instead of holding a connection proxy_connect_timeout 60s 2s A loopback connect is instant; failing fast lets nginx try the other instance proxy_read_timeout 60s 30s (API), 1h (WebSocket) Longest normal response, and long-lived sockets keepalive_timeout (client side) 75s 65s Idle client connections are cheap but not free keepalive_timeout (upstream) 60s default Must stay below Node's server.keepAliveTimeout (65 s in TaskFlow) so nginx closes idle upstream connections first

Failover between instances. In the upstream block, each server defaults to max_fails=1 and fail_timeout=10s: one failed attempt marks it unavailable for 10 seconds. proxy_next_upstream (default error timeout) retries a request on the other instance when a connection fails, but nginx does not retry non-idempotent requests such as POST once it has sent them upstream, and cannot retry anything once it has started sending the response to the client.

Reloading. nginx -t checks the configuration; systemctl reload nginx sends HUP, after which the master process applies the new configuration, starts new workers, and asks the old ones to "shut down gracefully", letting them finish their current requests. If the new configuration cannot be applied, nginx keeps running with the old one. Run nginx -t first anyway, because a broken file still breaks the next full restart or reboot.

Real client addresses. nginx passes the client address in X-Forwarded-For, and Express needs app.set("trust proxy", 1) to use it. If a load balancer or CDN sits in front of nginx too, use the realip module (set_real_ip_from with the balancer's ranges and real_ip_header X-Forwarded-For) so nginx itself logs and rate-limits by the real client.

docs.title: TLS with certbot
docs.text: Certificates come from Let's Encrypt through certbot, renewed by a systemd timer that runs certbot renew twice a day; the full lifecycle, challenge types, and monitoring are covered in obtaining and renewing certificates. Two details matter for this setup. The port 80 server keeps serving /.well-known/acme-challenge/ while redirecting everything else, so renewal works forever. And on the very first issuance the HTTPS server block cannot load yet, because the certificate files do not exist: start with the port 80 block only, obtain the certificate, then add the HTTPS block and reload.

docs.title: Zero-downtime deploys on one server
docs.text:
Node.js cannot swap its code in place, so on one server "reload" means replacing processes one at a time:

  1. Prepare the release in /srv/taskflow/releases/1.9.0: download the artifact CI built, verify its checksum, unpack it as root so the app cannot modify it. Nothing running is touched yet.
  2. Migrate the database with changes that the old version still understands, once (zero-downtime database migrations).
  3. Switch the current symlink atomically: create a new symlink and rename it over the old one. Running processes keep the directory they started in; new processes start in the new release.
  4. Restart instance 3001. It receives SIGTERM, drains, and closes; while it refuses connections, nginx sends everything to 3002.
  5. Wait until 3001 answers /readyz and reports 1.9.0 on /version, then restart 3002 the same way.
  6. Roll back automatically if an instance does not become ready: point current at the previous release and restart the instances again.

For a few seconds both versions serve requests at once, so every release must be compatible with its predecessor, the same rule as for any rolling deployment (rolling, blue-green, and canary). Two alternatives exist on one host: systemd socket activation keeps the listening socket open across a restart (described in the deploying backend services lesson), and a blue-green variant runs a second pair of instances on other ports and switches nginx's upstream with a reload, which lets old workers finish their requests on the old pair.

docs.title: systemd compared with PM2
docs.text:
systemd only PM2 (itself started by systemd) Supervisor The init system, PID 1 A Node.js daemon, started by a unit that pm2 startup generates Using several CPU cores One template instance per core, balanced by nginx Cluster mode: workers share one port Zero-downtime restart Rolling restart script (this lesson) or socket activation pm2 reload in cluster mode Logs journald: structured fields, rate limits, size caps Files under the user's ~/.pm2/logs, rotated with the pm2-logrotate module Memory limits Kernel-enforced cgroups (MemoryHigh=, MemoryMax=) max_memory_restart: restart when memory exceeds a threshold Sandboxing and secrets ProtectSystem=, SystemCallFilter=, LoadCredential=, and more None of its own Language Any program Built for Node.js, works for others License Part of the OS PM2 is AGPL-3.0

PM2 is convenient on a developer-friendly VM, and its cluster mode is the simplest way to use every core behind one port. systemd gives the same supervision with one fewer moving part, plus isolation and limits PM2 cannot provide. If you use PM2, still run it under systemd and keep its logs rotated.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended setup One small API on one VM systemd template with two instances, nginx in front, this lesson's deploy script A VM with many cores and CPU-bound load One instance per core as template units, or PM2 cluster mode under systemd Several VMs The same units on each VM behind a load balancer, deployed one VM at a time (from one server to many) Apps already packaged as containers Docker or Compose with restart policies, or an orchestrator; systemd then supervises the container runtime A team that does not want to operate servers A PaaS or serverless container platform

Avoid running a single instance where a restart must not drop requests, running the app as root or as a login user, and editing files under /srv/taskflow/current on the server instead of deploying a new release.

docs.title: The template unit
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-api@.service: one instance per port, e.g. taskflow-api@3001
[Unit]
Description=TaskFlow API on port %i
Documentation=https://docs.example.com/runbooks/taskflow-api
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
# Give up after 5 failed starts within 2 minutes (result: start-limit-hit)
StartLimitIntervalSec=120
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=exec
User=taskflow
Group=taskflow
WorkingDirectory=/srv/taskflow/current
# Shared settings first; per-instance values must not appear in api.env
EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/api.env
Environment=PORT=%i HOST=127.0.0.1
LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node --max-old-space-size=448 src/server.js
SyslogIdentifier=taskflow-api-%i

# Restart after crashes: 2 s, then growing to at most 60 s between attempts
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=2s
RestartSteps=5
RestartMaxDelaySec=60s

# Stop: SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after 30 s (the app's own deadline is 25 s)
KillSignal=SIGTERM
TimeoutStopSec=30s

# Resource limits for this instance
MemoryHigh=600M
MemoryMax=700M
TasksMax=128
LimitNOFILE=65536

# Sandbox
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/srv/taskflow/shared
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
PrivateDevices=yes
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
ProtectClock=yes
ProtectHostname=yes
ProtectProc=invisible
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_UNIX AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_NETLINK
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
RestrictSUIDSGID=yes
LockPersonality=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=
SystemCallArchitectures=native
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM
UMask=0027
# Never set MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes for Node.js: V8 compiles code at runtime

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
  • WorkingDirectory=/srv/taskflow/current follows the symlink when the process starts, so a restarted instance runs the newly linked release while the other keeps its old directory.
  • --max-old-space-size=448 keeps the V8 heap well under MemoryHigh=600M, leaving room for buffers and native memory.
  • SyslogIdentifier=taskflow-api-%i labels each instance's journal lines, so they are not all called node.

docs.title: Enable, start, and inspect
docs.text:
# Check the unit file for errors, then load it
sudo systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-api@.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload

# Start both instances now and at every boot
sudo systemctl enable --now taskflow-api@3001 taskflow-api@3002

systemctl status taskflow-api@3001
systemctl show taskflow-api@3001 -p NRestarts -p Result -p MemoryCurrent

Example output of systemctl status (trimmed):

● taskflow-api@3001.service - TaskFlow API on port 3001
     Loaded: loaded (/etc/systemd/system/taskflow-api@.service; enabled; preset: enabled)
     Active: active (running) since Fri 2026-11-13 09:12:41 UTC; 2h 3min ago
   Main PID: 41873 (node)
      Tasks: 11 (limit: 128)
     Memory: 182.4M (high: 600M, max: 700M, available: 417.6M, peak: 201.7M)
        CPU: 1min 12.904s
     CGroup: /system.slice/system-taskflow\x2dapi.slice/taskflow-api@3001.service
             └─41873 /usr/bin/node --max-old-space-size=448 src/server.js

NRestarts counts automatic restarts since the unit was started, and Result shows why it last stopped (success, exit-code, signal, oom-kill, start-limit-hit, and so on).

docs.title: Reading the logs
docs.text:
# Follow both instances live
journalctl -u 'taskflow-api@*' -f

# The last hour for one instance, without a pager
journalctl -u taskflow-api@3001 --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager

# Errors only: pino writes "level":50 for errors, and the journal stores everything as info
journalctl -u 'taskflow-api@*' --since today -g '"level":(50|60)' -o cat

# Why did it stop? systemd's own messages about the unit, including the exit status
journalctl -u taskflow-api@3001 -b -o short-iso | grep -E 'Main process exited|Failed|Scheduled restart'

# Machine-readable entries with fields, for scripts
journalctl -u taskflow-api@3001 -n 5 -o json --output-fields=MESSAGE,_PID,SYSLOG_IDENTIFIER

Example output of the stop-reason query:

2026-11-13T07:41:08+00:00 taskflow-app-1 systemd[1]: taskflow-api@3001.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
2026-11-13T07:41:08+00:00 taskflow-app-1 systemd[1]: taskflow-api@3001.service: Failed with result 'oom-kill'.
2026-11-13T07:41:10+00:00 taskflow-app-1 systemd[1]: taskflow-api@3001.service: Scheduled restart job, restart counter is at 1.

An oom-kill result with status=9/KILL means the instance hit MemoryMax; the troubleshooting lesson shows how to find out why.

docs.title: Measure the sandbox
docs.text:
# Every check with its exposure contribution, then the overall estimate on the last line
sudo systemd-analyze security taskflow-api@3001.service

# Compare with an unhardened unit on the same machine
sudo systemd-analyze security cron.service | tail -n 1

The report lists each sandboxing setting as enabled or not with its weight, and ends with a line of the form "Overall exposure level for unit: score label" (the manual's own example, for systemd-logind.service, scores 4.1 and is labelled OK). Read it as a to-do list: settings still open in this unit, such as network access (PrivateNetwork=, IPAddressDeny=), are open because an API that talks to MongoDB needs them.

docs.title: The nginx site
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/snippets/taskflow-proxy.conf: shared proxy settings, included in every proxied location
proxy_http_version 1.1;
proxy_set_header Host $host;
proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $request_id;

# /etc/nginx/sites-available/taskflow-api.conf (enable with a symlink in sites-enabled)
upstream taskflow_api {
    server 127.0.0.1:3001 max_fails=1 fail_timeout=10s;
    server 127.0.0.1:3002 max_fails=1 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 16;
}

# Connection header for WebSocket requests: "upgrade" when the client asks, otherwise "close"
map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
    default upgrade;
    ''      close;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name api.example.com;

    # Let's Encrypt HTTP-01 challenges must stay reachable over plain HTTP
    location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ {
        root /var/www/acme;
        default_type "text/plain";
    }

    location / {
        return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
    }
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name api.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem;

    server_tokens off;
    access_log /var/log/nginx/taskflow-api.access.log;
    error_log  /var/log/nginx/taskflow-api.error.log warn;

    # Limits: body size and slow clients
    client_max_body_size 10m;
    client_body_timeout 15s;
    client_header_timeout 15s;
    keepalive_timeout 65s;

    # Compress JSON and text responses (Ubuntu's nginx.conf only turns gzip on)
    gzip on;
    gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;
    gzip_min_length 1024;
    gzip_vary on;
    gzip_proxied any;

    # Upstream timeouts and failover to the other instance
    proxy_connect_timeout 2s;
    proxy_send_timeout 30s;
    proxy_read_timeout 30s;
    proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
    proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;

    # Job endpoints for local cron and timers only (they call 127.0.0.1:3001 directly)
    location ^~ /internal/ {
        return 404;
    }

    # Live task updates over WebSocket
    location /ws/ {
        include snippets/taskflow-proxy.conf;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;
        proxy_send_timeout 1h;
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
    }

    location / {
        include snippets/taskflow-proxy.conf;
        # Empty Connection header: keep upstream connections alive (nginx before 1.29.7)
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
    }
}

# Enable the site, test, and reload without dropping connections
sudo ln -s /etc/nginx/sites-available/taskflow-api.conf /etc/nginx/sites-enabled/
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

# Check what the outside sees: TLS, compression, and the proxied response
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %{size_download} bytes\n' \
    -H 'Accept-Encoding: gzip' https://api.example.com/tasks
curl -sSI https://api.example.com/tasks | grep -iE '^(content-encoding|vary|server):'
  • Each proxied location includes the snippet, because setting any proxy_set_header in a location discards the inherited ones.
  • proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503 retries on the other instance when a connection fails or an instance answers 502 or 503, which covers the moment an instance closes during a restart; proxy_next_upstream_tries 2 stops a failing request from being tried against both instances more than once.
  • With a CDN or load balancer in front, gzip_proxied any lets nginx compress responses to requests that arrive with a Via header.
  • location ^~ /internal/ keeps job endpoints off the public site; the ^~ modifier means no regular-expression location can override it. Scheduled jobs call them on 127.0.0.1 directly (see scheduled jobs and log rotation).

docs.title: Get the first certificate
docs.text:
# 1. Temporarily enable only the port 80 server block, then obtain the certificate
sudo install -d -m 755 /var/www/acme
sudo certbot certonly --webroot -w /var/www/acme -d api.example.com \
    --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx"

# 2. Enable the full site (with the 443 block), test, and reload
sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

# 3. Prove that renewal works end to end
sudo certbot renew --dry-run
systemctl list-timers | grep -i certbot

docs.title: The deploy script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/sbin/deploy-taskflow-api: release directory, symlink switch, rolling restart
# usage: deploy-taskflow-api 1.9.0   (runs as root, through sudo or the CI deploy key)
set -euo pipefail

VERSION="$1"
APP_DIR=/srv/taskflow
RELEASE="$APP_DIR/releases/$VERSION"
ARTIFACT_URL="https://artifacts.example.com/taskflow-api/taskflow-api-$VERSION.tar.gz"
PORTS=(3001 3002)
KEEP=5

log() { printf '%s %s\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "$*"; }

# Only one deploy at a time on this machine
exec 9> /run/lock/taskflow-deploy.lock
flock -n 9 || { log "another deploy is running"; exit 1; }

wait_until_serving() {   # port version: ready, and running the expected version
  local port="$1" want="$2"
  for _ in $(seq 1 30); do
    if curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://127.0.0.1:$port/readyz" > /dev/null &&
       curl -fsS --max-time 2 "http://127.0.0.1:$port/version" | grep -q "\"version\":\"$want\""; then
      return 0
    fi
    sleep 1
  done
  return 1
}

rolling_restart() {   # version
  local port
  for port in "${PORTS[@]}"; do
    log "restarting taskflow-api@$port"
    systemctl restart "taskflow-api@$port"
    if ! wait_until_serving "$port" "$1"; then
      log "taskflow-api@$port is not serving $1"
      return 1
    fi
  done
}

switch_to() {   # release directory: atomic symlink replacement
  ln -sfn "$1" "$APP_DIR/current.tmp"
  mv -T "$APP_DIR/current.tmp" "$APP_DIR/current"
}

previous="$(readlink -f "$APP_DIR/current" || true)"

# 1. Prepare the release once: download, verify, unpack as root, make it read-only to others
if [ ! -d "$RELEASE" ]; then
  tmp="$(mktemp -d "$APP_DIR/releases/.incoming.XXXXXX")"
  curl -fsSL "$ARTIFACT_URL" -o "$tmp/release.tar.gz"
  expected="$(curl -fsSL "$ARTIFACT_URL.sha256" | cut -d' ' -f1)"   # bare hash or sha256sum output
  echo "$expected  $tmp/release.tar.gz" | sha256sum -c -
  tar --no-same-owner -xzf "$tmp/release.tar.gz" -C "$tmp"
  rm "$tmp/release.tar.gz"
  chmod -R go-w "$tmp" && chmod 755 "$tmp"
  mv "$tmp" "$RELEASE"
fi

# 2. Backward-compatible migrations, once, with the same user, settings, and credential as the app
systemd-run --wait --pipe --collect --unit="taskflow-migrate-$VERSION" \
  --uid=taskflow --gid=taskflow --working-directory="$RELEASE" \
  -p EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/api.env \
  -p LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri \
  /usr/bin/node scripts/migrate.js

# 3. Switch, then restart instances one at a time
touch "$RELEASE"            # newest mtime: protects it from the cleanup below
switch_to "$RELEASE"
if rolling_restart "$VERSION"; then
  log "deployed $VERSION"
  ls -1dt "$APP_DIR"/releases/*/ | tail -n +$((KEEP + 1)) | xargs -r rm -rf
  exit 0
fi

# 4. Failure: point back at the previous release and restart again
log "deploy of $VERSION failed; rolling back to ${previous:-nothing}"
if [ -n "$previous" ] && [ "$previous" != "$RELEASE" ]; then
  switch_to "$previous"
  rolling_restart "$(basename "$previous")" || log "ROLLBACK FAILED: page the on-call engineer"
fi
exit 1

What each part guarantees:

  • Idempotent preparation. A release directory appears only after it has been downloaded, verified against its published SHA-256 sum, and unpacked, because mv renames the finished temporary directory in one step. Running the script twice reuses it.
  • Read-only code. tar --no-same-owner run as root leaves the files owned by root, and go-w removes write access for everyone else, so the taskflow user can run the code but never change it.
  • Migrations in the app's sandbox. systemd-run starts the migration as a transient service with the app's user, environment file, and credential, and --wait --pipe shows its output and returns its exit status, so a failed migration stops the deploy before any instance restarts.
  • Atomic switch. ln -sfn followed by mv -T replaces the symlink with a rename, so current always points at a complete release, never at nothing.
  • Verified rollout. Each instance must answer /readyz and report the new version on /version before the next one restarts; otherwise the script switches back and restarts onto the previous release.
  • Locking and cleanup. flock prevents two concurrent deploys; the five newest releases stay on disk for fast rollbacks.

docs.title: Roll back by hand
docs.text:
# Which releases exist, and which one is live?
ls -1t /srv/taskflow/releases/
readlink -f /srv/taskflow/current

# Redeploy the previous version: the script finds its directory and skips the download
sudo /usr/local/sbin/deploy-taskflow-api 1.8.0

Rolling back is just deploying an older version, which is why releases stay on disk and why every migration in the newer release must leave the schema usable by the older one.

docs.title: The PM2 equivalent, for comparison
docs.text:
# PM2 keeps its state in ~/.pm2, so the app user first needs a home directory
sudo npm install -g pm2
sudo install -d -m 750 -o taskflow -g taskflow /var/lib/taskflow
sudo usermod -d /var/lib/taskflow taskflow

# Generate and enable a systemd unit that starts PM2's daemon as taskflow at boot
sudo env PATH="$PATH" pm2 startup systemd -u taskflow --hp /var/lib/taskflow

# Start the app under PM2 as that user, then save the process list for the next boot
sudo -u taskflow env HOME=/var/lib/taskflow pm2 start /srv/taskflow/current/ecosystem.config.cjs --env production
sudo -u taskflow env HOME=/var/lib/taskflow pm2 save

The ecosystem file, cluster mode, and pm2 reload are shown in deploying backend services. Count the extra pieces: a global npm package, a home directory for the daemon's state, and a second supervisor between systemd and Node.js, which is why this lesson runs the app under systemd directly.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run every long-lived process as a systemd service with Type=exec, a dedicated user, and a restart policy with backoff.
  • Use a template unit and at least two instances on one server, behind nginx, so restarts never drop traffic.
  • Bind the app to 127.0.0.1; only nginx listens publicly.
  • Keep shared settings in an environment file, per-instance values in the unit, and secrets in LoadCredential=.
  • Cap memory with MemoryHigh= and MemoryMax=, and keep the V8 heap below them.
  • Sandbox with ProtectSystem=strict, an allow-list of writable paths, and the other Protect* settings; check with systemd-analyze security.
  • Set SyslogIdentifier=, log JSON to stdout, and ship the journal off the server.
  • In nginx, put common proxy headers in a snippet, set explicit HTTP/1.1 and keep-alive settings, raise timeouts only where needed, add JSON to gzip_types, and run nginx -t before every reload.
  • Deploy by preparing a release directory, switching a symlink atomically, and restarting instances one at a time with verification and automatic rollback.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A burst of 502 errors on every deploy. Detect: nginx's error log shows connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream at deploy times. Cause: both instances restarted together (systemctl restart 'taskflow-api@*'), or only one instance exists. Fix: restart one instance at a time and wait for readiness, keep proxy_next_upstream error, and make the app drain before closing.
  • Uploads fail with "413 Request Entity Too Large". Detect: the response comes from nginx (its error page, no app log line). Cause: client_max_body_size is still the 1 MB default. Fix: raise it in the server or the upload location only, and keep the app's own body limit in line.
  • WebSocket clients disconnect after exactly one minute of silence. Detect: the browser console shows close code 1006 at regular 60-second intervals. Cause: proxy_read_timeout defaults to 60 seconds and nothing is sent. Fix: raise it in the WebSocket location and send application-level pings more often than the timeout.
  • The app logs the proxy's address instead of the client's for some routes. Detect: req.ip is 127.0.0.1 only on /ws/. Cause: that location sets its own proxy_set_header lines and lost the inherited X-Forwarded-For. Fix: include the shared snippet in every proxied location.
  • The service stays down after a crash loop. Detect: systemctl status shows failed (Result: start-limit-hit). Cause: more than StartLimitBurst starts within StartLimitIntervalSec, often a bad release or a missing credential. Fix: read the journal for the first failure, fix it, then systemctl reset-failed taskflow-api@3001 and start it.
  • An instance restarts every few hours with result 'oom-kill'. Detect: journalctl -u taskflow-api@3001 shows Failed with result 'oom-kill' and the memory graph climbs steadily before each one. Cause: a memory leak reaches MemoryMax=. Fix: the restarts protect the server for now; take heap snapshots to find the leak.
  • Some log lines are missing during traffic peaks. Detect: the journal contains Suppressed N messages from taskflow-api@3001.service. Cause: the service exceeded journald's per-service rate limit. Fix: log less per request (sample debug lines), or raise LogRateLimitBurst= for that unit.
  • A new setting in api.env has no effect. Detect: systemctl show taskflow-api@3001 -p Environment and the app's behavior show the old value. Cause: the service was not restarted, or the unit itself was edited without systemctl daemon-reload. Fix: daemon-reload after unit edits, rolling restart after environment changes.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Unit / unit file: Something systemd manages, described by an INI-style file.
  • Template unit / instance: A unit file with @ in its name, and a running copy of it with a value for %i.
  • Drop-in: A .conf file in unit.d/ that overrides part of a unit without editing it.
  • cgroup: The kernel group systemd puts each service in, used for accounting, limits, and killing every process of a unit.
  • Start limit: The rate limit on starts that ends a crash loop.
  • Credential: A secret systemd passes to one service as a private, read-only file.
  • Upstream: nginx's name for the group of backend servers it proxies to.
  • Hop-by-hop header: A header such as Connection or Upgrade that applies to one connection and is not forwarded automatically.
  • Release directory: An immutable directory holding one version of the app.
  • Atomic symlink switch: Replacing the current link with a rename, so it is never missing or half-written.
  • Rolling restart: Restarting instances one at a time while the others serve.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Writing Restart=always # keep it up (the comment becomes part of the value) or editing a unit file and forgetting daemon-reload.
  • Putting PORT in a shared EnvironmentFile, which overrides the per-instance Environment=PORT=%i.
  • Believing Type=simple or Type=exec means the app is ready.
  • Setting MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes on a Node.js service.
  • Expecting journalctl -p err to show a Node.js app's errors.
  • Assuming a location inherits proxy_set_header lines after adding one of its own.
  • Thinking gzip on compresses JSON.
  • Restarting all instances at once and calling it a deploy.
  • Letting the app user write to its own release directory.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does %i expand to in taskflow-api@3002.service, and why does each instance need its own port?
  2. Explain the difference between Restart=on-failure and Restart=always, and what happens after 5 failed starts in 10 seconds.
  3. Why must TimeoutStopSec= be longer than the app's shutdown deadline, and what does systemd do when it expires?
  4. Why can a location /ws/ block lose the X-Forwarded-For header, and how does a snippet fix it?
  5. A service logs 2,000 lines per second and the journal's file system has 20 GB free. With journald's defaults, how many lines are dropped per 30-second window? (The burst is 10,000 x 5 = 50,000 per 30 s; the service writes 60,000, so about 10,000 are suppressed every 30 s.)
  6. Walk through the deploy script and explain what makes the symlink switch atomic and the rollout safe.
  7. Why does Ubuntu 26.04's nginx need proxy_http_version 1.1 and an empty Connection header for upstream keep-alive, while nginx 1.29.7 and later do not?
  8. Name three sandboxing settings that are safe for a Node.js API and one that breaks it, and explain why.
