docs.title: Scheduled Jobs and Log Rotation
docs.text:
Every production server runs work nobody triggers by hand: nightly reports, database dumps, cleanup of expired sessions, certificate renewal, and the rotation of the logs all of that produces. This lesson covers the two schedulers on an Ubuntu server, cron and systemd timers: cron's syntax and its classic traps (a minimal environment, PATH, the % sign, time zones and daylight saving time, overlapping runs), timers and why they are the better default, how to run a job exactly once when the same server image runs three times, log rotation with logrotate, journald's size limits, and how disk-full incidents happen and are handled.

Scheduling inside the application (job queues such as BullMQ, Agenda, and delayed jobs) is covered in background jobs and scheduling, and Kubernetes CronJobs in stateful workloads and jobs. This lesson is about the operating system's schedulers.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Scheduled jobs fail quietly. A cron job whose output goes nowhere can fail every night for months; nobody notices until the backup that was never taken is needed. Jobs also fail in ways interactive commands never do: a script that works in your shell cannot find node under cron, a job scheduled at 02:30 runs twice or not at all on the night the clocks change, and a job that usually takes 4 minutes takes 20 one day and piles up behind itself.

Logs are the other slow-motion failure. Without rotation and limits, a single chatty process fills the disk, and a full disk takes down the database, the web server, and the logging that would have explained it. Both problems are cheap to prevent and expensive to discover in production.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• systemd timers. The systemd.timer manual documents Persistent= (catch up on runs missed while the machine was off), RandomizedDelaySec= (spread load), and a built-in rule against overlap: if the unit is still running when the timer elapses, "it is not restarted, but simply left running. There is no concept of spawning new service instances in this case."
  • Kubernetes CronJobs. The CronJob documentation warns that "there are certain circumstances where two Jobs might be created, or no Job might be created", and concludes that "the Jobs that you define should be idempotent". The same advice applies to every scheduler.
  • Managed schedulers. Google Cloud Scheduler is "designed to provide at-least-once delivery", and Amazon EventBridge Scheduler provides "at-least-once event delivery to targets" with retries. Moving a job to a managed scheduler removes the "which server runs it" question but not the need for idempotent jobs.
  • logrotate. The logrotate manual states the cost of the convenient copytruncate option plainly: "there is a very small time slice between copying the file and truncating it, so some logging data might be lost".

Popular tools and providers: cron, systemd timers, anacron, logrotate, systemd-journald, Kubernetes CronJobs, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, Google Cloud Scheduler, BullMQ and Agenda for in-app scheduling, and dead man's switch monitors such as Healthchecks.io and Cronitor.

docs.title: cron: where jobs live and what a line means
docs.text:
Ubuntu 26.04 ships the classic Debian cron daemon. Jobs can live in four places:

Location Format Notes crontab -e (per user, stored under /var/spool/cron/crontabs/) Five time fields and a command Runs as that user /etc/crontab Five time fields, a user, and a command Edited by hand; avoid, packages own it /etc/cron.d/<name> Like /etc/crontab Best place for your own system jobs; file must be owned by root, not group- or world-writable, and its name must not contain dots /etc/cron.hourly/, daily, weekly, monthly Executable scripts run by run-parts Names may contain only letters, digits, underscores, and hyphens, so backup.sh here is silently ignored

Cron checks its tables every minute and reloads changed files by itself, so it never needs a restart after an edit. When both day-of-month and day-of-week are restricted, a job runs when either matches, which is how 0 0 13 * 5 runs every Friday as well as on the 13th.

docs.title: cron's traps
docs.text:
• A minimal environment. Cron runs commands with sh (on Ubuntu, dash, not bash), takes HOME and LOGNAME from the user's /etc/passwd entry, and sets PATH to /usr/bin:/bin when the crontab does not set one. Nothing from your login profile is loaded. A script that calls node, aws, or anything in /usr/local/bin works in your shell and fails under cron. Use absolute paths or set PATH= at the top of the crontab.
  • The % sign. In the command field, an unescaped % ends the command and everything after it is passed to the command on standard input. date +%F must be written date +\%F.
  • Output goes nowhere useful. Output is mailed to the crontab owner (or MAILTO). A typical cloud server has no mail transfer agent, so cron discards the output and logs "No MTA installed, discarding output". Send output to the journal instead (systemd-cat -t name command) and monitor success separately.
  • One time zone. Debian's cron runs every job in the system time zone (/etc/localtime); it "does not support per-user timezones", and setting TZ in a crontab affects only the commands' environment, not when they run.
  • Daylight saving time. For clock changes of less than three hours, Debian's cron runs jobs that fell into a skipped hour "soon after the change" and does not re-run jobs in a repeated hour; jobs with wildcards in the hour or minute fields simply follow the new time. A server on UTC never meets this logic, which is one more reason to keep servers on UTC.
  • Overlap. Cron starts a new copy on schedule whether or not the previous one finished.

flock from util-linux prevents overlap: flock -n /path/to/lockfile command takes an exclusive lock on the file and runs the command, or fails immediately (-n) with exit code 1 if another process holds it. The kernel releases the lock when the process exits, even if it crashes, so there are no stale lock files to clean up. flock -w 60 waits up to 60 seconds instead of giving up immediately.

docs.title: systemd timers
docs.text:
A timer is a .timer unit that starts a .service unit (by default the one with the same name) on a schedule. That split is the reason timers beat cron for anything important:

cron systemd timer Schedule syntax Five fields OnCalendar= calendar events, plus OnBootSec= and OnUnitActiveSec= for relative times Testing the schedule Reading carefully systemd-analyze calendar --iterations=5 'expression' Environment Minimal, set by cron Exactly what the unit declares: EnvironmentFile=, LoadCredential=, WorkingDirectory= Overlap New copy every time A still-running service is left running Missed runs (machine off) Lost (unless anacron) Persistent=true runs once at the next boot Spreading load By hand RandomizedDelaySec= Logs Mail or nothing The journal, per unit: journalctl -u name Failure handling Exit code lost Unit result recorded; OnFailure= starts another unit Limits and sandbox None Every systemd.exec and resource-control setting Time zones System zone only Optional zone per expression, for example ... 02:30:00 Europe/Berlin Running it now Copy the command systemctl start name.service

Calendar expressions read DayOfWeek Year-Month-Day Hour:Minute:Second, with * for any value, .. for ranges, , for lists, and / for repetition: Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00, *:0/15 (every 15 minutes), or shorthands such as daily (*-*-* 00:00:00). Two defaults surprise people: AccuracySec= is one minute, so systemd may start a timer up to a minute late to group wake-ups (lower it, down to 1us, when precision matters), and the start timeout is disabled for Type=oneshot services, so a hung job runs forever unless you set TimeoutStartSec=.

docs.title: Running a job once across several servers
docs.text:
When the API scales from one server to three built from the same image, every timer and crontab runs three times. Options, from simplest to most robust:

Approach How it works Trade-off A designated job server Only one machine gets the timers (a role in the provisioning code) Simple; if that server is down, jobs do not run A lock in a shared store Every server tries; whoever takes a lock in MongoDB or Redis runs No single point of failure; the lock must expire, and a job outliving its lock can run twice A managed or cluster scheduler EventBridge Scheduler, Cloud Scheduler, or a Kubernetes CronJob calls one endpoint or starts one job Reliable and observable; at-least-once delivery still means possible duplicates A job queue with repeatable jobs BullMQ, Agenda, or similar schedule jobs into a queue that one worker consumes Fits apps that already use a queue; the queue becomes critical infrastructure

Whatever chooses the runner, design the job to be idempotent: a digest records which users already received this week's email, a report overwrites the same output, a cleanup deletes by condition. Duplicates then cost a little work instead of a second charge or a second email. Statelessness across servers more broadly is covered in from one server to many.

docs.title: Log rotation with logrotate
docs.text:
Applications that log to stdout under systemd need no rotation of their own: journald stores, compresses, and caps their output. Files written by nginx, by older programs, or by apps configured to write files are rotated by logrotate. On Ubuntu, logrotate.timer runs logrotate /etc/logrotate.conf once a day (OnCalendar=daily with up to an hour of random delay and Persistent=true), and that file includes every rule in /etc/logrotate.d/. Its state file, /var/lib/logrotate/status, records when each log was last rotated.

Renaming a file does not affect a process that has it open: the process keeps writing to the same inode under the new name. So with the default create method, rotation must end by telling the program to reopen its log. nginx's own rule on Ubuntu does exactly that:

# /etc/logrotate.d/nginx (as shipped in Ubuntu's nginx package)
/var/log/nginx/*.log {
    daily
    missingok
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    notifempty
    create 0640 www-data adm
    sharedscripts
    prerotate
        if [ -d /etc/logrotate.d/httpd-prerotate ]; then \
            run-parts /etc/logrotate.d/httpd-prerotate; \
        fi \
    endscript
    postrotate
        invoke-rc.d nginx rotate >/dev/null 2>&1
    endscript
}

invoke-rc.d nginx rotate makes the nginx master process reopen its logs (the USR1 signal), after which "old files are almost immediately available for post processing, such as compression". delaycompress keeps yesterday's file uncompressed for one more day in case a process wrote to it late, and sharedscripts runs the postrotate script once for all matching files instead of once per file.

Directive Meaning daily, weekly, monthly Rotation interval (checked only when logrotate runs) rotate 14 Keep 14 rotated files, delete older ones maxsize 200M Also rotate as soon as the file exceeds 200 MB, even before the interval has passed size 200M Rotate by size only, ignoring the interval compress, delaycompress gzip rotated files, starting with the second-newest missingok, notifempty Skip missing or empty logs without errors create 0640 taskflow adm Mode, owner, and group of the new file copytruncate Copy then truncate in place, for programs that cannot reopen (lossy) su taskflow adm Rotate as this user and group; recommended when root rotates logs in a directory an unprivileged user controls dateext Suffix rotated files with a date (-20261114) instead of a number postrotate ... endscript Shell commands after rotation, typically a reopen signal

Size limits are only as fresh as the timer: maxsize 200M with a daily run can still let a log grow to several gigabytes in a bad hour. For busy logs, run logrotate hourly (an override of logrotate.timer shown below) rather than relying on daily runs.

docs.title: journald limits
docs.text:
The journal is size-capped by default, but the defaults are relative to the file system, so check what they mean on your disk:

Setting (journald.conf) Default Meaning Storage= persistent (recent systemd) Keep the journal under /var/log/journal across reboots SystemMaxUse= 10% of the file system, at most 4 GiB Total disk the journal may use SystemKeepFree= 15% of the file system, at most 4 GiB Free space journald leaves for everything else SystemMaxFileSize= One eighth of SystemMaxUse=, at most 128 MiB Size at which one journal file is rotated MaxRetentionSec= 0 (off) Delete entries older than this MaxFileSec= 1 month Rotate journal files at least this often RateLimitIntervalSec=, RateLimitBurst= 10,000 messages per 30 s per service Drop floods of messages and record how many

Override them with a drop-in in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/ and restart systemd-journald. journalctl --disk-usage shows the current size, and journalctl --vacuum-size= or --vacuum-time= deletes old data immediately, but only from archived files; combine with --rotate to archive the active files first.

docs.title: Disk-full incidents
docs.text:
Disks fill gradually and then everything fails at once: MongoDB stops accepting writes, nginx cannot buffer uploads or write its logs, journald stops persisting, apt breaks mid-upgrade, and some applications crash on their first failed write. The usual causes on an app server, roughly in order:

  1. Application or web server logs without rotation or limits, including Docker's default json-file log driver, which does not rotate unless configured (see structured logging).
  2. Database dumps and backups written to the local disk and never removed, or kept only there.
  3. Old release directories, container images, and package caches.
  4. A deleted log file still held open by a process (found with lsof +L1, see the troubleshooting lesson).
  5. Core dumps from a crash-looping process.

Prevention is a set of caps plus an alert: logs rotated or capped everywhere, backups shipped off the machine and pruned locally, the deploy script keeping a fixed number of releases, alerts on disk and inode usage at around 80% and 90%, and, on servers with large data, a separate volume for data so logs cannot starve the database.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use A job on one server that needs the app's configuration or secrets A systemd timer with a service that declares EnvironmentFile= and LoadCredential= A trivial job (call a local endpoint, prune a cache directory) cron in /etc/cron.d/, with absolute paths, flock, and journal output, or a timer A job that must run exactly once across a fleet A lock in the shared database, a managed scheduler, or a queue; plus an idempotent job Many jobs, retries, and visibility A job queue in the app, or a workflow tool, instead of OS schedulers Kubernetes CronJobs with concurrencyPolicy: Forbid and a .spec.timeZone Logs from services under systemd stdout to journald, with size limits and a log shipper Logs written to files logrotate with create and a reopen signal; copytruncate only when unavoidable

Do not run important jobs from a developer's personal crontab, depend on cron mail on a server without mail, or schedule the same job on every instance of an autoscaling group without a lock.

docs.title: A cron file done right
docs.text:
# /etc/cron.d/taskflow: system crontab format (the sixth field is the user)
SHELL=/bin/bash
PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin
MAILTO=""

# Every 15 minutes: ask the local API to expire old sessions; never two at once
*/15 * * * *  taskflow  systemd-cat -t taskflow-expire flock -n /srv/taskflow/shared/.expire.lock curl -fsS --max-time 600 -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3001/internal/jobs/expire-sessions

# 02:30 UTC on weekdays: % must be escaped as \% inside crontabs
30 2 * * 1-5  root  systemd-cat -t taskflow-archive tar -czf /var/backups/taskflow-uploads-$(date -u +\%F).tar.gz -C /srv/taskflow/shared uploads
  • The file name has no dot, it is owned by root, and it is not group- or world-writable, or cron ignores it.
  • PATH and SHELL are set explicitly; MAILTO="" disables mail because output goes to the journal through systemd-cat (journalctl -t taskflow-expire).
  • flock -n makes an overlapping run exit immediately instead of stacking up.
  • The first job calls an endpoint, so it uses the app's configuration without cron ever seeing a secret. The /internal/ path must never be reachable from outside: the nginx site in running apps with systemd and nginx answers it with 404, so only local callers on 127.0.0.1 reach it.
  • The archive job writes a local file; a real backup must also copy it off the server.

docs.title: The same idea as a systemd timer
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-nightly-report.service
[Unit]
Description=TaskFlow nightly report
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
OnFailure=notify-failure@%n.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
User=taskflow
Group=taskflow
WorkingDirectory=/srv/taskflow/current
EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/api.env
LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri
ExecStart=/usr/bin/node scripts/nightly-report.js
# A hung run must not last forever (oneshot services have no start timeout by default)
TimeoutStartSec=30min
Nice=10
NoNewPrivileges=yes
ProtectSystem=strict
ReadWritePaths=/srv/taskflow/shared
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes

# /etc/systemd/system/taskflow-nightly-report.timer
[Unit]
Description=Run the TaskFlow nightly report at 02:30 UTC on weekdays

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC
Persistent=true
RandomizedDelaySec=5min

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target

# Check the schedule, then enable the TIMER (not the service)
systemd-analyze calendar --iterations=3 'Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC'
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now taskflow-nightly-report.timer

systemctl list-timers 'taskflow-*'
sudo systemctl start taskflow-nightly-report.service     # run it now, once
journalctl -u taskflow-nightly-report --since today

Example output of systemd-analyze calendar (run on Saturday 2026-11-14):

  Original form: Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC
Normalized form: Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC
    Next elapse: Mon 2026-11-16 02:30:00 UTC
       From now: 1 day 14h left
       Iter. #2: Tue 2026-11-17 02:30:00 UTC
       Iter. #3: Wed 2026-11-18 02:30:00 UTC

The service declares the same environment file, credential, user, and sandbox as the API, so the job runs with exactly the app's configuration. Persistent=true runs a missed report once after a reboot, RandomizedDelaySec=5min keeps several servers from starting at the same second, and OnFailure= starts the notifier below whenever the job fails. The same pattern runs the nightly mongodump from database backups and point-in-time recovery.

docs.title: A failure notifier for any unit
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/notify-failure@.service: started by OnFailure= with the failed unit's name
[Unit]
Description=Report the failure of %i

[Service]
Type=oneshot
EnvironmentFile=/etc/taskflow/alerts.env
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/notify-failure %i

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/sbin/notify-failure: post the failed unit and its last log lines to a chat webhook
set -euo pipefail
unit="$1"
lines="$(journalctl -u "$unit" -n 15 --no-pager -o cat | tail -c 1500)"
payload="$(jq -n --arg text "$(hostname): $unit failed"$'\n'"$lines" '{text: $text}')"
curl -fsS --max-time 10 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "$payload" "$ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL"

%i carries the failed unit's name into the notifier (OnFailure= in the job used %n, the job's own full name). ALERT_WEBHOOK_URL lives in a root-only environment file, because a webhook URL is a credential. jq (sudo apt-get install jq) builds valid JSON from arbitrary log text. For jobs that silently stop running, add a dead man's switch: the job pings a monitoring URL on success, and the monitor alerts when the ping does not arrive.

docs.title: Running once across servers with a MongoDB lock
docs.text:
// scripts/lib/run-once.js: let exactly one server run a scheduled job at a time
import { hostname } from "node:os";

export async function withLock(db, name, ttlMs, job) {
  const locks = db.collection("locks");
  const owner = `${hostname()}:${process.pid}`;
  const now = new Date();

  try {
    // Matches only a missing or expired lock; otherwise the upsert's insert hits the unique _id
    await locks.updateOne(
      { _id: name, expiresAt: { $lt: now } },
      { $set: { owner, expiresAt: new Date(now.getTime() + ttlMs) } },
      { upsert: true },
    );
  } catch (err) {
    if (err.code === 11000) {
      console.log(JSON.stringify({ level: 30, msg: `lock ${name} is held elsewhere; skipping` }));
      return false;
    }
    throw err;
  }

  try {
    await job();
    return true;
  } finally {
    await locks.deleteOne({ _id: name, owner }); // release only our own lock
  }
}

// scripts/nightly-report.js (excerpt)
await withLock(db, "nightly-report", 30 * 60_000, async () => {
  await buildAndStoreReport(db, new Date()); // idempotent: overwrites the report for that date
});

If the lock document is missing or expired, the filter matches (or the upsert inserts) and this server owns the lock. If another server holds a live lock, the filter does not match, the upsert tries to insert a second document with the same _id, and MongoDB rejects it with error 11000. Choose a TTL longer than the job's worst-case runtime, and keep server clocks synchronized, because expiry is computed from each server's clock; even so, keep the job idempotent, since a job that outlives its lock can overlap with the next one.

docs.title: logrotate for an app that writes files
docs.text:
# /etc/logrotate.d/taskflow-worker
/var/log/taskflow/worker.log {
    daily
    maxsize 200M
    rotate 14
    compress
    delaycompress
    missingok
    notifempty
    create 0640 taskflow adm
    su taskflow adm
    postrotate
        systemctl kill --signal=SIGHUP --kill-whom=main taskflow-worker.service
    endscript
}

// src/logger.js (worker): a pino file destination that reopens on SIGHUP after rotation
import pino from "pino";

const destination = pino.destination({ dest: "/var/log/taskflow/worker.log", sync: false });
process.on("SIGHUP", () => destination.reopen());

export const logger = pino(destination);

# Dry run: show what would happen, change nothing
sudo logrotate -d /etc/logrotate.d/taskflow-worker

# Force one rotation now to test the whole cycle, including the reopen signal
sudo logrotate -f /etc/logrotate.d/taskflow-worker
ls -l /var/log/taskflow/

SIGHUP is used because Node.js reserves SIGUSR1 for its debugger, and pino's documentation uses the same signal for reopening. su taskflow adm makes logrotate rotate as the directory's owner, which its manual recommends when root rotates logs in a directory controlled by an unprivileged user (logrotate also refuses to work in a group- or world-writable directory without it). If the program cannot reopen its file, replace create and the postrotate block with copytruncate and accept the small loss.

docs.title: Rotate busy logs hourly
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/system/logrotate.timer.d/override.conf (create with: sudo systemctl edit logrotate.timer)
[Timer]
OnCalendar=
OnCalendar=hourly

The empty OnCalendar= clears the packaged daily schedule before adding the hourly one. Rules with daily still rotate once a day; rules with maxsize or size are now checked every hour.

docs.title: Cap the journal
docs.text:
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/50-limits.conf
[Journal]
SystemMaxUse=2G
SystemKeepFree=4G
MaxRetentionSec=30d

sudo systemctl restart systemd-journald
journalctl --disk-usage

# One-off cleanup: archive the active files, then delete down to 1 GiB
sudo journalctl --rotate --vacuum-size=1G

On a 40 GB root file system, the defaults would allow 4 GiB for the journal (10% is 4 GB, at the 4 GiB cap) and keep 4 GiB free (15% is 6 GB, capped at 4 GiB); the drop-in halves the journal's share and adds a 30-day retention.

docs.title: A disk-full runbook
docs.text:
# 1. What is full: blocks or inodes?
df -hT -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs; df -i -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs

# 2. Fast, safe wins (each prints or frees space it can account for)
sudo journalctl --rotate --vacuum-size=500M
sudo apt-get clean
sudo lsof +L1                       # deleted files still held open: restart or truncate them

# 3. Find the rest
sudo du -xh -d1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 10
ls -1t /srv/taskflow/releases/      # the deploy script should keep only five
docker system df 2>/dev/null        # images, containers, volumes, build cache

# 4. Confirm the services are healthy again, then fix the cause and add the missing cap or alert
systemctl --failed

Free space before you investigate deeply, and never delete files you cannot explain, such as a database's data files or the newest backup. After the incident, the fix is a limit or a rotation rule plus an alert, not a manual cleanup that will be needed again next month.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Prefer systemd timers for anything that matters: the service declares its environment, user, limits, and sandbox, and the journal keeps its output.
  • In cron, set PATH and SHELL, use absolute paths, escape %, send output to the journal, and wrap jobs in flock -n.
  • Keep servers on UTC so daylight saving time never touches your schedules; use per-timer time zones only when a business rule needs local time.
  • Make every scheduled job idempotent, and choose one runner explicitly when several servers exist.
  • Set TimeoutStartSec= on oneshot services and alert on failure with OnFailure=; add a dead man's switch for jobs that must run.
  • Log to stdout under systemd; rotate files with create plus a reopen signal; reserve copytruncate for programs that cannot reopen.
  • Cap the journal explicitly, run logrotate hourly for busy logs, and alert on disk and inode usage before 90%.
  • Ship backups and logs off the server; local copies are a cache.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A nightly job "works when I run it" but fails under cron. Detect: journalctl -t <identifier> shows node: not found or a missing environment variable. Cause: cron's minimal PATH and environment. Fix: absolute paths, PATH= in the cron file, or move the job to a timer whose service declares its environment.
  • A report ran twice on the night the clocks changed, or not at all. Detect: two runs (or none) at about 02:00 local time on the DST date. Cause: a server in a local time zone; jobs in skipped or repeated hours behave specially. Fix: run servers on UTC, or set an explicit time zone in the timer's OnCalendar= and test it with systemd-analyze calendar.
  • Database load spikes every 5 minutes and grows through the night. Detect: ps shows several copies of the same job; their start times are 5 minutes apart. Cause: runs take longer than the interval and cron starts new copies. Fix: flock -n, or a timer, and look at why the job slowed down.
  • Users receive the weekly digest three times. Detect: three runs logged at the same time, one per server. Cause: the same timer on every instance. Fix: a lock or a single scheduler, and record which users were already sent the digest.
  • The disk fills overnight although logrotate is configured. Detect: one log file is many gigabytes; /var/lib/logrotate/status shows it was last rotated yesterday. Cause: rotation is daily and maxsize is only checked when logrotate runs. Fix: run logrotate hourly, lower the log level, and alert on disk usage.
  • After rotation, the app keeps writing to worker.log.1 and the new worker.log stays empty. Detect: ls -l shows the rotated file growing; lsof -p <pid> shows worker.log.1 open. Cause: create without a reopen signal. Fix: add a postrotate signal the program handles, or use copytruncate for programs that cannot reopen.
  • A backup timer has failed silently for weeks. Detect: systemctl list-timers shows it ran; systemctl status shows Result: exit-code from the last run, and no recent backup exists. Cause: nobody watched the result. Fix: OnFailure= notifications plus a dead man's switch on success, and periodic restore tests.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• cron / crontab: The classic scheduler daemon and its tables of jobs.
  • System crontab: /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d/ files, which include a user field.
  • run-parts: The tool that runs every valid executable in a directory, used for /etc/cron.daily and friends.
  • systemd timer: A .timer unit that starts a service on a calendar or relative schedule.
  • Calendar event: systemd's schedule syntax, such as Mon..Fri *-*-* 02:30:00 UTC.
  • Persistent timer: A timer that catches up on runs missed while the machine was off.
  • flock: A command that runs another command while holding a file lock.
  • Idempotent job: A job that produces the same result when run more than once.
  • Dead man's switch: A monitor that alerts when an expected success signal does not arrive.
  • Log rotation: Renaming, compressing, and deleting old logs on a schedule or size.
  • copytruncate: Rotation by copying a log and truncating the original in place.
  • Vacuuming: Deleting archived journal files to meet a size or age target.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming cron runs commands with your login shell, PATH, and environment.
  • Writing date +%F in a crontab.
  • Naming a file backup.sh in /etc/cron.daily or taskflow.cron in /etc/cron.d, which are silently ignored.
  • Relying on cron mail on a server without a mail transfer agent.
  • Scheduling local-time jobs between 01:00 and 03:00 on a server that observes daylight saving time.
  • Deploying the same scheduled job to every server in a fleet.
  • Enabling the .service of a timer instead of the .timer.
  • Deleting a log file that a process still has open instead of rotating it.
  • Believing journald grows without bound, or that its defaults suit every disk size.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. When does 0 0 13 * 5 run, and why?
  2. Name four ways a command can behave differently under cron than in your shell.
  3. Why are systemd timers safer than cron for a job that needs the app's database credentials?
  4. A job runs every 10 minutes and occasionally takes 25 minutes. What happens under cron, under cron with flock -n, and under a systemd timer?
  5. Three servers run the same nightly timer. Describe two ways to make the job run once, and why the job should be idempotent anyway.
  6. Explain the difference between logrotate's create and copytruncate, and what each requires from the application.
  7. With default settings, how much space may the journal use on a 20 GB root file system, and how much free space will journald leave? (10% of 20 GB is 2 GB, and 15% is 3 GB; neither reaches the 4 GiB cap, so about 2 GB for the journal while keeping about 3 GB free.)
  8. A server's disk is 100% full at 03:00. List your first five commands and what each tells you.

docs.text:

  • systemd.time: calendar events
  • journald.conf
  • logrotate(8) on Ubuntu 26.04

docs.title: Setting Up a Production Server
docs.text:
A new VPS from any provider boots with sensible defaults, but defaults are written for convenience, not for an application that holds user data. This lesson turns a fresh Ubuntu Server 26.04 LTS machine into a production baseline for the TaskFlow API, in the order that avoids locking yourself out: updates, a named admin user, SSH hardening, a two-layer firewall, automatic security updates, time synchronization, swap, fail2ban, Node.js from a supported repository, an unprivileged app user with a sane directory layout, configuration and secret files with correct permissions, and backups.

Every step is shown as commands you can run by hand once, and the lesson ends with the same baseline as cloud-init user data, because a server you cannot rebuild from a script is a server you are afraid to touch.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A VM with a public IP address is probed by automated scanners within minutes of booting, and nothing about a default install knows that this machine will hold a production database password. What separates a safe server from a risky one is a short list of decisions: who can log in and how, which ports answer at all, whether security patches arrive without anyone remembering, whether the clock is right (TLS, JWT expiry, and log correlation all depend on it), and whether the application runs with the least privilege it needs.

Order matters as much as content. Disable password logins before your key works, or enable the firewall before allowing SSH, and the next step is a support ticket or a rebuild. Doing the risky access steps first, deliberately and with a second session open, makes everything after them routine.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Ubuntu Server documentation. The automatic updates guide states that unattended-upgrades is installed by default and applies security updates, and that since Ubuntu 24.04 LTS needrestart restarts affected services automatically after updates. Your service will therefore be restarted by the system at times you did not pick, which only works if it shuts down gracefully.
  • Docker documentation. The packet filtering and firewalls page warns that "Docker and ufw use firewall rules in ways that make them incompatible with each other": ports published by containers are routed before ufw's rules apply. A cloud firewall in front of the VM is what actually protects them.
  • Ubuntu's chrony guide. The chrony client documentation shows the 26.04 default: chrony with Network Time Security (NTS) against Ubuntu's time servers, which needs outbound TCP 4460 for the key exchange in addition to UDP 123.
  • Ubuntu Security Guide. For regulated environments, Canonical's Ubuntu Security Guide (part of Ubuntu Pro) audits and applies CIS benchmark hardening automatically, which turns a checklist like this one into a report an auditor accepts.
  • Node.js release schedule. The previous releases page lists Node.js 24 and 26 as LTS lines; per the release working group, Node.js 24 is in maintenance until April 2028 and Node.js 26 became Active LTS in October 2026. Ubuntu 26.04's own nodejs package is Node.js 22 from the community-maintained universe component, a line that reaches end of life in April 2027, which is why this lesson uses NodeSource's repository.

Popular tools and providers: cloud-init, Ansible, Terraform and Packer, ufw (on nftables), fail2ban, unattended-upgrades, Ubuntu Pro (ESM, Livepatch, USG), NodeSource, and VPS providers such as DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Akamai (Linode), Vultr, and AWS Lightsail and EC2.

docs.title: The order of the steps
docs.text: The first five steps change how you reach the machine. Each can cut off your current session, so each ends with a test from a second terminal before you close the first. The provider's browser console (or Session Manager) is your way back in if something goes wrong; make sure you know where it is before you start.

docs.title: Accounts: a named admin, an app user, and no shared root
docs.text:
Cloud images log you in as a default user (ubuntu on Ubuntu images) with a key the provider injected, and that user can run any command through sudo without a password. For production:

  • Create a named admin account per person (here ops), give it a password for sudo, and log in with keys only. Logs then show who ran what, and removing one person does not affect anyone else.
  • Keep root without a usable password and with SSH login refused. Ubuntu 26.04's sudo is sudo-rs, a Rust rewrite that reads the same /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d/ files.
  • Run the app as a system user (taskflow) with no login shell and no home directory. If the app is compromised, the attacker gets a user that cannot log in, cannot sudo, and cannot write its own code.

docs.title: SSH: keys only, applied as a drop-in
docs.text: The hardening options, why each matters, and how sshd reads drop-in files are covered in SSH and remote access. The short version for setup: put the settings in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf so they sort before the 50-cloud-init.conf file the installer writes, validate with sudo sshd -t, check the effective values with sudo sshd -T, reload, and test a fresh login before closing your session.

docs.title: Firewalls: two layers, and the Docker exception
docs.text:
• The cloud firewall (an AWS security group, DigitalOcean Cloud Firewall, Hetzner Firewall, or Google Cloud VPC firewall rule) filters traffic before it reaches the VM. It is managed through the provider's API, so it can live in Terraform with the rest of the infrastructure, and it keeps working even if someone on the server disables ufw.
  • ufw is Ubuntu's front end for the kernel's packet filter. It is disabled by default. Its rules are evaluated in order and the first match wins; the default policy decides everything that matches no rule. ufw limit denies an address that opens 6 or more connections within 30 seconds, a cheap brake on SSH guessing.
  • Docker publishes ports around ufw. Container port mappings are handled by Docker's own NAT rules before ufw sees the packets, so a database started with -p 27017:27017 is reachable from the internet even when ufw status says otherwise. Publish to loopback (-p 127.0.0.1:27017:27017) and rely on the cloud firewall.
  • Bind private services to loopback. TaskFlow's Node.js instances listen on 127.0.0.1, so even a firewall mistake cannot expose them; only nginx listens on public interfaces.

Network design across many servers (private subnets, security group references, and egress control) is covered in network security in the cloud.

docs.title: Automatic security updates
docs.text:
Two systemd timers drive APT on Ubuntu: apt-daily.timer refreshes the package lists and apt-daily-upgrade.timer runs unattended-upgrade, each at a randomized time. The defaults install updates from the release and its -security pocket (plus Ubuntu Pro's ESM origins when attached) but not the general -updates pocket, and never from third-party repositories such as NodeSource.

Three consequences shape the configuration:

  • Kernel and libc updates need a reboot. Their packages create /var/run/reboot-required, and unattended-upgrades does not reboot unless you set Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true". Choose a quiet time with Automatic-Reboot-Time, and stagger it across servers so two instances never restart together.
  • Services restart on their own. needrestart restarts services that still use replaced libraries. With two instances and graceful shutdown this is invisible; with one instance it is a short outage.
  • Patch policy lives elsewhere. Severity-based deadlines, handling a critical CVE, and reporting belong to the process described in vulnerability and patch management; automatic updates are only the mechanism.

docs.title: Time synchronization
docs.text: TLS certificate checks, JWT exp claims, TOTP codes, scheduled jobs, and log correlation across servers all assume an accurate clock. New Ubuntu 26.04 installations use chrony with NTS, which authenticates the time servers so an attacker on the path cannot shift your clock. The default sources are 1.ntp.ubuntu.com to 4.ntp.ubuntu.com plus a bootstrap server, defined under /etc/chrony/sources.d/. NTS performs its key exchange on TCP port 4460 and then uses UDP 123; if a restrictive egress firewall blocks 4460, chrony cannot authenticate its sources and the clock drifts. Keep servers in UTC: logs line up across regions and daylight saving time cannot run a job twice (see scheduled jobs and log rotation). The protocol itself is covered in NTP and time synchronization.

docs.title: Swap and memory headroom
docs.text:
Many cloud images ship without swap. On a small VM, a short memory spike (an npm ci during a deploy, a burst of large requests) then goes straight to the out-of-memory killer. A modest swap file gives the kernel somewhere to put rarely used pages, turning a crash into a slow moment. It is a safety net, not extra capacity: a server that swaps continuously is too small, and the troubleshooting lesson shows how to spot that with vmstat.

  • mkswap --file --size 2G /swapfile (util-linux 2.41 and later, as in Ubuntu 26.04) creates the file with safe permissions and fully allocated blocks. Files with holes, which cp and truncate create, are rejected by swapon.
  • vm.swappiness (0 to 200, default 60) sets the relative cost the kernel assigns to swapping compared with dropping page cache. Lower values keep application memory in RAM longer.
  • On Ubuntu 26.04, /tmp is a RAM-backed tmpfs (the upstream systemd tmp.mount, sized at up to 50% of RAM). Large temporary files consume memory, not disk; check with findmnt /tmp.

docs.title: fail2ban and connection penalties
docs.text:
With key-only SSH, password guessing cannot succeed, but it still fills logs and uses CPU. Two layers reduce it:

  • OpenSSH's PerSourcePenalties (on by default since 9.8) makes sshd itself refuse addresses that repeatedly fail.
  • fail2ban watches logs and adds firewall bans. On Ubuntu 26.04 the package enables the sshd jail out of the box, reading the systemd journal (backend = systemd) and banning through nftables. Defaults: 5 failures (maxretry) within 10 minutes (findtime) earn a 10-minute ban (bantime). Your own changes go in /etc/fail2ban/jail.local, never in jail.conf.

Add your office or VPN range to ignoreip, or one colleague with a stale key can ban the whole office behind its shared NAT address.

docs.title: Installing Node.js
docs.text:
Method What you get Fit for a production VM NodeSource apt repository One Node.js major per repository (node_24.x), updated by apt, pinned above Ubuntu's own package Good default: system-wide, scriptable, upgrades with apt Official binaries from nodejs.org A tarball for linux-x64 or linux-arm64 Good when you need an exact version; you handle updates Ubuntu archive nodejs Node.js 22 from universe on 26.04 Works, but the line ends in April 2027 and it is not the version the rest of this section uses nvm, fnm, or mise Per-user installs under a home directory Developer machines; awkward for system services Container image node:24 Node.js inside an image When you deploy containers instead of processes

NodeSource's setup script adds a signing key under /usr/share/keyrings/, a deb822 source file /etc/apt/sources.list.d/nodesource.sources with the nodistro suite, and an APT pin (priority 600) so its nodejs beats Ubuntu's. It supports amd64 and arm64. Read the script before running it as root; it is short. This section's examples use Node.js 24 to match the CI pipelines; the same steps with setup_26.x install the newer LTS line.

docs.title: The app user and the directory layout
docs.text: The layout follows one rule: the app can read its code but not change it. Releases are extracted by root-owned deploy tooling, the app writes only to shared/, and systemd's ProtectSystem=strict (next lesson) enforces the same rule at the kernel level. The release directories and the current symlink are what make the zero-downtime deploy in running apps with systemd and nginx possible.

docs.title: Configuration and secrets on the server
docs.text:
• Non-secret settings go in /etc/taskflow/api.env, read by systemd through EnvironmentFile=. systemd's parser accepts KEY=value lines and # comments but has its own quoting rules, so keep the file plain (the differences between .env parsers are in .env files and precedence). The file can be 0600 and owned by root, because systemd reads it before it starts the process as the service user.
  • Secrets are better passed as systemd credentials. The systemd.exec manual warns that "environment variables are not suitable for passing secrets": they are visible over D-Bus and inherited by every child process. With LoadCredential=, systemd reads a root-only file and gives the service a private, read-only copy under $CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY that only the service's user can read.
  • Neither belongs in the release directory or in Git. The source of truth for secrets is a secret manager; the file on the server is a delivery mechanism. Rotation and secret stores are covered in secrets management.

docs.title: Backups for a single server
docs.text:
What Where its backup comes from MongoDB data The managed service's continuous backups, or scheduled mongodump with point-in-time recovery (database backups) User uploads in /srv/taskflow/shared Better stored in object storage from the start; otherwise synced to it on a schedule /etc/taskflow configuration and secrets The secret manager and the provisioning code, not the server The server itself Rebuilt from cloud-init or Ansible; a provider snapshot before risky changes for a fast way back

A backup that lives only on the same disk, or that the server can delete with its own credentials, does not survive the incidents that matter (ransomware, a deleted volume, a compromised host). The scheduled job that runs the dumps is in scheduled jobs and log rotation; restore drills are in restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach One to a few long-lived VMs This checklist, captured as cloud-init user data or an Ansible playbook A fleet behind a load balancer or an autoscaling group A baked image (Packer) plus cloud-init for per-instance settings; never configure instances by hand (autoscaling server fleets) Compliance requirements (SOC 2, PCI DSS, HIPAA) The same baseline, verified by CIS benchmark tooling such as USG, with evidence kept A team that does not want to operate servers A PaaS or container platform; the provider owns this checklist (choosing where to run software) A quick throwaway experiment Still key-only SSH and a firewall; skip the rest

Do not configure production servers by hand and leave it at that. Hand steps drift between servers and are forgotten during the 2 a.m. rebuild. Run them by hand once to learn them, then encode them.

docs.title: Step 1: first login and updates
docs.text:
# From your laptop, with the key you gave the provider
ssh ubuntu@203.0.113.10

# Refresh package lists, apply all updates (dist-upgrade = apt's full-upgrade), check for a reboot
sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get dist-upgrade -y
[ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && echo "reboot required" && sudo reboot

# Name the machine and keep it on UTC
sudo hostnamectl set-hostname taskflow-app-1
sudo timedatectl set-timezone Etc/UTC

Scripts use apt-get rather than apt: the apt manual says its command line "may change behavior between versions" and points scripts to apt-get and apt-cache.

docs.title: Step 2: a named admin user with your key
docs.text:
# Interactive: sets a password (used by sudo) and creates the home directory
sudo adduser ops
sudo usermod -aG sudo ops

# Group that may log in over SSH (used by AllowGroups in step 4)
sudo groupadd sshusers
sudo usermod -aG sshusers ops

# Install your public key for ops (or run ssh-copy-id from your laptop)
sudo install -d -m 700 -o ops -g ops /home/ops/.ssh
echo 'ssh-ed25519 <ops-public-key> ops laptop 2026' | sudo tee /home/ops/.ssh/authorized_keys > /dev/null
sudo chown ops:ops /home/ops/.ssh/authorized_keys
sudo chmod 600 /home/ops/.ssh/authorized_keys

docs.title: Step 3: test the new login before changing anything else
docs.text:
# From a SECOND terminal on your laptop; keep the first session open
ssh -o IdentitiesOnly=yes -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow ops@203.0.113.10 'sudo -v && echo sudo works'

Only continue when this prints sudo works. The default ubuntu user is not in sshusers, so the next step also stops it from logging in over SSH.

docs.title: Step 4: harden SSH
docs.text:
Create /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf with the settings from the hardening drop-in, then:

sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|allowgroups) '
# From a second terminal: a fresh login as ops must still work

docs.title: Step 5: firewalls, SSH first
docs.text:
# Host firewall: deny inbound by default, allow outbound
sudo ufw default deny incoming
sudo ufw default allow outgoing

# SSH only from the office VPN range, rate-limited; HTTP and HTTPS for everyone
sudo ufw limit proto tcp from 198.51.100.0/24 to any port 22 comment 'SSH from office VPN'
sudo ufw allow proto tcp from any to any port 80,443 comment 'HTTP and HTTPS'

# Enable (ufw asks for confirmation because you are connected over SSH)
sudo ufw enable
sudo ufw status verbose

Example output of ufw status verbose:

Status: active
Logging: on (low)
Default: deny (incoming), allow (outgoing), disabled (routed)
New profiles: skip

To                         Action      From
--                         ------      ----
22/tcp                     LIMIT IN    198.51.100.0/24            # SSH from office VPN
80,443/tcp                 ALLOW IN    Anywhere                   # HTTP and HTTPS
80,443/tcp (v6)            ALLOW IN    Anywhere (v6)              # HTTP and HTTPS

If admins have no fixed address range, use sudo ufw limit 22/tcp instead and rely on keys, PerSourcePenalties, and fail2ban. Mirror the same rules in the cloud firewall, for example on AWS:

# Security group: SSH from the office range; repeat with --port 443 (and 80) and --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-0123456789abcdef0 \
    --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 198.51.100.0/24

docs.title: Step 6: automatic security updates with a reboot window
docs.text:
# Confirm the periodic settings (installed and enabled by default on Ubuntu Server)
cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades

Example output:

APT::Periodic::Update-Package-Lists "1";
APT::Periodic::Unattended-Upgrade "1";

// /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52unattended-upgrades-local
// Read after 50unattended-upgrades, so these values win. app-2 uses 04:30.
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "03:30";
Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-WithUsers "true";

# What would be installed right now, without installing it
sudo unattended-upgrade -v --dry-run

# What it did on previous runs
sudo ls -l /var/log/unattended-upgrades/
systemctl list-timers 'apt-daily*'

APT reads the files in /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/ in alphanumeric order and later values override earlier ones, so a local file with a higher number keeps your settings separate from the package's own file, which package upgrades may replace.

docs.title: Step 7: check time synchronization
docs.text:
timedatectl status | grep -E 'Time zone|synchronized|NTP service'
chronyc -N tracking
sudo chronyc -N authdata

Example output (trimmed):

                Time zone: Etc/UTC (UTC, +0000)
System clock synchronized: yes
              NTP service: active

Reference ID    : B97DBE7B (2.ntp.ubuntu.com)
System time     : 0.000000004 seconds slow of NTP time
Leap status     : Normal

Name/IP address             Mode KeyID Type KLen Last Atmp  NAK Cook CLen
=========================================================================
1.ntp.ubuntu.com             NTS     6   30  128  14d    0    0    8   64

Mode NTS with non-zero KeyID, Type, and KLen means the sources are authenticated. If authdata shows no NTS keys and the clock is not synchronized, check that outbound TCP 4460 and UDP 123 are allowed.

docs.title: Step 8: a swap file
docs.text:
# Create, enable, and persist a 2 GiB swap file
sudo mkswap --file --size 2G /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

# Prefer keeping application memory in RAM over swapping it out
echo 'vm.swappiness = 10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/90-swappiness.conf
sudo sysctl --system > /dev/null

swapon --show
free -h

Size it modestly: on a 2 GiB VM, 1 to 2 GiB of swap absorbs spikes; a larger file mostly lets a leaking process thrash longer before the OOM killer acts.

docs.title: Step 9: fail2ban
docs.text:
sudo apt-get install -y fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd

# /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
[DEFAULT]
# Never ban localhost or the office VPN range
ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 198.51.100.0/24
bantime = 1h
findtime = 10m
maxretry = 5

sudo systemctl restart fail2ban
sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
# Unban an address that was banned by mistake
sudo fail2ban-client set sshd unbanip 203.0.113.55

Example output of fail2ban-client status sshd:

Status for the jail: sshd
|- Filter
|  |- Currently failed: 2
|  |- Total failed:     341
|  `- Journal matches:  _SYSTEMD_UNIT=ssh.service + _COMM=sshd
`- Actions
   |- Currently banned: 3
   |- Total banned:     27
   `- Banned IP list:   203.0.113.55 203.0.113.81 203.0.113.140

docs.title: Step 10: Node.js 24 from NodeSource
docs.text:
# Download and read the setup script before running it as root
curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_24.x -o /tmp/nodesource_setup.sh
less /tmp/nodesource_setup.sh
sudo bash /tmp/nodesource_setup.sh

sudo apt-get install -y nodejs
node --version
apt-cache policy nodejs

Example output of apt-cache policy nodejs (versions abbreviated):

nodejs:
  Installed: 24.y.z-1nodesource1
  Candidate: 24.y.z-1nodesource1
  Version table:
 *** 24.y.z-1nodesource1 600
        600 https://deb.nodesource.com/node_24.x nodistro/main amd64 Packages
        100 /var/lib/dpkg/status
     22.22.1+dfsg+~cs22.19.15-1ubuntu1 500
        500 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 Packages

The priority 600 pin is why apt-get install nodejs picks NodeSource's build over the Ubuntu archive's Node.js 22. Because unattended upgrades ignore third-party origins by default, Node.js patch releases arrive when you run apt-get upgrade yourself; schedule that like any deploy, since needrestart will then restart the app.

docs.title: Step 11: the app user and directories
docs.text:
# System user and group: no login shell, no home directory
sudo adduser --system --group --no-create-home taskflow

# Code: root-owned, readable by everyone; data: writable only by the app
sudo install -d -m 0755 -o root -g root /srv/taskflow /srv/taskflow/releases
sudo install -d -m 0750 -o taskflow -g taskflow /srv/taskflow/shared

# Configuration and secrets: root only
sudo install -d -m 0700 -o root -g root /etc/taskflow /etc/taskflow/credentials

getent passwd taskflow

Example output of getent passwd taskflow:

taskflow:x:998:998::/nonexistent:/usr/sbin/nologin

docs.title: Step 12: configuration and secret files
docs.text:
# /etc/taskflow/api.env: non-secret settings shared by every instance (PORT is set per instance)
sudo install -m 0600 -o root -g root /dev/null /etc/taskflow/api.env
sudo tee /etc/taskflow/api.env > /dev/null <<'EOF'
NODE_ENV=production
APP_ENV=production
LOG_LEVEL=info
CORS_ORIGINS=https://app.example.com
EOF

# Secret: create the file with mode 0600 FIRST, then paste the value (Ctrl+D to finish)
sudo install -m 0600 -o root -g root /dev/null /etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri
sudo tee /etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri > /dev/null

Creating the empty file with install -m 0600 before writing means the secret is never readable by others, not even for a moment, and pasting it into tee keeps it out of your shell history. The unit file in the next lesson loads it with LoadCredential=mongodb-uri:/etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri, and the app reads it like this:

// src/config/credentials.js: read a systemd credential, falling back to an env var in development
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { join } from "node:path";

export function credential(name, envFallback) {
  const dir = process.env.CREDENTIALS_DIRECTORY;
  if (dir) return readFileSync(join(dir, name), "utf8").trim();
  const value = process.env[envFallback];
  if (!value) throw new Error(`missing credential ${name} (or env ${envFallback})`);
  return value;
}

// Usage: const mongoUri = credential("mongodb-uri", "MONGODB_URI");

docs.title: Step 13: backups and a snapshot
docs.text: Take a provider snapshot now that the baseline is complete; it is the fastest way back if a later change goes wrong. Then confirm the database backups exist and that a restore has been tested (the backups section), and schedule any server-side dumps with a systemd timer as shown in scheduled jobs and log rotation.

docs.title: Step 14: audit the baseline
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/audit-baseline.sh: print this server's security baseline (read-only checks)
set -u
. /etc/os-release
echo "== OS: $PRETTY_NAME, kernel $(uname -r)"
echo "== Listening sockets";   sudo ss -tlnp
echo "== Firewall";            sudo ufw status verbose
echo "== SSH";                 sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|kbdinteractiveauthentication|allowgroups) '
echo "== Automatic updates";   cat /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/20auto-upgrades
[ -f /var/run/reboot-required ] && echo "!! reboot required"
echo "== Time";                timedatectl status | grep -E 'Time zone|synchronized'
echo "== Swap";                swapon --show
echo "== fail2ban";            sudo fail2ban-client status sshd | grep -E 'Currently|Total'
echo "== Node.js";             node --version
echo "== App user";            getent passwd taskflow

Keep the output with the server's record; running it again later shows drift.

docs.title: The whole baseline as cloud-init user data
docs.text:
#cloud-config
# user-data.yaml: the baseline from this lesson, applied once at first boot
# (cloud-init requires "#cloud-config" as the very first line)
hostname: taskflow-app-1
timezone: Etc/UTC
package_update: true
package_upgrade: true
package_reboot_if_required: true
packages:
  - fail2ban

groups:
  - sshusers

users:
  - name: ops
    groups: [sudo, sshusers]
    shell: /bin/bash
    lock_passwd: true
    sudo: "ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL"
    ssh_authorized_keys:
      - ssh-ed25519 <ops-public-key> ops laptop 2026

ssh_pwauth: false
disable_root: true

write_files:
  - path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf
    permissions: "0644"
    content: |
      PermitRootLogin no
      PasswordAuthentication no
      KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
      AuthenticationMethods publickey
      AllowGroups sshusers
      MaxAuthTries 3
      LoginGraceTime 30
      AllowAgentForwarding no
      AllowTcpForwarding no
      X11Forwarding no
  - path: /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/52unattended-upgrades-local
    permissions: "0644"
    content: |
      Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "true";
      Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot-Time "03:30";
  - path: /etc/fail2ban/jail.local
    permissions: "0644"
    content: |
      [DEFAULT]
      ignoreip = 127.0.0.1/8 ::1 198.51.100.0/24
      bantime = 1h

runcmd:
  - [ufw, default, deny, incoming]
  - [ufw, default, allow, outgoing]
  - [ufw, limit, proto, tcp, from, 198.51.100.0/24, to, any, port, "22"]
  - [ufw, allow, proto, tcp, from, any, to, any, port, "80,443"]
  - [ufw, --force, enable]
  - [mkswap, --file, --size, 2G, /swapfile]
  - [swapon, /swapfile]
  - [sh, -c, "echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' >> /etc/fstab"]
  - [systemctl, try-reload-or-restart, ssh]
  - [systemctl, restart, fail2ban]
  - [sh, -c, "curl -fsSL https://deb.nodesource.com/setup_24.x -o /root/nodesource_setup.sh && bash /root/nodesource_setup.sh && apt-get install -y nodejs"]
  - [adduser, --system, --group, --no-create-home, taskflow]

Validate the file before you boot anything with it: cloud-init schema --config-file user-data.yaml. Two choices here differ from the manual walkthrough on purpose. The ops account has no password, so it gets passwordless sudo, like the default cloud user; compensate with hardware-backed keys or short-lived SSH certificates, or set a password at first login. And ufw --force enable skips the interactive prompt, which is only safe because the SSH rule is added first. Directory creation and secrets are left to the deploy tooling and the secret manager, which should never be baked into user data.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Script the baseline (cloud-init, Ansible, or a baked image) and run it for every server; treat hand changes as drift.
  • Do the access steps first, test each from a second terminal, and know where the provider console is before you start.
  • One named admin account per person, keys only, root login refused, AllowGroups set.
  • A cloud firewall in front of the VM plus ufw on the host, default deny inbound, and private services bound to 127.0.0.1.
  • Never publish container ports on all interfaces of an internet-facing host.
  • Automatic security updates with a staggered reboot window, and services that restart gracefully.
  • UTC everywhere, chrony with NTS, and an egress rule for TCP 4460.
  • A modest swap file on small VMs, with alerts on sustained swapping.
  • Node.js from a supported repository, upgraded deliberately.
  • The app as a system user that cannot write its own code; secrets as systemd credentials, never in Git or the release directory.
  • Backups stored off the server and restore-tested; a snapshot before risky changes.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Locked out right after enabling ufw. Detect: new SSH connections time out; the existing session froze or dropped. Cause: ufw enable ran before an SSH rule existed, or the rule allows a different source range than your current address. Fix: use the provider console to ufw allow your range or ufw disable; next time add the SSH rule first and keep a second session open.
  • A database container is reachable from the internet although ufw denies the port. Detect: an external port scan or a security alert shows 27017 open; ufw status does not list it. Cause: the container was published with -p 27017:27017, and Docker's rules handle published ports before ufw. Fix: publish to 127.0.0.1, close the port in the cloud firewall, rotate the database credentials, and check access logs.
  • The API restarted in the middle of the day with no deploy. Detect: the journal shows taskflow-api@3001 stopping and starting at the time an apt run finished; /var/log/apt/history.log lists upgraded libraries. Cause: needrestart restarted services that used replaced libraries. Fix: expected behavior; make shutdown graceful and run two instances so restarts are invisible, and run manual upgrades in a planned window.
  • Kernel security fixes installed weeks ago but not running. Detect: /var/run/reboot-required exists; uname -r is older than the installed kernel. Cause: automatic reboots are off. Fix: enable Automatic-Reboot with staggered times, or schedule reboots, and alert when the file has existed for more than a few days.
  • TLS handshakes and token validation fail on one server. Detect: errors such as "certificate is not yet valid" or JWTs rejected as expired only on that host; timedatectl shows System clock synchronized: no. Cause: chrony cannot reach its NTS sources because egress TCP 4460 is blocked. Fix: allow outbound TCP 4460 and UDP 123, or point chrony at internal time servers, then confirm with chronyc -N authdata.
  • The office cannot SSH in after one person's failed attempts. Detect: fail2ban-client status sshd lists the office's public address. Cause: everyone shares one NAT address and a stale key produced repeated failures. Fix: unban it, add the office range to ignoreip, and remove the stale key from the colleague's agent.
  • The server crawls, then the OOM killer stops the API. Detect: vmstat 1 shows non-zero si and so columns for minutes; journalctl -k shows an out-of-memory kill. Cause: the working set no longer fits in RAM; swap only delayed the failure. Fix: find the memory consumer, cap it with MemoryMax=, and resize the VM.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Baseline: The minimum, repeatable configuration every server must have before it runs anything.
  • Cloud firewall / security group: Provider-managed packet filtering in front of the VM.
  • ufw: Ubuntu's uncomplicated firewall, a front end for the kernel's packet filter.
  • unattended-upgrades: The service that installs security updates automatically on Debian and Ubuntu.
  • needrestart: The tool that restarts services still using replaced libraries after an upgrade.
  • NTS (Network Time Security): Authentication for NTP using a TLS key exchange on TCP 4460.
  • Swap file: Disk space the kernel can move rarely used memory pages into.
  • tmpfs: A RAM-backed file system; /tmp on Ubuntu 26.04.
  • System user: An account for a service, with no login shell and usually no home directory.
  • systemd credential: A secret that systemd reads as root and hands to one service as a private, read-only file.
  • cloud-init: The tool that applies user data (users, files, packages, commands) on a cloud instance's first boot.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hardening SSH or enabling the firewall without a tested second way in.
  • Believing ufw protects ports that Docker publishes.
  • Leaving automatic reboots off forever, so patched kernels never run.
  • Running the app as root, or as the admin user, "to avoid permission problems".
  • Installing Node.js with a per-user version manager and pointing a system service at a path in someone's home directory.
  • Writing secrets with echo on the command line, which stores them in shell history.
  • Making the release directory writable by the app.
  • Treating a provider snapshot as the backup strategy.
  • Assuming the clock is right because the VM is in the cloud.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why must steps 3 to 5 come first, and what do you do before closing the session after each of them?
  2. Explain why a port published by Docker can be reachable when ufw status does not allow it, and two ways to prevent it.
  3. A 2 GiB VM runs two Node.js instances capped at 700 MiB each with MemoryMax=, nginx using about 50 MiB, and system services using about 250 MiB. How much RAM is left for the page cache and spikes, and what does a 2 GiB swap file change? (About 2048 - 1400 - 50 - 250 = 348 MiB of headroom; swap absorbs short spikes but cannot fix a working set that no longer fits.)
  4. What does unattended-upgrades install by default, what does it not install, and what must you configure for kernel fixes to take effect?
  5. Why does chrony on Ubuntu 26.04 need outbound TCP 4460, and what breaks when it is blocked?
  6. Why should /etc/taskflow/credentials/mongodb-uri be passed with LoadCredential= rather than placed in api.env?
  7. Two servers both use Automatic-Reboot-Time "03:30". What can go wrong, and how do you fix it?
  8. Why does this lesson install Node.js from NodeSource rather than from the Ubuntu archive, and what keeps apt from picking the archive version?
