docs.title: SSH and Remote Access
docs.text:
SSH is how you reach a Linux server's shell, run commands on it from scripts and CI, copy files to it, and tunnel to services that are not exposed to the internet. This lesson goes past the basics in SSH and SFTP: what happens during a connection, Ed25519 keys and the agent, a client configuration that keeps many servers manageable, host key verification and what to do when it fails, hardening sshd on Ubuntu 26.04, jump hosts with ProxyJump, port forwarding, SSH certificates, cloud services that need no open SSH port, and copying files with scp and rsync.

Every example uses the TaskFlow servers: a bastion at 203.0.113.20 and private app servers 10.0.2.10 and 10.0.2.11, all running Ubuntu 26.04 LTS with OpenSSH 10.2.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Port 22 on a public address is scanned and hit with automated password-guessing attempts all day, every day, so SSH is the most attacked door on most servers. The defaults are reasonable, but a few settings decide whether a server can be broken into with a guessed password, whether a stolen laptop file is enough to log in, and whether someone on the network path can impersonate the server.

SSH mistakes also cause outages of a different kind. Disabling password logins before a key works locks you out. Changing the port without opening the firewall locks you out. A CI job with StrictHostKeyChecking=no will happily deploy to an impostor. And as a team grows, copying public keys into authorized_keys on every server turns offboarding into a hunt through dozens of machines. Knowing how keys, host keys, agents, jump hosts, and certificates fit together lets you avoid all of these.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Meta (Facebook). In Scalable and secure access with SSH (2016), Facebook's engineers explain that trust defined per key pair in authorized_keys "does not scale", so their servers trust a single SSH certificate authority instead. Certificates are issued on bastion hosts that require two-factor authentication, principals decide which accounts an engineer may use, and the post recommends short-lived certificates (for example 24 hours) to shrink an attacker's window.
  • GitHub Enterprise Cloud. The SSH certificate authorities documentation shows organizations signing developers' keys with ssh-keygen -s ... -V '+1d', and states that an issued certificate cannot be revoked, which is exactly why lifetimes must be short.
  • AWS Systems Manager Session Manager. The guide to SSH connections through Session Manager describes reaching instances "without opening inbound ports or maintaining bastion hosts", with IAM policies deciding who may connect. It also warns that Session Manager cannot log sessions used for SSH or port forwarding, because they are encrypted end to end.
  • OpenSSH 10.0. The OpenSSH release notes record the removal of DSA keys and the switch to the hybrid post-quantum key agreement mlkem768x25519-sha256 as the default. Ubuntu 26.04 ships OpenSSH 10.2, so new servers and laptops negotiate it without any configuration.

Popular tools and providers: OpenSSH (client and server), the OpenSSH client built into Windows, PuTTY, Teleport, Smallstep step-ca, HashiCorp Vault's SSH secrets engine, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager and EC2 Instance Connect, Google Cloud IAP TCP forwarding and OS Login, Azure Bastion, and Tailscale SSH.

docs.title: What happens when you run ssh
docs.text:
An SSH connection is built in three layers:

  1. Transport. After the TCP handshake, client and server agree on algorithms and run a key exchange. Since OpenSSH 10.0 the default is mlkem768x25519-sha256, which combines the post-quantum ML-KEM algorithm with classic X25519, so the session stays protected even if one of the two is broken later, including by a future quantum computer applied to recorded traffic. OpenSSH 10.1 and later print a warning when a connection falls back to a key agreement without post-quantum protection, which you will see when connecting to old network appliances. In the same step the server signs the exchange with its host key, proving it holds the matching private key.
  2. User authentication. The client checks the host key against ~/.ssh/known_hosts first; only then does it authenticate the user. With public key authentication, the client offers a public key, the server looks for it in the account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, and the client proves it holds the private key by signing data that includes the session identifier. The private key never leaves the client, and the signature is useless for any other session.
  3. Connection. One authenticated connection carries many channels: an interactive shell, a single command (ssh host uptime), forwarded TCP ports, and the SFTP subsystem used by sftp, scp, and rsync.

The order matters for security. A password is sent to whoever answers, so if you accept an impostor's host key, the impostor learns your password. With key authentication, the impostor receives a signature that only works for its own fake session. Host key checking plus key-only login closes both doors.

docs.title: Keys, passphrases, and the agent
docs.text:
Key type ssh-keygen -t When to use it Ed25519 ed25519 (the default) Everything new: short keys, fast, no parameter choices to get wrong Ed25519 on a FIDO2 security key ed25519-sk Admin access: the private key lives in the hardware token and every use needs a touch ECDSA ecdsa, ecdsa-sk Systems or tokens that lack Ed25519 RSA rsa Only for old systems that accept nothing newer DSA none Removed in OpenSSH 10.0

A private key file on disk is protected by its passphrase, which encrypts the file; ssh-keygen -a sets how many key-derivation rounds an attacker must pay for each guess (the default is 16). The ssh client refuses to use a private key that other users can read, and sshd refuses an authorized_keys file (or a ~/.ssh directory or home directory) that other users can write, unless StrictModes is turned off. Most "the key is right but it still asks for a password" problems are permissions: ~/.ssh should be 700, private keys and authorized_keys 600.

ssh-agent holds decrypted keys in memory so you type the passphrase once per login session. ssh-add -t 8h makes a key expire from the agent after a working day, ssh-add -c asks for confirmation on every use, and AddKeysToAgent yes in the client config adds a key the first time you use it.

Agent forwarding (ssh -A, ForwardAgent yes) gives the remote server a socket that talks back to your agent. The ssh_config manual spells out the risk: an attacker on that server "cannot obtain key material from the agent, however they can perform operations on the keys". Anyone with root on a shared bastion can use your keys to log in anywhere you can for as long as you stay connected. ProxyJump solves the same problem without that exposure.

docs.title: The client configuration file
docs.text:
~/.ssh/config turns a command like this one into ssh taskflow-app-1:

# Without a client configuration: key, jump host, user, and address every time
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow -J ops@203.0.113.20 ops@10.0.2.10

Two rules explain most surprises:

  • The first value wins. For each option, ssh uses the first value it finds, reading the command line, then ~/.ssh/config, then /etc/ssh/ssh_config, top to bottom. Put specific Host blocks first and a catch-all Host * block last.
  • The agent offers every key it holds. Servers allow MaxAuthTries attempts (6 by default), so a well-stocked agent can trigger Too many authentication failures before the right key is tried. IdentitiesOnly yes limits a host to the keys you name.

ControlMaster auto with ControlPath and ControlPersist reuses one TCP connection for later ssh, scp, and rsync runs to the same host, which makes scripts and tools such as Ansible much faster. ssh -G host prints the configuration that will actually be used.

docs.title: Host keys and known_hosts
docs.text:
The first connection to a server is trust on first use: ssh shows the host key fingerprint and asks. StrictHostKeyChecking controls this:

Value New host Changed host key ask (default) Ask the user Refuse accept-new Add automatically Refuse yes Refuse unless already in known_hosts Refuse no Add automatically Connect anyway (dangerous)

Answering "yes" without checking defeats the point. Verify the fingerprint through a channel the attacker cannot touch: cloud-init prints every host key fingerprint to the instance's console log on first boot by default, and most providers show that log in their console; or run ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub through the provider's browser console. Automation should use pre-seeded known_hosts entries (StrictHostKeyChecking yes) or accept-new, never no. ssh-keyscan fetches host keys conveniently, but its manual warns that a known_hosts file built from it without verifying the keys leaves you open to man-in-the-middle attacks.

A changed host key means one of two things: the server was rebuilt or its keys were regenerated, or someone is intercepting the connection. Confirm the new fingerprint out of band, then remove the old entry with ssh-keygen -R host and reconnect. For planned key rotation, UpdateHostKeys (on by default unless you changed UserKnownHostsFile) lets a server announce additional host keys so clients learn them before the old one is retired. Host certificates, covered below, remove trust on first use entirely.

docs.title: Hardening sshd on Ubuntu 26.04
docs.text:
Ubuntu's /etc/ssh/sshd_config includes /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf at the top, and for most keywords sshd uses the first value it reads. Two consequences:

  • Settings in drop-in files override the main file, so the main file can say PasswordAuthentication no while a drop-in silently re-enables it. The Ubuntu installer and cloud-init write /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf for exactly this setting.
  • Your own drop-in must sort first. Name it 00-hardening.conf, then confirm the result with sshd -T, which prints the effective configuration.
Setting Default Recommended Why PermitRootLogin prohibit-password no Log in as a named user, then use sudo; logs show who did what PasswordAuthentication yes no Guessable secrets are the main SSH attack KbdInteractiveAuthentication yes (Ubuntu's file sets no) no The other route to password prompts through PAM AuthenticationMethods any one method publickey States the policy explicitly AllowGroups everyone sshusers Only intended accounts can log in at all MaxAuthTries 6 3 Fewer guesses per connection LoginGraceTime 120 seconds 30 Unauthenticated connections close sooner AllowAgentForwarding yes no Nobody parks an agent socket on the server AllowTcpForwarding yes no on app servers, local on bastions Forwarding can bypass network controls X11Forwarding no (Ubuntu's file sets yes) no Not needed on servers

OpenSSH 9.8 and later also enable PerSourcePenalties by default: an address that fails authentication or connects without authenticating is refused for a while (5 seconds per authentication failure, up to 10 minutes, with longer penalties for causing crashes). Monitoring systems or office VPN ranges that should never be penalized go in PerSourcePenaltyExemptList. Together with key-only logins this makes brute force pointless; fail2ban, covered in setting up a production server, adds firewall-level bans.

Apply changes safely: validate with sudo sshd -t, reload, and test a new login from a second terminal while the first session stays open. Ubuntu's ssh.service runs sshd -t again before every reload and restart, and existing sessions survive both because they are separate processes. On current Ubuntu releases, socket activation is the default: systemd's ssh.socket owns the listening socket, and a generator derives it from sshd_config. After changing Port, ListenAddress, or AddressFamily you must therefore run sudo systemctl daemon-reload and sudo systemctl restart ssh.socket, as the comment in Ubuntu's sshd_config says. Open the new port in the firewall before you do.

docs.title: Jump hosts and bastions
docs.text:
A bastion (jump host) is the one machine that accepts SSH from outside; app servers and databases sit in private subnets and accept SSH only from the bastion's security group. With ProxyJump (ssh -J), the client opens an SSH session to the bastion, asks it to open a plain TCP connection to the target's port 22, and runs a second SSH session to the target through that connection. The inner session is authenticated with keys on your laptop and encrypted end to end, so the bastion never sees your keys or your commands. Compare the alternatives:

Approach Where keys live What a compromised bastion can do ProxyJump Your laptop only Relay or block traffic it cannot read Agent forwarding (-A) Your laptop, usable from the bastion Use your keys while you are connected Keys copied to the bastion The bastion's disk Steal the keys and use them forever

Keep the bastion boring: no other services, patched automatically, port 22 open only to known address ranges, AllowTcpForwarding local, and accounts that can forward but not get a shell. A Match Group block with PermitTTY no and ForceCommand /usr/sbin/nologin does that, because ForceCommand applies to shell, command, and subsystem sessions, while ProxyJump only opens a TCP forwarding channel; PermitOpen can limit which host:port destinations may be forwarded to. Where the network design is concerned (security groups, private endpoints, and the trade-offs between bastions and identity-aware proxies), see network security in the cloud.

docs.title: Port forwarding
docs.text:
• -L [bind:]port:host:hostport (local): your machine listens, and the SSH server connects onward to host:hostport. Use it to reach a private admin UI or database port without exposing it. host is resolved from the server's point of view, so 10.0.2.30 or localhost means the server's network, not yours.
  • -R [bind:]port:host:hostport (remote): the server listens and connections come back to your side. By default sshd binds remote forwards to the server's loopback address (GatewayPorts no), so only processes on the server can use them.
  • -D [bind:]port (dynamic): your machine runs a SOCKS proxy and the server dials whatever destination each request names.
  • -N runs no remote command (forwarding only) and -f sends ssh to the background once it has authenticated. In scripts add -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes so ssh fails loudly when the port is already taken.

ssh binds local forwards to the loopback address by default; keep it that way (no GatewayPorts yes, no 0.0.0.0 bind address), because a forward listening on all interfaces of your laptop shares the private service with everyone on the same Wi-Fi. Writing 127.0.0.1: in front of the port makes the intent explicit. On the server side, forwarding can carry traffic past network controls, which is why app servers that never need it should set AllowTcpForwarding no.

docs.title: SSH certificates
docs.text:
An SSH certificate is a public key signed by a certificate authority key, together with a key ID (recorded in the server's log), a list of principals (names the certificate may log in as), a validity window, and optional restrictions. OpenSSH certificates are not X.509 certificates; ssh-keygen creates and signs them.

  • User certificates: servers trust the CA with TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/taskflow_user_ca.pub, so no per-user authorized_keys lines are needed. AuthorizedPrincipalsFile maps principals to local accounts: /etc/ssh/auth_principals/deploy containing taskflow-ops lets any certificate carrying that principal log in as deploy.
  • Host certificates: the CA signs each server's host key (ssh-keygen -h), sshd presents it with HostCertificate, and clients trust every server the CA signed with one line in known_hosts: @cert-authority *.example.com ssh-ed25519 <ca-public-key>. Rebuilt servers no longer trigger host key warnings.
  • Revocation: RevokedKeys accepts a list or an OpenSSH key revocation list (KRL), but the practical control is a short lifetime. An 8-hour certificate expires before most incident responses even begin, which is the reasoning in Facebook's post and GitHub's warning that its certificates cannot be revoked.
  • Protect the CA key like the most powerful credential you own, since it can sign a login to every server. Keep it offline or in a secrets engine (step-ca, Vault, Teleport) that issues certificates only after SSO and MFA.

docs.title: Remote access without an open SSH port
docs.text:
Cloud providers offer access paths that need no public SSH port at all:

Service How you connect Inbound port 22 from the internet Identity and audit AWS Systems Manager Session Manager aws ssm start-session --target i-...; the SSM Agent on the instance connects outward to AWS Not needed IAM policies; shell sessions can be logged, SSH and port-forward sessions cannot EC2 Instance Connect Pushes your public key to the instance metadata for 60 seconds, then you SSH Needed, or use an EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint for private instances IAM; connection requests logged to CloudTrail Google Cloud IAP TCP forwarding gcloud compute ssh vm --tunnel-through-iap Only from Google's range 35.235.240.0/20 IAM role roles/iap.tunnelResourceAccessor Azure Bastion The Azure portal in a browser, or your own SSH client (Standard and Premium tiers), through a managed bastion in your virtual network Not needed; VMs need no public IP Azure RBAC; Microsoft Entra ID sign-in with the native client

Session Manager can also carry real SSH (useful for scp and rsync) and port forwarding with the AWS-StartPortForwardingSession documents. An EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint is an identity-aware TCP proxy into a VPC; each endpoint supports up to 20 concurrent connections, and a connection lasts at most one hour, so it suits management access rather than data transfer. These services are the network-level answer to "how do we get rid of the bastion", compared in network security in the cloud.

docs.title: Copying files: scp, sftp, and rsync
docs.text:
• scp has used the SFTP protocol for transfers by default since OpenSSH 9.0 (-O selects the legacy protocol for old servers). It copies whole files every time.
  • sftp gives an interactive or batch file-transfer session.
  • rsync compares source and destination and sends only what changed, over SSH by default, honoring your ~/.ssh/config (including ProxyJump). -a (archive) means -rlptgoD: recursive, symlinks, permissions, times, group, owner, and devices. A trailing slash on the source copies the directory's contents rather than the directory itself, and --delete removes destination files missing from the source, so always preview with -n (--dry-run) first.

For application deploys, copying source code to servers is the weakest pattern; CI should build an artifact once and the server should fetch a specific version, as in deploying backend services.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended access One or two VMs, small team Key-only SSH (Ed25519, passphrase), port 22 limited to known addresses where possible, a hardening drop-in, fail2ban or PerSourcePenalties for noise Several servers in private subnets A bastion with ProxyJump, or a cloud service with no open port AWS fleet Session Manager (IAM, no inbound ports); EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint when you need real SSH to private instances Google Cloud fleet IAP TCP forwarding with OS Login Growing team, compliance audits, frequent joiners and leavers SSH certificates from an issuer behind SSO and MFA, with lifetimes of hours CI deploying to a VM A dedicated deploy key restricted to one forced command, plus a pinned host key Immutable servers or containers No interactive SSH in normal operation; replace instead of fixing in place (immutable infrastructure)

Do not:

  • share one private key across a team; every person and every system gets its own key, so access can be removed one at a time;
  • disable host key checking to make a script "work";
  • use agent forwarding to reach servers behind a bastion;
  • treat a non-standard SSH port as protection.

docs.title: Create a key and prove it works before disabling passwords
docs.text:
# On your laptop: an Ed25519 key with a passphrase and 100 KDF rounds
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100 -C "ops laptop 2026" -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow

# Append the public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the server
ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow.pub ops@203.0.113.20

# Log in with the key only; password prompts are disabled for this attempt
ssh -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
    -o PasswordAuthentication=no ops@203.0.113.20 'echo key login works'

ssh-copy-id uses whatever access you already have (a password or the provider's initial key) and creates ~/.ssh/authorized_keys if it is missing. Only after the last command succeeds is it safe to turn off password authentication on the server.

docs.title: A client configuration for the TaskFlow servers
docs.text:
# ~/.ssh/config
Host taskflow-bastion
    HostName 203.0.113.20

Host taskflow-app-1
    HostName 10.0.2.10

Host taskflow-app-2
    HostName 10.0.2.11

Host taskflow-app-*
    ProxyJump taskflow-bastion

Host taskflow-*
    User ops
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Host *
    AddKeysToAgent yes
    ServerAliveInterval 30
    ServerAliveCountMax 4
    ControlMaster auto
    ControlPath ~/.ssh/cm-%C
    ControlPersist 10m

ssh taskflow-app-1 now picks up its HostName from the first matching block, ProxyJump from the second, the user and key from the third, and keep-alives and multiplexing from the last. Because the first obtained value wins, a User line in Host * would never override the one set above it. ServerAliveInterval 30 sends a keep-alive through the encrypted channel every 30 seconds and disconnects after 4 missed replies, which stops idle sessions from being cut by NAT gateways and detects dead connections in about two minutes. %C is a hash of the local host name, remote host, port, user, and jump host, which keeps control socket paths short and unique.

docs.title: One hardening drop-in for sshd
docs.text:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf
# Sorts before 50-cloud-init.conf; for most keywords sshd keeps the FIRST value it reads.
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
AuthenticationMethods publickey
AllowGroups sshusers
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 30
AllowAgentForwarding no
AllowTcpForwarding no
X11Forwarding no
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2

# Create the login group first, or AllowGroups locks everyone out
sudo groupadd sshusers
sudo usermod -aG sshusers ops
sudo usermod -aG sshusers deploy

# Validate, inspect the effective values, then reload (keep this session open)
sudo sshd -t
sudo sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|kbdinteractiveauthentication|authenticationmethods|allowgroups) '
sudo systemctl reload ssh

# From a SECOND terminal: a password attempt must now be refused
ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -o PreferredAuthentications=password ops@203.0.113.20

Example output of the sshd -T check (values are lowercased):

permitrootlogin no
passwordauthentication no
kbdinteractiveauthentication no
authenticationmethods publickey
allowgroups sshusers

The final command should end with Permission denied (publickey). On a bastion, use AllowTcpForwarding local instead of no, or ProxyJump through it stops working. ClientAliveInterval 300 with ClientAliveCountMax 2 makes the server drop clients that stop answering after about ten minutes.

docs.title: Reach a private admin UI through the bastion
docs.text:
# Forward 127.0.0.1:3300 on your laptop to Grafana on the private network; -N: no shell
ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -L 127.0.0.1:3300:10.0.2.30:3000 taskflow-bastion
# Then open http://127.0.0.1:3300 in a browser; Ctrl+C closes the tunnel

The bastion connects to 10.0.2.30:3000 on your behalf, so its sshd_config must allow local forwarding and its security group must reach Grafana. Nothing about Grafana is exposed to the internet.

docs.title: A deploy key that can run exactly one command
docs.text:
CI needs to trigger deploys, not to get a shell. A dedicated key in the deploy account's authorized_keys, restricted to a forced command, gives it exactly that:

# /home/deploy/.ssh/authorized_keys (one line per key)
restrict,command="/usr/local/sbin/taskflow-deploy-gate" ssh-ed25519 <ci-public-key> ci-deploy

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/sbin/taskflow-deploy-gate: the only command the CI key can run
set -euo pipefail

# What the client asked to run, for example "1.8.0"
version="${SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND:-}"

if [[ ! "$version" =~ ^[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+$ ]]; then
  echo "usage: ssh deploy@host <major.minor.patch>" >&2
  exit 2
fi

exec sudo /usr/local/sbin/deploy-taskflow-api "$version"

# /etc/sudoers.d/deploy-taskflow (edit with: sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/deploy-taskflow)
deploy ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/local/sbin/deploy-taskflow-api

restrict disables port, agent, and X11 forwarding and PTY allocation for this key, and future restrictions OpenSSH adds are included automatically. command= runs the gate whatever the client asked for; the requested text arrives in SSH_ORIGINAL_COMMAND and is validated before use. The sudoers rule lets the deploy account run one root-owned script (the release script from running apps with systemd and nginx) and nothing else. Ubuntu 26.04 uses sudo-rs as sudo, which reads the same /etc/sudoers.d files; check the result with sudo -l -U deploy.

docs.title: Pin the host key in a CI workflow
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy-vm.yml
name: deploy-vm
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      version:
        description: "Release version to deploy, for example 1.8.0"
        required: true

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    concurrency: deploy-production
    steps:
      - name: Install the deploy key and the pinned host key
        env:
          DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_SSH_KEY }}
          KNOWN_HOSTS: ${{ vars.PROD_KNOWN_HOSTS }}
        run: |
          install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "$DEPLOY_KEY" > ~/.ssh/deploy_key
          chmod 600 ~/.ssh/deploy_key
          printf '%s\n' "$KNOWN_HOSTS" > ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Trigger the deploy
        env:
          VERSION: ${{ inputs.version }}
        run: |
          ssh -i ~/.ssh/deploy_key -o IdentitiesOnly=yes \
              -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@203.0.113.10 "$VERSION"

PROD_KNOWN_HOSTS is a configuration variable holding the server's verified known_hosts line, so the job refuses to talk to anything else. The version is passed through an environment variable rather than pasted into the script, which prevents script injection through the input, and the forced command on the server validates it again. The production environment can require an approval, and concurrency stops two deploys from overlapping. Pipeline security in general is covered in pipeline and supply chain security.

docs.title: Sign a short-lived user certificate
docs.text:
# Once, on the CA machine (offline, or inside step-ca or Vault): the user CA key
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ./taskflow_user_ca -C "taskflow user CA"

# Per login session: sign an engineer's public key for 8 hours as principal taskflow-ops
ssh-keygen -s ./taskflow_user_ca -I "ops-laptop-2026-11-14" -n taskflow-ops \
    -V +8h ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow.pub

# Inspect the result (written as id_ed25519_taskflow-cert.pub next to the key)
ssh-keygen -L -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519_taskflow-cert.pub

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-user-ca.conf
TrustedUserCAKeys /etc/ssh/taskflow_user_ca.pub
AuthorizedPrincipalsFile /etc/ssh/auth_principals/%u

# On each server: the deploy account accepts certificates for principal taskflow-ops
sudo install -d -m 755 /etc/ssh/auth_principals
echo taskflow-ops | sudo tee /etc/ssh/auth_principals/deploy
sudo sshd -t && sudo systemctl reload ssh

ssh picks up <key>-cert.pub automatically when it sits next to the private key. In production an issuer service runs the signing step after SSO and MFA, and nobody handles the CA key directly.

docs.title: Copy a directory with rsync
docs.text:
# Preview: what would change? (trailing slash = copy the CONTENTS of dist/)
rsync -avzn --delete dist/ taskflow-app-1:/srv/taskflow-web/

# Apply, with resumable partial transfers and progress
rsync -avz --delete -P dist/ taskflow-app-1:/srv/taskflow-web/

Because rsync runs ssh, the jump through the bastion, the key, and multiplexing all come from ~/.ssh/config.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• One Ed25519 key per person and per device, protected by a passphrase; a FIDO2 (-sk) key for administrators.
  • Key-only logins, no root login, an AllowGroups list, and a hardening drop-in that sorts before anything cloud-init writes; verify with sshd -T.
  • Keep a second session open while changing SSH or firewall settings.
  • Verify host keys out of band; pin them in CI; never use StrictHostKeyChecking=no.
  • Reach private servers with ProxyJump, not agent forwarding.
  • Prefer no public SSH at all: Session Manager, IAP, or a bastion that only accepts known address ranges.
  • Move to SSH certificates with lifetimes of hours once more than a handful of people need access.
  • Give automation restricted keys with forced commands and narrow sudo rules.
  • Collect sshd logs centrally so a login can be traced to a person.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• "REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED" after a server rebuild. Detect: ssh refuses to connect and prints the old and new fingerprints. Cause: the rebuilt server generated new host keys, or someone is intercepting the connection. Fix: compare the new fingerprint with the console log or ssh-keygen -lf run through the provider console; if it matches, run ssh-keygen -R host and reconnect; move to host certificates to stop the warnings.
  • Locked out right after disabling passwords. Detect: Permission denied (publickey) for every account. Cause: the key was never installed for that user, ~/.ssh or authorized_keys is writable by others (StrictModes), or the user is missing from the AllowGroups group. Fix: get in through the provider's console or Session Manager, fix ownership and permissions (700 and 600), add the group membership, and next time test from a second session first.
  • "Too many authentication failures" before the right key is tried. Detect: ssh -v shows several keys offered and rejected. Cause: the agent offers every loaded key and the server stops at MaxAuthTries. Fix: IdentitiesOnly yes with the right IdentityFile for that host.
  • Password authentication still accepted after hardening. Detect: sudo sshd -T | grep passwordauthentication prints yes. Cause: /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-cloud-init.conf sets it first, and sshd keeps the first value. Fix: name your file 00-...conf (or correct the cloud-init file), reload, and check again.
  • The new SSH port does not take effect, or the server becomes unreachable. Detect: ss -tlnp still shows :22, or connections time out. Cause: on Ubuntu, systemd's ssh.socket owns the port and needs daemon-reload plus a socket restart; or the firewall or security group was not opened first. Fix: open the port in ufw and the security group, run both systemctl commands, and test before closing your session.
  • Idle SSH sessions freeze after a few minutes. Detect: the terminal stops responding after idle time; reconnecting works. Cause: a NAT gateway or firewall drops idle TCP flows. Fix: ServerAliveInterval 30 on the client (or ClientAliveInterval on the server).
  • The auth log fills with failed logins from all over the internet. Detect: journalctl -u ssh shows thousands of Invalid user lines per hour. Cause: port 22 open to the world. Fix: key-only authentication makes them harmless; restrict the source ranges in the security group, or remove public SSH and use Session Manager or IAP.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Host key: The server's key pair; proves the server's identity to clients.
  • known_hosts: The client's record of trusted host keys.
  • authorized_keys: The per-account list of public keys allowed to log in, optionally with restrictions such as command= and restrict.
  • Trust on first use (TOFU): Accepting a host key the first time it is seen and checking it on every later connection.
  • ssh-agent: A process that holds decrypted private keys and signs on request.
  • Agent forwarding: Exposing your agent to a remote server.
  • ProxyJump: Connecting to a target through a jump host with an end-to-end encrypted inner session.
  • Bastion (jump host): The single hardened entry point into a private network.
  • Port forwarding: Carrying TCP connections through an SSH session: local (-L), remote (-R), or dynamic SOCKS (-D).
  • SSH certificate: A public key signed by a CA with a key ID, principals, and a validity window.
  • Principal: A name in a certificate that maps to accounts a holder may use.
  • Forced command: A command that runs whenever a given key is used, regardless of what the client asked for.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a passphrase-less key "is fine on my laptop": a stolen backup or synced folder is enough to log in.
  • Copying the same private key to colleagues, CI, and servers, so it can never be revoked without breaking everything.
  • Fixing a changed host key with ssh-keygen -R without checking why it changed.
  • StrictHostKeyChecking=no in scripts and CI.
  • Editing /etc/ssh/sshd_config while a drop-in silently overrides it.
  • Thinking a different port, or fail2ban alone, is what secures SSH; key-only authentication is.
  • Using agent forwarding through a bastion "just this once".
  • Assuming scp and rsync bypass your ~/.ssh/config; they use it.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the steps of an SSH connection in order, and explain why key-based login protects you even if you accidentally accept an impostor's host key, while password login does not.
  2. Why does sshd on Ubuntu 26.04 keep accepting passwords when /etc/ssh/sshd_config says PasswordAuthentication no, and how do you prove which value is in effect?
  3. What does StrictHostKeyChecking accept-new do differently from ask, yes, and no, and which would you use in CI?
  4. Explain why ProxyJump is safer than agent forwarding when reaching private servers through a bastion.
  5. Write the command that makes a private Grafana at 10.0.2.30:3000 available on your laptop's port 3300 through the bastion, and explain which machine resolves 10.0.2.30.
  6. A team has 40 engineers and 30 servers, and every engineer's key is in authorized_keys on every server. How many entries must be managed, how many servers change when one person leaves, and how do 8-hour certificates change both numbers? (1,200 entries and 30 servers to edit; with certificates the servers trust one CA key and nothing changes on them, because access ends when the certificate expires.)
  7. Compare Session Manager, EC2 Instance Connect, and IAP TCP forwarding: which need an inbound port, and how is access granted?
  8. Why does changing Port in sshd_config on Ubuntu need systemctl daemon-reload and a restart of ssh.socket?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OpenSSH manual pages
  • sshd_config(5) on Ubuntu 26.04
  • ssh_config(5) on Ubuntu 26.04
  • Ubuntu Server: OpenSSH server
  • AWS: Start a Session Manager session
  • Google Cloud: Using IAP for TCP forwarding
  • AWS: EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint
  • Next: setting up a production server. Back to the Linux server operations overview.

docs.title: Troubleshooting CPU, Memory, Disk, and Network
docs.text:
When the TaskFlow API slows down or starts failing, the server itself is one of the first suspects and one of the fastest to rule in or out. This lesson is a working method for that: a one-minute snapshot of the whole machine, then a focused look at the resource that is short. It covers load average versus CPU utilization, top, vmstat, and pidstat; memory as free really reports it, swap, and the OOM killer; disk space, inodes, deleted-but-open files, and I/O latency; and the network from listening sockets to DNS, TCP, TLS, and the path between, with ss, curl, dig, and mtr. It ends with the "too many open files" family of failures.

Application-level profiling under load (CPU profiles, event-loop lag, slow queries during a load test) is covered in finding bottlenecks; this lesson stays on the host.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
During an incident, guessing is expensive. Restarting the app, resizing the VM, or blaming the network each takes minutes and destroys evidence, and each is right only some of the time. A few commands answer the real questions within a minute: is a resource saturated, which one, and which process is responsible.

Most host-level incidents are also repeats of a handful of patterns: a disk filled by logs, a memory leak ending in an OOM kill, a single-threaded process pinned at 100% of one core, a slow DNS lookup, a file descriptor limit. Recognizing the pattern from one or two numbers is what separates a ten-minute incident from a two-hour one.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix: the first 60 seconds. In Linux Performance Analysis in 60,000 Milliseconds, Netflix's performance engineering team lists the ten commands they run first on a misbehaving Linux instance: uptime, dmesg | tail, vmstat 1, mpstat -P ALL 1, pidstat 1, iostat -xz 1, free -m, sar -n DEV 1, sar -n TCP,ETCP 1, and top. This lesson's snapshot script is built on that list.
  • The USE method. Brendan Gregg's USE method checks every resource for utilization, saturation, and errors, which turns "the server is slow" into a short, complete checklist instead of a hunt.
  • Linux load averages. Gregg's Linux Load Averages: Solving the Mystery explains that Linux load averages "track not just runnable tasks, but also tasks in the uninterruptible sleep state", so a high load can mean slow disks rather than busy CPUs.
  • Google SRE book. The Effective Troubleshooting chapter frames debugging as forming and testing hypotheses, and insists that the first goal is to "make the system work as well as it can under the circumstances" before hunting for the root cause.
  • Linux kernel documentation. Pressure stall information reports the share of time tasks were stalled waiting for CPU, memory, or I/O, a direct measure of saturation.

Popular tools and providers: procps (top, vmstat, free), sysstat (mpstat, pidstat, iostat, sar), htop, iproute2 (ss), lsof, curl, dig, mtr, and on the platform side the Prometheus node exporter, Netdata, CloudWatch, and Datadog for the same signals over time.

docs.title: A method before commands
docs.text:
Three habits make host-level debugging fast:

  1. Stop the bleeding first. If one instance is broken, take it out of the load balancer or restart it after capturing evidence; if the disk is full, free space before investigating why.
  2. Capture before you change. A snapshot script (below) records the state in a file, so a restart does not erase the answer.
  3. Work through resources, not hunches. For CPU, memory, disk, and network, ask the USE questions: how busy is it (utilization), is work queueing (saturation), and are there errors?
Resource Utilization Saturation Errors CPU top / mpstat us + sy vmstat r above the CPU count; /proc/pressure/cpu Rare; kernel log Memory free -h used versus available vmstat si / so; /proc/pressure/memory OOM kills in journalctl -k Disk I/O iostat -xz %util (for spinning or serial devices) aqu-sz, await, vmstat b and wa I/O errors in the kernel log Disk capacity df -h, df -i n/a ENOSPC: "No space left on device" Network sar -n DEV 1 throughput TCP retransmits (sar -n TCP,ETCP 1), listen queue overflows Connection refused or reset, DNS failures

docs.title: The first minute
docs.text:
The snapshot uses the Netflix list. mpstat, pidstat, iostat, and sar come from the sysstat package (sudo apt-get install sysstat); the rest are installed on Ubuntu Server.

Command What it tells you What bad looks like uptime Load averages over 1, 5, and 15 minutes Load well above the CPU count, or a 1-minute value far above the 15-minute one (it is getting worse) sudo dmesg -T (read the last lines) Recent kernel messages OOM kills, I/O errors, dropped packets vmstat 1 5 Run queue, blocked tasks, swap, I/O, CPU split High r, non-zero b, si/so above 0, high wa or st mpstat -P ALL 1 Per-CPU utilization One CPU at 100% while others idle: a single-threaded bottleneck pidstat 1 CPU per process Which process is busy iostat -xz 1 Per-device latency, queue, utilization High r_await/w_await, growing aqu-sz free -h Memory, including available available near zero sar -n DEV 1 Network throughput per interface Close to the instance's bandwidth limit sar -n TCP,ETCP 1 Connections and retransmits Many retransmits top Everything at once, per process Confirms the suspect

The first line of vmstat and iostat output reports averages since boot; read the following lines, which cover each interval.

docs.title: CPU: load average is not CPU usage
docs.text:
On Linux, the load average counts tasks that are running, waiting to run, or in uninterruptible sleep (state D, usually waiting for disk or network storage). The three numbers are exponentially damped averages with 1, 5, and 15 minute time constants, so a load spike shows up in the first number before the others. Compare them with the number of CPUs (nproc):

  • Load 7.9 on 2 vCPUs, vmstat shows us 85 sy 10: the CPUs are saturated and work is queueing. Find the process with top or pidstat 1.
  • Load 7.9 on 2 vCPUs, vmstat shows us 5 wa 80 and b 6: the CPUs are mostly idle; tasks are stuck waiting for the disk. This is an I/O problem, and adding CPUs would change nothing.
  • Load 1.1 on 8 vCPUs, the API is slow, and top shows one node process at 100%: the machine is 12% busy, but Node.js runs JavaScript on one thread, so that instance is saturated. Add instances (one per core) or move CPU-heavy work to worker threads (worker threads, child processes, and cluster). mpstat -P ALL 1, or pressing 1 in top, shows the pinned core.

The CPU split in top and vmstat is diagnostic in itself:

Field Meaning When it is high us Running user code Application work: profile the process sy Running kernel code Many system calls, context switches, or network packets wa Idle while waiting for I/O Slow or saturated disks st Time "stolen from this VM by the hypervisor" The host or instance type is not giving you the CPU you ask for; check the provider's CPU credit or throttling metrics

docs.title: Memory: free, available, swap, and the OOM killer
docs.text:
Linux uses otherwise idle RAM as page cache for file data, so free is normally small on a healthy server. The column that matters is available, which the free manual defines as an "Estimation of how much memory is available for starting new applications, without swapping": free memory plus cache the kernel can drop. In the procps version on Ubuntu 26.04, used is calculated as total minus available.

When available memory runs out, the kernel tries, in order, to:

  1. Reclaim page cache, which costs re-reading files later.
  2. Swap anonymous memory out, if swap exists. vmstat shows it as non-zero si (swapped in) and so (swapped out). A little swap use is harmless; continuous si/so means the working set no longer fits and everything slows down.
  3. Kill a process. The OOM killer picks the process with the highest badness score (roughly its share of memory, adjusted by /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj from -1000 to +1000, where -1000 disables OOM killing for that process; systemd sets it with OOMScoreAdjust=).

There are two kinds of OOM kill, and the kernel log says which:

  • Out of memory: Killed process ... is the whole machine running out.
  • Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process ... is one service reaching its own MemoryMax=. systemd then reports the unit's result as oom-kill, and the rest of the machine is fine.

Two Ubuntu 26.04 details: /tmp is a tmpfs, so large files there use RAM (they appear in the shared column); and on Ubuntu, reading the kernel ring buffer with dmesg needs sudo, while journalctl -k reads the same messages from the journal. For a Node.js process, the RSS includes the V8 heap plus buffers and native memory; a heap that grows steadily across garbage collections is a leak, diagnosed with heap snapshots as described in errors, debugging, and performance.

docs.title: Disk: space, inodes, and files that are deleted but still open
docs.text:
A full disk breaks more than the app: MongoDB stops accepting writes, journald and nginx cannot write logs, nginx cannot buffer large request bodies to temporary files, and apt fails halfway through an upgrade. Four checks cover nearly every case:

  • Space: df -h per file system. ext4 reserves 5% of blocks for root by default, so that root-owned daemons keep working after ordinary processes can no longer write; df's Avail column already excludes that reserve.
  • Inodes: df -i. Millions of small files (cache entries, session files, mail queues) can exhaust inodes while gigabytes are free, with the same "No space left on device" error.
  • Where it went: du -xh -d1 / | sort -h walks one file system level by level. Usual suspects: /var/log (application files, the journal), /var/lib/docker (images, containers, unrotated container logs), old releases, /var/lib/apt caches, and core dumps.
  • Deleted but open: when df says the disk is full but du cannot find the space, a process is holding a deleted file open.

A file's name is only a directory entry pointing at an inode; the blocks are freed when the last name is removed and the last open file descriptor is closed. Deleting a log file that a process still writes to removes the name, so du stops counting it, but the process keeps the inode alive and growing. lsof +L1 lists open files whose link count is below one, that is, deleted ones. Restarting the process (or signalling it to reopen its logs) releases the space; truncating the file through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> frees it immediately without a restart.

I/O latency is the other disk problem. iostat -xz 1 reports r_await and w_await (average milliseconds per request, queue time included) and aqu-sz (average queue length). %util near 100% means saturation only for devices that serve one request at a time; for SSDs and RAID arrays the manual warns it "does not reflect their performance limits", so trust latency and queue length instead. Cloud volumes also have provisioned IOPS and throughput limits; when you hit them, latency rises while %util looks unremarkable.

docs.title: Network: listening, connecting, resolving, and the path
docs.text:
Work from the inside out:

  • Is the service listening where you think? ss -tulpn lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with the owning process. A service bound to 127.0.0.1:3001 is unreachable from other machines by design; one bound to 0.0.0.0 is reachable from everywhere the firewall allows.
  • What are the connections doing? ss -s summarizes sockets by state. Thousands of TIME-WAIT sockets are normal on a busy proxy; sockets piling up in CLOSE-WAIT mean the local application received the peer's close but never closed its side, which is a bug in the app or a library and eventually exhausts file descriptors.
  • Refused or timed out? "Connection refused" means a host answered with a reset: nothing listens on that port, or a firewall rejects rather than drops. A timeout means packets disappear: a firewall or security group drops them, routing is wrong, or the host is down.
  • Where does the time go? curl -w prints cumulative timestamps for each phase of a request.

Subtracting consecutive timestamps separates DNS, TCP, TLS, server time, and transfer. TCP's handshake costs one round trip and TLS 1.3 one more, so both should be close to the ping time; if the wait for the first byte dominates, as here, look at the server, its logs, and its queries rather than the network.

  • Is DNS the problem? On Ubuntu, applications ask the systemd-resolved stub at 127.0.0.53, which forwards to the configured upstream servers; resolvectl status shows which. dig queries a server directly: compare the stub with a public resolver, and use +trace to follow delegation from the root. The resolution process itself is covered in DNS.
  • Where on the path? mtr combines traceroute and ping, showing loss and latency per hop over many cycles. Loss at an intermediate hop that does not continue to later hops is usually a router rate-limiting its own ICMP replies, not real loss; loss that starts at a hop and persists to the destination is real. mtr -T -P 443 probes with TCP to the port you care about, which survives firewalls that drop ICMP (see ICMP).

docs.title: Too many open files
docs.text:
Every socket, file, and pipe a process holds is a file descriptor, and each process has a soft and a hard limit on how many it may hold (RLIMIT_NOFILE). Errors look like EMFILE: too many open files in Node.js or socket() failed (24: Too many open files) in nginx.

  • Read the limit that applies. ulimit -n shows only your shell's limit. For a service, read /proc/<pid>/limits, which shows the soft limit, hard limit, and units for each resource.
  • Count the descriptors. ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l, watched over time. A count that only grows is a leak (often sockets left in CLOSE-WAIT), and raising the limit only delays the failure.
  • Raise it at the right layer. systemd's default is 1024:524288 (soft:hard) for services. Node.js raises its own soft limit to the hard limit at startup, so a Node.js service mostly fails only when the hard limit is low (set with LimitNOFILE=) or there is a leak. nginx does not do this: its worker_connections (768 in Ubuntu's nginx.conf) counts both client and upstream connections, and its open-file limit is raised with worker_rlimit_nofile. When workers run out of connection slots, nginx logs "worker_connections are not enough".
  • System-wide limits are rarely the cause on modern kernels: /proc/sys/fs/file-nr shows allocated handles against fs.file-max, and fs.nr_open (default 1048576) caps how high any process's limit can be raised.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Symptom Start with Then Everything is slow uptime, vmstat 1 5 Follow the flowchart One API endpoint is slow Request logs with timings, curl -w Finding bottlenecks and query profiling The service keeps restarting systemctl status, journalctl -u ... -b Result oom-kill, exit codes, start limit "No space left on device" df -h, df -i du, lsof +L1, journal and Docker cleanup Clients cannot connect ss -tulpn on the server, curl -v from the client Firewall and security group rules, DNS Intermittent timeouts to an external service curl -w timings, dig, mtr -T Retries and timeouts in the app

Host tools show the present moment. For "why was it slow at 03:00 yesterday", you need metrics collected over time (node exporter, CloudWatch, or similar), as described in metrics and dashboards, and sar's own history once the sysstat collector is enabled.

docs.title: A one-minute snapshot script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/sbin/snapshot: capture the server's state to a file before changing anything
set -u
out="/var/tmp/snapshot-$(hostname)-$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt"
{
  echo "== uptime";         uptime
  echo "== dmesg (tail)";   dmesg -T | tail -n 25
  echo "== vmstat 1 5";     vmstat 1 5
  echo "== mpstat";         mpstat -P ALL 1 3
  echo "== pidstat";        pidstat 1 3
  echo "== iostat";         iostat -xz 1 3
  echo "== free";           free -h
  echo "== pressure";       grep -H . /proc/pressure/* 2>/dev/null
  echo "== df";             df -hT -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs; df -i -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs
  echo "== sockets";        ss -s; ss -tulpn
  echo "== top";            top -b -n 1 | head -n 25
  echo "== failed units";   systemctl --failed --no-pager
} > "$out" 2>&1
echo "saved $out"

Run it with sudo as the first thing in an incident and attach the file to the incident record. /var/tmp survives reboots, unlike /tmp on Ubuntu 26.04.

docs.title: Reading vmstat
docs.text:
vmstat 1 5

Example output on a 2-vCPU server that is waiting on its disk:

procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ---------cpu---------
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st gu
 1  0      0 312840  61200 2398112    0    0    35   220  410  690  4  2 93  1  0  0
 0  6      0 309112  61204 2398530    0    0 18432  9210 1890 2410  3  4 12 81  0  0
 1  5      0 306904  61210 2399010    0    0 17920  8800 1822 2302  5  3 10 82  0  0
 0  7      0 305760  61212 2399420    0    0 19104  9312 1950 2501  2  4  9 85  0  0
 2  6      0 304120  61218 2399808    0    0 18560  9001 1875 2390  4  3 11 82  0  0

Ignore the first line (averages since boot). Then: b 5 to 7 tasks blocked, wa above 80%, heavy bi/bo, and si/so at zero. The disk is the bottleneck, not CPU or memory; iostat -xz 1 and pidstat -d 1 (I/O per process) show which device and which process.

docs.title: Confirming an OOM kill
docs.text:
# Kernel messages about OOM kills today (the journal keeps them across reboots)
journalctl -k --since today -g 'Out of memory|oom-kill|invoked oom-killer'

# Did systemd see it for this unit, and how often has it restarted?
systemctl show taskflow-api@3001 -p Result -p NRestarts

Example output:

Nov 13 07:41:07 taskflow-app-1 kernel: node invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0xcc0(GFP_KERNEL), order=0, oom_score_adj=0
Nov 13 07:41:08 taskflow-app-1 kernel: Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process 4123 (node) total-vm:22941268kB, anon-rss:705312kB, file-rss:51200kB, shmem-rss:0kB, UID:998 pgtables:3104kB oom_score_adj:0
Result=oom-kill
NRestarts=3

"Memory cgroup out of memory" and Result=oom-kill mean the instance hit its own MemoryMax=; the machine as a whole was fine. A large total-vm is normal for V8 (reserved address space); anon-rss is the memory it actually used.

docs.title: Finding what fills the disk
docs.text:
df -hT -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs          # which file system is full
df -i -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs           # or out of inodes?
sudo du -xh -d1 / 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 10
sudo du -xh -d1 /var 2>/dev/null | sort -h | tail -n 10

# The usual suspects
sudo journalctl --disk-usage
sudo ls -lt /var/lib/systemd/coredump/ 2>/dev/null | head
ls -1t /srv/taskflow/releases/ | wc -l
docker system df 2>/dev/null

# Deleted files still held open
sudo lsof +L1

Example output of lsof +L1:

COMMAND  PID     USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE   SIZE/OFF NLINK    NODE NAME
node    4123 taskflow    3w   REG  259,1 8804682752     0    4711 /var/log/taskflow/api.log (deleted)

# Free the space now, without restarting: truncate the deleted file through the open descriptor
sudo truncate -s 0 /proc/4123/fd/3

# Then fix the cause: log to stdout and let journald or logrotate handle files

NLINK 0 means no directory entry points at the file any more; FD 3w is descriptor 3, open for writing. After truncation df shows the space again, and the process keeps writing at its current offset, so the file may later look sparse; restarting the process is the clean end state.

docs.title: Who is listening, and who is connected
docs.text:
# Listening sockets with their processes
sudo ss -tulpn

# Socket counts by state, and established connections to MongoDB
ss -s
ss -tn state established '( dport = :27017 )'

# Connections the app has not closed (a growing count is a leak)
ss -tn state close-wait | wc -l

Example output of ss -tulpn (IPv6 listeners trimmed):

Netid State  Recv-Q Send-Q Local Address:Port  Peer Address:Port Process
udp   UNCONN 0      0         127.0.0.54:53         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=612,fd=16))
udp   UNCONN 0      0      127.0.0.53%lo:53         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("systemd-resolve",pid=612,fd=14))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511          0.0.0.0:443        0.0.0.0:*     users:(("nginx",pid=1180,fd=8),("nginx",pid=1179,fd=8))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511          0.0.0.0:80         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("nginx",pid=1180,fd=6),("nginx",pid=1179,fd=6))
tcp   LISTEN 0      4096         0.0.0.0:22         0.0.0.0:*     users:(("sshd",pid=938,fd=3),("systemd",pid=1,fd=86))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511        127.0.0.1:3001       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("node",pid=41873,fd=21))
tcp   LISTEN 0      511        127.0.0.1:3002       0.0.0.0:*     users:(("node",pid=41902,fd=21))

The app listens only on loopback, nginx on all interfaces, and port 22 is held by systemd itself (socket activation) as well as sshd. For listening sockets, Send-Q shows the backlog limit and Recv-Q the number of connections waiting to be accepted; a Recv-Q near the limit means the process is not accepting fast enough.

docs.title: Timing an HTTPS request
docs.text:
# curl-format.txt: one line per phase, cumulative seconds since the request started
   namelookup: %{time_namelookup}\n
      connect: %{time_connect}\n
   appconnect: %{time_appconnect}\n
starttransfer: %{time_starttransfer}\n
        total: %{time_total}\n
         code: %{http_code}  remote: %{remote_ip}\n

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "@curl-format.txt" https://api.example.com/tasks

# Bypass DNS to test one specific server behind the name
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "@curl-format.txt" --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 \
    https://api.example.com/tasks

# Every step of the conversation: DNS answer, TCP, TLS certificate, request and response headers
curl -v https://api.example.com/readyz

Example output of the first command:

   namelookup: 0.012021
      connect: 0.048113
   appconnect: 0.084220
starttransfer: 0.312456
        total: 0.320030
         code: 200  remote: 203.0.113.10

DNS took 12 ms, TCP 36 ms, TLS 36 ms, and the server about 190 ms after subtracting one round trip for the request itself. --resolve pins the name to an address, which tests one server behind a load balancer and rules DNS out of the measurement.

docs.title: DNS checks
docs.text:
# What the system resolver returns, and which upstream servers it uses
resolvectl query api.example.com
resolvectl status | grep -E 'Current DNS Server|DNS Servers'

# Ask specific resolvers directly and compare
dig +short api.example.com A
dig +short @1.1.1.1 api.example.com A
dig +noall +answer api.example.com A     # includes the remaining TTL

# Follow delegation from the root servers (useful right after DNS changes)
dig +trace api.example.com

If the stub and a public resolver disagree right after a change, cached answers have not expired yet; the TTL in +noall +answer output tells you for how much longer. DNS changes and migrations are covered in DNS migrations and troubleshooting.

docs.title: Path checks with mtr
docs.text:
# 50 cycles, wide report, no DNS lookups for hop names
mtr -rwc 50 -n mongo.internal.example.com

# TCP SYN probes to port 443, for paths that drop ICMP
mtr -rwc 50 -T -P 443 api.example.com

Example output:

HOST: taskflow-app-1         Loss%   Snt   Last   Avg  Best  Wrst StDev
  1.|-- 10.0.2.1              0.0%    50    0.3   0.3   0.2   0.6   0.1
  2.|-- 198.51.100.1         40.0%    50    1.1   1.2   0.9   2.0   0.2
  3.|-- 198.51.100.33         0.0%    50    1.4   1.5   1.2   2.3   0.2
  4.|-- 203.0.113.10          0.0%    50    1.8   1.9   1.6   2.6   0.2

The 40% loss at hop 2 does not continue to hops 3 and 4, so it is that router limiting its own replies, not packet loss on the path.

docs.title: Checking file descriptor limits and usage
docs.text:
pid=$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value taskflow-api@3001)

grep 'open files' /proc/$pid/limits      # soft and hard limit for this process
sudo ls /proc/$pid/fd | wc -l            # descriptors in use right now
cat /proc/sys/fs/file-nr                 # system-wide: allocated, unused, maximum

# What kinds of descriptors? (sockets, regular files, pipes)
sudo lsof -p "$pid" | awk 'NR > 1 { print $5 }' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Example output of the first two commands:

Max open files            65536                65536                files
1873

If the count climbs steadily between samples while traffic is flat, something is leaking; ss -tnp | grep "pid=$pid" shows whether the descriptors are sockets and to where.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Capture a snapshot before restarting or resizing anything.
  • Read the kernel log and vmstat first; they rule whole resources in or out.
  • Compare load with the CPU count, and always look at the CPU split (us, sy, wa, st) and per-core usage.
  • Judge memory by available, swap activity, and OOM messages, never by free.
  • Alert on disk usage and inode usage well before 100%, and keep logs bounded (journald limits, logrotate, Docker log options).
  • Never delete a log file a process has open; rotate it or truncate it.
  • Time network requests by phase with curl -w before blaming "the network".
  • Treat a steadily growing descriptor count as a leak, not a limit problem.
  • Install sysstat and a metrics agent before you need them; history answers questions that a live view cannot.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Load average of 12 on a 4-vCPU server, but CPU is mostly idle. Detect: vmstat shows high wa, non-zero b; iostat -xz shows w_await in the hundreds of milliseconds. Cause: the volume hit its IOPS or throughput limit, often during a backup or log burst. Fix: find the process with pidstat -d 1, move heavy jobs off peak, or provision a faster volume.
  • The API is slow while the server shows 13% CPU. Detect: top shows one node process at about 100%; mpstat -P ALL shows one core pegged. Cause: the single JavaScript thread of one instance is saturated (a synchronous loop, JSON parsing of a huge payload, or simply too little capacity). Fix: profile it, move CPU work to worker threads, and run one instance per core.
  • An instance dies every few hours. Detect: Result=oom-kill and "Memory cgroup out of memory" in journalctl -k. Cause: the process grows until it reaches MemoryMax=, usually a leak. Fix: keep the limit (it protects the rest of the server), take heap snapshots, and fix the leak.
  • "No space left on device", but du finds only a few gigabytes. Detect: df -h shows 100% used; lsof +L1 lists a large deleted file. Cause: someone deleted a log the app still had open. Fix: truncate it through /proc/<pid>/fd/<n> or restart the process, then use proper log rotation.
  • "No space left on device" with plenty of free space. Detect: df -i shows 100% inode use. Cause: millions of small files, such as a cache directory nobody prunes. Fix: delete the files (or the directory), and add expiry to whatever creates them.
  • Requests to an external API intermittently take 5 seconds longer. Detect: curl -w shows namelookup near 5 s on some runs. Cause: one configured DNS server times out and the resolver waits before trying the next. Fix: check resolvectl status, remove or fix the bad server, and give app HTTP clients sensible timeouts.
  • Users get intermittent "connection reset" errors and the app logs EMFILE. Detect: the descriptor count in /proc/<pid>/fd is at the limit; ss -tn state close-wait shows thousands of sockets. Cause: the app leaks sockets that peers already closed. Fix: find the code path that never closes (often an HTTP client without timeouts), and only then consider raising LimitNOFILE=.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Load average: Exponentially damped averages of runnable plus uninterruptible tasks over 1, 5, and 15 minutes.
  • Uninterruptible sleep (D state): A task waiting in the kernel, usually for I/O, that cannot be interrupted by signals.
  • iowait (wa): CPU time spent idle while I/O is outstanding.
  • Steal time (st): Time the hypervisor gave your vCPU's turn to someone else.
  • Page cache: File data cached in RAM; reclaimable when memory is needed.
  • Available memory: The kernel's estimate of memory usable for new work without swapping.
  • OOM killer: The kernel mechanism that kills a process when memory cannot be reclaimed; global or per cgroup.
  • Inode: The file system object that holds a file's metadata and data blocks; names are directory entries pointing to it.
  • File descriptor: A process's handle to an open file, socket, or pipe.
  • CLOSE-WAIT: The TCP state of a socket whose peer has closed while the local application has not.
  • PSI (pressure stall information): Kernel counters of time lost to CPU, memory, and I/O contention.
  • USE method: Checking utilization, saturation, and errors for every resource.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Reading load average as CPU usage, or comparing it without knowing the CPU count.
  • Panicking at a small free number while available is large.
  • Restarting the app first and losing the evidence.
  • Deleting a large log file to free space while the writer is running.
  • Raising LimitNOFILE to hide a descriptor leak.
  • Trusting %util on SSDs and cloud volumes as a saturation measure.
  • Treating loss at a single intermediate mtr hop as packet loss.
  • Running ulimit -n in a shell and assuming a service has the same limit.
  • Blaming the network without measuring DNS, TCP, TLS, and server time separately.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why can a server with a load average of 8 on 4 CPUs have mostly idle CPUs, and which two numbers in vmstat prove it?
  2. free -h shows 0.2 GiB free and 2.6 GiB available on a 4 GiB server. Is it short of memory? What would make you say yes?
  3. What is the difference between "Out of memory: Killed process" and "Memory cgroup out of memory: Killed process", and what does each tell you to fix?
  4. df reports 97% used but du adds up to 30%. Give the most likely cause, the command that proves it, and two ways to release the space.
  5. curl -w shows namelookup 0.004, connect 0.110, appconnect 0.215, starttransfer 0.330, total 0.335. How long did each phase take, and where would you look first? (DNS 4 ms; TCP 106 ms; TLS 105 ms; first byte 115 ms after TLS; transfer 5 ms. TCP and TLS each cost about one round trip of roughly 105 ms, so the client is far from the server; the server's own time is small. Look at geography: a CDN or a closer region, not the app.)
  6. Why does a Node.js service rarely hit the 1024 soft file limit under systemd, while nginx can?
  7. In mtr, hop 3 shows 30% loss and hops 4 to 8 show 0%. Is there packet loss on the path?
  8. What does a growing number of CLOSE-WAIT sockets tell you about the application?
