docs.title: Autoscaling Server Fleets
docs.text:
The previous lesson spread the TaskFlow API across Availability Zones and regions (multi-AZ and multi-region architecture). This one makes each of those fleets size itself. An autoscaling group keeps a set of identical virtual machines running from a template, replaces the ones that fail their health checks, and adds or removes instances as load changes, so you pay for roughly the capacity you need instead of the peak, all day.

This lesson covers the three big implementations (AWS Auto Scaling groups, Google Cloud managed instance groups, and Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets), launch templates built on immutable machine images, the scaling policies (target tracking, step, scheduled, and predictive), how to choose the metric, why new capacity always arrives late and how warmup, warm pools, and headroom deal with it, lifecycle hooks, scale-in protection, and draining before termination, how fleet autoscaling relates to Kubernetes, and the cost guards that stop a scaling policy from running up a bill.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Traffic is rarely flat. A business application peaks during office hours and sleeps at night; a consumer app peaks in the evening; a shop peaks during a sale. A fleet sized for the peak wastes most of its money off peak, and a fleet sized for the average falls over at the peak. Autoscaling also gives you two things beyond cost: self-healing (failed instances are replaced automatically) and a safe way to roll out new machine images by replacing instances gradually.

It is also easy to get wrong in ways that only show up under load: scaling on a metric that does not track load, capacity that arrives ten minutes after the spike that needed it, scale-in that kills requests in flight, or a scale-out triggered by a retry storm that launches hundreds of instances and still does not help because the database is the real bottleneck.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix. The post Scryer: Netflix's Predictive Auto Scaling Engine (2013) explains why reactive autoscaling was not enough for Netflix: instance startup then took 10 to 45 minutes, leaving existing servers exposed during a rapid spike, and an outage that suddenly dropped traffic could make reactive policies scale in just before the traffic came back. Because daily and weekly patterns repeat, Netflix predicted demand and provisioned ahead of it.
  • Amazon Builders' Library. The article Static stability using Availability Zones argues that a service should be overprovisioned so it keeps working without launching any new instances if an Availability Zone becomes impaired, because reacting to an impairment depends on a control plane that may itself be affected.
  • AWS. The predictive scaling documentation describes forecasting from up to 14 days of history (after at least 24 hours of data), an hourly forecast for the next 48 hours refreshed every 6 hours, and a forecast-only mode to check accuracy before letting it scale.
  • Google Cloud. The managed instance group autoscaler documentation describes an initialization period during which new VMs' usage is ignored for scale-out decisions, and a stabilization period (10 minutes by default) during which the autoscaler keeps enough capacity for the peak it has just seen before deleting VMs.

Popular tools and providers: AWS EC2 Auto Scaling, Google Cloud managed instance groups, Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets, Packer and image pipelines for golden images, Terraform and other IaC tools, Spot and preemptible capacity, and Kubernetes node autoscalers (Cluster Autoscaler, Karpenter) built on the same groups.

docs.title: The building blocks
docs.text:
An autoscaling fleet has four parts:

  1. A template that says what to launch: the machine image, instance type, network and security groups, IAM role or service account, and a small user-data script.
  2. A group with a minimum, maximum, and desired size, spread over subnets in several Availability Zones, that launches instances from the template until the actual count matches the desired count.
  3. Health checks that decide when an instance is broken and must be replaced, ideally using the load balancer's application-level check rather than only "the VM is running".
  4. Scaling policies that change the desired size from metrics, schedules, or forecasts.

The same ideas have different names on each cloud:

Concept AWS Google Cloud Azure Fleet Auto Scaling group Managed instance group (zonal or regional) Virtual Machine Scale Set (Flexible orchestration recommended) Template Launch template (versioned) Instance template Scale set VM profile Replace unhealthy instances EC2 and ELB health checks Autohealing with a health check Automatic instance repairs Roll out a new template Instance refresh Rolling update (max surge, max unavailable) Rolling upgrades Pre-initialized capacity Warm pools (stopped, hibernated, or running) Standby pools of suspended or stopped VMs Standby pools (Flexible orchestration only) Predictive scaling Predictive scaling policies Predictive autoscaling (CPU only) Predictive autoscale (CPU only)

docs.title: Immutable images and launch templates
docs.text:
The faster and more predictable an instance's boot, the better autoscaling works. Teams therefore bake everything into a golden machine image (the OS patches, the runtime, the agents, and the application build) with a tool such as Packer, and keep user data to a few lines of environment-specific configuration. Installing packages at boot makes every launch slower and makes the fleet depend on package mirrors being reachable during an incident. Building images is covered in immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

A release then becomes: build image, create a new launch template version, and replace instances gradually. On AWS, an instance refresh does the replacement in batches controlled by a minimum and maximum healthy percentage (for example 90% and 110%: replace about 10% of the fleet at a time, launching before terminating), with optional checkpoints, a bake time, skip matching (leave instances already on the new configuration alone), and automatic rollback when CloudWatch alarms fire.

docs.title: Scaling policies
docs.text:
Policy How it decides Good for Target tracking Keeps a metric near a target value, like a thermostat; the provider creates and manages the alarms The default for most web fleets Step scaling Adds or removes a fixed or percentage amount per alarm breach band Precise control, such as adding more instances the further a metric overshoots Scheduled Changes min, max, or desired size at set times Known patterns: office hours, a planned sale, nightly batch windows Predictive Forecasts load from history and launches capacity ahead of it Strong daily or weekly cycles combined with slow boots

Policies combine. A common production setup is target tracking for the unexpected, plus scheduled or predictive scaling to have capacity ready before the expected morning ramp. When several policies are active, the group follows whichever asks for the most capacity, so the extra policies only ever add safety.

Two provider details matter. AWS target tracking scales in more gradually than it scales out, to protect availability when traffic fluctuates. AWS predictive scaling in forecast-and-scale mode only ever adds capacity; scale-in still needs a dynamic policy. Google Cloud's and Azure's predictive options forecast CPU only.

docs.title: Target tracking with numbers
docs.text: Target tracking assumes the metric moves in proportion to the number of instances. If 10 instances each see 1,500 requests per minute and the target is 1,000, the group needs roughly 10 × 1,500 / 1,000 = 15 instances to bring each one back to 1,000. The provider rounds conservatively, so with small groups the metric may settle a little below the target rather than exactly on it.

docs.title: Choosing the metric
docs.text:
Metric Works when Watch out for Average CPU utilization The service is CPU-bound and instances are identical I/O-bound services sit at low CPU while queues build; mixed instance sizes skew the average Request count per target Web services where each request costs about the same Expensive and cheap requests mixed; it says nothing about response time Backlog per instance (queue depth ÷ instances) Queue workers Raw queue length is not proportional to fleet size; divide by instances Custom business metric You can publish a per-instance load measure It must rise and fall in proportion to fleet size Latency Never as the target tracking metric Latency does not fall in proportion to instances; use it for alarms instead Memory Rarely Garbage-collected runtimes keep memory high when idle

For queue workers, derive the target from what users will tolerate. If a message takes 2 seconds to process and a message may wait at most 10 minutes, one instance can own a backlog of 600 / 2 = 300 messages. With 15,000 messages waiting, the fleet needs 15,000 / 300 = 50 instances, and the target tracking metric is "messages per instance" with a target of 300.

docs.title: Why capacity arrives late: detection, boot, warmup
docs.text:
A reactive policy can only respond after the metric has been high for long enough to trust it, and then the instance still has to boot, start the application, and pass health checks. For several minutes the existing fleet carries the new load alone. The defenses, in order of cost:

  • Headroom. A target of 50% to 60% CPU instead of 80% means the fleet absorbs a large jump while new instances start.
  • Faster boot. Golden images, small user data, and lazy loading of rarely used data.
  • Warmup. A warmup period (AWS default instance warmup, Google Cloud's initialization period) keeps freshly launched instances' noisy start-up metrics out of the average, so the group does not overreact.
  • Warm pools and standby pools. Pre-initialized instances kept stopped or hibernated (you pay for their disks, not their compute), so a scale-out resumes them instead of building them from scratch.
  • Scheduled and predictive scaling. Capacity that is already running when the expected ramp starts; AWS can launch ahead of the forecast by a configurable buffer.

docs.title: The instance lifecycle: hooks, protection, and draining
docs.text:
• Lifecycle hooks pause an instance in a wait state at launch or at termination so your code can act: finish bootstrapping before it takes traffic, or upload logs and finish a job before it disappears. A hook waits up to its heartbeat timeout (one hour by default on AWS, with a 48-hour overall limit) until your code calls complete-lifecycle-action. An instance can read its target state from the instance metadata item autoscaling/target-lifecycle-state.
  • Scale-in protection removes specific instances from scale-in selection, for example a worker in the middle of a long job that sets protection when it takes the job and clears it when done.
  • Termination policies decide which instance goes first; the default first balances instances across Availability Zones.
  • Draining. Deregistration from the load balancer stops new requests while the target group's deregistration delay (300 seconds by default on an Application Load Balancer) lets requests in flight finish. Set it close to your longest normal request, not to the default, or every scale-in and rollout waits five minutes per batch. The application must still handle SIGTERM gracefully, as described for containers in health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: Health checks and self-healing
docs.text: By default AWS only replaces instances whose EC2 status checks fail: a VM that is running but whose application is hung stays in service. Setting the group's health check type to ELB makes it replace instances the load balancer considers unhealthy, using the same /readyz-style check that controls traffic. A health check grace period (or Google Cloud's autohealing initial delay) prevents the group from killing instances that are still booting. Be careful with health checks that depend on shared dependencies: if the database is down and every instance fails, the group replaces the whole fleet in a loop and makes recovery slower.

docs.title: Multiple zones and static stability
docs.text:
A group spread over three Availability Zones keeps roughly a third of its instances in each. If one zone fails, the group launches replacements in the others, but only if the control plane can launch them and there is capacity to launch into. The statically stable alternative is to run enough capacity that losing a zone does not require launching anything.

Worked example: the API needs 12 instances at peak. Spread over 3 zones that is 4 per zone; losing a zone leaves 8, a third short. Running 6 per zone (18 instances, 50% overprovisioning) means losing any zone still leaves 12. With 4 zones, 4 per zone (16 instances) leaves 12 after a loss: more zones make static stability cheaper.

docs.title: Spot capacity and mixed instance types
docs.text: Spot (AWS), Spot VMs (Google Cloud), and Azure Spot VMs are spare capacity at a discount that the provider can reclaim; AWS gives a two-minute interruption notice. A mixed instances policy keeps a base of On-Demand instances and fills the rest with Spot across several instance types, so one type running out does not stop scaling. Use Spot for stateless, interruption-tolerant capacity behind a load balancer, never for the minimum capacity you need to survive.

docs.title: Autoscaling with Kubernetes
docs.text: On Kubernetes, scaling happens at two layers. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler changes the number of Pods, and a node autoscaler (Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter) adds nodes when Pods cannot be scheduled, usually through the same cloud groups this page describes (managed node groups are Auto Scaling groups, GKE node pools are managed instance groups, AKS node pools are scale sets). The ideas carry over: target tracking becomes the HPA formula, warmup becomes readiness and startup probes, and draining becomes Pod termination. See scaling and resource management.

docs.title: Cost guards
docs.text:
Autoscaling spends money automatically, so put limits around it:

  • A maximum size you would be willing to pay for and that downstream systems (database connections, third-party rate limits) can survive.
  • Alarms on group size and on scaling activity, and a budget alert.
  • Care with automatic maximum increases (AWS predictive scaling can raise the maximum when the forecast approaches it).
  • Scale on the bottleneck. If the database is saturated, adding API instances adds connections and makes it worse; fix or scale the database first.
  • Scale-in. A fleet that never scales in (a missing scale-in policy, or a metric that never falls) quietly costs as much as a fixed peak fleet.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Workload Approach Steady, predictable load A fixed-size group (min = max) for self-healing only Web API with daily cycles and boots under a few minutes Target tracking on request count or CPU, plus a scheduled minimum before the morning ramp Strong weekly patterns and slow boots Predictive scaling (start in forecast-only mode) plus target tracking Very slow boots (large caches, JIT warmup) Warm or standby pools, plus a lower target Queue workers Target tracking on backlog per instance, scale-in protection for long jobs Stateful nodes (databases, brokers) Do not autoscale on load; scale deliberately Containers already on Kubernetes HPA plus a node autoscaler Spiky, small workloads Serverless platforms that scale per request may be simpler

Do not autoscale to hide a bug (a memory leak "fixed" by replacing instances), do not let scaling policies fight manual changes, and do not use autoscaling for components whose state lives on the instance.

docs.title: A TaskFlow API fleet in Terraform
docs.text:
# infra/api-fleet.tf: launch template, group, warm pool, and draining hook
resource "aws_launch_template" "api" {
  name_prefix   = "taskflow-api-"
  image_id      = var.api_ami_id            # golden image built by Packer
  instance_type = "c7g.large"
  vpc_security_group_ids = [aws_security_group.api.id]

  iam_instance_profile {
    name = aws_iam_instance_profile.api.name
  }

  metadata_options {
    http_tokens = "required"                # IMDSv2 only
  }

  user_data = base64encode(templatefile("${path.module}/api-user-data.sh", {
    environment = var.environment
  }))
}

resource "aws_autoscaling_group" "api" {
  name_prefix               = "taskflow-api-"
  min_size                  = 6
  max_size                  = 40
  vpc_zone_identifier       = var.private_subnet_ids   # three AZs
  target_group_arns         = [aws_lb_target_group.api.arn]
  health_check_type         = "ELB"
  health_check_grace_period = 120
  default_instance_warmup   = 180

  launch_template {
    id      = aws_launch_template.api.id
    version = aws_launch_template.api.latest_version
  }

  # Replace ~10% at a time, launching before terminating; roll back on alarms
  instance_refresh {
    strategy = "Rolling"
    preferences {
      min_healthy_percentage = 90
      max_healthy_percentage = 110
      skip_matching          = true
      auto_rollback          = true
      alarm_specification {
        alarms = [aws_cloudwatch_metric_alarm.api_5xx.alarm_name]
      }
    }
  }

  warm_pool {
    pool_state                  = "Stopped"
    min_size                    = 4
    max_group_prepared_capacity = 12
    instance_reuse_policy {
      reuse_on_scale_in = true
    }
  }

  initial_lifecycle_hook {
    name                 = "drain"
    lifecycle_transition = "autoscaling:EC2_INSTANCE_TERMINATING"
    heartbeat_timeout    = 300
    default_result       = "CONTINUE"
  }

  lifecycle {
    ignore_changes = [desired_capacity]     # owned by the scaling policies
  }
}

Key choices: the ELB health check replaces instances whose application is broken, not just their VM; the warmup keeps new instances out of the averages for three minutes; any change to the launch template starts an instance refresh that rolls back if the 5xx alarm fires; four stopped instances wait in the warm pool; and the termination hook gives each instance up to five minutes to drain.

docs.title: Scaling policies: target tracking, schedule, and forecast
docs.text:
# infra/api-scaling.tf
resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "requests_per_target" {
  name                   = "requests-per-target"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.api.name
  policy_type            = "TargetTrackingScaling"

  target_tracking_configuration {
    predefined_metric_specification {
      predefined_metric_type = "ALBRequestCountPerTarget"
      resource_label         = "${aws_lb.public.arn_suffix}/${aws_lb_target_group.api.arn_suffix}"
    }
    target_value = 1000
  }
}

# Raise the floor before the weekday morning ramp, lower it in the evening.
# -1 means "leave unchanged"; the provider defaults these fields to 0.
resource "aws_autoscaling_schedule" "weekday_morning" {
  scheduled_action_name  = "weekday-morning"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.api.name
  recurrence             = "30 7 * * MON-FRI"
  time_zone              = "Europe/Berlin"
  min_size               = 12
  max_size               = -1
  desired_capacity       = -1
}

resource "aws_autoscaling_schedule" "weekday_evening" {
  scheduled_action_name  = "weekday-evening"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.api.name
  recurrence             = "0 20 * * MON-FRI"
  time_zone              = "Europe/Berlin"
  min_size               = 6
  max_size               = -1
  desired_capacity       = -1
}

# Learn the weekly pattern first; switch mode to "ForecastAndScale" once the
# forecast matches reality.
resource "aws_autoscaling_policy" "predictive_cpu" {
  name                   = "predictive-cpu"
  autoscaling_group_name = aws_autoscaling_group.api.name
  policy_type            = "PredictiveScaling"

  predictive_scaling_configuration {
    mode                   = "ForecastOnly"
    scheduling_buffer_time = 300           # launch 5 minutes ahead of the forecast
    metric_specification {
      target_value = 50
      predefined_metric_pair_specification {
        predefined_metric_type = "ASGCPUUtilization"
      }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Draining on termination from inside the instance
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# /usr/local/bin/asg-drain-watcher.sh: run every 5 s by a systemd timer
set -euo pipefail

IMDS=http://169.254.169.254
token=$(curl -sf -X PUT "$IMDS/latest/api/token" \
  -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token-ttl-seconds: 60")
md() { curl -sf -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $token" "$IMDS/latest/meta-data/$1"; }

state=$(md autoscaling/target-lifecycle-state || echo "InService")
[ "$state" = "Terminated" ] || exit 0

instance_id=$(md instance-id)
region=$(md placement/region)

# The load balancer has stopped sending new requests. Stop the service:
# systemd sends SIGTERM, and the API finishes in-flight work and exits.
systemctl stop taskflow-api
/usr/local/bin/flush-logs-and-metrics.sh

aws autoscaling complete-lifecycle-action \
  --region "$region" \
  --auto-scaling-group-name taskflow-api \
  --lifecycle-hook-name drain \
  --instance-id "$instance_id" \
  --lifecycle-action-result CONTINUE

The instance role needs permission for autoscaling:CompleteLifecycleAction on its own group. If the script fails, the hook's default_result continues termination when the heartbeat timeout expires, so a broken script delays but never blocks scale-in.

docs.title: The same fleet on Google Cloud and Azure
docs.text:
# Google Cloud: a regional MIG with autohealing and a CPU autoscaler
gcloud compute instance-groups managed create taskflow-api \
  --region=europe-west1 --template=taskflow-api-v7 --size=6 \
  --health-check=taskflow-api-readyz --initial-delay=120

gcloud compute instance-groups managed set-autoscaling taskflow-api \
  --region=europe-west1 --min-num-replicas=6 --max-num-replicas=40 \
  --target-cpu-utilization=0.6 --cool-down-period=120

# Azure: a Flexible scale set and a CPU autoscale rule pair
az vmss create --resource-group taskflow --name taskflow-api \
  --orchestration-mode Flexible --image <image-id> --instance-count 6 \
  --zones 1 2 3
az monitor autoscale create --resource-group taskflow \
  --resource taskflow-api --resource-type Microsoft.Compute/virtualMachineScaleSets \
  --name taskflow-api-autoscale --min-count 6 --max-count 40 --count 6
az monitor autoscale rule create --resource-group taskflow \
  --autoscale-name taskflow-api-autoscale \
  --condition "Percentage CPU > 60 avg 5m" --scale out 3
az monitor autoscale rule create --resource-group taskflow \
  --autoscale-name taskflow-api-autoscale \
  --condition "Percentage CPU < 30 avg 10m" --scale in 1

On Google Cloud the --cool-down-period flag sets the initialization period. On Azure, metric rules come in pairs, and the scale-in rule uses a lower threshold and a longer window than the scale-out rule so the two cannot chase each other.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Bake golden images and keep boot under a few minutes; measure it.
  • Spread every group over at least three Availability Zones, and size it so losing a zone does not require launching anything.
  • Use the load balancer's health check for replacement, with a grace period longer than boot.
  • Scale on a metric that falls in proportion to fleet size; keep latency for alarms.
  • Leave headroom in the target, and add scheduled or predictive scaling for known ramps.
  • Set warmup so new instances do not distort the averages.
  • Drain before termination: a deregistration delay that matches your longest requests, a termination hook, and graceful SIGTERM handling.
  • Roll out images with instance refresh or rolling updates, with alarms that stop and roll back.
  • Cap maximum size, alarm on fleet size, and scale the real bottleneck.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Latency spikes every weekday morning before the fleet catches up. Detect: p99 latency and CPU climb from 08:00, and scaling activity shows instances launching after the peak has started. Cause: reactive scaling plus a multi-minute boot cannot follow a steep, predictable ramp. Fix: raise the minimum with a scheduled action before the ramp, try predictive scaling in forecast-only mode, and lower the target.
  • The fleet oscillates: scale out, scale in, scale out. Detect: the activity history shows launches and terminations every few minutes. Cause: new instances' start-up CPU distorts the average (no warmup), or step and target tracking policies with overlapping thresholds fight each other. Fix: set a default warmup, keep scale-in slower than scale-out, and use one primary policy.
  • Every scale-in produces a burst of 502 errors. Detect: load balancer 5xx errors coincide with terminations. Cause: instances are terminated while requests are in flight: a deregistration delay of zero, no termination hook, or an app that exits immediately on SIGTERM. Fix: a delay that covers the longest normal request, a draining hook, and graceful shutdown in the application.
  • A broken application stays in service for hours. Detect: the load balancer marks targets unhealthy, but the group never replaces them. Cause: the group uses only EC2 status checks. Fix: switch the health check type to ELB with a sensible grace period.
  • A traffic spike launched 200 instances and the site still failed. Detect: the group hit its maximum while database CPU and connection counts were saturated. Cause: the bottleneck was the database, and each new instance opened more connections. Fix: a lower maximum, connection pooling or a proxy, load shedding at the edge, and scaling decisions based on the real bottleneck.
  • A new image rolled out and half the fleet failed to boot. Detect: an instance refresh stalls with new instances failing health checks. Cause: a broken image or user-data change. Fix: checkpoints, alarm-based automatic rollback, and testing new images in staging with the same refresh settings.
  • Scale-out silently stops in one zone. Detect: activity history shows "insufficient capacity" errors for one instance type. Cause: the provider has no spare capacity of that type in that zone. Fix: allow several instance types (a mixed instances policy) and keep static-stability headroom.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Autoscaling group: A set of identical instances kept between a minimum and maximum size from a template.
  • Launch template / instance template: The versioned definition of what each instance runs.
  • Golden image: A pre-baked machine image containing the OS, runtime, agents, and application.
  • Desired capacity: The instance count the group is currently working toward.
  • Target tracking: A policy that keeps a metric near a target value.
  • Step / scheduled / predictive scaling: Scaling by alarm bands, by time, or by forecast.
  • Warmup / initialization period: Time during which a new instance's metrics are ignored or not trusted.
  • Warm pool / standby pool: Pre-initialized stopped, hibernated, or suspended instances ready for fast scale-out.
  • Lifecycle hook: A pause at launch or termination for custom actions.
  • Scale-in protection: A flag that keeps an instance from being chosen for scale-in.
  • Deregistration delay: How long a load balancer lets in-flight requests finish on a deregistering target.
  • Instance refresh / rolling update: Gradual replacement of instances with a new template.
  • Static stability: Surviving an impairment without needing to make changes, such as launching instances.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Scaling on latency or raw queue length with target tracking.
  • Assuming new capacity arrives within seconds of a spike.
  • Installing software at boot instead of baking an image.
  • Leaving the health check type at EC2 status checks only.
  • Terminating instances without draining.
  • Setting no maximum, or a maximum the database cannot survive.
  • Relying on launching replacements during a zone failure instead of pre-provisioned headroom.
  • Running the minimum capacity on Spot instances.
  • Treating autoscaling as a fix for leaks and crashes.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are the four building blocks of an autoscaling fleet, and what is each called on AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure?
  2. A target tracking policy targets 1,000 requests per target per minute. Eight instances receive 14,000 requests per minute. About how many instances does the group need, and why does the metric have to be proportional to the fleet size?
  3. A worker takes 4 seconds per message, and messages may wait at most 5 minutes. What target backlog per instance would you choose, and how many instances does a backlog of 9,000 messages need?
  4. Walk through the minutes between a traffic spike and new instances taking traffic. Name four ways to shorten or hide that gap.
  5. How do a deregistration delay, a termination lifecycle hook, and graceful SIGTERM handling work together during scale-in?
  6. Why should a group use the load balancer's health check, and what can go wrong if that check depends on the database?
  7. Your API needs 18 instances at peak across 3 zones. How many must you run to stay statically stable through the loss of one zone? How many with 4 zones?
  8. Which cost guards would you put around an autoscaling group, and why can scaling out make a database bottleneck worse?

docs.title: Load Balancing and Multi-Server Architecture Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the load balancing and multi-server lessons, for use before an interview or a scaling task.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does nginx -t Test the Nginx configuration before a reload aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "<arn>" Target states: initial, healthy, unhealthy, draining, unused aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes --target-group-arn "<arn>" --attributes Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=30 Drain for 30 s instead of 300 s aws arc-zonal-shift start-zonal-shift --resource-identifier "<load-balancer-arn>" --away-from use1-az2 --expires-in 2h --comment "drain" Move load balancer traffic away from one zone dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com @1.1.1.1 One resolver's answer and its remaining TTL

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-api.conf (excerpt)
upstream taskflow_api {
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.1.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;  # passive checks
    server 10.0.2.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
    keepalive 32;
}

server {
    listen 80;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503;
        proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;  # one retry, never for a sent POST
    }
}

# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg (excerpt)
backend taskflow_api
    balance leastconn
    option httpchk
    http-check send meth GET uri /readyz
    default-server inter 2s fall 3 rise 2 slowstart 30s
    server api1 10.0.1.11:3000 check

// src/server.js (excerpt): behind exactly one load balancer
app.set("trust proxy", 1);         // req.ip: the address the balancer saw
const server = app.listen(3000);
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65_000;  // above the ALB's 60 s idle timeout

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why A public HTTP API A managed L7 balancer, least outstanding requests Per-request balancing, TLS, retries TCP or UDP, static IPs A managed L4 balancer with PROXY protocol v2 Any protocol, high throughput gRPC between services An L7 proxy, a mesh, or client-side round_robin L4 pins each HTTP/2 connection to one pod A cache tier Consistent hashing Adding a node moves about 1/N of keys Many independent balancers Power of two choices No herd behavior Sessions on many instances A shared Redis store or short-lived tokens Any instance serves any request A cron job on many instances A per-run claim, one scheduler, or a queue Runs once, not once per instance A production baseline Three zones, sized so two carry peak A lost zone needs no scaling Regional failover in seconds Anycast or a global L7 proxy No DNS caches to wait out Users on several continents A home region per user or tenant Local writes, no conflicts A flaky dependency Timeouts, retries at one layer with jitter, a breaker Fails fast without a retry storm

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value ALB health checks 30 s interval; out after 2 failures (~60 s), back after 5 passes (~150 s) ALB deregistration delay 300 s by default (0 to 3,600) ALB slow start 30 to 900 s; not with least outstanding requests Idle timeouts ALB 60 s; Nginx proxy_read_timeout 60 s; Node keep-alive 5 s Fail open ALB and NLB use every target when none is healthy Route 53 checks 10 s x 3 = ~30 s to detect; healthy above 18% of checkers CloudFront failover 3 attempts x 10 s = up to 30 s; GET, HEAD, OPTIONS only Light in fiber ~200 km per ms; Sydney to Virginia: 157 ms round trip or more Zone capacity Peak x N / (N - 1): 200% with 2 zones, 150% with 3 After losing k of N Utilization x N / (N - k): 3 at 60%, lose 1: 90% Database connections Instances x processes x maxPoolSize (MongoDB: 100) 4 to 5 servers Modulo hashing moves 80% of keys; consistent hashing ~20% Async RPO Lag x write rate: 2 s x 500/s = 1,000 writes Target tracking Current x metric / target: 10 x 1,500 / 1,000 = 15 AWS lifecycle hook 1 h heartbeat by default, 48 h limit Eureka Renew every 30 s; removed after 90 s without one Retries 3 tries at 5 layers: 3^5 = 243 calls; budget ~10%

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Keeping state on the instance. Move sessions, uploads, cron jobs, socket rooms, and counters off it before adding a second instance.
  • Health-checking a shared dependency. Check local readiness; when every target fails, balancers and Route 53 stop protecting you.
  • Keeping the 300 s deregistration delay. Set it just above the longest normal request, and drain on SIGTERM.
  • A keep-alive shorter than the balancer's idle timeout. Raise it above the balancer's, or reused connections end in 502s.
  • Retrying at every layer. Retry at one layer, idempotent requests only, with full jitter and a budget.
  • Trusting the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry. Trust only your own proxy hops.
  • Expecting DNS failover within one TTL. Lower TTLs in advance, recycle connections, or use anycast or a global proxy.

docs.title: From One Server to Many
docs.text:
Almost every service starts on one machine: Nginx, a Node.js API, a database, a folder of uploads, and a crontab, all on one VPS. That is the right choice at first. This lesson follows TaskFlow API from that single server to a multi-region deployment, one stage at a time, and shows what each stage fixes and what it breaks next. Most of what breaks is state hidden on the instance, so the second half of the lesson goes through each kind of state (sessions, uploads, in-process caches, scheduled jobs, WebSocket connections, counters) and where it has to live instead. It ends with the trade-off between scaling up and scaling out, with numbers.

The next lesson, load balancers in depth, covers the component that sits in front of every stage from the third one onwards.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Adding a second instance is the moment hidden assumptions surface. The code worked for a year because every request reached the same process: the session was in its memory, the uploaded avatar was on its disk, and the nightly email ran once because there was one crontab. With two instances behind a load balancer, users are logged out at random, avatars are missing half the time, and the nightly email goes out twice. None of this shows up in unit tests, and all of it shows up within minutes in production.

Knowing the stages also stops you from paying for the wrong one. A team with a slow query does not need a second region; a team whose only VM restarts during every deploy does not need Kubernetes first. Each stage costs money and adds failure modes, so the useful skill is recognizing which limit you have actually hit.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App. Factor VI, Processes, states that "twelve-factor processes are stateless and share-nothing", allows memory and the filesystem only as "a brief, single-transaction cache", says that sticky sessions "are a violation of twelve-factor and should never be used or relied upon", and recommends a datastore with time expiration, such as Memcached or Redis, for session state.
  • Express. The guide Production best practices: performance and reliability warns that separate app instances "do not share the same memory space", so "you cannot maintain state in the application code", recommends Redis for session data, and notes that this caveat "applies to essentially all forms of horizontal scaling". It also recommends running Express behind a reverse proxy and spreading traffic with a load balancer.
  • express-session. The express-session README says its default MemoryStore "is purposely not designed for a production environment": it "will leak memory under most conditions, does not scale past a single process".
  • Stack Overflow. Nick Craver's Stack Overflow: The Architecture - 2016 Edition lists the hardware behind the site at the time: 11 IIS web servers (9 of them serving production), 4 SQL Servers, 2 Redis servers, 3 tag engine servers, 3 Elasticsearch servers, and 4 HAProxy load balancers. A small fleet of powerful, well-tuned machines goes a long way before anything more elaborate is needed.

Popular tools and providers: Nginx, HAProxy, and cloud load balancers; Redis and Valkey (self-run or as a managed service such as Amazon ElastiCache or Google Cloud Memorystore); connect-redis for express-session; Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, and Azure Blob Storage for uploads; the Socket.IO Redis adapter; node-cron, BullMQ, Kubernetes CronJobs, and Amazon EventBridge Scheduler for scheduled work; and PM2 or the Node.js cluster module for using every CPU core of a machine.

docs.title: Six stages of growth
docs.text:
Stage What you add What it fixes What breaks or appears next 1. One server One VPS with Nginx, Node.js, MongoDB, uploads on disk, a crontab Nothing to coordinate; cheapest Any reboot, deploy restart, full disk, or hardware fault is an outage; the database and the API compete for memory and CPU 2. Separate database A managed database (or a dedicated database server) Backups, failover, and patching handled for you; the app server becomes disposable The app server is still one machine; every query now crosses the network 3. Load-balanced app tier A load balancer and two or more identical instances No single app server; rolling deploys; more capacity Anything stored on an instance: sessions, uploads, local caches, cron jobs, WebSocket rooms, counters 4. Cache and CDN Redis for hot reads; a CDN for static files and public responses Lower latency and database load Stale data, invalidation bugs, personalized responses cached for the wrong user 5. Multiple zones Load balancer nodes, instances, and database replicas in two or three Availability Zones Survives a data center failure Capacity must cover a lost zone; cross-zone latency and data transfer charges 6. Multiple regions A second region and global traffic management Survives a region outage; nearby service for distant users Replication lag, write conflicts, data residency, roughly double the infrastructure

Stage 2: separating the database. A managed database removes the most dangerous job from the app server, but three things change:

  • Latency per query. Each query now pays a network round trip, well under a millisecond inside one zone. An endpoint that runs 50 sequential queries notices; batch them ($in, bulkWrite) or run them in parallel.
  • Connections multiply. Every instance opens its own connection pool. The MongoDB Node.js driver's default maxPoolSize is 100 connections per server per MongoClient, so ten instances can open 1,000 connections to the primary. Size pools on purpose (see the worked example below).
  • Network security. The database must not be reachable from the internet: private subnets, security groups, and TLS (see cloud building blocks).

Stage 3: adding the load balancer. Instances must be identical (built from one image, configured by environment variables), expose a readiness endpoint, and shut down gracefully, as described in deploying backend services. Behind a TLS-terminating load balancer, the app must also trust exactly one proxy hop to see the real client IP and scheme (see TLS termination). The rest of this lesson is about the hidden state this stage exposes.

Stage 4: caches and a CDN trade freshness for speed; the rules are in cache fundamentals and HTTP and CDN caching.

Stages 5 and 6 are covered in multi-AZ and multi-region architecture and global traffic management. Scaling the database itself (read replicas, sharding) and moving slow work to queues are covered in database scaling and message queues.

docs.title: Statelessness: what must leave the instance
docs.text: A stateless instance holds nothing that another instance cannot rebuild or look up. It may cache things to go faster, but losing it must not lose data, log anyone out, or change what a user sees.

docs.title: Sessions
docs.text:
Option How it works Strengths Weaknesses In-memory sessions (MemoryStore) Session data in the process No setup Lost on every restart; not shared; leaks memory Sticky sessions The load balancer pins a client to one instance by cookie or IP hash No code change Uneven load; sessions lost when that instance dies or is deployed; fights autoscaling Shared session store Session ID in a cookie, data in Redis with a TTL Any instance serves any request; survives deploys Redis becomes a critical dependency and must be replicated Signed tokens (JWT) The client carries signed claims; no server lookup No session storage at all Hard to revoke before expiry; keep them short-lived with refresh tokens

A shared store is the usual default for browser sessions. The trade-offs of tokens are covered in sessions, cookies, and JWT. Sticky sessions still have legitimate uses (Socket.IO's HTTP long-polling fallback needs them, and they keep a warm per-instance cache warm), but never rely on them to keep data that matters.

docs.title: Uploaded files
docs.text: A file saved to ./uploads on instance 1 does not exist on instance 2, and disappears with the instance. Uploads belong in object storage: the API issues a short-lived presigned URL, the browser uploads directly to the bucket, and the API stores only the object key. Files are then served through a CDN or through presigned download URLs. The details are in file storage and uploads and object and file storage.

docs.title: In-process caches
docs.text: A small in-memory cache per instance is fine for data that rarely changes (feature configuration, lookup tables) if its TTL is short, because each instance invalidates on its own schedule and two instances can disagree for up to one TTL. Shared data that changes (a task, a user's permissions) belongs in Redis, where one delete invalidates it for everyone. If you need both, publish invalidation messages over Redis pub/sub so every instance drops its local copy.

docs.title: Scheduled jobs
docs.text:
A crontab or in-process scheduler runs on every instance, so three instances send the daily digest three times. The options:

Approach How Trade-off One designated instance An environment flag enables the scheduler on one instance only Simple; jobs silently stop when that instance is gone Claim each run Every instance tries SET key NX with an expiry; the key holds the job name and the scheduled time Any instance can run the job; needs Redis, and a Redis outage skips runs A separate scheduler Kubernetes CronJob, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler, or one worker deployment Jobs leave the web tier; one more component to run (see stateful workloads and Jobs) A queue with repeatable jobs BullMQ job schedulers or similar; workers consume the jobs Retries, history, and visibility; a queue to operate

Two details make the claim approach correct. First, the key must include the scheduled time (daily-digest:2026-11-13T07:00:00.000Z), so every instance computes the same key for the same run, even if their clocks differ by a few seconds. Second, the claim must not be deleted when the job finishes. If it were, an instance whose clock is ten seconds late would fire after the first one finished, find no key, and send the digest again. Let the key expire on its own, well after any plausible clock skew.

Claiming a run ("exactly one instance starts this occurrence") is different from mutual exclusion ("never two copies at the same time"), which needs a lock released by its owner. Redis locks expire, so a job that runs longer than its lease, or pauses for a long garbage collection, can lose the lock while still running. Keep jobs short, renew leases, or use a queue for work that must never overlap.

docs.title: WebSockets and fan-out
docs.text:
Each WebSocket connection lives on one instance. When a task changes, instance 1 can only push the update to the sockets it holds, so users connected to instance 2 never see it. The fix is a backplane: every instance publishes events to a shared channel (Redis pub/sub, Redis Streams, or a message broker) and delivers them to its own sockets. For Socket.IO this is an adapter such as the Redis adapter.

Two more consequences:

  • Socket.IO's HTTP long-polling transport sends several requests per session, and all of them must reach the process that created the session, so long-polling requires sticky sessions. Clients that use only the WebSocket transport do not.
  • Long-lived connections stay where they are while load changes. New instances get no existing sockets, so use a least-connections algorithm, and expect reconnect storms when an instance is drained (see load balancers in depth and rainbow deployments in advanced deployment patterns).

docs.title: Counters, rate limits, logs, and configuration
docs.text:
• Rate limits and counters kept in memory are per instance: a limit of 100 requests per minute becomes 300 with three instances. Keep counters in Redis or enforce limits at the edge (see rate limiting and throttling).
  • Logs written to local files vanish with the instance. Write structured logs to stdout and ship them to a central store (see structured logging).
  • Configuration and secrets must be identical across instances: one artifact, configured by the environment. A session secret that differs per instance logs users out as surely as an in-memory store.

docs.title: Scaling up compared with scaling out
docs.text:
Scale up (vertical) Scale out (horizontal) How A bigger instance More instances behind a load balancer Code changes None The app must be stateless Ceiling The largest machine your provider sells Usually the database or another shared dependency Failure impact One machine is the whole service Losing one of N instances removes 1/N of capacity Resizing Usually a restart, so downtime unless a second instance exists Add or remove instances while serving Node.js specifics One Node process runs JavaScript on one core; use cluster, PM2, or several containers to use more cores Small instances, one or two processes each

Scaling up is often the right first move: it needs no code change and buys time to remove state. Scaling out is what gives availability, because it is the only option where one failure does not take everything down.

A worked example for TaskFlow API:

Measured: one instance (2 vCPU, two Node processes) serves 300 req/s at 60% CPU
Peak traffic: 1,200 req/s

Instances for peak:            1,200 / 300 = 4
Plus one for failures/deploys: 4 + 1 = 5
After losing one of five:      1,200 / 4 = 300 req/s each (the measured safe level)

Utilization after losing k of N equal instances:  u_after = u x N / (N - k)
  3 instances at 60%, lose 1:  60% x 3 / 2 = 90%   (close to saturation)
  5 instances at 60%, lose 1:  60% x 5 / 4 = 75%

Database connections:
  5 instances x 2 processes x 100 (driver default maxPoolSize) = 1,000 possible connections
  With a 600-connection budget: maxPoolSize = 600 / 10 = 60 per process

The connection line is the one teams forget: autoscaling from 5 to 15 instances triples the possible connections to a database that did not grow. How spare capacity must be spread across zones is covered in multi-AZ and multi-region architecture.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Do this next Not yet Low traffic, brief deploy downtime is acceptable Stay on one server; automate backups and deploys Load balancers, clusters, or Kubernetes Deploys and reboots cause outages users notice Two instances behind a load balancer, with state moved out A second region One instance's CPU is saturated and the app is still stateful Scale up while you remove state Sticky sessions as a crutch for scaling out The database is saturated (CPU, connections) Indexes, query fixes, caching, read replicas More app instances, which add connections A zone outage would break your availability target Multiple zones with capacity for a lost zone Multi-region Distant users see high latency, or data must stay in a country A CDN first, then a region near those users Active-active writes without a measured need

docs.title: Sessions in Redis with express-session
docs.text:
// src/session.js: sessions in Redis, so any instance can serve any request
import session from "express-session";
import { RedisStore } from "connect-redis";
import { createClient } from "redis";

export async function sessionMiddleware() {
  const redis = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
  redis.on("error", (err) => console.error("redis:", err.message));
  await redis.connect();

  return session({
    store: new RedisStore({ client: redis, prefix: "taskflow:sess:" }),
    name: "tf.sid",
    secret: process.env.SESSION_SECRETS.split(","), // first one signs, all verify
    resave: false,
    saveUninitialized: false,
    rolling: true,                                  // extend the session on activity
    cookie: {
      httpOnly: true,
      secure: process.env.NODE_ENV === "production", // needs "trust proxy" behind the LB
      sameSite: "lax",
      maxAge: 8 * 60 * 60 * 1000,                   // 8 hours; connect-redis uses it as the TTL
    },
  });
}

// src/app.js
import os from "node:os";
import express from "express";
import { sessionMiddleware } from "./session.js";

export const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1);           // the load balancer is one hop away
app.use(await sessionMiddleware());

if (process.env.NODE_ENV !== "production") {
  // Development check: the counter keeps rising whichever instance answers
  app.post("/debug/visits", (req, res) => {
    req.session.visits = (req.session.visits ?? 0) + 1;
    res.set("X-Instance", os.hostname());
    res.json({ visits: req.session.visits });
  });
}
  • connect-redis 10 exports RedisStore as a named export and works with the official redis client. Sessions live under taskflow:sess:<id> with a TTL taken from the cookie's expiry.
  • secret accepts a list. The first secret signs new cookies and all of them verify, so you can rotate secrets without logging everyone out. Every instance must get the same list.
  • With secure: true, express-session sets the cookie only when it sees HTTPS. Behind a TLS-terminating load balancer that requires app.set("trust proxy", 1); without it, production sessions silently never stick.

docs.title: Running each scheduled job once across instances
docs.text:
node-cron 4.6 can coordinate runs across instances. With distributed: true, every instance still runs the schedule, but before each run it asks a run coordinator whether it should run. The key it passes is the task name plus the scheduled time, identical on every instance.

// src/jobs/scheduler.js: every instance runs the schedule; one instance runs each fire
import os from "node:os";
import cron from "node-cron";
import { createClient } from "redis";
import { sendDailyDigests } from "./daily-digest.js";

const redis = createClient({
  url: process.env.REDIS_URL,
  disableOfflineQueue: true, // fail fast while Redis is down instead of queueing the SET
});
await redis.connect();

cron.setRunCoordinator({
  // key looks like "daily-digest:2026-11-13T07:00:00.000Z" on every instance
  async shouldRun(key, ttlMs) {
    const claimed = await redis.set(`cron:${key}`, os.hostname(), {
      condition: "NX",                           // only the first instance succeeds
      expiration: { type: "PX", value: ttlMs },  // the claim expires on its own
    });
    return claimed === "OK";
  },
  // No onComplete that deletes the key: a late instance must still lose the claim.
});

cron.schedule("0 7 * * *", sendDailyDigests, {
  name: "daily-digest",
  timezone: "UTC",
  distributed: true,
  distributedLease: 10 * 60 * 1000, // far longer than any clock skew between instances
  noOverlap: true,
});

If Redis is unreachable, the SET fails at once (because of disableOfflineQueue; by default node-redis would queue it until Redis returns), node-cron skips the run (it fails closed), and it emits an execution:skipped event, so a missed digest is possible but a duplicate is not. Alert on skipped runs. Without a coordinator, node-cron's default reads NODE_CRON_RUN, which you set to true on exactly one instance: the designated-instance approach from the table above.

For work that must never run twice at the same time, use a lock that only its owner can release:

// src/jobs/lock.js: mutual exclusion with an owner token
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const RELEASE_IF_OWNER = `
if redis.call("GET", KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then
  return redis.call("DEL", KEYS[1])
end
return 0`;

export async function withLock(redis, name, leaseMs, work) {
  const key = `lock:${name}`;
  const token = randomUUID();
  const acquired = await redis.set(key, token, {
    condition: "NX",
    expiration: { type: "PX", value: leaseMs },
  });
  if (acquired !== "OK") return { ran: false };
  try {
    return { ran: true, result: await work() };
  } finally {
    // Delete only our own lock; it may have expired and been taken by someone else.
    await redis.eval(RELEASE_IF_OWNER, { keys: [key], arguments: [token] });
  }
}

The lease must be longer than the work. If it expires first, a second instance can take the lock while the first is still running, so this pattern limits overlap; it does not make it impossible.

docs.title: Real-time events across instances with Socket.IO
docs.text:
// src/realtime.js: board events reach every client, whichever instance holds its socket
import { createServer } from "node:http";
import { Server } from "socket.io";
import { createClient } from "redis";
import { createAdapter } from "@socket.io/redis-adapter";

const pubClient = createClient({ url: process.env.REDIS_URL });
const subClient = pubClient.duplicate();
await Promise.all([pubClient.connect(), subClient.connect()]);

const httpServer = createServer();
export const io = new Server(httpServer, {
  adapter: createAdapter(pubClient, subClient),
  transports: ["websocket"], // no long-polling, so no sticky sessions are needed
});

io.on("connection", (socket) => {
  // Check that the user may read the board before joining, in real code
  socket.on("board:join", (boardId) => socket.join(`board:${boardId}`));
});

// Any instance calls this after a task changes; Redis relays it to the others.
export function publishTaskUpdate(task) {
  io.to(`board:${task.boardId}`).emit("task:updated", task);
}

httpServer.listen(3001);

Clients must also connect with transports: ["websocket"]. If you keep the long-polling fallback for networks that block WebSockets, enable sticky sessions at the load balancer instead.

docs.title: A three-instance test environment
docs.text:
Running three instances locally flushes out hidden state before production does:

# compose.yaml: three API instances behind Nginx, to find hidden state early
services:
  api:
    build: .
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: development
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/taskflow
      SESSION_SECRETS: local-only-change-me
    deploy:
      replicas: 3
    depends_on: [redis, mongo]
  lb:
    image: nginx:1.30
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    volumes:
      - ./deploy/nginx-local.conf:/etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf:ro
    depends_on: [api]
  redis:
    image: redis:8
  mongo:
    image: mongo:8

# deploy/nginx-local.conf: round robin over every "api" container
upstream taskflow_api {
    zone taskflow_api 64k;
    resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=5s;     # Docker's embedded DNS server
    server api:3000 resolve;          # one upstream entry per container (nginx 1.27.3+)
}

server {
    listen 80;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
    }
}

// scripts/check-stateless.mjs: 30 requests with one session through the load balancer
const base = process.argv[2] ?? "http://localhost:8080";
const perInstance = new Map();
let cookie;

for (let i = 1; i <= 30; i += 1) {
  const res = await fetch(`${base}/debug/visits`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: cookie ? { cookie } : {},
  });
  cookie ??= res.headers.get("set-cookie")?.split(";")[0];
  const { visits } = await res.json();
  const instance = res.headers.get("x-instance");
  perInstance.set(instance, (perInstance.get(instance) ?? 0) + 1);
  if (visits !== i) {
    console.error(`request ${i} on ${instance}: expected visits=${i}, got ${visits}`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
}

console.log("requests per instance:", Object.fromEntries(perInstance));
console.log(perInstance.size > 1 ? "session shared across instances" : "only one instance answered");

docker compose up -d --build
node scripts/check-stateless.mjs http://localhost:8080
# requests per instance: { 'a1f3c9e2b7d4': 10, '7d20e4c1a9b8': 10, '3b9c51f0e2a6': 10 }
# session shared across instances

The resolve parameter makes Nginx re-resolve api and pick up every container as it starts or stops, which needs nginx 1.27.3 or later in the open-source build. Switch SESSION_SECRETS to a different value in one container, or remove the Redis store, and the script fails on the second or third request: exactly the bug users would have hit in production.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Scale up first when it buys time, but make the app stateless before you need to scale out.
  • Build every instance from one artifact and configure it only through the environment.
  • Keep sessions in a replicated shared store or short-lived tokens; do not rely on sticky sessions for correctness.
  • Put uploads in object storage, logs on stdout, and counters in Redis or at the edge.
  • Give every scheduled job one owner: a per-run claim, a separate scheduler, or a queue.
  • Add a pub/sub backplane before running real-time features on more than one instance.
  • Budget database connections across all instances and processes, and revisit the budget when autoscaling limits change.
  • Keep at least N+1 instances so one failure or deploy leaves enough capacity.
  • Run a multi-instance environment in CI or locally to catch hidden state before production.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Users are logged out at random after a second instance was added. Detect: sign-in rate jumps right after the scale-out, and requests alternate between instances in the logs. Cause: sessions in process memory, or a session secret that differs between instances. Fix: a shared Redis store and the same secret list on every instance.
  • Sessions never stick in production, although Redis is configured. Detect: responses carry no Set-Cookie header in production, while development works. Cause: cookie.secure is on, but the app does not trust the load balancer, so it thinks every request is plain HTTP. Fix: app.set("trust proxy", 1) for the single load balancer hop, and confirm the load balancer sends X-Forwarded-Proto.
  • Uploaded avatars return 404 about half the time. Detect: the 404s come from one instance; the file exists on another instance's disk. Cause: uploads written to local disk. Fix: object storage with presigned URLs, and a one-off migration of existing files.
  • The daily digest arrives three times. Detect: three log lines for the same scheduled time, one per hostname. Cause: the scheduler runs in every instance. Fix: claim each occurrence in Redis (key includes the scheduled time, never deleted early), or move the job to one scheduler.
  • Task board updates reach only some users. Detect: users connected to different instances see different boards; refreshing fixes it. Cause: events are emitted only to sockets on the local instance. Fix: a Redis pub/sub adapter so every instance relays events to its own clients.
  • Database connection errors appear after scaling out. Detect: the database reports its connection limit reached, and app logs show connection timeouts as instances are added. Cause: per-process pool size times process count exceeds the database's limit. Fix: set maxPoolSize from a connection budget, and cap the autoscaling maximum to match.
  • Rate limits stopped working after autoscaling. Detect: clients exceed documented limits by a factor equal to the instance count. Cause: in-memory counters per instance. Fix: a Redis store for the limiter, or limits enforced at the edge.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Vertical scaling (scaling up): Moving to a bigger machine.
  • Horizontal scaling (scaling out): Adding more machines that share the load.
  • Stateless service: A service whose instances keep no data that another instance cannot rebuild or look up.
  • Sticky session (session affinity): A load balancer rule that keeps a client on the same instance.
  • Shared session store: An external store, such as Redis, that holds session data for every instance.
  • Single point of failure: A component whose failure stops the whole service.
  • N+1 redundancy: Running one more instance than the load needs, so one can fail or be replaced.
  • Backplane: A shared pub/sub channel that relays real-time events between instances.
  • Lease: A lock or claim that expires automatically after a set time.
  • Connection budget: The total database connections all instances may open, divided among them.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a load balancer makes an application scalable; statelessness does.
  • Using sticky sessions to hide in-memory state instead of removing it.
  • Releasing a run-once claim when the job finishes, which lets a late instance run it again.
  • Adding app instances to fix a saturated database.
  • Forgetting that every instance and every process has its own connection pool, rate limiter, and cache.
  • Assuming a Redis lock guarantees exclusivity even when the work outlives the lease.
  • Jumping to multiple regions before using multiple zones well.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name the six stages of growth in this lesson and the main limit each stage removes.
  2. Why does adding a second instance expose bugs that tests did not catch? Give three examples and their fixes.
  3. Compare sticky sessions, a shared Redis session store, and signed tokens for session state.
  4. Three instances run at 65% CPU and one fails. What is the utilization of the other two? At the same total load, how many instances do you need so that losing one leaves the rest at or below 80%? (97.5%; four, which run at 48.75% and rise to 65%.)
  5. Why must a run-once claim include the scheduled time, and why must it not be deleted when the job finishes?
  6. What changes for the load balancer when Socket.IO clients may fall back to HTTP long-polling?
  7. Twelve instances each run two Node processes with the driver's default pool of 100 connections, and the database allows 1,500. What maxPoolSize keeps you under a 1,200-connection budget? (1,200 / 24 = 50.)
  8. When is scaling up a better next step than scaling out?
