docs.title: Global Traffic Management
docs.text:
Once a service runs in more than one region, something has to decide which region each user reaches, and how fast traffic moves when a region fails. That decision can be made by DNS (different answers for different users), by the network itself (anycast: one address announced from many places), or by a global layer 7 proxy at the edge (a CDN or global load balancer that picks a region for every request). This lesson explains each mechanism: GeoDNS and latency-based, weighted, and failover routing with Route 53, Google Cloud DNS, Azure Traffic Manager, and Cloudflare; anycast; global L7 load balancers and CDN edges; why DNS TTLs and resolver caches limit how fast failover can be; and why health checks for global routing run from many locations at once.

The previous lesson covered the load balancer inside one region; the next, multi-AZ and multi-region architecture, covers what has to be true of the application and its data before a second region can actually take traffic.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Distance is latency, and physics sets the floor. Light in optical fiber covers roughly 200,000 km per second, so the 15,700 km between Sydney and northern Virginia cost at least 157 ms per round trip before any real-world routing detours. A new HTTPS connection with TLS 1.3 needs two round trips before the first request byte (TCP, then TLS), so a user in Sydney waits over 300 ms for a server in Virginia to even start working, against about 20 ms for an edge location in their own city. Global traffic management is how users reach something nearby.

It is also how a regional outage becomes a short blip instead of a long one. If failover depends on DNS records with a one-hour TTL, users keep reaching the dead region for up to an hour. If it depends on an anycast address or a global proxy, new connections move within seconds of detection. The design choice made on a quiet day sets the length of the worst outage.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE book. The chapter Load Balancing at the Frontend describes DNS as Google's "first layer of load balancing", explains why "load balancing with DNS on its own is not sufficient", and follows it with a second level based on virtual IP addresses handled by network load balancers.
  • Amazon Route 53. The documentation on how Route 53 determines whether a health check is healthy explains that health checkers in several AWS Regions probe each endpoint independently and that "If more than 18% of health checkers report that an endpoint is healthy, Route 53 considers it healthy", which makes a false failover caused by one checker's network trouble very unlikely.
  • Amazon Builders' Library. In Reliability, constant work, and a good cup of coffee, AWS explains that Route 53 health check aggregators send "a fixed-size table of health check statuses" to the DNS servers every few seconds, whether or not anything changed, so a mass failure does not create a surge of extra work at the worst moment.
  • Netflix. The post Active-Active for Multi-Regional Resiliency describes users being "geo-DNS routed to the closest AWS Region, with a rough split of 50/50%", with Netflix's Zuul gateway in front of every edge service so traffic can also be proxied between regions.
  • AWS Global Accelerator. The how it works guide describes two static anycast IP addresses served from AWS edge locations; when an endpoint becomes unhealthy, Global Accelerator "instantly begins directing traffic for all new connections to another available endpoint", without any DNS change.

Popular tools and providers: Amazon Route 53 (with Application Recovery Controller), AWS Global Accelerator, and CloudFront; Google Cloud DNS routing policies, the global external Application Load Balancer, and Cloud CDN; Azure Traffic Manager and Azure Front Door; Cloudflare Load Balancing and CDN; and the dig tool for checking what each resolver sees.

docs.title: The layers of global routing
docs.text:
Layer Decides Granularity Reacts to failure in Examples DNS steering Which address a client receives Per resolver, cached for the TTL Detection plus TTL plus client caching: tens of seconds to hours Route 53, Cloud DNS routing policies, Traffic Manager, DNS-only Cloudflare load balancers Anycast Which location the packets for one address reach Per network path Seconds to minutes (BGP convergence); new connections first Global Accelerator, CDN and DNS networks, Google's global front end Global L7 proxy Which region or origin each request goes to Per request Seconds after detection Google global external Application Load Balancer, Azure Front Door, CloudFront, proxied Cloudflare load balancers Regional load balancer Which instance serves the request Per request or connection Seconds Covered in load balancers in depth

Most global services stack them: DNS hands out an anycast address, the anycast network delivers the user to a nearby edge, and the edge proxy chooses a healthy region for each request.

docs.title: DNS-based routing
docs.text:
An authoritative DNS server for api.taskflow.example.com can give different answers to different queries. The common policies, using Route 53 names (other providers offer the same ideas under other names):

Policy Answer chosen by Typical use Simple One fixed record One endpoint Weighted Configured weights (0 to 255) Gradual migrations between regions or providers; A/B infrastructure tests Latency Lowest measured latency from the user's network to each AWS Region Serving users from the closest region Failover A primary record while its health check passes, otherwise a secondary Active-passive disaster recovery Geolocation The user's continent, country, or US state Data residency, licensing, language-specific deployments Geoproximity Distance to each resource, with an adjustable bias Shifting the boundary between regions gradually IP-based Client IP ranges (CIDR blocks) you define Routing known networks, such as one ISP or a partner, to a chosen endpoint Multivalue answer Up to eight healthy records at random Simple client-side spreading with health checks

Other providers:

  • Google Cloud DNS routing policies offer weighted round robin, geolocation, and failover. Health checks are available for external endpoints in public zones and for internal load balancers in private zones.
  • Azure Traffic Manager is a DNS-based router with six methods (priority, weighted, performance, geographic, multivalue, subnet), probing endpoints every 30 seconds or every 10 seconds with "fast probing", and a configurable number of tolerated failures (default 3).
  • Cloudflare Load Balancing steers between pools by failover order, random weights, dynamic (measured latency), geography, proximity, or least outstanding requests. It runs either as DNS-only answers or proxied through Cloudflare's network, where it balances at layer 7 per request.

docs.title: Whose location? The resolver problem
docs.text:
The authoritative server never talks to the user: it receives the query from the user's recursive resolver. As RFC 7871 puts it, "the source address is that of the Recursive Resolver rather than of the query originator." Route 53 documents the consequence: when the resolver does not support the EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) option, it "uses the source IP address of the DNS resolver to guess where the user is"; when it does, the resolver sends "a shortened version of the user's IP address", which usually gives a more accurate location. A user whose resolver sits on another continent and sends no ECS is routed by the resolver's location, not their own.

Two more details matter in practice. Geolocation records need a default record: Route 53 cannot map every address to a location, and without a default it returns no answer for those queries. And every answer is cached by the resolver for the record's TTL, so a routing change reaches users only as caches expire.

docs.title: How fast can DNS fail over?
docs.text:
Failover time with DNS is the sum of several delays:

detection        request interval x failure threshold     10 s x 3 = 30 s (Route 53 "fast" checks)
DNS update       health-based answers switch at once; edited records propagate
                 to all Route 53 name servers "generally ... within 60 seconds"
resolver caches  up to the record TTL after the switch       60 s TTL -> until ~90 s
client caches    browsers, operating systems, and runtimes may keep answers longer
open connections keep-alive, HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSocket connections never re-resolve

Worked example, region A fails at t = 0:
  TTL 60 s:     most new requests move between t = 30 s and t = 90 s
  TTL 300 s:    between t = 30 s and t = 330 s
  TTL 3,600 s:  up to an hour, which is how a five-minute incident becomes a one-hour outage

Ways to make it faster:

  • Short TTLs on records that fail over, set long before an incident: lowering a TTL during an outage does not shorten caches that already hold the old value. Short TTLs cost more queries, which is usually cheap.
  • Expect stragglers. Some resolvers and clients cache longer than the TTL; RFC 8767 also lets resolvers serve stale answers when the authoritative servers are unreachable. Plan for a tail of minutes, not zero.
  • Recycle long-lived connections. Clients that hold one connection for hours never notice a DNS change. Close connections after a maximum age, and make clients reconnect (with jitter) when requests fail.
  • Avoid the cache entirely with anycast or a global proxy: the address never changes, so there is nothing to expire.

Health checks interact with failover in one more way. In Route 53, "If no record is healthy, all records are healthy": when every record in a group fails its check, Route 53 answers as if all were healthy rather than returning nothing. For failover records, if both the primary and the secondary are unhealthy, Route 53 returns the primary. A health check that fails everywhere at once (because it tests a shared dependency) therefore disables failover instead of triggering it.

docs.title: Anycast
docs.text:
With anycast, the same IP prefix is announced over BGP from many locations, and each network sends packets to whichever announcement its routing prefers, usually a nearby one. RFC 4786 (BCP 126) describes it as making a service address "available in multiple, discrete, autonomous locations."

  • Failover without DNS. When a location fails, it withdraws its announcement and routers converge on the next best location, typically within seconds to minutes, for every client at once.
  • Load and attack absorption. Traffic, including attack traffic, is spread across all locations instead of converging on one.
  • Routing, not geography. BGP chooses paths by policy and topology, so a user can reach a location that is not the closest on a map.
  • Long connections. A routing change in the middle of a TCP connection can deliver its packets to a different location that knows nothing about it; RFC 4786 warns that "especially for long running flows, there are potential failure modes using anycast". Providers engineer route stability, and many use anycast only for the first hop to their edge, where connections terminate.

AWS Global Accelerator, Google's global external load balancers, CDNs, and public DNS services all use anycast addresses.

docs.title: Global layer 7 load balancers and CDN edges
docs.text:
A global L7 proxy accepts connections at the edge location nearest the user (usually through anycast), terminates TLS there, and forwards each request over the provider's backbone to a region it chooses:

  • Faster connections. The TCP and TLS handshakes complete with a nearby edge (a few milliseconds per round trip), and the edge reuses warm, long-lived connections to the origin.
  • Per-request routing. Each request can go to a different region based on health, latency, weights, or capacity. Google's global external Application Load Balancer, for example, sends traffic to the closest region with capacity and lets it "overflow to the next closest region" when that region is full or unhealthy.
  • Failover without client involvement. The client keeps talking to the same edge address; only the edge's choice of origin changes.

The main options and their failover rules:

Service How it chooses an origin Failover detail Google global external Application LB Closest healthy region with capacity, overflowing to the next Health checks per backend; one anycast IP for all regions Azure Front Door Latency (the default), priority, weighted, or session affinity Health probes per origin; if every probe fails, it spreads traffic across all origins Amazon CloudFront origin groups A primary origin, then a secondary for each failed request Only GET, HEAD, and OPTIONS fail over, on the status codes you choose or on connection failures and timeouts Cloudflare proxied load balancing Steering policy across pools of origins Monitors run from three data centers in each chosen region; an origin is healthy when most regions agree AWS Global Accelerator (L4) Endpoint groups per region with traffic dials and weights New connections move once an endpoint is unhealthy; open connections stay until they close

CloudFront's defaults show why the details matter: it tries to connect to the primary origin three times with a 10-second connection timeout each, so a dead origin delays every affected request by up to 30 seconds before failover. One attempt with a short connection timeout makes failover fast, at the cost of failing over on a single slow connection.

docs.title: Comparing the three approaches
docs.text: DNS-based Anycast L4 (Global Accelerator) Global L7 proxy Failover speed Detection plus TTL plus client caches Detection, then new connections move Detection, then the next request moves Granularity Per resolver Per connection Per request Protocols Anything TCP and UDP HTTP(S), gRPC, WebSockets Client IP at the origin Unchanged Preserved for ALB, EC2 instance, and NLB-with-security-group endpoints In headers such as X-Forwarded-For Cost and lock-in Low, portable Per accelerator and data transfer Highest, provider-specific features Best for Simple multi-region and DR, non-HTTP protocols Static IPs, gaming, IoT, fast TCP and UDP failover Global web APIs and sites

docs.title: Health checks from many locations
docs.text:
Global routing decides the fate of a whole region, so a false alarm is expensive: it moves every user, may lose recent writes (see multi-AZ and multi-region architecture), and sends traffic to a region that may not have the capacity. Global health checks therefore:

  • Probe from many places. Route 53 runs checkers in eight Regions by default (you can pick at least three), and Cloudflare probes from three data centers in each region you select.
  • Require agreement. Route 53 marks an endpoint unhealthy only when fewer than 18% of checkers report it healthy; Cloudflare counts an endpoint healthy when the majority of regions do. A problem in one checker's network does not move your users.
  • Test what users need. A region-level endpoint (/health/region) should fail when the region cannot serve users (its database writer is unreachable, its critical queue is down), not when one instance is busy. Shared external dependencies do not belong in it, or every region fails together.
  • Combine and gate. Route 53 calculated health checks combine several checks, and Application Recovery Controller adds operator-controlled switches (routing controls, zonal shift, Region switch) for teams that want a person to decide on regional failover.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach One region, users mostly on one continent A CDN for static files; no global routing yet Active-passive disaster recovery, RTO of tens of minutes DNS failover records with short TTLs and a tested runbook Users on several continents, HTTP APIs A global L7 proxy (Front Door, Google global LB, Cloudflare) or latency-based DNS to regional load balancers Fixed IP addresses for clients or firewalls, TCP or UDP Anycast entry such as Global Accelerator Data must stay in one country or region Geolocation routing with a default record, plus enforcement in the application (DNS alone is not a control) Migrating between regions or providers Weighted DNS, moving weight in small steps Very fast failover for long-lived connections Anycast or a proxy plus client reconnect logic; DNS alone cannot do it

Do not rely on GeoDNS for anything that must be exact, such as legal data residency or licensing: resolvers lie about location, VPNs exist, and caches outlive changes.

docs.title: Latency-based routing with regional health checks (Terraform)
docs.text:
# dns/latency-routing.tf: send users to the lowest-latency region that can serve them
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.11"
  required_providers {
    aws = {
      source  = "hashicorp/aws"
      version = "~> 6.0"
    }
  }
}

provider "aws" {
  region = "us-east-1"
}

variable "zone_id" {
  description = "Hosted zone for taskflow.example.com"
  type        = string
}

variable "regions" {
  description = "Regional entry points, keyed by AWS Region"
  type = map(object({
    alb_dns_name = string
    alb_zone_id  = string
    health_fqdn  = string # for example api-eu-west-1.taskflow.example.com
  }))
}

resource "aws_route53_health_check" "region" {
  for_each = var.regions

  fqdn              = each.value.health_fqdn
  port              = 443
  type              = "HTTPS"
  resource_path     = "/health/region"
  request_interval  = 10 # fast checks; the default is 30
  failure_threshold = 3  # about 30 s to detect a failed region
  regions           = ["us-east-1", "us-west-2", "eu-west-1", "ap-southeast-1"]

  tags = {
    Name = "taskflow-api-${each.key}"
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "api" {
  for_each = var.regions

  zone_id         = var.zone_id
  name            = "api.taskflow.example.com"
  type            = "A"
  set_identifier  = each.key
  health_check_id = aws_route53_health_check.region[each.key].id

  latency_routing_policy {
    region = each.key
  }

  alias {
    name                   = each.value.alb_dns_name
    zone_id                = each.value.alb_zone_id
    evaluate_target_health = true
  }
}

# dns/terraform.tfvars: two regions behind one name
zone_id = "<hosted-zone-id>"
regions = {
  "eu-west-1" = {
    alb_dns_name = "<eu-alb-dns-name>"
    alb_zone_id  = "<eu-alb-hosted-zone-id>"
    health_fqdn  = "api-eu-west-1.taskflow.example.com"
  }
  "us-east-1" = {
    alb_dns_name = "<us-alb-dns-name>"
    alb_zone_id  = "<us-alb-hosted-zone-id>"
    health_fqdn  = "api-us-east-1.taskflow.example.com"
  }
}
  • Route 53 picks the record for the Region with the lowest latency from the user's network, then checks health. Both conditions must hold: the region's own /health/region check passes, and (because evaluate_target_health is true) the load balancer has healthy targets. If either fails, the next-lowest-latency region answers.
  • You cannot set a TTL on an alias record that points to an AWS resource; Route 53 uses the resource's default, which the Elastic Load Balancing guide gives as 60 seconds.
  • regions limits health checking to four checker Regions (the minimum is three); the default uses all of them.

docs.title: A region health endpoint
docs.text:
// src/routes/region-health.js: "can this region serve users?" for global health checks
import { Router } from "express";

const CACHE_MS = 5_000;   // many checkers probe every 10 s; do the real work at most every 5 s
let cached = { at: 0, ok: false, detail: "not checked yet" };
let inFlight = null;      // concurrent probes share one check

function withTimeout(promise, ms, what) {
  let timer;
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`${what} timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms);
  });
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

async function checkRegion(db) {
  // The region's own primary must answer quickly; shared external services are left out
  await withTimeout(db.command({ ping: 1 }), 1_000, "database ping");
  return { ok: true, detail: "database primary reachable" };
}

export function regionHealth(db, region = process.env.AWS_REGION) {
  const router = Router();
  router.get("/health/region", async (req, res) => {
    if (Date.now() - cached.at > CACHE_MS) {
      inFlight ??= checkRegion(db)
        .then((result) => ({ at: Date.now(), ...result }))
        .catch((err) => ({ at: Date.now(), ok: false, detail: err.message }))
        .finally(() => { inFlight = null; });
      cached = await inFlight;
    }
    res.set("Cache-Control", "no-store");
    res.status(cached.ok ? 200 : 503).json({ region, ok: cached.ok, detail: cached.detail });
  });
  return router;
}

// src/app.js (excerpt)
app.use(regionHealth(mongoClient.db("taskflow")));

Route 53 health checkers in several Regions each probe every 10 seconds, so the endpoint receives a steady stream of requests; caching the result for a few seconds, and letting concurrent probes share one check, keeps that load constant and small. The timeout lives in the application (Promise.race) because a ping to an unreachable primary can otherwise wait for the driver's server selection timeout (30 seconds by default). The endpoint checks only what makes this region unable to serve: a dependency every region shares would make them all fail at once, and Route 53 would then treat every record as healthy.

docs.title: Seeing what different resolvers answer
docs.text:
# Answer and remaining TTL from your own resolver, then from two public ones
dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com
dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com @8.8.8.8
dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com @1.1.1.1

# Ask the authoritative server directly, pretending to be a user in a given subnet (ECS)
dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com @<authoritative-name-server> +subnet=203.0.113.0/24
dig +noall +answer api.taskflow.example.com @<authoritative-name-server> +subnet=198.51.100.0/24

// scripts/dns-vantage.mjs: what does each resolver return, and for how long?
import { Resolver } from "node:dns/promises";

const name = process.argv[2] ?? "api.taskflow.example.com";
const resolvers = { system: null, google: "8.8.8.8", cloudflare: "1.1.1.1", quad9: "9.9.9.9" };

for (const [label, server] of Object.entries(resolvers)) {
  const resolver = new Resolver({ timeout: 2_000, tries: 2 });
  if (server) resolver.setServers([server]);
  try {
    const answers = await resolver.resolve4(name, { ttl: true });
    const list = answers.map((a) => `${a.address} (ttl ${a.ttl}s)`).join(", ");
    console.log(`${label.padEnd(10)} ${list}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log(`${label.padEnd(10)} ${err.code}`);
  }
}

Run it during a failover drill: the answers show which resolvers already switched and how many seconds each cached answer has left. Note that resolve4 queries DNS directly, while fetch and http.request use the operating system's resolver (dns.lookup), which may cache differently.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Put a CDN or global proxy in front of user-facing HTTP traffic before building multi-region DNS logic.
  • Keep TTLs short (60 seconds or so) on every record that may fail over, and set them well before any incident.
  • Health-check regions from many locations with a deep but region-local check; keep shared dependencies out of it.
  • Always define a default record for geolocation routing.
  • Make clients re-resolve and reconnect: cap connection age and retry with jitter after failures.
  • Prefer anycast or a global L7 proxy when failover must take seconds.
  • Shift traffic between regions in steps (weights), and confirm the target region has capacity before moving everyone.
  • Rehearse regional failover and measure the actual time from failure to traffic moved; compare it with your recovery time objective.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Failover worked, but users kept reaching the dead region for an hour. Detect: traffic to the healthy region rises slowly; some resolvers still return the old address. Cause: a 3,600-second TTL on the API record, or clients holding long-lived connections. Fix: lower TTLs ahead of time, cap connection age, and consider anycast or a global proxy.
  • Users in Asia are served from the US region. Detect: latency by country shows one country far above its neighbours; dig from that network returns the US answer. Cause: those users rely on a resolver far away that sends no client subnet, or a geolocation record set without a default that matches. Fix: latency-based routing or a global proxy that measures from the edge, and a default record.
  • Every region was marked unhealthy at once, and failover did nothing. Detect: all regional health checks failing together; Route 53 keeps answering with the usual records. Cause: the health endpoint checks a shared dependency, so all regions fail, and Route 53 treats a fully unhealthy group as healthy. Fix: region-local checks only; alert on shared dependencies separately.
  • Traffic flaps between regions. Detect: answers alternate every minute; logs show repeated failover and failback. Cause: a borderline health check with low thresholds, often under load that moves with the traffic. Fix: higher thresholds, a slower or manual failback, and capacity in the target region.
  • The failover region fell over too. Detect: errors and latency jump in region B right after failover. Cause: region B was sized for its own users only. Fix: keep spare capacity or warm standby, scale before shifting, and move traffic in steps.
  • CloudFront failover makes users wait 30 seconds. Detect: origin-failover requests have very long response times. Cause: default origin settings: three connection attempts of 10 seconds each before using the secondary. Fix: fewer connection attempts and a shorter connection timeout on the primary origin.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Authoritative DNS server: The server that holds a zone's records and answers for them.
  • Recursive resolver: The DNS server that looks up names on a client's behalf and caches the answers.
  • TTL (time to live): How long a resolver may cache an answer.
  • GeoDNS / geolocation routing: Answering based on the estimated location of the query.
  • Latency-based routing: Answering with the region that has the lowest measured latency from the user's network.
  • EDNS Client Subnet (ECS): A DNS option carrying part of the client's address from resolver to authoritative server.
  • Anycast: Announcing the same IP prefix from many locations so routing delivers each user to one of them.
  • BGP convergence: The time routers take to agree on new paths after a change.
  • Point of presence (PoP): An edge location of a CDN or network.
  • Global load balancer: An L7 proxy at the edge that chooses a region for each request.
  • Origin failover: A CDN retrying a request against a secondary origin.
  • Serve-stale: A resolver returning an expired answer when it cannot reach the authoritative servers.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a 60-second TTL means every client moves within 60 seconds.
  • Lowering the TTL during an incident and expecting it to help.
  • Using GeoDNS as a security or legal control.
  • Health-checking regions with a shallow endpoint, or with one that tests shared dependencies.
  • Forgetting the default record in geolocation routing.
  • Treating anycast as "nearest on the map".
  • Failing over to a region that cannot carry the extra load.
  • Assuming long-lived connections follow a DNS change.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why does a user in Sydney gain more from an edge location in Sydney than from a faster server in Virginia? Estimate the minimum handshake cost. (At least 157 ms per round trip; about 314 ms for TCP plus TLS 1.3.)
  2. Compare weighted, latency, failover, and geolocation routing. Which would you use for a gradual migration, and which for active-passive DR?
  3. Why can a GeoDNS server send a user to the wrong continent, and what does EDNS Client Subnet change?
  4. Route 53 checks every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3, and the record TTL is 120 seconds. When have most resolvers switched after a region fails at t = 0? (After about 30 + 120 = 150 seconds, with a tail.)
  5. What does Route 53 do when every record in a group is unhealthy, and why does that make shared dependencies in health checks dangerous?
  6. How does anycast fail over without DNS, and what is its risk for long-lived TCP connections?
  7. Compare DNS-based routing, Global Accelerator, and a global L7 proxy on failover speed, granularity, and protocols.
  8. Why do global health checks run from many locations, and why does Route 53 use an 18% threshold rather than a simple majority of failures?

docs.text:

  • Amazon Route 53: How Route 53 uses EDNS0 to estimate the location of a user
  • Google Cloud: Service load balancing policies

docs.title: How Top Companies Run at Scale
docs.text:
The previous lessons described load balancers, global traffic, multi-region designs, autoscaling, discovery, and resilience patterns in general terms. This lesson looks at how specific companies applied them, using only what they have published themselves: papers, engineering blog posts, and open-source projects. For each case the question is the same: what did they build, and why: what problem made the existing approach insufficient?

The cases cover software layer 4 load balancing (Google's Maglev, Meta's Katran, GitHub's GLB Director, Cloudflare's Unimog), edge gateways, discovery, and load-aware balancing (Netflix's Zuul and Eureka, Dropbox's Robinhood), multi-region active-active operation and region evacuation at Netflix, cells and shuffle sharding (Slack, AWS and Route 53, Shopify), and practicing failure. Two small Node.js programs reproduce the core algorithms (Maglev hashing and shuffle sharding) so you can see why they work.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Large-scale architectures are easy to misread as a list of products to copy. The useful part is the reasoning: which limit they hit, what they tried first, and what trade-off they accepted. That reasoning transfers to much smaller systems. You probably do not need a custom packet processor, but you may well need to drain a zone without knowing the root cause, make failover a DNS change instead of a 25-minute boot, keep one tenant's bad request from taking down every tenant, or stop a connection-level load balancer from overloading your slowest servers.

These cases are also standard material in system design and SRE interviews, where "how does Google load balance?" or "what is a cell?" expects an answer grounded in the published designs rather than guesses.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google. The NSDI 2016 paper Maglev: A Fast and Reliable Software Network Load Balancer describes the network load balancer that has served Google's traffic since 2008 and provides network load balancing for Google Cloud.
  • Amazon. The Builders' Library article Workload isolation using shuffle-sharding explains the technique and how Route 53 uses it, and the whitepaper Reducing the Scope of Impact with Cell-Based Architecture (2023) applies the isolation of Availability Zones and Regions inside a single workload.
  • Slack. Slack's Migration to a Cellular Architecture (2023) starts from a specific incident and explains how Slack made each Availability Zone a drainable cell.
  • Netflix. Project Nimble: Region Evacuation Reimagined (2018) breaks down why a region failover took about 50 minutes and how pre-started "dark capacity" brought it under 10.

Popular tools and providers: open-source descendants of these designs include Katran and GLB Director themselves, Envoy (which offers a Maglev consistent-hashing load balancer), Zuul and Eureka, Chaos Monkey, and cloud services built on the same ideas (Google Cloud's network load balancing on Maglev, AWS's cell-based services).

docs.title: Software L4 load balancing on ordinary servers
docs.text:
Four companies independently replaced dedicated load balancer hardware, or ECMP alone, with software running on ordinary servers. Their reasons overlap, and the differences are instructive.

Google Maglev. The Maglev paper lists four limitations of hardware network load balancers: capacity limited by a single unit, which could not keep up with Google's growth; only 1+1 redundancy, which did not meet Google's availability requirements; little flexibility to modify them; and costly upgrades that require buying and installing new hardware. Maglev runs on commodity Linux servers. Every Maglev machine announces a service's virtual IP to the routers over BGP with equal cost, so routers spread packets across all of them with ECMP; each machine picks a backend and forwards the packet inside GRE encapsulation, and responses go straight back to the routers (direct server return), so Maglev handles only the smaller incoming traffic. Capacity grows by adding machines, giving N+1 redundancy.

Two mechanisms keep connections stable. A connection table remembers the backend chosen for each recent flow. But when the set of Maglev machines changes (rolling upgrades, failures), ECMP moves flows to a different Maglev that has no entry for them, so Maglev also uses Maglev hashing, a consistent hashing scheme in which every machine builds the same lookup table from the backend list. The paper explains that existing consistent hashing schemes favored minimal disruption over even balance; Maglev hashing deliberately puts even balance first (so backends need not be overprovisioned) while keeping disruption small. The paper also describes bypassing the Linux kernel for packet processing to reach line rate.

Meta Katran. Meta's announcement of Katran (2018) describes a first-generation L4 load balancer built on the Linux IPVS module that served the company for well over four years but fell short on one goal: coexisting with other services on the same machines. Katran rebuilt the forwarding plane with XDP and eBPF so the load balancer can run on the backend servers themselves in Meta's points of presence. The rest of the design follows the same pattern as Maglev: ExaBGP announces the VIPs, switches spread packets with ECMP, a consistent hash of the 5-tuple sends every packet of a connection to the same backend without any state shared between load balancers, IP-in-IP encapsulation lets backends live in other racks, and direct server return keeps responses off the load balancer.

GitHub GLB Director. The GLB Director project, which GitHub uses to serve all traffic from its data centers, starts from a problem with plain ECMP: adding or removing a node disrupts flows, because no per-flow state is stored. Traditional solutions such as LVS store flow state on each director and share it between them. GLB Director stays stateless instead: it hashes each flow (with a variant of rendezvous hashing) to an ordered pair of proxy servers and, through a "second chance" mechanism, uses the state the proxies already hold so that flows can finish on a server that has started draining. Packets are encapsulated in Generic UDP Encapsulation, and responses use direct server return. Draining servers without breaking connections was the point.

Cloudflare Unimog. Cloudflare's post on Unimog (2020) explains that before Unimog it relied on ECMP alone, and lists ECMP's problems: changes in the set of servers cause rehashing that breaks connections, routers limit the size of ECMP groups, and ECMP cannot adjust the share of connections each server receives. Cloudflare needed both: to move servers in and out of service safely, and to balance load accurately across servers of different hardware generations. Unimog runs on the same general-purpose servers that run Cloudflare's services, making every server a load balancer, measures server load to adjust connection shares dynamically, uses XDP, and was, by Cloudflare's own description, strongly influenced by GLB.

Company Built Main reason Key techniques Google Maglev Hardware LBs could not scale with growth and gave only 1+1 redundancy ECMP to a software tier, Maglev hashing, connection tracking, GRE, DSR, kernel bypass Meta Katran First generation (IPVS) could not coexist with backends on the same hosts XDP and eBPF, ECMP, stateless 5-tuple consistent hashing, IP-in-IP, DSR GitHub GLB Director ECMP disrupts flows on membership change; avoid sharing flow state Stateless directors, rendezvous-style hashing to server pairs, "second chance" draining, GUE, DSR Cloudflare Unimog ECMP rehashing, group size limits, no dynamic load balancing Every server balances, load-based connection shares, XDP

The shared lesson: use ECMP for what routers do well (spreading packets), put the balancing logic in software you control, make flow placement consistent so that any balancer node gives the same answer, and keep responses off the load balancer.

docs.title: Netflix: an edge gateway and client-side discovery
docs.text:
• Eureka (2012). Netflix's announcement explains that in AWS "servers come and go", that AWS did not yet offer a middle-tier load balancer, and that putting mid-tier services behind internet-facing load balancers would have meant giving up security-group protection. Eureka is a registry, and clients balance load across the instances it lists: client-side discovery (see service discovery and service mesh).
  • Zuul. Netflix's edge gateway fronts its edge services. The 2018 post Open Sourcing Zuul 2 describes more than 80 Zuul 2 clusters sending traffic to about 100 backend clusters at more than a million requests per second, rebuilt on asynchronous Netty, with features such as HTTP/2, mutual TLS, adaptive retries, and dynamic routing rules used to shard traffic, onboard new services, run load tests on a slice of real traffic, and migrate gradually to new origins.
  • Resilience libraries. Netflix's Hystrix popularized circuit breakers and bulkheads; it is now in maintenance mode, with Netflix moving toward adaptive concurrency limits (see resilience patterns across servers).

docs.title: Dropbox: balancing on measured load
docs.text: Dropbox's Robinhood (deployed in 2020, described in 2024) addresses a problem simple balancing ignores: clients doing round robin over the subset of servers discovery gave them produced quite imbalanced load. Robinhood collects load information from servers and turns it into endpoint weights, delivered through Envoy's Endpoint Discovery Service so both Envoy and gRPC clients do weighted round robin. A PID controller per node steers each node's utilization toward the average. Dropbox reports reducing the fleet size of some of its largest services by 25%, because fewer servers need headroom for imbalance. Unimog's dynamic balancing follows the same logic at layer 4.

docs.title: Netflix: multi-region active-active and region evacuation
docs.text:
Netflix's regional design evolved in steps, each described publicly:

  1. Isthmus, resilience against a region-wide load balancer outage.
  2. Active-active across two US regions (2013): every service on the user call path deployed in both regions, with the requirements that services be stateless, use only in-region resources, make no cross-region calls on the user's path, and replicate data asynchronously (Cassandra and EVCache). Users were routed by geography with a roughly even split, DNS was controlled through Netflix's Denominator library across two DNS providers, and Zuul handled misrouted requests and load shedding during traffic shifts.
  3. Global cloud (2016): members in any region could be served from any region where Netflix was deployed, removing the single European region as a single point of failure.
  4. Project Nimble (2018): faster evacuation, below.

The Nimble post breaks the old 50 minutes down: about 5 minutes to decide, 3 to 5 minutes to provision, about 25 minutes for services to start (boot, download resources, connect to backends, register with Eureka and load balancers), 10 or more minutes of proxying traffic between regions through Zuul to cover DNS caching and let instances warm up, and about 5 minutes for DNS changes to reach most devices. The insight was that the long poles all happen after the decision. Netflix first considered keeping services permanently scaled high, then chose dark capacity: spare instances already running in a separate shadow group that the load balancers never see and that a shared library keeps in Eureka's STARTING state, so they receive no traffic until an evacuation. Failover then becomes flipping DNS. The post reports going from close to an hour to less than 10 minutes while staying cost neutral. Compare the warm pools and static stability ideas in autoscaling server fleets, and the architecture choices in multi-AZ and multi-region architecture.

docs.title: Cells, silos, and shuffle sharding
docs.text:
Slack. Slack's cellular migration began with an incident review. On 30 June 2021, a network link between Availability Zones in Slack's main US region had intermittent faults; the cloud provider removed it, it came back, and it failed again. Slack asked why a single impaired zone was visible to users at all, and found a gray failure: different components had different views of what was healthy, which is hard to detect and remediate automatically. Rather than try to solve gray failure automatically, Slack built a way for humans to act on it: a button that drains an Availability Zone. Its stated goals were to remove as much traffic as possible from a zone within 5 minutes (Slack's 99.99% availability SLA allows less than an hour of unavailability a year), cause no user-visible errors, drain and undrain incrementally (as little as 1% of traffic to test a recovered zone), and not depend on anything inside the zone being drained. Because Slack's services were written in several languages and used several discovery mechanisms (Envoy xDS, Consul, DNS), it did not change every client; instead it siloed services so that each only receives and sends traffic within its own zone, which makes draining the user-facing entry points enough to drain everything behind them.

AWS: cells and shuffle sharding. A cell is a complete, independent copy of a workload serving a subset of customers; a thin router sends each customer to its cell, so a bad deployment, a poison request, or a runaway customer affects only that cell (see advanced deployment patterns for cell-by-cell releases). Shuffle sharding refines this for shared fleets.

The Builders' Library article works through the arithmetic: eight workers in four shards means a problem customer affects a quarter of the service; giving each customer a pseudo-random pair of the eight workers creates 28 possible pairs, so only customers with exactly the same pair share the full impact, about 1/28, and customers who share one worker keep the other. Route 53 arranges its capacity into 2,048 virtual name servers and assigns every domain a shuffle shard of four, about 730 billion possible shards. The why was attacks: Route 53 hosts many domains, and a DDoS attack on one of them must not take down DNS for everyone else; buying enough scrubbing appliances to protect every domain was estimated at tens of millions of dollars and months of delay.

Shopify pods. Shopify's pods post (2018) explains that in 2015 a single, ever larger database server was no longer possible, so the database was sharded. That gained capacity but lost resilience: code that looped over every shard meant that one shard being down made an action unavailable across the whole platform. In 2016 Shopify introduced pods: a set of shops on a fully isolated set of datastores. Application servers, job workers, and load balancers are shared, but every unit of work (a web request or a background job) talks to exactly one pod, so serving a request only requires that pod to be up. A routing component in the load balancers, Sorting Hat, matches each request to its pod and adds a header that tells the application which datastores to use. Each pod has a pair of data centers, one active and one for recovery, and a tool called Pod Mover can move a pod to its recovery data center in about a minute without dropping requests or jobs, which also makes evacuating a whole data center a matter of moving its pods one at a time.

docs.title: Practicing failure
docs.text: Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates instances in production so that teams build services that tolerate it, and the 2013 active-active post lists larger exercises (Chaos Gorilla, Chaos Kong, and split-brain tests) used to verify that whole zones and regions can be lost. Regular evacuation drills are the reason an evacuation works on the day it is needed. Running such experiments safely is covered in chaos engineering and game days.

docs.title: What the stories have in common
docs.text: Problem Pattern Who A pair of load balancer appliances limits capacity and redundancy Scale-out software load balancing behind ECMP Google, Meta, GitHub, Cloudflare Membership changes break connections Consistent hashing everywhere, plus connection tracking or "second chance" Google, Meta, GitHub, Cloudflare Equal shares overload slower or busier servers Load-aware, dynamic weights Cloudflare, Dropbox Instances come and go faster than configuration can follow Registries and client-side balancing Netflix Failover is slow because capacity starts after the decision Pre-started, idle capacity; failover by DNS Netflix Gray failures inside one zone Siloed zones plus a human-operated drain Slack One customer or request can hurt everyone Cells, pods, and shuffle sharding AWS, Shopify, Slack Resilience decays without exercise Chaos experiments and evacuation drills Netflix

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Your situation Borrow Do not copy yet One region, a few services Managed load balancers, multi-AZ fleets, timeouts and retries Custom L4 balancers, cells Long-lived connections and frequent deploys Consistent hashing and connection draining (most managed and open-source balancers offer them) Writing your own forwarding plane Uneven servers or request costs Least-outstanding-requests or load-aware weights A PID-controlled control plane, until imbalance costs real money Strict availability targets in one region Zone silos and a tested zone-drain procedure Multi-region active-active Large multi-tenant SaaS Cells or pods by tenant, shuffle sharding for shared fleets One giant shared database Multi-region already justified Pre-provisioned capacity, regular evacuation drills Failover plans that start by booting servers

These companies built custom systems because nothing available met their scale or constraints at the time. Today, many of their ideas ship in managed cloud load balancers, Envoy, and service meshes; prefer those before building anything yourself.

docs.title: Maglev hashing in Node.js
docs.text:
// src/lb/maglev.js
// Maglev hashing (Eisenbud et al., NSDI 2016): every backend gets a preference
// order over the table slots; backends take turns claiming their next free slot.
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

function hash(text, seed) {
  return createHash("sha256").update(`${seed}:${text}`).digest().readUInt32BE(0);
}

export function buildTable(backends, size = 65_537) { // size must be prime
  const offsets = backends.map((b) => hash(b, "offset") % size);
  const skips = backends.map((b) => (hash(b, "skip") % (size - 1)) + 1);
  const next = backends.map(() => 0);
  const table = new Array(size).fill(-1);
  let filled = 0;
  while (filled < size) {
    for (let i = 0; i < backends.length && filled < size; i++) {
      let slot;
      do {
        slot = (offsets[i] + next[i] * skips[i]) % size; // i-th backend's permutation
        next[i]++;
      } while (table[slot] !== -1);
      table[slot] = i;
      filled++;
    }
  }
  return table.map((i) => backends[i]);
}

export function pick(table, flowKey) {
  return table[hash(flowKey, "flow") % table.length];
}

With five backends and the 65,537-slot table (the size Envoy's Maglev balancer also uses), each backend received 13,107 or 13,108 slots in a test run, an almost perfectly even split. Removing one backend changed 13,149 slots: the 13,107 that belonged to the removed backend and only 42 others, so almost every connection to a surviving backend stays where it is. That is the property that lets every Maglev machine compute the same answer independently, with no shared state.

docs.title: Shuffle sharding in Node.js
docs.text:
// src/lb/shuffle-shard.js
// Shuffle sharding: give each customer a small, deterministic, pseudo-random
// subset of workers, so two customers rarely share their whole subset.
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";

export function shuffleShard(customerId, workers, shardSize = 2) {
  const ranked = workers
    .map((w) => ({ w, score: createHash("sha256").update(`${customerId}|${w}`).digest().readUInt32BE(0) }))
    .sort((a, b) => a.score - b.score); // rendezvous-style ranking per customer
  return ranked.slice(0, shardSize).map((r) => r.w);
}

// How many distinct shards are possible: n choose k
export function combinations(n, k) {
  let result = 1n;
  for (let i = 0n; i < BigInt(k); i++) result = (result * (BigInt(n) - i)) / (i + 1n);
  return result;
}

combinations(8, 2) returns 28 and combinations(2048, 4) returns 730,862,190,080, the "730 billion" in the Route 53 example. In a test with 1,000 customers on 8 workers, poisoning one customer's pair took out both workers of 32 other customers (3.2%, close to 1 in 28), while 427 customers lost one worker and kept the other. In production, a client that tries the second worker when the first fails turns "lost one worker" into "no impact".

The same deterministic assignment works for cells: hash the tenant ID to pick a cell, store the result in a routing table so tenants can be moved, and route at the edge, as in the cell router example in advanced deployment patterns.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Learn the reason behind each design before borrowing the design.
  • Keep the data path simple and stateless where possible; move intelligence into control planes that can fail without stopping traffic.
  • Use consistent hashing so any node computes the same placement, and plan for membership changes (draining, second chance, connection tracking).
  • Balance on measured load when servers or requests differ.
  • Pre-provision what failover needs; a plan that boots servers after the decision is slow by design.
  • Build generic mitigations (drain a zone, evacuate a region, move a tenant) that work before the root cause is known.
  • Limit blast radius structurally: silos, cells, pods, shuffle shards.
  • Exercise failure on purpose and regularly.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Connections reset whenever the load balancer tier changes. Detect: resets spike during load balancer deploys or scaling, not during backend changes. Cause: ECMP rehashes flows to balancer nodes without state for them. Fix: consistent hashing that gives the same backend on every node, connection tracking, and gradual draining, as Maglev, Katran, and GLB do.
  • One zone's network trouble causes errors everywhere. Detect: errors appear in every zone while infrastructure metrics point at one. Cause: a gray failure plus cross-zone calls in every request. Fix: silo services within zones and build a tested zone-drain control at the entry points, like Slack.
  • A region failover takes most of an hour. Detect: drills show long waits for scaling, boot, and warmup after the decision. Cause: destination capacity is created during the failover. Fix: pre-started idle capacity and DNS-based failover, like Nimble.
  • One customer's traffic pattern takes down the shared fleet. Detect: an outage begins with a spike or malformed request from a single tenant. Cause: every tenant shares every worker. Fix: cells or pods per tenant group and shuffle sharding for shared tiers.
  • A loop over every shard makes one shard's outage platform-wide. Detect: a single database shard failure causes errors for all customers. Cause: code paths that touch all shards per request or job. Fix: assign every unit of work to exactly one shard or pod, like Shopify.
  • Newer servers sit idle while older ones overload. Detect: CPU differs widely between instance generations behind the same balancer. Cause: equal connection or request shares on unequal hardware. Fix: load-aware weights or least-outstanding-request balancing, like Unimog and Robinhood.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• ECMP (equal-cost multipath): Router feature spreading flows across several next hops with the same cost, using a hash of each flow.
  • VIP (virtual IP): An address served by many machines rather than one interface.
  • Direct server return (DSR): Responses go from the backend to the client without passing back through the load balancer.
  • GRE / IP-in-IP / GUE: Encapsulations used to forward packets from a load balancer to backends in other racks.
  • Maglev hashing: A consistent hashing algorithm that fills a lookup table evenly from per-backend preference lists.
  • Connection tracking: Remembering the backend chosen for each flow.
  • XDP / eBPF: Linux kernel facilities for fast, programmable packet processing.
  • Gray failure: A failure that some components see and others do not.
  • Silo: A service that only takes and sends traffic within its own zone.
  • Cell / pod: An isolated copy of a stack serving a subset of customers.
  • Shuffle sharding: Assigning each customer a pseudo-random subset of workers so customers rarely share a whole subset.
  • Dark capacity: Running instances held out of service until a failover needs them.
  • Region evacuation: Moving all users out of a region, usually by DNS.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Copying a big company's architecture without its problem or scale.
  • Believing these companies avoid failure; their designs assume it and limit its reach.
  • Thinking ECMP alone is a load balancer; it spreads flows but breaks them on membership changes and cannot weight by load.
  • Treating multi-region as automatically resilient without regular evacuation drills and pre-provisioned capacity.
  • Confusing cells with simple sharding: a cell includes the whole stack, not only the database.
  • Quoting numbers from these posts as if they were universal; they describe one system at one time.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What four limitations of hardware load balancers did the Maglev paper give, and how does Maglev address each?
  2. Why do Maglev, Katran, and GLB Director use consistent hashing even though they also track connections or flows?
  3. What problem with its first-generation load balancer led Meta to build Katran on XDP?
  4. What two capabilities did Cloudflare need that ECMP could not provide?
  5. Break down Netflix's old 50-minute failover. Which parts did dark capacity remove, and why is failover then mostly a DNS change?
  6. Why did Slack choose siloing plus a manual drain over automatic detection of gray failures? What were the drain's design goals?
  7. With 8 workers and shards of 2, what fraction of customers shares a given customer's entire shard? With 2,048 workers and shards of 4, how many shards are possible?
  8. What made Shopify's sharded database less resilient than expected, and how do pods fix it?
