docs.title: Load Balancing and Multi-Server Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review the move from one server to many, load balancers, global traffic management, multi-AZ and multi-region architecture, autoscaling, service discovery and meshes, resilience patterns, and how large companies apply them. They end with traffic-path design questions and production scenarios. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What are the usual stages of growth from one server, and what breaks at each?
docs.text: One server (any reboot is an outage) → a separate managed database (the app server is still a single point of failure) → several app instances behind a load balancer (instance-local state breaks) → caches and a CDN (staleness and invalidation) → multiple Availability Zones (capacity for a lost zone, cross-zone latency) → multiple regions (replication lag, write conflicts, data residency, cost).

docs.title: 2. What does "stateless" mean for an app tier, and what must leave the instance?
docs.text: Any instance can serve any request, and losing an instance loses nothing but in-flight work. Sessions move to a shared store such as Redis (or into signed tokens), uploads go to object storage, caches become shared or tolerant of misses, scheduled jobs run once across the fleet through a per-run claim or a single scheduler, and WebSocket messages fan out through a shared channel such as a Redis adapter.

docs.title: 3. Why are sticky sessions a weak substitute for shared session storage?
docs.text: They tie a user to one instance, so that instance's failure, scale-in, or deploy logs the user out or loses work, and load becomes uneven because long sessions pile onto old instances. They are acceptable as a temporary step, not as the design.

docs.title: 4. How do you make sure a cron job runs once when ten instances run the same code?
docs.text: Claim each scheduled run: every instance tries SET with NX and an expiry on a key made of the job name and the scheduled time, only the first succeeds, and the key is left to expire rather than deleted, so an instance whose clock is late cannot run the same occurrence again. Or move scheduling out of the app into a single scheduler (a Kubernetes CronJob, a cloud scheduler) that triggers one worker. Make the job idempotent in case two runs ever overlap.

docs.title: 5. When do you scale up and when do you scale out?
docs.text: Scale up (a bigger machine) when it is simple and the workload is hard to split, such as a primary database, accepting a hard ceiling and a single point of failure. Scale out (more machines) for stateless tiers: it adds redundancy and near-linear capacity but requires statelessness and a load balancer.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?
docs.text: An L4 balancer forwards TCP or UDP connections by address and port without reading the payload: fast, protocol-agnostic, balancing per connection. An L7 balancer terminates HTTP, reads paths, headers, and cookies, and balances per request: routing rules, retries, header injection, and gRPC awareness, at more cost per request.

docs.title: 7. Which balancing algorithm would you choose for an HTTP API, a cache tier, and WebSockets?
docs.text: For an HTTP API with varying request times, least outstanding requests (or least connections). For a cache tier, consistent hashing on the key so the same key reaches the same cache and only about 1/N of keys move when a node is added. For WebSockets, least connections, because connections are long-lived and request counts mean little.

docs.title: 8. Why does modulo hashing hurt when a node is added?
docs.text: With hash(key) mod N, changing N from 4 to 5 moves about 80% of keys, so every cache goes cold at once. Consistent hashing moves only the keys that now belong to the new node, about 1/5.

docs.title: 9. What is "power of two random choices", and why is it used?
docs.text: Pick two backends at random and send to the less loaded one. It gets almost the benefit of checking every backend while avoiding herd behavior, because independent balancers rarely sample the same pair. It suits large fleets with many independent balancers or sidecars.

docs.title: 10. How are health check detection and recovery times calculated?
docs.text: Roughly interval × unhealthy threshold (plus the probe timeout) to remove a backend, and interval × healthy threshold to restore it. A 10-second interval with a threshold of 3 means up to about 30 seconds of failed requests before removal, so pair active checks with passive outlier detection.

docs.title: 11. What does it mean that load balancers "fail open"?
docs.text: When every backend fails its health check, many balancers route to all of them rather than none (AWS ALB and NLB, Envoy below its panic threshold, Azure Front Door). It prevents a total outage caused by a bad health check, but it also means a check that depends on a shared dependency stops protecting you exactly when it fails everywhere.

docs.title: 12. What are connection draining and slow start?
docs.text: Draining (AWS calls it the deregistration delay, 300 seconds by default) stops new requests to a backend being removed while in-flight requests finish. Slow start ramps a new backend's share of traffic up gradually so cold caches and JIT compilers are not hit with a full share at once.

docs.title: 13. How does the application learn the real client IP behind a load balancer?
docs.text: An L7 balancer adds X-Forwarded-For (and X-Forwarded-Proto); the app must trust only the known proxy hops, or clients can spoof the header. An L4 balancer can preserve the client IP or send the PROXY protocol header at the start of the connection, which the backend must be configured to expect.

docs.title: 14. How do you keep the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure?
docs.text: Use a managed load balancer, which runs nodes in every enabled zone behind its DNS name; or a self-managed pair sharing a virtual IP through keepalived and VRRP; or an active-active L4 tier announcing one address over BGP with ECMP and consistent hashing, as in Maglev-style designs.

docs.title: 15. What DNS routing policies are available, and what is each for?
docs.text: Geolocation (answer by the resolver's location: data residency, local content), latency-based (the region with the lowest measured latency), weighted (gradual shifts, canary regions), and failover (primary and secondary with health checks). Route 53, Cloudflare load balancing, and Azure Traffic Manager offer equivalents.

docs.title: 16. How long does a DNS-based failover take?
docs.text: Detection (interval × threshold), the DNS change itself, then resolver caches for up to the TTL, plus clients that cache longer and long-lived connections that never re-resolve. With 30 seconds of detection and a 60-second TTL, most new requests move between 30 and 90 seconds; with a 3,600-second TTL a short incident can last an hour for some users.

docs.title: 17. What is anycast, and what are its trade-offs?
docs.text: The same IP prefix is announced over BGP from many locations, and each network routes to the one its routing prefers. Failover needs no DNS change and attack traffic spreads across locations, but routing policy, not distance, picks the location, convergence takes seconds to minutes, and route changes can break long-lived TCP flows.

docs.title: 18. Why can a global L7 proxy fail over faster than DNS?
docs.text: Clients keep talking to the same anycast edge address, and the edge chooses an origin per request based on health and capacity, so there are no resolver caches to expire. The trade-offs are HTTP-only protocols, provider lock-in, and cost.

docs.title: 19. Why should failover health checks run from many locations?
docs.text: A single checker can be cut off by its own network problem and declare a healthy region dead. Checks from several regions, combined with a rule that needs enough of them to agree, avoid false failovers caused by partial network failures. Route 53, for example, treats an endpoint as healthy when more than 18% of its checkers report it healthy.

docs.title: 20. Why can a shared dependency in a regional health check disable failover?
docs.text: If every region's check fails at once because they test the same shared dependency, providers such as Route 53 treat "all unhealthy" as "all healthy" and keep answering normally. Regional checks should test what is specific to that region.

docs.title: 21. What is the difference between a region and an Availability Zone?
docs.text: An Availability Zone is one or more data centers with independent power, cooling, and networking; a region is a group of zones close enough for low-latency, often synchronous replication. Zones protect against a data center failure, regions against a regional outage or disaster.

docs.title: 22. Why is multi-AZ considered the baseline for production?
docs.text: Zone failures happen, and spreading load balancer nodes, app instances, and a database standby across two or three zones costs little extra compared with multi-region. It removes the single data center as a single point of failure with almost no change to the application.

docs.title: 23. Compare pilot light, warm standby, and active-active.
docs.text: Pilot light keeps data replicated and infrastructure defined, with compute switched off, so recovery means starting and scaling it (slowest, cheapest). Warm standby runs a smaller full copy that can serve at reduced capacity immediately and scales up during failover. Active-active serves traffic from every region all the time: the fastest recovery and best latency, but the hardest data problems and the highest cost. Recovery objectives are covered in disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: 24. How do synchronous and asynchronous replication affect RPO?
docs.text: Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy before acknowledging a write, giving an RPO of zero but adding the round-trip latency to every write, which is practical within a region. Asynchronous replication acknowledges first, so the RPO equals the replication lag at the moment of failure; it is the usual choice between regions.

docs.title: 25. What problems does active-active across regions add?
docs.text: Write conflicts when the same record changes in two regions (solved by routing each user's writes to a home region, single-writer partitioning, or conflict-free data types; last-writer-wins rules also resolve them but silently discard one of the two updates), replication lag visible to users, data residency rules about where data may live, and roughly doubled infrastructure and cross-region transfer cost.

docs.title: 26. Why must failovers be drilled regularly?
docs.text: Untested failovers fail: runbooks drift, capacity in the other region is missing, DNS TTLs are too long, and dependencies are discovered on the day. Regular drills (and evacuations, as Netflix and Slack practice) prove the path works and keep the team practiced.

docs.title: 27. What are the parts of an autoscaling group?
docs.text: A template (image, instance type, user data, role), a group with minimum, maximum, and desired size across zones, health checks that replace broken instances, and scaling policies. AWS calls them launch templates and Auto Scaling groups, Google Cloud instance templates and managed instance groups, and Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets.

docs.title: 28. How does target tracking decide how many instances to add?
docs.text: It keeps a metric near a target, assuming the metric falls in proportion to the number of instances. Ten instances at 1,500 requests per target with a target of 1,000 need about 10 × 1,500 / 1,000 = 15. It scales out quickly and in gradually.

docs.title: 29. Which metrics make good scaling signals?
docs.text: Request count per target or CPU for web tiers, backlog per instance (queue depth divided by instances) for workers, or a custom per-instance load metric. Latency and raw queue length are poor target tracking metrics because they do not fall in proportion to the fleet size.

docs.title: 30. Why does new capacity arrive minutes after a spike, and how do you compensate?
docs.text: The alarm needs several datapoints, then the instance must boot, start the application, and pass health checks. Compensate with headroom (a lower target), golden images for fast boot, warm or standby pools, and scheduled or predictive scaling for known ramps.

docs.title: 31. What are lifecycle hooks and scale-in protection for?
docs.text: Hooks pause an instance at launch (finish setup before taking traffic) or termination (drain, flush, finish jobs) until code completes the action or the heartbeat timeout expires. Scale-in protection keeps specific instances, such as a worker mid-job, from being chosen for scale-in.

docs.title: 32. What is static stability, and how does it change capacity planning?
docs.text: A statically stable service survives an impairment without having to make changes, such as launching instances during a zone failure. You run enough capacity in the remaining zones in advance: needing 12 instances, you run 6 in each of 3 zones, so losing one still leaves 12.

docs.title: 33. Why is service discovery needed?
docs.text: Instances come and go with autoscaling, deploys, and failures, and get new addresses each time. Callers need a live list of healthy instances rather than hard-coded addresses.

docs.title: 34. What is the difference between client-side and server-side discovery?
docs.text: In client-side discovery the caller reads a registry and picks an instance itself (Eureka with Spring Cloud, gRPC with DNS or xDS): no extra hop, smarter balancing, but a library per language. In server-side discovery the caller uses a stable name and a load balancer or the platform picks (cloud internal load balancers, Kubernetes Services).

docs.title: 35. What are the pitfalls of DNS-based discovery?
docs.text: Caching: resolvers and clients keep answers until the TTL or longer, and open keep-alive or HTTP/2 connections keep going to old instances. Plain DNS also cannot express health, zones, or weights. Use short TTLs, cap connection age, and retry on another instance.

docs.title: 36. How do Consul and Eureka differ?
docs.text: Consul runs an agent on each node that health-checks services, keeps a consistent catalog with Raft, and offers DNS and HTTP interfaces, a key-value store, and a mesh. Eureka is a REST registry where instances renew leases (every 30 seconds, removed after 90 seconds) and clients cache the registry; it favors availability, with a self-preservation mode during mass renewal loss.

docs.title: 37. What does a service mesh provide, and what does it cost?
docs.text: Proxies on every hop, configured by a control plane, provide mutual TLS with workload identities, authorization policy, per-request load balancing, timeouts, retries, outlier detection, traffic splitting, and uniform telemetry without code changes. The costs are proxy CPU and memory, extra latency per hop, a control plane to operate, harder debugging, and possible retry amplification.

docs.title: 38. What is Istio's ambient mode?
docs.text: A sidecarless data plane: a per-node ztunnel provides mutual TLS, L4 authorization, and L4 telemetry for all Pods on the node, and optional waypoint proxies per namespace or service add L7 features only where needed. It has been generally available since Istio 1.24 (November 2024).

docs.title: 39. How do you choose a timeout for a remote call?
docs.text: From the dependency's measured latency and an acceptable false-timeout rate, for example its p99.9 latency for a 0.1% rate, with padding when the distribution is tight. Inner timeouts must fit inside outer ones, ideally by propagating the remaining deadline budget.

docs.title: 40. When is retrying a request safe?
docs.text: When the operation is idempotent (or carries an idempotency key) and the failure is likely transient: connection errors, timeouts, 429, 502, 503, 504. Never retry client errors such as 400 or 404.

docs.title: 41. Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
docs.text: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together, and each wave hits the recovering service at once. Full jitter waits a random time between zero and the exponential backoff, spreading the same retries over time.

docs.title: 42. What is a retry storm, and how do you prevent one?
docs.text: Load amplification when many clients or many layers retry at once: three attempts at each of five layers can multiply load up to 3⁵ = 243 times. Retry at one layer only, cap attempts, add jitter, and use a retry budget that keeps retries to about 10% of traffic.

docs.title: 43. Describe the circuit breaker states.
docs.text: Closed: calls pass and results are recorded. Open: after the failure rate crosses a threshold over a minimum number of calls, calls fail fast for a cool-down period. Half-open: a few trial calls are allowed; success closes the breaker, failure reopens it.

docs.title: 44. What is the difference between a bulkhead and load shedding?
docs.text: A bulkhead partitions capacity per dependency or workload, so one slow dependency can only exhaust its own share. Load shedding rejects excess work at the entrance when the whole service is saturated, so the requests it accepts still finish quickly (protecting goodput).

docs.title: 45. Where should rate limiting happen, and how is it different from load shedding?
docs.text: At the edge (CDN, WAF, gateway) to stop abusive clients before they cost compute, and inside services to enforce per-tenant fairness. Rate limits cap each client regardless of service health; load shedding reacts to the service's own overload.

docs.title: How top companies run at scale
46. Why did Google build Maglev instead of using hardware load balancers?
docs.text: The Maglev paper lists capacity limited by a single unit, only 1+1 redundancy, little flexibility, and costly upgrades. Maglev runs on commodity servers behind ECMP, uses consistent hashing and connection tracking so flows keep their backends, and uses direct server return.

docs.title: 47. What problem did GitHub's GLB Director and Cloudflare's Unimog solve that ECMP alone could not?
docs.text: ECMP rehashes flows when servers join or leave, breaking connections, and cannot weight by load. GLB Director adds stateless directors with a "second chance" so draining servers finish their flows; Unimog makes every server a load balancer and adjusts connection shares by measured load.

docs.title: 48. How did Netflix cut region failover from about 50 minutes to under 10?
docs.text: Most of the 50 minutes was spent after the decision: provisioning, starting services, and warming them up. With "dark capacity", instances already running but held out of service, failover became mostly a DNS change.

docs.title: 49. What is shuffle sharding?
docs.text: Each customer gets a small pseudo-random subset of workers, so customers rarely share their whole subset. With 8 workers and pairs there are 28 possible shards, so a poison customer fully affects about 1 in 28 customers instead of a whole shard; Route 53 gives each domain 4 of 2,048 virtual name servers.

docs.title: 50. What are Slack's AZ cells and Shopify's pods?
docs.text: Slack siloed services so each only talks within its own Availability Zone, making a zone a cell that operators can drain in minutes without knowing the root cause. Shopify's pods give each set of shops its own isolated datastores and route every request to exactly one pod, so one pod's failure stays inside it.

docs.title: 51. Design the traffic path for the TaskFlow API serving users in Europe and North America.
docs.text:
Requirements: low latency on both continents, survive a zone and a region failure, data residency for European users.

Traffic path: a global edge (anycast L7 proxy or CDN) terminates TLS near users → per-region load balancers in two regions (one in each continent) → app fleets across three zones per region → a database with each user homed in their continent's region, replicating asynchronously for disaster recovery to a second region the residency rules allow (a second European region for European users).

Key decisions: route by home region so writes have a single owner, health checks per region from many locations, short TTLs or a global proxy for failover, capacity in each recovery region to absorb the traffic it takes over during an evacuation.

docs.title: 52. Design the traffic path for a WebSocket chat service.
docs.text:
Requirements: millions of long-lived connections, messages delivered across instances, safe deploys.

Traffic path: DNS or anycast → an L4 or WebSocket-aware L7 balancer using least connections → stateless gateway instances holding connections → a shared pub/sub channel (such as Redis or a message broker) so a message published on one instance reaches subscribers on others.

Key decisions: generous idle timeouts, connection draining with client reconnects using jitter, deploys that drain slowly (rainbow or gradual), and capacity planned per connection, not per request.

docs.title: 53. Design internal traffic for 40 gRPC microservices in Kubernetes.
docs.text:
Requirements: per-request balancing, encryption between services, consistent timeouts and telemetry.

Traffic path: services call stable names; a mesh (sidecars or ambient mode with waypoints) or client-side round_robin over headless Services balances each request; mutual TLS everywhere.

Key decisions: deadlines propagated through calls, retries owned by one layer with budgets, outlier detection, one circuit breaker per dependency, and rollout of the mesh namespace by namespace in permissive mode first.

docs.title: 54. Design the traffic path for a flash sale expected to bring ten times normal traffic.
docs.text:
Requirements: stay up and keep checkout working while browsing may degrade.

Traffic path: CDN for static assets and cacheable pages → edge rate limits and bot protection → load balancer → API fleet scaled up ahead of time by a scheduled action → a queue or virtual waiting room in front of checkout if capacity is exceeded.

Key decisions: pre-provision instead of relying on reactive scaling, load shedding by priority (checkout over recommendations), bulkheads between checkout and browsing, database connection limits, and a load test of the whole path beforehand.

docs.title: 55. Users are logged out at random after the API moved behind a load balancer with three instances. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: where sessions are stored and whether the balancer uses sticky sessions.

How to confirm: the logout happens when a request lands on a different instance; session data exists in only one instance's memory.

Likely causes and fixes: in-memory sessions. Store sessions in Redis (or use signed tokens) so any instance can serve any request; avoid relying on stickiness. See from one server to many.

docs.title: 56. Every deploy causes a short burst of 502 errors. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the target group's deregistration delay and the application's SIGTERM handling.

How to confirm: the errors line up with instances being deregistered, and the instances exit before in-flight requests finish.

Likely causes and fixes: no draining, a delay of zero, or an app that exits immediately. Set the delay just above the longest normal request, fail readiness and finish in-flight work on SIGTERM, and close idle keep-alive connections. See load balancers in depth.

docs.title: 57. One backend receives far more traffic than the others behind an L4 balancer. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the protocol and connection lifetimes.

How to confirm: clients use HTTP/2 or gRPC with long-lived connections, and per-connection balancing put most of them on the oldest instances.

Likely causes and fixes: connection-level balancing of multiplexed protocols. Use an L7 balancer, client-side per-request balancing, or a mesh, and cap connection age. See load balancers in depth.

docs.title: 58. A region failed, DNS was switched within a minute, but users kept hitting the dead region for an hour. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the record TTL and how clients hold connections.

How to confirm: the record's TTL was 3,600 seconds, and many clients kept using cached answers or open connections.

Likely causes and fixes: a long TTL and connections that never re-resolve. Lower TTLs well before incidents, recycle connections, and consider a global proxy or anycast for failover. See global traffic management.

docs.title: 59. Failover did not happen although the primary region was clearly down. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the state of every health check in the failover group during the incident.

How to confirm: all checks failed at once because they tested a shared dependency, so the DNS service treated all records as healthy.

Likely causes and fixes: a health check that is not region-specific. Check what is unique to each region, from several locations with a quorum. See global traffic management.

docs.title: 60. After failing over to the secondary region, users saw recent changes missing. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the replication mode and lag at the time of the failover.

How to confirm: asynchronous replication was several seconds or minutes behind, so the last writes never reached the secondary.

Likely causes and fixes: RPO equal to replication lag. Monitor lag, decide the acceptable RPO in advance, reconcile lost writes from the old primary afterwards, and where zero loss across regions is required, use a synchronously replicated multi-region database in nearby regions. See multi-AZ and multi-region architecture.

docs.title: 61. Latency and errors spike every weekday morning until the fleet catches up. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: scaling activity timestamps compared with the traffic ramp.

How to confirm: new instances launch after the ramp starts and take several minutes to pass health checks.

Likely causes and fixes: reactive scaling cannot follow a steep, predictable ramp. Add a scheduled minimum before the ramp, try predictive scaling in forecast-only mode, lower the target, and use warm pools. See autoscaling server fleets.

docs.title: 62. A traffic spike scaled the API to its maximum, and the site still went down. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the database's CPU and connection count during the spike.

How to confirm: the database hit its connection limit as each new instance opened its own pool.

Likely causes and fixes: the bottleneck was the database, and scaling out made it worse. Cap the fleet size, pool or proxy connections, shed load at the edge, and scale on the real bottleneck. See autoscaling server fleets.

docs.title: 63. Errors spike for a minute after every scale-in, from calls to addresses that no longer exist. What is happening?
docs.text:
What to check first: how callers discover instances and how long they cache results.

How to confirm: callers use cached registry lists, DNS answers, or keep-alive connections to terminated instances.

Likely causes and fixes: stale discovery data. Drain before termination, shorten TTLs and cache lifetimes, cap connection age, and retry connection failures on another instance. See service discovery and service mesh.

docs.title: 64. Enabling strict mutual TLS in the mesh broke a nightly job and the metrics scraper. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which callers are outside the mesh.

How to confirm: connections from workloads without a mesh identity are reset.

Likely causes and fixes: strict mode rejects plaintext clients. Migrate in permissive mode, bring every client into the mesh or give it a certificate, then switch to strict. See service discovery and service mesh.

docs.title: 65. A short database blip turned into a 20-minute outage, with traffic several times normal. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: request rates at each layer and the retry configuration of each client.

How to confirm: traces show the same request retried at several layers, with retries arriving in synchronized waves.

Likely causes and fixes: a retry storm. Retry at one layer with full jitter and a retry budget, fail fast elsewhere, and add circuit breakers. See resilience patterns across servers.

docs.title: 66. A slow reports service made the whole API unresponsive, including login. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the API's concurrency and connection pool usage by dependency.

How to confirm: every request slot was occupied by calls waiting on reports.

Likely causes and fixes: no timeouts or bulkheads. Short per-try timeouts, a separate concurrency limit per dependency, a circuit breaker around reports, and a degraded response when it is unavailable. See resilience patterns across servers.

docs.title: 67. One zone has intermittent packet loss, and users in every zone see errors. What do you do now, and what do you build next?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether errors correlate with calls that cross into the impaired zone.

How to confirm: requests from all zones that touch services in the bad zone are slow or failing, while other paths are fine.

Likely causes and fixes: a gray failure amplified by cross-zone calls. Now: remove the zone from the load balancers and DNS. Next: silo services within zones and build an incremental zone drain at the entry points, as Slack did. See how top companies run at scale.

docs.title: 68. One tenant's malformed requests keep crashing the shared worker fleet. How do you limit the damage?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the crashes start with traffic from a single tenant.

How to confirm: worker crashes follow that tenant's requests and spread across every worker.

Likely causes and fixes: every tenant shares every worker. Fix the parsing bug, then contain future cases with shuffle sharding (each tenant on a small subset of workers) or cells per tenant group. See how top companies run at scale.

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Load balancing and multi-server overview
  • From one server to many · Load balancers in depth · Global traffic management · Multi-AZ and multi-region architecture · Autoscaling server fleets · Service discovery and service mesh · Resilience patterns across servers · How top companies run at scale
  • Google SRE book: Load Balancing in the Datacenter
  • Amazon Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

docs.title: Load Balancers in Depth
docs.text: A load balancer accepts connections or requests on one address and spreads them across a pool of backends, stops sending work to backends that fail, and lets backends join and leave without clients noticing. This lesson covers the difference between layer 4 and layer 7 balancing, the balancing algorithms and when each fits, health checks, connection draining and slow start, sticky sessions, TLS, passing the client's address to the backend (X-Forwarded-For and the PROXY protocol), HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets, the cloud load balancers of AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, the main software load balancers with working Nginx and HAProxy configurations, and how to keep the load balancer itself from becoming a single point of failure.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text: Every request crosses the load balancer, so its settings decide how a failure feels to users. With default settings, an AWS Application Load Balancer needs two failed checks 30 seconds apart before it stops sending traffic to a dead instance, and it reports a removed instance as draining for 300 seconds; a deploy tool that waits for each batch to finish draining turns a five-batch rolling deploy into a 25-minute one. A load balancer that only checks whether a TCP port is open happily routes to an instance whose database pool is exhausted. A layer 4 balancer in front of gRPC services pins every request from a client to one pod. Most "the load balancer is broken" incidents are really a mismatch between the balancer's settings and how the application behaves.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE book. The chapter Load Balancing in the Datacenter describes a "lame duck" state in which a backend "is listening on its port and can serve, but is explicitly asking clients to stop sending requests", subsetting (each client talks to a subset of typically 20 to 100 backend tasks rather than all of them), and weighted round robin in which backends report their query rate, error rate, and utilization so clients can favor the healthiest ones.
  • HAProxy. Willy Tarreau's Test Driving "Power of Two Random Choices" Load Balancing benchmarked algorithms on one load balancer and found that "Least Connections consistently performs better", while power of two choices matched round robin. The post also notes that HAProxy's random algorithm now draws two servers by default.
  • NGINX. The post NGINX and the "Power of Two Choices" Load-Balancing Algorithm explains the other half of that result: two random choices are "not as effective on a single load balancer", but avoid the "herd behavior" that appears when many independent load balancers each send work to whichever backend looks least loaded.
  • AWS Elastic Load Balancing. The target group health check documentation states the fail-open rule: "If a target group contains only unhealthy registered targets, the load balancer routes requests to all those targets, regardless of their health status."
  • Kubernetes and gRPC. The Kubernetes blog post gRPC Load Balancing on Kubernetes without Tears explains that because HTTP/2 multiplexes requests over one long-lived connection, connection-level balancing stops working: "All requests will get pinned to a single destination pod."
  • Dropbox. In Dropbox traffic infrastructure: Edge network, Dropbox describes scaling its layer 4 balancers with "BGP ECMP, DSR, and consistent hashing", with IPVS as the data plane.

Popular tools and providers: AWS Application, Network, and Gateway Load Balancers; Google Cloud Application and Network Load Balancers; Azure Load Balancer, Application Gateway, and Front Door; Nginx (and the commercial F5 NGINX Plus), HAProxy, Envoy, Traefik, and Caddy; keepalived for redundant pairs; Linux IPVS; and Katran and other Maglev-style layer 4 balancers.

docs.title: What a load balancer does
docs.text:
1. Accepts traffic on a stable address (a DNS name, a virtual IP, or an anycast address) so clients never need to know backend addresses.
  2. Chooses a backend with a balancing algorithm.
  3. Checks health actively (probes) and passively (watching real responses) and removes failing backends.
  4. Shapes traffic: terminates TLS, enforces timeouts and connection limits, retries, routes by host or path, and adds headers.
  5. Reports per-backend request counts, errors, and latency, which are often the best signal you have.

Load balancers appear at several places: at the edge facing the internet, internally between services, and client-side as a library or sidecar inside the caller (gRPC, Envoy, service meshes). A proxy balancer keeps two connections per request (client to balancer, balancer to backend); a pass-through balancer forwards packets, and with direct server return (DSR) the backend answers the client directly, so the balancer only handles the smaller inbound traffic.

docs.title: Layer 4 compared with layer 7
docs.text:
Layer 4 (transport) Layer 7 (application) Sees IP addresses, ports, TCP or UDP The whole HTTP request: method, path, headers, cookies Decides Once per connection (flow) For every request Connections Packets forwarded, or a TCP proxy Client side and backend side are separate; backend connections are pooled TLS Passed through, or terminated on a TLS listener Terminated, optionally re-encrypted Can do Any TCP or UDP protocol, very high throughput, static IPs, the original client IP Host, path, and header routing, retries, header injection, WAF, compression, per-request gRPC balancing Cannot do Route by URL, retry a request, balance requests inside one HTTP/2 connection Non-HTTP protocols (outside a TCP mode); it costs more CPU per request Examples AWS NLB, Azure Load Balancer, Google passthrough Network Load Balancers, HAProxy mode tcp, the Nginx stream module, Linux IPVS AWS ALB, Google Application Load Balancers, Azure Application Gateway and Front Door, Nginx http, HAProxy mode http, Envoy

Large systems usually use both: a layer 4 tier that spreads connections across a fleet of layer 7 proxies, which then route each request.

docs.title: Balancing algorithms
docs.text:
Algorithm How it picks Fits Watch out for Round robin Next backend in turn Identical backends, requests of similar cost Slow requests pile up on whichever backend gets them Weighted round robin In turn, in proportion to weights (5:3:2 sends 500, 300, and 200 of 1,000 requests) Mixed instance sizes, gradual traffic shifts, canaries Weights are static; a weight cannot know a backend is slow today Least connections Backend with the fewest open connections Long-lived connections (WebSockets), uneven request times Counts connections, not requests; a new backend with zero connections gets a burst Least outstanding requests Backend with the fewest requests in flight (AWS ALB; Envoy's least_request) HTTP APIs whose request times vary Needs per-request tracking, so it is a layer 7 feature Random, power of two choices Pick two backends at random, send to the less loaded one Many independent balancers or sidecars, large fleets Needs a load signal; on one balancer, least connections is usually as good IP hash Hash of the client address picks the backend Rough affinity without cookies Many users behind one NAT land on one backend; most clients move when backends change Consistent hashing Hash of a key (URL, user, tenant) on a ring; the key belongs to the next backend on the ring Caches and sharded backends, where the same key should reach the same server Hot keys still overload one backend; uneven rings need virtual nodes Least time Lowest average response time (Nginx least_time) Backends in different locations or of different speeds Open-source Nginx gained it only in the 1.31 mainline; earlier it was NGINX Plus only

Two results explain the hashing and random rows:

Modulo hashing (server = hash(key) mod N), going from 4 to 5 servers:
  a key stays put only if hash mod 4 == hash mod 5, true for 4 of every 20 values
  -> 80% of keys move, and every cache in the tier goes cold at once

Consistent hashing, going from 4 to 5 servers:
  only the keys that now belong to the new server move: about 1/5
  -> 20% of keys move; the other 80% keep hitting a warm cache

Random choices (balls into bins, one million of each):
  one random choice: the fullest bin usually holds about 9
  best of two random choices: it drops to about 4

The last result is from the balanced-allocations work surveyed in The Power of Two Random Choices (Mitzenmacher, Richa, and Sitaraman). It is why two choices are almost as good as asking every backend, and why they avoid herd behavior: two balancers rarely sample the same pair.

Which to choose: start with least outstanding requests (or least connections) for HTTP APIs, round robin when requests are uniform and cheap, weighted variants for mixed capacity or traffic shifting, and consistent hashing only when data placement matters. Many balancers combine these: Nginx's random two least_conn is power of two choices using connection counts.

docs.title: Health checks
docs.text:
Active checks probe each backend on a schedule. Passive checks (Envoy calls them outlier detection) watch real responses and eject a backend that returns errors or timeouts. Use both: active checks find a backend that is down before users do, passive checks react to errors between probes.

Detection and recovery times follow directly from the settings:

time to remove  ~ interval x unhealthy threshold (+ the probe timeout)
time to restore ~ interval x healthy threshold

AWS ALB defaults (interval 30 s, unhealthy 2, healthy 5):  remove ~60 s, restore ~150 s
Tuned ALB (interval 10 s, unhealthy 2, healthy 3):           remove ~20 s, restore ~30 s
HAProxy defaults (inter 2 s, fall 3, rise 2):                remove ~6 s,  restore ~4 s
Google Cloud defaults (interval 5 s, thresholds 2 and 2):    remove ~10 s, restore ~10 s

What the check should test:

  • Readiness, not liveness. The endpoint (/readyz) answers "should this instance get new requests now?": started, connected, not draining. It is cheap and has a timeout shorter than the probe interval. The difference between liveness and readiness is covered in deploying backend services.
  • Not every dependency. If /readyz fails whenever the database is slow, every instance fails at the same moment. Balancers then fail open: AWS ALB and NLB route to all targets when none are healthy, Envoy ignores health once fewer than 50% of hosts are healthy (its panic threshold), and Azure Front Door spreads traffic across all origins when every probe fails. Failing open is better than serving nothing, but it means the health check stopped protecting you. AWS lets you tune the threshold with the target_group_health.unhealthy_state_routing attributes.
  • Hysteresis. Requiring several consecutive failures and successes stops a backend from flapping in and out on a single slow response.

docs.title: Connection draining, deregistration delay, and slow start
docs.text:
• Draining removes a backend from rotation for new requests while its in-flight requests finish. On AWS this is the deregistration delay (default 300 seconds, range 0 to 3,600). The load balancer stops sending new requests at once; if the target has no requests in flight it finishes deregistering early, but it is still shown as draining until the delay ends, so tools that wait for the unused state wait the full delay. Set it a little above your longest normal request (30 seconds for TaskFlow API); the default makes every rolling deploy wait five minutes per batch.
  • The application must cooperate. On SIGTERM it fails readiness, keeps serving in-flight requests, and closes idle keep-alive connections, as shown in deploying backend services. A target that closes connections before the delay ends returns errors to the clients still using them.
  • Long-lived connections never "finish". WebSockets and streams are cut when the delay ends. Clients must reconnect with random jitter, or you need longer drains (see rainbow deployments in advanced deployment patterns).
  • Slow start ramps a backend's share of traffic up from zero so a cold instance (empty caches, unwarmed JIT, no pooled connections) is not hit with a full share at once. AWS ALB applies it to newly registered targets over 30 to 900 seconds, rising linearly. HAProxy's slowstart applies to a server returning after being seen as down, not at startup. In Nginx, slow_start is still an NGINX Plus feature. ALB cannot combine slow start with the least outstanding requests or weighted random algorithms.

docs.title: Sticky sessions
docs.text:
Stickiness (session affinity) sends a client back to the same backend:

  • Load balancer cookie: the balancer adds its own cookie (AWS ALB AWSALB, HAProxy cookie ... insert, Nginx sticky cookie).
  • Application cookie: the balancer follows a cookie your app sets (ALB application-based stickiness).
  • Source IP: hash or affinity by client address (NLB source_ip, Azure Load Balancer client IP persistence, Nginx ip_hash).

Stickiness has a real cost: load stays uneven (a scale-out helps only new users), sessions on a failed backend are lost, and some algorithms cannot use it (ALB's weighted random). Use it for performance or protocol reasons (Socket.IO long-polling, warm per-instance caches, keeping a canary user on one version) and never as the only copy of session data, as explained in from one server to many.

docs.title: TLS at the load balancer
docs.text: Most HTTP setups terminate TLS at the balancer with a managed certificate; re-encryption to backends adds encryption inside the network, and passthrough (a layer 4 balancer routing by SNI) keeps the private key off the balancer at the cost of all layer 7 features. The trade-offs, certificate handling, and troubleshooting are covered in TLS termination and troubleshooting. AWS ALB can also check client certificates itself (mutual TLS in verify mode) or pass them to targets in a header (passthrough mode).

docs.title: Passing the client's address: X-Forwarded-For and the PROXY protocol
docs.text:
Behind a proxy, the backend's TCP peer is the balancer, so the client's address must travel separately:

  • Layer 7: headers. The balancer appends the address it saw to X-Forwarded-For (client, proxy1, proxy2), and sets X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-Host; the standard Forwarded header (RFC 7239) carries the same information. Any client can send a fake X-Forwarded-For, so a backend must trust only the entries added by its own proxies: count hops from the right. In Express, app.set("trust proxy", 1) trusts exactly one hop; in Nginx, set_real_ip_from with real_ip_header and real_ip_recursive does the same.
  • Layer 4: the PROXY protocol. A TCP balancer cannot add HTTP headers, so it prepends a small header to the connection (text in version 1, binary in version 2) carrying the original addresses and ports. AWS NLB sends it when proxy_protocol_v2.enabled is true; HAProxy sends it with send-proxy-v2 and accepts it with accept-proxy; Nginx accepts it with listen ... proxy_protocol. Both sides must agree: a backend that does not expect the header sees garbage at the start of every connection, and one that expects it rejects connections that lack it. Some layer 4 balancers (AWS NLB with instance targets, for example) instead preserve the client's source IP, so no header is needed.

docs.title: HTTP/2, gRPC, and WebSockets
docs.text:
• HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one long-lived connection. Behind a layer 4 balancer, every request on that connection reaches one backend; a layer 7 balancer balances each request (stream) separately. AWS ALB sends HTTP/2 or gRPC to targets when the target group's protocol version is HTTP2 or GRPC.
  • gRPC clients keep one channel open for a long time, so behind a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service (connection-level balancing) a few pods do all the work. Fixes, from least to most infrastructure: client-side balancing (a headless Service, a dns:/// target, and the round_robin policy, since the default pick_first uses one address), a maximum connection age on the server (grpc.max_connection_age_ms in grpc-js) so clients reconnect and rebalance, or an L7 proxy or service mesh that balances per call (see service discovery and service mesh).
  • WebSockets start as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket and then become a long-lived tunnel; the balancer chooses a backend once, at connect time. Use least connections, set idle timeouts above your heartbeat interval (the ALB idle timeout defaults to 60 seconds, Nginx's proxy_read_timeout to 60 seconds), and send pings more often than that.

docs.title: Timeouts and retries at the balancer
docs.text:
Setting What it limits Typical value for TaskFlow API Connect timeout to backend Time to open a TCP connection 1 to 3 s; a healthy backend in the same region connects in milliseconds Response (read) timeout Time waiting for the backend to respond A little above the slowest normal endpoint, such as 30 s Client idle timeout Idle time on the client connection 60 s (ALB default) Backend keep-alive How long idle backend connections stay open The app's keepAliveTimeout must be longer than the balancer's, or requests fail with 502 Retries Sending a failed request to another backend One retry, for connection failures and idempotent requests only

Retries are where balancers differ most. Nginx retries on error and timeout by default (proxy_next_upstream), but never passes a POST, PATCH, or LOCK to the next server after it reached one, unless you add non_idempotent. HAProxy retries only connection failures by default (retry-on conn-failure); its manual warns that the other retry conditions replay requests whatever their method, so use them only when the API has replay protection such as idempotency keys. Retrying at several layers multiplies load during an outage; budgets and backoff are covered in resilience patterns across servers.

docs.title: Software load balancers
docs.text:
Nginx HAProxy Envoy Traefik Typical role Web server and reverse proxy that also balances Dedicated, very fast L4 and L7 balancer Sidecar, gateway, and mesh data plane, configured over APIs (xDS) Edge router that discovers backends from Docker or Kubernetes Algorithms Round robin, weights, least_conn, ip_hash, hash ... consistent, random two, least_time (1.31 mainline) roundrobin, static-rr, leastconn, first, source, uri, hdr, random, and more; random with two draws is the default since 3.3 Round robin, least request (two choices by default), ring hash, Maglev, random Weighted round robin (default), power of two choices, highest random weight, least time Health checks Passive (max_fails, fail_timeout) in open source; active checks in NGINX Plus Active HTTP and TCP checks, passive observation Active checks and outlier detection Active checks and passive health checks Runtime changes Reload; DNS re-resolution with resolve Runtime API (drain, weights, add servers) Full dynamic configuration Automatic from providers

Open-source Nginx gained several former NGINX Plus features recently: resolve in 1.27.3, sticky, route, and drain in 1.29.6, upstream keepalive by default in 1.29.7, and least_time in the 1.31 mainline. Distribution packages often ship older versions, so check nginx -v before relying on them.

docs.title: Making the load balancer highly available
docs.text:
• Managed cloud balancers are already a redundant fleet: AWS creates a load balancer node in every enabled Availability Zone and returns their addresses from the balancer's DNS name. Your job is to enable at least two zones, point DNS at the name (an alias record), not at an IP address, and let clients re-resolve.
  • A self-managed pair shares a virtual IP with keepalived, which implements VRRP (RFC 5798): the master holds the address and sends advertisements; when they stop, the backup claims the address and announces it with gratuitous ARP. Failover takes seconds, but the backup sits idle, and in most clouds moving an IP requires an API call rather than VRRP on the local network.
  • An active-active layer 4 tier announces the same address from many balancers over BGP; routers spread flows across them with equal-cost multipath (ECMP). Because a router may rehash flows when a balancer joins or leaves, the balancers use consistent hashing (and connection tracking) so that a flow keeps reaching the same backend. This is the design of Google's Maglev and similar systems, described in how top companies run at scale.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choose Avoid Public HTTP API or website on a cloud Managed L7 balancer (ALB, Google Application LB, Application Gateway) with least outstanding requests One public IP per instance; DNS round robin across instances Non-HTTP TCP or UDP protocol, static IPs, millions of connections Managed L4 balancer (NLB, Azure Load Balancer) with the PROXY protocol or client IP preservation An L7 balancer in TCP mode as a workaround for everything gRPC between services L7 proxy or mesh, or client-side round_robin with a headless Service A plain L4 Service with long-lived channels Cache tier keyed by URL or user Consistent hashing Round robin (every node caches everything) or modulo hashing Many balancers or sidecars choosing independently Power of two choices (random two, Envoy least_request) Every balancer chasing the globally least-loaded backend Self-hosted on VMs or bare metal Nginx or HAProxy, with keepalived for a redundant pair A single balancer with no standby Sessions in memory you cannot remove yet Sticky sessions as a temporary measure Relying on stickiness for correctness long term

docs.title: Nginx as a layer 7 balancer for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-api.conf: L7 balancing with TLS, retries, and WebSockets
upstream taskflow_api {
    zone taskflow_api 64k;                # shared state across worker processes
    least_conn;
    server 10.0.1.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s max_conns=200;
    server 10.0.2.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s max_conns=200;
    server 10.0.3.11:3000 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s max_conns=200;
    server 10.0.9.11:3000 backup;         # used only when all others are unavailable
    keepalive 32;
    keepalive_timeout 60s;
}

upstream taskflow_realtime {
    zone taskflow_realtime 64k;
    least_conn;
    sticky cookie tf_srv expires=1h path=/ httponly secure samesite=lax;  # nginx 1.29.6+
    server 10.0.1.11:3001;
    server 10.0.2.11:3001;
    server 10.0.3.11:3001 drain;          # keeps its sticky clients, gets no new ones
}

server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name api.taskflow.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/api.taskflow.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/api.taskflow.example.com/privkey.pem;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    proxy_connect_timeout 2s;
    proxy_read_timeout    30s;
    proxy_send_timeout    30s;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_api;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;           # default since 1.29.7; needed for keepalive before
        proxy_set_header Connection "";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $request_id;
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502 http_503 http_504;
        proxy_next_upstream_tries 2;      # the original attempt plus one retry
        proxy_next_upstream_timeout 5s;
    }

    location /realtime/ {
        proxy_pass http://taskflow_realtime;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
        proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_read_timeout 1h;            # idle sockets stay open; clients ping every 30 s
    }
}
  • max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s is passive health checking: three failed attempts within 10 seconds mark a server unavailable for 10 seconds. What counts as a failure is defined by proxy_next_upstream.
  • max_conns=200 caps concurrent connections per server, so one slow server cannot absorb unlimited work. backup cannot be combined with the hash, ip_hash, or random methods.
  • The /realtime/ upstream keeps Socket.IO clients on one server with a cookie and uses drain to empty a server before maintenance. Both need nginx 1.29.6 or later; on older open-source versions use hash $remote_addr consistent.

Two more upstream patterns:

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-cache-tier.conf: hashing and two random choices
upstream thumbnail_cache {
    hash $request_uri consistent;         # ketama: adding a server moves about 1/N of URLs
    server 10.0.5.11:8080;
    server 10.0.5.12:8080;
    server 10.0.5.13:8080;
}

upstream taskflow_api_fleet {
    zone taskflow_api_fleet 64k;
    random two least_conn;                # power of two choices on connection counts
    server 10.0.1.11:3000;
    server 10.0.1.12:3000;
    server 10.0.2.11:3000;
    server 10.0.2.12:3000;
}

docs.title: A layer 4 tier with the PROXY protocol
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/nginx.conf (stream section of the L4 tier): route TLS by SNI without decrypting
stream {
    map_hash_bucket_size 64;              # default follows the CPU cache line; long names need more
    map $ssl_preread_server_name $tls_pool {
        api.taskflow.example.com  taskflow_api_tls;
        default                   taskflow_web_tls;
    }

    upstream taskflow_api_tls {
        least_conn;
        server 10.0.1.11:8443;
        server 10.0.2.11:8443;
    }

    upstream taskflow_web_tls {
        server 10.0.1.21:8443;
        server 10.0.2.21:8443;
    }

    server {
        listen 443;
        ssl_preread on;                   # read the SNI name from the ClientHello
        proxy_pass $tls_pool;
        proxy_protocol on;                # prepend the client's address to each connection
        proxy_connect_timeout 2s;
    }
}

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/taskflow-api-node.conf: each API node accepts the PROXY protocol
server {
    listen 8443 ssl proxy_protocol;
    server_name api.taskflow.example.com;
    ssl_certificate     /etc/nginx/tls/api.taskflow.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/nginx/tls/api.taskflow.example.com/privkey.pem;

    set_real_ip_from 10.0.0.0/16;         # only the L4 tier may assert a client address
    real_ip_header   proxy_protocol;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;   # now the real client address
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto https;
    }
}

The node terminates TLS itself, so the L4 tier never holds a private key, yet the app still sees the real client address.

docs.title: HAProxy for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# /etc/haproxy/haproxy.cfg: TLS termination, health checks, and slow start (HAProxy 3.4)
global
    log stdout format raw local0
    stats socket /run/haproxy/admin.sock mode 660 level admin
    ssl-default-bind-options ssl-min-ver TLSv1.2

defaults
    mode http
    log global
    option httplog
    option forwardfor                  # append the client address to X-Forwarded-For
    option redispatch                  # a retry may go to another server
    retries 2
    retry-on conn-failure              # the default: never replay a request that was sent
    timeout connect 3s
    timeout client 60s
    timeout server 30s
    timeout http-request 10s
    timeout http-keep-alive 10s
    timeout tunnel 1h                  # WebSocket connections after the upgrade

frontend api
    bind :80
    bind :443 ssl crt /etc/haproxy/certs/api.taskflow.example.com.pem alpn h2,http/1.1
    http-request redirect scheme https code 301 unless { ssl_fc }
    http-request set-header X-Forwarded-Proto https if { ssl_fc }
    use_backend taskflow_realtime if { path_beg /realtime/ }
    default_backend taskflow_api

backend taskflow_api
    balance leastconn
    option httpchk
    http-check send meth GET uri /readyz ver HTTP/1.1 hdr Host api.taskflow.example.com
    http-check expect status 200
    default-server inter 2s fall 3 rise 2 slowstart 30s maxconn 200
    server api1 10.0.1.11:3000 check
    server api2 10.0.2.11:3000 check
    server api3 10.0.3.11:3000 check

backend taskflow_realtime
    balance leastconn
    cookie TFSRV insert indirect nocache httponly secure
    option httpchk
    http-check send meth GET uri /readyz ver HTTP/1.1 hdr Host api.taskflow.example.com
    http-check expect status 200
    default-server inter 2s fall 3 rise 2
    server rt1 10.0.1.11:3001 check cookie rt1
    server rt2 10.0.2.11:3001 check cookie rt2
  • inter 2s fall 3 rise 2 removes a server after about six seconds of failed checks and restores it after two passing checks; slowstart 30s then ramps its weight and connection limit up over 30 seconds.
  • retry-on conn-failure plus option redispatch retries only requests that never reached a server, on a different server, so a POST that timed out is not sent twice.
  • cookie TFSRV insert indirect nocache makes HAProxy add its own persistence cookie for the real-time backend only.

Draining a server through the runtime API before maintenance:

# Stop new traffic to api2; established connections finish, health checks continue
echo "set server taskflow_api/api2 state drain" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
echo "show servers state taskflow_api" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock
# ... patch or redeploy api2, wait until /readyz passes ...
echo "set server taskflow_api/api2 state ready" | socat stdio /run/haproxy/admin.sock

docs.title: Tuning an AWS target group
docs.text:
# Health checks: probe /readyz every 10 s; 2 failures remove, 3 successes restore
aws elbv2 modify-target-group \
  --target-group-arn "<target-group-arn>" \
  --health-check-path /readyz \
  --health-check-interval-seconds 10 \
  --health-check-timeout-seconds 5 \
  --unhealthy-threshold-count 2 \
  --healthy-threshold-count 3 \
  --matcher HttpCode=200

# Drain for 30 s instead of 300, and balance on requests in flight
aws elbv2 modify-target-group-attributes \
  --target-group-arn "<target-group-arn>" \
  --attributes \
    Key=deregistration_delay.timeout_seconds,Value=30 \
    Key=load_balancing.algorithm.type,Value=least_outstanding_requests

# Watch target states: initial, healthy, unhealthy, draining, unused
aws elbv2 describe-target-health --target-group-arn "<target-group-arn>"

To use slow start instead (slow_start.duration_seconds, 30 to 900), keep round_robin, because ALB does not combine slow start with least outstanding requests.

docs.title: Reading the client address in Express
docs.text:
// src/client-ip.js: the client address behind exactly one load balancer
import express from "express";

export const app = express();
app.set("trust proxy", 1);    // trust the last hop only: the load balancer

app.get("/whoami", (req, res) => {
  // X-Forwarded-For "203.0.113.9, 198.51.100.7" from the balancer at 10.0.1.5:
  // req.ip is "198.51.100.7", the address the balancer itself saw.
  // "203.0.113.9" may have been typed by the client, so it is ignored.
  res.json({ ip: req.ip, protocol: req.protocol });
});

Use the same rule anywhere the address matters, such as rate limits, audit logs, and allowlists: take the address added by your own outermost proxy, never the leftmost entry.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Prefer managed, multi-zone load balancers; self-manage only with a redundant pair or tier.
  • Use L7 balancing for HTTP and gRPC, L4 for other protocols or when you need static IPs and maximum throughput.
  • Default to least outstanding requests or least connections for APIs; use consistent hashing only where data placement matters.
  • Health-check a cheap readiness endpoint; keep dependencies out of liveness, and know what your balancer does when every target fails.
  • Tune check intervals and thresholds so detection takes seconds, not a minute, without flapping.
  • Set the deregistration delay just above your longest normal request, and make the app fail readiness and drain on SIGTERM.
  • Use slow start or a warm-up for instances with cold caches.
  • Keep app keep-alive timeouts longer than the balancer's idle timeout.
  • Retry at one layer only, and only for idempotent requests or requests that never reached a backend.
  • Trust forwarded client addresses only from your own proxies, and enable the PROXY protocol on both ends at once.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• One backend is overloaded while the others idle. Detect: per-backend request rate or CPU is very uneven, often for gRPC or HTTP/2 traffic. Cause: connection-level balancing of long-lived multiplexed connections, or sticky sessions. Fix: L7 per-request balancing, client-side round_robin, or a maximum connection age on the server; remove stickiness that is not needed.
  • Intermittent 502 errors during quiet periods. Detect: balancer logs show the backend closed the connection; 502s cluster on idle, reused connections. Cause: the app's keep-alive timeout (Node defaults to 5 seconds) is shorter than the balancer's idle timeout, so the app closes a connection the balancer is about to reuse. Fix: set server.keepAliveTimeout above the balancer's idle timeout.
  • Health checks pass while users get errors. Detect: targets show healthy, yet the 5xx rate is high. Cause: a TCP or / check that does not exercise what requests need. Fix: a /readyz that checks readiness cheaply, plus passive outlier detection.
  • Every target turned unhealthy at once, and traffic kept flowing to broken instances. Detect: all targets unhealthy at the same moment, often during a database incident, and the balancer failing open. Cause: the health check depends on a shared dependency. Fix: check only local readiness, and handle dependency failures inside the app with timeouts and degradation.
  • Deploys take 25 minutes. Detect: each batch waits in draining for five minutes. Cause: the default 300-second deregistration delay. Fix: set it just above the longest normal request, such as 30 seconds, after confirming the app drains on SIGTERM.
  • WebSocket users are disconnected every minute. Detect: reconnects every 60 seconds on idle sockets. Cause: the balancer's idle timeout with no traffic on the socket. Fix: heartbeat pings more often than the idle timeout, or a longer idle timeout for the real-time route.
  • All users share one rate limit, or logs show only the balancer's address. Detect: req.ip is the balancer's private address for every request. Cause: trust proxy is not set, or the PROXY protocol is enabled on one side only. Fix: trust exactly your proxy hops, and enable the PROXY protocol on the balancer and the backend together.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Layer 4 / layer 7 load balancing: Balancing per connection on addresses and ports, or per request on HTTP content.
  • Target, backend, upstream: A server the balancer can send traffic to.
  • Active health check: A probe sent to each backend on a schedule.
  • Passive health check (outlier detection): Removing a backend based on errors in real traffic.
  • Fail open (panic mode): Sending traffic to all backends when too few are healthy.
  • Connection draining (deregistration delay): Letting in-flight requests finish on a backend that gets no new ones.
  • Slow start: Ramping a new backend's share of traffic up gradually.
  • Sticky session (session affinity): Routing a client to the same backend repeatedly.
  • Consistent hashing: Mapping keys to backends so that adding or removing one moves only about 1/N of the keys.
  • Power of two choices: Picking the less loaded of two random backends.
  • PROXY protocol: A header at the start of a TCP connection that carries the client's original address.
  • VRRP / virtual IP: A protocol and shared address that let a standby balancer take over from a failed one.
  • ECMP: Equal-cost multipath routing, which spreads flows across several next hops, such as a tier of balancers.
  • Direct server return (DSR): Backends replying to clients directly, bypassing the balancer on the way back.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Thinking round robin spreads load evenly when request costs differ.
  • Health-checking / or a TCP port and calling the service healthy.
  • Putting database checks in the endpoint the balancer uses, so one database blip removes every instance.
  • Leaving the 300-second deregistration delay in place and blaming the pipeline for slow deploys.
  • Trusting the leftmost X-Forwarded-For entry for rate limits or access control.
  • Enabling the PROXY protocol on the balancer but not on the backend, or the reverse.
  • Expecting a layer 4 balancer to spread gRPC or HTTP/2 requests.
  • Retrying non-idempotent requests at the balancer and at the client.
  • Forgetting that the balancer itself needs redundancy.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What can a layer 7 balancer do that a layer 4 balancer cannot, and when would you still choose layer 4?
  2. A target group checks every 15 seconds with an unhealthy threshold of 3 and a healthy threshold of 4. Roughly how long does it take to remove a dead instance, and to restore a recovered one? (About 45 seconds; about 60 seconds.)
  3. Why does consistent hashing suit a cache tier better than modulo hashing? What share of keys move when a tier grows from 9 to 10 servers with each? (Modulo: about 90%; consistent: about 10%.)
  4. Why does power of two choices help most when there are many independent balancers?
  5. What does "fail open" mean, which balancers do it, and why does a health check that tests the database make it more likely?
  6. Explain connection draining, the deregistration delay, and slow start, and how each protects users during a rolling deploy.
  7. How does a backend learn the client's real address behind an L7 balancer, and behind an L4 balancer? What breaks if only one side enables the PROXY protocol?
  8. Compare a keepalived pair, a managed cloud balancer, and an ECMP tier as ways to keep the balancer itself available.
