docs.title: Multi-AZ and Multi-Region Architecture
docs.text:
A service in one data center fails with that data center. Cloud providers group data centers into Availability Zones (independent failure domains many kilometers apart; AWS keeps a region's zones within 100 km of each other) and regions (separate geographic areas, each with several zones). This lesson explains why running across several zones is the baseline for production and how to size it so that losing a zone needs no emergency scaling; when a second region is worth its cost; the active-passive and active-active designs; synchronous and asynchronous replication and what they mean for data loss (RPO); write conflicts and the global databases that handle them; routing users to a home region; data residency; failover runbooks and drills; and how each step multiplies the bill.

Traffic steering between regions is covered in global traffic management, and recovery objectives and DR strategies in disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO; this lesson connects them to the shape of the application and its data.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Zones fail: power, cooling, networking, or a bad change can take one out, and a service whose instances, NAT gateway, or database all sit in that zone goes down with it. Spreading across zones costs little: managed load balancers and databases support it out of the box, and the price is some spare capacity and cross-zone data transfer.

Regions are a different decision. The compute is easy to copy; the data is not. AWS's multi-Region guidance puts it bluntly: "Challenges around data consistency and latency make it very difficult to take an existing application that was designed for a single Region and make it multi-Region." A second region doubles much of the infrastructure, adds replication lag and conflicts, and introduces a failover procedure that fails in its own ways if it is not practised. Done for the right reasons it removes a whole class of outage; done by default it can lower availability.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon: static stability. The Builders' Library article Static stability using Availability Zones defines the goal ("In a statically stable design, the overall system keeps working even when a dependency becomes impaired") and explains that with three Availability Zones Amazon overprovisions by 50 percent, so the remaining zones absorb a lost one without launching new capacity during the event.
  • AWS multi-Region fundamentals. The guide Understanding the data frames the trade-off: "By definition, a multi-Region architecture includes network partitions between Regions, so you have to choose between availability and consistency." It warns that when writes replicate synchronously across Regions, "write latency increases by an order of magnitude", and that "Most workloads that use a multi-Region approach for resilience won't require an active-active approach."
  • Netflix: active-active. In Active-Active for Multi-Regional Resiliency Netflix lists its rules: services must be stateless, with "all data / state replication" handled in the data tier, and "there should not be any cross-regional calls on user's call path". The later post Project Nimble: Region Evacuation Reimagined describes cutting a full region evacuation to "8 minutes, as opposed to the 50 minutes it used to take", while remaining cost neutral.
  • Slack: zones as cells. In Slack's Migration to a Cellular Architecture Slack describes "siloed" services that only take traffic from and send traffic within their own zone, and a control that removes traffic from an Availability Zone "within 5 minutes", in steps as small as 1%.
  • Amazon DynamoDB global tables. The documentation on how global tables work shows the core trade-off in one product: multi-Region eventual consistency replicates "typically within a second or less" with a "last writer wins" rule for conflicts, while multi-Region strong consistency replicates synchronously, needs exactly three Regions, and offers an RPO of zero at the cost of higher write latency.

Popular tools and providers: multi-AZ managed databases (Amazon RDS and Aurora, Google Cloud SQL, Azure Database), MongoDB Atlas multi-region and global clusters, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB global tables, Google Cloud Spanner, Azure Cosmos DB, and CockroachDB; Amazon Application Recovery Controller (zonal shift and Region switch), AWS Fault Injection Service, and Kubernetes topology spread constraints and traffic distribution.

docs.title: Failure domains
docs.text:
Failure domain What fails What protects you Process or instance A crash, an out-of-memory kill, a bad host Several instances behind a load balancer, health checks Availability Zone Power, cooling, or networking in one data center group; a zonal deploy gone wrong Instances, load balancer nodes, NAT, and database members in every zone Region A regional service or control-plane outage A second region with replicated data Shared global dependency A global control plane, DNS or CDN provider, identity provider Avoiding global dependencies on the request path; fallbacks Change A bad deploy or configuration pushed everywhere at once Staged rollouts: one box, one zone, one region (see advanced deployment patterns)

The last row is a reminder that redundancy alone does not stop the most common outages: a bad change copied to every zone and region breaks all of them together.

docs.title: Multi-AZ is the baseline
docs.text:
AWS describes its Availability Zones as "within 100 km (60 miles) of each other" and connected by networking "sufficient to accomplish synchronous replication between AZs". That is what makes multi-AZ cheap: light needs about a millisecond for a 100 km round trip, so a database can wait for a copy in another zone before acknowledging a write.

What to spread across zones:

  • Load balancer nodes (enable at least two zones; three is common).
  • Application instances, evenly, so each zone carries its share (in Kubernetes, topology spread constraints; see scaling and resource management).
  • NAT gateways and other per-zone network pieces, one per zone, so a zone failure does not cut the others off (see cloud building blocks).
  • Database members. Managed relational databases keep a synchronous standby in another zone; a MongoDB replica set with one member per zone and w: "majority" acknowledges a write only after two of three members have it, so the loss of any one zone loses no acknowledged write.
  • Caches and queues with replicas in other zones, or at least the ability to start empty without overloading the database.

docs.title: Sizing for a lost zone
docs.text:
Static stability means the remaining zones already have enough capacity when one fails, because launching instances during a zonal incident is exactly when it is least reliable:

TaskFlow API needs 12 instances at peak.

Zones N    each zone must carry    instances per zone    total    spare capacity
  2        peak / 1 = 100%         12                    24       100%
  3        peak / 2 =  50%          6                    18        50%
  4        peak / 3 =  33%          4                    16        33%

total capacity = peak x N / (N - 1)

Three zones are the usual sweet spot: half the spare capacity of two zones, and a majority (two of three) survives for databases that elect a leader.

docs.title: Cross-zone traffic and zone affinity
docs.text: Traffic between zones is fast but not free: AWS notes that "Traffic that crosses an Availability Zone boundary typically incurs a data transfer charge." Chatty services can keep calls inside their zone: Kubernetes Services support trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone, load balancers can turn cross-zone balancing off per target group, and Slack's cellular design siloes whole request paths inside one zone. Zone affinity also contains "gray" failures, where a zone is degraded rather than down: you can drain it on purpose with a tool such as ARC zonal shift, which moves load balancer traffic away from one zone until you cancel it or it expires.

docs.title: Why go multi-region, and why not
docs.text:
Good reasons:

  • A regional outage is not acceptable for your recovery time objective, as agreed in a business impact analysis (see disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO).
  • Users on several continents need lower latency than one region can give, even with a CDN.
  • Data residency: some data must stay in a country or region.
  • Blast radius: regions as large cells, so one region's failure or bad deploy affects only its users.

Costs: roughly double the infrastructure for a hot second region, cross-region data transfer, replication lag or slower writes, conflict handling, a routing layer, and a failover procedure that must be rehearsed. If none of the good reasons apply, multi-AZ plus backups copied to another region is usually the right answer.

docs.title: Active-passive
docs.text:
In active-passive designs, one region serves users and a second waits. They differ in how much of the second region is running, which sets the recovery time:

Strategy Second region Typical recovery Notes Backup and restore Backups and infrastructure code only Hours Cheapest; depends on rebuilding everything from code Pilot light Live data replica, compute switched off Tens of minutes Start and scale compute during failover Warm standby Live data replica, a small running copy Minutes Scale up during failover

Failover means: promote the replica, scale compute, shift traffic, verify. The details, timings, and worked RPO and RTO examples are in disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: Active-active
docs.text:
In active-active designs every region serves users all the time. The differences are all about writes:

  1. Read local, write global. Reads are served from a local replica; every write goes to one primary region. Simple and conflict-free, but users far from the primary pay a cross-region round trip on writes, and a user who writes and then reads locally can see the old value. Aurora Global Database works this way (with optional write forwarding from secondary regions).
  2. Home region per user or tenant. Each record has one owning region: EU customers' data is written in the EU, US customers' data in the US, and each partition is replicated to the other region for recovery. Most writes are local and there are still no conflicts. This is the cell idea applied to regions, and it is what AWS's guidance suggests when it notes you can "shard clients so that half of the clients are aligned to Region one and half are aligned to Region two".
  3. Multi-writer. Every region accepts writes for the same records. Either replication is asynchronous and conflicts are resolved after the fact (DynamoDB global tables in eventual mode, Cosmos DB with multi-region writes), or writes reach a synchronous quorum across regions (Spanner, DynamoDB in strong mode, CockroachDB) and every write pays cross-region latency.

Most teams that need active-active should use the first or second pattern: one writer per record removes the hardest problem.

docs.title: Synchronous or asynchronous replication
docs.text:
Synchronous Asynchronous A write is acknowledged After a copy exists in another region (or a quorum of regions) After the local commit; the copy follows Data lost if the region is destroyed (RPO) None for acknowledged writes Whatever had not replicated: the replication lag Write latency Adds at least one cross-region round trip Unchanged Availability coupling Writes stall if the remote copy is unreachable (unless a quorum survives) Regions write independently

The latency floor comes from distance. Light in fiber travels about 200 km per millisecond:

Data centers about 480 km apart (northern Virginia to central Ohio): >= 4.8 ms per round trip
About 1,090 km apart (Dublin to Frankfurt):                           >= 10.9 ms
About 5,460 km apart (Dublin to northern Virginia):                   >= 54.6 ms

A request that makes 5 sequential writes, each waiting for a copy in the other region:
  nearby pair:          5 x  4.8 ms = 24 ms extra, at minimum
  transatlantic pair:   5 x 54.6 ms = 273 ms extra, at minimum

Asynchronous replication with 2 s of lag at 500 writes per second:
  losing the region loses about 2 x 500 = 1,000 acknowledged writes

That is why synchronous multi-region databases place regions in nearby pairs or triangles, and why asynchronous designs must monitor lag against the RPO: lag that quietly grows from one second to ten minutes turns a small data loss into a large one.

docs.title: Write conflicts
docs.text:
With asynchronous multi-writer replication, two regions can accept different updates to the same record before either sees the other's. If a user renames a task in the EU while a colleague renames it in the US a second later, both commits succeed locally, and replication must then choose:

  • Last writer wins (LWW): the update with the later timestamp survives and the other disappears silently. DynamoDB global tables (eventual mode) resolve conflicts "using the modification with the latest internal timestamp on a per-item basis", and Cosmos DB uses the _ts timestamp by default. Simple, but it loses data, and clock skew decides what "later" means.
  • Merge: application rules or data types designed to merge (counters, sets, CRDTs) combine both updates. Cosmos DB lets you register a merge procedure and writes unresolved conflicts to a conflicts feed.
  • Prevent: give each record a single writing region (the home-region pattern), use conditional writes with version numbers, or use a synchronous store that rejects concurrent updates (DynamoDB in strong mode returns a ReplicatedWriteConflictException that can be retried).

Some invariants cannot be enforced across asynchronous regions at all. "Every username is unique" needs a single place that decides, such as one region, a strongly consistent global table, or a naming scheme that makes collisions impossible.

docs.title: Global databases
docs.text:
Database Model Where writes go Across regions RPO if a region is lost Aurora Global Database One primary Region, up to 10 read-only secondary Regions The primary (secondaries can forward writes) Asynchronous storage-level replication, "typically under a second" The replication lag; a planned switchover loses nothing DynamoDB global tables, eventual (MREC) Multi-active replicas in any Regions Any replica Asynchronous, last writer wins per item The replication delay, "usually a few seconds" DynamoDB global tables, strong (MRSC) Exactly three Regions: three replicas, or two plus a witness Any replica Synchronous to at least one other Region Zero Spanner, multi-region configuration Typically read-write replicas in two regions plus a witness in a third; a default leader region Leader replicas, with a quorum across regions Strongly consistent Zero for committed writes Cosmos DB, multi-region writes Every region accepts writes Any region Asynchronous, conflicts resolved by LWW or a merge procedure Depends on configuration MongoDB Atlas global clusters Up to nine zones, each zone's shards with their primary in the zone's highest-priority region The zone that owns the document Replica sets can span regions Depends on write concern

Read the fine print for each: transactions, time-to-live deletes, and secondary indexes often behave differently across regions (DynamoDB's strong mode, for example, does not support transactions or TTL).

docs.title: Routing users to their home region
docs.text:
The home-region pattern needs three pieces:

  1. A directory: a small, globally replicated mapping from user or tenant to home region, read at sign-in.
  2. A routing signal: the home region travels with each request as a signed token claim or cookie, or the client is given a regional API address (api-eu-west-1.taskflow.example.com) at sign-in.
  3. A guard: a region that receives a request for a user it does not own refuses or forwards it, so a misrouted write never lands in the wrong partition.

The edge (a global proxy rule or edge function) can route on the signal so most requests never reach the wrong region; the guard catches the rest. Travelers keep their home region (their requests travel further); moving a tenant between regions is a data migration, not a routing change.

docs.title: Data residency
docs.text:
Some laws, regulators, and customer contracts restrict where personal data may be stored or processed; for example, the European Union regulates transfers of personal data outside the EU (see the European Commission's international dimension of data protection). Requirements differ by jurisdiction and contract, so get them from legal counsel, then design for them:

  • Partition by residency: data subject to a rule lives only in regions that satisfy it, and its disaster recovery region must satisfy it too.
  • Replicate globally only data that is not restricted, or that has been pseudonymized.
  • Remember the copies people forget: backups, logs, analytics exports, search indexes, caches, and support tools.
  • Enforce in the application and data layer. GeoDNS and edge routing steer traffic; they do not prove where data is stored.

docs.title: Failover runbooks and drills
docs.text:
A regional failover is a sequence of risky steps under pressure, so it is scripted and rehearsed:

  1. Detect and decide. Clear criteria (for example, error budget burn and provider status), a named decision-maker, and a time limit for waiting on the provider.
  2. Fence the old primary. Make sure the failed region cannot keep accepting writes if it comes back half-alive, or two primaries will diverge (split brain).
  3. Promote data. Promote the replica or run the database's managed failover; record the replication lag at that moment (your actual RPO).
  4. Scale the target region to carry the extra traffic before moving it.
  5. Shift traffic in steps with the routing tools from global traffic management, watching errors and latency.
  6. Verify and communicate: synthetic checks, key business flows, a status page update.
  7. Fail back later, deliberately: resynchronize the original region first; failback is a second failover, with the same risks.

Practise it. Regular game days that drain a zone or evacuate a region in production-like conditions turn a 50-minute scramble into an 8-minute routine, as Netflix's experience shows. AWS Fault Injection Service, ARC zonal shift, and chaos engineering tools make the exercises repeatable (see chaos engineering and game days and restore testing and runbooks).

docs.title: Cost multiplication
docs.text:
An illustrative model, not a price list: compute that needs 12 instance units at peak at 100 units of currency per month each, and a database node at 1,000 per month.

Design                                         compute              database               monthly
Single zone (no spare capacity)                12 x 100 = 1,200     1 node    = 1,000      2,200
Three zones, sized to lose one                 18 x 100 = 1,800     3 nodes   = 3,000      4,800
+ warm standby region (4 instances, 1 node)    +4 x 100 =   400     +1 node   = 1,000      6,200
Active-active, two regions, each able to
  carry all users (3 zones per region)         36 x 100 = 3,600     6 nodes   = 6,000      9,600

Plus: cross-zone and cross-region data transfer, a global routing layer,
duplicated observability, and the engineering time to build and rehearse failover.

The same rule as for zones applies to regions: if every region must survive the loss of another, two regions need 200% of peak capacity and three regions need 150%. The database lines grow fastest, which is why many designs keep compute warm in the second region but replicate data more cheaply, or keep only the most critical data multi-region.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Choose Avoid Any production service Multi-AZ: three zones, capacity for a lost zone, a multi-AZ database A single zone, a single NAT gateway Hours of regional downtime are acceptable Multi-AZ plus backups copied to another region A hot second region Recovery in tens of minutes, little data loss Pilot light or warm standby with continuous replication Active-active complexity Users on several continents, write-heavy per user Home region per user or tenant Multi-writer on the same records Read-heavy global product Read local, write global Synchronous replication across oceans Records that must never conflict, across regions A synchronous multi-region database, nearby regions Asynchronous last-writer-wins Residency rules Partitioned regions with in-jurisdiction DR Global replication of restricted data

docs.title: A replica set across three zones
docs.text:
// mongosh: one member per zone (self-managed; managed services such as Atlas do this for you)
rs.initiate({
  _id: "taskflow",
  members: [
    { _id: 0, host: "mongo-a.internal.example.com:27017", priority: 2, tags: { zone: "eu-west-1a" } },
    { _id: 1, host: "mongo-b.internal.example.com:27017", priority: 1, tags: { zone: "eu-west-1b" } },
    { _id: 2, host: "mongo-c.internal.example.com:27017", priority: 1, tags: { zone: "eu-west-1c" } },
  ],
});

// src/db.js: acknowledged writes survive the loss of any one zone
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";

export const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, {
  writeConcern: { w: "majority", wtimeoutMS: 5_000 }, // two of three members, in different zones
  readPreference: "primary",                         // users read their own writes
  retryWrites: true,                                 // one automatic retry after an election
  maxPoolSize: 50,
});

With w: "majority", a write that the driver reports as successful exists in at least two zones, so an election after a zone failure cannot roll it back. wtimeoutMS stops a write from waiting forever when a majority is unreachable; the write may still have been applied, so retried writes should be idempotent.

docs.title: Keeping Kubernetes traffic inside its zone
docs.text:
# k8s/api-service.yaml: prefer endpoints in the caller's zone, fall back to others
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  selector:
    app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
  trafficDistribution: PreferSameZone

PreferSameZone became stable in Kubernetes 1.35 (PreferClose is the older, deprecated name for the same behaviour). It cuts cross-zone traffic and contains a degraded zone's impact, but it needs pods spread evenly across zones, or one zone's pods take that zone's whole load.

docs.title: Draining a zone with ARC zonal shift
docs.text:
# Allow zonal shift on the load balancer once
aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes \
  --load-balancer-arn "<load-balancer-arn>" \
  --attributes Key=zonal_shift.config.enabled,Value=true

# Move traffic away from one zone (use the AZ ID, such as use1-az2, not the name)
aws arc-zonal-shift start-zonal-shift \
  --resource-identifier "<load-balancer-arn>" \
  --away-from use1-az2 \
  --expires-in 2h \
  --comment "elevated 5xx in use1-az2; draining while we investigate"

aws arc-zonal-shift list-zonal-shifts --status ACTIVE
aws arc-zonal-shift cancel-zonal-shift --zonal-shift-id "<zonal-shift-id>"

A zonal shift expires on its own (it can be set for up to 72 hours and extended), so a forgotten shift does not leave a zone drained forever. Check that the other zones have the capacity first: this is where sizing for a lost zone pays off.

docs.title: A home-region guard in Express
docs.text:
// src/middleware/home-region.js: serve each account only from its home region
const LOCAL_REGION = process.env.AWS_REGION; // for example "eu-west-1"

export const regionalApiUrl = (region) => `https://api-${region}.taskflow.example.com`;

// At sign-in: tell the client which regional API to use from now on
export function signInResponse(user) {
  return { userId: user.id, homeRegion: user.homeRegion, apiUrl: regionalApiUrl(user.homeRegion) };
}

// On every authenticated request; homeRegion comes from the verified token, never from input
export function requireHomeRegion(req, res, next) {
  const home = req.user?.homeRegion;
  if (!home || home === LOCAL_REGION) return next();
  res.set("Cache-Control", "no-store");
  return res.status(409).json({
    error: "wrong_region",
    message: `This account is served from ${home}`,
    apiUrl: regionalApiUrl(home),
  });
}

// src/app.js (excerpt): after authentication, before any route touches data
app.use("/tasks", authenticate, requireHomeRegion, tasksRouter);

The client switches to apiUrl when it sees wrong_region, and the edge routes by the same claim so this rarely happens. During a regional failover, the directory entry for affected tenants changes to the recovery region, new tokens carry the new home region, and the guard in the recovery region starts accepting them.

docs.title: A region evacuation runbook outline
docs.text:
Runbook: evacuate eu-west-1 to us-east-1 (TaskFlow API)          owner: on-call primary

Decide   Trigger: EU error budget burn > 14.4x over 1 h (5 min short window) AND provider status confirms a regional issue
         Decision: incident commander; record the time
Fence    Disable writes in eu-west-1: set the region's write switch off; confirm 0 write QPS there
Promote  Promote the EU partition replica in us-east-1; note the replication lag at promotion (actual RPO)
Scale    Raise us-east-1 minimum capacity to 200% of its normal peak; wait for instances to be healthy
Shift    Route EU users to us-east-1: 10% -> 50% -> 100%, 5 minutes per step, watching 5xx and p99
Verify   Synthetic sign-in, create task, list tasks for an EU test tenant; check the status page
Recover  Later: resynchronize eu-west-1 from us-east-1, then fail back with the same steps in reverse
Measure  Record time per step; compare the total with the RTO; file follow-ups

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run every production tier in at least two zones, preferably three, and size each so the others can absorb a lost zone without scaling.
  • Use managed multi-AZ databases and majority-acknowledged writes.
  • Keep chatty traffic inside a zone where you can, and be able to drain a zone on purpose.
  • Add a second region only for a stated reason: RTO, latency, residency, or blast radius.
  • Prefer one writer per record (read local and write global, or a home region) over multi-writer replication.
  • Monitor replication lag against the RPO, and alert before it grows.
  • Keep the routing directory, tokens, and edge rules consistent with the data's home region.
  • Fence the old primary during failover, and treat failback as a separate, rehearsed operation.
  • Rehearse zone drains and region evacuations, and measure them.
  • Budget for the multiplied cost before committing to a design.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• One zone failed and the service went down anyway. Detect: everything failed at the moment one zone was impaired. Cause: a hidden single-zone dependency: the database primary with no standby, a single NAT gateway, or all replicas scheduled in one zone. Fix: audit every tier for zone spread, one NAT gateway per zone, and spread constraints for pods.
  • A zone failed and the surviving zones fell over. Detect: errors and saturation spread to the healthy zones right after the first one failed. Cause: capacity sized for normal load, relying on autoscaling during the incident. Fix: static stability (peak x N / (N - 1) of capacity) and alarms on per-zone headroom.
  • Cross-zone data transfer dominates the bill. Detect: cost reports show inter-zone transfer growing with traffic. Cause: chatty service-to-service calls and caches crossing zones on every request. Fix: zone-aware routing, local replicas of hot read paths, and larger, less frequent calls.
  • After a regional failover, recent writes are missing. Detect: customers report updates from the minutes before the incident are gone. Cause: replication lag had grown far beyond the expected seconds before the failure. Fix: alert on replication lag against the RPO, and record the lag at every promotion.
  • Two regions both accepted writes after failback. Detect: duplicate or diverging records once the old region returned. Cause: the old primary came back and took writes before it was fenced (split brain). Fix: fencing as a runbook step, write switches per region, and resynchronizing before failback.
  • Edits disappear for users who work across regions. Detect: support tickets about changes that vanished; both regions show conflicting versions in logs. Cause: multi-writer replication with last-writer-wins on records edited in two regions. Fix: a single home region per record, or merge rules designed for that data.
  • EU personal data turned up in a US analytics export. Detect: an audit or data inventory finds restricted data outside its region. Cause: a global replication or export pipeline ignored residency. Fix: classify data, partition by residency, and enforce residency in pipelines and backups, not only in routing.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Availability Zone: One or more data centers in a region with independent power, cooling, and networking.
  • Region: A geographic area with several Availability Zones.
  • Static stability: Continuing to work through a failure without needing to create new resources.
  • Active-passive: One region serves users while another waits to take over.
  • Active-active: Several regions serve users at the same time.
  • Home region: The single region that owns a user's or tenant's data.
  • Synchronous replication: Acknowledging a write only after a copy exists elsewhere.
  • Asynchronous replication: Acknowledging a write after the local commit; copies follow.
  • Replication lag: How far a replica is behind its source; the RPO of an asynchronous design.
  • Write conflict: Two concurrent updates to the same record accepted in different places.
  • Last writer wins (LWW): Resolving conflicts by keeping the update with the latest timestamp.
  • Split brain: Two copies both acting as primary and accepting writes.
  • Fencing: Preventing a failed or old primary from accepting writes.
  • Data residency: Requirements on where data is stored or processed.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating multi-AZ as "spread the instances" while the database, NAT gateway, or cache stays in one zone.
  • Sizing for normal load and counting on autoscaling to replace a lost zone.
  • Going multi-region before getting multi-AZ, deployments, and backups right.
  • Assuming asynchronous replication means no data loss.
  • Using last-writer-wins for data where a lost update matters.
  • Forgetting that DR copies, backups, and logs are subject to residency rules too.
  • Writing a failover runbook and never running it.
  • Expecting two regions to cost twice as much; with spare capacity, data transfer, and tooling it is often more.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is multi-AZ the baseline for production while multi-region is a business decision?
  2. A service needs 20 instances at peak. How many does it need in total, and per zone, to survive the loss of one zone with two zones and with four? (40 with 20 per zone; about 27, rounded up to 28 with 7 per zone.)
  3. Compare read local and write global, home region per user, and multi-writer designs on latency, conflicts, and failover.
  4. Two regions are 1,090 km apart. What is the minimum added latency for a request that performs three sequential synchronous writes? (At least 3 x 10.9 ms, about 33 ms.)
  5. With asynchronous replication, the lag is 4 seconds and the region handles 300 writes per second. Roughly how many acknowledged writes are at risk if the region is destroyed? (About 1,200.)
  6. What is a write conflict, and what are three ways to deal with one?
  7. Describe the steps of a regional failover runbook. Why must the old primary be fenced?
  8. Which copies of data must a data residency design account for besides the primary database?

docs.text:

docs.title: Resilience Patterns Across Servers
docs.text:
Once a request crosses several servers, partial failure is normal: one dependency is slow, one instance is overloaded, one zone has packet loss. The goal of the patterns in this lesson is to stop a local problem from turning into a system-wide outage, the cascading failure that takes down healthy services because they waited, retried, and queued on a sick one.

This lesson covers timeouts and deadline budgets, retries with exponential backoff and jitter (and how retries cause storms), idempotency, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding and graceful degradation, rate limiting at the edge compared with inside services, backpressure, and how health and readiness checks fit in. Every pattern comes with Node.js code for the TaskFlow API; each module below runs as written on Node.js 22 and later, with Express 5 for the middleware.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The most damaging outages are often not caused by the first failure but by the reaction to it. A database slows down; every API instance keeps its requests waiting for 30 seconds, so the API's connection and memory limits fill up; clients time out and retry, tripling the load; the autoscaler adds instances, which open more database connections; and the database never recovers. Each of those steps was a reasonable local decision with a bad default.

The patterns here are cheap to add and change the shape of failures: slow dependencies fail fast, overloaded services reject some work instead of all of it, retries help with blips instead of amplifying outages, and users see a degraded page instead of an error page.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Amazon Builders' Library. The article Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter describes how Amazon picks a timeout from an acceptable false-timeout rate (for example 0.1%, so the downstream's p99.9 latency), shows that three retries at each of five layers can multiply load on a struggling database 243 times, recommends retrying at a single point in the stack, and explains the local token bucket that AWS added to its SDKs in 2016 to limit retries.
  • Amazon Builders' Library. The article Using load shedding to avoid overload distinguishes throughput (everything sent to a server) from goodput (the requests answered successfully and fast enough to be useful), and shows how shedding excess requests keeps goodput steady when offered load goes far beyond capacity.
  • Google SRE. The chapter Handling Overload describes a per-request retry budget of up to three attempts, a per-client budget that keeps retries below 10% of requests (limiting load growth to about 1.1 times instead of three), request criticality propagated through RPCs, and client-side adaptive throttling.
  • Netflix. The Hystrix README explains that the library that popularized circuit breakers and bulkheads in Java is in maintenance mode, because Netflix moved toward adaptive approaches such as adaptive concurrency limits and recommends projects like resilience4j for new work.
  • Google. The Tail at Scale (Dean and Barroso, 2013) explains why rare slow responses dominate latency in systems that fan out to many servers, and describes tail-tolerant techniques such as hedged requests.

Popular tools and providers: resilience4j (JVM), Polly (.NET), cockatiel and opossum (Node.js), Envoy and service meshes (timeouts, retries, outlier detection), API gateways and CDNs for rate limiting, and chaos tools for testing all of it.

docs.title: Timeouts: every remote call needs one
docs.text:
A call without a timeout can wait forever, and every waiting request holds a socket, memory, and often a database connection. Set three kinds:

Timeout Bounds Typical value Connect Establishing the TCP or TLS connection Short: tens to a few hundred milliseconds inside a data center Request (per try) One attempt, from sending to the last byte From the dependency's high-percentile latency, such as p99.9 Overall (deadline) The whole operation, including retries What the caller can afford

Choose the per-try timeout from measurements: pick the share of false timeouts you accept (0.1% means using the dependency's p99.9 latency) and add padding when p99.9 is close to the median.

Timeouts must also nest: an inner call's timeout must fit inside the outer one, or the outer caller gives up while the inner work continues. The robust way is to propagate a deadline: the edge sets a total budget, each hop subtracts what it used and passes the rest on, and no hop starts work it cannot finish in time. gRPC does this natively with deadlines; with HTTP you pass the remaining budget in a header. Passing a relative budget (milliseconds left) rather than an absolute timestamp avoids errors from clock skew between servers.

docs.title: Retries, backoff, and jitter
docs.text:
Retries turn transient failures (a dropped connection, an instance that was just terminated, a brief overload) into successes. They are also the most common amplifier of outages, so they need four guards:

  1. Only retry what is safe. Idempotent operations (GET, PUT, DELETE, or a POST with an idempotency key) and failures that may succeed next time: connection errors, timeouts, 429, 502, 503, and 504. Never retry 400-class client errors.
  2. Back off exponentially, with jitter. Wait longer after each failure (for example 100, 200, 400 ms, capped) and randomize the wait. With "full jitter" the wait is a random value between zero and the exponential backoff. Without jitter, every client that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment.
  3. Cap attempts and respect the deadline. Two or three attempts in total, never past the caller's deadline, and honor Retry-After.
  4. Spend from a retry budget. Limit retries to a fraction of normal traffic (around 10%), so when a dependency is down the retries stop instead of tripling its load.

Retry storms come from layering. If the API retries 3 times, the tasks service retries each call 3 times, and the database client retries 3 times, one user request becomes up to 27 database queries during a failure. Amazon's example of three retries at each of five layers gives 3⁵ = 243. Retry at one layer (usually the one closest to the user, or the service mesh, but not both) and make every other layer fail fast.

Hedged requests are a related technique for tail latency: if a read has not answered after, say, its p95 latency, send a second copy to another replica and use whichever answers first. Hedge only idempotent reads, and only a small fraction of requests.

docs.title: Idempotency: making retries safe
docs.text: A retried "create task" must not create two tasks. The client generates an idempotency key once per logical operation and sends it with every attempt; the server stores the key with the result and returns the stored result for repeats. Patterns and storage are covered in timeouts, retries, and idempotency in the Backend section, and the Builders' Library article Making retries safe with idempotent APIs explains how Amazon designs APIs around it.

docs.title: Circuit breakers
docs.text:
A circuit breaker watches calls to one dependency and stops calling it when it is clearly failing. While open, calls fail immediately, so the caller does not wait on timeouts, and the dependency gets breathing room to recover.

Design choices:

  • What counts as failure: timeouts, connection errors, 5xx, and 429; not 4xx errors caused by bad input.
  • When to open: a failure rate over a window with a minimum number of calls, so three failures out of three do not trip it at 3 a.m.
  • What callers do while open: a fallback (cached data, a default, a feature switched off) or a fast error. Amazon's article Avoiding fallback in distributed systems warns that rarely used fallback paths are hard to test and can fail or overload something else exactly when needed, so keep fallbacks simple and exercise them regularly.
  • One breaker per dependency (and sometimes per endpoint), never one for "everything downstream".

Load balancers and meshes implement a related idea per instance: outlier detection ejects a single misbehaving instance for a while, whereas a circuit breaker reacts to the dependency as a whole.

docs.title: Bulkheads
docs.text:
A ship's bulkheads keep one flooded compartment from sinking the ship. In software, a bulkhead is a separate, bounded pool of capacity per dependency or workload, so one slow dependency can only exhaust its own share.

The same idea works at every scale: concurrency limits and connection pools per dependency inside a process, separate worker fleets for batch and interactive traffic, separate load balancer target groups for expensive endpoints, and whole cells for groups of customers (see how top companies run at scale).

docs.title: Load shedding and graceful degradation
docs.text:
Past its capacity, a server that accepts everything gets slower for everyone until nearly every request times out: throughput stays high while goodput collapses. Load shedding rejects the excess early and cheaply, with 503 and Retry-After, so the requests it accepts still finish quickly.

  • Detect overload directly: in-flight requests above a measured limit, time spent queued, or (in Node.js) event loop delay. CPU alone reacts too late.
  • Shed by priority: keep health checks, logins, and checkout; shed analytics, prefetches, and batch traffic first. Google propagates a criticality value with every RPC for exactly this.
  • Reject at the edge of the work: shedding after the expensive work is done saves nothing.
  • Prefer adaptive limits: a concurrency limit that adjusts to measured latency (as in Netflix's concurrency-limits library) follows capacity changes better than a fixed number.

Graceful degradation keeps the core working by turning off what is optional: serve slightly stale cached data, hide recommendations, show a static page for a non-critical widget, or disable an expensive feature behind a flag while overloaded (a "brownout").

docs.title: Rate limiting at the edge compared with inside services
docs.text:
At the edge (CDN, WAF, API gateway, load balancer) Inside a service Protects against Abusive clients, bots, credential stuffing, floods One tenant or caller using more than its share; protecting capacity Keyed by IP, API key, user, path Tenant, user, caller service, operation Knows about service health Rarely Can combine with load shedding Response 429, challenge, or block 429 with Retry-After, or queueing

Use both: edge limits stop abuse before it costs you compute (see edge protection: WAF, DDoS, and bots), and service limits enforce fairness between legitimate callers. Algorithms such as token buckets are covered in rate limiting and throttling. A rate limit is not load shedding: it caps each client, but it does not know that the service as a whole is overloaded.

docs.title: Backpressure
docs.text:
Backpressure means a slow consumer tells the producer to slow down instead of silently buffering. Unbounded queues turn overload into memory exhaustion and hours-old work. Bound every queue and buffer, and make "full" visible:

  • HTTP services return 429 or 503 with Retry-After.
  • Node.js streams respect write() returning false and the drain event; pipeline() does this for you.
  • Message consumers fetch a bounded number of messages at a time and scale on backlog, and producers watch queue depth.
  • When a queue has fallen hopelessly behind, older work may be worthless: the Builders' Library article Avoiding insurmountable queue backlogs discusses strategies such as preferring newer work and dropping work whose caller has given up.

docs.title: Health checks, readiness, and the load balancer
docs.text:
Health checks decide which instances get traffic, so they are part of the resilience design (see health probes and rolling updates):

  • Liveness asks "should this process be restarted?" and must not depend on shared dependencies, or a database blip restarts the fleet.
  • Readiness asks "should this instance receive traffic now?"; it can fail during startup, shutdown, and local overload.
  • Do not let every instance fail readiness because of a shared dependency: the load balancer then has no healthy targets (many load balancers "fail open" and send traffic everywhere in that case, which is a deliberate safeguard). Prefer serving fast errors or degraded results.

docs.title: Putting it together
docs.text: A practical order around one dependency call, from outside in: deadline → retry (with budget) → circuit breaker → bulkhead → per-try timeout → the call, plus load shedding at the entrance of the service. The retry sits outside the breaker so that an open circuit stops retries immediately; the bulkhead sits inside so that waiting for a slot counts against the deadline.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Pattern Use Skip or be careful Timeouts Every remote call, always Never "no timeout" Deadline propagation Call chains of two or more hops Not needed for a single hop Retries with jitter Idempotent calls, transient errors Non-idempotent writes without keys; more than one layer Retry budget Any client making many calls Low-volume clients (use small attempt caps) Circuit breaker Dependencies that can fail or slow down as a whole In-process calls; dependencies already behind a mesh breaker Bulkhead Several dependencies with different reliability Single-dependency services Load shedding Any service that can be overloaded Never shed health checks Graceful degradation Optional features and data Correctness-critical data such as balances Hedged requests Idempotent reads with high tail latency Writes; services near capacity

docs.title: Deadline budgets
docs.text:
// src/resilience/deadline.js
// Propagate the remaining time budget so downstream calls never outlive the caller.
export const BUDGET_HEADER = "x-request-budget-ms"; // relative, avoids clock skew

export class DeadlineExceededError extends Error {
  constructor() {
    super("deadline exceeded");
    this.name = "DeadlineExceededError";
  }
}

// Express middleware: the deadline is the caller's budget or our own default
export function deadlineMiddleware({ defaultBudgetMs = 2_000, maxBudgetMs = 10_000 } = {}) {
  return (req, _res, next) => {
    const asked = Number(req.get(BUDGET_HEADER));
    const budget = Number.isFinite(asked) && asked > 0 ? Math.min(asked, maxBudgetMs) : defaultBudgetMs;
    req.deadline = Date.now() + budget;
    next();
  };
}

// Call a dependency with at most perTryMs, never past the deadline, and pass on
// what is left (minus a margin we keep for building our own response).
export async function fetchWithDeadline(url, { deadline, perTryMs = 1_000, marginMs = 50, ...init } = {}) {
  const remaining = deadline - Date.now() - marginMs;
  if (remaining <= 0) throw new DeadlineExceededError();
  const timeoutMs = Math.min(perTryMs, remaining);
  return fetch(url, {
    ...init,
    headers: { ...init.headers, [BUDGET_HEADER]: String(Math.floor(remaining)) },
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs),
  });
}

AbortSignal.timeout() aborts the fetch with a TimeoutError. Against a dependency that takes 1.5 seconds, a call with 400 ms of budget fails after about 350 ms and tells the dependency it has 350 ms to work with.

docs.title: Retries with full jitter and a retry budget
docs.text:
// src/resilience/retry.js
// Retries with capped exponential backoff, full jitter, and a retry budget.
import { setTimeout as sleep } from "node:timers/promises";

// Token bucket: every call earns `ratio` tokens, every retry spends one.
// With ratio 0.1, retries stay below about 10% of calls once the bucket is empty.
export function createRetryBudget({ ratio = 0.1, maxTokens = 10 } = {}) {
  let tokens = maxTokens;
  return {
    recordCall() {
      tokens = Math.min(maxTokens, tokens + ratio);
    },
    tryAcquire() {
      if (tokens < 1) return false;
      tokens -= 1;
      return true;
    },
  };
}

const RETRYABLE_STATUS = new Set([429, 502, 503, 504]);

export class HttpError extends Error {
  constructor(status, retryAfterMs) {
    super(`upstream returned ${status}`);
    this.name = "HttpError";
    this.status = status;
    this.retryAfterMs = retryAfterMs;
  }
}

// Connection failures, timeouts, and 429/502/503/504 are worth another try.
export function isRetryable(err) {
  if (err instanceof HttpError) return RETRYABLE_STATUS.has(err.status);
  return err.name === "TimeoutError" || err.name === "TypeError"; // fetch: network error
}

export function fullJitter(attempt, baseMs, capMs) {
  return Math.random() * Math.min(capMs, baseMs * 2 ** attempt);
}

export async function withRetries(fn, {
  attempts = 3, baseMs = 100, capMs = 2_000, budget, deadline, retryable = isRetryable,
} = {}) {
  budget?.recordCall();
  for (let attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
    try {
      return await fn(attempt);
    } catch (err) {
      const last = attempt + 1 >= attempts;
      if (last || !retryable(err)) throw err;
      if (budget && !budget.tryAcquire()) throw err; // budget spent: fail fast
      const waitMs = Math.max(fullJitter(attempt, baseMs, capMs), err.retryAfterMs ?? 0);
      if (deadline && Date.now() + waitMs >= deadline) throw err; // no time left
      await sleep(waitMs);
    }
  }
}

// Helper: turn a non-2xx fetch response into an error carrying Retry-After.
export async function checkResponse(res) {
  if (res.ok) return res;
  const header = res.headers.get("retry-after");
  const seconds = header === null ? NaN : Number(header);
  throw new HttpError(res.status, Number.isFinite(seconds) ? seconds * 1_000 : undefined);
}

Against an upstream that fails half of all requests, three attempts turn a 50% success rate into about 87% (1 − 0.5³). Against an upstream that is completely down, 100 calls without a budget would send 300 requests; with the budget above they sent 119 in a test run, because retries stop as soon as the bucket's initial tokens are spent.

For writes, generate the idempotency key once, outside the retry loop, so every attempt carries the same key:

// src/clients/create-task.js
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { withRetries, checkResponse } from "../resilience/retry.js";

export async function createTask(baseUrl, task) {
  const idempotencyKey = randomUUID(); // one key per logical operation
  return withRetries(async () => {
    const res = await fetch(`${baseUrl}/tasks`, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json", "idempotency-key": idempotencyKey },
      body: JSON.stringify(task),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1_000),
    });
    await checkResponse(res);
    return res.json();
  }, { attempts: 3 });
}

docs.title: A circuit breaker
docs.text:
// src/resilience/circuit-breaker.js
// Closed -> Open when the recent failure rate is too high; Open -> Half-open after
// a cool-down; Half-open lets a few trial calls decide between Closed and Open.
export class CircuitOpenError extends Error {
  constructor(name) {
    super(`circuit ${name} is open`);
    this.name = "CircuitOpenError";
  }
}

export class CircuitBreaker {
  constructor(name, {
    windowSize = 20,        // look at the last 20 calls
    minCalls = 10,          // never trip on a handful of calls
    failureRate = 0.5,      // open at 50% failures
    openMs = 10_000,        // stay open this long before probing
    halfOpenProbes = 2,     // successes needed to close again
    isFailure = () => true, // e.g. ignore 4xx client errors
  } = {}) {
    Object.assign(this, { name, windowSize, minCalls, failureRate, openMs, halfOpenProbes, isFailure });
    this.state = "closed";
    this.results = [];      // true = failure, oldest first
    this.openedAt = 0;
    this.probesInFlight = 0;
    this.probeSuccesses = 0;
  }

  async call(fn) {
    if (this.state === "open") {
      if (Date.now() - this.openedAt < this.openMs) throw new CircuitOpenError(this.name);
      this.#transition("half-open");
    }
    if (this.state === "half-open" && this.probesInFlight >= this.halfOpenProbes) {
      throw new CircuitOpenError(this.name); // enough trial calls already running
    }
    const probing = this.state === "half-open";
    if (probing) this.probesInFlight++;
    try {
      const result = await fn();
      this.#record(false, probing);
      return result;
    } catch (err) {
      this.#record(this.isFailure(err), probing);
      throw err;
    } finally {
      if (probing) this.probesInFlight--;
    }
  }

  #record(failed, probing) {
    if (probing) {
      if (failed) return this.#transition("open");
      if (++this.probeSuccesses >= this.halfOpenProbes) this.#transition("closed");
      return;
    }
    if (this.state !== "closed") return; // late result from before a transition
    this.results.push(failed);
    if (this.results.length > this.windowSize) this.results.shift();
    const failures = this.results.filter(Boolean).length;
    if (this.results.length >= this.minCalls && failures / this.results.length >= this.failureRate) {
      this.#transition("open");
    }
  }

  #transition(state) {
    this.state = state;
    if (state === "open") this.openedAt = Date.now();
    if (state === "half-open") this.probeSuccesses = 0;
    if (state === "closed") this.results = [];
    this.onStateChange?.(state);
  }
}

Export state changes as a metric (onStateChange is a hook for that) and alert when a breaker stays open: an open breaker is a symptom someone should look at, not a fix.

docs.title: A bulkhead
docs.text:
// src/resilience/bulkhead.js
// Cap how much of this process one dependency may occupy: at most maxConcurrent
// calls in flight and maxQueue waiting; anything beyond is rejected at once.
export class BulkheadFullError extends Error {
  constructor(name) {
    super(`bulkhead ${name} is full`);
    this.name = "BulkheadFullError";
  }
}

export function createBulkhead(name, { maxConcurrent = 10, maxQueue = 20, queueTimeoutMs = 500 } = {}) {
  let active = 0;
  const waiting = []; // { resolve, reject, timer }

  function release() {
    active--;
    const next = waiting.shift();
    if (next) {
      clearTimeout(next.timer);
      active++;
      next.resolve();
    }
  }

  function acquire() {
    if (active < maxConcurrent) {
      active++;
      return Promise.resolve();
    }
    if (waiting.length >= maxQueue) return Promise.reject(new BulkheadFullError(name));
    return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
      const entry = { resolve, reject, timer: null };
      entry.timer = setTimeout(() => {
        waiting.splice(waiting.indexOf(entry), 1);
        reject(new BulkheadFullError(name)); // waited too long: give up early
      }, queueTimeoutMs);
      waiting.push(entry);
    });
  }

  return {
    async run(fn) {
      await acquire();
      try {
        return await fn();
      } finally {
        release();
      }
    },
    stats: () => ({ active, waiting: waiting.length }),
  };
}

With maxConcurrent: 2 and maxQueue: 2, ten simultaneous calls to a slow dependency produce two running, two waiting, and six immediate BulkheadFullErrors: the caller learns at once instead of after a timeout, and the rest of the process keeps its capacity.

docs.title: Composing the guards around one dependency
docs.text:
// src/clients/tasks-client.js
// One dependency, all the guards: retries (outermost) -> circuit breaker ->
// bulkhead -> per-try timeout bounded by the request deadline.
import { CircuitBreaker, CircuitOpenError } from "../resilience/circuit-breaker.js";
import { createBulkhead } from "../resilience/bulkhead.js";
import { withRetries, createRetryBudget, checkResponse, HttpError } from "../resilience/retry.js";
import { fetchWithDeadline } from "../resilience/deadline.js";

const TASKS_URL = process.env.TASKS_URL ?? "http://tasks.internal:3000";

export const breaker = new CircuitBreaker("tasks", {
  openMs: Number(process.env.TASKS_BREAKER_OPEN_MS ?? 10_000),
  // 4xx (except 429) is the caller's fault, not a sign the dependency is sick
  isFailure: (err) => !(err instanceof HttpError) || err.status >= 500 || err.status === 429,
});
export const bulkhead = createBulkhead("tasks", { maxConcurrent: 20, maxQueue: 40 });
const budget = createRetryBudget({ ratio: 0.1 });
const cache = new Map(); // last good value per id, for graceful degradation

export async function getTask(id, { deadline = Date.now() + 2_000 } = {}) {
  try {
    const task = await withRetries(
      () => breaker.call(() => bulkhead.run(async () => {
        const res = await fetchWithDeadline(`${TASKS_URL}/tasks/${id}`, { deadline, perTryMs: 600 });
        await checkResponse(res);
        return res.json();
      })),
      { attempts: 3, baseMs: 50, capMs: 500, budget, deadline },
    );
    cache.set(id, task);
    return { task, stale: false };
  } catch (err) {
    // Degrade: a slightly old task beats an error page, if we have one
    if (cache.has(id) && (err instanceof CircuitOpenError || err.name === "TimeoutError")) {
      return { task: cache.get(id), stale: true };
    }
    throw err;
  }
}

In a test against a dependency that went down completely, the breaker opened after ten failures; the next 27 calls failed fast without touching the dependency; after the cool-down two trial calls closed it again; and while it was open, a task fetched earlier was served from the cache with stale: true. A production cache needs a size limit and an age limit (see cache fundamentals).

docs.title: Load shedding middleware for Express
docs.text:
// src/resilience/load-shedding.js
// Reject work early and cheaply when the process is saturated, so the requests
// it does accept still finish fast. Health checks are never shed; low-priority
// requests are shed first.
import { monitorEventLoopDelay } from "node:perf_hooks";

export function loadShedding({
  maxInFlight = 200,          // concurrent requests this instance handles well
  lowPriorityShare = 0.7,     // low-priority requests only below 70% of that
  maxEventLoopDelayMs = 200,  // p99 event loop delay that means "overloaded"
  isLowPriority = (req) => req.get("x-priority") === "low",
} = {}) {
  const loop = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 20 });
  loop.enable();
  let loopDelayMs = 0;
  setInterval(() => {
    loopDelayMs = loop.percentile(99) / 1e6; // nanoseconds -> milliseconds
    loop.reset();
  }, 1_000).unref();

  let inFlight = 0;

  return function shed(req, res, next) {
    if (req.path === "/healthz") return next();
    const limit = isLowPriority(req) ? maxInFlight * lowPriorityShare : maxInFlight;
    if (inFlight >= limit || loopDelayMs > maxEventLoopDelayMs) {
      res.set("Retry-After", "1");
      return res.status(503).json({ error: "overloaded, retry shortly" });
    }
    inFlight++;
    let done = false;
    const finish = () => {
      if (!done) {
        done = true;
        inFlight--;
      }
    };
    res.on("finish", finish);
    res.on("close", finish);
    next();
  };
}

// src/app.js (excerpt): shedding first, then the deadline, then routes
import express from "express";
import { loadShedding } from "./resilience/load-shedding.js";
import { deadlineMiddleware } from "./resilience/deadline.js";
import { getTask } from "./clients/tasks-client.js";

const app = express();
app.use(loadShedding({ maxInFlight: 200 }));
app.use(deadlineMiddleware({ defaultBudgetMs: 2_000 }));

app.get("/healthz", (_req, res) => res.send("ok"));
app.get("/tasks/:id", async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    const { task, stale } = await getTask(req.params.id, { deadline: req.deadline });
    if (stale) res.set("Warning", '110 - "stale task data"');
    res.json(task);
  } catch (err) {
    next(err);
  }
});

export default app; // src/server.js calls app.listen()

In a test with maxInFlight: 5 and twenty simultaneous slow requests, five were served and fifteen received 503 immediately, while /healthz kept answering 200. Measure the real limit with a load test (see performance and reliability testing) instead of guessing it.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Put a timeout on every remote call, derived from measured latency, and make inner timeouts fit inside outer ones.
  • Propagate a deadline budget through call chains.
  • Retry only idempotent operations and transient errors, with capped exponential backoff, full jitter, and a retry budget.
  • Retry at one layer only; everywhere else, fail fast.
  • Use idempotency keys for writes that may be retried.
  • One circuit breaker per dependency; alert on open breakers.
  • Give each dependency its own bulkhead: connection pool and concurrency limit.
  • Shed load early, by priority, with 503 and Retry-After; never shed health checks.
  • Design degraded modes for optional features, and exercise them regularly so they work when needed.
  • Bound every queue, and prefer dropping work whose caller has given up.
  • Test all of it with fault injection and game days (see chaos engineering and game days).

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A slow database took down every API instance. Detect: API latency equals its timeout, connection pools are exhausted, and memory grows, while CPU is low. Cause: long or missing timeouts let every request wait on the database, filling every slot. Fix: short per-try timeouts, a bulkhead per dependency, a circuit breaker, and load shedding so the API fails fast instead of queueing.
  • A brief failure turned into a 20-minute outage. Detect: traffic to the failing service is several times normal, and traces show the same request retried at several layers. Cause: a retry storm: each layer retried independently, with no jitter or budget. Fix: retry at one layer with full jitter and a retry budget, and fail fast elsewhere.
  • Duplicate tasks appeared after a network blip. Detect: two identical tasks created milliseconds apart with the same payload. Cause: a timed-out POST was retried although the first attempt had succeeded. Fix: idempotency keys stored with results, and retries only for idempotent requests.
  • Recovery stalls every time a dependency comes back. Detect: the dependency recovers, then falls over again as traffic floods back. Cause: every client's circuit closed at once, or queued work and retries arrived together. Fix: half-open trial calls, jitter on retries and reconnects, and gradual traffic restoration.
  • A circuit breaker stays open while the dependency is healthy. Detect: the breaker metric shows open, but direct calls succeed. Cause: client errors (400s for bad input) or the caller's own timeouts are counted as dependency failures. Fix: count only failures that reflect dependency health, and set timeouts from measured latency.
  • The site went down under a traffic spike instead of slowing down. Detect: goodput drops to near zero while CPU is at 100% and every request takes longer than the client timeout. Cause: the service accepted all work and nothing finished in time. Fix: load shedding by concurrency or queue time, priorities, and an autoscaling policy with headroom (see autoscaling server fleets).
  • All instances failed readiness when Redis restarted. Detect: the load balancer has no healthy targets while every instance is running. Cause: readiness checks depended on a shared cache. Fix: readiness based on the instance's own state, with the shared dependency handled by timeouts, breakers, and degraded responses.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Cascading failure: A failure that spreads because healthy parts of the system wait on, retry against, or take over load from a failing part.
  • Deadline / budget: The time left for a whole operation, passed from hop to hop.
  • Exponential backoff: Waiting longer after each failed attempt.
  • Jitter: Randomness added to waits so clients do not act in lockstep.
  • Retry budget: A cap on retries as a share of normal traffic.
  • Retry storm: Load amplification from many clients or layers retrying at once.
  • Idempotency key: A client-generated identifier that lets the server recognize repeated attempts of one operation.
  • Circuit breaker: A guard that stops calls to a failing dependency for a while.
  • Bulkhead: An isolated, bounded pool of capacity for one dependency or workload.
  • Load shedding: Rejecting excess requests early to protect the ones already accepted.
  • Goodput: Requests completed successfully and fast enough to be useful.
  • Graceful degradation / brownout: Keeping core functions working by switching off optional ones.
  • Backpressure: Signaling producers to slow down instead of buffering without limit.
  • Hedged request: A duplicate request sent to another replica after a delay, keeping the first response.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Remote calls with no timeout, or the library's default of minutes.
  • Inner timeouts longer than outer ones.
  • Retrying everything, including 400s and non-idempotent POSTs.
  • Exponential backoff without jitter.
  • Retries at every layer of the stack.
  • Treating a circuit breaker as a fix rather than a symptom to alert on.
  • Fallback paths that are never exercised until the outage.
  • Unbounded queues "so nothing is lost".
  • Health checks that depend on shared dependencies.
  • Believing autoscaling replaces load shedding; new capacity arrives in minutes, overload arrives in seconds.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why must every remote call have a timeout, and how would you choose its value from latency percentiles?
  2. A request has a 2,000 ms budget. The API spends 300 ms, keeps a 50 ms margin, and calls a service whose per-try limit is 1,000 ms. What budget does it pass on, and what timeout does it use for the call?
  3. A request passes through four layers, and each retries failed calls twice (three attempts). How many calls can reach the bottom layer for one user request during an outage? What would you change?
  4. Explain full jitter, and why synchronized retries can prevent a recovering service from recovering.
  5. Describe the circuit breaker states and what triggers each transition. What should not count as a failure?
  6. How do bulkheads and load shedding differ, and why do you want both?
  7. What is the difference between rate limiting at the edge and load shedding inside a service?
  8. Why should readiness checks avoid depending on shared dependencies?
