docs.title: Service Discovery and Service Mesh
docs.text:
In a fleet that autoscales, deploys several times a day, and replaces failed machines automatically, the set of addresses behind each service changes constantly. Service discovery is how a caller finds the healthy instances of the service it wants to call right now. A service mesh goes one step further and moves discovery, load balancing, encryption, retries, and telemetry for service-to-service traffic out of the application and into proxies managed by a control plane.

This lesson covers why hard-coded addresses fail, client-side and server-side discovery, self-registration and platform registration, DNS-based discovery and its caching pitfalls, the main registries (Consul, Eureka, etcd, ZooKeeper, cloud registries) and how Kubernetes does it, then service meshes: sidecar proxies, mutual TLS, retries, traffic splitting, observability, Istio and Linkerd, sidecarless designs such as Istio's ambient mode, and the real cost and complexity of running one.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
The first multi-server version of an application usually puts a list of IP addresses in a configuration file. That breaks as soon as instances come and go: callers keep sending requests to terminated instances, miss new ones, and every scaling event becomes a config change. Even with a registry, the details decide whether failures are invisible or painful: how quickly a dead instance disappears from callers' lists, what callers do when the registry itself is unreachable, and how connections that stay open for minutes interact with a list that changed seconds ago.

A mesh promises uniform encryption, retries, and metrics for every service without code changes, which is valuable with dozens of services written in several languages. It also adds a proxy to every hop, a control plane to operate, and new failure modes, so it should be adopted for concrete reasons.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Netflix. The 2012 post Netflix Shares Cloud Load Balancing And Failover Tool: Eureka! explains why Netflix built a registry: in AWS "servers come and go", AWS did not yet offer a middle-tier load balancer, and putting mid-tier services behind internet-facing load balancers would have given up the protection of security groups. Eureka let clients balance load across instances themselves.
  • Envoy. The What is Envoy page states the belief the proxy was built on: the network should be transparent to applications, and when network and application problems occur it should be easy to find the source. Envoy is the data plane of Istio's sidecar mode and of many other meshes and gateways.
  • Slack. In describing its migration to a cellular architecture, Slack lists the discovery interfaces its services used at the same time: the Envoy xDS API, the Consul API, and plain DNS, and notes that DNS has no way to express ideas such as "drain this zone".
  • Dropbox. The post Robinhood: in-house load balancing service explains that clients doing plain round robin over the subset of servers that discovery gave them produced imbalanced load, so Robinhood attaches load-based weights to endpoints through Envoy's Endpoint Discovery Service; Dropbox reports reducing fleet size by 25% for some of its largest services.

Popular tools and providers: Consul, Eureka (through Spring Cloud Netflix), etcd, ZooKeeper, AWS Cloud Map, Kubernetes Services and CoreDNS, Envoy and its xDS APIs, gRPC's built-in load balancing, Istio, Linkerd, Cilium, and Consul's service mesh.

docs.title: Why static addresses break
docs.text: Instances get new IP addresses whenever they are replaced, autoscaled, rescheduled, or redeployed. A list in a file or an environment variable has to be edited and redeployed for every change, and it says nothing about health. Discovery replaces the static list with a live one: a registry that knows which instances exist and are healthy, and a way for callers to read it.

docs.title: Client-side compared with server-side discovery
docs.text: Client-side discovery Server-side discovery Who picks the instance The caller, using a library A load balancer, proxy, or kernel rules Extra network hop No Usually one (a load balancer), or none with kernel rules (Kubernetes) Smart balancing (zone preference, least load) Easy, in the library Depends on the load balancer Languages A library per language, kept in sync Any client that can call a name Examples Eureka with Spring Cloud LoadBalancer, gRPC with DNS or xDS, Consul API clients Cloud internal load balancers, Kubernetes Services, Consul DNS behind a proxy

docs.title: How instances get registered
docs.text:
• Self-registration: the instance registers itself at startup and renews a lease with heartbeats (Eureka). Simple, but every service needs the client code, and a hung process may keep heartbeating.
  • Platform registration: something outside the instance registers it: the Auto Scaling group adds it to a target group, Kubernetes adds ready Pods to EndpointSlices, or a Consul agent on the host registers services from configuration and runs their health checks. The application does not need to know.

Either way, registration must be paired with health checking and deregistration: a registry full of dead instances is worse than no registry, because callers trust it.

docs.title: DNS-based discovery and its caching pitfalls
docs.text:
DNS is the most universal discovery interface: every language can resolve a name. A registry or platform publishes A or AAAA records for instance addresses, and SRV records (_http._tcp.tasks.example) can also carry ports and weights. The pitfalls all come from caching:

  • TTLs. Resolvers and operating systems cache answers until the TTL expires, so a short TTL (a few seconds to a minute) is needed for dynamic fleets, at the cost of more lookups.
  • Client caches. Some runtimes and libraries keep their own DNS cache longer than the TTL; check the defaults of yours.
  • Long-lived connections. A keep-alive or HTTP/2 connection opened to an instance keeps going to that instance whatever DNS now says. New instances receive no traffic from existing connections, and a removed instance keeps receiving it until the connection breaks. Cap connection age, or use a balancer that understands membership changes.
  • No health or zones in plain DNS. DNS returns a list; it cannot say "prefer your zone" or "send 1% here". That is why richer systems use APIs such as xDS.

docs.title: Registries
docs.text:
Registry Model Notes Consul An agent on every node runs health checks and gossips membership; servers keep the catalog consistent with Raft. Discovery via DNS (port 8600, name.service.consul) and an HTTP API Also a key-value store and a service mesh. Licensed under the Business Source License since version 1.17; HashiCorp, including Consul, is now part of IBM Eureka REST registry with client-side load balancing; instances renew leases every 30 seconds and are removed after 90 seconds without a renewal; clients cache the registry and refresh every 30 seconds Favors availability: in "self-preservation" mode during mass renewal loss it stops expiring instances. Community-maintained on GitHub, widely used through Spring Cloud Netflix etcd Strongly consistent key-value store (Raft) with leases and watches The store behind Kubernetes; registration is a key bound to a lease that expires if not kept alive ZooKeeper Consistent coordination service; ephemeral nodes disappear when the session ends Older but still common in data infrastructure (and behind older Kafka clusters; Kafka 4.0 removed it) AWS Cloud Map Managed registry with DNS and API discovery Integrates with ECS and other AWS services Kubernetes The API server stores Services and EndpointSlices; CoreDNS answers names Built in; see below

Worked example of staleness with Eureka's defaults: an instance crashes just after its last renewal. The server removes it after 90 seconds without a renewal, and a client may then use its cached list for up to 30 more seconds. For about two minutes, some calls go to a dead address, so callers must time out quickly and retry on a different instance. Faster heartbeats shorten the window but multiply registry traffic, and the Eureka documentation advises against changing the renewal interval because the server uses it to detect widespread renewal problems.

docs.title: Discovery in Kubernetes
docs.text: Kubernetes provides server-side discovery out of the box. Ready Pods are listed in a Service's EndpointSlices, CoreDNS resolves taskflow-api.taskflow.svc.cluster.local to a virtual IP, and kernel rules on every node spread connections across the endpoints (see Pods, Deployments, and Services). A headless Service returns the Pod addresses themselves, which is how gRPC clients do client-side balancing inside a cluster. Because the kernel balances per connection, long-lived HTTP/2 connections can pin traffic to a few Pods, one of the main reasons teams adopt a mesh or client-side balancing.

docs.title: xDS: discovery as an API
docs.text: Envoy introduced a family of discovery APIs, collectively called xDS: listeners, routes, clusters, and endpoints, each pushed from a control plane to the proxy as they change. Endpoints can carry health, zone, and weight, which plain DNS cannot. Istio and other meshes speak xDS to their proxies, and gRPC can consume xDS directly for proxyless client-side balancing.

docs.title: Service mesh: data plane and control plane
docs.text:
A mesh has two parts:

  • The data plane: proxies on the request path, traditionally a sidecar container in every Pod, which intercept inbound and outbound traffic.
  • The control plane: watches the platform for services and endpoints, turns your policies into proxy configuration, and runs a certificate authority that gives every workload a short-lived identity certificate (often in the SPIFFE format).

What the proxies provide without application changes:

Feature What it means Mutual TLS Every hop encrypted, both sides authenticated by workload identity, certificates rotated automatically Authorization policy Rules such as "only orders may call POST /tasks", based on identity rather than IP Load balancing Per request (not per connection), with least-request and zone-aware options Timeouts and retries Configured per route; see the warnings in resilience patterns across servers Outlier detection Temporarily ejecting instances that return errors Traffic splitting and mirroring Weighted routing for canaries, header-based routing, shadow traffic Telemetry Request rate, error rate, and latency for every service pair, plus trace spans (see distributed tracing)

docs.title: Istio, Linkerd, and sidecarless meshes
docs.text:
• Istio has a single control plane binary, istiod, and two data plane modes. In sidecar mode each Pod gets an Envoy proxy. In ambient mode, a per-node ztunnel proxy handles mutual TLS, L4 authorization, and L4 telemetry for every Pod on the node, and optional waypoint proxies (Envoy-based, per namespace or service) add L7 features only where they are needed. Ambient mode reached general availability in Istio 1.24 (November 2024); at the time of writing (November 2026) the current Istio release is 1.32.
  • Linkerd, a graduated CNCF project, keeps a sidecar design with its own small Rust proxy and puts simplicity first. Its release model changed in February 2024: the open source project now publishes edge releases (weekly or near-weekly), and stable releases come from vendors such as Buoyant, whose Buoyant Enterprise for Linkerd distribution is free for companies with fewer than 50 employees and paid for larger ones in production. Linkerd 2.20 was announced in June 2026.
  • Cilium offers sidecar-free mesh features built on eBPF in the kernel, with Envoy for L7 where needed, and Consul includes its own mesh using Envoy.

docs.title: What a mesh costs
docs.text:
• Resources. Every sidecar uses memory and CPU, multiplied by the number of Pods; size requests for it.
  • Latency. Each hop passes through extra proxies; usually small, but it adds up on deep call chains.
  • Operations. A control plane to upgrade and monitor, certificates to reason about, CRDs and policies to review, and proxy upgrades that in sidecar mode require restarting application Pods.
  • Debugging. A failed request may now be a proxy configuration problem, a policy denial, or a certificate issue.
  • Retry amplification. Mesh retries stack on top of application and client retries unless one layer owns them.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommendation A few services on one platform Platform discovery (Kubernetes Services, internal load balancers) and libraries for timeouts and retries VMs in autoscaling groups Internal load balancers per service, or Consul / Cloud Map Java estate already on Spring Cloud Eureka with client-side balancing remains reasonable gRPC services that need per-request balancing Headless Services with client-side balancing, or a mesh Many services, several languages, mTLS required everywhere A service mesh Need zero-trust identity between services Mesh (mTLS plus authorization policy) Small team, no clear driver No mesh yet

Adopt a mesh for a specific need (encryption and identity everywhere, per-request balancing, uniform telemetry, traffic splitting) and roll it out namespace by namespace. Do not adopt one because it is popular, and do not make the registry or mesh control plane a hard dependency of every request.

docs.title: Registering the API with Consul
docs.text:
# /etc/consul.d/taskflow-api.hcl: the local agent registers and health-checks the API
service {
  name = "taskflow-api"
  id   = "taskflow-api-1"
  port = 3000
  tags = ["v1.5.0"]

  check {
    id       = "readyz"
    name     = "HTTP readiness"
    http     = "http://localhost:3000/readyz"
    interval = "10s"
    timeout  = "2s"
    deregister_critical_service_after = "5m"
  }
}

consul reload
dig @127.0.0.1 -p 8600 taskflow-api.service.consul SRV +short    # healthy instances and ports
curl -s "http://127.0.0.1:8500/v1/health/service/taskflow-api?passing=true"

Only instances whose check passes are returned, and an instance that stays critical for five minutes is removed from the catalog.

docs.title: Client-side discovery in Node.js
docs.text:
// src/discovery/consul-client.js
// Client-side discovery: ask the local Consul agent for healthy instances,
// cache the list briefly, and round-robin across it.
export function createDiscovery({ consulUrl = "http://127.0.0.1:8500", ttlMs = 5_000 } = {}) {
  const cache = new Map(); // service name -> { instances, expiresAt, next }

  async function load(service) {
    const url = `${consulUrl}/v1/health/service/${encodeURIComponent(service)}?passing=true`;
    const res = await fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(1_000) });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Consul returned ${res.status}`);
    const entries = await res.json();
    return entries.map((e) => ({
      host: e.Service.Address || e.Node.Address,
      port: e.Service.Port,
    }));
  }

  async function lookup(service) {
    const cached = cache.get(service);
    if (cached && cached.expiresAt > Date.now()) return cached;
    try {
      const instances = await load(service);
      const entry = { instances, expiresAt: Date.now() + ttlMs, next: cached?.next ?? 0 };
      cache.set(service, entry);
      return entry;
    } catch (err) {
      if (!cached) throw err;
      // Registry unreachable: keep serving the last known list, retry in 1 s
      cached.expiresAt = Date.now() + 1_000;
      return cached;
    }
  }

  return {
    async pick(service) {
      const entry = await lookup(service);
      if (entry.instances.length === 0) throw new Error(`no healthy ${service} instances`);
      const instance = entry.instances[entry.next % entry.instances.length];
      entry.next += 1;
      return `http://${instance.host}:${instance.port}`;
    },
  };
}

// src/clients/tasks-via-consul.js (usage)
import { createDiscovery } from "../discovery/consul-client.js";

const discovery = createDiscovery();

export async function getTask(id) {
  const base = await discovery.pick("taskflow-api");
  const res = await fetch(`${base}/tasks/${id}`, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2_000) });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`tasks returned ${res.status}`);
  return res.json();
}

Two properties matter more than the code size: the list is cached, so the registry is not called on every request, and if the registry is unreachable the client keeps using the last list it saw instead of failing every call. Callers should still retry a failed call on a different instance, as shown in resilience patterns across servers.

docs.title: Per-request gRPC balancing over a headless Service
docs.text:
// src/clients/tasks-grpc.js: round robin across every Pod behind a headless Service
import grpc from "@grpc/grpc-js";

const serviceConfig = JSON.stringify({ loadBalancingConfig: [{ round_robin: {} }] });

export const channelOptions = {
  "grpc.service_config": serviceConfig,
  "grpc.keepalive_time_ms": 30_000,
};

// dns:/// re-resolves the headless Service name and balances per request
export const target = "dns:///tasks-grpc.taskflow.svc.cluster.local:50051";

export function createClient(ClientCtor) {
  return new ClientCtor(target, grpc.credentials.createInsecure(), channelOptions);
}

The headless Service (clusterIP: None) makes DNS return every ready Pod address, and the round_robin policy opens a connection to each and spreads requests across them, instead of pinning every request to the single connection a ClusterIP would give.

docs.title: Turning on Istio for the TaskFlow namespace
docs.text:
# Ambient mode: no sidecars; ztunnel provides mTLS for every Pod in the namespace
kubectl label namespace taskflow istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient

# Add a waypoint so L7 policies (routing, retries) apply to this namespace
istioctl waypoint apply -n taskflow --enroll-namespace

# Or sidecar mode instead: inject an Envoy proxy into each new Pod
# kubectl label namespace taskflow istio-injection=enabled
# kubectl rollout restart deployment -n taskflow

# k8s/mesh/peer-authentication.yaml: refuse plaintext traffic to the namespace
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT
---
# k8s/mesh/tasks-destination-rule.yaml: subsets and outlier detection
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  host: taskflow-api
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50
  subsets:
    - name: v1
      labels:
        version: v1
    - name: v2
      labels:
        version: v2
---
# k8s/mesh/tasks-virtual-service.yaml: a 90/10 canary with one timeout and few retries
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  hosts:
    - taskflow-api
  http:
    - route:
        - destination:
            host: taskflow-api
            subset: v1
          weight: 90
        - destination:
            host: taskflow-api
            subset: v2
          weight: 10
      timeout: 2s
      retries:
        attempts: 2
        perTryTimeout: 800ms
        retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream,unavailable,reset

Start with mode: PERMISSIVE while some callers are still outside the mesh, and switch to STRICT once every client sends mutual TLS. The retry policy retries only connection-level failures, not every 5xx, so a slow, overloaded service does not receive three times its traffic.

In ambient mode, Istio documents VirtualService support as Alpha and recommends the Gateway API (HTTPRoute, with weighted backendRefs) for traffic splitting, so prefer HTTPRoute for new ambient setups.

docs.title: Linkerd: inject and observe
docs.text:
kubectl annotate namespace taskflow linkerd.io/inject=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n taskflow      # new Pods get the proxy
linkerd viz stat deploy -n taskflow                 # success rate, RPS, latency per deployment

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Never hard-code instance addresses; use platform discovery or a registry.
  • Pair registration with health checks and automatic deregistration.
  • Cache discovery results in clients and keep working on the last known list when the registry is unreachable.
  • Keep DNS TTLs short for dynamic services and cap connection lifetimes so traffic follows membership changes.
  • Retry failed calls on a different instance, with timeouts short enough to notice dead instances quickly.
  • Prefer platform registration over self-registration where available.
  • Adopt a mesh for a concrete need, one namespace at a time, starting in permissive mTLS mode.
  • Decide which single layer owns retries: mesh, client library, or application.
  • Budget sidecar resources, and plan proxy upgrades as rollouts.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Errors spike briefly after every scale-in. Detect: connection-refused or timeout errors to addresses that no longer exist, right after terminations. Cause: clients use cached lists, DNS answers, or keep-alive connections to removed instances. Fix: drain before termination, shorten TTLs and cache lifetimes, limit connection age, and retry connection failures on another instance.
  • New instances receive almost no traffic. Detect: per-instance request rates are uneven, and recently started instances sit idle. Cause: long-lived HTTP/2 or keep-alive connections stay on the old instances. Fix: per-request balancing (client-side or a mesh), maximum connection age, or periodic reconnects.
  • The registry went down and every service failed. Detect: errors started when the registry became unreachable, although service instances were healthy. Cause: clients looked up the registry on every request and failed when it did not answer. Fix: cache results, serve stale lists, and treat the registry as a control plane that may be briefly unavailable.
  • Dead instances stay registered after a network blip. Detect: a Eureka server reports self-preservation mode, and its registry lists instances that no longer exist. Cause: many renewals were lost at once, so the server stopped expiring instances to avoid wiping the registry. Fix: retries on other instances in clients, alerting on self-preservation, and investigating the network problem.
  • Enabling strict mTLS broke a nightly job and the monitoring scraper. Detect: connections from workloads outside the mesh are reset. Cause: STRICT mode rejects plaintext clients. Fix: migrate with PERMISSIVE, bring every client into the mesh or give it a certificate, then switch to STRICT.
  • An overloaded service received three times its normal traffic. Detect: request rates at the service far exceed what callers sent; traces show repeated attempts. Cause: retries in the mesh plus retries in the client library. Fix: one owner for retries, retry budgets, and retries only on connection failures for non-idempotent calls.
  • Pods crash at startup with connection errors. Detect: the app's first outbound calls fail before the sidecar is ready. Cause: the application container started before its proxy. Fix: native sidecars or Istio's holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts, or ambient mode.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Service discovery: Finding the current, healthy instances of a service.
  • Service registry: A database of service instances and their health.
  • Client-side discovery: The caller reads the registry and picks an instance.
  • Server-side discovery: A load balancer or proxy picks the instance for the caller.
  • Self-registration / platform registration: The instance registers itself, or the platform registers it.
  • SRV record: A DNS record that carries a target host and port.
  • xDS: Envoy's family of discovery APIs for listeners, routes, clusters, and endpoints.
  • Service mesh: Proxies on every service-to-service hop, managed by a control plane.
  • Sidecar: A proxy container running next to the application in the same Pod.
  • Ambient mode: Istio's sidecarless data plane: per-node ztunnel for L4, optional waypoint proxies for L7.
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): TLS in which both client and server present certificates.
  • Outlier detection: Temporarily removing instances that return errors from load balancing.
  • Self-preservation: Eureka's mode that stops expiring instances when many renewals are lost at once.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Hard-coding IP lists in configuration.
  • Calling the registry on every request instead of caching.
  • Ignoring how DNS TTLs and keep-alive connections delay changes.
  • Trusting self-registration without health checks.
  • Assuming a mesh fixes application design problems such as missing timeouts or non-idempotent retries.
  • Enabling strict mTLS before every client is in the mesh.
  • Stacking mesh retries on top of library retries.
  • Treating "mesh" as mandatory for microservices; many systems do well without one.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why do hard-coded instance lists break in an autoscaling fleet?
  2. Compare client-side and server-side discovery. Which is a Kubernetes Service, and which is Eureka with Spring Cloud?
  3. With Eureka's defaults (30-second renewals, removal after 90 seconds, 30-second client refresh), roughly how long can clients keep calling a crashed instance? How should clients cope?
  4. Why can a keep-alive or HTTP/2 connection keep sending traffic to a removed instance, and what limits it?
  5. What does a service mesh's control plane do, and what do the data plane proxies do?
  6. How does Istio's ambient mode differ from sidecar mode, and when would you add a waypoint proxy?
  7. What changed in Linkerd's release model in 2024?
  8. Name three costs of a service mesh and one situation in which you would still adopt it.

docs.title: Alerting and On-Call
docs.text: An alert is a decision, made in advance, that a condition deserves a human's attention. Paging someone at 3 a.m. is the most expensive thing a monitoring system can do, so every alert has to earn it. This lesson covers alerting on symptoms rather than causes, the difference between a page and a ticket, severity levels, how to keep alerts actionable and avoid alert fatigue, how Alertmanager groups, deduplicates, inhibits, and routes alerts, why every alert needs a runbook, and how to run a humane on-call rotation: handoffs, escalation policies, follow-the-sun, and the metrics that show whether on-call is healthy.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Bad alerting fails in two directions. Too few alerts and users discover outages before you do. Too many and engineers learn to ignore them: when nine pages out of ten need no action, the tenth (the real one) is acknowledged and snoozed like the rest. Alert fatigue is a major reliability risk, and it also burns people out and makes on-call something everyone avoids.

Good alerting is small and precise. A team running TaskFlow API should be paged only when users are being hurt, or are about to be, and something can be done about it now. Everything else becomes a ticket, a dashboard, or automation. Combined with a fair rotation and good runbooks, that makes on-call sustainable.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE (philosophy of paging). The chapter Monitoring Distributed Systems says pages should be urgent, actionable, and require human intelligence, and that you should page on symptoms rather than causes; anything that can be handled by a robot should not page a human.
  • Google SRE (being on-call). The chapter Being On-Call describes primary and secondary rotations, caps the share of time an engineer spends on-call, and sets a target of at most two incidents per 12-hour shift so each incident gets proper follow-up.
  • Prometheus. The project's alerting best practices recommend keeping alerting simple, alerting on symptoms associated with end-user pain, alerting on latency and errors as high in the stack as possible, and having consoles that let you find the cause.
  • PagerDuty Incident Response. PagerDuty's public incident response documentation, including Being On-Call, describes on-call responsibilities, acknowledgement expectations, handoffs, and escalation in a form many companies adopt.

Popular tools and providers: Prometheus Alertmanager, Grafana Alerting, PagerDuty, Jira Service Management, incident.io, Splunk On-Call, and cloud-native alarms such as Amazon CloudWatch alarms with SNS.

docs.title: Alert on symptoms, not causes
docs.text:
A symptom is something a user experiences: errors, slowness, missing data. A cause is a reason it might happen: high CPU, a full disk, a restarted pod. Causes are many, change with the architecture, and often do not hurt anyone. Symptoms are few and always matter.

Cause-based alert (avoid paging) Symptom-based alert (page) CPU above 90% on an API pod Error budget burning 14x too fast One of six pods restarted p99 latency above SLO for the create-task journey MongoDB replica lag above 10 s Synthetic "create and read a task" check failing from two regions Queue depth above 1,000 Reminder emails more than 15 minutes late (freshness SLI) Memory above 80% Public TLS certificate expires in under 7 days with renewal failing

Cause-based signals are still valuable: they belong on dashboards, in tickets (a disk that will fill in five days), and in the runbook as diagnosis steps. The exception is a cause that predicts imminent, unavoidable user pain with no slack, such as a disk that will be full in two hours; that can page.

docs.title: Pages, tickets, and dashboards
docs.text:
The SRE book describes three kinds of monitoring output:

Output Meaning Response time TaskFlow examples Page A human must act now Minutes, any hour Fast error budget burn, site down from outside, data loss risk Ticket A human must act, but not now Hours to days, working hours Slow budget burn, certificate expiring in 20 days, disk full in 5 days, backup job failed once Dashboard or log Nobody needs to act; useful for diagnosis Never, unless investigating CPU, memory, individual pod restarts, cache hit ratio

Most alerts people create should be tickets or dashboard panels. A practical rule: if the right response is "look at it tomorrow", it must not page tonight.

docs.title: Severity levels
docs.text:
Severity labels on alerts drive routing. Keep the scheme small and written down:

Severity Definition Routing page (critical) User-facing SLO at risk now; needs action within minutes Pager service, primary on-call, escalation ticket (warning) Will become user-facing if ignored for days Ticket queue for the owning team info Context only Chat channel or dashboard, no notification

Do not invent more levels than you route differently; five severities that all go to the same channel are one severity.

docs.title: Actionable alerts and alert fatigue
docs.text:
Every paging alert should pass four tests:

  1. Urgent: waiting until morning would hurt users or the business.
  2. Actionable: the responder can do something (mitigate, roll back, fail over, scale), and the runbook says what.
  3. Requires judgement: if the fix is a fixed script, automate it instead of paging.
  4. Novel: it is not a duplicate of another page for the same problem.

Alert fatigue builds up from small exceptions: a flapping alert nobody fixed, a threshold set on a quiet week, a duplicate per pod. Counter it with process:

  • Review every page in a weekly on-call review: was it actionable? If not, fix, downgrade, or delete the alert that week.
  • Track the actionable rate: the share of pages that led to a real action. A healthy target is well above half; anything near zero means the alert is noise.
  • Use for: to require a condition to persist (for example 5 minutes) for threshold alerts, so momentary spikes do not page. SLO burn-rate alerts already have this built into their windows.
  • Delete alerts nobody would miss. An alert that has not fired in a year and has no clear owner is not protection, it is clutter.

docs.title: The alerting pipeline
docs.text:
Alerting rules live in Prometheus (or Grafana, or a cloud provider). Each rule has an expression, an optional for duration (the condition must hold that long; until then the alert is pending), optional keep_firing_for (keeps it firing briefly after the condition clears, to avoid flapping), labels such as severity, and annotations such as summary and runbook_url.

Alertmanager receives firing alerts from one or more Prometheus servers and decides who hears about them:

  • Deduplication: run two Prometheus servers for redundancy and both send the same alert; Alertmanager notifies once. Run Alertmanager itself as a small cluster (two or three instances) that shares state.
  • Grouping: group_by: [alertname, service] turns 40 pod-level alerts into one notification. group_wait (default 30 s) waits to collect the first batch, group_interval (default 5 m) controls updates to an existing group, and repeat_interval (default 4 h) re-sends while it is still firing.
  • Inhibition: suppress some alerts while others fire. If "TaskFlow API down" is paging, the latency and error-budget alerts for the same service add nothing.
  • Silences: temporary, time-limited mutes created by people (in the UI or with amtool) during maintenance or while an incident is already being worked. Every silence should have an author, a comment, and an expiry.
  • Routing: a tree of matchers on labels sends each group to a receiver (pager, ticket webhook, chat, email).

docs.title: Runbook links in every alert
docs.text:
A page at 3 a.m. should never leave the responder wondering what it means. Every alert carries a runbook_url annotation pointing to a page that answers:

  1. What this alert means, in one sentence, and what users experience.
  2. Impact and urgency: which journeys and how badly.
  3. Dashboards and queries to open first (linked, with the right variables).
  4. Diagnosis steps: the likely causes, how to tell them apart.
  5. Mitigation: the safe actions, such as rolling back the last deploy, scaling out, failing over, disabling a feature flag, in order of preference.
  6. Escalation: who to call when the runbook does not work.

Runbooks are reviewed after every incident that used them, and an alert without a runbook is not allowed to page.

docs.title: On-call rotations and handoffs
docs.text:
A rotation is the schedule of who responds:

  • Primary and secondary: the primary responds to pages; the secondary backs up the primary (escalation) and takes over if the primary is overloaded or unreachable.
  • Shift length: commonly one week, handing over on a weekday morning so the handoff happens during work hours.
  • Team size: with fewer than about six to eight people in a rotation, each person is on-call too often; small teams share a rotation with a neighbouring team or buy time with better automation.
  • Handoffs: a short written note (or meeting) at every change of shift: open incidents, active silences and why, noisy alerts, risky changes scheduled, anything half-finished.
  • Compensation and recovery: time off after a night of pages, and pay or time in lieu for being on-call, are part of a sustainable rotation.

docs.title: Escalation policies
docs.text: An escalation policy says what happens when a page is not acknowledged: page the primary; if no acknowledgement in 5 minutes, page the secondary; after 15 minutes, page the engineering manager. It ensures that a dead phone battery or a missed vibration does not turn a 10-minute incident into a 2-hour one. Acknowledgement only means "I am on it"; the responder then works the problem or declares an incident (see incident response and postmortems).

docs.title: Follow-the-sun
docs.text: Teams spread across time zones can split the day so nobody is paged at night: for example, a team in Europe covers 08:00 to 16:00 UTC, one in the Americas 16:00 to 24:00, and one in Asia-Pacific 00:00 to 08:00. This removes night pages but needs at least two or three sites with real expertise in the service, consistent runbooks, and excellent handoffs at each boundary.

docs.title: On-call health metrics
docs.text:
Measure on-call like any other system:

Metric What it tells you Healthy signal Pages per shift Load on the responder Low single digits per week; at most about two incidents per 12-hour shift Pages outside working hours Sleep disruption Trending down Actionable rate Alert quality Most pages led to action Time to acknowledge (MTTA) Responsiveness and paging reliability A few minutes Time to mitigate Effectiveness of runbooks and tooling Trending down Top alerts by count Where to invest The top three are fixed or deleted each quarter Repeat incidents Whether follow-ups get done Rare

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Condition Action SLO burn rate fast (14.4x or 6x) Page Service unreachable from external probes in two or more regions Page SLO burn rate slow (1x over days) Ticket Certificate expires in under 21 days Ticket; page only if under 7 days and renewal is failing Disk will be full within 4 hours at current rate Page (imminent, no slack) Disk will be full within 5 days Ticket One pod restarting, others healthy and SLO fine Dashboard; ticket if it persists CPU or memory high, SLO fine Dashboard Backup job failed once Ticket; page if no successful backup for over 26 hours on a critical database Prometheus or Alertmanager itself is down Page through an external watchdog

docs.title: Prometheus alerting rules
docs.text:
# prometheus/rules/taskflow-alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: taskflow-availability
    rules:
      - alert: TaskflowApiDown
        expr: sum(up{job="taskflow-api"}) == 0 or absent(up{job="taskflow-api"})   # absent(): no targets discovered at all
        for: 2m
        labels:
          severity: page
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "No TaskFlow API instance can be scraped"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/api-down"

      - alert: TaskflowSyntheticCheckFailing
        # Blackbox exporter probes from several regions; page only when two or more fail.
        expr: count(probe_success{job="blackbox-taskflow"} == 0) >= 2
        for: 3m
        labels:
          severity: page
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "External probes failing from {{ $value }} regions"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/synthetic-failing"

  - name: taskflow-capacity
    rules:
      - alert: TaskflowDbDiskFullSoon
        expr: predict_linear(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{job="node", mountpoint="/var/lib/mongodb"}[6h], 5 * 86400) < 0
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          service: taskflow-db
        annotations:
          summary: "MongoDB data disk on {{ $labels.instance }} will be full within 5 days"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-db/disk-full"

      - alert: TaskflowCertificateExpiringSoon
        expr: (probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry{job="blackbox-taskflow"} - time()) / 86400 < 21
        for: 1h
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "TLS certificate for {{ $labels.instance }} expires in {{ $value | humanize }} days"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/certificate-expiry"

  - name: meta
    rules:
      - alert: Watchdog
        # Always firing. An external service pages if it STOPS receiving this.
        expr: vector(1)
        labels:
          severity: none
        annotations:
          summary: "Alerting pipeline heartbeat"

The SLO burn-rate pages from SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets are the main symptom alerts; these rules cover total outages, outside-in checks, capacity tickets, and the pipeline itself. predict_linear extrapolates the last 6 hours of free space 5 days ahead. The Watchdog alert is a dead man's switch: it proves the whole path from Prometheus to the receiver works, and its absence is what pages.

docs.title: Alertmanager routing, grouping, and inhibition
docs.text:
# alertmanager/alertmanager.yml
global:
  resolve_timeout: 5m

route:
  receiver: team-chat            # default: anything not matched below
  group_by: [alertname, service]
  group_wait: 30s
  group_interval: 5m
  repeat_interval: 4h
  routes:
    - matchers: ['alertname="Watchdog"']
      receiver: heartbeat
      group_interval: 1m           # repeats are only sent at group_interval ticks
      repeat_interval: 1m
    - matchers: ['severity="page"']
      receiver: taskflow-pager
      repeat_interval: 1h
    - matchers: ['severity="ticket"']
      receiver: taskflow-tickets
      repeat_interval: 24h

inhibit_rules:
  # While the API is completely down, its other alerts add nothing.
  - source_matchers: ['alertname="TaskflowApiDown"']
    target_matchers: ['alertname!="TaskflowApiDown"', 'service="taskflow-api"']
    equal: [service]
  # A page for a service hides that service's tickets.
  - source_matchers: ['severity="page"']
    target_matchers: ['severity="ticket"']
    equal: [service]

receivers:
  - name: taskflow-pager
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/pagerduty-routing-key
        severity: critical
  - name: taskflow-tickets
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://tickets.example.com/hooks/alertmanager
  - name: team-chat
    slack_configs:
      - api_url_file: /etc/alertmanager/secrets/slack-webhook-url
        channel: "#taskflow-alerts"
        send_resolved: true
  - name: heartbeat
    webhook_configs:
      - url: https://heartbeat.example.com/ping/<check-id>

Parts: the route tree matches top to bottom and stops at the first matching child; group_by keeps one notification per alert name and service; the inhibit rules mute duplicates while a bigger alert is firing; secrets (the PagerDuty routing key and chat webhook URL) are read from files mounted from a secret store, not written in the config; the heartbeat receiver pings an external dead man's switch service every minute. Alertmanager rounds repeat_interval up to a multiple of group_interval, so the heartbeat route lowers both; with the inherited 5-minute group_interval it would ping only every 5 minutes.

docs.title: Validating and testing alerts
docs.text:
# Syntax and semantic checks, run in CI on every change
promtool check rules prometheus/rules/*.yml
amtool check-config alertmanager/alertmanager.yml

# Unit tests for alert rules
promtool test rules prometheus/tests/taskflow-alerts.test.yml

# Show which receiver an alert with these labels would reach
amtool config routes test --config.file=alertmanager/alertmanager.yml severity=page service=taskflow-api

# Silence an alert during planned maintenance, with an expiry and a reason
amtool silence add alertname=TaskflowDbDiskFullSoon service=taskflow-db \
  --duration=2h --comment="Disk resize in progress (change 4821)" \
  --alertmanager.url=http://alertmanager:9093

# prometheus/tests/taskflow-alerts.test.yml
rule_files:
  - ../rules/taskflow-alerts.yml

evaluation_interval: 1m

tests:
  - interval: 1m
    input_series:
      - series: 'up{job="taskflow-api", instance="api-1:9464"}'
        values: "1 1 0 0 0 0 0"
      - series: 'up{job="taskflow-api", instance="api-2:9464"}'
        values: "1 1 0 0 0 0 0"
    alert_rule_test:
      - eval_time: 3m
        alertname: TaskflowApiDown
        exp_alerts: []          # down for 1 minute: still pending
      - eval_time: 5m
        alertname: TaskflowApiDown
        exp_alerts:
          - exp_labels:
              severity: page
              service: taskflow-api
            exp_annotations:
              summary: "No TaskFlow API instance can be scraped"
              runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/api-down"

Testing alerts in CI catches typos in label names (which silently route a page to the wrong place) and checks that for durations behave as intended.

docs.title: A handoff note template
docs.text:
On-call handoff: taskflow, week 46 (primary: <name>, secondary: <name>)

Open incidents:        none / INC-123 (status, next step, owner)
Active silences:       TaskflowDbDiskFullSoon until Thu 14:00 (disk resize, change 4821)
Pages this week:       6 (4 actionable). Noisy: TaskflowSyntheticCheckFailing from ap-south (ticket TF-881)
Risky changes ahead:   MongoDB 8.0 upgrade Wed 10:00 UTC, rollback plan in change 4830
Follow-ups for review: runbook for certificate expiry was out of date (fixed), ticket TF-879

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Page on symptoms tied to SLOs; send causes to dashboards and tickets.
  • Make every page urgent, actionable, judgement-requiring, and novel.
  • Require a runbook_url and a dashboard link on every paging alert.
  • Use a small, written severity scheme that maps one-to-one to routing.
  • Group and inhibit aggressively so one problem produces one page.
  • Run Prometheus and Alertmanager redundantly, and watch them with an external dead man's switch.
  • Test rules and routes in CI with promtool and amtool.
  • Review every page weekly; fix or delete non-actionable alerts that week.
  • Keep rotations large enough, hand off in writing, compensate on-call, and give recovery time after bad nights.
  • Track pages per shift, actionable rate, and time to acknowledge.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The on-call engineer receives 40 pages in 2 minutes for one outage. Detect: the pager history shows one page per pod and per alert for a single database failure. Cause: group_by includes instance or pod, or no inhibition from the root-cause alert. Fix: group by alertname and service, add inhibit rules from "service down" to its dependent alerts, and alert on service-level symptoms rather than per-pod conditions.
  • A real outage was acknowledged and ignored. Detect: the postmortem timeline shows the page acknowledged within a minute but no action for 30 minutes. Cause: alert fatigue: the same alert had fired and self-resolved dozens of times that month. Fix: measure the actionable rate per alert, fix or delete flapping alerts, and tie paging to SLO burn rates.
  • Nobody was paged during a full outage. Detect: users reported the outage; the alert history shows the rule firing but no notification sent. Cause: Alertmanager was down, its pager secret had expired, or a route matcher had a typo in the severity label. Fix: an external dead man's switch on a Watchdog alert, amtool config routes test in CI, and a periodic end-to-end test page.
  • Alerts keep firing after the problem is fixed. Detect: the dashboard shows recovery, but the alert stays firing for an hour and re-pages. Cause: a long-window expression without a short window, or a repeat_interval that is too short for the receiver. Fix: use multiwindow burn-rate rules, and set repeat intervals per route.
  • A silence outlived the maintenance and hid a real failure. Detect: an incident review finds a matching silence created days earlier with no expiry note. Cause: broad silences (matching a whole service) with long durations. Fix: narrow matchers, short expiries, mandatory comments, and active silences listed in every handoff.
  • On-call engineers burn out and leave the rotation. Detect: rising pages outside working hours, people swapping shifts, and repeat incidents. Cause: noisy alerts, small rotations, and no time to fix root causes. Fix: cap on-call load, prioritize the top noisy alerts in planning, enlarge or merge rotations, and give recovery time.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Alert rule: An expression evaluated periodically; when true (for the for duration), it fires.
  • Pending / firing: States of an alert before and after its for duration has elapsed.
  • Page: A notification that interrupts a person immediately.
  • Ticket: A tracked task for non-urgent follow-up.
  • Symptom / cause: What users experience versus why it happens.
  • Grouping: Combining related alerts into one notification.
  • Inhibition: Suppressing alerts while a related, more important alert fires.
  • Silence: A time-limited, manual mute of matching alerts.
  • Runbook: A document describing how to diagnose and mitigate a specific alert.
  • Escalation policy: Rules for who is notified when a page is not acknowledged.
  • Follow-the-sun: Splitting on-call across time zones to avoid night shifts.
  • Dead man's switch: An always-firing alert whose absence triggers notification, proving the pipeline works.
  • MTTA / MTTR: Mean time to acknowledge, and to restore or resolve.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Paging on CPU, memory, or individual pod restarts.
  • Thinking that more alerts mean better coverage.
  • Alerts without runbooks, owners, or links to dashboards.
  • Copying thresholds from a blog post instead of deriving them from SLOs.
  • Grouping by instance, producing one page per pod.
  • Silences without expiry or comments.
  • Monitoring the alerting system with itself.
  • Treating on-call as a punishment, or expecting one person to carry it alone.
  • Muting a noisy alert instead of fixing or deleting it.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Give two cause-based alerts and rewrite each as a symptom-based alert for TaskFlow API.
  2. What four properties should every paging alert have?
  3. Explain Alertmanager's grouping, inhibition, and silences with an example of each.
  4. What do group_wait, group_interval, and repeat_interval control?
  5. What belongs in a runbook linked from an alert?
  6. A rotation of five engineers takes weekly shifts. How many weeks a year is each person on-call as primary, and why might that be too much? (52 / 5 = about 10.4 weeks, one week in five, which leaves little time to recover and is often combined with secondary duty as well.)
  7. In one week the primary received 18 pages, 11 outside working hours, and 5 led to an action. What would you change first?
  8. Why does a Watchdog alert need an external receiver?

import pino from "pino";

export const logger = pino({
  base: { service: "taskflow-api", env: process.env.NODE_ENV, version: process.env.APP_VERSION },

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why What happened to one request Logs by reqId or trace_id Per-event detail Exact counts, rates, alerts Metrics Cheap per series, never sampled Where a slow request spent its time A distributed trace Causal chain with timings Crashes grouped by release An error tracker Grouping, source maps, regressions Proof users can reach you Multi-region synthetic checks Sees DNS, TLS, and CDN failures Real users' page speed RUM, Core Web Vitals at p75 Real devices and networks Cheap, simple sampling Head sampling, parentbased_traceidratio Decided at the root span Every error and slow trace Tail sampling in the Collector Decides after the trace ends Pages that match user pain Multiwindow burn-rate SLO alerts Few, symptom-based, actionable Restart a stuck process Liveness /healthz, no dependencies A database blip must not restart pods Stop traffic to an instance Readiness /readyz, quick ping, 503 Drains without restarting

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Logging whole req objects or HTTP client errors. Log selected fields, redact in pino and the pipeline, rotate leaked secrets.
  • Logging 400 and 404 as error. Use info or warn; error means someone should look.
  • IDs or raw paths as metric or Loki labels. Label by route template; keep IDs in log lines and span attributes.
  • Averaging percentiles or summing before rate(). Use sum(rate(x[5m])), and sum histogram buckets before the quantile.
  • Loading instrumentation after the app. Load it first with --import or --require, plus the loader hook for ES modules.
  • Checking the database in liveness. Keep /healthz dependency-free and check MongoDB in /readyz.
  • Paging on causes or once per pod. Page on SLO burn, group by alertname and service, and inhibit dependent alerts.
  • Deploying source maps. Upload them in CI, delete them from dist/, and fail the build if any remain.
