docs.title: Distributed Tracing
docs.text: A distributed trace records the path of one request through every process it touches: the API, the services it calls, the database queries, and the messages it leaves on a queue. Each step is a span with a start time, a duration, and a link to the step that caused it. Put together, the spans show where time was spent and where the request failed. This lesson covers traces and spans, span attributes and events, how context crosses process boundaries (the W3C traceparent header, field by field), OpenTelemetry's API, SDK, auto-instrumentation for Node.js, and Collector, head and tail sampling, linking logs to traces, and the main tracing backends.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Metrics can tell you that POST /tasks got slower at 14:03. Logs can tell you that one request took 412 ms. Neither tells you which of the eleven things that request did took 308 of those milliseconds. In a single process you would reach for a profiler; once a request crosses services, a queue, and a database, a trace is the only view that shows the whole causal chain with timings.

Tracing also exposes design problems that are otherwise invisible: calls made one after another that could run in parallel, an N+1 pattern of fifty tiny queries, a retry loop against a slow dependency, or a "fast" endpoint that is fast only because it hands work to a worker that takes seconds. As TaskFlow grows from one API into an API, an auth service, a notifications service, and a queue worker, tracing turns "it's slow somewhere" into a specific span.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google (Dapper). The paper Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure (2010) describes Google's production tracing system: trees of spans linked by trace and span IDs, propagated automatically through shared RPC libraries, with sampling to keep overhead low. Most modern tracing systems follow its model.
  • W3C Trace Context. The Trace Context specification is a W3C Recommendation that standardizes the traceparent and tracestate HTTP headers, so a trace can cross services instrumented by different tools and vendors without breaking.
  • Jaeger. The Jaeger documentation describes an open-source tracing platform originally built at Uber and now a graduated CNCF project. Its current major version is built on the OpenTelemetry Collector and accepts OTLP natively.
  • OpenTelemetry. The What is OpenTelemetry? page explains that the project, formed from the merger of OpenTracing and OpenCensus, provides vendor-neutral APIs, SDKs, and the Collector for traces, metrics, and logs.

Popular tools and providers: OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Grafana Tempo, Zipkin, Honeycomb, Datadog APM, New Relic, Elastic APM, AWS X-Ray, Google Cloud Trace, and Azure Application Insights.

docs.title: Traces and spans
docs.text:
A trace is a tree of spans that share one trace ID. Each span represents one operation and records:

Field Meaning TaskFlow example Trace ID 16 random bytes shared by every span in the trace 4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736 Span ID 8 random bytes identifying this span 00f067aa0ba902b7 Parent span ID The span that caused this one (empty for the root) The server span for POST /tasks Name A low-cardinality operation name POST /tasks, find tasks Kind SERVER, CLIENT, PRODUCER, CONSUMER, or INTERNAL CLIENT for the call to the auth service Start and end time Gives the duration 44 ms to 352 ms Status Unset, Ok, or Error Error when the handler throws Attributes Key-value details http.route="/tasks", db.collection.name="tasks" Events Timestamped notes inside the span An exception with its stack trace Links References to spans in other traces A batch consumer linking to each message's producer

The service that produced a span is described by its resource (service.name="taskflow-api", service.version="1.42.0"), shared by all spans from that process.

Reading a waterfall:

  • Find the critical path: the chain of spans that determines the end time. Shortening a span off the critical path does not make the request faster.
  • Look for the longest bar: here, an unindexed find on the tasks collection takes 75% of the request.
  • Look for gaps: time inside a parent not covered by any child is either CPU work in that service or something uninstrumented.
  • Look for staircases: many short sequential spans (N+1 queries, sequential HTTP calls) that could be batched or run concurrently.
  • Remember async work: the worker span runs after the response; it does not slow the user's request but it is part of the outcome.

docs.title: Attributes, events, and status
docs.text:
Attributes make spans searchable ("all traces where http.route="/tasks" and http.response.status_code=500"). Use OpenTelemetry semantic conventions for common attributes so every backend understands them, and a project prefix (taskflow.) for your own.

Unlike metric labels, span attributes may have high cardinality: a task ID or tenant ID on a span is fine and is often exactly what you need when debugging. They must still never contain secrets or sensitive personal data, because traces are stored and shared like logs.

Events are timestamped annotations inside a span ("cache miss", "retrying after 503"). An exception is recorded as an event with the exception type, message, and stack trace, and the span's status is set to Error so the trace is easy to find.

docs.title: Context propagation
docs.text:
Spans become a tree only if each new span knows its parent. That knowledge is the span context (trace ID, span ID, trace flags), and moving it around is context propagation.

  • Inside a process, OpenTelemetry keeps the active context in a context manager. In Node.js it is built on AsyncLocalStorage, so the active span follows the request through await and callbacks.
  • Across processes, a propagator injects the context into the outgoing carrier (HTTP headers, message headers) and the receiver extracts it and starts a child span.

The default propagator uses the W3C traceparent header:

traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01
             |  |                                |                |
             |  trace-id (16 bytes, 32 hex)      |                trace-flags
             version                             parent-id (8 bytes, 16 hex)

Field by field:

  1. version (00): the format version. Version 00 is the only one defined today; ff is invalid.
  2. trace-id (32 lowercase hex characters): the ID of the whole trace, copied unchanged to every downstream span. All zeros is invalid.
  3. parent-id (16 hex characters): the span ID of the span that made the call, usually the caller's CLIENT or PRODUCER span. The receiver's new span records it as its parent. All zeros is invalid.
  4. trace-flags (2 hex characters, 8 bits): the lowest bit is the sampled flag. 01 means the caller recorded this trace, so the receiver should too; 00 means it did not.

Two companion headers exist. tracestate carries vendor-specific key-value data alongside traceparent. baggage (a separate W3C specification) carries application key-value pairs, such as a tenant ID, to every downstream service. Baggage is sent in plain headers, including to third parties you call, so never put secrets or personal data in it.

Context is lost whenever something in the chain does not propagate: an uninstrumented HTTP client, a proxy that strips unknown headers, a message queue whose producer does not write message headers, or work scheduled with setTimeout outside the active context. A broken chain shows up as several short, unconnected traces instead of one tree.

docs.title: OpenTelemetry: API, SDK, and instrumentation
docs.text:
OpenTelemetry deliberately separates three layers:

Layer Package examples (Node.js) Role API @opentelemetry/api Stable interfaces libraries call (trace.getTracer, startActiveSpan). Without an SDK it does nothing, at almost no cost. SDK @opentelemetry/sdk-node The implementation: creates real spans, applies sampling, batches, and exports. Configured once by the application. Instrumentation @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node Patches popular libraries (http, Express, MongoDB driver, undici/fetch, pino, Redis clients) to create spans and propagate context automatically. Exporters @opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto Send spans using OTLP (the OpenTelemetry Protocol) over HTTP (port 4318) or gRPC (port 4317).

The split matters: a library author depends only on the API, so their library is traced when the application installs an SDK and costs nothing when it does not.

Instrumentation must load before the libraries it patches, so it runs from a separate file loaded with a Node.js flag, not imported halfway through server.js. Most settings can be given as standard environment variables: OTEL_SERVICE_NAME, OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER, and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG.

docs.title: The OpenTelemetry Collector
docs.text:
The Collector is a separate process that receives, processes, and exports telemetry. A configuration defines:

  • Receivers: how data comes in (otlp, also Prometheus scraping, Jaeger, Zipkin, log files).
  • Processors: what happens in between (memory_limiter to avoid out-of-memory crashes, batch, attributes to delete or hash fields, tail_sampling, resource detection).
  • Exporters: where data goes (OTLP to Tempo, Jaeger, or a vendor; Prometheus remote write; debug output).
  • Pipelines: which receivers, processors, and exporters are wired together for each signal.

Common deployments are an agent (one Collector per node or as a sidecar, close to the apps) and a gateway (a central, horizontally scaled pool), often both. Benefits: applications send to one local endpoint and never hold vendor credentials; retries and batching happen outside the app; sensitive attributes are scrubbed in one place; and switching or adding a backend is a config change, not a redeploy of every service. Many components, including tail_sampling, ship in the "contrib" distribution of the Collector rather than the core one.

docs.title: Sampling
docs.text:
Recording every span of every request is expensive: TaskFlow at 200 requests per second with 8 spans each produces 1,600 spans per second, about 138 million per day. Sampling keeps a representative subset.

Head sampling decides when the trace starts, at the root span, and passes the decision downstream through the sampled flag.

  • TraceIdRatioBased(0.1) keeps 10% of traces, chosen from the trace ID so every service makes the same decision.
  • ParentBased respects the caller's decision, so a trace is never half recorded. The usual configuration is parentbased_traceidratio.
  • Cheap and simple, but blind: the decision is made before anyone knows whether the request will fail or be slow, so 90% of interesting traces are thrown away with the boring ones.

Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete, in the Collector.

  • Policies such as "keep all traces with an error", "keep all traces slower than 1 s", "keep 10% of the rest".
  • Keeps the traces you actually want, at the cost of buffering every span in memory for a decision window (for example 10 s) and sending 100% of spans from the apps to the Collector.
  • Every span of a trace must reach the same Collector instance, so a multi-instance gateway needs a load-balancing layer keyed by trace ID (the Collector's loadbalancing exporter).
Head sampling Tail sampling Decision point Root span, at request start Collector, after the trace ends Keeps all errors and slow traces No (only at the sampled rate) Yes, by policy Cost in apps Low (unsampled spans are not exported) Higher (export everything) Cost in the pipeline Low Memory for buffering; trace-aware load balancing Typical use Starting point; very high traffic When rare failures matter more than volume

Many teams combine them: a generous head-sampling rate in apps to bound volume, tail sampling in the Collector to keep the interesting part.

docs.title: Linking traces with logs and metrics
docs.text:
• Logs: the OpenTelemetry pino instrumentation adds trace_id and span_id to every log line written inside an active span (see structured logging), and backends turn the value into a link to the trace.
  • Metrics: exemplars attach a sample trace ID to a histogram bucket, so a spike on a latency graph links to a real slow trace. The Collector can also derive RED metrics from spans (the spanmetrics connector).
  • Errors: error trackers record the trace ID with each exception.

Because sampling drops most traces, a log line's trace_id may point to a trace that was not kept. Tail sampling that keeps all error traces makes the error case reliable.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
Backend Storage model Notes Jaeger Pluggable (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Cassandra, Badger, memory) Open source, CNCF graduated; native OTLP; good local development UI Grafana Tempo Object storage (S3, GCS, Azure Blob); indexes little Cheap at scale; TraceQL queries; integrates with Loki and Prometheus in Grafana Zipkin Pluggable The original open-source Dapper-style tracer; simple and mature Vendors (Datadog, Honeycomb, New Relic, cloud tracing services) Managed Rich analysis and correlation; priced by spans or hosts; accept OTLP

Because the apps speak OTLP to a Collector, the backend is a deployment choice you can change later.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Tracing value Requests cross several services, queues, or serverless functions High: the only end-to-end view Latency problems you cannot explain from per-service metrics High One monolith with one database Moderate: still useful for DB and outbound calls, but a profiler and good logs go far Batch jobs processing millions of records Low per record; trace the job and its phases, not each record You need exact counts (requests, errors) Use metrics; traces are sampled Debugging CPU hot spots inside one function Use a profiler

Start with auto-instrumentation: it covers HTTP, Express, MongoDB, and outbound calls with no code. Add manual spans only around business operations that matter (an import, a billing run) and around code the auto-instrumentation cannot see.

docs.title: Auto-instrumenting TaskFlow API
docs.text:
npm install @opentelemetry/api @opentelemetry/sdk-node \
  @opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node @opentelemetry/instrumentation \
  @opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto \
  @opentelemetry/resources @opentelemetry/semantic-conventions

// src/instrumentation.mjs
import { NodeSDK } from "@opentelemetry/sdk-node";
import { getNodeAutoInstrumentations } from "@opentelemetry/auto-instrumentations-node";
import { OTLPTraceExporter } from "@opentelemetry/exporter-trace-otlp-proto";
import { resourceFromAttributes } from "@opentelemetry/resources";
import { ATTR_SERVICE_NAME, ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION } from "@opentelemetry/semantic-conventions";

const sdk = new NodeSDK({
  resource: resourceFromAttributes({
    [ATTR_SERVICE_NAME]: "taskflow-api",
    [ATTR_SERVICE_VERSION]: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev",
    "deployment.environment.name": process.env.NODE_ENV ?? "development",
  }),
  // Default endpoint is http://localhost:4318/v1/traces
  traceExporter: new OTLPTraceExporter({
    url: process.env.OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT ?? "http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces",
  }),
  instrumentations: [
    getNodeAutoInstrumentations({
      // File-system spans are noisy and rarely useful in an API.
      "@opentelemetry/instrumentation-fs": { enabled: false },
    }),
  ],
});

sdk.start();

// Flush buffered spans on shutdown. Call this from the server's SIGTERM handler
// after server.close() has finished draining, or spans from the drain window are lost.
export const shutdownTracing = () => sdk.shutdown().catch(() => {});

# .env.production (sampling read by the SDK from standard variables)
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio
OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.25
# The SDK also exports logs and metrics over OTLP by default. Logs already flow
# stdout -> Collector and metrics are scraped from /metrics, so turn those off.
OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER=none
OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER=none

# TaskFlow API is an ES module app, so the loader hook is required
node --experimental-loader=@opentelemetry/instrumentation/hook.mjs \
     --import ./src/instrumentation.mjs src/server.js

Parts: the resource names the service and version on every span; the OTLP exporter sends batches to the Collector; the auto-instrumentations create spans for incoming HTTP requests, Express routing, MongoDB commands, outgoing fetch calls, and add trace IDs to pino logs; parentbased_traceidratio keeps 25% of new traces and always follows the caller's decision. server.js imports shutdownTracing and awaits it at the end of its SIGTERM handler, once server.close() has finished. For a CommonJS app, node --require ./instrumentation.js app.js is enough. The OpenTelemetry docs note that the ESM loader mechanism is expected to change, so check the current guidance when upgrading.

docs.title: Adding a manual span around a business operation
docs.text:
// src/tasks/import.js
import { trace, SpanStatusCode } from "@opentelemetry/api";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("taskflow-api");

export async function importTasks(db, userId, rows) {
  return tracer.startActiveSpan("tasks.import", async (span) => {
    span.setAttribute("taskflow.import.rows", rows.length);
    try {
      const valid = rows.filter((r) => typeof r.title === "string" && r.title.length > 0);
      span.addEvent("validation complete", { "taskflow.import.invalid": rows.length - valid.length });

      const result = await db.collection("tasks").insertMany(
        valid.map((r) => ({ title: r.title, userId, createdAt: new Date() }))
      );
      span.setAttribute("taskflow.import.inserted", result.insertedCount);
      return result.insertedCount;
    } catch (err) {
      span.recordException(err);
      span.setStatus({ code: SpanStatusCode.ERROR, message: err.message });
      throw err;
    } finally {
      span.end(); // a span that is never ended is never exported
    }
  });
}

startActiveSpan makes the new span the active context, so the MongoDB span created by auto-instrumentation inside it becomes its child.

docs.title: Propagating context through a queue by hand
docs.text:
If a queue library has no instrumentation, inject the context into the message and extract it in the worker:

// src/queue/trace-context.js
import { context, propagation, trace, SpanKind } from "@opentelemetry/api";

const tracer = trace.getTracer("taskflow-api");

// Producer: run inside the request's active span.
export function withTraceHeaders(payload) {
  const carrier = {};
  propagation.inject(context.active(), carrier); // adds traceparent (and tracestate)
  return { ...payload, traceHeaders: carrier };
}

// Consumer: continue the trace in the worker.
export function runWithJobContext(name, job, fn) {
  const parentContext = propagation.extract(context.active(), job.data.traceHeaders ?? {});
  return tracer.startActiveSpan(name, { kind: SpanKind.CONSUMER }, parentContext, async (span) => {
    try {
      return await fn();
    } finally {
      span.end();
    }
  });
}

// usage
await queue.add("task.created", withTraceHeaders({ taskId: task.id }));
// in the worker:
await runWithJobContext("process task.created", job, () => sendNotifications(job.data.taskId));

Making the consumer span a child suits one message per request. When a consumer processes a batch of messages from many traces, start a new trace and add links to each message's context instead.

docs.title: A Collector gateway with tail sampling
docs.text:
# otel-collector.yaml (contrib distribution)
receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_percentage: 80
    spike_limit_percentage: 25
  attributes/scrub:
    actions:
      - key: http.request.header.authorization
        action: delete
      - key: user.email
        action: hash
  tail_sampling:
    decision_wait: 10s
    policies:
      - name: keep-errors
        type: status_code
        status_code:
          status_codes: [ERROR]
      - name: keep-slow
        type: latency
        latency:
          threshold_ms: 1000
      - name: sample-the-rest
        type: probabilistic
        probabilistic:
          sampling_percentage: 10
  batch: {}

exporters:
  otlp/tempo: # recent Collector releases log "otlp" as a deprecated alias of "otlp_grpc"; both work
    endpoint: tempo.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true # plaintext inside the cluster network only

service:
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, attributes/scrub, tail_sampling, batch]
      exporters: [otlp/tempo]

memory_limiter comes first so the Collector refuses data before it runs out of memory; batch comes last so exports are efficient. A trace is kept if any policy matches. When tail sampling decides, apps should send all spans (sampler parentbased_always_on), otherwise the Collector only sees the head-sampled fraction.

docs.title: Running Jaeger locally
docs.text:
# compose.yaml (local development only)
services:
  jaeger:
    image: jaegertracing/jaeger:latest
    ports:
      - "16686:16686" # web UI
      - "4317:4317"   # OTLP gRPC
      - "4318:4318"   # OTLP HTTP

Point OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT at http://localhost:4318/v1/traces, send a few requests to TaskFlow API, and open http://localhost:16686 to see the waterfall. Pin an explicit image version outside a local experiment.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with auto-instrumentation and W3C Trace Context everywhere; load instrumentation before any other module.
  • Name spans by operation, with low cardinality (GET /tasks/:id, not GET /tasks/6650f1...); put IDs in attributes.
  • Use semantic conventions for standard attributes and a prefix for custom ones.
  • Record exceptions and set error status on failing spans; always end spans in finally.
  • Propagate context through queues and background jobs.
  • Send telemetry to a Collector, not straight to a vendor.
  • Choose sampling deliberately: parent-based head sampling to bound cost, tail sampling to keep errors and slow traces.
  • Scrub secrets and personal data from attributes, both in code and in the Collector.
  • Put trace_id in every log line and use exemplars to connect metrics.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Traces stop at the API; downstream services appear as separate traces. Detect: the auth service's spans have their own trace IDs and no parent. Cause: a hop does not propagate context: an uninstrumented HTTP client, a proxy or gateway that drops traceparent, or a different propagator configured in one service. Fix: use instrumented clients, allow the headers through proxies, and standardize on the W3C propagator.
  • No spans appear at all after deploying the instrumentation. Detect: the trace backend is empty; with OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug the SDK logs export errors or shows no instrumented modules. Cause: the instrumentation file loads after express and the MongoDB driver (or the ESM loader hook is missing), or the exporter points at the wrong endpoint or port. Fix: load it with --import or --require before the app, add the loader hook for ESM, and check the Collector's receiver address.
  • The Collector is OOM-killed under load. Detect: Collector restarts and gaps in all traces during traffic peaks. Cause: tail sampling buffering every span for the decision window without a memory limit, or a backend outage filling export queues. Fix: add memory_limiter first in the pipeline, size memory for spans per second times decision window, scale out with trace-ID load balancing, and alert on refused and dropped spans.
  • Error traces are missing when you need them. Detect: a log line's trace_id returns "trace not found" for most failed requests. Cause: head sampling at a low rate discards 90% or more of traces before anyone knows they fail. Fix: tail sampling with an error policy, or a higher head rate for error-prone routes.
  • The tracing bill jumps after a new feature ships. Detect: spans per second per service doubles at a deploy. Cause: a loop that creates a span per item (per task in a 5,000-task import) or a newly enabled noisy instrumentation such as file system calls. Fix: span the batch, not the item; record counts as attributes; disable noisy instrumentations.
  • Authorization tokens are visible in trace attributes. Detect: a review of span attributes finds full headers or query strings. Cause: instrumentation configured to capture all request headers, or custom code adding them. Fix: capture an allow-list of headers, delete sensitive keys in the Collector, and rotate exposed tokens.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Trace: All spans for one request or transaction, sharing a trace ID.
  • Span: One timed operation with a parent, attributes, events, and status.
  • Root span: The first span of a trace, with no parent.
  • Span kind: Whether a span is a server, client, producer, consumer, or internal operation.
  • Span context: Trace ID, span ID, and trace flags; what is propagated.
  • Context propagation: Passing span context within and between processes.
  • Propagator: Code that injects and extracts context into carriers such as headers.
  • traceparent: The W3C header carrying version, trace ID, parent ID, and flags.
  • Baggage: Application key-value data propagated with the context.
  • OTLP: The OpenTelemetry Protocol for exporting telemetry.
  • Collector: OpenTelemetry's standalone pipeline for receiving, processing, and exporting telemetry.
  • Head / tail sampling: Sampling decided at the start of a trace versus after it completes.
  • Critical path: The chain of spans that determines total latency.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Importing the tracing setup after the application code, so nothing is patched.
  • Expecting traces to replace metrics: sampled traces cannot count requests accurately.
  • Using IDs or full URLs as span names.
  • Forgetting to end manual spans, or to propagate through queues.
  • Head sampling at 1% and expecting to find the trace for a specific failed request.
  • Putting secrets or personal data into attributes or baggage.
  • Sending spans directly from every app to a vendor with embedded API keys instead of through a Collector.
  • Believing tracing requires microservices; even a monolith benefits from database and outbound call spans.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What are a trace, a span, and a span context? How does a span know its parent?
  2. Decode 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-01. Which part changes on each hop, and what does 01 mean?
  3. Why does OpenTelemetry separate the API from the SDK?
  4. A request crosses three services, but the trace shows only the first. List three places propagation could be breaking.
  5. TaskFlow handles 300 requests per second with 10 spans per request and 500 bytes per span. How many spans per day are stored with head sampling at 10%, and roughly how much data? (300 x 10 x 0.10 = 300 spans/s, about 25.9 million spans and about 13 GB per day.)
  6. Compare head and tail sampling. Why does tail sampling need trace-aware load balancing?
  7. What does the Collector add compared with exporting straight from each service?
  8. How do you get from a slow request on a latency graph to its trace and its log lines?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• OpenTelemetry: Traces
  • OpenTelemetry: Context propagation
  • OpenTelemetry: Node.js getting started
  • OpenTelemetry: Sampling
  • OpenTelemetry Collector
  • Tail sampling processor
  • W3C Trace Context

docs.title: Error Tracking and Uptime Monitoring
docs.text: Metrics say the error rate rose; logs hold the details of individual requests. Two more tools complete the picture. Error tracking captures every unhandled exception, in the API and in users' browsers, groups thousands of identical failures into one issue with a readable stack trace, the release that introduced it, and how many users it hit. Uptime and synthetic monitoring test the service from the outside, the way users reach it, through DNS, TLS, CDNs, and load balancers. This lesson covers both, plus frontend real-user monitoring with Core Web Vitals, health endpoints (/healthz liveness compared with /readyz readiness), and status pages.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Many failures never show up as server-side 5xx responses. A JavaScript error in TaskFlow Web's task editor makes the Save button do nothing: the API never receives the request, so no server metric moves. An expired certificate or a broken DNS record stops every user before they reach your infrastructure, so internal dashboards stay green. A crashed process that the orchestrator keeps restarting may look "up" most of the time.

Error trackers turn scattered exceptions into a prioritized list tied to releases, so you notice a bad deploy from the first few users instead of the first support ticket. Outside-in checks are the only way to see what users see when the problem is between them and your code. Health endpoints, done right, let load balancers and orchestrators route traffic away from broken instances automatically; done wrong, they cause cascading restarts.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Sentry (issue grouping). Sentry's documentation on issue grouping explains how events are fingerprinted, primarily by stack trace, and grouped into issues, and how to customize fingerprints when the default grouping is too coarse or too fine.
  • Google web.dev (Core Web Vitals). The Web Vitals guide defines the current Core Web Vitals (Largest Contentful Paint, Interaction to Next Paint, and Cumulative Layout Shift), their "good" thresholds, and the recommendation to evaluate them at the 75th percentile of page loads.
  • Kubernetes (probes). The guide Configure Liveness, Readiness and Startup Probes explains that a failed liveness probe restarts a container while a failed readiness probe only removes the pod from Service endpoints, and warns that liveness probes must be configured carefully. Kubernetes' own API server exposes separate /livez and /readyz endpoints.
  • Prometheus blackbox exporter. The blackbox exporter probes endpoints over HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, TCP, ICMP, and gRPC and exposes results such as probe_success and the certificate expiry time as metrics, which is the open-source building block for synthetic checks.

Popular tools and providers: Sentry, Rollbar, BugSnag, Honeybadger, Datadog Error Tracking, and Grafana Faro for errors and real-user monitoring; Checkly, Grafana Synthetic Monitoring, Datadog Synthetics, Amazon CloudWatch Synthetics, Pingdom, and UptimeRobot for synthetic checks; Atlassian Statuspage, Instatus, and Better Stack for status pages.

docs.title: Error tracking compared with logs
docs.text:
A log line records that something happened. An error tracker is built around exceptions and adds:

  • Grouping: 12,000 occurrences of the same TypeError become one issue with a count, first-seen and last-seen times, and the number of distinct users affected.
  • Rich context: stack trace with source code, breadcrumbs (what happened just before), browser and OS, release, environment, request, and trace ID.
  • Release awareness: which release introduced an issue, whether a fix release resolved it, and whether it came back (a regression).
  • Workflow: assign, link to a ticket, mark resolved, ignore, and alert on new or regressed issues.

Use both: the tracker for exceptions and crashes, logs for the request story around them, linked by the trace ID.

docs.title: Anatomy of an error event
docs.text: Part Example for TaskFlow Web Exception TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'dueAt') Stack trace TaskList.tsx:42 in formatDue, TaskList.tsx:88 in TaskRow (after symbolication) Breadcrumbs Navigation to /tasks, GET /api/tasks returned 200, click on "Edit" Release and environment taskflow-web@1.42.0, production Context and tags Browser, OS, route /tasks, feature flag new-editor=on User A pseudonymous ID such as u_42, never an email by default Trace ID Links to the backend trace and logs for the same action

docs.title: Grouping and fingerprinting
docs.text:
The tracker computes a fingerprint for each event and groups events with the same fingerprint into one issue. The default is based mainly on the stack trace (especially frames in your own code), falling back to the exception type and message.

Grouping goes wrong in two directions:

  • Too fine: messages that contain IDs or timestamps (Task 6650f1c2 not found), or stacks that differ only by minified names, create thousands of one-event issues. Fix with stable messages and source maps, or a custom fingerprint.
  • Too coarse: a generic wrapper such as fetchJson() that throws for every API failure puts unrelated failures in one issue. Fix by adding the endpoint or error code to the fingerprint.

docs.title: Source maps for minified frontend code
docs.text:
The production bundle of TaskFlow Web is minified: one line, short variable names, no file structure. A stack frame like main.3f9a.js:1:4821 is useless. A source map maps positions in the bundle back to the original file, line, and name (TaskList.tsx:42 in formatDue).

How it should work:

  1. The build generates source maps (Vite: build.sourcemap).
  2. CI uploads them to the error tracker, tagged with the release, before deploying.
  3. CI deletes the .map files from the build output, so they are never served to the public.
  4. The tracker uses the uploaded maps to symbolicate incoming stacks.

Why source maps must not be public:

  • They contain your original source code, often including comments, internal API routes, feature flags for unreleased features, and business logic, making it much easier to study the app for weaknesses.
  • Any secret that was (wrongly) embedded at build time is easier to find.
  • They are large and slow down nothing for users, so there is no benefit to serving them.

Vite's build.sourcemap: "hidden" generates maps without adding the //# sourceMappingURL= comment to bundles, so browsers do not request them; deleting the files is still required, because a predictable URL such as main.3f9a.js.map could otherwise be fetched directly.

docs.title: Releases, release health, and environments
docs.text:
Every event carries a release identifier (taskflow-web@1.42.0, or a commit SHA) set at build time. That enables:

  • "New in this release" views to spot regressions right after a deploy.
  • Resolving an issue "in the next release", so it reopens automatically as a regression if it appears in a newer release.
  • Release health: the share of sessions or users that ended without a crash in each release, compared across releases, as a signal to halt a rollout (see rollbacks and safe releases).

The environment (production, staging, development) keeps test noise out of production alerts. Alert only on production; review staging issues before releasing.

docs.title: Scrubbing personal data before it leaves
docs.text:
Error events can carry sensitive data: request bodies, headers, cookies, form inputs in breadcrumbs, and local variables. Defend in layers:

  • Limit what the SDK collects. Sentry's JavaScript SDK v11 sends user data such as IP addresses, cookies, and request bodies by default, so turn off what you do not need with its dataCollection option (it replaced sendDefaultPii), and set a pseudonymous user ID yourself.
  • Strip known sensitive fields in a beforeSend (and beforeBreadcrumb) hook in the SDK, so the data never leaves the user's browser or your server.
  • Enable server-side scrubbing rules in the tracker as a second net (passwords, tokens, card-number patterns).
  • If you use session replay, keep text and inputs masked by default.
  • Treat the tracker as a data processor in your privacy policy and set retention deliberately.

docs.title: Real-user monitoring and Core Web Vitals
docs.text:
Real-user monitoring (RUM) collects performance data from actual users' browsers. Synthetic checks measure a lab-like path from a few locations; RUM measures every device, network, and region you actually serve.

Google's Core Web Vitals, evaluated at the 75th percentile of page loads (separately for mobile and desktop):

Metric Measures Good Poor LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) Loading: when the main content appears 2.5 s or less Over 4 s INP (Interaction to Next Paint) Responsiveness: delay from a click or key press to the next frame 200 ms or less Over 500 ms CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) Visual stability: unexpected movement of content 0.1 or less Over 0.25

INP replaced First Input Delay (FID) as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. The open-source web-vitals library measures all three in the browser so you can send them to your own endpoint or RUM tool; split them by route and release to catch a frontend regression the same way you catch a backend one.

docs.title: Synthetic and uptime checks
docs.text:
Synthetic monitoring runs scripted requests on a schedule from locations you choose:

Check type What it tests TaskFlow example HTTP(S) Status code, response body, latency, redirects GET https://api.example.com/healthz returns 200 and "status":"ok" in under 2 s TLS certificate Validity, chain, days until expiry Certificate on api.example.com valid for more than 14 days DNS Records resolve to the expected values app.example.com points to the CDN Multi-step API A short user journey through the API Log in, create a task, read it back, delete it Browser (scripted) The real UI in a headless browser, often with Playwright Log in to TaskFlow Web, create a task, see it in the list

Design rules:

  • Probe from several regions and alert on a quorum. A single probe location fails for its own network reasons; requiring two or more regions to fail, on consecutive runs, removes most false alarms.
  • Probe from outside your infrastructure, so a cloud-region or network outage that takes down your servers does not also take down the checks.
  • Check the journeys that matter, not just the home page. A static home page from the CDN can be "up" while the API is down.
  • Use dedicated test accounts and clean up the data synthetic checks create, and exclude their traffic from business metrics and SLIs if it would distort them.
  • Keep checks fast and frequent (every 1 to 5 minutes) so they detect outages within minutes and double as a steady source of SLI data for low-traffic services.

docs.title: Health endpoints: liveness and readiness
docs.text:
Health endpoints let machines (load balancers, Kubernetes, uptime checkers) decide what to do with an instance. They answer different questions, and mixing them up causes outages:

Endpoint Question Should check Must not check On failure /healthz (liveness) Is this process alive and not stuck? That the HTTP server responds; optionally that the event loop is not blocked Databases or other services The orchestrator restarts the container /readyz (readiness) Can this instance serve traffic right now? Startup finished, not shutting down, required dependencies reachable (a quick MongoDB ping) Optional or third-party dependencies; slow deep checks The instance is removed from load balancing until it recovers Startup (often reuses /healthz) Has a slow-starting app finished starting? Same as liveness Same as liveness Liveness checks wait until startup succeeds

The classic mistake is a liveness check that queries the database. When MongoDB has a brief problem, every pod fails liveness, Kubernetes restarts every pod, and the restarts add load and time to the outage. A database problem should make pods not ready (stop sending traffic), not dead (restart).

Other guidelines:

  • Make checks cheap and bounded by a short timeout; the probe may run every few seconds on every instance.
  • Return 503 when not ready, and flip readiness to failing at the start of graceful shutdown so the load balancer drains the instance before it stops.
  • Do not expose detailed health output (versions, dependency hosts) on the public internet; keep detailed diagnostics on an internal port or behind authentication.

The probe configuration itself is covered in health probes and rolling updates.

docs.title: Status pages
docs.text:
A status page tells users what is happening during an incident, which cuts support load and builds trust:

  • Host it separately from your own infrastructure (a hosted status page service or a different provider), so it stays up when you are down.
  • Model components the way users see them: API, web app, reminders and email, integrations.
  • Post early, update on a cadence (for example every 30 minutes during a major incident), and close with a summary and, for significant incidents, a public postmortem.
  • Automate carefully: automatic "degraded" updates from synthetic checks are fast but can be wrong; most teams let a human confirm before posting.
  • Announce maintenance windows in advance.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Need Use Not a substitute for Find and prioritize crashes in API and browser code Error tracker Metrics-based SLO alerts Know the user's actual page speed by device and region RUM with Core Web Vitals Synthetic checks (lab data) Know the service is reachable from the internet Multi-region synthetic checks Internal metrics Let orchestrators route around broken instances /readyz and /healthz Monitoring dashboards Communicate with customers during incidents Status page Direct support for affected customers

An error tracker is not a log store (do not send every handled warning as an "error"), and a synthetic check is not an SLI on its own unless it runs often enough and represents real traffic.

docs.title: Error tracking in TaskFlow API (Express)
docs.text:
// src/instrument.mjs (loaded with --import before the app)
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";

Sentry.init({
  dsn: process.env.SENTRY_DSN,
  environment: process.env.NODE_ENV ?? "development",
  release: `taskflow-api@${process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev"}`,
  // SDK v11 collects everything by default: turn off automatic user data
  // (IP address), cookies, and request and response bodies.
  dataCollection: { userInfo: false, cookies: false, httpBodies: [] },
  // Tracing is handled by OpenTelemetry in this service, so tracesSampleRate
  // stays unset; errors are attached to the active OpenTelemetry trace.
  integrations: [Sentry.openTelemetryIntegration()],
  beforeSend(event) {
    // Defence in depth: remove headers that must never leave the server.
    if (event.request?.headers) {
      delete event.request.headers.authorization;
      delete event.request.headers.cookie;
      delete event.request.headers["x-api-key"];
    }
    return event;
  },
});

// src/app.js
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";
import express from "express";
import { tasksRouter } from "./tasks/router.js";

export const app = express();
app.use(express.json());
app.use("/tasks", tasksRouter);

// After all routes: reports unhandled errors, then passes them on.
Sentry.setupExpressErrorHandler(app);

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  res.status(500).json({ error: "Internal Server Error", requestId: req.id });
});

// src/tasks/errors.js: group duplicate-key failures by collection, not by message
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/node";

export function reportDuplicateTask(err, collection) {
  Sentry.withScope((scope) => {
    scope.setFingerprint(["mongo-duplicate-key", collection]);
    scope.setTag("collection", collection);
    Sentry.captureException(err);
  });
}

Parts: instrument.mjs must run before Express is imported (with node --import ./src/instrument.mjs src/server.js), just like the OpenTelemetry setup; setupExpressErrorHandler captures errors that reach Express's error handling; openTelemetryIntegration() puts the request's trace ID on each error event; the custom fingerprint keeps every E11000 duplicate key error for the tasks collection in one issue even though each message contains a different key value. Only report errors that need attention: expected client errors such as validation failures are not issues.

docs.title: Error tracking and source maps in TaskFlow Web (React and Vite)
docs.text:
// src/sentry.js (TaskFlow Web)
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/react";

Sentry.init({
  dsn: import.meta.env.VITE_SENTRY_DSN, // a DSN is public by design; it only allows sending events
  environment: import.meta.env.MODE,
  release: `taskflow-web@${import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION}`,
  dataCollection: { userInfo: false, cookies: false, httpBodies: [] },
  integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration()],
  tracesSampleRate: 0.05,
  // Only attach trace headers to our own API, not to third parties.
  tracePropagationTargets: [/^https:\/\/api\.example\.com/],
});

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";
import { sentryVitePlugin } from "@sentry/vite-plugin";

export default defineConfig({
  build: {
    sourcemap: "hidden", // generate maps, without sourceMappingURL comments in the bundles
  },
  plugins: [
    react(),
    // Keep the Sentry plugin last. It uploads maps for this release at build time.
    sentryVitePlugin({
      org: "example",
      project: "taskflow-web",
      authToken: process.env.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN, // CI secret, never committed
      release: { name: `taskflow-web@${process.env.VITE_APP_VERSION}` },
      sourcemaps: {
        filesToDeleteAfterUpload: ["./dist/**/*.map"], // never deploy maps
      },
    }),
  ],
});

# CI: build with the release version; the plugin uploads and deletes the maps
VITE_APP_VERSION="1.42.0" SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN="<token>" npm run build
test -z "$(find dist -name '*.map')" || { echo "source maps left in dist/"; exit 1; }

The final check fails the pipeline if any .map file would be deployed. The auth token used for uploads is a secret with write access to your project; it belongs only in CI, unlike the DSN.

docs.title: Health endpoints with graceful shutdown
docs.text:
// src/health.js
let shuttingDown = false;

export function markShuttingDown() {
  shuttingDown = true;
}

function withTimeout(promise, ms) {
  let timer;
  const timeout = new Promise((_, reject) => {
    timer = setTimeout(() => reject(new Error(`timed out after ${ms} ms`)), ms);
  });
  return Promise.race([promise, timeout]).finally(() => clearTimeout(timer));
}

export function registerHealthRoutes(app, mongoClient) {
  // Liveness: the process answers HTTP. No dependency checks.
  app.get("/healthz", (req, res) => {
    res.status(200).json({ status: "ok" });
  });

  // Readiness: safe to receive traffic right now.
  app.get("/readyz", async (req, res) => {
    if (shuttingDown) {
      return res.status(503).json({ status: "shutting_down" });
    }
    try {
      await withTimeout(mongoClient.db("admin").command({ ping: 1 }), 500);
      res.status(200).json({ status: "ready" });
    } catch {
      res.status(503).json({ status: "not_ready", reason: "database" });
    }
  });
}

// src/server.js (shutdown part)
import { markShuttingDown } from "./health.js";

process.once("SIGTERM", () => {
  markShuttingDown(); // readiness fails, the load balancer stops sending new requests
  setTimeout(() => {
    server.close(() => mongoClient.close().then(() => process.exit(0)));
  }, 10_000); // wait for endpoints to update before refusing connections
});

The 10-second delay before closing the server gives load balancers time to notice the failing readiness check; tune it to your probe period and failure threshold.

docs.title: Multi-region probes with the blackbox exporter
docs.text:
# blackbox/blackbox.yml (deployed in each probe region)
modules:
  taskflow_health:
    prober: http
    timeout: 5s
    http:
      method: GET
      valid_status_codes: [200]
      fail_if_not_ssl: true
      fail_if_body_not_matches_regexp:
        - '"status":"ok"'

# prometheus/prometheus.yml (one job per probe region)
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: blackbox-taskflow
    metrics_path: /probe
    params:
      module: [taskflow_health]
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["https://api.example.com/healthz"]
        labels:
          region: eu-west
    relabel_configs:
      - source_labels: [__address__]
        target_label: __param_target
      - source_labels: [__param_target]
        target_label: instance
      - target_label: __address__
        replacement: blackbox-eu-west.monitoring.example.com:9115

The relabeling turns the listed URL into the target query parameter and sends the scrape to the regional exporter, which performs the probe and returns probe_success, probe_duration_seconds, and probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry. The quorum alert (count(probe_success == 0) >= 2) is shown in alerting and on-call. Host at least some probes outside the cloud region and provider that runs TaskFlow.

docs.title: Reporting Core Web Vitals from TaskFlow Web
docs.text:
// src/vitals.js (TaskFlow Web)
import { onCLS, onINP, onLCP } from "web-vitals";

function send(metric) {
  const body = JSON.stringify({
    name: metric.name,         // "LCP" | "INP" | "CLS"
    value: metric.value,
    rating: metric.rating,     // "good" | "needs-improvement" | "poor"
    id: metric.id,
    route: window.location.pathname.replace(/\/[0-9a-f]{24}(?=\/|$)/g, "/:id"),
    release: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
  });
  // sendBeacon survives page unload; fall back to fetch with keepalive.
  if (!navigator.sendBeacon?.("https://api.example.com/rum", body)) {
    fetch("https://api.example.com/rum", { method: "POST", body, keepalive: true });
  }
}

onCLS(send);
onINP(send);
onLCP(send);

The route is normalized (MongoDB ObjectIds replaced by :id) before it becomes a metric label on the server, for the cardinality reasons explained in metrics and dashboards.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Report unhandled exceptions from both the API and the browser, tagged with release and environment.
  • Upload source maps privately at build time and make the pipeline fail if any map would be deployed.
  • Keep personal data out of error events: limited SDK data collection, beforeSend scrubbing, server-side rules.
  • Fix grouping early: stable error messages and custom fingerprints where needed.
  • Alert on new and regressed issues in production, and watch release health during rollouts.
  • Measure Core Web Vitals from real users at p75, per route and release.
  • Run synthetic checks for critical journeys from several regions outside your infrastructure, with a quorum rule.
  • Keep liveness checks dependency-free; put dependency checks in readiness; fail readiness during shutdown.
  • Host the status page independently and update it on a fixed cadence during incidents.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every pod restarts at once during a short database blip. Detect: restart counts jump across all pods at the same moment as a MongoDB failover, and the outage lasts longer than the failover itself. Cause: the liveness endpoint checks the database. Fix: make /healthz dependency-free, move the database check to /readyz, and give probes sensible thresholds.
  • Error stack traces are unreadable after a frontend deploy. Detect: new issues show frames like main.3f9a.js:1:4821. Cause: source maps were not uploaded for this release, or the release name in the SDK does not match the uploaded one. Fix: upload maps in the same CI job that builds, use one release variable for both, and fail the build if the upload fails.
  • Source maps are publicly downloadable. Detect: a request for https://app.example.com/assets/main.3f9a.js.map returns 200. Cause: maps were left in the build output and deployed to the CDN. Fix: delete maps after upload, add a CI check, purge them from the CDN, and review the exposed code for embedded secrets.
  • The uptime check says 100% while users cannot log in. Detect: support reports login failures; the check on the home page stays green. Cause: the home page is static and served by the CDN, while the API behind login is down. Fix: check /healthz on the API and run a multi-step login journey.
  • Synthetic alerts fire every few nights and then clear. Detect: pages from a single probe location with timeouts while other regions are fine. Cause: network problems near that probe. Fix: require two or more regions to fail on consecutive runs before paging.
  • The error tracker quota runs out by mid-month. Detect: the tracker drops events; one issue accounts for most volume. Cause: a noisy error (often from a browser extension or a bot) or a loop that reports the same error repeatedly. Fix: fix or ignore the noise, filter third-party script errors, sample very frequent events, and set rate limits per project.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Error tracking: Capturing, grouping, and managing application exceptions with context.
  • Issue: A group of events with the same fingerprint.
  • Fingerprint: The value used to decide which events belong together.
  • Breadcrumbs: The trail of events (navigation, requests, clicks, logs) recorded before an error.
  • Source map: A file mapping minified code positions to original source.
  • Symbolication: Translating a minified or compiled stack trace into original files and lines.
  • Release health: Crash-free session or user rates per release.
  • RUM: Real-user monitoring, measured in users' browsers.
  • Core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, and CLS.
  • Synthetic monitoring: Scripted checks run on a schedule from chosen locations.
  • Liveness / readiness: Whether a process should be restarted, and whether it should receive traffic.
  • Status page: A public page reporting service status and incidents.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Shipping source maps to production, or not uploading them at all.
  • Leaving request bodies, cookies, or emails in error events.
  • Reporting expected errors (validation failures, 404s) as issues, which buries real bugs.
  • Using the home page as the only uptime check.
  • Probing from one location, or from inside the same cloud region as the app.
  • Checking dependencies in liveness probes.
  • Treating a green synthetic check as proof that all users are fine.
  • Hosting the status page on the infrastructure it reports on.
  • Measuring Core Web Vitals only in the lab, on a fast laptop.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does an error tracker add compared with logging the exception?
  2. Why do error messages that include IDs cause poor grouping, and how do you fix it?
  3. Walk through how a minified stack frame becomes TaskList.tsx:42. Where must the source map live, and why?
  4. What are LCP, INP, and CLS, and what are the "good" thresholds at the 75th percentile?
  5. Four probe regions run every minute, and each region independently fails 0.5% of runs for local reasons. Roughly how many false alerts per day would a single-region rule give, compared with a rule requiring two regions to fail together? (Single region: 1,440 x 0.005 = 7.2 per day per region. Two specific regions together: about 0.000025 per run, with 6 region pairs about 0.00015 per run, or about 0.2 per day; adding "two consecutive runs" reduces it much further.)
  6. What should /healthz and /readyz each check, and what happens when each fails?
  7. Why should readiness start failing before the server closes during a graceful shutdown?
  8. Where should a status page be hosted, and how often should it be updated during a major incident?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Sentry: Express guide
  • Sentry: Source maps
  • Sentry: Scrubbing sensitive data
  • web.dev: Interaction to Next Paint
  • web-vitals library
  • Vite: Build options (build.sourcemap)
  • Kubernetes: Liveness, readiness, and startup probes
  • Next: incident response and postmortems. Back to the monitoring and logging overview.

docs.title: Incident Response and Postmortems
docs.text: Alerts and dashboards tell you something is wrong. What happens next, in the minutes when users are affected and everyone is under pressure, decides whether an outage lasts ten minutes or three hours. Incident response is the practised process for that moment: declare the incident, assign clear roles, communicate on a schedule, mitigate first, and fix the root cause later. The postmortem afterwards turns the incident into lasting improvements without blaming individuals. This lesson covers what counts as an incident, severity levels, the lifecycle (detect, triage, mitigate, resolve, learn), roles, communication, blameless postmortems with a complete worked example, the "5 whys" and its limits, and tracking action items to completion.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Unmanaged incidents follow a familiar pattern: five engineers debug in parallel in different directions, two of them restart the same service, nobody updates customers, the support team learns about the outage from social media, and the one person who knows the database is not told. The technical problem may be simple; the coordination failure makes it long. Google's SRE book opens its incident chapter with exactly such a story.

After the incident, the instinct is to find who made the mistake. That teaches people to hide mistakes, so the next postmortem has less information and the same failure happens again. Organizations that learn fastest from failure treat incidents as evidence about the system (tooling, processes, defaults, alerts) and fix that.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE (managing incidents). The chapter Managing Incidents describes an incident management process based on the Incident Command System, with separate incident commander, operations, communication, and planning roles, a live incident document, and clear handoffs.
  • Google SRE (postmortem culture). The chapter Postmortem Culture: Learning from Failure explains blameless postmortems, when to write them, and how to review and share them; the book also includes an example postmortem.
  • PagerDuty Incident Response. PagerDuty's open documentation on incident roles defines the incident commander, deputy, scribe, subject matter experts, and customer and internal liaisons, and is widely reused as a starting point.
  • Public postmortems. GitLab's postmortem of its January 31, 2017 database outage and Amazon's summary of the February 2017 S3 disruption show real timelines, contributing factors, and action items. The AWS summary also notes that the service health dashboard itself could not be updated at first because it depended on the failing service.

Popular tools and providers: PagerDuty, incident.io, FireHydrant, Rootly, Jira Service Management, Atlassian Statuspage, chat tools (Slack, Microsoft Teams) with incident channels, and shared documents for the live incident record.

docs.title: What counts as an incident
docs.text:
An incident is an unplanned event that disrupts or threatens a service and needs a coordinated response. Write the declaration criteria down so nobody has to argue in the moment. For TaskFlow, declare an incident when any of these is true:

  • A user-facing SLO is burning fast (a burn-rate page fired), or users cannot complete a core journey (sign in, create or view tasks).
  • Data may be lost, corrupted, or exposed, or there is a suspected security breach.
  • The problem needs more than one person or team to fix.
  • It is not clearly mitigated within 15 to 30 minutes of the first page.

The rule of thumb from experienced teams: declare early, downgrade later. Declaring costs a channel and a few messages; not declaring costs coordination when it matters most.

docs.title: Severity levels
docs.text:
Severity Definition TaskFlow example Response SEV1 (critical) Most users cannot use the product, data loss or a security breach API down for everyone; tasks deleted All hands; IC and comms lead immediately; status page within 15 minutes; updates every 30 minutes; executive notification SEV2 (major) A core feature broken or severely degraded for many users Creating tasks fails for 30% of requests IC and responders; status page; updates every 30 to 60 minutes SEV3 (minor) Partial degradation with a workaround, or a small group affected Reminder emails delayed by 20 minutes On-call handles in working hours; internal updates SEV4 (low) Cosmetic or internal-only issues An admin report is slow Normal ticket

Severity can change during an incident; say so explicitly in the channel when it does. Severity drives response, communication, and whether a postmortem is required, not blame.

docs.title: The incident lifecycle
docs.text:
1. Detect. An alert, a synthetic check, an error-tracker spike, or a customer report. Good monitoring makes this minutes, not hours.
  2. Triage. Acknowledge, assess impact, declare the incident, set the severity, open the incident channel, and assign an incident commander.
  3. Mitigate. Stop or reduce user impact as fast as possible, even before the cause is understood.
  4. Resolve. Fix the underlying cause (or make the mitigation permanent), verify the SLIs are back to normal, and close the incident.
  5. Learn. Write and review a blameless postmortem, and complete its action items.

Measure the clocks: time to detect (impact start to first alert), time to acknowledge, time to mitigate (impact start to user impact ending), and time to resolve. "MTTR" is used for both "mitigate/restore" and "resolve", so define which you mean.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
Role Responsibilities Does not Incident commander (IC) Owns the incident: sets priorities, assigns work, makes decisions (roll back or not), keeps the big picture, declares severity changes and the end of the incident, hands off explicitly Debug or type commands; that is how coordination gets lost Communications lead Writes status page updates and internal briefings on a fixed cadence, handles support and stakeholder questions, shields responders from interruptions Speculate about causes in public Operations lead and subject matter experts Investigate and change production: roll back, fail over, scale, run queries; report findings to the IC Make large changes without telling the IC Scribe Keeps the timeline in the incident document: what was observed, decided, and done, with UTC timestamps Filter out "unimportant" events; the postmortem needs them

In a small team, the first responder is IC until someone takes over, and one person may hold several roles in a SEV3. For SEV1 and SEV2, separate the IC from the people fixing. Handoffs are explicit ("I am handing IC to Priya; Priya, please confirm"), and long incidents rotate people before they are exhausted.

docs.title: Communication
docs.text:
Communication has two audiences with different needs:

  • Internal (the incident channel): every observation, hypothesis, action, and decision, posted in one place so newcomers can catch up by reading. Side conversations in direct messages are how facts get lost.
  • External (status page, customer support, leadership): what users experience, what you are doing, and when you will update next. No internal jargon, no blame, no guesses about root cause.

A status update always includes the current impact, what is being done, and the time of the next update, and the next update is sent on time even if there is nothing new ("still investigating" is information). Cadence by severity: every 30 minutes for SEV1, every 30 to 60 minutes for SEV2.

docs.title: Mitigate first, then find the root cause
docs.text:
The first goal is to stop user pain, not to understand it. Common mitigations, roughly in order of preference:

  1. Roll back the most recent deploy or configuration change (the most common cause of incidents is change).
  2. Turn off a feature flag for the new code path.
  3. Fail over to a healthy replica, zone, or region.
  4. Scale out or add capacity when the problem is load.
  5. Shed or block traffic: rate-limit an abusive client, disable a non-essential feature, serve a degraded page.

Mitigation buys time to find the real cause calmly. Two cautions:

  • Preserve evidence before destroying state: take a heap snapshot or a few thread dumps, save logs, snapshot a disk, before restarting everything.
  • Know what cannot be rolled back. A database migration that dropped a column makes a code rollback unsafe; that is why migrations are written to be backward compatible (see zero-downtime database migrations).

docs.title: Blameless postmortems
docs.text:
A postmortem (also called an incident review or retrospective) is a written record of an incident: what happened, its impact, why it happened, and what will change. Blameless means it focuses on how the system (code, tools, processes, defaults, incentives) allowed or amplified the failure, and assumes people acted reasonably with the information they had at the time.

Why blameless works: engineers who fear punishment hide details, and the details are what make the analysis useful. "An engineer ran the wrong command" is never the end of the analysis; the questions are why the command was possible, why it looked right, and why nothing stopped it. Blameless does not mean nobody is accountable: owners are accountable for completing the action items.

When to write one (agree on this in advance): every SEV1 and SEV2, any data loss, any incident needing on-call intervention beyond a runbook step, any incident where monitoring failed to detect the problem, and any incident consuming more than a set share (for example 20%) of the error budget.

A postmortem template:

  1. Summary: two or three sentences anyone in the company can understand.
  2. Impact: who and what was affected, for how long, with numbers (failed requests, users, error budget consumed, revenue or support tickets where relevant).
  3. Timeline: UTC timestamps from the triggering change through detection, response, mitigation, and resolution.
  4. Root causes and contributing factors: the conditions that together produced the incident, including detection and response gaps.
  5. What went well: practices to keep (fast rollback, a good runbook).
  6. What went wrong and where we got lucky.
  7. Action items: each with an owner, a priority, a due date, and a tracking link, grouped as detect, mitigate, and prevent.
  8. Lessons learned and supporting information: graphs, links to the incident channel and document.

docs.title: Root causes, contributing factors, and the "5 whys"
docs.text:
The 5 whys technique repeatedly asks "why?" to move from a symptom to deeper causes:

Why did task creation fail?        The API returned 500 for POST /tasks.
Why did it return 500?             A new index made inserts violate a unique constraint.
Why was the index unique?          The migration defined it as unique by mistake.
Why was the mistake not caught?    Tests ran on an empty database with no duplicates.
Why do tests use empty data?       No realistic test data set exists for migrations.

It is useful for pushing past the first answer, but it has known limits:

  • It produces a single linear chain, while real incidents almost always have several contributing factors that were each necessary and only jointly sufficient (the code bug, and the missing test data, and the deploy at peak traffic, and an alert that took 10 minutes).
  • Different people asking the same "why" reach different answers, and the chain tends to stop at whatever the facilitator already believed.
  • It easily stops at "human error", which is a starting point for analysis, not a cause.

Better practice is to list contributing factors across categories (technical trigger, detection, response, process, organizational) and ask "what made this action make sense at the time?" for every human decision in the timeline. Richard Cook's short paper How Complex Systems Fail explains why post-accident attribution to a single "root cause" is fundamentally wrong for complex systems.

docs.title: Action items that get done
docs.text:
Postmortems that produce no change are ceremonies. Good action items are:

  • Specific and verifiable: "Add a migration test that runs against a sanitized copy of production data", not "be more careful with migrations".
  • Owned and dated: one owner (a person, not a team), a due date, a priority, and a ticket in the normal backlog.
  • Balanced: some improve detection (an alert that would have fired sooner), some mitigation (a faster rollback), some prevention (a guardrail that makes the failure impossible).
  • Tracked: a recurring review of open postmortem actions, and a metric for completion rate. Repeat incidents with the same contributing factor are a sign that actions are not being completed.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Response SLO burn-rate page, users affected Declare an incident; IC; status page for SEV1/SEV2 Suspected security breach or data exposure Declare; involve the security team; follow the security incident process, including legal and regulatory notification duties A bug found in development or staging Normal bug process, not an incident A single failed background job retried successfully Ticket; no incident Near miss: a dangerous situation caught before impact Short postmortem is worthwhile; near misses are cheap lessons Planned maintenance Change management and status page notice, not an incident (unless it goes wrong)

docs.title: Declaring an incident: a checklist for the first 10 minutes
docs.text:
1. Acknowledge the page. Look at the SLO and RED dashboards: what is the user impact?
2. Declare: open #inc-<date>-<short-name>, post "Declaring SEV2: <impact>. I am IC until handoff."
3. Assign roles: ops lead, comms lead (SEV1/SEV2), scribe. Page experts you need.
4. Start the incident doc from the template; pin it in the channel.
5. Ask: "What changed?" Check deploys, config changes, feature flags, and infrastructure events.
6. Choose the fastest safe mitigation (roll back, flag off, fail over). Say it, then do it.
7. Comms lead posts the first status update and sets the next update time.
8. Every 15 minutes the IC summarizes: impact, current hypothesis, actions in flight, next steps.

docs.title: Status update templates
docs.text:
Internal update (incident channel), SEV2, 14:30 UTC
Impact: ~30% of POST /tasks requests failed from 14:02 to 14:29 UTC. Reads unaffected.
Current state: Mitigated at 14:29 by dropping a unique index added by release 1.42.0.
               Error ratio back to baseline. App rolled back to 1.41.3 (did not help alone).
Working on: confirming no tasks were lost; preparing a corrected migration.
Next update: 15:00 UTC or sooner if anything changes.
IC: <name>  Ops: <name>  Comms: <name>

Status page update, 14:35 UTC: Monitoring
Between 14:02 and 14:29 UTC, some attempts to create tasks failed with an error.
We have applied a fix and task creation is working normally. Existing tasks were not affected.
We are monitoring closely and will post another update by 15:30 UTC.

docs.title: A blameless postmortem for TaskFlow
docs.text:
Postmortem: Task creation failures after release 1.42.0
Status: Action items in progress   Severity: SEV2   Incident date: 2026-11-10
Authors: <IC name>, <ops lead name>   Review meeting: 2026-11-12

Summary
Release 1.42.0 added a unique index on (userId, title) to the tasks collection by
mistake. For 27 minutes, users creating a task with a title they had used before
received an error. Dropping the index restored service. No data was lost.

Impact
- 14:02 to 14:29 UTC (27 minutes): 31% of POST /tasks requests returned 500.
- 6,840 failed task creations from 2,310 users; 37 support tickets.
- 14% of the 30-day error budget for API availability consumed.
- Reads and updates were not affected.

Timeline (UTC)
14:00  Release 1.42.0 rollout starts (index build included in the migration).
14:02  Rollout completes; E11000 duplicate key errors begin on POST /tasks.
14:05  TaskflowErrorBudgetBurnFast pages the primary on-call.
14:06  Error tracker alerts on a new issue: MongoServerError E11000 in createTask.
14:08  On-call acknowledges, sees errors started with the deploy.
14:12  SEV2 declared; IC, ops lead, and comms lead assigned.
14:15  Decision: roll back the application. Index left in place for now.
14:17  First status page update posted.
14:21  Rollback to 1.41.3 complete... errors continue at the same rate.
14:24  Ops lead identifies the unique index (not the code) as the cause.
14:29  Index dropped; error ratio returns to baseline. Impact ends.
15:40  Corrected migration (non-unique index) shipped in 1.42.1.
       Incident resolved.

Root causes and contributing factors
- The migration declared the new index { userId: 1, title: 1 } with unique: true.
  The intent was a non-unique index to speed up search.
- Migration tests ran against an empty database, so no duplicate titles existed.
- Code review covered the application diff; the migration file was reviewed
  quickly because "it only adds an index".
- The runbook for "errors after deploy" said to roll back the application, which
  does not undo schema changes, so the first mitigation did not help (8 extra minutes).
- Detection was good: the burn-rate alert fired 3 minutes after impact began.

What went well
- Burn-rate alert and the error tracker identified the deploy as the trigger within minutes.
- Roles were assigned quickly; customers received an update within 15 minutes of the page.

What went wrong / where we got lucky
- The rollback did not include schema changes.
- We were lucky the index was additive; a destructive migration could have lost data.

Action items
| # | Action | Type | Owner | Priority | Due | Ticket |
| 1 | Run migration tests against an anonymized production-like data set | Prevent | <name> | P1 | 2026-11-24 | TF-901 |
| 2 | Lint migrations: flag unique indexes and require explicit approval | Prevent | <name> | P2 | 2026-12-01 | TF-902 |
| 3 | Update the "errors after deploy" runbook: check schema changes before rollback | Mitigate | <name> | P1 | 2026-11-14 | TF-903 |
| 4 | Ship schema changes as a separate, earlier deploy step with its own rollback | Prevent | <name> | P2 | 2026-12-15 | TF-904 |
| 5 | Add a canary step so 5% of traffic sees a release for 10 minutes first | Detect | <name> | P2 | 2026-12-15 | TF-905 |

Note how the timeline exposes the 8 minutes lost to an ineffective first mitigation, and how every contributing factor is about the system (tests, review focus, runbook, deploy design), not the engineer who wrote the migration. Action item 5 would have limited the impact to a small share of users; see rolling, blue-green, and canary deployments.

docs.title: Postmortem template
docs.text:
# Postmortem: <short title>
Status: Draft | In review | Action items in progress | Complete
Severity: SEV<n>    Incident date: <YYYY-MM-DD>    Authors: <names>    Reviewers: <names>

## Summary            (2-3 sentences, for any reader)
## Impact             (who, what, how long, numbers, error budget consumed)
## Timeline           (UTC; trigger, detection, response, mitigation, resolution)
## Root causes and contributing factors   (technical, detection, response, process)
## What went well
## What went wrong / where we got lucky
## Action items       (# | action | type: detect/mitigate/prevent | owner | priority | due | ticket)
## Lessons learned
## Supporting information   (graphs, links to channel, incident doc, related postmortems)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write down declaration criteria and severity definitions before you need them; declare early.
  • Separate the incident commander from the people fixing the problem.
  • Keep one incident channel and one live document as the record.
  • Communicate on a fixed cadence with impact, actions, and next update time, internally and externally.
  • Mitigate first: roll back, flag off, fail over; investigate after users are safe, preserving evidence.
  • Host the status page and incident tooling independently of the production systems they report on.
  • Write blameless postmortems for every qualifying incident, review them in a meeting, and share them widely.
  • List contributing factors across technical, detection, response, and process categories; never stop at "human error".
  • Give every action item one owner, a due date, and a ticket, and review completion regularly.
  • Practise: run incident drills and game days so roles feel familiar before a real SEV1.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Everyone is debugging and nobody is coordinating. Detect: the incident channel is a stream of conflicting theories, two people restart the same service, and no decision is recorded. Cause: no incident commander, or the IC is also debugging. Fix: assign an IC who does not touch production, and have them summarize the state every 15 minutes.
  • Customers hear about the outage from social media first. Detect: support tickets reference posts made before the first status update. Cause: no communications lead, or status updates wait until the cause is known. Fix: post an initial update within minutes of declaring ("we are investigating errors creating tasks") and update on a fixed cadence.
  • The same incident happens again three months later. Detect: a new postmortem lists the same contributing factor as an old one. Cause: action items were vague, unowned, or deprioritized. Fix: concrete, owned, dated action items in the normal backlog, reviewed for completion; leadership treats overdue P1 actions as risk.
  • The first mitigation does not work and nobody knows why. Detect: errors continue after a rollback. Cause: the change was not in the application code (a schema change, a configuration or feature flag, an infrastructure change). Fix: check every kind of change in the "what changed?" step, and record all changes in one place with timestamps.
  • People stop reporting their mistakes. Detect: postmortems become vague ("a configuration issue occurred"), timelines have gaps, and near misses are never reported. Cause: a postmortem or manager blamed an individual. Fix: reaffirm blameless principles from leadership, focus reviews on system changes, and thank people for candid accounts.
  • A long incident degrades as responders tire. Detect: after several hours, decisions slow and mistakes increase. Cause: no rotation of the IC and responders. Fix: plan handoffs every few hours for long incidents, with a written handoff summary.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Incident: An unplanned disruption, or threat of one, needing a coordinated response.
  • Severity (SEV): A level describing impact and the response it requires.
  • Incident commander (IC): The person coordinating the response and making decisions.
  • Communications lead: The person responsible for internal and external updates.
  • Scribe: The person recording the timeline.
  • Mitigation: An action that reduces or stops user impact, even if the cause remains.
  • Resolution: Fixing the underlying cause and confirming normal service.
  • Postmortem: A written analysis of an incident with action items.
  • Blameless: Focusing on system causes rather than individual fault.
  • Contributing factor: One of several conditions that together produced an incident.
  • 5 whys: A technique that asks "why?" repeatedly to look past the first explanation.
  • Near miss: A situation that could have caused an incident but did not.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Waiting to declare an incident until the cause is understood.
