  • An incident commander who also debugs.
  • Discussing the incident in many private chats instead of one channel.
  • Investigating the root cause while users are still affected and a rollback is available.
  • Restarting everything and destroying the evidence needed later.
  • Postmortems that name and blame individuals, or that stop at "human error".
  • Treating the 5 whys as finding the root cause in a complex system.
  • Action items like "be more careful" or "improve monitoring" without an owner or date.
  • Writing postmortems that nobody reads, reviews, or follows up.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What criteria would you use to decide that a problem is an incident? Why "declare early, downgrade later"?
  2. Describe the five phases of the incident lifecycle and what "done" means for each.
  3. Why should the incident commander not debug?
  4. What must every status update contain?
  5. Give three mitigations you could apply before knowing the root cause, and one situation in which a rollback is unsafe.
  6. In the TaskFlow example, impact began at 14:02, the alert fired at 14:05, the incident was declared at 14:12, and impact ended at 14:29. What were the time to detect and the time to mitigate? How many minutes were lost to the ineffective first mitigation? (3 minutes; 27 minutes; 8 minutes, from 14:21 to 14:29.)
  7. What are the limits of the 5 whys, and what would you use instead or alongside it?
  8. What makes an action item likely to be completed?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Google SRE book: Managing Incidents
  • Google SRE book: Postmortem Culture
  • Google SRE Workbook: Incident Response
  • Google SRE Workbook: Postmortem Culture
  • PagerDuty Incident Response documentation
  • Atlassian: Blameless postmortems
  • Next: monitoring and logging interview questions and answers. Back to the monitoring and logging overview.

docs.title: Monitoring and Logging Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review observability fundamentals, structured logging, metrics and dashboards, distributed tracing, SLOs and error budgets, alerting and on-call, error tracking and uptime monitoring, and incident response. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
docs.text: Monitoring checks known conditions you defined in advance ("is the error rate above 1%?") and produces dashboards and alerts. Observability is how well you can answer new questions about the system from its telemetry without shipping new code, which requires rich, high-cardinality context on logs and spans. Monitoring detects known failure modes; observability helps explain novel ones.

docs.title: 2. What are the main telemetry signals, and what question does each answer?
docs.text: Logs record discrete events ("what happened to this request?"). Metrics are numeric time series ("how much, how fast, is it getting worse?"). Traces follow one request across services ("where did the time go or fail?"). Profiles sample CPU and memory by function ("which code is expensive?"). Change events record deploys and config changes ("what changed?").

docs.title: 3. Why are metrics cheap at high traffic while logs are not?
docs.text: Metric cost depends on the number of time series (label combinations), not on how many events are counted: a counter incremented a million times is still one series. Log cost grows with every request, multiplied by bytes per line. That is why identifiers go in logs and spans, and metrics keep small, bounded label sets.

docs.title: 4. What are Google's four golden signals?
docs.text: Latency (time to serve requests, with successes and failures measured separately), traffic (demand, such as requests per second), errors (rate of failed requests, including wrong answers and policy violations such as too-slow responses), and saturation (how full the most constrained resource is). They come from the "Monitoring Distributed Systems" chapter of the Google SRE book.

docs.title: 5. Compare the RED and USE methods.
docs.text: RED (rate, errors, duration) is applied to every service or endpoint and describes health as users experience it. USE (utilization, saturation, errors) is applied to every resource (CPU, memory, disks, connection pools, the Node.js event loop) and finds bottlenecks. RED tells you a service is unhealthy; USE tells you which resource is the cause.

docs.title: 6. What is the difference between white-box and black-box monitoring?
docs.text: White-box monitoring uses internal telemetry (metrics, logs, traces) and explains causes and early warnings. Black-box monitoring tests external behaviour as a user would, such as an HTTPS probe from several regions, and catches failures outside the code, like an expired certificate or a DNS error. Use both: black-box confirms user impact, white-box explains it.

docs.title: 7. Why should every signal carry service.name and service.version?
docs.text: Shared identity lets you join signals: filter logs, traces, and metrics for the same service, and split errors and latency by release. "Did the deploy cause this?" becomes one query instead of an investigation.

docs.title: 8. Why log JSON instead of plain text?
docs.text: JSON lines are machine-parseable records with named fields, so you can filter by level, route, or userId, group by error code, and join on trace_id without fragile regular expressions. The message stays short and constant while variable data moves into fields.

docs.title: 9. Which fields should every log line include?
docs.text: An ISO 8601 UTC timestamp, level, service, environment, version, a short message, request ID, trace and span IDs, and contextual fields such as route, method, status, duration, and a pseudonymous user ID. Errors are serialized as objects with type, message, stack, and code.

docs.title: 10. When should a failed request be logged at error versus warn or info?
docs.text: error means someone should look: server-side failures and unhandled exceptions. Client errors such as a 400 for invalid input or a 404 for a missing task are expected behaviour; log them at info or warn on the request line. Otherwise real errors drown in noise.

docs.title: 11. What is a correlation ID, and how is it propagated?
docs.text: A value attached to all work caused by one request. A request ID is generated (or validated and accepted) at the edge, returned in X-Request-Id, passed on outgoing HTTP calls and queue messages, and logged on every line. With tracing, the W3C trace ID plays the same role across services.

docs.title: 12. How does AsyncLocalStorage help with request logging in Node.js?
docs.text: It keeps per-request context (such as the request's child logger and ID) available to any code running for that request, including after await, so service functions can log with the request ID without passing a logger through every function signature.

docs.title: 13. How do you keep secrets and personal data out of logs?
docs.text: Never log whole objects such as req, headers, bodies, or HTTP client errors; use the logger's redaction (pino redact) for known paths; mask patterns again in the log pipeline; log pseudonymous IDs instead of emails; restrict access and set retention. If a secret leaks, rotate it, because copies may already exist in archives.

docs.title: 14. Why must containerized applications log to stdout?
docs.text: The platform captures stdout and stderr, stores them on the node with rotation (the kubelet rotates container logs), and an agent ships them. The app needs no log files, rotation, or shipping code, which is the Twelve-Factor approach. Writing files inside a container loses logs on restart and can fill disks.

docs.title: 15. How can you cut log volume without losing what matters?
docs.text: Run production at info, skip health-check and metrics-scrape logs, log one canonical line per request, never log large payloads, and sample fast successful requests while keeping all errors and slow requests. Counts should come from metrics, so sampling logs does not break dashboards.

docs.title: 16. Why should high-cardinality values not be Loki labels?
docs.text: Loki indexes only labels, and every unique label set is a separate stream. Request or user IDs as labels create huge numbers of tiny streams that overload ingestion and queries. Keep them in the log line and filter with | json | reqId="...".

docs.title: 17. Describe the four Prometheus metric types.
docs.text: A counter only increases (resets on restart) and counts events. A gauge goes up and down for current state. A histogram counts observations into cumulative buckets plus _sum and _count, and can be aggregated across instances. A summary computes quantiles in the client, which cannot be aggregated across instances.

docs.title: 18. Why does Prometheus pull metrics, and when do you push?
docs.text: Pulling lets Prometheus know which targets should exist (up == 0 shows a dead target), keeps targets simple, and lets you inspect any /metrics endpoint by hand. Short-lived batch jobs that may finish between scrapes push to a Pushgateway, ideally a success timestamp, and nothing else should.

docs.title: 19. What is cardinality, and how does it explode?
docs.text: The number of distinct series a metric produces: the product of the value counts of its labels. 5 methods x 40 routes x 10 statuses x 14 histogram series x 10 pods is 280,000 series; adding a user_id label with 50,000 users multiplies that by 50,000. Raw URL paths, IDs, and free-text labels are the usual causes.

docs.title: 20. Why can't you average percentiles?
docs.text: A percentile depends on the whole distribution. If pod A's p99 is 100 ms over 900 requests and pod B's is 2 s over 100 requests, the average of 1,050 ms describes no request, and the true combined p99 is 2 s. Combine the raw data first: sum histogram buckets across pods, then compute the quantile.

docs.title: 21. How does histogram_quantile work, and what limits its accuracy?
docs.text: It takes cumulative bucket rates, finds the bucket containing the target rank, and linearly interpolates inside it. Accuracy depends on the bucket layout; if the quantile falls in the +Inf bucket, the result is the highest finite boundary. Put bucket boundaries at important thresholds such as the SLO latency target.

docs.title: 22. What does rate() do, and why apply it before sum()?
docs.text: It computes the per-second average increase of a counter over a range, handling counter resets. Summing raw counters first hides resets from individual pods and produces huge spikes, so the correct form is sum(rate(x[5m])), never rate(sum(x)[5m:]).

docs.title: 23. How long should the range in rate(x[...]) be?
docs.text: Several times the scrape interval, commonly at least four, so each window has enough samples. With a 15 s scrape interval, [1m] is a practical minimum and [5m] is typical for dashboards and alerts.

docs.title: 24. Why are averages misleading for latency?
docs.text: Latency distributions are skewed. An average of 96 ms can hide that 1 in 50 requests takes 2 seconds, and it barely moves when the tail worsens. Percentiles (p50, p95, p99) or "fraction of requests under 300 ms" show what users actually experience.

docs.title: 25. How would you label an Express request-duration histogram?
docs.text: With method, the route template from req.baseUrl + req.route.path (such as /tasks/:id, or a single value like unmatched for 404s), and status_code. Never the raw URL, user ID, or request ID.

docs.title: 26. What makes a good service dashboard?
docs.text: The same RED layout for every service (rate, error ratio, latency percentiles, SLO status) at the top, details by route and version below, dependency and saturation panels after that, deploy annotations, units and threshold lines on every panel, template variables instead of copies, and the JSON kept in version control.

docs.title: 27. What are recording rules for?
docs.text: They evaluate expensive PromQL expressions on a schedule and store the results as new series, so dashboards and alerts read precomputed values. They are named level:metric:operations, for example job_route:http_requests:rate5m.

docs.title: 28. What are a trace, a span, and a span context?
docs.text: A trace is a tree of spans sharing one trace ID for a single request. A span is one timed operation with a name, kind, parent, attributes, events, and status. The span context (trace ID, span ID, trace flags) is what is propagated so the next span can name its parent.

docs.title: 29. Explain the W3C traceparent header field by field.
docs.text: 00-<trace-id>-<parent-id>-<flags>: the version (00), a 16-byte trace ID as 32 hex characters shared by every span, the 8-byte span ID of the calling span as 16 hex characters, and trace flags where the lowest bit means sampled (01). The trace ID stays the same on every hop; the parent ID changes.

docs.title: 30. How does context propagation work inside and between processes?
docs.text: Inside a Node.js process, OpenTelemetry's context manager (built on AsyncLocalStorage) keeps the active span across await. Between processes, a propagator injects the context into HTTP or message headers and the receiver extracts it to start a child span. Any hop that does not do this breaks the trace.

docs.title: 31. Why does OpenTelemetry separate the API from the SDK?
docs.text: Libraries depend only on the stable, lightweight API, which does nothing without an SDK. The application installs and configures the SDK (sampling, exporters). This lets libraries be instrumented once and cost almost nothing when tracing is not enabled.

docs.title: 32. Why must instrumentation load before the application code?
docs.text: Auto-instrumentation works by patching modules such as http, Express, and the MongoDB driver when they are loaded. If they are imported first, they are not patched and no spans appear. Load it with --require or --import (plus the loader hook for ES modules).

docs.title: 33. What does the OpenTelemetry Collector add?
docs.text: A separate pipeline of receivers, processors, and exporters. Apps send OTLP to one endpoint; the Collector batches, retries, limits memory, scrubs sensitive attributes, applies tail sampling, and exports to one or more backends. Changing vendors becomes a config change and apps never hold vendor credentials.

docs.title: 34. Compare head sampling and tail sampling.
docs.text: Head sampling decides at the root span (for example parent-based 10%), which is cheap but drops most error and slow traces. Tail sampling decides in the Collector after the trace completes, keeping all errors and slow traces plus a share of the rest, at the cost of buffering spans and routing every span of a trace to the same Collector instance.

docs.title: 35. How do you link logs, metrics, and traces?
docs.text: Log the trace and span IDs on every line (OpenTelemetry's pino instrumentation does this), attach exemplars (sample trace IDs) to histogram buckets, record the trace ID in error-tracker events, and use the same service resource attributes everywhere.

docs.title: 36. Define SLI, SLO, SLA, and error budget.
docs.text: An SLI is a measurement, usually good events over valid events. An SLO is a target for it over a window (99.9% over 30 days). An SLA is a contract with consequences such as service credits. The error budget is 1 - SLO, the failure the SLO allows. SLAs should be looser than internal SLOs.

docs.title: 37. How much downtime does 99.9% allow in 30 days? And 99.99%?
docs.text: 30 days is 43,200 minutes. 99.9% allows 0.1%, which is 43.2 minutes (43 min 12 s); 99.99% allows 4.32 minutes (about 4 min 19 s); 99% allows 7 hours 12 minutes.

docs.title: 38. What makes a good SLI?
docs.text: It reflects what users experience (availability, latency, freshness, correctness), is measured as close to users as practical (load balancer or synthetic checks, not only inside the app), has a clear definition of valid events, and uses latency thresholds rather than averages.

docs.title: 39. What is burn rate?
docs.text: Observed error ratio divided by the error budget ratio. A burn rate of 1 uses exactly the whole budget over the window; 14.4 on a 30-day window uses 2% of the budget per hour and exhausts it in about two days.

docs.title: 40. Explain multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting.
docs.text: Alert when both a long and a short window exceed a burn-rate threshold. The SRE Workbook suggests paging at 14.4 over 1 hour and 5 minutes, and at 6 over 6 hours and 30 minutes, and opening a ticket at 1 over 3 days and 6 hours. The long window proves the burn is significant; the short one (one-twelfth of it) makes the alert resolve quickly after a fix.

docs.title: 41. What is an error budget policy?
docs.text: An agreed document that states what happens as the budget is consumed, such as extra review below 50% and a freeze on non-critical releases below 25% or when exhausted, with exceptions for security fixes. It turns the SLO into decisions without debates.

docs.title: 42. Why alert on symptoms rather than causes?
docs.text: Symptoms (errors, latency, failed journeys) always matter to users and are few. Causes (CPU, restarts, replica lag) are many, change with the architecture, and often hurt nobody. Causes belong on dashboards, in tickets, and in runbooks as diagnosis steps.

docs.title: 43. What qualities should every paging alert have?
docs.text: It should be urgent, actionable (the responder can do something), require human judgement (otherwise automate it), and be novel (not a duplicate of another page). It needs a runbook link and a dashboard.

docs.title: 44. What do Alertmanager grouping, inhibition, and silences do?
docs.text: Grouping combines related alerts (by alertname and service) into one notification. Inhibition suppresses alerts while a related, more important alert fires, such as all TaskFlow alerts while "API down" is paging. Silences are time-limited manual mutes for maintenance, with an author and a comment.

docs.title: 45. What is a dead man's switch in alerting?
docs.text: An always-firing alert (often called Watchdog) sent to an external service, which pages if it stops arriving. It proves the whole chain from Prometheus through Alertmanager to the receiver works, which the system cannot verify about itself.

docs.title: 46. What makes an on-call rotation healthy?
docs.text: Enough people (commonly six to eight or more), primary and secondary roles, written handoffs, a clear escalation policy, a low and declining number of pages (at most about two incidents per 12-hour shift), a high actionable rate, compensation, and recovery time after bad nights.

docs.title: 47. What does an error tracker provide beyond logs?
docs.text: Grouping of identical exceptions into issues with counts and affected users, readable stack traces with source context, breadcrumbs, release and environment tracking, regression detection, and a triage workflow, all linked to traces and logs.

docs.title: 48. Why upload source maps but never serve them publicly?
docs.text: Without maps, minified stacks are unreadable; with them, the tracker can symbolicate to original files and lines. Public maps expose your original source code, comments, internal routes, and unreleased features. Upload them privately in CI for each release, then delete them from the build output.

docs.title: 49. What are the Core Web Vitals and their thresholds?
docs.text: LCP (loading) should be 2.5 s or less, INP (responsiveness) 200 ms or less, and CLS (visual stability) 0.1 or less, evaluated at the 75th percentile of page loads. INP replaced First Input Delay in March 2024.

docs.title: 50. What is the difference between /healthz and /readyz?
docs.text: Liveness (/healthz) answers "is the process alive?" and must not check dependencies; failure restarts the container. Readiness (/readyz) answers "can it serve traffic now?" and may check required dependencies with a short timeout; failure removes the instance from load balancing. Checking the database in liveness causes mass restarts during a database blip.

docs.title: 51. How do you avoid false alarms from synthetic checks?
docs.text: Probe from several regions outside your infrastructure and alert only when two or more regions fail on consecutive runs. Check real journeys (API health, login and create task), not just a static home page.

docs.title: 52. What are the phases of the incident lifecycle?
docs.text: Detect, triage (declare, set severity, assign roles), mitigate (stop user impact), resolve (fix the cause and verify), and learn (postmortem and action items). Measure time to detect, acknowledge, mitigate, and resolve.

docs.title: 53. What does the incident commander do, and what do they not do?
docs.text: The IC coordinates: sets priorities, assigns work, makes decisions, tracks the overall state, and hands off explicitly. The IC does not debug or change production, because coordination collapses when the coordinator is heads-down in a terminal.

docs.title: 54. Why mitigate before finding the root cause?
docs.text: Users are hurt while you investigate. Rolling back, turning off a flag, failing over, or shedding load stops the damage quickly, and the root cause can then be found calmly, after preserving evidence such as logs and heap snapshots.

docs.title: 55. What makes a postmortem blameless, and why does it matter?
docs.text: It analyses how the system (tools, defaults, processes) allowed the failure and assumes people acted reasonably with what they knew. Blame makes people hide details, and the details are what make the analysis useful. Accountability remains: owners must complete action items.

docs.title: 56. What are the limits of the 5 whys?
docs.text: It produces one linear chain while incidents usually have several contributing factors, different people reach different answers, and it often stops at "human error". Use it alongside a contributing-factors analysis across technical, detection, response, and process categories.

docs.title: 57. Dashboards are green, but customers report that TaskFlow is down. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: external synthetic checks and a request from outside your network to the public URL; certificate expiry and DNS records.

How to confirm: curl -v https://api.example.com/healthz from outside; ingress or load balancer logs show few or no requests compared with normal.

Likely causes and fixes: a failure before requests reach the app (DNS change, expired certificate, CDN or load balancer misconfiguration). Fix the edge issue, then add multi-region black-box probes and measure SLIs at the edge. See observability fundamentals.

docs.title: 58. After a deploy, Prometheus memory doubles and it starts restarting. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: prometheus_tsdb_head_series over time and the TSDB status page's top metrics by series count.

How to confirm: the series count jumps at the deploy time and one metric, such as http_request_duration_seconds, has a label with thousands of values.

Likely causes and fixes: a new unbounded label, usually the raw path instead of the route template, or an ID. Fix the instrumentation, drop the label with metric_relabel_configs as a stopgap, and review new labels in code review. See metrics and dashboards.

docs.title: 59. Average latency is 90 ms and stable, yet users complain that task lists are slow. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: p95 and p99 from the duration histogram per route, not the average.

How to confirm: p99 for GET /tasks is several seconds, and slow traces share an attribute such as very large task counts or one tenant.

Likely causes and fixes: a tail problem hidden by the mean, often an unindexed query or unbounded result size for heavy users. Add the index or pagination, and set SLOs on percentiles or thresholds. See metrics and dashboards.

docs.title: 60. Traces show the API span but downstream services appear as separate, parentless traces. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether outgoing requests carry a traceparent header and whether the downstream service uses the W3C propagator.

How to confirm: capture a request at the downstream service; the header is missing or stripped by a proxy, or a different propagation format is configured.

Likely causes and fixes: an uninstrumented HTTP client, a gateway that drops unknown headers, or mismatched propagators. Use instrumented clients, allow trace headers through proxies, and standardize on W3C Trace Context. See distributed tracing.

docs.title: 61. You deployed OpenTelemetry to TaskFlow API but no spans arrive. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the instrumentation is loaded and the exporter endpoint.

How to confirm: set OTEL_LOG_LEVEL=debug; logs show export errors, or show that Express and MongoDB were never patched.

Likely causes and fixes: the instrumentation file is imported after the app modules, the ES module loader hook is missing, or the OTLP endpoint or port (4318 for HTTP, 4317 for gRPC) is wrong. Load it with --import or --require before the app and verify the Collector address. See distributed tracing.

docs.title: 62. The on-call engineer got 40 pages in two minutes during a database failover. How do you fix the alerting?
docs.text:
What to check first: the alert rules that fired and Alertmanager's group_by and inhibit rules.

How to confirm: the pages are one per pod or per instance, all for the same underlying problem.

Likely causes and fixes: grouping by instance, per-pod cause alerts, and no inhibition. Group by alertname and service, inhibit dependent alerts while "database down" fires, and page on service-level SLO burn instead. See alerting and on-call.

docs.title: 63. A burn-rate alert pages every night for a few minutes and resolves on its own. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: request volume during those minutes and the number of failed requests behind the error ratio.

How to confirm: at night only a few dozen requests arrive, so two or three failures exceed the 1.44% threshold.

Likely causes and fixes: low traffic makes ratios noisy. Require a minimum count of failed requests, add steady synthetic traffic, or use longer windows for low-traffic services. See SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets.

docs.title: 64. During a 10-minute MongoDB failover, every TaskFlow pod restarted and the outage lasted 25 minutes. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the liveness probe endpoint and what it checks.

How to confirm: pod restart counts jump on all pods at the same time, and /healthz runs a database query.

Likely causes and fixes: a liveness probe with a dependency check, so a database problem kills healthy processes and restarts add time. Make /healthz dependency-free and move the database ping to /readyz. See error tracking and uptime monitoring.

docs.title: 65. Frontend error reports show only main.3f9a.js:1:4821 frames after the latest release. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether source maps were uploaded for this release and whether the SDK's release name matches the uploaded one.

How to confirm: the tracker's release page shows no artifacts, or artifacts under a different release string.

Likely causes and fixes: the upload step failed or ran with a different version variable. Upload in the same CI job that builds, use one release variable for both, fail the build if the upload fails, and keep deleting maps from dist/. See error tracking and uptime monitoring.

docs.title: 66. A security review finds access tokens in the log store. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: which service and log statement wrote them, and how long they have been stored.

How to confirm: search for the token pattern; it appears inside a serialized HTTP client error or a headers object.

Likely causes and fixes: logging whole request or error objects that bypassed redaction paths. Rotate the exposed tokens, purge or restrict the affected streams, log selected fields only, add pipeline masking and a redaction test. See structured logging.

docs.title: 67. Log ingestion costs doubled overnight with no traffic increase. How do you find the cause?
docs.text:
What to check first: ingestion volume by service and by log level.

How to confirm: one service's debug lines or one message dominate, starting at a deploy time.

Likely causes and fixes: debug level left on in production, or a log statement inside a loop. Restore info, remove the noisy statement, sample high-volume success logs, and alert on ingestion per service. See structured logging.

docs.title: 68. During a SEV1, five engineers debug in parallel, two of them restart the same service, and customers learn about it from social media. What changes do you make?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether an incident commander and a communications lead were assigned, and where the discussion happened.

How to confirm: the incident channel has no recorded decisions, and the first status update came long after the first page.

Likely causes and fixes: an unmanaged incident. Declare early, assign an IC who does not debug, keep one channel and document, have a comms lead post an initial status within minutes and update on a cadence. See incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: 69. Postmortems keep listing the same contributing factor, and the incident repeats. What is going wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: the status of action items from earlier postmortems.

How to confirm: the earlier items are vague ("improve monitoring"), unowned, or still open past their due dates.

Likely causes and fixes: action items are not concrete, owned, or tracked. Write specific, verifiable items with one owner and a due date in the normal backlog, review completion regularly, and treat overdue high-priority items as accepted risk that leadership must sign off. See incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: 70. Users report slow page loads in TaskFlow Web, but API latency is fine. How do you investigate?
docs.text:
What to check first: real-user Core Web Vitals (LCP and INP at p75) by route, device type, and release.

How to confirm: LCP or INP regressed with a specific frontend release, or only on mobile devices.

Likely causes and fixes: a larger bundle, render-blocking resources, or heavy main-thread work in the browser. Fix the frontend regression and track Web Vitals per release like backend latency. See error tracking and uptime monitoring.

docs.title: Metrics and Dashboards
docs.text: A metric is a number measured over time: requests per second, the 95th percentile of request latency, connections in use. Metrics are the cheapest signal to keep and the fastest to query, which makes them the backbone of dashboards and alerts. This lesson covers the four metric types, the Prometheus pull model and its text format, labels and the cardinality trap, why averages lie and percentiles cannot be averaged, how histograms and histogram_quantile work, rate() over counters, instrumenting TaskFlow API with prom-client, PromQL you will use every day, and how to design Grafana dashboards people can read during an incident.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
When TaskFlow API slows down, the first question is not "what happened to request 7f3a?" but "how bad is it, since when, and for whom?". Metrics answer that in seconds across months of history: error ratio by route, latency percentiles by version, saturation of the MongoDB pool. They feed every alert, every SLO, and every capacity plan.

Metrics are also easy to get subtly wrong. A label holding user IDs can take down the monitoring system, an average can show 96 ms while one request in fifty takes two seconds, and summing percentiles across pods produces numbers that describe nothing. Understanding the mechanics is the difference between a dashboard that tells the truth and one that hides the incident.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Prometheus (SoundCloud and the CNCF). The Prometheus overview describes a monitoring toolkit originally built at SoundCloud, with a multi-dimensional data model (metric name plus key-value labels), PromQL, and pull-based collection over HTTP. It joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation in 2016 as its second hosted project after Kubernetes.
  • Google SRE (Borgmon). The SRE book chapter Practical Alerting from Time-Series Data describes Borgmon, Google's internal time-series monitoring system, whose design (scraping a standard metrics endpoint, labels, rule evaluation) Prometheus closely resembles.
  • Prometheus histogram guidance. The official Histograms and summaries page explains why quantiles from summaries cannot be aggregated across instances, how histogram_quantile estimates quantiles from buckets, and how bucket layout affects the error of the estimate.
  • Grafana Labs. Grafana's dashboard best practices recommend RED dashboards for services and USE dashboards for infrastructure, consistent layouts, and managing dashboards as code to avoid sprawl.

Popular tools and providers: Prometheus, Grafana, Grafana Mimir, Thanos, VictoriaMetrics, the OpenTelemetry metrics SDK, prom-client for Node.js, Datadog, Amazon CloudWatch, Google Cloud Monitoring, and Azure Monitor.

docs.title: What a time series is
docs.text:
A Prometheus time series is identified by a metric name and a set of labels, and holds samples: (timestamp, float value) pairs.

http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", instance="api-1:9464",
                                    method="POST", route="/tasks", status_code="201"}
  @1763042400  10250
  @1763042415  10281
  @1763042430  10309

Every distinct combination of name and label values is a separate series. job and instance are added by Prometheus at scrape time; the others come from the application.

docs.title: Metric types
docs.text:
Type Behaviour Use for TaskFlow example Counter Only goes up (resets to 0 when the process restarts) Counting events taskflow_tasks_created_total, requests, errors Gauge Goes up and down Current state mongodb_pool_connections_in_use, queue depth, memory Histogram Counts observations into cumulative buckets, plus _sum and _count Distributions you aggregate: latency, payload size http_request_duration_seconds Summary Computes quantiles in the client over a sliding window, plus _sum and _count Precise quantiles for one instance only Rare in services; avoid for aggregated latency

Rules of thumb: never read a counter's raw value (wrap it in rate() or increase()); never use a gauge for something that only increases; use a histogram, not a summary, for latency you want to aggregate across pods. OpenTelemetry has the same ideas under slightly different names (Counter, UpDownCounter, Gauge, Histogram).

Naming conventions from the Prometheus docs: a prefix for the domain (taskflow_, http_), base units in the name (_seconds, _bytes, never milliseconds), and _total on counters.

docs.title: The pull model
docs.text:
Prometheus pulls: on every scrape interval it discovers targets (static lists, Kubernetes pods, cloud instances), sends GET /metrics to each, and stores the samples it receives. Each scrape also produces a synthetic up series: 1 if the scrape succeeded, 0 if not.

Why pull:

  • Prometheus knows which targets should exist, so a dead target shows up immediately as up == 0 instead of silently going quiet.
  • Targets stay simple: they only expose current values over HTTP.
  • You can curl any target's /metrics to see exactly what it reports.
  • The scrape interval, not the application, controls load on the monitoring system.

The trade-off is that Prometheus must be able to reach every target over the network, and a process that lives for a few seconds may finish between scrapes. That is what the Pushgateway is for, and only that (see Practical examples).

The default scrape_interval is one minute; 15 to 30 seconds is common for services. A query looks back at most five minutes for a series' latest sample, and series that vanish from a scrape (or whose target disappears) are marked stale, so they drop out of queries quickly.

docs.title: The exposition format
docs.text:
GET /metrics returns plain text. A trimmed example from TaskFlow API:

# HELP http_request_duration_seconds HTTP request duration in seconds
# TYPE http_request_duration_seconds histogram
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.05",method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 9120
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.1",method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 9700
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="0.25",method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 9950
http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf",method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 10000
http_request_duration_seconds_sum{method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 512.7
http_request_duration_seconds_count{method="GET",route="/tasks",status_code="200"} 10000
# HELP mongodb_pool_connections_in_use MongoDB connections currently checked out of the pool
# TYPE mongodb_pool_connections_in_use gauge
mongodb_pool_connections_in_use 3
# HELP taskflow_tasks_created_total Tasks successfully created
# TYPE taskflow_tasks_created_total counter
taskflow_tasks_created_total{source="web"} 48211

# HELP and # TYPE describe each metric. Histogram buckets are cumulative: le="0.1" counts every request that took at most 0.1 s, including those already counted in le="0.05", and le="+Inf" always equals _count. The OpenMetrics format is a closely related standardization of the same text format.

docs.title: Labels and the cardinality trap
docs.text:
Labels make metrics useful (error ratio per route) and also make them expensive, because the number of series is the product of the number of values of each label.

Worked through:

method (5) x route (40) x status_code (10)          = 2,000 label sets
x 14 series per histogram label set                  = 28,000 series per pod
x 10 pods (the instance label)                       = 280,000 series

Each active series costs memory in Prometheus's head block
(on the order of a few KB including index overhead).

Add user_id with 50,000 active users                 = 14,000,000,000 series

In practice actual counts are lower (not every route returns every status), but the multiplication is what matters. Real explosions usually come from:

  • Raw URLs as labels: /tasks/6650f1c2... instead of the template /tasks/:id. Every task becomes a series.
  • IDs: user, tenant, request, session, or trace IDs.
  • Unbounded strings: error messages, user agents, email domains.
  • Too many histogram buckets multiplied by many labels.

Find the culprits with prometheus_tsdb_head_series (total active series), Prometheus's TSDB status page (top metrics and labels by series count), or topk(10, count by (__name__) ({__name__=~".+"})). Fix them at the source, or drop labels at scrape time with metric_relabel_configs.

docs.title: Counters and rate()
docs.text:
A counter's raw value depends on when the process started, so it is almost never what you want. rate() computes the per-second average increase over a time window:

counter at 14:00:00 = 12,000      counter at 14:05:00 = 12,600
rate(...[5m]) = (12,600 - 12,000) / 300 s = 2 requests per second
increase(...[5m]) = 600 requests

rate() also handles counter resets: if a pod restarts and the counter drops from 12,400 to 0 and climbs to 150, rate() treats the drop as a reset and counts 150 more, instead of a negative rate.

Two rules prevent most mistakes:

  • rate() first, then sum(). sum(rate(x[5m])) is correct; rate(sum(x)[5m:]) (a subquery; rate(sum(x)[5m]) does not even parse) is not, because summing first hides individual counter resets.
  • Make the range a few times the scrape interval (a common guideline is at least four), so each window contains enough samples. With a 15 s interval, [1m] is the practical minimum and [5m] is typical for dashboards.

irate() uses only the last two samples; it reacts faster but is noisy, and is meant for graphs of fast-moving counters, not alerts.

docs.title: Percentiles compared with averages
docs.text:
The p95 (95th percentile) is the value that 95% of observations are less than or equal to. Latency distributions are skewed: most requests are fast and a long tail is very slow. The mean mixes them into a number no request experienced, and it barely moves when the tail gets worse. The tail matters because heavy users make many requests per page and will hit the p99 often, and because the slowest requests are frequently the most valuable (the largest task lists, the busiest customers).

You cannot average percentiles. Suppose two pods serve GET /tasks:

Pod A: 900 requests, all ~100 ms                 -> p99 = 100 ms
Pod B: 100 requests, 50 at ~100 ms, 50 at ~2 s   -> p99 = 2,000 ms

avg(p99) = (100 + 2,000) / 2 = 1,050 ms     <- describes no request

Actual combined distribution: 950 at ~100 ms, 50 at ~2 s
  true p99 (request 990 of 1,000) = 2,000 ms
  true p95 (request 950 of 1,000) = 100 ms

Percentiles depend on the whole distribution, so the only correct way to combine them is to combine the underlying data first. This is exactly what histogram buckets allow, and what client-side summaries do not.

docs.title: Histograms and histogram_quantile
docs.text:
Because buckets are counters, you can rate() them, sum() them across pods, and then estimate a quantile from the combined distribution:

histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

The function finds the bucket containing the target rank and linearly interpolates inside it. Worked example with rates per second summed over all pods:

le="0.1"   9,000      le="0.25"  9,700      le="0.5"  9,950      le="+Inf"  10,000

target rank for p95 = 0.95 x 10,000 = 9,500  -> falls in (0.1, 0.25], which holds 700
position inside the bucket = (9,500 - 9,000) / 700 = 0.714
estimate = 0.1 + 0.714 x (0.25 - 0.1) = 0.207 s

The true p95 could be anywhere between 0.1 and 0.25 s; the estimate assumes observations are spread evenly in the bucket. Consequences:

  • Choose buckets around the values you care about, especially your SLO threshold. With a bucket boundary at exactly 0.3 s, "fraction of requests faster than 300 ms" is exact, not estimated: sum(rate(..._bucket{le="0.3"}[5m])) / sum(rate(..._count[5m])).
  • If the quantile lands in the +Inf bucket, the result is the highest finite boundary, so a top bucket of 10 s caps every estimate at 10 s.
  • More buckets mean more accuracy and more series (cardinality again).
  • Prometheus also supports native histograms, which pick exponentially spaced buckets automatically and store them compactly; check that your Prometheus server and client library versions support them before adopting them.
Histogram Summary Quantiles computed At query time, on the server In the client process Aggregate across pods Yes No (quantiles are not additive) Accuracy Depends on bucket layout Precise within its configured error, for that one process Change quantile later Yes, any quantile No, fixed at instrumentation time Client cost Cheap (increment a bucket) Higher (streaming quantile estimation)

docs.title: Dashboards that work during incidents
docs.text:
A dashboard is a tool for answering questions under pressure. Design them in layers:

  1. Service overview (RED): one row per service with request rate, error ratio, and p50/p95/p99 latency, plus SLO status. Every service dashboard has the same layout, so on-call engineers can read any of them.
  2. Service detail: the same RED panels split by route, status code, and version; dependency panels (MongoDB latency, outbound call errors); runtime saturation (event loop lag, heap, CPU throttling).
  3. Resource dashboards (USE): nodes, databases, queues, connection pools: utilization, saturation, errors.

Design rules:

  • Put the most important panel top-left; read top to bottom from symptom to cause.
  • Use template variables ($env, $service, $route) instead of copying dashboards per service.
  • Show deploys as annotations so every graph answers "did a release cause this?".
  • Set units (seconds, requests/s, percent) and SLO threshold lines on every panel.
  • Prefer percentiles and ratios to raw counts; avoid pie charts and gauges for time-based questions.
  • Keep dashboards in version control (provisioned JSON or code), reviewed like any other change, and delete the ones nobody opens.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Choose Why Request latency across many pods Histogram Aggregatable; any quantile later Exact quantile inside one process, no aggregation Summary Precise for that process Current value (queue depth, connections) Gauge Goes up and down Number of events Counter with rate() Robust to restarts Per-user or per-request detail Logs or spans Unbounded values destroy metrics Long-running service Prometheus scrape Built-in liveness via up Batch job that runs for seconds Pushgateway (or the job's completion timestamp in logs) It may never be scraped Many services and vendors, one instrumentation API OpenTelemetry metrics, exported to Prometheus or OTLP Vendor-neutral

Do not use metrics for data that must be exact per event (billing, audits); Prometheus is designed for operational monitoring, where a few lost samples or an estimated quantile are acceptable.

docs.title: Instrumenting TaskFlow API with prom-client
docs.text:
// src/metrics/http.js
import client from "prom-client";

export const register = client.register;
client.collectDefaultMetrics({ register }); // CPU, memory, event loop lag, GC, handles

export const httpDuration = new client.Histogram({
  name: "http_request_duration_seconds",
  help: "HTTP request duration in seconds",
  labelNames: ["method", "route", "status_code"],
  // Boundaries around TaskFlow's targets, including the 300 ms SLO threshold.
  buckets: [0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5],
});

export function metricsMiddleware(req, res, next) {
  const end = httpDuration.startTimer();
  res.on("finish", () => {
    // Route template ("/tasks/:id"), never the raw URL; one value for 404s.
    const route = req.route ? req.baseUrl + req.route.path : "unmatched";
    end({ method: req.method, route, status_code: String(res.statusCode) });
  });
  next();
}

// src/metrics/server.js: metrics on a separate, internal-only port
import express from "express";
import { register } from "./http.js";

export function startMetricsServer(port = 9464) {
  const metricsApp = express();
  metricsApp.get("/metrics", async (req, res) => {
    res.set("Content-Type", register.contentType);
    res.end(await register.metrics());
  });
  return metricsApp.listen(port);
}

// src/server.js
import express from "express";
import { metricsMiddleware } from "./metrics/http.js";
import { startMetricsServer } from "./metrics/server.js";
import { tasksRouter } from "./tasks/router.js";

const app = express();
app.use(metricsMiddleware); // before the routers, so every request is timed
app.use(express.json());
app.use("/tasks", tasksRouter);

app.listen(3000);
startMetricsServer(9464);

Parts: startTimer() returns a function that observes the elapsed seconds with the labels you pass; req.route is only set when a route matched, so unmatched paths collapse into one label value; the histogram's _count series doubles as the request counter. Port 9464 is not exposed through the public load balancer, so internal metrics are not visible to the internet.

docs.title: Prometheus configuration and recording rules
docs.text:
# prometheus/prometheus.yml
global:
  scrape_interval: 15s
  evaluation_interval: 15s

rule_files:
  - /etc/prometheus/rules/*.yml

alerting:
  alertmanagers:
    - static_configs:
        - targets: ["alertmanager:9093"]

scrape_configs:
  - job_name: taskflow-api
    static_configs:
      - targets: ["api-1:9464", "api-2:9464"]
        labels:
          env: production
    metric_relabel_configs:
      # Safety net: drop a label that must never reach storage.
      - action: labeldrop
        regex: user_id

# prometheus/rules/taskflow-recording.yml
groups:
  - name: taskflow-http
    rules:
      - record: job_route:http_requests:rate5m
        expr: sum by (job, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

      - record: job_route:http_request_errors:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum by (job, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum by (job, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count[5m]))

      - record: job_route:http_request_duration_seconds:p95_5m
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            sum by (job, route, le) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))

Recording rules precompute expensive expressions every evaluation interval and store the results as new series, so dashboards and alerts stay fast. Their names follow the level:metric:operations convention from the Prometheus docs.

docs.title: A PromQL cookbook for TaskFlow
docs.text:
# Requests per second, whole service
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[5m]))

# Error ratio per route (5xx / all)
job_route:http_request_errors:ratio_rate5m{job="taskflow-api"}

# p99 latency by version during a rolling deploy (version from build_info)
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le, version) (
    rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="taskflow-api"}[5m])
    * on (instance) group_left (version) taskflow_build_info))

# Share of requests faster than the 300 ms SLO threshold
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="taskflow-api", le="0.3"}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[5m]))

# Targets that failed their last scrape
up{job="taskflow-api"} == 0

# Tasks created in the last hour compared with the same hour a week ago
sum(increase(taskflow_tasks_created_total[1h]))
  /
sum(increase(taskflow_tasks_created_total[1h] offset 1w))

The version query joins each pod's latency buckets with its taskflow_build_info series (from observability fundamentals) so latency can be compared between the old and new release.

docs.title: Provisioning Grafana from files
docs.text:
# grafana/provisioning/datasources/prometheus.yaml
apiVersion: 1
datasources:
  - name: Prometheus
    type: prometheus
    access: proxy
    url: http://prometheus:9090
    isDefault: true

# grafana/provisioning/dashboards/taskflow.yaml
apiVersion: 1
providers:
  - name: taskflow
    folder: TaskFlow
    type: file
    options:
      path: /var/lib/grafana/dashboards

Dashboard JSON files exported from Grafana are committed to the repository and mounted at /var/lib/grafana/dashboards, so every environment gets the same reviewed dashboards and a broken edit can be reverted.

docs.title: Pushing from a batch job
docs.text:
A nightly backup job finishes in minutes and may never be scraped. It pushes one gauge to the Pushgateway on success:

# scripts/backup.sh (last step, only reached when the backup succeeded)
cat <<EOF | curl --fail --silent --show-error --data-binary @- \
  "http://pushgateway.monitoring.internal.example.com:9091/metrics/job/taskflow_backup"
# TYPE taskflow_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds gauge
taskflow_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds $(date +%s)
EOF

# Alert when the last successful backup is older than 26 hours
time() - taskflow_backup_last_success_timestamp_seconds{job="taskflow_backup"} > 26 * 3600

Pushing a timestamp of success is deliberate: if the job stops running entirely, the value goes stale in an obvious way and the alert fires. The Pushgateway never forgets a pushed series on its own, which is why it is not a substitute for scraping long-running services.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Follow RED for every service and USE for every resource; give every service dashboard the same layout.
  • Use histograms for latency, with bucket boundaries at your SLO thresholds.
  • Label with bounded values only: method, route template, status code, version. Never IDs, raw paths, or free text.
  • Always rate() counters before aggregating; choose ranges of at least a few scrape intervals.
  • Never average percentiles; aggregate buckets, then compute quantiles.
  • Use base units and Prometheus naming conventions (_seconds, _bytes, _total).
  • Precompute heavy queries with recording rules.
  • Keep /metrics off the public internet.
  • Watch Prometheus itself: active series, scrape failures, rule evaluation time.
  • Keep dashboards in version control and annotate deploys.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Prometheus memory doubles after a deploy and it restarts in a loop. Detect: prometheus_tsdb_head_series jumps at the deploy time; the TSDB status page shows one metric with millions of series. Cause: a new label with unbounded values, typically the raw URL path when req.route was not used. Fix: label by route template, add a labeldrop or drop rule as a stopgap, and add a review checklist item for new labels.
  • The p99 graph shows exactly 5 s during an outage, every time. Detect: the latency panel flattens at a round number while users report 20-second waits. Cause: the quantile fell in the +Inf bucket, and histogram_quantile returns the highest finite boundary. Fix: add buckets that cover realistic worst cases (and your client timeout) and also chart the fraction of requests over the SLO threshold.
  • Request rate spikes at every deploy. Detect: sawtooth artefacts in rate graphs aligned with pod restarts. Cause: the query sums counters before applying rate(), so when one pod restarts the sum drops, and rate() misreads that drop as a counter reset and adds a false spike. Fix: use sum(rate(counter[5m])), never rate(sum(counter)[5m:]).
  • A pod is broken but dashboards look fine. Detect: users see intermittent errors; up{job="taskflow-api"} shows one target at 0. Cause: the broken pod cannot be scraped, so its errors never reach the aggregate, and no alert covers up. Fix: alert on up == 0 for longer than a few scrape intervals, and on SLO metrics measured at the load balancer.
  • The dashboard is too slow to load during an incident. Detect: panels time out exactly when traffic is high. Cause: heavy histogram_quantile queries over many series and long ranges, run on every refresh by every viewer. Fix: recording rules for dashboard queries, sensible default time ranges, and fewer panels per dashboard.
  • A batch job's metric says it succeeded, but it has not run for days. Detect: the job's last-success gauge in the Pushgateway is old, yet nothing alerted. Cause: the alert checks for failure values, and a job that never runs never pushes a failure. Fix: push a success timestamp and alert on its age.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Time series: A metric name plus a unique set of label values, with timestamped samples.
  • Label: A key-value pair that adds a dimension to a metric.
  • Cardinality: The number of distinct series a metric produces.
  • Counter / gauge / histogram / summary: The four Prometheus metric types.
  • Scrape: One HTTP pull of a target's /metrics endpoint.
  • Exposition format: The text format served at /metrics.
  • Percentile (quantile): The value below which a given fraction of observations fall (p95 = 0.95 quantile).
  • Bucket: A cumulative histogram counter for observations at or below a boundary (le).
  • rate(): Per-second average increase of a counter over a range, adjusted for resets.
  • Recording rule: A query evaluated periodically and stored as a new series.
  • Pushgateway: A cache that holds metrics pushed by short-lived jobs until Prometheus scrapes them.
  • PromQL: Prometheus's query language.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Using raw paths, IDs, or error messages as label values.
  • Alerting on or charting average latency.
  • Averaging or summing percentiles across instances.
  • Reading raw counter values or applying rate() after sum().
  • Using a summary for latency that must be aggregated across pods.
  • Default buckets that do not include the SLO threshold or realistic timeouts.
  • Measuring in milliseconds in one service and seconds in another.
  • Using the Pushgateway to turn Prometheus into a push system for services.
  • Building one dashboard per person instead of a shared, layered set.
  • Exposing /metrics publicly, leaking internal details.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. When would you use a counter, a gauge, and a histogram? Give a TaskFlow example of each.
  2. Why does Prometheus pull, and what problem does the up metric solve?
  3. A histogram with 9 buckets has labels method (4 values), route (25 values), and status_code (8 values), on 6 pods. How many series is that? (Each label set has 9 + 1 + 2 = 12 series; 4 x 25 x 8 = 800 label sets; 800 x 12 x 6 = 57,600 series.)
  4. A counter goes from 30,000 to 31,800 in 10 minutes. What do rate(x[10m]) and increase(x[10m]) return? (3 per second and 1,800.)
  5. Why is the average of two pods' p99 latencies not the service's p99?
  6. Using cumulative bucket rates le="0.2" = 800, le="0.5" = 960, and +Inf = 1,000, estimate the p90. (Rank 900 falls in (0.2, 0.5], which holds 160; (900 - 800) / 160 = 0.625; 0.2 + 0.625 x 0.3 = 0.3875 s.)
  7. When is a Pushgateway appropriate, and what should a batch job push?
  8. How would you lay out a dashboard for TaskFlow API so an on-call engineer can find the cause of a latency spike?
