docs.title: Observability Fundamentals
docs.text:
Monitoring tells you when something you anticipated has gone wrong. Observability is the wider ability to ask new questions about a running system, from the outside, without shipping new code to answer them. Both rest on telemetry: the logs, metrics, traces, profiles, and change events that software emits while it runs.

This lesson explains what each signal is good at and what it costs, the standard checklists engineers use to decide what to measure (Google's four golden signals, the RED method, and the USE method), the difference between white-box and black-box monitoring, and a concrete instrumentation plan for TaskFlow API, the Express and MongoDB task service used across this site.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Production fails in ways tests never see: a slow disk on one node, a connection pool that fills only at peak, a third-party API that times out for one region, a deploy that doubles memory use. Without telemetry the team learns about these from angry users, then guesses. With good telemetry the team sees the symptom first, follows it to a cause in minutes, and can prove the fix worked.

Telemetry is also how you make decisions with data instead of opinion: whether a release is safe to continue, whether you have capacity for next month's traffic, and whether reliability is good enough to keep shipping features. The cost is real (storage, licences, engineering time, and alert fatigue), so the skill is choosing the right signals, not collecting everything.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE (four golden signals). The chapter Monitoring Distributed Systems in Google's Site Reliability Engineering book defines latency, traffic, errors, and saturation as the four signals to measure for a user-facing system if you can measure only four. It also argues for alerting on symptoms rather than causes and for keeping monitoring simple.
  • Brendan Gregg (USE method). Gregg's USE Method page describes checking utilization, saturation, and errors for every resource (CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, and software resources such as locks and pools) as a fast way to find performance bottlenecks.
  • Grafana Labs (RED method). Tom Wilkie's post The RED Method: How to instrument your services proposes measuring rate, errors, and duration for every service, so every service dashboard looks the same and on-call engineers can read any of them.
  • OpenTelemetry (signals as a standard). The OpenTelemetry project's Signals documentation defines traces, metrics, logs, and baggage as vendor-neutral signals, and lists profiles as a signal under development. It is the reason instrumentation written today can be sent to almost any backend.

Popular tools and providers: Prometheus, Grafana (with Loki, Tempo, Mimir, and Pyroscope), OpenTelemetry, the Elastic Stack, Jaeger, Datadog, New Relic, Honeycomb, Sentry, Amazon CloudWatch, Google Cloud Observability, and Azure Monitor.

docs.title: Monitoring compared with observability
docs.text:
Monitoring is built from questions you already know to ask: "Is the error rate above 1%?", "Is the disk more than 90% full?". You write the check in advance, and it answers yes or no. That works well for known failure modes.

Observability matters for failures nobody predicted. When POST /tasks is slow only for users of one tenant whose task lists are huge, no pre-built dashboard has a "tenants with huge lists" panel. You need telemetry rich enough (high-cardinality fields such as tenant ID, request ID, and route on logs and spans) to slice the data in a way you did not plan.

Monitoring Observability Question type Known in advance ("is X above Y?") New, exploratory ("what do the slow requests have in common?") Main output Dashboards and alerts Ad-hoc queries over rich events Typical data Aggregated metrics Structured logs and traces with many fields, plus metrics Good at Detecting known failure modes cheaply Explaining novel failures Risk when missing You find out from users You know something is wrong but cannot find why

They are not rivals. Monitoring detects; observability explains. A mature team has a small set of reliable alerts plus telemetry that is good enough to debug what those alerts find.

docs.title: The signals and what each answers
docs.text:
Signal Shape Strength Weakness Logs One record per event, with a timestamp and fields Full detail of individual events; easy to add Volume and cost grow with traffic; hard to aggregate if unstructured Metrics Numeric time series identified by a name and labels Cheap to store and query over months; ideal for alerts and trends Aggregated: cannot tell you about one specific request Traces A tree of spans (timed operations) for one request across services Shows where time is spent and how calls relate Needs context propagation everywhere; usually sampled Profiles Sampled stack traces of CPU, memory allocation, or locks Points to the exact function using resources Language-specific tooling; less mature standards Events Deploys, config changes, feature flag flips, failovers Answers "what changed?", the first question in most incidents Often not recorded at all

The three core signals are covered in depth in structured logging, metrics and dashboards, and distributed tracing. Profiles are usually collected by a continuous profiler such as Grafana Pyroscope or Parca; OpenTelemetry's profiles signal is still in development. Change events are the cheapest high-value signal: record every deploy with its version and show it on every dashboard.

The signals are most useful when they are linked. A log line carries a trace_id, a trace carries the same service.name and service.version as the metrics, and a metric graph can show exemplars (sample trace IDs) for its slowest points. Linking is what turns three separate tools into one investigation.

docs.title: Cost and cardinality
docs.text:
Each signal scales differently, which drives most architecture decisions.

  • Metrics cost by the number of time series, not by traffic. A counter incremented a million times a second is still one series. What makes metrics expensive is cardinality: the number of unique combinations of label values. Adding a user_id label creates one series per user.
  • Logs cost by volume: bytes ingested, indexed, and retained. They grow linearly with traffic and with how chatty the code is.
  • Traces cost by span count, which is traffic times the number of spans per request, so they are almost always sampled.

A worked estimate for TaskFlow API at 200 requests per second:

Logs: 1 request log line of ~600 bytes per request
  200 req/s x 600 B = 120 KB/s
  120 KB/s x 86,400 s = ~10.4 GB/day; 30-day retention = ~311 GB

Traces: 10% sampled, ~8 spans per request, ~500 bytes per span
  200 x 0.10 x 8 x 500 B = 80 KB/s = ~6.9 GB/day

Metrics: 5,000 active series scraped every 15 s
  5,000 / 15 = ~333 samples/s
  Prometheus stores roughly 1-2 bytes per sample after compression
  333 x 2 B x 86,400 = ~58 MB/day

Double the traffic and logs and traces double; metrics stay the same as long as the label sets do not change. This is why the rule of thumb is: put high-cardinality detail (user IDs, request IDs, task IDs) in logs and spans; keep metric labels to small, bounded sets (method, route template, status class). The cardinality trap is worked through in metrics and dashboards.

docs.title: The four golden signals
docs.text:
Google's SRE book names four signals to watch on every user-facing service:

  1. Latency: the time to serve a request. Measure successful and failed requests separately: a fast 500 can drag the average down and hide slow successes, while a slow error (a timeout) is worse than a fast one. Use percentiles, not averages.
  2. Traffic: demand on the system, in a unit that fits it. For TaskFlow API it is HTTP requests per second, split by route; for a queue worker it is jobs per second.
  3. Errors: the rate of failed requests. Count explicit failures (HTTP 5xx), implicit ones (a 200 with the wrong body), and policy failures (a response slower than a committed limit counts as an error if your SLO says so).
  4. Saturation: how "full" the service is, focused on its most constrained resource. For a Node.js API that is often the event loop (one thread) or the MongoDB connection pool, not CPU. Many systems degrade before 100% utilization, so saturation is also about predicting trouble: "the pool will be exhausted at 1.5x today's peak".

docs.title: The RED method and the USE method
docs.text:
The golden signals overlap with two checklists that divide the work by what you are looking at.

RED, for every service or endpoint (request-driven things):

  • Rate: requests per second.
  • Errors: failed requests per second (or as a ratio of rate).
  • Duration: the distribution of request latency, as a histogram.

USE, for every resource (things that have capacity):

  • Utilization: the fraction of time or capacity the resource is busy.
  • Saturation: the extra work it cannot serve yet, usually a queue.
  • Errors: error events for that resource.
Resource in TaskFlow Utilization Saturation Errors CPU (container) CPU seconds used / CPU limit CFS throttling time, run-queue length n/a Memory RSS / memory limit Swapping, GC time rising OOM kills Node.js event loop Event loop utilization (ELU) Event loop lag n/a MongoDB connection pool Checked-out / max pool size Requests waiting for a connection Checkout timeouts, pool cleared Disk (database host) Percent busy I/O wait queue I/O errors Job queue Workers busy / workers Queue depth, age of oldest job Failed jobs

RED tells you that a service is unhealthy as its users experience it; USE tells you which resource is the bottleneck. Build RED dashboards per service and USE dashboards per resource, and link from one to the other.

docs.title: White-box and black-box monitoring
docs.text:
• White-box monitoring uses telemetry emitted from inside the system: metrics, logs, and traces from the code, runtime, and dependencies. It explains why something is happening and can warn early (the pool is at 90% and climbing).
  • Black-box monitoring tests externally visible behaviour the way a user would: an HTTP probe from several regions that requests https://api.example.com/healthz or runs a login-and-create-task flow. It sees failures that never reach your code, such as an expired certificate, a DNS mistake, or a CDN outage.

The SRE book recommends heavy use of white-box monitoring with modest but critical use of black-box monitoring: black-box tells you a problem is happening now and affecting users; white-box lets you diagnose it and spot problems before they become user-visible. See error tracking and uptime monitoring for synthetic checks.

docs.title: An instrumentation strategy for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
Instrument by layer, starting where users are, and give every signal the same identity attributes so they can be joined later.

Layer What to emit Signal Tool Edge Request logs and status codes at the load balancer or ingress; external probes Logs, metrics, black-box checks Load balancer logs, Blackbox exporter or a synthetic service Service (RED) Request count, errors, duration histogram per route template Metrics prom-client or OpenTelemetry metrics Requests One structured log line per request with request ID and trace ID Logs pino and pino-http Call graph Spans for HTTP server, Express routes, MongoDB, outgoing HTTP, queue publish Traces OpenTelemetry auto-instrumentation Runtime (USE) Event loop lag and utilization, heap, GC, CPU, RSS Metrics prom-client default metrics Dependencies (USE) MongoDB pool checkouts and wait time, queue depth Metrics Driver events, queue metrics Business Tasks created, reminders sent, sign-ups Metrics Custom counters Change Deploys with version and commit, flag flips Events CI/CD annotations, a build_info metric Errors Unhandled exceptions with stack traces and release Error events An error tracker such as Sentry

Three rules keep this coherent:

  1. One identity everywhere. Every log line, metric, and span carries service.name (taskflow-api), service.version (the release), and the environment (deployment.environment.name in OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions). This makes "errors by version" a one-line query.
  2. Follow conventions instead of inventing names. Use OpenTelemetry semantic conventions (http.request.method, http.route, http.response.status_code) for spans, and Prometheus naming conventions (_total for counters, base units such as _seconds and _bytes) for metrics.
  3. Label by route template, never by raw path. /tasks/:id is one value; /tasks/6650f1... is one value per task and will explode cardinality.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Pick the signal that answers the question at the lowest cost:

Question Best first signal Then Are users affected right now? Metrics (error ratio, latency SLO) and black-box probes Alerts on SLO burn Why did this specific request fail? Logs filtered by request ID The linked trace Which service or call added latency? Traces Metrics for that dependency Which code path burns CPU or memory? Profiles Load test to confirm Did the deploy cause it? Change events plus metrics split by version Roll back, then investigate Is a resource running out? USE metrics and their trend Capacity plan What do slow requests have in common? Structured logs or spans with many fields Add a metric if it recurs

When not to reach for more telemetry:

  • A single-process side project does not need a tracing backend on day one. Structured logs with request IDs and a handful of metrics go a long way; add tracing when requests cross process boundaries.
  • Do not add a metric per user, tenant, or task ID. Put those identifiers in logs and spans.
  • Do not keep debug-level logging on in production "just in case"; turn it on temporarily and per component when you need it.
  • Do not build a dashboard for every metric. Build dashboards for questions people actually ask during incidents.

docs.title: Runtime and dependency saturation metrics
docs.text:
prom-client's default metrics cover the Node.js runtime (event loop lag, heap, GC, CPU, open handles). The MongoDB Node.js driver emits connection pool monitoring events, which make a direct USE metric for the pool.

// src/metrics/runtime.js
import client from "prom-client";

export const register = client.register;

// process_cpu_seconds_total, process_resident_memory_bytes,
// nodejs_eventloop_lag_seconds, nodejs_heap_size_used_bytes, nodejs_gc_duration_seconds, ...
client.collectDefaultMetrics({ register });

const poolInUse = new client.Gauge({
  name: "mongodb_pool_connections_in_use",
  help: "MongoDB connections currently checked out of the pool",
});
const checkoutFailures = new client.Counter({
  name: "mongodb_pool_checkout_failures_total",
  help: "Failed attempts to check out a MongoDB connection",
  labelNames: ["reason"],
});

// Call once with the shared MongoClient after creating it.
export function instrumentMongoPool(mongoClient) {
  mongoClient.on("connectionCheckedOut", () => poolInUse.inc());
  mongoClient.on("connectionCheckedIn", () => poolInUse.dec());
  mongoClient.on("connectionCheckOutFailed", (event) =>
    checkoutFailures.inc({ reason: event.reason })
  );
}

reason comes from a small, fixed set defined by the driver (such as timeout or connectionError), so it is a safe label. Utilization is then mongodb_pool_connections_in_use / maxPoolSize, and any increase in mongodb_pool_checkout_failures_total is a saturation error.

docs.title: Recording deploys as change events
docs.text:
Expose the running version as a metric so every graph can be split by release, and post an annotation to Grafana from the deploy pipeline so the deploy appears as a vertical marker on dashboards.

// src/metrics/build-info.js
import client from "prom-client";

new client.Gauge({
  name: "taskflow_build_info",
  help: "Build information; value is always 1",
  labelNames: ["version", "commit"],
}).set({ version: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev", commit: process.env.GIT_SHA ?? "unknown" }, 1);

# deploy step: record the deploy in Grafana (HTTP API, service account token)
curl -sS -X POST "https://grafana.example.com/api/annotations" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $GRAFANA_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d "{\"time\":$(date +%s)000,\"tags\":[\"deploy\",\"taskflow-api\"],\"text\":\"taskflow-api ${APP_VERSION} deployed\"}"

time is in epoch milliseconds. Annotations tagged deploy can then be shown on every dashboard through an annotation query. A query such as count by (version) (taskflow_build_info) then shows how many instances run each version during a rolling deploy.

docs.title: RED and USE queries for the TaskFlow dashboard
docs.text:
# RED: request rate per route
sum by (route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[5m]))

# RED: error ratio (5xx share of all requests)
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
  /
sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[5m]))

# RED: p95 duration per route
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le, route) (rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="taskflow-api"}[5m])))

# USE: event loop lag (seconds) and pool utilization (max pool size 10)
max(nodejs_eventloop_lag_seconds{job="taskflow-api"})
max(mongodb_pool_connections_in_use{job="taskflow-api"}) / 10

These assume the request-duration histogram built in metrics and dashboards; a histogram's _count series doubles as the request counter, so you do not need a separate one.

docs.title: A business counter
docs.text:
Technical health does not prove the product works. A counter for the core action catches failures that return 200 but do nothing:

// src/tasks/metrics.js
import client from "prom-client";

export const tasksCreated = new client.Counter({
  name: "taskflow_tasks_created_total",
  help: "Tasks successfully created",
  labelNames: ["source"], // "web" | "mobile" | "api": a bounded set
});

// in the POST /tasks handler, after the insert succeeds:
// tasksCreated.inc({ source: req.get("x-client") === "mobile" ? "mobile" : "web" });

A sudden drop in rate(taskflow_tasks_created_total[10m]) against the same hour last week is often the first sign of a broken frontend release that server-side error rates never show.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start from the user: define what "working" means for TaskFlow (tasks can be created and listed quickly), measure that first, then add internals.
  • Apply RED to every service and USE to every resource; make all service dashboards look the same.
  • Give every signal the same service.name, service.version, and environment, and put the trace ID in every log line.
  • Keep metric labels bounded; push identifiers into logs and spans.
  • Use histograms and percentiles for latency; never alert on averages.
  • Record deploys and configuration changes as events.
  • Combine black-box probes (is it working for users?) with white-box telemetry (why not?).
  • Monitor the monitoring: alert if Prometheus cannot scrape targets, if log ingestion stops, or if the alerting pipeline itself is down.
  • Review telemetry cost monthly; delete dashboards, metrics, and log fields nobody uses.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• All dashboards are green while users report errors. Detect: support tickets and social media complaints with no matching spike in server metrics; an external probe would show failures. Cause: only white-box telemetry exists, and the failure is outside the application (expired certificate, DNS change, CDN or load balancer misconfiguration). Fix: add black-box probes from several regions against the public URL, and measure SLIs at the edge (load balancer logs), not only inside the app.
  • The metrics backend runs out of memory after a release. Detect: prometheus_tsdb_head_series jumps at the deploy time and Prometheus memory climbs until it restarts. Cause: a new label with unbounded values, such as the raw URL path or a user ID. Fix: label by route template, drop the offending label with metric_relabel_configs, and move the identifier into logs or spans.
  • Average latency looks fine, but users say the app is slow. Detect: p99 latency from the histogram is many times the average, or slow-request logs cluster on certain routes. Cause: averages hide the tail; a few very slow requests (often the biggest customers) disappear in the mean. Fix: chart p50, p95, and p99 from histograms and set SLOs on percentiles or on "fraction of requests faster than X".
  • An incident cannot be traced from a user report to the cause. Detect: engineers grep several services' logs by timestamp and guess. Cause: no request ID or trace ID is propagated and logged. Fix: generate or accept a request ID at the edge, propagate W3C trace context, and log trace_id on every line.
  • Monitoring goes down together with the application. Detect: during a cluster or region outage, dashboards and alerts are also unavailable, so the outage is discovered by users. Cause: Prometheus and Alertmanager run on the same cluster they monitor. Fix: run an external watchdog: an always-firing alert whose absence pages (a "dead man's switch"), plus at least one black-box probe hosted outside your infrastructure.
  • The log bill doubles overnight. Detect: ingestion volume per service jumps after a deploy. Cause: debug logging left on in production, or a log statement inside a hot loop. Fix: set log levels per environment, sample high-volume success logs, and alert on ingestion volume per service.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Telemetry: Data a system emits about its own behaviour.
  • Monitoring: Collecting telemetry and checking it against known conditions, producing dashboards and alerts.
  • Observability: How well you can understand a system's internal state from its outputs, especially for questions you did not plan for.
  • Signal: A category of telemetry: logs, metrics, traces, profiles, events.
  • Cardinality: The number of unique values (or label combinations) a field or metric has.
  • Golden signals: Latency, traffic, errors, and saturation.
  • RED method: Rate, errors, and duration for each service.
  • USE method: Utilization, saturation, and errors for each resource.
  • White-box monitoring: Monitoring from internal telemetry.
  • Black-box monitoring: Testing external behaviour as a user would.
  • Exemplar: A sample trace ID attached to a metric data point, linking the aggregate to a concrete request.
  • Semantic conventions: OpenTelemetry's standard names for attributes such as http.route and service.name.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing observability is a tool you buy. It is a property of the telemetry your code emits; a vendor only stores and queries it.
  • Treating "three pillars" as three separate systems with no links between them. Without shared IDs, you cannot move from a metric spike to the failing request.
  • Measuring only CPU and memory. Users feel errors and latency; resources are causes, not symptoms.
  • Averaging latency, or mixing fast errors with successful requests.
  • Using user IDs, emails, or raw URLs as metric labels.
  • Assuming that more data is always better. Unused telemetry costs money and slows queries.
  • Monitoring from inside the cluster only, so DNS, certificate, and CDN failures are invisible.
  • Never recording deploys, which makes "what changed?" the slowest question in every incident.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the difference between monitoring and observability with an example of a failure that monitoring alone would not explain.
  2. Which signal would you use first to answer "where did the 400 ms go in this request?", and why?
  3. TaskFlow API serves 500 requests per second and writes one 800-byte log line per request. How much log data is that per day, and per 30 days? (Answer: 400 KB/s, about 34.6 GB per day, about 1.04 TB per 30 days.)
  4. Why do metrics costs depend on cardinality rather than traffic, while log costs depend on traffic?
  5. Name the four golden signals and give a TaskFlow measurement for each.
  6. Apply the USE method to a MongoDB connection pool: what are its utilization, saturation, and errors?
  7. Give two failures that only black-box monitoring would catch.
  8. Why should every signal carry service.version?

docs.title: SLIs, SLOs, and Error Budgets
docs.text: "Is TaskFlow reliable enough?" is an argument until you put numbers on it. A service level indicator (SLI) measures one aspect of the service as users experience it, a service level objective (SLO) sets a target for that measurement over a time window, and the error budget is the amount of unreliability the target still allows. This lesson defines SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs, shows how to choose good SLIs, computes the "nines" correctly, works through error budget math, explains error budget policies, and builds the multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts recommended by Google's SRE Workbook, ending with an SLO document for TaskFlow API.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without an agreed target, reliability work is driven by whoever shouts loudest: product wants features, operations wants stability, and every incident triggers a debate about whether things are "bad enough" to slow down. An SLO turns that into a shared, measurable contract inside the team. If the service is meeting its SLO, you ship; if it is burning the budget too fast, you stop and fix reliability. Nobody has to win an argument.

SLOs also fix alerting. Instead of paging on CPU, memory, or every error spike, you page when users are being hurt fast enough to threaten the objective. That single change removes most alert noise, as the next lesson on alerting and on-call shows.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google SRE book. The chapter Service Level Objectives defines SLIs, SLOs, and SLAs, explains why 100% is the wrong target, and recommends choosing a small number of indicators that reflect what users care about.
  • Google SRE Workbook: error budgets in practice. The chapter Implementing SLOs walks through choosing SLIs, measuring them, and using error budgets to make decisions, and the Example Error Budget Policy shows a policy that halts non-critical releases when a service exceeds its budget.
  • Google SRE Workbook: alerting. The chapter Alerting on SLOs compares six alerting approaches and recommends multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts, with a table of burn rates (14.4, 6, and 1) and windows for a 99.9% SLO.
  • Cloud provider SLAs. Public SLAs such as the Amazon Compute Service Level Agreement promise a monthly uptime percentage and define service credits when it is missed, which is the contractual layer that sits on top of internal SLOs.

Popular tools and providers: Prometheus recording and alerting rules, Sloth and Pyrra (generate SLO rules for Prometheus), the OpenSLO specification, Grafana SLO, Datadog SLOs, Google Cloud Service Monitoring, Nobl9, and Amazon CloudWatch Application Signals.

docs.title: SLI, SLO, and SLA
docs.text:
Term What it is Who it is for TaskFlow example SLI (indicator) A measurement, usually a ratio of good events to valid events Engineers Proportion of /tasks requests that return a non-5xx response SLO (objective) A target for an SLI over a window The team and its stakeholders 99.9% of requests succeed over a rolling 30 days SLA (agreement) A contract with consequences, usually money or service credits Customers and lawyers 99.5% monthly availability or a 10% credit Error budget 1 - SLO: how much failure the SLO allows The team, to make decisions 0.1% of requests may fail: about 50,000 of 50 million a month

An SLA should always be looser than the internal SLO. If TaskFlow promises customers 99.5%, the team aims for 99.9% so it notices and reacts long before the contract is at risk. Many internal services have SLOs and no SLA at all.

docs.title: Choosing good SLIs
docs.text:
The SRE books recommend expressing SLIs as a ratio:

SLI = good events / valid events   (x 100%)

Common SLI types:

Type Question TaskFlow SLI Availability Did the request succeed? Non-5xx responses / all API requests (excluding health checks) Latency Was it fast enough? Requests served in under 300 ms / all requests Freshness Is the data recent enough? Reminder emails sent within 5 minutes of the due time / reminders due Correctness Was the answer right? Synthetic task reads that return the expected content / synthetic reads Throughput or coverage Did the batch process everything? Nightly export jobs that complete by 06:00 / jobs scheduled

Guidelines that make SLIs trustworthy:

  • Measure as close to the user as practical. Load balancer or ingress logs and metrics see requests that never reached the app (a crashed pod, a full connection queue). Application metrics miss those. Real-user or synthetic measurements from outside catch DNS and CDN failures too.
  • Define "valid" carefully. Exclude health checks and synthetic traffic you do not want to count. Decide deliberately how to treat 4xx: a 404 for a missing task is the client's problem (good, or not valid), but a 429 caused by your own overloaded rate limiter may well be a failure.
  • Use thresholds, not averages, for latency. "99% of requests faster than 300 ms" is understandable and directly measurable from a histogram bucket at le="0.3". Some teams use two thresholds (p90 under 100 ms and p99 under 500 ms).
  • Few SLIs per user journey. Two or three (availability, latency, maybe freshness) for each critical journey such as "create a task" and "list my tasks". Twenty SLIs is a dashboard, not an objective.

docs.title: SLO targets and the nines
docs.text:
Allowed full-outage time per window:

SLO Error budget Per 30 days (43,200 min) Per year (365 days) 99% 1% 432 min = 7 h 12 min 3.65 days 99.5% 0.5% 216 min = 3 h 36 min 1.83 days 99.9% 0.1% 43.2 min = 43 min 12 s 8.76 hours 99.95% 0.05% 21.6 min = 21 min 36 s 4.38 hours 99.99% 0.01% 4.32 min = 4 min 19 s 52.6 minutes 99.999% 0.001% 0.432 min = 26 s 5.26 minutes

How to compute any row: window length times (1 - SLO). For 99.95% over 30 days: 43,200 min x 0.0005 = 21.6 min.

Choosing a target:

  • Each extra nine costs far more than the last in engineering and infrastructure (the SRE book warns an increment may cost 100x more): redundancy across zones, faster detection, automated rollback, on-call staffing.
  • You cannot be more reliable than your dependencies without redundancy. If TaskFlow depends on a single managed database with a 99.95% SLA and a single region, a 99.99% SLO is fiction.
  • Users cannot tell the difference above a point. Their own Wi-Fi and mobile networks fail more often than 0.01% of the time.
  • Start from current performance. Measure the SLI for a few weeks, set the SLO slightly below what you already achieve, and tighten it as the service improves.
  • Prefer request-based SLOs over time-based ones for APIs: "0.1% of requests may fail" handles partial outages (one bad pod out of ten) better than "the service is up or down each minute".

docs.title: Error budget math
docs.text:
A worked example for TaskFlow API:

SLO: 99.9% of API requests succeed, rolling 30 days
Traffic: ~50,000,000 requests per 30 days (about 19 requests/second on average)

Error budget = 50,000,000 x (1 - 0.999) = 50,000 failed requests

Incident A: full outage for 15 minutes at 20 requests/second
  failed = 15 x 60 x 20 = 18,000            -> 36% of the budget

Incident B: bad deploy, 5% of requests fail for 2 hours at 25 requests/second
  failed = 2 x 3,600 x 25 x 0.05 = 9,000     -> 18% of the budget

Background: 0.02% of requests fail all month
  failed = 50,000,000 x 0.0002 = 10,000      -> 20% of the budget

Total used = 37,000 of 50,000 = 74%; 26% remaining

The burn rate is how fast the budget is being consumed relative to the rate that would use exactly all of it over the window:

burn rate = observed error ratio / (1 - SLO)

0.1% errors on a 99.9% SLO  -> burn rate 1    -> budget lasts exactly 30 days
0.5% errors                 -> burn rate 5    -> budget gone in 30 / 5 = 6 days
1.44% errors                -> burn rate 14.4 -> budget gone in about 2.1 days (50 h)
100% errors (full outage)   -> burn rate 1,000 -> budget gone in about 43 minutes

Burn rate is the bridge between SLOs and alerting: a burn rate of 1 is exactly on budget, anything far above it is an emergency.

docs.title: Error budget policies
docs.text:
An SLO without consequences is a dashboard. An error budget policy is a short, agreed document saying what the team does as the budget runs low. A typical policy for TaskFlow:

Budget remaining (rolling 30 days) Action More than 50% Normal development; experiments and risky migrations allowed 25% to 50% Extra review for risky changes; prioritize reliability bugs from recent incidents Below 25% Freeze non-critical feature releases; only fixes and reliability work ship Exhausted Freeze continues until the SLI is back within the SLO over the window; postmortem required for any single incident using more than 20%

Good policies are agreed in advance by engineering and product leadership, apply automatically (no meeting needed to decide), define exceptions (security fixes always ship), and are reviewed when they do not seem to work. The budget is also permission: with 70% left near the end of the window, the team can afford a risky but valuable migration.

docs.title: Alerting on SLOs: multiwindow, multi-burn-rate
docs.text:
The naive alert "error ratio over 0.1% for 5 minutes" fires on every small blip and resolves before anyone looks. The opposite, "budget below 10%", fires days too late. The SRE Workbook's recommendation is to alert on burn rate, over two windows at once:

  • A long window proves the burn is significant (not a 30-second spike).
  • A short window, one-twelfth of the long one, proves it is still happening, so the alert resolves soon after a fix instead of firing for another hour.

Recommended starting parameters for a 99.9% SLO over 30 days, from the SRE Workbook:

Severity Budget consumed Long window Short window Burn rate Error ratio threshold Page 2% 1 hour 5 minutes 14.4 14.4 x 0.1% = 1.44% Page 5% 6 hours 30 minutes 6 6 x 0.1% = 0.6% Ticket 10% 3 days 6 hours 1 1 x 0.1% = 0.1%

Where 14.4 comes from: 2% of a 30-day budget consumed in 1 hour means burning at 0.02 x 720 hours / 1 hour = 14.4 times the sustainable rate. Likewise 0.05 x 720 / 6 = 6 and 0.10 x 720 / 72 = 1.

Properties of this scheme:

  • Detection time scales with severity. A full outage (100% errors, burn rate 1,000) trips the 1-hour condition after about 0.0144 x 60 min = 52 s; a 2% error ratio takes about 43 minutes; a slow 0.2% leak never pages but opens a ticket within days.
  • Fast reset. The short window drops below the threshold minutes after a fix.
  • Precision. A page always means at least 2% (or 5%) of the monthly budget is being lost, which is worth waking someone for.

Low-traffic services need care: with 20 requests an hour, one failure is a 5% error ratio. Options are synthetic traffic to keep a steady denominator, longer windows, or a minimum count of failed requests before alerting.

docs.title: SLO documents
docs.text: An SLO is written down and versioned, like code. The SRE Workbook's example SLO document includes the service overview, the SLIs and SLOs with their exact measurement, the rationale for each target, the error budget, clarifications and caveats, and links to the error budget policy and dashboards. Keep it in the service's repository and review it at least quarterly.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach User-facing API or website Availability and latency SLOs per critical journey Asynchronous pipeline (reminders, exports) Freshness and completeness SLOs Internal platform used by other teams SLOs agreed with those teams; they are your users Prototype or internal tool with no users yet Skip formal SLOs; basic alerts are enough Hard regulatory or safety guarantees SLOs help operations, but they do not replace formal requirements and testing Contract with customers An SLA, backed by a stricter internal SLO

SLOs are not a tool for ranking teams or punishing incidents, and they do not replace debugging telemetry; they decide when to act, not what is broken.

docs.title: SLI recording rules for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# prometheus/rules/taskflow-slo-recording.yml
groups:
  - name: taskflow-slo-sli
    rules:
      # Availability SLI: share of requests that failed (5xx), per window.
      # Health checks and unmatched routes are not valid events.
      - record: taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[5m]))
      - record: taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate30m
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[30m]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[30m]))
      - record: taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[1h]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[1h]))
      - record: taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate6h
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[6h]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[6h]))
      - record: taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate3d
        expr: |
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[3d]))
          /
          sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[3d]))

      # Latency SLI: share of valid requests slower than 300 ms (bucket boundary at 0.3).
      - record: taskflow:slo_latency_bad:ratio_rate1h
        expr: |
          1 - (
            sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", le="0.3"}[1h]))
            /
            sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[1h]))
          )

Tools such as Sloth or Pyrra generate exactly this kind of rule set from a short SLO definition, which avoids copy-paste mistakes across windows.

docs.title: Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts
docs.text:
# prometheus/rules/taskflow-slo-alerts.yml
groups:
  - name: taskflow-slo-alerts
    rules:
      - alert: TaskflowErrorBudgetBurnFast
        expr: |
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
          and
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "TaskFlow API is burning its 30-day error budget at 14x or more"
          description: "1h error ratio {{ $value | humanizePercentage }}; at this rate 2% of the monthly budget is gone every hour."
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/error-budget-burn"

      - alert: TaskflowErrorBudgetBurnSustained
        expr: |
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
          and
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: page
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "TaskFlow API has burned 5% of its error budget in 6 hours"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/error-budget-burn"

      - alert: TaskflowErrorBudgetBurnSlow
        expr: |
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate3d > (1 * 0.001)
          and
          taskflow:slo_errors:ratio_rate6h > (1 * 0.001)
        labels:
          severity: ticket
          service: taskflow-api
        annotations:
          summary: "TaskFlow API is on track to exhaust its error budget this month"
          runbook_url: "https://runbooks.example.com/taskflow-api/error-budget-burn"

No for: clause is needed: the windows already provide the smoothing, and adding for only delays detection. The severity label is what Alertmanager routes on (pager versus ticket queue), covered in alerting and on-call.

docs.title: Error budget remaining
docs.text:
# Budget remaining over the last 30 days, as a fraction (1 = untouched, 0 = exhausted)
1 - (
  (
    sum(increase(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz", status_code=~"5.."}[30d]))
    /
    sum(increase(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api", route!~"unmatched|/healthz|/readyz"}[30d]))
  ) / 0.001
)

A query over 30 days of raw data is expensive; in production compute it from a recording rule, or from long-term storage such as Mimir or Thanos, and show it as the headline panel on the service dashboard.

docs.title: An SLO document for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
# docs/slo/taskflow-api.yaml (team-owned, reviewed quarterly)
service: taskflow-api
owner: tasks-team
window: rolling 30 days
user_journeys:
  - name: create and list tasks
    endpoints: ["POST /tasks", "GET /tasks", "GET /tasks/:id", "PATCH /tasks/:id"]
slos:
  - name: availability
    sli: share of valid requests that do not return 5xx, measured at the ingress
    valid_events: all API requests except health checks and synthetic probes
    objective: 99.9%
    error_budget: 0.1% of requests (about 50,000 per 30 days at current traffic)
  - name: latency
    sli: share of valid requests served in under 300 ms, measured at the ingress
    objective: 99%
rationale: >
  Current performance over the last quarter is 99.95% availability and 99.4% under
  300 ms. Targets leave headroom for planned migrations. The managed database
  plan's SLA is stricter than 99.9%, so it does not cap these objectives.
alerting: multiwindow multi-burn-rate (14.4 / 6 page, 1 ticket), see taskflow-slo-alerts.yml
error_budget_policy: docs/slo/error-budget-policy.md
dashboard: https://grafana.example.com/d/taskflow-slo
review: quarterly, or after any incident consuming more than 20% of the budget

The format is illustrative; the content follows the structure of the SRE Workbook's example document. The OpenSLO project defines a standard YAML schema for the same information if you want tooling to read it.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write SLIs as good events divided by valid events, measured as close to users as practical.
  • Pick two or three SLIs per critical user journey; leave the rest to dashboards.
  • Set SLOs from measured current performance and real user needs, never 100%, and keep SLAs looser than SLOs.
  • Use request-based SLOs for APIs; time-based ones hide partial failures.
  • Align histogram buckets with latency SLO thresholds.
  • Alert on burn rate with long and short windows; page only for fast burns.
  • Agree an error budget policy in advance with product leadership, and follow it.
  • Version the SLO document with the service and review it regularly.
  • Report budget remaining on the main dashboard and in planning meetings.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The SLO dashboard is green while customers complain. Detect: support tickets and social media reports of errors, while the application-level SLI stays above target. Cause: the SLI is measured in the app, so requests that fail before reaching it (crashed pods, ingress timeouts, DNS or certificate problems) are invisible. Fix: measure at the load balancer or ingress, add synthetic checks from outside, and include those failures in the SLI.
  • The burn-rate page fires every night for a few minutes. Detect: repeated short pages at low-traffic hours, each with a handful of failed requests. Cause: tiny denominators make a few errors look like a high error ratio. Fix: add a minimum event count to the alert, generate steady synthetic traffic, or use longer windows for low-traffic services.
  • The budget is always exhausted, and nothing changes. Detect: budget remaining sits at zero for months while features keep shipping. Cause: an SLO set above what the system can deliver, or no error budget policy with agreed consequences. Fix: reset the target to measured performance, agree a policy with leadership, and invest in the top causes of budget burn.
  • The budget is never touched, and the team is still afraid to deploy. Detect: 95% of the budget remains every month, yet releases are slow and heavily gated. Cause: the SLO is looser than needed, or the team is not using the budget as permission. Fix: spend it deliberately on faster releases and experiments, or tighten the SLO if users need more.
  • Latency SLI values jump when the dashboard is changed from 5m to 1h. Detect: the "requests under 300 ms" ratio looks different across panels and the alert disagrees with the dashboard. Cause: the histogram has no bucket at 0.3 s, so the ratio is interpolated, or panels average ratios instead of dividing summed rates. Fix: add a le="0.3" bucket and compute ratios as sum(rate(good[1h])) / sum(rate(valid[1h])), with the same range for both.
  • A dependency outage burns the whole budget and the team argues about whether it counts. Detect: a postmortem debate over excluding the incident. Cause: the SLO document did not define how dependency failures are treated. Fix: users felt it, so it counts; record the decision in the SLO document and invest in redundancy or graceful degradation for that dependency.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• SLI: A measured indicator of service level, usually good events / valid events.
  • SLO: A target value for an SLI over a time window.
  • SLA: A contract with customers that includes consequences for missing a target.
  • Error budget: 1 - SLO; the allowed amount of failure in the window.
  • Burn rate: Observed error ratio divided by the error budget ratio; 1 means on budget.
  • Rolling window: A window that moves with time (the last 30 days), as opposed to a calendar month.
  • Error budget policy: Agreed actions taken as the budget is consumed.
  • Multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alert: An alert that requires both a long and a short window to exceed a burn-rate threshold, at several severities.
  • The nines: Shorthand for availability levels (three nines = 99.9%).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Targeting 100%, which forbids change and is impossible anyway.
  • Using SLA numbers as internal SLOs, leaving no margin before contractual breaches.
  • Measuring SLIs only inside the app.
  • Averaging latency instead of using thresholds and histograms.
  • Having dozens of SLOs, so none of them drives decisions.
  • Alerting on raw error ratios with a short for: instead of burn rates.
  • Computing nines wrongly: 99.9% is 43 minutes a month, not 4.3, and 99.99% is about 4 minutes, not 43.
  • Defining SLOs and never agreeing what happens when they are missed.
  • Treating error budgets as a quota to be avoided rather than spent.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Explain the difference between an SLI, an SLO, and an SLA with a TaskFlow example of each. Why must the SLA be looser than the SLO?
  2. How much full downtime does a 99.95% SLO allow in 30 days, and in a year? (21 min 36 s; about 4.38 hours.)
  3. TaskFlow serves 80 million requests in 30 days with a 99.9% SLO. How many requests may fail? A 25-minute outage at 40 requests per second uses what share of that budget? (80,000; 25 x 60 x 40 = 60,000, which is 75%.)
  4. The current error ratio is 0.3% on a 99.9% SLO. What is the burn rate, and when will a fresh budget run out? (3; in 10 days.)
  5. Where does the burn-rate threshold 14.4 come from, and why does the alert need both a 1-hour and a 5-minute window?
  6. Why should the availability SLI be measured at the ingress rather than inside the Express app?
  7. Should a 429 Too Many Requests count as a good or bad event? Argue both sides.
  8. What should an error budget policy say, and who must agree to it?

docs.title: Structured Logging
docs.text: A log is a timestamped record of something that happened. A structured log writes that record as data (usually one JSON object per line) instead of a sentence, so machines can filter, group, and join it. This lesson covers log levels, the fields every line needs, correlation IDs that tie a request together across services, a production pino setup for TaskFlow API with request logging and redaction, keeping secrets and personal data out of logs, controlling volume and cost, and the pipeline that carries logs from a container's stdout to a searchable store.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
During an incident, logs are where you go to answer "what exactly happened to this request?". Plain text lines such as Error creating task for user 42 look readable, but you cannot reliably filter them by user, count them by route, or find every line belonging to one request across four services. Every team that grows past one server eventually rewrites its logging to be structured, usually during a painful incident.

Logs are also the most common place for data leaks and runaway costs. One console.log(req.headers) can write every user's session token into a system dozens of people can search, and a debug statement inside a loop can double a logging bill overnight. Good logging is as much about what you leave out as what you put in.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The Twelve-Factor App. The Logs factor says an app should treat logs as event streams and write them, unbuffered, to stdout, leaving routing and storage to the execution environment. This is exactly how container platforms collect logs today.
  • Stripe (canonical log lines). Stripe's engineering post Fast and flexible observability with canonical log lines describes emitting one information-dense line per request at the end of the request, with the key facts (route, status, duration, user, rate limit decisions) as fields, so most questions can be answered by querying a single line type.
  • OWASP. The Logging Cheat Sheet lists which security events to log and which data must never be logged directly (session identifiers, access tokens, passwords, encryption keys, and sensitive personal data), and recommends removing, masking, hashing, or encrypting such data.
  • Grafana Loki. Loki's label best practices explain that Loki indexes only labels, so labels must be few and low cardinality; high-cardinality values such as request IDs belong in the log line itself, where queries can still filter on them.

Popular tools and providers: pino, winston, and Bunyan for Node.js; Fluent Bit, Fluentd, Vector, Logstash, and the OpenTelemetry Collector as agents; Grafana Loki, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Amazon CloudWatch Logs, Google Cloud Logging, Azure Monitor Logs, Datadog, and Splunk as stores.

docs.title: From text lines to structured events
docs.text:
Compare the same event written two ways:

2026-11-13 14:03:12 ERROR Failed to create task for user 42: duplicate key

{"level":"error","time":"2026-11-13T14:03:12.481Z","service":"taskflow-api","env":"production","version":"1.42.0","reqId":"7f3a9c2e-0b1d-4d6e-9a51-2f0c8b6e1d44","trace_id":"4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736","span_id":"00f067aa0ba902b7","userId":"u_42","route":"/tasks","method":"POST","err":{"type":"MongoServerError","message":"E11000 duplicate key error","code":11000},"msg":"failed to create task"}

The text line needs a regular expression for every question, breaks when someone rewords the message, and has no request or trace ID. The JSON line can be filtered with level="error" and route="/tasks", grouped by err.code, and joined to the trace for that request. The message becomes a short, stable description; the variable parts move into fields.

docs.title: Log levels and when to use each
docs.text:
pino uses numeric levels, with names that most loggers share:

Level pino value Use it for TaskFlow example fatal 60 The process cannot continue and is about to exit Cannot connect to MongoDB at startup after retries error 50 A request or job failed and needs attention Unhandled exception in POST /tasks; a job exhausted its retries warn 40 Something unexpected that was handled, or a degraded mode Retrying a timed-out call; serving from a fallback; deprecated API used info 30 Normal, significant events Request completed (one line each); server started; task reminder sent debug 20 Detail for developers diagnosing a problem Query filters used, cache hit or miss trace 10 Very fine-grained flow Entering and leaving functions

Rules that keep levels meaningful:

  • Production runs at info. debug is turned on temporarily, ideally for one service or component, and turned off again.
  • error means someone should look. A 404 for a missing task or a 400 for invalid input is the client's mistake: log it at info or warn on the request line, not as error. Otherwise the error count becomes noise and real failures hide in it.
  • Log an error once, where it is handled. Logging at every layer that rethrows produces five copies of one failure.
  • Level is not severity for alerting. Alerts should come from metrics and SLOs; a spike of error lines is a useful signal, but paging on single log lines creates alert fatigue.

docs.title: The fields every line needs
docs.text:
Field Example Why time 2026-11-13T14:03:12.481Z ISO 8601 in UTC with milliseconds; sortable and timezone-safe level "error" Filtering; a string label is easier to query than 50 service "taskflow-api" Which service wrote it (same value as service.name in traces and metrics) env "production" Never mix staging and production lines by accident version "1.42.0" Did this start with a release? msg "failed to create task" Short, constant description of the event reqId UUID Every line of one request, within and across services trace_id, span_id 32 and 16 hex characters Jump from a log line to the distributed trace Context route, method, status, duration_ms, userId, tenantId The dimensions you will filter by err { type, message, stack, code } Serialized errors, not "[object Object]"

Keep field names consistent across services: if one service writes user_id and another userId, every query has to handle both. Many teams publish a small shared logging package. OpenTelemetry's log data model defines standard top-level fields (timestamp, severity, body, trace and span IDs, resource, and attributes) that collectors can map JSON lines onto.

docs.title: Correlation IDs
docs.text:
A correlation ID is a value attached to everything that happens because of one request, so all of it can be found together.

  • A request ID identifies one inbound HTTP request. It is generated at the edge (ingress or load balancer) or by the first service, returned to the client in an X-Request-Id response header (so a user or support agent can quote it), and passed to downstream calls.
  • A trace ID comes from distributed tracing. It is carried in the W3C traceparent header and covers the whole tree of calls, including asynchronous work. With OpenTelemetry in place, the trace ID can serve as the correlation ID, and the request ID becomes a user-facing handle.

Three details make correlation work in practice:

  1. Propagate on every hop, including message queues: put the IDs in message headers or job metadata so the worker's lines join the same story.
  2. Do not pass the logger through every function. In Node.js, AsyncLocalStorage keeps per-request context available to any code running for that request, including after await.
  3. Treat incoming IDs as untrusted input. Accept an X-Request-Id only if it matches a strict pattern (length and characters), or only from your own edge. Otherwise a client can inject newlines, huge values, or another request's ID into your logs.

docs.title: Never log secrets or personal data
docs.text:
Logs are copied to agents, stores, backups, and laptops, and are readable by far more people than the production database. Treat anything written to a log as widely visible and long-lived.

Never log:

  • Passwords, password reset tokens, API keys, OAuth access and refresh tokens, session cookies, and Authorization headers.
  • Private keys, connection strings with embedded passwords, and webhook signing secrets.
  • Full payment card numbers, CVVs, and bank account numbers.
  • Health or other special-category data, and government identifiers.

Minimize personal data (names, email addresses, phone numbers, IP addresses): log a stable internal user ID (u_42) rather than an email address, and only keep IP addresses if you need them for security, with a short retention period. Privacy laws such as the GDPR treat these as personal data with rules on purpose and retention.

Defend in layers:

  • Do not log whole objects such as req, req.headers, req.body, or third-party error objects. HTTP client errors (for example from axios) often contain the request configuration, including the Authorization header.
  • Redact at the source with the logger's redaction feature (pino's redact option), which replaces values at known paths before serialization.
  • Scrub again in the pipeline with agent rules that mask patterns such as Bearer <token> or card-number-like digit runs.
  • Restrict and audit access to the log store, and set retention deliberately.
  • If a secret leaks, rotate it. Deleting log lines is not enough; copies may already exist in archives and backups.

docs.title: Controlling volume and cost
docs.text:
Logging cost grows with traffic times bytes per request, so small habits compound:

  • Levels per environment: debug locally, info in production.
  • One canonical line per request instead of five lines at each layer.
  • Skip noise: health checks, readiness probes, and metrics scrapes can be thousands of requests an hour per instance; do not log them.
  • Sample successful requests, keep everything else: log all errors, all slow requests, and a fraction of fast 2xx requests.
  • Never log large payloads (full task lists, file contents); log sizes and counts instead.
  • Watch for loops: a log call inside a per-item loop or a retry loop is the classic cause of sudden volume spikes.

Worked example: TaskFlow API at 300 requests per second, 700 bytes per request line.

Before: 300 x 700 B = 210 KB/s = ~18.1 GB/day

After:
  health checks and /metrics scrapes removed: 10% of requests  -> 270 req/s
  errors (1%) and slow requests (2%) always kept: 3% of 270     -> 8.1 req/s
  fast 2xx lines sampled at 10%: 97% of 270 x 0.10             -> 26.2 req/s
  total 34.3 req/s x 700 B = ~24 KB/s = ~2.1 GB/day  (about 88% less)

Request counts and latency are still exact, because they come from metrics, not from counting log lines. Sampling only works if your dashboards do not depend on counting logs.

docs.title: Logging in containers
docs.text:
In containers, the application writes to stdout and stderr and nothing else: no log files, no rotation logic, no shipping code.

  • The container runtime captures the streams. On Kubernetes nodes, logs are written to files under /var/log/pods/, and the kubelet rotates them (its containerLogMaxSize and containerLogMaxFiles settings default to 10 MiB and 5 files). kubectl logs reads those files.
  • Docker's default json-file logging driver does not rotate logs unless you set max-size and max-file; unbounded log files are a classic cause of full disks. Docker's local driver rotates by default.
  • Pretty-printing (for example pino-pretty) is for local development only. In production, emit raw JSON lines and let tools format them.
  • Write logs synchronously or flush on shutdown. If the process crashes with logs still buffered in memory, the most important lines (the ones just before the crash) are lost. pino's default stdout destination is asynchronous; logger.fatal() always flushes synchronously, and pino.destination({ sync: true }) makes every write synchronous.

docs.title: Aggregation pipelines
docs.text:
A typical pipeline has three stages:

  1. Agent on each node (Fluent Bit, Vector, or the OpenTelemetry Collector, usually as a Kubernetes DaemonSet) tails container log files, parses JSON, adds metadata (namespace, pod, container, node), applies redaction and filtering, and buffers on disk so a store outage does not lose data.
  2. Optional aggregator tier (another Vector or Collector deployment, or a queue such as Kafka) for heavy processing, fan-out to several destinations, or absorbing bursts.
  3. Store and query layer that indexes, retains, and searches.
Store Indexing model Strengths Watch out for Grafana Loki Indexes only labels; scans compressed chunks for content Cheap storage on object stores; fits Grafana and Prometheus-style labels High-cardinality labels create too many streams; broad text searches scan a lot of data Elasticsearch / OpenSearch Full-text inverted index of fields Fast, flexible search and aggregations Index size, memory, and cluster operations cost; mapping explosions from inconsistent fields Cloud logging (CloudWatch Logs, Cloud Logging) Managed No servers to run; IAM integration Ingestion and query pricing; per-region and per-account setup

Delivery is normally at least once: the agent retries until the store acknowledges, so occasional duplicates are possible, and a long store outage can fill the agent's buffer. Monitor agent buffer usage and dropped records.

docs.title: Retention and querying
docs.text:
Retention is a cost and compliance decision, set per stream:

  • Hot, searchable: 7 to 30 days for application logs, enough to investigate incidents and recent bugs.
  • Archive: compressed objects in cheaper storage for months or years when audit or regulation requires it, restored to a searchable tier only when needed.
  • Security and audit logs often have longer, legally defined retention and stricter access than application logs.

Example queries for the same question, "show TaskFlow errors on POST /tasks":

# Grafana Loki (LogQL): select streams by label, then parse and filter
{service="taskflow-api", env="production"} | json | level="error" | req_method="POST"

# LogQL metric query: error lines per minute, per environment
sum by (env) (count_over_time({service="taskflow-api"} | json | level="error" [1m]))

# Amazon CloudWatch Logs Insights
fields @timestamp, msg, reqId, trace_id
| filter level = "error" and req.method = "POST"
| sort @timestamp desc
| limit 50

LogQL's json parser flattens nested fields with underscores, so req.method becomes req_method. Use queries like these to investigate; for dashboards and alerts, prefer real metrics, which are cheaper and exact.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
You want to know Use Not What happened to request 7f3a? Logs filtered by request or trace ID Metrics (they are aggregated) How many requests failed in the last hour? A metric counter Counting log lines (sampled, slower, costlier) Which service made the request slow? A trace Comparing timestamps across services' logs Who changed a task's owner, and when? An audit log with its own retention and access rules Debug lines in the application log What did the user send? Log the shape (field names, sizes), not the content Logging req.body

Logs are the right tool for discrete, detailed events and for exploring unanticipated questions. They are the wrong tool for counting, alerting on rates, or storing business records: a log store is not a database or an audit system unless it is designed and retained as one.

docs.title: A production pino logger
docs.text:
// src/logger.js
import pino from "pino";

const isProd = process.env.NODE_ENV === "production";

export const logger = pino({
  level: process.env.LOG_LEVEL ?? (isProd ? "info" : "debug"),
  // Fields added to every line. Replaces pino's default pid and hostname;
  // the log agent adds pod and node metadata instead.
  base: {
    service: "taskflow-api",
    env: process.env.NODE_ENV ?? "development",
    version: process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev",
  },
  timestamp: pino.stdTimeFunctions.isoTime, // "time":"2026-11-13T14:03:12.481Z"
  formatters: {
    level(label) {
      return { level: label }; // "error" instead of 50
    },
  },
  redact: {
    paths: [
      "req.headers.authorization",
      "req.headers.cookie",
      'res.headers["set-cookie"]',
      "password",
      "token",
      "*.password",
      "*.token",
      "*.refreshToken",
    ],
    censor: "[REDACTED]",
  },
});

redact paths use dot notation with wildcards; *.password matches a password key one level down in any logged object, such as { body: { password } }, so top-level keys (password, token) are listed separately. Redaction is a safety net for known paths, not a licence to log whole objects.

docs.title: Request logging with request IDs and request context
docs.text:
// src/http-logger.js
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { AsyncLocalStorage } from "node:async_hooks";
import pinoHttp from "pino-http";
import { logger } from "./logger.js";

const SAFE_ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,64}$/;
const SKIP = new Set(["/healthz", "/readyz", "/metrics"]);
const context = new AsyncLocalStorage();

export const httpLogger = pinoHttp({
  logger,
  quietReqLogger: true, // req.log binds only reqId, not the whole request
  genReqId(req, res) {
    const incoming = req.headers["x-request-id"];
    const id = typeof incoming === "string" && SAFE_ID.test(incoming) ? incoming : randomUUID();
    res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", id);
    return id;
  },
  customLogLevel(req, res, err) {
    if (err || res.statusCode >= 500) return "error";
    if (res.statusCode >= 400) return "warn";
    return "info";
  },
  autoLogging: { ignore: (req) => SKIP.has(req.url) },
});

// Makes the request's child logger available to any code running for it.
export function requestContext(req, res, next) {
  context.run({ log: req.log, requestId: req.id }, next);
}

export function getLog() {
  return context.getStore()?.log ?? logger;
}

export function getRequestId() {
  return context.getStore()?.requestId;
}

// src/app.js
import express from "express";
import { httpLogger, requestContext } from "./http-logger.js";
import { tasksRouter } from "./tasks/router.js";

export const app = express();
app.use(httpLogger);      // first, so every request gets an ID and a completion line
app.use(requestContext);
app.use(express.json());
app.use("/tasks", tasksRouter);

// Error handler: attach the error to the request's completion line
// instead of logging a second, separate line.
app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  res.err = err;
  res.status(500).json({ error: "Internal Server Error", requestId: req.id });
});

// src/tasks/service.js: no logger parameter needed
import { getLog } from "../http-logger.js";

export async function createTask(db, userId, input) {
  const result = await db.collection("tasks").insertOne({ ...input, userId, createdAt: new Date() });
  getLog().info({ taskId: result.insertedId.toString(), userId }, "task created");
  return result.insertedId;
}

pino-http writes one completion line per request with reqId, the serialized request (method, URL, headers after redaction) and response (status), and responseTime in milliseconds. Returning requestId in the error body lets a user quote it to support. When the OpenTelemetry Node.js auto-instrumentation is loaded (see distributed tracing), its pino instrumentation adds trace_id, span_id, and trace_flags to every line written while a span is active, with no code changes.

docs.title: Propagating the request ID downstream
docs.text:
Outgoing fetch calls get the traceparent header automatically from the OpenTelemetry instrumentation; the request ID is passed explicitly.

// src/clients/notifications.js
import { getRequestId, getLog } from "../http-logger.js";

export async function scheduleReminder(task) {
  const requestId = getRequestId();
  const res = await fetch("https://notifications.internal.example.com/reminders", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: {
      "content-type": "application/json",
      ...(requestId ? { "x-request-id": requestId } : {}),
    },
    body: JSON.stringify({ taskId: task.id, dueAt: task.dueAt }),
    signal: AbortSignal.timeout(2000),
  });
  if (!res.ok) {
    // Log the status, not the response body or the request headers.
    getLog().warn({ status: res.status, taskId: task.id }, "reminder scheduling failed");
  }
}

For queue jobs, store the request ID in the job's data or message headers and bind it to the worker's child logger: logger.child({ reqId: job.data.requestId, jobId: job.id }).

docs.title: Shipping logs with Vector on Kubernetes
docs.text:
# vector.yaml (agent running as a DaemonSet)
sources:
  k8s:
    type: kubernetes_logs

transforms:
  parse:
    type: remap
    inputs: [k8s]
    source: |
      parsed, err = parse_json(.message)
      if err == null && is_object(parsed) {
        . = merge(., object!(parsed))
        del(.message)
      }
      # Label values must exist for every event, including non-JSON lines.
      if !exists(.service) { .service = "unknown" }
      if !exists(.env) { .env = "unknown" }
      # Second line of defence: mask bearer tokens that slipped through.
      if exists(.msg) {
        .msg = replace(string!(.msg), r'Bearer [A-Za-z0-9._~+/=-]+', "Bearer [REDACTED]")
      }

  drop_debug:
    type: filter
    inputs: [parse]
    condition: '.level != "debug" && .level != "trace"'

sinks:
  loki:
    type: loki
    inputs: [drop_debug]
    endpoint: http://loki.monitoring.svc.cluster.local:3100
    encoding:
      codec: json
    labels:
      namespace: "{{ kubernetes.pod_namespace }}"
      container: "{{ kubernetes.container_name }}"
      service: "{{ service }}"
      env: "{{ env }}"

Parts: the kubernetes_logs source tails node log files and attaches pod metadata; the remap transform (Vector Remap Language) parses the JSON line into fields and masks tokens; the filter drops debug lines; the Loki sink uses only bounded values (namespace, container, service, environment) as labels. reqId and trace_id stay inside the line, queryable with | json | trace_id="...".

docs.title: Bounded Docker logs on a single host
docs.text:
# compose.yaml
services:
  api:
    image: ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:1.42.0
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      LOG_LEVEL: info
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options:
        max-size: "10m"
        max-file: "5"

Without max-size, the json-file driver keeps one ever-growing file per container until the disk fills.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Log JSON to stdout, one event per line, with ISO 8601 UTC timestamps.
  • Use a short, constant msg and put variable data in fields.
  • Include service, env, version, reqId, and trace_id on every line, with the same names in every service.
  • Write one canonical completion line per request; log errors once, where they are handled.
  • Validate incoming request IDs; generate one when missing; return it in X-Request-Id.
  • Never log secrets; minimize personal data; redact at the source and in the pipeline; rotate anything that leaks.
  • Run production at info; skip health-check noise; sample fast successes but keep all errors and slow requests.
  • Keep log store labels low-cardinality; keep identifiers in the line.
  • Set retention per stream and restrict access to the log store.
  • Count and alert with metrics; use logs to explain.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• An access token appears in the log store. Detect: a secret-scanning rule on the log pipeline, or someone noticing Authorization values in search results. Cause: a handler logged a raw HTTP client error or req.headers, bypassing redaction paths. Fix: rotate the exposed credentials, purge affected streams where possible, log only selected fields from errors, and add pipeline masking rules plus a test that asserts redaction.
  • The last lines before a crash are missing. Detect: the container restarted with an uncaught exception, but the log ends seconds earlier with nothing explaining it. Cause: logs were buffered asynchronously in-process and lost when the process died, or the crash happened before the logger was configured. Fix: write to stdout synchronously, flush on shutdown signals, and register uncaughtException handlers that log with logger.fatal() (which pino writes synchronously) before exiting.
  • Loki queries time out and ingestion is throttled. Detect: Loki reports a very high number of active streams, and queries touching a few hours fail. Cause: a high-cardinality label such as reqId, userId, or the raw path was added in the agent config. Fix: remove the label, keep the value in the log line, and filter with | json | reqId="...".
  • A node runs out of disk space. Detect: disk usage alerts; du shows huge files under /var/lib/docker/containers/. Cause: the json-file driver without max-size, plus a chatty container. Fix: set rotation options (or use the local driver), lower the log level, and find the noisy source.
  • Stack traces arrive as dozens of separate entries. Detect: in the log UI, each line of a stack trace is its own event, out of order with other lines. Cause: plain-text logging (console.error(err)) writes multi-line output. Fix: log errors through the JSON logger so the stack is one escaped string field.
  • Logs from different services cannot be correlated. Detect: investigations rely on matching timestamps by eye. Cause: services use different ID fields, or the ID is not forwarded to downstream calls and queue messages. Fix: adopt a shared logging package with standard field names and propagate IDs on every hop.
  • Log timestamps from two services disagree by minutes. Detect: a downstream service appears to log a call before the caller made it. Cause: local-time strings without offsets, or clock drift on a host without time synchronization. Fix: log UTC ISO 8601 times and run NTP or chrony on every host.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Structured log: A log record written as data with named fields, usually JSON.
  • Log level: The importance of a record (fatal to trace), used for filtering.
  • Correlation ID: A value attached to all work caused by one request.
  • Request ID: A per-request correlation ID, often returned in X-Request-Id.
  • Canonical log line: One information-dense line per request summarizing it.
  • Redaction: Replacing sensitive values before they are written.
  • Log agent / shipper: A process that collects, processes, and forwards logs (Fluent Bit, Vector).
  • Stream (Loki): A unique set of labels; each stream is stored and indexed separately.
  • Retention: How long logs are kept before deletion.
  • Sampling: Keeping only a fraction of similar records to reduce volume.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Logging sentences with values embedded instead of fields.
  • console.log of whole objects such as req, req.body, or error objects from HTTP clients.
  • Logging client errors (400, 404) at error level.
  • Logging the same error at every layer that rethrows it.
  • Thinking redaction makes it safe to log everything.
  • Using the log store for counting and alerting that metrics should do.
  • Putting request IDs or user IDs into Loki labels or Elasticsearch index names.
  • Writing log files inside containers instead of to stdout.
  • Leaving debug on in production after an investigation.
  • Trusting client-supplied request IDs without validation.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Rewrite the line User 42 failed login from 203.0.113.9 with password hunter2 as a safe structured log entry. What do you remove, and why?
  2. When should a failed request be logged at warn rather than error?
  3. What is the difference between a request ID and a trace ID, and when would you keep both?
  4. How does AsyncLocalStorage help with request-scoped logging in Express?
  5. A service at 400 requests per second logs 900 bytes per request. Health checks are 20% of requests. If you drop health-check logs and sample fast successes (95% of the remaining requests) at 10%, keeping everything else, what is the daily volume before and after? (Before: about 31.1 GB/day. After: 320 req/s, of which 16 are kept in full and 304 are sampled to 30.4, so 46.4 req/s, about 3.6 GB/day.)
  6. Why should high-cardinality values not be Loki labels, and how do you still query them?
  7. Why must applications in containers log to stdout, and what rotates the logs?
  8. A token leaked into the logs. Why is deleting the log lines not enough?
