docs.title: Chaos Engineering and Game Days
docs.text:
A load test proves the system is fast enough while everything works. Chaos engineering asks the next question: what happens when parts of it fail? It runs controlled experiments that inject real faults (a killed instance, a slow dependency, a lost zone) and checks whether users still get what they need. A game day rehearses the human side: the people who would handle the failure practise detecting, diagnosing, and recovering from it while everyone is awake and watching.

This lesson covers the principles of chaos engineering, steady state and hypotheses, blast radius and safety controls, which faults to inject and the tools that inject them (Chaos Monkey, AWS Fault Injection Service, Gremlin, LitmusChaos, Chaos Mesh, Toxiproxy, and others), how to start small, how to run a game day, and what to do with the findings. The patterns that experiments verify (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, load shedding) are explained in resilience patterns across servers, and restore and failover drills for data in restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Resilience features are code paths that run only when something fails: the timeout that fires, the retry that backs off, the failover that promotes a replica, the autoscaling that replaces an instance. Code that rarely runs rots quietly. A configuration change disables a health check, a new dependency is added without a timeout, a runbook refers to a dashboard that no longer exists, and nobody finds out until the real failure, usually at night.

Distributed systems also fail in combinations nobody designed for: a slow dependency fills a connection pool, which fails health checks, which removes healthy instances from the load balancer. Experiments surface these interactions in daylight, with a small blast radius and people ready to stop. And because incidents are handled by people, practising the response is as important as testing the software.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Principles of Chaos Engineering. The community statement at principlesofchaos.org defines chaos engineering as "the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production", and describes the experiment: define steady state as a measurable output, hypothesize that it continues in a control and an experimental group, introduce real-world events, and try to disprove the hypothesis. Its advanced principles add running in production, automating experiments, and minimizing the blast radius.
  • Netflix. Chaos Monkey "randomly terminates virtual machine instances and containers that run inside of your production environment", so that engineers build services that survive it; it requires the Spinnaker delivery platform. It was part of the Simian Army (2011), whose repository was archived in 2021; Chaos Monkey now lives on as a standalone service. Netflix later described its Chaos Automation Platform in A Platform for Automating Chaos Experiments, which runs failure-injection experiments in production to verify that failures in non-critical services do not cause outages. How Netflix's wider architecture is built is covered in how top companies run at scale.
  • Google DiRT. In Building resilient systems to weather the unexpected (2020), Google's Ben Treynor Sloss describes Disaster Recovery Testing (DiRT), "a regular, coordinated set of both real and fictitious incidents and outages across the company", that tests "everything from our technical systems to processes and people". It uses capacity that is not needed at the time, and stops a test before that capacity is needed if engineers cannot find the fix quickly.
  • AWS Well-Architected. The Reliability Pillar's REL12-BP04 Test resiliency using chaos engineering gives a hypothesis template, recommends stop conditions as guardrails and running experiments as part of CI/CD, and warns not to run an experiment you already know will fail; REL12-BP05 Conduct game days regularly lists anti-patterns such as documenting procedures but never exercising them.
  • Shopify. The Toxiproxy README says Shopify has used it "in all development and test environments" since October 2014, to prove with tests that applications do not have single points of failure.

Popular tools and providers: Netflix Chaos Monkey, AWS Fault Injection Service, Azure Chaos Studio, Gremlin, LitmusChaos, Chaos Mesh, Chaos Toolkit, and Toxiproxy.

docs.title: The principles in practice
docs.text: Principle What it means for TaskFlow API Build a hypothesis around steady state Define "working" as user-visible outputs: task creation success rate, p99 of GET /tasks, not CPU or pod counts Vary real-world events Inject what actually happens: instances die, MongoDB elects a new primary, the notification service slows down, a zone degrades Run experiments in production The real system is the only fully accurate test bed, but only after the same experiment has passed in lower environments Automate experiments to run continuously An experiment that passed becomes a regression test in CI or a scheduled job Minimize the blast radius One pod, one instance, 1% of traffic, a few minutes, with an abort that works

docs.title: Steady state and the hypothesis
docs.text:
Steady state is a measurable output that shows the system is healthy from the user's point of view, usually an SLI from SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets: request success rate, a latency percentile, tasks saved per minute. Measure it before the experiment; if the system is not in steady state, do not start.

A hypothesis says what will happen and why, and must be falsifiable. AWS's template works well: If [specific fault] occurs, the [workload] will [mitigation] to maintain [business or technical metric]. For TaskFlow:

  • If one of three API instances is terminated, the load balancer stops routing to it within 30 seconds and the Auto Scaling group replaces it, so the 5xx rate rises by less than 0.1 percentage points.
  • If the notification service responds 3 seconds slower, POST /tasks still succeeds in under 1 second, because the call has a 300 ms timeout and failed notifications are retried later.
  • If the MongoDB primary steps down, writes fail for less than 20 seconds and the driver's retryable writes absorb most of them.

An experiment either supports the hypothesis (confidence grows) or disproves it (you found a weakness, which is the valuable outcome). Experiments you already expect to fail are not experiments: fix the known weakness first.

docs.title: Blast radius and safety controls
docs.text:
The blast radius is how much of the system, and how many users, an experiment can affect. Keep it small and make it smaller when in doubt:

  • Where: a local test, then a staging or performance environment, then production.
  • What: one pod or instance, a small percentage of traffic, one zone; never everything at once.
  • How long: minutes, with the fault removed automatically at the end (Toxiproxy toxics are removed by the test, Chaos Mesh faults have a duration, FIS actions restart or replace what they stopped).
  • Stop conditions: automatic guardrails that end the experiment when a metric crosses a threshold. AWS FIS ties them to CloudWatch alarms (up to five per experiment template); in other tools, an alert on the steady-state metric plus a person with a tested abort command.
  • When: working hours, off-peak, with the owning team watching and support informed; never during an incident or a release freeze.
  • Rollback: know how to restore the system to a known-good state, and check it is there at the end.

docs.title: What to inject
docs.text:
Choose faults from your own history (postmortems, near misses) and from the dependencies on your architecture diagram, ranked by how often they happen and how much they would hurt.

Fault Real event it models What it verifies Typical tools Kill an instance, container, or pod Hardware failure, OOM kill, a bad node Redundancy, health checks, rescheduling, graceful shutdown Chaos Monkey, FIS (aws:ec2:terminate-instances, aws:eks:pod-delete), Chaos Mesh PodChaos Add latency to a dependency A slow database, network congestion, a struggling service Timeouts, connection pools, bulkheads, user-facing fallbacks Toxiproxy latency, Chaos Mesh NetworkChaos, FIS network-latency actions for ECS and EKS Make a dependency unavailable or reset connections A crashed service, a firewall change Fallbacks, circuit breakers, retries with backoff, error messages Toxiproxy down, reset_peer, timeout; Chaos Mesh partition Drop packets A flaky network Retries, idempotency Toxiproxy packet_loss, Chaos Mesh loss Stress CPU or memory Noisy neighbours, a runaway process Autoscaling, resource limits, load shedding FIS CPU stress through Systems Manager, Chaos Mesh StressChaos, LitmusChaos pod-cpu-hog Throttle cloud API calls Provider throttling during an event Backoff in automation and SDK calls FIS aws:fis:inject-api-throttle-error Fail over the database A primary crash or maintenance Driver reconnection, retryable writes, timeouts FIS RDS and Aurora failover actions; rs.stepDown() on a MongoDB replica set in staging Lose a zone A data-centre or power event Capacity in the remaining zones, failover runbooks Several faults combined in one experiment, as a game day

docs.title: Tools
docs.text:
Tool What it is Where it injects Status in November 2026 Chaos Monkey Netflix's open-source instance and container killer Production fleets managed with Spinnaker Open source, lifecycle marked active; requires Spinnaker AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS) Managed service: experiment templates with actions, targets, and stop conditions EC2, ECS, EKS, RDS, networking, API faults; can run Chaos Mesh and Litmus resources on EKS Generally available; renamed from AWS Fault Injection Simulator in 2023 Azure Chaos Studio Managed chaos service for Azure Service-direct and agent-based faults; Scenarios such as a zone outage Workspaces and Scenarios in public preview, replacing classic Experiments Gremlin Commercial reliability platform Services, hosts, and containers; Failure Flags for application-level and serverless faults Commercial, with reliability scoring and GameDays LitmusChaos Kubernetes-native chaos platform with a hub of experiments Pods, nodes, applications in Kubernetes CNCF incubating project since January 2022 Chaos Mesh Kubernetes chaos platform driven by custom resources PodChaos, NetworkChaos, StressChaos, and more CNCF incubating project since February 2022 Toxiproxy A TCP proxy controlled over HTTP, built for tests Any TCP connection your code makes (databases, caches, HTTP services) Open source (MIT) from Shopify; release 2.13.0 added optional API tokens

For a team on one cloud account, the managed service of that cloud is the easiest start; for Kubernetes, LitmusChaos or Chaos Mesh; for code-level and CI experiments, Toxiproxy. Costs follow the same split: open-source tools are the cheapest to adopt but cost the time to run and secure them; a managed service such as AWS FIS bills for the minutes its actions run, so short, targeted experiments stay cheap; commercial platforms add a subscription on top, which buys support, a fault catalogue, and safety features.

docs.title: Starting small
docs.text:
A sensible order for a team that has never done this:

  1. Tabletop exercise. Walk through "the notification service is down" on paper with the people who would respond. It costs an hour and finds gaps in alerts and runbooks.
  2. Fault-injection tests in CI. Toxiproxy in integration tests proves that timeouts and fallbacks behave as designed, on every build.
  3. Experiments in a performance environment under load. Combine a k6 load test with pod kills or network delay; this is where most surprises appear (see load testing with k6).
  4. A game day in staging, then production, with stop conditions and a tested abort.
  5. Automate the experiments that passed and run them on a schedule or with releases, widening the scope slowly.

docs.title: Game days
docs.text:
A game day is a planned exercise in which a team injects a failure into a real system and practises the full response. It tests what automated experiments cannot: whether alerts reach the right person, whether dashboards answer the questions people ask, whether the runbook works when followed by someone who did not write it, and whether communication with stakeholders happens.

Good game days share a few traits:

  • A written plan: scenario, hypothesis, success criteria, blast radius, abort conditions, and who does what.
  • Real roles: the facilitator injects and can abort; the operators are the people normally on call, not the system's authors; a scribe records timestamps (time to detect, time to mitigate) for the review.
  • Announced, not secret, at least for the first ones; surprise drills come later, when the basics work.
  • A blameless review within a week, using the same format as an incident postmortem (see incident response and postmortems).

Data-recovery drills (restoring a database to a point in time, failing over to another region) follow the same format and are covered in restore testing and runbooks.

docs.title: What to do with findings
docs.text:
An experiment or game day is wasted if nothing changes afterwards:

  • Record the outcome: hypothesis supported or disproved, with the evidence (graphs, timestamps, logs).
  • Turn every weakness into a tracked action with an owner and a date: a missing timeout, an alert that did not fire, a runbook step that was wrong, a dashboard that was missing.
  • Re-run the experiment after the fix, then automate it so the weakness cannot return unnoticed.
  • Update runbooks, alerts, and dashboards with what the responders actually needed.
  • Share the results beyond the team; other services often have the same weakness.
  • Track coverage over time: which critical dependencies and failure modes have a passing experiment, and how recently.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach A new dependency or resilience pattern (timeout, fallback, retry) A Toxiproxy test in CI Before a big launch or seasonal peak A game day in the performance environment under a k6 load After a major architecture change (new region, new database) Experiments in staging, then a production game day Mature service with SLOs, good observability, tested aborts Small automated experiments in production On-call team new to a service A tabletop exercise, then a game day

Do not run chaos experiments (yet) when:

  • There is no monitoring that shows steady state; you could not tell whether the experiment hurt users. Fix observability first.
  • You already know the system will fail; fix the known weakness instead.
  • The system has a single point of failure by design; an experiment only causes an outage.
  • An incident is in progress, a release freeze is on, or the owning team is unavailable.
  • There is no stop condition or rollback you have tested.

docs.title: An experiment card
docs.text:
Experiment:   Slow notification service, TaskFlow API (staging)
Owner:        TaskFlow team; facilitator on duty this week
Steady state: POST /tasks success rate > 99.9%, p95 < 300 ms (k6 at 120 requests/s)
Hypothesis:   If the notification service responds 3 s slower, POST /tasks still
              succeeds in under 1 s, because the call has a 300 ms timeout and
              deferred notifications are retried later.
Fault:        Toxiproxy latency toxic, 3000 ms, on the notifications proxy
Blast radius: staging only; one service; 10 minutes
Stop if:      POST /tasks success rate < 99% for 1 minute, or p95 > 2 s
Abort:        toxiproxy-cli toxic remove --toxicName latency_downstream notifications
Result:       (filled in afterwards: supported or disproved, with graphs and timestamps)
Follow-ups:   (actions with owners and dates)

docs.title: A non-critical call with a timeout and a fallback
docs.text:
The hypothesis above depends on code like this:

// src/notifications.js: a non-critical call with a short timeout and a fallback
const NOTIFY_URL = process.env.NOTIFY_URL ?? "http://localhost:4000/notifications";

export async function notifyTaskCreated(task, { timeoutMs = 300, log = console } = {}) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(NOTIFY_URL, {
      method: "POST",
      headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
      body: JSON.stringify({ type: "task.created", taskId: task.id }),
      signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs), // never wait longer than this
    });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`notification service returned ${res.status}`);
    return "sent";
  } catch (err) {
    // Non-critical: the task is already saved; a background job retries deferred notifications.
    log.warn({ err: err.message, taskId: task.id }, "notification deferred");
    return "deferred";
  }
}

AbortSignal.timeout() bounds the wait, and the catch turns any failure (a timeout, a refused connection, a 5xx) into a logged, deferred notification instead of a failed request. A more robust design writes the notification to a queue or an outbox in the same transaction as the task (see messaging fundamentals); the experiment is what tells you whether the simpler version is enough.

docs.title: A chaos test with Toxiproxy
docs.text:
Toxiproxy sits between the API and the notification service. The API is started with NOTIFY_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4100/notifications, the proxy listens on port 4100 and forwards to the real service on port 4000, and the test changes the network between them through Toxiproxy's HTTP API on port 8474:

// test/chaos/notifications.test.js: creating a task survives a slow or dead notification service
import { test, before, after } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";

const TOXIPROXY = process.env.TOXIPROXY_URL ?? "http://localhost:8474";
const API = process.env.BASE_URL ?? "http://localhost:3000";

async function toxiproxy(path, method = "GET", body) {
  const res = await fetch(`${TOXIPROXY}${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
    body: body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(body),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`toxiproxy ${method} ${path}: HTTP ${res.status} ${await res.text()}`);
  return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json();
}

async function createTask(title) {
  const started = performance.now();
  const res = await fetch(`${API}/tasks`, {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "content-type": "application/json", authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.API_TOKEN}` },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
  });
  await res.arrayBuffer(); // read the body so the timing includes it
  return { status: res.status, ms: performance.now() - started };
}

before(async () => {
  // The API under test runs with NOTIFY_URL=http://127.0.0.1:4100/notifications.
  await toxiproxy("/populate", "POST", [
    { name: "notifications", listen: "127.0.0.1:4100", upstream: "127.0.0.1:4000" },
  ]);
});

after(async () => {
  await toxiproxy("/reset", "POST"); // remove every toxic and re-enable every proxy
});

test("steady state: a task is created in under 500 ms", async () => {
  const { status, ms } = await createTask("steady state");
  assert.equal(status, 201);
  assert.ok(ms < 500, `took ${ms.toFixed(0)} ms`);
});

test("notification service 3 s slower: still created in under 1 s", async () => {
  await toxiproxy("/proxies/notifications/toxics", "POST", {
    name: "slow_notifications",
    type: "latency",
    stream: "downstream",
    attributes: { latency: 3000 },
  });
  try {
    const { status, ms } = await createTask("slow dependency");
    assert.equal(status, 201);
    assert.ok(ms < 1000, `took ${ms.toFixed(0)} ms`);
  } finally {
    await toxiproxy("/proxies/notifications/toxics/slow_notifications", "DELETE");
  }
});

test("notification service down: still created", async () => {
  await toxiproxy("/proxies/notifications", "PATCH", { enabled: false });
  try {
    const { status } = await createTask("dependency down");
    assert.equal(status, 201);
  } finally {
    await toxiproxy("/proxies/notifications", "PATCH", { enabled: true });
  }
});

$ node --test test/chaos/
✔ steady state: a task is created in under 500 ms (64.3956ms)
✔ notification service 3 s slower: still created in under 1 s (366.6143ms)
✔ notification service down: still created (46.5578ms)
ℹ tests 3
ℹ pass 3
ℹ fail 0

The output is from a local run against a stand-in API that uses the notifyTaskCreated() function above: with 3 seconds of injected latency the task was still created in about 370 ms, which is the 300 ms timeout plus normal work. Details worth copying:

  • /populate creates the proxy, or leaves it alone if it already exists with the same addresses, so the test can run repeatedly.
  • A latency toxic on the downstream stream delays the service's responses; one on upstream delays requests.
  • Proxy updates use PATCH: Toxiproxy 2.13 logs that updating a proxy with POST is deprecated.
  • finally blocks and POST /reset remove the faults even when an assertion fails, so one failed test does not poison the next.
  • The Toxiproxy API is unauthenticated by default and can proxy to any address: keep it on localhost or a private test network, or start it with TOXIPROXY_AUTH_TOKEN set.

docs.title: Exploring by hand with toxiproxy-cli
docs.text:
toxiproxy-server &                      # API on localhost:8474
toxiproxy-cli create --listen localhost:4100 --upstream localhost:4000 notifications
toxiproxy-cli toxic add --type latency --attribute latency=1000 notifications
toxiproxy-cli inspect notifications     # shows latency_downstream, latency=1000
toxiproxy-cli toxic remove --toxicName latency_downstream notifications
toxiproxy-cli toggle notifications      # disabled: new connections are refused
toxiproxy-cli toggle notifications      # enabled again

A toxic added without --toxicName is named <type>_<stream>, here latency_downstream; a toxic is applied to the downstream stream unless you pass --upstream. In a local check, a request through the proxy took about 1,035 ms with the 1,000 ms latency toxic, and a disabled proxy refused connections outright, which is how a crashed service looks to its callers.

docs.title: Kubernetes: Chaos Mesh experiments for TaskFlow
docs.text:
# k8s/chaos/taskflow-api-pod-kill.yaml: kill one TaskFlow API pod
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: PodChaos
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-pod-kill
  namespace: taskflow-staging
spec:
  action: pod-kill
  mode: one                         # one random pod that matches the selector
  selector:
    namespaces:
      - taskflow-staging
    labelSelectors:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api

# k8s/chaos/taskflow-mongodb-delay.yaml: 200 ms extra latency from the API to MongoDB for 5 minutes
apiVersion: chaos-mesh.org/v1alpha1
kind: NetworkChaos
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api-mongodb-delay
  namespace: taskflow-staging
spec:
  action: delay
  mode: all
  selector:
    namespaces:
      - taskflow-staging
    labelSelectors:
      app.kubernetes.io/name: taskflow-api
  direction: to
  target:
    mode: all
    selector:
      namespaces:
        - taskflow-staging
      labelSelectors:
        app.kubernetes.io/name: mongodb
  delay:
    latency: "200ms"
    jitter: "50ms"
    correlation: "25"
  duration: "5m"

kubectl apply -f starts an experiment and kubectl delete -f ends it early. mode chooses how many matching pods are affected (one, all, fixed, fixed-percent, or random-max-percent), and direction with target limits the delay to traffic between the API and the database. For a database outside the cluster, such as a managed MongoDB service, externalTargets takes IP addresses or domain names instead of a pod target. The pod kill expects the Deployment's other replicas, readiness probes, and graceful shutdown (see health probes and rolling updates) to keep the 5xx rate flat.

docs.title: AWS: a Fault Injection Service experiment
docs.text:
An experiment template for TaskFlow's EC2 fleet, saved as fis/taskflow-terminate-one-instance.json. It terminates one running API instance in one zone and stops automatically if the 5xx alarm goes off:

{
  "description": "Terminate one TaskFlow API instance in us-east-1a; the Auto Scaling group should replace it",
  "targets": {
    "taskflowApi": {
      "resourceType": "aws:ec2:instance",
      "resourceTags": { "app": "taskflow-api", "env": "production" },
      "filters": [
        { "path": "Placement.AvailabilityZone", "values": ["us-east-1a"] },
        { "path": "State.Name", "values": ["running"] }
      ],
      "selectionMode": "COUNT(1)"
    }
  },
  "actions": {
    "terminateOneInstance": {
      "actionId": "aws:ec2:terminate-instances",
      "description": "lose one API instance",
      "targets": { "Instances": "taskflowApi" }
    }
  },
  "stopConditions": [
    {
      "source": "aws:cloudwatch:alarm",
      "value": "arn:aws:cloudwatch:us-east-1:111122223333:alarm:taskflow-api-5xx-rate"
    }
  ],
  "roleArn": "arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/fis-taskflow-experiments",
  "tags": { "Name": "taskflow-terminate-one-instance" }
}

aws fis create-experiment-template --cli-input-json file://fis/taskflow-terminate-one-instance.json
aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id <template-id>
aws fis get-experiment --id <experiment-id>    # state: initiating, running, completed, stopped, failed ...
aws fis stop-experiment --id <experiment-id>   # the manual abort switch

The template follows the shape of AWS's own examples: targets found by tags and filters, selectionMode to limit them (COUNT(1), PERCENT(25), or ALL), actions that reference targets by name, and CloudWatch alarms as stop conditions. The IAM role in roleArn must allow FIS to terminate instances, and nothing else; keep it as narrow as the experiment. Account 111122223333 is the placeholder AWS uses in its documentation.

docs.title: A game day plan
docs.text:
Game day:     TaskFlow API loses a zone (staging), Thursday 14:00-16:00 UTC
Scenario:     Terminate every API instance in one of three zones; MongoDB primary unaffected
Hypothesis:   Requests keep succeeding (5xx < 1% for at most 2 minutes) because the load
              balancer routes to the two healthy zones and autoscaling restores capacity in
              under 10 minutes; the on-call engineer is paged and follows the "zone loss"
              runbook.
Load:         k6 average-load test at 120 requests/s, started at 13:45
Stop if:      5xx > 5% for 2 minutes, p95 > 2 s for 5 minutes, or the facilitator calls it
Roles:        facilitator (injects, can abort), operators (this week's on-call pair),
              scribe (timestamps), comms lead (status channel)
Schedule:     13:30 briefing; 13:45 load starts; 14:00 baseline check; 14:05 inject;
              14:05-14:45 respond and observe; 14:50 restore and verify; 15:00 hot debrief
Measure:      time to detect, time to mitigate, peak 5xx rate, time until capacity restored
Afterwards:   written review within a week; every surprise becomes an action with an owner

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Start with a hypothesis about steady state that users would notice, and measure steady state before injecting anything.
  • Begin where failure costs nothing (tests, CI, staging) and widen the blast radius only after the smaller experiment has become boring.
  • Always have stop conditions and a tested abort; know how to restore a known-good state.
  • Inject faults that really happen, ranked by frequency and impact; reuse your postmortems.
  • Run experiments under realistic load; many weaknesses appear only when pools and queues are busy.
  • Announce experiments and game days, and involve the people who would respond for real.
  • Treat every disproved hypothesis as a success: it found a weakness before users did.
  • Automate experiments that passed and re-run them after changes.
  • Keep chaos tooling locked down: its APIs and roles can break production on purpose.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• An experiment caused a real outage. Detect: the steady-state metric fell beyond the expected range and users reported errors during the experiment. Cause: the blast radius was too large, or stop conditions were missing or never tested. Fix: run a blameless review, shrink the scope, test the stop condition in a dry run, and climb back up the ladder from a lower environment.
  • Nobody noticed the injected failure. Detect: the game day scribe records no alert and no human reaction while the fault was active. Cause: alerts on the wrong signals, or routed to the wrong place. Fix: alert on SLO burn and symptoms, test paging during the next game day, and add the missing dashboard panels (see alerting and on-call).
  • A timeout exists, but requests still hang. Detect: with latency injected, the API's response time equals the dependency's delay. Cause: the timeout is set on a different client, is longer than the request budget, or wraps only part of the call (DNS and connect excluded). Fix: set an explicit timeout on every outbound call and verify it with a Toxiproxy test in CI.
  • Killing one instance causes a burst of errors. Detect: 5xx spikes for tens of seconds after a pod or instance is terminated. Cause: no graceful shutdown, health checks that react too slowly, or clients without retries for idempotent requests. Fix: handle SIGTERM by draining connections, tune readiness and load-balancer health checks, and retry idempotent requests with backoff.
  • The experiment would not stop. Detect: the fault remains after the abort command, or a proxy stays in place after the test run. Cause: a cleanup step that depended on the test passing, or an abort path that was never exercised. Fix: remove faults in finally blocks and after hooks, give every fault a duration, and practise the abort before the real run.
  • Findings were recorded but never fixed. Detect: the same weakness appears in the next game day. Cause: no owners, no dates, no tracking. Fix: treat game-day findings like postmortem actions, with owners and due dates, and re-run the experiment to close them.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Chaos engineering: Experimenting on a system to build confidence that it withstands turbulent conditions.
  • Steady state: A measurable, user-visible output that shows normal behaviour.
  • Hypothesis: A falsifiable statement of what will happen to steady state when a fault occurs, and why.
  • Blast radius: How much of the system, and how many users, an experiment can affect.
  • Stop condition: A guardrail that ends an experiment automatically when a metric crosses a threshold.
  • Fault injection: Deliberately introducing a failure such as latency, errors, or termination.
  • Control group / experimental group: Comparable parts of the system with and without the fault.
  • Game day: A planned exercise in which a team handles an injected failure as it would a real incident.
  • Tabletop exercise: A discussion-only walk-through of a failure scenario.
  • Toxic: A Toxiproxy fault, such as latency or a reset connection.
  • Experiment template: In AWS FIS, the blueprint of actions, targets, and stop conditions.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "Chaos engineering means breaking production at random." It means controlled experiments with hypotheses, small blast radiuses, and stop buttons.
  • Starting in production before the same experiment has passed in lower environments.
  • Running experiments without observability, so nobody can tell whether users were hurt.
  • Injecting faults you already know the system cannot handle.
  • Measuring infrastructure (CPU, pod counts) instead of the user-facing steady state.
  • Treating a passed experiment as permanent; systems change, so re-run them.
  • Running game days with the system's authors as responders, which tests memory instead of runbooks.
  • Collecting findings without owners and dates.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define steady state for TaskFlow API and write a hypothesis for "the MongoDB primary steps down".
  2. What controls keep the blast radius of an experiment small? Name at least four.
  3. Why should a chaos experiment usually run under load?
  4. When should you not run a chaos experiment?
  5. Which tool would you use to test a timeout in CI, to kill pods in Kubernetes, and to terminate an EC2 instance with an automatic stop condition?
  6. An experiment injects 3 s of latency into a dependency that is called with a 300 ms timeout and no retries, on an endpoint whose SLO is p95 under 1 s. If the rest of the request takes 40 ms, what latency do you expect, and what would it mean if you measured 3 s? (About 340 ms; a 3 s result means the timeout is not applied to that call.)
  7. What roles does a game day need, and why should the responders not be the system's authors?
  8. What should happen to a finding from a game day?

docs.title: Performance and Reliability Testing Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the performance and reliability testing lessons, for the day before an interview, a load test, or a game day.

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
// perf/average-load.js (the shape of an open-model test with an SLO gate)
export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    list_tasks: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate", // open model: N iterations per second
      startRate: 10,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 50,              // rate x iteration time, plus headroom
      maxVUs: 200,
      stages: [
        { target: 120, duration: "5m" },  // ramp up
        { target: 120, duration: "20m" }, // plateau: read the results here
        { target: 0, duration: "2m" },    // ramp down and watch recovery
      ],
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],
    "http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks}": ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"],
    checks: ["rate>0.999"],             // checks alone never fail a run
    dropped_iterations: ["count==0"],   // the planned load was delivered
  },
};

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text: Command What it does k6 run -e BASE_URL=<url> perf/average-load.js Runs a test; exits 0 if all thresholds pass, 99 if one fails k6 run --scenario browse,write <script> Runs only the named scenarios (k6 2.3+) k6 run --once <script> One VU, one iteration: checks a script before a long run K6_WEB_DASHBOARD=true K6_WEB_DASHBOARD_EXPORT=results/report.html k6 run <script> Dashboard on port 5665 and an HTML report k6 run -o opentelemetry --tag testid=nightly-42 <script> Streams metrics to a Collector or Prometheus node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles src/server.js Writes a .cpuprofile when the process exits db.tasks.find(...).explain("executionStats") Compare nReturned with keys and docs examined toxiproxy-cli toxic add --type latency --attribute latency=1000 notifications Adds 1 s of latency (latency_downstream) aws fis start-experiment --experiment-template-id <id> Starts an FIS experiment; stop-experiment aborts it

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why "Can we serve 120 requests/s?" constant-arrival-rate or ramping-arrival-rate Open model: load holds when the server slows A fixed pool of users or workers constant-vus or ramping-vus Closed model: the real system waits too A script and environment check Smoke test, 1-2 VUs, 1-2 minutes Cheap before a long run The SLO at the expected peak Average-load test Ramp, plateau, ramp down The real capacity Step or breakpoint test, read per minute Thresholds are cumulative Slow leaks Soak test for hours Memory, connections, disk stay flat ELU near 100% CPU profile under load (--cpu-prof, 0x) CPU-bound JavaScript or GC ELU low, latency high Pool waits, slow query log, explain() Waiting on I/O, not CPU A timeout tested in CI Toxiproxy Real TCP faults on every build Pod faults in Kubernetes Chaos Mesh or LitmusChaos CNCF incubating, custom resources An AWS fault with an automatic stop AWS FIS with CloudWatch alarms Up to five alarms per template Practised responders A tabletop, then a game day Tests alerts, runbooks, and roles

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text:
• Little's law, L = λ × W: a closed model needs 120/s × (0.15 + 4.85 s) = 600 VUs; at 1.15 s the same VUs send 600 / 6.0 = 100/s, 17% less.
  • Arrival-rate VUs ≈ rate × iteration time: 200/s × 0.25 s = 50 plus headroom; 200/s × 1.5 s = 300 for maxVUs.
  • Busy pool connections = requests/s × queries per request × seconds per query: 120 × 2 × 0.080 = 19.2 of a pool of 20.
  • k6 exit codes: 0 passed, 99 a threshold failed, 97 a cloud run aborted for another reason (since 2.0), 107 a script error, 108 test.abort().
  • k6 defaults: gracefulStop 30 s; compact summary; trend stats avg, min, med, max, p(90), p(95); http_req_failed counts statuses outside 200-399; dashboard updates every 10 s.
  • k6 2.0 (May 2026) removed externally-controlled, k6 login, and --no-summary (use --summary-mode=disabled); 2.4 deprecated the influxdb and experimental-prometheus-rw outputs.
  • Load generator: CPU under about 80% and dropped_iterations at 0.
  • Node.js: --cpu-prof samples every 1,000 µs; an idle loop's delay is about the sampler resolution (10 ms; 15.6 ms on Windows).
  • MongoDB: slowms 100 ms; Node.js driver maxPoolSize 100 and waitQueueTimeoutMS 0 (no limit).

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Closed-loop VUs for a rate question. Use an arrival-rate executor; a closed loop eases off and hides slow periods (coordinated omission).
  • Gating on checks alone. Add a checks threshold; a failed check only counts.
  • Raw URLs as metric names. Tag route templates (GET /tasks/:id) or use http.url.
  • Ignoring dropped iterations. Gate on count==0 and size VUs with Little's law.
  • Reading capacity from the abort time. Read the knee from the time series; abortOnFail is only a safety stop.
  • An unpinned k6 in CI. Pin k6-version in grafana/setup-k6-action and run mkdir -p results first: a failed summary write still exits 0.
  • A bigger pool for a saturated database. Fix the slow query (an ESR index), then size the pool.
  • Chaos without a stop. Start in CI and staging, watch steady state, and test the abort first.

Back to the performance and reliability testing overview.

docs.title: Finding Bottlenecks
docs.text:
A load test tells you that something broke: p95 jumped at 230 requests per second, or errors appeared at twice the peak. This lesson is about finding out why. It covers a repeatable triage loop, the USE method applied during a load test, finding the knee of the latency curve, event-loop delay and utilization in Node.js, CPU profiling with --cpu-prof (and where Clinic.js and 0x fit), garbage-collection pressure, slow MongoDB queries and missing indexes, connection pool exhaustion, N+1 queries, and a worked investigation from symptom to fix.

Operating-system tools (top, vmstat, iostat, ss) are covered in troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network, and the Node.js basics behind this page (the event loop, heap snapshots, worker threads) in the event loop and errors, debugging, and performance.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Without a method, teams guess, and the usual guesses are expensive or harmful: add instances, double the connection pool, raise the heap limit. Each can make things worse. A bigger pool pushes more concurrent queries into a database that is already saturated; more instances multiply the connections the database must hold; a bigger heap only delays a leak.

A bottleneck is the first resource to saturate as load rises, and it caps the throughput of the whole system. Fixing it moves the limit to the next bottleneck, so capacity grows in steps, one diagnosis at a time. Knowing exactly which resource saturates decides whether the fix is a line of code, an index, a configuration value, or more hardware, which is the difference between a cheap fix and a recurring bill.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The USE method. Brendan Gregg's USE method is a checklist for performance investigations: "For every resource, check utilization, saturation, and errors." It applies to software resources too: for a thread pool or a lock, saturation is the number of requests waiting.
  • Discord: GC pauses. In Why Discord is switching from Go to Rust (2020), Discord describes latency and CPU spikes roughly every two minutes in its Read States service. The cause was Go's garbage collector, which runs at least every two minutes and had to scan a very large in-memory cache. Shrinking the cache cut the spikes but raised p99, because more lookups went to the database; the team load-tested cache sizes before rewriting the service in Rust, which removed the spikes.
  • Netflix: flame graphs for Node.js. Node.js in Flames (2014) describes rising request latency on Netflix's Node.js website. CPU flame graphs showed the time growing inside Express's route handling; the cause was route handlers being registered again and again, so every request walked an ever longer list.
  • Node.js documentation. The official flame graphs guide recommends 0x for a single-step flame graph locally, and Linux perf with V8's --perf-basic-prof options for production systems.

Popular tools and providers: node --cpu-prof with Chrome DevTools or VS Code, 0x, Linux perf, Clinic.js (no longer actively maintained), perf_hooks and prom-client's default metrics, OpenTelemetry traces, MongoDB explain() and the database profiler, the Atlas Query Profiler and Performance Advisor, and continuous profilers such as Grafana Pyroscope.

docs.title: The triage loop
docs.text:
Investigations go wrong in two ways: chasing the first thing that looks odd, and changing several things at once. A fixed order avoids both:

  1. Reproduce the symptom under load with the same test, at the step where it starts.
  2. Rule out the test itself. If the generator is saturated or dropping iterations, nothing else you read is trustworthy.
  3. Check saturation, cheapest signals first: event-loop utilization, then connection pools and the database, then dependencies seen in traces.
  4. Measure the suspect directly: a CPU profile, an explain() plan, a pool wait-time metric.
  5. Change one thing, re-run the same test, and compare with the baseline. The next bottleneck appears at a higher load.

docs.title: The USE method during a load test
docs.text:
For every resource on the request path, check utilization (how busy it is), saturation (how much work is waiting), and errors. Build the checklist before the test, so the dashboards are ready when it runs.

Resource Utilization Saturation Errors CPU (host or container) CPU % per core Run-queue length; CPU throttling in containers - Node.js event loop Event-loop utilization (ELU) Event-loop delay Request timeouts Memory and heap Heap used against the limit GC time and frequency Out-of-memory restarts Database connection pool Connections in use / maxPoolSize Requests waiting; checkout wait time Checkout timeouts MongoDB server CPU, disk I/O, cache use Queued operations, slow operations Errors, failovers Downstream API In-flight calls against its limit Calls waiting for a socket Timeouts, 429, 5xx File descriptors Open sockets and files - EMFILE errors Load generator CPU, network Dropped iterations Request errors at the client

USE complements the RED view of each service (rate, errors, duration per route) described in metrics and dashboards: RED tells you which endpoint hurts, USE tells you which resource is behind it. Container CPU throttling is explained in scaling and resource management.

docs.title: Finding the knee
docs.text:
Run a step test: raise the offered load in steps and hold each one long enough to read steady-state numbers (a few minutes in a real test). For each step, compare the achieved throughput with the offered load, and watch p95. Below the limit, throughput follows the offered load and latency stays flat. At the knee, throughput stops following and latency turns sharply upward, because every extra request now waits in a queue. The last step before the knee that still meets the SLO is the measured capacity; plan to run well below it (see capacity planning for the queueing math and headroom).

The chart comes from the step-test script in the practical examples, run with shortened holds against a local stand-in server. Little's law predicted the plateau before the test: a pool of 5 connections whose queries take about 0.0215 s can complete at most 5 / 0.0215, about 233 queries per second. Event-loop utilization stayed at 4-6% throughout, so adding CPU would not have helped; the queue was in front of the pool.

docs.title: Event-loop delay and utilization
docs.text:
Node.js runs all JavaScript on one thread. Two built-in measurements describe how busy it is:

  • Event-loop utilization (ELU): the share of time the loop spent running code rather than waiting for I/O, from performance.eventLoopUtilization(). Near 100% means the process is CPU-bound.
  • Event-loop delay: how late timers fire, from perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay(). Long synchronous work (a huge JSON.parse, a deep copy, synchronous crypto) delays every other request in the process.

Each event-loop-delay sample includes the sampling interval itself: an idle loop reports values close to the resolution (10 ms in the sampler below), and on Windows, where timers are coarser, about 15.6 ms. Judge the delay by how far p99 and the maximum rise above that baseline. A 200 ms block, in a local check, showed up as a 200 ms maximum.

Read the two together:

ELU Event-loop delay Request latency Likely bottleneck High (above about 80%) High High CPU-bound JavaScript or GC in this process Low At the baseline High Waiting on I/O: a pool, the database, a dependency, a lock Low Occasional spikes Occasional spikes Rare long synchronous tasks

Measured on the local lab server with the sampler from the practical examples:

Run Throughput p95 latency ELU Event-loop delay p99 Healthy: 100 requests/s to a cheap endpoint 100/s, no errors 11 ms 3-5% about 20 ms CPU-bound: 150/s offered to an endpoint doing heavy synchronous work 131/s achieved, 341 dropped iterations 1.58 s 99-100% 110-403 ms Pool-bound: the 250/s step of the knee test 232/s achieved 726 ms 4-6% about 16-23 ms

The second and third runs are both slow, for opposite reasons; only the second would improve with more CPU. When the event loop is saturated, timers and I/O callbacks also run late, so pools and queries look slow too: check ELU before blaming the database.

docs.title: CPU profiling under load
docs.text:
When ELU is high, find out which functions use the CPU. Node's built-in sampling profiler records the stack every millisecond by default (--cpu-prof-interval, in microseconds) and writes a .cpuprofile file when the process exits:

node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles src/server.js
# run the load test against it, then stop the server with SIGINT or SIGTERM;
# the file is named like CPU.20261114.012039.16912.0.001.cpuprofile

The process must exit normally for the profile to be written, so the server needs a shutdown handler that closes and calls process.exit() on SIGTERM and SIGINT (as in a graceful-shutdown handler). Open the file in Chrome DevTools (the Performance panel's load-profile button) or VS Code to see a flame chart, which puts time on the x-axis, or summarize it from the command line with the script in the practical examples. Profile under the realistic load from your test, for a bounded time, against one instance: profiling a process with no traffic shows only start-up code.

How to read a flame graph: the x-axis is the population of samples sorted alphabetically, not the passage of time; the y-axis is stack depth, with callers below callees. A box's width is how often that frame was on the stack. The top edges are what was actually running, so wide plateaus at the top are where the CPU time goes. A flame chart (the DevTools view) keeps time on the x-axis instead, which is better for finding one long task.

Two well-known tools wrap this workflow:

  • 0x profiles a process and writes an interactive flame graph in a single command (npx 0x -o src/server.js, then Ctrl+C); its README lists Node.js 20 and later.
  • Clinic.js (Doctor, Flame, Bubbleprof, Heap Profiler), originally developed by NearForm, carries a notice that it is not being actively maintained and that its results may be inaccurate on current Node.js versions; its last npm release dates from 2023. Prefer --cpu-prof, 0x, or a continuous profiler on new projects.

In production, use short, targeted captures, Linux perf with --perf-basic-prof, or a continuous profiler that samples all the time at low overhead, rather than leaving --cpu-prof running.

docs.title: Memory and garbage-collection pressure
docs.text:
Every allocation must eventually be collected, and collection takes time on the same thread. GC pressure shows up as:

  • latency spikes that line up with major collections;
  • a large share of ELU spent in GC (the (garbage collector) frame in a profile, or nodejs_gc_duration_seconds from prom-client);
  • a heap that saws up and down at a high rate, or a floor that keeps rising (a leak).

Typical causes in an API are per-request allocations that scale with data (serializing huge result sets, deep copies, building large strings) and caches without bounds. The fixes are to allocate less (smaller pages, projections, streaming), to bound caches, and to find leaks with heap snapshots taken minutes apart under load. Raising --max-old-space-size is right only when the working set is genuinely larger; for a leak it only delays the crash.

docs.title: Slow queries and missing indexes
docs.text:
Most API latency under load is database time. Three tools find it:

  • The slow query log. mongod logs operations slower than slowms (100 ms by default). Lower it in a performance environment to see more.
  • The database profiler. db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 20 }) records slow operations into the capped system.profile collection. MongoDB's documentation warns that the profiler can degrade performance and suggests the Atlas Query Profiler, the Performance Advisor, or the $queryStats stage first; on a self-managed test environment it is fine for a short run.
  • explain("executionStats") on a suspect query, comparing nReturned with totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined. A query that returns 20 documents after examining 40,000 is the classic missing index. A COLLSCAN stage is a full collection scan; a SORT stage means an in-memory sort the index could not provide.

For compound indexes, MongoDB's ESR guideline puts Equality fields first, then Sort fields, then Range fields. TaskFlow's main list query, { ownerId, status: "open" } sorted by dueDate, therefore wants { ownerId: 1, status: 1, dueDate: 1 }. Index basics are covered in MongoDB index design and explain and query plans.

docs.title: Connection pool exhaustion
docs.text:
Every query needs a connection from the driver's pool. Little's law gives the number of connections busy on average:

busy connections = requests/s × queries per request × seconds per query

When that approaches maxPoolSize, requests queue for a connection. The MongoDB Node.js driver's defaults are a maxPoolSize of 100 and a waitQueueTimeoutMS of 0, meaning no limit on the wait; the driver does not limit the number of waiters either, so a saturated pool shows up as rising latency, not errors, until your own request timeout fires. Setting waitQueueTimeoutMS makes the driver fail a checkout that waits too long with a MongoWaitQueueTimeoutError, which turns a hidden queue into a visible error.

A full pool is usually a symptom. If the queries are slow because the database is saturated, a bigger pool sends more concurrent work into it and makes every query slower. Raise maxPoolSize only when the database has headroom and the queries are already fast, and remember that every instance has its own pool: 10 instances with maxPoolSize: 100 can open 1,000 connections to one server.

docs.title: N+1 queries
docs.text: An N+1 pattern runs one query for a list and then one more per item, so the query count grows with the page size and the data. The pattern and its fixes (one batched $in query, $lookup, embedding, DataLoader for GraphQL) are explained in performance and latency. Under load it shows up as database operations per second rising faster than requests per second. The cheapest guard is a test that counts the commands one request sends, shown in the practical examples.

docs.title: Other common limits
docs.text:
• Dependencies: a slow downstream service holds sockets and memory for every waiting request. Traces show it (see distributed tracing); timeouts and bulkheads contain it (see resilience patterns across servers).
  • No connection reuse: a client or proxy that opens a new TLS connection per request spends CPU on handshakes; k6's http_req_tls_handshaking and the server's CPU show it.
  • Rate limiters and quotas: a wall of 429 responses at a round number is a limiter, not a capacity limit.
  • File descriptors: EMFILE errors mean the process hit its open-file limit; see the Linux troubleshooting page.
  • Autoscaling lag: new instances arrive after the spike; see autoscaling server fleets.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Symptom under load First tool Then Latency rises with ELU near 100% CPU profile under load (--cpu-prof, 0x) Optimize the hot functions or move work to worker threads Latency rises with ELU low Pool wait time, slow query log explain(), indexes, N+1 checks Periodic latency spikes GC timing, event-loop delay maximum Reduce allocations, find the long synchronous task Memory grows during a soak test Heap snapshots minutes apart Fix the leak; bound caches One endpoint slow, others fine Traces for that route Its queries and dependencies Everything slow, servers idle Load-generator health, network Fix the test or the network path

Do not profile or tune before you have a reproducible symptom under a realistic load: micro-optimizing code that is not on the critical path costs time and readability for nothing. And do not tune production by experiment; reproduce the problem in a performance environment first.

docs.title: A runtime health sampler
docs.text:
// src/runtime-stats.js: event-loop delay, event-loop utilization, and GC pauses every 10 s
import { monitorEventLoopDelay, performance, PerformanceObserver, constants } from "node:perf_hooks";

export function startRuntimeStats({ intervalMs = 10_000, log = console.log } = {}) {
  const delay = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 10 }); // samples every 10 ms
  delay.enable();
  let lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
  const gc = { pauses: 0, major: 0, totalMs: 0, maxMs: 0 };

  const gcObserver = new PerformanceObserver((list) => {
    for (const entry of list.getEntries()) {
      gc.pauses += 1;
      gc.totalMs += entry.duration;
      gc.maxMs = Math.max(gc.maxMs, entry.duration);
      if (entry.detail?.kind === constants.NODE_PERFORMANCE_GC_MAJOR) gc.major += 1;
    }
  });
  gcObserver.observe({ entryTypes: ["gc"] });

  const ms = (ns) => Number((ns / 1e6).toFixed(1)); // the histogram records nanoseconds
  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    const elu = performance.eventLoopUtilization(lastElu); // only the last interval
    lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
    log({
      eluPercent: Math.round(elu.utilization * 100),
      loopDelayP50Ms: ms(delay.percentile(50)),
      loopDelayP99Ms: ms(delay.percentile(99)),
      loopDelayMaxMs: ms(delay.max),
      gcPauses: gc.pauses,
      gcMajor: gc.major,
      gcTotalMs: Math.round(gc.totalMs),
      gcMaxMs: Number(gc.maxMs.toFixed(1)),
      heapUsedMb: Math.round(process.memoryUsage().heapUsed / 1048576),
    });
    delay.reset();
    Object.assign(gc, { pauses: 0, major: 0, totalMs: 0, maxMs: 0 });
  }, intervalMs);
  timer.unref(); // never keeps the process alive on its own

  return function stop() {
    clearInterval(timer);
    delay.disable();
    gcObserver.disconnect();
  };
}

// src/server.js (excerpt): log runtime stats next to the request logs
import { startRuntimeStats } from "./runtime-stats.js";
import { logger } from "./observability.js";

startRuntimeStats({ log: (stats) => logger.info({ runtime: stats }, "runtime stats") });

# two samples from the lab runs (5-second interval)
CPU-bound:  {"eluPercent":100,"loopDelayP50Ms":88.7,"loopDelayP99Ms":403.2,"gcPauses":57,"gcMajor":1,"gcTotalMs":255,"heapUsedMb":33}
Pool-bound: {"eluPercent":5,"loopDelayP50Ms":11.5,"loopDelayP99Ms":23.2,"gcPauses":13,"gcMajor":2,"gcTotalMs":13,"heapUsedMb":37}

Each line covers only the last interval: eventLoopUtilization(lastElu) returns the difference since the previous reading, and the histogram and GC counters are reset after each log. In production, export the same values as metrics (prom-client's collectDefaultMetrics() already provides nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds and nodejs_gc_duration_seconds) and put them on the dashboard you watch during load tests. The samples above are trimmed to the most telling fields.

docs.title: Profiling under load and summarizing the profile
docs.text:
# terminal 1: the API under the profiler, on a performance host
node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles src/server.js

# terminal 2: steady load on the suspect endpoint for 60 seconds
k6 run --vus 20 --duration 60s -e BASE_URL=http://localhost:3000 perf/smoke.js

# terminal 1: stop the server with Ctrl+C (its shutdown handler exits cleanly), then
node perf/tools/cpuprofile-top.js profiles/CPU.*.cpuprofile

// perf/tools/cpuprofile-top.js: the functions with the most CPU samples in a .cpuprofile
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const profile = JSON.parse(readFileSync(process.argv[2], "utf8"));
const totalSamples = profile.samples.length;
const msPerSample = (profile.endTime - profile.startTime) / 1000 / totalSamples; // times are in µs

const selfSamples = new Map();
for (const { callFrame, hitCount = 0 } of profile.nodes) {
  const file = callFrame.url ? ` ${callFrame.url.split("/").pop()}:${callFrame.lineNumber + 1}` : "";
  const name = `${callFrame.functionName || "(anonymous)"}${file}`;
  selfSamples.set(name, (selfSamples.get(name) ?? 0) + hitCount);
}

console.log("self %   self ms  function");
for (const [name, hits] of [...selfSamples].sort((a, b) => b[1] - a[1]).slice(0, 10)) {
  const pct = ((hits / totalSamples) * 100).toFixed(1).padStart(6);
  const ms = (hits * msPerSample).toFixed(0).padStart(8);
  console.log(`${pct}  ${ms}  ${name}`);
}

self %   self ms  function
  78.2     18809  (idle)
  13.8      3316  buildTaskStats stats.mjs:2
   5.2      1254  (anonymous) stats.mjs:5
   0.9       215  (garbage collector)
   0.3        83  (program)
   0.3        71  writeUtf8String

The output is from a 24-second profile of the lab server while k6 sent 60 requests per second to an endpoint with a deliberately wasteful statistics builder. (idle) is time the loop waited for I/O; among the busy samples, buildTaskStats and its map callback dominate, so that is the function to fix. Each profile node records hitCount, the samples in which it was the running (top) frame, which is exactly the self time a flame graph shows as top edges. On a real API run, the same script points at the busiest handlers in seconds and works in CI, where no browser is available.

docs.title: Finding the knee with a step test
docs.text:
// perf/find-the-knee.js: step the arrival rate up and watch where latency turns upward
import http from "k6/http";

const steps = [100, 150, 200, 250, 300]; // requests per second, held for 2 minutes each

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    steps: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: steps[0],
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 100,
      maxVUs: 1000,
      stages: steps.flatMap((rate) => [
        { target: rate, duration: "10s" }, // move to the next step
        { target: rate, duration: "2m" },  // hold it
      ]),
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: [{ threshold: "rate<0.05", abortOnFail: true }],
  },
};

export default function () {
  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/tasks?limit=20`, {
    headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}` },
    tags: { name: "GET /tasks" },
  });
}

// perf/tools/k6-steps-report.js: throughput and latency per time window from k6 --out json
import { createReadStream } from "node:fs";
import { createInterface } from "node:readline";

const [file, windowSeconds = "60"] = process.argv.slice(2);
const bySecond = new Map(); // epoch second -> request durations in ms

for await (const line of createInterface({ input: createReadStream(file) })) {
  if (!line.includes('"type":"Point"') || !line.includes('"metric":"http_req_duration"')) continue;
  const { data } = JSON.parse(line);
  const second = Math.floor(Date.parse(data.time) / 1000);
  if (!bySecond.has(second)) bySecond.set(second, []);
  bySecond.get(second).push(data.value);
}

// Windows start at the first sample, so each one lines up with a step of the test.
const first = Math.min(...bySecond.keys());
const windows = new Map();
for (const [second, durations] of bySecond) {
  const w = Math.floor((second - first) / Number(windowSeconds));
  windows.set(w, (windows.get(w) ?? []).concat(durations));
}

const pick = (sorted, q) => sorted[Math.min(sorted.length - 1, Math.ceil(q * sorted.length) - 1)];
console.log("window   req/s    p50 ms   p95 ms   p99 ms");
for (const w of [...windows.keys()].sort((a, b) => a - b)) {
  const d = windows.get(w).sort((a, b) => a - b);
  const cols = [d.length / Number(windowSeconds), pick(d, 0.5), pick(d, 0.95), pick(d, 0.99)];
  console.log(`${String(w + 1).padStart(6)}  ${cols.map((v) => v.toFixed(0).padStart(7)).join("  ")}`);
}

$ k6 run --out json=results/knee.json perf/find-the-knee.js
$ node perf/tools/k6-steps-report.js results/knee.json 25
window   req/s    p50 ms   p95 ms   p99 ms
     1       98       20       30       36
     2      144       21       29       44
     3      194       21       40       91
     4      232      336      726      772
     5      209     2365     4589     5029
     6       43     6003     6375     6389

This output is from the lab run behind the knee chart, with each step held for 20 seconds instead of 2 minutes, so 25-second windows line up with the steps. Window 4 is the knee. In window 5 the achieved rate falls below the offered 300 per second because k6 reached its 1,000 VUs and dropped iterations; window 6 is the queue draining after the test ended. With real 2-minute holds, use 130-second windows and read the steady part of each.

docs.title: Reading the database side
docs.text:
// mongosh, in the performance environment: record operations slower than 20 ms
db.setProfilingLevel(1, { slowms: 20 })

// the slowest recent operations on the tasks collection
db.system.profile.find(
  { ns: "taskflow.tasks", millis: { $gt: 20 } },
  { op: 1, millis: 1, planSummary: 1, keysExamined: 1, docsExamined: 1, nreturned: 1, hasSortStage: 1 }
).sort({ millis: -1 }).limit(5)

// the suspect query, with execution statistics
db.tasks.find({ ownerId: ObjectId("<user-id>"), status: "open" })
  .sort({ dueDate: 1 }).limit(20)
  .explain("executionStats")

db.setProfilingLevel(0) // switch the profiler off again

# trimmed and illustrative: field names as documented, layout varies by version
before  winning plan: SORT <- FETCH <- IXSCAN { ownerId: 1 }
        nReturned: 20, totalKeysExamined: 41200, totalDocsExamined: 41200, executionTimeMillis: 85
after   winning plan: LIMIT <- FETCH <- IXSCAN { ownerId: 1, status: 1, dueDate: 1 }
        nReturned: 20, totalKeysExamined: 20, totalDocsExamined: 20, executionTimeMillis: 1

Before, the only index was on ownerId: a heavy user's 41,200 tasks were fetched, filtered by status, and sorted in memory to return 20. After an ESR index, the index delivers the 20 open tasks already in dueDate order. Build indexes on large collections as a planned change (see zero-downtime database migrations).

docs.title: Watching the connection pool
docs.text:
// src/db/pool-stats.js: connection pool use and checkout waits, from MongoDB driver events
export function trackPoolWaits(client, { intervalMs = 10_000, log = console.log } = {}) {
  let inUse = 0;
  let waitsMs = [];
  let timeouts = 0;

  client.on("connectionCheckedOut", (event) => {
    inUse += 1;
    waitsMs.push(event.durationMS); // how long this checkout waited for a connection
  });
  client.on("connectionCheckedIn", () => {
    inUse -= 1;
  });
  client.on("connectionCheckOutFailed", (event) => {
    if (event.reason === "timeout") timeouts += 1; // waitQueueTimeoutMS was exceeded
  });

  const timer = setInterval(() => {
    waitsMs.sort((a, b) => a - b);
    const p99 = waitsMs.length ? waitsMs[Math.ceil(0.99 * waitsMs.length) - 1] : 0;
    log({ poolInUse: inUse, checkouts: waitsMs.length, checkoutWaitP99Ms: Math.round(p99), checkoutTimeouts: timeouts });
    waitsMs = [];
    timeouts = 0;
  }, intervalMs);
  timer.unref();
}

// src/db/client.js (excerpt): one client per process, with a bounded wait
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import { trackPoolWaits } from "./pool-stats.js";
import { logger } from "../observability.js";

export const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, {
  maxPoolSize: 20,
  waitQueueTimeoutMS: 2000, // fail a checkout after 2 s instead of waiting forever
});
trackPoolWaits(client, { log: (stats) => logger.info({ pool: stats }, "pool stats") });

The driver emits connection pool events on the client by default. connectionCheckedOut carries durationMS, the time the checkout took (in current driver versions), which is the wait a request spent in front of the pool; its p99 rising while poolInUse sits at maxPoolSize is the signature of a saturated pool. A non-zero checkoutTimeouts means requests are now failing with MongoWaitQueueTimeoutError instead of waiting silently.

docs.title: A test that catches N+1 queries
docs.text:
// test/integration/tasks-query-count.test.js: fail the build when GET /tasks queries per item
import { test, before, after } from "node:test";
import assert from "node:assert/strict";
import request from "supertest";
import { MongoClient } from "mongodb";
import { createApp } from "../../src/app.js";

const client = new MongoClient(process.env.MONGODB_URI, { monitorCommands: true });
const commands = [];
let app;

before(async () => {
  await client.connect();
  client.on("commandStarted", (event) => commands.push(event.commandName));
  app = createApp({ db: client.db() });
});

after(() => client.close());

test("GET /tasks sends the same number of queries for 5 and 50 tasks", async () => {
  commands.length = 0;
  await request(app).get("/tasks?limit=5").expect(200);
  const forFive = commands.filter((name) => name === "find" || name === "aggregate").length;

  commands.length = 0;
  await request(app).get("/tasks?limit=50").expect(200);
  const forFifty = commands.filter((name) => name === "find" || name === "aggregate").length;

  assert.equal(forFifty, forFive, `query count grew with page size: ${forFive} -> ${forFifty}`);
});

Command monitoring is off by default; monitorCommands: true makes the client emit commandStarted for every command. With one request at a time there is no doubt which request sent which command, which makes this a reliable guard in the integration suite from testing and quality gates. It needs seeded data with at least 50 tasks for the test user.

docs.title: A worked investigation
docs.text:
An example investigation on TaskFlow API, with illustrative numbers. The setup: three API instances, maxPoolSize: 20 each, one MongoDB replica-set primary.

  1. Symptom. A breakpoint test shows p95 of GET /tasks flat around 45 ms up to 300 requests per second, then 900 ms at 360, with timeouts from 400. Achieved throughput plateaus near 370 per second. dropped_iterations is zero and the generator's CPU is 35%: the test is sound.
  2. USE. On the API instances, ELU is about 30% and event-loop delay is at its baseline: not CPU. The pool sampler shows poolInUse at 20 of 20 and a checkout-wait p99 of 600 ms: the pool is saturated. MongoDB's CPU is at 92%.
  3. Little's law. At 360 requests per second, each instance serves 120, each request runs 2 queries, and queries now take about 80 ms: 120 × 2 × 0.080 = 19.2 busy connections, which is the whole pool. A larger pool would push more concurrent queries into a database already at 92% CPU, so the pool is the symptom.
  4. The database. The profiler shows the list query on top, with hasSortStage: true and docsExamined in the tens of thousands for heavy users; explain() confirms an in-memory sort after scanning every task the user owns.
  5. The fix. A single ESR index, { ownerId: 1, status: 1, dueDate: 1 }, built in the performance environment and then rolled out as a planned change. The query now examines 20 documents and takes about 2 ms; busy connections at the same load fall to 120 × 2 × 0.002 = 0.48.
  6. Re-run. The same breakpoint test now holds p95 under 50 ms to 800 requests per second, MongoDB's CPU is about 35% at 360, and the new knee appears near 850, where ELU on the API instances reaches 95%. The next bottleneck is CPU: a profile under load is the next step.

The pattern generalizes: rule out the test, read utilization and saturation for each resource, use Little's law to check that the numbers agree, fix the cause rather than the symptom, and expect the next bottleneck.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Investigate in a fixed order: the test, then CPU, then pools and the database, then dependencies.
  • Prepare RED and USE dashboards for the request path before the test, including event-loop utilization, delay, GC, pool waits, and database saturation.
  • Find capacity with a step test and read it where throughput stops following the offered load.
  • Use Little's law to check that pool sizes, concurrency, and throughput agree before changing any of them.
  • Profile under realistic load, for a bounded time, on one instance.
  • Fix causes, not symptoms: a slow query, not a bigger pool; a leak, not a bigger heap.
  • Bound every wait: request timeouts, waitQueueTimeoutMS, and timeouts on dependencies.
  • Change one thing per run and re-run the same test against the baseline.
  • Keep a regression guard for each bottleneck you fix: an index check, a query-count test, a threshold.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• p95 rises with load while the CPU looks idle. Detect: ELU and CPU are low, latency grows with the request rate, and the pool's checkout wait rises. Cause: requests queue for database connections because queries are slow or the pool is too small for rate × queries × query time. Fix: find and fix the slow queries first; then size the pool with Little's law, within the database's connection budget.
  • Every endpoint slows down at once. Detect: event-loop delay p99 and ELU jump together, on unrelated routes. Cause: synchronous CPU work in one handler (large serialization, deep copies, synchronous crypto) blocks the whole process. Fix: profile under load, optimize or move the work to worker threads (see worker threads, child processes, and cluster), and paginate large responses.
  • Latency spikes at regular intervals. Detect: p99 spikes that line up with major GC events or with a timer. Cause: large heaps with many live objects, or a periodic job running on the request thread. Fix: allocate less per request, bound caches, and move periodic jobs out of the API process.
  • Raising maxPoolSize made things worse. Detect: after the change, database CPU and query time rise and p95 gets worse at the same load. Cause: the database was the real bottleneck; more connections meant more concurrent work on it. Fix: revert, find the slow queries with the profiler and explain(), and add the missing index.
  • Database load grows faster than traffic after a release. Detect: database operations per request jump at the deploy time. Cause: a new N+1 query pattern. Fix: batch the queries, and add a query-count test so it cannot come back unnoticed.
  • Requests hang instead of failing during an overload. Detect: requests take as long as the client timeout, with no errors logged by the API. Cause: unbounded waits: no waitQueueTimeoutMS, no timeouts on dependencies. Fix: bound every wait so overload turns into fast, visible errors that load shedding and retries can handle.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Bottleneck: The first resource to saturate as load rises; it caps the system's throughput.
  • USE method: Checking utilization, saturation, and errors for every resource.
  • Saturation: Work waiting for a resource, such as a queue length or a wait time.
  • Knee: The load where throughput stops following the offered load and latency rises sharply.
  • Event-loop utilization (ELU): The share of time the Node.js event loop is busy running code.
  • Event-loop delay: How late the event loop runs scheduled callbacks.
  • CPU profile: A sampled record of which functions were running.
  • Flame graph: Aggregated stacks with width for sample share and height for stack depth.
  • Flame chart: Stacks drawn against time.
  • Self time: Samples in which a function itself, not its callees, was running.
  • GC pressure: Latency and CPU lost to garbage collection because of heavy allocation.
  • Connection pool exhaustion: All pool connections busy, so requests queue for one.
  • N+1 queries: One query for a list plus one per item.
  • ESR guideline: Equality, Sort, Range order for compound index fields.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Adding instances or connections before finding the saturated resource.
  • Trusting the results of a test whose generator was saturated or dropping iterations.
  • Profiling an idle process, or a different version from the one tested.
  • Reading a flame graph's x-axis as time.
  • Treating event-loop delay values as pure lag, without subtracting the sampling interval.
  • Blaming the database when the event loop is saturated and every callback runs late.
  • Raising the heap limit to "fix" a memory leak.
  • Fixing several things between runs, so nobody knows what helped.
  • Stopping after the first fix, without re-testing for the next bottleneck.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Apply the USE method to a Node.js API and its MongoDB database: name the utilization, saturation, and error signal for four resources.
  2. In a step test, how do you recognize the knee, and what is the measured capacity?
  3. ELU is 8% and p95 is 2 seconds. What kind of bottleneck is likely, and where do you look next?
  4. An instance serves 150 requests per second, each with 3 queries of 40 ms. How many connections are busy on average? What happens with maxPoolSize: 10, and is raising it the right fix? (150 x 3 x 0.040 = 18 busy connections; with 10 the pool saturates and requests queue; first check why queries take 40 ms and whether the database has headroom.)
  5. Why must a process exit normally for --cpu-prof to write its profile, and how do you arrange that for a server?
  6. What do the x-axis, y-axis, and box width mean in a flame graph?
  7. How does explain("executionStats") reveal a missing index? Which fields do you compare?
  8. How would you stop an N+1 pattern from reaching production again?
