docs.title: Performance and Reliability Testing Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review load-testing fundamentals, load testing with k6, finding bottlenecks, and chaos engineering and game days. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What are smoke, average-load, stress, spike, soak, and breakpoint tests?
docs.text: They are the same script driven by different load shapes. A smoke test runs minimal load for a minute or two to prove the script and environment work. An average-load test holds the expected peak to check the SLO. A stress test goes above the peak to see how the system degrades. A spike test jumps to several times normal in seconds. A soak test holds normal load for hours to find leaks. A breakpoint test ramps until something breaks, to find capacity.

docs.title: 2. Why run a smoke test before any bigger test?
docs.text: A broken script, missing test data, or a misconfigured environment wastes a 30-minute run and produces meaningless numbers. A smoke test with one or two VUs and strict checks (every check passes, no failed requests) proves the plumbing in a minute.

docs.title: 3. What is the difference between an open and a closed workload model?
docs.text: In a closed model, a fixed number of virtual users each send a request, wait for the response, think, and repeat, so throughput is VUs / (response time + think time) and drops when the server slows. In an open model, requests (or sessions) arrive at a set rate regardless of responses, so a slow server accumulates requests in flight, as it would with real independent users.

docs.title: 4. Which model fits a public API, and why?
docs.text: An open model. Internet users arrive independently and do not wait for each other, so the arrival rate does not fall when the API slows down. A closed model eases off exactly when the server struggles and understates the problem. Closed models fit fixed populations, such as a pool of 20 worker processes or a team using an internal tool.

docs.title: 5. What is think time, and why does it matter?
docs.text: The pause between one user's actions, such as reading a page before clicking. Without it, each VU sends requests back to back, so a few VUs generate as much traffic as thousands of real users and the VU count stops meaning anything. Think time should be randomized (for example 2-6 seconds) and taken from production where possible.

docs.title: 6. What is coordinated omission?
docs.text: A measurement error in closed-loop load generators. When the server pauses, each VU is stuck on one request and sends nothing else, so the pause is recorded once per VU instead of once for every request real users would have sent. In a local test against a server pausing 500 ms every 5 seconds, a 2-VU closed loop reported p99 of 22-36 ms while an open model at 120 requests per second reported 468-475 ms.

docs.title: 7. How do you avoid coordinated omission?
docs.text: Use an open model (arrival-rate executors) when the question is a rate; check that the planned load was delivered (achieved against intended throughput, dropped_iterations at zero); distrust p99 values from closed-loop benchmarks with few connections and no think time; or use tools that measure from the intended send time, as wrk2 does.

docs.title: 8. State Little's law and use it to size a closed-model test.
docs.text: L = λ × W: the number in the system equals the arrival rate times the time each one stays. To offer 200 requests per second when each iteration is one request with 0.1 s of response and 2.9 s of think time, W = 3.0 s, so L = 200 × 3.0 = 600 VUs. If responses slow to 1.1 s, W = 4.0 s and the same 600 VUs send only 600 / 4.0 = 150 requests per second.

docs.title: 9. How many VUs does an arrival-rate scenario need?
docs.text: About the rate times the iteration duration, plus headroom; k6 documents it as preAllocatedVUs = median iteration duration × rate + a constant for variance. At 200 iterations per second and 0.25 s per iteration that is 50 VUs plus headroom, but if iterations slow to 1.5 s it needs 300, so set maxVUs for the slowest latency you want to measure honestly.

docs.title: 10. Where should the endpoint mix, peak rate, and think time come from?
docs.text: From production: request counts per route during the busiest hour, the busiest five-minute rate over recent weeks, and the time between requests within user sessions from logs. Guessed mixes miss expensive endpoints, and planning from averages misses the peak.

docs.title: 11. Why does the size of the test data matter?
docs.text: With small data, every index and document fits in memory, caches hit almost every time, and queries are fast. Production-sized data (including heavy users with thousands of records) exercises disk, index selectivity, and memory pressure. A test on a tiny dataset can pass at a rate that production cannot sustain.

docs.title: 12. What should you measure during a load test?
docs.text: On the client side: achieved throughput against the target, latency percentiles per endpoint, error rate by type, failed checks, and dropped iterations. On the server side: RED metrics per route and USE metrics per resource (CPU, event loop, memory and GC, connection pools, database, dependencies). Read time series, not only the end-of-test summary.

docs.title: 13. How do you know the load generator is not the bottleneck?
docs.text: Watch its CPU (keep it below roughly 80%), memory, and network; check that dropped_iterations is zero and the achieved rate matches the target. A large gap between client-side and server-side latency, with idle servers, also points to the generator or something in front of the application.

docs.title: 14. How do you compare two load-test runs fairly?
docs.text: Same script, data snapshot, environment sizes, configuration, and warm-up; compare the same steady-state window and exclude the ramps; run important tests at least twice to know the run-to-run spread; record the version of the system under test; and change one thing at a time.

docs.title: 15. What runs in k6's init code, setup(), VU code, and teardown()?
docs.text: Init code (top level) runs once per VU: imports, options, open() of files, SharedArray. setup() runs once before the load, for example to log in test users, and returns JSON data. The VU code runs once per iteration and receives a copy of that data. teardown() runs once at the end. Init code cannot make HTTP requests.

docs.title: 16. Is k6 Node.js? What follows from that?
docs.text: No. k6 is a Go binary with its own JavaScript runtime, one per VU. Node built-ins and npm packages are not available directly; k6 has its own modules and can import local files, remote modules such as jslib, and bundled code. k6 2.x runs TypeScript files directly by stripping the types. Memory grows with VUs, so large data belongs in a SharedArray.

docs.title: 17. Which executors does k6 2.x have?
docs.text: Six: constant-arrival-rate and ramping-arrival-rate (open model), and constant-vus, ramping-vus, shared-iterations, and per-vu-iterations (closed model). The externally-controlled executor was removed in k6 2.0.

docs.title: 18. What is a threshold, and how does it fail a build?
docs.text:
A pass/fail condition on a metric, such as http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"] or http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"]. If any threshold fails, k6 exits with code 99, which fails the CI step; when all pass, it exits with 0.

// perf/thresholds-example.js: the SLO as thresholds
export const options = {
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],
    "http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks}": ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"],
    dropped_iterations: ["count==0"],
  },
};
export default function () {}

docs.title: 19. Do failed checks fail a k6 test?
docs.text: No. A check records a pass or fail in the checks metric and the iteration continues. To gate on checks, add a threshold such as checks: ["rate>0.999"]. Use fail() or throw when an iteration cannot continue, for example after a failed login in setup().

docs.title: 20. Why give requests a name tag?
docs.text: By default the name tag holds the full URL, so /tasks/<id> creates one metric series per task: an unreadable summary and a cardinality problem for any metrics backend. A route-template name such as GET /tasks/:id, or the http.url template tag, groups them into one series that thresholds and dashboards can use.

docs.title: 21. How do you set a threshold for one endpoint or one scenario?
docs.text: Put a tag filter in the metric name to create a sub-metric: "http_req_duration{name:POST /tasks}": ["p(95)<400"] or "checks{scenario:write}": ["rate>0.999"]. The summary then prints that sub-metric too, which is why always-true thresholds are sometimes added just to display per-scenario numbers.

docs.title: 22. What does abortOnFail do, and why can it fire late?
docs.text: It stops the test as soon as a threshold is crossed, optionally after delayAbortEval so warm-up samples do not trigger it. It can fire late because thresholds are computed over every sample since the start of the test, not a sliding window: a long healthy ramp dilutes the slow samples. In a local check, a median threshold tripped 20 seconds after the server actually degraded.

docs.title: 23. What is dropped_iterations, and how do you gate on it?
docs.text: A counter of iterations an arrival-rate executor could not start on time, usually because it ran out of VUs; k6 also logs "Insufficient VUs". A run with dropped iterations did not deliver the planned load. Gate with dropped_iterations: ["count==0"] and size preAllocatedVUs and maxVUs with Little's law.

docs.title: 24. How do you share test data between VUs efficiently?
docs.text: Load it once in a SharedArray in the init context: new SharedArray("users", () => JSON.parse(open("./data/users.json"))). Without it, every VU holds its own copy of the file. Keep secrets out of the data files and pass them through environment variables.

docs.title: 25. How would you run k6 in CI?
docs.text: A short smoke test on every pull request against the API started inside the job, and longer average-load tests on a schedule against a dedicated performance environment. Install a pinned k6 version with grafana/setup-k6-action, run k6 run, rely on exit code 99 to fail the job, create the results directory first, and upload the summary and HTML report as artifacts. Use a concurrency group so two tests never share the environment.

docs.title: 26. How do you get k6 results into Grafana dashboards?
docs.text: Use the OpenTelemetry output (-o opentelemetry) to send metrics to an OpenTelemetry Collector or to Prometheus's OTLP receiver (Prometheus started with --web.enable-otlp-receiver), then chart them next to the application's own metrics. Tag each run with --tag testid=.... The InfluxDB and Prometheus remote-write outputs were deprecated in k6 2.4 and are planned for removal in k6 3. For a single run, the built-in web dashboard can export a self-contained HTML report.

docs.title: 27. What changed in k6 2.0 that can break a pipeline?
docs.text: The externally-controlled executor, k6 login, --no-summary (use --summary-mode=disabled), the legacy summary mode, and the k6 cloud script.js form (use k6 cloud run) were removed; every k6 cloud command needs a stack; and cloud runs aborted for reasons other than thresholds now exit with 97 instead of 0. Pin the k6 version in CI and upgrade deliberately.

docs.title: 28. How does k6 compare with JMeter, Gatling, Locust, and Artillery?
docs.text: k6 uses JavaScript or TypeScript tests, one Go binary, open and closed executors, and thresholds with an exit code for CI. JMeter uses XML test plans built in a GUI and run in CLI mode, with a huge plugin ecosystem. Gatling uses Java, Kotlin, Scala, or JavaScript code with explicit open and closed injection profiles and assertions. Locust uses Python users with wait times. Artillery uses YAML scenarios with arrival-rate phases and ensure thresholds. Choose the one your team will maintain.

docs.title: 29. What is a bottleneck, and why does fixing one reveal another?
docs.text: The first resource to saturate as load rises; it caps the throughput of the whole system. Once it is fixed, load can rise until the next resource saturates, so capacity grows in steps and each fix should be followed by the same test again.

docs.title: 30. Explain the USE method and apply it to a database connection pool.
docs.text: For every resource, check utilization, saturation, and errors. For a connection pool: utilization is connections in use against maxPoolSize, saturation is the number of requests waiting and their checkout wait time, and errors are checkout timeouts. USE complements RED, which tells you which endpoint hurts.

docs.title: 31. How do you find the knee of the latency curve?
docs.text: Run a step test that raises the offered rate and holds each step. Below the limit, achieved throughput follows the offered load and latency is flat; at the knee, throughput stops following and p95 rises sharply. In a local step test against a 5-connection pool with roughly 21 ms queries, throughput plateaued at about 232 requests per second (5 / 0.0215 is about 233) while p95 rose from 40 ms to 726 ms.

docs.title: 32. What are event-loop utilization and event-loop delay?
docs.text: ELU is the share of time the Node.js event loop is busy running code, from performance.eventLoopUtilization(). Event-loop delay is how late timers fire, from monitorEventLoopDelay(); long synchronous work delays every request in the process. Each delay sample includes the sampling interval, so an idle loop reports roughly the resolution.

docs.title: 33. ELU is low, but latency is high under load. Where do you look?
docs.text: The process is waiting, not computing: look at connection pool waits, slow queries and database saturation, slow dependencies in traces, and locks. A CPU profile would show mostly idle time. More CPU will not help.

docs.title: 34. How do you CPU-profile a Node.js service under load?
docs.text: Start it with node --cpu-prof --cpu-prof-dir=./profiles, apply a steady realistic load, then stop it so it exits normally; the profile is written before exit, so the server needs a shutdown handler that calls process.exit(). Open the .cpuprofile in Chrome DevTools or VS Code, or summarize self time per function with a script.

docs.title: 35. How do you read a flame graph?
docs.text: The x-axis is the population of samples sorted alphabetically, not time; the y-axis is stack depth, with callers below callees; width is how often a frame was on the stack. The top edges are what was running, so wide plateaus at the top are where CPU time goes. A flame chart, as in DevTools, puts time on the x-axis instead.

docs.title: 36. What are Clinic.js and 0x, and should you use them?
docs.text: Both build on Node's profiling. 0x writes an interactive flame graph from a single command and supports Node.js 20 and later. Clinic.js (Doctor, Flame, Bubbleprof, Heap Profiler) carries a notice that it is not being actively maintained and may give inaccurate results on current Node.js; its last release was in 2023. Prefer --cpu-prof, 0x, or a continuous profiler for new work.

docs.title: 37. How do you recognize garbage-collection pressure?
docs.text: Latency spikes that line up with major collections, a large share of time in the (garbage collector) frame or in nodejs_gc_duration_seconds, and a heap that saws up and down fast or keeps a rising floor. Allocate less per request, bound caches, and use heap snapshots for leaks; raising the heap limit only delays a leak.

docs.title: 38. How does explain() reveal a missing index, and what is ESR?
docs.text: Compare nReturned with totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined: returning 20 documents after examining 41,200 means the index does not fit the query; COLLSCAN is a full scan and SORT is an in-memory sort. The ESR guideline orders compound index fields as Equality, Sort, Range, so { ownerId, status } sorted by dueDate wants { ownerId: 1, status: 1, dueDate: 1 }.

docs.title: 39. How does Little's law apply to a connection pool?
docs.text: Busy connections = requests per second × queries per request × seconds per query. At 100 requests per second, 2 queries each, and 50 ms per query, 100 × 2 × 0.05 = 10 connections are busy on average, so a pool of 10 is saturated and requests queue; if the queries drop to 5 ms, only 1 connection is busy.

docs.title: 40. Why can raising maxPoolSize make things worse?
docs.text: If queries are slow because the database is saturated, a bigger pool sends more concurrent work to it, and every query gets slower. More instances multiply the effect, since each has its own pool. Fix the slow queries first, and raise the pool only when the database has headroom.

docs.title: 41. How do you catch N+1 queries before production?
docs.text: Count database commands per request in an integration test, with command monitoring enabled (monitorCommands: true and commandStarted events), and assert that the count does not grow with the page size, for example the same number of find commands for 5 and 50 tasks. Fix N+1 with a batched $in query, $lookup, or embedding.

docs.title: 42. What is chaos engineering?
docs.text: In the words of principlesofchaos.org, "the discipline of experimenting on a system in order to build confidence in the system's capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production". You define steady state, hypothesize that it holds, inject real-world faults, and try to disprove the hypothesis.

docs.title: 43. What is steady state, and what makes a good hypothesis?
docs.text: Steady state is a measurable, user-visible output such as a success rate or a latency percentile. A good hypothesis is specific and falsifiable: "If one of three API instances is terminated, the 5xx rate rises by less than 0.1 percentage points because the load balancer and Auto Scaling group replace it." Do not run experiments you already expect to fail; fix the known weakness first.

docs.title: 44. What is the blast radius, and how do you limit it?
docs.text: How much of the system, and how many users, an experiment can affect. Limit it by environment (test, staging, then production), scope (one pod, one instance, a small percentage of traffic), duration, stop conditions, a tested abort, timing (working hours, off-peak), and announcing the experiment.

docs.title: 45. What are stop conditions?
docs.text: Guardrails that end an experiment automatically when a metric crosses a threshold. AWS FIS uses CloudWatch alarms, up to five per experiment template; with other tools, an alert on steady state and a person with a tested abort command play the same role.

docs.title: 46. Which faults would you inject first for an API like TaskFlow?
docs.text: Faults that really happen, ranked by frequency and impact: losing one instance or pod, latency and failure in a non-critical dependency (such as a notification service), a database primary failover, and later the loss of a zone. Past incidents are the best source of experiments.

docs.title: 47. Compare the main chaos tools.
docs.text: Chaos Monkey randomly terminates instances and containers in production and requires Spinnaker. AWS Fault Injection Service is a managed service with experiment templates and CloudWatch stop conditions. Azure Chaos Studio is the Azure equivalent. Gremlin is a commercial platform. LitmusChaos and Chaos Mesh are CNCF incubating projects for Kubernetes. Toxiproxy is a TCP proxy for injecting network faults in tests and CI.

docs.title: 48. How does Toxiproxy work?
docs.text: It is a TCP proxy placed between your code and a dependency, controlled through an HTTP API (port 8474) or toxiproxy-cli. You create a proxy (listen address and upstream) and add toxics such as latency, timeout, reset_peer, bandwidth, or packet_loss, or disable the proxy to make the dependency unreachable. It is ideal for integration tests that prove timeouts and fallbacks work.

docs.title: 49. What is a game day, and how do you run one?
docs.text: A planned exercise where a team injects a failure into a real system and practises the response. It needs a written plan (scenario, hypothesis, blast radius, abort rules), roles (facilitator, operators who are normally on call, a scribe, a communications lead), a baseline, the injection, a hot debrief, and a written blameless review within a week.

docs.title: 50. How should a team start with chaos engineering?
docs.text: Small: a tabletop exercise, then fault-injection tests with Toxiproxy in CI, then experiments under load in a performance environment, then a game day in staging and production with stop conditions, and finally automated small experiments in production. Climb to the next rung only when the current one has become boring.

docs.title: 51. What do you do with the findings of an experiment or game day?
docs.text: Record the outcome with evidence, turn every weakness into a tracked action with an owner and a date, fix it, re-run the experiment, and automate it as a regression test. Update runbooks, alerts, and dashboards with what responders needed, and share the lessons with other teams.

docs.title: 52. When should you not run a chaos experiment?
docs.text: When there is no monitoring of steady state, when you already know the system will fail, when it has a single point of failure by design, during an incident or freeze, or without a tested stop condition and rollback.

docs.title: 53. A load test passed at 300 requests per second, but production failed at 200 during a launch. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the test differed from production: data volume, endpoint mix, cache state, and workload model.

How to confirm: compare the failing endpoints and queries in production with the test's request mix, and the test database's size with production's.

Likely causes and fixes: a small dataset that fit in memory, a missing expensive endpoint, warm caches, or a closed model that eased off. Use production-sized data, the real mix and peak, an open model, and a cold-cache test. See load testing fundamentals.

docs.title: 54. k6 reports a p99 of 40 ms, but users complain about multi-second freezes. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the executor type and the run's maximum latency.

How to confirm: a closed executor with few VUs and no think time, a maximum far above the p99, and server-side event-loop delay or GC spikes at the same times.

Likely causes and fixes: coordinated omission: the closed loop recorded each freeze once per VU. Re-run with an arrival-rate executor, check dropped_iterations, and find the source of the freezes (a long synchronous task or GC). See load testing fundamentals.

docs.title: 55. Throughput plateaus at 180 requests per second while the API servers sit at 20% CPU. What is the bottleneck?
docs.text:
What to check first: the load generator's health and dropped_iterations, then ELU and the connection pool.

How to confirm: if k6 drops iterations or its CPU is saturated, the test is the limit; if pool checkout waits rise while ELU stays low, the pool or the database is.

Likely causes and fixes: too few VUs or generator hosts, or requests queueing for database connections because of slow queries. Fix the test first, then use Little's law, the profiler, and explain(). See finding bottlenecks.

docs.title: 56. A k6 smoke test in CI fails on some runs and passes on others, with no code change. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: which thresholds fail, and their margins.

How to confirm: latency thresholds fail by small amounts on shared runners, while checks and errors stay clean.

Likely causes and fixes: noisy shared runners and tight latency budgets. Keep PR smoke tests strict on correctness and loose on latency, run latency budgets on dedicated runners or the performance environment, and compare against a baseline rather than a hard number. See load testing with k6.

docs.title: 57. During a four-hour soak test, p99 and memory creep up after the third hour. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: heap used, GC time, open handles and connections, and disk usage over the run.

How to confirm: heap snapshots taken minutes apart show a growing object type, or connection counts rise steadily.

Likely causes and fixes: a memory leak (an unbounded cache, listeners added per request), a connection leak, or logs filling a disk. Fix the leak, bound caches, and keep the soak test in the release checklist. See finding bottlenecks.

docs.title: 58. During a load test, ELU sits at 100% and every endpoint is slow, not just one. What now?
docs.text:
What to check first: a CPU profile of one instance under the same load.

How to confirm: the profile shows one function dominating self time, such as a deep copy or large JSON serialization in one handler.

Likely causes and fixes: synchronous CPU work blocking the event loop for all requests. Optimize the hot function, paginate or project large responses, or move the work to worker threads. See finding bottlenecks.

docs.title: 59. Raising maxPoolSize from 20 to 100 made p95 worse. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: database CPU and query times before and after the change.

How to confirm: the database's CPU and the duration of the slowest queries rose with the extra concurrency.

Likely causes and fixes: the database was the bottleneck; more connections meant more concurrent work on a saturated server. Revert, find the slow queries with the profiler and explain(), and add the missing index. See finding bottlenecks.

docs.title: 60. A breakpoint test aborted at minute 40, but dashboards show latency degrading from minute 25. Which is the real limit?
docs.text:
What to check first: per-minute throughput and p95 from the run, not the summary.

How to confirm: the time series shows throughput flattening and p95 rising at minute 25.

Likely causes and fixes: k6 thresholds are cumulative over the whole test, so the healthy early samples delayed the abort. Read the knee from the time series and treat abortOnFail as a safety stop. See load testing with k6.

docs.title: 61. The nightly k6 job is green, but its summary artifact is missing. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the k6 log for "failed to handle the end-of-test summary".

How to confirm: the results/ directory did not exist when the run ended.

Likely causes and fixes: k6 does not create directories, and a failed handleSummary() write is logged while the exit code stays 0. Run mkdir -p results before the test and fail the job if the artifact is missing. See load testing with k6.

docs.title: 62. After the CI runner picked up a new k6 version, load tests fail with unknown flags or executors. What changed?
docs.text:
What to check first: the k6 version in the job log and the release notes.

How to confirm: the scripts use externally-controlled, --no-summary, k6 login, or k6 cloud script.js, all removed in k6 2.0.

Likely causes and fixes: an unpinned upgrade across a major version. Pin k6-version in grafana/setup-k6-action, migrate to --summary-mode=disabled, k6 cloud login, and k6 cloud run, and upgrade deliberately. See load testing with k6.

docs.title: 63. A chaos experiment kills one API pod and a burst of 502 errors follows. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the pod shuts down and how fast the load balancer and readiness checks react.

How to confirm: errors start when the pod receives SIGTERM and stop when it is removed from the endpoints.

Likely causes and fixes: no graceful shutdown, slow readiness or health checks, or no retries for idempotent requests. Drain connections on SIGTERM, tune readiness probes and deregistration, and retry idempotent requests with backoff. See chaos engineering and game days.

docs.title: 64. You inject 3 s of latency into the notification service, and POST /tasks takes 3 s. What does that tell you?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether the outbound call has a timeout.

How to confirm: the API's response time follows the injected delay exactly.

Likely causes and fixes: a missing timeout, a timeout on a different client, or one longer than the request budget. Add AbortSignal.timeout() with a fallback for this non-critical call, and keep the Toxiproxy test in CI. See chaos engineering and game days.

docs.title: 65. During a game day, the injected failure went unnoticed for 20 minutes. What do you fix?
docs.text:
What to check first: which alerts should have fired and where they were routed.

How to confirm: the scribe's timeline shows no page; the alert rules watch CPU rather than user-facing symptoms.

Likely causes and fixes: alerts on the wrong signals or the wrong routing. Alert on SLO burn rates and symptoms, test paging in the next game day, and add the dashboards responders needed. See chaos engineering and game days.

docs.title: 66. A chaos experiment in production caused a real outage. What do you change?
docs.text:
What to check first: the blast radius, the stop conditions, and whether the same experiment had passed in a lower environment.

How to confirm: the experiment's scope and timeline, and whether the stop condition fired.

Likely causes and fixes: too large a blast radius, a stop condition that was missing or never tested, or skipping lower environments. Run a blameless review, shrink the scope, test the abort, and climb back up the ladder from staging. See chaos engineering and game days.

docs.text:

docs.title: Load Testing Fundamentals
docs.text:
A load test sends realistic traffic to a system on purpose and measures what happens: how fast it answers, how much it can do, and what fails first. This lesson covers how to design one that answers a real question: the main test types and their load shapes, open and closed workload models, think time and pacing, realistic scenarios and test data, where to run tests, what to measure on both sides of the wire, coordinated omission (the measurement error that makes many load tests look far better than reality), and Little's law for sizing a test.

The measurement basics (percentiles, tail latency, the utilization knee) are covered in performance and latency and capacity planning; this page applies them to test design. The tool comes next, in load testing with k6.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Most load-testing failures are design failures, not tool failures. A test that runs 50 virtual users in a tight loop against a staging database with a thousand rows will report excellent numbers, and the launch will still fall over: production has millions of rows that no longer fit in memory, a different mix of endpoints, and users who keep arriving whether or not the site is slow. Capacity decisions (instance counts, database tiers, autoscaling limits) are made from these numbers, so a wrong workload model turns directly into a wrong plan.

A well-designed test is cheap insurance. It finds the limit on a Tuesday afternoon in a performance environment instead of on launch day in front of customers, it shows whether the system degrades gracefully or collapses, and it gives every later change a baseline to be compared against.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Shopify. In Pummelling the Platform: Performance Testing Shopify (2020), Shopify separates load tests (can a service handle a known level of traffic, such as 1 million requests per minute for 15 minutes) from stress tests (raise the load until the service fails). It turns browser sessions recorded as HAR files into load-test flows, shapes the traffic to match the extreme spikes of flash sales, and runs simulated sales against representative test shops dozens of times a day.
  • Google SRE. The SRE book chapter Addressing Cascading Failures says to "load test components until they break", to test both gradual and impulse (sudden) load patterns because they can give different results, and to check whether a component returns to normal without human intervention once the load drops.
  • wrk2 and coordinated omission. Gil Tene's wrk2 README explains why load generators that wait for each response before sending the next one "coordinate" with the server and skip measuring exactly the slow periods. wrk2 sends at a constant rate and measures latency from when each request should have been sent; in the README's example with a server pause, the corrected 99th percentile is about 200 times higher than the uncorrected one.
  • Grafana k6. The k6 documentation on open and closed models notes that in a closed model the iteration rate depends on the target's response time, recommends the arrival-rate executors when you need a fixed rate, and names the problem coordinated omission.

Popular tools and providers: Grafana k6 and Grafana Cloud k6, Apache JMeter, Gatling, Locust, Artillery, wrk2 for single-endpoint benchmarks, and managed runners such as Azure Load Testing (JMeter and Locust scripts) and Distributed Load Testing on AWS (JMeter, k6, and Locust).

docs.title: Test types and their load shapes
docs.text:
Every load test is the same script driven by a different load shape, and each shape answers a different question. The names below follow the k6 documentation's test-types guide; other tools use the same ideas.

Type Question it answers Shape Typical length Passes when Smoke Do the script and the environment work? 1-2 VUs or requests per second 1-2 minutes Zero errors, every check passes Average-load Does the system meet its SLO at the expected peak? Ramp up, hold the expected peak, ramp down 5-60 minutes at the plateau p95, p99, and error-rate thresholds hold Stress How does it behave above the expected load? Ramp to the peak, then step to 1.5-2 times it and hold 5-60 minutes It slows or sheds load with 429/503 instead of collapsing, and recovers afterwards Spike Does it survive a sudden surge, and recover? Jump to several times normal in seconds, hold briefly, drop A few minutes No crash; autoscaling or load shedding reacts; latency returns to normal Soak Does it degrade over time? Expected load held for hours 2-12 hours Latency, errors, memory, connections, and disk stay flat Breakpoint Where is the limit, and what breaks first? One continuous ramp until thresholds fail As long as needed It records the highest throughput that met the SLO and the first resource to saturate

The overview page draws all six shapes side by side. Two details make them trustworthy:

  • Ramp up. A cold system is slower than a warm one: JIT compilation, connection pools, caches, and autoscaling all need time. Ramping over a few minutes avoids measuring the start-up, and the steady part of the run (the plateau) is where you read the results.
  • Ramp down and keep watching. Recovery is part of the answer. A system that is still slow five minutes after the load dropped has a queue, retry storm, or leak that the plateau alone would not show.

docs.title: Open and closed workload models
docs.text:
A workload model describes how new work arrives. It decides what your numbers mean.

In a closed model, a fixed number of virtual users (VUs) each run a loop: send a request, wait for the response, think, repeat. The arrival rate is an output: VUs / (response time + think time). When the server slows down, every VU waits longer, so the test sends less. It models a fixed population that waits for answers: a call-centre team on an internal tool, a pool of 20 worker processes, a mobile app that retries only after a response.

In an open model, new requests (or user sessions) arrive on a schedule, for example 120 per second, whatever the server does. When the server slows down, requests keep arriving and pile up in flight, exactly as they do on a public website where thousands of independent users never coordinate with each other. A partially open model combines both: sessions arrive at a rate, and each session makes several requests with think time between them.

Closed model Open model You set The number of concurrent users (VUs) The arrival rate (requests or sessions per second) Throughput is A result: VUs / (response + think time) An input: fixed by the schedule When the server slows The test sends less; pressure drops Requests queue, concurrency grows, timeouts appear Realistic for Fixed populations that wait for answers Public APIs and websites with many independent users k6 constant-vus, ramping-vus, per-vu-iterations, shared-iterations constant-arrival-rate, ramping-arrival-rate Gatling constantConcurrentUsers, rampConcurrentUsers constantUsersPerSec, rampUsersPerSec JMeter Thread Group Open Model Thread Group, or the Precise Throughput Timer

For a question phrased as a rate ("can we serve 120 requests per second?") use an open model. Use a closed model only when the real system has a fixed population, and say so when you report the results.

docs.title: Think time and pacing
docs.text:
Think time is the pause between one user's actions: reading the task board, typing a title. Without it, every VU becomes a request cannon and the VU count stops meaning anything about real users; 50 VUs with no think time can send more traffic than 5,000 people.

  • Randomize it. Fixed sleeps make VUs march in lock-step and produce artificial waves; a range such as 2-6 seconds spreads them out.
  • Take it from production where you can: the time between requests in a session, from logs or real-user monitoring.
  • Pacing fixes the duration of a whole iteration ("start a session every 10 seconds per user") rather than the pause; it keeps per-user rates stable when response times vary, until a response takes longer than the pacing interval.
  • In an open model a single-request iteration has no think time; the arrival rate already spaces the requests. Think time belongs inside multi-request sessions.

docs.title: Realistic scenarios and test data
docs.text:
A load test is only as realistic as its traffic and its data.

  • Use the production mix. Count requests per route during the busiest hour (see the PromQL in the practical examples) and reproduce the proportions. A test that hammers only GET /tasks misses the expensive POST /tasks path and its index updates.
  • Use the peak, not the average. Plan from the busiest five minutes of a typical busy day, plus known events; peak-to-average ratios of 2-5 are common (see capacity planning).
  • Use production-sized data. With a hundred tasks every query is fast and every index fits in memory. Copy the real data volume and shape (anonymized or synthetic), including heavy users with thousands of tasks.
  • Vary the inputs. Many test users and many task IDs, distributed like production, so caches and the database see realistic hit ratios instead of one hot document.
  • Handle writes. Tests that create data change the dataset. Use a dedicated test tenant, clean up after each run, or restore a snapshot so runs stay comparable.
  • Authenticate realistically. Log in at the rate real users do, not once per request, and not with one shared token if the server caches per token.
  • Stub what you do not own. Never send load to a payment provider, email service, or partner API. Point those calls at sandboxes or stubs, and make sure no real email or charge can leave the test environment.

docs.title: Where to run load tests
docs.text:
Environment Good for Watch out for Laptop Writing scripts, smoke runs Numbers say nothing about capacity CI runner with service containers Short regression budgets, comparing a change with its base branch Shared runners are noisy; use relative comparisons Dedicated performance environment Average-load, stress, spike, soak, breakpoint Must match production sizes and configuration; reset data between runs Shared staging Occasional tests Your test disturbs other teams, and theirs disturbs yours Production Final proof of the real path (CDN, load balancer, database) Real users share the capacity: off-peak, small steps, marked traffic, an abort switch

The load generator must never be the bottleneck. Watch its CPU, memory, and network during every run; when its CPU stays above roughly 80%, its own scheduling delays leak into the latency you measure. Put it close to the system (same region) to measure the service, or near users to include the network, and say which you did. Very high rates need several generator hosts or a managed cloud runner. Tell security teams and CDN or DDoS-protection providers before you send heavy traffic from a few IP addresses; otherwise the test may be blocked as an attack, or worse, it may be measuring the rate limiter.

docs.title: What to measure
docs.text:
Measure from both sides, and compare them:

Side Signals Why Client (load tool) Achieved throughput against the target, latency percentiles per endpoint, error rate by type, failed checks, dropped iterations What users would experience, end to end Server (application) RED per route: request rate, errors, duration histograms What the service itself saw Server (resources) USE: CPU and throttling, memory and GC, event-loop delay, connection pools, database CPU, I/O, and slow queries, queue depth Which resource is saturating, and why Generator CPU, memory, network, dropped iterations Whether the numbers can be trusted at all

A large gap between client-side and server-side latency means time is being spent before the application: in the load balancer, a TCP backlog, a connection pool in front of the app, or the generator itself. Read time series, not only the end-of-test summary: a run whose summary passes can still contain a two-minute meltdown in the middle. Percentiles must come from histograms and must never be averaged across instances (see metrics and dashboards). Turning a saturated resource into a root cause is the subject of finding bottlenecks.

docs.title: Coordinated omission
docs.text:
Real users do not wait for each other. If the server freezes for half a second, every user who arrives during that half second waits. A closed-loop load generator behaves differently: each VU is stuck on its one outstanding request, sends nothing else, and so records one slow sample per VU instead of one per request that real users would have sent. The generator has "coordinated" with the server and omitted the slow period from its own measurements. The result is a p99 that looks excellent while users suffer.

The table in the diagram comes from the script in the practical examples, run three times against a local stand-in server that froze for 500 ms every 5 seconds. Both scenarios saw the same pauses (their maximum latencies are similar), yet the closed loop reported a p99 of 22-36 ms and the open model 468-475 ms. The closed loop also sent fewer requests than the open model in the same 30 seconds (3,249-3,468 against 3,600), without any error to warn you.

How to avoid it:

  • Use an open model (k6's arrival-rate executors) when the question is about a rate.
  • Check that the planned load was delivered. Compare achieved and intended throughput, and treat k6's dropped_iterations metric above zero as a failed test setup: k6 could not start iterations on time, usually because it ran out of pre-allocated VUs.
  • Distrust benchmark p99s from closed loops with few connections and no think time; they measure the server when it is fast.
  • Correct where you cannot change the model. wrk2 measures from the intended send time, and HdrHistogram can compensate when the expected interval between requests is known.

docs.title: Little's law for sizing a test
docs.text:
Little's law states that in a stable system the average number of items inside equals the arrival rate times the time each one stays: L = λ × W. The definition and its capacity uses are covered in performance and latency; here it sizes the test itself.

Worked example. TaskFlow's busiest five minutes reach 120 requests per second, typical responses take 0.15 s, and users pause about 4.85 s between requests:

Closed model (each VU iteration = 1 request + think time)
  W = 0.15 s + 4.85 s           = 5.0 s per iteration
  L = λ × W = 120/s × 5.0 s     = 600 VUs to offer 120 requests/s

  If responses slow to 1.15 s:
  W = 1.15 s + 4.85 s           = 6.0 s
  λ = L / W = 600 / 6.0 s       = 100 requests/s   (17% less load, silently)

Open model (each iteration = 1 request, no think time)
  in flight at 0.15 s: 120/s × 0.15 s = 18 requests
  in flight at 1.15 s: 120/s × 1.15 s = 138 requests
  -> pre-allocate at least 138 VUs (plus headroom) or k6 drops iterations

The k6 documentation gives the same rule for arrival-rate executors: preAllocatedVUs = median iteration duration × rate + a constant for variance. Size for the slowest latency you want to test honestly, not the fastest.

docs.title: Baselines and comparing runs
docs.text:
A single number means little; a change against a baseline means a lot.

  • Keep the script, data snapshot, environment sizes, and configuration under version control, and record the git SHA of the system under test.
  • Warm up, then compare the same steady-state window of each run; exclude the ramps.
  • Run important tests at least twice; differences smaller than the run-to-run spread are noise.
  • Change one thing at a time between runs, or you will not know what helped.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Your question Test to run Model Does my script, or this new endpoint, work under load at all? Smoke Either, 1-2 VUs Will the next release meet the SLO at the weekday peak? Average-load Open What happens on Black Friday at twice the normal peak? Stress Open Will a push notification to every user knock us over? Spike Open Do memory, connections, or disk creep up over a day? Soak Open, at the expected load How many requests per second can one instance take within the SLO? Breakpoint Open, ramping Is a fixed pool of 20 workers fast enough for its queue? Average-load Closed (the real system is closed)

Do not load test (yet) when:

  • There is no agreed question or SLO. Write the pass criteria first.
  • The target is a dependency you do not own, such as a third-party API.
  • You want to know which function is slow. A profiler or a micro-benchmark answers that faster; see finding bottlenecks.
  • The environment is so unlike production that the numbers would only mislead. Fix the environment, or run relative comparisons only.

docs.title: A test plan for TaskFlow API
docs.text:
Test:        TaskFlow API average-load, release 2.14
Question:    Does the API meet its SLO at the expected weekday peak?
Pass:        p95 < 300 ms, p99 < 800 ms, errors < 0.1%, per scenario
             dropped_iterations = 0, generator CPU < 80%
Workload:    open model, 120 requests/s at the plateau
             GET /tasks 62%, GET /tasks/:id 23%, POST /tasks 9%,
             PATCH /tasks/:id 5%, POST /auth/login 1%
Shape:       5 min ramp, 20 min plateau, 2 min ramp down
Data:        perf environment restored from the nightly anonymized snapshot
             (2.1 million tasks, 40,000 users); 500 test users
Environment: same instance types and counts as production (3 API, M30 cluster),
             autoscaling pinned off, third-party email and payments stubbed
Watch:       Grafana "TaskFlow API" and "MongoDB" dashboards, k6 output
Baseline:    release 2.13 run of 2026-11-02

At 120 requests per second the mix becomes 74.4 requests/s for GET /tasks, 27.6 for GET /tasks/:id, 10.8 for POST /tasks, 6.0 for PATCH /tasks/:id, and 1.2 for logins. Autoscaling is pinned off so the test measures fixed capacity; a separate spike test checks autoscaling.

docs.title: Deriving the workload from production metrics
docs.text:
With the request histogram from metrics and dashboards in Prometheus, two queries give the peak rate and the mix:

# Peak request rate over the last 30 days (5-minute resolution)
max_over_time(sum(rate(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[5m]))[30d:5m])

# Share of each route during one busy hour (set the dashboard range to that hour)
sum by (method, route) (increase(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[1h]))
  / scalar(sum(increase(http_request_duration_seconds_count{job="taskflow-api"}[1h])))

The first query returns one number, the busiest five-minute rate. The second returns the fraction of traffic per method and route template for the selected hour. Use the same hour for think-time estimates from your logs.

docs.title: Sizing the test with Little's law
docs.text:
// perf/tools/size-test.js: turn production numbers into load-test settings
const peakRps = 120;            // busiest 5 minutes of the last 30 days, requests/s
const responseS = 0.15;         // typical response time at that load, seconds
const thinkS = 4.85;            // average pause between one user's requests, seconds
const degradedResponseS = 1.15; // a slow day we still want to test honestly

// Little's law: L = lambda x W
const closedVUs = peakRps * (responseS + thinkS);      // users needed in a closed model
const inFlight = peakRps * responseS;                  // requests in flight, open model
const inFlightDegraded = peakRps * degradedResponseS;  // ... when responses slow down
const closedRpsDegraded = closedVUs / (degradedResponseS + thinkS); // what the closed model really sends

const r = (n) => Math.round(n);
console.log(`closed model: ${r(closedVUs)} VUs to offer ${peakRps} requests/s`);
console.log(`open model: ${r(inFlight)} requests in flight at ${responseS} s, ${r(inFlightDegraded)} at ${degradedResponseS} s`);
console.log(`closed model at ${degradedResponseS} s: only ${r(closedRpsDegraded)} requests/s`);

$ node perf/tools/size-test.js
closed model: 600 VUs to offer 120 requests/s
open model: 18 requests in flight at 0.15 s, 138 at 1.15 s
closed model at 1.15 s: only 100 requests/s

docs.title: One session with think time, as a closed or an open model
docs.text:
The same user journey (open the board, read it, open one task, read it) can run as a fixed population or as arriving sessions:

// perf/board-session.js: one user session with think time, as a closed or an open model
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, sleep } from "k6";

const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL;
const params = { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}` } };

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    // Closed: a fixed population of 400 users who read between clicks.
    team_users: {
      executor: "ramping-vus",
      startVUs: 0,
      stages: [
        { duration: "5m", target: 400 },
        { duration: "20m", target: 400 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 0 },
      ],
      exec: "session",
    },
    // Open: 60 new sessions start every second, however slow the API gets.
    arriving_users: {
      executor: "ramping-arrival-rate",
      startRate: 0,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 450, // 60 sessions/s x about 6.8 s per session = 408 busy VUs
      maxVUs: 700,
      stages: [
        { duration: "5m", target: 60 },
        { duration: "20m", target: 60 },
        { duration: "2m", target: 0 },
      ],
      exec: "session",
    },
  },
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300"],
  },
};

export function session() {
  const list = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/tasks?status=open&limit=20`, params);
  check(list, { "list is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  sleep(2 + Math.random() * 4); // reads the board for 2-6 s

  const tasks = list.json("tasks") ?? [];
  if (tasks.length > 0) {
    const task = tasks[Math.floor(Math.random() * tasks.length)];
    const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/tasks/${task.id}`, {
      ...params,
      tags: { name: "GET /tasks/:id" }, // one metric series for every task id
    });
    check(res, { "task is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
    sleep(1 + Math.random() * 3); // reads the task for 1-4 s
  }
}

# Run one scenario at a time (the --scenario flag needs k6 2.3 or later)
k6 run --scenario arriving_users -e BASE_URL=https://perf.taskflow.example.com \
  -e API_TOKEN="$PERF_TEST_TOKEN" perf/board-session.js

Each session makes two requests and lasts about 6.8 s (6.5 s of average think time plus two responses), so both scenarios offer roughly 120 requests per second while the API is healthy: 400 VUs / 6.8 s is about 59 sessions per second, and the open scenario starts 60. The difference appears when the API slows: the closed scenario backs off, the open one does not. If the open scenario runs out of VUs, k6 logs a warning such as Insufficient VUs, reached 700 active VUs and cannot initialize more and counts the skipped sessions in dropped_iterations.

docs.title: Seeing coordinated omission for yourself
docs.text:
This script produced the numbers in the diagram above. Run it against a local test server that blocks its event loop for 500 ms every 5 seconds:

// perf/coordinated-omission-demo.js: one server, a closed and an open workload model
import http from "k6/http";

export const options = {
  scenarios: {
    closed: {
      executor: "constant-vus", // like a classic benchmark: 2 VUs, each waits for its response
      vus: 2,
      duration: "30s",
      exec: "request",
    },
    open: {
      executor: "constant-arrival-rate", // 120 new requests every second, whatever happens
      rate: 120,
      timeUnit: "1s",
      duration: "30s",
      preAllocatedVUs: 100, // Little's law: 120/s x 0.5 s stall = 60 in flight, plus headroom
      maxVUs: 150,
      startTime: "35s", // starts after the closed scenario has finished
      exec: "request",
    },
  },
  // Thresholds on tagged sub-metrics make the summary show each scenario separately.
  thresholds: {
    "http_req_duration{scenario:closed}": ["p(99)>=0"],
    "http_req_duration{scenario:open}": ["p(99)>=0"],
    "http_reqs{scenario:closed}": ["count>=0"],
    "http_reqs{scenario:open}": ["count>=0"],
  },
  summaryTrendStats: ["med", "p(90)", "p(99)", "max"],
};

const params = { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${__ENV.API_TOKEN}` } };

export function request() {
  http.get(`${__ENV.BASE_URL}/tasks?limit=20`, params);
}

# Excerpt from one run (k6 2.4.0)
http_req_duration{scenario:closed}
✓ 'p(99)>=0' p(99)=22.43ms
http_req_duration{scenario:open}
✓ 'p(99)>=0' p(99)=475.16ms
http_reqs{scenario:closed}
✓ 'count>=0' count=3468
http_reqs{scenario:open}
✓ 'count>=0' count=3601

The always-true thresholds (p(99)>=0) are a common trick to make k6 print per-scenario numbers; they never fail. The two VUs of the closed scenario saw the same pauses, but recorded only a handful of slow samples and quietly sent fewer requests than the 3,600 the open scenario delivered.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Write the question and the pass criteria, derived from the SLO, before writing the script.
  • Use an open model for anything phrased as a rate; document it whenever you use a closed one.
  • Take the endpoint mix, peak rate, and think time from production metrics and logs, not from guesses.
  • Test against production-sized data in a production-like environment, and reset the data between runs.
  • Run a smoke test before every bigger test.
  • Ramp up, hold a steady plateau, ramp down, and keep watching recovery.
  • Monitor the load generator and treat dropped_iterations above zero as an invalid run.
  • Read time series on both sides, not only the summary.
  • Size VUs with Little's law for the slowest latency you want to measure.
  • Keep scripts, data, environment details, and results versioned, and compare against a baseline.
  • Stub third parties and warn anyone who could mistake your test for an attack.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The test passed, but production failed at lower traffic. Detect: an incident at a request rate below the tested one; the failing endpoint or query never appeared in the test results. Cause: an unrealistic test: small data that fit in memory, a missing endpoint in the mix, warm caches, or a closed model that eased off. Fix: production-sized data, the mix and peak from real metrics, an open model, and a test of the cold-cache case.
  • The load test shows a fine p99, yet users report multi-second freezes. Detect: real-user monitoring or support tickets disagree with the test; the test's maximum latency is far above its p99. Cause: coordinated omission in a closed-loop test, or percentiles averaged over instances. Fix: rerun with an arrival-rate executor, check dropped_iterations, and compute percentiles from merged histograms.
  • Throughput plateaus below the target while the servers are idle. Detect: achieved requests per second stay under the target, server CPU is low, and the generator's CPU is high or dropped_iterations grows. Cause: the generator is the bottleneck: too few VUs, too little CPU, or connection reuse disabled. Fix: pre-allocate more VUs, add generator hosts, and watch generator metrics in every run.
  • Identical runs differ by 30%. Detect: p95 and throughput vary widely between back-to-back runs of the same commit. Cause: shared or noisy environments, autoscaling starting from different sizes, data growth from earlier runs, or no warm-up. Fix: a dedicated environment, data reset, fixed instance counts, a warm-up period, and at least two runs per comparison.
  • Latency creeps up after three hours of a soak test. Detect: p99 and memory rise slowly while the load is flat; restarts "fix" it. Cause: a memory, connection, or file-handle leak, an unbounded cache, or a disk filling with logs. Fix: chart heap, handles, pool sizes, and disk during soaks, then find the leak with heap snapshots (see finding bottlenecks).
  • The test is blocked, or measures the wrong thing. Detect: a sudden wall of 403 or 429 responses from the edge, not from the application. Cause: a WAF, rate limiter, or DDoS protection treating the generator's few IP addresses as an attack. Fix: agree on allow-listed sources with the security team and provider, or test behind the edge when the edge is not what you are measuring.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Load test: Sending controlled, realistic traffic to a system to measure its behaviour.
  • Smoke, average-load, stress, spike, soak, breakpoint test: Load shapes that answer different questions, from "does it work" to "where does it break".
  • Virtual user (VU): One simulated client running the test script in a loop.
  • Workload model: How new work arrives in a test: closed, open, or partially open.
  • Closed model: A fixed number of users who wait for each response; the arrival rate depends on response time.
  • Open model: Work arrives at a set rate regardless of response time.
  • Think time: The pause between one user's actions.
  • Pacing: Fixing how often an iteration starts rather than how long the pause is.
  • Arrival rate: New requests or sessions per second.
  • Coordinated omission: Missing the slow periods because the load generator waits for the server before sending more.
  • Little's law: L = λ × W; items in the system equal arrival rate times time in the system.
  • Dropped iterations: Iterations an arrival-rate executor could not start on time, usually for lack of VUs.
  • Baseline: A stored earlier result that later runs are compared with.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• "More VUs means more realistic." With no think time, a few VUs send more than thousands of real users; with a closed model, VUs hide slowness.
  • Measuring the average latency, or the p99 of a closed-loop benchmark, and calling it the user experience.
  • Testing against a tiny or unrealistic dataset.
  • Treating the load generator as infinitely fast.
  • Reading only the end-of-test summary and missing a meltdown mid-run.
  • Running a single test once and drawing conclusions from small differences.
  • Load testing a third-party API or a shared environment without permission.
  • Starting with a stress or breakpoint test before a smoke test has shown the script works.
  • Assuming a passing test still holds after the code, data, or infrastructure changed.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Name six load-test types and the question each one answers.
  2. What is the difference between an open and a closed workload model, and which fits a public API?
  3. Why does a closed-loop load generator under-report tail latency? Explain coordinated omission with an example.
  4. A test must offer 300 requests per second. Each user iteration makes one request with a 0.2 s response time and 2.8 s of think time. How many VUs does a closed model need? If responses slow to 1.2 s, what rate does that closed test actually send? How many VUs would an arrival-rate executor need at 1.2 s? (900 VUs; 900 / 4.0 = 225 requests/s; 300 x 1.2 = 360 VUs.)
  5. Where would you get a realistic endpoint mix and peak rate for a test?
  6. Which signals tell you the load generator, not the system, limited a test?
  7. Why should a soak test chart memory, connections, and disk, and not only latency?
  8. Your client-side p95 is 900 ms but the application's own p95 is 120 ms. Where is the time going?

docs.text:
