docs.title: Load Testing with k6
docs.text:
Grafana k6 is an open-source load-testing tool: you describe the traffic in a JavaScript (or TypeScript) file, and a single Go binary generates it, measures every request, and decides pass or fail from thresholds you write. This lesson builds a complete k6 suite for TaskFlow API: the test lifecycle, scenarios and executors, thresholds, checks, tags and groups, test data, one shared workload driven by several load shapes, running in GitHub Actions with a pass/fail gate, and sending results to dashboards. It ends with a short comparison with JMeter, Gatling, Locust, and Artillery.

The examples use k6 2.x: version 2.0.0 was released in May 2026 and 2.4.0 is current at the time of writing. Choosing the load shape and the workload model is covered in load testing fundamentals; a short smoke test as a CI quality gate is introduced in testing and quality gates.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
A load test is only useful if it is repeatable, reviewable, and able to fail a build. k6 treats a test as code: scripts live in the repository next to the API, changes go through pull requests, and thresholds turn the SLO into an exit code that CI understands. Because it is one binary with no runtime to install, the same command runs on a laptop, in a GitHub Actions job, and on a dedicated load-generator host.

The flip side is that k6 does exactly what the script says. A script that uses the wrong executor, forgets to group URLs, or has no thresholds will produce confident, useless numbers. Knowing how k6 schedules work, aggregates metrics, and evaluates thresholds is what makes the results trustworthy.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• GitLab. The GitLab Performance Tool is "built upon" k6 and provides tests of GitLab's server performance; GitLab uses it to continuously validate the performance of its published reference architectures through scheduled pipelines.
  • Grafana Labs. In How we use the k6 load-testing tool for developing Grafana (2021), Grafana engineers describe using k6 to test token refresh across several Grafana instances before shipping, to reproduce a spike of 500 errors behind an authentication proxy and verify the fix, and to compare a slow database query against different indexes and a rewrite.
  • k6 itself. The k6 v2.0.0 release notes list what changed in the current major version: the externally-controlled executor, k6 login, and the --no-summary flag were removed, and cloud runs that abort for reasons other than thresholds now exit with code 97 instead of 0, so CI cannot mistake them for a pass.

Popular tools and providers: k6 (open source, AGPL-3.0), Grafana Cloud k6 for managed and distributed runs, the k6 Operator for distributed tests in Kubernetes, the grafana/setup-k6-action and grafana/run-k6-action GitHub Actions, Apache JMeter, Gatling, Locust, and Artillery.

docs.title: The test lifecycle
docs.text:
A k6 script has four stages, and knowing which code runs when prevents most surprises:

Stage Runs Typical use Init code (top level of the file) Once per VU Imports, options, open() of local files, SharedArray setup() Once, before the load Log in test users, create fixtures; the return value is passed on VU code (default or a scenario's exec function) Once per iteration The requests, checks, and custom metrics teardown(data) Once, after the load Delete data the test created handleSummary(data) Once, at the very end Write the summary to files or the terminal

Two rules follow from the table. Init code cannot make HTTP requests, so logins belong in setup() or in the VU code. And setup() can only pass data (JSON), not functions; each VU receives its own copy.

docs.title: Not Node.js
docs.text:
k6 runs scripts in its own JavaScript runtime (Sobek) inside a Go binary, and each VU has its own copy of that runtime. That has consequences:

  • Node built-ins (fs, process, Buffer from Node) and npm packages are not available directly. k6 has its own modules (k6/http, k6/data, k6/metrics, k6/execution), imports local files and remote modules such as the jslib libraries at jslib.k6.io, and accepts code bundled from npm.
  • k6 2.x runs .ts files directly; the TypeScript types are stripped, not checked, so run tsc separately if you want type checking.
  • Memory grows with VUs. Data loaded with open() is copied into every VU; wrap large test data in a SharedArray so it is stored once, and set discardResponseBodies when the script never reads the bodies.
  • Environment values arrive through __ENV: -e NAME=value on the command line, or the real environment variables of the process (passed through by default).

docs.title: Scenarios and executors
docs.text:
A scenario describes one workload: which function to run, with which executor, at what load, starting when. A script can run several scenarios at once, each with its own executor, tags, and environment. k6 2.x has six executors:

Executor Model You set Good for constant-arrival-rate Open Iterations per time unit, duration, VU budget A fixed request rate (average-load, soak) ramping-arrival-rate Open Stages of target rates, VU budget Ramps, stress, spike, breakpoint constant-vus Closed VUs and duration A fixed population of users or workers ramping-vus Closed Stages of target VUs A population that grows and shrinks shared-iterations Closed Total iterations shared by VUs Running a fixed amount of work as fast as possible per-vu-iterations Closed Iterations each VU must run Each VU processing its own slice of data

The externally-controlled executor, which let k6 scale and k6 pause change a running test, was removed in k6 2.0. Every scenario also accepts startTime, gracefulStop (30 seconds by default), exec, env, and tags.

Arrival-rate executors need a VU budget: preAllocatedVUs are created before the test, and k6 adds more up to maxVUs when iterations last longer than expected. Creating VUs mid-test costs CPU and time, so a sudden spike served by VUs that are still starting drops iterations. Size the budget with Little's law (rate times iteration duration, see load testing fundamentals) and watch dropped_iterations; when k6 runs out it logs Insufficient VUs, reached N active VUs and cannot initialize more.

From k6 2.3, --scenario name1,name2 runs only the named scenarios of a script, and --once runs the script (or each selected scenario) with one VU and one iteration, which is handy for checking a script before a long run.

docs.title: Metrics k6 records
docs.text:
Every HTTP request produces several built-in metrics:

Metric Type Meaning http_reqs Counter Requests made http_req_duration Trend Total request time: sending + waiting + receiving http_req_waiting Trend Time to first byte, the server's share http_req_blocked, http_req_connecting, http_req_tls_handshaking Trend Waiting for a connection slot, TCP connect, TLS handshake http_req_failed Rate Share of responses not marked as expected (by default, statuses outside 200-399) checks Rate Share of successful checks iterations, iteration_duration Counter, Trend Completed iterations and their length dropped_iterations Counter Iterations an arrival-rate executor could not start vus, vus_max Gauge Active and allocated VUs

Which statuses count as expected is configurable with http.setResponseCallback(http.expectedStatuses(...)) or a per-request responseCallback; a 404 your test expects should not raise http_req_failed. Custom metrics come from k6/metrics (Counter, Gauge, Rate, Trend).

docs.title: Thresholds: the pass/fail gate
docs.text:
A threshold is a condition on a metric, in the form <aggregation> <operator> <value>. The aggregations depend on the metric type: count and rate for counters, value for gauges, rate for rates, and avg, min, max, med, and p(N) for trends (in milliseconds).

http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"]                          fewer than 0.1% failed requests
http_req_duration: ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"]           latency SLO
"http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks}": ["p(95)<300"]      one endpoint only (tag filter)
"checks{scenario:write}": ["rate>0.999"]                 one scenario only
dropped_iterations: ["count==0"]                         the planned load was delivered
http_req_duration: [{ threshold: "p(95)<1000", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "1m" }]

When any threshold fails, k6 marks it with a cross and exits with code 99; when all pass, it exits with 0. That exit code is the whole CI integration. Three behaviours are worth knowing:

  • Thresholds are cumulative. k6 computes each one from every sample since the start of the test, not over a sliding window. In a local check where the server slowed from 8 ms to 300 ms per query 20 seconds into a run, a median threshold with abortOnFail tripped at 40 seconds, when half of all samples were slow. For breakpoint tests, read the knee from the time series, not from the moment of the abort.
  • abortOnFail stops the test early when a threshold is crossed; delayAbortEval waits until enough samples exist, so a few slow requests during warm-up do not end the run.
  • Thresholds on tagged sub-metrics (metric{tag:value}) are how you hold each endpoint or scenario to its own target. They also make the summary print those sub-metrics.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text: A check asserts something about a response (status, a header, a field in the body) and records the result in the checks metric. A failing check does not fail the test or stop the iteration; it is a counted observation. To gate on checks, add a threshold such as checks: ["rate>0.999"]. Use fail() from k6 (or throw) when the iteration genuinely cannot continue, such as a failed login in setup().

docs.title: Tags, groups, and URL grouping
docs.text:
Every metric sample carries tags. k6 adds system tags such as method, status, url, name, group, check, scenario, and expected_response; you add your own per request (tags: { name: ... }), per scenario (tags in the scenario), or for the whole run (--tag testid=nightly-42 or options.tags). Tags drive thresholds, summaries, and dashboards.

The name tag matters most. By default it holds the full URL, so /tasks/6650f1c2... and /tasks/6650f1c3... become different series, one per task: useless in a summary and expensive in a metrics backend. Give requests a route-template name (tags: { name: "GET /tasks/:id" }) or build the URL with the http.url template tag, which strips the dynamic parts from the name. This is the same cardinality rule as for application metrics (see metrics and dashboards).

group() nests requests under a name (for example one user journey) and records group_duration; the group tag holds the path such as ::checkout.

docs.title: Results and outputs
docs.text:
At the end of a run k6 prints a summary in compact mode by default; --summary-mode=full adds per-group and per-scenario results, and --summary-mode=disabled replaces the --no-summary flag removed in 2.0. --summary-trend-stats chooses the statistics shown for trends (the default is avg, min, med, max, p(90), p(95)), and --summary-export writes the summary as JSON. A handleSummary() function replaces the default output entirely and can write any files you like.

Output How Use Web dashboard K6_WEB_DASHBOARD=true (or --out web-dashboard); HTML report with K6_WEB_DASHBOARD_EXPORT Watch a run live on port 5665; attach a self-contained report to CI JSON or CSV files --out json=results/metrics.json, --out csv=results/metrics.csv Every sample, for offline analysis OpenTelemetry -o opentelemetry, configured with K6_OTEL_* variables Stream metrics to a collector or Prometheus and view them in Grafana Grafana Cloud k6 k6 cloud run, or k6 cloud run --local-execution Managed storage, comparison, and distributed load Prometheus remote write, InfluxDB experimental-prometheus-rw, influxdb Deprecated in k6 2.4, planned for removal in k6 3; migrate to OpenTelemetry

k6 does not create output directories. A missing results/ directory makes --out csv fail at start-up, and makes handleSummary() log "failed to handle the end-of-test summary" while the run still exits with code 0, so create the directory first. The dashboard report is skipped for very short runs (it needs more than three update periods, 10 seconds each by default).

docs.title: Running k6 in CI
docs.text:
The usual split, as in testing and quality gates:

When Test Against Gate Every pull request Smoke, 1 VU for a minute The API started inside the CI job Fails the PR on any failed check or request Nightly or before a release Average-load, 25-30 minutes The dedicated performance environment Fails the run on SLO thresholds; report as an artifact Before big events, monthly Stress, spike, breakpoint, soak The performance environment Reviewed by a person; results feed capacity planning

Two GitHub Actions help: grafana/setup-k6-action installs k6 (pin the version with k6-version), and grafana/run-k6-action wraps k6 run with glob patterns, parallel and fail-fast options, a k6 inspect check of each script before it runs, and Grafana Cloud k6 integration when K6_CLOUD_TOKEN is set. Plain k6 run after the setup action is enough for most pipelines.

docs.title: Bigger loads and distributed runs
docs.text:
One k6 process can generate a lot of load, but every request still costs CPU on the generator. When one host is not enough:

  • split the test across hosts with --execution-segment and --execution-segment-sequence, so each host runs its share of every scenario;
  • run it in Kubernetes with the k6 Operator, whose TestRun custom resource describes one test that the operator runs distributed across the cluster;
  • or use Grafana Cloud k6, which runs the load from managed load zones.

docs.title: k6 compared with other tools
docs.text:
k6 Apache JMeter Gatling Locust Artillery Tests written as JavaScript or TypeScript XML test plans (.jmx), usually built in a GUI Java, Kotlin, Scala, or JavaScript/TypeScript code Python code YAML scenarios with JavaScript hooks Runs on A single Go binary The JVM The JVM (plus a JavaScript SDK) Python Node.js Open model Arrival-rate executors Open Model Thread Group, Precise Throughput Timer injectOpen (users per second) Not built in: users loop with a wait_time arrivalRate phases (new VUs per second) Closed model VU executors Thread Groups injectClosed (concurrent users) Users with wait_time Not built in; maxVusers only caps concurrency CI pass/fail Thresholds, exit code 99 No built-in gate: parse the results file or use a wrapper such as Taurus Assertions fail the simulation --exit-code-on-error on any failure ensure thresholds, non-zero exit Licence AGPL-3.0 Apache 2.0 Apache 2.0 (Community Edition) MIT MPL-2.0 (most of the code)

All five are mature. Choose k6 when the team writes JavaScript and wants tests as code with thresholds in CI; JMeter when you need its very wide protocol support and plugin ecosystem, and run it in CLI mode (its own documentation says not to load test in GUI mode); Gatling for JVM teams and explicit open and closed injection profiles; Locust when the team works in Python; Artillery for YAML-first scenarios and browser tests with Playwright. Latest releases at the time of writing: JMeter 5.6.3, Gatling 3.16, Locust 2.47, and Artillery 2.0.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Use k6? Notes HTTP, WebSocket, or gRPC APIs, tests reviewed as code Yes The core use case Pass/fail performance budgets in CI Yes Thresholds and exit code 99 Load from many regions or very high rates Yes, distributed Execution segments, the k6 Operator, or Grafana Cloud k6 Real browser timings (Web Vitals) under light load Yes, with the browser module Browsers are heavy; keep browser VUs few and generate load with protocol VUs A team fluent in Python or the JVM only Consider Locust or Gatling Use the language the team will maintain Protocols k6 does not support natively Check extensions, or JMeter k6 extensions (xk6) cover some protocols Finding which function is slow No Use a profiler; see finding bottlenecks

docs.title: Project layout
docs.text:
perf/
  lib/
    taskflow.js       HTTP helpers: one function per endpoint, with checks and name tags
    workload.js       the production mix, setup(), and a load-shape helper
    summary.js        handleSummary(): terminal output plus results/summary.json
  data/
    users.json        test accounts (emails only; the password comes from the environment)
  smoke.js            1 VU for a minute, every endpoint
  average-load.js     the weekday peak for 20 minutes
  stress.js           twice the peak, then recovery
  spike.js            five times the peak in 30 seconds
  breakpoint.js       ramp until the SLO breaks
  soak.js             the peak for four hours

One workload, many shapes: the endpoint functions and the traffic mix live in lib/, and each test file only states its load shape and thresholds. perf/data/users.json is a JSON array of objects such as { "email": "perf-user-1@example.com" }.

docs.title: Endpoint helpers with checks and route names
docs.text:
// perf/lib/taskflow.js: HTTP helpers shared by every TaskFlow load test
import http from "k6/http";
import { check, fail } from "k6";

export const BASE_URL = __ENV.BASE_URL || "http://localhost:3000";
const JSON_HEADERS = { "Content-Type": "application/json" };

function params(token, name) {
  return {
    headers: { ...JSON_HEADERS, Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
    tags: { name }, // a route template, so /tasks/<id> URLs share one metric series
  };
}

export function login(email, password) {
  const res = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/auth/login`, JSON.stringify({ email, password }), {
    headers: JSON_HEADERS,
    tags: { name: "POST /auth/login" },
  });
  if (!check(res, { "login is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 })) {
    fail(`login failed for ${email}: HTTP ${res.status}`); // aborts setup, so the test stops
  }
  return res.json("token");
}

export function listTasks(token) {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/tasks?status=open&limit=20`, params(token, "GET /tasks"));
  check(res, {
    "list is 200": (r) => r.status === 200,
    "list has a tasks array": (r) => Array.isArray(r.json("tasks")),
  });
  return res;
}

export function getTask(token, id) {
  const res = http.get(`${BASE_URL}/tasks/${id}`, params(token, "GET /tasks/:id"));
  check(res, { "get is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  return res;
}

export function createTask(token, title) {
  const res = http.post(`${BASE_URL}/tasks`, JSON.stringify({ title }), params(token, "POST /tasks"));
  check(res, { "create is 201": (r) => r.status === 201 });
  return res;
}

export function updateTask(token, id, status) {
  const res = http.patch(`${BASE_URL}/tasks/${id}`, JSON.stringify({ status }), params(token, "PATCH /tasks/:id"));
  check(res, { "update is 200": (r) => r.status === 200 });
  return res;
}

Every request gets a route-template name, so thresholds and dashboards can address GET /tasks/:id as one series. res.json("tasks") reads one field of the JSON body with a path selector.

docs.title: The shared workload
docs.text:
// perf/lib/workload.js: the TaskFlow production mix, shared by every load shape
import { SharedArray } from "k6/data";
import exec from "k6/execution";
import { login, listTasks, getTask, createTask, updateTask } from "./taskflow.js";

// Loaded once and shared by all VUs; passwords come from the environment, never the file.
const users = new SharedArray("test users", () => JSON.parse(open("../data/users.json")));

export function setup() {
  const tokens = [];
  for (const user of users) tokens.push(login(user.email, __ENV.TEST_USER_PASSWORD));
  return { tokens };
}

function tokenFor(data) {
  return data.tokens[exec.vu.idInTest % data.tokens.length];
}

// Reads: GET /tasks (62% of traffic), followed 37% of the time by GET /tasks/:id (23%).
export function browse(data) {
  const token = tokenFor(data);
  const tasks = listTasks(token).json("tasks") ?? [];
  if (tasks.length > 0 && Math.random() < 0.37) {
    getTask(token, tasks[Math.floor(Math.random() * tasks.length)].id);
  }
}

// Writes: POST /tasks (9%), followed 56% of the time by PATCH /tasks/:id (5%).
export function write(data) {
  const token = tokenFor(data);
  const res = createTask(token, `load test ${exec.scenario.iterationInTest}`);
  if (res.status === 201 && Math.random() < 0.56) updateTask(token, res.json("id"), "done");
}

// One load shape for both kinds of traffic. `peak: 1` is the weekday peak:
// 74 browse + 11 write iterations per second, about 120 requests/s.
export function scenarios(stages, { preAllocatedVUs = 50, maxVUs = 300 } = {}) {
  const at = (perSecondAtPeak) =>
    stages.map((s) => ({ duration: s.duration, target: Math.round(s.peak * perSecondAtPeak) }));
  const base = { executor: "ramping-arrival-rate", startRate: 0, timeUnit: "1s" };
  const quarter = (n) => Math.ceil(n / 4); // writes are 11 of every 85 iterations
  return {
    browse: { ...base, exec: "browse", preAllocatedVUs, maxVUs, stages: at(74) },
    write: { ...base, exec: "write", preAllocatedVUs: quarter(preAllocatedVUs), maxVUs: quarter(maxVUs), stages: at(11) },
  };
}

// The SLO as thresholds, plus a guard that the planned load was really delivered.
export const sloThresholds = {
  http_req_failed: ["rate<0.001"],
  "http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks}": ["p(95)<300", "p(99)<800"],
  "http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks/:id}": ["p(95)<200"],
  "http_req_duration{name:POST /tasks}": ["p(95)<400"],
  checks: ["rate>0.999"],
  dropped_iterations: ["count==0"],
};

What each part does:

  • SharedArray reads users.json once for all VUs. open() resolves the path relative to the module that calls it, so ../data/users.json from lib/ finds perf/data/users.json.
  • setup() logs every test user in once, before the load starts, and returns their tokens; each VU then uses one token chosen by its test-wide VU number (exec.vu.idInTest).
  • browse and write reproduce the production mix: 74 browse and 11 write iterations per second give about 74 + 27 + 11 + 6 = 118 requests per second at the peak.
  • scenarios(stages) turns a list of stages, written as multiples of the peak, into two ramping-arrival-rate scenarios, so every load shape keeps the same mix.
  • sloThresholds is the SLO, endpoint by endpoint, plus dropped_iterations: ["count==0"], which fails the run when k6 could not deliver the planned load.

docs.title: The average-load test
docs.text:
// perf/average-load.js: the expected weekday peak, held for 20 minutes
import { scenarios, sloThresholds } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { setup, browse, write } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { handleSummary } from "./lib/summary.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: scenarios([
    { duration: "5m", peak: 1 },  // ramp up to about 120 requests/s
    { duration: "20m", peak: 1 }, // hold: read the results from this window
    { duration: "2m", peak: 0 },  // ramp down and watch recovery
  ]),
  thresholds: sloThresholds,
  tags: { test: "average-load" },
};

// perf/lib/summary.js: keep the terminal summary and also write a JSON file for CI
import { textSummary } from "https://jslib.k6.io/k6-summary/0.1.0/index.js";

export function handleSummary(data) {
  return {
    stdout: textSummary(data, { indent: " ", enableColors: true }),
    // k6 does not create directories: run `mkdir -p results` first
    "results/summary.json": JSON.stringify(data, null, 2),
  };
}

mkdir -p results
k6 run -e BASE_URL=https://perf.taskflow.example.com perf/average-load.js
# TEST_USER_PASSWORD is read from the environment, never typed on the command line

The scenario functions are re-exported from the shared module, which is how k6 finds setup, browse, and write by name. handleSummary() replaces the default terminal output, so it prints the standard text summary itself (with the jslib textSummary helper) as well as writing the JSON file.

docs.title: A smoke test
docs.text:
// perf/smoke.js: one user touching every endpoint for a minute
import { sleep } from "k6";
import { login, listTasks, getTask, createTask, updateTask } from "./lib/taskflow.js";

export const options = {
  vus: 1,
  duration: "1m",
  thresholds: {
    checks: ["rate==1"],        // every check must pass
    http_req_failed: ["rate==0"],
  },
};

export function setup() {
  return { token: login(__ENV.TEST_USER_EMAIL, __ENV.TEST_USER_PASSWORD) };
}

export default function ({ token }) {
  listTasks(token);
  const created = createTask(token, `smoke ${Date.now()}`);
  const id = created.json("id");
  getTask(token, id);
  updateTask(token, id, "done");
  sleep(1);
}

A smoke test is strict on correctness (every check, no failed requests) and loose on latency; its job is to prove that the script, the test data, and the environment work before anyone spends 30 minutes on a bigger run.

docs.title: Stress, spike, breakpoint, and soak with the same workload
docs.text:
// perf/stress.js: twice the weekday peak for 20 minutes; it may degrade, it must not fall over
import { scenarios } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { setup, browse, write } from "./lib/workload.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: scenarios([
    { duration: "5m", peak: 1 },
    { duration: "5m", peak: 2 },  // step to 2x (about 240 requests/s)
    { duration: "20m", peak: 2 },
    { duration: "5m", peak: 0 },  // recovery is part of the test
  ], { preAllocatedVUs: 100, maxVUs: 600 }),
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.01"],    // degraded but serving: under 1% errors
    http_req_duration: ["p(95)<1000"],
    dropped_iterations: ["count==0"],
  },
  tags: { test: "stress" },
};

// perf/spike.js: a push notification sends five times the peak in 30 seconds
import { scenarios } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { setup, browse, write } from "./lib/workload.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: scenarios([
    { duration: "2m", peak: 0.5 },
    { duration: "3m", peak: 0.5 },
    { duration: "30s", peak: 5 },   // the surge
    { duration: "2m", peak: 5 },
    { duration: "30s", peak: 0.5 }, // back to normal: does latency recover?
    { duration: "5m", peak: 0.5 },
  ], { preAllocatedVUs: 400, maxVUs: 1500 }), // VUs started mid-spike arrive too late
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: ["rate<0.05"],
  },
  tags: { test: "spike" },
};

// perf/breakpoint.js: ramp until the SLO breaks, then stop on our own
import { scenarios } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { setup, browse, write } from "./lib/workload.js";

export const options = {
  // 0 to 8 times the peak (about 960 requests/s) over 30 minutes
  scenarios: scenarios([{ duration: "30m", peak: 8 }], { preAllocatedVUs: 200, maxVUs: 2000 }),
  thresholds: {
    http_req_failed: [{ threshold: "rate<0.01", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "1m" }],
    http_req_duration: [{ threshold: "p(95)<1000", abortOnFail: true, delayAbortEval: "1m" }],
  },
  tags: { test: "breakpoint" },
};

// perf/soak.js: the weekday peak for four hours, looking for slow leaks
import { scenarios, sloThresholds } from "./lib/workload.js";
export { setup, browse, write } from "./lib/workload.js";

export const options = {
  scenarios: scenarios([
    { duration: "10m", peak: 1 },
    { duration: "4h", peak: 1 },
    { duration: "5m", peak: 0 },
  ]),
  thresholds: sloThresholds,
  tags: { test: "soak" },
};

Notes on the shapes:

  • Stress relaxes the thresholds to "degraded but serving", because the question is how the system fails, not whether it meets the normal SLO.
  • Spike pre-allocates 400 VUs: at five times the peak, 370 browse iterations per second that slow to about a second each need roughly 370 VUs, and VUs created during the surge start too late.
  • Breakpoint stops itself when 1% of requests fail or p95 passes 1 second. Because thresholds are cumulative, find the real knee in the time series (throughput against p95 per minute) rather than at the moment of the abort.
  • Soak reuses the normal SLO; what you watch is the trend of memory, connections, and latency over the four hours, not the final summary.

docs.title: A pull-request smoke test in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/perf-smoke.yml
name: perf-smoke
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["src/**", "perf/**", "package-lock.json"]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  k6-smoke:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    services:
      mongo:
        image: mongo:8.0
        ports: ["27017:27017"]
    env:
      MONGODB_URI: mongodb://localhost:27017/taskflow_perf
      PORT: "3000"
      BASE_URL: http://localhost:3000
      TEST_USER_EMAIL: perf-user-1@example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - name: Create a throwaway password for the seeded test users
        run: |
          pw="$(openssl rand -hex 16)"
          echo "::add-mask::$pw"
          echo "TEST_USER_PASSWORD=$pw" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Seed test data and start the API in the background
        run: |
          npm run seed:perf          # the project's seed script: test users and sample tasks
          npm start > api.log 2>&1 &
          curl --retry 30 --retry-connrefused --retry-delay 1 -fsS "$BASE_URL/healthz"
      - uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
        with:
          k6-version: "2.4.0"
      - name: k6 smoke test (exit code 99 fails the job)
        run: |
          mkdir -p results
          k6 run --summary-export=results/smoke-summary.json perf/smoke.js
      - if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: k6-smoke
          path: |
            results/
            api.log
          retention-days: 7

The job starts its own MongoDB service container and TaskFlow API, so the test never touches a shared environment and fork pull requests need no secrets: the password for the seeded users is generated in the job and masked in the logs. curl --retry-connrefused waits until the API answers its health check. Pinning k6-version keeps a k6 upgrade from changing results or breaking scripts without a reviewed change.

docs.title: A nightly average-load test against the performance environment
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/perf-nightly.yml
name: perf-nightly
on:
  schedule:
    - cron: "30 1 * * 1-5"   # 01:30 UTC, Monday to Friday
  workflow_dispatch:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: perf-environment     # never two load tests against the same environment
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  average-load:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 45
    environment: perf
    env:
      BASE_URL: https://perf.taskflow.example.com
      TEST_USER_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.PERF_TEST_PASSWORD }}
      K6_WEB_DASHBOARD: "true"
      K6_WEB_DASHBOARD_PORT: "-1"                  # no live server in CI, only the report
      K6_WEB_DASHBOARD_EXPORT: results/report.html
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: grafana/setup-k6-action@v1
        with:
          k6-version: "2.4.0"
      - name: Average-load test
        run: |
          mkdir -p results
          k6 run --tag testid="nightly-${{ github.run_id }}" perf/average-load.js
      - if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: k6-average-load
          path: results/
          retention-days: 30

The concurrency group queues runs instead of letting two tests share the performance environment and spoil each other's numbers. The artifact holds summary.json (from handleSummary()) and the HTML dashboard report, which can be opened without any server. With grafana/run-k6-action@v1 the test step becomes:

# excerpt of a job using grafana/run-k6-action instead of a run step
      - run: mkdir -p results          # k6 still does not create it
      - uses: grafana/run-k6-action@v1
        with:
          path: perf/average-load.js
          flags: --tag testid=nightly-${{ github.run_id }}
          disable-analytics: true   # the action reports anonymous usage by default

docs.title: Sending results to Prometheus and Grafana
docs.text:
# Prometheus started with --web.enable-otlp-receiver accepts OTLP at /api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics
export K6_OTEL_EXPORTER_PROTOCOL=http/protobuf
export K6_OTEL_HTTP_EXPORTER_ENDPOINT=prometheus.perf.example.com:9090   # host:port, no scheme
export K6_OTEL_HTTP_EXPORTER_URL_PATH=/api/v1/otlp/v1/metrics
export K6_OTEL_HTTP_EXPORTER_INSECURE=true    # plain HTTP inside the private network
export K6_OTEL_METRIC_PREFIX=k6_
k6 run --tag testid=nightly-2026-11-14 -o opentelemetry perf/average-load.js

k6 exports trends as OpenTelemetry histograms and rates as counters with a condition attribute; Prometheus stores them under k6_-prefixed names (its OTLP translation adds unit and type suffixes). The testid tag, sent as an attribute on every metric, lets a Grafana dashboard show one run at a time, and putting k6 panels next to the API's own RED and saturation panels is what turns "p95 rose at 300 requests per second" into a cause. The same variables work with an OpenTelemetry Collector (the default protocol is gRPC on localhost:4317).

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Keep load tests in the repository, reviewed like code, with one shared workload module and one small file per load shape.
  • Express the SLO as thresholds, per endpoint where it matters, and add dropped_iterations: ["count==0"] to every arrival-rate test.
  • Give every request a route-template name tag; never let raw URLs with IDs become metric names.
  • Use arrival-rate executors for rate questions and size VUs with Little's law; pre-allocate enough for spikes.
  • Gate on thresholds, not on checks alone; add a checks threshold.
  • Pin the k6 version in CI and upgrade deliberately, reading the release notes (k6 2.0 removed commands, flags, and an executor).
  • Create output directories before the run and upload the summary and HTML report as artifacts.
  • Tag each run (--tag testid=...) and stream metrics next to the application's dashboards.
  • Keep secrets out of scripts and data files; pass them through the environment.
  • Smoke test every script change before running long tests.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Scripts stop working after a k6 upgrade. Detect: CI fails with an unknown executor, flag, or command right after the runner picked up a new k6 version. Cause: k6 2.0 removed externally-controlled, --no-summary, k6 login, and k6 cloud script.js, and requires a stack for every k6 cloud command. Fix: pin k6-version, migrate to --summary-mode=disabled, k6 cloud login, and k6 cloud run, and upgrade on purpose.
  • The run "passed" but the planned load never arrived. Detect: dropped_iterations above zero, achieved requests per second below the plan, "Insufficient VUs" warnings in the log. Cause: too small a VU budget, or VUs created too late during a spike. Fix: raise preAllocatedVUs and maxVUs using Little's law, and add dropped_iterations: ["count==0"] so this fails the run.
  • The metrics backend slows down or runs out of memory during tests. Detect: the number of k6 series in Prometheus jumps by thousands per run. Cause: requests without a name tag, so every task ID is a new series, or high-cardinality custom tags. Fix: route-template names or http.url, and no IDs in tags.
  • Latency gets worse as the load generator gets busier. Detect: the generator's CPU is near 100%, http_req_blocked grows, and server-side latency stays flat. Cause: the generator is saturated: heavy JSON parsing in checks, large response bodies, too many VUs per host. Fix: discardResponseBodies where bodies are not needed, lighter checks, and more generator hosts (execution segments, the k6 Operator, or Grafana Cloud k6).
  • The CI artifact with the summary is missing. Detect: the upload step finds no results/summary.json, while the k6 step was green. Cause: the directory did not exist; handleSummary() logged an error but k6 still exited with 0. Fix: mkdir -p results before the run, and fail the job if the artifact is missing.
  • A breakpoint test aborts long after the system broke. Detect: per-minute dashboards show p95 rising well before the abort time. Cause: thresholds aggregate every sample since the start, so a long healthy ramp dilutes the slow tail. Fix: take the knee from the time series; use tighter percentiles for abortOnFail; keep the thresholds as a safety stop, not as the measurement.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Virtual user (VU): One k6 JavaScript runtime executing iterations.
  • Iteration: One run of the scenario's function.
  • Scenario: A named workload: function, executor, load, timing, tags.
  • Executor: The scheduler that decides how VUs and iterations run.
  • Threshold: A pass/fail condition on a metric; a failure makes k6 exit with code 99.
  • Check: An assertion on a response, counted in the checks metric, which does not stop the test by itself.
  • Tag: A key-value label on every metric sample, used for filtering.
  • Sub-metric: A metric filtered by tags, such as http_req_duration{name:GET /tasks}.
  • Group: A named block of requests with its own group_duration.
  • SharedArray: Read-only test data stored once and shared by all VUs.
  • setup() / teardown(): Functions that run once before and after the load.
  • handleSummary(): A function that replaces the end-of-test summary output.
  • Output: A destination for metrics during the run (files, OpenTelemetry, the web dashboard).
  • Dropped iteration: An iteration an arrival-rate executor could not start on time.
  • k6 Operator: A Kubernetes operator that runs distributed k6 tests from a TestRun resource.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating checks as assertions that fail the test; without a threshold they only count.
  • Using constant-vus with no think time to answer "can we handle 500 requests per second?".
  • Leaving raw URLs as the name tag and drowning the summary and the metrics backend in series.
  • Assuming k6 is Node.js and trying to import npm packages or fs.
  • Loading large data with open() in every VU instead of a SharedArray.
  • Reading a breakpoint result from the abort time instead of the time series.
  • Running the latest k6 in CI without pinning, and finding out about breaking changes from a red pipeline.
  • Forgetting that handleSummary() replaces the terminal summary unless it prints one itself.
  • Writing passwords or tokens into scripts and data files.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. In which lifecycle stage would you log in test users, and why not in the init code?
  2. Which executor would you use to hold 150 requests per second for 30 minutes, and which to model a pool of 20 workers?
  3. An arrival-rate scenario runs 200 iterations per second. Iterations take 250 ms at the median and up to 1.5 s when the system struggles. How many VUs should you pre-allocate, and what maxVUs keeps the load honest when it struggles? (About 200 x 0.25 = 50 plus headroom, say 60-80; at least 200 x 1.5 = 300 for maxVUs.)
  4. Write thresholds for "p95 of POST /tasks under 400 ms, fewer than 0.1% failed requests, and all planned iterations delivered".
  5. Why does a failing check not fail a k6 test, and how do you make it?
  6. What does the name tag do, and what goes wrong without it?
  7. A nightly k6 job is green but uploads no summary file. What happened?
  8. Why might abortOnFail stop a breakpoint test much later than the moment the system actually broke?

docs.title: Backup and Restore Drill
docs.text: Schedule encrypted MongoDB backups to object storage with a retention policy and an immutable copy, then prove they work: drop a collection, restore to the minute before the mistake, verify the data, and compare the time it really took with the RPO and RTO you would promise users.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds backup and recovery skills: full and incremental backups, point-in-time recovery, retention, and immutability.
  • Improves resilience: a backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a plan; this project turns it into a measured procedure.
  • Improves ransomware and mistake protection: an immutable copy survives an attacker or an admin with delete rights.
  • RPO and RTO questions, and "tell me about a restore you have done", come up in interviews for any backend or operations role.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A MongoDB replica set (local containers, or a managed cluster whose continuous backup supports point-in-time restore).
  • The MongoDB Database Tools (mongodump, mongorestore) or restic for encrypted, deduplicated backups.
  • An object storage bucket with versioning, lifecycle rules, and Object Lock (or your provider's equivalent).
  • Builds on Infrastructure from Code for the bucket, and any earlier project that runs TaskFlow.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read backup fundamentals and strategies and write down the RPO and RTO you are aiming for.
  2. Schedule backups with mongodump --oplog (or restic, or the managed service's continuous backup), encrypted before or as they reach storage; see database backups and point-in-time recovery.
  3. Add a retention policy (daily, weekly, monthly) with lifecycle rules or restic's forget options.
  4. Copy backups to a separate account or bucket with Object Lock so they cannot be deleted before their retention ends.
  5. Seed test data, note the time, and drop a collection.
  6. Restore into a scratch environment to the minute before the drop, by replaying the oplog with mongorestore --oplogReplay and a stop point, or with the managed point-in-time restore.
  7. Verify with document counts per collection and a smoke test of the API, then switch over or copy the data back; see restore testing and runbooks.
  8. Record each step's duration and compare the totals with your RPO and RTO; see disaster recovery, RPO, and RTO.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Backups run on a schedule, are encrypted, and follow the retention policy.
  • An immutable copy exists that cannot be deleted during its retention.
  • The dropped collection is restored to the minute before the mistake.
  • Counts and the smoke test match the expected data.
  • A runbook records the real restore time and data loss next to the RPO and RTO targets.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Automate a monthly restore test in CI that fails if the restore breaks.
  • Restore into another region and time it.
  • Back up uploads in object storage as well; see backup and archive storage.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Backups and Disaster Recovery
  • MongoDB security and operations

Back to all projects.

docs.title: Canary Release Lab
docs.text: Release TaskFlow API the way large teams do: shift traffic to a new version in steps, stop automatically when it misbehaves, expose a new endpoint to a stable 10% of users with a feature flag, and rename a database field across three deploys without downtime.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds progressive delivery skills: canaries, automated analysis, feature flags, and backward-compatible schema changes.
  • Improves release safety: a bad version reaches only a small share of users and is rolled back by the system, not by a tired human.
  • Improves deployment frequency: separating deploy from release lets you ship small changes often.
  • "How would you roll out a risky change?" is a standard interview question.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The Kubernetes setup from TaskFlow on Kubernetes, plus Argo Rollouts (or Gateway API routes with weights).
  • Prometheus metrics for request errors, which the analysis reads (see Observability Lab; basic request counters are enough).
  • A feature flag SDK through OpenFeature, with a simple local provider.
  • A load generator such as k6.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read rolling, blue-green, and canary and convert the API Deployment into an Argo Rollouts canary.
  2. Define steps with setWeight of 5, 25, 50, and 100, with pauses between them, and send steady traffic with k6.
  3. Add an AnalysisTemplate that queries the canary's error rate in Prometheus and fails above a threshold.
  4. Ship a deliberately broken version (for example one endpoint returns 500) and watch the rollout abort and return traffic to the stable version.
  5. Add an OpenFeature flag for a new endpoint and enable it for 10% of users with stable bucketing (a hash of the user ID); see feature flags and progressive delivery.
  6. Plan the field rename with expand and contract from zero-downtime database migrations.
  7. Deploy 1: add the new field and write both; backfill existing documents.
  8. Deploy 2: read the new field. Deploy 3: stop writing the old field, then remove it once nothing reads it.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Traffic moves through 5%, 25%, 50%, and 100% with pauses you can see.
  • The broken version is rolled back automatically within one analysis interval.
  • The same user always gets the same flag decision, and about 10% of users see the new endpoint.
  • The field is renamed across three deploys with no failed requests and no lost data.
  • Each step and its rollback command are written down.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Compare the canary against a blue-green switch for the same change.
  • Add a kill switch flag that disables the new endpoint instantly.
  • Practice a rollback that also needs a data fix; see rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Deployment Strategies
  • Environments and promotion
  • Advanced deployment patterns

Back to all projects.

docs.title: Config and Secrets Hardening
docs.text: Make TaskFlow API refuse to start with bad configuration, fetch its database password from a secret store instead of a file, and rotate that password with no downtime. You also rehearse the full response to a leaked secret on a throwaway repository.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the habits behind twelve-factor configuration: everything in the environment, validated once, with clear errors.
  • Improves security: no credentials in code, images, or Git, and a practiced answer to "a key just leaked".
  • Improves reliability: a missing variable fails fast at startup instead of breaking one request at 3 a.m.
  • Interviewers often ask how you rotate a secret without an outage; you will have done it.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A secret store: AWS Secrets Manager on a free-tier account, or HashiCorp Vault in dev mode on your laptop (vault server -dev).
  • A validation library such as zod or envalid.
  • git filter-repo and a separate test repository.
  • Builds on Ship It Pipeline; works with the image from Production Image.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. List every setting the API reads and move each hard-coded value into an environment variable; see configuration fundamentals.
  2. Validate all variables once at startup with a zod or envalid schema and exit with a clear message when one is missing or malformed.
  3. Keep local values in an untracked .env file and know which source wins; see env files and precedence.
  4. Store the MongoDB password in the secret store and let the app fetch it at startup with its own identity, caching it and retrying on failure; see secrets management.
  5. Rotate with an overlap window: create a second database user (or second password), point new instances at it, wait, then remove the old one.
  6. Run a load test during the rotation and confirm no request fails.
  7. In a test repository, commit a throwaway credential you can revoke, then practice the order: revoke and rotate first, check its usage, and only then purge it with git filter-repo; see undoing mistakes and recovery.
  8. Turn on secret scanning and push protection, and add a gitleaks pre-commit hook so the next leak is stopped before it is pushed.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Starting the API with a variable removed prints a clear error and exits.
  • No credential exists in the code, the image, or the repository history.
  • The app reads the database password from the secret store at startup.
  • A password rotation completes while traffic flows, with zero failed requests.
  • The leak drill is written down with the time each step took.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Use dynamic database credentials from Vault with a one-hour lease.
  • Encrypt a config file for GitOps with SOPS.
  • Separate build-time and runtime settings for TaskFlow Web; see build-time vs runtime configuration.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Environment Variables and Secrets
  • Configuration and secrets in Kubernetes
  • Pipeline and supply chain security

docs.title: Infrastructure from Code
docs.text: Create TaskFlow's cloud resources with Terraform: a network with public and private subnets, versioned storage for uploads, and the permissions the app needs, with remote state and locking. Plans run on pull requests, applies run after merge, and you prove it all by destroying and recreating it.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds infrastructure-as-code skills: providers, resources, modules, state, and plans that reviewers can read.
  • Improves repeatability: environments can be rebuilt from code, and nothing depends on someone remembering console clicks.
  • Improves change safety: every infrastructure change is a reviewed pull request with a plan attached.
  • Remote state, locking, and drift are standard interview topics for DevOps and platform roles.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Terraform (a version that supports S3-native state locking) and a cloud account with a budget alert.
  • A state bucket for the S3 backend, and an OIDC-assumable role for CI.
  • GitHub Actions with hashicorp/setup-terraform@v4.
  • Builds on Ship It Pipeline.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Learn the core workflow (terraform init, plan, apply) in IaC fundamentals.
  2. Configure an S3 backend with use_lockfile = true so state is remote and locked; see Terraform in practice.
  3. Create a VPC with public and private subnets across two zones (the community VPC module is fine); see cloud building blocks.
  4. Add an uploads bucket with versioning and public access blocked.
  5. Add a role for the API with a least-privilege policy for that bucket and nothing else.
  6. In CI, run terraform plan -out=tfplan on every pull request and post it for review, authenticating with OIDC instead of stored keys.
  7. Run terraform apply tfplan only after merge to main, behind a protected environment.
  8. Destroy everything, recreate it from code, and run terraform plan again: it should report no changes.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• State lives in the remote backend, and a second concurrent run waits for the lock.
  • Every pull request shows a plan, and applies happen only after merge.
  • The bucket is versioned and private, and the API role can reach only that bucket.
  • No cloud keys are stored in the repository or CI secrets.
  • After destroy and recreate, terraform plan reports no changes.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Split code into modules with separate state per environment.
  • Add a policy check (Checkov, Trivy, or OPA) to the plan job; see Secure the Pipeline.
  • Reconcile infrastructure continuously with GitOps; see immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Infrastructure as Code
  • Identity and access management
  • Pipeline and supply chain security

docs.title: Load Test and Break It
docs.text: Write k6 tests for TaskFlow's main user journeys with thresholds, run a short version in CI as a performance gate, push the load until latency bends, find and fix the bottleneck, and finish with a small game day that injects latency between the API and MongoDB.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds performance engineering skills: realistic load tests, thresholds, profiling, and the USE method.
  • Improves capacity planning: you learn where TaskFlow breaks and what limits it, before real users find out.
  • Improves release safety: a CI threshold catches performance regressions like any failing test.
  • Interviewers ask how you would find a bottleneck; you will have a real story with numbers.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• k6 on your laptop and the Grafana k6 GitHub Actions (setup-k6-action and run-k6-action).
  • Node's built-in profiler (node --cpu-prof) and system tools such as top and vmstat.
  • Toxiproxy for fault injection.
  • A test environment you own, from Production Image or TaskFlow on Kubernetes.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Pick the main journeys (sign in, list tasks, create a task) and the load model using load testing fundamentals.
  2. Write k6 scenarios with checks and thresholds on p95 latency and error rate; see load testing with k6.
  3. Run a short version in CI so the job fails when a threshold is crossed.
  4. Ramp the load in steps and plot latency against throughput to find where it bends upward.
  5. Apply the USE method to CPU, memory, disk, network, and the database, and record a CPU profile with node --cpu-prof at peak load; see finding bottlenecks.
  6. Fix the biggest bottleneck (for example a missing index or an N+1 query) and run the same test again to measure the gain.
  7. Plan a game day: write your hypothesis, then add a latency toxic between the API and MongoDB with Toxiproxy; see chaos engineering and game days.
  8. Compare what happened with what you expected, and turn the gaps into tasks.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• k6 tests cover the main journeys with thresholds on p95 latency and error rate.
  • CI fails when a threshold is crossed and passes when it is not.
  • You know the throughput at which latency bends, and why.
  • One bottleneck is fixed, with before and after numbers from the same test.
  • The game day notes compare the hypothesis with the observed behavior.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Run a soak test for an hour and look for memory growth.
  • Use an arrival-rate executor and compare it with a fixed number of virtual users.
  • Add timeouts and a circuit breaker where the game day showed a gap; see resilience patterns across servers.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Performance and Reliability Testing
  • Performance testing basics

docs.title: Measure Your Delivery
docs.text: Compute the DORA metrics for your own TaskFlow work with a small script over git history, deployment records, and the incidents from earlier projects. Choose one metric to improve, write a one-page team charter, and record one architecture decision as an ADR.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the habit of measuring delivery instead of guessing: throughput and stability, from data you already have.
  • Improves team practices: ownership, on-call, and change approval are written down instead of assumed.
  • Improves decision memory: an ADR explains why something was built a certain way long after the people who decided have moved on.
  • DORA metrics and "how would you improve this team's delivery?" are common interview topics for senior and platform roles.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The repositories, pipelines, and deployment records from earlier projects (for example Ship It Pipeline and Version Everything).
  • The postmortems from Observability Lab and any other incidents you recorded.
  • git, the GitHub CLI (gh run list) or your CI's API, and a scripting language you like.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read measuring delivery performance for the definitions and their pitfalls.
  2. Export commits and merges with git log, deployments from your CI or deployment records, and incidents from your postmortems.
  3. Compute deployment frequency and change lead time (commit to production) with a small script.
  4. Compute change fail rate, failed deployment recovery time, and deployment rework rate from deployments linked to incidents and hotfixes.
  5. Choose one metric to improve, explain why it matters most right now, and name one change you would try first.
  6. Write a one-page charter covering ownership, on-call, and how changes are approved; see team practices and ownership.
  7. Record one real decision from your projects (for example canary releases or a hosting choice) as an ADR with context, decision, and consequences.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• A script prints all five metrics for a chosen period.
  • Each metric's definition and data source are written next to its value.
  • One metric is chosen for improvement, with a reason and a first step.
  • A one-page charter exists covering ownership, on-call, and change approval.
  • One ADR is committed to the repository.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Track the metrics weekly and chart the trend.
  • Compare your numbers with the ranges published in the latest DORA report.
  • Sketch a golden path for a new service; see platform engineering and developer portals.

docs.title: Observability Lab
docs.text: Instrument TaskFlow API with structured logs, metrics, and traces, define SLOs with a dashboard and a burn-rate alert, then break something on purpose, follow the alert to the cause, and write a blameless postmortem.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the three signals every on-call engineer relies on: logs, metrics, and traces, connected by a request ID.
  • Improves detection and recovery time: you find problems from alerts and traces instead of from users.
  • Improves prioritization: SLOs and error budgets turn "is this bad?" into a number.
  • "Walk me through debugging a latency spike" is a staple interview question; you will have done it end to end.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• pino and pino-http for logs, prom-client for metrics, and the OpenTelemetry Node.js SDK with auto-instrumentations for traces.
  • A local stack: Prometheus, Grafana, Alertmanager, and a trace backend such as Jaeger or Grafana Tempo (Docker Compose is enough).
  • Builds on Production Image.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read observability fundamentals and decide which questions each signal must answer.
  2. Emit JSON logs with pino-http and a request ID on every line; see structured logging.
  3. Expose request rate, errors, and duration with prom-client and scrape them with Prometheus; see metrics and dashboards.
  4. Start the OpenTelemetry SDK before the app so traces follow requests into MongoDB, and put the trace ID in the logs; see distributed tracing.
  5. Define an availability SLO and a latency SLO and build a Grafana dashboard for them; see SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets.
  6. Add a multiwindow burn-rate alert in Prometheus with a runbook link in its annotations, routed through Alertmanager; see alerting and on-call.
  7. Break something on purpose (a slow query or an error in one route), and go from the alert to the trace and the log line that explain it.
  8. Write a blameless postmortem with a timeline and action items using incident response and postmortems.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Every log line is JSON and carries a request ID and trace ID.
  • The dashboard shows request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, and remaining error budget.
  • A trace shows the HTTP request and the MongoDB calls inside it.
  • The burn-rate alert fires during the incident and links to a runbook.
  • A postmortem names the trigger, the root causes, and owned action items.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Add error tracking and an external uptime check; see error tracking and uptime monitoring.
  • Sample traces by tail latency instead of at random.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Monitoring and Logging
  • Logging and monitoring in the backend

docs.title: Pick a Host and Price It
docs.text: Write down what TaskFlow actually needs, estimate three hosting setups at three traffic levels with the providers' official calculators, deploy the two cheapest, and compare deploy time, cold starts, and the real bill after a month. Budget alerts are in place before anything is created.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the judgment to choose where software runs: static hosts, container platforms, managed databases, all-in-one platforms, and plain virtual servers.
  • Improves cost control: you learn what drives a bill (compute hours, data transfer, database size, requests) and catch surprises early.
  • Improves decision quality: choices are backed by requirements and measurements instead of habit.
  • "Which host would you pick and why?" is a common design and interview question; you will have numbers of your own.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Accounts with the providers you compare, each with a budget alert set up first (for example AWS Budgets, or the budget tools in Google Cloud and Azure).
  • The AWS Pricing Calculator, Google Cloud Pricing Calculator, Azure Pricing Calculator, or the pricing pages of the platforms you choose.
  • The image from Production Image and TaskFlow Web.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. List the requirements: expected traffic, data size, regions, compliance, and how much operations work you can take on; see choosing where to run software.
  2. Pick three setups, for example a static host plus a container platform plus a managed database, an all-in-one platform, and one virtual server.
  3. Model each at 10,000, 1 million, and 50 million monthly page views with the official calculators, writing down your assumptions.
  4. Compare which setup is cheapest at each level and why; costs usually cross over as traffic grows. Use cost optimization and cloud bills.
  5. Set budget alerts on every account before creating any resource.
  6. Deploy the two cheapest setups, following hosting websites and frontends and running backend servers and APIs.
  7. Measure deploy time, cold start latency, and response times with the same test on both.
  8. After a month, compare the real bills with your estimates and explain the differences.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• A one-page requirements list exists.
  • A table shows all three setups at all three traffic levels, with assumptions.
  • Budget alerts exist on every account and one test alert has fired.
  • Both deployed setups serve TaskFlow, with measured deploy time and cold starts.
  • You can say which setup you would choose at each traffic level and why.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Price the database separately with managed databases and compare it with self-hosting MongoDB.
  • Estimate storage and transfer costs for uploads with object and file storage.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Hosting and Cloud Platforms
  • AWS

docs.title: Production Image
docs.text: Package TaskFlow API as a small, non-root container image that shuts down cleanly and reports its health, built and scanned in CI and pushed to a registry with the commit SHA as its tag. A Docker Compose stack starts the API, MongoDB, and a database UI in the right order.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the core container skills: multi-stage builds, layer caching, users and signals, health checks, tags, and registries.
  • Improves security: a non-root, minimal image scanned on every build has far fewer ways to be exploited.
  • Improves reliability: graceful SIGTERM handling and health checks are what let orchestrators restart and roll out without dropping requests.
  • Covers interview favorites: image size, why latest is dangerous, and what PID 1 does with signals.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Docker Engine or Docker Desktop with BuildKit and Docker Compose v2.
  • A registry account; GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api) is free for public images.
  • Trivy (or Grype or Docker Scout) for scanning.
  • Builds on Ship It Pipeline.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Write a multi-stage Dockerfile: install and build in one stage, copy only production files into a slim Node 24 runtime. See writing production Dockerfiles.
  2. Run as a non-root user (USER node) and keep a .dockerignore so secrets and node_modules never enter the build context.
  3. Handle SIGTERM in the app (stop accepting connections, finish requests, close MongoDB), and run with --init or tini so signals reach Node.
  4. Add a HEALTHCHECK that calls a lightweight health endpoint.
  5. In CI, build with docker/build-push-action@v7 and tag the image sha-<commit>; see images, registries, and tagging.
  6. Scan the image before pushing (for example trivy image --severity HIGH,CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1); see container security.
  7. Push to the registry only from main, and record the image digest.
  8. Write compose.yaml with the API, MongoDB, and mongo-express, using health checks and depends_on with condition: service_healthy; see Docker Compose for development.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• The runtime image is small, runs as a non-root user, and has no build tools.
  • docker stop finishes in seconds and in-flight requests complete.
  • docker ps shows the container as healthy.
  • CI pushes ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-<commit> only after a clean scan.
  • docker compose up starts MongoDB first and the API only when it is healthy.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Switch the runtime stage to a distroless image and compare size and CVE count.
  • Pin the base image by digest and let Dependabot propose updates.
  • Sign the image with cosign and verify it before running.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Docker
  • Container fundamentals
  • Debugging and operating containers

docs.title: Production Server from Scratch
docs.text: Turn a fresh Ubuntu LTS virtual server into a hardened home for TaskFlow API: locked-down SSH, a firewall, automatic security updates, a hardened systemd service behind Nginx, one-command rollbacks, rotated logs, and a nightly job that never overlaps. Then break the server on purpose and diagnose it.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the Linux operations skills that sit under every platform: users, SSH, firewalls, systemd, Nginx, cron, and logs.
  • Improves security: key-only SSH, a default-deny firewall, and automatic patches remove the most common ways servers are taken over.
  • Improves recovery speed: release folders with a symlink switch make a rollback one command, and practiced troubleshooting shortens outages.
  • "The disk is full, what do you do?" is a classic interview question.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The smallest virtual server from any cloud or VPS provider, on a current Ubuntu LTS image, and an SSH key pair.
  • The TaskFlow API code and a MongoDB it can reach (a managed free tier or a local container).
  • Builds on Ship It Pipeline.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Create a non-root user with sudo, copy your public key, and set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no; see SSH and remote access.
  2. Follow setting up a production server: enable ufw with default deny incoming, add fail2ban, and confirm unattended-upgrades applies security updates.
  3. Install Node.js 24 by a supported method (the lesson uses NodeSource) and create a dedicated app user and directories.
  4. Run TaskFlow under a systemd unit with restart, an environment file, and hardening options, and check it with systemd-analyze security; see running apps with systemd and Nginx.
  5. Put Nginx in front as a reverse proxy, with timeouts and body size limits.
  6. Deploy into timestamped release folders and switch a current symlink with ln -sfn; a rollback points it back and restarts the service.
  7. Add a logrotate rule and limit journald's disk use; schedule the nightly job with flock -n (or a systemd timer) so runs cannot overlap; see scheduled jobs and log rotation.
  8. Fill the disk with fallocate and exhaust memory with a test process, then diagnose with df -h, du, free -h, dmesg, and journalctl using troubleshooting CPU, memory, disk, and network.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• SSH accepts only keys for the non-root user; root and password logins fail.
  • Only SSH, HTTP, and HTTPS are reachable from the internet.
  • TaskFlow restarts automatically after a crash or a reboot.
  • A deploy and a rollback each take one command and drop no requests.
  • The nightly job never runs twice at once, and logs rotate.
  • You found the cause of the full disk and the memory exhaustion from the tools, not from memory.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Script the whole setup with cloud-init or Ansible and rebuild the server.
  • Add a second server and move to Three Servers, One Address.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Linux Server Operations
  • Servers and Nginx

docs.title: Publish These Notes
docs.text: Deploy a MkDocs site like this one to GitHub Pages with a workflow that builds on every push to main, fails on broken links, and publishes only from the default branch, plus a pull-request check that builds without deploying.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds a complete, small delivery pipeline you can finish in an afternoon: build, validate, and deploy a static site.
  • Improves release safety: strict builds stop broken links and missing pages before readers see them.
  • Improves separation of checks and releases: pull requests prove the site builds, and only main can publish.
  • A live site with a clean pipeline is a useful portfolio item to show in interviews.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A GitHub repository with Markdown pages and an mkdocs.yml.
  • Python with MkDocs and the Material theme (pip install mkdocs-material).
  • GitHub Pages enabled with GitHub Actions as the source (free for public repositories).
  • Helpful but not required: Ship It Pipeline.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Build locally with mkdocs serve, then run mkdocs build --strict and fix every warning, because strict mode turns warnings such as broken links into errors.
  2. In the repository settings, set GitHub Pages to deploy from GitHub Actions.
  3. Add a workflow on pushes to main with actions/checkout@v7, actions/setup-python@v7, and a pip install of the site's requirements.
  4. Build with mkdocs build --strict, then upload the site/ folder with actions/upload-pages-artifact@v5.
  5. Deploy in a separate job with actions/deploy-pages@v5, with permissions of pages: write and id-token: write and the github-pages environment; see deploying frontends and static sites.
  6. Restrict the deploy job to the default branch (an if: on github.ref, or environment branch rules), so other branches can never publish.
  7. Add a pull-request workflow that runs the same strict build and uploads nothing; see pipeline design.
  8. Make the pull-request build a required check on main.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• A push to main publishes the site within minutes.
  • A broken internal link fails the build and nothing is published.
  • Pull requests show a passing or failing build check and never deploy.
  • Only the default branch can deploy, even if someone edits a workflow on another branch.
  • The site is reachable at its GitHub Pages address, or a custom domain.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Add a custom domain with HTTPS; see Your Own Domain, Properly.
  • Check external links on a weekly schedule instead of on every build.
  • Deploy a preview of each pull request to a separate host.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• CI/CD
  • GitHub Actions in depth
  • Deployment Strategies

docs.title: Secure the Pipeline
docs.text: Add security checks to TaskFlow's delivery pipeline that catch real problems without drowning the team, replace stored cloud keys with OIDC, test the running API on staging, rate-limit the login endpoint at the edge, and triage findings by severity and real-world exploitation.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds DevSecOps skills: SAST, dependency and secret scanning, IaC and image scanning, DAST, and workload identity.
  • Improves security: known vulnerabilities, leaked secrets, and risky infrastructure changes are caught before they reach production.
  • Improves signal quality: gating only on new, fixable, serious findings keeps the checks trusted instead of ignored.
  • Interviewers ask how you would secure a pipeline and how you prioritize a flood of CVEs; this project gives you concrete answers.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The pipeline from Ship It Pipeline, the image from Production Image, and the Terraform from Infrastructure from Code.
  • Free tools: CodeQL or Semgrep, Dependabot or OSV-Scanner, GitHub secret scanning, Checkov or Trivy, and ZAP.
  • A staging deployment you own, and a WAF in front of it (a cloud WAF or a CDN's rate limiting rules).

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read security in the delivery pipeline and decide which findings block a merge.
  2. Enable CodeQL (or Semgrep), Dependabot alerts, and secret scanning with push protection; pin third-party actions to full commit SHAs.
  3. Scan the Terraform code with Checkov or trivy config on pull requests.
  4. Scan the image and fail only on fixable critical findings, for example trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1.
  5. Replace stored cloud keys with OIDC and a least-privilege deploy role; see identity and access management.
  6. Run a ZAP baseline or API scan against staging after each deploy, never against production.
  7. Add a WAF rate-limit rule on the login path; see edge protection.
  8. Triage findings with CVSS for severity, EPSS for exploitation likelihood, and the CISA KEV catalog for confirmed exploitation; see vulnerability and patch management.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• A pull request that adds a vulnerable dependency or a test secret is blocked with a clear message.
  • Terraform and image scans run on every change, and only fixable critical image findings fail the build.
  • No long-lived cloud keys remain in CI secrets.
  • A ZAP report exists for staging, with each alert fixed or justified.
  • Repeated failed logins from one address are blocked at the edge.
  • Every open finding has a priority based on CVSS, EPSS, and KEV, and an owner.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Generate an SBOM and provenance for the image and verify them before deploy; see pipeline and supply chain security.
  • Write a custom Semgrep rule for a TaskFlow convention.
  • Restrict outbound traffic from the API; see network security in the cloud.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• DevSecOps and Cloud Security
  • Container security
  • Secrets management

docs.title: Ship It Pipeline
docs.text: Put TaskFlow API under a real team workflow: main is protected, every change arrives through a pull request with a passing check, and a GitHub Actions pipeline lints, type checks, and tests the code in under five minutes. You finish with a tagged release and a generated changelog.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the everyday Git and CI skills every team expects: branches, pull requests, required checks, and a pipeline you can read and fix.
  • Improves release safety: nothing reaches main without review and green tests, including integration tests against a real MongoDB.
  • Improves pipeline speed: lockfile-keyed caching and parallel jobs keep feedback fast, which is what keeps people from skipping CI.
  • Gives you concrete answers for interview questions on branch protection, caching, flaky tests, and how a release is cut.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A GitHub account and the TaskFlow API repository (Express and MongoDB) from the Backend section; GitHub Actions minutes on the free plan are enough for a public repository.
  • Node 24 and a test runner the project already uses, plus ESLint and TypeScript (or JSDoc type checks).
  • No earlier projects: this is the first one.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Create a branch ruleset (or classic branch protection) for main that requires a pull request, one approval, and a passing check. See pull requests and code review.
  2. Pick a branching model (trunk-based with short-lived branches works well) from branching strategies.
  3. Add .github/workflows/ci.yml triggered on pull_request and pushes to main, with permissions: contents: read; use actions/checkout@v7.
  4. Install with actions/setup-node@v7 (node-version: 24, cache: npm) and npm ci, so dependencies are cached on the lockfile hash. See pipeline design.
  5. Run lint and type check in one job and tests in another so they run in parallel; see GitHub Actions in depth.
  6. Start MongoDB as a service container for integration tests, as shown in testing and quality gates.
  7. Mark the jobs as required checks in the ruleset, then open a pull request that fails and one that passes to prove the gate works.
  8. Measure the pipeline's duration in the run summary and remove the slowest steps until it stays under five minutes.
  9. Cut a release with a tag and a generated changelog using release-please or gh release create <tag> --generate-notes; see versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• A direct push to main is rejected.
  • A pull request cannot merge until lint, type check, and tests pass.
  • Integration tests run against MongoDB in a service container.
  • A cached run finishes in under five minutes.
  • A tagged release exists with a changelog generated from commits.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Shard the slowest test suite across a matrix and compare durations.
  • Add a weekly scheduled run and a status badge to the README.
  • Require signed commits on main.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Git and GitHub and CI/CD
  • Continuous integration fundamentals
  • Pipeline and supply chain security
