docs.title: TaskFlow on Kubernetes
docs.text: Run TaskFlow API on a local Kubernetes cluster with proper configuration, probes, resource settings, and autoscaling. Under load you watch it scale, roll out a new image, roll back, and keep serving requests the whole time; the result is packaged as a Helm chart.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds working knowledge of the objects every Kubernetes job uses: Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes, and autoscalers.
  • Improves availability: readiness probes and rolling updates are what keep requests succeeding during deploys and failures.
  • Improves cost and capacity control: requests, limits, and an HPA match resources to real load.
  • Gives you a live demo for interviews: "here is a rollback under load".

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• kind or minikube, kubectl, and Helm on your laptop (all free).
  • metrics-server installed in the cluster, because the HPA needs it.
  • A load-testing tool such as k6.
  • Builds on Production Image.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Create a cluster with kind create cluster (or minikube start) and load or pull the TaskFlow image.
  2. Write a Deployment and a Service for the API and a StatefulSet or simple Deployment for MongoDB; see pods, Deployments, and Services.
  3. Move settings into a ConfigMap and the database password into a Secret, as in configuration and secrets.
  4. Add readiness and liveness probes with sensible thresholds; see health probes and rolling updates.
  5. Set CPU and memory requests and limits, install metrics-server, and add an autoscaling/v2 HorizontalPodAutoscaler; see scaling and resource management.
  6. Generate load with k6 and watch kubectl get hpa -w as replicas are added and later removed.
  7. Roll out a new image tag, follow it with kubectl rollout status, then run kubectl rollout undo while the load test keeps running.
  8. Package the manifests as a chart with helm create, check it with helm lint and helm template, and deploy with helm upgrade --install; see ingress, networking, and Helm.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• kubectl get pods shows all replicas ready and the API answers through the Service.
  • No value in the manifests is hard-coded that belongs in a ConfigMap or Secret.
  • Under load, the HPA adds replicas and removes them afterwards.
  • A rollout and a rollback complete with zero failed requests in the load test results.
  • helm upgrade --install reproduces the whole deployment.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Add an Ingress or Gateway API route with a hostname.
  • Add a PodDisruptionBudget and drain a node during the load test.
  • Run a Job that seeds the database before the API starts.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Kubernetes
  • Orchestration fundamentals
  • Stateful workloads and Jobs
  • Load testing with k6

docs.title: Three Servers, One Address
docs.text: Run three TaskFlow API instances behind one load balancer so that any instance can serve any request, any one can be stopped under load without errors, deploys drain connections cleanly, scheduled jobs run once, and a slow dependency cannot take the API down with it.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds the core skills of horizontal scaling: stateless services, load balancing, health checks, draining, and distributed jobs.
  • Improves availability: losing one instance, or deploying, no longer means losing requests.
  • Improves resilience: timeouts, jittered retries, and a circuit breaker stop one slow dependency from cascading into a full outage.
  • These are exactly the topics of system design and on-call interviews.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• Three instances: containers on your laptop with Docker Compose, or three small virtual servers.
  • Nginx or HAProxy as the load balancer, Redis for sessions and locks, and object storage for uploads (a cloud bucket or MinIO locally).
  • k6 to generate load.
  • Builds on Production Server from Scratch or Production Image.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Find the state that ties a user to one instance (sessions, uploads on local disk, in-memory caches, cron jobs) using from one server to many.
  2. Move sessions to Redis (for example with connect-redis) and uploads to object storage with presigned URLs.
  3. Put Nginx or HAProxy in front of the three instances with health checks; see load balancers in depth.
  4. Run k6 and stop instances one at a time; watch the load balancer remove them and the error rate stay flat.
  5. For rolling deploys, drain each instance first (for example HAProxy's set server ... state drain), wait for connections to finish, then update and re-enable it.
  6. Make the scheduled job run once per scheduled time with a Redis lock (SET key NX with an expiry) or a single scheduler.
  7. Wrap calls to a slow dependency with timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter, and a circuit breaker (opossum or cockatiel); see resilience patterns across servers.
  8. Inject slowness into that dependency and confirm the API degrades gracefully instead of hanging.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Requests are spread across all three instances, and a logged-in user stays logged in whichever instance answers.
  • Stopping any single instance under load causes no failed requests.
  • A rolling deploy of all three instances drops no requests.
  • The scheduled job runs exactly once per scheduled time across the fleet.
  • With the dependency slowed down, the circuit breaker opens and the API answers quickly with a fallback or a clear error.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Add autoscaling for the fleet; see autoscaling server fleets.
  • Spread the instances across two zones and fail one zone.
  • Read how large companies design their traffic path in how top companies run at scale.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Load Balancing and Multi-Server Architecture
  • Load balancing
  • Load testing with k6

Back to all projects.

docs.title: TLS Everywhere
docs.text: Serve TaskFlow over HTTPS with a Let's Encrypt certificate that renews itself, redirect all HTTP to HTTPS, add HSTS, alert before a certificate can expire, and practice diagnosing a broken certificate chain with openssl s_client.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds working knowledge of certificates, ACME, renewal, and TLS termination, which every public service needs.
  • Improves security: encrypted traffic everywhere, with HSTS preventing downgrade to plain HTTP.
  • Improves reliability: expired certificates cause real outages, and automated renewal with alerts prevents them.
  • "The site shows a certificate error for some users" is a common incident and interview scenario.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A server with a public IP and a domain pointing at it; see Production Server from Scratch and Your Own Domain, Properly.
  • Nginx with certbot, or Caddy (which handles certificates automatically).
  • openssl and curl on your laptop; an uptime or monitoring tool for the expiry alert.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Read TLS and certificate fundamentals for chains, SNI, and ACME challenges.
  2. Request a certificate against Let's Encrypt's staging environment first (certbot --staging, or Caddy's acme_ca setting), and switch to production once it works; see obtaining and renewing certificates.
  3. Configure Nginx (or Caddy) to terminate TLS for TaskFlow and redirect port 80 to HTTPS; see TLS termination and troubleshooting.
  4. Add a Strict-Transport-Security header, starting with a short max-age and raising it once everything works.
  5. Prove renewal works with certbot renew --dry-run (Caddy renews on its own), and check that the renewal timer is active.
  6. Add an expiry alert from your monitoring, because Let's Encrypt no longer sends expiry emails and certificate lifetimes are getting shorter.
  7. Break the chain on purpose (serve only the leaf certificate without the intermediate) and diagnose it with openssl s_client, passing -servername for SNI and -showcerts to see what the server sends.
  8. Fix the chain and confirm with curl -v and an online TLS checker.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• http:// requests redirect to https:// with a permanent redirect.
  • Responses carry an HSTS header.
  • certbot renew --dry-run succeeds (or Caddy shows automatic renewal).
  • An alert fires in a test when a certificate is within your warning window.
  • You can explain the broken-chain error from the openssl s_client output and show the fix.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Re-encrypt traffic from Nginx to the app on the internal hop.
  • Require client certificates (mTLS) for an internal admin endpoint.
  • Test with a certificate from a second ACME CA.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• SSL Certificates
  • TLS and SSL
  • Reverse proxy

docs.title: Version Everything
docs.text: Give every TaskFlow artifact a version a person can trace from a running system back to a commit, deprecate an API field properly, make open browser tabs pick up new frontend releases safely, and make the API refuse clients older than a minimum supported version with a clear upgrade message.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds release engineering skills: version schemes, build metadata, deprecation policies, and client compatibility.
  • Improves debuggability: "which version is running?" has an exact answer for the API, the web app, and every image.
  • Improves compatibility during deploys: old clients and new servers keep working together while versions are mixed.
  • Version skew and forced upgrades are common interview and on-call topics.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The repository and pipeline from Ship It Pipeline and the image from Production Image.
  • TaskFlow Web (React and Vite), and a desktop or mobile client (a simple script that sends a version header is enough).
  • release-please, semantic-release, or Changesets for tags and changelogs.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Choose what gets which version (API SemVer, web build ID, image digest) using versioning patterns.
  2. Automate tags and changelogs with release-please or semantic-release; see versioning, tags, and releases.
  3. Bake a build ID into TaskFlow Web with a Vite define constant such as __APP_VERSION__, and expose the API's version on /version.
  4. Record the image digest, version, and commit in each deployment record.
  5. Deprecate one API field: send the Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers, document the dates, and keep the field working until the sunset passes.
  6. Make the web app check /version (or a manifest) and offer a reload, and recover from ChunkLoadError after deploys; see keeping frontend and backend in sync.
  7. Have the client send its version (for example X-App-Version), and make the API answer clients below the minimum with 426 and an error code the client turns into an upgrade message.
  8. Test it with an old client build and confirm the message appears.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• From a request in production you can name the API version, image digest, and commit.
  • Every release has a tag and a generated changelog.
  • Responses using the deprecated field carry Deprecation and Sunset headers, and the field still works.
  • An open browser tab notices a new release and reloads without errors.
  • An outdated client gets a 426 with a clear upgrade message.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Add a release train calendar for the mobile client; see release trains and release management.
  • Roll out a desktop update to 10% of users first; see update mechanisms and updaters.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Release Engineering
  • Releasing desktop and mobile apps
  • Images, registries, and tagging

docs.title: Your Own Domain, Properly
docs.text: Point a domain you own at TaskFlow with clean records: the apex and www (one redirecting to the other), an api subdomain, and a CAA record. Put a CDN in front of TaskFlow Web, rehearse a DNS provider move, and send transactional email that passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC at p=reject.

docs.title: Why this project helps
docs.text:
• Builds DNS and email skills that every production system depends on and few developers practice: records, TTLs, CDNs, and email authentication.
  • Improves performance: a CDN with sensible cache rules serves the web app close to users and offloads the origin.
  • Improves deliverability and trust: authenticated mail stops landing in spam and stops others from spoofing your domain.
  • DNS migrations and "why is our email in spam?" come up in interviews and on real teams.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A domain from any registrar (a cheap TLD is fine) and a DNS provider.
  • A CDN with a free plan, and a transactional email provider's free tier.
  • dig on your laptop.
  • Builds on Production Server from Scratch or any hosted TaskFlow from earlier projects.

docs.title: How to do it
docs.text:
1. Learn the record types and TTLs in domains and DNS records.
  2. Point the apex and www at the frontend (ALIAS, ANAME, or flattening at the apex), redirect one to the other, and add api for the backend; see connecting domains to hosting.
  3. Add a CAA record naming your certificate authority, for example 0 issue "letsencrypt.org".
  4. Put the CDN in front of TaskFlow Web with cache rules per path (long for hashed assets, short or none for HTML) and a purge step in the deploy pipeline; see CDN setup and edge caching.
  5. Rehearse a provider move: lower TTLs days ahead, copy every record (including MX and TXT), compare answers with dig @<nameserver>, then switch nameservers; see DNS migrations and troubleshooting.
  6. Send transactional email through your provider with SPF and DKIM records and a DMARC record at p=none with reporting.
  7. Read the DMARC reports, fix any sender that fails, then move to p=quarantine and finally p=reject; see email deliverability.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• example.com and www.example.com resolve, and one redirects to the other.
  • api.example.com reaches the backend, and the CAA record is visible with dig CAA.
  • CDN responses show cache hits for assets, and a deploy purges stale HTML.
  • The rehearsed migration copied every record with no resolution gap.
  • Test messages pass SPF, DKIM, and DMARC, and the policy is p=reject.

docs.title: Stretch goals
docs.text:
• Turn on DNSSEC at the registrar and DNS provider.
  • Add MTA-STS for inbound mail.
  • Serve a per-pull-request preview subdomain.

docs.title: Lessons to use
docs.text:
• Domains, DNS and Email
  • DNS and CDN

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Comparing versions as strings. Use a SemVer library.
  • Contracting the API while old clients remain. Measure, then contract.
  • Deleting old assets on deploy. Keep hashed files for days.
  • Calling per-request throttling a rollout. Bucket by install ID and release.
  • Fixing only the release branch. Fix main, then cherry-pick -x.
  • Rebuilding the final release. Promote the last candidate's build.
  • Deploying a monorepo diff against HEAD^1. Use the last successful deploy and fetch-depth: 0.
  • Undeclared env vars in task hashes. Declare them (VITE_*).

docs.title: Deploying Microservices
docs.text:
Splitting TaskFlow into services (a tasks API, a notification service, a search service, and the web app) only pays off if each one can be changed, tested, and deployed on its own. That property, independent deployability, is the real goal of a microservice architecture, and it is easy to lose: one shared database, one breaking API change, or one "release night" in which every service must deploy in a fixed order, and you have all the cost of a distributed system with none of the independence.

This lesson covers independent deployability as the goal, one pipeline per service and clear ownership, contracts between services (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, and schema registries for events), backward-compatible changes across services and event schemas, deployment ordering without lock-step releases, per-service databases and migrations, environments and ephemeral test environments, GitOps with one deployable unit per service, observing a deploy across services, and when microservices make deployment harder than a modular monolith. The architecture side (boundaries, sagas, gateways) is covered in microservices patterns.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Independent deployability is the payoff. Teams choose microservices to ship without waiting for each other, to deploy small changes many times a day, and to limit the blast radius of a bad deploy. All three depend on deploying one service without coordinating with the others.
  • The distributed monolith is the common failure. Services that must be released together, in order, during a window, are a monolith whose function calls now cross a network: slower, harder to debug, and still coupled.
  • More deployables multiply release work. Ten services mean ten pipelines, ten sets of dashboards, and ten things that can be on the wrong version. Without shared templates and contracts, release engineering effort grows faster than the number of services.
  • Compatibility becomes a network problem. In a monolith the compiler catches a renamed field; between services, nothing does unless contract checks run in CI.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• The original definition. James Lewis and Martin Fowler's Microservices (2014) describes services that are "independently deployable by fully automated deployment machinery", each managing its own database, and recommends designing services as tolerant readers so that versioning is a last resort.
  • Amazon. Clare Liguori's Builders' Library article Automating safe, hands-off deployments describes a typical microservice with several pipelines (application code, infrastructure, operating system patches, configuration and feature flags, operator tools), deploying multiple times a day, and stresses that new code must be backward compatible with both the current code and the service's dependencies.
  • Segment. Alexandra Noonan's Goodbye Microservices (2018) describes more than 140 services whose shared libraries drifted apart, so that a change to a shared library meant testing and deploying every service; consolidating into one service removed the operational load.
  • Shopify. Kirsten Westeinde's Deconstructing the Monolith (2019) explains why Shopify chose a modular monolith, with components by business domain behind public interfaces, instead of splitting into services.
  • Event contracts. Confluent's schema evolution and compatibility documentation defines BACKWARD (the default), FORWARD, FULL, their transitive variants, and NONE, and states which side must be upgraded first for each.

Popular tools and providers: Argo CD and Flux for GitOps, Helm and Kustomize, the Pact Broker and PactFlow, Confluent Schema Registry and Apicurio Registry, OpenAPI and AsyncAPI with diff tools such as oasdiff, Backstage for service ownership, OpenTelemetry for tracing by version, and Spinnaker or Argo Rollouts for progressive delivery.

docs.title: Independent deployability is the goal
docs.text:
A simple test: can the notification team deploy the notification service on a Tuesday afternoon, without asking anyone, and without anything else deploying? If yes, the conditions below hold:

Condition What breaks it Its own pipeline and artifact A shared build that produces every service's image at once Its own data Another service reading or writing its tables Compatible contracts A change that requires a consumer to deploy at the same moment No shared runtime state Shared in-process libraries with behaviour that must match across services No deploy-time ordering "Deploy search before tasks, or indexing breaks" A rollback that touches only itself A migration other services already depend on

docs.title: One pipeline per service, owned by one team
docs.text:
Each service gets its own pipeline: test, contract checks, build one image, deploy to staging, can-i-deploy, production with a canary, and a record of what was deployed. Writing that pipeline ten times invites drift, so most organizations keep one reusable pipeline (a GitHub Actions reusable workflow, versioned like any other dependency) that each service calls with a few inputs. The platform team improves the template; services adopt new versions deliberately. Reusable workflows are explained in GitHub Actions in depth.

Ownership must be explicit and machine-readable: a team per service in a service catalog (for example Backstage's catalog-info.yaml), the same team in CODEOWNERS, and the same team in the alert routing. When a deploy breaks something at night, "whose service is this?" must have one answer.

docs.title: Contracts between services
docs.text:
Services talk through contracts, and each kind of contract has its own tool for describing it and checking changes:

Interaction Contract Breaking-change check Synchronous HTTP OpenAPI document in the provider's repository Diff against the version in production (oasdiff or similar) in CI Asynchronous events AsyncAPI document plus a schema per event type A schema registry rejects incompatible schemas under the topic's compatibility mode gRPC and Protobuf .proto files Field-number and type rules (never reuse a field number; reserve deleted ones) Any of the above, consumer's view Consumer-driven contracts (Pact), for HTTP and messages Provider verification against every deployed consumer version, and can-i-deploy

Provider-side diffs catch changes that break the documented contract; consumer-driven contracts catch changes that break what consumers actually use, and they tell the provider which fields are safe to remove. Mature setups use both.

The mechanics of Pact (publishing, verification selectors, can-i-deploy, record-deployment) are shown with full workflows in keeping frontend and backend in sync; between backend services they work the same way, with each service being a consumer of some and a provider for others.

docs.title: Backward-compatible changes across services and event schemas
docs.text:
The rules for HTTP APIs carry over to service-to-service calls: add fields instead of changing them, never repurpose a field, make new request fields optional, and have consumers ignore unknown fields. Events add two complications:

  • Events outlive deploys. A Kafka topic with seven days of retention holds events written by last week's producer. A consumer that replays the topic (after a bug fix, or a new consumer starting from the beginning) reads every schema version still stored there.
  • Producers and consumers deploy at different times, and which one may go first depends on the compatibility mode.

For a change no compatibility mode allows (a new required field, a changed meaning), publish a new event version next to the old one:

  1. The producer publishes task.assigned v2 alongside v1 (same event ID in both, so consumers that read both can deduplicate).
  2. Each consumer team moves to v2 on its own schedule.
  3. When no consumer reads v1 (no consumer group's committed offsets on the v1 topic still move), the producer stops publishing it.

The event envelope (ID, type, version, source, time) is described in event-driven architecture.

docs.title: Deployment ordering without lock-step releases
docs.text:
Lock-step releases have recognizable symptoms: a spreadsheet of deploy order, a "release night", a version matrix that pins exact versions of other services, and pull requests in several repositories that must merge together. The cure is the same expand-and-contract sequence used between frontend and backend, applied service by service:

  1. The provider deploys support for the new behaviour, keeping the old (a new optional field, a new endpoint, a new event version).
  2. Each consumer deploys its change whenever it is ready, possibly behind a flag.
  3. The provider removes the old behaviour once contracts and usage show no consumer needs it.

Each step is one service, deployable alone, and can-i-deploy checks each step against what is actually running. If a change truly cannot be split this way, the two services probably belong together.

docs.title: Per-service databases and migrations
docs.text:
Each service owns its data store; other services get data through its API or its events, never by reading its tables. A shared table is a hidden, untested contract: a column rename in the tasks service breaks the search service at runtime, and no contract test notices.

Migrations live in the service's repository and run in its pipeline, following the rules in zero-downtime database migrations: every migration must work with the previous version of the same service, because both run side by side during its rolling deploy. Data another service needs is copied through events into that service's own store (the search index is built from task events), which is also what lets each side change its schema independently.

docs.title: Environments and ephemeral test environments
docs.text:
A single shared staging environment becomes a bottleneck as services multiply: teams queue for it, one broken service blocks everyone's tests, and "it worked in staging" stops meaning much because staging rarely matches the mix of versions in production. Options, in order of cost:

  • Contract tests first. They replace most cross-service integration testing and need no environment at all.
  • Ephemeral environments per pull request that run the changed service and use the production versions of everything else (from images already in the registry). Previews are covered in environments and promotion.
  • Shared baseline with request routing: one environment runs the current version of every service, and a header on test requests routes calls for the service under test to its preview instance (service meshes and some platforms support this kind of header-based routing).
  • A small end-to-end suite on the few journeys that matter most, run against staging and production, not a full regression suite.

docs.title: GitOps with one deployable unit per service
docs.text: In a GitOps setup each service has its own directory in the deployment repository, generated into its own Argo CD Application (for example by an ApplicationSet with a Git directory generator). Promotion is a commit that changes one service's image digest; history, review, and rollback all happen per service. One Application that deploys every service together recreates the lock-step release in YAML. The mechanics of Argo CD and Flux are in immutable infrastructure and GitOps.

docs.title: Observing a deploy across services
docs.text:
When several services deploy independently, "what changed?" needs data:

  • Every signal carries service.version. With the OpenTelemetry resource attribute set from the image's version, metrics, logs, and traces can be split by version, so a canary of the notification service can be compared with its stable version directly.
  • Deploy markers on dashboards. Each pipeline records a deployment event (service, version, environment, time); dashboards show them as annotations, so an error spike lines up with the deploy that caused it.
  • Traces by version. A trace shows which version of each service handled each hop. If errors appear only on traces that pass through search-service 4.2.0, the culprit is found without a meeting.
  • The deployment history across services answers "what changed in the last hour anywhere?", which is the first question of most incidents.

See distributed tracing for propagation and the resource attributes.

docs.title: When microservices make deployment harder
docs.text:
Delivery concern Modular monolith Microservices Deployables One One per service Atomic change across modules One commit, one deploy Several deploys in a compatible order Contract checks The compiler and tests Contract tests, schema registries, can-i-deploy Rollback One version One service, if contracts hold Local development Run one process Run several, or use stubs and shared environments Independent scaling and release cadence No Yes Blast radius of a bad deploy Everything One service, if isolation holds

Signs that two services should be one: they are always deployed together, they share a database, the same team owns both, or every change to one needs a change to the other. Segment's and Shopify's posts are public examples of teams deciding that a well-structured single deployable served them better; the trade-offs are discussed in monolith, modular monolith, and microservices.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Approach Several teams that need to ship independently Microservices with one pipeline each, contracts in CI, can-i-deploy gates One team, one product A modular monolith with internal boundaries; split later if teams grow Services that always change together Merge them, or make the contract between them stable first Event-driven integration A schema registry with an explicit compatibility mode per topic, and new event versions for breaking changes Shared staging is a bottleneck Contract tests and per-pull-request environments before more shared environments Kubernetes with Argo CD or Flux One Application per service, promotion by digest, rollback per service

docs.title: One reusable pipeline that every service calls
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/service-pipeline.yml (in the example/pipelines repository)
name: service-pipeline
on:
  workflow_call:
    inputs:
      service:
        type: string
        required: true              # image name and Pact participant, e.g. notification-service
    secrets:
      PACT_BROKER_TOKEN:
        required: true
      DEPLOY_REPO_TOKEN:
        required: true

permissions:
  contents: read

env:
  PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL: https://pact-broker.example.com

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test                   # unit tests, consumer pacts, provider verification
        env:
          PACT_BROKER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}

  image:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    outputs:
      digest: ${{ steps.push.outputs.digest }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - id: push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/example/${{ inputs.service }}:sha-${{ github.sha }}
          build-args: |
            VERSION=sha-${{ github.sha }}

  promote:
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
    needs: image
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production              # reviewers, if production needs them
    env:
      SERVICE: ${{ inputs.service }}
      DIGEST: ${{ needs.image.outputs.digest }}
      PACT_BROKER_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.PACT_BROKER_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - name: Is this version compatible with everything in production?
        run: |
          docker run --rm -e PACT_BROKER_BASE_URL -e PACT_BROKER_TOKEN \
            pactfoundation/pact-cli:latest \
            pact-broker can-i-deploy --pacticipant "$SERVICE" \
            --version "$GITHUB_SHA" --to-environment production
      - name: Pin the new digest for this service only (GitOps)
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_REPO_TOKEN }}
        run: |
          gh repo clone example/taskflow-deploy deploy -- --depth 1
          cd deploy
          yq -i '.images[0].digest = strenv(DIGEST)' "apps/$SERVICE/overlays/prod/kustomization.yaml"
          git config user.name "taskflow-release-bot"
          git config user.email "release-bot@example.com"
          git commit -am "deploy($SERVICE): $DIGEST"
          gh auth setup-git
          git push

# .github/workflows/pipeline.yml (in the notification-service repository)
name: pipeline
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  pipeline:
    uses: example/pipelines/.github/workflows/service-pipeline.yml@v3
    with:
      service: notification-service
    secrets: inherit
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
  • The caller pins the shared pipeline to @v3, so the platform team can publish v4 without changing every service at once.
  • Inputs reach shell scripts through env, never through ${{ }} inside run, so a crafted input cannot inject commands.
  • The promote job changes only this service's directory in the deploy repository; Argo CD syncs that one Application. After the sync is healthy (for example from an Argo CD notification), the pipeline or a webhook runs record-deployment so can-i-deploy knows what is live.

docs.title: Describe the event contract with AsyncAPI
docs.text:
# asyncapi.yaml (tasks-api repository): the event contract other teams build against
asyncapi: 3.1.0
info:
  title: TaskFlow task events
  version: 2.1.0
channels:
  taskAssignedV2:
    address: taskflow.task.assigned.v2
    messages:
      taskAssigned:
        $ref: "#/components/messages/TaskAssignedV2"
operations:
  publishTaskAssigned:
    action: send
    channel:
      $ref: "#/channels/taskAssignedV2"
components:
  messages:
    TaskAssignedV2:
      name: task.assigned
      contentType: application/json
      payload:
        type: object
        required: [id, type, version, occurredAt, data]
        properties:
          id: { type: string, format: uuid }
          type: { const: task.assigned }
          version: { const: 2 }
          occurredAt: { type: string, format: date-time }
          data:
            type: object
            required: [taskId, assignee]
            properties:
              taskId: { type: string }
              assignee:
                type: object
                required: [id]
                properties:
                  id: { type: string }
                  team: { type: string }
              due:
                type: object
                properties:
                  date: { type: string, format: date }
                  timezone: { type: string }

The document lives next to the producer's code, is reviewed with it, and is published to the service catalog, so consumer teams discover topics and payloads without reading the producer's source.

docs.title: Let the schema registry refuse breaking changes
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/check-schema.sh: fail CI if a schema change would break a deployed reader
set -euo pipefail
REGISTRY="https://schema-registry.example.com"
SUBJECT="taskflow.task.assigned.v2-value"
CT="Content-Type: application/vnd.schemaregistry.v1+json"

# Once per subject: consumers may replay a week of history, so check every version
curl -fsS -X PUT "$REGISTRY/config/$SUBJECT" -H "$CT" \
  --data '{"compatibility": "BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE"}'

# On every pull request that touches the schema
jq -n --rawfile schema schemas/task-assigned-v2.schema.json \
  '{schemaType: "JSON", schema: $schema}' > /tmp/schema-request.json
curl -fsS -X POST "$REGISTRY/compatibility/subjects/$SUBJECT/versions/latest" \
  -H "$CT" --data @/tmp/schema-request.json | jq -e '.is_compatible == true'

jq -e exits non-zero when the registry answers "is_compatible": false, which fails the pull request before the producer can deploy a schema that the deployed consumers cannot read. (In practice the compatibility setting is managed as configuration, not run on every build.)

docs.title: Publish two event versions during a migration
docs.text:
// src/events/task-assigned.js (tasks-api): v1 and v2 until no consumer reads v1
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";
import { publish } from "./bus.js"; // a thin wrapper around the message broker client

export async function publishTaskAssigned(task, assignee) {
  const id = randomUUID();                 // the same ID in both versions: consumers dedupe
  const occurredAt = new Date().toISOString();
  const envelope = { id, type: "task.assigned", source: "tasks-api", occurredAt };

  await publish("taskflow.task.assigned.v2", task.id, {
    ...envelope,
    version: 2,
    data: { taskId: task.id, assignee: { id: assignee.id, team: assignee.teamId }, due: task.due },
  });
  await publish("taskflow.task.assigned.v1", task.id, {   // remove when v1 has no consumers
    ...envelope,
    version: 1,
    data: { taskId: task.id, assigneeId: assignee.id, dueDate: task.due?.date ?? null },
  });
}

Keying both messages by task ID keeps per-task ordering within each topic. Two separate publishes are not atomic; if losing one of them is unacceptable, write both to an outbox table in the same database transaction as the change (the transactional outbox pattern) and publish from there.

docs.title: One Argo CD Application per service
docs.text:
# clusters/prod/taskflow-services.yaml: one Application per service directory
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: taskflow-services-prod
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - git:
        repoURL: https://github.com/example/taskflow-deploy.git
        revision: main
        directories:
          - path: apps/*/overlays/prod
  template:
    metadata:
      name: "{{index .path.segments 1}}-prod"     # e.g. notification-service-prod
    spec:
      project: taskflow
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/example/taskflow-deploy.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: "{{.path.path}}"
      destination:
        server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
        namespace: "{{index .path.segments 1}}"
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
        syncOptions:
          - CreateNamespace=true

Adding a service is adding a directory; each service syncs, fails, and rolls back on its own, and the Argo CD history shows deploys per service.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Treat independent deployability as a requirement and test it: any service, any day, alone.
  • Give every service one owner, one pipeline (from a shared, versioned template), and one deployable artifact.
  • Keep each service's data private; share data through APIs and events.
  • Describe contracts (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, schemas) next to the code, and check changes in CI against what is deployed, not just against the last commit.
  • Choose a compatibility mode per event topic deliberately, and use the transitive modes where consumers replay history.
  • Ship breaking changes as expand, migrate consumers, contract, with new event versions published alongside old ones.
  • Gate production deploys with can-i-deploy and record every deploy.
  • Promote per service in GitOps; never bundle all services into one release unit.
  • Tag every signal with service.version and mark deploys on dashboards.
  • Merge services that always deploy together.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Every release needs a deploy-order spreadsheet. Detect: releases happen in windows; pull requests across repositories must merge together; rollbacks involve several teams. Cause: breaking contracts or a shared database couple the services. Fix: make each change backward compatible (expand, migrate, contract), move shared tables behind one owner's API, and gate deploys with can-i-deploy.
  • Search results go stale after a tasks deploy, with no errors. Detect: the search service's consumer lag is zero but documents stop updating; its logs show events skipped as unparseable. Cause: the producer changed the event payload in a way the consumer's parser rejects, and the registry's compatibility mode was NONE. Fix: set BACKWARD or FULL (transitive where history is replayed), add contract tests for messages, and replay the skipped events after the fix.
  • A consumer crashes when it replays a topic from the beginning. Detect: a new consumer, or one reset to an old offset, fails on events from weeks ago. Cause: compatibility was checked only against the latest schema, not every version still stored in the topic. Fix: use a _TRANSITIVE mode, and test consumers against samples of every stored version.
  • A rollback of one service breaks another. Detect: errors in a dependent service immediately after rolling back. Cause: the dependent already relied on the new endpoint or field, so the rollback removed something in use. Fix: consumers adopt new provider features behind a flag, and can-i-deploy is run for rollbacks too.
  • Staging is always broken. Detect: teams wait for staging; failures there are usually someone else's service. Cause: one shared environment for many independently deployed services. Fix: contract tests in each pipeline, per-pull-request environments that use production versions of the other services, and a small end-to-end suite.
  • Nobody can say which deploy caused an error spike. Detect: incident time is spent asking every team what they shipped. Cause: no deploy markers and no version on telemetry. Fix: record every deploy as an event, annotate dashboards, and add service.version to every signal.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Independent deployability: the ability to deploy one service without deploying or coordinating with others.
  • Distributed monolith: services that must be released together, combining the costs of distribution with monolith coupling.
  • Lock-step release: deploying several services together in a fixed order.
  • Contract: the agreed shape and behaviour of an interface between services.
  • Consumer-driven contract: a contract derived from what consumers actually use.
  • Schema registry: a service that stores event schemas and enforces a compatibility mode on changes.
  • Compatibility mode: the rule (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL, transitive variants, NONE) a new schema must satisfy.
  • Event version: a distinct, published shape of an event type, run side by side with older versions during migrations.
  • Ephemeral environment: a short-lived environment created for one change.
  • ApplicationSet: an Argo CD resource that generates one Application per item, such as one per service directory.
  • Deploy marker: a recorded deploy event shown on dashboards.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Equating "many services" with "independent services".
  • Sharing a database between services "temporarily".
  • Writing a separate, hand-made pipeline for every service.
  • Checking only the producer's documented contract, not what consumers use.
  • Leaving the schema registry's compatibility mode at NONE, or checking only against the latest version for replayed topics.
  • Coordinating releases in a meeting instead of making changes compatible.
  • Deploying all services from one GitOps Application.
  • Splitting a system into services before the team or the product needs it.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Define independent deployability and list four conditions it needs.
  2. What are the symptoms of a distributed monolith, and how do you remove them?
  3. Which contract checks would you run for an HTTP API, an event, and a gRPC interface?
  4. Under the BACKWARD compatibility mode, which side deploys first, and which changes are allowed? What about FORWARD?
  5. Why does a topic with 30 days of retention push you towards a transitive compatibility mode?
  6. Plan the deploys needed to replace assigneeId with an assignee object in the task.assigned event without breaking any consumer.
  7. Why should each service be its own Argo CD Application rather than part of one Application for the whole system?
  8. Ten services each deploy about twice a day. Roughly how many production deploys happen per week, and what must the observability setup provide to make an error spike attributable? (About 100 on a five-day week; deploy markers and service.version on every signal.)

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• James Lewis and Martin Fowler: Microservices
  • AWS Builders' Library: Automating safe, hands-off deployments
  • Confluent: Schema evolution and compatibility
  • AsyncAPI specification
  • Pact: can-i-deploy
  • Argo CD: Git generator for ApplicationSets
  • Protocol Buffers: dos and don'ts
  • Next: monorepo builds and deployments. Back to the release engineering overview.

docs.title: Release Engineering Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review versioning patterns, keeping frontend and backend in sync, update mechanisms and updaters, release trains and release management, deploying microservices, and monorepo builds and deployments. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. Why does one product need several version numbers?
docs.text: Different things change at different times and are read by different audiences: an SDK's consumers ask "is upgrading safe?" (SemVer), the deploy pipeline asks "which exact build?" (commit SHA and digest), the migration tool asks "which order?" (migration IDs), stores ask "is it newer?" (an integer build number), and event consumers ask "which payload shape?" (an event version). One number cannot answer all of them.

docs.title: 2. Compare SemVer, CalVer, build numbers, commit SHAs, and digests.
docs.text: SemVer orders versions and signals compatibility. CalVer orders by date but says nothing about compatibility. A CI build number orders builds within one workflow. A commit SHA identifies the source exactly but does not order anything, and a content digest identifies the exact artifact. Pipelines record several of them because no single one gives ordering, identity, and meaning together.

docs.title: 3. What is SemVer build metadata, and why can it not order builds?
docs.text: It is the part after +, as in 2.4.1+build.873.g3f2a1c. SemVer ignores it for precedence, so 2.4.1+build.873 and 2.4.1+build.874 are equal to an updater or package manager. Some systems also drop or reject it: Docker tags cannot contain +, and the semver package's valid() returns 2.4.1. Use it for traceability, not ordering.

docs.title: 4. How should development builds between releases be versioned?
docs.text: As pre-releases of the next version, for example 2.4.2-dev.5 (five commits after v2.4.1). A name like 2.4.1-dev.5 is a pre-release of 2.4.1 and sorts before the release it was built after, so updaters treat a newer build as older. With the next-version scheme, precedence matches build order: 2.4.1 < 2.4.2-dev.5 < 2.4.2-rc.1 < 2.4.2.

docs.title: 5. What are display versions and build numbers on Android and iOS?
docs.text: Android has versionName (any string, shown to users) and versionCode (a positive integer, at most 2,100,000,000, never reused on Google Play, and used by the system to block downgrades). Apple has CFBundleShortVersionString (three integers, user-visible) and CFBundleVersion (the build, one to three integers); App Store Connect identifies a build by bundle ID, version, and build string together.

docs.title: 6. How do you produce monotonic build numbers in CI, and what goes wrong?
docs.text: Common sources are the CI run number plus an offset, a timestamp, a commit count, or a value derived from SemVer. Traps: run numbers restart when the build moves to another workflow, commit counts differ between branches and are 1 in a shallow clone, and long timestamps overflow store limits (YYMMDDHHmm exceeds Android's 2,100,000,000). Whatever the source, it must never go backwards.

docs.title: 7. Where should a running service expose its version, and how is it set?
docs.text: In image tags and OCI labels, a GET /version endpoint, an X-App-Version response header, the startup log, the OpenTelemetry service.version attribute, and the error tracker's release name. CI computes the version once and passes it to every step as a build argument; computing it at runtime from Git fails because containers have no .git directory.

docs.title: 8. Why must versions never be compared as strings?
docs.text: Because "1.10.0" < "1.9.0" and "rc.10" < "rc.2" as strings. Use a SemVer library (semver.compare, semver.gt) and compare build numbers as integers. Also know that semver.satisfies("2.4.2-dev.5", ">=2.4.1") is false unless includePrerelease is set.

docs.title: Keeping frontend and backend in sync
9. What is version skew, and why can you not avoid it?
docs.text: Skew is two interdependent components running different versions at the same time. A rolling deploy serves old and new versions side by side for minutes, open browser tabs keep old JavaScript for hours, and installed apps keep old builds for months. At 50% new pods, 20 requests from one page all reach the same version with probability 2 x 0.5^20, about two in a million.

docs.title: 10. What is the difference between backward and forward compatibility here?
docs.text: A backward-compatible server works with older clients: it accepts their request shapes and keeps the fields they read. A forward-compatible client keeps working against a newer server: it ignores unknown fields and treats unknown enum values safely. During a rollout a new client can also hit an old server, so it must not depend on new server features until they are deployed everywhere.

docs.title: 11. Which changes look additive but still break clients?
docs.text: A new enum value (clients with exhaustive switches or strict validation), a new required request field, tightened validation, a repurposed field (same name, new meaning or unit), new response fields for clients that reject unknown fields, and changed defaults such as sort order or page size.

docs.title: 12. In what order do you deploy a breaking API change?
docs.text: Expand the server so it accepts and returns both the old and the new shape; switch the clients; wait while measuring usage of the old shape (old tabs reload, app users update, the minimum version rises); then contract the server. Reversing the first two steps breaks new clients on old pods, and contracting early breaks old clients still in use.

docs.title: 13. Compare API versioning strategies.
docs.text: Path versions (/v2) are easy to route, log, and cache but version the whole API at once. Header versions (dated, like GitHub's X-GitHub-Api-Version) allow fine-grained changes but need Vary for caches and are easy to forget. Media-type versions fit content negotiation but are awkward for tools. Account pinning (Stripe) never breaks a client by default but requires transforms for every version. GraphQL avoids versions by adding fields and deprecating old ones with @deprecated, removing them when usage stops.

docs.title: 14. Why do single-page apps hit chunk-load errors after a deploy?
docs.text: An open tab's index.html references hashed route chunks from its own build. If the deploy deleted those files, the next lazy navigation fails ("Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" in Vite apps, ChunkLoadError in webpack apps). Keep old assets for days, serve HTML with no-cache, reload once on a missing chunk with a loop guard, and prompt long-open tabs to update.

docs.title: 15. How does a long-open tab learn that a new version is deployed?
docs.text: By polling a version.json served with no-cache (on an interval and when the tab becomes visible), by comparing a version header on API responses with its own build, or through a waiting service worker. It then prompts the user or turns the next navigation into a full page load. Builds are compared for inequality, so a rollback also moves tabs.

docs.title: 16. What does platform skew protection do, and where does it stop?
docs.text: It routes requests from an open page to the deployment that served it. On Vercel the deployment ID travels as ?dpl=, an x-deployment-id header, or a __vdpl cookie, depending on the framework. Full-page navigations always get the latest deployment, some frameworks pin only framework-managed requests, and pinning ends at the maximum age (12 hours by default on Pro). It does not protect a separately deployed API or installed apps.

docs.title: 17. How do you enforce a minimum supported client version?
docs.text: Clients send their platform and version on every request. The API keeps a minimum and a recommended version per platform in configuration, returns a documented error (often 426 with a code such as client_update_required) below the minimum, adds a soft X-Client-Update header below the recommended one, exempts the endpoints the update screen needs, and never blocks requests whose version it cannot parse. For browser clients on another origin, CORS must allow the custom request headers and expose X-App-Version and X-Client-Update with Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

docs.title: 18. How do consumer-driven contract tests protect old clients?
docs.text: Each consumer records the requests it makes and the fields it uses. The provider verifies the pacts of the consumers' main branch and of every deployed or released version, and can-i-deploy checks a version against what is in the target environment. Mobile and desktop versions recorded with record-release stay in the verification set until support ends, so the API cannot drop a field a supported app reads.

docs.title: 19. How do you size the support window for installed clients?
docs.text: From the update decay curve. If 25% of an old version's users update each week, 0.75^n remain after n weeks, so falling below 2% takes 14 weeks. Publish the policy (which releases, how long), measure the version distribution, and raise the floor only when the remaining share is small and the update path works on every supported OS.

docs.title: 20. Static manifest on a CDN or dynamic update server?
docs.text: A static manifest (latest.yml, a Sparkle appcast, Tauri JSON) is cheap, cacheable, and highly available, but gives everyone the same answer, so rollout logic lives in the client and halts wait for caches. A dynamic server decides per request from version, platform, channel, install ID, and tenant, enabling instant halts, cohorts, tenant pinning, and forced updates, at the cost of running a highly available service.

docs.title: 21. Describe the service worker update lifecycle.
docs.text: On navigation (or a push or sync event if no check happened in 24 hours), the browser fetches sw.js, ignoring the HTTP cache by default, and installs it if it is byte-different. The new worker installs (precaching), then waits while the old worker controls open pages, then activates (cleaning old caches) and controls new page loads. The wait keeps one version per set of pages.

docs.title: 22. When is skipWaiting() safe, and what is the usual alternative?
docs.text: It is safe only when the new worker works with pages already open. It makes the new worker active immediately, and with clients.claim() it controls pages built from old code, which can break them. The usual pattern: detect the waiting worker, show "Update available", on click post a message so it calls skipWaiting(), and reload once on controllerchange.

docs.title: 23. Why verify update signatures when downloads already use HTTPS?
docs.text: HTTPS protects the connection, not the content of a compromised bucket, CDN, or update server. The app verifies a signature with a public key built into it before installing. TUF's security model also lists rollback attacks (older files), indefinite freeze attacks (stale files forever), and mix-and-match attacks, which need version checks and signed metadata with expiry.

docs.title: 24. How do you rotate an update-signing key safely?
docs.text: Ship the app with the current public key and a backup key from the first release. To rotate, publish an update signed with the old key that adds the new public key; switch signing only after that update reaches every supported install. Keep private keys in an HSM or signing service, and test the update path from the oldest supported version.

docs.title: 25. Compare full, delta, and block-based updates.
docs.text: Full packages are simple and large. Binary deltas (Sparkle's .delta files) are tiny but generated per source version, and a mismatched delta falls back to the full download. Block-based updates (electron-updater's blockmap, MSIX's 64 KB blocks) download only changed blocks from any older version. For 1,000,000 installs of a 150 MB app, cutting the average download to 15 MB saves 135 TB per release.

docs.title: 26. What is the difference between bucketing installs and throttling requests?
docs.text: Bucketing hashes the install ID with the release version, so a 10% rollout means a fixed 10% of installs, and raising it only adds installs. Throttling requests (Balrog's backgroundRate is a percentage of requests) is a dice roll per check: a client checking six times a day at 10% is offered the release within a day with probability 1 - 0.9^6 = 47%.

docs.title: 27. A bad desktop release reached 20% of installs. What do you do?
docs.text: Halt it, disable the broken feature with a remote flag if possible, and roll forward: offer the fix immediately to every install on the bad version (they are already affected) and ramp everyone else normally. Avoid downgrades, because the bad version may have migrated local data that older code cannot read.

docs.title: 28. What mechanisms exist for forced and optional updates?
docs.text: Optional: background download, install on quit or restart (electron-updater's default). Recommended: a banner or Android's flexible flow. Required: MSIX UpdateBlocksActivation, Sparkle critical updates, Android's immediate flow, or a server-side minimum version. Force only for security fixes and versions the API can no longer serve.

docs.title: 29. What can over-the-air JavaScript updates change, and what limits them?
docs.text: They replace the JavaScript bundle and assets of a React Native app, delivered only to builds with a matching runtime version; native code needs a store build. Apple's license agreement allows downloaded interpreted code only if it does not change the app's primary purpose, bypass OS security, or create a storefront, and Google Play forbids downloading executable code outside Play except code running in an interpreter such as JavaScript. Microsoft retired App Center, including CodePush, on March 31, 2025.

docs.title: 30. How do you keep an update service available?
docs.text: Make clients fail open with short timeouts; jitter check times (2 million installs every four hours average 139 requests per second, but a morning launch peak can reach thousands); return cheap 204 answers; keep artifacts immutable on a CDN; and keep a static manifest as a fallback.

docs.title: 31. Which telemetry shows that an update rollout is healthy?
docs.text: The funnel per target version (offered, downloaded, verified, installed, healthy first launch), crash-free sessions of the new version against the old, the version distribution of active installs, and time to reach 50% and 90%. A spike in verification failures usually means a key or file problem, not a code bug.

docs.title: 32. When is a release train better than continuous deployment?
docs.text: When releases cannot reach users continuously: mobile apps behind store review, desktop and on-premises software, browsers, and public API changes that need notice. Web services usually deploy continuously and use trains only for client apps or versioned API changes. Trains cost lead time: with a two-week train and a week each of stabilization and rollout, a change takes two to four weeks to reach everyone. Public examples: Chrome ships a milestone every two weeks since Chrome 153 (September 2026), Firefox moved to two-week releases from Firefox 155, and Rust releases every six weeks.

docs.title: 33. Describe the parts of a release train.
docs.text: A fixed cadence; a cut that creates release/<version> from main; stabilization in which only fixes enter and each produces a release candidate for beta users; a go/no-go decision on agreed numbers; a phased rollout that promotes the last candidate's build; and support with hotfixes. A feature that misses the cut takes the next train or ships dark behind a flag.

docs.title: 34. What are the rules for release branches?
docs.text: Branch from main at the cut and never merge back; fix on main first, then cherry-pick with -x; accept only fixes; protect release/* with rulesets; and promote candidate builds instead of rebuilding. Fixing only the branch brings the bug back in the next release cut from main.

docs.title: 35. Walk through a hotfix for a bug in 2.4.0 and in the LTS line 2.3.
docs.text: Decide whether a rollback or flag is faster. Otherwise fix on main with a test, cherry-pick into release/2.4 and release/2.3 (adapting the older one), tag v2.4.1 and v2.3.7, build each once, ship through a shortened but still staged rollout, communicate, and follow up with a postmortem.

docs.title: 36. How do release notes differ from changelogs?
docs.text: A changelog lists every notable change per version for developers and is generated from commits or labels. Release notes are written for users and customers: what changed for them, upgrade steps, known issues, and deprecations, in the app, the store listing, or email.

docs.title: 37. What should a long-term support policy state, and what does it cost?
docs.text: Which versions are supported, for how long, which fixes qualify (security only or critical bugs too), and the end-of-life dates. Examples: Kubernetes maintains three minor releases; GitLab backports security fixes to the previous two monthly releases; Node.js 24 is in maintenance until April 2028. Each supported line multiplies backports: monthly releases with three supported lines turn 12 security fixes into 36 patch releases a year.

docs.title: 38. What do the Deprecation and Sunset headers communicate?
docs.text: Deprecation (RFC 9745) says a resource is or will be deprecated, as a structured date such as @1796083200; it does not change behaviour. Sunset (RFC 8594) gives the HTTP date after which the resource is likely to stop responding. A Link with rel="deprecation" points to details, and the sunset must not be earlier than the deprecation.

docs.title: 39. What is a brownout, and why run one?
docs.text: A short, announced, scheduled period (an hour, then a day) in which a deprecated endpoint fails exactly as it will after the sunset. Clients that ignored every notice discover the dependency while there is still time, and usage numbers usually drop sharply after each one.

docs.title: 40. What belongs in a go/no-go decision?
docs.text: Agreed criteria with numbers and sources: open release blockers, crash-free sessions of the candidate against the current release with a minimum sample, API error rates by client version, reviewed migrations, flag defaults, a rollback or roll-forward plan, and communication ready. Missing data counts as no-go, and the decision is recorded with its evidence.

docs.title: 41. What is independent deployability, and how do you test for it?
docs.text: The ability to deploy one service without deploying or coordinating with any other. Test it literally: can the owning team deploy it on a Tuesday afternoon, alone? That requires its own pipeline and artifact, its own data, backward-compatible contracts, no deploy ordering, and a rollback that touches only itself.

docs.title: 42. What is a distributed monolith?
docs.text: Services that must be released together, in order, during a window, usually because of shared databases or breaking contracts. Symptoms: a deploy-order spreadsheet, release nights, version matrices pinning other services, and multi-repository pull requests that must merge together. It combines the costs of distribution with monolith coupling.

docs.title: 43. Which contract checks fit HTTP, events, and gRPC?
docs.text: HTTP: an OpenAPI document diffed against production for breaking changes. Events: an AsyncAPI document and a schema registry enforcing a compatibility mode. gRPC: Protobuf rules (never reuse or retype a field number, reserve deleted ones). Consumer-driven contracts (Pact) cover what consumers actually use, for HTTP and messages, with can-i-deploy as the gate.

docs.title: 44. Explain schema registry compatibility modes.
docs.text: BACKWARD (Confluent's default): consumers on the new schema read data written with the previous one, so consumers upgrade first; fields may be deleted and added only with defaults. FORWARD: old consumers read new data, so producers upgrade first. FULL: both, in any order, with only optional fields added or removed. Transitive variants check every earlier version, which matters when consumers replay long-retention topics.

docs.title: 45. How do you make a breaking change to an event?
docs.text: Publish a new event version alongside the old one with the same event ID, so consumers can deduplicate; let each consumer move on its own schedule; stop publishing the old version when no consumer group still reads it. Use a transactional outbox if both publishes must succeed together.

docs.title: 46. How should GitOps be structured for many services?
docs.text: One Argo CD or Flux application per service (for example generated by an ApplicationSet from one directory per service), promotion as a commit that changes one service's digest, and rollback per service. A single application for every service recreates the lock-step release.

docs.title: 47. How do you find which service's deploy caused an error spike?
docs.text: Record every deploy as an event and show deploy markers on dashboards, put service.version on every metric, log, and trace, and split errors by version. Traces show which version handled each hop, so errors that appear only through search-service 4.2.0 point straight at it.

docs.title: 48. When is a modular monolith the better delivery choice?
docs.text: When one team owns the system, services always change and deploy together, or they share a database. One deployable gives atomic changes, one rollback, and compiler-checked boundaries. Segment consolidated more than 140 services into one, and Shopify chose a modular monolith with enforced component boundaries.

docs.title: 49. How does affected detection work?
docs.text: The tool builds a project graph from declared workspace dependencies, maps changed files to projects, and selects those projects plus all their dependents. Nx (nx affected -t build) selects tasks whose inputs changed; Turborepo (turbo run build --affected) selects whole packages by default; Bazel queries reverse dependencies with rdeps. Changes to global inputs such as the lockfile affect everything.

docs.title: 50. Which base commit should affected detection use?
docs.text: For pull requests, the merge base with the target branch. For deploys on main, the last successfully deployed commit: with HEAD^1, a change whose deploy failed is skipped forever by the next run. The checkout must include history (fetch-depth: 0), or every package looks changed.

docs.title: 51. How does a remote build cache work, and what are its risks?
docs.text: A task's hash covers its files, dependency hashes, declared environment variables, configuration, and resolved dependencies; outputs and logs are stored under that hash and restored on a hit. Risks: undeclared inputs cause wrong hits (a staging bundle served to production), and writable caches can be poisoned, so only CI writes and entries are signed (Turborepo's HMAC signatures, Bazel's read-only clients).

docs.title: 52. Why are path filters a poor fit for required checks in a monorepo?
docs.text: A workflow skipped by paths leaves its checks pending, which blocks merging, and the filter does not follow the dependency graph. Use an always-running workflow that decides inside it what to run (affected detection), and keep path filters for non-required workflows such as per-app deploys.

docs.title: 53. One deploy workflow per app, or one matrix?
docs.text: Per-app workflows give clear triggers, environments, approvals, and ownership, and a shared reusable workflow removes duplication. One workflow with a computed matrix (or turbo run deploy --affected) avoids duplication and handles required checks easily, but mixes credentials and approvals for every app in one place.

docs.title: 54. How do you version shared packages in a monorepo?
docs.text: Internal-only packages use workspace:* and have no meaningful version. Published packages need SemVer: fixed versioning keeps a group on one version, linked versioning aligns changed packages to the group's highest version, and independent versioning lets each move alone. Changesets records bumps in files, changeset version applies them, and changeset publish publishes and tags.

docs.title: 55. Does an atomic commit across the API and the web app make the release atomic?
docs.text: No. The commit is reviewed and tested together, but the API and web app deploy separately, old tabs and installed apps keep running, and published client packages live in customers' lockfiles. Wire changes still need expand, migrate, contract.

docs.title: 56. How do you keep dependencies consistent across a monorepo?
docs.text: Define workspaces, keep one version per external dependency (pnpm catalogs define a range once and packages reference it with catalog:), group dependency updates so one pull request upgrades a library everywhere, and detect duplicates with pnpm why before they reach bundles.

docs.title: 57. Users on an old desktop build start failing after an API deploy. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: errors by X-Client-Version before and after the deploy, and the diff of the API's request and response shapes.

How to confirm: failures come only from versions older than a certain release, start at the deploy time, and show parsing or validation errors for one endpoint.

Likely causes and fixes: a removed or renamed field, a new enum value or required field, or tightened validation. Roll the API back or restore the old shape (expand), add contract tests for every supported desktop release with record-release and deployedOrReleased, and remove the field only after usage reaches zero. See keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: 58. A deploy causes ChunkLoadError for users with open tabs. How do you fix it?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether old hashed assets still exist on the host, and the Cache-Control header of index.html.

How to confirm: the errors come only from sessions that started before the deploy, and the failing URLs are chunk names from the previous build that now return 404.

Likely causes and fixes: the deploy deleted the previous build's assets (a sync with delete), or a cached index.html references old chunks. Keep old assets for days, serve HTML with no-cache, reload once on a missing chunk with a loop guard, and prompt long-open tabs to reload. See keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: 59. For a few minutes during every deploy, the newest web build gets 400 errors. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the timing (only while the API rollout runs) and which client builds see the errors.

How to confirm: the failing requests contain a new field, and they fail only when served by API pods still on the old version.

Likely causes and fixes: the web app started sending a new field before every API pod accepted it. Deploy the API change first (expand), keep the client behaviour behind a flag until the API rollout completes, and make the pipeline enforce server-first ordering. See keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: 60. Users on 1.9.4 are never offered the 1.10.0 desktop update. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: the update server's or client's version comparison and the manifest content.

How to confirm: the check for 1.9.4 returns "no update" while 1.9.4 and 1.10.0 are both in the manifest; a unit test comparing them fails.

Likely causes and fixes: versions compared as strings, so "1.10.0" < "1.9.4". Compare with a SemVer library, and add tests with two-digit minor versions and pre-releases. See versioning patterns.

docs.title: 61. The Play Console rejects the Android upload on release day. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the versionCode of the bundle and of the last upload, including uploads to test tracks.

How to confirm: the code was already used, or the new scheme produces a value above 2,100,000,000.

Likely causes and fixes: a hand-edited build number, a pipeline re-run that reused the number, a CI migration that restarted the run counter, or a timestamp scheme that overflowed. Derive codes from CI with an offset above every code ever shipped, and never reuse one. See versioning patterns.

docs.title: 62. A new desktop release is offered to thousands of installs but installed by none. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the update funnel: offered, downloaded, verified, installed.

How to confirm: downloads complete but verify_ok stays at zero, and client logs show signature failures.

Likely causes and fixes: the release was signed with a different key than the one built into the app, or the manifest carries a signature path instead of its content. Halt, re-sign or fix the manifest, add a CI check that verifies each artifact against the shipped public key, and keep the signing key in one managed place. See update mechanisms and updaters.

docs.title: 63. A halted desktop rollout keeps gaining installs for an hour. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the Cache-Control of the manifest and the CDN's cached copy.

How to confirm: the CDN still serves the previous manifest content, and new installs of the halted version stop exactly when it expires.

Likely causes and fixes: the manifest was cached with a long lifetime. Serve manifests with no-cache or a short max-age, purge them on every change, or move the decision to a dynamic update server. See update mechanisms and updaters.

docs.title: 64. A "10%" update rollout reached most active users within three days. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: how the server decides who gets the update.

How to confirm: the code or configuration rolls a random number per request, and frequent checkers dominate the new version's population.

Likely causes and fixes: per-request throttling instead of bucketing: with 10% per request and six checks a day, 1 - 0.9^18 is 85% after three days. Bucket by a hash of install ID and release so the percentage means a share of installs. See update mechanisms and updaters.

docs.title: 65. After raising the minimum app version, old clients show a blank screen instead of an update prompt. What went wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: responses to the requests the update screen makes (configuration, links, token refresh).

How to confirm: those requests also receive the client_update_required error, so the screen cannot render.

Likely causes and fixes: the version gate covers every path. Exempt the endpoints the update flow needs, test the floor change with the oldest supported build before applying it, and keep the floor in configuration so it can be lowered again quickly. See keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: 66. A bug fixed two weeks ago is back in the new release. How did that happen?
docs.text:
What to check first: where the fix was committed: the release branch, main, or both.

How to confirm: the fix commit exists only on the old release branch, and no commit on main references it.

Likely causes and fixes: a branch-only hotfix; the new release was cut from main, which never had it. Apply the fix on main, require fixes on main first with cherry-pick -x into branches, and check that every release-branch commit references its main source. See release trains and release management.

docs.title: 67. Customers break on the API v1 sunset date despite months of notice. What should have happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: v1 traffic by API client in the weeks before the sunset, and how the deprecation was communicated.

How to confirm: several clients were still calling v1 the day before; responses carried Deprecation and Sunset headers that nobody watched.

Likely causes and fixes: notices without measurement or contact. Count usage per client, contact the remaining users directly, run announced brownouts before the deadline, and keep the sunset date no earlier than the deprecation date. See release trains and release management.

docs.title: 68. Search results stop updating after a tasks-service deploy, with no errors in tasks. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the search consumer's logs and lag, and the event schema change in the tasks deploy.

How to confirm: the consumer skips events as unparseable since the deploy, and the registry's compatibility mode for the topic is NONE.

Likely causes and fixes: an incompatible event change slipped through. Set BACKWARD or FULL (transitive for replayed topics), publish breaking changes as a new event version alongside the old one, add message contract tests, and replay the skipped events after the fix. See deploying microservices.

docs.title: 69. A change merged to the monorepo's main last week never reached production. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the deploy runs for that commit and for the commits after it, and the base each run used.

How to confirm: the change's own deploy failed, and the next run compared with HEAD^1, saw only unrelated files, and deployed nothing.

Likely causes and fixes: the wrong base for affected detection. Use the last successfully deployed commit as the base (TURBO_SCM_BASE, or nx-set-shas), fetch enough history, and alert on failed deploy runs. See monorepo builds and deployments.

docs.title: 70. After a deploy, the production web app calls the staging API. The build log shows a cache hit. Explain.
docs.text:
What to check first: the task's declared inputs and environment variables, and the cache key of the restored build.

How to confirm: VITE_API_URL differs between the staging and production builds, but it is not part of the task's hash.

Likely causes and fixes: an undeclared input, so the staging artifact was restored for production. Declare environment variables in the task configuration (for example VITE_*), clear the affected cache entries, and move per-environment values to runtime configuration. See monorepo builds and deployments.
