docs.title: Monorepo Builds and Deployments
docs.text:
A monorepo keeps many projects in one repository: for TaskFlow, the API, a background worker, the web app, the desktop app, and the packages they share. One repository does not mean one build or one deploy. The work of release engineering in a monorepo is to build, test, and deploy only what a change affects, to reuse every result that has not changed, and to keep each app on its own release path even though the code lives together.

This lesson covers monorepo versus polyrepo from a delivery point of view; what changes in CI: affected-project detection (Nx affected, Turborepo --affected and --filter, Bazel), choosing the base commit, task graphs with local and remote caching, path filters in GitHub Actions, one workflow per deployable app versus a matrix; per-app deploys from one repository; shared packages and their versioning (fixed versus independent, Changesets, publishing internal packages); atomic cross-cutting changes; CODEOWNERS per directory; and dependency hygiene with pnpm workspaces and a one-version policy. Repository mechanics (partial clones, sparse checkout, large files) are covered in hooks, .gitignore, and large repositories.

The example repository:

taskflow/
  apps/
    api/            TaskFlow API (Express) -> container image
    worker/         background jobs -> container image
    web/            TaskFlow Web (React + Vite) -> static site
    desktop/        TaskFlow Desktop (Tauri) -> installers, released on a train
  packages/
    shared-types/   TypeScript types used by api and api-client, published with the client
    api-client/     typed client for the API, used by web and desktop, also published to npm
    ui/             React components used by web and desktop
  pnpm-workspace.yaml
  turbo.json

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• CI time grows with the repository unless it is scoped. If every pull request lints, tests, and builds every project, 40 tasks of two minutes each cost 80 runner-minutes per push, for a change that may touch one file in one app.
  • Deploys must stay per app. A documentation fix should not redeploy the API, and a change to the API should not rebuild the desktop installers.
  • Atomic commits are not atomic deploys. One pull request can change the API, its client, and the web app together, but the API and the web app still deploy separately, so the version skew rules from keeping frontend and backend in sync still apply.
  • Shared code needs a versioning decision. Internal packages can always track the latest source; packages published to npm need SemVer and changelogs, and a choice between one version for all and one per package.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Google. Rachel Potvin and Josh Levenberg's Why Google Stores Billions of Lines of Code in a Single Repository (Communications of the ACM, 2016) describes one repository serving as the source of truth for tens of thousands of developers, the custom tooling that makes it workable, and the trade-offs of the model.
  • Microsoft. Brian Harry's The largest Git repo on the planet (2017) describes moving the Windows codebase, about 3.5 million files and 300 GB, with about 4,000 engineers, to Git, which needed GVFS to virtualize the repository so developers download only what they use.
  • Meta. Meta's Sapling announcement (2022) describes source control built to serve an internal repository with tens of millions of files, commits, and branches for tens of thousands of developers.
  • Nx and Turborepo. Nx's affected command runs only the tasks whose inputs changed between a base and a head commit, and recommends using the last successful commit on main as the base. Turborepo's --affected flag is equivalent to --filter=...[main...HEAD], and its documentation warns that a too-shallow checkout makes every package look changed.
  • Vercel. Vercel's monorepo documentation creates one project per app directory and skips builds for projects that a commit did not change, based on the workspace's declared dependencies and the lockfile.

Popular tools and providers: Nx, Turborepo, Bazel, pnpm, npm, and Yarn workspaces, Changesets, release-please in manifest mode, Vercel and Netlify monorepo support, GitHub CODEOWNERS and merge queues, and remote caches (Vercel Remote Cache, Nx Cloud, self-hosted HTTP caches, Bazel remote execution services).

docs.title: Monorepo or polyrepo, from a delivery point of view
docs.text:
Delivery concern Monorepo Polyrepo Cross-project change One pull request, reviewed and tested together Several pull requests merged in order Shared code Consumed from source (workspace:*), always current Published packages, upgraded by each consumer CI cost Needs affected detection and caching, or it grows with the repository Naturally scoped to one project Deploy independence Must be designed (per-app workflows or affected deploys) The default Ownership CODEOWNERS per directory Repository permissions Tooling Workspaces, a task runner, remote caching Standard per-repository tooling

Neither model is better in general. A monorepo trades per-project simplicity for cheap cross-project changes and one set of tools; the build system is what makes that trade work.

docs.title: The project graph and affected detection
docs.text:
Workspace tools build a project graph from each package's declared dependencies ("@taskflow/api-client": "workspace:*" in package.json). A change is mapped to the projects that own the changed files, and the affected set is those projects plus everything that depends on them, directly or transitively.

Tool Command Granularity and notes Nx nx affected -t lint test build Task-level: selects tasks whose inputs include a changed file; base defaults to main, override with --base and --head or NX_BASE and NX_HEAD Turborepo turbo run lint test build --affected Package-level by default: any changed file selects all of that package's tasks; base and head from TURBO_SCM_BASE and TURBO_SCM_HEAD Turborepo filters turbo run build --filter=...[origin/main] ... before a selector adds dependents; --filter=@taskflow/ui... selects a package and its dependencies Bazel bazel query "rdeps(//..., set(//packages/shared-types:lib))" Target-level reverse dependencies within a universe; the most precise, at the cost of declaring everything in BUILD files

Global inputs need special handling: a change to the root lockfile, the task runner's configuration, or a shared compiler configuration can affect every project. Turborepo lists such files in globalDependencies; Nx treats workspace configuration as an input to every project.

docs.title: Choosing the base commit
docs.text:
Affected detection is a diff, so its answer depends on what you diff against:

  • Pull requests: the merge base with the target branch (what the pull request would add to main).
  • Pushes to main that deploy: the last commit that was successfully deployed, not the previous commit.

Nx documents a GitHub action, nrwl/nx-set-shas, that uses the GitHub API to find the last successful workflow run on main and sets NX_BASE and NX_HEAD; with Turborepo you set TURBO_SCM_BASE yourself (the deploy workflow below does it with gh run list). Either way the checkout needs history: fetch-depth: 0 (Turborepo also suggests filter: blob:none to keep it fast), because without the base commit every package counts as changed.

docs.title: Task graphs and build caching
docs.text:
Inside the affected set, tasks form a graph: web#build needs api-client#build and ui#build first (dependsOn: ["^build"]), while lint and unit tests can often run in parallel. The task runner schedules that graph across CPU cores and, crucially, skips tasks whose result is already known.

How caching works:

  • The hash is the cache key. It covers the files the task reads, the hashes of the internal packages it depends on, the declared environment variables, the task's configuration, and the resolved versions of external dependencies.
  • Outputs and logs are stored. Turborepo treats logs as artifacts, so a cache hit replays the original output; Bazel stores an action cache (action hash to result) and a content-addressable store of output files.
  • Remote caches share results between CI runs and developers. A task built on one pull request is a hit on the next pull request and on main after the merge.
  • Trust matters. A poisoned cache entry would ship in every build that hits it. Let only CI write to the remote cache (Bazel's documentation suggests exactly that, and --remote_upload_local_results=false makes a client read-only), and sign entries: Turborepo can sign artifacts with HMAC-SHA256 using TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY and treats any artifact that fails verification as a miss.
  • Undeclared inputs cause wrong hits. If the web build reads VITE_API_URL but the task does not declare it, staging and production builds have the same hash, and production can receive the staging bundle. Declare environment variables explicitly (Turborepo's env, with wildcards such as VITE_*), and prefer runtime configuration for values that differ per environment (see build-time versus runtime configuration).

docs.title: Path filters in GitHub Actions
docs.text:
GitHub's own paths filter is the simplest scoping tool: a workflow runs only if at least one changed file matches. Three properties shape how to use it (details and a required-check workaround are in pipeline design):

  • A workflow skipped by a path filter leaves its checks pending, which blocks merging if those checks are required.
  • The filter does not know the dependency graph: apps/web/** misses a change in packages/ui that web depends on, unless you list every dependency path by hand and keep the list current.
  • GitHub documents limits: if a push contains more than 1,000 commits the workflow always runs, and for very large diffs only the first 3,000 files are considered.

A good split: workflow-level paths filters for non-required, per-app deploy workflows, and an always-running CI workflow that uses the task runner's affected detection for required checks.

docs.title: One workflow per deployable app, or one matrix
docs.text:
One workflow per app One workflow, matrix of affected apps Triggers paths per app (or a call from a shared workflow) One trigger; the matrix is computed from the affected set Environments and approvals Natural: each app has its own environment and reviewers Possible per matrix entry, but less clear in the UI Ownership CODEOWNERS can assign each workflow file to its team One file that every team edits Duplication Avoided with a reusable workflow None Required checks Hard with path filters (pending checks) Easy: one job always reports

A common combination: one always-running CI workflow with --affected for required checks, and one deploy workflow per app (each a thin caller of a shared reusable workflow) or a single deploy job that runs turbo run deploy --affected when all apps deploy the same way.

docs.title: Per-app deploys from one repository
docs.text:
• Vercel: one project per app directory (the Root Directory setting). Vercel skips builds for projects that a commit did not change, when the repository is on GitHub and uses npm, Yarn, pnpm, or Bun workspaces with unique package names and explicit dependencies between packages; other repositories can use the Ignored Build Step setting.
  • Netlify: one site per app, with the package directory pointing at the app. By default any change in the base directory (the repository root) builds every connected site, so monorepos add an ignore command that checks only the relevant paths.
  • Containers: each app has its own image, built from the repository root as context so it can include workspace packages. turbo prune <package> --docker produces a pruned copy of the workspace (the package.json files separately from the full source, plus a pruned lockfile), so the Docker build installs and caches only what that app needs.
  • Desktop and mobile: built and tested on every affected change, but released on their own train with their own version numbers (see release trains and release management).

docs.title: Shared packages and versioning
docs.text:
There are two kinds of shared package, and they need different rules:

  • Internal-only packages (ui) are consumed from source with workspace:*. They have no meaningful version; every app always builds against the current code, and affected detection decides what to rebuild. This is the "one version" model: there is never an old copy of ui in use.
  • Published packages (@taskflow/api-client on npm for customers, and @taskflow/shared-types, whose types the client exposes) need SemVer, changelogs, and tags, because consumers outside the repository upgrade on their own schedule. Inside the repository the apps still consume them from source.

For published packages, choose how versions relate:

Strategy Meaning Fits Fixed Every package in the group always shares one version; all are bumped and published together even without changes (Changesets fixed) SDKs whose packages are always used together Linked Packages keep their own versions, but a release bumps changed ones to the highest current version in the group plus the highest bump type (Changesets linked) Related packages whose versions should line up when they change Independent Each package versions itself Unrelated libraries

Changesets makes versions explicit: each pull request adds a small changeset file naming the packages and bump types, changeset version applies the bumps and updates changelogs, and changeset publish publishes to npm and creates tags like @taskflow/api-client@2.5.0. Its GitHub action opens a versioning pull request that collects pending changesets, so releasing is merging that pull request. release-please's manifest mode is the alternative driven by Conventional Commits (see versioning, tags, and releases).

docs.title: Atomic cross-cutting changes
docs.text:
A monorepo's strongest feature is one reviewed, tested commit that changes a shared package and every consumer: rename a field in shared-types, update api-client, the API, and the web app, and CI proves they still compile and pass together. Large-scale refactors and codemods depend on this.

The trap is assuming the deploy is atomic too. After the merge, the API and the web app deploy separately, old web tabs keep running, desktop and mobile users update over weeks, and published api-client versions live in customers' lockfiles. So a cross-cutting change that alters a wire format still needs the expand, migrate, contract sequence; the monorepo only makes each step easier to review.

docs.title: Ownership with CODEOWNERS
docs.text: CODEOWNERS maps directories to teams, and a branch rule that requires code owner review makes each team approve changes to its area. The last matching pattern wins, so a general owner goes first and specific directories after it. Give the platform team ownership of .github/workflows/ and the build configuration, since a change there affects every project.

docs.title: Dependency hygiene
docs.text:
• Workspaces (pnpm-workspace.yaml, or workspaces in package.json for npm and Yarn) define which directories are packages, and the workspace: protocol links them from source.
  • One version per external dependency. Two versions of React in one app, or tests running against a different version than production, are classic monorepo bugs. pnpm catalogs define a version range once in pnpm-workspace.yaml and let packages reference it with catalog:, so an upgrade is one edit and package files stop conflicting in merges.
  • Group dependency updates (Renovate or Dependabot groups) so one pull request upgrades a library everywhere, with affected detection testing every consumer.
  • Find duplicates with pnpm why <package> and fix them before they reach production bundles.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Approach Several apps sharing a lot of code, one or a few teams Monorepo with workspaces, affected detection, and remote caching Independent services owned by separate teams with little shared code Polyrepo, or a monorepo only if tooling investment is acceptable Shared packages consumed only inside the repository workspace:*, no versions Packages published to npm Changesets or release-please with SemVer and changelogs Required checks in a monorepo An always-running workflow with affected detection, not path filters Per-app deploys Per-app workflows calling a shared reusable workflow, or turbo run deploy --affected with the base set to the last successful deploy Very large, polyglot codebases Bazel or a similar build system with fine-grained targets and remote execution

Avoid a monorepo without investing in affected detection and caching; the first months feel fine, and then every pull request takes an hour.

docs.title: The workspace, with a catalog
docs.text:
# pnpm-workspace.yaml
packages:
  - "apps/*"
  - "packages/*"

catalog:
  react: ^19.2.0
  react-dom: ^19.2.0
  typescript: ^5.9.0
  vite: ^7.0.0
  vitest: ^3.2.0

{
  "name": "@taskflow/web",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "scripts": {
    "build": "vite build",
    "test": "vitest run",
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "deploy": "node ../../scripts/deploy-web.mjs"
  },
  "dependencies": {
    "@taskflow/api-client": "workspace:*",
    "@taskflow/ui": "workspace:*",
    "react": "catalog:",
    "react-dom": "catalog:"
  },
  "devDependencies": {
    "typescript": "catalog:",
    "vite": "catalog:",
    "vitest": "catalog:"
  }
}

The second file is apps/web/package.json. The deploy script is what the deploy workflow below runs for every affected app that defines one; apps/desktop deliberately has none, because it is released by its train.

docs.title: Tasks, inputs, and a signed remote cache
docs.text:
{
  "$schema": "https://turborepo.dev/schema.json",
  "globalDependencies": ["tsconfig.base.json"],
  "remoteCache": { "signature": true },
  "tasks": {
    "build": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
      "inputs": ["$TURBO_DEFAULT$", "!**/*.test.ts", "!**/*.md"],
      "outputs": ["dist/**"],
      "env": ["VITE_*", "APP_VERSION"]
    },
    "test": {
      "dependsOn": ["^build"],
      "outputs": []
    },
    "lint": {},
    "deploy": {
      "dependsOn": ["build", "test", "lint"],
      "cache": false
    }
  }
}

This is turbo.json at the repository root. ^build builds internal dependencies first; inputs keeps tests and docs out of the build hash, so editing a test does not invalidate the bundle; env puts every VITE_* variable into the hash; and deploy is never cached, because its job is a side effect.

docs.title: CI that runs only affected tasks
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/ci.yml: always runs, so required checks always report
name: ci
on:
  pull_request:

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  affected:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      TURBO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TURBO_TOKEN }}
      TURBO_TEAM: ${{ vars.TURBO_TEAM }}
      TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0              # affected detection needs the base commit
          filter: blob:none
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6    # pnpm version from "packageManager" in package.json
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm turbo run lint test build --affected
        env:
          TURBO_SCM_BASE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}

A pull request that touches only apps/web runs web's three tasks; one that touches packages/shared-types runs the affected projects from the diagram; a re-run after a flaky failure restores every task that already passed from the remote cache.

docs.title: Deploy every app changed since the last successful deploy
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/deploy.yml
name: deploy
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false            # never cancel a deploy halfway

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    permissions:
      contents: read
      actions: read                    # read earlier runs of this workflow
      id-token: write                  # OIDC for the cloud deploy scripts
      packages: write
    env:
      TURBO_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.TURBO_TOKEN }}
      TURBO_TEAM: ${{ vars.TURBO_TEAM }}
      TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY: ${{ secrets.TURBO_REMOTE_CACHE_SIGNATURE_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          filter: blob:none
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Find the commit of the last successful deploy
        id: base
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
        run: |
          sha=$(gh run list --workflow deploy.yml --branch main --status success \
                --limit 1 --json headSha --jq '.[0].headSha')
          # First deploy ever: compare with the root commit, so everything deploys
          echo "sha=${sha:-$(git rev-list --max-parents=0 HEAD | tail -n 1)}" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - name: Build, test, and deploy every affected app
        env:
          TURBO_SCM_BASE: ${{ steps.base.outputs.sha }}
        run: pnpm turbo run deploy --affected
  • The base is the last successful run of this workflow, so a failed deploy's changes are picked up again by the next run, as in the diagram above.
  • concurrency serializes deploys, so two merges in quick succession cannot deploy out of order.
  • One job holds credentials for every app. When apps need separate approvals or separate cloud roles, use one workflow per app instead, each calling a reusable deploy workflow.

docs.title: Version published packages with Changesets
docs.text:
{
  "changelog": "@changesets/cli/changelog",
  "commit": false,
  "fixed": [],
  "linked": [["@taskflow/api-client", "@taskflow/shared-types"]],
  "access": "public",
  "baseBranch": "main",
  "updateInternalDependencies": "patch"
}

That is .changeset/config.json. A pull request that changes the client adds a changeset file such as .changeset/brave-tasks-sing.md:

---
"@taskflow/api-client": minor
"@taskflow/shared-types": minor
---

Add the `due` object to tasks. `dueDate` is deprecated and will be removed in 3.0.0.

# scripts/release-packages.sh: what the release pull request and its merge run
pnpm changeset version    # apply pending bumps, update CHANGELOG.md files and internal ranges
pnpm changeset publish    # publish changed packages; tags such as @taskflow/api-client@2.5.0
git push --follow-tags

linked keeps the two packages' versions aligned when both change, without forcing a release of one when only the other changed (that would be fixed). Apps are private packages and are not published; they get their versions from the release process of each app.

docs.title: Ownership per directory
docs.text:
# .github/CODEOWNERS: the last matching pattern wins
*                          @example/platform
/apps/api/                 @example/tasks-team
/apps/worker/              @example/tasks-team
/apps/web/                 @example/web-team
/apps/desktop/             @example/desktop-team
/packages/ui/              @example/web-team @example/desktop-team
/packages/shared-types/    @example/tasks-team
/packages/api-client/      @example/tasks-team
/.github/workflows/        @example/platform
/turbo.json                @example/platform

With "Require review from Code Owners" enabled, a change to ui needs one approval from either team that owns it, and a change to the workflows or the task configuration always reaches the platform team.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Run CI on the affected set, not the whole repository, and keep a workflow that always runs for required checks.
  • Use the merge base for pull requests and the last successful deploy as the base on main; check out enough history.
  • Cache task results locally and remotely; let only CI write, sign the entries, and declare every input, including environment variables.
  • Keep deploys per app: per-app workflows or an affected deploy task, never "deploy everything on every merge".
  • Consume internal packages from source with workspace:*; version and changelog only what you publish.
  • Keep one version of each external dependency with catalogs and grouped updates.
  • Assign every directory an owner with CODEOWNERS, and give the platform team the build configuration.
  • Treat atomic commits as a review tool, not a deploy guarantee; keep wire changes backward compatible.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Pull requests take an hour although most change one app. Detect: CI duration grows month by month; logs show every package building on every push. Cause: no affected detection or remote caching. Fix: run tasks with --affected (or nx affected), add a remote cache, and track the cache hit rate.
  • A merged change never reached production. Detect: the feature is on main but not live; the deploy log of the next run shows no affected apps. Cause: the deploy compared with HEAD^1, and the run for the change itself had failed. Fix: use the last successful deploy as the base, and alert when deploy runs fail.
  • Every package rebuilds on every push to main. Detect: the affected set is always everything; the log notes that no base commit was found. Cause: a shallow checkout. Fix: fetch-depth: 0 (with filter: blob:none for speed).
  • Production served a bundle pointing at the staging API. Detect: the production web app calls the staging URL right after a deploy; the build log shows a cache hit. Cause: VITE_API_URL was not part of the task's hash, so the staging build was restored. Fix: declare env (for example VITE_*), invalidate the cache, and move per-environment values to runtime configuration.
  • A required check stays "Expected" forever on docs-only pull requests. Detect: merging is blocked; the workflow never started. Cause: a paths filter skipped the workflow that provides a required check. Fix: make the required workflow always run and decide inside it what to test.
  • Two versions of React end up in the web bundle. Detect: the bundle grows; hooks fail with errors about invalid hook calls. Cause: ui and web declared different React ranges. Fix: move React to the catalog, run pnpm why react, and add a duplicate check to CI.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Monorepo: one repository containing many projects.
  • Project graph: the dependencies between projects in a workspace.
  • Affected projects: projects changed by a commit range plus all their dependents.
  • Base and head: the two commits whose difference defines what changed.
  • Task graph: the order in which tasks must run, derived from task dependencies such as ^build.
  • Task hash: the cache key computed from a task's inputs.
  • Remote cache: a shared store of task outputs and logs keyed by hash.
  • Workspace protocol: workspace:*, a dependency on the in-repository version of a package.
  • Catalog: a pnpm workspace feature that defines dependency versions once for all packages.
  • Fixed, linked, and independent versioning: ways to relate the versions of published packages in one repository.
  • Changeset: a file describing which packages a change bumps, and by how much.
  • CODEOWNERS: a file mapping paths to the owners whose review is required.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing a monorepo means one build and one deploy.
  • Running every task on every pull request.
  • Using HEAD^1 as the deploy base.
  • Shallow checkouts in jobs that compute affected projects.
  • Letting every developer machine write to the remote cache, or not signing cache entries.
  • Forgetting environment variables in task inputs.
  • Path filters on required checks.
  • Versioning internal-only packages, or not versioning published ones.
  • Assuming a cross-cutting commit deploys atomically.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does "affected" mean, and how does a workspace tool compute it?
  2. Why should the base for a deploy on main be the last successful deploy rather than HEAD^1? Describe the failure the wrong base causes.
  3. Which inputs go into a task hash, and what happens when one is missing?
  4. A repository has 40 tasks of 2 minutes each. With affected detection a typical pull request runs 9 of them, and the remote cache hits 6 of those 9. How many task-minutes does the pull request use? (3 x 2 = 6 minutes, plus a few seconds per restore.)
  5. Why are path filters a poor fit for required checks, and what do you use instead?
  6. Compare fixed, linked, and independent versioning for published packages.
  7. A pull request changes the API response and the web app together. Why must the change still be backward compatible?
  8. What should CODEOWNERS assign to the platform team in a monorepo, and why?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• Nx: Run only tasks affected by a change
  • Turborepo: run reference (--affected, --filter)
  • Turborepo: Remote caching
  • Bazel: Remote caching
  • pnpm: Catalogs
  • Changesets: Linked packages and fixed packages
  • GitHub Docs: About code owners
  • Vercel: Using monorepos
  • Next: release engineering interview questions and answers. Back to the release engineering overview.

docs.title: Release Trains and Release Management
docs.text:
Continuous deployment answers "how does a change reach production?" Release management answers the questions around it: when does a version ship, what is in it, who decides it is ready, how a fix reaches versions that already shipped, how long each version is supported, and how a feature is retired without breaking the people who still use it. Teams that ship to app stores, to customers' own servers, or to millions of installed browsers cannot avoid these questions; teams that deploy a web service continuously still face them for their public API.

This lesson covers continuous release versus release trains (fixed cadence, cut-off, stabilization), release branches and cherry-picked fixes, the hotfix process end to end, release notes versus changelogs, long-term support and several supported versions, deprecation and sunset policies with the Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers, release checklists and go/no-go decisions, and coordinating one release across web, API, and mobile. Branch mechanics are in branching strategies, and version numbers and changelog automation in versioning, tags, and releases.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Releases without a schedule grow. "One more feature" delays the release, the delay attracts more features, and the eventual release is large, late, and risky. A fixed cadence keeps each release small.
  • Not everything can ship continuously. App store review, customers who install software on their own servers, regulated approvals, and browsers on billions of devices all need versions that are prepared, stabilized, and shipped on a known date.
  • Shipped versions need fixes. A security fix may have to reach the current release and every supported older one, quickly and without dragging in unrelated changes.
  • Retiring things is part of releasing. Without a deprecation policy, old endpoints either break customers when removed or are never removed and cost you forever.
  • Lead time is set by the cadence. With a two-week train, a change merged right after a cut waits two weeks for the next cut, a week of stabilization, and about a week of rollout: up to four weeks to reach everyone, three on average.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Chrome. Chrome moved to four-week milestones starting with Chrome 94 in 2021, alongside an Extended Stable channel with a new milestone every eight weeks. Google then announced a two-week release cycle that started with the stable release of Chrome 153 on September 8, 2026, while Extended Stable keeps its eight-week cycle. The Chromium release cycle document describes a milestone branch that is stabilized for three weeks, with weekly refreshes for security fixes once it is stable.
  • Firefox. Firefox ships through Nightly, Beta, Release, and ESR channels, and Mozilla's support blog announced a move to a two-week release cycle starting with Firefox 155 on September 1, 2026. Mozilla's What Train Is It Now? page publishes the schedule.
  • Rust. The Rust book's chapter on release channels describes the train model directly: nightly builds every night, a beta branch every six weeks, fixes landing on main and backported to beta, and a stable release six weeks after each beta; a feature that misses one train simply takes the next.
  • Kubernetes. The Kubernetes release cycle produces about three releases a year, with an enhancements freeze about four weeks in and a code freeze around week 12 after which only critical fixes merge; the project maintains the three most recent minor releases with about a year of patch support each.
  • Meta. Chuck Rossi's Rapid release at massive scale (2017) describes facebook.com moving from a weekly release branch with daily cherry-picks to continuous push from master in tiers (employees, 2% of production, then everyone), while mobile apps kept a weekly branch-and-cherry-pick train with daily release candidates for beta users.
  • Google. The SRE book's Release Engineering chapter states the branch rule most teams follow: branch from the mainline at a specific revision, never merge the branch back, and submit fixes to the mainline first, then cherry-pick them into the branch.
  • GitLab. GitLab's maintenance policy ships a monthly minor release on the third Thursday, patch releases twice a month, and backports security fixes to the previous two monthly releases as well as the current one.

Popular tools and providers: release-please, semantic-release, and Changesets for versions and notes; GitHub milestones, rulesets for release/* branches, and backport automation; feature flag services to keep unfinished work dark; fastlane, App Store Connect, and the Play Console for mobile trains; and status pages and changelog sites for release communication.

docs.title: Continuous release versus release trains
docs.text:
Continuous deployment Release train Feature-based release A release happens On every merge that passes the pipeline On a fixed schedule (weekly, every two weeks, monthly) "When it is ready" Unfinished features Hidden behind flags Hidden behind flags, or they miss the train Delay the release Size of a release One change One cadence's worth of changes Unbounded Predictability for users and support High frequency, low ceremony Known dates Low Fits Web services and web apps you host Mobile apps, desktop apps, on-premises software, browsers, platforms Rarely a good choice

The train metaphor is precise. The train leaves on schedule whether or not your feature is aboard; if it misses the train, it takes the next one. That removes the pressure to rush a half-finished change into a release, and it turns the release date from a negotiation into a fact. Trains and continuous deployment combine well: TaskFlow's API deploys continuously, while its mobile apps and the public API's versioned changes follow trains.

docs.title: Anatomy of a train
docs.text:
• Cadence: the fixed interval between trains, for example every second Monday.
  • Cut (branch point): the moment the release branch is created from main. Everything merged before it is aboard; everything after waits.
  • Stabilization: a period in which only fixes enter the branch. Each fix produces a release candidate (2026.11.2-rc.2) that goes to beta testers, TestFlight, or Play testing tracks.
  • Go/no-go: a decision, based on agreed numbers, that the last candidate becomes the release. The candidate build is promoted, never rebuilt.
  • Rollout: a phased release to users, gated on crash-free sessions and error rates.
  • Support: after release, the branch receives only hotfixes until it goes out of support.

With overlapping trains, several versions are always active: one rolling out or supported, one stabilizing, one in development on main. The cost of a train is lead time (the two to four weeks computed above); the benefits are predictability and a stabilization period that catches problems before users do.

docs.title: Release branches and cherry-picks
docs.text:
The rules that keep release branches healthy:

  1. Branch from main at the cut; never merge the branch back. The branch is a stabilizing copy, not a place for development.
  2. Fix on main first, then cherry-pick. If a fix is made only on the branch, the next release, cut from main, brings the bug back. The exception is a fix for code that no longer exists on main; then the branch gets its own reviewed change, linked to the issue.
  3. Use git cherry-pick -x. It appends "(cherry picked from commit ...)" to the message, so anyone can trace the backport to its source.
  4. Only fixes enter a stabilizing branch. Every change is reviewed against the question "would we hold the release for this?"
  5. Protect release/* branches with a ruleset: pull requests only, required checks, and a release owner's approval.

Squash merging (one commit per pull request on main) makes backports simple: there is exactly one commit to pick. A label such as backport:release/2.4 on the pull request lets automation open the backport pull request (example below).

docs.title: The hotfix process end to end
docs.text:
1. Decide whether this is a hotfix at all: severity, number of users affected, and whether a rollback, a feature flag, or a server-side change solves it faster.
  2. Fix on main through a normal, reviewed pull request with a test that reproduces the bug.
  3. Backport to every supported branch that has the bug, adapting the change where an older line diverged.
  4. Build and verify each patch release from its branch: tag v2.4.1, build once, run the release pipeline, and smoke-test it.
  5. Ship fast, but still in stages. Shorten bake times rather than skipping them; for mobile, request an expedited review and use the fastest phased rollout you can tolerate.
  6. Communicate: release notes, a status page update, and notes to customers on older supported lines.
  7. Follow up with a postmortem when the bug reached users (see incident response and postmortems).

For hosted services, rolling back to the previous version is usually faster than a hotfix; for installed software it is not an option, which is why client hotfixes go through this whole sequence.

docs.title: Release notes versus changelogs
docs.text:
Changelog Release notes Audience Developers and integrators Users, customers, support staff Content Every notable change per version, grouped by type What changed for the reader, upgrade steps, known issues, deprecations Produced by Generated from Conventional Commits or pull request labels Written or edited by a person, often from the same labels Where CHANGELOG.md, GitHub Releases In-app "what's new", store listings, a docs page, email

Generate the changelog (see the Git lesson), and write release notes for humans. Deprecations and breaking changes belong in both.

docs.title: Long-term support and several supported versions
docs.text:
Supporting several versions at once is sometimes unavoidable: enterprises upgrade slowly, on-premises installs lag, and mobile users stay on old builds. Public projects show the common shapes:

  • The last N releases: Kubernetes maintains release branches for the three most recent minor versions, each with about a year of patches.
  • Current plus recent, for security only: GitLab backports security fixes to the previous two monthly releases.
  • Designated long-term support lines: until Node.js 26, even-numbered Node.js releases became LTS lines, actively supported for 12 months and maintained for another 18; Node.js 24 entered maintenance in October 2026 with support until April 2028. The project's release schedule changes from Node.js 27: one new release line a year, and every line becomes LTS.

Every supported line multiplies work. With monthly releases, a policy of "current plus the two previous for security" turns each security fix into three backports, three patch releases, and three test runs on three toolchains. Twelve such fixes a year are 36 patch releases. That is why an LTS policy states exactly which versions, for how long, and which fixes qualify (security only, or also critical bugs), and announces each end-of-life date in advance.

docs.title: Deprecation and sunset policies
docs.text:
A deprecation policy turns "we will remove this" into a predictable process:

  1. Announce with a date: docs, changelog, release notes, email to the owners of clients that still use it.
  2. Mark responses. RFC 9745 defines the Deprecation header, whose value is a structured-field date such as @1796083200 (seconds since 1970); deprecation itself changes nothing about how the resource behaves. A Link header with rel="deprecation" points to the migration guide. RFC 8594 defines the Sunset header, an HTTP date after which the resource is likely to become unresponsive, and RFC 9745 requires the sunset not to be earlier than the deprecation.
  3. Measure who still calls it, per API client, and contact them.
  4. Brown out before the deadline: announced, short, scheduled periods (an hour, then a day) in which the deprecated endpoint fails exactly as it will after the sunset. Clients that ignored every notice find out while there is still time.
  5. Remove at the sunset date: return 410 Gone with a pointer to the replacement, then delete the code.

Public policies give a sense of scale: GitHub supports a previous REST API version for at least 24 months after a new one; Kubernetes keeps serving a deprecated beta API for 9 months or 3 minor releases after the deprecation (whichever is longer) and never removes a GA API within a major version; GraphQL marks fields @deprecated(reason: "...") and removes them when usage stops. For installed clients, the equivalent is the minimum supported version described in keeping frontend and backend in sync.

docs.title: Release checklists and go/no-go
docs.text:
A checklist makes the release independent of who runs it; the go/no-go decision makes it independent of who argues loudest. Useful criteria, each with a number and a source:

Criterion Example threshold Source Open release blockers 0 The issue tracker's release-blocker label Crash-free sessions of the candidate Not worse than the current release by more than 0.1 percentage points, with at least 2,000 beta sessions Crash reporting API error rate from the candidate's clients Not above the current release's Metrics by client version Migrations Reviewed and backward compatible with the previous version The migration pull requests Feature flags Default states agreed for every new flag The flag service Rollback or roll-forward plan Written, with an owner The release document Support and communication Release notes, support briefing, status page text ready The release document Store metadata (mobile) Screenshots, "what's new", phased release enabled App Store Connect, Play Console

Typical roles in the meeting are the release captain (runs the train for this cycle), engineering owners of risky changes, QA, product, support, and the on-call engineer. The decision is recorded with the numbers behind it. The checklist for an individual risky deploy is in rollbacks and safe releases.

docs.title: Coordinating a release across web, API, and mobile
docs.text:
A feature that touches TaskFlow's API, web app, and mobile apps follows the compatibility order from the previous lessons, laid over the train calendar:

When What Why this order Monday, week 1 Database migration (expand) and API 2.5.0 with the new endpoint, behind a flag Servers learn new things first Tuesday, week 1 TaskFlow Web with the feature, flag off The web app can ship any day Monday, week 2 Mobile train cut: iOS and Android 3.4.0 with the feature, flag off Store review needs time; the client must not depend on the flag being on Week 2 to 3 Stabilization, TestFlight and Play testing; submit for review The candidate is verified against production APIs Week 3 Phased rollout of 3.4.0 Crash-free sessions gate each step Week 4 Turn the flag on for web and for app versions 3.4.0 and later Both sides are ready Later Remove the flag and any old code paths Contract step

One person, the release captain, owns this calendar and a single release document that lists the versions, the flags, the go/no-go numbers, and who to call. Rotating the role spreads the knowledge and keeps the process honest.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Context Recommended cadence and process Hosted web service and web app Continuous deployment; flags for unfinished work; trains only for public API version changes Mobile apps Weekly or two-week trains with a cut, stabilization on test tracks, and phased rollout Desktop apps with an updater Trains plus a beta channel; staged rollouts on the update server On-premises or self-hosted product Monthly or quarterly trains, an LTS line, documented upgrade paths Public API Continuous additive changes; breaking changes only through versioning and a published deprecation policy Small team, one product, few users Release from main with tags; skip trains and LTS until customers need them

Avoid long-lived release branches for hosted services (roll back instead), stabilization periods longer than the cadence (they overlap until nothing ships), and LTS promises nobody has budgeted for.

docs.title: Cut a train and tag release candidates
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/cut-release.sh: cut the train branch and tag its first candidate
# usage: cut-release.sh 2026.11.2
set -euo pipefail
TRAIN="$1"

git fetch origin --tags
git switch -c "release/$TRAIN" origin/main
git push -u origin "release/$TRAIN"

git tag -a "v$TRAIN-rc.1" -m "TaskFlow $TRAIN release candidate 1"
git push origin "v$TRAIN-rc.1"
# CI builds the candidate once from the tag and ships it to beta testers.
# Later fixes arrive as cherry-picks and produce rc.2, rc.3, ...
# After go/no-go, tag the SAME commit as the final release (no rebuild):
#   git tag -a "v$TRAIN" -m "TaskFlow $TRAIN" "v$TRAIN-rc.3^{commit}"

2026.11.2 is CalVer that is also valid SemVer (and a valid display version on both stores), and -rc.N pre-releases sort before the final release. Tagging the release on the last candidate's commit means the binary users get is the one beta testers already ran.

docs.title: Automate backports with a label
docs.text:
# .github/workflows/backport.yml: label a merged PR "backport:release/2.4" to backport it
name: backport
on:
  pull_request:
    types: [closed]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  backport:
    if: github.event.pull_request.merged == true
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: write
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0                               # all branches for cherry-pick
          token: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_TOKEN }}      # App token: CI runs on the new PRs
      - name: Cherry-pick into every labelled release branch
        env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.RELEASE_BOT_TOKEN }}
          LABELS: ${{ toJSON(github.event.pull_request.labels.*.name) }}
          MERGE_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.merge_commit_sha }}
          PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
          PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}
        run: |
          git config user.name "taskflow-release-bot"
          git config user.email "release-bot@example.com"
          for target in $(jq -r '.[] | select(startswith("backport:")) | sub("^backport:"; "")' <<<"$LABELS"); do
            branch="backport/$PR_NUMBER-to-${target//\//-}"
            git switch -c "$branch" "origin/$target"
            if git cherry-pick -x "$MERGE_SHA"; then
              git push origin "$branch"
              gh pr create --base "$target" --head "$branch" \
                --title "[$target] $PR_TITLE" \
                --body "Backport of #$PR_NUMBER to \`$target\`."
            else
              git cherry-pick --abort
              gh pr comment "$PR_NUMBER" \
                --body "Automatic backport to \`$target\` failed. Please cherry-pick it by hand."
            fi
            git switch --detach "$MERGE_SHA"
          done
  • It assumes squash merging, so merge_commit_sha is the single commit to pick; a true merge commit would need cherry-pick -m 1.
  • Pull request titles and labels arrive through environment variables, never pasted into the script with ${{ }}, which would allow script injection (see pipeline and supply chain security).
  • Pull requests opened with the default GITHUB_TOKEN do not trigger other workflows, so the bot uses a GitHub App or fine-grained token and the backport pull request gets the normal checks and reviews.

docs.title: Announce deprecation with headers, brownouts, and a sunset
docs.text:
// src/middleware/deprecate-v1.js: mark, measure, brown out, and finally retire /v1
import client from "prom-client";

const DEPRECATED_AT = Date.parse("2026-12-01T00:00:00Z");
const SUNSET_AT = Date.parse("2027-06-30T23:59:59Z");
const GUIDE = "https://docs.example.com/taskflow/v1-migration";
const BROWNOUTS = [
  ["2027-03-16T14:00:00Z", "2027-03-16T15:00:00Z"],   // announced: one hour
  ["2027-05-18T00:00:00Z", "2027-05-19T00:00:00Z"],   // announced: one day
].map(([from, to]) => [Date.parse(from), Date.parse(to)]);

const v1Requests = new client.Counter({
  name: "taskflow_api_v1_requests_total",
  help: "Requests to the deprecated v1 API, by API client",
  labelNames: ["client_id"], // registered API clients, a bounded set
});

const inBrownout = (t) => BROWNOUTS.some(([from, to]) => t >= from && t < to);

export function deprecateV1(req, res, next) {
  const now = Date.now();
  v1Requests.inc({ client_id: req.auth?.clientId ?? "anonymous" });

  if (now > SUNSET_AT || inBrownout(now)) {
    return res.status(410).json({
      error: "api_version_retired",
      message: "TaskFlow API v1 is retired (sunset 2027-06-30). Use /v2.",
      documentation: GUIDE,
    });
  }
  res.set("Deprecation", `@${Math.floor(DEPRECATED_AT / 1000)}`); // RFC 9745: @1796083200
  res.set("Sunset", new Date(SUNSET_AT).toUTCString());           // Wed, 30 Jun 2027 23:59:59 GMT
  res.set("Link", `<${GUIDE}>; rel="deprecation"`);
  next();
}

// src/app.js: app.use("/v1", deprecateV1, v1Router);

The counter, broken down by client_id, is the list of customers to contact before each brownout; the brownouts return exactly the response clients will get after the sunset, so nothing about the final removal is a surprise.

docs.title: A go/no-go check that reads the numbers
docs.text:
// scripts/go-no-go.mjs: print the go/no-go criteria; exit 1 on no-go
// usage: node scripts/go-no-go.mjs <candidate> <current>   e.g. 2026.11.2-rc.3 2026.11.1
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";

const [candidate, current] = process.argv.slice(2);
const PROM = process.env.PROMETHEUS_URL ?? "https://prometheus.example.com";

async function promValue(expr) {
  const res = await fetch(`${PROM}/api/v1/query?query=${encodeURIComponent(expr)}`);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`Prometheus returned ${res.status}`);
  const { data } = await res.json();
  return data.result.length ? Number(data.result[0].value[1]) : NaN; // NaN fails every check
}

const sessions = (v) =>
  promValue(`sum(increase(taskflow_app_sessions_total{version="${v}"}[48h]))`);
const crashFree = (v) =>
  promValue(
    `1 - sum(increase(taskflow_app_crashed_sessions_total{version="${v}"}[48h]))` +
      ` / sum(increase(taskflow_app_sessions_total{version="${v}"}[48h]))`,
  );

const blockers = JSON.parse(
  execFileSync("gh", ["issue", "list", "--label", "release-blocker",
    "--milestone", candidate.split("-")[0], "--state", "open", "--json", "number,title"],
    { encoding: "utf8" }),
);
const [candSessions, candCrashFree, curCrashFree] = await Promise.all([
  sessions(candidate), crashFree(candidate), crashFree(current),
]);

const checks = [
  ["no open release blockers", blockers.length === 0, `${blockers.length} open`],
  ["at least 2,000 beta sessions", candSessions >= 2000, String(candSessions)],
  ["crash-free sessions within 0.1 pp of the current release",
    candCrashFree >= curCrashFree - 0.001,
    `${(candCrashFree * 100).toFixed(2)}% vs ${(curCrashFree * 100).toFixed(2)}%`],
];

for (const [name, ok, detail] of checks) {
  console.log(`${ok ? "GO   " : "NO-GO"}  ${name}: ${detail}`);
}
process.exit(checks.every(([, ok]) => ok) ? 0 : 1);

The metric names stand for whatever your crash reporting exports. The important properties are that missing data counts as no-go (a NaN comparison is always false), and that the output is pasted into the release document, so the decision is recorded with its evidence.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Pick a cadence and keep it; move features to the next train instead of moving the train.
  • Hide unfinished work behind flags so the train can always leave.
  • Cut release branches from main, accept only fixes, fix on main first, and cherry-pick with -x.
  • Promote the last release candidate's build; never rebuild the final release.
  • Ship hotfixes through the same pipeline with shorter stages, not around it.
  • Write release notes for people and generate changelogs for tools.
  • Publish which versions are supported, for how long, and which fixes each receives, and budget for the backports that implies.
  • Deprecate with dates: announce, mark responses with Deprecation, Sunset, and a Link, measure usage per client, brown out, then remove.
  • Decide go/no-go on agreed numbers, record them, and rotate the release captain role.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• A fixed bug comes back in the next release. Detect: a regression report for a bug closed weeks ago, right after a new train ships. Cause: the fix was made only on the release branch, not on main. Fix: re-apply it on main, add a check that every commit on a release branch references a main commit (the -x line), and make "fix on main first" part of the hotfix checklist.
  • The release slips every cycle. Detect: the cut date moves for "one more feature"; releases grow and the stabilization period lengthens. Cause: features are not independently releasable, so the release waits for them. Fix: fix the cut date, put unfinished work behind flags, and let features ride the next train.
  • The final release behaves differently from the candidate testers approved. Detect: different checksums or image digests for the RC and the release; issues that never appeared in beta. Cause: the release was rebuilt from the branch with newer dependencies or a different base image. Fix: tag and promote the candidate's artifacts; never rebuild a release.
  • A security fix takes weeks to reach older supported versions. Detect: the fix ships on the current line but older lines stay vulnerable; backport pull requests pile up. Cause: old branches no longer build, or nobody owns them. Fix: keep CI green on every supported branch, automate backports, and reduce the number of supported lines to what you can actually maintain.
  • Customers break on the sunset date despite months of notice. Detect: a burst of 410 responses and support tickets on the sunset day. Cause: notices went to documentation nobody read, and nobody measured usage per client. Fix: count usage by client, contact the heavy users directly, and run brownouts before the deadline.
  • Two hotfixes collide on the same release branch. Detect: a patch release contains a half-tested second fix; the release notes do not match the change. Cause: several people cherry-picked into the branch without coordination. Fix: one release captain owns each branch's patch releases, and every backport goes through a reviewed pull request.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Release train: releases on a fixed schedule, carrying whatever is ready at the cut.
  • Cadence: the interval between releases.
  • Cut (branch point): the moment a release branch is created from main.
  • Stabilization: the period in which only fixes enter the release branch.
  • Release candidate (RC): a build that becomes the release if it passes go/no-go.
  • Go/no-go: the recorded decision to ship a candidate, based on agreed criteria.
  • Cherry-pick: applying one commit's change to another branch.
  • Backport: a fix carried from main to an older supported branch.
  • Hotfix: an urgent fix released outside the normal cadence.
  • LTS (long-term support): a release line supported for a longer, published period.
  • Deprecation: an announcement that something will be removed; it does not change behaviour.
  • Sunset: the date after which a deprecated resource stops working.
  • Brownout: a scheduled, temporary disablement that rehearses the sunset.
  • Release captain: the person who runs a release cycle.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating the train as a deadline to rush features into, instead of a schedule features can miss.
  • Fixing bugs only on the release branch.
  • Merging release branches back into main.
  • Rebuilding the final release instead of promoting the tested candidate.
  • Supporting every old version "just in case", with no end-of-life dates.
  • Announcing a deprecation without measuring who still uses the API.
  • Removing an endpoint on the sunset date without brownouts or contact with remaining users.
  • Running go/no-go meetings on opinions rather than numbers.
  • Confusing changelogs (for tools and developers) with release notes (for people).

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. When is a release train a better choice than continuous deployment, and how do the two combine in one product?
  2. With a two-week train, one week of stabilization, and a one-week rollout, what are the shortest, longest, and average times from merge to full rollout? (About 2, 4, and 3 weeks.)
  3. State the rules for release branches and explain why fixes land on main first.
  4. Walk through a hotfix for a bug present in 2.4.0 and in the LTS line 2.3.
  5. What do the Deprecation, Sunset, and Link: rel="deprecation" headers each communicate, and what ordering rule applies to their dates?
  6. Why run brownouts before a sunset?
  7. A product releases monthly and supports the current release plus the two previous ones for security. How many patch releases do 12 security fixes a year require? (36.)
  8. Which criteria would you put in a go/no-go check for a mobile release, and where does each number come from?
