docs.title: Update Mechanisms and Updaters
docs.text:
Server software is updated by deploying it. Everything else updates itself: a web app when the browser loads new files, a service worker when the browser notices a changed script, a desktop app through its updater, and a mobile app through its store or, for some code, over the air. Each mechanism has its own rules for when the new version is found, verified, installed, and started, and each one needs a way to stop a bad version from spreading.

This lesson explains how software updates itself on each platform (web, desktop, and mobile) and then the architecture of an updater: a static manifest on a CDN or a dynamic update server, signature verification and key rotation, full and delta updates, channels, percentage and cohort rollouts with stable bucketing, halting and rolling forward, forced and optional updates, keeping the update service available, and adoption telemetry. Code signing, notarization, store review, and a basic update server are covered in releasing desktop and mobile apps.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• An updater is a deployment system for machines you do not control. It needs the same safety as a server pipeline (stages, health gates, a stop button), but it cannot roll back what it already installed.
  • It is a remote code execution channel by design. Whoever controls the update feed controls every install. Signatures are what make that acceptable.
  • A broken updater strands users. If a release breaks the update path itself, those installs never receive the fix. They stay on the broken version until users reinstall by hand.
  • Adoption speed sets your support window. The faster installs move to new versions, the sooner the API can drop old behaviour (see keeping frontend and backend in sync).
  • Bandwidth is real money. A 150 MB desktop app updated on 1,000,000 installs moves 150 MB x 1,000,000 = 150 TB per release; if deltas average 15 MB, the same release moves 15 TB.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Electron's built-in updater. Electron's autoUpdater is built on Squirrel.Mac on macOS and uses Squirrel.Windows (or the MSIX updater for MSIX packages) on Windows; it has no Linux support, and on macOS the app must be signed. Electron's updates tutorial describes update.electronjs.org, a free service for apps with a public GitHub repository that publish builds to GitHub Releases.
  • Sparkle. Sparkle's publishing guide documents appcast feeds with EdDSA signatures, delta updates, channels, critical updates that users cannot skip, and phased rollouts in seven groups released one interval apart; phased rollout does not apply to critical updates or to manual checks.
  • Mozilla Balrog. Firefox's update server, Balrog, matches each update request against rules on fields from the update URL (channel, version, build ID, OS version, and others), picks the highest-priority match, and uses a backgroundRate that sets the percentage of requests served the new release.
  • Google Omaha. Omaha is the open-source version of Google Update, the Windows updater that keeps Chrome and other Google products up to date.
  • Android in-app updates. Google Play's in-app updates offer a flexible flow (background download) and an immediate flow (full-screen, blocking), with an update priority from 0 to 5 set per release through the Play Developer API and a staleness count in days.
  • Over-the-air JavaScript. Expo's EAS Update updates the JavaScript, styling, and images of a React Native app without a store build, and only for builds with a matching runtime version. Microsoft's App Center retirement notice confirms App Center, including CodePush, was retired on March 31, 2025; the standalone CodePush server Microsoft published instead was archived as read-only, without support, on May 20, 2025.

Popular tools and providers: Squirrel.Mac and Squirrel.Windows, electron-updater (electron-builder), the Tauri updater plugin, Sparkle, MSIX with App Installer, the Microsoft Store's gradual package rollout, Google Play in-app updates and staged rollouts, App Store phased release, Expo EAS Update, Workbox for service workers, Balrog, and Omaha.

docs.title: Web apps: a reload is the update
docs.text: A plain single-page app updates when the browser loads a new index.html. Everything that makes that safe (hashed assets kept for days, no-cache HTML, reload prompts for long-open tabs, chunk-error recovery) is covered in keeping frontend and backend in sync. A service worker adds a real install step with its own lifecycle.

docs.title: Service worker updates
docs.text:
A service worker sits between the page and the network, often serving the app shell from a cache. Updating it follows fixed rules:

  • Finding the update. The browser checks the worker script on navigation, and on functional events such as push and sync unless it checked within the previous 24 hours. By default it ignores HTTP caching headers for that check (the updateViaCache registration option changes this), and the worker counts as updated only if the script is byte-different. Embedding the build ID in sw.js guarantees that.
  • Why it waits. The browser runs only one version of a worker for a set of pages at a time. While any tab is controlled by v1, v2 waits.
  • skipWaiting() trade-off. Calling it makes the waiting worker active immediately. As Jake Archibald's service worker lifecycle article puts it, the new worker is then likely controlling pages loaded with an older version; if that can break things, don't use it. A page built from v1 HTML and code, served by a v2 worker that deleted v1's caches, is exactly the mixed state that produces missing chunks.
  • The usual compromise. Detect the waiting worker, show "Update available", and on click tell the worker to skipWaiting(), then reload once when controllerchange fires. The user chooses the moment, and the page and the worker change together.
  • Long-open tabs. A tab that never navigates never checks. Call registration.update() on an interval (the article suggests hourly for sites kept open a long time).

docs.title: Desktop update frameworks
docs.text:
Framework Platforms Update metadata Worth knowing Electron autoUpdater macOS (Squirrel.Mac), Windows (Squirrel.Windows, or the MSIX updater for MSIX packages) A feed URL from an update server or static storage No Linux support; the macOS app must be signed electron-updater (electron-builder) Windows (NSIS), macOS (DMG plus ZIP), Linux (AppImage, DEB, RPM, Pacman) latest.yml, latest-mac.yml, latest-linux.yml stagingPercentage for staged rollouts, blockmap-based differential downloads, Windows code-signature checks; Squirrel.Windows is not supported Tauri updater plugin Windows, macOS, Linux A static JSON file, or a dynamic server answering 200 with JSON or 204 Signatures are mandatory and cannot be disabled; Windows install mode passive (default), basicUi, or quiet Sparkle 2 macOS An RSS appcast EdDSA signatures, delta updates, channels, critical updates, phased rollout in seven groups MSIX with App Installer Windows An .appinstaller XML file Checks on launch (HoursBetweenUpdateChecks, 0 to 255, default 24) or in the background every 8 hours; UpdateBlocksActivation forces the update; only changed 64 KB blocks are downloaded

They all follow the same shape: ask whether a newer version exists, download it, verify it, install it at a convenient moment, and restart. The differences that matter for release engineering are where the rollout decision is made, how signatures work, whether partial downloads exist, and whether a downgrade is possible.

docs.title: Mobile: stores, in-app updates, and over-the-air code
docs.text:
• Store updates. Most users update through automatic store updates. You control the pace with Apple's phased release and Google Play's staged rollouts (details in the desktop and mobile lesson), and in Google Play halting stops further users from getting the version.
  • Android in-app updates. The Play Core library tells the app that an update exists, how many days ago it appeared (clientVersionStalenessDays), and its priority (0 to 5, set with inAppUpdatePriority when the release is rolled out, and not changeable later). A common policy: prompt with the flexible flow (download in the background, restart when the user agrees) after a few days of staleness, and use the immediate flow (full screen until updated) only for priority 4 and above.
  • iOS. There is no equivalent API. Apps compare their version with a minimum and a recommended version from your server and open their App Store page.
  • Over-the-air JavaScript updates. In React Native apps, the JavaScript bundle and assets can be replaced without a store build. With EAS Update, a build belongs to a channel, the channel points to a branch of updates, and an update is delivered only to builds whose platform and runtime version match exactly; native code changes need a new runtime version and a new store build. By default the app checks for an update when it opens; if the download finishes within the configured timeout it runs immediately, otherwise on the next launch.

Store policies limit what over-the-air code may do. Apple's Developer Program License Agreement (section 3.3.1(B)) allows downloaded interpreted code only if it does not change the app's primary purpose, does not bypass signing, sandbox, or other OS security features, and, for App Store apps, does not create a storefront for other apps; App Review guideline 2.5.2 forbids downloading code that introduces or changes features. Google Play's Device and Network Abuse policy forbids an app updating itself outside Google Play and downloading executable code such as dex or .so files, with an exception for code running in a virtual machine or interpreter with indirect access to Android APIs, such as JavaScript in a WebView. In practice: use over-the-air updates for fixes and small adjustments, and ship new features through review.

docs.title: Static manifest or dynamic update server
docs.text:
A static manifest is a file per channel and platform (latest.yml, an appcast, a Tauri JSON document) uploaded next to the installers. It is cheap, cacheable, and as available as your CDN. Its limits: everyone gets the same answer, so any rollout logic must run inside the installed app (electron-updater's stagingPercentage, Sparkle's phased groups), and a halt takes effect only when caches expire, so serve the manifest with a short cache lifetime or purge it on every change.

A dynamic update server receives the installed version, platform, architecture, channel, an install ID, and often a tenant ID, and decides per request. That is how you get instant halts, cohort targeting, tenant pinning ("this customer stays on 1.8 until their admin approves 1.9"), blocklists of known-bad versions, and a log of every check. Mozilla's Balrog and Google's Omaha are public examples. The cost: the server is on every client's update path, so it needs high availability, caching, and a fallback.

A common hybrid keeps the decision dynamic and everything heavy static: the service returns a small manifest that points to immutable, versioned artifact URLs on a CDN, and if the service is down the client simply tries again later.

docs.title: The update sequence as a state machine
docs.text: Two properties make an updater safe. Every failure before the install leaves the old version untouched (download to a temporary location, verify, and only then replace anything). Every failure after the install is reported quickly enough to stop the rollout for everyone else. A healthy first launch of the new version, reported back, is the most important signal an updater sends.

docs.title: Signatures, key rotation, and attacks on updaters
docs.text:
There are two separate layers of trust:

  1. Operating system code signing (Authenticode, Apple Developer ID, notarization) tells the OS who published the binary.
  2. Update signatures let the installed app check that a download came from you, using a public key built into the app. Tauri requires them, Sparkle uses EdDSA (ed25519) keys created with its generate_keys tool, and electron-updater checks Windows code signatures before installing.

HTTPS alone is not enough: it protects the connection, not the content of a compromised bucket, CDN, or update server. The TUF security model lists the attacks an update system must resist, including arbitrary software installation, rollback attacks (serving files older than the client has already seen), indefinite freeze attacks (serving the same stale files forever), and mix-and-match attacks (combining files that never existed together). Verifying a signature over the artifact handles the first; refusing versions lower than the installed one and signing the metadata, including its expiry, address the others.

Keys need a lifecycle plan before the first release:

  • Keep private keys in a hardware security module or a managed signing service, never on a laptop or in the repository.
  • Ship the app with the current public key and a backup key from day one, so losing or retiring the primary does not strand installs.
  • Rotate by publishing an update, signed with the old key, that adds the new public key; switch signing to the new key only after that update has reached every supported install.
  • Test the update path from the oldest supported version on every release, because that is the path a key or format mistake breaks.

docs.title: Full and delta updates
docs.text:
Approach How it works Trade-off Full package Download the whole new installer or archive Simple and robust; largest downloads Binary delta A patch from one specific old version to the new one (Sparkle's .delta files) Very small, but you generate one per supported source version, and a delta whose checksum does not match the installed copy is ignored in favour of the full download Block-based differential Compare block hashes and download only changed blocks (electron-updater's blockmap with HTTP range requests; MSIX's 64 KB blocks) Works from any older version that shares blocks; needs range-request support and good layout of files

With 1,000,000 installs and a 150 MB app, cutting the average download to 15 MB saves 135 TB of transfer per release and makes updates finish on slow connections, which directly raises the adoption rate.

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Channels let different audiences run different streams of versions: stable, beta, and often nightly or canary. Browsers are the best known examples: Chrome ships Canary, Dev, Beta, Stable, and Extended Stable; Firefox ships Nightly, Beta, Release, and ESR (the cadences are in release trains and release management). Design points:

  • Staff and volunteers run beta. They are the first ring of every rollout.
  • Moving from beta back to stable usually means waiting until stable catches up, because the beta version is higher and updaters do not downgrade by default.
  • Enterprise channels let administrators pin a version or delay updates, which a dynamic server implements as tenant rules.

docs.title: Percentage and cohort rollouts with stable bucketing
docs.text:
Each install gets a bucket from a hash of its install ID and the release version, for example hash("1.9.2:" + installId) mod 10000. The release is offered when the bucket is below percent x 100. Raising the percentage only adds installs, and because the release version is part of the hash, each release starts with a different set of early users. The same technique is used for feature flags.

Percentage of installs and percentage of requests are different things. Balrog's documented backgroundRate is the percentage of requests that receive the new release: a dice roll per check. A client that checks six times a day at a 10% rate is offered the release within a day with probability 1 - 0.9^6 = 47%, and within three days 1 - 0.9^18 = 85%. Per-request throttling is therefore a way to slow a rollout down, not a stable cohort; if you need a fixed share of installs (to compare crash rates against a control group), bucket by install ID.

Cohorts are ordered rings: internal users, the beta channel, then 1%, 5%, 20%, 50%, and 100% of stable, each step gated on crash-free sessions and error rates for the new version compared with the old.

docs.title: Pausing, rolling back, and rolling forward
docs.text:
You cannot uninstall software from users. Halting a rollout stops new installs only; electron-updater's documentation is explicit that pulling a bad staged release means publishing a version higher than the broken one. The Microsoft Store works the same way: going back to an older package stops new acquisitions, but customers who received the bad package keep it until a higher-versioned package arrives.

The roll-forward has an important asymmetry: installs that already have the bad version should get the fix first and all at once (they are already affected), while everyone else gets it through the normal staged ramp. Downgrades are possible in some frameworks (electron-updater's allowDowngrade, App Installer's ForceUpdateFromAnyVersion, a custom version comparator in Tauri), but they are risky: the newer version may already have migrated local data that the older one cannot read. Roll forward, and use remote kill switches to disable a broken feature in the meantime.

docs.title: Forced and optional updates, and when to install
docs.text:
Mode Example mechanisms Use for Optional Background download, install on quit (electron-updater's default install moment is on quit) Almost every release Recommended A dismissible banner; Android's flexible flow Releases with important fixes Required MSIX UpdateBlocksActivation, Sparkle critical updates, Android's immediate flow, a server-side minimum version Security fixes and versions the API can no longer serve

Installing on quit or restart is the least disruptive moment, but apps that are never closed (a desktop client left running for weeks) need a nudge: a prompt after a few days, or a silent install while the app is idle. Never install over a running process holding unsaved work.

docs.title: Keeping the update service available
docs.text:
• Fail open. The app must start and work normally when the update check fails; time it out after a few seconds and try later.
  • Spread the load. Two million installs checking every four hours is 2,000,000 / 14,400 s = 139 requests per second on average, but if 1.2 million of them start between 08:55 and 09:05 and check at launch, the peak is 1,200,000 / 600 s = 2,000 requests per second. Add random jitter to timers and delay the first check after launch.
  • Make "no update" cheap. A 204 with no body, cached decisions per version and channel, and rules held in memory.
  • Keep artifacts immutable. Versioned URLs on a CDN, never overwritten, so a cached manifest can never point at different bytes.
  • Have a static fallback. If the decision service is down for long, serving the last known-good static manifest is better than serving nothing.

docs.title: Telemetry for update adoption
docs.text:
Track each step of the funnel per target version: offered, download started and completed, verified, installed, first launch healthy. For example:

offered 100,000 -> downloaded 92,000 -> verified 91,900 -> installed 88,000 -> healthy 87,600
install failures: (91,900 - 88,000) / 91,900 = 4.2%   <- investigate before raising the rollout

Watch three more numbers: the version distribution of active installs, the time for a release to reach 50% and 90% of active installs, and spikes in verification failures, which usually mean a key, file, or CDN problem rather than a code bug.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Decision Choose When Manifest Static file on a CDN Small user base, one channel, no per-customer targeting Manifest Dynamic update server Staged rollouts with instant halt, tenants who pin versions, forced updates, adoption telemetry Download Full packages Small apps, or until bandwidth or slow connections become a problem Download Deltas or block maps Large apps, many installs, users on slow or metered networks Install On quit or restart The default Install Forced Security fixes and versions below the supported floor, never as routine Mobile change Over-the-air JavaScript update Bug fixes and small changes within store policy, same runtime version Mobile change Store build Native code changes, new features that need review, new permissions Web Prompted service worker activation PWAs and apps whose old pages would break with a new worker Web Immediate skipWaiting() Only when the worker change is compatible with pages already open

docs.title: A service worker update prompt for TaskFlow Web
docs.text:
// src/sw-register.js: detect a waiting worker, prompt, activate, reload once
export function registerServiceWorker(onUpdateReady) {
  if (!("serviceWorker" in navigator)) return;
  const hadController = Boolean(navigator.serviceWorker.controller);

  navigator.serviceWorker.register("/sw.js").then((registration) => {
    // A new worker may already be waiting from an earlier visit
    if (registration.waiting && hadController) {
      onUpdateReady(() => registration.waiting.postMessage({ type: "SKIP_WAITING" }));
    }

    registration.addEventListener("updatefound", () => {
      const worker = registration.installing;
      worker?.addEventListener("statechange", () => {
        // "installed" while another worker controls the page means "waiting"
        if (worker.state === "installed" && navigator.serviceWorker.controller) {
          onUpdateReady(() => worker.postMessage({ type: "SKIP_WAITING" }));
        }
      });
    });

    // Tabs that stay open for days never navigate, so check every hour
    setInterval(() => registration.update(), 60 * 60 * 1000);
  });

  // Reload once when the new worker takes over (not on the very first install)
  let reloading = false;
  navigator.serviceWorker.addEventListener("controllerchange", () => {
    if (!hadController || reloading) return;
    reloading = true;
    window.location.reload();
  });
}

// src/main.jsx (excerpt)
// registerServiceWorker((activate) => showBanner("A new version is ready.", "Reload", activate));

// public/sw.js (excerpt): activate only when the page asks
const BUILD = "873";                 // replaced at build time, so every build changes the bytes
const CACHE = `taskflow-${BUILD}`;
const PRECACHE = ["/", "/index.html"]; // plus the hashed assets listed by the build

self.addEventListener("install", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then((cache) => cache.addAll(PRECACHE)));
  // No skipWaiting() here: the page decides when to switch
});

self.addEventListener("message", (event) => {
  if (event.data?.type === "SKIP_WAITING") self.skipWaiting();
});

self.addEventListener("activate", (event) => {
  event.waitUntil(
    caches.keys().then((keys) =>
      Promise.all(
        keys
          .filter((key) => key.startsWith("taskflow-") && key !== CACHE)
          .map((key) => caches.delete(key)),
      ),
    ),
  );
});

Deleting the old caches in activate is safe here because activation only happens right before every controlled page reloads. Tools such as Workbox generate the precache list and the same message handling for you.

docs.title: Publishing a static manifest for TaskFlow Desktop
docs.text:
// scripts/make-manifest.mjs: build the Tauri static update manifest from CI outputs
import { mkdirSync, readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const { version } = JSON.parse(readFileSync("src-tauri/tauri.conf.json", "utf8"));
const base = `https://downloads.taskflow.example.com/desktop/${version}`;
const signature = (file) => readFileSync(`artifacts/${file}.sig`, "utf8").trim();

// File names as collected (and renamed per architecture) by the build jobs
const files = {
  "windows-x86_64": `TaskFlow_${version}_x64-setup.exe`,
  "darwin-aarch64": "TaskFlow_aarch64.app.tar.gz",
  "darwin-x86_64": "TaskFlow_x64.app.tar.gz",
};

const manifest = {
  version,
  notes: process.env.RELEASE_NOTES ?? "",
  pub_date: new Date().toISOString(),
  platforms: Object.fromEntries(
    Object.entries(files).map(([target, file]) => [
      target,
      { url: `${base}/${encodeURIComponent(file)}`, signature: signature(file) },
    ]),
  ),
};

mkdirSync("dist-updates/stable", { recursive: true });
writeFileSync("dist-updates/stable/latest.json", JSON.stringify(manifest, null, 2));

# .github/workflows/desktop-release.yml (publish job; the build matrix is not shown)
name: desktop-release
on:
  release:
    types: [published]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  # build: a matrix job that builds, signs, and uploads desktop-* artifacts

  publish:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: desktop-stable            # required reviewers before users get it
    permissions:
      contents: read
      id-token: write                      # OIDC to AWS: no stored access keys
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
      - uses: actions/download-artifact@v8
        with:
          pattern: desktop-*
          path: artifacts
          merge-multiple: true
      - uses: aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials@v6
        with:
          role-to-assume: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/taskflow-desktop-publish
          aws-region: eu-west-1
      - name: Upload installers first (versioned, immutable paths)
        run: |
          VERSION=$(node -p "require('./src-tauri/tauri.conf.json').version")
          aws s3 cp artifacts/ "s3://taskflow-downloads/desktop/$VERSION/" --recursive \
            --exclude "*.sig" --cache-control "public, max-age=31536000, immutable"
      - name: Then the manifest that points at them
        env:
          RELEASE_NOTES: ${{ github.event.release.body }}
        run: |
          node scripts/make-manifest.mjs
          aws s3 cp dist-updates/stable/latest.json \
            s3://taskflow-downloads/desktop/stable/latest.json \
            --cache-control "no-cache" --content-type application/json

The order is the same as for a web deploy: artifacts first, the pointer last, so no client is ever told about a file that does not exist yet. To halt, re-upload the previous latest.json: installs still on the old version see no update, and installs that already took the new version are not downgraded because the default comparison only moves forward.

docs.title: A rules-based update decision service
docs.text:
// src/update-service.js: rules decide per check; artifacts stay on the CDN
import express from "express";
import semver from "semver";
import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
import { loadReleases } from "./releases.js"; // version -> { notes, pub_date, platforms }

// Loaded from reviewed configuration; the first matching rule wins
const rules = [
  { name: "replace-bad-1.9.1", match: { channel: "stable", versions: "1.9.1" }, release: "1.9.2", percent: 100 },
  { name: "tenant-pinned", match: { tenant: "tenant-042" }, release: "1.8.4", percent: 100 },
  { name: "beta", match: { channel: "beta" }, release: "1.10.0-beta.3", percent: 100 },
  { name: "stable", match: { channel: "stable", versions: "<1.9.2" }, release: "1.9.2", percent: 25 },
];
const halted = new Set(["1.9.1"]);          // never offered, whatever a rule says
const releases = await loadReleases();

function bucket(installId, release) {
  const digest = createHash("sha256").update(`${release}:${installId}`).digest();
  return digest.readUInt32BE(0) % 10_000;   // 0..9999, stable per install and release
}

function matches({ match }, ctx) {
  if (match.channel && match.channel !== ctx.channel) return false;
  if (match.tenant && match.tenant !== ctx.tenant) return false;
  if (match.versions && !semver.satisfies(ctx.version, match.versions, { includePrerelease: true })) {
    return false;
  }
  return true;
}

const app = express();

// Tauri endpoint template: /desktop/{{target}}/{{arch}}/{{current_version}}
app.get("/desktop/:target/:arch/:version", (req, res) => {
  const ctx = {
    version: semver.valid(req.params.version),
    platform: `${req.params.target}-${req.params.arch}`,
    channel: req.get("X-Channel") ?? "stable",
    tenant: req.get("X-Tenant-Id"),
    installId: req.get("X-Install-Id"),
  };
  if (!ctx.version) return res.status(204).end();

  const rule = rules.find((r) => matches(r, ctx));
  if (!rule || halted.has(rule.release)) return res.status(204).end();

  const release = releases.get(rule.release);
  const asset = release?.platforms[ctx.platform];
  const inRollout =
    rule.percent >= 100 || (ctx.installId && bucket(ctx.installId, rule.release) < rule.percent * 100);

  if (!asset || !inRollout || !semver.gt(rule.release, ctx.version)) {
    return res.status(204).end();           // nothing for this install right now
  }
  res.json({ version: rule.release, notes: release.notes, pub_date: release.pub_date, ...asset });
});

app.listen(Number(process.env.PORT ?? 3001));

The rule order encodes the roll-forward from the diagram: installs on the halted 1.9.1 match the first rule and get 1.9.2 immediately; a pinned tenant stays on 1.8.4 regardless of the stable ramp; everyone else follows the 25% bucket. Installs without an ID are only offered releases at 100%, so they never skew a staged rollout's comparison group. Every decision should also be logged (version, rule, offered or not) to feed the adoption funnel.

docs.title: Over-the-air updates with EAS Update
docs.text:
{
  "expo": {
    "runtimeVersion": { "policy": "fingerprint" }
  }
}

The fingerprint policy (in app.json) changes the runtime version whenever anything that affects native code changes, so an over-the-air update can never reach a build whose native code it does not match.

# Publish a JavaScript fix to 10% of the production branch
eas update --branch production --message "Fix crash when opening a board" --rollout-percentage=10

# Watch crash-free sessions, then raise the percentage (100 finishes the rollout)
eas update:edit

# Or undo: send everyone in the rollout back to the previous update
eas update:revert-update-rollout

docs.title: Measuring adoption
docs.text:
-- adoption.sql: version share among desktop installs active in the last 7 days
WITH latest AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT ON (install_id) install_id, version
  FROM client_events
  WHERE platform = 'desktop'
    AND occurred_at > now() - interval '7 days'
  ORDER BY install_id, occurred_at DESC
)
SELECT version,
       count(*) AS installs,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 1) AS pct
FROM latest
GROUP BY version
ORDER BY installs DESC;

-- update-funnel.sql: where updates to 1.9.2 stop
SELECT event, count(DISTINCT install_id) AS installs
FROM client_events
WHERE platform = 'desktop'
  AND attributes ->> 'target_version' = '1.9.2'
  AND event IN ('update_offered', 'download_complete', 'verify_ok', 'install_ok', 'first_run_ok')
GROUP BY event
ORDER BY installs DESC;

Both queries assume a PostgreSQL table of anonymous client events keyed by install ID; any analytics store with the same fields works.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Treat the updater as a deployment pipeline: stages, health gates, a halt switch, and telemetry for every step.
  • Verify an update signature with a public key built into the app before installing anything; keep private keys in an HSM or signing service and ship a backup public key from the first release.
  • Download to a temporary location, verify, and only then replace files, so every failure before the install leaves a working version.
  • Upload artifacts first and the manifest last, at immutable versioned URLs; keep manifest caching short.
  • Bucket installs by a hash of install ID and release for staged rollouts; when rolling forward, replace the bad version first.
  • Prefer roll-forward to downgrades, and build remote kill switches into the app.
  • Install on quit or restart by default; force updates only for security and for versions below the supported floor.
  • Make the update check fail open, jitter its timing, and keep a static fallback for the decision service.
  • Test the update path from the oldest supported version on every release.
  • For service workers, prompt before skipWaiting() and reload once on controllerchange.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The new version is installed nowhere after a release. Detect: offers rise but verify_ok stays at zero; clients log signature errors. Cause: the release was signed with a different key than the one built into the app, or the manifest carries a signature path instead of the signature content. Fix: halt, re-sign with the correct key, add a CI step that verifies each artifact against the shipped public key, and keep the signing key in one managed place.
  • A halt does not stop new installs for an hour. Detect: installs of the halted version keep growing after the manifest was replaced. Cause: the CDN cached latest.json with a long lifetime. Fix: serve manifests with no-cache or a short max-age, and purge the manifest path on every change.
  • The update server falls over every Monday morning. Detect: request rate spikes at the start of the working day; app launches slow down. Cause: every install checks at launch with no jitter, and the app waits for the check. Fix: delay and jitter the first check, make the check asynchronous with a short timeout, cache "no update" answers, and scale for the launch peak.
  • Users with a tab open all week report a broken app after a deploy. Detect: errors only from sessions older than the last service worker update; requests for chunks that no longer exist. Cause: skipWaiting() and clients.claim() let the new worker control pages built from the old code, and the old caches were deleted. Fix: activate only after a user prompt and reload, and keep old hashed assets on the server.
  • A 10% rollout reached most users within days. Detect: the share on the new version far exceeds the configured percentage. Cause: the server rolled dice per request, so frequently checking clients eventually won. Fix: bucket by install ID and release, so the percentage means a share of installs.
  • An over-the-air update crashes on launch for some users. Detect: crash reports rise right after an update, only on older store builds. Cause: the update needed native code those builds lack, with a runtime version that did not change. Fix: revert the rollout, switch to the fingerprint runtime version policy, and test updates against every store build still in use.
  • Installs stop updating after a release. Detect: the version distribution freezes at the new version; update checks from it fail or never happen. Cause: the release broke the updater itself (endpoint, key, or install code). Fix: reach those users through the in-app minimum-version screen or a download page, and add an "update from N to N+1" test to the release pipeline.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Update manifest: the document that tells installs which version is available and where to download it.
  • Static manifest: a manifest file served unchanged to every client.
  • Dynamic update server: a service that decides per request which update, if any, to offer.
  • Update signature: a signature over the artifact, verified by the installed app with an embedded public key.
  • Delta update: a patch from one specific old version to the new one.
  • Block map: a list of block hashes that lets a client download only changed blocks.
  • Channel: a stream of versions for an audience, such as stable or beta.
  • Stable bucketing: assigning each install a fixed bucket from a hash, so rollout percentages mean a fixed share of installs.
  • Halt: stopping a rollout so no further installs receive a version.
  • Roll forward: replacing a bad version with a newer, fixed one.
  • Runtime version: in over-the-air systems, the identifier of the native code an update is compatible with.
  • Waiting worker: a newly installed service worker that cannot activate while the old one controls open pages.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing HTTPS makes update signatures unnecessary.
  • Thinking a halt removes a bad version from devices.
  • Downgrading installs whose local data was already migrated.
  • Rolling dice per request and calling it a percentage rollout.
  • Caching the manifest for hours, so halts are slow.
  • Blocking app startup on the update check.
  • Calling skipWaiting() by default in every service worker.
  • Using over-the-air updates to ship features that need store review.
  • Keeping the only copy of the update signing key on one machine.
  • Never testing the update path from old versions.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Why is an updater a deployment system, and which property of server deployments does it lack?
  2. Describe the service worker lifecycle and explain why a new worker waits. When is calling skipWaiting() safe?
  3. Compare a static manifest with a dynamic update server for halting, targeting, and availability.
  4. Which attacks on update systems does a signature over the artifact stop, and which need signed metadata and version checks?
  5. A rollout throttles 10% of requests, and clients check eight times a day. What share of active clients is offered the update within one day? (1 - 0.9^8 = 57%.)
  6. A bad 1.9.1 reached 20% of installs before the halt. How should the rules for 1.9.2 treat those installs compared with everyone else?
  7. When would you choose an over-the-air JavaScript update, and when a store build?
  8. Two million installs check every four hours. What is the average request rate, and why is the real peak higher?

docs.title: Versioning Patterns
docs.text:
A product does not have one version; it has many. The TaskFlow API image, the public API contract, the database schema, the events on the message bus, the shared npm packages, the Helm chart, and every desktop and mobile build each carry their own number, and each number is read by a different audience asking a different question. Getting these identifiers right is what lets you answer "what exactly is running, and is it compatible with that?" in seconds.

This lesson covers what gets a version and why the schemes differ; SemVer, CalVer, build numbers, Git SHAs, and monotonic build IDs, and how to combine them in one string; store version codes versus display versions; embedding the version in every artifact; one version for the whole product versus one per component; and when to bump what. SemVer rules, Git tags, and changelog automation are covered in versioning, tags, and releases; this page builds on them.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Incidents start with "which version?" If the API, the web bundle, and the crash reports all name their versions consistently, you can match a spike of errors to one build in a minute. If they do not, the first hour of the incident is archaeology.
  • Compatibility decisions need comparable numbers. A minimum supported client version, an updater deciding whether 1.10.0 is newer than 1.9.0, and a migration tool deciding which scripts to run all depend on versions that sort correctly.
  • Stores and operating systems enforce rules. Google Play rejects a reused version code, Android refuses to install a lower version code over a higher one, and App Store Connect identifies a build by its version and build string. A careless scheme can block a release on the day you need it.
  • Dashboards group by release. Crash-free rates, error budgets, and canary comparisons are only meaningful when every build has a distinct, correctly formatted release name.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Android version codes. Android's versioning guide defines versionCode as a positive integer used to decide which build is newer, used by the system to block downgrades, never reusable on Google Play, and capped at 2,100,000,000; versionName is the string shown to users and is not used for comparisons.
  • Apple bundle versions. Apple documents CFBundleShortVersionString as the user-visible release version (three period-separated integers) and CFBundleVersion as the build version (one to three integers). App Store Connect's app information reference says a build is uniquely identified by the bundle ID, version number, and build string together.
  • Chromium. The Chromium project's version numbers page explains its four-part MAJOR.MINOR.BUILD.PATCH scheme: BUILD is an ever-increasing number for a point on the trunk, PATCH increases on a branch, and MAJOR and MINOR reflect scheduling and marketing decisions rather than the code itself.
  • Microsoft Store. The MSIX app package requirements require four-part versions whose sections are integers from 0 to 65535, with the fourth section reserved for the Store and left at 0.
  • Sentry release names. Sentry's naming releases guide recommends package@version or package@version+build, and forbids slashes, newlines, and names over 200 characters.

Popular tools and providers: the semver npm package, git describe, release-please, semantic-release, Changesets, docker/metadata-action, Gradle's versionCode and versionName, Xcode's agvtool, and the release features of Sentry and other error trackers.

docs.title: What gets a version, and why the schemes differ
docs.text:
Each versioned thing has a different consumer, and the number exists to answer that consumer's question.

Thing Who reads the version The question it answers Typical scheme Library or SDK (@example/taskflow-sdk) Other developers' package managers Is upgrading safe? SemVer Public HTTP API Client developers Which contract am I calling? A major version in the path (/v2) or a dated version (2026-11-01) Service build (TaskFlow API image) Deploy pipeline, on-call engineers Exactly which build is this? Commit SHA and image digest, optionally a SemVer or CalVer label Database schema Migration tool, the app at startup Which migrations have run, in what order? A monotonic migration ID (sequence or timestamp) Events and messages Consumers on the bus Which payload shape is this? A version per event type, or a schema registry ID Infrastructure modules (Helm charts, Terraform modules) Other teams' configuration Is upgrading safe? SemVer (a Helm chart has a chart version and a separate appVersion) Desktop and mobile builds Users, stores, update servers What do I call it, and is it newer? A display version plus a strictly increasing build number Web bundle Browsers and CDNs Which files belong together? Content hashes in file names plus a build ID

The mistake to avoid is forcing one scheme onto everything. SemVer on a database schema says nothing useful, and a commit SHA on a public SDK tells consumers nothing about compatibility.

docs.title: Version identifiers compared
docs.text:
Identifier Example Orders builds? Unique? Signals compatibility? Generated by SemVer 2.4.1 Yes, by precedence rules Only if never reused Yes People, or tools reading Conventional Commits CalVer 2026.11.2 Yes With a counter segment No The release date CI run number 873 Within one workflow Within one workflow No The CI system Commit SHA 3f2a1c9 No Yes No Git git describe v2.4.1-5-g3f2a1c9 Relative to the last tag Yes No Git Content digest sha256:9f2c... No Yes No The registry or build tool

Three properties matter, and no single identifier has all of them: ordering (is this newer?), identity (exactly which bits?), and meaning (is it compatible?). That is why mature pipelines record several identifiers for every build and combine them where one string is needed.

docs.title: Combining identifiers in one string
docs.text:
SemVer leaves room for this: a pre-release after a hyphen, and build metadata after a plus sign.

Two consequences follow from the SemVer rules:

  • Build metadata does not order builds. 2.4.1+build.873 and 2.4.1+build.874 have equal precedence, so an updater that compares SemVer will not treat the second as newer. If two builds can both be "the latest", they need different version cores or pre-release parts, not just different metadata.
  • Some systems reject or drop the plus sign. Docker tags allow only letters, digits, _, ., and -, so you tag the image 2.4.1 and keep the full string in a label or environment variable. The semver npm package's valid() returns 2.4.1 for 2.4.1+build.873, silently dropping the metadata.

Development builds between releases need care. A build made on Tuesday after 2.4.1 shipped on Monday must sort after 2.4.1. Naming it 2.4.1-dev.5 gets that wrong, because a pre-release sorts before its release:

The fix is to name development builds as pre-releases of the next version: 2.4.2-dev.5, where 5 is the number of commits since the v2.4.1 tag. Precedence then matches build order all the way to the release:

2.4.1 < 2.4.2-dev.5 < 2.4.2-dev.12 < 2.4.2-rc.1 < 2.4.2

docs.title: Monotonic build numbers
docs.text:
Stores, update servers, and some operating systems compare builds with a single integer that must only ever increase. Common sources and their traps:

Source Monotonic? Trap CI run number (github.run_number) Within one workflow Moving the build to a different workflow or CI system starts again at 1; add a fixed offset when you migrate Commit count (git rev-list --count HEAD) On one branch Differs between branches, and a shallow clone (fetch-depth: 1) counts 1 Timestamp (YYYYMMDDHH) Yes, if builds are not parallel Two builds in the same hour collide; long formats overflow store limits Derived from SemVer (major*1000000 + minor*10000 + patch*100 + n) Yes, while parts stay under their caps A minor version above 99 breaks the encoding A counter in a database or build service Yes One more service to keep available

Limits turn this into arithmetic. Google Play allows version codes up to 2,100,000,000:

YYYYMMDDHH   2026111310  = 2,026,111,310   fits, until the year 2100
YYMMDDHHmm   2611131042  = 2,611,131,042   too large: the upload is rejected
SemVer-based 3.2.0 build 1 -> 3*1,000,000 + 2*10,000 + 0*100 + 1 = 3,020,001

MSIX sections are smaller still: each of the first three must be between 0 and 65535 (and the first cannot be 0), so 20261113 cannot be a section. A Windows build usually puts a counter in the third section, for example 1.9.873.0.

Whatever source you choose, it must never go backwards. Android blocks installing a lower version code over a higher one, so a scheme change must start above the largest code ever shipped.

docs.title: Store version codes versus display versions
docs.text:
Every client platform separates the name users see from the number machines compare.

Platform Display version Build number Rules for the build number Android versionName, any string (3.2.0) versionCode, an integer (30200) Positive, at most 2,100,000,000, never reused on Google Play; the system blocks downgrades iOS and macOS CFBundleShortVersionString, three integers (3.2.0) CFBundleVersion, one to three integers (412) A build is identified by bundle ID, version, and build string, so each upload of a version needs a new build string Windows (MSIX) Your marketing name Package version Major.Minor.Build.Revision Sections 0 to 65535, fourth section 0 for the Store; the Store serves the highest applicable version Directly distributed desktop (Tauri, Electron) The app version (1.9.1) Usually the same SemVer string The updater compares SemVer, so pre-release and metadata rules apply

Keep the display version meaningful for people and let CI own the build number. Humans should never type a build number into a project file.

docs.title: Embedding the version in every artifact
docs.text:
Compute the version once, early in the pipeline, and pass the same values to every later step. Never compute it at runtime from a Git checkout: production containers have no .git directory.

Where How Who reads it Container image Tags (2.4.1, sha-<commit>), OCI labels org.opencontainers.image.version and .revision, the digest Deploy tools, registry users, scanners Running service GET /version, an X-App-Version response header, a startup log line, the OpenTelemetry service.version resource attribute On-call engineers, clients, dashboards Web bundle A build-time define (__APP_VERSION__) or a VITE_APP_VERSION variable, plus a version.json file served with no-cache The app itself, support staff, update prompts Error tracking The release name, for example taskflow-api@2.4.1+build.873.g3f2a1c Crash and regression analysis Deployment record Version, commit, digest, environment, time Audits, DORA metrics, rollback

A version header on every response looks redundant, but it pays off: in the browser's network panel anyone can see which server version answered a failing request, and a client can notice that the server changed underneath it (the next lesson uses this). The GET /version endpoint and image labels are shown in versioning, tags, and releases, and service.version in distributed tracing.

docs.title: One version for the product, or one per component
docs.text:
One product version One version per component Example "TaskFlow 2026.11" for API, web, and desktop together API 2.4.1, web build 873, desktop 1.9.1 Communication Simple for customers and support Needs a mapping to say what shipped together Releases Every component gets a new version even if unchanged, or the version lies Each component releases when it changes Fits On-premises bundles, desktop apps with an embedded server, a monorepo with one deployable Independently deployed services and clients

Most products that deploy continuously use a hybrid: each component keeps its own version for machines, and a product release name (often CalVer) points to a manifest of component versions for humans, like the manifest on the release engineering overview. Large platforms publish the compatibility rules between their components' versions; Kubernetes's version skew policy is a good model.

docs.title: When to bump what
docs.text:
Change App or service version API version Schema version Event version Client build number Bug fix in a handler Patch No No No (new client build: +1) New optional response field Minor No, it is additive Only if stored No Renamed or removed response field Major for SDKs New API version, or expand and contract within one Expand first New column for a feature Minor No New migration Breaking change to an event payload Minor or major New event version, published alongside the old one Any new client build uploaded to a store Display version only when releasing Always +1

The rule underneath the table: bump a version only for its own audience. An internal refactor does not change the API version; a new migration does not change the event version; and a build number changes on every build because the store, not a human, is its audience.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text: Situation Use Avoid Public npm SDK or library Strict SemVer, automated from commits CalVer, or breaking changes in minor releases Internal service deployed many times a day Commit SHA and digest per build; SemVer or CalVer tags for milestones if humans need them Inventing SemVer bumps that nobody reads Public API Major versions in the path, or dated versions in a header; additive changes without a bump A new API version for every release Database schema Monotonic migration IDs SemVer for migrations Mobile app SemVer or CalVer display version plus a CI-owned build number Hand-edited build numbers Desktop app with an updater SemVer, because updaters compare it; dev builds as pre-releases of the next version Build metadata as the only difference between builds Product release shared with customers CalVer release name pointing to a component manifest One synthetic number bumped on every component change

docs.title: Compute every version once in CI
docs.text:
// scripts/version.mjs: compute every version identifier once, in CI
import { execFileSync } from "node:child_process";
import { appendFileSync, readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import semver from "semver";

const git = (...args) => execFileSync("git", args, { encoding: "utf8" }).trim();
const tryGit = (...args) => {
  try {
    return git(...args);
  } catch {
    return "";
  }
};

const pkg = JSON.parse(readFileSync("package.json", "utf8")); // e.g. 2.4.1
const sha = git("rev-parse", "HEAD");
const build = process.env.GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER ?? "0";

// A commit tagged v<package version> is a release. Anything else is a
// pre-release of the NEXT patch, so it sorts after the last release.
const releaseTag = `v${pkg.version}`;
const tagsHere = tryGit("tag", "--points-at", "HEAD").split("\n");
let version = pkg.version;
if (!tagsHere.includes(releaseTag)) {
  const since = tryGit("rev-list", "--count", `${releaseTag}..HEAD`) || "0";
  version = `${semver.inc(pkg.version, "patch")}-dev.${since}`; // 2.4.2-dev.5
}

const out = {
  version,                                         // 2.4.1 or 2.4.2-dev.5
  full: `${version}+build.${build}.g${sha.slice(0, 7)}`,
  build,
  sha,
};
console.log(out);
if (process.env.GITHUB_OUTPUT) {
  const lines = Object.entries(out).map(([k, v]) => `${k}=${v}\n`).join("");
  appendFileSync(process.env.GITHUB_OUTPUT, lines);
}

# .github/workflows/build.yml
name: build
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  version:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    outputs:
      version: ${{ steps.v.outputs.version }}
      full: ${{ steps.v.outputs.full }}
      sha: ${{ steps.v.outputs.sha }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0              # tags and history for rev-list
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 24
          cache: npm
      - run: npm ci
      - id: v
        run: node scripts/version.mjs

  image:
    needs: version
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4
      - uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          build-args: |
            VERSION=${{ needs.version.outputs.full }}
            GIT_SHA=${{ needs.version.outputs.sha }}
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:${{ needs.version.outputs.version }}
            ghcr.io/example/taskflow-api:sha-${{ needs.version.outputs.sha }}
  • fetch-depth: 0 matters: with the default shallow clone the release tag is missing, the count falls back to 0, and every dev build would be 2.4.2-dev.0.
  • The image tags use version (no +), and the full string with build metadata travels as the VERSION build argument, which the Dockerfile in versioning, tags, and releases turns into the APP_VERSION environment variable and the OCI version and revision labels. Setting labels in one place avoids two sources disagreeing.
  • The version is computed in one job and consumed by the others through job outputs, so every artifact of this run carries identical values.

docs.title: Stamp the version into responses, traces, and the web bundle
docs.text:
// src/middleware/version-header.js
const VERSION = process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev";

export function versionHeader(req, res, next) {
  res.set("X-App-Version", VERSION); // visible in every response
  next();
}

// src/app.js (excerpt)
// app.use(versionHeader);

# Dockerfile (excerpt): one source for the version inside the container
ARG VERSION=dev
ENV APP_VERSION=$VERSION \
    OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=taskflow-api \
    OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES=service.version=$VERSION

OTEL_SERVICE_NAME and OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES are standard OpenTelemetry SDK variables, so every span, metric, and log the API exports carries service.version without code changes. (If the platform also sets OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, merge the values instead of overwriting them.)

// vite.config.js: TaskFlow Web
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

const version = process.env.APP_VERSION ?? "dev";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react(),
    {
      name: "emit-version-json",
      apply: "build",
      generateBundle() {
        // dist/version.json: served with Cache-Control: no-cache
        this.emitFile({
          type: "asset",
          fileName: "version.json",
          source: JSON.stringify({ version, builtAt: new Date().toISOString() }),
        });
      },
    },
  ],
  define: {
    __APP_VERSION__: JSON.stringify(version), // replaced in the code at build time
  },
});

The app reads __APP_VERSION__ (declare it in a .d.ts file for TypeScript) for its own release name, and the deployed version.json tells an open tab whether a newer build exists, which the next lesson uses for "new version available" prompts.

docs.title: Set store build numbers from CI
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/set-ios-version.sh: run in CI before archiving the iOS app
set -euo pipefail
cd ios
xcrun agvtool new-marketing-version "$APP_VERSION"   # CFBundleShortVersionString, e.g. 3.2.0
xcrun agvtool new-version -all "$BUILD_NUMBER"        # CFBundleVersion, e.g. 412

agvtool requires the project's versioning system to be set to Apple Generic. On Android, read both values from the environment in the Gradle build so that CI, not a person, owns them:

// app/build.gradle.kts (excerpt)
android {
    defaultConfig {
        versionName = providers.environmentVariable("APP_VERSION").getOrElse("0.0.1-dev")
        versionCode = providers.environmentVariable("VERSION_CODE").map { it.toInt() }.getOrElse(1)
    }
}

# In the Android job: an offset keeps codes above those from the old CI system
export VERSION_CODE=$(( 30000 + GITHUB_RUN_NUMBER ))

docs.title: Compare versions correctly
docs.text:
// scripts/compare-versions.mjs
import semver from "semver";

const versions = ["1.10.0", "1.9.0", "1.9.0-rc.2", "1.9.0-rc.10", "2.0.0-dev.3"];

console.log([...versions].sort());
// [ '1.10.0', '1.9.0', '1.9.0-rc.10', '1.9.0-rc.2', '2.0.0-dev.3' ]   string order: wrong

console.log([...versions].sort(semver.compare));
// [ '1.9.0-rc.2', '1.9.0-rc.10', '1.9.0', '1.10.0', '2.0.0-dev.3' ]   precedence order

semver.gt("1.10.0", "1.9.0");                                // true
semver.compare("2.4.1+build.873", "2.4.1+build.874");        // 0: metadata ignored
semver.compareBuild("2.4.1+build.873", "2.4.1+build.874");   // -1: metadata compared
semver.satisfies("2.4.2-dev.5", ">=2.4.1");                  // false: pre-releases excluded
semver.satisfies("2.4.2-dev.5", ">=2.4.1", { includePrerelease: true }); // true

// Store build numbers are integers: compare them as numbers, never as strings
Number("1000") > Number("412");                               // true ("1000" > "412" is false)

The satisfies behaviour surprises people: by default a range only matches pre-releases of the same major.minor.patch, so a dev build will not satisfy a minimum-version range unless you opt in.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Give each versioned thing the scheme its consumer needs; do not force SemVer onto schemas or SHAs onto SDKs.
  • Compute versions once per pipeline run and pass them along as outputs; never recompute them in later jobs or at runtime.
  • Name development builds as pre-releases of the next version so precedence follows build order.
  • Let CI own build numbers, make them strictly increasing, and plan for store limits before you need them.
  • Stamp the version into image labels, a response header, telemetry resource attributes, error-tracking release names, and the web bundle.
  • Compare versions with a SemVer library and build numbers as integers.
  • Keep product release names (CalVer) separate from component versions, and link them with a release manifest.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The store rejects the upload on release day. Detect: the Play Console refuses the bundle because the version code was already used, or App Store Connect rejects a duplicate build string. Cause: a build number typed by hand, or a pipeline rerun that rebuilt with the same number. Fix: derive the number from CI, add an offset if it ever went backwards, and treat every upload as a new build.
  • The updater never offers 1.10.0. Detect: installs stay on 1.9.x after a release; update-check logs show "no update" for 1.9.4. Cause: versions compared as strings, so "1.10.0" < "1.9.4". Fix: compare with a SemVer library and add a unit test with a two-digit minor version.
  • Development builds look older than the release before them. Detect: beta-channel users are offered 2.4.1 again after installing a later dev build. Cause: dev builds named 2.4.1-dev.N, which sort before 2.4.1. Fix: name them 2.4.2-dev.N, a pre-release of the next patch.
  • /version says dev in production. Detect: the endpoint, the header, and error reports show dev or unknown. Cause: the build argument was not passed, or the version was read from a Git checkout that does not exist in the container. Fix: pass the computed version as a build argument, and fail the pipeline if the built image reports dev.
  • Crash reports mix two different builds under one release. Detect: a "regression" that appears to come and go within one release; symbol uploads overwrite each other. Cause: the release name omits the build number, so a rebuild reused it. Fix: use package@version+build names and never rebuild a released version under the same name.
  • Every dev build gets the same version. Detect: consecutive builds are all 2.4.2-dev.0 (or -dev.1); image tags are overwritten. Cause: a shallow clone, so the release tag is missing and the commit count is 0 or 1. Fix: fetch-depth: 0, or fetch tags explicitly before computing.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• Version core: the MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH part of a SemVer string.
  • Pre-release: a hyphenated suffix (-rc.2) that sorts before the release it belongs to.
  • Build metadata: a + suffix that identifies a build but is ignored for precedence.
  • Precedence: SemVer's rules for ordering versions.
  • Build number: a strictly increasing integer that identifies a build to stores, updaters, or operating systems.
  • Display version: the human-facing version (versionName, CFBundleShortVersionString).
  • Version code: Android's integer build number, versionCode.
  • Monotonic: never decreasing; required for build numbers.
  • Content digest: a hash of an artifact's content that identifies it exactly.
  • Release name: the identifier an error tracker or deploy record uses for a build, such as taskflow-api@2.4.1+build.873.
  • Release manifest: a document that lists every component version in one product release.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Believing one version number can serve every audience.
  • Using build metadata as the only difference between two builds and expecting tools to order them.
  • Naming development builds after the last release instead of the next.
  • Sorting versions as strings, or comparing build numbers as strings.
  • Typing build numbers by hand, or letting them reset when CI changes.
  • Computing the version at runtime from Git inside a container.
  • Bumping the API version for internal changes, or not bumping it for a removed field.
  • Encoding dates into build numbers without checking store limits.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Which three properties can a version identifier have, and which identifiers provide each one?
  2. Why does 2.4.1+build.873 not count as newer than 2.4.1+build.872?
  3. A build is made two days after v2.4.1 shipped. What version should it carry, and why not 2.4.1-dev.7?
  4. A team proposes Android version codes in YYMMDDHHmm form. Calculate the code for 2026-11-13 10:42 and decide whether Google Play accepts it. (2,611,131,042 is above the 2,100,000,000 limit, so no.)
  5. What are the display version and the build number on Android and iOS, and what rules apply to each build number?
  6. List four places the TaskFlow API version should appear at runtime, and who reads each one.
  7. When does one product version make sense, and when should each component be versioned separately?
  8. Why does semver.satisfies("2.4.2-dev.5", ">=2.4.1") return false?

docs.title: SSL Certificates Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Quick revision of the SSL certificates lessons, for a last look before an interview or a certificate task.

docs.title: Key commands
docs.text:
Command What it does openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -showcerts </dev/null Shows the chain the server really sends (always pass SNI) openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -tls1_2 </dev/null Tests whether TLS 1.2 is accepted openssl x509 -in fullchain.pem -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName Names, issuer, and validity of the first (leaf) certificate openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem leaf.pem Checks that the leaf chains up to the root curl -v --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://api.example.com/healthz Tests one server directly, without changing DNS sudo certbot certonly --webroot -w /var/www/acme -d api.example.com --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx" HTTP-01 issuance; the hook reloads nginx after every renewal sudo certbot renew --dry-run Proves renewal works end to end without a real certificate sudo certbot certificates Lists the certificates certbot manages and their expiry sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx Validates the config, including the key match, before reloading kubectl -n taskflow describe certificate taskflow-api-tls cert-manager status and events for one certificate 
# Does this private key belong to this certificate? The two hashes must match.
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl pkey -in privkey.pem -pubout | openssl sha256

docs.title: Key configuration
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/api.example.com.conf (excerpt): TLS termination with HSTS
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name api.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem;
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;

    # Start with a small max-age, then raise it to two years
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains" always;
}

docs.title: Decision guide
docs.text: If you need Choose Why HTTPS on one server certbot with webroot and a deploy hook, or Caddy Free ACME certificates with automatic renewal A wildcard certificate DNS-01, for example certbot-dns-route53 Wildcards need DNS validation TLS on a cloud load balancer or CDN The provider's managed certificates The platform renews and deploys them Kubernetes ingress cert-manager with an ACME issuer Certificates as resources, renewed automatically Internal service names A private CA (step-ca, Vault PKI, a cloud private CA) Public CAs cannot validate internal names Service-to-service identity mTLS with short-lived certificates or a mesh Proves who is calling; authorization stays separate Testing automation Let's Encrypt staging Avoids production rate limits HTTPS from a CDN to the origin Full (strict) or an equivalent verify mode Plain "Full" accepts any certificate

docs.title: Numbers and defaults to remember
docs.text: Item Value Public maximum validity (SC-081v3) 398 days, then 200 from March 15, 2026, 100 from March 15, 2027, 47 from March 15, 2029 Domain validation reuse 200 days, then 100 days, then 10 days (2029) Let's Encrypt lifetimes 90 days by default; 64 days from February 10, 2027; 45 days from February 16, 2028 Let's Encrypt options Opt-in 45-day tlsserver profile since May 2026; optional 6-day certificates certbot renewal Runs twice a day; renews with a third of the lifetime left (30 of 90 days); follows ARI since 4.1 Alert thresholds 90-day certificates: ticket below 21 days, page below 7; 45-day: below 10 and 4 Let's Encrypt rate limit 5 certificates for the same set of names in 7 days HSTS max-age Seconds; 63,072,000 is two years; roll out with a small value such as 300 OCSP Let's Encrypt removed OCSP URLs and ended OCSP in 2025; stapling does nothing for its certificates Renewal pace at 47 days About once a month when renewing at two-thirds of the lifetime

docs.title: Top mistakes
docs.text:
• Serving cert.pem instead of fullchain.pem. Browsers may cope, but curl, Java, and mobile clients report an unknown issuer; serve the chain.
  • Renewing without reloading. nginx keeps the old certificate in memory; add a deploy hook such as systemctl reload nginx.
  • Redirecting the ACME path to HTTPS. Let /.well-known/acme-challenge/ win on port 80, or HTTP-01 fails.
  • A CAA record that omits your CA. Issuance fails even though the challenge passes; list every CA your automation and platforms use.
  • Hard-coded renewal intervals. A 60-day timer breaks with 45-day certificates; renew by remaining lifetime or ARI.
  • Watching files instead of served certificates. Probe every hostname and listener from outside, for example probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry.
  • Requesting a new certificate on every container start. Persist the ACME storage, or rate limits stop issuance.
  • Re-encrypting without verifying. nginx defaults to proxy_ssl_verify off; turn it on, and use Full (strict) at CDNs.
