docs.title: SSL Certificates Interview Questions and Answers
docs.text: These questions review TLS and certificate fundamentals, obtaining and renewing certificates, and TLS termination and troubleshooting. Try answering each one before reading the answer.

docs.title: 1. What is the difference between SSL and TLS?
docs.text: SSL is the original protocol (SSL 2.0 and 3.0), now prohibited because of serious weaknesses. TLS replaced it; TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are also deprecated (RFC 8996), so modern servers offer TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only. "SSL certificate" is a historical name: the same X.509 certificate is used with any TLS version.

docs.title: 2. What three security properties does TLS provide?
docs.text: Confidentiality (traffic is encrypted with keys from the handshake), integrity (each record carries an authentication tag, so tampering is detected), and authentication (the server proves, with its certificate and a signature, that it is the named host; mutual TLS also authenticates the client).

docs.title: 3. What does TLS not hide from a network observer?
docs.text: The IP addresses, the size and timing of traffic, and, unless Encrypted Client Hello is used, the hostname in the SNI field of ClientHello. It also says nothing about whether the server itself is trustworthy or secure.

docs.title: 4. Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake.
docs.text: The client sends ClientHello with supported versions, cipher suites, signature algorithms, SNI, ALPN, and a key share. The server replies with ServerHello and its key share; both derive handshake keys via ECDHE. The server then sends, encrypted, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify (a signature over the handshake), and Finished. The client verifies everything and sends Finished, and application data can flow after one round trip.

docs.title: 5. Why is TLS 1.3 faster and more private than TLS 1.2?
docs.text: TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for a full handshake instead of two, because the client sends its key share in the first message. It encrypts the certificate and most handshake messages, removes static RSA key exchange and legacy ciphers, and makes forward secrecy mandatory.

docs.title: 6. What is forward secrecy?
docs.text: Session keys are derived from ephemeral (EC)DHE key shares that are discarded after the handshake, so an attacker who records traffic and later steals the server's long-term private key still cannot decrypt the recorded sessions.

docs.title: 7. What is 0-RTT early data, and what is its risk?
docs.text: With session resumption, a TLS 1.3 client can send application data in its first flight. That data can be replayed by an attacker, so it is safe only for idempotent requests, and many servers leave it disabled.

docs.title: 8. What are the most important fields in an X.509 server certificate?
docs.text: The subject alternative name list (the hostnames it is valid for), the validity period (notBefore and notAfter), the issuer, the public key, key usage and extended key usage (serverAuth), basic constraints (CA:FALSE), and the issuer's signature. Clients match the hostname against the SAN entries, not the subject CN.

docs.title: 9. Explain the chain of trust.
docs.text: The leaf certificate is signed by an intermediate CA, which is signed by a root CA. Roots are self-signed and trusted because they are in the client's trust store (browser, OS, runtime). The client verifies each signature up the chain and checks that it ends at a trusted root.

docs.title: 10. Why must the server send intermediate certificates, and why not the root?
docs.text: Clients have the roots but not necessarily the intermediates, so the server sends the leaf plus all intermediates (fullchain.pem). The root is already on the client and sending it adds bytes without adding trust. Browsers can sometimes fetch missing intermediates; most API clients cannot.

docs.title: 11. What are DV, OV, and EV certificates?
docs.text: Domain validation proves control of the domain only and is issued automatically (Let's Encrypt issues only DV). Organization validation and extended validation also verify the organization, with stricter checks for EV. The encryption is identical, and browsers no longer show special EV indicators.

docs.title: 12. What does a wildcard certificate for *.example.com cover?
docs.text: Exactly one label: api.example.com and app.example.com, but not example.com and not v2.api.example.com. It is convenient for many subdomains, but one private key then protects them all. Let's Encrypt requires the DNS-01 challenge for wildcards.

docs.title: 13. What is Certificate Transparency, and why should you monitor it?
docs.text: Public, append-only logs where CAs record every publicly trusted certificate; browsers require proof of logging (SCTs). Monitoring the logs for your domains reveals certificates you did not request. It also means every hostname in a public certificate is public, so internal names belong on a private CA.

docs.title: 14. How do HSTS and the preload list work?
docs.text: The Strict-Transport-Security header tells browsers to use only HTTPS for the domain for max-age seconds, optionally for all subdomains. The preload list builds this into browsers so even the first visit is protected; it requires a long max-age, includeSubDomains, and HTTPS on every subdomain, and it is slow to undo.

docs.title: 15. How long can a public TLS certificate be valid today?
docs.text: Under CA/Browser Forum Ballot SC-081v3, certificates issued from March 15, 2026 may be valid for at most 200 days, falling to 100 days from March 15, 2027 and 47 days from March 15, 2029 (it was 398 days before). Let's Encrypt issues 90-day certificates by default, moving to 64 days on February 10, 2027 and 45 days on February 16, 2028.

docs.title: 16. Why is revocation considered unreliable, and what replaces it?
docs.text: Many clients soft-fail when they cannot check CRLs or OCSP, OCSP has privacy and availability problems, and Let's Encrypt shut down its OCSP service in 2025. Browsers use aggregated revocation data (CRLSets, CRLite), and the main mitigation is short certificate lifetimes.

docs.title: 17. What are SNI and ALPN?
docs.text: Server Name Indication is the hostname the client puts in ClientHello so a server hosting many names can choose the right certificate. ALPN (Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation) lets client and server agree on the protocol inside TLS, such as h2 or http/1.1, without an extra round trip.

docs.title: 18. Should you use RSA or ECDSA certificates?
docs.text: Both are secure at recommended sizes (RSA 2048 bits or more, ECDSA P-256). ECDSA keys and signatures are much smaller and faster, and all modern clients support them. Many sites serve ECDSA, and some serve both an ECDSA and an RSA certificate for very old clients.

docs.title: 19. What are PEM, DER, and PKCS#12 files?
docs.text: PEM is Base64 text between -----BEGIN ...----- lines and can hold several certificates or a key (fullchain.pem, privkey.pem). DER is the same data in binary. PKCS#12 (.p12, .pfx) is a password-protected bundle of a certificate chain and its private key, common on Windows and in Java.

docs.title: 20. What is ACME, and what are its main steps?
docs.text: The protocol (RFC 8555) for automated issuance: the client registers an account key, creates an order for identifiers, completes a challenge for each authorization, finalizes the order with a CSR, and downloads the certificate chain. Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, and other CAs support it.

docs.title: 21. Compare HTTP-01, DNS-01, and TLS-ALPN-01 challenges.
docs.text: HTTP-01 serves a token file on port 80 and is simplest for public servers. DNS-01 creates a TXT record at _acme-challenge.<domain>, works for internal hosts, and is required for wildcards. TLS-ALPN-01 answers on port 443 with a special certificate and suits TLS-terminating proxies when port 80 is blocked. Only DNS-01 issues wildcards.

docs.title: 22. What are the risks of DNS-01, and how do you reduce them?
docs.text: The client needs DNS API credentials, often able to change the whole zone, stored on a server. Reduce the risk with tokens limited to TXT records, delegating _acme-challenge via CNAME to a dedicated validation zone, or running issuance on a separate, hardened host. Also allow for DNS propagation delays.

docs.title: 23. How does certbot renew certificates, and what is a deploy hook?
docs.text: A systemd timer or cron job runs certbot renew twice a day; since certbot 4.0, certificates are renewed by default when a third of their lifetime remains (30 days for a 90-day certificate), or earlier when the CA's ARI suggests it. A deploy hook runs only after a successful renewal, for example systemctl reload nginx, so the server actually starts using the new certificate.

docs.title: 24. What is ACME Renewal Information (ARI)?
docs.text: An ACME extension (RFC 9773) where the CA tells the client when to renew a specific certificate. It lets the CA spread load and ask for early renewal before a mass revocation, and at Let's Encrypt, ARI-driven renewals are exempt from rate limits.

docs.title: 25. What does Caddy do differently from nginx with certbot?
docs.text: Caddy obtains and renews certificates automatically for every site address that is a domain, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and loads renewed certificates itself. There is no separate client, timer, or reload to configure; you only persist its data directory.

docs.title: 26. How does cert-manager work in Kubernetes?
docs.text: Issuers and ClusterIssuers describe how to get certificates (ACME, private CA, cloud CAs). A Certificate resource, created directly or from an Ingress annotation, declares names and a Secret name. cert-manager runs the order and challenges, stores tls.crt and tls.key in the Secret, and renews at about two-thirds of the lifetime by default.

docs.title: 27. What are managed certificates, and what can still go wrong with them?
docs.text: Certificates issued and renewed by a cloud provider for its load balancers and CDNs, such as AWS Certificate Manager with DNS validation. The private key never leaves the provider. Renewal can still fail if the validation DNS record is deleted or a name on the certificate stops resolving.

docs.title: 28. When should you use a private CA?
docs.text: For internal services and mutual TLS: internal names should not appear in public CT logs, public CAs cannot validate internal names, and private CAs can issue very short-lived certificates at high volume. Tools include step-ca, Vault PKI, cloud private CAs, cert-manager CA issuers, and service meshes.

docs.title: 29. Why do certificate expiries still cause outages?
docs.text: Renewal fails silently (port 80 closed, broken redirects, expired DNS tokens, removed names), renewal succeeds but the server is not reloaded, some certificates are outside the automation, monitoring checks the file rather than the served certificate or only one network path, and teams relied on CA expiry emails that no longer exist.

docs.title: 30. How should certificate expiry be monitored?
docs.text: Probe the served certificate from outside, on every hostname and network path, with thresholds scaled to the lifetime (for 90-day certificates, a ticket under 21 days and a page under 7). Also alert directly on renewal failures, keep an inventory with owners, and monitor CT logs for certificates you did not expect.

docs.title: 31. What is the ACME staging environment for?
docs.text: Testing issuance and renewal automation without hitting production rate limits. Its certificates are not trusted by browsers, but it exercises the same flow, which makes it ideal for new setups and CI.

docs.title: 32. Why do CAs validate domain control from several network locations?
docs.text: An attacker who hijacks one network path (for example with a BGP route leak) could otherwise answer a challenge and obtain a certificate. Multi-perspective validation requires the challenge to succeed from several vantage points, and CA/Browser Forum rules now require it of public CAs.

docs.title: 33. Where can TLS be terminated, and how do you choose?
docs.text: At a CDN, a cloud load balancer, a reverse proxy or ingress, or the application; or passed through to the app by an L4 load balancer. Choose based on where plaintext may exist, who should hold keys, whether you need HTTP-aware routing or a WAF at the edge, and where certificates can be automated.

docs.title: 34. What is re-encryption, and what makes it secure?
docs.text: Terminating TLS at the load balancer and opening a new TLS connection to the backend. It is only meaningful if the load balancer verifies the backend certificate (for example proxy_ssl_verify on in nginx or a strict mode at a CDN); without verification it stops passive eavesdropping but not an active attacker.

docs.title: 35. What does an app need when TLS terminates at a proxy?
docs.text: The original scheme and client IP from X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For (or Forwarded), and configuration to trust only its proxy for those headers, such as app.set("trust proxy", 1) in Express. Otherwise it sees every request as plain HTTP, causing redirect loops and missing Secure cookies.

docs.title: 36. What are the key settings in a modern nginx TLS server block?
docs.text: listen 443 ssl with http2 on, ssl_certificate pointing at the full chain, the private key, ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3, ECDHE AEAD cipher suites for TLS 1.2, a shared session cache, session tickets off unless keys are rotated, HSTS with always, and a port 80 server that redirects to HTTPS except for the ACME challenge path.

docs.title: 37. What is mutual TLS, and where is it used?
docs.text: TLS in which the server requests a certificate from the client and verifies it against a trusted CA, so both sides are authenticated. It is used for service-to-service traffic (often via a service mesh with SPIFFE identities), partner APIs, and devices. It proves identity; authorization is still a separate decision.

docs.title: 38. Which openssl s_client options matter most when debugging?
docs.text: -connect host:443, -servername host (send SNI), -showcerts (print the chain), -verify_return_error and -verify_hostname (fail on problems), -tls1_2 or -tls1_3 (test a protocol), -alpn h2, and -brief for a summary. Pipe the output into openssl x509 -noout -dates -ext subjectAltName to decode the leaf.

docs.title: 39. What do OpenSSL verify errors 10, 18, 19, 20, and 21 mean?
docs.text: 10: certificate has expired. 18: the leaf is self-signed. 19: a self-signed certificate (an untrusted root) is in the chain. 20: unable to get the local issuer certificate, and 21: unable to verify the first certificate, both usually meaning a missing intermediate or an unknown CA.

docs.title: 40. Why does forgetting SNI cause confusing results?
docs.text: A server hosting several names chooses the certificate by SNI. Without it, the server returns its default certificate, so you see a hostname mismatch or a different certificate than real clients get.

docs.title: 41. How do you test one backend server behind a load balancer for TLS problems?
docs.text: Use curl -v --resolve api.example.com:443:<backend-ip> https://api.example.com/ (or openssl s_client -connect <backend-ip>:443 -servername api.example.com), which connects to that IP while sending the real hostname for SNI and verification.

docs.title: 42. How do you check that a private key matches a certificate?
docs.text: Compare the public keys: hash the output of openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -pubkey and of openssl pkey -in key.pem -pubout; the hashes must be identical. This works for RSA and ECDSA keys.

docs.title: 43. Why is NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 dangerous?
docs.text: It disables certificate verification for every TLS connection in the process, so any attacker on the path can impersonate any server. Fix the real cause instead: serve the full chain, or trust a private CA with NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS or the ca option.

docs.title: 44. How can add_header in nginx silently drop HSTS?
docs.text: A location block inherits add_header directives from the server level only if it defines none of its own. Adding any header in a location drops the inherited HSTS header there. Repeat security headers in such locations (or use an include), and use always so they appear on error responses too.

docs.title: 45. How do you rotate a certificate in a Node.js HTTPS server without a restart?
docs.text: Call server.setSecureContext({ key, cert }) with the new files, for example when a file watcher sees cert-manager update the mounted Secret. New connections use the new certificate; existing connections are unaffected.

docs.title: 46. Browsers load https://api.example.com, but the mobile app and Node.js clients fail with certificate errors. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the chain the server sends, with openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -showcerts.

How to confirm: only the leaf appears, and the verify return code is 21 (unable to verify the first certificate); Node.js reports UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE.

Likely causes and fixes: the server uses cert.pem instead of fullchain.pem; browsers fill the gap from caches, other clients cannot. Configure the full chain and reload. See TLS and certificate fundamentals.

docs.title: 47. The site went down at midnight with "certificate expired", although certbot is installed. What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: sudo certbot certificates and the certbot log in /var/log/letsencrypt/.

How to confirm: either renewals have been failing for weeks (challenge errors), or a renewed certificate exists on disk while openssl s_client shows the old notAfter.

Likely causes and fixes: a broken challenge (port 80 closed, redirect, DNS change) or a missing deploy hook so nginx never reloaded. Fix the challenge, add --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx", and monitor the served certificate with ticket and page thresholds. See obtaining and renewing certificates.

docs.title: 48. After moving TLS termination from nginx on the VM to a cloud load balancer, the site loops on redirects. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: what scheme the app thinks requests use, and the X-Forwarded-Proto header arriving at the app.

How to confirm: app logs show http requests and 301 redirects to https for every request.

Likely causes and fixes: the app redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS but now receives HTTP from the load balancer and does not trust its forwarded headers. Configure trust proxy for the load balancer, or do the redirect only at the load balancer. See TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 49. A new subdomain v2.api.example.com shows NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID, even though you have a *.example.com certificate. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the SAN list of the served certificate.

How to confirm: it contains *.example.com only, which matches one label, not v2.api.

Likely causes and fixes: wildcards do not cover deeper subdomains. Issue a certificate that includes v2.api.example.com or *.api.example.com. See TLS and certificate fundamentals.

docs.title: 50. A cert-manager Certificate has been stuck in "Issuing" for an hour. How do you debug it?
docs.text:
What to check first: kubectl describe on the Certificate, CertificateRequest, Order, and Challenge.

How to confirm: the Challenge shows a failing self-check (HTTP-01 path not reachable, wrong ingress class, a network policy blocking the solver) or DNS-01 permission or propagation errors.

Likely causes and fixes: fix the solver configuration or credentials, test against the staging issuer, and alert when Certificates are not Ready. See obtaining and renewing certificates.

docs.title: 51. Let's Encrypt returns a rate-limit error for a service that restarts often. What is wrong?
docs.text:
What to check first: how often new certificates are issued for the same names, and where the client stores its certificates and account.

How to confirm: each container start creates a new account or order because the data directory is ephemeral; the limit of 5 certificates for the same set of names in 7 days is hit.

Likely causes and fixes: persist the ACME data (a volume or a Kubernetes Secret), rely on renewal instead of re-issuance, and use the staging environment for tests. See obtaining and renewing certificates.

docs.title: 52. Only one VM reports "certificate is not yet valid" for a certificate issued an hour ago. What do you check?
docs.text:
What to check first: the VM's clock (date -u, timedatectl status).

How to confirm: the clock is behind by hours or days compared with other hosts.

Likely causes and fixes: NTP is not running or blocked. Enable chrony or systemd-timesyncd, allow NTP traffic, and alert on clock offset. See TLS and certificate fundamentals.

docs.title: 53. Users behind one corporate network report certificate warnings for your site, but nobody else does. Why?
docs.text:
What to check first: the issuer of the certificate those users see.

How to confirm: the issuer is the company's proxy CA, not your CA.

Likely causes and fixes: a TLS-intercepting proxy re-signs traffic and some devices lack the proxy's root, or a pinned client rejects it. This is outside your server; the network's administrators must fix their trust distribution or exempt your domain. See TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 54. A security review finds that the load balancer forwards to backends over HTTPS but accepts any backend certificate. Is that acceptable?
docs.text:
What to check first: the backend TLS verification settings of the load balancer, proxy, or CDN mode.

How to confirm: proxy_ssl_verify is off (the nginx default), or the CDN uses "Full" rather than "Full (strict)".

Likely causes and fixes: re-encryption without verification protects only against passive eavesdropping. Issue backend certificates from an internal CA and enable verification, or use a service mesh with mTLS. See TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 55. After rotating the internal CA, one service's mTLS calls fail with "bad certificate". What happened?
docs.text:
What to check first: which CA issued the failing client's certificate and which CAs the server trusts.

How to confirm: the client has a certificate from the new intermediate, and the server's CA bundle contains only the old one.

Likely causes and fixes: trust was not distributed before issuance from the new CA. Add new trust anchors first, keep old and new during the overlap, then rotate issuance in stages. See TLS termination and troubleshooting.

docs.title: 56. Certificate expiry probes are green, yet some users get an expired certificate. How can that be?
docs.text:
What to check first: whether every network path is probed: IPv4 and IPv6, each region or edge location, each load balancer listener.

How to confirm: probing the failing path directly (for example over IPv6 or from the affected region) shows a different, expired certificate.

Likely causes and fixes: a separate proxy or edge configuration with its own certificate outside the automation. Probe every path separately and bring it under the same automation. See obtaining and renewing certificates.

docs.title: 57. HSTS was enabled with includeSubDomains, and an old HTTP-only subdomain is now unreachable in browsers. What do you do?
docs.text:
What to check first: the HSTS header served on the apex domain and the affected subdomain's HTTPS support.

How to confirm: browsers refuse HTTP for the subdomain and it has no valid HTTPS endpoint.

Likely causes and fixes: includeSubDomains forces HTTPS everywhere, and browsers cache the policy for max-age. The quick fix is to serve HTTPS on that subdomain; in future, roll out HSTS with a short max-age first and preload only when all subdomains support HTTPS. See TLS and certificate fundamentals.

docs.title: 58. An internal hostname such as admin.internal.example.com appears in a public certificate search. Is that a problem?
docs.text:
What to check first: crt.sh results for your domain and which team requested the certificate.

How to confirm: a publicly trusted certificate lists the internal name.

Likely causes and fixes: internal services were given public certificates, which are logged in Certificate Transparency. Treat the names as public, move internal services to a private CA or a wildcard, and keep monitoring CT for unexpected certificates. See TLS and certificate fundamentals.

docs.title: Obtaining and Renewing Certificates
docs.text: A certificate is only useful while it is valid, and public certificates now live for months, soon weeks. The job is therefore not "buy a certificate" but "run a system that keeps every certificate valid forever". This lesson covers the ACME protocol and Let's Encrypt, the HTTP-01, DNS-01, and TLS-ALPN-01 challenges and when each is required, certbot and its renewal timers, Caddy's automatic HTTPS, cert-manager in Kubernetes, managed certificates at cloud load balancers and CDNs, private CAs for internal services, and why certificate expiry still causes outages, with a monitoring setup and a renewal automation checklist.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
An expired certificate is a total outage for every client that verifies certificates, which is all of them: browsers show a full-page warning, mobile apps and API clients refuse to connect, and webhooks from partners start failing. It happens to well-run companies because renewal is a background process that runs rarely, depends on things that change (DNS records, firewall rules, hosting providers, API tokens), and fails silently.

Shorter lifetimes (a 200-day maximum since March 2026, 47 days by 2029) make this both worse and better. Renewal now happens many times a year, so a manual process is impossible, but a broken automation is discovered sooner and practised constantly. The goal of this lesson is automation that renews early, verifies what is actually served, and alerts long before users notice.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Let's Encrypt and ACME. Let's Encrypt's How It Works page explains how an ACME client proves control of a domain and obtains certificates automatically and for free. The protocol is standardized as RFC 8555, and ACME Renewal Information (ARI), which lets the CA suggest when to renew, as RFC 9773.
  • Tailscale (March 2024). In TLS certificate outage, Tailscale describes how the certificates for its website expired and took it down for about 90 minutes: automatic renewal had been broken by a workaround from a hosting migration, and its probes checked only the IPv6 path, which served a different, valid certificate.
  • Bazel (December 2025). The Bazel team's post-mortem explains how a managed certificate for several subdomains expired, breaking builds for hours: renewal failed after one subdomain on the certificate was removed from DNS, and nothing alerted on the failures.
  • cert-manager. The cert-manager documentation describes the de facto standard Kubernetes controller that issues and renews certificates from ACME CAs, private CAs, and cloud issuers, storing them as Secrets.

Popular tools and providers: certbot, acme.sh, lego, Caddy, Traefik, cert-manager, AWS Certificate Manager, Google Cloud Certificate Manager, Azure Key Vault and App Service certificates, Cloudflare, step-ca, HashiCorp Vault PKI, and AWS Private CA.

docs.title: The ACME protocol
docs.text:
ACME (Automatic Certificate Management Environment) is how a client and a CA automate issuance:

  1. Account: the client creates an account key pair and registers it with the CA. Every later request is signed with this key.
  2. Order: the client asks for a certificate for a set of identifiers (api.example.com).
  3. Authorizations and challenges: for each identifier, the CA offers challenges that prove control of the domain.
  4. Validation: the client fulfils one challenge and tells the CA; the CA checks it, from several network vantage points (multi-perspective validation, now required of public CAs by CA/Browser Forum rules) so one hijacked network path cannot fool it.
  5. Finalize: the client sends a CSR for a fresh key pair; the CA issues the certificate.
  6. Download: the client fetches the certificate chain and installs it.

Authorizations are cached for a while, so renewals often skip step 4. The CA/Browser Forum schedule also shortens how long a validation may be reused, down to 10 days in 2029, so challenges will run more often.

docs.title: HTTP-01, DNS-01, and TLS-ALPN-01
docs.text:
HTTP-01 DNS-01 TLS-ALPN-01 Proof File at http://<domain>/.well-known/acme-challenge/<token> TXT record at _acme-challenge.<domain> Special self-signed certificate offered on port 443 with ALPN acme-tls/1 Port 80 (redirects to 80 or 443 are followed) None; DNS only 443 Wildcards (*.example.com) No Yes (required) No Server must be publicly reachable Yes No: works for internal hosts Yes Many servers behind a load balancer Every server must serve the file (or route the path to one) Easy: validation is independent of servers Every server must answer Main risk Port 80 blocked, or a redirect rule breaks the path DNS API credentials on servers; propagation delay Few clients support it Typical users certbot on a single server, cert-manager HTTP solver Wildcards, internal services, CI-issued certificates TLS-terminating proxies such as Caddy and Traefik

Decision rules:

  • Need a wildcard? DNS-01 is the only option.
  • Server not reachable from the internet (internal dashboard)? DNS-01.
  • Single public server or ingress, port 80 open? HTTP-01 is simplest.
  • Port 80 blocked, but you terminate TLS yourself? TLS-ALPN-01.

DNS-01 security tip: an API token that can edit your whole DNS zone is a powerful secret to leave on a web server. Limit it to TXT records where the provider allows, or delegate _acme-challenge.example.com with a CNAME to a separate zone used only for validation. Some hosting platforms ask for an NS delegation of the same name instead, so they can issue wildcards while your DNS stays where it is (see connecting domains to hosting).

CAA records decide which CAs may issue at all. Before issuing, a public CA looks up the domain's CAA records and must refuse if they exist but do not list it. A CAA set that omits your CA (common after moving to a platform or CDN that uses a different one) makes issuance and renewal fail with a CAA error even though the challenge would pass. The record format and lookup rules are in domains and DNS records.

docs.title: certbot and renewal timers
docs.text:
certbot, from the Electronic Frontier Foundation, is the reference ACME client for single servers:

  • Plugins decide how the challenge is answered and how the certificate is installed: --nginx and --apache edit the web server config, --webroot writes files into an existing site, --standalone runs a temporary server on port 80, and DNS plugins (for example certbot-dns-route53) create TXT records.
  • Files live in /etc/letsencrypt/live/<name>/: fullchain.pem (leaf plus intermediates, what servers should use), privkey.pem, cert.pem, and chain.pem. They are symlinks to the latest versions in /etc/letsencrypt/archive/.
  • Renewal runs from a systemd timer (or cron) installed with the package, which runs certbot renew twice a day. Since certbot 4.0 a certificate is renewed by default when a third of its lifetime remains (30 days for a 90-day certificate; configurable as renew_before_expiry in its renewal file), and since certbot 4.1 it also follows the CA's ARI suggestion when the CA provides one.
  • Deploy hooks run only after a successful renewal, for example systemctl reload nginx. Without one, nginx keeps serving the old certificate from memory until something reloads it.

docs.title: Caddy: automatic HTTPS
docs.text: Caddy obtains and renews certificates by default for every site address that is a domain name: no separate client, no timer, no reload. It redirects HTTP to HTTPS, solves HTTP-01 or TLS-ALPN-01 challenges itself, uses Let's Encrypt and ZeroSSL as issuers, staples OCSP where the CA still offers it, and stores certificates in its data directory. For a small deployment of TaskFlow API on one or two VMs, Caddy as the reverse proxy removes most certificate operations.

docs.title: cert-manager in Kubernetes
docs.text:
cert-manager adds Kubernetes resources for certificates:

  • Issuer / ClusterIssuer: how to obtain certificates (an ACME account with HTTP-01 or DNS-01 solvers, a private CA, Vault, or cloud CAs).
  • Certificate: the desired certificate: names, Secret name, key algorithm, duration. It can be created explicitly or from an Ingress or Gateway annotation.
  • CertificateRequest, Order, Challenge: the in-progress steps, useful when debugging (kubectl describe them).
  • Secret: the result, holding tls.crt and tls.key, which the ingress controller or application mounts.

By default cert-manager renews when two-thirds of a certificate's lifetime has passed (configurable with renewBefore), and it updates the Secret in place, so ingress controllers that watch Secrets pick up the new certificate without a restart. The Kubernetes side (Ingress, Gateway, controllers) is covered in ingress, networking, and Helm.

docs.title: Managed certificates at load balancers and CDNs
docs.text:
Cloud providers can own the whole lifecycle when TLS terminates on their infrastructure:

  • AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) issues public certificates at no charge for use with integrated services (Application and Network Load Balancers, CloudFront, API Gateway). With DNS validation, ACM renews them automatically while they are in use, keeping the same ARN. Certificates are regional, and CloudFront only uses certificates from us-east-1.
  • Google Cloud Certificate Manager, Azure (App Service managed certificates, Front Door), and CDNs such as Cloudflare offer the same model.

The trade-off: you never touch a private key (good), but you can only use those certificates on that provider's services, and renewal can still fail if the DNS validation record is deleted or a name on the certificate stops resolving, as the Bazel incident shows.

docs.title: Private CAs for internal services
docs.text:
Service-to-service traffic inside TaskFlow's network (the API calling an internal reports service, mutual TLS between services) should not use public certificates: internal names would be published in CT logs, public CAs cannot validate internal names, and public lifetimes and rate limits do not fit thousands of short-lived workloads. Use a private CA:

  • step-ca (Smallstep), HashiCorp Vault PKI, AWS Private CA, Google Cloud CA Service, or cert-manager's CA issuer.
  • A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) runs its own CA and rotates workload certificates automatically, often every day.
  • Distribute the private root to every client's trust store (for Node.js, NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS), protect its key offline, and issue from an intermediate.
  • Keep lifetimes short (hours to days) and automate renewal, just as with public certificates.

docs.title: Why expirations still cause outages
docs.text:
Common causes, roughly in order of frequency:

  1. Renewal fails silently: port 80 closed by a new firewall rule, an HTTP to HTTPS redirect that breaks the challenge path, an expired DNS API token, a name on the certificate that no longer resolves, a CAA record that does not list the CA, a CA rate limit hit after repeated failures.
  2. Renewal succeeds but the old certificate is still served: no deploy hook to reload nginx, a Java keystore or appliance that needs a manual import, a copy of the certificate baked into a container image or another server.
  3. The certificate was never in the automation: one manually issued certificate on a forgotten host, an internal service, a client certificate used for a partner integration, or a code-signing or push-notification certificate with its own expiry.
  4. Monitoring checks the wrong thing: checking the file on disk, not the certificate served; probing one of several paths (IPv4 versus IPv6, one of several edge locations).
  5. Notification gaps: relying on CA expiry emails. Let's Encrypt stopped sending expiration emails in June 2025, so any process that depended on them now depends on nothing.

docs.title: Monitoring expiry the right way
docs.text:
• Measure the certificate actually served, from outside, on every hostname and every path (IPv4 and IPv6, each region or edge, each load balancer listener). The Prometheus blackbox exporter exposes probe_ssl_earliest_cert_expiry; synthetic monitoring services offer the same.
  • Scale thresholds to the lifetime. For 90-day certificates renewed at 30 days left: a ticket below 21 days (renewal has been failing for over a week) and a page below 7. For 45-day certificates renewed at 15 days left: a ticket below 10 days and a page below 4.
  • Alert on renewal failures directly where you can: failed certbot or cert-manager runs, Certificate resources not Ready.
  • Inventory every certificate, including internal, client, and third-party ones, with an owner. Certificate Transparency monitoring finds public ones you forgot.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Recommended approach One or two VMs running TaskFlow behind a reverse proxy Caddy, or nginx with certbot (--nginx or --webroot) and a deploy hook Kubernetes cluster cert-manager with an ACME ClusterIssuer; DNS-01 for wildcards TLS terminates at a cloud load balancer or CDN The provider's managed certificates (ACM, Google Certificate Manager, Cloudflare) Wildcard for many tenant subdomains DNS-01 (certbot DNS plugin, cert-manager DNS solver, or the provider) Internal services and mutual TLS Private CA or service mesh with short-lived certificates Environments that cannot reach a public CA Private CA, or DNS-01 run from a host that can Testing your automation The CA's staging environment (Let's Encrypt staging) to avoid production rate limits

Avoid manually purchased certificates installed by hand unless something truly prevents automation, and if you must, put them in the inventory with calendar reminders and monitoring, as Tailscale did after its outage.

docs.title: certbot with nginx
docs.text:
# Install certbot (snap is the method recommended by the certbot project)
sudo snap install --classic certbot
sudo ln -s /snap/bin/certbot /usr/bin/certbot

# Option 1: let certbot edit the nginx server block for api.example.com
sudo certbot --nginx -d api.example.com

# Option 2: keep nginx config under your control; certbot only writes challenge files
sudo certbot certonly --webroot -w /var/www/acme -d api.example.com \
  --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx"

# Prove renewal works end to end without issuing a real certificate
sudo certbot renew --dry-run

# Where renewal is scheduled, and what certbot manages
systemctl list-timers | grep -i certbot
sudo certbot certificates

# /etc/nginx/conf.d/acme-challenge.conf (included in the port 80 server block)
location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ {
    root /var/www/acme;
    default_type "text/plain";
}

The location must take precedence over any HTTP to HTTPS redirect on port 80 (or the redirect must keep the path), otherwise HTTP-01 validation breaks. The deploy hook given at issuance is saved in the certificate's renewal configuration under /etc/letsencrypt/renewal/ and runs after every successful renewal.

docs.title: A wildcard certificate with DNS-01 (Route 53)
docs.text:
sudo snap install certbot-dns-route53
sudo snap set certbot trust-plugin-with-root=ok
sudo snap connect certbot:plugin certbot-dns-route53

# Credentials come from the instance role or the standard AWS environment/profile;
# the IAM policy needs route53:ListHostedZones, route53:GetChange, and
# route53:ChangeResourceRecordSets on the hosted zone.
sudo certbot certonly --dns-route53 \
  -d example.com -d "*.example.com" \
  --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx"

*.example.com does not cover example.com, so both names are listed.

docs.title: Caddy as an automatic-HTTPS reverse proxy
docs.text:
# Caddyfile
{
    email ops@example.com
}

api.example.com {
    reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}

app.example.com {
    root * /srv/taskflow-web
    file_server
}

That is the whole TLS configuration: Caddy obtains certificates for both names, redirects HTTP to HTTPS, and renews automatically. Persist its data directory (in containers, mount a volume at /data) so certificates and the ACME account survive restarts; losing it means re-issuing everything on every restart and running into rate limits.

docs.title: cert-manager with Let's Encrypt
docs.text:
# k8s/cluster-issuer.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-staging
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-staging-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: ops@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-staging-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx   # your ingress controller's class
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: ops@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-prod-account-key
    solvers:
      - http01:
          ingress:
            ingressClassName: nginx

# k8s/ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: taskflow-api
  namespace: taskflow
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: letsencrypt-prod
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts:
        - api.example.com
      secretName: taskflow-api-tls   # cert-manager creates and renews this Secret
  rules:
    - host: api.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service:
                name: taskflow-api
                port:
                  number: 3000

# Watch issuance and debug failures
kubectl -n taskflow get certificate,certificaterequest,order,challenge
kubectl -n taskflow describe certificate taskflow-api-tls

Test a new setup against letsencrypt-staging first (its certificates are not trusted by browsers, but its rate limits are far higher), then switch the annotation to letsencrypt-prod.

docs.title: An explicit wildcard Certificate with a DNS-01 solver
docs.text:
# k8s/wildcard-certificate.yaml
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: letsencrypt-dns
spec:
  acme:
    server: https://acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org/directory
    email: ops@example.com
    privateKeySecretRef:
      name: letsencrypt-dns-account-key
    solvers:
      - dns01:
          route53:
            region: us-east-1   # credentials from the pod's cloud identity, not static keys
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: wildcard-example-com
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  secretName: wildcard-example-com-tls
  dnsNames:
    - example.com
    - "*.example.com"
  privateKey:
    algorithm: ECDSA
    size: 256
  issuerRef:
    name: letsencrypt-dns
    kind: ClusterIssuer

docs.title: A managed certificate with AWS Certificate Manager (Terraform)
docs.text:
# infra/certificate.tf
resource "aws_acm_certificate" "api" {
  domain_name       = "api.example.com"
  validation_method = "DNS"

  lifecycle {
    create_before_destroy = true
  }
}

resource "aws_route53_record" "api_validation" {
  for_each = {
    for o in aws_acm_certificate.api.domain_validation_options : o.domain_name => o
  }

  zone_id = var.zone_id
  name    = each.value.resource_record_name
  type    = each.value.resource_record_type
  records = [each.value.resource_record_value]
  ttl     = 300
}

resource "aws_acm_certificate_validation" "api" {
  certificate_arn         = aws_acm_certificate.api.arn
  validation_record_fqdns = [for r in aws_route53_record.api_validation : r.fqdn]
}

The validation CNAME records must stay in DNS for ACM's automatic renewal to keep working; deleting them during a DNS cleanup is a classic way to break renewal months later. See Terraform in practice for managing this in code.

docs.title: A private CA issuer for internal services
docs.text:
# k8s/internal-ca-issuer.yaml (cert-manager CA issuer; the CA key pair lives in a Secret)
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: ClusterIssuer
metadata:
  name: internal-ca
spec:
  ca:
    secretName: internal-ca-key-pair   # tls.crt and tls.key of an internal intermediate CA
---
apiVersion: cert-manager.io/v1
kind: Certificate
metadata:
  name: reports-internal
  namespace: taskflow
spec:
  secretName: reports-internal-tls
  duration: 72h
  renewBefore: 24h
  dnsNames:
    - reports.internal.example.com
  issuerRef:
    name: internal-ca
    kind: ClusterIssuer

Clients of the reports service trust the internal root (for example with NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS), and three-day certificates make a leaked key short-lived.

docs.title: Checking expiry from a script
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# scripts/check-cert-expiry.sh: fail if any served certificate expires within WARN_DAYS
set -euo pipefail
WARN_DAYS="${WARN_DAYS:-21}"
status=0

for host in api.example.com app.example.com; do
  cert="$(openssl s_client -connect "${host}:443" -servername "${host}" </dev/null 2>/dev/null)"
  end="$(printf '%s' "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -enddate | cut -d= -f2)"
  if printf '%s' "$cert" | openssl x509 -noout -checkend $(( WARN_DAYS * 86400 )) >/dev/null; then
    echo "OK    ${host} expires ${end}"
  else
    echo "WARN  ${host} expires ${end} (within ${WARN_DAYS} days)" >&2
    status=1
  fi
done
exit "$status"

openssl x509 -checkend N exits non-zero if the certificate expires within N seconds. Run a script like this from CI on a schedule as a cheap second check, but rely on continuous probes (blackbox exporter or a synthetic monitoring service) with alerts as the main defence; the alert rule is shown in alerting and on-call.

docs.title: Renewal automation checklist
docs.text:
• Every certificate is issued and renewed by automation (ACME client, cert-manager, or a managed provider), and listed in an inventory with an owner.
  • Renewal starts at about two-thirds of the lifetime and retries daily; the client supports ARI where available.
  • A successful renewal reloads or redeploys every consumer (deploy hook, Secret watch, or managed attachment).
  • The challenge path is protected: port 80 and the /.well-known/acme-challenge/ path for HTTP-01, a scoped DNS token or delegated zone for DNS-01, validation records left in place for managed certificates.
  • CAA records list every CA your automation and platforms use, and are checked with every hosting or CDN change.
  • Changes to DNS, firewalls, redirects, and hosting trigger a review of certificate automation for the affected names.
  • certbot renew --dry-run (or staging issuance) runs in CI or on a schedule.
  • Served certificates are probed from outside on every hostname and path, with ticket and page thresholds scaled to the lifetime.
  • Renewal failures alert directly, not only through the expiry check.
  • ACME account keys and data directories are persisted and backed up.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Automate everything; treat a manual certificate as an incident waiting to happen.
  • Prefer HTTP-01 for simple public servers and DNS-01 for wildcards and internal names; scope DNS credentials tightly.
  • Test against the CA's staging environment before production.
  • Reload consumers after renewal, and verify the served certificate.
  • Monitor every hostname and network path from outside; alert days left scaled to lifetime.
  • Use managed certificates where TLS terminates at a cloud load balancer or CDN, and keep their validation records.
  • Use a private CA or service mesh for internal traffic, with short lifetimes.
  • Keep an inventory, including client certificates and certificates in third-party systems.
  • Plan now for 100-day (2027) and 47-day (2029) maximums.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• The site serves an expired certificate although certbot renewed it. Detect: openssl s_client shows the old notAfter, while certbot certificates shows a fresh certificate. Cause: no deploy hook, so nginx never reloaded and keeps the old certificate in memory. Fix: add --deploy-hook "systemctl reload nginx" (or a script in /etc/letsencrypt/renewal-hooks/deploy/) and monitor the served certificate, not the file.
  • HTTP-01 renewal starts failing after a security hardening change. Detect: certbot renew logs a connection or 404 error for /.well-known/acme-challenge/. Cause: port 80 was closed, or a new redirect rule sends the challenge path elsewhere. Fix: allow port 80 for the challenge path (redirect everything else), or switch to DNS-01 or TLS-ALPN-01.
  • cert-manager Certificate stuck at "Issuing" for hours. Detect: kubectl describe challenge shows a failed self-check or a DNS propagation wait. Cause: the solver Ingress uses the wrong class, a network policy blocks the solver pod, or the DNS-01 credentials lack permission. Fix: fix the solver configuration, test with the staging issuer, and alert when Certificates are not Ready.
  • Too many certificates issued: rate limited. Detect: the ACME error says a rate limit was hit, for example 5 certificates for the same set of names in 7 days at Let's Encrypt. Cause: containers that request a new certificate on every start because their certificate storage is not persistent, or a retry loop. Fix: persist the ACME data directory or Secret, use staging for tests, and rely on renewal, not re-issuance.
  • A managed certificate silently stopped renewing. Detect: the provider console shows renewal pending or failed; expiry approaches. Cause: a DNS cleanup deleted the validation CNAME, or one name on the certificate no longer resolves. Fix: restore the record or remove the dead name, and alert on the provider's renewal status as well as on days left.
  • One region serves an expired certificate while others are fine. Detect: probes from one region or over IPv6 fail with certificate has expired. Cause: a separate server, proxy, or edge configuration with its own certificate outside the automation. Fix: probe every path separately and bring the outlier under the same automation.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• ACME: The protocol for automated certificate issuance (RFC 8555).
  • ACME account key: The key pair that identifies the client to the CA.
  • Order / authorization / challenge: The request for a certificate, the proof needed per identifier, and the method used to prove it.
  • HTTP-01 / DNS-01 / TLS-ALPN-01: Challenge types using a web file, a DNS TXT record, or a special TLS certificate.
  • Key authorization: The challenge token joined to the account key thumbprint.
  • ARI: ACME Renewal Information, the CA's suggested renewal window (RFC 9773).
  • Deploy hook: A command run after a successful renewal.
  • ClusterIssuer / Certificate (cert-manager): Resources describing how to obtain certificates and which certificate is wanted.
  • Managed certificate: A certificate issued and renewed by a cloud provider for use on its services.
  • Private CA: A CA you run for internal names, trusted only by your clients.
  • Staging environment: A CA endpoint for testing that issues untrusted certificates with relaxed rate limits.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Treating renewal as solved because "certbot is installed".
  • Monitoring the certificate file instead of what clients receive.
  • Relying on CA expiry emails (Let's Encrypt no longer sends them).
  • Redirecting all of port 80 to HTTPS in a way that breaks HTTP-01.
  • Storing a DNS API token with full zone access on every web server.
  • Requesting new certificates on every container start without persistent storage, hitting rate limits.
  • Using public certificates for internal hostnames, publishing them in CT logs.
  • Deleting "unused" DNS validation records for managed certificates.
  • Hard-coding a 60-day renewal interval that will break with 45-day certificates.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Describe the ACME flow from account creation to installing a certificate.
  2. When must you use DNS-01, and what are its security risks?
  3. Why can a valid renewal still leave users with an expired certificate?
  4. What does cert-manager create when you annotate an Ingress, and where does the certificate end up?
  5. For a 45-day certificate renewed at two-thirds of its lifetime, on which day does renewal start, and how many days does a failing renewal have before expiry? (Day 30; 15 days.)
  6. Why should internal services use a private CA rather than public certificates?
  7. Your team has 60 certificates on 90-day lifetimes. How many renewals happen per year, and what changes when lifetimes drop to 47 days with renewal at two-thirds? (About 60 x 365 / 60 = 365 per year when renewed every 60 days; at roughly every 31 days it becomes about 700 per year.)
  8. List four reasons certificate expiry still causes outages, and one control for each.
