docs.title: TLS and Certificate Fundamentals
docs.text: TLS (Transport Layer Security) is the protocol that puts the "S" in HTTPS. It encrypts traffic, detects tampering, and lets the client confirm it is talking to the right server using a certificate: a document signed by a certificate authority (CA) that binds a domain name to a public key. This lesson explains the SSL and TLS naming, what TLS does and does not protect, the TLS 1.3 handshake step by step, the fields of an X.509 certificate, the chain of trust from leaf to root, validation levels, wildcard and multi-domain certificates, Certificate Transparency, HSTS, revocation, and the shrinking maximum lifetime of public certificates.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
Every request from TaskFlow Web to TaskFlow API carries a session token. Without TLS, anyone on the same Wi-Fi network, ISP, or compromised router could read it and take over the account, or silently change responses. With TLS, they see only encrypted bytes, and a forged server cannot present a valid certificate for api.example.com.

Understanding the mechanism matters operationally too. Most "SSL problems" in production are not cryptography failures but configuration ones: a missing intermediate certificate, a hostname that is not in the certificate, an expired certificate, a client with an outdated trust store, or a clock that is wrong. You cannot debug those quickly without knowing what the client checks and in what order.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• IETF TLS 1.3. RFC 8446 (2018) defines TLS 1.3: a one-round-trip handshake, encryption of most handshake messages including the certificate, removal of static RSA key exchange and legacy ciphers, and forward secrecy for every connection. RFC 8996 (2021) formally deprecates TLS 1.0 and 1.1.
  • CA/Browser Forum. Ballot SC-081v3 (2025) introduced a schedule that reduces the maximum validity of publicly trusted TLS certificates from 398 days in steps starting in March 2026 and ending at 47 days in March 2029, and shortens how long domain validation results may be reused.
  • Certificate Transparency. The Certificate Transparency project describes public, append-only logs of issued certificates that browsers require for publicly trusted certificates, and that anyone can monitor (for example through crt.sh) to spot certificates issued for their domains.
  • Let's Encrypt root transition. Let's Encrypt's post Help with chaining covers the planned expiry of the DST Root CA X3 cross-signature in September 2021, after which some outdated clients and OpenSSL configurations failed to build a valid chain: a real example of chain of trust problems at internet scale.

Popular tools and providers: OpenSSL, mkcert for local development, Let's Encrypt, ZeroSSL, Google Trust Services, DigiCert, Sectigo, AWS Certificate Manager, the Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator, Qualys SSL Labs, and crt.sh.

docs.title: SSL or TLS?
docs.text:
"SSL" is the name of the original Netscape protocol. It was replaced by TLS, but the old name stuck in product names ("SSL certificate", "SSL termination").

Version Year Status SSL 2.0 1995 Prohibited (RFC 6176) SSL 3.0 1996 Prohibited (RFC 7568); broken by the POODLE attack TLS 1.0 1999 Deprecated (RFC 8996) TLS 1.1 2006 Deprecated (RFC 8996) TLS 1.2 2008 Still widely supported; acceptable with modern cipher suites TLS 1.3 2018 Current; preferred

The certificate itself is not "SSL" or "TLS": the same X.509 certificate works with any protocol version. Servers today should offer TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only.

docs.title: What TLS provides, and what it does not
docs.text:
Property How TLS provides it Confidentiality Symmetric authenticated encryption (AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305) with keys derived during the handshake Integrity Every record carries an authentication tag; modified bytes fail decryption Server authentication The certificate binds the name to a public key; the server proves it holds the private key by signing the handshake Forward secrecy Session keys come from ephemeral (EC)DHE key shares, so stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt recorded traffic Client authentication (optional) Mutual TLS: the client also presents a certificate

TLS does not hide which IP address you connect to, the size and timing of traffic, or (without Encrypted Client Hello, which is being deployed by browsers and some CDNs) the hostname in the SNI field. It also says nothing about whether the server itself is secure or honest.

docs.title: The TLS 1.3 handshake, step by step
docs.text:
1. ClientHello. The client sends the versions it supports (the supported_versions extension lists TLS 1.3), cipher suites, the signature algorithms it accepts, the server name (SNI) so one IP can host many certificates, the application protocols it wants (ALPN: h2, http/1.1), and, importantly, a key share: an ephemeral public value for a key exchange group it guesses the server supports, usually X25519.
  2. ServerHello. The server picks the version and cipher suite and sends its own ephemeral key share. Now both sides can compute the same shared secret (ECDHE) and derive handshake keys. If the server does not support the client's guessed group, it sends a HelloRetryRequest and the handshake takes one extra round trip.
  3. Encrypted server flight. Everything after ServerHello is encrypted:
  4. EncryptedExtensions: the remaining negotiated settings, such as the chosen ALPN protocol.
  5. Certificate: the leaf certificate and intermediates.
  6. CertificateVerify: a signature, made with the certificate's private key, over the whole handshake so far. This proves the server holds the private key and binds the certificate to this handshake.
  7. Finished: a MAC over the handshake, proving nothing was tampered with.
  8. Client verification. The client builds and checks the chain, checks the hostname against the SAN list and the validity dates, verifies the CertificateVerify signature and the server's Finished.
  9. Client Finished, and the client can send its first HTTP request in the same flight. One round trip after the ClientHello, application data is flowing, encrypted with application traffic keys.

Compared with TLS 1.2, which needs two round trips for a full handshake, sends the certificate in clear text, and allows static RSA key exchange without forward secrecy, TLS 1.3 is faster and leaks less.

TLS 1.3 cipher suites are short because key exchange and signatures are negotiated separately:

Cipher suite Notes TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 Mandatory to implement; fast with AES hardware TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 Larger key TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256 Fast on devices without AES acceleration

Two related features:

  • Session resumption: a returning client presents a pre-shared key (session ticket) and skips certificate processing.
  • 0-RTT early data: with resumption, the client may send data in its very first flight. That data can be replayed by an attacker, so it is only safe for idempotent requests; many deployments leave it off.

Key exchange is also evolving: major browsers and CDNs now commonly negotiate a hybrid post-quantum group (X25519 combined with ML-KEM, named X25519MLKEM768) so that traffic recorded today cannot be decrypted by a future quantum computer. Certificates and signatures are unchanged by this.

docs.title: What a certificate contains
docs.text:
Points that trip people up:

  • The SAN list is what counts. Browsers match the hostname against the subject alternative name (SAN) entries; the subject common name (CN) is ignored for that purpose. A certificate with only a CN fails in modern clients.
  • The private key is not in the certificate. The certificate holds the public key and is public information; the private key stays on the server (file mode 600, never in Git) or in a hardware security module or cloud key service.
  • Key types: RSA (2048 bits or more) is universally supported; ECDSA P-256 keys and signatures are much smaller and faster and are supported by all modern clients. Many sites serve ECDSA certificates.

Common file formats:

Format Looks like Holds PEM (.pem, .crt, .key) Base64 between -----BEGIN ...----- lines Certificates, keys, CSRs; can concatenate several DER (.der, .cer) Binary One certificate or key PKCS#12 (.p12, .pfx) Binary, password-protected Certificate chain plus private key in one file CSR (.csr) PEM A certificate signing request: public key plus requested names, signed by the private key fullchain.pem PEM Leaf followed by intermediates: what a server should serve

docs.title: The chain of trust
docs.text:
• A root CA certificate is self-signed. Clients trust it only because it is shipped in a trust store: Mozilla's root store (Firefox and most Linux distributions' ca-certificates), the Chrome Root Store, Apple's and Microsoft's stores, Java's cacerts, and the Mozilla-derived list compiled into Node.js. Root programs audit CAs and can remove them.
  • Root private keys are kept offline. Day-to-day issuance uses intermediate CAs, signed by the root, which can be rotated or revoked without touching every device's trust store.
  • The server sends its leaf and all intermediates; the client supplies the root. Browsers can sometimes fetch a missing intermediate using the Authority Information Access URL or a cache, but many clients (Node.js, curl, Java, mobile apps) cannot, which is why a missing intermediate "works in my browser" but fails for API clients.
  • Cross-signing lets a new root be trusted by older devices: the new root's intermediate is also signed by an older, widely trusted root. When that cross-signature expires, old clients without the new root break, as happened with DST Root CA X3 in 2021.

docs.title: Validation levels: DV, OV, and EV
docs.text:
Level What the CA verifies Typical use DV (domain validation) Control of the domain only, automatically (ACME challenges) Almost all websites and APIs; Let's Encrypt issues only DV OV (organization validation) Domain control plus that the organization exists Some corporate policies; details visible only when inspecting the certificate EV (extended validation) Stricter organization checks Formerly shown as a green bar; major browsers removed special EV indicators around 2019

The encryption is identical at every level. For TaskFlow, DV certificates issued automatically are the right choice.

docs.title: Wildcard and multi-domain certificates
docs.text:
• A multi-domain (SAN) certificate lists several names explicitly, such as example.com, www.example.com, and api.example.com.
  • A wildcard certificate for *.example.com covers exactly one label: api.example.com and app.example.com, but not example.com itself and not v2.api.example.com. List example.com as a second SAN if you need it.

Wildcards are convenient for many subdomains and keep individual hostnames out of Certificate Transparency logs, but the same private key then protects every subdomain: one compromised server exposes them all. Let's Encrypt issues wildcards only with the DNS-01 challenge (see obtaining and renewing certificates).

docs.title: Certificate Transparency
docs.text:
Publicly trusted CAs submit every certificate (as a precertificate) to several Certificate Transparency (CT) logs, which return signed certificate timestamps (SCTs) embedded in the final certificate. Browsers such as Chrome and Safari reject publicly trusted certificates without enough valid SCTs.

Consequences for you:

  • You can monitor CT logs for your domains (crt.sh, or monitoring services) and detect certificates you did not request: mis-issuance, a forgotten team's shadow infrastructure, or an attacker who briefly controlled DNS.
  • Every hostname in a public certificate becomes public. Internal names such as jenkins.internal.example.com in a public certificate reveal infrastructure; use a wildcard or a private CA for internal services.

docs.title: Revocation
docs.text:
A certificate can be revoked before it expires (for example if its key leaks). Clients learn about revocation through:

  • CRLs (certificate revocation lists) published by the CA.
  • OCSP, an online per-certificate status check, and OCSP stapling, where the server attaches a recent OCSP response to the handshake.
  • Browser-aggregated revocation data such as Chrome's CRLSets and Firefox's CRLite, built from CA data and pushed to browsers.

Revocation has always been unreliable because many clients "soft fail" (accept the certificate if they cannot check). Let's Encrypt removed OCSP URLs from its certificates and shut down its OCSP service in 2025, relying on CRLs. The industry's main answer is short certificate lifetimes: a leaked key is only useful until the certificate expires.

docs.title: HSTS
docs.text:
HTTP Strict Transport Security tells browsers to use HTTPS only for a domain, for a period, even if the user types http:// or clicks an old link:

Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload
  • max-age is in seconds (63,072,000 is two years).
  • includeSubDomains applies the rule to every subdomain.
  • preload signals consent to be included in the HSTS preload list built into browsers (submitted at hstspreload.org), which protects even the first visit. Preload requires a valid certificate, an HTTP to HTTPS redirect on the same host, HTTPS for all subdomains, and a max-age of at least one year with includeSubDomains.

HSTS is effectively irreversible for its duration: if any subdomain still needs plain HTTP, includeSubDomains breaks it. Roll out with a short max-age (for example 300 seconds), verify, then increase; treat preload as a long-term commitment because removal takes months to reach users.

docs.title: Certificate lifetimes are shrinking
docs.text:
Public certificate lifetimes are capped by the CA/Browser Forum's Baseline Requirements and browser root programs. The maximum was 398 days from 2020 until Ballot SC-081v3 introduced this schedule:

Certificates issued on or after Maximum validity Domain validation reuse March 15, 2026 200 days 200 days March 15, 2027 100 days 100 days March 15, 2029 47 days 10 days

Let's Encrypt already issues 90-day certificates by default, offers optional 6-day short-lived certificates, and has announced shorter defaults: 64-day certificates from February 10, 2027 and 45-day certificates from February 16, 2028, with domain validation reuse cut to 10 days and then 7 hours (opt-in 45-day certificates through its tlsserver profile became available in May 2026). These rules cover publicly trusted TLS certificates; a private CA for internal services sets its own policy, though short lifetimes are good practice there too.

The practical consequence: renewal must be fully automated. At 47 days with renewal at about two-thirds of the lifetime, each certificate is renewed roughly every month.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Situation Choice Public website or API (TaskFlow Web, TaskFlow API) DV certificate from a public CA via ACME, or a managed certificate at the load balancer or CDN Many subdomains created dynamically Wildcard via DNS-01, or on-demand issuance per host Internal service-to-service traffic Private CA (or a service mesh) with short-lived certificates; do not put internal names in public CT logs Machine clients that must prove identity Mutual TLS with client certificates from a private CA Local development mkcert (a locally trusted development CA); never disable verification instead Requirement to show the organization's verified identity OV or EV, knowing browsers no longer display EV specially

Do not use self-signed certificates in production for anything users or other teams connect to: every client then has to disable verification or pin a one-off certificate, which defeats the point.

docs.title: Generate a private key and CSR with SANs
docs.text:
# OpenSSL 3: ECDSA P-256 key and a CSR for two names (use -nodes on OpenSSL 1.1.1)
openssl req -new \
  -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:P-256 -noenc \
  -keyout api.example.com.key \
  -out api.example.com.csr \
  -subj "/CN=api.example.com" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:api.example.com,DNS:app.example.com"

chmod 600 api.example.com.key
openssl req -in api.example.com.csr -noout -text | grep -A1 "Subject Alternative Name"

With ACME clients you rarely do this by hand (they generate keys and CSRs for you), but private CAs and some commercial CAs still take a CSR.

docs.title: Inspect a certificate file
docs.text:
openssl x509 -in fullchain.pem -noout \
  -subject -issuer -serial -dates \
  -ext subjectAltName,keyUsage,extendedKeyUsage,basicConstraints

# Full decoded dump, including SCTs and the public key
openssl x509 -in fullchain.pem -noout -text

openssl x509 reads only the first certificate in a file, which in fullchain.pem is the leaf. To see every certificate, split the file or use openssl crl2pkcs7 -nocrl -certfile fullchain.pem | openssl pkcs7 -print_certs -noout.

docs.title: Verify a chain and match a key to a certificate
docs.text:
# Does the leaf chain up to this root through this intermediate?
openssl verify -CAfile root.pem -untrusted intermediate.pem leaf.pem
# leaf.pem: OK

# Does this private key belong to this certificate? (works for RSA and ECDSA)
openssl x509 -in leaf.pem -noout -pubkey | openssl sha256
openssl pkey -in privkey.pem -pubout | openssl sha256
# The two hashes must be identical.

A key and certificate mismatch is a common cause of a server refusing to start after a manual renewal.

docs.title: Trusted certificates for local development
docs.text:
# mkcert creates a local CA, installs it in the system and browser trust stores,
# and issues certificates signed by it. Development machines only.
mkcert -install
mkcert localhost 127.0.0.1 ::1
# Created localhost+2.pem and localhost+2-key.pem

Never share the mkcert root key or install it on servers; anyone with it can issue certificates your machine trusts.

docs.title: Trusting a private CA from Node.js
docs.text:
# Adds a private CA to Node's built-in Mozilla roots for https, tls, and fetch
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/taskflow/internal-ca.pem node src/server.js

// src/clients/reports.js: a client for an internal service with a private CA
import https from "node:https";
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";

const ca = readFileSync("/etc/taskflow/internal-ca.pem");

export function getReport(id) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const req = https.request(
      { host: "reports.internal.example.com", path: `/reports/${id}`, ca, timeout: 3000 },
      (res) => {
        let body = "";
        res.on("data", (chunk) => (body += chunk));
        res.on("end", () => resolve(JSON.parse(body)));
      }
    );
    req.on("timeout", () => req.destroy(new Error("timeout")));
    req.on("error", reject);
    req.end();
  });
}

Passing ca replaces the default trust store for that request, so only the private CA is trusted there; NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS adds to the defaults for the whole process. Both keep verification on, unlike rejectUnauthorized: false.

docs.title: Sending HSTS from Express
docs.text:
// src/app.js (when TLS terminates in front of the app, the proxy can set this instead)
import express from "express";
import helmet from "helmet";

const app = express();
app.use(
  helmet({
    strictTransportSecurity: {
      maxAge: 63072000,        // seconds; start small (e.g. 300) when first rolling out
      includeSubDomains: true,
      preload: true,
    },
  })
);

Browsers ignore HSTS headers received over plain HTTP, so the header only takes effect once users reach the site over HTTPS.

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Offer TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only; prefer TLS 1.3 and AEAD cipher suites with forward secrecy.
  • Serve the leaf plus all intermediates (fullchain.pem), never just the leaf.
  • Use SAN entries for every hostname; do not rely on the CN.
  • Prefer ECDSA P-256 keys where clients allow; keep private keys out of Git, with tight permissions, or in a key management service.
  • Automate issuance and renewal; plan for 47-day certificates.
  • Monitor Certificate Transparency for your domains.
  • Keep internal hostnames out of public certificates; use a private CA internally.
  • Roll out HSTS gradually; preload only when every subdomain is HTTPS.
  • Keep client trust stores and OpenSSL versions up to date.
  • Never disable certificate verification to make an error go away.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• Browsers are fine, but API clients fail with "unable to verify the first certificate". Detect: Node.js reports UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE, curl reports "unable to get local issuer certificate", while Chrome loads the site. Cause: the server sends only the leaf, and browsers fill in the missing intermediate from their cache or the AIA URL. Fix: configure the server with the full chain (fullchain.pem) and verify with openssl s_client -showcerts.
  • Some users get certificate errors and others do not. Detect: errors only for some regions, devices, or old Android versions. Cause: different servers or edge nodes serve different certificates, or old clients lack a newer root after a cross-sign expired. Fix: check every endpoint behind the load balancer, align certificates, and decide which old clients you still support.
  • NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID on a new subdomain. Detect: the browser error names the hostname; the certificate's SAN list does not include it. Cause: the subdomain was added to DNS but not to the certificate, or a wildcard was expected to cover a second-level name (v2.api.example.com). Fix: reissue with the name in the SAN list or add a matching wildcard.
  • Internal hostnames appear in public search tools. Detect: a crt.sh search lists admin.internal.example.com. Cause: internal services were given publicly trusted certificates, which are logged in CT. Fix: use a private CA for internal services, or a wildcard, and assume any logged name is public.
  • A subdomain becomes unreachable after enabling HSTS. Detect: users cannot open legacy.example.com, which only serves HTTP. Cause: includeSubDomains forced HTTPS on every subdomain. Fix: serve HTTPS on that subdomain (the only quick fix while browsers hold the policy), and roll out HSTS with short max-age first next time.
  • TLS handshakes fail on one host with "certificate is not yet valid". Detect: errors on a single VM or container host, with a recently issued certificate. Cause: the host clock is wrong (behind by hours or days). Fix: run NTP or chrony and alert on clock offset; see NTP and time synchronization.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• TLS: The protocol that secures connections; SSL is its obsolete predecessor.
  • Handshake: The negotiation that authenticates the server and derives session keys.
  • Forward secrecy: Past sessions stay secret even if the long-term private key later leaks.
  • SNI: Server Name Indication, the hostname sent in ClientHello.
  • ALPN: Application-Layer Protocol Negotiation, choosing h2 or http/1.1 during the handshake.
  • X.509 certificate: The standard certificate format binding names to a public key, signed by an issuer.
  • SAN: Subject Alternative Name, the list of names a certificate is valid for.
  • CA: Certificate authority; root CAs are trusted directly, intermediate CAs are trusted through roots.
  • Trust store: The set of root certificates a client trusts.
  • CSR: Certificate signing request.
  • DV / OV / EV: Validation levels of a certificate.
  • Certificate Transparency: Public logs of all publicly trusted certificates.
  • SCT: Signed certificate timestamp, proof that a certificate was logged.
  • HSTS: A header telling browsers to use HTTPS only.
  • Revocation: Invalidating a certificate before its expiry (CRL, OCSP).

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Calling the protocol SSL and assuming SSL 3.0 or TLS 1.0 are acceptable.
  • Serving only the leaf certificate because "it works in Chrome".
  • Expecting a wildcard to cover the apex domain or deeper subdomains.
  • Believing EV or paid certificates are more secure cryptographically.
  • Assuming HTTPS hides which site a user visits; IPs and, without ECH, SNI are visible.
  • Disabling verification in clients to work around errors.
  • Relying on revocation to protect against a leaked key instead of short lifetimes and fast rotation.
  • Enabling HSTS preload before every subdomain supports HTTPS.
  • Committing private keys to repositories or baking them into images.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. What does TLS provide, and what does it leave visible to a network observer?
  2. Walk through the TLS 1.3 handshake. When can the client send its first HTTP request, and why is the certificate encrypted?
  3. What is forward secrecy, and which part of the handshake provides it?
  4. Why does a server need to send intermediate certificates but not the root?
  5. Which of these does a certificate for *.example.com cover: example.com, api.example.com, v2.api.example.com? (Only api.example.com.)
  6. A publicly trusted certificate is issued on March 20, 2026. What is the latest possible expiry date under the current CA/Browser Forum rules? (200 days later: October 6, 2026.)
  7. With 47-day certificates renewed at about two-thirds of their lifetime, roughly how many renewals per year does each certificate need, and for 150 certificates? (About every 31 days, so roughly 12 per year per certificate, about 1,800 for 150.)
  8. Why can enabling HSTS with includeSubDomains break a site, and how do you roll it out safely?

docs.title: Further learning
docs.text:
• RFC 8446: TLS 1.3
  • Mozilla: Server Side TLS guidelines
  • CA/Browser Forum: Baseline Requirements
  • Let's Encrypt: Certificate lifetime rationale and plans
  • Let's Encrypt: Chains of trust
  • HSTS preload list
  • TLS and SSL in the Networking section
  • Next: obtaining and renewing certificates. Back to the SSL certificates overview.

docs.title: TLS Termination and Troubleshooting
docs.text: TLS termination is the point where an encrypted connection is decrypted. Where you put it (CDN, load balancer, reverse proxy, or the application itself) decides who holds private keys, where plaintext exists, and what can inspect or route traffic. This lesson compares the options, covers re-encryption to backends and mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic, walks through a modern nginx TLS server block with an HTTP redirect and HSTS, and then gives a systematic way to debug TLS failures with openssl s_client, curl -v, and online scanners, including the error messages for incomplete chains, hostname mismatches, expired and self-signed certificates, clock skew, and missing SNI.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
TaskFlow API runs behind something: a cloud load balancer, an ingress controller, nginx, or a CDN. Each hop may terminate TLS, re-encrypt, or pass it through, and each choice changes your security posture and your failure modes. A load balancer that terminates TLS and forwards plain HTTP across a shared network leaves tokens readable inside your environment. A backend connection that is "encrypted" but never verifies the backend's certificate can be intercepted. A proxy that strips the original scheme makes the app generate http:// links and insecure cookies.

When something does break, TLS errors are cryptic ("handshake failure", "unable to verify the first certificate") and often client-specific. A repeatable troubleshooting method turns a two-hour mystery into a five-minute diagnosis.

docs.title: Real-world usage
docs.text:
• Mozilla. The Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator and the Server Side TLS guidelines publish "modern", "intermediate", and "old" configurations for nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and others, the starting point most teams use for protocol and cipher settings.
  • Cloudflare. The documentation on SSL/TLS encryption modes shows the termination choices in practice: "Flexible" (HTTPS to the edge, plain HTTP to the origin), "Full" (HTTPS to the origin without validating its certificate), and "Full (strict)" (HTTPS to the origin with certificate validation), recommending strict modes.
  • nginx. The guide Configuring HTTPS servers explains certificate chains (the leaf must come before the intermediates in the file), SNI-based virtual hosting, and session caching.
  • Qualys SSL Labs. The SSL Server Test grades public endpoints on protocol support, key exchange, cipher strength, chain completeness, and HSTS, and is a standard check before and after TLS changes.

Popular tools and providers: nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, Traefik, AWS Application and Network Load Balancers, Google Cloud Load Balancing, Azure Application Gateway, Cloudflare, Istio and Linkerd for mutual TLS, OpenSSL, curl, testssl.sh, and SSL Labs.

docs.title: Where to terminate TLS
docs.text:
Termination point Holds the private key Typical use Watch out for CDN or edge (Cloudflare, CloudFront) The CDN Static sites, global APIs, DDoS protection The edge-to-origin leg needs its own TLS with validation Cloud load balancer (ALB, Google HTTPS LB) The provider (managed certificates) Most cloud deployments Traffic to targets is plain HTTP unless you re-encrypt Reverse proxy or ingress (nginx, Envoy, ingress controllers) Your proxy VMs, Kubernetes, self-managed Certificate renewal and reload are your job Application (Node.js https.createServer) Every app instance Small services, end-to-end requirements, mTLS between services Key distribution to every instance; TLS work in the app process Passthrough (L4 load balancer, SNI routing) The application Strict end-to-end encryption, client certificates checked by the app No HTTP-level routing, caching, or WAF at the load balancer

For TaskFlow, the common setup is TLS at the cloud load balancer or ingress with a managed or cert-manager certificate, plus re-encryption or a service mesh inside the cluster if the network is shared or compliance requires encryption in transit everywhere.

docs.title: Re-encryption to backends
docs.text:
Re-encrypting means the load balancer or proxy opens a new TLS connection to the backend. Two rules make it meaningful:

  1. Verify the backend certificate against a CA you trust (usually an internal CA) and check the name. Encryption without verification protects against passive eavesdropping only; an active attacker inside the network can present any certificate. Some managed load balancers do not validate target certificates at all, and Cloudflare's "Full" mode (as opposed to "Full (strict)") does not either, so check what your provider does.
  2. Reuse connections. A full handshake per request adds latency and CPU; keep-alive connection pools to backends make re-encryption cheap.

docs.title: What the application needs to know after termination
docs.text:
When TLS ends before the app, the app sees plain HTTP from the proxy and must learn the original details from headers the proxy sets:

  • X-Forwarded-Proto: https (or the standard Forwarded header): the original scheme, used for redirects, absolute URLs, and Secure cookies.
  • X-Forwarded-For: the client IP chain.
  • In Express, app.set("trust proxy", 1) (or the proxy's address) makes req.secure, req.protocol, and req.ip use these headers. Only trust them from your own proxy: a client can send fake ones directly. See production and performance in the Express section.

docs.title: A modern nginx TLS configuration, explained
docs.text:
The practical example below configures TaskFlow API behind nginx. The key directives:

Directive Purpose listen 443 ssl; and http2 on; TLS on port 443 and HTTP/2 (the separate http2 directive replaced the listen ... http2 parameter in nginx 1.25.1) ssl_certificate fullchain.pem: leaf first, then intermediates ssl_certificate_key The private key, readable only by root ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; Disable SSL and TLS 1.0/1.1 ssl_ecdh_curve Key exchange groups in preference order ssl_ciphers TLS 1.2 cipher suites (ECDHE with AES-GCM or ChaCha20); TLS 1.3 suites are configured separately and are safe by default ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off; With only strong ciphers offered, let clients pick (mobile devices prefer ChaCha20) ssl_session_cache / ssl_session_timeout Resume sessions to skip full handshakes ssl_session_tickets off; Avoid long-lived ticket keys that weaken forward secrecy unless you rotate them add_header Strict-Transport-Security ... always; HSTS on every response, including errors Port 80 server with return 301 https://... Redirect HTTP to HTTPS, except the ACME challenge path

A classic nginx pitfall: add_header directives are inherited by a location block only if that block defines no add_header of its own. Adding a header in one location silently drops HSTS there; repeat it or use an include file.

OCSP stapling (ssl_stapling on) only helps if your CA runs OCSP; Let's Encrypt certificates no longer include OCSP URLs, so stapling does nothing for them.

docs.title: Mutual TLS for service-to-service traffic
docs.text:
In ordinary TLS only the server is authenticated. In mutual TLS (mTLS) the server also sends a CertificateRequest, and the client must present a certificate and prove it holds the key. The server verifies the client certificate against a CA it trusts (normally a private CA) and uses an identity from it, such as a SAN URI, to authorize the request.

Where it fits:

  • Service-to-service calls inside TaskFlow (API to reports service, worker to API): strong workload identity without shared API keys. Service meshes such as Istio and Linkerd issue short-lived workload certificates (often with SPIFFE IDs like spiffe://example.com/ns/taskflow/sa/worker) and do mTLS transparently in sidecars or node proxies.
  • Partner and B2B APIs, IoT devices, and admin endpoints, where each caller gets a client certificate.

Costs: you run a private CA, distribute and rotate client certificates (short lifetimes, automated), and need a way to revoke or block a compromised identity quickly. Browsers support client certificates, but the user experience is poor, so mTLS is mostly for machines.

docs.title: A troubleshooting method
docs.text:
Work from the bottom of the stack up:

  1. Can you connect and complete a handshake? If not, the issue is below certificates: DNS, port, firewall, a protocol or cipher mismatch, or a server that needs SNI.
  2. Does the chain verify? openssl s_client prints a verify return code; 0 (ok) means the chain built to a trusted root.
  3. Does the name match? The hostname must be in the SAN list.
  4. Is it one client? Then look at that client: its trust store, its clock, a corporate proxy re-signing traffic, or certificate pinning in a mobile app.

Always pass -servername to openssl s_client. Without SNI, a server hosting several names returns its default certificate, and you debug the wrong one.

docs.title: Common errors and what they mean
docs.text:
Problem OpenSSL Node.js curl / browser Fix Incomplete chain verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate, num=21:unable to verify the first certificate UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE curl (60) SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate; browsers may work Serve fullchain.pem Hostname mismatch Fails with -verify_hostname ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID curl no alternative certificate subject name matches target host name; Chrome NET::ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID Add the name to the SAN list; check SNI routing Expired num=10:certificate has expired CERT_HAS_EXPIRED Chrome NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID Renew, reload, and fix the automation Not yet valid num=9:certificate is not yet valid CERT_NOT_YET_VALID NET::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID Fix the clock (NTP) on the client or server Self-signed or unknown CA num=18:self-signed certificate, num=19:self-signed certificate in certificate chain DEPTH_ZERO_SELF_SIGNED_CERT, SELF_SIGNED_CERT_IN_CHAIN NET::ERR_CERT_AUTHORITY_INVALID Use a publicly trusted CA, or add the private root to the client's trust store Protocol or cipher mismatch alert handshake failure or protocol version alerts, no protocols available ERR_SSL_... errors such as unsupported protocol ERR_SSL_VERSION_OR_CIPHER_MISMATCH Align TLS versions and cipher suites; upgrade old clients SNI missing Default certificate returned, then a name mismatch Rare (Node sends SNI for hostnames) Old clients, scripts connecting by IP Send SNI (-servername), or give the default server the right certificate Key does not match certificate Server fails to start (key values mismatch) ERR_OSSL_... key errors Site down Compare public key hashes; reinstall the matching pair

curl -k, rejectUnauthorized: false, and NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=0 hide every one of these errors by turning off verification. They are diagnostic switches for a lab, never fixes.

docs.title: When to use and when not to use
docs.text:
Requirement Recommended termination Standard public web app or API on a cloud provider Cloud load balancer or ingress with managed or ACME certificates Compliance requires encryption in transit inside the network Terminate at the edge and re-encrypt with verification, or use a service mesh Load balancer must never see plaintext TCP passthrough with SNI routing; TLS in the app Service-to-service authentication without shared secrets Mutual TLS from a private CA or service mesh Global static content CDN termination with a strict, validated origin connection Local development Plain HTTP on localhost, or mkcert certificates when features need HTTPS

Avoid terminating TLS in every Node.js process when a proxy or load balancer can do it: key distribution and renewal multiply with each instance. Avoid "Flexible"-style setups (HTTPS to the edge, HTTP over the internet to the origin) for anything with logins or personal data.

docs.title: nginx: HTTPS for TaskFlow API with redirect and HSTS
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/api.example.com.conf
# Port 80: ACME challenges and a redirect to HTTPS for everything else
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;
    server_name api.example.com;

    location ^~ /.well-known/acme-challenge/ {
        root /var/www/acme;
    }

    location / {
        return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
    }
}

# Port 443: TLS termination in front of the Node.js app on 127.0.0.1:3000
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    listen [::]:443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name api.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/api.example.com/privkey.pem;

    # Based on Mozilla's "intermediate" profile; regenerate from ssl-config.mozilla.org
    ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3;
    ssl_ecdh_curve X25519:prime256v1:secp384r1;
    ssl_ciphers ECDHE-ECDSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256:ECDHE-ECDSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384:ECDHE-ECDSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305:ECDHE-RSA-CHACHA20-POLY1305;
    ssl_prefer_server_ciphers off;

    ssl_session_timeout 1d;
    ssl_session_cache shared:TLS:10m;
    ssl_session_tickets off;

    # Start with a small max-age when first rolling out HSTS, then raise it.
    add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains" always;

    location / {
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
        proxy_http_version 1.1;
        proxy_set_header Host $host;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
        proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $request_id;
    }
}

sudo nginx -t && sudo systemctl reload nginx

nginx -t validates the configuration (including that the key matches the certificate) before the reload, so a mistake does not take the site down. With a recent OpenSSL (3.5 or later) you can also list the hybrid post-quantum group X25519MLKEM768 first in ssl_ecdh_curve; check your nginx and OpenSSL versions before doing so.

docs.title: Express behind the proxy
docs.text:
// src/app.js
import express from "express";

export const app = express();

// Trust exactly one proxy hop (nginx on the same host or the load balancer).
app.set("trust proxy", 1);

app.get("/whoami", (req, res) => {
  // With trust proxy: req.protocol === "https" and req.secure === true behind nginx
  res.json({ protocol: req.protocol, secure: req.secure, ip: req.ip });
});

Without trust proxy, req.secure is false behind a TLS-terminating proxy, and libraries that set Secure cookies or build absolute URLs behave as if the site were plain HTTP.

docs.title: Re-encrypting to a backend and verifying it
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/reports-upstream.conf (fragment inside a server block)
location /reports/ {
    proxy_pass https://reports.internal.example.com:8443;

    proxy_ssl_verify              on;    # off by default: without it, any certificate is accepted
    proxy_ssl_verify_depth        2;
    proxy_ssl_trusted_certificate /etc/nginx/tls/internal-ca.pem;
    proxy_ssl_server_name         on;    # send SNI to the backend
    proxy_ssl_name                reports.internal.example.com;
    proxy_ssl_protocols           TLSv1.3;

    # Optional: present a client certificate to the backend (mutual TLS)
    proxy_ssl_certificate         /etc/nginx/tls/gateway-client.crt;
    proxy_ssl_certificate_key     /etc/nginx/tls/gateway-client.key;
}

proxy_ssl_verify defaults to off in nginx, which is exactly the "encrypted but not authenticated" trap described above.

docs.title: Requiring client certificates (mTLS) at nginx
docs.text:
# /etc/nginx/conf.d/partners.example.com.conf
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    http2 on;
    server_name partners.example.com;

    ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/partners.example.com/fullchain.pem;
    ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/partners.example.com/privkey.pem;

    ssl_client_certificate /etc/nginx/tls/partner-ca.pem;  # CA that issues partner client certs
    ssl_verify_client      on;
    ssl_verify_depth       2;

    location / {
        # Overwrite (never pass through) identity headers for the app.
        proxy_set_header X-Client-Subject $ssl_client_s_dn;
        proxy_set_header X-Client-Verify  $ssl_client_verify;
        proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
    }
}

The app trusts X-Client-Subject only because nginx always overwrites it and the app is reachable only through nginx.

docs.title: Mutual TLS and certificate reload in Node.js
docs.text:
// src/reports-server.js: an internal service that requires client certificates
import https from "node:https";
import { readFileSync, watch } from "node:fs";
import express from "express";

const dir = "/etc/taskflow/tls";
const load = () => ({
  key: readFileSync(`${dir}/tls.key`),
  cert: readFileSync(`${dir}/tls.crt`),
});

const app = express();
app.get("/reports/:id", (req, res) => {
  const peer = req.socket.getPeerCertificate();
  // subjectaltname looks like "URI:spiffe://example.com/ns/taskflow/sa/worker"
  if (!req.socket.authorized || !peer.subjectaltname?.includes("/sa/worker")) {
    return res.status(403).json({ error: "forbidden" });
  }
  res.json({ id: req.params.id });
});

const server = https.createServer(
  {
    ...load(),
    ca: readFileSync(`${dir}/internal-ca.pem`), // trusted issuer of client certificates
    requestCert: true,
    rejectUnauthorized: true,
    minVersion: "TLSv1.2",
  },
  app
);

// Pick up renewed certificates (for example from cert-manager) without a restart.
watch(dir, () => {
  try {
    server.setSecureContext({ ...load(), ca: readFileSync(`${dir}/internal-ca.pem`) });
  } catch {
    // keep serving the previous certificate if files are mid-update
  }
});

server.listen(8443);

setSecureContext replaces the key and certificate for new connections, which matters when certificates live for days.

docs.title: A troubleshooting session
docs.text:
# 1. Handshake, chain, and certificate details (always send SNI with -servername)
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -showcerts </dev/null

# 2. Fail on verification errors and check the hostname explicitly
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com \
  -verify_return_error -verify_hostname api.example.com -brief </dev/null

# 3. Protocol and ALPN checks
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -tls1_2 </dev/null
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com -alpn h2 </dev/null 2>/dev/null | grep -i alpn

# 4. Dates on the served leaf certificate
openssl s_client -connect api.example.com:443 -servername api.example.com </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -dates -subject -ext subjectAltName

# 5. The client's view, step by step
curl -v https://api.example.com/healthz

# 6. Test one backend behind DNS or a load balancer without changing DNS
curl -v --resolve api.example.com:443:203.0.113.10 https://api.example.com/healthz

# 7. Trust a private CA for this request only
curl --cacert /etc/taskflow/tls/internal-ca.pem https://reports.internal.example.com:8443/healthz

# 8. Clock check on the machine that reports "not yet valid"
date -u && timedatectl status

A healthy -showcerts result (OpenSSL 3) looks like this:

Certificate chain
 0 s:CN=api.example.com
   i:C=US, O=Example Trust Services, CN=Example TLS CA R1
   v:NotBefore: Oct 31 09:12:44 2026 GMT; NotAfter: Jan 29 09:12:43 2027 GMT
 1 s:C=US, O=Example Trust Services, CN=Example TLS CA R1
   i:C=US, O=Example Trust Services, CN=Example Root X1
---
New, TLSv1.3, Cipher is TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384
Verify return code: 0 (ok)

An incomplete chain shows only certificate 0 and ends with:

verify error:num=20:unable to get local issuer certificate
verify error:num=21:unable to verify the first certificate
Verify return code: 21 (unable to verify the first certificate)

For a full configuration audit of a public endpoint, run the SSL Labs Server Test, or for internal endpoints testssl.sh:

docker run --rm -t ghcr.io/testssl/testssl.sh https://api.example.com

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
• Terminate TLS as few times as practical, at a layer with automated certificates; re-encrypt or use mTLS inside when the network is shared or compliance requires it.
  • Always verify backend certificates when re-encrypting (proxy_ssl_verify on, strict modes at CDNs).
  • Serve fullchain.pem, TLS 1.2 and 1.3 only, ECDHE with AEAD ciphers.
  • Redirect HTTP to HTTPS (keeping the ACME path), and send HSTS with always.
  • Set X-Forwarded-Proto at the proxy and configure the app to trust exactly that proxy.
  • Use mTLS with short-lived certificates for service identity; prefer a mesh or automated issuer to hand-made client certificates.
  • Debug with openssl s_client -servername and curl -v before changing anything; never "fix" errors by disabling verification.
  • Re-run SSL Labs or testssl.sh after every TLS configuration change.

docs.title: In production
docs.text:
• API clients fail while browsers work. Detect: openssl s_client -showcerts lists only one certificate; Node.js clients report UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE. Cause: the server is configured with cert.pem instead of fullchain.pem. Fix: point ssl_certificate at the full chain, reload, and add a synthetic check from a non-browser client.
  • Infinite redirect loop after moving TLS to the load balancer. Detect: the browser reports too many redirects; logs show the app redirecting every request to HTTPS. Cause: the app receives plain HTTP from the load balancer and does not trust X-Forwarded-Proto, so it thinks every request is insecure. Fix: set trust proxy (or the framework equivalent) for the load balancer, or redirect only at the load balancer.
  • A multi-tenant host serves the wrong certificate to some clients. Detect: openssl s_client without -servername returns a different certificate than with it; old clients or IP-based health checks report name mismatches. Cause: the client does not send SNI and gets the default server's certificate. Fix: make the default server's certificate correct for health checks, and upgrade or reconfigure clients to send SNI.
  • HSTS is missing on some responses. Detect: curl -sI on different paths shows the header only on some. Cause: a location block with its own add_header does not inherit the server-level HSTS header, or the header lacks always and is missing on error responses. Fix: use always and repeat or include security headers in locations that add headers.
  • Internal traffic is "encrypted" but an attacker could intercept it. Detect: a review finds proxy_ssl_verify off (the default), CDN mode "Full" rather than "Full (strict)", or clients with rejectUnauthorized: false. Cause: re-encryption configured without verification. Fix: issue backend certificates from an internal CA and enable verification end to end.
  • Only one service's mTLS calls fail after a CA rotation. Detect: certificate verify failed or bad certificate alerts from one client; its certificate was issued by the new intermediate. Cause: the server's trusted CA bundle was not updated with the new intermediate or root. Fix: distribute new trust anchors before issuing from a new CA, keep old and new in the bundle during the overlap, and rotate in stages.

docs.title: Important terminology
docs.text:
• TLS termination: Decrypting TLS at a proxy, load balancer, or app.
  • Re-encryption (TLS bridging): Terminating TLS and opening a new TLS connection to the backend.
  • Passthrough: Forwarding encrypted traffic without terminating it, usually routed by SNI.
  • Mutual TLS (mTLS): TLS where the client also presents a certificate.
  • SPIFFE ID: A URI-form workload identity (spiffe://...) often carried in mTLS certificates.
  • X-Forwarded-Proto: A header carrying the original scheme to the app.
  • SNI: The hostname the client requests in ClientHello, used to pick a certificate.
  • Verify return code: OpenSSL's result of chain verification (0 is OK).
  • Full chain: Leaf plus intermediate certificates, as served.
  • SSL Labs / testssl.sh: Tools that audit a TLS endpoint's configuration.

docs.title: Common mistakes and misconceptions
docs.text:
• Assuming traffic inside a VPC or cluster cannot be read.
  • Re-encrypting to backends without verifying their certificates.
  • Using the leaf-only certificate file in the server configuration.
  • Debugging with openssl s_client but forgetting -servername.
  • Disabling verification "temporarily" and shipping it.
  • Not telling the app that TLS was terminated upstream, causing redirect loops and insecure cookies.
  • Losing HSTS on some paths because of add_header inheritance.
  • Rotating a CA without first distributing the new trust anchor.
  • Treating mTLS as authorization; it proves identity, and the app or mesh policy must still decide what that identity may do.

docs.title: Revision questions
docs.text:
1. Compare terminating TLS at the load balancer, re-encrypting, and passthrough. What does each mean for who can read plaintext?
  2. Why is re-encryption without certificate verification weak, and which nginx directive enables verification?
  3. What must an Express app configure when TLS terminates at a proxy, and what breaks if it does not?
  4. Explain each directive in the nginx TLS server block and why session tickets are often disabled.
  5. How does mutual TLS work, and how does the server decide who the client is?
  6. A Node.js client reports UNABLE_TO_VERIFY_LEAF_SIGNATURE while Chrome works. What do you run, what do you expect to see, and what is the fix?
  7. With a 60 ms round trip time, how long does it take before the first HTTP request can be sent on a new HTTPS connection with TLS 1.3, and with TLS 1.2? (TCP needs 1 RTT; TLS 1.3 adds 1 RTT, so about 120 ms; TLS 1.2 adds 2 RTTs, so about 180 ms. Session resumption and keep-alive avoid most of this.)
  8. A certificate error appears only on one VM: "certificate is not yet valid". What is the likely cause and fix?
